## Near Me Search Optimization for St. Louis: The Guide to Getting Found
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/near-me-search-optimization-for-st-louis-2026-guide
It’s a weekday afternoon. Someone in Florissant pulls out their phone and types “plumber near me.” A family in Belleville searches “tacos near me open now.” A stressed parent in Wentzville asks out loud, “urgent care near me.” In the three seconds it takes those results to load, a handful of local businesses win the customer — and everyone else may as well not exist. Three seconds decides it. So when your customer runs that search tomorrow, are you one of the handful who wins them — or one of the everyone-else?
That’s the whole game of “near me” search. People aren’t browsing; they’re ready to act, right now, close to home. The only question is whether your business is one of the few they see. This is the complete playbook for making sure it is — across Google, Maps, and the AI assistants people increasingly ask.
“Near me” search optimization means making your business the one Google — and now AI assistants — surface when someone nearby searches for what you offer. It comes down to three things Google weighs (relevance, distance, and prominence), powered by a complete Google Business Profile, consistent listings, and recent reviews. Nail those and you show up in the map pack, in “open now” results, and in the AI answers 45% of consumers now rely on.
### What “Near Me” Search Really Is
A “near me” search is any search with local intent — whether the person types the words “near me” or not. When someone searches “coffee shop,” “emergency electrician,” or “tacos open now,” Google assumes they mean near them and serves local results built around their location. That behavior isn’t new, and it isn’t slowing down. When the trend first exploded, Google reported that mobile searches for “___ near me now” grew more than 150%, and “open now near me” searches more than 200%, between 2015 and 2017 (Think with Google). By 2018, 82% of smartphone shoppers had done a “near me” search (Uberall, 2018), and Google has said roughly 46% of all searches carry local intent (Google, 2018).
Those numbers are years old — and that’s exactly the point. “Near me” searching stopped being a trend and became the default long ago. What’s changed since is where people do it, and how ruthlessly the top results get rewarded. The businesses in the top three map results capture the overwhelming majority of clicks and calls; everyone below the fold splits the scraps.
### The 2026 Shift: People Ask AI “Near Me” Too
Here’s the update most St. Louis businesses haven’t caught. 45% of consumers now use AI tools like ChatGPT to find local businesses — up from just 6% a year earlier (BrightLocal, 2026), making AI the third most popular way people get local recommendations, behind only search engines and maps. When someone asks an assistant “who’s the best [your service] near me,” you’re either in that short answer or you don’t exist to them.
The good news: AI doesn’t invent its picks. It reads the same signals Google does — complete profiles, consistent listings, real reviews, and presence on trusted local sources. So “near me” optimization in 2026 isn’t two separate jobs. It’s one job that pays off in two places at once. Do the fundamentals well and you win the map pack and the AI answer with the same effort.
### Watch: The Secret to Dominating Near-Me Search
### How “Near Me” Ranking Actually Works
Google is unusually clear about how it ranks local results. Per Google’s own Business Profile documentation, three factors decide who shows up — and understanding what each one rewards tells you exactly what to do.
### Relevance — do you match the search?
Relevance is how well your profile matches what someone typed. You raise it by choosing the single most accurate primary category (a “taqueria” should not be filed under “restaurant” if taqueria is an option), adding every relevant secondary category, listing your real services in plain language, and writing a description that uses the words customers actually search. Most businesses lose here simply by leaving their profile half-filled.
### Distance — how close are you?
Distance is how far you are from the person searching. You can’t move your building, but you can make sure Google knows precisely where you are and how far you travel: a verified, exact address, or — for service-area businesses like plumbers and cleaners — a properly configured service area listing the suburbs you cover. A vague or wrong location quietly caps how often you appear.
### Prominence — how established do you look?
Prominence is how well-known and trusted your business appears across the web, and it’s the biggest lever most owners ignore. It’s built from the volume and recency of your reviews, the consistency of your listings everywhere they appear, links and mentions from other reputable sites, and your overall reputation. Two businesses the same distance from a searcher will rank very differently based on prominence — and prominence is almost entirely earnable.
Distance is largely fixed. Relevance and prominence are entirely in your control — which is where every win in this guide comes from.
### Near-Me Search, by the Numbers
### The Near-Me Optimization Playbook
Do these in order — each one feeds the next, and together they cover relevance, prominence, and the AI layer at once.
### 1. Complete and verify your Google Business Profile
Non-negotiable, and free. Claim your profile, verify it, then actually finish it: exact hours (including holidays), the most accurate primary category, relevant secondary categories, your full service list, real photos of your work and space, attributes, and answered questions. A complete profile is the single biggest driver of whether you appear in the map pack — and “complete” beats “merely claimed” every time.
### 2. Build a steady stream of recent reviews
Reviews are pure prominence, and 97% of consumers read them before choosing (BrightLocal, 2026). Recency matters as much as volume — a wall of five-star reviews from two years ago reads as stale. Build a simple, repeatable habit of asking every happy customer, make it one tap easy, and reply to every review, good or bad. A business earning a few fresh reviews a month will steadily out-rank a quiet competitor with more old ones.
### 3. Make your listings identical everywhere
Your name, address, and phone must match exactly across Google, your website, the major maps and review sites, and a strong local directory. Google trusts a business whose details line up everywhere and discounts one that contradicts itself — an old suite number here, a disconnected phone there. You don’t need 100 listings; you need the handful customers actually use, kept perfectly consistent. That same consistency is what feeds the AI answers.
### 4. Add local signals to your own website
Your site reinforces relevance. Name the neighborhoods and suburbs you serve, build a real page for each core service, publish genuinely useful local content, and mark up your pages with local-business schema so search engines and AI can read your details cleanly. A generic site with no location signals leaves relevance on the table.
### 5. Show up where AI looks
The 45% asking AI get answers pulled from your profile, your reviews, and reputable directories. There’s no separate “AI strategy” — steps 1 through 4 done well are what get you cited. The businesses investing now are getting a head start their competitors haven’t noticed yet.
Hard left turn: your stomach will thank you for Troy’s dinner list.
### Near-Me Search Looks Different for Every Business Type
The fundamentals are universal, but how “near me” plays out — and where you should focus — depends on what you do.
Restaurants & cafes: “Open now” and photos rule. Keep hours flawless (including holidays), post fresh food photos, and stay on top of reviews — a hungry searcher in Maplewood decides in seconds, and stale hours or dark photos lose them.
Home & trades services (HVAC, plumbing, roofing): These are service-area businesses. Nail your service-area setup across the metro, lean hard on reviews (trust is everything for someone letting you into their home in Kirkwood or O’Fallon), and win the “emergency ___ near me” and “open now” searches with accurate 24/7 hours if you offer them.
Retail & shops: Product-level relevance and in-store photos matter. Someone searching “bike shop near me” in Webster Groves wants to see you have what they need before they drive over.
Professional services (legal, accounting, agencies): Prominence and reputation carry the most weight. Reviews, consistent citations, and authoritative local content build the trust these higher-consideration searches demand.
Healthcare & wellness: Accurate categories, insurance/attribute details, and recent reviews decide who a patient in Chesterfield or Belleville books.
### The Mobile Reality (and the Voice Question)
“Near me” is a mobile behavior first and foremost — these searches happen on phones, on the move, with intent to act immediately. That means the experience after the click matters: a mobile-friendly site, a tap-to-call button, and directions that actually work. If your site is slow or clunky on a phone, you lose the customer even after winning the search.
Voice search — “Hey Google, find a bakery near me” — layers on top of this, and it pulls from the exact same local signals. You’ll see a lot of eye-popping voice statistics online; be skeptical, because most trace back to circular citations with no primary source. What’s reliably true is simpler: voice results lean heavily on your Google Business Profile and structured data, so the work you’re already doing covers it. Don’t chase voice as a separate project — just keep your profile and site clean.
### What to Actually Publish: Near-Me Content That Works
Content is how you compound relevance over time. The pages that earn near-me visibility aren’t clever — they’re useful and specific:
Service-plus-location pages: a real page for each core service, naming the areas you serve, written for humans (not stuffed with “plumber St. Louis plumber Kirkwood plumber”).
Neighborhood and suburb guides: genuinely helpful local content that signals you know and serve the area.
Answer-style FAQs: the real questions customers ask, answered plainly — the format both Google’s features and AI assistants love to quote.
Quality beats quantity every time. One thorough, honest, genuinely local page outperforms ten thin ones — and it’s the kind of page an AI assistant will happily cite.
### Why You’re Not Showing Up
If you’re invisible for “near me” searches, it’s almost always one of a handful of fixable reasons: an unclaimed or half-finished Google profile; a name, address, or phone that differs across your listings; a vague or wrong primary category; too few recent reviews; or a thin website with no local signals. None of these cost money to fix — they cost an afternoon and then consistent upkeep. The businesses beating you usually aren’t spending more; they’re just more complete and more consistent.
### What It Costs — and How Long It Takes
Two fair questions. On cost: every fundamental above is free if you do it yourself — your time, not your money. Done for you, local SEO runs roughly $300 to $2,000 a month across the industry (WebFX). On time: it’s not overnight. Plan on three to six months for meaningful movement — Google itself says SEO changes can take four months to a year to fully register. Anyone promising the top of the map next week is selling something.

## Your Door Hangers Are in a Recycling Bin: Promoting a Business Across St. Louis County’s 88 Towns
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-county-business-promotions-the-2026-playbook-for-real-local-growth
Your door hangers are in a recycling bin in Hazelwood. All hundred of them, tossed with the junk mail, and the printer billed you for every porch whether anybody behind those doors needed you or not. Meanwhile the bell over your door in Florissant hasn’t rung since eleven on a Saturday, and the 15-percent-off sign is curling at the corners where you taped it to the glass.
Here’s the fact that explains your Saturday: St. Louis County isn’t one market. It’s 88 municipalities, and by the County’s own description each one runs its own planning and zoning, sign rules included. Florissant’s sign code alone charges $50 to permit a person waving a sign on the corner. A promotion built for “the county” fits none of those 88 rulebooks. The flyer printer bills by the porch and the county-wide ad package sells all 88 towns as one, and both get paid whether a single customer walks in or not.
Three free moves before next Saturday:
Ask every customer this week which town they live in and jot it in a notebook by the register. In seven days you’ll know where your money really comes from.
Pick your 20. Google lets a Business Profile carry up to 20 service areas, set by city or ZIP code, never a radius. In a county of 88 towns, spend those slots on the ones your notebook says pay the bills.
Book a free one-on-one with the Missouri SBDC’s St. Louis office (314-241-1005), which helps owners plan exactly this at no cost.
So what if the porches came sorted, and free? A St. Louis County Library card unlocks Reference Solutions, a database of millions of business and household listings with search tools built for making a list of potential customers. Open it from the library’s online resources, sign in with your card, and pick the U.S. New Movers/Homeowners module. The screen narrows to Florissant and homes sold in the last month, a list built partly from the same deeds county recorders file. Ask the reference desk how many records the library’s license lets you download at a time. Then do the math. Two hundred postcards to those households at the 65-cent postcard stamp is $130. The Post Office’s Every Door Direct Mail is cheaper per piece, 26 cents with a 200-piece minimum, but it lands on every door on the route, new neighbors or not. The $130 reaches the family that just moved to Florissant, boxes still stacked in the garage, with no plumber, no barber and no pizza place yet. A dated offer in their first weeks isn’t junk mail. It’s the welcome nobody else sent. The printer charges for every porch. The library costs nothing and points you at the porches that matter.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. How can a business get more customers?
A.  Be easy to find at the moment someone is ready to buy, then give them a reason to choose you. For a St. Louis County business that means a complete Google Business Profile, the same name, address and phone everywhere you’re listed, recent reviews you actually answer, and a specific offer with a real end date. Then show up locally: back the causes your neighbors care about and keep your St Louis Near Me Directory listing current with coupons, events and photo albums (all part of the Gold Plan). Ask every new customer how they found you, and do more of whatever they name.
### Q. What are 5 promotional strategies?
A.  Five that pull their weight for a local business: (1) local search, meaning a complete Google Business Profile and consistent listings; (2) reviews, asked for after every good job and answered every time; (3) offers, like a first-visit coupon or a seasonal deal with a deadline; (4) community promotion, such as sponsoring a youth team, co-hosting an event or cross-promoting with the shop next door; and (5) email to past customers, the cheapest repeat sale you will ever make. Run at least three at once, so a customer keeps running into your name between the first search and the sale.
### Q. What are four common methods of promotion?
A.  The classic four are advertising (paid placements), personal selling (direct outreach and relationships), sales promotion (discounts, coupons, limited-time offers) and public relations (community involvement, press, word of mouth). Most marketing textbooks now add direct marketing and digital marketing to that list. For a local St. Louis County business, the highest-return mix usually leans on public relations and community engagement plus a strong, consistent online presence before much money goes to paid ads. If you are weighing whether to hire that out, read what a PR firm actually does for a St. Louis business first.
### Q. What is a promotion strategy?
A.  It’s your plan for getting the right message in front of the right customers: who you want to reach, what you want them to do, which channels and offers you’ll use, what you’ll spend and how you’ll know it worked. For a small business it should fit on one page. A real example: reach homeowners within ten miles, get them to book a first cleaning, put a first-visit coupon on your listings and mail a postcard to past customers, spend $300 this quarter, and count the bookings that mention the coupon. If you can’t measure it, it isn’t a strategy yet.
### Q. What is the rule of 7 in advertising?
A.  It’s an old marketing rule of thumb that a potential customer needs to run into your message about seven times before they buy. Nobody has proven the number is exactly seven, and it isn’t research, but the lesson holds: one ad, one post or one sponsorship rarely makes the sale. That’s why the local businesses that grow run several channels at once (search, listings, reviews, community events and email), so the name keeps turning up until the day the customer needs you.
### Q. How much should a small business spend on marketing?
A.  A common benchmark is 5–10% of revenue, though there’s no hard rule; the SBA itself says there’s no hard and fast answer. For a local business the smarter first move costs almost nothing: your Google Business Profile, consistent listings and reviews are free and drive the most local customers. Spend money only after those fundamentals are solid, and put it toward the channels where your specific customers already are.
### Q. Do I need a business license in St. Louis County?
A.  Not in the way most people mean. St. Louis County says it doesn’t issue a business license as such, but every business has to register with the county Assessor for personal property tax, and retailers, wholesalers and manufacturers need a merchant’s or manufacturer’s license through the Assessor, with a $5 fee paid to the Collector of Revenue. Some activities, like selling liquor or street vending, need separate county licenses. If your business sits inside a city rather than unincorporated county, that city has its own license rules, so check with city hall too.
### Q. Are there government programs that help St. Louis County businesses?
A.  Yes. The St. Louis Economic Development Partnership (STL Partnership) is the economic development agency for the city and county, with low-interest loan programs, SBA 504 financing, incubator space and help navigating it all. The Missouri SBDC’s St. Louis office offers free, confidential one-on-one consulting, and your local chamber of commerce adds networking. Cheaper capital and free advice stretch the promotion budget you do have.

## Where to List Your Business Online: The Listing Sites That Actually Matter
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/the-ultimate-guide-to-seo-local-business-listings-2025
Refreshed September 2026
Somewhere in your inbox is an offer promising to “list your business on 100+ directories!” It sounds productive — more places, more visibility, right? So you start submitting to sites you’ve never heard of, and… nothing happens. No calls, no traffic, just your business name scattered across a hundred pages nobody visits, half of them with your old phone number. There’s a better way, and it starts with doing less, not more.
You don’t need 100 business listings — you need the right ten or so, kept perfectly consistent. The listing sites that actually matter are the ones your customers and Google actually use: Google Business Profile, your website, the major maps and review platforms, your industry’s niche sites, and your local directory. Spraying yourself across random directories doesn’t help, and can even hurt. Here’s the honest 2026 playbook for St. Louis businesses.
And the stakes here are local: 99.4% of Missouri businesses are small businesses (SBA Office of Advocacy, 2025), and the St. Louis region adds more than 6,000 new businesses a year (Greater St. Louis, Inc.). In a field that crowded, the business that’s easiest to find — consistently, everywhere customers look — is the one that wins.
### Why “More Directories” Is a Myth
The people who built the citation playbook say so themselves. David Mihm, one of the early champions of citation building, has written that citations have been losing ranking weight since 2014, and that the ones worth chasing are directories that already show up for your keywords (Near Media). Whitespark’s 2026 Local Search Ranking Factors survey lists mismatched name, address and phone details as a negative ranking factor, and ranks citation consistency on the major platforms well above the raw number of citations (Whitespark, 2026). Every extra low-quality listing is one more place your information can go stale and contradict the others — which is worse than not being there at all. Which flips the usual instinct on its head: instead of asking where else you can get listed, when did you last check that the listings you already have all agree?
### Consistency Is the Real Lever
One signal outweighs nearly everything else here. Consistent name, address, and phone (NAP) data across the major sources is how search engines and AI assistants confirm you’re real and located where you say — Whitespark’s survey counts mismatched NAP against you, and finds that three of the top five factors for AI search visibility are citation factors (Whitespark, 2026). Even small mismatches — “Street” vs “St.,” an old suite number, a disconnected phone — erode Google’s confidence in where you actually are. Chase the same listing everywhere that counts, not more of them.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. How many business directories should I list on?
A.  Fewer than you’ve been told. Focus on the platforms customers and Google actually use — Google Business Profile, your website, Apple Maps, Bing, Facebook, Yelp, the BBB, and your industry’s niche sites — and keep them perfectly consistent. Whitespark’s 2026 ranking-factors survey puts citation consistency on the major platforms well ahead of the raw number of citations, so a short, accurate list beats a long, sloppy one every time.
### Q. What is a business directory listing?
A.  It’s your business’s entry on a site that sorts businesses by category and location, so people can look you up by what you do and where you are. A basic listing carries your name, address, phone, hours and website; a fuller one adds photos, reviews, services and posts. Google Business Profile, Bing Places, Apple Maps, Yelp and the BBB are all directory listings in that sense. On St Louis Near Me Directory, the free basic listing holds your name, address, phone, three images and an About section, and the Gold Plan turns it into a listing that works like your own website, in up to 10 categories across 40 locations.
### Q. What is NAP in SEO?
A.  NAP stands for name, address and phone number, the three details search engines use to confirm a business is real and located where it says. Google, Bing and AI assistants compare your NAP across your website, your Google Business Profile, the data aggregators and every directory that lists you. When they all agree, letter for letter, that agreement works as a trust signal; when they don’t, each mismatch is a small vote of doubt about which version is right.
### Q. Why is NAP consistency important?
A.  Because inconsistency costs you twice. Customers who find an old phone number or a former address call the wrong line or drive to the wrong place, and search engines that see conflicting details lose confidence in where you actually are. Whitespark’s 2026 survey lists mismatched NAP as a negative ranking factor, and AI assistants lean on the same citations when they decide whether to name you. The fix costs nothing but attention: pick one canonical version and make every listing match it.
### Q. How to check NAP consistency?
A.  Search your business name, then your phone number, then your street address, and note every listing that comes up. Put each one in a spreadsheet next to your canonical version and look for the small drift: St. vs Saint, Ste 200 vs Suite 200, an old number, a former location, a call-tracking number. Fix the platforms that matter most first (Google, Bing, Apple Maps and the data aggregators), then the rest. The 20-minute audit above walks through it, and it’s worth repeating a couple of times a year.
### Q. Are the yellow pages still used?
A.  Yes, by a smaller crowd. The printed book is fading while YP.com and its listing data live on. ## Day Nine, No Postcard: Don't Touch Your Google Business Profile Yet
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/the-ultimate-guide-to-google-local-business-listing-2025
Day nine. The mail truck pulls away from the curb on your South City block, and the box holds a water bill, a pizza coupon and nothing from Google.
Maybe you told a customer last week it was “all set on Google.” Now you’re flipping envelopes on the front steps, hearing yourself say it. Just a postcard that may or may not be coming, and a profile that sits half-finished until it lands.
And here is the trap the process sets for you: the two moves that feel like action are the two that cost you time. Clicking for a new code feels like doing something. Google says don’t: if you request a new one, it invalidates the code already in the mail and sends another, and that can make the process longer. Tidying your business name, address or category while you wait feels responsible. Google says don’t do that either, because the code it sent you won’t work. Day nine is a waiting day. Leave the profile alone.
That knot in your stomach is what a process feels like when it keeps its rules to itself and hands you a form instead of a person. Two of those rules matter tonight. You can’t choose how Google verifies you: its page says the method is picked for you and “can’t be changed.” And you can’t pay to rank higher: its ranking page says there’s no way to request or pay for a better local ranking. Adding or claiming the profile costs nothing. So when a smooth voice on a spoofed local number calls offering to switch your verification method or buy you the top of the map, ask yourself one question: who is selling what Google says can’t be bought? Hang up and keep the money.
The paper is where St. Louis gets specific, and where it can save you real money. Say you bake out of a Tower Grove South kitchen, flour on the counter and the oven still ticking, under a name that isn’t your own. Missouri’s Secretary of State wants that trade name registered: $7, good for five years, per its fictitious name FAQ.
Inside the City limits, the City’s own opening-a-business page says a license is required for every business. Here is the sentence to forward to every friend who works from home: the initial Graduated Business License fee is $200, unless it’s a City home-based business, and then it’s $25. Same city, same kitchen table, a very different check to slide under the window. Timing matters too: open between January 1 and May 31 and that year’s license is $100, but the renewal is still due June 1 for another $200. Call the Business Assistance Center in City Hall, Room 421, at (314) 622-4120 before you pay for the wrong one.
Drive across the river, tires humming on the bridge deck, and the rules change again. St. Clair County says it doesn’t issue business licenses at all, so the answer comes from the town where the work happens. Wherever you file, keep one name on the truck, the invoice, the state paperwork and the profile. If Google asks you to verify by video, its examples of proof include a business permit, invoice or utility bill that matches the name on your Business Profile.
Now, tonight. Three moves, and none of them needs a phone call. First, open your profile and read which verification options Google is showing you. Second, leave the code button and the name field alone, however long day nine feels. Third, mark two dates: most codes arrive within 14 days, and a code expires after 30 days. If today is day nine, circle day 14 on the calendar by the back door.
### What does a stranger in a flooded basement see when your business comes up?
It’s 11 at night after a hard rain, and a woman in Affton stands in two inches of cold water in her basement, phone lit in one hand. She isn’t reading anybody’s website. She’s tapping the first few names that come up and checking three things: the stars, the phone number, one photo of a truck.
The profile card holds your name, hours, photos, reviews and a button that rings your phone, and it shows up in Google Search and Google Maps. BrightLocal’s local consumer survey of 1,002 US adults found that 97% of consumers read reviews for local businesses, and 74% only care about reviews written in the last three months.
That second number is the quiet one. Last year’s five-star praise won’t carry you forever, and a quiet profile starts to look like a quiet business. Is it worth having a Google Business Profile? For a business that wants local customers, the survey leans one way: nearly every shopper reads local reviews, and the profile costs nothing.
### Can you pay to come up first?
No. Its local ranking page says local results are mainly based on relevance, distance and popularity, and it calls that last one prominence: how well-known a business is, “based on info like how many websites link to your business and how many reviews you have.” Then comes the sentence every burned owner should have framed: “There’s no way to request or pay for a better local ranking on Google.”
That’s the second half of the line from the top of this guide: you can’t choose how Google verifies you, and you can’t pay to rank higher. When someone promises you a guaranteed top spot, you now know what they’re really selling. What you can do is earn your place the slow way: accurate details, steady reviews, and other places on the web that point to you. Google adds that “More reviews and positive ratings can help your business’s local ranking,” which is why the review habit below isn’t busywork.
### Are you eligible for a Google Business Profile if you drive to your customers?
A van with a ladder rack sits in the driveway. The “office” is a kitchen table, a laptop and a coffee ring on last Tuesday’s estimate. Does that count as a business Google will list? If you travel to your customers where they are, yes. That’s the test.
Google’s guidelines say a profile is for “a physical location that customers can visit, or travels to customers where they are.” Online-only businesses, brands, organizations and artists aren’t eligible. Neither are addresses that only look like locations. A P.O. box or a mailbox at a remote location isn’t acceptable, and a virtual office “isn’t eligible.”
### Storefront, service-area or both?
Service-area businesses, like a plumber who runs the business from home, play by a different address rule. Google says that “If you’re a service-area business, you should hide your business address from customers.” If you run a shop and also drive out to jobs, a hybrid business “can show their storefront address.”
For the service area itself, you can list up to 20 areas, by city, postal code or another area. They “shouldn’t be more than about 2 hours of driving time,” and there’s no radius option. So pick real places by name: Kirkwood, Florissant, Belleville, Edwardsville. Don’t try to draw a circle. If you hid your address, nothing is wrong.
### Do you need an LLC? What Google checks, and why the paper has to match
It’s ten at night, and you’ve typed “do I need an LLC for Google” into the search bar because the last person you asked said “probably” and then mentioned their rate.
Do you need an LLC for a Google Business Profile? No. Google’s eligibility test is in-person contact with customers during your stated hours, not an LLC or any other business structure. Where LLC does come up, it’s in the naming rules, which list “irrelevant legal terms (e.g. LLC, LTD, INC)” among the things your business name must not include.
### Every filing in one place
When Google reads your paper, what matters is whether it matches the profile. Here is every filing from this guide in one list, so you can screenshot it. Fees and phone numbers change, so confirm them on the call.
Missouri trade name: $7.00, good for five years, filed at bsd.sos.mo.gov. The rule is Missouri statute section 417.200. A sole proprietor using their own name can skip it.
Madison County, Illinois: an assumed name goes through the county clerk for $31.00, plus a newspaper notice that runs three weeks and carries its own publication fee. Call (618) 296-6200.
St. Clair County, Illinois: assumed names go through the County Clerk at 618-277-6600 ext. 2363. The county doesn’t issue business licenses, so ask your municipality.
City of St. Louis: a license is required for all businesses. Home-based businesses pay $25, while the initial graduated fee is $200. Ask zoning about a home occupation waiver at (314) 622-3666, and expect a City Tax Clearance. The Business Assistance Center, at 1200 Market St., Room 421, answers at (314) 622-4120.
Outside the city limits, we haven’t verified every town’s rules, so call the one where you work. Then do the cheap, unglamorous thing that helps against a silent process. Keep one name on the truck, on the invoice, in the state filing and on the profile. That’s our advice, not a Google rule. But Google’s examples of proof include an official business registration, a business license, tax certificates and utility bills, and the name and address on them have to match. An afternoon spent lining them up now is an afternoon you won’t have to spend scrambling later.

### Start at your own sign: how to make a business listing on Google
Walk out to your own sign, or the door of your truck, and read the name out loud. Sun on the vinyl lettering, maybe a smudge from last week’s rain. That’s the name to start from, and every other step builds on it.
### Start with the name on your door
One older guide tells you to pack your business name with keywords. Please don’t. “Best Cheap Plumber St. Louis 24 Hours” isn’t a name. It’s a search. Google’s naming rules list marketing taglines and phone numbers or website URLs among the things a name must not include, and “Including unnecessary information in your business name isn’t permitted, and could result in the suspension of your Business Profile.” Keywords belong in your categories, services and description.
### When the name on your profile isn’t the name on your truck
It happens. You search yourself, and the card shows an old name, an extra phrase, a version you never chose. We couldn’t find a Google page that explains why names change, so we won’t guess. What the pages do cover is the fix. Edit the name from the profile itself, and don’t create a new profile to dodge the problem. Google says edits “usually take up to 10 minutes to review, but sometimes it can take up to 30 days,” so check back before you panic. And make sure the name you submit follows the rules above, because a name with a tagline or a service stuffed into it is the kind that can get a profile suspended.
### Search first, then claim or add
Search your business name on Google before you add anything. If a card already exists, claim it. If it doesn’t, add it. Is a Google Business Profile free? In Google’s own words: “You can add or claim your business at no charge.”
You’ll enter your name, then your address or your service areas, your phone number and a category. One rule is worth a sticky note on your monitor: do not create a new Business Profile for the same business. And if someone else has already verified your listing and you’re authorized to manage the business, you can request ownership from the current profile owner, who “has 3 days to respond.”
### Pick categories, write the description, add the details
Choose a primary category: Google says to pick a specific category that represents your main business. Google lets you add up to 9 more, and it warns: “Do not use categories solely as keywords.” Pick the ones that are true.
The description has a hard ceiling: “Do not exceed 750 characters.” No links of any type are allowed, and Google asks you to focus on your business instead of promotions, prices or sales. Write it the way you’d explain your work to a neighbor: what you do, who for, where. Save the sale for a post.
Attributes describe who you are and what you offer. Google’s list includes Women-owned, Veteran-owned and Small business. Finish with your hours, holiday hours included. A customer who drives to a dark shop on a holiday remembers it.
### What if the postcard never comes?
Some owners get offered a text. Some end up on the sidewalk recording a video, phone held out like a flashlight. Some wait on a postcard. You don’t get to choose, because Google says “Verification methods are automatically determined by Google and can’t be changed.” The options you see depend on your business type, public info, region or business hours, so a postcard-only screen isn’t a setting you missed.
Google’s verification page describes these options: phone or text, email, a live video call, a video recording and a postcard. Most codes arrive within 14 days, and they expire after 30 days. While you wait, resist the urge to ask for another. Google’s instruction is blunt: “Do not request a new code.” Verification reviews take up to 5 business days.
What if day 15 comes and goes? We couldn’t find a Google instruction for that exact day, and we won’t guess. What the page does say is that codes last 30 days and a second request is the wrong move.
Use the wait. Draft your description in a notes app and trim it under 750 characters. Gather the photos you’re proudest of. When the code lands, you can finish the rest that night.
### If Google asks for a video
For a live video call, Google’s tip is simple: “Show outside signs, nearby businesses, or a street sign that confirms your business location.” We’d start on the sidewalk, let the camera find the name on your sign or door, then walk in. You’re proving you’re really standing where the pin says you are.

A promise of an exact go-live date is a guess dressed as a fact.

### What do you do when your profile is suspended on a Monday?
Monday, 7 a.m., coffee still too hot to drink. You type your own business name into Google, and the card you’ve been feeding for months doesn’t look the way it did on Friday. The stomach drop comes first. The anger comes second. Both are fair.
Now do the slow thing, because the order of your next moves matters more than speed. Start by reading your business name against the naming rules above, because Google says unnecessary information in a business name could result in suspension. Then work through this list, which quotes Google’s suspension and appeal pages. Screenshot it. It’s the part owners tend to learn the hard way.
Don’t start over. Google says it flatly: “Do not create a new Business Profile for the same business.” A fresh start feels like control.
Gather proof before you appeal. Google’s examples include an official business registration, a business license, tax certificates and utility bills, with your name and address matching. This is where the paperwork we talked about earlier earns its keep.
Appeal once, and make it count. “Appeals can only be submitted once.” Don’t fire one off at 7 a.m. just to feel busy.
Wait out the review. “Appeal reviews and decisions can take up to 5 business days.” That’s a long time to stare at your phone, so keep working.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Is a Google Business Profile free?
A.  Yes. Google says it in plain words: “You can add or claim your business at no charge.” If someone quotes you a fee, it’s for their time, not Google’s permission. The real price is attention: an evening to set it up well, then a few minutes now and then to keep it current.
### Q. Do I need an LLC for a Google Business Profile?
A.  No. Google’s test is in-person contact with customers during your stated hours, not an LLC or any other entity type, and its naming rules list irrelevant legal terms like LLC, LTD and INC among the things a name must not include, unless real-world proof shows they’re part of your business name. Missouri does ask you to register a fictitious name with the Secretary of State if you trade under one: $7.00, good for five years.
### Q. Who is eligible for a Google Business Profile?
A.  Any business with “a physical location that customers can visit, or travels to customers where they are.” Online-only businesses, brands, organizations and artists aren’t eligible, and a P.O. box, a mailbox at a remote location or a virtual office won’t work. Service-area businesses hide their address and can list up to 20 service areas.
### Q. Is it worth having a Google Business Profile?
A.  For a business that wants local customers, yes. BrightLocal’s survey found 97% of consumers read reviews for local businesses, and the profile is free to add. But it isn’t the only place to be seen. A listing on St Louis Near Me Directory gives neighbors and AI tools a second source to read about you.
### Q. How long does it take for your business to show up on Google Maps?
A.  Most verification codes arrive within 14 days, a verification review takes up to 5 business days, and later edits usually take up to 10 minutes to review but can take up to 30 days. Codes expire after 30 days, and Google says not to request a new one while you wait.
### Q. How much does it cost to put a location on Google Maps?
A.  Google says you can add or claim your business at no charge. A Maps listing comes from that Google Business Profile, and Google says there’s no way to pay for a better local ranking. Apple Business and Bing Places are free too. If someone charges to “put you on Google Maps,” ask exactly what the fee buys.
### Q. How much does it cost to set up Google My Business?
A.  Nothing. Whether you call it Google My Business or Google Business Profile, Google lets you add or claim your business at no charge. Paying for help is your call. If you want a second home on the web, Gold on St Louis Near Me Directory is $357 a year, under a dollar a day, with a 7-day trial and no charge until day 8.

Across the river, a pen scratches across an assumed-name form at the Madison County clerk’s counter: $31.00 plus the cost of a newspaper notice, and then your business name sits in small type in the legal notices once a week for three consecutive weeks. The clerk’s number is (618) 296-6200. On the Missouri side, if you operate under a name that isn’t your own legal name, the fictitious name registration is $7.00, good for five years, and filed online at bsd.sos.mo.gov. Same metro, two counters, two price tags.
Then the license, and this is where St. Louis gets strange: cross a city limit and the rules change under your tires. Missouri law, RSMo 71.990, says no political subdivision shall require a person, as a condition of operating a home-based business, to obtain a home-based business license. Webster Groves puts it in capital letters: home-based businesses are “NOT required to obtain a business license,” though they still need a residential occupancy permit. Brentwood’s FAQ says “Home businesses also need a license.” Inside the City of St. Louis, a home-based business pays $25 for one. One state law, three answers.
We’re not lawyers, and the statute itself says whether a local rule complies “is a judicial question.” So call the office before you pay or skip anything. Not sure you’re inside the City line? The City will check for you: “Use the form below to see if your address is in the City.”
Why does any of this matter for search? If your profile is ever suspended, Google lists an official business registration and a business license among the evidence that can help your appeal. A name that matches on every page is a name you can prove.
### What Is Local SEO? The Short List Read Out Loud on Gravois
At a red light on Gravois, the passenger reads the short list out loud: a name, a star rating, another name, another rating. Local SEO is the work of being one of the names she reads, and a chart of impressions can’t tell you whether you are.
The search doesn’t stop at a town line, either. In this metro, the calls in your report can come from the city (in the Census Bureau’s words, “an independent city outside of any county”), a Missouri county or an Illinois one. Your customer’s phone doesn’t know where one jurisdiction ends. Your paperwork does.
Google’s Business Profile help page says local results are “mainly based on relevance, distance, and popularity.” Under prominence, it names two things you can grow: how many websites link to your business and how many reviews you have. Distance depends on where the customer is standing. The other two you can work on.
Remember the line from the top: no retainer and no special package can buy the spot. What Google does say is that “more reviews and positive ratings can help your business’s local ranking.” Its advice on hiring help is just as blunt: no one can guarantee you a top ranking on Google. So a pitch that promises to buy you page one is promising something Google says can’t be bought.
What local SEO isn’t: a one-time trick, a pile of keywords in your footer, or a stack of cheap directory submissions you’ll never look at again. It’s a handful of things kept complete, consistent and current. Boring? A little. That’s the good news, because boring is something you can do on a Tuesday night.
### When a Neighbor Asks ChatGPT for a Plumber, Is SEO Dead?
A homeowner asks ChatGPT who to call about a leaking roof. Not Google. ChatGPT. In BrightLocal’s survey of 1,002 US adults, use of ChatGPT and other generative AI tools for local recommendations rose from 6% last year to 45% (BrightLocal). In that same survey, 97% of consumers read reviews for local businesses, and 74% only care about reviews written in the last three months.
### Dead, or just spread out?
So, is SEO dead now with AI? No. The asking spread out. Nearly all of those same consumers still read reviews, and most want them recent. You can’t fix that with a keyword. You fix it by being a business with a complete profile and fresh reviews that shows up in more than one place.
Now the part that’s opinion, so we’ll label it. Whitespark’s local ranking factors survey of 47 experts ranks the factors the experts believe matter most, and it says plainly that none of them has special access to the internal workings of Google’s local search algorithm. The same panel puts the primary Business Profile category at number one. The report also says citations as a local search strategy “have been decreasing in importance for the past decade,” yet 3 of the top 5 AI Search visibility factors are citation factors. A citation is any site that lists your name, address and phone. Both can be true at once. Treat it as a reason to keep your details tidy, not as a rule.
### Replaced by what?
What is replacing SEO? As far as we can tell, nothing. A second place to be recommended opened up next to the first. What’s fading is the old recipe: a website, one listing and a monthly report. The need to be easy to recommend isn’t going anywhere.
### What can a chatbot actually do?
Can ChatGPT do SEO for you? Partly. It can draft wording, like a reply to a review or a first pass at your business description. Read every line before you post it. The parts that need you still need you: claiming the profile, fetching the postcard from the mailbox, and doing work good enough that a customer wants to write about it. And the page-one shortcut doesn’t exist. Reread that Google line above.

### Which Five Things Sit Behind That Little Map Card?
Stand at the curb outside your own door, pull your business up on Google Maps, and it looks small: a name, a pin, a star rating, a row of photos. Here’s what sits behind that small card, in the order we’d work on it.
### 1. Your Google Business Profile
It’s free: Google calls it a free Business Profile. If you go to the customer, Google treats you as a service-area business, one that provides “service at the customer’s location (for example, a locksmith or plumber),” so you list the areas you serve instead of a storefront address. Then you verify, and the method can be a postcard with a PIN, a phone call or an email.
Then the details. Choose the primary category that matches what you actually do. Use your real business name and nothing else. Google’s guidelines for the name are plain: “Don’t include marketing taglines,” and the same list rules out phone numbers, website URLs and location details.
### 2. Reviews, asked for on purpose
Ask on purpose: text customers a review link, or put a QR code by the register. Two habits to skip: asking only the customers you expect to be happy, and trading a discount or a gift for a review. Reply to every review anyway; Google says that when you reply, “it shows that you value their feedback.” Recent ones carry weight, since 74% of consumers in BrightLocal’s survey only care about reviews written in the last three months. A steady trickle of fresh reviews beats a big pile of old ones.
### 3. Details that match everywhere
Same name, same address, same phone on your website, Facebook, Bing Places and Apple Business. Bing Places is free and imports from Google. Apple says the brand management tools previously available in Apple Business Connect will now be available through Apple Business. None of this is a Google ranking promise. It’s hygiene: a customer shouldn’t have to guess which number is real. Keep the handful of listings that matter perfectly consistent instead of scattering your business across a pile of junk directories.
### 4. Pages that name the town and the job
Your website should say what you do and where you do it. One page for each service. The towns you cover, named. Written for a person standing in their driveway, not for a robot. Put your name, address and phone in the footer. If whoever built your site can add local-business schema, a bit of code that, in Google’s words, lets “you tell Google about business hours” and similar details, ask them to. If not, skip it for now.
### 5. Links and local mentions
Google names links to your website as part of prominence. The honest ones come from being a neighbor: your chamber of commerce, a local news mention, a supplier or partner who lists you. They arrive slowly. That’s the nature of other people vouching for you.

### How to Start SEO as a Beginner When You Only Have Four Evenings
Four weeks, one evening a week, a phone and a coffee going cold. How to start SEO as a beginner? In this order.
### Week 1: Claim and complete your profile
Finish what you started tonight. Set it up as a service-area business if you go to the customer, and verify by whichever method Google offers. Fill in your hours, services and primary category. Add real photos of your work and your place. Write the description in the words customers actually use.
### Week 2: Make the details match
Pick one version of your name, address and phone, and fix every mismatch. Start with your website, Facebook, Bing Places and Apple Business. Then pull out whichever filings from the paperwork section near the top apply to you. The name on each should read exactly like the name on your profile.
A few more St. Louis details belong in that file. Inside the city, a home-based business also needs a home occupation waiver from zoning at (314) 622-3666 and a City Tax Clearance, and the Business Assistance Center at (314) 622-4120, 1200 Market St., Room 421, can walk you through the license. St. Clair County doesn’t issue business licenses, so ask your municipality. For a Missouri sales tax license, the Department of Revenue’s number is 573-751-5860.
### Week 3: Turn on reviews
Text every happy customer your review link, or put the QR code where they’ll see it. Don’t screen who you ask, and don’t offer a discount for a review. Then reply to every review you already have, good and bad. Google says “positive reviews and helpful replies can help your business stand out,” and a calm, specific reply to a rough one shows the next reader how you handle a problem.
### Week 4: Strengthen your site
Make sure your site names your services and the towns you cover, and put your name, address and phone in the footer. Publish one genuinely helpful local page: a neighborhood guide, an FAQ, a “what to expect” article. Then open Performance and write down this month’s calls, directions and website clicks. That’s your baseline. Thirty days of this beats a year of good intentions.

## What Local SEO Actually Is (and Isn’t)

Local SEO is search optimization aimed at a place. Regular SEO tries to rank a page nationally or globally; local SEO tries to make *your* business the answer for people in *your* area. It’s what decides whether you appear when someone searches “electrician near me,” “best tacos in Maplewood,” or just “plumber” from a phone in Kirkwood.

What it isn’t: a one-time trick, a pile of keywords stuffed into your footer, or a stack of cheap directory submissions. Google got wise to all of that years ago. Modern local SEO is about being genuinely complete, consistent, and trusted — signals you build and maintain, not games you play.

## Why Local SEO Matters More Than Ever

Search is how people find local businesses now, full stop. Google has said roughly **46% of all searches carry local intent** (Google, 2018), and by 2018 **82% of smartphone shoppers had run a “near me” search** (Uberall, 2018). Those numbers are years old and have only intensified — local search is the default, not a trend.

What’s genuinely new is the AI layer. **45% of consumers now use AI tools like ChatGPT to find local businesses, up from just 6% a year earlier** (BrightLocal, 2026). And **97% read reviews before choosing** (BrightLocal, 2026). The through-line: whether a customer uses Google, Maps, or an AI assistant, they’re pulling from the same local signals — which means one well-run local SEO effort now pays off everywhere at once.

## The Building Blocks of Local SEO

Five pieces do almost all the work. Get them in this order:

- **Google Business Profile**— the foundation. Claim it, verify it, and complete every field: hours, the most accurate primary category, services, photos, attributes, and Q&A. This single asset is the biggest driver of whether you appear in the local map pack.
- **Reviews**— recent, plentiful, and answered. They’re both a ranking signal and the thing 97% of customers read before choosing you. A steady trickle of fresh reviews beats a big pile of old ones.
- **Citations & NAP consistency**— your name, address, and phone, identical everywhere they appear. Google trusts a business whose details line up and discounts one that contradicts itself.
- **Local website content**— pages that name the areas and services you cover, written for humans, marked up with local-business schema.
- **Links & local reputation**— mentions and links from other reputable local sources (chambers, directories, press, partners) that vouch for you.

## On-Page, Off-Page & Technical: The Three Layers

Local SEO work sorts into three layers, and a strong effort touches all three:

- **On-page**— what’s on your own site: title tags and headings with your service and location, dedicated pages per service, local content, internal links, and schema. This is where you control relevance directly.
- **Off-page**— what happens elsewhere: your Google Business Profile, reviews, citations, and links from other sites. This is where prominence is built, and it’s usually the bigger lever for local.
- **Technical**— the plumbing: a mobile-friendly, fast-loading site, clean crawlable structure, and valid structured data so search engines and AI can read you cleanly. You don’t need to be an engineer — you need a site that isn’t actively broken on a phone.

## How Google Ranks Local Results

Google spells it out. Per its own Business Profile documentation, local rankings come down to three factors: **relevance** (how well your profile matches the search — driven by categories, services, and content), **distance** (how close you are to the searcher — managed through an accurate address or service area), and **prominence** (how established and trusted you look — built from reviews, citations, and links). Distance you can’t change; relevance and prominence are entirely yours to earn, and that’s where local SEO lives.

## What Local SEO Costs — and How Long It Takes

The fundamentals are free if you do them yourself; they cost time, not money. Done for you, local SEO runs roughly **$300 to $2,000 a month** across the industry (WebFX), depending on scope. And it isn’t instant: plan on **three to six months** for meaningful movement — Google itself says SEO changes can take four months to a year to fully register. Anyone guaranteeing page one next week is selling smoke.

## DIY or Hire It Out?

Every building block above is genuinely DIY-able, and if you’ve got the time, do it. The catch is never the *knowing* — it’s the *consistency*: the weekly review asks, the monthly listing checks, the fresh content, the AI-visibility monitoring. That’s the part that slips when you’re busy running the business, and it’s exactly the part worth handing off. Do it yourself if you’ll keep it up; hire it out if you know you won’t.

## Common Local SEO Mistakes

The usual reasons a St. Louis business stays invisible: an unclaimed or half-finished Google profile; a name, address, or phone that differs across listings; a vague or wrong primary category; too few recent reviews; a thin website with no local pages; and chasing volume — dumping your business into 100 junk directories — instead of keeping the handful that matter perfectly consistent. Every one of these is fixable, and none require a big budget.

## Local SEO vs. Regular SEO: What’s the Difference?

Regular (or “organic”) SEO competes for ranking on a topic anywhere — a national blog trying to rank for “best running shoes.” **Local SEO competes for customers near you**, in the Map pack, on Google Maps, and in “near me” and AI answers. The levers overlap but the emphasis differs: local leans heavily on your Google Business Profile, consistent name-address-phone, reviews, and location relevance, while classic SEO leans more on broad content and links. For a St. Louis business serving local customers, local SEO is where nearly all the return is — you’re not trying to beat the whole internet, just to be the obvious choice in your own city.

## The One Signal That Tells You It’s Working

If you track just one thing, track **real contacts from your Google Business Profile** — calls, direction requests, and website clicks, visible right in your profile insights. Rankings bounce around and impressions can flatter you, but calls and visits are customers actually choosing you. When that number trends up month over month, your local SEO is working, full stop. When it’s flat, revisit the fundamentals: is the profile complete and active, is your name-address-phone consistent everywhere, are fresh reviews coming in? Nail those and the contacts follow — because they’re the same things that decide whether you appear in that first ten-second search in the first place.

## She Was Half a Block Away. The Map Sent Her Somewhere Else.
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/hyperlocal-seo-platform-benefits-how-st-louis-businesses-win-their-neighborhood
She’s half a block from your door. Saturday morning in Tower Grove South, phone out, thumb typing “coffee near me” while the smell of your espresso drifts onto the sidewalk. The map loads three pins. None of them is you. She walks six minutes to the shop that showed up. Twenty minutes later she strolls back past your window holding somebody else’s cup, and you’re wiping down a counter nobody’s leaning on, wondering why Saturdays feel slower than they should.
That’s not a you problem. It’s a map problem. Google decides who’s “near” from the signals you hand it, not from where your front door actually sits. So what does the map think is on your corner?
Run the parking-lot test this week. Drive to the Schnucks lot in the neighborhood you most want to win, sit in the car, open your phone and search your trade the way a customer would. Screenshot whose names come up. Google weighs distance, so that screen, not the one at your desk, is your real ranking in Affton or Florissant or Soulard. Here’s why that screen looks the way it does. The St. Louis map is unusually fine-grained, 79 city neighborhoods and 88 county towns, and the map’s names aren’t even the ones people say out loud.
Dogtown isn’t on the city’s official list of 79 neighborhoods. Your customers still search for it.
The city’s map calls that corner Clayton-Tamm. The Grove isn’t on the list either; it’s a strip of Manchester Avenue inside Forest Park Southeast. People type the name they use at the bar, so put both on your profile: “serving Dogtown (Clayton-Tamm) and The Grove.”
Then there’s the county’s third kind of place: no city at all. A mom in Affton types “shoe repair Affton” while her kid’s cleat flaps loose at the toe. Nearly a third of St. Louis County’s roughly 1 million people live in unincorporated places like these, governed directly by the County, per its own financial report. The map can’t learn a name you never say, so put it in your description and your posts.
Your receipt says St. Louis. Your customer typed Affton.

If you drew a 25-mile circle around your shop years ago, Google’s help page says you can’t edit it now; you have to replace it with named places. Around here, 20 slots go fast, so start with the towns and ZIP codes where your actual customers live.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Should I do my own marketing or hire it out?
A.  Both work. Every core task — Google Business Profile, reviews, listings — is DIY-able if you’ll keep it up consistently. The moment the weekly upkeep starts slipping (which is when most owners fade), that’s the signal it’s worth hiring out.
### Q. How much does done-for-you marketing cost in St. Louis?
A.  Industry-wide, local SEO runs about $300 to $2,000 a month (WebFX), with fully-managed services often $800 to $1,300 per location (BrightLocal). The honest first step is free, though: run an AI audit to see where you stand before paying to fix anything.
### Q. How long before it works?
A.  Plan on three to six months for meaningful movement in local rankings and leads. Google itself says SEO changes can take four months to a year. Anyone guaranteeing page one within days isn’t being straight with you.
### Q. What does a done-for-you service actually include?
A.  The ongoing fundamentals on a schedule: Google Business Profile management, review generation and response, consistent listings, AI-visibility monitoring, and plain reporting. It’s the weekly maintenance, not a one-time setup.
### Q. What are the red flags in a marketing provider?
A.  Promises of “500 citations” or “18x listings,” guaranteed #1 rankings, long lock-in contracts, and no clear reporting. Real providers focus on fundamentals, stay transparent, offer month-to-month terms, and know your local market.
### Q. Can I switch marketing providers later without losing my work?
A.  Yes — as long as you own your accounts. If your Google Business Profile, listings, and website are in your name from the start, you can change providers and keep everything you’ve built. Problems only arise when a provider holds those assets hostage, which is exactly why ownership is the first thing to confirm before you sign.
### Q. How do I measure the ROI of local marketing?
A.  Track outcomes, not vanity metrics: calls, direction requests, form fills, and new customers — most visible right in your Google Business Profile insights. Ask new customers how they found you. If contacts and customers trend up over three to six months, it’s working. Impressions and rankings are supporting signals, not the scoreboard.
### Q. Is SEO or paid advertising better for a small local business?
A.  They do different jobs. Local SEO (your profile, listings, reviews) is a durable, mostly-free foundation that keeps paying off; paid ads buy fast, temporary visibility that stops when the budget does. For most small St. Louis businesses, build the free foundation first, then use ads to fill specific gaps — a slow season, a new service — rather than as a substitute.
### Q. How much does done-for-you local marketing cost in St. Louis?
A.  It varies widely with scope, but honest local providers typically price monthly and are transparent about exactly what’s included. Be wary of both extremes — suspiciously cheap offers usually mean automated, low-value work, while premium prices should come with premium reporting and results. Judge cost against the value of the customers it brings, and insist on month-to-month terms until they’ve earned your trust.

## What Movers Actually Cost in St. Louis (and the Question That Makes Quotes Comparable)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/moving-cost-st-louis
You have a closing date, a lease that ends on the 31st, and a vague sense that movers cost either four hundred dollars or four thousand.
So you search it, and the top results tell you what movers cost in Oregon. Then Indianapolis. Then Houston, then Los Angeles. Which is a strange way to answer a question nobody asked.
### How much do movers actually cost?
For a local move, most households land somewhere between $500 and $2,500, driven almost entirely by how much stuff you have and how hard it is to carry.
But before you compare a single quote, know the two things that make quotes incomparable:
Hourly rates are quoted two different ways. Some companies quote per mover, some quote per crew. A “$50 an hour” quote and a “$100 an hour” quote can be the identical price.
Travel time is usually billed and rarely mentioned. Many companies charge for driving from their yard to you and back again, which can add an hour or two to a job you thought was three.
Ask these four before comparing a single price:
Is that rate per mover, or for the whole crew?
When does the clock start — when you leave your shop, or when you arrive at my house? And when does it stop?
Are there separate charges for the truck, equipment, blankets, boxes or tape?
Is the estimate binding, non-binding, or binding not-to-exceed?
That third one matters more than it sounds, because the hourly figure is often labor only. A three-person crew quoted at $175 an hour can arrive and bill the truck, the blankets, the boxes and the tape as separate line items on top of it. Nothing about “$175 an hour” tells you which arrangement you are in, and the difference across a full day is substantial. Ask what the rate covers and what it does not, item by item, and get the answer before the truck is loaded rather than when the invoice appears.
### Why the published numbers are useless
Line up what the top results actually say and the problem is obvious — they are not measuring the same thing.
A storage company: $25 to $50 an hour per mover, roughly $200 to $600 for two, with totals from $550 to $12,000.
A consumer review site: $80 to $100 an hour for a team of two.
An Indianapolis page: $95 to $110 an hour per mover.
A Los Angeles page: $100 to $170 an hour for two movers and a truck.
A moving-quote site: local average $1,400, long distance $5,450 at a thousand miles.
Read those again and notice the unit switching underneath. $25–$50 per mover is the same money as $80–$100 for a team of two. They look like wildly different markets and they are describing the same job.
The other problem is geography. Those pages are city templates — the same article with the city name changed. Rates genuinely differ between Los Angeles and the Midwest, so a number calculated for LA tells you nothing useful about moving from Affton to St. Peters.
### What actually determines your bill
Four things, roughly in order of impact.
Volume. How much you own is the whole game. Crews and trucks are sized to it, and hours follow from it. This is also the one variable you can genuinely change — every item you get rid of beforehand is money you do not spend moving it.
Access. Stairs, elevators, long carries from the truck to the door, and narrow streets where the truck cannot park close. A second-floor walk-up on both ends can add hours to an otherwise ordinary move. Say this up front; it is the most common reason a quote gets revised on the day.
Packing. Full-service packing is a separate line and often a large one, because it is labor plus materials. Partial packing — where they do the kitchen and the fragile things and you do the rest — is frequently the sensible middle.
Specialty items. Pianos, gun safes, treadmills, pool tables, oversized appliances and anything requiring disassembly get priced separately. Mention them when you book, not when the crew arrives.
### The travel-time charge nobody warns you about
This is the single most resented line on a moving invoice, and it is worth understanding before you see it rather than after.
The specific thing to pin down is when the clock starts and stops. Some companies start billing the moment the truck leaves their yard and stop when it returns — which means you are paying for their commute at both ends. Others bill door to door. The difference on a metro this spread out can be an hour or two of crew time on an otherwise ordinary job.
Many companies bill for getting the truck to you and back to their yard. Some charge a flat trip fee. Some add a fixed amount of time to the clock. Some bill actual drive time at both ends, which on a metro this spread out — a crew based in one county working a job in another — can be a genuinely significant chunk of the bill.
None of that is a scam. The truck and crew really are on the clock, and they cannot take other work. What makes people angry is discovering it at the end. Ask exactly how travel is billed, get the answer in writing, and factor it in when comparing two quotes — because a lower hourly rate with heavy travel billing frequently loses to a higher rate without it.
### Binding, non-binding, and why it matters
Ask which kind of estimate you are being given. It is the most important sentence in the whole transaction.
A non-binding estimate is a guess. The final price is what the job actually takes, which means it can go up. Most local hourly moves work this way, and that is normal — but it means your quote is a forecast, not a price.
A binding estimate is a fixed price for the agreed inventory. If the crew works slower than expected, that is their problem. If you add three rooms of furniture on the day, the binding estimate is void.
A binding not-to-exceed estimate is the best of both: you pay the actual cost if it comes in lower, and never more than the quoted ceiling. If it is offered, take it.
For any move crossing into Illinois, the company must be registered with the federal regulator and carry a USDOT number. That number is public and checkable, and a company that will not give you one is telling you something.
Nothing to do with movers — but Gillespie’s food lineup is worth the drive.
### Getting a real quote without the phone call
A common and entirely reasonable complaint about this industry: every site demands a phone call before it will say a number.
You can usually get around it. Most companies will now do a video survey — you walk through the house on a video call, they see the actual inventory, and you get a real quote instead of a range. It takes fifteen minutes and it is dramatically more accurate than describing it over the phone.
Whatever the format, get every quote to include the same things so they are actually comparable: hourly rate and whether it is per mover or per crew, how travel is billed, minimum hours, what packing materials cost, fees for stairs or long carries, and the estimate type. Two quotes that do not cover the same list are not two quotes.
### When to move, if you have any choice
Timing moves the price more than most people realize, because the industry has severe peaks.
Summer is peak season, and it is not close — leases and school calendars concentrate demand into a few months. The end of the month is peak within that, because leases end then. Weekends are peak within that.
Which means the cheapest slot is broadly the opposite: a weekday, mid-month, outside summer. A Tuesday in the middle of October is a different market from the last Saturday in July, with better crews available because they are not stretched.
If you cannot choose the date, book early anyway. Late bookings in peak season get whoever is left.
### What movers will not take
Every company refuses a similar list, and finding out on the morning of is a genuine problem because these things do not fit in the car with the plants and the cat.
Anything flammable or pressurized — propane tanks, gasoline, kerosene, lighter fluid, aerosols, paint thinner. Drain the mower and the grill tank in advance.
Paint and chemicals, including most cleaning products and pool chemicals.
Ammunition, and often firearms depending on the company.
Perishable food, and anything from the freezer.
Plants, frequently — they do not survive a hot truck, and some companies simply will not carry them.
Irreplaceable items — documents, jewelry, medication, hard drives. Not because they are banned, but because you should carry them yourself.
Paint and chemicals go to household hazardous waste, which every county in the region runs, not into the truck and not into the trash.
### The cheapest ways to move
Full service is one option on a spectrum, not the only one.
Labor-only — you rent the truck, they load and unload it — is the biggest single saving for most people, because loading is the skilled part and driving is not.
Portable containers get dropped at your house, you fill them on your own schedule, and they are collected and delivered. Useful when the two dates do not line up.
Truck rental with friends is genuinely cheapest and genuinely worst, and the calculation people forget is the risk: your furniture, your walls, your backs, and no insurance on any of it.
And the free one that beats all of them: move less. Sell, donate or dispose of things before the estimate, not after — and check whether your city will haul the bulky items for free before paying anyone to take them.
### Insurance, and what “covered” means
The word insurance gets used loosely here, and the default coverage is far thinner than people assume.
Basic liability, which is included at no charge on interstate moves, pays by weight rather than value. That means a heavy, cheap item and a light, expensive one are compensated the same way — and for anything genuinely valuable, the payout will not come close to replacing it. Full value protection costs extra and obligates the company to repair, replace or pay the actual value.
Two things worth doing regardless of which you choose: photograph anything valuable before it goes on the truck, and check whether your homeowner’s or renter’s policy covers goods in transit, because some do and it changes what you need to buy.
And note what voids coverage: boxes you packed yourself are generally not covered for internal damage, since nobody but you saw what went in or how. If a box holds something you would be upset to lose, let them pack it.
### Finding movers here
Get three quotes, insist they cover the same list, and ask every one of them the per-mover-or-per-crew question. Browse local movers on the home services coverage map, which covers both sides of the river.
If the move is into an older home, it is worth knowing what you are moving into — what an inspection does and does not cover is a useful read before closing day.

### Q. What is the cheapest day to hire movers?
