## Jiu-Jitsu in St. Louis: Every Academy, What It Costs, and What to Check
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/jiu-jitsu-and-bjj-in-st-louis
Almost every article about jiu-jitsu in St. Louis tells you it costs $150 to $250 a month. We checked every academy in the metro that actually publishes its rates.
They charge $50, $120 and $160.
That number appears to be a national guess that got repeated until it sounded local. It’s a decent illustration of why this guide exists: the useful information about training here — what it costs, who’s actually qualified, and what to look at before you put your bare feet on a mat — mostly isn’t written down anywhere.
### Where can I train jiu-jitsu in St. Louis?
The metro has around eighteen verifiable academies — a specialized corner of the region’s independent gyms and studios. The deepest credentials are at Vaghi BJJ in Ellisville — Rodrigo Vaghi is a sixth-degree black belt under Rickson Gracie and the highest-ranked black belt in the region. BJJ Lifestyle Academy in South County is the strongest competition room, run by Mike Rethmeyer, a Pan-American champion. For structured beginner curricula, the Gracie and Gracie Barra schools run defined fundamentals programs. For cheap, no-contract, no-gi training, Nomad Jiu Jitsu on South Grand is $50 a month.
### What it actually costs here
Only three academies in the metro publish their prices. Here they are.
Nomad Jiu Jitsu — $50 a month, or $10 a class, no contract. Arnold BJJ — $120 a month for one person, $216 for two, $324 for three; wrestling-only $100; six months $648; a year $1,224. They advertise no long-term contracts. Gracie Jiu-Jitsu St. Louis — $160 a month unlimited for the Combatives program, with 25% off for military, first responders and law enforcement, and family discounts.
So the honest range for published St. Louis rates is roughly $50 to $160 — not $150 to $250.
Most academies here don’t publish anything and want you to call. That’s not sinister, but it does mean you should ask three specific questions on the phone: is there an enrollment or registration fee, how long is the contract, and what does cancellation require. A gym that won’t answer those plainly is telling you something.
### The part nobody mentions: nobody is checking
Missouri does not license, register or inspect martial arts gyms. There is no state credential to teach jiu-jitsu here. Anyone can lease a space, buy mats, and call themselves an instructor.
The state does regulate professional combat sports — the Office of Athletics licenses promoters, fighters, referees, judges and physicians for boxing, kickboxing and MMA contests held in Missouri. But that authority covers events, not schools. It licenses the people running a fight card. It has nothing to do with the gym where your kid takes class on Tuesday.
Which means credential-checking and hygiene assessment are entirely on you. That’s the reason the two sections below exist, and the reason this guide lists lineage and belt rank wherever they could be verified.
### Academies by area
City. Watson Martial Arts, 2737 Papin St — BJJ gi and no-gi, Muay Thai, wrestling and kids, first visit free. North Broadway BJJ, 2324 Marconi Ave on the Hill, run by Bryan Guidry, a black belt under Rodrigo Vaghi, open since 2006. Maelstrom BJJ, 2500 Ohio Ave, where Jason Smith is a second-degree black belt under Leonardo Peçanha. Nomad Jiu Jitsu, 3139 S. Grand Blvd — no-gi focused, beginner classes, open mat, and the cheapest published rate in the metro.
Mid-county. Gracie Jiu-Jitsu St. Louis, 7545 Ravensridge Dr — a certified Gracie University training center running Combatives, the Master Cycle, Bullyproof for kids from age three, and Women Empowered. Wise Warriors MMA & Fitness in Brentwood, though jiu-jitsu is one offering among many there.
South County and Jefferson County. BJJ Lifestyle Academy, 4274 Telegraph Rd — Mike Rethmeyer, fourth-degree black belt under Leo Peçanha, Pan-American champion, third at Worlds, twenty-time IBJJF medalist. Free trial. Finney’s MMA, 9744 Watson Rd, which runs a genuine judo program alongside BJJ. Arnold BJJ in Arnold, which publishes its pricing and asks you to bring a gi for the free class. Absolute Martial Arts on Gravois, a general martial arts school where BJJ sits alongside karate and kickboxing.
West County. Vaghi BJJ, 15739 Manchester Rd in Ellisville. More on this one below — it’s the root of most jiu-jitsu in this city. Free week for new students, which is the most generous trial we found.
St. Charles County. Gracie Humaitá St. Louis, 1039 Wolfrum Rd in Weldon Spring, under Professor JW Wright, a fourth-degree black belt, affiliated through Royler Gracie and David Adiv, and a partner of the We Defy Foundation for veterans. Gracie Barra O’Fallon in Lake St. Louis, running the standard GB1 through GB3 curriculum with age-banded kids classes. Revive Brazilian Jiu Jitsu in St. Peters. Onyx Grappling in St. Peters, which is what the former Gracie Barra St. Peters became — their address isn’t published, so call.
Metro East. Gracie Barra Collinsville, 2539 Vandalia St, with kids, women’s and law-enforcement programs. BJJ Lifestyle Academy Illinois, 1556 Frontage Rd in O’Fallon. Fathom Brazilian Jiu Jitsu, 919 Washington St in Highland, with a Friday women’s class and a competition team.
North County: we could not verify a single dedicated jiu-jitsu academy. Searches surface only landing pages built by gyms located elsewhere. If you’re in Florissant, Hazelwood or Ferguson, the realistic options are the city gyms or driving to St. Charles County. We’d rather say that than invent an entry to balance the map.
### Why so much of this traces to one man
Rodrigo Vaghi started training at fourteen at the original Gracie Academy in Rio de Janeiro, under Grandmaster Hélio Gracie and his sons — Rickson, Royce, Royler and Rolker. In the mid-1990s he was offered a place training at Rickson Gracie’s school in California. He came to St. Louis instead, specifically because he liked the idea of bringing jiu-jitsu somewhere it didn’t exist yet.
He is a sixth-degree black belt under Rickson Gracie, the highest-ranked Rickson representative outside Brazil, and a 2010 black belt world champion.
Within his first years here he taught the students who became this city’s next generation of black belts — Mike Rogers, Ed Shobe, Bryan Guidry and Bill Krieg, all promoted by him. Guidry went on to found North Broadway BJJ in 2006. If you train in St. Louis, there is a good chance your instructor’s instructor learned from Vaghi.
A second, independent line runs through Leo Peçanha — Mike Rethmeyer at BJJ Lifestyle and Jason Smith at Maelstrom both trace there. Rethmeyer’s competition record is the strongest in the metro after Vaghi’s, and BJJ Lifestyle took Best Academy Overall at the St. Louis CXBJJ Championships.
### What to bring to your first class
Don’t buy a gi before you go. Most academies lend one for a trial class, and a gi is a real purchase — a basic one runs about $70 to $90, midrange $90 to $170, and the market stretches past $300. Budget $150 to $300 for a full starter kit once you know you’re staying. Arnold BJJ is the exception; they ask you to bring one.
For no-gi, wear a fitted rash guard or synthetic athletic shirt and pocketless shorts. That’s not a style rule — fingers and toes catch in pockets, and that’s a real way people break things.
A rash guard is worth owning even for gi classes; it cuts friction and reduces skin-to-skin and skin-to-mat contact, which matters for reasons covered below. A mouthguard usually isn’t required on day one but you’ll want one before you start live rolling.
Bare feet on the mat, shoes off, sandals for walking anywhere else — especially the bathroom. Trim your nails. Both sets.
Total swerve — an hour of rolling earns you dinner in Mascoutah.
### The belts, and how long blue actually takes
Adult belts run white, blue, purple, brown, black. Blue belt requires a minimum age of sixteen.
Here’s the thing most articles get wrong. The IBJJF — the sport’s main governing body — sets minimum time-in-grade at the upper belts: two years at blue before purple, eighteen months at purple, a year at brown. It sets no minimum at all for white to blue.
So the widely repeated “two years to blue belt” is convention, not a rule. Promotion at that stage is entirely at your instructor’s discretion, based on attendance and skill. One to two years of consistent training is typical. Some people take longer, and that is genuinely fine.
### Skin infections: the risk that's actually documented
Grappling means sustained skin-to-skin contact with strangers on a shared surface. That carries a real, measured infection risk, and it’s worth understanding rather than ignoring.
The CDC reports that skin infections including MRSA are most common in high-contact sports, with wrestling at the top, and that skin infections account for roughly 8.5% of all adverse events among wrestlers. Three families of infection come up: fungal (ringworm, called tinea gladiatorum in this context), viral (herpes gladiatorum), and bacterial (impetigo, staph, MRSA).
A 2022 review in the Journal of Clinical Medicine found reported ringworm prevalence among wrestlers ranging from 2.4% to 100% depending on the population studied, with a single organism responsible for about 92% of cases. Transmission runs through both skin contact and contaminated mats, and abraded skin makes it worse. It’s most common in ages ten to twenty, which is worth knowing if you’re enrolling a child.
None of that means don’t train. It means the gym’s hygiene practices matter, and since no state agency inspects them, you have to look yourself.
### Seven things to look at on your free trial
All of these are observable in ten minutes, and every one maps to published guidance from the CDC or wrestling’s governing bodies.
1. Is there a shoe barrier — a rack, sandals at the mat edge, a stated no-shoes rule? Nobody should be walking from the bathroom onto the mat barefoot. 2. Do you see the mat actually get mopped between classes, and is there a labeled disinfectant kept at the mat? 3. Are there working showers, and does anyone use them? Showering immediately after training is the single most repeated recommendation in the literature. 4. Does the coach look people over before class and turn away visible skin lesions? 5. Is there a written skin and hygiene policy, posted or in the intake paperwork? 6. Is the mat surface intact, with no tears or open seams holding moisture? 7. Are people in clean gis? A gym where yesterday’s gi is normal has a culture problem, not a laundry problem.
You are allowed to ask about all of this on a trial visit. A well-run academy will be pleased you asked — it means you’re the kind of student who won’t train with ringworm.
### Choosing by what you actually want
You’ve never done this and want structure. Gracie Jiu-Jitsu St. Louis, Gracie Barra Collinsville or O’Fallon, or Vaghi’s fundamentals class. Defined beginner curricula rather than being thrown into the general class.
You want to compete. BJJ Lifestyle or Vaghi. Both have current records rather than reputations.
It’s for your kid. Gracie Jiu-Jitsu St. Louis runs age bands from three; Gracie Barra bands 4–6, 7–9, 10–12 and 13–15; Finney’s adds youth judo; Vaghi covers 6–15 — and if grappling turns out not to be their thing, the metro has plenty of kids’ music, art and dance classes instead.
You want a women’s class. Vaghi, Gracie Humaitá, Gracie Jiu-Jitsu St. Louis, both Gracie Barra locations, and Fathom all run women’s-specific programming.
You want to try it cheaply. Nomad at $50 a month or $10 a class, no contract. Or take the free trials — almost every academy here offers one, and Vaghi offers a full free week.
### Before you commit
Every academy above was verified operating in July 2026 through its own website or booking platform. A few notes on what we left out and why.
Gracie Barra St. Peters no longer exists under that name — its domain now redirects to Onyx Grappling. We also excluded four Gracie Barra “locations” that turned out to be search-landing pages rather than physical gyms; Gracie Barra O’Fallon is one academy, in Lake St. Louis. One St. Charles gym was left out because its website has a broken security certificate and we couldn’t verify it directly.
Class schedules change more often than websites do. Call before you show up.

### Q. Where is the best jiu-jitsu in St. Louis?

BJJ Lifestyle Academy in South County is the strongest competition room. For structured beginner programs, the Gracie and Gracie Barra schools; for cheap no-contract training, Nomad on South Grand.
### Q. Do martial arts gyms need a license in Missouri?
A.  No. Missouri does not license, register or inspect martial arts gyms or instructors — there is no state credential required to teach jiu-jitsu. The state’s Office of Athletics regulates professional combat sports contests, licensing promoters, fighters, referees and physicians for events, but that authority does not extend to training academies.
### Q. How long does it take to get a blue belt in BJJ?
A.  Commonly one to two years of consistent training, but that’s convention rather than a rule. The IBJJF sets no minimum time for white to blue — promotion is at the instructor’s discretion. Minimum times only apply at higher belts: two years at blue, eighteen months at purple, one year at brown. Blue belt does require a minimum age of sixteen.
### Q. What do I need for my first jiu-jitsu class?
A.  Usually nothing — most academies lend a gi for a trial class, so don’t buy one first. For no-gi, wear a fitted rash guard and pocketless shorts; pockets catch fingers and toes. Bare feet on the mat, sandals off it, and trimmed nails. A basic gi costs about $70 to $90 when you’re ready to buy.
### Q. Is jiu-jitsu safe from a hygiene standpoint?
A.  Grappling carries a documented skin-infection risk — ringworm, impetigo, staph and MRSA — because of sustained skin contact on shared mats. The CDC reports skin infections account for about 8.5% of adverse events among wrestlers. It’s manageable: look for mats being disinfected between classes, a no-shoes rule, working showers, and a coach who checks for skin lesions before class.

## Eco-Friendly Cleaning Services: How to Tell Who Actually Means It
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/eco-friendly-cleaning-services
You come home to a spotless house, and the first thing that hits you is not how clean it looks. It is the smell — that sharp chemical bite that makes your eyes water a little and hangs in the air for hours.
Then the baby crawls across the just-mopped floor. Or the dog stretches out on it and rolls. And a small thought nags at you: what exactly did they wipe all of this down with?
Whether your place is a bungalow in Affton, a rental in Belleville, a farmhouse outside Wentzville or a shared office suite in Maryland Heights, it is a fair question — and a surprisingly hard one to get a straight answer to.
### What does eco-friendly cleaning actually mean?
By itself, almost nothing. “Eco-friendly” and “green” are marketing words, not regulated terms — anybody can print them on a van.
What separates a real green cleaner from a claim is verifiable, and it comes down to two things:
EPA Safer Choice — certifies the products. Every ingredient is screened, including fragrance.
Green Seal GS-37 — certifies the service company, not just what is in the bottle.
Ask which of those a company can point to. That single question does more than an hour of reading reviews, because it is the one thing a business cannot answer with adjectives.
### Why the label alone tells you nothing
Search for a green cleaner and look at what comes back: cleaning companies. All of them. A map pack of three, then a page of firms with “eco” or “green” in the business name, then two booking aggregators.
Every result is a company applying the label to itself. Not one of them explains how you would check. That is not a conspiracy — it is just what happens when a term has commercial value and no definition behind it.
The practical consequence shows up in an unexpected place. Look at what people actually do when they need one of these services, and you find neighborhood groups full of posts like this, from the last few weeks alone: “I have searched and haven’t seen anyone advertising green, non-toxic products, and it’s very important to me.” “I searched the group with no luck.” “Looking for a house cleaner — need eco-friendly products.”
People who want this cannot find it by searching, so they fall back on asking a neighbor. That is a failure on both sides of the transaction: the customer cannot find the cleaner, and the cleaner — who may well be doing everything right — is invisible to the exact person looking for them.
### The two certifications that mean something
### EPA Safer Choice (the products)
This is the one worth knowing about, and it is stricter than most people assume. To carry the Safer Choice label, every single ingredient in a product is evaluated against the EPA’s Safer Chemical Ingredients List and rated on a traffic-light system — green for preferred, yellow for use with caution, red for not allowed. A product containing any red-rated ingredient cannot be certified. Nearly 2,000 products currently qualify.
Here is the detail that matters most in a house with a kid or an asthmatic in it: the screening includes fragrance components. Fragrance is normally exempt from ingredient disclosure — a manufacturer can list “fragrance” and stop there, covering dozens of compounds. Safer Choice does not permit that shortcut. Given that scent is what most people actually react to, this is the difference between a real standard and a nice-sounding one.
It is also not a boutique label. Under the fiscal year 2025 National Defense Authorization Act, the Department of Defense is required to purchase Safer Choice-certified products to the maximum extent possible — a procurement standard, not a marketing badge.
You can look products up yourself on the EPA’s searchable list, which is the fastest way to check whether the products your cleaner named are actually certified.
### Green Seal GS-37 (the company)
The distinction people miss: Safer Choice certifies bottles. Green Seal GS-37 certifies the cleaning service itself — how the company works, not only what it buys.
That matters because a crew can carry excellent products and still undo the benefit: over-applying, cross-contaminating cloths between the bathroom and the kitchen, running a vacuum that pushes fine dust straight back into the room. Products are the easy half. Practice is the half that shows up in your air.
### The questions to ask before you book
Five minutes on the phone settles it. Ask these in this order:
“What products do you actually use?” You want brand names, not categories. A company doing this properly answers immediately, because they chose those products on purpose.
“Are any of them Safer Choice certified?” Then look them up. It takes a minute and it is the whole ballgame.
“What do you use for disinfecting, specifically?” This is where honest companies get precise and vague ones get uncomfortable.
“How do you handle cloths between rooms?” Microfiber, color-coded or separated by area, laundered between homes. A shrug here tells you about the practice half.
“Do your vacuums have HEPA filtration?” For allergies this matters as much as anything in a bottle.
And say the specific thing out loud — a child with asthma, a chemical sensitivity, a new baby, a cat that licks the floor. A good company will adjust, tell you exactly what they will change, and sometimes tell you honestly that one particular job needs a product they would rather you were out of the house for. That last answer is the most reassuring one you can get.
### What green cleaning does not mean
This part gets skipped in the enthusiasm, and skipping it is how people end up worse off.
Green does not mean anything goes. Gentle plant-based products are excellent for routine cleaning — floors, counters, glass, dust, the ordinary weekly work that is most of what a cleaner does. They are not always the right tool when someone in the house has a stomach virus, or after a raw-chicken spill, or in a bathroom during a norovirus week. Real disinfection sometimes calls for a registered disinfectant used correctly, with the contact time the label specifies.
The good news is that Safer Choice includes disinfecting products, so this is rarely an either/or. But a company that claims it never needs anything stronger, in any circumstance, is telling you something about its willingness to say inconvenient things.
“Natural” does not automatically mean safe, either. Plenty of natural substances irritate lungs and skin. And two common household staples should never be combined — never mix bleach with ammonia, or bleach with vinegar. That is not a green-cleaning rule, it is a basic safety one, and it sends people to the emergency room every year.
Unrelated, and we know it: Hi Pointe, block by block.
### What you can handle yourself between visits
A professional cleaner is not an all-or-nothing decision, and a surprising share of routine work needs almost nothing.
White vinegar handles glass, hard water spots and a lot of kitchen surfaces. Baking soda handles scrubbing and odors. A good microfiber cloth, used dry, picks up more dust than any spray does — most dusting sprays exist to make dust stick to the cloth, which is a job the cloth already does. Between them, those three cover a large share of ordinary weekly cleaning without a cabinet full of sprays.
Two caveats worth carrying: vinegar should stay off natural stone, where the acid etches the surface, and it belongs nowhere near bleach. And ventilation is free — open a window while you clean and for half an hour after, whatever you are using. In this climate that is easy for a good part of the year and worth remembering in January anyway.
### For the businesses on the other side of this
If you run a cleaning company that genuinely uses non-toxic products, the neighborhood-group posts above are worth reading twice. Those are customers with money in hand, actively looking, who could not find you.
What fixes that is boring and specific: say the words they are typing. “Eco-friendly” in your business name is not enough. Name the certifications you actually hold, name the products, say plainly that you accommodate asthma, allergies, pets and infants, and list every town you cover. Those are the phrases people search and the phrases they ask their neighbors in — and if none of them appear anywhere you can be found, the search simply fails.
It is also worth remembering that this is a two-audience service. Offices, salons, daycares and clinics increasingly want the same thing for the people who spend forty hours a week in the building, and that is a different pitch to a different buyer.
### Finding one around here
The most efficient approach is to compare several local companies at once, then make the five-minute call to the two or three that look right.
For an office, salon, daycare or clinic, the commercial cleaning map covers janitorial services across the metro on both sides of the river. For your own home, search the directory for cleaning companies serving your area, shortlist two or three, and ask each one the five questions above. If a company has taken the trouble to list its certifications and the towns it covers, that is already a signal about how it runs.
A clean home and a healthy one should be the same thing. Ask what is in the bottle, look the products up, speak up about sensitivities, and you can have floors clean enough for the baby to crawl on without the chemical cloud that used to come with them.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is considered green cleaning?
A.  Cleaning that uses non-toxic, often plant-based products in place of harsh chemicals, combined with practices that keep dust and residue out of your air — microfiber instead of disposables, HEPA vacuums, sensible ventilation. The term itself is unregulated, so the meaningful markers are EPA Safer Choice for products and Green Seal GS-37 for the company.
### Q. Is green cleaning more expensive?
A.  Not inherently. Certified products cost a little more per bottle than commodity chemicals, but products are a small share of what you pay for — most of a cleaning bill is labor. Where you may see a difference is with companies that market green as a premium tier. Get two or three quotes and compare like for like.
### Q. How much do 2 hours of cleaning cost?
A.  It depends on the size of the home, how many bathrooms, whether it is a first deep clean or ongoing upkeep, and whether one cleaner comes or a team. Any number quoted online before someone has asked those questions is a guess. Ask for a written quote based on your actual home — reputable companies give one readily.
### Q. Is $50 an hour for cleaning good?
A.  Compare the total job, not the hourly figure. A team of two at a lower rate each can finish in half the time; an experienced solo cleaner may charge more per hour and need fewer of them. Ask what the whole job costs, how long it should take, and what is included — inside the oven, inside the fridge, and baseboards are the usual line items people assume and should not.
### Q. Do I tip a house cleaner?
A.  It is not required and it is genuinely appreciated. Common practice is to tip for one-off deep cleans or move-out jobs, and to give something at the holidays for a regular cleaner rather than every visit. If you use a company rather than an independent cleaner, ask whether tips reach the crew — sometimes they do not.
### Q. What is the 20 minute rule of cleaning?
A.  Setting a timer and cleaning for twenty focused minutes rather than waiting for a free afternoon that never arrives. It works because most household mess is accumulation, not catastrophe. It also reduces how often you need heavy products at all, which is the cheapest form of green cleaning there is.

## DIY Interior Painting in St. Louis: Lead, Plaster, and What It Really Costs
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/diy-interior-painting-in-st-louis
Federal lead-paint rules do not apply to you painting your own house.
That is the actual text of the EPA rule, and almost nobody says it plainly — the guidance you find is written for contractors, so homeowners come away thinking they need certification to paint a bedroom.
But before you reach for the sander: 87% of houses in the City of St. Louis were built in 1979 or earlier — before the 1978 lead-paint ban. The rule doesn’t bind you. The dust doesn’t care.
### Do I need to be certified to paint my own house?
No. EPA states that the Renovation, Repair and Painting Rule “does not apply to homeowners doing RRP projects in their own home.” The rule governs anyone paid to disturb painted surfaces in pre-1978 housing. There are three exceptions that pull you back in: it does apply if you rent out all or part of your home, operate a childcare center in it, or buy and renovate homes to sell for profit. If any of those describe you, you are inside the rule and need a certified firm.
### The square-footage numbers are not your permission slip
You’ll see thresholds quoted everywhere: more than 6 square feet of paint disturbed inside a room, or more than 20 square feet outside, makes a job a regulated renovation. Below that it’s “minor repair and maintenance.”
Those numbers decide whether a paid contractor’s job is regulated. They are not a homeowner safety line. A homeowner painting their own primary residence is outside the rule at 6 square feet and at 600.
Two details worth knowing anyway, because they catch people hiring out small jobs: window replacement and demolition of painted surfaces are always covered regardless of square footage, and multiple jobs in the same room within 30 days count as one job for the threshold.
### Why 1978 matters so much here
Lead in consumer paint was banned effective February 1978. The ban stopped new sales; it did not require anyone to remove what was already on the walls.
Which is why the date lands so hard in this market. About 87% of St. Louis city housing units were built in 1979 or earlier, and the median city home dates to 1938 — forty years before the ban. The Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services designates the entire city a high-risk area for lead poisoning.
And this is not only a city story, which is where most coverage gets it wrong. St. Louis County’s median home was built in 1970 — also pre-1978 — and about 67% of county housing predates 1980. Florissant, Webster Groves, Kirkwood, Maplewood, Overland, Ferguson: all inside the frame.
### Before you sand anything, check this
Here is the most useful thing in this article, and it is buried on a page almost nobody reads.
The City of St. Louis offers free lead inspections on residential property where a child under six or a pregnant woman lives. Call the Building Division’s lead program at 622-4800. There is also remediation assistance, income- and occupancy-based.
If that describes your household and you are about to disturb paint in a pre-1978 house, make the call first. It costs nothing and it changes what you should do next.
### Test kits work in one direction only
EPA recognizes exactly three lead test kits: LeadCheck, D-Lead, and a Massachusetts state kit that works on drywall and plaster only. The first two work on wood, ferrous metal, drywall and plaster.
Now the part that changes how you should read your result. EPA says plainly that “to date no lead test kit has met both of the performance criteria outlined in the RRP rule.” The recognized kits satisfy only the negative-response criterion — a demonstrated false-negative rate of no more than 5% at 95% confidence.
In plain terms: a negative result is reasonably trustworthy. A positive result is not independently validated. A swab turning red is a signal to stop and get real testing — not a confirmed measurement.
Real testing means one of two things a homeowner can’t do at the kitchen table: XRF analysis, which reads lead concentration through multiple layers without damaging anything, or paint chips sent to an accredited lab.
And know which service you’re buying. An inspection tells you whether the building has lead-based paint and where it is. A risk assessment tells you whether there are actual hazards right now and what to do about them — usually the more useful product for someone deciding whether to start a project.
### How to work without making it worse
The rule doesn’t bind a homeowner, but EPA’s practices are the practices for a reason. The whole game is not turning paint into airborne dust.
Don’t dry sand and don’t dry scrape. Mist the surface first and use wet-dry sandpaper. Don’t use a heat gun above 1,100°F, and never open flame. Don’t use power tools without HEPA exhaust control — an ordinary shop vac spreads fine lead dust rather than capturing it.
Contain the room with plastic sheeting and an airlock at the door. Wear a respirator, coveralls, gloves and shoe covers. Clean at the end of every day rather than at the end of the project, because you are still living in the house while the work goes on — the same reason it’s worth knowing how long to wait before sleeping in a freshly painted room. Finish by HEPA-vacuuming and then wet-wiping until the cloths come away clean.
One more, which people get wrong constantly: painting over a lead hazard with ordinary paint is not abatement. It is a temporary encapsulation at best, and if the underlying surface is failing it will fail again through your new paint.
Nothing to do with paint — but Columbus Square is a neighborhood worth knowing.
### Plaster is not drywall, and it changes the job
A house built in 1938 almost certainly has lath-and-plaster walls, and if you have only ever painted drywall, some of what you know doesn’t transfer.
Here is how plaster actually holds on, which explains everything else. Thin wood lath was nailed across the studs with gaps between the strips. A rough basecoat about three-quarters of an inch thick was applied and squeezed into those gaps, forming “keys” behind the lath. Those keys are what hold the whole surface up, including on ceilings.
So there are two completely different problems that look similar from the front. Surface cracking is cosmetic. Plaster that has pulled loose from the lath is structural — the keys have broken — and the National Park Service describes that as requiring specialized restoration rather than patching. Press gently on a suspect area: if it moves or sounds hollow, you are looking at the second problem, and painting over it accomplishes nothing.
Before you decide to tear it out, know what you have. Multi-coat plaster is extremely durable, fire resistant, and it reduces sound transmission in ways drywall does not, and federal preservation standards strongly recommend repair over wholesale replacement. The instinct to strip to the studs and hang sheetrock produces a flatter wall and a worse house.
Two practical notes. Old plaster is rarely perfectly flat, so a flat or matte sheen hides what satin and eggshell reveal under raking light. And ask an experienced local plasterer which patching material suits your specific substrate — the compatible-compound question depends on what kind of plaster you have, and it’s worth a real answer rather than a guess from a blog.
### What it costs, honestly
There is no St. Louis-specific pricing source for painting from any government or research body. The best national figure we could verify directly puts professional interior painting at roughly $4.22 to $8.19 per square foot as of spring 2026 — a national marketplace estimate, not a St. Louis quote, and our market generally runs below national labor rates.
On the materials side, the math is simple. A gallon covers about 350 to 400 square feet in one coat on a smooth surface, less on texture. Most interiors need two coats, so plan on roughly 175 to 200 square feet of finished wall per gallon.
And on paint quality: Consumer Reports’ testing spans interior paints from about $17 to $105 a gallon, and their finding is worth internalizing — a higher price does not guarantee better paint. Mid-priced lines routinely score within a few points of flagship products. Buy on tested performance, not on the shelf position.
The honest structural point about DIY savings: on a small, simple room you save roughly half, because materials and labor run close to even. On a complicated room you save much less, because prep is the part that scales with difficulty and it’s the part you cannot skip. A pro is fast at prep. That’s most of what you’re paying for.
### When to hire it out
Genuinely call someone when you are disturbing lead paint at scale in a pre-1978 house — the homeowner exemption removes your legal duty, not your exposure. When you rent out part of the house, run a daycare in it, or are flipping it, in which case the exemption doesn’t apply at all. When plaster has pulled away from the lath or there’s long-term moisture damage. And when the work is high ceilings or a stairwell — that’s ladder work over a drop, and it is where DIY painting projects turn into emergency room visits.
Spraying deserves its own mention. In a pre-1978 house, spraying atomizes coating in a room where you may have just created lead dust. If you’ve never sprayed, an old house is the wrong place to learn — that is the point to start comparing painting contractors across the St. Louis metro.
### The question to ask any painter you hire
Missouri’s Division of Professional Registration lists no painting license — painters are not a licensed profession in this state. Missouri’s health department licenses lead abatement, and it says explicitly that incidental disturbance of lead paint during remodeling doesn’t meet its definition of abatement, so no state lead license is required for ordinary repainting.
But federal law fills that gap, and this is the one thing to remember:
Missouri does not license painters — but if someone takes your money to disturb paint in a pre-1978 St. Louis home, federal law requires their firm to be EPA Lead-Safe certified. And roughly 87% of city housing is pre-1978.
So the question is simply: “Are you EPA Lead-Safe certified, and can I see the certificate?” A legitimate firm answers instantly. EPA maintains a public list of certified firms you can check yourself.
Separately, the City of St. Louis requires contractors to hold a Construction Industry business license, which involves a clearance from the Collector of Revenue and proof of workers’ compensation coverage. The City’s page names general and sub-contractors without listing painting specifically, so call the License Collector at (314) 622-4528 to confirm how your trade is classified.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Do I need a lead certification to paint my own house?
A.  No. EPA states the Renovation, Repair and Painting Rule does not apply to homeowners working on their own home. It does apply if you rent out all or part of the house, operate a childcare center in it, or buy and renovate homes to sell for profit — in those cases you are treated as a regulated renovator.
### Q. How do I know if my St. Louis house has lead paint?
A.  Assume it does if it was built before 1978, which covers roughly 87% of city housing and about two-thirds of the county. Confirm with an EPA-recognized test kit — LeadCheck or D-Lead — or with professional XRF testing or lab-analyzed paint chips. If a child under six or a pregnant woman lives there, the City offers a free lead inspection.
### Q. Are lead paint test kits accurate?
A.  Only in one direction. EPA states that no lead test kit has met both of its performance criteria; the recognized kits satisfy only the negative-response standard, meaning a false negative no more than 5% of the time. So a negative result is reasonably reliable, but a positive is not independently validated — treat it as a signal to get real testing.
### Q. What if I accidentally sanded lead paint?
A.  Stop, and do not dry-sweep or reach for a shop vac — both throw the dust back into the air. Keep children and pets out of the room. Clean with wet methods and a HEPA vacuum rather than a broom, wipe down horizontal surfaces and window wells, and bag the debris. If anyone, especially a child or someone pregnant, may have been exposed, that is a question for a doctor rather than a website. For anything beyond a small patch, bring in a certified firm.
### Q. Can I just paint over lead paint?
A.  Painting over a lead hazard with ordinary paint is not abatement, and EPA is explicit about that. Intact, undisturbed lead paint in good condition is generally lower risk than damaged paint, but if the surface underneath is failing, it will fail again through your new coat. The hazard is deteriorating paint and the dust from disturbing it.
One limit worth knowing: encapsulation works on surfaces that stay still. It is a poor answer for friction surfaces — window sashes that slide, doors that rub, stair treads — because those grind through any coating and start making dust again. Those are the components a certified firm will usually recommend replacing rather than sealing.
### Q. How do you paint plaster walls?
A.  First determine whether the problem is cosmetic cracking or structural. Plaster holds on via “keys” squeezed through gaps in wood lath; when plaster has pulled loose from the lath, that is a structural failure requiring specialized repair, not patching. Press gently — movement or a hollow sound means stop. Flat or matte sheens hide old plaster’s irregularity better than satin.
### Q. How much paint do I need for a room?
A.  A gallon covers roughly 350 to 400 square feet in one coat on a smooth surface, less on texture. Since most interiors need two coats, plan on about 175 to 200 square feet of finished wall per gallon. Measure wall length times height, subtract large openings, and buy one extra quart for touch-ups.
### Q. Is expensive paint worth it?
A.  Not automatically. Consumer Reports tests interior paints ranging from about $17 to $105 a gallon and has found that a higher price does not guarantee better performance — mid-priced lines often score within a few points of flagship products. Buy on tested hiding and durability rather than on price.
### Q. Does Missouri license painters?
A.  The Missouri Division of Professional Registration lists no painting license. However, any firm paid to disturb paint in a pre-1978 home must be EPA Lead-Safe certified under federal law — which covers most St. Louis housing. Ask any painter you hire for their certification, and check the City’s business license requirements at (314) 622-4528.

## How to Choose a Commercial Cleaning Service in St. Louis (Cost Guide)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/top-rated-commercial-cleaners-in-st-louis-your-ultimate-guide
It’s 7:45 on a Monday morning. You unlock the office ahead of a 10 a.m. client meeting and it hits you before the lights are even on — the trash from Friday is still at every desk, the breakroom smells like it, and the glass door has a week of fingerprints. You’re paying a cleaning company for exactly this not to happen. Maybe you’ve lived it, whether you run a suite in Clayton, a storefront on The Hill, or a warehouse out in Earth City. Wherever you sit, the question that saves the most regret comes before the price: do you actually know what “clean” means in writing — or are you about to learn it the hard way?
A clean, professional space isn’t vanity — it’s how clients judge you and how you keep employees healthy. But commercial cleaning is a crowded field where the quality gap between companies is enormous, and the wrong choice quietly costs you in bad impressions and constant babysitting. Here’s how a St. Louis business owner actually vets one — starting with what it should cost.
### How Much Does Commercial Cleaning Cost in St. Louis?
Commercial cleaning is usually priced one of two ways: per square foot or per hour. For standard recurring office cleaning in 2026, expect roughly $0.10 to $0.18 per square foot, with the full market spanning about $0.07 to $0.20 depending on frequency, layout, and building type. Priced hourly, most janitorial work runs $35 to $60 per hour, though rates can reach $30 to $75 depending on scope and labor. Two things drive your number more than anything: frequency (weekly is cheaper per visit than nightly) and layout — ten thousand square feet of open office cleans far faster (and cheaper) than the same footage chopped into private offices, exam rooms, closets, and multiple restrooms. Because of that, a walk-through and a written, itemized quote for your space beat any per-foot average.
### First, Define the Job
“Commercial cleaning” ranges from nightly janitorial (trash, restrooms, vacuuming, wipe-downs) to periodic deep cleaning, floor and carpet care, window work, and specialized disinfection. Before you call anyone, write a simple scope: what needs doing, how often, and on what schedule (after-hours is standard for offices). A clear scope is what makes quotes comparable instead of apples-to-oranges — and it becomes the checklist you hold them to later. It also stops you from overpaying for services you don’t need or, worse, discovering the restrooms weren’t in the deal after you’ve signed.
### The Vetting That Actually Protects Your Business
This is where choosing a commercial cleaner differs from hiring for your home — these people are in your space, often after hours, with access to everything. Confirm liability insurance and bonding: liability insurance covers accidental damage, while bonding protects you against theft by cleaning staff — for a company handling your keys and alarm code after dark, both are non-negotiable, so ask for proof. Get a written scope and checklist, which is your recourse when standards slip. Ask for references from similar businesses — a medical office, a restaurant, and a law firm have very different needs, so ask for references that look like you. And make sure there’s a real point of contact: when there’s a problem, you want an account manager who answers, not a voicemail box.
### Employees vs. Subcontractors: Why It Matters
One question separates consistent companies from chaotic ones: are your cleaners the company’s own W-2 employees, or are they subcontracted out? W-2 employees typically come with background checks, training, and direct accountability — the company owns the quality and answers for it. Subcontracted labor can be fine, but it introduces variability in who actually shows up, how they’re vetted, and who’s responsible when something goes wrong or goes missing. It also affects consistency of crew: the same team night after night learns your space, remembers that the conference room needs extra attention on Thursdays, and simply does better work than a rotating cast of strangers. Ask directly, and favor companies that staff with their own trained employees.
### Green Cleaning, Supplies, and the Details That Separate Good From Great
A few details reveal a company’s real quality. Ask about green cleaning options if that matters to your brand or your employees’ health — low-VOC products and safer chemicals are widely available and worth requesting. Clarify supplies: do they provide their own equipment and restroom consumables (paper towels, soap, liners), or is that on you? Unclear supply terms are a common source of friction. And ask how they handle quality control — do they do periodic walk-throughs, supervisor checks, or a simple way for you to flag misses? A company that has a system for catching its own mistakes is one that takes the work seriously.
### Contract Terms: Start on a Short Leash
On contracts, understand whether you’re signing month-to-month or into a longer commitment, and what the cancellation terms are if the service disappoints. A confident company will happily start you on a short leash — a trial period or month-to-month arrangement — because they expect to earn the renewal with good work. Be cautious of anyone who insists on a long, hard-to-exit contract before they’ve proven themselves. Read the terms for automatic renewals and price-escalation clauses too, so a fair starting rate doesn’t quietly climb. The goal is a relationship you stay in because the work is good, not because you’re locked in.
Random, but: West County’s whole dinner lineup is right here.
### Types of Commercial Cleaning to Know
It helps to know the categories so your scope is precise. Janitorial is the routine recurring service — trash, restrooms, vacuuming, dusting, and surface wipe-downs, usually nightly or several times a week. Deep cleaning is a periodic, more intensive service that reaches the buildup routine cleaning doesn’t. Floor and carpet care (buffing, waxing, carpet extraction) is often scheduled separately on a rotation. Window cleaning and specialized disinfection (important for medical, dental, and food-service spaces) round out the menu. Many businesses combine a nightly janitorial contract with periodic deep cleans and floor care — spelling out which is which, and how often, keeps everyone honest and your quotes comparable.
### Red Flags When Hiring a Cleaning Company
Watch for the warning signs. Be cautious of a company with no proof of insurance or bonding, no written scope, vague answers about who actually does the cleaning, a bid dramatically below the others (often a sign of undertrained, high-turnover labor), pressure to sign a long contract immediately, no references from businesses like yours, and no clear point of contact. A cleaning company is a quiet extension of your brand and a set of after-hours keys to your space — so professionalism, accountability, and transparency matter as much as the nightly checklist. The good ones welcome every one of these questions.
### Why the Right Cleaner Is a Business Investment
It’s easy to treat cleaning as a line item to minimize, but a professional space quietly does real work for you. Clients form an impression the moment they walk in — a spotless lobby and fresh-smelling restroom signal competence and care before you say a word, while fingerprinted glass and an overflowing bin undercut everything else you’re trying to project. Inside, a consistently clean, sanitized workplace reduces the spread of illness, which means fewer sick days and steadier productivity, and it tells your employees you take their environment seriously. The wrong cleaner costs you twice: once in the bad impressions and health effects, and again in the hours you spend babysitting the service and re-explaining the same misses. Viewed that way, paying a little more for an accountable, consistent company is usually the cheaper choice.
### How Often Should Your Office Be Cleaned?
The right frequency depends on your space, your traffic, and your industry — and it’s the biggest lever on your bill, so it’s worth thinking through. A busy office with heavy foot traffic, shared kitchens, and customer-facing areas usually warrants nightly or several-times-a-week janitorial service, especially the restrooms and breakroom, where hygiene and smell are most noticeable. A smaller, lower-traffic office might do fine with cleaning two or three times a week, or even weekly, with restrooms and trash handled more often. Medical, dental, and food-service spaces have higher hygiene and disinfection needs and often stricter requirements. The common pattern is a nightly or few-times-weekly janitorial base plus periodic deep cleans and floor care on a rotation. A good company will right-size this with you rather than upselling a nightly contract you don’t need — and being able to scale up or down as your needs change is a fair thing to ask for.
### Questions to Ask Before You Hire
Before you sign, ask: Are you insured and bonded, and can I see proof? Are your cleaners W-2 employees or subcontractors, and are they background-checked? Can you provide a written scope and checklist? Do you have references from businesses like mine? Who’s my point of contact if there’s a problem? Do you provide supplies and restroom consumables? Do you offer green cleaning? Is this month-to-month, and what are the cancellation terms? How do you handle quality control and missed items? A professional company answers all of these clearly and welcomes them — the questions themselves are a filter, because the accountable, well-run companies expect them, while the ones to avoid get vague exactly where it matters most.
The fastest way to a shortlist you can trust is to compare a few local companies side by side. ### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. How much does commercial cleaning cost in St. Louis?
A.  Standard recurring office cleaning runs roughly $0.10 to $0.18 per square foot in 2026 (the full market spans about $0.07 to $0.20), or $35 to $60 per hour for janitorial work. Your price depends most on frequency (weekly is cheaper per visit than nightly) and layout — open space cleans faster and cheaper than the same footage split into offices, exam rooms, and restrooms. Get a walk-through and an itemized written quote.
### Q. What’s the difference between insurance and bonding for a cleaning company?
A.  Liability insurance covers accidental damage the cleaners cause to your property; bonding protects you financially against theft by their staff. For a company handling your keys and alarm code after hours, both are non-negotiable — ask for written proof of each. A reputable commercial cleaner carries both and provides documentation without hesitation.
### Q. Should cleaners be employees or subcontractors?
A.  Favor companies that use their own W-2 employees, who typically come with background checks, training, and direct accountability — the company owns the quality. Subcontracted labor can work but adds variability in who shows up and who’s responsible if something goes wrong. Employees also mean a more consistent crew, and the same team night after night learns your space and does better work.
### Q. Should I sign a long-term cleaning contract?
A.  Start on a short leash. A confident company will offer a trial period or month-to-month arrangement because they expect to earn the renewal with good work. Be cautious of anyone insisting on a long, hard-to-exit contract before proving themselves, and read for automatic renewals and price-escalation clauses. The goal is a relationship you stay in because the work is good, not because you’re locked in.
### Q. How do I compare commercial cleaning quotes fairly?
A.  Write a clear scope first — what needs cleaning, how often, and on what schedule — then have each company quote against that same scope. This turns apples-to-oranges bids into a real comparison and becomes your checklist to hold them to. Confirm insurance and bonding, ask who does the work, get supplies and consumables spelled out, and favor an itemized written quote over a vague flat number.

## St. Louis Coffee Shops: How to Pick One by Neighborhood and Errand
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/the-best-coffee-shops-in-st-louis-a-local-guide
Imagine it’s a Saturday morning and you have exactly one free hour. Maybe you’re in Maplewood with a book you keep meaning to start. Maybe you’re killing time in Kirkwood before a kid’s game, or you’ve driven into the Central West End early for an appointment and you’d rather not sit in the parking garage.
You could pull into the drive-thru you always pull into. Or you could spend that hour somewhere that actually feels like St. Louis — a roaster in a hundred-year-old bank building where the seating is inside the old vault, a coffee bar in a converted filling station, a cafe built inside a working greenhouse.
All three of those are real, all three are open, and all three are within a short drive of most of this metro. This guide is where to find them.
### What is the best coffee shop in St. Louis?
People ask it as What’s the most popular coffee shop in St. Louis? and the honest answer is that popularity moves by neighborhood and by hour, which is why this guide is organized by what you are actually doing rather than by rank.
There isn’t one answer, and anyone who gives you one is selling something. St. Louis has an unusually deep bench of independent roasters — shops that buy green coffee and roast it themselves rather than order it in. For a third-wave roaster with a national reputation, that’s Sump Coffee in Marine Villa. For the shop that arguably started the city’s specialty coffee scene, it’s Kaldi’s on DeMun, roasting since 1994. For the most memorable room, it’s Shaw’s Coffee on the Hill, where you can sit inside a former bank vault.
What follows is organized the way people actually decide: by what you want out of the hour.
### Which St. Louis coffee shops roast their own beans?
This is where St. Louis genuinely punches above its weight. A surprising number of local shops are roasteries first and cafes second, which means the coffee in your cup was likely roasted a few miles away, sometimes in the same room.
Sump Coffee — 3700 S. Jefferson Ave. A third-wave pioneer that put St. Louis on the specialty-coffee map and has since expanded to Nashville. Known for flash-brewed iced coffee. The room is spare and serious; the coffee is the point.
Blueprint Coffee — four locations including 6225 Delmar, 4206 Watson, and inside High Low at 3301 Washington. A roaster with proper coffee bars attached, and patios at the Watson and High Low locations.
Coffeestamp — 2511 S. Jefferson Ave, Fox Park. Honduran brothers Patrick and Spencer Clapp run a micro-roastery inside an old auto shop, original conveyor belt still in place. They also make empanadas, which is a better breakfast than most coffee shops attempt.
La Cosecha Coffee Roasters — 7360 Manchester Rd, Maplewood. Roasting since 2006 with relationship-based sourcing, and a house roast called City Limits.
Northwest Coffee Roasting Company — 4251 Laclede Ave, Central West End. A long-standing Black-owned roaster that hand-roasts low and slow, and one of the few good options open until 7 p.m. daily.
Goshen Coffee Roasters — 6120 Shoger Dr, Edwardsville, plus a Soulard cafe at 910 Geyer Ave. Twenty years of roasting out of southern Illinois; the Soulard location is a two-story historic building with a garden patio.
Coma Coffee Roasters — 1034 S. Brentwood Blvd, Richmond Heights. Siblings Corbin and Macy Holtzman have run it since 2016, and they host latte-art competitions and public cuppings — a genuinely good way to learn what you like.
### Which coffee rooms are worth the drive?
Some places you go for the coffee. Some you go because the building is doing something no other building does.
Shaw’s Coffee Ltd. — 5147 Shaw Ave, the Hill. A micro-roastery operating since 1999 inside an old bank, with a Probat roaster and seating inside the vault. Take someone from out of town here.
Maypop Coffee & Garden Shop — 803 Marshall Ave, Webster Groves. A coffee shop inside a working garden center and greenhouse. House-made syrups, and vegan and gluten-free pastries that aren’t an afterthought.
Fiddlehead Fern Cafe — 4066 Russell Blvd, Botanical Heights. A converted gas station, and the only shop in town running an under-counter La Marzocco Modbar. Botanical syrups, which sounds precious until you try one.
Comet Coffee & Microbakery — 5708 Oakland Ave, with a second location on Shaw Blvd. Come for the croissants; the coffee is very good but the pastry case is the reason.
### Which shops are the neighborhood institutions?
Every good coffee town has shops that function as living rooms. These have been doing it for decades.
MoKaBe’s Coffeehouse — 3606 Arsenal St, South Grand. More than 25 years old, a longtime LGBTQ+ safe haven, a Sunday brunch buffet, and views into Tower Grove Park. Large water bowls on the patio for dogs.
Hartford Coffee Company — 3974 Hartford St, Tower Grove South. Air-roasted daily since 2004, with a dedicated kids’ section that makes it survivable with small children, and about ten dog-friendly outdoor tables.
Meshuggah Cafe — 6269 Delmar Blvd, the Delmar Loop. A quarter-century Loop fixture. Order a cinnamon scone.
Kaldi’s Coffee, DeMun — 700 DeMun Ave, Clayton. The 1994 flagship. Kaldi’s has grown to more than a dozen metro cafes, so it’s no longer a small independent — but it is St. Louis-born and it roasts its own, and the DeMun store is still the one to sit in.
### Which new arrivals are worth knowing?
The scene moves. Two openings are worth putting on your list.
Kentzo Koffee — 2500 Sutton Blvd, Maplewood. Brothers John and Hunter Iffland opened in July 2025, air-roasting their own. That Sutton address has a history: it held Stone Spiral for fifteen years, then Looking Meadow, and both closed. Kentzo is the current occupant and, so far, a well-loved one.
Shortwave Coffee — 33 N. Sarah St, Central West End. A Columbia, Missouri roaster that opened here in February 2026, partnering with women-led farms. It took over the space Quarrelsome Coffee used to occupy — worth knowing, because several coffee guides still list Quarrelsome as if it were open.
### What should you order, and what is it actually?
Specialty menus can be intimidating in a way that keeps people ordering the same drip coffee for years. The vocabulary is simpler than it looks, and it’s nearly all about the ratio of espresso to milk.
Espresso is not a special bean. It’s a brewing method — finely ground coffee, hot water forced through under pressure, producing a small concentrated shot. Many roasters do sell an “espresso roast,” but that’s a roasting choice, not a different plant.
Americano — espresso plus hot water. It is not coffee with cream. It drinks closer to drip coffee but with an espresso backbone, and it’s the safe order at a shop whose drip has been sitting.
Macchiato — espresso “marked” with a spoonful of foam. Traditionally tiny and strong. Note that the large sweet caramel drink of the same name at national chains is a different animal entirely.
Cortado — roughly equal parts espresso and steamed milk. Flat white — more milk, thin velvety microfoam, stronger coffee flavor than a latte. Latte — the most milk of the group, and the mildest. Cappuccino — the thick airy foam cap.
Chai latte — spiced tea concentrate with steamed milk, and no coffee at all unless you ask for it “dirty,” which adds a shot.
If you’re unsure at a roaster, ask what they’re proud of that week. People who roast their own coffee generally enjoy the question.
Off-topic entirely: what to do in Belleville, Illinois.
### Where are the coffee shops concentrated?
A mid-century corner shop on Watson Road in St. Louis, MO, photographed by Lane Forman on August 31, 2026 for St Louis Near Me Directory.
The metro’s coffee is not evenly distributed. Maplewood, the Central West End, Webster Groves, and Kirkwood are dense with good options. Downtown, honestly, thinned out after 2020 and hasn’t fully recovered — Park Avenue Coffee at 417 N. 10th St, known for its gooey butter cake, is the reliable anchor there.
Two suburbs have enough of their own to be worth a separate trip — see our guides to coffee shops in Maplewood and Wentzville.
In Webster Groves, Maypop is joined by The Clover and The Bee on W. Lockwood, The Annex Coffee & Foods on Big Bend, 23 West Coffee, and the Webster Groves Garden Cafe, where the owners perform music. In Kirkwood, Kaldi’s on S. Kirkwood Rd has a large patio and free garage parking behind it, and Teleo Coffee on W. Monroe runs a charitable sourcing model. In St. Charles, Picasso’s anchors Main Street with live music on weekends, Course Coffee Roasters micro-roasts out of a historic home, and Bike Stop Cafe sits right on the Katy Trail with a bike service station.
If you’re out in St. Charles County, we have a separate guide to coffee shops in Wentzville.
### Can you bring the dog, or stay a while?
A few shops actively welcome dogs rather than tolerating them. MoKaBe’s keeps large water bowls on the patio. Hartford Coffee has roughly ten dog-friendly outdoor tables. Shaw’s has five outdoor tables and welcomes dogs. Shameless Grounds in Benton Park, at 1901 Withnell Ave, goes furthest — water bowls and a menu item they call puppy bacon.
If you need to actually work, the roaster-cafes with real seating — Blueprint’s larger locations, Coma, Hartford — tend to be more forgiving than the small bars built for a quick shot and out. It’s worth a quick call if you’re planning to camp for three hours.
### Where can you find Black-owned coffee in St. Louis?
Northwest Coffee Roasting Company in the Central West End is the metro’s flagship Black-owned coffee business, and a serious roaster by any measure. The Drip Community Coffeehouse at 3615 Potomac St in Tower Grove South opened in September 2023 after founder LaTosha Baker rehabbed a derelict building, and it was built deliberately around community conversation. Latte Lounge operates in Florissant and Midtown, the Midtown location adding a full brunch menu. SweetArt on S. 39th St pairs Reine Bayoc’s vegan and gluten-free bakeshop with Cbabi Bayoc’s art studio.
### Why do coffee guides go stale?
Coffee shops close, and coffee guides usually don’t notice. While putting this together we found several widely-read St. Louis coffee lists still recommending Rise Coffee House in the Grove, which closed in 2022; Stone Spiral and C Oliver, both closed in 2022; Coffee Cartel, closed in 2018; and Quarrelsome Coffee, whose space is now Shortwave. One well-known guide still prints an address for Catalyst Coffee Bar that the shop left in 2024.
Every shop named above was verified open as of July 2026. Hours change, though, and small shops change them quickly — if you’re making a drive for a specific place, call ahead.
### Frequently asked questions about St. Louis coffee shops
### Q. What is the best coffee shop in St. Louis?
A.  It depends what you want from the visit. For a nationally regarded third-wave roaster, Sump Coffee on S. Jefferson. For the shop that started the city’s specialty scene, Kaldi’s on DeMun, roasting since 1994. For the most distinctive room, Shaw’s Coffee on the Hill, where the seating is inside a former bank vault.
### Q. Which St. Louis coffee shops roast their own beans?
A.  Quite a few, which is unusual for a metro this size. Sump, Blueprint, Coffeestamp, La Cosecha, Northwest Coffee Roasting, Goshen, Coma, Shaw’s, Kentzo Koffee and Course Coffee Roasters in St. Charles all roast in-house. Kaldi’s roasts its own as well, though it now runs more than a dozen cafes.
### Q. Is espresso made from a special kind of bean?
A.  No. Espresso is a brewing method — finely ground coffee with hot water forced through under pressure. Roasters often sell an “espresso roast,” but that describes how the bean was roasted, not a different plant or species.
### Q. Is an Americano just coffee with cream?
A.  No. An Americano is espresso with hot water added and no milk unless you ask. It drinks somewhat like drip coffee but with an espresso base, which makes it a good order at a shop whose drip pot has been sitting a while.
### Q. Which St. Louis coffee shops are dog friendly?
A.  MoKaBe’s on Arsenal keeps large water bowls on its patio, Hartford Coffee has around ten dog-friendly outdoor tables, and Shaw’s on the Hill welcomes dogs at its outdoor seating. Shameless Grounds in Benton Park offers water bowls and a puppy bacon menu item.
### Q. Where can I find Black-owned coffee shops in St. Louis?
A.  Northwest Coffee Roasting Company in the Central West End is the metro’s flagship. The Drip Community Coffeehouse in Tower Grove South opened in 2023 and is built around community gathering. Latte Lounge operates in Florissant and Midtown, and SweetArt on S. 39th St combines a vegan bakeshop with an art studio.
### Q. What St. Louis coffee shop has the best atmosphere?
A.  Atmosphere is the most personal thing on this list, so treat it as a set of tradeoffs rather than a ranking. Hard surfaces and high ceilings look beautiful and carry every conversation across the room. Soft seating and rugs feel calm but fill up early. A shop with a roaster running in back smells extraordinary and is loud for twenty minutes at a time. Decide which of those you want before you decide where to go.
### Q. What is the best coffee shop to do work in St. Louis?
A.  The ones that welcome it say so plainly — posted hours for laptops, outlets along the wall, and tables meant for one. The ones that do not will tell you in other ways: no outlets, tall stools, and a line out the door at 9 a.m. We cover that in more detail in our guide to coffee shops you can actually work in.
### Q. What does Gen Z look for in a coffee shop?
A.  Broadly the same things everyone does, with more weight on a few: somewhere comfortable to sit for a while, reliable wifi, non-dairy milk treated as normal rather than a surcharge to apologize for, and a room that photographs well. Shops that added oat milk and better seating did not narrow their audience — they widened it.
### Q. What’s the average cost to start a coffee shop?
A.  We deliberately do not publish a figure. The range is enormous and the average is useless to you: a counter inside an existing building with used equipment and a shop built out from bare walls with a new roaster are not the same business. What actually drives it is the space, the build-out, the espresso machine, and how many months of payroll you can carry before the morning regulars appear. Price those four for the specific room you are looking at.
### Q. Which St. Louis neighborhoods have the most coffee shops?
A.  Maplewood, the Central West End, Webster Groves and Kirkwood have the deepest concentration of independent shops. Downtown thinned considerably after 2020 and has fewer independent options than its size suggests.

## St. Louis AC Repair: How to Choose a Pro and When to Replace
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/smart-ac-repair-your-eco-friendly-guide
It’s the third day of a July heatwave, the kind where the air outside feels like a wet wool blanket. You come home, the house is 84 degrees and climbing, and the vents are blowing… nothing. Or barely-cool nothing. Maybe you’ve lived it — your parents’ ranch in Ballwin, a rental you manage up in north county, or your own place across the river in Belleville.
In a St. Louis summer, a dead air conditioner isn’t just uncomfortable — with our humidity it gets genuinely miserable fast, and for older folks and little kids it can be a real health risk. So the pressure to call the first company you find and say “yes” to whatever they quote is enormous. That pressure is exactly how people overpay. Here’s how to slow down for ten minutes, choose an AC pro you can trust, and tell when repairing the old unit is throwing good money after bad — including the simple rules the pros use to make that call.
### What Is the $5,000 Rule for AC?
The $5,000 rule is a quick gut-check for whether to repair or replace: multiply your AC unit’s age (in years) by the estimated repair cost. If the result is under $5,000, repairing is usually worth it. If it’s over $5,000, replacement is generally the smarter move. So a 6-year-old unit needing a $500 repair scores 3,000 — fix it. A 14-year-old unit needing a $600 repair scores 8,400 — lean toward replacing. It’s a rule of thumb, not gospel, but it captures the real math: pouring money into an old, inefficient system rarely pays off when a new one will be more reliable and cheaper to run. For context, a full central-AC replacement generally runs about $3,000 to $7,500 installed for a typical home, so weigh the repair against that.
### What Does an AC Service Call Cost?
Most HVAC companies charge a service-call or diagnostic fee of about $75 to $200 to come out, identify the problem, and quote the fix — and many will credit that fee toward the repair if you approve the work on the same visit. Once diagnosed, common AC repairs nationally average $300 to $600, with most jobs falling between $150 and $1,500 depending on the part and complexity. The big-ticket exception is the compressor (more on that below), which runs well into the thousands. When you book, ask the two questions that protect you: what’s the diagnostic fee, and is it applied to the repair if I move forward today?
### Is It Worth Fixing a 20-Year-Old AC Unit?
Usually not. Central AC units generally last around 12 to 15 years in our climate, so at 20 years a unit is well past its expected life — you’re maintaining borrowed time, and units that old typically need service calls twice a year just to limp along. There’s also a hidden cost trap: a system that old may still run on R-22 (the old “Freon”), whose production was banned in the U.S. in 2020. Because the remaining supply is shrinking, recharging an R-22 system after a leak has become very expensive — which often tips the math decisively toward replacement. A 20-year-old unit is also far less efficient than a modern one, quietly inflating every summer’s electric bill. Barring a cheap, minor fix, replacement almost always wins at that age.
### How to Tell If an AC Compressor Is Blown
The compressor is the heart (and the most expensive part) of your AC, so knowing the warning signs helps. Classic symptoms of a failing or blown compressor include warm air blowing from the vents even though the system is running, loud clunking, grinding, or rattling noises from the outdoor unit, the circuit breaker tripping repeatedly when the AC kicks on, hard starting (the unit struggles or hesitates to turn on), and noticeable vibration or shaking of the outdoor unit. A compressor replacement typically costs $1,800 to $2,800 — which is exactly the kind of high repair figure that, on an older unit, sends the $5,000 rule toward replacement. If a tech diagnoses a blown compressor on a unit over ten years old, seriously weigh a new system before sinking that much into the old one.
### What Is the 3-Minute Rule for AC?
The 3-minute rule (some techs say five) is a simple habit that protects your compressor: after your AC shuts off, wait at least three minutes before turning it back on. When the system cuts out, pressure inside the compressor needs time to equalize; restarting too quickly forces the compressor to work against that trapped pressure, which strains it and can shorten its life or trip the breaker. Most modern thermostats build in a delay for exactly this reason, but if you’re manually flipping the system or the power, give it those few minutes. It’s a small discipline that helps you avoid the most expensive repair on the list.
### Check Credentials the St. Louis Way
Missouri has no statewide HVAC license — it’s handled locally, and both St. Louis City and St. Louis County license mechanical (heating and cooling) contractors. So step one is confirming the company is licensed to work in your jurisdiction and carries insurance (which protects you if something goes wrong during the repair). Beyond the license, two industry certifications are worth looking for because they’re real and earned, not marketing badges: NATE (North American Technician Excellence), the leading certification for HVAC technicians, and ACCA (Air Conditioning Contractors of America) membership, a sign the company follows recognized industry standards.
Nothing to do with air conditioning — people eat in Sauget, surprisingly well.
### Repair or Replace? The St. Louis Math
Beyond the $5,000 rule, a few honest signals point toward replacement. Age: past that 12–15-year mark, you’re on borrowed time. Refrigerant: an R-22 system is increasingly costly to service. Repair frequency: if you’re calling every summer, those repairs are adding up to a down payment on a new, efficient system. Creeping bills: a unit losing efficiency quietly raises your electric bill every hot month. A trustworthy tech walks you through this honestly instead of automatically pushing the most expensive option — and if someone inspects a five-year-old unit and immediately insists on a full replacement, get a second opinion.
### The Eco Angle That Also Saves You Money
With air conditioning, “green” and “cheaper to run” are the same thing — less energy in means a smaller bill and a smaller footprint. A few things genuinely move the needle. Right-sizing matters more than raw power: an oversized unit short-cycles, blasting cold then shutting off before it can pull the humidity out, so the house feels clammy and the equipment wears faster — a good contractor sizes the system to your home, not by rule of thumb. High-efficiency systems (check the SEER2 rating) and heat pumps cost more up front but less to run. And a smart or programmable thermostat stops you from cooling an empty house all day. Before you buy, check whether Ameren Missouri has a current rebate and whether any federal energy tax credits apply — these change year to year, so confirm what’s active and ask your contractor to help you claim it. It can knock real money off a high-efficiency upgrade.
### Simple Maintenance That Prevents the 84-Degree Afternoon
Most heatwave breakdowns are preventable. You can do these yourself: change the air filter monthly during cooling season, keep the outdoor condenser clear of grass, leaves, and our infamous spring cottonwood fluff, and don’t block indoor vents with furniture. Then have a pro do a tune-up in the spring, before the first hot spell — it’s far cheaper than an emergency call in July, when every company in town is slammed. Booking that spring visit is the single best way to avoid ever coming home to an 84-degree living room.
### Signs It’s Time to Call a Pro (Not Just Change a Filter)
Some AC problems are DIY-fixable — a clogged filter, a tripped breaker, a thermostat set wrong — but others are clear signals to call a licensed tech before a small issue becomes a compressor bill. Call a pro if you notice warm air despite a correct thermostat setting, weak airflow from the vents, short-cycling (the unit turning on and off rapidly), water pooling or ice on the indoor unit or refrigerant lines, strange smells or noises, or a sudden jump in your electric bill. Ice on the lines in particular is a common one homeowners misread — it usually signals low refrigerant or airflow problems, and running the system that way can damage the compressor. When in doubt during a heatwave, it’s cheaper to have a pro check something minor than to run a struggling system until it dies.
### Getting Quotes Without Getting Burned
For any big repair or replacement, get a few estimates and get them itemized in writing. Be wary of a quote dramatically lower than the rest — it often hides add-ons or thin work — and just as wary of one dramatically higher. Ask about warranties on both parts and labor; a company that stands behind its work says so in writing. And notice how they communicate: a pro who explains the problem in plain English, shows you the failed part, and returns your calls is telling you how the whole job will go. The people who stay cool and spend the least aren’t lucky — they’re prepared: they book the tune-up early, know their unit’s age and refrigerant, ask for the license, and keep a trusted local pro bookmarked.
Sweating through a heatwave is the worst time to research contractors from scratch. Browse and compare local heating-and-cooling companies across the metro on the St. Louis HVAC Map - see who serves your neighborhood, compare reviews, and line up a spring tune-up before the rush.
