### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What does an AC service call cost?
A.  Most HVAC companies charge a $75 to $200 diagnostic or service-call fee to come out and quote the fix, and many credit it toward the repair if you approve the work same-visit. Once diagnosed, common AC repairs average $300 to $600, with most jobs between $150 and $1,500 depending on the part. Ask whether the diagnostic fee applies to the repair if you proceed.
### Q. Is it worth fixing a 20-year-old AC unit?
A.  Usually not. Central AC lasts about 12 to 15 years here, so at 20 it’s well past its life and often needs twice-yearly service to limp along. It may also run on R-22 refrigerant, banned from production in 2020 and now costly to recharge, and it’s far less efficient than a modern unit. Barring a cheap minor fix, replacement almost always wins at that age.
### Q. How can you tell if an AC compressor is blown?
A.  Warning signs include warm air from the vents while the system runs, loud clunking or grinding from the outdoor unit, the breaker tripping repeatedly when the AC starts, hard starting or hesitation, and heavy vibration. A compressor replacement runs about $1,800 to $2,800 — a high figure that, on an older unit, tips the $5,000 rule toward replacing the whole system rather than the compressor alone.
### Q. What is the 3-minute rule for AC?
A.  After your AC shuts off, wait at least three minutes before turning it back on. When the system cuts out, pressure inside the compressor needs time to equalize; restarting too soon forces the compressor to work against trapped pressure, straining it and possibly tripping the breaker. Most modern thermostats build in this delay automatically, but if you’re manually cycling the system, give it those few minutes.
### Q. What is the $5000 rule for HVAC?
A.  Multiply the unit’s age in years by the estimated repair cost. Under $5,000 and repairing is usually worth it; over $5,000 and replacement is generally the smarter move. It is a gut-check rather than a formula — efficiency gains and refrigerant type can push the answer either way.
### Q. Is it better to run AC all day or just when home?
A.  A modest setback while you are out beats switching it off entirely in a St. Louis summer — a house that gets deeply heat-soaked costs more to pull back down, and the humidity comes with it. Programmable setbacks of a few degrees are the practical middle.
### Q. What is the 3-minute rule for air conditioners?
A.  Wait about three minutes before restarting a compressor after it shuts off, so refrigerant pressures can equalise. Short-cycling is hard on the compressor, which is the expensive part — most modern thermostats enforce the delay for you.
### Q. Is there a big difference between a 5000 and 6000 BTU air conditioner?
A.  About one room’s worth. Roughly, 5,000 BTU suits around 150 square feet and 6,000 around 250. Oversizing is the more common mistake — an over-large unit cools fast, shuts off, and never runs long enough to pull the humidity out, which is what actually makes a room comfortable here.

## DIY Lawn Care vs. Hiring a Pro in St. Louis: What the Science Says
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/diy-lawn-care-vs-hiring-a-pro-in-st-louis
University of Missouri Extension has a sentence about seeding a lawn in spring that ought to be printed on every bag of grass seed sold in this state:
“In some cases, complete failure should be expected.”
That is a land-grant university telling you that the seed everyone buys in April is largely money in the trash. Timing, not effort and not equipment, is what separates a good St. Louis lawn from a bad one — and it’s also what decides whether you should be doing this yourself.
### Should I do my own lawn care in St. Louis?
Mostly yes, with two exceptions. Missouri law lets you apply any general-use product to your own lawn with no license, and the highest-value task — seeding in the August 25 to October 10 window — requires timing rather than skill. Hire out core aeration, where renting the machine barely beats the roughly $107–$202 a service charges, and hire out anything on a neighbor’s property, because applying pesticide on someone else’s land for money legally requires a certified commercial applicator’s license.
### Why nothing quite works here
St. Louis sits in what turf scientists call the Transition Zone — and MU Extension defines it exactly as bluntly as it deserves: an area “where neither warm- nor cool-season grass species are completely adapted.”
There is no perfect grass for this city. There are only trade-offs, and picking one means choosing which season you’re willing to lose.
Cool-season grasses grow best between 60 and 75 degrees — spring and fall — and struggle through a St. Louis August. Warm-season grasses want 80 to 95 degrees and go dormant in the cold.
MU’s recommendation for Missouri lawns has been the same for decades: turf-type tall fescue, ideally as a mix of 90% tall fescue and 10% Kentucky bluegrass. It has a deep root system and handles heat and drought better than other cool-season options. It is green in April and green in November and it suffers in high summer.
Zoysia is the other legitimate choice, adapted to the southern two-thirds of Missouri. It is genuinely tough — durable, weed-resistant, heat- and drought-tolerant, easy to mow. The price is that it goes straw-colored from mid-fall to mid-spring. Roughly half the year, your lawn is brown while your neighbor’s is green.
Neither is wrong. But bermudagrass is, at least here — MU says flatly that it is “not recommended for lawns in Transition Zone,” and is best adapted to the southern third of the state.
One number worth having if you pay a water bill: properly managed, tall fescue needs about 25% less water and zoysia about 50% less than Kentucky bluegrass to stay green and growing here.
### The three weeks that decide your year
If you take one thing from this article, take this. For cool-season grass in Missouri, the seeding window is August 25 to October 10, and lawns seeded around Labor Day outperform ones seeded in October.
Spring seeding fails because spring moisture feeds weeds that outcompete your seedlings, and then summer heat kills whatever survived. Fall works because the soil is still warm enough for fast germination while the air is cooling, rain is more regular, and weed pressure has dropped.
The seeding rates make the point by themselves. MU specifies 7 pounds of tall fescue per 1,000 square feet in fall — and 10 pounds in spring. Forty percent more seed, for a result the same publication says may fail completely.
And here is what makes that window so efficient: the three highest-value jobs of the entire lawn year all land in it. Aeration is best in early fall. Seeding runs August 25 to October 10. And September is, in MU’s words, the most important time to fertilize — 1 to 1½ pounds of nitrogen per 1,000 square feet.
Done as one operation, the sequence is: mow low, aerate, seed, lightly rake in, fertilize, water. One weekend in early September does more for your lawn than everything you will do in April, May and June combined.
### The rest of the calendar
For tall fescue: half a pound to a pound of slow-release nitrogen in early-to-mid April, the big feeding in September, and a moderate application in late October or November once temperatures drop below 50 degrees to push root growth.
Mowing height matters more than people think. MU gives 2 to 3½ inches in spring, 3 to 4 inches in summer, and 2½ to 3½ in fall. Cutting tall fescue short in a St. Louis July is a self-inflicted wound — taller grass shades its own roots and holds soil moisture.
If you have zoysia, throw all of that out, because the calendar is nearly the mirror image. Fertilize from late May through mid-August only — MU is explicit: do not fertilize into September, because the plant is heading for dormancy. Plant it in mid-May to early June, not fall. Mow it short, 1½ to 2 inches.
Applying the fescue program to a zoysia lawn is actively harmful, and a lot of people do it without realizing they have zoysia at all. If your lawn browns out every October while the neighborhood stays green, that’s your answer.
### Clay, and what actually helps
Heavy clay compacts, restricts water and air movement, and produces shallow roots that stress fast in drought. Two things about it are worth knowing before you spend money.
Do not add sand. This is the single most common expensive mistake. MU is unambiguous: sand mixed into clay “can set up into a bricklike mixture,” and you need 75% or more sand by volume before you see any improvement in aeration, drainage or texture. Anything less makes it worse. A few bags of sand on a clay lawn is money spent making the problem harder.
What does work is organic matter — compost, peat or well-rotted manure, 1 to 3 inches worked into the top 6 inches, aiming for 2.5 to 3% organic matter. And note this carefully: MU says topdressing with topsoil “does not generally improve” heavy clay “unless it is done in combination with core aerification.” The aeration is what makes the amendment reach anything.
Test your drainage before you diagnose anything. Dig a hole and fill it with water. Gone within 18 to 24 hours is satisfactory. Two days or longer and you have a drainage problem that no fertilizer program will fix.
One thing in clay’s favor, since it gets a uniformly bad press: it holds water and nutrients well — ammonium, potassium, calcium, magnesium — which makes it naturally fertile. It’s a mixed blessing, not a curse.
### Aeration is the one to hire out
Core aeration — pulling plugs rather than poking holes — is the highest-value service on this list, and it’s the one where DIY math stops working.
Early fall is the best timing for cool-season lawns, which conveniently puts it in the same window as seeding. Coring also stresses the lawn less than dethatching with a power rake, and it reduces compaction at the same time.
A service runs roughly $107 to $202 nationally, with a second independent source putting it at $100 to $300 — those ranges corroborate each other, which is more than can be said for most home-services pricing. Against that: renting the machine, getting it home, running it, and returning it. The margin is thin and the machine is heavy. This is where hiring wins on the merits, and where it pays to compare the lawn and landscaping crews working your part of the metro before you book one.
Whoever does it, leave the plugs on the lawn to dry and crumble. Mowing them once dry redistributes the soil microbes that break down thatch. Raking them up throws away half the benefit.
Unrelated, and we know it — but Ellendale is worth a scroll.
### What you can legally do yourself
There is a clean legal line here, and almost no local lawn content states it correctly.
On your own lawn: MU Extension puts it plainly — general-use pesticides “may be used by anyone, so long as the pesticide is used only on lands owned or rented by that person,” and “homeowners do not need a private applicator license.” Anything you can buy off the shelf at a hardware store is general-use. Read the label, follow it, and you’re fine.
On anyone else’s lawn, for money: Missouri law states that no individual shall use any pesticide “on the lands of another at any time without a certified commercial applicator’s license.” That’s $65 a year, under Category 3, Ornamental and Turf Pest Control, plus proof of financial responsibility through bond or insurance.
Which means the mowing side-hustle is fine, and the moment it becomes a spraying side-hustle it isn’t — not even once, not even as a favor with twenty dollars attached.
It also gives you a way to vet a lawn company in one sentence: “What’s your Missouri commercial applicator license number and category?” A legitimate operator has it ready. Certified applicators also recertify on a three-year cycle and must keep application records for three years, so a company that treats your yard should be able to tell you exactly what went down and when.
### What hiring costs
There is no government or research source for lawn service pricing — not the Bureau of Labor Statistics, not the Department of Agriculture, not Extension. Every figure available comes from lawn-service marketplaces, which have an obvious interest in the framing. So treat these as national marketplace estimates, not St. Louis quotes:
Mowing: roughly $42 to $68 per visit. Core aeration: $107 to $202. Fertilization: $67 to $405 depending on program. Full-service monthly: $100 to $410.
Mowing is the biggest line item in any full-service quote, because it’s the highest-frequency task. It’s also the lowest-skill one. If you want to cut a lawn bill in half without learning anything, mow it yourself and buy the rest.
### The honest split
DIY genuinely wins on mowing, and on seeding and fertilizing your own lawn — where the law is entirely on your side and where timing beats technique. A homeowner who seeds on Labor Day weekend beats a professional who seeds in April, because MU says the April job risks complete failure regardless of who does it.
Hiring genuinely wins on core aeration, on anything touching a property you don’t own, on a lawn you suspect is zoysia and can’t confirm, and on a drainage failure — if water sits in that test hole past two days, you need grading and soil work, not a fertilizer program.
And if you do nothing else this year: put the seed and the fertilizer down in the first half of September. That single decision outweighs everything else on this page.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. When should I seed my lawn in St. Louis?
A.  Between August 25 and October 10, with Labor Day weekend the sweet spot — MU Extension finds Labor Day seedings outperform October ones. Spring seeding is far riskier; MU states that with spring seeding “in some cases, complete failure should be expected,” because weeds outcompete seedlings and summer heat finishes them.
### Q. What is the best grass for St. Louis?
A.  Turf-type tall fescue, ideally in a 90% fescue / 10% Kentucky bluegrass mix, is MU Extension’s long-standing recommendation for Missouri lawns. Zoysia is the warm-season alternative — tougher in summer but straw-colored from mid-fall to mid-spring. Bermudagrass is explicitly not recommended for our transition zone.
### Q. How much seed do I need per 1,000 square feet?
A.  For tall fescue, MU specifies 7 pounds per 1,000 square feet when seeding in fall, and 10 pounds in spring. That 40% increase for spring seeding — for a worse expected result — is itself the strongest argument for waiting until late August.
### Q. When should I fertilize my lawn in Missouri?
A.  For cool-season grass, September is the most important application at 1 to 1½ pounds of nitrogen per 1,000 square feet, with a half to one pound of slow-release in early-to-mid April and a moderate rate in late fall once temperatures fall below 50 degrees. Zoysia is the opposite — feed late May through mid-August and never into September.
### Q. Should I add sand to clay soil?
A.  No. MU Extension warns that sand mixed with clay “can set up into a bricklike mixture,” and you would need 75% or more sand by volume before seeing any improvement. Use organic matter instead — 1 to 3 inches of compost worked into the top 6 inches — and note that topdressing generally does not help heavy clay unless combined with core aeration.
### Q. Do I need a license to spray my own lawn in Missouri?
A.  No. General-use pesticides may be used by anyone on land they own or rent, and MU Extension states plainly that homeowners do not need a private applicator license. But applying pesticide on someone else’s property for compensation requires a certified commercial applicator’s license — $65 a year, Category 3 Ornamental and Turf.
### Q. How much does lawn care cost per month?
A.  National marketplace estimates put full-service programs at roughly $100 to $410 a month, with mowing at $42 to $68 per visit and core aeration at $107 to $202. No government or research source publishes lawn service pricing, so treat all of these as national estimates rather than St. Louis quotes.
### Q. When should I aerate my lawn in St. Louis?
A.  Once the mowing is handled, a bigger plan may be worth it — see what goes into hiring a landscape architect in St. Louis.
Early fall is best for cool-season lawns, which conveniently overlaps the seeding window — aerate, then seed, then fertilize in one operation. Zoysia and bermuda are different: mid-June is preferred, and only while actively growing. Leave the soil plugs on the lawn to dry and crumble rather than raking them up.

## The St. Louis Homeowner Starter Toolkit (and Knowing Your Limits)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/must-have-handyman-tools-for-st-louis-homeowners
There’s a small, specific pride in fixing something yourself. The picture finally hung straight. The kitchen drawer that glides again. The wobbly chair made solid. You don’t need to be handy by nature — you just need a handful of the right tools and the confidence to start. Whether you just bought your first bungalow in south city or you’ve rented the same place in Overland for years, a basic toolkit turns “I should call someone” into “I’ll just do it.”
Here’s the honest starter kit — what actually earns its place in a St. Louis home, a couple of things our older houses specifically demand, the first projects to cut your teeth on, and, just as importantly, where to put the tools down and call a pro.
### The starter kit at a glance
The honest starter kit is short: a claw hammer, a screwdriver set (or a multi-bit driver), a retractable tape measure, a level, pliers, an adjustable wrench, a utility knife, and a stud finder — plus one cordless drill/driver. That handful covers the overwhelming majority of everyday household fixes. What St. Louis adds to the standard list is proper wall anchors for plaster, because so much of our housing stock has plaster-and-lath walls rather than drywall. Buy quality on the few tools you’ll use most, and add the rest as real projects call for them.
### The core hand tools every homeowner should own
Claw hammer — comfortable grip, solid head. The workhorse; a 16-ounce is the do-everything size.
Screwdriver set — a range of flathead and Phillips sizes, or a good multi-bit driver that stores the tips in the handle.
Tape measure — retractable, with a lock. “Measure twice” is real, and a 25-foot tape reaches across a room.
Level — so shelves and pictures are actually straight, not just close. A torpedo level fits a drawer; a longer one is better for shelving.
Pliers — needle-nose for fiddly work, standard for gripping, and a pair of channel-locks once you start on plumbing fixtures.
Adjustable wrench — for the nut the pliers keep slipping off.
Utility knife — with spare blades; a sharp blade is safer than a dull one you have to force.
Stud finder — cheap, and it saves you from anchoring a heavy shelf into thin air.
Round it out with the small consumables that live in the same box: a tape measure’s useless without a pencil, and a starter assortment of screws, nails, and wall anchors, a roll of painter’s tape, and a tube of caulk will handle half the little jobs a house throws at you. None of it is expensive, and buying it once means you’re never stuck mid-project driving to the hardware store.
### The two power tools to add first
You don’t need a garage full of machines. Start with a cordless drill/driver and a set of bits — it drills holes and drives screws and will earn its keep the first weekend. Look for one with two batteries so you’re never waiting on a charge. When your projects grow, a circular or reciprocating saw covers most cutting and light demolition. Add tools as real projects call for them, not before — a tool you bought for one job and never touch again is just clutter with a cord.

### What a St. Louis old house specifically demands
Here’s the local twist most tool lists miss. A huge share of our housing stock — the brick bungalows, two-families, and century homes — has plaster-and-lath walls, not modern drywall. Plaster is brittle and behaves differently: a standard drywall anchor can crack it, and screws don’t bite the same way. So stock proper wall anchors (toggle or molly bolts for heavy items), use that stud finder, and drill a pilot hole rather than muscling a screw in. Get that right and you’ll hang a heavy mirror on 1920s plaster with total confidence.
Two more worth having in our climate: a plunger and a basic drain auger for the inevitable clog, and, if you’ve got the kind of basement a lot of St. Louis homes have, a wet/dry shop vac is a genuine hero after a heavy rain. Older homes here also tend to have quirks worth a few dollars of prevention — painted-shut windows, settling that leaves nothing quite plumb, and galvanized or cast-iron plumbing that’s less forgiving than modern PVC. None of that changes the starter kit; it just means going gently and expecting a house with history to have opinions.
### Your first five projects
The fastest way to get comfortable is to actually use the kit on small, forgiving jobs. A good progression:
Hang a picture or a shelf — find the stud or set the right anchor, check it with the level, done. The confidence-builder.
Tighten everything loose — cabinet knobs, door hinges, a wobbly toilet-paper holder, the handrail. A ten-minute lap of the house with a screwdriver.
Fix a sticky drawer or door — a little sanding, a new glide, or a tightened hinge, and something that annoyed you daily just stops.
Re-caulk a tub or sink — peel the old bead, run a clean new one; it looks pro and it keeps water where it belongs.
Clear a slow drain — plunger first, then the auger. You’ll never dread a clog the same way again.
Each one teaches a tool and a little patience, and none risks much if it goes sideways. String a few of these together and the mental shift happens on its own — the house stops feeling like a series of things to call about and starts feeling like something you can actually take care of.
### A few safety basics
None of this kit is dangerous if you respect it, and a couple of cheap habits keep it that way. Grab a pair of safety glasses and wear them any time something might fly — drilling into masonry, cutting, or hammering. Keep blades sharp (a dull utility knife slips and cuts you, not the box), unplug or remove the battery before you change a drill bit or saw blade, point a fan out the window on any paint job and know how long to wait before sleeping in a freshly painted room, and before you put a screw or a nail into any wall, be sure there’s no electrical or plumbing line behind it — a basic wall scanner that flags wires and pipes is a few dollars well spent in an older home. Small stuff, but it’s the difference between a satisfying afternoon and a trip to urgent care.
### Buy once, cry once: quality over quantity
The temptation with a first toolkit is to grab the cheapest big-box “100-piece homeowner set” and call it done. Resist it a little. Those kits are mostly filler — a dozen sockets you’ll never use around a few tools that strip and bend the first time you lean on them. You’re better off spending the same money on fewer, better versions of the tools you’ll actually reach for: a solid hammer, a good driver, a tape that doesn’t rattle apart, and a drill from a name-brand line.
The old carpenter’s line — “buy once, cry once” — is exactly right for the handful of tools that get daily use. Where cheap is fine: consumables and the odd single-job specialty tool you might never touch again. Where it isn’t: anything with a moving part or a cutting edge you’re trusting with your knuckles. A quality core kit will outlast the house’s next three owners; a bargain-bin one lives in a landfill by spring.
Random, but: put the drill down and eat in Mt Olive instead.
### Where to buy it around St. Louis
You’ve got options at every price point. The big-box stores — Home Depot, Lowe’s, and Menards, scattered across the metro — carry everything on this list under one roof and are open early and late for the mid-project run. For advice with your purchase, the neighborhood hardware stores and local Ace and True Value shops are worth the slightly higher sticker: the person helping you has usually done the exact repair you’re describing and will steer you to the right anchor or bit in two minutes.
Don’t overlook the secondhand route, either. Estate sales, resale shops, pawn shops, and online marketplace listings around St. Louis are full of good old hand tools — a solid vintage hammer or wrench often outclasses a new budget one for a few dollars. For anything with a battery or a motor, though, buy new and stick to a major brand so batteries and parts stay easy to find down the road.
### The most important tool is knowing your limits
Confidence is great; overconfidence with the wrong job is expensive. Cosmetic and mechanical fixes — hanging, patching, assembling, tightening, unclogging — are exactly what this kit is for. But electrical work, plumbing beyond a simple fixture, anything with a gas line, and structural changes aren’t DIY territory here — those need the appropriate licensed St. Louis contractor and, often, a permit pulled with your municipality. Knowing which side of that line you’re on is the mark of a genuinely handy homeowner, not a limitation.
The stakes make the rule easy to remember. A botched shelf falls down; a botched electrical or gas job can burn a house down or void your insurance, and unpermitted work can come back to bite you at resale. When a job crosses into wiring, the main plumbing stack, gas, or the structure of the house, the smart, handy move is to hire the right licensed trade — and to know how to pick a home repair company in St. Louis well enough to tell a straight quote from a scary one.
### When a project’s bigger than the toolbox
Some jobs are a quick fix; others are a “call a pro” the moment you open the wall and see what’s really going on. When that happens, St Louis Near Me Directory is where you find the right person fast — browse the map of local handymen and licensed trades across the metro, compare reviews, and reach out. Start small, buy quality over quantity, respect the plaster and the licensed-trade line, and add tools as you grow. The toolkit is really just permission — permission to look at a small problem and think, “yeah, I’ve got this.”
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What tools should every homeowner have?
A.  The essential starter kit: a claw hammer, a screwdriver set or multi-bit driver, a retractable tape measure, a level, pliers, an adjustable wrench, a utility knife, a stud finder, and one cordless drill/driver. Add a plunger, a small drain auger, and — for St. Louis’s plaster walls — proper toggle or molly wall anchors. That handful handles most everyday household fixes.
### Q. How do I hang things on plaster walls?
A.  Many older St. Louis homes have plaster-and-lath walls, which are brittle. Use a stud finder to hit framing where you can, drill a pilot hole instead of forcing a screw, and for heavier items use toggle or molly bolts rated for the weight rather than standard drywall anchors. Go slowly — plaster can crack if you rush — and it’ll hold a heavy mirror with confidence.
### Q. What home repairs should I not do myself?
A.  Leave electrical work, plumbing beyond a simple fixture swap, anything involving a gas line, and structural changes to licensed professionals — these carry real safety, insurance, and permit consequences in St. Louis. Cosmetic and mechanical fixes like hanging, patching, assembling, tightening, and unclogging are exactly what a homeowner’s starter kit is for.
### Q. What’s the one power tool to buy first?
A.  A cordless drill/driver. It drills pilot holes and drives screws, which covers the majority of small projects, and it pays for itself the first weekend. Get one with two batteries so you’re never waiting on a charge, and add a circular or reciprocating saw only later, once real cutting or demolition projects call for it.

## How to Choose an Interior Painter in St. Louis (Cost & Checklist)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/7-smart-tips-for-choosing-the-best-interior-painting-company-in-st-louis
You’ve been staring at that room for a year. The color’s dated, there’s a scuff by the light switch you’ve stopped seeing, and every time you say “we should repaint” you picture the version that goes wrong — drips on the trim, crooked cut-in lines, tape that peels the paint right off with it. A good interior paint job is one of the highest-return, most satisfying things you can do to a home. A bad one you look at every single day. Whether your place is in Webster Groves, Florissant, or a loft downtown, choosing the right painter is the whole ballgame.
This guide covers what interior painting actually costs in 2026 — by room and by whole house — whether the season matters, the one certification most St. Louis homeowners forget to ask about, and the checks that separate a pro who’ll make you happy from one who’ll make you repaint.
### What Is the Average Cost to Paint an Interior Room?
For a direct answer: professional interior painting runs about $300 to $1,000 per room, with a national average around $624 for a standard 12×12 room — most 12×12 rooms land between $400 and $950. Priced by area, painters generally charge $2 to $6 per square foot for walls alone, or roughly $4.70 to $6.75 per square foot when ceilings and trim are included. What moves a room toward the high end: tall or vaulted ceilings, heavy prep (patching, sanding, priming bare or damaged walls), trim and doors, dark-to-light color changes needing extra coats, and premium paint. Remember that labor is 70 to 85 percent of the total — which is exactly why the prep and skill you’re paying for matter more than the paint on the shelf.
### How Much Does It Cost to Paint a Full House Interior?
Painting a whole home’s interior ranges widely — roughly $1,800 to $12,000 — because it depends entirely on square footage, how many rooms, ceiling height, and how much trim and prep are involved. For a typical 2,000-square-foot home, most homeowners spend around $4,200 to $9,500 for a full interior repaint including walls, ceilings, and trim. Doing the whole house at once usually earns a better per-room price than one room at a time, since the crew mobilizes, masks, and sets up only once. If you’re on a budget, a good painter can help you phase it — the main living areas now, bedrooms later — or focus on the walls and skip the ceilings where they’re still in good shape.
### How Much Does It Cost to Repaint a 3-Bedroom House?
A three-bedroom home is right in that typical-house range. Depending on size and scope, repainting the interior of a three-bedroom house generally falls somewhere around $4,000 to $9,500 for a full, professional walls-ceilings-and-trim job — less if you’re doing walls only or a lighter refresh, more for a large home with lots of trim, tall ceilings, or extensive prep. Individual bedrooms typically run $350 to $850 each (a large primary bedroom can reach $650 to $1,400), while a small bathroom might be as little as $150 to $350. The single biggest cost lever is prep and condition — smooth, sound walls paint fast; cracked plaster and heavy patching add labor.
### Can I Paint My House in October?
Yes — and for interior painting, fall is actually one of the best times. Because you’re painting inside, you control the temperature and humidity year-round, so you’re not at the mercy of the weather the way exterior painting is. October in St. Louis brings mild temperatures and lower humidity than our sticky summers, which helps paint dry and cure well, and you can crack windows for ventilation without the swampy air or deep freeze that summer and winter bring. It’s also often a slightly quieter season for painters than the spring-and-summer rush, which can mean better availability. The only real rule for any season is ventilation and reasonable indoor temperatures while painting and drying — conditions a good pro manages regardless of the month, and that same airflow is what decides how long you should wait before sleeping in a freshly painted room.
### EPA Lead-Safe Certification — Critical in St. Louis
This is the check most homeowners don’t know to ask about, and it matters enormously here because so many of our homes are old. Under federal law, any paid firm disturbing paint in a home built before 1978 must be an EPA Lead-Safe Certified firm and follow lead-safe work practices — because sanding or scraping old lead paint releases dust that’s genuinely dangerous, especially to kids and pregnant women. Given how much of St. Louis’s housing stock predates 1978, this is not a technicality. If your home is that old, ask the painter directly whether they’re Lead-Safe Certified and how they contain the dust. A real pro says yes and explains their process; anyone who waves the question off is a company to avoid.
### Insurance and What “Licensed” Really Means Here
Painting isn’t a state-licensed trade in Missouri the way electrical or plumbing is, so don’t assume a “license” means much on its own. What actually protects you is liability insurance (and workers’ compensation if they run a crew). Ask for proof. If a ladder goes through a window or a worker is hurt on your property, insurance is the difference between their problem and yours. Pair that with a local track record — a painter who works St. Louis knows our old plaster walls, the humidity that affects dry times, and the quirks of a century-old surface versus new drywall — and you’ve covered the two things that matter most before you even talk color.
Nothing to do with paint — but every metro carpet cleaner is mapped here.
### The Prep, the Quote, and the Warranty
Three more checks separate great jobs from regrets. First, the prep is the job: patching, sanding, caulking, priming, and careful taping are what make the difference between “wow” and “you can tell” — and a suspiciously cheap quote almost always cuts the prep, so ask exactly what’s included in writing. Second, get a detailed written quote that spells out the paint brand and quality, number of coats, which surfaces, the prep, and cleanup — “two coats of a quality paint after full prep” and “we’ll slap a coat on” are very different jobs at similar-looking prices. Third, insist on a warranty: a painter confident in their prep and product will stand behind the work for a period afterward, in writing. Add a portfolio and specific reviews (clean lines, respected the home, finished on schedule), and you have a reliable shortlist.
### Common Painting Mistakes a Pro Avoids
Knowing what goes wrong helps you judge a bid. The classics: skipping prep (painting over dust, grease, or glossy surfaces so the new coat won’t bond), not priming bare patches or big color changes, using cheap paint or too few coats, bad cut-in lines from rushing rather than cutting in carefully, peeling tape too late or too early, and painting in poor ventilation. There are also things worth not repainting carelessly — factory-finished surfaces, certain woodwork, and anything that really needs refinishing rather than a quick coat. A seasoned painter talks about prep and product before they talk about how fast they’ll be done; that emphasis is the tell of someone whose work will still look sharp in five years.
### Flat, Eggshell, or Semi-Gloss: Choosing the Right Finish
Sheen matters as much as color, and a good painter will guide you — but knowing the basics helps. Flat/matte hides wall imperfections beautifully and suits low-traffic ceilings and formal rooms, but it’s harder to clean. Eggshell and satin are the everyday workhorses for living rooms, bedrooms, and hallways — a soft, low-luster finish that wipes down reasonably well and hides minor flaws. Semi-gloss and gloss are durable and scrubbable, making them the right call for trim, doors, kitchens, and bathrooms where moisture and cleaning are constant — though the shine highlights surface imperfections, so prep matters even more. In St. Louis’s older homes with imperfect plaster walls, many owners land on eggshell for walls and semi-gloss for trim. If a painter recommends a finish, ask why for that room; the reasoning tells you whether they know their craft.
### Should You DIY or Hire a Pro?
Painting is one of the more DIY-friendly home projects, so it’s a fair question. A single small, simple room with sound walls is a very reasonable weekend DIY if you’re patient with prep and cutting in. Where hiring a pro pays off: large jobs, high or vaulted ceilings, heavy prep or damaged plaster, extensive trim, dark-to-light color changes, and any pre-1978 home where lead-safe practices apply. Pros are faster, their lines are cleaner, and their prep makes the finish last — and for a whole-house repaint, the time and do-over risk you save often justify the cost. A useful middle path: DIY the easy bedrooms and hire out the tricky, high-visibility spaces like the stairwell, the living room, and all the trim. And be honest with yourself about time — a room that takes a pro crew a day can eat an entire DIY weekend once you account for moving furniture, taping, two coats, and cleanup.

## Dog Boarding and Daycare in St. Louis: Real Prices, and How to Check a Kennel
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/dog-boarding-and-daycare-in-st-louis
Missouri licenses and inspects dog boarding kennels. The inspections are unannounced, they happen at least once a year, and the reports are public records.
Almost nobody knows this, because there is no website to search. You have to ask the state for the file.
Every “best boarding in St. Louis” list ranks by star rating. None of them mention the inspection reports. Here’s how to actually check a kennel, what boarding really costs here based only on facilities that publish their rates, what their cancellation rules actually say, and the one vaccine question that separates them.
### How much does dog boarding cost in St. Louis?
Based only on metro facilities that publish rates on their own websites, standard overnight boarding for one dog runs about $34 to $60 a night, with suites and luxury rooms from about $54.50 to $90. Full-day daycare runs about $21 to $48, dropping toward $17 a day with an unlimited membership. The cheapest published boarding we found is Muttropolitan at $34; the low end for daycare is also Muttropolitan at $21. Holiday surcharges are common, typically $5 to $10 a night where they’re disclosed. Every rate below was checked on the facility’s own site in October 2026, so confirm the current price when you book.
### The thing nobody tells you: the state inspects these
Under Missouri’s Animal Care Facilities Act, a boarding kennel must hold a state license, a separate one for each physical location. Every license runs one year and expires January 31, and the law covers boarding operations regardless of what they call themselves.
The Missouri Department of Agriculture states that routine inspections happen at least once yearly, that they are unannounced, and that they occur between 7am and 7pm on weekdays. Complaint-driven inspections, and unannounced reinspections after multiple or repeat violations, happen on top of that.
Inspection reports, complaints and investigative reports are all obtainable through a Missouri Sunshine Law records request. The Department says so plainly.
But there is no public database. You cannot type a kennel’s name into a state website and see its record. You have to submit a records request, or call the Animal Care Facilities Program at (573) 751-3076 or email acfa@mda.mo.gov.
That friction is the whole reason this matters. The reports exist, they’re legally yours, and essentially nobody asks, so a facility’s inspection history plays no part in the reviews you read.
The program has teeth, too. In May 2025 the state denied a license to St. Louis County’s own animal shelter in Olivette after three failed inspections that turned up crates too small for the dogs, expired medications and insects. The shelter passed on June 30, 2025 and got its license; two more failures and the state could have shut it down. That’s a county shelter rather than a private boarding kennel, a different kind of facility under the same licensing program, but it shows the inspections are real.
### One honest caveat about daycare
We want to be precise here, because this is where other write-ups would overreach.
Overnight boarding clearly requires a license. The Department’s own guidance frames the trigger as animals being cared for overnight away from the owner’s home for consideration, and that includes a sitter who boards dogs in their own house. It also says training and grooming on their own are not regulated in Missouri, only if the animals stay overnight.
What the guidance never addresses is a daycare-only facility where no dog stays the night. The underlying regulation is worded broadly enough that it might apply; the Department’s published FAQ doesn’t say. So we’re not going to tell you every dog daycare in St. Louis is inspected, because that isn’t established. If it matters to you, ask the Department directly about that specific facility.
### What the metro actually charges
Fifteen facilities publish rates openly. That is genuinely useful, and it is also a decent proxy for how a business treats customers. Cheapest first:
Muttropolitan, 5280 Fyler Ave in south city: $34 a night, $62 for two dogs, $96 for three; daycare $21 full day, $16 half. The lowest published rates we found.
Creve Coeur Animal Hospital, 12550 Olive Blvd: priced by weight, from $40 for a dog under 20 pounds up to $53.50 for one near 88 pounds, with suites to $71 and a playroom at $86.50. Vet-attached boarding, which is worth considering for a senior dog or one on medication. No daycare.
Baronwood Kennels, 17220 New Halls Ferry Rd in Florissant: $43 for one dog in a regular kennel, $78 for two sharing, $55 for a larger room.
Silver Maple Pet Center, 2014 N Ballas Rd in Des Peres: $44 small, $49.50 medium, $54.50 large, villas $78; daycare $42.75, Monday through Thursday only.
WestInn Kennels, in Wentzville and Dardenne Prairie: $45 a night, with 10% off for three or more pets; daycare $30.
Holly Hills Pet Hotel, 4152 Toenges Ave in south city: $45 for one dog, $80 for two.
No Leash Needed, with St. Louis-area locations including Hampton Ave: $50 to $64 a night depending on the play package, XL rooms $10 more; daycare $35.50. It notes seasonal or peak rates may apply.
Williamsburg Pet Hotel, 13998 Manchester Rd in Ballwin, operating since 1962: $50 for a standard room, $70 with all-day play, suites up to $90; daycare $40 drop-in, with an unlimited membership working out near $16.66 a day.
Kennelwood Pet Resorts, the biggest local chain, boarding at Page & Lindbergh, South County, Mason Lane in Ballwin, St. Peters and Maryville, Illinois: $51 for a patio or studio room, $62 for a standard suite, up to $87 for a private villa, plus a required $15 resort fee per pet, per visit that covers up to $500 of vet care if your dog gets sick or hurt during the stay.
Arch City Dog Boarding, 6256 Gravois Ave: $53 for the first dog, $43 for each additional; holidays add $5.
The Watering Bowl, with locations in Brentwood, on Manchester in the city, and in St. Peters: $53 standard, $59.50 suite, plus $10 on holidays; daycare $37 full day, and multi-day packages down to about $30 a day.
Petropolis, in Chesterfield and St. Charles: $53 to $73 by room size, but every dog must book at least one activity a day at $22 or more, so the real floor is about $75 a night. Daycare is $48, and a 30-day daycare card is $1,258.20. Stays of 14 to 29 nights get 10% off the room, 30 nights or more 25% off.
Dogtopia of Ellisville, 15400 Manchester Rd: $58 a night if you’re on a daycare plan, $68 if not, private suite $15 more, with a full day of daycare included.
Sled & Breakfast, 1051 Old Gravois Rd in Fenton: $60 standard, $70 luxury suite, with 15% off additional dogs.
Happy Tails STL, in St. Ann near the airport: one flat $67 a night for any size, covering group play, meals and medication.
Read those with the extras in mind. The sticker isn’t the bill at Kennelwood ($15 a visit on top) or Petropolis (a required daily activity), while Dogtopia and Happy Tails fold play into the nightly price. Price out a real three-night stay at your top two before you decide.
A note on the numbers you’ll see elsewhere: the widely quoted St. Louis “average” nightly price comes from a sitter marketplace and prices in-home pet sitters, not commercial kennels. Different product, different rules. Don’t compare them.
Boarding a cat too? Cat rooms run far less, from $24 a night at Baronwood to $42 for a Kitty Suite at Kennelwood, and our guide to cat boarding in St. Louis covers that side; to keep the dog home instead, see what a pet sitter costs in St. Louis.
### What cancellation policies do St. Louis boarding kennels have?
Most St. Louis kennels don’t publish a cancellation policy at all. The few that do save their strictest terms for holidays, and the fee that catches the most owners isn’t for canceling. It’s for picking up late.
Here is what each says on its own site as of October 2026. Policies change, and the binding version is the agreement you sign, so get the terms in writing before you pay a deposit.
Camp Bow Wow Crestwood is the strictest we found. Over six major holidays (New Year’s Day, Memorial Day, Independence Day, Labor Day, Thanksgiving and Christmas) it requires a three-night minimum and a 50% deposit when you book, and any stay of seven nights or more takes the same 50% deposit. Deposits become nonrefundable two weeks before the stay.
Arch City Dog Boarding runs on prepayment: a stay isn’t reserved until it’s paid in full. Cancel by the day before the invoice is due and you get everything back; after that, canceled nights are refundable up to 50%, and nights you add cost $10 more than the regular rate. It will also cancel the stay, or charge $85 a night, if your dog is diagnosed with something contagious in the seven days before.
The Watering Bowl takes a $50 deposit to hold a boarding reservation, and the deposit becomes nonrefundable once the facility is fully booked. Holiday drop-off and pickup hours are limited.
Petropolis says flatly that there are no fees for canceling. The catch is on the calendar instead: most weekends and the Thanksgiving and Christmas weeks are peak dates, and it doesn’t publish how much more peak nights cost.
Kennelwood takes payment at pickup, not up front, so there’s no boarding deposit to lose; its published deadline is for DayCamp, which must be canceled by noon the day before or you pay for the day. Happy Tails STL sells 10-, 20- and 30-day boarding packages at 10% to 20% off and states that they’re nonrefundable. Muttropolitan asks for a couple of weeks’ to a month’s notice for holidays.
Now the fee people actually hit: the pickup clock. Sled & Breakfast and The Watering Bowl both charge half a day of daycare for a boarding pickup between 10am and 1pm and a full day after 1pm. Dogtopia Ellisville’s nightly rate covers you until noon, then it’s a $30 half day. Happy Tails adds $33.50 for checkout after 1pm. Kennelwood checks out at noon, bills the check-in day as a full day, and charges $25 for check-in or pickup after hours. Creve Coeur Animal Hospital bills by the quarter day at both ends. WestInn charges $75 per family to drop off or pick up on a holiday. A relaxed Sunday-afternoon pickup can quietly add half a night to the bill.
So before you pay anything, ask three things. Is the deposit refundable, and until when? Which dates count as holidays, and is there a minimum stay? What time is checkout, and what does a late pickup cost?
### How do you compare St. Louis boarding kennels on safety, not stars?
Star ratings tell you how customers felt about the visit they saw. The state file tells you what an inspector found on a weekday nobody was warned about. Five checks, most of them a phone call:
1. Ask for the license, and make sure it hasn’t expired. Every Missouri boarding kennel needs an Animal Care Facilities Act license for each location, and every one expires January 31. Most kennel websites never mention it (Arch City and Holly Hills are exceptions), so ask for the license number and confirm it with the program at (573) 751-3076.
2. Request the inspection reports. As of October 2026 the Department’s Animal Care Facilities Act program page offers no license search, so use its online open-records request form and ask for the facility’s recent routine inspection reports, any complaints and any investigative reports. Complaints, names and allegations included, are public records.
3. Read for patterns, not one bad day. A clean routine report is the baseline. Reinspections are the tell: the Department schedules one, unannounced, when an inspector finds multiple, direct or repeat violations. A trail of them says something a five-star review can’t.
4. Ask who the kennel’s vet is. Every licensed boarding kennel must keep a written program of veterinary care signed by an attending veterinarian, who has to visit the premises at least once a year. Ask for that vet’s name and where your dog goes in an emergency. Some answer in writing: Arch City says a dog at risk of losing life or limb goes straight to a veterinary hospital, and Kennelwood’s required resort fee covers up to $500 of vet care during a stay.
5. Count the dogs per person. Group play is where scrapes happen, so ask how many dogs one staff member watches. Happy Tails publishes an average of nine dogs per staff member, Holly Hills takes dogs out in groups of five to eight, and Arch City keeps the whole building to roughly 12 to 15 dogs.
### The vaccine that tells you something
Nearly every facility here requires the same three: rabies, distemper/parvo (DHPP or DHLPP), and bordetella. That’s the baseline and it isn’t a differentiator.
The differentiator is canine influenza. Of everything we checked, two facilities require it: Silver Maple requires H3N2, and has since 2017, and Creve Coeur Animal Hospital requires either strain. Petropolis, WestInn, The Watering Bowl and Kennelwood recommend it without requiring it. Nobody else we checked mentions it.
Neither approach is wrong. Requiring it is stricter and recommending it is more accommodating, but it tells you how a facility thinks about contagion, and it’s a concrete question you can ask.
A few other requirements worth knowing before you show up: The Watering Bowl and Creve Coeur ask for a negative fecal test, and Creve Coeur wants new patients examined by one of its vets at least 14 days before boarding. Most places require a temperament evaluation before a first stay: Petropolis runs a one-to-two-hour assessment, The Watering Bowl a 45-minute session, Holly Hills a quick 15-minute meet and greet. Several require spay or neuter: Holly Hills for every dog (and it takes none under six months), Happy Tails for dogs over twelve months; Petropolis doesn’t require it but keeps intact males over a year out of group play. Sled & Breakfast states plainly that it has no breed restrictions for boarding, which not every facility can say.
### Is anybody there overnight?
This is the question most owners assume they know the answer to, and most facilities simply don’t address it.
Six say something concrete on their own sites. Sled & Breakfast is the clearest: someone is on site 24/7. Kennelwood says its boarding staff care for pets around the clock, 365 days a year. WestInn advertises around-the-clock care staff. Happy Tails in St. Ann is open 24/7, with drop-off and pickup at any hour. At Arch City Dog Boarding the owner lives on site. And Baronwood Kennels in Florissant, family owned since 1971, has owners who live on the property and generators for power outages, which for overnight monitoring and severe weather is arguably better than a staffed shift.
Read the wording, though. Williamsburg describes its round-the-clock care in terms of 24/7 surveillance and security cameras, so ask whether a person is also in the building overnight. Everyone else is silent on it. That silence is not evidence that dogs are left alone; plenty of good facilities simply never thought to put it on the website. But it does mean the answer isn’t published, so you have to ask. It’s a fair question and a reasonable business will answer it directly.
Totally unrelated, but Fairground has more going on than you’d guess.
### Where the metro is thin
Coverage is wildly uneven, and it’s worth knowing before you start calling.
West county is saturated: Silver Maple, Petropolis, Williamsburg, Dogtopia Ellisville, Kennelwood’s Mason Lane resort, Country Acres in Manchester and Creve Coeur Animal Hospital all sit within a short drive. St. Charles County is well served too. The city has real options: Muttropolitan on Fyler, The Watering Bowl on Manchester, No Leash Needed on Hampton, Arch City Dog Boarding at 6256 Gravois, which keeps its numbers small and states plainly that it’s licensed, and Holly Hills Pet Hotel at 4152 Toenges.
North county is the weakest part of the metro. We verified three: Baronwood in Florissant, Happy Tails in St. Ann and Kennelwood’s Page & Lindbergh resort. South county is thin as well: Camp Bow Wow in Crestwood, Kennelwood South County and Sled & Breakfast in Fenton. The Metro East has a handful: Kennelwood in Maryville, All Paws Inn in Belleville, No Leash Needed in O’Fallon, and Traveling Tails Inn in Edwardsville, which boards only dogs that are regular daycare guests and, as of October 2026, isn’t taking new guests other than young puppies.
Jefferson County is thin but not empty. We found Playful Paws in Arnold and, in Imperial, Black Creek Boarding and the pet lodge at Imperial Animal Hospital. We couldn’t find published rates for any of the three, so call.
One thing to watch if you’re searching from north county: a facility called North of the River Pet Resort comes up on those searches and is in Bakersfield, California. We nearly listed it ourselves.
### What to ask before you book
Five questions, each of which has a right answer somewhere above.
1. Are you licensed under the Missouri Animal Care Facilities Act, and when was your last inspection? A boarding kennel should answer this without hesitating. 2. Is a person physically in the building overnight? 3. Do you require canine influenza vaccination, or only recommend it? 4. What happens if my dog stops eating or seems sick? At what point do you call me, and at what point do you call a vet? 5. Is the deposit refundable, is there a holiday surcharge or minimum stay, and what time is checkout?
Then, if you want the thing nobody does: call the state at (573) 751-3076 and ask for the facility’s inspection record. It is a public document and it costs you a phone call.
And on drop-off morning, run the dog tired. A long walk or an hour at one of the dog-friendly places in St. Louis makes the first night in a strange room a lot easier.
### A word on webcams and touring
Several places offer live cameras: the Dogtopia locations, Kennelwood’s private villas, Williamsburg, and Traveling Tails Inn in Edwardsville with nineteen streams. Cameras are genuinely reassuring and also genuinely limited: they show you the playroom during the day, which is rarely where the questions are.
Tour in person, and ask to see where the dogs actually sleep, not just where they play. Kennelwood takes walk-in tours daily from 10am to 2pm. Dogtopia’s Rock Hill location publishes something specific and checkable: three fully separated playrooms on separate HVAC systems, so the rooms don’t share air. Country Acres in Manchester gives each dog its own area with a window and direct access to a covered outdoor patio. Those are the kinds of details you can verify with your own eyes in ten minutes.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much does it cost to board a dog in St. Louis?
A.  Among metro facilities that publish rates, standard overnight boarding runs about $34 to $60 a night for one dog, and suites about $54.50 to $90. Muttropolitan on Fyler Ave is the cheapest published at $34; Sled & Breakfast in Fenton is $60 standard. Watch the extras: Kennelwood adds a required $15 fee per visit, Petropolis requires a paid daily activity, and holiday surcharges of $5 to $10 a night are common.
### Q. How much should dog boarding cost per day?
A.  Based on published St. Louis rates, a fair price for a standard night is about $43 to $60 for one dog. Under $40 is rare, and $65 and up usually buys a suite or an all-inclusive rate like Happy Tails’ flat $67. For a long trip, $34 to $60 a night works out to about $1,020 to $1,800 for 30 days before discounts, and some places cut that: Petropolis takes 25% off the room for stays of 30 nights or more.
### Q. Is it stressful for a dog to be boarded?
A.  It can be, particularly on a first stay, which is why most St. Louis facilities require an evaluation first, from a 15-minute meet and greet at Holly Hills to a one-to-two-hour assessment at Petropolis. A trial daycare day or one test night before a long trip is the standard way to reduce it; Kennelwood offers a free orientation sleepover on Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Thursdays.
### Q. Do dogs feel abandoned when boarded?
A.  What boarded dogs show is separation stress: pacing, skipped meals, extra clinginess at pickup. For most dogs it fades as the routine takes over; Happy Tails in St. Ann says most dogs settle in within the first day. Something that smells like home helps, and several kennels here allow one or two items from home, such as a blanket or a worn T-shirt.
### Q. Are dogs usually tired after being boarded?
A.  Yes, and it’s usually a good sign: days of group play and nights in a new place leave most dogs sleeping hard for a day or two. What isn’t normal is a dog that won’t eat, stays lethargic past a couple of days, or develops a honking cough, the classic sign of kennel cough, which the required bordetella vaccine helps prevent. Call your vet if you see any of those.
### Q. Is it better to leave a dog at home or board?
A.  It depends on the dog. A social dog often does well in group-play boarding; an anxious, senior or medicated dog may do better at home with a sitter, or at a vet-attached facility like Creve Coeur Animal Hospital. One legal difference: a sitter who comes to your house isn’t licensed by the state, while anyone who boards dogs overnight for pay outside your home, including in their own house, is supposed to hold the same state license as a kennel.
### Q. How do I check if a St. Louis boarding kennel is licensed?
A.  Ask the kennel for its Animal Care Facilities Act license number (one per location, renewed every January 31), then confirm it with the Missouri Department of Agriculture at (573) 751-3076 or acfa@mda.mo.gov. There is no searchable public database, but inspection reports, complaints and investigative reports are public records you can request through the Department’s online Sunshine Law request form.
### Q. Does someone stay overnight at dog boarding facilities?
A.  Only some St. Louis facilities say so. Sled & Breakfast states someone is on site 24/7, Kennelwood says staff care for pets around the clock, WestInn advertises around-the-clock staff, Happy Tails is open 24/7, and the owners of Arch City and Baronwood live on the property. Most others say nothing either way, which means you have to ask; it is not evidence dogs are left alone.

## How to Choose a Roofing Contractor in St. Louis (Homeowner Guide)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-roofing-contractor-your-digital-edge
The morning after one of those violent St. Louis spring storms, the kind that rolls through with hail the size of marbles, a dark stain is spreading across your bedroom ceiling. Your stomach drops. You need a roofer fast, and by afternoon there’s a truck in the driveway and a stranger on your roof telling you the whole thing needs replacing. Is he honest? Skilled? Going to be around next year if something fails?
Few hiring decisions carry this much weight. The roof is expensive, it shields everything underneath it, and after big weather the St. Louis area fills up with out-of-town “storm chasers” hunting for exactly this moment. Here’s how to pick a good roofer in this market: the signs of a reputable one, the questions worth asking, the red flags that should end a conversation, and when to schedule the work.
### How Do You Pick a Good Roofer in St. Louis?
The short answer: hire a licensed, insured, established local roofer with strong reviews and a detailed written estimate — and never sign under pressure. The single most important filter is local track record. A contractor with a real St. Louis address, years of history here, and a trail of verifiable reviews has a reputation to protect and will still be around if a repair is needed years down the line. A crew that showed up from three states away after a hailstorm has neither. Beyond that, it comes down to verifying credentials, comparing a few detailed bids, and trusting your gut if something feels off. The rest of this guide is how to do each of those well.
### Signs a Roofer Is Reputable
Reputable roofers tend to look alike in a few concrete ways. Start with the paperwork: a good one is properly licensed and insured for both liability and workers’ compensation, and hands you proof without hesitation. That last part matters more than it sounds. If a worker gets hurt on your property and the roofer carries no coverage, the bill can land on you. They’re established and local too, with a physical St. Louis-area address and a real history behind them, not a magnetic sign and an out-of-state plate. Their reputation holds up when you dig: recent reviews, references you can actually call, a rating that stays consistent across sources. The estimate arrives detailed and in writing, spelling out materials, scope, timeline, and cost rather than a number scribbled on a business card. There’s a clear warranty on materials and workmanship. And the communication feels professional from the very first call. Hit all of those, and you’re almost certainly in good hands.
### What Questions Should You Ask a Roofing Contractor?
Ask these out loud before you sign, and watch how they land. Are you licensed and insured, and can I see proof? How long have you been in business in the St. Louis area, and do you have a local address? Can you provide recent local references? Is this estimate detailed and in writing, with materials and scope spelled out? What warranty do you offer on materials and on your workmanship? Who exactly will do the work — your own crew or subcontractors? How will you protect my property and handle cleanup? And, if it’s storm damage, how do you handle the insurance claim process? The answers matter, but so does the tone. Calm and specific is a good sign. Hesitation, vagueness, or irritation at being asked tells you plenty on its own.
### Red Flags: What to Watch Out For With Roofers
Some behaviors should simply end the conversation. The classic one is the door-knocking storm chaser: appears right after bad weather, pushes you to sign on the spot, and can’t point to a local address or any history. Then there’s money. Walk away from anyone who demands large payment up front or wants cash before a single shingle is touched. A reasonable deposit is normal; paying in full before the work is not. Other warning signs stack up fast: no written contract, a bid dramatically lower than everyone else’s (usually cut corners or a coming bait-and-switch), no verifiable license or insurance, high-pressure “today only” deadlines, and offers to “waive your deductible” on an insurance job, which is fraud you don’t want your name near. Heavy storm season makes St. Louis prime territory for these operators. Slow down and verify. A real roof is worth a few days of due diligence.
### When Is the Cheapest — and Best — Time for a New Roof?
Roofers are slammed right after storm season and through the peak of summer and early fall, so demand, and usually pricing, runs highest then. The quiet stretch is late winter and early spring, before the storm rush. Contractors are hungrier for work, which tends to mean better availability and more competitive bids. One caveat, and it’s a big one. Never let a leak wait for a deal. Active water intrusion does fast, expensive damage, so an urgent repair beats a seasonal bargain every single time. Handle emergencies the moment they happen; save any non-urgent full replacement for the off-peak window, and line up your quotes a little ahead of when you actually need the work.
### Repair or Replace? How to Tell
Not every roof problem calls for a full tear-off, and an honest roofer will tell you which camp you’re in. A contractor who insists on total replacement for what looks like a minor issue is waving a red flag of his own. A repair usually makes sense when the roof is otherwise sound and the damage stays local: a few missing or lifted shingles, a small leak around a vent or flashing, one patch of storm damage. A replacement is the smarter money when the roof is near the end of its lifespan (most asphalt roofs last roughly 20–30 years), when the damage is widespread, when you’re chasing multiple leaks or seeing sag, or when the repair bills are creeping past what a new roof would cost. Not sure which you’re looking at? Get an honest assessment from a reputable local roofer, ideally two, and stay suspicious of anyone who jumps straight to “you need a whole new roof” without really looking.
Random, but: every licensed electrician in St. Louis, mapped.
### Handling a Storm-Damage Insurance Claim
So much St. Louis roof work follows a storm that the insurance side is worth understanding up front. Suspect damage? Document it first, photos and dates, then call your insurer to open a claim. An adjuster comes out to assess the damage and decide coverage. A reputable local roofer can meet that adjuster, offer a professional assessment, and make sure legitimate damage doesn’t get missed. Here’s the line you don’t cross: never let a roofer pressure you into signing over your insurance rights, and treat any promise to “waive your deductible” as a warning, not a favor. Pick your roofer on reputation and credentials, not on who knocked first, and keep the claim in your own hands. A trustworthy contractor helps you through it honestly. He doesn’t try to take it over.
### The St. Louis Roof Reality: Storms, Hail, and Older Homes
Roofing in St. Louis carries a few wrinkles you won’t find everywhere. This is a genuinely storm-prone region. Spring and summer bring high winds, hail, and the occasional severe event, so roofs take a beating and storm-damage claims are common, which is precisely why the storm-chaser problem bites so hard here. The metro also holds a huge stock of older brick homes, plenty of them with steep slopes, complicated rooflines, and materials like slate or older tile that demand a roofer who actually knows historic St. Louis construction. A one-size-fits-all crew will get it wrong. Winter piles on too: freeze-thaw cycles turn small problems into big ones fast. All of it argues for hiring deep local experience. Someone who reads St. Louis weather and housing stock will make sharper calls than a national outfit passing through on the storm.
### Always Get More Than One Quote
However urgent it feels, don’t hire the first roofer up your driveway. Get at least two or three detailed written estimates before you commit. Price is only part of what those bids reveal. Line them up and you see the range of what different professionals think the job actually needs, which is exactly where you catch someone over-selling a replacement you don’t need, or under-scoping one that comes back to haunt you. Read them side by side. Same materials? Same scope? Same warranty? The cheapest number isn’t automatically the best value, and the priciest isn’t automatically the most thorough. You want the roofer who explains the work clearly, stands behind it, and has the local reputation to back it up. A day or two spent gathering bids is cheap insurance on a purchase this size, and a reputable contractor will never push you to skip it.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What are some signs a roofer is reputable?
A.  They’re properly licensed and insured (and show proof without hesitation), established and local with a physical address, backed by recent verifiable reviews and callable references, and they provide a detailed written estimate and a clear warranty on materials and workmanship. Professional communication from the first contact is another strong sign. A roofer who checks all these boxes is almost certainly trustworthy.
### Q. What questions should I ask a roofing contractor?
A.  Ask whether they’re licensed and insured (and to see proof), how long they’ve worked in the St. Louis area and whether they have a local address, for recent local references, whether the estimate is detailed and in writing, what warranty they offer on materials and workmanship, who does the actual work, how they protect your property, and — for storm damage — how they handle insurance claims. Clear, calm answers are a good sign.
### Q. What should I watch out for with roofers?
A.  Be wary of storm-chasing door-knockers who pressure you to sign fast, demands for large upfront or cash payment, no written contract, a bid far below everyone else’s, no verifiable license or insurance, “today only” deadlines, and offers to “waive your deductible” (that’s insurance fraud). St. Louis’s heavy storm season attracts these operators, so slow down and verify before committing.
### Q. What is the cheapest time of year to get a new roof?
A.  Typically late winter and early spring, before the storm-season rush, when roofers are less busy and more competitive on price and availability. Summer and early fall — peak demand after storms — run higher. That said, never let an active leak wait for a seasonal deal; urgent water damage gets expensive fast. Handle emergencies immediately and schedule non-urgent replacements for the quieter off-peak window.
### Q. How do I find roofers near me in St. Louis?
A.  Start with the St. Louis roofing map to browse and compare local contractors by area, then vet your shortlist using the criteria above — license and insurance, local history, reviews, and a detailed written estimate. Focusing on established local roofers (rather than out-of-town storm crews) is the single best way to protect yourself on one of the biggest home investments you’ll make.
### Q. What to look for when selecting a roofer?
A.  Missouri registration, proof of insurance, a written scope naming the shingle and the underlayment, and a local address you can drive to. Since January 1, 2023 under Senate Bill 326, roofing contractors operating in the state must register with the Department of Commerce and Insurance.
### Q. How to know if a roofer is good?
A.  They put the whole job in writing before asking for money, and they can produce registration and insurance in an afternoon. If someone doing a $12,000 job on your house cannot produce those documents quickly, that is the answer to a different question you were about to ask.
### Q. How to spot a bad roofing company?
A.  Door-knocking after a storm, a discount that expires today, a large deposit up front, and no written scope. The bid that is thousands below the others is usually not the same job — fewer layers, cheaper underlayment, or no permit.
### Q. Is $30,000 too much for a roof?
A.  For a typical St. Louis asphalt replacement, yes — most land between $8,000 and $15,000. Thirty thousand is a different job: slate, tile, standing-seam metal, a steep multi-level roof, or structural repair bundled in. Ask which of those you are buying.

## How to Find a Good Handyman in St. Louis (Homeowner Guide)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/choose-a-top-rated-handyman-essential-tips-for-st-louis
Every home has a running list of them: the leaky faucet, the door that won’t latch, the ceiling fan still in its box, the fence board that’s been loose since spring. Individually they’re small; together they’re the low hum of a to-do list that never ends — and none of them is big enough to justify calling a specialized contractor. What you need is a good handyman: a skilled, reliable jack-of-all-trades who can knock out a dozen small jobs in an afternoon and actually show up when they say they will.
The catch is that “handyman” covers everyone from a true craftsman to a guy with a truck and a Facebook post, and telling them apart before you hand over your list (and your key) isn’t easy. This guide walks through how to find a good handyman in St. Louis: the best way to find one, what they typically charge, the red flags to avoid, what they can and can’t legally do, and how to hire someone you’ll want to call again.
### What Is the Best Way to Find a Good Handyman?
Two things find you the best handyman: reputation and verification. Strong reviews or a personal referral get you a name; a quick check of their work and reliability confirms it. Start with recommendations. A neighbor’s trusted handyman or a well-reviewed local pro beats a random ad every time. Then verify: read recent reviews, ask for references, and have a plain conversation about your specific jobs. Skill matters, but consistency and communication matter just as much. You want someone who returns calls, shows up on time, quotes fairly, and does tidy work you don’t have to redo. And because a handyman often works inside your home with little oversight, trust counts for a lot. Favor an established local pro with a track record over the cheapest unknown quote.
### What Do Most Handymen Charge?
There’s no single magic rate. Handyman pricing shifts with region, experience, and the job itself, so pay attention to how someone charges. Many bill by the hour, usually with a minimum, a first hour or a service-call fee, because small jobs still take showing up and setting up. Others quote a flat rate per job when the task is well defined. Here’s the counterintuitive part: a more experienced handyman may charge more per hour, then work faster and better and cost you less overall. So describe your full list up front and get an estimate. Bundling several small jobs into one visit almost always drops the per-task cost versus calling again and again. Ask what’s included, whether materials are billed separately, and whether there’s a minimum. Then compare a couple of quotes on value, not the lowest hourly figure.
### What Is the Most Requested Handyman Service?
A handful of jobs come up over and over. They’re the everyday fixes and installs most homeowners can’t or would rather not do themselves: minor plumbing (leaky faucets, running toilets, new fixtures), drywall repair and painting (patching holes, touch-ups), furniture and fixture assembly and mounting (TVs, shelves, ceiling fans, blinds), door and window fixes (sticking doors, broken latches, weatherstripping), general carpentry (trim, decking boards, small repairs), and a long tail of odd jobs from caulking to gutter cleaning to hanging pictures. One person, the whole pile of small tasks that don’t each warrant a specialist. That’s why a reliable handyman on speed dial feels like such a find. Share the whole list when you call. You’ll often be surprised how much gets done in a single visit, and how much cheaper that is than tackling each job on its own.
### What Are Red Flags When Hiring a Handyman?
Handyman work is largely unregulated compared to the licensed trades, so the vetting is on you. The same warning signs that get homeowners burned hiring a home repair company apply just as much here. Watch for anyone who demands full payment upfront (a reasonable deposit for materials is fine; paying in full before the work is done is not), has no reviews or references you can check, won’t put the scope or price in writing, quotes far below everyone else, or gets vague about their experience with your kind of job. Poor communication is its own red flag. Missed calls and a no-show for the estimate only get worse once you’ve paid. And here’s the big one: a handyman willing to take on work that legally requires a licensed pro, major electrical, gas, or structural work, is telling you something about how they operate. A good one knows the limits of what they should touch and refers you out when a job needs a licensed electrician or plumber. Honesty about scope is the real tell.
### What a Handyman Can — and Can’t — Legally Do
Knowing where the line falls keeps you safe and keeps your work legal. A handyman is the right call for small, non-specialized repairs and installations, the kinds of jobs listed above. Some work, though, legally requires a licensed specialist, and a trustworthy handyman won’t cross that line. Significant electrical work (new circuits, panel work), gas line work, major plumbing, and structural changes usually need a licensed electrician, plumber, or contractor, both for safety and to keep the job insurable. Depending on local rules, there may also be a cap on the total dollar value of work a handyman can do without a contractor’s license. So use a handyman for the many small things they do well. When a job is big, specialized, or safety-critical, hire the licensed pro. A good handyman will tell you honestly which is which, and that honesty is exactly what you want to see.
### How to Get the Most From Your Handyman
A little prep makes a visit far more efficient, and cheaper. Because many handymen charge by the hour with a minimum, the smart move is to save up a list and clear several tasks in one visit instead of calling for each little thing. The second and third jobs cost far less per task once someone’s already standing in your kitchen. Before they arrive, write down every job clearly, gather any parts or fixtures you’ve already bought, and clear access to the work areas. If painting is on the list, plan around the fumes, since there’s a real wait before it’s safe to sleep in a freshly painted room. Be upfront about the full scope so the estimate is accurate and nobody’s caught off guard. Then, when you find a good one, keep them. A handyman who already knows your home and its quirks gets faster and more useful over time, and being an easy, organized, fair-paying customer keeps you near the top of their call-back list. Treat the relationship well and it pays off every time the to-do list grows again.

And the honesty test: Is there anything on my list you’d refer to a licensed specialist instead? A trustworthy handyman answers plainly, gives a fair estimate without pressure, and readily admits when a job is outside their lane. How they handle that last question in particular separates the reliable pros from the ones who’ll take on anything for a paycheck and leave you with a mess.

A handyman who’s worked on older St. Louis homes handles those quirks smoothly where someone used only to new builds might stall. ### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What do most handymen charge?

A more experienced handyman may cost more hourly but work faster and better.
