## No Flags, No Dig: How to Pick a St. Louis Landscaper
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/transform-your-space-top-landscaping-services-in-st-louis
A skid steer idles at the curb, shovels come off the trailer, and there isn’t a single paint flag in your lawn. Remember that bare grass. Clay grabs a spade like wet cement here. You push, it holds, and when it finally lets go it comes up in a gray-brown slab that keeps the exact shape of the blade. Anyone who has tried to plant one shrub in a St. Louis yard knows that feel in the shoulders. It is also the quickest way to sort the landscapers worth hiring from the ones who will hand you a pretty drawing and a dead hedge by August.
Here is the part nobody puts on a flyer: the good ones start talking about what is under your yard before they talk about what goes on top of it. The soil. The water. The lines buried in it. A crew that skips straight to plant names and patio colors is selling you the picture. A crew that kneels down, pushes a thumb into the dirt and asks where the downspouts drain is selling you a yard that is still alive in three summers.
### How to pick a good landscaper?
Start with one question at the first visit and listen to how the answer sounds: “Who calls 811, and when?” Missouri’s underground facility law, section 319.026, says notice goes in at least two working days, but not more than ten working days, before the dig starts. That second number is the one almost nobody knows. If the crew can’t start within ten working days of the request, the law says they have to make a relocate request before they dig. So a landscaper who calls in your locate, then gets rained out for two weeks and shows up anyway, is digging on a stale ticket. A landscaper who answers right away, names who files the request and explains that window has done real installs here. One who shrugs, or says they “just dig around it,” has told you everything about how they treat the parts of the job you cannot see.
Better still, you get to check their work with your own eyes. The locate is free: request it by calling 811 or at missouri-811.org. A few days later little paint lines and flags appear across your grass, each color its own buried danger: red for electric, yellow for gas, blue for water, orange for communications, green for sewer. Those marks show the approximate location of the lines, which is why careful crews switch to hand tools near them. So here is the tell to text every neighbor who is about to hire someone: if the morning of the dig arrives and your lawn has no colored flags in it, nobody called. Stop the job right there, before the first machine bites into the clay.
After that, match the crew to the job (mowing, planting and hardscape are sorted out further down) and keep the checklist short; the full version sits at the bottom of this page. The question on it that matters most: what happens if a tree they planted is dead next spring, after its first St. Louis August in clay? A pause there is an answer too.
### Walk the Garden before you sign anything
Gravel crunches underfoot, the air smells like wet mulch, and for the first time you can see what a ten-year-old planting actually looks like instead of a nursery tag. That is the best hour you can spend before hiring a landscaper, and it starts with a parking spot on Tower Grove Avenue. The William T. Kemper Center for Home Gardening at the Missouri Botanical Garden spreads 23 demonstration gardens over 8.5 acres, planted for the same heat, the same humidity and the same clay you are fighting at home. Walk it slowly. Feel the shade drop ten degrees under a mature tree. Notice which plants look tired in late summer and which still look crisp. Take pictures of what you love, with the plant tags in the frame.
Stuck on a question before you even call anyone? The Garden runs a Horticulture Answer Service by phone, Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to noon, at (314) 577-5143, staffed by Garden staff and Master Gardeners. Ask them whether the plant a bidder suggested will handle your wet corner or your hot south wall. It is a neutral second opinion from people with nothing to sell you, and it takes one phone call. If you are buying some of the plants yourself, read what to know before you buy them in St. Louis first. Zone, frost dates and the clay underneath all decide what survives.
Now you are not walking into a sales conversation with a vague wish for “something nice.” You are walking in with a phone full of plants that already proved they survive here, at full size, so you can see exactly how big that “compact” shrub really gets. Show the photos to every landscaper who bids and ask which of those plants they would put in your yard, and why. The good ones dig into it with you, because you just did half their homework. The weak ones steer you back toward whatever they already had in mind.
### The quote that should make you nervous
Lay three written estimates on the kitchen table and one of them will be a lot lower than the others. It feels like relief for about a minute. Then read what is missing. Usually it is soil prep, grading, drainage, haul-away, or a plant list that just says “shrubs.” On clay those are not extras. Water that has nowhere to go sits around roots until they rot, or runs toward your foundation, and you only find out after the first hard rain when the bed looks like a bathtub.
So compare scope, not totals. Same plants, same sizes, same depth of new soil, same cleanup, same guarantee. Once the lines match, the price gap usually shrinks or disappears. If it does not, ask the high bidder what they are doing that the low bidder is not. Sometimes the answer is “nothing,” and you have saved real money. Often it is the drainage work that keeps the whole project alive.
A few other things should stop you cold: a big cash deposit before any materials show up, no address or insurance paperwork, pressure to sign today, and anyone who waves off your worry about water. Good crews are busy. They do not need to rush you.
### Go stand in the rain first
The next time a real storm rolls across the city, put on boots, grab an umbrella and walk your yard while it is still coming down. Listen to the gutters. Watch where the water sheets off the roof, where it pools against the foundation, where it cuts a little brown channel across the lawn toward the alley. Wait an hour after it stops and walk it again. The low spot that is still holding water, still squishing under your heel, is the spot that will drown whatever gets planted there.
Take photos and short videos of all of it. This is the most useful thing you can hand a landscaper, and almost nobody does it, because the bids happen on dry, sunny afternoons when every yard looks fine. A dry yard hides its problems. A wet one confesses them.
When the landscaper comes out, show them the videos before they show you their portfolio. A good one will want to see every clip, ask where the downspouts empty and start sketching how to move that water away from the house, whether that means regrading, a dry creek bed, a rain garden or simply extending a downspout ten feet. A weak one will glance at the phone, nod and go back to talking about mulch color. You have just learned which crew to hire, and it cost you a wet pair of socks.
If that brown channel runs toward the house, ask every bidder whether a rain garden makes sense. The Metropolitan St. Louis Sewer District’s Project Clear Rainscaping pages explain how a rain garden gives runoff a safe place to go and keeps it away from your foundation, and the program also lists a Small Grants Program with a program area map. Check whether your address falls inside it before you sign, and ask whether the landscaper has built one before. Most homeowners never hear the word rainscaping until after the bed has already flooded.
Do the same with sun. Stand in the spot where you want the new bed at nine in the morning, at noon and at five, or just snap a photo at each time from the back door. Full sun, part shade and deep shade need completely different plants, and the honest answer to “how much sun does it get?” is almost never the one you guess.
### Mowing crew, design crew, or both?
The Saturday you finally stop pushing a mower in July heat is a real kind of freedom, and a maintenance contract buys it. That is a different hire from the crew who rebuilds your front yard. For upkeep, you want consistency: the same people, the same day, a fair seasonal price, and someone who notices when a shrub starts browning. For a project, you want a portfolio and a designer who asks about how you actually use the yard, where the kids run, where the dog wears a path, where you want to sit with coffee in the morning.
Many homeowners end up wanting both, a one-time build and then steady care so it stays that way. Some full-service companies handle the whole thing. Others are honest that they only do one side, which is worth respecting. What you want to avoid is hiring a mow-and-go outfit to design a patio, or paying design-firm rates for someone to edge your sidewalk.
Match the kind of company to the job. Weekly mowing and cleanup, design-and-install work like new beds and plantings, and hardscape like patios, walkways and retaining walls are three different trades with three different sets of tools. Plenty of companies do two of them well. Very few do all three well. Ask which kind of job fills most of their calendar, and make sure it matches the thing you actually want built.
When you are ready to build a shortlist, start on the St. Louis landscaping map and compare local companies by area, or widen out to every trade on the home services coverage map.

### What to ask at the first walk-through
Bring these questions on paper and write the answers down while the landscaper is still standing in your yard. The smell of cut grass and the friendly handshake fade fast. The notes do not.
Who files the Missouri 811 request, and how many working days does that add to the schedule?
Can I see a job you finished two or three years ago, and can I call that homeowner?
What will you do about drainage and soil before anything goes in the ground?
Which plants are you proposing, at what size, and how big will they be at maturity?
Do you guarantee plants, and for how long? What does the guarantee require of me?
Is it your own crew doing the work, and who do I call if something goes wrong?
Can I have a certificate of insurance and a written, itemized estimate?
A good landscaper answers every one of these without flinching and usually adds something you did not think to ask. That is the person you want leaning on the shovel.
Before you sign, walk the Kemper Center gardens and bring the photos to every bid. Then shortlist two or three local crews on the St. Louis landscaping map and ask each one who calls 811.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the rule of 3 in landscaping?
A.  Plant in odd-numbered groups, threes, fives and sevens, because the eye reads them as natural and pairs as stiff. It also works for layers: something tall, something mid-height and something low in each bed, so the planting reads as one picture instead of a row of soldiers.
### Q. What are common landscaping mistakes to avoid?
A.  Putting sun plants in shade, ignoring how big plants get, skipping soil prep and drainage on heavy clay, and building more than you have time to maintain. The other classic is digging before the utilities have marked their buried lines. A good landscaper plans around all of it before the first shovel goes in.
### Q. What to look for when hiring a landscaper?
A.  Insurance, references you can call, finished work that is a few years old, and a written estimate with the plant list on it. Ask what they do about clay soil and drainage. The answer separates people who plant here from people who plant anywhere.
### Q. Is $100 an hour too much for landscape work?
A.  It depends on what that hour buys. For a crew with equipment, insurance and disposal, an hourly rate covers several people and a truck. For one person with a mower, the same number is a lot. Compare crew size and what is included, not the hourly number on its own.
### Q. How much tip should you give a landscaper?
A.  Tipping a company owner is not expected. Many homeowners thank a crew that did hard work in the heat with cold drinks, a cash thank-you split among the workers, or a strong review with the crew members named. On a big install, a referral to a neighbor is often worth more to the business than cash.
### Q. What are some reputable landscape companies in St. Louis, Missouri?

## How to Choose a Carpet Cleaner in St. Louis (Homeowner Guide)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/best-carpet-cleaners-in-st-louis-for-a-spotless-home
The traffic path down the hallway has gone gray. A mystery stain sits by the couch, and a faint pet smell lingers no matter how often you vacuum. Carpet takes a beating in a busy St. Louis home — kids, pets, muddy shoes, a whole season tracked across the floor — and every so often it needs a real professional cleaning that a rented machine can’t match. So you start searching. Almost immediately you hit a wall of “$29 whole-house special!” ads that sound too good to be true. They usually are.
Choosing a good carpet cleaner is trickier than it looks. The industry runs on bargain-bait pricing, and the gap between a quality job and a cheap one shows up later: in whether your carpets actually come clean, dry right, and stay fresh. This guide covers how to choose a carpet cleaner in St. Louis: the cleaning methods and which to pick, what it really costs, how often to clean, the bait-and-switch to sidestep, and how to find a trustworthy pro near you.
### How Do You Choose a Good Carpet Cleaner?
Hire an experienced, well-reviewed, insured carpet cleaner who gives you an honest, upfront price and uses the right method for your carpet. Treat suspiciously cheap ads with real skepticism. The single biggest tell of a good carpet cleaner is transparent pricing: a reputable company quotes from the actual square footage and condition, explains what’s included, and doesn’t bait you with a rock-bottom number only to pile on charges once they’re inside your home. Beyond price, check the reviews, the years in business, and the insurance that covers you if something gets damaged. Ask how they clean, how long it dries, and whether the work is guaranteed. Heavy stains and pet odor need more than a quick surface pass, so a good cleaner tailors the approach to your carpet and your problem.
### Steam Cleaning vs. Dry Cleaning: Which Method?
Two methods cover almost every professional job. Hot water extraction — what most people call steam cleaning — sprays hot water and solution deep into the pile, then immediately pulls it back out along with the dirt. It’s the method most manufacturers recommend, and the most thorough for lifting stubborn dirt and allergens. The tradeoff is drying time, often several hours. Low-moisture or “dry” cleaning uses far less water with specialized compounds or pads, so carpets dry fast. That’s handy for quick turnarounds or moisture-sensitive rooms, but it doesn’t clean as deep. For a genuine deep clean, hot water extraction is the default. Low-moisture wins when speed matters most. A good cleaner picks the method that fits your carpet and explains why, instead of running the same process on every floor.
### What Does Carpet Cleaning Cost?
Price tracks the square footage, the number of rooms, the carpet’s condition, and any add-ons: heavy stain treatment, pet-odor removal, protectant. That’s exactly why the flashy flat-rate ads mean nothing. Get a real quote instead. Reputable cleaners price by the room or by the square foot and give an honest estimate up front, usually after asking about your space or seeing it. The classic warning sign is the absurdly low advertised price that exists only to get a technician in your door, where the “real” price for anything past a token surface pass suddenly appears. Do what you’d do for any home service: get two or three clear quotes for the same scope, ask exactly what’s included (pre-treatment, spot treatment, moving furniture, drying), and pick on value and trust, not the lowest headline number. A fair price for good work beats a bait price every time.
### How Often Should You Have Carpets Cleaned?
For most homes, plan on a professional cleaning about once a year. Bump that to every six months or so if you have pets, kids, allergies, or heavy foot traffic. The payoff goes past a fresher look. A deep clean pulls out the set-in dirt, allergens, and dust mites that vacuuming leaves behind, which helps indoor air quality, and it stretches the carpet’s lifespan by clearing the abrasive grit that grinds down the fibers. Many carpet warranties actually require periodic professional cleaning to stay valid, so skipping it can cost you the coverage too. Between visits, vacuum often and hit spills fast. The sooner you treat a spill, the less likely it sets into a permanent stain. Regular cleaning is maintenance that pays for itself in carpet that lasts longer and stays healthier.
### Red Flags: The Bait-and-Switch and Other Warning Signs
The carpet-cleaning industry has a well-known bad-actor problem, so vet carefully. The biggest red flag is the bait-and-switch: an unbelievably low advertised price (“3 rooms for $49!”) built to get a technician in your door. Once inside, he decides your carpets need “deep cleaning,” “pet treatment,” or “protectant” at several times the quoted price, and leans on you hard if you hesitate. Watch for the rest of the pattern too: no verifiable reviews or business history, no insurance (which matters the moment furniture or flooring gets damaged), vague answers about their method or what’s included, a demand for full payment upfront, and pressure to add services on the spot. A trustworthy cleaner does the opposite. Straight quote, clear process, no ambush charges, and a guarantee behind the work. If a price seems too good to be true, it is. Letting that operator into your home usually costs more in the end, not less.
### DIY Rental vs. Hiring a Pro
You’ve seen the rental machines parked by the grocery-store exit. For a light freshen-up, they earn their keep. They are not professional cleaning, though, and the difference is worth knowing. A rental unit has far less suction and heat than truck-mounted equipment, so it pulls out less dirt and leaves more water in the pile. Carpet that stays over-wet and dries slowly can turn mildewy or musty, and St. Louis humidity only makes that worse. A rental also can’t match a pro’s pre-treatment and stain know-how. Between professional visits, a rental or a decent spot cleaner handles routine touch-ups fine. For a real deep clean, set-in stains, pet odor, or a carpet warranty you need to protect, professional hot water extraction cleans far better and dries the way it should. DIY for touch-ups, a pro for the real thing. And whatever you use, never leave the carpet soaked.
Random, but: Belleville storefronts, here’s the visibility playbook.
### What to Do Before the Cleaner Arrives
A few minutes of prep makes the visit faster and cheaper, and the result better. Vacuum first if the company asks you to, and many do; it lifts the loose surface dirt so the crew can focus on the deep cleaning. Clear the floor. Pick up toys, cords, and small items, and move any small or fragile furniture you can, because some companies charge to move furniture and all of them work faster with open access. Point out problem areas and specific stains before they start, and say what caused them if you know (pet accidents, wine, grease), since different stains call for different treatment. Put pets somewhere safe and out of the way. Then plan for drying time: keep foot traffic off the fresh carpet for several hours, and run fans or the AC to speed things along. That small bit of prep helps the cleaner do their best work, and it protects you from surprise charges for extra labor.
### St. Louis-Specific: Allergens, Pets, and Older Homes
A few local realities make professional carpet cleaning especially worth it here. St. Louis’s humid climate and notorious allergy seasons — the region regularly ranks among the tougher places for seasonal allergies — leave carpets holding a lot of pollen, dust, and allergens. A deep clean noticeably helps indoor air quality in allergy-prone households. The area’s many pet-loving homes add dander and the occasional odor that only proper extraction and treatment fully clear. Then there are the metro’s countless older homes, where you find aging carpet, delicate fibers, or wall-to-wall laid straight over hardwood: the kind of floor a careless cleaner over-wets and ruins. That’s one more reason to hire an experienced pro who matches method to material. A cleaner who knows St. Louis homes, seasons, and allergy patterns leaves you with a healthier result than a bargain crew rushing through on a single setting.

Given St. Louis’s humid, allergy-heavy climate and many pet-owning and older homes, an experienced local cleaner who matches the right method to your carpet delivers a genuinely healthier, longer-lasting result than a bargain bait-price crew ever will.
### Q. What are the common mistakes in carpet cleaning?
A.  Over-wetting, too much detergent left behind, and rushing the dry. Residue is the one that bites later — carpet that was cleaned cheaply attracts dirt faster afterwards, which is why it looks worse three months on than it did before.
### Q. Is it better to shampoo or steam clean carpets?
A.  Hot water extraction — what most people call steam cleaning — is the method most manufacturers specify, because it rinses rather than leaving detergent in the pile. Shampooing can look good immediately and re-soil quickly for exactly that reason.
### Q. What is the most recommended carpet cleaner?
A.  Method matters more than brand: look for hot water extraction, a written price before the truck arrives, and no upsell at the door. The classic trap is the “3 rooms for $49” advert — that price exists to get a technician into the house, not to do the job.
### Q. Who are some good carpet cleaners in St. Louis?
A.  Rather than name one, use the test that works: a company quoting in writing from room measurements, using hot water extraction, with no bait pricing. Search the directory by category and compare on those three points — they separate the real operators quickly.

## How to Choose a Pest Control Company in St. Louis (Guide)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/top-pest-control-options-in-st-louis-easy-guide
It usually starts small. A trail of ants across the kitchen counter, a single mouse dropping behind the pantry, a wasp nest tucked under the eaves. Then comes the one that makes every St. Louis homeowner tense up: the first sign of termites in a region where they thrive. The pest changes. The reaction doesn’t. You want it gone, gone safely, and gone for good. So you start searching, and within minutes you’re staring at a wall of companies all promising the same fix.
Which one you pick matters more than most people think. The gap between a good exterminator and a bad one is the gap between a solved problem and a recurring nightmare, plus a real question of what chemicals end up sprayed around your kids and pets. This guide walks through how to choose a pest control company in St. Louis: what to look for, the types of pest control, which pests are genuinely hard to beat, the red flags to avoid, and how to find a trustworthy local pro.
### What Should You Look for When Choosing a Pest Control Company?
The essentials come down to a short, non-negotiable list. Start with licensed and insured. Pest control means regulated chemicals, and a licensed operator is trained to apply them safely and legally, so ask to see proof. Next, look for experience with your specific pest; treating termites, bed bugs, and mice each calls for different expertise.
You also want a strong local reputation, the kind that shows up in recent reviews and references you can actually check. Insist on a clear plan and written estimate that explains what they’ll treat, how, what it costs, and what happens if the pests come back. Ask about safety, meaning the products they use and how they protect children and pets. And favor a company that offers a guarantee or warranty and stands behind its work. Check those boxes and you hire someone who solves the problem instead of spraying once and driving off.
### What Are the Types of Pest Control?
Knowing the main approaches helps you judge what a company is actually offering. There are four broad categories. Chemical control is the pesticides and baits most people picture. Biological control uses natural predators or organisms to manage pests, and it shows up more in gardens and on farms. Physical or mechanical control covers traps, barriers, and exclusion, sealing the gaps pests use to get in. Cultural or preventive control removes the food, water, and shelter that draw pests in to begin with.
The best modern companies practice Integrated Pest Management (IPM). They combine those methods on purpose: identify the pest, use the least-toxic effective treatment, seal entry points, and head off the next wave, instead of blasting everything with chemicals. So when a company leads with prevention and exclusion rather than a quick spray, take it as a sign you’ve found a real professional.
### What Is the Hardest Pest to Get Rid Of?
Some pests are simply tougher, and knowing which ones keeps your expectations honest. Bed bugs top the list. They hide in tiny cracks, shrug off many treatments, and usually take specialized, repeated effort. Termites are both hard to eliminate and genuinely destructive, which is why they demand a specialist and why prevention matters so much around St. Louis. Cockroaches, German cockroaches especially, breed fast and build resistance, so full eradication becomes a persistent job. Rodents keep coming back whenever the entry points stay open.
The lesson runs through all four: a cheap one-time spray rarely holds. You want specific expertise, a thorough plan, and a company willing to follow up. If someone promises to wipe out bed bugs or termites in a single quick visit for a bargain price, be skeptical.
### What Are the 3 C’s of Pest Control?
One useful frame is the “three C’s.” Control is dealing with the active infestation you have right now. Correction is fixing the underlying conditions, the gaps, moisture, and food sources, that let the pests in. Continuity is the ongoing monitoring and prevention that keeps them from coming back. A good company works all three.
Anyone can spray to knock down what you can see. The professionals also trace how the pests got in and make it harder for the next batch. So when you’re comparing companies, ask how they’ll keep pests out, not only how they’ll kill the ones you’ve got. A real answer to that question is the mark of a company worth hiring.
### Red Flags When Hiring a Pest Control Company
Watch for warning signs before you let anyone spray around your home. A company that’s not licensed or insured, or won’t show proof. One that pressures you to sign a long contract on the spot. A price far below everyone else, which often means a quick spray that never touches the real problem. Vague answers about what chemicals they use or how they’ll protect your family and pets. Guarantees that sound too good to be true, like “100% gone forever in one visit.” And door-to-door outfits that turn up out of nowhere with a high-pressure pitch.
A trustworthy pest professional is transparent about methods, honest about what the job takes, and easy to talk to about safety. Feel rushed, kept in the dark about the products going into your home, or pushed toward a big contract before anyone has diagnosed the problem? Keep looking.
### One-Time Treatment vs. an Ongoing Plan
People often ask whether they need recurring service or just a single visit. The honest answer depends on the pest and the situation. A one-time treatment can be plenty for a specific, contained problem, a single wasp nest or an occasional invader, especially when you also fix the conditions that caused it. An ongoing plan, quarterly or seasonal, earns its keep against steady pressure, tough recurring pests, or the plain peace of mind of regular monitoring. In a long-season, termite-prone metro like St. Louis, that preventive service genuinely pays off for a lot of homeowners.
The real test is whether a company recommends what your situation needs instead of defaulting to the priciest plan. Be wary of anyone pushing a costly long-term contract for a minor one-off. Be just as wary of a one-time spray sold as a permanent fix for something that clearly needs follow-up.
Random, but: Maryland Heights restaurants are better than the town gets credit for.
### What Does Pest Control Cost?
Costs swing widely with the pest, the severity, the size of your home, and whether you pick one-time or ongoing service. Rather than chase a single number, get clear itemized quotes. A simple one-time treatment for a common pest usually runs modest. Specialized work like termite treatment or bed-bug eradication costs considerably more, given the expertise and repeat visits it takes. Recurring plans tend to be priced per visit or as an annual agreement.
Get two or three detailed estimates for the same scope so the comparison is fair, and make sure each quote spells out what’s treated, how many visits are included, and what the guarantee covers. The cheapest bid isn’t automatically the best value. A slightly higher price from a company that actually solves the problem, and stands behind it, beats a bargain spray you end up redoing.
### Questions to Ask Before You Hire
Before you let anyone treat your home, run a short list out loud. Are you licensed and insured, and can I see proof? Do you have experience with my specific pest? What products will you use, and how will you keep my kids and pets safe? What’s your plan — and how will you keep the pests from coming back? Is the estimate detailed and in writing? Do you offer a guarantee, and what does it cover? Is this a one-time treatment or an ongoing plan, and why? A professional answers every one clearly and without pressure. How a company handles the questions, patient and transparent versus vague and rushed, tells you most of what you need to know before they set foot inside.
### St. Louis-Specific: Termites, Humidity, and Old Homes
A few local realities make pest control here its own beast. The region’s humid summers and mild shoulder seasons stretch the pest calendar long and active. This is genuine termite country, where subterranean termites pose a real and costly threat to homes, so termite inspections and prevention deserve extra attention, and a termite specialist beats a generalist. The metro’s many older brick homes, deep basements, and mature trees hand pests plenty of entry points and harborage, everything from ants and spiders to mice and the occasional bat.
The calendar drives predictable invasions, too. Ants and wasps push in through the warm months; rodents come looking for heat as things cool. A local company that knows St. Louis’s specific pests and seasons sees problems coming that a generic outfit won’t. That’s a strong reason to hire a pro who actually knows the area.

### Q. What are the 3 C’s of pest control?

Control (handling the active infestation), Correction (fixing the underlying conditions — gaps, moisture, food sources — that let pests in), and Continuity (ongoing monitoring and prevention so they stay out). ## Your $28 Sewer Fee and the Best Plumbers in St. Louis, Ranked
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-top-plumbers-in-st-louis-now
If you own a home in the city of St. Louis with six or fewer units, there’s a $28 sewer lateral fee on your property tax bill every year, and almost nobody reads that line. Here’s what it buys: when your sewer line breaks under the public right of way, the street side of the pipe, the city repairs it at no fee, as long as your taxes are paid. You learn what that line is worth on the night the floor drain gurgles, the basement smells like the street, and cold water creeps across the concrete toward the furnace.
The catch is who you call. The city wants a report and video from a plumber licensed in the city of St. Louis before it will look at your claim. A perfect score from a few dozen customers is a coin toss with good lighting. A 4.9 that has held steady across nearly 12,000 Google reviews is a track record, built one flooded basement at a time by people who had every reason to complain and mostly didn’t.

The license is where St. Louis gets particular, and where most out-of-town advice goes quiet. Inside the city limits, plumbing permits are issued to licensed plumbing contractors who are certified by the City of St. Louis, and a sewer lateral replacement is one of the jobs that needs a permit and an inspection. Back to that $28 sewer lateral fee. It funds the city’s Sewer Lateral Repair Program, and when your sewer line breaks under the public right of way, the street side of the line, there is no fee for the repair as long as your taxes are paid. The catch is the paperwork. The city wants a report and video from a plumber licensed in the city of St. Louis before it will look at your claim. Many of the city’s sewer lines are over 100 years old and made of clay, so this is not a rare situation. A plumber with a camera and a city license can save you the most expensive check you’ll ever write for a pipe you never see. The program doesn’t cover clogs, tree roots or the part of the line under your own yard.

## 7 Up Was Born in St. Louis, and Its Famous First Name Never Existed
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-where-flavor-tells-a-story
Crack open a cold 7 Up and the fizz prickles your nose before the lemon-lime lands on your tongue. That soda was born here: a St. Louis firm, the Howdy Co., applied for the SEVEN UP trademark on Oct. 4, 1928.
Now the part your trivia friend gets wrong. More than 150 websites say its first name was “Bib-Label Lithiated Lemon-Lime Soda.” Bottle historians Bob Brown and Bill Lockhart dug through the trademarks, the ads and the old paper labels looking for it. They found bib-labels, all right: paper cards hung on a string over the bottles like bibs, one of them bright orange and promising to take the ‘ouch’ out of grouch. The long name, never. Their verdict, in their study of the company and its bottles: “The obvious answer is that it never existed.” The name was Seven-Up from the start; “Lithiated Lemon Soda” was only a descriptive second line on labels from about 1931 to 1935.
So the soda story everyone repeats is a myth. The best dare in town is real, and it’s printed on the menu. The line under the malts on Crown Candy Kitchen’s own menu calls it “our policy since 1913”: five malts lined up in front of you, cold enough to ache in your teeth, a 30-minute clock, and if every one is gone in time, they’re free. The house rules read like a referee wrote them: all five ordered at once, nobody helps, no bathroom trips, no stepping outside, and no attempts during the lunch rush or whenever the staff decide it’s too busy. At $5.75 a regular malt, that’s $28.75 of ice cream riding on a policy dated seven years before Prohibition began. Send this to the friend who still quotes the Bib-Label name.
Make a Saturday of it, four stops in this order.
11 a.m.: Balkan Treat Box, 8103 Big Bend in Webster Groves, open 11 to 8 every day, (314) 733-5700. Get the pide. It comes out of the wood-fired oven blistered at the edges, slicked with red-pepper ajvar and cool, tangy kajmak, and you’ll burn your fingers on the first piece because you can’t wait. The chef, Loryn Nalić, won the James Beard Award for Best Chef: Midwest cooking there.
12:30 p.m.: Berix, 2201 Lemay Ferry Road, open 9 to 7 on Saturdays, (314) 845-3711. Bosnian coffee, dark and unfiltered, the grounds settling at the bottom of the cup.
2:30 p.m.: Crown Candy Kitchen, 1401 St. Louis Ave. in Old North, open 10:30 to 5 Monday through Saturday, (314) 621-9650. Call ahead and ask whether it’s a good hour for the dare. Two friends from Greece, Harry Karandzieff and Pete Jugaloff, opened the counter in 1913, and Harry’s grandsons Andy, Tommy and Mike run it now, the shop’s own history says.
5 p.m.: Charlie Gitto’s On the Hill, 5226 Shaw Ave., opens at 5 on Saturdays, (314) 772-8898. Order the toasted ravioli the house calls its signature, if the malts left you any room, and listen for the breading to crackle.
### Does St. Louis have a dining scene?
Yes, and the awards are the least of it. Nalić’s win was only the third Best Chef: Midwest for a St. Louis chef, after Gerard Craft of Niche and Kevin Nashan of Sidney Street Cafe, as FOX 2 reported, and it came on her fifth nomination, years after she started out running catering at Pappy’s Smokehouse.
Under the trophies sit the plates nobody else makes: toasted ravioli with the breading still crackling, Provel turning glossy on a cracker-thin crust cut into squares, pork steaks going sticky with sauce on a backyard grill. Then whole neighborhoods built by immigrant cooks: pho steam and torn injera on South Grand, a flat-top hissing on Cherokee Street, Bosnian coffee poured thick around Bevo Mill. A town that gave the world 7 Up, and still hands out free malts under a rule from 1913, doesn’t need a critic to settle the question. Is St. Louis a foodie city? Esquire once found a line down the block on Big Bend at 11 in the morning. That’s your answer.
### From meat-and-potatoes town to a Beard winner on Big Bend
St. Louis spent decades as a meat-and-potatoes town, and plenty of those plates are still worth ordering. What changed is the range. At Vicia, a James Beard finalist for Outstanding Restaurant, the menu turns with whatever the farms are pulling out of the ground that week. At Balkan Treat Box, the ćevapi come on wood-fired somun that soaks up the sausages’ peppery juices, and the restaurant now ships its pide across the country.
### Taquerias on Cherokee, Bosnian coffee near Bevo Mill
Walk Cherokee Street and the taquerias set the soundtrack: a flat-top hissing, a radio in Spanish, a stack of warm tortillas on every table. Head south to the Bevo Mill area, home to one of the largest Bosnian communities outside Bosnia, and the coffee at Berix Coffeehouse on Lemay Ferry Road comes thick and strong, the Bosnian way. Nearby, a Bosnian refugee family, the Grbićs, turned an old Gravois dive into Lemmons by Grbic, where the ćevapi come hot off the grill.
At Meskerem Restaurant on South Grand, you tear the injera with your fingers, sour and spongy, and scoop up the stews with it. Seoul Taco folds Korean barbecue into tortillas, and on The Hill, Zia’s still sends out the Italian-American plates the neighborhood was built on.
### Slow pour-overs and a cocktail called In A Pickle
At Sump Coffee and Blueprint Coffee, the pour-over drips slowly enough that you smell it long before the first sip, and the conversation at the next table is usually about the Cardinals. After dark, Planter’s House in Lafayette Square pours from a list of 350-plus spirits, 39 of them bottled just for the bar, and its house cocktail In A Pickle is exactly the conversation starter it sounds like.

### Institutions and immigrant kitchens worth the trip
Some of the best St. Louis food stories aren’t trends at all - they’re institutions that have fed the city for generations. In Old North, Crown Candy Kitchen has run since 1913, founded by Macedonian immigrant Harry Karandzieff and still family-owned four generations later; its malts, sundaes, and BLT are a genuine piece of living history. Just as important are the kitchens that arrived with newer waves of immigrants. Mai Lee in Brentwood opened in 1985 as St. Louis’s first Vietnamese restaurant - a refugee family’s enterprise that now runs a menu of two hundred-plus dishes - and it helped introduce a whole city to pho. For barbecue, Pappy’s Smokehouse in Midtown carries the Memphis-style-rib torch that made St. Louis a serious smoke town. And at the fine-dining end, chef Nick Bognar’s Indo in Botanical Heights blends his Thai heritage with sushi craft - work that has earned repeated James Beard recognition. Together they trace the whole arc: a century-old soda fountain, a pioneering immigrant kitchen, a smokehouse, and a nationally acclaimed fusion room, all in one metro. What ties them together is the thing this whole city does best with food: it holds onto its history while constantly making room for the next wave of cooks and cultures, so the story on the plate keeps getting richer without ever forgetting where it started.
### How restaurants helped bring South Grand back
The growth of the restaurant industry has a positive ripple effect on St. Louis’s economy. These establishments create jobs for chefs, servers, bartenders, and countless others, revitalizing the local workforce. The economic impact is substantial, with restaurants contributing significantly to the St Louis City GDP and tax revenue.
This growth also spurs ancillary industries, such as food suppliers, local farmers, and artisanal producers, creating a multiplier effect that benefits the entire regional economy. The continuous development and expansion of the culinary sector are crucial for St. Louis’s economic vitality, attracting investment and fostering a climate of entrepreneurship.

Faced with unprecedented challenges, St. Louis restaurants embraced creative solutions like delivery and outdoor dining, ensuring the survival of their businesses and the continuation of their culinary stories.
Many pivoted to offering meal kits, virtual cooking classes, and expanded take-out services, demonstrating an adaptability that has become a hallmark of the St. Louis culinary community. This period highlighted the deep connection between residents and their local eateries, with many patrons actively supporting restaurants through various means, underscoring the integral role these establishments play in the city’s social fabric.

The future of St. Louis’s restaurant scene is brimming with promise. A focus on sustainability, community, and culinary exploration ensures a constant evolution. Chefs are increasingly partnering with local farmers, minimizing their environmental impact and highlighting the region’s fresh produce.
The farm-to-table movement is a fundamental shift towards a more responsible, ethical food system rather than a passing trend, and it benefits both the environment and the local economy. The emphasis on seasonality and local sourcing results in fresher, more flavorful dishes and supports the livelihoods of regional agricultural producers.
Community Supported Agriculture (CSA) programs and farmer’s markets are thriving, fostering a deep connection between diners and the source of their food. ### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What food is St. Louis known for?
A.  Its own hyper-local specialties: toasted ravioli, gooey butter cake, the pork steaks and St. Louis-cut ribs of its German-rooted barbecue, Provel-topped St. Louis-style pizza and the frozen custard concrete. Beyond those, the city is known for a deep immigrant food scene, from Bosnian to Vietnamese to Ethiopian, and a growing list of James Beard-recognized chefs.
### Q. What is the signature dish of St. Louis, Missouri?
A.  Toasted ravioli is the usual answer: breaded, deep-fried ravioli born on The Hill and served with marinara for dipping. Gooey butter cake and cracker-thin St. Louis-style pizza with Provel are close behind. Our guide to the dishes this city actually invented tells each origin story.
### Q. What are some unique and unusual foods from St. Louis?
A.  The slinger, a late-night pile of hash browns, eggs and a burger patty under chili; snoots, crisp-fried pig snouts from the city’s barbecue joints; the St. Paul sandwich, an egg foo young patty on white bread; Provel, the processed cheese blend on local pizza; and Red Hot Riplets, the spicy chips locals put on everything.
### Q. Is St. Louis known for its barbecue?
A.  Yes, for a specific style. St. Louis gave its name to the trimmed St. Louis-cut spare rib, and backyard cooks here grill and sauce pork steaks, a habit tied to the region’s German pork tradition. Smokehouses like Pappy’s in Midtown carry the rib torch. Our local’s guide to St. Louis barbecue covers the rest.
### Q. Where do locals eat in St. Louis?
A.  In the neighborhoods, where they can park once and graze. South Grand for Vietnamese, Ethiopian and Thai; Cherokee Street for Mexican; the Bevo Mill area for Bosnian; The Hill for Italian; and walkable suburbs like Maplewood for chef-driven independents. Old institutions such as Crown Candy Kitchen and Mai Lee still draw regulars who have been going for decades.
### Q. Where can I find international food in St. Louis?
A.  Several neighborhoods each tell a culinary story: South Grand for Vietnamese, Ethiopian, and Thai; The Hill for Italian; Cherokee Street for Mexican and Latino food; and the Bevo Mill area (“Little Bosnia”) for Balkan cooking. It’s genuinely possible to take a world tour of flavors without leaving the city.

## Streamline Your Life: Master St. Louis Services in One Place
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/streamline-your-life-master-st-louis-services-in-one-place
Imagine it’s a Tuesday night in Webster Groves, or Florissant, or out in O’Fallon. Somewhere on your kitchen counter there’s a sticky note that says “call gutter guy.” It has said that for three weeks now, quietly judging you. Your phone holds a screenshot of a dog groomer a friend recommended in April, a reminder to find a new dentist that you’ve snoozed eleven times, and a photo of the water heater’s serial number you took “just in case” — though you no longer remember in case of what.
None of these things are hard. That’s the maddening part. Each one is a ten-minute task. But they live in six different places — a note here, a screenshot there, a vague intention everywhere — and so the mental load of running a household ends up heavier than any single job on the list. Somebody in every house is carrying that invisible clipboard, and somehow it never quite gets any shorter.
This guide is about putting the clipboard down. Not with an app subscription or a productivity system you’ll abandon by August like the last three — just a seasonal rhythm that matches how St. Louis actually works, one page that holds your people, and one place to look when you need someone new.
### The St. Louis household service calendar
The single best trick for streamlining services is to stop treating them as surprises. Most of what a metro home needs follows the seasons here, and the seasons are predictable:
Spring: Air conditioning checkup before the first 90-degree week, when every HVAC company’s phone melts. Gutter cleaning after the maple seeds drop. A slow walk around your foundation to spot what winter’s freeze-thaw opened up — clay soil moves in this region, and small cracks are cheaper conversations than big ones, every single time. Storm season also starts: if your trees haven’t been assessed in a few years, our tree storm-proofing guide is the place to start.
Summer: Exterior work season — painting, decks, concrete, roofing. The good crews book out, so summer projects are really late-spring phone calls. It’s also peak season for discovering your AC’s limits; if it’s struggling, the AC repair guide covers repair-or-replace honestly.
Fall: Furnace checkup before the first cold snap (same phone-melting rule as spring, in reverse). Gutters again once the leaves finish. Chimney sweep if you burn wood. Fall is also the sweet spot for interior projects — painters and remodelers often have more room in the calendar before the holidays.
Winter: Planning season. Get estimates for next year’s big project while contractors have time to talk, watch for basement dampness during the January thaw (our waterproofing guide explains what’s normal and what isn’t), and keep an eye on ice dams after heavy snow.
Put those eight-or-so recurring items on your actual calendar — the one that already runs your life — and half the sticky notes never get written in the first place.
### One page that holds your people
Here’s the lowest-tech system that actually survives contact with real life: a single page — a note on your phone, a doc, a sheet of paper on the fridge, it genuinely doesn’t matter — with four columns:
Who: Your vetted pros. One plumber, one electrician, one HVAC company, one handyman, plus the household regulars — dentist, vet, groomer, hair stylist, mechanic.
When: The last time each one came, and roughly when they’re due again.
What: Model numbers and install dates for the big stuff — furnace, AC, water heater, roof. (That mystery screenshot of the water heater serial finally has a home.)
Paper: Where the warranties and receipts live — a folder, a drawer, an email label. One answer, not four.
Building the “who” column is the real work, and it’s worth doing before anything breaks. Our step-by-step guide to hiring home repair pros walks the full vetting process — insurance certificates, three estimates, red flags — and it works for every trade on your list.
### Beyond the house: the whole-life version
The same system runs the rest of your life’s services, and it’s arguably more valuable there — because nobody sends you a reminder that the dog is overdue for the groomer.
The people services: dentist, doctor, hair stylist, barber. Most run on six-month or six-week rhythms; book the next visit before you leave the current one and the slot problem disappears — it’s the single highest-leverage habit on this whole page. (Choosing well is its own skill — our personal care guide covers how to pick salons, spas, and stylists you’ll keep.)
The pet services: vet, groomer, boarding. Boarding especially rewards planning — the good kennels fill up for holidays months out, and the scramble always lands the week before Thanksgiving. A standing row on your page — vet in spring, boarding booked by September — beats the annual panic.
The machine services: your mechanic and your oil-change rhythm. A trusted mechanic found before the check-engine light is the automotive version of the vetted plumber — same logic, same one-page slot, and the same relief the first time you skip the frantic where-do-I-even-take-it search.
House rows, people rows, pet rows, car rows — it’s still just one page. That’s the point.
### Finding someone new without the twelve-tab spiral
When a slot on your page is empty — new to town, groomer retired, plumber stopped answering — the search usually turns into twelve open tabs, three conflicting phone numbers, and a review site argument from 2019. A cleaner sequence, whether you’re in Kirkwood or Granite City:
Start local and browsable. A metro directory like St Louis Near Me Directory lets you browse by category and location across Missouri and Illinois, so you’re comparing businesses that actually serve your area rather than whoever bought the most ads.
Cross-check one candidate, not ten. Pick the two or three most promising, then read their recent reviews and their own site. Depth on a shortlist beats skimming a longlist.
Call before you commit. Hours shift, service areas change, and no listing anywhere — ours included — beats a thirty-second phone call. How a business handles that first call tells you plenty about the fifth one.
### The handoff test
Here’s how you know the system works: could someone else run the house from your page? If your partner, your house-sitter, or your kid home from college can find the plumber’s number, the furnace filter size, and the location of the water shutoff without texting you — you’ve actually put the clipboard down. If every answer still lives in your head, you’ve just written the clipboard a nicer cover.
Three things to add for a passing grade: where the main water shutoff, breaker panel, and gas valve are; which pro to call for which emergency; and where the spare key and the wifi password live. It’s ten minutes of writing that turns a 2 a.m. burst-pipe panic into a checklist — for whoever happens to be home when it happens, whether that’s you, your teenager, or the neighbor watching the cat.
Wildly off-topic: St. Louis commercial cleaning crews, all on one map.
### The services people forget until they’re urgent
Every St. Louis homeowner learns a few of these the expensive way. Learn them the calendar way instead:
Dryer vent cleaning. Lint-clogged vents are a genuine fire risk and a quiet energy drain. If drying takes two cycles, that’s the symptom.
Water heater flush. Sediment shortens the tank’s life, and this region’s hard water accelerates it. A periodic flush is cheap; a Saturday-night tank failure is not.
Sump pump test. The pump that sat silent all winter meets its first real test during an April downpour. Test it before the storm does.
Sewer lateral check. In the metro’s older neighborhoods, the clay pipe between house and main is often original — and tree roots love it. If you’re buying an older home or have slow drains, a camera inspection answers the question before the backup does. Some municipalities in the area run lateral repair programs — worth a call to yours before paying out of pocket.
Chimney and fireplace inspection. If you burn wood even occasionally, an annual look is the standard safety advice — and fall booking beats December scrambling.
None of these are monthly worries. All of them fit on the seasonal calendar from the top of this page, which is exactly where they stop being emergencies.
### DIY or call someone? A thirty-second rule
Streamlining includes knowing which jobs never belong on your list at all. A simple split that serves most households well: if it’s cosmetic, ground-level, and reversible — paint, caulk, hardware, filters — it’s fair DIY game. If it involves the electrical panel, gas, anything structural, the roof, or plumbing beyond a trap — call your person. The math rarely favors heroics: a botched Saturday repair often costs more to undo than the pro would have charged to do it once, and anything permit-worthy done off the books can surface at sale time. Your one page isn’t just who to call — it’s permission to stop pretending you were ever going to fix the sub-panel yourself.
### The payoff: what “streamlined” actually feels like
It isn’t a perfectly optimized home — nobody has one. It’s smaller than that, and better: the AC gets checked in April instead of failing in July. The gutter guy is a name on your page instead of a sticky note on the counter. When the water heater finally does quit, you make one call to a plumber you already trust, with the model number already in your notes, instead of starting a research project at 9 p.m. with wet socks. That’s the whole promise of one place: fewer surprises, faster answers, and a home that runs on a rhythm instead of a series of small emergencies.
The mental load doesn’t vanish. It just gets a place to live that isn’t your head — and everyone in the house feels the difference, from Arnold to Alton, Chesterfield to Collinsville.
Ask most owners what the most common home service call is and the answer is seasonal HVAC work — the spring cooling check and the autumn furnace check. Both are predictable enough to sit on a calendar rather than a crisis list.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. How often should HVAC be serviced in St. Louis?
A.  The standard advice from most manufacturers and technicians is twice a year: cooling checked in spring, heating in fall. St. Louis summers and winters both work systems hard, and the off-season timing matters — book before the first heat wave or cold snap, when good companies still have open slots and aren’t charging peak-demand urgency.
### Q. What maintenance does a St. Louis home need that other places don’t?
A.  Three regional specials: foundation attention, because the area’s expansive clay soil swells and shrinks with the weather; masonry care, because so much local housing is century-old brick that eventually needs tuckpointing; and sewer lateral awareness in older neighborhoods, where original clay pipes meet mature tree roots. Hard water is the fourth, quieter one — it shortens the life of water heaters and fixtures.
### Q. How do I find service providers I can trust?
A.  Referrals from neighbors first, then verification: recent reviews, proof of liability insurance and workers’ compensation, and a written estimate before work starts. Browse candidates by category and location on a local directory, shortlist two or three, and let the first phone call be part of the test. The full vetting checklist is in our step-by-step hiring guide.
### Q. What is the most common home service?
A.  Seasonal HVAC work, by a wide margin — and it is predictable here, which is the useful part. Spring is the air-conditioning check, autumn the furnace. Anything you can put on a calendar is something you stop scrambling for.
### Q. What are some good apps to keep track of household items?
A.  Whatever you will actually open twice a year. A note with the trade, the company, the date and the price beats a dedicated app you abandon in March. The value is in having the last person’s number when the same thing breaks again.
### Q. How do I keep track of all my expenses?
A.  Separate recurring from one-off. Recurring home services — lawn, pest, HVAC contract — belong on a calendar with renewal dates, because those are the ones that quietly auto-renew at a higher rate. One-off repairs only need the receipt and the warranty term.
### Q. How far back can I trace my house's history?
A.  In St. Louis, often a long way — city directories, assessor records and building permits go back generations, and the Missouri Historical Society holds more. Start with the assessor’s parcel record for the build year, then work backward through permits.

## How to Check If a Contractor Is Licensed in Missouri (the Answer Surprises People)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-check-if-a-contractor-is-licensed-in-missouri
### How do you check if a contractor is licensed in Missouri?
Search that question and you will get a wall of official-looking answers, nearly all of them useless to you. We pulled the live results for this exact phrase from a Missouri location, and page one was nine different state license lookup portals — California, Washington, Florida, South Carolina, New Jersey, Tennessee, Virginia, Minnesota, North Carolina.
Missouri was not among them. Not lower down, not on page two. Missouri has no statewide licensing board for general contractors, plumbers, or HVAC contractors, so there is no state database to search. The advice everyone gives — “just check the state license board” — describes a thing that does not exist here.
That is not a loophole or an oversight anyone is hiding. Bills to create statewide contractor licensing have been introduced in Jefferson City repeatedly and have not passed. So the verification job falls to you, and it works differently than it does almost anywhere else.
### What Missouri does license, and what it doesn’t
The distinction matters, because “unlicensed” sounds alarming until you understand it is often just how the state is organized.
The state does license a long list of professions through its Division of Professional Registration — electricians in some contexts, elevator mechanics, engineers and architects, cosmetologists, and many health professions. If your project needs a licensed design professional, there is a state record to check.
The state does not license general contractors, remodelers, plumbers, HVAC contractors, roofers, painters, or handymen. There is no state exam, no state number, no state complaint history. Home inspectors are not licensed by the state either — a fact worth knowing before you rely on an inspection report.
So when a roofer tells you they are “fully licensed,” the honest follow-up is: licensed by whom? The answer should be a city. If they cannot name one, that is your first real signal.
### Where the license actually lives: your city hall
Missouri pushes this work down to local government, and in the St. Louis metro that means it is fragmented to an unusual degree.
The City of St. Louis licenses contractors directly through its License Collector, with its own application and its own requirements. If work is happening inside the city limits, that is where the record is.
St. Louis County is not one jurisdiction. It holds more than eighty separate incorporated municipalities — the published count runs 84 or 88 depending on whether villages are counted — plus unincorporated territory. Kirkwood, Clayton, Florissant, Webster Groves, Chesterfield and the rest each write their own contractor rules. Some require a bonded registration or a master’s card. Some require little.
The practical consequence: a contractor can be perfectly licensed for the job they did last week and not licensed for yours, purely because your house sits in a different municipality. This is not misconduct. It is the structure. It also means the only license that matters to you is the one valid where your address is.
### How to actually verify a contractor here
Since there is no portal, the sequence is manual. It takes about twenty minutes and it works.
1. Find out which city governs your address. Do not assume. A “St. Louis, MO” mailing address frequently sits in a county municipality with entirely separate rules. Get this right first or every other step points at the wrong office.
2. Call that city’s permit or building office and ask two questions. Does this trade require a license or registration here? And is this specific company current? Permit desks answer this routinely — it is not an unusual request, and they will tell you.
3. Ask who is pulling the permit. This is the highest-value question on this page. A licensed contractor pulls the permit in their own name. If they suggest you pull it as the homeowner, understand what that means: liability shifts to you, inspections become your responsibility, and the arrangement is frequently a sign the contractor cannot pull one. Occasionally there are legitimate reasons. Usually there are not.
4. Verify insurance directly with the insurer, not the contractor. Ask for the certificate, then call the number on it. A certificate is a PDF; anyone can edit a PDF. The insurer will confirm the policy is active in about a minute. Ask for general liability and, if they have employees, workers’ compensation — without the latter, an injury on your property can become your problem.
5. Check the paper trail that does exist. No state board does not mean no record. Look at Better Business Bureau complaint history, Missouri Attorney General consumer complaints, and county court records for judgments and mechanic’s liens. Court records are public and are far more revealing than reviews.
6. Ask for two recent local addresses. Not a reference list — specific jobs in your area within the last year. A contractor working steadily nearby can produce them without effort. One who hesitates is telling you something.
### What to weigh instead of a state license
Because the state signal is missing, other signals carry more weight here than they would in California or Florida:
Whether they pull permits as a matter of course. The single strongest indicator of a legitimate operation.
Insurance you confirmed yourself. Not a certificate you were handed.
How long they have worked in this metro. A contractor who has been doing this in the same municipalities for a decade has passed inspections there repeatedly.
Trade certifications the state doesn’t require. Manufacturer certifications, trade association membership, EPA certification for refrigerant work. Voluntary credentials mean more where mandatory ones are absent.
A written contract with a defined scope. Missouri does not hand you a licensing board to complain to, so your contract is your protection.
### The lien notice: a verification test almost nobody knows
This one is worth the whole page, and most homeowners have never heard of it.
Under Chapter 429 of the Missouri statutes, a general contractor is required to give the property owner a conspicuous written notice about mechanic’s liens — in at least 10-point type — at the front end of the project. Not at the end. Not buried in an invoice. Up front, as a matter of law.
Which hands you a clean test. A contractor who gives you that notice unprompted is running a real operation. One who has never heard of it is telling you how they work, without meaning to. You do not have to be confrontational about it — just notice whether it arrives.
And here is why it exists, which is the part that should get your attention: in Missouri, a subcontractor who does not get paid can place a lien on your house even if you already paid the general contractor in full. Your payment to the contractor only offsets the claim to the extent of what was actually paid through. If your GC pockets the money and stiffs the drywall crew, the drywall crew’s claim can land on your title. Subcontractors must give you ten days’ notice before filing, stating the amount and who owes it — so if a letter like that ever arrives, it is not junk mail.
The protection is straightforward and you should ask for it every time: lien waivers from every subcontractor and supplier, collected before you release final payment. A contractor who works this way already has a process for it. A contractor who reacts badly to the request has just answered a question you were going to have to ask eventually.
Nothing to do with permits — cross the river and eat in Collinsville.
In a state with a licensing board, some of this gets screened out before you ever meet the person. Missouri does not have that filter. Which is exactly why the paperwork habits — permits, notices, waivers — carry so much more signal here than a friendly estimate does.
### Red flags that matter more in a no-license state
Some warning signs are universal. These three are sharper here, precisely because there is no board doing any screening for you:
A large deposit up front. Materials deposits are normal. Half the job before anyone shows up is not. Without a licensing authority, there is no fast administrative remedy if the crew never returns — your recourse is civil court.
Storm-chasers after severe weather. Hail and wind events reliably bring out-of-state crews into the metro. They are often not licensed in your municipality, may not be insured locally, and are gone before problems surface. Ask where their office is and how long they have worked in your city.
Cash-only, no contract, no permit. Any one of these is a caution. All three together is not a discount — it is an operation with nothing to lose. If the work fails inspection later, or shows up as an unpermitted improvement when you sell, the cost lands on you.
### If you are the contractor reading this
The same gap cuts against you. Homeowners here have no state directory that proves you are legitimate, which means an established, insured, permit-pulling business looks identical online to someone who started last Tuesday. Nothing sorts you apart automatically.
So the sorting has to be something you do. Name the municipalities you are licensed in. Say plainly that you pull your own permits. Put your insurance status and your years in the metro where people can see them before they call. In a state with no license lookup, being easy to verify is the competitive advantage — and most of your competitors are not bothering.
Worth knowing what you owe on the paperwork side too: our guide to business licenses in St. Louis covers the city versus county split and what each actually costs.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Does Missouri require a contractor license?
A.  Not at the state level. Missouri issues no statewide license for general contractors, plumbers, or HVAC contractors, and has no state board that maintains a lookup. Licensing is handled by individual cities and counties, so requirements change from one municipality to the next — and a contractor may hold several.
### Q. How do I verify a contractor in St. Louis?
A.  Identify the municipality your address falls in, then call that city’s permit or building office and ask whether the trade requires licensing there and whether the company is current. Confirm insurance by calling the insurer directly rather than trusting the certificate. Then check BBB history, Missouri Attorney General complaints, and county court records for liens or judgments.
### Q. Is it legal to hire an unlicensed contractor in Missouri?
A.  Because there is no statewide license, “unlicensed” usually means not registered with a specific city rather than breaking state law. The real risk is practical: work that never gets permitted or inspected can fail, may surface as an unpermitted improvement when you sell, and leaves you with civil court as your only recourse.
### Q. Should I pull the permit myself as the homeowner?
A.  Generally no. Homeowner-pulled permits shift responsibility for inspections and code compliance to you, and a contractor who asks for this is often unable to pull one themselves. There are occasional legitimate reasons, but treat the request as a question to be answered rather than a convenience.
### Q. What should I check if there is no state license to look up?
A.  Weight shifts to what you can verify yourself: whether they pull permits in their own name, insurance you confirmed with the insurer, how long they have worked in your specific municipalities, voluntary trade certifications, and a written contract with a defined scope. Court records and complaint history fill in the rest.
### Q. Can a subcontractor put a lien on my house if I already paid the contractor?
A.  Yes. Under Missouri's Chapter 429, payment to the general contractor only offsets a claim to the extent it was actually paid through. If your contractor doesn't pay a subcontractor or supplier, that party can pursue a lien against your property. Subcontractors must give you ten days' notice before filing. Collect signed lien waivers from every sub and supplier before releasing final payment.
### Q. Does Missouri license home inspectors?
A.  No. Home inspector does not appear among the state’s licensed professions, and bills to create licensing have not passed. Look for ASHI or InterNACHI certification instead, since those impose exams and continuing education that state law does not require.
