## Master Home Repair in St. Louis: A Step-by-Step Guide to Hiring the Right Pro
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/master-home-repair-your-step-by-step-guide-to-top-services
Updated June 21, 2026.
The water heater quits on a Sunday. Or a storm drops a branch through the gutter, or that “I’ll get to it” repair finally can’t wait another week. However it starts, you end up staring at your phone, about to hand a stranger your house, your money, and your trust, and hoping you pick a good one.
The steps below find you a home repair pro in St. Louis you can actually count on, and help you spot the ones you can’t. They work the same for a century-old brick two-family in the city and a newer build out in the county.
### 1. Get clear on what you need
Before you call anyone, name the job: plumbing, electrical, roofing, HVAC, drywall, general handyman work — and be honest about which of those needs a licensed pro and which you could handle yourself with a basic St. Louis homeowner toolkit. The clearer you are, the easier it is to find a specialist instead of a jack-of-all-trades who dabbles — and the more accurate your quotes will be.
### 2. Ask the people you trust
A neighbor who just had the same work done is worth more than any ad — they’ve seen the crew’s punctuality, the cleanup, and the final invoice. Ask friends, family, and your neighborhood Facebook group who they’d use again — and, just as useful, who they’d warn you away from.
### 3. Do a little homework online
Look the company up: their website, recent reviews across Google and other sites, and a local directory listing. You’re looking for a real, consistent track record — and recent reviews, since a company can change a lot in a year.
### 4. Check the credentials that protect you
This is the step that saves people thousands. Confirm the company is licensed for the work (and that any required St. Louis city or county permits will be pulled), and — this is the big one — that they carry liability insurance and workers’ compensation. Ask for a certificate of insurance. If an uninsured worker is hurt on your property, you don’t want to be the one holding that bill.
### 5. Get at least three written estimates
Don’t take the first number. Get three, in writing, and read them closely — the cheapest bid often leaves something out, while a higher one may include better materials or a step the others skipped. Price is one factor; understanding exactly what each includes is the real goal. Be especially wary of a quote that’s dramatically lower than the rest.
### 6. Test how they communicate
Call the office. Does a real person answer, or does it ring out? How quickly do they call back? The way a company communicates before they have your money is a pretty good preview of how they’ll treat you after. Prompt, clear, patient communication is a green flag.
### 7. Ask about warranties — and get it in writing
A confident pro stands behind their work with a warranty on parts and labor. Ask what’s covered and for how long, and make sure the scope, price, timeline, and warranty all land in a signed written agreement before work starts.
### 8. Trust your gut
You’ll know. The right pro listens, answers your questions in plain English without hiding behind jargon, doesn’t pressure you, and makes you feel like a customer rather than a transaction. If something feels off, keep looking — there are plenty of good ones in this town.
One quiet tell: look at how a company keeps its online presence and directory profile. A business that takes the time to maintain a complete, professional profile tends to bring that same care to the work itself.
### Reading three estimates side by side
Once the three written quotes are in hand, don’t just compare the bottom lines — compare what each one actually commits to:
Scope: Does each bid describe the same job? A cheaper bid that quietly omits haul-away, patching, or a code-required upgrade only looks cheaper. You pay the difference later.
Materials: Brand and grade matter. “Water heater” tells you nothing; a specific model with a specific warranty tells you plenty.
Allowances and exclusions: The fine print where surprises live. What happens if they open the wall and find rot, old wiring, or a surprise from a previous owner’s handiwork? A good estimate says how change orders get priced and approved.
Timeline and payment schedule: Start date, duration, and payments tied to completed milestones — not the calendar.
If a bid is dramatically lower than the other two, ask the contractor to walk you through it line by line. Sometimes there’s an honest reason — lighter overhead, a slower season, a simpler approach. Often, though, the walkthrough answers the question for you: something was missing, and you’d have paid for it later as a change order.
### The St. Louis homework: what makes repairs here different
Generic hiring advice misses the things this metro’s housing actually throws at you. A few local realities worth knowing before you talk to anyone:
Clay soil moves. The region’s expansive clay swells when wet and shrinks in drought, which is why foundation cracks, sticking doors, and bowing basement walls are such common calls here. For anything structural, you want a contractor who works with St. Louis soil for a living — and for water in the basement, start with our basement waterproofing guide.
This is a brick town. Much of the city’s housing stock is century-old brick, and old mortar joints eventually need tuckpointing. It’s a specialty trade — done badly, it’s ugly and traps moisture; done well, it buys your walls decades.
Old houses carry old systems. Knob-and-tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, and undersized panels still hide in older homes across the city and inner suburbs. If your house predates the 1950s, budget for surprises behind the walls — and hire accordingly (our electrician guide covers what to ask).
Storm season brings storm chasers. After every big hail or wind event, out-of-town crews sweep neighborhoods knocking on doors. Some are legitimate; plenty are not. The safest rule: never sign anything on your doorstep the day of the knock, and run any roofer through the checks above first — our roofing contractor guide goes deeper.
### Build your bench before you need it
The single best home-repair habit costs nothing: assemble your shortlist while nothing is broken. One plumber, one electrician, one HVAC company, one handyman pulled from the St. Louis handyman services map — each vetted with the steps above, on a calm afternoon, with time to check reviews and make an unhurried call. Save the numbers in your phone, and note who answered fast and who explained things clearly — that’s your tiebreaker later.
Then, when the sump pump quits during an April downpour or the furnace gives up on the coldest night of January, you’re not vetting strangers under pressure — you’re calling someone you already chose. Every step in this guide works twice as well when you run it before the emergency instead of during one — calm decisions are cheaper than panicked ones, in this trade more than most. (For the household-wide version of that habit — a seasonal calendar and one page for every service you use — see our streamline-your-services guide.)
### Emergency or can-it-wait? A quick triage
Half of hiring well is knowing how much time you actually have. A rough triage:
Call now, tonight if needed: active water leaks you can’t shut off, no heat in winter or no AC in a St. Louis heat wave, sparking outlets or burning smells, sewage backup. Pay the emergency rate — it’s cheaper than the damage. (Guides: plumbers, AC repair.)
This week: a roof leak you’ve bucketed, a water heater limping along, a tree limb resting where it shouldn’t. Urgent, but you still have time to get two or three quotes — use it.
This season: peeling paint, drafty windows, that gutter run that overflows. These reward patience: off-season scheduling often gets you better attention and sometimes better pricing. (Guides: interior painters, window companies, handymen.)
The emergencies are where bad decisions happen — which is exactly why it pays to keep a short list of vetted pros before the water heater dies on a Sunday.
Nothing to do with contractors — but Brighton’s dinner lineup is right here.
### Storm damage and insurance: a St. Louis rite of passage
Sooner or later, hail or straight-line winds will find your roof — it’s practically a metro tradition, from Arnold to Alton and every zip code in between. When it happens, the order of operations matters: document the damage with photos before anything is touched, call your insurance company before signing with any contractor, and be careful with paperwork that assigns your insurance benefits to the contractor — read anything called an “assignment of benefits” closely, and ask your insurer about it before signing.
Legitimate local roofers work with insurance claims every week and will walk the adjuster’s report with you. The crews that pressure you to sign on the doorstep “so we can get you on the schedule” are the ones this guide exists to help you avoid. Slow down by one day; a real company will still be there tomorrow — and the good ones will respect you more for checking.
### Red flags that end the conversation
Any one of these is reason enough to keep looking:
Cash only, no paperwork. No written estimate, no contract, no receipt — no job.
A huge deposit up front. Materials deposits are normal; demanding most of the money before work starts is not. Be wary of anyone who needs the bulk of payment to begin.
Pressure to sign today. “This price is only good right now” is a sales tactic, not a deadline. Good contractors are busy, not desperate.
No local footprint. No verifiable local address, no local reviews, a magnetic sign on the truck door — especially after a storm, that pattern deserves extra scrutiny.
Vague about permits. “We don’t really need one” for electrical, plumbing, or structural work is a red flag; the permit protects you. Requirements vary by municipality, so a quick call to your city or county building department settles it.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Do contractors need a license in Missouri?
A.  Missouri has no statewide general-contractor license — licensing happens at the city and county level, and requirements differ between St. Louis city, St. Louis County, and each municipality. Electricians, plumbers, and mechanical contractors are typically licensed locally. The practical move: ask which license the work requires in your municipality and verify it with your local building department.
### Q. When does a home repair need a permit in St. Louis?
A.  Rules vary by municipality, but electrical, plumbing, structural, and most roofing or HVAC replacement work commonly require permits in both the city and county, while cosmetic work like painting generally doesn’t. A reputable contractor pulls the permit themselves and builds it into the quote — a contractor who asks you to pull the permit is shifting liability onto you, and that’s worth questioning.
### Q. How do I find a trustworthy contractor in St. Louis?
A.  Start with referrals, check recent online reviews, confirm the company is licensed and carries liability insurance and workers’ compensation, get at least three written estimates, and make sure everything — scope, price, timeline, and warranty — is in a signed agreement.
### Q. Why does insurance matter when hiring a home repair company?
A.  If a worker is injured on your property or your home is damaged and the company isn’t properly insured, you could be left responsible. Always ask for a certificate of liability insurance and workers’ compensation before work begins.
### Q. Should I always choose the lowest bid?
A.  No. Get three written estimates and compare what each actually includes. A very low bid may use lower-grade materials or skip a needed step, so weigh value and what’s covered, not just the price.

## Home Inspections in St. Louis: What They Miss, and Why It Matters Here
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/home-inspections-in-st-louis
Missouri does not license home inspectors.
No exam, no state registration, no required insurance, no board to complain to. The legislature has been asked to change this at least three times and has declined every time. Anyone in this state can print a business card tomorrow and inspect the largest purchase of your life.
Then there’s the second half, which is worse: the inspection you do get is contractually excused from looking at almost everything that’s actually wrong with old St. Louis houses.
### What does a home inspection cover in St. Louis?
A standard inspection is a visual, non-invasive examination of accessible areas — roof, foundation, structure, plumbing, electrical, heating and cooling, and visible components on the day of the inspection. Under both major national standards, it explicitly does not include radon, lead paint, asbestos, mold, termites, anything underground, remaining life expectancy of any system, repair costs, or code compliance. In a metro where the median city home was built in 1938, those exclusions cover most of what you actually need to know — which means the specialty tests have to be ordered separately.
### Nobody licensed the person inspecting your house
This surprises almost everyone, so here is how it checks out. “Home inspector” does not appear anywhere on the Missouri Division of Professional Registration’s list of licensed professions — a list that runs to 57 occupations and includes barbers, cosmetologists, tattoo artists, private investigators and real estate appraisers. And Chapter 339 of the Missouri statutes, which licenses real estate professionals, contains no home inspector provisions at all.
Sit with the comparison for a second. The person selling you the house is licensed and can be disciplined by a state commission. The person inspecting it is not regulated at all.
One caution while we’re here, because we nearly got this wrong ourselves: you may find claims online that Missouri created a home inspector registration board. Those cite statute numbers that come from a bill introduced in 2019 that never passed. It isn’t law. Similar bills failed in 2011 and 2013.
### What to check instead of a license
Since the state isn’t vetting anyone, the private certifications carry the weight. Two matter, and they are not equivalent.
ASHI Certified Inspector (ACI) is the higher experience bar. It requires passing the National Home Inspector Examination and completing a minimum of 250 fee-paid inspections, with a sample of reports reviewed and verified by ASHI, plus 20 hours of continuing education a year.
InterNACHI Certified Professional Inspector (CPI) requires passing an exam, completing ethics and standards courses, and submitting four mock inspection reports — then 24 hours of continuing education annually and re-passing the exam every three years at 80% or better.
Both impose a code of ethics and continuing education that Missouri law does not. Neither, as far as we could verify, requires errors and omissions insurance — so ask whether they carry it and ask to see the certificate. Ask for a sample report too. A good one runs to dozens of photographed pages; a bad one is a checklist.
### The exclusion list is the whole story
Here is where this gets specific to St. Louis, and where most buyers get hurt.
Both national standards of practice state plainly that an inspection is not technically exhaustive and will not identify concealed or latent defects. Then they list what the inspector is not required to determine. Among the items on those lists: the presence of pests, mold or fungus; airborne hazards including radon; environmental hazards including lead paint and asbestos; the remaining life expectancy of anything; the cause of any condition; the cost of any correction; compliance with codes; and anything underground.
Now line that up against what defines housing here. Radon. Lead paint in a city where most homes predate 1978 by forty years. Asbestos. Termites. The sewer lateral and the water service line, both underground.
Every hazard St. Louis is known for is on the excluded list. That isn’t a criticism of inspectors — it’s their published rulebook, and a general inspection was never meant to do those jobs. But a buyer who orders “a home inspection” and assumes it covered them is wrong, and will find out later.
### Radon: everyone gets the zone wrong
You will read locally that St. Louis sits in EPA Radon Zone 1, the highest-risk category. We checked EPA’s own map of Missouri. St. Louis City and St. Louis County are both Zone 2 — moderate potential, a predicted average indoor screening level between 2 and 4 picocuries per liter. Missouri’s Zone 1 counties are mostly clustered in the northwest corner of the state.
That is not a reason to skip testing, for three reasons. EPA says on the map itself that it should not be used to decide whether an individual home needs testing, and that all homes should be tested regardless of zone. The zones are county averages, and radon varies enormously house to house. And Missouri’s Department of Health reports that one in three Missouri homes tested came back above the 4.0 action level.
Here’s the useful part: Missouri DHSS gives away free radon test kits. Request one through the state health department’s radon page using the coupon code MO TESTING — one per household while supplies last. A radon test as an inspection add-on typically runs a hundred dollars or more. This one is free.
### The two things underground that nobody inspects
Remember that both standards exclude anything underground. In St. Louis that exclusion covers two expensive problems.
The sewer lateral. Order a separate sewer scope — a camera run down the line. It is the single add-on most worth buying on an older house here, because a collapsed lateral is a five-figure problem that a visual inspection cannot see.
Both the City and the County run lateral repair programs funded by a $28 annual fee on the property tax bill, and they are separate programs with different rules. The City’s covers repairs under the public right of way only — not breaks under your yard, and not clogs or tree roots — and requires a licensed plumber’s written statement and video documenting the break. Eligibility also requires that the property taxes be fully paid. Many individual municipalities — Maplewood, Clayton, Creve Coeur, Chesterfield, Florissant, Bridgeton and others — run their own versions with different terms. Which program covers you depends on which municipality you’re buying in, so check before you assume you’re covered.
The water service line. The City states plainly that service lines are entirely owned by the property owner, and that owners are currently responsible for replacing them. The City is working through a federally required inventory of which lines contain lead — and a large share of the system is still classified as unknown. A standard inspection does not test your water and does not excavate the line. If you’re buying a pre-war house, ask the water division what your address’s service line status is.
Unrelated, and we know it — here’s dinner in Cedar Hill.
### Lead paint, and the ten days you can waive
Federal law requires the seller of any pre-1978 home to give you the “Protect Your Family from Lead in Your Home” pamphlet, disclose any known lead-based paint and hazards, hand over any records and reports they have, include a lead warning statement in the contract, and give you ten days to conduct a lead inspection or risk assessment. A seller or agent who fails to disclose can be sued for triple damages.
Two things about that rule matter enormously in this market. First, it requires disclosure of what the seller already knows — it does not require anyone to test for lead or remove it. Second, that ten-day window is your actual protection, and it is routinely waived in the rush of a contract.
In a city where the median home dates to 1938, nearly the entire housing stock falls under this rule.
### The permit that isn’t an inspection
This one confuses people constantly, and the confusion is expensive.
Many St. Louis-area municipalities require an occupancy inspection before a home can be sold or occupied. In the City of St. Louis, every property sits in a Housing Conservation District, and a Certificate of Inspection must be obtained before occupancy is permitted on a residential sale. It costs $120, is valid twelve months, and if it comes back with violations you generally get 30 days to fix them. Webster Groves charges $75 for the inspection plus a $30 permit. Kirkwood ties the occupancy permit to your utility transfer, which means you cannot quietly skip it.
Here is the trap. That municipal inspection is a minimum property-maintenance code check, conducted by a city inspector, that also sets an occupancy load limit. It is not an assessment of whether your furnace has five years left in it.
So when someone says “the house passed inspection,” find out which inspection they mean. One is a city code baseline that protects the city’s housing stock. The other is a private, unregulated, voluntary examination that protects you. Passing the first says almost nothing about the second.
### Nobody is required to find problems for you
Worth understanding before you rely on anyone else’s diligence.
Missouri law puts a disclosure duty on the real estate licensee: they must disclose adverse material facts actually known, or that should have been known. But the same statute says the agent owes no duty to conduct an independent inspection or discover any adverse material facts for a customer’s benefit.
So it is a duty not to conceal. It is not a duty to investigate. Combine that with an unregulated inspection profession and a standards document that excludes the six things most likely to be wrong, and the conclusion is uncomfortable but clear: the only person in this transaction whose job is to find out what’s wrong with the house is you.
One more distinction, straight from HUD’s own buyer notice: “The appraisal is not a home inspection.” An appraisal tells your lender the house is worth what they’re lending. It is not a condition assessment and it is not for you.
### What it costs, and what to actually order
There is no official or government source for inspection pricing in Missouri — unsurprisingly, since the state doesn’t regulate the trade. Inspectors in this metro commonly advertise somewhere around $300 to $500 for a standard single-family inspection, with add-ons priced separately. Treat that as market-advertised, not as a regulated rate, and call three.
For an older St. Louis house, the general inspection is the starting point, not the whole job. Add the sewer scope — the highest-value add-on here by a distance. Add a termite or wood-destroying organism inspection, since pests are excluded from the standard. Get the free state radon kit rather than paying for the add-on, if timing allows. Ask about the water service line status. And if the house predates 1978, decide deliberately whether you’re using your ten-day lead window or waiving it.
Then get contractor quotes for anything flagged, because your inspector is explicitly not required to tell you what a repair costs — and in a house built in 1938, that number is the one that decides whether you should buy it.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What's not included in a home inspection?
A.  Both national standards of practice explicitly exclude radon, lead paint, asbestos, mold and fungus, pests, anything underground, remaining life expectancy of systems, the cost of repairs, and code compliance. In St. Louis that covers nearly every hazard the housing stock is known for, so those tests must be ordered separately.
### Q. What is the biggest red flag in a home inspection?
A.  In older St. Louis homes, findings around structural movement, active water intrusion, and the electrical system tend to carry the largest costs. But the biggest red flag is often what isn’t in the report — a thin, photo-free checklist, or an inspector who won’t provide a sample report or proof of errors-and-omissions insurance. Missouri does not license inspectors, so that vetting is yours.
### Q. What are the most common things found on a home inspection?
A.  Roof wear, grading and drainage problems, aging HVAC equipment, plumbing leaks, and electrical issues are the usual categories. In St. Louis, add settling and foundation movement in older homes, plus wiring findings tied to the era — the median city home was built in 1938 and most of the county’s stock dates to the aluminum-wiring years.
### Q. Do sellers usually fix everything on home inspections?
A.  No. Missouri sellers generally have no obligation to repair inspection findings, and the report itself carries no enforcement. Findings become negotiation — repairs, a credit, a price reduction, or nothing. Note this differs from a municipal occupancy inspection, where code violations typically must be cured within 30 days.
### Q. What is a deal breaker in a home inspection?
A.  That depends on your budget, not on a standard list. The findings that most often end St. Louis deals are ones a general inspection doesn’t even cover — a collapsed sewer lateral found on a separate scope, or a lead water service line the owner is responsible for replacing. Get repair quotes before deciding; your inspector is not required to estimate costs.
### Q. What am I supposed to do during a home inspection?
A.  Ask when you book whether you can attend and what the inspector prefers — policies vary and no rule guarantees attendance. If you do attend, follow along, ask what a finding means in practice, and note what the inspector says is outside their scope. Those out-of-scope items are your list of specialty tests to order.
### Q. Does Missouri license home inspectors?
A.  No. Home inspector does not appear on the Missouri Division of Professional Registration’s list of licensed professions, and the state’s real estate statutes contain no inspector provisions. Bills to create licensing have been introduced and have not passed. Look for ASHI or InterNACHI certification instead, since those impose exams, experience and continuing education that state law does not.
### Q. Is St. Louis a high radon area?
A.  The city runs its own inspection too, and it is not the one you are paying for — here is how St. Louis occupancy and code inspections actually work.
St. Louis City and County are EPA Radon Zone 2 — moderate potential, not the highest category, despite claims otherwise in some local content. Test regardless: EPA says the zone map should not be used to decide whether an individual home needs testing, and Missouri reports one in three homes tested exceeded the action level. The state offers free test kits.

## How to Choose a Home Repair Company in St. Louis (Without Getting Burned)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/10-must-know-tips-for-finding-top-home-repair-services
Picture a Saturday morning gone wrong: a ceiling stain spreading in Webster Groves, a furnace that won’t light in Florissant, a deck board that finally gave way in St. Charles. You need someone good, you need them soon, and the internet coughs up fifty names with no obvious way to tell the pros from the problems. Hiring the wrong contractor can cost you far more than the repair itself — in money, in do-overs, and in stress.
This is an honest, St. Louis-specific guide to choosing a home-repair company you can actually trust: what to check, which credentials matter here in Missouri (and across the river in Illinois), the red flags that should end a conversation, and the questions that separate a real pro from a smooth talker. The good news is that vetting a contractor isn’t complicated — it’s a short, repeatable set of checks, and the small amount of time it takes is the cheapest insurance you’ll ever buy on a home project.
It matters more here than a lot of homeowners realize. The St. Louis metro’s housing skews older — century-old brick in the city, mid-century ranches across the county — and older homes hide more surprises, which means the gap between a careful pro and a careless one shows up fast. Add our clay soil, hard water, and freeze-thaw winters, and the quality of the work you hire genuinely determines whether a repair holds for a decade or fails by next season.
### Start by knowing exactly what you need
Before you call anyone, get clear on the job. Is it plumbing, electrical, roofing, HVAC, or general handyman work? The clearer you are, the better your quotes will be and the harder it is for anyone to pad the scope. A specialist in the exact problem — a roofer for a roof, not a general contractor who “does roofs too” — usually does better work at a fairer price, and can spot the underlying cause a generalist might miss. Write down what you’re seeing (the symptom, when it started, any photos) so you can describe it consistently to everyone you call and get comparable quotes back. If you’re not sure whether a job needs a licensed trade or a handyman, our home-services hiring guide breaks the trades down.
### The credential check — and how licensing actually works here
This is where St. Louis homeowners get tripped up, because Missouri’s licensing is local, not statewide. A few honest facts to arm you:
Missouri has no statewide general contractor license, and plumbers and general contractors are licensed at the city or county level. Most electricians are too (there’s an optional statewide electrical contractor license). So “licensed” means licensed where your job is — ask which municipality issued the license and confirm it with that city or county building department.
Illinois (the Metro East) is stricter on paper. Under the Illinois Home Repair and Remodeling Act, contractors must carry public liability and property-damage insurance, and jobs over a set dollar amount require a written contract. If you’re in Belleville, Edwardsville, or O’Fallon IL, hold them to it.
Insurance is non-negotiable everywhere. Ask for a current certificate of liability insurance, and workers’ comp if they bring a crew. If a worker is hurt on your property or your home is damaged and there’s no coverage, the exposure can land on you.
A legitimate contractor hands over license and insurance details without flinching. Hesitation, excuses, or “I’ll get that to you later” when you ask for basic license and insurance proof is your first real red flag, and one worth taking seriously no matter how good the rest of the pitch sounds.
Ready to find someone? Browse vetted home-repair and trade pros across the metro in the St Louis Near Me Directory - start with our step-by-step guide to hiring home services, which links out to plumbers, roofers, HVAC, and more by trade.
If you run a business in this line of work, list your business. Run a home-repair business? A complete, well-maintained directory profile is how careful homeowners find you - and the same attention to detail that fills out a good profile is what signals you’ll bring that care to their home.
### Do your homework: reviews, references, and real work
Reputation is the best predictor you have. Work three angles:
Read reviews across platforms, not just the star average. Look at how the company responds to criticism — a gracious, specific reply to a bad review tells you more than a wall of five stars. Check Google, and directories that show real local businesses.
Ask for local references and call them. A reputable pro will gladly share recent nearby clients. Ask those homeowners the real questions: did the work hold up, did they stick to the quote, would you hire them again?
See comparable work. Photos are fine; a similar job you can actually look at is better. Recent, local, visitable work beats any brochure.
Check how long they’ve been around. Longevity in the same metro isn’t everything, but a company with years of local history and a real address is easier to hold accountable than a name that appeared last month.
### Get multiple written estimates — and read them closely
Never hire off a single quote. Get at least two or three, in writing and itemized, so you can compare apples to apples. When you read them:
Be wary of the lowball. An unusually cheap bid often means cut corners, unlicensed labor, or a scope that’s missing steps you’ll pay for later. The lowest number rarely wins in the end.
Be wary of the highball, too. The most expensive bid isn’t automatically the best — make them justify the difference.
Look for what’s missing. Does the quote include materials, cleanup, permits, and disposal? Vague quotes hide surprises.
### Red flags that should end the conversation
Some warning signs are worth walking away over, no matter how charming the pitch:
Demanding a large payment up front. A modest deposit is normal; being asked for half or more before work begins — especially in cash — is a classic warning sign that a contractor may be underfunded. Tie payments to progress milestones instead, so the money follows the finished work.
Door-to-door pressure and “today only” deals. Storm-chasers and high-pressure closers who need an answer right now are protecting themselves, not you.
No written contract, or a vague one. Get scope, price, timeline, payment schedule, and warranty in writing before anyone starts. If they resist paper, resist them.
No physical address or a brand-new, review-less presence. Everyone starts somewhere, but be extra careful and verify hard.
Cash-only, no receipts. That’s a setup for zero recourse if the job goes sideways.
### Questions that reveal a real pro
The estimate visit is your interview. A few questions cut through the polish fast:
“Are you licensed for this work, and which city or county issued it?” Then verify it. A real pro knows exactly where they’re licensed.
“Can I see a current insurance certificate?” Not a promise — the document.
“Who actually does the work — your crew or subcontractors?” If they sub it out, you want the subs vetted and insured too.
“Will you pull the permit?” For work that needs one, a reputable contractor pulls it in their name and says so. Being asked to pull your own permit for a pro’s work is a warning sign.
“What does the warranty cover, and for how long?” In writing, on both labor and materials.
“What’s the payment schedule?” You want milestones tied to progress, not a big lump sum up front.
One quiet tip on the other side of the table: don’t hand a contractor your absolute maximum budget on the first call. Describe the job and let them price it; leading with your ceiling only invites a quote that rises to meet it. Get the scope and the number first, then talk money.
Completely different errand — dinner, dry cleaning, all of Creve Coeur.
### The conversation: communication is a preview
How a contractor communicates before you’ve paid a dime is the best preview of the whole job. Do they call back promptly, answer questions plainly, and show up when they said they would for the estimate? A pro who’s scattered and hard to reach while they’re trying to win your business will not magically get better once they have your deposit. Trust that signal.
Finally, get everything in a signed contract, keep a folder of every document and receipt, and don’t make the final payment until the work is genuinely complete and, where required, has passed inspection. Careful up front, calm at the end.
### Protecting yourself once the work begins
Vetting doesn’t stop when you sign. A few habits keep a good hire from turning into a bad experience:
Pay by traceable method. Check or card leaves a record; large cash payments don’t. Keep receipts for every payment and tie them to the milestones in your contract.
Document the work. Snap photos before, during, and after. If a dispute ever arises, a clear visual record is worth more than anyone’s memory.
Don’t pay for the whole job before it’s done. Hold a meaningful final payment until you’ve inspected the finished work in daylight and confirmed any required inspection passed. That last payment is your leverage to get punch-list items fixed.
Get lien waivers on bigger jobs. On larger projects where subcontractors or suppliers are involved, a lien waiver confirms they’ve been paid, so you can’t be surprised by a claim against your home later.
None of this signals distrust — good contractors expect and respect a homeowner who keeps clean records. The ones who bristle at reasonable documentation are telling you something.
### Where St. Louis homeowners should look
Between a strong referral, honest online reviews, and a directory map of St. Louis handyman and home-repair pros that shows real local businesses with their details and service areas in one place, you can build a shortlist quickly — then run the checks above on your top two or three. The goal isn’t to find a contractor; it’s to find the right one, and a little diligence at the start is what turns a stressful repair into a job you barely have to think about. Whether the fix is in the city, out in St. Charles County, or across the river in the Metro East, the same fundamentals apply: verify, compare, get it in writing, and trust the pro who makes all three easy rather than the one who rushes you past them.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What are red flags when hiring a contractor?
A.  Big warning signs: demanding a large cash payment up front, high-pressure “today only” sales tactics, no written contract or a vague one, no proof of license or insurance, no verifiable address or reviews, and cash-only with no receipts. Any one of these is reason to slow down; several together is reason to walk away and find someone else.
### Q. Should I pay a contractor 50% upfront?
A.  Generally no. A reasonable deposit — often a smaller percentage to cover initial materials — is normal, but being asked for half or more before work begins, especially in cash, is a red flag. Tie payments to completed milestones and hold the final payment until the job is finished and, where required, inspected. That structure protects you and is standard with reputable pros.
### Q. How do I check if a contractor is licensed in St. Louis?
A.  Ask which city or county issued their license, then confirm it directly with that local building or licensing department — Missouri licenses plumbers, general contractors, and most electricians locally, not statewide. In the Illinois Metro East, contractors must carry liability insurance under the Home Repair and Remodeling Act. Always ask for a current insurance certificate too, regardless of the trade.
### Q. How many estimates should I get for home repairs?
A.  Get at least two or three written, itemized estimates so you can compare scope and price fairly. Be cautious of both the unusually low bid (which may signal cut corners or hidden costs) and the highest one (make them justify it). The goal isn’t just the cheapest number — it’s the clearest scope from the most trustworthy pro.

### The student scheduling playbook
The difference between a job that supports your degree and one that eats it is usually scheduling strategy, not the job itself:
Ride the semester rhythm. Load up hours over winter and summer breaks — warehouse and delivery work pay best exactly then — and throttle back to a sustainable base during the term.
Protect finals in writing. Tell your manager your exam weeks at the start of the semester, not the week before. Employers near campuses expect this; the ones who won’t accommodate it are telling you to keep looking.
Guard a realistic ceiling. Academic advisors commonly suggest keeping term-time work in the range of 10–20 hours a week — beyond that, grades tend to pay the overtime. The whole point of working through school is finishing it.
Stack complementary gigs, not competing ones. Tutoring afternoons plus event-staff weekends beats two jobs fighting over the same evenings.

SLU, WashU, UMSL, SIUE, and the STLCC campuses all run active career offices; they are the single most under-used free resource in the entire student job hunt.

### Q. What jobs fit best around a class schedule?

### Q. How much can a student realistically earn part-time in St. Louis?
A.  Based on the ranges local employers post: roughly 4–7 an hour in retail, 7–0 in warehouses, and 5–5 in delivery depending on tips and timing — so 15 steady hours a week lands most students in the several-hundred-dollars-a-month range, with break-time sprints earning meaningfully more. Treat these as ballparks; actual offers vary by employer and shift.
### Q. Should I use my campus career center?
A.  Yes — first, before anything else. ### Q. What is the $1000 a month rule for retirees?
A.  It’s a rough retirement-savings guideline: for every $1,000 a month of income you want, you need roughly $240,000 saved (assuming about a 5% withdrawal rate). Part-time work can bridge the gap — even $500–$1,000 a month of earned income eases the pressure on your savings.

## Top 10 Companies in St. Louis: The Giants That Call the Metro Home
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/top-10-company-st-louis-picks-for-2025
Refreshed September 2026
Here’s a bar-trivia question that stumps people who’ve lived here their whole lives: how many Fortune 1000 companies are headquartered in greater St. Louis? Most folks guess four or five — the beer, the brokerage, maybe the pet food. The actual answer, last time the count was published by Greater St. Louis, Inc., is seventeen and growing — and that count doesn’t even include the privately held giants that never appear on Fortune’s revenue-ranked lists at all.
Whether you’re a job seeker sizing up the market, a business owner wondering who anchors the local economy, or just someone who likes knowing what’s behind the logos on the highway, this is the honest tour: the ten biggest corporate names that call the metro home, what each actually does, and why they matter to the rest of us. Every fact here traces to the companies themselves or to Greater St. Louis, Inc.’s headquarters data — no padding, no guesswork, and no ranking anyone paid for.
### 1. Centene
The biggest company most St. Louisans have never bought anything from. Centene is a healthcare insurance giant — managed care, government health programs — and at #23 on the Fortune 500, it’s the highest-ranked company headquartered in the metro. Its Clayton campus reshaped that suburb’s skyline, and its scale makes it one of the region’s most consequential employers for healthcare, technology, and corporate roles alike — when Centene sneezes, Clayton commercial real estate catches a cold.
### 2. Enterprise Mobility
You know it as the rental counter, but Enterprise is quietly one of the largest privately held companies in America — which is why it never shows up on the Fortune 500 despite belonging in any conversation about it. Founded here and still family-owned and headquartered in the metro, Enterprise runs a global mobility business from St. Louis, and its name is on the Blues’ arena downtown.
### 3. Edward Jones
The investment firm built on the one-broker-office model — there’s probably a branch in a strip mall near you, and that’s the point. A Fortune 500 firm headquartered in the metro, Edward Jones runs one of the region’s largest corporate campuses and hires steadily across finance, technology, and operations. For St. Louis job seekers in financial services, it’s the anchor tenant of the whole local industry — and its steady hiring across technology and operations surprises people who only picture brokers.
### 4. World Wide Technology
The metro’s great under-the-radar success story. WWT is a technology solutions company — enterprise IT, cloud, AI infrastructure — with roughly $20 billion in revenue and a global headquarters at Westport Plaza in Maryland Heights (WWT). Privately held, founded here, and one of the largest Black-founded companies in the country, WWT is the biggest reason “St. Louis tech” is a serious phrase rather than a hopeful one.
### 5. Anheuser-Busch
The one everybody knows. The historic Soulard brewery complex has anchored the city since the 1850s, and it remains the U.S. brewing headquarters — One Busch Place, where the Budweiser Clydesdales still live part of the year and the brewery lights still draw crowds every December. Whatever has changed about global ownership, the brewing, the jobs, and the civic identity are still very much here — ask anyone who’s taken the brewery tour, or anyone whose grandfather worked the bottling line.
### 6. BJC Health System
Not a household “brand” so much as the place half the metro was born, treated, or employed. BJC — anchored by Barnes-Jewish Hospital and its Washington University medical partnership — is the largest private employer in Missouri, with a workforce around 47,000 after its merger with Kansas City’s Saint Luke’s (BJC). If employment is the measure, this is the biggest name on the list — and its hiring reach runs from surgeons to schedulers to software teams.
### 7. Emerson
A St. Louis industrial institution since 1890. Emerson builds automation technology and software for industries worldwide, sits at #238 on the Fortune 500, and runs its global operations from its longtime campus in the metro. It’s the classic quiet giant: little consumer visibility, enormous engineering payroll — and a name on more automation systems worldwide than most people will ever notice.
### 8. Nestlé Purina PetCare
If you have a dog or cat, Purina is probably in your pantry right now. The pet care giant’s North American headquarters sits at 800 Chouteau Avenue downtown — Purina has been a St. Louis company since its Ralston Purina days more than a century ago, and its checkerboard logo is as local as the Arch. It remains one of downtown’s largest corporate anchors and a major employer in marketing, R&D, and operations.
### 9. Reinsurance Group of America (RGA)
The metro’s most invisible giant: RGA sells reinsurance — insurance for insurance companies — from its Chesterfield headquarters, and at #196 on the Fortune 500 it outranks almost everything on this list in revenue while remaining unknown at most dinner tables — the corporate equivalent of the bassist who’s secretly the best musician in the band. For actuarial, finance, and data careers in St. Louis, it’s a destination employer.
### 10. Bunge
The newest heavyweight. The global agribusiness and food company — roughly $53 billion in revenue — moved its headquarters to the St. Louis area in 2019, instantly becoming one of the metro’s largest companies by revenue and deepening the region’s claim as an ag-tech capital alongside the plant-science corridor at Danforth and Bayer’s crop-science operations. A company that size choosing St. Louis in this decade is the strongest possible counter-argument to the decline narrative.
### How St. Louis built this bench
None of this is accidental. The metro’s corporate depth grew out of four historic strengths that still shape who headquarters here:
The river made it a trade town. Grain, goods, and beer moved through St. Louis before they moved through almost anywhere else west of the Mississippi — the lineage that runs from the 1850s brewery in Soulard straight to Bunge’s modern agribusiness headquarters and the region’s plant-science corridor.
Aviation left an engineering deep bench. The McDonnell Douglas legacy lives on in Boeing’s major defense operations near the airport — and in generations of engineers whose skills seeded companies across the region.
Medicine became an industry. The Washington University–BJC medical center didn’t just treat the region; it built one of the country’s premier academic-medical economies, with Centene’s insurance empire and a health-tech scene steadily growing up around it.
Family ownership kept companies home. Enterprise, Edward Jones’ partnership model, WWT — St. Louis’s giants skew unusually private and founder-rooted, which is a big reason they never merged their way out of town the way so many public companies eventually do.
### The bench: five more worth knowing
The list could honestly run twenty deep. Rounding out the picture from the same Fortune 1000 data: Post Holdings (the cereal-and-consumer-foods company, #477), Energizer (yes, the battery bunny is a St. Louis company), Graybar (electrical and industrial distribution), Core & Main (waterworks distribution, #497), and Build-A-Bear, whose world headquarters sits downtown on 18th Street. Seventeen Fortune 1000 headquarters, plus the private giants — for a metro our size, that’s a remarkably deep bench — deeper per capita than most metros twice our size, and the quiet engine behind everything from charity galas to stadium naming rights.
### Where the headquarters actually sit
The corporate map clusters more tightly than people expect. Clayton is the boardroom of the region — Centene’s towers, Enterprise’s home base, Emerson nearby. West County stacks the rest of the suburban giants: Edward Jones’ sprawling campus, RGA out in Chesterfield, and World Wide Technology at Westport Plaza in Maryland Heights. Downtown holds the makers and the mascots — Purina on Chouteau Avenue, Build-A-Bear on 18th Street — with Anheuser-Busch just south at One Busch Place in Soulard.
That geography matters practically: it’s why Clayton lunch spots survive on expense accounts, why Highway 40 westbound at 5 p.m. is what it is (a parking lot with exits), and why “where do you work?” in St. Louis is half a question about your commute.
Hard pivot, no apology — the Clayton restaurants worth the parking hassle.
### The next chapter: what’s growing
The bench isn’t static. A few currents worth watching, stated honestly: the region’s plant-science and ag-tech corridor keeps compounding — Bunge’s arrival, Bayer’s crop-science operations, and the Danforth Plant Science Center give St. Louis a legitimate claim to the ag-innovation capital conversation. Geospatial is the newest gravity well: the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency’s massive new western headquarters in north St. Louis has drawn a growing cluster of mapping and data firms around it. And the startup layer — Cortex in Midtown, T-REX downtown, the TechSTL community — keeps working to turn all that corporate depth into founder pipelines and the next generation of names on this list.
None of that is guaranteed to mint the next Fortune 500 name. But it’s the same recipe that built the current list: institutions, engineers, and companies that decided staying home was a strategy.
### What this means if you live here
Three practical takeaways from all this corporate geography:
For job seekers: these headquarters mean the metro hires for national-scale roles — finance at Edward Jones and RGA, tech at WWT and Centene, brand marketing at Purina and Post, healthcare across BJC and Mercy — at a cost of living well below the coasts. Our guide to the best jobs near St. Louis maps the strongest career paths, and the marketing jobs guide digs into what those corporate marketing seats actually pay.
For small business owners: giants create ecosystems. Every headquarters on this list is surrounded by caterers, contractors, cleaning crews, IT shops, and coffee spots that live on its gravity. The corporate map is also a customer map: a catering company that lands one corporate campus account changes its whole year, and the vendors who serve these giants are hiding in every strip mall from Maryland Heights to Chesterfield.
For everyone else: civic bragging rights, properly sourced. Next time someone calls St. Louis a flyover town, you have seventeen Fortune 1000 headquarters, the country’s biggest rental-car company, a $20 billion tech firm, and the beer — all with local addresses, and all hiring your neighbors.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What Fortune 500 companies are headquartered in St. Louis?
A.  The metro’s Fortune 500 headquarters include Centene (#23), Emerson (#238), Reinsurance Group of America (#196), Edward Jones, and Post Holdings among a larger group — Greater St. Louis, Inc. counts seventeen Fortune 1000 headquarters in the region in its most recent tally. Privately held giants like Enterprise Mobility and World Wide Technology don’t appear on Fortune’s revenue lists but rank with the largest of them.
### Q. Who is the largest employer in St. Louis?
A.  By headcount, BJC Health System — the largest private employer in the entire state of Missouri, with a workforce of roughly 47,000 following its merger with Saint Luke’s. Among non-healthcare employers, the giants include Edward Jones, Enterprise Mobility, World Wide Technology, and the region’s major universities and government bodies.
### Q. Is St. Louis a good city for corporate careers?
A.  Honestly, yes — and it’s underrated. Seventeen Fortune 1000 headquarters plus major private companies means national-scale roles in insurance, finance, technology, healthcare, consumer brands, and agribusiness, without coastal living costs. The trade-off is concentration: certain industries (healthcare, finance, ag-tech) run deep here, while some others cluster elsewhere.
### Q. What products made by St. Louis companies do I probably own?
A.  Check your house: Purina pet food, Energizer batteries, Post cereals, and Anheuser-Busch beverages are all made by companies headquartered in the metro — and if you’ve ever rented a car, there’s a good chance the receipt said Enterprise, National, or Alamo, all one St. Louis-based company.

### A City with a Story: What St. Louis Has to Offer
St. Louis is one of the oldest major cities in the Midwest, founded in 1764 by French fur traders Pierre Laclède and Auguste Chouteau. Its location at the confluence of the Mississippi and Missouri Rivers made it a vital hub for trade, exploration, and migration. This is why St. Louis became known as “the Gateway to the West”—it was the launching point for countless pioneers heading into the American frontier. Today, exploring St. Louis means discovering a metropolis where history, innovation, and community spirit come together.
Historic Landmarks: Stand in awe at the Gateway Arch, stroll through Soulard, Lafayette Square, and the lush Tower Grove Park, where 19th-century brick homes and gardens whisper stories of the past.
Modern Marvels: Marvel at the St. Louis Aquarium and ride the St. Louis Wheel for sweeping city views.
Neighborhood Vibes: Each area, from The Hill to The Delmar Loop, South City St. Louis, North St. Louis, Downtown St. Louis, and Forest Park, has its own flavor—literally and figuratively.
Fun for Kids: Discover family adventures with 25 Things Every St. Louis Kid Must Do.
Revitalization: See how the city is evolving at PlanSTL.
### Making a Living: Jobs and the Economy
What’s it like to build a life here? Look around and you’ll find a city with a resilient, diverse economy. From Fortune 500 giants like Anheuser-Busch and Emerson Electric to biotech startups and creative agencies, opportunity is everywhere.
Major Employers: Centene, Enterprise Holdings, World Wide Technology, and more.
City of St Louis: Explore career opportunities with the City of St. Louis—enjoy steady employment and excellent benefits.
Cost of Living: Your dollar stretches further here than in most big cities—think more home, more fun, more savings.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. How many days do you need in St. Louis?
A.  A long weekend covers the icons — the Gateway Arch, City Museum, Forest Park’s museums, and a neighborhood food crawl. Give it four or five days and you can add the day trips: Missouri wine country in Augusta and Hermann, historic St. Charles, or Cahokia Mounds just across the river.
### Q. Is there anything fun to do in St. Louis?
A.  Plenty — climb through the City Museum, a playground for all ages built from salvaged architecture, ride the St. Louis Wheel, catch a Cardinals game at Busch Stadium, then pick a neighborhood: The Hill for Italian, the Delmar Loop for music, Soulard for its market and nightlife.
### Q. Is it safe to walk around downtown St. Louis?
A.  Downtown is generally fine in the daytime and around the event districts — the Arch grounds, Ballpark Village, and stadium crowds keep things lively. Like any big city, use common sense after dark: stay where the activity is, park in lit lots, and don’t wander somewhere unfamiliar alone.
### Q. What is a must do in St. Louis?
A.  The Gateway Arch for the view, then Forest Park for a whole day — the Zoo, the Art Museum and the History Museum are all free and all inside it. Add Soulard or Lafayette Square if you want the older architecture rather than the postcard.
### Q. Is it safe to ride the MetroLink in St. Louis?
A.  Generally yes, particularly during the day and on event trains, and it is the easiest way to reach downtown from the airport. Use ordinary city sense — stay on populated platforms, keep valuables put away late at night — the same as any transit system.
### Q. Why are so many people leaving St. Louis?
A.  The city proper has lost population for decades while the metro has broadly held, which is a suburbanisation story more than a decline story. Cost of living stays low and the metro spans two states, so much of the movement is people relocating within it.
### Q. What are the biggest issues in St. Louis?
A.  Population loss in the city core, uneven investment between neighborhoods, and the fragmentation of dozens of separate municipalities across the county. Founded in 1764, it carries a lot of history and a lot of inherited boundaries — the second is the harder problem.
Come fall, the metro fills with Halloween events and haunted attractions.

## What It Actually Costs to Start a Business in St. Louis (Missouri vs. Illinois)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/cost-to-start-a-business-missouri-illinois
### What does it actually cost to start a business in the St. Louis metro?
Less than almost anyone expects on the Missouri side, and the gap between the two states is bigger than most people in this metro realize. Which is worth pausing on: if the gap between the two states is that big, are you about to register on the wrong side of the river out of pure habit?
A Missouri LLC costs $50 to file online ($105 by mail), and then Missouri asks for nothing again — no annual report, no annual fee. Across the river, an Illinois LLC runs $150 to form and $75 every single year after that. Same metro, same drive to work, three times the setup cost and a recurring bill that never appears in Missouri.
Add a free federal EIN and, if you are inside St. Louis city limits, a $200 business license, and a genuinely lean Missouri startup can be legally standing for well under $300.
### The state filing, side by side
Run that forward. Five years in, the Missouri LLC has paid $50 total. The Illinois LLC has paid $525. Neither number is large in the scheme of a business, but the structural difference is worth knowing before you assume the states are interchangeable — particularly if you are choosing where to register a business that could sit on either side.
To be clear about what that does not mean: you do not get to form in Missouri to dodge Illinois obligations for an Illinois business. Where you actually operate drives what you owe. But for a genuinely mobile or online business, it is a real consideration.
### The thing Missouri quietly gets right
The no-annual-report rule deserves its own moment, because it removes an entire failure mode.
In most states, the way small LLCs die is not dramatic. The owner forgets an annual filing, the fee goes unpaid, late penalties stack, and the entity is administratively dissolved — often discovered months later when a bank or a client asks for proof of good standing. Missouri does not require LLCs to file an annual report, and does not impose a franchise tax on them, which puts it among only four states with no recurring annual LLC fee at all.
So the single most common paperwork trap in American small business simply does not apply to a Missouri LLC. That is worth more than the $50 saved.
Corporations and other structures have their own requirements, and this is one of the few places where twenty minutes with an accountant genuinely pays for itself. But for the ordinary one-or-two-person LLC, Missouri is about as low-maintenance as it gets.
### What you do not have to pay for
A large share of what people spend forming a business is optional, and the upsells are aggressive because the margins are good.
You do not need a formation service. Filing directly with the Secretary of State is the same filing. Services are a convenience purchase, not a legal requirement, and the “$0 + state fees” offers typically recover their margin on the registered agent renewal.
You may not need a paid registered agent. You can generally serve as your own if you have a physical address in the state and are available during business hours. The real reasons to pay for one are privacy — your address becomes public record — or not having a reliable street address. Those are legitimate. “It is required” is not.
You do not need to buy a “business license package.” There is a whole industry selling Missouri business licenses. Missouri does not issue a general statewide business license, so what these products actually do is fill out local forms you could file yourself. Our guide to what licensing you actually need in St. Louis covers which office to go to and what each one charges.
You almost certainly do not need a trademark on day one. Worth doing eventually if the brand matters. Not a startup cost.
### The local layer, which is where it gets uneven
The state fee is the predictable part. Local licensing is where two identical businesses pay different amounts for no reason other than geography.
Inside the City of St. Louis, a Graduated Business License runs $200 to start — or $100 if you begin between January 1 and May 31 — and renews from $200 a year for a business with up to two city employees, on a license year running June 1 to May 31.
In St. Louis County, there is no single county-wide equivalent. The county holds more than eighty separate municipalities, each with its own rules and its own fees. Two competitors five miles apart can face entirely different requirements.
Budget for this rather than being surprised by it, and find out which municipality actually governs your address before you assume. A “St. Louis, MO” mailing address very often is not in the City of St. Louis.
### The $7 filing almost nobody mentions
If you plan to operate under any name that is not your own legal name or your LLC’s exact registered name, Missouri wants a fictitious name registration — what most people call a DBA, for “doing business as.” It is Form Corp-56 with the Secretary of State, and it costs $7.
Seven dollars. It is almost certainly the cheapest line item in your entire startup, and it is the one most commonly skipped — usually by sole proprietors who assume that because there was no formation filing, there is no filing at all.
Two situations catch people:
Sole proprietors using a trade name. If you are Maria Alvarez and you answer the phone as “Alvarez Cleaning Co.,” that is a fictitious name.
LLCs operating a second brand. If your LLC is registered as “Gateway Services LLC” but the truck and the website say “Gateway Gutter Pros,” the second name needs registering too.
The practical reason to bother, beyond compliance: banks generally want to see the DBA before they will open an account in the trade name or deposit checks made out to it. People discover this at the bank counter, which is a bad time to discover it. Missouri takes roughly five to ten business days to process one and offers no expedited option, so file it before you need it, not after.
Total tangent — but North Riverfront rewards an afternoon of curiosity.
### The costs that actually surprise people
Formation is cheap. These are the ones that show up in month two:
Insurance. General liability is the real first bill for most service businesses, and if you have employees, workers’ compensation on top. Premiums vary enormously by trade — a bookkeeper and a roofer are not in the same universe, which is worth weighing if you are still deciding which services to build the business around — so get two or three actual quotes rather than trusting any number you read online, including a range in an article like this one.
A business bank account. Not legally mandatory for a sole proprietor, but the moment you have an LLC, mixing personal and business money is how people quietly undermine the liability protection they just paid for. Many local banks and credit unions offer free small business checking.
Accounting help. Cheaper than the first mistake. Especially around sales tax, which catches new retail and food businesses constantly.
Getting found. The one nobody puts in the startup budget. You can be fully licensed, insured and legally perfect — right down to the legal pages your website is supposed to carry — and still have a silent phone, because none of that paperwork is visible to a customer searching for what you sell.
### Do you even need an LLC?
Honest answer: not always, and the $50 is not the deciding factor.
A sole proprietorship is the default the moment you start doing business under your own legal name, which is where most people going solo as a freelancer in St. Louis begin. There is generally no formation filing to make with the Secretary of State, and no fee. You will still handle local licensing and taxes, but the entity itself costs nothing.
What the LLC buys is separation — a legal line between business liabilities and personal assets. That matters more as you take on risk: going into people’s homes, handling their property, having employees, signing leases, carrying inventory. It matters less for a low-risk side business with no employees and no premises.
The mistake in both directions is common. People form an LLC for a hobby that will never generate a claim, and people skip one while doing work in strangers’ houses. If you are unsure which side you are on, that is a specific question worth asking an attorney or accountant once, rather than guessing permanently.
And before spending anything at all: it is usually worth confirming somebody wants to buy this. We wrote a guide on testing a business idea before you spend money for exactly that reason.
### A realistic first-year floor
For a one-person Missouri service business, formed online, acting as its own registered agent, based in the City of St. Louis:
LLC filing — $50
EIN — $0
Graduated Business License — $200 ($100 if you start after January 1)
Missouri annual report — $0, because there isn’t one
That is roughly $250 to exist legally, before insurance and before anything that actually brings in customers. In St. Louis County the license line changes to whatever your municipality charges. In Illinois, swap the $50 for $150 and add $75 a year forever.
Which is genuinely good news, and also the part worth sitting with: the cheap part is becoming legal. The expensive part is becoming findable. Most businesses that fail quietly in this metro were perfectly registered the whole time.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much does an LLC cost in Missouri?
A.  $50 to file articles of organization online with the Secretary of State, or $105 by mail. After that Missouri requires no annual report and imposes no franchise tax on LLCs, so the recurring state cost is $0 — one of only four states with no ongoing annual LLC fee. Local licensing and any professional licenses are separate.
### Q. Does Missouri require an annual report for an LLC?
A.  No. Missouri LLCs have no annual report obligation to the Secretary of State and no annual fee. This removes the most common way small LLCs get administratively dissolved in other states — a missed yearly filing. Other entity types have their own requirements, so confirm what applies to your specific structure.
### Q. Is it cheaper to form an LLC in Missouri or Illinois?
A.  Missouri, substantially. Formation is $50 online in Missouri versus $150 in Illinois, and Illinois charges a $75 annual report fee that Missouri does not have at all. Over five years that is $50 versus $525. But you cannot form in Missouri to escape Illinois obligations for a business actually operating in Illinois — where you do business governs what you owe.
### Q. Do I need a business license to start an LLC in Missouri?
A.  They are separate things. Forming an LLC registers a legal entity with the state; a business license is local permission to operate. Missouri issues no general statewide business license, but your city may require one — the City of St. Louis does, at $200 to start. Forming the LLC does not license you anywhere.
### Q. Can I be my own registered agent in Missouri?
A.  Generally yes, if you have a physical street address in the state and are available during normal business hours. A commercial registered agent is worth paying for when you want to keep your address off the public record or lack a reliable street address — but it is a convenience, not a legal necessity, despite how formation services present it.
### Q. What does it cost to start a business if I skip the LLC?
A.  A sole proprietorship operating under your own legal name generally has no state formation filing and no fee, so the entity itself is free. You would still handle local licensing, taxes, and any professional licensing. What you give up is the liability separation an LLC provides, which matters more as you take on employees, premises, or work inside customers' homes.

## The Heart of Community: Why Local Matters
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/the-heart-of-community-why-local-matters
Sit with me for a moment. Picture lunchtime on a Saturday: the sun soft on the corner of Main Street, the warm smell of fresh barbecue drifting from a small café or food truck, and you hear the low, satisfied rumble of a lawn mower being tuned at a family-run garage down the block.
That feeling — of places that know your name, of streets threaded together by familiar faces and dependable services — is what the St. Louis Near Me spirit is about.
This is not a sales pitch; it's an invitation to hold a door open for neighbors and friends, to make daily life a little easier for the people who make our neighborhood, city, and region hum.
### Why Choosing Local Is an Act of Community
When you choose a local barbecue restaurant instead of a chain, you're doing more than buying a sandwich. You're making possible the sound of the smoker timer, the restaurant or food truck owner's family who remembers your order, and the teenager saving for college who works the register.
Have you patronized a business like this? That single, small act ripples: dollars that stay close by, jobs that support families, and the authentic character of neighborhoods from Warrenton to Highland and from Bonne Terre to Jerseyville. The human economy is woven from these small local choices we make to support our friends and neighbors.
Think about the sensory memory of a place you love: the softness of a storefront's worn wooden sign and the creak in the store's old wooden floors, the spicy tang of a food truck's simmering sauce that you remember from your last visit, the distant rhythm of a band tuning up at a town festival that you've been looking forward to for weeks.
Those layers — sight, smell, sound, texture, taste — are the town's real capital. It's where life is made and experiences are photographed, and those photos are sent to friends and remembered forever.
You're not just shopping or buying a barbecue sandwich; you're supporting local businesses, which keeps those delicate layers of interaction alive. Those businesses train the younger generation and teach the skills that are necessary to lead a long, productive, and happy life right here in our community.
Whether those businesses support a single mother, an older couple, or a larger business with many employees, you know that all of us are in this community together and that we need to continue to support each other. St Louis Near Me Directory is the connector — pointing neighbors to the businesses that serve them, and businesses to the neighbors looking for exactly what they do.
Let's call it a hyperlocal collaboration, or more simply call it helping each other. Sound good?
### The Directory as More Than a List — A Quietly Humming Community
There's a difference between a directory and a community. A directory can be a database; a community is a conversation. On our pages, you'll find more than phone numbers — you'll find voices. People leave notes about a florist's careful arrangements in Ferguson, praise for a mechanic's honest assessment in Millstadt, or a tip about the best late-night sandwich in Sappington. These small, human insights turn discovery into trust.
When you talk to a friend about an experience with a business and they use words like “reliable,” “friendly,” “on time,” that language is a kind of local shorthand. It tells you who to trust without a hard sell. The St Louis Near Me Directory amplifies those real conversations so neighbors can make better choices faster.
### How Supporting Local Businesses Strengthens Our Regional Fabric
Dollars spent locally recirculate. A resident or business that hires a gardener or landscaper from the neighborhood spends more locally on supplies; a plumber who hires an apprentice keeps wages within the community. It means the person who fixes your roof might also be the one coaching at the local youth league in the evening. This kind of local recirculation builds an economic web that's resilient — and intimately affects each one of us.
Beyond economics, local businesses hold the civic memory of a place. The mural outside a family shop in Dupo, IL, the annual block party in Bellefontaine Neighbors, MO, the outdoor farmers' table on a Saturday in Columbia, IL — these are the textures that make our towns distinct. ### For Business Owners: How the Directory Helps You Be Found and Chosen
If you own a shop, a studio, or a service business, the St Louis Near Me Directory is designed to be practical: it helps customers find you, understand what you do, and decide to reach out. Make it easy for them. So make it easy in the most literal way: if a neighbor who would love what you do has never once heard your name, how are they ever going to find you?

### FAQs — Quick Answers for Neighbors and Owners
### Q. Do I need a storefront to be listed?
A.  No. Mobile and home-based businesses can list and set service areas so customers know where you operate without exposing private addresses.
### Q. How do reviews work?
A.  Reviews are posted to your directory page. If you subscribe to our Gold Plan, you can and should respond to every review. Honest feedback helps others choose and helps owners improve.
### Q. How quickly will I see results?
A.  Results vary — there are no guarantees in local search. In our experience, the owners who see movement first are usually the ones who complete their profile, add real photos, and post a coupon, then give it a few weeks. Every business is different and every profile is different. Make yours stand out and make sure everyone knows about your St Louis Near Me Directory listing.
### Q. What are some benefits of buying local?
A.  More of your money stays in St. Louis — local owners hire neighbors, buy from nearby suppliers, and sponsor the Little League teams and school fundraisers that chains rarely touch. You also get faster, more personal service, and neighborhoods that keep their lights on and their character intact.
### Q. Why do people say “shop local”?
A.  It began as a response to chains and online giants pulling spending out of neighborhoods. “Shop local” is shorthand for keeping St. Louis dollars in St. Louis — supporting the businesses that give our streets their character, our neighbors their jobs, and our community its identity.
### Q. Is buying local always better?
A.  Honestly, not always — sometimes a chain or an online store genuinely is cheaper or more convenient, and nobody should feel guilty about a tight budget. The point is intention, not perfection: when price and convenience are close, choosing the local option is where the community payoff happens.
