## When a Contractor Won't Finish the Job (Missouri vs. Illinois Rules)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/contractor-wont-finish-the-job-missouri-illinois
### What do you do when a contractor takes your money and disappears?
Search that and you will be sent to a licensing board. Which board depends on the day: we pulled the live results from a Missouri location and page one was California’s CSLB, Arizona’s Registrar of Contractors, Tennessee, Florida, Massachusetts, North Dakota, Maryland, Louisiana.
Not one of them has any authority over a contractor in Missouri. Missouri has no statewide contractor licensing board, which means there is no state agency that can suspend a license, order restitution, or make anyone come back and finish your kitchen. The complaint form everyone tells you to file does not exist here.
That is genuinely worse for homeowners than it is in most states, and it is worth knowing before you hire rather than after. But “no board” does not mean no recourse. It means your leverage is in different places, and the order you use them in matters.
### First: stop and write things down
Before you make a single angry phone call, spend twenty minutes building a record. Everything below depends on it, and it gets harder to reconstruct the longer you wait.
The contract, plus any change orders, texts, and emails where scope or timing was discussed. Texts count.
Every payment — amount, date, method. Cancelled checks and card statements are stronger than memory.
Dated photographs of the current state of the work. Take more than you think you need.
A timeline: promised dates, actual visits, when contact stopped.
The permit status. Call your municipality and ask whether a permit was pulled, in whose name, and whether any inspections passed.
That last one is often the moment things become clear. A contractor who never pulled the permit has usually left you with unpermitted work as well as unfinished work — and that is a problem that resurfaces years later when you sell.
### Second: send a written demand, and send it properly
A phone call is not a record. A letter is. Send a short, unemotional written demand that states what was agreed, what was paid, what is incomplete, exactly what you want done, and a specific deadline. Send it by certified mail with return receipt, and email a copy.
This is not a formality and it is not about being polite. Every step after this one goes better when you can show a judge that you asked plainly and gave them a chance. Some contractors also simply reappear at this point, because a certified letter reads differently than a voicemail.
Keep it factual. Do not threaten things you are not going to do, and do not describe your feelings about the situation. Dates, dollars, deliverables.
### Third: the leverage Missouri actually gives you
With no licensing board in the picture, these are the levers that exist:
### Small claims court — up to $5,000
Missouri’s small claims division handles civil claims where the amount in controversy does not exceed $5,000, under RSMo 482.305. It is designed to be used without a lawyer, and for a deposit that vanished or a job abandoned partway, it is frequently the right tool.
One useful wrinkle: if your damages exceed $5,000, you can choose to waive the excess and stay in small claims for the speed and the simplicity. You give up the difference permanently, so it is a real trade — but for a $6,500 loss, many people decide that recovering $5,000 in a few months beats chasing $6,500 for a year.
### Associate circuit court, above that
Larger claims move up to associate circuit court, where the process is more formal and a lawyer starts to make sense. If the number is big enough that you are weighing this, talk to a construction attorney before filing anything — the strategy differs and the deadlines are real.
### The Missouri Attorney General’s consumer complaint
The Attorney General accepts consumer complaints, and filing one is worth doing. Be clear-eyed about what it is, though: it builds a public record and can contribute to a pattern that draws enforcement attention. It is not a mechanism that gets your money back, and no one should wait on it instead of filing suit.
### Your municipality’s permit office
Underused, and in Missouri it is closer to a regulator than anything the state offers. If the contractor is registered in that city, the city has a relationship with them and an interest in how they behave. If the work was done without a required permit, the city wants to know that too. Call and describe what happened.
### The Better Business Bureau
No legal power, but a real effect on a business that depends on reputation, and the complaint stays visible to the next homeowner researching them. Low effort, worth the fifteen minutes.
### Across the river: Illinois plays by different rules
If your house is in Belleville, Edwardsville, O’Fallon, Collinsville, Alton or anywhere else on the Illinois side, almost everything above changes — in your favor. Illinois regulates this work at the state level in ways Missouri simply does not, and metro-east homeowners routinely do not realize how much more leverage they have.
### Illinois requires a written contract over $1,000 — and a pamphlet before you sign
Under the Home Repair and Remodeling Act (815 ILCS 513), a contractor doing home repair or remodeling work over $1,000 must give you a written contract, and it must state the total cost, the materials and parts, any charge for estimates, and how to contact the company.
More useful still: before any contract is signed, the contractor must hand you a copy of the state pamphlet “Home Repair: Know Your Consumer Rights.” They must also disclose up front if the contract forces arbitration or waives your right to a jury trial.
Think about what that gives you. If the contractor never produced a written contract, or never gave you that pamphlet, they were out of compliance from the first day — before any of the work went wrong. That is a concrete statutory failure you can point at, not a matter of opinion about workmanship. And the Act lets a damaged homeowner sue directly, or have the Illinois Attorney General or the county State’s Attorney pursue the violation.
### Illinois licenses roofers. Missouri doesn’t license anyone.
Roofing is the clearest example. The Illinois Roofing Industry Licensing Act (225 ILCS 335) requires a state license to do roofing work — with an examination, a designated qualifying party who actually participates in day-to-day operations, and a surety bond that must be filed and maintained before the license issues or renews.
So on the Illinois side there is a real state license to verify, a real regulator to complain to, and a bond that may be reachable. Cross the river into Missouri and none of that exists for the same trade. Same metro, same contractor driving between both, completely different consumer protection.
The practical takeaway for metro-east homeowners: ask for the Illinois license before you hire, and if a roofer is working your side of the river without one, that alone is worth stopping over.
### Which state’s rules apply?
Where the property is — not where the contractor is based. A contractor headquartered in St. Louis County working on a house in Belleville is doing Illinois work and owes you the Illinois protections. Plenty of crews work both sides and default to the looser habits of the Missouri side. That is your problem to catch, and it is easiest to catch before you sign.
Illinois also has its own small claims process with a different dollar limit than Missouri’s $5,000. Confirm the current threshold with the circuit clerk in the county where the property sits before you decide where to file.
### The lien problem nobody warns you about
Here is the part that turns a bad situation into a much worse one, and it catches Missouri homeowners constantly.
Under Chapter 429, a subcontractor or supplier who was not paid can place a mechanic’s lien on your property even if you already paid the general contractor in full. Your payment offsets the claim only to the extent it actually reached them. So a contractor who took your money, did half the work, and never paid the lumberyard can leave you facing a lien for materials you already bought once.
Two things follow from that:
If you receive a notice from a subcontractor or supplier, do not ignore it. They are required to give you ten days’ notice before filing, stating the amount and who owes it. That notice is your window to act — talk to a lawyer, and do not assume it will resolve itself.
Stop paying, and get advice before you pay more. If a job has gone wrong, additional payments to the general contractor may not protect you from the subs at all. This is the point where an hour of a construction attorney’s time is genuinely cheap.
Nothing to do with contractors — here’s Wydown Skinker, top to bottom.
The preventive version, for next time: collect signed lien waivers from every subcontractor and supplier before you release final payment. Contractors who run real operations already do this.
### What actually gets money back
Honest answer, in rough order of how often it works:
A credit card chargeback, if you paid that way and are still inside the dispute window. This is the single fastest remedy available and it is the one most people forget. It is also a strong argument for paying deposits by card rather than check or transfer — and a strong hint about contractors who insist on cash.
Small claims. Slower, but effective for amounts in range, and a judgment is a real thing that follows a business around.
A demand letter from a lawyer. Often cheaper than people assume, and the response rate is very different from a letter you sent yourself.
Their next job. A contractor who wants to keep working in your municipality has more to lose from a permit-office complaint and a BBB record than from a letter.
What generally does not get money back: online reviews, angry phone calls, social media posts, and waiting. Post the review if it is true — but do not mistake it for a remedy.
### Hiring the person who finishes the job
If you are now looking for someone to fix or complete the work, be honest with the next contractor about what happened and what condition the job is in. Many will not take over another crew’s unfinished work, and the ones who will need to see it before quoting. Hiding it wastes everyone’s time and yours most of all.
Then vet this one properly, because the state will not do it for you. Our guide to checking whether a contractor is licensed in Missouri covers how verification actually works here — which municipality to call, why the permit question matters most, and how to confirm insurance without taking anyone’s word for it.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it worth suing a contractor?
A.  Often yes for amounts within Missouri’s $5,000 small claims limit, where you can file without a lawyer and resolve it in months. Above that, weigh legal costs against the amount and, importantly, against whether the contractor has assets worth collecting from — a judgment against a business that has dissolved is paper. Ask a lawyer that question before filing.
### Q. Can I call the police on a contractor?
A.  Usually this is a civil matter, not a criminal one, and police will say so. It can cross into criminal territory when there is clear fraud — a fake identity, a pattern of taking deposits with no intent to perform, forged documents. If you believe that describes your situation, report it and also file with the Attorney General, since patterns across multiple victims are what draws enforcement.
### Q. What should you not say to a contractor?
A.  Once a dispute starts, avoid saying anything that could read as accepting incomplete work or agreeing to a new deal verbally. Do not threaten actions you will not take, and do not negotiate significant changes by phone. Put scope, money, and deadlines in writing — a text thread is a record, and a phone call is not.
### Q. How to get money back from a bad contractor?
A.  Fastest is a credit card chargeback if you paid by card and are within the dispute window. After that: a written demand sent certified, then small claims for amounts up to $5,000, or a lawyer’s demand letter for larger sums. In Missouri there is no licensing board that can order restitution, so recovery comes from the card issuer or the courts.
### Q. Does Illinois require a written contract for home repair?
A.  Yes. Under the Home Repair and Remodeling Act, work over $1,000 requires a written contract stating total cost, materials and parts, any estimate charge, and company contact information. The contractor must also give you the state's “Home Repair: Know Your Consumer Rights” pamphlet before you sign, and disclose any arbitration clause or jury-trial waiver. Missing any of that is a statutory violation independent of the workmanship.
### Q. Who do you complain to about a contractor in Missouri?
A.  There is no state contractor board, so complaints go to three places instead: the municipality that licenses or permits the work, the Missouri Attorney General’s consumer protection process, and the Better Business Bureau. The permit office is the one most people skip and the one closest to having real leverage.
### Q. Can a subcontractor lien my house if I paid the contractor?
A.  Yes. Under Missouri’s Chapter 429, your payment to the general contractor offsets a claim only to the extent it was actually paid through. An unpaid subcontractor or supplier can pursue a lien against your property regardless. They must give ten days’ notice before filing — treat that notice as urgent, and get advice before making further payments.

## Business Licenses in St. Louis: What You Actually Need (City vs. County)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/business-license-st-louis-what-you-need
### Do I need a business license in St. Louis?
Here is the part that trips people up, and it is worth saying plainly before anything else: Missouri does not issue a general, statewide business license. There is no single form you fill out with the state that makes your business legal to operate. Google’s own answer panel for this question says as much, pointing to the Secretary of State, and Wolters Kluwer puts it the same way — the state does not require a state-issued general business license.
So when someone tells you they “got their Missouri business license,” they almost certainly mean one of three different things: they registered an entity with the Secretary of State, they registered for taxes with the Department of Revenue, or they got a license from their city. Those are three separate offices, three separate forms, and only the third one is actually called a license.
Where you sit on the map decides most of it. A bakery on South Grand and a bakery in Kirkwood follow different rules, not because the state treats them differently, but because their city halls do.
### What the state of Missouri actually requires
Strip away the license question and the state layer is short. Depending on how you are set up and whether you have employees, you are looking at some combination of:
Entity registration with the Secretary of State — if you are forming an LLC or a corporation, or operating under a name that is not your own legal name. A sole proprietor working under their own name generally has no filing to make here.
Tax registration with the Department of Revenue — a sales tax license if you sell taxable goods, and employer withholding if you have employees.
A federal EIN from the IRS — free, and needed if you have employees or a multi-member entity.
A professional or occupational license — but only for regulated fields. Cosmetology, healthcare, real estate, liquor, childcare and similar work go through state boards.
Notice what is missing from that list. There is no line item that says “business license.” If your trade is not one the state regulates, the state does not have a license to sell you.
### The City of St. Louis: the Graduated Business License
Inside the city limits, the answer flips. Any person engaged in business within the City of St. Louis is required to have a business license, and unless specifically exempt, that means a Graduated Business License — the GBL. This one is real, it is annual, and it has teeth. Which is exactly why the real question isn’t whether you need a license — it’s whether you know which of the eighty-plus local rulebooks yours falls under.
What makes it “graduated” is that the renewal amount scales with your number of city employees in the previous calendar year, not with your revenue. That surprises people who assume a small shop with high sales pays more than a quiet office with a large staff. It is the opposite.
The first year works on a different rule — a flat amount that depends only on when in the license year you started:
After that first year, renewals follow the employee-count schedule. A representative slice of it:
Source: the City’s own Graduated Business License fee schedule. For most small operations — a solo consultant, a two-person shop — the number that matters is the one at the top: $200 a year.
### The dates matter more than the dollars
The license year runs June 1 through May 31. It does not follow the calendar year, and it does not follow your fiscal year. Renewal is due before June 1, and late filing carries a penalty of 5% per month up to a 25% cap, with an additional 20% if payment runs more than 60 days behind. That is how a $200 license quietly becomes a $290 problem.
### Three things people forget until they are stuck
The license itself is rarely the whole errand. The city also expects:
A state sales tax number first, if you sell a product. You need it in hand before you can register for the GBL — so the Department of Revenue step comes before the city step, not after.
A clearance statement from the Collector of Revenue confirming your city taxes are paid. Owe anything, and the license stalls until you do not.
An Occupancy Permit from the Building Division if your business is physically located in the city.
And a separate GBL is required for each business location or trade name. Two storefronts means two licenses, even under one owner.
### St. Louis County: it is not one license, it is more than eighty
This is the single biggest source of confusion in the region, and it is why generic online guides are close to useless here. “St. Louis County” is not one jurisdiction for licensing purposes. It contains more than eighty separate incorporated municipalities — the exact count depends on whether you tally cities only or include villages and towns, which is why you will see both 84 and 88 quoted — plus unincorporated territory administered by the county itself.
Each of those municipalities sets its own business licensing. Clayton, Kirkwood, Webster Groves, Florissant, Chesterfield, Maplewood: separate city halls, separate ordinances, separate fees, separate renewal dates. There is no county-wide equivalent of the city’s GBL that covers you everywhere.
Which produces a genuinely strange practical result. A mobile service business — a house cleaner, a handyman, a mobile groomer — working across ten municipalities may technically owe licensing in several of them. Most one-person operations never learn this until a city sends a letter. The honest advice is to license where you are based first, then check the ordinance in any city where you keep a physical presence or do steady, repeat work.
### The merchant license, and who actually needs it
Separate from city licensing, Missouri has an old category worth knowing: the merchant license, governed by Chapter 150 of the Revised Statutes. The statute defines a merchant as someone who deals in selling goods, wares and merchandise at a store, stand or place occupied for that purpose. In St. Louis County it runs $5 through the Collector of Revenue, and businesses are also required to register with the County Assessor.
Read that definition closely, because the word doing the work is goods. A consultant does not sell goods. Neither does a lawn service, a bookkeeper, a massage therapist, or a dog walker. Plenty of service businesses get talked into hunting for a merchant license they were never required to hold. If you sell physical things, look into it. If you sell your time and skill — the way most freelancers going solo in St. Louis do — this is probably not your form.
### If you are in the trades, the licensing question is different again
Here is where Missouri gets genuinely unusual, and it is worth stating clearly because national guides get it wrong constantly: Missouri has no statewide license for HVAC contractors, plumbers, or general contractors. There is no state board to register with and no state license number to put on your truck. Bills to create one have been introduced repeatedly and have not passed.
That work is licensed at the city and county level instead. The City of St. Louis licenses contractors directly. Individual county municipalities set their own requirements, and some require a master’s card or a bonded contractor registration on top of the ordinary business license.
For owners, that means the answer to “am I licensed?” depends entirely on where you work, and you may need more than one. For customers, it means the usual advice to “check the state license board” simply does not apply in Missouri — there is nothing to check. We wrote a separate guide on how to verify a contractor here, since the process is nothing like what most people expect.
### The mistakes that cost people money
Four patterns come up again and again:
Assuming an LLC is a license. It is not. Forming an LLC with the Secretary of State creates a legal entity; it says nothing about your right to operate in a given city. Plenty of people finish their LLC paperwork, feel done, and are still unlicensed where they actually work — the same blind spot that leaves a new website missing the legal pages a small business site is expected to carry.
Assuming an EIN is a license. Also no. An EIN is a federal tax identifier from the IRS. It is free, it takes minutes, and it has no bearing on local licensing.
Getting the jurisdiction wrong. A St. Louis mailing address does not mean you are in the City of St. Louis. Enormous numbers of addresses that say “St. Louis, MO” sit in county municipalities with entirely different rules. Check which city actually governs your address before you file anything.
Missing the June 1 renewal. In the city, this is the most common avoidable expense on this page. Put it in your calendar the day you get the license.
Total tangent — Troy, Illinois, business by business.
### A sane order of operations
If you are starting fresh in the metro — still working out which services are worth building a business around — this sequence avoids most of the backtracking:
Confirm your jurisdiction. City of St. Louis, a named county municipality, or unincorporated county. Everything downstream depends on this.
Register the entity with the Secretary of State, if you are forming one or using a trade name.
Get the EIN from the IRS. Free, same day.
Register with the Department of Revenue for sales tax and withholding as they apply. Do this before the city step if you sell products.
Apply for the local license at the city that governs your address — the GBL if you are in the city, your municipality’s license otherwise.
Handle the extras: occupancy permit, tax clearance, and any trade-specific registration.
None of it is difficult. It is just spread across more desks than anyone expects, and no single office will tell you about all the others.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Do I need a local business license if I have an LLC?
A.  Usually yes, and they are unrelated things. An LLC is a legal structure registered with the Secretary of State — it limits liability and defines ownership. A business license is permission from a city to operate there. Forming an LLC does not license you anywhere, and in the City of St. Louis you would still need a Graduated Business License.
### Q. How much does a business license cost in mo?
A.  There is no statewide fee, because Missouri has no statewide business license. Cost is set locally. In the City of St. Louis, the initial Graduated Business License is $200 if you start between June 1 and January 1, or $100 between January 1 and May 31; renewals begin at $200 for businesses with 0–2 city employees and rise with headcount. County municipalities each set their own.
### Q. Do I need a business license in Missouri?
A.  Not from the state — Missouri does not issue a general one. Whether you need a local license depends on your city. In the City of St. Louis, anyone engaged in business within the city limits is required to have one unless specifically exempt. In St. Louis County, it depends on which of the 80-plus municipalities your address falls in.
### Q. How to look up a business license in Missouri?
A.  Because licensing is local, there is no single statewide lookup. Check the licensing office of the specific city — the City of St. Louis License Collector for city businesses, or the relevant municipal clerk in the county. For entity records rather than licenses, the Secretary of State’s business search shows registered LLCs and corporations.
### Q. Can I use my EIN as a business license?
A.  No. An EIN is a federal tax identification number issued free by the IRS for tax and payroll purposes. It grants no authority to operate and is not accepted in place of a local license. You may well need both, and they come from different governments entirely.
### Q. Is your business license number the same as your EIN number?
A.  No. They come from different issuers and serve different purposes — the EIN from the IRS for federal tax identification, the license number from your city as proof of local authorization. If a form asks for one, do not substitute the other.

## The Real Cost of Living in St. Louis (It's the Housing, Not Everything Else)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/cost-of-living-in-st-louis
### What does it actually cost to live in St. Louis?
About 10% below the national average — and almost all of that discount is one category.
Missouri’s own state agency, the Missouri Economic Research and Information Center, puts the St. Louis MO-IL metro at a composite cost-of-living index of 89.8 for the first quarter of 2026, where 100 is the national average. Statewide, Missouri sits at 88.6, tied with Iowa for the seventh-lowest cost of living in the country.
But the composite hides the interesting part. Break it into components and St. Louis stops looking uniformly cheap:
Source: MERIC Cost of Living Data Series, Q1 2026.
So the honest summary is not “everything is cheap in the Midwest.” It is: your housing costs drop sharply, your grocery bill barely moves, and your health care costs go up.
### Why every website gives you a different number
If you have already searched this, you have noticed the answers do not agree. We pulled the current page one and counted:
Salary.com — about 2% below national
Payscale — 6% below
MERIC — 10.2% below
Apartments.com — 10.4% below
Google’s own summary panel currently repeats the 2% figure. That is a five-fold spread on the same question, and none of these sources is lying.
They differ because a cost-of-living index is a basket, and everyone builds the basket differently. How much weight goes on housing versus groceries? Is it the city or the whole metro? Renting or owning? Change those and the answer moves several points.
Which is why we lead with MERIC here: it is a state agency, it is dated to a specific quarter, and it publishes the components rather than one blended number. You can see which parts are cheap instead of taking a single percentage on faith.
The practical takeaway is not to trust any one figure — including ours. Look at the category that dominates your budget. If you rent modestly and have a chronic condition, the health line matters more to you than the housing line, and your personal index looks nothing like 89.8.
### What earning a living actually requires here
The MIT Living Wage Calculator estimates the living wage in the St. Louis metro at $21.79 an hour for one adult with no children. Missouri’s minimum wage is $15.00 as of January 1, 2026.
That gap — roughly $6.79 an hour, or about $14,000 a year at full time — is the honest shape of affordability here. St. Louis is genuinely inexpensive compared with the coasts, and a full-time minimum-wage job still does not reach a single adult’s baseline. Both things are true, and most cost-of-living pages only tell you the first one.
### How St. Louis compares inside Missouri
Every participating Missouri city sat below the national average in Q1 2026:
Joplin — 83.7, the lowest in the state, with housing at 59.8
Springfield — 89.7
St. Louis MO-IL — 89.8
Columbia — 91.3
What driving school costs in St. Louis
St. Louis and Springfield are effectively tied, which surprises people who assume a large metro must cost more than a smaller city. It does not, here — because the housing stock is old, plentiful, and spread across a very large area.
That last point deserves its own note, because it is where the metro’s averages become almost meaningless in practice.
### The average is not a place you can live
A hillside block of brick homes in south St. Louis, MO, photographed by Lane Forman on August 31, 2026 for St Louis Near Me Directory.
“St. Louis” in these indexes means the whole MO-IL metro — the city, all of St. Louis County’s eighty-plus municipalities, St. Charles County, and the Illinois side. The spread inside that area is enormous.
Housing in Clayton and housing in Florissant are not the same market. A house in Belleville, Illinois and a house in Chesterfield are not the same purchase, and they are not even in the same state for tax purposes. The index averages all of it into one number that describes no actual neighborhood.
So use the index for the question it answers — is this metro cheaper than where I live now? — and then look at specific municipalities for the question you actually care about. Our guide to why St. Louis real estate is so affordable goes deeper on the housing side, which is where most of your savings live.
### How to actually use this if you are comparing a job offer
Here is where most people misuse a cost-of-living index, and it can cost them real money in a negotiation.
The instinct is to take the composite and apply it to the whole salary — “St. Louis is about 10% cheaper, so I can accept about 10% less.” That is the wrong calculation, and depending on your situation it is wrong in either direction.
The composite is a weighted blend of six categories, and your household does not spend like the blend. Do it this way instead:
Split your current spending into the same six buckets — housing, groceries, utilities, transportation, health, everything else. Rough percentages are fine. Then apply each index to its own bucket rather than applying one number to everything.
Unrelated, and we know it — North Pointe, if you’re curious.
Two examples of how differently that lands, both clearly hypothetical:
Someone spending half their income on rent gets most of the benefit. Housing at 80.4 is doing the heavy lifting, and it is the biggest slice of their budget, so their personal saving lands well above the headline 10%.
Someone with modest housing costs and high medical spending gets almost none of it. Their largest categories are groceries at 98.7, utilities at 98.0, and health at 103.6 — that is roughly break-even or slightly worse. For that household, moving here on a 10% pay cut is a real pay cut.
Same city, same quarter, same official numbers, opposite conclusions. Which is why the component table above matters more than any single percentage anyone quotes at you.
Two practical notes if you are running this exercise. Renting and buying are not the same bet. The 80.4 housing index reflects both, and a renter feels it immediately while a buyer feels it over years — alongside the maintenance costs of older housing stock. And health care weighting rises with age and household size. A 103.6 index on a small share of a young single person’s budget is noise; on a retired couple’s budget it is the headline.
### Costs the index does not really capture
A few things surprise people who move here, none of which show up cleanly in a composite number.
Personal property tax on vehicles. Missouri counties assess an annual tax on cars, trucks and boats. Newcomers from states without it are reliably caught out by the first bill. Rates are set locally, so check with the assessor for the county you are moving to rather than assuming a figure.
Two states, two tax systems. The metro spans Missouri and Illinois, and where you live determines your income tax, your property tax, and your sales tax — while your commute may cross the river daily. If you are weighing sides, that comparison is worth doing properly rather than by rule of thumb.
Sales tax stacking. Missouri layers state, county, city and special district rates, so the rate at one shopping center differs from another a few blocks away. It is a small effect on a coffee and a real one on a car.
Older housing stock. The savings on the purchase price are real. So are the maintenance costs of a house built in the 1930s — sewer laterals, original wiring, foundations on clay soil. Budget for the house you are actually buying, not the index.
Utilities are an annual average hiding two extremes. The 98.0 index is a yearly figure, and St. Louis does not have a mild year. Summers are hot and genuinely humid, winters get cold, and the bills follow — so a household that budgets by the monthly average will be caught out twice a year. If you are moving from a temperate climate, ask a prospective landlord or seller for twelve months of actual utility bills rather than a typical month. In an older, poorly insulated house the gap between July and October is not small.
Car dependence outside the core. Transportation scores well at 88.8, but that assumes driving. Much of the metro has limited transit, so a household running two cars will not feel the transport discount the way the index implies.
### So is it affordable?
For most people moving from a larger or coastal metro, yes — and the reason is specific rather than general. You will spend meaningfully less on housing, slightly less on getting around, about the same on food and utilities, and somewhat more on health care.
If you are moving here from elsewhere in the Midwest, the difference narrows to very little. And if you are already here on a lower income, the state ranking is cold comfort: a low cost of living and a wage that does not reach the local living wage still leaves a gap.
Both of those are the honest answer, and it is a more useful one than a single percentage.
For the tax side of a St. Louis budget, see how the St. Louis sales tax rate changes by address, what the St. Louis County personal property tax adds every year, and the Missouri state income tax rate.
Turning these numbers into a plan? Start with how to budget on a St. Louis paycheck, and what causes inflation explains why the prices keep moving.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it expensive to live in St. Louis, MO?
A.  By the numbers, no — it is cheaper than most of the country. The metro sits at a cost-of-living index of 89.8 against a national average of 100, and Missouri as a whole is tied for the seventh-lowest in the country. But the discount is concentrated in housing, at 80.4. Groceries and utilities run close to national, and health care is above it at 103.6.
### Q. What salary do you need to live in St. Louis?
A.  There is no single honest figure, and published estimates vary widely because each uses a different basket. A useful floor: the MIT Living Wage Calculator puts the living wage for one adult with no children in this metro at $21.79 an hour. Comfort above that depends most on whether you rent or own, and in which municipality.
### Q. What is middle class income in St. Louis?
A.  Definitions vary by source and none is authoritative, so treat any specific bracket cautiously. What is measurable is that local costs run roughly 10% below the national average overall, driven by housing, meaning a given income stretches further here than the same income in a coastal metro — but less far than the headline suggests once health care is included.
### Q. Is $40 an hour good in Missouri?
A.  It is well above both the state minimum wage of $15.00 and the MIT living-wage estimate of $21.79 an hour for a single adult in the St. Louis metro. Whether it is comfortable depends on household size and municipality — the same wage supports a very different life in Joplin, at an index of 83.7, than in a higher-cost pocket of St. Louis County.
### Q. Why do different websites give different costs of living for St. Louis?
A.  Because each builds a different basket and weights it differently. Current published estimates for St. Louis range from about 2% below national to about 10.4% below. MERIC, a Missouri state agency, is the one that publishes the underlying components by quarter, which is why its 89.8 composite is the most inspectable figure rather than simply the most favorable.
### Q. Is the cost of living the same across the St. Louis metro?
A.  No, and the average can be misleading. The index covers the whole MO-IL metro — the city, more than eighty municipalities in St. Louis County, St. Charles County and the Illinois side. Housing costs, property taxes and sales tax rates all vary considerably between them, and the Illinois side sits under a different state tax system entirely.

### Q. What is a livable salary in St. Louis?
A.  The MIT Living Wage Calculator puts the living wage for one adult in the St. Louis metro at $21.79 an hour, against a Missouri minimum wage of $15.00. That is a floor for one person covering their own costs, not a comfortable salary and not a household figure - add children or a second earner and the number moves substantially.

A.  Housing is where nearly all of the savings live. MERIC puts the metro’s housing component at 80.4 against a national 100 - roughly 20% cheaper - while groceries (98.7) and utilities (98.0) run about national and health care is above it at 103.6. That is why a single “10% cheaper” figure applied to your whole salary will mislead you.

## Marketing Jobs in St. Louis: What They Pay and How to Land One
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/top-8-marketing-job-st-louis-opportunities-for-2025
Refreshed September 2026
Imagine it’s a Tuesday night and you’re at a coffee shop in Maplewood with your laptop open, scrolling marketing listings. One says a “St. Louis” marketing director role pays $230,000. The next says a marketing assistant in Earth City pays $17 an hour. A third wants eight years of experience, four certifications, and calls itself entry-level. If you’ve been trying to make sense of the marketing job market here — from Florissant to Fenton, Edwardsville to O’Fallon — you already know the listings don’t add up.
Here’s the thing: they don’t add up because they’re not describing the same market. Some of those postings are real St. Louis jobs at real St. Louis companies. Others are national remote roles wearing a St. Louis costume, benchmarked to coastal salaries you will rarely see from a local employer.
This guide separates the two — with real government wage data for our metro, the honest gap between national medians and local offers, who actually hires marketers here, and the doors (some of them literal, with name tags and free appetizers) that get people hired.
### What Marketing Jobs in St. Louis Actually Pay
Start with the most reliable numbers available: the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics wage survey for the St. Louis metro area. In its most recent published metro table, the BLS counted about 6,960 marketing specialists and market research analysts working in greater St. Louis at a mean wage of $78,660, and about 2,330 marketing managers at a mean of $136,680. Public relations specialists — a close cousin — averaged $73,450 across roughly 3,780 jobs.
Marketing specialist / market research analyst: ~$78,660 mean (about 6,960 jobs in the metro)
Marketing manager: ~$136,680 mean (about 2,330 jobs)
Advertising & promotions manager: ~$81,930 mean (a small field — only about 170 jobs)
Public relations specialist: ~$73,450 mean (about 3,780 jobs)
Those are averages across all experience levels, pulled up by senior people — not starting offers. Look at what employers are actually posting and the picture gets more grounded: Indeed pegs the average St. Louis marketing manager posting around $81,000, and ZipRecruiter’s middle range for the same title runs roughly $58,000 to $95,000. For marketing specialists, current local postings commonly land in the $40,000–$69,000 band. (Sources: BLS OEWS, St. Louis MSA; Indeed; ZipRecruiter.)
One more number worth knowing: nationally, the median marketing manager earns about $161,030 per the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook. Which brings us to the trap.
### The Remote-Listing Trap
Search “marketing jobs St. Louis” on any national board and you’ll see six-figure director and VP roles that seem wildly out of step with the local numbers above. Most aren’t St. Louis jobs at all — they’re remote-national roles at companies headquartered in San Francisco, New York, or Denver, shown to you because remote listings render in every city’s search results. The pay is real, but you’re competing against the entire country for it, and the company has no St. Louis office, no local network, and no local ladder.
The remote market is also smaller than the listings make it feel. Staffing firm Robert Half analyzed 376,200 U.S. marketing and creative postings and found only about 21% advertised as hybrid — and across all occupations, only around 12% of new postings are fully remote (Robert Half research). Apply to remote roles if they fit — just don’t let a $230K remote listing convince you a $75K offer from a solid Clayton employer is an insult. In a metro where the cost of living sits well below the national average, that local offer often lives better.
### Who Actually Hires Marketers in St. Louis
The good news: this metro has an unusually deep bench of major employers with real, local marketing teams. Greater St. Louis is home to a long list of Fortune 1000 headquarters (Greater St. Louis, Inc.), and most of them market consumer or business brands at national scale from right here: (For the full tour of the metro’s corporate giants — who they are and where they sit — see our top companies in St. Louis guide.)
Consumer brands: Anheuser-Busch (Soulard), Nestlé Purina (downtown), Post Holdings, Energizer, Build-A-Bear (downtown)
Healthcare & insurance: Centene, BJC Health System — the largest private employer in Missouri — and Mercy
Finance & B2B: Edward Jones, Enterprise Mobility, Emerson (Clayton), RGA (Chesterfield), World Wide Technology (Maryland Heights), Graybar, Bunge
On the agency side, be honest with yourself about the landscape: the traditional ad-agency world here has consolidated hard. Rodgers Townsend — for years one of the city’s biggest shops — closed its doors in 2024. Independent shops like HLK (downtown, founded 1977) and Obata are still working, and healthcare-marketing specialists maintain a presence here, but agency seats are fewer than they were a decade ago. Brand-side and healthcare-side is where most of the local headcount lives now.
And demand is genuinely there: as of mid-2026, Indeed alone listed over 1,200 marketing jobs in the St. Louis area, with LinkedIn showing 400+ at the entry level.
### Where the Jobs Sit on the Map
Marketing work here clusters in a handful of corridors, and knowing them helps you target a commute you can live with. Downtown holds consumer-brand headquarters — Nestlé Purina on Chouteau, Build-A-Bear on 18th Street — with Anheuser-Busch just south in Soulard. Clayton is corporate territory, anchored by Emerson. West County stacks up quickly: Edward Jones’s sprawling campus, RGA out in Chesterfield, and World Wide Technology’s headquarters at Westport Plaza in Maryland Heights. Centene sits in Clayton and north county; BJC and the medical-center marketing teams concentrate in the Central West End. And the Metro East is not empty — regional healthcare systems, banks, and manufacturers across Edwardsville, Belleville, and O’Fallon, Illinois all staff their own marketing seats.
One underrated pocket: small business. Beyond the Fortune 1000 names, thousands of St. Louis-area small companies — contractors, medical practices, restaurants groups, professional firms — hire their first in-house marketer once word-of-mouth stops scaling. These jobs rarely make the national boards. They show up on company sites, in chamber newsletters, and through referrals, which is exactly why the networking rooms below punch above their weight.
### The Two-Rung Ladder: Specialist, Then Manager
Nationally, the BLS projects marketing manager roles to grow about 6% and market research/marketing specialist roles about 7% through 2034 — both faster than average, with a combined 120,000+ openings a year (BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook). The practical read for St. Louis: the specialist tier is where the volume is — nearly 7,000 metro jobs versus 2,330 manager seats — so plan your first three to five years there, building a portfolio of measurable wins, then compete for the manager tier where the pay jumps sharply.
Skills that move you up the ladder here are the same ones employers list everywhere: analytics and reporting you can actually defend, hands-on experience with a major CRM or automation platform, and increasingly, fluency with AI tools as an accelerant rather than a novelty. Certifications in Google Analytics or HubSpot won’t land a job alone, but they get resumes past filters.
### How People Actually Get Hired Here
St. Louis is a warm-introduction town. Two organizations put working marketers in the same room regularly, and both are active right now:
AMA Saint Louis — the local American Marketing Association chapter runs regular networking events and an annual “Art & Science of Marketing” conference.
AAF-STL — the Advertising Club of Greater St. Louis, host of the annual American Advertising Awards show, where the region’s creative community gathers in one building.
Beyond the name-tag circuit: tailor every application to the posting, lead your resume with numbers (“grew email list 40%” beats “managed email marketing”), and build a portfolio even if your current title isn’t “marketing” — a campaign you ran for a family business or a nonprofit counts. If you’re starting from zero, our guide to St. Louis entry-level jobs covers adjacent first rungs, and the broader 9 best jobs near St. Louis shows how marketing pay compares to other local careers.

### Search Beyond the Word “Marketing”

Communications specialist / coordinator — common at hospitals, universities, and nonprofits, and often marketing in everything but name

Brand manager — the consumer-products ladder at places like Purina and Post
Demand generation, growth, lifecycle — the tech-company dialect for revenue-side marketing, common at WWT and the software firms
Development or membership coordinator — the nonprofit world’s version, and a genuine portfolio-builder
Recruiters filter by titles; job seekers who search by skills find the postings their competitors never see. Set one alert per title above and let the boards prove it to you within a week.
### A Week-One Search Plan
If you’re starting cold, here’s a first week that beats a hundred scattershot applications:
Day 1: Set alerts on Indeed, LinkedIn, Glassdoor, and Built In for “marketing specialist,” “marketing coordinator,” and “marketing manager” within 25 miles. Let the boards work for you overnight.
Day 2: Build a target list of ten local employers from the names above, and bookmark each careers page — many post there before (or instead of) the boards.
Day 3: Check the AMA Saint Louis and AAF-STL calendars and register for the next event on either one. A name tag beats a cover letter.
Day 4: Assemble a one-page portfolio — three campaigns or projects with a number attached to each. If you don’t have three, that’s this month’s assignment, not a disqualification.
Day 5: Send three informational-interview requests to St. Louis marketers on LinkedIn — alumni of your school first. Ask about their path, not for a job. The jobs follow.
Repeat the rhythm weekly: applications go out steadily, but the compounding returns come from the target list, the rooms, and the conversations. For the wider toolkit — workforce agencies, library job clubs, and every free metro resource — see our St. Louis local-jobs roadmap.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the average salary for a marketing specialist in St. Louis, MO?
A.  Posting platforms put it in the mid-$60,000s — Indeed’s current figure is about $67,324 — while the BLS metro survey, which includes senior specialists, shows a mean of $78,660. A realistic read: entry offers commonly start around $40,000–$50,000, mid-career specialists cluster in the $60,000s–$70,000s.
### Q. Which marketing job pays the most?
A.  Management. Marketing managers in the St. Louis metro average about $136,680 per the BLS — roughly $58,000 more than the specialist tier — and director and VP roles at the region’s Fortune 1000 headquarters climb from there. The catch is scarcity: the metro has roughly one manager seat for every three specialist jobs.
### Q. Is it hard to get a marketing job right now?
A.  The honest answer: entry and coordinator level is crowded — popular postings draw large applicant pools — but the field itself is growing faster than average, with the BLS projecting 6–7% growth through 2034. Candidates who show measurable results and a real portfolio, and who network through groups like AMA Saint Louis, consistently outperform resume-blasters.
### Q. Are marketing jobs still in demand?
A.  Yes — the BLS projects both marketing manager (+6%) and marketing specialist (+7%) roles to grow faster than the average occupation through 2034, and the local boards bear it out: over 1,200 St. Louis-area marketing listings on Indeed alone as of mid-2026. What has changed is the skill mix — employers increasingly expect analytics fluency and comfort with AI-assisted tools alongside the creative fundamentals.
### Q. What is considered a good salary in St. Louis?
A.  Because the metro’s cost of living sits well below the national average, salaries stretch further here than the raw number suggests. A mid-career marketing specialist income in the $60,000s–$70,000s supports a comfortable life in most of the metro, and a marketing manager’s six-figure income here buys what considerably more would on either coast.

### Q. What is the highest paying job in St. Louis?
A.  Physicians and specialists top every local pay list — anesthesiologists, surgeons, and other medical specialists routinely clear $200,000 a year in the metro. Outside medicine, the biggest paychecks cluster in executive management, actuarial and finance leadership, and senior software or cybersecurity roles at employers like Mastercard, Edward Jones, and World Wide Technology.
### Q. How can I make $100,000 a year without a college degree?
A.  In St. Louis, the realistic no-degree paths run through the skilled trades and logistics: experienced CDL-A drivers on the right routes, journeyman electricians and plumbers, elevator mechanics, A-level automotive technicians, and commission sales roles can all reach six figures. None of it is guaranteed — these paths trade a degree for years of licensure, apprenticeship, and hustle.
### Q. What is the happiest 6-figure job?
A.  Surveys consistently point to technology roles — software engineering and data science — where autonomy, problem-solving, and flexible schedules drive satisfaction alongside the salary. In St. Louis specifically, those roles come with a bonus: six-figure tech pay stretches much further against the metro’s below-average cost of living.

### What to Expect in Your First Interview
If you've never been through a job interview before, or if it's been so long that you can barely remember the experience, let me walk you through what to expect so you can feel prepared rather than nervous.
Picture yourself walking into a clean, professional office where you can smell fresh coffee and hear the quiet hum of productive work happening. The interviewer will likely greet you with a warm handshake and a smile, trying to put you at ease because they want you to succeed. They're not looking for reasons to reject you - they're hoping you'll be the perfect fit for their team.
Most interviews follow a predictable pattern. You'll start with small talk to help everyone relax, then move into questions about your background, experience, and interest in the position. The interviewer cares less about your task list and more about how you think, solve problems, and work with others.
Common questions include variations of “Tell me about yourself,” “Why are you interested in this position,” and “Describe a challenge you've faced and how you handled it.” These aren't trick questions - they're opportunities for you to share your story and help the interviewer understand what you'd bring to their team.
You'll also have the chance to ask questions, which is actually one of the most important parts of the interview. This is when you can demonstrate your genuine interest in the role and the company. Ask about training opportunities, team dynamics, or what success looks like in the position.
### What to Expect in Your Next Resume
If you haven't written a resume in several years - or maybe decades - the process might feel completely different from what you remember. Modern resumes focus more on accomplishments and results rather than just listing job duties and responsibilities.
Today's employers want to see what you've achieved, not the duties you were handed. Instead of saying “Responsible for customer service,” you might write “Resolved customer issues with 95% satisfaction rate, resulting in increased repeat business and positive reviews.”
The format might feel unfamiliar too. Many modern resumes include a professional summary at the top that gives hiring managers a quick snapshot of your qualifications. You might see skills sections that highlight technical competencies, or achievement sections that showcase quantifiable results from your work experience.
If this feels overwhelming, remember that professional resume services exist specifically to help people navigate these changes. They can help you translate your experience - whether it's from decades ago or from non-traditional work like volunteering, parenting, or military service - into a document that makes hiring managers excited to meet you.
### Building Confidence Through Preparation

If you can tell your professional story to a friend over coffee, you can tell it to a hiring manager in an interview.
Remember that employers are looking for people who can do the job and fit well with their team. You don't need to be perfect - you just need to be genuine, prepared, and enthusiastic about the opportunity to contribute to their organization.

## The Best Free Local Business Listing Sites (and How to Use Them Right)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/top-10-free-local-listing-sites-to-boost-your-business-in-2025
Refreshed September 2026
Most “top 10” listing posts hand you a long checklist and call it a strategy. This one runs in the right order instead. First, the list you came for: the free listing sites that actually matter in 2026, and how to use each one. Then the part those roundups skip: why a short, consistent list beats a long one, which sites to ignore, and where all of this fits in a real St. Louis growth plan.
Short version: you don’t need to be on 50 directories. You need to be on a handful that actually feed the search-and-AI ecosystem — with identical information on every one. Ten accurate, consistent listings beat a hundred half-filled, contradictory ones every time. Below are the free sites worth your time, in rough order of impact. Get these right and stop chasing the rest.
### Why a Short, Consistent List Wins
The old advice was “submit your business to as many directories as possible.” That’s a relic. Citation volume barely moves the needle anymore — an analysis of thousands of sites found that appearing in hundreds of directories barely out-performed appearing in none (Near Media). What matters now is consistency: the same name, address, and phone (your “NAP”) on every platform that counts. Every extra no-name directory is one more place your information can drift out of date and start contradicting the others — which actively hurts you. So the goal isn’t a long list. It’s a right list, kept identical everywhere. Quick gut-check: if you searched your own business name right now, would every listing agree — or would the mismatches quietly tell Google you’re not quite who you claim to be?
### The Best Free Local Business Listing Sites in 2026
Here are the ones genuinely worth claiming, and what each one does for you:
Google Business Profile — start here, full stop. This is the single biggest lever in local search: it controls how you appear in Google Search, Google Maps, and the local “3-pack.” Claim it at google.com/business, verify, and fill in everything — categories, hours, service area, photos, and regular posts. If you do only one thing on this list, do this.
Bing Places for Business — free, and it feeds AI. Bing’s local data powers Microsoft Copilot, Edge’s AI answers, and DuckDuckGo — and Yahoo Search runs on Bing too. Claim it at bingplaces.com and, in two clicks, import it straight from your Google Business Profile. One of the highest-value ten minutes you can spend.
Apple Business — don’t forget the iPhone crowd. Every “near me” search on an iPhone runs through Apple Maps and Siri. Apple Business (formerly Apple Business; business.apple.com) is free and lets you control your Apple Maps place card — name, hours, photos, and offers. For a huge share of mobile customers, this is your storefront.
Yelp — still matters, and it feeds others. Beyond its own traffic, Yelp supplies business data and reviews to Yahoo and Apple Maps. Claim your page at biz.yelp.com, complete it, and never fake a review — but do make it easy for happy customers to leave real ones. A strong Yelp profile does quiet double duty across the web.
Facebook Business Page — free reach and social proof. A complete Facebook Page is a free listing that shows up in search, gives customers a familiar place to check you out, and collects recommendations. Keep the NAP identical to your other listings and post enough to look active.
Nextdoor Business Page — the hyper-local one. Nextdoor is where neighbors ask “who do you recommend for…” every single day. A free business page puts you in those neighborhood conversations — especially powerful for home services, and for anyone whose customers are literally down the street.
A strong local directory — the location-centric anchor. A well-run local directory (for St. Louis, that’s St Louis Near Me Directory) reinforces your NAP and puts you in front of people specifically searching your metro, not the whole country. More on why this one punches above its weight in a moment.
That’s the core. Notice what it is: the platforms that own the maps, the search engines, the AI assistants, the reviews, and the neighborhood — plus a local anchor. Cover those with identical information and you’ve done 95% of what listings can do for you. The other 5% is industry-specific — the two or three directories that matter for your trade.
### What to Skip
Just as useful as knowing where to list is knowing where not to spend your time. Skip pay-to-blast services that promise to “submit your business to 500 directories” — volume was never the point, and half those sites are ghost towns that only create more places for your info to go stale. Skip obscure, no-name directories with no real traffic and no data relationships; a listing there does nothing but add maintenance risk. The Better Business Bureau, Foursquare and Manta come up on almost every “best free listing sites” roundup, so they deserve a straight answer. Foursquare is the one worth ten minutes: its location data still feeds a long list of apps and devices that never ask you directly, so a correct record there quietly fixes your address in places you would never think to check. A BBB profile is free to claim and buys credibility with a certain kind of customer — but accreditation is a paid membership, and paying for it is a reputation decision, not an SEO one. Manta is a general B2B directory that costs nothing to claim and does very little; claim it for the citation, then forget it. None of the three belongs ahead of the core list above. General directories like EZlocal and Cylex are legitimate and free to claim, but treat them as minor extras, not a substitute for the core list — and the old print Yellow Pages is a legacy channel, not a strategy. And be wary of anyone selling a “Yahoo listing” or similar — you can usually get that coverage for free by claiming Yelp and Bing. If a site isn’t on the core list above and can’t explain what ecosystem it feeds, it’s probably not worth the ten minutes.
### The Honest Verdict, at a Glance
### What Actually Moves Your Ranking
Listings are table stakes, not the game. Rank the work honestly and it comes out like this: the Google Business Profile does the heavy lifting; real reviews, arriving steadily rather than in one old cluster, do the next most; and a name, address, and phone that agree across the places that count does the rest (a well-documented edge in the local pack, per Whitespark, 2026). The sites above serve all three — they are the raw material consistency gets built from. But it is the reviews and the Google profile that convert a listing into a ringing phone, and no amount of listing volume substitutes for either.
And here’s the math these roundups never show you: listings do not pay off evenly. The second one is worth a great deal — it’s the first time two independent sources agree on your name, address, and phone, and that agreement is the entire signal. The sixth still helps. The twenty-sixth is doing something close to nothing. The fiftieth is a login you’ll forget, on a site you’ll never revisit, holding a phone number that will eventually be wrong. The return curve flattens fast; the risk curve doesn’t, because every additional listing is one more place your information can quietly go stale while you assume it’s working for you. That’s why the list above is short on purpose. Six finished profiles beat thirty opened ones, and it isn’t close.

### The 3 Mistakes That Make Listings Backfire
None of this is difficult. It just rewards a little discipline, and punishes three habits in particular. One: opening accounts instead of finishing them. A profile with no hours, no categories, and no photos is a placeholder with your phone number on it, and it competes with your real presence in the results. Finish the sites above — every field, every hour, real photos — before you go looking for a seventh. Two: treating a listing as finished. Hours change at holidays. Suites get renumbered. Numbers get ported. A short list is only an advantage if you actually revisit it — and six sites is few enough that a twice-a-year pass over all of them takes one coffee. Three: chasing quantity over quality. Ten accurate, consistent listings on the sites that matter beat a hundred half-filled ones on sites nobody uses. Depth on the core list beats a scattershot blast every time.
### How to Keep It All Consistent (the Part Everyone Skips)
Claiming the listings is the easy afternoon; keeping them aligned is the quiet work that actually pays off. Start by writing down your business details once — the exact name, the exact address format (decide “Suite” vs. “Ste.” and never waver), the exact phone number, your hours, and your primary categories — and treat that as the master copy every listing must match. When anything changes — a new phone line, a move, new holiday hours — update the master copy first, then walk it across every platform the same day, because a half-updated set of listings is exactly the contradiction that confuses search engines. Set a reminder to spot-check your core listings a couple of times a year; five minutes of maintenance prevents the slow drift that quietly buries a business. And where a platform lets you sync — like importing Bing from Google — use it, so you’re maintaining one source of truth instead of six.

Work the short list — Google, Bing, Apple, Yelp, Facebook, Nextdoor — with identical information, then anchor it locally. A verified listing on St Louis Near Me Directory is the local anchor at the end of that short list — the one that ties the other five together by carrying the same name, address, and phone, and the one that puts you in front of a homeowner in Oakville looking for a handyman rather than a shopper three states away. It’s also what AI assistants reach for when the question is local. The national platforms make you findable. A local listing makes you the answer. You want both. And the highest-return move here isn’t adding a seventh site — it’s going back to the six and finishing every field on each one: hours, categories, real photos, a current phone number, and the same address characters throughout. Most businesses that feel invisible aren’t missing listings at all; they’re carrying six half-built ones.

## Your Old Half-Page Ad Is Propping Open a Garage Door in Mehlville
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/7-essential-free-business-listing-yellow-pages-for-2025-success
Your shop phone sits on the counter, quiet. Across town, a woman in the Schnucks parking lot, engine running, a dishwasher leaking onto her kitchen floor at home, says “plumber near me” to her phone. Whoever the map shows in the next four seconds gets the call.
Your old half-page ad? It’s propping open a garage door in Mehlville.
Remember the thud of that book on the front porch, the rubber band, the pages so thin they tore if you flipped too fast? Getting “in the book” was the whole marketing plan. A bold-print line if you felt flush. A half-page ad if you felt brave. Then you waited for the phone on the wall to ring.
Now even the Yellow Pages has given up on paper. The company that owns it agreed to sell the print book for $142 million and keep only the website.
Tonight, before you close the laptop: search your trade plus your suburb on your phone the way she would, say “roofer Kirkwood” or “florist Florissant,” and count the reviews and photos on the three businesses the map shows against yours. Then claim the free listings that feed most phones: your Google Business Profile first, then Bing Places, which can import your Google profile in a few clicks and also feeds Microsoft’s Copilot answers, then Apple Maps through Apple Business Connect. Two of the three take less time than this article.
Still paying for a print ad? Find one date this week. Open your print-directory contract and look for the words “Close Date.” In one major publisher’s current standard agreement, if the publisher doesn’t receive your written cancellation by that date, it may renew your ad for the next issue, which typically runs 18 to 24 months, at the then-current undiscounted rate. That same kind of clause makes finding the date your job. Call the customer-care number printed on your contract, ask for the Close Date on your directory, and circle it on the calendar.
St. Louis has lived through a split like this once. In 1897 the city got a second phone company, Kinloch, and for more than two decades its lines didn’t connect to Bell’s. A Kinloch customer couldn’t call a Bell subscriber.
So a shop that wanted every customer kept two phones on the counter, one of each, until Southwestern Bell bought Kinloch in 1923.
Today the networks are Google, Apple Maps, Bing and ChatGPT, and nobody sent a notice when the switch happened. When your next customer asks her phone, which phone is on your counter? The happy difference from 1923: joining every network is free.
Here’s the part the old ad reps never had a reason to tell you. Even the company that owns the Yellow Pages doesn’t want the book anymore, and almost every listing that matters now is free. The book charged you by the size of your ad. Google Business Profile, Apple Maps and Bing Places charge nothing. The only people still charging you for a spot in the new book are the ones selling ads around it.
The rule nobody mailed you: the old book rewarded bigger and bolder, so the habit makes sense. Google plays it the other way. Its own guidelines say extra words in the name field, like “Joe’s Plumbing, Best Plumber St. Louis,” can get a free profile suspended. The name painted on your truck is all it wants.
Then run the index-card test before that Close Date. For one month, tape a card by the phone, ask every new caller “how’d you hear about us?” and make a tick mark under the answer. If “the book” gets fewer ticks than Google, you have your answer, and your budget back.

If the old goal was to be “in the book,” the new goal is to be complete and consistent across a handful of free platforms.

This is why the old “get listed on 500 sites” pitch backfires: it multiplies inconsistency across junk directories. A tight, perfectly consistent set of listings is far more powerful than a sprawling, sloppy one. Before you add a new listing, make sure the ones you already have all agree.
