## How to Remove a Google Review (Mostly You Can't - Here's What Works)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-remove-a-google-review
### Can you actually remove a Google review?
Almost never, if you are the business. That is the honest answer, and it is not the one most of page one is selling. Which raises the question worth more than the removal itself: if you can’t delete it, what can you do that the next customer will actually see?
A business owner cannot delete a customer’s review. There is no button, no account level, no support tier that grants it. You can report a review to Google for violating its content policies, and Google decides. Only two parties can actually remove a review: the person who wrote it, and Google.
Search the question and you will find the flag-button instructions repeated a dozen ways, alongside companies promising permanent removal on a no-win-no-fee basis. What none of page one mentions is that this whole area became federally regulated in October 2024, and some of what gets sold as review management is now the kind of conduct the FTC can fine you for.
So this page covers three things in order: what genuinely works, what the new rule changed, and the thing that outperforms removal anyway.
### What actually gets a review taken down
Google removes reviews that break its content policies — not reviews that are unfair, wrong, or written by someone having a bad day. That distinction is the whole game, and it is why most reports fail.
Reportable, broadly: spam and fake engagement, content posted by someone with a conflict of interest, off-topic content that is not about a customer experience, profanity and harassment, impersonation, and personal information. A competitor review-bombing you, a review that is plainly about a different business, an ex-employee’s rant, five one-star ratings from accounts created the same afternoon — those are policy arguments and worth making.
Not reportable: “this is unfair,” “they misremembered,” “we did nothing wrong,” or a one-star rating with no text. A negative opinion from a real customer is exactly what the platform is for, and no amount of escalating gets it removed.
To report one: open your Google Business Profile, go to reviews, find it, use the three-dot menu, choose to report it, and pick the policy it violates. Then screenshot everything — the review, the profile of who wrote it, the date — because if you escalate later, the review may already be edited.
Pick the specific policy, not the closest emotional match. “This review is spam because the account has posted identical text on four unrelated businesses today” is a reviewable claim. “This review is unfair” is not.
### What changed in October 2024, and why it matters more than the flag button
The FTC’s Rule on the Use of Consumer Reviews and Testimonials took effect on October 21, 2024, passed on a 5–0 vote. It is the first time the agency has had civil penalty authority here, and the numbers are not symbolic: up to $51,744 per violation for knowing violators, plus consumer restitution.
What it prohibits, in plain terms:
Fake reviews and testimonials — written by people who never used the business, or by AI, presented as genuine.
Buying reviews, positive or negative. Both directions. Paying for a rival’s bad reviews is squarely covered.
Incentivizing reviews that express a particular sentiment — conditioning a reward on the review being positive.
Undisclosed insider reviews, including from officers and managers, that do not clearly and conspicuously disclose the connection. Your manager reviewing your business without saying so is now a rule problem, not just bad taste.
Review suppression — using unfounded legal threats, intimidation, or similar pressure to force a review down, or presenting your displayed reviews as if they were all the reviews when negative ones have been withheld.
Read that last one against how review removal is often sold. A service promising that bad reviews will “disappear in seven days” is either flagging genuine policy violations, which you can do yourself for free, or doing something else. If the something else involves pressuring reviewers, you are the client whose name is on it.
To be clear, because the opposite reading would be worse: reporting a review that genuinely violates Google’s policies is completely legitimate. Nothing in the rule discourages that. The line is between contesting content on the platform and leaning on a human being to retract it.
### When the reviewer was never a customer
This is the most common version of the problem for small businesses, and it is genuinely maddening: reviews from people who were never there. Sometimes it is mistaken identity — two businesses with similar names in the metro, and the reviewer picked the wrong pin. Sometimes it is a competitor. Sometimes it is one person with several accounts.
Mistaken identity is the most fixable, because it is provable. Say so plainly in your public response — “we have no record of this visit and we think you may have us confused with a similarly named business on Manchester” — and report it as off-topic. Reviewers often delete these themselves once they realize, and a reviewer deleting their own review is the fastest removal available.
Coordinated fake reviews are harder but more reportable. Document the pattern before you file: account ages, whether the same phrasing appears elsewhere, whether they arrived in a cluster. A pattern is a policy argument. A single suspicious review is just a claim.
If a review contains a factual assertion that is false and damaging — not an opinion, an assertion — that is a legal question, and it is one for a Missouri attorney rather than an article. Be aware that legal threats made without a real basis are exactly what the suppression provision addresses, so this is not a bluff to make casually.
### When it is not one review but twenty
A coordinated attack is a different problem from a bad review, and it needs a different response. Go and read what small business owners are actually posting about this and the pattern is always the same: several one-star ratings arriving together, from accounts that look new, sometimes all carrying the same person’s name, occasionally tied to someone impersonating the business entirely.
The instinct is to reply to each one. Do not. Ten defensive replies in a row is a wall of noise that makes the profile look worse than the ratings did, and it buries the real reviews underneath.
Do this instead:
Document the whole cluster before you touch anything. Screenshot every review with its date and the reviewer’s profile. Note account ages, how many other reviews each account has posted, whether the wording repeats, and how tightly the timestamps group. That collection is your case. Individually these look like opinions; together they look like coordination, and coordination is a policy violation.
Report them as a pattern, not as twenty separate grievances. Each report should point at the same specific policy and describe the cluster, because a reviewer of your report needs to see the shape of it to act.
Respond once, publicly, to the most visible one. Calm, factual, no accusations you cannot support: that you have no record of these visits, that you have reported the activity, and how a real customer can reach you. Readers can tell the difference between a business under attack and a business with a problem — but only if you sound like the former.
If someone is impersonating your business — spoofing your number, using your name on another listing — that is a separate and more serious report, and worth raising with Google as impersonation rather than burying it in a review complaint.
Expect this to take weeks rather than days, and expect partial results. Some come down, some do not, and some return later. That is genuinely frustrating and it is still better than the alternative of paying someone to pressure the people who wrote them.
### The response is worth more than the removal
Here is the part owners resist and then find true.
Your reply is not for the person who wrote the review. It is for the next several hundred people who read it while deciding whether to call you. That audience is not judging whether the complaint was fair — they are judging how you behave when something goes wrong, which is precisely what they are worried about before hiring a stranger.
A good reply is short, specific, unemotional, and offers a way to resolve it offline. It does not relitigate, does not blame the customer, and does not sound like a form letter. A defensive paragraph confirms every fear the reader arrived with; a calm two-line response quietly disproves it.
And a business with a wall of unbroken five-star reviews reads as suspicious to a lot of people now. A handful of imperfect reviews with thoughtful responses is a stronger signal than perfection, because perfection is what bought reviews look like.
Unrelated, and we know it — dinner in Ellisville beats arguing with strangers online.
### Before you pay anyone
Ask three questions of any removal service, and take the silence as an answer:
What specific policy will you cite? If they cannot name one, they are not doing the thing you can do free.
Will you contact the reviewer? If yes, ask exactly what will be said. This is where the suppression rule lives.
What happens if Google reinstates it? Reviews come back. “Permanent” is a marketing word.
For most St. Louis businesses the honest sequence is: report the ones that genuinely break policy, respond well to the ones that do not, and put the remaining energy into being findable in the first place. One bad review among many recent, real ones is close to invisible. One bad review on a profile with four total reviews is the whole picture.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it possible to remove Google reviews?
A.  Only two parties can remove one: the author, and Google. A business owner cannot delete a review, only report it for violating Google’s content policies. Reviews that break a policy — spam, conflict of interest, off-topic, harassment, impersonation — can come down. Reviews that are merely negative or unfair will not.
### Q. How do I delete someone else's review?
A.  You cannot delete it, only report it. In your Google Business Profile, open reviews, use the three-dot menu on the review, choose to report it, and select the specific policy it violates. Screenshot everything first. Naming the exact policy and the evidence for it matters far more than how strongly you word the complaint.
### Q. How do I remove a negative review?
A.  If it is negative but genuine, you generally cannot, and that is by design. Report it only if it actually breaches a policy. Otherwise the productive move is a short, calm public reply offering to resolve it — which is read by future customers rather than by the reviewer, and does more for you than removal would.
### Q. Can I delete a review I wrote?
A.  Yes. Open Google Maps signed in, go to your contributions, then reviews, find it, and choose to edit or delete. This is also the fastest route when a reviewer has confused your business with another — point it out politely in your response and they will often remove it themselves.
### Q. How much does it cost to have a Google review removed?
A.  Reporting a policy-violating review costs nothing and you can do it yourself. Paid removal services charge per review, often on a no-win-no-fee basis, and what you are buying is someone filing the same report you could file. Before paying, ask which specific policy they intend to cite.
### Q. Can you hire someone to remove bad Google reviews?
A.  Services exist, but be careful what you are buying. Since October 21, 2024 the FTC’s consumer reviews rule prohibits review suppression — including using unfounded threats or intimidation to force a review down — with civil penalties up to $51,744 per violation for knowing violators. Legitimately reporting a policy breach is fine. Pressuring a reviewer is not, and it is your business name attached.

## St. Louis Hotels with Indoor Pools: The Verified List by Area
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-st-louis-top-hotels-with-indoor-pools-for-year-round-fun
Picture a gray St. Louis Saturday in February. The kids are bouncing off the walls, the forecast is hopeless, and everyone needs to burn energy somewhere warm. Or maybe it’s a July scorcher and the last thing anyone wants is a sun-baked outdoor deck. Either way, the answer is the same: a hotel with a real, heated, indoor pool — open year-round, weather be damned, and ready whether it’s a snow day or a heat wave outside.
An indoor pool is quietly one of the most useful things a hotel can offer a family. It turns a rained-out afternoon into the highlight of the trip, tires the kids out before bed, and gives everyone a reason to stay put after a long day of sightseeing. It’s also a genuine year-round amenity in a city that swings from icy Januaries to swampy Julys — the water’s the same perfect temperature either way.
The catch is that plenty of hotel listings blur “pool” and “indoor pool,” and a family can arrive to find a seasonal outdoor deck that’s closed for the season. So here’s a local’s guide to St. Louis-metro hotels with confirmed year-round indoor pools, sorted by area, plus a quick honest list of popular hotels whose pools are outdoor-only — so you book the right one the first time.
### St. Louis Hotels With Confirmed Indoor Pools, by Area
### Downtown: Pool Plus Everything Within Walking Distance
If you want a swim and the Arch, the ballpark, and City Museum on foot, downtown delivers. The Drury Plaza Hotel St. Louis at the Arch has a year-round indoor pool plus two whirlpools, and it stacks Drury’s trademark free hot breakfast and free evening food and drinks on top — a genuinely good family value a short walk from Busch Stadium and the Gateway Arch. Nearby, the Hilton St. Louis at the Ballpark keeps a climate-controlled indoor pool in a glass atrium, with views toward the Arch and the ballpark, right across from Ballpark Village.
One important correction for downtown: the St. Louis Union Station Hotel is a wonderful, historic place to stay, but its pool is a seasonal outdoor one, not an indoor pool — so if a winter swim is the goal, steer to the Drury or the Hilton instead.
### Forest Park: Pool After the Zoo and the Museums
The Forest Park area is the sweet spot for families, because you can pair the free Saint Louis Zoo, Science Center, and Art Museum with an indoor pool for the after-nap wind-down. The Drury Inn & Suites St. Louis Forest Park has a heated year-round indoor/outdoor pool and a hot tub, plus the usual free Drury extras. And the Hampton Inn & Suites St. Louis at Forest Park — the closest hotel to the zoo with an indoor pool — adds a hot tub and free hot breakfast. Both put you minutes from the park, so the kids can chase penguins in the morning and cannonball in the afternoon — the ideal family one-two punch.
### Clayton: A Quieter, Upscale Home Base
For a calmer, more upscale base a few miles west, the Clayton Plaza Hotel & Extended Stay runs a year-round heated pool and offers extended-stay suites — handy for longer trips or families who want a bit more room and a kitchen. Clayton itself is a walkable district of restaurants and shops, and you’re a short drive from Forest Park and the zoo. (Note: some older listings still show a “Sheraton” or “Crowne Plaza” name for this property; the current brand is the independent Clayton Plaza Hotel & Extended Stay.)
### West County: Chesterfield and Creve Coeur
Out in West County, indoor-pool options are plentiful. The Drury Plaza Hotel St. Louis Chesterfield has a heated year-round indoor/outdoor pool; Hyatt Place St. Louis/Chesterfield keeps an indoor pool open daily; and the Drury Inn & Suites St. Louis Creve Coeur offers a heated indoor pool and a large jacuzzi. This area is convenient to Chesterfield’s shopping and the Creve Coeur/Maryland Heights corridor — a good pick if your trip centers on the west side of the metro rather than downtown. (One to skip if you need indoor: Homewood Suites Chesterfield’s pool is outdoor and seasonal.)
### By the Airport: Easy Flights, Warm Water
If you’re flying in and out, or just want an easy in-and-out stay, the airport cluster in Bridgeton has solid indoor pools. The Embassy Suites by Hilton St. Louis Airport has an indoor pool, all-suite rooms, free made-to-order breakfast, and a free airport shuttle; the Renaissance St. Louis Airport Hotel offers a year-round indoor/outdoor pool and its own free shuttle. Both make an early flight painless and still give the kids a swim the night before.
### St. Charles: History Plus a Swim
The Ameristar resort tower in St. Charles — note its pool is seasonal. Photographed by Lane Forman, July 26, 2026.
Across the Missouri River, historic St. Charles pairs its charming brick Main Street with a reliable indoor-pool option: the Embassy Suites by Hilton St. Louis St. Charles has an indoor pool and whirlpool, all-suite rooms, and free breakfast, right by the riverfront and the shops. It’s a scenic, slightly-out-of-the-way base that still keeps a warm pool on tap. (Heads-up: the Ameristar casino’s pool in St. Charles is seasonal, so don’t count on it for a winter swim.)
Zero connection to pools — go poke around DeBaliviere Place sometime.
### Across the River: Metro East, Illinois
Don’t forget the Illinois side. If you’re staying east of the river — for the casinos, a Gateway Center event, or just a cheaper base close to downtown — the Drury Inn & Suites St. Louis Fairview Heights is a reliable indoor-pool pick, with a separate indoor pool plus an outdoor pool and the usual free Drury breakfast and evening extras. It’s an easy highway hop back across to the Arch and the ballpark, and it keeps the whole metro in play for a pool weekend.
### A Quick Honesty Check: Popular Hotels That Are Outdoor-Only
Because this trips people up, here are well-known St. Louis hotels whose pools are not year-round indoor pools, so you don’t book them expecting a winter swim: the St. Louis Union Station Hotel (seasonal outdoor), Homewood Suites Chesterfield (seasonal outdoor), and the Ameristar St. Charles (seasonal). And the Hyatt Regency St. Louis at the Arch, despite some confusing listings, does not have a guest pool at all. When in doubt, the safest bet in St. Louis for a guaranteed indoor pool is a Drury or an Embassy Suites property — both chains reliably build indoor pools into their St. Louis hotels.
### How to Book a Pool Weekend That Actually Delivers
A few habits save a ruined afternoon. Confirm the pool is open when you book — call or check the hotel’s own site, since pools close for occasional maintenance or renovation. Ask “indoor or outdoor?” directly; aggregator icons don’t always distinguish. Check the hours — some indoor pools close by 10 p.m. or open only by reservation. And match the area to your trip: pick Forest Park for the zoo, downtown for the Arch and a ballgame, the airport for an early flight, and Chesterfield or St. Charles for the west and north sides of the metro. One more tip for families: ask whether the pool has a shallow end or a hot tub, and what the posted hours are — a pool that closes at 9 p.m. is little help if you don’t roll in from dinner until after that. A two-minute call before you book beats a disappointed carful of kids at check-in.
### St. Louis Tourism Is Climbing — Reserve Ahead
Demand is real: St. Louis set a tourism record in 2025, with future hotel bookings up sharply and direct visitor spending in the billions. Family-friendly indoor-pool hotels near the big draws — Forest Park and downtown especially — fill first on weekends and school breaks. If your trip depends on that pool, book as soon as your dates are set rather than hoping for a last-minute room. And because the truly close-in indoor-pool cluster is small in each area, a little lead time is the difference between the hotel you want and a longer drive to the one that’s left. Booking directly with the hotel, rather than through a third-party site, also makes it easier to confirm the pool is actually open and heated during your stay — worth a quick phone call before you commit.

## Chimi’s Fresh-Mex in Wentzville: A Family Mexican Favorite
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-the-authentic-flavors-of-chimi-s-wentzville
Imagine a Friday night in Wentzville: the workweek finally behind you, a table full of people who can’t agree on anything except that they want tacos and a good margarita. There’s a family-run spot right off the Wentzville Center that has quietly become the answer to exactly that — Chimi’s Fresh-Mex, the kind of place that settles the “where do you want to eat” debate before it even gets going.
Maybe a coworker in Lake Saint Louis swears by the fajitas. Maybe you’ve driven past it a dozen times and never stopped. Either way, this is an honest look at what Chimi’s is, what to order, and where to find it — a genuinely local Mexican kitchen that has grown across the St. Louis region without losing the family behind it. In a stretch of the metro dominated by familiar franchise signs, that’s worth knowing about, because the independent, family-run places are usually the ones actually worth the drive.
### What Chimi’s Fresh-Mex actually is
Chimi’s Fresh-Mex is a St. Louis-area family-owned local chain — run by the Casillas family — serving fresh, made-to-order Mexican food. That “Fresh-Mex” label is the key: this is fresh, from-the-kitchen Mexican rather than heavy, gloppy Tex-Mex. The Wentzville location is one of several across the metro, from St. Charles County out into St. Louis County, and each carries the same menu and the same family standards.
One quick note to avoid confusion: there’s a separate, unrelated restaurant in St. Peters with a similar name. The spot in this guide is Chimi’s Fresh-Mex in Wentzville, at 8 Wentzville Center Drive — that’s the one to plug into your maps.
### What to order
The menu covers all the Mexican classics, made fresh. A few that regulars reach for:
Sizzling fajitas — steak or chicken, arriving loud and fragrant; a crowd favorite, an easy first order, and half the fun is watching the plate arrive still sizzling.
Street-style tacos — al pastor, carne asada, and more, built the simple, flavorful way with fresh toppings rather than a pile of filler, and easy to order a few of to compare.
Enchiladas and carnitas — the enchiladas verdes and the trio plate get called out often, and the carnitas are a reliable comfort order for anyone who wants something rich and slow-cooked.
Steak and shrimp — when you want a heartier plate off the grill and a bit of everything on one order.
Fresh guacamole and salsa — the fundamentals, made in-house, which is the real test of a fresh-Mex kitchen, and a good sign of everything else on the menu.
Margaritas — genuinely part of the draw, and the reason a lot of tables linger. Save room for the fried ice cream, a fun, crispy-warm finish the table always ends up sharing.
Given the “Chimi’s” name, chimichangas are a natural order too — if that’s your craving, it’s worth a quick look at the current menu or a question when you order. Menus evolve, so check what’s on offer tonight rather than counting on any one dish.
Vegetarians and lighter eaters are looked after too. Between the fresh guacamole, bean-and-cheese options, veggie fajitas, and build-your-own tacos, a meatless meal here isn’t an afterthought, which makes Chimi’s an easy call for mixed groups where one person wants a hearty steak plate and another doesn’t eat meat at all. That range — something genuinely good for everyone at the table — is a big part of why it works as a family restaurant rather than a special-occasion-only spot.

### What “Fresh-Mex” actually means here
It’s worth pausing on that name, because it sets expectations. A lot of what passes for Mexican food in the suburbs is the heavy, cheese-blanketed, everything-tastes-the-same kind. “Fresh-Mex” is a deliberate step away from that: produce that reads as produce, salsa and guacamole made in the kitchen rather than scooped from a bucket, proteins grilled to order. You can taste the difference in the small things — a squeeze of real lime, cilantro that’s actually green, a char on the fajita steak instead of a steam-table gray. It’s not fancy food, and it doesn’t pretend to be; it’s honest, well-made Mexican that respects the ingredients, which is exactly what you want from a neighborhood spot you’ll come back to on a random weeknight.
That approach is why Chimi’s works for a range of appetites at the same table. ### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. How much does the average wedding cost in St. Louis?
A.  A St. Louis wedding often runs in the low-to-mid five figures — roughly $25,000–$35,000, generally below the national average — though it swings widely with guest count and venue. The venue is usually the single biggest line item, which is why choosing among St. Louis options (from Union Station to a brewery taproom) drives most of the budget.
### Q. What is a realistic budget for a wedding?
A.  A realistic wedding budget hinges on guest count, with the venue and catering typically eating up about half of it. In St. Louis, a modest wedding is very doable for well under $20,000 with an affordable venue and a trimmed guest list, while a larger celebration at a marquee space runs $30,000 or more.
### Q. Is $10,000 enough for a wedding?
A.  Yes — $10,000 can host a St. Louis wedding if you keep the guest list tight and choose the venue wisely. Non-traditional spaces (a brewery taproom, a restaurant’s private room, a park pavilion) and off-peak dates stretch the budget furthest. The venue choice is where a smaller budget wins or loses.
### Q. Is $5,000 enough for a wedding?
A.  It’s tight but doable for an intimate St. Louis wedding — think a small guest list, a low-cost or free venue (a park, a family space, an off-peak restaurant room), and DIY touches. At $5,000 the strategy is fewer guests and a venue that includes tables, chairs, and catering so you’re not renting each piece separately.
### Q. What do the groom’s parents typically pay for?
A.  Traditionally the groom’s family covers the rehearsal dinner, and often the officiant, marriage license, and sometimes the honeymoon or bar — but modern couples split costs however works for them. When touring St. Louis venues, ask what’s included (tables, catering, coordination) so families can divide the real line items clearly.
### Q. What is the 50/30/20 rule for weddings?
A.  The 50/30/20 wedding rule is a budgeting guide: about 50% toward the reception (venue, food, drink), 30% toward the “experience” (attire, photography, flowers, music), and 20% for everything else (stationery, favors, contingency). Since the venue anchors that biggest 50%, picking the right St. Louis space is the highest-leverage decision.

## Filthy Knees, Free Museums: Indoor St. Louis When It Pours
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-the-best-indoor-activities-in-st-louis-for-any-weather
Your kid is gone. Vanished up a multi-story slide somewhere over your head, and you’re on scraped knees in a tunnel deep in City Museum’s caves, jeans filthy, laughing too hard to care. You can’t even hear the rain pounding the roof of this 600,000-square-foot former shoe warehouse downtown, which a sculptor turned into tunnels, caves and slides built from salvaged scrap. Bring clothes you can crawl in.
Then the good news lands: four of the best rainy-day stops in town cost nothing to walk into. The Saint Louis Science Center, the Saint Louis Art Museum and the Missouri History Museum charge no general admission, because since 1971 City and County property owners have paid for them through the Zoo-Museum District tax, and the Contemporary Art Museum in Grand Center is free on its own. Most big cities charge $20 or more a head at their flagship museums, so a family of four is out $80 before anyone sees a dinosaur. Here they spend the whole gray day in Forest Park and pay for nothing but parking. In St. Louis, the rainy day is the cheap day.
Live in the City or County? Two more freebies most residents never use. The steamy rainforest under the Climatron dome at the Missouri Botanical Garden is free on Wednesday and Saturday mornings until noon, and the Butterfly House in Chesterfield lets residents in free for the first two hours on the first Tuesday of every month, butterflies landing on your sleeve while it sleets outside.
One more that visitors walk right past: after dark, step into the Grand Hall at Union Station and look up. On the hour from 5 to 10 p.m., a 3D light show plays across the 65-foot ceiling, flowers swaying and fireworks bursting overhead, with John Goodman narrating the old station’s story. It costs nothing to stand there and watch, except on nights the hall is booked for a private event.
Before you grab the umbrella: check the day. The Art Museum and History Museum are typically closed Mondays, the Science Center on Tuesdays. For City Museum, buy tickets online because the morning ticket line gets long, park in the serpent-fenced lot at 16th and Delmar for a flat $15, and write your phone number on your kid’s wristband before they vanish into a tunnel. Knee pads are for sale in the gift shop by the door. Then dry off at Union Station with the aquarium’s shark tank and a ride on the 200-foot St. Louis Wheel, which is climate-controlled and runs in a downpour.
### The Rainy-Day Cheat Sheet
### The Free Big Three, Paid For Before You Walked In
Start on the glass Sky Bridge at the Saint Louis Science Center, wet I-64 traffic hissing past beneath your feet while the kids aim radar guns at it. The rest of the building is experiments, dinosaurs and the McDonnell Planetarium (the Omnimax and some simulators are paid add-ons; note it’s closed Tuesdays). Across Forest Park, run up Art Hill and shake the rain off inside the Saint Louis Art Museum, thousands of years of art in one free building. The Missouri History Museum tells the city’s story, from the 1904 World’s Fair to Chuck Berry, at no charge.
Add a fourth free stop in Grand Center: the Contemporary Art Museum St. Louis is always free, with rotating modern and experimental shows that can be strange in the best way. From there you’re a short walk from the Fabulous Fox and the rest of the arts district if the rain hangs on into the evening.
### City Museum: Wear Jeans You Can Ruin
You hear it before you find your way in: kids hollering through tunnels somewhere over your head, sneakers squeaking on metal. If you do one paid indoor thing in St. Louis, make it the City Museum. Housed in a 600,000-square-foot former shoe warehouse and dreamed up by the late artist Bob Cassilly, it works as a museum and a playground at once, though neither word quite covers it: caves and tunnels, multi-story slides, a rooftop school bus hanging off the edge, and endless salvaged-material art to climb through. It’s as fun for adults as for kids (wear clothes you can crawl in). On a miserable-weather day, you can lose three or four hours here without noticing. A tip from locals: it’s busiest on weekend afternoons, so go at opening or on a weekday if you can, and know that much of the fun is physical - this is a climb-crawl-slide kind of place, not a look-with-your-eyes museum. There’s even a pinball and arcade room tucked inside if your crew needs a breather from the tunnels, and if that ends up being everyone’s favorite part, the city’s barcades and pinball halls are worth a trip of their own.
### For the Kids: Sharks, a 200-Foot Wheel and 2,000 Butterflies
Families have easy wins downtown. The St. Louis Aquarium at Union Station brings touch pools and a shark tank under one roof, and the St. Louis Wheel right outside is a climate-controlled, 200-foot observation wheel that runs year-round - a fun, dry way to see the skyline even in a downpour. Out in Kirkwood, The Magic House (the St. Louis Children’s Museum) is a beloved hands-on playground for younger kids, and in Chesterfield, the Sophia M. Sachs Butterfly House is a warm indoor tropical conservatory with roughly 2,000 free-flying butterflies - a real mood-lifter on a gray day. Little kids tend to love it: butterflies land right on you, it’s warm and calm, and it’s an easy hour that doesn’t require a nap-time meltdown recovery afterward.
Total tangent - St. Louis Hills, quietly one of the best neighborhoods in the city.
### For Grown-Ups: a Rainforest Dome, a Food Hall and the Fox
Indoor doesn’t have to mean kid-focused. The Missouri Botanical Garden’s Climatron - a geodesic-dome rainforest conservatory - is a lush, humid escape when it’s cold and gray outside (and St. Louis city and county residents get in free on Wednesday and Saturday mornings). City Foundry STL in Midtown packs a food hall, the Alamo Drafthouse cinema, Puttshack’s high-tech mini golf, and more under one roof - a whole indoor date without moving your car. And for a classic grown-up rainy afternoon, the free Art Museum plus a long lunch is hard to beat. Grand Center, the arts district around the Contemporary Art Museum, is also home to theaters, jazz at the Dark Room, and the Fabulous Fox - so a gray day can easily turn into a culture-packed evening if you let it, and those same theaters and music rooms turn up again when the city makes its New Year’s Eve plans.
### Retro Bowling on the Loop, Mini Golf at the Foundry
When you just want to do something, St. Louis delivers. Pin-Up Bowl in the Delmar Loop pairs retro bowling with a cocktail lounge; Puttshack at City Foundry does tech-tracked mini golf; and Main Event in Chesterfield stacks bowling, laser tag, and a big arcade for an all-day rainy-weather option. If your crew wants active indoor fun - escape rooms, climbing, arcades - St. Louis has a whole scene for that, too (see our separate guide to active indoor things to do), and come October that same appetite for a scare fills the region’s haunted houses and Halloween events.
A rainy-day outing is better with the right lunch or coffee stop nearby - and that’s what a local directory is for. You can search St Louis Near Me Directory to find spots near any of these attractions before you head out.
If you run a café, a lunch spot or an escape room within a few minutes of Forest Park or Union Station, list your business with us and turn the soaked families coming out of the Science Center into customers.
### A Rainy Weekend Plan: One Free Day, One Paid Day
The beauty of St. Louis for bad weather is how the attractions cluster, so you can chain several without much driving. In Forest Park, the free Art Museum, History Museum, and Science Center sit within a few minutes of each other - you could spend an entire rainy day going museum to museum and never pay admission. Downtown, the City Museum and Union Station (aquarium, wheel, mini golf, ropes course, mirror maze) are a short hop apart, enough to fill a family weekend on their own, and Union Station turns into a holiday destination in its own right once the Christmas lights and seasonal events arrive. And Grand Center / Midtown pairs the free Contemporary Art Museum with City Foundry’s food hall and entertainment for an easy adult day.
A smart rainy-weekend plan looks like this: one day of free museums (Forest Park’s big three plus the Contemporary Art Museum), one day of paid play (City Museum in the morning, Union Station in the afternoon). Mix in a warm break at the Climatron or the Butterfly House if the gray really sets in, and the worst-weather weekend of the year turns into one of the more memorable ones.
### Know Before You Go: Closed Mondays, Closed Tuesdays
A couple of planning notes save headaches. Hours and prices drift, so it’s worth a quick check of each attraction’s website before you drive out - especially the Science Center, which is closed Tuesdays, and the Art Museum and History Museum, which are typically closed Mondays. The free museums can get busy on rainy weekends and school breaks, so arrive early for parking. And remember that “free admission” sometimes still means paid parking, paid special exhibitions, or paid add-ons like the Science Center’s Omnimax - the core visit is free, but budget a little for extras.
### Which Indoor Day Is Right for You?
Free rainy day: the Science Center, Art Museum, History Museum, and Contemporary Art Museum - all $0. Restless kids who need to move: City Museum or The Magic House. Toddlers: the Butterfly House or the Magic House. A whole family day under one roof: Union Station’s aquarium and wheel. An adult rainy date: the Climatron or City Foundry. Something active indoors: Pin-Up Bowl, Puttshack, or Main Event. There’s no such thing as a washed-out day here - only an indoor one, and usually a cheap one at that. Keep this list handy on your phone; the day the forecast falls apart is exactly when you’ll be glad you already knew where to go. And most of these spots are close enough together that you can chain two or three into a single day if the rain really settles in - a museum in the morning, lunch, and a bowling alley or aquarium in the afternoon.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What can we do inside when it's raining?
A.  In St. Louis, plenty. Climb through the City Museum, explore the free Saint Louis Science Center, Art Museum, or History Museum, visit the St. Louis Aquarium at Union Station, or warm up in the Missouri Botanical Garden’s Climatron rainforest. City Foundry STL adds a food hall, cinema, and mini golf under one roof.
### Q. What are 5 indoor activities?
A.  Five great St. Louis indoor activities: climb through the City Museum, explore the free Saint Louis Science Center, tour the free Saint Louis Art Museum, meet the sharks at the St. Louis Aquarium in Union Station, and walk the humid Climatron rainforest at the Missouri Botanical Garden. All work rain or shine.
### Q. What are some fun indoor activities to do in Saint Louis?
A.  The free institutions carry the day here - a major art museum, a history museum and a science center that cost nothing to walk into. Add City Museum for something no other city has, plus aquariums, bowling and indoor mini golf when you want the day structured around one stop.
### Q. What can couples do together on a rainy day?
A.  Go somewhere steamy first. Walk the rainforest under the Climatron dome at the Missouri Botanical Garden, which is free for City and County residents on Wednesday and Saturday mornings until noon. Then head to City Foundry STL in Midtown for the food hall, a movie at the Alamo Drafthouse or a round of Puttshack. If it’s still pouring, finish with jazz at the Dark Room in Grand Center. Three stops, zero ball pits.
### Q. What to do when I'm bored on a rainy day?
A.  Pick the format first: something to look at, something to climb or something to eat and linger over. Look: the free Art Museum on Art Hill. Climb: the tunnels and slides at City Museum. Linger: the food hall at City Foundry. Or go somewhere warm. At the Butterfly House in Chesterfield, City and County residents get in free for the first two hours on the first Tuesday of every month.
### Q. What are some fun indoor activities to do in Missouri?
A.  Go underground. Missouri has roughly 7,500 recorded caves, which is why it’s called the Cave State, and about 20 are show caves with guided tours. Meramec Caverns in Stanton, the largest commercial cave in the state, is an easy day trip down I-44, and a cave holds the same temperature all year, so the rain up top stops mattering. Check tour times before you drive.

## Remember the Warrenton Denny’s? It’s a Family Cantina Now: Casa Tequila
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/experience-authentic-flavors-at-casa-tequila-cantina-grill-winghaven
Remember the Warrenton Denny’s? Seventeen years of coffee refills and Grand Slams on Veterans Memorial Parkway, and then one afternoon the signs came down and the doors were locked. “Well guys, after 17 years at Warrenton Denny’s... We are closed for good,” a longtime employee wrote on Facebook.
It didn’t stay dark. Walk into that room now and it smells like charred peppers and lime; a skillet of fajitas comes hissing past your booth, steak and onions still spitting, and somebody at the next table turns to look. Jessenia Lopez and Leo Carmona, who run Casa Tequila Cantina & Grill, didn’t lease the old Denny’s. They bought it. “If this is like the long haul, and we’re gonna do this for the rest of our lives, we might as well just buy something,” Lopez told the Warren County Record. It’s the small-town turn people forward to each other: the diner closes, and the family down the road buys it so they never have to leave.
That move trips people up, so text this part to whoever’s driving: map apps may still send you to the family’s old unit in the Shoppes at Warrenton outlet center, and that unit is closed. The Warrenton kitchen is 429 E Veterans Memorial Pkwy now, the former Denny’s, and the sister kitchen is 905 Caledonia Dr in the Winghaven neighborhood of O’Fallon. Both open at 11 every morning.
Then order like a regular. Street tacos, carne asada, al pastor, barbacoa or shrimp. A skillet of fajitas for the table. The Trash Can Nachos, exactly as over-the-top as the name promises, with a margarita on the rocks, salt crusted on the rim and cold against your lip. Ask which tequilas behind the bar say “100% agave” on the label, because the word “tequila” alone promises less than people think: under Mexico’s official tequila standard, a bottle labeled just “Tequila” only has to get 51 percent of its sugars from blue agave, and up to 49 percent can come from other sugars, as the Tequila Regulatory Council spells out. Same glass, same salt, same lime, and nearly half the sugar that tequila was distilled from can be something other than agave. Screenshot that for whoever always orders the house margarita without asking. Those nachos are the dish people post about: Atly’s review-based roundup of Missouri’s best queso and nacho spots lists the Winghaven kitchen first. Ask for a to-go box early, because the portions win. And if you’re the one planning the graduation party or the backyard birthday, the same family will roll a taco truck up your driveway: email casatequilawinghaven@gmail.com with the date, the place and a head count.
### Two kitchens, one family, one new address
Walk into Winghaven on a warm night and the patio is the first thing you hear. Casa Tequila Cantina & Grill is one restaurant with two kitchens on the western edge of the metro. Winghaven: 905 Caledonia Dr, O’Fallon, (636) 284-7385. Warrenton: 429 E Veterans Memorial Pkwy, (636) 377-1269. Both run 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. Sunday through Thursday and until 10 on Fridays and Saturdays. “Winghaven” isn’t a separate town, just the name of the O’Fallon store’s neighborhood.
The Warrenton story is the one locals repeat. The couple’s first home there, in the outlet center, came with little more than tables and booths; they built out a bar and bought about 90 percent of the restaurant equipment themselves before the Denny’s down the road came up for sale.
And if a friend says Casa Tequila closed, they’re thinking of Casa Tequila Bar & Grill in St. Peters, a different restaurant. Both Casa Tequila Cantina & Grill kitchens are open and cooking.
Both kitchens answer to the same couple, so the menu and the standards travel between them, and regulars order the same plate at either door without a second thought.
### What to order when the skillet hits the table
Five things on the menu earn the drive out I-70 or down Caledonia:
Street tacos: carne asada, al pastor, barbacoa or shrimp, small enough that you order three and argue over the last one.
Sizzling fajitas: steak or chicken, arriving loud enough that the whole room knows what you ordered.
The Trash Can Nachos: the signature, and big; Atly’s review roundup calls the portion large, and it’s the plate that gets photographed before anyone touches it.
Carne asada and chunky guacamole: the guac comes cold and bright with lime against warm chips.
The margaritas: the reason the place is named for tequila, poured from a deep shelf that runs from a clean blanco to a slow-sipping añejo.
Portions run big enough that the to-go box is part of the meal, and the chips keep coming warm while you decide.
Eating at home? Both kitchens do takeout and deliver through the major apps, and tacos and fajitas ride out the drive across O’Fallon or out to Wright City better than most food does. On a weeknight when nobody wants to cook and everyone is tired of the pizza rotation, that’s the call.
### Tequila: why “100% agave” on the bottle matters
The name isn’t an accident. Casa Tequila leans into its bar with a deep tequila selection - the kind of range that lets you drink your way from a familiar blanco to a smoky, sipping-quality añejo. If tequila has only ever meant the burn of a bad college shot, this is a good place to be gently corrected. Two label words do most of the work. “100% agave” means every sugar in the bottle came from blue agave; without it, the rules allow up to 49 percent other sugars. Then the age: under the same standard, a reposado rests at least two months in oak, an añejo at least a year, and an extra añejo at least three years, so the darker the pour, the longer it sat in the barrel.
The margaritas are the headliner for most tables, and regulars are loyal to them - classic on the rocks, blended with fruit, or built up into something more ambitious. Pair one with the Trash Can Nachos to start and you’ve got the platonic ideal of a St. Charles County Friday night. For anyone not drinking, the usual Mexican-restaurant standbys and soft options are on hand too, so the designated driver isn’t stuck with water. It’s the kind of bar program that makes the place work equally well for a casual weeknight and a birthday worth celebrating - you can keep it simple or make a night of it, and the room flexes to match.
### A patio, a pitcher and a game on in Winghaven
Casa Tequila leans into a warm, upscale-casual feel - comfortable enough for a family dinner, lively enough for a night out with friends. The Winghaven location in particular plays up the social, patio-and-sports side of things, with outdoor space and an easygoing atmosphere that suits a summer evening and a pitcher of margaritas. It’s the kind of place where a quick weeknight dinner and a leisurely celebration both feel right at home.
Service gets consistent praise, which matters as much as the food for a neighborhood restaurant. When people describe why they keep returning, it’s usually some combination of the flavors, the generous plates, the drinks, and staff who make you feel like a regular even on a first visit - a rare combination that’s harder to find than it should be. That’s the quiet advantage of a family-run place: the owners are often on the floor, and it shows in how the room is run.
Waiting on the skillet? Lewis Place, back in the city, has a story worth the ten minutes.
### Why the names over the door matter
It’s easy to default to a national chain when you’re hungry and don’t want to think. But there’s a real case for a place like Casa Tequila instead. When Jessenia Lopez and Leo Carmona own the restaurant, the quality is personal - their name is on it, their neighbors are the customers, and a bad night isn’t a data point on a corporate dashboard, it’s a face they’ll see at the grocery store. That accountability is exactly why independent restaurants so often out-cook their chain competition on flavor and care.
It’s also where your money goes further for the community. Dollars spent at a locally owned restaurant circulate back through the local economy far more than dollars spent at a chain, and the character it adds to a place like Winghaven or Warrenton - a real gathering spot, not an interchangeable box - is the kind of thing a suburb misses only after it’s gone. Choosing the family-run taco spot over the drive-thru is a small vote for the kind of town you want to live in.
### First visit: chips, guac, then the nachos
Never been? Keep it simple. Start with chips and the chunky guacamole while you look at the menu, and put in an order of the Trash Can Nachos if you’re with a group - it’s built to share and it’s the signature for a reason. For the main event, the street tacos are the easiest crowd-pleaser (get a mix - carne asada, al pastor, barbacoa), while the sizzling fajitas make the whole table turn to look when they arrive. Add a margarita, pace yourself, and you’ve had the full Casa Tequila experience on the first try. Bring the family or a crew - the portions are generous and the room is built for a good time, not a hushed one. And if the weather’s good, ask about patio seating at the Winghaven location; a margarita outdoors on a warm St. Charles County evening is hard to beat, and it’s exactly the sort of small, local pleasure that’s easy to overlook until you make a habit of it.
Craving another basket of warm chips somewhere else in the metro? Our guide to the best Mexican food in St. Louis rounds up local favorites across the region - real places, real reviews, no algorithm deciding what you see.
If you’re the taqueria, the cantina or the family kitchen behind the sizzling skillets, the Gold plan keeps your address, hours and photos in front of more customers, so a move like Casa Tequila’s sends diners to the new door, not the old one.
### Winghaven or Warrenton: which one to drive to
The two locations quietly cover a lot of ground on the western side of the metro. The O’Fallon store sits in Winghaven, a master-planned community of homes, offices, and green space in one of the fastest-growing parts of the metro - the kind of neighborhood with plenty of families looking for a go-to dinner spot that isn’t a chain. It draws easily from O’Fallon, Lake Saint Louis, Dardenne Prairie, and Wentzville, which has its own family-run favorite in Chimi’s Fresh-Mex on Wentzville Center Drive.
The Warrenton location, the original, anchors the western edge of the metro along the I-70 corridor, where good sit-down Mexican is genuinely harder to come by. For folks out that way - Warrenton, Wright City, and the surrounding towns - having a from-scratch, family-run cantina nearby is no small thing. Between the two, Casa Tequila has become the reliable answer to “where should we get Mexican tonight” across a wide stretch of the western suburbs and the I-70 towns beyond them.
### The food truck, for your backyard party
Casa Tequila also runs a food truck for private events - a fun way to bring the tacos, fajitas, and margarita energy to a birthday, office party, graduation, or backyard get-together without anyone having to cook or clean up. There’s something about a taco truck pulling up to your own driveway that turns an ordinary afternoon into an occasion; guests remember it in a way they don’t remember a tray of grocery-store sandwiches. Rates and availability vary by date and event size, so the move is to email casatequilawinghaven@gmail.com with your date, time, location, and rough head count, and let them put together a menu that fits. It’s a simple way to make a gathering feel like a party without you doing the work.

## $9.60 Toasted Ravioli, All Day Sunday: Why Sunday Beats Friday at Satchmo’s
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-satchmo-s-chesterfield-mo-a-taste-of-local-flavor
The toasted ravioli steams when you break one open, the breading crackles, and the draft beside it sweats onto the bar while a game murmurs on the TV overhead. At Satchmo’s, in the Woodchase Shopping Plaza at 13375 Olive Boulevard, that basket is $9.60 during happy hour: 2 to 6 p.m. Monday through Saturday, and all day Sunday from the 11 a.m. open.
That’s why Sunday beats Friday here. Happy hour means 20 percent off every appetizer, $2 off drafts, $3 wells and $4 house wine, and on the current online menu that turns the $12 toasted ravioli into $9.60 and the $16 eggroll trio, buffalo chicken, pizza and taco, into $12.80, so two people can split both with two well drinks on a Sunday for $28.40 before tax and tip. Send that to whoever’s picking the Sunday spot. And if you’re reading old reviews, check the dates: new owners took over in mid-2024, and their operating manager, Matt Mitchell, had opened 27 restaurants for chains like Applebee’s and Red Robin before this one, St. Louis Restaurant Review reported.
The name over the door is Louis Armstrong’s. In 1919 he came up the Mississippi on a Streckfus excursion steamer with Fate Marable’s band, looked up at downtown St. Louis and asked whether all those tall buildings were colleges, historian William Howland Kenney recounts in Jazz on the River; on those boats, the National Mississippi River Museum notes, he learned to read music. Satchmo’s says on its own site that it’s named for him and quotes him there: “What a wonderful world.” When the second basket lands, raise a $3 well drink to the kid on the steamer deck.
Then pick your night by how you want it to sound. Monday, the chicken and steak fajita skillet hisses across the room. Wednesday, kids eat free and the turkey melt comes off the grill. Thursday at 7, free trivia starts and a Philly cheesesteak sits next to your answer sheet until 8:30. Most Saturdays at 6, a local act plugs in, no cover. Tuesday’s steakhouse salad and Friday’s golden fish and chips fill in the week. Specials rotate, so call (314) 392-9401 before you build a night around one.
### A riverboat name on a bar-and-grill menu
Powdered sugar is the first clue: the Monte Cristo comes deep-fried and dusted with it, and some of it ends up on your shirt. The rest of the menu is built for a bar stool: a double cheeseburger called the Big Mo, an 8-ounce sirloin, a full bar and TVs for the game. Its current site is satchmosgrill.com, and the old satchmosbarandgrill.com address is dead, so ignore any listing that still points there.
### Toasted ravioli first, then the eggrolls
Toasted ravioli ($12). The breading cracks and the filling steams when you bite through. This is St. Louis, so order the city’s own appetizer first; at happy hour it’s $9.60.
The eggroll trio ($16). Grilled buffalo chicken, pepperoni pizza with marinara, and beef taco with avocado crema, one of each; the wrappers shatter, and the buffalo one is the plate St. Louis Restaurant Review gave five stars.
The Big Mo ($17). The menu’s signature double cheeseburger, American cheese and thousand island running toward your wrist, with tots or onion rings on the side.
Prices are from the restaurant’s own menus and can change. Sides run $5. Save room for the apple wontons ($8): fried, filled with apple pie filling, and dusted in cinnamon sugar under a drizzle of caramel.
### A game on, a draft in hand
Come on a Thursday at 7 and you’ll hear the room before you see it: free trivia, hosted by Unleashed Entertainment, with prizes every round until 8:30. Wednesday is the night to bring the kids, because they eat free, and the turkey melt special comes off the grill with the cheese still sliding. Save room for the chocolate chip cookie skillet, baked to order and slumping under vanilla ice cream, fudge and caramel ($8).
Saturdays are getting louder. The owners are booking local musicians for most Saturdays at 6, no cover and all ages, so a bar named for a trumpet player gets live music in the room; the lineup goes up on the bar’s Facebook page first. Before 6 on any day, a $4 glass of house wine or a $3 well drink is the cheapest seat in the house.
### The 2 o’clock rule
Two questions come up every time: what’s actually included in the happy hour, and what time it starts. Plenty of places advertise one and then discount two drafts and a basket of fries, and most don’t start until you’ve already left work.
That 2 p.m. start is the part people miss. Most happy hours wait until 3 or 4; this one catches the early shift, the retirees and the parents between school pickup and practice, with 20% off all appetizers, $2 off drafts, $3 wells and $4 house wine, and Sunday running all day. It turns an ordinary weeknight into an affordable one, and it’s a smart window to try the place for the first time without committing to a full dinner.
Monday’s fajitas are the special you hear coming, still hissing on the skillet as they cross the room.

## Old St. Louis Chop Suey & the St. Paul Sandwich: A Hometown Tradition Worth Tasting
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/a-taste-of-tradition-exploring-the-enduring-appeal-of-old-st-louis-chop-suey
Maybe you grew up with it. A little corner carry-out with a glowing “CHOP SUEY” sign, a bulletproof lazy-susan window, and a paper sack that came back warm with something you’d never find on a menu anywhere else in the country. Or maybe you’ve lived in St. Louis for years and never once ordered the one sandwich that’s pure hometown.
The old St. Louis chop-suey house — and its signature, the St. Paul sandwich — is one of the most quietly St. Louis things you can eat. It’s cheap. It’s a little strange to outsiders. And it carries a century of city history in a couple slices of white bread. Below is what it actually is, where it came from, and where you can still get one — because once you know the story, that strange little sandwich starts to taste like the city itself.
### Where to Get One, at a Glance
### What the St. Paul Sandwich Actually Is
If you’ve never had one: the St. Paul sandwich is a hot egg foo young patty — egg, bean sprouts, and minced onion, bound with a little flour and fried — served between two slices of plain white bread with mayonnaise, dill pickle, lettuce, and tomato. That’s the classic build. Order it “with meat” and you can add chicken, pork, shrimp, or beef mixed into the patty; a “Special” usually piles on a combination.
It sounds odd written out — a fried egg patty on cold white bread with mayo and pickle — and that’s exactly the point. It’s comfort food invented at the intersection of a Chinese-American kitchen and a Midwestern lunch counter, and it tastes like nowhere else because it exists almost nowhere else.
How you eat one is part of the ritual. It comes wrapped in paper, warm and a little messy, best eaten in the car or straight out of the sack. The contrast is the whole appeal: the hot, savory, fried egg patty against cool mayo, crisp lettuce, and the sharp bite of dill pickle. Most shops let you customize — extra meat, no tomato, hot mustard or soy on the side — and each carry-out’s version is a little different, which is exactly why St. Louisans argue about whose is best.
### The name: fact, legend, and a little mystery
Nobody can prove where the “St. Paul” name truly came from, and that’s part of its charm. The most-repeated story ties it to Steven Yuen and his Minnesota hometown. Food writers have floated other ideas over the years — including that the sandwich is a cousin of the egg-based “Denver” or “Western” sandwich, which some historians believe Chinese cooks helped create from egg foo young. There’s even a bit of folklore about a cook aboard a Mississippi steamboat named the St. Paul. Treat all of it as the kind of tale that grows up around a beloved local food: fun to trade, impossible to pin down. None of it matters much once the sandwich is in your hands.
### A Taste With Deep St. Louis Roots
To understand the St. Paul sandwich, you have to know a little about Hop Alley — St. Louis’s original Chinatown. It sat downtown, roughly bounded by Seventh, Tenth, Walnut, and Chestnut streets. The city’s first Chinese resident, a man recorded as Alla Lee, arrived in 1857, and the community really took shape after 1869, when a wave of roughly 250 immigrants came seeking factory work. By 1900 the neighborhood was home to several hundred people, with laundries, groceries, restaurants, and shops.
Hop Alley didn’t survive the twentieth century. Between the late 1950s and the mid-1960s it was condemned and cleared in the name of urban renewal — the ground was needed for Busch Memorial Stadium, which opened in 1966. The heart of St. Louis’s first Chinatown literally became a stadium and its parking. But the city’s Chinese-American families and their restaurants didn’t disappear; they scattered and put down new roots across the metro, and the neighborhood carry-out — the “chop suey” — became a fixture in working-class neighborhoods all over town.
Over the following decades, the community’s new center of gravity shifted west, to the stretch of Olive Boulevard in University City that St. Louisans now call the “unofficial Chinatown” — today lined with dumpling houses, Cantonese barbecue, and Asian groceries. So the story runs in a straight line: a downtown Chinatown razed for a ballpark, families rebuilding across the region, and a humble egg-foo-young sandwich carrying a piece of that history forward on every corner-store menu. When you bite into a St. Paul, you’re tasting the legacy of a neighborhood that no longer exists.
The sandwich itself came later than Hop Alley. As local legend has it, the St. Paul was created in the early 1940s by a cook named Steven Yuen, who is said to have named it after his hometown of St. Paul, Minnesota, and put it on the menu at Park Chop Suey. That origin story is repeated everywhere in St. Louis, though it’s passed down as lore rather than hard documented fact — which feels about right for a sandwich this beloved. What’s certain is that by the 1970s and ’80s, nearly every neighborhood chop-suey house in St. Louis had one on the menu.
### Why “St. Louis chop suey” means something specific
“St. Louis chop suey” names a whole category of small, family-run Chinese-American carry-outs that spread across the city in the mid-twentieth century, not a single dish. These were counter-service spots, often with a spinning bulletproof window, serving Americanized classics: egg foo young, fried rice, egg rolls, crab rangoon, and — the local signature — the St. Paul sandwich. Cheap and fast, they were part of the daily rhythm of the neighborhoods they served.
The food mattered, but the neighborhood role mattered more. For decades the corner chop suey was where you grabbed a cheap, filling dinner on the way home, where the same family knew your order, where a five-dollar sandwich fed a hungry kid after practice. These were small businesses in the truest sense, family-run and stitched into daily life.
Many of the classic old shops have closed over the years as owners retired and neighborhoods changed. But the tradition is far from dead — a handful of beloved spots are still turning out St. Pauls today, and a new order tastes exactly like the ones people remember.
Nothing to do with sandwiches — but the home-services map is right here.
### Where to Get a St. Paul Sandwich Today
Park Chop Suey (1321 Chouteau Ave, near downtown) is the sentimental first stop — the spot most often credited with inventing the sandwich. It’s open Monday through Saturday and still serves the St. Paul that (by legend) started it all.
Mai Lee in Brentwood is a St. Louis institution — the region’s first Vietnamese restaurant, open for four decades — and it has served the St. Paul for nearly that entire run, now offering around six variations, from barbecue pork to shrimp. It’s the sit-down way to experience the sandwich.
Chinese Express in Richmond Heights (on Clayton Ave) is known for a loaded “Special” St. Paul topped with an amalgam of chicken, roast pork, and shrimp — a heartier take for a bigger appetite.
Lisa’s Chop Suey in Jennings rounds out the list with a giant, famously affordable Special St. Paul — the kind of old-school neighborhood counter where the value is as memorable as the sandwich.
Half the fun is comparing them. No two St. Pauls are quite alike — the ratio of egg to filling, how much mayo, whether the bread is toasted, how loaded the Special gets — so trying a few around town is a genuinely enjoyable little St. Louis food quest. Ask five locals for their favorite and you’ll get five answers, usually tied to whichever shop they grew up near.
### The Ones That Are Gone
Part of what makes the St. Paul feel precious is how many of the old shops have closed. Longtime neighborhood chop-suey houses have quietly shut their windows over the years as families retired — and even recently, spots that served a well-loved St. Paul have gone dark. It’s worth calling ahead before you make a special trip, because this is a tradition kept alive by a shrinking number of small, independent kitchens. Every order you place at one of the survivors is a small vote to keep it going.
### Craving more real St. Louis food?
The St. Paul sandwich is one thread in a much bigger, more delicious St. Louis food story. If it’s the authentic, family-run Chinese cooking you’re after, the metro has that too - and you can search St Louis Near Me Directory to find restaurants, carry-outs, and neighborhood spots across the area, with hours and details, before you head out.

### Q. Why is it called a St. Paul sandwich?

### Q. Where can I get a St. Paul sandwich in St. Louis?

### Q. What does “St. Louis chop suey” mean?

Their menus feature Americanized classics like egg foo young and fried rice, and their signature item is the St. Paul sandwich.
### Q. Was there really a Chinatown in St. Louis?
A.  Yes. St. Louis’s original Chinatown, known as Hop Alley, sat downtown near Seventh through Tenth streets, dating to the mid-1800s and growing after 1869. It was demolished between the late 1950s and mid-1960s to build Busch Memorial Stadium, which opened in 1966, and the community resettled across the metro.

## Ring In The New Year: Your Ultimate Guide to New Year's Eve in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/ring-in-2026-your-ultimate-guide-to-new-year-s-eve-in-st-louis
Midnight in St. Louis can mean six open bars in Soulard, a balloon drop timed for bedtime, or a tasting menu eight floors above the Arch. The city runs the full range on December 31, from black-tie dinners to pajama parties. Here are the celebrations worth planning around for new years eve st louis.
### Key Takeaways
Big crowds and open bars: NYE Live! at Ballpark Village and Molly's In Soulard both go large on drinks and entertainment.
Refined dinners: Ramsay's Kitchen serves it with Arch views, and Casa Don Alfonso runs an Italian feast.
Something offbeat: the St. Louis Symphony Orchestra, a burlesque show at The Boom Boom Room, or stand-up at Helium Comedy Club.
Family plans: City Museum runs a kid-friendly countdown, and Winterfest's Neon Nights adds ice skating and entertainment.
Two ends of the spectrum: rooftop views at 360 St. Louis and a pajama party at Work & Leisure both welcome the new year in their own way.
### Grand Celebrations For New Year's Eve St. Louis
The biggest rooms in town go all out on December 31. If you want scale, noise, and a Champagne toast at midnight, start here.
### NYE Live! At Ballpark Village
Ballpark Village bills its bash as the most legendary New Year's Eve party in town. The draw: all-inclusive premium drink packages, multiple VIP options, and several venues, each with its own DJ. Add themed party favors and a Champagne toast at midnight. It's built for people who want to let loose without watching a tab.
### Molly's In Soulard's Extravaganza
Molly's in Soulard throws a party every year, and the numbers tell the story. Their annual extravaganza is a Soulard institution — six open bars pour beer, wine, and cocktails. Three DJs, two balloon drops, and a Champagne toast keep the night moving. The largest patio in St. Louis gets covered and heated for the crowd. VIP tables and cabanas are there if you want to splurge.
### The Ultimate Celebration At Hyatt Regency St. Louis
The Hyatt Regency St. Louis at The Arch calls its version the “Ultimate New Year's Eve Celebration.” Things start at 8 p.m. with a dinner buffet and an open bar stocked with beers, wines, and cocktails. Local bands play live later, and there's a photo booth, a balloon drop, and a Champagne toast. Book the room package and you can celebrate, then head upstairs. No cab, no cleanup.
### Culinary Delights For New Year's Eve St. Louis
Some people want the last meal of the year to matter more than the countdown itself. Several St. Louis kitchens build special menus for December 31, and a handful of them require booking weeks out.
### Ramsay's Kitchen's Elevated Dining
Ramsay's Kitchen, Gordon Ramsay's spot on the eighth floor of the Four Seasons Hotel, runs a New Year's Eve dinner with clear views of the Gateway Arch. ### Casa Don Alfonso's Sorrento-Style Feast
Casa Don Alfonso at The Ritz-Carlton puts on a five-course prix fixe menu it calls a Sorrento-style feast. It's a strong pick for a romantic dinner built on authentic Italian flavors. Book a room at the hotel and the night gets even easier.

Union 30, inside Hotel St. Louis, adds a three-course prix fixe menu to its regular list. These prix fixe menus sell out, so book the seat you actually want a few weeks ahead, not the week of.

### Jazz St. Louis With Victor Goines
Jazz St. Louis swings into the new year with Victor Goines, the organization's president and CEO, leading a band of first-rate players. The set mixes jazz standards, beloved classics, and a few originals. It's a direct line into the city's vibrant jazz scene.
### A Big Night At Live! By Loews
Live! By Loews goes big on entertainment for New Year’s Eve — one recent year starred St. Louis’s own Cedric The Entertainer. The night runs dinner, hors d'oeuvres, and an open bar, all capped by a Champagne toast at midnight. That's a strong way to close out the year.
### Hometown Bands At Delmar Hall
Delmar Hall usually rings in the year with a hometown favorite — St. Louis’s own The Mighty Pines have headlined recent New Year’s Eves there. The band trades in layered harmonies and thoughtful songs that capture the spirit of the city. It's built for dancing, and it stays a notch more relaxed than a full-blown bash. Showtimes and ticket links shift as December 31 nears, so confirm with the venue before you commit.
### Exclusive New Year's Eve St. Louis Experiences
A few of these nights come with a story attached, not just a menu. You'll find rich food experiences around town, like Casa Don Alfonso for a taste of Sorrento.
### Wheelhouse Midnight Soirée
The Wheelhouse Midnight Soirée runs on good music and an all-inclusive setup. DJ Nabbs spins the tunes, premium drinks are covered, and late-night snacks keep you going. There's a photo booth to capture the memories. Go VIP and you can snag a private booth or mezzanine access with bottomless bottle service.

Work & Leisure has turned its New Year’s Eve Pajama Party with chef Liz Schuster into a tradition. Dress code: your comfiest PJs. From 8 p.m. to 1 a.m., expect light bites, an open bar, and a Champagne toast right at midnight. Then it keeps going. A huge breakfast buffet starts the year off, complete with a waffle bar and an omelet station, plus games, dancing, and a balloon drop.
### Grand Tavern's Prohibition Era Cocktails
Grand Tavern at the Angad Arts Hotel has hosted “The Walsh Experience” on recent New Year’s Eves, a nod to the legendary parties thrown by St. Louis socialite Clara Bell Walsh. Chef Robert Cantu builds a five-course tasting menu. The signature, though, is the Prohibition Era cocktails mixed by Beverage Director Meredith Barry. It plays like a night pulled from another era.

The one thing every option here shares is a booking deadline. Open bars, tasting menus, and VIP tables sell out well before December 31, and the marquee events go first. Figure out the kind of night you're after, then reserve it weeks ahead instead of hoping for a walk-in. St. Louis supplies the range. The calendar is the part you actually control.

## A Locked Door at 3:05: When (and What) to Eat at Thai Kitchen Florissant
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-authentic-flavors-at-thai-kitchen-florissant
3:05 p.m. on a Wednesday, and the door at 8458 N. Lindbergh won’t open. There’s still lemongrass and chili on the air, your stomach growls in the parking lot, and nobody warned you about the gap.
At 4 the lock turns, and by 4:15 the wait has paid for itself. Order the khao soi first. The crispy noodles on top crackle when your spoon breaks through to the yellow curry, and then the heat arrives late: Riverfront Times critic Cheryl Baehr found this one spicier than most, its warmth “more haunting than assertive,” creeping up the back of your palate and staying. Then the Gang Quah shrimp, a tangier, tomato-forward curry with chunks of pineapple warmed through in the broth, spooned over rice so the sweet and the sour hit together.
Those recipes have a name behind them. They’re Andie Ongartsutthikue’s, passed down through her mother’s family for generations, Baehr wrote when she put this kitchen on her list of St. Louis County favorites. What the menu doesn’t say: this is a family branch. Andie, as the Thai Kitchen founder is known, ran her own restaurant in Bangkok for five years before coming to the U.S. in 1995, and the Florissant kitchen, opened in April 2018, belongs to her brother and sister-in-law, St. Louis Restaurant Review reported. That’s why the family’s group site, thaikitchenco.com, takes online orders for its other kitchens, from O’Fallon to Overland, but not this one. Order Florissant on its own page or by phone. One more for the table: the Nam Tok Beef with sticky rice. Nam tok means waterfall in Thai, for the juices that drip off the grilled beef.
So you only learn it once: closed Tuesdays; Monday and Wednesday through Friday, 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. and 4 to 8:30; Saturday and Sunday, noon to 8:30 straight through. On the Saturday we checked, online orders stopped at 8:15. Call (314) 695-5039 if you’re cutting it close.
Here’s the North County twist. Two Thai kitchens share this stretch of Lindbergh, and both go dark in the afternoon: Pearl Cafe, a few doors down at 8416, breaks from 2:30 to 5 on weekdays. Thai Kitchen’s one-hour gap is the short one. And if the lock still beats you, or it’s a Tuesday, the founder’s own new carryout kitchen, Thai Kitchen Overland at 9440 Midland Blvd, cooks from 11 a.m. to 11 p.m. every day, Ladue News reported when it opened, with moo ping pork skewers and sticky rice you can only get there. Send that to the friend who always suggests Thai at 3:30.
Then the surprise. This Thai kitchen in North County keeps a whole section of pho, big bowls that come with bean sprouts, basil, jalapeños and cilantro on the side. And on its own online ordering page, the most-liked item isn’t a curry at all. It’s the crispy spring rolls, still crackling when the box opens, with pad Thai right behind them.
Ask how much heat you want; the staff will dial a dish up or down. Plan on a box for tomorrow, because portions run big. Budget-wise, most curries, noodles and fried rice list at $17.94 on the online ordering page and the spring rolls at $8.34, so two plates and a starter run about $44 before tip.
### Lunch on a clock
Weekday lunch runs 11 to 3, and plates come out fast enough for a lunch hour. Order the Thai basil stir fry and the basil still smells green when it lands. Get the last order in by about 2:45, before the gap.
### The bowls and plates regulars come back for
### Tom yum, Crying Tiger and the specialties page
The tom yum noodle soup arrives so hot you lean back from the steam, and the first spoonful, sour with lime and lemongrass, clears your sinuses on the way down. The rest of the house specialties run to Panang grouper, spicy catfish and Crying Tiger, and the duck spicy basil fried rice is the plate to split when the table can’t decide.
### Big soup bowls, pho included
With the pho, you build the bowl yourself: tear the basil, push the bean sprouts under the broth, and drop the jalapeño slices in one at a time until it bites back. There’s chicken pho, rare-beef pho and a seafood noodle soup beside the tom yum, and the steam on your face is the point.
Red curry over rice
### The curry that comes home in a box
The red curry arrives orange-red and glossy with coconut milk, deep and slightly sweet, with your choice of meat and fresh vegetables over rice. Panang runs thicker and nuttier, green brighter and sharper. Whatever’s left goes home in a box, and tomorrow’s lunch is handled.
### A long menu, and a pho section nobody expects
The spring rolls are the sound of this place: the box opens, the wrappers crackle, and somebody at the table has already taken two. They’re the most-liked thing on the online ordering page, and the pho bowls and a kids’ menu mean the whole table gets fed, including the friend who only eats pho.
### Delectable Appetizers and Salads
Before the main courses arrive, start with a few appetizers. Crispy spring rolls, flavorful chicken satay, or a plate of Thai dumplings all make an easy opener. If you want something lighter to lead off, the salads are a strong choice. The Papaya Salad, for one, brings a bright mix of textures and a chili kick that wakes up your palate before the bigger dishes land. It’s a smart first move, especially on a warm afternoon. And if you’re weighing whether Thai is healthier than Chinese takeout, this end of the menu, the salads and the broth-based soups, is where Thai cooking runs lightest; the coconut-milk curries and fried rice are the rich end.
### Rich Curry Selections
Curry is the heart of this menu, and Thai Kitchen Florissant handles it well. You can pick from several rich, aromatic options, each with its own distinct profile. The Red Curry runs creamy and slightly sweet, the Green Curry brings a brighter, sharper spice, and the Panang leans thick and nutty. Each one arrives with your choice of protein and a generous pile of rice, which makes for a genuinely comforting meal. Pick based on how much heat you’re after, then work through the rest on later visits.
Rich Curry Selections
### Flavorful Fried Rice Varieties
Don’t sleep on the fried rice, because they do it exceptionally well here. There are several variations worth ordering, including the popular Spicy Basil Fried Rice, which hits hard with heat and herbs, and the sweet-and-savory Pineapple Fried Rice, which plays fruit against fluffy grains. It’s hard to go wrong with any of them; each one lands as a filling, satisfying order. The full menu is posted online, which is handy when you’re deciding ahead of time. It’s an easy way to taste the range of St. Louis flavors without ever leaving Florissant.
