## Tell a Joke, Get the Candy: St. Louis Halloween Events, Haunts and Pumpkin Patches
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/unforgettable-halloween-event-st-louis-your-guide-to-spooky-fun
“Why didn’t the skeleton go to the party? He had no body to go with.” A seven-year-old in a cape delivers it on your porch, dead serious, and only then holds out the pillowcase. That’s Halloween in St. Louis. Here, trick-or-treaters tell a joke before they get the candy, a habit that goes back to just after World War II and still baffles every transplant on the block. Teenagers do it too, usually with the worst pun they can find. New in town? Have the kids practice one before the 31st, because a St. Louis porch expects it.
The rest of October piles on around it: screams leaking out of The Darkness onto the sidewalk near Soulard, a haunted hayride rattling through the dark at Creepyworld in Fenton, the glow of Jack’s Lighted Trail at Eckert’s in Belleville while your breath fogs and your kid clutches a pumpkin bigger than their head.
Pick by the most nervous person in the car.
Wants to be genuinely scared? Strobe light, a scream right behind you, a hand on your shoulder that isn’t your friend’s. That’s The Darkness, at 1525 South 8th Street next to Soulard Market, or Creepyworld’s scream park at 1400 South Old Highway 141 in Fenton. One combo pass covers both. Everyone walks through a metal detector, and ticket sales are final, no refunds. Both go from weekends in late September to nightly as Halloween gets close, and the last two weekends sell out, so buy timed tickets ahead or go on a weeknight.
Is five years old? Glow sticks bobbing through Forest Park after dark: Boo at the Zoo, select October nights from 5 to 8:30 p.m. (last entry at 8). It’s $16 this season, $13 for members and free under age 2, parking in the park is free, scary costumes stay home, and there’s a sensory-friendly night with quiet areas and sensory maps. The insider catch: on Boo nights the zoo clears everyone out at 4 p.m. and reopens at 5, so a daytime zoo visit can’t just roll into the party.
Just wants a pumpkin and something warm? Mud on your boots and a hay wagon bumping out to the field: Eckert’s in Belleville, about 25 minutes east of downtown, or Thies Farm’s Pumpkinland, Stuckmeyer’s in Fenton and Rombachs in Chesterfield, generally late September through October 31. Go early on a weekend, before the best pumpkins are picked over.
Before you plan around an old list, four things have changed. Union Station’s Trick or Train isn’t on the calendar anymore; the St. Louis Aquarium’s Pirates and Pumpkins, with underwater pumpkin carving, runs there from mid-September into November 1 instead. Six Flags St. Louis is now Mid America Adventure, and Fright Fest still takes over the park after dark. Purina Farms’ kids’ Halloween event is on hold while tornado damage keeps its visitor center closed. And St. Charles turns Main Street into Legends & Lanterns on October weekends, free.
### The whole season at a glance, scary to not-scary
Here’s a Saturday in late October. The line outside The Darkness stretches down the sidewalk near Soulard, fog rolling out every time the doors open. Out in Fenton, Creepyworld’s hayride wagons rumble past in the dark to a soundtrack of screams. And in Forest Park the zoo’s lights come up at 5 for a crowd of very small superheroes. Most of it runs from late September through late October or early November.
### For the fearless: haunted houses and scream parks
You hear the flagship before you see it: screams leaking out the doors and a line of people laughing a little too loudly to prove they aren’t nervous. Then you’re in the first black corridor, hand on the shoulder in front of you, fog thick enough to taste. The Darkness, in the Soulard area near Ballpark Village, has been terrifying visitors for more than three decades, and it has been featured on the History Channel’s Modern Marvels and on the Travel Channel. Haunt owners in town for the industry’s Transworld trade show have toured it to see how it’s done. A short distance away, the same company’s Lemp Haunted House on Lemp Avenue leans into the neighborhood’s real haunted lore for a second, distinct scare.
Need something to wear first? Here’s how to choose a Halloween costume.
For a bigger, outdoor-heavy experience, Creepyworld in Fenton (off Highway 141) is a sprawling “scream park” with multiple attractions including a haunted hayride - a full night out rather than a single walk-through. And for scares wrapped inside a theme park, Fright Fest at Mid America Adventure (the former Six Flags St. Louis) in Eureka overlays the whole park with haunted mazes and scare zones after dark while the coasters keep running. These ramp up from weekend nights in late September to nightly as Halloween approaches, so buy timed tickets ahead and expect lines on the closest weekends.
### For families: not-scary Halloween fun
Plenty of the best local Halloween is built for little ones: tiny bumblebees and dinosaurs waving glow sticks, costumes encouraged, scares dialed all the way down. The classic is Boo at the Zoo, the Saint Louis Zoo’s after-hours family event in Forest Park, where costumed kids ride the Emerson Zooline Railroad in the dark and the Primate House stays open after sunset. It’s a themed evening rather than a trick-or-treat event, scary costumes stay home, and guests 14 and older can’t wear full-face masks or face-covering makeup. It runs select evenings through most of October and is a beloved rite of the season for St. Louis families.
Halloween Nights at Grant’s Farm in Grantwood Village is another family favorite - an after-dark experience with a haunted tram ride (watch for the headless horseman), decor, and shows, plus a daytime Fall Fest at the Clydesdale stables for the younger set. Downtown at St. Louis Union Station, the St. Louis Aquarium’s Pirates and Pumpkins season runs from mid-September into the first day of November, with underwater pumpkin carving plus a Trick or Treat Night and a Trick, Treat & Toast evening on the aquarium’s calendar. Purina Farms in Gray Summit used to run a not-so-scary kids’ Halloween event, but its visitor center has been closed since the March 2025 tornadoes, so check the farm’s own site before you plan around it.
### For the harvest crowd: pumpkin patches and farms
Some of the most reliable fall fun around St. Louis skips the scares completely: hayrides, corn mazes, and the annual hunt for the perfect pumpkin. The regional heavyweight is Eckert’s in Belleville, Illinois (about 25 minutes east of downtown), an eighth-generation family farm with pick-your-own pumpkins and “Ecktoberfest” festival weekends; its newer Jack’s Lighted Trail, a walkable illuminated pumpkin path, has become a fresh evening draw.
On the Missouri side, Thies Farm & Market’s Pumpkinland brings a straw castle, corn maze, and rides; Stuckmeyer’s Farm in Fenton (near the junction of Highways 141 and 21) runs Saturday “Halloween Family Fun Days” with farm animals and hayrides; and Rombachs Farm in Chesterfield opens daily in October with its “Great Pumpkin Pyramid.” These are the low-key, daytime, all-ages side of the season - perfect for younger kids, photos, and a wagon full of pumpkins - and they generally run from late September through October 31.
Random, but: every O’Fallon business worth knowing is one click away.
### The St. Louis Halloween calendar, week by week
It starts with fog machines in Soulard and ends with kids counting candy on the living-room floor. The exact dates slide a little each year, but the rhythm holds. Mid-to-late September: The Darkness opens, Creepyworld kicks off with a late-September “Slasher Weekend,” and the aquarium’s Pirates and Pumpkins season starts at Union Station. Late September into October 1: the farms open their pumpkin fields and corn mazes, and Stuckmeyer’s Saturday fun days get rolling. The first full weekends of October: Boo at the Zoo opens for select nights, Grant’s Farm’s Halloween Nights are in full swing, and St. Charles turns historic Main Street over to Legends & Lanterns, a free festival of storybook villains, ghost stories and a Day of the Dead plaza that runs on October weekends. The last two weekends: everything is open at once, the haunts go nightly, and the best tickets sell out. Halloween and just after: trick-or-treat hours are set town by town, and the St. Louis rule still holds on every porch: tell a joke, get the candy, a habit that goes back to just after World War II. Fright Fest at Mid America Adventure runs through the first day of November.

### Trick-or-treating and neighborhood happenings
Beyond the ticketed attractions, the oldest Halloween tradition of all is still going strong across the metro: door-to-door trick-or-treating. One thing that surprises newcomers - there’s a local wrinkle to it. In much of the St. Louis area, kids are expected to tell a joke before they get their candy, a “St. Louis trick” that generations here grew up with and that puzzles visitors from anywhere else. It’s a small, charming piece of local culture worth knowing before your first Halloween in town.
Because trick-or-treat night and its hours are set locally, they vary by municipality - each city and suburb tends to announce its official window, so check your city’s page or social media as the date nears. Many neighborhoods, churches, and business districts also host trunk-or-treats and fall festivals - safer, contained, weather-friendly alternatives that are great for younger kids - and shopping centers and malls sometimes run daytime candy events. A quick local search in the days before Halloween usually turns up several within a short drive.
For the grown-ups, the season has its own nightlife: costume parties and Halloween-themed events pop up at bars, breweries, and event spaces across the city and suburbs in the days around the holiday, and the metro’s genuine haunted-history spots lean into the season with tours and special evenings - a seasonal turn on the unique, offbeat St. Louis outings adults seek out year-round. Between the daytime family traditions and the after-dark options, the only real question left is how spooky you want to get.
### What to expect at a haunt (and how to survive it)
If you’re new to the big haunted attractions, a little know-how makes the night better. The premium haunts are a real production: expect elaborate, multi-room sets, live actors whose whole job is to make you jump, plenty of fog, strobe effects, and loud sound design. They’re intense by design - genuinely too scary for young children, and worth being honest with yourself about if you spook easily. A scream park like Creepyworld bundles several attractions and a hayride into one ticket, so plan for a couple of hours on your feet, outdoors, in whatever the late-October weather is doing.
The practical playbook: buy timed tickets online in advance (the closest weekends to Halloween sell out and the lines are long), wear comfortable closed-toe shoes, dress for the actual temperature after dark, and go earlier in October or on a weeknight if you want smaller crowds. If you’re bringing a group with mixed nerves, know that most haunts don’t let you bail mid-attraction easily - so match the outing to the least brave person in your party, or split up and regroup after.
### A morning at the pumpkin patch
The harvest farms deserve a little extra attention because they’re the most flexible, all-ages option of the season. A typical visit is a half-day out: a hayride to the pumpkin field, a corn maze to get lost in, a straw-bale playground or barnyard animals for the little kids, and cider, kettle corn, or apple-cider donuts on the way out. They’re built for photos - the wagons, the pumpkin pyramids, the fall color - and they’re a gentle, no-scares way to mark the season with toddlers and grandparents alike.
A few tips make the morning smoother: go early on weekends before the crowds and the best pumpkins thin out, bring cash for the stands that prefer it, dress the kids for mud after any recent rain, and check the farm’s page for whether admission, the maze, and hayrides are separate tickets or bundled. Weekdays, if you can swing them, are dramatically calmer than sunny Saturday afternoons.
### How to plan your Halloween season
With this much on offer, a little planning goes a long way. Match the outing to your crew first: a genuine haunt like The Darkness or Creepyworld for teens and thrill-seekers, Boo at the Zoo or Grant’s Farm for families with young kids, and a pumpkin-patch morning at Eckert’s, Thies, Stuckmeyer’s, or Rombachs for the harvest crowd. Many families do one of each over the month - a patch early, a family night mid-month, and a scarier outing for the older kids as Halloween nears.
A few practical notes: the haunted attractions get busiest on the weekends closest to Halloween, so go early in October or on a weeknight if you can, and buy tickets in advance. The farms are weather-dependent and busiest on sunny weekend afternoons, so it pays to keep a few indoor St. Louis attractions built for a rainy day in your back pocket in case the forecast turns. And because exact dates, hours, and ticket prices change every year, always confirm on each venue’s official page before you head out - the events are annual, but the calendar isn’t identical two years running.
The range is what makes the metro so easy to plan around. Within a short drive you can go from a gentle pumpkin-patch morning to a genuinely terrifying scream park to a friendly night at the zoo, mixing and matching by the weekend. Book the haunts the day tickets go on sale - the weekends nearest Halloween are the first to sell out, and those are exactly the ones your teenagers will want.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the best haunted house in St. Louis?
A.  The Darkness, next to Soulard Market about a mile from Ballpark Village, is the region’s most famous haunted house, running for more than three decades and regularly ranked among the best in the country. Its sister attractions, the Lemp Haunted House and Creepyworld scream park in Fenton, round out the top tier, and Fright Fest at Mid America Adventure in Eureka adds scares inside a theme park.
### Q. What events are happening in St. Louis in October?
A.  October in St. Louis is Halloween season: The Darkness, Creepyworld and the Lemp Haunted House for scares, Fright Fest at Mid America Adventure, Boo at the Zoo on select nights, Halloween Nights at Grant’s Farm, Pirates and Pumpkins at the St. Louis Aquarium, pumpkin patches all month, and the free Legends & Lanterns festival on historic Main Street in St. Charles.
### Q. What events are happening in St. Charles, Mo. for Halloween?
A.  The big one is Legends & Lanterns, a free festival on historic Main Street over several October weekends. Costumed storybook and folklore villains like Lizzie Borden, the Big Bad Wolf and the Queen of Hearts roam the street, you can write a scary story with Edgar Allan Poe, and a self-guided video tour points out Main Street’s paranormal hotspots.
### Q. What can adults do for fun on Halloween?
A.  Go get scared: The Darkness, the Lemp Haunted House and Creepyworld are built for grown-ups, and Fright Fest at Mid America Adventure adds coasters after dark. Bars and breweries across the city throw costume parties in the days around the holiday, and the Lemp Mansion leans into its own haunted history with paranormal tours and a Halloween bash.
### Q. What to do on Halloween that isn’t partying?
A.  Make it a pumpkin-patch morning at Eckert’s, Thies, Stuckmeyer’s or Rombachs, then go back after dark for Eckert’s Jack’s Lighted Trail. Boo at the Zoo is a costumed family night with no trick-or-treating, Legends & Lanterns in St. Charles is free, and on Halloween itself there are trunk-or-treats and the old St. Louis rule of telling a joke for your candy.

## The Best Fishing Spots in St. Louis: A Local Guide to Free Public Water
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-the-best-good-fishing-spots-in-st-louis
Everybody who fished here as a kid has the same morning stored somewhere. It started too early. A styrofoam cup of nightcrawlers sweated in the cupholder. The rod was cheap — maybe your dad’s, maybe a garage-sale special — and the bobber sat dead-still on flat water until, out of nowhere, it twitched, then plunged, and your whole small world narrowed to that one red-and-white dot. Maybe a grandpa in Affton taught you. Maybe an uncle out past St. Charles. Maybe it’s a memory you’ve been meaning to hand down to a kid of your own.
None of that required a bass boat or a lake-house membership, and it still doesn’t. A rod, a few bucks of bait, and a spot will do. This metro is quietly loaded with free, public, genuinely good water. From Florissant to south county to Valley Park to the city itself, there’s honest fishing within about fifteen minutes of your front door.
So here’s where to actually go, what you’ll catch, the one permit rule that trips people up, and a St. Louis secret most folks don’t know: you can catch trout here, in the city, in the dead of winter.
The best public fishing spots in the St. Louis area include Creve Coeur Lake (one of the largest natural lakes in Missouri), the 32 lakes of the August A. Busch Conservation Area near Weldon Spring, Simpson Lake in Valley Park, Bee Tree and Suson Parks in south county, and Jefferson Lake in Forest Park — all free and public. Anglers ages 16 to 64 need an inexpensive Missouri fishing permit; kids 15 and under and residents 65 and up fish free.
### First, the One Rule Everyone Trips On: Your Fishing Permit
Settle this before you load the car, because it’s the single most common St. Louis fishing question. In Missouri, anyone ages 16 through 64 needs a valid fishing permit to fish public water. It’s cheap. A resident annual permit runs around $14, and you can buy it in minutes online through the Missouri Department of Conservation, in the MDC app, or at nearly any Walmart, Bass Pro, or bait shop in the region.
Two exemptions worth knowing: kids 15 and under fish free, and so do Missouri residents 65 and older — which makes this a genuinely cheap outing for a grandparent taking the grandkids. One catch: if you want to keep trout (outside a designated trout park), you need a separate trout permit. For a full day of catch-and-release bluegill with the kids, the basic permit is all you’ll ever touch. When in doubt, the MDC website spells out current rules and prices — check it before your first trip of the year.
The same agency runs two staffed public shooting ranges in the metro — Jay Henges near Eureka and August A. Busch near Defiance — with staff on site for rifle, pistol, shotgun and archery. If that is more your idea of a Saturday outdoors, here is what a first range visit actually involves.
### The St. Louis Secret: You Can Catch Trout in the City in January
Almost nobody outside serious anglers knows this one. The MDC runs a St. Louis Urban Fishing Program that stocks a handful of city and county lakes with fish all year — channel catfish through the warm months (roughly March to September), hybrid sunfish, and, best of all, rainbow trout in the winter. While everyone else is inside complaining about the cold, you can stand at a lake inside the city limits and reel in trout, a fish most people assume you have to drive to the Ozarks to catch.
Only a few local lakes get the winter trout treatment — the Boathouse Lake in Carondelet Park is one of the standouts — and MDC even runs a fish-stocking hotline and online schedule so you can time your trip to a fresh stocking. It turns the deadest, grayest part of the St. Louis calendar into fishing season. Pack gloves, bring a thermos, and go.
### Where to Fish in St. Louis, by Where You Live
St. Louis fishing spreads across the whole metro, so the smartest move is usually the closest good water to you. Here’s the honest rundown, grouped by area, with what each is known for.
### West County & St. Charles: The Big Water
Want room to spread out? Head northwest. Creve Coeur Lake in Maryland Heights is the big one — at roughly 320 acres it’s one of the largest natural lakes in Missouri, ringed by a county park with trails and boat rentals. You’ll find crappie, bass, channel catfish, and even gar. It’s electric-motor only and there’s no swimming, which keeps it calm and fishable. A little farther out sits the August A. Busch Memorial Conservation Area near Weldon Spring, the region’s best bet for sheer variety: roughly 7,000 acres holding 32 fishable lakes, stocked by MDC with everything from bass and crappie to catfish, muskie, and winter trout. You could fish there a dozen weekends and not repeat a lake. The adjacent Weldon Spring area adds Prairie Lake and Fire Lake to the list.
### South County: Docks, Kids, and a Quiet Morning
South county is stacked with family-friendly water. Simpson Lake in Valley Park — a 72-acre former quarry — holds largemouth and spotted bass, catfish, and crappie, with a fishing dock and an electric-motor boat ramp. Bee Tree Park in Oakville pairs a stocked ~9-acre lake and fishing dock with gorgeous bluff views over the Mississippi, one of the prettiest places to wet a line in the metro. And Suson Park in Sappington is the pick for little kids: a few small, easy lakes plus a working animal farm right there, so when the fish stop biting, the goats and cows save the day.
### In the City: You Don’t Have to Leave Town
City-dwellers, you’ve got real options too. In Forest Park, aim for Jefferson Lake — the one Forest Park lake MDC actually stocks (bass, crappie, catfish, and winter trout), with a fishing dock and dead-center convenience. One honest heads-up so you don’t waste a trip: the scenic Post-Dispatch Lake by the Boathouse is not open to fishing, so don’t set up there — walk over to Jefferson Lake instead. On the south side, the Boathouse Lake in Carondelet Park (just off I-55) is a five-acre gem with a boathouse and fishing jetties, holding bass, catfish, crappie, sunfish, and carp — and it’s one of the select few lakes stocked with winter trout.
Totally unrelated, but — Southwest Garden is the neighborhood you keep driving past.
### Where to fish the Mississippi in St. Louis
And then there are the giants. The Mississippi fishes nothing like the park lakes above: no stocking truck, no fishing dock, just current, rock and a lot of very large catfish. The Missouri Department of Conservation’s own surveys on the St. Louis stretch turn up good numbers of blue and flathead catfish, many of them 20 to 30 inches, and several over 70 pounds. Here’s where the public can actually reach the water, as of October 2026.
North Riverfront Park, north city. The city calls its northernmost park “the spot most popular with fishermen,” and the usual catch off its banks is buffalo. Park in the north lot (70 spaces) or the south lot (20) and walk to the water.
Below Melvin Price Locks and Dam, Missouri side. The public access just below the dam, off Riverlands Way, puts you on the tailwater, where the churned water stays open in the hardest winters and anglers fish from the bank while eagles work the same water. No fishing from the lock walls or the dam itself. Our guide to Melvin Price Locks and Dam covers the free lock tours next door.
Confluence Point State Park. Bank fishing on both rivers, but not within 300 feet of the point itself. Open 7 a.m. to a half hour after sunset.
Cliff Cave Park, south county. St. Louis County lists fishing there, and Great Rivers Greenway says you can fish the Mississippi from the park. No boat ramp. Open a half hour before sunrise to a half hour after sunset.
Riverlands and Ellis Bay. From Oct. 1 to April 30, Ellis Bay is bank fishing only, so the waterfowl refuge stays quiet.
Two spots people still ask about need a caveat this fall. Columbia Bottom Conservation Area has been closed since Sept. 8, 2026 for levee work, except its boat ramp, and that ramp is on the Missouri River, not the Mississippi. Chouteau Island, on the Illinois side, is reached over a canal bridge that has been closed since June 22, 2026. Check both before you load the truck.
What bites, and where. Blue cats hold at current breaks below the tips of the rock dikes and along fast riprap banks; MDC’s bait list is fresh cut carp, shad or skipjack herring. Flatheads like moderate current around dikes and woody cut banks, and they want live sunfish. Channel cats sit in slower side channels and take nightcrawlers, chicken livers and stinkbait. In fall, white bass and hybrid stripers gang up near tributary mouths, dam tailwaters and the Chain of Rocks area.
Is there walleye in the Mississippi at St. Louis? Yes. MDC says walleye and sauger both turn up here, best on a minnow-tipped jig drifted near wing dikes and rocky shorelines. It doesn’t say which is more common, so treat either one as a bonus.
Your license works from either bank. Missouri and Illinois honor each other’s fishing licenses on the Mississippi itself, its backwaters and shared oxbow lakes, from a boat or from either bank. The deal stops at the tributaries: an Illinois creek needs an Illinois license. The center of the navigation channel is the state line, and on the other state’s side the stricter rule applies. That matters for walleye and sauger: Missouri allows 8 a day with no length limit on the river, while Illinois allows 6 with a 14-inch minimum. Catfish limits match, 20 blue and channel combined plus 10 flatheads. Missouri also caps you at two poles on the Mississippi.
Before you keep one. Missouri’s fish advisory for the Mississippi says no more than one meal a week of catfish over 17 inches, one a month of buffalo or shovelnose sturgeon, and never eat sturgeon eggs. Pallid and lake sturgeon go straight back in the river. The Missouri and Meramec fish the same way on a smaller scale, and both are open to public bank and boat fishing too. Mind the current and your footing on every one of them. Curious what else swims out there, from alligator gar to the one bull shark ever recorded near here? Read up on sharks in the Mississippi.
### What You’ll Catch — and What They Want to Eat
Half the fun is knowing your quarry. Here’s the short course on the fish you’ll actually meet in St. Louis water.
Largemouth & spotted bass — the glamour fish. And since people always ask: a bass’s favorite foods are crayfish, shad, and small fish like bluegill, which is exactly why crankbaits, jigs, and spinnerbaits that look like those work so well. Fish the edges and structure early and late in the day.
Channel catfish — the workhorse of the urban program, stocked spring through fall. Nightcrawlers, chicken liver, or stinkbait on the bottom, and patience. Great for kids because they bite willingly.
Crappie — spring is prime, around brush and docks; a small jig or minnow is all you need, and they’re excellent eating.
Bluegill & sunfish — the perfect beginner fish. A worm under a bobber, a dock, and a kid — that’s the whole recipe for a lifelong hobby.
Winter trout — the cold-weather bonus at Carondelet, Jefferson, and the Busch lakes. Small spinners, dough bait, or a bit of corn. (Trout permit required to keep them.)
### The Angler “Rules” People Google — Explained
Search fishing tips for five minutes and you’ll run into these two, so here’s the plain-English version. The 80/20 rule says that about 80% of the fish are holding in about 20% of the water. Translation: don’t just fan casts randomly across a whole lake. Find the structure — a drop-off, a weed edge, submerged timber, the fishing jetty, the shady side of a dock — and work it, because that’s where the fish stack up. The 90/10 rule is just the stricter cousin (90% of the fish in 10% of the water), making the same point even harder: a handful of prime spots out-produce everything else combined. Spend your time finding the good water, not covering all of it. That one idea will out-fish a fancier rod every time.
### Which St. Louis Spot Is Best for You?
Taking little kids: Suson Park (animal farm backup) or Bee Tree Park (easy dock, pretty views).
Chasing bass: the Busch Conservation Area lakes or Creve Coeur.
Winter trout: Boathouse Lake in Carondelet, Jefferson Lake in Forest Park, or the Busch lakes.
The most variety in one trip: Busch CA — 32 lakes, take your pick.
Staying in the city: Jefferson Lake (Forest Park) or Carondelet Boathouse Lake.
Big-river catfish and a good story: the Mississippi, Missouri, or Meramec.
West county convenience: Simpson Lake in Valley Park.
### When to Go: A St. Louis Fishing Calendar
There’s no closed season on the fun here — only different fish. Spring is crappie time, with fish moving shallow around brush and docks; it’s many locals’ favorite few weeks of the year. Late spring through summer is prime for bass (early morning and evening, when it’s cooler) and for the stocked channel catfish that show up in the urban lakes from about March through September. Fall keeps the bass and catfish going as the water cools. And winter, as we said, is trout season in the city. If you want to time it perfectly, MDC’s stocking schedule and hotline tell you when fresh fish hit each lake.
### Before You Head Out: A Quick Checklist
Grab your permit (ages 16–64) — online or at any bait shop or big-box store. Add a trout permit if you plan to keep trout.
Check the rules for your lake — many are electric-motor-only, most have no swimming, and some have length or catch limits posted at the ramp.
Keep it simple to start — a rod, hooks, bobbers, split shot, and a cup of nightcrawlers will catch fish almost anywhere on this list.
Mind the river. If you fish the big rivers, respect the current and check consumption advisories before eating your catch.
Pack it out. Leave the bank cleaner than you found it — cut line and hooks are brutal on wildlife.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Where can I fish in St. Louis for free?
A.  Plenty of public spots cost nothing to access: Creve Coeur Lake (Maryland Heights), the Busch Conservation Area lakes (Weldon Spring), Simpson Lake (Valley Park), Bee Tree and Suson Parks (south county), Jefferson Lake in Forest Park, and Carondelet’s Boathouse Lake. You’ll still need a Missouri fishing permit if you’re 16 to 64, but the water itself is free.
### Q. Can I fish in Missouri without a license?
A.  Only if you’re 15 or under, or a Missouri resident 65 or older. Everyone 16 to 64 needs a Missouri fishing permit (about $14 for a resident annual), and a separate trout permit is required to keep trout outside designated trout parks. Buy permits online, in the MDC app, or at most bait and big-box stores.
### Q. Can you really catch trout in St. Louis?
A.  Yes — the MDC stocks rainbow trout in select city and county lakes in winter through its St. Louis Urban Fishing Program. The Boathouse Lake in Carondelet Park, Jefferson Lake in Forest Park, and the Busch Conservation Area lakes are among the spots to try. Check the MDC stocking schedule to time your trip, and get a trout permit if you plan to keep any.
### Q. What is the best fishing spot near St. Louis for bass?
A.  The 32 lakes of the August A. Busch Conservation Area near Weldon Spring are a top bass destination for their sheer variety, and Creve Coeur Lake and Simpson Lake are strong closer-in options. Fish structure and edges early and late in the day, using lures that imitate a bass’s favorite foods — crayfish, shad, and bluegill.
### Q. What is the 80/20 rule in fishing?
A.  The 80/20 rule says roughly 80% of the fish hold in about 20% of the water. The takeaway: don’t cast randomly across a whole lake — find the structure (a drop-off, a weed edge, submerged timber, the shady side of a dock, the fishing jetty) and work it, because that’s where fish stack up. The stricter 90/10 version makes the same point even harder: find the good water, don’t just cover all of it.
### Q. What bait is irresistible to bass?
A.  Whatever looks like what they already eat: crayfish, shad, and small fish like bluegill. That’s exactly why lures that imitate them (crankbaits, jigs, and spinnerbaits) work so well in St. Louis lakes. Fish the edges and structure early and late in the day, when bass move shallow to feed, for your best shot.
### Q. Where can I fish in the Mississippi River near St. Louis?
A.  North Riverfront Park in north city, the Missouri bank just below Melvin Price Locks and Dam, Confluence Point State Park (not within 300 feet of the point) and Cliff Cave Park in south county all put you on the Mississippi. As of October 2026, Columbia Bottom is closed except a Missouri River ramp, and Chouteau Island’s canal bridge is closed. A Missouri or Illinois license works from either bank.
### Q. What fish are in season around St. Louis right now?
A.  There’s good fishing year-round: crappie in spring, bass and stocked channel catfish spring through fall, and rainbow trout stocked in select lakes in winter. Because it shifts by season and stocking date, MDC’s online stocking schedule and hotline are the best way to see what’s biting this week.

## Finding Low Income Apartments in St. Louis: Your Guide to Affordable Housing
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/finding-low-income-apartments-in-st-louis-your-guide-to-affordable-housing
Affordable units in St. Louis move fast, and the listings sit scattered across housing-authority rolls, nonprofit lists, and a handful of rental sites. This guide pulls that search into one place. You'll see where low income apartments get posted, the paperwork to have ready, the programs that lower your rent, and what to check at a viewing. Start with what ‘low income’ actually means here.
### Key Takeaways
Understand what makes housing qualify as low income and the advantages of opting for affordable places.
Explore various online platforms, local housing authorities, and community groups that list low income apartments in St. Louis.
Prepare for the application process by gathering necessary documents and understanding income verification.
Learn about government programs like Section 8 vouchers that can help cover rent costs.

### Understanding Low Income Apartments in St. Louis
‘Low income’ apartments carry rents set below the local market because they're meant for households under a certain earnings level. In St. Louis that covers public housing, units that accept Housing Choice Vouchers, and privately owned income-restricted buildings. Eligibility usually turns on how your income compares to the area median. Here's how to find each type and prove you qualify.
### Resources for Finding Low Income Apartments
### Online Listing Platforms for Affordable Rentals
A few rental sites are built specifically for low-income and subsidized housing, which spares you from wading through market-rate listings. Most let you filter by location, price, and even specific programs like Section 8. You can often create an account to save your favorite listings and get alerts when new places become available. It's a good idea to check these sites regularly because affordable apartments can get snapped up quickly.
Some popular platforms include:
AffordableHousing.com
Rent.com (look for their affordable housing section)
Apartments.com (use their filters for income-restricted units)
### Local Housing Authorities and Agencies
Your local government plays a big role in affordable housing. In St. Louis, the St. Louis Housing Authority (SLHA) is a key resource. They manage public housing and administer programs like the Housing Choice Voucher program (often called Section 8). These agencies often have their own lists of available properties or can guide you on how to apply for their programs. It's worth visiting their website or giving them a call to see what they offer. They can also tell you about other local initiatives that might not be advertised on general listing sites.
### Community Organizations and Non-profits
Beyond official government agencies, many non-profit groups and community organizations in St. Louis are dedicated to helping people find housing. These groups might offer services like:
Housing counseling to help you understand your options.
Assistance with filling out applications.
Information on local resources and support services.
Sometimes, they even have their own housing developments.
These organizations often have a deep connection to the community and can provide personalized support. A quick search for “St. Louis housing non-profits” should give you a starting point for finding these helpful groups.

### Eligibility and Application Process
Getting approved for a low-income apartment runs on a few clear steps, and knowing them ahead of time keeps things smooth. Finding a place you like is only the start. You still have to document that you meet the requirements, then get the application in before someone else does.
### Income Verification Requirements
Landlords and housing programs need to confirm your income to make sure you qualify for affordable housing. This usually means providing proof of what you earn. This is often the most important part of the application.
Here's what you might need to show:
Pay stubs: Recent ones, usually from the last 30-60 days.
Tax returns: Your most recent federal tax return.
Benefit statements: If you receive Social Security, disability, or unemployment benefits, you'll need official award letters.
Bank statements: These can show regular income deposits.
Letter of employment: From your employer, stating your position and salary.
Sometimes, there are limits on how much you can earn to qualify for certain programs. These limits are often based on a percentage of the Area Median Income (AMI) for St. Louis. For example, you might see terms like “30% AMI” or “50% AMI,” meaning your rent should be no more than 30% or 50% of that median income.
Hard left turn: nobody expects this many good restaurants in New Haven.
### Completing Rental Applications
Once you've gathered your income documents, you'll fill out the actual rental application. Be thorough and honest. Missing information or errors can cause delays or even lead to your application being rejected.
Most applications will ask for:
Personal information: Names, dates of birth, Social Security numbers for all adults who will live there.
Employment history: Where you've worked and for how long.
Rental history: Previous addresses and landlord contact information.
References: Personal or professional contacts who can vouch for you.
Consent for background checks: This is standard for most rentals.
It's a good idea to have a copy of your identification, like a driver's license or state ID, ready to go. Some applications might be online, while others are paper forms. If you're looking at properties listed on sites like affordable housing listings, you might find online application options built right in.
### Understanding Waiting Lists
For many low-income housing options, especially those with subsidies or in high demand, there might be a waiting list. This means you apply, get approved, and then wait for an available unit. Waiting lists can sometimes be long, so patience is key.
How they work: Applications are usually processed in the order they are received, or based on specific criteria set by the housing provider.
What to expect: You might be given an estimated wait time, but this can change. It's important to keep your contact information updated with the housing authority or property manager so they can reach out when a unit is ready.
Staying informed: Don't hesitate to check in periodically (but not too often!) to see where you are on the list. Some programs have online portals where you can track your status.
Remember to keep copies of everything you submit. This helps you stay organized and provides a backup if any documents go missing.
### Government Programs and Assistance
### Section 8 Housing Choice Vouchers
Section 8, officially known as the Housing Choice Voucher Program, is a big deal for many people looking for affordable housing. It's a federal program that helps very low-income families, the elderly, and the disabled afford decent, safe, and sanitary housing in the private market. Basically, you find a place you like, and if it meets program standards, your Public Housing Agency (PHA) pays a portion of your rent directly to the landlord. You'll typically pay about 30% of your adjusted income for rent. It's a way to make market-rate apartments accessible when your budget is tight. Getting a voucher can take time, as waiting lists are often long, but it's a significant resource if you qualify.
Tired of Waiting for SEO?
### Other Federal and State Aid Programs
Beyond Section 8, there are other programs that can help make housing more affordable. The Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) can help with utility bills, which is a huge relief for many households. There are also state and local initiatives, sometimes run through the Missouri Housing Development Commission or specific St. Louis city agencies, that might offer rental assistance, down payment assistance for first-time homebuyers, or support for specific groups like veterans or people with disabilities. It's worth looking into what's available specifically in the St. Louis area, as these programs can change and have different eligibility rules.
### How to Apply for Housing Assistance
Applying for housing assistance programs can feel like a lot, but breaking it down makes it manageable. Here’s a general idea of what you might need to do:
Identify the Right Program: Figure out which program best fits your needs. Is it Section 8, a local rental subsidy, or something else? Your local housing authority is a good place to start asking questions.
Gather Your Documents: You'll likely need proof of income (pay stubs, tax returns), identification (driver's license, social security card), and possibly birth certificates for all household members. Sometimes, proof of disability or veteran status is also required.
Complete the Application: Fill out the application forms completely and accurately. Missing information can cause delays or disqualification. Many applications can be found online or picked up in person.
Submit and Wait: Submit your application by the deadline. Be prepared for waiting periods, especially for programs like Section 8. You might be placed on a waiting list.
Finding affordable housing often involves using multiple resources. You can explore various listing platforms, including those focused on affordable rentals, which can sometimes integrate with government programs like Section 8. Checking out sites like St Louis Near Me Directory can also help you find local resources and listings.
### Tips for Securing Your Apartment
Preparation is what separates the applicants who land a unit from the ones who keep missing out. The process isn't always quick, but a little groundwork, documents ready and questions prepared, moves you toward the front of the line.
### Preparing Your Documentation
Before you even start looking at places, get your paperwork in order. This will make you look organized and ready to rent when you find a place you like. You'll likely need several things:
Proof of Income: This could be pay stubs, a letter from your employer, or documentation for any public assistance you receive. Make sure these are recent.
Identification: A valid government-issued ID, like a driver's license or state ID card, is a must.
Credit Report: Some landlords may check this, so it's good to know where you stand. You can often get a free report annually.
References: Have contact information ready for previous landlords or employers who can vouch for you.
Bank Statements: A few months of recent statements can show you manage your money well.
Having these documents ready to go can make a huge difference when you're competing for a desirable apartment.
### What to Expect During Viewings
When you tour an apartment, slow down and pay attention. Looks are the surface. What matters more is the condition of the unit and whether it feels right for you. Take your time, and don't let anyone rush you.
Inspect the Unit: Look for any signs of damage, like water stains on the ceiling, cracks in the walls, or issues with plumbing. Test the faucets, flush the toilet, and check the appliances if they're included.
Check the Building and Neighborhood: Walk around the common areas. Are they clean? Is there adequate lighting? How does the neighborhood feel at different times of the day? Consider proximity to public transportation and essential services.
Ask Questions: Don't be shy. Ask about utility costs, any building rules, parking availability, and the landlord's maintenance policies.
### Tenant Rights and Responsibilities
Once you secure an apartment, it's important to know your rights as a tenant and what your responsibilities are. This helps prevent misunderstandings down the road.
Your Rights: You have the right to a safe and habitable living space. Landlords must make necessary repairs in a timely manner and cannot enter your unit without proper notice, except in emergencies.
Your Responsibilities: You are responsible for paying rent on time, keeping the unit clean, and not disturbing your neighbors. You also need to follow the terms of your lease agreement.
Remember, being a responsible tenant can lead to a positive renting experience and good relationships with your landlord.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. How much of your income should go to rent?
A.  The common rule of thumb is about 30% of your gross (pre-tax) income — so if you earn $3,000 a month, aim for roughly $900 in rent. It’s a guideline, not a law: you might go higher short-term in a pinch, but staying near 30% leaves room for utilities, food, and emergencies. Income-restricted apartments can bring rent below that line.
### Q. How do I find affordable apartments in St. Louis?
A.  Search the big rental sites with price and “low income/affordable” filters — Apartments.com, Zillow, and AffordableHousing.com all list St. Louis units. For income-based options, apply through the St. Louis Housing Authority (slha.org) and the Housing Authority of St. Louis County. Apply to several at once, and act fast when something in budget opens.
### Q. Do you need good credit to rent an apartment?
A.  It helps but isn’t always required. Many market-rate landlords check credit, but income-restricted and affordable properties often weigh income and rental history more than a score. If your credit is thin, offer references, proof of steady income, or a co-signer, and look at affordable-housing programs that tend to be more flexible.
### Q. What is the maximum income to qualify for rent assistance?
A.  It varies by program and household size, but most rent-assistance and affordable-housing options cap income around 50% of the Area Median Income, with tax-credit (LIHTC) apartments often allowing up to 60–80%. Check the current AMI limit for your household size before applying — it’s on the housing authority or property’s site.
### Q. How can I help someone find an affordable apartment?
A.  Set a realistic budget together (aim near 30% of income), then search Apartments.com, Zillow, and AffordableHousing.com with price filters, and apply to income-based options through the housing authorities. Help gather documents (ID, proof of income, references) so applications move fast. Community Action Agencies and Beyond Housing offer free help if it feels overwhelming.
### Q. What makes an apartment count as 'low income' housing?
A.  Low income housing usually means places where the rent is set lower because it's meant for people or families who don't make a lot of money. Often, there are rules about how much you can earn to qualify for these kinds of apartments in St. Louis.
### Q. Where can I find listings for affordable places to live in St. Louis?
A.  You can check out websites that focus on affordable rentals. Also, local housing groups and government offices in St. Louis often have lists or can point you in the right direction. Sometimes, community centers have helpful information too.
### Q. What kind of paperwork do I need to apply for a low income apartment?
A.  You'll likely need to show proof of your income, like pay stubs or tax forms. They might also ask for identification and possibly references. Having these documents ready makes the application process smoother.
### Q. How does the Section 8 program work for finding an apartment?
A.  Section 8, also called the Housing Choice Voucher program, helps pay part of your rent. You find an apartment that accepts these vouchers, and the program pays the landlord the difference between the rent and what you can afford based on your income.
### Q. What should I do if there's a waiting list for an apartment?
A.  If there's a waiting list, get on it as soon as possible! Make sure you understand how long it might be and what your spot on the list is. Keep your contact information updated with the housing provider so they can reach you when a unit becomes available.
### Q. Are there specific neighborhoods in St. Louis that are generally more affordable?
A.  Yes, some areas in St. Louis tend to have lower rent prices than others. It's a good idea to research different neighborhoods to see which ones fit your budget and also offer things you need, like access to public transport or nearby shops.

### At a Glance: What to Order
### What Millwoods Actually Is
Millwoods is a full-on sports bar and grill in Maryland Heights — think roughly forty TVs, pool tables, darts, Golden Tee, and a downstairs taproom that essentially makes it two bars in one. It’s the kind of place built for a game day: plenty of screens, a big menu of shareable bar food, and enough going on that a group can settle in for hours. On value, MeYou generally serves good-sized portions. You won't leave hungry. The amount of food per dollar feels fair, and you can eat well here without spending a lot. Quality and quantity stay in balance, plate after plate.

Appetizers: Usually a good size for sharing or starting your meal.
Entrees: Generous servings that often leave room for a small doggy bag.
Value: Prices are reasonable, especially considering the quality and portion sizes. You're getting a good deal for authentic Thai food in the St. Louis area.

MeYou doesn't shout for attention. Find it once, though, and you’ll wonder how you drove past for so long. Locals guard it; visitors are glad they stumbled in. It sits off the main drag, but the food earns the detour.

## Hotels Near Busch Stadium: Where to Stay for a St. Louis Cardinals Game
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/top-rated-hotels-close-to-busch-stadium-for-your-next-st-louis-visit
The buzz outside the window starts hours before first pitch. Grab your coffee, and the walk to the gate is short enough that “getting to the game” never turns into a parking nightmare. After the ninth inning, you’re back in your room in ten minutes instead of sitting in a garage line with 40,000 other people.
That’s the whole case for staying near Busch Stadium: the walk to the ballpark becomes part of the fun instead of a logistics headache. Some fans drive in from Columbia or Cape Girardeau. Some fly in for a weekend series, and some are building a birthday around one game. However you get here, where you stay decides how good the day feels. What follows is a local’s guide to the hotels closest to the ballpark, ranked by how far you’ll actually walk, plus the game-day booking tips that save money and hassle.
### At a Glance: Closest Hotels to Busch Stadium
### Right Across the Street: Ballpark Village
Want to fall out of bed and into your seat? Live! by Loews — St. Louis gets you closest. It sits inside Ballpark Village, the dining-and-entertainment district directly across from Busch Stadium, roughly a tenth of a mile from the gates. It’s Cardinals-themed by design. Many suites face the stadium, and the hotel’s terrace carries a live video feed from inside Busch. Nothing on a game day stays closer to the action, which is exactly why it books up first.
Ballpark Village itself is worth knowing about even if you stay elsewhere: developed by the Cardinals and The Cordish Companies next to the stadium, it’s packed with bars, restaurants, and the Cardinals Nation venue, and it’s where the pre- and post-game crowd gathers. Staying here means the party is downstairs.
### A Few Blocks Away: The Reliable Big-Brand Picks
Just west of the stadium, in the historic Cupples Station district, The Westin St. Louis is an upscale option a couple of blocks from the gates — close enough that the hotel calls itself steps from Busch and Ballpark Village. A short walk north, the Hilton St. Louis at the Ballpark (about 0.3 mile, roughly two blocks) is a Cardinals preferred hotel partner, with the popular Three Sixty rooftop bar looking out over the field — a genuine game-day amenity. Both are dependable, full-service downtown hotels that put you within an easy stroll of first pitch.
### The Arch District: A Short, Scenic Walk
A few blocks east toward the Gateway Arch, two more hotels put you within a comfortable walk of the ballpark and the riverfront at once. The Drury Plaza Hotel St. Louis at the Arch (about 0.3 mile) is a local favorite for its free extras — the Drury chain is known for free hot breakfast and evening drinks — and, handy for families, it has an indoor pool. Nearby, the Hyatt Regency St. Louis at The Arch (about 0.4 mile) is a large hotel steps from Gateway Arch National Park, an easy walk to both the game and the Arch grounds.
One heads-up: the old Millennium Hotel on the riverfront is closed and being demolished as part of a major redevelopment — don’t confuse it with the fully-operating Hyatt Regency, which is a separate building. If an old listing points you to the Millennium, skip it.
### A Little Farther, Still Walkable
If the closest hotels are booked or your budget wants options, several more sit within about a 10-to-15-minute walk along the Washington Avenue corridor. The Magnolia Hotel St. Louis, a Tribute Portfolio hotel (about 0.5 mile), is a stylish boutique choice; the Embassy Suites by Hilton St. Louis Downtown (about 0.6 mile) offers all-suite rooms with free breakfast; the Courtyard by Marriott Downtown/Convention Center (about 0.9 mile) is a solid mid-range pick; and the Marriott St. Louis Grand (about 0.9 mile), housed in the historic former Statler hotel, is a grand old downtown landmark. All keep you downtown and walkable to the ballpark, the Arch, and the convention center.
### Getting to the Game (and Skipping the Parking Mess)
Here’s the underrated reason to stay close: parking. On a Cardinals home date, downtown garages and lots fill up and prices spike, and the post-game exit crawl can eat 30 to 45 minutes before you even reach a highway. Stay within a few blocks of Busch and that whole problem disappears — you walk to the gate, and you walk home. If you’re driving in for the day instead, plan to park once, early, and treat the ballpark district as a walkable zone; many visitors leave the car at the hotel entirely. The MetroLink light rail also has a stop right at the stadium (Stadium Station), which is handy if you’re staying near a line or coming from the airport.
Total tangent — where to eat in South County, since you’re already hungry.
### Budget, Mid-Range, or Splurge
The ballpark district covers every budget. For a splurge or a special occasion, Live! by Loews and the Westin put you in the thick of it with full-service amenities. For a reliable mid-range stay, the Drury Plaza at the Arch is hard to beat — the free breakfast and evening drinks genuinely lower the trip’s total cost, and there’s that indoor pool for the kids. For more room or a suite, the Embassy Suites Downtown gives you two-room suites and free breakfast a short walk out. The trick is matching the hotel to your trip: a couple doing a game-and-Arch weekend wants something different than a family of five with a pool-loving seven-year-old.
### Game-Day Tips for Booking Downtown
A few things save first-timers real money and stress. Book early for home stands. St. Louis just posted a record tourism year — future hotel room-nights booked jumped about 46% — and the closest ballpark hotels (Live! by Loews, the Westin, the Hilton at the Ballpark) sell out first on Cardinals weekends and marquee events. Watch for hotel-plus-ticket packages; the Cardinals’ preferred partners sometimes bundle rooms with tickets. Weigh walking versus a shuttle: the hotels above are all walkable, but some downtown properties a bit farther out run game-day shuttles, which can be worth it if you’re staying wider. And if you’re coming for a big series or a concert at the nearby Enterprise Center too, lock your room in as far ahead as you can.
### Make a Weekend of It
The best part of staying downtown is that a Cardinals game is only the start. From these hotels you can walk to Gateway Arch National Park and ride the tram to the top, spend an afternoon getting lost in the wonderfully weird City Museum, catch a St. Louis Blues game or a concert at the Enterprise Center, or wander America’s Center and the Washington Avenue restaurant-and-nightlife strip. The Dome at America’s Center pulls in stadium-sized concerts and events too, so a summer weekend can easily stack a ballgame, a show, and a riverfront morning back to back.
And of course, downtown is full of places to eat and drink within a few blocks of every hotel here — from Ballpark Village’s sports bars to Washington Avenue’s restaurants to the historic spots tucked around Laclede’s Landing. Pair a ballgame with the Arch and a great dinner, and one hotel booking turns into a full St. Louis weekend on foot — no car, no parking hassle, just the ballpark and the city all within a few blocks.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What hotel is closest to Busch Stadium?
A.  Live! by Loews is the closest, sitting inside Ballpark Village directly across the street from Busch Stadium — roughly a tenth of a mile from the gates. It’s Cardinals-themed, many suites face the field, and it books up fastest on game days, so reserve early for home stands.
### Q. Where to stay for a St. Louis Cardinals game?
A.  Stay downtown, within walking distance of the ballpark. Top picks by proximity are Live! by Loews (across the street), the Westin, the Hilton at the Ballpark (a Cardinals preferred hotel), and the Drury Plaza and Hyatt Regency near the Arch. Staying downtown lets you walk to the game and skip game-day parking.
### Q. Where should I park for a Cardinals game?
A.  If you’re staying downtown near the ballpark, the easiest answer is to not drive at all — walk from your hotel. If you’re commuting in, park once in a downtown garage or lot early, since prices rise and spaces vanish close to first pitch, or take MetroLink to the Stadium Station stop right at Busch.
### Q. Can you walk from Union Station hotel to Busch Stadium?
A.  Yes, roughly. The St. Louis Union Station Hotel is about a mile from Busch Stadium — a walkable 15-to-20 minutes, or a short rideshare. It’s a good option if the closest ballpark hotels are booked, and Union Station has its own attractions like the aquarium and the St. Louis Wheel.
### Q. Is there a hotel with an indoor pool near Busch Stadium?
A.  Yes. The Drury Plaza Hotel St. Louis at the Arch, about a quarter-mile from Busch, has a year-round indoor pool and whirlpools — a good pick for families. The Hilton St. Louis at the Ballpark also has a climate-controlled indoor pool. Both keep you within an easy walk of the ballpark.
### Q. How far ahead should I book a hotel for a Cardinals game?
A.  As early as you can for weekend series and marquee events. St. Louis set a tourism record in 2025 and future hotel bookings are up sharply, so the closest, best-value rooms near Busch Stadium sell out first on game days. For a popular home stand, booking several weeks to months ahead is wise.
### Q. Do hotels near Busch Stadium have shuttles?
A.  Some do. The hotels closest to the ballpark are easy walks, so they typically don’t need shuttles, but several downtown hotels a bit farther out run game-day or general downtown shuttle service. If you’re staying beyond a comfortable walk, ask the hotel directly whether it shuttles to the stadium.
### Q. How early should you get to Busch Stadium?
A.  Gates open well before first pitch, and arriving in that first window is the difference between walking in and standing in a line. If you are driving, add time for downtown traffic; if you are staying within a few blocks, you can leave much later than a driver can and still beat them in.
### Q. Is Busch Stadium in a good area?
A.  The stadium sits at the edge of downtown next to Ballpark Village, and the blocks immediately around it are busy and well lit on game nights. Like any downtown core it is quieter when nothing is on, so pick your hotel for the walk you will actually make after the game.
### Q. What are some affordable hotels near Busch Stadium in St. Louis?
A.  The cheaper rooms are usually a few blocks out rather than across the street, and the walk is flat and short. Rates swing hard with the schedule — a weekday against a low-draw opponent costs a fraction of a weekend series, so shift the date before you shift the hotel.
### Q. Which hotels in St. Louis offer shuttle service to Busch Stadium?
A.  Shuttle arrangements change season to season and are usually offered by properties farther from the core, so confirm it with the hotel directly when you book rather than trusting a listing. Downtown, most people find the walk faster than waiting for a van anyway.

## Escape Rooms, Rock Climbing, VR & Barcades in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/top-indoor-activities-in-stl-beat-the-boredom-indoors
Some days you don’t want to look at things in a museum — you want to do something. Maybe it’s a first date that needs a spark, a group of friends who can never agree on a plan, a birthday, or just a restless Saturday when the weather won’t let you outside. You want to move, compete, and laugh a little.
St. Louis has a deep bench of active indoor entertainment — escape rooms, rock climbing, virtual reality, retro barcades, bowling, and axe throwing — all under a roof and open whatever the sky is doing. This is a local’s guide to the best active indoor things to do in St. Louis, sorted by the mood you’re after. Some nights call for a puzzle and a team. Some call for a wall to climb, others for a cocktail and a pinball machine. St. Louis covers all of them within a short drive.
### St. Louis Active-Indoor Spots at a Glance
### Escape Rooms: Turn a Night Into a Team Sport
Escape rooms are the perfect active indoor plan for a date or a small group — an hour of puzzles, teamwork, and a ticking clock. St. Louis Escape in Soulard runs eight themed rooms and even adds blacklight 3D mini golf and a pinball arcade if you want to make a night of it. Downtown in the Loft District, Escape the Room STL offers several themed rooms for around $35 a person. Both are ideal for four-to-eight people who want to laugh, argue about clues, and (maybe) beat the clock together. They’re also a great equalizer for mixed groups — there’s a job for the detail-spotter, the big-picture thinker, and the person who just enjoys yelling “try that key in that lock.” Book a slot ahead, show up a few minutes early, and plan to grab food or drinks afterward to rehash how you did.
### Indoor Rock Climbing: Surprise Yourself
You don’t need to be an athlete to have fun on a climbing wall — the good gyms are built for beginners. Upper Limits in Maryland Heights is a big, well-equipped gym with 45-foot walls and auto-belays, so you can climb even without a partner. Climb So iLL runs a dramatic downtown location inside a former power plant (plus a St. Charles gym), pairing climbing with yoga and fitness. Rent shoes, take the intro, and you’ll be surprised how quickly a rainy afternoon turns into a real workout you actually enjoyed. Climbing is also a sneaky-great date or group activity: you’re cheering each other up the wall, there’s a built-in sense of accomplishment, and no experience is required to have a genuinely good time.
### Barcades: Beer, Quarters, and Zero Boredom
For grown-ups, St. Louis’s barcades are some of the best nights out in the city. Up-Down STL in the Central West End is the flagship — more than 60 retro arcade games, pinball, skee-ball, and console classics, with a rooftop bar (it’s 21+ in the evenings, with family hours during the day). Over in The Grove, Purple Quarters is a newer cocktail-and-arcade bar from a well-loved local team, with comedy and karaoke nights mixed in. Both nail the same trick: cheap games, good drinks, and the instant nostalgia of a machine you haven’t touched since childhood.
### Bowling and Games, Grown-Up Edition
Bowling still holds up, and St. Louis does it with character. Pin-Up Bowl in the Delmar Loop pairs retro lanes with a full cocktail lounge and runs late into the night — a great low-key date or group hang. For a bigger, do-it-all option, Main Event in Chesterfield stacks bowling, multi-story laser tag, and 100-plus arcade games under one roof, open late daily — ideal for families or big groups who want variety without venue-hopping.
### Virtual Reality: The Group Adrenaline Hit
VR has grown up, and St. Louis has real options now. Sandbox VR, which opened inside City Foundry in late 2025, is the premium pick — full-body motion capture and haptics that drop your group into a shared virtual world (zombies, space, the works). In south county, STL Virtual Reality in Oakville is an all-ages spot where up to six players can team up or compete across co-op, competitive, and escape-style games. Either way, it’s a genuinely modern, high-energy activity that groups and older kids love.
### Axe Throwing and Other Ways to Blow Off Steam
If your idea of active indoor fun involves throwing something, St. Louis has you covered. Top Notch Axe Throwing runs locations in St. Louis and St. Charles where a coach gets you sticking axes into a target in minutes — a surprisingly fun group or date activity. Amp Up Action Park combines an axe range with other action attractions under one roof. It’s the kind of thing that sounds intimidating and turns out to be the highlight of the night.
Nothing to do with axes — there are surprisingly good restaurants in Hazelwood.
### City Foundry STL: When You Can’t Agree on One Thing
If your group can’t settle on a single activity, City Foundry STL in Midtown solves it. This food-hall-and-entertainment complex — which drew more than two million visitors in 2025 — packs Puttshack’s tech-tracked mini golf, Sandbox VR, The Escape Game, and the Alamo Drafthouse cinema around a huge food hall. You can throw an entire evening together here: dinner, a game, a movie, a drink, all without moving the car. It’s the easiest answer to “what do you want to do?” in the whole city — and because it keeps adding new tenants, there’s usually something you haven’t tried yet. For a group with mixed ages and interests, it’s hard to beat: the little kids do mini golf, the teens do VR, and the adults get a proper dinner and a drink, all in one building.
### The Deeper Pinball and Games Scene
St. Louis has a genuinely serious pinball culture worth knowing about if you catch the bug. Beyond the big barcades, spots like the Silver Ballroom in Bevo (a punk-rock pinball bar in a former bowling alley) and Lazarus Pinball Museum in Fenton (all-ages) draw dedicated players, and there are league nights around the metro. The point is that “playing some games” in St. Louis can be a five-dollar lark with a beer or a genuine hobby — the machines and the community are here either way. If arcades and pinball are your thing, it’s worth exploring the full lineup across the city and into the Metro East.
### Know Before You Go
A few quick tips make an active-indoor night smoother. Book escape rooms and VR ahead — they run on timed slots and sell out on weekends. Check age policies: barcades like Up-Down STL and Purple Quarters are 21+ in the evenings (Up-Down adds daytime family hours), while family centers like Main Event and all-ages spots like STL Virtual Reality welcome kids. Wear the right clothes for climbing or City Museum-style crawling. And call ahead for the smaller venues — independent spots occasionally change hours or host private events, so a two-minute check saves a wasted drive.
### Which Active Indoor Plan Fits Tonight?
A memorable date: an escape room or Up-Down’s barcade. A group or party: Main Event or Sandbox VR. Actually getting active: rock climbing at Upper Limits or Climb So iLL. Can’t agree on one thing: City Foundry. Low-key and cheap: Pin-Up Bowl or a barcade with a roll of quarters. Whatever the mood, there’s an active indoor plan in St. Louis that beats sitting at home. And most of these are surprisingly affordable — an escape room, a climb, or a night at the barcade runs about the price of a movie and popcorn, but you’ll actually remember it. When the group text asks “what should we do?”, you’ll have a real answer.

## Cate Zone Chesterfield: Authentic Northeastern Chinese in West County
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/cate-zone-chesterfield-a-culinary-gem-you-can-t-miss
For years, if you wanted the real thing — authentic Northeastern Chinese cooking, not the Americanized takeout most of the metro grew up on — you drove to a small, perpetually-packed cafe in University City and waited for a table. Cate Zone earned that kind of devotion. So when the family behind it opened a second, roomier location in Chesterfield, west-county food lovers took notice. If the strip-mall takeout version is all you’ve ever eaten, one meal here can change your mind about the whole cuisine.
West-county diners no longer have to drive across town for this food, which is why it now earns a spot in any local’s guide to west county dining. Cate Zone brought its Dongbei-style cooking to the Four Seasons Shopping Center, into a bigger, more modern room made for the shared, family-style meals this cuisine is built around. Same food that built the reputation, now with elbow room. The expansion never watered down what made the original special.
### A real second location — and the original is still going
The geography trips people up, so here it is plainly. Cate Zone Chesterfield is a genuine second location, opened in February 2024 — not a relocation. The original in University City is still open and running, so you can visit either. Co-owner Daniel Ma runs the Chesterfield restaurant, while his partner stayed on at the University City cafe, keeping both kitchens in the same family’s hands.
You’ll find the Chesterfield location at 24 Four Seasons Shopping Center, Chesterfield, MO 63017, phone (314) 392-9624. The owners hail from Liaoning province in Northeastern China, and the whole concept is built around sharing: as Daniel Ma has put it, in China you share food and bring the family, and the bigger Chesterfield dining room was designed to let more people do exactly that. It’s a place that makes the most sense with a crowd, a lazy Susan turning, and a dozen dishes in the middle of the table.
### What is Northeastern Chinese food?
“Dongbei” cuisine comes from Northeastern China, a cold, hearty region, and it tastes noticeably different from the Cantonese-derived American-Chinese takeout most people know. Expect bold, savory, generously spiced dishes: hand-crafted dumplings, cumin-scented lamb, chili-oil-slicked fish, rich braises. This is food for a table of people passing plates around, not a single takeout carton. The region borders Korea and Russia and cooks with its own accent — wheat instead of only rice, mountains of dumplings, hearty stews, and a fearless hand with cumin and chili. Traveled in China, or have friends from the north? It’ll taste like home. If not, consider it a very good place to learn.
For a lot of St. Louis diners, Cate Zone was their first taste of this regional style, and it’s converted plenty of skeptics who thought they knew what “Chinese food” meant. If your idea of the cuisine stops at sweet-and-sour and fried rice, this is a genuinely eye-opening upgrade.
Love real regional Chinese food? Cate Zone’s original University City location put Northeastern Chinese cooking on the St. Louis map - and our guide to the best Chinese food in St. Louis rounds up more across the metro.

### The cafe that started it
It began in University City in 2016 as a small cafe, and it didn’t stay a secret long. International students and adventurous local eaters found it fast — a word-of-mouth run built on genuinely authentic cooking, not marketing. The owners, from Liaoning in Northeastern China, were serving the food they grew up on, and St. Louis diners who’d never tasted real Dongbei cuisine got hooked. Long waits, a devoted following: the kind of place people drive out of their way for and then talk about to anyone who’ll listen.
The Chesterfield location grew directly out of that success. Demand outstripped the little cafe, and west-county fans were tired of the drive, so the family opened a larger, more comfortable room — with space for the shared, celebratory meals this cuisine is built around. An immigrant family’s honest cooking, earning enough love to expand across the metro on its own terms. Hard not to root for that.
### What to order
The menu rewards a little adventure, and portions are generous — many dishes are built to feed two to four people, so come with a group and share. A few standouts:
Handcrafted dumplings and potstickers — a Northeastern staple and the classic starting point; order a couple varieties, pan-fried or boiled, and don’t skip the dipping sauce.
Cumin lamb with cilantro — a Dongbei signature, fragrant and savory with a warm cumin backbone, and a must-try for first-timers.
Hot, crispy fish — battered fish under fragrant chili oil and dried chiles, crispy and numbing-spicy, one of the dishes regulars come back for.
Sweet and sour pork — golden, battered cutlets done the real way, a world apart from the gloppy mall-food-court version.
Beef and ox tripe in chili sauce, and crisp sweet potato with egg yolk — for the table that wants to go deeper into the regional menu.
The deeper you go into the menu, the more it rewards you — but there’s no shame in easing in. Dumplings and sweet-and-sour pork are approachable enough for the most cautious eater at the table. The cumin lamb, crispy fish, and tripe give the adventurous crowd plenty to chase. That range is why Cate Zone works for a mixed group: it can feed the “I’ll just have what I always get” diner and the “order me the weirdest thing on the menu” one at the same table.
Finish with the sweet red-bean egg rolls if they’re available — a fun, dessert-style ending. Because the menu is deep and portions are large, the smart move is to over-order variety with a group and pass everything around; that’s how this food is meant to be eaten — a spread of contrasting textures and flavors that add up to more than any single plate. If you have a specific dish in mind, glance at the current online menu or ask when you order, since offerings can shift with the seasons and the kitchen’s specials.
### A first-timer’s game plan
Never had Northeastern Chinese food? Here’s the low-stakes way in. Bring at least three or four people so you can order broadly and share, because this is not a cuisine that rewards a single entree for one person. Start with a round of dumplings while you read the menu; they’re familiar enough to settle anyone nervous, and genuinely excellent here. Then branch out. The cumin lamb is the gateway dish that converts skeptics, the hot crispy fish is the showstopper, and the sweet and sour pork gives a hesitant eater something recognizable, done far better than they expect.
Pace yourselves — portions are large and it’s easy to over-order, which is half the fun but leaves you rolling out the door. Leftovers reheat well and often taste even better the next day, so don’t be shy about boxing up whatever you can’t finish. And don’t treat spice as a dare; ask your server about heat levels if you’re sensitive, since some Dongbei dishes carry real chili punch. Go in curious and hungry, and you’ll leave understanding why this small family’s cooking earned two locations and a metro-wide following — and, most likely, planning which dishes you’ll work through on the next visit.
