## The Dome Has No Parking Lot: How 30,000 Fans Get Into America's Center
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/america-s-center-convention-complex-a-hub-for-innovation-and-events
Thirty thousand people, one sound. It starts as a single voice high in the upper deck, then the whole bowl throws up the Battlehawks “caw” at once, and you feel it through the soles of your shoes and the plastic seat under you. Spring Saturday, downtown St. Louis. The dome the Rams walked away from now draws the biggest crowds in the UFL, roughly double the next-best home average.
Now the part nobody prints on the ticket: America’s Center has no parking lot of its own. Not one. Every car in that crowd found a private garage, a surface lot or a meter, and on a Saturday when a convention is also loading in next door, the closest decks are gone early. Here’s the whole game-day playbook first, because it decides how your day starts.
### Where to park near America’s Center
The good news inside the bad news: Explore St. Louis counts more than 30,000 parking spaces within a 10-minute walk of The Dome, in the garages and surface lots that ring Washington Avenue and Eighth Street. On a Battlehawks Saturday the closest decks still fill first, and circling Washington Avenue in a line of brake lights while kickoff ticks closer is a miserable way to start the day.
The train move. Leave the car free at a Metro Park-Ride lot: North Hanley or Fairview Heights on the Red Line, Brentwood I-64 on the Blue Line. Both lines stop at the Convention Center station, and you climb out of it into a river of blue jerseys with the gate right there. MetroLink is $2.50 a ride or $5 for a one-day pass; kids 5 to 12 ride half fare, 4 and under free.
The counterintuitive part: for a family, the train isn’t cheaper than a garage. It’s faster out. The math for two adults, a grade-schooler and a toddler:
Park-Ride lot: free.
Two adult day passes: $10.
The grade-schooler, half fare both ways: $2.50.
The toddler: free.
That’s $12.50 all in, about what one garage spot near the Dome costs. So don’t ride it to save money. Ride it for the exit: when the clock hits zero you’re on the platform with a kid asleep on your shoulder, while the garage ramps are still a single-file crawl of red taillights onto Washington Avenue.
Driving anyway? Reserve ahead. SpotHero and ParkWhiz sell prepaid spots within a few blocks; SpotHero’s posted event averages near the complex have run roughly $10 to $18, with some closer decks higher.
Don’t trust “free after 7.” City meters normally charge Monday through Saturday, 8 a.m. to 7 p.m., and are free on Sundays and city holidays. But near big downtown events the city Treasurer’s Office flips meters into “Event Mode” two hours before start time: a flat $5 for the whole event, reaching up to six blocks from the venue. No sign on the pole tells you. Only the meter screen or the parking app does, and St. Louis Magazine found fans walking back to $30 “contrary to sign” tickets. We couldn’t confirm whether Event Mode skips Sundays, so read the screen before you walk away, any day.
Bring a card and a little cash. The Dome is cash-free inside, but some parking facilities may still want cash.
Don’t aim for Convention Plaza. The block between 7th Street and Broadway closes on game days from four hours before kickoff until an hour after the game.
Coming from Illinois? Explore St. Louis routes Poplar Street Bridge traffic up 9th Street and 7th Street to Washington Avenue, and Stan Musial Bridge traffic via Tucker Boulevard.
At the gate: doors open 90 minutes before kickoff, there’s no re-entry, and the quickest way through security is empty-handed, which Explore St. Louis recommends outright. If you carry anything, it’s a clear tote no bigger than 12 by 6 by 12 inches or a one-gallon clear zip bag, plus a clutch up to 4.5 by 6.5. Kids 3 and under get in free on a lap. And the one the regulars know: beer sales end with the third quarter, so time your last round.
The whole game day on one line: park free at North Hanley, Red Line to Convention Center, no bag or a clear one, through the gate 90 minutes early, last beer before the fourth quarter.
And the Dome is only one room. The same complex at Washington Avenue and Eighth Street holds 574,000 square feet of exhibit halls, a 1,400-seat theater and a 28,000-square-foot ballroom. Here’s what’s under that roof.
### What is the America’s Center Convention Complex?
The America’s Center Convention Complex is downtown St. Louis’s largest event venue - about 2.2 million square feet at 701 Convention Plaza, managed by Explore St. Louis, the region’s convention and visitors organization. Explore St. Louis counts four facilities under one roof (the Cervantes Convention Center, The Dome, the St. Louis Executive Conference Center and the Ferrara Theatre), and these are the spaces most visitors walk into:
The Cervantes Convention Center - 574,000 square feet of contiguous exhibit space across seven halls, plus 95 meeting rooms.
The America’s Ballroom - a 28,000-square-foot ballroom for galas and large banquets.
The Ferrara Theatre - an intimate theater seating about 1,400.
The Dome at America’s Center - the 67,000-seat domed stadium most St. Louisans just call “The Dome.”
Put together, the complex hosts more than 350 events and around 1.8 million attendees in a single year. That’s a lot of lanyards, rolling suitcases and folding-chair graduations, and a lot of proud families squinting for one face in a sea of caps. Here’s the complex at a glance:
### The Dome at America’s Center: from the Rams to the Battlehawks
The Dome has worn a few names. It opened in 1995 as the Trans World Dome (TWA Dome), became the Edward Jones Dome in 2002, and is now simply The Dome at America’s Center. For two decades it was the home of the NFL’s St. Louis Rams, who played there from 1995 until the franchise left for Los Angeles after the 2015 season - a wound St. Louis football fans still feel.
But the story didn’t end there. The Dome found a new heartbeat with the St. Louis Battlehawks, whose electric, sold-out crowds turned it into a genuine phenomenon. The Battlehawks play their UFL home games at The Dome, and the spring schedule runs from late March into June, so check the team’s site for this season’s home dates. Beyond football, the venue hosts concerts, motocross and monster-truck rallies, large graduations, and convention overflow - a flexible big-room that keeps downtown busy year-round.
### What’s new: the AC Next Gen expansion
In 2024, America’s Center completed its first major expansion in more than 30 years - the roughly $240 million AC Next Gen project. It was a real modernization, not a coat of paint:
A brand-new 72,000-square-foot exhibit hall, expanding total exhibit space to 574,000 square feet.
The 28,000-square-foot America’s Ballroom.
More than double the enclosed loading docks (a big deal for the trade shows that live and die by move-in logistics).
An on-site culinary garden, refreshed restrooms, and a refurbished Washington Avenue entrance.
The upgrade keeps St. Louis competitive for the national conventions that shop cities against each other - and those events are what fill downtown hotels and restaurants.
### What happens at America’s Center?
On any given week the complex might host a medical convention in the exhibit halls, a corporate meeting in the conference center, a touring concert in The Dome, and a wedding reception in the ballroom - all at once. The regular lineup includes:
Conventions, trade shows, and conferences - the core business, from national association meetings to regional expos.
Battlehawks UFL football - spring Saturdays at The Dome.
Concerts and touring shows, motocross, and monster-truck events.
Graduations and community events for the region’s schools and universities.
What ties it all together is flexibility. A single week can pair a 20,000-person medical convention in the exhibit halls with a sold-out concert at The Dome and a black-tie gala in the ballroom - each running independently, none in the other’s way. That range is exactly what lets St. Louis compete for national events while still hosting hometown graduations and community gatherings; the complex is built to do both at once.
Total tangent - getting more customers in Highland, IL is its own puzzle.
### Game day at The Dome
If your trip is for a Battlehawks game, know that you’re walking into one of the best atmospheres in pro football. The team’s rabid fan base - and the signature “Battlehawks” caw that rolls around the bowl - draws the biggest crowds in the UFL, roughly double the next-best home average, remarkable for a spring league. It’s an affordable, family-friendly day out compared to an NFL ticket, and the indoor Dome means weather never cancels the fun.
A few game-day tips: take MetroLink if you can and skip the garage scramble, arrive early to soak in the tailgate energy around the complex, and check the team’s page for the current bag policy before you leave home. Concerts and other big shows follow the same playbook - downtown fills up, so plan your parking or transit in advance.
### Make a day of it downtown
The America’s Center sits in the middle of everything downtown, which makes it easy to build a full day around your event. You’re a short walk or quick ride from the Gateway Arch and its riverfront grounds, Ballpark Village and Busch Stadium, City Museum for families, and the restaurants and rooftop bars along Washington Avenue. Before or after a convention session or a game, it’s a genuinely walkable stretch of the city.
And if you’re staying overnight, the walkable core means you can leave the car parked. Plenty of attendees never move theirs from Friday check-in to Sunday checkout, hopping between the show floor, dinner on Washington Avenue, and a rooftop nightcap on foot or a two-minute MetroLink ride. It’s one of the underrated perks of a downtown convention center - the city is the venue, not just the building.

### Getting there: the address, the train and the bag rules
The complex sits in the heart of downtown, and getting there is easier than parking-anxiety suggests:
Address: 701 Convention Plaza, St. Louis, MO 63101.
Transit: the Convention Center MetroLink station is right at the complex - for a Battlehawks game or a big convention, the train beats fighting for a garage spot.
Hotels: nearly 8,000 hotel rooms are within walkable downtown distance, and you’re minutes from the Gateway Arch grounds and downtown dining.
Bags: large events at The Dome typically use a clear-bag policy - check your specific event’s page before you go, since rules vary by show.
### Bringing an event here
For meeting and event planners, the appeal is simple: one connected campus that can flex from a 50-person breakout to a 40,000-seat general session without anyone leaving the building. The 574,000 square feet of contiguous exhibit space, 95 meeting rooms, the ballroom, the theater, and The Dome share a downtown footprint wrapped by nearly 8,000 walkable hotel rooms - so attendees can land, check in, and walk to the show floor. Explore St. Louis handles booking and event services for the whole complex, and the 2024 expansion’s doubled loading docks and new hall were built specifically to win the large national shows that used to size St. Louis up and pick somewhere else.
### Why it matters to St. Louis
This isn’t just a big building - it’s an economic engine. Conventions, meetings, and events at America’s Center generate about $258 million in direct spending for the region, filling hotel rooms, restaurants, and rideshares far beyond the show floor. When a national convention comes to town, thousands of local jobs and small businesses feel it - the coffee shop, the caterer, the tour guide, the boutique.
For locals, that’s not an abstraction on a spreadsheet. A big convention means a busy Friday for a downtown restaurant, a booked-solid weekend for a hotel’s housekeeping staff, extra runs for rideshare drivers, and steady work for the florists, AV crews, and security teams who make events happen. A thriving convention complex is one of the quiet ways a downtown pays for itself - and why the city keeps investing to keep it competitive.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What events are happening at America’s Center St Louis?
A.  Something almost every week: national conventions and trade shows in the exhibit halls, Battlehawks UFL football at The Dome in spring, plus concerts, dirt-track and monster-truck shows, and big graduations. Explore St. Louis’s CEO has said The Dome alone is in use about two of every three days. Its America’s Center page lists upcoming public events, so check there before you plan a trip.
### Q. What is the St. Louis Dome called now?
A.  It’s The Dome at America’s Center. It opened in 1995 as the Trans World Dome (TWA Dome), became the Edward Jones Dome in 2002, and took back its original name in 2016 after the Rams left and Edward Jones ended its sponsorship. Locals still call it the Dome, and Battlehawks fans call it the BattleDome.
### Q. What team plays at the Dome at America’s Center?
A.  The St. Louis Battlehawks of the UFL play their home games at The Dome. Their spring season runs from late March into June, and their crowds have led the UFL in attendance, often around double the next-best team. The NFL’s Rams played there from 1995 until they left after the 2015 season.
### Q. Who owns America’s Center in St. Louis?
A.  It’s publicly owned, not a private venue. Explore St. Louis, the region’s convention and visitors commission, runs the whole complex. A state law Gov. Mike Kehoe signed put The Dome and the convention center under one combined board, with equal seats for the State of Missouri, the City of St. Louis and St. Louis County.
### Q. Where can I park near America’s Center convention Complex in St. Louis?
A.  There’s no single dedicated lot, so you use the downtown garages and surface lots around Washington Avenue and Eighth Street. Explore St. Louis lists preferred providers, and apps like SpotHero sell prepaid event spots nearby. On Battlehawks and concert days, book ahead or ride MetroLink to the Convention Center station, which lets you off at the complex.
### Q. Which is the biggest convention center in the USA?
A.  It depends on how you measure. McCormick Place in Chicago advertises about 2.6 million square feet of exhibit halls and is usually called the largest in North America, while Las Vegas claims more exhibit space overall. America’s Center is smaller, with 574,000 square feet of contiguous exhibit space, which keeps the show floor walkable.

## Explore the Delicious Osteria Forto Menu
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/explore-the-delicious-osteria-forto-menu-for-2026
The pasta at Osteria Forto is rolled and cut by hand in the kitchen, not shaken out of a box. Here’s a closer look at the food and the drinks.

### Discover Osteria Forto's Signature Dishes

### Pork Rib Chop Saltimbocca

### Tre Amici Cake
Don’t even think about skipping dessert. The Tre Amici Cake is a multi-layered creation built from peanut butter cream, rich chocolate ganache, and a salted caramel sauce.
Peanut Butter Cream: Adds a nutty, smooth layer.

### Chef Fortunato Pietoso's Culinary Vision

### Family Restaurant Roots
The restaurant is literally named for him — Fortunato “Forto” Pietoso grew up in Aversa, Italy, and spent decades cooking in some of St. Louis’s most storied Italian kitchens, including John Mineo’s, Giovanni’s on the Hill, and Café Napoli. The osteria itself is co-owned by spouses Dominic and Liz Pietoso, and it started as a happy experiment: a once-a-week, regularly sold-out “osteria night” at the Cecil Whittaker’s pizzeria they ran in Creve Coeur. Demand kept growing, and in December 2023 the family opened Osteria Forto’s doors in O’Fallon. That arc — from pizzeria side-project to a destination the St. Louis Post-Dispatch praised for “classic Italian, subtle twists” — tells you most of what you need to know about how seriously this kitchen takes its food.

## Sweetie Cup Thai Cafe: Valley Park’s Thai Dessert Gem
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-authentic-flavors-at-sweetie-cup-thai-cafe-your-new-favorite-spot
Some restaurants win you over with one thing you can’t get anywhere else. For Sweetie Cup Thai Cafe, tucked into a west St. Louis County shopping center, that thing is dessert — the namesake Thai “sweetie cups” of fruit, jelly, coconut milk, and shaved ice that the whole place is named for. But it would be a mistake to file it away as just a sweets stop. This is a genuine, family-owned Thai kitchen with real Lao roots, and it’s worth the drive whether you come for the drunken noodles or the dessert.
Here’s an honest look at what Sweetie Cup is, where to find it, and what to order on a first visit.
### What Sweetie Cup Thai Cafe is
Sweetie Cup Thai Cafe sits at 2961 Dougherty Ferry Road in Valley Park, MO 63122 — in the Shoppes at Seven Oaks, next to Tavern Kitchen & Bar — phone (636) 529-8690. (A quick note for your GPS: the 63122 ZIP is shared with Kirkwood, so some listings say Kirkwood or even just “St. Louis,” but the restaurant is in Valley Park.) It’s a sit-down Thai restaurant that opened in the spring of 2019, family-owned and run, and it’s built a loyal following in the years since.
The story behind it is part of the charm. Co-owner Saengchan Inthichak was born in Laos and moved to northern Thailand as a child, and that background gives the kitchen a Lao accent alongside the Thai menu — the cooking comes from real memory and heritage rather than a corporate template. The name, meanwhile, comes from the restaurant’s signature: the Thai dessert cups that are its calling card. It’s a Thai street-food-and-dessert spot with a personality all its own.
### What to order
Start with the savory food, because it’s genuinely good. The dish that gets the most love is the pad kee mao — drunken noodles — wide rice noodles stir-fried with holy basil, a plate that’s equal parts comforting and punchy. It’s the one to order if you want to understand why regulars keep coming back for more than the sweets.
Then, of course, the reason for the name. The Sweetie Cup dessert cups are layered creations of fruit, jelly, coconut milk, syrup, and shaved ice, with several varieties on the menu. The owners’ standout is the Lod Chong Singapore — green tapioca noodles in coconut milk with fragrant pandan syrup and jackfruit. Other Thai desserts round it out: Tub Tim Grob (water chestnuts in sweet coconut milk over ice), bua loi (glutinous rice balls in coconut milk), and more coconut-milk classics. To drink, the Thai iced tea is the essential order — strong black tea with condensed milk over crushed ice — and there’s a lineup of fruit and tea shakes (mango, honeydew, strawberry, green tea) plus bubble tea if you want the boba experience.
A good first-visit strategy: order a savory dish like the drunken noodles, a Thai iced tea, and at least one sweetie cup to share — that trio shows off exactly what makes the place special. The menu covers the wider range of Thai standards too, but the noodles, the desserts, and the drinks are the signatures worth building an order around.

### The desserts, explained
If Thai desserts are new to you, they’re worth the small leap of faith — they’re unlike the heavy, sugary desserts a lot of American menus default to. The through-line is coconut milk: subtly sweet, a little savory, cool and refreshing rather than cloying. Add chewy textures (tapioca, jelly, water chestnut, glutinous rice) and fresh fruit, pile it over shaved ice, and you get something that feels light even when it’s indulgent. On a hot, humid St. Louis afternoon, a sweetie cup is close to the perfect thing.
It’s also a genuinely fun order for a group or a family — the cups are colorful, a little theatrical, and easy to pass around and compare. For anyone who’s only ever thought of Thai food as pad thai and curry, the dessert side is a whole world, and Sweetie Cup is one of the few places in the metro that treats it as the main event rather than an afterthought.
### Why it’s worth the trip
West county isn’t always where people think to look for authentic, owner-run ethnic food — the conversation tends to center on the city neighborhoods. That’s exactly why a place like Sweetie Cup deserves a shout. It’s proof that some of the metro’s most distinctive cooking is tucked into unassuming suburban storefronts, made by a family cooking the dishes they grew up with rather than chasing a trend.
There’s real value in supporting that kind of independent kitchen, too. When the people cooking your food own the place and are serving their own community’s recipes, the care shows — and every dollar spent there stays close to home and keeps a small local business going. For anyone in Valley Park, Kirkwood, Ballwin, or the surrounding suburbs, it’s an easy, rewarding local pick — and one worth keeping on your short list of where to eat in Valley Park; for a serious eater from elsewhere in the metro, it’s a good reason to point the car west.
It’s also the kind of place that rewards becoming a regular. A family-run kitchen serving its own heritage tends to get better the more you go — you learn the menu, the staff learn your order, and a good meal turns into a standing habit. Independent restaurants live and die on exactly that: word of mouth and neighbors who keep coming back. When you find one doing something genuinely distinctive, like Thai desserts done as the main attraction, the best thing you can do is show up and bring a friend the next time.
### A quick primer on Thai flavor
If Thai food beyond pad thai is new to you, the thing to understand is balance. A good Thai kitchen chases the interplay of five tastes at once — sweet, sour, salty, spicy, and savory umami — and the magic is in how they play against each other in a single bite. That’s why a dish like drunken noodles can taste bright, herbal, a little sweet, and a little fiery all together, and why it’s so easy to keep eating. Fresh herbs like holy basil, lime, garlic, chili, and fish sauce are the building blocks, and a place cooking from real heritage layers them with a confidence you can taste.
Spice is usually adjustable, so don’t let heat scare you off — ask for it mild if you’re unsure and work your way up on the next visit. And Thai cuisine is naturally friendly to a range of eaters: there are typically vegetarian-friendly options, and the noodle and rice dishes give picky eaters an easy on-ramp while the more adventurous chase the herbs and chilies. It’s a cuisine built for sharing and for curiosity, which makes it a great choice for a table with different tastes.
### A first-timer’s game plan
Bringing someone who’s never had much Thai food, or new to it yourself? Keep it simple and let the signatures do the work. Anchor the meal with the drunken noodles — it’s approachable, satisfying, and a fair test of the kitchen. Add a Thai iced tea, which is basically a dessert in a glass and an instant crowd-pleaser, and one savory dish you’re curious about from the wider menu so the table gets some variety.
Total tangent — but Academy Sherman Park has a guide worth a look.
Then, whatever else you do, order at least one sweetie cup to finish and pass it around. It’s the thing you can’t get at most restaurants and the whole reason the place exists, and sharing a couple of the different varieties is the best way to find your favorite. Go in ready to try the desserts as seriously as the entrees, and you’ll leave understanding exactly what makes Sweetie Cup its own thing rather than one more Thai spot.
### Good for a group, a date, or a sweet stop
Part of what makes Sweetie Cup versatile is that it fits a lot of occasions. It works as a full dinner out, an easy family meal where the kids can chase noodles and a colorful dessert, a low-key date with something a little different to talk about, or simply a mid-afternoon sweet-and-drink stop when you want a Thai iced tea and a dessert cup and nothing more. That flexibility — a real restaurant that’s also a genuine dessert destination — is rarer than it sounds, and it’s a big part of why regulars fold it into their rotation. It’s equally at home as the main event or the sweet ending to an afternoon of errands in west county, and that range is hard to beat.
If you’re making an afternoon of it, the Shoppes at Seven Oaks setting helps — it’s an easy, low-key stop to fold into other plans on that side of the metro, whether you’re coming from Kirkwood, Ballwin, or off the highway. Park once, grab a table or a to-go cup, and you’ve got a genuinely distinctive bite that most of the metro hasn’t discovered yet.

Closed Mondays. It runs a split schedule the rest of the week — generally late morning through early afternoon, then again in the evening, with an afternoon break in between.
Call ahead to confirm hours. Because of that mid-afternoon gap, it’s worth a quick call to (636) 529-8690 so you don’t arrive during the break — posted hours can shift.
Dine-in, carryout, and delivery. There’s dine-in and online ordering, plus takeout and the major delivery apps, and catering is available; reservations generally aren’t taken.
One location. This is the only Sweetie Cup — if you see it filed under Kirkwood or St. Louis online, it’s the same Valley Park spot.
It holds strong local ratings — around 4.7 stars on Yelp over roughly a hundred-plus reviews — the kind of steady, high mark that tells you a family-run kitchen is doing right by its regulars. If you’ve been meaning to branch out beyond the usual Thai order, this is a good place to do it.

## Beyond the Arch: Unique & Offbeat Things to Do in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/beyond-the-arch-uncovering-unique-things-to-do-in-st-louis-for-adults
Everyone who visits St. Louis sees the Arch, and they should — it’s magnificent. But the Arch is the beginning of what makes this city interesting, not the end of it. Scratch the surface and St. Louis turns out to be one of the quirkiest, most surprising cities in the country: a place where you can climb through a ten-story art playground, stand next to the world’s largest chess piece, and eat frozen custard so thick they hand it to you upside down.
This is a guide to the most unique and offbeat things to do in St. Louis — the “wait, that’s here?” stuff that sticks with you. It’s built for visitors who want more than the postcard, and for locals ready to rediscover their own city. These are the places people bring out-of-town guests to show off, the spots that turn a skeptical visitor into someone who suddenly gets why this underrated city has such a hold on the people who live here. Think of it as the natural next step once you’ve taken a broader tour of the vibrant St. Louis metro.
### City Museum: Not Just for Kids (Especially at Night)
Start with the strangest, best thing in the city. The City Museum is a 600,000-square-foot former shoe warehouse that the late sculptor Bob Cassilly turned into a climbable, crawlable fever dream — caves, tunnels, ten-story slides, a rooftop school bus dangling over the edge, and salvaged-material art everywhere you look. It opened in 1997 and still feels like nothing else on earth. Come during the day with kids, or come on a weekend night when it’s open late and 21+ energy takes over — either way, wear clothes you can crawl in. People try to describe it and fail; it’s part playground, part sculpture, part obstacle course, all built from salvaged industrial scraps — old chimneys, airplane fuselages, bank vaults, miles of rebar bent into tunnels. You will get a little lost, you will find slides you didn’t expect, and you will leave sore in muscles you forgot you had. There is nothing else like it in America, and it’s reason enough to visit St. Louis on its own.
### The World Chess Hall of Fame (and a 20-Foot King)
In the Central West End, St. Louis quietly became the chess capital of America — home to the Saint Louis Chess Club and the World Chess Hall of Fame, a legitimately fascinating museum of the game’s history and art. Out front stands the star attraction: the world’s largest chess piece, a Guinness-record king that towers about 20 feet tall. It’s free to photograph, endlessly Instagrammed, and the kind of only-in-St.-Louis oddity this list exists for.
### The Budweiser Brewery Experience: Beer, History, and Clydesdales
The Budweiser Brewery Experience in Soulard is the historic Anheuser-Busch brewery, founded in 1852, and its tours are a genuine St. Louis rite. Walk the beautiful old brew house, learn how the beer is made, meet the famous Clydesdales at their stables, and (if you’re of age) sample a fresh pour. There are several tour tiers, from a free general tour to deeper behind-the-scenes options — a great, very St. Louis way to spend a couple of hours. The brewery has been part of the city’s identity for well over a century, and standing inside the ornate old Brew House — a National Historic Landmark — is genuinely impressive whether or not you drink the beer. Kids come for the Clydesdales; adults come for the history (and the sample). It’s a rare tour that works for a whole family.
### City Foundry STL: A Whole Date Under One Roof
City Foundry STL in Midtown took an old industrial foundry and turned it into a buzzing food hall and entertainment complex. Beyond the dozens of food vendors, it’s home to Puttshack — high-tech mini golf from the founders of Topgolf — plus a cinema and more, which makes it an easy pairing with a night at the city’s best arcades and barcades. It’s the easy answer when you want dinner, a game, and a movie without hopping between venues, and it’s become one of the city’s most popular gathering spots.
### Cherokee Street and the Delmar Loop: Two One-of-a-Kind Strips
For the real texture of St. Louis, walk its signature streets. Cherokee Street in south city is a six-block run of antique shops (Antique Row), murals, vintage stores, and a vibrant Mexican dining-and-culture corridor — a browser’s and eater’s paradise. The Delmar Loop in University City packs a dozen nights into one strip: the bronze-star St. Louis Walk of Fame set into the sidewalks, Chuck Berry’s old haunt Blueberry Hill (with its music-club Duck Room), restaurants, record shops, and theaters. Both are free to wander and impossible to replicate — the kind of streets where the browsing is the activity. Give yourself an unhurried afternoon on either one: poke into the shops, grab a taco or a slice, listen to whatever’s spilling out of a doorway, and let the block set the pace. This is the version of St. Louis that no landmark can show you.
### Ted Drewes: A Sweet St. Louis Ritual
Ted Drewes Frozen Custard is the sweet ending this list needs. A family institution since 1929, its Chippewa Street stand has sat on an old Route 66 alignment since 1941, and ordering a “Concrete” — a custard so thick it’s handed to you upside down to prove it won’t fall out — is a genuine local rite of passage. The Chippewa shop is open most of the year (closed in January); the South Grand location runs seasonally. Get in the line; it moves fast, and it’s worth it. Order a Concrete in a flavor you can’t get anywhere else, watch them flip it upside down at the window, and you’ll understand why generations of St. Louisans measure summer by trips to Ted Drewes.
### The Ultimate “Wait, That’s Here?”: Cahokia Mounds
Here’s the one that stuns even lifelong locals. Just across the river in Illinois, Cahokia Mounds is a UNESCO World Heritage Site — the largest pre-Columbian settlement north of Mexico. At its peak around 1050–1150 AD, it was a city of tens of thousands, larger than London was at the time, and you can still climb Monks Mound, the largest prehistoric earthwork in the Americas, for a view over the whole site. (The Interpretive Center is currently closed for renovation, but the mounds and grounds remain open.) It’s free, it’s astonishing, and most visitors have never heard of it. Bring water and decent shoes for the climb up Monks Mound’s four terraces, and take a minute at the top to grasp what you’re looking at: the center of a civilization that thrived here a thousand years ago, on the flat Mississippi bottomland with the modern St. Louis skyline hazy in the distance. Few day trips anywhere pack this much history into a short drive.
### Only-in-St.-Louis Quirks
Some of the best offbeat moments here are small and free. At St. Louis Union Station, find the Whispering Arch in the Grand Hall: stand at one corner of the archway, have a friend stand at the other, and whisper — the curve carries your voice perfectly across the room, an acoustic trick that delights kids and adults alike. Down on Cherokee Street, the Venice Cafe is a bar so thoroughly covered in mosaics, broken mirrors, and salvaged oddities that it feels like stepping inside a kaleidoscope — a year-round taste of the strangeness this city leans all the way into at its Halloween haunts and pumpkin patches. And at City Foundry, the Museum of Illusions packs in mind-bending optical rooms and photo tricks — a quick, fun stop that’s pure “how did they do that?”
Random, but: Collinsville keeps its own list of good stuff.
### A Few More Hidden Gems
If you want to go deeper, St. Louis keeps rewarding you. The newly reopened Old Courthouse downtown — part of Gateway Arch National Park, reopened in 2025 after a major renovation — is free and tells the story of the landmark Dred and Harriet Scott case in new galleries. The Griot Museum of Black History in north city preserves Black history and culture through wax figures and artifacts, and the Moto Museum in Midtown displays rare vintage motorcycles from around the world (call ahead, as it often hosts events). And if you have a car and a free afternoon — the same combination that opens up the region’s free public fishing spots — the Busch family’s Grant’s Farm offers a free-admission animal preserve with a tram ride, Clydesdales, and (for the grown-ups) a beer sample. Each is the kind of place you leave saying, “how did I not know about this?”

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the world’s largest chess piece in St. Louis?
A.  It’s a Guinness World Record king piece standing about 20 feet tall, located outside the World Chess Hall of Fame and Saint Louis Chess Club in the Central West End. St. Louis is a hub of American chess, and the giant piece is a free, popular photo stop that captures the city’s quirky side.
### Q. Is Cahokia Mounds worth visiting?
A.  Absolutely. Cahokia Mounds, just across the river in Illinois, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and the largest pre-Columbian settlement north of Mexico — once larger than London. You can climb Monks Mound, the largest prehistoric earthwork in the Americas. The grounds are free and open; the Interpretive Center is temporarily closed for renovation.
### Q. What is a St. Louis Concrete at Ted Drewes?
A.  A Concrete is Ted Drewes’ signature frozen custard blended so thick that it’s served upside down to prove it won’t drip out. Ted Drewes has been a St. Louis institution since 1929, and its Chippewa Street stand sits on a historic Route 66 alignment. It’s a beloved local ritual, especially on a warm evening.
### Q. What can you do in St. Louis besides the Arch?
A.  Plenty. Beyond Gateway Arch National Park, visit the City Museum, the World Chess Hall of Fame, the Budweiser Brewery Experience, City Foundry STL, Cherokee Street, the Delmar Loop, Ted Drewes, and Cahokia Mounds. The free, newly reopened Old Courthouse and museums like the Griot and the Moto Museum round out a city full of offbeat surprises.
### Q. What free unique things are there to do in St. Louis?
A.  Several of St. Louis’s most unique attractions are free: the world’s largest chess piece, the grounds at Cahokia Mounds, the St. Louis Walk of Fame on the Delmar Loop, the newly reopened Old Courthouse, and wandering Cherokee Street’s murals and antique shops. You can build a full, memorable offbeat day for the cost of parking and a Concrete.
### Q. What are some quirky things to do in St. Louis?
A.  The City Museum is the headline — a 600,000-square-foot former shoe warehouse the late sculptor Bob Cassilly turned into a climbable sculpture. It opened in 1997 and still feels like nothing else on earth. Daytime with kids, weekend nights when 21+ energy takes over; two different experiences.
### Q. What is there to do near the arch in St. Louis?
A.  The Gateway Arch museum sits underground at the base and is free to enter; the tram ride to the top is ticketed and worth booking ahead. Laclede’s Landing and the riverfront are walkable from there, and downtown restaurants are a short walk west.
### Q. What is a must do in St. Louis?
A.  If you only get one: the Arch for the view, the City Museum if you would rather climb than look. Forest Park is the answer for a whole day — the Zoo, the Art Museum and the History Museum are all free and all inside it.
### Q. What is the main attraction in St. Louis?
A.  The Gateway Arch, by visitor numbers and by a mile. But locals will point you at Forest Park, which is larger than Central Park and holds several free museums plus the Zoo. The Arch is the postcard; the park is where the city actually spends its weekends.

## Pop’s Kitchen Maryland Heights: Fried Catfish, Jack Salmon & Wings Worth the Trip
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/pop-s-kitchen-maryland-heights-your-guide-to-delicious-fried-chicken-and-fish
It’s Friday, you’re wiped, and cooking is the last thing on the list. What you want is a paper bag going translucent at the bottom, still warm, packed with something fried that was worth the drive home. Maybe you’re headed back toward Bridgeton or out to Creve Coeur. Maybe you just need to feed a hungry house without standing over the stove for an hour.
In Maryland Heights, a small counter-service spot tucked into the Dorsett Village plaza has quietly built a reputation for exactly that. No dining room, no frills — just made-to-order fish, chicken, and sandwiches that come out fast and come out big. That’s Pop’s Kitchen. Here’s what to order, what to know before you go, and the family story behind the counter.
### At a Glance: What to Order
### What Pop’s Kitchen Actually Is
Pop’s Kitchen is a fast, order-at-the-counter comfort-food shop — fried fish, fried chicken, and grilled sandwiches, made to order. There’s no dine-in room; this is a pick-up spot, so you order ahead or wait a few minutes and carry it home. Regulars keep coming for huge portions, flavorful food, and a fair price. Ambiance was never the pitch.
It’s also a genuine family business. Pop’s is run by the Qasem family, who came to St. Louis from Palestine — founder Mohammed Qasem immigrated in 1997, opened the original shop on St. Charles Rock Road in 2013, and grew it into a second Maryland Heights location in 2021, where his brother Fayez runs the counter. That’s the “Pop” energy people feel here: a spot built by one family, one fryer basket at a time, feeding their corner of the metro.
It’s a very St. Louis story: a family that crossed an ocean and built something real out of a strip-mall storefront, serving the fried catfish and wings their neighbors grew up on. There’s no corporate playbook behind the counter, no test kitchen deciding the recipes. Because everything is cooked to order rather than sitting under a heat lamp, what you carry out is genuinely fresh from the fryer — the trade-off being that you wait a few minutes, which is exactly why calling ahead is the regular’s move. That combination — family-run, made-to-order, big portions, fair prices — is why a small counter with no dining room has earned the loyalty it has.
### A St. Louis kind of shop
If you’re not from here, the fried-fish-and-chicken counter might need a little explaining — because in St. Louis, it’s practically its own food group. All over the metro you’ll find small, independent shops doing exactly this: catfish and whiting in the fryer, wings tossed to order, and, more often than not, a Philly cheesesteak on the same menu. Longtime institutions like King Edward’s Chicken & Fish have been working this template since 1966. Pop’s sits squarely in that tradition — the neighborhood fry counter where dinner comes in a paper bag and nobody leaves hungry.
It’s the kind of food that shows up at St. Louis fish fries and Friday-night dinner tables year-round — fried fish is close to a regional love language here — and a shop like Pop’s turns it into a weeknight option you don’t have to cook yourself. Pairing a Philly cheesesteak with a catfish dinner might sound odd on paper, but in St. Louis it’s a familiar combination: the neighborhood fry counter is where a lot of these menus grew up, adding hot sandwiches and wings until there was something for everybody in the car. Pop’s carries that tradition forward without overthinking it. The goal is a hot, generous meal handed across the counter in a couple of minutes.
### Fried fish is a St. Louis love language
To really understand a place like Pop’s, it helps to know how seriously St. Louis takes fried fish. For generations, the Friday fish fry has been a regional institution — rooted in the Catholic tradition of skipping meat on Fridays, especially during Lent, and turned into a community event in church basements and social halls across the metro. Some have been running for decades; the fish fry at St. Ferdinand in Florissant has been going since 1953. Learning to love a paper plate of fried cod or catfish is, only half-jokingly, part of becoming a true St. Louisan.
A shop like Pop’s takes that seasonal, once-a-week ritual and puts it on the menu six days a week. You don’t have to wait for Lent or a parish calendar — the fryer’s already going.
### What to Order at Pop’s Kitchen
The fried catfish is the headliner — crisp cornmeal crust, moist inside, the plate people make the drive for. You can get it as a fillet, or go for catfish nuggets if you want all crunch. Right next to it, order the jack salmon (more on that name below) for the true St. Louis experience — available as a fillet or whole. There’s also fried tilapia and shrimp, from regular to jumbo, for anyone who wants to mix the box up.
On the chicken side, the party wings come fried to order with a genuinely long list of sauces — buffalo, honey glazed, sweet chili, honey BBQ, garlic parm, and more — so you can build a box exactly how you like it. There are also chicken tenders, nuggets, and gizzards for the fried-chicken crowd. The Philly cheesesteak is loaded and generous, a fan favorite for anyone who wants a hot sandwich instead of a fish plate, and it shares the menu with burgers, a gyro, and other grilled sandwiches. Round it all out with sides — hush puppies, cheese fries, fried pickles, onion rings, or a loaded potato bowl — and, if you’ve got any room left, the banana pudding that regulars rave about.
### Wait — what is “jack salmon”?
Here’s a fun one for out-of-towners: jack salmon isn’t salmon at all. In St. Louis, “jack salmon” means fried whiting — a mild, flaky whitefish — and the name is pure local history. As St. Louis Magazine’s George Mahe has explained, the term traces back to a St. Louis restaurant that billed whiting as “jack salmon” as far back as the 1920s, and the name simply stuck around town. Order it bone-in and whole and you’ll get the old-school version many locals swear is the moistest and most flavorful. When you see “jack salmon” on Pop’s menu, now you’re in on the St. Louis secret.
Off in a totally different direction — Barnhart’s best plates, no context needed.
### Before You Go: Hours & How It Works
Pop’s Kitchen in Maryland Heights sits in the Dorsett Village plaza — the Schnucks-anchored strip center at the corner of Dorsett Road and McKelvey Road, just off I-270 (63043). It’s open Monday through Saturday, 11 a.m. to 8 p.m., and closed Sundays. Remember there’s no seating — this is a takeout counter, so the move is to call your order ahead at (314) 628-1996 or order and wait a few minutes for it to come out hot. It earns a solid rating in the 4.4–4.5-star range across more than 130 Google reviews, which for a no-frills fry counter tells you the food does the talking.
### Make It a Maryland Heights Meal
Pop’s is perfectly placed for a bigger outing. It’s minutes from Creve Coeur Park and Lake — a 320-acre lake with paddleboarding, kayaking, biking, and miles of trails — so you can grab a catfish plate and eat lakeside after a walk or a paddle. It’s an easy stop before a concert at the Hollywood Casino Amphitheatre, the metro’s big outdoor music venue just up the road, where a real dinner beats a $20 venue hot dog every time. And Westport Plaza — a cluster of restaurants, hotels, and entertainment — is right nearby if you’re making a night of it, one of the many places to eat in Maryland Heights worth the stop. Pop’s is the kind of fast, filling, no-fuss stop that anchors a Maryland Heights afternoon without slowing it down.
That versatility is a big part of the appeal. Nobody comes here to linger over a long dinner. You hit Pop’s when real food, fast, is the whole point: a work lunch, a car full of hungry kids, a lake day, a tailgate before a show. Order a big box, split it around, and everyone’s happy for well under what a chain sit-down would cost.

## Explore the Cosmos at the McDonnell Planetarium in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/explore-the-cosmos-at-the-st-louis-science-center-planetarium
Look up almost anywhere in Forest Park and you’ll spot it: a great white hourglass of a building, curving up against the sky like something that landed rather than was built. That’s the James S. McDonnell Planetarium, one of St. Louis’s most beloved landmarks — and after a major upgrade, it’s better than ever. This is your honest guide to exploring the cosmos right here in St. Louis: what it is, what you’ll see, and how to plan a visit.
The timing couldn’t be better. The planetarium reopened in July 2026 after a nearly six-month renovation, emerging with cutting-edge technology that has it billed as one of the most advanced hybrid planetariums in the country. If you haven’t been in a while — or ever — now is the moment. The upgrade was significant enough to make national news, and locals who grew up with the old star projector are discovering a genuinely transformed experience under the same iconic roof.
### A St. Louis icon, reborn
The McDonnell Planetarium is part of the Saint Louis Science Center in Forest Park, and it’s been the city’s home for all things space for more than 60 years. It first beamed a star show on April 16, 1963, and its unmistakable shape — a thin-shell concrete hyperboloid designed by celebrated St. Louis architect Gyo Obata of HOK — has been a landmark on the Forest Park skyline ever since. It’s named for aviation pioneer James Smith McDonnell, whose aerospace legacy is woven through the whole building and, in a real sense, through the whole city.
For generations of St. Louisans, a trip here was a childhood rite of passage — the school field trip where space suddenly felt close enough to touch. The reopening gives a whole new generation that same first moment of looking up in the dark and feeling small in the best possible way.
What makes the reopening a genuine event is what’s now inside. The renovation installed a first-of-its-kind-in-the-U.S. hybrid star projector paired with a state-of-the-art full-dome digital system, letting the theater fly you through more than 100 million stars in immersive, 360-degree detail under what the Science Center calls the largest artificial sky in the Western Hemisphere. It’s a serious leap, and it earned national recognition even before the upgrade — the McDonnell Planetarium was named the best planetarium in the country in a recent USA TODAY 10Best Readers’ Choice poll.
Planning a St. Louis day around the planetarium? Pair it with the rest of Forest Park - the free Zoo, Art Museum, and History Museum are all a short walk away. Our guide to exploring St. Louis maps a full day out.
If you run a business in this line of work, list your business. Run a St. Louis business families would love to find? A directory listing puts you in front of people searching “things to do near me” and planning their next outing.
### Six decades of looking up
The planetarium’s history is a real part of its charm. When it opened in 1963, its space-age silhouette felt like a promise about the future — fitting, in a city that built the Mercury and Gemini capsules that carried the first Americans into orbit. That aerospace heritage isn’t decoration here; it’s local history. James McDonnell’s company put St. Louis at the center of the space race, and the planetarium that bears his name has spent generations turning that legacy into wonder for kids and adults alike.
Gyo Obata’s hyperboloid design — that graceful, curving concrete shell — has aged into one of the most recognizable pieces of mid-century architecture in the region. It’s the kind of building that makes an impression before you ever walk inside, and it’s been a fixture in the memories of St. Louisans who came here on childhood field trips and now bring their own kids. Few attractions manage to be both a genuine scientific institution and a nostalgic landmark; this one has been both for over 60 years.
### What you’ll experience
The heart of a visit is a live or immersive show in the Bill and Laura Orthwein StarBay Theater, under the big dome. Current programs cover a real range:
The Sky Tonight — a live, educator-guided tour of the current night sky, so you’ll actually know what you’re looking at when you step outside.
The Earth Today: A Changing Planet — a striking look at our own world using real-time geospatial data.
The Little Star That Could 360 — a gentle, immersive show made for younger kids and families, and a great first planetarium experience for the smallest visitors.
Because programming rotates and new shows debut over time, it’s worth checking the current lineup before you visit — there’s usually something for both the serious space enthusiast and the kid who just wants to see the stars swirl overhead.
Beyond the dome, the planetarium campus is packed with space and flight exhibits: the Boeing Space Station gallery, a Liftoff Gallery with real Mercury and Gemini space capsules, a Mission: Mars area with a touchable Martian meteorite (yes, you can put your hand on a rock from Mars), and hands-on displays throughout. Public telescope-viewing events are offered too, for anyone who wants to look through the eyepiece at the real thing. Between the shows and the exhibits, it’s easily a half-day for a curious family. And the reopening added more than a new projector — the whole experience of a show is different now, with sharper, more immersive visuals that genuinely put you inside the scene rather than watching it from a distance. It’s the closest most of us will get to flying through a nebula, and it lands with a real sense of awe even for grown-ups who thought they were too jaded for a planetarium.
### Especially good for families
If you’re looking for an outing that genuinely works for a range of ages, this is one of the best in the metro. Little kids get wide-eyed at the immersive dome and the gentle shows made just for them; grade-schoolers get hands-on space and flight exhibits that make science feel like play; and teens and adults get the awe of the upgraded full-dome technology and the real spacecraft on display. It’s the rare attraction where nobody in the group is just tagging along — there’s something to spark curiosity at every level.
It’s also a reliable rainy-day or beat-the-heat plan, since so much of it is indoors and climate-controlled. On a bitter January afternoon or a sweltering July day, a couple of hours under the artificial sky is a small piece of magic that doesn’t depend on the weather cooperating. Pack a little patience for the popular new shows, arrive with tickets in hand, and it’s a smooth, wonder-filled few hours.
### The free part (and the ticketed part)
Here’s the practical bit that surprises a lot of first-time visitors: general admission to the Saint Louis Science Center — including the planetarium building and its exhibits — is free. That makes it one of the best budget-friendly outings in the metro, on par with the free Zoo and Art Museum a short walk away in Forest Park.
The exception is the star shows: the immersive planetarium shows (and the Science Center’s OMNIMAX films and laser shows) are ticketed separately, at a modest cost. Members receive free planetarium-show tickets with each visit, which is a nice perk if you go often. Because prices and showtimes change, buy or check ahead at the Science Center’s site rather than counting on same-day availability for the popular shows. Given how much attention the reopening has drawn, the new star shows in particular have been in high demand, so a little advance planning goes a long way. Even if you skip the ticketed show entirely, the free exhibits alone justify the trip — but the immersive dome is the headliner, and it’s worth the modest ticket.
Unrelated, and we know it — Princeton Heights rewards a slow drive.
### Planning your visit
The Saint Louis Science Center sits at 5050 Oakland Avenue, St. Louis, MO 63110, with the planetarium building on the Forest Park side, reachable off Clayton Avenue. One of the genuinely fun details: the two halves of the Science Center are joined by a Sky Bridge that spans Interstate 64 (Highway 40) — walking across it, watching traffic rush beneath your feet, is a small thrill in itself, and there’s an engineering exhibit built right into the crossing that turns the walk itself into a lesson on how bridges work. Kids tend to remember the bridge as much as the shows.
Check current hours. The Science Center generally runs daytime hours (around 9:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.) and is closed on Tuesdays, but it’s worth confirming at slsc.org or (314) 289-4400 before you go.
Book star-show tickets ahead. The newly upgraded shows are popular; reserve online so you’re not turned away at the door.
Make a Forest Park day of it. The Zoo, Art Museum, History Museum, and miles of park are all right here — and most are free.
### Make a whole Forest Park day of it
The planetarium’s location is a gift, because it drops you into the middle of one of the great urban parks in America. Forest Park — larger than New York’s Central Park — surrounds the Science Center, and a remarkable number of its top attractions are, like the Science Center, free to enter. You could pair a morning of star shows and space exhibits with an afternoon at the Saint Louis Zoo, the Saint Louis Art Museum, or the Missouri History Museum, all within the park, and never pay for general admission to any of them.
That makes the planetarium an ideal anchor for a low-cost, high-wonder day out — the kind of outing that’s become genuinely rare in an era when a family trip to an attraction can cost a small fortune. Bring comfortable shoes, budget the ticketed star show as your one splurge, and let the free stuff fill in the rest. It’s St. Louis at its most quietly generous — a full, memorable day for a family that costs less than a single ticket to many big-city attractions.
Whether you’re a lifelong space nerd, a parent looking for a genuinely wondrous outing, or a visitor wanting the real St. Louis, the McDonnell Planetarium delivers — now more than ever. It’s proof that some of the best experiences in the city are hiding in plain sight, right under that great white curve in Forest Park.

## Hiring a Personal Injury Lawyer in St. Louis: Deadlines, Fees and the State Line
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/hiring-a-personal-injury-lawyer-in-st-louis
Two cars crash the same way on the same afternoon. One wreck happens on Kingshighway, the other on a street in Belleville, twenty minutes east.
The Missouri driver has five years to file. The Illinois driver has two. And if a jury later decides each driver was 60% at fault, the Missouri driver still collects a substantial check while the Illinois driver collects nothing at all.
St. Louis straddles a state line, which means the single most important fact about an injury claim here is one almost nobody explains: which side of the river it happened on.
### How long do I have to file an injury claim in St. Louis?
In Missouri, generally five years for personal injury, three years for wrongful death from the date of death, and two years for medical malpractice. In Illinois, it’s two years for personal injury and wrongful death, and only one year for a claim against a local public entity. If your claim is against the City of St. Louis for a street or sidewalk defect, written notice must reach the mayor within 90 days. And a work injury must be reported to your employer in writing within 30 days. Which deadline applies is a legal question — don’t self-diagnose it.
### Missouri’s five years is a trap
Missouri’s general five-year window is unusually generous, and that generosity is exactly what hurts people. Someone hears “five years,” relaxes, and blows through every shorter deadline that actually governs their case.
Because the five years is the exception in this list, not the rule:
Wrongful death: three years from the date of death, not from the injury. Medical malpractice: two years from the act, with a ten-year outer limit. A work injury: 30 days to notify your employer in writing. Street or sidewalk defect in the City of St. Louis: 90 days written notice to the mayor. Anything that happened in Illinois: two years — or one year against a municipality.
One more that surprises people: for a minor, the Missouri clock is paused until the disability is removed — and the statute sets that at age twenty-one, not eighteen. Medical malpractice has its own separate rule for minors.
### The 90-day rule almost nobody knows
If you were hurt by a defect in a street, sidewalk, bridge, boulevard or thoroughfare in a Missouri city of 100,000 or more — which in this metro essentially means the City of St. Louis — you must give written notice to the mayor within 90 days of the occurrence. The notice has to state the place, the time, the character and circumstances of the injury, and that you will claim damages.
Two limits worth being precise about, because they get blurred constantly. It applies only to cities over 100,000 — St. Louis County is a county, not a city, so this particular provision doesn’t reach it. And it applies only to those specific kinds of defects, not to every claim against a city.
Suing a public entity is harder in another way, too. Missouri governments are generally immune, with narrow exceptions — principally the negligent operation of a motor vehicle by a public employee on the job, and injuries caused by a dangerous condition of public property. Outside those windows the claim often does not exist at all.
Where immunity is waived, damages are capped, and the cap is adjusted for inflation every year. For 2026 the Department of Commerce and Insurance publishes it at $532,148 for any one person and $3,547,658 for all claims from a single occurrence. Those numbers change every January 1 — if you see them quoted without a year attached, they’re probably stale.
### Partly your fault? It depends which state
This is the single biggest practical difference across the river, and it’s the reason people who assume they have no case sometimes do.
Missouri uses pure comparative fault. There is no cutoff. Your recovery is reduced by your share of the blame, and that’s all. (Worth noting for accuracy: for ordinary negligence this comes from a 1983 Missouri Supreme Court decision rather than a statute, so anyone citing “the Missouri comparative fault statute” for a car wreck is misinformed.)
Illinois uses modified comparative negligence with a bar. If you are found more than 50% responsible, you recover nothing at all. At 50% or less, your damages are reduced proportionally.
Put actual numbers on it. Say your damages are $100,000 and a jury finds you 60% at fault:
Missouri: you recover $40,000. Illinois: you recover $0.
Same facts. Same injury. Same jury. Opposite outcomes, decided by geography. Which state’s law applies is a choice-of-law question and depends on more than your home address — another reason not to talk yourself out of a claim because you think you were partly to blame.
### Why the other driver’s insurance usually isn’t enough
Missouri requires drivers to carry $25,000 per person, $50,000 per accident, and $25,000 for property damage. That is the floor the state demands of an at-fault driver. It is not a measure of what an injury costs.
An ambulance ride, an emergency room visit, imaging and a single surgery can exhaust $25,000 before anyone counts a lost paycheck. If the at-fault driver carries the minimum and has nothing worth pursuing, that policy is effectively the ceiling on your recovery.
Which is why the coverage that matters most is often your own. Missouri requires uninsured motorist coverage on every auto policy, at the same $25,000/$50,000 limits. Missouri does not require underinsured motorist coverage — that one is optional, and it is precisely the coverage that carries a serious claim when the at-fault driver is insured but nowhere near adequately.
Go read your own declarations page tonight. Ten minutes, and it tells you more about your protection than the other driver’s policy will.
### Hurt at work? Two clocks, running at once
A work injury runs on an entirely separate track, and the first deadline is brutally short.
Written notice to your employer within 30 days. Missouri’s Division of Workers’ Compensation says plainly that failing to report within 30 days may jeopardize your benefits — and advises keeping a copy of the notice with the date, time, and who received it. There is a narrow exception where the employer wasn’t prejudiced, but the burden falls on you. Treat 30 days as hard.
The claim itself must be filed with the Division within two years, extended to three if your employer never filed its report. The Division also notes the period can run from the last payment made on account of the injury — which matters if you received benefits for a while.
Now the part most injured workers never hear. Workers’ compensation is generally your exclusive remedy against your employer — that’s the trade. But it does not bar a claim against a negligent third party: another driver who hit you while you were working, a subcontractor on the site, the manufacturer of a machine that failed.
Those third-party claims run on the ordinary injury clock, not the comp clock. So you can have two live cases at once, with different deadlines, and the third-party case is frequently where the real recovery is.
Apropos of nothing: Rock Hill, Missouri is tiny and eats surprisingly well.
### The one sentence in the fee agreement that costs you thousands
Injury lawyers work on contingency — a percentage of what they recover, nothing if they lose. We are deliberately not going to tell you what percentage is “normal” in Missouri, because no neutral source establishes one. Every number you’ll find comes from law firm marketing.
You don’t need the average anyway, because Missouri’s rules of professional conduct require your contract to spell it out. A contingency agreement must be in writing, signed by you, and must state:
• the percentages for settlement, trial and appeal, separately — they are often different • the litigation and other expenses to be deducted • whether those expenses come off before or after the fee is calculated • any expense you owe even if you lose
That third item is the one to read twice, because Missouri sets no default. The contract decides — and the rule requires the contract to say which. Here is what it’s worth, on a $100,000 settlement with a one-third fee and $10,000 of case expenses:
Expenses first, then the fee: $10,000 comes off, the fee is one third of $90,000 — $30,000 — and you net $60,000. Fee first, then expenses: the fee is one third of the full $100,000 — $33,333 — then $10,000 of expenses, and you net $56,667.
Same settlement, same percentage, same expenses. A $3,333 difference, decided entirely by one sentence. If a fee agreement doesn’t address it, that agreement doesn’t comply with the rule.
Expenses are separate from the fee and typically include filing fees, depositions and court reporters, expert witnesses, medical records, investigators and exhibits.
### Why your settlement shrinks, and the cap that protects you
A $100,000 settlement never lands in your account as $100,000, and the reason isn’t just the fee.
When someone injures you, your health insurer or the hospital usually pays the bills up front. If you later recover from the at-fault party, those payers can claim reimbursement out of your settlement — otherwise the same bill gets paid twice. That’s a lien.
Missouri law puts a real limit on it, and it is stated correctly almost nowhere. Health care provider liens are capped at 50% of the net proceeds — and “net” is defined as what remains after attorney fees and the expenses of recovery. Providers do not get to take the settlement. Where the liens exceed the cap, they share the available amount proportionally.
If MO HealthNet paid your bills, the state has its own lien, with no fixed percentage cap — but attorney’s fees take priority over the state’s claim, and courts apportion based on equitable factors including your age, the permanence of the injury and your future needs.
### Can a lawyer call you after a crash? No.
This is the question people actually have after a wreck, and it has an unambiguous answer.
Missouri’s rules prohibit a lawyer from initiating in-person, telephone, or real-time electronic solicitation of legal business under any circumstance — with narrow exceptions for existing clients, other lawyers, close friends and relatives. Not “discouraged.” Prohibited.
Written solicitation has rules too. In an injury or wrongful death matter, a lawyer may not send one within 30 days of the accident. And any solicitation letter must be marked ADVERTISEMENT on the envelope and at the top of the first page.
So: a call or a knock at the door from a lawyer you don’t know is a violation. A letter that shows up a week after your crash is a violation. A letter at six weeks with no ADVERTISEMENT marking is a violation. You can report any of them to the Office of Chief Disciplinary Counsel.
Related, and worth knowing: Missouri lawyers generally may not pay anyone for recommending them, and may not practice through a business a non-lawyer owns or controls. If a “case manager” from a marketing company signs you up and then assigns you a lawyer, ask directly who owns the firm.
### Checking a lawyer, and what the lookup won’t tell you
For Missouri, the Office of Chief Disciplinary Counsel is the Supreme Court agency that investigates lawyer misconduct, and public discipline imposed since January 1, 2006 is posted through the courts. The Missouri Bar maintains an official directory to confirm someone is a member and authorized to practice. For Illinois, use the ARDC lawyer search.
Three limits to understand, because misreading these does real harm:
The Missouri Bar’s LawyerSearch tool is opt-in — it lists only lawyers who asked to be listed and are taking new clients. A lawyer’s absence from it means nothing. Use the official directory for the “is this person licensed” question.
Public discipline online runs from 2006 forward. Older matters aren’t in that set.
And pending, dismissed and confidential complaints are not public — so a clean record means no public discipline, not that nobody ever complained.
For a Metro East crash, check both states. A Missouri license is not an Illinois license.
### You probably don’t need legal aid
This surprises people, so it’s worth saying directly: legal aid organizations in this metro generally do not handle personal injury cases — and that isn’t a gap in the system.
Injury work is done on contingency, which means someone with a real claim can hire a lawyer without any money up front. Cost isn’t the barrier here the way it is for an eviction or a custody fight.
Where legal aid matters enormously is the wreckage that follows an injury — the eviction when you can’t work, the debt collectors, the denied benefits. Legal Services of Eastern Missouri covers 21 counties of eastern Missouri; Land of Lincoln Legal Aid covers the entire Metro East from its East St. Louis office. The Missouri Bar also runs a free, confidential fee dispute resolution program if you end up in a disagreement with your own lawyer over a bill.
This is general information about Missouri and Illinois law, not legal advice, and deadlines have exceptions that turn on facts specific to your case. If you were injured, talk to a lawyer licensed in the state where it happened — most will tell you where you stand at no charge.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What percentage do most injury lawyers take?
A.  There is no Missouri cap and no neutral source establishing a local norm — every percentage you will find online comes from law firm marketing. What Missouri’s rules do require is that your written agreement state the percentages for settlement, trial and appeal separately, since they often differ. Ask for those three numbers in writing.
### Q. How much will I get from a $50,000 settlement?
A.  It depends on the fee percentage, the case expenses, whether expenses come off before or after the fee, and any medical liens. On a $50,000 settlement with a one-third fee and $5,000 of expenses, expenses-first nets you about $30,000 while fee-first nets about $28,333. Missouri also caps health care provider liens at 50% of your net proceeds after fees and costs.
### Q. What not to say to a personal injury lawyer?
A.  Don’t guess or minimize. Saying “I’m fine” or estimating speeds and distances you aren’t sure of can follow a case for years. Also avoid assuming you have no claim because you were partly at fault — Missouri uses pure comparative fault, so being 60% responsible reduces recovery rather than ending it.
### Q. How hard is it to win a personal injury lawsuit?
A.  Most injury claims settle rather than going to trial. The harder practical questions are usually whether the deadline was met, whether fault can be proven, and whether there is enough insurance to collect against — Missouri only requires $25,000 per person in liability coverage, which frequently becomes the real ceiling.
### Q. How long do I have to file an injury claim in Missouri?
A.  Generally five years for personal injury, three years for wrongful death from the date of death, and two years for medical malpractice. Shorter deadlines override these: 30 days to report a work injury in writing, and 90 days’ written notice to the mayor for a street or sidewalk defect claim in the City of St. Louis.
### Q. Is the deadline different if my accident happened in Illinois?
A.  Yes, and dramatically. Illinois allows two years for personal injury and wrongful death, against Missouri’s five and three. A claim against an Illinois local public entity must be filed within one year. For a Metro East crash the Illinois clock is the one that likely matters.
### Q. Can I still recover money if the accident was partly my fault?
A.  In Missouri, yes — it uses pure comparative fault, so if you are 60% at fault on $100,000 of damages you still recover $40,000. In Illinois, being more than 50% at fault bars recovery entirely, so the same facts would yield nothing. This is the sharpest legal difference across the river.

Facing charges rather than a claim? Here’s what a criminal defense attorney costs in St. Louis.
If the harm came from treatment rather than a crash, start with whether you have a medical malpractice case in St. Louis.
Hurt on the job rather than on the road? Here is when to call a workers’ compensation attorney in St. Louis.
No. Missouri’s rules prohibit a lawyer from initiating in-person, telephone or real-time electronic solicitation, with narrow exceptions for existing clients, other lawyers, friends and relatives. Written solicitation is also barred within 30 days of an accident, and any solicitation letter must be marked ADVERTISEMENT.
