## Kicked Out at 1:30? The Grove Is Just Getting Loud. Where to Dance in St. Louis Tonight
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-the-best-dance-clubs-in-stl-your-ultimate-guide-for-2026
1:30 on a Saturday night in a bar out in St. Charles. The house lights slam on mid-chorus, the bartender is already stacking stools, somebody is still clutching a half-finished Busch Light, and a bouncer is holding the door open to the cold. Your shirt is still damp. Your feet are still going. And twenty-some miles east, in the Grove, the bass is only now getting loud.
Same city, same night. The difference is a line on a map, and almost nobody explains it until you’ve been kicked out on the wrong side of it. The scene moves fast, too: Attitudes, the Grove’s longtime staple, is closed for good, Europe on Washington Avenue lost its 3am permit, and Pop’s in Sauget isn’t the 24-hour club the old lists swear it is. And the cheapest good night out costs nothing at the door: Soulard’s DJ bars skip the cover and the velvet rope, and Club Viva throws in a free salsa lesson at 8:15. Here’s where the floor is full tonight, and how late it stays that way.
Last call, by zone: most of the Missouri metro, 1:30am. Licensed clubs in the City and St. Louis County, 3am. Sauget, Illinois, somewhere between 5 and 8 in the morning.
The best places to go dancing in St. Louis span a few districts: Washington Avenue downtown (EDM and hip-hop at Europe, dressy dancing at Pepper Lounge), The Grove (the heart of LGBTQ+ nightlife and Latin nights), Soulard’s DJ bars, Latin dancing at Club Viva, country line-dancing at PBR in Ballpark Village, and true after-hours clubs across the river in Sauget, Illinois. Most are 21+.
### The Local Quirk That Shapes Your Whole Night: Last Call by Zone
Here’s how it plays out on a real Saturday. At 1:30 the lights come up in a Soulard bar without the late license, and you spill onto the sidewalk smelling like beer and somebody else’s cologne. Ten minutes later you’re on Manchester in the Grove, Just John is open until 3, and the bass is only getting louder. When the music stops depends entirely on which side of which line you’re standing on. Across most of the Missouri metro, last call is 1:30am. But qualifying high-volume venues in the City of St. Louis and St. Louis County can serve until 3am, which is why the downtown and Grove spots keep going after the suburbs have gone dark. And if you’re still not ready to quit? Cross the Mississippi into Sauget, Illinois, where the clubs run until 5 or 6am, and one legendary spot keeps the music going until 7 or 8 in the morning.
So the shape of your night comes down to one early choice. A normal-hours neighborhood bar, a 3am downtown club, or a dawn run across the river and a drive home over the Poplar Street Bridge with the sun at your back and the Arch catching it. Plan the finish before you plan the start, and line up your rides accordingly.
### Which St. Louis Dance Clubs Are Open Tonight?
It depends on the night, and weeknights are where people get burned: you show up dressed and ready, the door is dark, and the only sound on the block is your own shoes. Here’s the rhythm, taken from the venues’ own posted hours:
Sunday and Monday: the Grove carries it. Just John opens in the afternoon and runs until 1:30am, Rehab has something going seven days a week, and HandleBar stays open until 2:30am. Pepper Lounge also opens at 10pm on Sundays.
Tuesday: the quietest night. Just John (open until 3am) and Rehab are your best bets; HandleBar is closed Tuesdays. And yes, Pop’s in Sauget still runs its overnight party from midnight to 7am, even on a Tuesday.
Wednesday: reggae night at Club Viva from 8pm, plus the Grove.
Thursday: Latin night and the free lesson at Club Viva, PBR from 8pm, and Oz in Sauget from 11pm until 5am.
Friday and Saturday: everything. Club Viva and PBR open at 8pm, the Soulard DJ bars get going around 9 or 9:30, Europe and Pepper Lounge open at 10pm, and Oz and Pop’s run from 11pm until 6 to 8 in the morning.
Want a club that’s already open at 9pm? Head to the Grove, Club Viva or PBR. The big downtown rooms don’t open their doors until 10, so skip the 9:15 wait on an empty sidewalk. Sauget doesn’t start until 11. And if it’s a Sunday-through-Thursday night and you’re still going at midnight, Pop’s runs its overnight party every night of the week. Hours shift for holidays, private events and big game nights, so check the venue’s socials the day you go.
### Downtown & Washington Avenue: The Club District
Washington Avenue was St. Louis’s marquee club strip for years, and while it’s thinned out, its anchor is still standing and still packed. Europe Night Club (710 N 15th St) is the survivor - a proper nightclub running house, techno, bass, hip-hop, and Latin nights, open Friday and Saturday nights, and big enough to land touring names when the trance and EDM crowd comes to town. It inherited the crowds from the downtown clubs that have closed around it, which is exactly why it still feels alive on a Saturday at midnight. One caution: the city’s excise commissioner has revoked Europe’s 3am permit, so check its current closing time before you plan to finish the night there.
For something a little dressier, Pepper Lounge brings an all-night dance floor with hip-hop, R&B, house, and EDM and a cocktail-and-heels crowd - a good pick if you want to dance but also want the night to feel like an occasion. On Clark Avenue a couple of blocks from Ballpark Village, Tin Roof mixes live bands and DJs for a rowdier, no-pretense party, and a short walk away sits the metro’s wildest curveball (more on that below).
### The Grove: St. Louis’s Nightlife Heart (and LGBTQ+ Home Base)
If you want the densest concentration of dance floors in one walkable stretch, go to The Grove on Manchester Avenue - the center of St. Louis’s LGBTQ+ nightlife and one of the most welcoming, high-energy scenes in the region for absolutely everyone. Just John Nightclub (4112 Manchester) is the flagship: a real dance floor, a performance stage, rotating DJs and theme parties, and doors open until 3am Tuesday through Saturday. A few doors down, the bike-themed HandleBar pairs a real dance floor and a two-story patio with DJ sets, karaoke, drag shows and regular Latin dance nights.
Round out the Grove crawl with Rehab Bar & Grill on Chouteau (drag shows, a big patio, DJ nights, open seven days a week). If an old guide sends you to Attitudes, the Grove’s longtime staple, skip it: it’s closed for good. One geography note so you find it: the beloved Grey Fox Pub - a gay pub and drag venue going strong since 1988 - is just south in Tower Grove South, not in the Grove proper, but it’s well worth the short hop.
Nothing to do with nightlife: nobody talks enough about the Southampton neighborhood.
### Soulard: Where the DJ Sets Sneak Up on You
Soulard is famous for its bar-crawl energy, and several of its spots turn into genuine dance parties after dark. Social Bar & Grill on South 7th throws a bass-heavy EDM night on Thursdays and an industry party on Sundays. Duke’s hides a Friday-and-Saturday DJ dance party upstairs (Cajun food downstairs, if you need fuel), and Molly’s spins DJ sets on its patio on weekend nights. It’s the move when you want dancing without a cover charge or a velvet rope - just wander until you hear the beat.
### Latin Night: Salsa, Bachata, and Free Lessons
St. Louis has a warm, growing Latin dance scene, and the anchor is Club Viva at 408 N Euclid in the Central West End - salsa, bachata, merengue and cha-cha on its Thursday and Saturday Latin nights (Wednesdays are reggae, Fridays Afro-Caribbean), with a free intro salsa and bachata lesson around 8:15pm so first-timers aren’t thrown in cold. It’s 21+ with a small cover, and its Thursday and Saturday Latin nights are the reliable heart of the scene. Add La Calle on Manchester for its Saturday Latin dance night and HandleBar’s Latin nights, and you’ve got a full rotation. Can’t dance a lick? That’s what the free lesson is for - show up early.
### Boots and a Mechanical Bull: Country Line Dancing
Want to two-step instead of two-turntable? PBR St. Louis: A Cowboy Bar in Ballpark Village (601 Clark Ave) is the big, loud answer - live country and southern rock, a giant dance floor, a mechanical bull, and hours that run to 2am on Thursdays and 3am on Fridays and Saturdays. It’s the perfect pairing with a Cardinals game or a bachelorette party, and no, you don’t need to know how to line dance before you get there - you’ll pick it up (or fake it) by the second song.
### Across the River: The After-Hours Clubs of Sauget, Illinois
This is the part where St. Louis stops playing by Missouri’s clock. Because Sauget, Illinois sits outside Missouri’s closing laws, its clubs run when everything else is locking up. Oz Nightclub (300 Monsanto Ave) is the big EDM-and-hip-hop room, open until 5am on Thursdays and 6am on weekends, pulling touring DJs and the crowd that isn’t ready to call it. And then there’s Pop’s (1403 Mississippi Ave), the legendary concert venue and nightclub whose overnight party runs from midnight to 7am Sunday through Thursday and 11pm to 8am on Fridays and Saturdays, with cover bands and DJs still going at 5:30 in the morning for the diehards. Cross the river when the metro closes and the night simply keeps going.

If you would rather sing every word than dance to them, here’s what to expect at a piano bar in St. Louis.
Out in St. Charles, RYSE Nightclub inside Ameristar Casino brings a modern, LED-drenched EDM room for a Vegas-style night without leaving the metro. And when you’d rather sip than sweat, the rooftop lounges deliver a different kind of night: Three Sixty atop the Hilton at the Ballpark serves Arch-and-river views with DJ nights, and ART Bar runs its own rooftop DJ events. Great for a date, a birthday, or easing into the evening before the real dancing starts.

## Local SEO for Contractors in St. Louis: What Google Actually Says
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/local-seo-for-contractors-in-st-louis
Google publishes a sentence that most of the marketing industry would rather you didn’t read:
“There’s no way to request or pay for a better local ranking on Google.”
That is Google’s own help documentation, not our opinion. And it is worth starting there, because if you search the question this article answers, every single result on the first page is written by someone selling the service. Including a block of ads for SEO agencies.
We sell directory listings, so we have our own interest — and we’ll be upfront about where it shows up. But most of what follows is Google telling you how this works, and Missouri law telling you something about your license that a lot of websites are getting flatly wrong.
### How does local search ranking actually work?
Google says local results are ranked on three things. Relevance is “how well a Business Profile matches what someone is searching for.” Distance is “how far each business is from the customer who’s searching.” Prominence is “how well-known a business is.” You can influence relevance and prominence. You cannot influence distance, and you cannot buy position — Google states plainly there is no way to request or pay for better local ranking. Sit with that for a second: if nobody can buy their way to the top, then the contractor beating you isn’t paying for it — he’s doing something you’re not. What?
### The thing about being a service-area business
Most trades don’t have a shop customers walk into. You drive to them. Google calls that a service-area business, and the rules are specific, published, and routinely violated by people trying to game them.
You can list up to 20 service areas, defined by city, postal code, or similar. You cannot set a radius — “thirty miles around Kirkwood” is not an option; you name places. Google says your service area should not exceed about two hours of driving time from your base, which in this metro means the whole thing, Illinois included, is fair game.
If customers don’t come to you, Google says to remove your address from your profile. If you have a showroom and also go out, you can run as a hybrid and keep the address visible.
Now the rules that get businesses penalized, all in Google’s own words:
“Do not create more than one page for each location of your business.” That kills the scheme somebody will eventually pitch you — a separate listing for Ballwin, one for Florissant, one for O’Fallon. It is against the rules, in writing, and it is the most common reason a trade business gets its profile suspended.
A rented mailing address you don’t operate from — a virtual office — “isn’t eligible for a Business Profile.” Neither are P.O. boxes or remote mailboxes.
And your business name has to be your actual business name, “as used consistently on your storefront, website, stationery, and as known to customers.” Not Smith Plumbing — Emergency Plumber St. Louis Ballwin Kirkwood.
### The uncomfortable math nobody selling you services will explain
Put those three facts together and you get a conclusion worth sitting with.
Distance from the searcher is a confirmed ranking factor. A service-area business has to hide its address. And you are allowed exactly one listing.
Which means you cannot rank equally across the whole St. Louis metro, and no amount of money changes that. A plumber based in Affton will have a harder time surfacing for someone searching in St. Peters than a plumber based in St. Peters will — not because of effort or budget, but because of geometry.
That is not a reason to do nothing. It is a reason to be skeptical of anyone promising metro-wide dominance, and a reason to think hard about which twenty areas you actually name.
### The Missouri license thing that half the internet gets wrong
If you have searched for what license you need in Missouri, you may have read that the state has a statewide HVAC or mechanical contractor license, and possibly that it took effect in early 2026.
That is not true.
The Missouri Statewide Mechanical Contractors Licensing Act has been introduced and has failed in at least six sessions — 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2025, and the current one, where it sits in committee. Bills carry conditional effective dates, and websites keep mistaking those for law.
Here is what Missouri actually licenses at the state level, per the Division of Professional Registration’s own list of professions:
Electrical contractors: yes — and it’s the only construction trade on the list. Optional, statewide, available since July 2019. It licenses the contractor, not individual electricians. Plumbers: no state license. Missouri statute delegates plumbing regulation to cities over 15,000 and to first-classification counties — which is exactly why St. Louis County runs its own plumbing board. HVAC and mechanical: no state license. General contractors: no state license.
So in this metro, licensing is municipal, and there are a lot of municipalities. The City of St. Louis requires a Construction Industry Contractor business license, with a separate one for each location or trade name, plus a Collector of Revenue clearance and proof of workers’ compensation. St. Louis County issues trade permits only to contractors it has licensed.
And there’s a genuinely useful wrinkle for electricians. Missouri law says political subdivisions must recognize the statewide electrical license in lieu of a local one and may not make a statewide licensee sit another local exam. In a region carved into dozens of municipalities, that portability is the practical argument for holding the optional state license — and almost nobody frames it that way.
### Free credibility you already qualify for
Something most licensed trades never think about: the government publishes lists with your name on them.
St. Louis County maintains public rosters of certified mechanical contractors, licensed plumbing contractors, and licensed master plumbers. The state maintains a searchable license lookup for electrical contractors.
Two things follow. First, a careful homeowner can check you in about a minute — so make sure your entry is correct and current, because a name that doesn’t match or a lapsed status reads as a red flag. Second, that is third-party government verification of your credential, free, and worth pointing customers toward when they’re deciding between you and someone cheaper.
### Reviews: what Google says, versus what you’ll be told
Google’s entire published statement on reviews and local ranking is one sentence: “More reviews and positive ratings can help your business’s local ranking.” It also says responding to reviews can help your business stand out.
That’s it. No threshold. No number you need. No recency formula. Anyone quoting you a specific figure — “you need 40 reviews to rank” — is not quoting Google, because Google has never published one.
What Google does publish in detail is what gets you punished. Prohibited: reviews “paid for, directly or in kind.” Reviews posted “from multiple accounts by or at the request of one person.” Reviews obtained “due to an incentive offered by a business — such as payment, discounts, free goods and/or services.” And content showing “unusual volumes or patterns of review contributions.”
The documented consequences: your profile can be blocked from receiving new reviews for a period, or have existing reviews unpublished.
Read that twice before you buy a review package, or before you offer a customer a discount for a five-star. The gift card feels harmless. It is explicitly the prohibited case.
Asking satisfied customers to leave an honest review, with no incentive attached, is fine and is what every legitimate operator does.
Hard left turn: the work van still has to stop for lunch in Jennings.
### About those local SEO statistics
A short digression, because it will save you money.
In researching this piece we tried to verify the statistics that appear in nearly every contractor-marketing pitch. “72% of consumers who performed a local search visited a store within five miles.” “46% of all Google searches are local.” “97% of people go online to learn about a local company.”
We could not trace a single one of them to an original study. They cite each other in circles and dead-end at marketing blogs — no methodology, no sample size, no publication date, no Google document.
That doesn’t mean local search is unimportant. It means the case for it is routinely made with numbers nobody can source. When someone quotes one at you, ask where it came from. The answer is informative either way.
You will also see a widely-cited ranking-factors study assigning percentage weights to Google Business Profile signals, reviews, on-page factors and links. Worth knowing what it actually is: a survey of 47 local search practitioners scoring factors on a five-point scale — expert opinion, not measured correlation and certainly not Google confirmation — published by a company that sells local SEO software. Useful as a read on what practitioners believe. Not evidence.
### The AI question, answered honestly
You are being told that AI is changing how customers find you. Here is what is actually documented.
Pew Research surveyed 5,119 U.S. adults in February 2026 and found that 49% now use AI chatbots, up from 33% in 2024. Of those, 42% use them for searching for information, and 60% of Americans report reading AI-generated search summaries.
That is real, it is large, and it is moving fast.
Here is what is not documented, and we looked: there is no credible survey showing that people are hiring plumbers or roofers through AI assistants. Pew measured general information-seeking, not local-service hiring. Anyone telling you customers are picking contractors via ChatGPT is extrapolating, not citing.
What we can say without overreaching: the structured business information these assistants draw on is largely the same information that feeds local search results — your profile, your hours, your service area, your reviews, your presence in local sources. Getting that right serves both. That’s reasoning, not a measured claim, and we’d rather label it than dress it up.
### When St. Louis actually breaks things
A note on timing, from the National Weather Service rather than from a marketing calendar.
St. Louis averages about 47 days a year at or above 90°F (1991–2020 normals) and fewer than 25 days at or below freezing. It gets 40 to 50 thunderstorm days a year and about 18 inches of snow. Severe storms — the large hail and damaging winds that generate roofing and siding work — cluster in April and May.
We are not going to tell you search volume spikes by a specific percentage in those windows, because we could not find data supporting it. What we can tell you is when the weather here breaks things, which is the part that actually drives the phone call. Your profile, hours and service areas should be correct before the storm, not after it.
### What’s actually worth your time
Stripping out everything unsourceable, here is what survives — all of it free, all of it grounded in Google’s own documentation.
Verify your profile. All of Google’s verification methods are free — phone, email, video recording, postcard, live call. Note that video verification must be captured live; pre-recorded footage isn’t accepted. Until you verify, you can’t edit your information or interact with customers.
Complete every field, accurately. Relevance is one of the two things you can influence, and it’s determined by how well your information matches what someone searched.
Choose your 20 service areas deliberately. That is a real constraint. Name the places you actually want work, not the places you could theoretically reach.
Ask for honest reviews and respond to them. Never incentivize. Google says responding helps you stand out, and it is the one thing on this list your competitors mostly skip.
Claim Bing too. It’s free, it takes twenty minutes, and it feeds Copilot — which matters more now than it did two years ago.
Check your government listing. If St. Louis County or the state lists you, make sure it’s accurate.
And be skeptical of anyone whose pitch requires a statistic they can’t source, a review shortcut Google explicitly prohibits, or a promise of a ranking that Google says cannot be bought.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Can you pay Google for a better local ranking?
A.  No. Google states in its own help documentation that “there’s no way to request or pay for a better local ranking on Google.” You can pay for ads, which appear separately and are labeled as ads, but the local results themselves cannot be bought. Any pitch promising a purchased position is misrepresenting how the system works.
### Q. Do I need a state license to be an HVAC contractor in Missouri?
A.  No. Missouri has no statewide HVAC or mechanical contractor license, despite claims to the contrary on several websites. A statewide mechanical licensing bill has been introduced and has failed in at least six sessions. Licensing is municipal — the City of St. Louis and St. Louis County each have their own requirements. Electrical contractors are the only construction trade Missouri licenses at the state level, and that license is optional.
### Q. Should a contractor hide their address on Google?
A.  If customers do not come to your location, yes — Google instructs service-area businesses to remove their address from the profile. If you have a showroom customers visit and you also travel to jobs, you can operate as a hybrid and keep the address displayed. Virtual offices and P.O. boxes are not eligible for a Business Profile at all.
### Q. Can I create separate Google listings for each suburb I serve?
A.  No. Google states directly: “Do not create more than one page for each location of your business.” Separate listings for Ballwin, Florissant and O’Fallon violate the guidelines and are a common cause of suspension. Instead, define up to 20 service areas on your single profile — by city or postal code, since a mileage radius is not an option.
### Q. How many Google reviews does a contractor need to rank?
A.  Google has never published a number. Its entire public statement is that “more reviews and positive ratings can help your business’s local ranking.” Anyone quoting a specific threshold is not citing Google. What Google does document in detail is what gets penalized — paid or incentivized reviews, and unusual review patterns.
### Q. Can I offer a discount for a Google review?
A.  No. Google explicitly prohibits reviews obtained through an incentive “such as payment, discounts, free goods and/or services.” The documented consequence is that your profile can be blocked from receiving new reviews, or have existing reviews unpublished. Asking satisfied customers for an honest review with nothing attached is fine.
### Q. Are customers really finding contractors through AI?
A.  AI adoption is documented — Pew Research found 49% of U.S. adults use AI chatbots and 42% of those use them to search for information. But we found no credible survey showing people hire local trades through AI assistants specifically. The reasonable position is that the same profile data feeding local search also feeds these tools, so accuracy serves both.
### Q. How can a homeowner verify my contractor license in St. Louis?
A.  St. Louis County publishes public lists of certified mechanical contractors, licensed plumbing contractors and licensed master plumbers, and Missouri maintains an online license search for electrical contractors. These are free and government-hosted — which makes them worth pointing customers toward, and worth checking to confirm your own entry is accurate.

## How to Choose a Real Estate Agent in St. Louis (After the 2024 Rule Change)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-real-estate-agent-in-st-louis
The rules for hiring a real estate agent changed in August 2024, and the lawsuit that changed them was decided in a Missouri federal courtroom — the Western District, in Kansas City.
If you are buying a house in St. Louis right now, you will be asked to sign something before you are allowed to walk through your first front door. Most people sign it without reading it.
Here is what actually changed, what didn’t, and the specific things worth checking before you pick anyone.
### How do you choose a real estate agent in St. Louis?
Start by verifying the license. Missouri’s public lookup is at mopro.mo.gov, and disciplinary actions since 2011 are posted separately at pr.mo.gov/realestate-disciplines.asp — both free, both take a minute. Then interview at least three, and before signing anything, get the compensation figure written as an actual number. Since August 2024 a buyer must sign a written agreement before touring a home, and that agreement’s compensation term must be, in the National Association of Realtors’ own words, “objectively ascertainable” and “not open-ended.” A blank, or “standard rate,” or “whatever the seller offers” does not meet that standard.
### What actually changed in 2024
The case was Burnett v. National Association of Realtors. NAR agreed to pay $418 million, and a judge granted final approval in November 2024. The practice changes took effect on August 17, 2024. Two of them matter to you.
One: offers of buyer-agent compensation came off the MLS. This is the change that gets described wrong more than any other. Compensation was not banned. Sellers can still offer to pay a buyer’s agent — it just can’t be advertised through the multiple listing service anymore. Seller concessions toward your closing costs can still appear there, though nothing in a listing tells you what movers actually cost in St. Louis, which stays its own line in your budget.
Two: you sign before you tour. An agent working with you must have a signed written agreement in place before showing you a home. There are exceptions — an open house hosted by the seller’s agent doesn’t require one, and neither does a showing where you’re unrepresented.
What did not change: commissions were always negotiable. The settlement didn’t create that, cap anything, or set a rate. NAR now requires agents to conspicuously disclose that compensation “is not set by law and is fully negotiable” — which was true before, and is now something they have to say out loud.
### Commissions did not go down
You will read that the settlement drove commissions down. The data doesn’t support it, and you should know that before you sit across from anyone.
Redfin’s research tracked the average buyer’s-agent commission at 2.38% in the second quarter of 2024, dipping to 2.36% in the third quarter as the rules took effect — and back to 2.42% by the third quarter of 2025. Slightly higher than before the change. A separate analysis by AccountTECH, covering more than 224,000 closed transactions across roughly 1,300 offices, found the same shape: a real dip in late 2024 that round-tripped within about five months.
Two independent datasets, same conclusion. Anyone telling you the market has settled this for you is wrong.
And there’s a detail in that data that lands directly on St. Louis. Broken out by price, the average buyer-agent commission in the third quarter of 2025 ran 2.52% on homes under $500,000, 2.32% between $500,000 and $999,000, and 2.22% above a million. The cheaper the house, the higher the percentage. Nearly every St. Louis transaction sits in that first tier — so buyers and sellers here are in the segment paying the most, proportionally, and have the most to gain from asking.
Which almost nobody does. A survey conducted by Ipsos for Redfin in spring 2025 found 37.4% of sellers negotiated or tried to negotiate commission — against just 27.2% of buyers. Buyers are leaving the most on the table, in the tier where the percentage is highest.
### Verify the license in about a minute
Two free public tools, and almost nobody uses either.
License status: the Missouri Division of Professional Registration portal at mopro.mo.gov/license/s/license-search. You can confirm the license is real, active, and whether the person is a salesperson or a broker. (If you find an older link floating around, note that Missouri migrated portals — the legacy address redirects here.)
Disciplinary history: a separate page, pr.mo.gov/realestate-disciplines.asp, which posts actions taken since June 30, 2011 as downloadable PDFs you can search by name.
Know the limits of what you’re seeing. You cannot see pending or unresolved complaints, sales volume, transaction history, or anything before mid-2011 without digging into archives. A clean record means no public discipline — not that someone is good at the job.
### Agent, REALTOR, broker — three different things
These get used interchangeably and they are not interchangeable. There are actually two separate systems running at once.
The state licensing system. Under Missouri law, a broker is licensed to conduct real estate business, and a salesperson must be affiliated with a broker who is responsible for their conduct. A salesperson cannot operate independently. That’s state law, and violating it is a licensing matter.
The trade association. “REALTOR” is a registered membership mark belonging to the National Association of Realtors. It is not a license and not a job title — it means the person pays dues and is bound by NAR’s Code of Ethics, first adopted in 1913. A licensed agent who isn’t a member is not bound by that code.
The practical consequence is that you have two different complaint paths. Legal violations go to the Missouri Real Estate Commission, which can act against a license. Ethics complaints against a REALTOR go to the local association — here, St. Louis REALTORS — which can only discipline membership. Knowing which is which saves you months.
### The word that decides how much they owe you
Missouri law draws a line between a client and a customer. A client has entered a brokerage relationship. A customer is involved in the transaction but has not.
There is also a role called a transaction broker, who assists with the deal without an agency or fiduciary relationship to either side. That is a legitimate, legal arrangement — and it means nobody in the room owes you a fiduciary duty.
Ask the question directly: Am I your client or your customer, and are you acting as a single agent, a limited agent, or a transaction broker? If the answer is vague, that is the answer.
Unrelated, and we know it — where to eat in Creve Coeur.
### What a seller has to tell you in Missouri — and what they don’t
Missouri leans toward caveat emptor. There is no broad statutory duty for a seller to volunteer every defect. There are specific exceptions in both directions, and they surprise people.
Must be disclosed: if methamphetamine was produced on the property and the seller knew, that has to be disclosed in writing — and it applies whether or not anyone was ever convicted.
Need not be disclosed: Missouri law says a property is not required to be disclosed as “psychologically impacted.” That covers a homicide, felony or suicide having occurred there, and an occupant having had a disease unlikely to be transmitted by living in the house. The statute goes further and bars a cause of action against an agent for not telling you.
Now the part worth reading twice. The agent’s duty is broader than the seller’s. A Missouri licensee must disclose adverse material facts actually known, or that should have been known — to clients and customers both. But the same law says the licensee has no duty to conduct an independent inspection, no duty to discover adverse facts for a customer, and no duty to verify what the seller told them.
So it is a duty not to conceal. It is not a duty to investigate. Nobody in the transaction is required to go find the problems for you. Get your own inspection.
### Which St. Louis number are they quoting you?
If an agent quotes “the St. Louis median” without saying which geography, they may not be misleading you on purpose — but the figures differ enormously.
For June 2026: the median sale price in St. Louis City was about $261,000, up roughly 0.8% year over year, on 292 homes sold. In St. Louis County, about $325,000, up roughly 6.6%. Meanwhile the median list price across the whole St. Louis MO–IL metro area ran about $290,000, down 3.3% — and that one is an asking price, not a sale price. They are not the same measurement and should never be compared to each other.
Two more metro figures worth having: median days on market around 44, four days longer than a year earlier, and active listings up about 10.3%. More inventory, sitting slightly longer. We’re reporting those as recorded, not predicting where they go.
City and county are different markets. An agent who closes constantly in one may know very little about the other — so ask which municipalities they actually close in.
### What to ask before you sign
Do the license and discipline lookups first, quietly, before the meeting. Then:
1. What exact rate or dollar figure goes in the compensation blank, and how long does this agreement run? 2. Can I cancel it, and on what terms? 3. If the seller offers compensation off-MLS, does that reduce what I owe you dollar for dollar, or do you keep the difference? 4. Am I your client or your customer, and what is your agency role? 5. Will you show me homes where the seller offers little or no buyer-agent compensation? 6. Are you a REALTOR, or licensed only? 7. Which municipalities do you actually close in?
Question three is the sharpest one on the list, because it is precisely the ambiguity the off-MLS change created — and a straight answer to it tells you most of what you need to know about the person.
Two red flags worth naming: anyone who tells you the commission is standard or set by law, and anyone who pressures you to sign before you’ve read it. The signature is required. The terms in it are not.
This is general information about Missouri real estate practice, not legal advice. For advice about your situation, talk to a Missouri attorney.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the best way to choose a real estate agent?
A.  Verify the license at mopro.mo.gov and check disciplinary history at pr.mo.gov/realestate-disciplines.asp, then interview at least three. Before signing, get the compensation written as an actual number — NAR requires it to be “objectively ascertainable” and “not open-ended,” so a blank or “standard rate” does not qualify.
### Q. How much does a realtor make off of a $300,000 house?
A.  At the 2.52% average buyer-agent commission for homes under $500,000, a $300,000 sale is about $7,560 to the buyer’s agent, before their brokerage takes a share. A listing agent is paid separately. Nothing sets these rates — they are negotiable, and St. Louis sits squarely in the price tier where the percentage runs highest.
### Q. What not to say to a real estate agent?
A.  Avoid revealing your maximum budget or your deadline pressure before you understand who the agent represents. Under Missouri law a transaction broker owes no fiduciary duty to either party, and a “customer” is owed less than a “client” — so establish your agency relationship in writing first, then share strategy.
### Q. What is the 3-3-3 rule in real estate?
A.  It is an informal rule of thumb that circulates online in several conflicting versions — sometimes about touring three homes, sometimes about savings or budgeting. It is not a Missouri regulation, an NAR rule, or a lending standard, and no authoritative source defines it. Treat it as folklore rather than guidance.
### Q. What annoys real estate agents?
A.  Common complaints are touring homes far outside your approved budget, working with several agents at once without disclosing it, and missing scheduled showings. Note that since August 2024 the multiple-agent question is more concrete — buyers now sign written agreements before touring, so overlapping agreements can create real obligations.
### Q. What is the hardest month to sell a house?
A.  Winter months are traditionally slowest, though it varies by market and we would not predict any particular month for St. Louis. What is documented locally: metro median days on market was about 44 in June 2026, four days longer than a year earlier, with active listings up roughly 10.3%.
### Q. How do I check if a real estate agent is licensed in Missouri?
A.  Use the Missouri Division of Professional Registration lookup at mopro.mo.gov/license/s/license-search to confirm the license is active and whether the person is a salesperson or a broker. Disciplinary actions since June 30, 2011 are posted separately at pr.mo.gov/realestate-disciplines.asp. Both are free.
### Q. Does a seller in Missouri have to disclose a death in the house?
A.  If reading about how agents get paid made you consider the other side of the table, here is what real estate school costs in Missouri.
Thinking of renting the place out short-term instead? Know the rules first with our guide to short-term rental rules in St. Louis.
Before the listing photos get taken, it helps to know what home staging does for a St. Louis sale and when it’s worth paying for.
No. Missouri law states that property is not required to be disclosed as “psychologically impacted,” which includes a homicide, felony or suicide having occurred there, and it bars a cause of action against an agent for not disclosing it. Methamphetamine production on the property, by contrast, must be disclosed in writing if the seller knew.

## Old-House Wiring in St. Louis: Knob-and-Tube, Aluminum, and Your Panel
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/old-house-wiring-in-st-louis
The median house in the City of St. Louis was built in 1938. Nearly 58% of the city’s housing went up in 1939 or earlier, per the Census Bureau’s five-year American Community Survey estimates.
In St. Louis County the median is 1969, and about a third of the housing stock was built between 1960 and 1979.
Those two numbers, both from the Census Bureau, mean the city and the county have completely different electrical problems hiding in their walls. City houses are knob-and-tube country. County houses are aluminum-wiring and questionable-panel country. Here’s how to tell what you have, what actually matters, and what you can ignore.
### What is knob-and-tube wiring, and is it dangerous?
Knob-and-tube was the standard wiring method from roughly the 1880s through the 1940s — two separate conductors run several inches apart, supported by white porcelain knobs and passing through porcelain tubes where they cross framing. It has no ground wire, and its cloth-and-rubber insulation gets brittle with age. But the single biggest hazard isn’t age at all: it was engineered to shed heat into open air, so burying it in insulation is what makes it dangerous. The National Electrical Code prohibits concealed knob-and-tube in spaces filled with loose, rolled or foamed-in insulation for exactly that reason.
### The city problem: knob-and-tube
A 1938 median puts the typical city house dead in the middle of the knob-and-tube era. If you own a brick house in south city, Tower Grove, Dutchtown, Baden or the north side, there is a genuine chance some original wiring is still in service somewhere in it.
Go look, and don’t touch anything. In an unfinished basement or attic you’re looking for white porcelain spools nailed to the joists with a single wire running through each, porcelain tubes where wire passes through wood, and — the giveaway — two separate wires running parallel several inches apart instead of one modern cable. The sheathing is cloth or rubber, often cracked.
The thing you are actually hunting for is knob-and-tube buried under or inside blown-in insulation. That is the combination the Code specifically bans, and it is the realistic fire scenario. It usually happens innocently: somebody insulated the attic decades after the wiring went in and had no idea it mattered.
Two more clues that you’re on an ungrounded system: two-prong outlets throughout the house, and no third slot anywhere.
### So is it legal?
Yes. Existing knob-and-tube is generally grandfathered — the electrical code is not retroactive, and neither Missouri nor the federal government bans living with it. You are not breaking a law by owning it.
Where it bites is the moment you touch it. The Code permits knob-and-tube only as an extension of an existing installation, typically with the local inspector’s approval, and new installation isn’t allowed at all. Insulating over it is prohibited outright. The City of St. Louis enforces the 2017 edition of the National Electrical Code; St. Louis County runs on its own adopted edition, so confirm with the County before planning work out there.
### The county problem: aluminum branch wiring
If your house went up in the late sixties or early seventies — which describes about a third of St. Louis County — your risk is different and better documented.
Between roughly 1965 and 1973, a copper shortage pushed builders to aluminum branch circuit wiring. The Consumer Product Safety Commission estimates about two million homes got it. And the CPSC finding is blunt: homes built before 1972 wired with aluminum are 55 times more likely to have one or more connections at outlets reach what the agency calls “Fire Hazard Conditions.”
That phrase has an actual definition, which almost nobody quoting the statistic bothers to include. It means the cover plate screws on a receptacle reaching 300°F, or sparks coming out of the receptacle, or the material around it charring.
The important nuance: the danger is at the connections, not in the wire itself. Aluminum expands, contracts and oxidizes where it terminates at a switch or outlet, and those spots turn into high-resistance hot spots over decades.
To spot it, look at the cable sheathing in your basement or at the panel for printed “AL” or “ALUMINUM,” and at conductor color — dull silver rather than copper.
CPSC accepts two permanent repairs short of a full copper rewire: COPALUM crimp connectors and AlumiConn connectors. What it does not accept as a permanent fix is ordinary pigtailing with twist-on wire nuts — which is unfortunately the cheap fix people are sometimes sold.
### What your panel is telling you
Read the label on the outside of the panel. Do not remove the cover. The conductors feeding the main are energized and are not protected by any breaker inside that box — this is the one part of a house where amateur curiosity genuinely kills people.
Federal Pacific / FPE Stab-Lok. Here the internet is far more confident than the evidence, so here is the careful version. CPSC ran a two-year investigation and closed it in 1983 without reaching a conclusion, saying the data available did not establish that the breakers posed a serious risk — while also explicitly citing its budget and noting it had insufficient data to accept or refute the manufacturer’s test results. So: no recall, no finding of a defect, and no finding of safety either. Anyone who tells you CPSC cleared these, or that CPSC condemned them, is overstating. What is on the record since: a 2002 New Jersey class action concluded the manufacturer had issued UL labels to products it knew did not meet UL testing requirements, and at least one insurer — The Hanover — publishes guidance saying the safest course is full replacement of the panelboard.
Zinsco (also branded GTE-Sylvania or Sylvania-Zinsco) gets grouped with FPE, but be aware the evidence is weaker: there was never a CPSC investigation, and what exists is home-inspector field reporting rather than formal testing. Widely flagged, worth having looked at, not federally documented.
### Fuse boxes: obsolete, not automatically unsafe
A fuse is a perfectly effective overcurrent device — arguably faster-acting than a breaker. A fuse box is mostly obsolete rather than inherently dangerous: low total capacity, few circuits, no ground, no modern arc-fault or ground-fault protection, and you have to keep spares.
The real hazard has a name, and it’s over-fusing. A 30-amp screw-in fuse physically fits the same socket as a 15-amp fuse. Somebody gets tired of a circuit tripping, puts in a bigger fuse, and the nuisance stops — because the protection stopped. A fuse protects the wire, not the appliance. Put a 30-amp fuse on wiring rated for 15, and the wire inside your wall becomes the weakest link and the thing that overheats.
The Code names this failure mode directly: screw-in Edison-base fuses are permitted only as replacements in existing installations where there is no evidence of over-fusing or tampering.
And there is a cheap fix almost no one mentions, because it doesn’t sell a panel. Type S fuses and adapters are made so tampering is difficult — the adapter screws into the existing fuseholder and cannot be removed, after which only a correctly-rated fuse will fit. An adapter kit costs very little and makes an old fuse panel tamper-resistant.
Nothing to do with fuse boxes — dinner in Glendale, Missouri is quietly excellent.
### Do you actually need 200 amps?
Often, no — and this is where you’ll be told otherwise by people selling panels.
Amperage is your whole house’s simultaneous capacity, not a quality grade. The Code sets 100 amps as the minimum service for a one-family dwelling — a floor, not a deficiency. Whether you need more is decided by a load calculation, and there’s a specific method in the Code for existing homes that exists precisely to answer “can what I have carry what I want to add.” Plenty of existing houses calculate out in the eighties of amps and pass comfortably on a 100-amp service.
100 amps is genuinely fine when your heat is gas, the range, dryer and water heater are gas, there’s one central air unit, and no EV charger or hot tub. That describes an enormous number of St. Louis houses.
200 amps is genuinely driven by an electric range plus electric dryer plus electric water heater; central air added to an already-loaded panel; a heat pump, especially with electric backup heat, which counts at full nameplate in the calculation; a hot tub; and EV charging — a 48-amp charger alone claims a 60-amp circuit, which is most of the way through a 100-amp service.
Ask for the load calculation. A contractor who won’t run one and just quotes an upgrade is guessing on your dollar.
### The permit rule that surprises St. Louis homeowners
This one is worth knowing before you plan a DIY weekend.
The City of St. Louis does let a homeowner pull an electrical permit — but you have to pass a short test given by the Building Division’s Electrical Section, the work must be on an owner-occupied single-family home, and it’s limited to a room addition, repair, or modification of an existing system. Then comes the line that matters: in the City’s own words, you may not apply for permits for service changes, rehab, or new construction — those require a licensed contractor.
Which means the two jobs this entire article is about — rewiring, and upgrading your service or panel — are precisely the two you cannot permit yourself. Application fee is $25; the Building Division is at 1200 Market.
St. Louis County also requires licensed electrical contractors registered with the County, with a homeowner exception tied to an examination. Confirm the current rules with County Public Works before relying on it.
### Checking that your electrician is real
Missouri’s setup is unusual and worth understanding, because “licensed” means two different things here.
Since July 2019 Missouri has offered a statewide electrical contractor license — but it is optional, and it is a business credential rather than a replacement for local licensing of individual electricians. A statewide licensee can work in any jurisdiction without passing a local proficiency exam. Permits and inspections still happen locally; the state issues neither.
So verify in two places: the state license lookup at mopro.mo.gov, and then the local registration — a City of St. Louis certified electrical contractor license for city work, or County electrical licensing for county work.
### Insurance, and the right you actually have
You will read a lot of confident claims about which insurers refuse to cover knob-and-tube. We’re not going to repeat any of them, because carrier underwriting guidelines are not published and every specific claim we found traced back to marketing content rather than a carrier document. Ask your own agent — that is the only reliable answer, and it’s free.
What we can tell you is a right Missouri law gives you. If an insurer cancels a policy, it must give at least 30 days’ written notice (10 for non-payment), and the notice must state the actual reason clearly and specifically enough that an ordinary person can identify the basis — vague language is expressly prohibited.
That letter is useful. If wiring is the reason, you now have it in writing, which is exactly what your electrician needs to scope the remediation the carrier wants.
### What it costs, honestly
We looked for St. Louis rewiring figures from any credible source and could not find any. There is no government, academic or research-body data on residential rewiring costs — only home-services marketplaces.
For rough scale, those national marketplaces put full knob-and-tube replacement somewhere around $12,000 to $35,000, with a panel upgrade adding roughly $1,500 to $4,000 and wall repair another $1,000 to $5,000. Treat those as national estimates, not St. Louis quotes.
One local factor does push the repair line item up: St. Louis’s older housing is full of plaster walls, and opening and patching plaster costs meaningfully more than drywall. Get three itemized local bids from electricians working across the St. Louis metro, and make sure each one separates the electrical work from the wall repair, because that is where quotes diverge most.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is knob and tube wiring still legal?
A.  Existing knob-and-tube is generally grandfathered and legal to keep using — the electrical code is not retroactive, and Missouri has no ban. New installation is not permitted, extensions of existing runs require the local inspector’s approval, and covering concealed knob-and-tube with loose, rolled or foamed insulation is prohibited outright.
### Q. Can you live in a house with knob and tube wiring?
A.  Yes, and a great many St. Louis households do — the median city home dates to 1938. Intact knob-and-tube that has not been buried in insulation, overloaded, or badly spliced can function. The realistic hazards are insulation covering it, brittle cloth insulation, amateur splices, and the absence of any ground.
### Q. How much does it cost to rewire a house with knob and tube?
A.  No government or research source publishes rewiring costs. Home-services marketplaces put full replacement at roughly $12,000–$35,000 nationally, plus about $1,500–$4,000 for a panel and $1,000–$5,000 for wall repair. Those are national estimates, not St. Louis quotes, and plaster walls here push the repair side higher. Get three itemized local bids.
### Q. Is it worth buying a house with knob and tube wiring?
A.  It can be, but price it in before you close. Have an electrician assess how much original wiring is still live, whether any of it is buried in insulation, and what the panel is. Also ask your insurance agent what they will require, since that answer varies by carrier and is worth knowing before your financing is committed.
### Q. Can I sell my house if it has knob and tube wiring?
A.  Yes. There is no legal barrier to selling a home with knob-and-tube in Missouri. Expect it to surface in the buyer’s inspection, expect some buyers’ insurers to ask questions, and expect it to become a negotiating point. Having a recent electrician’s assessment in hand tends to help more than it hurts.
### Q. Can you run Romex off knob and tube?
A.  This is exactly the work that requires a licensed electrician and a permit rather than a weekend. The code allows knob-and-tube only as an extension of an existing installation and typically requires the local inspector’s approval, and the splice between old and new is a common failure point when done improperly. In the City of St. Louis, rewiring counts as “rehab,” which homeowners cannot permit themselves.
### Q. How do I know if I have aluminum wiring?
A.  Look at the cable sheathing in your basement or at the panel for printed “AL” or “ALUMINUM,” and at conductor color — dull silver rather than copper. Aluminum branch wiring was installed roughly 1965–1973, which covers about a third of St. Louis County housing. CPSC accepts COPALUM or AlumiConn connectors as permanent repairs; ordinary twist-on pigtailing is not accepted.
### Q. Do I need to upgrade from 100 amp to 200 amp service?
A.  Often not. The electrical code sets 100 amps as the minimum service for a single-family home, and a load calculation — not the age of the house — decides whether you need more. If your heat, range, dryer and water heater are gas and you have one central air unit, 100 amps is frequently adequate. Electric heat, a heat pump, a hot tub or EV charging are what genuinely drive 200.

## Kaslik Mediterranean Cuisine: A Hazelwood Middle Eastern Favorite

There’s a particular kind of restaurant that a neighborhood quietly falls in love with: unassuming from the street, packed with regulars, serving food made with obvious care. This is an honest look at what it is, what to order, and why it’s spent more than a decade earning a loyal Hazelwood following.

### What Kaslik is
Kaslik Mediterranean Cuisine sits at 7847 North Lindbergh Boulevard in Hazelwood, MO 63042, phone (314) 972-8282. It’s a family-owned Mediterranean and Middle Eastern restaurant serving Levantine classics — the shawarma, kebabs, and mezze of the eastern Mediterranean. It first opened in Florissant around 2013 and moved to its Hazelwood home a couple of years later, and it’s been a north-county fixture ever since.
A note on the name and the food, because it’s a nice story: “Kaslik” is a town in Lebanon, and the menu draws on that whole Levantine tradition — but the family behind the restaurant is Palestinian, having come to St. Louis from the West Bank. ### What to order
The menu covers the Levantine greatest hits, and a few dishes anchor any good order:

Falafel and vegetarian options — crisp, herby falafel and a genuinely good veggie platter make this an easy call for meatless eaters.
Baklava — the classic sweet, flaky finish. Save room.
The kebabs and the hummus are the fundamentals that tell you whether a Middle Eastern kitchen is the real deal, and Kaslik passes the test — the grilled meats come off the fire juicy and well-seasoned, and the dips taste made-that-day because they are. If you’re new to the cuisine, a mixed grill with a couple of mezze and warm pita is the perfect introduction. ### A quick primer on Levantine food
If Middle Eastern food is new to you, here’s the short version of what makes it so satisfying. The Levantine tradition — the cooking of the eastern Mediterranean, from Lebanon and Syria through Palestine and Jordan — is built on fresh, bright, generous flavors: grilled meats seasoned simply and well, fresh herbs, lemon and garlic, olive oil, and a whole family of dips and salads meant for sharing with warm bread. It’s food that feels both healthy and deeply comforting, which is a rare combination — you can eat well here without the heavy, over-full feeling a lot of restaurant meals leave you with, and still walk out satisfied.
It’s also a cuisine built for the table, not the individual plate. A proper Middle Eastern meal is a spread — several mezze in the middle, a platter of grilled meats, a stack of pita, everyone reaching and passing. That communal, unhurried style is part of what makes a place like Kaslik feel welcoming, and it’s why it works so well for a group. You don’t just eat here; you graze, you share, you linger.
### Great for takeout, catering, and feeding a crowd
One underrated thing about this style of food: it travels beautifully. ## Candicci’s: A 40-Year St. Louis Italian Favorite, Reinvented

### What Candicci’s is today
Candicci’s Catering & Express operates from 14870 Clayton Road, on the Chesterfield/Ballwin border in west St. Louis County (ZIP 63017), phone (636) 220-8989. It moved here in 2024 into the former Chirco’s Pizza space at Clayton and Baxter — not in Old Town Chesterfield or the Valley, but along the Clayton Road corridor between the two communities, an easy hop from the rest of Chesterfield’s shops and services.

## Your Casino Floor Is Floating: All 6 St. Louis Casinos, Compared
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-the-best-casinos-in-st-louis-mo-a-comprehensive-guide
The river wind is still in your collar when the doors slide shut behind you, and here’s what almost nobody on this floor knows: you’re standing on water. Warm air, carpet soft enough to swallow your footsteps, a wall of slot chimes, and somewhere past the cashier cage a table goes up in one big shout. You walked here over the cobblestones of Laclede’s Landing with the Arch at your back. No boarding pass. No resort fee. No $18 airport beer.
The water part is literal. Missouri only allows casinos on or right beside the Mississippi and Missouri rivers, so even the big land-style rooms are built on barges in concrete basins of river water, no more than 1,000 feet from the main channel. Missourians nicknamed them “boats in moats.” It plays like any Vegas floor. Legally, it floats.
Most St. Louisans price out a Vegas weekend, close the tabs somewhere around the resort fee, and forget there are six casino floors within about 40 minutes of downtown. One you can walk to from Busch Stadium, and the Caesars Rewards card still in your wallet from that last Vegas trip works there. One is an honest-to-goodness riverboat in Alton. And the south-county favorite everyone assumes has a poker room doesn’t.
Going tonight? Do it in this order.
Pick by where you are. Downtown or at a Cardinals game: Horseshoe. South county: River City. West county or St. Charles: Hollywood or Ameristar. Metro East: DraftKings at Casino Queen or Argosy.
Bring a photo ID. You must be 21, and it’s checked at the door and again at the tables.
Park free or ride. Parking is generally free, with valet at the bigger resorts. Or take MetroLink to the Laclede’s Landing or East Riverfront stop: $2.50 a ride, or $5 for a one-day pass.
Get the players card before your first spin. It’s free at the desk (Penn for Hollywood and River City, Caesars Rewards for Horseshoe, Boyd for Ameristar), and the free play and dining comps cost you nothing.
Check the clock. The big Missouri floors generally run around the clock; little Argosy keeps shorter hours, roughly 9am to 2am.
Set your number before you sit down. If it ever stops being fun, the free, confidential National Problem Gambling Helpline is 1-800-GAMBLER.
### What’s the Nearest Casino to Downtown St. Louis?
Horseshoe St. Louis. It sits at 999 N. 2nd Street on the north end of Laclede’s Landing, a short walk from the Arch grounds, and it’s the only casino in downtown proper. Staying at a hotel near Busch Stadium or catching a show downtown? You can walk it, finishing over the Landing’s cobblestones with the casino lights ahead and the river on your right, or ride MetroLink to the Laclede’s Landing stop.
The runner-up is just over the water. DraftKings at Casino Queen sits on the East St. Louis riverfront right beside the East Riverfront MetroLink station, one stop across the Eads Bridge, and it’s usually a five-to-ten-minute drive. Two casinos, two states, one MetroLink stop apart. Everything else is a real drive: River City in Lemay runs roughly 20 minutes south, Hollywood in Maryland Heights and Ameristar in St. Charles are each about 25 to 30 minutes west, and Argosy in Alton is roughly half an hour north. Rush hour and Cardinals game days stretch every one of those.
### Why You Don’t Need Vegas (or Biloxi)
Do the honest math. A Vegas weekend is a flight, two burned vacation days, a resort fee and a $700 card statement before you’ve touched a chip. A St. Louis casino night is a tank of gas and whatever you decide to lose. Drop a hundred bucks at the tables and that’s the whole night, and you’re asleep in your own bed by two.
And the Strip can’t sell you the river. Up in Alton, Argosy is an honest-to-goodness riverboat on the Mississippi, the same water that built this city. Downtown, you can play blackjack two blocks from the Gateway Arch, then step out of Horseshoe into the damp river air and the quiet of the Landing after midnight. Turn a Cardinals afternoon at Busch into a casino evening without moving the car, and still make it home for a plate of toasted ravioli.
### Six Casinos, Two States, One River
The St. Louis area has six casinos inside about a 40-minute drive of downtown: four in Missouri, Hollywood Casino (Maryland Heights), River City Casino (Lemay), Horseshoe St. Louis (downtown, formerly Lumière Place) and Ameristar (St. Charles), plus two in Illinois, DraftKings at Casino Queen (East St. Louis) and Argosy Casino Alton. You must be 21, and Missouri now allows legal sports betting, too. That state line matters more than you’d guess, and it explains the floor you were standing on a minute ago.
Every Missouri casino is, technically, a floating casino. State law requires gaming to sit on or right beside the Mississippi or Missouri River, so even the sleek, land-style rooms like Hollywood and Ameristar are actually built atop enormous concrete barges set in water basins. You’d never feel it on the floor - it plays like any Vegas room - but that quirk is why every one of them hugs the riverfront. Illinois plays it more literally still: up in Alton sits an honest-to-goodness riverboat.
### All Six Side by Side: Slots, Poker, Hotels, Sportsbooks
### Hollywood Casino & Hotel - The Biggest Night Out (Maryland Heights)
If you want the works - a giant floor, a hotel, a real night - Hollywood in Maryland Heights is the metro’s heavyweight. More than 1,700 slots and video poker machines, 40-plus table games, a 20-table poker room, a 502-room hotel, and the Hollywood Casino Amphitheater next door, with a shuttle on concert nights. There’s a fitness center, valet, and a free airport shuttle, which makes it the natural landing pad for out-of-towners flying into Lambert. Best for: a big floor with a real poker room, a concert-and-casino weekend, and groups who want everything under one roof.
### River City Casino & Hotel - The South County Favorite (Lemay)
Down in Lemay, right on the Mississippi in south county, River City is the pick for anyone on the south side who’d rather not fight downtown or trek to Maryland Heights. More than 1,600 slots and video poker machines, a full table pit, and an eight-table baccarat room that runs around the clock. One thing it doesn’t have is a poker room, so card players drive to Hollywood, Horseshoe or Ameristar. Add a 200-room hotel, several restaurants, and Judy’s Velvet Lounge with live music on Saturday nights, and it’s a full night without the long drive. Best for: south-county players, baccarat, and a strong all-around floor with a friendlier, less-touristy crowd.
### Horseshoe St. Louis - Downtown by the Arch (formerly Lumière Place)
The only casino in downtown proper, Horseshoe sits about two blocks from the Gateway Arch - and if the name throws you, that’s because Caesars rebranded the old Lumière Place to Horseshoe St. Louis back in 2022. It’s a more compact, upscale floor (around 950 slots, about 30 table games, a 10-table WSOP poker room), and the real magic is what’s attached: two hotels, including the boutique Hotel Lumière and the genuinely luxurious Four Seasons Hotel St. Louis, plus a 453-seat theater. It runs on Caesars Rewards, so a card from Vegas works here too. Best for: a downtown stay, pairing a casino night with a Cardinals game or the Arch, poker, and higher-end play.
### Ameristar Casino Resort Spa - The Weekend Getaway (St. Charles)
The Ameristar tower in St. Charles, MO, photographed for St Louis Near Me Directory by Lane Forman on July 26, 2026.
Across the Missouri River in St. Charles, Ameristar is the one that feels like a destination instead of just a casino. The floor is enormous - more than 1,700 slots and video poker machines, a live poker room and a private high-limit room, all on 130,000 square feet - but the extras are the sell: an all-suite, AAA Four-Diamond hotel, the 7,000-square-foot aRa Spa, seven dining venues, a Topgolf Swing Suite, and the Hi-Vi Arcade for the kids. Add St. Charles’s historic cobblestone Main Street a few minutes away and you’ve got a whole weekend without a boarding pass. Best for: a couples’ or spa getaway, St. Charles-area players, and resort amenities with your gaming.

### DraftKings at Casino Queen - Across the River (East St. Louis, IL)
Just across the Mississippi from downtown - with a postcard view of the Arch and skyline - sits the longtime Casino Queen, now branded DraftKings at Casino Queen. It’s a full casino with a hotel and dining on the riverfront, and because Illinois legalized sports betting all the way back in 2019, its DraftKings sportsbook has been running years longer than any Missouri book. It’s a quick hop over the river. Best for: Metro East residents, a fast trip from downtown, and DraftKings sportsbook fans.
### Argosy Casino Alton - The Real Riverboat (Alton, IL)
About 25 minutes upriver in Alton sits the metro’s throwback: an actual riverboat casino on the Mississippi, the riverboat operation that first opened as the Alton Belle. It’s the smallest of the six - roughly 500 slots and about nine tables, dining on board, no hotel - and that’s exactly the charm. Low-key, easy to navigate, and a genuine riverboat experience the big barges can’t fake. Make a day of it with pretty, antique-lined downtown Alton. Best for: a relaxed, smaller visit, a true riverboat feel, and folks up in the River Bend.

Biggest floor / most slots: Ameristar or Hollywood. Both run 1,700-plus machines, and Ameristar’s 130,000-square-foot floor is the largest in the metro.
Poker: Hollywood, Horseshoe and Ameristar all run live poker rooms. River City doesn’t have one.
Downtown, near the Arch or a Cardinals game: Horseshoe St. Louis, two blocks away.
A resort, a spa, a full weekend: Ameristar in St. Charles.
A true riverboat: Argosy Casino Alton.
From the Metro East: DraftKings at Casino Queen or Argosy Alton - no bridge-into-downtown hassle.
Best all-arounder without the crowds: River City in south county.

### The Slot Machine Questions Everyone Googles
Be honest - you’ve typed at least one of these into your phone in a parking lot. Here are straight answers, no mysticism.
What’s the “$20 method”? It’s a bankroll trick, not a loophole: you put $20 in a machine, play a set number of spins, and if you don’t hit a target you cash out the ticket and move on - protecting whatever’s left instead of feeding it all back. It won’t beat the house math, but it’s a genuinely good way to make a small budget last and stay in control.
Which slot machines “hit” the most? No machine is ever “due,” and none in a licensed casino is warm because the last person left. Every spin is independent and random. As a rule of thumb, higher-denomination and simpler machines tend to carry a better return-to-player rate than the flashy penny games with a dozen bonus features - but the house keeps an edge on all of them. Play the ones you enjoy, set a limit, and treat any win as a happy surprise.
Are the machines rigged? Not in the cheating sense. Slots in Missouri and Illinois are regulated and independently tested for fairness, and the house edge is built into the math legally and openly - that’s just how casinos make money, the same way the lottery does. The only truly rigged machines are on unlicensed, offshore apps. At the six casinos above, the game is square; the odds simply favor the house, which is exactly why you set a budget.
### Sports Betting Is Finally Legal in Missouri
This is the big recent change. Missouri voters narrowly passed Amendment 2 in November 2024, and legal sports betting - both at retail sportsbooks inside the casinos and through online apps - officially launched on December 1, 2025. For the first time, you can place a legal wager on the Cardinals, the Blues, or a Sunday NFL slate from inside a Missouri casino or from your phone in-state. Illinois books were taking bets years before Missouri’s, so the Casino Queen and Argosy books have a long head start. Minimum age is 21 for sports betting in both states, same as the casino floor. (Physical sportsbook counters can open in phases, so if the in-person book is your goal, a quick check that it’s fully live is worth it.)
### Before You Go: ID at the Door, Free Parking, a Players Card
You must be 21 for casino gaming and sports betting in both Missouri and Illinois. Bring a valid photo ID - it’s checked at the door and the tables.
Hours: the larger Missouri casinos generally run around the clock, especially on weekends; little Argosy keeps shorter hours (roughly 9am–2am). Check the property before a late-night run.
Parking is generally free, with valet at the bigger resorts - one more Vegas headache you get to skip.
Join the players club. Every casino has a free rewards program (Penn’s for Hollywood and River City, Caesars Rewards for Horseshoe, Boyd for Ameristar). Sign up before you play - the free play, dining comps, and parking perks add up fast and cost you nothing.
Gamble responsibly. Set a budget before you walk in and treat it as entertainment money, not income. If it ever stops being fun, the free, confidential National Problem Gambling Helpline is at 1-800-GAMBLER.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Does St. Louis have gambling?
A.  Yes - the St. Louis area has six casinos (four in Missouri, two in Illinois) plus, since December 2025, legal sports betting in Missouri. You’ll find slots, table games, poker, and sportsbooks all within about a 40-minute drive of downtown, so there’s no need to travel to Vegas for a night out.
### Q. Is River City Casino in downtown St. Louis?
A.  No. River City sits in Lemay, south of the city, not downtown. Horseshoe St. Louis is the only casino in downtown proper, about two blocks from the Gateway Arch.
### Q. Is there a Caesars casino in St. Louis?
A.  Yes, under a different name. Caesars rebranded the old Lumière Place to Horseshoe St. Louis in 2022, and it runs on Caesars Rewards - so a card earned in Las Vegas works downtown.
### Q. Is there a Harrahs casino in St. Louis?
A.  Not anymore. Hollywood Casino in Maryland Heights was Harrah’s St. Louis until Penn bought it from Caesars and renamed it. Today the metro’s Caesars casino is Horseshoe St. Louis downtown, alongside Hollywood, River City and Ameristar on the Missouri side and two casinos in Illinois.
### Q. Is River City Casino worth visiting?
A.  It is the pick if you want a strong all-around floor without the downtown crowd: 1,600-plus slots, a 24-hour baccarat room, a 200-room hotel and a friendlier, less-touristy room. There’s no poker room, though. South-county players tend to make it their regular rather than a night out.

## 9 St. Louis Restaurants Locals Actually Love (Not the Chains)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-the-top-fast-food-spots-in-st-louis-a-2025-guide
Refreshed September 2026
Picture a Friday night when nobody at the table wants a drive-thru. Maybe you’re showing an out-of-town friend around, or you’re just tired of the same three chains off the highway in Chesterfield, Kirkwood, or Florissant. You want somewhere that actually tastes like St. Louis — a place a local would send you, not a logo you could find in any city in America.
This is that list. A quick honesty note first: despite how it sometimes gets labeled, none of these are “fast food” in the drive-thru sense. They run the range from order-at-the-counter barbecue to sit-down, special-occasion kitchens — the common thread is that they’re independent, they’re beloved, and they’re the opposite of an interchangeable chain. Here are nine St. Louis spots worth going out of your way for.
### Nine St. Louis restaurants worth the drive
St. Louis’s most beloved local restaurants span every price point and craving: Pappy’s Smokehouse for Memphis-style barbecue, Hi-Pointe Drive-In and Stacked STL for standout burgers, The Frisco Barroom in Webster Groves for elevated tavern food, Havana’s Cuisine in the Central West End for a real Cuban sandwich, Menya Rui for Tokyo-style shoyu ramen, The Golden Hoosier for sandwiches with a side of taxidermy, and, when you want something more refined, Acero in Maplewood and Peppe’s Apt. 2 in Kirkwood. Below is what to order at each.
### 1. Pappy’s Smokehouse
If you only eat at one place on this list, make it Pappy’s. This is the St. Louis barbecue institution — old-school, Memphis-style, and worth every minute of the line that regularly forms out the door. The dry-rubbed ribs are the headliner: smoked low and slow, tender without turning to mush, with that deep bark that tells you someone who cares was tending the pit.
Don’t stop at ribs, though. The brisket comes off moist and thinly sliced, the pulled pork is smoky and piled high, and the sides pull their weight — rich baked beans, sweet potato fries, and applesauce that tastes homemade. Go early; the most popular cuts sell out, and when the meat’s gone for the day, they close. It’s casual, family-friendly, and about as St. Louis as a plate of food gets.
### 2. Hi-Pointe Drive-In
Part burger joint, part retro movie set, Hi-Pointe Drive-In leans into a fun, nostalgic vibe — pop-culture touches everywhere and a menu built around genuinely excellent burgers. You can build your own or order one of the signature creations, and the staff are happy to walk a first-timer through it.
A few crowd favorites to point you in the right direction: the Frisco Melt, a rich, melty burger on sourdough; the Arch D-Lux, a stacked, bold-flavored classic; the Taco Burger for something crunchy and a little different; and the Cowboy Burger loaded with fixings. Add a thick shake — the flavors get creative — and you’ve got the whole experience. It’s a burger a step above the usual, in a room that makes you smile.
### 3. Stacked STL
Stacked STL is for the person who wants their burger built exactly their way. You pick the patty — beef, pork, turkey, or a beef-pork blend — then the bun (brioche, pretzel, gluten-free, or a lettuce wrap), the cheese, the sauces, and a genuinely long list of toppings. If decision fatigue sets in, there’s a lineup of a dozen signature burgers ready to go.
People rave about the juicy patties and the crispy fries, and the vibe is laid-back and friendly, with customer artwork on the walls. It gets busy at peak hours and parking can take a lap or two, but for a burger made precisely to your spec, that’s a small price. Not in the mood to go out? It’s an easy one to get delivered.
### 4. The Frisco Barroom
Over in Webster Groves, on Big Bend Boulevard near Webster University, The Frisco Barroom does elevated tavern food in a warm, rustic room — and its upstairs patio is one of the better places in the area to lose an afternoon. There are heaters up there, so it works well past the first cold snap, too.
Curious why a griddle patty beats a grilled one? This is what actually makes a good burger.
The kitchen keeps it fresh and consistent: the burgers get real praise (the double cheeseburger with horseradish cheese has a following), the salads are surprisingly good, and they turn out solid pierogies and kielbasa when you want something heartier. There’s a deep whiskey list with generous pours, and live music turns up now and then. It’s the kind of place you settle into for a few hours.
