### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Where do I go if I have nowhere to stay?
A.  In St. Louis, call 2-1-1 or St. Patrick Center at (314) 802-0700 for tonight’s shelter options. On a weekday, walk into St. Patrick Center’s Welcome Center at 800 N. Tucker Blvd. at 8 a.m. or 1 p.m. It runs coordinated entry for the City and County, so one intake gets you assessed for housing. Veterans can call 314-356-0657.
### Q. How to apply for emergency housing assistance in Missouri?
A.  Dial 2-1-1, the United Way line that covers Missouri, and ask for emergency housing or shelter near you. In St. Louis City and County, the application is an in-person intake: go to St. Patrick Center’s Welcome Center on a weekday at 8 a.m. or 1 p.m., bring an ID and proof of your situation if you have them, and a specialist will refer you.
### Q. What is the rental assistance program in St. Louis?
A.  There isn’t one standing program; rent help in St. Louis comes and goes with funding. St. Patrick Center says it has no rental assistance available right now and points people to 2-1-1 or (314) 802-0700 for current options. If you’re facing eviction, Missouri Tenant Help (motenanthelp.org) builds free court forms, and Legal Services of Eastern Missouri defends low-income tenants.
### Q. How to get immediate rental assistance?
A.  Call 2-1-1 the same day you fall behind, because rent funds go fast, and have your lease, ID, proof of income and the past-due notice ready. Then ask your landlord for a payment plan in writing, which Missouri Tenant Help suggests as a first step. If court papers arrive, don’t skip the hearing: once a judge orders you out, you get 10 days.
### Q. What are the four types of homelessness?
A.  HUD, which funds most homeless programs, uses four categories: literally homeless (sleeping outside, in a car or in a shelter), at imminent risk of losing housing within 14 days, homeless under other federal laws (mainly unaccompanied youth and families with children), and fleeing domestic violence. Which one fits you shapes which programs you qualify for, so say it plainly at intake.
### Q. How does St. Patrick Center help veterans?
A.  Through Project HERO, which pairs housing with one-on-one case management, and a Supportive Services for Veteran Families program for veterans who are homeless or about to be; call 314-356-0657 to reach it. The newly refurbished Caritas St. Matthews, formerly McFarlane Place and Visitation House, also houses veterans and Hospital to Healthy Housing clients.

## Free Meals in St. Louis: An Honest Guide to Soup Kitchens & Meal Programs
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/finding-nourishment-a-guide-to-soup-kitchens-in-st-louis
If you or someone you know needs a meal in St. Louis, help is out there — and you don’t have to be homeless to use it. Soup kitchens, community meal programs, and food pantries across the metro serve free food to anyone facing a hard stretch, no judgment attached. This is an honest, practical guide to finding nourishment in St. Louis: who serves meals, who supplies groceries, and — most importantly — the single best way to find help that’s open right now.
One thing to know up front: meal programs change. Hours shift, locations move, and programs open and close. So rather than a list of addresses that might be out of date by the time you read it, this guide points you to the organizations that are genuinely operating and the master resource that always has the current details.
### Start here: dial 2-1-1
Before anything else, the most useful thing you can do is call 2-1-1 (or 1-800-427-4626), or visit 211.org. It’s a free, confidential, around-the-clock service from United Way of Greater St. Louis that connects people to food, shelter, and other help across Missouri and Illinois. A real person — or the online search — can tell you which meal or pantry near you is open today, which no static list can guarantee.
Why lead with 211 instead of a fixed list? Because it absorbs the one risk that matters most for someone who’s hungry: a program that quietly changed its hours or closed. 211 stays current so you don’t make a trip for nothing. Save the number in your phone; it’s the backbone of finding help in this region.
For housing, employment, and health services, see our guide to St. Patrick Center.
Need a meal today? The fastest way to find one near you right now is to dial 2-1-1 (or visit 211.org) - United Way’s free, confidential, 24/7 line connects you to current meal programs, food pantries, and shelter across the St. Louis metro. Because hours and locations change, 211 is the most reliable single place to start. For more local help - food stamps, pantries, rent and shelter assistance - see our St. Louis help and assistance resource hub.
If you run a soup kitchen, a pantry or a church supper, list it on St Louis Near Me Directory so the person calling around for a hot meal tonight can find you.
### Places that serve hot meals
Several St. Louis organizations serve prepared meals to people in need. Because serving times and details change, we’ve described what each one does and pointed you to its official contact — call ahead or check 211 for current hours before you go.
### St. Patrick Center
A cornerstone of homeless services in downtown St. Louis, St. Patrick Center provides a wide range of help — outreach, shelter, housing, and employment support — and also serves a daily free lunch. It’s more of a full-service agency than a stand-alone soup kitchen, which means that if you need more than a meal, this is a place that can connect you to it: the same visit that feeds you can start you toward stable housing or a job. That wraparound approach is exactly why it’s worth knowing about even if all you need today is lunch. Reach them through stpatrickcenter.org.
### Peter & Paul Community Services (PPCS)
Based in the Soulard area, PPCS runs emergency shelter and, through a recently expanded community campus, provides nutritious meals along with housing programs — it served tens of thousands of meals over the last winter season. It’s a shelter-and-meals nonprofit rather than a walk-up meal line, so contact them directly (ppcsinc.org, 314-588-7111) to understand what’s available.
### Sts. Peter and Paul Parish meal program
Distinct from the nonprofit above (though historically related), the Sts. Peter and Paul parish in Soulard runs its own free meal program serving shelter residents and low- and fixed-income neighbors. It’s a separate front door, so if one is full or closed, the other may help — a good reminder that it’s always worth checking more than one program when you’re looking for a meal. Details are at stspeterandpaulstl.org, and 211 can confirm the current schedule.
### Trinity “Soup Alley”
Trinity Church in Soulard operates “Soup Alley,” offering window-service free hot meals along with a food pantry. It’s a straightforward, no-barrier way to get a meal in that part of the city, and the pantry means you may be able to pick up groceries as well as eat. Check trinitystlouis.com for current details, since window-service hours can change.
### Gateway 180
One of Missouri’s largest emergency shelters for women, children, and families, Gateway 180 provides three hot meals a day to the people staying there. It’s a residential shelter rather than a public walk-up soup kitchen, so it’s the right call if you need shelter along with food — a safe place to sleep and regular meals together, which is exactly what a family in crisis needs most. Learn more at gateway180.org, or ask 211 about family shelter openings.
### St. Vincent de Paul (parish programs)
The Society of St. Vincent de Paul operates through local parish “conferences” across the region, running food pantries, some sandwich windows, and home food deliveries. Because it’s decentralized, the best way to find the nearest help is through their locator or 211. Start at svdpstlouis.org.
### Food pantries and distributors (groceries, not hot meals)
It’s worth understanding an important distinction, because it saves a wasted trip. Some of the biggest names in St. Louis hunger relief are food distributors and pantry networks — they supply groceries through hundreds of partner sites rather than serving meals at a counter:
St. Louis Area Foodbank supplies a network of hundreds of pantries across the bi-state region and runs mobile and pop-up distributions. Its website has a pantry locator to find a partner pantry with groceries near you — stlfoodbank.org.
Operation Food Search distributes food to 600-plus partner pantries and programs and runs mobile markets. It’s a distributor and mobile-market operator, not a walk-up meal line, but a powerful way to find groceries — operationfoodsearch.org.
If what you need is groceries to cook at home rather than a prepared meal, a food pantry is your best bet — and these two organizations, plus 211, are how you find the closest one that’s open. Many pantries are open to anyone in need; you generally don’t need to prove anything beyond a rough sense of your household size and where you live.
Total tangent — Southampton is a good walk on a slow afternoon.
### Other resources worth knowing
A few more paths to food and support in the St. Louis area:
Church and community meal programs — a number of local congregations serve weekly lunches or hand out to-go meals. Because these come and go, 211 or a call to the church is the way to confirm one is running.
SNAP (food stamps) — for longer-term help buying groceries, see our guide to applying for SNAP in Missouri.
WIC — for pregnant women, new mothers, and young children, WIC provides free food and nutrition help.
Free food giveaways — pop-up distributions happen around the metro; our guide to free food giveaways can help you spot them.
### Who these programs are for
There’s a common misconception worth clearing up: you don’t have to be homeless, or hit some rock bottom, to use a food program. These resources are for anyone going through a hard stretch — a lost job, a medical bill that ate the grocery budget, a fixed income that doesn’t stretch to the end of the month, a sudden crisis. Working families, seniors, students, and people between paychecks all use them. Food insecurity is far more common than most people realize, and it’s usually temporary; a meal program or pantry can be exactly the bridge that gets a household through a rough patch without falling further behind.
If you’re hesitating because you feel like someone else needs it more, know that these programs are built for exactly this moment. Using help when you need it, and paying it forward when you’re able, is how a community takes care of its own. The people running these services would far rather feed you than have you go without out of pride.
### Seasonal and emergency help
Some help ramps up when the need is greatest. During dangerously cold weather, St. Louis activates additional winter shelter and outreach — volunteers and city programs distribute warm meals, blankets, and supplies and help people reach a warm place to sleep. If you or someone you see is out in the cold, 211 and the City of St. Louis’s winter-outreach information are the fastest way to find an open warming site or emergency shelter that night. Don’t wait for a regular meal program’s hours in an emergency — call 211 and say plainly what you need.
### Want to help? Give food, time, or money
If you’re reading this from the other side — fortunate enough to want to help rather than needing help — the organizations above make it easy. The food banks and meal programs always need volunteers to sort, pack, and serve, and monetary donations stretch remarkably far because these groups buy in bulk. A modest gift to the St. Louis Area Foodbank or Operation Food Search translates into many meals, and an hour of volunteering at a meal program is genuinely useful. Supporting the local hunger-relief network is one of the most direct ways to make a difference in your own community, and it keeps these doors open for the neighbors who need them.
### A few honest notes
First, you belong here. Needing a meal is common and human, and these programs exist precisely so that no one in our community goes hungry. Volunteers and staff run them because they want to help; there’s no shame in walking through the door. Nearly everyone hits a hard stretch at some point, and accepting a meal when you need one isn’t failure — it’s exactly what these programs were created to do.
Second, always confirm before you travel. Meal programs are often run by small nonprofits and churches with limited resources, and their schedules genuinely do change. A two-minute call — or a check with 211 — can save you a long trip to a locked door. And if one place can’t help today, ask them who can; the people running these programs know the network and will usually point you to the next open door.
Finally, if you’re in a deeper crisis — no place to sleep, or an emergency — tell 211 that too. The same line that finds you a meal can connect you to shelter, especially during extreme weather, and to the broader safety net that exists to help you get back on your feet.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Can anyone go to a food pantry or soup kitchen?
A.  Generally, yes. Most St. Louis food pantries and meal programs serve anyone in need, and you don’t have to be homeless or prove much beyond your household size and area. Some pantries have a service-area or once-a-month limit, so it helps to call ahead or check with 211, but the default is that help is available to people who need it, no judgment.
### Q. How do I find food help right now in St. Louis?
A.  Dial 2-1-1 (or 1-800-427-4626), or visit 211.org — United Way’s free, confidential, 24/7 service connects you to meal programs, food pantries, and shelter that are currently open across the St. Louis metro. It’s the most reliable way to find help today, because it stays current when static lists go out of date.
### Q. What’s the difference between a food pantry and a soup kitchen?
A.  A soup kitchen or meal program serves prepared, ready-to-eat food on site. A food pantry gives you groceries to take home and cook. Big organizations like the St. Louis Area Foodbank and Operation Food Search are distributors that supply pantries rather than serving meals directly — use their pantry locators (or 211) to find groceries, and the meal programs above for a hot meal.
### Q. Where can I get free food in St. Louis?
A.  Dial 2-1-1 first, or 1-800-427-4626. It is the fastest route to what is actually open today, because pantry and meal schedules change constantly and a printed list goes stale within weeks. They can also route you to help you did not know to ask for.
### Q. Is there a free food giveaway in St. Louis today?
A.  That changes daily, which is exactly why 2-1-1 is the answer rather than a fixed list. Call or text and they will tell you what is distributing today and where. Church and school pantries in particular rarely appear on any searchable directory.
### Q. How can I get free food if I have no money?
A.  2-1-1 connects you to pantries, hot-meal sites and emergency boxes at no cost and without a referral. Ask about SNAP at the same time — many people eligible for it never apply, and the two work together rather than one excluding the other.
### Q. What are those places that give free food?
A.  Food pantries, which give groceries to take home, and meal programs, which serve a hot meal on site. Both are commonly run by churches, community centers and nonprofits. Hours vary week to week, so confirm before traveling — 2-1-1 will do that for you.

## Court Sent Someone You Love to 5351 Delmar: What Happens Next, and Who to Call
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/exploring-services-at-5351-delmar-blvd-st-louis-forensic-treatment-center
“The court found them not fit to proceed. They’re going to 5351 Delmar.” You wrote the address on the back of an envelope while the lawyer was still talking, and the other words slid past you. Forensic. Competency. Committed. Now the house is quiet, the phone is face-down on the kitchen table, and you want to know two things before anything else: what kind of place this is, and how you reach the person you love.
Start with one number: 314-877-0502. That’s the main line for the North Campus of the St. Louis Forensic Treatment Center at 5351 Delmar Boulevard, a psychiatric hospital run by the Missouri Department of Mental Health. Family visits on Delmar have to be scheduled ahead, and they happen on Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Saturdays. Visiting times change, so call before you drive over, not from the parking lot.
What the place is. It’s a secure state psychiatric hospital, and the people there are patients. The Delmar campus has 75 beds for adults a criminal court has sent for competency restoration, which is treatment meant to help someone understand the charges and work with their lawyer. It also runs outpatient evaluations a judge has ordered. The 180-bed South Campus at 5300 Arsenal Street (314-877-6501) is a different track, for people found not guilty by reason of mental disease or defect or permanently incompetent to stand trial.
What usually comes next. Competency treatment usually combines medication, intensive therapy and plain-language lessons on how court works. When staff report that competency has been restored, the judge decides whether the case moves forward. The court, not the hospital, sets that larger timeline, so the lawyer on the case is your best source on dates. If someone mentioned a 96-hour hold, that’s Missouri’s civil clock, and it doesn’t run here. That’s why nobody can hand you a release date yet, and it isn’t because anyone is hiding one. Missouri law does build in a checkpoint: six months after commitment, the court orders the hospital to report whether your loved one is fit to proceed, and if not, it can continue treatment for up to six more months before checking again. Attorneys reach the center’s Forensic Evaluation Services at 314-877-0775.
Three things families rarely hear. Under Section 552.020 of Missouri law, nothing your loved one says during the exam or in treatment can be used as evidence of guilt in the criminal case. The exam report isn’t a public record. And if the case is still early, the state pays for the first one: the Department of Mental Health provides one pretrial evaluation at no charge to the defendant.
Forward this to the rest of the family: North Campus, 5351 Delmar Blvd., 314-877-0502, family visits scheduled ahead on Tue, Wed or Sat. South Campus, 5300 Arsenal St., 314-877-6501. Forensic Evaluation Services, for attorneys and courts: 314-877-0775. If the weight of this is too much tonight, 988 answers by call or text, any hour.
### Key Takeaways
5351 Delmar is the North Campus of the St. Louis Forensic Treatment Center, a 255-bed hospital the Missouri Department of Mental Health runs for adults committed by a criminal court.
Delmar handles competency restoration and outpatient court-ordered evaluations; the longer-term programs are on the South Campus at 5300 Arsenal Street.
Care is a team effort: doctors, nurses, social workers and therapists work the same case, and a Deaf Services Program serves Deaf and hard-of-hearing patients.
Family visits on Delmar are scheduled ahead, on Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Saturdays. Call 314-877-0502 first.
The criminal court, not the hospital, decides when a case moves forward.
### What Happens at 5351 Delmar?
One note on layout before the programs below: the Forensic Treatment Center runs two campuses. The North Campus at 5351 Delmar Boulevard handles inpatient competency restoration and outpatient forensic evaluation, while most of the longer-term, living-area rehabilitation programs described here are based at the South Campus, 5300 Arsenal Street. Both are part of the same Missouri Department of Mental Health facility.
The programs at 5351 Delmar Blvd each target a specific point in the forensic mental health system. Some restore a person’s fitness for court. Others build the skills someone needs after release.
### Competency Restoration Program
Competency restoration helps a person understand the legal proceedings against them and assist in their own defense. The work is practical: reach the point where you can take part in your own court case. Once competency is restored, the legal process can move forward.
### Forensic Responsibility Program
The Forensic Responsibility Program centers on understanding and managing behavior in relation to the legal system. Participants work on accountability and on the concrete steps that meet legal requirements. The aim is greater personal responsibility, one decision at a time.
### New Outlook Program
New Outlook is about a fresh perspective and stronger coping skills. You look at your situation from a different angle and build habits that support a steadier future. Much of the work targets managing mental health and lowering the chance of re-offending.
### Social Learning Program
The Social Learning Program puts social skills into practice instead of leaving them on a worksheet. You work on reading social cues and improving day-to-day interactions. Activities build toward healthier relationships and steadier handling of tense moments. For many people, it is a real step toward life outside the facility.
### What Treatment Looks Like, Day to Day
At the St. Louis Forensic Treatment Center, you'll find a strong focus on providing robust clinical support and treatment tailored to individual needs. The work reaches past managing conditions toward real recovery and steadier well-being.
### Evidence-Based Practice Enhancement
The center is committed to using treatment methods that are proven to work. This means constantly looking at current research and updating practices to make sure you're getting the most effective care possible. They regularly assess and improve their existing evidence-based approaches, aiming to integrate new ones as they become available. This dedication to staying current helps ensure that treatment plans are as effective as they can be.
### Group and Individual Therapy
You'll have access to both group and individual therapy sessions. Group therapy offers a chance to connect with others facing similar challenges, sharing experiences and learning from one another in a supportive environment. Individual therapy provides a more private setting to work through personal issues with a dedicated clinician. These sessions are designed to help you develop coping strategies and work through personal challenges.
### Clinical Training and Development
Part of the center's commitment to high-quality care involves ongoing training and development for its clinical staff. This ensures that the professionals working with you are up-to-date on the latest therapeutic techniques and best practices. They also collaborate with outside providers to bring in fresh perspectives and specialized training, which benefits everyone involved. This continuous learning environment helps maintain a high standard of care.
Here's a look at how clinical support is structured:
Assessment and Planning: Clinicians conduct thorough assessments to understand your specific needs.
Treatment Implementation: Based on assessments, they use evidence-based practices in individual and group settings.
Progress Monitoring: Your progress is regularly reviewed and discussed, with treatment plans adjusted as needed.
Staff Development: Continuous training for staff ensures they are equipped with the latest skills and knowledge.
This structured support system is designed to help you make meaningful progress. For a complete change of subject, our guide to the St. Louis culinary scene is here when you want it.
### The Team Working With Your Loved One
At 5351 Delmar Blvd, care runs as a team effort. Different professionals work the same case together rather than leaving it to one person. This approach means you get a more complete picture of what's going on and a better plan for moving forward.
### Collaboration With Social Workers
Social workers are a big part of the team here. They connect with you, help sort out practical issues, and work with everyone else to make sure your treatment plan is actually working. They're often the ones helping to bridge the gap between what happens here and what needs to happen in the community.
### Integration With Healthcare Professionals
Social workers are only part of the team. You'll see doctors, nurses, therapists, and other specialists involved too. This means that if you have physical health issues alongside your mental health needs, those are being looked at too. This integrated care helps make sure all aspects of your well-being are considered. The goal is treating the whole person, physical health alongside mental health.
### Patient Record Review and Assessment
Part of this team approach involves looking closely at your records and doing regular assessments. Those reviews are how the team stays on the same page. They review what's been done, what's working, and what might need to change. This constant check-in helps tailor your treatment, making sure it stays relevant to your current situation. It's a good way to track progress and adjust the clinical training as needed.
Here's a look at how different roles contribute:
Physicians: Provide medical oversight and manage psychiatric medications.
Nurses: Offer direct patient care, monitor vital signs, and administer medications.
Social Workers: Focus on psychosocial assessments, case management, and community resource connection.
Therapists: Conduct individual and group therapy sessions tailored to specific needs.
### Getting Ready to Come Home
Patient Care and Rehabilitation
At the St. Louis Forensic Treatment Center, your journey toward recovery and improved well-being is supported through a variety of specialized services. Its programs focus on helping each patient build skills and manage challenges so they can move forward.
### Transitional Rehabilitation Services
These services are designed to help you transition back into the community. It's about getting you ready for life outside the facility, step by step. Staff work with patients to develop practical skills needed for daily living, like managing a household, using public transportation, and handling personal finances. The goal is to make your return to the community as smooth as possible.
### Deaf Services Program
Communication is key to care, which is why the center runs a dedicated Deaf Services Program for Deaf and hard-of-hearing patients who need intermediate to long-term inpatient treatment. This program ensures that individuals who are deaf or hard of hearing receive the support they need in a way that makes sense to them. This includes providing qualified interpreters and ensuring that all treatment and information is accessible.
### Risk Assessment and Management
Safety is a top priority, both for you and for the community. The treatment team conducts thorough risk assessments to understand any potential challenges. Based on these assessments, it develops personalized management plans.
Regular reviews of your progress and behavior.
Development of strategies to address specific concerns.
Coordination with external agencies when necessary.
If you're looking for services in the St. Louis area, you can find more information about local resources at local business directory. This can help you connect with various support systems available.
### Professional Roles and Qualifications
When you're looking into the services at 5351 Delmar Blvd, it's helpful to know who's providing that care and what makes them qualified. The staff here are a mix of dedicated professionals, each bringing their own set of skills to the table. You'll find a variety of roles, all working together to support patient recovery.
### Registered Nurse Responsibilities
Registered nurses are on the front lines of patient care. They're responsible for a lot, from administering medications to monitoring vital signs and providing direct patient support. They also play a key role in educating patients and their families about health conditions and treatment plans. It's a demanding job that requires a sharp mind and a caring heart.
### Clinical Social Work Specialist Duties
Clinical social work specialists are vital to the multidisciplinary team. They conduct assessments, develop treatment plans, and provide individual and group therapy. They also collaborate with other professionals to coordinate care and connect patients with community resources. Their work often involves helping patients navigate complex social and emotional challenges. You can find more information about social work roles in Missouri through the state's career pages.
### Licensure and Experience Requirements
To ensure the highest quality of care, specific qualifications are necessary for many roles. For instance, clinical social workers typically need to be licensed in the state, often holding an LCSW (Licensed Clinical Social Worker) designation. This usually requires a master's degree in social work and a certain number of supervised clinical hours. Experience working with individuals who have severe and persistent mental health diagnoses is also frequently a requirement. These standards help make sure that the professionals you interact with are well-prepared for their roles.
Here's a general idea of what's expected:
Education: Master's degree in Social Work (MSW) or equivalent.
Licensure: Must be licensed in Missouri (e.g., LCSW, LMSW, or provisionally licensed).
Experience: Prior experience in mental health settings, particularly with forensic populations, is often preferred.
Skills: Strong abilities in assessment, treatment planning, therapy, and interdisciplinary collaboration.

### Facility Operations at 5351 Delmar Blvd
When you visit the St. Louis Forensic Treatment Center at 5351 Delmar Blvd, you'll find it operates as a significant inpatient psychiatric setting. This facility is dedicated to adult care, focusing on providing specialized services within the mental health system. It's important to know that the center is structured with two main locations, often referred to as the North and South Campuses, to manage its operations effectively.
### Inpatient Psychiatric Setting
The 5351 Delmar Blvd location functions as a key part of the Missouri Department of Mental Health. It's designed to provide intensive, round-the-clock care for adults who require psychiatric treatment. This means you're in a place where individuals receive structured support and therapeutic interventions in a secure environment. The focus here is on stabilization and treatment for those with serious mental health conditions.
### Adult Facility Operations
As an adult facility, the operations at 5351 Delmar Blvd are tailored to meet the specific needs of adult patients. This includes everything from daily routines and therapeutic programming to the administrative aspects that keep the center running smoothly. The goal is to create an environment that supports recovery and rehabilitation for adults navigating complex mental health challenges. You'll see a coordinated effort to manage patient care across various programs.
### North and South Campus Structure
To manage its extensive services, the St. Louis Forensic Treatment Center utilizes a dual-campus structure. The 5351 Delmar Blvd address represents one of these key locations, often referred to as the North Campus. This division helps in organizing patient populations and services, allowing for more focused care within each area. Understanding this structure can give you a clearer picture of how the center is organized to serve its patients. Job openings for both campuses are posted on the center’s opportunities page.
### Who Runs the Forensic Treatment Center, and How Do You Reach It?
The State of Missouri runs it. The St. Louis Forensic Treatment Center is a state-funded, 255-bed psychiatric hospital operated by the Missouri Department of Mental Health’s Division of Behavioral Health, and its patients are adults committed by a criminal court under Chapter 552 of Missouri law. It used to be the St. Louis Psychiatric Rehabilitation Center, and it took its current name when it absorbed 75 beds from the Metropolitan St. Louis Psychiatric Center.
The North Campus at 5351 Delmar Boulevard has those 75 beds and handles competency restoration plus outpatient court-ordered evaluations. If a judge has just sent someone you love there, start with its main line, 314-877-0502. Family visits on Delmar must be scheduled ahead, on Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Saturdays. The South Campus at 5300 Arsenal Street has 180 beds for people found not guilty by reason of mental disease or defect or permanently incompetent to stand trial; call 314-877-6501. Attorneys and courts reach Forensic Evaluation Services at 314-877-0775. Visiting times change, so call the main number before you go, not from the car after you’ve already made the drive.
### What 5351 Delmar Comes Down To
Two campuses, one Missouri Department of Mental Health facility. The North Campus at 5351 Delmar handles competency restoration and forensic evaluation; the South Campus on Arsenal Street runs the longer-term rehabilitation programs. Between them sit court-ordered patients, the nurses and social workers who staff the units, and programs built to move people back toward the community. Trying to reach a patient, apply for a role, or point someone toward help? Start with the Department of Mental Health directly.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What does the term “forensic patient” mean?
A.  A forensic patient is someone placed in psychiatric treatment by a criminal court rather than by choice or a civil order. In Missouri that happens under Chapter 552: to restore competency to stand trial, after a verdict of not guilty by reason of mental disease or defect, or after a finding of permanent incompetence. Nearly every patient at this center is one.
### Q. What is a forensic inpatient ward?
A.  It’s a secure hospital unit for patients sent by a court, where treatment and security run side by side. At the St. Louis Forensic Treatment Center, the North Campus on Delmar has 75 such beds for competency restoration, and the South Campus on Arsenal Street has 180 for longer-term treatment and rehabilitation of people the court has committed.
### Q. What do forensic services do?
A.  They work where mental health and criminal law meet. Forensic evaluators examine defendants on a judge’s order to answer two questions: is this person competent to stand trial, and were they criminally responsible? Inpatient programs then treat the people the court commits. In St. Louis, the center’s Forensic Evaluation Services handles those outpatient exams (314-877-0775).
### Q. What does forensic mean in mental health?
A.  Forensic means connected to the courts. Forensic mental health covers evaluations and treatment ordered as part of a criminal case, so a judge sets part of the goal: restoring someone’s ability to understand their charges, or showing the stability a court needs before it approves release. Ordinary psychiatric care, by contrast, is a matter between the patient and the treatment team.
### Q. How long is a psychiatric hold in Missouri?
A.  A civil hold in Missouri starts at up to 96 hours, not counting weekends and certain holidays. If the treatment team thinks more care is needed, it can ask a court for 21 days, then 90 days or one year of mental health treatment. Forensic commitments at this center are a separate track, set by the criminal court rather than that clock.
### Q. Where is the St. Louis Forensic Treatment Center located?
A.  It has two St. Louis campuses. The North Campus is at 5351 Delmar Blvd. (63112, 314-877-0502) and handles competency restoration and outpatient evaluations. The South Campus is at 5300 Arsenal St. (63139, 314-877-6501) and runs the longer-term inpatient programs. Both belong to the Missouri Department of Mental Health; call the main number before visiting either one.

## Got a Shut-Off Notice? A LIHEAP Pledge Counts as Payment, and Heat Up St. Louis Pays Past-Due Bills
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-heat-up-st-louis-essential-utility-assistance-programs
The Spire disconnection notice has been sitting on the kitchen counter for three days. Looking at it doesn’t make the number any smaller. Outside, the wind off the river is hard enough to rattle the storm door. You’ve got the thermostat at 62 and a sweatshirt pulled on over your pajamas, and every time the furnace clicks on you catch yourself listening to it run, doing the math again.
Nobody prints this part on the notice: in Missouri, a LIHEAP pledge for the amount due counts as the payment your utility asks for on a Cold Weather Rule plan. One application can keep the gas on while the rest gets sorted out.
Tonight, with the notice next to the keyboard, you can start on two doors. One is Heat Up St. Louis, the volunteer charity that pays past-due heating bills straight to the utility. The other is LIHEAP, Missouri’s heating program, which also pays the utility directly. If anyone in your home is 60 or older or has a disability, LIHEAP opened to you on October 1; everyone else can apply starting November 1, the same day the Cold Weather Rule kicks in.
Start online, not on the phone. Heat Up’s lines are for questions after you apply, and the charity warns they get busy in extreme weather.
Pass this to a neighbor: for LIHEAP, use this season’s form, MO 886-4576, because CAASTLC can’t accept last year’s. Funds run out, so apply early.
### What is Heat Up St. Louis, and who does it help?
If you’ve ever sat on hold listening to the furnace click off behind you, you already know why this charity exists. Heat Up St. Louis is an all-volunteer regional charity that has been keeping the lights and heat on for a quarter century. Founded by Gentry W. Trotter in 2000, it works through a network of roughly three dozen partner agencies to pay past-due utility bills for the people who feel a cold snap the hardest: seniors, people with physical disabilities, and low-income families with children.
Two things have changed since a lot of older guides were written, and both matter:
It now helps with natural gas. Older information said Heat Up couldn’t assist with gas bills. That is out of date. The program now provides grants toward natural gas, electric, propane, and home heating oil. Which bills it can pay at any given moment depends on donations, so read the notice at the top of the application form before you apply.
It reaches far past the city. Heat Up St. Louis and its sister program serve a network spanning 40-plus Missouri and Illinois counties - from North County and Jefferson County to St. Charles, Franklin County, and the Metro East. Live in Ferguson, De Soto, Washington, or Granite City? There’s a form for your area.
According to the organization’s own history, it has impacted more than 660,000 people since it began. It runs on donations and community fundraising, so grants are limited and awarded as pledges directly to your utility company - the money doesn’t come to you, it goes to the bill.
### How do I apply to Heat Up St. Louis?
You apply online first. Sit down with the notice next to the keyboard or the phone, because the form asks for the numbers printed on it. Heat Up St. Louis wants the web application for your region before you call anyone. The phone lines are for questions, not intake. Here’s how it works, step by step:
Go to heatupstlouis.org and open the application. Choose the form that matches where you live: St. Louis City, St. Louis County, or Outstate Missouri & Metro East.
Have your utility details ready. You’ll need your utility company’s name, your account number, and the amount you owe.
Upload proof of income. Accepted documents include a year-to-date check stub, an SSI or Social Security award letter, an unemployment statement, a pension award letter, or an official child-support form. Screenshots are not accepted - upload the actual document.
Tell your utility company you’ve applied. As a courtesy, let your provider know you’ve submitted an application and are waiting on a pledge. This is honest, and it can buy you a little time.
Call only if you have a question. After you’ve applied online, the General Office (314-657-1599) and the Senior Automated Line (314-241-7668) are there for follow-up.
If your utility provider or local community-action agency isn’t showing up on the program’s list, call the resource hotline at 314-241-0001 and they’ll point you to the right place. Apply early in the season - funds are limited and go fast once the cold sets in.
### What if nobody answers the phone at Heat Up St. Louis?
The shut-off notice is on the counter, the house is getting colder, and you still can’t get through. That’s common, and it doesn’t mean your application is lost. Heat Up is an all-volunteer charity, its phone lines are meant for follow-up questions rather than intake, and its own client notice warns that the 24/7 automated hotline at 314-241-0001 gets busy during extreme weather. It asks callers to try again at off-peak times or to go straight to a partner agency. Here’s what works while you wait:
Send your paperwork without the phone. Upload it on the form, or email scanned documents to clientserv@heatupstlouis.org. You can also fax them (314-241-1860 for the City form, 314-454-3180 for County and outstate) or drop them off: City applicants at the lobby lock-box at 1520 Market Street, County and outstate applicants at 8960 Jennings Station Road or Suite 111, 1408 North Kingshighway. No screenshots.
Call your utility first. Heat Up asks every applicant to tell the utility they can’t pay and that a pledge application is pending. That call is what buys you time.
Go to a partner agency directly. CAASTLC (314-863-0015) serves St. Louis County, People’s Community Action (314-353-1457) serves south city, and the Urban League answers at 314-615-3600 in the city and 314-388-9840 in the county.
Read the banner on the form. Lately the application pages have said Heat Up is only helping with Ameren bills and is sending Spire gas customers to partner agencies that still have LIHEAP funds.
Ask for the waiting list. If an agency’s money is gone for now, ask to be put on its list, then dial 2-1-1 for anything else.
Helping a neighbor through a shut-off notice tonight? Send them our guide on how to apply for LIHEAP in Missouri, and keep the St. Louis Help & Assistance Resources hub open for the next call.
If you’re the agency, the church pantry or the contractor who helps families keep the heat on, list it with us so more neighbors facing a shut-off notice can find you.
### LIHEAP: the biggest heating-help program in Missouri
Unlike the charities above, the largest source of heating assistance is federal. It’s a program called LIHEAP (the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program), run in Missouri through the Department of Social Services. (For the full walkthrough, see our guide to how to apply for LIHEAP in Missouri.) It has two parts:
Energy Assistance (EA) - a one-time payment each season toward one heating fuel. On the current state application the most it pays is $326 for natural gas, $318 for electric, and $495 for tank propane. Those caps are adjusted each year.
Energy Crisis Intervention Program (ECIP) - emergency help when you’ve gotten a shut-off notice or already been disconnected. Winter crisis help can be worth up to $800; summer cooling crisis help up to $300.
Who qualifies: Eligibility is based on your household size and income, using Missouri’s income guideline of 60% of the state median income, plus a resource test - generally $3,000 or less in bank, retirement, and investment accounts. The agency counts everyone’s gross income, before taxes, from last month. Here are the monthly limits on the state’s current chart. They are adjusted each year, so check the Benefit Program Income Limits chart on dss.mo.gov before you rule yourself out.
When to apply: If anyone in your home is 60 or older or has a disability, you can apply for heating help starting October 1. Everyone else can apply starting November 1, the same day the Cold Weather Rule begins. Energy Assistance applications are taken through May 31. Winter crisis help opens November 1 for senior and disabled households and December 1 for everyone else.
How to apply: Apply online on the state’s LIHEAP page at dss.mo.gov, or print the application and bring, mail, or fax it to the agency that serves your address. Call 855-373-4636 (855-FSD-INFO) if you’d rather have a paper application mailed to you. Use this season’s form, MO 886-4576. The application changed, and CAASTLC says it can’t accept versions from previous years. Send proof of everyone’s income from last month (anyone already on SNAP can skip it), proof of a Social Security number for everyone in the home, and your current gas and electric bills, plus any shut-off notice. Applications are typically reviewed within about 30 business days - faster if you’re in an active crisis - so don’t wait for the disconnection date to loom.
Where to apply in St. Louis: LIHEAP runs through one agency per area, so send your application to the one that covers your address.
City of St. Louis and Wellston: Urban League of Metropolitan St. Louis, 1408 N. Kingshighway Blvd., 314-615-3632. It takes applications weekdays from 8 a.m. to noon, and a drop box is open from noon to 5 p.m. You can also mail it there.
St. Louis County: Community Action Agency of St. Louis County (CAASTLC), 2709 Woodson Road in Overland, energy line 314-446-4420. Mail it, fax it to 314-446-4480, email it to energyhelp@caastlc.org, or drop it off at Woodson Road or at 26B North Oaks Plaza in Northwoods.
### Help straight from your utility company
Most people skip this step entirely: your own utility company has assistance programs, and many agencies want you to contact your provider before they process an application anyway. Call them first - it can open doors, and sometimes a payment plan alone is enough to keep the heat on.
Learn more directly from each provider: Ameren Missouri energy assistance, Spire assistance programs, and Missouri American Water payment assistance.
### The agencies that take your application in person
If you’d rather sit across from a real person - or you don’t have easy internet access - local social-service agencies handle utility-assistance intake all over the metro. Call ahead to ask about their hours and what to bring; some will ask you to notify your utility company first. A few of the main ones:
Urban League of Metropolitan St. Louis - utility assistance line 314-615-3632; takes LIHEAP applications for the City of St. Louis and Wellston
The Salvation Army - Greater St. Louis - 314-646-3000
Community Action Agency of St. Louis County (CAASTLC) - 314-863-0015 (energy assistance line 314-446-4420); handles both energy and water services and takes LIHEAP applications for St. Louis County
People’s Community Action Corporation - 314-353-1457 (6827 S. Broadway, St. Louis 63111)
Society of St. Vincent de Paul - St. Louis - reachable through 211
Not sure which one covers your ZIP code, or need help you don’t see here? Dial 2-1-1 (or 1-800-427-4626). United Way’s 211 line is free, confidential, staffed 24/7, and can connect you to utility, rent, food, and medical help anywhere in the region - from Lincoln County down to Ste. Genevieve and across the river into Illinois.
Looking for more local resources? A tool like findhelp.org can point you to food, housing, and health programs near you, and you can search the St Louis Near Me Directory for St. Louis businesses and community organizations.
If you run a nonprofit that helps families across the metro keep the heat on, list it with us so more neighbors and customers who need what you do can reach you without fighting a busy line.
### Know your rights: the Missouri Cold Weather Rule
Missouri law puts a seasonal brake on winter shut-offs. Under the Cold Weather Rule, which runs from November 1 through March 31, regulated electric and natural gas utilities can’t disconnect you when the temperature is forecast to drop below 32°F within the next 72 hours. That 72-hour window is new as of 2025 - Senate Bill 4 tripled it from the old 24-hour rule, giving families more breathing room during a cold stretch. (See our full guide to the Missouri Cold Weather Rule and how to stop a winter shutoff.)
Two important limits to understand: on days that aren’t forecast to freeze, staying connected generally means telling the utility you can’t pay in full and signing a payment agreement with an initial payment (it delays disconnection, it doesn’t erase the bill), and it only covers investor-owned utilities regulated by the Missouri Public Service Commission. Municipal utilities, rural electric cooperatives, and truck-delivered propane are not under PSC jurisdiction, so check your provider’s own winter policy if you’re served by one of those.
The PSC’s written rule has two more details worth knowing. First, a LIHEAP pledge for the amount due counts as the payment the utility asks for on a Cold Weather Rule agreement. Second, if someone in your home is 65 or older or has a disability, register with your utility, and renew it by October 1 each year. A registered household with income under 150% of the poverty line that signs a Cold Weather Rule payment plan can’t be cut off for nonpayment from November 1 through March 31, as long as it keeps paying at least half of each bill (or half the plan amount, if that’s less).
If you believe a regulated utility is treating you unfairly, you have somewhere to turn:
Missouri Public Service Commission consumer hotline - 1-800-392-4211
Missouri Attorney General consumer protection - 1-800-392-8222
### When the heat becomes the danger: Cool Down St. Louis
St. Louis summers can be just as deadly as its winters, and the same organization runs a warm-weather counterpart. Cool Down St. Louis - also founded by Gentry Trotter - provides window air-conditioning units and electric-bill help to at-risk seniors, people with disabilities, and critically ill children, in partnership with Ameren. The program reports distributing roughly 25,000 A/C units over the years. If you’re reading this in July instead of January, that’s your door - same website, same phone numbers.
### Are Heat Up St. Louis and Cool Down St. Louis the same organization?
Yes. One nonprofit, Heat-Up St. Louis, Inc., a 501(c)(3) charity, runs both: Heat Up is the winter side and Cool Down St. Louis is its summer program, so the charity you call about a cold radiator in January is the same one you call about a sweltering upstairs bedroom in July. Type CoolDownStLouis.org into a browser and you land on HeatUpStLouis.org, and the hotlines are shared. The charity also works under the names Heat Up Missouri and Cool Down Missouri.
The founder is Gentry W. Trotter, a two-time Emmy-winning producer who spent 24 years as a public relations consultant for a Missouri natural gas company, where he ran community outreach for its customer check-off fund. More than 25 years ago, he and a group of volunteers started Heat-Up St. Louis to reach families that one utility’s program never could, across the river into Illinois and into electric, propane and heating oil bills. He has since stepped down as board president and now serves as interim executive director. The board is all volunteer, and the charity says every donated dollar goes to families because its administrative costs are underwritten.
### Don’t wait for the shut-off date
The single biggest mistake people make is waiting until the power is already off. Every program on this page works better - and some only work - when you reach out before the disconnection date. So here’s the short version to act on today:
Call your utility company and ask about payment plans and assistance.
Apply to Heat Up St. Louis online, and to LIHEAP through myDSS or an agency.
Gather your documents - proof of income, household size, and any disconnection notice.
Dial 2-1-1 if you’re stuck, and follow up if you haven’t heard back in a couple of weeks.
Reaching out is the hard part, and reading this far means you’ve mostly done it. Make the call to your utility company today, and dial 2-1-1 the moment you feel stuck.
More St. Louis help: This guide is part of our St. Louis Help & Assistance Resources hub - one trusted place for housing, food, jobs, health coverage, utility bills, and legal aid, for yourself or for someone you’re helping.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What’s the number to Heat Up St. Louis?
A.  Heat Up St. Louis lists its General Office at 314-657-1599 and a Senior Automated Line at 314-241-7668. The organization asks that you complete the online application at heatupstlouis.org first, then call only if you have a question. If you’re not sure which agency serves your area, the resource hotline is 314-241-0001.
### Q. Is there a Heat Up St. Louis application online?
A.  Yes. The application is filled out online at heatupstlouis.org, with a separate form for each region: St. Louis City, St. Louis County, and Outstate Missouri & Metro East. Have your utility company name, account number, and amount owed ready, and upload proof of income - screenshots are not accepted.
### Q. How do I apply for LIHEAP in Missouri?
A.  Apply online on the state’s LIHEAP page at dss.mo.gov, or send this season’s paper form (MO 886-4576) to your local agency: the Urban League (314-615-3632) for the City of St. Louis and Wellston, or CAASTLC (314-446-4420) for St. Louis County. Call 855-373-4636 (855-FSD-INFO) to get a paper application by mail. Households with someone 60 or older or disabled can apply from October 1, and everyone else from November 1. Reviews take about 30 business days, faster in a crisis, so do not wait for the disconnection date to loom.
### Q. What is the income limit for LIHEAP in Missouri?
A.  It depends on household size. On the state’s current chart, gross monthly income can be up to $2,942 for one person, $3,847 for two, $4,752 for three, and $5,657 for four. That is 60% of Missouri’s state median income, and the limits are adjusted each year, so check the current Benefit Program Income Limits chart on dss.mo.gov before you rule yourself out. You also need $3,000 or less in bank, retirement, and investment accounts.
### Q. Does Ameren Missouri have payment assistance?
A.  Yes, several programs. Keeping Current gives monthly bill credits when you pay on time, Keeping Cool adds up to five $50 credits from May through September, Dollar More can cover up to $600, and New Start Energy Relief offers up to $1,000 for neighbors coming out of homelessness. Veterans and active-duty military can get up to $600; dial 2-1-1. Call 1-800-552-7583 or start at AmerenMissouri.com/EnergyAssistance.
### Q. What are the ways I can get help paying my gas bill in Missouri?
A.  Start with Spire’s DollarHelp, worth up to $1,000 a year toward a past-due gas bill for households up to 300% of poverty. Dial 2-1-1 to reach a DollarHelp agency, or call Spire at 800-887-4173 about payment arrangements. Stack it with LIHEAP through myDSS. Heat Up St. Louis can cover gas when funds allow, but check the banner on its form, which lately has pointed Spire customers to partner agencies.

## When Sunday Night Means Dad Leaves Again: How St. Louis Dads Start Over
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/empowering-dads-how-the-fathers-and-families-support-center-strengthens-communities
The overnight bag is zipped and waiting by the front door. The TV is still going, it’s Sunday, it’s almost six, and nobody in the room wants to be the one who says it’s time. Then the drive back over the Poplar Street Bridge, and the quiet in the car once you’re alone.
If that drive is your Sunday, there’s a free six-week class on the other side of one phone call: 314-333-4170, the Fathers & Families Support Center.
One St. Louis-area teenager, Machil, 19, summed up what those years feel like from the other side, in a story the Fathers & Families Support Center tells on its own site: “I used to hate Sunday nights because it meant Dad had to leave again.” For 14 years his father, Malcome H., was the weekend dad. Nearly $30,000 went to legal fees and child support, and whenever things got tense with the twins’ mother he shut down and stopped talking. He heard about the center during a court proceeding, took its six-week Family Formation class at the East St. Louis site, and learned to keep the conversation going when it got hard. Now Sunday night isn’t goodbye. The twins live with him every other week.
The class that changed it costs $0. So does the family-law help inside it, for child support modifications, visitation and custody, the same fights that ate those court years. If your hours were cut, ask about it early: in Missouri a judge can change only the payments that come due after the other parent is served with the request, and a recalculated amount that differs by 20% or more counts as the kind of change a court looks for.
And if the Sunday visits keep getting canceled, Missouri hands you a tool most dads never hear about: the family access motion. When a parent blocks court-ordered time without good cause, ask the circuit clerk for the state’s simple form. The clerk has to explain how to file it, you don’t need a lawyer, and it costs the regular court filing fee. A judge can order make-up time at least as long as the time you lost, plus a fine of up to $500 paid to you, and the law calls for a decision within 60 days after the other parent is served. Check your own order: Missouri now requires every order that sets or changes custody to spell this right out. In the City, self-represented filings go to the Clyde S. Cahill Courts Building, 10 North Tucker. Illinois runs its own process, so dads on the East St. Louis side should ask the case manager which rules apply.
### What the six weeks actually look like
Ask Malcome what mattered and it isn’t the curriculum. It’s the room: men learning from him, and him learning from them, five days a week. Family Formation is 30 hours of classes and services over six weeks, and you’re not handed a workbook and left alone. Each parent works with a team: a parenting facilitator, a social services case manager, an employment case manager and a family therapist. The class covers parenting and co-parenting, financial literacy, job readiness and, in Malcome’s words on the center’s site, everyday things like cooking and nutrition. The part he credits most is simpler: a room of men learning from each other.
Week four has its own moment. Participants get to browse the center’s clothing closet, stocked with donated suits, jackets, shirts, ties, slacks and shoes, and what fits goes home with them at no cost. The center’s own Family Formation page says the last two weeks are strictly jacket-and-tie, because job interviews are coming, and its outreach coordinator says some participants have never owned a suit before. Graduates then get a year of follow-up support. By the center’s own published count, Family Formation parents paid a combined $5.9 million in child support in a single year.
Your first call, and what happens next
The call takes about a minute. Say: “I’m a dad, I want to get into Family Formation, and I’d like to talk to a case manager.” They take it from there.
Call 314-333-4170 and ask for a case manager. You’ll set an appointment, and the case manager sits down with you to sort out what you need and which class fits. Bring whatever paperwork you have, like a child support order or court papers, so they can see where things stand. Classes start in numbered sessions several times a year, and each one has its own enrollment window that opens about two weeks before the start date, so ask which window is open now. Calls and emails are returned Monday through Friday during business hours, or use the Get Started form at fatherssupportcenter.org.
Behind on child support, or fighting over visitation? That’s part of the program, not a reason to stay away. Family Formation’s legal help covers modifications, visitation and custody. Missouri’s Family Support Division will also review an order every 3 years on request: write to P.O. Box 6790, Jefferson City, MO 65102, or fax 573-635-7545.
Stuck arguing over the schedule? M.A.R.C.H. (marchmediation.org), a Missouri nonprofit, mediates custody and parenting-plan disputes and offers free pre-mediation coaching, so the next conversation with your kids’ mom isn’t in a courtroom.
Three places to take the class: the downtown headquarters at 1601 Olive St.; a room inside St. Peter’s United Church of Christ at 1433 Stein Rd. in Ferguson; or 8601 Washington St. in East St. Louis, where the center points out there’s plenty of lot parking. Classes run Monday through Friday, days or evenings.
Can’t do six weeks? Fathers’ Rap meets Tuesdays and Thursdays, 5 to 7 p.m., at 1601 Olive, with family therapists, social workers and job developers in the room.
Coming home from prison? The Re-Entry Project starts inside, at the Transition Center of St. Louis on North 1st Street and several Missouri prisons, and the center reports that 7% of its graduates go back, against a Missouri average of about 35%.
Know a dad who keeps saying he’ll figure it out alone? The number is 314-333-4170.
### The other doors at 1601 Olive Street
Family Formation is the main door, but the Fathers and Families Support Center runs four more: a job program with a mentor assigned to you, the Re-Entry Project, a youth program for ages 14 to 24, and the Neighborhood Healing Network for families hurt by crime or violence.
### Workforce Development and Career Path Guidance
The Employment Development & Mentoring program pairs each job seeker with a trained mentor and works through mock interviews, resume writing, career coaching and training that leads to a certification and a placement. The center’s figures for 2025: 267 participants got or kept a job, at an average of $18.65 an hour, against a Missouri minimum wage of $13.75.
### Reentry Support for Incarcerated Fathers
For a dad finishing his time at the Missouri Eastern Correctional Center in Pacific, or at the Transition Center of St. Louis on North 1st Street, the work starts before the gate opens. The Re-Entry Project, run with the Missouri Department of Corrections, brings parenting and relationship classes, job-readiness training, housing help and job placement inside, so there’s a plan waiting on the outside. The center reports that its graduates go back to prison at an average rate of 7%, against a Missouri average of about 35%.
### Direct Services for Fathers, Youth, and Mothers
The center’s door opens wider than the word “fathers” suggests. Support reaches the youth and mothers in a dad’s life too, because a father’s progress rarely happens in isolation. Services run from relationship training to plain, practical guidance, whatever a family needs to steady itself.
Here’s a look at some of the ways they help:
Skill Building: Learn practical skills for employment and personal growth.
Mentorship: Connect with experienced individuals who can guide you.
Relationship Support: Get help improving connections with your children and their mothers.
Resource Connection: Access information and support for housing, health, and other needs.
The center meets fathers where they are and builds from there, and its footprint shows up across the St. Louis organizations it works alongside.
### Why St. Louis employers hire these dads
Community Impact and Partnership Initiatives
### Fostering Strong Families as Societal Cornerstones
Strong families tend to produce stronger communities, and the Fathers and Families Support Center builds on that link deliberately. Keep fathers anchored in the family unit and the surrounding blocks hold steadier too. A supported dad sends a ripple outward, first to his kids, then to the street, then to the whole neighborhood.
### Business Partnerships for Workforce and Community Growth
Employers have real leverage here. A company that partners with the Fathers and Families Support Center helps fathers gain skills and land better jobs, and it gets something back: a steadier, more reliable workforce and a stronger local economy. Call it enlightened self-interest rather than charity. Businesses looking to connect with that talent can start with the directory of local business listings.
Here’s a look at how businesses can get involved:
Sponsorship Tiers: Different levels of support, like funding training for one dad for a year or contributing to entire programs.
Employee Engagement: Encouraging employees to volunteer or mentor fathers in the program.
Workforce Integration: Partnering to offer internships or job opportunities to fathers completing training.
### Allyship Programs for Enhanced Family Relationships
The Center looks past job skills to the relationships around a dad. Its allyship programs help fathers become better partners to the mothers of their children, sharing the load and respecting each other’s role at home. The idea is a working team inside the family, not two adults negotiating from opposite corners.
That relationship work often anchors everything else, long before a new paycheck does.

### A Father of the Year, and the numbers behind him
### Inspiring Journeys of Fatherhood Transformation
What does the work look like in practice? Often it looks like a dad who arrived unsure of himself and now runs his household with confidence. Antonio Davis, the center’s 2026 Father of the Year, earned that recognition for exactly this kind of growth, achieved with the center’s support. His story doesn’t end with him. The changes a father makes ripple out to his kids, his co-parent, and the people around him.
### Measurable Improvements in Family and Community Well-being
The impact reaches past individual stories. The Center tracks its outcomes, and the trend points the same direction: more involved fathers, kids doing better in school, families carrying less stress. That steadiness acts like a cornerstone for the block. Employers notice it too. A worker whose home life is stable tends to show up, focus, and stay, which is worth as much to the business as it is to the family.
Here's a look at some of the outcomes:
Increased Father Involvement: Dads participating in programs report spending more quality time with their children.
Improved Family Relationships: Partners often note better communication and a more supportive home environment.
Enhanced Employability: Many fathers find better jobs or advance in their careers after completing training.
### The Fathers and Families Support Center's Proven Effectiveness
The recognition isn’t self-declared. Experts and community leaders point to the Center’s consistency and its results. Timing is part of it: the right support arrives when a father actually needs it, at a job search or during a hard stretch at home. The Center also connects local employers with fathers who finish its job training, and in its most recent annual report those graduates averaged $18.65 an hour.

### What your kids get when you stay
Addressing Root Causes Through Fatherhood Engagement
Too many programs treat symptoms and leave the source untouched. Involved fathers change that math. When a dad is present and engaged, he addresses several problems at once, at the root rather than the surface. Being there for the kids is a big piece of it. The bigger piece is a family unit sturdy enough to hold together when life gets rough.
### Combating Family Instability and Its Societal Effects
A stable home underpins a healthy society, and the reverse holds just as firmly. When fathers are absent or checked out, families tend to struggle, and the effects spread, from a child’s grades to their long-term well-being. Supporting fathers attacks that instability directly. Fewer kids grow up without a consistent male role model, and research ties that consistency to better outcomes.
Reduced likelihood of children experiencing poverty.
Lower rates of juvenile delinquency.
Improved academic achievement for children.
### Cultivating Essential Character Traits in Fathers
Showing up is step one. Showing up with the right skills is the harder, more useful part. Fatherhood programs spend real time on character: responsibility, patience, steady communication, the knack for solving a problem instead of escalating it. Those traits carry past the living room. A dad who learns to defuse a conflict at home tends to handle one at work better too, and the family, the job, and the block all gain from it.
### Reducing Crime and Improving Worker Productivity
The connection is less of a leap than it sounds. Children with engaged fathers are less likely to end up in the justice system, a straight gain for public safety. And a father who has steadied his own life usually brings that to the job, showing up reliable and focused. That lifts the local economy and the workplace at the same time, and it all traces back to supporting dads in the role.
Fix the root and the surface problems tend to ease with it. Engaged fathers make families and communities stronger, and that is the entire premise the center runs on. It is also why the programs stack employment, reentry, and relationship help together instead of treating each one in isolation.
### How to Get Started at the Fathers & Families Support Center
Call 314-333-4170 or fill out the Get Started form at fatherssupportcenter.org. The headquarters is downtown at 1601 Olive Street, and services run at several locations around St. Louis. Moms are welcome too: the flagship Family Formation program enrolls men and women.
Family Formation is the big commitment, and the center doesn’t hide it. It’s a no-cost, six-week, Monday-through-Friday program, with day and evening classes, covering parenting and co-parenting, family therapy, job skills, health, legal help and substance-use prevention, followed by a year of follow-up support. Can’t take six weeks of weekdays? Fathers’ Rap, a peer support group at 1601 Olive, meets Tuesdays and Thursdays from 5 to 7 p.m. and covers child support, custody and visitation, relationships and work. That’s a slot a dad can make straight off a shift, still in his work boots.
The other doors: Employment Development & Mentoring pairs job seekers with trained mentors and works toward placement; the Re-Entry Project runs with the Missouri Department of Corrections at the Transition Center of St. Louis; and the Youth Leadership & Development Program mentors young people ages 14 to 24. Since its first class more than 25 years ago, the center has worked with nearly 23,000 fathers, and it reports a 7% recidivism rate for its graduates, against a Missouri average of about 35%.
### Know a dad who needs this?
The Fathers and Families Support Center turns uncertain dads into the role models their kids need, steadies families, and leaves whole neighborhoods better off. A more present father, a calmer household, a more connected block: that is the sequence, and it starts with support. You can add to it. Volunteer an hour, send a donation, or point one father toward the door. Any of those keeps the work going and helps build stronger families, one dad at a time.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What types of family support services are available?
A.  In St. Louis, the Fathers & Families Support Center alone offers parenting and co-parenting classes, family therapy, job training and placement, legal assistance, substance-use prevention, reentry help after prison, youth mentoring for ages 14 to 24 and a twice-weekly support group for dads. For food, housing or utility help on top of that, dial 2-1-1 to reach United Way’s referral line.
### Q. What support groups are available in St. Louis?
A.  For fathers, Fathers’ Rap meets Tuesdays and Thursdays from 5 to 7 p.m. at the Fathers & Families Support Center, 1601 Olive Street, with talk on child support, custody and visitation, relationships and work. The center’s Neighborhood Healing Network also runs monthly trauma workshops for people hurt by crime or violence. For other kinds of groups, 2-1-1 keeps a current list.
### Q. What are the legal rights of a father in Missouri?
A.  If you’re married to the mother, you’re presumed the legal father. If not, paternity has to be established first, by both parents signing an acknowledgment of paternity or through a court or child support order. Once it is, Missouri law presumes that equal or roughly equal parenting time is in the child’s best interest, though a judge can find otherwise.
### Q. How do I contact child support services in Missouri?
A.  Call the Missouri Department of Social Services’ Child Support Customer Service line at 866-313-9960 about a case with an order, or 800-859-7999 for general information. You can also manage a case through the Child Support Customer Portal at dss.mo.gov. The state program serves both parents, including help establishing paternity and changing an existing order.
### Q. How to cope with being a father?
A.  Don’t do it alone. Talk with other dads who’ve been there, like the men at Fathers’ Rap, keep a simple routine with your kids even on hard weeks, and look after your own sleep and health. If stress turns into hopelessness, call or text 988, the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, any time. Asking for help is part of the job.
### Q. What kind of job help does the center offer?
A.  Its Employment Development & Mentoring program covers job readiness, resume writing and interview coaching, occupational training, financial education and job placement, with trained mentors for career guidance. It shows up in paychecks: in its most recent annual report, the center says 267 participants gained or kept a job, at an average of $18.65 an hour.

💥Organizations, advocacy groups, and community partners are welcome to link to and share this blog with their members, clients, and friends if they believe it will help more women in St. Louis find safe shelter, support, and local resources.
Leaving an unsafe situation often happens fast, with no time to plan. If you’re in St. Louis and need a women’s shelter or somewhere to turn, this guide lays out what’s available and how to reach it.
Below you’ll find the services these programs offer, who they serve, and the numbers to call first.
### Key Takeaways
St. Louis offers various shelters and resources for women, providing emergency housing, safety planning, and crisis intervention.
Accessing help is made easier through directories, food assistance programs, and specific support for immigrants and refugees.
Specialized services like counseling, mental health support, and job training are available to aid in recovery and independence.
