### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the difference between an HOA and an association?
A.  A homeowners association (HOA) is mandatory — membership and dues are a binding condition of owning the property, and it can enforce rules and fees. A neighborhood association is voluntary; it advocates and organizes but can’t force you to join or fine you. Most of the City of St. Louis has voluntary neighborhood associations, while mandatory HOAs are more common in newer county subdivisions.
### Q. Is a neighborhood association a nonprofit?
A.  Many are. Neighborhood associations often incorporate as nonprofit organizations so they can hold a bank account, accept donations and grants, and operate formally — but not all do, and it isn’t required to function. Smaller or newer groups may operate informally with volunteer leaders and optional dues before ever filing for nonprofit status.
### Q. How do I find my neighborhood association in St. Louis?
A.  Enter your address on the City of St. Louis neighborhood lookup at stlouis-mo.gov to find your neighborhood, ward, and contacts, then check the city’s Neighborhood Organization Registry and its list of association websites and social media. SLACO (slaco-mo.org) and Nextdoor help too. If the info is outdated, email NAM@stlouis-mo.gov to update it.
### Q. What ward am I in in St. Louis?
A.  The easiest way to find your ward is the address lookup on stlouis-mo.gov — entering your address returns your neighborhood, your ward, and your local officials in one place. Knowing your ward matters because your alderperson is a key ally for neighborhood issues, from vacant buildings to traffic calming to city-service requests.
### Q. Can you legally refuse to join an HOA?
A.  Generally no — if a property is already governed by a mandatory HOA, membership and dues run with the deed and you accept them when you buy. You can avoid HOA obligations by buying a property that isn’t in one, which describes most homes in the City of St. Louis, where neighborhood associations are voluntary rather than binding.
### Q. What is the difference between an HOA and a neighborhood association?
A.  Membership and power. An HOA is tied to your deed, membership is mandatory, dues are enforceable and it can place a lien. A neighborhood association is voluntary, has no legal authority over your property, and works by organizing rather than by rule.
### Q. What is the purpose of a neighborhood association?
A.  To give a block collective voice — on zoning cases, city services, traffic and safety — and to organize the things nobody owns individually, like clean-ups and events. Its power is attention and turnout, not enforcement.
### Q. Can you refuse to join an HOA?
A.  Generally not, if the covenants run with the land; buying the property means accepting them. That is the key difference from a neighborhood association, which you can join or ignore freely. Read the covenants before closing, not after.
### Q. What are the pros and cons of a homeowners association?
A.  Pros: maintained common areas, consistent standards, and a mechanism for dealing with a genuinely bad neighbor. Cons: dues that can rise, rules on what you may do with your own property, and enforcement that varies enormously with whoever is on the board that year.

## The Times Called It Drab: Where to Eat in Maplewood, MO, Block by Block
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/where-to-eat-in-maplewood-mo-a-local-s-guide-to-st-louis-s-tastiest-small-town-2026
“Drab.” That’s what The New York Times called this strip of Manchester Road, in the same write-up that named Robin, at 7268 Manchester, one of America’s best restaurants. Argue with it from a two-top at Robin. The Dorothy’s Potatoes arrive crowned with sour cream, herbs and trout roe, the roe pops cold and salty against the hot potato, and outside the window Manchester Road goes dark blue. Down the block, Bolyard’s fries its potatoes in beef tallow, and Acero has been rolling house-made pasta on the same street for nearly 20 years. Chef Alec Schingel argued with the Times too.
Maplewood is its own town of about 8,000 people, just outside the city line in St. Louis County, and it’s tiny: 1.56 square miles by the Census count, so the whole town would fit inside Forest Park, about two square miles, with room to spare. The city line hasn’t moved since 1876, and the city’s own history says it once ran straight through the old Maplewood Theater, projection booth in Maplewood, screen in St. Louis. Everything worth eating fits into a few walkable blocks of Manchester Road and Sutton Boulevard, almost all of it locally owned. Park once and eat your way around the world on foot.
### Why Maplewood is St. Louis’s tastiest few blocks
Here’s the brag nobody hangs on a sign. In a storefront at 7458 Manchester, Side Project Brewing ages saisons and wild ales in barrels, and RateBeer, weighing more than 4.2 million reviews of over 33,000 brewers, ranked it the No. 2 brewer in the world, behind only Vermont’s Hill Farmstead, Feast Magazine reported. The owner called it “our tiny brewing operation here in Maplewood.” Hold the cold stemmed glass up to the window and the pour glows amber; that’s what an affordable inner-ring lease buys a brewer, a chef or a butcher with something to prove. Text that to the friend who thinks good beer means a road trip. Here’s the route, from first coffee to last pour.
### Coffee first, with cats underfoot
At Mauhaus Cat Café & Lounge, St. Louis’s original cat café, an adoptable cat settles across your lap and your latte goes cold while you decide whether you’re allowed to move. A few doors down, La Cosecha Coffee Roasters roasts its beans on-site, so the room smells like the roaster before you even order.
### Duck-ham DLTs and tallow fries
Break the yolk on The Blue Duck’s DLT and it runs into the smoked duck ham and house sourdough; that sandwich, and a daily brunch, are why the room fills on weekends. At Bolyard’s Meat & Provisions, a whole-animal butcher shop with a sandwich counter, the fries are cooked in beef tallow and leave honest grease spots on the paper. Want lighter? BLK MKT Eats rolls burrito-sized sushi and poke bowls, and Revel Kitchen does gluten-free bowls and cold-pressed juice.
### Robin, Acero and the dinner blocks
At Robin, chef Alec Schingel’s four-course prix fixe is short enough that, as St. Louis Magazine’s critic put it, a table of four can cover the whole menu, so pass the plates and fight over the last spoonful of trout roe. A few doors away, Acero has rolled its pasta in house for nearly 20 years, and the bowls arrive steaming beside a long wine list. At Robata, the tonkotsu broth fogs your glasses before the robata-grilled skewers arrive, and at Michael’s Bar & Grill the braised lamb shank comes apart under a fork, next to the moussaka.
Booking Robin: reservations open on Resy 60 days out, on a rolling basis, and a James Beard finalist nod for Best New Restaurant means they go fast, so set a reminder. Missed it? The bar takes walk-ins and serves the full menu. Dinner runs Tuesday through Saturday, 5 to 10; a no-show can cost $25 a guest; and corkage is $40, waived if you also buy a bottle off the list.
### Pibil, khao soi and Memphis fried chicken
Sabroso Cocina Mexicana brings chef Miguel Pintor’s Yucatán-style cochinita pibil, the achiote-red pork the Yucatán traditionally roasts in banana leaves, plus birria and a full bar. Thai Table pours khao soi, the northern Thai curry noodle soup that traditionally arrives under a nest of crispy fried noodles, and Gus’s World Famous Fried Chicken delivers the Memphis-born, spicy-crisp kind that leaves your fingertips stinging.
### Side Project and the barrel-aged pour
Maplewood is a genuine craft-beer destination. Side Project - both the Brewing tasting room and the Side Project Cellar - pours nationally acclaimed saisons and barrel-aged ales. Schlafly Bottleworks is the brewpub home of St. Louis’s original craft brewery, with pizza, beer-cheese soup, and weekend brunch. Catch a game with loaded tots at The Post Sports Bar & Grill, or settle in with comfort food and cheese curds at The Crow’s Nest.
### A few more stops worth knowing
Maplewood keeps rewarding the wanderer, so leave room for these. Living Room Coffee & Kitchen on Sutton is a family-owned café roasting its own beans with a full breakfast-and-lunch menu - a calmer alternative when La Cosecha is packed. Foundation Grounds (now also branded the Maplewood Deli & Coffeehouse) pairs organic coffee with a deli counter and breakfast burritos. Coffee is deep enough here to deserve its own map, and our guide to Maplewood coffee shops goes shop by shop. And between courses, Vom Fass lets you taste and fill your own bottles of imported olive oils, aged balsamics, and small-batch spirits - a browse-worthy stop that makes an easy gift.
Walked home past a porch that needs a new roof? Here’s the whole home-services map.
### How to plan your Maplewood crawl
The trick to a great Maplewood day is treating it as one long, unhurried grazing session rather than a single sit-down meal. Start with coffee at La Cosecha, Living Room, or Foundation Grounds. Graze mid-day - a Blue Duck sandwich, a Bolyard’s counter plate, a sushi burrito from BLK MKT - so you leave room to keep going. Break up the eating with browsing at The Book House or Vom Fass, which is half the charm of a walkable district. Then anchor the evening with a proper dinner (Robin if you planned ahead, Acero, Robata, or Sabroso if you didn’t) and a nightcap flight at Side Project. Because it’s all within a few blocks, you can adjust on the fly - follow the smell of something good, and you won’t go wrong.
### Parking and getting around
One of Maplewood’s quiet advantages is that you really can park once. There’s free street parking along Manchester Road and Sutton Boulevard and a few small public lots, and the whole restaurant core is an easy, flat walk end to end. Weekend evenings get busy, so arrive a little early or be ready to circle a block; once you’re parked, though, you’re set for the night. The district is also an easy hop from Kirkwood, Webster Groves, the Hill, and the city’s southwest neighborhoods, which is part of why it draws such a mixed, food-loving crowd - and why reservations at the marquee rooms are worth making in advance. If you’re coming from farther out, the district also sits right off Interstate 44 and Highway 40, so it’s an easy detour on the way home from downtown or the airport - another reason a “quick coffee in Maplewood” has a way of turning into the whole evening.
Hungry for more? Browse the Food & Dining listings in the St Louis Near Me Directory to find independent restaurants across the metro.
If you’re the kitchen, the coffee counter or the little bakery on these blocks, this one’s for you. The Gold plan puts your menu, hours and photos in front of more customers who park once and graze.
### How one small town got this good
Maplewood’s food scene didn’t happen by accident. It’s a small, affordable inner-ring suburb with a walkable historic main street - exactly the kind of place where an ambitious chef can take a lease they couldn’t afford in Clayton and a butcher or baker can build a following one neighbor at a time. Over the last decade that combination drew a critical mass of independent, owner-operated spots, and success there bred more of it: a great butcher next to a great bakery next to a great brewery makes the whole strip a destination, so the next talented person wants in too. The result is a district with almost no chains and an unusual density of James Beard-caliber cooking in a few flat blocks. It’s the same virtuous cycle you see in the city’s best food neighborhoods, just concentrated into a town you can cross on foot in fifteen minutes - which is exactly why it punches so far above its size.
That local-ownership DNA is also why the food tastes like somewhere. The people cooking here mostly live here; the menus reflect real heritage (Yucatán, northeastern Thai, Greek, modern Midwestern) rather than a corporate playbook; and the same faces are behind the counter year after year. When you eat in Maplewood, your money stays in Maplewood - and you can usually thank the owner on your way out.
### More than restaurants
Part of what makes a Maplewood evening work is that the eating is woven through with browsing and small pleasures, so it never feels like a food march. Duck into The Book House for an hour among the stacks, taste your way through oils and spirits at Vom Fass, pet an adoptable cat over coffee at Mauhaus, or just window-shop the independent storefronts between bites. The district hosts seasonal events and a genuinely neighborly street life, and because everything is so close together, plans stay flexible: a coffee can turn into lunch, lunch into a browse, a browse into dinner and a nightcap, all without ever moving the car. That easy, unscripted rhythm - eat a little, walk a little, discover something - is the real reason locals keep coming back, and it’s what a strip mall can never replicate.
### Maplewood by craving
Know what you’re in the mood for? Here’s the shorthand. Coffee: La Cosecha, Living Room, Foundation Grounds. Breakfast all day: Living Room Coffee & Kitchen, which roasts its own beans. A great sandwich: The Blue Duck’s DLT or a Bolyard’s counter plate. Global flavors: Sabroso (Mexican), Thai Table (Thai), Robata (Japanese), Michael’s (Greek). Special-occasion dinner: Robin, Acero. Craft beer: Side Project, Schlafly Bottleworks. Casual and comfort: The Crow’s Nest, The Post, Gus’s fried chicken, Revel’s gluten-free bowls. Something different: a latte with cats at Mauhaus or a tasting at Vom Fass. Whatever the craving, it’s almost certainly within a three-block walk - and our directory guide to where to eat in Maplewood lists the addresses for the strip’s marquee stops. That range is the whole point: a group that can never agree on one cuisine can still park in Maplewood and each get exactly what they want, then meet back up for a beer - which makes it one of the easiest places in the metro to feed a crowd with different tastes.
### Make a day of it
The beauty of Maplewood is that the food sits shoulder-to-shoulder with browsing. Wander into The Book House - a beloved shop with hundreds of thousands of new, used, and rare titles - between courses, and the afternoon takes care of itself. If this walkable, independent food scene is your speed, you’ll also love our guide to eating your way through South Grand, the city’s International District.
Maplewood is one chapter in a much bigger story - see our look at St. Louis food culture, where flavor tells a story.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Where is Maplewood, and is it walkable?
A.  Maplewood is a small city on the southwest edge of St. Louis, centered on Manchester Road and Sutton Boulevard. Its restaurants, bakeries, and breweries are clustered within a few blocks, so you can park once and explore on foot.
### Q. Is Maplewood considered St. Louis City?
A.  No. Maplewood is its own city in St. Louis County, with its own mayor, council and city hall at 7601 Manchester Road, and about 8,000 residents. It borders the City of St. Louis, which is why it feels like part of town, and some business addresses still read St. Louis, MO 63143.
### Q. Where do locals eat in St. Louis?
A.  Wherever they can park once and graze. Maplewood is a good example: locals walk Manchester and Sutton for a Blue Duck sandwich, a Bolyard’s counter plate or a Side Project pint instead of driving to a chain. The same pattern holds on South Grand, The Hill and Cherokee Street, where independents outnumber franchises.
### Q. What food is associated with St. Louis?
A.  Toasted ravioli, gooey butter cake, Provel-topped St. Louis-style pizza, pork steaks and frozen custard are the classics, and our guide to the dishes this city actually invented tells the backstory. Maplewood shows the next chapter: whole-animal butchery at Bolyard’s and modern Midwestern cooking at Robin.
### Q. What is considered the best restaurant in St. Louis?
A.  There’s no single answer, but recent James Beard lists make a fair shortlist: Vicia has been a nominee for Outstanding Restaurant, and Maplewood’s Robin a finalist for Best New Restaurant. For the wider field by neighborhood and budget, see our local’s guide to where to eat in St. Louis.

## The Dog Pond Is Gone, and One St. Louis Dog Park Costs $30 or $80
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/the-best-dog-parks-in-st-louis-2026-a-local-guide-for-every-corner-of-the-metro
A dog named Red loved the diving board at Broemmelsiek Park. A ball went out over the water, Red ran the board and went in after it with a splash, his owner, Jamie Kelly, told KMOV. Officials decided to remove the pond, and crews drained it.
For 17 years it was the dog pond at the Defiance park, an acre-sized splash of water. Then toxic blue-green algae kept shutting it. “Sometimes it’s closed a week, sometimes, like this year, it’s been closed three months,” county parks director Ryan Graham said at the time. The county gave up: crews drained the pond and started hauling out years of mud, with plans to fill it in and plant grass.
Defiance still earns the drive. The county describes the nearly 5-acre area with “a covered shelter and grove of shade trees,” and there is no charge to use it. Throw an old towel over the back seat for the muddy ride home, and bring the one thing the county asks for: your dog’s updated immunization record.
### Where is the dog lake coming back?
The splash is coming back. On 68 acres north of New Melle, the late Mary and David Wolk trained golden retrievers. They donated the land, and St. Charles County is now designing what it calls the biggest dog park in Missouri: Sundust Preserve, with some 50 acres where dogs can “run free, chase frisbees or jump in a lake.” “They weren’t born on a leash,” Parks Director Ryan Graham says. Construction “could begin as soon as this winter.”
### Why does one Creve Coeur gate cost $30 or $80?
Punch in the code, hear the latch give, and two acres of big-dog room in Conway Park open up in front of you. At Creve Coeur Dog Park that entry code comes in the mail from the city, and what you paid for it depends on your street address. Same first dog, same gate: $30 a year if you live in Creve Coeur, $80 if you don’t.
The calendar flips it again. Sign up in Creve Coeur during a July heat wave, shirt stuck to your back, and the city cuts you a break: membership fees paid July 1 through December 31 are prorated 50 percent. Try that late start at Southwest City Dog Park on Hampton or Lucas Park Dog Park downtown and you pay full price, because neither one prorates.
### Pea soup or spilled paint? Leash on, walk away.
A still pond on a hot afternoon, a skin of green on top, and your dog already leaning into the leash: that is the moment to turn around. Missouri’s Department of Natural Resources says a toxic bloom can make the water “look like pea soup” or the surface look “as if paint has been spilled on it,” and as the bacteria die they can give off an odor like rotting plants. Your dog won’t care how it looks or smells. Pets can get very sick and die within hours to days after swallowing the toxins, and a dog can get sick just from licking its fur after touching the scum.
If your dog gets in anyway, rinse it with fresh water right away, before the licking starts, and call your vet.
### Who do you call before the leash comes off the hook?
Creve Coeur, at 314-432-6000. Press zero for the operator between 8 a.m. and 5 p.m., pay by phone, and email your dog’s rabies, Bordetella and spay or neuter papers. Then listen for the mail truck: the city mails back the gate code and a tag for your dog to wear, typically within one day of receipt.
Going free instead? Call the St. Charles County rainout line at 636-707-0011 first to check the park is open before the dog hops in.
### Which park stays open all night?
Your shift ends at midnight, the dog has been pacing by the door since dinner, and downtown at St. Charles Street and 13th the gate still opens: Lucas Park Dog Park says it “is open 24/7 year round.” Members only, and blunt about it: “No tag, No admittance, No exceptions.” Big and little dogs share one yard, so the dachshund and the shepherd chase the same ball.
“There is no separation of big dogs and little dogs,” the park says, so watch the play closely. Membership is $80 a year for the first dog and $40 each for a second and third. Retractable leashes are not permitted, outside sanctioned events no more than 25 dogs may be inside at once, and the board “does have the final say if a dog is a good fit.” Lucas is honest about who should apply: “The dog park is not a place to find out if your dog will be aggressive or not.” The rules even cover the humans: “Having a bad day? Go home, come back later.”
### A gate in a Soulard alley
You find Frenchtown Dog Park by turning into an alley: “The entrance to the park is in the alley behind the intersection of 10th Street & Emmet,” the park says. Park on Emmet or a nearby street, and don’t block the neighbors’ garages. Inside is over 3/4 of an acre of fenced green, which the association calls one of the largest fully fenced green spaces in the city, open 6 a.m. to 9 p.m. every day.
The minimum annual donation is $60 for the first dog and $20 for each additional dog, which the park points out is “just $5 per month.” Bring Rabies, Bordetella and DHLPP records (current titer results are accepted), and a puppy must be at least 6 months old. Then comes the hard part. One of the park’s own FAQs asks, “I just submitted my application, can I bring my dog to the park in 15 minutes?” Its answer: the park is “typically able to process applications within 48 business hours.” Its liability insurance rules out day passes, and there are no trials. Write to membership@frenchtowndogpark.com.
### Why does the grass at Southwest City get a spring break?
A dog flat on its back, legs in the air, rolling in cool grass: that is what the members at Southwest City Dog Park are protecting. They say their “pooches love to run on and roll in the grass,” the turf takes very heavy foot and paw traffic, and the soil is heavily compacted by season’s end, so each spring they excavate the busiest spots, aerate, fertilize and seed, “Closing in late March and reopening around June 1.” The park sits in Willmore Park at 7351 Hampton, next to a ball field and directly across from Lake #1, and it closes Tuesdays from 8 a.m. to noon during mowing season.
The harder wait is for a spot. Registrations were temporarily closed when we checked, with a waitlist that emails you the moment they reopen, so check the park’s membership page first. When they open, a first dog is $70 for a city resident and $80 for a non-city resident, with vet-administered rabies and Bordetella proof, a signed waiver and a solo photo of each dog. Don’t ask for a test run: the park’s FAQ answers “Can I try out the dog park before I pay?” with a flat “No,” citing City Ordinance 66595. Questions go to the message line at 314-567-2012.
### Which free county park suits a small or shy dog?
Out in Wentzville, Quail Ridge Park gives little dogs their own side. The county lists a 2.5-acre area with “two separate areas for large and small dogs, covered shelter, and water available near the parking lot.” Veterans Tribute Park on Kisker Road in St. Charles splits its 3-acre area the same way, and its water is outside the main fence, so fill the bowl before you go in. Like Broemmelsiek, both are free.
The county’s dog park rules: a limit of three dogs per person, no children under 8 inside the off-leash area, no food, treats or glass, and no puppies under four months. Doggie bags are provided inside the parks. Use them, because the county says dog feces are one of the most common carriers of hookworms, roundworms and parvo, and pet waste washes into storm drains, creeks and rivers.
### Leave the treats in the car at Creve Coeur
A pocket full of biscuits is a problem here. Inside the Creve Coeur fence, the city’s dog park rules ban “Alcoholic beverages, food, dog treats, rawhide or glass containers.” Pinch, spike and choke collars come off before the fenced area, and if your dog digs, you fill the hole. All dogs must be spayed or neutered, puppies under six months stay out, no children under ten are allowed, and the person handling the dog must be 16. Dogs smaller than 30 pounds get their own half-acre. Prefer to sign up in person? The Government Center at 300 N. New Ballas Road sells memberships on weekdays, by card or check, and cash is not accepted.
Out west, Queeny Park has the Tails and Trails Dog Park; check St. Louis County’s park page for its current rules before you drive out. Dog people will like the history: the American Kennel Club once ran its Museum of the Dog in the park’s Jarville House, before the museum returned to New York.
### Which parks are free, and which charge at the gate?
In North County the fee drops to single digits. Slide your dog’s rabies and DHLPP records across the counter at the JFK or JJE community center, pay $8 a dog if you live in Florissant or $14 if you don’t, and the fenced off-leash area in Duchesne Park is yours on a permit that is good until December 31.
Some gates swing open for any vaccinated dog; others stay shut until your paperwork clears. St. Charles County’s three dog parks, Broemmelsiek, Quail Ridge and Veterans Tribute, charge nothing, though dogs must have an updated immunization record. The rest charge, and the first-dog prices run like this: Florissant $8 for a resident, Creve Coeur $30 for a resident, Frenchtown a $60 minimum donation, Southwest City $70 for a city resident, and Lucas $80.
If you’re still testing whether your dog even likes a crowd, start free in St. Charles County. Frenchtown says it is unable to offer day passes or trials, and Southwest City’s answer to a try-before-you-pay request is no.
### How do St. Louis seasons change a dog’s park day?
Summer pavement and dark turf soak up heat, so press the back of your hand to the ground before your dog’s pads find out the hard way. Go early or late in the heat, carry more water than you think you need, and watch for heavy panting. Shade matters: the grove of shade trees at Broemmelsiek is the place to be on a sticky afternoon.
Spring is the season of closed gates. Southwest City shuts for its reseeding from late March, and it also closes for wet weather when the grounds are too saturated for play. In winter, wipe your dog’s paws after walks on salted streets so the salt isn’t licked off later. Fall is the easy stretch: cooler mornings, dry grass, and a dog that wants to run until it drops in the back seat.
### Where is a dog actually allowed off-leash?
The grass looks inviting and the trail looks empty, but in the city the rule is clear. The City of St. Louis Department of Health says the city’s code requires dogs to be leashed on a public street, park or other public place, on a leash no more than six feet long, and the only exception is a City-designated dog exercise park. In St. Charles County, dogs must stay on-leash outside the dog park facility, and at Creve Coeur every dog stays leashed until it is inside the fenced area.
So the fenced park is where your dog gets to be a dog. Pick the one that fits your dog and your weekend, unclip at the inner gate, and let them run where they’re actually allowed to.
Nothing to do with dogs - the Central West End is worth an afternoon.
### What should your dog’s first park trip look like?
And for the day an old dog finally stops pulling toward the gate, here’s what pet cemetery burial in St. Louis involves.
Records in hand, water jug full, leash on until the inner gate clicks shut behind you. Go at a quiet hour the first time, so your dog meets a few dogs instead of a pack at the fence line. Use the small-dog side if your pup is little, timid or older. Watch your dog, not your phone, and step in early if play tips from bouncy to stiff and silent. Leave while your dog still wants more; Lucas asks members to “leave promptly once your dog is finished” when others are waiting to come in. And always pick up after your dog. A few good habits from every owner are the whole reason a good dog park stays good.
Need a groomer, trainer, vet, boarder or daycare for the rest of your dog’s week? Browse the Pet Services listings in the St Louis Near Me directory.
If you’re the groomer, the trainer or the one-person crew behind a dog business, list your business with us and turn more of the regulars at your neighborhood dog park into customers.
### What are the ground rules before you go?
At the gate, the first thing a membership park wants is your dog’s vaccination record, and the rest differs by park. On spaying and neutering, Creve Coeur says all dogs must be spayed or neutered, Lucas requires it for any dog after the age of 1 year, Southwest City calls it recommended but not required, and Frenchtown doesn’t require it but highly encourages it. On kids, Creve Coeur allows no children under ten, while Lucas, Southwest City and the St. Charles County parks allow none under 8. Mind the small-dog and large-dog separations where they exist, and check each park’s own page before you go, because fees and hours change.
Still looking for the dog to bring to these parks? See our guide to St. Louis pet rescues and adoption.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Do St. Louis dog parks require a membership?
A.  Many do. Creve Coeur is open to registered members only, Florissant admits only dogs registered with its dog park, Southwest City is a membership-based park, Lucas is for active members only, and Frenchtown’s insurance requires a paid membership. The free exception is St. Charles County, whose three dog parks charge nothing as long as your dog has an updated immunization record.
### Q. Are dogs allowed at Forest Park St. Louis?
A.  Yes, on a leash: Forest Park Forever says that per City ordinance, pets must be on leashes no more than six feet long, held by a responsible party capable of controlling the animal. Pick up after your dog, and save off-leash play for a fenced dog park.
### Q. Are dog parks good for dogs?
A.  For a healthy, vaccinated, social dog, yes - a fenced park gives the kind of flat-out running a sidewalk walk can’t. They’re a poor fit for fearful or reactive dogs, puppies that haven’t finished their shots, and dogs that guard toys. Lucas Park Dog Park puts it plainly: “Off leash does not mean out of control.” Match the park to your dog, not the other way around.
### Q. How long is enough time at the dog park?
A.  Long enough for a good run, short enough to end on a happy note. Keep the first visit short and leave while your dog is still having fun. Heavy panting, ignoring you, or play that keeps getting rougher all mean it’s time to go, and in a St. Louis summer, go early or late and keep it shorter. If others are waiting at the gate, Lucas asks members to be mindful of how long they stay.
### Q. What diseases are commonly found in dog parks?
A.  Dog feces are one of the most common carriers of hookworms, roundworms, tapeworms, whipworms, parvo and salmonellosis. Frenchtown’s required DHLPP shot covers canine distemper, hepatitis, parvovirus, parainfluenza and leptospirosis. Current vaccines, parasite prevention, and skipping shared puddles cut the risk a lot.
### Q. What do vets say about dog parks?
A.  Ask your own vet, and bring the park’s vaccine list to the appointment, because the park will want the vet’s paperwork anyway. Southwest City, for one, wants proof of current vet-administered rabies and Bordetella vaccines with the vet’s name, the date, the dog’s name and the vaccine on it. Wait until a puppy’s shots are finished, stay on parasite prevention, and watch your dog instead of your phone.
### Q. Why don’t dog trainers recommend dog parks?
A.  The worry is the mix - strange dogs of every size and temperament, owners who aren’t watching, and nobody stepping in before play turns into a scuffle. One bad experience can make a dog fearful. If you go, pick quiet hours, keep your eyes on your dog, and leave at the first sign of trouble; Lucas sums it up as “Having a bad day? Go home, come back later.”
### Q. What do I need to bring to a St. Louis dog park?
A.  Bring your dog’s vaccination records. Creve Coeur and Southwest City ask for rabies and Bordetella. Florissant asks for rabies and DHLPP. Frenchtown asks for rabies, Bordetella and DHLPP. The St. Charles County parks ask for an updated immunization record. At a membership park, bring the tag or gate code too, plus water, waste bags, and a leash for the walk from the car. Your dog stays leashed until you’re inside the fenced off-leash area.

## No Pointing, a Piano and a 40-Book Limit: St. Louis’s Best Independent Bookstores
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-s-best-independent-bookstores-a-2026-guide-for-book-lovers
Nobody at Left Bank Books is allowed to point. Ask for poetry and a bookseller walks you there, between tables of new hardcovers, until the book is in your hands. It’s a house rule at the city’s oldest independent bookstore, employee-owned and opened in 1969 by Washington University graduate students at Euclid and McPherson in the Central West End. It tells you most of what you need to know about buying books in St. Louis.
Across town on South Grand, somebody is playing the piano on the main floor of Dunaway Books. That’s allowed, if you’re good. Records wait at the foot of the stairs, modern first editions up on the mezzanine, mysteries and science fiction down in the basement, all inside an old gallery space where the aisles keep going longer than you planned to stay.
A weekend route: start at Left Bank, 399 N. Euclid (10 a.m. to 8 p.m. Monday through Saturday, 10 to 6 on Sunday), and check the events page on left-bank.com for that week’s free author talks. Ask a bookseller for a staff pick and let them walk you to it.
Then drive to 3111 S. Grand, where Dunaway has been since 2000 after opening near the Loop in 1965. Climb to the mezzanine for the modern first editions, then walk a block down to Leviathan at 3211 S. Grand. Dunaway is closed Mondays, and its own site notes the parking meters out front aren’t checked on Sundays.
Selling instead of buying? Call before you load the trunk. Dunaway (314-771-7150) buys selectively, looks at books on Saturdays and Sundays by appointment, and caps a load at 40 books, so describe what you have before you drive over. Left Bank Books also takes used books by appointment. Clean copies of in-demand, collectible or out-of-print titles are what these shops want most.
### The anchors: where booksellers walk you to the shelf
At a Left Bank Books author event the room is small enough that you can ask a national name a question, and most of the 300-plus events a year are free. It is the anchor of the city’s bookstore scene, and it had the first women’s studies, LGBT and African American sections in town, long before other stores caught up.
In Webster Groves, The Novel Neighbor is a community hub with events, classes and book clubs on the calendar, and it recently spun off Open Door Romance, a sister shop devoted entirely to the genre. Out on the Delmar Loop, Subterranean Books has been championing indie bestsellers and small presses since 2000.
### Bookstores with a mission
Walk into EyeSeeMe in University City and the faces on the covers look like the kids reading them. A few of these shops exist to fill one specific gap. EyeSeeMe bills itself as the country’s largest African American children’s bookstore, Black-owned and dedicated to positive representation. A husband-and-wife team built it because they couldn’t find enough books showing their own kids in a positive light, and it has become a national destination for African American children’s literature. Story time is a favorite there.
A comics-obsessed nine-year-old has a home at Betty’s Books in Webster Groves, the place for comics, graphic novels, and manga, now in a bigger space with a café. A cook has one on Cherokee Street: Anchovy Book Co. is a cookbook lover’s dream, and it’s expanding to a larger Cherokee Street storefront, so check the current address before you go.
### Used, rare and out of print: where the afternoon disappears
You walk into The Book House in Maplewood for one book and lose a Saturday. Used-book country smells like old paper and floor polish, and the shelves run higher than you can reach, with 300,000-plus new, used and rare titles packed into every corner. The shop was founded in 1986 and has been on Manchester Road since 2013, and it makes a perfect stop on our Maplewood food crawl.
On South Grand, Dunaway Books has built a deep used and antiquarian collection, while the newer Leviathan Bookstore brings a sharply curated literary selection to the same stretch - both easy add-ons to a South Grand dining day. For affordable secondhand finds, Read A Book STL on Meramec Street in Dutchtown is worth a browse. Both The Book House and Dunaway buy used stock too, so call ahead before you haul a box over.
### Across the river: Metro East
Children’s story times put Afterwords Books in Edwardsville on the map, a family-owned shop of new and used titles. In 2024, downtown Belleville got an independent of its own, Belleville Books, with new and used shelves too. Illinois readers aren’t left out.
### Cobblestones in St. Charles, consignment shelves in Benton Park
On the cobblestone stretch of South Main Street in historic St. Charles, Main Street Books has been the go-to indie since 1993, recently moving just a few doors down. It’s a general new-book shop with a steady events calendar, in the kind of walkable, coffee-and-antiques district that makes an afternoon of it.
Every shelf at Spine Indie Bookstore & Café in Benton Park holds independent authors or small presses, stocked on consignment. A café sits alongside a busy calendar of poetry readings, author showcases, and even comedy. Between the two shops they round out the map: St. Charles County to the west, the near-south side in the city. Odds are a real bookstore sits closer to you than the nearest big-box.
Nothing to do with books - St. Louis HVAC contractors, all mapped.
### How to get the most out of an indie bookstore
Find the little handwritten shelf-talkers first. Each one is a note from someone who actually read the book, which makes staff picks the whole point of an independent, so start there instead of the bestseller table. Most shops will special-order nearly anything and have it in a few days, often for the same price as ordering online, which quietly makes the “but they didn’t have it” excuse disappear.
A good independent gives you things an app never will, if you know to ask. Get on the events calendar: Left Bank alone runs hundreds of author signings a year, and The Novel Neighbor and Spine keep the literary community humming with launches and book clubs. Bring the kids to a story time (Afterwords in Edwardsville and EyeSeeMe are favorites), ask about a loyalty or membership program, and remember that many of these shops buy used stock - so the used-and-rare stores like The Book House and Dunaway are a place to sell as well as browse.
### A quick map by neighborhood
Walk a block down South Grand and you’ve gone from Dunaway to Leviathan on a single parking spot, and the rest of the shops cluster nicely too. Central West End: Left Bank Books at 399 N. Euclid. Delmar Loop / U. City: Subterranean and EyeSeeMe. Webster Groves: The Novel Neighbor, Open Door Romance, and Betty’s Books - three within a short drive. South Grand: Dunaway at 3111 S. Grand and the newer Leviathan at 3211 S. Grand, a natural pairing with the neighborhood’s international restaurants. Maplewood: The Book House on Manchester Road. Cherokee Street: Anchovy. Dutchtown: Read A Book STL on Meramec Street. Benton Park: Spine. St. Charles: Main Street Books on South Main Street. Metro East: Afterwords (Edwardsville) and Belleville Books. Stack two or three in a single neighborhood and you’ve got an afternoon.
### Before you drive: shops that changed space or are about to
Anchovy Book Co. is expanding to a larger Cherokee Street storefront. Betty’s Books in Webster Groves already has its bigger space and its café. Main Street Books in St. Charles slid a few doors down South Main Street. Drive to an old address and you’ll circle the block, so check each current address before you go. The settled stops are Dunaway, at 3111 S. Grand since 2000, and The Book House, on Manchester Road since 2013. Mind the day, too: on a Monday, Left Bank is open until 8 p.m. while Dunaway is closed.
### Why can two bookstores a mile apart feel like different countries?
Two St. Louis bookstores a mile apart can feel like different countries: one all literary fiction and staff obsessions, the next all cookbooks or comics or romance. The theme across all of them is curation with a human behind it. A chain orders by the algorithm and the sales rep; an independent orders by what the person at the front counter believes in.
On South Grand, Dunaway’s deep antiquarian stacks and the sharply curated Leviathan sit within a block of each other, so one parking spot buys you both the hunt and the discovery. Finding the shop whose taste matches yours is half the fun, and once you do, its recommendations become more reliable than any five-star rating.
### The right shop for the reader you’re shopping for
The comics-obsessed nine-year-old on your list belongs at Betty’s Books. For everyone else, match the shop to the person. For a literary-fiction devotee, Left Bank, Subterranean, or Leviathan will have the sharp new releases and the staff picks to go with them. For a kid, EyeSeeMe and Afterwords are built around young readers. For a home cook, Anchovy on Cherokee Street is the easy gift. For the collector or the hard-to-shop-for reader who has everything, the used-and-rare stacks at The Book House and Dunaway turn up first editions and out-of-print oddities you couldn’t plan for. For a romance reader, The Novel Neighbor’s Open Door is the whole genre under one roof. And when in doubt, a gift card plus a staff recommendation beats guessing every time - walk in, describe the person, and let a bookseller do what the internet can’t.
Ask a bookseller who’s writing about St. Louis right now, and the answer is a short walk to a shelf and a story you didn’t know you wanted. Many of these shops actively champion St. Louis and Missouri authors, hosting local launches and stocking regional writers you won’t find featured on a national homepage. Buying a local author’s book from a local store is about the most direct way there is to keep the region’s literary scene alive: the writer gets the sale, the shop gets the foot traffic, and you get a book with a genuine sense of place.

### Why it's worth leaving the couch
An algorithm can sell you a book. It can’t hand you the one a bookseller couldn’t stop thinking about. In St. Louis, the nearest shop that can is closer than you’d guess.
Make an evening of it: after browsing, a lot of these shops sit a short walk from a great bar, so pair the trip with our guide to St. Louis’s best craft cocktail bars and speakeasies.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the oldest independent bookstore in St. Louis?
A.  Left Bank Books in the Central West End, open since 1969, is widely considered St. Louis’s oldest and largest independent bookstore. You’ll find it at 399 N. Euclid Ave., with hours of 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. Monday through Saturday and 10 to 6 on Sunday. Booksellers walk you to the shelf instead of pointing, and alongside new books and a busy author-event calendar it sells used books and takes used-book appointments.
### Q. What are the best used bookstores in Saint Louis, Missouri?
A.  Start with The Book House on Manchester Road in Maplewood, which mixes 300,000-plus new, used and rare titles, and Dunaway Books at 3111 S. Grand, a deep used and antiquarian shop that is closed Mondays. Read A Book STL on Meramec Street in Dutchtown is the budget pick for affordable secondhand finds, and Left Bank Books keeps a used section too.
### Q. What is a good way to sell used books?
A.  Call before you load the trunk. Dunaway Books on South Grand buys selectively, asks sellers to phone first (314-771-7150), caps a visit at about forty books and prefers to look on weekends by appointment. Left Bank Books also takes used books by appointment. Clean copies of in-demand, collectible or out-of-print titles are what these shops want most.
### Q. Is there a Barnes & Noble in the St Louis area?
A.  Yes. Barnes & Noble’s store locator lists stores at the Saint Louis Galleria in Richmond Heights, Ladue Crossing in Ladue, Chesterfield Oaks in Chesterfield and St. Clair Square in Fairview Heights, Illinois. For staff picks, author events and used or rare books, the independents in this guide are the better trip.
### Q. What was the other big bookstore besides Barnes and Noble?
A.  Borders. It was the other national superstore chain until it went out of business in 2011 and closed every location, its St. Louis-area stores included. Since then the local independents, from Left Bank Books to The Book House, have carried much of the in-person browsing that a superstore used to cover.

## A $2 Carousel Survived a Fire: St. Louis Indoor Play Places
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/the-best-indoor-play-places-for-kids-in-st-louis-2026-rainy-day-and-winter-lifesavers
The carousel didn’t burn. On the night of July 19, 1963, flames swept through the Forest Park Highlands amusement park and took almost everything else, but its carousel came through, and today its 65 hand-carved animals and 2 chariots turn indoors at Faust Park in Chesterfield. Two dollars buys a ride, and that goes for parents too. On a sleet-gray Saturday that’s the best $2 you’ll spend: a painted horse rising and falling, a few minutes of music, and a four-year-old who has forgotten what the crying was about.
Union Station has a carousel too, and it costs $5 a ride. The $2 one is the one that survived the fire. It runs Tuesday through Sunday, shuts for Easter, July 4, Thanksgiving, Christmas, New Year’s Day and the first few weeks of January, and posts two different sets of closing times, roughly 4 to 4:30 on weekdays and 3:45 to 4 on weekends. Call (314) 615-8345 before you drive.
The free version is louder, and it comes with a catch. The Science Center’s own posts show kids on the Sky Bridge aiming radar guns at the cars roaring along I-64 below. General admission is always free, so when the meltdown comes you just leave, no ticket to mourn. Parking is $15, card only (free for members), and the building is closed every Tuesday.
The Magic House math: admission is $15 for everyone age 1 and up (under 1 is free), parking is free, and there’s no need to buy advance tickets. But from 3 to 5 p.m. it’s $3 a person for residents of St. Louis City and County and Jefferson, Franklin, St. Charles, Warren and Lincoln counties (bring proof of residency). A family of four pays $12 instead of $60. And on the third Friday of every month, Free Family Night runs 5 to 8 p.m. for up to two adults and four children, first come, first served.
Mind the day. On Mondays the Butterfly House and the carousel are closed, and so is the Magic House during the school year. On Tuesdays it’s the Science Center that’s dark. A rainy Monday belongs to the Science Center and the Aquarium. A rainy Tuesday belongs to Faust Park and the Magic House.
A few rules nobody tells you until you’re at the door. The Butterfly House restricts strollers and wagons because of limited space and USDA containment requirements, so bring a baby carrier and leave the big rig in the car. Sky Zone in Fenton requires its own socks to jump, and they’re $4.99 on top of the ticket, so dig last visit’s pair out of the cup holder. Go Play! in Chesterfield charges $21 for ages 1 to 15, and adults are always free.
The sleet-day game plan: carousel and butterflies at Faust Park while the kids are fresh, lunch, then The Magic House in Kirkwood once the nap window closes, timed for the $3 hour after 3 p.m. if you live in a qualifying county. Older kids who need to burn it off can skip straight to the trampoline and slide parks below, sorted by energy, age and part of town.
### Hands-on museums: a three-story slide and a free science center
Follow the shrieking. At the City Museum, 750 N. 16th St. downtown, it echoes out of caves and tunnels, down slides and across a rooftop that thrills toddlers and teenagers alike. Everything is built from salvaged materials, so every corner is a surprise; wear closed-toe shoes, bring knee-friendly clothes, and plan on a few hours because nobody leaves quickly.
Tickets are $20 each, and buying online runs more than 10% cheaper than the ticket window. Children 2 and under are free. There’s no fixed closing time, so check the online calendar: the late-fall schedule lists Wednesday, Thursday and Sunday 10 to 6 and Friday and Saturday 10 to 9, with some days closed (314-231-2489). The Gold Pass is $39.99, less than two $20 tickets, so it pays off on the second visit, and it takes $5 off main-lot parking.
A three-story slide is the headline at The Magic House (St. Louis Children’s Museum), 516 S. Kirkwood Rd. in Kirkwood. The rest is a make-believe grocery, a pretend construction site, and rooms that change with the seasons. School-year hours: closed Monday, 10:30 to 5 Tuesday through Friday and Sunday, 9:30 to 5 Saturday. Call (314) 822-8900.
Its maker-focused offshoot, The Magic House @ MADE for Kids on Delmar, suits a slightly older crowd, roughly ages six to thirteen, who build, sew, print, and tinker with real tools. Memberships run $175 for Family (Magic House only), $250 for Family Plus (which adds MADE for Kids) and $25 for a Kids Club pass (one child). At $60 a visit for four, the Family tier wins on the third trip.
The Saint Louis Science Center, 5050 Oakland Ave. in Forest Park, has galleries of hands-on science and general admission that is always free. Hours are 9:30 to 4:30 Monday and Wednesday through Saturday and 11 to 4:30 Sunday, closed Tuesdays, with last entry 30 minutes before close (314-289-4400).
The extras cost money. OMNIMAX is $11.50 for adults and $9.50 for children and seniors. The Blue Whale exhibit is $16 for adults 13 to 59, $14 for seniors and $12 for ages 5 to 12 ($8 for members), with timed entry every 15 minutes; children 4 and under are free but still need a ticket. The Discovery Room is $6 for non-members, and the planetarium needs a ticket too.
(Note: another local favorite, Myseum in Town and Country, has been temporarily closed while it relocates, so check its status before you drive out.)
### Sharks, butterflies and a $2 carousel
Cold fingers in a touch pool fix a lot of moods. The St. Louis Aquarium at Union Station brings touch tide pools, sharks, and river-to-ocean galleries under one roof, with a train-station theme kids love. It no longer uses timed ticketing, strollers are allowed, and doors are open 9 to 5 Sunday through Thursday and 9 to 6 Friday and Saturday. Parking is a $5 flat rate with validation.
For something gentler, the Sophia M. Sachs Butterfly House at Faust Park in Chesterfield is a warm tropical conservatory with more than a thousand free-flying butterflies. Admission is $8 for ages 13 and up and $5 for ages 3 to 12 and seniors 65 and up. It’s closed Mondays and for a few weeks each January. St. Louis City and County residents get in free for the first two hours on the first Tuesday of the month, with proof of residency at the door. Right next door, the historic indoor St. Louis Carousel gives little ones their $2 spin.
### For kids bouncing off the walls: trampolines, slides and auto-belays
When the couch cushions are already on the floor, it’s time to jump. Trampoline parks lead the way: Sky Zone in Fenton (631 Gravois Rd., 636-364-4444) and Urban Air Adventure Park - with locations in Sunset Hills, Cottleville, and Fairview Heights on the Illinois side - pack in trampolines, foam pits, obstacle courses, and climbing walls, with dedicated toddler times at slower hours. Socks are required at both. Sky Zone allows only its own, and Urban Air doesn’t publish its prices, so call your location.
Slick City Action Park is an all-indoor slide park - think a dozen giant slides plus air-jump courts - with metro locations in Chesterfield and St. Peters, and it suits kids who’ve outgrown the ball pit. For climbers, Climb So iLL (downtown St. Louis and St. Charles) has walls and auto-belays sized for families.
Older kids and tweens gravitate to Amp Up Action Park in Town and Country (indoor go-karts, laser tag, a ninja course) and Puttshack at City Foundry, which reinvents mini-golf with tech-enabled scoring and a full menu. That makes it a rare spot that entertains a squirrelly nine-year-old and a couple of adults at the same table.
### Little ones and play cafés
Got toddlers? Go Play! in Chesterfield (140 Long Rd., Suite 108, with a second spot in Lake St. Louis) offers a three-story play structure, slides, and ball pits with coffee for the grown-ups. Ages 1 to 15 are $21, ages 6 to 12 months are $10, under 6 months are free, and adults are always free. Sessions run 9 to 1 and 2 to 7. The site lists Wednesday as the closed day while another page says Tuesday, so call 636-893-8134 before you go.
TotSpot Social in Clayton’s DeMun neighborhood is a play-space-and-café built for newborns through age six, with timed sessions. And We Rock the Spectrum in Fenton is a sensory-inclusive gym designed so kids of all abilities - including those with autism or sensory needs - can play side by side. These smaller spots are the sanity-savers when you have a napper and a runner in the same stroller.
### Union Station: a rainy day in one building
St. Louis Union Station is more than the aquarium. Under the same historic roof you’ll find a mirror maze, a ropes course, mini-golf, a carousel that costs $5 a ride (not the $2 survivor at Faust Park), a Build-A-Bear Workshop, and the giant St. Louis Wheel just outside. That’s enough to build a whole rainy day around without going back to the car. The Wheel is $18 and up for ages 13 and older, $12 and up for ages 3 to 12, and free at 2 and under.
An Aquarium-plus-Wheel combo ticket exists, but its price appears only at checkout and no savings figure is published, so price it against buying each separately before you commit. Aquarium members get unlimited visits for less than the cost of two general admission tickets, plus 15% off Union Station rides and a parking voucher.
### Indoor playgrounds near you, by part of town
Nobody types “indoor playground near me” with time to spare. There’s a kid bouncing off the couch cushions and maybe twenty minutes of patience left in the house. So here’s the metro sorted by drive, not by brand. Downtown: City Museum, Union Station’s aquarium, mirror maze and ropes course, and the climbing walls at Climb So iLL are a short hop apart, the easiest answer for an indoor play place downtown. Midtown and the central corridor: the free Science Center in Forest Park, Puttshack at City Foundry, and TotSpot Social on Clayton Road in DeMun. South County and Fenton: Sky Zone on Gravois Road, Urban Air in Sunset Hills, and We Rock the Spectrum. Kirkwood and Town and Country: The Magic House and Amp Up Action Park.
West County: Go Play! and Slick City in Chesterfield, plus the Butterfly House and the Carousel at Faust Park. St. Charles County: Urban Air in Cottleville, Slick City in St. Peters, and the second Go Play! in Lake St. Louis. Metro East: Urban Air in Fairview Heights. Pick the cluster closest to home and your backup is one exit away.
Nothing to do with kids - but Soulard is worth a wander.
### What to check before you load the car
Two checks save every indoor-play outing. First, check the ticket rules before you leave the driveway. The Magic House sells admission at the front desk and the Aquarium no longer uses timed ticketing, so neither needs an advance purchase. City Museum is cheaper online, and the Science Center’s Blue Whale exhibit sells timed entry every 15 minutes. Second, pack the right gear: Sky Zone and Urban Air require socks (Sky Zone allows only its own), closed-toe shoes make City Museum far more fun, and a change of clothes is never a bad idea.
### Go early, keep a backup, pack the bag
Go early. The Aquarium opens at 9, the Science Center at 9:30 (11 on Sundays), and the Magic House at 10:30 (9:30 on Saturdays). Have a backup that’s open the same day. The Monday and Tuesday closures above are the easiest way for a plan to fall apart, and the carousel and Butterfly House also close for a few weeks each January. Pack a bag. Water bottles, a snack, your Sky Zone socks, and a change of clothes cover most disasters, and they keep you from paying concession prices for a forgotten juice box.
It also helps to match the venue to your window of time. If you’ve got ninety minutes before a nap, a play café or the Carousel is perfect; if you’ve got a whole miserable-weather afternoon to fill, City Museum or Union Station will happily eat all of it. And don’t underestimate the smaller neighborhood spots - a quiet play café on a weekday morning can save your sanity just as well as a big-ticket attraction on a Saturday.
### By age: what actually works when
The right indoor spot depends a lot on who’s in the back seat. For babies and young toddlers, the winners are the calm, contained spaces: TotSpot Social, the soft-play areas at Go Play!, the Carousel at Faust Park, and the toddler hours at the trampoline parks, where the big kids aren’t bouncing them off the mats. For preschoolers and early grade-schoolers, The Magic House is a strong pick, and the Aquarium, Butterfly House, and City Museum’s lower levels hit the sweet spot of “amazing but not overwhelming.”
Still a few months out from the play-place years? Here’s when to start buying maternity clothes in St. Louis.
Once you’re into the grade-school years, the whole map opens up: City Museum top to bottom, Science Center experiments, Slick City’s slides, Climb So iLL’s walls, and the trampoline parks all land. And for tweens and teens - the age that’s hardest to impress - lean on Amp Up’s go-karts and laser tag, Puttshack’s tech mini-golf, Climb So iLL, and the Union Station attractions, which feel less “little-kid” and more like an outing they’d actually choose. Mixed-age group? City Museum and Union Station are the two spots where a three-year-old and a thirteen-year-old can both have a good time.

### Budgets, memberships, and keeping it cheap
Indoor play adds up fast with a couple of kids, so start with the cheap doors. The Science Center is free to enter, though parking is $15 (card only, free for members). The Magic House drops to $3 a person from 3 to 5 p.m. for residents of the counties listed above, and Free Family Night covers up to two adults and four children on the third Friday of the month. The Butterfly House is free for St. Louis City and County residents during the first two hours on the first Tuesday of each month.
Memberships come down to arithmetic. The Magic House Family tier is $175 against $60 at the door for four, so it wins on the third visit. The Magic House also honors the ACM Reciprocal Network at 50% off, not free, for Family, Family Plus and Grandparent memberships, up to six people with the cardholder present. Because Science Center entry is free, its membership is really about parking and shows: the $100 Family tier includes free parking plus four free OMNIMAX, planetarium and Discovery Room tickets per visit. The ASTC Passport program excludes venues within 90 miles and never covers the planetarium, the large-screen theater or special exhibits.
The other passes follow the same math. City Museum’s $39.99 Gold Pass costs less than two $20 tickets, and an Aquarium membership gives unlimited visits for less than two general admission tickets. For the pay-to-play spots, buy Sky Zone socks once and reuse them.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What are the best indoor activities for kids in St. Louis on a rainy day?
A.  Top picks are the City Museum ($20, children 2 and under free), The Magic House in Kirkwood ($15 for age 1 and up), the Saint Louis Science Center (free admission, closed Tuesdays) and the St. Louis Aquarium at Union Station. All four are indoors, but their closed days differ, so check before you go. For high energy, add a trampoline or slide park like Sky Zone, Urban Air, or Slick City.
### Q. What are some fun indoor activities to do in Saint Louis on a rainy day?
A.  Sort it by energy. Curious kids: the Saint Louis Science Center (free admission, $15 parking) or The Magic House in Kirkwood. Kids bouncing off the walls: Sky Zone, Urban Air or Slick City, with the right socks on. Toddlers: Go Play! or TotSpot Social. Can’t decide? Union Station puts an aquarium, a mirror maze, a ropes course and mini-golf under one roof, so one parking spot covers the whole wet day.
### Q. Is there an indoor playground for kids in St. Louis?
A.  Yes, several, and they are not interchangeable. Go Play! in Chesterfield and Lake St. Louis has a three-story play structure for younger kids, TotSpot Social in DeMun is a play café with a soft area for babies, and Sky Zone, Urban Air and Slick City are big trampoline and slide parks for older kids. Match the venue to the age, not the drive time.
### Q. How much does it cost for an indoor playground?
A.  Prices are per person, and some places charge adults while others don’t. Go Play! in Chesterfield is $21 for ages 1 to 15 with adults always free, Sky Zone Fenton requires $4.99 socks on top of the ticket, the Saint Louis Science Center is free to enter with $15 parking, and The Magic House is $15 for everyone age 1 and up, or $3 a person from 3 to 5 p.m. for qualifying local residents.
### Q. What are some fun winter games for kids to play indoors?
A.  The ones that work are the ones with a physical outlet: obstacle courses down a hallway, indoor bowling with soft balls, scavenger hunts with written clues for readers. Save screens for the recovery hour. If the walls are closing in, the venues above exist for exactly that afternoon.

## Hot Towel, Straight Razor, Cash Only: South City Barbershops Since 1907
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/the-best-barbershops-in-south-city-st-louis-2026
The hot towel lands first, heavy and steaming, and Union Barbershop on Gravois goes quiet except for the scrape of a straight razor making its first pass along your jaw. Then the second pass. That two-pass hot-towel shave is the house ritual near Benton Park; its booking listing on Squire prices it at about $50 to $80 for 45 to 75 minutes, so call 314-328-2411 before you go.
Over on South Grand, at Wyoming Barber Shop, you wait your turn on a bench that looks like it came out of a church, under vintage photos from the day the shop opened in 1907. Every station has its own retro sink. The South Grand business district calls 3192 S. Grand the oldest barber shop in Missouri, and the man behind the first chair, Marco, has been cutting hair for 45 years and has owned the place since 2000. His daughter Reece, who grew up in the shop and learned the trade from him, works the next chair over. It’s cash only, and they’d rather you call ahead at 314-772-6675.
Here’s the move most people never make: before a stranger puts a straight razor to your throat, look the barber up. Missouri’s Board of Cosmetology and Barber Examiners licenses every barber in the state, and the free MOPRO license search at mopro.mo.gov shows whether a license is active. Almost nobody checks. It takes a minute.
Then the nick. It stings, the razor stops mid-stroke, and in Missouri what happens next is spelled out by rule: the barber has to stop, glove up, clean the cut and reach for antiseptic and liquid or spray styptic, without letting the bottle touch the wound. The chalky styptic pencil old-time barbers rubbed on a razor cut is banned in Missouri barbershops. The same rules want a clean towel or paper on the headrest, a fresh towel or neck strip between your skin and the cape, and every tool disinfected before it touches you. That fresh paper behind your head is the rule, not a courtesy.
Tip math worth a screenshot: 15 to 20 percent is about $4 to $5 on a $25 cut and $12 to $16 on an $80 shave.
### The old-school chairs: a shop open since 1907
Wyoming Barber Shop is the reason to walk South Grand with a few twenties in your pocket: classic cuts, clean skin fades and straight-razor shaves from a father and daughter who know most of the room by name. Make it part of a stroll through the South Grand International District, where lunch can be pho or falafel down the block. When it’s Sunday morning and the interview is Monday, head to Bevo Mill: St. Louis Barber & Beauty Salon takes walk-ins seven days a week, so the clippers are already buzzing when everyone else is at brunch.
### Hot towels and two passes of a straight razor
Union Barbershop, on Gravois near Benton Park, builds its shave the slow way: hot towels, lather, two passes with a straight razor, then a beard trim and skin products, with sharp fades in the next chair for everyone else. In Tower Grove South, Yasser’s Barbershop does the full routine, cuts, shampoo, facials and hot-towel shaves, from a barber with one of the better reputations on the south side. Bring cash; Yasser’s doesn’t take cards.
### Fades, appointments and a design-forward chair in Shaw
The cape snaps around your neck and the clippers start their low buzz at SOHA Barbershop in Southampton, opened by two longtime barbers who cut for years before going out on their own. It runs by appointment, so book instead of dropping in. In historic Shaw, Idle Hands Grooming Company is co-owned and pairs barbering with high-end styling, the kind of appointment where you talk through the cut in the mirror before the first snip. On Cherokee Street, Nisus Barbershop is the walk-in stop: sit down, listen to the clippers in the chair ahead of you, and you’re next for a fade or an everyday cut. In Dutchtown, Legacy Barber & Beauty handles clean cuts, shaves and razor lining, that crisp edge along the hairline you keep touching for days.
### A few more South City chairs worth knowing
Out toward Macklind, on the St. Louis Hills edge of Southampton, Angelo’s Barber Collective literally brands itself “south city barbers,” with sharp fades in a different pocket than the Grand and Cherokee crowd. Back on Cherokee Street, Latin Barber Shop is the long-tenured mainstay, open seven days and walk-in friendly, the place to walk in on a Sunday and walk out with the sides tight again before Monday’s meeting.
### Walk-in or appointment? Know before you go
South City shops split fairly cleanly into two camps, and knowing which is which saves you a wasted trip. The walk-in mainstays - St. Louis Barber & Beauty in Bevo Mill (open seven days), Nisus and Latin on Cherokee Street (long daily hours) - are built for “I need a cut today.” The appointment shops - SOHA in Southampton and Idle Hands in Shaw - run on a booked schedule and are worth planning around, especially for a first visit or a more involved cut-and-style. A few, like Wyoming and Yasser’s, take walk-ins but book up fast, so a quick call ahead is the move. When in doubt, check the shop’s Instagram or booking page; most post their current hours and their booking link right there.
Random, but: Alton across the river is worth a Saturday.
### What a real barbershop cut costs - and how to tip
South City barbering is still a bargain compared with a salon. A standard men’s cut at these shops generally runs in the range of a chain price to modestly above it, a beard trim or lineup adds a little, and a full hot-towel straight-razor shave - the real ritual, hot lather and all - is priced as the small luxury it is. The unwritten rule: tip like you would at a good restaurant, around fifteen to twenty percent, more if your barber squeezed you in or nailed a tricky cut. Cash is always appreciated and, at a cash-only shop like Yasser’s, required - so hit the ATM first. And the single best money-saving habit is also the best-grooming habit: rebook on a regular cadence (every two to four weeks depending on your style) so you’re never walking in shaggy and hoping for a miracle.
### Why South City is a barber town
There’s a reason the south side has this many good shops. South City is a dense grid of walkable, fiercely local neighborhoods - Tower Grove, Southampton, Bevo, Cherokee, Shaw, Dutchtown - where a corner storefront still means something and people are loyal to businesses within a few blocks of home. That’s exactly the soil a great barbershop grows in: repeat customers who come every three weeks for years, know the barber’s kids’ names, and send their brothers and coworkers. It also reflects the area’s mix. You’ll find century-old straight-razor traditions a few blocks from a design-forward grooming lounge, an immigrant-run shop that’s anchored a block for a generation, and a brand-new studio built by two barbers who trained under the old guard before striking out on their own. A barbershop isn’t just where you get a haircut here - it’s one of those third places where the neighborhood actually talks to itself.
That density is good news for you, the customer, because it means competition on craft rather than just price. When there are eight excellent shops within a couple of miles, the way a barber keeps your business is by genuinely being good - listening, remembering how you like it, and sending you out looking sharp enough that someone asks where you got it done. It’s worth trying a couple before you settle, precisely because the bar is high enough that you can afford to be picky.

### Getting the cut you actually want
The single biggest predictor of a good haircut is communication, not the shop. Bring a photo - two, ideally: one of the length and shape you want, one of a look you want to avoid. Learn a little vocabulary so you and the barber mean the same thing: a fade blends from skin up gradually, a taper is a subtler version around the edges, and “scissors on top” versus “clippers” makes a real difference in how a cut grows out. Be specific about the parts people usually get wrong - how tight you want the sides, whether you want the neckline squared or rounded (a “blocked” vs. “natural” nape), and how much to take off the top, in inches or fingers rather than a vague “not too much.” Speak up early if something’s going a direction you don’t love; a good barber would much rather adjust mid-cut than send you home unhappy. And when they nail it, tell them what you liked and book your next visit before you walk out - that’s how you become a regular who never has to re-explain your head again.
### Between visits: making a good cut last
The chair is only half of it. A sharp cut that grows out fast is worth less than a slightly simpler one you can maintain, so ask your barber what to do at home - most will happily tell you which products and routine suit your hair. For beards, a little oil or balm keeps things from getting scraggly between trims; for the neckline, a cheap trimmer and a mirror will buy you an extra week before the “forgot” stage. And if you like the straight-razor shave, know that it’s as much relaxation as grooming - the hot towels, the ritual, twenty minutes of doing nothing - which is exactly why plenty of South City regulars book one not because they need it, but because it’s the best twenty dollars of self-care in the neighborhood.
A quick word for anyone new to the ritual: a real straight-razor shave is a multi-step process - hot towels to soften the beard, a pre-shave oil, a careful pass with the grain, more lather, and a second pass - so it takes time and shouldn’t be rushed. Book it when you’re not squeezing it between errands, mention any skin sensitivity up front, and let the barber work. Done right, it’s the closest, most comfortable shave you’ll ever get, and it’s a genuinely different experience from dragging a cartridge razor across a dry jaw at seven in the morning.

### How to pick your barber
The best barber is the one who listens. Bring a reference photo, be clear about how short you want the sides, and ask whether a shop prefers walk-ins or appointments - some of these book up fast. And once you find someone who nails it, do what every well-groomed local does: tip well and rebook before you leave.
