### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the best coworking space in St. Louis for startups?
A.  T-REX downtown (a nonprofit incubator tied to Arch Grants) and CIC St. Louis in the Cortex district are the metro’s leading startup-focused spaces, with mentorship, events, and room to grow.
### Q. Are there boutique or creative coworking spaces in St. Louis?
A.  Yes — TechArtista (with rotating art and several locations), Nebula on Cherokee Street (the city’s oldest), and NexCore in Fox Park all offer a more creative, community-driven vibe.
### Q. How much does coworking cost in St. Louis?
A.  It varies widely — flex memberships often start around $120 to $300 a month depending on the space and whether you want a shared desk or a private office. Most spaces offer a free day pass so you can try before you commit.
### Q. Is there coworking in St. Charles or the suburbs, or only in the city?
A.  Both. OPO Startups anchors St. Charles with a multi-building startup campus on South Main Street, NexCore has a new South County campus on Tesson Ferry Road, and professional-flex brands like ThriveCo, Office Evolution, and Regus cover Clayton, Creve Coeur, and Chesterfield. You rarely need to drive downtown to find a desk.
### Q. Coworking or a coffee shop — which is better for remote work?
A.  For occasional light work, a coffee shop is fine. For anything with client calls, private meetings, or a full workday, coworking wins: a guaranteed seat, reliable and backed-up internet, real meeting rooms and phone booths, a professional address, and other people around you — without the noise, seat-hunting, and privacy gaps of a cafe.
### Q. How do I choose the right coworking space for me?
A.  Start from who you are: solo founders and freelancers do best at startup hubs like T-REX, CIC, or OPO Startups; remote employees want a quiet professional-flex space with reliable internet and phone booths; small teams want a private office with room to grow. Then take the free day pass, sit in the space at the hour you’d actually use it, and check the access hours, meeting-room availability, and what’s included before you commit.

## How to Choose a Financial Advisor in St. Louis: What to Ask Before You Trust Anyone With Your Money
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-financial-advisor-in-st-louis-2026-what-to-ask-before-you-trust-anyone-with-your-money
Maybe you just started a job with a 401(k) you don’t understand. Maybe you came into some money, or you’re staring down retirement and realizing “wing it” is no longer a plan. Whatever brought you here, handing your financial future to a stranger is a big leap — and not everyone who calls themselves an “advisor” has your best interests at heart.
Here’s how to choose a financial advisor in St. Louis you can actually trust — and the questions that separate the real ones from the salespeople.
### First, understand who you’re hiring
“Financial advisor” isn’t a protected title — it can mean a fee-only fiduciary planner or a commissioned product salesperson. Two terms matter most:
Fiduciary. A fiduciary is legally required to act in your best interest at all times — an ongoing duty of loyalty. Brokers who aren’t fiduciaries are held to the SEC’s Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI), in force since 2020: they must act in your “best interest” when they make a recommendation, but that’s a lighter, point-of-sale standard than a fiduciary’s constant duty. Ask, “Are you a fiduciary, 100% of the time?” — and get the answer in writing.
How they’re paid. There are three models, and they’re easy to mix up. A fee-only advisor is paid only by you — a flat fee, hourly rate, or a percentage of assets — and earns no product commissions. A fee-based advisor charges you a fee and can also collect commissions, a dual model with a built-in conflict. A commission advisor is paid by the products they sell you. Fee-only is the cleanest of the three; with the other two, always ask exactly how a recommendation makes them money.
### Check the credentials (it takes five minutes)
Look for real designations: a CFP (Certified Financial Planner) has met rigorous education, exam, and ethics requirements, and a CFA is the gold standard for investment analysis and portfolio management (note: that’s a different job than comprehensive financial planning). A ChFC (Chartered Financial Consultant), issued by The American College of Financial Services, is a planning-focused credential similar in scope to the CFP. The credential names the specialty; a CFP or ChFC signals planning, a CFA signals investing.
### Verify anyone in ten minutes (three free tools)
Before a second meeting, run any advisor through the free public databases — it takes minutes and it’s the single best fraud check you can do:
FINRA BrokerCheck (brokercheck.finra.org) — brokers and brokerage firms: licenses, employment history, and any disclosures or complaints.
SEC Investment Adviser Public Disclosure / IAPD (adviserinfo.sec.gov) — investment advisers and their Form ADV, which spells out fees, conflicts, and disciplinary history in plain sight.
CFP Board “Verify a CFP Professional” (cfp.net) and the consumer site LetsMakeAPlan.org — confirms a planner’s current CFP status and any disciplinary or bankruptcy history.
For a Missouri-specific check, the Missouri Secretary of State’s Securities Division registers and regulates investment advisers who operate in the state (generally those managing under $100 million; larger firms register with the SEC). You can confirm an adviser’s registration status and file a complaint through the Division — a real, local layer of protection worth knowing about.
### Do you even need a human advisor?
Not everyone does, and it’s worth being honest about that before you pay for one. A robo-advisor — an automated service that builds and rebalances a portfolio for a low fee, often around a quarter percent of assets — is a perfectly good fit for someone with a straightforward situation who mainly needs disciplined, low-cost investing. Where a human advisor (ideally a CFP) earns their fee is complexity and life transitions: an inheritance, selling a business, navigating retirement drawdown, a divorce, equity compensation, or a tangled tax and estate picture. If your finances are simple, a robo-advisor or a one-time hourly planning session may be all you need; if your life has gotten complicated, that’s exactly when a good local advisor is worth the cost. Paying an ongoing 1%-of-assets fee for a situation a robo-advisor could handle is one of the quieter ways people overpay.
### The questions to ask in the first meeting
A good advisor welcomes these; a bad one dodges them:
Are you a fiduciary 100% of the time?
How exactly do you get paid — and what will I pay in total, including fund fees?
What are your credentials, and can I verify them?
Who is your typical client, and do you work with people in my situation?
How and how often will we communicate?
Who is the custodian actually holding my money?
### What a good advisor actually does for you
It helps to know what you’re paying for, because “financial advisor” covers a lot of ground. At the narrow end, some advisors mainly manage investments — building and rebalancing a portfolio. A good comprehensive planner does much more: mapping your goals, building a retirement and savings plan, coordinating taxes, insurance, and estate documents, talking you off the ledge when markets drop, and adjusting the plan as your life changes. That last part — the behavioral coaching that keeps you from panic-selling at the bottom or lifestyle-creeping past your goals — is often where an advisor quietly earns their fee many times over. When you interview someone, get clear on which kind they are. If you want a full financial quarterback and they only pick funds, or you just want low-cost investing and they’re selling a comprehensive-planning retainer, it’s a mismatch no matter how likable they are.
### Red flags and money-safety rules
Most bad outcomes are avoidable if you know the warning signs. Walk away from anyone who guarantees returns — no honest advisor can, and “can’t-lose” language is the oldest tell in the book. Be wary of pressure to act fast, vagueness about fees, or a pitch built around a single hot product. And the non-negotiable rule that has protected investors from Madoff-style fraud for decades: never write a check payable to the advisor personally. Your money should be held by an independent, third-party custodian (a firm like Schwab or Fidelity), and your statements should come from that custodian, not from the advisor’s own spreadsheet — so if the two ever don’t match, that’s your signal to stop and investigate. This matters especially for older investors and their families, who are disproportionately targeted; a good practice is to loop in a trusted family member or second set of eyes before moving a large sum. If something feels off, you can report suspected fraud to the Missouri Secretary of State’s Securities Division. Trustworthy advisors are transparent, patient, and happy to put everything in writing — and they never rush you.
### When it’s actually time to hire one
You don’t need an advisor for every stage of life, and knowing when the value shows up saves money. The common triggers are moments of change or complexity: starting a job with a 401(k) and stock options you don’t understand, coming into an inheritance or a windfall, buying a first home, getting married or divorced, starting or selling a business, or approaching retirement and realizing “wing it” is no longer a plan. Each of these is a point where a wrong move is expensive and a right one compounds for decades — exactly where advice pays for itself. If you’re earlier and simpler — steady paycheck, employer 401(k), no dependents — you may only need a one-time hourly planning session to set a course, not an ongoing relationship. And you can scale up later: many people start with a single flat-fee financial plan, implement it themselves, and only move to ongoing management when their situation grows complicated enough to warrant it. The goal isn’t to hire the most advisor you can; it’s to match the level of help to the actual complexity of your money. And there’s no penalty for starting small: an advisor who’s worth hiring will tell you honestly when you don’t need them yet, which is one more reason to interview two or three before you commit — the one who talks you out of over-buying is often the one worth hiring when you genuinely do.
Total swerve — nobody regrets knowing where to eat in O’Fallon, Illinois.
### Watch for the red flags
Walk away from anyone who guarantees returns, pressures you to act fast, is vague about fees, or wants you to write checks directly to them rather than a third-party custodian like Schwab or Fidelity. Trustworthy advisors are transparent, patient, and happy to put everything in writing.
### Local matters more than you’d think
A St. Louis-based advisor you can sit across the table from understands the things a 1-800 number never will — Missouri taxes, the local cost of living, the realities of buying a home here, and your actual life. Many area advisors offer a free introductory consultation, so meet two or three before you commit; the right fit is as much about trust and communication as it is about returns. A local advisor also tends to know the regional landscape you’re actually planning around — Missouri’s tax quirks, the cost of living here, the realities of the local housing and job markets — in a way a distant call center never will. That context won’t replace credentials and a clean regulatory record, but paired with them, it’s a real advantage: the person across the table understands the life the plan is supposed to fit.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the difference between a fiduciary and a regular financial advisor?
A.  A fiduciary is legally obligated to act in your best interest at all times. A non-fiduciary (typically a broker) is held to the SEC’s Regulation Best Interest — a “best interest” standard that applies only at the moment of a recommendation, which is weaker than a fiduciary’s ongoing duty of loyalty and can leave room for higher-commission choices. Always ask if an advisor is a fiduciary 100% of the time.
### Q. How do I check a financial advisor’s background?
A.  Use FINRA’s free BrokerCheck tool and the SEC’s Investment Adviser Public Disclosure site to verify an advisor’s licenses, employment history, and any disciplinary actions or complaints.
### Q. How much does a financial advisor cost?
A.  It depends on the model: fee-only advisors may charge a flat or hourly fee, or about 1% of assets managed per year; others earn commissions on products they sell. Always ask for the all-in cost, including underlying fund fees, in writing.
### Q. How do I verify a financial advisor’s background for free?
A.  Use three free tools: FINRA BrokerCheck (brokercheck.finra.org) for brokers, the SEC’s IAPD site (adviserinfo.sec.gov) for investment advisers and their Form ADV, and the CFP Board’s “Verify a CFP Professional” tool for planners. In Missouri, the Secretary of State’s Securities Division can confirm an adviser’s state registration and take complaints.
### Q. Do I need a financial advisor, or is a robo-advisor enough?
A.  If your situation is straightforward, a low-cost robo-advisor (often around 0.25% of assets) or a one-time hourly planning session may be all you need. A human advisor — ideally a CFP — earns their fee during complexity and transitions: an inheritance, a business sale, retirement drawdown, divorce, equity compensation, or a complicated tax and estate picture.
### Q. What’s the difference between fee-only, fee-based, and commission advisors?
A.  A fee-only advisor is paid only by you (flat, hourly, or a percentage of assets) and takes no commissions — the cleanest model. A fee-based advisor charges you a fee and can also earn commissions, a dual model with a built-in conflict. A commission advisor is paid by the products they sell. With fee-based and commission advisors especially, always ask exactly how a given recommendation makes them money.
### Q. Who regulates financial advisors in Missouri?
A.  Investment advisers operating in Missouri are generally registered with the Missouri Secretary of State’s Securities Division (those managing under about $100 million; larger firms register with the SEC). The Division can confirm an adviser’s registration status and takes complaints, so it’s a useful local check alongside FINRA BrokerCheck and the SEC’s IAPD site.

## Crash in Belleville? Your Deadline Is 3 Years Shorter. How to Find the Right St. Louis Lawyer
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-find-the-right-lawyer-in-st-louis-2026
Glass crunches under your shoes on the shoulder of I-64. Hazard lights tick. The other driver is already on the phone, talking fast. Or it’s the envelope you had to sign for: heavy paper, the name of a law firm you’ve never heard of, a deadline you don’t understand. Either way, the same question lands in your chest: who do I even call?
Your thumb is already over the number from the billboard. Wait one minute. Here’s what to do instead, in the order that matters.
Tonight, before bed: put every paper in one folder. The envelope, the police report number, the adjuster’s card, the photos of the car. Then write down what happened while it’s still loud in your head: the time, the exit, who said what. A lawyer works from details, and you’ll never remember them better than tonight.
Tomorrow morning: go to stllawyersearch.org, the free lawyer search run by the Bar Association of Metropolitan St. Louis; older guides still list a phone line for it, but the referral service now runs online. Pick your legal issue and it matches you with metro attorneys who handle it. Shortlist three or four.
Before you sign anything: look each one up with the Missouri Bar to confirm good standing. Missouri’s bar is mandatory, so every practicing lawyer in the state has to be a member. If the Missouri Bar can’t find them, walk away. Ask who will actually work your file, because some heavily advertised firms sign cases and refer them out to other lawyers. And get the fee in writing.
Then mind the river. Illinois generally gives you two years to file an injury lawsuit and Missouri generally gives you five, so the deadline for a crash in Belleville comes three years sooner than for the same crash in Brentwood.
Save this for the morning: Free lawyer match by legal issue: stllawyersearch.org. Check good standing: the Missouri Bar. Low income with a civil problem like an eviction? Hurt in Illinois: generally two years to file. In Missouri: generally five.
### How Do You Choose a Lawyer When You’ve Never Hired One?
Two first phone calls tell you most of what you need. In one, you describe the crash and the voice on the line says, “We handle everything.” In the other, the lawyer asks which side of the river it happened on, whether the case would land downtown in the City’s 22nd Circuit or out in Clayton at the County’s 21st, and when your doctor first saw you. Hire the second one.
That’s the whole idea. The best way to choose a lawyer is to match the right specialist to your exact problem, then check that person’s experience and standing. Law is narrow work. The defense attorney who was brilliant for your cousin is the wrong call for your divorce, and the estate lawyer who drew up your parents’ wills won’t help with a crash claim. So step one is naming the issue: family, criminal, personal injury, estate, business, employment, landlord-tenant. That one word decides who you need.
After that it comes down to four things: real experience in that exact area, a clean record, straight talk about fees, and fit, meaning someone you can sit across a desk from and tell the embarrassing part of the story. Most people find their lawyer one of three ways: a referral from someone they trust, the bar association’s free search, or an online search. Each one works if you do it carefully.
### The Paper in Your Hand Names the Lawyer You Need
Look at the paper in your hand. Its heading usually tells you who you need. A summons means a court case has started and the clock to answer is already running. A petition for dissolution of marriage calls for a family law attorney. A notice to vacate is landlord-tenant. A letter from the other driver’s insurance adjuster is personal injury. The other everyday areas are criminal defense, estate planning and probate, business and employment. Then there’s immigration, where the stakes run high enough that it’s worth reading how to find a trustworthy immigration lawyer in St. Louis before you make a single call.
One thing most people miss: a lawyer who works your specific area day in and day out will almost always beat a generalist. They know the local courts, the judges, the opposing attorneys, and the shortcuts that come only from repetition. So pin down which practice area your problem falls under before you search. Not sure? BAMSL’s free lawyer search below starts by asking you to pick the legal issue, which sorts most people out fast.
Wildly off-topic: someone still has to figure out dinner in Bethalto tonight.
### Why Should You Hire a Local Lawyer in St. Louis?
Because the courthouse, the license and the deadline are all local, and a St. Louis lawyer already knows all three. Start with the courthouse. The City of St. Louis is the 22nd Judicial Circuit and St. Louis County is the 21st, two separate courts with their own judges, clerks and habits. A lawyer who files there every week knows how its judges run a docket and which opposing firms settle. An out-of-town firm learns that on your bill.
Then the license. Missouri and Illinois license lawyers separately, so if the crash happened in Belleville or your landlord is in Edwardsville, you need someone admitted in Illinois. Plenty of St. Louis firms carry both licenses, so ask on the first call. The clock differs across the river too: Illinois generally gives you two years to file an injury lawsuit, Missouri generally five, so a Metro East crash runs on the shorter one.
And the meetings. A divorce or an injury case means months of document drops and sit-downs, and a lawyer twenty minutes away is one you’ll actually see, across a desk with the papers spread out between you. Those meetings are also where you learn whether the lawyer you hired is the one doing the work.
### Where Do You Actually Find a Lawyer in St. Louis?
St. Louis has an excellent, underused resource for exactly this: the Bar Association of Metropolitan St. Louis (BAMSL), whose old Lawyer Referral & Information Service now runs as St. Louis Lawyer Search, a free online directory at stllawyersearch.org. You pick the legal issue, and it matches you with metro-area attorneys who list that practice area, whose profiles you can read and contact directly. The search costs nothing. The lawyers charge their normal fees, and a match doesn’t promise anyone will take your case. BAMSL also says it doesn’t vouch for a matched lawyer’s fit, so still run the Missouri Bar check below. Questions about the service go to BAMSL at 314-421-4134.
Beyond BAMSL, three more paths work well: the Missouri Bar’s statewide “Find A Lawyer” search, which lets you look up private attorneys by practice area and location; personal referrals from friends, family, or another professional (an accountant or a lawyer in a different field is often a great source); and online directories and reviews, useful for building a shortlist as long as you verify what you find. Cast a small net - three or four names - then vet them, rather than hiring the first ad you see.
### How Do You Check If a Lawyer Is Any Good?
Before you hire anyone, do fifteen minutes of homework - it’s the single highest-value step most people skip. Start with the Missouri Bar: every practicing attorney in the state is licensed through it, and you can confirm a lawyer is in good standing and check their public disciplinary record. A lawyer who isn’t properly licensed in Missouri, or who has a history of discipline, is an immediate red flag.
Then look at experience and reputation: how long have they practiced in your type of case, and what do past clients say? Read reviews across a few sources rather than trusting a single glowing testimonial, and look for patterns - consistent praise for communication and results, or repeated complaints about being ignored. Finally, use the free consultation (most offer one) as your real test: a good lawyer explains your options in plain English, gives an honest read on your case rather than guaranteeing a win, and answers your questions without making you feel rushed or small. How they treat you in that first meeting tells you a lot about how they’ll treat your case.
### What Are the Red Flags When Hiring a Lawyer?
Trust your gut, and watch for a few warning signs. Be cautious of a lawyer who guarantees a specific outcome. No honest attorney can promise you’ll win, and the ones who do are selling, not advising. Other red flags: vague or evasive answers about fees (you should get costs in writing before you commit), poor communication from the very start (if they’re slow to respond while courting you, it rarely improves later), pressure to sign immediately, no clear written fee agreement, and a lawyer who talks over you or can’t explain your situation in language you understand.
A disciplinary history, an unwillingness to put terms in writing, or a bedside manner that leaves you uneasy are all good reasons to keep looking. You’re hiring someone for one of the hardest moments of your life. Being choosy is completely fair.
### What Does a Good Lawyer Cost?
Legal fees vary widely by the type of case and the lawyer’s experience, but they generally follow a few structures, and knowing them helps you compare. Hourly rates are common for business, family, and general matters. Flat fees are typical for well-defined jobs like a simple will, an uncontested divorce, or a basic contract. Contingency fees are standard in personal-injury cases - the lawyer takes an agreed percentage of your settlement and you generally pay nothing up front (and nothing if you don’t recover). Some matters also involve a retainer, an up-front deposit the lawyer bills against.
The most important cost rule has nothing to do with the number. Get it in writing. Before you hire anyone, ask for a clear written fee agreement that spells out the structure, the rate or percentage, and what expenses are extra. A reputable lawyer will happily provide one, and that free initial consultation is the right time to talk money openly. Don’t let an awkward fee conversation cost you later.

### What If You Can’t Afford a Lawyer?
If cost is the barrier, you still have real options in St. Louis - don’t assume you’re on your own. Legal Services of Eastern Missouri provides free civil legal help to people who qualify (based on income) across the St. Louis region, and it’s one of Missouri’s established legal-aid programs. For criminal cases where you can’t afford counsel, you have the right to a public defender. Many private attorneys also offer free consultations, work on contingency (so there’s no up-front cost) for injury cases, or can arrange payment plans. Law-school clinics and periodic free legal-advice events are additional resources. Being short on money doesn’t mean going without help here. You do have to ask, though, and early, because these programs run on limited capacity.
### What Should You Bring to the First Consultation?
Specifically facing a DWI? Here’s what a DUI lawyer costs in St. Louis.
Once you’ve booked that first meeting, a little preparation turns it from a nervous chat into a real evaluation. Bring the key documents (the accident report, the contract, the court papers, the lease) and a short written timeline of what happened, so the lawyer can give you an informed read instead of a guess. Write down your questions in advance - how many cases like mine have you handled, what are the likely outcomes, what will it cost, who will actually work on my file, and how will you keep me updated. Take notes, and pay attention to how they make you feel: a good lawyer leaves you clearer and calmer than you walked in, not more confused. And remember you’re interviewing them as much as they’re assessing you - it’s completely appropriate to meet two or three before deciding who earns your trust and your case.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. How do you look up if a lawyer is good?
A.  Start with the Missouri Bar, where every practicing Missouri attorney has to be a member: confirm they’re in good standing and look for any public discipline. Then read client reviews across several sources, looking for consistent patterns rather than a single testimonial, and use the free consultation to judge how clearly they explain your options. Experience in your exact type of case matters more than a flashy ad.
### Q. What are red flags when hiring a lawyer?
A.  Be cautious of anyone who guarantees a specific outcome, is vague about fees, pressures you to sign at the first meeting, or won’t put the fee agreement in writing. Poor communication early is another: if calls go unreturned while they’re winning your business, that rarely improves once they have it. A disciplinary history, or an inability to explain your situation in plain English, is a reason to keep looking.
### Q. What is the average cost of a good lawyer?
A.  It varies widely by case type and experience, and follows a few structures: hourly rates (common for business and family matters), flat fees (for defined jobs like a simple will or uncontested divorce), and contingency fees (standard in injury cases, where the lawyer takes a percentage of any settlement, often with nothing up front). The key rule is to get the fee structure in writing before you hire anyone.
### Q. What not to tell the attorney?
A.  Nothing about the facts. Conversations with your own lawyer are protected by attorney-client privilege, and hiding facts, even embarrassing ones, only handicaps their ability to help you. What to hold back is your bottom line in a fee negotiation. The real caution is what you say to others: don’t discuss the case with the other side or post about it online.
### Q. What is the 80/20 rule for lawyers?
A.  It’s the Pareto principle applied to legal work: roughly 80 percent of the results come from 20 percent of the effort, and in a practice a small share of cases or clients drives most of the work. For you as a client, the useful version is that a handful of facts and documents usually decide most of a case, so bring those to the first meeting.
### Q. Where can I get free legal advice in St. Louis?
A.  Legal Services of Eastern Missouri gives free civil legal help to low-income Missourians who qualify. BAMSL also points people to two free programs, the St. Louis Bankruptcy Pro Se Assistance Program and the St. Louis Federal Court Legal Advice Clinic. Free help is usually income-tested, so ask about eligibility first. If you’re charged with a crime and can’t afford counsel, you have the right to a public defender.
Injury cases work differently from most legal matters, particularly on fees and timelines. Hiring a Personal Injury Lawyer in St. Louis: Deadlines, Fees and the State Line covers what to ask before signing anything.

## St. Louis Furnaces Die in January. The Mistake Was October: A Seasonal Home Maintenance Checklist
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/a-seasonal-home-maintenance-checklist-for-st-louis-homeowners-2026
Click. Then nothing. It’s 5 a.m. in January in a brick two-family off Gravois, and you lie there listening for the furnace to catch, and the only sound in the house is the refrigerator and your own breath, which you can see. The thermostat says 58 and falling. You start calling HVAC numbers in the dark, and so does every neighbor whose furnace got ignored in October.
That night almost never starts in January. It starts on a mild Saturday in the fall when the furnace still works and nobody wants to spend money on something that isn’t broken. Most of the ugly surprises in a St. Louis house work the same way: a wet basement in April was a clogged gutter in November, and a cracked mortar joint in March was water that froze and thawed inside the brick a dozen times while you weren’t looking. The fix is not a heroic weekend. It’s a short list, done four times a year, at the moment it actually matters.
### What are some important seasonal home maintenance checklists for homeowners?
The good ones fit on an index card taped inside the basement door. For a St. Louis house, four checks carry most of the weight: the cooling system looked at in spring and the heating system in fall, a clean HVAC filter every month, water moved away from the foundation (gutters, downspouts, grading), and brick and mortar protected from the freeze-thaw swings that pry it apart. The timing is the whole trick. ENERGY STAR’s maintenance checklist notes that contractors get busy once summer and winter come, and here that means the first heat wave and the first January cold snap. So borrow the clock change. Clocks forward, call about the AC. Clocks back, call about the furnace.
### The job nobody remembers until the water heater is standing in it
Gutters and grading. It sounds boring because it is, right up until you’re standing in two inches of cold water by the water heater, socks soaked, the bottom of every cardboard box gone soft. In a clay-soil city, water that isn’t carried well away from the foundation is the beginning of most of the big repair bills. A downspout that dumps right at the corner of the house, or a flower bed that slopes back toward the wall, quietly feeds the problem every time it rains.
Here’s the part almost nobody knows. The moment you grab a shovel to regrade that bed or trench a downspout line out to the yard, you’re digging, and the state’s one-call center says it plainly on its page for homeowners: safe digging is everyone’s responsibility. State law says to give notice before you excavate, at least two working days, but not more than ten working days, ahead. Call too late and you’re stuck waiting with a pile of dirt on the lawn; call three weeks early and you’re outside the window. 811 is the free national before-you-dig service, so the call costs nothing. A gas line under a flower bed costs a great deal.
And before you rent a trencher at all, know this: the sewer district may pay you to keep that water in the yard instead. MSD will reimburse single-family households up to $4,000 for rainscaping, the rain gardens and plantings that drink a downspout’s runoff before it ever reaches the basement wall. Check MSD’s Project Clear rainscaping pages, or call MSD customer service at 1 (314) 768-6260, to see whether your address qualifies before you spend a dollar on regrading.
### Why a St. Louis house wears out differently
Walk down almost any block in Soulard, Tower Grove South or Benton Park and run your hand along the walls. Red brick, warm in the afternoon sun, gritty where the mortar has started to sand away. That brick is not an accident of taste. It traces back to a mattress. On May 17, 1849, a fire most likely started by a mattress airing out on the moored steamboat White Cloud broke loose with the burning boat, which drifted down the river setting 22 other steamboats alight before the flames reached the levee. Afterward, a new building code required new structures to be built of stone or brick. The city that grew out of those ashes is still standing, and a lot of us live in it.
Brick is tough, but it is not waterproof. Water soaks into old, soft mortar, freezes overnight, expands, thaws by lunch and soaks in a little deeper. Do that enough winters and a joint you could once scratch with a key turns to dust in your palm. The soil underneath plays its own game. Much of the region sits on clay that swells when it’s wet and shrinks when it’s dry, so a foundation here gets squeezed in a soggy spring and left hanging in a bone-dry August. And the summers are thick, the kind of humid where the basement smells like a wet towel by July.
Put those together and the pattern is obvious. Almost every expensive failure in a St. Louis house traces back to water in the wrong place or a system that ran too long without a look. The seasons below are built around that, nothing more.
### Spring, when winter sends the bill
The first warm Saturday is when you find out what the winter did. Walk the outside of the house slowly with your coffee. Look up at the gutters for sagging runs, look along the foundation for new hairline cracks, and look at the mortar joints at eye level. Then go down to the basement after the next hard rain and use your nose before your eyes. A musty smell that wasn’t there in February is the house telling you water found a way in. That’s also the week to call about the AC, before the first heat-wave forecast sends everyone to the phone at once.
Once nights stay above freezing, it’s caulk and paint season, and if the brushes come indoors the same weekend, check how long to wait before sleeping in a freshly painted room before you move the beds back.
### Summer, and the ground pulling away
In a long dry spell you can sometimes see it: a dark gap opening between the soil and the foundation wall, wide enough to slide a finger into. That’s the clay shrinking. Gentle, even watering along the foundation during a drought helps keep it from pulling away, but flooding it does the opposite and pushes water at the basement wall. Keep the AC filter on its monthly schedule, because the system is working its hardest now, and keep mulch and soil from piling up against siding and wood trim, where termites and rot both like to start.
The filter is the cheap one people forget. Once a month, slide it out of the return in the basement and hold it up to the kitchen window. Gray felt that blocks the sun is costing you on the electric bill and wearing on the blower. If you can’t see daylight through it, you already know.
### Fall is the season you can’t skip
If you only do one season well, make it this one. Clean the gutters after the leaves come down, not before, or you’ll do it twice. Disconnect hoses and drain the outdoor spigots before the first hard freeze. Book the furnace check when you set the clocks back. Air-seal and insulate the attic, which cuts the heating bill and is the best defense against ice dams. And if you use the fireplace, have the chimney looked at before the first fire; here is what a chimney sweep costs in St. Louis.
If the basement is too full to reach the furnace filter, start with the decluttering mistakes to skip before you call an organizer.
If you have an in-ground irrigation system, don’t skip the fall blow-out; our guide to sprinkler repair and winterizing explains why it matters in our freeze-thaw climate.
Hand the furnace, the tuckpointing and the roof to a pro. Book them in the shoulder months, when crews have openings, and search St Louis Near Me Directory for HVAC techs, masons and roofers before something breaks, not after.
If you’re the HVAC tech, the mason or the one-person handyman crew homeowners are searching for this fall, a listing puts your name in front of more customers right when they’re ready to book. See how it works or claim your spot.
### Is your old brick quietly turning to sand?
Here is a test you can do this afternoon. Pick a mortar joint on the north side of the house, where the sun barely reaches and the wall stays damp longest after a rain. Press a house key into it and drag. If it scratches a clean little line, the joint is doing its job. If it crumbles out in a soft trickle onto your shoe, that joint has been taking on water for years, and the brick on either side of it is next.
A lot of older St. Louis houses were laid with soft mortar on purpose. Soft mortar is meant to be the sacrificial part of the wall: it gives a little, lets moisture move out, and wears away before the brick does. The mistake people make is patching it with a hard, rigid modern mix because it seems stronger. Stronger is the problem. When the mortar is harder than the brick, the wall can’t breathe the way it was built to, moisture gets trapped, and the face of the brick can start to flake and pop off in winter. You’ll see it as chips of red on the sidewalk in March.
So when you hire for tuckpointing, ask one question before price: what mortar will you match to this house, and how? A mason who knows old brick will have an answer right away. And before anyone touches the front of the house, find out whether your block is in a local historic district. The Cultural Resources Office (CRO) of the City of St. Louis governs local historic districts, and those districts typically come with design codes enacted by ordinance, so the mortar, the windows and even the brick color on a street-facing wall can be someone else’s call. Ask the CRO first. Finding out after the scaffolding goes up is the expensive way to learn it. Look too at the chimney, the parapet and the spots under leaky gutters, because that’s where walls fail first. Fixing a few joints every year or two costs far less than rebuilding a whole face of a wall later, and it keeps a house that has already stood for a century standing for the next one.
### Winter, and the sharp drop
St. Louis winters swing. A soft forty-degree week, then a night that drops hard and fast, and that’s when exposed pipes in a crawl space or an outside wall let go. Before the cold snap, insulate exposed lines, keep the heat on even when you travel, and on the hardest nights let a faucet on an exposed line drip. Ice dams form when attic heat melts roof snow that refreezes at the cold eaves; chipping at the ice won’t fix it, the attic work you did in fall will. Test the smoke and carbon monoxide detectors while the furnace is running daily. And after any midwinter thaw, when the snow melts off in one gray afternoon and the yard turns to soup, go down and listen for the sump pump. That hum is the sound of the system working. Silence, with water in the pit, is the sound of a long night ahead.
Side trip while the coffee’s hot: every business service in the metro, on one map.
### A quick list to tape inside the basement door
Spring (clocks forward): AC check, gutters, foundation walk, sump pump test with a bucket of water.
Summer: filter monthly, even watering in drought, soil and mulch off the siding.
Fall (clocks back): furnace check, gutters after leaf drop, spigots drained, attic sealed, chimney.
Winter: pipes insulated, heat never off, detectors tested, sump pump checked after a thaw.
Tie each season to something you already notice, the first mow, the clock change, the first hard freeze on the forecast. It’s the same habit behind managing your St. Louis services in one place, and it stops depending on memory.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What are 5 items that regularly scheduled maintenance will check?
A.  The HVAC filter and the system itself, the water heater, the sump pump, gutter flow and downspout discharge, and the seals around windows and doors. Notice how many of them come down to keeping water where it belongs.
### Q. What maintenance items should be checked during a seasonal startup?
A.  Before cooling season: the filter, a professional AC check and a test run before the first hot week rather than during it. Before heating season: the filter again, a furnace check, the flue and the smoke and carbon monoxide detectors. ENERGY STAR suggests timing those visits to the spring and fall clock changes.
### Q. What is included in a maintenance checklist?
A.  Seasonal work grouped by system: roof and gutters, HVAC filters and service, plumbing and the water heater, exterior caulk, paint and masonry, and the safety items like detectors and the sump pump. The point of a list is that none of it depends on remembering.
### Q. What’s the most overlooked home maintenance task?
A.  Gutters and grading, together. Here, with clay soil and freeze-thaw swings, water that isn’t carried away from the foundation is where the expensive problems start. Most people notice the basement first, and by then the fix is no longer an afternoon with a downspout extension.
### Q. Why do St. Louis homes need special masonry care?
A.  So much of the city is old brick, and freeze-thaw slowly breaks down mortar joints. Older homes often used soft mortar, and repointing them with a hard, rigid mix can trap moisture and damage the brick. That’s why tuckpointing an older house belongs with someone who knows historic masonry.

## The Best Kids' Music, Art, and Dance Classes in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/the-best-kids-music-art-and-dance-classes-in-st-louis-2026
Every parent knows the moment: your kid won’t stop drumming on the table, can’t stop drawing, or twirls through the kitchen like the floor is a stage. That spark is worth feeding — and St. Louis is full of places ready to turn it into a real skill (and a whole lot of confidence).
Whether your child is into music, art, dance, theater, or robotics, here are some of the best places for kids’ classes and lessons across the metro.
### Music lessons
The Community Music School of Webster University — now over a century old, with locations in Webster Groves and Chesterfield — offers private lessons on just about every instrument, plus Suzuki strings and Kindermusik for the littlest ones. For something more rock-and-roll, Shock City School of Music runs group and private lessons on guitar, drums, piano, and more, starting as young as preschool.
### Art classes
Craft Alliance on Delmar (in the Delmar Maker District) puts kids’ hands on real clay, fiber, glass, and printmaking, with summer camps and free Family Saturdays. In Dutchtown, the South Broadway Art Project is a full ceramics studio with kids’ pottery classes — wheel and hand-building — for ages seven and up.
### Dance studios
For ballet and beyond, the Saint Louis Ballet School in Chesterfield (affiliated with the professional company) teaches ages two through eighteen across ballet, jazz, tap, and hip-hop. The Dance Center of Kirkwood brings classical ballet, tap, jazz, and pointe in a nurturing setting, and Central Studio Academy (Central West End and Webster Groves) adds aerial arts and tumbling to the mix.
### Theater, multi-arts, and STEM
The crown jewel of the metro’s arts education is COCA (Center of Creative Arts) in University City — a multidisciplinary center offering dance, theater, visual art, and music for preschoolers through teens, plus twelve weeks of summer camps. For the stage, Metro Theater Company in Grand Center runs acting and improv camps, and the Gateway Center for Performing Arts offers musical-theatre classes for grades K-12. And for the future engineers, Smart Kids Robotics (a West County program) and Wize Computing Academy turn coding and robotics into hands-on fun.
### For the littlest ones (and a few more picks)
The list above skews toward school-age kids, so here are a few that widen the range — especially down toward babies and toddlers, plus a makerspace and a second music option. For infants through age five, Music Together classes (offered around the metro by providers like Little Music Makers) are early-childhood music-and-movement done with a caregiver in the room — the sweet spot before formal lessons make sense. For a music program with a band, STL Rock School in Olivette teaches guitar, drums, piano, bass, and vocals and runs rock-band camps that end in a real concert — a different energy than one-on-one lessons. And for a hands-on STEAM crossover, MADE for Kids (from the team behind the Magic House, on Delmar) is a genuine makerspace where kids screen-print, 3D-print, work with clay, and build stop-motion films — art and technology under one roof. Any of these fills a gap the core list leaves open, so start from your child’s age and interest and work outward.
One more note for families weighing a bigger commitment: several of the metro’s marquee programs run pre-professional or company tracks for kids who fall hard for their art — a serious ballet trainee path, an advanced COCA track, a rock-band ensemble that gigs. You don’t need to think about any of that on day one, but it’s reassuring to know the ceiling is high here. A kid who starts with a tentative trial class at seven can, if the love takes hold, find a genuine pathway a few years later without leaving St. Louis to do it.
### Matching the class to your kid’s age
Age is the fastest way to narrow the field. For babies and toddlers (0–4), look for play-based, caregiver-involved programs — Music Together, Kindermusik through the Community Music School, and Suzuki strings, which can start as young as four. For early elementary (5–8), the world opens up: intro art at Craft Alliance, first dance classes at the Saint Louis Ballet School or Dance Center of Kirkwood, beginner instruments, and multidisciplinary sampling at COCA, which lets a kid try a bit of everything before committing. For older kids and tweens (9–13), look for skill-building and performance — pottery at the South Broadway Art Project, rock-band camps at STL Rock School, theater and improv at Metro Theater Company, and pre-pointe or company-track ballet. And for teens, seek out programs with a serious or pre-professional path (COCA’s advanced tracks, Gateway’s musical-theatre classes, a dance company’s trainee program). The right level keeps a kid challenged without overwhelming them, which is most of what keeps them coming back.
### Choosing well: the teacher matters more than the building
When you tour a program, it’s tempting to be sold by a shiny lobby or a long trophy shelf, but the thing that actually determines whether your kid thrives is the teacher in the room. Watch how an instructor talks to the children mid-class: are they warm, patient, and quick to praise effort, or focused only on the most advanced kid? Ask who will actually teach your child — the founder in the brochure, or a rotating staff — and whether it’s the same person each week, because continuity builds the trust a shy kid needs to take risks. A few practical questions cut through the marketing: How big are the classes? (smaller means more individual attention). Are there performance or recital opportunities, and are they low-pressure or high-stakes? What’s the make-up policy when you miss for illness or travel? And crucially, use the free trial almost every studio offers — let your child sit in on a real class and read their face afterward. A kid who bounces out excited found the right fit; a kid who’s quiet and drained probably didn’t, no matter how good the program looks on paper.
Random, but: The Hill is a good excuse to skip cooking.
### Keeping it fun (and avoiding burnout)
The goal at this age isn’t a prodigy — it’s a kid who loves the thing enough to stick with it, and that’s easy to accidentally undermine. Resist the urge to over-schedule: one or two activities a child is genuinely into beats five they’re dragged to, and unstructured downtime is where a lot of creativity actually happens. Let them sample before they commit — the six-week “maybe I’ll like guitar” trial is exactly what these intro classes are for, and quitting something that isn’t clicking to try something that might is a feature, not a failure. Praise effort and enjoyment over results (“you worked really hard on that” lands better than “you’re so talented”), and keep the practice-at-home conversations light, because the fastest way to kill a love of piano is to turn it into a nightly fight. And watch for the real win, which usually isn’t a ribbon: a kid who starts doing the thing on their own, unprompted, because they want to. That’s the whole point — and it’s worth far more than early mastery.
### A quick map by discipline
If you already know what your kid’s into, here’s the shorthand. Music: Community Music School of Webster University (Webster Groves + Chesterfield), Shock City School of Music (Benton Park, Maplewood, Maryland Heights), STL Rock School (Olivette), plus Music Together for the littlest. Visual art / making: Craft Alliance (Delmar), South Broadway Art Project (Dutchtown, ceramics), and MADE for Kids (Delmar, STEAM makerspace). Dance: Saint Louis Ballet School (Chesterfield), Dance Center of Kirkwood, and Central Studio Academy (CWE + Webster Groves). Theater: Metro Theater Company (Grand Center) and Gateway Center for Performing Arts. STEM: Wize Computing Academy and Smart Kids Robotics (West County). A bit of everything: COCA in University City, the metro’s multidisciplinary anchor, where a kid can try dance, theater, art, and music in one place. Whatever the spark is, there’s a St. Louis program built for it.
### Camps vs. year-round classes: which to try first
If you’re not sure whether to commit, a camp is the low-risk way in. Many of these programs — COCA, Metro Theater Company, Craft Alliance, STL Rock School, the Saint Louis Ballet School — run summer or school-break camps that pack a week or two of immersion into a single burst, with a showcase or a finished project at the end. It’s a perfect trial balloon: your kid gets a real taste of an art form without a year-long tuition commitment, and you find out whether the spark is real before you sign up for the season. Year-round classes, by contrast, are where actual skill compounds — the weekly rhythm is what turns a curious beginner into a capable young musician, dancer, or artist over time. A sensible path for a lot of families is camp first, then, if your kid comes home lit up, roll into the fall session at the same place, where they’ll already know the space and a teacher. Watch the calendar, too: popular camps and fall classes at the marquee programs fill early, so the parents who plan a season ahead get the spots and the schedules they want.
### How to find the right fit
Weighing a class that is less about art and more about safety? Read the age most St. Louis parents get swim lessons wrong.
Picking the studio itself is its own decision, and it works differently for grown-ups than for a six-year-old — here is how to choose a dance studio in St. Louis.
Most studios offer a trial class or a no-pressure tour, so let your child sample a couple before committing — the right teacher matters more than the fanciest space. Ask about class sizes, recital opportunities, and make-up policies. And keep it fun: the goal at this age is a love of the craft, not perfection. ### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Where can my child take music lessons in St. Louis?
A.  The Community Music School of Webster University (Webster Groves and Chesterfield) offers lessons on nearly every instrument plus Suzuki and Kindermusik, and Shock City School teaches group and private lessons starting in preschool.
### Q. What is the best all-around arts program for kids in St. Louis?
A.  COCA (Center of Creative Arts) in University City is the metro’s premier multidisciplinary arts center, offering dance, theater, visual art, and music for ages preschool through high school, plus summer camps.
### Q. Where can kids take dance classes in St. Louis?
A.  The Saint Louis Ballet School in Chesterfield (ages 2-18), the Dance Center of Kirkwood, and Central Studio Academy in the Central West End and Webster Groves all offer strong kids’ dance programs.
### Q. Where can babies and toddlers take classes in St. Louis?
A.  For ages 0–5, look for caregiver-involved, play-based programs: Music Together (offered around the metro by providers such as Little Music Makers) and Kindermusik through the Community Music School of Webster University are the go-to early-childhood music options. Suzuki strings, also at the Community Music School, can begin as young as four.
### Q. How much do kids’ classes cost in St. Louis, and what should I ask?
A.  Costs vary widely by discipline and format — group classes and camps are generally more affordable than private lessons or company-track programs. Most studios offer a free trial class or tour, so use it. Ask about class sizes, recital or performance opportunities, make-up policies for missed classes, and any recital, costume, or materials fees on top of tuition before you enroll.
### Q. Should I start my child in a camp or a year-round class?
A.  A camp is the lower-risk way to test interest — programs like COCA, Metro Theater Company, Craft Alliance, and STL Rock School run week-long summer and break camps that end in a showcase, so your child gets real immersion without a season-long commitment. If they come home excited, roll into the year-round classes, where weekly practice is what actually builds skill over time. Popular camps and fall sessions fill early, so plan ahead.

## New to St. Louis? Your Move-In Setup Checklist
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/new-to-st-louis-your-move-in-setup-checklist-2026
You found the place, you’ve got the keys, and there’s a mountain of boxes by the door. Welcome to St. Louis! Before you collapse onto the couch, there’s a short list of get-set-up tasks that’ll save you headaches later — and as a new resident, a couple of them come with real deadlines and penalties, so they’re worth doing in the first week or two.
Here’s your move-in checklist for getting settled in the St. Louis metro, from utilities and inspections to the local quirks nobody tells you about.
### Turn on the utilities
Electric: Ameren Missouri is the electric utility for the St. Louis area — set up service before your move-in date so you’re not unpacking in the dark.
Natural gas: Spire (formerly Laclede Gas) is the area’s gas provider for the city and eastern Missouri.
Water: It depends where you live. Inside the city, it’s the City of St. Louis Water Division; across most of the county, it’s Missouri American Water. A few small municipalities run their own systems, so confirm by your address.
Sewer: The Metropolitan St. Louis Sewer District (MSD) handles wastewater and stormwater for the city and most of the county, and it’s billed separately from your water.
One city-specific wrinkle: in the City of St. Louis, your water and trash are combined on a single water/refuse bill through the Collector of Revenue, while sewer (MSD) comes as its own bill. In the county, water and trash are usually separate. Set up whichever accounts apply before day one.
### Get connected: internet
For home internet, the metro is well covered. AT&T Fiber has the widest fiber footprint in the city with fast symmetrical plans; Spectrum offers cable almost everywhere with no data caps; and T-Mobile 5G Home Internet is a no-contract, no-installation option that’s handy for renters or anyone who doesn’t want to wait on a technician. Availability is address-specific, so plug your new address into each provider’s checker to see what actually reaches your block.
### Sort out trash and recycling
In the City of St. Louis, trash service is run by the city’s Refuse Division for a flat fee of $14 a month per dwelling unit that shows up on your water/refuse bill — not your property taxes. That fee bundles in trash, recycling, yard waste, monthly bulk pickup, and 12 transfer-station drop-offs a year. Recycling changed in August 2025: the city ended alley-dumpster recycling, so homes with blue roll carts still get curbside pickup while alley households now use an expanded network of drop-off sites. Check the current setup for your address.
In St. Louis County, it varies by municipality — some cities contract a single hauler for all residents, and in others you arrange service with a private hauler yourself. When in doubt, ask your municipality’s office or a neighbor which hauler and day you’re on.
### Get your Missouri license, plates, and inspections
This is the part with a clock on it. The Missouri Department of Revenue expects you to switch to a Missouri driver’s license as soon as you establish residency, and you have 30 days from becoming a resident to title and register your vehicle. Don’t let it slide: the inspections and tax paperwork below take longer than the license office visit.
For the license: if you’re moving in with a valid out-of-state license (or one expired 184 days or less), you skip the written and driving tests — you’ll take the vision and road-sign tests and bring proof of identity, lawful status, your Social Security number, and a Missouri address. If you want a REAL ID (required to board domestic flights since May 7, 2025), bring two documents from two different sources proving your Missouri address.
For the vehicle, there are two St. Louis-area inspection catches plus a tax step:
Emissions testing: Vehicles registered in the City of St. Louis and St. Louis, St. Charles, and Jefferson counties need a Gateway Vehicle Inspection Program emissions test. It’s every two years (even model years in even years, odd in odd), for gas vehicles from model year 1996 on and diesels from 1997 on, at 8,500 pounds or less. It’s also required whenever a title changes hands.
Safety inspection: Missouri still requires a state safety inspection, separate from emissions, every two years. Vehicles are exempt for their first ten model years if they’re under 150,000 miles, so an older car will need both. Even an exempt car needs a quick VIN and odometer check (an ID/OD inspection) when a new resident titles it here; a safety inspection covers it.
Statement of non-assessment: Because Missouri charges personal property tax on vehicles, new residents who didn’t own property here on January 1 first get a statement of non-assessment (a tax waiver) from their county or city Collector or Assessor, then use it to register. Budget a little time for the paperwork.
### Don’t forget the personal property tax
Here’s the one new arrivals are most likely to miss. Missouri charges an annual personal property tax on things like vehicles, and you have to declare what you owned as of January 1 each year with your county (or city) Assessor. In the City, the declaration is due April 1, and late filers pay a 10% penalty; St. Louis County’s 2026 notice asked for it by April 30, and the state penalty for a late county return runs $15 to $105. Deadlines can shift, so check your Assessor’s site rather than assuming. The actual bill arrives from the Collector in the fall and is due by December 31. Put a reminder on your calendar now; it’s an easy thing to forget in your first year and an annoying one to be penalized for.
Unrelated, and we know it — where to eat in Cool Valley.
### Register to vote and grab a library card
To vote in the next election, register through your local election authority or the Missouri Secretary of State’s online portal — the deadline is 27 days before Election Day. You can also register by mail or at the DMV while you’re handling your license. And don’t sleep on the libraries: both the St. Louis Public Library (city) and the St. Louis County Library offer free cards to area residents, with far more than books — events, museum passes, tools, seeds, and streaming media among them.
### Save the number that fixes things: 311
If you’re in the City of St. Louis, program in the Citizens’ Service Bureau: dial 311 (or 314-622-4800) to report a pothole, a missed trash pickup, a broken streetlight, graffiti, or other non-emergency issues. They log it, route it, and let you track it. St. Louis County municipalities have their own non-emergency lines, so find your city’s once you know where you are.
### A few more first-week tasks
File a change of address with USPS so mail follows you, then update the address on your bank, insurance, employer, and subscriptions.
Line up renters or homeowners insurance before move-in day — many leases and all mortgages require it.
Know your flood and sewer-backup risk. Parts of the metro sit in low, older areas prone to basement backups; ask about a backwater valve or a rider on your policy, especially if you’re near a creek or the rivers.
Find your trash, recycling, and street-sweeping days so you’re not the house with cans out on the wrong morning.
### Getting around your first weeks
St. Louis is a driving town for most people, but it’s worth knowing your options. MetroLink light rail connects the airport, downtown, the Central West End, and Shrewsbury, and MetroBus fills in the rest — genuinely useful if you live or work near a line, and a cheap way to get to a Cardinals game without parking downtown. Most of the metro, though, is spread out enough that a car is the default, and street parking rules vary by neighborhood (watch for permit zones and street-sweeping days in the city). If you’re carless for a stretch between moving trucks, rideshare and the region’s bike- and scooter-share options cover short trips downtown and in the Central West End. One local quirk worth learning early: the metro is a patchwork of nearly ninety municipalities in St. Louis County alone, so speed limits, parking rules, and even trash days can change the moment you cross a street. When in doubt, your municipality’s website is the fastest way to get the specifics for exactly where you live.
### Budget for the setup costs
A move always costs more than the truck. In your first few weeks, plan for utility deposits or connection fees (some providers waive them with good credit or autopay), the title, registration, plate, and inspection fees for your vehicle, and that first combined water/refuse bill in the city. Renters should budget a security deposit and renters insurance; buyers will see the personal property tax bill land in the fall. None of it is huge on its own, but it stacks up, so it helps to keep a small cushion for the “welcome to town” expenses rather than spending every dollar on furniture the first week. For the taxes that follow you after move-in week, from the yearly bill on your car to the city earnings tax, see our St. Louis money guide. A good rule of thumb: knock out the deadline items (utilities, license, registration, insurance) first, since those are the ones that cost you money or a penalty if you wait, and let the nice-to-haves like the perfect couch come later once the essentials are handled and the bills are predictable.
### Then go meet your neighbors
Once the boxes are unpacked, the best way to feel at home is to plug in. Find your neighborhood association, explore the local restaurants and shops, and start collecting your own list of go-to spots — that’s where St. Louis really wins you over. A quiet corner bakery, a park you didn’t know about, a mechanic you trust: those are the things that turn a new address into home.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the first thing you should do when moving to another state?
A.  Get the house running, then start the clocks. Set up electric (Ameren Missouri), gas (Spire), water and sewer before move-in day and file a USPS change of address. Then turn to the state deadlines: Missouri expects you to switch your driver’s license as soon as you’re a resident, and you have 30 days to title and register your car, which in the St. Louis area can mean an emissions test, a safety inspection and a personal property tax waiver first.
### Q. What documents do I need to switch my license to Missouri?
A.  Bring your out-of-state license, proof of identity, proof of lawful status, your Social Security number and proof of your Missouri address; for a REAL ID, that means two address documents from two different sources, dated within the past year. With a valid license, or one expired 184 days or less, Missouri waives the written and driving tests, but you’ll still take the vision and road-sign tests. A REAL ID is what you need to board domestic flights.
### Q. What is considered proof of residency in Missouri?
A.  For a Missouri license or REAL ID, the Department of Revenue accepts documents like a utility bill, a bank or credit card statement, government mail, an insurance document, a lease or mortgage statement, or a voter registration card, as long as each shows your name and Missouri address and is dated within the past year. A REAL ID needs two of them from two different sources, and only one can be a housing document like a lease. P.O. boxes don’t count.
### Q. How much does a new license plate cost in Missouri?
A.  For a passenger car it depends on taxable horsepower: a one-year registration runs $18.25 to $51.25 (two years, $36.50 to $102.50), plus a $9 processing fee per year. Titling adds $8.50 and another $9 processing fee. Sales tax generally isn’t due on a car you’ve owned for 90 days or more before you title it here. Budget for your emissions and safety inspections too, and bring your personal property tax waiver to the license office.
### Q. Is Missouri going away from vehicle inspections?
A.  Not as of October 2026. A 2026 bill to end safety inspections died in the Senate, an attempt to attach it to another bill was dropped before that bill was signed, and the Department of Revenue has called the “no more inspections” posts misinformation. Missouri still requires a safety inspection every two years once a vehicle is past ten model years or 150,000 miles, and the St. Louis area still requires Gateway emissions tests. Check dor.mo.gov before you skip one.
### Q. Why do you have to pay personal property tax?
A.  Because Missouri lets counties and cities tax personal property, mainly cars, trucks, boats and RVs, and that money helps fund local schools, libraries, fire districts and other services. You declare what you owned on January 1 to your county or city Assessor each spring, and the bill is due December 31. New arrivals feel it twice: you need a waiver (a statement of non-assessment) to register a car you didn’t own here on January 1, and your first full bill lands the following fall.
### Q. What is the 183 day rule in Missouri?
A.  It’s part of how Missouri decides who owes state income tax as a resident. You’re a resident if Missouri is your domicile, or if you keep a permanent place to live here and spend more than 183 days of the year in the state. For a move, that usually means filing as a part-year resident for the year you arrive, reporting the income you earned after you moved in.
### Q. When is the voter registration deadline in Missouri?
A.  The fourth Wednesday before an election, which works out to 27 days before a Tuesday election; for the November 3, 2026 general election that was October 7. You can register online through the Missouri Secretary of State, by mail (postmarked by the deadline), in person at your local election authority, or at a license office while you switch your driver’s license.

## A First-Time Homebuyer's Guide to St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/a-first-time-homebuyer-s-guide-to-st-louis-2026
The sticker shock runs backwards here. A typical St. Louis home sells for far less than the national median, so it remains one of the most affordable major metros in the country, and ownership stays within reach for first-timers who’d be priced out almost anywhere else. Affordable isn’t the same as easy, though — not in this market. Going in prepared is what separates the buyers who close from the ones who keep getting outbid.
This guide runs through it in plain English: what the market looks like right now, the down-payment help that actually exists, the older-home quirks worth knowing, and where to find honest guidance before you sign anything. Start with the market, because it shapes every decision that follows.
### St. Louis is affordable — but it’s a seller’s market
The U.S. median home sells for around $400,000. In the city of St. Louis, it’s been running closer to $250,000 — one of the best affordability pictures of any large metro. Tight inventory is the catch. Homes have been going in about a month, selling at roughly 98% of asking, and better than a third close above list price. Cheap and competitive, in the same breath. Line up your financing before you fall for a place, not after.
Price alone can mislead you. Some of the lowest numbers sit in North County and North City neighborhoods that have absorbed decades of disinvestment, so read a price next to schools, commute, and the home’s condition rather than on its own. Property taxes deserve a line in the budget too. St. Louis County’s effective rate lands on the higher end for Missouri, and it feeds straight into your monthly payment.
### Get help with the down payment
First-timers here leave more money on the table at this step than anywhere else, usually because nobody told them the help exists. The programs worth knowing:
Missouri Housing Development Commission (MHDC) — its First Place and Next Step programs pair a competitive 30-year fixed mortgage with down-payment assistance of up to about 4% of the loan amount, given as a second loan that’s fully forgiven after 10 years in the home. You can take the forgivable assistance or a discounted interest rate. What you cannot do is combine a First Place loan with a Mortgage Credit Certificate (MCC) — MHDC’s First Place operations manual states plainly that the two may not be used together. An MCC turns a chunk of your annual mortgage interest into a federal tax credit, so if that is worth more to you than the down payment help, it is a decision to make before you apply rather than after. Minimum credit score is generally 640. First Place is aimed at first-time buyers; Next Step allows higher incomes and repeat buyers. Income and price limits apply (roughly a $510,000 purchase-price cap and household income limits in the low-to-mid $100,000s for the St. Louis area — check the current figures).
HomeSTL (City of St. Louis, via the St. Louis Development Corporation) — relaunched in 2026 and much bigger than it used to be: a forgivable, 0% interest loan of up to $40,000 citywide, or up to $50,000 in a HUD Qualified Census Tract, with no monthly payments and forgiveness over ten years. You need to be a first-time buyer (no ownership in three years), at or below 80% of area median income, buying within the City of St. Louis, and completing HUD-approved homebuyer education. It’s funded from a fixed pot and reservations run until the money is gone (or the program’s 2026 deadline), so move early and use one of its approved lenders.
Beyond Housing — the metro’s largest HUD-approved counseling agency and its biggest down-payment-assistance provider, offering roughly $7,000–$10,000 as a 5-year forgivable loan. Important: Beyond Housing serves St. Louis County, St. Charles County, and Jefferson County — not the City. You’ll need to finish its homebuyer education and one-on-one counseling first.
St. Charles County runs its own Down Payment Loan Program — up to $10,000, 0% interest, forgivable after five years, for buyers in the county’s program area (first-time status isn’t even required).
USDA, FHA, and VA loans — if you’re buying in an outer county (Franklin, Lincoln, Warren and similar), a USDA loan can mean zero down. FHA lets first-timers put down as little as 3.5% with a 580+ score (lenders often want ~620–640 in practice), and VA loans give eligible veterans 0% down with no monthly mortgage insurance.
Because terms, income limits, and availability change, work with an MHDC-approved lender and confirm the current details before you count on any single program.
### Which program works where
A quick map, since eligibility is mostly about location:
City of St. Louis: HomeSTL + MHDC (+ possible MCC).
St. Louis County: Beyond Housing + MHDC.
St. Charles County: the county HOME program + Beyond Housing + MHDC.
Outer/rural counties: USDA zero-down + MHDC.
MHDC is the common thread almost everywhere, so it’s a smart first call no matter which county you’re shopping.
### Know the steps
The sequence rarely surprises anyone. Check your credit and budget, get pre-approved for a mortgage (St. Louis sellers rarely take an offer seriously without a pre-approval letter), find a buyer’s agent, tour homes, make an offer with earnest money, get a home inspection and a lender appraisal, then close — usually about a month after your offer is accepted. Plan for closing costs of roughly 2–5% of the price on top of your down payment.
A couple of Missouri specifics work in your favor. Missouri has no real-estate transfer tax — a genuine savings compared with many states. And most closings here are handled by a title company; a real-estate attorney is not required, though you’re free to hire one.
### Figure out your real budget first
Get clear on what you can actually carry each month before you tour a single house. Sticker price is the least of it. Lenders weigh your debt-to-income ratio (many programs cap it around 45%), so your car payment, student loans, and credit cards all shape how much home you qualify for. The monthly payment covers principal and interest, then keeps going: PITI — principal, interest, taxes, and insurance — plus PMI if you put less than 20% down.
Those extras add up fast around here. In higher-tax St. Louis County municipalities, taxes and insurance can pile on a few hundred dollars a month, so run the full number, not just the mortgage. Keep a cushion after closing, too. Older St. Louis homes have a way of needing a water heater or a furnace the week after you’ve spent everything, so don’t drain your savings to the last dollar for the down payment.
### Making a competitive offer without overpaying
When a third of homes sell above asking, first-timers tend to do one of two things: overbid in a panic, or keep losing out. A good buyer’s agent threads that needle. They pull recent comparable sales so you know what a home is really worth, advise on earnest money, and shape an offer that stands out without wrecking your budget. Your single biggest advantage is a strong, current pre-approval letter — it tells a seller the financing is solid.
Price is not the only lever, either. Flexibility on the closing date, a slightly larger earnest deposit, or trimming small repair requests can all make an offer more appealing without raising the number. One move to skip: waiving the inspection to win a bid. On a century-old brick home, that’s how a “deal” turns into a five-figure surprise. Assistance programs like MHDC and HomeSTL work with normal financed offers, so getting help and staying competitive aren’t a trade-off.

### Two St. Louis quirks to budget for
Older homes need a real inspection. St. Louis has one of the largest stocks of pre-1940 brick homes in the Midwest. They’re charming and solid, but watch for foundation movement (our clay soil swells and shrinks), aging knob-and-tube wiring, old plumbing, and lead paint. A thorough inspection — and sometimes a specialist for the foundation or electrical — is money well spent. Once you’re in, our seasonal home maintenance checklist helps you protect the investment, and if repairs are looming, see our guide to government home improvement grants.
Occupancy inspections. Some St. Louis-area municipalities require a point-of-sale occupancy inspection before a home can change hands — separate from your buyer’s inspection. Rules vary city by city and the waits can run several weeks, so ask early which apply to your address.
### Get free, honest guidance first
Sit down with a HUD-approved housing counselor before you talk to a single lender. It’s low-cost or free, and it’s often required to unlock the assistance programs above anyway. In St. Louis, Justine Petersen (314-533-2411) and Beyond Housing both run homebuyer education and one-on-one counseling that connects you to lenders, agents, and down-payment help. Habitat for Humanity St. Louis offers a sweat-equity path to ownership for qualifying families. A counselor reads your real numbers, flags what could trip up your loan, and gets you shopping on facts instead of guesswork.
### Where first-timers are buying
First-timers cluster in a handful of value pockets. North County suburbs like Florissant and Hazelwood, mid-county Overland, and in-city neighborhoods like Tower Grove South and Dutchtown all pull them in; over in St. Charles County, growing suburbs such as St. Peters and O’Fallon trade a higher price point for newer homes. Dozens of metro neighborhoods still list homes under $200,000, rare for a major city. Inventory is tight, though, so move fast and lean on that pre-approval when the right one surfaces.
