## Best Tutoring and Learning Centers Across the St. Louis Metro
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/best-tutoring-and-learning-centers-across-the-st-louis-metro
Report cards come home, and suddenly the kitchen table turns into a battleground. Maybe it is fractions in third grade, or chemistry that stopped making sense in October, or the looming ACT that decides which scholarships your high schooler qualifies for. If you have ever Googled “math help near me” at 9 p.m. on a Sunday, you are in very good company across the St. Louis metro.
The good news: the region is loaded with quality tutoring and learning centers, and they are spread out from St. Charles County to the Illinois Metro-East. You do not have to drive downtown or settle for whoever a neighbor happened to mention. Here is a practical look at where to find help, how to choose, and what it actually costs.
### When it is time to get a tutor
A rough patch on one quiz is normal. The signs that point toward outside help are more persistent: grades sliding two quarters in a row, homework that triggers tears or shutdowns, a kid who says “I am just bad at math” (a confidence problem, not an ability one), or a standardized test on the calendar with real stakes attached. Tutoring is not a punishment or an admission of failure. It is the same logic as hiring a swim coach. Some skills are easier to build with a trained outside eye.
The other common trigger is timing. Reading and math gaps compound. A second grader who never locked in place value will struggle with long division in fourth grade and algebra in eighth. Catching it early is almost always cheaper and faster than catching it late.
### The national learning centers, town by town
The familiar chains run on proven systems, and the St. Louis suburbs have plenty of them. What matters is finding the specific location near you, because quality and hours vary by franchise owner.
Mathnasium focuses purely on math, K-12 through pre-calculus, with a free assessment that maps a student's exact gaps before any lessons begin. You will find centers in St. Charles, St. Peters (the St. Peters North location on Mexico Road), and Kirkwood (technically on Manchester Road in Des Peres, serving Kirkwood and Webster Groves families). Across the river, Mathnasium of O'Fallon, Illinois serves the Metro-East including Belleville families.
Kumon takes a different angle: a worksheet-based, self-paced method in both math and reading that builds independent study habits over the long haul. Metro centers include Chesterfield (on Olive Boulevard), Wildwood, Manchester (located in Ballwin on Manchester Road), and Clayton (on Ladue Road). Kumon tends to reward consistency. It is a marathon, not a quick fix.
Sylvan Learning covers the widest subject range: math, reading, writing, science, and ACT/SAT prep, with personalized plans tied to local school curriculum. The Ballwin center serves Ballwin, Chesterfield, and Kirkwood, there is a dedicated Chesterfield location, and Sylvan of O'Fallon, Illinois serves the Metro-East. Sylvan is a strong pick when a student needs help across several subjects rather than just one.
### Local independents and specialized programs
The national chains aren’t the whole picture. St. Louis has homegrown independents and specialty programs that fill gaps the big brands don’t. Mackler Associates in Frontenac is a longtime local name in academic tutoring and ACT/SAT prep, the kind of established, one-location practice families pass along by word of mouth. Huntington Learning Center, another established brand with metro locations, runs K-12 tutoring and intensive, diagnostic-driven test prep, and is often a fit when a student needs a structured, results-focused plan rather than casual help.
A different category worth knowing: Brain Balance, which has a presence in the metro, is not subject tutoring at all — it’s a drug-free program aimed at focus, attention, and behavior for kids who struggle to sit still and absorb material in the first place. If the real obstacle is attention rather than the algebra itself, a focus-and-executive-function program can matter more than another hour of math. Beyond any brand, plenty of independent one-on-one tutors — retired teachers, graduate students, and subject specialists — work across the metro, and they often cost less and flex around your schedule.
### Match the help to the subject
The best choice depends on what’s actually hard. For reading struggles or dyslexia, look specifically for a tutor or center trained in a structured, multisensory method like Orton-Gillingham — it’s the researched approach for stubborn reading gaps, and not every general tutor offers it. For math, a diagnostic center that pinpoints the exact missing building block usually beats generic homework help. For writing, you want someone who’ll coach the process, not just fix a paper the night before it’s due. And for ACT and SAT prep, ask about real practice tests, score tracking, and whether the tutor knows the current test format cold. Naming the specific problem before you shop saves money and false starts.
Unrelated, and we know it — Collinsville’s local-search page is right here.
### Lower-cost and free options first
Before you commit to a monthly membership, know that real help exists for little or nothing. Most St. Louis County Library and St. Louis Public Library branches offer free homework help and, in many cases, free live online tutoring with a library card. Many high schools run National Honor Society peer tutoring at no cost, and area universities often have students who tutor affordably. Online, Khan Academy is genuinely free and strong for math and test prep. None of this replaces a dedicated center when a student has a deep, persistent gap — but for a single tough unit or a confidence dip, the free tier is often all you need, and it’s the honest first stop before spending real money.
### Making tutoring actually work at home
The center does the teaching, but whether it sticks is decided at your kitchen table. Kids read the adults around them, so the single most useful thing a parent can do is frame tutoring as normal and even a little enviable — the academic version of a coach — rather than a punishment for a bad report card. Protect the sessions like any other commitment; the families who see results are almost never the ones who cancel every time something else comes up. Ask your tutor what to reinforce between visits, and keep it light: ten focused minutes a night beats a tense hour on Sunday. And watch for the real early win, which usually isn’t a grade at all — it’s a kid who stops saying “I’m bad at this” and starts asking questions again. Confidence tends to arrive before the A does, and it’s the thing that keeps the A coming.
### What to ask on the free assessment
Nearly every center offers a free assessment or trial, and it’s the best hour you’ll spend before committing a dime. Go in with questions. Ask who will actually work with your child — a certified teacher, a trained staffer, or a college student — and whether it’s the same person each week, because continuity matters more than credentials for a nervous kid. Ask how they measure progress and how often you’ll hear about it. Ask about the total cost, including any registration, assessment, and materials fees stacked on top of the monthly rate, and about the cancellation policy before you sign anything. Then watch the room: are the other kids engaged or bored, is the staff warm or rote? Trust your read on how your own child responds in that first session — it tells you more than any brochure.
### In-person versus online
Most of these centers now offer both. In-person wins for younger kids, students who are easily distracted, and anyone who needs the structure of a dedicated space away from home and phones. Online works well for busy high schoolers, families juggling several activities, and rural-edge towns where the nearest center is a 25-minute drive. Online math tutoring has improved a lot. Shared digital whiteboards mean a tutor can watch a student work a problem in real time, the same as sitting beside them. If you are unsure, many centers let you start in person and shift online later, or mix the two.
### How to choose the right one
Match the method to the kid. A worksheet system like Kumon suits a disciplined child who needs reps. A diagnostic, plan-driven center suits a student with specific gaps to close. Ask how they assess and how they measure progress.
Ask about the tutors. Are they certified teachers, college students, or trained staff? There is no single right answer, but you deserve a clear one.
Visit before you commit. Take the free assessment most centers offer. Watch how they talk to your child. Warmth matters as much as credentials.
Check the contract. Understand the monthly cost, the minimum commitment, and the cancellation policy before you sign.
Mind the drive. A center two towns over with a perfect program still loses if you cannot reliably get there twice a week. Convenience drives consistency, and consistency drives results.
### What it costs
Expectations help. Center-based memberships in the St. Louis metro generally run in the range of a few hundred dollars a month for two to three sessions a week, depending on the brand, subject, and session length. Private one-on-one tutors often charge by the hour, which can be cheaper for a quick fix but adds up fast for ongoing help. Intensive ACT or SAT prep packages are usually priced separately and can be a meaningful investment, though a score bump that unlocks scholarship money frequently pays for itself many times over. Always ask about assessment fees, materials fees, and any registration cost on top of the monthly rate.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much does tutoring cost in the St. Louis area?
A.  Center memberships commonly fall in the few-hundred-dollars-per-month range for two or three weekly sessions, while private hourly tutors vary widely. Test-prep packages are typically priced on their own. Always confirm the total, including any assessment or materials fees, before enrolling.
### Q. What age should my child start tutoring?
A.  There is no single right age. Some families start as early as kindergarten to build reading and number sense, while others wait until a specific subject becomes a struggle. The better question is whether a real gap exists. If it does, earlier is almost always easier and less expensive than later.
### Q. Is online tutoring as effective as in-person?
A.  For motivated, focused students, yes. Online sessions with shared whiteboards let a tutor watch and guide work in real time. Younger children and easily distracted students usually do better in person, where the structure of a dedicated space keeps them on task.
### Q. How long until I see results?
A.  Most families notice improved confidence within a few weeks, with grade improvements typically following over a semester of consistent attendance. Worksheet-based programs reward the long haul. Targeted gap-closing and test prep can move faster. Consistency is the biggest single factor.
### Q. Should I pick a chain or an independent tutor?
A.  Chains offer proven systems, structured assessments, and accountability. Independent tutors can offer more flexibility and a personal touch. Neither is automatically better. Match the format to your child's needs, your budget, and your schedule.
### Q. How do I find help for a specific need like reading, dyslexia, or ACT prep?
A.  Match the specialist to the problem. For reading struggles or dyslexia, look for a tutor trained in a structured, multisensory method such as Orton-Gillingham. For the ACT or SAT, ask about full practice tests and score tracking, and confirm the tutor knows the current format. Longtime local independents like Mackler Associates and diagnostic centers like Huntington are common starting points for test prep.
### Q. Are there free or low-cost tutoring options in St. Louis?
A.  Yes. St. Louis County and St. Louis Public Library branches offer free homework help and often free live online tutoring with a library card, many high schools run free National Honor Society peer tutoring, and Khan Academy is free online for math and test prep. These are a smart first stop for a single tough unit before you pay for a monthly membership.

## The Best Local Credit Unions in the St. Louis Metro
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/the-best-local-credit-unions-in-the-st-louis-metro
The bank statement finally lands on a Saturday morning. There it is: a $12 “maintenance” fee, an ATM charge, a savings rate that rounds to nothing. Then a neighbor in Florissant mentions the car she just financed through her credit union — a full point below what your big bank quoted. You start doing the math on how many years you’ve been leaving money on the table.
St. Louis is a good place to fix that. Both sides of the river are thick with strong, member-owned credit unions, several founded right here for local workers and neighborhoods. This guide walks through the best of them across the metro: who’s allowed to join each one, and why so many St. Louisans quietly bank this way.
### What Makes a Credit Union Different From a Bank
The short version: a credit union is a not-for-profit financial cooperative that’s owned by its members, not by outside shareholders. When you open an account, you become a part-owner with a vote. Because there are no stockholders to pay, the money a credit union earns flows back to members as lower loan rates, higher savings rates, and fewer fees. A bank, by contrast, answers to investors who expect a profit.
That difference shows up in real numbers. According to the National Credit Union Administration (NCUA), the federal regulator, credit unions nationally averaged a 6.27% rate on a 60-month new-car loan versus 7.50% at banks, and paid 3.26% on a one-year $10,000 CD versus 2.41% at banks (NCUA, 2025). On a car loan or a mortgage, a point or more adds up to real money over the life of the loan.
And your money is just as safe. Deposits at federally insured credit unions are protected up to $250,000 by the NCUA — the credit-union equivalent of FDIC insurance, backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government. The coverage amount is identical to a bank’s; only the insuring agency’s name changes.
### The St. Louis–Headquartered Credit Unions
These are the home-grown institutions — founded and headquartered in the St. Louis area, most now open to anyone who lives or works in the metro.
First Community Credit Union (Chesterfield) is the largest credit union headquartered in St. Louis — roughly $4.78 billion in assets, more than 408,000 members, and about 42 branches. It celebrated its 90th anniversary in 2024, and its community charter covers St. Louis City plus a wide sweep of Missouri and Illinois counties, so most metro residents can join.
Together Credit Union (St. Louis) began in 1939 as the Anheuser-Busch Employees’ Credit Union — a beer-industry credit union that grew into a roughly $2.64-billion institution with about 145,000 members and 26 branches. It rebranded to Together in 2020 and is now a founding and official banking partner of St. Louis CITY SC. Membership is open to people who live or work across the core metro counties, plus employees of partners like Anheuser-Busch, Nestlé Purina, and BJC, and their families.
Vantage Credit Union (Bridgeton) runs about 14 metro branches and has one of the friendliest community charters around: you can join if you live, work, worship, or attend school in St. Louis, St. Charles, Jefferson, or Franklin counties in Missouri, or St. Clair or Madison counties in Illinois.
Neighbors Credit Union (St. Louis), with about 8 branches, leans on a “once a member, always a member” promise and serves the core Missouri and Illinois metro counties, plus select employer groups like Costco and Bi-State/Metro.
Alliance Credit Union (Fenton) was founded in 1948 and carries deep labor-union and skilled-trades roots — its field of membership includes dozens of employer groups and several labor organizations alongside the usual live-or-work-here counties on both sides of the river.
### A Metro That Keeps Growing: Recent Mergers
The St. Louis credit-union map has shifted recently, and it’s worth knowing so you don’t go looking for a branch that’s changed its sign.
West Community Credit Union (O’Fallon, MO) completed a legal merger with Gateway Metro Federal Credit Union on April 7, 2026, creating a roughly $670-million credit union with 43,000-plus members and about 16 branches under the West Community name. Alltru Credit Union (Wentzville) is another rebrand to know: it was 1st Financial Federal Credit Union until late 2020, and it started life in 1968 as the McDonnell Douglas Credit Union — a nod to St. Louis’s aerospace heritage. Alltru is a certified Community Development Financial Institution (CDFI) serving St. Louis City, St. Louis County, and St. Charles County.
And there’s a big new entrant: CommunityAmerica Credit Union, Missouri’s largest credit union at roughly $5 billion in assets, planted its flag in St. Louis by merging in Electro Savings Credit Union on January 1, 2025. It now runs branches in Maryland Heights, Manchester, South County, and St. Peters, with membership eligibility inherited from Electro’s metro charter.
### The Metro East (Illinois) Anchors
Cross the river and the Metro East has its own strong, locally rooted credit unions.
Scott Credit Union (Edwardsville) is the Metro East’s largest home-grown credit union, with roots at Scott Air Force Base and a field of membership spanning more than 30 Illinois and Missouri counties; a $5 minimum share opens the door. 1st MidAmerica Credit Union (Bethalto) serves around 64,000 members across some 21 Illinois counties from about 10 branches, and recently expanded into Granite City through a local merger. Both are worth a look if you live or work on the Illinois side of the river, and both reflect a whole-metro reality: “local” in St. Louis stretches well into Illinois.
### A St. Louis Story Worth Telling: St. Louis Community Credit Union
If you want a credit union that doubles as a force for the neighborhoods, St. Louis Community Credit Union is the standout. With about $427 million in assets and more than 51,000 members across 14 branches, it’s the region’s largest CDFI and one of the nation’s larger Minority Depository Institutions — meaning it deliberately banks underserved parts of North City and North County that big banks have long overlooked.
The impact is concrete: more than $40 million in business loans, roughly 90% of them to Black-owned businesses, plus payday-loan alternatives and its “Sure Rides” affordable auto-loan program. It even reopened a historic Gateway branch honoring one of the nation’s first African American–owned banks. For a lot of St. Louisans, joining here is as much a vote for the community as it is a smart financial move.
### How to Choose — and How Membership Works
The old idea that you need a special connection to join a credit union is mostly history. Every credit union has a “field of membership” — the rules for who can join — but most of the St. Louis institutions above now hold a community charter, which typically means anyone who lives, works, worships, or attends school in a given county is eligible. In practice, nearly every metro resident qualifies for several of these.
To choose, start with what you actually do at a bank. Want branches near your home and work? Compare locations. Carry a car loan or plan to buy a house? Compare loan rates. Keep a big savings balance? Compare CD and savings rates. Also ask whether the credit union participates in the CO-OP shared-branching and ATM network, which lets members use thousands of other credit unions’ branches and surcharge-free ATMs nationwide — a quiet perk that makes a local credit union feel a lot bigger than its branch count. Opening an account usually takes a small deposit (often $5 to $25) that represents your ownership share.
Wildly off-topic — here’s downtown St. Louis, block by block.
### Are There Any Downsides?
To be fair, credit unions aren’t perfect for everyone. Because membership is tied to a field of membership, you have to be eligible to join — though, as noted, most metro residents qualify for several. A single local credit union also has fewer branches than a national megabank, so if you travel constantly or move out of state, that can matter (the CO-OP shared-branch network softens this a lot). And historically, some smaller credit unions lagged big banks on app features and digital tools, though most St. Louis institutions have closed that gap and now offer solid mobile banking, Zelle, and online account opening.
The honest takeaway: for the vast majority of St. Louisans — anyone who wants better loan and savings rates, lower fees, and a say in how their institution is run — the tradeoffs are minor next to the upside. It’s worth pulling up two or three of the credit unions above, comparing their rates and branch maps against your current bank, and seeing for yourself what a switch would save you.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the biggest credit union in Missouri?
A.  CommunityAmerica Credit Union is Missouri’s largest credit union, at roughly $5 billion in assets; it planted its flag in St. Louis in 2025 by merging in Electro Savings. Among credit unions actually headquartered in St. Louis, First Community is the largest, with about $4.78 billion in assets and over 408,000 members.
### Q. What is the best credit union in Missouri?
A.  There’s no single best — it depends on what you need. By size, CommunityAmerica is Missouri’s largest. In the St. Louis metro, First Community and Together lead on branches, Vantage has an especially open charter, and St. Louis Community Credit Union stands out for community impact. Compare rates, branches, and eligibility.
### Q. What credit union is the highest recommended?
A.  No single credit union is universally the highest recommended — the right one depends on your priorities. For branch access, First Community and Together stand out; for the most open membership, Vantage; for community impact, St. Louis Community Credit Union; and on the Illinois side, Scott and 1st MidAmerica. Compare rates and locations for your situation.
### Q. What are the top 3 credit unions?
A.  By asset size in the St. Louis area, the three largest are CommunityAmerica (Missouri’s largest, roughly $5 billion), First Community (about $4.78 billion, the largest headquartered in St. Louis), and Together Credit Union (about $2.64 billion). Bigger isn’t always better, though — the best fit depends on your rates, branches, and eligibility.
### Q. What is the hardest credit union to get into?
A.  In today’s St. Louis metro, almost none are truly hard to join. Most local credit unions now hold a community charter, so anyone who lives, works, worships, or attends school in a covered county is eligible. A few still lean on employer or labor-union groups, like Alliance’s trades roots, but most residents qualify somewhere easily.
### Q. How safe is it to keep $500,000 in a credit union?
A.  Very safe, if you structure it right. The NCUA insures up to $250,000 per depositor, per credit union, per ownership category. To fully cover $500,000, spread it across different ownership categories — individual, joint, retirement — or across two credit unions. Every dollar within those limits is backed by the U.S. government.
### Q. Can anyone join a credit union in St. Louis?
A.  Almost anyone can. Most St. Louis credit unions now hold a community charter, meaning anyone who lives, works, worships, or attends school in a covered county can join — and between them they cover the entire metro on both sides of the river. Opening an account usually requires a small share deposit, often $5 to $25.
### Q. Do credit unions have better interest rates than banks?
A.  Generally, yes. Because credit unions are not-for-profit and member-owned, they tend to pay more on deposits and charge less on loans. NCUA figures for 2025 show credit unions averaging 6.27% on a 60-month new-car loan versus 7.50% at banks, and 3.26% versus 2.41% on a one-year $10,000 CD.

## Best Wedding & Event Caterers Across the St. Louis Metro
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/best-wedding-and-event-caterers-across-the-st-louis-metro
The guest list hits 130 names. The venue is locked for a Saturday next fall. Then it sinks in: you have to feed every one of them. Maybe the event is a wedding in Kirkwood. Maybe a milestone anniversary in St. Charles, or a company party out in the Metro East. Either way, the food is what guests will actually remember, and it’s usually the single biggest line on the budget. No pressure.
St. Louis rewards the search. The catering scene here runs deep, from white-glove wedding houses that have been at it for half a century to barbecue teams turning brisket into burnt-end toasted ravioli. This guide walks through the best wedding and event caterers across the metro, on both sides of the river, plus what catering actually costs here and the questions that save you from an expensive surprise.
### What Wedding & Event Catering Costs in St. Louis
Catering is almost always the largest single expense at a wedding, so it helps to walk in with real numbers. Nationally, the average wedding ran about $34,200 in The Knot’s 2026 Real Weddings Study, but Missouri comes in well below that — a median closer to $17,470 — and St. Louis is one of the more affordable major metros for a celebration.
For catering specifically, budget expectations vary widely by service style. At the low end, drop-off or prepared-food-only catering can run roughly $15 to $18 per person (Thumbtack). Full-service wedding catering — with staff, plated or attended-buffet service, and bar — is more commonly planned around $225 to $325 per guest once you add service and beverages, and independent estimates put the St. Louis average near $263 to $292 per guest (wedding.report). Local venue guides peg a typical 75-to-125-guest St. Louis wedding at roughly $18,000 to $35,000 all-in, with catering the biggest slice. Treat these as planning ranges, not quotes — your number depends on menu, guest count, and bar.
A few things move that number the most: service style (plated dinners cost more than buffets, which cost more than drop-off), whether you add a hosted bar, your guest count, and the season — peak spring and fall dates command premium pricing and book out first. Rentals like linens, china, and glassware, plus staffing and the service charge, can add 20% to 30% on top of the food itself, which is exactly why an itemized quote matters so much when you’re comparing caterers side by side.
### Full-Service vs. Drop-Off: Know What You’re Buying
Before you compare caterers, get clear on the two main models, because a “cheap” quote and an “expensive” one often aren’t the same product. Full-service catering means the team handles it all: setup, plated or attended-buffet service, bartending, and teardown and cleanup at the end of the night. It’s the widest menu range and the least work for you. Drop-off catering means the caterer cooks, delivers, and sets out ready-to-serve trays — then you and your people handle serving and cleanup. It’s meaningfully cheaper and perfect for casual events, but it’s not the same as having a staffed reception.
### The Full-Service Wedding Heavyweights
St. Louis couples have leaned on these staff-everything wedding houses for decades. The established names first.
Butler’s Pantry (Lafayette Square) has catered St. Louis weddings and events since 1966. It’s the exclusive caterer at venues like The Coronado, 18Rails, and The Reverie, and a preferred caterer at 40-plus more — the Missouri History Museum, The Muny, and Third Degree Glass among them. If your venue has a caterer list, Butler’s Pantry is often on it.
Ces & Judy’s Catering (Frontenac) has been an elegant-wedding mainstay for 40-plus years and runs its own exclusive venue, The Venue at Maison du Lac. Russo’s Catering (St. Louis) brings roughly 60 years of experience and all-inclusive bridal packages, comfortably scaling from an intimate dinner to a 10,000-guest event. Catering St. Louis Events is chef-owned and has been since 1980, pairing full-service catering with 14 boutique event venues — a one-stop option if you still need a space. And Callier’s Catering (Warson Woods/Ballwin), family-owned since 1983, spans everything from plated weddings to drop-off and BBQ, handling events from 15 to 2,000-plus.
### Barbecue, Comfort Food & Crowd-Pleasers
Not every great St. Louis reception is black-tie. Some of the most-loved catering in town comes off a smoker.
Salt + Smoke (University City and beyond) caters weddings and corporate events with post-oak-smoked brisket and a signature only St. Louis could invent: burnt-end toasted ravioli. Food service starts around $15 per person, with vegan, vegetarian, and gluten-free options and a 4.9-star WeddingWire rating. Grace Meat + Three (The Grove) caters Southern comfort food from chef Rick Lewis, a James Beard Rising Star Chef semifinalist known for some of the city’s best fried chicken. Championship Catering has 30-plus years catering St. Louis weddings, private parties, and corporate events, and Pasta House Catering brings a 50-year St. Louis tradition of full-service Italian catering — a familiar, crowd-pleasing choice.
### Boutique Venues, Bistros & the Sweet Stuff
Some events are smaller, or just want more character. St. Louis has the caterers for that.
SqWires Restaurant & Annex (Lafayette Square) is a women-owned spot in a former wire factory — 18-foot ceilings, exposed brick — that handles weddings, rehearsal dinners, and showers on-site and off. Herbie’s (Central West End) is a French-American bistro with private rooms, patios, and off-site catering for rehearsal dinners and events. For dessert and favors, Kakao Chocolate (Maplewood) makes handcrafted truffle place settings and chocolate displays, while Cravings (Webster Groves), founded in 1984 by James Beard–award chef Tim Brennan, specializes in catering, gourmet desserts, and wedding cakes.
Totally unrelated, but — the whole St. Louis city guide is worth a bookmark.
### The Metro East (Illinois) Caterers
Cross the river and the Metro East holds its own. Cygan-Delaney Catering brings 50-plus years of full-service weddings, banquets, and BBQ across St. Louis, the Metro East, and Southern Illinois. Bella Milano (Edwardsville) caters Italian menus for weddings and corporate events and is the exclusive caterer for the historic Leclaire Room. As with everything in St. Louis, “local” here means the whole metro — don’t rule out an Illinois caterer for a Missouri event, or vice versa.
### The St. Louis Twist — and One Rule to Remember
Two things make catering here distinctly St. Louis. First, the hometown flavors: toasted ravioli (a St. Louis original) and gooey butter cake show up on cocktail-hour and dessert menus all over town — Salt + Smoke’s burnt-end toasted ravioli is a documented local mashup worth asking about. Adding a regional signature dish is an easy way to make a reception feel unmistakably St. Louis — a gooey butter cake dessert bar or a toasted-ravioli passed appetizer gives out-of-town guests a taste of the city and gives locals something to smile about.
Second, the rule that trips up the most couples: many St. Louis venues require you to use a preferred or exclusive caterer. Butler’s Pantry, Ces & Judy’s, and Bella Milano all hold exclusive relationships at specific venues, and Catering St. Louis Events comes with its own spaces. So before you fall in love with a caterer, confirm your venue’s catering rules — and before you book a St. Louis wedding venue, ask which caterers you’ll be allowed to hire. And book early: popular St. Louis caterers and venues fill 9 to 12 months out, more for peak spring and fall dates.
### A Few More Worth a Look
Beyond the names above, a few other St. Louis caterers show up again and again in local searches and reviews. Championship Catering and The Fifth Wheel Catering both rate highly for weddings and private parties, Seed Sprout Spoon earns strong marks for creative, from-scratch menus, and 612North Event Space + Catering pairs a downtown venue with in-house catering. As always, confirm each one is available for your date and approved at your venue before you commit — the best caterers book up first.
### Questions to Ask Any Caterer Before You Book
A little due diligence up front prevents the most common day-of headaches. Before you sign, ask each caterer:
What’s included — and what’s extra? Get an itemized quote separating food, staff, bar, rentals (linens, china, glassware), delivery, service charge, and gratuity. A low headline price often leaves several of these out.
Are you approved at my venue? Many St. Louis venues require a preferred caterer, so confirm before you fall for a menu.
Who staffs and cleans up? Ask the staffing ratio, who buses tables, and when load-out happens — especially with buffet or drop-off service.
Can you handle our dietary and cultural needs? Vegan, vegetarian, gluten-free, halal, kosher-style, allergy accommodations — ask before you assume.
Is there a tasting, and what’s your deposit and cancellation policy? Reputable caterers offer tastings and put terms in writing.
Answers that are clear, itemized, and in writing are a good sign. Vague quotes and “we’ll figure it out later” are not.

Two decisions do most of the work before you ever book a tasting: which caterer fits once you know your format, and which red flags to catch when every quote looks reasonable on its own. Full-service versus drop-off settles the rest.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. How much does wedding catering cost in St. Louis?
A.  It depends on service style. Drop-off or prepared-food-only catering runs about $15 to $18 per person, while full-service catering with staff and bar is more commonly planned around $225 to $325 per guest, with local estimates near $263 to $292. A typical 75-to-125-guest St. Louis wedding often totals $18,000 to $35,000 all-in.
### Q. What is a reasonable budget for wedding catering?
A.  Expect catering to be your single biggest wedding expense, often 30% to 40% of the total. In St. Louis, budgeting somewhere between $15 to $18 per person for drop-off and $225 to $325 per guest for full-service with bar covers most scenarios. Get itemized quotes to compare food, staff, bar, and rentals separately.
### Q. How much would it cost to feed 50 people at a wedding?
A.  Using St. Louis per-guest ranges, feeding 50 guests costs roughly $750 to $900 for drop-off catering at $15 to $18 per person, or about $11,250 to $16,250 for full-service at $225 to $325 per guest. Full-service adds staff, bar, and cleanup; drop-off is delivery only. Menu and bar move the final number.
### Q. What is the cheapest way to feed 100 people at a wedding?
A.  The cheapest route is drop-off or prepared-food-only catering, roughly $15 to $18 per person in St. Louis, so feeding 100 guests lands near $1,500 to $1,800 for food. You and your people handle serving and cleanup, which is why it beats full-service. Buffets also cost less than plated dinners.
### Q. Is $10,000 a small wedding budget?
A.  By local benchmarks, yes, $10,000 is a modest budget. It sits below Missouri’s median wedding of about $17,470 and well under the national average near $34,200, plus the $18,000 to $35,000 a typical 75-to-125-guest St. Louis wedding runs. It’s workable here, especially with drop-off catering and a smaller guest count.
### Q. What’s the difference between full-service and drop-off catering?
A.  Full-service catering includes setup, plated or attended-buffet service, bartending, and end-of-night cleanup, so the team handles everything. Drop-off catering means the caterer cooks and delivers ready-to-serve food, but you handle serving and cleanup. Drop-off is significantly cheaper and great for casual events; full-service is the norm for staffed wedding receptions.
### Q. How far in advance should you book a caterer in St. Louis?
A.  Aim for 9 to 12 months ahead, and even earlier for peak spring (April–June) and fall (September–October) dates or guest counts above 150. Popular St. Louis caterers and venues book out fast, and because many venues require a preferred caterer, locking both in early keeps your options open.
### Q. How to pick a wedding caterer?
A.  Decide full-service or drop-off first, because that choice changes everything after it. Then compare on what is actually included — staff, rentals, cake cutting, bar service and gratuity — rather than on the per-plate figure, which is the number most likely to be quoted without them.
### Q. What are the red flags to look for in wedding catering?
A.  A quote without an itemised scope, reluctance to do a tasting, vague answers on staffing ratios, and no written plan for dietary restrictions. The biggest one is a caterer who has never worked your venue and does not ask about the kitchen, the power, or where they can stage.
### Q. What are common catering mistakes to avoid?
A.  Booking before the guest count is real, forgetting that service staff and rentals are separate lines, and not confirming who handles setup and teardown at the venue. The other one is skipping the timeline conversation — food that is ready before the photos are done gets served cold.
### Q. How much should catering cost for a 50 person wedding?
A.  Build it per head and then add the fixed costs, rather than trusting a headline figure. Drop-off is a fraction of full service. Staffing, rentals, bar and gratuity often total as much as the food itself, so ask for the all-in number before you compare two quotes.

## What to Do After a Car Accident in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-do-after-a-car-accident-in-st-louis
One second you are merging onto I-64 thinking about lunch. The next, there is a crunch, your heart is pounding, and a stranger is walking toward your window. The minutes right after a crash are loud, confusing, and easy to fumble — and what you do in them can shape the weeks that follow. Whether your fender-bender happened downtown, out in St. Charles County, across the river in the Metro-East, or on a quiet road in Jefferson County, the same calm checklist applies. The goal in those first minutes is simple: keep everyone safe, capture what happened while it’s fresh, and avoid the handful of mistakes that make the aftermath harder than it needs to be. Do that, and you’ll be in a far stronger position whether the whole thing wraps up with a quick insurance claim or turns into something more complicated.
This is general information to help you stay organized after a wreck. It is not legal advice, and every accident is different. For guidance on your specific situation, talk with a licensed Missouri attorney.
### First, Get Safe
Before anything else, check yourself and your passengers for injuries. If anyone is hurt, call 911 right away. If the cars are drivable and blocking traffic, move them to the shoulder or a nearby lot so you are not sitting in a live lane — St. Louis interstates do not slow down for a stopped car. Turn on your hazard lights. If you cannot move the vehicle safely, leave it, get yourself to a safe spot away from traffic, and wait.
### When to Call the Police
Call the police for any crash involving an injury, a death, or noticeable property damage. In Missouri you must report a crash that causes injury, death, or more than $500 in property damage, and you may also need to file a written accident report with the Missouri Department of Revenue within 30 days. A police report gives you an official, neutral record of what happened. Even for a minor bump, a report is worth having. If officers respond, ask how to get a copy of the report and write down the report number. If police do not come to the scene — which happens with smaller crashes — you can still document everything yourself.
### Document the Scene
Your phone is your best tool here. Take wide shots and close-ups of:
Damage to every vehicle involved, from several angles
License plates
The position of the cars before anyone moves them, if it is safe to photograph
Skid marks, debris, traffic signals, and street signs
Any visible injuries
The overall scene, so the road and weather conditions are clear
If there are witnesses, politely ask for their names and phone numbers. A neutral bystander who saw the whole thing can matter a great deal later.
Unrelated, and we know it — every rug eventually meets a St. Louis carpet cleaner.
### Exchange Information — Carefully
Swap names, phone numbers, addresses, driver’s license numbers, license plate numbers, and insurance details with the other driver. Stay civil, but keep it factual. This is the moment people often slip up: do not apologize, do not say “it was my fault,” and do not argue about who caused it. You may be rattled and not have the full picture yet. Stick to exchanging information and let the facts come out later.
### See a Doctor, Even If You Feel Fine
Adrenaline is a powerful painkiller. Plenty of people walk away from a crash feeling okay, only to wake up the next morning with a stiff neck, a pounding headache, or back pain that will not quit. Whiplash and concussions often show up hours or days after impact. Getting checked out by a doctor — even a visit to urgent care or your primary care office — protects your health and creates a medical record that ties any injuries to the accident. If you skip care and symptoms appear later, an insurer may argue your injury had nothing to do with the crash.
### Report It to Your Insurance
Notify your own insurance company promptly, even if the other driver was clearly at fault. Most policies require you to report accidents within a reasonable time, and reporting does not mean you are admitting blame. Give your insurer the facts you have. Be honest, but you do not need to volunteer guesses or speculate about fault. If the other driver’s insurance company calls and asks for a recorded statement, you are allowed to slow down, ask questions, and get advice before agreeing to one.
### How Fault Works in Missouri
Missouri is an at-fault state, which means the driver responsible for a crash (and their insurer) is generally on the hook for the resulting damages. Missouri also follows what is called pure comparative fault. In plain terms: if you are found partly to blame, your compensation is reduced by your share of the fault, but you are not automatically locked out of recovering. For example, if your damages were $10,000 and you were found 20 percent at fault, you could recover $8,000. Missouri courts have applied this approach to car accident cases for decades. Importantly, the other side has to actually prove you share blame — it is not assumed.
### Missouri’s Insurance Basics
It helps to know the coverage rules before you ever need them. Missouri requires every driver to carry at least $25,000 in bodily-injury liability per person, $50,000 per accident, and $25,000 in property-damage liability (often written “25/50/25”). Missouri also requires uninsured-motorist coverage of at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident, which protects you if the at-fault driver has no insurance — a real risk on any given day. Underinsured-motorist coverage, which covers the gap when the other driver’s limits are too low, is optional but worth asking your agent about. These are only minimums; many drivers carry more because a serious injury claim can blow past $25,000 quickly. Knowing your own limits — and whether you have collision, medical-payments, and rental coverage — makes the days after a crash far less stressful.
### The Deadline to Take Action
Missouri law sets a time limit, called the statute of limitations, for filing a personal injury lawsuit. For most personal injury claims, that window is five years from the date of the injury under Missouri statute (RSMo 516.120). Some claims are different — wrongful death and medical malpractice, for instance, have shorter deadlines — so do not assume five years applies to every situation. Deadlines are firm, and missing one can permanently end your right to sue. If you are unsure how the deadline applies to you, confirm the current timeline with an attorney or The Missouri Bar.
### Watch Out for Quick Lowball Offers
Sometimes an insurer calls within days with a settlement check and a friendly tone. It can be tempting to sign, especially with a car in the shop and bills coming. But an early offer is often made before anyone knows the full extent of your injuries or the real cost of repairs. Once you accept and sign a release, you usually cannot go back and ask for more — even if a problem surfaces weeks later. There is no rule that says you must accept the first number. Take your time, get your medical care, and understand what your claim is actually worth before you agree to anything.
### When It Is Worth Talking to an Attorney
Not every fender-bender needs a lawyer. But it is reasonable to consult one when there are serious or lasting injuries, when fault is genuinely disputed, when multiple vehicles are involved, when an insurer denies a fair claim or pressures you, or when you simply feel out of your depth. Most personal injury attorneys offer a free initial consultation, so a conversation costs you nothing and can clarify your options. The Missouri Bar (mobar.org) offers a lawyer referral service and consumer information if you want a starting point.
### Keep Your Records Together
From the day of the crash forward, hold on to everything: the police report number, photos, medical bills and notes, repair estimates, a log of missed work, and any letters from insurers. Jot down how you are feeling each day while it is fresh. Organized records make every later step — an insurance claim, a repair dispute, or a conversation with an attorney — far smoother.
### Common Mistakes to Avoid
A few missteps trip people up again and again in the days after a crash. Steer clear of these:
Admitting fault at the scene. “I’m so sorry, I didn’t see you” feels polite, but in a comparative-fault state it can be used against you before anyone knows what really happened. Be kind and factual, not self-blaming.
Skipping medical care because you “feel fine.” Adrenaline hides injuries, and a gap in treatment gives insurers a reason to deny that your injury came from the crash.
Giving the other insurer a recorded statement right away. You’re not required to, and it’s easy to say something — while shaken — that gets twisted later. It’s fine to slow down and get advice first.
Accepting the first check. Once you sign a release, the claim is closed, even if a problem shows up next month.
Throwing away records. The photo you almost deleted or the estimate you tossed can be the thing that settles a dispute in your favor.
### Handling the Repair and Getting Back on the Road
Once the immediate steps are done, there’s the practical side: getting your car fixed. You generally have the right to choose your own repair shop — an insurer can recommend one, but it can’t force you to use it. Get your own estimate, ask whether the shop offers a warranty on the work, and keep every invoice. If your policy includes rental coverage, ask how to set up a loaner while your car is in the shop. And if the other driver was at fault and their insurer accepts liability, your repairs and a rental may be handled through their policy — but don’t let a repair drag on unaddressed while the two insurers sort out who pays. A little persistence here keeps a bad day from turning into a bad month.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What should I do first after a car accident in St. Louis?
A.  Get to safety. Check for injuries and call 911 if anyone is hurt, move drivable cars out of live traffic, and turn on your hazards. Then call the police, document the scene with photos, and exchange information with the other driver — without admitting fault.
### Q. Do I have to call the police after a minor accident in Missouri?
A.  You’re required to report a crash involving injury, death, or more than $500 in property damage, and you may need to file a report with the Missouri Department of Revenue within 30 days. Even for a small bump, a police report gives you a neutral official record, so it’s usually worth calling.
### Q. Is Missouri a no-fault or an at-fault state?
A.  At-fault. The driver responsible for the crash and their insurer generally pay the damages. Missouri also uses pure comparative fault, so if you’re found partly to blame, your recovery is reduced by your share — but you’re not automatically barred from recovering.
### Q. How long do I have to file a claim after a car accident in Missouri?
A.  For most personal-injury claims, Missouri gives you five years from the date of the injury (RSMo 516.120). Some claims, like wrongful death, have shorter deadlines, so don’t assume five years applies to every situation — confirm your timeline with an attorney if you’re unsure.
### Q. What is Missouri’s minimum car insurance?
A.  At least 25/50/25 — $25,000 bodily injury per person, $50,000 per accident, and $25,000 property damage — plus uninsured-motorist coverage of 25/50. Many drivers carry more, since a serious injury can exceed those minimums.
### Q. Should I accept the insurance company’s first offer?
A.  If the other vehicle was a commercial rig, the claim works differently from the start — see who is liable in a St. Louis truck accident before you talk to any adjuster.
Not automatically. Early offers often come before anyone knows the full extent of your injuries or repair costs, and signing a release usually ends your claim for good. Get your medical care, understand what your claim is worth, and take your time before agreeing to anything.

## Two O’Fallons, One Wrong Click, $1,650 a Year: St. Louis Suburbs Compared
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-suburbs-compared-find-the-right-town-for-you
It’s 11 p.m., the laptop is the only light in the kitchen, your coffee went cold an hour ago, and two O’Fallon listings look perfect. Then you notice one is in St. Charles County, Missouri, and the other is across the Mississippi in Illinois. Troy pulls the same trick. Click the wrong one and you haven’t just picked a house. You’ve picked a state, a tax system and a bridge you’ll be sitting on every morning.
So you open another tab, and one number stops you. At typical rates, the same $300,000 house runs about $5,490 a year in property tax in St. Clair County, Illinois, and about $3,180 in St. Charles County, Missouri: 1.83% of value versus 1.06%, per the Tax Foundation’s county figures. Even after Missouri’s yearly tax on a $30,000 SUV, about $657, the Illinois side costs roughly $1,650 a year more. Houses are cheaper over there. The tax bill isn’t.
Same $300,000 house: St. Clair County, IL, about $5,490 a year. St. Charles County, MO, about $3,180 a year, plus about $657 on a $30,000 SUV.
That car bill is Missouri’s catch. In November the envelope lands on the kitchen counter, one bill for every car you owned on January 1, due by December 31.
Each car is assessed at a third of its value and taxed at your local rate. The $657 comes from running St. Charles County’s own published example rate on a $30,000 SUV.
Illinois abolished personal property taxes in 1979, so no envelope waits on that side of the river.
And inside the City of St. Louis, 1% of every paycheck goes to the earnings tax, even for people who only work there.
Before you close the laptop, add one line to the moving list. Missouri won’t title your car without a statement of non-assessment from your county assessor: St. Louis County takes requests online or in Clayton, St. Charles County online or at 201 N. Second St., and the City of St. Louis assessor answers at 314-622-4800. Request it as soon as you have your title or current out-of-state registration in hand, bring both to the license office, and you won’t sit in its plastic chair twice.
Shop by school district, not town name. Two houses a mile apart can sit in different districts, so ask for the exact district on every listing and check it against that district’s own boundary map. Then drive the commute for real: leave the open house at 7:30 on a weekday morning, merge onto I-270 or I-64 with everyone else, watch the brake lights stack up red, and check the clock when you park.
### West County: walkable main streets, big lots and the price of both
Friday night in downtown Kirkwood, the patios are full, a freight train rumbles past the old depot and kids on bikes cut across the sidewalk. West County is the part of St. Louis County most people picture when they think suburbs: bigger lots, strong schools and home prices toward the top of the metro.
Dinner smells drift out onto the sidewalk, and you can walk home after. That’s Kirkwood and Webster Groves, the walkable-downtown stars, with historic main streets and school districts that consistently rank among the best in Missouri. You pay for that combination of charm and schools.
Drive west and the lots get bigger, until in Wildwood you hear tree frogs instead of traffic at night. Chesterfield, Town and Country, Wildwood and Des Peres lean more spread-out and newer, with larger homes and a higher price point. Chesterfield Valley is where the big-box shopping and a lot of the jobs are; Wildwood is the greener, more rural one.
Cul-de-sacs, basketball hoops over the garage and kids on scooters until the streetlights come on: that’s Ballwin and Ellisville, generally a step more affordable than Town and Country or Chesterfield, with access to the same well-regarded districts.
Out where the subdivisions give way to wooded hills along I-44, Eureka and Manchester stretch the dollar further still. Eureka is more rural and newer, out toward Mid America Adventure (the former Six Flags) with Rockwood schools. Manchester sits between Ballwin and Kirkwood at a middle price, with Parkway and Rockwood access and none of the Town and Country premium.
### Mid County: Clayton, Ladue and a shorter drive to work
Every September the white tents of the Saint Louis Art Fair fill the streets of downtown Clayton. The rest of the year you can walk to lunch, the county courthouse and a MetroLink platform without touching your car keys. Mid County sits between the city and West County, and it trades big lots for shorter commutes and walkable, character-rich neighborhoods.
Clayton is where the county does business: the county seat, a true walkable downtown, and one of the very top school districts in Missouri (Ladue and Clayton routinely trade the number-one and number-two spots). It’s also one of the most expensive places to live in the area, so it fits buyers who put schools and walkability ahead of square footage.
A few minutes west the streets go quiet and the driveways get long. Ladue, Frontenac and Huntleigh are the prestige addresses: estate-scale lots, the highest household incomes in the metro and, in Ladue’s case, the top-ranked school district in Missouri for several years running. Close-in luxury, big, private and expensive, for buyers who want space without leaving Mid County.
Independent restaurants and shops line the revitalized main streets of Maplewood and Brentwood, compact, older streetcar suburbs where city energy comes with a short commute, and you can walk it all.
University City, Richmond Heights, Creve Coeur and Maryland Heights round out the area: U. City has the Loop and a diverse, urban feel, Creve Coeur skews more upscale and corporate, and Maryland Heights is convenient to the airport and Westport.
### St. Charles County: new subdivisions and the metro’s fastest growth
Fresh sod, a new elementary school with the paint barely dry, and a longer drive across the Missouri River every morning. St. Charles County is where much of the metro’s new construction and population growth has gone: since 2020 the county has grown about 5% while the City of St. Louis shrank almost 8%, per the Census Bureau. Expect newer subdivisions, newer schools and a longer-but-manageable commute to downtown.
St. Charles itself anchors the county with its historic brick Main Street along the riverfront.
O'Fallon (Missouri), St. Peters, Wentzville, Lake St. Louis, Cottleville, and Dardenne Prairie are the growth engines. Wentzville has been among the fastest-growing school districts in the entire state. Lake St. Louis is built around its lakes; Cottleville and Dardenne Prairie are smaller and newer.
If you want a newer home and a yard for a more reasonable price than West County, this county is usually the first place to look - just budget for the extra drive time.
Total tangent - driveways crack, patios sag, and St. Louis concrete crews fix both.
### South County and Jefferson County: more house for less, down I-55
Down I-55, a stretched budget finally gets room to breathe. South St. Louis County offers steady, established neighborhoods at gentler prices than West County.
Oakville, Mehlville, Affton, and Sunset Hills are dependable, family-oriented communities. Sunset Hills sits a bit higher on price; Affton and Mehlville are among the more budget-friendly inner-ring choices.
Further south, Jefferson County stretches the dollar further. Arnold is the county's largest community and a common landing spot for first-time buyers; Festus and Imperial offer a more semi-rural feel with highly rated Festus schools. (One common mix-up: Fenton is actually in St. Louis County, not Jefferson County, though it borders the line.)
### North County: lower prices and a short drive to the airport
The mid-century house you would pay far more for in West County is often the one you can afford in Florissant, Hazelwood and Ferguson. North County offers some of the most affordable housing in the metro.
The region has historically carried economic and racial divides (some describe a similar divide along Olive Boulevard, echoing the city’s Delmar Divide), and headlines have shaped outside perceptions.
The fair, accurate take: these are real communities with engaged residents, established housing stock, and genuine value. Visit the specific neighborhoods, talk to people who live there, and judge each block on what you actually see.
Narrowing it down? Explore the metro city by city in our local guides, and find the dentist, mechanic, and coffee shop that make a new neighborhood feel like home.
If you run a business in one of these towns, list it with us and turn the new neighbors shopping for a dentist, a mechanic and a coffee shop into customers.
### Illinois Metro-East: more house for the money
The Illinois listing from your 11 p.m. search wins on sticker price: across the river, your budget often goes further. The tax bill is another story, because property taxes work differently in Illinois. Factor the full monthly cost, not just the sticker price.
Edwardsville and Glen Carbon are the Metro-East's standouts - Edwardsville District 7 is one of the most respected districts in the region, and Edwardsville's walkable, historic Main Street (home to the restored Wildey Theatre) gives it real downtown life.
Waterloo and Columbia in Monroe County are known for low crime, strong homeownership, and well-rated schools, just south of the river.
Belleville, Collinsville, O'Fallon (Illinois), and Highland round out the choices - Belleville has a large historic district and Main Street, Collinsville is central and convenient, and O'Fallon, Illinois, the other O’Fallon, is a growing community near Scott Air Force Base.
### Property taxes: the Missouri-vs-Illinois math
The sticker price is only half the story. Illinois leans more heavily on property taxes than Missouri, so a house that looks cheaper across the river can cost about the same - or more - once the monthly tax bill is baked in.
Two homes at the same list price can carry very different payments depending on the county, the school district, and any special assessments. Before you fall for a bargain on either side of the river, ask your lender or agent to run the full monthly cost - principal, interest, taxes, and insurance - for the specific address, not the town average.
Within Missouri, too, rates vary between the City, St. Louis County municipalities, and the outer counties, and don’t forget Missouri’s separate annual personal-property tax on vehicles.
### New construction vs. historic character
One of the clearest dividing lines in the metro is new versus old. St. Charles County and the outer edges are where you’ll find newer subdivisions: bigger closets, open floor plans, low early maintenance, and often an HOA - at the cost of smaller lots and a longer commute. Kirkwood, Webster Groves, Maplewood, University City, and much of South City offer the opposite: brick, character, mature trees, and walkable streets, but also older systems that need upkeep. Neither is better; it’s a genuine trade-off between move-in-ready convenience and established charm. Be honest about which one actually fits how you live before you tour a single house, because it quietly rules half the map in or out.
### Match the town to where you are in life
It helps to think in terms of who’s buying. First-time buyers stretching a budget tend to land in North County, Jefferson County (Arnold, Festus), or the Illinois side. Move-up families chasing space and newer schools gravitate to St. Charles County. Schools-first buyers aim for Clayton, Ladue, Kirkwood, or Webster Groves and accept the price. And downsizers or walkability-seekers love Maplewood, Webster, Kirkwood, and Edwardsville, where you can park once and live on foot. There’s no wrong answer - just the one that fits your stage and your commute.
### How to actually choose
Personality aside, four practical filters narrow the field fast:
Schools: Even if you do not have kids, district reputation drives resale value. Look up the specific district (not just the town) and check current ratings - you can also see where schools sit across the metro on our St. Louis area schools map.
Commute: Drive your real route at your real rush hour before you commit. Ten miles in West County can feel very different from ten miles across the river.
Budget: Compare total monthly cost, including property taxes, which vary a lot between Missouri and Illinois.
Walkability: If a walkable downtown matters, Kirkwood, Webster Groves, Clayton, Maplewood, and Edwardsville should be near the top of your list.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Which suburbs in St. Louis are considered the best to live in?
A.  It depends what matters most to you. For schools and walkable downtowns, Kirkwood, Webster Groves, Clayton and Ladue lead. For space and newer homes, look at Chesterfield, Wildwood and St. Charles County towns like O’Fallon and Wentzville. For value, Arnold, Florissant and the Illinois side. Edwardsville is the Metro-East standout. Pick the school district first, then the town.
### Q. Which St. Louis suburbs have the best schools?
A.  Ladue, Clayton, Kirkwood, and Webster Groves consistently rank near the top in Missouri, and Edwardsville District 7 leads the Metro-East. Always confirm current ratings for the exact district that serves a specific address, because one town can be split between districts.
### Q. What is the most expensive suburb in St. Louis?
A.  Ladue, with tiny Huntleigh and Frontenac next door, sits at the top: estate-size lots, the highest household incomes in the metro and, in Ladue’s case, a top-ranked Missouri school district. Clayton and Town and Country follow close behind. In all of them you pay for the address and the district as much as the house.
### Q. What city is 30 minutes from St. Louis, Missouri?
A.  Plenty. With no traffic, St. Charles, Chesterfield, Edwardsville, Belleville and Arnold are all roughly 25 to 35 minutes from downtown St. Louis, and inner suburbs like Clayton, Kirkwood and Webster Groves are closer. Rush hour on I-64, I-70 or a river bridge can stretch any of those, so drive it at your real commute time before you decide.
### Q. Is St. Louis growing or shrinking?
A.  Both, depending on where you draw the line. Census Bureau estimates, adjusted each year, show the City of St. Louis down about 7.7 percent since the 2020 census, to roughly 278,000 people, while St. Charles County grew about 5 percent to roughly 426,000. The growth is in the suburbs, which is why the newest subdivisions and schools are out there.

## A Guide to St. Louis Metro Farmers Markets by Town
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/a-guide-to-st-louis-metro-farmers-markets-by-town
There is a particular kind of Saturday morning that makes summer in the St. Louis area feel worth it. You are up a little earlier than you wanted to be, there is coffee in a paper cup, and you are walking past a folding table piled with tomatoes still warm from someone’s field that morning. A grower hands you a peach. Somewhere a band is tuning up. This is farmers market season, and the good news is that you do not have to drive into the city to find it. From Kirkwood to Edwardsville, nearly every town in the metro has its own market, each with its own personality.
There’s a real payoff to shopping this way beyond the freshness. Your money stays with a neighbor instead of a distant supply chain, the produce was usually picked within a day so it lasts longer in your fridge, and you get to actually talk to the person who grew it — which is how you end up trying a vegetable you’d never have picked up under fluorescent lights. For families, it’s a cheap, screen-free Saturday outing; for cooks, it’s the best way to let the season decide dinner. Once you find your regular market, it tends to become a weekly habit rather than a chore. The vendors start to recognize you, they set aside the thing you always buy, and a routine grocery errand quietly turns into the best part of the weekend.
Here is a by-town guide to where you can find fresh local produce across the suburbs and the Illinois Metro-East. Markets are seasonal and schedules shift year to year, so always check the current schedule before you go.
### Mid-County and South County, Missouri
Kirkwood. The Kirkwood Farmers’ Market on East Argonne is one of the oldest in the region and runs most of the year, with peak local-grower season in the warmer months. Unlike weekend-only markets, it keeps daily hours, which makes it an easy weekday stop. Saturday mornings are busiest, so arrive early if you want first pick of the produce.
Maplewood. The market formerly sponsored by Schlafly now runs as the SOL Food Farmers Market on Sutton Boulevard in downtown Maplewood. It is a producer-only, vendor-owned market on Wednesday evenings during the growing season, which means the people behind the tables actually grew or made what they are selling. Expect pastured meats and eggs, mushrooms, honey, preserves, and seasonal produce.
### North County, Missouri
Ferguson. The Ferguson Farmers Market at the Plaza at 501 on South Florissant is a Saturday-morning staple that serves the whole North County area, including nearby Florissant. Produce here is often picked within a day of the market. One standout: Ferguson participates in SNAP and Double Up Food Bucks, a program that matches what you spend with your EBT card on fruits and vegetables, dollar for dollar up to a limit. It is a quiet way to stretch a grocery budget while eating better. Check the current schedule for token details.
### West County and Far West, Missouri
Wildwood. The Wildwood Farmers Market on Plaza Drive opens later in the spring, usually around late May, and runs Saturday mornings through early fall. It pairs fresh produce, eggs, and meats with handmade soaps, honey, and crafts.
Lake St. Louis. The Lake Saint Louis Farmers & Artists Market at The Meadows shopping center runs Saturday mornings across a long season, rain or shine, and leans into both local growers and local artisans. Vendors are drawn from within roughly 100 miles, so what you buy is genuinely regional.
St. Charles. The Saint Charles Market on Historic Main Street is one of the longer-running seasons in the metro, stretching well into late fall on Saturday mornings. With farmers, bakers, crafters, and artisans together on a brick-lined street, it doubles as a morning out.
Wildly off-topic — 40,000 Illinois-side businesses, mapped, and not a tomato among them.
### Illinois Metro-East
O’Fallon, Illinois. Note the state — there is an O’Fallon in Missouri too. The Vine Street Market at O’Fallon Station has become one of the most popular markets in the Metro-East, with 60-plus vendors at peak, live music, and food trucks. It focuses on food grown or made within about 100 miles and runs roughly May through October.
Edwardsville. The Land of Goshen Community Market is a beloved Saturday-morning fixture. For the 2026 season it temporarily moved to City Park while its usual downtown home is rebuilt as a new park, so confirm the current location before you go. It is large, lively, and worth the drive.
Alton. The Alton Farmers’ & Artisans’ Market, organized by Alton Main Street, runs Saturday mornings near the downtown historic district from late spring into mid-fall. Expect locally grown fruits and vegetables alongside handmade crafts, specialty foods, and even pet goods.
Belleville. Belleville’s Old Town area hosts a long-running market with both outdoor and indoor space, and several vendors accept SNAP, EBT, WIC, and the Farmers Market Nutrition Program. Hours and exact dates shift, so check the city’s current schedule.
### City and inner-ring markets worth the trip
This guide leans toward the suburbs, but a few close-in markets are too good to leave off — especially if you want something running outside the peak summer window.
Soulard. The Soulard Farmers Market, just south of downtown, is the region’s oldest and the one to know when every suburban market is closed for the season: it’s open year-round, Wednesday through Saturday. It’s a bustling, historic public market with produce, meats, cheeses, spices, flowers, and prepared food under one roof — as much an experience as a grocery run. Go early on a Saturday for the fullest stalls and the best people-watching, and bring a rolling cart if you plan to stock up.
Tower Grove. The Tower Grove Farmers Market, held in the park, is one of the metro’s largest and most popular. It’s producer-focused (the people selling grew or made it), with Saturday hours spring through fall plus a weekday market in the height of summer, live music, and a family-friendly crowd. It doubles as a morning in the park, so bring a blanket, grab breakfast from a stall, and let the kids run around while you take your time shopping the stalls.
University City. The U. City Farmers Market fits the by-town frame on the inner-suburb side, running multiple days a week deep into the fall with a strong lineup of local growers — a handy mid-week option when you miss the Saturday markets. It has a loyal neighborhood following and a good mix of produce, prepared food, and local makers.
Richmond Heights. The Boulevard Market brings a Sunday option to mid-county, which is a nice fit if your Saturday mornings are already spoken for by soccer and swim lessons.
### What’s in season, roughly by month
Part of the fun of shopping local is eating with the calendar. Here’s the rough St. Louis rhythm so you know what to look for:
April–May: asparagus, spinach, lettuces, radishes, green onions, strawberries, and the first herbs and bedding plants. This is when the suburban markets open.
June: strawberries give way to cherries and the first zucchini and cucumbers; peas and green beans arrive.
July–August: the peak. Sweet corn, tomatoes still warm from the field, peaches, blackberries, melons, peppers, and eggplant. If a market has a busy week, this is it — go early.
September–October: apples, winter squash, pumpkins, greens, sweet potatoes, and the last tomatoes. Cooler mornings, smaller crowds, great color.
November–March: most suburban markets close, but Soulard and a few winter markets carry root vegetables, greens, eggs, meats, honey, and preserves right through the cold months.
### It’s not just produce
A good market is a whole local pantry. Alongside the fruit and vegetables you’ll typically find pastured eggs and meats, local honey, artisan bread and pastries, cheese, mushrooms, jams and pickles, cut flowers, coffee, and prepared foods for breakfast on the spot. Many markets also host craft and artisan vendors — soaps, candles, pottery, pet treats — which makes a Saturday stroll double as gift shopping. Producer-only markets like SOL Food and Tower Grove are especially good if you care that the person behind the table actually raised or made what they’re selling.
### How to shop a farmers market like you mean it
Go early. The best tomatoes, berries, and sweet corn sell out fast. The first hour is where the good stuff lives.
Bring cash and small bills. Many smaller vendors are cash-first, and breaking a twenty for a three-dollar bunch of radishes is nobody’s favorite moment.
Bring your own bags. Reusable totes save you from juggling an armload of peaches across a gravel lot.
Ask the growers. They will tell you what was picked yesterday, what is at its peak this week, and how to cook the weird-looking green thing you have never tried. A two-minute conversation with a grower will teach you more than an hour of recipe scrolling.
Use SNAP and Double Up Food Bucks where offered. Markets like Ferguson and several Metro-East markets accept EBT and may match your produce dollars. Ask at the information table.
Expect a spring-to-fall season. Most markets run roughly April or May through October. A few keep winter or year-round hours, but the peak produce window is summer into early fall.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. When does farmers market season start in the St. Louis area?
A.  Most metro markets open between early April and late May and run through October, with a handful stretching into November. A few, like Kirkwood, keep hours much of the year. Always confirm opening day on the market’s current schedule, since dates move.
### Q. Which farmers markets accept SNAP or Double Up Food Bucks?
A.  The Ferguson Farmers Market participates in SNAP and Double Up Food Bucks, which matches your EBT spending on fruits and vegetables up to a limit. Several Metro-East markets, including Belleville, accept SNAP, EBT, WIC, and the Farmers Market Nutrition Program. Ask at the market’s information table for current details.
### Q. What time should I arrive for the best selection?
A.  Aim for the first hour. Popular items like sweet corn, berries, heirloom tomatoes, and fresh-cut flowers often sell out early, especially on busy Saturdays.
### Q. Is there a difference between O’Fallon, Missouri and O’Fallon, Illinois markets?
A.  Yes — they are two different towns in two different states. This guide highlights the Vine Street Market in O’Fallon, Illinois. If you are searching online, include the state so you do not drive the wrong direction across the river.
### Q. Do I need cash, or can I use a card?
A.  Bring some cash, ideally small bills. Many larger markets have card and token systems at an information booth, but plenty of individual growers still prefer cash, and small bills keep the line moving.
### Q. Are farmers markets more expensive than the grocery store?
A.  Sometimes, sometimes not. Specialty items like pastured meat, artisan bread, and cut flowers can cost more than a big-box store, but in-season staples — sweet corn, tomatoes, zucchini, greens — are often competitive or cheaper at peak, and far fresher. Shopping what’s in season, buying in bulk when something is at its cheapest, and using SNAP or Double Up Food Bucks where offered all stretch the dollar further.
### Q. Can I bring my kids and my dog?
A.  Kids, yes — markets are a great, low-pressure outing, and many have music, samples, or activities. Dogs depend on the market: some welcome leashed, well-behaved dogs, while others (especially those with lots of open food) don’t allow them. Check the individual market’s rules before you bring the pup.
### Q. Which market is best for a first-timer?
A.  For sheer variety and a can’t-miss experience, start with Soulard (year-round) or Tower Grove in peak season. If you want something closer to home, pick the market in your own town from the list above — the beauty of the metro is that a good one is usually just a few minutes away.
When the markets are closed for the season, the same shopping instinct moves indoors — this is how to shop a health food store in St. Louis without paying for the label.
Thinking of working those markets from your own kitchen on wheels? Start with what a St. Louis food truck really costs.
Turn it into a day out — after the market, try one of these easy family-friendly hiking trails around St. Louis.
