## Google Business Profile Posts: What to Post & Why (St. Louis)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/google-business-profile-posts-st-louis
You’ve claimed your Google Business Profile, filled it out, and gathered some reviews. Then you notice a feature you’ve been ignoring: the ability to publish posts — little updates that appear right on your profile in Search and Maps. Most St. Louis business owners glance at it, think “I don’t have time for another thing to post,” and move on. And in doing so, they leave one of the easiest free tools on the table. So the honest question is small but stubborn: what’s really stopping you from spending five minutes a week on a tool that’s free and already yours?
Google Business Profile posts won’t single-handedly transform your business, but they’re a genuinely useful, no-cost way to keep your profile active, promote what matters, and give a searching customer one more reason to choose you. This is a straightforward 2026 guide: what these posts are, whether they’re worth your time, exactly what to post, and how to write one that works.
### How Do Google Business Profile Posts Work?
Google Business Profile posts are short updates — a bit of text, usually an image, and often a button — that you publish directly to your profile, where they appear in Google Search and Maps when someone looks up your business. Think of them as mini-announcements built into your listing: an offer, an event, a piece of news, a new product. You create them free from your profile through Google Search or Maps, and they show up in a dedicated area of your listing. Some post types (like specific offers or events) run for a set window, while general updates stay visible for a while before rolling off. There’s no cost, no approval delay for normal posts, and no technical skill required — if you can write a social media caption, you can publish a Google post.
### Is It Worth Posting on Google Business Profile?
Yes. The effort is small and the upside is real, as long as you keep expectations honest. Posting won’t rocket you up the rankings on its own, but it earns its keep in three ways. It keeps your profile looking active, so the listing reads as open and attentive to customers and to Google alike. It promotes what matters, putting your offer, event, or news right where a ready-to-buy customer is already looking you up. And it drives conversion, because a well-timed post can be the exact nudge that turns a browser into a caller. The catch is consistency. A single post from a year ago does nothing. But a post or two a week, taking only minutes, is one of the better returns on time a local business can get for free.
### What Should I Post on My Google Business Profile?
You have more to post about than you think. The most effective types for a local business: offers and promotions (a discount, a seasonal special, a limited-time deal — with a clear expiration); events (a sale, a workshop, an open house, anything with a date); news and updates (a new service, extended hours, a remodel, an award, a staff addition); products or featured services with a photo and a short description; and seasonal or timely content tied to holidays, the weather, or local happenings. When you’re stuck, answer a question customers always ask, or spotlight a single popular product. The rule of thumb: post things a potential customer would find useful or appealing, not filler. Every post should give someone a reason to choose you or an easy next step to take.
### How to Write a Good Google Business Profile Post
A strong post is short, visual, and action-oriented. Lead with the point — the offer, the event, the news — in the first sentence, since space is limited and attention is short. Keep the writing clear and friendly, skip the jargon, and always include a good image, because posts with photos draw far more eyes than text alone. Add a call to action button where it fits (Call now, Learn more, Book, Order) so the reader has an obvious next step. If it’s an offer or event, state the details plainly: what it is, the dates, and how to claim or attend. And write it for a real person on the sidewalk deciding whether to walk in, not for a search engine.
### Where Do Google Business Profile Posts Show Up?
Your posts appear on your Business Profile itself — the panel that shows up when someone searches your business name on Google or finds you in Maps. They surface in a dedicated “Updates” or posts area of that profile, where a person checking you out will see your latest news alongside your reviews, photos, and hours. Offer and event posts can also appear more prominently at the relevant moment. The important thing to understand is the audience: these posts are seen mainly by people who are already looking you up — which is exactly the high-intent moment you want to influence. Someone reading your post is often seconds from calling or visiting, so a timely offer or a reassuring update lands at the perfect time. That’s what makes the feature valuable despite its modest reach: the reach is small, but the intent is high.
### A Week of Post Ideas for a St. Louis Business
If a blank posting box stalls you, work from a simple rotation. Monday: feature a popular product or service with a nice photo and a “Learn more” button. Midweek: share a current offer or seasonal special with clear dates and a call to action. Later in the week: post a piece of news — extended weekend hours, a new team member, an award, a completed project — or promote an upcoming event. Tie posts to the local rhythm when you can: a Cardinals-weekend special, a back-to-school offer, a holiday reminder, a “beat the heat” note in July. You don’t need all of these every week; rotating through a couple keeps your profile fresh without becoming a burden. The point is a steady drumbeat of useful, specific updates that make your business look active and give nearby customers a reason to act.
Total tangent — when hunger hits, Herculaneum’s dinner lineup is right here.
### Are Google Posts the Same as Social Media Posts?
Not quite — and treating them identically is a common mistake. Social media posts chase engagement (likes, shares, comments) from your followers; Google Business Profile posts inform and convert people who are actively searching for a business like yours. The audience and the goal are different. That said, they can share content: a promotion or event you post to social can often be repurposed as a Google post in a few minutes. The key difference in tone is that Google posts should be more direct and utility-focused — less “look at this fun thing” and more “here’s a reason to choose us, and here’s the next step.” Reuse the content, but sharpen the intent for the searcher who’s ready to buy.
### How Often Should You Post?
Consistency beats volume. Aim for at least one post a week, and up to a few, so your profile always shows recent activity — that freshness is much of the value, since a post from months ago signals a dormant business. You don’t need to agonize over each one; a quick weekly rhythm (this week’s special, an upcoming event, a featured product) keeps things moving without eating your time. Batching helps: sit down once and rough out a few posts for the coming weeks. The goal isn’t to go viral — these aren’t social media posts chasing likes — it’s to keep a steady, useful presence in front of the customers already searching for you. A little, done regularly, is the entire game — the businesses that keep a steady rhythm quietly stay visible while the ones that posted once and stopped fade into the background.
### Common Posting Mistakes to Avoid
A few habits waste the feature’s potential. Posting once and quitting is the biggest, since a lone stale post is worse than none: it signals abandonment. Text with no image gets far less attention. Vague content (“great deals available!”) gives no reason to act, so be specific. Treating it like Twitter with hot takes or off-topic musings misses the point; keep posts about your business and useful to customers. And letting an expired offer linger looks careless. Avoid those, keep posts specific, visual, current, and customer-focused, and this small free tool pulls its weight. Paired with a fully optimized profile (see our guide to optimizing your Google Business Profile), regular posts help keep you the active, obvious choice in local search, and it becomes a small, free habit that compounds alongside your reviews and your complete profile.
Posts keep your profile active - a consistent presence keeps you found. ## That Box Fan Won’t Save You in the High 90s. A Free AC Unit Can.
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/cool-down-st-louis-free-ac-units-summer-cooling-assistance-2026
At midnight the back bedroom of a one-story house in Spanish Lake is still hot enough that the sheets stick to your legs. The window unit quit in June. The box fan just pushes the same thick air from one wall to the other, and the cicadas outside are louder than the fan. For the 80-year-old who lives there on a fixed income, rationing the AC to keep the Ameren bill down, that isn’t a bad night’s sleep. In a St. Louis heat wave it can turn dangerous within hours.
Free window AC units exist for exactly that bedroom, with one catch: Cool Down St. Louis gives them only to seniors and people with severe disabilities who have no working unit at home, through partner agencies, while supplies last. Apply before the first heat advisory, not in the middle of it.
That box fan is the trap. The CDC puts it plainly: once the temperature is in the high 90s, an electric fan may feel like relief, but it won’t prevent heat-related illness. A cool shower or an air-conditioned room does.
First, the rule that buys you time: from June 1 through September 30, Missouri law bars Ameren from cutting your power when the forecast calls for more than 95 degrees, or a heat index over 105, anytime in the next 72 hours. Being behind on the bill doesn’t mean the AC goes dark in a heat wave.
The protection almost nobody uses works in any month. Under the Missouri Public Service Commission’s rules, a utility it regulates, like Ameren Missouri, has to postpone a shut-off for up to 21 days if cutting service would aggravate an existing medical emergency for anyone who lives in the home. Call before the shut-off date and be ready to show proof, like a letter from the doctor. That’s three more weeks to get bill help lined up.
Then the unit itself. Heat kills more Americans than any other kind of weather, and there’s a St. Louis charity that hands out free window air conditioners for exactly that bedroom: Cool Down St. Louis, the summer twin of Heat Up St. Louis, run by the same nonprofit. Call early in the season, because once the summer’s supply of units is gone, it’s gone.
Tonight, while you wait: sleep on the lowest floor, keep a cool, wet cloth on your neck and wrists, and if the house is still hot after dark, dial 2-1-1 for the nearest cooling center.
When you apply at CoolDownStLouis.org or 314-241-0001, have your household and income information ready, plus any paperwork on a medical condition. Worth passing to the neighbor whose window unit just died.
### What is Cool Down St. Louis?
For a lot of St. Louis seniors, the most important sound in July is a window unit kicking on in the back bedroom. Cool Down St. Louis is a regional charity - the summer counterpart to Heat Up St. Louis, founded by Gentry Trotter - that helps at-risk residents survive dangerous heat. It provides free ENERGY STAR window air-conditioning units and cooling-related electric-bill assistance for the people who are most at risk when the temperature spikes: seniors, people with disabilities, and low-income households, especially families with critically-ill children.
The program leans on community partners to do it. Ameren Missouri has backed it for more than 20 summers, and its most recent donation was 950 ENERGY STAR window air-conditioning units for the whole state. Like its winter sibling, Cool Down serves a wide footprint - dozens of counties across Missouri and Illinois - so help isn’t limited to the city. Over its two decades, the program reports distributing roughly 25,000 air-conditioning units to the region’s most vulnerable residents. That number climbs every time the forecast turns dangerous.
### Who to call: a quick summer reference
When the heat is bearing down and you’re not sure where to start, here’s the short list:
### Who qualifies for cooling help?
If the pill bottles on the kitchen windowsill carry warnings about heat, that’s the household this program was built for. Cool Down focuses its limited supply of AC units on the households most likely to suffer a medical emergency in the heat. You’re a strong candidate if you are:
A senior, especially on a fixed income
A person with a disability or a health condition that heat makes dangerous
A low-income household, particularly one with a critically-ill child or a medically fragile family member
Why these groups specifically? Older adults and people with chronic conditions can’t shed body heat as easily, and plenty take medications that make a hot day even harder on the body. In a Missouri heat wave, a home without working air conditioning can push a fragile body past its limit within hours. That is why the program exists, and why it prioritizes the people it does.
If that describes you or someone you love, don’t wait for a crisis - supplies are limited and go fast once the first heat wave hits. Apply early in the season.
### How to apply for Cool Down St. Louis
Applying is simple, and you can do it online or by phone:
Online - apply at CoolDownStLouis.org (or CoolDownMissouri.org).
By phone - call 314-241-0001 or 314-834-0034.
Have your basic household and income information ready, along with any documentation of a medical condition if that’s part of your situation. The program partners with Ameren Missouri and area agencies to distribute units, so where and when you pick up may depend on supply in your area - the intake staff will walk you through it. Because demand always outruns the number of donated units, being early in the season matters more than almost anything else. If the current year’s supply is exhausted when you apply, ask to be added to the list so you’re first in line for the next round.
Checking on someone who lives alone this summer? Send them this page, and keep the St. Louis Help & Assistance Resources hub handy for the other bills a hot month brings.
If you’re the agency, the HVAC shop or the volunteer crew that helps neighbors stay cool, put it on the map with us so more neighbors can find you before the next heat wave.
### Where do you pick up a free AC unit from Cool Down St. Louis?
When the back bedroom is still sticky-hot at midnight, you want to know exactly where to go. There’s no warehouse you can walk into. Cool Down St. Louis hands its donated window units to partner agencies, and the agency that serves your ZIP code handles the paperwork and tells you when and where to get the unit. The charity says it works with more than 38 agencies, and the Urban League of Metropolitan St. Louis has helped hand out air conditioners since the program began. Start with the hotlines for seniors and people with disabilities, 314-241-0001 or 314-834-0034, and ask which agency is yours.
Know the catch before you call. In its most recent client notice, the charity says units go only to seniors and people with severe disabilities while supplies last, and it won’t provide one if anyone in the household already has a working unit. Ameren’s latest donation was 950 units for the entire state, so the line forms early, often before the first heat advisory.

### Prepare before the next heat wave
A little planning turns a dangerous day into a manageable one. Do these on a cool day, so a hot one never becomes an emergency:
Get your fan or AC unit now, before the first advisory - supplies run out fast.

Ask your pharmacist whether any of your medications are affected by heat or need cool storage.
Set up a daily check-in with someone if you live alone - even a quick text counts.
### Your rights: the Missouri Hot Weather Rule
Just as winter has the Cold Weather Rule, Missouri summers have a Hot Weather Rule that limits when your electricity can be shut off - and it’s broader than most people realize.
From June 1 through September 30, an electric utility cannot disconnect your service when the National Weather Service forecasts the temperature above 95°F, or the heat index above 105°F. Thanks to the same 2025 law (Senate Bill 4) that updated the winter rule, the forecast window was extended from 24 hours to 72 hours. The statute protects residential customers whose cooling runs on electricity, and it covers gas service too when gas powers the only cooling equipment in the home. The Missouri PSC enforces it for the utilities it regulates, like Ameren Missouri; if a city utility or rural co-op serves you, call it to confirm how it applies the rule.
If you’re behind on your bill and a heat wave is coming, that protection buys you time - use it to apply for the help below. If you believe a utility is violating the rule, call the Missouri PSC Consumer Services line at 1-800-392-4211.
### More cooling help: bill assistance and cooling centers
Cool Down isn’t the only summer resource. Stack these on top:
Summer energy crisis assistance (ECIP): Missouri’s LIHEAP program offers up to $300 toward summer cooling costs for income-eligible households. It’s the same application as winter heating help - see our guide to applying for LIHEAP in Missouri.
Cooling centers: during declared heat emergencies, both the City of St. Louis and St. Louis County open air-conditioned cooling centers - community centers, libraries, and senior centers where anyone can escape the heat for free. To find the nearest one open today, dial 2-1-1 (United Way).
Your utility’s programs: Ameren’s Budget Billing and payment plans can smooth out those brutal July and August bills before they become a crisis.
Ameren’s summer credits and grants: Keeping Cool gives income-eligible seniors, households with children under 5, and people with a documented medical condition or disability up to five $50 bill credits from May through September. Dollar More can cover up to $600, and Cool Down’s own Ameren-funded bill help runs up to $600 as well; call 314-241-0001.
### Warning signs of heat illness (and when to call 911)
Knowing the warning signs can save a life - especially for the seniors and medically fragile neighbors this program serves. Heat exhaustion shows up as heavy sweating, cold or clammy skin, dizziness, headache, nausea, and a fast, weak pulse. Move the person somewhere cool, loosen their clothing, have them sip water, and apply cool, damp cloths. If it doesn’t improve within an hour, get medical help.
Heat stroke is the emergency. The signs: hot, red skin that may be dry or damp; a body temperature above 103°F; confusion or slurred speech; and fainting. Call 911 immediately, move the person into shade or air conditioning, and cool them with whatever you have - but do not give fluids to someone who is unconscious. When a heat advisory hits, check on elderly neighbors and anyone living alone. A two-minute knock on the door is the simplest life-saving thing you can do all summer.
Looking for more local resources? A tool like findhelp.org can point you to food, housing, and health programs near you, and you can search the St Louis Near Me Directory for St. Louis organizations and community resources.
If your nonprofit checks on seniors or keeps fans and window units moving when the heat index climbs, list it with us so more neighbors and customers who need you can reach you before the next heat advisory.
### Lower your summer electric bill
A few moves keep the summer bill from becoming the emergency in the first place. Ask Ameren about Budget Billing to flatten those brutal July and August spikes into a steady monthly amount. Apply for free weatherization through your Community Action Agency - the same insulation and air sealing that keeps heat inside in winter keeps it out in summer, cutting cooling costs for good. And simple habits add up: close the blinds on the sunny side during the day, run fans so you feel comfortable at a higher thermostat setting, and change your AC filter monthly so the unit doesn’t have to strain.
### Don’t wait for the heat to win
The hardest part of a heat wave is that it doesn’t look like an emergency until it becomes one. A stuffy apartment feels survivable right up until it isn’t - and for a senior or someone with a heart or lung condition, that line comes fast. So make the call on a normal day, not a 105-degree one. Get the fan or the unit in the window before you need it, apply for the bill help while there’s still funding, and know where your nearest cooling center is.

Seniors and people with disabilities should apply to Cool Down St. Louis for a free unit.
### Q. Is a broken AC considered an emergency?
A.  For a senior, a baby, or anyone with a heart, lung or other heat-sensitive condition, a dead AC during a heat advisory is a health emergency. Get to a cooling center (dial 2-1-1), call Cool Down at 314-241-0001 about a replacement unit, and if you rent, tell your landlord in writing. Call 911 for confusion, fainting or a body temperature above 103°F.
### Q. What types of grants are available in St. Louis, Mo.?
A.  For cooling and utility costs, the main ones are Cool Down St. Louis (free window AC units plus Ameren-funded bill help up to $600), LIHEAP crisis help (up to $300 in summer and $800 in winter), and Ameren’s Dollar More (up to $600) and Keeping Cool credits. For rent, food or medical bills, dial 2-1-1 for current programs.
### Q. What are signs that your AC unit is going out?
A.  Warm air from the vents, weak airflow, a unit that runs nonstop or keeps clicking on and off, water leaking indoors, ice on the coils, and a power bill that jumps for no reason. Change the filter first. If it still struggles and you are a senior or have a disability, apply to Cool Down St. Louis before it quits in July.

## Things to Do at St. Louis Union Station: The Complete Guide
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-at-st-louis-union-station-the-complete-2026-guide
Ask a St. Louis parent where to take the kids on a hot Saturday or a rainy Sunday, and there’s a good chance the answer is Union Station. What used to be the world’s busiest train terminal — and, for a while, a fading shopping mall — is now one of the metro’s most packed family destinations, with an aquarium, a giant observation wheel, ropes courses, mini golf, and a free fire-and-light show all under and around one gorgeous 1894 roof.
The trouble is there’s so much to do that first-timers don’t always know where to start — or which parts cost money and which are free. So here’s the complete, up-to-date guide to everything there is to do at St. Louis Union Station in 2026, with real prices, hours, parking tips, and a plan to make a full day of it.
Save this guide and share it with whoever you’re bringing - then check the official site for the exact prices and hours on your date, since ticketed attractions use dynamic pricing. Planning the aquarium too? Start with our aquarium visit guide.
If you run a shop, a bar or a lunch counter within walking distance of the station, put it on the directory where people planning a day downtown can see it.
### What is there to do at Union Station?
Union Station packs a full lineup of attractions, dining, and free shows into one downtown campus at 1820 Market Street, one anchor of a metro with plenty more to explore. Here’s the whole menu at a glance:
Prices are approximate and set dynamically — combo “bundle” tickets cover several attractions for less. Check stlouisunionstation.com for current prices and hours on your date.
### The St. Louis Aquarium
The anchor of the whole complex, the St. Louis Aquarium fills the space where the old mall used to be with six galleries that follow water from a Missouri creek to the deep ocean. The showstopper is Shark Canyon, a 250,000-gallon habitat of sharks, rays, and sea turtles you walk right up to. Kids gravitate to the hands-on touch tanks — stingrays, jellyfish, doctor-fish — and the whole visit runs about 1.5 to 2.5 hours. It’s the one attraction worth building your day around. For the full details on tickets, hours, and tips, see our guide to visiting the St. Louis Aquarium.
### The St. Louis Wheel
Rising 200 feet over the lake, The St. Louis Wheel is the city’s best easy view. Its 42 enclosed, climate-controlled gondolas keep you comfortable in heat, cold, or drizzle across a smooth 15-minute turn, with downtown and the Gateway Arch on the horizon. It runs late, typically to 10 p.m. That makes a sunset or after-dark ride, city lights flickering on, the one to catch. Each gondola holds a small group. There’s no height requirement and no thrills, so grandparents and toddlers ride just as happily. Pair it with the aquarium on a combo ticket and you’ve got the two marquee experiences in one visit.
### Rides, ropes, and mazes for the whole family
Past the aquarium and the Wheel, the campus keeps mixed-age groups busy for hours.
Ropes Course — a multi-level indoor course with 45-plus obstacles and a 100-foot SkyRail, plus a Sky Tykes junior version for little ones.
Mini Golf — an 18-hole indoor course, weatherproof and fun for all ages.
Mirror Maze — a disorienting, delightful maze themed to the 1904 World’s Fair.
Carousel — a classic ride the youngest visitors love.
Selfie Express and seasonal outdoor rides — photo experiences and warm-weather rides that rotate through.
Nearly all of it sits indoors and climate-controlled. That’s exactly why Union Station becomes the metro’s default plan when it’s 100 degrees outside or pouring rain.
### Free things to do at Union Station
Some of the best things at Union Station are free. A lot of visitors never realize it. You can spend a whole evening here and never buy a ticket.
The Fire & Light Show — a spectacular, multi-million-dollar show of fire, water, and light out on the lake, free to watch nightly from the outdoor plaza. It’s the single best no-cost date-night or family moment at Union Station.
The Grand Hall 3D Light Show — more than 30 video vignettes projected across the 65-foot barrel-vaulted ceiling of the historic Grand Hall, set to music. Grab a drink, lean back, and look up.
The Grand Hall itself — just walking through the restored 1894 headhouse, a genuine cathedral of the railroad age, costs nothing and is worth the trip on its own.
### Where to eat at Union Station
You never have to leave the property to eat. Options run from a quick sweet treat to a full sit-down dinner.
The Soda Fountain — retro diner classics and famously over-the-top “Freak Shakes.”
The Train Shed — American plates and cocktails under the historic train-shed canopy.
Landry’s Seafood House — Gulf Coast seafood with lakeside boardwalk seating.
Station Grille — breakfast and lunch in the restored Fred Harvey restaurant space.
The Grand Hall — dinner and drinks beneath the 65-foot archways, plus The Pitch Athletic Club & Tavern, Cookies and Cupcakes, and seasonal outdoor stands.
### Where to stay: the Union Station Hotel
You can sleep inside the landmark, too. The St. Louis Union Station Hotel, part of Hilton’s Curio Collection, occupies the historic headhouse, and its lobby lounge sits right inside the Grand Hall. Railroad-age grandeur meets modern rooms. Wake up steps from the aquarium, the Wheel, and the nightly light shows, and it becomes a natural base for a downtown weekend, a conference at the nearby America’s Center convention complex, or a special-occasion stay.
### Planning your visit
A few details make the day run smoother. Sort these out before you leave the house.
Address: 1820 Market Street, St. Louis, MO 63103, in the heart of downtown.
Parking: the South Lot offers a $5 flat rate when you validate at a gift shop (credit card only); the West Lot serves the hotel and dining.
Transit: the Union Station MetroLink stop (Red and Blue lines) is a short walk from the door — an easy car-free option from downtown or the airport.
Tickets: buy combo “bundle” passes to cover the aquarium, the Wheel, and the rides for less than à la carte, and buy online ahead on busy weekends.
Hours: they vary by attraction and season — the aquarium closes at 5 (6 on weekends) while the Wheel and rides run later — so check the official site before you go.
Good to know: after 3 p.m., guests 16 and under need an adult 21+ with them, per Union Station’s code of conduct.
One more money tip: the free experiences do a lot of heavy lifting here. Pair a couple of paid attractions with the free Fire & Light Show, the Grand Hall light show, and a walk through the historic building, and a family can have a full, memorable day without buying a ticket to everything. And if you’ll visit more than a couple of times a year, an aquarium membership pays for itself fast — it throws in free parking and discounts across Union Station’s shops, restaurants, and attractions.
Unrelated, and we know it — St. Charles restaurants, for when dinner sneaks up.
### Union Station by the type of trip
The best plan depends on who’s along for the day.
With young kids: the aquarium touch tanks, the carousel, Sky Tykes, and the free light shows are the sweet spot.
With teens and tweens: the ropes course, mini golf, the mirror maze, and a Wheel ride after dark hit different.
Date night: the free Fire & Light Show, dinner under the Grand Hall archways, and a sunset Wheel ride make a genuinely romantic evening without spending much.
Out-of-town visitors: it’s the easiest one-stop taste of St. Louis — history, an aquarium, a skyline view, and dinner, all without moving the car.
A rainy or brutally hot day: nearly everything is indoors and climate-controlled, which is exactly why locals treat Union Station as the all-weather backup plan.
### Seasonal events at Union Station
On top of the everyday attractions, Union Station runs a calendar of its own. The holidays bring the beloved Polar Express Train Ride and festive lights; summer adds outdoor rides and lakeside food stands; and the free Fire & Light Show glows nightly whatever the season. It’s always worth a look at the events calendar before you go — there’s often something special layered on top of the regular lineup, and plenty of it is free to enjoy.
### A quick history
This is a saved piece of St. Louis history, not a purpose-built theme park, and that changes how it feels. Opened in 1894 and designed by architect Theodore Link, it was once the largest and busiest passenger rail terminal in the world. Generations of travelers passed beneath that soaring Grand Hall ceiling. Then the trains stopped, a shopping-mall era came and faded, and a major redevelopment reinvented the building as today’s entertainment destination, anchored by the aquarium that opened on Christmas Day 2019. ### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is there to do at Union Station in St. Louis?
A.  Union Station offers the St. Louis Aquarium, the 200-foot St. Louis Wheel, a ropes course, mini golf, a carousel, and a mirror maze, plus restaurants and a historic hotel. Two of the best experiences — the nightly Fire & Light Show on the lake and the Grand Hall 3D light show — are completely free.
### Q. Is Union Station in St. Louis worth visiting?
A.  Yes, especially for families and visitors. Between the aquarium, the Wheel, the indoor rides, the free light shows, and the beautifully restored 1894 Grand Hall, it’s an easy half- or full-day out, and much of it is weatherproof. Even if you only came for the free shows and a meal, it’s worth the trip downtown.
### Q. Is there anything free to do at Union Station?
A.  Yes. The nightly Fire & Light Show on the lake and the 3D light show projected across the Grand Hall’s 65-foot ceiling are both free, and simply walking through the historic Grand Hall costs nothing. The aquarium, the Wheel, and the rides are ticketed, but you can enjoy a full evening at Union Station for free.
### Q. How much are tickets for the St. Louis Wheel and attractions?
A.  The St. Louis Wheel runs about $15, mini golf and the ropes course around $12–$15, and the carousel about $5, while aquarium admission is roughly $25–$30 for adults. Prices are dynamic, so buy combo “bundle” passes to save across multiple attractions and check the official site for current rates.
### Q. How much is parking at Union Station?
A.  The South Lot at Union Station offers a $5 flat rate when you validate at a gift shop (credit card only), a bargain for downtown. You can also skip parking by taking MetroLink to the Union Station stop on the Red or Blue line, a short walk from the entrance at 1820 Market Street.
### Q. How long should I spend at Union Station?
A.  Plan on a half to full day if you want to do it right. The aquarium alone takes about 1.5 to 2.5 hours; add the Wheel, a ride or two, a meal, and the free evening light shows and you’ve got a satisfying full day. Combo tickets and the walkable layout make it easy to fit a lot in.

## Started With No Factory, Now in Every Target: 10 St. Louis Businesses to Watch
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/top-10-businesses-in-st-louis-to-watch
“Power outages, equipment breaks. We aren’t making our numbers.” That was the Katie’s Pizza & Pasta team with 50 days left on a 400,000-pizza order for Target, every crust stretched by hand and slid into a wood-fired oven at 800 degrees, heat you feel on your face before you smell the char. They went from 1,000 pizzas on day one to 7,000 a day by day 45, and they made the deadline in 96 days. The frozen line started during the pandemic, when the St. Louis dining room became an assembly line and the servers and bartenders became delivery drivers. No factory, no funding. Now it’s a reported $20 million retail deal and a pizza in every Target in the country. That’s what a business to watch looks like up close. It rarely looks like the old standbys that already anchor the metro’s economy: the brewery, the pet food, the bread.
The other nine are just as easy to miss from the street: a fence line along Cass Avenue, a startup rebuilding seeds inside the chloroplast, a WashU cancer spinout under a new name. Every one earned its spot with a recent win you can check yourself, and one once-hyped name, Benson Hill, got cut after its bankruptcy, because yesterday’s buzz doesn’t count.
One St. Louis secret hides in these stories: the city pays founders to stay. Arch Grants gives winners of its startup competition $75,000 with no equity taken, plus $25,000 more to relocate, and asks one thing back: headquarter in the City of St. Louis for at least a year. Buck Surgical, No. 6 below, won one, then a $100,000 Growth Grant. Arch Grants hasn’t announced its next window; the last one ran about six weeks, Feb. 18 to March 31. If you’re building something that can scale, sign up for the reminder at archgrants.org tonight.
Run something smaller? Here’s the night these ten never have. Your phone face-down on the counter at 9 p.m. A homeowner in Florissant tapping a request into a lead-farm app. Three other contractors’ phones lighting up in three other trucks, because the app sold that one request to all of them and will bill every one. That middleman is standing in the doorway the ten companies below made sure to own: when a customer, an investor or a new hire went looking, the search ended at their door. Your work was never the question. So here’s the question worth asking: when a neighbor in Kirkwood asks her phone for what you do, does the answer reach you, or an app that resells her request?
Five minutes, tonight, free: what would you find if you searched your own trade plus your neighborhood the way that neighbor does, on Google, on the map, and in the AI app on her phone? How many of the names that come back are apps reselling the job instead of people who’d do it? And if you’d rather sell to companies like the ten below, they gather in two places worth a visit: T-REX downtown for geospatial startups and the 39 North district in Creve Coeur for agtech.
### 1. Next NGA West & T-REX (geospatial): a $1.7 billion campus in north city
Lunch hour at Jefferson and Cass, traffic easing past a security fence that runs around 97 acres of the St. Louis Place neighborhood. Behind it sits the new $1.7 billion Western headquarters of the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, opened in September 2025. NGA turns satellite images, drone footage and maps into geospatial intelligence, the analysis of anything tied to a place on Earth, used by the military and disaster-response teams; it helped pinpoint Osama bin Laden’s compound. With T-REX, the downtown tech incubator, and the geospatial startups it’s pulling in, NGA is pulling mapping and location companies to the city that used to have to court them. For owners: a campus that size changes who’s driving down Jefferson at lunch. If you feed, fix or move people on the north side, add St. Louis Place and the streets around Jefferson and Cass to the places your profile and listings name.
### 2. Katie’s Pizza & Pasta (food): 400,000 pizzas in 96 days
Early on, the phone rang and a federal agent was on the line: pull the pizzas off the grocery shelves. The pepperoni meant USDA inspection, a detour most founders never hear about. Chef Katie Lee went through it and kept going. Her premium frozen line, a consumer packaged goods brand sold on grocery shelves, is now in all roughly 1,800 Target stores nationwide, after her team hand-made a reported 400,000 pizzas in 96 days. Frozen-entrée sales are up 82% and sauces 91%, more major retailers are signed, a dedicated plant in Bridgeton should triple frozen-pizza output, and a fourth restaurant is open in Crestwood.
### 3. Plastomics (agtech): a better seed, built inside the chloroplast
Hold a leaf up to a window and every green speck you see is a chloroplast, the tiny structure where photosynthesis happens. It carries its own strand of DNA, and that’s where Plastomics loads new traits. Most genetically modified crops get the new gene in the plant’s main genome, its complete set of DNA. Putting it in the chloroplast instead makes the trait more stable, lets several traits stack together, and keeps it from drifting to other plants through pollen. The St. Louis startup raised roughly $6 million in Series B funding to push toward commercial seeds.
### 4. Pivot Bio (agtech): fertilizer pulled out of thin air
Those white anhydrous tanks parked at the edge of spring cornfields along I-70 hold one of farming’s biggest costs and pollutants: nitrogen fertilizer. Pivot Bio wants to shrink that bill. The company engineers microbes - microscopic soil bacteria - that perform nitrogen fixation, pulling nitrogen straight out of the air to feed a corn plant the way nature intended, so farmers can use less synthetic fertilizer. The company has committed to a $7 million-plus expansion adding about 40 jobs, with manufacturing in Hazelwood and R&D in the 39 North agtech district in Creve Coeur. Its global headquarters now sits in the Twin Cities, but the lab work and the production run here, another sign St. Louis is the center of gravity for the future of farming. For owners: forty new jobs in Hazelwood means forty more people looking for lunch, a mechanic and a barber near the plant.
### 5. Allotera Therapeutics, formerly Wugen (biotech): cancer-fighting cells, off the shelf
Allotera Therapeutics, the company most of St. Louis still knows as Wugen, is a spinout of WashU Medicine chasing a holy grail of cancer treatment. It’s developing CAR-T therapy - treatment that re-engineers a patient’s own immune cells to hunt and kill cancer - but in an “off-the-shelf” version. Today CAR-T is custom-built for each patient, which is slow and enormously expensive; Allotera is working on a universal, ready-to-use form that any eligible patient could receive. Its lead therapy, sofi-cel, is now in a global pivotal Phase 2 clinical trial for hard-to-treat T-cell leukemia and lymphoma, backed by roughly $150 million in Series C money. If it works, it’s a very big deal - and it’s happening here.
### 6. Buck Surgical (medtech): tools for vessels thinner than spaghetti
Buck Surgical builds tools for microvascular surgery - operating on blood vessels and structures thinner than a strand of spaghetti, the delicate work behind reconstructive and transplant procedures. Precision at that scale is brutally hard, and Buck’s technology aims to make it faster and more reliable. The startup was named a 2026 “Startup to Watch” by the St. Louis Business Journal, raised $4.2 million, and won a growth grant from Arch Grants, the St. Louis nonprofit that hands promising startups equity-free cash to stay and build in the city. Buck reads like a case study in how the region’s medtech pipeline works: a highly technical, patient-serving company born from St. Louis’s deep bench of surgeons, engineers, and university research.
Totally unrelated, but if you’re suddenly hungry - where to eat in Chesterfield.
### 7. DeepSight (medtech): ultrasound that steers the needle
DeepSight, an imaging company with offices in Clayton and California’s Bay Area, tackles a problem every clinician knows: guiding a needle to exactly the right spot inside the body. Its NeedleVue system uses medical ultrasound - imaging that bounces sound waves off tissue to see beneath the skin in real time - to help doctors place a needle accurately for procedures like biopsies and injections. In 2025 the company earned FDA clearance for the device, the regulatory green light that lets it actually reach patients - a milestone many medtech startups never hit. For patients, better needle guidance can mean fewer failed attempts and less pain during a routine biopsy or injection; for the company, clearance is what turns a promising idea into a real product.
### 8. Take Root Hospitality, Vicia (food): a Beard finalist that got leaner
If one of these companies is where you want to work next, start with where working adults in St. Louis build new skills.
On the culinary side, few St. Louis names carry the weight of Vicia, the vegetable-forward, farm-driven restaurant from chefs Michael and Tara Gallina under their Take Root Hospitality group. Vicia was a 2026 James Beard Award finalist for Outstanding Restaurant - the culinary world’s equivalent of an Oscar nomination - and while Philadelphia’s Kalaya took the medal, making that final five puts St. Louis’s food scene squarely on the national stage. The group has gotten leaner, not bigger: Taqueria Morita has closed, and Take Root now runs two restaurants, Vicia and Winslow’s Table. Fewer rooms, sharper focus.

If you run something smaller, start here. Katie’s frozen pizza started as a pandemic plan to keep one restaurant’s doors open, with no factory and no funding. Now it’s in every Target. ### 9. Orise Distribution (logistics): 40 new jobs in medical supply
Not every business to watch is a lab or a kitchen. Orise Distribution, a medical-supply distributor, announced a $6.2 million expansion adding about 40 new jobs in 2025 as it builds out nationwide distribution and adds textile-manufacturing lines. It’s the kind of quiet, job-creating growth - real facilities, real hires - that keeps a regional economy healthy underneath the flashier headlines. Medical-supply distribution is a steady, recession-resistant business, and Orise’s move to add its own manufacturing means more of that supply chain runs through St. Louis.
### 10. HJ Enterprises (manufacturing): 150 jobs headed to High Ridge
St. Louis’s comeback runs well past the downtown redevelopment story, out into the exurbs. HJ Enterprises broke ground on an expansion set to bring roughly 150 jobs to Jefferson County, in High Ridge, in 2025 - a meaningful boost for a part of the metro that doesn’t always get the spotlight, and a vote of confidence in local manufacturing. For families in Jefferson County towns like High Ridge, Arnold, and House Springs, a growing local employer means good jobs close to home - the kind of win that rarely makes national headlines but genuinely changes a community.
### A note on who’s not here
A “to watch” list is only useful if it’s honest, so we vetted every entry - and deliberately left off some names you might expect. The clearest example: Benson Hill, once one of St. Louis’s most-hyped agtech companies. It filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in March 2025, was delisted from the Nasdaq, and converted to liquidation later that year, with its assets sold off. Including a company on the way down would defeat the purpose. Every business above was checked for real, current momentum - a recent raise, expansion, approval, or award. Yesterday’s buzz didn’t count.
### Why St. Louis - the bigger picture
Notice the pattern: plant science, biotech, medtech, and geospatial keep coming up. That’s not a coincidence. St. Louis has quietly assembled one of the country’s densest innovation ecosystems, and these companies are its output:
The Donald Danforth Plant Science Center and the 39 North district make the region a global hub for agtech - the science of feeding the world.
The Cortex Innovation Community in the Central West End anchors tech and biotech startups near Washington University and its medical school.
T-REX downtown and the new NGA headquarters are building a national geospatial cluster.
Arch Grants and BioSTL pour equity-free funding and support into founders who agree to build here.
Add it up and you get a city that punches far above its size in exactly the industries that will define the next decade. The businesses above aren’t flukes - they’re the product of a machine St. Louis has been quietly building for years. For a city long known mostly for what it used to be - the gateway west, the brewery town - that’s a genuine shift: St. Louis is increasingly known for what it’s building next. The proof is the ten companies above, each with a 2025 or 2026 milestone already on the board.
One more name worth watching is yours. Remember the habit from the top: every company above made sure that when someone went looking, it was there. The Florissant bakery pulling its first trays at 5 a.m. and the two-truck HVAC crew in Fenton deserve the same shot, and too often a middleman takes it. Nobody there is bad at the work. They’re just hard to see. ## Why Downtown St. Louis Is Ripe for Development
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/why-downtown-st-louis-is-ripe-for-development
Here is downtown St. Louis in a single building. In 2006, the 44-story tower at 909 Chestnut — the former AT&T Center, the tallest office building in Missouri — was worth about $205 million. In 2025 it sold for roughly $3.6 million. That’s under two cents on the dollar for the biggest building in the state. Two cents on the dollar. So the real question for anyone paying attention: is that a city in decline — or the best entry price a developer will see in a generation?
You can read that number two ways. One: proof of collapse. Two: the buy of the decade. This guide makes the honest case for the second reading — that downtown St. Louis, after decades of disinvestment and a rough reputation, is genuinely ripe for development in 2026: unusually cheap, newly incentivized, historically rich, and finally sitting on the pieces of a comeback. It’s not a boom yet. But the setup for one is more real than it has been in twenty years.
We’re not going to cheerlead. Downtown’s problems are real and we’ll name every one of them. But the opportunity is real too, and most people haven’t noticed — so let’s walk through it with clear eyes and sourced facts.
Bookmark this - we keep it current as the downtown story develops. If you build things for a living, read to the end. For the money side, see how the downtown incentives work.
If you run a contracting firm, a design studio or a brokerage that works downtown, list your business with us so the people pricing a project can find you.
### First, the honest part: the reputation
Ask the internet about St. Louis and you get a wall of doubt: Is St. Louis still in decline? Why is it so run down? Will it ever come back? Those questions are fair, and pretending otherwise would insult you. The City of St. Louis has lost population year over year — it slipped to roughly 278,000 residents in 2025, continuing a decline that’s run for decades — and that shrinking tax base is exactly why the mayor and aldermen are working so hard to reverse it. Downtown’s office towers emptied out, storefronts went dark, and the “everyone left for the suburbs” story became the whole story.
All of that is true. But three big pieces of the reputation deserve a much closer look — the “run-down” label, the crime numbers, and the city’s industrial bones — because each one is more hopeful, and more interesting, than the headline.
### “Run-down” vs. old: they’re not the same thing
Start with the word people use most: run-down. Here’s some context that changes the picture. St. Louis was founded in 1764 — it’s 262 years old, one of the oldest cities west of the Mississippi. Its housing and building stock is routinely 100-plus years old: brick rowhouses, terra-cotta storefronts, and grand stone warehouses built when the city was one of the largest in America.
That age gets misread. A lot of what a visitor calls “run-down” is really just old — historic architecture that a newer Sun Belt city simply doesn’t have. Century-old brick and carved stone read as “worn” to an eye trained on beige subdivisions, but that same building stock is exactly what makes St. Louis beautiful, walkable, and cheap to own. Old is not a synonym for decayed. Much of it is character that money can restore.
Now the honest flip side: some parts of the city genuinely are run-down — disinvested blocks, vacant lots, buildings past saving. The city is working to clear those obstacles, from demolition of the truly dangerous to incentives for the salvageable. But reversing real disinvestment takes the one thing a shrinking tax base can’t manufacture on its own: good-paying jobs and outside money. Which is the whole point of this article. Employers and developers are exactly who the city is holding the door for, and at these prices the invitation is hard to ignore. St. Louis is, frankly, waiting.
### A blue-collar town that made things
To understand why downtown looks the way it does — grand old buildings, cheap prices — you have to know what St. Louis was. This is a former Rust Belt city, and it made things the whole country used. St. Louis was one of America’s great manufacturing hubs: it was a shoe-making capital (the Brown Shoe Company, maker of Buster Brown shoes, was founded here in 1878 and still runs from suburban Clayton as Caleres), a brewing giant, an aircraft builder, and a car town — the Chevrolet Corvette was assembled at a St. Louis plant for its first three decades, from 1954 to 1981, before production moved to Kentucky.
That industrial wealth is why the city has such spectacular building stock — the warehouses, factories, and headquarters of an economy that employed hundreds of thousands. And the collapse of that manufacturing base, from the 1960s on, is why so much of it sits empty and cheap today. St. Louis isn’t rust-belt anymore — its growth sectors now are agtech, biotech, and geospatial technology — but it still carries a blue-collar, make-things-with-your-hands DNA. That heritage is a feature: it’s a city that knows how to build, sitting on the physical infrastructure of a much larger economy, waiting for the next thing to fill it.
### The crime reputation vs. the crime numbers
St. Louis’s heaviest reputational weight is crime, so let’s deal with it directly, with sourced facts instead of spin. Violent crime in St. Louis has fallen for four straight years. Homicides dropped to 141 in 2025 — a 12-year low — down from a peak of about 260 in 2020, and overall crime fell 16% in that single year, with shootings down 28% (SLMPD 2025 statistics). Since Police Chief Robert Tracy took over in 2023, the department reports homicides down roughly 31% and violent crime down about 42%. Mayor Cara Spencer re-signed Tracy through 2029 and made a downtown public-safety task force one of her stated priorities.
Now the part almost every “most dangerous city” ranking gets wrong. Those rankings measure the City of St. Louis’s tiny boundary — a 62-square-mile city of about 290,000 people that split from its county in 1876 and never annexed its suburbs — while the actual metro holds around 2.8 million. Only about one in ten metro residents lives inside the lines those rankings use.
Do the math and the distortion is stark. Roughly 141 homicides against the city’s ~290,000 residents produces a rate near 50 per 100,000 — the scary number that fuels the lists. But spread those same deaths across the full 2.8-million metro — the way a city like Indianapolis, Jacksonville, or Nashville, which swallowed their suburbs, effectively counts — and the rate falls to roughly 5 per 100,000, right around the national average. It’s an illustration, not a perfect measurement (the suburbs have their own, lower crime counted separately) — but it shows how much a frozen 1876 border, not present-day danger, drives St. Louis’s ranking.
The honest bottom line: crime is falling, meaningfully and by the city’s own numbers — but a 12-year low is still not a low rate, a few categories like carjacking have seen upticks, and the improvement isn’t uniform across every neighborhood. It’s a real trend in the right direction, not a finished job. For anyone weighing downtown, “getting safer, fast” is a very different bet than “dangerous and getting worse” — and the data says it’s the former.
### We’ve done this before — and it worked
Here’s the part St. Louis forgets: downtown has already staged one comeback, and the playbook still exists. In 1998, Missouri created a state Historic Tax Credit — a tax break covering 25% of the cost of rehabbing a historic building — that stacks on top of the federal 20% credit. Together they can cover close to half the rehab cost of an old building, which is what turns a money-losing renovation into a deal that pencils out.
The result was the Washington Avenue loft district running through Downtown West: from about 1998 to 2008, dozens of empty garment-district warehouses became loft apartments and condos, pulling thousands of new residents into a downtown everyone had written off. STLPR later called it a “wildfire” of development. That same tax-credit toolkit is still on the books — the exact lever that makes converting today’s empty office towers financially possible. St. Louis isn’t guessing whether this can work. It has the receipts.
### What’s different now: money, will, and a $670 million signal
Three things shifted in 2025–2026 that weren’t true a few years ago.
1. Real public money is on the table. In July 2026, the Board of Aldermen passed a $255 million spending plan — the city’s share of the settlement from the Rams’ departure to Los Angeles — and carved out $55 million specifically for downtown (STLPR). That downtown slice includes $15 million to acquire vacant buildings, $15 million for the riverfront, $15 million for infrastructure, and $7.5 million in retail and restaurant incentives. Like every public commitment, the figure is current as of 2026 and subject to the usual political process — but it’s passed, and it’s real today. (For the full breakdown of the money and the tax-credit stack behind it, see our guide to St. Louis’s downtown development incentives.)
2. City leadership made downtown the priority. Mayor Cara Spencer, who took office in 2025, has named downtown revitalization a formal strategic priority, pushing office-to-residential conversion and downtown safety at the same time. When City Hall’s attention and its checkbook point the same direction, developers notice.
3. A $670 million vote of confidence at the riverfront. The old twin-tower Millennium Hotel by the Arch — vacant and decaying for years — is being demolished now and replaced with a roughly $670 million mixed-use campus of housing, offices, retail, and public space, a short walk from the America’s Center convention complex, and backed by the Gateway Arch Park Foundation and Cordish Companies. You don’t spend $670 million on a district you think is dying.
And it’s already working in places. The Butler Brothers building reopened as “The Victor,” a 384-unit apartment conversion. The long-vacant Jefferson Arms — empty for 19 years — is finishing a roughly $104 million conversion into apartments, a hotel, and retail. These aren’t renderings; they’re leased buildings with residents in them, proof the conversion model works in downtown St. Louis right now.
Total tangent — here’s how Florissant businesses get found online.
### The empty-building math: why cheap is the opportunity
Downtown’s office vacancy hit 31.7% at the end of 2025 — the highest since 1999 (CBRE), and that figure doesn’t even count the two fully-empty giants, the AT&T Tower and the Railway Exchange. On the surface, that’s a crisis. Underneath, it’s the entire investment thesis: a glut of grand old buildings selling for a fraction of what they’d cost to build, in a city that will help pay to rehab them.
Nationally, the smart-money move of this decade is office-to-residential conversion — turning obsolete office space into apartments people actually want. The Brookings Institution literally used St. Louis as its case study for reversing an “urban doom loop” this way. St. Louis has the raw material (beautiful, cheap, empty buildings), the tool (the tax-credit stack), and now the public money to prime it. That combination is genuinely rare.
### The catalyst that hasn’t fired yet: NGA
The wild card is the Next NGA West campus — the $1.7 billion National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency headquarters that opened in north St. Louis in 2025, the largest single federal investment in the region’s history. On paper it should be a gold mine: thousands of high-paying jobs and a magnet for the contractors and geospatial startups that cluster around a facility like this. It may well be the leash that eventually leads the dog — the anchor that pulls a whole new economy into the city.
But here’s the honest part: that spillover hasn’t fully happened yet. The campus is open; the surrounding boom is still mostly potential. And that’s the pattern across downtown right now — the ingredients are assembled, but the reaction is waiting on a spark.
### The chicken-and-egg problem — and who breaks it
If it’s all so cheap and incentivized, why isn’t everyone already here? Because downtown is stuck in a classic chicken-and-egg standoff. Residents hold off until there are more shops, restaurants, and street life. Retailers and restaurants won’t open until the residents show up first. Developers want proof of demand before they commit. Everyone is watching the door, and nobody wants to be first through it. Which is the oldest question in every rising market: the reward goes to whoever moves before the crowd agrees it’s safe. So — do you watch this one from the sidelines, or step through the door first?
That standoff is the opportunity. The public money, the tax credits, the falling crime, the $670 million riverfront project — those are the tools designed to break the logjam and make being first pay off. Whoever moves while it’s cheap gets in before the curve, not after. A developer. A small business. A resident who wants a real loft for a third of what one costs in Denver or Nashville. First movers in an undervalued market are the ones who look like geniuses in ten years.
### The bigger picture: cheap, and quietly on the rise
Zoom out from downtown and the case gets stronger. The St. Louis metro’s median home price is around $285,000 — against roughly $404,000 nationally and $1.5 million in San Jose — and the overall cost of living runs about 16% below the U.S. average. That’s why Redfin flagged St. Louis as a market poised to heat up, and why U.S. News lists it among the country’s most undervalued housing markets. (For the full affordability case, see our guide to why St. Louis real estate is so affordable.)
The economy underneath is stronger than the reputation suggests: metro GDP grew 7.1% over two years, the region ranked #3 in the nation for job growth, and St. Louis is quietly a national hub for agtech, biotech, and geospatial technology. (For the companies proving it, see our guide to the top St. Louis businesses to watch.) None of that erases the challenges — workforce is a real concern here, as it is across the entire country right now — but “cheap and declining” and “cheap and undervalued” are very different things, and the data increasingly points to the second.
Line up the facts — a 262-year-old city with irreplaceable architecture, buildings selling for pennies on the dollar, a tax-credit stack that covers half a rehab, $55 million in fresh public money, a $670 million riverfront project, crime falling four years running, and a $1.7 billion federal anchor already in the ground — and you have a downtown that isn’t dying. It’s waiting. The only missing ingredient is the people and the capital willing to move before everyone else figures it out.
