### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What restaurants are in Soulard?
A.  The anchors are Bogart’s Smokehouse (barbecue), Molly’s in Soulard (huge patio, brunch, New American) and John D. McGurk’s (Irish pub with live music and a big garden). For Cajun food with live music, 1860 Saloon & Hardshell Cafe is the signature spot, with Great Grizzly Bear nearby for scratch pub fare. The 9th Street corner of iTap, Epic Pizza and Session Taco is a great casual cluster.
### Q. What is the best food in Soulard?
A.  Barbecue and burgers lead. Bogart’s apricot-glazed, blowtorch-finished ribs are the neighborhood’s signature plate, and they sell out, so go early. For burgers, Big Daddy’s half-pound Angus burgers, Eat Crow’s quadruple cheeseburger and Jack Nolen’s smash burgers all have loyal fans. Add a bowl of gumbo with live music at 1860 Saloon and a Saturday-morning graze through the Soulard Farmers Market.
### Q. Where is the Soulard neighborhood in St. Louis?
A.  Soulard is a historic neighborhood just south of downtown St. Louis, near the Mississippi riverfront, in ZIP 63104. The Soulard Farmers Market at 730 Carroll Street anchors its northern end, and south of Lynch Street the land is mostly the Anheuser-Busch brewery and headquarters. The whole neighborhood covers about six-tenths of a square mile, with Benton Park right next door, so park once and explore on foot.
### Q. What is Soulard known for?
A.  Soulard is known for its historic Farmers Market (with roots back to 1779), red-brick 19th-century architecture, and a lively nightlife of blues bars, Irish pubs, and Cajun kitchens. It hosts the largest Mardi Gras celebration outside New Orleans, drawing huge crowds each winter. Saturday mornings belong to the market crowd. Saturday nights belong to the blues bars.
### Q. What is the Soulard Farmers Market?
A.  The Soulard Farmers Market is a historic public market at 730 Carroll Street with more than 100 vendors selling produce, meat, baked goods, honey, spices and prepared foods. Its roots trace to 1779, making it the oldest operating public market in St. Louis. It’s open Wednesday through Saturday, roughly 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., and Saturday is the busiest and best day to visit. Bring cash and a tote bag.
### Q. What are the best bars in Soulard, St. Louis?
A.  Start with McGurk’s for live Irish music and a pint in the garden, then 1860 Saloon for live music every night. iTap pours 44 rotating craft taps, the cozy Bastille is a classic neighborhood tavern, Great Grizzly Bear has a brick patio, and Big Daddy’s is the party bar and a Mardi Gras hub. It’s all walkable, so you can bar-hop on foot all night.
### Q. What are some fun things to do in Soulard?
A.  Graze the Soulard Farmers Market on a Saturday morning, then wander the red-brick blocks of 19th-century rowhouses. Catch a live set at 1860 Saloon or McGurk’s, and plan around the calendar: Mardi Gras season, with the Barkus dog parade and the Grand Parade, is the big one, and Oktoberfest follows in the fall. A bar crawl on foot is the classic finish.
### Q. What are some good restaurants near Soulard, St. Louis?
A.  Just outside Soulard proper, Benton Park and the downtown edge add excellent options a short walk or drive away: Blues City Deli (po’boys, lunch only, Benton Park), Sidney Street Cafe (romantic fine dining, Benton Park), Frazer’s (eclectic dinners, Benton Park), and downtown’s Broadway Oyster Bar (Cajun food and live music). Within Soulard itself, stick with the anchors: Bogart’s, Molly’s, McGurk’s, and 1860 Saloon.

## Why Is Tony’s Dark Tonight? Where to Eat on St. Charles Main Street, Monday Included
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/where-to-eat-on-st-charles-main-street-a-locals-guide
Why is Tony’s dark? You’re standing on the bricks of Historic Main Street in St. Charles, dressed for dinner, with a reservation-shaped hole in your evening, and the answer is simple: it’s Monday. The Main House, Jalea and Bella Vino are dark too, and nobody warned you. So walk down the bricks to Lewis & Clark’s. The door’s open, the kitchen’s going, and there’s prime rib on the menu. It’s the street’s best Monday dinner.
Come back Saturday and it’s everything people promised. Steak butter sliding off a ribeye at Tony’s. Gas lamps glowing on brick storefronts built between 1807 and the 1890s. The Missouri River a few steps away in the dark, and the rooftop crowd at Lewis & Clark’s looking down on all of it. It’s a favorite for date nights, strolls, holiday visits and long lunches, and it runs on its own clock.
Two things nobody tells you: the steak butter everyone drives out for is sold by the tub at Dierbergs, and upstairs at Tony’s on Top, late Friday and Saturday nights came with buy-one-get-one drinks and $10 St. Louis-style pizzas when we checked.
And the street’s nightlife has a record. In May 1804, William Clark and about 42 men tied up here for six days to wait for Meriwether Lewis, and some of them celebrated the trip ahead a little too hard. Three were court-martialed for slipping off without leave; John Collins drew 50 lashes for going AWOL, misbehaving at a ball and mouthing off to Clark. The National Park Service tells the story because these bricks are a stop on the Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail. Main Street’s first big night out ended in lashes. Yours can end with steak butter.
### Steak, Lunch or a Monday? Who’s Open on Main Street
Noon on a Tuesday: a hanger steak and fries under chimichurri at The Main House. Monday night: prime rib at Lewis & Clark’s while Tony’s sits dark. Main Street rewards whoever knows the schedule. This is what the restaurants’ own sites and listings showed when we checked:
Monday night: prime rib at Lewis & Clark’s, or barbecue on South Main at Salt + Smoke ($$) in the old Little Hills building or Hendricks BBQ ($$) near the Katy Trail end, both open from 11. By day, Magpie’s, Novellus, Picasso’s, Frontier Perk and La Vie stay open.
Monday, dark: Tony’s, The Main House, Jalea, Bella Vino and St. Charles Coffee & Creperie.
Steak: Tony’s, dinner only: 4 to 9:30 Tuesday through Thursday, from 3 on Friday and Saturday, 4 to 8:30 on Sunday. When we checked, a 6-ounce filet was $38 and a 14-ounce ribeye $44, each with the butter melting on top. For a steak at noon, The Main House, Tuesday through Sunday.
Lunch: Lewis & Clark’s (every day but Tuesday), The Main House (Tuesday through Sunday), Magpie’s (from 11 daily), Novellus, Picasso’s and La Vie French Cafe. Jalea and Tony’s don’t serve lunch, and Bella Vino only does on weekends.
Hours shift with the seasons, so call before a special trip. Parking is the easy part: spaces along Historic Main Street and in the surrounding lots are free, and the free ParkSTC app from the city and county shows open spots in real time.
### Steak Butter, a Rooftop and Ceviche: The Sit-Down Anchors
The ribeye lands with a pat of house steak butter already melting into it. That’s Tony’s on Main Street ($$$), the family steakhouse since 1998, where the butter is so requested it’s sold by the tub, and upstairs Tony’s on Top keeps a DJ going until 1 a.m. on Friday and Saturday nights. Climb above the three levels of Lewis & Clark’s ($$), the American tavern down the street, and the rooftop patio puts the bricks and the gas lamps below you and the river out past them. At The Main House ($$$), a newer New American room in the historic former Mother-in-Law House building at 500 S. Main, an 8-ounce filet or a 16-ounce ribeye comes with steak butter even at lunch, next to toasted ravioli in the kitchen’s own tomato sauce. And at Jalea ($$-$$$), a chef-driven Peruvian bistro, the ceviche comes bright with lime and the lomo saltado comes off a hot wok, Thursday through Saturday nights. These are the reservations to make.
### Date Night on Main Street
Fire pits glowing on a heated patio, small plates, a glass of red: that’s Bella Vino Wine Bar & Tapas ($$-$$$), where Spanish and Italian tapas come out a few plates at a time and nobody rushes you off the patio. Novellus ($$) is a book-themed spot at 201 N. Main, shelves and all, that serves breakfast and lunch most days, then turns into an Italian dinner house on Friday and Saturday nights. The Main House’s historic rooms and heated patio, Jalea’s small bistro and a cocktail at Tony’s on Top round out the lineup. Finish with a walk under the gas lamps on the bricks and you’ve got the evening. (For more, see our guide to the best date-night restaurants in St. Louis.)
Not about dinner at all: Clayton’s local-SEO guide lives over here.
### Crepes, Coffee and a Slow Morning on the Bricks
Main Street shines for a daytime bite or a coffee break. Magpie’s Cafe ($$) has been a beloved fixture since 1984 - baked-potato soup, homemade quiche, cocktails, and weekend live music. Picasso’s Coffee House ($) is the iconic independent coffeehouse (since 2003), with micro-roasted coffee, local art, river views, and evening wine and live music. For breakfast, Frontier Perk ($) does scratch-made coffee and morning fare, and St. Charles Coffee & Creperie ($) pairs house-roasted organic coffee with sweet and savory crepes. For a fully plant-based option, La Vie French Cafe ($$) is now a 100% vegan French concept. And just off Main on Riverside Drive, by the Katy Trail, Bike Stop Cafe ($) does sandwiches, espresso, and vegan options.
### Wine, Beer & Bars
Main Street rewards a relaxed drink, too. Beyond Bella Vino’s tapas-and-wine setup, the Old Millstream Inn ($$) is a laid-back south-end tavern with a list of 100-plus beers, upstairs and basement bars, and a patio. The revived St. Charles Wine Garden ($$-$$$) - a restored landmark winery - pours Missouri-inspired house wines with small bites and event terraces (it’s open Wednesday through Sunday). And Tony’s on Top is the spot for a craft cocktail with a view. Whether you want a big beer list, a glass of local wine, or a well-made cocktail, Main Street has a comfortable perch for it. Many of these spots offer live music on weekends and patios that make the most of the historic streetscape, so it’s easy to turn a single drink into a long, pleasant evening watching the district go by.
Nothing deflates a Main Street day like a dark window and a locked door on the cobblestones. Planning a day on Main Street? Search St Louis Near Me Directory for St. Charles restaurants, shops and services, and check hours before you go, since Monday closures catch a lot of visitors.

### Just Off Main
A couple of worthy spots sit just beyond the core cobblestone blocks. Arzola’s Fajitas & Margaritas ($$) - a second location of the Benton Park favorite - brings family Mexican and brunch to North Main. And a short drive east, at the modern Streets of St. Charles development near the riverfront, Prasino ($$-$$$) does farm-to-table dining (worth knowing, though it’s not on Historic Main Street itself). These give you a little more range without straying far from the district.
### The Historic District: More Than Food
Main Street is on the National Register of Historic Places, the local tourism bureau calls it Missouri’s first and largest historic district, and it markets itself as home to more than 25 restaurants.
The gas lamps and restored brick storefronts on North Main. Photographed by Lane Forman, July 26, 2026.
Part of what makes eating on Main Street special is everything around it. The cobblestone district is packed with boutique shops, antique stores, and galleries - just a slice of the local businesses listed across St. Charles, MO - perfect for a browse before or after a meal. The Missouri Riverfront and the start of the Katy Trail sit at the south end, ideal for a walk or bike ride to work up an appetite. And in winter, the district hosts the famous Christmas Traditions festival, when costumed characters roam the gas-lit streets and the whole corridor glows - a magical time to visit (and to eat). It’s a rare place where the meal is just one part of a genuinely lovely outing.
### Making a Day of It on Main Street
The nicest way to enjoy Main Street is to make a whole day (or evening) of it. Start with coffee and a pastry at Picasso’s or St. Charles Coffee & Creperie, then browse the shops - antiques, boutiques, candy stores, and galleries line the cobblestones. Work up an appetite with a walk along the riverfront or a stretch of the Katy Trail at the south end, then settle in for lunch at Magpie’s or Lewis & Clark’s rooftop. In the evening, a candlelit dinner at The Main House, Bella Vino, or Jalea as the gas lamps flicker on is hard to beat. During the Christmas Traditions season, add the festive lights and costumed characters, and it becomes genuinely magical. It’s a rare district where the meal is just one part of a lovely, unhurried outing.

### A Note on What’s Closed
One honest update, because old guides still point people to closed doors. A few longtime favorites are gone: Little Hills Restaurant & Winery has closed, as has the roughly 50-year Mother-in-Law House (its building is now The Main House). The south-end brewpub Trailhead Brewing became Schlafly Bankside and then closed in early 2025, and Cafe Beignet and the nearby Miss Aimee B’s Tea Room have also closed. Main Street evolves quickly, with new spots regularly replacing old ones, so - as always - call ahead to confirm hours before a special trip, since things change. ### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Where to eat on Main Street St. Charles?
A.  The Main Street anchors are Tony’s on Main Street (steakhouse), Lewis & Clark’s (historic American tavern with a rooftop), The Main House (New American), Jalea (Peruvian), and Novellus (book-themed breakfast and lunch, Italian dinners on weekends). For a date, Bella Vino Wine Bar & Tapas is the quintessential pick. For cafes and sweets, Magpie’s, Picasso’s Coffee House, and St. Charles Coffee & Creperie. Hours change, so call before you go.
### Q. What is the best restaurant in St. Charles, Mo.?
A.  It depends on the night. For a classic steak dinner, Tony’s on Main Street has been the call since 1998. For something you won’t find elsewhere in town, Jalea’s Peruvian ceviche and lomo saltado. For a long lunch, Lewis & Clark’s or Magpie’s. Just outside the city, Noto Italian Restaurant in St. Peters is known for Neapolitan pizza, but Main Street is the most walkable corner of the scene.
### Q. What are some top-rated restaurants in St. Charles?
A.  On Main Street, the names that come up again and again are Tony’s on Main Street for steak, Lewis & Clark’s for a meal above the street, The Main House for New American, Bella Vino for tapas and wine, and Magpie’s, a lunch fixture since 1984. Ratings move with every new review, so skim the recent ones and confirm hours before you drive.
### Q. What are the most unique restaurants in St. Charles?
A.  Jalea, a chef-driven Peruvian bistro doing ceviche and lomo saltado. Novellus, a book-themed cafe that turns Italian on weekend nights. La Vie French Cafe, a plant-based French spot on South Main. And the St. Charles Wine Garden, a restored landmark winery pouring house wines with small bites. Add Lewis & Clark’s three floors in a historic building, and dinner comes with a side of history.
### Q. What is a must eat in St. Louis, Missouri?
A.  The classics are toasted ravioli, gooey butter cake, thin-crust St. Louis-style pizza with Provel cheese, and barbecue. Out on St. Charles Main Street, the local version of that list is a steak with Tony’s house steak butter, a slow-smoked plate at Salt + Smoke or Hendricks BBQ on South Main, and Magpie’s baked-potato soup at lunch.

## Root Beer Behind Glass, a Free Trolley and Five Spots Gone: Where to Eat on the Delmar Loop
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/where-to-eat-on-the-delmar-loop-a-locals-guide
A vintage streetcar rattling down Delmar, storefronts sliding past, and the ride costs you nothing. The Loop Trolley is free, no ticket and no fare at any age, Thursday through Sunday from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m., late April through late October, on a 2.2-mile line from the University City Library to the Missouri History Museum in Forest Park. The cars have no air conditioning and no heat, so pick your season.
Look down and there’s a brass star in the sidewalk. Look left and a bottling line is filling root beer behind a glass wall at Fitz’s. Walk a block and the noodles at Corner 17 are being pulled by hand, while down the street at Sakatanoya, St. Louis’s first double-tier conveyor-belt sushi bar, the plates ride past on two levels. That’s the Delmar Loop, a six-block neighborhood strip straddling the city and University City line, where Chuck Berry played 209 monthly shows in the Duck Room at Blueberry Hill and a 1972 burger joint sits a few doors from Korean-Mexican tacos. It’s been named one of the “10 Great Streets in America,” and the food is a big reason why.
Before you go, cross five names off the old list. Three Kings hasn’t returned to Delmar since its 2023 fire, Guerrilla Street Food’s Loop counter is gone, Strange Donuts doesn’t have a Delmar shop, Kimchi Guys is only at Laclede’s Landing now, and the Fountain on Delmar has closed. What came in: conveyor-belt sushi at Sakatanoya and African cooking at Africana.
Then plan around two clocks the old lists never mention:
Blueberry Hill turns 21-and-over at 9 p.m. (all-ages shows excepted), so bring the kids for the early burger. After 9, table service stops and late-night food is ordered at the bar, until 11 Sunday through Tuesday and midnight Wednesday through Saturday.
Blueprint Coffee’s Delmar bar closes at 4 p.m. After that, the sweet stop is a root beer float at Fitz’s.
The Loop in one walk:
A burger under the memorabilia: Blueberry Hill, the 1972 original.
A float made with root beer bottled on-site: Fitz’s, 6605 Delmar.
Hand-pulled noodles and soup dumplings: Corner 17, 6623 Delmar.
Korean-Mexican tacos where the chain started: Seoul Taco, 6665 Delmar.
Omakase or conveyor sushi: Nobu’s (6253) or Sakatanoya.
Hot pot you cook yourself: Umami Seasons (6602) or Movoc (6329).
### The Institutions: A 1972 Burger and Root Beer Behind Glass
Start where the Loop started. At Blueberry Hill ($$), Joe Edwards’ 1972 landmark, you eat the “Famous Burger” under walls of pop-culture memorabilia, and downstairs is the Duck Room where Chuck Berry played his monthly shows. At Fitz’s ($$), the root beer is bottled on-site behind a glass wall, so you can watch the line run while you wait on a burger and one of the famous floats. And Salt + Smoke ($$) brings St. Louis-style BBQ right by the bronze Chuck Berry statue.
### The International Row: Noodles, Banh Mi and a Gyro Since 1982
Walk west from the statue and the smells change every storefront: chili oil, fryer, lemongrass, charred lamb. For Korean-Mexican fusion, Seoul Taco ($) got its start here, with K-Bop ($) nearby for Korean rice bowls. For ramen and pho, Nudo House ($$); for hand-pulled noodles and soup dumplings, Corner 17 ($$); and for a newer Chinese noodle spot, Noodle Story ($$). Add Thai (Fork & Stix, Thai Gai Yang), Vietnamese banh mi (Paris Banh Mi), Lebanese-Syrian mezze at Ranoush ($$), 40-year-old Greek gyros at Gyro House ($), plus Indian (Gokul, Turmeric) and African (Africana).
### Sushi, Ramen & Japanese
The Loop does Japanese two ways: a chef laying down omakase one piece at a time, or plates gliding past you on a belt. Nobu’s ($$$) does multi-course omakase (reservations via Tock), the Loop’s date-night splurge. For fun, Sakatanoya ($$) is St. Louis’s first double-tier conveyor-belt sushi bar (plus ramen), and Katsuya ($$) does Japanese katsu in tidy bento-style presentations. Grab a plate as it glides past on either level.
### Hot Pot & Interactive
Broth bubbling in the middle of the table, thin-sliced meat going in with chopsticks: that’s the cook-it-yourself meal, and the Loop has two good ones. Umami Seasons Hotpot ($$), across from Blueberry Hill, does Taiwanese tabletop hot pot, and Movoc ($$) offers DIY individual hot pots and malatang. Gather a group, pick your broth, and cook your way through the meal while the steam fogs everybody’s glasses.
A detour, then back to the noodles: how St. Charles businesses win more customers.
### Coffee, Sweets & Floats
The Loop is great for a sweet or caffeinated stop, too. Blueprint Coffee ($) is a beloved third-wave roaster (its Delmar bar runs 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.), the longtime Meshuggah Cafe ($) keeps the bohemian coffeehouse tradition alive, and Paris Banh Mi ($) at the east end pours Vietnamese coffee and boba next to its pastries. For dessert, a Fitz’s root beer float is the classic, made with root beer bottled on-site behind a glass wall, and Nudo House finishes a bowl of ramen with soft serve. Between a proper cup of coffee, a boba tea, and an old-fashioned float, the Loop covers the sweet side as well as it does the savory.
### More Than Food: The Loop Experience
Eating on the Loop comes with a built-in show. The St. Louis Walk of Fame runs down the sidewalks - brass stars and bronze plaques honoring Missouri greats from Chuck Berry to Maya Angelou to Tennessee Williams. The Chuck Berry statue stands across from Salt + Smoke, and the historic Tivoli Theatre, the Pageant, and Delmar Hall keep live music and film central to the strip. Make a night of it: dinner and a show, with a stroll past the stars in between. Few dining districts anywhere pack this much culture into a few walkable blocks.
### How to Do a Delmar Loop Food Crawl
The best way to eat the Loop is to graze it, so here’s a game plan. Start with a snack - a Korean-Mexican taco at Seoul Taco or a gyro at Gyro House - to warm up. Move to the international row for the main event: a bowl of ramen at Nudo House, hand-pulled noodles at Corner 17, or mezze at Ranoush, sharing plates as you go. If you’re making a night of it, book a sushi dinner at Nobu’s or grab a spot at the Sakatanoya conveyor belt. Between stops, walk the St. Louis Walk of Fame and snap a photo at the Chuck Berry statue. And finish sweet with an old-fashioned root beer float at Fitz’s (or, before 4 p.m., a coffee at Blueprint). Because the strip is so compact and walkable, you can hit three or four spots in an evening without ever moving your car - ideally capped with a show at the Pageant, Delmar Hall, or the Duck Room. It’s a food-and-culture crawl unlike anywhere else in the metro.

### What the Loop Does Best
A few things define this strip. The international row is the headline - an unmatched density of independent global kitchens, especially new Asian dining. The iconic institutions (Blueberry Hill, Fitz’s) give it soul and history. The live-music-and-dinner combination, thanks to the Pageant, Delmar Hall, and the Duck Room, is a signature. And it’s wonderfully walkable, with the Walk of Fame turning a stroll between restaurants into a mini-tour. The Loop rewards the curious eater who’s willing to skip the obvious and try the noodle shop, the hot pot, or the banh mi.
### Tips for Visiting the Loop
A few practical notes. The Loop straddles the St. Louis city and University City line, so addresses run along Delmar Boulevard on both sides - it’s all one continuous, walkable strip. Parking can get tight on weekend nights and around concerts, so arrive a little early, use the side streets and lots, or take the MetroLink (the Delmar Loop station is right there). Many spots are counter-service and quick, which is perfect for a pre-show bite, while the sit-down rooms reward a reservation on busy nights. And because the strip changes, it’s always worth a quick look at current hours before a special trip. Go with an open mind and a plan to walk, and the Loop delivers one of the most fun, flavorful evenings in the metro.
### A Note on What’s Closed
One honest update, because the Loop turns over and old lists mislead. The beloved Peacock Loop Diner closed in early 2025 (its neon peacock sign remains). Pi Pizzeria’s Loop spot is gone (the whole Pi chain has since closed), the longtime Italian-and-music venue Cicero’s closed back in 2017, and the Melting Pot location has closed as well. Also off the list now: Three Kings Public House, which hasn’t returned to Delmar since its 2023 fire (its owners say they’ll come back when the right space turns up), Guerrilla Street Food’s Loop counter, the daytime Strange Donuts shop, Kimchi Guys (now only at Laclede’s Landing), and the Fountain on Delmar, which closed in January 2026. The flip side is genuinely exciting: the Loop keeps filling those spaces with independent noodle shops, hot pot, and sushi. Because the strip changes fast, call ahead to confirm hours before a special trip, since things change - and when a Loop spot wins you over, become a regular.
The Delmar Loop is one of the most fun, eclectic places to eat in the entire St. Louis region - iconic burgers, an international row that never stops evolving, live music, and the Walk of Fame underfoot. For the bigger picture, see our guide to the best restaurants in St. Louis - then spend an evening on Delmar: a bowl of ramen or a plate of hand-pulled noodles, a stroll past the brass stars, and a show at the Pageant. The best of the Loop isn’t any one restaurant - it’s the whole eclectic, music-filled, keep-wandering street.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What are the best restaurants near the Delmar Loop in St. Louis?
A.  The iconic anchors are Blueberry Hill (burgers, Chuck Berry history) and Fitz’s (root beer and floats), with Salt + Smoke (BBQ) close by. But the Loop’s real strength is its international row: Seoul Taco (Korean-Mexican), Corner 17 (hand-pulled noodles), Nudo House (ramen/pho), Ranoush (Lebanese), Gyro House (Greek), plus omakase at Nobu’s and conveyor sushi at Sakatanoya. It’s a strip built for adventurous eating.
### Q. What is the Delmar Loop known for?
A.  The Delmar Loop is known for its eclectic mix of independent restaurants, live-music venues, and shops along a six-block stretch of Delmar Boulevard. It’s home to the St. Louis Walk of Fame (brass stars honoring Missouri notables), Blueberry Hill and its Chuck Berry legacy, the Pageant and Delmar Hall concert venues, and the historic Tivoli Theatre. It’s been named one of the “10 Great Streets in America.”
### Q. Why do they call it the Delmar Loop?
A.  The name comes from the streetcars. Starting in the late 1800s, trolley lines out of the city looped around at this stretch of Delmar to turn back east, and the name stuck long after the streetcars were gone. The modern revival began in 1972, when Joe Edwards opened Blueberry Hill on a block that had gone quiet.
### Q. What neighborhood is Delmar Loop in?
A.  Two cities share it. The western blocks, around Blueberry Hill and Fitz’s, are in University City, and the eastern blocks around the Pageant and Delmar Hall are in the City of St. Louis, spilling into the Skinker-DeBaliviere neighborhood. It’s one continuous, walkable strip, and the Delmar Loop MetroLink station drops you right in it.
### Q. Is Delmar Loop safe?
A.  For most visitors, yes, especially in the evening, when the restaurants, the Pageant and Blueberry Hill keep the sidewalks busy. It’s an urban entertainment district, so use normal city sense: park on lit, busy stretches or take MetroLink to the Delmar Loop station, keep valuables out of sight in the car, and stick to the main strip late at night.

## Best Restaurants in Edwardsville, IL: A Local's Guide to the Metro East
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/best-restaurants-in-edwardsville-il-a-locals-guide
Just 25 minutes across the river from downtown St. Louis, Edwardsville, Illinois has quietly become one of the Metro East’s best places to eat. This walkable college town — home to Southern Illinois University Edwardsville (SIUE) — has a compact, historic downtown along North Main Street packed with chef-driven independents, cozy cafes, brewpubs, and a genuinely growing food scene.
What sets Edwardsville apart is how independent it is. The town’s reputation was built by scratch kitchens, not chains — led by the acclaimed Cleveland-Heath, which put Edwardsville on the regional food map — and 2026 keeps bringing new local spots. A student-and-neighbor crowd keeps the coffeehouses busy and the Main Street taverns lively.
This guide covers the best of Edwardsville (plus nearby Glen Carbon and Maryville in Madison County): the acclaimed anchor, the Italian and international spots, BBQ, cafes, and brewpubs. As always with a growing scene, a quick call to confirm hours before you go is smart. Come explore — it’s worth the short drive across the river.
📌 Love the Metro East food scene? Keep this — and share it.
Bookmark this guide and send it to the SIUE student or parent, the friend on the Illinois side, or the St. Louisan who doesn’t realize how good Edwardsville dining has gotten.
Every share points one more hungry person to a great meal in Edwardsville. That’s the whole idea.
### The Acclaimed Anchor
Start with the restaurant that made Edwardsville a food destination. Cleveland-Heath ($$-$$$), open since 2011 at 106 N Main, is a nationally-noticed New American spot doing seasonal, from-scratch cooking that rivals anything in the metro. Its founders sold to local owners in 2025, but the name, direction, and quality continue. Whether it’s a special dinner or a great weeknight meal, this is the Edwardsville table to book first. It anchors a downtown that has grown up around it — and it’s the reason the town punches so far above its weight.
### Downtown Main Street
Edwardsville’s walkable downtown is the heart of the scene. Beyond Cleveland-Heath, Foundry Public House ($$) is a gastropub with a seasonal menu and weekend brunch (in the former Erato space), and the classic North Main Diner ($) does old-school American comfort right on Main. The stretch of North Main and St. Louis Street forms a genuine restaurant row — easy to stroll, with shops and the historic Wildey Theatre woven in. It’s the kind of downtown where you can park once and wander between coffee, dinner, and a drink.

### Italian & Pizza
Edwardsville does Italian and pizza well. Sugo’s Spaghetteria ($$) makes third-generation Sicilian recipes, fresh pasta, and Neapolitan pizza. Mio Osteria ($$) is a small, modern neighborhood Italian spot. And for wood-fired pizza, the award-winning Peel Wood Fired Pizza ($$) and the contemporary Bella Milano ($$) round out the options (both are small regional groups, not national chains). Whether you want handmade pasta or a blistered pizza, the town has you covered.
### International Flavors
The international bench is deeper than you’d expect for a town this size. Bann Thai ($$) does authentic Thai with adjustable heat, Wang Gang Asian Eats ($$) is a chef-driven pan-Asian spot (Thai, Chinese, Vietnamese), and Wasabi Sushi Bar ($$) covers Japanese. For Mexican, family-owned Chava’s ($) does Guadalajara recipes, and for Indian, both Taj Indian Cuisine ($$) and Mr. Curry’s do a traditional lunch buffet. It’s a globe-spanning lineup that keeps Edwardsville dining interesting well beyond the American classics.
### BBQ, Cafes & Bakeries
For smoke, Salt + Smoke ($$) brought its St. Louis-style BBQ to an old Edwardsville fire station in 2026, and Doc’s Smokehouse ($$) — a competition-winning pitmaster on old Route 66 — is a longtime favorite. For coffee and pastries, Sacred Grounds Cafe ($) has anchored Main Street for 30-plus years as a student and artist hub, and 222 Artisan Bakery ($) does daily artisan breads with local Goshen coffee. These are the everyday, come-often spots that give the town its rhythm.
### Date Night & Drinks
For a special evening, 1933 House of Bourbon ($$$) pairs Iowa Angus steaks with a 120-bottle bourbon bar — the upscale-casual date-night pick alongside Cleveland-Heath. For drinks, Global Brew Tap House ($$) pours 50 taps and 200-plus bottles, the historic Stagger Inn ($) is the town’s oldest tavern with live music, Big Daddy’s ($) has a downtown beer garden, and Bin 51 ($$) is a wine shop with a tasting bar. Nearby in Collinsville, Old Herald Brewery & Distillery ($$) is a full brewpub-and-distillery in a historic newspaper building. There’s a good drink for every mood.

### A Growing Scene: Restaurant Week & What’s New
One of the best things about eating in Edwardsville right now is that the scene is actively expanding. The town’s downtown has been on a genuine growth streak, with new independent restaurants opening regularly — recent arrivals span BBQ, poke, and reinvented bar-and-burger concepts — so there’s always something new to try on Main Street. ### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What are the best restaurants in Edwardsville, IL?
A.  The acclaimed anchor is Cleveland-Heath, a nationally-noticed New American spot downtown. For Italian, Sugo’s Spaghetteria and Mio Osteria; for pizza, Peel Wood Fired. International standouts include Bann Thai, Wang Gang, and Taj Indian. For a special night, 1933 House of Bourbon (steaks and bourbon). Add BBQ at Salt + Smoke and Doc’s, plus cafes like Sacred Grounds — a deep, independent lineup for a town this size.
### Q. What is Edwardsville, IL known for?
A.  Edwardsville is known as a charming, walkable college town in Illinois’ Metro East, home to Southern Illinois University Edwardsville (SIUE) and a historic downtown along North Main Street. It’s about 25 minutes from downtown St. Louis and has built a strong reputation for independent, chef-driven dining — anchored by Cleveland-Heath — along with the Wildey Theatre, local shops, and an annual restaurant week.
### Q. Where should I go for a nice dinner in Edwardsville?
A.  For a special dinner, Cleveland-Heath (acclaimed seasonal New American) and 1933 House of Bourbon (steaks with a big bourbon list) are the top picks. For upscale-casual Italian, Sugo’s or Mio Osteria; for a lively downtown gastropub, Foundry Public House. Pair dinner with a stroll down Main Street and a drink at Global Brew or Bin 51, and you’ve got a great evening.
### Q. Is Edwardsville good for a date night?
A.  Yes — the walkable historic downtown makes it a lovely date destination. Book Cleveland-Heath or 1933 House of Bourbon for dinner, stroll Main Street’s shops and the Wildey Theatre, and finish with a glass of wine at Bin 51 or a craft beer at Global Brew. The compact, park-once downtown makes it easy to build a full, relaxed evening without moving the car.
### Q. What is there to do in downtown Edwardsville besides eat?
A.  Downtown Edwardsville pairs its restaurants with local boutiques, shops, and galleries, plus the historic Wildey Theatre for concerts and films. The town hosts events year-round, including a popular restaurant week, and SIUE brings college-town energy nearby. The Madison County Transit trails and nearby parks are good for a walk or bike ride, making downtown an easy all-day or evening destination.

## Gooey Butter Cones by a British Warship’s Cannons: Where Lafayette Square Eats Now (and What Closed)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/where-to-eat-in-lafayette-square-a-locals-guide
Seven o’clock on Park Avenue. The brick sidewalk tilts under your heels, the townhomes lean close behind their wrought iron, and the park across the street smells like cut grass. You have twenty minutes before the reservation, so you slow down outside the windows where 33 Wine Shop & Bar poured for 25 years, and nobody is pouring now. Later, walking back with a square of gooey butter cake from Park Avenue Coffee, you’ll find powdered sugar on your sleeve. Let it stay.
Two date-night rooms have gone dark. 33 Wine closed after 25 years, citing rising costs, St. Louis Public Radio reported in its monthly openings-and-closings roundup, and the same roundup listed Baileys’ Chocolate Bar (the candlelit chocolate-and-martini lounge that ran for two decades) as closed too. Mayo Ketchup has moved to Midtown. Older lists still send couples to all three, so if your plan came off one of them, fix it before the weekend. Everything below is open.
Thursday is the cheap night. Hamilton’s own website lists its Thursday bar special: half off bottles of wine under $75, from 3 p.m. to close. Split a steak and it’s the best-value dinner in the Square. Specials change, so check first.
The best table in Lafayette Square isn’t in a restaurant. Carry a cone of Clementine’s gooey butter cake ice cream, its most popular flavor, into Lafayette Park and find the three black cannons just west of the playground. The iron is cool under your palm while the cone drips. Those were guns on the British frigate Actaeon, scuttled in Charleston harbor during the Battle of Sullivan’s Island in 1776. They sat underwater for more than a century, until St. Louis veterans bought them and gave them to this park in 1897, as the city’s own Lafayette Park page records. Tell your date that between bites. Clementine’s scoops until 10 p.m., and until 11 on Fridays and Saturdays.
Don’t plan it for a Monday. The Bellwether, Planter’s House and Extra Wavy are all closed Mondays, and The Bellwether and Extra Wavy skip Sunday dinner too. Tuesday through Saturday is the only stretch when every room on this page is serving dinner.
📌 Planning an anniversary in the Square? Send this to whoever’s booking.
The night in four stops: a drink at Planter’s House, whose 350-plus spirits include 39 bourbons, ryes and rums bottled just for the bar; dinner at Eleven Eleven Mississippi, SqWires or The Bellwether (reserve on weekends); a lap of Lafayette Park; and that cone at Clementine’s.
### Four tables for the big night
The first thing you smell at Eleven Eleven Mississippi is the wood fire under the Poached Pear & Fig Flatbread; then the Char Crust Ribeye arrives, its dry rub seared dark. It has anchored the Square since 2003 from a restored shoe factory, and it books through its website ($$$). At SqWires the fireplace throws warmth across the room, and on weekends a jazz or blues set plays under the conversation; call 314-865-3522 ($$-$$$). On The Bellwether’s rooftop, the first forkful of cacio e pepe is all pepper and pecorino, and the evening air is on your arms; it serves dinner Tuesday through Saturday, so call 314-380-3086 ($$$, thebellwetherstl.com). Its sister, Polite Society at 1923 Park Ave., is the gastropub where the Jimmy Burger is the order ($$-$$$).
### Bourbon, steak and a raw bar on Chouteau
Out on the Chouteau edge it’s the clink of ice in a bourbon glass and the smell of beef on a hot grill. Hamilton’s Urban Steakhouse & Bourbon Bar ($$$) serves heritage-breed Black Angus with greens from its own hydroponic greenhouse; ask about the edible candle St. Louis Magazine once called the city’s best, and wear sleeves. Down the block, Extra Wavy ($$$), at 2017 Chouteau since late 2025, sends out cold, briny plates off the raw bar and tropical cocktails; text 314-346-1165 for the fastest answer on a table.
### Saturday and Sunday brunch, then a lap of the park
The cream cheese icing on The Bellwether’s whisk cinnamon roll is still soft when it hits the table, and the Cinnamon Toast Crunch French toast with maple praline sounds like a dare and tastes like Saturday-morning cartoons. The bacon fried rice is the grown-up order. Brunch there runs Saturday and Sunday, 10 to 2, indoors or on the patio; SqWires and Polite Society do weekend brunch too, and Eleven Eleven Mississippi opens for brunch on Saturdays. Afterward, take the long way home through Lafayette Park, under the shade of the old trees.
### Gooey butter cake in more than 70 flavors
Save room, because the Square’s dessert game is distinctive. Park Avenue Coffee is a must - the St. Louis original serves gooey butter cake in more than 70 flavors alongside house-roasted coffee. Just up the way, Clementine’s Naughty & Nice Creamery ($) does boozy and vegan microcreamery ice cream (including a gooey-butter-cake flavor - peak St. Louis). Baileys’ Chocolate Bar, the Square’s candlelit chocolate-and-martini lounge for two decades, has closed. For a sweet nightcap now, order dessert where you ate or walk back to Clementine’s, which scoops until 10 p.m. (11 on Fridays and Saturdays). Gooey butter cake two ways within a couple of blocks: that’s a St. Louis sweet tooth’s dream.

### Where to drink now that 33 Wine is gone
The Square is one of the best drinking neighborhoods in the city. 33 Wine Shop & Bar poured its last glass after 25 years, citing rising costs, so the wine crowd now leans on Winnie’s and the restaurant lists. Planter’s House is a nationally regarded craft-cocktail bar with an intimate upstairs room (the Bullock Room) and food to match. Winnie’s Wine Bar pours flights in a retro-aviation setting near Hamilton’s. And Square One Brewery & Distillery keeps it casual as the neighborhood brewpub (and Missouri’s first post-Prohibition microdistillery). Whether you want a wine flight, a perfect cocktail, or a house-brewed pint, the Square has your pre- or post-dinner drink.
### Handmade pasta and a pint, no occasion needed
Not every meal here is a splurge. One change from older lists: Mayo Ketchup, chef Mandy Estrella’s Puerto Rican and Dominican spot, has moved to Midtown. These are the everyday, come-as-you-are spots that balance out the district’s special-occasion reputation - proof that Lafayette Square is a real neighborhood, not just a date-night stage set.

### The 1836 park that sets the mood
Part of what makes eating here special is the setting. Trivia for the table: the Marquis de Lafayette himself visited St. Louis in 1825, eleven years before the park that carries his name was laid out. Lafayette Park, established in 1836, anchors the neighborhood with its Victorian bandstand, ponds, and old-growth trees - perfect for a pre- or post-dinner stroll. The surrounding streets are lined with painstakingly restored Second Empire and Italianate mansions, many rebuilt after an 1896 tornado and revived again through decades of preservation. Wandering the brick sidewalks past the grand old homes, with the park at the center, gives a Lafayette Square meal a sense of occasion that few other neighborhoods can match. Come early and take a walk before your reservation.
### One evening, four blocks: an itinerary
Because Lafayette Square is so compact and walkable, it’s easy to build a whole romantic evening within a few blocks. Start with cocktails at Planter’s House’s intimate upstairs Bullock Room or a wine flight at Winnie’s. Move to dinner at Eleven Eleven Mississippi, SqWires, or The Bellwether - candlelit rooms in restored brick warehouses, exactly the setting an anniversary calls for. Take a stroll between courses or after the meal through Lafayette Park, past the Victorian bandstand and the grand old mansions, especially lovely at dusk. And finish with dessert: a scoop of boozy ice cream at Clementine’s, or a shared plate where you had dinner. The whole arc, from first drink to last bite, happens on foot in one beautiful historic neighborhood. That density of romance is exactly why Lafayette Square is the metro’s go-to for a special night - a little planning turns dinner into a genuinely memorable evening.

Historic ambiance, from converted warehouses to Victorian streetscapes, sets the mood. The wine and cocktail scene (Planter’s House, Winnie’s) is genuinely excellent. And the St. Louis-pride sweets, gooey butter cake at Park Avenue and in Clementine’s ice cream, give it a distinctive local finish. ### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What are the best restaurants in Lafayette Square?
A.  The anchors are Eleven Eleven Mississippi (Tuscan and California wine-country cooking, the neighborhood standard), SqWires (New American in a historic factory), The Bellwether (contemporary American) and Polite Society (New American gastropub). For steaks and something new, Hamilton’s Urban Steakhouse and the Extra Wavy raw bar. For drinks, Planter’s House and Square One round out a standout district.
### Q. What is Lafayette Square in St. Louis?
A.  It’s a historic neighborhood just south of downtown, built around Lafayette Park and known for its restored Victorian mansions and townhomes. The park was established in 1836 and is generally cited as one of the oldest public parks west of the Mississippi River. Today the Square is also a dining destination, with a notable wine, cocktail, and dessert culture.
### Q. What is Lafayette Park known for?
A.  Its age and its Victorian look. Lafayette Park dates to 1836 and still has its Victorian bandstand, ponds and old-growth trees, ringed by restored 19th-century mansions worth admiring on foot. It’s the neighborhood’s front yard for a stroll before or after dinner, and the setting for seasonal events and historic house tours.
### Q. Who is Lafayette Square named after?
A.  The neighborhood takes its name from Lafayette Park, which honors the Marquis de Lafayette, the French general who fought beside George Washington in the American Revolution and visited St. Louis in 1825. The park came first, and the grand Second Empire and Italianate homes grew up around it later in the 1800s.
### Q. What is the zip code for Lafayette Square in St. Louis?
A.  Most of Lafayette Square uses 63104, the ZIP code for SqWires, Square One, Polite Society and the shops along Park Avenue. A few businesses on the Chouteau Avenue edge, like Extra Wavy and Hamilton’s, carry 63103, so double-check the full address when you plug a restaurant into your GPS.

## Last Call Is 1:30. Some Grove Bars Pay $300 to Pour Till 3: Where to Eat and Drink Now
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/where-to-eat-in-the-grove-a-locals-guide
Friday night on Manchester Avenue, between Kingshighway and Vandeventer: murals lit up by neon, bass leaking out of a dance-club door, beer smell drifting from Urban Chestnut’s bierhall. Officially it’s Forest Park Southeast. Everybody calls it The Grove, and with Just John, Rehab and Prism on the same few blocks, it’s the center of the city’s LGBTQ nightlife.
At 1:30 a.m., most of Missouri goes dark. State law makes every bar stop pouring and lock its doors. On Manchester, some doors keep thumping until 3, and here’s why: a City of St. Louis bar can buy a state permit for $300 a year to stay open two more hours, if it sits in a city-designated convention trade area and grossed at least $150,000 the year before. The tell is the posted hours. HandleBar, at 4127 Manchester, lists 2:30 a.m. (closed Tuesdays), and from opening until 6, and all night on Mondays, its pizza is half price. A posted close past 1:30 means a permit; anywhere else, order your last round by 1.
The street did lose a kitchen it loved. Grace Meat + Three, where cracklin’ cornbread came under caramelized honey butter and the fried chicken was too hot to hold, served its last dinner after nine years. The chicken didn’t die, though. Owners Rick and Elisa Lewis still fry it at Grace Chicken + Fish, 8654 Watson Road in Crestwood, with cornmeal-crusted catfish on the side. Chao Baan, Everest Cafe and the late-night standbys Little Lucy and Pie Guy closed too; the full list is in the note at the end.
So here’s a night in order: wood-fired pizza at Fordo’s inside Urban Chestnut’s bierhall, then kabobs and a warm bolani at Sameem, then a drag show at Rehab, and after midnight, Wednesday through Sunday, the Atomic Eats kitchen inside Atomic by Jamo, which cooks until 1 a.m. Hours change often here, so call before a special trip. Then start walking.
### Start at the Wood Smoke: Pizza, a Mediterranean Feast and a Tasting Menu
Follow the wood smoke first. At Fordo’s Killer Pizza ($$), Gerard Craft’s Niche Food Group pulls wood-fired sourdough pies, blistered at the edges, inside Urban Chestnut’s bierhall, so the pizza and the pint come from the same room. Down the street, Sultan Mediterranean ($$) is the family-owned, critically praised kitchen where a Mediterranean spread takes over the whole table, back after a months-long renovation. Aperi ($$$) has turned into a Spanish-leaning tapas and wine bar: paella, papas bravas and a glass of something red. And the newest wave is the boldest: Malo ($$$$) sends out a Mexican tasting menu course by course, and Baia ($$) twirls pasta Thursday through Monday nights.
### Keep Walking: Afghan Kabobs to LA-Style Tacos
Keep walking and the smells change every storefront. Smoke off a kabob grill and a warm bolani torn in half at the table mean Sameem ($$), Missouri’s first Afghan restaurant (kabobs, bolani, stews). Seoul Taco ($), just off Manchester on Chouteau, brings its Korean-Mexican fusion, Chico Bueno ($) is a newer LA-style taqueria open daily, and La Crazy Margarita ($$) does Tex-Mex at 4353 Manchester. La Calle ($$) does Mexican with a patio, but only Thursday through Sunday nights. For a bowl of ramen that fogs your glasses, or sushi, Oni ($$) serves lunch and dinner Wednesday through Sunday. Creole With a Splash of Soul has closed, too.
The Grove right now, by the clock:
New: Malo’s Mexican tasting menu, Baia’s pasta (Thursday through Monday nights), Oni’s sushi and ramen (Wednesday through Sunday) and Chico Bueno’s LA-style tacos, open daily.

### Breweries & Bars
Pints clink down the long tables at Urban Chestnut’s Grove Bierhall ($$), the 400-seat German-style flagship at 4465 Manchester (314-222-0143), in a 1920s paper-company building, now with Fordo’s pizza in the kitchen. ### The LGBTQ Heart of St. Louis
The Grove is the center of St. Louis’s LGBTQ nightlife, and its bars are neighborhood institutions. Just John ($) is the city’s largest and most popular gay club - multiple rooms, a big patio, and in-house pizza. Rehab Bar & Grill ($) is queer-owned with drag shows, DJs, and food daily. Prism ($$) does cocktails and a Sunday drag brunch. These spots are so central to LGBTQ life here that Grove bar owners publicly pushed back when the city floated early-closure rules during Pride weekend. Welcoming, loud and proud, it’s a defining part of what makes The Grove, The Grove.
### Coffee & Dessert
For a daytime or sweet stop, The Grove delivers. La Finca ($) does Colombian specialty coffee, and JAVA ($) is a coffee bar by day that turns into an open-mic music venue by night. For dessert, Serendipity Homemade Ice Cream ($) does classic and vegan scoops. Between a great cup of coffee and a scoop of ice cream, the Grove’s lighter side is just as thoughtful as its nightlife.
### The Grove From Afternoon to After-Hours
The Grove rewards a plan that follows the day into the night. Afternoon is for a relaxed start: coffee at La Finca, lunch at Sameem, Sultan or Neon Greens, and a wander to admire the murals. Early evening is prime dinner time: book Sultan for a Mediterranean spread, Aperi for Spanish-style tapas, or Baia for pasta, then settle in at Urban Chestnut’s bierhall or Rockwell’s patio for a craft beer. Night is when the neighborhood truly comes alive: whiskey at The Vandy, a drag show at Prism or Rehab, dancing at Just John. And after hours, refuel at Atomic Eats, whose kitchen runs until 1 a.m. Wednesday through Sunday. Because it’s all walkable along Manchester Avenue, you can flow from a nice dinner to a wild night to a midnight snack without ever calling a car. That easy afternoon-to-after-hours arc is the Grove’s superpower, and why it’s the metro’s go-to for a full night out.

## Best Restaurants in Belleville, IL: A Local's Guide to the Metro East
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/best-restaurants-in-belleville-il-a-locals-guide
About 20 minutes across the river from downtown St. Louis, Belleville, Illinois is one of the Metro East’s most characterful small cities — a place with deep German roots, a large walkable historic downtown built around a Public Square and fountain, and a food scene anchored by one of the best barbecue joints in the entire region.
Founded in 1814 and settled heavily by German immigrants (by 1870, roughly 90% of residents were German-born or descended), Belleville wears its history well. Today its downtown Main Street district mixes cozy taverns, wine bars, pizza pubs, and cafes among the old brick storefronts, while the real destination draw — Beast Craft BBQ — pulls hungry St. Louisans across the river.
This guide covers the best of Belleville and the surrounding St. Clair County area (O’Fallon IL, Fairview Heights, Swansea): the barbecue anchor, the downtown sit-down spots, the international kitchens, and the cafes. As always, a quick call to confirm hours before you go is smart. It’s worth the short drive — let’s dig in.

Bookmark this guide and send it to the friend on the Illinois side, the BBQ lover who hasn’t made the Beast Craft pilgrimage, or the St. Louisan who’s never explored historic downtown Belleville.
Every share points one more hungry person to a great meal in Belleville. That’s the whole idea.
### The Anchor: Beast Craft BBQ
Let’s start with the destination. Beast Craft BBQ Co. ($$), from pitmaster David Sandusky, is a nationally acclaimed live-fire barbecue chophouse with in-house butchery, white-oak-smoked brisket, and a legendary St. Louis-style pork steak. For many across the metro, it’s simply the best barbecue in the region — worth crossing the river for on its own. If you make one trip to Belleville, make it here, and go early before the good cuts sell out. It’s the reason Belleville lands on serious eaters’ maps. For the metro-wide picture, see our guide to the best BBQ in St. Louis.
### Downtown Main Street
Belleville’s historic downtown, centered on the Public Square fountain, is a genuine walkable dining district. Tavern on Main ($$) is a cozy brick-lined spot for pasta, pizza, and upscale entrees with a patio. Copper Fire Bar & Eatery ($$) does contemporary bar-and-grill fare with live music and weekend brunch. And the wine bars shine: Grüv Bistro & Wine Bar ($$) offers approachable-upscale shareables and flatbreads, and Grafted Wine Bar & Lounge ($$) is a rustic, cozy lounge. It’s an easy park-once evening among the historic storefronts.
### Italian, Pizza & Beyond
Belleville does casual Italian and pizza with character. Papa Vito’s ($) serves thin-crust pizza in an 1852 historic home, with live music on weekends, and Bennie’s Pizza Pub ($) does creative slice-by-slice pies (the Hawaiian Hog, a dill-pickle pizza) plus Bloody Marys and live music. Nearby in O’Fallon, IL, the small regional favorites Bella Milano ($$) and Peel Wood Fired Pizza ($$, with its own on-site brewery) add more options a short drive away. Casual, fun, and full of personality — that’s the Belleville pizza vibe.

### International Flavors
The international bench is solid across Belleville and its neighbors. For Mexican, family-run Casa Maria ($$) does authentic downtown cooking with fresh-lime margaritas, and in Fairview Heights, Rio Grande MX Cocina ($$) is a top-ranked independent (try the prickly-pear margarita). For Thai, Sala Thai ($$) and the west-side Banana Leaf ($$) both do authentic, customizable-spice cooking. And across in Swansea, India’s Oven ($$) covers Indian with butter chicken, tandoori, and fresh naan. It’s a well-rounded global lineup for the area.
### Cafes, Breakfast & a Famous Orchard
Belleville does mornings and casual well. Downtown, Clara B’s Kitchen Table ($) does standout brunch (the smothered chicken biscuit), Main Street Cafe ($) is the classic breakfast diner, and coffee-and-treat stops like Sugar High Bakery ($) and Pour @322 ($) dot Main Street. And don’t miss Eckert’s Country Restaurant ($$) — the restaurant at what’s billed as the largest pick-your-own orchard in the country, famous for fried chicken, a hearty farm breakfast, and seasonal fun. It’s a destination in its own right, especially in apple season.
### Bars & Brewpubs
For a drink, downtown Belleville has independent options. Shoehorn Brewing ($) is a veteran-and-homebrewer-owned taproom on Main (bring your own food, stay for trivia), and 4204 Main Street Brewing Co. ($$) is an established brewpub pairing food with house beer. In O’Fallon, Edley’s Bar-B-Que ($$) adds Nashville-style smoke, and Peel Brewing Co. pours above its pizza kitchen. Between the taprooms and the wine bars downtown, there’s a comfortable spot for a pre- or post-dinner drink among the historic storefronts.
### German Heritage: The Honest Picture
Belleville’s German roots run deep — but here’s the honest truth: its two marquee German-name restaurants are both gone. The 80-year institution Fischer’s closed in 2017, and the big Bavarian beer hall Hofbräuhaus closed amid a 2024 legal dispute. So the German story here lives on through history and atmosphere rather than a currently-operating German restaurant: the 1814 Public Square, the wave of educated “Forty-Eighter” German settlers who crossed from St. Louis after 1848, the Veterans Memorial Fountain, and Illinois’s first brewery. Fittingly, Beast Craft’s St. Louis-style pork steak is itself a German-immigrant barbecue tradition — a tasty bridge to the past.
### Making a Day of It in Historic Belleville
Belleville is worth a whole day, not just a barbecue run. Start with breakfast at Clara B’s or Main Street Cafe, or make a morning of it at Eckert’s orchard (especially in apple or pumpkin season, when you can pick your own before eating). Midday, explore the walkable downtown around the Public Square — the boutiques, galleries, and the historic Veterans Memorial Fountain, plus the rest of the shops and services in our Belleville, IL city guide — and grab a coffee or a sweet at Sugar High or Pour @322. For lunch or an early dinner, that’s your Beast Craft BBQ pilgrimage (go before the good cuts sell out) or a pizza at Papa Vito’s in its 1852 home. In the evening, settle into a downtown wine bar like Grüv or Grafted, or a taproom like Shoehorn, with live music at Copper Fire or Bennie’s on the weekend. It’s an easy, pleasant day trip from St. Louis — history, shopping, and genuinely great food, all in one walkable historic city just across the river. Pack a little curiosity and an appetite.
### What Belleville Does Best
A few things define this scene. World-class barbecue at Beast Craft is the headline — a genuine regional destination. The historic walkable downtown, built around the Public Square and fountain, makes for a pleasant park-once evening of taverns and wine bars. The area’s German heritage gives it real character (even if the German restaurants have moved into the history books). And Eckert’s offers a farm-to-table, orchard-side experience you won’t find in the city. For a Metro East city, Belleville delivers a surprisingly rich day out.
### Nearby: St. Clair County Beyond Belleville
Belleville anchors a wider St. Clair County dining area worth exploring. Just a short drive away in O’Fallon, Illinois, you’ll find Edley’s Bar-B-Que (Nashville-style smoke), the contemporary Italian Bella Milano, and Peel Wood Fired Pizza with its own on-site brewery. These towns sit close enough to fold into a single outing, so a Belleville trip can easily become a broader Metro East food tour. Getting there is simple — Belleville is about 20 minutes from downtown St. Louis via I-64 and Route 15, with easy parking around the historic Public Square. Whether you come just for Beast Craft or make a day of the whole district, the St. Clair County side rewards a little exploring beyond the interstate exits and chain corridors.

## Ćevapi by 5 on Sunday, Dark on Monday: The Best Restaurants in South County
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/best-restaurants-in-south-county-a-locals-guide
Fifteen minutes. That’s what’s left before Taste of Bosnia locks its door on a Sunday, and the ćevapi are still coming off the grill, tucked into soft lepinja with raw onion and a smear of the house’s creamy spread, $7.99 for a small order. You made it. Show up on Monday and you’d be standing at a dark window on Union Road, wondering why nobody warned you. That’s South County eating in one scene: honest family kitchens in strip malls along Lindbergh, Gravois, Telegraph and Lemay Ferry, each with its own day off, none of it on a chain menu.
South County is the big southern half of St. Louis County: Affton, Mehlville, Oakville, Lemay, Concord, Sunset Hills and Crestwood. You drive here. The best food hides between the chains, in long-tenured family independents (steakhouses and Irish pubs that have fed the same neighborhoods for decades) and in a Bosnian food scene that spills south from Bevo Mill into Affton, thanks to one of the largest Bosnian communities outside Bosnia.
So skip the chains. And before you spend a dollar, take the one South County perk the restaurant lists leave out: the beer at Grant’s Farm is free. Off Gravois Road, the old Busch family farm charges nothing for general admission, and guests 21 and up get complimentary Anheuser-Busch samples at the Hospitality Bar in the Bauernhof courtyard, poured cold next to the brat and pretzel stands. You pay only to park (buy the pass online ahead), and bring a card, because the farm is cashless. Check its calendar first, since it runs by the season.
Then know the one thing that trips up everybody down here, locals included.
### Who’s Closed When: A South County Cheat Sheet
Plenty of South County’s family kitchens close one or two days a week, and it’s never the same day from one place to the next. This is what the restaurants’ own sites and listings showed when we checked:
Sunday: Tucker’s Place South and Berix are closed. Taste of Bosnia runs short hours, 11 to 5, and Sharpshooter Pit & Grill opens at noon.
Monday: Taste of Bosnia, Sharpshooter and Nubby’s Telegraph are closed, and Roberto’s in Concord Village is dark Sunday and Monday.
Tuesday: Thai Racha takes its day off, and Taste of Bosnia and Sharpshooter still haven’t reopened.
Any day: La Oaxaqueña and Tequila in Oakville open seven days, and Dave’s Diner is listed as open around the clock. Bring cash for that one.
The rule worth texting a friend: Sunday is Bosnian, Monday is Oaxacan, and on Tuesday, skip Thai. Taste of Bosnia runs 11 to 5 on Sundays, La Oaxaqueña never takes a day off, and Thai Racha rests on Tuesdays. Small family spots change hours with the season, though, so treat this as a starting point and call before a special trip.
### Order Like a Regular: Ćevapi on Union Road and Lemay Ferry
Here’s how to do it. At Taste of Bosnia ($) on Union Road, ask for ćevapi: small grilled beef sausages packed into a split, warm lepinja with raw onion and the house’s creamy spread. The full order is $14.99 on the restaurant’s menu, a small one $7.99, and a coiled burek, flaky and filled with ground beef, is $10.49. Go on a Thursday and add mantije, the little baked meat dumplings the kitchen only makes that day. And if you fall for that creamy spread, it’s kaymak, and the menu sells it by the 11-ounce tub for $6.99. Over on Lemay Ferry Road, Berix ($) is the longtime kitchen people drive to for ćevapi and doner. The historic heart of Bosnian St. Louis is Bevo Mill in South City, but the cooking spills straight into Affton and South County. (An honest note: two names people still ask about, Grbic and Bosna Grill, are no longer sit-down restaurants, so head to Berix or Taste of Bosnia.)
### Steak, an Irish Patio and the Oakville Regulars
Start with the steak. One block off South Lindbergh on Union Road, Tucker’s Place South ($$) grills Omaha Black Angus sirloins and strips, USDA Choice or better, in a cozy pub-style room, and the Post-Dispatch’s Best of St. Louis named Tucker’s Best Steak two years running; Riverfront Times readers have voted it Best Steakhouse every year since 1998. A Post-Dispatch columnist once put the value plainly: you could eat at Tucker’s twice for what one dinner costs at Morton’s. The South County kitchen runs until 10 on Friday and Saturday and takes Sundays off. Out on Lindbergh, Helen Fitzgerald’s ($$) is the sprawling Irish grill and pub with a huge patio, live music and a wing sauce so popular they bottle it, a landmark since 1992. And in Oakville, family-owned Crusoe’s ($$) does a big, reliable American menu, with Croc’s sports bar next door for the game.

### How to Eat Like a South County Local
A few tips to eat well down south. Skip the chains - South County is thick with national fast-food and casual chains along the arterials, but the real rewards are the family independents in the same strip malls. ### What South County Does Best
A few things define this area’s food. Long-tenured family institutions - Tucker’s, Bartolino’s, Crusoe’s, Helen Fitzgerald’s - are the backbone, trusted spots that have fed generations.
