## Coffee Shops in Chesterfield and West County: What’s Actually Open
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/coffee-shops-in-chesterfield-and-west-county
If you search for a coffee shop in Chesterfield, you will still find results pointing at Chesterfield Mall.
The mall is gone. Demolition finished in May 2025, and the site is now a $2 billion redevelopment that won’t open its first phase until late 2026. Any list still sending you there hasn’t been touched in over a year.
Here’s what’s actually open across Chesterfield, Ballwin, Ellisville, Creve Coeur and the rest of west county — checked one shop at a time against each business’s own website, including the three towns where the honest answer is “nothing.”
### What are the best coffee shops in Chesterfield, MO?
Four independents are verified open in Chesterfield proper: Kaldi’s Chesterfield (17211 Chesterfield Airport Rd), the only shop in the region that advertises free wifi and a reservable meeting room on its own site; Café Fermata (16626 Old Chesterfield Rd), inside a historic house shared with a music studio; The Tea Spout (17712 Chesterfield Airport Rd), organic coffee alongside tea with rentable event space; and Corner Cafe at Greentrails (14276 Ladue Rd), certified Kosher and open late most nights. Just over the line in Ballwin, The Wolf Cafe runs to 9pm Tuesday through Friday and The Ground STL opens at 6am.
### The one that will surprise you
Café Fermata at 16626 Old Chesterfield Rd occupies the historic Edward L. Schmidt house and shares the building with the 89th Key Music Studio. There are pianos on site, and the baristas perform while they make drinks.
That is not a marketing line someone wrote about the room — it’s how the place operates, stated by the business itself. Open 8am to 6pm Monday through Thursday and 8 to 3 Friday through Sunday. If you have ever wanted your latte accompanied, this is the only address in the county that does it — and it makes an easy stop before or after anything on our local’s guide to where to eat in Chesterfield.
### Chesterfield
Kaldi’s Coffee — Chesterfield, 17211 Chesterfield Airport Rd, 6:30am to 5pm daily. Kaldi’s is a St. Louis company rather than a national chain, and this location is the most useful room in west county if you actually need to get work done: it states free wifi and ample parking on its own site, and it has a cupping room you can reserve for a meeting or a training session. That’s the clearest work-friendly claim any coffee shop in this region publishes. It also opens earlier than anything else in Chesterfield.
The Tea Spout by Aquene Amora, 17712 Chesterfield Airport Rd. Organic coffee served alongside a full tea program, Tuesday to Friday 7 to 3 and Saturday 10 to 3. The space is available for events during and after hours, which is unusual for a shop this size.
Corner Cafe at Greentrails, 14276 Ladue Rd, is certified Kosher by the Vaad — the only kosher-certified cafe in this guide — and its hours follow that. Open until 8:30pm Sunday through Thursday, closing at 5pm Friday, then opening at 10:30pm Saturday night and running to midnight. Read that twice before you drive over on a Friday evening — after 5pm that day, one of Chesterfield’s restaurants is the fallback.
### Ballwin and Ellisville
This is where west county’s coffee actually lives.
The Wolf Cafe, 15480 Clayton Rd, Suite 210, Ballwin. Open 7am to 9pm Tuesday through Friday — one of only six independents in the whole metro open that late — then 8 to 3 Saturday, closed Sunday and Monday.
The Ground STL, 109 Ballpark Dr, Ballwin. A coffeehouse and a plant shop in the same room, open at 6am on weekdays, one of the earliest in the metro. Worth noting that several listing sites place it in Wildwood; its own site says Ballwin.
6 North Cafe, 14438 Clayton Rd, Ballwin. Family-owned, free-standing building with a drive-thru, weekdays 7 to 3. They’re straightforward that they pour Kaldi’s rather than roasting their own, and they bake their own cookies, muffins and pastries in house.
Kaldi’s Ellisville Drive-Thru, 147 Clarkson Rd, 6am to 4pm every day. This was Kaldi’s first drive-thru, with an express menu and a little outdoor seating.
Qahwatea Coffee, 15957 Manchester Rd, Ellisville, is the most interesting room out here and the hardest to pin down. It’s a Yemeni coffeehouse built as a deliberately alcohol-free late-night alternative — hand-stitched Yemeni wicker chairs, cushion seating, carved Moroccan panels, murals of Yemeni life — and it’s reported open to 10pm on weeknights and midnight on Friday and Saturday, which would make it the latest-closing coffeehouse in the metro. The catch: the business has no website, so those hours come from a magazine feature rather than the owners, and listings disagree about Sunday. Call before you go, and then go.
### Creve Coeur
La Bonne Bouchée, 12344 Olive Blvd, has been a French patisserie here since 1981 — older than most of the neighborhood around it. The bakery and café run to 8:30pm Tuesday through Saturday; the restaurant side closes at 2:30pm. Two schedules, one building, and people get caught by it.
Gateway Coffee Company, 12806 Olive Blvd, opened in December 2022 and sources its baked goods from Trolley Stop Bakery. Weekdays 7 to 6, Saturday 8 to 6, Sunday 8 to 3.
### Just over the line
Two more worth knowing if you’re willing to cross a municipal boundary, which nobody in an actual car cares about.
Rosemary Coffee Co. sits at 1316 Big Bend Rd, technically in Twin Oaks right at the Manchester line — which is why half the listings put it in one town and half in the other. It has patio seating, a lending library, and a wall of products from mostly women-owned local vendors. The one thing we can’t give you is hours: their own site posts them as an image rather than text, so call. Listings put the weekday open at 6am, which would make it one of the earliest in the region.
Deer Creek Coffee at 9820 Clayton Rd is a real independent, but the address is Ladue, not west county proper. It gets tagged to Des Peres constantly in search results. If you’re coming from Des Peres or Town and Country, it’s likely closer than anything actually inside your own city limits — which says something about the state of coffee in those two towns.
Total tangent: the Tiffany neighborhood is smaller than you’d guess.
### Where west county has nothing
Three of the towns in this search have no independent coffee shop at all, and no guide seems willing to say it.
Wildwood has none. The City of Wildwood’s own food and drink listing names four cafe-type businesses in the entire municipality: a Starbucks, a St. Louis Bread Co, Letty Lou’s Cafe & Diner and Sunny Street Cafe. There is no independent coffee house in Wildwood Town Center. If you live there, the nearest real options are in Ellisville and Ballwin, five to ten minutes east — the same direction as most of west county’s restaurants.
Town and Country and Des Peres have none either. Every shop that gets tagged to those two in search results — 6 North, The Ground, Deer Creek — is physically in Ballwin or Ladue. That’s not a technicality if you’re deciding whether to drive.
For two of the wealthiest municipalities in Missouri to have no independent coffee shop between them is a genuinely strange fact, and if you were considering opening one, it’s the most interesting sentence in this article.
### What’s not there anymore
Beyond the mall, a few things worth knowing before you trust another list.
“thePerk” turns up in Creve Coeur coffee results, but it’s Missouri Baptist University’s campus cafe — real, and not a public coffee shop you’d plan a morning around. One Chesterfield roaster that appears in AI-generated summaries traces back to a business in Dubai with a similar name. And Course Coffee Roasters, which shows up constantly in west county results, is in St. Charles, across the river.
We name these because the pattern matters more than any one entry: most coffee lists are assembled by copying other coffee lists, and mistakes compound rather than get corrected.
### Does Kaldi’s count?
Two of the eleven shops here are Kaldi’s, and a third pours their coffee, so it’s worth being straight about it.
Kaldi’s is a St. Louis company, founded here, roasting here, with locations across the region. It is not a national chain and it is not a one-off neighborhood shop either — it sits in between, and where you land on that is a matter of taste rather than fact. We’ve included it because in west county it is frequently the only thing open at 6am, and because pretending otherwise would make this guide less useful than it should be. If your definition of independent is stricter, the single-location shops here are The Wolf Cafe, 6 North, The Ground STL, Café Fermata, The Tea Spout, Corner Cafe, Gateway, La Bonne Bouchée, Qahwatea and Rosemary.
### A note on hours, and on working here
Every time above came from the business’s own website on the day this was written, with two exceptions we’ve flagged in place — Qahwatea, which has no site, and La Bonne Bouchée, whose site blocks automated reading. West county shops keep short and seasonal hours, and several close two days a week. Call ahead if you’re driving.
And if you’re looking for somewhere to work: Kaldi’s Chesterfield is the only shop in west county that publishes anything about wifi, parking or meeting space. Nobody else mentions outlets or a laptop policy on their own site. Every “great for remote work” claim you’ll read elsewhere is someone’s impression. Thirty seconds on the phone is worth more than any of them.

## What Junk Removal Actually Costs in St. Louis (Check Your City First)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/junk-removal-cost-st-louis
The couch has been in the garage for four months. The old treadmill is holding coats. There is a dead water heater behind the shed that you have stopped seeing.
At some point you search what it costs to make it all go away, and the answers come back $99, $210, $400, $950. All for the same job, apparently.
### How much does junk removal actually cost?
Most households land somewhere between $150 and $400. But the number you get depends almost entirely on two things nobody explains up front:
It is priced by volume, not weight or time. You are buying a fraction of a truck — an eighth, a quarter, a half. Not an hour of labor.
The advertised low price is a minimum charge. The $99 headline exists to get the truck to your driveway. Very little actually fits inside it.
And before you book anything: in a lot of this metro, your own municipality will haul bulk items for free or close to it. That option is invisible on every pricing page you will find, for reasons worth understanding.
### Why every site gives you a different number
Line up the results and the spread stops looking random. Each source is describing a different business, and none of them mentions it:
A storage company says $75 to $800.
A national booking platform says $150 to $350, national average $210.
A moving-comparison site says $100 to $400.
A regional hauler publishes $100–$199 for an eighth of a truck and $700–$950 for a full one.
An operator in another state prices it at $0.85 per cubic foot.
The last two are the honest ones, because they are quoting the unit the industry actually uses. The middle ones are averages across job sizes that have nothing to do with each other — a single mattress and a full basement cleanout are both “junk removal.”
The most useful number on that whole page comes from a forum, where somebody reported what they were actually billed: charged by the truckload, told their load was three-eighths of a truck, about $260. That is what this looks like in practice.
### How the pricing actually works
Almost every full-service hauler charges by how much of the truck bed your stuff fills. The crew looks at the pile, quotes a fraction, and that is the price.
Roughly what the fractions mean in real objects: an eighth is a couple of large items — a mattress and a chair. A quarter is a small room’s worth, or a bedroom set. A half is a garage’s worth of accumulated things. A full truck is a basement, an estate cleanout, or a whole apartment.
Two things break that model and cost extra, so ask about them by name:
Heavy material. Concrete, dirt, brick, roofing tear-off and tile are priced by weight, not volume, because the truck hits its weight limit long before it fills up. A small pile of concrete can cost more than a truckload of furniture.
Items with disposal fees. Appliances with refrigerant, televisions and monitors, mattresses, tires and paint carry per-item charges at the transfer station, and those get passed to you.
Labor is usually included, but stairs, long carries and anything requiring disassembly can add to the quote. Say up front that the couch is in a walk-out basement.
### Check your city first
Here is the option the pricing pages cannot mention, because all of them make money sending you to a hauler.
The St. Louis metro is not one city. It is roughly ninety municipalities on the Missouri side alone, plus the Metro East, and many of them include bulk-item pickup in the trash service you already pay for. Some run it on a schedule, some on request, some a set number of times a year. For a couch, a mattress or a grill, that is frequently the entire answer — at no additional cost.
Because the rules genuinely differ from one municipality to the next, the only reliable move is to check your own. Search your city name plus “bulk pickup” or call the number on your trash bill, and ask four things:
Is bulk pickup included, and how often?
Do I need to schedule it, or is there a set week?
What is excluded — appliances, electronics, tires, construction debris?
Is there an item limit per pickup?
That call takes five minutes and regularly saves a couple hundred dollars. Where it does not work: exclusions are common for the exact items you most want gone, volume limits are real, and if you are on a deadline — a closing, a move-out, a landlord — a scheduled municipal pickup three weeks out is no help. That is when you hire someone.
### The other free and cheap routes
Before paying for volume, some of the pile may not be junk at all.
Donation pickup. Several charities collect furniture and household goods from the curb or the house at no charge, and will give you a receipt for the deduction. The catch is condition — they turn down anything torn, stained, water-damaged or missing parts, and they will not take your mattress. Book well ahead; free pickup runs a wait.
Give it away. Marketplace and local groups will clear a working appliance or decent furniture within a day, usually with the person carrying it out themselves. Put “curb alert” and the cross streets in the post and it often disappears before you get back inside.
Scrap metal. Anything substantially metal — old appliances, swing sets, cast iron, water heaters — has scrap value. Some haulers will take metal at a reduced rate because they resell it, and scrap yards accept drop-offs.
Household hazardous waste. Paint, chemicals, oil and batteries are handled separately by every program in the region and cannot go in regular trash. Your county runs collection for this; look up its schedule rather than hiding it in a hauler’s load, where it will either be refused or surcharged.
Unrelated, and we know it — every place to eat in Richmond Heights.
### When a dumpster beats a hauler
Roll-off dumpster rental is the other model, and the trade is straightforward: you do the loading, and you keep it for several days.
It wins for renovations and long projects, where debris accumulates over a week and one truck visit would not cover it. It also wins for heavy construction material, where volume-based hauling pricing works against you.
It loses when the job is one afternoon, when you cannot or would rather not carry it yourself, or when there is nowhere legal to put a container — a real constraint on the narrower city streets and in neighborhoods with permit requirements for anything sitting on the street.
### The awkward items, specifically
A few things come up constantly and price differently from everything else, so it is worth knowing before you call.
Hot tubs are their own category. They have to be cut apart to move, they are heavy, and the job usually takes a crew a few hours. Expect it to be quoted separately rather than as a fraction of a truck.
Pianos — particularly uprights — are heavy, awkward and hard to give away, because almost nobody wants one. Removal is a specialist job and stairs make it dramatically worse.
Sheds, decks and fencing are demolition plus hauling, which are two different services. Get clear about which one you are being quoted for.
Refrigerators, freezers and air conditioners contain refrigerant that must be recovered before disposal, which is why every program charges extra for them and why they are the most common exclusion from municipal bulk pickup.
Mattresses carry a disposal fee almost everywhere, are refused by donation programs as a rule, and take up more truck volume than their weight suggests.
Paint is not junk, it is household hazardous waste, and latex can often be dried out and disposed of with regular trash once solid. Check your county program before paying anyone to take it.
### Getting an honest quote
Three habits get you a price you can trust.
Photograph the pile and send it. Most companies will quote from photos. It takes two minutes and it prevents the conversation where the crew arrives, re-prices upward, and you feel cornered because they are already standing in your driveway.
Ask what the number includes. Labor, disposal fees, taxes, and any per-item charges. “Starting at” pricing is a minimum, not an estimate.
Get two quotes. Volume assessment is a judgment call, and two crews will genuinely see the same pile differently — sometimes by a full fraction of a truck.
One more that matters more than people expect: ask what happens to it. Reputable operators separate metal, sort donatable goods, and take electronics to proper recycling rather than sending everything to a transfer station. It costs them time, which is part of why the cheapest bid is sometimes cheap.
### Finding someone here
Once the municipal option is ruled out and the giveaway pile is separated, compare a few local companies and send the same photos to each. Browse local pros on the home services coverage map, which covers both sides of the river.
If the cleanout is tied to something larger — a move, an estate, a renovation — it is usually cheaper to sequence it: give away and donate first, let the city take what it will, and hire the truck for whatever is genuinely left.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Why is junk removal so expensive?
A.  Because you are paying for three things, not one: a crew, a truck, and disposal. Transfer stations charge by weight and add per-item fees for appliances, mattresses, electronics and tires. A quote that seems high for “taking away a couch” is mostly labor and landfill cost, and the cheapest bids usually cut the sorting and recycling.
### Q. What is the minimum charge for junk removal?
A.  Most companies have one, commonly in the $100–$150 range, and it applies even to a single item. That is why hauling one mattress can cost nearly as much as hauling three. If you only have one or two things, check municipal bulk pickup or a donation collection first — the minimum charge is exactly where those options save the most.
### Q. What’s included in a $99 junk removal service?
A.  Usually the minimum load — roughly one or two items, sometimes a strict cubic-foot cap — with labor included and disposal fees often not. Treat $99 as the price of getting a truck to your address. Ask specifically whether the figure covers dump fees and per-item surcharges, because that is where the quote grows.
### Q. What is the cheapest way to get rid of junk?
A.  In this metro, usually your own city. Many municipalities include bulk-item pickup in the trash service you already pay for. After that: donation pickup for anything in good condition, giving it away locally, and scrapping metal. Paying a hauler is the right answer for volume, deadlines, and things nobody else will take.
### Q. How to get junk removed for free?
A.  Municipal bulk pickup, charity collection for usable furniture and household goods, and curb-alert giveaways cover most of it at no cost. Scrap metal can even pay slightly. What genuinely will not go free is anything damaged, mattresses, construction debris, and hazardous material — those have real disposal costs behind them.
### Q. What is the cheapest way to get rid of junk for free?
A.  Sort the pile before you do anything else. Usable items go to donation pickup or a curb alert, metal goes to scrap, hazardous material goes to your county collection, and whatever your city accepts goes out on bulk day. What survives all four of those is normally small enough that the remaining decision is easy.

## Repair It or Replace It? An Honest Guide to St. Louis Appliance Repair
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/appliance-repair-or-replace
The dryer is making a noise. Not a dramatic noise — a rhythmic one, the kind you can talk yourself into ignoring for a week.
Then it stops heating, and you are standing in the basement with wet towels doing math you have no basis for. Is this a $200 fix or a $900 mistake?
### Is it worth repairing, or should you replace it?
Two rules settle most of these, and between them they cover almost every appliance in the house:
The 50% rule. If the repair costs more than about half the price of a comparable new unit, replace it.
The age rule. If the appliance is past roughly three-quarters of its expected life, replace it — even if the repair is cheap. You are about to meet the next failure.
And the question to ask before anyone comes out: is the diagnostic fee credited toward the repair if I go ahead? Many companies credit it. Some do not. That single answer is the difference between paying once and paying twice to be told bad news.
### The diagnostic fee, and why it feels like a trap
Nearly every repair company charges a call-out or diagnostic fee. That is legitimate — someone drove to your house with a van full of parts and spent time working out what is wrong.
What makes it feel unfair is the sequence. You pay the fee, the technician tells you the control board is dead and the part costs most of what a new machine costs, and you have now spent money to be told to buy a different thing entirely.
You cannot avoid the fee, but you can avoid the sting. Ask three things when you book:
Is the fee credited toward the repair if I approve the work? Frequently yes, and it should be stated plainly.
Will you quote the full repair before starting? You want the total — parts and labor — not a running clock.
Do you service this brand, and can you get parts for it? This is the one people skip, and it is the most common reason a repair stalls.
Describe the symptom precisely when you call. “It runs but does not heat” and “it will not turn on” are different problems, and a good dispatcher can sometimes tell you on the phone that it is not worth the visit.
### What actually drives the price
Repair quotes vary far more than people expect, and it is not arbitrary.
Which part failed. This is most of it. A thermostat, igniter, belt, valve or heating element is usually a modest repair. A control board, compressor, sealed refrigeration system or transmission is usually the one that ends the conversation.
Whether the part still exists. Manufacturers stop making parts. On older or discontinued models the part may be unavailable, back-ordered for weeks, or only available refurbished — and a two-week wait for a refrigerator part is its own kind of expensive.
How the machine is built. Some units require pulling the whole appliance apart to reach a cheap component. The part is $40 and the labor is three hours.
Whether it is a sealed system. Refrigerant work on refrigerators, freezers and air conditioners requires certification and specialized recovery equipment, which is why those repairs sit in a higher bracket than anything mechanical.
### Rough lifespans, and where yours sits
The age rule needs a denominator. These are the widely published general ranges — treat them as orientation, not prophecy, because usage matters enormously. A washer running two loads a day in a house of six is not on the same clock as one running twice a week.
Refrigerators: commonly cited around 10 to 15 years, with the compressor the usual terminal failure.
Washers and dryers: commonly around 10 to 13 years. Dryers often outlast washers because they do less mechanical work.
Dishwashers: commonly around 9 to 12 years.
Ranges and ovens: often the longest-lived in the house, particularly gas, which has fewer electronics to fail.
Microwaves: commonly under 10 years, and rarely economical to repair.
Find the model number — usually on a plate inside the door, behind the kick panel, or on the back — and look up its manufacture date. Knowing whether the machine is six years old or fourteen changes the whole calculation, and most people genuinely do not know.
### When repair is clearly the right call
Fix it, without much agonizing, when:
The appliance is young. Under about five years, repair almost always wins.
It is a known consumable. Belts, igniters, thermostats, door seals, filters and heating elements are wear items, not death sentences.
It is a high-end unit. On a built-in or professional-grade appliance, a repair that would be irrational on a builder-grade machine is often obviously worth it — replacement is a different order of cost.
It is built in. Panel-ready and integrated appliances have to fit the cabinetry. Replacement can mean cabinet work, which the quote never includes.
### When to stop spending
Replace it when:
It has already been repaired recently. Two failures in a year on an aging machine is a pattern, not bad luck.
The compressor or sealed system has gone on a refrigerator past its middle age.
The control board is dead and the board is a large share of replacement cost, which it frequently is.
The part is discontinued or weeks out. A working appliance you do not have is worth less than it sounds.
It is genuinely inefficient. A twenty-year-old machine costs money every month it runs, and that quietly changes the math.
One honest caveat against replacing reflexively: new does not automatically mean more reliable. Modern appliances carry more electronics, and a board failure out of warranty on a three-year-old machine is a common and infuriating experience. Replacement buys efficiency and a warranty — not certainty.
Random, but: is your Waterloo, IL shop showing up in search?
### Check the warranty before you call anyone
People skip this and pay for covered repairs constantly.
Look for three things. The manufacturer warranty may still be running, and many carry longer coverage on specific components — sealed systems and motors often run well past the general term. Your credit card may have extended the warranty automatically if you bought the appliance with it. And your homeowner’s policy will not cover the appliance itself, but it may cover the damage it caused — a failed washer hose or a leaking refrigerator line is a water-damage claim even when the machine is not covered.
If any of those apply, use the manufacturer’s authorized service channel rather than an independent shop, because outside repairs can void what remains.
### Before you book: the free checks
A meaningful share of service calls turn out to be something you could have found in ten minutes.
Check the obvious power path — breaker, outlet, and whether the plug is actually seated. Dryers that will not heat are often a tripped breaker on one leg of a 240-volt circuit, which is confusing because the drum still turns. A dishwasher that will not drain is frequently a clogged filter or a garbage disposal knockout plug that was never removed. A refrigerator running warm is very often condenser coils packed with dust, particularly in a house with pets. A washer that will not spin may simply be unbalanced.
None of this is a substitute for a technician on a real failure. It is the ten minutes that occasionally saves the fee entirely.
### A word on extended warranties
You will be offered one at the register on the replacement, and the honest answer is that it depends on what you are buying.
The case against them is simple arithmetic. On a mid-range appliance, the plan often costs a meaningful fraction of the machine, covers a window when failure is least likely, and excludes the things that actually go wrong — cosmetic damage, wear items, and anything the manufacturer already covers. Set the same money aside and you have self-insured with better terms.
The case for them is narrower but real. On an expensive, electronics-heavy or built-in appliance, one control board or sealed-system failure can exceed the plan cost outright, and on integrated units the replacement headache is worse than the repair. If you are buying at the high end, the math flips.
Either way, read two things before deciding: who actually performs the service — the manufacturer, the retailer, or a third-party network you have never heard of — and whether the plan pays out in repairs or in store credit. A plan that resolves to a gift card is a different product than the one you thought you were buying.
Check what you already have first. Many credit cards extend the manufacturer warranty automatically on anything bought with the card, which quietly covers the same window the paid plan is selling you.
### Finding someone here
Have the model number and the symptom ready before you call — it gets you a better answer and sometimes an honest “that one is not worth fixing” before anyone charges you. Browse local repair pros on the home services coverage map, which covers both sides of the river.
And if the answer turns out to be replacement, the old unit is mostly metal, which means it has scrap value and does not belong at the curb by default. Many retailers will haul the old machine away when they deliver the new one, sometimes at no charge — ask about that at purchase rather than after, because it is far easier to arrange in advance than to solve on your own afterwards.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it worth repairing an appliance?
A.  Usually, if the repair is under half the cost of a comparable new unit and the appliance is not past about three-quarters of its expected life. Under five years old, repair nearly always wins. Past twelve, on a major component failure, it rarely does.
### Q. How much does appliance repair cost?
A.  It depends almost entirely on which part failed, not on the appliance. Wear items — belts, igniters, thermostats, seals, heating elements — sit at the affordable end. Control boards, compressors and sealed refrigeration systems sit at the end where replacement usually wins. Always ask for the full quote, parts and labor, before work starts.
### Q. Is the diagnostic fee credited toward the repair?
A.  Often yes, but not always, and it is the single most useful question to ask when booking. If it is not credited, you will pay the fee even when the answer is “replace it” — which is a reasonable charge for the technician’s time, but you should know it going in.
### Q. How long do appliances last?
A.  Broadly: refrigerators around 10 to 15 years, washers and dryers around 10 to 13, dishwashers around 9 to 12, ranges often longer, microwaves usually under 10. Usage moves these a lot. Find the model number and look up the manufacture date — knowing the real age changes the decision more than any other single fact.
### Q. Should I repair or replace a refrigerator?
A.  If the compressor or sealed system has failed and the unit is past its middle age, replace it. If it is a fan, thermostat, defrost element or door seal, repair it — those are ordinary wear items. Before either, pull the unit out and check whether the condenser coils are packed with dust, which causes a lot of “failures.”
### Q. Why is my dryer not heating but still running?
A.  Commonly a tripped breaker on one leg of the 240-volt circuit — the drum turns on one leg while the heat needs both, which is why it looks alive but runs cold. It can also be a failed heating element, thermal fuse or thermostat, all of which are ordinary repairs. Check the breaker first; it costs nothing.

## Hardwood, Laminate or Vinyl? Start by Looking Under Your Carpet
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/hardwood-vs-laminate-st-louis
The carpet in the back bedroom has to go. That much is settled.
What replaces it is less settled, and an hour of reading turns up confident people telling you hardwood is the only real answer, laminate is a scam, vinyl plank has solved everything, and engineered wood is either the smart compromise or a marketing exercise.
### Hardwood or laminate — which should you actually put down?
It depends far less on taste than the comparison articles suggest, and far more on three questions:
What room is it, and is it below grade? Solid hardwood does not belong in a basement. That is not a preference, it is moisture physics.
What is already under the carpet? In a lot of houses around here, the answer is original hardwood — and refinishing beats buying.
Who lives there? Large dogs, small children and heavy traffic push the answer toward wear resistance over authenticity.
The short version: hardwood for main living areas above grade, especially in an older home. Laminate or luxury vinyl for basements, high-traffic rooms, rentals, and houses with big dogs. Engineered wood when you want real wood over a concrete slab or in a room with some humidity swing.
### Look under the carpet first
Before you price a single square foot, pull up a corner in a closet.
This metro is full of houses built long before wall-to-wall carpet existed, and a great many of them have original hardwood underneath — oak, usually, installed when the house was built and covered over sometime in the second half of the last century. If your house predates the carpet by decades, there is a genuine chance the floor you want is already in the room.
Refinishing existing hardwood is usually cheaper than buying and installing new flooring, and the material is frequently better than what you would buy today: old-growth, tighter grain, and thick enough to sand more than once. It also keeps the house consistent with itself, which matters in a period home more than people expect.
What to check when you look: whether the boards are actually wood rather than a thin veneer; how much thickness is left above the tongue, since that determines whether it can be sanded at all; whether there is water staining, cupping or crowning; and how much damage the carpet tack strips and staples did around the perimeter. A flooring contractor will tell you in one visit whether it is refinishable, and that visit is worth more than any amount of online comparison.
If you have recently worked out that your house is older than the listing claimed, this is the practical payoff — that age makes it much more likely there is something worth uncovering.
### The basement rule
This is the one place where the choice is not really a choice.
Basements are below grade, which means the slab passes moisture upward continuously, humidity swings hard by season, and the risk of standing water is never zero. Solid hardwood in that environment cups, gaps and eventually fails — not because it is poor quality, but because wood moves with moisture and a basement never stops supplying it.
What works below grade is waterproof by construction rather than by finish: luxury vinyl plank, tile, or sealed concrete. Laminate is a middle case — better than hardwood, but its core is wood-based, and a genuine water event will swell it permanently unless it is a specifically waterproof product.
And the sequencing point that saves people the most money: fix the water before you buy the floor. A finished basement floor installed over an unresolved moisture problem is a floor you will pay for twice. If the space has ever taken water, deal with that first.
### What each material is actually good at
Solid hardwood. Real wood, sandable several times over a lifetime, and the only option that genuinely adds to a period home rather than sitting inside it. Weaknesses: moisture, scratching, and cost. It should stay above grade.
Engineered wood. A real wood veneer over a dimensionally stable core. It handles humidity swings better than solid, can go over concrete, and looks identical because the surface is wood. The catch is the veneer thickness — a thick wear layer can be refinished once or twice, a thin one never can. Ask for that number before buying anything.
Laminate. A photographic layer under a hard wear surface. Modern laminate is genuinely scratch-resistant — often more so than real wood — and inexpensive. Weaknesses: it cannot be refinished, ever, and water at the seams is its failure mode. It also sounds different underfoot, which some people never stop noticing.
Luxury vinyl plank. Fully waterproof, quiet, comfortable underfoot, and the most forgiving of everything the household throws at it. Weaknesses: it can dent under heavy point loads, quality varies enormously between cheap and good, and it does not add the character an older home wants.
### If you have dogs
This deserves its own answer because it is asked constantly and answered badly.
Two different problems get conflated: scratching and liquid. Dog nails scratch, and accidents, water bowls and wet paws soak. A material can be excellent at one and poor at the other.
Solid hardwood loses on both counts — it scratches visibly and standing liquid stains it if it sits. Laminate resists scratching very well and handles liquid poorly at the seams. Luxury vinyl plank handles both, which is why it wins most dog-household recommendations honestly rather than as a sales pitch.
Two practical notes worth more than the material choice: matte and textured finishes hide scratches dramatically better than glossy ones, and lighter or heavily grained looks hide them better than dark uniform ones. And whatever you install, keeping nails trimmed does more for the floor than any product feature.
Nothing to do with flooring — here’s where to eat in Byrnes Mill.
### Where each one belongs
Living room, dining room, bedrooms, above grade: hardwood if the house suits it, engineered if there is a slab.
Kitchen: tile or luxury vinyl. Wood in a kitchen is a decision about looks, made knowing the dishwasher will eventually leak.
Bathrooms and laundry: tile or vinyl. Nothing wood-based.
Basement: vinyl, tile or sealed concrete. Never solid hardwood.
Rentals and high-traffic: laminate or vinyl. Durability and replaceability beat authenticity when you are not the one living on it.
Stairs: wood or carpet. Vinyl and laminate on stairs is a specialist installation and frequently done badly.
Entryways and mudrooms: tile or vinyl. This is where road salt, slush and grit arrive every winter, and grit is what actually destroys a finish — it works like sandpaper underfoot. A mat inside and out does more for whatever you install here than the material choice does.
### Pick one of each up and look at the edge
If you take one thing into the showroom, take this: hold a solid oak plank next to a laminate plank and look at them edge on.
The oak will be around three quarters of an inch thick, and it is wood the whole way through. The laminate will be somewhere near three sixteenths — roughly a quarter of the thickness — with a thin decorative layer over a dense core.
That difference is the entire argument, and it explains everything else. Three quarters of an inch of real wood can be sanded down and refinished several times across a lifetime, which is why hundred-year-old floors in this city are still in service. There is nothing to sand on a laminate plank; the surface you buy is the only surface it will ever have, and once it wears through or a seam swells, the plank gets replaced rather than repaired.
Engineered wood sits between them, and the same test applies — look at the edge and find the real wood layer on top. A thick one can be refinished once or twice. A paper-thin one is, functionally, laminate with a nicer surface and a higher price.
### How it goes down matters too
Installation method is not a detail. It affects cost, how the floor sounds, and whether it survives.
Nail-down is traditional solid hardwood over a wood subfloor. It is the most permanent and the most expensive in labor, and it is not an option over concrete.
Glue-down bonds the floor to the subfloor. It is quiet underfoot and stable, common for engineered wood over slab, and it is the hardest to remove later.
Floating means the planks lock to each other rather than to the floor beneath. It is fast, it is what most laminate and vinyl use, and it is the most forgiving of a subfloor that is not perfectly flat — up to a point. Past that point it separates at the seams, which is why levelling gets skipped and then regretted.
Ask what goes underneath, too. Underlayment handles sound, minor levelling and — over concrete — the moisture barrier. On a slab that last one is not optional, and a floor installed without it is a warranty claim waiting to happen.
And ask about acclimation. Wood and many laminates need to sit in the room for a few days before installation so they reach the humidity they will live in. A crew that wants to deliver and install the same day is skipping a step that shows up months later as gaps or buckling — and in a climate with our humidity swing, that step earns its delay.
### The costs nobody quotes
The number you are given per square foot is rarely the number you pay, and the gaps are predictable.
Removal and disposal of the old floor is labor plus a dumpster or a hauler, and old carpet is bulky. Subfloor repair only reveals itself once the old floor is up, and in an older house it frequently reveals something. Levelling matters more than people expect, because click-together floors installed over an uneven subfloor separate at the seams later.
Then the finishing details: transitions and trim at every doorway, quarter round or new baseboard, and door undercutting if the new floor sits higher than the old. Each is small and they add up.
Get every quote itemized to the same list, and ask specifically what happens if the subfloor turns out to need work — whether that is a change order, and at what rate. That is the line that surprises people mid-project.
### Finding an installer here
Have the room measured and know what is underneath before you call, and get the refinishing question answered before you price replacement — those two facts change the entire budget. Browse flooring pros on the home services coverage map, which covers both sides of the river.
If the job is tile rather than plank, that is a different trade with different skills — how to choose a tile installer covers what to ask there.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is hardwood or laminate better?
A.  Neither, in the abstract. Hardwood is better above grade in a home where character and long-term value matter, because it can be refinished for decades. Laminate is better where scratching, budget or traffic dominate. The room decides it more than preference does — and below grade, neither is the right answer.
### Q. What is the best flooring for dogs?
A.  Luxury vinyl plank, for most households, because it handles the two separate problems — scratching and liquid — that other materials only solve one of. Choose a matte, textured finish rather than gloss, since texture hides scratches far better. Laminate is a close second if accidents are not a concern.
### Q. Can you put hardwood in a basement?
A.  You should not. Below-grade slabs pass moisture upward continuously and humidity swings by season, which makes solid wood cup, gap and eventually fail. Use luxury vinyl, tile or sealed concrete. And resolve any water problem before installing anything, or you will buy the floor twice.
### Q. Is it cheaper to refinish hardwood or replace it?
A.  Refinishing is usually cheaper, and in older homes it is frequently an option people do not realize they have. Pull up a corner of carpet in a closet before pricing replacement. What matters is whether enough thickness remains above the tongue to sand — a flooring contractor can tell you in one visit.
### Q. Does laminate flooring add value to a home?
A.  Less than hardwood, more than worn carpet. In a period home, original or new hardwood is what buyers respond to. In a rental, a basement, or a house where the floor takes real abuse, laminate or vinyl is the sensible choice and nobody is penalizing you for it.
### Q. What is engineered hardwood?
A.  A real wood veneer bonded to a stable core. The surface is genuine wood, so it looks identical to solid, but it handles humidity better and can go over a concrete slab. The number that matters is the wear-layer thickness — thick enough and it can be refinished, thin and it never can. Ask before buying.
Before you price new flooring, look under the carpet. In an older home there is a real chance the floor you want is already there, and refinishing usually costs less than replacing. Browse flooring pros across the metro on the home services coverage map or on St Louis Near Me Directory.

## Your Auto Body Estimate Will Probably Change. Here Is Why That Is Normal
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/auto-body-repair-estimate-st-louis
The estimate lands in your inbox and the number looks oddly specific. Then the shop calls two weeks later with a second number, and the specificity starts to feel like a magic trick.
Nothing has gone wrong. That is close to how the process is built to work — but almost nothing you will find online explains it, because most of what ranks for this question is a form pretending to be a calculator.
### How does an auto body repair estimate actually work?
The first estimate is written from damage somebody can see. It is a starting position, not a final price.
Once the vehicle is disassembled — the bumper cover comes off, the fender liner comes out — hidden damage may or may not turn up. If it does, the shop writes a supplement: a revised estimate for what was not visible the first time. That is normal, and it is why the number moves.
Three things follow from that, and they are the whole article:
The shop negotiates the supplement with the carrier, not you. That is in your favor, and it is the opposite of what most advice suggests.
“Get three estimates” is the wrong instruction when insurance is paying. Interview shops instead. You are choosing a contractor, not shopping a price.
Almost every answer here depends on your specific policy, on which state you are in, and on case law that can shift quickly. Anyone giving you a flat answer is guessing.
### Why the shop should do the negotiating
When a supplement is needed, the body shop or mechanic takes it directly to the carrier. Left alone, that arrangement works better for you than getting in the middle of it.
Consider what the negotiation is actually about. Whether a particular bracket is compromised. Whether a sensor housing behind the bumper still meets spec. Whether a panel can be repaired or has to be replaced. Most vehicle owners do not know what those parts are or how they are supposed to function, and there is no reason they should — they want the vehicle fixed correctly and returned.
The shop, meanwhile, has a powerful reason to fight for the right repair: it does not want liability for workmanship that could contribute to a future accident. A shop that lets a carrier talk it into a cheaper repair it does not believe in is the shop holding the risk afterward.
So the incentives line up. Your interest and a good shop's interest point the same direction, and the shop speaks the language.
### What “advocate for yourself” should actually mean
The advice is not wrong, it is aimed at the wrong target. The chain runs owner to shop, then shop to carrier — not owner to carrier.
Here is what that looks like. The carrier authorizes repainting the two front fenders and the hood. The work is done and the paint does not match the rest of the car, because paint ages and fresh paint on three panels of an older finish is visibly newer.
The thing to say is simple, and you say it to your shop: this car did not have two-tone paint before the accident, and I do not accept it now. Then the shop takes that to the carrier and argues for the money to blend adjacent panels and do it properly.
The standard underneath that argument is pre-loss condition — the idea that a settlement should restore you to roughly the condition you were in before the damage. That is what it means to indemnify a claim. A mismatched paint job plainly falls short of it, and that is an argument worth making through someone who makes it every week.
### Why “get three estimates” is the wrong instruction
Collecting three prices is comparison shopping. That is exactly right when you are buying a vacuum cleaner, or when you are paying for the repair yourself.
When the carrier is paying, price comparison is not working for you. It is working for them.
None of that requires believing carriers are villains. It is arithmetic. An insurer settling on the order of a hundred thousand claims a year, saving two dollars per claim, has covered the annual salaries of several full-time employees. At that scale, small per-claim savings are a genuine business line rather than a conspiracy. Anyone would run it that way.
Which tells you what your job is. You already know who is paying. Your job is deciding who they pay.
So interview and research three or more shops rather than collecting three numbers from them. Ask how long they have been doing this, whether they have worked on your make, what their workmanship warranty covers, whether they will handle the supplement conversation directly, and what happens if you are unhappy with the paint match. Then take your decision to the carrier: based on my research I want this shop to do the repairs, and I expect you to work with them to indemnify my claim.
### Whether you can insist on manufacturer parts
This is where people are most often surprised, and the honest answer is that the statute gives you less than you would expect — while your policy may give you more.
Neither Missouri nor Illinois gives you a right to demand OEM parts. Both states require disclosure, not consent. Consent statutes exist in only a handful of states nationally, and neither of ours is among them.
What both states do require is that you be told, in writing, before the work happens:
Every non-OEM part intended for the repair must be clearly identified on the written estimate.
A separate disclosure must explain that warranties on those parts come from the part manufacturer or distributor, not from the manufacturer of your vehicle. Missouri specifies the wording and requires it in ten-point type or larger; Illinois requires the customer be advised in writing.
The parts themselves must carry the maker's logo or name, visible after installation where practicable.
Your policy is the other half, and it may or may not be more generous than the statute. Policies generally fall into one of three shapes: some allow OEM parts only; some give you the choice, though if you pick the cheaper aftermarket part you will not be permitted to pocket the difference; and some let the carrier choose. Which one you have is on your declarations page, and it decides the outcome far more than the statute does.
Read the declarations page, not the estimate.
Nothing to do with fenders — Clayton, MO local SEO lives over here.
### Deductibles, depreciation and what “indemnify” buys you
Most carriers pay up to the cost of repair, minus your deductible, minus any non-recoverable depreciation. Depreciation on a claim is typical, not a slight.
What tends to get non-recoverable depreciation — meaning you do not get the held-back money, ever — is high-wear items: tires, hoses, wipers, a battery. The reasoning is that you were not going to get brand-new ones for free out of a collision. Whether it applies, and how much, depends on your policy.
There is a consequence people do not see coming. If you take the money and never do the repair, the carrier has indemnified the claim. The obligation has been met. Whether that has other effects is genuinely uncertain: an insurer or a lender may or may not report to a licensing bureau, and you may never be told either way. Those communications happen out of sight and tend to surface later — at refinance, at trade-in, at sale.
The same pattern exists on the property side, where a carrier may be required to notify a mortgage company above a damage threshold, depending on state statute. Anyone who tells you flatly that taking a settlement without repairing leaves no trace is overstating what they know.
### Do I have to use the body shop my insurance company recommends?
No. You choose the repair facility. A carrier is allowed to recommend a shop. It is not allowed to require one.
There is a name for pushing you past a recommendation into a decision: steering. It is worth knowing the word, because most people have never heard it and assume a firm nudge from their own insurer is simply how the process works.
It is not. Steering is treated as an improper claims practice rather than ordinary salesmanship, and the reason is a conflict of interest you are usually not told about: a carrier may have a standing pricing arrangement with the shops it recommends. Those arrangements can be perfectly legitimate, and plenty of those shops do excellent work. But the shop is being recommended to you by the party paying the bill, and that party has an interest in the bill being smaller. You are entitled to weigh that yourself.
In practice it rarely sounds like pressure. It sounds reasonable, because it often is:
“Many of our customers choose that shop — they are close by, they are well known, and they are the only shop nearby that handles your brand of vehicle.”
“You can choose any shop you want, but we do not pay towing or mileage to move your vehicle to a shop that far away when there is one this close.”
Here is the part most consumer articles will not tell you: that may be steering, and it may also be entirely true. The nearby shop may genuinely be the better choice. The towing limitation may genuinely be what the policy says.
Which is why the answer is not suspicion, it is homework. If you have interviewed shops and have a reasoned preference, say so plainly and expect it to be honored — that is your call to make, not a favor being granted. If you have not done that homework, the recommendation you are being given may well be the right one anyway.
The line to listen for is the difference between advising and discouraging. “Here is a shop we work with often” is a recommendation. Being told your chosen shop will delay the repair, void something, or cost you money out of pocket — when your policy does not actually say that — is closer to pressure. If it feels like the latter, you can put your choice in writing, and the Missouri Department of Commerce and Insurance takes consumer complaints about claims handling.
### Repairable or totaled, and who decides
Less negotiable than people expect. Most carriers now use applications tied to national databases: photographs, the VIN and the vehicle's vitals upload on the spot, and the underlying calculation returns repairable or total loss.
You can contest a valuation. Unless the vehicle is exotic, it is usually a losing battle.
When an estimate lands genuinely on the cusp, many carriers will ask you which you prefer — repair it or total it. That choice deserves more thought than it usually gets, because totaling a vehicle will typically brand the title through the state licensing bureau, and that brand follows the vehicle for the rest of its life.
Hail is where this gets interesting locally, and hail is not a rare event here. Missouri has recently ranked second in the country for hail claims paid by State Farm, behind only Texas, according to the carrier's own 2025 figures. Missouri is, by any measure anyone publishes, a top hail state.
Consider a vehicle that cost around forty thousand dollars new, is a year old, is worth roughly thirty thousand today, and takes fifteen thousand dollars in hail damage. Mechanically it is exactly as reliable as it was the day before the storm. The dents are cosmetic.
Some owners take the payout and simply do not repair it. They keep a dependable vehicle and keep the money. Resale and trade-in become meaningfully harder afterward, and depending on how the claim is settled a branded title may follow — but for somebody who does not mind driving a dimpled truck, it can be a sound financial decision rather than a mistake.
It is a real trade-off with real consequences on both sides, which is exactly why it should be your decision and not a default.
### Choosing a shop here
Ask how long they have worked on your make, what their workmanship warranty actually covers and for how long, whether they will handle the supplement conversation with your carrier directly, and how they approach paint blending on adjacent panels. That last question tells you a great deal quickly.
Then browse body shops and mechanics across the metro on the home services coverage map, which covers both sides of the river.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much does body repair usually cost?
A.  It depends almost entirely on the vehicle, which is why the calculators are so unreliable. Parts pricing has changed dramatically: a headlight for a pickup from a decade ago might run a little over a hundred dollars, while a xenon headlight assembly for a current model of the same truck can exceed a thousand — and there are several of them. Sensors behind bumpers and in windshields add calibration work that did not exist before. Get a real estimate on your actual vehicle.
### Q. Will a body shop give me an estimate?
A.  Yes, and most will do it at no charge. Understand what you are receiving: an estimate written from visible damage, which may or may not change once the vehicle is disassembled. If it does, the shop writes a supplement and takes it to your carrier. A first estimate that later moves is normal rather than a sign something is wrong.
### Q. What is the current labor rate for auto repair?
A.  It varies by shop, by location, and by the experience of the technicians doing the work — and any figure that is accurate today may not be the going rate tomorrow. Rather than chase a number, ask a prospective shop directly what their rate is and whether your carrier has agreed to it. Where a carrier and a shop disagree on rate, that is a conversation for the two of them.
### Q. What is steering in an insurance claim?
A.  Steering is when a carrier pushes you past recommending a shop into effectively choosing one for you. It is treated as an improper claims practice, not ordinary salesmanship, because the shop is being recommended by the party paying the bill — and there may be a pricing arrangement between them. You choose the repair facility. A recommendation is fine; being discouraged from your own choice is not.
### Q. Can I demand original manufacturer parts in Missouri or Illinois?
A.  Not by statute. Both states require disclosure of non-OEM crash parts rather than your consent, so each such part must be identified on your written estimate along with a warranty disclosure. Your policy may give you more than the law does — some allow OEM only, some let you choose without pocketing any savings, and some leave the choice to the carrier. Check your declarations page.
### Q. Can I recover diminished value after a repair?
A.  Check your policy first, because that is where the answer lives. Diminished value coverage is generally not included unless it was purchased, so it should be easy to spot on your declarations page. Mass-market carriers often do not offer it at all, while carriers serving high-net-worth clients sometimes will for additional premium. If you believe it applies and are getting nowhere, have an attorney read the policy — and bear in mind that litigation, even pending litigation, can change this area quickly.
Interview shops, do not just collect prices. When your carrier is paying, three quotes is comparison shopping that works for them - your real leverage is choosing a shop you trust and asking your carrier to work with it. ## That Warm Outlet: The Best Electricians in St. Louis, Ranked
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-st-louis-best-electricians-your-easy-guide
The outlet behind the couch is warm. Not hot, just warm, like a mug somebody set down an hour ago, and there’s a faint smell you can’t place, part dust and part pennies. You pull the lamp plug and the prongs feel warmer than metal should. That’s the moment a St. Louis homeowner starts typing “electrician” into a phone with the lights still on and a knot under the ribs.
Here’s something most people in the city never learn. Inside St. Louis city limits, you can get a permit to do some of your own electrical work, if the house is your owner-occupied single-family home and you pass a short test given by the Building Division’s Electrical Section. What no homeowner can pull a permit for is a service change, a rehab or new construction. In this city you can wire your own room addition. You can’t pull a permit to change your own electrical service. That job belongs to a licensed contractor every single time, which makes the contractor you pick the most important decision in this whole story.
So we did the sorting you can’t do with a warm outlet in the next room. We pulled Google’s electrician listings across the metro, ranked them on rating and review count together, and split the results into two honest groups: electrical specialists, whose own websites lead with electrical work, and the big home-service companies that send an electrician one day and a furnace tech the next. Nobody paid to be here, and St Louis Near Me Directory vouches for no one. The numbers and the companies’ own words do the talking.
### Who are some good residential electricians in St. Louis, Missouri?
On our October 12 snapshot of Google’s listings, the highest-rated electrical specialists were Grasser Electric & Home Services at 5.0 stars from 636 reviews, Loveland Home Solutions at 4.9 from 1,117 and Anytime Electric at 4.9 from 701. Among the big home-service companies, Hoffmann Brothers stood at 4.9 from 11,999 reviews.
Stars won’t keep the panel from arcing, though, so check the license for the place the job is. Electrical permits in the city are issued to licensed electrical contractors certified by the City of St. Louis. In the county, ask which license they carry anyway, and write the number on something you won’t throw away, like the back of the electric bill. If your house is in the city and you want to ask about a permit or a contractor, the Building Division’s Electrical Section is at 314-622-3313, Room 425 in City Hall. Ask your electrician which license they hold before they set a ladder against your house. The good ones answer like you asked their name.
### The code your electrician works to has a number
Open the panel door in an older St. Louis house and you can usually read its history: breakers in three different colors, a handwritten label that just says kitchen with a question mark, a cable somebody’s uncle ran in a hurry. The city keeps a single standard over all of it. St. Louis builds to the 2017 National Electrical Code as the city adopted it, by Ordinance #70802, and permitted work gets inspected against it. An electrician who works here every week knows that without looking it up.
That’s why the cheapest bid is so often the most expensive one. Work done without a permit can sail along fine until you sell the house, file an insurance claim, or smell that warm-penny smell again. Then you pay twice: once for the shortcut and once for the electrician who has to undo it. If your attic still has the old cloth-wrapped knob-and-tube wiring on porcelain posts, ask for someone who replaces it regularly. Mr. Electric of St. Louis, for one, lists knob-and-tube replacement among its services.
### How we ranked them
A perfect score from a dozen friendly customers tells you a company has nice friends. Thousands of reviews holding steady near five stars tell you how it behaves on its worst Tuesday. So our score starts every company at the average rating of all the St. Louis electrician listings we pulled and lets its own reviews move it from there. Small samples barely budge. Big, steady ones carry the day.
Then read the reviews the way an inspector reads a panel: slowly, looking for the thing that doesn’t belong. Skip the ones that only say great guy. Look for the ones that mention a permit, a basement left cleaner than it was found, a price that matched the estimate, a callback that came the same day. Give extra weight to people with old houses, the brick two-flats and bungalows where wiring from several decades meets in one junction box. Those customers have seen bad work up close, and when they rave about an electrician, it means something.

### What should you ask before anyone opens your panel?
The panel door squeaks, the electrician’s flashlight clicks on, and you’re standing in the basement doorway trying to look like you know what a bus bar is. You don’t need to. You need three answers, and you should get them before a single screw comes out.

A good electrician answers all three without a pause, and that’s how to tell if an electrician is good long before the work is done. Watch how they test, too. A trained electrician probing a live circuit keeps one hand away from the equipment, a habit that keeps current from crossing the chest. If someone grabs a panel with both hands and a shrug, that tells you plenty.

### Frequently asked questions about St. Louis electricians
### Q. How to tell if an electrician is good?
A.  A good electrician tells you which license they hold, pulls the permit when the job needs one, and puts a detailed estimate in writing before starting. Look for a deep, steady review record rather than a handful of perfect scores, and notice whether they explain the work plainly. Evasive answers about credentials are the clearest warning sign.
