A.  Start with companies that have strong ratings across hundreds or thousands of reviews, like the ones ranked above, then confirm the city or county license for your address. The St. Louis Electricians Map on St Louis Near Me Directory shows electricians across the metro, so you can compare a few before the next emergency.
### Q. What type of electrician is best?
A.  For a house, a licensed residential electrician who does your kind of job every week. For a service change in the city of St. Louis, it has to be a licensed contractor, because homeowners can’t pull that permit. For low-voltage work like networking or audio, pick a shop that lists it as a specialty.
### Q. What is the one-hand rule for electricians?
A.  When testing or working on a live circuit, an electrician uses only one hand to hold the meter probes and keeps the other hand away from the equipment. That prevents a hand-to-hand current path across the chest, which could be fatal if a shock happens. Seeing it done is a small sign of real training.
### Q. How much do electricians charge per hour in St. Louis?
A.  It depends on the job, the electrician’s license level and whether it’s an emergency, and many price by the job instead of the hour. Get two written estimates for the same scope. Our St. Louis electrician cost guide breaks down typical local rates and what common jobs run.

## Shutoff Notice in St. Louis? The Rule Is 72 Hours, Not 24
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-help-and-assistance-resources
Seventy-two hours, not 24. Hold on to that number while the shutoff notice sits on the counter beside your phone.
You’ve read the date on it a dozen times. The radiator in the old brick flat ticks, the refrigerator hums, and every search you try opens ten more tabs. You don’t have to solve all of it tonight. You have to dial one number.
Pick up the phone and dial 211. A trained resource specialist answers 24/7, works out the area you’re calling from and what services you need, then gives you contact and program information for the help near you. It is not an emergency line: the 211 help site’s FAQ says to keep calling local emergency numbers for medical emergencies, fires and police.
Now pick up the paper. Smooth it flat and keep it within reach, because it isn’t only bad news. It’s also your key. A disconnect notice that shows a specific disconnect date is one way to qualify for the state’s winter crisis energy aid, ECIP, which can pay up to $800, based on funding; 211 can point you to where to apply. And if you appear on the eviction court docket, HELP STL, the free eviction legal help the City offers its renters, wants that information with you when you call. So don’t hide it, and don’t throw it out.
Then turn it over and read the date again. On a January night in a south city three-family, with frost creeping up the inside of the storm windows and the furnace cycling on and off, that date may not be the one that counts.
If it’s a shutoff notice from Ameren Missouri or Spire, remember that from November 1 to March 31, Missouri’s Cold Weather Rule bars a heat-related shutoff for nonpayment on any day when the National Weather Service forecast for the following seventy-two hours predicts a temperature below thirty-two degrees. The state law now says seventy-two hours, while the Public Service Commission’s older rule text still prints twenty-four. If anyone quotes you 24, the law says 72.
The rule covers gas and electric utilities under the Public Service Commission. Municipal systems, cooperatives and propane delivered by truck are not under the Commission, so it doesn’t reach them. And if you just moved in, here’s one worth repeating to a neighbor: you can’t be shut off for the previous occupant’s unpaid bill, unless that person still lives there.
Then make the call, pen in hand, the notice face-up where you can see it. Write down the name of whoever answers; tomorrow it’s the one thing you’ll wish you had. A utility notice goes to the utility itself, at the number printed on the bill, and you tell them you can’t pay in full.
### What is the fastest way to get housing assistance?
The fastest way to get housing assistance is to call the line built for the paper you were handed, with your lease, photo ID and anything that shows your income already on the table. The person who picks up will ask what the paper says and what date is on it. Read it out loud, date first, with a finger under the line so the words stop swimming.
For a court summons or eviction notice, call the City’s Department of Human Services for HELP STL at (314) 657-1671 or (314) 657-1654, with the paper in front of you. It’s for renters living in the City of St. Louis, and the City works with Legal Services of Eastern Missouri to offer the legal help free.
Outside the City, or if you want a second option, Legal Services of Eastern Missouri gives free civil legal help to low-income people and older adults in 21 eastern Missouri counties, including landlord and tenant problems.
If you’re behind but nothing has been filed, spread the lease and anything that shows your income across the kitchen table. Then start with 211. Ask Beyond Housing, Guardian Angel and Doorways the same plain question: what is open this month? Guardian Angel serves people at risk of eviction, foreclosure or utility shut-off. We couldn’t confirm which of the three has money right now, and their numbers are in the list further down.
Help paying rent comes from a patchwork of agencies and nonprofits, which is why one call beats a night of refreshing tabs until your eyes sting. Our guide to emergency rent assistance in St. Louis covers the hotlines and programs that pay back rent.
Is Missouri rental assistance still available? Not the way it was. When we last checked, the City of St. Louis listed no current emergency assistance programs; its past programs are on hold or completed and not available. What remains is smaller and local: the agencies above, and whatever 211 finds for your ZIP code.
For the longer game, housing help runs on a spectrum. Emergency shelter is for tonight. Transitional housing is a supported bridge of up to two years. Income-based, low-income and affordable apartments are longer-term homes where rent is often tied to what you earn. Long waiting lists are common, so apply to several at once and apply early. Learn the difference between income-based (Section 8) housing (and the full Section 8 voucher guide), low-income (tax-credit) housing, and how to find and afford an apartment that fits your budget.
### Where Do I Sleep Tonight?
By late afternoon you’re watching the light go orange over the brick two-families across the street. A bag sits by the door, and there’s no address to give yet. The hours before dark are the hardest. For emergency housing, start with the same 211 call, or the St. Louis Housing Helpline. Those are the two numbers the City of St. Louis gives on its winter housing and emergency shelter page for anyone who needs shelter.
The Housing Helpline number is (314) 802-5444. Call earlier in the day and you’ll know where you’re headed before dark.
Need a safe place tonight? Our guide to emergency homeless shelters in St. Louis shows who to call and which shelters serve families, women, men and youth, including Gateway180, Hope House, Haven of Grace and Covenant House.
In crisis or rebuilding? Start with how transitional housing works and helps you build stability, then the directory of local transitional-housing programs (who to call, what each offers).
Fleeing domestic violence? See our guide to St. Louis women’s shelters and safety resources. Confidential shelter is open to women and their children.
Nowhere to go during the day? Daytime drop-in & day centers offer showers, meals and computer access, usually free, during the day.
### Which Paper Goes With Which Number?
Lay everything that came in the mail out on the counter. Each paper has its own number, and the person on the line will ask what yours says.
A shutoff notice from your gas or electric company. Pick up the bill and find the account number. Call the utility before the date on it and say you can’t pay in full.
An eviction notice or court summons. Put the paper where you can see it. HELP STL, for renters in the City of St. Louis: (314) 657-1671.
Outside the City, or you want a second option. Legal Services of Eastern Missouri’s general number is 314-534-4200.
Behind on rent, nothing filed yet. Sit down with the lease and dial 211, then ask each of these what is open this month: Beyond Housing: 314-533-0600
Guardian Angel, for people at risk of eviction, foreclosure or utility shut-off: 314-773-9027
Doorways: 314-535-1919
No bed tonight. Grab the phone before the light goes and call the St. Louis Housing Helpline, (314) 802-5444.
Food running out. Open the cabinet, count what’s left, then dial 211 for a pantry near you and apply for SNAP today. Expedited SNAP must be on your card by the seventh calendar day after you apply.
Searching for “$500 help.” Before you tap that link, know that the City’s $500 Direct Cash Assistance has completed, and so has its $500-a-month basic income pilot. Anyone charging a fee to unlock “free money” is not the help you need.
Not safe at home. When you have a few minutes alone, call the National Domestic Violence Hotline: 1-800-799-7233. In danger right now, call 911.
Worried about an older adult. Sit down beside them with the phone and call the Missouri Senior Resource Line, 1-800-235-5503, then enter your ZIP code.
Suspect abuse or neglect of an adult. The state hotline is 1-800-392-0210, 7 days a week, 7 a.m. to 8 p.m.
All of the above, or none of them. That’s what 211 is for, or its long number, 800-427-4626.
Would you rather search on your own at 2 a.m.? FindHelp.org lets you enter your ZIP code and browse local food, housing and health programs. Here’s how FindHelp.org works. Either way, save these numbers in your phone, and put them in the phone of anyone you’re helping.
### The Lights Are Still On. How Long?
The envelope from Ameren or Spire is still face-down on the counter, and it feels heavier than paper should. The furnace kicks on, and you catch yourself counting how long it runs. If you can’t pay your utility bill, how long you have depends on two things: the date on the notice and, in winter, the forecast. Call early, with the bill and your account number in front of you, and tell them you can’t pay. Heat Up St. Louis says it plainly: call your utility first.
Here is what the Cold Weather Rule asks of you. Contact the utility. Say you can’t pay in full. Make the initial payment. Enter a payment agreement. The utility must first offer a 12-month budget plan that covers what you owe and the bills ahead. If you haven’t defaulted on a cold weather plan, the initial payment can be no more than 12% of that budget amount unless you and the utility agree to something else, and a pledge from the agency that runs LIHEAP counts as the payment.
Already cut off between November 1 and March 31? Contact the utility, ask it to reconnect you, say you can’t pay in full, make the initial payment and enter the agreement. The utility must reconnect you without requiring a deposit. If your heat comes from a co-op, a municipal system or propane, the rule doesn’t apply, so call them anyway and ask what help they offer.
Other protections work outside the winter rule. A utility must postpone a shutoff for up to 21 days if it would aggravate an existing medical emergency. Shutoffs can happen only between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m., and only after written notice mailed at least 10 days ahead. If you think the bill is wrong, call the Public Service Commission’s consumer hotline at 1-800-392-4211. During an informal complaint, and for at least 31 days after the Commission’s letter, the utility can’t shut you off over the disputed amount. Not paying the part that isn’t in dispute can still get you cut off.
Money for the bill itself comes from two places. The state’s crisis energy aid, called ECIP, helps when you have a disconnect notice with a specific disconnect date or a propane or fuel oil tank under 20% full. Winter ECIP runs November through May based on funding, and the most you could get is $800. You need $3,000 or less in bank, retirement or investment accounts. The state explains it on its LIHEAP page. Ameren Missouri’s Dollar More program now reaches households with income up to 300% of the federal poverty level and provides up to $600 per calendar year. Ameren runs it with United Way of Greater St. Louis and local Community Action Agencies.
Heat Up St. Louis and LIHEAP energy assistance help pay past-due heating and cooling bills.
The Missouri Cold Weather Rule guide walks through the winter steps, and Cool Down St. Louis helps qualifying seniors, people with a disability and low-income households get an air conditioner while supplies last.
No safe place to wait out the cold? See warming centers across the St. Louis metro: where to go, when they open, and who to call.
Behind on your water or sewer bill? Water & sewer bill assistance in St. Louis covers the City, County and MSD programs that keep your water on.
Cold air coming through the walls? Older and low-income homeowners can get free home repair and weatherization help to stay safe and warm.
### What Do I Do About the Fridge?
The refrigerator hums over a shelf of condiments. At the register, you watch the total climb and start putting things back. Open the cabinet, count what’s left, then dial 211 for a pantry near you and start the SNAP application the same day.
Expedited SNAP has to be on your EBT card by the seventh calendar day after you apply. Missouri gives it to households whose monthly gross income is under $150 with $100 or less in cash and bank accounts, to households whose income and cash together come to less than monthly shelter costs, and to destitute migrant or seasonal farm worker households with $100 or less. Otherwise, you’ll typically know within 30 days. Start with how to apply for SNAP (food stamps) in Missouri. If your benefits are ever cut, reduced or run out before the month’s end, what to do when food benefits get cut or run out shows how to appeal and where to get food today.
For groceries today, grab your photo ID before you leave for a standing pantry, since most ask for one. Food distribution events are different: the St. Louis Area Foodbank says an ID is usually not required there. Our guide to free food giveaways and pantries happening today maps where to get groceries and meals near you. Need a hot meal right now? Our guide to free meals and soup kitchens in St. Louis covers where to find hot food and how to reach the 211 helpline.
A few more pieces of the food puzzle. Ask about WIC if you’re pregnant or have young children. Low-income families with little ones can also get free diapers through the St. Louis Area Diaper Bank. And if you’re feeding a pet on a tight budget, our guide to pet food pantries in St. Louis covers where to get free pet food and what to bring.
### Is That $500 Offer Real?
You’ve seen the ad: free cash, just apply. For a second, your chest loosens. Then the facts. The City of St. Louis ran $500 Direct Cash Assistance as a one-time payment for households hit by the pandemic, and it has completed. The Guaranteed Basic Income pilot paid $500 a month for 18 months to 540 families, and the City Treasurer has announced its completion. If anyone asks you for a fee to unlock “free money,” hang up and dial 211 to check what’s real.
So how can you get money if you’re struggling? Not in one lump from one office. Real help arrives in pieces: one-time rent or utility aid from the agencies above, crisis energy aid of up to $800, unemployment if you lost a job, and Temporary Assistance, a monthly cash benefit for families with children. We didn’t list its eligibility rules here, so ask 211 to walk you through them before you apply. Our guide to emergency cash & TANF help in Missouri covers one-time rent, utility and crisis funds plus monthly Temporary Assistance. If a disability keeps you from working, applying for disability benefits (SSI & SSDI) walks through the process and the free local help available.

### What If Home Isn’t Safe, or a Parent Isn’t Fine?
You may have only a few minutes alone with your phone. You’re listening to the next room while you read this. If you’re afraid of someone at home, call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233. The Hotline is free, confidential and open 24/7, and it offers support in over 200 languages.
If talking isn’t safe, text START to 88788 or chat with a live advocate.
Deaf and hard of hearing callers can use the Hotline’s video phone at 855-812-1001. If you feel you are in immediate danger, call 911. For local hotlines, shelters and safety, see domestic violence help in St. Louis.
A parent says “I’m fine” while the mail piles up on the table. Look at the mail. Call the Missouri Senior Resource Line, 1-800-235-5503, and enter your ZIP code when prompted to reach your local Area Agency on Aging, which connects older adults and their caregivers to local help.
If you suspect abuse or neglect of an adult, the state’s Adult Abuse & Neglect Hotline is 1-800-392-0210, open 7 days a week from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m.
Relay Missouri is 1-800-735-2966. Our guide to senior services and aging in place explains how to help someone stay independent at home.

### I Want to Help. Where Do I Start?
You’re sitting beside someone while the line rings, and neither of you says much. The coffee between you has gone cold. That counts. The best help is small and specific. Make the first call with them. Read the notice out loud so they don’t have to. Write the name of whoever picks up, plus the number, on a card. Then offer something concrete: a ride to an appointment, help gathering ID, income proof and the lease, or an hour with the kids while they fill out forms.
You don’t need special training. You need to point toward real help and stay beside the person while they reach for it. Bookmark this page and pass it on. When the worst has passed, a plain night out can matter more than another list, because sitting down to a meal says the crisis didn’t change how you see them. If you’re looking for a table, our guide to North County restaurants is a place to start.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the $500 direct cash assistance program in Missouri?
A.  The City of St. Louis paid $500 Direct Cash Assistance once, as a one-time payment for households hit by the pandemic, and the program has completed. A separate Guaranteed Basic Income pilot paid $500 a month for 18 months to 540 families, and the City Treasurer has announced its completion. Never pay a fee to unlock “free money.” Call 211 instead, where a trained specialist gives you contact and program information for the services available in your community.
### Q. Can I get $500 rental assistance in St. Louis?
A.  When we last checked, the City of St. Louis listed no current emergency assistance programs; its past programs are on hold or completed and not available. Call 211, then ask Beyond Housing (314-533-0600), Guardian Angel (314-773-9027) and Doorways (314-535-1919) what rent funds are open this month. If you appear on the eviction court docket, call HELP STL at (314) 657-1671.
### Q. How can I get money if I'm struggling?
A.  Pick up the phone and dial 211, then build help in pieces. Guardian Angel, for one, gives direct help to people at risk of eviction, foreclosure or utility shut-off. Winter crisis energy aid can pay up to $800 when you have a notice with a specific disconnect date, and Ameren Missouri’s Dollar More provides eligible households up to $600 per calendar year. Temporary Assistance is a monthly cash benefit for families with children. Never pay a fee for “free money.”
### Q. What resources can I use to get help paying rent in Missouri?
A.  Start with 211 (or 800-427-4626), then call the local rent agencies: Beyond Housing at 314-533-0600, Guardian Angel at 314-773-9027 and Doorways at 314-535-1919. Ask each what is open right now, since we couldn’t confirm current funds. If you’ve been served court papers, HELP STL at (314) 657-1671 connects City renters with free legal help, and Legal Services of Eastern Missouri takes calls at 314-534-4200.
### Q. What do I do if I can't pay my utility bill?
A.  Call the utility before the shutoff date and say you can’t pay in full. From November 1 to March 31, the Cold Weather Rule limits heat shutoffs by gas and electric utilities under the Public Service Commission if you make an initial payment and enter a payment agreement. Then ask 211 about winter crisis energy aid of up to $800. For more on the rule, call the Public Service Commission’s consumer services hotline at 1-800-392-4211.
### Q. What low-income assistance programs are available in Missouri?
A.  Start with one call to 211 (800-427-4626), then work through the groups: rent and shelter help, SNAP and WIC for food, Medicaid (MO HealthNet) for health coverage, LIHEAP for heating and cooling bills, and Temporary Assistance for families with children.

## Asking for Help Is a Strength, Not a Failure

Before anything else, hear this: needing help doesn’t mean you’ve done something wrong. Jobs disappear, rent climbs, health falters, relationships break, and hard seasons come for good people who were doing everything right. The programs on this page exist precisely because your neighbors, your city, and dozens of local nonprofits believe no one should face a rough stretch alone. Reaching out early — before a small problem becomes a crisis — is one of the smartest, bravest things a person can do. And if you’re reading this for someone else, the fact that you’re looking already tells them they matter. Whatever brought you here, you belong in this city’s circle of care — and there is no shame in taking what’s offered.

## Start Here: The Numbers to Call First

When you’re not sure where to begin, these free, confidential lines connect you to the right local program:

- **2-1-1 (or 800-427-4626)**— United Way’s 24/7 helpline for housing, food, utilities, and more across the St. Louis region. One call, many resources.
- **National Domestic Violence Hotline: 1-800-799-7233**(text START to 88788) — 24/7 and confidential. In immediate danger, call 911.
- **Missouri Senior Resource Helpline: 1-800-235-5503**— connects older adults to local aid. Report elder abuse at 1-800-392-0210.
- **St. Louis County Emergency Shelter Hotline**— for anyone facing a housing crisis or homelessness.
- **FindHelp.org**— a free national tool: enter your ZIP code for local food, housing, and health programs. See how FindHelp.org works.

Save these numbers in your phone even if you don’t need them today — the best time to know where help lives is before you’re in the middle of a crisis. And if you’re helping someone else, program them into their phone too, or write them somewhere they’ll find them. A single number, dialed at the right moment, has changed the course of many hard nights.

## Housing & Shelter

Whether you need a safe place tonight or an affordable place for the long term, the path is different for each situation — so we wrote a clear guide for each:

- **Behind on rent or facing eviction?**See emergency rent assistance in St. Louis — the hotlines and programs that pay back rent and stop evictions before you lose your home.
- **Need a safe place tonight?**Our guide to emergency homeless shelters in St. Louis shows who to call for a bed and which shelters serve families, women, men, and youth.
- **In crisis or rebuilding?**Start with how transitional housing works and helps you build stability, then the directory of local transitional-housing programs (who to call, what each offers).
- **Fleeing domestic violence?**See our guide to St. Louis women’s shelters and safety resources — free, confidential, and open to you and your children.
- **Looking for affordable long-term housing?**Learn the difference between income-based (Section 8) housing, low-income (tax-credit) housing, and how to find and afford an apartment that fits your budget.

A quick orientation: housing help runs on a spectrum. Emergency shelter is for tonight; transitional housing is a supported bridge of up to two years; and income-based, low-income, and affordable apartments are longer-term homes where rent is often tied to what you earn. Most long-term programs have waitlists, so the single best move is to apply to several at once and apply early — being on a list costs nothing and keeps your options open. Each guide above walks you through eligibility, the documents you’ll need, and exactly who to call.

## Utility Bills & Staying Safe at Home

Behind on a heating or cooling bill? Help exists, and shutoffs can be prevented:

- Heat Up St. Louis and LIHEAP energy assistance help pay past-due heating and cooling bills.
- The Missouri Cold Weather Rule can stop a winter shutoff, and Cool Down St. Louis provides free fans and AC units in summer.

One important thing to know: you don’t have to wait until the power is off. Assistance programs and the Cold Weather Rule work best when you call *before* a shutoff date, and many utilities will set up a payment plan or apply a credit even mid-crisis. If a bill is piling up, treat it like any other emergency — reach out now, and let these programs do what they were built to do.

## Legal Help

Free civil legal aid is available for older and low-income residents — for housing, benefits, guardianship, wills, and protection from abuse. Start with our guide to free legal services for seniors and where to find them. Free legal aid covers civil (non-criminal) matters — housing and eviction, benefits denials, guardianship, powers of attorney, wills, and protection from fraud or abuse — and eligibility usually depends on income. You don’t need to know the legal terms; just describe your problem, and an advocate will point you to the right help. For older adults especially, getting advice before a crisis often saves money, stress, and heartache.

## If You’re the One Helping

So much of the help in this city flows through people who simply care — family members, friends, neighbors, teachers, faith communities, volunteers, and donors. If that’s you: **bookmark this page and pass it on.** Every guide here is written to be handed to someone in need or read alongside them. Share the one that fits, make the call together, and offer the concrete things that matter most — a ride, help with paperwork, or just showing up.

You don’t need special training to make a real difference — you just need to care enough to point someone toward help and stay beside them while they reach for it. Sometimes the most valuable thing you offer isn’t money or answers; it’s hope, a listening ear, and the reminder that they’re worth the effort. That’s the whole spirit of this page: a broad net, cast wide, because this city takes care of its own.

And if you **run an organization** — a nonprofit, shelter, pantry, clinic, or ministry that offers housing, food, jobs, or support — the more visible you are, the more neighbors you reach. List your services on St Louis Near Me Directory so the people searching these pages can find your door.

**Need help right now?** Call **2-1-1** (or 800-427-4626) — it’s free, confidential, and open 24/7. For domestic violence, call 1-800-799-7233; for older adults, 1-800-235-5503.

**Helping others?** Bookmark and share this page — and if your organization offers help, list it on St Louis Near Me Directory so families can find you.

## Emergency Rent Assistance in St. Louis: How to Get Help Paying Rent
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/emergency-rent-assistance-in-st-louis-how-to-get-help-paying-rent
Falling behind on rent is one of the most stressful places a person can be — and one of the most common. A car repair, a missed shift, a medical bill, and suddenly the month comes up short. If that’s you right now, take a breath: St. Louis has real programs that pay back rent and stop evictions, and this guide walks you straight to them. And if you’re helping someone else — a family member, a friend, a tenant, a client — you’re in the right place too.
The fastest path: call 2-1-1 or the St. Louis Housing Resource Hotline at (314) 802-5444 to be matched with open rent-assistance funds near you. The main local programs are run by the Community Action Agency of St. Louis County (CAASTLC), the City and County Departments of Human Services, the Salvation Army, and the Urban League. Funding is limited and opens in cycles, so apply early, to more than one program, with your paperwork ready. Here’s exactly how.
📌 Found this helpful? Keep it — and pass it on.
Bookmark this page and share it with anyone who could use it — a friend or neighbor, or a caseworker, social worker, counselor, donor, or nonprofit walking alongside someone who’s rebuilding.
Every share puts real help in one more person’s hands. That’s exactly why we made it.
### Start Here: Get Matched to Open Funds
You don’t have to figure out which program has money right now — these lines do it for you:
2-1-1 (United Way) — free, 24/7; tell them you need rent help and your ZIP code, and they’ll route you to open programs.
St. Louis Housing Resource Hotline: (314) 802-5444 — connects city and county residents to housing and eviction-prevention resources.
St. Louis County call center: (314) 806-0910 — for county residents to check open funding portals.
### St. Louis Rent-Assistance Programs
These local organizations help pay back rent and prevent eviction. Because funding opens and closes as money runs out, call several — don’t stop at one:
Community Action Agency of St. Louis County (CAASTLC) — rent and utility assistance for county residents; call (314) 446-4438 (offices in Overland and beyond).
City of St. Louis Department of Human Services — emergency assistance for city residents facing eviction or behind on rent, covering back rent and utilities.
The Salvation Army (Midland Division) — rent and utility assistance based on income limits and Fair Market Rent; contact your local corps.
Urban League of Metropolitan St. Louis — HUD-certified housing counseling and eviction/foreclosure prevention through its Housing Empowerment program.
Beyond Housing — housing support and stabilization for the 24:1 community and beyond; (314) 533-0600.
Doorways — housing assistance for people affected by HIV/AIDS; (314) 535-1919.
Franciscan Connection — limited help (up to about $75) for ZIP codes 63111, 63116, and 63118; (314) 773-8485.
Missouri DMH Rental Assistance Program (RAP) — one-time-per-year help for eligible individuals connected to behavioral-health services.
### Rent Help by Where You Live
Which program helps you depends heavily on your address — the metro is split across two states and many jurisdictions, and funds are usually tied to residency. Start with the one that matches where you live:
City of St. Louis — City Department of Human Services emergency assistance, plus CAASTLC and the Urban League.
St. Louis County (Hazelwood, Overland, Ballwin, University City, Crestwood, and beyond) — County DHS call center (314) 806-0910 and CAASTLC (314) 446-4438.
St. Charles County (St. Charles, O’Fallon, Lake Saint Louis, Cottleville) — the Community Council of St. Charles County and Sts. Joachim & Ann Care Service (636) 441-1302 are the go-to for rent and utility help.
Jefferson and Franklin Counties — the East Missouri Action Agency (EMAA) serves rural MO residents south and west of the metro.
Metro East, Illinois (East St. Louis, Granite City, Edwardsville, Cahokia Heights) — the St. Clair County and Madison County Community Action agencies handle Illinois rent and energy assistance; call 2-1-1 for the right office.
Not sure which applies? 2-1-1 sorts it out for you in one call, no matter which side of the river you’re on.
### Don’t Forget Utility Assistance
Rent and utilities often come due together, and getting your gas and electric covered frees up cash for rent. Missouri’s LIHEAP / Energy Assistance program (applied for through your local Community Action agency) helps with heating and cooling bills, and both Ameren Missouri and Spire run their own assistance and budget-billing programs. Ask about utility help in the same call — many agencies process rent and energy assistance together.
### Help for Specific Situations
Some of the most reliable help is targeted to a situation rather than a ZIP code:
Veterans — the Supportive Services for Veteran Families (SSVF) program provides rapid rehousing and rent help; the St. Patrick Center administers SSVF locally.
Survivors of domestic violence — ALIVE (314-993-2777) and the Women’s Safe House offer emergency housing and can fast-track safety-related assistance.
Families with children — ask about Temporary Assistance (TANF) and school social workers, who often know quiet local funds.
Seniors and people with disabilities — the Aging Ahead area agency and disability service organizations can layer help on top of the programs above.
### What You’ll Need to Apply
Having your documents ready makes the difference between getting help this week and waiting weeks. Gather what you can:
Photo ID for the lease holder (and IDs or names for everyone in the household)
Your lease and a current past-due or eviction notice from your landlord
Proof of income (recent pay stubs, benefits letters) — or an explanation if you have none
Your landlord’s name, address, and a W-9 or payment details (most programs pay the landlord directly)
Missing something? Don’t let that stop you from calling — case managers help people replace documents and work around gaps every day.
### If You’re Facing Eviction, Act Now
Time matters enormously in an eviction. The moment you get a notice: don’t move out on your own (you may have more time and rights than you think), respond to any court date (missing it almost always means you lose), and get free legal help. Legal Services of Eastern Missouri (lsem.org) and the courts’ eviction-prevention resources can represent or advise you at no cost if you’re income-eligible. Pairing a rent-assistance application with legal help is the strongest way to keep your home.
### The Honest Reality — and How to Beat It
Here’s the straight talk: rent-assistance money in St. Louis is limited, and the large pandemic-era programs have mostly wound down, so funds open in cycles and run out. That doesn’t mean help is gone — it means strategy matters. Apply to several programs at once rather than waiting on one. Call 2-1-1 weekly, since new funding opens regularly. Keep talking with your landlord and get any payment agreement in writing. And treat the documents above like a go-bag — ready to send the moment a portal opens. Persistence, not luck, is what gets most families across the line.
### Need a Deposit or First Month, Not Back Rent?
Not every rent crisis is about being behind — sometimes the barrier is getting into a place. If you have housing lined up but can’t cover the security deposit or first month, ask agencies specifically about rapid rehousing and deposit assistance. CAASTLC, the St. Patrick Center, and homeless-services programs coordinated through the St. Louis Continuum of Care can sometimes cover move-in costs for people leaving shelters, doubling up with family, or fleeing unsafe situations. Say plainly what you need — “first month and deposit” is a different funding bucket than “back rent,” and naming it gets you to the right program faster.
Total tangent — ever wondered what Kings Oak is actually like?
### Know Your Rights as a Missouri Renter
Knowing what a landlord can and can’t do keeps you from being pushed out unfairly while you line up help. In Missouri, a landlord generally cannot lock you out, remove your belongings, or shut off your utilities to force you to leave — only a court and a sheriff can carry out an eviction, and only after a judge’s order. You’re entitled to proper written notice before an eviction case is even filed, and you have the right to show up to court and tell your side. If you paid a security deposit, the landlord must return it (minus lawful deductions) within the timeframe the law requires after you move out. If a landlord tries an illegal “self-help” eviction, call the police and contact Legal Services of Eastern Missouri right away — these protections exist precisely so a hard month doesn’t cost you your home overnight.
### What Happens After You Apply
Knowing the rhythm of the process takes some of the fear out of it. Here’s the typical path:
Intake. You call or apply online and answer questions about your household, income, and situation. This is where 2-1-1 or the hotline points you to an agency with open funds.
Documents. The agency requests your ID, lease, past-due notice, and your landlord’s payment info. Sending these quickly is the single biggest thing that speeds approval.
Review and landlord contact. A caseworker verifies eligibility and reaches out to your landlord, since most programs pay the landlord directly rather than paying you.
Payment. Approved funds go to the landlord, and you get confirmation. Timelines range from days to a few weeks depending on funding and volume.
Throughout, keep your phone on and respond fast — a missed callback can send limited funds to the next family in line.
### Protect Yourself While You Wait
Desperation attracts scammers, so guard against them: legitimate rent-assistance programs never charge a fee to apply, never ask for gift cards, and never guarantee approval up front. Apply only through 2-1-1, your Community Action agency, established nonprofits, or official city and county offices. Meanwhile, communicate with your landlord in writing and keep copies of everything — a documented good-faith effort to pay can matter in housing court. And if the stress is overwhelming, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline is there any hour; a housing crisis is survivable, and you are not alone in it.
Need rent help now? Call 2-1-1 or the St. Louis Housing Resource Hotline at (314) 802-5444, and reach the Community Action Agency (CAASTLC) at (314) 446-4438. Also see our guides to free food, income-based housing, and all St. Louis help resources.
If you run a program that helps families keep a roof overhead, this part is for you. If your nonprofit or ministry offers rent, housing, or financial assistance, list it on St Louis Near Me Directory so families searching for help can find you.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. How do I get help with rent in St Louis County?
A.  County residents can call the St. Louis County call center at (314) 806-0910 to check open funding, and contact the Community Action Agency of St. Louis County (CAASTLC) at (314) 446-4438 for rent and utility assistance. Calling 2-1-1 also routes you to whatever county programs currently have funds. Have your ID, lease, and past-due notice ready.
### Q. How to get immediate rent assistance?
A.  Call 2-1-1 and the St. Louis Housing Resource Hotline (314-802-5444) first — they match you to programs with open funds today. Apply to several at once (CAASTLC, the Salvation Army, the City or County Department of Human Services), and if you have an eviction court date, get free legal help from Legal Services of Eastern Missouri right away. Speed and applying broadly matter most.
### Q. Is Missouri rental assistance still available?
A.  Yes, but it looks different now. The large federal pandemic program (ERAP) has mostly ended, so today’s help comes through local agencies — CAASTLC, the Salvation Army, the Urban League, the City and County Departments of Human Services, and Missouri’s DMH Rental Assistance Program — whose funds open in cycles. Call 2-1-1 regularly, since availability changes week to week.
### Q. What is the maximum rent assistance I can receive?
A.  It varies by program, your income, and available funding — some offer one month or a set dollar amount, others cover several months of back rent up to Fair Market Rent. Smaller programs (like Franciscan Connection) may cap help around $75, while agency programs can cover more. Ask each program what it offers; applying to several can add up to what you need.
### Q. How can I help someone facing eviction?
A.  Help them call 2-1-1 and apply to several rent programs the same day, and gather their documents (ID, lease, past-due notice, proof of income). Make sure they respond to any court date and connect with free legal aid (Legal Services of Eastern Missouri). Sometimes the biggest help is sitting with them through the calls and reminding them this is survivable.

## The Ground Beef Goes Back First: Missouri Food Stamps Now Want Proof of Your Rent
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-apply-for-food-stamps-snap-in-missouri-a-st-louis-guide
You put the ground beef back first. The total on the screen at the Schnucks register still makes your stomach drop, so the coffee goes back too, and the cashier is kind about it, which somehow makes it worse. In the car you sit for a minute with the receipt in your lap before you turn the key. Maybe you tell the kids you already ate. That moment is exactly what SNAP is for. Most people still call it food stamps, and it isn’t charity to feel small about; your own paychecks helped pay for it. If you’re filling out the forms for a parent or a neighbor, this works for you, too.
Then know this before you apply: since October 1, Missouri no longer takes your word for your rent, your utilities, your child care or your bank balance. Whatever you can’t prove on paper gets left out, and your monthly benefit comes out smaller than it should. It’s Missouri’s own rule, not a federal one, and a lot of guides haven’t caught up.
The short version: apply online at mydss.mo.gov (or mydssapp.mo.gov from your phone), by phone at 855-373-4636, or on paper by mail, fax or in person. You have the right to apply the same day you need it. A short interview follows, by phone or in person, and if you miss that call you can dial 855-823-4908 to finish it. Approved benefits land on an EBT card you use like a debit card at grocery stores and many farmers markets. Rather hand your papers to a person? The Family Support Division’s resource centers at 3101 Chouteau Ave. in the city and 9900 Page Ave. in the county take them in person, and Operation Food Search in Overland and the St. Louis Area Foodbank will walk you through the application for free.
Before you hit submit, lay these four papers on the kitchen table:
Your lease, or a rent receipt with your landlord’s name and phone number. Your latest electric, gas or water bill. A receipt or a signed note from whoever watches your kids while you work. Your most recent bank statement.
Upload them at mydssupload.mo.gov. Then send this list to anyone you know who’s applying.
### Three Ways to Apply
Most people start on a phone at the kitchen table after the house goes quiet, and that works. Missouri lets you apply however fits your night:
Online (fastest) - go to mydss.mo.gov and start an application, or use mydssapp.mo.gov from your phone. Available 24/7.
By phone - call the Family Support Division Information Center at 855-373-4636 for help starting an application.
By paper - print the application from mydss.mo.gov and submit it by mail, by fax to 573-526-9400, or in person at your local FSD Resource Center.
After your application is received, the state contacts you for a required interview, which can be done by phone or in person. If you miss the call, you can call back at 855-823-4908 to complete it.
### Who Qualifies in Missouri?
Before you talk yourself out of it, look at the numbers below with last month’s pay stubs in hand. SNAP is based mainly on household size and income - generally, your gross monthly income must be at or below about 130% of the federal poverty level. On the federal chart in use since October 1, that’s $1,729 a month for one person, $2,345 for two, $2,960 for three and $3,575 for a household of four, with higher limits for larger households. The figures are adjusted each year, so don’t rule yourself out over a close call. Deductions for rent, utilities, child care, and medical costs (for seniors and people with disabilities) can bring a household that looks “over” back under the limit.
### What You’ll Need to Apply
Dig the lease out of whatever drawer it landed in when you moved in, and pull up last month’s bank statement while you’re at it. Gathering these ahead of time makes the interview quick:
A valid photo ID
Social Security numbers for household members (or proof you’ve applied)
Proof of where you live (a lease, utility bill, or mail)
Proof of income - recent pay stubs, and any benefits letters (earned and unearned)
Proof of your rent or mortgage, utility bills, any child or dependent care you pay for, and your bank balances (now required - see the next section), plus medical costs if you’re 60 or older or have a disability
Proof of citizenship or eligible immigration status
Don’t have everything? Apply anyway. You have the right to apply at any time, and a caseworker will tell you what’s still needed.
Wildly off-topic - Franz Park is one of the city’s quieter corners.
### What proof does Missouri SNAP ask for now?
Since October 1, Missouri wants paper proof of your housing costs, your utility bills, any child or dependent care you pay for, and your bank balances. It applies to new applications filed on or after October 1, renewals due on or after that date, and requests to add someone to your case. Your word used to cover most of these. Not anymore. This is Missouri’s own choice, not a new federal USDA rule.
Rent: a lease signed by your landlord, or a rent receipt with the landlord’s contact information, the amount and the date
Own your home: your latest mortgage or property tax statement
Utilities: electric, gas, water, sewer, trash or heating fuel bills
Care you pay for so you can work, look for work or go to training: the provider’s itemized receipt, a signed note from an informal caregiver with the hours and pay, or canceled checks and e-payment receipts
Bank accounts: your most recent statements
Pay your aunt rent with no lease, or a neighbor to watch the kids? A signed note from that person works if it gives their name, phone, address, the amount and how often you pay. Most of the rest is already in the kitchen drawer with the Ameren bill.
Missing a piece? FSD still processes your case, but it leaves that cost out, and that can shrink your benefit. Send the proof later and it can be added back. When FSD asks for something, you get 10 days to answer. Upload it at mydssupload.mo.gov, fax it to 573-526-9400, mail copies (never originals) to Family Support Division, PO Box 2700, Jefferson City, MO 65102, or drop it off at any FSD Resource Center. Already getting SNAP? Unless you’re adding someone, nothing is due until your next renewal.
### Need Food This Week? Ask for Expedited SNAP
If your household has very little income and few resources, you may qualify for expedited SNAP - benefits within about 7 days instead of the usual 30. Say clearly when you apply that you have an emergency need for food; it flags your case for the faster track. In the meantime, no one in St. Louis should go hungry waiting on paperwork - see our guide to free food giveaways and pantries happening now.
### What Happens Once You’re Approved
When your application is approved, Missouri issues an EBT (Electronic Benefits Transfer) card - it works like a debit card, loaded automatically each month on a set date based on your case number. You can use it at grocery stores, most Schnucks and Dierbergs and Aldi locations, corner stores, and many area farmers markets (some even double your dollars on fresh produce through programs like Double Up Food Bucks). Benefits cover food staples - bread, milk, produce, meat, seeds and plants that grow food - but not hot prepared meals, alcohol, or non-food items.
A few things keep your benefits flowing smoothly: report major changes (income, address, household size) to the Family Support Division, and complete your recertification when the renewal notice arrives, usually every 6 to 12 months. Set a phone reminder for that date - missing a recert is the most common reason benefits lapse for families who still qualify.
### How Much Will I Get?
Your benefit depends on household size, income, and expenses, but it helps to know the ceiling. The maximum monthly SNAP allotment since October 1 is $306 for one person, $562 for two, $808 for three and $1,023 for a household of four, rising with each additional person and adjusted each year. Households with very low or no income tend to receive close to the maximum; those with some income receive less, because SNAP is designed to fill the gap between what you can afford to spend on food and what a healthy diet costs. Even a “small” monthly benefit adds up to real groceries over a year - and it frees up cash for rent, utilities, and everything else.
### Stretch Your SNAP Dollars in St. Louis
Once your benefits arrive, a few local moves make them go further. Many St. Louis-area farmers markets - including Tower Grove, Schlafly, and University City - participate in Double Up Food Bucks, which matches your SNAP spending on fresh fruits and vegetables dollar for dollar, effectively doubling your produce budget. Some grocery stores offer senior or student discount days you can stack with SNAP. You can also use benefits to buy seeds and food-producing plants, turning a few dollars into a season of homegrown vegetables. And if you’re 60 or older or have a disability, ask about the Restaurant Meals Program and home-delivery grocery options that accept EBT online. Small habits like these can add a week or more of groceries to every month’s benefit - real money back in a tight budget.
### SNAP for Specific Situations
The program flexes to fit real lives:
Seniors (60+) and people with disabilities - often have a simpler application and higher deductions for medical and shelter costs. The work rule now reaches able-bodied adults through age 64, so a healthy 62-year-old without kids at home may be asked for proof of hours. Over 64, or unable to work for a health reason? You’re exempt.
Working families - you can work and still qualify; earned income gets a 20% deduction, so a paycheck doesn’t automatically disqualify you.
College students - may be eligible if they meet an exemption, such as working 20+ hours a week, caring for a young child, or being in a work-study program.
Adults without dependents - if you can work, Missouri may ask for proof of 80 hours a month of work, training or the free SkillUP program. Since November 1 that rule covers ages 18 to 64, and a parent is exempt only with a child under 14 in the home. You’re still exempt if you already work 30 hours a week, are pregnant, are in treatment, go to school 20 hours a week, or can’t work for a physical or mental health reason. Send proof the same ways as any SNAP document.
People experiencing homelessness - can still apply using a shelter address or the address of someone who receives your mail; you don’t need a permanent home to get SNAP.
### Avoid the Three Things That Stall Applications
Most delays come down to fixable slip-ups. First, a missed interview - keep your phone on around your application date and call back at 855-823-4908 if you miss it. Second, missing documents - upload whatever proof you have at mydssupload.mo.gov, and answer any FSD request inside its 10 days. Third, an out-of-date address or phone number - the state can’t approve a case it can’t reach. Stay reachable and responsive, and most Missouri applications move from submitted to approved within 30 days - or 7 with an expedited emergency need.

### Myths That Keep People From Applying
A lot of families who qualify never apply because of things they’ve heard that simply aren’t true. Let’s clear a few up. “It’ll hurt my credit” - it won’t; SNAP is not a loan and never touches your credit report. “I have a job, so I can’t qualify” - plenty of working households receive SNAP, since the program is designed to supplement low and moderate wages. “I own a car or a home, so I’m out” - Missouri doesn’t count your home, and a vehicle you need for work or daily life generally doesn’t disqualify you. “I’m taking food from someone who needs it more” - SNAP is a federal entitlement, not a fixed local pot; your approval doesn’t reduce anyone else’s benefits. If you’re unsure, the honest answer is almost always the same: apply and let them decide. The worst outcome is a “no” that costs you twenty minutes.
### While You’re At It, Ask About These Too
One application can open several doors. When you apply for SNAP, ask the same office about WIC (for pregnant women and young children), Temporary Assistance (TANF), free and reduced school meals, and MO HealthNet (Medicaid) for health coverage. If rent is also tight, our guide to emergency rent assistance covers programs that pay back rent. It’s all part of the same safety net - and you’re allowed to use it.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the income limit to get food stamps in Missouri?
A.  Most households need gross monthly income at or below 130% of the federal poverty level. On the federal chart in use since October 1, that’s $1,729 for one person, $2,345 for two, $2,960 for three and $3,575 for four, with more for larger households. The limits are adjusted each year, and deductions for rent, utilities and child care can still help you qualify, so apply even if you’re close.
### Q. What disqualifies you from getting food stamps in Missouri?
A.  Having income or resources above the limits is the main disqualifier. Certain drug-related felony convictions after August 22, 1996, being a fleeing felon in violation of probation or parole, or not meeting citizenship/immigration and work requirements can also affect eligibility. Rules have exceptions, so apply and let a caseworker review your specific situation rather than assuming you don’t qualify.
### Q. What supporting documents do I need for food stamps in Missouri?
A.  Bring a valid ID, Social Security numbers for household members, proof of where you live, proof of earned and unearned income, and proof of citizenship or immigration status. Since October 1, Missouri also requires proof of rent or mortgage, utility bills, child or dependent care you pay, and bank balances. Missing something? Apply anyway. A cost you can’t prove is left out until you send the paper.
### Q. What are the new SNAP rules in Missouri?
A.  One big change started October 1. New applications, renewals due on or after that date and requests to add someone now need proof of housing costs, utility bills, dependent care costs and bank balances. Without it, FSD still processes your case but leaves the cost out, which can lower your benefit. People already on SNAP send nothing until their next renewal. This one is Missouri’s own choice, not a federal rule.
### Q. How long does it take to get approved for SNAP in Missouri?
A.  Most people hear back within 30 days. If your household has very little income and few resources, ask for expedited SNAP, which can put benefits on your card in seven days or less. Two things slow it down: a missed interview call (call back at 855-823-4908) and proof that shows up late. When FSD asks for a document, you have 10 days to answer.
### Q. What is the maximum food stamp amount?
A.  Since October 1, the most a household can get each month in Missouri and the other contiguous states is $306 for one person, $562 for two, $808 for three and $1,023 for four, adjusted each year. Households with little or no income get close to the maximum. Everyone else gets less, because SNAP expects about 30% of your net income to go toward food.
### Q. What income is not counted for SNAP?
A.  Some money doesn’t count as income for SNAP - generally one-time payments like lump-sum insurance settlements, refunds of rental security deposits, and one-time stipends. Recurring payments such as monthly public-assistance grants are counted. Because the rules are detailed, let your caseworker sort out what counts; you may qualify even if a rough income total looks too high.
### Q. How can I help someone apply for food stamps?
A.  Help them start an application at mydss.mo.gov or call 855-373-4636, and gather their ID, proof of income, and proof of residence for the interview. You can be an authorized representative and apply on their behalf if needed. Local nonprofits like Operation Food Search and the St. Louis Area Foodbank offer free help too - sometimes the biggest gift is just getting them started.

## Three Ways to Apply

Missouri lets you apply however works best for you:

- **Online (fastest)**— go to- **mydss.mo.gov**and start an application, or use- **mydssapp.mo.gov**from your phone. Available 24/7.
- **By phone**— call the Family Support Division Information Center at- **855-373-4636**for help starting an application.
- **By paper**— print the application from mydss.mo.gov and submit it by mail, by fax to- **573-526-9400**, or in person at your local FSD Resource Center.

After your application is received, the state contacts you for a required **interview**, which can be done by phone or in person. If you miss the call, you can call back at **855-823-4908** to complete it.

## Who Qualifies in Missouri?

SNAP is based mainly on household size and income — generally, your gross monthly income must be at or below about **130% of the federal poverty level**. As a rough guide for the current year, that’s roughly $1,632/month for one person, $2,215 for two, $2,798 for three, and $3,380 for a household of four, with higher limits for larger households. These numbers change yearly, so check **mydss.mo.gov** for the current figures — and don’t rule yourself out over a close call. Deductions for rent, utilities, child care, and medical costs (for seniors and people with disabilities) can bring a household that looks “over” back under the limit.

## What You’ll Need to Apply

Gathering these ahead of time makes the interview quick:

- A valid photo ID
- Social Security numbers for household members (or proof you’ve applied)
- Proof of where you live (a lease, utility bill, or mail)
- Proof of income — recent pay stubs, and any benefits letters (earned and unearned)
- Proof of certain expenses (rent, utilities, child care, medical) that can raise your benefit
- Proof of citizenship or eligible immigration status

Don’t have everything? Apply anyway. You have the right to apply at any time, and a caseworker will tell you what’s still needed.

## Need Food This Week? Ask for Expedited SNAP

If your household has very little income and few resources, you may qualify for **expedited SNAP** — benefits within about **7 days** instead of the usual 30. Say clearly when you apply that you have an emergency need for food; it flags your case for the faster track. In the meantime, no one in St. Louis should go hungry waiting on paperwork — see our guide to free food giveaways and pantries happening now.

## What Happens Once You’re Approved

When your application is approved, Missouri issues an **EBT (Electronic Benefits Transfer) card** — it works like a debit card, loaded automatically each month on a set date based on your case number. You can use it at grocery stores, most Schnucks and Dierbergs and Aldi locations, corner stores, and many area farmers markets (some even double your dollars on fresh produce through programs like Double Up Food Bucks). Benefits cover food staples — bread, milk, produce, meat, seeds and plants that grow food — but not hot prepared meals, alcohol, or non-food items.

A few things keep your benefits flowing smoothly: report major changes (income, address, household size) to the Family Support Division, and complete your **recertification** when the renewal notice arrives, usually every 6 to 12 months. Set a phone reminder for that date — missing a recert is the most common reason benefits lapse for families who still qualify.

## How Much Will I Get?

Your benefit depends on household size, income, and expenses, but it helps to know the ceiling. The **maximum monthly SNAP allotment** for the current year is roughly **$292 for one person, $536 for two, $768 for three, and $975 for a household of four**, rising with each additional person. Households with very low or no income tend to receive close to the maximum; those with some income receive less, because SNAP is designed to fill the gap between what you can afford to spend on food and what a healthy diet costs. Even a “small” monthly benefit adds up to real groceries over a year — and it frees up cash for rent, utilities, and everything else.

## SNAP for Specific Situations

The program flexes to fit real lives:

- **Seniors (60+) and people with disabilities**— often have a simpler application, higher deduction allowances for medical and shelter costs, and no strict work requirement.
- **Working families**— you can work and still qualify; earned income gets a 20% deduction, so a paycheck doesn’t automatically disqualify you.
- **College students**— may be eligible if they meet an exemption, such as working 20+ hours a week, caring for a young child, or being in a work-study program.
- **Adults without dependents**— may face a time limit tied to work or training requirements; ask about exemptions, which are common.
- **People experiencing homelessness**— can still apply using a shelter address or the address of someone who receives your mail; you don’t need a permanent home to get SNAP.

## How to Apply for Medicaid (MO HealthNet) in Missouri: A St. Louis Guide
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-apply-for-medicaid-mo-healthnet-in-missouri-a-st-louis-guide
Putting off a doctor’s visit because you’re uninsured is a gamble too many St. Louis families are forced to make — in Dogtown, in Bridgeton, out in St. Charles, across the river in Granite City. A nagging cough, a lump you keep meaning to check, a kid’s ear infection at 2 a.m. Here’s the good news a lot of people missed: since Missouri expanded Medicaid, hundreds of thousands more adults now qualify for free or low-cost health coverage through MO HealthNet — and you might be one of them without realizing it. This guide shows you how to apply, and if you’re helping a parent, a patient, or a friend get covered, it’s written for you too.
For years, the hardest part wasn’t the paperwork — it was being told you earned a little too much to qualify but nowhere near enough to buy insurance on your own. That gap trapped a lot of hardworking people. Expansion closed it. If you looked into Medicaid before and got turned away, the rules that turned you down may not apply anymore. It is genuinely worth a fresh look.
To apply for MO HealthNet (Missouri Medicaid), go online to mydss.mo.gov/healthcare/apply, call the Family Support Division at (855) 373-9994, apply in person at a local Family Support Division Resource Center, or mail a paper application to the Family Support Division, P.O. Box 2700, Jefferson City, MO 65102. You’ll provide your Social Security number and proof of identity, residency, and household income. Eligibility is usually decided within about 45 days — and coverage can be backdated to cover recent medical bills.

Every share puts real help in one more person’s hands. That’s exactly why we made it.
### Four Ways to Apply
Online (fastest) — apply at mydss.mo.gov/healthcare/apply and upload your documents through the myDSS Document Uploader. Available any time.
By phone — call the Family Support Division at 855-373-9994 to apply or ask questions.
In person — visit your local Family Support Division Resource Center for hands-on help.
By mail — download and print the single Missouri application and mail it to the Family Support Division, P.O. Box 2700, Jefferson City, MO 65102.
Missouri now uses one application form for all Medicaid programs, so you don’t have to figure out which category you fit — the state sorts that out from your answers.
### Who Qualifies Now — Medicaid Expansion Changed the Rules
This is the part people miss. Thanks to Medicaid expansion, adults ages 19–64 can qualify based on income alone — you no longer have to be pregnant, disabled, or a parent to get covered. The cutoff is roughly 138% of the federal poverty level: about $1,730 a month for one person or roughly $3,588 a month for a family of four (higher for larger households). Children and pregnant women qualify at higher income levels still. These figures shift yearly, so if you’re anywhere close, apply — MO HealthNet checks the current numbers for you at mydss.mo.gov.
### What You’ll Need to Apply
Social Security numbers for those applying
Proof of identity (a driver’s license or state ID)
Proof of Missouri residency (a lease, utility bill, or mail)
Proof of household income (recent pay stubs, benefit letters, or a statement if you have none)
If you’re 65 or older, blind, or disabled — the Aged, Blind, and Disabled (ABD) Supplement form
Immigration or citizenship documentation, if applicable
Applying online lets you send these straight through the myDSS Document Uploader, which is the quickest way to avoid back-and-forth.
### What MO HealthNet Covers
Coverage is comprehensive — not a stripped-down plan. MO HealthNet includes doctor visits, hospital and emergency care, prescriptions, lab and X-ray, maternity and newborn care, mental health and substance-use treatment, and preventive care like checkups and immunizations. Most members pick a managed-care health plan — in the St. Louis area that includes Home State Health, Healthy Blue, and UnitedHealthcare Community Plan — which comes with a member card, a network of local doctors, and a nurse line. Kids get extra benefits through MO HealthNet for Kids (Missouri’s CHIP), including dental and vision.
### Special Paths to Coverage
Beyond the standard adult pathway, Missouri has targeted programs worth asking about:
Pregnant women — MO HealthNet for Pregnant Women and Show-Me Healthy Babies cover prenatal care, delivery, and postpartum at higher income limits; coverage can start quickly so care isn’t delayed.
Children — MO HealthNet for Kids (Missouri’s CHIP) covers children in families that earn too much for regular Medicaid but can’t afford private insurance, and includes dental and vision.
Adults 65+, blind, or disabled — the Aged, Blind, and Disabled programs cover long-term care, in-home services, and help with Medicare costs.
Working people with disabilities — the Ticket to Work Health Assurance program lets you earn more and keep coverage.
Young adults who aged out of foster care — may qualify for coverage up to age 26 regardless of income.
### Need Care Before You’re Approved?
Don’t skip a real emergency waiting on paperwork. By federal law, hospital emergency rooms must screen and stabilize anyone with an emergency, insured or not. If you deliver a baby or face a medical crisis while your application is pending, tell the hospital — MO HealthNet coverage can often be backdated up to three months before your application date, wiping out bills you thought you’d be stuck with. Community health centers also treat patients on a sliding fee scale, so a lack of coverage today never has to mean no care today.
Changing the subject completely: somebody in Granite City is making your next favorite meal.
### What Does It Cost?
For most people, MO HealthNet is free or nearly free — there’s no monthly premium for the majority of members, and copays for covered services are small or zero. Some programs (like MO HealthNet for Kids at higher income tiers, or Ticket to Work) may involve a modest monthly premium on a sliding scale, but nothing like private insurance. That’s the whole point of the program: cost should never be the reason you skip the care you need. Compared with a marketplace plan’s premiums and deductibles, Medicaid is by far the most affordable coverage available to those who qualify — which is exactly why it’s worth ten minutes to find out if you do.
### What If You Don’t Qualify?
Even if your income is a little too high for MO HealthNet, you’re not out of options — and you should never assume “no coverage” is the end of the road. Most people who don’t qualify for Medicaid do qualify for subsidized private insurance through the Health Insurance Marketplace at HealthCare.gov, where tax credits can bring premiums down to a few dollars a month; a free Cover Missouri navigator can walk you through it. Your children may still qualify for MO HealthNet for Kids even when you don’t. And regardless of insurance, St. Louis community health centers like Affinia Healthcare, CareSTL Health, and Family Care Health Centers treat everyone on a sliding fee scale based on income — so a checkup, a prescription, or a dental visit stays affordable while you sort coverage out. Ask; the door is rarely fully closed.
### Get Free Help Enrolling in St. Louis
If the forms feel overwhelming, trained local navigators will walk you through it for free — no cost, no pressure:
Community health centers like Affinia Healthcare, CareSTL Health, Family Care Health Centers, and People’s Health Centers have enrollment specialists on site and will see you whether or not you’re insured yet.
Cover Missouri navigators offer free, unbiased enrollment help by phone and in person.
Your hospital’s financial counselor — if you have unpaid bills, ask; they can often help you apply and backdate coverage.
### Already Applied? What Happens Next
After you submit, the Family Support Division reviews your case and requests anything missing — respond fast to keep it moving. A decision usually comes within about 45 days (longer for disability-based cases that need medical review). If approved, you’ll get a MO HealthNet ID and choose or be assigned a managed-care plan. Keep your address and phone current, and watch for your annual renewal notice — returning that form on time is the single most important thing you can do to avoid a coverage gap. If you’re ever denied, you have the right to appeal, and a community health center or legal aid can help.
### Myths That Stop People From Applying
Plenty of eligible Missourians never apply because of outdated fears. A few worth retiring: “I make too much money” — expansion raised the limit dramatically, and many full-time workers now qualify. “I own a car and a home, so I’m out” — for expansion adults, eligibility is based on income, not assets, and your home and vehicle don’t count. “Applying will hurt my immigration case” — using Medicaid you’re entitled to does not, on its own, make you a “public charge,” and emergency Medicaid is available regardless of status. “It’s charity I shouldn’t take” — MO HealthNet is coverage your taxes already fund, built so a health scare doesn’t become a financial one. When in doubt, apply and let the state decide.
### Cover the Rest of the Basics Too
Health coverage is one piece of the safety net. While you’re getting set up, it’s worth checking whether you also qualify for SNAP food benefits — many households qualify for both — and if rent is tight, our guide to emergency rent assistance points you to programs that pay back rent. Applying for one often makes the others easier, since much of the same information carries over.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the income limit to receive Medicaid in Missouri?
A.  For adults under Medicaid expansion, the limit is about 138% of the federal poverty level — roughly $1,730 a month for one person or about $3,588 for a family of four, with more for larger households. Children and pregnant women qualify at higher income levels. Limits change yearly and deductions apply, so apply at mydss.mo.gov even if you’re close — the state checks the current figures for you.
### Q. How long does it take to get approved for Missouri Medicaid?
A.  Most MO HealthNet applications are decided within about 45 days. Cases based on disability can take longer because they require a medical review. Applying online and submitting your documents through the myDSS Document Uploader is the fastest route, and responding quickly to any request for more information keeps your case from stalling. Approved coverage can often be backdated to help with recent bills.
### Q. What are the requirements for Medicaid in Missouri 2026?
A.  You generally must be a Missouri resident, a U.S. citizen or eligible immigrant, and have household income within the program limits — about 138% of the poverty level for expansion adults, higher for kids and pregnant women. You’ll verify identity, residency, income, and Social Security numbers. Adults 65+, blind, or disabled also complete an ABD supplement. Missouri uses one application form for all these programs.
### Q. What will disqualify you for Medicaid?
A.  Income or countable assets above the program limits are the main reasons for denial, along with not being a Missouri resident or lacking eligible citizenship/immigration status. For aged, blind, and disabled programs, resource limits also apply. Missed documents or interviews can lead to a denial that’s easily fixed by reapplying. If you’re denied, you can appeal — a community health center or legal aid can help.
### Q. How can I help someone apply for MO HealthNet?
A.  Help them apply online at mydss.mo.gov/healthcare/apply or call 855-373-9994, and gather their ID, proof of income, and residency. You can assist as an authorized helper, and community health centers like Affinia Healthcare and CareSTL Health offer free enrollment help. For someone who is homebound, elderly, or ill, sitting with them through the online application is often the most valuable help of all.
