### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it worth paying for an interior designer?
A.  It depends on what is wrong. If your rooms function well and simply look unresolved, a few paid hours or a decorator engagement is usually enough and it is worth it. If you are moving walls, redoing a kitchen, or building, a designer earns the fee by preventing expensive mistakes—the wrong layout, the appliance that does not fit, the wall that turns out to be carrying the floor above. In a century St. Louis house, that risk-catching function is the strongest argument for hiring one.
### Q. Is it cheaper to use an interior designer?
A.  On furnishings, sometimes yes. Designers buy at trade pricing that commonly runs 20 to 60 percent below retail, and even after a 20 to 25 percent markup you can end up paying less than showroom price for the same piece. On the total project, usually no—you are adding a professional fee. The honest framing is that a designer rarely makes the project cheaper, but frequently makes it better per dollar and prevents the costly reversal.
### Q. What are red flags when hiring a designer?
A.  A designer who will not disclose the furniture markup percentage. A quote with no written scope, deliverables, or revision count. A large retainer with no milestone schedule attached. Refusal to show trade cost alongside billed cost under a cost-plus arrangement. Charging a percentage of project cost and a furniture markup on the same items without disclosing both. Vagueness about whether your permitted work needs an architect or engineer. And, in an older house, a designer who never asks about plaster, radiators, or the age of the electrical panel.
### Q. What is the 70/30 rule in interior design?
A.  It is a styling guideline, not a budget rule, and the two get mixed up constantly. The idea is that roughly 70 percent of a room commits to one dominant style, palette, or material, and the remaining 30 percent provides contrast—a secondary color, a different era of furniture, an unexpected texture. It exists to stop rooms from reading either monotonous or chaotic. It has nothing to do with what a designer charges, and no designer will price a job off it.
### Q. Do I need a registered interior designer in Missouri?
A.  Not for decorating or most furnishing work. Registration matters when drawings need to be signed and sealed for a permit. Under Senate Bill 1233, signed July 13, 2026, registered Missouri interior designers can stamp their own drawings within their scope of practice rather than routing everything through an outside architect or engineer. Registration requires passing the full NCIDQ exam plus roughly six years of combined education and experience. Structural changes still require a structural professional, so ask early which category your project falls into.
### Q. How much should I pay for an interior designer?
A.  Hourly runs roughly $100 to $500, with junior designers starting near $75. Flat fees per room land between $1,000 and $12,000, though most firms cluster at $1,500 to $4,900. Design-only work, with no furnishing procurement attached, typically runs $450 to $1,500 per room. Per square foot, most homeowners pay $7 to $12.
### Q. What is a normal budget for interior design?
A.  For one room, most people land between $1,500 and $4,900 in designer fees, with design-only work at $450 to $1,500 per room. Per square foot, $7 to $12 is the common band. Furnishings sit on top of all of that and are usually the larger number by a wide margin.
### Q. What is the 3-5-7 rule in interior design?
A.  Group objects in odd numbers — threes, fives and sevens — because the eye reads odd groupings as intentional and even ones as symmetrical and static. It applies to vases on a mantel, cushions on a sofa, and art in a gallery wall. It is a styling habit, not something you pay a designer to apply.

## How Much Does Pest Control Cost in St. Louis? (2026 Numbers)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-much-does-pest-control-cost-in-st-louis
Imagine it’s a warm Tuesday in April in Affton. You come down for coffee and there is a small drift of what look like insect wings on the sill above the kitchen sink, and a few more stuck in the window track. You sweep them up, think about it all morning, and call somebody. The company sends a technician out that Thursday, he pulls back the mulch along the south foundation wall, finds a mud tube the width of a pencil, and hands you a number just under two thousand dollars.
That same week a friend in Florissant has ants marching along the kitchen baseboard. Her quote is $180 for a one-time treatment, or $49 a month if she signs up for a plan — except the plan also carries a first-visit charge she does not notice until the invoice arrives. And across the metro in Webster Groves, a couple under contract on a 1912 brick two-story gets a wood-destroying insect report back with mud tubes noted on the foundation, and by closing there is a termite bond in the paperwork with an annual renewal nobody sat down and explained to them.
Three houses, three completely different bills, and not one of those companies did anything wrong. Pest control around St. Louis gets priced on at least five different meters — per visit, per month, per linear foot of foundation, per room and per square foot — and the number you are handed depends far more on which pest you have and which meter is running than on which company you called. Here is what each of those jobs actually costs in this metro, and what makes one quote double another on what looks like the same house.
### The short answer
How much does pest control typically cost in St. Louis? For routine general pest work — ants, spiders, roaches, the ordinary stuff — local pricing runs roughly $85 to $189 per visit with an average near $133, which sits a little under the national one-time range of $100 to $300 and its roughly $171 average. A heavy or unusual infestation can push a single visit to $600.
Recurring service is a different animal. Monthly plans commonly run $40 to $70 a month, quarterly service lands around $100 to $175 per quarter nationally and $100 to $275 per visit in this market, and a full year of quarterly coverage typically totals $400 to $800.
Then there are the specialty jobs, which are the ones that actually wreck a budget. Termite treatment runs $500 to $1,500 for a liquid barrier on a typical house and $1,800 to $3,500 for a bait system on a 2,000-square-foot home. Bed bugs run $1,000 to $2,500 chemically or $2,000 to $4,000 for whole-home heat. A season of mosquito control is $300 to $700. Real rodent exclusion — not just trapping — is $600 to $1,400.
Those are wide bands on purpose. The rest of this is about which end of each one your house is on.
### What a one-time treatment actually buys
A one-time visit is an inspection, a treatment of the interior and the exterior perimeter, and usually a short callback window — often thirty days — during which the company will come back once if the problem is still there. That is the whole product. It is the right purchase when you have a defined, contained problem: one ant trail, wasps under a soffit, a single mouse.
What it is not is a fix for anything that lives in the structure. Roach populations, established rodent colonies, carpenter ants nesting in a damp joist, and anything termite-related do not resolve in one visit, and a company that sells you a single spray for those is selling you a delay.
Typical one-time numbers by pest, nationally:
General ants, spiders and seasonal invaders: about $100 to $300, with roughly $170 in the middle
Carpenter ants: $150 to $500, averaging near $300, and past $800 when satellite colonies mean drilling into wall voids
Cockroaches: $100 to $400 with an average around $160, rising to $300 to $700 per visit on a heavy infestation
Mice: about $200 to $600 for inspection, trapping and basic rodent-proofing
Rats: $150 to $600 using traps or bait, before any exclusion or cleanup work
One quiet detail worth knowing before you compare bids: some companies price a one-time visit high on purpose, because the visit is really a lead for the plan. If the one-time number and the plan’s first-year total are close, you are being steered, and that is fine as long as you can see it happening.
Random, but: here’s what Mark Twain / I-70 Industrial is actually like.
### Plans, and the initial fee nobody quotes over the phone
Most recurring pest control in this metro is sold three ways. Monthly plans run about $40 to $70 a month. Bimonthly and quarterly plans are billed per visit, generally $100 to $275 locally, with the exterior treated every time and the interior only when you ask. Annual agreements bundle four visits and land at $400 to $800 for the year.
The line that surprises people is the initial or setup visit. That first treatment is longer, uses more product and often includes a full perimeter granule application and a web sweep, and it is priced separately — commonly $150 to $190 in the St. Louis market, and $150 to $300 more broadly. Some companies waive it if you sign an annual agreement. Some discount it if you commit to monthly. Nearly all of them leave it out of the number they say on the phone.
So when you compare two plans, do not compare the monthly figures. Compare twelve months plus the setup fee, minus any waiver, and compare what each visit includes. A $39 plan with a $299 start and exterior-only service costs more in year one than a $55 plan with no start fee and interior treatment on request.
Is $50 a month good for pest control? For an average St. Louis home on a real recurring program — exterior perimeter every visit, interior on request, unlimited callbacks between scheduled visits, and rodent stations included — yes, that is a fair market price and slightly better than the national midpoint. For a small condo or a townhouse it is a bit rich. And if $50 buys exterior spray only, with callbacks billed as extra visits, it is not a bargain at all, it is a subscription to a spray schedule.
The callback policy is where the actual value hides. A plan that includes unlimited return visits between scheduled services is worth noticeably more than one that does not, because that is the clause you use in July when the ants come back three weeks after a treatment.
### Termites: the line item St. Louis cannot skip
This region is genuine termite country, and that is not marketing. According to University of Missouri Extension, Missouri has four native termite species, all subterranean, and the most common house-infesting termite in the country — the eastern subterranean termite, Reticulitermes flavipes — is the one at work here. Extension notes that swarming flights happen in Missouri during the spring months, usually on a warm sunny day following rain, which is exactly the pile of wings on the Affton windowsill.
It matters more here than in much of the country because of what we build on and what we build with. Subterranean termites invade from the soil around and beneath the structure, and MU Extension points out that consistently moist soil along a foundation wall makes good termite habitat. Heavy clay that holds water against a foundation, century-old brick homes with rubble or stone foundations, unvented crawl spaces, wood siding or porch posts sitting too close to grade, and mulch piled against the house are the local recipe. The same moisture problem that fills a basement is the one that feeds a termite colony, which is why our guide to basement waterproofing in St. Louis and this article keep pointing at the same downspouts.
### Termite inspection and the WDI report
A standalone termite inspection runs $0 to about $277, with an average near $130. Many companies inspect free when they expect to bid the treatment, and that is legitimate as long as you understand the incentive.
The real estate version is a different document. A wood-destroying insect report for a home sale runs $200 to $500, though many purchase inspections land in the $0 to $150 range, and the NPMA-33 form that VA and FHA lenders require adds roughly $50 to $100. Worth knowing if you are buying with a VA loan: the borrower is not permitted to pay for that report — it has to come from the seller, the lender, the agent, the closing agent or another third party.
### Termite treatment: liquid barrier versus bait
There are two mainstream approaches, and they are priced completely differently.
Liquid soil barrier. Priced per linear foot of foundation perimeter at roughly $3 to $20 a foot, with $6 to $10 typical. Most homes total $500 to $1,500, and a 2,000-square-foot house with an active subterranean infestation generally runs $700 to $2,200. It works fast and leaves residual protection in the soil.
Bait and monitoring systems. Stations are installed around the perimeter, usually fifteen to twenty-five of them. Installation runs $800 to $2,000 with $300 to $600 a year in monitoring and maintenance, and a 2,000-square-foot home commonly totals $1,800 to $3,500. Slower to work, less invasive, more expensive over time, and dependent on somebody actually showing up to service the stations.
The national average for termite treatment overall sits around $750 to $850, but averages are close to useless here, because a slab ranch in Maryland Heights and a Webster Groves foursquare with a stone foundation and a crawl space are not the same job.
One thing MU Extension is blunt about and worth repeating: there are no do-it-yourself termite control measures that effectively achieve the desired results. Whatever you spend, spend it on somebody licensed.
### Termite bonds: what you are actually buying
A termite bond is a service contract, not insurance. Typically it covers an initial treatment, scheduled annual inspections, and free re-treatment if termites come back during the term. Expect $500 to $2,000 up front, with initial bonds commonly landing at $700 to $1,000 when they include that first full treatment, then $200 to $400 a year to renew — and sometimes as little as $100 to $350 depending on the tier.
The distinction that matters is retreat-only versus repair coverage. A retreat-only bond means they will treat again for free; you pay for the damage. A repair bond adds structural repair coverage up to a stated limit. The difference in annual cost between the two is usually $200 to $500, and given that termite damage repairs average $3,000 to $8,000 and can exceed $25,000 in severe structural cases, that is often the cheapest gap you will ever close on an older St. Louis house.
Read the conditions before you assume you are covered. Bonds generally require the annual inspection to actually happen, and they can be voided by things like inaccessible crawl spaces, added structures, or moisture conditions you were told to fix and did not.
### Bed bugs: heat versus chemical, and why the cheap number is not the total
Bed bug work is priced per room or per square foot, and it is the single most expensive routine pest job most households will ever face.
Chemical treatment: roughly $200 to $400 per room, or $1,000 to $2,500 for a typical whole home
Heat treatment: roughly $400 to $900 per room, or $2,000 to $4,000 whole home, generally $2.00 to $6.50 per square foot, with a common $1,000 minimum
Chemical looks cheaper on the quote and frequently is not, because it takes two to three visits over four to six weeks, and you are living with bed bugs for that entire stretch. Heat is usually one day. Run the math on visits rather than on the per-visit price, and ask whether follow-up treatments are included in the quoted figure or billed separately — that single question changes the real total more than the choice of method does.
### Mosquitoes: what a program costs, and what the public agencies already do
Mosquito pressure is real here, especially in the bottoms and on properties near the Missouri, the Mississippi and the Meramec, and anywhere with shade, standing water and dense plantings.
A single barrier spray runs $75 to $150 per visit for an average suburban lot, with some providers quoting $125 to $165. A full-season program — usually five to eight treatments every three to four weeks from late spring into early fall — runs $300 to $700, which brings the effective per-visit cost down to roughly $60 to $90. Across all property types and program lengths the average lands near $350, on a full range of $50 to $2,500.
Before you buy a program, know what already exists. St. Louis County runs a Vector-Borne Disease Prevention program that conducts nighttime ultra-low-volume truck-mounted adulticide applications in unincorporated St. Louis County and in contracted municipalities, targeting areas where arboviral disease is detected or where medically significant mosquito species are abundant. Residents can report an overabundance of mosquitoes or a suspected breeding site at 314-615-0680. The City of St. Louis runs its own Vector Control program covering mosquitoes and rats, reachable at 314-657-1500.
Public spraying is a population-level tool and it is not a substitute for treating your own yard, but it does mean the honest first move is a phone call about the standing water two doors down, before you sign a seven-treatment agreement.
### Rodents: why exclusion costs more than trapping, and why it is worth it
Every fall, when nights drop into the forties, mice come inside. In this housing stock they have plenty of doors: gaps around utility penetrations, unsealed rim joists, garage door sweeps that no longer touch the slab, crumbling mortar joints on century brick, and the space behind a porch that nobody has looked at in thirty years.
Straight extermination — trapping and bait, with a couple of return visits — runs $200 to $600 for most homes. That solves the mice that are in the house today. It does not touch the reason they got in.
Exclusion is the other product. A full rodent-eviction plan with entry points sealed, one-way exclusion doors on active openings, repairs and a month or more of follow-up visits runs $600 to $1,400. Individual exclusion doors run $200 to $400 each. If droppings have accumulated in an attic or crawl space, cleanup and disinfection is separate again at $600 to $1,000, or $200 to $260 an hour.
Some of the sealing work is carpentry rather than pest control, and if your company does not do it, a qualified handyman runs roughly $67 to $190 an hour. Paying twice for trapping every autumn is the expensive way to own the problem.
### What actually moves your number in this metro
Square footage and stories. Almost every plan is tiered by home size, and a three-story with a walkout costs more to treat than a ranch of the same square footage.
Foundation type. Stone, rubble and unvented crawl spaces are slower and riskier to treat than a poured slab, and they show up directly in a termite bid’s linear-foot count.
Moisture. Clay soil, flat lots, short downspout extensions and a sump that runs constantly all raise both the risk and the price.
Age and materials. Century brick with soft mortar joints, original wood windows and balloon framing give insects and rodents more paths than 1990s construction does.
Which pest. The single largest factor. General pest, termites and bed bugs are three different businesses that happen to share a truck.
Access. Finished basements, storage stacked against foundation walls, and crawl spaces you cannot get into add labor or get excluded from coverage entirely.
### Licensing in Missouri, and why it belongs in a cost conversation
Applying pesticides for compensation on someone else’s property in Missouri is a licensed activity, and the license categories map neatly onto the price tiers above. The Missouri Department of Agriculture certifies commercial applicators in category 7A for general structural pest control, 7B for wood-destroying organisms including termites, carpenter ants and powderpost beetles, and 7C for fumigation. Applicators pass a core standards exam plus at least one category exam through Pearson VUE, licenses renew annually at $65, and recertification is required every three years. For 7A, 7B and 7C specifically, the state also wants documented supervised experience or an associate degree in biology, chemistry, agriculture or entomology. A solo operator with no employees needs both an applicator license and a pesticide business license.
The practical version: when you get a termite bid, ask whether the person doing the work holds a 7B, not just a 7A. Ask about the business license too. The state Pesticide Control Program can be reached at 573-751-5504. It is a two-minute question that separates a real termite company from a general pest company taking a swing at a termite job.
### Seven questions that make three quotes comparable
What is the initial or setup fee, and is it waived if I sign an annual agreement?
Does each scheduled visit include the interior, or exterior only unless I request it?
Are callbacks between scheduled visits included, or billed as additional visits?
For termites, is this bid liquid barrier or bait, how many linear feet, and what is the annual cost after year one?
Is the bond retreat-only, or does it include repair coverage, and what is the limit?
What voids the guarantee — missed inspections, moisture conditions, inaccessible areas?
Who is licensed for this specific work, in which category, and can I see it in writing?
Ask all seven of every company. The quotes stop being three numbers and start being three offers you can actually rank.
If you are still deciding who to call rather than what to spend, our companion piece on how to choose a pest control company in St. Louis covers red flags, guarantees and the questions to ask before anyone treats your home. ### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is $50 a month good for pest control?
A.  For an average St. Louis home, yes — provided that price includes the exterior perimeter every visit, interior treatment on request, rodent stations, and unlimited callbacks between scheduled visits. Monthly plans nationally run $40 to $70, so $50 sits right in the normal band. Check the setup fee before you judge it, though: a $50 plan with a $299 initial visit costs more in year one than a $60 plan with no start fee.
### Q. Why is my monthly pest control bill so high?
A.  Usually one of four reasons. The initial or setup visit was billed on top of the first month, commonly $150 to $190 here. The plan is tiered by square footage and your home moved up a tier. Callbacks are billed as extra visits rather than included. Or add-on programs — mosquito service at $300 to $700 a season, a termite bond renewal at $200 to $400 a year, rodent stations — got bundled into one monthly draft. Ask for an itemized statement showing the base plan, the setup fee and each add-on separately.
### Q. Is it expensive to get rid of termites in your house?
A.  It is the most expensive routine pest job most St. Louis homeowners face, and still far cheaper than the alternative. A liquid soil barrier runs $3 to $20 per linear foot of foundation, typically $6 to $10, putting most homes at $500 to $1,500 and a 2,000-square-foot house with an active infestation at $700 to $2,200. Bait systems run $800 to $2,000 to install plus $300 to $600 a year to maintain. For comparison, termite damage repairs average $3,000 to $8,000 and can exceed $25,000.
### Q. How many years does a termite treatment last?
A.  A liquid termiticide barrier generally protects for about five years, and often five to ten depending on soil type, moisture and the product — EPA labeling requires these products to provide at least five years of protection. Annual inspections are still recommended throughout. Bait systems work differently: they protect only as long as the stations are monitored and refilled, typically checked every three to six months and maintained indefinitely.
### Q. Will insurance pay for termite treatment?
A.  Almost never. Homeowners insurance treats insect damage as a preventable maintenance issue rather than a sudden accidental loss, and insect damage is a named exclusion on most policies, so neither the treatment nor the repairs are typically covered. The rare exceptions involve a covered peril causing the infestation, or hidden damage leading to a collapse. That gap is exactly what a termite bond exists to fill, which is why the repair-coverage tier at $200 to $500 more a year is worth pricing on an older home.
### Q. How much should you spend on pest control?
A.  For routine ant, spider and roach work in St. Louis, $85 to $189 a visit is normal, averaging near $133. Monthly plans run $40 to $70 and quarterly service $100 to $275 a visit in this market. Spending well past that usually means a specific problem — termites, bed bugs or rodents — priced separately.
### Q. Is it worth paying for pest control?
A.  For recurring problems, generally yes. Routine ant, spider and roach service runs $85 to $189 a visit here, or $40 to $70 a month on a plan. Weigh that against what the alternative costs: termite treatment is $500 to $1,500 for a liquid barrier, and bed bugs run $1,000 to $2,500 chemically.
### Q. What is the hardest pest to get rid of?
A.  Bed bugs, by most accounts — they hide in seams and outlets, survive months without feeding, and usually need whole-home heat at $2,000 to $4,000 to finish properly. Termites are the more expensive surprise, since colonies are invisible until damage shows. Neither is a one-visit problem, whatever a quote implies.

## What New Flooring Costs in St. Louis (2026 Price Guide)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-much-does-new-flooring-cost-in-st-louis
Picture three St. Louis households on the same Saturday morning, all of them staring at a floor. In a century brick two-family in south city, a homeowner peels back the corner of a bedroom carpet with a pair of pliers and finds narrow-strip oak underneath — gray at the edges, a little dinged near the doorway, but solid all the way across. The question in that room is not what new flooring costs. It’s whether the floor already there is worth saving.
A few miles west, in a 1958 Kirkwood ranch, a different family has decided the wall-to-wall carpet is done. They want luxury vinyl plank running through the living room, hall, and three bedrooms. Then somebody notices that the hallway dips slightly toward the center of the house, and the closet door has been sticking since the last dry summer. That dip is going to show up on the quote, and it has nothing to do with the flooring itself.
Out in St. Charles, a 2003 two-story has builder-grade carpet upstairs and a finished basement that took water one spring. The family wants something down there that can get wet again without becoming a disaster. Three houses, three completely different numbers — and that’s the honest answer to what flooring costs in this metro. What follows is the price range for each material, plus the St. Louis-specific line items that turn a tidy estimate into a real one.
### The short version: installed cost per square foot
These are 2026 national installed ranges — material plus labor, before removal, subfloor work, or stairs. St. Louis labor tends to sit at or slightly below the national middle, which is good news, but our housing stock adds prep work that flatter markets don’t need.
Carpet with pad: roughly $1.75 to $7.50 per square foot installed, with most homeowners landing between $3 and $6. Mid-grade nylon or triexta runs about $4 to $8.50 all in.
Luxury vinyl plank (LVP): about $4.50 to $12 per square foot installed.
Laminate: roughly $6.90 to $11.80 per square foot installed.
Solid hardwood: $6 to $25 or more per square foot installed, with most jobs settling in the $10 to $16 range.
Engineered wood: about $7 to $20 per square foot installed.
Ceramic and porcelain tile: $10 to $31 per square foot installed, averaging around $18.
Blend all of that together and the broad national average for flooring installation is close to $12.50 per square foot, based on a 500-square-foot project running roughly $1,529 to $4,860. That average is nearly useless for budgeting a specific room, which is why the per-material ranges above matter more.
### How much does it cost to floor 1000 sq ft fully installed?
A thousand square feet is roughly the main level of a small ranch or the first floor of a south city bungalow, so it’s a useful yardstick. Run the ranges out and here is what you get for material and labor only:
Carpet and pad: about $3,000 to $6,000 for most mid-grade choices.
LVP: about $4,500 to $12,000, with a lot of St. Louis jobs landing near $6,000 to $8,000.
Laminate: about $6,900 to $11,800.
Solid hardwood: about $10,000 to $16,000 for a typical grade and layout.
Engineered wood: about $7,000 to $20,000 depending on veneer thickness and finish.
Tile: about $10,000 to $31,000, which is why almost nobody tiles a whole main level.
Then add the prep. Old flooring removal, subfloor repair, and leveling can easily add $2 to $6 per square foot on an older home, which on a thousand square feet is another $2,000 to $6,000. In a century house that prep is not optional and it is not a small rounding error. Budget for it before you fall in love with a sample.
Totally unrelated — but Troy’s restaurant lineup is right here.
### Solid hardwood, and the floor you may already own
Solid hardwood is the default in a huge share of St. Louis housing built before about 1950. Red oak strip flooring went into brick two-families, bungalows, and four-families across the city by the acre, and in a startling number of them it is still down there under carpet, under padding, sometimes under a layer of vinyl tile from the 1970s.
That changes the math completely. New solid hardwood installed runs $10 to $16 per square foot for most jobs. Refinishing what you already have runs $3 to $8 per square foot nationally, and in the St. Louis market whole-project refinishing commonly lands between about $1,153 and $3,051, with an average near $2,055. Dustless refinishing sits at the higher end, roughly $5 to $8 per square foot.
So the first thing to do in an older home is not to shop flooring. It is to pull a vent cover, lift a closet carpet corner, or check the edge of a heat register and see what is actually under there. If you want the full walkthrough on choosing between wood, laminate, and vinyl once you know what you have, our guide on hardwood, laminate, or vinyl in St. Louis homes starts exactly there.
### Is it cheaper to refinish hardwood floors or replace them?
Almost always, yes. Is it cheaper to refinish hardwood floors or replace them? Refinishing typically costs a third to a half of what new solid hardwood costs on the same square footage, and it keeps the original material — which in a 1910 house means quartersawn or tight-grained old-growth oak that you simply cannot buy at that price today.
Refinishing stops making sense in a few specific situations:
The boards have already been sanded down to the tongue. Old floors have a finite number of sandings in them, and a house that has changed hands six times may be out of them. A flooring pro can check this at a doorway or a floor register cut.
There is water damage with cupping or crowning that did not flatten out after the source was fixed.
Large sections are missing — a wall was moved, a chimney was pulled, a bathroom was added — and matching old strip width and species would cost more than starting over.
Pet damage has soaked through the boards into the subfloor. Surface stains sand out. Saturation does not.
Partial replacement plus a full refinish is a real middle path and it is common here. A crew laces in new boards where the old ones are gone, then sands and finishes the whole room so it reads as one floor. It costs more than a straight refinish and far less than a full tear-out.
### LVP and why it suits St. Louis basements
Luxury vinyl plank has taken over the lower-cost end of this market, and in St. Louis it earns the spot for a specific reason: quality LVP is genuinely waterproof, not merely water resistant. A plank can be submerged, dried, and still be fine. Laminate and engineered wood cannot make that claim — laminate’s fiberboard core swells and does not come back.
That matters in a metro where finished basements are standard and where a slab is always wicking moisture up from the ground even when it feels bone dry to the hand. If you are putting a floating floor over a basement slab, a vapor barrier is not an upgrade, it is a requirement. Skip it and you get trapped vapor under the underlayment, which is how mold starts in an otherwise dry-looking basement.
If your lower level has ever taken water, fix that before you spend a dollar on flooring. Our St. Louis basement waterproofing guide covers the drainage and grading side, and the order of operations is not negotiable: water first, then floor.
Expect $4.50 to $12 per square foot installed. The spread inside that range is mostly wear layer thickness and plank rigidity. Thin, floppy, cheap LVP telegraphs every imperfection in the slab underneath and its wear layer gives out in a hallway within a few years.
### Laminate, tile, and carpet in short
Laminate installs for roughly $6.90 to $11.80 per square foot. It looks better than it used to and it handles foot traffic well, but it is the wrong call anywhere that floods, and that includes a lot of St. Louis lower levels.
Tile is the most expensive square foot in the house at $10 to $31 installed, averaging around $18. That price buys a floor that outlives everything else in the room, which is why it stays sensible in baths, entries, and mudrooms even when it is unaffordable everywhere else. Substrate prep drives a big share of tile cost in older homes; if you want the detail, see our guide to choosing a tile installer in St. Louis.
Carpet remains the cheapest way to cover a floor: about $1.75 to $7.50 per square foot with pad and labor, with most projects between $3 and $6. Carpet material alone runs $1 to $12 per square foot, pad with installation adds $0.75 to $3.75, and labor lands between about $0.50 and $3.00. Ask for those three numbers separately. Cheap pad under good carpet is a false economy that shows up in eighteen months.
### The line items that blow up a flooring quote
Material price is the number people shop. Prep is the number that decides whether the project comes in on budget.
### Removal and disposal of the old floor
General flooring removal runs about $2.42 to $4.47 per square foot. By material:
Carpet: $1 to $5 per square foot. If you tear it out yourself, disposal alone is roughly $0.40 to $0.50 per square foot.
Sheet vinyl: about $0.75 to $1.50 per square foot.
Laminate: about $2 to $3 per square foot.
Hardwood: about $2 to $4 per square foot.
Ceramic tile: $2 to $7 per square foot, averaging around $3.50 — tile set in a mud bed is the worst of them.
Disposal is separate and real. A dumpster averages about $380 and ranges from roughly $200 to $800 per week, and hauling by a contractor typically runs $100 to $400. Ask whether the quote includes the dumpster or whether it appears later as a change order.
### Subfloor repair
Replacing subfloor averages $2.20 to $4.75 per square foot, though jobs that need framing attention run $5 to $7 and can reach $10. This is the line item that catches St. Louis homeowners in pre-war houses, because the assembly under an old floor is not what is under a modern one. Many century homes have one-by planks laid diagonally over the joists rather than sheet goods, and after a hundred-plus years those planks have shrunk, cupped, and opened gaps. That surface is fine under a nailed hardwood floor. It is not flat enough for a floating LVP or laminate floor without an added underlayment layer.
### Leveling for clay-soil movement
Missouri clay expands when wet and shrinks hard in a dry August, and it moves foundations with it. In practice that shows up indoors as a floor that dips toward the center beam, or a room that slopes a half inch across twelve feet. Floating floors are unforgiving about this — too much deflection and the locking joints separate and click underfoot.
Self-leveling compound runs about $1 to $5 per square foot for material, and $3 to $9 per square foot professionally installed on a slab. Over a wood subfloor it needs seam sealing and mesh, adding $1 to $5 per square foot. Whole-house leveling projects average around $2,800 and commonly range from $1,000 to $8,000.
One caution: leveling treats the symptom. If a floor has moved recently, or doors that used to close have stopped closing, get the foundation looked at before you cover the evidence with new flooring.
### Radiator, register, and trim cuts
Old St. Louis houses fight back at the edges. Cast iron radiators either get drained and pulled or the new floor gets scribed around each foot. Floor registers in original hardwood are framed openings that a new floor has to be cut and trimmed to meet. Add pocket door tracks, curved bay window walls, and baseboard with a shoe mold that a previous owner caulked to the floor, and you have hours of finish carpentry that a 1990s subdivision simply does not generate. Expect an older-home labor premium, and expect the crew that quotes it lowest to be the one that has not looked closely.
### Stairs are priced by the step, not the square foot
Every flooring quote that includes a staircase should break the stairs out separately, because stairs are labor, not square footage.
Carpet on stairs: roughly $14 to $36 per step installed, with wider figures of $15 to $55 per step depending on carpet grade and whether the stairs are boxed or open on one side. A typical fourteen-step run comes in a few hundred dollars.
Hardwood treads and risers: commonly $60 to $360 per step. A retro-fit overlay over existing stringers runs about $100 to $200 per step; a full replacement with demolition runs $150 to $300 per step. Treads themselves cost roughly $35 to $50 each, and can range from $20 to $160 for premium species.
Refinishing existing stairs: a standard twelve to seventeen step staircase costs about $344 to $1,322, with a national average near $800 and a wide overall range of roughly $120 to $3,000.
In a south city two-family or a Central West End rowhouse, the staircase is often the single nicest piece of woodwork in the building. If the treads are original oak under carpet, refinishing them is almost always the better spend than covering them again.
### How to read a flooring quote before you sign
A quote you can actually compare has these lines broken out. If they are bundled into one number, ask for them separately.
Material cost per square foot, by product name and wear layer or thickness.
Labor per square foot, stated separately from material.
Old flooring removal and haul-away, including whether a dumpster is in the price.
Subfloor inspection, repair allowance, and what happens if they open the floor and find more.
Leveling or underlayment, with the compound and depth specified.
Transitions, thresholds, quarter round, and shoe mold — and whether existing baseboard is being reused or replaced.
Stairs, priced per step.
Furniture moving and appliance disconnects.
Acclimation time for wood products, which matters here because our humidity swings hard between a St. Louis July and a January with the furnace running.
Get three quotes on the same scope. If one is dramatically lower, look at what it left out rather than assuming you found a bargain — the low bid on an old house is usually the crew that skipped the subfloor conversation.

Comparing quotes is how you find out what a St. Louis flooring project actually costs in your house - century subfloor, clay-soil dip, radiator cuts and all. ### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it cheaper to refinish hardwood floors or replace them?
A.  Refinishing is cheaper in nearly every case. Refinishing runs about $3 to $8 per square foot against $10 to $16 for new solid hardwood installed, and in the St. Louis market a typical refinishing project lands between roughly $1,153 and $3,051. Replacement only wins when the boards have been sanded down to the tongue, when water damage has permanently cupped them, or when large sections are missing and cannot be matched.
### Q. Can I stay in my house while floors are refinished?
A.  You can, but most people are happier if they don’t. Sanding produces fine dust even with dust-containment equipment, and oil-based polyurethane fumes are strong for several days while the finish cures. Water-based finishes have less odor and dry faster. If you stay, plan to keep off the finished floors entirely for at least a day or two, longer before furniture goes back, and expect to live around a sealed-off work zone.
### Q. How much does a contractor charge to install LVP?
A.  Installed luxury vinyl plank runs about $4.50 to $12 per square foot including material and labor, and many St. Louis jobs land near the $6 to $8 mark for a good mid-grade product. Labor alone is the smaller share; most of the spread comes from wear layer thickness and plank rigidity. Add a vapor barrier over any basement slab and add leveling if the subfloor is not flat, because a floating floor over a wavy surface will separate at the joints.
### Q. What are the downsides of luxury vinyl plank flooring?
A.  It is a plastic product, so it can dent under heavy furniture, it can fade in a room with strong direct sun, and it will not add resale value the way real wood does. It also cannot be refinished — when the wear layer goes, the floor is replaced rather than restored. And it is unforgiving of a bad substrate: every hump and dip in an old St. Louis subfloor shows through a thin floating plank.
### Q. How do I find out if there is original hardwood under my carpet?
A.  Pull up a floor register or a heat vent cover and look at the cut edge of the opening — you will usually see the whole floor assembly in cross section. Failing that, lift a corner of carpet in a closet where the tack strip is easy to pry and nothing shows afterward. In St. Louis homes built before about 1950, narrow-strip red oak is common, and finding it changes your project from a several-thousand-dollar replacement into a refinishing job at a fraction of the price.
### Q. How much to install 2000 sq ft of laminate flooring?
A.  At roughly $6.90 to $11.80 per square foot installed, 2,000 square feet of laminate runs about $13,800 to $23,600. Most of that spread is the plank itself and whatever the subfloor needs. Carpet over the same area lands closer to $3,500 to $15,000, and luxury vinyl plank $9,000 to $24,000.
### Q. How much to install 2000 sq ft of hardwood floor?
A.  Solid hardwood runs $6 to $25 per square foot installed, with most jobs settling between $10 and $16. Across 2,000 square feet that is roughly $20,000 to $32,000 for the typical band. Engineered wood at $7 to $20 per square foot lands lower and tolerates a St. Louis basement far better.
### Q. How much does Home Depot charge to lay a floor?
A.  Big-box installation is subcontracted to local crews, so the price follows your market rather than a national rate card. In this market the installed ranges hold either way: carpet $1.75 to $7.50 per square foot, luxury vinyl plank $4.50 to $12, laminate $6.90 to $11.80. Confirm whether subfloor prep and haul-away are included.

## What Self Storage Actually Costs in St. Louis (and Why Month Four Is Different)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-much-does-self-storage-cost-in-st-louis
A couple in Ballwin sells the house where they raised three kids and buys a condo with half the square footage. The dining set that seated ten does not fit anywhere in the new place. Neither does the workbench, or the cedar chest, and no one in the family is ready to say out loud that these things are going away.
Across the metro, someone in the Central West End has a lease that ends on the 31st and a new one that starts on the 15th. That is two weeks with an entire life in boxes and nowhere to set it down.
And in Florissant, a daughter stands in her mother’s house the week after the funeral, looking at four decades of accumulation, with a brother flying back east on Sunday and a closing date that will not move.
Three different problems. One storage unit answers all three — and depending on which of those people you are, the same answer costs anywhere from about $44 a month to well over $200. Here is what the sizes actually cost around here, what each one honestly holds, and why the number on the sign is so often not the number on your fourth invoice.
### How much is a storage unit in STL?
Average monthly rates across the St. Louis market in July 2026, for standard units without climate control:
5x5 — about $44 a month
5x10 — about $67 a month
10x10 — about $108 a month
10x15 — about $143 a month
10x20 — about $179 a month
The same sizes with climate control:
5x5 — about $47 a month
5x10 — about $75 a month
10x10 — about $120 a month
10x15 — about $161 a month
10x20 — about $218 a month
Those are metro averages, and the spread underneath them is genuinely wide. A national operator’s own St. Louis pricing page put the local 10x10 average nearer $92. A separate market tracker had the same size around $117.80 in mid-July 2026. For national context, the average street rate across the country was $133 a month in May 2026, down about 2.2 percent from a year earlier.
So the honest version of the answer is a range, not a figure. A 10x10 in this metro is roughly a hundred dollars, plus or minus thirty, before anything else lands on the bill. Everything below is about that phrase — before anything else lands on the bill.
### What each size actually holds
Renting one size too large is the most common and most expensive mistake, and it happens because square footage is abstract while a pile of furniture in a driveway is not. Translate the numbers first.
5x5 (25 square feet) — a hall closet. Seasonal decorations, a few dozen boxes of books and papers, a set of golf clubs, small tools. Not furniture.
5x10 (50 square feet, roughly 400 cubic feet) — the furniture from a studio or a light one-bedroom. A queen mattress set, a love seat, a dresser, a television, a bicycle, and a stack of boxes.
10x10 (100 square feet) — the size of a small bedroom. Commonly used for the contents of two full bedrooms or one large family room, and it is the standard recommendation for a full one-bedroom apartment.
10x15 (150 square feet, roughly 1,200 cubic feet) — the contents of a two- or three-bedroom house, including the awkward things: a sectional, an entertainment center, a dining table with its chairs, a refrigerator.
10x20 (200 square feet) — a one-car garage. A two- to three-bedroom house with the appliances, or a household plus a project car’s worth of parts.
The step from 10x10 to 10x15 costs about $35 a month here, which is $420 a year, and it is the step people take out of anxiety more than arithmetic. Should I get a 10x10 or 10x15 storage unit? Stack the boxes in the garage first and measure the footprint of the pile. If the answer is close, the 10x10 with a walkway left down the middle usually wins, because you will need to get to the back of it in February and you will not want to unload the whole unit onto the pavement to do it.
### Is a 10x10 storage unit enough for a one bedroom apartment?
For most one-bedroom apartments, yes, with room left over. The 10x10 is sized for roughly two bedrooms of furniture, so a single bedroom plus a living room plus a kitchen usually fits with a path down the center.
Where it stops fitting is not bedrooms — it is bulk. A full-size sofa sectional, a treadmill, a washer and dryer, and a dining table for six will fill a 10x10 on their own no matter how few bedrooms they came out of. Count the large rigid objects, not the rooms.
And remember the ceiling. Most units run about eight feet tall, which is where the cubic-foot figures come from, but that capacity only exists if you actually stack. Mattresses on end, boxes to shoulder height, nothing heavy on top of anything that can be crushed.
Random, but: Marthasville’s whole food scene is one click away.
### Why the advertised rate is rarely the rate you pay in month four
This is the part almost nobody explains, and it is the single most useful thing to understand before you sign anything.
The self-storage industry runs on two separate prices. The street rate is what a new customer is quoted today, and it is set low and moved constantly to fill empty units. The in-place rate is what you are already paying, and it drifts upward through what the industry openly calls existing customer rate increases.
The gap between the two is not a rumor. Street rates have been soft nationally — down a couple of percent year over year as of spring 2026 — while operators lean harder on raising rents for tenants who are already moved in. In a lot of markets, what existing customers pay now sits above what the same unit is advertised for on the website.
What that means for you, practically:
Ask, before signing, whether the quoted rate is promotional, when it expires, and what the standard rate for that unit is.
Expect a rate letter. Many tenants see their first increase somewhere in the first six to twelve months.
Check the website rate for your own unit size at your own facility every few months. If a new customer can get your unit cheaper than you are paying, call and ask for the current rate. It is a month-to-month agreement, and the facility would rather adjust you than have an empty unit.
If the answer is no, moving your things two doors down the road is a real option, and the staff know it.
None of this is dishonest on the operator’s part. It is simply how the pricing works, and the only people it costs money are the ones who never look at the bill again after move-in day.
### The extras nobody quotes you
The monthly rate is the headline. Here is the rest of the bill, in the order you will meet it:
Administrative or setup fee — a one-time charge, commonly $10 to $30, applied at move-in. This is the fee that quietly cancels out a free-month promotion on a cheap small unit.
A lock — most facilities require an approved lock and sell it at the counter, typically $10 to $30. Some accept a disc lock you bring yourself; ask before you buy one twice.
Tenant insurance — frequently required, not optional. Facility plans generally run $10 to $30 a month depending on coverage. Some facilities will waive it if you show a homeowners or renters policy that already covers off-premises property, so check your existing policy before you agree to a second one.
Late fees — commonly $10 to $50, or a percentage of the monthly rent, and they compound with the lien timeline described further down.
Add it up honestly. A $108 non-climate 10x10 with a $20 admin fee, a $20 lock, and $15 a month of required insurance is not $108. It is $163 in month one and $123 every month after — roughly fourteen percent above the advertised number, permanently.
### How to get the actual lowest price
A few things reliably move the number, and they cost nothing but attention:
Reserve online rather than at the counter. Most operators publish a lower web rate than their walk-in rate, and first-month-free offers are very often web-exclusive. Walking in and asking for the internet price does not always work; booking the internet price does.
Read what the free month actually covers. It usually applies to rent only. Admin fee, lock, and insurance are still due at move-in. Some promotions require a two- or three-month minimum stay and claw the discount back if you leave early.
Take the autopay discount if there is one. Some facilities tie the promotional rate to enrolling in automatic payment, and it also removes the late-fee risk entirely.
Move mid-month if you can. Demand concentrates at month-end when leases turn over, which is exactly when the cheap units are gone.
Take the upper floor. Inside a climate-controlled building, ground-floor units near the door are priced above upper-floor units reached by elevator. If you are storing rather than shopping the unit weekly, the elevator is a fair trade.
### Is climate-controlled storage worth the cost?
Sometimes clearly yes, sometimes clearly no, and the deciding factors are what is in the box and how long it will sit there — not how expensive the contents were.
Start with the local weather, because that is the whole argument. A St. Louis July averages a high near 89 degrees with relative humidity around 68 percent, and a metal building with a roll-up door runs considerably hotter than the air outside it. A climate-controlled space is generally held somewhere between 55 and 85 degrees, with the humidity swings flattened out.
Things that genuinely need that:
Solid wood furniture — repeated moisture cycling is what warps, splits, and loosens glued joints. The heirloom dresser is the classic loss.
Electronics — condensation on cold circuit boards, swollen batteries, and failed capacitors after a summer in a hot box.
Photographs and paper — preservation guidance puts photographs below 75 degrees with humidity held in a moderate band. Prints stick to each other and to album sleeves when they get hot and damp, and that damage is permanent.
Vinyl records — a stable 60 to 70 degrees with humidity near the middle of the range. Heat warps the discs and the sleeves grow mold.
Leather, musical instruments, artwork, wine, and anything upholstered that will sit through more than one summer.
Things that mostly do not need it:
Yard tools, bicycles, ladders, patio furniture, plastic bins of hardware.
Sealed plastic totes of clothing and linens for a short stay.
Anything already living in your garage year-round without complaint.
A move-gap stay of a few weeks in spring or fall, when the temperature swing is small.
The premium here is smaller than people assume — roughly $3 a month on a 5x5, about $12 on a 10x10, and about $39 on a 10x20. On the 10x10 that is a hundred and forty-four dollars a year to keep a bedroom set from cupping. So ask it plainly. Is climate-controlled storage worth the cost? If wood, electronics, photographs, or records are going in, and the stay will cross a Missouri summer, it is a straightforward yes. If it is lawn equipment for six weeks, it is a straightforward no.
One caution worth stating plainly: climate control is not a mold guarantee. Damp items sealed into a unit will grow mold in a conditioned building the same as anywhere else. Anything that goes in wet — a rug, a mattress, a tent, a cooler — needs to be fully dry first.
### Drive-up versus interior
Drive-up units are the ones you back a truck to and open like a garage. Interior units live inside a conditioned building down a hallway.
Pricing between the two is less consistent than you would expect and varies facility to facility. At many sites the drive-up units are simply the unconditioned concrete boxes and sit at the low end of the rate card. At others, the convenience of loading straight from the tailgate carries a small premium over an interior unit of the same size. One published comparison showed a 10x10 drive-up at $95 against $110 for the interior equivalent, with similar gaps at the smaller sizes.
Choose on how you will use it, then compare prices:
Drive-up if you are loading heavy furniture or appliances, visiting often, or moving in and out on one busy weekend.
Interior if the contents need conditioning, if security matters more than convenience, or if the unit will simply sit.
Also account for the walk. An upstairs interior unit reached by elevator adds ten or fifteen minutes to every single visit, which is invisible on move-in day and extremely visible on the ninth trip.
### The month-to-month reality, and the lien
Almost all self-storage in this market is month-to-month with no minimum term and no maximum. That flexibility is real and it is the best thing about the product.
Two details people miss:
Leaving requires notice. Facilities typically want somewhere between ten and thirty days before you vacate, and the requirement is in your lease, not in the industry. Emptying the unit and driving away does not always stop the billing.
Missing payments has a legal timeline. Under Missouri law, once an occupant has been in default for more than thirty days the operator may enforce a lien against the stored property and sell it. The operator must give at least forty-five days of notice before disposing of anything, with a second notice sent no sooner than ten days after the first, and any surplus from a sale is held for the occupant for a year.
That is not a scare story, it is a calendar. If money gets tight, the worst move is silence. Call the office early — partial payments and short extensions are common, and a sale is expensive and unpleasant for the facility too.
### The three-month rule and the two-year problem
Here is the arithmetic almost nobody runs before renting, and it is the reason people are still paying in year three.
Take a climate-controlled 10x10 at roughly $120 a month, plus $15 of required insurance, plus a $20 admin fee and a $20 lock at the start.
Three months: about $445. Against a closing delay, a renovation, or a death in the family, that is cheap. It buys time to make decisions properly instead of under pressure, and time is genuinely what you are purchasing.
One year: about $1,660, and probably more, because a rate increase has likely landed by then.
Two years: north of $3,300. At that point the question is no longer whether storage is affordable. It is whether the contents of that unit are worth $3,300 to you, because that is what you have spent to avoid deciding.
The national average tenancy is now somewhere around eighteen months, roughly double what it was a decade ago. That is not because people plan eighteen-month stays. It is because a unit is easy to open and emotionally difficult to close.
So set the exit date on the day you set the start date. Write it on the calendar, put a reminder on your phone for two weeks before, and decide then. Storage is an excellent bridge and a poor destination. If what is inside is a dining set nobody wants and a workbench nobody uses, the honest comparison is not storage versus keeping it. It is storage versus what it costs to clear it out, once.
### What items should not go in storage?
Every lease has a prohibited list, and it is broadly the same everywhere:
Flammables and pressurized containers — gasoline, propane tanks, aerosols, paint thinner, fireworks. Drain the mower and leave the grill tank behind.
Perishable food — it draws pests, and pests are a problem for the whole building, which is why leases treat it seriously.
Living things — plants and animals, without exception.
Hazardous or toxic materials, chemicals, and in most leases ammunition.
Anything you cannot afford to be without — passports, titles, medication, tax records, hard drives. Not because they are banned, but because a unit you cannot reach after hours is a bad place for them.
And to answer the question people ask but rarely say out loud: you cannot live in a storage unit, or sleep in one, day or night. It is prohibited by every lease and by building and occupancy code, the units are not habitable spaces, and getting caught means eviction from the unit. If housing is the actual problem, that is a different search and there is real help in this metro for it.
### Before you sign, ask these
Is this rate promotional, and what does it become? Get the standard rate for the unit, not just today’s number.
What is due at move-in beyond the first month? Admin fee, lock, insurance — itemized.
Is insurance required, and will you accept my existing homeowners or renters policy?
How much notice do I owe when I leave, and how do I give it?
What are your access hours, and are gate hours different from office hours?
Is this unit climate controlled or only temperature controlled? The two are marketed interchangeably and are not the same thing.
Not sure a unit is the answer? Here is what hiring a home organizer costs in St. Louis.
Get the answers by phone or email before move-in day, when you have leverage and time, rather than at the counter with a loaded truck idling outside. It is the same discipline that makes moving quotes comparable — ask every facility the identical questions and the prices finally line up next to each other.
