### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much should jewelry cost?
A.  It depends on metal weight, stone quality and labor, so there is no single right number — but you can price it structurally. Ask for the quote split into metal, stones and bench time, ask what changes if you drop one grade of color or clarity, and compare two shops on the same specification rather than on a headline price. A piece you wear daily justifies more metal; a piece you wear twice a year does not.
### Q. Is $3,000 cheap for an engagement ring?
A.  No, it sits in normal territory. The Knot’s 2026 Real Weddings Study put average engagement ring spend at $4,600 for weddings held in 2025, with 61% of rings using a lab-grown center stone, and averages get pulled upward by a small number of very large purchases. What matters more than the number is where it goes: cut quality and a setting built to hold the stone outlive an extra tenth of a carat.
### Q. What are the 5 C’s of jewelry?
A.  Officially there are four. GIA founder Robert M. Shipley coined the four Cs — color, clarity, cut and carat weight — in the 1940s as a teaching device, and the earliest GIA course material naming them dates to 1949. The commonly cited fifth C is certification, meaning an independent grading report, but it was never part of GIA’s system. Treat it as good buying advice rather than a grading standard.
### Q. What is the 2:1:1 rule in jewelry?
A.  It is a styling ratio, not a valuation rule. The idea is to balance a look by mixing impact levels instead of piling everything in one place — commonly two quieter pieces, one medium and one statement, or two rings on one hand and one on the other. Interpretations vary by stylist, which tells you it is a guideline. It has nothing to do with quality, price, or how a jeweler quotes a repair.
### Q. What is the hottest jewelry right now?
A.  Lab-grown center stones are the clearest shift in the numbers: The Knot’s 2026 study found 61% of engagement rings now use one, a 239% jump since 2020, with average center size at 1.9 carats. Beyond bridal, gold’s run to record levels has pushed buyers toward lighter hollow chains, vintage and estate pieces, and remounting stones they already own instead of paying for new metal.
### Q. How often should I have my rings checked?
A.  Every six months to a year if you wear them daily, which matches GIA’s guidance on professional cleaning and inspection. The check takes minutes: a jeweler looks at prong tips, tests whether stones move under a probe, and inspects the shank for thinning. If your ring came with a service plan, read the interval — many require a documented inspection on a schedule to keep the coverage alive.
### Q. Can a local jeweler repair a ring I bought online?
A.  Usually yes, and this is where a bench relationship pays for itself. Sizing, prong work and stone tightening do not care where the ring came from. Two limits worth raising up front: full eternity bands and some tension settings cannot be sized conventionally, and repairs done elsewhere can void an online retailer’s own warranty, so check that policy before you hand the ring over.

## Hearing Aids in St. Louis: How to Get Tested, Fitted and Covered
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/hearing-aids-st-louis-what-to-expect
Imagine it’s a Sunday afternoon and you’re at the long table at a family birthday in Affton. Somebody down at the far end tells a story. Everybody laughs. You laugh a beat late, because you caught maybe half of it and filled in the rest. You blame the room. The room is loud.
Then it happens again over dinner in Kirkwood. Then in the car back to St. Charles, when your daughter has to say it twice. Your spouse has started mentioning the TV volume in a tone that isn’t really a question, and at some point you began aiming your good ear at the table without ever deciding to.
This is where most people stall — not because they don’t care, but because nobody tells them what the first step is. Who is qualified to test you. Whether the device advertised online for a couple hundred dollars is the same thing a clinic in Florissant or Belleville would fit. Below is the map. It is not medical advice, and nothing on this page can tell you whether your hearing loss is serious. Only a clinician who tests your ears can answer that.
### Who is the best hearing aid supplier?
There isn’t one, and any list that names a winner is ranking products, not your ears. What separates providers in the St. Louis metro is checkable in about ten minutes: whether the person holds a current state license, whether they verify the device’s output inside your ear canal instead of trusting the fitting software, what the written trial period and return terms say, and what the quoted price still includes after you walk out the door.
Two people with identical audiograms can end up with wildly different outcomes from the same model of hearing aid, because the fitting is the treatment. The device is just hardware. So the questions worth asking on the phone before you book are boring, specific, and revealing:
Are you a licensed audiologist or a licensed hearing instrument specialist — and can I have your license number?
Do you do real-ear (probe microphone) verification at the fitting?
How many follow-up visits are included in the price, and for how long?
What is the trial period, and what is nonrefundable if I return the aids?
If I buy through my insurance plan, what changes about the service I get?
Missouri and Illinois both publish licensee lookups, and both are free. The Missouri Board of Examiners for Hearing Instrument Specialists sits inside the state’s Division of Professional Registration and takes consumer complaints directly. In Illinois, hearing instrument dispensers are licensed through the Illinois Department of Public Health.
### What is the difference between an audiologist and a hearing instrument specialist?
Training and scope. An audiologist holds a graduate degree — typically an AuD or a PhD — and performs diagnostic hearing and balance evaluations. A hearing instrument specialist (you’ll also see hearing aid dispenser, fitter, or dealer) is a state-licensed professional who conducts basic hearing tests, then fits and dispenses hearing aids. Both can sell you a hearing aid. Only audiologists can bill insurance, including Medicare, for medically necessary hearing and balance evaluations, per the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association.
The two states license them through different doors, which trips people up crossing the river. In Missouri, hearing instrument specialists fall under Chapter 346 and their own Board of Examiners, while audiologists are licensed under Chapter 345 through the Board of Registration for the Healing Arts. In Illinois, dispensers answer to the Department of Public Health and audiologists to the Department of Financial and Professional Regulation.
Neither title is a verdict on quality. A meticulous specialist who runs real-ear measurements on every fitting will serve you better than an audiologist who skips them. The credential says what someone may do; the protocol says what they actually do.
### How are OTC hearing aids different from prescription ones?
Over-the-counter hearing aids are for adults 18 and older with perceived mild to moderate hearing loss, and you can buy them in a store or online with no exam, no prescription, and no professional fitting. That category took effect on October 17, 2022. A prescription hearing aid is, by the FDA’s definition, any hearing aid that is not an OTC hearing aid — available only through a licensed hearing health care professional who programs it to your specific loss, at any age and any severity.
The FDA is blunt about the ceiling: OTC devices are limited in maximum output and are not intended for severe or profound hearing loss. Anyone under 18 needs a prescription device. And the box has to earn its keep — FDA labeling rules require the outside packaging to show the words “OTC” and “hearing aid,” the warning conditions, battery information, whether a phone or remote is needed, whether the unit is used or rebuilt, and the manufacturer’s return policy. The FDA does not require a warranty at all, so read that panel before you pay.
One detail almost nobody knows: you can be tested by a professional and still buy elsewhere. The FDA says outright that you may request your hearing evaluation records and purchase your hearing aid somewhere else. A test and a purchase are two separate decisions.
### What happens at a hearing evaluation?
Expect roughly an hour, most of it sitting down. The clinician takes a history, looks in your ear canals, and then puts you in a sound-treated booth with headphones to find the softest tones you can detect across pitches, usually followed by word-repetition testing and a quick pressure test of the eardrum. Results land on an audiogram — a chart, not a diagnosis — and the clinician walks you through it.
Bring somebody whose voice you struggle with, because their presence changes what gets tested and what gets discussed. Bring a written list of the rooms that defeat you: the church basement in Maryland Heights, the shop floor, the restaurant with the tin ceiling, a tented graduation party in the yard. That last one is its own species of hard room — if you’re hosting it, our rundown of what to ask before booking party rentals in St. Louis covers the tent end of it.
If it goes as far as a fitting, ask about verification. Professional guidance from ASHA and the American Academy of Audiology says the prescribed output should be verified with a probe microphone placed in the ear canal — real-ear measurement — rather than assumed from the manufacturer’s software. Ear canals differ in length and shape, and a device set correctly on a screen can be badly off inside a particular ear.
### What are the red flags for audiology referrals?
The FDA prints a specific list on OTC hearing aid packaging under the heading “When to See a Doctor,” and it is the closest thing to an official answer. See a doctor, preferably an ear-nose-throat physician, if any of these apply to you:
Your ear has a birth defect or unusual shape, or was injured or deformed in an accident.
You saw blood, pus, or fluid coming out of your ear in the past six months.
Your ear feels painful or uncomfortable.
You have a lot of ear wax, or you think something could be in your ear.
You get really dizzy, or have a feeling of spinning or swaying.
Your hearing changed suddenly in the past six months.
Your hearing changes: it gets worse, then gets better again.
You have worse hearing in one ear.
You hear ringing or buzzing in only one ear.
That list is a routing instruction, not a diagnosis. It exists because hearing loss can come from something as ordinary as impacted wax or as consequential as a growth on the hearing nerve, and an amplifier fixes neither. Nobody reading a web page can tell you which you have.
### How much should a decent hearing aid cost?
It depends almost entirely on what is folded into the price, which is why quotes swing so hard. The National Council on Aging puts the typical cost of a pair of prescription hearing aids at roughly $2,500 to $3,690, citing published research, while OTC devices can start around $200. Neither number is a St. Louis price list. Both are a starting point for the only question that matters: what am I buying besides the plastic?
Traditional practices bundle. The FDA said as much in the 2022 rule, expecting OTC availability to lower costs by unbundling hearing aids from professional advice, fitting, adjustment, and maintenance. In a bundled quote, the device price is also paying for the fitting appointment, the tweaks at week six, cleanings, tubing changes, and often a loss-and-damage warranty for several years. In an unbundled quote, the device is cheaper and each visit has a fee. Neither is a scam. They are different structures, and comparing one to the other on the sticker alone will mislead you every time.
What genuinely moves the number: one device or two, the technology tier within a manufacturer’s lineup, rechargeable versus disposable batteries, years of follow-up included, warranty length, and whether an insurance contract sets the fee. What matters less than people assume: the physical style of the aid.
Nothing to do with ears — where to find St. Louis plumbers.
### How much does Medicare cover for a hearing aid?
Original Medicare covers nothing toward hearing aids, and nothing toward the exams used to fit them. Medicare.gov states it plainly: you pay all costs. What Part B does cover is diagnostic hearing and balance exams ordered by your doctor or other provider to determine whether you need medical treatment. After the Part B deductible you pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount, plus a copayment if the service happens in a hospital outpatient setting.
There is one useful wrinkle. Since January 1, 2023, you can see an audiologist once every 12 months without an order from a provider — but only for non-acute hearing conditions, such as hearing loss that developed over many years, and not for exams meant to prescribe or fit hearing aids. That distinction is the whole game with Medicare and hearing.
Medicare Advantage plans are a different animal and may add hearing benefits Original Medicare leaves out. Call your plan and ask three things: the hearing allowance, which providers are in network, and whether the benefit resets annually. Open enrollment runs October 15 to December 7, with new coverage starting January 1. Veterans have another road entirely — through VA audiology, hearing aids, repairs and batteries come at no charge to eligible enrolled veterans, and the VA St. Louis Health Care System keeps main campuses on North Grand Boulevard in the city and at Jefferson Barracks in south county.
### What does the trial period actually protect in Missouri and Illinois?
In Illinois, quite a lot. Under the Hearing Instrument Consumer Protection Act, every hearing instrument offered for sale must come with a 30-business-day return privilege, and the receipt or contract has to state your right to return it for a refund within 30 business days of delivery. If a nonrefundable dispensing fee or restocking fee will be withheld, those terms must be stated in writing too. Business day there excludes Saturdays, Sundays, and federal holidays — so 30 business days is closer to six weeks on the calendar.
Missouri takes the disclosure route instead of setting a minimum. Section 346.020 requires the purchase agreement to carry the licensee’s signature, business address and license number, the make, model and serial number, the exact down payment, the length of any trial period, any fees tied to that trial, and any right you have to return the instrument. If no right of return exists, the seller has to say so in writing. Used, recased or reconditioned instruments must be marked. Read that page before you sign, because in Missouri the agreement is the protection.
One more Missouri rule worth knowing for families: for a purchaser under eighteen, state law requires an examination by an otolaryngologist, a Missouri-licensed physician, or a licensed audiologist, with a written recommendation issued within ninety days before the fitting.
### What does this look like from behind the counter?
Hearing practices don’t make money the way customers picture. Under the bundled model the FDA described in its 2022 rule, years of service are priced into one transaction — the fitting, the reprogram at week six, the remake when a dome won’t seat, the tubing change three winters later. All of it was paid for on day one and never again. Meanwhile Medicare reimburses nothing for the fitting exam, so the single appointment that most determines whether a patient succeeds is the one no insurer pays for. The calendar is lumpy too: with Medicare open enrollment ending December 7 and new plan benefits starting January 1, a quiet autumn turns into a January of people arriving with a freshly reset allowance. Owners talk to each other about the returns and about patients who never wore the aids long enough to adapt. Being findable when a neighbor finally searches is the other half of it, which is where a complete directory listing earns its keep.
Ready to stop guessing at the dinner table? Browse hearing aid providers across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two of them and ask the same five questions from the top of this page. Hospital billing has its own rules worth knowing before any procedure: charity care and the billing rights nobody mentions.
If you run a hearing practice, list it on St Louis Near Me Directory so the family tired of repeating themselves at dinner can find you.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the Trump hearing aid act?
A.  That phrase refers to the Over-the-Counter Hearing Aid Act of 2017, introduced in the Senate as S.670 and folded into the FDA Reauthorization Act of 2017, signed August 18, 2017. It directed the FDA to create a category of hearing aids adults could buy without a prescription. The agency finalized those regulations in August 2022, and the OTC category took effect October 17, 2022.
### Q. What is the best hearing aid available right now?
A.  No honest answer names a model. Hearing aids are matched to a specific pattern of loss, a specific ear canal, and a specific set of listening situations, so a device that changes one person’s life underperforms for the next. Round-up articles rank features and prices, which is real information, but they haven’t tested your ears. Only a clinician who measures your hearing can say what fits your loss.
### Q. What hearing aid do most audiologists recommend?
A.  There is no consensus brand. A clinic’s shelf is shaped by manufacturer relationships, buying groups, insurance contracts, and which fitting software the staff knows cold — worth knowing rather than resenting. Ask directly: which manufacturers do you fit, and why that one for my results? A provider who answers specifically about your audiogram tells you more than any brand name would.
### Q. What is the number one rated hearing aid?
A.  Ratings come from reviewers comparing features, app quality, battery life and price, and they change every year. None of them ranks the thing that decides your outcome: how accurately the device is programmed to your ears, and how consistently you wear it. Treat a top rating as a shortlist, not a prescription, and get the trial terms in writing before money changes hands.
### Q. What is the average cost of a behind-the-ear hearing aid?
A.  No official average exists by style, and style is a weak predictor of price. Behind-the-ear housings span the whole range, from basic to premium, because the cost tracks the technology tier and the services bundled with it. The National Council on Aging cites roughly $2,500 to $3,690 for a pair of prescription aids nationally, with OTC options starting near $200. Ask for an itemized quote instead of a style-based estimate.
### Q. Do I need a doctor’s order to see an audiologist?
A.  Not necessarily. Medicare beneficiaries can see an audiologist once every 12 months without an order for non-acute hearing conditions, though that exception does not extend to hearing aid fitting exams. Private plans set their own referral rules, so call the number on your card first. If you have ear pain, drainage, sudden change, or loss in only one ear, start with a physician instead.
### Q. Can I buy hearing aids online in Missouri?
A.  Yes for OTC devices, if you’re 18 or older and believe your loss is mild to moderate. The FDA allows purchase in a store or online with no exam or prescription. Prescription devices still run through a licensed professional. Before ordering, read the manufacturer’s return policy printed on the outside of the box, since FDA rules require it to appear there and do not require any warranty.

## When You Actually Need a Family Law Attorney in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/when-you-need-a-family-law-attorney-st-louis
Imagine it’s a Wednesday night in Affton and you’re sitting in your own driveway with the engine off, because walking through the door means the same conversation you have already had four times this month. Nobody threw anything. Nobody is a villain. You just know, in the flat way people know these things, that it is over.
Or maybe it isn’t a marriage at all. Maybe you’re a dad in Florissant whose name is on the birth certificate, who just learned that is not the same thing as a custody order. Maybe you’re in Belleville and a parenting schedule from three years ago stopped matching anybody’s real life. Maybe you’re in Kirkwood and your ex quit a job the week after the support order landed.
Those are four different problems, and only some of them need a lawyer. One thing first: this article is general information about how family law works in Missouri and Illinois. It is not legal advice, it is not about your case, and nothing here predicts what a judge will do with your facts. What it can do is hand you the vocabulary before a consultation, so the hour you pay for goes to your situation instead of definitions.
### When do you actually need a family law attorney?
You need one when the other side disputes something, when a court order has to be created or changed, or when the money is complicated. No children, no house, no retirement accounts, both of you agreeing on paper — that is the narrow case people handle themselves. The facts that reliably mean hire someone: children whose schedule you two do not agree on; a business, a pension or a 401(k) to divide; a self-employed spouse who controls the books; any allegation of abuse; an order somebody is ignoring; or a case where the other side already has counsel and you don’t.
Missouri builds in one deadline that catches people flat. Under RSMo 452.310, in any proceeding involving custody or visitation, the petitioner and respondent each have to submit a proposed parenting plan — individually or jointly — within thirty days after service of process or the filing of an entry of appearance, whichever comes first. That is not much time to design the next several years of a child’s life, and the clock runs whether or not you have found help.
Where abuse or neglect is alleged, Missouri removes the discretion: RSMo 452.423 says the court shall appoint a guardian ad litem in any proceeding in which child abuse or neglect is alleged. In other contested custody or support matters that appointment is optional. Either way the guardian ad litem is a third attorney in the room representing the child, and the court can order the parties to pay those fees.
### Is Missouri a 50/50 state for divorce?
No. Missouri divides marital property equitably, not equally. RSMo 452.330 directs the court to divide the marital property and marital debts “in such proportions as the court deems just” after considering the listed factors — and just is not a synonym for half.
The statute names the factors: the economic circumstances of each spouse when the division takes effect, including whether the family home should go to the parent who has custody; each spouse’s contribution to acquiring the marital property, expressly including the contribution of a spouse as homemaker; the value of non-marital property set apart to each spouse; the conduct of the parties during the marriage; and custodial arrangements for the minor children. No formula, no fixed weighting. The trial judge weighs them.
What even counts as marital is its own argument. RSMo 452.330 defines marital property as everything acquired after the marriage except property acquired by gift, bequest, devise or descent, property acquired in exchange for property owned before the marriage, property excluded by a valid written agreement, and the increase in value of premarital property. The house you owned in Maryland Heights before the wedding starts outside the pot; mixing it with marital money is how it gets pulled in. There is one place 50/50 has real footing here, and it is not the bank accounts.
### What rights do fathers have in Missouri?
The same rights mothers have, in writing. RSMo 452.375.8 says that as between the parents of a child, no preference may be given to either parent in the awarding of custody because of that parent’s age, sex, or financial status, nor because of the age or sex of the child. That language has been in the statute for decades.
What moved recently is the starting point on parenting time. Senate Bill 35 took effect August 28, 2023, and put into RSMo 452.375.2 a rebuttable presumption that an award of equal or approximately equal parenting time to each parent is in the best interests of the child. Rebuttable matters — it is a default evidence can overcome, not a guarantee. But the default moved, and it surprises fathers who assumed every other weekend was the ceiling.
For unmarried fathers the real gap is paternity, not parenting. Signing a birth certificate is not a custody order. Under RSMo 210.823 a signed acknowledgment of paternity is treated as a legal finding of paternity, and either party may rescind it by filing with the bureau within sixty days of the last signature; after that, undoing it takes fraud, duress or a material mistake of fact. Legal fatherhood and an enforceable schedule are two separate pieces of paper, and you can hold the first while owning nothing a school will act on.
### How long does a Missouri divorce take?
Missouri sets a floor, not an average. Under RSMo 452.305 the court may enter a judgment of dissolution only if one of you has been a resident of the state for the ninety days immediately preceding the commencement of the proceeding, thirty days have elapsed since the filing of the petition, and the court finds there remains no reasonable likelihood that the marriage can be preserved — that it is irretrievably broken.
Thirty days is the earliest a genuinely agreed case can close. Contested cases run on discovery, appraisals, evaluations and the circuit’s docket, and a year is ordinary. Child support carries its own machinery: Missouri Supreme Court Rule 88.01 presumes a correctly calculated Form 14 amount is the correct amount, and a court departing from it must find, in writing or on the record, that the Form 14 figure is unjust or inappropriate.
Unrelated, and we know it — a dead outlet needs a licensed electrician.
### What is different on the Illinois side?
Illinois runs on a different statute, and this metro straddles the line. Illinois also requires ninety days of residence before a judgment under 750 ILCS 5/401, and it also runs on irreconcilable differences causing an irretrievable breakdown. Parenting is where the two states part company.
Illinois stopped using the word custody in 2016. What Missouri calls legal and physical custody, Illinois splits into significant decision-making responsibility and parenting time, under 750 ILCS 5/602.5 and 5/602.7. And Illinois has no equal-time presumption. Section 602.7 presumes both parents are fit and bars restricting parenting time unless the court finds by a preponderance of the evidence that a parent’s exercise of it would seriously endanger the child’s physical, mental, moral, or emotional health. Allocation itself turns on best interests, with no thumb on the scale toward an even split.
Spousal support diverges the same way. Under 750 ILCS 5/504(b-1), where the parties’ combined gross annual income is under $500,000 and the payor has no prior support obligation, Illinois guideline maintenance is 33 1/3 percent of the payor’s net annual income minus 25 percent of the payee’s net, capped so the payee keeps no more than 40 percent of combined net income. Missouri publishes nothing of the kind — RSMo 452.335 is a list of factors a judge weighs case by case. If one of you lives in Belleville and the other in Kirkwood, where the case lands is not a small detail.
### How much does a divorce attorney cost in Missouri?
There is no honest single number, and any figure pinned to a named firm would be stale within weeks. Four variables do almost all of the work.
Contested versus uncontested. The biggest factor by a wide margin. An agreed case with a signed settlement is essentially a drafting job; a contested case is discovery, depositions, motions and hearings, every hour billed.
Retainer versus hourly. The retainer is usually an advance deposit held in a client trust account and billed against in tenths of an hour, with a clause requiring you to top it up. It is not the price of the divorce. It is the opening balance.
Whether children are involved. A disputed parenting plan, a guardian ad litem, a custody evaluation, a later modification — each adds hours, plus outside fees separate from your attorney’s bill.
How complicated the money is. A closely held business, a pension needing a qualified domestic relations order, self-employment income, or a spouse who controls the records. Each adds an expert, and experts bill too.
Worth raising in the first call: Missouri allows limited scope representation. Rule 4-1.2(c) lets a lawyer limit the work with the client’s written, signed consent setting out the essential terms and the lawyer’s limited role, and Rule 43.01(b), effective July 1, 2010, recognizes an entry of limited appearance. So you may be able to hire someone to draft the parenting plan or appear at one hearing without buying the whole case. Not every firm offers it. Asking is free.
### How do I find a good family law lawyer?
Start with fit, not badges. You want someone who practices family law regularly in the county where the case will actually sit — St. Louis County, St. Charles, Jefferson, Franklin, St. Clair, Madison — because the local judge, the local guardians ad litem and the local docket habits are half the job.
Verify the license first. The Missouri Bar publishes an official directory of Missouri lawyers in good standing with the Supreme Court of Missouri, updated daily and free to search. Illinois attorneys register with the Attorney Registration and Disciplinary Commission of the Supreme Court of Illinois, which runs its own free public lookup. Two minutes, both sides of the river.
Then use the consultation properly. Bring three years of tax returns, recent pay stubs, a list of accounts and debts, and any existing order. Ask how many cases like yours this attorney handled last year, who will work the file day to day, how fast calls get returned, and what the written fee agreement says before you sign. Anyone who guarantees an outcome twenty minutes after hearing your facts is telling you something. If a company the two of you built is tangled in the split, that is a different bench — our guide to when a St. Louis business needs an attorney covers that side.
### What does this look like from the other side of the desk?
Family law bills in tenths of an hour against an advance held in a client trust account — and the household that funded that advance is becoming two households. The final invoice lands when money is tightest, and withdrawing after counsel has entered takes leave of court. That arithmetic sits behind every fee agreement in this metro.
The calendar is lopsided too. Julie Brines and Brian Serafini of the University of Washington, studying filings from 2001 to 2015, found divorce filings peaked in March and August, right after the winter and summer holidays; the pattern repeated in Ohio, Minnesota, Florida and Arizona. December is quiet. The people who file in March mostly decided in December.
What separates the strong operators is what they do with the hours that do not need a lawyer: routing the venting to a paralegal, flat-quoting genuinely uncontested work, offering limited scope help instead of turning someone away. Nobody browses for this the way they browse for dinner — they search the night it lands. Firms can add or claim a listing so that search finds them.
### What if you cannot afford a lawyer at all?
Free civil legal help exists on both sides of the river, income-qualified rather than first-come. Legal Services of Eastern Missouri serves low-income Missourians across 21 eastern Missouri counties, St. Louis City, St. Louis County, St. Charles, Jefferson and Franklin among them. Its general intake does not take routine family law, but its Lasting Solutions program handles family law matters for survivors of domestic violence in St. Louis City, St. Louis County, St. Charles County and Jefferson County. The main line is 314-534-4200.
On the Illinois side, Land of Lincoln Legal Aid serves 65 counties across central and southern Illinois. Its East St. Louis office covers St. Clair, Monroe, Randolph, Clinton and Washington counties; the Alton office covers Madison, Jersey, Macoupin and Bond, among others. Its Legal Advice and Referral Center number is 877-342-7891.
If safety is the immediate problem, that is a faster and separate track from a divorce. Missouri’s Adult Abuse Act, Chapter 455, provides orders of protection, and RSMo 455.025 states that the duties of the clerk prescribed in that section are performed without cost to the litigants. Illinois has a parallel path under its Domestic Violence Act. Neither requires you to have hired an attorney first.
Ready to say it out loud to someone who does this every week? Browse family law attorneys across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then shortlist three, check each license, and book the consultations in one week so you can compare the answers while they are fresh. Family budgets get stretched by more than legal fees - how orthodontic costs and insurance actually work is worth reading early.
If you’re the family law attorney people trust with the hardest conversation of their year, list your practice so they can find you.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is a divorce lawyer worth the cost?
A.  It depends on what is in dispute. With no children, no real estate, no retirement accounts and a signed agreement, a lawyer mostly buys correct drafting. Add children, a house, a pension or a spouse who controls the money, and the mistakes an unrepresented party makes tend to cost more than the fee. Some, like a vague parenting plan, follow you for a decade.
### Q. Who is the top-rated family law attorney in St. Louis?
A.  No official ranking exists, and no bar association issues one. The badges you see mix paid directories, peer-nomination lists and review counts, and none of them knows your facts, your county or your budget. A better screen: confirm the license through The Missouri Bar directory or the Illinois ARDC lookup, then judge fit yourself in a consultation.
### Q. What are the three C’s of divorce?
A.  It is a coaching phrase, not a legal standard — usually given as communication, cooperation and compromise. No Missouri or Illinois statute uses it, and no judge applies it. The statutory tests are different animals: Missouri asks whether the marriage is irretrievably broken and divides marital property in the proportions the court deems just, while Illinois runs on irreconcilable differences.
### Q. What is the 80/20 rule for lawyers?
A.  It is the Pareto principle applied to a law practice: roughly 80 percent of results come from roughly 20 percent of inputs, so a small share of clients or tasks drives most of the revenue. That is practice-management shorthand for firm owners, not a rule of law, and it has no bearing on how a judge decides a case.
### Q. Do I still need a lawyer if the divorce is uncontested?
A.  Not necessarily, but uncontested is stricter than most people use it. It means you agree on every item: property, debt, support, and a complete parenting plan you have both signed. If one line is unresolved, it is a contested case with a polite tone. Missouri also permits limited scope representation, so you can pay someone to review the agreement without retaining them for everything.
### Q. Can a Missouri custody order be changed later?
A.  It can be modified, but not because somebody changed their mind. RSMo 452.410 requires facts arising since the prior decree, or unknown to the court then, showing a change in the circumstances of the child or the custodian, plus a finding that modification is necessary to serve the child’s best interests. Informal side agreements are not orders and are not enforceable.
### Q. Does it matter which Missouri county I file in?
A.  Practically, yes. Venue follows residence, and the local circuit sets the rhythm: which judge hears family matters, how parenting plans and Form 14 worksheets are presented, whether mediation gets pushed early, how long the wait for a hearing runs. St. Louis County is a different experience from St. Charles or Jefferson County under identical statutes.
### Q. We live on opposite sides of the river. Which state hears the case?
A.  Worth an early consultation, because Missouri and Illinois answer several of these differently — the parenting-time presumption and spousal maintenance most of all. Both states require ninety days of residence before a dissolution judgment. Which court decides the children’s issues turns on the child’s home state under the interstate custody act both states have adopted.
None of this makes the year easier. It does make the first phone call shorter, and it keeps you from paying by the tenth of an hour to have a parenting plan explained. Write down what you actually want on the other side of this — the schedule, the house, the retirement account, the holidays — before anybody asks you in a conference room.

## Party Equipment Rentals in St. Louis: What to Ask Before You Book
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-ask-before-booking-party-rentals-st-louis
Imagine it’s the middle of April and the graduation party in Affton just became your problem. The date is fixed. Forty-some people said yes. The backyard is a backyard — a grill, a swing set, a patch of grass that has never held a crowd.
Maybe your version is a fall wedding on a rented lawn in St. Charles, where the ceremony chairs have to be dry at four o’clock. Maybe it’s a church picnic in Florissant, a company family day in Maryland Heights, or a sixtieth birthday in Belleville where half the guests will not stand for three hours. Same phone call.
Here’s the part nobody warns you about. Picking the tent is the easy half. The half that decides how the day runs is a short list of questions asked before any money changes hands.
### What should you ask before you book party equipment rentals?
Six questions, before the deposit. What is the delivery and pickup window? Does the crew set up and tear down, or is this a drop-off? What surface will the tent sit on? What is the weather and cancellation policy, in writing? Who pulls the permit? And what does the damage waiver actually cover?
Those six aren’t arbitrary. They map to the six ways a rental goes sideways. The truck shows up at 7 a.m. Saturday when you wanted Friday. The chairs land stacked on the driveway and setup was extra. The tent can’t be staked because the only flat ground is asphalt. It rains and the deposit is gone. An inspector wants a permit nobody applied for. Get the answers by email.
### What size tent do you need for 100 guests?
For 100 guests seated at round tables, plan on roughly 1,200 square feet of tent — a 30x40 is the bare minimum, and most rental companies will move you up to a 40x60 once you add a buffet line, a bar and any dance floor. A standing cocktail crowd of 100 fits in far less, closer to 600 square feet, because nobody needs a chair or a place to set a plate.
The arithmetic is simple enough to do yourself. Companies size from square feet per person, not headcount: roughly 12 square feet for a guest at a round table, about 8 for ceremony rows, 5 or 6 for standing. Multiply, then add the footprint of anything that isn’t a person.
What size tent do I need for 50 guests? Half the people, roughly half the ground: about 600 square feet seated, which puts a 20x30 at the floor and a 20x40 in comfortable territory. Give them the guest count, the seating style and the extras, then ask them to confirm it fits your yard with room to stake.
### What are the most rented items for parties?
Tables, chairs, linens and tents carry most of the volume in this trade, in that order. They are what nearly every event needs, which is why a rental yard’s chair count is the truest measure of how big it is.
After that come the things that make an event feel finished. Sidewalls and tent lighting for anything running past dusk. Cocktail tables, which quietly reduce how many chairs you need. Chafing dishes, ice tubs, dance floors, portable restrooms for open ground. Heaters in October and fans in July, both of which sell out the same week the weather turns.
Then the family category: inflatables, concession machines, yard games and a sound system somebody’s uncle will take over. If the party is for kids, the bounce house gets booked first — and it carries the most rules.
### Does the price include setup, or is it a drop-off?
Ask directly, because both are common and they price differently. A drop-off means the crew unloads at the curb and leaves; you carry, unfold and stack. Full setup means they place the tables, open the chairs, stake the tent, and return to break it down. Plenty of companies do setup on tents and drop-off on everything else.
Then pin down the window. Most companies deliver on a range, not a time — a four-hour block, sometimes an all-day one. For a Saturday event that often means a Friday delivery and a Monday pickup, and that weekend-long possession is baked into the rate whether you use it or not. Say so up front if your park shelter has to be clear by dark.
### Do you need a permit for a tent in St. Louis?
Inside the City of St. Louis, yes, above a size threshold. The city’s tent and temporary structure policy requires a permit for tents greater than 800 square feet in total area, including multiple tents attached to one another with an aggregate area greater than 800 square feet. Any tent that affects, covers or obstructs a required means of egress needs approval regardless of size. Tents under 800 square feet that block nothing are exempt, as are tents for a private family event on the same residential lot.
Notice where that leaves a 20x40. It is exactly 800 square feet, right on the line, and attaching a 10x10 caterer’s canopy puts the aggregate over. Two other city rules catch people out: fabric has to be flame resistant with a certificate, and tents must be placed on grass so they can be staked — not on pavement. If your only flat ground is a parking lot, the conversation shifts to ballast, and ballast means weight, labor and a different price.
Outside the city limits, the threshold is whatever the local building or fire office says it is — St. Louis County, St. Charles County, Kirkwood and the Illinois municipalities all run their own. Ask the rental company who pulls it. Good operators handle it routinely, but the customer is responsible for all permits is a real sentence in real contracts.
Wildly off-topic — the graduate needs a haircut before the photos.
### Do bounce houses need a permit in Missouri or Illinois?
This is a genuine state-line split, and it matters if your event is in Belleville rather than Ballwin. Illinois regulates inflatables by name: the Illinois Department of Labor’s Amusement Ride and Attraction Safety Division lists inflatable attractions — moonwalks and bounce houses — among equipment that must be inspected before initial operation and annually after, with a permit decal affixed to each unit. Illinois permits run the calendar year.
The rule follows public use, not the equipment. IDOL’s FAQ is explicit that someone who rents an inflatable for a private party does not need a permit; the obligation sits with the owner operating it publicly. IDOL also sets a minimum operator age of 16 and a $1,000,000 per occurrence, $2,000,000 aggregate insurance requirement for permitted operations.
Missouri is different. Its Amusement Ride Safety Act, at RSMo 316.203, defines an amusement ride as mechanical devices that carry passengers, dry slides over 20 feet, trams and motorized wagons, bungee attractions, and climbing walls over 10 feet. Inflatables are not named. So in Illinois, ask to see the current decal. In Missouri there is no state decal — ask instead for the certificate of insurance, the manufacturer’s posted rider limits, and whether an attendant stays.
### What happens if it rains on the day of your event?
Usually the event goes on and the deposit does not come back. Most rental contracts treat a deposit as non-refundable once equipment is loaded, since the item was off the shelf and unavailable to anyone else. That is why the tent is the rain plan rather than a casualty of it.
Three things to settle in writing: how late you can move the date and whether the deposit travels with it, what happens if the crew judges conditions unsafe, and whether sidewalls can be added last minute. Wind is the real decision point, not rain — crews will strike or refuse to raise a tent in gusts, and no reputable operator negotiates that.
If the site is a park, a rented lawn or one of the campgrounds around St. Louis, check its own rules on staking and vehicle access first.
### How can I reduce the cost of party rentals?
Shrink the tent, shrink the chair count, and widen the delivery window — in that order. Those are the three biggest levers, and none of them costs you anything the guests will notice.
It helps to know what drives the number. Tent size and anchoring is the largest single factor: staking into grass is quick, ballasting on pavement adds weights, labor and time. A tight delivery window costs more than a flexible one. Weekend dates carry a premium in peak months because inventory is finite. Damage waivers are usually a percentage add-on, so they scale with everything else on the order.
Practical cuts: move the buffet and the bar outside the tent so you are not renting square footage to shelter a table. Swap a third of the seating for cocktail tables. Use one vendor rather than two delivery fees. And ask what is already going out that weekend — a size sitting idle sometimes prices better.
### How far ahead should you book for graduation and wedding season?
As soon as the date is fixed, and earlier than feels necessary. Late April through early June is graduation season across the metro, and September and October carry the fall weddings. Those weekends are when tent inventory runs out first, and a rental yard cannot conjure a second 40x60 the way a caterer adds a tray.
Chairs and tables usually survive a late request. Tents, dance floors, heaters and specialty linen colors do not. Weekday and Sunday dates hold availability much longer. If the event is a wedding, the rental calendar and the bridal shop timeline in St. Louis run on the same months, and both reward booking early for the same reason: finite stock, fixed dates.
### Are event rentals profitable?
They can be, and the shape of it surprises people. The American Rental Association’s May 8, 2026 forecast, built with S&P Global Market Intelligence, put the U.S. event rental industry on track to grow 8 percent in 2026 to $6.1 billion. But the margin isn’t where customers assume. A big frame tent is capital that pays back across seasons, not on one weekend. Linens carry the best percentage and the worst labor, because somebody launders and folds every one between events. The money is really made or lost on the truck — how many stops a two-person crew clears in a window.
The year is made in two stretches, graduations and fall weddings, and January is quiet enough to hurt. What operators grumble about is short: the Saturday-in-May call placed ten days out, and the tent booked for a driveway that cannot be staked. ### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it cheaper to rent a tent or a venue?
A.  A tent is cheaper on the invoice and more expensive in everything else. A venue rolls tables, chairs, restrooms, power, parking and a rain plan into one number. A tent covers ground and nothing more, so the honest comparison adds everything you put under it plus the labor of running the day yourself.
### Q. How much does it cost to rent a 20x20 event tent?
A.  Ask for a written quote rather than trusting a number off the internet. The same 20x20 prices differently depending on how it is anchored, how tight the delivery window is, and whether the date falls in peak season. Staking into grass is cheapest; ballasting on pavement adds weights and labor. Sidewalls, lighting and the damage waiver move it further.
### Q. How much do chair rentals typically cost?
A.  Chairs price per chair, and that figure is only part of it. Style matters most — a white folding chair, a resin garden chair and a wooden crossback are three tiers. Then delivery, whether the crew sets them out or leaves them stacked, the waiver, and quantity. Ask for the all-in total, delivered.
### Q. Is it cheaper to buy or rent a bounce house?
A.  Renting wins unless you use one many times a year. A purchased inflatable brings storage, a blower, cleaning, patching and the setup you were paying someone else to do. It also brings the liability: a rental company carries insurance, checks anchoring, and in Illinois must hold a current state permit for public use.
### Q. Are bounce house rentals worth it?
A.  For a party with young kids it is usually the one item that earns its price, because it occupies the guests you were most worried about. The value drops fast if the yard is wrong — not enough flat space, no anchor points, a long carry from the truck. Confirm footprint, power and surface before booking.
### Q. What age is appropriate for a bounce house?
A.  Go by the unit, not a general rule. Every commercial inflatable carries a manufacturer placard listing age, height and weight limits and the maximum riders at once, and that placard governs. The practical rule operators use is to keep sizes separated, since little kids and big kids bouncing together is where injuries come from.
### Q. Where can I rent an event tent in St. Louis, MO?
A.  Search party equipment rentals by your municipality rather than the whole metro, since delivery zones and fees are drawn tightly around a company’s yard. A vendor twenty minutes closer often quotes better than a bigger name across the river. Ask each the same three things: tent size, anchoring, and their written weather policy.
### Q. How much does an inflatable bounce house cost to rent?
A.  Ask for the number as a day rate plus delivery, because those are quoted separately and the delivery half moves with your address. Size and type drive the rest: a plain bounce unit sits at the bottom, combo units with a slide cost more, and water units and larger obstacle setups cost the most. Expect the quote to change with the length of the rental window, whether an attendant is included, generator rental if the yard has no outlet within reach, and a surcharge for stairs or a long carry. Get all of it in writing before you put down a deposit.

## How to Book a Campsite Near St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-book-a-campsite-near-st-louis
Imagine it’s a Wednesday in March and somebody in the group chat types “let’s camp Memorial Day weekend.” Six people react with a thumbs up. Nobody books anything. Then it’s the second week of May, you finally open the reservation site, and every electric site within ninety minutes of Kirkwood is spoken for.
Maybe your version is different. You bought a used travel trailer off a driveway in Florissant over the winter and you still aren’t sure whether the cord coming out the back is 30 amp or 50. Or the kids are seven and four, nobody in the house has ever slept in a tent, and you want a first night out close enough to Affton that bailing at midnight is still an option.
Camping around here is genuinely easy. The booking is where people get burned, because the two states on either side of the river run separate systems, open their calendars at different times, cap your stay differently, and price a night outdoors far enough apart that the bridge is worth crossing.
### What is the best campground near St. Louis?
There isn’t a single best one, and any list that names one is guessing for you. The best campground near St. Louis is whichever one matches three things: what you sleep in, how far ahead you booked, and whether you need a shower. Sort by those and the field narrows fast.
On the Missouri side, the close ring of state park campgrounds includes Dr. Edmund A. Babler Memorial State Park at 800 Guy Park Drive in Wildwood, Robertsville State Park where the Meramec River and Calvey Creek meet in Franklin County, and Meramec State Park at 115 Meramec Park Drive in Sullivan, which puts Fisher Cave and river access in the same trip. Cuivre River State Park north of Troy and Washington State Park south of De Soto fill out the arc.
Cross the river and the math changes. Pere Marquette State Park in Grafton runs 80 reservable Class A sites with 20, 30 and 50 amp service and a shower building, plus non-reservable Class B tent sites. Eldon Hazlet State Recreation Area on Carlyle Lake is bigger than anything close on the Missouri side: 328 Class A sites with 30 and 50 amp hookups, 36 walk-in Class C tent sites and three shower buildings. Closest of all is Horseshoe Lake State Park in Madison, Illinois — 26 tent or trailer sites, a dump station, pit toilets and water hydrants, normally open May 1 through September 30 with no reservations taken. Heads up: IDNR has the campground and its road closed until May 2027 for causeway work, so check its alerts before you plan on it.
### How much does it cost to camp at a Missouri state park?
On the 2026 on-season chart, which covers April 1 through October 31, most Missouri state parks charge $15 a night for a basic or walk-in site, $27 for a 30-amp electric site and $29 for 50-amp. Electric and water together runs about $35. A full sewer, electric and water site lands between $42 and $57 depending on the park.
Backcountry sites are $10. A few parks sit below the common rate — Echo Bluff starts at $13 basic, St. Joe at $12 — and a few sit a dollar or two above. Off-season, November 1 through March 31, the same tiers drop to roughly $14 basic, $23 for 30 amp and $25 for 50 amp.
Add the booking cost on top. Missouri charges $6.50 per campsite reserved online, $8 through the call center at 877-422-6766, $5.25 to change a reservation and $10 to cancel one, with the original reservation fee forfeited either way. A $2 per night discount applies year-round for campers 65 and older, people with disabilities, and current, former and active-duty military families.
### How far ahead do campsite reservations open?
Missouri opens 12 months out. Illinois opens six. That one difference decides more summer weekends than anything else on this page. Missouri State Parks takes reservations starting at 7 a.m. Central Time exactly one year before your first night, so a Memorial Day site is claimable the previous May.
Illinois DNR releases sites 180 days ahead through ExploreMoreIL, also at 7 a.m. Central. Illinois also refuses last-minute bookings: a reservation has to be made at least three days before you need the site. Missouri goes the other direction and accepts same-day reservations up to 7 p.m. on your arrival date, with no reservation fee charged on those.
Length of stay is capped on both sides. Missouri limits you to any 15 days within a 30-consecutive-day period at one park under 10 CSR 90-2.030. Illinois caps reservations at 14 nights per 30-day period, and Horseshoe Lake tightens that to seven days in 30. The Illinois reservation fee is $5, non-refundable, and camping fees are refunded if you cancel three days out.
### What does a campsite fee actually include?
A basic Missouri state park site buys you a parking pad, a table, a grill and a lantern post. That is the whole list. Electric adds a 30- or 50-amp power supply, electric and water adds a private water hookup, and the top tier adds a sewer connection. Everything else — shelter, bedding, light, water containers, a way to cook — comes out of your car.
Illinois builds the fee the same way but shows the math on the receipt. Its published schedule splits each night into a camping fee plus a $10 utility fee, so a Class A site with showers, electricity and vehicle access is $10 plus $10, or $20 a night. Class B/E, electricity and vehicle access without showers, is $18. Class B/S, showers without electricity, is $10. Class C is $8 and Class D primitive tent sites are $6. Holiday weekends push Class A to $30.
Neither state charges you to drive through the gate. Illinois DNR says outright that it “does not charge an Entrance Fee to any state owned or operated land.” Missouri funds about three-fourths of its state park budget with the one-tenth of 1% Parks, Soils and Water Sales Tax, which voters renewed in 2026 with roughly 82% approval.
Nothing to do with tents — St. Louis gyms are here too.
### Do you need 30 amp or 50 amp, and does water come with it?
Check the cord before you book, not at the pedestal. A 50-amp rig plugged into a 30-amp site through an adapter is still limited to 30 amps, which in a St. Louis August usually means one air conditioner instead of two. Missouri lists more than 1,200 campsites with 50-amp service, and those pedestals carry 30 amp too, so the bigger site fits either rig.
Water is the part newcomers misread. On Missouri electric/water and sewer/electric/water sites, the private hookup runs only during the park’s on-season. Book one of those in February and you have paid for a spigot that isn’t running. Electric hookups, by contrast, stay live year-round at most Missouri parks.
Illinois handles the same problem with a price cut. Its published rule is that when cold weather forces buildings closed and water shut off in Class AA, A, A-P, B/S or B/S-P campgrounds, the fee drops to match what is actually available for use. Call the park office before any winter trip; that is the only reliable way to learn which shower house is open.
### What closes for the season, and what stays open?
Most campgrounds within reach of St. Louis stay open all winter at the lower off-season rate. What closes is the plumbing. Missouri’s 2026 off-season chart lists Babler, Robertsville, Meramec, Cuivre River, Hawn, Washington, St. Francois, Onondaga Cave and Graham Cave as available every day of the off-season. The system runs more than 3,500 campsites in all.
Illinois splits its year into a May 1 through September 30 spring and summer period and an October 1 through April 30 fall and winter period, and says camping is generally available year-round, weather permitting. Individual campgrounds are the exception that matters — Horseshoe Lake State Park’s campground runs May 1 to September 30 and nothing else, and it is closed until May 2027 for causeway work.
Three Missouri parks start early rather than late. Roaring River, Bennett Spring and Montauk open their on-season February 25 because trout season does, and Table Rock runs March through November. None are day trips from the metro, but they answer the March weekend where you want the water actually on.
### What does a first-time camper actually need?
Sleep warm, then worry about the rest. Ground pulls heat out of a body far faster than air does, so an insulated sleeping pad does more for an April or October night around here than upgrading your sleeping bag. Add a tent with a full rainfly, two light sources per person, and more water than you think you need — the site’s hydrant may be a walk away, or shut off entirely.
Know the site’s limits before you pack. A typical Missouri state park campsite allows two sleeping units, only one of which can be wheeled, two non-sleeping vehicles and six people. Quiet hours run 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. Check-in starts at 3 p.m., checkout is 2 p.m., and you have to arrive within the first 24 hours of the stay. Leashes are capped at 10 feet, with two dogs per site recommended.
Buy firewood, don’t forage it. Missouri State Parks asks campers not to gather or cut firewood in the parks, so plan on a bundle from the park store or a stand down the road. If you are planning a bigger trip around a camping leg, lock the campsite dates first — those are the ones with a release date you cannot negotiate.
### What campground owners around here wish campers knew
A campground makes its year in roughly fourteen weekends. Memorial Day through Labor Day carries the season, a few October leaf weekends help, and a rained-out Fourth of July cannot be made up in November. That is why monthly and seasonal sites exist: they fill Monday through Thursday when transient campers don’t come. A monthly site near $800 works out around $27 a night, well under a summer weekend rate. That trade buys stability, not profit.
Booking the site is the easy half — here is what outdoor gear you actually need in St. Louis before you go.
The margin lives in the small stuff — firewood, ice, propane, laundry, the store — because the site itself has to cover a septic system, a well, gravel and mowing whether anyone is on it or not. What operators complain about to each other is holiday no-shows and August electric bills, when every rig on the property runs air conditioning at once. Being listed with accurate hookup amperage, pad length and season dates saves both sides that phone call, which is most of why owners keep a complete listing current.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the 200 rule for camping?
A.  It’s the Leave No Trace guideline to camp at least 200 feet from lakes and streams — described as 70 to 80 adult steps — so riparian ground stays intact and wildlife keeps its access routes to water. The same buffer applies to washing dishes and burying waste. It governs backcountry and dispersed camping, not developed campgrounds, where you pitch on the pad the park assigns you.
### Q. What is the 3-3-3 rule for camping?
A.  It’s an RV travelers’ rule of thumb, not a regulation anybody enforces: drive no more than 300 miles in a day, be parked by 3 p.m., and stay at least three nights before moving again. The enforceable limits are different. Missouri caps camping at any 15 days within 30 consecutive days at one park, and Illinois caps reservations at 14 nights per 30-day period.
### Q. Are there any free campgrounds near St. Louis, Missouri?
A.  Not inside the metro. The closest genuinely free option is dispersed camping in Mark Twain National Forest, where you camp outside any developed campground with no fee and no permit required, typically for up to 14 days in a 30-day span. The nearest ground is the Potosi/Fredericktown Ranger District south of the metro. There is no pad, no toilet and no water, so check the district’s motor vehicle use map first.
### Q. What is the cheapest campground?
A.  Among developed sites near St. Louis, Illinois undercuts Missouri. A Class D primitive tent site on Illinois DNR land is $6 a night and a Class C site with vehicle access is $8, against $15 for a typical Missouri basic site and $10 for a Missouri backcountry site. Add $5 to reserve in Illinois or $6.50 online in Missouri. Free means dispersed national forest camping, with nothing provided.
### Q. How much do campsites cost per week?
A.  Public parks don’t discount by the week — it’s the nightly rate times seven, plus one reservation fee. Seven nights on a Missouri 30-amp electric site works out to about $189 plus $6.50 online. Seven nights on an Illinois Class A site is about $140 plus $5. Private RV parks around the metro do post weekly rates, commonly between $175 and $375 depending on hookups, as advertised in August 2026.
### Q. How much do most campgrounds cost per month?
A.  Around $800 a month for a full-hookup site at a private RV park in the St. Louis area, checked in August 2026, with electricity often metered separately on top. Public campgrounds are not an option for monthly stays at all: Missouri state parks cap you at 15 days in any 30, and Illinois caps reservations at 14 nights per 30-day period.
### Q. Can I just show up, or do I have to reserve?
A.  It depends on which side of the river. Missouri State Parks accepts same-day reservations up to 7 p.m. on your arrival date and waives the reservation fee on those. Illinois requires bookings at least three days ahead, so a spur-of-the-moment Illinois trip means a first-come campground — Horseshoe Lake State Park in Madison takes no camping reservations at all, May 1 through September 30, once its campground reopens in May 2027.

## When a Travel Agent Is Worth It in St. Louis (and When to Book It Yourself)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/when-to-use-a-travel-agent-st-louis
Imagine it’s a Sunday night in Kirkwood and there are eleven browser tabs open. Two of them are the same hotel at two different prices. Your mother-in-law needs a ground-floor room, your brother is flying in from Denver, and the whole thing has to land in one week in June or it doesn’t happen at all.
Maybe your version starts in Belleville, where a cruise deposit is due Friday and nobody agrees on the cabin. Maybe it’s St. Charles, and you’re pricing nine days in Italy for four adults and a nine-year-old. Maybe you’re in Florissant holding a passport that expires in five months, with a wedding in Mexico already on the calendar.
Here’s the honest part. For a nonstop to Phoenix and three nights at a chain hotel, you do not need a travel agent, and anyone who says otherwise is selling. You’ll book it faster yourself. The trips above are a different animal — many moving parts, real money, and a decent chance of a 2 a.m. problem somewhere you don’t speak the language. Here’s how to tell which trip you have.
### How can I choose a reliable travel agency?
Ask three questions before you hand over a deposit: how do you get paid, what do you book most, and what happens if something goes wrong while I’m gone. A working advisor answers all three in about a minute. Vague answers on money are the loudest warning sign in this business.
Then check the mechanics. Pay by credit card — never by wire, Zelle, Venmo or personal check, which strip away your dispute rights. Ask for the supplier’s own confirmation number, not just the agency invoice, and log in to the cruise line or tour operator site yourself to confirm the booking exists. Get cancellation and change penalties in writing before you pay.
Finally, hire for the trip you’re taking. An advisor who books forty river cruises a year knows which cabins sit above the engine, and may be no better than you at a national-park road trip. Specialization is the real credential.
### How does a travel agent actually get paid?
Two ways, and most advisors use both. The first is commission paid by the supplier — the cruise line, tour operator, hotel or insurer — out of the price you were going to pay anyway. The second is a fee you pay directly, usually called a planning, consultation or service fee. Neither is a markup on the published fare.
The timing is the part almost nobody knows. Supplier commission is generally paid after you travel, not when you book, and if you cancel it is clawed back. It also applies only to the commissionable portion of a fare — port charges, taxes and prepaid gratuities usually pay nothing. Most independent advisors work under a host agency that holds the industry accreditation and keeps a slice of every commission.
Air is the exception that explains the planning fee. Delta ended base commissions on tickets sold in the United States and Canada in March 2002, and the rest of the industry followed within months. More than twenty years later, booking your domestic flights still pays an advisor essentially nothing — which is why fee-charging became normal rather than rude.
### Is it actually cheaper to use a travel agent?
Usually it’s the same price, sometimes it’s better value, and if you pay a planning fee the trip costs more by exactly that fee. Cruise lines, tour operators and most hotel brands hold advisors to the same published rates you see online, so the fantasy of a secret cheaper price is mostly a fantasy. What does move is what comes bundled with the price.
Where an advisor earns it back is in extras and errors. Onboard credit, a group amenity, a cabin upgrade at the same fare, a resort credit — those are real and supplier-funded. So is the mistake you didn’t make: the connection that was legal on paper and impossible in practice, the visa nobody mentioned, the shore excursion booked so tight a late tender leaves you on the dock. Say your budget plainly. An advisor who won’t work inside a number is telling you something useful.
### When is booking direct genuinely the better call?
Book it yourself when the trip is one flight and one hotel, when you’d happily rebook the whole thing in eight minutes, when you’re chasing status that only credits on a direct booking, or when a planning fee would be a meaningful slice of the trip. A weekend in Chicago or Branson does not need a professional.
Booking direct with the airline also gets you one rule an agency cannot. Under 14 CFR 259.5, a covered U.S. carrier must either hold a reservation at the quoted fare without payment, or allow cancellation without penalty, for at least 24 hours — but only if you booked seven or more days before departure. That obligation sits on the airline, not on ticket agents, so the same 24-hour grace is not guaranteed on a third-party booking.
### What do ASTA, IATA and CLIA after a name actually mean?
They are trade credentials, not government licenses, and knowing the difference protects you. ASTA is the American Society of Travel Advisors, the industry’s main trade association; members agree to its code of ethics, and membership is voluntary. An IATA or IATAN number is supplier accreditation, not a consumer safeguard — IATA’s own ID card eligibility rules ask only that a U.S. applicant work at least 20 hours a week in travel sales and have earned $5,000 in salary or commission over the past 12 months. CLIA is the cruise trade body and runs its own cruise-selling certifications.
Only four states register sellers of travel — California, Florida, Washington and Hawaii — and neither Missouri nor Illinois issues a travel agent license the way it licenses a real estate broker. Illinois does regulate the money, though. Under the Travel Promotion Consumer Protection Act, a travel promoter must deposit 90 percent of all sums received into a trust account at a federally insured bank, and may not draw on it except to pay the carriers and suppliers you contracted for or to issue refunds. Missouri has no travel-specific statute like it, which is a real difference between an agency in Edwardsville and one in Chesterfield.
Unrelated, and we know it — that airline-seat backache may want a chiropractor.
### What does travel insurance cover, and what does it not?
A comprehensive policy typically pays for trip cancellation and interruption for a list of named covered reasons, emergency medical treatment and medical evacuation abroad, and baggage problems. The National Association of Insurance Commissioners puts typical policy cost at 5 to 10 percent of the trip price. The medical piece is underrated: standard Medicare generally does not travel outside the United States, and an air ambulance home from a cruise port is a five-figure event.
The exclusions are broader than people expect. The NAIC lists pre-existing health conditions, pandemics, civil and political unrest, pregnancy and childbirth, and high-risk activities among the common ones. Changing your mind, or a storm already named when you bought, is usually out too. Some plans waive the pre-existing exclusion, but only if you buy soon after your first trip payment and insure the full nonrefundable cost — the insurer sets that window, so ask for it in writing.
Two traps worth naming. Cancel For Any Reason is an optional upgrade that reimburses a portion of your nonrefundable cost, not all of it — NAIC puts the usual range at 50 to 75 percent — and it carries its own purchase deadline. And the Illinois Department of Insurance warns that a cancellation waiver sold at checkout is not an insurance policy and is not regulated by the department. No policy and no advisor can guarantee a claim gets paid; the policy language decides that.
### What happens when something goes wrong mid-trip?
Federal rules cover the airline half, and they reach your travel agent too. Under the U.S. Department of Transportation’s 2024 refunds rule, now at 14 CFR Part 260, you are owed a refund when a flight is cancelled or significantly changed and you don’t accept what’s offered instead. Significant means departure or arrival moved three or more hours domestically, six or more internationally, plus different airports, added connections or a downgrade. Refunds are due within seven business days on a credit card and 20 calendar days on other payment methods — and when the ticket agent took your payment, the rule makes the airline push the money back to them.
Your credit card is the second layer. The Fair Credit Billing Act gives you the right to dispute a billing error in writing within 60 days of the statement on which it appeared, and the issuer must acknowledge and investigate. That is why a big tour deposit belongs on a card, and what a wire transfer throws away.
The third layer is a person. Rules do not rebook you; someone has to. When a sailing is cancelled or a hurricane closes an airport, an advisor works a trade line while you stand in a queue of four hundred people dialing the same number. That is what you’re buying on a multi-generation trip, a destination wedding, or a cruise where a missed connection means the ship leaves without you.
### What running a travel agency actually looks like
The money arrives long after the work does. An advisor sells a November cruise in January, does every hour of the labor in January, and collects commission after the ship sails — and if the client cancels, that commission is recalled. That single fact shapes the trade. It is why wave season, roughly January through March, is the stretch that makes or breaks the year, and why air-only requests are the quiet complaint in every agent group chat: since base commissions ended in 2002, four hours rebuilding your flights pays nothing. Most independents run under a host agency that holds the accreditation and keeps a share of each commission, so take-home is smaller than the headline percentage. The client good operators dread is the one who asks for a full itinerary and then books it online. Because people search for this help locally, keeping a complete listing is how a small agency gets found at all.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it actually cheaper to use a travel agent?
A.  Rarely cheaper on the sticker price, often better value, and more expensive by exactly the fee if you pay one. Cruise lines, tour operators and hotel brands hold advisors to the same published rates you can see yourself. The gap shows up as supplier-funded extras — onboard credit, a better cabin at the same fare — and as the expensive mistake you avoided.
### Q. What is a normal fee for a travel agent?
A.  There isn’t one national number, and treat any figure you read as a guess about somebody else’s business. Fees are set per advisor and scale with complexity: a flat charge for one hotel booking, more for a multi-country itinerary or a group. Ask how much, what it covers, and whether it is credited back if you book — before any research starts.
### Q. What is the average cost of using a travel agent?
A.  For most leisure bookings the direct cost is zero, because the advisor is paid a commission by the cruise line, tour operator or hotel out of the fare you were already paying. Where a planning fee applies, it is disclosed up front, before work begins. The real question is not the average — it is what this advisor charges you, in writing.
### Q. How much does a travel agent make on a $10,000 trip?
A.  It depends entirely on what the $10,000 is made of. Only the commissionable portion pays — port charges, taxes and prepaid gratuities usually don’t, and domestic airfare pays essentially nothing since base commissions ended in 2002. Whatever the supplier does pay is split with the host agency and lands after travel, not at booking. Cancel and it is taken back.
### Q. Who are the best travel agents in St. Louis?
A.  There is no single best one, because the right advisor depends on the product. Pick for specialization: someone who sells river cruises weekly, or Disney weekly, or Italy weekly, beats a generalist on your specific trip. Ask how many of your exact product they sold this year, how they are paid, and who answers at 2 a.m. overseas.
### Q. Who are some good travel agents in St. Charles, MO?
A.  Search by your side of the metro, then screen on the same three questions rather than on the storefront. Plenty of advisors in St. Charles County work from home under a host agency and never open a storefront — normal in 2026, not a red flag. What matters is who they book, how they charge, and whether they hand you the supplier’s own confirmation number.
### Q. Do I need travel insurance if my credit card already has it?
A.  Sometimes, but read the card benefit guide first. Card coverage is usually secondary, capped well below a big trip’s cost, and often triggered only if you charged the full fare to that card. It also rarely includes medical evacuation, the expensive part of an overseas emergency. Compare the card’s covered reasons and limits against a standalone policy.

## St. Louis Auction Houses: What to Know Before You Bid or Consign
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-auction-houses-work-st-louis
Picture a Thursday night in Affton. Laptop open on the kitchen table, a timed online auction closing in eleven minutes, and a walnut dresser sitting at $85 with two other bidders circling it. Your pulse is doing something ridiculous over a piece of furniture you have never touched.
Now picture the other end of the same business. A family in Florissant has to have a parent’s house empty by the thirtieth. Forty years of belongings, three siblings with three opinions, nobody sleeping well. Somebody says the word “auction” and everyone nods, because it sounds like a plan and nobody has a better one.
Both of those people are about to agree to the same document without reading it: the terms of sale. That one page decides what the dresser actually costs, what the family actually nets, and when the money lands. Here is how auction houses work across the St. Louis metro from both sides of the paddle — buying and selling — and what to check before you commit to either.
### How do I find a reputable auction house?
Start with the license, because that is the piece you can verify in about five minutes. In Illinois, auctioneers and auction firms are licensed by the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation under the Auction License Act, 225 ILCS 407, and IDFPR runs a public license lookup. In Missouri, auctioneers are licensed county by county under RSMo Chapter 343 rather than by a state board, so you ask the county, not Jefferson City.
Missouri’s rule is not decorative.
