Under Section 144.049, RSMo, the exemption covers clothing at $100 or less per item, school supplies up to $50 per purchase, computers and peripherals up to $1,500, computer software at $350 or less, and graphing calculators at $150 or less.
The second is the Show Me Green sales tax holiday, April 19 through 25 every year under Section 144.526.1, RSMo. It exempts qualifying new ENERGY STAR certified appliances from all state and local sales and use taxes, up to $1,500 per appliance, covering clothes washers and dryers, water heaters, trash compactors, dishwashers, conventional ovens, ranges, stoves, air conditioners, furnaces, refrigerators and freezers. If you have been limping along on a dying washer, that is the week to walk an appliance floor.
Both are Missouri laws, so they apply to purchases made in Missouri. They do not follow you across the river. A family in Belleville or Edwardsville that wants the break on a laptop or a refrigerator has to buy on the Missouri side during those dates, which is worth a look at the map before you pick a store.
### What does this look like from behind the counter?
The ticket price was never the plan. Buyers set initial markup knowing a large share of the goods will sell at markdown, so the number that decides a season is maintained margin at the end of it, not what the tag says in week one. Cosmetics and fragrance carry the floor — fast turns, repeat customers, and counters frequently staffed or subsidized by the brand rather than the store. Fine jewelry and appliances are where one sale rescues a slow afternoon. The store card is no courtesy either; the credit program is its own profit line. November and December decide the year, January is returns and re-ticketing, and back-to-school is the second season. What operators grumble about to each other is return abuse and the pickup counter, where online orders turn floor staff into pickers without adding an hour of payroll. Independents feel all of it harder, which is why a complete listing matters — it is how a shopper finds a store that is not on a mall directory board.
Not sure which store still carries what you need? Browse department stores across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call the one nearest you and ask for the department, not the front desk. A new kitchen usually starts long before the appliance floor - see what a kitchen remodel actually costs here.
If you run a store that still has real departments and people in them, list your store with us so shoppers calling around can find you.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What were some of the old department stores in St. Louis?
A.  Famous-Barr is the name most people reach for — a St. Louis institution under the May Department Stores Company. Stix, Baer & Fuller was the other local giant; Dillard’s took over its stores and the South County location carried the Dillard’s name from 1984. Lord & Taylor anchored West County Center until it closed in June 2006, and Sears anchor boxes across the metro have since gone dark, including the one at Mid Rivers Mall.
### Q. What happened to Famous Barr?
A.  It became Macy’s. Federated Department Stores acquired the May Department Stores Company on August 30, 2005, and on September 9, 2006 the Famous-Barr nameplate was retired along with Filene’s, Foley’s, Hecht’s, Kaufmann’s, Marshall Field’s and the rest of the May regional banners, all converted to Macy’s. The stores did not close that day; the sign changed. Several of those buildings, including the Galleria store that opened as Famous-Barr in 1991, still operate as Macy’s.
### Q. Is Macy’s or Dillard’s higher end?
A.  Neither is a clean answer, because it depends on the store and the department. Dillard’s tends to run a deeper better-brand assortment and less aggressive everyday discounting, so full-price tickets often read higher. Macy’s runs a heavier promotional and coupon cadence and folds a Backstage clearance shop into some locations. Compare the specific department you care about at the specific address, not the logos.
### Q. Which mall in St. Louis is considered the best?
A.  It depends what you need. The Saint Louis Galleria in Richmond Heights is the largest at about 1.2 million square feet and pairs the metro’s biggest department-store footprints, with Dillard’s near 330,000 square feet and Macy’s around 265,000. West County Center in Des Peres is the only one still listing a Nordstrom. On the Illinois side, St. Clair Square in Fairview Heights keeps three department stores under one roof.
### Q. What are the best shopping areas in St. Louis?
A.  For department stores, the clusters are Richmond Heights, Des Peres, Mehlville, St. Peters and Fairview Heights, Illinois. For independent shops it is a different map: the walkable business districts in Kirkwood, Maplewood, Webster Groves, the Delmar Loop, Cherokee Street and Historic Main Street in St. Charles. Most locals end up using both — the anchors for services and sizes, the districts for anything they want to be unusual.
### Q. Can I return an online order at a department store counter?
A.  Usually yes for items the retailer sold itself, and that is the fastest refund you will get. Bring the packing slip or pull up the order in the app. The exceptions worth knowing: marketplace items shipped by a third-party seller often have to go back by mail, and large items such as appliances and mattresses typically follow a separate policy with its own window and possible fees. Check the order confirmation before you load the car.
### Q. Do department stores still do alterations and gift wrap?
A.  Many do, but it varies store by store and is no longer a safe assumption. Alterations are usually attached to menswear and formalwear, with a fee schedule and a turnaround measured in days rather than hours — call before a wedding week. Gift wrap desks come and go with seasonal staffing. Phone the department directly and ask about cost and turnaround before you buy the garment.

## How to Buy a Mattress in St. Louis Without Getting Worked Over
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/mattress-buying-guide-st-louis
Imagine it’s a Tuesday night in Affton and you’ve rolled, again, into the trench your body carved down the middle of the bed. Your partner has done the same from the other side. You meet in the valley. Nobody sleeps. Somebody finally says it out loud — we need a new mattress — and the room goes quiet, because you both know what Saturday looks like.
Saturday goes like this. A showroom in Kirkwood, where a pleasant person walks you to three beds and quotes a number already marked down twice. A stop on Mid Rivers in St. Charles, where a bed that feels identical carries a different model name and a different number. Then a laptop in Florissant, full of foam rectangles that ship in a box.
By dinner you have three model names that line up against nothing and a growing suspicion the whole thing is rigged. You’re not imagining it. The trade spent decades building a pricing system designed to stop you comparing anything. Here is how it works, and how to walk into a store in Belleville or Maryland Heights and buy well anyway.
### How do I know what type of mattress is right for me?
Start with how you actually sleep, not with a category name. Side sleepers generally want more give at the shoulder and hip; back and stomach sleepers generally want less. Heavier bodies compress every layer further, so the same bed can read medium to one person and soft to another. Then test it by lying down in your normal sleeping position for a full ten minutes.
After that it’s a short list of filters. Sleep hot? Coil units and open-cell foams move more air than dense memory foam, which holds heat by design. Partner moves a lot? Pocketed coils isolate motion better than a connected innerspring. Sit on the edge to pull on shoes? Ask about the reinforced perimeter. Want the head to raise? Confirm the bed flexes on an adjustable base.
One thing this guide will not do is tell you a mattress fixes anything. If pain, numbness or a diagnosed sleep condition is pushing you into the store, talk to your doctor or a physical therapist first. Firmness is a comfort choice; anything past that belongs to someone with a license.
### Why does the same mattress have a different name at every store?
Because it stops you from price matching, and that is the entire point. Manufacturers build a core mattress, then let each retailer attach its own exclusive model name and cover, so the bed you liked in Kirkwood is technically a different product from the near-identical bed in St. Charles. The industry site GoodBed calls this the name game, and it is the biggest reason mattress shopping feels dishonest.
You beat it by shopping construction instead of names. Ask for the spec sheet: coil count and gauge, whether the coils are individually pocketed, the thickness of each comfort layer, foam density in pounds per cubic foot, whether latex is natural or blended. Two beds with the same coil unit, layer thicknesses and densities are the same bed in different pajamas.
Then ask the blunt version out loud: what is the manufacturer’s base model this one is built from? Some will tell you, and that answer beats any discount.
### What actually drives the price of a mattress?
Materials and build, first — then the cost of getting the thing into your bedroom. On the build side it’s the coil unit, the density and thickness of the foams, whether latex is in the stack, the quilting and the fire barrier. Foam density in pounds per cubic foot is the durability number almost nobody asks for, and the one that best predicts whether a bed holds its shape in year six.
Some of that cost is federally required. Since July 1, 2007, every mattress set sold in the United States has had to meet the Consumer Product Safety Commission’s open-flame standard at 16 CFR Part 1633, which caps how large a fire a bed can produce during a 30-minute burner test. NIST reported in 2020 that open-flame bed fires and their casualties fell sharply afterward.
The rest of the ticket is everything that isn’t the mattress: the lease, the truck, the two people carrying it up your stairs, the financing program and the markdown structure. That last piece deserves suspicion. A compare-at number only means something if the bed genuinely sold at that price. Ask what it costs today and the week after the sale ends. If those match, the sale was scenery. Warranty length works the same way: 25 years that turns prorated after year ten is often worth less than a plain ten-year non-prorated warranty.
Wildly off-topic — but here are nail salons across the metro.
### What does a comfort trial actually commit the store to?
Less than the advertisement implies. A comfort trial is a store policy, not a legal right, and the fine print stacks conditions: a break-in period of roughly three to four weeks before you may exchange, one exchange rather than unlimited swaps, a restocking fee, a pickup charge, a required protector, and a bed that comes back clean with its law tag attached.
The federal cooling-off rule will not rescue you. Under the Federal Trade Commission rule at 16 CFR Part 429, the three-day right to cancel covers sales at your home for $25 or more and sales at temporary locations like a hotel ballroom for $130 or more. It does not cover a purchase at a seller’s permanent place of business. Buy in a showroom and there is no federal window.
State law doesn’t fill the gap. Neither Missouri nor Illinois has a statute forcing a retailer to take back merchandise a buyer simply doesn’t like — refunds are store policy on both sides of the river. The policy is the protection. Get five things written on the invoice before you sign:
How many nights before an exchange is allowed, and when the trial expires.
The dollar amount of any restocking, comfort or pickup fee.
Whether you get one exchange or more, and whether a refund is possible.
Whether a protector purchase is a condition, and which one qualifies.
Who comes to get the bed, and how long that takes.
Returned and floor-model beds don’t vanish, and both states regulate what comes next. Missouri’s bedding law at RSMo 421.038 requires bedding made with previously used material to be sanitized and labeled — wording beginning “THIS BEDDING CONTAINS PREVIOUSLY USED MATERIALS WHICH HAVE BEEN CLEANED AND SANITIZED…” plus the method, date and permit number of whoever treated it. Illinois regulates used bedding under its Bedding and Upholstered Furniture Act, requiring sanitizing by an approved method and clear labeling as used. If a price looks impossible, read the tag before the sign.
### What should you check before delivery day?
Measure the path, not just the room. A bed that fits your bedroom may not survive the turn at the top of the stairs in a South City flat or a Dogtown four-family. Check doorway width, stair width and the landing. A king foundation often ships as two split pieces for that reason.
Then confirm three line items in writing: delivery, setup and old-mattress haul-away. Haul-away is where metro shoppers get surprised. Four states — California, Connecticut, Oregon and Rhode Island — run statewide mattress recycling programs funded by a checkout fee. Missouri and Illinois are not among them. Here, removal is a store service priced by the store, and some only take the old set if the new one arrives the same trip.
Handle disposal yourself and the rules turn local. The City of St. Louis Refuse Division runs bulk item pickup for city residents, at 314-622-4800. In St. Louis County and most Illinois suburbs, bulky pickup follows whichever hauler your municipality contracts with, so the answer in Ballwin isn’t the answer in Belleville. Call before you drag anything to the curb. If the frame and linens are on the same list, our guide to department stores around the metro is the companion trip.
### How long should a mattress last?
Plan to re-evaluate the bed at about seven years. The Better Sleep Council, the consumer education arm of the International Sleep Products Association, puts the useful life of a mattress set at roughly seven to ten years depending on use and build quality. ISPA’s mattress age study found the average mattress is 13.9 years old when discarded — most people sleep on a worn-out bed for years past noticing.
The warranty covers manufacturing defects, not the fact that you stopped liking it. Most programs only recognize a body impression once it exceeds a stated depth measured with nothing on the bed — commonly around an inch and a half, though some brands set the bar lower. Stains are a routine denial reason even when unrelated to the defect, and a missing law tag is another. Use a protector, keep the receipt, and use the foundation the maker specifies.
### Is a local store or a bed-in-a-box the better buy?
It depends on whether you trust your own back more than a product photo. A showroom lets you feel two beds back to back inside ten minutes and gives you someone to call when the crew is late. A boxed mattress usually offers a longer trial.
The difference shows up when something goes wrong. A trial is only as good as its return mechanics, and many online sellers ask you to arrange a local donation or haul-off and send proof rather than sending a truck. Around here that means finding a charity that accepts mattresses at all — many won’t. Price both as a delivered, hauled-away, set-up total instead of comparing stickers.
### What does the mattress business look like from behind the counter?
A sleep shop runs on an odd equation: strong margin per ticket, very few tickets. A store might write a handful of sales on a Tuesday and pay the same rent as a place ringing up hundreds. The promotional queen set in the window is the door-opener; the profit lives in the attach — adjustable base, protector, pillows — and in the finance terms. Presidents Day, Memorial Day, the Fourth, Labor Day and Black Friday carry the year. ISPA’s 2026 trends report put 2025 U.S. mattress unit shipments down 13.2% and market value down 6.5% — fewer beds, higher tickets. Owners complain to each other about one thing above all: they didn’t invent the model-name shell game, but they explain it all day. People search this category locally and late, so a complete listing — hours, delivery radius, financing, haul-away — is how a shop built on trust gets found at all.
Ready to shop the spec instead of the sign? Browse mattress stores across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two with the same build question - coil count, foam density, delivered price with haul-away - and see who answers plainly.
If you run a mattress store that answers the build question plainly, list it with us so the shopper tired of the sales floor finds you.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much should I pay for a good mattress?
A.  There isn’t an honest single number, because the same build carries different names and tags at different stores. Budget by construction: decide what you want in coil count, foam density and warranty terms, then ask two or three retailers to quote that build delivered and hauled away. The percentage off the sign tells you nothing.
### Q. What is the average cost for a good mattress?
A.  Averages mislead here for a structural reason: exclusive model names mean no two stores quote the same product, so an average blends beds that aren’t comparable. Industry data shows direction, though. ISPA’s 2026 trends report says U.S. mattress units fell 13.2% in 2025 while market value fell only 6.5%, because selling prices rose. Judge your purchase on build and delivered cost.
### Q. What mattresses should I stay away from?
A.  Any bed a store won’t give you specs for. If nobody can name the coil count, the foam density or what’s in the comfort layers, you can’t compare it or judge how it ages. Skip anything missing its law tag, anything sold as used without the sanitizing label Missouri and Illinois require, and any trial whose fees outweigh the discount that sold you.
### Q. Who has the best prices on mattresses right now?
A.  It shifts by weekend and by model, and the exclusive-name system exists so you can’t answer it by comparing tags. Answer it yourself: fix your build spec, then collect quotes from three stores on that spec, delivered and hauled away, financing included. The deepest promotions usually land on long holiday weekends.
### Q. What type of mattress do 5 star hotels use?
A.  Luxury hotels generally buy hospitality lines built to a contract spec, not the retail models sold under the same brand name, which is why hotel beds skew medium-firm and agreeable rather than distinctive — they must suit every guest and survive daily housekeeping. Much of what you remember may be the topper, linens and blackout curtains.
### Q. Where is the best place to buy a mattress in St. Louis?
A.  The best store does three things: shows you a real spec sheet, writes the trial and fee terms on your invoice, and quotes a delivered-and-hauled-away price rather than a sticker. That test works in Chesterfield, Florissant, O’Fallon and Belleville alike. Shortlist a few shops nearby, call each with the same build question, and buy from whoever answers straight.
### Q. Does removing the law tag void a mattress warranty?
A.  The warning on that tag is aimed at sellers, not at you — the label itself typically says the consumer may remove it. Practically, leave it on. Manufacturers use the law tag to identify the exact bed, build date and plant, and warranty programs routinely decline claims when it is gone.

## What Truck Repair Really Costs in St. Louis (and Why Downtime Costs More)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/heavy-duty-truck-repair-cost-st-louis
Imagine it’s 4:40 on a Tuesday morning and you’re parked on the shoulder off I-70 near Wentzville with the dash lit amber and a load that has to be in Indianapolis by two. The truck still runs. That’s what makes the decision hard. That’s the real question idling on the shoulder, isn’t it — not what the repair costs, but what every hour that truck sits still is quietly costing you?
Maybe your version is a straight truck in Maryland Heights that lost its air compressor overnight. Maybe two dump trucks in Belleville whose inspection stickers came due the same week. Maybe a reefer in Earth City that won’t hold temperature while a broker keeps texting. Same arithmetic every time: an hour parked earns nothing, and the note is still due on the first.
Most repair-cost articles get one thing backward. They quote a number as if the invoice were the expense. On a commercial truck it usually isn’t — the invoice is the smaller half. Here’s how heavy-duty pricing actually gets built around St. Louis, what the federal inspection rules require, and where Missouri and Illinois part ways.
### How much do truck repairs cost?
Repair and maintenance on a Class 8 tractor averaged about 22 cents per mile across the industry in 2025, up 8.6 percent from roughly 19.8 cents in 2024, according to the American Transportation Research Institute’s operational costs report released July 15, 2026. On a truck turning 100,000 miles a year that’s roughly $22,000 in parts and labor — and ATRI counts tires, towing and recovery separately, so those sit on top.
The average hides a spread, and the spread is the useful part. A burned-out trailer marker lamp and an in-frame engine overhaul both file under truck repair. Four things move a heavy-duty bill more than anything else: whether the fault is mechanical or emissions-related, whether the part is on a shelf in this metro or two days out, whether the truck can be worked where it sits, and how many diagnostic hours the code burns before anyone picks up a wrench. Emissions work is the category that surprises owner-operators most, because a particulate filter, an SCR catalyst, a doser and their sensors throw overlapping codes and the failure rarely announces itself cleanly.
### Why does downtime cost more than the repair invoice?
Because a truck is a revenue machine whose fixed costs don’t pause. ATRI put the industry-average marginal cost of operating a truck at $2.336 per mile in 2025, the highest in that report’s history, with $1.854 of it being everything other than fuel. Insurance, the payment, plates, permits and driver pay keep accruing while the tractor sits in a bay in Fenton doing zero miles.
Then there’s the load you couldn’t cover — the day’s gross, plus the repositioning move to get back under freight, plus whatever the broker remembers next month. A three-truck operation that loses one truck loses a third of its capacity, and the other two can’t absorb it. That’s why a slightly higher rate at a shop with your parts already in the building routinely beats a lower rate at one that has to order everything.
### What actually drives a heavy-duty shop’s hourly rate?
Six things, and none of them are greed. Lift and bay capacity comes first: putting a loaded tandem-axle tractor in the air takes equipment a two-post car lift can’t substitute for, and that bay costs the same empty as full. Second, diagnostic software — engine and chassis makers each license their own tool, so a shop covering several makes renews several subscriptions plus interface hardware, forever. Third, technician qualification, because federal rules put real requirements on who may perform annual inspections and brake work.
Fourth, parts inventory: air dryers, wheel seals, slack adjusters, glad hands and common sensors on a shelf are money standing still, and they are exactly what makes a same-day repair possible. Fifth, liability on work that puts an 80,000-pound vehicle back on I-270. Sixth, whether the shop runs mobile or after-hours service, which means paying somebody to be awake at 2 a.m.
So a rate by itself tells you almost nothing. Ask what it includes, whether diagnostic time applies to the repair if you approve the work, and what the current parts lead time looks like. A rate quoted next to a realistic completion time is information. A rate quoted alone is a fragment.
Nothing to do with air brakes — the family car needs St. Louis auto repair too.
### What does a DOT annual inspection actually cover?
Under 49 CFR 396.17, every commercial motor vehicle must pass an inspection covering at minimum the components in Appendix A to Part 396 at least once during the preceding 12 months, and the documentation has to be on the vehicle. The rule counts each unit separately: for a tractor, semitrailer and full trailer combination, the tractor, the semitrailer and the full trailer — including the converter dolly if it’s so equipped — each get inspected.
Who signs it matters. Section 396.19 requires the person performing the annual inspection to understand the criteria in Part 393 and Appendix A, to have mastered the methods and tools, and to have either completed a federal or state training program, hold a qualifying state or provincial certificate, or have training and experience totaling at least one year. Section 396.25 sets a separate bar for anyone responsible for brake work. A carrier may self-inspect, or under 396.17(e) use a commercial garage, fleet leasing company or truck stop as its agent — provided that business maintains facilities appropriate for commercial vehicle inspections and employs qualified inspectors.
The paperwork has its own rules. The inspection report is retained fourteen months from its date under 396.21, kept where the vehicle is housed or maintained. Separately, 396.3 requires a systematic inspection, repair and maintenance program with records for every vehicle you control for 30 consecutive days, held one year and for six months after the vehicle leaves your control. Auditors ask for that first, and it is the cheapest thing on this page to get right.
### How do Missouri and Illinois differ on truck inspections?
Missouri leans on the federal rule and applies it to everybody. RSMo 307.400 makes it unlawful to operate a commercial motor vehicle unless it’s equipped and operated as required by Parts 390 through 397 of Title 49, and the statute says it plainly — “whether intrastate transportation or interstate transportation.” A dump truck that never leaves St. Louis County is still on the annual clock. The same statute adopts CVSA’s North American Uniform Out-of-Service Criteria as the standard for parking a truck or driver roadside.
Missouri’s own biennial state safety inspection under RSMo 307.350 carves interstate trucks out: vehicles engaged in interstate commerce and proportionately registered with the Missouri highway reciprocity commission are excepted, as are vehicles registered above 24,000 pounds for less than twelve months.
Illinois adds a state layer. Under 625 ILCS 5/13-101, second division vehicles must pass a safety test and carry a Certificate of Safety, and 13-109 sets the schedule: at least every 6 months by default, with truck tractors, semitrailers and property-carrying vehicles registered for more than 10,000 but less than 26,001 pounds on a 12-month cycle. Tests happen at an official testing station or through an official mobile safety testing company. Pull a Certificate of Safety and an orange triangular decal goes on the vehicle until it passes again; a lesser violation gets a yellow sticker and three working days. If you run a yard in Granite City or Cahokia Heights, ask a prospective shop whether it does the federal annual, the Illinois safety test, or both.
### Where can I find semi-truck repair services near Saint Louis, MO?
Heavy-duty service here sorts into five lanes, and knowing which one you need saves a wasted trip. Dealer service departments carry factory diagnostic tools and warranty authority for their make. Independent heavy-duty shops handle mixed fleets and usually price diagnostic labor more flexibly. Trailer and reefer specialists work the box, doors, landing gear and refrigeration unit — a different trade from tractor work. Commercial tire service runs its own trucks and inventory. Mobile and roadside outfits come to the shoulder or your yard.
Geography helps. The St. Louis Regional Freightway counts four interstates plus the I-270 and I-255 loop serving this region, with Chicago, Memphis, Kansas City and Indianapolis all within a five-hour drive or less. That freight density supports a deeper parts distribution network than a metro this size would otherwise carry, so the odds of a common Class 8 part sitting in the region today are better here than most places you break down. Search by capability, not proximity: a shop three miles away that can’t take your GVWR is farther away than one in Hazelwood that can.
### Is scheduled maintenance actually cheaper than break-down repair?
Almost always, and the roadside data shows why. In CVSA’s 2025 International Roadcheck — 56,178 inspections across the U.S., Canada and Mexico on May 13–15, results published October 7, 2025 — the vehicle out-of-service rate was 18.1 percent and the driver rate 5.9 percent. Brakes led: 3,304 brake system violations, 24.4 percent of all vehicle out-of-service violations, plus 2,257 more for 20 percent defective brakes — together 41.1 percent. Tires came second at 2,899, or 21.4 percent, then lights and cargo securement.
Every one of those four is something a preventive-maintenance interval or an honest pre-trip catches for a fraction of what it costs on the shoulder. An out-of-service order isn’t a repair bill — it’s a repair bill plus a tow plus a missed delivery plus a mark on your safety record. A workable rhythm for a small fleet: a PM service on the engine maker’s interval, brakes and tires checked at every PM, the federal annual scheduled in a slow week you choose rather than discovered at a scale house, and a written pre-trip the driver actually performs.
### What should you ask before handing over the keys?
Six questions, one phone call. What’s the heaviest GVWR you can lift and work on? Do you have the factory diagnostic software for my engine and chassis? Is your annual inspection performed by an inspector qualified under 396.19, and can you handle brake work under 396.25? What’s your current parts lead time for my make? Do you offer mobile or roadside service, and in what radius? Will you estimate in hours out of service, not just dollars? Then two habits: ask for photos of the failed component, and keep your own maintenance file, because 396.3 puts that obligation on you rather than on the shop.
### What running a heavy-duty shop looks like from the other side
The constraint in this trade isn’t customers — it’s technicians and bay hours. A heavy-duty bay is a fixed cost that either turns or doesn’t, and a shop covering several makes renews each manufacturer’s diagnostic subscription every year whether business is good or not. Parts margin is thinner than outsiders assume, because fleet buyers price-shop parts online; the money is in labor hours sold and in having the right part on the shelf so the truck leaves today. Seasonality is brutal and predictable — the first hard freeze brings gelled fuel, dead batteries and frozen air lines at once, spring brings the pre-Roadcheck inspection rush, and late in the year carriers defer everything they can. What owners complain about to each other is the truck that arrives with no service history and an instruction to just fix the noise, which is how a comeback gets built. People search for diesel and heavy-duty service locally, usually in a hurry, so a complete listing is how a shop gets found on the worst morning of a stranger’s week. Getting listed takes a few minutes.
Need a shop that can actually take your GVWR? Browse truck repair shops across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two of them today - before you need one - and ask what they can lift and how long parts take.
If you run a truck shop with the lift for the big stuff, put it on the directory so a fleet owner calls you before the breakdown, not after.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is $100 an hour fair for mechanic labor?
A.  The number alone can’t answer it, because heavy-duty rates carry costs a car bay never does: lifts rated for a loaded tractor, a separate diagnostic subscription for each engine and chassis maker, federally qualified inspectors and brake technicians, and parts inventory sitting on a shelf. Judge a rate against what it includes, the diagnostic policy, and the shop’s parts lead time. A rate quoted without a completion time is half a quote.
### Q. What’s the going rate for a mechanic right now?
A.  It varies by shop, by specialty, and by whether the work happens in a bay, in your yard or on the shoulder — after-hours and mobile calls price differently from scheduled bay time everywhere. Rather than chase one number, compare quotes on total hours out of service. The industry benchmark worth knowing is ATRI’s: repair and maintenance averaged about 22 cents per mile across the industry in 2025.
### Q. What is the most expensive thing to fix on a truck?
A.  On a Class 8 truck, the powertrain and the emissions aftertreatment. An in-frame engine overhaul or a transmission replacement sits at the top, with the aftertreatment system — particulate filter, SCR catalyst, doser and sensors — close behind, partly because those faults take diagnostic hours to isolate. Frame and collision damage can exceed both. Brakes, tires and air system parts are far cheaper, which is exactly why deferring them is a bad trade.
### Q. What is it called when you fix up an old truck?
A.  Depends on the goal. Cosmetic and mechanical work on a classic pickup is a restoration. On a working commercial truck the vocabulary differs: an in-frame overhaul rebuilds the engine in the chassis, a repower swaps in a different engine, refurbishment or reman covers component-level rebuilding, and a frame-off job is a rebuild. Shops quote these very differently, so use the term that matches what you actually want done.
### Q. Where can I find car and truck repair services in St. Louis?
A.  Usually two different searches. Passenger cars and light trucks go to general automotive shops; anything above roughly 10,000 pounds GVWR needs heavy-duty lifts, air brake capability and commercial diagnostic tools. Some shops do both and many don’t, so ask about maximum GVWR before you drive over. If you need the federal annual inspection, confirm the shop performs it with a qualified inspector under 49 CFR 396.19.
### Q. Where can I find semi-truck repair services near Saint Louis, MO?
A.  Sort by what you need: a dealer service department for warranty and factory tooling, an independent heavy-duty shop for mixed fleets, a trailer and reefer specialist for the box, commercial tire service, or mobile and roadside for a truck that can’t move. Because four interstates and the I-270 and I-255 loop converge here, the metro carries a deeper parts network than its size suggests. Ask any shop its lead time on your make.
### Q. Do I need a DOT annual inspection if I only drive in Missouri?
A.  Yes, if you operate a commercial motor vehicle. RSMo 307.400 applies Parts 390 through 397 of Title 49 to commercial motor vehicles in Missouri and specifies that it holds whether the transportation is intrastate or interstate, so the periodic inspection requirement in 49 CFR 396.17 rides along. The statute carries narrow exceptions for certain intrastate solid-waste and farm-plated vehicles under stated weight limits.
### Q. Is a used truck bought at auction worth the repair risk?
A.  Sometimes, but budget for a full inspection before it hauls anything. Fleet units and municipal equipment turn up at regional sales priced for an unknown maintenance history. Read how St. Louis auction houses work before you register to bid, then have a heavy-duty shop go through the truck against 49 CFR 396.17 standards rather than trusting the sticker on the door frame.

## When a Small Business Actually Needs a Lawyer in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/small-business-attorney-st-louis-when-you-need-one
Imagine it’s a Tuesday in October and you’re standing in a half-empty storefront in Affton with a lease in your hand. Eleven pages. You understood page one, because page one is the rent. Pages four through nine are the ones you skimmed, and one of them is the reason you might still owe money on this space in 2031. That’s the quiet cost of the pages you skimmed. So which decision in front of you right now is the kind you’ll wish you’d run past a lawyer — before, not after?
Maybe that’s not you. Maybe you and the friend you started this thing with are three years in, drawing the same paycheck, except one of you now works every Saturday and neither of you has said it out loud. Maybe you’re in Belleville about to hire your first real employee and somebody at the counter says the word “contractor” like it settles the question. Maybe a customer in St. Charles quit answering the phone about an invoice from March.
None of those feel like legal problems on the day they happen. That is exactly what makes them expensive later. The moments where a lawyer is worth real money are almost never the dramatic ones — they’re the quiet Tuesdays when a document gets signed and nobody reads page six.
One thing before anything else: this article is general information about how business law works in Missouri and Illinois. It is not legal advice, it is not a recommendation about your situation, and no article can tell you what your facts require. That part takes a licensed attorney who hears them.
### Why would someone need a business lawyer?
Because a handful of ordinary moments create liability that costs very little to prevent and a great deal to unwind: forming the entity, signing a lease, putting a partnership in writing, making the first hire, chasing a contract that went bad, and selling. Most owners call during the fifth one.
The order matters more than the list. The first four are cheap, scheduled and boring. You know they’re coming, you can shop for help, and the work is mostly drafting. The fifth is a dispute, which means somebody else now controls half your calendar and most of your costs. A lawyer you meet at formation is doing prevention. A lawyer you meet mid-dispute is doing damage control, and damage control is priced accordingly.
There’s a quieter reason too. Missouri law says members and managers of an LLC are not liable, solely by reason of being a member or manager, for the debts and obligations of the company (RSMo 347.057). That shield is not self-maintaining. It holds up because the company behaves like a separate company — its own bank account, contracts signed in the company’s name, filings kept current. Much of what a business attorney does is protect the thing you already paid to create.
### What exactly does a business lawyer do?
Three jobs, mostly. They draft and negotiate the documents that define your relationships — leases, operating agreements, customer contracts, employment terms, buy-sell provisions. They keep the entity in good standing so the liability shield stays intact. And when a relationship breaks, they either settle it or take it to court.
In practice the trade splits into transactional work and litigation, and those are nearly different careers. Transactional lawyers build things: the entity, the agreement, the deal. Litigators fight about things other people built. Plenty of small-firm business attorneys do the first and refer the second to someone who lives in courtrooms. Ask which one you’re hiring. The answer tells you how the engagement will be priced and how long it will run.
What a business lawyer does not do: run your books, file your taxes, or promise you a result. If a contract dispute has three plausible endings, a straight answer describes all three and what each is likely to cost. It does not pick the winner.
### Do you need a lawyer to form an LLC in Missouri or Illinois?
No. Neither state requires one. Missouri charges $50 to file articles of organization for a domestic LLC online and $105 on paper, according to the Secretary of State schedule of fees revised January 2025. Illinois charges $150 to file articles of organization, or $400 for a series LLC, under 805 ILCS 180/50-10. You can do either yourself in an afternoon.
The filing isn’t the part that matters. The operating agreement is, and the two states treat it differently. Missouri’s statute says the member or members of a limited liability company shall adopt an operating agreement (RSMo 347.081). Illinois says all members may enter into one, and where they don’t, the LLC Act itself governs relations among members and managers (805 ILCS 180/15-5). Either way, the default rules were written for a generic company. They decide what happens when a member wants out, dies, divorces or simply quits showing up — and they will decide it without knowing anything about your business.
The compliance calendars differ too, which catches people who move a business across the river. An Illinois LLC files an annual report with a $75 fee, delivered to the Secretary of State within the 60 days immediately preceding the first day of its anniversary month; let it go delinquent and the penalty is $100, plus another $100 for each year or fraction of a year after the first (805 ILCS 180/50-1 and 50-15). Missouri does not put LLCs on that treadmill at all — its annual registration report is a corporation obligation, $20 online or $45 on paper, filed in the month of incorporation, with a new corporation’s first report due within 30 days of incorporating (RSMo 351.120). And in Missouri, if you do business under any name other than your true name, the fictitious name registration costs $7, is supposed to be filed within five days of starting, and expires after five years unless you renew it (RSMo 417.210).
### What are the four types of business law?
There’s no official list of four — different textbooks give different sets, and some swap tax in for one of these. But the legal life of a small company really does fall into four buckets, and knowing which bucket you’re in tells you who to call.
Entity and governance. Who owns what, who can sign, how profits get split, what happens when someone leaves. This is the operating agreement, the bylaws, the buy-sell provision. It is the cheapest legal work you will ever buy and the most expensive to skip, because the price of skipping it only shows up when two owners disagree.
Contracts and commercial. Your customer agreement, vendor terms, lease, equipment financing. Missouri gives you ten years to sue upon a writing for the payment of money or property (RSMo 516.110) and five years on contracts and obligations not in writing (RSMo 516.120). Illinois splits it the same way: ten years on written contracts, five on unwritten ones (735 ILCS 5/13-206 and 13-205). That gap is the entire argument for getting it on paper.
Employment. Classification, wage and hour, handbooks, and the agreements that follow people out the door. This is where the two states diverge hardest. Illinois bars a non-compete unless the worker’s annualized earnings exceed $75,000, rising to $80,000 on January 1, 2027, and bars a non-solicit below $45,000, rising to $47,500 — and it requires the employer to advise the worker in writing to consult an attorney and to allow 14 calendar days to review the covenant (820 ILCS 90). Missouri sets no salary floor. Instead it treats a covenant not to solicit as conclusively reasonable when its post-employment duration is no more than one year, and it carves out employees who provide only secretarial or clerical services (RSMo 431.202).
Property, real and intellectual. The lease and the build-out on one side; trade names, trademarks, and whatever your software, recipes or customer list are actually worth on the other. Owners underweight this one right up until a competitor two towns over opens under a confusingly similar name.
Unrelated, and we know it — the metro’s Mexican food deserves a Friday.
### What type of lawyer do you need for a small business?
For most small companies, a business or corporate generalist — someone whose practice is entity work, contracts and commercial disputes for owner-operated companies. One attorney like that handles the large majority of what a ten-person business ever needs, and knows who to hand off the rest to.
The rest is specialists. An employment lawyer when you’re firing someone or writing a handbook. A real estate lawyer for a purchase or a complicated build-out. An intellectual property lawyer for trademarks and licensing. A tax attorney for anything involving an election or an audit. A litigator once a dispute becomes a lawsuit. There’s overlap you don’t expect, too: a divorce can put a co-owned business squarely in play, which is why some owners end up sitting down with a family law attorney and a business attorney in the same month.
One note specific to this metro: attorneys are licensed by state, and the St. Louis area sits in two of them. If your company operates on both sides of the river, ask early whether the attorney is admitted in Missouri, Illinois or both. Each state also publishes a free license and discipline lookup, which takes about a minute and almost nobody uses.
### How much can a small business attorney cost?
It depends far less on the individual lawyer than on the shape of the work. Defined, repeatable matters — forming an entity, a standard operating agreement, a trademark application, a lease review — are increasingly quoted as a flat fee, because the attorney can predict the hours. Open-ended matters get billed hourly, because nobody can.
Four things move the number. Whether the work is transactional or contested. How much of it a paralegal can carry. The attorney’s years and specialty. And whether the other side is cooperating. Litigation is the expensive one for a structural reason: the opposing party controls half the calendar. A deposition you didn’t want, a motion you didn’t file, a continuance you didn’t ask for — all of it lands on your invoice.
Filing fees sit on top of the legal fee and aren’t negotiable by anyone: $50 or $105 for the Missouri LLC filing depending on whether you file online or on paper, $150 in Illinois, $7 for a Missouri fictitious name. Get the fee arrangement in writing before work starts, and ask specifically who will do the work and at what rate. The same result staffed by a senior partner and staffed by an associate with paralegal support produces two very different invoices.
One more thing worth knowing before you hire anybody: if the entire fight is small, you may not need to. In Missouri, a small claims judge has original jurisdiction over civil cases, tort or contract, where the amount in controversy does not exceed $5,000, exclusive of interest and costs (RSMo 482.305), and you don’t need an attorney to file one. Illinois runs its own small claims track with a different ceiling set by court rule. Equipment disputes land there constantly — which is its own argument for reading the fine print before you sign for a copier, as anyone who has compared buying against leasing office equipment can tell you.
### How to find a good small business lawyer?
Start with fit rather than credentials. You want an attorney whose regular clients look like you, because if the practice is built around companies with 300 employees, your six-person shop becomes the file that waits.
Five questions, asked in the first call, sort most of it out:
Who actually does the work, and what does each person on the matter bill?
Is this a flat fee or hourly, and what specifically is excluded from it?
Are you admitted in Missouri, Illinois, or both?
What is a realistic response time on a normal email from me?
Have you handled this exact thing in the past year, and roughly what did it run?
Then pay attention to the meeting itself. A business attorney who is any good asks about your customers, your margins and how money actually moves through the company before offering an opinion, because the answer changes with those facts. And no attorney can guarantee an outcome — anyone who implies otherwise has just told you something useful about how they work.
### What this work looks like from the other side of the desk
A small-firm business practice sells one thing it cannot restock: hours. So the real economics aren’t in the rate, they’re in the hours that never get billed. The conflicts check that kills a matter the firm wanted. The 20-minute call written off because invoicing it would feel petty. The receivable that ages 90 days because a client had a slow quarter. Formation work is often priced flat and close to cost on purpose — it’s the door, not the room. The money is in year three, when that same client has a lease, a partner buyout and a deal. Retainers aren’t revenue either: unearned funds sit in a client trust account until the work is done, so a big check is an obligation, not a good month. What clients get wrong, nearly universally, is calling after signing. And because most of this work begins with an owner searching locally for someone who handles companies their size, being listed and easy to verify is not a vanity exercise.
Not sure which of those six moments you’re actually in? Browse business attorneys across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two of them and ask each the same thing: flat fee or hourly, and what falls outside it. Fleet owners face a version of this every week - see what heavy-duty truck repair really costs.
If you’re the business attorney who quotes a flat fee and means it, list your practice so owners at a crossroads can find you.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much does a lawyer cost for a small business?
A.  There’s no single number, and the fee structure matters more than the rate anyway. Flat fees are common for defined work such as entity formation, an operating agreement, or a lease review. Hourly is the norm for anything contested, because the other side controls part of the timeline. Ask for the arrangement in writing, ask what is excluded, and remember state filing fees are separate — $50 or $105 in Missouri, $150 in Illinois.
### Q. Is $400 an hour a lot for a lawyer?
A.  On its own, that number means very little. Rates move with the market, the practice area, the attorney’s experience and how much of the work a paralegal can carry. A higher rate that closes a matter in four hours costs you less than a lower rate that takes fifteen. The more useful request is an estimate of total hours and a written fee agreement, not a rate comparison between two firms.
### Q. What is the 80/20 rule for lawyers?
A.  It isn’t a rule of law and no court applies it. It’s the Pareto observation borrowed into practice management: roughly a fifth of clients or matters generate most of the revenue, and a small share of preventive work avoids most of the disputes. Owners usually hear it in the second sense — that the modest document work done early is what keeps the expensive argument from happening at all.
### Q. What type of lawyer is needed for business?
A.  For day-to-day company matters, a business or corporate attorney who works with owner-operated companies. Bring in specialists as the facts require: employment for hiring and firing, real estate for leases and purchases, intellectual property for trademarks and licensing, tax for elections and audits, and a litigator once a dispute becomes a lawsuit. In this metro, also ask whether the attorney is admitted in Missouri, Illinois or both.
### Q. Can the same lawyer represent me and my business partner?
A.  Often not, and it surprises people. When two owners want different things from the same document — a buy-sell, a departure, a valuation — their interests conflict, and one attorney advocating for both may not be able to advocate properly for either. Firms run conflict checks before accepting a matter for exactly this reason. Expect to be told that one of you needs separate counsel.
### Q. How long do I have to sue over an unpaid invoice?
A.  In Missouri, an action upon a writing for the payment of money or property must be brought within ten years (RSMo 516.110), while contracts and obligations not in writing get five (RSMo 516.120). Illinois divides it the same way: ten years on written contracts, five on unwritten ones (735 ILCS 5/13-206 and 13-205). Deadlines turn on when the claim accrued and on your specific facts, so confirm yours with an attorney rather than counting backward on a calendar.
### Q. Should I use an online filing service instead of a lawyer?
A.  For the filing itself, the state doesn’t care who typed it — Missouri charges $50 for LLC articles of organization filed online, Illinois charges $150 under 805 ILCS 180/50-10. What a filing service will not do is tell you which entity structure fits, write an operating agreement around your real ownership split, or catch the clause in your lease. Plenty of owners use a service for the filing and still pay an attorney for the agreement.

## How Hospital Billing Works in St. Louis: Networks, Estimates and Charity Care
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-hospital-billing-charity-care
Imagine you’re at the kitchen table in Florissant on a Thursday night, holding an envelope you already know you don’t want to open. The procedure went fine. The hospital was in your network — you checked, twice. And yet here is a bill from a physician group whose name you have never heard, for someone you met for ninety seconds while you were counting backward from ten.
Or maybe it’s the other version of the same story. You live in Belleville, a doctor just put an outpatient procedure on the calendar six weeks out, and nobody has said one word about money. You have a vague feeling you’re supposed to ask something. You just don’t know what, or who, or when.
This is about the paperwork side of hospital care across the St. Louis metro: how the billing actually works, what federal rules already hand you for free, and the four or five questions that change the outcome. It does not rank hospitals and it does not name a best one. And if you are trying to decide right now whether something is an emergency, stop reading and call 911 or your own clinician. That call belongs to them, not to a webpage.
### How do I choose the right hospital?
Do three checks, in this order. Call the number on the back of your insurance card and confirm the facility is in network for the specific service, not just in network generally. Look the hospital up on CMS Care Compare, which covers more than 4,000 Medicare-certified hospitals. Then ask the scheduler which physician groups will bill you separately. Those three answers decide most of what lands in your mailbox later.
People search “Which is the best hospital in St. Louis?” and “Which hospital in Missouri offers the best healthcare?” constantly, and no honest local directory can answer either. Best for a hip replacement is not best for a stroke, and neither is best if the surgeon you trust only operates across town. What you can check is concrete: whether the facility is Medicare-certified and accredited, what its Care Compare measures show for the service line you need, and whether it sits inside your plan’s network.
### What’s the difference between an ER, an urgent care and a nurse line?
They are three different businesses with three different legal obligations. A hospital emergency department operates under EMTALA, the 1986 federal law now at Section 1867 of the Social Security Act: a Medicare-participating hospital that offers emergency services must give you a medical screening examination when you ask for one, regardless of your ability to pay, then provide stabilizing treatment, then arrange an appropriate transfer if it cannot stabilize you itself.
An urgent care is a walk-in clinic. It carries no EMTALA screening duty, it cannot admit you upstairs, and it keeps posted hours. A nurse line is neither — most health plans and many clinics run a 24-hour line, and the number is usually printed on your card or on the practice’s after-hours voicemail. Two national numbers are worth writing on the refrigerator right now, before you need them: Poison Help at 1-800-222-1222 and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.
One naming trap deserves a flag on both sides of the river. A freestanding emergency department can sit in a strip center, look exactly like an urgent care, and bill like a hospital emergency room, because that is what it is licensed as. If the sign says emergency, ask at the desk which one you are checking into before you hand over the card. Nobody is hiding it. Almost nobody asks.
### What does “in-network” actually cover at a hospital?
The hospital’s contract with your insurer and the doctor’s contract with your insurer are two separate pieces of paper. A building can be in network while the anesthesiologist, the radiologist reading your scan, the pathologist reading your tissue and the hospitalist rounding on you every morning are all employed by independent groups that negotiated their own deals — or negotiated none at all. That gap is the single most common way a carefully planned procedure turns into an unexpected bill.
Federal law closed much of it. The No Surprises Act took effect January 1, 2022 and protects you from unexpected out-of-network bills for emergency room visits, for non-emergency care connected to a visit to an in-network hospital, hospital outpatient department or ambulatory surgical center, and for air ambulance services. You pay your in-network cost sharing, and the provider and the plan argue about the rest without you in the middle.
Here is the part almost nobody knows. There is a consent form that asks you to waive those protections, and it legally cannot cover certain services no matter what you sign. Under 45 CFR 149.420(b), the waiver never applies to items and services related to emergency medicine, anesthesiology, pathology, radiology or neonatology; to assistant surgeons, hospitalists or intensivists; to diagnostic services including radiology and laboratory work; or to any out-of-network provider when no in-network provider at that facility could have done the job. It also never applies to unforeseen, urgent needs that come up mid-procedure. When a waiver does apply, the written notice has to reach you at least 72 hours before a scheduled appointment, or at scheduling if the appointment is inside that window, and never later than three hours before care.
So the question to ask the scheduler is narrow and specific: which groups practicing inside this hospital bill separately, and are they in my plan’s network? The same contract-versus-provider gap shows up well outside hospital walls — it’s the reason people are blindsided by what their plan does and doesn’t pay toward hearing aids and audiology visits, too.
Unrelated, and we know it — sometimes you just want toasted ravioli.
### What is a good faith estimate, and who gets one?
If you don’t have insurance, or you have it and choose not to use it for a service, providers generally must give you a good faith estimate of what the care will cost. You get one automatically when you schedule at least three business days in advance, and you can request one any time. Keep it. If the final bill comes in at least $400 more than the estimate, you may be able to dispute it through the federal patient-provider dispute resolution process.
Ask whether the estimate includes the physician charges or only the facility charges — that one clarifying question is worth more than an hour on hold later. CMS staffs a No Surprises Act help line seven days a week at 1-800-985-3059, with language support, and that is where a complaint goes if a facility refuses you an estimate you are entitled to.
### Where do I find a hospital’s prices?
Every hospital in the country has been required since January 1, 2021 to publish its prices online in two forms: a comprehensive machine-readable file covering all items and services, and a consumer-friendly display of standard charges for at least 300 shoppable services that can be planned in advance — imaging, lab tests, outpatient visits, bundled procedures. The file includes the rates negotiated with insurers and the discounted price the hospital will accept in cash directly from a patient.
That last number is the one people miss. The discounted cash price is sometimes lower than what an out-of-network claim would leave you owing, which is why the phrase “self-pay rate” is worth saying out loud at registration. The rule has teeth: CMS audits a sample of hospitals, investigates complaints, can impose civil monetary penalties, and publishes which hospitals have been penalized. Enforcement of updated requirements from the CY 2026 outpatient payment rule started April 1, 2026.
We don’t publish hospital prices here and neither should anyone else who isn’t the hospital. A price file is a starting point for a conversation, not a quote. The quote is the good faith estimate with your name on it.
### What is charity care, and how do I ask for it?
Every nonprofit hospital in the country is required to have a written financial assistance policy, and most patients never find out. Under Section 501(r)(4) of the Internal Revenue Code, added by the Affordable Care Act with final regulations released December 29, 2014, a tax-exempt hospital facility must maintain a written financial assistance policy, or FAP, and widely publicize it. The policy has to spell out who qualifies, whether the help is free care or discounted care, how to apply, and what happens if you don’t pay.
Two more pieces of that rule matter to you directly. Section 501(r)(5) says a hospital cannot charge a FAP-eligible patient more than the amounts generally billed to patients who have insurance — the industry calls it AGB, and it is calculated from what Medicare and private insurers actually allowed on past claims, not from the sticker price. Section 501(r)(6) says the hospital must make reasonable efforts to determine whether you qualify before it takes an extraordinary collection action. Those actions have a legal definition: selling your debt, reporting you to a credit bureau, suing you, garnishing wages, placing a lien, seizing a bank account, or requiring payment before providing further medically necessary care.
The FAP also has to include a list of the providers other than the hospital itself who deliver emergency or medically necessary care inside that building, specifying which of them are covered by the policy and which are not. Read that list. It is the plainest answer you will find anywhere to the question of who else is going to bill you.
Illinois goes further than federal law. Under the Hospital Uninsured Patient Discount Act, a non-rural Illinois hospital must discount charges for uninsured patients with family income up to 600% of the federal poverty level — $132,300 for a family of four, per the state’s own Hospital Report Card — and up to 300% at rural and critical access hospitals. It covers medically necessary services above $300 in a single admission or encounter, caps the bill at the cost of services plus 35%, and limits what a hospital can collect from you in any 12 months to 25% of family income.
Two more Illinois details worth knowing: every bill or invoice sent to an uninsured patient has to state that the discount exists and how to apply, and you generally have 60 days from discharge or service to apply. Missouri’s hospital licensing chapter carries no equivalent uninsured-discount statute, so on the Missouri side the enforceable floor is the federal 501(r) rules plus whatever the hospital’s own policy adds on top.
What to actually say: ask for a financial counselor and ask for the financial assistance policy by name. Apply in writing, keep a copy, note the date. Ask whether the hospital screens patients presumptively, because many do, and ask what the policy says about the physician groups that billed you separately. If a bill is already in collections, the FAP may still apply.
### How do I get my medical records?
You have a federal right of access under HIPAA, at 45 CFR 164.524, and it comes with a clock. The provider must act on your request within 30 days. It can take one 30-day extension, and only one, and it has to tell you in writing why and give you a date. Any fee has to be reasonable and cost-based, covering only labor for copying, supplies, postage if you asked for mail, and preparing a summary if you agreed to one.
Two practical notes. Ask for an electronic copy through the patient portal where the records already live — it’s faster and usually cheaper than paper. And ask for the itemized bill separately, in writing, because an itemized statement is a billing document, not a medical record, and it goes through a different department. The itemized bill is where duplicate charges and services you never received become visible.
### What should I bring for a scheduled procedure?
Photo ID and your insurance card, plus a secondary card if you have one.
The good faith estimate or written cost estimate, on paper, with the physician charges question already answered.
A current medication list with doses, and your allergy list.
Your advance directive or durable power of attorney for healthcare if you have one, and the name and cell number of the person who will drive you home.
Prior imaging on disc or the portal login, so nothing gets repeated and rebilled.
Your medical record number, and the name of the scheduler you spoke with.
Leave the rest at home. And if a form appears at registration asking you to consent to out-of-network care, that is the moment to slow down and ask what it covers, not after.
### What this looks like from the hospital’s side of the counter
The same questions that shrink a hospital bill also decide what a scan costs before it is ever run. It is worth reading what an MRI costs in St. Louis and how to pay less while you still have room to ask.
Hospital finance runs unlike almost any other business in a local directory. The emergency department is a door that legally cannot close — EMTALA requires the screening exam regardless of ability to pay — so the least predictable part of the operation is also the part with the least control over who walks in. Scheduled outpatient work is what can be planned, staffed and forecast. Layered on top is a compliance stack patients never see: a community health needs assessment, a written financial assistance policy and emergency medical care policy, community benefit reported on Form 990 Schedule H, and a public price file CMS audits with civil monetary penalties behind it. CMS is now asking the field how to clean up the free-text fields in those files, which is exactly what revenue-cycle staff have muttered about for years. And the complaint you hear in any billing office: the policy already names which provider groups are covered and which are not, and hardly anyone reads it before the bill lands. Being listed clearly where neighbors search is part of closing that gap.
Not sure which hospitals are even near you? Browse hospitals across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call the number on your insurance card and ask whether the one you picked is in network for the exact service you need - and whether the physicians there are too.
If you run a clinic or a billing advocacy practice, you can add or update a listing through the join page.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are the main hospitals in St. Louis?
A.  The metro is served by several large nonprofit systems operating multiple campuses on both sides of the river, plus independent, specialty, psychiatric, rehabilitation and government hospitals. Rather than take anyone’s list on faith, pull the authoritative one: CMS Care Compare covers more than 4,000 Medicare-certified hospitals and filters by ZIP code, so you can see every certified facility within a radius of your address in Missouri and Illinois alike.
### Q. What is the number one hospital in St. Louis?
A.  We don’t rank hospitals and won’t. Ranking lists weight things that may have nothing to do with your situation. Check three things instead: whether the facility is Medicare-certified and accredited, what its Care Compare measures show for the specific service line you need, and whether it and the physicians who practice there are in your plan’s network. A hospital that fails the third test is the wrong hospital for you regardless of any list.
### Q. Which hospital system is considered the best in St. Louis?
A.  Different lists reach different conclusions because they measure different things, so this article doesn’t pick one. What is worth comparing system by system is concrete and public: accreditation status, Care Compare measures for the service you need, whether the system is in your plan’s network, and what its published financial assistance policy says about eligibility and about which physician groups inside its buildings are covered by it.
### Q. What is the biggest hospital in St. Louis, Missouri?
A.  Size is usually measured in licensed beds, and that count changes as facilities open, close or convert units, so any number published in an article goes stale fast. The current figure for a specific hospital comes from that hospital or from state licensing records — Missouri licenses hospitals under Chapter 197 of the Revised Statutes of Missouri, and Illinois hospitals are licensed by the Illinois Department of Public Health. Bigger also doesn’t mean better for any particular procedure.
### Q. How expensive is the hospital without insurance?
A.  Nobody can quote you a real number without knowing the service, the facility and your income, and we won’t publish one. What you can do is get a good faith estimate before scheduled care, ask for the discounted cash price from the hospital’s published price file, and apply for financial assistance. If you qualify under a nonprofit hospital’s policy, federal law caps what you can be charged at the amounts generally billed to insured patients.
### Q. How much does an average 3 day hospital stay cost?
A.  An average is close to useless here, because the same three nights can differ enormously depending on the unit, the procedure, the drugs and your coverage. Get your own number instead of a national one: request a good faith estimate in writing if you are uninsured or self-paying, ask whether it includes physician charges, and if the final bill exceeds that estimate by at least $400, you may be able to dispute it through the federal process.
### Q. What is the #1 hospital in Missouri?
A.  There is no single authoritative answer, and a statewide winner is the wrong thing to chase anyway. Ranking lists disagree because they weight different inputs, and a hospital that scores well statewide may be hours from you or outside your plan’s network. Filter CMS Care Compare to your own ZIP code, look at the measures for the service line you actually need, and confirm the facility and the physicians who practice there are in network before anything else.
### Q. Which hospital in Missouri offers the best healthcare?
A.  Best healthcare is not one thing, it is care for a particular condition. A hospital with a strong cardiac program is not automatically the right place for a complex birth or a spine procedure, so match the facility to the diagnosis rather than to a reputation. Compare accreditation, the Care Compare measures for that specific service, and how much of that work the program does. Then check the two things that decide what you pay: network status for both the building and the doctors, and what the published financial assistance policy says about who qualifies.

## Copier Leases and Office Equipment in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/copier-lease-traps-office-equipment-st-louis
Imagine it’s a Tuesday in Florissant and the copier throws a code nobody recognizes. Not a paper jam — a code. The rep who sold it to you has moved on, the tech says the part is back-ordered, and somebody digs out the folder. You know that folder feeling. So before you ever sign the next one, which clause in it would you most regret not reading out loud first?
The folder is worse than the copier. There are two contracts in it, not one, with different end dates. One renewed itself in March, and nobody in the building signed anything in March.
Maybe your version is a four-person insurance office in St. Charles, a dental practice in Webster Groves, or a contractor’s trailer in Belleville. Office equipment is the one purchase small businesses commit to for five years while shopping for it like an errand.
### How does a copier lease work?
A copier lease is usually two contracts and three parties. You sign an equipment lease with a finance company and a separate service agreement with the dealer who delivers the machine. The dealer is paid in full up front by the finance company. Every payment after that goes to the finance company, which never touched your copier.
That split is why copier leases go wrong. Under Article 2A of the Uniform Commercial Code, adopted on both sides of the river, an arrangement built that way is often a “finance lease.” Missouri’s RSMo 400.2A-407, effective August 28, 1992, says that in a finance lease that is not a consumer lease the lessee’s promises become “irrevocable and independent upon the lessee’s acceptance of the goods,” and are then “not subject to cancellation, termination, modification, repudiation, excuse, or substitution” without the other side’s consent. Illinois carries the same language at 810 ILCS 5/2A-407.
So a machine sitting dead in your lobby is a dispute with your dealer, not a reason the finance company stops expecting a check. That is what these statutes say, not a legal conclusion about your paperwork — have a business attorney read it first.
The rest is structure worth knowing by name. A term, usually 60 months. A return provision. A notice window, which quietly runs everything. And an end-of-term purchase option: fair market value means you own nothing and buy the machine at whatever it is then worth, while a nominal or one-dollar buyout means the deal was a purchase all along.
### What does cost-per-copy actually cover, and what is an overage?
Cost-per-copy — also written as “cost per image” or a click charge — bills a set amount for every page the machine counts, against a monthly allowance folded into your payment. Print past it and extra pages bill at the overage rate. Color meters separately, and a page counts whether or not it came out right.
What drives that rate is your volume, your color mix, whether toner and parts are bundled in, how fast the dealer commits to showing up, and the class of machine. Price a floor-standing unit like a desktop and you buy capacity you never use.
Three questions save real money, and all three belong in writing. Does an unused allowance roll over, or evaporate? Does a legal or tabloid sheet count as one click or two? And is there an escalator letting the payment or the per-page rates rise annually? Buried on page four, it compounds across 60 months.
### Why does a 60-month lease turn into 66 or 72?
Because most equipment agreements renew themselves unless you deliver written notice inside a specific window before the end date, and that window closes months before your last payment. Miss it and the contract rolls — month to month, or into another full term at the same payment.
These are evergreen clauses. They are legal, they are ordinary, and the consumer protections owners half-remember do not reach them. The Illinois Automatic Contract Renewal Act (815 ILCS 601) requires an automatic renewal clause and its cancellation procedure to be disclosed clearly and conspicuously — to consumers. It does not apply to business-to-business contracts.
Missouri arrives in a similar place by another route. The private civil action under the Missouri Merchandising Practices Act, RSMo 407.025, belongs to a person who purchases or leases merchandise “primarily for personal, family or household purposes.” An office copier is not that. The Missouri Attorney General’s consumer division takes complaints, but do not build your exit around one.
So the fix is calendar discipline. The day you sign, find the notice provision, count backward from the end date, and set two reminders: 30 days before the window opens, and the day it opens. Then send notice exactly as the contract says.
### What does the service agreement really cover?
The service agreement is where toner, parts, labor and response time live — a separate contract from the lease, with its own term and renewal clause. The two can end on different dates. That is how an office pays for service on a machine picked up in March, or loses coverage on one it still owes 14 payments on.
Read it for exclusions before price. Common carve-outs: network and driver setup, moving the machine to another suite, damage traced to paper or toner the dealer did not supply, and anything a user did to the finisher. Response time is a target, not a guarantee, unless the contract says so.
Then ask in writing: does coverage follow the machine if you relocate, what happens if the dealer is acquired, and is color toner included, metered separately, or excluded?
Wildly off-topic — if your loading dock is crumbling, start with concrete contractors.
### What are your real options for getting out early?
There are four. Buy the lease out, roll it into an upgrade with the same dealer, assign or sublease it with the lessor’s written consent, or ride the term out and hit the non-renewal date on time. Only the last is cheap. Almost all leverage sits before signature: ask for a shorter term, a purchase option stated in dollars, and the evergreen renewal struck.
A buyout quote is typically the remaining payments plus any residual, sometimes discounted. Ask for it in writing with a good-through date, then ask what the return costs — packing and freight are frequently yours, and a machine that arrives damaged can be billed back.
The upgrade rollover deserves suspicion, not because dealers are dishonest but because of the arithmetic. Rolling a remaining balance into a fresh 60-month agreement keeps the payment looking reasonable while your total obligation grows. Do it twice and you are paying on a machine that left two copiers ago.
### Should you buy, lease, or go refurbished?
Buying outright is usually cheaper across the machine’s life, because you are not paying a finance charge on top of the hardware. Leasing costs less in month one and bundles service plus a scheduled replacement. Refurbished contract-grade equipment splits the difference.
Buy if your volume is modest, cash is comfortable, and somebody will handle toner and service calls. Lease if you print heavily, need color to be reliable, or value one predictable number. The mistake is rarely picking wrong — it is picking on the monthly payment without multiplying by the term and adding clicks.
Refurbished machines come off lease from larger offices, get reconditioned, and often sell with a limited warranty. Ask for the lifetime meter reading, what was replaced, and whether parts and toner are still in normal supply. Then ask your CPA how each option lands on your return.
### Where should you buy office furniture around St. Louis?
