Adult vision benefits are set state by state: a National Eye Institute-supported study published in Health Affairs on August 5, 2024 found that fee-for-service Medicaid in 20 states covered no eyeglasses for adults at all. MO HealthNet in Missouri and HFS in Illinois each write their own optical rules, and managed-care plans layer more on top. Check your plan, not a general article.
Paying cash? No number goes here, because it swings with the practice, the testing and whether a procedure happens. Ask for the self-pay rate before you book, and ask whether the refraction is billed on its own. If cost is the barrier, three doors are worth knowing: federally qualified health centers, which use sliding-scale fees; university optometry teaching clinics; and EyeCare America, the American Academy of Ophthalmology’s public-service program, which connects people who qualify with volunteer ophthalmologists for a medical eye exam at no out-of-pocket cost to the patient. Eligibility rules change, so check the program rather than assume.
### What do eye practices wish patients understood?
If you’re weighing surgery instead of glasses, start with who is a good candidate for laser eye surgery in St. Louis.
From behind the counter, an ophthalmology practice is two businesses stapled together. The surgical side is priced by Medicare, and the number moves: for 2026, CMS set the physician payment for routine cataract surgery, CPT 66984, at $462.94, down roughly 11% from $521.75 in 2025, after a work RVU cut and a steeper cut to facility practice expense. The office side runs on volume — refractions, the optical dispensary, elective lens upgrades. Fourth quarter is a crush, because deductibles are met and flexible spending dollars expire December 31. January is dead air. The recurring frustration is mismatch: a patient books a “routine” exam for a medical problem, or no-shows a dilated slot that held a chair, a tech and an hour. Practices get found by town and by symptom now, so a complete, current listing is not vanity, it is intake.
Holding a referral card and no idea who to call? Browse ophthalmologists across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two offices and ask the same three things: subspecialty, wait time, and what they need from your referring doctor.
If you run an eye practice, list it with us so the person squinting at a referral card can find you.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it better to go to an ophthalmologist or optometrist?
A.  Neither is better; they answer different questions. An optometrist is the right first stop for a vision exam, a glasses or contact lens prescription, and routine monitoring. An ophthalmologist is a medical doctor who diagnoses and treats eye disease and performs surgery. Most people start with an optometrist and get referred when something medical surfaces. If you already know the issue is disease, injury or surgical, book the ophthalmologist directly.
### Q. Can an ophthalmologist treat floaters?
A.  Yes. Ophthalmologists evaluate floaters and treat the conditions behind them, which is why they are the specialist to see when floaters change suddenly. Most floaters are a normal age-related change and get monitored rather than treated. The National Eye Institute treats a sudden burst of new floaters, especially alongside flashes of light, as a reason to seek emergency care, because it can point to a retinal tear.
### Q. Should I see an ophthalmologist for astigmatism?
A.  Astigmatism by itself is a refractive error, and an optometrist can usually diagnose it and prescribe glasses or contacts. An ophthalmologist enters the picture when the astigmatism is tied to a corneal condition, when you are weighing refractive surgery, or when it is being corrected during cataract surgery with a toric lens. Ask which of those situations you are actually in.
### Q. What diseases can be detected by an ophthalmologist?
A.  Eye disease first: glaucoma, cataracts, macular degeneration, diabetic retinopathy, retinal tears and corneal disease among them. A dilated exam also shows blood vessels and the optic nerve directly, which is why an eye exam sometimes surfaces signs of systemic conditions such as diabetes or high blood pressure. That is a finding to carry to your primary care doctor, not a diagnosis to make yourself.
### Q. What is the most common surgery performed by ophthalmologists?
A.  Cataract surgery. It is the most commonly performed intraocular surgery in the United States, and most ophthalmology practices are built around it. The clouded natural lens is removed and replaced with an artificial intraocular lens. Medicare covers the procedure when it is medically necessary, and Medicare beneficiaries account for the large majority of the national volume.
### Q. Are ophthalmologists covered by insurance?
A.  Medically necessary eye care is generally covered by health insurance, Original Medicare included. What often is not covered is the routine refraction that produces a glasses prescription, which tends to be a vision-plan benefit instead. HMO-style plans may require a referral before they pay anything. Confirm the practice is in network for your medical plan, not only your vision plan. Those two networks frequently differ.
### Q. How much does it cost out of pocket to see an ophthalmologist?
A.  It depends on the practice, the visit type, and whether testing or a procedure happens, so ask for the self-pay rate before booking. Ask three things specifically: the office visit charge, whether the refraction is billed separately, and what imaging or testing could be added. Many offices will quote a self-pay price over the phone.
### Q. Where is the least expensive place to get an eye exam?
A.  Usually a federally qualified health center on a sliding-scale fee, a university optometry teaching clinic, or a retail optical chain running an exam promotion. If you qualify, EyeCare America connects patients with volunteer ophthalmologists for a medical eye exam at no out-of-pocket cost to the patient. Cheapest is not automatically right, though — a medical problem needs a medical exam, which is a different visit than a glasses check.
### Q. Where can I find an ophthalmologist in St. Louis?
A.  Start with your health plan’s provider directory, then verify the license in Missouri at pr.mo.gov or in Illinois through IDFPR. If you hold a referral, the referring office usually works with two or three practices regularly and can tell you which takes your plan. A local directory helps you sort by town when the drive matters.

## How to Pay for a Retirement Home in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-pay-for-a-retirement-home-in-st-louis
Imagine it’s a Sunday afternoon in Affton and you’re standing in your mother’s kitchen holding a shoebox of unopened mail. She’s fine. Mostly. But she went down on the back steps in June, the stairs are a real problem now, and last week she called you twice about the same doctor’s appointment.
So you start looking. Within an hour you’ve toured a website in Kirkwood, priced something in Florissant, and found a place near Belleville quoting a number so low you assume you misread it. Nobody explains what the price includes, or why one building calls itself assisted living and the one three miles away calls itself residential care. And the question under all of it — the one you haven’t said out loud — is who pays for this.
That question has a real answer. Not a comfortable one, but a clear one. Here’s how senior living actually gets paid for in the St. Louis metro, on both sides of the river.
### How do families in St. Louis actually pay for a retirement home?
Five sources cover almost every bill: private pay from income and savings, a long-term care insurance policy if one exists, VA Aid and Attendance for wartime veterans and surviving spouses, Medicaid — MO HealthNet in Missouri, Illinois Medicaid across the river — and subsidized senior housing for people whose problem is rent rather than daily care.
Which door opens depends less on how much help your parent needs than on what license the building holds and which state it sits in. Order matters too: private pay and insurance work across the widest range of settings, VA money attaches to a pension, Medicaid is the deepest benefit and the narrowest gate, and subsidized housing is cheapest and slowest. Families who start at the Medicaid end learn the hard way that eligibility takes months of paperwork nobody has begun.
### What is the difference between independent living, assisted living, memory care and skilled nursing?
They are four products at four prices, and only one is a medical facility. Independent living is an apartment with meals and activities. Assisted living adds hands-on help with daily tasks. Memory care is assisted living in a secured setting built around dementia. Skilled nursing is licensed nursing care under a physician’s direction.
Missouri makes the distinction legal. Its Department of Health and Senior Services, through the Section for Long-Term Care Regulation, licenses residential care facilities, assisted living facilities, intermediate care facilities and skilled nursing facilities. In a residential care facility, residents are generally expected to reach safety on their own in an emergency. An assisted living facility helps with eating, dressing, bathing, toileting, transferring and walking, oversees medications, and must have a licensed nursing home administrator.
Illinois uses its own categories — sheltered care, assisted living establishments, supportive living facilities and skilled nursing — under the Illinois Department of Public Health, with supportive living run by Healthcare and Family Services. Two buildings that look identical from the parking lot, one in Maryland Heights and one in Fairview Heights, can sit under different rules and different funding. Ask what license a building holds before you ask what it costs.
### Does Medicare pay for a retirement home?
No. Medicare does not pay for long-term custodial care, which is exactly what most retirement homes provide — help with bathing, dressing, eating, and getting in and out of bed. Medicare.gov says it plainly: Medicare doesn’t cover custodial care if that is the only kind of care you need. This is the most expensive misunderstanding families carry onto a tour.
What Medicare covers is short, skilled and medical. After a qualifying hospital stay, Part A can pay for skilled nursing facility care up to 100 days in a benefit period, and only while the person genuinely needs skilled nursing or therapy. Coverage is full early in that window and carries a daily coinsurance later. When the skilled need ends, coverage ends, even with days left on the counter.
Three weeks of rehab after a hip fracture in Florissant may well be covered. The following year in the same building, with the same person needing help getting dressed, is not. Confirm your own coverage at 1-800-MEDICARE, or free through Missouri’s CLAIM counselors or the Illinois Senior Health Insurance Program.
### What does private pay really look like, and is long-term care insurance worth using?
Private pay is the default, and it is almost never one number. Most communities charge monthly rent for the apartment, add a care level fee based on an assessment of how much help the resident needs, then charge a one-time community fee on top. Skilled nursing is the exception and is usually quoted as a daily rate.
Ask for the current rate sheet in writing. Ask what triggers a move to the next care tier and what it costs. Ask what the increases have been three years running — that number decides whether this is affordable in year three. Two communities can quote similar base rent and land far apart once care tiers are added. The Genworth Cost of Care Survey publishes regional figures by care type; use it to sanity-check a quote.
Nothing to do with senior living — St. Louis auto repair shops.
If a long-term care policy is sitting in a drawer, read it before you tour anything. Most policies pay once the insured needs help with two or more of six activities of daily living, or has a cognitive impairment requiring substantial supervision, and many require the inability be expected to last roughly 90 days. Then comes the elimination period, a waiting stretch chosen at purchase during which the family pays out of pocket. Check the benefit cap, whether the policy covers assisted living or only nursing care, and whether it carries an inflation rider. A policy written in the 1990s without one may cover a small fraction of a 2026 bill.
### What is VA Aid and Attendance, and who qualifies?
Aid and Attendance is not a standalone program. It is an increased monthly amount added to an existing VA pension for qualified wartime veterans and surviving spouses who need another person’s help with daily activities — bathing, feeding, dressing — or who are largely confined to bed, in a nursing home from lost physical or mental ability, or severely visually impaired.
The detail most families miss: because Aid and Attendance raises the pension rate itself, someone whose income was once too high for a basic VA pension may still qualify at the increased rate. A household told no five years ago should ask again once care costs enter the picture.
Applications go to a VA Pension Management Center or regional benefit office, usually with VA Form 21-2680 completed by a physician. Rates change every year, so take the current one from va.gov, not a placement website. County veterans service offices on both sides of the river handle these claims at no cost.
### When does Medicaid pay, and how do Missouri and Illinois differ?
Medicaid is the country’s largest payer of long-term nursing facility care, and in Missouri that program is MO HealthNet. It can cover room, board and care in a Medicaid-certified nursing facility for people who meet a medical level-of-care standard and strict financial rules. Residents put nearly all of their monthly income toward the cost, keeping a small personal needs allowance plus allowances for insurance premiums and a spouse still at home.
Here is the Missouri catch. MO HealthNet generally does not pay assisted living room and board. The state’s Aged and Disabled Waiver funds in-home services — personal care, homemaker help, home-delivered meals, adult day care, respite — for people in their own home or a relative’s, not in a facility. For residents of licensed residential care and assisted living facilities, Missouri offers Supplemental Nursing Care instead, a modest monthly cash grant. It narrows a gap. It does not cover a bill.
Illinois built a different door. The Illinois Supportive Living Program is a Medicaid waiver alternative to nursing home care: a private apartment with personal care, medication assistance, housekeeping, meals and 24-hour staff, for people 65 and older or adults 22 to 64 with physical disabilities. Illinois Healthcare and Family Services reports more than 150 operational supportive living settings statewide and publishes a provider list by county. If your parent lives in Madison, St. Clair, Monroe or Clinton County, call before writing off assisted living.
Every income figure, asset limit and look-back period in both states changes over time. Confirm your own numbers with the Missouri Family Support Division or Illinois Healthcare and Family Services before you move money or retitle an account.
### What happens if the money runs out?
The practical answer is spend-down: private funds pay until they are gone, then the resident applies for Medicaid. Whether that happens without another move depends on a question to ask on the first tour — does this building accept Medicaid, and does it hold Medicaid-certified beds? Many assisted living communities do not, and a family that skips it can face a second move at the worst moment.
If the real need is affordable housing rather than daily care, look at subsidized senior housing. HUD’s Section 202 Supportive Housing for the Elderly serves households with at least one member 62 or older and very low income, generally under 50 percent of area median income, with residents typically paying 30 percent of adjusted income toward rent.
For free, unbiased help, call your Area Agency on Aging. The St. Louis Area Agency on Aging serves the City of St. Louis. Mid-East Area Agency on Aging covers St. Louis, St. Charles, Franklin and Jefferson counties. AgeSmart Community Resources serves Bond, Clinton, Madison, Monroe, Randolph, St. Clair and Washington counties in Illinois. All three do benefits counseling. If a coverage gap is part of the squeeze, our guide to getting health insurance in Missouri covers the marketplace and MO HealthNet basics.
### What should you ask before you sign anything?
Start with the license and the money, in that order. What license does this building hold? What does the current written rate sheet say? What triggers a move to a higher care level, and what does it cost? Is the community fee refundable? Does the building accept Medicaid, and for which residents? And what happens if a resident’s needs exceed what the license allows — who makes that call, and how much notice does the family get?
Check the record yourself. Missouri publishes facility information through the Department of Health and Senior Services, Illinois through the Department of Public Health, and Medicare’s Care Compare covers certified nursing homes nationwide. Both states run a long-term care ombudsman program that takes resident complaints, and Missouri operates an Elder Abuse and Neglect Hotline at 1-800-392-0210.
Visit twice — once on a scheduled tour, once unannounced around dinner. And if staying home a while longer is realistic, our guide to where to get medical supplies in St. Louis covers grab bars, shower chairs and walkers.
### What does this look like from the operator’s side of the desk?
Senior living runs on two numbers nobody prints in a brochure: occupancy and payer mix. A community running near full with a healthy private-pay share works; the same building with empty apartments and a census that has spent down to Medicaid rates below the cost of care does not. Labor is the largest line by a wide margin, and an agency-filled shift costs a multiple of one filled in-house.
Seasonality is real too. Families put decisions off through the holidays, then January and February bring a wave of move-ins after adult children visit and see the decline. What operators complain about to each other is referral commissions — placement services are commonly paid between half and a full month’s rent per move-in. Families search this category by neighborhood, and a complete, accurate directory listing is how a community gets found without paying a commission on the introduction.
Ready to tour instead of scroll? Browse retirement homes across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call three of them and ask the same two questions: what license do you hold, and do you accept Medicaid?
If you run a retirement community, list it on St Louis Near Me Directory so families planning a tour can find you.
Paperwork that helps long before a move: power of attorney in Missouri, so someone you trust can sign when you can’t.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Does Medicare cover retirement homes?
A.  Not for long-term stays. Part A can pay for skilled nursing facility care up to 100 days in a benefit period after a qualifying hospital stay, with a daily coinsurance later. It stops when the skilled need stops. Room, board and daily personal help are custodial care, which Medicare does not cover.
### Q. How much does a retirement home cost per day?
A.  Most communities bill monthly, so a per-day figure is really rent divided by days in the month, and it leaves out the care level fee and the one-time move-in fee. Skilled nursing is the exception and is normally quoted daily. Ask three communities for a current written rate sheet.
### Q. What happens to the elderly if they can’t afford assisted living?
A.  They typically spend down private funds, then apply for Medicaid, which in Missouri pays for care in Medicaid-certified nursing facilities rather than assisted living. Illinois residents may qualify for the Supportive Living Program instead. Other routes include VA Aid and Attendance, subsidized senior housing and in-home waiver services. Start early.
### Q. What is the 80/20 rule in a retirement community?
A.  It comes from federal fair housing law. To qualify as housing for older persons and claim the exemption from familial status rules, a 55-plus community must have at least 80 percent of its occupied units housing at least one person 55 or older, publish policies showing that intent, and verify ages periodically.
### Q. Is it cheaper to live in a 55 and over community?
A.  Sometimes, though not for the reason people assume. A 55-plus community is housing, not care, so you are not paying for meals, staffing or personal assistance. Costs usually bundle exterior maintenance, lawn care and amenities into an association fee. Compare the total monthly outlay against what the current house costs you.
### Q. At what age do most people go into a retirement home?
A.  No single age, and it splits by care type. Independent living draws people in their seventies and early eighties. Assisted living skews much older — AHCA/NCAL data has long shown roughly half of assisted living residents are 85 or older, with reported average stays of about 22 to 28 months. The trigger is usually a fall or a diagnosis, not a birthday.
### Q. Where can I find affordable senior living in St. Louis?
A.  Start with your Area Agency on Aging — the St. Louis Area Agency on Aging for the city, Mid-East Area Agency on Aging for St. Louis, St. Charles, Franklin and Jefferson counties, AgeSmart Community Resources on the Illinois side. All do free benefits counseling. Then look at HUD Section 202 properties, vouchers and tax-credit senior apartments.
### Q. Is there low-income senior housing in St. Charles, MO that has no waiting list?
A.  Rarely. Income-based senior housing in St. Charles County and across the metro almost always runs a waiting list, and some properties close the list once it gets long. What works is applying to several properties at once rather than waiting on one, and asking each manager how the list is ordered.
### Q. What is the downside of living in a retirement community?
A.  Cost and inflexibility, mostly. Fees rise, care levels add charges as needs grow, and a building licensed for one level may not be able to keep a resident whose needs outgrow it. Some residents also feel the loss of a neighborhood they knew for forty years.

## How Pawn Shops Work in St. Louis: A Plain Guide to Pawn Loans
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-pawn-shops-work-in-st-louis
Imagine it’s a Thursday in Affton, rent clears Friday, and the alternator on your car picked this week to quit. There’s $180 in checking and a paycheck six days out. In a drawer somewhere is a guitar you haven’t touched since 2019, a set of impact drivers, and a ring from a marriage that ended.
Maybe it’s Florissant instead and the furnace. Maybe it’s Belleville and a vet bill nobody budgeted for. The details move around; the arithmetic doesn’t. You need a few hundred dollars for a short stretch, and every option on the table — a card near its limit, asking a brother-in-law, a storefront lender out on Gravois — carries a different kind of cost.
A pawn shop is one of those options, and it is built differently from all of them. Nobody pulls your credit. Nobody calls your job. If the loan goes sideways you lose the guitar, and that is the entire consequence. Whether that trade suits you comes down to details nobody explains, so here they are.
### What should I know before visiting a pawn shop?
Bring a current government-issued photo ID, bring the item complete — case, charger, cords, paperwork — and decide before you walk in whether you want a loan against it or an outright sale. Those are two different transactions at two different prices. Then ask for one number: the total dollars you must hand back, and the exact date.
The ticket you sign is the contract. It should name the item, list the amount you’re getting, state the finance charge and any service or storage fee, and give a maturity date. If a clerk quotes you a percentage instead of a dollar figure, ask again in dollars. People get hurt on pawn loans mostly by misunderstanding the payoff and the date, not by the rate itself.
You also don’t owe anyone your story. A pawnbroker is pricing the item, not you. Nobody needs to know why you’re standing there, and a shop that pushes for a reason is telling you how it operates.
### How does a pawn loan actually work, start to finish?
A pawn loan is a small loan secured by an object you hand over. The shop appraises the item, offers an amount, writes a ticket, and locks the item in the back. You get cash that day. Pay the principal plus the charges by the maturity date and you walk out with your property. Miss it, and the shop keeps the item.
That last part is the whole design. A pawn loan is non-recourse: the collateral is the only thing on the hook. There is no credit check going in, and no report to Equifax, Experian or TransUnion coming out — not when you take the loan, not when you repay it, and not when you walk away from it. No collector calls. No judgment. No garnishment. You forfeit the item, and the shop resells it to get its money back.
What you pay for that convenience is set by state law and varies by state, by loan size and by shop, so treat any rate you read online as a rumor until you see your own ticket. Missouri regulates pawnbrokers under Chapter 367 of the Revised Statutes of Missouri. Illinois regulates them through the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation under the Pawnbroker Regulation Act of 2023, amended by Public Act 103-0585, which Governor Pritzker signed on March 22, 2024. That act set new financing rate caps, required additional disclosures and posted fee displays, clarified how shops handle pledges of allegedly stolen property, and mandated annual training for pawn employees.
One federal rule is worth knowing by name. The Military Lending Act caps the military annual percentage rate at 36% for active-duty service members and their dependents, bars mandatory arbitration in covered loans and requires specific disclosures. It gets enforced. In July 2025 the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau settled with FirstCash, Inc. and its subsidiaries over allegations the company charged above that 36% cap on 42,698 loans originated between October 2016 and August 2024; the settlement set aside an estimated $5 million to $7 million in redress for affected service members and dependents, plus a $4 million civil penalty. If you or your spouse is active duty — and plenty of families around Scott Air Force Base are — say so at the counter.
### Is it better to pawn or sell?
Sell if you don’t want the item back. Pawn if you do and you’re confident about the date. Selling almost always pays more cash on the spot, because the shop takes ownership and the resale risk immediately. Pawning pays less and adds a finance charge, and what that charge buys you is the right to get your property back.
Here is the version nobody says out loud. If you already know the money will not be there by the maturity date, pawning is just the expensive way to sell. You take the smaller loan amount, you pay the charge, and you lose the item anyway. Two minutes with a calendar before you choose is worth real dollars.
Sentiment is the honest exception. A grandmother’s ring, a father’s watch, an instrument a kid still plays — those get pawned rather than sold on purpose, and shops see it every week.
### How much will a pawn shop give you for a $1,000 item?
Far less than $1,000, and the reason is arithmetic rather than insult. The offer keys off what the shop believes it can resell the item for, locally and reasonably fast, then discounts that again to leave room for margin and risk. The National Pawnbrokers Association puts typical offers at roughly 25% to 60% of an item’s resale value, and the average pawn loan in the U.S. at around $150.
The trap is the word “value.” A $1,000 item usually means $1,000 at retail when it was new. A three-year-old laptop that stickered at $1,000 might carry $350 of realistic used resale value today, and the loan offer comes off that $350, not off the sticker. Gold is the cleanest case, because scrap weight and purity set a hard floor under the number no matter what the piece looks like.
What moves the offer up: the item is complete and testable, it powers on at the counter, you brought the box and the paperwork, it’s a brand the shop moves quickly, and the shelf isn’t already holding four of them. What moves it down: missing chargers, cracked housings, dead batteries, activation locks nobody can clear, and bad seasonal timing.
Unrelated, and we know it — St. Louis Korean food is worth the drive.
### What sells at a pawn shop, and what gets turned away?
Shops take what they can resell in the St. Louis market without babysitting it. That means gold and jewelry first, then power tools, musical instruments, current-generation electronics and consoles, coins and bullion, lawn equipment, and firearms at shops holding a federal firearms license. Anything bulky, dated, or hard to prove ownership on gets a polite no.
Usually welcome: gold and diamond jewelry, watches, power tools, guitars, amps and brass, laptops, tablets, game consoles, cameras and lenses, bullion, mowers, designer handbags with authentication.
Usually declined: furniture, older televisions, printers, car seats, most clothing, opened cosmetics, medical equipment, recalled goods, defaced serial numbers, and devices locked to someone else’s account.
Tools deserve their own note. They are among the easiest items to pawn and the most painful to lose, because losing them can cost you work. If it’s a tool you use twice a year, weigh the loan against renting equipment when you need it instead.
### What do you need to bring, and how do the rules differ in Missouri and Illinois?
You need a valid photo ID, you need to be 18, and you need to actually own the item. In Missouri, statute 367.031 requires the pawnbroker to record the pledgor’s name, address and physical description along with a driver’s license, military identification or other official identifying number, plus a description of the goods and serial numbers where they are reasonably available.
Missouri law also bars a pawnbroker from taking a pledge from anyone under eighteen, and it makes the paperwork visible to police by design. Licensed Missouri pawnbrokers must transmit a business day’s reportable transaction data to the state database by the end of the next business day, and must hand over paper copies of any transaction on request from law enforcement. Section 367.047 lets an officer with probable cause place a hold order on property, and a shop cannot sell an item while that hold stands.
Cross the river and the framework changes, though the spirit does not. Illinois pawnshops must hold a license from the state, operating without one is unlawful, and the 2024 amendments layered on posted fee displays, additional customer disclosures and a clearer process for pledges of allegedly stolen goods. Pawn in Belleville and redeem while living in Missouri, and you are dealing with two rulebooks.
Practically: expect your ID to be scanned, expect a thumbprint at some counters, and expect the transaction to be searchable by detectives. None of that is aimed at you. It exists because the fastest way to close a burglary case in St. Charles County is a serial-number match against last week’s pawn uploads.
### What happens if you cannot pay the loan back on time?
You forfeit the item, and that is where it ends. The shop takes ownership and puts it on the sales floor. Nobody sues you, nobody sends a balance to collections, and nothing lands on your credit report. That is the fundamental difference between a pawn loan and nearly every other loan you can get in a single afternoon.
Before the date arrives, though, call the shop. Extensions and renewals are common, and are usually handled by paying the accrued charges to move the maturity date out. Some shops also take partial payments toward the principal, which lowers what you owe at the end. Every one of those conversations goes better a week early than a day late.
Keep the ticket somewhere you will find it. Losing it is not fatal, since your ID and the shop’s own record usually sort it out, but it slows a redemption that should take four minutes.
### What this looks like from the owner’s side of the counter
A pawn shop runs on two engines: service fees on loans that get redeemed, and retail margin on the items that do not. The loan book is the steadier one, and it breathes on a schedule. FirstCash, the largest U.S. pawn operator, tells investors in SEC filings that pawn loan balances fall in the first and second quarters as customers receive federal tax refunds around February, then rebuild later in the year, while retail sales peak in the fourth quarter. Jewelry anchors the book because scrap value floors the collateral. And the complaint owners trade with each other is not margin — it is being treated as a fence by people who never see them upload every transaction to a police database, on deadline, at their own expense.
Sitting on an old coin collection instead? Here’s how to sell coins in St. Louis without getting ripped off.
The quieter frustration is being invisible. Somebody in Maryland Heights searching at 9 p.m. for a shop that takes instruments is a real customer with a real item, and a complete listing with hours and specialties turns that search into a walk-in. Shops can get listed on St Louis Near Me Directory.
Want to compare offers before you hand anything over? Browse pawn shops across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two or three with the make, model and condition in hand before you drive anywhere.
If you own a pawn shop that quotes straight over the phone, list your shop with us so the person comparing offers can find you.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the point of a pawn shop?
A.  It is a lender and a resale store in one building. The lending side hands people cash the same day against an object, with no credit check and no consequence beyond losing it. The retail side sells what was forfeited or sold outright. That combination is why a pawnshop can approve someone a bank will not touch.
### Q. What items do pawnshops usually buy?
A.  Gold and diamond jewelry, watches, power tools, musical instruments, laptops and tablets, game consoles, cameras, coins and bullion, lawn equipment, and firearms where the shop is federally licensed. The common thread is a known resale market and easy verification. If a buyer exists in the St. Louis metro this month, a shop will usually make an offer.
### Q. What will a pawn shop not take?
A.  Furniture, older televisions, printers, car seats, most clothing, opened cosmetics and medical devices are typical refusals — too bulky, too dated or too regulated to resell. Shops also decline anything with a defaced serial number, anything under a manufacturer recall, and phones or tablets still locked to another person’s account, because those cannot be sold.
### Q. Can I pawn something at 17?
A.  No. Missouri law prohibits a pawnbroker from receiving a pledge from anyone under eighteen, and it is a criminal offense in Missouri for a pawnbroker to buy personal property from an unemancipated minor without written consent from a custodial parent or guardian. Illinois shops apply adult identification requirements too. Bring a parent, or wait.
### Q. What to pawn for $50?
A.  Small gold items are the reliable answer, because the offer keys off metal weight rather than fashion — a broken chain still weighs what it weighs. Beyond that: a name-brand cordless drill with a working battery, a solid set of hand tools, an entry-level guitar, or a console controller bundled with a few current games.
### Q. What sells for $100 at a pawn shop?
A.  On the retail side, the $100 shelf is mostly mid-tier power tools, older game consoles with a controller, entry-level guitars and amps, smaller gold chains, and used tablets a generation or two back. On the loan side, an item has to carry roughly $200 to $400 of resale value before an offer reaches $100.
### Q. How much will a pawn shop give you for a $500 item?
A.  Expect an offer well under $500, because the shop works from used resale value and then discounts it. If $500 was the retail price when new, current resale might be $175 to $250, and the loan comes off that figure. Gold is the exception again: weight and purity set a floor the shop cannot argue below.
### Q. Is it worth selling items to a pawn shop?
A.  Often yes, when speed matters. You get cash immediately, with no shipping, no meeting a stranger in a parking lot and no waiting on a marketplace buyer. You will net less than a patient private sale would bring. For common items, or when the money is needed this afternoon, that spread is usually worth paying.
### Q. Which pawn shop gives you the most money?
A.  There is no permanent winner — it shifts by item and by week, depending on what each shop already has too much of. Call three, describe the exact make, model and condition, and ask for a range over the phone. For gold, ask what they pay per gram at current spot, which makes the quotes directly comparable.
### Q. What are some good pawn shops in Saint Louis, Missouri?
A.  Rather than crowning one, judge shops on what predicts a fair transaction: a posted fee schedule, a clerk who states the payoff amount and date out loud, real testing at the counter, and reviews that mention redemptions going smoothly. Compare pawn shops across the metro and the Metro East, then call two or three before you go.

## How to Find Good Breakfast and Brunch in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-find-good-breakfast-and-brunch-in-st-louis
Imagine it’s Saturday and you volunteered to handle breakfast for four people. It’s 9:40. You’re somewhere on Manchester between Maplewood and Brentwood, three phones are buzzing, and the place you half-remembered doesn’t open until ten. Not a disaster. Just forty minutes you didn’t plan to spend in a parking lot.
Or it’s Sunday and your parents drove in from Florissant. You promised brunch. The first spot quotes ninety minutes. The second won’t seat a party of six. The third stopped serving eggs at noon, and you’re circling a block in Soulard on the one morning when the market has every curb space spoken for.
None of that is bad luck. Breakfast and brunch are the two hardest meals in this metro to simply show up for. The serving windows are short, the rush is squeezed into about three hours, and the words breakfast and brunch describe two different kinds of business running two different sets of rules. Sort that out first and the morning gets easy.
### How do you find good breakfast and brunch in St. Louis?
Work in this order: decide if you want a diner or a brunch, confirm the hours yourself the same week you’re going, then pick a neighborhood that has three options inside a two-block walk. Most ruined breakfast mornings are an hours problem or a parking problem. Neither one shows up in a review.
Four checks take about ninety seconds between them. What time does the kitchen open on this specific day — weekend hours often shift an hour in either direction from weekday hours. Is there a separate weekend-only menu, and when does it stop. Will they seat a party your size. And can you join a waitlist from the car instead of standing at the host stand.
Then build in a fallback before you leave. Pick the block, not the restaurant. If your first choice quotes an hour, a second kitchen within walking distance turns a blown morning into a two-minute adjustment.
### What timeframe is considered brunch?
Brunch generally runs from about 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. In practice around St. Louis, weekend brunch menus most often start at 9 or 10 a.m. and stop somewhere between 1 and 3 p.m., and plenty of kitchens run brunch on Saturday and Sunday only. Anything served at 6 a.m. is breakfast, not brunch.
The word is older than the habit. Guy Beringer coined it in an 1895 essay titled Brunch: A Plea, published in Hunter’s Weekly, arguing for one cheerful late-morning meal in place of the heavy post-church spread. He called it talk-compelling, which is still the honest reason a table lingers.
What matters for planning is the cutoff, not the start. Kitchens change over in the middle of service — the griddle goes down, the brunch board comes off the wall, and the last order for eggs may be called fifteen or twenty minutes before the posted end time. If you’re arriving inside the final half hour of a brunch window, call first. That is the most common way people end up eating a lunch they didn’t want.
### What’s the difference between a diner and a brunch spot?
A diner opens early, serves the same breakfast menu seven days a week, turns tables fast and keeps the check low. A brunch spot opens late, runs a weekend-only menu, usually pours alcohol, and expects you to sit a while. They look like the same meal in a photo. They are completely different mornings.
Diners and counters tend to open the door between 5 and 7 a.m., seat walk-ins only, and hand you a two-egg plate with potatoes and toast. Service is quick because the kitchen is cooking off a flat top it has run ten thousand times. You don’t need a plan to eat at one. You need to get there before the after-church wave, which across most of this metro lands around 11.
Brunch kitchens are the opposite economy: fewer covers, longer tables, plates built to order and a drink list. Expect a waitlist app, a bigger check and a room that is loud by 11:30. Two more categories are worth knowing. Bakeries and coffee houses will feed you well for a fraction of the price when you don’t need table service. And weekend morning food here isn’t only eggs — taquerias along Cherokee Street, Bosnian kitchens around Bevo Mill and the international row on South Grand all run morning and midday menus that have nothing to do with pancakes.
### Which St. Louis neighborhoods are best for breakfast and brunch?
Aim for a walkable commercial strip rather than a single address. In the city, Soulard, Benton Park, Lafayette Square, Tower Grove South and South Grand, the Central West End, The Grove, the Delmar Loop and downtown each put several breakfast and brunch kitchens within a few blocks of one another. Park once, walk to plan B.
In the county, the old downtowns do the same job: Maplewood along Manchester, Webster Groves, Kirkwood, Clayton, University City, Florissant, Ferguson and Affton. West county and Chesterfield lean toward shopping-center breakfast, which is less charming and much easier to park at with a group. St. Charles County has Main Street in St. Charles, plus O’Fallon, St. Peters and Wentzville along the highway corridors.
Don’t skip the Illinois side. Belleville, Edwardsville, Collinsville, O’Fallon and Alton all have compact downtown blocks with weekend brunch, and from south city or downtown the drive is often shorter than the run out to west county on a Sunday. The metro east also tends to run shorter waits at the same hour, which is worth knowing on Mother’s Day weekend.
One more anchor worth planning around. The City of St. Louis lists Soulard Market as open Wednesday through Saturday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., with full vendor participation on Saturday and the market closed Sunday through Tuesday. That makes Saturday morning in Soulard excellent for a market-plus-breakfast plan and rough for parking. Go early or walk in from several blocks out.
### How long is the wait, and can you reserve a table?
Assume 10:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. on Saturday and Sunday is the peak, and assume many breakfast houses take no reservations at all. Walk-in with a waitlist is the norm for diners. Reservations are more common at brunch kitchens with a bar program, and for holidays those books open weeks ahead.
Treat a quoted wait as a range, not a promise. Twenty minutes means the host is estimating how fast four tables will pay and leave, and one lingering party moves everybody. If the quote runs past forty-five minutes, put your name in anyway, then add it at the next block too. Whichever texts first wins.
Nothing to do with pancakes — St. Louis drugstores, if you need one.
Mother’s Day is the exception to every rule here. The National Restaurant Association projects 80 million American adults will dine out on Mother’s Day 2026, up from 75 million in 2025, and OpenTable reported noon as the most-booked hour of that Sunday. If your plan involves that weekend, book in April, ask what the fixed menu is, and confirm the party size in writing.
### Can you order a mimosa at 9 a.m. in Missouri and Illinois?
In Missouri, yes, statewide. Senate Bill 126 took effect August 28, 2021 and moved Sunday alcohol sales — including sales by the drink at restaurants — from an 11 a.m. start to a 6 a.m. start, matching the rest of the week. A 9 a.m. Sunday mimosa in the city, the county or St. Charles is legal.
Illinois is a local question. The statewide Sunday-hours provision, 235 ILCS 5/6-14, was repealed in 2015 by Public Act 99-46, and hours are now set by the municipality and its local liquor commissioner. Belleville, Edwardsville and Collinsville can each run a different Sunday start time, and license classes can differ inside the same town.
Either way, the law only sets the outer edge. A restaurant can start pouring later than it is allowed to, and many do. If the drink is part of why you are going, ask when you call about the table.
### How do you take a group or a couple of kids to brunch?
Call ahead for six or more, and give the real number. Small weekend kitchens frequently cap party size or refuse to seat a table until every guest has arrived, and a group that trickles in one car at a time loses the table you waited for. With kids, the friendliest window is 8 to 9:30 a.m., before the room fills and the noise makes everyone tense.
Ask about split checks before anybody orders. Plenty of places split six ways happily and a few flatly will not, and finding out at the end is nobody’s favorite moment. Ask about high chairs the same way. Old storefront dining rooms in Soulard, Maplewood or Main Street St. Charles are charming and often tight — if someone uses a wheelchair or a walker, confirm the entrance and the restroom instead of assuming.
Parking rules change by municipality, so read the meter rather than trusting what worked last time. And once the group runs past about a dozen people you have left brunch territory for private-room territory — a different search entirely, and this guide to booking a banquet hall in St. Louis covers how those bookings actually work.
### Where do you get a good breakfast without paying brunch prices?
Go on a weekday, sit at a counter, and skip the two things that inflate the check: the specialty coffee drink and the brunch cocktail. A standard two-egg plate at a diner that opens before seven is the cheapest sit-down breakfast in the metro, and frequently the best one.
Bakeries and coffee houses are the next tier — pastry and coffee for a few dollars, no wait, no table-service tip pressure. Taquerias and international groceries with a hot counter sit under that, concentrated along Cherokee Street, South Grand, Bevo Mill and stretches of north county. A farmers market run plus something cooked at home lands cheaper still, and Soulard Market’s Saturday hours make that a real plan rather than a theoretical one.
It helps to know where the money goes at a brunch. Two eggs and toast is a low-cost plate anywhere. A made-to-order entree plus a cocktail can double that check without doubling the food, which isn’t a trick — it is how the daypart pays for itself.
### What does a breakfast house look like from behind the counter?
Craving something else? Here’s what to order at a creperie.
Breakfast is the cheapest food cost of any daypart and the lowest average check, so the whole model is volume and table turns. Coffee carries the margin, and alcohol is what made weekend brunch worth staffing at all. Ingredient shocks land hard here — the federal Bureau of Labor Statistics average for a dozen Grade A large eggs hit $6.23 in March 2025, and a kitchen going through cases a week can’t reprice a printed menu that fast. The rush compresses into roughly three hours on Saturday and Sunday, so a full crew works a shift that is dead at 8:45 and drowning at 10:45. Mother’s Day is the single biggest day of the year, and January is the month that hurts. Owners trade the same two complaints: no-shows, and tables that camp an hour after paying while twelve people wait at the door. Nearly all of those searches start on a phone in a parking lot, which is the honest argument for a complete listing with current hours.

If you run the brunch spot with the line out the door on Saturday, put it on the directory so the next hungry table finds you.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the difference between breakfast, brunch, and lunch?
A.  Breakfast is a menu and a time slot — eggs, griddle items and coffee, served from opening until late morning. Brunch is a weekend hybrid that adds lunch plates and often alcohol, usually between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m. Lunch is the midday menu: sandwiches, salads, entrees, no griddle. One restaurant can serve all three and still keep them in separate windows.
### Q. Is brunch just a late breakfast?
A.  Not quite. A late breakfast is the same food eaten later. Brunch is a different menu built to bridge two meals, which is why you see pancakes sitting next to a burger, plus a drink list that breakfast service usually doesn’t carry. It is also a longer sit. Brunch tables turn slower than breakfast tables, and that is why the wait feels so different.
### Q. What is the correct time to have brunch?
A.  There is no rule, but the social default around St. Louis is 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. on Saturday or Sunday. Aim before 10 if you want to be seated immediately, after 1:15 if you want a calmer room and a server who has caught her breath. When people are driving in from opposite ends of the metro, 11 a.m. is the safest split.
### Q. Who has the best breakfast in St. Louis?
A.  No single place wins, because breakfast splits into categories that barely compete with one another: counter diners, weekend brunch kitchens, bakeries, taquerias and pancake houses. Decide which one you actually want, then sort by hours, wait and distance. Recent reviews for the day of the week you plan to go are worth more than a best-of list written two years ago.
### Q. Where can I find the best brunch in Saint Louis, MO?
A.  Start with a neighborhood you can park in, then check which kitchens there run a weekend-only menu and what time it ends. Comparing brunch spots by area beats chasing one recommendation, because the moment your first choice quotes ninety minutes you want the second and third option already picked out on the same block.
### Q. What do you serve at a breakfast brunch?
A.  If you are hosting, a workable spread is one hot egg dish, one griddle or bread item, one savory protein, something fresh, and two drinks — coffee plus something cold. Casseroles, stratas and sheet-pan eggs hold heat far better than plated eggs, which is why they turn up at every brunch that has to feed more than six people at once.
### Q. What are the rules of brunch?
A.  There are no formal rules, only practical ones. Show up as the party you booked, and tell the host your full count before they seat you. Don’t linger an hour past the check while a line stands at the door. Ask about split checks before anyone orders rather than after. And tip on the pre-discount total when a coupon is involved.
### Q. Where’s the cheapest place to get breakfast?
A.  Counter diners, then bakeries, then taquerias and the hot counters inside international groceries — and on a weekday rather than a weekend. The cheapest sit-down breakfast is nearly always the standard two-egg plate at a place that opens before seven. Dropping the specialty coffee drink and the cocktail can cut a check close to half without changing the food.
### Q. Is there a black-owned brunch restaurant in St. Louis?
A.  Yes. The metro has Black-owned breakfast and brunch restaurants, with clusters in north St. Louis city and north county and along the Delmar and Grand corridors, plus locations out in the county and across the river. Local Black-owned business guides, and the ownership details a restaurant posts on its own site or social profile, are the reliable way to confirm before you drive.

## What Happens When You File Bankruptcy in Missouri
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-happens-when-you-file-bankruptcy-in-missouri
Imagine it’s a Tuesday in Affton and the mail has something in it you already knew was coming. A garnishment notice. Your employer got a copy too, which somehow lands harder than the number on the page. You’ve been paying something to somebody every single month for two years, and the balances have barely moved.
Or picture a different version in Belleville. Hours got cut in the spring, an emergency room visit showed up in the summer, and the two events found each other. You’re not reckless with money. You’re current on the mortgage and behind on everything else, and the phone rings from numbers you stopped answering a while ago.
Both people stall in the same spot, and it isn’t pride. Nobody has laid out the mechanics — what happens, in what order, once a petition gets filed. So here is that machinery for the St. Louis metro, both sides of the river. This is general information, not legal advice. Only an attorney who reviews your income, debts and property can tell you whether filing is right for you.
### What happens when you file bankruptcy in Missouri?
The moment your petition hits the docket, the automatic stay under section 362 of the Bankruptcy Code takes effect and collection stops. Wage garnishments stop. Collection calls stop. A scheduled foreclosure sale stops. A repossession stops. The court opens a case number, assigns a trustee, and sets a date for a meeting of creditors. Your creditors get notice from the court, not from you.
The stay is a pause, not a ruling. Nothing about your debts has been decided. It also has holes: criminal proceedings continue, most child support and alimony collection continues, and a secured lender can ask the court for permission to move on a car or a house. Filers with recent prior cases may get a shortened stay, or none, unless the court extends it.
### Does Chapter 7 wipe out all debt?
No. A Chapter 7 discharge erases most ordinary unsecured debt — credit cards, medical bills, personal loans, old utility balances, deficiency balances left over after a repossession. Congress carved out categories that survive, and they survive whether or not you knew about them.
The usual survivors are child support and alimony, most recent income taxes, most student loans, criminal fines and restitution, debts traced to fraud, and debts from a willful and malicious injury — which is why drunk-driving injury judgments typically stay. Student loans have a narrow undue-hardship route, but it means a separate lawsuit inside the bankruptcy. A debt you forget to list can also be left out.
One distinction does more damage than the rest: a discharge wipes your personal liability, not the lien. If a lender holds a mortgage on the house in Maryland Heights or a title on the truck, that lien rides through the case. Keep the collateral, keep paying. Give it back, and the debt goes with it. Medical bills are plain unsecured debt and go out with the credit cards, which is why closing a coverage gap belongs on the same list — here is how to get health insurance in Missouri.
### Chapter 7 or Chapter 13 — what’s the actual difference?
Chapter 7 is a liquidation. A trustee reviews everything you own, sells anything an exemption doesn’t protect, distributes the proceeds, and the qualifying debt is discharged. In practice most consumer Chapter 7 cases are no-asset cases: the exemptions cover what the filer owns and the trustee sells nothing at all.
Chapter 13 is a court-supervised repayment plan measured in years, not months. You keep your property and make one monthly payment to a standing trustee, who distributes it under a plan the judge confirms. People land there for concrete reasons: they’re behind on a mortgage and want to catch up the arrears over time, they have vehicle equity they’d rather not risk, their income is too high for the means test, or they owe priority debt like recent taxes.
Nationally the split leans toward Chapter 7. The American Bankruptcy Institute, citing Epiq data in January 2026, reported 332,706 consumer Chapter 7 filings in calendar year 2025 against 200,055 consumer Chapter 13 filings, with total consumer filings of 533,949 — a 12 percent rise over 2024’s 478,752. Neither chapter is the “better” one. They solve different problems.
### What is the means test, and what does it measure?
The means test is an arithmetic screen, not a character assessment. Step one compares your household’s income to the median family income for the same household size in your state — Missouri and Illinois each have their own figures, published by the U.S. Trustee Program and revised periodically. The Bankruptcy Code measures that income over the six calendar months before the month you file, which is why timing a filing around a bonus or a severance check is a real conversation.
Come in below the median and you’re presumed eligible for Chapter 7, test over. Come in above it and you move to step two, where allowed living expenses and secured payments get subtracted to see what’s genuinely left each month. Plenty of people who assume they earn too much clear it at step two on the strength of a mortgage payment, a car note or childcare. The figures move. Have an attorney run the current ones.
### What can you keep? Missouri’s bankruptcy exemptions
Usually, everything. Exemptions mark out property a Chapter 7 trustee can’t sell, and in a typical consumer case they cover all of it. Missouri doesn’t let you swap in the federal list. RSMo 513.427 takes it off the table, so a St. Louis filer works from the state’s own numbers. Those numbers are about to jump. A new state law raises most of them for cases filed on or after January 1, 2027, and the date your petition hits the docket decides which set you get.
Every figure is measured against what the property would sell for on your filing date, not what you paid for it, and only your equity counts. A car worth $9,000 with $7,500 still owed is $1,500 of equity, and only that $1,500 needs covering.
Say an illustrative single filer with no kids owns a paid-off older sedan that would bring about $4,000 in a private sale, though she paid $17,000 for it new, and has roughly $20,000 of equity in her house. If she files before January 1, 2027, the $3,000 vehicle exemption plus the $600 wildcard leave $400 of the car unprotected, and the $15,000 homestead leaves $5,000 of the house exposed. If she files on or after that date, the $5,000 vehicle figure covers the car and the $40,000 homestead covers the house. Same person, same property, different filing date. Chapter 13 sells nothing, though unprotected equity roughly sets the minimum the plan pays unsecured creditors. When to file, with a garnishment running or a sale date set, is a question for an attorney.
So will Chapter 7 take your car if you own it outright? Usually not. On a paid-off car the whole resale value is equity, so the real test is whether that number fits inside the vehicle exemption plus any wildcard or head-of-family allowance you haven’t spent elsewhere. The head-of-family addition is $1,250, plus $350 for each unmarried dependent child under 21 or disabled dependent. If the car’s value runs past all of that, the trustee can sell it and hand you the exempt share in cash, or you can offer to pay the unprotected amount and keep driving it.
Retirement money gets the strongest shield on the list. RSMo 513.430 exempts qualified accounts like 401(k)s, 403(b)s and traditional and Roth IRAs, inherited ones included, with no dollar cap. The exceptions are narrow: certain divorce and child support orders, and money put into a plan to defraud creditors in the three years before filing. Your right to receive Social Security, unemployment, public assistance, veterans and disability benefits is exempt too, as is alimony or support up to $750 a month.
Metro East filers on the Illinois side use Illinois’s exemptions, not these. And if collectors are the pressure point and bankruptcy is still a maybe, read up on debt collectors, the statute of limitations and wage garnishment in Missouri and compare debt consolidation in St. Louis before you pick a path.
### Where do St. Louis metro filers actually file?
Which side of the river you live on decides your court. Missouri residents of St. Louis City, St. Louis County, St. Charles, Jefferson, Franklin, Lincoln and Warren counties file in the Eastern Division of the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Eastern District of Missouri, whose clerk’s office sits in the Thomas F. Eagleton U.S. Courthouse at 111 South 10th Street downtown. Metro east residents in St. Clair, Madison and Monroe counties file in the Southern District of Illinois, whose East St. Louis division is in the Melvin Price Federal Courthouse at 750 Missouri Avenue.
The bigger difference isn’t the address — it’s the exemptions. Both states opted out of the federal exemption list, Missouri by statute at RSMo 513.427, so the federal one is off the table. Missouri’s covers categories like a homestead, a motor vehicle, household goods, tools of your trade, a general wildcard and an extra allowance for a head of family. Illinois has its own structure, and Public Act 104-0120 raised several Illinois exemption figures effective January 1, 2026. Two neighbors with identical debts and nearly identical cars, one in Collinsville and one in Kirkwood, can get different answers about what they keep.
That matters most if you’ve moved. Federal law has a residency look-back deciding which state’s exemptions you may claim, and a household that crossed from Granite City to Florissant recently may be stuck with the old state’s list. It isn’t intuitive and it isn’t optional.
Wildly off-topic — St. Louis real estate agencies, for entirely different paperwork.
### What does the process look like from start to finish?
Every consumer case runs on the same spine: credit counseling, petition, trustee, meeting of creditors, a second course, discharge. Chapter 13 adds a confirmation hearing and years of plan payments. Here it is in the order you’ll live it.
Credit counseling first. Federal law requires a briefing from an approved nonprofit agency before you file, and the U.S. Trustee Program maintains the approved list by district. It’s usually done online or by phone, and the certificate goes into the court file.
The petition and schedules. Every debt, every asset, income, expenses, recent transfers, lawsuits, prior addresses. You sign under penalty of perjury. Nearly everything that goes wrong goes wrong here — a forgotten co-signed loan, a car titled in a relative’s name.
Filing day. The clerk opens a case, a trustee is assigned, and the automatic stay begins. Creditors get formal notice with your case number.
Documents to the trustee. Pay stubs, tax returns, bank statements, sometimes vehicle valuations. Missing paperwork is the usual reason a routine case turns slow.
The meeting of creditors. The 341 meeting. Not a court hearing, and no judge — the Bankruptcy Code bars judges from attending. You’re sworn in, show photo ID and proof of your Social Security number, and the trustee asks about your schedules. Creditors may attend and usually don’t. Many districts hold these by video, so read the notice.
A second course. After filing and before discharge you complete a personal financial management course. Skipping it is a painful way to lose a discharge you already earned.
Discharge. The court issues an order permanently barring creditors from collecting the discharged debts. In Chapter 13 that arrives at the end of the plan.
There is a court filing fee, and courts allow installments and, for filers who qualify, waivers. Ask at the consultation rather than assuming it’s out of reach.
### Who should you call, and what should you ask?
Start with someone who files consumer cases regularly in your own district, because local practice and local trustees differ between the Eastern District of Missouri and the Southern District of Illinois. Most consumer bankruptcy attorneys offer a free first consultation, with no obligation attached.
Four questions do most of the sorting. What does the flat fee cover, and what falls outside it — amendments, motions, reaffirmation agreements? Do you recommend Chapter 7 or Chapter 13 for my facts, and why? Who will appear with me at the meeting of creditors? And what should I stop doing right now? That last one is worth the whole meeting.
Two checks worth running. Bankruptcy petition preparers are not attorneys and cannot give legal advice; federal law limits them to typing what you tell them. And both states publish licensing and discipline records — Illinois through the Attorney Registration & Disciplinary Commission, Missouri through the Missouri Bar’s lawyer search. Bring pay stubs, two tax returns, a credit report, vehicle titles, your mortgage statement and any lawsuit papers, plus the parts you’d rather not mention.
Bankruptcy is one chapter of our St. Louis money guide, which covers the everyday money questions most of us had to learn the hard way.
### What this looks like from the attorney’s side of the desk
Consumer bankruptcy is a flat-fee practice with a strange economic wrinkle. In Chapter 7 the lawyer generally must collect the whole fee before filing, because any unpaid balance on the filing date is a pre-petition debt and gets discharged along with the credit cards. Chapter 13 flips it: most districts let counsel take a deposit and collect the rest through the plan, often under a court-approved “no-look” amount. That single rule shapes the practice. It is why the person who most needs Chapter 7 sometimes can’t afford the door, and why March and April are the busy months while November and December go quiet — tax refunds are what pay retainers. The complaint you hear between bankruptcy lawyers isn’t about clients. It’s timing: people arrive after the garnishment, after the repossession, after they’ve paid a brother back. Most of that is fixable two months earlier, which depends on whether someone searching locally finds a complete, current listing worth calling. That is what getting listed is for.
