## What Real Estate School Costs in Missouri
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-real-estate-school-costs-in-missouri
Picture a woman in Arnold sitting in the elementary school pickup line with her phone propped against the steering wheel and a real estate school’s enrollment page open on it. She has been half-thinking about this for two years. Every page she finds says the same thing, 72 hours, as if that were the whole answer. What she actually wants to know is what those hours cost, what arrives in the mail after them, and whether her household can survive the stretch between passing an exam and getting paid for anything.
The same month, other people around the metro are reading the same page with the same expression. A man in Florissant who has given fifteen years to a warehouse job that keeps getting reorganized around him. A parent in Wentzville whose youngest just started kindergarten, who wants work that bends around a school calendar. Somebody in Washington who flipped one house with a brother-in-law, enjoyed every part of it, and quietly wondered whether the agent was the one having the better week. A retiree in Granite City who wants a few closings a year, not a second career.
They all want the same three answers. What does this cost in total, how long until money actually comes in, and is it worth doing at all. Here is what the 72 hours contain, how the Missouri exam is built and why so many people stumble on the state half, the bills that start the day after you pass, and the brokerage decision that will shape your first year far more than anything you learn in a classroom.
### How much does it cost to get your realtor license in Missouri?
Missouri requires 72 hours of pre-license education, then an exam, fingerprinting and a criminal background check, and a license application. Those are the one-time bills, and they are the ones everybody counts. The larger column starts after you pass: brokerage fees, insurance, dues, MLS access, marketing, a car, and the self-employment taxes of a 1099 worker.
Nobody can hand you a real total, and you should be a little suspicious of any page that tries. Course prices change. State fees get revised. Brokerages differ from one another far more than schools do, and the brokerage line is the big one. What you can do instead is build your own number in an afternoon, which is more useful anyway, because the number you build belongs to your situation rather than to an average of strangers.
### The two columns nobody puts side by side
Draw two columns on a sheet of paper. The left one is getting licensed: the 48-hour Missouri Real Estate Practice course, the 24-hour Missouri Real Estate Principles course, exam prep if you decide to use it, the exam fee, fingerprinting and the background check, and the license application. That column has a bottom. You will reach it, pay it, and be done with it.
The right column is staying in business, and it has no bottom. Brokerage desk or monthly fees. Transaction or franchise fees taken off each closing. Errors-and-omissions insurance. Local, state and national association dues if you join. MLS access. Lockbox or key access. Marketing and signage. Mileage and a vehicle. Self-employment tax and health insurance. Most people fill in the left column carefully and leave the right one blank, which is exactly backward.
### How to build your own number this week
Three conversations and one website. Get current fees straight from the Missouri Real Estate Commission, which sits inside the Missouri Division of Professional Registration and sets and administers the licensing requirements. Get the course total in writing from the school, including whether books, exam prep and any retake sit inside that price or outside it. Then ask two or three brokerages for their full fee schedule before you sign a thing.
That last one is the step people skip, and it is the one that matters most. Not the split. The whole schedule, written down: what you pay monthly whether or not you close anything, what comes off the top of a closing, what technology or franchise fees ride along, and what insurance and dues you are required to carry. In our experience that single document changes people’s plans more than any course price ever does.
### What do the 72 hours of Missouri pre-license education actually cover?
Missouri’s 72 hours arrive in two pieces: a 48-hour Missouri Real Estate Practice course and a 24-hour Missouri Real Estate Principles course. You complete both before sitting the salesperson exam, and the Missouri Real Estate Commission sets the requirement. The split between the two courses tells you something honest about the job you are signing up for.
Principles is the law-and-vocabulary half. Ownership, agency, contracts, disclosure, fair housing, and the rules that govern how a licensee is allowed to behave. Practice is closer to the daily work: how a transaction moves from showing to contract to closing, what each piece of paperwork does, and what you owe a client at every step. Neither course teaches you how to find your first client. That surprises almost everybody.
### Online self-paced, or a classroom?
Both formats satisfy the same requirement, so the real difference is not quality. It is accountability. Self-paced online costs you less time, fits around a shift or a nap schedule, and lets you move at whatever speed your week allows. A classroom, live or virtual, puts you on somebody else’s calendar and gives you an instructor you can interrupt with a question the moment it forms.
### Who each format actually suits
Self-paced suits people who have finished a self-directed course before and know from experience that they will finish this one. Shift workers. Parents of small kids. Anyone whose week refuses to look the same twice. The failure mode is quiet rather than dramatic: you enroll, you do two sessions in the first week, and then the login sits untouched until the enrollment window closes.
A classroom suits people who want the calendar to supply the discipline, people who learn by asking things out loud, and career-changers who get value from sitting next to others in the same position. Ask any school two questions before you pay: how long do I have to finish, and what happens if I do not. Both answers are perfectly fair to ask, and the way they are answered tells you plenty.
### Why do so many people fail the state portion of the exam?
The Missouri salesperson exam has two parts, a national portion and a Missouri state portion, and people fail them for different reasons. The national portion rewards general real estate vocabulary and math, which courses drill heavily. The state portion covers Missouri’s own rules, and that is where under-prepared candidates most often come unstuck.
The reason is not mysterious. General material is everywhere, in every practice app and every video, so people over-study it and feel confident. State material is narrow, dry, and easy to skim on a tired Tuesday night. If you are budgeting study time, weight it toward the part that has the fewest study aids, not the part that has the most. That is the opposite of what most people do naturally.
There is more than an exam standing between you and a license, too. You complete fingerprinting and a criminal background check as part of the process. And once you pass, your license has to be held by a licensed broker. A new salesperson cannot practice independently in Missouri, which means choosing a brokerage is not a decision for later. It is part of becoming licensed at all.
One more piece nobody mentions in the enrollment brochure. New licensees complete required post-license education within their first licensing period, and continuing education after that. Get the current requirement from the Missouri Real Estate Commission rather than from a forum thread, because rules like this get revised and a stale answer costs you either money or a scramble at renewal.
### Is a Missouri license the same thing as being a Realtor?
No, and this is precisely where the after-the-exam bills begin. A license comes from the state and is what legally lets you practice. “Realtor” is a trademarked membership term for members of the National Association of Realtors, a private association you choose to join and pay to stay in. Holding a Missouri license does not make you one.
In practice the two get tangled, because membership usually arrives as a bundle. Local association dues, state dues and national dues, often billed together, frequently with MLS access sitting alongside them. Plenty of brokerages expect or require membership as a condition of hanging your license there, which means the choice may effectively be made for you the moment you pick an office.
So ask it early, and ask it in this exact shape: if I join you, what am I required to join, what does each piece cost per year, and when is it billed. Annual dues that land in January are a very different problem for somebody who got licensed in November than for somebody who got licensed in February.
### Which bills start the day after you pass?
The recurring column decides whether your first year works, and it starts immediately. Brokerage fees come first, usually as some mix of a monthly desk fee and a cut of each closing. Then errors-and-omissions insurance, association and MLS dues, lockbox or key access, marketing and signage, a vehicle, and the self-employment tax that nobody withholds for you.
Take them one at a time. Desk or monthly fees are charged whether you close anything or not, which is exactly why they sting in month three. Transaction or franchise fees come off each closing before your share is calculated. Errors-and-omissions insurance, often abbreviated E&O, protects against claims arising from your work, and how it is billed varies: some brokerages charge it monthly, some per transaction, some fold it into another line.
Then the working costs. Lockbox or key access is its own fee in most markets. Signs, photography, mailers and whatever you spend to be visible all come out of your pocket, not the brokerage’s. And the car: you are about to put serious miles on a vehicle, driving from Jefferson County to St. Charles County and back for a showing that lasts eleven minutes. Fuel, wear and insurance are business costs now.
Finally, the two that ambush every new 1099 worker. Self-employment tax, because nobody is withholding anything on your behalf and the bill arrives whether you set money aside or not. And health insurance, if you are leaving a job that provided it. That second one has quietly ended more real estate careers around this metro than any exam ever has.
Buyers ask about the furnace. Here is how HVAC estimates work.
### How do you choose a brokerage without guessing?
This is the single biggest financial decision of your first year, and it is not close. Brokerages differ on splits, caps, desk fees, training, mentorship, lead access and floor time, and those things trade against each other constantly. Shortlist two or three worth interviewing, then compare what you need against what each one is actually prepared to provide.
Start by saying plainly what you want. Do you need structured training, or have you sold something before and just need a place to hang a license? Do you want a mentor on your first three contracts? Are you hoping for leads, or bringing your own? Are you full-time, or working evenings while a W-2 job pays the mortgage? And how many months of runway do you have. Say that number out loud.
Here is the tension nobody at a recruiting lunch will name for you. The most generous split in the metro is worth nothing to an agent who is getting no training. A large share of zero closings is still zero. A smaller share of a year in which somebody sat beside you through your first four contracts is a real number, and it compounds, because you come out of that year knowing how to do the job.
### What to ask, and what to listen for
Six questions, asked the same way at each office. What do I pay whether or not I close anything? What comes off each closing, and in what order? Is there a cap, and what happens after I hit it? What training happens in my first ninety days, and who runs it? Is there a mentor, and what does the mentor take from my transactions? Do you provide leads, and what do those cost me?
Then listen to the gaps rather than the numbers. One office describes a training calendar with names attached to it. Another says training is available and changes the subject to the split. A third says you will learn by doing and offers you a desk. Those three answers are not variations on a theme. They are three different first years, and the gap between what you asked for and what came back is the signal.
### How long is the runway before your first commission lands?
Longer than the course calendar makes it look. People ask how long it takes to get a real estate license in Missouri, which is the wrong question. A license is not income. The gap between activating a license and depositing a first check is the stretch that decides who is still doing this a year from now.
Walk the whole sequence. You enroll and complete the 72 hours at whatever pace your life permits. You schedule and sit the exam. You complete fingerprinting and the background check. You submit the application. You find a broker willing to hold your license and you activate it. Then onboarding and training. Only after all of that do you begin, from zero, with no clients, no listings and nobody in the metro aware that you do this now.
And a closing is not fast. You find a client, then wait for the right property or the right offer, then go under contract, then wait out inspection, appraisal and financing before anyone signs anything. Commission is paid at closing, not at contract. Add those weeks to everything above and the honest planning horizon is measured in months of household expenses, not weeks.
Which is why plenty of people around the metro start this part-time and keep a paycheck coming while the pipeline fills. It is slower, and some brokerages are better set up for it than others. Ask about that directly during your interviews, because a brokerage built around full-time floor time will treat an evenings-and-weekends agent very differently than one that expects it.
### How much money does a real estate agent make in Missouri?
There is no salary to quote, and that is the truthful answer rather than a dodge. Missouri agents are almost always independent contractors paid per closing, so income is a function of how many transactions you close, what you keep from each, and what your overhead costs. Two agents in the same office can have completely different years.
If you want a reference point, look at published labor statistics for real estate sales agents rather than a figure from a recruiting video, and read it knowing what it contains. Any average blends full-time veterans with a long tail of licensees who closed almost nothing, and it rarely subtracts the overhead column above. The median in that kind of data is describing two very different populations at once.
### Who this actually works for
People with a financial runway, a network they are genuinely willing to talk to, real tolerance for irregular income, and enough self-direction to make calls nobody asked them to make. It rewards consistency more than charisma. The agents who last are usually the ones who did unglamorous follow-up in month four, when nothing was happening and nobody would have noticed if they stopped.
### Who it does not work for
Anyone who needs a predictable amount of money next month. Anyone who dislikes prospecting enough to avoid it, since prospecting is most of the job for the first two years. And anyone hoping for something part-time and easy, which is the version sold on social media and almost nobody’s actual experience. If the runway math does not work, the same comparison habits apply to any training path, and how to choose a college or trade school in St. Louis walks through that. Going in clear-eyed is not pessimism. It is the difference between a plan and a wish.
### For real estate schools and brokerages in the metro
If you are on the other side of this, notice that every person described above starts with a search and a fear, not with a school name. They are trying to work out the total, and the pages that answer them plainly are the ones they call. Being findable when somebody in Franklin County types the question at ten at night is most of the work.
Publish the specifics. Which courses you offer, the format, how long the enrollment lasts, what is included, and what a retake involves. Brokerages, the same instruction applies to your fee schedule: the offices willing to put the whole thing in front of a new licensee before signing day earn a reputation for it quickly, and new agents talk to each other constantly.
Interview two or three before you commit to either decision. You can compare real estate schools across the metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then do the same with brokerages: say plainly what training, mentorship and lead support you need and how many months of runway you have, and ask for the full fee schedule in writing. The gap between what you asked for and what came back is the signal, not the split.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How long does it take to get a real estate license in Missouri?
A.  It depends mostly on how fast you complete the 72 hours, since self-paced students set their own pace and classroom sections run on a fixed calendar. After the coursework you schedule and sit the exam, complete fingerprinting and a criminal background check, submit your application, and find a licensed broker to hold your license. Motivated full-time students move through it briskly. People studying around a job should plan in months rather than weeks.
### Q. How hard is it to become a realtor in Missouri?
A.  The coursework is manageable for most adults and the exam is passable with honest preparation, though the Missouri state portion trips up people who over-study the national material. The genuinely hard part comes after you pass. You are building a business from nothing while overhead runs from day one, and no one hands you clients. Getting licensed is a hurdle. Staying in business through the first year is the real test.
### Q. Is it hard starting out as a realtor?
A.  Yes, and the difficulty is financial and emotional more than technical. There is no salary, no withholding and no guaranteed first closing, while desk fees, insurance, dues and mileage start immediately. You are prospecting people who did not ask to hear from you, often for months before anything closes. Training and a real mentor make an enormous difference here, which is why the brokerage you choose matters more than the school you attend.
### Q. Is being a real estate agent still worth it in 2026?
A.  That depends entirely on your runway and your fit for the work, and anybody promising a universal answer is selling something. The honest test is arithmetic plus temperament. Can you cover household expenses for months without commission income, and will you keep prospecting when nothing is happening? If both answers are yes, the licensing path is straightforward and worth exploring. If either is no, fix that first rather than enrolling and hoping.
### Q. Is 30 too late to become a real estate agent?
A.  Not remotely. Career-changers are extremely common in this field, and thirty is early by the standards of most offices around this metro. An adult who has already worked somewhere else brings a network, a track record of showing up, and judgment about people that a twenty-two-year-old is still developing. What matters is your runway and your willingness to prospect, not your birth year. Plenty of people start considerably later than thirty.
### Q. How much would a real estate agent make on a $300,000 house?
A.  Less than the headline suggests, and there is no standard rate to quote. Commission is negotiable on every transaction. Whatever total is agreed is typically divided between the brokerages involved, then divided again between the agent and their broker under the split in your agreement, then reduced by transaction or franchise fees, then taxed as self-employment income. What a new agent actually keeps is a fraction of a fraction. Ask any brokerage to walk that chain with you before you sign.

## The $1,911 Soccer Year: What St. Louis Clubs Really Cost
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-club-soccer-actually-costs-in-st-louis
$1,911. That is the year one St. Louis club, St. Louis Legends, prints on its own fee page as the estimated cost for a U9 to U14 player who plays fall, winter and spring. It is laid out line by line, which is more than most clubs give you. And it still is not the number you will pay, because the hotel in March, the gas, the cooler of Gatorade and the second pair of cleats never make it onto anybody’s sheet.
You usually meet that gap at the edge of a tryout field in Fenton on a warm weeknight, the grass freshly cut, a folded club packet going soft in your hand while your daughter jogs past in a numbered pinnie. She is grinning. That is the problem. You already want to say yes, and you would like to know what you are saying yes to before somebody asks for a deposit.
Here is the part almost nobody at that folding table will tell you. In St. Louis, the top of the soccer ladder is not always the expensive part. St. Louis CITY SC’s own academy FAQ says the club will pay for all fees and expenses for academy participation. The pros pay for the best boys in the region. The middle of the ladder, where most families actually live, is where the invoices are. Say that out loud on a sideline and watch three parents start doing arithmetic.
So the question is not whether club soccer is expensive. It is which bills, from whom, and when. A mother in Maryland Heights whose son aged out of rec and just got invited to something called “select.” A couple in Dardenne Prairie doing the math on two kids in two age groups. A family in Columbia, Illinois weighing a river crossing twice a week against a nearer club with a thinner reputation. A grandmother in Ballwin who quietly pays for one of the two seasons. They all need the same thing: a number they built themselves, from paper, before the first payment clears.
Tonight, before anyone asks for a deposit, open the Legends fee page and use it as your template: registration, coaching, league and uniforms, each on its own line. Email every club on your list for that same breakdown in writing, plus one question that saves real money: how many players are on this team’s roster, and what gets billed on top of the coaching fee? The next section shows why that question matters.
### How much does youth club soccer cost?
Plan on club fees near $1,911 a year, then uniforms and travel on top. St. Louis Legends estimates $1,911 for a U9 to U14 player playing year-round: $202 in registration fees, a $1,309 coaching fee and about $400 in fall, winter and spring league costs. The coaching fee can be paid in a lump sum due July 1 or as $119 a month for 11 months, July through May. For that, a team player gets two training sessions a week, usually one indoor and one outdoor.
Now look at the line most families skim. Legends divides league and tournament fees equally between every rostered player and invoices them separately from the coaching fee, and it says plainly that the league costs may be more or less depending on roster size. Translation: a short roster, or a team vote to add one more tournament, shows up on your kitchen counter as a second envelope. Nobody is hiding it. It is just on page two, and page two is where seasons go sideways.
Every club prices differently, by age group, by team and by how far a particular coach likes to drive. Two families in the same club can pay very different amounts because their kids landed on different teams. That is exactly why one published fee page is worth more than any metro-wide average: it shows you what a real line-item year looks like, so you know what to demand from every other club you talk to.
### Build your number from the club’s own paper
Ask for the fee schedule in writing before tryouts, not after the offer call, when your kid is already over the moon and you are not thinking straight. Then sit at the kitchen table with a pen and draw two columns. The left column is everything the club bills: registration, coaching, league fees, field use, the uniform kit. That column has a bottom, and the club can tell you where it is. The right column is everything you pay to somebody who is not the club: hotels, gas, food eaten out of a paper bag in a parking lot, tournament gate fees, shin guards lost twice, and the Saturday shift you did not work.
Most families fill in the left column carefully and leave the right one blank, which is exactly backward. The right column decides whether the season still feels affordable in February, when the heater in the van is running and the next tournament is three hours away. Write it out even if the figures are rough. A guess you wrote down beats a number you were avoiding.
### Rec, select and club are different seasons, not different prices
Rec is local, seasonal and built around participation: short drives, volunteer coaches, everybody plays. Select and club sit above it, with tryouts, rostered teams, paid coaching, a longer calendar and real travel. The labels are not standardized across this metro, so two organizations can use the same word for very different commitments. Read the calendar, not the label.
The mistake families make is not picking the wrong rung. It is picking a rung nobody explained. A nine-year-old who loves soccer and hates pressure can be miserable on a team that trains four nights a week, and a twelve-year-old who is ready for more can quietly lose interest in a league that never asks anything of her. Match the rung to the child in the back seat, not to the player you are hoping she becomes.
Crossing into club changes three things at once. The season stops ending, so fall bleeds into winter indoor and spring bleeds into summer. Playing time stops being guaranteed, because the roster is built to win. And your family calendar starts taking orders from a schedule somebody else publishes, often late. If you have another child in gymnastics, those two calendars now negotiate every single week.
### The bills that never touch the invoice
Uniforms first, because they ambush people. Many clubs run a kit cycle, where every player buys the full package on a set schedule. At Legends, it is a new uniform every two years. Ask which year of the cycle you are joining. A family that joins in the final year buys the whole kit, then buys it again twelve months later, and nobody at tryouts mentions it because it simply does not occur to the person behind the table.
Travel is the line that separates a manageable season from a hard one, and it is decided team by team, not club by club. Ask how many tournaments this specific team entered last year, how many needed a hotel, and how far the farthest league game was. A team that plays mostly inside the metro is a different financial animal than one that drives to Kansas City. Both can be excellent. Only one of them costs a family in Troy several nights of motel ice machines and continental waffles.
Then the small things that add up quietly. Cleats outgrown mid-season. A ball in the exact size the coach specified. Goalkeeper gloves, which a family often discovers it is buying only after the kid volunteers to go in goal. A canopy, a folding chair, a cooler that actually holds ice through a July afternoon. If you are stocking up, where to buy sporting goods in St. Louis covers the metro’s options.
And the refund policy. Ask, in writing, what happens if your child is injured in week three, if you relocate, if the team folds, or if the coach you signed up for leaves in December. Most answers are perfectly reasonable. It is the not-knowing that turns a bad break into an argument in a parking lot.
Ask two or three clubs for their fee sheet before you sign anything. You can browse soccer clubs and programs across the metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then tell each one plainly how many weeknights you can do and how many hotel weekends you can absorb. The club that emails the paperwork the same afternoon is telling you something. So is the one that never does.
If you run the club, coach the team or train keepers out of a rented gym, these parents are looking for you tonight. Put your fee sheet, your training nights and your travel plan where they search, and let the honest page win you more customers than the slick one. Get listed and be the club they call first.
### What a season takes out of your calendar
More than the training schedule suggests. Two weeknight sessions, a weekend game that may be an hour away, and a few tournaments that eat a whole Saturday and Sunday. Add drive time, the arrive-early rule and the little brother who has to come along with his tablet and his complaints, and a club season becomes a part-time job for a parent.
Do the honest arithmetic. Time the drive from your door to the training field at five thirty on a Tuesday, which is not the same drive as noon on a Sunday. A family in Des Peres training up in St. Charles County has signed up for something quite different from a family ten minutes away. Then count the weekends between August and June that will not be yours, and say that number out loud to whoever else lives in your house.
The cost nobody budgets is that everything else stops. Birthday parties, a cousin’s wedding that lands on a tournament weekend, the other kid’s recital. Some families make that trade happily for a few years. Others discover in year two that they gave up more than they meant to. Both are easier if you saw it coming in July.
### How to interview a club before you hand over a deposit
You are not negotiating the price. You are finding out whether this club is built for your child, your budget and your driving radius. Start by stating your situation, because a club cannot answer a question you never asked: she is ten, she has played rec for three years, we can do two weeknights, not four, and two hotel weekends a year, not six. Then stop talking and listen.
Ask the same six things everywhere. The full fee, the payment schedule and what is not included. How many tournaments this age group entered last season, and how many needed a hotel. Who coaches this team and how long they have been there. The playing-time philosophy at this age. What happens if your child is injured or you leave mid-season. And what the summer looks like, week by week.
Then listen to the gaps. One club emails a fee schedule and last season’s tournament list the same afternoon. Another says it depends and steers back to how much your daughter impressed everyone at tryouts. A third answers everything cheerfully and cannot produce a single document. Those are three different seasons. If a club treats a request for a written fee schedule as an insult, you just learned something valuable for the price of one uncomfortable pause.
### When to step down a rung instead of quitting
Watch for three signals. The kid who used to ask when practice is and now asks whether she has to go. The parent doing quiet math in the car about a tournament six weeks away. And the house that is organized around a schedule nobody in it chose. Any one of those is worth a conversation. Two together usually means the rung is wrong, not the sport.
Girls play better in gear that fits. Here is how to get a bra that fits.
There is a middle option people forget. You can drop a rung without leaving. Legends, for one, runs an academy track for players who take a season off but want to keep training: $99 a month for one session a week. Rec, a school team or a summer off entirely work too. A kid who steps back at eleven and comes back at thirteen wanting it is in a better place than one pushed through to burnout. And if soccer is not the thing, the metro is full of alternatives, from a martial arts school to music, art and dance classes.
### For soccer clubs and coaches in the metro
If you are on the other side of the table, notice that every family on this page starts with a fear about money, not a club name. The clubs that publish a plain fee sheet, a realistic tournament count and a refund policy get the call first, because the parent at the kitchen table in Dardenne Prairie has already crossed off everyone who made her guess. Publish the specifics, including which teams travel and which stay local. You will keep the families who knew exactly what they were signing.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. At what age can you start playing club soccer?
A.  Rostered team play usually starts in the early elementary years; at St. Louis Legends, the team-player coaching fee applies to teams U9 and older. Before that, it is mostly rec and small-sided play. Ask any club for its youngest competitive age group and what a week actually looks like there. If the answer is four nights and a travel schedule for a seven-year-old, keep looking.
### Q. Why are youth soccer clubs so expensive?
A.  You are paying for things a rec league does not buy: paid coaching, field and indoor space through a St. Louis winter, league and state association registration, referees and insurance. Then tournaments charge entry, and travel adds hotels and gas that never touch the club’s invoice. Some of that is unavoidable. Some of it is a club spending your money in ways you would not choose. The fee sheet tells you which.
### Q. Is youth club soccer worth it?
A.  It depends on what you are buying. If your child loves the game and wants better coaching and stronger teammates, club delivers that and it is hard to get elsewhere. If you are buying a college scholarship, most families will spend more than they ever get back. Buy the coaching, the friendships and the years. Treat anything beyond that as a bonus.
### Q. Is it better to play high school or club soccer?
A.  For most players it is not either-or. High school gives a short, intense season, a local team and games grandparents can walk to. Club gives year-round training and stronger competition. Some clubs schedule around it: Legends runs its high school girls from July 1 to mid-November and its high school boys from November 1 through June 1, at $960 a year either way. Ask any club how it handles the school season before you commit.
### Q. What’s better, academy or club soccer?
A.  Academy generally means tighter rosters, more training days and a stricter development focus; club covers a much broader range of teams. Academy suits a player who is already ahead of her age group and hungry for more. Club suits most everybody else, including many very good players. The better question is which one matches your child’s appetite, your driving radius and what your household can sustain for a full year.
### Q. At what age do kids quit soccer?
A.  The drop-off tends to arrive in the early teen years, when school sports, friends, a first job and a year-round schedule all land at once. It usually builds slowly rather than overnight. If your child still asks when practice is, you are fine. When she stops asking, pay attention.
### Q. Is age 9 too late to start soccer?
A.  No. Nine is early, and plenty of players pick the game up later and do well. A nine-year-old beginner needs a team where she is not the only one learning, a coach who teaches rather than sorts, and a season short enough to find out whether she actually likes it. Start in rec or a lower competitive tier, give it a full year, then decide.

## Your 2-Year-Old Pulls You to the Fridge Instead of Asking? In Missouri, You Can Make the Call
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/signs-your-toddler-needs-speech-therapy-in-st-louis
A small warm hand closes around your wrist and pulls, hard, toward the fridge. No word. Just the pull, and a look up at you, and then the whine when you guess wrong. In a St. Louis County kitchen or a South City flat, the next thing you hear is usually a grandparent or a friend across the table: “He’ll talk when he’s ready.” Sometimes that is even true. But you are the one hearing the quiet at bath time, and you are allowed to want an answer instead of a guess.
Here is what most families are never told. On Missouri’s official list of who can refer a child to First Steps, the state’s early intervention program for children under three, the first entry is not a doctor. It is parents. You do not need anyone’s permission to find out. Call 866-583-2392, extension 3, and you are connected to the office for your area, or enter the referral online. Federal rules say the evaluation is one of the steps that cannot be billed to you. At three and older, federal law lets a parent request the evaluation from the public school system directly.
In St. Louis County, which office answers depends on your district. Special School District runs early childhood special education for 14 of the county’s 22 public school districts. The other eight run their own programs, and SSD tells parents in those eight to start with their district’s Parents as Teachers staff. So the first question on the phone is a short one: does SSD serve my district, or do you? Ask it first. It can save you a week of being transferred.
Not sure it is worth a referral yet? There is a gentler door. Parents as Teachers, the home-visiting program whose national office is right here in St. Louis, is voluntary and free for all Missouri families through their local school district, and it offers annual developmental screenings. It is a trained second pair of eyes on your child, on your own living room floor, with no waiting room.
### What are the signs that a toddler needs speech therapy?
The signs most worth raising with your pediatrician are about communication as a whole, not clear pronunciation alone. Very few words compared with other children the same age. Little pointing or gesturing. Losing words your child once used. Real frustration when trying to be understood. Speech that people outside the family cannot follow. None of those is a verdict.
Now picture where those signs actually show up. In the grocery aisle, a two-year-old in the cart seat strains toward the bananas and grunts, and when you hold up the bunch and ask “banana?” she just keeps reaching. At daycare pickup, the other kids run to the door shouting a name; yours runs, grabs your knee and says nothing at all, and the teacher’s smile holds a half-second too long. Those are the moments to write down. What is not on the list matters too. Not being a chatterbox is not a sign. Being shy around strangers is not a sign. Being a second or third child with older siblings who answer every question first is not, by itself, a sign either, though it is the reason a lot of parents wait longer than they meant to. The signs that matter are about whether your child has a way to tell you things, and whether that way is growing month over month.
### Which signs are worth a phone call
At the front door, she hands you a shoe instead of saying the word. Write down moments like that for a week before the appointment, because specifics travel better than worry. How many different words does your child use, not counting the sounds you interpret generously? Does she point at things to show you, or only to get them? Does he bring you objects, take your hand, shake his head, wave? Can a neighbor understand him, or only you? Does she follow a simple instruction when you are not gesturing at the same time? Has anything gone backward, meaning words or skills that were there a few months ago and are not now?
That last one deserves its own sentence. If your child used words and no longer does, raise it promptly rather than saving it for the next well visit. Not because it means any particular thing, since it does not, but because it is the kind of change an evaluator wants to hear about while it is recent. The same goes for anything worrying you enough to search at nine at night. That feeling is information too, and pediatricians are used to hearing it.
### Understanding and talking are two different questions
Speech-language pathologists separate what a child understands from what a child can produce, and parents almost never do. A toddler who follows directions, finds the shoes, points to the dog in the book and clearly gets the joke is showing you a great deal, even with very few words. A toddler who seems to miss instructions is showing you something different. Both are worth describing to your pediatrician, and neither is something you can sort out yourself from a chart. That sorting is exactly what an evaluation is for.
### Who do you call first in Missouri?
It depends on the birthday. Under three, the call goes to Missouri First Steps. From three to five, your local school district’s early childhood special education program is responsible for finding and evaluating children. Tell your pediatrician what you are doing, since the medical side still matters, but the referral itself is yours to make.
### Under three: Missouri First Steps
First Steps is Missouri’s early intervention system for infants and toddlers, and it runs through the state rather than through your school. You contact the program, describe your concerns, and go through an intake and evaluation process that determines whether your child is eligible for services and what those services would look like. For a child without a diagnosed condition, eligibility turns on whether the child is functioning at half the developmental level expected for their age in an area such as communication. That is a high bar, which is why a “not eligible” letter at two is not the last word. Ask for the current criteria in writing when you call.
### Three and older: your school district
At three, responsibility shifts to the public school district where you live, and it does not matter whether your child attends any school yet. Districts across the metro run early childhood special education, and each one has somebody whose job is intake for exactly this. Call the district office and ask who handles early childhood special education evaluations. If your child is already in a preschool, those teachers usually have useful observations to hand over, and how to choose a preschool in St. Louis covers what to look for in that setting.
### Where your pediatrician fits
Your pediatrician is still the front door for everything medical, and a good one will want to check things on their side while an evaluation runs in parallel. If you have felt brushed off more than once, take that seriously as information about the fit. How to choose a pediatrician in St. Louis goes through what to look for and how to switch without drama. Private therapy billed to insurance is a third route, and the questions to ask about that are in the FAQ below.
### What actually happens in an evaluation?
Less testing than parents expect, and a great deal more playing. An evaluation usually combines a long conversation with you about your child’s history and daily communication, direct observation of your child at play, and some structured tasks. The evaluator is watching how your child communicates overall, not only whether the words come out clearly.
You are part of it, not a spectator in the hallway. Expect questions about pregnancy and birth history, ear infections, feeding, family history, which languages are spoken at home, and what a normal hour looks like in your house. Bring the notes you made. “He has about ten words and three of them are for the dog” is far more useful than “he does not talk much,” and it saves everybody a round of guessing.
Then they play. Bubbles, blocks, picture cards, a toy that requires asking for help to work. The evaluator is looking at receptive language, meaning what your child understands, and expressive language, meaning what your child can produce, along with how sounds are formed and how your child uses gestures, eye contact and turn-taking to get things done. A toddler who refuses to perform on cue is completely normal, and a decent evaluator plans for it.
You come out with a report and a recommendation, and the report is worth reading slowly with somebody who can translate it. If services are recommended through the school route, a plan document and a meeting come with it, and you are a member of that team rather than an audience for it. Special education in St. Louis: what parents need to know walks through how those plans and meetings work, which is a genuine relief to read before your first one.
Long therapy weeks need a break. Here is how to get cheap movie tickets.
### What can you do at home while you wait?
Waiting lists are real, and the weeks between a phone call and a first appointment are not wasted time. Most of what helps at home is not a drill or an app. It is a change in how you talk during the hours you already spend together: in the car, at the sink, in the bath, at the bottom of the stairs.
Narrate, then stop talking. Say what you are doing in short, plain phrases, then leave a gap long enough to feel awkward. Adults fill silence quickly, and a toddler who is working hard to produce a word needs more room than we naturally give. Count to five in your head before you jump in. That pause does more than most of what gets sold to parents in this situation.
Offer choices instead of yes-or-no questions. “Milk or water?” invites a word. “Do you want milk?” invites a nod. Repeat back what your child meant with one word added, so “ball” becomes “big ball.” Respond to gestures rather than ignoring them, because pointing and reaching are communication, and shutting them down teaches a child that trying does not work. Read together, and let your child pick the book and skip half the pages.
And one caution, because it comes up constantly in parent groups. Do not withhold a cup or a toy to force a word out. It turns something your child needs into a negotiation. In our experience families who try it end up with more meltdowns and less talking, not more. If a specific prompting technique is right for your child, the person who evaluates them can teach it to you properly, with the reasoning attached.
### How do you choose a speech-language pathologist?
Shortlist two or three and interview them the way you would interview a doctor. Credentials are the floor, not the decision. What separates one speech-language pathologist from another for a two-year-old is experience with this age group, whether they coach parents or only work with the child, and whether the schedule on offer is one your family can actually keep.
Start by saying plainly what you want. Say how old your child is and what you are seeing at home. Say whether you need somebody who can work around a preschool day, a night shift, or a drive in from Troy. Say whether you want to be in the room. Say what you hope will be different in six months, even if you are not sure it is realistic. Then listen carefully to what comes back.
### What to ask
Six questions, asked the same way at each place. How much of your caseload is toddlers this age? Will I be in the session, and will you teach me what to do between sessions? How do you decide what to work on first? How will I know it is working, and when would you tell me it is not? How often would you want to see us, and for roughly how long? And what happens if we turn out not to be the right fit for you?
### What to listen for
The gaps, more than the answers themselves. One person describes how they coach parents and tells you what the first month tends to look like. Another says every child is different and moves on to scheduling. A third promises a specific result on a specific timeline, which is the answer that should worry you most, because nobody can promise that for a toddler. Those are three different years. The distance between what you asked for and what came back is the signal.
Ask about the practical side too. Where the office is, whether teletherapy is offered, what happens when your child is sick, how cancellations are handled, and whether you are billed for missed visits. Families who quit therapy usually quit over logistics rather than over the therapy, and a drive that looked fine in September looks very different in January.
### What if you are told to wait and see?
You are allowed to ask for an evaluation anyway. Wait-and-see is sometimes sound advice and sometimes just a habit, and from the outside the two look identical. A parent can make the referral without a doctor, and a First Steps evaluation cannot be billed to you, so the price of checking is a few phone calls and some paperwork.
Some children who are slow to talk do catch up on their own. That is true, and any honest page has to say it. What nobody can tell you is which children those are, in advance, from the outside, at the age when knowing would actually be useful. That is the entire reason evaluations exist. An evaluation that finds nothing is not a wasted morning. It is an answer, and you get to stop carrying the question around.
If you disagree with a result, ask what your options are and ask in writing. Both routes have processes for questions, re-referral and review, and the people who run intake will tell you what those are if you ask directly. Keep a folder. Dates, names, what was said, what you were told to do next. Parents who keep a folder get better outcomes from systems, and that holds well beyond this one.
### For speech-language pathologists in the metro
If you are on the provider side of this, notice that every parent described above starts with a fear and a search box, not with your name. They are trying to work out whether this is worth a phone call at all. The pages that answer that plainly, in words a worried parent can absorb at nine at night, are the ones that get the call the next morning.
Publish the specifics. The ages you serve, whether you coach parents inside the session, which insurance you take, where you are and whether teletherapy is an option, and roughly how a first appointment goes. Say what you do not do, as well. A family in Jennings or St. Ann choosing between two options will pick the one that already answered three of their questions before anybody picked up the phone.
Make the First Steps or district call first, then interview two or three therapists. You can browse speech therapists across the metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then say plainly what you are seeing at home, what schedule your family can keep, and whether you want to be coached in the session.
If you’re the speech-language pathologist a worried parent is searching for at nine at night, make sure they can find you before they find a waiting list. Put your practice on St Louis Near Me Directory and let new customers see your ages, insurance and openings before they ever call.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. When should a toddler get speech therapy?
A.  There is no single age that switches it on, and any page handing you one is guessing about your child. The practical trigger is concern: yours, your pediatrician’s, or a preschool teacher’s. Because a parent can refer directly to either Missouri route, the threshold for asking is low. Raise it at your next well visit, and call the program yourself if the worry is not going away on its own.
### Q. Is 3 too late for speech therapy?
A.  No. Three is not a cutoff, it is the age where the route changes hands. Before three, Missouri First Steps handles early intervention for the state. At three, your local public school district’s early childhood special education program becomes the place to call, whether or not your child attends school anywhere yet. Plenty of children start therapy at three, four or later. The only thing waiting costs you is time nobody can give back.
### Q. What is done in speech therapy for toddlers?
A.  It looks like play, and that is deliberate. A therapist follows the child’s interest into an activity, then builds language into it: modeling words, waiting for attempts, adding gestures or pictures, shaping sounds, and rewarding any attempt to communicate rather than only perfect words. Good toddler therapy also coaches the adult, because an hour a week matters far less than what happens across the other hundred and sixty-seven. Expect homework for you, not worksheets for your child.
### Q. Can a child outgrow speech delay?
A.  Some children who talk late do catch up without any help, which is why wait-and-see survives as advice. The problem is that nobody can identify those children in advance, and a family living it has no way to tell the difference from the inside. An evaluation is how the question gets answered instead of guessed. If the answer turns out to be that nothing is needed, you have spent a morning and gained back every evening after it.
### Q. What qualifies a kid for speech therapy?
A.  Eligibility is decided by the program or the insurer, not by a checklist online, and the criteria differ between Missouri First Steps, school district early childhood special education, and private therapy billed to insurance. Each one uses its own evaluation and its own standards, and those standards get revised. Ask the specific program for its current criteria when you call. A child can be turned down by one route and be a good fit for another.
### Q. Do insurances cover speech therapy?
A.  Coverage varies a great deal by plan, so the answer has to come from your own policy. Call the number on the card and ask precise questions: is speech therapy covered, is a referral or prior authorization required, is there a visit limit per year, what is the copay, and is this provider in network. Ask the clinic to verify benefits too, then compare the two answers. For MO HealthNet, how to apply for Medicaid in Missouri covers the application itself.
### Q. At what age do late talkers talk?
A.  There is no reliable single age, and the ranges you find online disagree with each other because they come from different sources measuring different things. Some children who are slow to start pick up speed quickly. Others need support to get going at all. That variation is exactly why an average is useless for planning your own child’s year. Use an evaluation to answer it for your child rather than a chart written about other people’s.
### Q. Why is my 2.5 year old not talking but understands?
A.  That gap between understanding and speaking is a familiar pattern to speech-language pathologists, and it is one of the most common reasons families get referred for an evaluation. It can have several different explanations, and sorting between them is precisely the work a qualified evaluator does. It is not something to settle from a search result or a relative’s story. Call Missouri First Steps, or your district if your child has turned three, and describe exactly what you just described here.

## What Taxidermy Costs in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-taxidermy-costs-in-st-louis
Picture a man in Hillsboro standing in his driveway at first dark with a buck in the bed of the truck and his phone in his hand. The animal is better than anything he has taken in twenty years of hunting, his hands are still cold, and he has never once needed a taxidermist. What he wants to know, right there in the driveway, is what this is going to cost him and whether he is about to ruin it by doing the wrong thing for the next four hours.
The same week, other people around the metro are typing something close to the same question. A first-time hunter in Pacific who took a doe and is not sure a mount is even the right call. A woman in Bethalto whose father died in the spring and left her a shoulder mount that has been sitting in a shed since June. An angler in De Soto with a fish in a chest freezer and a photograph of it on his phone. A parent in Warrenton whose eleven-year-old took a first deer on a cold Saturday and wants that Saturday on a wall for the next fifty years.
They all want the same three answers. What does this cost, how long will it take, and what do I do with the animal in the meantime. Here is what actually moves the price of a mount, how the deposit and balance structure works, why the wait is measured in months rather than weeks, how to get a cape to the shop without ruining it, and how to pick a taxidermist before you hand anything over.
### What is the average cost to mount a deer head?
There is no honest average to quote, and you should be a little wary of any page that hands you one. The price of a mount moves with the species, the mount type, the pose, the form the shop uses, and the condition of the cape that comes through the door. Two men can drop off two whitetails on the same morning and leave with two different numbers.
That is not evasion. It is how the trade actually prices work. A taxidermist is quoting labor, a form, a tanned hide, glass eyes, a habitat base if there is one, and the finish work that happens after the mount dries. Change any of those and the number changes with it. What you can do, in a single phone call, is get the shop’s own current price list and a written figure for the exact thing you are asking for.
### The three numbers to ask for
Ask for three, not one. The price of the mount as you have described it. The deposit due at drop-off. And what happens to the price if the cape turns out to be damaged and needs repair or replacement. That third question is the one almost everybody skips, and it is the one that changes bills.
Most shops take a deposit up front and the balance when you collect the mount. The deposit generally covers the shop’s hard costs, the form and the tanning, which get spent months before you ever see anything on a hanger. Ask when the balance is due, what payment they take, and what their policy is on a finished mount that sits uncollected. Every shop has one, because every shop has a shelf of them.
### Why a written number beats a range you found online
A range you found online was written by somebody in another state, pricing a different animal, in a different year. Materials cost what they cost this season. Tanneries charge what they charge. A shop already booked solid prices differently than one with open bench space. The written number from the shop you are actually going to use is the only one worth planning around.
### What actually moves the price of a mount?
Six things, roughly in order of how much they matter. The species. The mount type. The pose. The form. The condition of the cape. And anything the shop has to do that sits outside its normal run of work. Understand those six and you can read a price list instead of guessing at it.
### Mount type is the biggest lever
This is the largest single choice, and it is entirely yours. A European or skull mount is the simplest thing a shop does: the skull cleaned, whitened and set on a plaque or a stand, with no cape involved at all. A shoulder mount is the classic wall piece, head, neck and shoulders built on a form. A wall pedestal turns the animal outward so it reads more like sculpture. A pedestal mount stands on a base, on a table or on the floor, and gets viewed from every side. A full body or life-size mount is the whole animal, and it is a different order of work entirely.
Those are not small differences in labor. A skull mount and a life-size mount are not the same job with a different sticker on it. They are related crafts sharing a building. If your budget is the real constraint, mount type is where you have the most control, and a good shop will tell you that plainly rather than talk you upward.
### The pose, the form, and the eyes
Within a shoulder mount there are still choices to make. Straight ahead, turned left or right, a sneak pose with the head low, upright and alert. Some poses need a different form and more work at the seam, and the shop will tell you which ones. The form itself matters too, because shops buy forms in different grades, and a better one fits a specific cape with less altering.
Ask what form and what tanning they use, and why. It is a fair question and taxidermists like answering it, because the form is the thing underneath everything and it is exactly where a careless shop cuts corners. The eyes, the ear liners, the nose and the finish work around the eye are where a mount either looks like the animal or just looks like a mount.
### The cape, which is the part you control
The cape is the hide from the head, neck and shoulders, and its condition on arrival is the single biggest variable you personally influence. A cape cut too short cannot be stretched back into existence. A cape that slipped, meaning the hair came loose because it got warm and stayed warm, may not be usable at all. A bullet hole or a fight tear can often be repaired, but repair is labor, and labor gets billed.
If the cape cannot be saved, the shop can usually buy a replacement cape in, and that cost gets passed along to you. Nothing about that is a scam. It is a purchase the shop makes on your behalf so you still get a mount. But it is precisely why the question “what happens to the price if the cape is damaged” belongs in your first phone call, not in a conversation eight months later.
### Rush work, storage and the extras
Two more lines that catch people out. Some shops charge for rush work if you want something moved up the queue, and most have a policy on storage if a finished piece sits past a certain point. Habitat bases, driftwood, custom panels and engraved plates are extras. None of it is hidden, and none of it is in the headline number either.
### Why does a mount take the better part of a year?
Because a hide has to be tanned before it can be mounted, and because a taxidermist takes in most of a year’s work inside a few weeks. Both halves of that sentence matter. The first is chemistry, and it cannot be hurried. The second is arithmetic, and it is the reason a busy November drop-off is not first in line.
Walk the sequence. The cape comes in and is fleshed, turned and prepared. It goes to a tannery, or through the shop’s own tanning process, and that step takes as long as it takes. It comes back and waits for bench time. The mount is built on the form, sewn, set and groomed. Then it dries, which is its own stretch of weeks. Then the finish work: eyes, nose, ear butts, paint. Only after all of that does it get a hanger and a phone call.
Now add the season on top. Missouri deer season fills a shop’s year in a matter of weeks. Everybody drops off inside the same narrow window, and the work comes back out in the order the bench allows. A shop quoting you a long turnaround is usually telling you the truth about its workload. A shop promising something suspiciously fast in December deserves a follow-up question.
Ask for their current turnaround before you leave the counter, and ask how they will contact you when it is ready. Do not carry an old number around in your head because a friend quoted it three seasons ago. Turnarounds move with workload, tannery and staffing. The people who handle the wait best treat it like any other seasonal booking around here, where the good dates go early, which is the same instinct behind how to book a campsite near St. Louis.
### What do you do with the animal before the shop opens?
Keep it cool, keep it out of the sun, and get it to a taxidermist or into a freezer as fast as you reasonably can. Hair slips when a hide gets warm and stays warm, and a slipped cape is the most common avoidable loss in this entire process. Nearly everything else can be worked around. That one frequently cannot.
### Cape it long, or do not cape it at all
If you are not confident caping an animal, do not learn on the one you want mounted. Bring the whole head and cape to the shop, or cape it long, taking far more hide than you think you need from well behind the shoulders. A taxidermist can always trim. Nobody can add. The most common damage a shop sees all season is a cape cut short by somebody trying to be tidy.
Do not cut the throat. Do not split up the front of the neck. If you are field dressing an animal you intend to have mounted, the cuts you make in the first ten minutes decide what is possible eight months later. When in doubt, stop, take a photo, and call somebody.
### Freezing, bagging, and the things not to do
If the shop is closed, or you are two hours from home, the freezer is your friend. Get the cape and skull cool first, then double-bag it, press the air out, and freeze it. Label the bag with your name and the date. A chest freezer beats a kitchen freezer for a whole head, and a frozen cape holds far better than a cool one sitting in a garage.
Do not salt it, and do not treat it with anything, unless your taxidermist has specifically told you to. Salting is a real step in a real process and it is easy to do badly. Do not leave a head in a truck bed in the sun while you finish out the day. And do not seal a warm cape into a plastic bag and walk away, because you have just built an incubator.
Here is the call worth making, and it costs you nothing. Ring a shop before the season opens and ask what they want you to do. Every taxidermist has preferences, and every one of them would rather spend four minutes on the phone in September than open a bag in November and deliver bad news. Getting the rest of your season squared away early is the same instinct that makes a list of outdoor gear you actually need in St. Louis worth writing down before opening weekend.
### What does Missouri law require before you move a head?
Check the current year’s regulations before you move a carcass, and ask the taxidermist what paperwork they need at drop-off. The Missouri Department of Conservation sets the rules on possessing and transporting wildlife, and it publishes carcass-movement restrictions tied to chronic wasting disease that change from season to season and by county.
You will not find a list of those rules on this page, deliberately. A list written today is wrong next year, and a hunter acting on a stale one has a real problem. What is stable is the habit: look up the current regulations before you drive a head anywhere, know whether the county you hunted has restrictions attached to it, and know what the shop is required to record when you walk in the door.
Taxidermists deal with this every season and they are used to being asked. Most will tell you exactly what to bring, what to write on the tag, and how they want the animal presented when you arrive. Ask them, and ask the department, rather than a forum thread from four years ago. It takes one search, and it protects both of you.
Another long wait worth planning: how to get into nursing school in St. Louis.
### How do you interview a taxidermist before you hand anything over?
Shortlist two or three worth interviewing, then go and look at their finished work in person. Photographs flatten everything. Standing in front of a real mount tells you in ten seconds what a gallery page never will: whether the eyes look alive, whether the ear butts sit right, whether the seam disappears, whether the whole thing carries the animal’s posture or just its parts.
Then say plainly what you want. The mount type, the pose, where it is going to hang, what the animal means to you, and roughly what you are able to spend. A taxidermist who hears all of that can tell you what is realistic and what is not, and will often suggest something better than what you walked in asking for. One who cannot get past a number is telling you something too.
### What to ask
Six questions, asked the same way at every shop. What is your current turnaround, and how will you contact me? What is the deposit, and when is the balance due? What form and what tanning do you use? What happens to the price if the cape turns out to be damaged? Can I see finished work in person rather than photos? And what do you want me to do with the animal between the field and your door?
### What to listen for
Listen to the gaps rather than the numbers. One shop answers all six plainly, hands you a price list, and shows you a mount in progress on the bench. Another answers two and goes vague on the rest. A third quotes fast and cheap and does not want to discuss the tannery. Those are not three versions of the same shop. The gap between what you asked for and what came back is the signal.
In our experience, the shops people are happiest with a year later are rarely the cheapest ones. They are the ones that were straight about the wait. A long honest turnaround, stated up front, is a far better sign than a short one offered casually. Ask, too, how they handle it if you are not happy with the finished mount. That conversation is much easier before any money changes hands.
### What about a fish, a bird, or a pet?
Different work, different shops, different conversations. Not every taxidermist handles every category, and plenty specialize on purpose. A shop that builds beautiful whitetails may not touch a fish, and a bird specialist may carry a waiting list of their own. Ask before you drive across the county with a cooler in the back.
### Fish
Fish split into two paths. A skin mount uses the actual fish. A reproduction is built from a blank and painted to match your fish, which means the fish itself can go back in the water or into a pan. For a reproduction the shop typically needs good measurements, length and girth, plus clear photographs taken quickly before the color fades. If you fish the water around the metro and think a wall fish is in your future, learn the measurement routine now and keep a tape in the boat alongside your notes on the best fishing spots in St. Louis.
### Birds and small game
Birds are delicate and the handling advice changes again. Smooth the feathers down, tuck the head under a wing, slide the bird into a smooth bag or a stocking so nothing bends or breaks, and freeze it. Do not gut it. Do not cram it into a game pouch for the rest of the afternoon and hope for the best.
### Pets
Pet preservation is a real service, and emotionally it is a very different thing from game work. Shops differ on whether they take it at all, and some decline it for perfectly good reasons of their own. If it is something you are considering, have that conversation directly and in advance, rather than making an assumption during a bad week.
### For taxidermists in the metro
If you are on the other side of the counter, notice that every person described above is hunting for two things you can simply publish. A current price list, and a current turnaround. Shops that put both on a page get called by people who have already decided, instead of by people shopping a number they found in another state.
The field care question is the other open opportunity, and it costs nothing. One clear page on how you want an animal handled between the field and your door will get shared in every hunting group from Imperial to Troy by the second week of November. It cuts down your ruined capes, it saves you hours on the phone, and it is probably the most useful thing a shop can put on the internet.
Interview two or three before you hand anything over. You can compare taxidermists across the metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then go and look at finished work in person, say plainly what mount type and pose you want and where it is going to hang, and ask each one for a written price, the deposit, the current turnaround, and what changes if the cape is damaged. The gap between what you asked for and what came back is the signal, not the price.
If you’re the taxidermist whose finished work speaks for itself, list your shop so hunters comparing mounts can find you.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much does it cost to get a deer shoulder mounted?
A.  There is no single figure worth quoting, because a shoulder mount is priced from the species, the pose, the form the shop uses, and the condition of the cape you bring through the door. Call two or three shops, ask for the current written price list, and ask what the deposit is and when the balance falls due. Then ask the question most people forget: what changes if the cape needs repair or has to be replaced?
### Q. How long does it take a taxidermist to shoulder mount a deer?
A.  Longer than most first-timers expect, and the shop will give you their own current number at drop-off. The hide has to be tanned before anything can be mounted, the mount has to dry before finish work can start, and shops take in most of a year’s work during the few weeks of deer season. Ask for their current turnaround, ask how they will contact you, and do not rely on a figure a friend quoted three seasons ago.
### Q. Can you freeze a deer head before taxidermy?
A.  Yes, and freezing is usually the right move if you cannot reach a shop quickly. Cool the cape and skull first, double-bag it, press the air out, and freeze it, ideally in a chest freezer rather than a kitchen one. Label the bag. Do not salt it or treat it with anything unless your taxidermist told you to, and call the shop to confirm how long they are comfortable with it sitting frozen.
### Q. How long will a taxidermy animal last?
A.  A well-built mount kept in reasonable conditions can last for decades, which is why inherited mounts turn up in families all the time. What shortens that life is environment rather than age: direct sunlight fading the hair, damp, heat, smoke, and insect damage. Keep it out of a sunny window and out of an unconditioned shed or attic, dust it gently, and have a taxidermist look at anything that is fading, shedding or coming loose.
### Q. Do the ears on a deer mount look better forward or back?
A.  That is taste rather than a rule, and it is worth settling before the shop starts instead of after. Ears forward reads alert and attentive, the way a deer looks when it has caught something. Ears back, or one back, reads tense and aggressive, which suits a rut pose. Ask to see finished examples of both in the shop, decide which matches the animal and the room it is going in, and put your choice in writing.
### Q. What is the most popular pose for a deer mount?
A.  The standard shoulder mount with a slight turn is the one most people picture, because it hangs well on a wall and shows the rack cleanly from the front. Beyond that, sneak poses with the head low, upright alert poses, and wall pedestals that turn the animal outward all have their followings. Popularity should not decide it for you. Look at where the mount will hang, how the light falls, and what you will see from your chair.
### Q. Can you wipe down deer mounts with WD-40?
A.  You will hear this passed around, and it is worth asking your own taxidermist before you try it on a mount you care about. Shops differ on what they recommend for cleaning and conditioning, and the wrong product can attract dust, dull the hair, or affect the finish work around the eyes and nose. For routine care, gentle dusting in the direction of the hair is the safe default. For anything beyond that, ask the person who built it.
### Q. Are taxidermied animals killed?
A.  Not by the taxidermist. A taxidermist works on animals that are brought to them, and for game work that means legally harvested animals brought in by hunters and anglers under state regulations. Shops also work on animals found dead, on livestock and pets, and on legally acquired specimens, with the paperwork rules varying by species. If you are curious about a particular mount, ask where it came from. Reputable shops are used to the question and answer it plainly.
