## Bike Rentals in St. Louis: Cost and Routes
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/bike-rentals-st-louis-what-they-cost-and-where-to-ride
The wedding was at six and Priya had the whole afternoon free. She was staying out near Chesterfield, she had no car of her own that day, and somebody at the front desk told her the thing to do was rent a bike and go ride Forest Park. So she called a shop and asked the only question she knew to ask: what does it cost for an hour? She got a number. Then she started doing arithmetic in her head, because she did not want one hour, she wanted three or four, and four times that number sounded like real money. The man on the phone stopped her. Nobody rents by the hour for a whole afternoon, he said. Ask me about the day rate. She had not known there was one.
Two weekends later, a family in Kirkwood was trying to get four people onto bikes for a Saturday on Grant’s Trail: two adults, a nine-year-old, and a cousin visiting from Edwardsville who had not been on a bike since college. The first shop they called asked how tall the kid was, how many hours they wanted, and whether they were driving to a trailhead or riding from the shop. The second shop quoted a rate and waited. Same trail, same Saturday, roughly the same money. One of those calls mentioned that a helmet and a lock came with the bike. The other let them find that out at the counter.
Here is what this covers. How rental pricing is actually built, hour by hour, half day, full day and weekend, and why the day rate almost always wins once you cross a certain number of hours. How app-based dockless bikes price themselves differently, with an unlock fee and a per-minute charge that is cheap for a quick hop and punishing for an afternoon. What tends to be included and what tends to be an add-on. What the counter will want from you: an ID, a card hold or a deposit, and a size. The arithmetic to run before you book. Where a rental bike is genuinely worth pointing around St. Louis. What Missouri actually says about helmets, and what your city says about sidewalks. And at the end, a note to the shops themselves about the one page most of them have never published.
### How much is it to rent a bike for an hour in St. Louis?
There is no honest single number, and any article handing you one is quoting a price it saw once. Rates move with the shop, the bike and the season. What holds steady is the structure: an hourly rate with a minimum rental period, a far better per-hour price once you buy a half day or a full day, and app-based bikes that charge an unlock fee plus a per-minute rate. E-bikes cost more everywhere. Confirm the current number with the shop before you go.
That is not a dodge, it is the actually useful answer. Prices shift between spring and August, between a beach cruiser and a full-suspension mountain bike, and between a shop with twelve bikes and one with sixty. If you learn the shape of the pricing instead of memorizing a figure, you can call any shop in the metro, hear their numbers, and know within ten seconds whether you are being quoted the cheap way or the expensive way for the ride you have in mind.
### How does bike rental pricing actually work?
Almost every rental operation in the region prices along one of two models. Traditional shops sell blocks of time: an hour with a minimum, a half day, a full day, sometimes a weekend or a multi-day rate. App-based dockless bikes sell minutes: a fee to unlock the bike, then a charge that runs for as long as the ride does. The two models are cheap in completely different situations, and that is the whole game.
### The hourly rate and the minimum that comes with it
Hourly pricing is the headline number, and it is also the one people misuse. Shops usually attach a minimum, often two hours, because a bike that goes out for thirty minutes still has to be checked, adjusted, cleaned and put back. So the real floor on an hourly rental is the minimum, not the hour. Hourly is the right buy when you genuinely want a short spin: a loop of a park, a ride down to the river and back, an hour to kill before dinner.
### Half day, full day and weekend
The half day and full day rates are where the value hides. A day rate is almost never the hourly rate multiplied out, it is a flat number that works out to a much lower cost per hour, which is why the shop will often steer you there before you ask. Weekend and multi-day rates go further in the same direction and usually assume you keep the bike overnight, which means you also inherit responsibility for storing it somewhere it will not walk off. Ask where they expect you to keep it.
### Unlock fee plus per minute, and where that flips
Dockless and app-based bikes are built for short trips, and they are excellent at them. Unlock, ride twenty minutes across town, park, done, and the total is small. The trouble is that the meter never stops. Lock it up while you eat lunch and you are usually still paying, or paying a pause rate. For a three-hour ride along the river the per-minute model is the most expensive way to do it in the metro, and for a ten-minute hop from a hotel to a restaurant it is the cheapest. Same product, opposite answers.
### What is included, and what costs extra?
This is where two quotes that sound identical stop being identical. Helmets, locks, racks, baskets, water bottle cages, trailers and child seats are sometimes bundled into the rate and sometimes billed separately. Bike type matters more than anything: an e-bike costs more than an analog bike at every shop in every season. Get the list of what is included in the same breath as the price, or you are not comparing the same thing.
### Helmets, locks and racks
A helmet is the first thing to ask about and the easiest one to forget. Some shops include one with every bike, some rent them for a small add-on, and some assume you brought your own. Locks are the same story, and a lock matters more than people expect, because a rental left unlocked outside a coffee shop is your problem, not the shop’s. Then there is the rack. If you are driving to a trailhead rather than riding from the shop, ask whether they rent a rack, whether it will fit your car, and who installs it.
### E-bikes, kids’ bikes and trailers
E-bikes sit at the top of every rate sheet, and for a mixed-fitness group they can still be the right call, because they let one rider keep up with three others instead of turning back after twenty minutes. Kids’ bikes are usually priced lower than adult bikes and are limited by inventory rather than by cost, which is exactly why sizes run out first on a nice Saturday. Trailers, child seats and trail-a-bikes are typically separate line items, and there are never many of them.
### What do you need to bring to rent a bike?
Expect to hand over a driver’s license or another photo ID, and expect a credit card. Most shops place a hold on the card or take a refundable deposit against the value of the bike, and that hold can be meaningfully larger than the rental itself. You will also sign a liability waiver, and if riders under eighteen are along, an adult usually has to sign for them.
Two practical notes. A card hold ties up available credit until it clears, which can take a few days after you return the bike, so it is worth knowing the amount before you plan the rest of the trip around that card. And bring the rider, not just the rider’s measurements. Sizing a bike takes about two minutes in person and produces a much better afternoon than guessing over the phone, particularly for a teenager who grew four inches since the last time anybody checked.
### How do you run the numbers before you book?
Do it in three quick steps, honestly. First, estimate how long you will really have the bike, including the coffee stop and the wrong turn, then add an hour, because everybody underestimates. Second, multiply that by the hourly rate and compare it against the flat day rate. Third, if an app bike is in the running, multiply the per-minute charge by your estimate in minutes and add the unlock fee.
The pattern that falls out is consistent. Short and purposeful favors per-minute. Two hours or less favors hourly. Anything that looks like an afternoon favors the day rate, and it usually is not close. Multiply the whole thing by the number of riders before you decide, because a family of four turns a modest per-person difference into a real one. Then add the extras you actually need, not the ones you might.
One more line item people skip: the return. If the shop closes at five and you are riding an out-and-back, your usable window is shorter than the day rate implies, and a late return can carry a fee. Ask what time the bike has to be back, and ask what happens if it rains at two o’clock. Cancellation and weather policies vary wildly from shop to shop, and the answer costs you one sentence on the phone.
### Where is a rental bike actually worth pointing in St. Louis?
At flat, paved, mostly car-free paths, which the region has an unusual amount of. Between Forest Park, the Riverfront Trail, Grant’s Trail, the greenway network built out by Great Rivers Greenway, and the Katy Trail west of the river, a visitor with a rented bike and an afternoon has more good options here than in most cities of this size. Match the trail to the bike you rented.
### Forest Park and Tower Grove Park
Forest Park is the default for a reason. The paved bike path makes a comfortable loop, the scenery changes every few minutes, and you can stop at museums and the zoo without ever getting in a car. It is also the busiest place to ride in the city on a warm weekend, so expect walkers, strollers and other rentals, and ride like it. Tower Grove Park is the quieter cousin: smaller, shaded, and a pleasant, easy spin if you are staying on the south side.
### The Riverfront Trail and the Chain of Rocks Bridge
The Riverfront Trail runs north along the Mississippi and delivers a genuinely different St. Louis than the one visitors see downtown: industry, floodwall murals, barges, big open sky. At its northern end sits the Chain of Rocks Bridge, an old highway crossing that is now a walking and cycling bridge over the Mississippi, and riding out to the middle of it is the kind of thing people remember about a trip. It is an out-and-back, it is exposed, and it is hot in July. Carry water. Our guide to the St. Louis Riverfront Trail has the trailheads, parking counts and this fall’s detours.
### Grant’s Trail, Creve Coeur Lake and Castlewood
Grant’s Trail is the easy family answer in south county: paved, flat, and separated from traffic for most of its run, which is why it fills with kids and casual riders every weekend. Creve Coeur Lake Memorial Park offers a paved loop around the water and is a good pick when you want somewhere to park a car, unload four bikes and not think about it. Castlewood State Park is the opposite errand entirely, with dirt and real climbing, and it wants a mountain bike and a rider who wanted one.
### The Katy Trail, and getting across town
The Katy Trail is the region’s marquee ride, a crushed-limestone rail trail whose eastern end is at Machens, north of St. Charles. Most casual riders start in St. Charles and go out and back for as long as they feel like, which is exactly the right way to use it. A hybrid or comfort bike handles the surface fine, a skinny-tired road bike is less happy on it. And if your plan involves crossing the metro rather than looping one park, MetroLink allows bikes and can turn a one-way ride into a sane afternoon instead of a forced march back.
Furniture shopping later? Here is how to tell if Amish furniture is real.
### Do you need a helmet, and can you ride on the sidewalk?
Missouri has no statewide bicycle helmet law for adults, and some municipalities in the region have their own ordinances, often covering minors. Wear one anyway, and check the rule where you are actually riding. Sidewalk riding is governed by municipal ordinance too, so it differs from city to city and is commonly restricted in downtown business districts. Look up the town you are in rather than assuming one rule covers the metro.
That municipal patchwork is easy to underestimate here, because a single afternoon can cross several city lines without you noticing. What is permitted in one suburb may not be in the next, and a business district downtown may have a different rule from the residential streets six blocks away. The reliable habit is simple: on a trail or a park path, ride the path. On streets, ride the street, with traffic, and treat the sidewalk as a last resort rather than a default.
The rental counter is a decent place to ask, since staff field the question all summer and know their own neighborhood. Ask them how they would ride from the shop to the trailhead. Ask about lights if there is any chance you are out near dusk, because a rental that goes out at four in October comes back in the dark. Ask what to do if you get a flat, and whether the bike carries a spare tube and a pump.
### How do you shortlist shops worth calling?
Pick two or three, call them, and say the same short thing to each one. Four riders, one is nine years old, one has not ridden in a decade, we want about four hours on a paved trail on Saturday, and we can drive to a trailhead. Then stop talking and listen to what comes back. That thirty-second summary does more work than any list of questions.
One shop will start solving it: they will ask the kid’s height, tell you the day rate beats four hourly hours, mention that helmets come with the bikes, warn you that the child sizes go first on Saturday morning, and suggest a trail. Another will confirm they have bikes and quote a rate. Neither one is doing anything wrong. But the gap between what you plainly described and what each shop is set up to deliver is the signal, and it shows up long before money does.
Riding your own bike instead of a rental? Here is what a bike tune up costs in St. Louis.
You are not asking anybody for a written estimate or an itemized quote. That is not how a rental counter works, and asking for it mostly signals that you have never done this. In our experience the shops that ask you questions back are the shops whose bikes are set up right, whose helmets fit, and whose staff will spend three minutes raising a saddle instead of handing you a bike and pointing at the door.
Ready to get a bike under you this weekend? You can browse bike rentals on St Louis Near Me Directory, shortlist two or three worth a phone call, and ask each one the same four things: what is the day rate versus the hourly rate, what comes with the bike, what do you hold on my card, and where would you send us to ride. How readily those answers come back tells you most of what you need.
If you’re the one doing this for a living, list yours.
### For St. Louis bike shops and rental outfitters
Think about Priya on the phone, quietly multiplying an hourly rate by four and getting ready to talk herself out of the whole afternoon. She was not haggling. She simply did not know that a day rate existed, and there was nowhere online for her to find that out. That call could just as easily have ended with a polite thank you and no rental.
So publish the rate sheet. A plain page with hourly, half day, full day and weekend rates, the minimum rental period, and the difference between an analog bike and an e-bike. Say what is included: helmet, lock, basket, rack, or none of the above. Say what the deposit or card hold is and what ID you need. Say what sizes you carry, adult and kids, and note that the small sizes go early on weekends. Prices change, and a line that reads “rates updated for the current season, call to confirm” costs you nothing and keeps the page honest.
Then add the thing almost nobody publishes: a route card. Two or three short suggested rides with a starting point, a rough duration, the surface, and whether it suits kids. A visitor holding a rented bike and no plan is the single most common customer you have, and the shop that hands them a printed route earns the review. Add your hours, your last return time, and your rain policy, because those three questions eat your phone all summer. A family from University City deciding between your shop and an app on their phone is deciding on that page, not at your counter.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Does St. Louis have rental bikes?
A.  Yes. The region has bike shops and outfitters that rent by the hour, the half day and the day, and app-based dockless bikes have operated here at various times as well. Seasonal availability is real: some rental operations run heavier hours in spring through fall and lighter ones in winter. Because operators and hours change, confirm availability by phone before you build an afternoon around it.
### Q. Does St. Louis have city bikes?
A.  App-based, dockless share bikes have come and gone in the metro depending on the operator and the year, so treat coverage as something to verify in the app rather than assume. They shine for short one-way hops across a neighborhood. For a planned two-hour or four-hour ride, a shop rental is both more predictable and, once the per-minute meter runs long enough, usually cheaper.
### Q. Can you rent bikes in Forest Park, St. Louis?
A.  Renting a bike to ride Forest Park is a normal thing to do, and rental options in and around the park have operated seasonally for years. Hours track the weather and the calendar, and warm weekends are the busiest time of the week. Call ahead the same day, ask about sizes if kids are riding, and ask whether a helmet and lock come with the bike.
### Q. How much is bicycle rent?
A.  It depends on the model you are buying. Shops charge an hourly rate with a minimum, then flat half day and full day rates that work out much cheaper per hour. App bikes charge an unlock fee plus a per-minute rate. E-bikes cost more than analog bikes everywhere. Rates move by season and operator, so confirm the current number with the shop before you go.
### Q. How much to bike in one day?
A.  A full day rental is a flat rate, and it is the cheapest way to buy a lot of hours, typically well below what the same hours would cost at the hourly rate. Add-ons change the total: an e-bike costs more, and a trailer, child seat, rack or helmet may be extra. Expect a card hold or deposit on top, refundable when the bike comes back.
### Q. Can an adult ride a bicycle on the sidewalk in the city of St. Louis?
A.  Sidewalk riding is set by municipal ordinance, so it varies across the metro and is commonly restricted in downtown business districts. Because a single ride can cross several city limits, the safe habit is to ride the street with traffic or use a trail, and to check the ordinance for the specific municipality you are riding in rather than assuming one regional rule.
### Q. Are bicycle helmets required in Missouri?
A.  Missouri has no statewide bicycle helmet law for adults. Some municipalities have adopted their own ordinances, and those often apply to riders under a certain age, so check the rule where you are riding. Wear one regardless. Ask the rental shop whether a helmet is included or an add-on, and make sure it actually fits before you leave the counter.
### Q. Which bikes are best for rent?
A.  Match the bike to the surface and the group. A hybrid or comfort bike is the right default for paved paths and crushed limestone, and it suits most casual riders. An e-bike is worth the premium when fitness levels differ or the ride is long. Choose a mountain bike only for dirt at somewhere like Castlewood State Park, and check kids’ sizes and trailer availability early.

## Candle Making Classes in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/candle-making-classes-st-louis-what-to-expect
Rachel had run out of date nights. She and Dev had eaten at everything within ten minutes of their place in Maplewood, and a Friday that starts with “where do you want to go” had stopped being fun sometime last winter. Someone at work mentioned pouring candles. Sit at a bench, smell a hundred little bottles, pick two, make something. She booked it mostly to break the pattern. What she could not find anywhere on the studio’s page was the one thing she actually wanted to know: does the candle come home with you that night, or do you drive back across town later to collect a jar you already paid for? She booked anyway and hoped.
A few weeks earlier, out in St. Charles, Nadia was trying to fill an afternoon. Her sister’s bridal shower needed something between brunch and dinner. Twelve women, two of them in their seventies, one very pregnant, and a mother-in-law who gets a headache from strong perfume. Nadia called two places. The first talked about availability and a deposit. The second asked how many people, what ages, how long she had, and whether anyone was sensitive to scent, then said the room seats fourteen, the fragrance table can sit on the far wall, and they open the back door between pours. Nadia booked the second one before she hung up. Same activity, roughly the same money. One of them had obviously done this for a group before.
Here is what this covers. What a pour-your-own session actually looks like from the minute you sit down, and how much of the hard work the studio has already finished before you walk in. What you personally do: choose a fragrance, weigh it, stir, pour, wait. Why the waiting matters, and the difference between a candle being cool enough to carry out and cured enough to burn well. Why wick sizing is the genuinely difficult part of candle making, and why that is the strongest argument for a class over a first kit. How sessions are priced and what is usually included. How to pick one for a date night, a birthday, a group of twelve, or a serious first run at the hobby. The safety rules worth knowing before you light anything. And at the end, a note to studios and shops around the metro about the handful of details people search for and almost never find.
### Is a candle making class worth it in St. Louis?
It is worth it when you want the session as much as the candle. The studio has already chosen the wax, sized the wick and picked the vessel, so you leave with a jar that burns properly on the first try, plus an evening out that is not another dinner.
The honest comparison is not class versus store candle. If a candle is all you want, buying one is faster and cheaper per jar, because a studio is charging you for a seat, a teacher, a clean bench and a room, not for wax. The comparison that makes sense is class versus a restaurant table, class versus a paint night, class versus a birthday party you have to run yourself in your own kitchen. Judged that way it holds up. You sit with people, you do something with your hands, nobody is on a phone, and at the end there is an object with your name on the bottom of it.
The second kind of value is instructional, and it is easy to underrate. A first candle kit at home usually fails in a specific, predictable way, and the person holding the jar has no way to tell whether the wax, the wick, the fragrance or the pour temperature caused it. In a class every one of those variables is locked down by somebody who has poured a few hundred jars. You get to watch a correct pour before you develop any bad habits, and you find out what melted wax at the right temperature actually looks like, which is surprisingly hard to learn from a photo.
### What actually happens in a candle making class?
Most of the technical work is done before you arrive. The studio has selected the wax, matched a wick to the vessel, and set the melt and pour temperatures. Your part is the enjoyable part: smell your way through a fragrance library, build a blend you like, weigh it, stir it into hot wax, pour, and wait for the jar to set.
### What the studio has already decided for you
Four decisions are made before the door opens. The wax, which might be soy, a coconut blend, a soy and paraffin blend or straight paraffin, each behaving differently in the jar. The vessel, chosen for its diameter as much as its looks, because diameter drives everything downstream. The wick, sized and centered for that wax in that vessel. And the temperatures, meaning how hot the wax gets, at what point the fragrance goes in, and how cool it should be when it hits the jar. None of that is glamorous and all of it is why the candle works.
### What you actually do at the bench
You start at the fragrance table with scent strips, which is where most of the session’s pleasure lives. Sniff broadly, narrow to a few, then usually blend two or three into something that is yours. From there it is measurement, not guesswork. Fragrance is dosed as a percentage of the wax weight, and every wax has a maximum load its manufacturer publishes, so the staff will weigh your oils on a digital scale against the wax going into your jar. Then you stir, and you stir longer than feels necessary, because that is how the fragrance binds into the wax instead of sitting on top of it. Then you pour, straighten the wick, and label the bottom.
### The wait, and then the longer wait
This is the part nobody explains and everybody wants to know. A freshly poured candle is too hot and too liquid to move, so it has to sit before you can carry it out. Some studios build that into the session with a drink, a snack or a label-making break. Others have you come back for it. Ask which, because it changes your evening. Then there is the second wait. A poured candle needs days to cure before it burns and smells its best, and if you light it on the drive home it will underperform and you will blame yourself. Set it somewhere with the lid off, be patient, and let the scent settle in.
### Why is wick sizing the hardest part of candle making?
Because the wick has to match the wax, the jar diameter and the fragrance all at once, and the only way to know you got it right is to burn a test candle and watch. That is the single job a class does for you, and it is the reason a first kit at home so often disappoints.
A wick that runs too small tunnels. It burns a narrow well straight down the middle and leaves a thick ring of unmelted wax stuck to the glass, and once that happens you rarely recover it. A wick that runs too large burns hot, mushrooms a carbon ball on the tip, soots the jar, and can make the glass uncomfortably warm. In between there is a narrow band where the melt pool reaches the edge in a reasonable time and stays there. Change the fragrance and that band moves. Change the jar and it moves again. Serious makers keep test logs for exactly this reason.
So a class hands you a solved problem. If you later want to pour at home, the transferable lesson is not the recipe, it is the method: change one variable at a time, write down what you did, and burn the result before you make twenty of them. In our experience that is the difference between people who keep the hobby and people who put the kit in a closet.
### What does a candle making class cost and what is included?
Sessions are almost always priced per person, and that price usually covers the vessel, the wax, your fragrance selection and the instruction. Bigger vessels and add-ons cost more. Private group bookings are typically quoted per head with a minimum number of guests. Prices move, so confirm the current one when you book rather than trusting a number in an article.
What pushes the number around is worth knowing, because it lets you read two quotes as either a discount or a different experience. Vessel size and style is the biggest lever, followed by how many candles you are making. A walk-in pour bar priced by jar size works differently from a scheduled class with a set start time. Private rooms, weekend evenings, holiday dates and anything involving food or drink all add. So do extras like wax melts, room sprays or a second small jar. None of that is a markup trick, it is just a longer list of things you are taking home.
When you call, ask what is included at the base price, whether there is a minimum for a private booking, and what happens if two people cancel the day before. Those three answers make quotes comparable in a way that the headline number never does.
### How do you pick a session for a date night, a birthday or a first try?
Match the format to the occasion, not the other way round. A walk-in pour bar suits two people with a loose evening. A scheduled class with a teacher suits a birthday or a shower where somebody has to be in charge. A small hands-on workshop suits the person who wants to keep doing this at home afterward.
### For a date night
Flexibility beats structure here. A pour bar or open studio night lets you arrive, take your time at the fragrance table, and talk while you work, which is most of the point. Check two things: whether the studio is next to somewhere you would happily eat afterward, and whether the candle can leave with you. Couples in Webster Groves and Maplewood are often within a short drive of both. Nobody wants a romantic evening that ends with a scheduled return trip.
### For a group, a birthday or a shower
Now you want structure and a person running it. Ask about the minimum and maximum group size, the age policy if kids are coming, whether the room is private, and how long the whole thing takes from arrival to leaving. Say out loud if anyone in the party is pregnant, asthmatic or scent-sensitive, because a room full of open fragrance oils is a lot, and a studio that has thought about it will tell you where to sit and how they ventilate. Groups traveling in from Belleville, Granite City or Cottleville should also ask about parking, which sounds trivial until twelve cars arrive at once.
### For a genuine first try at the hobby
Look for a smaller class where you can actually ask questions. The things you want explained are the wax type and why they chose it, how they matched the wick to that jar, the fragrance percentage and where they found the maximum, and the pour temperature. If the answers come easily, you have found a teacher. If the format is more party than instruction, that is fine, just book it knowing what it is.
### Shortlist two or three, then call them
Pick two or three studios worth an actual phone call and give each one the same short summary. Here is the group size, here is the occasion, here are the ages, here is how long we have, and here is who is sensitive to scent. Then listen. One will ask you three questions back and describe the room. One will send you to a booking page. One will tell you they can do it and get vague when you press. You are not asking anyone to itemize a quote or produce estimates in writing. You are comparing the gap between what you plainly said you wanted and what each place is set up to deliver, and that gap shows up in about four minutes.
Booking a kid’s birthday next? Swim lessons have their own right age.
### What is the 3-hour rule for candles?
Burn a candle no more than about three to four hours at a time, then put it out and let it cool before you relight it. Trim the wick each time, back to a short stub. Long burns overheat the container, let the wick mushroom and soot, and shorten the life of the candle you just made.
The companion rule matters just as much, and it applies the very first time you light it. Let that first burn run until the melted wax reaches the edges of the jar all the way around. Wax has a memory. If you blow it out early, the candle will keep tunneling down that same narrow channel for the rest of its life. So plan the first burn for an evening when you will be home and sitting down.
The rest is ordinary fire sense. Never leave a burning candle unattended. Keep it away from drafts, vents and open windows, since moving air makes the flame flicker, smoke and burn unevenly. Keep it well clear of curtains, paper, bookshelves, kids and pets, and on a stable, heat-safe surface. Stop burning when a small amount of wax is left in the bottom, rather than running it dry against the glass.
### Is candle making a profitable hobby?
It can be, but a class is not a business course, and the gap between the two is wide. Selling candles means buying wax, vessels, wicks, fragrance, labels and packaging at volume, testing every combination until it burns safely, and pricing your own labor into a product that customers compare against mass-produced jars.
Want another hands-on hobby? Here’s how to learn cake decorating.
The part people underestimate is testing. Every new vessel, every new fragrance, every new wax lot potentially changes how a wick performs, and a candle sold to the public needs to burn safely in someone else’s house. That is burn logs, discarded batches and time before a single sale. There are also labeling and safety expectations for anything sold, which are worth researching properly for your state and your sales channel before you list anything. Take the class because it is fun. Treat the business question as a separate project with its own homework.

How readily those come back tells you most of what you need.
If you’re the one people should be calling, don’t stay invisible - list your business.
### For St. Louis candle studios and shops
Think about Rachel scrolling a booking page at eleven at night, trying to work out whether she drives home with a candle or drives back for it. She was not being difficult. She was trying to plan an evening, and the answer was not written anywhere. Nadia had the same problem and solved it by calling, which most people will not do.
So write it down. Session length, start to finish, including the setting time. Exactly what the price includes and what counts as an add-on. Minimum and maximum group size for a private booking. A short page covering those seven things answers the questions your staff repeat all week and wins the bookings from families in Ferguson, Granite City and Cottleville who are choosing between you and a restaurant. If private groups need lead time, post the honest current lead time and keep it current. Someone planning a shower around a date will forgive a long wait far more readily than a missed one.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How long do candle making classes take?
A.  It varies a lot by format, so confirm it when you book. A drop-in pour bar can be quick, while a taught class with a set start time runs longer. The question that trips people up is whether the posted length includes the time your jar needs to set before you can carry it out, or whether that is extra.
### Q. Is candle making difficult?
A.  Pouring one is easy. Designing one is not. In a class the hard decisions, wax, wick size, vessel and pour temperature, are already made, so the skill you use is choosing a scent and following instructions. Doing it from scratch at home is harder, because you have to test wicks and pour temperatures yourself and burn the results to find out what worked.
### Q. Where can I make my own candle in St. Louis, Mo?
A.  Look at a few venue types rather than one. Dedicated candle studios and pour bars run open sessions and private bookings. Craft and paint studios often add candle nights to their calendar. Some gift and home goods shops host workshops in a back room, and independent makers take private group bookings. Community centers and event spaces sometimes bring a maker in for a one-off.
### Q. Is it cheaper to make your own candles or buy them?
A.  Buying is cheaper for one candle, every time. Making becomes competitive only at volume, once you have bought wax, wicks, vessels, fragrance and equipment and spread that across many jars, and only if you do not count your own time. A class is priced as an experience, not as a cheaper way to get a candle, and it is fair to judge it that way.
### Q. How many candles does a 10 lb bag of soy wax make?
A.  It depends entirely on your vessel, not on the wax brand. The arithmetic is simple: divide the usable wax weight by the fill weight of one jar. A small tin takes a fraction of what a wide three-wick vessel takes, so the same bag might fill a lot of little containers or far fewer big ones. Weigh one filled jar and do the division.
### Q. What not to do when making candles?
A.  Do not eyeball the fragrance. It is a percentage of wax weight, and every wax has a published maximum you should stay under. Do not pour at a guessed temperature, do not skip stirring after the fragrance goes in, and do not move or chill a jar to speed setting. Never leave melting wax unattended, and never assume an untested wick is safe.
### Q. Where can I find a candlemaking course?
A.  Beyond one-off studio sessions, check community college continuing education catalogs, city and county parks and recreation class listings, and library maker spaces, which run seasonal craft classes. Online, wax and fragrance suppliers publish detailed technical guides and structured courses, and independent makers sell recorded curricula. For safety and testing method, supplier documentation is usually the most reliable reading.
### Q. Can kids do a candle making class?
A.  Often yes, but age policies differ and you must ask first. Some studios set a minimum age for anyone handling hot wax, some let younger children choose the fragrance and decorate while an adult pours, and some run family sessions built around that split. Confirm the policy and the adult-to-child ratio before you promise a birthday party.

## Aerial Silks Classes: How Hard Is It?
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/aerial-silks-classes-st-louis-how-hard-is-it
Dana went to the show for somebody else’s birthday. Folding chairs, a low stage, a converted warehouse space with exposed beams, and she spent the whole second act with her head tilted back. Two performers climbed a pair of red silks to the ceiling, wrapped themselves in the fabric, and dropped. She got a ride back to Tower Grove and could not stop thinking about it. The next morning she looked up classes and talked herself out of it before lunch. She had not done a pull-up since middle school. She was thirty-four. Everyone in the videos looked like they had been doing this since they were nine, and none of them looked like her.
The same week, a mom in Kirkwood was working on a different version of the question. Her daughter had spent one week of summer camp on a low trapeze and a fabric hammock and had talked about almost nothing else since. The mom wanted the boring answers. How young is too young. Whether anyone stands underneath the kid. What happens the first time she is eight feet up and gets scared. She had signed this family up for enough activities to know that a five-minute phone call would tell her more than the website did.
Here is what this covers. What a beginner aerial silks class actually asks of your body, and why grip and skin, not upper-body strength, are what stop most people in the first month. What happens in a first class, including the two or three foundation skills nearly every studio teaches first. What to wear and what to leave in the car. How recreational circus programs are structured, and what lyra, aerial sling, static trapeze and floor acrobatics feel like next to silks. The honest answer to the weight question, which is a rigging question rather than a body question. The real risks, and the health conditions a studio will ask about before you climb. How pricing tends to be structured. How to shortlist two or three studios worth visiting. And at the end, a note to studios around the metro about the beginner page most of them have not written yet.
### How hard is it to learn aerial silks in St. Louis?
Hard in an unglamorous way, and easier to start than it looks. A beginner class is mostly conditioning plus two or three foundation skills. Grip strength and skin tolerance limit you first, not upper-body power. Progress arrives in months rather than weeks, and twice-a-week attendance beats occasional long sessions.
That is the part the videos hide. What looks like a strength sport from the audience is, for the first few months, mostly a patience sport. Nobody walks into a beginner class and gets asked to muscle their bodyweight up a rope. They get asked to hold on, to squeeze fabric between their feet, and to stop gripping so hard with their hands that their forearms quit before the drill does.
### Grip and skin, not biceps
Ask anyone in their first month what hurts and you will hear the same two answers. Forearms, and skin. Grip endurance is the true early limiter, because everything on silks starts with holding fabric that wants to slide. Your hands give out well before your back or shoulders do, and that feels like failure when it is really just a very trainable weakness.
Skin tolerance is the second one, and it surprises people more. Fabric under load rubs, and the classic beginner marks show up on the insides of the upper arms, the backs of the knees, and the tops of the feet where a footlock sits. Bruises and raw patches are normal. They fade, and the same spots stop complaining as tolerance builds, which is a real physical adaptation and not just toughness. In our experience the people who quit in week three quit because nobody told them this was expected.
### What progress actually looks like
Measure it in months. A reasonable arc for an adult beginner attending consistently looks something like this: the first few weeks are conditioning and learning to trust the fabric, the next stretch is a climb that finally works without a fight, and somewhere after that come clean inverts and the first wrapped shapes that look like something. Two shorter sessions a week beat one long weekend session almost every time, because grip and skin adapt to frequency rather than duration.
One honest note about plateaus. Almost everybody hits a wall right where the climb should be getting easy, and almost everybody thinks it is a strength problem. Usually it is technique: feet in the wrong place, hands too high, or a body trying to pull when it should be standing up. Good instructors spot that in about four seconds. That is most of what you are paying for.
### What happens in your first aerial silks class?
Less flying than you expect and more floor work. A typical beginner session opens with a warm-up and conditioning, then teaches two or three foundation skills that everything else is built from: a climb, a basic footlock, and an invert. You stay low. You repeat things. You leave sore in places you did not plan for.
The climbs have names, and you will hear them on day one. A French climb uses the fabric wrapped around the body and is often taught first because it is forgiving. A Russian climb, sometimes taught alongside it, uses a foot lock created by the fabric and moves faster once it clicks. A footlock is exactly what it sounds like: a wrap that secures one foot so you can hang and shape without holding your whole weight in your hands. Inverting is turning upside down from a hang, and it is a core skill dressed up as a trick.
### What to wear, and what to leave in the car
Leggings and a fitted top with sleeves. That is the standard answer everywhere, and it is not a dress code, it is friction. Bare skin slips against fabric and then burns when it stops slipping, so covering the backs of the knees and the insides of the arms makes a real difference on day one. Fitted matters too, because loose fabric gets caught in wraps.
Leave the rest in the car. No jewelry, especially rings and dangling earrings, and no watches. No zippers, buttons or hardware that can snag or tear silk. No lotion, oil or heavy moisturizer that day, because slick skin is genuinely dangerous on fabric. Long hair tied back and off the neck. Nails short enough that you can grip without them digging in. Most studios go barefoot, so no socks unless the studio says otherwise.
### Mats, spotting and how crowded the class is
Crash mats under the apparatus and a spotter nearby are standard practice for beginners, and their absence is worth asking about rather than assuming. Beginner classes are usually capped, because one instructor cannot spot six people at once and everyone needs their own fabric. If a beginner class is large, ask how many instructors are on the floor. That single number tells you a lot about how much correction you will actually receive.
### How does circus school work?
Recreational circus runs on levels, not seasons. You start in a beginner or intro class, learn a fixed set of foundation skills, and move up when an instructor says you are ready rather than when a calendar says so. Most adults never audition for anything. They take class the way other people take yoga.
There is usually a split worth understanding. Recreational tracks are open enrollment, ability-mixed and built around fitness and fun. Pre-professional or performance tracks add training hours, technique requirements, sometimes an audition, and a student showcase at the end of a term. A studio may run both under the same roof, and the beginner door is the same door. Youth programs run on their own ladder with age minimums, and if you are also weighing a tumbling class for a kid, the same evaluation habits apply as when you are signing a kid up for gymnastics.
### The rest of the apparatus family
Silks are one member of a family, and trying the others early is smart. Aerial sling, also called hammock, is a loop of the same fabric rather than two tails, and it is often the gentlest entry point because it supports more of you and asks less of your grip. Lyra, the aerial hoop, is a steel ring that gives you something rigid to hold, which many beginners find far less intimidating than fabric that moves.
Static trapeze is a bar and two ropes, and it is deceptively demanding on the shoulders and the hands. It is a different animal from flying trapeze, which needs a rig, a net and a catcher and is far less common as a weekly drop-in. Floor acrobatics, handstands and partner acro round out the family, and they are the least glamorous and most useful thing you can add, because almost every aerial problem is a core and shoulder problem in disguise. Plenty of people end up loving an apparatus they only tried because silks class was full.
### Is there a weight limit for aerial silks?
This is a rigging question, not a body question. Aerial equipment is engineered and rated, and the rated capacity belongs to the rigging point, the hardware and the apparatus, not to a rule of thumb someone repeats online. Some studios publish a policy, many have none, and the only reliable answer comes from asking the studio.
Say it plainly, because people are anxious to ask and often just quietly do not sign up. Properly installed aerial rigging is rated well above what a person weighs, with a substantial safety factor built in, because equipment has to handle dynamic load, which is the force of a drop, not just the static weight of a body hanging still. That engineering margin is why the honest answer is about hardware.
So ask it as a hardware question when you call. What is your rigging rated for, who installed it, and do you have a stated policy? A studio that answers clearly and without weirdness is telling you exactly what kind of room it is. And if a studio has a published limit, that is not a judgment, it is a specification that comes from their building and their gear. Aerial classes around the metro are full of adults of every build who could not do a single climb in January.
### What are the risks of aerial silks?
Real but manageable, and mostly ordinary. The everyday stuff is skin abrasion, bruising, and sore forearms and shoulders. The overuse injuries that show up later cluster in the shoulders, wrists and elbows. The serious risk is a fall, which is exactly why crash mats, spotting and a coached progression from low heights are standard for beginners.
The everyday risks resolve themselves. Fabric burns and bruises are the cost of admission and they fade, though it helps to know that a hot shower over a fresh fabric burn is its own small education. Nobody warns you about that one twice.
Overuse is the one that quietly ends people’s first year, and it comes from doing too much too soon. Shoulders take a lot of load in a hang, and wrists take it in inverts and acro. Adding a third or fourth class a week the moment things start clicking is the classic mistake. Build slowly, rest, and tell an instructor when something aches rather than working around it silently.
### The health conditions a studio will ask about
Studios commonly ask new students to disclose a short list, and inversion is the reason for most of it. Typical categories include recent surgery, pregnancy, uncontrolled high blood pressure, glaucoma or other eye conditions affected by being upside down, heart conditions, vertigo, osteoporosis, a recent concussion, and existing shoulder or wrist injuries.
None of that is a list of disqualifications, and none of it is something you should decide from an article. These are conversations to have with the studio and with your physician, in that order or the reverse, and a good instructor will often have a modification ready that keeps you upright while everyone else inverts. What matters is that you say it out loud on the intake form instead of hoping it will not come up.
### How much do aerial silks classes cost?
Pricing follows a predictable shape even though the numbers move. An intro or trial class is usually priced below a regular drop-in. Class packs and monthly memberships cost less per class than drop-ins. Small-group and private lessons cost more. Apparatus rental or open-gym time is often sold separately. Confirm current pricing with the studio.
Anybody quoting you a firm number for this category is quoting one studio they saw once. What is stable is the structure, and once you know the structure you can read any price sheet in about a minute. The intro class exists to get you in the door and is the right first purchase for almost everyone. A pack makes sense only once you know you will use it before it expires, so ask about expiration dates before you buy one.
Two costs people forget. Open-gym or practice time, where you work on your own without instruction, is frequently a separate line and is often the single best value once you have skills worth drilling. And gear is minimal, which is a genuine relief: leggings, a fitted top, maybe grip aids later. There is no equipment purchase standing between you and a first class.
Chasing a stage life, not a hobby? See how St. Louis performers get signed.
### How do you pick a studio worth a first month?
Shortlist two or three worth visiting, then go interview them. Say plainly what you want and where you are starting from: your goal, your current fitness, any injury history, and the nights you can realistically show up. Then compare that against what each studio is actually set up to provide. The gap is the signal.
You are not asking anyone for three written estimates. Nobody in this world works that way and asking for it tells the room you have never taken a class. What you are doing is much simpler. You describe your situation the same way to each place, and you notice which one asks a follow-up question, which one recommends the sling class instead because you mentioned a cranky wrist, and which one just sends you a link to the schedule.
### The four questions worth asking
Ask who rigs and inspects the equipment, and how often. Ask what the instructor’s training and certification path was, since aerial has several recognized instructor pathways and the answer should come easily. Ask how many students per instructor in a beginner class. Ask whether crash mats and spotting are standard for beginners, or only sometimes. Four questions, five minutes, and the difference in how the answers arrive is worth more than any price comparison.
Then go stand in the space. Ceiling height, floor surface, how the mats look, whether the room is hot in August, and whether the class before yours looked like people having a good time. Aerial studios sit in the same category as the metro’s independent gyms and studios in one important way: the room’s culture decides whether you come back in week four.
Ready to find an intro class near you? You can browse circus and acrobatics studios on St Louis Near Me Directory, shortlist two or three worth a visit, and bring the same four questions to each one: who rigs and inspects the equipment, what training the instructors have, how many students are in a beginner class, and whether mats and spotting are standard. How readily those answers come back tells you most of what you need.
If you run a business in this space, get on the directory.
### For St. Louis aerial and circus studios
Think about Dana at eight in the morning, phone in hand, three tabs open, talking herself out of the thing she wanted to do. She was not shopping on price. She was looking for one page that told her she would not be the only beginner in the room, and nobody had written it.
So write it. Describe an actual beginner class minute by minute: the warm-up, the conditioning, the two or three skills you teach first, how low the fabric stays. Say what to wear in plain words, and say the leave-it-at-home list too, because no jewelry, no zippers and no lotion is exactly the kind of detail that removes anxiety before it starts. Name the path from intro class to level one, and say who decides when someone moves up.
Then publish the operational facts that people are too polite to ask. Which apparatus you offer and which are open to beginners. Age minimums by program, stated as numbers. Who rigs your equipment, who inspects it, and on what schedule. Your beginner class cap and your instructor-to-student ratio. Whether mats and spotting are standard. If you have a rigging capacity policy, publish it as a specification with the reason attached, because how you word that sentence decides whether a whole group of people ever emails you.
And write one honest paragraph about what the first month feels like. Sore forearms. Bruises on the insides of the arms and the tops of the feet. A climb that does not work for three weeks and then suddenly does. Studios worry that honesty scares people off. It does the opposite: it is the paragraph a nervous adult in Maplewood or Florissant screenshots and sends to a friend with the words “ok, doing this.”
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Where can I take trapeze classes in St. Louis?
A.  Look for studios with a rigged ceiling that list trapeze on their schedule, and check which kind they mean. Static trapeze, a fixed bar on two ropes, is the common recreational class and often shares a class slot with lyra or silks. Flying trapeze needs a dedicated rig, a net and a catcher, so it is far rarer and usually offered as a session or a special event rather than a weekly class. Ask before you book.
### Q. Where can I find aerial classes in St. Louis?
A.  Start with the circus and acrobatics category in the directory, then filter by what your week can hold: distance, evening availability, and whether the studio runs a true intro class rather than dropping newcomers into a mixed level. Aerial spaces need high ceilings, so they are often tucked into converted industrial buildings and gyms rather than storefronts, which means map searching alone tends to miss several of them.
### Q. What is the best age to start aerial classes?
A.  There is no single right age, and studios set their own minimums by program, commonly starting somewhere in the elementary years for youth classes and around the teen years for adult-track classes. What matters more than age is whether a child can follow safety instructions reliably and listen when an instructor says stop. Adults start at every age, including in their fifties and sixties. Ask each studio for its stated minimum.
### Q. Is aerial silks a good hobby?
A.  For a lot of people, yes, and for reasons beyond fitness. It builds real strength and body awareness, it has a visible skill ladder that keeps motivation high, and the social side is unusually warm because everyone in the room remembers being terrible at it. The honest counterweights are the time it takes to progress, the bruising, and the fact that you cannot practice at home without proper rigging.
### Q. What are people who do aerial silks called?
A.  An aerialist. That covers anyone working on hanging apparatus, so silks, lyra, sling and trapeze performers are all aerialists, and someone may specify further by naming the apparatus. The silks themselves go by several names: aerial silks, tissu, and simply fabric. You will hear all three in the same class, sometimes in the same sentence, and none of them is more correct than the others.
### Q. Who should not do aerial yoga?
A.  Because aerial yoga involves inversions, studios commonly ask about recent surgery, pregnancy, uncontrolled high blood pressure, glaucoma or other eye conditions affected by being upside down, heart conditions, vertigo, osteoporosis, recent concussion, and shoulder or wrist injuries. None of these is automatically disqualifying. They are conversations to have with the studio and your physician, and instructors can often offer an upright modification rather than turning someone away.
### Q. Is aerial silk harder than pole dancing?
A.  They are hard in different places, so most people find one clicks faster than the other. Pole gives you a rigid surface and lets you build from standing, and skin contact and grip strength are still central. Silks give you a moving surface, more height early, and more work in the hands and shoulders before anything looks graceful. Try one class of each if you can before committing to a pack.
### Q. Do I need to be flexible to start aerial silks?
A.  No. Flexibility makes shapes look prettier later, but it stops nobody at the beginning, and beginner classes are built for average range of motion. What helps far more on day one is being willing to hang on when your forearms complain, and being fine with looking clumsy in front of strangers. Flexibility improves as a side effect of showing up, which is the easiest kind of progress to get.
