## Your Coffee Should Smell Like Highway 40: Where to Buy Fresh Beans in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/where-to-buy-fresh-coffee-beans-in-st-louis
Highway 40 smells like coffee. Crack the window where it runs past the Kaldi’s and Ronnoco roasteries and the car fills with it, warm and toasty. Kaldi’s own marketing director calls that little stretch “roasters row.” Then you get home, slit open the bag you grabbed at the grocery store, lean in, and smell almost nothing. Same city. Same week. Two completely different cups.
Here is the part most of us never learned in school. In 1920, St. Louis was considered the largest inland coffee hub in the United States, with green beans coming up the Mississippi from New Orleans to be roasted here. Ronnoco, still based in town, is the O’Connor brothers’ last name spelled backward, and they started it after watching a gas-powered roaster at the 1904 World’s Fair. A century later this is still a roasting town. You can buy a bag that came out of a roaster a few miles from your kitchen this week. You just have to know which counter to walk up to, and which date to read on the bag.
St. Louis Public Radio spent a morning at Sump Coffee on South Jefferson and described the fruity smell of fresh-brewed coffee filling the room. The pour-over menu tells you where each coffee grew, Sumatra or Colombia or Kenya, and every bean brewed there is roasted a few miles north in an unassuming warehouse in Old North. Owner Scott Carey loads about 20 pounds of beans at a time, and as he told the station, if you listen closely you can hear them cracking as they roast. That is what fresh means. Not a word on a shiny bag. A sound, a smell, a date.
### Where can I buy decent coffee beans in St. Louis?
Buy from the people who roast it. Sump Coffee at 3700 S. Jefferson Ave. sells beans roasted in its own Old North roastery. Goshen Coffee Roasters is at 910 Geyer Ave., La Cosecha Coffee Roasters is at 7360 Manchester Road in Maplewood, and Blueprint Coffee pours on Watson Road. Pick the bag with the most recent roast date, keep it whole, and buy only enough for a week or two.
That last line is the one that saves you money. The National Coffee Association says coffee begins to lose freshness almost immediately after roasting, and that roasted beans keep their freshness for about one to three weeks at room temperature. Do the math on the big “value” bag. If it takes you six weeks to finish, you spend at least the last three of them paying for flat coffee. The cheapest bag in the aisle per ounce is often the most expensive one per good cup. The association’s own advice is to buy smaller batches, enough for one or two weeks. A roaster’s counter is the one place in town where the bag in your hand might have been roasted days ago, and where the person behind the register can tell you the exact day without looking it up. Ask. A good roaster loves that question.
The map is wider than one neighborhood. Northwest Coffee has a cafe at 8650 Big Bend Blvd. in Webster Groves and another at 4251 Laclede Ave. in the city. Coffeestamp sits at 2511 S. Jefferson Ave., a short drive up the street from Sump. Out in St. Charles, Picasso’s Coffee is at 101 N. Main St. on the old brick street. If Maplewood is your corner of the map, the walkable stretch of Manchester Road gets its own write-up in our local guide to coffee in Maplewood.
### The Saturday market run
Some of the best bean shopping in town happens on a folding table. The Tower Grove Farmers’ Market runs Saturdays from 8 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. in Tower Grove Park during the season. If a roaster has a table that morning, you can taste before you commit, ask how last week’s batch turned out, and carry home a bag that was roasted days earlier. That is also where you meet the smallest roasters, the ones too new to have a storefront.
The habit that pays off here is simple. Ask which roaster your favorite coffee bar pours, then buy a retail bag of that exact coffee to take home. You already know you like it. Now you can drink it in your own kitchen, in your own mug, at six in the morning before anyone else is awake.
### How to read a coffee bag in ten seconds
Flip the bag over and look for a roast date first. A far-off “best by” stamp only tells you when the seller stops vouching for it. The roast date tells you when the clock started. If a bag shows no roast date at all, that silence is your answer, and it belongs back on the shelf.
Then read the rest. A useful bag tells you where the coffee grew, how it was processed, and roughly how dark it was roasted. Process, whether washed, natural or honey, shapes flavor as much as origin does. Lighter roasts lean bright and fruity, darker roasts lean bold and bittersweet, and neither one is better. Buy toward the flavors you already enjoy. Words like “gourmet” and “premium” in a fancy font tell you nothing about the cup. A plain bag from a small roaster with a clear date and a few honest details will almost always beat the glossy one beside it.
Whole bean or ground? Whole bean, nearly every time. The oils and gases that carry coffee’s smell stay locked inside the bean until you break it open, and grinding exposes all of it to the air at once. That is why the same coffee tastes bright at the bar and dull at home: the shop ground it seconds before brewing. If you have no grinder, buy smaller bags more often and ask the roaster to grind for your specific brewer.
Wide awake and looking for a Saturday that isn’t errands? Here’s how hard aerial silks really is in St. Louis.
### Keeping a good bag good at home
Air, moisture, heat and light are what turn a great bag flat. Keep beans in an opaque, airtight container in a cool, dark cupboard, and keep them away from the cabinet over the oven or next to the dishwasher, which the National Coffee Association flags as spots that get too warm. That pretty clear jar on the counter? It lets in light. The association’s own advice is to use jars of beans as decor only.
The freezer is the eternal argument. According to the association, roasted beans keep their freshness for about one to three weeks at room temperature and three to four months frozen, but only in a truly airtight container, because coffee soaks up moisture and odors from the air around it. If you freeze, pull out no more than a week’s worth at a time and put the rest back before condensation forms. For most people finishing a bag in a week or two, the cupboard is all you need.
### What coffee gear actually improves your cup at home?
A burr grinder does more for your coffee than any brewer you can buy. It crushes beans between two burrs to an even size, so the grounds brew evenly, while a blade grinder just chops them into chunks and dust. If your budget stretches to a single upgrade, make it the grinder and keep your old brewer.
Everything after that is polish. A small kitchen scale lets you use the same coffee-to-water ratio every morning, so a good cup becomes repeatable instead of lucky. A gooseneck kettle gives you control for pour-over. A drip machine, a pour-over cone and a French press all make excellent coffee for very little money. Dial in a pour-over and a good plate and you’ve nearly recreated the city’s best breakfast and brunch at your own counter.
### Why a river town has so many roasters
The modern chapter started small. Howard Lerner and Suzanne Langlois opened the first Kaldi’s Coffee on DeMun Avenue in 1994, one of the first modern coffeehouses in the area, and Kaldi’s now runs 13 cafes around St. Louis. Its marketing director says plenty of people now working at roasters around town got their start in its training program. Scott Carey opened Sump in 2011 and began roasting his own beans in 2012, back when, as he puts it, there was specialty coffee in New York but it didn’t feel like that was happening here.
The door is wider now. Co-roasting spaces like First Crack walk newcomers through the roasting process and give them access to the equipment, which is how a lot of very small roasters get going. Firaol Ahmed used First Crack to sample coffee while he built Moii Coffee from his dorm room at St. Louis University, and Moii now helps local roasters connect with coffee farmers in Ethiopia. So when you pick up a bag at a market table with a hand-written label, it may well have started in a shared roaster like that, run by someone still learning your name. That is a good bag to buy. You are early.
Katie Moon, who curated a coffee exhibit at the Missouri History Museum, put the whole guide in one line: “I don’t know if I’ve ever had bad coffee in St. Louis. So if there’s one by you, just go.”
### Keep the roaster in business
Buy direct and buy often. When you buy beans at the roaster’s counter, a market table or their own website, more of your money stays with the person who stood next to that loud machine. Tag the roaster when you post your pour-over. Leave an honest review. Bring a bag as a host gift instead of a bottle of wine. None of it costs much, and all of it adds up for a small shop on thin margins.
Many roasters also run a coffee bar, which turns a bean run into a good hour. You can taste the whole range in one sitting and grab a bag on the way out. Some of those rooms double as solid places to get work done, which we sorted through in our guide to the best coffee shops to work remotely.
Want a bag roasted this week, not this season? Browse coffee stores across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick the roaster or shop closest to you, and walk in with one question ready: when were these roasted?
If you own a roastery, a coffee bar or a little cafe that smells like this at 7 a.m., this part is for you. The people reading this page are your next regulars, and they are deciding where to buy before they ever leave the house. List your shop, then step up to Gold so your roast days, your bags and your hours sit right where those customers are already looking.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How do I know which coffee beans to buy?
A.  Start with the roast date, then match the label to your taste. Origin, process and roast level tell you far more than words like “premium.” Lighter roasts lean bright and fruity, darker roasts lean bold and bittersweet. Pick the flavors you already enjoy, and favor the bag roasted most recently.
### Q. How can you tell if coffee beans are high quality?
A.  Quality shows in specifics, not slogans. A good bag names the origin, the process, the roast level and a recent roast date. The beans should look even in size and color and smell fresh when you open the bag. Vague words and glossy packaging are not quality signals.
### Q. Is it okay to store coffee beans in a Ziploc bag?
A.  It works in a pinch, but it isn’t ideal. A zip bag is clear, so it lets in light, and it rarely seals out all the air. If you use one, squeeze out the air, seal it tight and keep it in a dark cupboard. An opaque, airtight container does better.
### Q. How long do coffee beans stay fresh in a sealed bag?
A.  An unopened retail package keeps until its best-by date, according to the National Coffee Association. Once opened and moved to an airtight container, roasted beans hold their freshness for about one to three weeks at room temperature. That is why buying a week or two at a time beats buying in bulk.
### Q. What is the best way to store coffee beans for long-term storage?
A.  Freeze them in a truly airtight container. Frozen roasted beans keep their freshness for about three to four months. Take out no more than a week’s worth at a time and return the rest quickly, before condensation forms, because coffee soaks up moisture and odors from the air.
### Q. Is it really worth buying an expensive coffee bean?
A.  Often yes, but price isn’t the point, freshness is. A pricey bag that sat for months loses to a cheaper bag roasted last week. Spend a little more for a specific origin, careful processing and a recent roast date, and you’ll taste it. Skip the premium that is really just packaging.

## How to Sell Coins Without Getting Ripped Off
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-sell-coins-in-st-louis-without-getting-ripped-off
Imagine clearing out your father’s house in Florissant on a Saturday and finding a coffee can of old silver dollars tucked behind the water heater. Under it sits a cigar box of foreign coins, a few folded stamps, and a blue folder with pennies pressed into little holes. You have no idea if any of it is worth ten dollars or ten thousand.
A week later, a woman in Affton is doing the same quiet math over her late aunt’s stamp albums, wondering whether the neat rows mean money or just memories. Across the river in Belleville, someone else has a rolled-up sock of wheat pennies. In St. Charles, a roll of Kennedy halves sits on a kitchen counter next to an open laptop.
Here is where it usually goes wrong. The instinct is to search “sell coins near me,” drive to the first shop that pops up in Kirkwood, and take whatever number the person behind the counter says. That single move, one offer with no homework, is exactly how ordinary people leave real money on the table. This guide is about not doing that.
Here is what this covers. How to tell whether your coins are actually worth money, and the difference between melt value and collector value that trips up almost everyone. How to check a value at home without fooling yourself, apps included. Where you can actually sell in the metro, dealer versus pawn versus auction versus online, and what each one is good and bad at. How to handle an inherited collection without wrecking its value. The red flags that mean a buyer is lowballing you. And a short section on stamps, because they follow different rules than coins.
### How do you get coins appraised without getting ripped off?
Most old coins are worth their metal or their face value, and a small minority are worth far more because of rarity, date, mint mark, or condition. The honest first step is separating the two. Age alone means almost nothing. A worn old cent can be common, while a specific date-and-mint pairing in high grade is a different story entirely.
### Melt value versus collector value
Melt value is what the metal is worth if the coin were melted down, and it moves with the daily spot price of silver and gold. In the United States, dimes, quarters, and half dollars struck in 1964 or earlier are 90% silver, which is why people sort by date first. Collector value, sometimes called numismatic value, is what a buyer pays above melt because a coin is scarce or beautifully preserved. A common silver quarter is a melt coin. A rare key date is a collector coin.
Why does this matter so much? Because a fair melt-based offer and a fair collector offer can differ enormously on the very same coin. If a buyer treats everything you brought as scrap metal, you might be fine for a jar of worn silver and badly shortchanged on the one piece that mattered. Knowing which pile a coin belongs in is most of the game.
### Key dates, mint marks, and condition
Three things push a coin above melt: the date, the mint mark, and the grade. A mint mark is the small letter showing where a coin was struck, and certain year-and-mint combinations were made in tiny numbers. Condition matters just as much, and it is ranked on a grading scale from heavily worn to pristine. A coin that looks “really old and shiny” to you may be an ordinary date in average shape, while a dull-looking coin can be a quiet standout.
In our experience the pieces people are most excited about, the giant old-looking dollar or the foreign coin with a king on it, are usually the common ones. The sleeper value tends to hide in a small, boring-looking cent nobody bothered to photograph. Don’t assume anything from size or shine. Sort by date and mint mark, then check the ones that stand out.
### What is the best way to check a coin’s value at home?
Start with a free coin-identifying app to name the coin, then confirm the number against a published price guide before you believe it. Apps are good at telling you what a coin is. They are weaker at telling you what yours is worth, because value depends on condition, and a phone photo cannot grade a coin the way a human can.
### Free apps and what they get right and wrong
Several free apps let you photograph a coin and get an instant identification, and a few sync to recent sales data. That is genuinely useful for sorting a big pile fast. The catch is the estimate. App values often quote a wide range, or the top of the range, and they cannot see a scratch, a cleaning, or the wear that knocks a coin down several grades. Treat the app as a naming tool, not a pricing oracle.
### Reading a price guide without fooling yourself
Once you know the date and mint mark, look the coin up in a recognized price guide or a completed-sales listing. The trick is matching your coin’s condition honestly to the price column, not the best-case one. It helps to compare against sold prices rather than asking prices, because anyone can list a coin for a dream number that nobody actually pays. Realized prices are the truth; wish prices are noise.
### Where can you sell coins in St. Louis, dealer, pawn, or auction?
You have four realistic paths in the metro: a coin and stamp dealer, a pawn shop, an auction house, or an online or mail-in buyer. Each fits a different situation. The right choice depends on what you have, how fast you need the cash, and whether your collection leans toward common silver or genuine rarities.
### Coin and stamp dealers
A dedicated dealer is usually the best starting point for anything beyond loose silver, because they know the market and can price collector coins on the spot. Good ones explain how they reached a number and separate melt from collector value in front of you. The trade-off is that a dealer buys to resell, so their offer sits below full retail. That is normal, not a scam.
### Pawn shops
A pawn shop is built for speed and convenience, not specialist coin knowledge. It can be fine for common silver you just want turned into cash today, but pawn staff rarely grade rare coins accurately, so a genuine key date can get bought as scrap. If you go this route, know your melt value first. It helps to understand how pawn shops work in St. Louis before you walk in.
### Auction houses
For a collection with real rarities, an auction can reach collectors nationwide and let them bid each other up, which sometimes beats any single dealer offer. The trade-offs are time and fees. You wait weeks for a sale and settlement, and the house takes a commission. Learning how auction houses work in St. Louis tells you whether your material is worth consigning.
### Online and mail-in buyers
National mail-in buyers and online marketplaces widen your audience, and for standardized bullion or already-graded coins they can be competitive. The risks are shipping valuables, slower payment, and offers you cannot question face to face. For an inherited jumble of unknowns, sell locally first, where someone can look you in the eye and answer questions in real time.
Coin fatigue setting in? Here’s where to rent a bike and ride St. Louis.
### What is the best way to sell an inherited collection?
Go slow, inventory everything, and get at least one professional opinion before you sell a single coin. Inherited collections are where the worst rip-offs happen, because grief and a full house create pressure to just be done. The collection is not going anywhere. A week of patience routinely pays for itself many times over.
### Do not clean anything
This is the mistake that costs people the most. Cleaning a collectible coin, even gently, scratches the surface and can slash its collector value, sometimes by most of it. Collectors prize original surfaces, toning and all. That dull, dirty coin might be worth more untouched than a shiny one you scrubbed. Resist the urge, and leave every coin exactly as you found it.
### Inventory before you sell
Lay everything out and make a simple list: dates, denominations, mint marks, and anything already sealed in a plastic grading holder. Photograph the standouts. This does two things at once. It tells you roughly what you have, and it protects you, because a written inventory makes it far harder for anyone to quietly set a coin aside or underquote the lot.
### Consider a paid appraisal first
For a large or clearly valuable collection, a paid written appraisal from an independent appraiser, someone who is not also trying to buy it, gives you a baseline you can trust. It costs money, but it removes the conflict of interest that appears when the person valuing your coins is the same person hoping to buy them cheaply. For a small jar of common silver, skip it. For a real collection, it is cheap insurance.
### What red flags mean a buyer is lowballing you?
The clearest warning signs are pressure to decide right now, a single price for a whole mixed lot, and a flat refusal to explain how an offer was reached. A fair buyer expects you to shop around and will happily walk you through the math. A buyer who needs you to sign today, before you can compare, is telling you something.
### The pressure close
“This offer is only good right now” is a sales tactic, not a market fact. Coin and metal prices move slowly day to day, so a legitimate offer will still be roughly good tomorrow. Manufactured urgency exists to stop you from getting a second opinion. Any time you feel rushed, treat it as your cue to slow down and leave.
### One price for everything
Beware the buyer who weighs your whole pile, quotes one lump number, and never separates the common silver from the potential key dates. That single number is convenient for them and expensive for you. Insist that anything unusual be looked at individually. A buyer unwilling to do that is either not equipped to, or would rather you didn’t notice.
### No explanation, no breakdown
A trustworthy offer comes with a reason: this much for melt at today’s spot price, this much extra for the collector pieces. If you ask how a number was reached and get a shrug or a vague “that’s just what it’s worth,” treat the offer as a starting point at best. Transparency is the whole tell. Get more than one number, always.
### What about selling old stamps?
Stamps follow different rules than coins, and most common stamps are worth far less than people hope, while a small number are genuinely valuable. Condition is everything. Original gum, centering, and whether a stamp has been hinged or postmarked all swing the value hard. A specialist buyer matters even more here than with coins.
Here is the uncomfortable part most sellers learn late. The thick, satisfying album full of canceled stamps that a relative saved for decades is often a labor of love with modest resale value, because canceled common stamps are everywhere. The value, when it exists, tends to hide in a handful of items: early issues, printing errors, unused stamps with original gum, or complete sets. Don’t soak them, don’t rearrange them, and don’t peel anything off an old envelope, since the whole cover can be the valuable part.
Because so few buyers specialize in both, look for dealers who handle coins and stamps together, and get the stamps in front of someone who actually trades them. The same not-so-fun rule from resale markets applies here, where knowing your item beats hoping a stranger is honest. The habits in our guide to flea market shopping in St. Louis transfer neatly to selling.
Ready to get a real number on what you found? You can browse coin & stamp dealers across the St. Louis metro, shortlist two or three, and bring the same coins to each one. Ask every buyer to separate melt value from collector value and to explain how they reached the number. The offer that comes with a clear breakdown, not the biggest promise, is usually the one to trust. Weighing a quick loan instead of a sale? See how pawn shops work in St. Louis.
If you’re the coin dealer who separates melt value from collector value out loud, list your shop with us.
### Before you hand over the coffee can
Think back to that Saturday in Florissant, the coffee can in one hand and your phone in the other, a single search result glowing on the screen. The most valuable thing you can do is refuse to sell to that first result on that first day. Sort, check, and get more than one offer. Nothing else protects you as reliably.
The pattern holds whether you inherited a shoebox in Affton or found a roll of halves in St. Charles. Separate the melt coins from the collector pieces. Never clean anything. Ask each buyer to explain the number out loud. And treat pressure to decide immediately as the reddest flag there is. Do those four things and the odds of getting ripped off drop sharply, no numismatics degree required.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How can I check if my old coins are worth anything?
A.  Start by identifying each coin’s date and mint mark, then separate common dates from possible key dates. A free coin app names a coin fast, but confirm value against recent sold prices or a dealer, since condition drives worth far more than age or size alone.
### Q. What is the best way to sell your old coins?
A.  Sort them into melt coins and possible collector coins, check the standouts against sold prices, then take the lot to two or three buyers for competing offers. Never accept the first number, and ask each buyer to break down melt versus collector value. Patience and comparison protect you more than any single expert can.
### Q. How can I find out if my old coins are worth money?
A.  Identify each coin’s date and mint mark, then check whether that exact combination is scarce and what condition yours is in. Common dates are worth metal or face value; specific key dates in strong grades carry collector premiums. A free app names the coin fast, but a dealer or price guide confirms the real value.
### Q. Where can I lookup the value of a coin?
A.  Look up the exact date and mint mark in a recognized price guide, then cross-check it against completed sales rather than asking prices. Realized prices show what buyers actually pay, while open listings can chase dream numbers. Match your coin’s true condition to the right column, not the best-case one.
### Q. What is the best free app to check the value of coins?
A.  Several free coin-identifier apps let you photograph a coin for an instant name and a rough value range, and they are excellent for sorting a pile quickly. Treat the price as a ballpark only, since a photo cannot grade condition. Confirm anything promising against recent sold listings or a dealer before you believe the number.
### Q. What year of coins are worth money?
A.  In the United States, dimes, quarters, and half dollars dated 1964 or earlier are 90% silver, so their year alone gives them melt value. Beyond that, specific key-date-and-mint combinations across many years carry collector premiums. Year matters, but date, mint mark, and condition together decide real worth.

## $5.75 to Laugh, 18% on the Food: St. Louis Comedy Clubs
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-comedy-clubs-what-to-expect-and-what-it-costs
The cocktail comes in a souvenir cup, and it is a double. That is printed right on the Funny Bone’s drink menu at Westport Plaza, a few lines above a shot called the Tanquerschäger and the menu’s own verdict on it: “It’s that kinda night!” The house lights drop. Chairs scrape. A spotlight finds a stool and a mic stand, and for the next hour a stranger is going to try to make a room full of St. Louisans laugh at things they would never say out loud.
That is the part everybody pictures. Nobody pictures the check. It slides onto a table the size of a dinner plate, in a room too dark to read it, while the headliner is still mid-bit. You tilt it toward the stage light, squint, and find a line you never budgeted for.
Better to know it now. Every price, minimum and rule below comes straight from the St. Louis clubs’ own pages: the two Funny Bone rooms at Westport Plaza and the Streets of St. Charles, Helium, and The Improv Shop in The Grove, the one that promises in writing not to pick on you.
### How much is it to go to a comedy club in St. Louis?
Cheap on a weeknight, more once a touring name and a minimum stack up. The Funny Bone’s Tuesday open mic at Westport Plaza is listed at $5.75, and its Wednesday open mic at the Streets of St. Charles is listed at $3.45. The Improv Shop says most of its shows are under $12. Helium adds a two-item per person minimum in the showroom on top of the ticket.
The ticket is the cheap part on a Tuesday. At Westport that is a five-dollar bill and three quarters, and you are in. So price the exact show you want, not the club. The good news is that the two Funny Bone rooms post their prices the way you wish everyone did: the club’s own pages say “All in pricing includes taxes and fees,” so the number you see is the number you pay at checkout.
Helium works a little differently. Its FAQ says ticket prices “include all fees (before taxes),” so expect the total to tick up once tax hits. Neither one is a trick. You just want to know which kind of price you are looking at before the group text starts doing math. Questions about a specific show go to the box office: Helium lists 314.727.1260, and the Funny Bone at Westport Plaza lists (314) 469-6692.
### The 18 percent nobody mentions at the door
Here is the line most people only find on the receipt. Helium’s own FAQ says “there will be an 18% administrative fee on all food and beverage purchases.” Same FAQ, same answer: “Food and drinks purchased in our bar and lounge do not count towards the two-item minimum.”
Read those two sentences together and the move is obvious. That cold beer you grabbed at the bar while you waited for the doors, the one sweating a ring onto the counter, does not count. You still owe two items once you sit down in the showroom. So wait. Order your first drink from your seat, and every sip counts toward the minimum instead of sitting on top of it.
That is the tip worth texting the friend who is buying. The two items do not have to be cocktails, either: Helium says the minimum “can be fulfilled with any food or drink items from the menu,” so a basket of something fried and a soda clears it. And if you want a real dinner first, Helium says food and drinks bought with a pre-show dinner reservation for the Thursday, Friday and Saturday early shows count toward the two-item minimum.
### Which room fits the night you want?
Four very different evenings hide under the word comedy, and picking the wrong one is how a good night goes flat. It almost never has anything to do with the club.
### The cheap, loud, hit-or-miss night: open mic
The Funny Bone calls Tuesday “our weekly Open Mic Night” at Westport Plaza, a room the club says has hosted St. Louis talent and nationally touring comedians since 1984. Open mic is where jokes get tested in front of strangers. Some land so hard the table shakes. Some die in a silence so complete you can hear the ice settle in your glass. For a few dollars, that swing is the whole show, and comics who love the craft will tell you it is the most honest hour in the building.
### The night where nobody gets picked on: improv
The Improv Shop sits at 3960 Chouteau in The Grove, and its FAQ answers the question every nervous first-timer is quietly asking: will they pick on me? “No. We may ask for audience suggestions, but that’s about it.” Then the line worth repeating: “we won’t single you out. We think that’s annoying.” Seating is open, parking is free in the club’s own lot east of the building, and after the show there is a fire pit on the patio. The shop rates its shows like an R movie, and says 17 is probably the minimum recommended age.
### The big-name night: touring headliners
This is the polished hour from someone you might have seen in a special or on TV. Helium says its shows usually run between 90 and 105 minutes, and it gives advice more clubs should: research the comedian first, because comedy is subjective and certain comics are not for everybody. Watch one clip before you buy four tickets. If the clip makes you wince, the live set will too.
### The sampler night: showcases
A showcase stacks several comics on one bill. It is the safest bet for a mixed group, because if one voice is not your thing, a different one is up in ten minutes. It is also how you find the local comic you will be telling people about next year.
### Do you need a reservation, and how old do you have to be?
For a weekend headliner, buy ahead. For age, it depends on the room, so check the exact show. Helium says plainly, “We are an 18+ venue.” The Improv Shop leaves kids to your discretion but calls its shows rated R. Wherever you go, bring a valid ID even if nobody has carded you in a decade.
Seats are the other surprise. At Helium, general admission is “first-come, first-sat,” and the club recommends arriving no later than 30 minutes before showtime, adding that late arrivals are not guaranteed seats. Want your whole party at one table? Helium says general admission groups should arrive at least an hour early and walk into the showroom together. It also says all sales are final, so be sure of the date before you click.
Prefer a mellower night out? Try a St. Louis candle-making class instead.
### Where to park
Helium’s FAQ says parking right outside is limited, with more on the east side of the building near Dillard’s and in the parking garage. The Improv Shop has its own free lot. Downtown and Soulard nights are a different story, so give yourself ten extra minutes to circle.
### How do you find comedy shows in St. Louis this week?
Go straight to the club calendars, because lineups change weekly and the clubs post their own prices there. Then follow the two or three comics you like, since touring dates get announced on their feeds first. When you want to compare rooms side by side by neighborhood and night, the unique things to do for adults guide pulls the city’s grown-up nights into one place.
Read the listing before you buy. Look for the words headliner, showcase or open mic, note whether there is an early and a late show, and check the age rule on that show’s own page rather than the venue’s homepage. The show is where the real rules live.
### What the clock looks like on show night
Timing is where first-timers lose the good seats. The clubs publish their own schedules, and they are more specific than most people expect.
At The Improv Shop, the first shows start at 8 p.m. on Fridays and Saturdays and at 7 p.m. on Thursdays, with a later 10 p.m. show on Fridays and Saturdays. Doors open at 6 p.m., the box office opens thirty minutes before showtime, and the shop says its shows typically last around 60 to 90 minutes. The kitchen runs until 11 p.m. on Thursdays and until midnight on Fridays and Saturdays, so you can order a burger from your seat while the scene builds.
At Helium, the venue opens two hours before shows that start between 6 and 8 p.m., and 45 minutes before shows that start at 8:30 p.m. or later. The box office closes between shows, so a late show ticket cannot be picked up during the early one. At the Funny Bone at Westport Plaza, the Tuesday open mic lists doors at 7 p.m. and the show at 7:30 p.m.
Put those together and the rule is simple. Get there early, eat or drink from your seat so it counts, and leave your phone in your pocket once the lights go down. The comic can see the glow from the stage, and so can everyone behind you.
Plan the whole night, not just the hour in the dark. Browse comedy clubs across the St. Louis metro, pick the room that fits your crowd, and check that show’s price, minimum and age rule before you leave the house.
If you run the club, the bar next door or the late-night kitchen where the crowd lands after the show, the people reading this are deciding where to spend tonight. Put your business where they are looking and turn that crowd into customers.
### Make the hour on either side count
Eat first, and eat somewhere you love, because a comedy-club kitchen is built for a dark room and a minimum, not a long meal. If this is a date, pair the show with one of the city’s best date night restaurants and let the jokes be dessert.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is there a drink minimum at St. Louis comedy clubs?
A.  At Helium, yes: a two-item per person minimum in the showroom, which any food or drink from the menu can fill. Items bought in the bar and lounge do not count, and an 18% administrative fee applies to all food and beverage. Rules differ by club, so check each show page.
### Q. How early should you get to a comedy show?
A.  Helium recommends arriving no later than 30 minutes before showtime and says late arrivals are not guaranteed seats. Groups who want to sit together should come at least an hour early. The Improv Shop opens its doors at 6 p.m. and its box office thirty minutes before each show.
### Q. What are some fun adult activities in St. Louis?
A.  Comedy is one of the easiest, because a single ticket buys you a room full of strangers laughing at the same moment. Beyond the clubs, the city has dance floors, cocktail bars, live music, trivia nights and late-night kitchens. ### Q. Where do 40 year old singles go on a Friday night in St. Louis?
A.  A comedy show is a low-pressure pick, because the room does the talking and you get an easy opener afterward. Improv works especially well if you are nervous about being singled out, since The Improv Shop says it will not do that. Catch an early show, then grab a nightcap.

## The Upload Box Won't Take Your Resume: Free St. Louis Computer Help Before You Pay for a Class
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/computer-classes-in-st-louis-beginner-to-job-ready
Where did the resume go? At a public computer in a St. Louis library, the box on the screen says “Upload your resume,” and you have no idea where the file went. You saved it. You know you saved it. The cursor blinks, the little wheel spins, and somewhere behind you a printer coughs out somebody else’s pages. Your neck is hot. You close the tab and tell yourself you’ll try again tomorrow, which is what you said yesterday. Your bus comes in twelve minutes. The application doesn’t care.
Before you pay anyone to fix that, know this: the City of St. Louis runs a job agency, SLATE, that offers financial assistance for training programs in high-demand, high-growth occupations, help that can cover tuition, books and supplies. Its Missouri Job Center also runs no-cost workshops on resume writing, online job search and succeeding on hiring tests, the timed online test that can stand between you and an interview.
Screenshot that before you pay for any computer course in St. Louis: the city may help cover it. Ask first. Pay second.
### Where can I learn basic computer skills for beginners in St. Louis?
Start at the library. The St. Louis Public Library’s Tech Connect program books in-person or virtual one-on-one appointments for technology help, scheduled for one hour, and its listed topics include searching for jobs online and basic resume writing. The St. Louis County Library has Digital Navigators who take appointments for computer and mobile device learning; fill out the form and they contact you within four weekdays to schedule. Neither one expects you to know anything when you walk in.
One change most guides haven’t caught, at the city library: St. Louis Public Library announced its hotspot checkout would end on February 28. Over $4 million in federal Emergency Connectivity Fund grants paid for it, and that federal funding has ended. If your cousin is about to ride the bus downtown for a library hotspot, text her this first, and tell her to reserve a library computer instead.
One-on-one beats a big class when you’re nervous, because the whole hour is your problem, not the room’s. Bring your own phone or laptop and a written list: the email you can’t open, the password you keep losing, the resume file that vanishes every time you hit save. Sit down, put the list on the table between you, and work it from the top.
Start one rung lower than you think you need to. There’s no shame in sitting through “this is a folder, and this is where your saved file actually goes.” That one lesson ends more of the upload-box panic than any spreadsheet class ever will.
### The free training money most people never ask about
If you are aiming past the basics, at a certificate or a real career change, go to SLATE before you pay anybody. The Missouri Job Center at 1520 Market Street downtown has resource rooms with computers, internet, printers and phones for your job search, plus workforce staff who specialize in career transitions. Register on MoJobs first, which SLATE calls the first step for job seekers, then call (314) 589-8000 and ask one plain question: “Do I qualify for training assistance?” If the answer is no, you’ve spent one phone call.
SLATE says its training programs help St. Louisans who are minorities, women and long-term unemployed get into careers in growing industries. If that’s you, the money is meant for you. Walk in with your ID, a rough resume on a thumb drive, and the one job posting that made you think “I could do that if I knew Excel.” That posting is your syllabus. Fold it in half, set it next to the keyboard in the resource room, and let every question you ask start with a line on that page.
### The handful of skills worth learning first
Every application that ever beat you has one of these five underneath it. The mouse that skates off the edge of the form, so learn mouse and keyboard control until clicking stops eating your attention. The resume that vanished, so learn files and folders. The job site that wanted you to search, filter and scroll, so learn a web browser. The “attach your resume” email that went out naked, so learn email with attachments. And the too-good message from a “recruiter” at 11 p.m., so learn internet safety: real passwords, and which links never to click.
Files and folders comes first for a reason. The afternoon you click Downloads and the resume is just sitting there, where it was the whole time, you’ll laugh out loud in a quiet library and nobody will mind. Tell anyone stuck at that upload box what took you weeks to learn: the upload box was never the test. The folder was.
### How much does a computer course cost in St. Louis?
It ranges from free to a few thousand dollars, and the price tracks the goal. SLATE’s workshops are no-cost. Community-college continuing-education courses usually carry a modest fee. Job-focused certificates cost more, and multi-week bootcamps sit at the top. Confirm current pricing directly with the provider before you commit, and ask SLATE about assistance before you pay a dime toward anything job-focused.
Two costs people forget. First, a device: a class teaches the skill, but you still need somewhere to practice. Second, time. A free class you can actually reach two evenings a week beats an expensive one across town that you’ll quietly stop attending by week three. Match the schedule to the shift you actually work. If you close at the restaurant and open at the store, a Saturday-morning appointment you can keep is worth more than a weeknight class you’ll miss twice and then drop. Look at the bus route too. A class that takes two transfers in January stops being a class by February. Choosing among options works a lot like weighing tutoring and learning centers across the metro: fit and pace matter more than the brochure.

### Where can seniors learn basic computer skills for free?
The same library appointments work beautifully for older beginners, because nobody rushes you and nobody grades you. Bring the grandkid’s text you couldn’t open and the bank login that locked you out. Write each step in a spiral notebook while the helper talks, then do it again yourself before you leave. The second time is when it sticks.
Ask a grandkid or a neighbor to sit with you for the first practice session at home, but keep your hands on the mouse. Helpers mean well and then do it for you, fast, and you’re left watching instead of learning. Say it kindly and out loud: “Tell me, don’t touch.” It feels awkward for about four minutes and then it works. Practice the same small task three days in a row, open the email, open the attachment, save it, find it again, before you move on to anything new.

Staying connected online is also part of flexible work and earning for seniors, if that’s where you’re quietly heading.
### Work backward from the job, not forward from the course catalog

## Discount Stores and Outlets in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discount-stores-and-outlets-in-st-louis
Imagine stretching one paycheck across back-to-school for three kids, a birthday party, and a winter coat that finally quit. It is Tuesday in Florissant because Tuesday is payday, and the list folded in your pocket runs longer than the money in your account. You are not looking for a treat. You are looking for a plan.
So you map it in your head. Notebooks and socks come from a dollar or variety store on the way home. The good sneakers, the ones that have to last, might come cheaper from the outlet shopping out in the Chesterfield Valley area, or from an off-price chain closer to South County. A gently used winter coat could turn up at a thrift or consignment shop in St. Charles for a third of the price of new. Bulk snacks and paper towels? A warehouse-club run once a month, split with your sister in Belleville who keeps the membership.
That instinct, matching the store type to the thing you are buying, is the whole game. This guide walks through the kinds of discount shopping the St. Louis metro actually has: dollar and variety stores, off-price and closeout chains, warehouse clubs, outlet-mall shopping, and the deep thrift, consignment, and deadstock scene. It covers what each one is genuinely good for, where the cheapest everyday shopping usually hides, how to stack savings without burning a whole Saturday, and the times of year the markdowns run deepest. We will keep the specifics general on purpose, because prices and hours at any one shop change constantly. The strategy does not.
### Is there a factory outlet in St. Louis?
The metro carries every major branch of the discount family, spread from the city out through the county and across the river into the Metro East. In broad strokes there are five: dollar and variety stores for cheap consumables, off-price chains for brand-name overstock, warehouse clubs for bulk, outlet centers for end-of-line goods, and thrift or consignment for secondhand. Each one solves a different problem, and knowing which is which is most of the skill.
### Dollar and variety stores
These are your consumables engine. Cleaning supplies, party goods, greeting cards, gift wrap, snacks, storage bins, and seasonal odds and ends, the stuff you burn through and do not want to overpay for. The trick is knowing what is a real deal and what only looks like one. A tiny bottle of name-brand detergent can cost more per ounce than the big jug at a regular grocery store. Buy the true bargains here, then skip the pantry staples that are cheaper by volume elsewhere.
### Off-price and closeout chains
Off-price is where brand-name clothing, shoes, home goods, and toys land when department stores overbuy or a season ends. Inventory is a treasure hunt, different every week, so the people who win here shop often and buy the thing the moment they see it. There is no rain check on a one-off pallet. If a winter coat in your kid’s size shows up in October at a good price, that is the coat. It will not be waiting for you on Saturday.
### Warehouse clubs
Warehouse clubs trade a yearly membership fee for low per-unit prices on bulk goods, fuel, and a surprising slice of the household budget. They pay off for larger families, for anyone who can store bulk, and for the paper-goods-and-protein core of a grocery run. They also punish impulse hard. The single best warehouse-club habit is a list plus a rule you say out loud: if it was not on the list, it does not go in the cart.
### Which store type is right for what you’re buying?
The savings come from matching, not from loyalty to one banner. A quick mental sort saves more than any single coupon ever will. Ask what you are buying, send it to the store type built for it, and the price mostly takes care of itself. That is the habit that separates a plan from a wander.
Everyday consumables go to dollar and variety. Brand-name clothes and shoes go to off-price first, then outlets for the labels that run their own stores. Bulk food and paper go to a warehouse club. Furniture, coats, and kids’ clothes that get outgrown in a season go to thrift and consignment. Specialty runs have their own homes too. For hair and nail products, a dedicated beauty supply store usually beats a big-box aisle on both price and selection.
One honest caveat from years of doing this. The cheapest sticker is not always the cheapest outcome. A five-dollar tool that breaks in a month is more expensive than a fifteen-dollar one that lasts. Discount shopping is not about buying the lowest number. It is about buying the lowest cost per use. Kids’ shoes that fall apart before the growth spurt were never a bargain.
### Where does outlet-mall shopping live in the metro?
Yes, the St. Louis area has outlet shopping, most visibly in the western suburbs. Outlet stores sell brands directly, often end-of-line, overstock, or made-for-outlet lines, at prices set below the flagship store. The appeal is buying labels you already know for less, in one concentrated trip, rather than hunting them piecemeal across off-price racks all over town.
### The Chesterfield Valley area
The outlet shopping out in the Chesterfield Valley area is the one most locals name first, a cluster of brand outlet stores along the western edge of the county. It is a destination trip, not a quick errand, so it rewards a plan. Go with a short list of the brands you actually wear, check each shop’s own posted hours before you drive out, and treat the food court as the reward rather than the reason. Outlet pricing is real, but a made-for-outlet item is not always the same garment as the flagship version, so check the make before you fall for the logo.
A quick word on the phrase factory outlet. It once meant a store attached to a factory selling seconds. Today it mostly means a brand-run discount store inside an outlet center, which is perfectly fine, as long as you know that outlet and flagship stock can differ. For which specific brands have a presence and what their current hours are, the shops post their own details, and those are the numbers to trust over anything you read secondhand.
### Where do thrift, consignment, and deadstock fit in?
Secondhand is where the metro’s deepest discounts hide, and St. Louis has a thick scene of it, from charity thrift stores to curated consignment to sneaker resale. This is the corner where patience pays the most, because pricing is inconsistent and the inventory is one-of-one. What is on the rack today is genuinely gone tomorrow, which is both the frustration and the whole appeal.
### Thrift and consignment
Thrift stores, often charity-run, price low across the board and are hard to beat for coats, furniture, books, and kids’ clothes that get outgrown anyway. Consignment shops are the curated cousin: someone has already sorted for quality and brand, so you pay a little more but dig a lot less. For furniture and one-off household pieces, the metro’s flea markets and resale spots are worth a slow Saturday. Go often, go early, and keep a running list of sizes so you can buy on sight.
### Deadstock and resale
Deadstock, in the modern sense, means unworn, older-release sneakers and streetwear, usually sold through resale shops and consignment sneaker stores rather than one big outlet. St. Louis has a resale and vintage scene that carries this, concentrated in the city’s shopping districts. If you are hunting a specific pair, call ahead, because inventory turns fast and no two shops carry the same wall. For a wider look at the independent scene, the guide to unique finds shopping downtown makes a good companion.
### How do you save the most at discount stores?
The biggest savings come from a handful of unglamorous habits, not from any one magic store. Shop with a list, shop the store type that fits the item, buy multiples of the true bargains, and let go of brand loyalty. In our experience, the households that save the most treat the whole thing like a route, not a wander through whatever is nearby.
Build the route around the errand you already have. If you are near South County for something else, that is when you swing the off-price stop. Stacking trips saves gas and time, which are real costs a coupon never shows you. Bring a list, bring your own bags where it matters, and set a number before you walk in. A budget spoken out loud before the door is worth more than any sign inside it.
### Stack the small stuff
Sign up for the free loyalty programs at the stores you already visit, because the digital coupons there are the closest thing to free money in this category. Check the clearance end-caps first, not last. Buy off-season on purpose: coats in spring, patio gear in fall, wrapping paper the morning after the holiday. And keep a small stockpile of the consumables you know you will use, because a deal is only a deal if you actually needed the thing.
Here is the counterintuitive part. The single most expensive habit in discount shopping is the extra trip you did not plan, the one where you walk in for one item and leave with a full cart. Every store in this category is engineered to sell you the unplanned thing. The list is not a suggestion. The list is the whole defense, and the day you treat it as optional is the day the savings quietly leak out.
### When is the best time to shop for deals?
Timing beats luck in this category. The deepest markdowns follow a predictable calendar: end-of-season clearance, post-holiday resets, and the quieter mid-week hours when shelves are freshly stocked and lines are short. Shopping against the crowd, early morning or a weekday, gets you to the racks before they are picked over.
Seasonal clearance is the big lever. Retailers mark down to clear floor space for the next season, so winter coats bottom out in late winter, summer gear in late summer, and holiday everything the morning after. Off-price and outlet stores restock constantly, so a fresh visit beats a giant one. The person who pops in weekly beats the person who makes one enormous trip a year. For groceries and bulk, a mid-month, mid-week run dodges the payday-weekend crush.

### For St. Louis discount and thrift shops
Think about that parent in Florissant on payday Tuesday, phone open, mapping a route in her head because no single page laid it out for her. ### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are the key differences between an outlet mall and a regular mall?
A.  An outlet mall gathers brand-run discount stores selling end-of-line, overstock, or made-for-outlet goods below flagship prices, while a regular mall carries the current in-season collections at full retail. Outlet centers are often open-air and sit in outlying areas like the Chesterfield Valley, so they read as destination trips rather than quick errands.
### Q. What is the best day to go to an outlet mall?
A.  Weekday mornings usually win. Go early on a Tuesday, Wednesday, or Thursday and you beat the weekend crowds, reach freshly stocked shelves, and shop picked-over racks less. If you can time it, the days right after a major holiday bring the deepest resets, when stores mark down to clear floor space for the next season.
### Q. Are outlets supposed to be cheaper?
A.  Yes, outlet stores are meant to price below the flagship, usually because the goods are end-of-line, overstock, or made specifically for the outlet channel. The catch is that a made-for-outlet item is not always the same garment as the flagship version, so check the make and fabric before you fall for a familiar logo.
### Q. What should you always buy at thrift stores?
A.  Thrift stores are hard to beat for coats, furniture, books, and kids’ clothes that get outgrown in a season anyway. These are the items where secondhand pricing saves the most and the wear barely matters. Skip anything with hidden condition risks, and inspect zippers, seams, and electronics closely before you commit to the buy.
### Q. What are some tips for successful thrift shopping?
A.  Go often and go early, because thrift inventory is one-of-one and what is on the rack today is gone tomorrow. Keep a running list of the sizes your family wears so you can buy on sight. Inspect each piece for wear, and treat the whole trip as a slow hunt rather than a quick errand.
### Q. What are the downsides of outlet shopping?
A.  Outlet centers sit on the metro’s edge, so a trip out to the Chesterfield Valley area costs real gas and time before you save a dollar. Made-for-outlet stock can differ from the flagship, discounts are not guaranteed, and the concentrated setting is engineered to sell you the unplanned extras. A short list is your defense.

## Electronics Repair in St. Louis: Fix It or Replace It?
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/repairing-electronics-in-st-louis-fix-or-replace
Imagine it’s a Tuesday evening in Maplewood Park. You set your laptop down to reheat dinner, come back, and the screen stays black. No fan, no chime, nothing. It’s four years old, it holds every photo and tax file you own, and a small voice says just buy a new one. Another voice, the one that remembers what a decent laptop costs now, says wait. Somewhere between those two voices is the right answer, and it depends on details you haven’t checked yet.
Across the metro the same standoff is playing out in a dozen kitchens. A student in St. John is staring at a phone with a spiderwebbed screen, wondering whether a repair is throwing good money after bad. A dad in Brooklyn is weighing a repair quote against a shiny new game console. Someone in Brighton is coaxing a five-year-old tablet through one more school year, and a couple in Freeburg is deciding whether their cracked TV is worth a house call. Same question, different gadgets: fix it, or let it go?
Here is what this guide covers. Whether repairing an aging device is actually worth it, and the simple math that settles most cases. What common electronics repairs tend to cost around St. Louis, in honest ranges rather than fake precision. Which repairs come up most often, and which ones signal a device on its last legs. Why repair bills can feel steep even when the fix looks small. When age alone should tip you toward replacing. And how to find a repair shop across the metro you can actually trust with your data and your money.
### Is it worth repairing old electronics?
Often it is, and the test is simpler than it feels. Repair usually wins when the fix costs less than half of a comparable replacement and the device still does what you need. Three things decide it: the price of the repair, the age of the gadget, and whether a newer model offers something you genuinely want. A cheap battery or screen swap almost always beats buying new. A pricey repair on an already-old machine usually does not.
### The half-cost rule most techs use
Most repair shops lean on a rough rule: if a fix costs more than half the price of a solid replacement, replacing usually makes more sense. Picture a repair that lands in the low hundreds against a comparable new device that sells for a few hundred more. That is close to a coin toss, and age breaks the tie. Come in well under half, though, and the repair is almost always the smart money. You keep a machine you already know, and you skip the whole setup headache.
### When the numbers say replace
The math flips when a device is old, slow, or on its second or third major failure. Pouring a big repair into a machine that will likely need another one soon is the definition of throwing good money after bad. Watch for a pattern: one part fails, then another follows a few months later. That cascade is the device telling you it is tired. At that point, even a fair repair price is money better saved toward something new.
### The costs that never show on the quote
A repair quote only counts part of the picture. Replacing a device also means hours of setup, moving your files, re-installing apps, and relearning quirks you had finally mastered. Your data alone can be priceless if it isn’t backed up somewhere safe. Repair keeps all of that intact. So even when a fix looks a little steep on paper, the time and hassle it spares you can tip the scale right back toward keeping what you have.
### How much does electronics repair cost in St. Louis?
It depends on the part, but most everyday repairs fall into predictable ranges. Small jobs like a phone screen or a laptop battery tend to be the cheapest, while logic-board and water-damage work can run into several hundred dollars. As a loose guide, a repair that costs less than half of a replacement is usually worth doing. Anything creeping toward the price of a new device rarely is.
### Phones and tablets
Cracked screens and dying batteries are the bread and butter of phone repair, and they are usually the most affordable fixes on the menu. A screen swap on a common model tends to land somewhere in the low-to-mid hundreds, depending on the phone and whether the glass alone or the whole display needs replacing. Battery replacements are typically cheaper still. Charging-port and camera repairs sit somewhere in the middle. Premium and folding phones cost more across the board.
### Laptops and desktops
Laptop repairs cover a wide spread. A new battery, a keyboard, a fan, or a memory and storage upgrade usually sits at the friendly end. Cracked screens climb higher, and anything touching the motherboard, or logic board, sits at the top, because the part is expensive and the labor is delicate. Data recovery from a failed drive is its own line item and can run into serious money. A tune-up or virus cleanup is often the cheapest visit you will make.
### TVs, consoles, and the rest
Bigger gear follows the same logic. Game-console fixes, like a new HDMI port or a replacement drive, are frequently worth doing because a new console costs a lot more. TV repairs depend heavily on the part: a power board or a handful of components can be reasonable, while a cracked or failed panel usually costs so much that replacing the whole set makes more sense. Smaller electronics, from headphones to smartwatches, often cost nearly as much to fix as to replace, so weigh those carefully.
### What are the most common electronics repairs?
Screens and batteries top the list by a mile. For laptops and phones alike, cracked or dead screens and worn-out batteries are the repairs shops see day in and day out, because both wear from ordinary use. After those come charging ports, keyboards, overheating from clogged fans, and software gunk that slows a machine to a crawl. Most of these are routine, affordable, and well worth doing.
Screen damage is the classic. A phone slides off a couch arm, a laptop lid meets a stuffed backpack, and suddenly the glass is a mosaic. The good news is that screen work is one of the most common jobs a shop handles, so parts and know-how are easy to come by. Batteries are the quieter problem. Every rechargeable battery fades, and a phone that dies by lunchtime or a laptop chained to its charger is almost always a battery issue, not a reason to replace the whole device.
The rest of the list is mostly wear and grime. Charging ports loosen from thousands of plug-ins. Keyboards lose keys to crumbs and spills. Fans choke on dust until the machine runs hot and throttles itself. And software slowdowns, from a cluttered drive or a lurking virus, fool plenty of people into buying new hardware when a cleanup would have done the trick. If your gadget feels tired, the fix is often smaller and cheaper than you fear.
Fixing the machine is step one. Learn to actually use it here.
### When should you replace instead of repair?
Replace when the device is old, when the fix costs close to a new one, or when it has already failed more than once. Age matters because older machines struggle with current software and lose support. A seven-year-old laptop, for instance, is usually past the point where a big repair pays off. And when repairs start stacking up one after another, the device is telling you it is done.
### The seven-year question
A seven-year-old laptop sits right at the edge. By that age the battery has cycled thousands of times, the operating system may no longer get security updates, and the machine feels slow against everyday apps. A small, cheap fix, like a battery or a fresh drive, can buy a year or two for light use. But a costly repair on a machine that old rarely makes sense, because you are propping up hardware that is near the end of its useful life anyway.
### How long devices really last
Most laptops are built to last somewhere in the range of three to five years of daily use, though a well-kept machine used gently can stretch well past that. Phones tend to run four to five years before batteries and software support give out. Tablets often last longest, because they work less hard. Knowing roughly where your device sits on that curve is the single most useful input to the repair-or-replace call. A fix early in a device’s life is money well spent. The same fix near the end usually isn’t.
### How do you find a repair shop you can trust in the St. Louis metro?
Look for clear pricing, a warranty on the work, and honest reviews from neighbors. A trustworthy shop diagnoses the problem before quoting, tells you plainly when a repair isn’t worth it, and stands behind the fix for at least a few months. The metro has independent shops on both sides of the river, so you rarely have to drive far to find one with a real track record.
Start with the same instincts you would use for any home fix. Read recent reviews, ask what the diagnostic costs, and get the quote in writing before anyone opens your device. A good repair tech explains the problem in plain language and points out when replacing beats repairing, even though it costs them the sale. That honesty is the whole game. The same reflexes that help you pick a plumber or electrician apply here, which is why our roundup of must-know tips for finding top home repair services travels well from the furnace to the phone.
It helps to treat electronics like any other system in your life that eventually needs a repair-or-replace call. Homeowners run the same math on a furnace or air conditioner every season, and the logic barely changes when the device is a laptop instead of a condenser. One more habit protects you no matter where you go: back up your data before you hand over any device. A reputable shop takes care with your files, but the safest file is the one you already copied somewhere else. Ask whether the repair risks wiping your storage, and whether they can recover data if the worst happens. The best shops answer both questions without flinching, and a straight answer there tells you a lot about the rest.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it cheaper to get a laptop fixed or replace it?
A.  Usually cheaper to fix, as long as the repair costs less than half of a comparable new laptop. A battery, keyboard, or screen swap almost always beats buying new. Once the quote climbs toward the price of a fresh machine, or the laptop is several years old, replacing tends to win. Run the half-cost test first.
### Q. How expensive is it to repair a laptop?
A.  It varies widely by part. Batteries, keyboards, fans, and memory upgrades sit at the friendly end. Cracked screens cost more, and motherboard or logic-board work is the priciest, because parts are costly and labor is delicate. Data recovery is its own charge. A cleanup or tune-up is usually the cheapest visit you will make.
### Q. What is the most common laptop repair?
A.  Screen and battery replacements top the list. Screens crack from drops and pressure, and every rechargeable battery eventually fades until the laptop cannot hold a charge. After those, shops see plenty of keyboard fixes, fan cleanings for overheating, and charging-port repairs. Software slowdowns are common too, and often mistaken for hardware failure.
### Q. Why are electronic repairs so expensive?
A.  Three reasons stack up. Parts are often proprietary and priced high by manufacturers, especially screens and boards. The labor is skilled and slow, since modern devices are glued, sealed, and packed tight. And diagnosis takes time before any fix begins. Add short warranties and specialized tools, and even a small repair carries real cost behind it.
### Q. Should a 7 year old laptop be replaced?
A.  Usually yes, unless the fix is small and cheap. By seven years the battery is worn, security updates may have stopped, and the machine lags on everyday tasks. A low-cost battery or drive swap can stretch it for light use. But any repair approaching a couple hundred dollars is money better spent toward a newer machine.
### Q. What is the average lifespan of a laptop?
A.  Most laptops last about three to five years of daily use, with well-kept machines running longer. Batteries and cooling fans usually wear first, followed by aging software support. Lighter use, good ventilation, and the occasional cleanup all add time. Business-grade and premium models often outlast budget ones, but even those slow down as software demands grow.

## $4,000 Back for a Soggy Yard? Talk to a Landscape Architect Before Anyone Digs
