The low corner of the yard in Pagedale is a brown pond again, and that water could be worth up to $4,000 back from MSD, if nobody touches a shovel too soon. You heard it start after dark: the downspout choking, then a steady gurgle at the corner of the house. By morning, mulch has floated up against the fence like driftwood, the grass squelches under your slippers, and the basement has that faint wet-cardboard smell again.
So the questions pile up. Do you need a landscape architect, a designer, or just a crew with a skid steer? What does any of it cost? Here’s the turn: in St. Louis, the most expensive mistake has nothing to do with who you hire. It’s letting anyone start digging too soon.
### Is a landscape architect worth it?
Often, yes, when the yard has slope, standing water, walls to hold back or a big hardscape budget, because that’s the work the license covers. Under Missouri law, professional landscape architecture includes site plans, landscape grading and landscape drainage plans, irrigation plans, planting plans and construction details. You can see the difference from the back step after a storm: water sheeting across a patio toward the door, or water sliding into a planted swale and disappearing. A plan drawn by someone trained in grading costs less than ripping out a patio that was poured the wrong way.
Missouri also guards the title. No one may hold themselves out as a professional landscape architect in this state unless they’re licensed, yet the same law lets people in nursery occupations, gardeners and landscape contractors prepare planting plans, as long as the project doesn’t put public health, safety and welfare at risk. Translation: the garden center can sketch your new beds. For grading that decides where a storm goes, hire someone licensed.
### Before anyone digs: MSD’s rainscaping money
Here’s the St. Louis piece to know before you sign anything. The Metropolitan St. Louis Sewer District runs a Rainscaping Small Grants Program that reimburses homeowners after they add rainscaping to better manage stormwater runoff, and residential projects can request up to $4,000. A rain garden that gives runoff a safe place to go, away from your foundation, is the kind of fix it was built for.
A local TV news report told the story of a homeowner near Tower Grove Park whose small backyard had patches of grass and steep brick slopes that sent rainwater straight into the alley. A landscaper added permeable pavers and native plants with deep roots, and MSD reimbursed her family several thousand dollars.
Now the line worth taping to the fridge. MSD’s program page puts it bluntly: do NOT begin installation until your application is approved and you have received a Notice to Proceed. Applications go by mail or hand delivery, because electronic applications are not accepted. MSD recommends applying by January for a spring installation and by June for a fall one, and the Rainscaping Team takes questions at (314) 577-0202. Money depends on your program area, and some areas fill up and waitlist new applications, so check your address on the program’s eligibility map first.
### What does hiring a landscape architect cost in St. Louis?
There’s no posted price list, and anyone who names a firm number before walking your yard is guessing. Landscape architects generally charge one of three ways: by the hour, as a flat design fee, or as a percentage of construction cost. An hourly consultation and a full master plan for a steep, wooded lot sit at very different price points, and the scope of your yard moves the number far more than your zip code does.
For a floor under any quote, look at what the profession earns here. O*NET’s local wage data puts the median landscape architect in the St. Louis, MO-IL area at $31.77 an hour, with the 90th percentile at $47.91. That’s the paycheck, not the bill. A firm’s billed hour also has to carry insurance, licensing, software and the evening spent redrawing your patio, so expect the invoice rate to sit above the wage, and ask what each billed hour includes.
### What pushes the price up or down
Lot size and slope matter most, because a flat yard is far simpler to plan than a hillside that sheds water toward the house. Complexity adds design time too: drainage fixes, retaining walls, outdoor kitchens, lighting and irrigation each need their own details. So does the level of drawing you want. A rough concept sketch costs much less than a full set of construction documents a contractor can build straight from.
### Hourly, flat fee or percentage
Each model fits a different job. Hourly billing suits a consultation or one defined question, like where to put a rain garden. A flat design fee suits a clearly scoped project, since you know the cost before the work starts. A percentage of construction cost shows up on big, involved builds, where the design effort scales with the budget. Whatever the model, get the fee, the scope and the number of revision rounds in writing.
### What the fee actually pays for
You’re paying for thinking, not just drawings: measuring and mapping the yard, reading how water moves across it, solving grade problems, and producing a plan detailed enough to price and build. Good documents also let several contractors bid the exact same scope, so you compare apples to apples instead of three guesses scribbled on the back of a business card.
### Does the design fee count toward the build?
Sometimes, but don’t assume it. Some design-build firms credit part of the design fee if you hire them for the installation. Independent landscape architects who only design usually bill separately, which keeps their advice free of any pull toward a bigger build. Ask early, so the total holds no surprises at signing.
### Architect, landscape architect or designer: who does what here
An architect designs buildings. A landscape architect designs the land around them, and Missouri’s definition draws the line clearly: the practice of professional landscape architecture does not include the design of structures or facilities ordinarily included in the practice of engineering or architecture. A designer, a nursery or a landscape contractor can prepare planting plans, but can’t call themselves a landscape architect without the license.
All of those licenses sit under one roof: the Missouri Board for Architects, Professional Engineers, Professional Land Surveyors, Professional Landscape Architects, and Licensed Interior Designers. Before you sign, run the name through the state’s Professional Registration licensee search. It takes a minute at the kitchen table, and it’s the cheapest insurance in the whole project.
Check the map before the shovel. Look up your address on MSD’s rainscaping eligibility map, then compare local crews in our roundup of top landscaping services in St. Louis.
If you’re the landscape architect, the designer or the install crew a soggy-yard homeowner calls next, those homeowners are your next customers, so see who AI names instead of you.
### St. Louis clay doesn’t forgive a bad plan
Clay is the quiet reason so many local yard projects go sideways. It’s the slick gray stuff that clings to your boots; dig a hole in July and the walls come out smooth as pottery, dig the same hole in April and it holds water like a bowl. Much of the soil in St. Louis is high in clay, the Missouri Botanical Garden notes, and clay tends to compact into a hard, dense layer that keeps water, air and fertilizers from moving downward, which is why a rain garden or a new bed here needs a plan for where the water goes, not just a pretty plant list.
That’s also why the heaviest storms do so much damage on a badly graded lot. Water that can’t sink in has to go somewhere, and without a plan it finds the lowest point, which is too often your foundation or the neighbor’s side yard. A landscape architect’s grading and drainage plan is, at bottom, a decision about where every heavy rain will end up.
### What should you expect during the design process?
Expect phases, not one visit. Most landscape architects move from a consultation to a concept or master plan, then to detailed construction documents, and each phase ends with something you review and approve before the next begins. That rhythm protects your budget, because you never commit to the whole project on the strength of one hopeful conversation in the yard.
### The first walk-through
It starts on your property, ideally after a rain. The architect walks the yard, watches where water collects, asks how you actually use the space, and takes rough measurements and photos. Talk budget honestly here. A good professional is listening for the real problem, which often isn’t the one you called about.
### Concept, master plan and the MSD packet
Next comes the plan on paper: a scaled drawing of the whole property with patios, plantings, paths and drainage laid out. If you’re applying to MSD, its application resources include a sample landscaping plan and blank grid paper for your own drawing, so ask your designer for a version you can submit. Expect a round or two of revisions; this is the document you’ll live with for years.
### Construction documents and bidding
For anything built, the last phase turns the plan into instructions: materials, dimensions, grades and details a contractor needs to price and build accurately. With them, several contractors can bid the same scope. Some landscape architects will also review bids and check the work as it goes in, usually for an added fee.
The dig itself has a clock too. Missouri law says whoever excavates must notify the notification center at least two working days, but not more than ten working days, before the digging starts, so the buried lines get marked. A careful landscape architect builds both clocks into the schedule. A rushed crew skips them.
### When a designer is the smarter call
Hire a designer, or a strong install crew, when the job is mostly plants and looks on flat, well-draining ground: fresh beds, a new plant palette, a front yard that finally matches the house. Save the licensed architect for grading, drainage, retaining walls and anything structural, where one wrong elevation turns into a muddy, expensive redo. A modest patio on level ground may not need one at all; the same patio on a steep Roxana lot probably does.
Pavers, plants and a rain barrel add up fast. Here’s where St. Louis bargain hunters stretch the rest of the budget.
### How do you choose the right landscape architect in St. Louis?
Choose on license, portfolio and how well they listen, not on price alone. Ask to see projects a few years old, since a landscape only proves itself once it has grown in and weathered a couple of hard summers. Ask who does the installation, because some firms design only and hand off to contractors while others run the whole build. Then get the scope, the fee and the schedule in writing, including who files the utility-locate request before anyone digs.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What does a landscape architect charge per hour?
A.  There’s no standard billed rate, so get it in writing before the first visit. For context, the median landscape architect in the St. Louis, MO-IL area earns $31.77 an hour in wages, and a firm’s billed hour sits on top of that. Bigger projects often move to a flat design fee or a percentage of construction cost. Ask whether the first site visit is billed.
### Q. Is $100 an hour too much for landscape work?
A.  It depends on what the hour buys. For licensed design time, where someone is solving the grading and drainage that decide where a storm goes, a professional rate can pay for itself by preventing a single tear-out. For mowing or planting labor, the same rate would be steep. Judge it against the skill the task needs and the cost of getting it wrong.
### Q. What’s the difference between an architect and a landscape architect?
A.  An architect designs buildings; a landscape architect designs the land around them. Missouri’s definition of professional landscape architecture covers site plans, grading, drainage, irrigation and planting plans, and it leaves out the design of structures ordinarily included in engineering or architecture. Architects and landscape architects fall under the same Missouri licensing board.
### Q. Do I need a landscape designer or architect?
A.  Choose by the problem. Missouri law lets gardeners, nursery staff and landscape contractors prepare planting plans, so new beds and curb appeal on flat ground rarely need more. When water, slope, retaining walls or a big patio are in play, a licensed landscape architect’s grading and drainage plan is the safer place to spend.
### Q. What should I ask a landscape architect before hiring?
A.  Ask whether they hold a Missouri license, then check it on the state’s licensee search. Ask how they charge, what’s included and how many revision rounds come with the fee. Ask who installs and who requests the utility locates. And if water is the problem, ask whether they’ve designed rainscaping for an MSD grant before.
### Q. What are the common landscape design mistakes?
A.  Ignoring where the water goes until it pools against the foundation. Planting for how things look today, not how big they’ll grow. Building in disconnected weekend pieces with no master plan. Fighting St. Louis clay instead of planning around it. And, in MSD territory, starting installation before the grant approval and Notice to Proceed arrive.

## $65 Patent Pending? What a St. Louis Patent Attorney Really Costs
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/patent-attorney-cost-in-st-louis-what-inventors-pay
Sixty-five dollars. That’s what the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office charges a micro entity to file a provisional patent application, and it’s the last number anybody expects to hear in a Wellston garage at midnight. The shop light buzzes. On the bench sits a phone bracket that clamps onto a wheelchair arm, gray plastic still warm from the printer, the latest try after the others snapped. This one holds. Your hands smell like sanded plastic and cold coffee from the shift you just finished at the other job.
So what if the $65 isn’t the expensive part? The expensive part is the noise built to sell to inventors: the late-night ad offering to patent and market your idea for you, the myth that mailing yourself the drawings makes a poor man’s patent, the attorney quote that arrives as one lump sum with no stages in it. None of it is aimed at your invention. This page takes the inventor’s side, with the real fees, two St. Louis doors those ads never mention, and the question that makes an invention promoter go quiet.
### How much do patent attorneys charge?
Most patent attorneys bill by the hour or quote a flat fee for each stage: the search, the drafting, and the back-and-forth with the examiner after filing. A lump-sum quote with no stages in it is the one to push back on, because you can’t compare it to anything. A hinged bracket is a different job than software or a chemical formula, so get every quote in writing, broken out by stage.
The government’s side is printed in the USPTO’s fee schedule. To file a provisional, a micro entity pays $65, a small entity $130 and a large company $325. A full utility application stacks a basic filing fee, a search fee and an examination fee: $70, $154 and $176 for a micro entity, $400 together. The same three fees cost a large company $2,000. If the patent is allowed, the micro entity issue fee is $258, and the first maintenance fee, due at 3.5 years, is $430.
Read those columns again with the coffee going cold beside you. The gap between them is the gap between a weekend of overtime and a month of it, and “micro” is roomier than it sounds. The gross income ceiling is adjusted each year, and the USPTO’s micro entity page currently lists it at $262,380. The other condition trips people up: no applicant or inventor on the filing can have been named as an inventor on more than four previously filed applications.
### Before any attorney: two St. Louis doors
The St. Louis Public Library has been designated a Patent and Trademark Resource Center by the USPTO. It sits in the Science & Technology Room on the first floor of Central Library, 1301 Olive Street, quiet except for keyboards ticking and a stranger’s patent drawings glowing on the screen in front of you. A librarian offers assistance with searching; the library cannot provide legal advice or searching services, so you dig with a guide at your elbow. Call 314-539-0390 to schedule an appointment or check when librarian assistance is available.
The second door is a law school clinic. The USPTO’s Missouri page lists Washington University in St. Louis School of Law among the clinics where Missouri inventors and entrepreneurs can get free legal help on patents, and it points inventors to the Inventors Association of St. Louis to connect with local inventors.
### The one question that makes an invention promoter go quiet
Here’s the line worth screenshotting. Under 35 U.S. Code § 297, an invention promoter must tell you in writing, before you sign, the total number of customers it knows received a net financial profit as a direct result of its services. Not a testimonial. Not a glossy success story. A number.
So ask for it, out loud, across their conference table, along with the total number of customers who contracted with them, because the law requires that one too. A promoter who has made inventors money has every reason to show you that page. One who hasn’t has to hand it over anyway.
Then read the complaints before you write any check. The USPTO publishes complaints concerning invention promoters and promotion firms in a public forum, along with the promoters’ responses, and its scam-prevention page puts the rule of thumb bluntly: if a website is offering services for a price that is too good to be true, it is highly likely that it is.
### What the attorney’s fee actually buys
Three jobs hide inside a patent attorney’s bill, and the drafting fee everybody fixates on is only the middle one. Knowing all three is how you read a quote without your stomach dropping.
### The search
A professional patentability search digs through issued patents and published applications to see whether your invention is actually new, and a good one comes back with a frank read on what the results mean for you. Your own first pass at Central Library doesn’t replace that, but it can sharpen the questions you bring to the attorney so the paid hours go further.
It also protects you from the most expensive surprise in patent work: paying to draft an application for something already patented. Find your bracket in someone else’s drawings at a library terminal and you’ve lost an afternoon. Find it after the drafting invoice and you’ve lost the invoice too.
### The drafting
A patent protects what its claims say, word for word. Write them too broad and the examiner rejects them; too narrow and a competitor changes one bolt and walks right around you. This is the craft you’re really hiring, and it’s where a cheap, rushed application quietly costs the most, because you won’t feel the weakness until someone copies you and your lawyer reads the claims out loud in a cold conference room.
### The prosecution
Filing starts a conversation with the USPTO, not a countdown to a certificate. An examiner often pushes back in writing with what’s called an office action, and your attorney answers, argues and amends. Every round is billed time. When a flat-fee package covers a round or two, get that in writing; when it doesn’t, ask what a typical response costs before the first one lands in your inbox.
### Provisional first, or straight to a utility patent?
For most first-time inventors, the provisional is the on-ramp. The USPTO built it to provide a lower-cost first patent filing, and it does real work: it establishes an official United States patent application filing date for your invention, and it permits use of the “Patent Pending” notice for 12 months. That year is breathing room to test the market, raise money or fix the prototype before the big spend.
Two hard edges. Provisional applications are not examined on their merits, and to benefit from one you must file the corresponding nonprovisional application during its 12-month pendency period, which cannot be extended. And provisional applications may not be filed for design inventions at all, so if your product’s value lives in how it looks rather than how it works, that on-ramp is closed to you.
One more clock ticks quietly in the background. Under federal patent law, your own public disclosure, the demo at a pitch night or the post with the prototype in it, isn’t prior art against your claim if you file within one year of it. Treat that year as a safety net with holes in it, not a plan. About to pitch, post or sell? Make the call the week before, not the week after.
Know the number before the other guy names it. It works on a promoter, and it works on a coin buyer too: how to sell coins in St. Louis without getting ripped off.
### Free legal help Missouri inventors can actually use
If money is the wall, the federal pro bono route deserves a call before anything else. The USPTO says Missouri inventors are served by the Pro Bono Patent Program, part of its nationwide program that matches inventors who qualify, based on income, with volunteer attorneys and patent professionals who help file the application. Each regional program screens for its own income limit, generally based on the inventor’s gross household income, so ask before you assume you’re over it.
The Washington University clinic from earlier is the other half of that picture. Expect an intake process and some patience, and apply before you’re up against a deadline you set for yourself, like a pitch night or a trade show.
Vetting any lawyer, free or paid, runs on the same instincts. Ask who will actually do the work, what the fee includes, and what happens when the examiner says no. Our guide to finding a trustworthy immigration lawyer in St. Louis walks through those instincts for a different specialty, and they carry over almost word for word.
### When does an inventor actually need a patent attorney?
When the stakes are real and the claims are hard. If you plan to raise money, license the invention, sell a physical product at scale or compete in a crowded field, professional claim drafting usually pays for itself, because the claims decide what the patent is worth. If it’s a hobby you’ll never sell, or the idea still changes shape every weekend, spending big before a single buyer says yes is the more common way to get hurt.
A sensible middle path exists. Some inventors write their own provisional to lock in a date, then bring in an attorney for the utility application once there’s money or real interest behind the product. Others pay for one consultation to pressure-test the claims before deciding anything. You don’t have to choose all-in or all-alone on day one.
### Can you file a patent application yourself?
Yes, and the USPTO has a whole program for you. Its Pro Se Assistance Program provides outreach and education to applicants who file patent applications without the assistance of a registered patent attorney or agent. USPTO employees cannot give legal advice, though, so you get training and resources, not someone telling you your claims are good. The forms are manageable. The claims are the part that keeps you up.
If your invention lives online, as an app, a download or a subscription, the paperwork doesn’t stop at the patent office. Terms, privacy and disclosure pages protect you in ways a patent never will, and our rundown of the essential legal pages for B2C websites covers what a patent can’t.
### Patent pending keeps copycats out. It doesn’t bring a single customer in.
Here’s the part the promoters and the paperwork both skip. A patent is a fence. It doesn’t walk your product to anybody’s door. When a neighbor asks ChatGPT where to buy a wheelchair phone mount in St. Louis, or a shop owner searches for a local maker, the answer comes from wherever your product is already described online, and a carton stamped “Patent Pending” stacked against your garage wall isn’t on that list.
You’re not doing anything wrong. The old belief that a website and a Google listing are enough was built for a different decade, and it leaves good products invisible. ### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is a patent attorney worth it?
A.  For anything you plan to sell, license or raise money on, usually yes, because a patent protects only what its claims say and claim drafting is a specialist’s craft. For a hobby project, or an idea that still changes every week, start smaller: a library search, then a provisional, then a paid consultation once someone actually wants to buy.
### Q. Is it worth patenting an idea?
A.  A patent doesn’t cover a bare idea. Federal law offers one for a new and useful process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter, or an improvement to one, which means a specific invention you can describe in detail. If yours is new, useful and headed to market, protection can pay. If it’s vague or easy to design around, the money buys little.
### Q. Does a poor man’s patent work?
A.  Not as a patent. Mailing yourself a sealed description gets you a postmark, and a postmark isn’t an application. A provisional application is the low-cost tool that counts: the USPTO says it establishes an official United States patent application filing date for the invention, and the micro entity filing fee is $65.
### Q. What are the downsides of getting a patent?
A.  Cost, time and the fight afterward. Government fees keep coming after the grant, starting with a maintenance fee due at 3.5 years, and the attorney hours can outrun them. A patent is also only as strong as your willingness to enforce it, and enforcement costs money too. For some products, secrecy and speed fit better than a filing.
### Q. Can I sell my idea without a patent?
A.  Yes. Inventors license and sell products without a patent, leaning on a working prototype, a signed nondisclosure agreement and speed. Filed protection can make a buyer more comfortable, because it fences out copycats. Either way, a product nobody can find doesn’t sell, which is why a garage maker can list on St Louis Near Me Directory with no public address and get more customers from St. Louis searches.
### Q. What is better than a patent?
A.  Sometimes a different tool fits. The St. Louis Public Library’s patent center puts it simply: patents protect inventions and trademarks protect brands, and other forms of intellectual property are protected by copyrights and trade secrets. A recipe nobody can reverse-engineer may be safer as a secret. Often the strongest move pairs one of those with speed to market.

## She Didn’t Turn Around: Where St. Louis Deaf Kids Learn
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/schools-for-the-deaf-in-st-louis-a-parents-guide
You can hear. That is the strange part nobody warns you about. The pots clanking in the sink, the furnace kicking on, your own voice saying her name a little too loud from the doorway, and she keeps stacking blocks with her back to you. Then the audiologist turns the screen around, and the line on the chart sits low where you hoped it would sit high, and the room goes very quiet for everybody except you.
If that is where you are, you are in big company. St. Joseph Hearing + Speech, one of the St. Louis schools in this guide, puts the number plainly on its own front page: 90% of children with hearing loss are born to parents with typical hearing. So most parents reading this did not grow up signing, did not grow up around deaf adults, and did not know until this year that a city could have a whole map of schools built for one kind of child. You are standing where nine out of ten families start. And deaf school starts sooner than anyone tells you: St. Joseph reports serving 335 infants and toddlers in a single school year, babies too small for a backpack.
Here is what nobody says out loud in that waiting room, and it is worth repeating to the grandparents on the drive home. The two fears that keep parents awake are money and distance, and around here both are smaller than they look. Central Institute for the Deaf on South Taylor Avenue is a private school, yet its own tuition page says no family need pay a penny for a child who qualifies. How that works is the part almost nobody explains: school districts contract with CID for children ages 3 to 12, donors fund full tuition scholarships, and for babies under three, Missouri First Steps, or Illinois Child and Family Connections across the river, supports the Family Center. The Missouri School for the Deaf in Fulton is a boarding school, yet its own FAQ says there is no cost to parents, and students travel home almost every weekend. Read that twice. The hard part is not finding a school or paying for it. It is knowing which fork comes first.
And the fork is not “which school.” It is “which language.” Spoken English with hearing technology, or American Sign Language with English in writing, or some blend of the two. Pick that, with your audiologist and early-intervention team at the table, and the list of schools shrinks on its own.
You can start tomorrow morning, before the coffee goes cold. If your child is under three, ask your audiologist or pediatrician for a referral to First Steps, Missouri’s early intervention system for infants and toddlers from birth to age three, and know that the handoff to school services happens around the third birthday, so it pays to ask early. Then three calls. Central Institute for the Deaf, 314.977.0132: what ages they take right now, how tuition support would work for your child, and when you can sit in on a class. The Missouri School for the Deaf, 573-592-4000, whose outreach list includes Families First early intervention, audiology and hearing tests, and American Sign Language. Special School District in St. Louis County, 314.989.8100: ask how to request an evaluation, then send that request by email so it carries a date. Write down who you talked to, and when.
### How many deaf schools are there in Missouri?
Missouri’s state school for the deaf is the Missouri School for the Deaf in Fulton, which has served deaf and hard-of-hearing students since 1851. Around St. Louis, families also have private listening-and-spoken-language schools, Central Institute for the Deaf, the Moog Center for Deaf Education and St. Joseph Hearing + Speech, plus public-school support through Special School District of St. Louis County.
So the real count has two halves. The state school sits at 505 East Fifth Street in Fulton, out in mid-Missouri, far enough that the drive gets quiet somewhere past the last St. Louis exit and you start doing the math on Sunday nights and dorm goodbyes. It serves students ages 5 to 21, and it teaches in ASL. Then, back home, there is the cluster of private schools that teach children to listen and talk, each with its own front door and its own feel.
Stand in any hallway for ten minutes and you will know more than any count could tell you. Walk into a spoken-language classroom and you hear small voices, teachers leaning in close, the soft click of a hearing-aid battery door. Walk into a signing classroom and it can be almost silent while the room is loud with conversation, hands moving fast, faces doing half the grammar. Both rooms are full of kids learning. They are just learning in different languages, and that difference decides which building is yours.
### The school on South Taylor that pays the tuition
Central Institute for the Deaf, which everybody in town calls CID, sits at 825 S. Taylor Avenue in the city, on the edge of the medical campus. Its own words are simple: at CID, children who are deaf and hard of hearing learn to listen, talk, read and succeed. The approach is listening and spoken language, usually alongside hearing aids or cochlear implants.
Back to that line most parents miss, the one worth forwarding to the grandparents who are quietly worried about money. CID states on its home page that 100% of CID students with hearing loss receive full tuition support. Right beside that line, the same page asks donors to help a child learn to listen and talk, which is how a private school in the Central West End can make that promise. That one fact changes the conversation at a lot of kitchen tables. Here is the move most families never hear about. CID’s tuition page says families of qualified candidates receive school district funding or full tuition scholarships, and that CID assists families in accessing all available third-party resources. So the question to bring to your district is not “can we afford CID?” It is “would you contract with CID for my child?” Then call 314.977.0132 and ask CID to confirm whether your child qualifies and what the support covers.
The Moog Center for Deaf Education, on South Forty Drive, is another spoken-language school. Its curriculum, in its own words, focuses on accelerating the development of spoken language so children can develop sufficient language skills to be full participants in the general education setting. Translation for a tired parent: the goal is a child who can walk into a regular classroom and hold her own. Moog answers at (314) 692-7172. St. Joseph Hearing + Speech, on Strassner Drive, works toward the same goal, reports serving 169 students in that same school year, and answers at (314) 918-1369.
### Hands, not ears: the state school that costs parents nothing
Some families sit in that audiology booth and decide their child should have a full language right now, one that does not depend on a device staying charged. That road leads mostly to Fulton. The Missouri School for the Deaf calls itself bilingual: the earliest possible access to American Sign Language, with English in reading and writing alongside it. Its outreach list includes Families First early intervention, audiology and hearing tests, hearing aids and FM systems, and American Sign Language. You can reach the campus at 573-592-4000.
The draw is immersion. A deaf kid there is not the only deaf kid in the building. The bus driver, the coach, the kid in the next bunk, everyone signs, and language comes at her from every side the way spoken English comes at a hearing child. The cost is distance, and it is smaller than the map makes it look. On home-going weekends, students leave campus by 1:30 p.m. on charter buses, with dorm staff riding along as chaperones, to drop-off points close to home, and families who live far from a stop get their mileage reimbursed. A typical year still has 4 to 6 ‘stay weekends’ on campus, usually built around home games. So the goodbye in the dorm hallway is real. So is the afternoon the bus pulls up near home and she comes down the steps already signing about her week. Families weigh that differently, and none of them are wrong.
You do not have to drive to Fulton to start signing, though. DEAF, Inc., based in St. Louis and bridging communication access since 2008, runs ASL classes and youth and family education. A parent who can sign “milk,” “more” and “I love you” by the end of the month has given a toddler something no waiting list can.
And here is the part that surprises a lot of parents who think they have to pick a team. Plenty of families do both for a while. A child can wear hearing aids at a spoken-language school during the day and sign “bath” and “book” with Mom at night. Some kids lean hard toward one language as they grow and show you which one feels like home. Others stay comfortable in both. Nobody hands you a grade for this, and the early years are for watching your child closely, not for winning an argument you read about online at two in the morning.
### Can my child stay in a local public school?
Yes, and many deaf and hard-of-hearing kids do, with services written into an Individualized Education Program, or IEP. In St. Louis County that help often comes through Special School District of St. Louis County, which calls itself the largest specialized education provider in the state. Families in the city and outside the county start with their own district.
What a plan can hold depends on the child: an interpreter, a teacher of the deaf who visits, speech services, captioning, a seat near the front away from the humming radiator, a microphone the teacher clips to her collar. The trade is real. Your kid rides the same bus as the neighbor kids and sleeps in her own bed every night, but she may be the only deaf child in her grade.
The first move is a written request for an evaluation. Put it in an email so there is a date on it. The evaluation drives the IEP, and the IEP drives the services. Bring a notebook to the meeting and remember you are a member of that team, not a guest at it. If you want a wider way to size up any school, our guide on how to choose a school in St. Louis pairs well with this one, and for homework help after the bell, see the best tutoring and learning centers across the St. Louis metro.
You have read audiology reports at midnight for weeks. Take one Saturday back and laugh at a St. Louis comedy club.
### Stand in the back of the classroom
Make the language call first, with your audiologist and early-intervention team. Then make the school calls, two or three of them, and ask to visit on a normal day, not an open house. Stand in the back. Listen to the room. Watch whether the adults get down to kid height when they talk, or sign, to a child.
Questions worth bringing: how big are the classes, how are parents involved, what does a regular Tuesday look like, how often do children move on to a neighborhood school, and how will they tell you if it is not working. Ask a current parent the same questions in the parking lot. They will tell you the truth faster than the brochure.
Keep one folder for all of it, paper or a phone note, it does not matter which. The audiogram, the evaluation request with its date, the names of the people you talked to and what each one promised. Three months from now, when a meeting gets tense and somebody says “we never got that,” you will slide the page across the table and the tone in the room will change. Parents who keep the folder are not being difficult. They are being the one person at that table who has been there for every single meeting, and that matters more than any title on a badge.
Then give yourself permission to change your mind. Kids grow, technology changes, families reassess at the IEP table every year. The first choice is a starting line. ### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Where is the Missouri school for the deaf?
A.  The Missouri School for the Deaf is at 505 East Fifth Street in Fulton, Missouri. It has served deaf and hard-of-hearing students since 1851, teaches in American Sign Language and serves students ages 5 to 21. There is no cost to parents, and students travel home almost every weekend. Call 573-592-4000 for admissions, and talk with your local district about how a placement would work.
### Q. What types of careers are available at Missouri School for the Deaf?
A.  A school with classrooms, dorms and outreach needs teachers of the deaf, ASL-fluent staff, speech and audiology staff, residential staff, counselors, nurses and office and support workers. Openings change, so check the Careers link on the school’s website for current positions.
### Q. Do most deaf children go to deaf schools?
A.  Not necessarily. Many deaf and hard-of-hearing children attend their neighborhood public schools with an IEP that adds interpreters, a teacher of the deaf or speech services. Deaf schools remain the choice for families who want full ASL immersion or an intensive spoken-language program. The right setting depends on the child.
### Q. Why are deaf schools declining?
A.  Families have more choices than they once did. Cochlear implants and better hearing aids, plus laws that guarantee services in public schools, let more deaf children stay close to home. I could not find a current Missouri enrollment figure to put a number on it. Deaf schools still matter for children who need a full signing community every day.
### Q. What is the oldest school for the deaf in the United States?
A.  The American School for the Deaf in Connecticut is the oldest permanent K-12 school for the deaf in the United States. Missouri’s own state school came later, in 1851, and still anchors ASL-based education in the state.
### Q. What states have schools for the deaf?
A.  Many states run a public school for the deaf, and the names and services differ from place to place. Missouri’s is the Missouri School for the Deaf in Fulton. If you are moving, or helping family in another state, start with that state’s department of education.

## The 3% Fee St. Louis Hosts Owe While Permits Are Frozen
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/short-term-rental-rules-in-st-louis-what-hosts-need-to-know
Three percent. That is the license fee the City of St. Louis now charges on the rent from every booking. It shows up nowhere in the payout notification that buzzes on your phone while you strip the bed, the old sheets still warm and smelling of somebody else’s shampoo. The app says the money landed. It doesn’t say part of it was never yours to keep. And the rules over your head split in two, with only one half frozen.
Here is the split, plainly. The permit law the city passed, Ordinance 71729, has been frozen by a judge, and the city is not enforcing its permit requirements while that order stands. But a second law, Ordinance 72095, went the other way. It requires every short-term rental operator in the city to hold a Short-Term Rental Business License and to pay a license fee of three percent of the rent, quarterly, to the License Collector. One door closed. The other one opened, and it has a meter on it. The city’s own notice says the fee is figured on the base nightly rate, before cleaning charges, platform service fees and taxes, so $3,000 in base rent for a quarter means $90 owed, not a cut of your cleaning fee. It is due April 30, July 31, October 31 and January 31, each for the quarter just ended, and the return asks for two numbers: nights rented and base rent collected. The License Collector’s short-term rental page has the form. City Hall’s main line is 314-622-4800.
The enemy here is the half-told headline. “Permits paused” ran everywhere, and a host in a Tower Grove two-family who read only that would fairly think the whole question went away. It didn’t. The pause covers the permit and its $150 annual application fee, which the lawsuit called a hidden tax. It does not cover the license fee voters asked for through Proposition S and aldermen finally passed into law about 15 months later, with the money going to affordable housing and the Right to Counsel program for tenants facing eviction. A spare room in Soulard and a whole unit in Dutchtown land on the same desk at City Hall, 1200 Market Street.
One detail the headlines skipped entirely: the ordinance lets the city sign collection agreements with rental platforms, and until one covers you, the operator is the one who pays. The fee took effect in late February. If your platform hasn’t mentioned it, that silence is not the same as an exemption. The first move is small: open the License Collector page and download the form before the next due date.
### What are the Airbnb rules for St. Louis?
Two laws, two very different states. Ordinance 71729, the permit law, has been blocked by a court order since April 22, 2025, and the city is not taking new permit applications. Ordinance 72095 is fully alive: it requires a Short-Term Rental Business License from the License Collector and a 3% license fee on rent, paid every quarter.
They sound like one law when a neighbor describes them over the fence. They are not. The permit ordinance reached anyone renting a home that is not their primary residence for less than 30 days at a time. Judge Joseph Whyte wrote that the company challenging it had “a likelihood of success on the merits” and granted a temporary restraining order.
On May 5, 2025, the court extended that order, and the city’s own notice still says it will not enforce the permit requirements while the order is in effect. That is a pause, not a repeal. A ruling can end it.
The license is the one in force. The city’s License Collector page says operators “must obtain a Short-Term Rental Business License and quarterly remit a 3% license fee.” Hold the two side by side. The permit is the law you’ve heard about. The license fee is the one with a due date.
### The address on your tax bill decides which rulebook you live under
Everything above is the City of St. Louis. The city and St. Louis County are two separate governments that share a name and nothing else on this question. A unit with a “St. Louis” mailing address can sit in unincorporated county land or inside one of dozens of small municipalities, each writing its own rules. A license from the city’s License Collector means nothing across that line, and a county approval means nothing inside it.
So before you buy another throw pillow, look at your property tax bill and find out who actually governs the lot. Hosts in Lake St. Charles, East Alton, Fairmont City, Foristell or Jerseyville answer to their own local offices, and some of those sit across a state line where Missouri law doesn’t reach at all. If you are still choosing where to buy a unit, our side-by-side look at St. Louis suburbs helps you weigh towns before the closing table.
Inside the city, the quiet part is that the fee runs on rent you already collected. Three percent of a booking is small on one weekend and real money across a year of weekends. Set it aside the day the payout lands, in its own account, so the quarterly filing never comes out of the grocery money.
A rental unit changes what your family loses if you’re gone. Compare term and whole life insurance.
### Why a frozen permit law still deserves your attention
The lawsuit leaned on Missouri’s Hancock Amendment, the state rule that bars government from raising taxes without voter approval. The plaintiff’s argument was simple: the $150 annual permit fee was a tax in disguise. Notice what that does and doesn’t touch. The fight is about the permit fee and the permit program. The 3% license fee came out of a ballot measure voters already approved, which is exactly the kind of approval Hancock asks for.
I could not confirm a final ruling in the permit case as of this writing. That uncertainty is the whole point. It is the feeling of a lease you signed with a clause still blank: you can live there, you just don’t know the last line yet. If the court lifts the order, the permit requirements can snap back, and hosts who spent the pause doing nothing will be the ones scrambling for inspections while their calendar fills. Keep the city’s court-order notice bookmarked, keep a copy of anything the city tells you in writing, and check it before each quarterly filing.
### What taxes should a short-term rental host understand?
There is the tax you collect and the tax you owe, and they live in different drawers. One is a shoebox of receipts you dread opening in March; the other is a quarterly line you can keep small if you file it on time. The city license fee is the first kind of headache. Your federal income tax is the second, and a few rules people repeat on video are much narrower than they sound.
### The 14-day rule, or Augusta rule
The IRS says that if you use a dwelling as a residence and rent it for fewer than 15 days in the year, you don’t report any of the rental income and you don’t deduct any of the expenses as rental expenses. Fourteen nights, then the door shuts. Rent the fifteenth and you are back in ordinary rental reporting. It suits the homeowner who rents out the whole house for one big weekend, not the host with a unit booked most of the month.
### The 80/20 rule and the short-term rental “loophole”
These two travel together in host chatter and both hinge on how your stays are classified and how much you personally participate. They can change how losses flow on your return, and they are easy to misapply. Bring them to a CPA with your booking history in hand instead of diagnosing yourself from a thirty-second clip.
### When a guest stops being a guest
A weekend visitor leaves a towel on the floor and a five-star review. A person who has been in your unit for weeks, with groceries in the fridge and mail coming to the door, can start to look like a tenant under Missouri law, and tenants carry protections a nightly host never planned for. Missouri, for one, says a landlord may not demand or receive a security deposit of more than two months’ rent, and must return it, or send a list of damages, within thirty days after the tenancy ends.
You can feel the shift before you can name it. The suitcase never gets repacked. A second toothbrush shows up by the sink, a parcel with their name sits on your porch, and the checkout date in the app keeps sliding a week at a time. Nothing about it is dramatic. That is exactly why hosts miss the line until they are standing on the wrong side of it, keys in hand, unsure what they are allowed to do next.
If you plan to allow long stays, put the terms in writing before the guest arrives, and talk to a local attorney before you ever touch a lock. Stuck? City Hall’s main line is 314-622-4800 if you need to be pointed to the right desk.
Then be the host nobody calls the city about. Cap guest counts, post the parking rules on the fridge, and give the neighbors a number that actually rings. ### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are the Airbnb regulations in Missouri?
A.  Start with your property tax bill, not the state, because the government named on it writes your rules. Inside the City of St. Louis, permit enforcement under Ordinance 71729 is paused by court order, while Ordinance 72095 requires a Short-Term Rental Business License and a 3% quarterly license fee.
### Q. What is the short-term rental loophole?
A.  It is a federal tax idea, not a way around city rules. It describes how income from short stays can sometimes be treated differently from ordinary rental income depending on stay length and how much you participate. It changes how losses flow, so ask a CPA before you count on it.
### Q. What is the 80/20 rule for Airbnb?
A.  In host tax talk, it points to how a stay is classified and how much service you provide, which can affect how the income is treated. Interpretations vary. Treat it as a question for a tax professional, and bring a full year of booking records when you ask.
### Q. What is the 14 day rental rule called?
A.  It’s called the Augusta rule, also known as Section 280A(g) of the tax code. The IRS says that if you use a dwelling as a residence and rent it for fewer than 15 days in a year, you don’t report the rental income or deduct rental expenses. A fifteenth night ends the exemption.
### Q. What are the tenant laws in St. Louis, Missouri?
A.  Longer stays can fall under Missouri landlord-tenant law. One example: a landlord may not take a security deposit above two months’ rent and must return it or itemize damages within thirty days after the tenancy ends. ### Q. What can landlords not do in Missouri?
A.  Missouri law limits what landlords can demand, starting with a security deposit cap of two months’ rent. When a guest who has stayed for weeks won’t leave, don’t improvise with locks or utilities. Call a local attorney first; St Louis Near Me Directory can help you find one by category.

## What a Taxi Costs in St. Louis (and When It Beats a Rideshare)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-taxi-costs-in-st-louis
It’s 11:05 on a Tuesday night at St. Louis Lambert. Your bag was the last one off the belt, the person who was supposed to pick you up isn’t answering, and your phone is sitting at two percent and falling. No app, no map, no way to send a text. Forty feet away, under the terminal overhang, a short line of cabs sits with their lights on and someone waving passengers forward. You have no idea what that ride is going to cost. You get in anyway, because the alternative is a dead phone and a cold bench.
That curb scene repeats in quieter forms all over the metro. A grandmother in Pine Lawn needs a ride to a morning appointment and has never installed a rideshare app. A wedding party in Pontoon Beach needs three cars at one in the morning, exactly when app pricing goes vertical. Someone out in New Melle is far enough from the core that the nearest app driver is twenty minutes away, if one accepts at all. A second-shift worker in Washington Park gets off after the buses thin out. A family in Winchester just wants one car, one price, and no surprises.
Here’s what this guide covers. What a metered cab fare in St. Louis is actually built from, and why nobody can quote you an exact number in advance. What a twenty-minute ride tends to run. How airport trips price differently from everything else. When a cab beats a rideshare, and when it clearly doesn’t. How to get one at the airport curb or from a hotel lobby. What to tip. And how to figure out, in one short phone call, whether a company is worth using twice.
### How much is a taxi in St. Louis, MO?
Most St. Louis cab rides run on a meter: a flag drop when you get in, a per-mile rate after that, plus waiting time when you’re stopped in traffic. Short in-town trips often land in the low double digits. Airport runs cost more, since a pickup surcharge is common. Ask about a flat rate.
The honest answer past that is a range, not a number. Two riders leaving the same downtown corner ten minutes apart can pay noticeably different amounts, because one hits every light and the other doesn’t. Distance sets the floor. Time stuck in traffic sets the ceiling. A quick two-mile hop across the Central West End is a different animal from a fifteen-mile run out to the edge of the county, and the meter treats them that way.
What a meter does give you is predictability of a different kind. The rate card doesn’t change because it’s a Cardinals home game, or because it started raining, or because it’s bar close on a Saturday. That’s the whole trade. You give up the up-front number on a screen, and in exchange the price of the ride doesn’t move with demand.
### What goes into a metered cab fare?
Four pieces, in most cases: the drop, the mileage, the waiting time, and the extras. Knowing those four lets you estimate a fare within a few dollars before you ever get in the car. It also lets you tell right away whether the number on the meter at the end of the trip makes sense.
### The drop, or flag charge
This is the base amount that appears the moment the meter starts, before the car has moved an inch. It covers the driver coming to get you. It’s the reason a six-block ride never feels cheap: you’re paying for the dispatch, not the distance. On very short trips, the drop is most of the fare.
### The per-mile rate
After the drop, the meter adds a set amount for every fraction of a mile. This is the piece that dominates on longer trips. If you know roughly how far you’re going, you can do the math yourself. Ten miles at a typical per-mile rate is the bulk of what you’ll owe on a cross-town run.
### Waiting time
When the car is stopped or crawling below a certain speed, the meter switches from counting miles to counting minutes. That’s why a rush-hour trip downtown costs more than the same trip at ten at night. It’s also why asking the driver to wait while you run inside for two minutes shows up on the final total.
### Surcharges and extras
Airport pickups commonly carry a surcharge, and many companies charge a small amount for each additional passenger beyond the first. Some add fees for oversized luggage, tolls, or scheduled pickups. None of that is hidden, but you do have to ask. “Is there anything on top of the meter?” is a fair question and a fast one.
### How much should a 20 minute taxi cost?
It depends almost entirely on how many miles fit inside those twenty minutes. Twenty minutes moving freely on the interstate might cover twelve or fifteen miles and produce a substantial fare. Twenty minutes of stop-and-go downtown might cover four, with much of that time billing as waiting rather than distance.
So the useful way to ask isn’t “how much for twenty minutes.” It’s “how much to get from here to there.” A dispatcher can usually give you a solid estimate for a named destination, because they know the route and they know the traffic. Give them the actual street address, not a neighborhood. Two addresses in the same neighborhood can sit four miles apart.
One more thing worth knowing: a longer route isn’t automatically the worse deal. Highway miles at speed accrue on the mileage rate and clear quickly. Surface streets at five in the afternoon accrue on the clock. If a driver suggests going around instead of straight through, that’s often the cheaper choice, not the pricier one.
### What does a taxi to or from the airport cost?
More than an equivalent in-town trip, for two reasons. Lambert sits roughly fifteen miles northwest of downtown, so the mileage alone adds up. And airport pickups commonly carry a surcharge on top of the meter. That’s a standard part of how cab pricing works at airports, not an upcharge aimed at you.
This is also the trip where a flat rate is most likely to exist. Cab companies frequently run set prices between the airport and common destinations, downtown hotels especially, precisely because it’s such a repeated route. Ask the dispatcher or the driver directly: do you run a flat rate from Lambert to this address? If the answer is yes, you know the number before you leave the curb.
Weigh it against the alternatives before you commit. If you’re traveling alone with one bag, MetroLink runs straight from the terminals and costs a fraction of any car; our guide to getting around St. Louis by ride, shuttle, and MetroLink lays those options out side by side. And if what you’re really pricing is leaving your own car at the airport for a week, compare two cab fares against what it costs to park at St. Louis Lambert. Round trips in a cab often beat a long-term parking bill.
### Which is cheaper, Uber or taxi?
Neither one wins every time, and that’s the real answer. Rideshare pricing is dynamic, so it’s often cheaper on an ordinary weekday afternoon and considerably more expensive during surge. Metered cab pricing is fixed by the rate card, so it doesn’t spike. The cheaper option depends on when you happen to be standing there.
On a quiet Wednesday at two in the afternoon, the app usually wins on price. At bar close, in a downpour, when a concert lets out, or on New Year’s Eve, the meter frequently wins, sometimes by a lot. If you’ve ever watched an app quote climb while you were still deciding, you already understand the difference. A meter simply doesn’t do that.
There’s also a reliability dimension that never shows up in the price. In dense parts of the city, app cars are everywhere. Farther out, in New Melle for instance, driver supply thins and a dispatched cab may be the more dependable call even when it isn’t the cheapest one. Cheap doesn’t help you if nobody accepts the ride.
Pricing a bigger project at home too? See what a landscape architect costs.
### When does a cab beat the app?
In predictable situations, mostly. Surge periods, weather events, big-event crowds, very early scheduled airport runs, riders who don’t use smartphones, cash payments, and trips outside the dense core. In each case the fixed rate card or the dispatch model does something an app can’t reliably do for you.
The scheduled pickup deserves its own mention. If you need to be at Lambert at 4:45 in the morning, a cab company will take that booking days ahead and hold it. Apps schedule rides too, but a scheduled app ride still has to find a driver at 4:15 a.m. A dispatcher assigns a car instead. That difference matters most exactly when the stakes are highest.
Group size and access needs matter as well. If you need a wheelchair-accessible vehicle, or you’ve got six people and a pile of luggage, calling ahead and describing the situation gets you a car that fits. And when the occasion is bigger than a single ride, a wedding or a milestone birthday, pricing it as a limo or car service in St. Louis is often the more sensible comparison.
### How do you actually get a taxi in St. Louis?
Three reliable ways: the stand at the airport, the front desk at a hotel, or a phone call to a dispatcher. Street hailing barely works here. St. Louis isn’t a city where empty cabs cruise looking for a raised hand, so standing on a corner waving is mostly wasted time.
### At St. Louis Lambert
Follow the signs for ground transportation and walk to the taxi stand outside baggage claim. There’s usually a starter directing passengers to the next car in line. You don’t book anything and you don’t pick a driver; you take the car at the front. Before you load bags, that’s the moment to ask about a flat rate.
### At a hotel
Ask the front desk or the bell stand. Hotels keep working relationships with cab companies and can usually have a car out front within minutes. This is the easiest option downtown and around the convention hotels, and the staff generally know what the common runs cost, which is a useful sanity check before you go.
### By phone or by the company’s own app
Call and book it. Give the pickup address, the destination address, the number of passengers, and the time you need the car. Ask for a fare estimate and how they take payment. Plenty of cab companies now run their own booking apps too, which pair dispatch reliability with the tracking you’re already used to.
### How much should you tip a taxi driver?
Fifteen to twenty percent is the customary range, the same as most service tipping in the United States. Round up to a whole dollar to keep it simple. Tip toward the higher end if the driver loaded heavy bags, waited on you, drove through bad weather, or got you somewhere on a tight schedule.
Tips can go on the card in most cabs, but not every reader makes that obvious, so it helps to carry a few singles. On a very short ride, percentage math gets silly; a couple of dollars is a normal minimum no matter what the meter says. And if a driver genuinely saved your evening, nobody has ever been offended by more.
### How do you choose a cab company worth calling?
Shortlist two or three that serve your area, then call and ask plainly for what you want. How is the fare structured? Do you run a flat rate to my destination? What payment methods do you take? How wide is the pickup window? The answers, and how readily they come, tell you most of it.
Pay attention to the gap between what you asked for and what they’re prepared to provide. A dispatcher who handles all four questions in thirty seconds without hedging runs an organized operation. One who won’t discuss payment methods, or can’t commit to a pickup window, is telling you something about the ride you’re about to book. That gap is the signal, not the quote.
Then check the boring things. Is the company licensed to pick up where you actually are, which matters when a trip crosses between Missouri and Illinois. Do recent reviews mention on-time pickups, or the opposite. Will they confirm a scheduled booking the night before. Save the number of whoever handles it well, because the second call is always easier than the first.
