### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the most famous Spanish dish?
A.  Paella, the saffron rice cooked in a wide, shallow pan and shared straight from it, is the dish most people name first. Close behind are tortilla española, the thick potato omelet, plus gazpacho, jamón ibérico and churros with thick hot chocolate.
### Q. How to eat tapas for beginners?
A.  Share everything and order in rounds. Start with quick cold plates like pan con tomate, olives or jamón, then add hot ones such as gambas al ajillo, croquetas and patatas bravas. Eat as they arrive and order more only if you’re still hungry. Ask the server what the kitchen is proudest of that night.
### Q. What is a typical tapas menu?
A.  Cold plates like olives, jamón, Manchego, pan con tomate, boquerones and tortilla española, then hot plates like patatas bravas, croquetas, gambas al ajillo, pimientos de padrón, albondigas and pulpo. Paella usually sits in its own rice section, followed by a short dessert list with churros and crema catalana.
### Q. What is the proper etiquette when eating tapas?
A.  Share every plate, take a modest portion, and ask before claiming the last croqueta. Use the serving spoon when there is one. Dragging bread through the garlic oil left in the gambas dish is expected, not rude. Splitting the bill evenly is the usual move for a shared table.
### Q. How many tapas should you order?
A.  Fewer than you think, at first. Order a small first round for the table, see how big the plates run, then add a second round. If paella is coming, go light, because the rice fills you up. The server can tell you how hungry a table usually needs to be for their portions.
### Q. What do Spanish people eat daily?
A.  The Spanish day runs late. Breakfast is light, often coffee with toast rubbed with tomato and olive oil. Lunch is the big meal of the day, eaten in the afternoon. Dinner comes late and lighter, and tapas with a drink often fill the stretch in between.

## $65,000 Down to $1: When You Need a St. Louis Tax Attorney, Not a CPA
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/when-you-need-a-tax-attorney-in-st-louis-not-a-cpa
Sixty-five thousand dollars, down to one. That is not a late-night radio promise. It is what a tax clinic at the Washington University School of Law reports doing for a St. Louis woman it calls Katie. Medical setbacks pushed her out of a long career. She pulled all of her retirement money to buy a home, didn’t have enough withheld, and ended up owing a large tax bill. Then came a lien against the house she had bought with every retirement dollar she had, and the threat of her Social Security being garnished. Think about what that does to a person: the home that was supposed to be the safe place becomes the thing with a claim on it. The clinic built an offer in compromise, and the debt went from over $65,000 to $1.
That story carries the whole lesson of this page. Katie didn’t need someone to redo her math. The math was done. She owed it. What she needed was someone who could stand between her and the government and argue about what should happen next. That is a different job from preparing a return, and it is the line between a CPA and a tax attorney.
You probably know the feeling that sends people searching for this. The envelope with the IRS eagle sits on the kitchen counter in Bridgeton for two days before you open it. Your thumb tears the flap crooked. The first page is fine. The second has a number on it with a comma in the wrong place, and your chest goes tight, and the coffee goes cold while you read it a third time. You call the CPA who filed the returns. They are good at what they do. But there is a pause on the line before they answer, and that pause is the thing you’re really asking about.
Here is the plain truth, before anything else: most tax trouble does not need a lawyer. Some of it does, and guessing wrong costs you in either direction. Hire an attorney for a routine notice and you pay lawyer rates for a letter an accountant could have answered over lunch. Bring only an accountant into something that turns criminal and you may have handed the government a witness who has to talk.
So here is tonight’s order of operations, with the letter still on the counter. If your household income is at or below 250% of the federal poverty line, your first call is not a firm at all. It is the Low Income Taxpayer Clinic at WashU Law, the same clinic that handled Katie’s case. Its own report says its student attorneys, working with faculty, have represented or consulted with nearly 500 taxpayers and corrected or compromised over $1.5 million in federal tax liabilities, penalties and interest. That is a St. Louis door most people walk past on the way to a radio ad. If you earn more than that and the letter is about numbers, call your CPA or an enrolled agent in the morning. If the letter or the person at your door uses the word criminal, call a lawyer and nobody else. The federal trial court for St. Louis is the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri, at the Thomas F. Eagleton U.S. Courthouse on South 10th Street downtown, and nobody should walk up those steps with only an accountant beside them.
### Why might you seek the help of a tax attorney rather than a CPA?
You seek a tax attorney when the problem has turned legal rather than arithmetic. A lawyer brings four things a CPA can’t: attorney-client privilege that holds even if the matter turns criminal, the right to argue your case in court, the training to defend anything with a fraud or criminal angle, and legal opinions on how a sale, business or estate should be structured. If your problem touches one of those, the lawyer is not a luxury.
Privilege is the one people don’t see coming. There is a federal rule that gives conversations with a CPA or enrolled agent some of the same protection a lawyer gets, but the statute itself spells out the hole: it can only be raised in a noncriminal tax matter before the IRS or a noncriminal tax case in federal court. The day a matter crosses into criminal territory, your accountant can be made to describe what you said and what you handed over. Your lawyer generally can’t.
That is why a good tax lawyer, once hired, will sometimes ask you to stop calling your accountant. It feels rude. It is protection. If the accountant’s help is needed, the lawyer arranges it so the work is done for the lawyer, and they make that call, not you.
The rest of the line is simpler. A CPA works in numbers: what you owe, why, and how to owe less next year. A tax attorney works in rights and consequences: what the government can prove, what it can take, and what it can do to you. Both read the same code. They ask it different questions. If you’re weighing the accountant route first, our guide to what a tax preparer costs in St. Louis sorts the tiers.
### The quiet audit, and other signs the lawyer’s turn has come
Most audits are paperwork, and they end with a folder closing. Watch for the shift. The agent stops asking what you did and starts asking why you did it. The questions reach into years nobody said were under review. Or a friendly exam goes silent for weeks, the phone just doesn’t ring, and the silence feels heavier than the questions did. Any of those can mean the file is being looked at by someone else. A restaurant owner in Sunset Hills who notices that silence should stop answering questions and call a lawyer before the next contact.
If people with badges who call themselves special agents show up at your door or your business, or a letter mentions a criminal investigation, a grand jury or a summons, you have a legal matter and nothing else. Be polite. Take their cards. Say your attorney will contact them. Don’t explain, and don’t call your CPA first, for the privilege reason above.
Money alone can tip it too. A balance you can pay in a few years with a payment plan is usually an accountant’s job. A balance you can never realistically pay, especially once a lien has landed on your house in Ballwin or a levy has hit your paycheck, turns into a negotiation, and Katie’s story shows how much room a negotiation can have. Several unfiled years need care as well, because the order and the way you file can change what you face. The same goes for a partnership breaking up, payroll taxes the government wants to collect from the owners personally, the sale of a business, or an estate fight over what something was worth. And a serious dispute with the state deserves the same respect as a federal one.
### When a CPA or enrolled agent is plenty
For most notices, routine audits and payment plans, you don’t need a lawyer and you shouldn’t pay for one. The IRS itself says enrolled agents, CPAs and attorneys all have unlimited representation rights before the IRS, which covers audits, payment and collection issues, and appeals. If nobody is questioning your honesty and the fight is about what the numbers should be, an accountant can carry it.
Enrolled agents are the option most people in St. Louis have never heard of. Representing taxpayers is their whole trade, and for a confusing notice or a manageable balance, a good one is often the best value in the room. A retired nurse in Hazelwood holding a notice about a rental she sold most likely needs one of these, not a litigator.
The rule of thumb is short. If your CPA or enrolled agent reads your letter and says it’s routine, believe them. If they read it and go quiet, or say “you might want to talk to an attorney,” take that sentence home and act on it. Good accountants know where their protection ends.
If the pause on the phone has already happened, start your shortlist tonight. Browse tax attorneys across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick two or three to call, and put your letters in date order before the first meeting.
If you’re the tax attorney, the enrolled agent or the one-person practice that takes these calls, the people holding those envelopes are your next customers, and a listing for your practice is a quiet way to get more customers who already know they need you.
### How do you tell a real lawyer from a tax relief ad?
A real tax attorney is a named person licensed in Missouri who signs a written engagement letter and never promises a result. A tax relief ad is a phone number. Many of those spots are lead generation: a call center takes your details and passes them along, and the “pennies on the dollar” line that hooked you was never said by anyone who will do the work. Katie’s $1 result is real, but it came from a clinic that looked at her actual facts, not from a jingle.
Three checks before you hand over a dime. Get a name: ask which attorney will handle your matter, then confirm that person’s license with the state’s public lawyer lookup. If the answer is “one of our tax professionals,” hang up. Get the engagement letter before you pay, with the scope and fee in writing. And listen for guarantees, because nobody can promise the IRS will accept an offer.
Treat the first meeting as an interview. Say plainly what you have and what you want: “I have three years of proposed changes and a balance I can’t pay in full, and I want my realistic options.” One lawyer will describe a process. Another will describe an outcome. Hire the process. Then ask the question that tells you the most: “What would you tell me if my case were weak?” A lawyer with a ready answer has said it to other clients.
### What the bill looks like, and what to carry in
Tax attorneys bill by the hour, by a flat fee for a defined job, or against a retainer you refill as it’s used. Hourly fits open-ended matters like an audit nobody has sized yet. Flat fees fit defined jobs, like an offer in compromise or a set of late returns. Retainers are common for litigation and criminal work. Expect a lawyer’s rate to sit above an accountant’s, and confirm every number with the attorney, because rates vary widely across the metro. The real comparison isn’t rate against rate. It’s the fee against the outcome you’re trying to avoid.
Bring every letter, with its envelope, in date order. Bring the returns for the years in question, or the preparer’s name. Bring notes on who you talked to at the IRS or the state, with dates. For a collection problem, bring a rough picture of what you own, earn and owe, because the options depend on it. Then sit at the Bridgeton kitchen table for ten minutes and write a one-page timeline; it can save an hour of billed time. Retirees should bring pension and Social Security figures too, and our guide to how Missouri taxes retirement income covers the basics before you sit down.
### What if you cannot afford a tax attorney?
Go back to Katie. She didn’t hire a downtown firm. She got help from a Low Income Taxpayer Clinic, and the WashU LITC helps people at or below 250% of the federal poverty line, with student attorneys working alongside faculty on real IRS disputes. If your household fits, call before you call anyone else. The contractor in Ballwin with four unfiled years and thin cash flow is exactly who these clinics were built for.
There is one more door. The Taxpayer Advocate Service is an independent organization within the IRS that helps taxpayers resolve problems. When a file has gone dead and nobody calls back, that silence is exactly what to bring them. For the filing side, free volunteer programs prepare returns for eligible households, and our guide to free tax preparation in St. Louis explains who qualifies. Getting late returns filed is usually the first thing any representative asks for.

You can also split the work. A lawyer can take only the piece that needs privilege or a courtroom and hand the rest to an enrolled agent. Say that out loud in the interview; most good attorneys would rather scope a matter small than lose a client who couldn’t afford the whole thing. ### Frequently asked questions
### Q. When should you use a tax attorney?
A.  Use a tax attorney when the matter is adversarial, criminal, headed to court, or too large to pay. That means an audit that has turned hostile, any contact from IRS special agents, a lien or levy on a balance you can’t realistically pay, several unfiled years, or a business or estate dispute. Routine notices and simple payment plans usually don’t need one.
### Q. Do you need a lawyer to negotiate with the IRS?
A.  No. The IRS says enrolled agents, CPAs and attorneys all have unlimited representation rights before it, covering audits, collection issues and appeals. A lawyer adds the most on large balances, offers in compromise, and anything where privilege or a courtroom could come into play.
### Q. Are tax relief attorneys worth it?
A.  A real tax attorney is worth it for the right problem. A “tax relief” ad promising pennies on the dollar often isn’t a law practice at all. Ask for the named Missouri-licensed attorney who will handle your case, a written engagement letter, and an honest read on your odds. If you get a guarantee instead, walk away.
### Q. What exactly does a tax attorney do?
A.  A tax attorney handles the legal side of tax: disputes with the IRS or the state, negotiations over large balances, offers in compromise, liens and levies, appeals, court cases, defense in criminal investigations, and legal opinions on structuring a business, sale or estate. The federal privilege for a non-lawyer “federally authorized tax practitioner” can only be raised in noncriminal tax matters, so a criminal case is lawyer territory.
### Q. How much does a tax lawyer cost in the US?
A.  Tax lawyers bill hourly, by flat fee for a defined job, or against a retainer. Rates sit above an accountant’s and vary with experience, city and complexity. A single offer in compromise is often quoted flat; litigation and criminal matters usually run on a retainer. Get the structure and the numbers in writing before work starts.
### Q. What if I can’t afford a tax lawyer?
A.  In St. Louis, the Low Income Taxpayer Clinic at the Washington University School of Law helps people at or below 250% of the federal poverty line, and it is where one woman’s debt went from over $65,000 to $1. The Taxpayer Advocate Service, an independent organization within the IRS, helps taxpayers resolve problems. For simpler pieces, an enrolled agent costs a fraction of a lawyer.

## Two Inches of Wrist: What a Tux Rental Costs in St. Louis and When to Book
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-tuxedo-rental-costs-in-st-louis-and-when-to-book
Two inches of wrist. That’s what shows when your son shrugs on the black jacket from his cousin’s wedding, the one that fit fine eighteen months ago, and lifts his arms in the hallway mirror. The sleeve rides up past the bone. The trousers stop above his ankle, and you can see the white of his gym socks. Prom is three Saturdays away. He told his group he already had a tux. You stand there with the jacket still warm from his shoulders and feel a small, cold drop in your stomach: this is going to cost something, and nobody will tell you what until you’re already standing at a counter.
Breathe. Three Saturdays is enough, if you spend them in the right order. Tonight, call two shops and ask what’s in the package and what costs extra. This week, get him measured by a person holding a tape, not by you at the kitchen table. If the group wants photos at the Missouri Botanical Garden, here’s the move almost nobody makes: don’t book that permit now. The Garden requires one for prom photos, it’s nonrefundable, and it only asks for 24 hours’ notice. So book it Thursday night, once the forecast is in and the tux is hanging in the closet. Pick up two days early, make him raise his arms in the store, and drop everything back the morning after. That’s the whole plan. The rest of this page is for the parent in that hallway, the groom in St. Peters counting six groomsmen on his fingers, and the husband in Manchester holding a black-tie invitation and a sport coat that won’t cut it.
### How much do tux rentals usually cost?
The first number you hear at the counter is rarely the last one. Plan on roughly $100 to $250 for the tux itself. One national rental company puts the average basic rental tux at about $140, with most rentals between $100 and $250 depending on style, brand and accessories. A basic standard-fit black package sits at the bottom, a designer or slim-fit package in better fabric in the middle, and a full package with shoes, vest, cufflinks and studs at the top. Ask the shop to read you its package line by line.
Then add the St. Louis line nobody quotes you: the photo stop. A Missouri Botanical Garden photo permit includes admission for your entire party, so call (314) 577-5100 and get the price before you split it six ways. The city’s Jewel Box in Forest Park charges $1 per person, and it’s free on Monday and Tuesday from 9 a.m. until noon. A dollar a head and a wall of glass. That’s the line to send the group chat.
For a high-schooler, the basic tier almost always wins. He’ll outgrow it by graduation, and after four hours of dancing and one spilled fountain soda, you’ll be glad it’s going back. Grooms tend to land in the middle tier, a slim navy or charcoal cut that still looks crisp at the end of a sticky St. Louis evening on a Forest Park lawn. And if your family already owns good black dress shoes, ask to drop them from a full package. That one question can move the total more than switching shops.
### The St. Louis step after the tux is on
So many prom groups in this city want the same photo: the whole crew in their rentals and gowns, lined up by the fountains at the Missouri Botanical Garden, 4344 Shaw Blvd. Corsages wilting in their plastic boxes. A dad holding three phones. Somebody’s mom fixing a bow tie in the parking lot. And then the question nobody planned for: do you have a photo permit?
You need one. The Garden’s formal and group photography policy says a permit is required for formal photography for private personal use, and it names prom, weddings, family sessions and quinceañera photos as examples. Reservations should be made at least 24 hours in advance, they aren’t accepted during the Garden’s Signature Events, and the permit is for the selected date only and is nonrefundable. Read those two rules together and the smart timing falls out: a nonrefundable permit that only needs a day’s notice should be bought late, after the last fitting and a look at the Saturday radar. Questions about the permit go to the Garden at (314) 577-5100.
A few rules shape the afternoon, too. Photos are allowed only in the Garden’s outdoor, public areas, never inside the buildings or the Climatron. Lighting equipment and reflectors aren’t permitted. Props are limited to one per person, no larger than two feet by two feet. So the group that planned a balloon arch and a ring light gets turned around, while the group that read the policy walks straight to the fountain.
If the Garden is booked, or the budget is already spent on four tuxes, the Jewel Box is the St. Louis backup most families forget, all glass and tropical green. The city says it can be reserved by permit by calling 314-289-5330, so a group that wants the space to itself should call before Saturday, not during it.
Why does this belong in a tux guide? Because the rental and the photo run on the same clock. If the photos happen Saturday at four, the tux has to be picked up, tried on and fixed before Friday night. Lock the tux early, buy the permit late, and the whole day stops being a scramble.
### What really moves the price
Two shops can quote wildly different totals for what looks like the same black jacket. The gap almost always hides in five places: the label, the fabric, what’s bundled versus added on, the fees in the rental agreement, and whether you rent as a group.
Fabric matters most for weather. Wool breathes. Polyester holds heat against the skin, and on a St. Louis August afternoon, with the air thick enough to drink, a groomsman in a polyester jacket on an outdoor lawn will be wiping his neck before the vows. For an indoor evening event, the cheaper blend is fine.
Add-ons are where the surprise lives. Shoes come first, then cufflinks and studs, then the vest, and at a few shops even the shirt. A sign that looks cheap can end up costing more than the shop down the road once you add what you actually need. Say this out loud at the counter: “What’s in the package, and what costs extra?” Write down the answer.
Then the fine print. Rush fees kick in when you order inside the shop’s normal lead time. A damage waiver is a small charge that covers a spilled punch or a split seam, and skipping it can leave you on the hook for the garment itself. Late-return fees usually run by the day. Every shop sets these differently, so ask before you sign.
### Group discounts for wedding parties
Most formalwear shops discount or waive the groom’s rental once enough groomsmen commit to the same shop. Some extend the deal to fathers and ring bearers. The catch is that everyone rents from one shop in one window. If the party is scattered from St. Peters to Valley Park, ask whether out-of-town groomsmen can be measured elsewhere and still count toward the group.
### When should you book and get fitted?
For a wedding, the groom should settle the style and color and line up the shop a few months out, then get the groomsmen measured over the following weeks. That leaves room for an out-of-town measurement to arrive, for the shop to confirm every size is in stock, and for a swap if a color gets discontinued. The final fitting belongs in the last couple of weeks. The bride’s side runs on a far longer clock, which our wedding dress shopping timeline lays out, and if the date is still open, choosing from the best wedding venues in St. Louis comes before everything else.
Prom is the tight one. Schools across the metro hold their proms in the same few spring weeks, and the slim sizes and popular colors go first. The parent who books early gets a rack of choices. The one who walks in two weeks out gets whatever’s left, in whatever length. Ask the shop for its prom order deadline and treat it like a flight time.
Call two shops this week, before the slim sizes thin out. Start with the tuxedo rental shops across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, ask each one what’s in the package and what costs extra, and save the Garden permit for the Thursday before.
If you’re the formalwear shop, the tailor or the one-person alterations crew who saves a prom on Friday night, those worried parents are searching for you right now, so put your shop where those customers already look.
### Fittings, pickup and return
A shop’s tape measure beats a sewing tape at the kitchen table every time. Get measured when you order and again a week or two before the event, especially for a teenager who seems to grow overnight. Pick up a day or two early. Then do the thing everyone skips: put on the whole outfit in the store, shoes and all, and raise your arms. That’s where you find the missing cufflink or the vest in the wrong shade, while there’s still a rack behind the counter. Return it the day after, bagged, and the late fee never happens.
### Should you rent in a store or online?
Rent in a store if the event matters and you can get there. Rent online if no shop is close or you know your exact measurements cold. The tuxedo is the same either way. What changes is who fixes it when it doesn’t fit, and how fast.
When a groomsman shows up Friday with sleeves an inch short, a local shop pulls another jacket off the rack and he walks out in ten minutes. A mail-order replacement takes days. That same national renter ships its tux to arrive two weeks before the date and wants it back three days after, which is generous until the first box is wrong. If the second box is wrong too, you’re out of runway. Online works best for a gala guest with a stable size or a groomsman living far from St. Louis. It works worst for a sixteen-year-old who grew after the tape came off. The middle path: have a local shop or tailor measure you in person, then order online with enough margin to send the box back once.
### When buying beats renting
Buy if the tux will come out of the closet more than a handful of times. Rent for a one-off. A rental costs a fraction of a purchase, so it takes several wearings before ownership pays. For a musician, a regular gala guest or anyone on the black-tie circuit, buying wins within a few years. For one prom or one wedding, rent and don’t look back.
Bodies change, and that tips it too. A teenager or an adult halfway through a fitness push will outgrow a purchase before it earns its keep. Owning also means dry cleaning, a garment bag in the closet that smells faintly of mothballs, and the odd re-hem. A rental hands all of that back to the shop the next morning.
Plenty of “formal” events are really suit events. A rented navy or charcoal suit often costs about the same as a basic tux and looks more natural at a daytime wedding. Some grooms buy a good suit they’ll wear to work again and rent only the tux for the reception. ### How to read a formalwear shop in five minutes
Walk in and say it plainly: the event, the date, how many people, the color and your budget tier. Then watch. A good shop answers the hard questions without flinching, because it hears them every week. What’s in the package? What happens if a piece doesn’t fit the day before? Is backup stock on-site? What’s the return window and the late fee? Is the damage waiver built in?
Notice who holds the tape and how. A fitter who measures twice, tugs the shoulder seam and asks how he’ll stand at the altar is a fitter who gets it right. One who eyeballs a size from across the counter is telling you something too. The mistakes renters make most are the same every season: guessing measurements at home, ordering late, skipping the try-on, forgetting shoes and studs, mixing shops inside one wedding party, and returning late. Every one is fixed by a real measurement, an early order and a calendar reminder.
