### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are the requirements to go to business school?
A.  Most programs want a bachelor’s degree, transcripts, a resume showing work experience, essays, and one or two recommendations from people who supervised you. Some want a standardized test, and many now waive it under certain conditions. Requirements differ by format, so confirm the current list with each program for the cycle you are applying to.
### Q. How many years is a business school?
A.  A full-time MBA typically runs about two academic years, and accelerated formats finish faster. Part-time, evening, and online programs stretch longer because you take fewer courses at a time, so the real length depends on the pace you keep. Executive formats usually run a fixed length. Ask each program what its realistic completion time looks like.
### Q. Is a part-time MBA worth it?
A.  It is worth it when you want the credential and the coursework without giving up your income, and your industry recognizes the degree. You keep earning, so the financial math is far gentler than a full-time program. The cost is years of evenings and weekends. It is worth less if you are trying to switch industries, since recruiting access tends to be thinner.
### Q. Are online MBAs taken seriously?
A.  Generally yes, when the program is properly accredited and the same school grants its on-campus degree. What employers question is not the format but the rigor and the accreditation behind it. Verify accreditation in the accrediting body’s own public directory, and ask whether the diploma distinguishes the online program from the residential one.
### Q. What are the downsides of an MBA?
A.  Cost, time, and the income you give up while studying. The degree does not guarantee a promotion, and its signal is strong in some industries and meaningless in others. Employer-funded seats can carry clawback clauses that hold you in a job. And if the gap you are closing is narrow, a full degree is an expensive way to close it.
### Q. At what age do most people get an MBA?
A.  Most students arrive in the middle stretch of a career, after several years of work but before senior leadership. It clusters there for a reason: you need enough experience for the coursework and the classroom discussion to mean anything, and enough working years left for the degree to pay back. Executive formats skew later, since they target people already leading.
### Q. Should I go to school if I want to start a business?
A.  Often not, at least not to an MBA first. Owners need customers, pricing, cash flow, and a credential or license if the trade requires one, and those come faster and cheaper elsewhere. School makes more sense if you will raise outside capital or sell to large companies. Name the gap first, then buy the smallest thing that closes it.
### Q. Is business school a lot of math?
A.  There is quantitative work, but it is applied rather than abstract: accounting, statistics, finance, and operations, mostly arithmetic, algebra, and spreadsheets. Calculus is not required by most programs. If your quantitative background is thin, taking a college-level statistics or accounting course beforehand both prepares you and strengthens the application.

## Medical Marijuana Cards in Missouri: What a Cannabis Clinic Actually Does
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/medical-marijuana-card-in-missouri-what-a-cannabis-clinic-does
On a Sunday morning in Barnhart, a 57-year-old named Ray spreads a year of dispensary receipts across his kitchen table. He has a chronic condition that brings persistent muscle spasms, and he buys at a licensed dispensary two or three times a month. He isn’t adding up the flower. He’s adding up the tax lines. A neighbor mentioned that the medical card Ray never bothered with, because recreational is legal now, might have been worth the paperwork the whole time. Ray isn’t even sure who he’d call. His regular doctor? A dispensary? Something called a cannabis clinic?
That confusion is the normal starting point. Missouri legalized adult-use marijuana, and plenty of people concluded the medical program had quietly become pointless. For an occasional buyer, close to true. For someone buying regularly, buying a lot at once, or wanting to grow at home, the arithmetic runs the other way.
Here is the short version. The state’s patient ID card costs $28.92 and lasts three years. Before you can apply, a Missouri-licensed physician or nurse practitioner has to certify that you have a qualifying condition, and that appointment is a separate private cost the state does not set or publish. Medical purchases are taxed at 4%. Adult-use purchases are taxed at 6% by the state, plus local sales tax and a possible local add-on. Whether the card pays for itself comes down to how much you buy.
What follows is what a cannabis clinic actually is, what the state charges versus what the clinic charges, how the application works, and how to decide if the card earns its keep for you. If what you want is how dispensaries operate and how Missouri and Illinois rules compare, that’s a different guide: what to know about cannabis dispensaries in St. Louis.
### How much does a medical marijuana card cost in Missouri?
Missouri charges $28.92 for a patient ID card, and that same $28.92 covers a renewal. The card is valid for three years. A patient cultivation authorization card costs $57.83 on top of it. Those figures come from the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services fee schedule for the fiscal year running July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027.
They also move. Article XIV of the Missouri Constitution ties these fees to the Consumer Price Index, and the department applied a 2.69% adjustment for the current fiscal year. Treat the number as this year’s number, not a permanent one, and check the published schedule before you budget.
### What the state charges
Patient ID card: $28.92, new or renewal. Caregiver ID card: $28.92. Patient cultivation authorization ID card: $57.83. Caregiver cultivation authorization ID card: $57.83. And for a non-patient adult who wants to grow under the adult-use side of the law, a consumer personal cultivation authorization ID card runs $115.68. A patient who wants to grow pays the patient card plus the cultivation card, not one or the other.
### What the clinic charges
The state fee is not the whole cost, and this is where people get surprised. The certification appointment with a physician or nurse practitioner is a separate, private charge set by the clinic. DHSS does not set it and does not publish it. Anyone quoting you a single all-in figure is quoting their own price stacked on the state’s. Ask what the appointment costs, ask whether that price includes the visit you’ll need at renewal, and ask whether it’s refundable if the clinician doesn’t certify you. Ask before you book, not after.
### What does a cannabis clinic actually do?
A cannabis clinic runs one appointment: a certification visit. A clinician evaluates whether you have a qualifying condition and, if so, signs a state certification form. That is the entire product. It is not a dispensary, nothing is sold there, and it is not a pharmacy, so nothing is dispensed there either.
Who can do it is defined narrowly. A qualifying patient may be certified by an MD, a DO, or a nurse practitioner licensed and in good standing with the state of Missouri. That clinician registers with DHSS and submits the form electronically through the state registry portal. You then select that submitted form inside your own application. If it hasn’t been filed, you cannot finish, which is why how fast the clinic files is a fair thing to ask on the phone.
One more distinction worth holding onto: this is a certification, not a prescription. Nobody in Missouri prescribes cannabis. The clinician is attesting that a qualifying condition exists, and the state, not the clinician, issues the card. Language matters here because the wrong word sets the wrong expectation about what the visit will feel like.
### Who qualifies for a medical card in Missouri?
The qualifying conditions are written into Article XIV of the Missouri Constitution. They include cancer, epilepsy, glaucoma, intractable migraines unresponsive to other treatment, HIV or AIDS, and a terminal illness. They also include a chronic medical condition that causes severe, persistent pain or persistent muscle spasms, with multiple sclerosis, seizures, Parkinson’s disease and Tourette’s syndrome named as examples rather than as the full list.
Two more categories matter. Debilitating psychiatric disorders, including post-traumatic stress disorder, qualify when diagnosed by a state-licensed psychiatrist. And a chronic condition normally treated with prescription medications that could lead to physical or psychological dependence qualifies when a physician determines cannabis could be effective and a safer alternative.
Then there is the catch-all, and it is broad on purpose. In the professional judgment of a physician, any other chronic, debilitating or other medical condition can qualify, with hepatitis C, ALS, inflammatory bowel disease, Crohn’s disease, Huntington’s disease, autism, neuropathies, sickle cell anemia, agitation of Alzheimer’s disease, cachexia and wasting syndrome all listed as examples. If your condition isn’t documented anywhere yet, that’s the piece to solve first. Our guide to free and low-cost health clinics in St. Louis is a reasonable starting point for getting a diagnosis on paper.
### How does the application actually work?
Applications go through the state’s online registry portal at mo-public.mycomplia.com. You need three things in hand: a color digital photo of yourself taken within the previous three months, a government-issued photo ID, and the electronic certification form signed by your clinician less than 30 days before you submit.
The photo trips people up most. It has to be a photo of you, not a photo of your driver’s license or passport. Scanning the ID and uploading that image is a common reason an application comes back. Proof of residency is no longer an application requirement, so skip the utility bill hunt.
After you submit, the department has 30 days to process a patient application. If you’re also applying to cultivate, the application asks for the location of the growing space, its security, and who has access to it. If you plan to share a cultivation space, you must list the name and Patient ID number of the one additional patient sharing it. One, not several.
### What goes wrong with an application?
Incomplete applications are the usual failure, and Missouri gives you exactly one chance to fix one. If an application is incomplete, it is returned once, and you have about ten days from notification to correct and resubmit. Miss that window and it’s denied. The practical advice is simple: act on the notification the day it arrives instead of counting days.
The second common problem is timing on the certification form. It has to be signed within the last 30 days. People get certified, then sit on the paperwork for six weeks while life happens, and discover they need the visit again. Book the appointment when you’re ready to apply, not months ahead of it.
Two things that surprise people in a good way. Previous convictions do not disqualify someone from getting a patient ID card. And if you are denied, the denial can be appealed to the Missouri Administrative Hearing Commission within 30 days, so a no is not automatically the end of it.
Not every price needs a clinic visit. Here is what a custom trophy costs.
### Is the card still worth it now that recreational is legal?
It depends almost entirely on volume, and you can settle it with your own receipts. Medical purchases are taxed at 4%. Adult-use purchases are taxed at 6% by the state, plus ordinary local sales tax, and a local government may add up to a further 3% on top of that. The gap is real, and it compounds with every purchase.
Work out your own break-even instead of trusting anyone’s average. Pull twelve months of receipts and total the pre-tax spend. Multiply that by the difference between the two tax rates where you actually shop, since the local add-on varies. Compare the result against $28.92 spread over three years plus the certification appointment. Heavy buyers clear that bar fast. Someone who shops twice a year won’t.
Tax isn’t the only difference, though. An approved patient may purchase up to six ounces of dried, unprocessed marijuana or its equivalent in a 30-day period, and more than that if the certification states compelling reasons and specifies the amount. Adult-use buyers are capped at three ounces in a single transaction and three ounces of possession at any time. Patients who don’t cultivate may possess up to a 60-day supply, which is 12 ounces or the equivalent. Patients with cultivation authorization may possess up to a 90-day supply, with anything over the 60-day amount kept in an enclosed, locked facility.
Then there’s growing. A patient cultivation authorization card is $57.83, and for someone in Cedar Hill or High Ridge with the space and the patience, that changes the math more than the tax rate does. A non-patient adult can also apply for a consumer personal cultivation authorization at $115.68, which is worth knowing before you assume the medical card is the only route to a legal plant.
### What the card does not do
Cannabis remains illegal under federal law. Federal law may still prohibit firearm possession or purchase by people who use marijuana regardless of state law. DHSS says it cannot say how that is enforced and directs people to an attorney, and that is exactly how carefully it should be stated. If you own firearms, this is a conversation with a lawyer, not with a clinic.
The card also doesn’t extend to products sold outside the licensed system. DHSS does not regulate delta-8, delta-10, THCA or similar products sold outside licensed dispensaries, and those have not been tested by a licensed testing facility. That matters if you’ve been buying from a counter in Dellwood or Bevo Mill that isn’t a dispensary. For what those stores do and don’t carry, see what a smoke shop actually sells.
A few more limits. Sales are only legal at a DHSS-licensed dispensary. Public consumption is generally not permitted, though local governments may designate areas. Driving under the influence is not permitted, card or no card. Curbside pickup is currently not an option, while drive-through and delivery are available where the department has approved them at that location. A rule amendment on curbside went out for public comment from September 1 to October 1, 2026, but a proposal is not law. One bit of good news for visitors: Missouri dispensaries may accept out-of-state-issued patient cards.
### How do you pick a certifying clinic?
Shortlist two or three certifying clinics and call each one. You’re not asking for an itemized quote. You’re asking four plain questions and listening to how readily they’re answered. What does the appointment cost? Does that price include the certification visit I’ll need at renewal in three years? What happens, financially, if you don’t certify me? How quickly after the appointment do you file the form in the state portal?
Then compare what you said you needed against what each clinic is prepared to deliver. The gap is the signal. A clinic that answers all four without hesitation has answered them a thousand times. One that gets vague about the refund question, or can’t say how fast the form goes in, is telling you something about how the rest of the process will go.
Distance counts too. Someone in Crystal City may find the nearest certifying clinic is a drive into the city, toward Southampton or the Central West End. Ask whether the visit is in person, and plan the trip once rather than twice.
### What happens when the card expires?
Patient and caregiver ID cards, and patient, caregiver and consumer cultivation authorization cards, are all valid for three years. Renewal applications may be submitted up to 60 days before expiration and must be submitted at least 30 days before the expiration date. That is a real window, and the back end of it is the one that bites.
You can still renew an expired card, but the card stays inactive until the renewal is fully processed and approved. Inactive means you are buying at adult-use rates and limits in the meantime. Set a reminder for the 60-day mark, because renewal also requires a new certification form signed within the last 30 days by a Missouri-licensed physician or nurse practitioner in good standing. That means a new appointment, which is why the question of whether your clinic’s price includes the renewal visit is worth asking on day one.
Back to Ray in Barnhart. He doesn’t need anyone’s opinion about whether the medical program still matters. He needs his twelve-month total, the tax rates where he shops, and two phone calls. That’s an afternoon’s work, and it answers the question for him specifically.
This is general information, not medical or legal advice. Fees, forms and rules change, and the fee schedule is adjusted every year, so confirm anything here with the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services before you act on it.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are the rules for medical marijuana in Missouri?
A.  You need a state-issued patient ID card, obtained after a Missouri-licensed physician or nurse practitioner certifies a qualifying condition. Cards last three years. Approved patients may buy up to six ounces of dried, unprocessed marijuana or the equivalent in a 30-day period, taxed at 4%. Sales are legal only at a DHSS-licensed dispensary. Public consumption is generally not permitted, and driving under the influence is not permitted.
### Q. Can I get a medical marijuana card online in Missouri?
A.  The application itself is online, through the state registry portal at mo-public.mycomplia.com. What you cannot skip is the certification: a Missouri-licensed physician, osteopathic physician or nurse practitioner in good standing has to evaluate you and file the certification form electronically. Whether that appointment can happen remotely depends on the individual clinic, so ask when you call. Upload a recent photo of yourself, not a scan of your ID.
### Q. What is the daily limit of marijuana in Missouri?
A.  Missouri doesn’t set a daily limit. It sets a 30-day purchase allotment and separate possession limits. An approved patient may purchase up to six ounces of dried, unprocessed marijuana or its equivalent in a 30-day period, or more if the certification states compelling reasons and specifies the amount. Adult-use buyers are limited to three ounces per transaction and three ounces of possession at any time.
### Q. How much does it cost to renew your medical marijuana card in Missouri?
A.  The state renewal fee for a patient ID card is $28.92, the same as a new application, under the DHSS fee schedule for the fiscal year running July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027. These fees adjust annually for inflation under the state constitution. Renewal also requires a new certification form signed within the last 30 days, and that appointment is a separate charge set by the clinic.
### Q. What does a medical card get you?
A.  A 4% tax rate instead of 6% plus local add-ons, a 30-day purchase allotment of six ounces or the equivalent rather than a three-ounce transaction cap, and possession of up to a 60-day supply. It also opens the door to a patient cultivation authorization card at $57.83, which raises possession to a 90-day supply, with the amount over 60 days kept in an enclosed, locked facility.
### Q. Do all doctors prescribe medical marijuana?
A.  No, and strictly speaking no doctor prescribes it. Missouri clinicians certify a qualifying condition; they do not write a prescription. No physician or nurse practitioner is required to participate, and many do not, which is why dedicated certifying clinics exist. The clinician must be licensed and in good standing in Missouri and must register with the department to submit certification forms through the state portal.
### Q. What are the requirements to buy marijuana in Missouri?
A.  For adult-use purchases, you must be 21 or older with a valid government-issued photo ID, and you’re capped at three ounces per transaction. For medical purchases at the 4% rate, you need an active patient ID card. Missouri dispensaries may accept out-of-state-issued patient cards. Either way, the purchase is legal only at a dispensary licensed by the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services.
### Q. Is recreational or medical marijuana better?
A.  Neither is universally better; it turns on how much you buy. Adult-use is simpler with no fees and no appointment. Medical costs $28.92 every three years plus a private certification fee, and returns a lower 4% tax rate, a six-ounce 30-day allotment, higher possession limits, and access to home cultivation. Run your own twelve months of receipts against those numbers and the answer becomes obvious.

## Car Security Systems in St. Louis: Alarms, Trackers, and Immobilizers
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/car-security-systems-in-st-louis-alarms-trackers-and-immobilizers
Marcus parks his truck in the driveway of a brick bungalow in Hanley Hills, nose out, same spot every night. On a Tuesday morning in September he came out at 6:40 and found the passenger door hanging open, the glove box emptied onto the seat, and his sunglasses gone. No broken glass. No pry marks. The alarm never made a sound, because the alarm never had a reason to. He had left the doors open, the way he had a thousand times before.
That is the shape of a lot of car crime around here, and it is the reason the siren is usually the least useful thing you can buy. Everybody on the block has heard a car alarm go off. Nobody has ever gone outside to look. A noise that people have been trained to ignore is not a deterrent. It is a habit nobody has, aimed at a problem it was never designed to solve.
Car security works as layers instead. Each layer stops one kind of theft and does nothing about the others. Once you know which layer answers which attack, you stop buying hardware on faith.
What follows: the attacks a car owner actually faces, what beats each one, what a factory immobilizer does and does not do, how trackers differ from one another, what a good aftermarket alarm install adds beyond noise, where Missouri law sits on leaving a car running, and how to interview an installer before you hand over your keys and your money.
### What deters thieves from stealing your car?
Layers deter thieves, and each layer is aimed at a different person. The one walking down a street in Bevo Mill pulling door handles is stopped by a locked car with a bare seat. The one working a keyless car is stopped by distance between your fob and your driveway. The one who wants to drive your car away is stopped by a starter kill. The one with a flatbed is stopped by none of it, which is what a tracker is for.
Notice what is missing from that list: noise. A siren is a reaction, not an obstacle. It tells you something already happened. Everything that actually works either removes the opportunity, adds time and effort, or makes the car harder to keep once it is gone.
Time is the currency. Nobody working a residential street in Dutchtown or Southampton wants to spend four minutes on one vehicle when the next one takes forty seconds. Your goal is not an untakeable car. There is no such thing. Your goal is to be the slower option on your own block.
### Why do so many car break-ins involve no breaking?
Because a door that was never secured does not need to be forced. Plenty of what gets reported as a break-in is an open door, an open window, or a car left running for two minutes while somebody ran back inside. That category of loss is beaten by habit, not by hardware, and no product you buy fixes it.
The habit is short. Lock it every time, including in your own driveway and including the garage. Take the bag, the laptop, the tools, and the loose change off the seat, because visible value is the entire reason your car got picked instead of the one behind it. Leave the glove box empty and the center console closed. Park where there is light.
One more thing belongs in that habit: never leave a garage door opener clipped to the visor with your registration in the glove box. That pairing turns a car break-in into a house problem, which is where vehicle security and what a home security system actually includes start overlapping more than people expect.
### What is a relay attack, and what stops it?
A relay attack exploits the one thing a keyless car is designed to do: recognize a fob that is nearby. Your fob is broadcasting a short-range radio signal more or less constantly. A relay setup captures that signal wherever the fob is sitting, inside your hallway, and carries it out to the car, which then behaves as though you are standing beside it. Nothing is forced and nothing is broken.
Distance is the first defense. A fob on a hook by the front door is close to the driveway. A fob in a back bedroom, or in a metal box, is not. The physics of a signal-blocking pouch is simple: the fob transmits radio energy, and a conductive enclosure wrapped fully around it attenuates that energy. A sealed metal tin does the same job. The catch is that the enclosure has to close completely, every time, on every fob in the house, including the spare in the junk drawer.
Check whether your fob has a motion-sleep mode. Many newer ones stop transmitting after a few minutes of sitting still, which solves the overnight problem without any pouch at all. The owner’s manual will say, usually under the keyless-entry section, and it costs nothing to look.
### Diagnostic port attacks and what a port lock does
The other common attack skips the fob entirely and goes after the car’s diagnostic port, the same connector a shop uses, to convince the vehicle to accept a new key. Two things push back. A physical port lock puts a barrier and extra minutes between somebody and that connector. An aftermarket immobilizer sits between the car and the starter circuit, so even a freshly programmed key gets a car that cranks and does not run.
### What does a factory immobilizer actually do?
A factory immobilizer keeps the engine from running unless the car reads the correct transponder code from your key. No valid code, no fuel and no spark. That is why hot-wiring in the old sense stopped working on mainstream vehicles years ago, and it is genuinely one of the most effective things ever built into a car.
Here is the honest limit. An immobilizer raises the effort required; it does not make a car untakeable. Attacks that produce a key the car will accept defeat it by definition, because at that point the car is not being tricked, it is being told the truth by a key it recognizes. An immobilizer also does nothing about a smashed window and a stolen bag, and nothing about the catalytic converter under the car.
And a car on a flatbed does not care about an immobilizer at all. The engine never needs to start. That single fact is the argument for a wheel clamp, for a tracker, and for parking in a way that makes a tow awkward.
Same instinct, different asset: what a financial planner costs in St. Louis.
### Do steering wheel locks and cameras still work?
They work for exactly one reason: they are visible, and visible means your car gets skipped before anyone touches it. A steering wheel bar, a wheel clamp, a lit driveway, a camera with an obvious lens. None of these are unbeatable and none of them claim to be. They move the decision from your car to the next one, which is the only outcome that matters to you.
Light is the cheapest layer on the list. A motion fixture aimed at the driveway of a house in Glendale or on a side street in Fox Park does more per dollar than most electronics, because it removes the cover the whole thing depends on. A camera is a recovery tool more than a deterrent, but footage is what turns a police report from a paragraph into something with a description attached.
### Do GPS trackers stop a theft or just help you get the car back?
Recovery, not prevention. A tracker does not stop anyone from taking the car. It gives you a location to hand to police afterward, and that is a real thing worth paying for, as long as you buy it understanding what it is. A tracker plus a fast, accurate police report is the combination that gets vehicles home.
Three types, and the differences matter. A hardwired unit is spliced into the vehicle’s wiring by an installer and hidden somewhere that takes effort to find. A port unit plugs into the diagnostic connector, installs in seconds, and sits in plain sight of anyone who knows to look. A battery-powered unit is self-contained, magnetic or tucked into a cavity, and needs recharging on a schedule you will forget.
The question to ask about any of them is what happens with the ignition off. A hardwired tracker draws from the vehicle’s power and a battery unit carries its own, so both can keep reporting while the car sits. Some port-connected units go to sleep when the vehicle does and wake on movement or on a schedule, which means there can be a gap in the trail at exactly the wrong moment. Ask before you buy, and ask about reporting interval too.
Nearly all of them ride on a cellular connection, which means a subscription. A tracker with no active plan is a plastic brick. And know in advance that the tracker’s value is the report you attach it to: police act on a location tied to a filed case, not on a screenshot you text a friend.
### What does a good aftermarket alarm install actually add?
A bare siren adds nothing. A good install adds sensors that detect the right events and a way to stop the car from moving. That usually means a shock sensor tuned so it does not fire at every passing bus, a tilt sensor that reacts to the car being jacked up or loaded onto a truck, a starter kill or relay interrupt, and a second siren mounted somewhere that takes time to reach.
The install matters more than the box. Two identical systems in two identical cars perform completely differently depending on where the control module was hidden, how the wiring was run and loomed, whether the connections were soldered, and whether the sensitivity was actually tuned in the vehicle rather than left at the factory setting. A well-hidden module that takes twenty minutes to reach is a security feature. A module zip-tied under the dash in plain view is decoration.
Push-to-start vehicles are a different job from a turn-key car, and modern electrical architecture means a sloppy installer can create problems that outlast the alarm: parasitic battery drain, dash warnings, or a warranty conversation you do not want to have. Ask specifically how the system interfaces with your car’s network, and ask what they do differently on your model.
### Is it illegal to leave your car running in Missouri?
Not under state statute. Missouri once had a law requiring a driver to stop the engine and remove the key from an unattended vehicle, RSMo 304.150, and the Revisor of Statutes records it as repealed by L. 1996 H.B. 1047 section C. So there is no current state offense for warming up your car in your own driveway.
Two caveats, and the second one is the real one. Municipalities write their own ordinances, and a city in the metro may still have something on the books, so check your own before you assume. More to the point: no statute has ever stopped a running car from being driven away. A vehicle idling with the keys in it in Berkeley, Dupo, or Pontoon Beach is the single easiest target on the street, and an insurer may take a dim view of a claim where the keys were in the ignition. The law is not your protection here. Your habits are.
### Does insurance cover a stolen car or a smashed window?
Theft and break-in damage fall under comprehensive coverage, not collision. Collision is for crashes. Comprehensive is the part of the policy that handles theft of the vehicle, a broken window, a stolen catalytic converter, vandalism, hail, and similar. If you carry liability only, none of that is covered, which surprises people at the worst possible moment.
Your deductible then decides whether filing is even worth it. A broken window and a stolen bag can total less than what you would pay out of pocket before coverage starts, in which case you file a police report for the record and pay for the glass yourself. Read your declarations page now, while nothing has happened, and find out which coverages you actually carry.
### How do you interview a car security installer?
Shortlist two or three shops worth talking to, then walk in with your own list rather than asking what they recommend. Say plainly what you want: a starter kill or immobilizer that stops the car from being driven, a tracker that keeps reporting with the ignition off, sensors tuned for your vehicle, and a clean install that does not void anything on a car still under warranty.
Then listen to how they answer. Have they done your exact year, make, and model, and what did they do differently on it? Where does the control module go, and why there? How do they prevent battery drain? If a tracker is involved, what is the reporting interval and what happens when the car is off? What do they warrant, and who fixes it if a dash light appears next month?
Compare what you said you wanted against what each shop is prepared to deliver. The gap is the signal. A shop that reaches straight for a louder siren and cannot explain how the module gets hidden is telling you what kind of work you would be buying. A shop that asks about where you park, how many fobs are in the house, and whether the car ever sits for weeks is thinking about your actual risk.
One last piece of timing. If you are about to buy a used vehicle, sort the security question during the inspection rather than after, and give the wiring a look while you are already under the hood. Our guide to how to check a used car before buying covers what else belongs on that walkaround. And if the worst happens and the car turns up impounded rather than gone, what to do when your car is towed in St. Louis is the next phone call.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Can I install a car alarm myself?
A.  You can, on an older turn-key vehicle, if you are comfortable with wiring diagrams and patient about hiding the module. On a modern push-to-start car it is a poor idea. The system has to interface with the vehicle’s network, and mistakes show up later as battery drain, dash warnings, or a warranty argument. The value of a professional install is the hiding, the tuning, and somebody to call when something acts up.
### Q. How much does it cost to put a car alarm on your car?
A.  It depends on your vehicle and on what the system actually does. A basic siren and shock sensor on a simple car is a short job. A push-to-start vehicle, a starter kill, tilt sensors, a second siren, or a hardwired tracker all add labor and parts. Ask a shop to quote your exact year, make, and model, and ask which parts of the price are labor and which are hardware.
### Q. Can thieves bypass car alarms?
A.  Yes, and more often they simply ignore them. A siren only matters if somebody responds, and on most streets nobody does. That is why the useful parts of an alarm system are the ones that are not noise: a starter kill that stops the car from being driven, a tilt sensor that reacts to a tow, and a hidden module that takes real time to find and disable.
### Q. Can someone break into your car without the alarm going off?
A.  Easily, if the car was never secured in the first place, since an open door is not an alarm event. Even on an armed car, a system with only a door trigger may not react to a window, and a shock sensor turned down to stop false alarms may not react to much at all. Sensor coverage and tuning decide this, not the brand on the box.
### Q. Can a car be stolen without the key fob?
A.  Yes. Relay attacks use your own fob’s signal from inside the house, so the fob never leaves your hallway. Attacks through the diagnostic port aim to produce a key the car will accept. And a flatbed removes the question entirely, because the engine never has to start. Distance from the fob, a port lock, an aftermarket immobilizer, and a wheel clamp each answer a different one of those.
### Q. Does wrapping a key fob in foil prevent theft?
A.  It can reduce the signal, because a conductive layer wrapped fully around the fob attenuates the radio energy it transmits. The problem is coverage: a loose or partial wrap leaves gaps, and foil tears. A proper signal-blocking pouch or a sealed metal tin is more reliable, and it only works if you use it every night on every fob, including the spare in a drawer.
### Q. Do car trackers work when the car is off?
A.  It depends on the type. A hardwired unit draws from the vehicle’s power and a battery-powered unit carries its own, so both can keep reporting while the car sits. Some units plugged into the diagnostic port sleep when the vehicle sleeps and wake on movement or on a schedule, which can leave a gap. Ask about off-ignition reporting and the reporting interval before you buy.
### Q. Do you have to pay monthly for a GPS tracker?
A.  Almost always, because the tracker reports over a cellular connection and that connection needs a plan. Some are billed monthly, some annually, and some bundle the first stretch into the purchase price. Without an active plan the device stops reporting, so confirm the billing terms, the cancellation terms, and who answers the phone if you need a location at two in the morning.

## 180 Days, Not Dollars: What a Civil Rights Attorney Costs in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-civil-rights-attorney-costs-in-st-louis
180 days. Not dollars - days. For a discrimination claim in Missouri, that is the number that quietly ends more cases than any price tag, and almost nobody hears it in time.
This is for the person reading with sore wrists, or with a cardboard box from the office still on the passenger seat, the desk plant tipped over on the floor mat. Before anything about fees: if what happened was discrimination at work or in housing, a complaint under the Missouri Human Rights Act has to reach the Missouri Commission on Human Rights within 180 days. Federal law gives you 300 days for a job discrimination charge with the EEOC and one year for a housing complaint with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. Police force and wrongful arrest cases run on different clocks, so ask a lawyer which one is yours. Money can be worked out. A missed deadline usually can’t.
Your one step today is small. Write the date it happened on the back of an envelope while it is still sharp, then call Legal Services of Eastern Missouri at 314-534-4200 or book a free consultation with a civil rights lawyer. This page is general information, not legal advice; the person on that call can tell you what applies to you.
The kitchen-table math goes the same way for nearly everyone. You sit there that night with the TV on mute and the light from the fridge, and you add up a number you don’t have. Then you let it go. The math leaves out one thing: the law was built so the person with the least money in the room could still bring the fight. And the scariest number at that table, the other side’s lawyer bill if you lose, is mostly a ghost here: under Missouri’s own civil rights law, an employer or landlord that wins can collect its attorney fees only by showing your case was without foundation. More on that below.
St. Louis has its own wrinkles, and they change where you go first. If the harm came from a city police officer, know that the state of Missouri took over the St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department, and complaints of police misconduct now go through SLMPD’s Internal Affairs division, not the city’s Civilian Oversight Board. The board still takes complaints against employees of the City Justice Center, the downtown jail, at (314) 657-1600. A complaint is not a lawsuit, though, and filing one does not stop any court clock. If your case goes federal, the city’s court is the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri, at the Thomas F. Eagleton U.S. Courthouse, 111 South 10th Street, where you empty your pockets into a gray plastic tray at security before you ever see a courtroom.
### What happens if you can’t afford an attorney in a civil case?
In a civil rights case, often nothing stops you. Many of these cases run on contingency, so the lawyer is paid only out of a recovery, and Section 1988 lets a court make the losing defendant pay the winner’s reasonable attorney fees. Many clients pay nothing upfront. If a private lawyer won’t take the case, free legal aid is the next door to knock on.
Unlike a criminal case, a civil case does not come with a lawyer the court appoints for you. That surprises people, and it is the reason the fee rules matter so much. The money to pay a civil rights lawyer has to come from somewhere, and the law points it at the defendant when you win.
When a private firm passes, Legal Services of Eastern Missouri is the free civil legal aid office for this region. Its St. Louis office is at 701 Market Street, Suite 1100, downtown, and the number is 314-534-4200. It serves people under income limits, and while it does not take every kind of case, calling costs you only the time on hold. A free first consultation with a private civil rights attorney costs the same: an hour of telling your story out loud, maybe for the first time, to someone whose job is to tell you whether it is a case.
### The three ways a civil rights lawyer gets paid
Sooner or later a lawyer slides a fee agreement across the table, and your hand hovers over it with the pen. Before you sign, know what kind it is. There are really only three: a contingency fee, an hourly rate, or a flat fee for one defined task. For the serious cases - excessive force, a firing after you complained, a landlord who refused you - contingency is the one you will hear most, because it lets a person with an empty checking account hire a capable lawyer anyway.
### Contingency: they bet their own time on you
On contingency, the lawyer takes a percentage of what you recover, and only if you recover. No envelope with a law firm’s return address sitting on the counter every month. No retainer check. Every firm sets its own percentage, and many charge more if the case goes to trial or appeal, so get the exact number in the written agreement before you sign anything.
Read the offer as information, too. A firm willing to take your case on contingency looked at your facts and decided they are worth its own unpaid hours. A firm that wants a large check just to start on a case that plainly fits contingency may be telling you what it really thinks of your odds.
### Section 1988: why a small-dollar case can still get a lawyer
This is the part almost nobody knows walking in. Say the arrest was wrong but you had no hospital bill and missed only one shift of work. On a percentage alone, that case might not pay a lawyer’s rent. Section 1988 changes that, because the fee can come from the defendant on top of whatever you recover. A case about the principle - the sore wrists, the neighbors watching from their porches - can still be worth a good lawyer’s time. The statute was written to pay for exactly that.
### Missouri’s own version, and the line that protects you if you lose
Missouri law has a twin to Section 1988, and most fee explainers skip it. Under Section 213.111 of the Missouri Revised Statutes, a court hearing a Missouri Human Rights Act case may award court costs and reasonable attorney fees to the prevailing party. Then comes the sentence that should loosen the knot in your stomach: a prevailing employer or landlord may be awarded its attorney fees only upon a showing that the case was without foundation. In plain words, losing an honest discrimination case in Missouri does not hand you the other side’s legal bill. The fear of that bill is what keeps a lot of people at the kitchen table. The statute takes most of it off the table.
### Hourly and flat fees, and when they show up
Some civil rights work doesn’t fit a percentage. If what you need is a court order making someone stop, rather than a check, there may be little money for a percentage to attach to. That work, and some defensive matters, can run hourly. Ask in the first meeting which structure applies to your case and why.
Ready for a different kind of fresh start? See what Missouri requires to bartend.
### What you might pay out of pocket, and what happens if you lose
Two kinds of money move through a case, and people blur them. The fee is the lawyer’s pay for the work. Costs are the hard expenses: court filing fees, deposition transcripts, expert witnesses, records requests, getting papers served. Many contingency firms advance those costs and take them back out of any recovery, which is why a lot of clients never write a check while the case is live.
Now the fear that keeps people up at 2 a.m., staring at the ceiling fan: what if I lose? On a typical contingency agreement, there is no fee to pay because there was no recovery to take a percentage of. The advanced costs are different, and the contract decides them. Some firms absorb them. Some agreements put them on the client. Ask which, and get the answer in writing, not in a friendly handshake at the door.
### Picking the lawyer: two or three calls, not twenty
Choose the way you would choose a surgeon: by fit for this exact problem, not by the loudest billboard on I-64. Make a shortlist of two or three attorneys who actually practice civil rights law, not a general office that takes one now and then. The same rule holds any time you hire a legal specialist, which is the whole point of our guide to when you need a tax attorney and not a CPA. Match the lawyer to the problem.
Maybe you ride MetroLink downtown for the consult, a folder flat on your knees, rehearsing the first sentence under your breath. Make that folder simple. Bring a single page: the date, what happened, who saw it, the names on any badge or letterhead, and what you want out of this. Keep any photos, texts, discharge papers or letters in one folder on your phone. Then say it plainly and watch how each lawyer answers. One will walk you through steps, risks and a realistic range. Another will talk about a big number. Hire the first kind.
Ask four things. How many cases like mine have you handled? Who will do the day-to-day work on my file? How are costs advanced, and who owes them if we lose? And the hard one: what would you tell me if my case were weak? A lawyer with a calm, ready answer to that last question has given it before.
Walk away from anyone who guarantees a result, because nobody can promise what a judge or jury will do. And if you can’t get a straight answer about fees and costs in the first meeting, you won’t get one later, when it matters far more.
You don’t need money to make the first call - you need the date it happened. Write it down, then browse civil rights attorneys across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick two or three, and use the free consultation to ask your real questions before the 180-day clock runs down.
If you’re the civil rights attorney, the small firm or the solo practice that takes these cases, the people above are searching for you tonight. A listing for your practice is a quiet way to get more customers who already know exactly what they need.
### When it’s a civil rights case and not just a bad day
You usually know it in your gut before you know the word for it: the badge, the HR door that closes a little too softly, the landlord’s smile that drops when the dog steps in. The thread through every one of these cases is power. Two neighbors arguing over a fence is a private dispute. It turns into a civil rights matter when the other side is the government, an employer or a landlord, and it used that position to take away a right the law protects: excessive force or a wrongful arrest, discrimination or retaliation at work, a housing refusal, a denied disability accommodation.
Job discrimination has an extra step people miss. Before you can sue, you usually file a charge with an agency first. In St. Louis, the EEOC’s district office sits in the Robert A. Young Federal Building at 1222 Spruce Street, Room 8.100; the phone is (314)-798-1960. Miss the 180-day state window or the 300-day federal one and even a strong case can close for good. That alone is a reason to make the call this week, before you have finished agonizing over whether you can afford to.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How do I get an attorney if I have no money?
A.  For a strong civil rights claim, an empty bank account is rarely the barrier people fear. Contingency fees and Section 1988 fee-shifting mean the lawyer gets paid from the recovery or by the defendant. If no private lawyer will take it, call Legal Services of Eastern Missouri at 314-534-4200 to see if you qualify for free help.
### Q. Can I hire a lawyer and pay later?
A.  Often, yes. Civil rights lawyers frequently work on contingency, so there is no fee upfront and the lawyer is paid a percentage only if you recover money. Many firms advance case costs and repay them from a settlement. Confirm the exact terms in the written fee agreement first.
### Q. Why would someone need a civil rights lawyer?
A.  Because the other side usually has one. When police, an employer or a landlord violates a protected right - excessive force, a wrongful arrest, discrimination, retaliation, a denied accommodation - the case turns on federal and state law and strict filing deadlines. Taking that on alone rarely works.
### Q. What is the most common civil rights violation?
A.  I could not find one official ranking that settles it. The cases lawyers see most fall into a few groups: discrimination and retaliation at work, police misconduct such as excessive force or wrongful arrest, and housing discrimination. Which one applies to you matters more than which is most common, because each has its own deadline.
### Q. Where is the best place to get free legal help?
A.  In St. Louis, start with Legal Services of Eastern Missouri at 701 Market Street, Suite 1100, phone 314-534-4200. It handles civil matters for people under income limits. Many private civil rights attorneys also give a free first consultation, so ask when you call.
### Q. What are the odds of winning a civil lawsuit?
A.  There is no honest single number. Outcomes swing with the facts, the evidence and the court. A capable lawyer will tell you how strong your case looks before you commit, and if a firm offers contingency, that is its own read on your odds.
### Q. Who pays the attorney fees if I win a civil rights case?
A.  Under 42 U.S.C. Section 1988, a court may let the prevailing party recover a reasonable attorney’s fee as part of the costs. In practice, that can put your legal bill on the defendant, which is why a case with modest damages can still be worth a lawyer’s time.

## What College Counseling Costs in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-college-counseling-costs-in-st-louis
It is a Sunday night in Hamel, and the kitchen table has become a command center. There is a laptop open to a college portal, a printed checklist gone soft at the folds, and a wall calendar with three deadlines circled in red. Priya, a junior, is scrolling. Her mother is doing the thing parents do at this hour, which is trying to look calm while quietly counting the cost of everything on the table.
Somewhere in that pile is the question almost every St. Louis family reaches eventually. Should we pay someone to help with this? A private college counselor can cost a few hundred dollars or many thousands, and the price tag says surprisingly little about the result. That gap is the whole problem, and it is worth slowing down before you spend a dollar.
This guide names no counselors, quotes no company, and prints no exact price, on purpose. Every real number is attached to one specific provider and one specific family, which means you can look it up yourself once you know what to ask. We cover what the help is actually worth, how counselors charge, the free option most families forget, when to start, what admissions officers really respond to, and how to interview two or three people before you hand anyone a check.
### Is it worth paying for a college counselor in St. Louis?
It is worth it when you can name what you need, a counselor reliably supplies it, and your high school cannot. For a family drowning in deadlines or aiming at selective schools, paid help often earns its keep. For a strong student with a good school counselor, it often does not.
The trouble starts when the reason goes vague. “We want her to have an edge” is vague. “She is applying to eight schools, four of them reaches, and nobody at home has done this before” is not vague, and it points straight at what help would do. Name the job first. The price only means something once the job is clear.
Paid counseling tends to earn its money in a handful of situations. The student is aiming at highly selective schools where essays and positioning carry real weight. The family is applying to a long list and cannot track the moving parts. A parent and a teenager keep colliding, and a neutral outsider lowers the temperature. Or the student simply will not start for a parent but will for a stranger with a calendar.
It tends not to be worth it when the plan is a couple of in-state schools with clear, published admission standards, or when the high school counselor is engaged and has the time. Paying for reassurance is a real thing people do, and there is no shame in it. Just call it what it is, so you can decide whether the calm is worth the cost.
If that reasoning sounds familiar, it should. It is the same worth-it math behind any big education purchase, the one we walk through for whether business school in St. Louis is worth it: name the specific thing you want, confirm the purchase reliably supplies it, then check whether anything cheaper supplies it too.
### How do college counselors charge, and what does it cost?
College counselors in the St. Louis area typically charge one of three ways, and the total swings from a few hundred dollars to many thousands depending on the model and the length of the relationship. There is no single going rate. The right question is not “what does it cost” but “which model fits the help we actually need.”
### By the hour
Hourly help is the lightest touch and the easiest to control. You pay for the time you use, so a family that just needs an essay read, a school list sanity-checked, or one strategy session can spend relatively little. Rates vary widely by experience and demand. Ask what a typical session covers and how many the counselor thinks your situation really needs, then you can multiply it out yourself.
### Blocks or packages of hours
Many counselors sell hours in bundles, sometimes at a gentler per-hour rate than one-off sessions. A package might cover a defined slice of the work: essay coaching, a school list, application review across a season. This suits a family that wants steady help through senior year without signing up for everything. Ask exactly what is inside the block, and what happens if you run out of hours or do not use them all.
### Comprehensive, multi-year packages
Comprehensive packages sit at the top of the market and carry the biggest checks. They often start in freshman or sophomore year and run through submission, covering course planning, activities, testing strategy, the school list, and every essay. Because they bundle years of work, the total can reach well into the thousands. For a family aiming high and starting early, the structure can be worth it. For a junior with a short list, it is usually far more than the job requires.
Two things move the price in every model: the counselor’s track record and how much of the work you hand over. A veteran with a long history of selective admissions charges more than someone newer. And a family that wants the counselor to run the whole process pays more than one that just wants a second read. Neither choice is wrong. They are simply different jobs at different prices.
### What about the counselor your high school already provides?
Every public high school in the St. Louis metro already employs counselors, and their help costs your family nothing. Before you pay anyone, find out what your own school offers, because for a lot of students it is genuinely enough. School counselors write the recommendations, send the transcripts, and know the local admissions patterns cold.
The honest catch is caseload. A single school counselor may be responsible for hundreds of students, and college advising is only one part of a job that also covers schedules, crises, and testing. That does not make the help worse. It makes it thinner. A family in Caseyville or Gillespie with an organized, self-starting teenager may need nothing more than a few well-timed appointments and a parent who books them early.
So use the free help first and measure the gap. Sit down with the school counselor, ask what they can realistically do for your student this year, and see what is left over. Maybe the answer is nothing, and you have saved thousands. Maybe it is one specific thing, an essay, a reach-school strategy, a calendar nobody is keeping, and now you know exactly what to pay for instead of buying the whole package blind.
Prefer a price you can look up? See what building inspections in St. Louis cost.
### When should you hire a college counselor?
The most useful time to start is earlier than most families think, typically sophomore or early junior year, while course choices and activities can still be shaped. Hiring in the fall of senior year is common, but by then the calendar is doing the negotiating, and a counselor is mostly triage rather than strategy.
What you are buying changes with the timing. Start early and the help is about direction: which classes, which activities, which tests, which schools to even consider. Start late and it narrows to execution: essays, deadlines, and keeping the application from falling apart. Both are valuable. They are just not the same purchase, and early help usually costs more because it lasts longer.
There is also a signal worth watching at home. If application talk keeps ending in a slammed door, or if a capable student in Fayetteville simply freezes every time the laptop opens, an outside deadline-keeper can be worth it for the household peace alone. Sometimes the value is not admissions expertise at all. It is that a teenager will do for a stranger what they will not do for a parent.
### What actually impresses admissions officers?
Admissions officers respond to depth, rigor, and a real voice far more than to a long list of shallow activities. They read for a student who challenged themselves in the courses available, went deep on a few things they genuinely care about, and wrote an essay that sounds like a person instead of a committee. No counselor, paid or free, can manufacture that.
This is the part families most often get backward. There is a temptation to pile on clubs, titles, and one-week summer programs, hoping volume reads as ambition. It usually reads as thin. A student in Eagle Park who spent two years deep in one thing, a job, a sport, a cause, tends to land harder than one with a dozen memberships and nothing behind them.
Rigor matters too, measured against what the school offered. Admissions readers look at whether a student took the harder classes available to them, not whether their school happened to offer twenty of them. A good counselor helps a student make honest, strong choices here. A counselor cannot go back and rewrite three years of transcript, which is exactly why starting early is worth more than starting expensive.
### How do you interview a college counselor before you hire one?
Shortlist two or three counselors and interview them before you commit to any. Not tour them, interview them, the same way you would interview a doctor before agreeing to treatment. Before each call, write one short paragraph stating plainly what you want: your student’s year, the kinds of schools on the list, the specific help you think you need, and your budget. Read it out loud, then ask what they would actually do against it.
Ask the practical questions. How do you charge, and what is the full cost for a student like mine? What exactly is included, and what is not? How many families do you work with at a time? How do you communicate, and how fast? Who does the work, you or an associate? And what do you not do, so nobody is surprised in November?
Then set what you asked for beside what each person answered. A counselor built for your situation answers specifically and quickly. One who dodges the cost question, reframes your goals into an easier version, or promises results no honest advisor can promise has told you something useful. A family in Gratiot comparing three calls this way usually knows the right fit within a day, and walking away from a bad one is the entire point of the exercise.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How expensive is a college counselor?
A.  It ranges widely, from a few hundred dollars for a handful of hourly sessions to many thousands for a comprehensive package that runs for years. The total depends on the model you choose, the counselor’s experience, and how much of the process you hand over. Ask any counselor to price your specific situation rather than trusting a general figure.
### Q. How much should I pay for a college advisor?
A.  Pay for the specific job you need done, not for a package built for someone else. If you only need essay help or a school-list review, hourly work often costs the least. If you want years of guidance starting early, a comprehensive package costs more but does more. Decide the job first, then judge whether the price fits it.
### Q. When should I hire a college counselor?
A.  Earlier helps more, often sophomore or early junior year, while course choices and activities can still be shaped. Hiring in senior fall is common but limits the counselor to triage on essays and deadlines. If your student is organized and your school counselor is engaged, you may not need to hire one at all. Start with the free help.
### Q. Is a college advisor worth it?
A.  Sometimes clearly yes, sometimes clearly no. It is worth it when you can name a specific need, an advisor reliably meets it, and your high school cannot. It is worth less for a strong student with a short in-state list and an engaged school counselor. Name the need before you decide, because the price alone tells you little.
### Q. What impresses college admissions officers?
A.  Depth, rigor, and an authentic voice impress far more than a long list of shallow activities. Officers look for students who took the harder courses their school offered, went deep on a few genuine interests, and wrote essays that sound like real people. A strong record built over years beats a padded resume assembled in a hurry.
### Q. Is a 60% acceptance rate high?
A.  A 60% acceptance rate is fairly high and usually signals a less selective school, where most qualified applicants are admitted. It is not a reach school for a solid student. Reach schools tend to admit a much smaller share. Use the published rate as a rough gauge of how much positioning help an application there actually needs.
### Q. Can a college counselor guarantee my child gets in?
A.  No, and any counselor who promises a specific admission is a reason to walk away. Admissions decisions rest with the colleges, and they weigh factors no advisor controls. A good counselor improves how a student presents a genuine record and manages the process well. That is real value, but it is help, not a guarantee. Be wary of anyone who claims otherwise.
### Q. What is the difference between a school counselor and a private college counselor?
A.  A school counselor works for the high school, helps every student, and costs your family nothing, but carries a large caseload across many duties. A private college counselor works for you alone, gives focused time, and charges for it. Many families use the free school counselor first and hire private help only for the gaps that remain.

## “Nonrefundable” Isn’t Final: What a Criminal Defense Attorney Costs in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-criminal-defense-attorney-costs-in-st-louis
“Nonrefundable.” It’s printed in capital letters halfway down the fee agreement, and your thumb keeps landing on it while the coffee goes cold beside the arrest paperwork. Somebody you love is charged with a crime. A lawyer wants money before they’ll file a single page. And that one word makes your stomach drop, because if the case ends in a month, that money looks gone for good.
In Missouri, that word does not mean what it seems to mean. The Missouri Bar’s own ethics guidance says agreements that call a flat fee “nonrefundable,” or say the lawyer earns it the moment it is paid, violate the rules and are not enforceable. If the lawyer is let go before the work is done, the unearned part comes back. Most people sign that page without ever hearing this. Some of them are signing it tonight.
That is the leverage point of this whole page. Defense fees feel like a black box because the charge is scary, the clock is loud and nobody slows down to explain the money. But the money has rules. There are rules about where a lawyer must hold it, rules about when it becomes theirs, and, if you cannot pay at all, a public defender office inside the downtown courthouse. Knowing those rules does not make a lawyer cheaper. It makes you harder to rush.
If the charge is filed in the City of St. Louis and there is no money for a private lawyer at all, write this down before anything else: the Missouri State Public Defender’s St. Louis City office, District 22, Mel Carnahan Courthouse, 1114 Market St, Ste 602, St. Louis, MO 63101, phone (314) 340-7625. You do not need to know anything else to make that call. You only need the case paperwork in your hand when you do.
And if a private lawyer is the plan, and a parent or grandparent is the one writing the check, know that Missouri gives the person paying a way to push back later. The Missouri Bar runs a Fee Dispute Resolution program that offers facilitation, mediation, and binding arbitration, at no cost to either party. The client starts it, and someone who paid the fee may join the client in the process. Nobody wants to need it. Knowing it exists changes how the first conversation feels.
### What is the average retainer fee for a criminal defense attorney?
There is no honest single average, and a confident number online deserves a raised eyebrow. A retainer is a deposit the lawyer draws against as they work, not the price of the case. A misdemeanor that ends in a plea and a felony headed for a jury are both “criminal cases,” but averaging them gives you a figure that fits nobody’s situation.
Think about what the lawyer is actually pricing. A first appearance. Reading the police report. Calls with the prosecutor. Maybe motions, maybe a suppression hearing, maybe a trial with witnesses sitting in the hallway at the Carnahan Courthouse waiting their turn. A case that resolves early takes a sliver of those hours. A case that fights to the end takes all of them, and the quote has to guess which one yours will be.
So when you hear a retainer figure, ask one question before you react to the size of it: is this the whole fee, or is it the starting balance? On a flat-fee misdemeanor it may be the whole thing. On an hourly felony it is the opening deposit, and you may be asked to top it up as the hours pile on. That single answer tells you more than any average ever could.
### The two ways a defense lawyer prices your case
Most defense lawyers quote one of two ways, or a mix of both. A flat fee is one agreed price for a defined piece of work. It is common for misdemeanors, many first-time DWI cases and anything likely to end in a plea. You know the number going in, which matters when the rent is due on the first. Read the scope line slowly, though, because a flat fee often stops at the courtroom door and a trial is priced separately.
Hourly billing is for cases nobody can size up front: several charges, a co-defendant, forensic evidence, a case that may go to trial. The lawyer names an hourly rate, asks for a retainer to start and bills their time against it. When the balance runs low, you get a letter asking for more. It costs more because it usually is more work, and an honest lawyer will tell you that up front instead of letting the second invoice surprise you.
Missouri adds a rule most clients never hear about. Under the Missouri Bar’s reading of Comment 20 to Rule 4-1.15, which took effect on Jan. 1, 2019, flat fees exceeding $2,000 paid in advance must remain in the lawyer’s trust account until earned. Smaller flat fees can go straight into the office account, but even then, any unearned part must be refunded if the relationship ends early. Your money is not the lawyer’s money just because it cleared.
### Does “nonrefundable” really mean you never see it again?
Not in Missouri. The Missouri Bar spells it out plainly: lawyers sometimes try to escape the refund obligation by calling a flat fee nonrefundable, or by saying it is earned on receipt or when they file an “Entry of Appearance,” and such agreements violate the rules and are not enforceable. A client agreeing to it does not fix it. A Missouri lawyer has to be able to explain which part of a flat fee has been earned and which part has not.
That does not mean you get everything back if you change your mind after months of work. It means the lawyer keeps what the work was reasonably worth, and the rest is yours. If you end the relationship, do it in writing, keep a copy, and in the same letter ask for an itemized accounting of what was earned and a refund of the rest. If the answer doesn’t sit right, the client can file with the Missouri Bar’s Fee Dispute Resolution program instead of hiring a second lawyer to fight the first. The quiet click of sending that email is a lot easier than the knot of never asking.
If the case is filed across the river in Illinois, the Missouri rules on this page may not be the ones that apply, so ask the lawyer to explain how a refund would work there before you sign. The question is the same. Only the rulebook changes.
### If you can’t pay at all, start on the sixth floor of the Carnahan Courthouse
Suite 602 in the Carnahan Courthouse is the public defender’s District 22 office, and (314) 340-7625 is the line. Bring the charging papers, the next court date and a rough picture of your income and bills. The people up there are trial lawyers who handle criminal cases every working day, and asking for one is not asking for a favor. It is what the office is there for.
Under Missouri law, anyone claiming they cannot afford a lawyer files an affidavit with the court with the financial information the public defender system requires. Eligibility looks at your whole situation, not just one paycheck. If the court later finds you are not indigent, the public defender stops representing you, so be accurate on the form. Missouri law also sets a penalty for false statements on it.
Here is the part almost nobody mentions at the window. Under section 600.090, the reasonable value of public defender services can become a lien on property you have or later acquire, and the public defender shall file that lien whenever the value appears to exceed one hundred fifty dollars. Free at the door is not always free forever. That is not a reason to refuse help when you need it. It is a reason to know the deal before you take it.

If you’re the defense lawyer, the solo practice or the two-attorney firm that takes new criminal cases, the frightened people reading this are your next customers. Listing your practice puts your name in front of them the night they start calling.
### How should you interview a criminal defense attorney about cost?
Treat the first meeting as an interview, because it is one. Shortlist two or three lawyers, tell each the charge in plain words, and say what scares you most. Then listen to how they explain the money and the likely path of the case, not just the number at the bottom.
Ask which structure applies, flat or hourly, and why. Ask what the fee covers and what it leaves out, so a separate trial fee doesn’t land on you later. Ask where the money will sit until it is earned. Ask what happens to the unearned part if the case ends early. Ask who does the day-to-day work and how fast they return calls. A lawyer who answers all of that without sighing is showing you how they will treat you for the next six months.
Listen for the difference between a process and a promise. One lawyer walks you through how cases like yours usually unfold. Another leads with a result that sounds guaranteed. Nobody can promise an outcome in criminal court, and the honest ones say so early. The same instinct helps any time you hire a lawyer for trouble you didn’t ask for.
