### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How many years does it take to become a fashion designer?
A.  Anywhere from about one to four years of formal training, depending on the route, plus the time it takes to build a portfolio and land work. A bachelor’s degree takes four years, an associate degree about two, and a certificate a semester to a year. Self-taught and apprenticeship paths take as long as it takes to build the skills and the samples that prove them.
### Q. What jobs can I do if I love fashion?
A.  More than design. In the St. Louis area, people with fashion training work in costume and wardrobe shops, bridal and alterations, uniform and workwear companies, technical design, sample making, merchandising, buying, visual display, styling, and small-batch production. Others run their own label or custom-sewing business, and some do remote technical or product-development work for brands based in other cities.
### Q. What GPA do I need for fashion school?
A.  It depends on the program, and at most fashion programs the portfolio matters more than the GPA. Certificate programs and many community-college tracks have open or minimal GPA requirements. Four-year degree programs usually require general admission to the college first, which may set a minimum GPA, and then a separate portfolio review for the design major. Confirm current requirements directly with each school.
### Q. Can I study fashion designing for free?
A.  You can learn a lot of the fundamentals for free. Free online courses cover sewing basics, pattern drafting and introductory CAD. Public libraries carry pattern and textile books, and some offer maker spaces or tool lending. Formal programs cost money, but community colleges keep it lower, and most programs offer scholarships and financial aid. Ask each program what it offers before you assume you can’t afford it.
### Q. Can I be a fashion designer if I can’t draw?
A.  Yes. Drawing is a way to communicate a design, not the design itself. Technical flats are drawn digitally now and follow learnable rules, draping lets you create directly in fabric, and construction skill matters more to most employers than sketching ability. Many programs teach illustration from scratch and don’t expect polished drawing at admission. Put your energy into sewing and fit, and let digital tools cover the rest.
### Q. What qualifications do you need to be a fashion designer?
A.  No license or required degree exists. What you need is proof that you can build a garment to spec, communicate a design clearly, and use the tools a shop relies on. A bachelor’s degree, associate degree or certificate is one way to show that. A portfolio of finished, photographed garments and work samples is another, and for many local employers it’s the one that counts.
### Q. Is it hard to get a job in fashion?
A.  Designing for a national label is highly competitive and mostly means living in a few large cities. Working in apparel in the St. Louis metro is more open, particularly for people who can sew, fit and write a tech pack. Costume shops, uniform companies, bridal and alterations businesses, and remote technical-design roles all hire locally. The harder part is usually the first job, not the ones after it.
### Q. Is fashion design a hard major?
A.  It’s demanding in a different way than most majors. The hard part isn’t exams; it’s hours. Construction and pattern-making projects take far longer than students expect, and a single garment can mean a week of late nights in the sewing lab. You also get critiqued in public and have to keep going. Students who like working with their hands and can take feedback usually do fine.

## Is Food Delivery Worth It in St. Louis?
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/is-food-delivery-worth-it-in-st-louis
It’s a quarter past seven on a Tuesday, and a nurse in Venice has just come off a twelve-hour shift. Her feet hurt, the fridge holds half a lemon and some yogurt, and the app on her phone is promising hot food at the door in forty minutes. Her thumb hovers over the button. Then she sees the total, and it’s a good deal more than the price of the meal. Is this worth it? Or is she about to pay real money for the privilege of not driving three miles?
That same pause is happening all over the St. Louis area tonight. In Maryville, two parents with three kids and a school night are staring down homework, baths, and a seven-thirty bedtime. In Marthasville, a retiree who no longer drives after dark wants something warm that isn’t another can of soup. A college student in Marine has a paper due at midnight and a food budget that’s already thin. And a couple who just moved into a place in Sauget has a kitchen full of boxes and not one pan unpacked.
Every one of them is asking the same question, and the honest answer isn’t a flat yes or no. Food delivery around St. Louis can be a genuine bargain or a quiet money leak, depending on the night, the household, and what you’re really buying. This guide walks through what you actually pay for when you order in, when delivery earns its cost and when pickup or cooking wins, how tipping works, what to know about meal programs for seniors, and a simple test you can run in ten seconds before you tap order. We won’t quote you a fee or a percentage, because those change by app, by restaurant, and by the hour. We’ll show you how the pieces fit instead.
### Is it worth getting food delivered in St. Louis?
Often, yes, but not every time. Delivery around St. Louis earns its cost when it buys back an hour you truly don’t have, when you can’t get out, or when the weather or an illness makes driving a bad idea. On an ordinary night with time to spare, pickup or cooking almost always wins on price.
The reason it’s not a flat yes is that delivery sells you two different things at once. One is the food. The other is an hour of your evening, brought to your door, and that second item has a price tag most people never look at directly. The nurse in Venice after a twelve-hour shift is buying that hour at a moment when it’s worth a lot to her. The college student in Marine on an ordinary Wednesday is buying the same hour when it’s worth almost nothing, because he has the time and the car.
So the question isn’t really “is delivery worth it?” It’s “is delivery worth it tonight, for us?” That’s a question you can answer well once you understand what the total on your screen is actually made of. Let’s take it apart.
### What are you actually paying for when you order in?
When you order through a third-party delivery app, the number at the bottom of the screen is a stack of separate charges, not one price. The food is only the first layer. Above it sit several fees that each have a different job, and most of them never reach the person who carries your bag to the door.
### The fee stack, layer by layer
Start with the menu itself. Many restaurants list higher prices on the app than on the menu in their own dining room, because the platform takes a cut of every order and the restaurant has to recover some of it somewhere. So before a single fee appears, you may already be paying more for the same sandwich. Then comes the delivery fee, which is the charge for getting the food to you. Then a service fee, which is the platform’s own charge for running the app and processing the order. If your order is small, a small-order fee may land on top. Then sales tax on all of it. Then the tip. And at busy times, like a rainy Friday night or a game night in the city, the app may add a surge or peak-time charge because drivers are stretched thin.
### Why the total surprises people
Each of those pieces looks small on its own. Stacked together, they can turn a modest meal into something that costs closer to a sit-down dinner, and that’s the moment the parents in Maryville do a double take. The trick is that the app shows you the menu prices first and the fees last, after you’ve already decided what you want. By then, you’re hungry and committed. The best defense is simple: look at the final total before you decide, not the menu price, and ask whether that number is what the meal plus the hour is worth to you tonight.
### The restaurant’s own delivery is a different animal
Some St. Louis restaurants still run their own delivery, with their own driver and their own phone line. Ordering that way usually skips the app markup and the service fee, though there may still be a delivery charge and you’ll still tip the driver. It also means the restaurant keeps far more of your money, which matters if you’d like the place to still be there next year. Try the “interview the provider” approach: call the restaurant, ask whether they deliver themselves or through an app, and ask whether their in-house prices match the app’s. It’s a two-minute call, and you’ll often learn something useful.
### Is pickup cheaper than delivery?
Almost always, yes. Pickup drops the delivery fee, the surge charge, and usually the service fee, and if you order straight from the restaurant you dodge the app markup, too. What you pay instead is your own time and gas for the round trip, which on a short drive is a small price for a real saving.
Pickup has a second advantage people forget: the food is usually better. It goes from the kitchen to your car in minutes, instead of sitting in a bag on a passenger seat while the driver makes two other stops. Fries stay crisp. Soup stays hot. You also get to check the bag before you leave, which solves the wrong-order problem before it happens.
### When pickup isn’t really cheaper
Pickup stops being a bargain when the drive is long, when you’d have to wrestle three kids into car seats to make it, or when the restaurant is across a bridge at rush hour. If the round trip eats forty-five minutes and you value your evening, the delivery fee can look like a fair trade. For the retiree in Marthasville who doesn’t drive at night, pickup isn’t an option at all, and that changes the math completely. The question is never “which is cheaper in dollars” alone. It’s “which is cheaper once I count what my time and effort are worth tonight.”
### A middle path: pick up on the way home
One trick that works well for a lot of St. Louis households is ordering ahead for pickup from a place that’s already on your route. The nurse in Venice passes half a dozen restaurants on her drive home. If she orders when she clocks out and grabs it on the way, she gets the hot meal, keeps the fees, and adds maybe five minutes to her trip. That’s the cheapest hot dinner there is, short of cooking.
### When does delivery earn its cost?
Delivery is worth paying for when the alternative is worse than the fee. That sounds obvious, but it’s the whole test. If skipping delivery means driving on ice, dragging a sick kid to a restaurant, or a new parent going hungry at nine at night, the fee is buying something real, and it’s usually a fair price for it.
### The nights it clearly pays
There’s a short list of situations where we’ve found delivery is almost always the right call. Illness, whether it’s you or someone you’re caring for. A new baby in the house, when nobody has slept and nobody is leaving. Bad weather, especially the kind of ice storm that makes St. Louis roads a bad bet. Mobility limits, permanent or temporary, like a broken foot or a recent surgery. And the plain end of a rope: the twelve-hour shift, the day that ran over, the evening where the only alternative to delivery is cereal. On those nights, paying to skip the drive is money well spent, and you shouldn’t feel bad about it.
### The nights it quietly doesn’t
The trouble starts when delivery becomes the default instead of the exception. Ordering in on an ordinary Tuesday, with time to spare and a car in the driveway, means paying the whole fee stack for an hour you didn’t need back. Do that three or four times a week and the total is real money, the kind that shows up on a bank statement and makes you wince. The college student in Marine felt this the hard way when the semester’s food budget was gone by October. Delivery didn’t do that alone, but it helped.
### What about meal kits and prepared-meal boxes?
Meal-kit subscriptions and prepared-meal services sit somewhere between cooking and ordering in. A meal kit sends ingredients and a recipe, so you still cook, but you skip the planning and the grocery run. A prepared-meal service sends food you only reheat. Both tend to cost less per meal than restaurant delivery and more than groceries, and both work best for people who want less deciding, not less eating at home. The couple in Sauget with no pans unpacked won’t get much out of a meal kit this week, but a box of ready meals might be exactly right until the kitchen is set up. Watch for the subscription trap, though: the boxes keep coming whether you eat them or not, and skipping a week takes a deliberate click. If you’re trying to eat better, not just faster, our guide to how to eat healthy at a St. Louis restaurant covers the ordering side of that.
Feeding a college student on a budget? See scholarships for St. Louis students.
### What are the disadvantages of food delivery?
The biggest downsides are the ones you notice after you pay: food that arrives lukewarm, orders that arrive wrong, and the slow realization that the restaurant you love is losing a slice of every order to the app. None of these is a dealbreaker on its own, but together they explain why the experience so often feels worse than the price.
### Cold food and wrong orders
Delivery food spends time in a bag, in a car, often alongside someone else’s order. Anything fried loses its crunch. Anything with sauce on the side may arrive with sauce everywhere. And when something is missing or wrong, the fix runs through the app, not the kitchen, which can mean a partial refund and no dinner rather than a quick remake. Dishes that travel well, like curries, pasta, sandwiches, and anything braised, hold up far better than the crispy stuff. Order accordingly and you’ll be disappointed less.
### What it does to the restaurant
This is the part diners rarely see. When you order through a third-party app, the platform keeps a portion of the sale, and the restaurant absorbs it. For a small, independent kitchen already working on thin margins, that cut can be the difference between a good month and a bad one. That’s why so many places quietly nudge you toward ordering direct, and why the same meal can cost less on the restaurant’s own site or over the phone. If you care about the locally owned spots we round up in our locals’ guide to the best restaurants in St. Louis, ordering direct is the single easiest way to help them keep the lights on.
### The habit problem
The last disadvantage isn’t about any single order. It’s that delivery removes every bit of friction between wanting food and having it, and friction is what used to make you cook. The app remembers your last order, your card is saved, and the whole transaction takes fifteen seconds. That’s a gift on a hard night and expensive as a lifestyle. In our experience, the households that come out ahead are the ones that treat delivery as a tool they reach for on purpose, not a reflex.
### Do I tip if there is a delivery fee?
Yes. On most third-party apps, the delivery fee goes to the platform, not the driver, so it isn’t a tip and the driver doesn’t see it. Tipping the person who brings the food is customary in St. Louis just as it is everywhere else in the country, and skipping it because you already paid a fee is a common and costly misunderstanding.
### How much is reasonable
There’s no rule written anywhere, but a common rule of thumb people use is a percentage similar to what you’d tip for sit-down service, with a small-order floor so that a single sandwich doesn’t turn into a tip of pocket change. Bad weather, a long drive, a big order, or a walk-up to a third-floor apartment are all good reasons to go higher. The driver in the ice storm outside Marthasville is doing something you decided not to do yourself, and the tip is the honest price of that.
### Is it ok to not tip delivery?
Not really, if the service was done. A driver who brought your food on time and intact earned the tip regardless of how the app handled its fees. The exception is real, documented bad service, and even then, remember that a cold order is often the restaurant’s or the platform’s fault, not the driver’s. If you’re tipping in the app before the food arrives, you can adjust afterward on most platforms. If the restaurant runs its own delivery, ask whether the driver gets the delivery charge; sometimes they do, and you can tip with that in mind.
### Can you get hot meals delivered for the elderly?
Yes, and not only through restaurant apps. Home-delivered meal programs, the kind most people know as Meals on Wheels, operate across the St. Louis region through the Area Agency on Aging network and bring hot or chilled meals to older adults who can’t easily cook or get out. Eligibility varies, so the first step is a phone call.
### Home-delivered meal programs
These programs typically serve adults over a certain age who are homebound or have trouble preparing meals, and some also serve younger people with disabilities. Meals are often free or offered for a suggested contribution, and the driver’s regular visit doubles as a wellness check, which the family of the retiree in Marthasville values as much as the food. Rules on age, income, frequency, and waiting lists differ between the Missouri and Illinois sides of the metro and between counties. Call the Area Agency on Aging that covers your address and ask what’s available, how to apply, and how long the wait is.
### Medicare Advantage and post-hospital meals
Some Medicare Advantage plans include a short-term meal benefit after a hospital discharge, sending prepared meals for a set number of days while someone recovers at home. Not every plan offers it, the details change every plan year, and it usually has to be requested rather than arriving automatically. If a parent or spouse is coming home from the hospital, call the plan and ask directly. Original Medicare doesn’t typically cover meals, so confirm what applies to your situation before you count on it.
### Prepared-meal delivery for seniors who don’t qualify
For older adults who don’t meet program requirements, or who simply want more choice, the private options include prepared-meal subscriptions built for seniors, grocery delivery, and the restaurant apps everyone else uses. A family member can set up the account, save the address, and place orders from anywhere, which is a practical way to help a parent across town. The same fee stack applies, so use the same judgment: it’s worth it on the nights it’s the only way a warm meal shows up.
### A simple way to decide before you tap order
Here’s the ten-second test we’ve found works better than any budget spreadsheet: look at the final total, subtract what the meal would cost picked up or cooked, and ask, “Would I pay that difference for the hour I’m saving tonight?” If the answer is a clear yes, order. If you hesitate, that hesitation is your answer.
The reason it works is that it pulls the two things you’re buying apart. On the night the nurse in Venice gets home from a twelve-hour shift, the hour is worth a lot, and she should order without guilt. On a slow Sunday with a full pantry, the same hour is worth almost nothing, and the fee is just a fee. The test doesn’t tell you delivery is good or bad. It tells you whether it’s good or bad right now.
### Three habits that keep delivery from becoming a leak
First, order direct when you can. Call the restaurant, ask if they deliver themselves or through an app, and compare. Second, favor pickup on your route home and save delivery for nights that truly need it. Third, when you do order in, choose food that travels well, so the meal you paid a premium for actually tastes like the meal you wanted. None of this is complicated. It’s just deciding on purpose instead of by reflex, which is the difference between delivery as a lifesaver and delivery as a habit that quietly eats your grocery budget.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are the disadvantages of food delivery?
A.  The main ones are food that arrives cooler and softer than it left the kitchen, wrong or missing items that get fixed with a refund instead of a remake, a fee stack that can push a modest meal toward sit-down prices, and the cut the app takes from the restaurant. Ordering food that travels well and going direct to the restaurant softens most of these.
### Q. Do I tip if there is a delivery fee?
A.  Yes. On third-party apps the delivery fee usually goes to the platform, not the driver, so it isn’t a tip. The person who brings your food is typically paid in part through tips, and in St. Louis, as elsewhere, tipping is customary. If a restaurant runs its own delivery, ask whether the driver receives the delivery charge and tip with that in mind.
### Q. Is it ok to not tip delivery?
A.  If the driver did the job, skipping the tip isn’t fair, since the app’s fees typically don’t reach them. Genuinely bad service is the exception, though a cold or wrong order is often the restaurant’s or the platform’s fault rather than the driver’s. Most apps let you adjust a tip after delivery, so tip normally up front and change it only if something truly went wrong.
### Q. Is delivery or pickup better?
A.  Pickup is better on price and on food quality, because you skip most of the fees and the food doesn’t sit in a car. Delivery is better when you can’t or shouldn’t drive, when you’re sick or caring for someone, or when the hour you’d spend on the round trip is worth more to you than the fees. Choose by the night, not by habit.
### Q. How much should I tip on a $20 pizza delivery?
A.  There’s no set rule, but most people use a percentage similar to sit-down service, with a small-order floor so a single pizza doesn’t leave the driver with pocket change. Go higher for bad weather, a long drive, or stairs. Remember that the delivery fee on the receipt usually doesn’t go to the driver, so the tip is the only part they actually see.
### Q. Can you get hot meals delivered for the elderly?
A.  Yes. Home-delivered meal programs in the Meals on Wheels tradition operate across the St. Louis region through the Area Agency on Aging network, often free or for a suggested contribution, and some Medicare Advantage plans cover short-term meals after a hospital stay. Eligibility, waiting lists, and coverage vary by county and by plan, so call your local agency or the plan to confirm.
### Q. What are the downsides of meal delivery?
A.  For meal kits and prepared-meal subscriptions, the main downsides are a cost per meal that runs above groceries, packaging waste, portions that may not fit your household, and a subscription that keeps shipping unless you actively skip a week. They shine when the problem is deciding and shopping, not cooking. If you already enjoy cooking and have the time, groceries usually win.
### Q. Should I order directly from a restaurant instead of through an app?
A.  When you can, yes. Ordering direct often means the restaurant’s own menu prices without the app markup, no platform service fee, and far more of your money staying with a local business. Call and ask whether they deliver themselves or through an app. If they only use an app, ordering pickup direct is the next-best way to help them keep more of the sale.

## What a Foreclosure Attorney Does in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-foreclosure-attorney-does-in-st-louis
A warehouse worker in Spanish Lake got laid off in March and has been three payments behind since early summer. A widow in Ste. Genevieve just found a late notice in a stack of mail her husband always handled. A family in Hillsboro spent their savings on a hospital stay, and the mortgage is what slipped. A self-employed contractor in De Soto is between jobs, and the servicer stopped returning his calls. A retiree in Herculaneum with a reverse mortgage got a letter about unpaid property taxes and doesn’t know that can trigger a foreclosure too.
Different stories, same knot in the stomach. Each of them is asking the same two questions: is it too late, and do I need a lawyer? Around St. Louis the honest answer depends on how far along the process is, which is exactly why the first thing a foreclosure attorney does is figure out where you actually stand.
This guide covers what a foreclosure attorney really does, why Missouri’s process moves faster than most people expect, what you can do yourself before you spend a dollar, how these lawyers charge, and where to turn if you can’t afford one. We won’t quote you a price, because fees depend on the case and the firm. We will explain how the pricing works, what to ask, and how to tell a real lawyer from a rescue scam.
### Do I need a lawyer to stop foreclosure in St. Louis?
Not always, but the sooner you talk to one, the more options you keep. Missouri lets most lenders foreclose without a court case, so the clock runs fast. If you can catch up or qualify for a loan modification on your own, you may not need a lawyer. Once notices arrive, or the servicer stonewalls you, call one.
Here’s the reason timing matters so much. In many states a lender has to sue you, and a judge oversees every step. Missouri is different. Most home loans here are secured by a deed of trust with a power-of-sale clause, which means the lender’s trustee can sell the house at a public sale after the required notices go out, without ever filing a court case. There’s no judge automatically checking the paperwork, and no built-in hearing where you get to explain yourself.
That changes what “getting help” means. Early on, help might be a phone call to your servicer and a free session with a HUD-approved housing counselor. Later, once a notice of sale has been mailed or published, help usually means a lawyer, because the tools that can actually stop a sale on short notice, like a bankruptcy filing or a court challenge to a defective foreclosure, are legal tools. The widow in Ste. Genevieve who is one payment behind and the contractor in De Soto whose sale date is three weeks out are not in the same situation, and they don’t need the same kind of help.
The practical test: if you can afford the house going forward and you’re just behind, start with the servicer and a counselor. If the servicer won’t engage, denies your application without explanation, or a sale date exists, talk to a foreclosure attorney that week. Most offer a consultation, and even one meeting will tell you whether the house can be kept and what it would take.
### How does foreclosure actually work in Missouri?
Missouri is primarily a non-judicial foreclosure state. The lender doesn’t have to sue you. Instead, the trustee named in your deed of trust sends the notices your loan documents and state law require, publishes notice of the sale, and then auctions the property at a public sale. Because there’s no lawsuit, the whole thing can move faster than homeowners expect.
### Deed of trust, not a court case
When you signed your loan, you almost certainly signed a deed of trust alongside the note. That document names a trustee and gives the trustee the power to sell the home if you default. It’s the reason the process skips the courthouse. The lender or its servicer declares the default, the trustee handles the notices and the sale, and the winning bidder gets a trustee’s deed. A judge only gets involved if someone, usually the homeowner, files something to bring the case into court. That’s part of what a lawyer is for.
### The 120-day rule
Before any of that starts, a federal mortgage-servicing rule generally bars the servicer from making the first notice or filing to begin foreclosure until you’re more than 120 days delinquent. That window exists so you have time to apply for loss mitigation, meaning a repayment plan, forbearance, modification, or another workout. If you submit a complete application during that period, the servicer generally has to review it before moving forward. The rule has exceptions and details, so confirm how it applies to your loan with a lawyer or a HUD-approved counselor. The takeaway is simple: the first four months are your best window, and they go quickly.
### From missed payment to sale, in general terms
The path usually looks like this. You miss a payment and the servicer starts calling and sending late notices. Somewhere along the way you get a formal demand or notice of default that says how much it takes to catch up. After the 120-day mark, the servicer can refer the loan to foreclosure, and the trustee mails a notice of sale and publishes it as required. Then comes the auction. The gap between that first missed payment and the sale can be months, but the gap between the sale notice and the sale itself is short. Timelines depend on your loan documents and the notices you received, so treat every date in a letter as real until a lawyer tells you otherwise.
If you’re on the Illinois side of the metro, the process is different, because Illinois runs foreclosures through the courts. The general advice in this guide still applies, but the deadlines and defenses don’t translate one for one. Ask a lawyer licensed where the house is.
### What does a foreclosure lawyer do?
A foreclosure attorney reads your notices and loan documents, checks whether the servicer followed the rules, negotiates with the lender for a workout, files bankruptcy when that’s the right tool, and defends against a foreclosure that was done wrong. After a sale, the same lawyer handles what comes next, like a deficiency claim or the timing of an eviction. Which of those you need depends on where you are.
### Reads the notices and the loan file
The first job is unglamorous: reading. The note, the deed of trust, every letter the servicer sent, the payment history, and any modification paperwork you already signed. The lawyer is looking for two things, where you stand on the calendar and whether the numbers the servicer is claiming are right. Servicers make mistakes on fees, escrow, and payment posting, and those mistakes sometimes inflate the amount you supposedly owe to reinstate.
### Checks whether the servicer followed the rules
Federal servicing rules and Missouri’s notice requirements set out what a servicer has to do before and during a foreclosure. Did they send the required notices to the right address? Did they review a complete loss-mitigation application before pushing ahead? Did the trustee publish the sale properly? A process that skipped a required step can sometimes be stopped or unwound, and even a small violation gives your lawyer real bargaining power in a negotiation.
### Negotiates loss mitigation
Most foreclosure work is negotiation, not courtroom drama. The lawyer packages your financials, submits the loss-mitigation application, escalates when the servicer loses documents (they do), and pushes for the option that fits your situation: reinstatement, a repayment plan, forbearance, a loan modification, a short sale, or a deed in lieu of foreclosure. Homeowners can apply on their own, and many do. A lawyer earns the fee when the servicer stalls, denies without a clear reason, or offers terms that don’t actually work.
### Files bankruptcy when it’s the right tool
A Chapter 13 bankruptcy filing triggers an automatic stay, which halts the foreclosure sale the moment the case is filed. The plan then lets you catch up the missed payments over time while staying current on the regular ones. It’s a powerful tool, and for the warehouse worker in Spanish Lake who is back on the job with a steady paycheck but can’t write one big reinstatement check, it’s often the tool that saves the house. It’s not right for everyone, and it only works if you can afford the plan. A good foreclosure attorney will tell you honestly which side of that line you’re on.
### Defends against a defective foreclosure
If the servicer or trustee got the process wrong, the lawyer can go to court to stop the sale or, in some cases, challenge one that already happened. That’s where Missouri’s non-judicial process cuts both ways. Nobody was checking the paperwork on the way in, so a homeowner who gets a lawyer to check it on the way out sometimes finds real problems.
### Handles what happens after a sale
If the house does sell, the questions don’t end. Can the lender come after you for the difference if the sale price didn’t cover the loan? How long do you have before you must move out, and can that be negotiated? Are there surplus funds owed to you if the sale brought more than the debt? These are the post-sale issues an attorney handles, and they matter for your finances long after the keys change hands. If your problem is more about title, a contract, or a closing than a missed payment, our guide on whether you need a real estate attorney in Missouri sorts out which kind of lawyer fits.
### How to stop foreclosure once it starts?
Start with the things that cost nothing: call the servicer, ask for the loss-mitigation department, and request the application. Then call a HUD-approved housing counselor, whose help is free. Do both in the same week. If those two paths stall, or a sale date is already set, that’s when a foreclosure attorney becomes the right next call.
### What you can do yourself first
Servicers can’t help someone who won’t pick up the phone, and they don’t know why you fell behind unless you tell them. Ask what it takes to reinstate, what programs you qualify for, and what the deadline is to apply. Write down the name of every person you talk to and the date. Then send in a complete application, every page, every pay stub, and keep proof it was received. The family in Hillsboro whose income has recovered after the medical bills is exactly who a repayment plan or modification is designed for, and they can apply without a lawyer.
### The options a lawyer or counselor will walk through
Reinstatement means paying everything past due in one lump sum. A repayment plan spreads the arrears over several months on top of your regular payment. Forbearance pauses or reduces payments for a set time. A loan modification permanently changes the terms, often by extending the loan or lowering the rate, so the payment fits your income. If keeping the house isn’t realistic, a short sale or a deed in lieu of foreclosure lets you exit with less damage than a completed foreclosure. Chapter 13 is the backstop when a sale is imminent and you have income to fund a plan.
### When a lawyer becomes necessary
Call a foreclosure attorney when a notice of sale exists, when the servicer denies your application without a clear explanation, when the amount they say you owe looks wrong, when you suspect a required notice never came, or when you’re weighing bankruptcy. Also call one if you’ve already been through a modification and are falling behind again, because second chances get harder. The rule of thumb: the closer the sale date, the fewer non-legal options remain.
### Watch for foreclosure-rescue scams
Once a notice of sale is published, your name is public, and the letters and door-knockers follow. Be suspicious of anyone who asks for an upfront fee to “save” your house, guarantees a result, tells you to stop paying the servicer and pay them instead, or asks you to sign the deed over to them “temporarily.” HUD-approved housing counselors don’t charge for foreclosure counseling, and a real lawyer will put the fee agreement in writing and explain what it covers. The retiree in Herculaneum who signs a deed over to a stranger loses the house faster than the foreclosure would have taken it.
Rights violated, not just a missed payment? See what a civil rights attorney costs.
### How much does it cost for a foreclosure attorney?
Fees vary widely, so confirm every number with the attorney. Most foreclosure lawyers around St. Louis charge one of three ways: a flat fee for a defined job like a loan-modification package, an hourly rate against a retainer for court work, or, for Chapter 13, attorney fees that are largely folded into the bankruptcy plan and paid over time.
### Flat fees for defined work
A flat fee suits work with a known scope. Preparing and submitting a loss-mitigation package, negotiating a modification, or handling a deed in lieu can each be priced as a single number. Ask exactly what the fee includes and what happens if the servicer denies the first application and you need to reapply. A flat fee that covers one submission and a flat fee that covers the whole negotiation are different products.
### Hourly and retainer for litigation
If the plan is to go to court, to stop a sale on the grounds that the servicer broke the rules or to challenge a completed sale, most attorneys bill hourly against a retainer. You pay a deposit up front, the lawyer bills time against it, and you replenish it if the case runs long. Litigation is harder to predict, which is why it’s rarely flat-fee work. Ask for a realistic range of hours for your situation and what would push it higher.
### Chapter 13 fees inside the plan
Bankruptcy attorneys often structure Chapter 13 so that a portion of the fee is paid up front and the rest is paid through the plan itself, alongside your mortgage arrears, over the life of the case. That’s a big reason Chapter 13 is reachable for homeowners who couldn’t write a large check the week before a sale. The court reviews the fee, and it varies by district and by case, so ask the attorney how much is due before filing and how much rides in the plan.
### Cheaper alternatives, and what to do if you can’t afford one
You have more options than you might think. HUD-approved housing counselors offer free foreclosure counseling and can help you apply for loss mitigation, and that’s the right first stop for most people. On the Missouri side, Legal Services of Eastern Missouri provides free civil legal help, including foreclosure defense, to people who qualify; eligibility is income-based, so confirm with them directly. On the Illinois side, Land of Lincoln Legal Aid plays the same role. Some private attorneys also offer a reduced-fee consultation or payment plans, and a bar-association referral service can point you to a lawyer who takes cases like yours at a rate you can manage. Not having money is not the same as not having options.
### How do you choose a foreclosure attorney in St. Louis?
Treat the first meeting as an interview. Shortlist two or three foreclosure attorneys, sit down with each, and say plainly what you want: to keep the house, or to get out cleanly with as little damage as possible. Then compare what you asked for against what each lawyer is prepared to deliver. That gap is your signal.
Say it straight. “I’m four payments behind, my income is back, and I want to keep the house.” Or, “I can’t afford this house anymore and I want to leave without owing anything afterward.” One lawyer will lay out a process: here’s what your notices say, here’s the loss-mitigation path, here’s where Chapter 13 fits if the servicer won’t deal, here’s what I’d do this week. Another will promise to save the house before opening the folder. Nobody honest guarantees an outcome against a lender.
Bring your notices, your loan documents, your last few months of income, and a list of everything the servicer has told you. Ask each attorney how much of their practice is foreclosure and mortgage work, whether they handle Chapter 13 themselves or refer it out, who will actually be dealing with your servicer, and how the fee is structured. The same instincts apply to any legal hire, and our guide to how to find the right lawyer in St. Louis walks through them in more detail. And if the end of this story is a fresh start with a new loan someday, how to choose a mortgage lender in St. Louis is the next thing to read once you’re back on your feet.

### Q. How long can a home stay in foreclosure?

After that, Missouri’s non-judicial process can reach a sale in a matter of months, since there’s no lawsuit. A loss-mitigation application, a bankruptcy filing, or litigation can extend that, sometimes considerably. Confirm the dates with a lawyer.
### Q. Can I save my house if it’s in foreclosure?
A.  Often, yes, if you act before the sale and you can afford the house going forward. Reinstatement, a repayment plan, forbearance, and a loan modification all keep you in the home. If the sale is days away, a Chapter 13 filing halts it through the automatic stay and lets you catch up over time. Once the trustee’s sale happens, your options narrow sharply, so don’t wait.
### Q. What is the 120 day rule for foreclosure?

The purpose is to give you a window to apply for loss mitigation before the trustee is involved. If you submit a complete application during that window, the servicer generally has to evaluate it first. There are exceptions, so confirm how it applies to your loan.
### Q. Are there cheaper alternatives to a foreclosure lawyer?

A HUD-approved housing counselor offers free foreclosure counseling and can help you prepare and submit a loss-mitigation application, which is enough for many homeowners who are behind but can afford the house. ## Written Up for Organizing? When a St. Louis Labor Relations Attorney Is Worth the Call
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/labor-relations-attorney-in-st-louis-when-you-need-one
Folded in quarters, soft at the creases, the write-up has been in your jacket pocket since Thursday. It showed up two weeks after you started asking people in the break room whether a union might fix the overtime schedule, and you’ve touched it through the fabric about forty times since. Take it out. On the back, write Room 8.302. That’s the St. Louis office of the National Labor Relations Board, Region 14, on the eighth floor of the federal building at 1222 Spruce Street downtown. Walk down the same hallway and you reach Room 8.100, the EEOC’s St. Louis District Office in the Robert A. Young Federal Building. Two federal doors, one elevator ride.
You probably didn’t know that, sitting in the car after the shift with the engine off and the phone lighting up your face. What you knew was that the paper felt heavier than paper should. That your stomach dropped when the supervisor said “we need to talk” and shut the door. That the radio in the shop kept playing like nothing happened. And the question underneath all of it: do I need a lawyer, which kind, and how fast?
Behind the NLRB door is the group: your right to act with co-workers on work issues, from a shared complaint about pay to a union drive. The EEOC door handles what happens to one person because of who they are: race, sex, age, disability and the rest. Which door you’re standing at decides which kind of lawyer you call.You can knock on either one yourself, and the NLRB’s own page tells you to call or visit and ask for the Information Officer on duty. The catch is the clock, and the clocks are not the same. So tonight, do one small thing: write the date on the write-up in pen and put a reminder in your phone six months out. Tomorrow, between 8:00am and 4:30pm, you can call Region 14 at (314) 539-7770 with the write-up, your dates and the names of who was in the room in front of you.
### What is the difference between a labor lawyer and an employment lawyer in St. Louis?
Labor law covers the collective side of work: organizing, collective bargaining, strikes and unfair labor practice charges under the National Labor Relations Act, enforced by the NLRB, whose Region 14 office sits at 1222 Spruce Street. Employment law covers one worker’s claim: discrimination, harassment, retaliation, unpaid wages or a firing. A labor lawyer works the first kind of problem, an employment lawyer the second. Quick test: a group, or one worker?
Put it the way you’d say it over the kitchen table. Is this about us, or about me? If two or more of you talked about pay, signed cards, circulated a petition for better hours or have a union contract, you’re in labor law. The NLRB’s plain-English page on concerted activity gives examples, starting with talking with one or more co-workers about your wages and benefits. That protection doesn’t wait for a union to exist. The crew that grumbled together at the loading dock had rights the moment they grumbled together.
If it’s about you alone, and something about you that the law protects, you’re usually in employment law. That’s the Room 8.100 side, or a complaint under the Missouri Human Rights Act filed with the MCHR.
Now the clocks, the part worth counting on the calendar stuck to your fridge. Federal law says no complaint can issue on an unfair labor practice that happened more than six months before the charge was filed and served. Six months from the write-up, not from the day you finally got angry enough to do something. A discrimination charge with the EEOC runs on a different meter: 180 calendar days, stretched to 300 where a state agency enforces a similar law. Missouri’s own clock is shorter. The Missouri Commission on Human Rights says complaints under the Missouri Human Rights Act must be filed with it within 180 days, while federal law allows 300 days at the EEOC. Miss the 180 and, under Missouri law, the commission loses the power to act on the complaint.
That’s the thing almost nobody tells you at the start. The same bad week can carry three deadlines, and the shortest one is the one that bites. If your write-up smells like punishment for organizing and also like punishment for your age, you may have a door on each end of that eighth-floor hallway, each with its own clock. The first meeting with a good lawyer is mostly sorting: which door, which clock, which claim to lead with.
One St. Louis wrinkle for public workers. The NLRB’s reach covers the great majority of non-government employers. The federal law itself says “employer” does not include any state or political subdivision, so if you work for a school district, a city department or the state, that federal door generally isn’t yours. Missouri’s constitution answers instead: Article I, Section 29 says employees have the right to organize and to bargain collectively through representatives of their own choosing. Tell any lawyer which sector you’re in during the first thirty seconds of the call.
### The meeting where you ask for your steward
The fluorescent light hums. HR has a legal pad, your supervisor has your file, and there’s a chair with nobody in it. If you’re in a union shop, that empty chair can be filled. The NLRB describes it as the right of employees, upon request, to have their representative present during an interview that the employee reasonably believes could lead to discipline. The agency files it under Weingarten Rights, after NLRB v. J. Weingarten, Inc., the Supreme Court case that first spelled it out. The representative can be a steward, a business agent or officer, or a fellow employee.
The catch: you have to ask. Out loud, plainly, before or during the meeting, even if your mouth has gone dry. Something like, “If this could lead to discipline, I’d like my steward here before I answer questions.” Under current Board law this right belongs to union-represented employees, so if your workplace has no union, ask anyway in a calm voice and write down what they said back.
Then keep it short. HR works for the company, and everything you say can land in a file. Don’t guess at anyone’s motives out loud. Don’t name coworkers who have been talking union. Don’t share medical details nobody asked for. Don’t sign a statement, a last-chance agreement or a separation agreement at that table; ask for a copy and a day to read it. And skip the line people blurt when they’re scared, the “my lawyer will hear about this.” Retaliating against you for a protected complaint is unlawful, but announcing a lawyer in a heated meeting changes every conversation after it, and it’s better decided with that lawyer first.
Same day, at the kitchen table, write it down while the coffee goes cold: the date, who sat where, what was said, what you were handed. Ask follow-up questions by email so the answers live in email. Keep your reviews and pay stubs somewhere other than a company laptop. If the meeting ended in a firing rather than a write-up, our guide to what your rights actually are when you’re fired in Missouri picks up from there.
### What does a labor relations lawyer do?
A labor relations lawyer handles the relationship between an employer and a group of workers, usually through a union. That covers organizing campaigns and elections, bargaining and reading contracts, grievances and arbitration, unfair labor practice charges, and the legal edges of a strike or lockout. What the work looks like depends on which side of the table you sit on.
For workers and unions, the lawyer files election petitions, answers employer objections, presses unfair labor practice charges and argues grievances at arbitration when the contract steps run out. Most unions keep counsel for exactly this, so a member with a scheduling grievance usually starts with the steward and the business agent, and they decide when a lawyer needs to be in the room.
For employers, the useful work starts before the petition lands. The NLRB lists what employers may not do in response to an organizing drive: threaten, interrogate or spy on pro-union employees, or promise benefits if they forget about the union. A supervisor can cross that line in one sentence on a Tuesday morning without meaning to. A labor attorney trains the supervisors, runs the election process, answers charges and sits at the bargaining table if a union is certified. If you run a small shop that has never had a lawyer on call, our guide to when a small business needs an attorney covers how that relationship usually gets set up.
### Should I get a labor lawyer?
Not always, and a good one will say so. A union member with a grievance has the steward, the business agent and the union’s own counsel. A worker punished for organizing can call Region 14 at (314) 539-7770 and talk to the Information Officer before deciding anything. You need your own lawyer when the union won’t move, a second claim rides along, or you’re the employer.
The two systems exist so ordinary people can use them without hiring anyone. Your contract’s grievance steps are the first. The NLRB is the second: the Region 14 office lists its status as open, with hours of 8:00am to 4:30pm Central, and the agency says it can arrange for someone to speak with you in the language of your choice. That matters if the words you reach for first, when you’re upset, aren’t English. The EEOC’s St. Louis office takes calls at (314) 798-1960.
Hire your own attorney when one of these is true. The union declined to carry your grievance and you think that decision was arbitrary. A discrimination claim sits next to the labor problem and the contract process won’t touch it. You’re part of a group trying to organize and people have started getting disciplined. Or a charge is being drafted and you want someone shaping it, because what goes into the first filing tends to define the case.
If you’re the owner who just slit open an envelope from the NLRB at your desk, the answer is yes, this week. The rules on what a supervisor can say are technical, and getting them wrong can cost you the election you were trying to win fairly.
Bring the paper, not just the story. Browse labor relations attorneys across the St. Louis metro, shortlist two or three, and carry the write-up, the contract or the petition to the first meeting, along with the date it all started so the six-month clock is on the table from minute one.
If you’re the labor-law firm or the solo attorney who takes these calls, the worker reading this at 11 p.m. is one of your next customers. Listing your practice puts you in front of more of those customers before they pick a name off a billboard.
### The verbs employers trip over during a drive
Threaten. Interrogate. Promise. Spy. Those four verbs cover most of what goes wrong on the employer side when cards start circulating. Telling workers the plant could close if the union wins. Asking someone in the hallway how they plan to vote. Floating a raise that appears only after the petition does. Noting who parked near the union hall on Saturday. Threatening, interrogating, spying and promising benefits to make the union go away are all named on the NLRB’s page about interfering with employee rights.
On the worker side, the charge that shows up again and again is the one this page opened with: discipline that follows people acting together. A group complaint gets read as insubordination, and a write-up follows. That’s why the date on that folded paper matters so much. It starts the clock, and it’s also the first piece of evidence about timing.
Once a union represents the workers, the law sets a mutual obligation of the employer and the union to meet at reasonable times and confer in good faith. Refusing to meet, changing wages on your own while talks are open, or going through the motions can each draw a charge. Disputes over what a contract sentence means usually go to an arbitrator instead, and that’s where a lawyer who knows the local arbitrators earns the fee.
### How the bill usually works
Employers and unions usually pay labor attorneys by the hour, often against a retainer, with arbitrations and litigation billed on top. Ask what the retainer covers and what triggers more billing. Individual workers rarely pay hourly for a claim against an employer, because few could. Contingency fees, where the lawyer takes a share of any recovery and nothing if there isn’t one, are common for discrimination, retaliation and wage claims, and some arrangements mix a smaller hourly rate with a smaller share. We won’t print a number, because nobody can give you an honest one from a blog. Any lawyer you interview can tell you theirs in one sentence, and you’ll feel your shoulders drop when they do.
Odds and timelines get the same honesty. Nobody truthful quotes a win rate. Outcomes turn on the evidence, the claim and how well the record was built early, which is why the kitchen-table notes matter. At the NLRB, the agency says a decision on the merits of a charge typically comes within 7 to 14 weeks, though some cases take much longer, and a lawsuit that goes the distance can take years. Be wary of anyone who answers “how long?” with a promise.
### Picking the lawyer across the desk
Treat the first meeting as an interview, because it is one. Put the folded paper on the desk between you and say it straight: “I was written up two weeks after I started talking to coworkers about a union. Do I have a charge, and what’s my deadline?” One lawyer will lay out a process, the clock and the next three steps. Another will hand you a guarantee. That gap is your answer.
Ask which side of the table they usually sit on. Labor law is unusual: most attorneys represent management or unions and workers, rarely both, and you want years on your side. Ask how many elections or arbitrations they’ve handled in this region, who will actually do the work, and what they’d tell you if your case were weak. For a broader vetting checklist, see how to find the right lawyer in St. Louis.
If the trouble is a criminal charge and not a write-up, start with what a criminal defense attorney costs here.
Let go outright, and not sure it was legal? Read when to call a wrongful termination attorney in St. Louis. And if money is tight, ask whether the first consultation is free or low-cost, and whether your problem belongs with the union or with an agency on the eighth floor of 1222 Spruce before you hire anyone. A good labor attorney will tell you when you don’t need them. Remember that one.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Should I get a labor lawyer?
A.  Not always. A union member with a grievance has the steward and the union’s counsel, and a worker disciplined for organizing can call the NLRB’s St. Louis office and ask for the Information Officer on duty. Get your own lawyer when the union won’t carry your case, a separate claim like discrimination is involved, or you’re an employer facing a petition or charge.
### Q. Should I tell HR I’m getting a lawyer?
A.  Talk to the lawyer first, then decide together. Telling HR isn’t wrong, and retaliation for a protected complaint is unlawful, but it changes every conversation afterward, and sometimes the lawyer would rather make contact. If you do say it, say it calmly and in writing, never as a threat in a heated meeting.
### Q. What not to disclose to HR?
A.  Don’t speculate about motives, name coworkers involved in organizing, or share medical details beyond what an accommodation request needs. Don’t sign a statement, last-chance or separation agreement in the meeting; ask for a copy and time. In a union workplace, if the meeting could lead to discipline, ask for your steward before answering.
### Q. What is the most common labor law violation?
A.  On the labor side, it’s discipline that follows protected concerted activity, like a write-up after coworkers complained together about pay. During organizing drives, the frequent employer mistakes are threatening, interrogating or spying on pro-union employees, or promising benefits to make the union go away.
### Q. Is it expensive to sue an employer?
A.  It depends on how the lawyer is paid. Many individual claims are taken on contingency or a hybrid fee, so the upfront cash can be low. The real costs are time, stress and the chance of no recovery. At the NLRB, once the agency issues a complaint, it becomes a representative for the charging party, and Board attorneys help prepare the case.
### Q. What are the odds of winning an employment lawsuit?
A.  No honest lawyer will quote a rate. The odds depend on the evidence, the type of claim, how well the record was built early and whether the case settles. Ask an attorney for a candid read on your facts, not a percentage.
### Q. How long does it take to settle an employment lawsuit?
A.  Months to years. An agency charge runs through investigation first, which takes months by itself. If a lawsuit follows, discovery, motions and mediation add more time, and a case that goes to trial can run years. Ask for a realistic range for your claim type.

## Do You Need a Lactation Consultant in St. Louis?
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/do-you-need-a-lactation-consultant-in-st-louis
Day four in Dardenne Prairie. The baby has been on and off the breast for most of an hour, the pain is sharp enough that she flinches before the latch even happens, and the pediatrician’s office cannot see them until Thursday. She has watched nine videos on her phone since 3 a.m. None of them were about her baby.
In Festus, a mother going back to work in three weeks has a pump she does not really understand and a freezer stash she is certain is too small. In Shrewsbury, a dad is doing 2 a.m. math on wet diapers, because the discharge paperwork said to call if there were fewer than a certain number and nobody explained what you are supposed to do about that in the middle of the night.
A second-time parent in Frontenac assumed this round would be easier and it is not: different baby, different mouth, different problem entirely. In Glen Carbon, a grandmother who nursed four of her own is offering advice that contradicts everything the hospital nurse said, which somehow makes the whole thing harder instead of easier.
None of those people are failing at anything. They are all hitting the same gap: feeding a newborn is a skill, and almost nobody is taught it. This guide covers what a lactation consultant actually does, when to call one and when to call your pediatrician instead, what the letters after their name mean, what drives the cost, how insurance coverage generally works under federal rules, and how to interview two or three before you pick. No invented prices and no scare tactics, because you have had enough of both.
### Do you really need a lactation consultant in St. Louis?
Often yes, and sooner than most people think. If feeding hurts, if the baby is not gaining, if the latch keeps slipping, or if you are pumping and unsure, a lactation consultant is the person whose whole job is that problem. Most families need one or two visits, not a long course of care.
The more useful framing is that you probably do not need an ongoing relationship with a consultant. You need one good visit at the right moment. Breastfeeding gets described as natural, and parents hear that as “should be easy,” so when it is not easy on day four the conclusion they reach is that something is wrong with them. Usually something is just mechanical. Mechanical problems tend to have mechanical fixes.
A consultant is not a replacement for your baby’s doctor. Weight, jaundice, tongue anatomy, reflux, anything that is a medical question about the baby belongs to the pediatrician, and a good consultant will say that out loud and send you there. If you have not picked a pediatrician yet, our guide to how to choose a pediatrician in St. Louis is worth reading before the birth rather than after.
So who does not need one? A parent whose baby latches without pain, gains steadily, makes the diapers the doctor expects, and who feels genuinely fine about the arrangement. That happens, and it is allowed to happen without anyone auditing it. Nearly everyone else is one phone call away from a better week.
### When should you call a lactation consultant?
Call sooner than feels justified. The three highest-value windows are the last few weeks of pregnancy, the first two weeks after birth, and any moment something changes: a return to work, a supply dip, a baby who suddenly refuses the breast. Waiting to see whether it sorts itself out is the regret parents describe most often.
### Before the baby arrives
A prenatal consult is badly underused. It earns its keep most after a hard experience with an earlier baby, if you are expecting twins, if you have had breast surgery, if you have a condition that can affect supply, or if you already know you will be pumping at work. The point is not to rehearse feeding. The point is to know exactly who you are calling, and to have that number in your phone before you are too tired to look for it.
### The first two weeks
This is where one visit changes the most. Latch habits set quickly, and early supply responds to how often and how well milk gets removed. If feeding hurts past the first few seconds, if the baby nurses an hour and seems hungry immediately after, if your nipples are cracked or come out misshapen, if diaper counts are low, or if you were told to supplement and are not sure how to protect supply while you do it, that is a call today. Not Monday.
### Later than people think is allowed
Month three, month six, month nine. Biting, bottle refusal, plugged ducts, a slow drop in pumped output after a schedule change, or a decision to wean on purpose instead of by accident. Consultants work on all of it. Nobody is going to inform you that you missed your window, because there is not one.
### When to call the pediatrician first
If the baby is lethargic, will not wake to feed, has a fever, is making far fewer wet diapers than you were told to expect, or is losing weight, that is a medical call and it goes to the doctor first. A consultant helps you feed the baby. The pediatrician decides whether the baby is okay. Those are two different questions, and you are allowed to ask both on the same day.
### What does a lactation consultant actually do in a visit?
They take a long history, weigh the baby, watch an entire feed start to finish, look at the baby’s mouth and at your breasts, often weigh again to estimate how much milk actually moved, and then leave you with a written plan. A first visit commonly runs one to two hours. It is far more hands-on and far less lecture than most parents expect.
### The history
Birth details, medications, how the first hours went, what the baby has eaten since, how often, for how long, what the diapers look like, what hurts and exactly where. Then your side: previous babies, surgeries, thyroid, fertility treatment, anything that can move supply. This part feels long and slightly invasive. It is also where the actual answer usually hides.
### The feed
Then they watch you feed, which is awkward for about ninety seconds and then stops mattering. They are watching how wide the baby opens, how deep the latch goes, whether the chin is buried, how the swallows sound, whether your posture is fighting you, and whether the baby can hold suction. Small adjustments, a different hold, a change of angle, one pillow moved, sometimes fix in a single visit what a month of late-night videos did not.
### The plan
You should walk away with something written down: how often to feed, whether and how much to supplement, a pumping schedule if you need one, flange sizing if you are pumping, comfort measures, and a clear trigger for when to call the pediatrician instead. If you are still assembling gear at this stage, our rundown of what baby gear is worth buying secondhand covers where saving money makes sense and where it does not. Before the consultant leaves, ask when the follow-up should happen and whether it is already included.
### What credentials should you look for, and what do the letters mean?
IBCLC is the credential with the highest bar. It stands for International Board Certified Lactation Consultant, and earning it requires health sciences coursework, a substantial number of supervised clinical hours, a board exam, and recertification over time. CLC, CLE and similar certificates involve shorter training and no comparable clinical-hour requirement. Both can help. They are not the same thing.
### When you want an IBCLC
Start here if the situation is complicated: poor weight gain, suspected tongue restriction, low supply, oversupply, relactation, a premature baby, breast surgery in your history, or pain that has not budged with the basic fixes. IBCLCs work inside hospitals, inside pediatric and OB practices, in private practice doing home visits, and increasingly over video. Many also hold a nursing or dietitian license on top of the certification.
### CLC, CLE and the shorter certificates
A counselor or educator with a shorter certificate can be genuinely useful for common, uncomplicated problems: positioning, engorgement, normal newborn behavior, what a good latch looks and sounds like, how to start pumping. Plenty work in clinics, WIC programs and hospital classes. The honest guidance is to match the credential to the difficulty of the problem, and to ask any provider straight out what they do when a case sits outside their scope. The good ones answer that without flinching.
### Peer counselors and groups
Peer support is a separate category and it is worth more than people assume. A mother-to-mother group will not diagnose anything. But sitting in a room with six other people in the same week of the same problem does something an appointment cannot. In our experience, families who use both, a clinical visit for the mechanics and a group for the morale, come out of the first three months in better shape than families who only do one.
Planning a career change once the baby sleeps? See what fashion design school expects.
### What does a lactation consultant cost, and who pays?
Cost tracks setting and length: a home visit runs more than an office visit, which usually runs more than a video consult, and first visits are longer than follow-ups. The bigger question is coverage. Under the Affordable Care Act, most non-grandfathered plans must cover breastfeeding support, counseling and supplies as preventive care, generally without cost sharing when you stay in network.
### What actually drives the price
Travel and time, mostly. A consultant driving out to Festus and spending two hours in your living room is selling a different product than a thirty-minute video follow-up. After that: whether follow-up texts, calls and a written plan are bundled into the first fee or billed separately, whether a rental scale comes with it, and whether the practice bills your insurer directly or hands you a superbill to submit yourself. Ask for the current fee when you call. Any number printed in an article goes stale, and a stale number is worse than no number.
### What the federal rule does and does not promise
The preventive-services requirement is real, and it is not a blank check. Plans keep meaningful latitude over which providers count as in network, how many visits are covered, and where those visits may happen. Grandfathered plans and certain other arrangements sit outside the rule entirely. Before you book, call the number on your card and ask three things: is lactation counseling covered without cost sharing, who is in network for it, and how many visits are allowed. Write down who told you and when. If you are between plans or shopping, our guide to how to get health insurance in Missouri walks through the options.
### Free and lower-cost routes
Hospitals frequently provide lactation support to families who delivered there, and many host free breastfeeding groups that anyone can attend. WIC offers breastfeeding counseling and peer support to eligible families at no cost. Volunteer-led groups meet regularly around the metro. Some private practices run a free phone triage before any paid visit, which can tell you whether you need the visit at all. Availability shifts, so confirm before you drive anywhere.
### How do you choose a lactation consultant in St. Louis?
Interview two or three before you commit. Say plainly what you have and what you want, then measure that against what each one is prepared to actually deliver. The gap between those two things is the signal. Price is the last item on the list, not the first, because the cheapest visit that does not solve your problem ends up costing the most.
Say it straight on the phone. “My baby is nine days old, feeding hurts the entire time, we are supplementing after every feed and I want to stop, and I need someone who can come to me in Glen Carbon this week.” Or: “I go back to work in three weeks, I have never used this pump, and I want a plan for the first month back.” Then listen. One consultant will describe how the visit runs, what they will look at, and what happens afterward. Another will promise you an outcome. Outcomes are not promisable here, and confidence is not the same as a plan.
Questions worth asking before you book: Are you an IBCLC, and how long have you held it? Do you come to the home, or is this an office or video visit? How long is the first appointment? What support is included afterward, and for how long? Do you bill insurance directly, or do I submit a superbill? Do you bill under me or under the baby? What do you do when a problem is outside your scope? And how soon can you get here?
That last one matters more than new parents expect. A brilliant consultant with a three-week wait is no help on day five. Ask about availability first and let it shorten the list for you. Then notice the tone. If someone makes you feel judged during a fifteen-minute phone call, that will not improve when they are sitting in your living room watching you feed at the worst hour of your day. Pick the person who asks good questions and does not react to your answers.
