### Q. How much do birthday party bus packages cost?
A.  Birthday packages usually price off the same hourly meter, so the four to five hour minimum sets the floor. A smaller bus for a shorter evening sits at the low end, while a big bus on a Saturday runs higher. Some operators bundle decorations or a set route, so get the package itemized before you commit.
### Q. How much to rent a 40 seater bus?
A.  A forty-seater is a large vehicle, so it sits near the top of the hourly range and sometimes crosses into charter-coach pricing rather than classic party-bus pricing. Expect a higher hourly rate, the usual four to five hour minimum, and a real premium on weekends. Confirm whether you are quoted a party bus or a coach, because they price differently.
### Q. How much to rent a 50 seater bus?
A.  A fifty-seater is usually a full coach rather than a true party bus, so it is priced like charter transportation. That often means a higher hourly or flat day rate, a firm minimum, and gratuity on top. For a group that big, ask specifically for a coach quote and confirm whether the layout is party-style or standard seating.
### Q. How many people do you need to rent a party bus?
A.  Usually just enough to justify renting the whole vehicle, since you pay for the bus, not per head. Most operators rent to any size group up to the vehicle’s capacity, so a group of eight can book a twenty-passenger bus. The real question is cost per person: the more riders you split the bill across, the better the deal feels.
### Q. Is it cheaper to rent a party bus or limo?
A.  Per hour, a limo is usually cheaper, commonly in a lower hourly range. Per person, a party bus often wins once your group passes eight or ten, because you split a bigger vehicle across more riders. So the cheaper option depends entirely on headcount. Price both for your exact group and compare the cost per person, not the hourly rate.
### Q. Is a party bus worth the cost?
A.  For the right occasion, most groups say yes. You are paying for safety, convenience, and the party being the ride, not just transportation from one place to another. Nobody drives, nobody drinks and drives, and the group stays together. For a milestone birthday, a bachelorette, or prom, that combination usually justifies the hourly rate, especially split across a full bus.

## $0 or 75 Percent: How Payday Loans Work in Missouri and What They Really Cost
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-payday-loans-work-in-missouri-and-what-they-cost
$0, or 75 percent of what you borrowed. Those are the two ends of a payday loan in Missouri, and the state’s own rules set both. Repay before the close of the lender’s next full business day and you owe no interest and no fees, only the principal, according to the Division of Finance’s payday lender page. Let it ride through all six renewals the law allows and the lender can collect interest and fees worth up to 75 percent of what you borrowed, on top of the loan itself. Same loan, same counter. The gap between those two numbers is mostly timing, and a couple of phone calls.
The weeks that send people to a payday counter tend to look alike. The alternator quits in a grocery lot in Richmond Heights and the key gets one dry click back. A disconnect notice from Ameren lies on a kitchen table in a flat off Tower Grove Park, the date on it four days ahead of payday. Someone is riding the Grand bus before sunrise, thumbs cold on the phone screen, running the same math again and getting the same answer, with a knot under the ribs that won’t loosen.
Before any counter, two calls cost nothing. Dial 211, or 800-427-4626, to reach United Way 211, the number the City of St. Louis housing help page lists for anyone who needs a shelter bed for the night. It handles far more than beds: housing and shelter, utilities and food are among the top requests people bring to 211, United Way says. Then call the number printed on the notice itself. Ameren Missouri says a customer with an outstanding balance can make an arrangement to avoid disconnection, and a landlord or repair shop can be asked for the same thing. An arrangement like that is not a loan. If you belong to a credit union, or can join one, ask about a small loan or a Payday Alternative Loan the same morning. At a federal credit union, a PAL can charge up to 28 percent, which is covered further down.
When the paper on the table is a shutoff notice, the city’s utility assistance page names people to call directly. Guardian Angel Emergency Assistance Program, 314-773-9027, helps families, seniors and individuals at risk of eviction, foreclosure or utility shut-off. Heat Up/Cool Down St. Louis, 314-241-0001, helps elderly and disabled people and low-income families with delinquent energy bills. Franciscan Connection, 314-773-8485, gives up to $100 toward a utility bill for people living in the 63111, 63116 or 63118 zip codes. Each one is a phone call that might shrink the amount you would otherwise borrow, or erase it.
If you have already signed, the free window still works for you. Keep those calls going the next morning. If the credit union approves, a manager agrees to a paycheck advance, or one of those agencies helps with the Ameren bill, take the cash back to the lender before its next full business day closes, and the loan cost you nothing but the trip. The calls made after a loan can save as much as the ones made before it.
For anyone who keeps the loan, the price should be on the wall, readable from the line while the clerk photocopies your ID and the printer warms up. Read it there, out loud if you have to, before your pay stub goes under the glass. The state watches this industry too, in the Division of Finance’s payday lender survey.
### What are the rules for payday loans in St. Louis?
Payday loans in St. Louis follow Missouri law: lenders need a Division of Finance license, each loan is capped at $500 for 14 to 31 days, renewals stop at six, and interest and fees cannot exceed 75 percent of the original principal. Repay before the lender’s next full business day closes and you owe no interest or fees.
The Division of Finance says three sections of state law, 408.500, 408.505 and 408.506, make up the entire payday loan law, and every licensed lender in Missouri works under them. If a lender offers you more than $500 on one loan, or a term shorter than two weeks, that’s your first sign something is wrong.
Two quieter rules deserve more attention than they get. Lenders have to post their rates conspicuously, so the price should be readable on the wall, in letters you can see from the doorway, before anyone slides a warm sheet of paper across the counter. And interest is calculated daily. Since the meter runs by the day, paying early should shrink the bill, so ask out loud what you would owe if you came back on day six instead of day fourteen.
The city adds its own layer. On March 7, 2017, about 60 percent of St. Louis city voters approved Proposition S, which put a $5,000 annual fee on short-term lenders inside the city limits, required them to clearly post what they charge in interest and fees, and required them to offer a guide to alternatives to short-term loans, St. Louis Public Radio reported. At a counter in the city, it is fair to ask for that alternatives guide before you hand over a pay stub.
The 75 percent ceiling is the one to carry in your head, the number to say back when the renewal form slides out a third time and your stomach drops. It isn’t a limit per pay period. It covers interest and fees on the first loan and every renewal added together, for the life of the loan. A lender can reach it fast on a short loan that keeps rolling over, which is why the renewal math below matters more than the fee on any single loan.
### Three things Missouri lets you know before you sign
The Division of Finance conducts a biennial survey of Missouri payday lenders, and its payday lender surveys are worth a look if you want the industry’s averages. But the counter you’re standing at isn’t cheaper because it’s the only sign on the block. The fluorescent hum, the laminated rate card, the pen on a chain: none of it tells you the price until you ask. Comparing two or three lenders is the one habit that protects you.
Here’s the part worth repeating to a cousin who’s thinking about it: Missouri caps the total, Missouri lets you hand the cash back before the lender’s next full business day closes and owe no interest or fees, and Missouri makes the lender post its rates. You’re allowed to know all three before you sign.
### How much would a $500 payday loan cost?
The legal worst case is the $500 you borrowed plus interest and fees equal to 75 percent of it, the full amount Missouri allows across the original loan and all six renewals. It’s a ceiling, not a suggestion.
Week to week, the cost depends on the rate your lender posts. Interest is figured by the day, so the same loan at the same rate costs more held 31 days than held 14. Ask for your own number in dollars, not a percent, and ask for it twice: once for the due date, once for paying early.
Where people get hurt is the second due date. A renewal, sometimes called a rollover, means you pay the fee, maybe some of the principal, and the lender writes a fresh loan with a new due date. If you only manage the fee, you can walk out having paid real money and still owe nearly what you borrowed, with the clock reset and the same dread waiting two weeks out. Do that a few times and the fees start to rival the loan.
That’s also why the APR on Missouri payday paperwork runs into the hundreds. A fee that sounds small on one short loan turns enormous when it’s stretched across a whole year, which is all an APR does. The number isn’t a typo. It’s the price of the money, written the way every car loan and credit card writes theirs.
One test before you sign. Sit at your kitchen table and say the worst case out loud: what you borrowed, plus three-quarters of it again. Could you survive paying that back over the next few months, on top of rent and the light bill? If the honest answer is no, the loan isn’t a bridge. It’s a hole with a fee attached, and every option in the next section is worth trying first.
### What is the best alternative to a payday loan?
Usually, the cheapest money is the money you never borrow, so the best alternative is a payment plan with whoever you owe. After that comes a small loan from a credit union, an advance from your employer, or a local emergency fund. Every one of them takes a phone call or two more than a storefront. Every one of them costs less.
Start with the envelope. Whether it’s a landlord or a utility, the company on that notice handles late payments every day and would usually rather set up an arrangement than start a shutoff or an eviction. Utilities often have hardship programs and budget billing that nobody brings up until you ask. Ten minutes on hold, the same tinny music looping in your ear, can turn a shutoff date into a payment plan that costs nothing extra.
Next, the credit union. Federal credit unions can offer Payday Alternative Loans, called PALs, at up to 28 percent APR plus an application fee of no more than $20, according to the CDFI Fund, and the NCUA says that fee can only cover the credit union’s actual processing cost. Under the original PALs program you need to have been a member for at least a month. The newer PALs II version has no minimum membership period, so ask which one a credit union offers before you assume you have to wait. Our guide to joining a credit union in St. Louis walks through the membership part.
Even outside a formal PAL, many credit unions make small personal loans to members with dented credit at ordinary consumer rates. If that alternator bill is $450, paying it back over several months instead of in one lump sum on payday is the difference that keeps one bad week from turning into a bad season.
Ask your employer about a paycheck advance. Plenty of small businesses will do it quietly, without a fee, for a worker they trust, and some larger employers offer earned-wage access through payroll. Then look at local help: utility assistance programs, church and nonprofit emergency funds, and county resources built for a one-time crisis. None of them move as fast as a storefront. All of them cost less.
If you own something worth pawning, a pawn loan has one structural advantage: if you can’t pay, you lose the item and nothing else. Read how pawn shops work in St. Louis before you carry anything in. What not to do is trade a payday problem for a bigger one. A title loan puts your car on the line, and title loans in Missouri and car repossession spells out how that can end. And if your real trouble is a paper check you can’t get cashed rather than a shortfall, read how check cashing works in Missouri and what it costs first.
Different worry entirely: a parent relearning to button a coat? What occupational therapy costs here.
### When the due date comes and the account is short
Can you get in trouble for not paying back a payday loan? Yes, but the usual path runs through civil court: a failed debit, collections, possibly a lawsuit, and, if the lender sues and gets a money judgment, garnished wages. That’s serious. It also moves slowly, and every stage of it can be negotiated.
It usually starts small and ugly. The lender deposits your check or pulls the debit, it fails, and your bank charges an overdraft or returned-item fee, often with a fee from the lender on top. Then the phone starts buzzing face down on the counter, the same unfamiliar number at dinner and again at eight the next morning. A licensed lender can send the account to collections or sue for the balance up to the legal ceiling, and after a judgment it can pursue garnishment through the court.
If anyone tells you a warrant is coming, that you’ll be arrested, or that you committed check fraud, write down the date, the name and exactly what was said, then file a complaint with the Division of Finance, which accepts complaints against lenders under its jurisdiction. Before you return a single collection call, read what debt collectors in Missouri can and can’t do, including how garnishment and the statute of limitations work.
### How do you get out of a loan that keeps renewing?
To legally get out of payday loans, take the cleanest exit first: pay the loan on its terms if you possibly can, because that ends it. If you can’t, ask the lender in writing for a payment plan and keep a copy. Then check your own math against the ceiling. Add up every fee and every dollar of interest you’ve paid since the first loan. If it’s already near 75 percent of what you originally borrowed, the lender is close to the legal limit, and you have every right to say so.
A nonprofit credit counselor can call lenders for you, which matters when your voice goes thin every time you pick up the phone. If it’s several debts tangled together, compare debt consolidation in St. Louis before you take on one more loan to pay the others.
And if the payday loan is one debt among many you can’t climb out of, it’s worth looking at the option nobody wants to say out loud. What happens when you file bankruptcy in Missouri explains it plainly, without the shame.
### Get two numbers before you sign
Whether you’re standing at a counter or reading a screen at midnight, you need exactly two numbers before you sign: the total you will pay back, in dollars, and the calendar date it’s due. A licensed Missouri lender can give you both in ten seconds. A shrug is an answer too.
Call two or three licensed lenders and ask each one the same short set of questions:
What is the total I’ll repay, in dollars, and on what date?
If I bring the money back before your next full business day closes, do I owe anything besides what I borrowed?
Since interest is figured daily, what would I owe if I paid early?
If I can’t pay on the due date, what does a renewal cost?
Are you licensed with the Missouri Division of Finance?
Borrow what the bill actually is, not the cap. If the alternator is $450, you don’t need $500 just because $500 is allowed, and you don’t need a 31-day term when your paycheck lands in nine. A lender who pushes the maximum is selling, not helping. Write the answers on the back of the envelope the bill came in, and let the numbers make the call your nerves can’t.

### Frequently asked questions from St. Louis borrowers
### Q. How much would a $200 payday loan cost?
A.  In Missouri, interest and fees on a $200 loan can never top 75 percent of that $200, across the first loan and all renewals combined. Inside that cap, the price depends on the rate the lender posts and how many days you keep the money, since interest is figured daily. Repay before the lender’s next full business day closes and you owe no interest or fees.
### Q. Is a payday loan ever a good idea?
A.  Rarely, and only when three things are true: the amount is small, you know the exact paycheck that will repay it, and every cheaper option has said no. A single loan repaid on the first due date costs one fee and ends. The danger is the second due date. If renewing is likely, the honest answer is no.
### Q. Can you get in trouble for not paying back a payday loan?
A.  It can. Expect bank fees from a failed debit, collection calls, possibly a lawsuit, and, if the lender sues and gets a money judgment, garnished wages. If anyone threatens arrest or a warrant, write down who said it and when, and report it to the Missouri Division of Finance.
### Q. How many payday loans can you have at once in Missouri?
A.  Missouri’s payday rules are written per loan: each loan must be $500 or less, with no more than six renewals. Ask each lender its own policy on holding more than one, and treat a second loan as a warning, not a fix.
### Q. Are payday loans illegal in Missouri?
A.  No. Missouri law authorizes these loans and requires anyone in the business of making these loans to obtain a license from the Division of Finance, under sections 408.500, 408.505 and 408.506. The law caps each loan at $500 for 14 to 31 days, allows six renewals, and limits interest and fees to 75 percent of the original principal. Ask to see the license before you sign.
### Q. How to legally get out of payday loans?
A.  Pay on the original terms if you can, because that ends it cleanly. If not, ask the lender in writing for a payment plan and keep copies. A nonprofit credit counselor can negotiate for you. Check that total interest and fees never top the 75 percent cap. If payday loans are one debt among many, ask a nonprofit counselor or a bankruptcy attorney whether bankruptcy fits.

## Pet Funeral and Cremation in St. Louis: What It Costs and What to Expect
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/pet-funeral-and-cremation-in-st-louis-what-it-costs-and-what-to-expect
A man in University City woke up on a Sunday to find his fourteen-year-old shepherd mix gone, curled on the dog bed by the back door as if he had simply decided not to get up. There was no vet appointment to cancel and nobody on the other end of a phone at seven in the morning. He sat on the kitchen floor for a while. Then he started wondering what you are actually supposed to do with a dog that weighs seventy pounds, and who you call on a weekend.
In Clayton, a family has a Friday appointment they have been dreading for a month. Their cat is nineteen, her kidneys are failing, and the vet has been gentle but clear that it is time. When the clinic called to confirm, the receptionist asked a question nobody in the house was ready for: what would they like done afterward? The parents said they would think about it. They have been thinking about it every night since.
Their ten-year-old has his own answer. He wants a real goodbye, not a cat that leaves in a carrier and never comes back. He has asked whether she can be buried in the yard, whether he can keep something of hers, and whether there is a place where people go to say things out loud. His parents want to say yes to all of it. They just do not know what any of it costs, or what is even allowed inside the city limits.
Every one of them has landed on the same set of questions in the same order: what happens right now, what are the choices, and what is this going to cost? This guide walks through it in that order. We will not quote you a firm price, because rates vary by provider, by the size of your animal, and by what you decide to take home. We will show you how the cost is built, what the options actually mean, and what to ask so you can choose without second-guessing yourself later.
### How much do pet funerals cost in St. Louis?
There is no single price, because the cost depends on what you choose. Communal cremation, where ashes are not returned, often runs under a couple hundred dollars. Private cremation with ashes returned commonly costs a few hundred, rising with the weight of the animal. Urns, paw prints, viewings, and pickup add to it. Confirm every figure with the provider.
The reason there is no single number is that you are choosing from a menu, not buying one thing. The least expensive choice is communal cremation, where your pet is cremated with others and the ashes are scattered by the provider rather than returned. The next step up is private cremation, where your pet is cremated alone and you receive the ashes. Each step adds cost, and each is a legitimate choice.
Then there is everything around the cremation itself. A basic urn or a scatter box is often included; a nicer wooden or ceramic urn is not. A clay paw print, a fur clipping, a viewing before the cremation, and pickup from your home or the clinic are commonly offered as add-ons. None of it is required. The Clayton family might want the paw print and a short viewing for their son. The man in University City might want only the ashes back, or nothing at all.
One honest note before the details. Any range you read online, including the one above, is a starting point. Prices differ from one provider to the next, and a pet aftercare company will usually tell you the exact figure over the phone once you describe your animal and what you want. That call is the only number that counts.
### What happens in the first hours after a pet dies?
The practical answer is simple: keep the body cool, and call someone the same day. You do not have to decide anything permanent in the first hour. You do have to keep your pet in a condition where a vet or crematory can accept them, and in most cases that means a cool room, a towel or blanket, and a phone call before the day is over.
### If your pet dies at home
Start by moving your pet somewhere cool, ideally a basement, a garage in the cooler months, or the coolest room in the house. Wrap them in a towel or blanket, then place that inside a bag or a lined box. If you cannot get them to a provider within a few hours, ice packs around the body help. This is not pleasant to think about, but it protects your options. A pet that has been kept cool can usually be transferred the next morning without any problem.
Then make the call. Your regular vet is often the easiest first contact, because most clinics will accept a pet that died at home and arrange cremation through the crematory they already work with. You can also call a pet crematory directly, and many offer home pickup for an added fee. The man in University City would likely find that a Sunday call reaches an answering service at the clinic but a real person at some crematories. Either route works; pick the one that reaches a human first.
### If your pet dies at the clinic
When a pet is put to sleep at the clinic, the aftercare conversation usually happens before the appointment, which is exactly the question the Clayton family was asked. The clinic will offer communal or private cremation through its partner crematory, and you can usually add an urn or a paw print through the same arrangement. You may also ask to take your pet home for burial. If you have not settled on a regular clinic yet, our guide to choosing a vet in St. Louis for routine pet care covers what to look for, including how a practice handles end-of-life care.
### If the death is sudden and it is after hours
Not every loss comes with a Friday appointment. If a pet dies unexpectedly at night, or is failing fast and you are not sure whether anything can be done, an emergency clinic is the right first call. They handle euthanasia and aftercare arrangements around the clock, and they can tell you honestly whether treatment is still an option. Our guide on finding reliable emergency veterinarian service near you explains how to reach one quickly and what to expect when you arrive.
### What are the options: burial, cremation, or aquamation?
You have four real choices in the St. Louis area: communal cremation, private cremation, aquamation, and burial, either at home where it is allowed or in a pet cemetery. Cremation in one form or another is by far the most common, largely because it is simple and the clinic can arrange it. But the others exist for good reasons, and it helps to know what each one actually means before you pick.
### Communal cremation
Communal, sometimes called group cremation, means your pet is cremated alongside other animals and the ashes are not returned to you. The provider scatters or handles them respectfully, often in a garden or a designated area. It is the least expensive option, commonly under a couple hundred dollars, and it is a perfectly dignified choice. Plenty of owners who do not want ashes in the house choose it deliberately, not just for the price.
### Private or individual cremation
Private cremation means your pet is cremated alone and you receive their ashes, usually within a few days to a week. This is the choice for anyone who wants something to keep, bury, or scatter themselves. It costs more than communal, commonly a few hundred dollars, and the price rises with the weight of the animal because a larger pet takes more time and fuel. Ask whether the provider offers a witnessed or attended option if being present matters to you.
### Aquamation, or water cremation
Aquamation, formally alkaline hydrolysis, uses warm water and a gentle alkaline solution instead of flame to reduce the body to bone, which is then processed into a fine ash and returned to you. It is legal, it is offered by some pet aftercare providers in the region, and many families choose it because it uses less energy and feels gentler. Cost is usually comparable to or somewhat above flame cremation. We will not quote a figure, because it varies; ask any provider that offers it.
### Home burial and pet cemeteries
Home burial is the oldest option and the one the ten-year-old in Clayton asked about first. The catch is that rules vary by municipality. Many cities around St. Louis regulate or restrict burying animals on residential lots, and it is generally not allowed on rented property or near wells and water lines. Before you dig, check your city’s ordinance or call city hall. If it is permitted, bury deep, commonly advised at least three feet, well away from utilities, and mark the spot. A pet cemetery is the alternative for families who want a permanent place to visit; costs vary widely with the plot and the marker, so ask directly.
### What drives the price up or down?
Three things move the number more than anything else: the size of your pet, whether you want the ashes back, and what you add on top. A small cat with communal cremation and no extras sits at the bottom of the range. A large dog with private cremation, a wooden urn, a paw print, home pickup, and a viewing sits near the top. Everything else is rounding by comparison.
### Size and weight
Almost every provider prices private cremation by weight bracket, so a guinea pig, a cat, a beagle, and a seventy-pound shepherd mix each land in a different tier. The jump between tiers can be meaningful. When you call, have a rough weight ready. It is the first thing they will ask, and it lets them quote you accurately instead of guessing.
### What you take home
Ashes returned versus not returned is the single biggest fork in the price. After that, the container matters. A simple scatter box or basic urn is often included with private cremation; an engraved wooden box, a ceramic urn, or a piece of memorial jewelry is extra. Paw prints in clay or ink, nose prints, and fur clippings are usually modest add-ons that families with kids tend to value most. The boy in Clayton would probably treasure a paw print more than any urn.
### Pickup, timing, and viewing
Home pickup adds a fee, and it is often worth it if you cannot lift or transport your pet. Some providers charge more for after-hours or weekend pickup, and some offer a faster turnaround for a premium. A private viewing or a short goodbye room before the cremation is another add-on. None of these are hidden costs so much as choices. A good provider will tell you what each one adds before you commit.
Grief wearing you down? Learn what a DO is and when to see one.
### How do you plan a pet funeral or memorial?
A pet funeral does not have to be formal to be real. Most families do something small: a few words at the burial spot, a photo and a candle on the table, or a walk to the dog’s favorite park with the people who loved him. What matters, especially for children, is that the goodbye happens on purpose rather than by accident. Decide what you want, then build the practical steps around it.
### Giving kids a real goodbye
Children grieve pets fully, and they do better when they are included. Let them see the body if they want to and are old enough, help pick the urn or the burial spot, write a note to go with the pet, or choose a photo for the memorial. The ten-year-old in Clayton is not asking for a production. He is asking to be there when it happens and to have something to hold afterward. A paw print and five minutes of everyone sharing one memory each will do more than any ceremony.
### A simple order of events
If it helps to have a shape, here is one many families use. First, a short viewing or a last hour at home before the transfer. Second, the cremation or burial itself, attended if the provider allows it and you want to be there. Third, a gathering: a meal, a walk, or a few words when the ashes come home. Fourth, something lasting, like a framed photo, a planted tree, or a donation in your pet’s name. If that last one appeals, our guide to what St. Louis animal shelters do and how to help explains where a gift actually goes.
Give yourself permission to skip any of it. The man in University City may want nothing more than the ashes on a shelf beside a leash. That is a memorial too. The goal is not to perform grief. It is to mark that something real ended and that it mattered.
### How do you choose a pet cremation provider?
Interview the provider. Shortlist two or three, whether that is your vet’s partner crematory or companies you call directly, and ask each the same handful of questions. What is included in the price? Is the cremation communal or private? Are ashes returned, and in what container? Can I add a paw print, and is it included or extra? Do you offer pickup, and when? How long until I have the ashes back? Then compare what you want with what each is prepared to provide.
Listen for how the answers are given, not only what they are. A provider who explains the difference between communal and private plainly, tells you the weight tier your pet falls into, and gives you a clear turnaround is doing this well. One who is vague about whether the ashes you receive are your pet’s alone is telling you something. It is fair to ask how they keep private cremations private; established providers have a tracking process and are glad to describe it.
Do not feel obligated to take the first option offered. Your vet’s arrangement is convenient and usually fine, but you are allowed to ask which crematory they use and to call that company yourself, or to choose a different one and have the clinic release your pet to them. Most clinics are used to this. In our experience, families who make one or two calls feel more settled about the decision than those who simply nod at the counter.
Finally, ask about aquamation if it interests you, and ask about attended cremation if being present matters. Not every provider offers either. Knowing that before you commit saves you from finding out after, when there is no going back.

### Q. What is the average cost of cremating an individual pet?

Private, individual cremation with ashes returned commonly costs a few hundred dollars, and the price climbs with the weight of your pet. A small cat sits at the low end; a large dog sits well above it. Urns, paw prints, and pickup add to the base. The exact number comes from calling a provider with your pet’s weight and what you want back.
### Q. What should I do if my pet dies at home?
A.  Keep the body cool and call someone the same day. Move your pet to the coolest room, wrap them in a towel, and place them in a bag or lined box; add ice packs if the transfer will take more than a few hours. Then call your vet or a pet crematory. Most vets will accept a pet that died at home and arrange cremation, and many crematories offer home pickup. You do not have to decide everything right away.
### Q. Can you legally bury a pet on your property?
A.  It depends on where you live. Rules vary by municipality, and many cities around St. Louis regulate or restrict burying animals on residential property. It is generally not permitted on rented property or near wells and water lines. Check your city’s ordinance or call city hall before you dig. Where it is allowed, bury at least three feet deep, well away from utilities, and mark the spot so nobody disturbs it later.
### Q. Is it better to cremate or bury a pet?
A.  Neither is better; they answer different needs. Cremation is simpler, available everywhere, and gives you ashes you can keep, scatter, or bury later. Burial gives you a permanent place to visit but depends on local rules, whether you own the property, and whether you plan to stay. Families who move often lean toward cremation. Families with a yard they will keep for decades sometimes prefer burial. Choose the one you will not regret.
### Q. Is aquamation cheaper than cremation for pets?
A.  Usually not. Aquamation, also called water cremation or alkaline hydrolysis, typically costs about the same as flame cremation or somewhat more, depending on the provider and the size of your pet. Families choose it for the gentler process and lower energy use, not for savings. It is legal and offered by some pet aftercare providers in the region, though not all. Ask any provider you are considering whether they offer it and what it adds.
### Q. How long after a pet dies can you cremate them?
A.  There is no strict deadline, but sooner is easier. If the body is kept cool, a pet can usually be transferred the next day without any issue, and providers regularly accept pets that died a day or two earlier. Cremation itself typically happens within a few days of arrival, and ashes from a private cremation are commonly returned within several days to a week. If you need more time to say goodbye, tell the provider; many can accommodate it.
### Q. Will a vet cremate a dog that died at home?
A.  In most cases, yes. Vets do not usually operate a crematory themselves, but nearly all work with a partner crematory and will accept a pet that died at home, hold them appropriately, and arrange communal or private cremation on your behalf. Call ahead so they are ready when you arrive. If your regular clinic is closed, an emergency clinic or a pet crematory that offers pickup can do the same thing.
### Q. What if I can’t afford to cremate my dog?
A.  Start by asking for communal cremation, which is the least expensive option and often under a couple hundred dollars. Tell your vet or the crematory honestly what you can afford; some will work with you or point you toward help. Local animal welfare groups occasionally know of assistance. Home burial, where your city allows it and you own the property, costs nothing beyond the effort. A dignified goodbye does not require the most expensive choice.

## $4 or $50 Before Puppy Class: What Dog Training Really Costs in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/dog-training-in-st-louis-what-it-costs-and-how-to-choose-a-trainer
Four dollars or fifty. That is the first bill a St. Louis puppy runs up, and it doesn’t go to a trainer. It goes to the City. Under the City of St. Louis pet registration rule, every dog kept in the city has to be vaccinated for rabies and registered, and a puppy has to get that first rabies shot and be registered between 3 and 4 months old. Registration costs $4.00 for a spayed or neutered dog and $50.00 for an intact one. No training quote will ever mention that $46 swing.
It happens on a cold steel exam table. The puppy scrabbles for grip, the shot is over before he notices, and on the way out your vet should hand you the City registration certificate and the tag. The tag clicks onto the collar or harness and stays there. The City says to keep it on the dog at all times. The certificate goes in a folder you can find in the dark, because an Animal Care and Control Officer or a police officer can ask to see it, and letting it lapse can bring a ticket and a fine. Just adopted? New arrivals get a 30-day grace period. Tonight, pull out the adoption or breeder paperwork, find the birth date, count forward three months and four months, and write both dates on the fridge. That is your window.
A week later that new tag jingles against the D-ring on a sticky evening in Tower Grove Park. Cicadas grind in the trees. Sweat crawls down the back of your shirt, your pocket is greasy with cut-up hot dog, and a ten-week-old corkscrews at the end of the leash because a squirrel just crossed the path. The leash zips through your fist and leaves a thin red line across your palm. This is the moment most people decide to pay someone to fix the dog. They have it backwards. The dog is the fast learner. The slow, expensive student is the one holding the leash: the timing, the tone, the hand that reaches for the treat half a second after the sit instead of during it.
That one truth rearranges every training price in this city. A modest class you actually practice beats a pricey program that sends home a dog who only listens to somebody else. A two-week stay that skips the lesson for you is the most expensive way there is to borrow good manners.
Cross Skinker into the County and the clock stays the same while the numbers shrink. A copy of St. Louis County Ordinance 611.050 posted by PETA sets the same window, on or before 4 months and not before 3, and lists a three-year certificate and tag at $20.00 for a spayed or neutered dog and $40.00 if not. Here is the line worth saying out loud at the dog park: in the City, an intact puppy’s tag costs twelve and a half times what a neutered one pays, and in the County a neutered dog is covered for three years for half the intact price. Those County figures come from that outside copy, so confirm them by phone before you budget.
### How much does dog training cost in St. Louis?
Dog training is sold by format, not by the dog: group classes commonly run in the low-to-mid hundreds for a full course, private sessions bill per hour, and board-and-train commonly reaches the low thousands. In the City of St. Louis, budget for the rabies shot and registration too: $4 for a spayed or neutered dog, $50 if intact. Trainers set their own rates, those ranges are rules of thumb I could not verify against any published St. Louis price list, and I could not find a local average worth repeating, so here is how to get your real number in one evening.
Pick one format first, say a group puppy class, then call two or three trainers who offer it and ask each for the same three numbers: the price per session, how many sessions the course runs, and the total, in writing, with anything extra spelled out. Ask what vaccine proof they want for puppies, and keep it in the same folder as the City certificate. Then compare totals, not hourly rates. A cheap hour inside a long package can cost more than a pricey hour in a short one.
If you went hunting for the average cost of training a dog and came back with a few hundred for a weeknight class and a few thousand for a two-week stay, nobody is necessarily gouging you. A group class buys a spot on the floor one evening a week. A private session buys one trainer’s full attention, often sold as a bundle of visits. Board-and-train buys room, board and daily sessions for a couple of weeks or more. Different products, same word.
While you have each trainer on the phone, ask three more things. What happens when the dog gets it right, and what happens when he gets it wrong? You want food, play, praise and management, not pain or intimidation. What exactly does the price include: written homework, help between visits? And what happens if your dog does not progress? A plan is a green light. A guarantee is a red one, because nobody controls a living animal on a schedule.
### Does the County rule apply in Maplewood and Chesterfield?
Maplewood and Chesterfield sit in St. Louis County, not the City, so the County rule is the one to read. A copy of County Ordinance 611.050 posted by PETA requires a puppy to be vaccinated for rabies and registered on or before 4 months old, and not before 3. It lists combined certificate-and-tag fees of $8.00 for one year or $20.00 for three if the dog is spayed or neutered, and $16.00 or $40.00 if not. Those fees come from an outside copy, so call the County before you budget, and ask your city hall too, in case it adds a license of its own.
### Group class, private hour or a two-week stay?
The formats differ in who holds the leash, where the work happens and how many of the trainer’s hours you are buying. Pick the one you will actually show up for. The cheap course you quit after two weeks is the priciest line on the list.
### Group classes
Usually a course with one session a week, with a handful of dogs and owners sharing a room. You handle and the trainer coaches. It suits puppies who need to meet the world and adult dogs who need basic manners and can stay calm near other dogs. It is a poor fit for the dog who spends the hour trembling under your chair or lunging at the beagle across the room. You will know which dog you have within a minute of walking in.
### Private sessions
Priced per hour or per session. The trainer comes to the problem: your front door, your stoop, the stretch of Soulard sidewalk where the mail truck squeals to a stop and your dog loses his mind. That is exactly what a dog who is an angel indoors and a freight train on a leash needs. Private work costs more per hour and often needs fewer hours, because none of them are spent waiting your turn.
### Day training and board-and-train
Day training means the trainer works your dog while you are at work, then hands off what they taught. Board-and-train goes further: the dog lives with the trainer for a couple of weeks or more. It is the most expensive format because you are paying for housing, daily sessions and round-the-clock care. The quiet house is real. So is the risk that the dog comes home polished for a voice that is not yours. If your dog already stays somewhere when you travel, our guide to dog boarding and daycare in St. Louis breaks down how that side of the bill is built.
### Three things push a quote up
What you are trying to fix, where the work happens, and what the trainer brings in training and accountability. A puppy learning sit on a rubber mat and an adult dog with a bite history working privately with a behavior specialist are not the same job, and they should not cost the same.
### The problem you are solving
Manners are cheaper than behavior problems. Sit, down, stay and loose-leash walking are predictable work that fits a class. Fear, aggression, separation anxiety and guarding a food bowl are slower and riskier, and usually call for private sessions or a specialist. If the barking at the mail carrier is pure excitement, a few sessions may settle it. If the hair along his spine stands up and his mouth clamps shut, that is a different job, and a trainer who quotes it cheap and fast should make your stomach drop a little.
### Where the work happens
A trainer who drives to your house is selling drive time along with training time, so in-home sessions commonly cost more than the same hour at a facility. A facility carries rent, insurance and the mop bucket, and that shows up in class prices. Packages usually lower the per-session cost.
### Credentials
A credential is the check you can actually run. The CCPDT, which issues the CPDT-KA, says its certificants are tested on humane, science-based training knowledge and skill, must keep earning continuing education credits, and follow its Standards of Practice and Code of Ethics. The CPDT-KA renews every three years, so ask when the trainer last renewed. For true behavior problems, a veterinary behaviorist is a veterinarian with specialty training, and the fee reflects that.
Unrelated, but tempting on a clear fall weekend: renting a motorcycle in St. Louis, explained.
### When should training start?
Sooner than most people think, and later than most people fear. Puppies can start socialization and basic classes once the vet clears them, and the veterinary behavior specialists of the AVSAB say a puppy can begin socializing, perhaps in a puppy class, as early as 7 to 8 weeks old, with only one set of vaccinations needed first. Adult dogs can be trained at any age. An older dog is not untrainable. He just needs more repetition to overwrite habits he has rehearsed for years.
A chewing ten-week-old is not too young for class. He is right on time. The stretch when a puppy takes in new people, the hiss of bus brakes, the clank of a storm grate and the cold of wet grass without fear closes faster than the window for teaching sit, and a good puppy class spends as much time on that exposure as on commands. Those dates on the fridge help here too: book the class and the rabies appointment in the same week. Before the first session, our list of what to buy at a pet store for a new puppy covers the leash, treats and crate you will be asked to bring.
Rescues run on a different clock. Rescue groups point to the 3-3-3 rule: roughly three days to decompress, three weeks to learn the routine, three months to feel at home. It is a rule of thumb, not a schedule. A dog three weeks out of the shelter is still learning which hook the leash hangs on. Start gentle basics right away, but judge the pulling after he settles.
Brace for the middle, too. For a lot of households the hardest stretch comes a few months in: teething, short nights, house training almost done but not quite, and the new-puppy glow worn thin. Waiting for a problem to get bad before you pay someone only makes it pricier. If it already annoys you, he has already practiced it plenty.
Your next step tonight: open the list of dog trainers across the St. Louis metro, pick two or three who offer the same format, and ask each for the per-session price, the number of sessions and the written total. Keep a notepad by the phone. The trainer who gets curious about your dog before quoting a package is usually the one worth paying.
If you’re the trainer, the training school or the one-person crew these owners should be calling, put your business where they are already looking and get more customers.
### How do you interview a trainer before you pay?
Treat the first call like a job interview, because it is one. Ask everyone on your shortlist the same questions, then compare answers, not price tags.
### Listen hard to the methods answer
You want plain words: food, play, praise, and management for mistakes. A trainer who leans on prong collars, shock collars or “showing the dog who’s boss” is not the trainer you want holding the leash of a fearful dog. If the answer is vague, ask again. If it stays vague, thank them and hang up.
### Pin down the handoff
For board-and-train, ask how many hours a day the dog is actually worked, where he sleeps, who else handles him and how the training gets handed back to you. That handoff decides everything, because the dog learned the trainer, not you. A program that skips it is renting you a well-behaved dog for two weeks.
### Run the ordinary checks
Read recent reviews and notice whether owners describe what their dog can do now, not just how nice the trainer was. Ask for proof of insurance. Ask to watch a class before you enroll. A package pitched before you finish your first sentence is a sales call.
### The rest of the week belongs to you
A trainer sees your dog for an hour a week at best. You get every other hour. Short daily sessions, a few minutes several times a day, beat one long weekly marathon, because dogs learn in reps and lose focus fast. That is the honest answer to how often you should train a dog: every day, briefly, tied to things you already do. A sit before the bowl hits the floor. A stay before the door swings open.
St. Louis summers make that easier to stick to. When the air is thick enough to drink and the sidewalk is hot under your palm, a long session helps nobody. Run your reps in the cool of the kitchen and save the leash work for dawn or after dark.
Use the trainer’s homework, not your own ideas, at least at first. If class taught a hand signal and a marker word, everyone in the house uses those. A dog will never learn loose-leash walking if one person lets him tow them down the block and another stops dead every time the leash goes tight.
Manage what you cannot train yet. Gate off the room with the good trim. Keep chargers on the counter. Walk the puller at a quieter hour. When the leash work is ready for a final exam, take it to one of the best dog parks in St. Louis and finish the walk there. Once the manners hold, our guide to dog-friendly places in St. Louis shows where a well-mannered dog can come along.
Keep a two-line log each day. A dog who barked at the mail carrier for forty seconds on Monday and eight on Friday is improving, even if Friday still rattled the windows.
### When it stops being a training problem
Some dogs need more than a trainer. Stiff freezes, hard stares, growling over a toy, panic that shreds a crate, a bite that broke skin: those can point to fear or a medical issue, not manners. Start with your vet, then read our guide on when to call a dog behaviorist in St. Louis. It may cost more up front. It is also the road most likely to hand you back a dog you can relax around, and a walk you actually look forward to.
### Frequently asked before you hire a trainer
### What is the average cost of training a dog?
Training is priced by format, so one average hides more than it shows. A group class commonly runs in the low-to-mid hundreds, private sessions are billed per hour or in packages, and board-and-train commonly reaches the low thousands. Ask each trainer for the total in writing, including what happens between sessions.
### How much will it cost to train a dog?
Budget beyond the trainer. Add a leash, treats and a crate, plus the rabies shot and registration. In the City of St. Louis, a puppy’s registration is $50 if intact and $4 if spayed or neutered, due between 3 and 4 months old. Then choose the format you will actually practice, because skipped homework is wasted money.
### Is it worth it to send a dog to training?
It can be, but a board-and-train stay only holds if the handoff is done well. The dog learns the trainer, not you, so the program must include lessons for your family afterward. With time to practice, a class or private sessions can teach the same skills.
### How many training sessions does a dog need?
It depends on the dog and the goal. Basic manners commonly fit one group course. A single problem like leash pulling might take a handful of private sessions plus daily homework. Fear or aggression can take months. A good trainer estimates after meeting your dog, and the number usually shrinks when you practice at home.
### What is the 3-3-3 rule for dog training?
Rescue groups use it for newly adopted dogs: roughly three days to decompress, three weeks to learn the household routine and three months to feel at home. It is not a schedule, and many dogs move faster or slower. Start gentle basics early, but judge a rescue’s behavior after he settles, not in week one.
### At what age should you start puppy training classes?
As soon as your vet clears it. The AVSAB says puppy socialization can begin as early as 7 to 8 weeks, after one set of vaccinations. Early weeks teach a puppy whether the world is safe, so socialization matters as much as commands. In the City of St. Louis, pair the class with the rabies shot and registration due between 3 and 4 months old.
### At what age is it harder to train a dog?
Training gets harder as a habit gets older, not as the dog does. A young puppy soaks up everything, good lessons and bad. An adult who has pulled or barked for years needs more repetition to overwrite it. Seniors learn fine but may tire sooner. Practice, not age, is the obstacle.
### How often should you train a dog?
Daily, in short bursts. A few minutes several times a day beats one long weekly session, because dogs learn by repetition and lose focus quickly. Tie practice to routines you already have: a sit before the bowl, a stay before the door, a few loose-leash steps as every walk begins. Let one weekly class supply the coaching.
### What is the hardest month for a puppy?
It depends on the puppy and the house. The hard month is the one where the puppy is teething, nights are short, house training is almost done but not quite, and the new-puppy patience has worn thin. It gets better, faster with a class and a steady routine. If you are there now, you are not failing.

## Buying an RV in St. Louis: What First-Time Buyers Should Know
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/buying-an-rv-in-st-louis-what-first-time-buyers-should-know
A young family in Webster Groves rented a small camper last summer for a week at a state park, and they came home with the bug. The kids slept through two thunderstorms, the parents drank coffee outside every morning, and nobody looked at a screen for five days. Now the parents are scrolling listings at night, and every unit looks reasonable right up until the payment calculator loads.
A couple in St. Louis County is six months from retirement and pricing a motorhome for a long loop west, the trip they have talked about for twenty years. They want a real bed, a real bathroom, and enough room that a rainy day does not turn into an argument. What they don’t have yet is a clear picture of what that motorhome costs to own once it is sitting in the driveway with the engine off.
Then there is the guy with a half-ton pickup who is not sure what it can actually tow. His neighbor says the truck will pull anything on the lot. The sticker in his door jamb says something more specific, and he has never read it. He is one confident salesperson away from buying a trailer his truck should not be pulling down a long grade on the interstate.
All three are asking the same structural question, even if it sounds different in each driveway: what kind of RV fits a first-time buyer, and what does it really take to own one? This guide walks through it in order. The types, the true cost of ownership, new versus used, how to inspect a unit on the lot, how to interview a dealer, and what Missouri needs from you at title time. We won’t quote a price you should trust over a written one, and we won’t name a brand. We will show you how to think it through.
### What type of RV is best for a first-time buyer?
For most first-time buyers, a modest travel trailer or a small Class C motorhome is the right fit. Both are forgiving to drive or tow, easier to store, and cheaper to insure and maintain than a big fifth wheel or Class A. Match the unit to the vehicle you already own and the trips you will actually take.
The reasoning is simple once you see what goes wrong for first-timers. Most buyers who regret an RV bought too much of one. A large fifth wheel needs a heavy-duty pickup. A Class A needs a place to park it and a comfort level with driving something the size of a bus. A modest trailer or a small Class C asks much less of you while you learn what you actually like.
It also keeps your exit cheap. RVs lose value quickly in their first few years, and the bigger the unit, the bigger the number you lose. If the Webster Groves family discovers after two seasons that they really want a camper van, a used travel trailer is far easier to sell or trade than a forty-foot motorhome they financed for fifteen years.
That said, the right type depends on three things: what you already drive, where you will store it, and how you will use it. The retiring couple heading west for months at a time has a different answer than a family doing long weekends within a few hours of St. Louis. Start with those three facts, and the type usually picks itself.
### What are the main types of RV and who are they for?
RVs split into two families: towables you pull behind a vehicle, and motorized units you drive. Towables include pop-ups, travel trailers, and fifth wheels. Motorized units are sold as Class A, Class B, and Class C. Each one trades off cost, space, and how demanding it is to drive, park, and store, so the honest first step is knowing which family fits your life.
### Towables: pop-ups, travel trailers, and fifth wheels
A pop-up is the lightest and cheapest way in, with canvas sides that fold out into sleeping areas. Many mid-size SUVs can pull one. A travel trailer is a hard-sided box on its own axles, from tiny teardrops to units longer than a city bus, and it needs a tow vehicle with a proper hitch and enough capacity to handle the loaded weight.
A fifth wheel is the biggest towable, and it needs a pickup with a hitch mounted in the bed, not on the bumper. Fifth wheels tow more steadily than a long travel trailer, but they take the whole truck bed, and the truck has to be rated for the weight. That is not a first-timer rig for most people, and that is fine.
### Motorized: Class A, Class B, and Class C
Class A is the big bus-style motorhome, built on a heavy chassis, with the most living space and the highest running costs. Class B is a camper van, easy to drive and park anywhere a van fits, with the tightest quarters. Class C sits in the middle: a cab-over bunk on a truck or van chassis, with a real bathroom and kitchen, and a driving feel closer to a moving truck than a bus.
Motorhomes let passengers stretch out on the road, and there is no hitching or unhitching at the campsite. The trade is that the whole home goes wherever you go, including to the grocery store, unless you tow a car behind it. That is why the retiring couple should be honest about how they will run errands on a two-month loop.
### The tow vehicle question
This is where the guy with the half-ton pickup needs to slow down. Three numbers have to line up: the tow rating of his truck, the loaded weight of the trailer, known as its GVWR, and the tongue weight pressing down on the hitch. Salespeople can be optimistic about all three. The only figure that counts is the label on his own door jamb, and he should read it before he reads a single listing.
A trailer that fits the rating on paper when empty can exceed it once you add water, propane, gear, and a family. In our experience, a comfortable margin under the rating makes for a calmer drive and far less wear on the truck. If the numbers are close, look at a lighter trailer, not a bigger truck payment.
### What does an RV really cost to own, beyond the sticker?
Plan on the purchase price being the beginning, not the whole story. An RV carries financing, insurance, Missouri personal property tax every year, registration and title fees, storage if you cannot keep it at home, maintenance and winterizing, campground fees, fuel, tires, and depreciation. None of those show up on the hang tag, and together they change what you can actually afford.
### Taxes, title, insurance, and financing
In Missouri, RVs and trailers are taxed as personal property, assessed by the county where you live, and the bill arrives every year for as long as you own the unit. You pay sales tax to the Missouri Department of Revenue when you title it, and you register it much like a vehicle. Check the Department of Revenue for current fees rather than trusting a number from a forum post.
Insurance is its own line, and it runs higher on motorhomes than on trailers because a motorhome is also a vehicle. RV loans often stretch longer than car loans, which keeps the monthly payment down but means you can owe more than the unit is worth for years. Ask yourself whether you would be comfortable selling in year three. If the answer is no, borrow less.
### Storage, maintenance, and winterizing
Ask where the RV will live before you buy it, because that answer has a price. Many municipalities and HOAs restrict driveway RV parking, and the Webster Groves family should read their city code and their covenants before assuming the side yard works. If it does not, you are paying a monthly storage bill. Our guide to how much self storage costs in St. Louis explains how that market prices space, and RV lots follow similar logic.
Maintenance is steady rather than dramatic. Roof seals need checking, tires age out before they wear out, and every fall the water system has to be winterized so a January freeze does not split a line. Skip that step once, and you learn what a plumbing repair costs on a unit built for weight, not for access.
### Fuel, campgrounds, and depreciation
Motorhomes get single-digit to low-teens miles per gallon, so the retiring couple’s loop west has a fuel line that can rival the campground line. A trailer drags your truck’s mileage down too. Campground fees vary widely by park and season. Our guide to how to book a campsite near St. Louis walks through how reservations and pricing work at parks close to home.
Depreciation is the quiet one. RVs lose value quickly in the first years, and the drop is steepest on new units. That is not a reason to skip buying. It is a reason to buy what you will actually use, so the value you lose is paid back in trips you took instead of weekends the rig sat under a tarp.
### New or used: which makes more sense for a first buyer?
For most first-timers, a well-kept used unit a few years old is the sensible answer. Someone else has absorbed the steepest depreciation, and the early build issues have usually been found and fixed. New wins on warranty, current layouts, and the peace of mind that nobody has ignored a roof seal. The trade is that you pay for that peace of mind twice: once at the counter and again when you sell.
Timing matters on both. Late fall through winter is commonly a slower sales period around St. Louis, and end-of-model-year clearances put pressure on dealers to move the units they have. RV shows bundle promotions in the same way. None of that guarantees a specific discount, and we won’t pretend it does, but a buyer who shops in the slow months usually finds a dealer more willing to talk.
Used carries one rule that is not optional: get it inspected. The logic is the same one we lay out in what to know before buying a used boat in Missouri. A unit that spends its life outdoors hides water damage well, and water damage is the expensive defect. A few hundred dollars for a professional look is cheap next to a delaminated wall.
Big group, one night? See what a party bus costs in St. Louis.
### How do you inspect an RV on the lot?
Start with water, because water intrusion and delamination are the most expensive common defects in an RV. Walk the roof seals, press on the floors and walls for soft spots, open every cabinet, and breathe in. A musty smell is a finding, not a mood. If you are serious about a used unit, hire an independent inspector. NRVIA-certified inspectors exist and do exactly this for a living.
### Roof, seals, and soft spots
Get on a ladder if the dealer allows it, or ask them to show you the roof. Look at every seam, vent, and antenna base for cracked or lifted sealant. Inside, push on the floor near the door, around the shower, and under the windows, where leaks show up first. A bubble or ripple in the exterior wall is delamination, which means water got behind the fiberglass. Walk away, or price it as a project.
### Systems, tires, and the underside
Run everything. Water pump, water heater, furnace, air conditioner, refrigerator on every mode it has, slides in and out, awning out and in. Then crouch and look underneath for rust, hanging wires, damaged tanks, and tired tires. Check the date code on the sidewall, because RV tires often age out while still showing tread. The dealer should let you do all of this. If they rush you, that is information.
### How do you interview an RV dealer before you sign?
Shortlist two or three dealers, then treat each visit like an interview where you are the one hiring. State plainly what you want: the type, your out-the-door budget, what you will tow with, and how you will actually use it. Then compare that with what each dealer is prepared to provide. The gap between what you asked for and what they steer you toward is the signal.
A good dealer hears “a modest travel trailer, this truck, long weekends” and shows you units that match. A less good one hears the same thing and walks you to the biggest fifth wheel on the lot. Neither is dishonest, exactly, but only one is listening. The guy with the half-ton pickup should bring his door-jamb numbers written down and watch what happens when he says them out loud.
Ask practical questions and notice how they land. Can you have a unit inspected by someone you hire? What does their pre-delivery inspection cover? How does service scheduling work in spring, when every owner in St. Louis County wants an appointment the same week? Who do you call the first time a slide sticks at a campground? A dealer who answers those without flinching is the one you want a relationship with, and buying an RV is a relationship.
The financing conversation deserves the same discipline. Our guide to buying a car from a St. Louis dealership covers keeping the vehicle price and the loan terms separate, and the same rule applies here, only with a longer loan. Know your out-the-door number, know your payment ceiling, and don’t let one blur the other.
One thing not to do: don’t walk in expecting a dealer to hand over a breakdown of their cost or margin. They won’t, and asking sours the room. Ask instead for the out-the-door price in writing, with every fee named, and compare that across your shortlist. That is a fair question, and a dealer who is proud of their number answers it quickly.
### What paperwork does Missouri require?
Missouri treats a motorhome like any other vehicle: it is titled and registered through the Department of Revenue, and you pay sales tax when you title it. Trailers are titled and registered too. You have 30 days from the purchase date to title the unit, and missing that window brings penalties. Check the Missouri Department of Revenue for current fees rather than trusting any figure you read online, including here.
Buying from a dealer usually means they handle the title application and gather the paperwork. Buying from a private seller means you carry the signed title, a bill of sale, and proof of insurance to a license office yourself. Either way, confirm the title is clean and the seller’s name matches before money moves. Then budget for the personal property tax bill, because the county will find you either way.
