### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Can I use Dawn dish soap to clean my hat?
A.  A plain, dye-free dish soap is the standard home method, and any basic one in that category does the job, since what you need is something that lifts body oil in cool water. Skip anything with added dye, bleach, brighteners, or heavy scent. Use a few drops swirled into a sink of water rather than soap applied straight to the fabric, and test the underside of the brim first on a colored or reproduction cap.
### Q. What’s the best way to get sweat stains out of a baseball cap?
A.  Pretreat the band before you soak anything. Work a thin baking soda paste or a dab of mild soap into the stained area with a soft brush, let it sit fifteen minutes, then soak the cap in cool water and rinse. Repeat once if it helps. Stay away from bleach and hot water, which set the discoloration and can yellow white fabric permanently. Old salt rings lighten; they usually do not disappear.
### Q. Will washing a cap ruin the brim?
A.  Hand washing in cool water, no. Machines and dryers, often yes. The brim is a stiffener sandwiched between fabric, pressed cardboard in older caps and thin plastic in most modern ones. Heat softens plastic until it warps and saturates cardboard until it buckles, and agitation creases both. Keep the water cool, avoid bending the brim while it is wet, and dry it curved over a bowl so it sets in the shape you want.
### Q. Is it better to wash baseball caps in the dishwasher or washer?
A.  Neither, honestly. Dishwasher detergent is harsh on dyes and fabric, and the heat in that cycle is what deforms a brim. A washing machine adds agitation and a spin cycle that are rough on stitching and shape. Hand washing in a sink takes about ten minutes of actual effort and risks almost nothing. If you are going to use a machine anyway, a cold gentle cycle with the cap in a frame, then air drying, is the least damaging version.
### Q. How do I convert hat size to inches?
A.  Multiply the hat size by pi, about 3.14, to get head circumference in inches, and divide to go the other direction. A size 7 works out to roughly 22 inches around. Each eighth of a size is a bit under half an inch of circumference, so small steps matter. Centimeters are simpler, since European sizes are just the circumference in centimeters. Land between sizes and you go up, then add sizing tape inside the band.
### Q. What’s the average adult head size?
A.  There is no single figure worth quoting, and published numbers vary depending on the population measured and how the measurement was taken. The useful part is that most adult heads land in a fairly narrow band, which is why the common run of sizes covers nearly everyone and why small, medium, and large sells at all. Your own measurement is the only number that helps you at the counter, so take it before you shop.
### Q. How to make a hat keep its shape?
A.  Handle it by the brim, front and back, instead of pinching the crown every time you pick it up, since that pinch wears one spot thin over years. Store it upside down on the crown or on a stand. Stuff the crown when you pack it. Keep it out of hot cars and attics, let it air dry on its own when it gets wet, and have felt steamed and reshaped occasionally rather than once it is badly crushed.
### Q. Should hats be stored upside down?
A.  For stiff-brim felt and straw hats, yes. Resting on the crown keeps all the weight off the brim, so the curl holds instead of slowly flattening. Caps and soft bucket hats do not need it, and a shelf or a rack is fine for them, as long as you stop hanging them by the visor. If a hat has a fragile or decorated crown, a hat stand or a stuffed crown on a shelf beats both options.

## What a Juice Bar Actually Sells in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-juice-bar-actually-sells-in-st-louis
Five mornings a week, same order. A woman in Truesdale had been buying the same green juice on her way to work since spring, and she couldn’t have told you what was in it past “kale and something.” She felt better on the days she drank it. She also felt the cost of it. When she finally asked the guy behind the counter what made his juice different from the bottle at the grocery store, he gave her a real answer, and it took about four minutes.
Down in Pine Lawn, a man bought a three-day cleanse as a reset after a rough stretch of eating out. Six bottles a day, numbered, drink them in order. By the second afternoon he had a headache and was standing in his kitchen thinking about a turkey sandwich the way other people think about a vacation. Nobody had warned him that the hardest part usually isn’t hunger. It’s the missing coffee.
And a mom in Wilbur Park buys her kid an acai bowl after Saturday practice because it reads as the healthy pick on the menu board. Sometimes it is. Sometimes it carries more sugar than a scoop of ice cream, and the acai has nothing to do with it. The sugar comes from the sweetened sorbet base, the fruit juice blended in, the honey drizzle, and the granola on top.
Three customers, one counter, three completely different products. What follows is what a juice bar is really selling you: how cold-pressed juice gets made and why it costs what it costs, how it differs from fresh-squeezed and from the bottles in a cooler, what a cleanse package actually consists of and how the pricing is built, what a smoothie or an acai bowl is nutritionally once you strip the marketing off, what the add-ins and wellness shots do and don’t do, and who should be careful. No brand names. No promises. Just the parts that decide whether the juice counter earns a spot in your week.
### Are cold-pressed juices actually good for you?
Fresh juice delivers real vitamins, potassium, and plant compounds, and for someone who eats almost no produce it’s a genuine upgrade. But juicing removes the fiber and leaves the sugar behind. A vegetable-forward green juice is worth the money. A big fruit juice behaves a lot like soda with a better reputation.
Here’s the part that gets skipped at the register. Fiber is most of what makes whole fruit behave well in your body. It slows the sugar down, feeds gut bacteria, and fills you up. Juicing throws that away by design, since the pulp is the fiber and the pulp goes in the bin. What’s left is water, sugar, acids, minerals, and a load of vitamins and polyphenols. That mix is not junk. It is also not a salad in a cup.
Ratio decides almost everything. A juice built on cucumber, celery, kale, and lemon with a single small apple lands in a very different place than one built on apple, pineapple, orange, and a garnish of spinach. Both are green. Only one is a vegetable drink. Ask what the first two ingredients are by volume, because ingredients are usually listed heaviest first, and the front of the list is where the sugar hides.
There’s a real upside worth saying out loud. Most Americans fall short of the daily produce recommendation, according to the CDC’s own surveillance reporting, and getting a concentrated hit of vegetables in a form you’ll actually swallow beats the vegetables you meant to cook and didn’t. Juice also hydrates. For someone recovering from a stomach bug, or working outside in August, that matters more than the macro argument.
The honest limits: it will not detoxify you, because your liver and kidneys already do that around the clock and don’t take requests. It will not cure anything. Raw juice is unpasteurized, so public-health guidance has long steered pregnant women, young children, older adults, and anyone immunocompromised toward pasteurized products instead. And if you’re managing blood sugar, a fruit juice on an empty stomach is one of the faster ways to spike it.
### How is cold-pressed juice actually made?
Produce gets ground into a wet mash, packed into a heavy filter bag, and squeezed under a hydraulic press at extreme pressure. No blade spinning at speed, so almost no friction heat and much less air whipped into the liquid. The result is denser, separates less violently, and takes a lot more produce per bottle.
Compare that to a centrifugal juicer, which is what most people own at home. A flat blade spins fast against a mesh basket, shredding the produce and flinging the juice out through the screen. It’s quick and it’s loud. It also drags in oxygen and a little heat, which is why centrifugal juice foams on top, browns faster, and tastes flatter an hour later. Neither method is a scandal. They’re just different tools with different yields.
### Cold-pressed, fresh-squeezed, and bottled are three different things
Fresh-squeezed usually means citrus on a reamer or a lever press, made in front of you, drunk within the hour. Nothing wrong with it. It’s simply a narrower category, since you can’t squeeze kale on a citrus press. Cold-pressed covers the whole produce aisle and needs the grinder-and-press setup, which is expensive equipment and part of what you’re paying for.
Bottled juice sold off a shelf is where the label gets slippery. Some of it is heat pasteurized, which kills microbes and dulls flavor. Some is treated with high pressure processing, sometimes shown as HPP, where sealed bottles sit in a cold water chamber under enormous pressure to knock down bacteria without heat. HPP juice can legitimately call itself cold-pressed, because it was pressed cold, and it can still be weeks old. Raw, untreated juice usually carries a short refrigerated shelf life measured in days, which is exactly why a real juice bar makes small batches.
### Why one bottle costs what it costs
Pounds of produce go in and a modest volume of liquid comes out. Leafy greens are the worst offenders, since a heaping bag of kale yields a splash. Add the labor of washing and prepping, the press itself, the short shelf life that guarantees some waste, and the fact that good produce isn’t cheap. That is the whole pricing story. The same math is why an independent grocery charges what it does, which the rundown of what a health food store actually sells gets into. A counter sourcing from metro-area farmers markets in summer has an ingredient cost that moves week to week.
### What is really in a juice cleanse, and how is it priced?
A cleanse is a numbered set of bottles for each day, usually five or six, meant to be drunk in a set order. Greens early, sweeter blends midday, something creamy like a nut milk at night, often a ginger or lemon-cayenne shot. Strip away the packaging and it’s a short, low-protein, low-calorie liquid diet.
The sequencing isn’t random, and most shops will explain it if you ask. Green juices go early because they’re lowest in sugar and easiest on an empty stomach. Root-vegetable blends with beet or carrot land mid-afternoon when energy sags. The nut milk sits at the end because fat and a little protein make the evening survivable. Some packages add a broth or a raw soup, which is a sensible upgrade for anyone doing more than one day.
### How cleanse pricing is usually structured
Pricing is built one of three ways, and shops mix them. Per day is the most common, with a per-day rate that often drops slightly on a three-day or five-day package. Per bottle count matters because a six-bottle day costs more than a four-bottle day. Bottle size is the quiet variable, since a 12-ounce and a 16-ounce program can be advertised the same way. Delivery, glass bottle deposits, and subscriptions add another layer. Published figures vary all over the map, so ask the counter directly: how many bottles, what size, per day or per package, and what happens to the price if you do three days instead of one.
### What a cleanse actually does, and doesn’t
People report feeling lighter and sleeping better. Some of that is real, since you’ve stopped eating fried food and drinking alcohol for three days. The scale moves, mostly water and gut contents, and it moves back. The headaches that show up on day one or two are frequently caffeine withdrawal rather than toxins leaving, which is why tapering coffee the week before makes the whole thing easier. Protein intake during a juice-only stretch is very low, and that’s the piece that argues against running one for a long time.
A guy in North Venice told his counter he wanted to break a fast-food habit. They talked him down to one cleanse day plus two days of juice with real meals. That’s the conversation worth having. If the shop’s only answer is a longer package, you’ve learned something.
### Are smoothies and acai bowls actually healthy?
A smoothie blends the whole fruit, so the fiber stays in, which makes it fundamentally different from juice. That’s a real advantage. The trouble is everything else in the cup: fruit juice as the liquid base, sherbet or frozen yogurt, honey, agave, and portions that ran up to 24 and 32 ounces years ago and never came back down.
Ask what the liquid is. Water, unsweetened almond milk, or plain dairy milk keeps a smoothie sane. Apple juice or a fruit-punch base doubles the sugar before a single berry goes in. Ask whether there’s added sweetener, because plenty of recipes carry honey or agave by default and most shops will leave it out if you say so. Greek yogurt or a protein scoop turns a sugar drink into something that holds you until lunch.
### The acai bowl, honestly
Acai itself is a dark purple palm berry, low in sugar and genuinely bitter on its own. Almost nobody serves it that way. The standard frozen pack comes sweetened, and sorbet-style bases add more. Then the toppings stack up: granola with its own added sugar, banana, berries, coconut flakes, nut butter, a honey drizzle, maybe chocolate. Each one is defensible. Together, in a bowl the size of your face, they add up to a dessert with excellent public relations.
None of that means skip it. It means order it like you know what it is. Ask for the unsweetened pack if they carry one, take half the granola, skip the drizzle, and eat it as a meal rather than a snack between meals. A bowl after a hard workout is a reasonable thing. A bowl at three in the afternoon on top of lunch is a second dessert.
### What do the add-ins and wellness shots really do?
Add-ins fall into two buckets. The ones that reliably change the drink are protein powder, Greek yogurt, chia or flax, nut butter, and oats, because they add protein, fat, or fiber you can measure. The second bucket, spirulina, maca, collagen, wheatgrass, and most wellness shots, ranges from lightly supported to mostly hopeful.
Protein is the one worth paying for. Whey, pea, or hemp turns a fruit smoothie into something that doesn’t leave you starving in ninety minutes. Chia and flax put back some of the fiber a juice base strips out, and they thicken things nicely. Nut butter adds fat and staying power, plus calories, which is great if you’re trying to gain and less great if you’re not. Oats do the same job more cheaply.
### The shot wall
Ginger, turmeric with black pepper, cayenne, apple cider vinegar, wheatgrass, oil of oregano, elderberry. Ginger has a decent research base for nausea. Turmeric has been studied a lot, and the black pepper is there because piperine improves absorption of curcumin. The catch with both is dose. The amount in a two-ounce shot is small compared with what studies use, so treat it as a pleasant jolt rather than medicine. No shot prevents a cold. Anyone taking blood thinners, anyone pregnant, and anyone on regular medication should run high-dose ginger or turmeric past a pharmacist first.
Add-ins also multiply fast. Two upgrades and a shot can push a smoothie past the price of a decent lunch. Pick the one that changes the drink for you, usually protein or fiber, and let the rest go. If you want a structured plan rather than a menu guess, that’s a job for a professional, and seeing a nutritionist costs less confusion than a year of guessing at the counter.

### How do you tell a serious juice bar from a sugar shop?
Ask four questions and listen to how fast the answers come. What kind of press do you use. When was this pressed. Is the acai base sweetened. What are the first two ingredients in this juice by volume. A counter that knows its product answers all four without flinching. A sugar shop gets vague.
Look at the room while you wait. Is there actual produce visible, crates of celery and lemons and greens, or only frozen bags and pump bottles of syrup? Is there a press in sight, or is everything arriving in cases? Does the menu list ingredients in order, or does it list moods? A shop that names the farm in July and admits it buys wholesale in February is being straight with you, and that’s the tell you want.
A retired teacher in Elsberry does something smart: she orders the smallest size the first visit and asks for it unsweetened. If the plain version tastes like the vegetables it’s made from, she goes back. If it tastes like nothing without the apple juice, she’s learned what she was really buying. Cheap test. Takes one trip.
Shortlist two or three counters worth interviewing rather than settling on the closest one. Say plainly what you want: a low-sugar green juice, an unsweetened acai base, a cleanse you can do over a weekend, a smoothie with real protein in it. Then compare that against what each place is prepared to provide. One will reformulate on the spot. One will tell you they can’t do it, which is honest and useful. One will hand you the sweet version anyway. The gap between what you asked for and what showed up in the cup is the whole signal. The same instinct applies across plant-based menus around St. Louis, where a label and a recipe aren’t always the same conversation.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are the disadvantages of cold press juice?
A.  You lose the fiber, which is a large part of what makes produce good for you, and the sugar stays behind in a form your body absorbs quickly. Raw juice is unpasteurized and spoils in days, so it costs more and wastes more. It’s low in protein and fat, meaning it rarely keeps you full. And a bottle takes several pounds of produce, which is why the price lands where it does.
### Q. Is cold-pressed juice healthier than fresh-squeezed juice?
A.  Not dramatically. Pressing avoids the friction heat and aeration of a spinning blade, so the juice oxidizes more slowly and often tastes fresher longer, and the method handles leafy greens a citrus press can’t touch. Nutritionally, both are fresh raw juice with the fiber removed. What’s in the bottle matters far more than how it was extracted. Celery and kale beat apple and pineapple no matter which machine made it.
### Q. Can I drink cold-pressed juice every day?
A.  Most healthy adults can, as long as it’s a vegetable-forward juice in a modest size and it sits alongside real food rather than replacing it. Daily large fruit juices are a different story, since that’s a steady sugar load. Anyone managing diabetes, kidney disease, or blood pressure medication should check with their own clinician first. Raw unpasteurized juice also isn’t advised for pregnancy, young kids, or anyone immunocompromised.
### Q. Is juicing hard on the kidneys?
A.  For healthy kidneys, normal amounts are fine. Two cautions matter. Heavy juicing of high-oxalate greens like spinach, along with beets and rhubarb, has been linked in case reports to kidney trouble and stone formation, especially without enough water. And juice concentrates potassium, which people with chronic kidney disease are often told to limit. If you have any history of stones or reduced kidney function, ask your doctor before making juice a daily habit.
### Q. How much does a juice cleanse cost?
A.  Pricing is structured, not standard. Shops charge per day, by bottle count, and by bottle size, and the same “three-day cleanse” can mean four 12-ounce bottles or six 16-ounce ones. Multi-day packages often carry a lower per-day rate, and delivery, glass deposits, or subscriptions change the total again. Published figures vary widely, so ask the counter directly how many bottles, what size, and what the per-day rate is at each package length.
### Q. Is doing a juice cleanse worth it?
A.  As a detox, no, since your liver and kidneys handle that continuously. As a short circuit-breaker on a bad eating stretch, some people find it genuinely useful, mostly because it interrupts a habit for a few days. Expect water weight that returns, very little protein, and possible caffeine headaches. A gentler version, one cleanse day plus two days of juice with real meals, gets most of the reset with far less misery.
### Q. What to avoid during a juice cleanse?
A.  Skip alcohol entirely, and taper caffeine the week before instead of quitting cold, which prevents most cleanse headaches. Avoid hard workouts, since calories and protein are both low. Don’t drive or work a demanding shift on day one if you feel lightheaded. Keep drinking plain water alongside the juice. And don’t break the cleanse with a heavy fried meal; ease back with soup, eggs, or cooked vegetables.
### Q. Are acai bowls high in sugar?
A.  Usually yes, though the acai isn’t the culprit. Pure acai puree is low in sugar and quite bitter, so shops use sweetened frozen packs or sorbet-style bases, blend in fruit juice, then top the bowl with granola, banana, and a honey drizzle. Portion size finishes the job. Ask for an unsweetened base, water or milk instead of juice, half the granola, and no drizzle, and eat it as a meal.

## What to Expect at a Karaoke Bar in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-expect-at-a-karaoke-bar-in-st-louis
The clipboard sat at the end of the bar next to a stack of binders as thick as old phone books. A woman in Clifton Heights printed her name on line fourteen, wrote down a song she had sung in her kitchen maybe four hundred times, and then spent the next forty minutes quietly deciding she was going to leave before her turn came up. She didn’t leave. Around 10:40 the guy running the night said her name into the microphone, the intro came up loud on the house speakers, and the room did what that room does for a first-timer: it got noisy on purpose, so she couldn’t hear herself being nervous.
She was fine. Nobody remembers whether she was fine.
South of there, in House Springs, four friends split two hours of a private room on a Saturday for somebody’s fortieth. Completely different night. Door shut, their own screen, a tambourine somebody found in a drawer, no line behind them, a server knocking every twenty minutes with another round. Same hobby. Almost nothing else in common.
Both of those are karaoke, and nobody ever explains the gap between them to the person walking in cold. So here’s the whole thing from the door in: who the KJ is and what they actually control, how the sign-up list and the rotation really work, how long you sit before your name comes up, when a private room beats the open floor, the shapes the cost can take, what the regulars will quietly hold against you, how to pick a song you can survive, what to wear, and how to bring a group without becoming the group everybody resents.
### What happens in a karaoke bar?
You write your name and a song on a slip or a tablet, a host called a KJ runs the rotation, and you sing when your name gets called. Between turns you drink, talk, and clap for strangers. Some places run an open floor for the whole bar. Others rent private rooms by the hour.
KJ stands for karaoke jockey, and the job is closer to a DJ than to a host with a clipboard. They own the gear, the music library, the mixer, and the pace of the night. They cue your track, ride your volume, add a little reverb so your voice doesn’t sit naked in the room, and decide whether the night runs tight or drifts. A good one will pull your level up when you sing quiet and duck the backing track when you’re carrying it. Most of them have been doing this for years and have heard every song in the book several thousand times.
The shape of a night is pretty consistent. Sign-ups open before the music starts, often an hour or so before the first singer. Early is thin: five or six names, quick turnaround, half the room still eating. By eleven the list is deep and the vibe has changed, and by last call the KJ is cutting people off because the license and the lease say so. Everything gets louder and more forgiving as the night goes.
Physically it’s simple. A screen or two with the lyrics scrolling, one or two wireless microphones, a monitor speaker so you can hear yourself, and a small stage or just a taped-off corner of floor. You’ll get the mic handed to you. Sometimes there’s a spot marked where you should stand so you don’t walk into feedback. And if you want a sense of which rooms in town even run nights like this, it helps to understand the different types of bars around St. Louis before you pick one.
### How does the sign-up list actually work?
You fill out a slip with your first name and the song, usually title plus artist, and hand it to the KJ. Names go into a rotation in the order they arrive. You sing one song per turn, then you go back to the bottom of the list and wait for the wheel to come around again.
The slip matters more than people think. Write legibly, because the KJ has to read it at arm’s length in bad light, and a name they can’t decode gets skipped or mangled into something you don’t answer to. Include the artist. Half a dozen songs share the same title, and the wrong one starting is your fault, not theirs. If you want a specific version, live, acoustic, the radio edit, say so on the slip instead of arguing about it once the track is rolling.
### How long will you wait?
Do the math on the room. Each turn eats roughly four to five minutes with the handoff and the intro chatter, so a list of twelve names means most of an hour between your songs. Show up early and you might sing twice before the crowd lands. Walk in at midnight on a busy night and you may get exactly one turn, if that. This is the single biggest thing first-timers get wrong: the wait is the night, not an interruption of it.
### Things that quietly move you up or down
KJs balance the rotation. A brand-new singer often gets slotted a little kindly, and someone who just sang a nine-minute epic might sit a beat longer. Disappear to the parking lot when your name comes up and you get passed; you’ll go back in a slot or two, but you’ve also just cost the room four dead seconds. Don’t ask to be bumped ahead because you’re leaving soon. Everyone is leaving soon.
### Should you book a private room or take the open floor?
Take the open floor if you want an audience and a cheap night out. Book a private room if you want control: your own queue, no waiting, a closed door, and a group that can be as bad as it wants. Rooms are rented by the hour, priced by the room rather than by the head.
The open floor is the version most people picture. You’re singing to a bar of strangers who are mostly half-watching, which sounds worse than it is, because a half-watching bar is an extremely gentle audience. Cheap to try. You buy a drink, you sing, you clap for the next person. The trade is the wait and the loss of control: you can’t pick when you go on, you can’t restart a song you flubbed, and you might sit through forty minutes of a regular working through his entire catalog.
Private rooms flip every one of those. Your group books a block of time, usually one to three hours, and inside that block the queue belongs to you. Sing four songs in a row. Restart the one that went sideways. Skip the bridge. Bring people who would never in a hundred years take a microphone in front of strangers, because in a private room there are no strangers. Service is normally a server checking in rather than a bar you walk up to, and food and drinks tend to be ordered by the table.
A rough rule from watching this play out: under four people, the open floor is usually more fun, because the room supplies the energy you don’t have. Six or more, book the room. Groups of eight on an open floor end up dominating the rotation, annoying the regulars, and still only getting one turn each. Somebody in Hanley Hills learns that the hard way roughly every weekend.
### How do you pick a song you can actually sing?
Pick something you know all the way through, that sits in a comfortable part of your range, and that the room recognizes within about five seconds. Those three filters knock out most bad choices. Ambition is what wrecks first attempts, not nerves.
Know the verses. Everybody knows the chorus, which is exactly why the verses are where people fall apart, standing there reading words they’ve never actually said out loud while the tempo leaves without them. Screen lyrics help, but they scroll at the recording’s pace, not yours. A song you’ve sung in the car a hundred times is a song you know. A song you like is not the same thing.
### Range beats taste
That enormous note in the last chorus is enormous because a professional with a vocal coach hit it in a studio, possibly on the eleventh take. Sing along to the recording at home first and notice where you start straining. If you’re reaching at home, you’ll be shouting at a bar. Lower and steady lands far better with a room than high and heroic. Nobody claps for accuracy anyway. They clap for commitment.
### The traps
Long songs test a room’s patience and burn a slot fourteen other people are waiting on. Rap punishes anyone who hasn’t practiced the timing, because the lyrics arrive faster than you can read them. Slow ballads early in a quiet night can die on the floor. Duets are great and also a promise: if your friend bails, you’re singing both parts. And that deep cut nobody knows might be the best song in the book, but a room that doesn’t recognize it can’t sing along with you, which is most of what makes this fun.
### What does a karaoke night cost?
It depends entirely on the format, and the honest answer is that you should call ahead. Costs here take four shapes: free to sing with a drink purchase or a minimum, a cover at the door, a private room billed by the hour, and a tip for the KJ. Some nights involve one of those. Some involve three.
Open-floor karaoke is usually the cheapest entertainment in any bar, because the bar isn’t selling the singing, it’s selling drinks on a slow weeknight. Singing is often free with a purchase. Some rooms add a cover on their busiest night, or a drink minimum per person, which functions like a cover you get to drink. Private rooms work differently: you’re renting a space by the hour, the rate is for the room rather than per person, peak weekend hours cost more than a Tuesday afternoon, and food and drink are usually extra on top.
### Tipping the KJ
There’s almost always a tip jar on the KJ’s table, and it’s worth using. Many of them are independent contractors hauling in thousands of dollars of their own gear and getting a flat rate from the bar. A tip when you sing is a small, normal courtesy. What a tip should not buy is a jump to the front of the line. Some hosts will bend the rotation for cash; plenty flatly won’t, and the regulars notice either way. Tip your bartender too, especially if you’re parked at a table for four hours drinking two beers.
Before you commit a group to anything, call two or three places worth interviewing and just say plainly what you want: eight people, a Saturday, two hours, we want to be able to order food. Then compare that against what each one is prepared to provide. One will quote you a rate and a deposit without blinking. Another will get vague about whether the room is really yours. That gap is the whole signal. Same approach works for a comedy club night, where covers and minimums stack the same way.
### What should you wear, and how do you handle a group?
Wear whatever you’d wear to that bar on a normal night. Karaoke isn’t a dress code event, and there is no costume expectation. The only real consideration is comfort under warm lights with a room looking at you, which argues for layers you can shed and shoes you can stand in.
A dive bar in Washington Park and a polished lounge with private rooms sit at opposite ends of the same hobby, and each one has its own normal. Jeans and a decent shirt clear the bar essentially everywhere. Private rooms run casual to the point of pajamas, since the only people seeing you are people who already know you. If you’re unsure, look at the venue’s own photos, or just think about which end of the dive bar spectrum you’re heading toward.
### Bringing a group
Big groups on an open floor need one rule and one volunteer. The rule: your group doesn’t stack the list. Put in two or three names at a time instead of nine, and let the rotation breathe, or the regulars will spend an hour watching people they don’t know monopolize a night they attend every week. The volunteer: one person owns the tab and the slips, so nine people aren’t individually bothering the KJ.
Call ahead for anything over six, even at an open-floor place. You’re asking about tables, not permission. Somebody planning a birthday in Crystal City who calls Wednesday gets a table by the stage; the same group walking in cold on Saturday stands in the back all night holding drinks.
Eating out with the kids first? Here is how to make that work.
### What do the regulars expect from you?
Be ready when your name is called, sing your one song, hand the mic back, and clap for whoever follows you. That’s the entire social contract, and the regulars enforce it through body language rather than confrontation. Nobody there cares how well you sing. They care whether you respect the rotation.
Heckling is the fastest way to become unwelcome. A karaoke room runs on a shared agreement that everyone is allowed to be bad, and one loud table breaking that agreement can shut down a night for the people who came to sing. So clap for the guy who forgets the second verse. Clap harder, honestly. He’s the reason you feel safe getting up there.
Mic handling is the other tell. Hold it a few inches from your mouth, aimed at your face, not straight out like an award. Keep it away from the speakers unless you enjoy feedback. Don’t tap it, blow into it, or swing it by the cable. And when you’re done, hand it back to the KJ instead of setting it on a table where it picks up every conversation in the room.
A few more that regulars notice without saying a word. Don’t sing along loudly from your seat while somebody else is up; a little crowd support is great, a second unofficial vocalist is not. Don’t grab the extra mic and join a stranger’s song uninvited. Don’t sign up and then vanish. Don’t demand your song get moved up. And if you’re genuinely good, which some people in these rooms are, keep the showcase pieces occasional, because a night where one person performs and everyone else participates is a night people stop coming to. The same unwritten rules travel to neighborhood live music venues, where the crowd polices the room more than the staff ever does.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is karaoke night at a bar?
A.  It’s a recurring night, usually the same weeknight or weekend slot every week, where a bar brings in a host and a sound system so customers can sing recorded backing tracks with the lyrics on a screen. Anyone in the room can sign up. There’s no audition and no performance requirement. The bar runs it because it fills seats on nights that would otherwise be quiet, which is why it’s often free to participate.
### Q. Can anyone sing karaoke?
A.  Yes, and the rooms are built on that assumption. You need to be old enough to be in the venue and willing to put your name down. No experience, no training, no ability to carry a tune required. Regulars are far more forgiving of a shaky voice than of bad manners, and a nervous first-timer usually gets the loudest applause in the room. If standing in front of strangers is the obstacle, a private room removes the strangers entirely.
### Q. What are the 10 rules of karaoke?
A.  There’s no official canon, but ten practical ones cover most of it. One, sign up early. Two, write your name and the artist legibly. Three, pick a song you know past the chorus. Four, be in the room when you’re called. Five, one song per turn. Six, don’t ask to be bumped up the list. Seven, applaud every singer, especially the bad ones. Eight, never heckle. Nine, tip the KJ and your bartender. Ten, hand the mic back when you’re done.
### Q. What is the golden rule of karaoke?
A.  Clap for everybody. Every other rule follows from it. The whole thing only works because a room full of people has agreed that being bad in public is fine tonight, and that agreement holds exactly as long as everyone keeps supporting the person holding the microphone. Withdraw the applause and the next four people stop signing up. Commitment beats talent in these rooms, and generosity beats both.
### Q. What not to do at karaoke?
A.  Don’t heckle, don’t grab a second mic and join a stranger’s song uninvited, and don’t argue with the KJ about the rotation. Beyond that: don’t stack the list with your whole group, don’t disappear after signing up, don’t pick a nine-minute song on a packed night, and don’t keep the mic to make a speech. Wandering off with the microphone is the one that genuinely costs the host money.
### Q. How much does karaoke usually cost?
A.  It varies enough that you should call ahead rather than assume. The cost takes a few recognizable shapes: free to sing with a drink purchase or a per-person drink minimum, a cover charge at the door on busier nights, or a private room rented by the hour with food and drinks billed separately. A tip for the KJ sits on top of any of those. Ask about minimums, deposits, and peak-hour rates when you call.
### Q. How to dress for karaoke night?
A.  Dress the way you’d dress for that venue on any other night. There’s no karaoke dress code, and showing up in a costume mostly just makes you conspicuous before you’ve sung a note. Jeans and a decent shirt work nearly everywhere. Rooms get warm under lights and body heat, so layers you can take off help, and comfortable shoes matter more than anything else if you’re standing for four hours.
### Q. Do karaoke bars have cameras in the rooms?
A.  Some venues with private rooms do run cameras, typically for security and to monitor for damage or underage drinking, and practice varies a lot from place to place. Many rooms also have large windows in the door for exactly that reason. If it matters to you, ask the venue directly when you book: whether cameras are in the rooms, whether anything is recorded, and how long footage is kept. A straight answer to that question tells you something about how the place is run.

## What a Midwife Does and How to Choose One in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-midwife-does-and-how-to-choose-one-in-st-louis
The appointment ran eleven minutes. A woman in Mascoutah, nine weeks along with her second, had six questions written on the back of a grocery receipt and got through two of them before the door opened and shut again. She wasn’t angry about it. She drove home with the receipt still in her coat pocket and the distinct feeling that nobody in that room had asked her a single thing.
An hour west in New Haven, a couple expecting their first had the opposite trouble. Too many words, no definitions. Somebody at work said get a midwife. Somebody else said doula, using it like the same word. A cousin over in Bethalto had a baby at home and talks about it constantly. A neighbor called that reckless. Everyone had an opinion ready. Nobody had a job description.
Both households are circling the same question, and it isn’t really hospital or house. It’s who do I want in the room with me, what is that person trained and permitted to do, and what happens at two in the morning if the plan changes. That question has actual answers.
One thing up front, and it matters more here than on most topics: this is general information, not medical advice, and it is not a coverage determination. Your provider and your health plan are the only authorities on your specific pregnancy and your specific benefits. What follows covers what a midwife does month to month, what the credential letters mean, the three places you can give birth with one, the clinical reasons a pregnancy moves into obstetric care, how payment tends to be structured, when to start looking, and the interview questions that actually separate one practice from another.
### What is the difference between a midwife and an OB-GYN?
A midwife is trained in pregnancy, birth, and well-person care, and most midwifery practices center on healthy, lower-risk pregnancies. An OB-GYN is a physician and surgeon who covers the full range, including high-risk pregnancy and cesarean birth. Plenty of families work with both, with the physician stepping in if something changes.
The cleanest way to hold the difference is surgery. An obstetrician can perform a cesarean, manage a pregnancy with serious medical complications, and handle the situations that call for an operating room. A midwife does not perform surgery. That single line explains most of the rest: who gets referred where, why some practices decline certain pregnancies, and why a midwife needs a working relationship with a physician no matter where she attends births.
The other real difference is the shape of the visit. Midwifery visits tend to run longer and cover more ground, including sleep, food, work, fear, and what home looks like. That isn’t a knock on physicians, who are often carrying a much heavier and sicker caseload. It’s a description of two different models. One is built around watching a normal process closely. The other is built around catching and treating what goes wrong.
And a third term keeps getting mixed in. A doula is not a clinician at all. No exams, no monitoring, no delivery, no prescriptions. A doula provides continuous labor support: positioning, counterpressure, coaching, and a steady voice while the clinical staff does clinical work. Some families hire one alongside a midwife. Some hire one alongside an obstetrician. The roles sit side by side, not on a ladder.
### What does a midwife actually do across a pregnancy?
A midwife handles routine prenatal care, orders and reviews standard labs and screenings, attends labor and delivery, and manages the postpartum weeks. Many also provide well-person care outside pregnancy entirely. It is ongoing primary care for a whole reproductive life, not a single appearance in a delivery room.
### Before the birth
Prenatal care with a midwife looks a lot like prenatal care anywhere: blood pressure, weight, fundal height, heart tones, the standard schedule of labs and screenings, and referrals for imaging. What tends to differ is time. A longer appointment means the conversation reaches things a short one never does. Whether you’re eating. Whether you’re sleeping. Whether the last birth went badly and you’ve been carrying that around for three years without telling anyone.
This is also where your birth preferences get built, revised, and pressure-tested. Not a laminated wish list. A real conversation about pain management, movement, monitoring, who’s in the room, and what you want to happen if the plan has to change. A good midwife will walk you through the change-of-plan scenarios on purpose, early, while you’re calm enough to think.
### During labor and delivery
Midwives monitor labor, support the person through it, catch the baby, manage the delivery of the placenta, and repair tearing where that’s needed and within their scope. In a hospital they work with nursing staff and have anesthesia and physician backup down the hall. Outside a hospital they bring equipment with them and work under a transfer plan. The scope of what a given midwife can administer varies by credential, by setting, and by state rules, which is a question to ask directly rather than assume.
### After the baby comes
Postpartum is the stretch families underestimate most. Bleeding, healing, feeding difficulty, blood pressure that misbehaves after delivery, and the mental health slide that can start quietly around week three. Midwifery practices generally build in postpartum contact, sometimes including visits at your house in the first days. Ask exactly how many visits, on what days, and how you reach someone at 3 a.m. Then ask what they screen for and when.
### The years that aren’t a pregnancy
Well-person care is the part people miss. Depending on credential and setting, a midwife may provide annual exams, cervical cancer screening, contraception counseling and prescriptions, and care through perimenopause. If you’ve been putting off building a regular care team, this is a reasonable on-ramp, and it pairs with finding a primary care doctor in St. Louis rather than replacing it.
### What do CNM, CM and CPM mean?
Those letters describe different training paths and different legal authority, and the difference is practical rather than cosmetic. Credential affects where a midwife can attend births, what she can prescribe, whether a hospital will credential her, and how insurers tend to treat the claim. Ask for the letters and what they permit.
### Certified nurse-midwife (CNM)
A CNM is a registered nurse who then completed graduate-level midwifery education and passed a national certification exam. This is the credential you most often find inside hospitals and in practices that work alongside physicians. CNMs generally hold prescriptive authority, so medications and contraception are typically on the table. Many also see patients for routine gynecologic care between pregnancies. If you want a midwife-led birth in a hospital, this is usually the credential attached to it.
### Certified midwife (CM)
A CM completes comparable graduate midwifery education and the same certification exam without coming in through nursing first. The training standard is the point of the credential. The catch is recognition: states differ on whether and how a CM can be licensed and practice, so the credential is more common in some parts of the country than others. Ask what the provider is licensed to do here, today.
### Certified professional midwife (CPM)
A CPM holds a credential built specifically around birth outside a hospital, with training requirements that include attending out-of-hospital births. CPMs are the midwives you typically find attending home births and working in freestanding birth centers. Legal status and licensure requirements for CPMs vary quite a bit from state to state, and insurance treatment varies right along with it.
Titles alone are not proof. Anyone can say midwife in casual conversation. Ask which credential, which certifying body, whether the license is current, and how to confirm it independently. A midwife who has nothing to hide will hand you that information without a flicker of irritation. Hesitation there is worth more than any review you’ll read.
### Where can you give birth with a midwife?
Three settings, broadly: a hospital, a freestanding birth center, or your own home. The setting determines how fast an operating room and anesthesia can reach you, what equipment is in the room, and which credentials can practice there. Not every midwife works in every setting.
### Hospital
Midwife-attended hospital birth gives you the midwifery model with surgical and anesthesia backup in the same building. Epidurals are available. So is an operating room, immediately, if something turns. Hospital policy shapes some of the experience, including monitoring practices and how long you stay, so ask what the unit’s standard routine looks like rather than assuming your preferences travel automatically.
### Freestanding birth center
A birth center is its own facility, not a wing of a hospital. Expect a home-like room, tubs, freedom to move, intermittent monitoring, and a short stay after delivery, often measured in hours. No epidurals, no surgery. Birth centers screen carefully, because their whole model depends on only accepting pregnancies that stay low-risk. Ask for the transfer plan in plain words: which hospital, how far, by what vehicle, who calls ahead, and who goes with you.
### Home
Planned home birth means the midwife comes to you with her equipment and stays through labor, delivery, and the first hours after. Families choose it for continuity, privacy, and control over the environment. The trade is distance. A family in Sullivan is farther from an operating room than a family inside the city, and that distance belongs in the decision honestly, not as an afterthought. Ask how the practice screens, what it carries, what it monitors, and exactly when it transfers.
### What moves a pregnancy out of midwifery care?
Certain clinical findings move care to a physician, either as consultation alongside your midwife or as a full handoff. Midwifery and birth-center practices screen for these throughout pregnancy, not just at intake. Each practice sets its own criteria, and a good one will tell you exactly what its list contains before you enroll.
The categories that come up most often include certain multiple pregnancies, a baby in breech or another non-vertex position near term, some prior surgical histories including previous cesarean, preeclampsia and other blood pressure disorders of pregnancy, gestational diabetes that stops responding to management, preterm labor, bleeding, and certain pre-existing conditions that need specialist management the whole way through. Some of these are absolute for a given practice. Others trigger consultation and a joint plan.
Here is the part worth saying out loud. A transfer is not a failure and it is not a punishment. It’s the system doing the thing it was built to do. Screening exists precisely so that the low-risk model stays low-risk, and a practice that transfers appropriately is a practice that is paying attention. The warning sign runs the other direction, toward anyone who talks like risk is a marketing problem.
Ask two questions and listen closely to both. What would make you send me to a physician? And what happens to my care, my records, and my money if that happens in month eight? The answers tell you whether a practice has thought this through.
### How does paying for midwifery care work?
Coverage depends on three things: the provider’s credential and license, whether that provider is in your plan’s network, and the birth setting. Licensed midwives practicing in hospitals are the most routinely covered arrangement. Out-of-hospital birth is treated less consistently. Get it confirmed by your plan in writing, well before the third trimester.
Structure first, because the structure is what confuses people. Prenatal care and delivery from a practice are often billed as one bundled maternity fee covering the visits, the birth, and a defined postpartum window. That fee is separate from the facility. A hospital bills its own charges for the room, the nursery, anesthesia, and anything else that happens under its roof, and those are itemized on their own. So two families can pay the same provider the same amount and end up in very different places, because their facility charges and their plan benefits were never the same.
In-network versus out-of-network does more work than almost any other variable. An out-of-network provider can leave you responsible for a much larger share, or for the whole thing, even though the service itself is a covered benefit. Medicaid coverage for maternity care exists, and specifics on which provider types and which settings are included change over time, so the answer has to come from the plan rather than from a forum post or a friend’s memory of 2021. If you’re still sorting out your plan at all, start with how to get health insurance in Missouri before you shortlist providers.
Call the number on your card and ask a specific set of questions. Is this named provider in network for maternity care. Is this specific setting a covered place of service. What is my deductible, coinsurance, and out-of-pocket maximum for the plan year the birth falls in. Is any prior authorization required. Then ask for it in writing, by portal message or email, and keep it. Verbal confirmation from a call center has a way of evaporating.
The other budget reality arrives with the baby, and it is not the provider’s bill. Gear, furniture, a bigger car seat, all of it lands at once. Some of that is worth buying used, some of it genuinely isn’t, which is its own separate homework on what baby gear to buy secondhand around St. Louis.

### What should you ask when you interview a midwife?
Shortlist two or three practices and interview them. Say plainly what you want from your care and what you expect when things change, then compare that against what each one is prepared to provide. The gap between those two answers is the signal. Most families start looking in the first trimester.
### Timing
Earlier is easier. Practices fill by due date, birth centers screen at intake, and a midwife who is already full for March cannot make room for you in February. Starting somewhere in the first trimester leaves time to interview more than one and still switch if the fit is wrong. Later is not hopeless, though. People change providers in the second trimester and sometimes the third, especially after a transfer, and it is allowed.
### The questions that actually separate practices
Who attends my birth if you’re unavailable, and will I meet that person first. How many clients do you take per month. What is your consulting physician arrangement and who is it with. What is your transfer plan, step by step. What are your screening criteria, and what would take me out of your care. How many postpartum visits, and how do I reach you overnight. What is included in the fee and what isn’t. How do you handle a client who wants something you don’t recommend.
### What you’re listening for
Specificity, mostly. Vague reassurance is the thing to distrust, from any provider, in any setting. You want someone who answers the hard scenario without flinching and without selling. Watch whether they ask you questions back. Watch whether they write things down. And pay attention to whether you’d feel comfortable disagreeing with this person while exhausted and scared, because you may need to. ### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is a doula the same as a midwife?
A.  No. A midwife is a trained clinician who provides prenatal care, attends the birth, delivers the baby, and manages postpartum care. A doula provides continuous non-clinical support: comfort measures, positioning, coaching, and advocacy during labor. A doula does not perform exams, monitor the baby medically, prescribe, or deliver. The two roles work well together, and many families hire a doula in addition to a midwife or an obstetrician rather than instead of one.
### Q. How many weeks pregnant should you get a midwife?
A.  Most families start looking in the first trimester, often between roughly six and twelve weeks, because practices fill by due date and the popular ones close out early. Starting then leaves room to interview more than one and still change your mind. Later is not a lost cause. People switch providers in the second trimester regularly, and sometimes in the third, particularly after a move or a change in their health plan.
### Q. Are midwives covered by insurance?
A.  Often, though coverage turns on the provider’s credential and license, whether they are in your plan’s network, and the birth setting. Licensed midwives practicing in hospitals are the most routinely covered arrangement; out-of-hospital care is handled less consistently across plans. Never rely on a general answer. Call your plan with the specific provider name and place of service, ask what is covered, and get the confirmation in writing before your third trimester.
### Q. Is it cheaper to have a baby with a midwife?
A.  It can be, and the reason is structural rather than about the provider’s fee. Midwifery care is often billed as a bundled maternity fee, while the facility bills separately, so a setting with lighter facility charges changes the total. Network status changes it again, sometimes dramatically. The only way to know your number is to have your plan confirm benefits for that provider and that place of service in writing.
### Q. Are home births legal in Missouri?
A.  Yes. Home birth is legal in Missouri, and Missouri law permits certified professional midwives to attend births outside a hospital. What changes over time is the detail around licensure requirements and how insurers treat out-of-hospital claims, so confirm the individual provider’s current credential and license with them directly rather than relying on general information. Ask which certifying body issued it and how you can verify it yourself.
### Q. Am I allowed to choose a home birth instead of hospital birth?
A.  Yes. Where you give birth is your decision, and a planned home birth with a qualified attendant is a legitimate choice in Missouri. The practical limits are clinical, not legal: midwifery and birth-center practices screen pregnancies and will decline or transfer care when specific risk factors appear. Talk through the transfer plan, the distance to a hospital from your address, and the screening criteria before you commit to a setting.
### Q. What disqualifies you from a home birth?
A.  Each practice sets its own criteria and will give you its list, but the risk factors commonly screened for include certain multiple pregnancies, breech or other non-vertex presentation near term, some prior surgical histories including previous cesarean, preeclampsia and other blood pressure disorders, gestational diabetes that stops responding to management, preterm labor, and bleeding. Some are absolute for a given practice. Others trigger physician consultation and a shared plan instead of a full handoff.
### Q. Does insurance pay for home births?
A.  Sometimes, and it is the least consistent category of the three settings. Payment usually depends on the attendant’s credential and license, whether that provider participates in your network, and how your plan classifies home as a place of service. An out-of-network attendant can leave most of the cost with you. Ask your plan about that named provider and that setting specifically, request written confirmation, and keep it.

## When to See a Periodontist in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/when-to-see-a-periodontist-in-st-louis
The sink told her first. A woman in Dellwood had been spitting pink into it most mornings for the better part of a year, and every morning she told herself the same thing: she’d brushed too hard again. Then one Tuesday her front teeth looked longer than she remembered. Not dramatically longer. Just enough that she went and dug out an old photo to compare, and stood there holding her phone up next to the mirror.
Across the metro in Glendale, a man sat through a cleaning listening to his hygienist call numbers out to an assistant. Three, three, two. Four, five, five. Six. A pause, then another six. He had no idea what any of it meant, only that the numbers sounded bigger than last time and the room had gone quiet in a way it hadn’t before. At the end his dentist said the word periodontist, wrote something on a card, and slid it across the counter.
And there’s a guy in High Ridge who has been working a lower molar with his tongue for a month. It moves. Barely, but it moves, and it wasn’t moving in the spring. Nothing hurts. That’s what keeps throwing him, because he figures anything serious would announce itself.
Gum disease is quiet, which is the whole problem with it. What follows is what a periodontist is trained to do that a general dentist usually isn’t, the warning signs worth acting on this month rather than next year, how pocket depths get measured and roughly what those numbers say, which stages can still be turned around and which can only be stopped where they are, what the common treatments actually involve in plain language, how referrals and insurance tend to work, and what to ask when you finally sit down in the chair.
### What doctor should I see for gum disease?
A periodontist. That’s the dental specialist trained in the gum tissue and the bone that holds your teeth in place, with several years of residency beyond dental school. Your general dentist may treat early gum disease well. Once pockets deepen or bone is involved, a specialist is the right call.
Periodontists finish dental school and then spend years in a residency built around one narrow subject: everything surrounding a tooth. They diagnose and stage gum disease, perform the surgical procedures most general offices refer out, place and repair dental implants, and treat recession, bone loss, and the occasional lesion that turns up on the gums. They also tend to catch the complicated cases. Patients on blood thinners. Patients whose diabetes will not sit still. Patients whose gums keep flaring back up after everything reasonable has already been tried.
None of that means your regular dentist was doing it wrong. Plenty of general offices treat early disease well, and a hygienist who has watched your mouth for a decade is the person most likely to notice the first change. The handoff usually happens for one of three reasons: the numbers stopped responding to ordinary cleanings, the x-rays show bone that is no longer where it belongs, or the case needs a procedure that office doesn’t perform.
### How a periodontist differs from the other dental specialists
Dentistry splits up by which part of the tooth is in trouble. An endodontist works inside the tooth, on the nerve and the root canal system, which is what an endodontist does and when you need one. An oral surgeon handles extractions, impacted teeth, and jaw work, covered in what an oral surgeon does. A periodontist works outside the tooth, on the foundation. Deep, throbbing pain in one tooth points one direction. Bleeding, recession, and movement point another.
There’s a second route into a periodontal office that has nothing to do with disease. Implants. If you lost a tooth years ago and want it replaced, or the site needs bone rebuilt before anything can go in, that work often lands on a periodontist’s schedule alongside oral surgeons. It’s worth understanding how dental insurance generally treats implants before you commit to a treatment plan built around one.
### What are the signs your gums need a specialist?
Blood in the sink is the signal people ignore longest. Healthy gums don’t bleed from ordinary brushing. Add persistent bad breath, gums pulling back so teeth look longer, or a tooth that has shifted or feels loose, and you are past the point where watching and waiting is a reasonable plan.
Start with the bleeding, because almost everybody misreads it. Bleeding is inflammation. It means bacteria have set up along the gumline and the tissue is reacting, not that your hand is heavy on the brush. Then the trap springs: people brush and floss more gently exactly where it bleeds, which leaves that spot dirtier, which makes it bleed more. A year of that quiet feedback loop does real damage without a single moment of pain.
Breath is the next tell. Not morning breath, and not garlic. A persistent bad smell or a metallic taste that survives brushing usually means bacteria are living somewhere a brush cannot physically reach, which is a fair description of a deep pocket. Mouthwash covers it for an hour. It does nothing to what’s causing it.
Recession is the one people notice in the mirror. Teeth look longer. A notch or a ledge appears where the enamel ends. Cold water hits a spot it never used to hit, because the exposed root surface has no enamel over it and reacts to everything. Dark triangles open between the front teeth. That last one sends more people in than the bleeding does, honestly, because it is the first sign that shows up in photographs.
Movement is the urgent category. A tooth that shifts, drifts, or wobbles has lost support underneath it. Same for a bite that suddenly feels off, a gap that wasn’t there in July, food packing between two teeth every single meal, or a partial denture that stops seating the way it did. Swelling, tenderness, or anything that looks like pus along the gumline should get a call that week, not at the next six-month visit.
A few things stack the deck. Smoking, uncontrolled diabetes, a family history of losing teeth early, pregnancy, dry mouth, and several common medications all make gum disease more likely or harder to control. Smoking is the cruel one. Nicotine narrows the small vessels in the gums, so smokers often bleed less while the underlying disease runs further. Less blood, worse disease. That combination fools people for years.
### What do the pocket numbers actually mean?
Your hygienist is measuring the space between gum and tooth with a slim probe marked in millimeters, at six spots around every tooth. One to three millimeters is healthy territory. Four is a flag. Five and six mean the pocket is deeper than a brush or floss can reach, and seven or more is advanced.
Picture the gum as a collar around each tooth rather than a seal. There’s a shallow groove where the collar meets enamel, and a probe slides into it until the tissue stops it. In a healthy mouth that stop comes fast. When disease breaks down the attachment and the bone beneath it, the probe travels further before anything resists, and the number goes up. That’s the whole measurement. No magic to it.
Depth alone never tells the story, though, and this is where patients fixate on the wrong thing. A five that bleeds at every visit is more worrying than a five that has been stable and quiet for three years. So the chart carries more than depths. Whether the site bleeds when probed. How far the gum has receded, which gets measured separately and added to the depth to describe the real attachment loss. How much a tooth moves under pressure. Whether the probe can slip into the space between the roots of a molar, which is its own bad sign. Then x-rays, because bone level is the thing a probe can only infer.
Pattern matters too. One deep pocket on one back molar is often a local problem, a cracked filling or a spot nobody can reach with floss. Fives and sixes scattered across the whole mouth describe something systemic. Ask which one you have. Ask to see the chart, and ask what those same teeth read the last two times, because the direction of travel is more useful than any single visit.
### Which stages of gum disease can still be reversed?
Gingivitis is genuinely reversible. It’s inflammation without attachment or bone loss, and it responds to a thorough cleaning plus consistent home care over a few weeks. Once the disease crosses into periodontitis and bone starts disappearing, the goal changes. You stop the loss and hold the line. Bone doesn’t regrow on its own.
Gingivitis looks like red, puffy gum margins that bleed easily and feel tender when you floss. The bone is intact. The attachment is intact. Clean the surfaces properly, keep them clean, and the tissue settles down and quits bleeding. That’s a real reversal, and it’s the only stage that gets one.
Early periodontitis is where the attachment starts letting go. Pockets read four and five, an x-ray shows the first bone loss between teeth, and most people still have no symptoms beyond bleeding. Moderate disease brings fives and sixes, visible recession, occasional soreness, and sometimes the beginning of that gap between molar roots. Advanced disease is sevens and up, teeth that move, teeth that drift into new positions, recurring abscesses, and the conversation nobody wants about which teeth are worth saving.
A retiree in Gray Summit found out in the worst order. He’d gone years between visits because nothing hurt, then went in about a tooth that felt funny while chewing, and the chart came back full of sixes and sevens. Treatment stabilized most of his mouth. Two teeth were already past stabilizing. That’s the practical difference between catching it at a four and catching it at a seven.
Be careful with the word “reversed.” Pockets do get shallower after treatment, and they get shallower two different ways. Inflammation resolves and the tissue tightens back against the root, which is what you want. Or the swollen gum shrinks down, which lowers the number while exposing more root, and that is a trade rather than a win. Grafting is the procedure that rebuilds tissue, and specific bone defects can sometimes be treated with regenerative techniques. Whether your particular sites qualify is a judgment your clinician makes after looking at the imaging and the shape of the defect, not something worth deciding from a web page.
### What does periodontal treatment involve?
Most people start with scaling and root planing, a deep cleaning below the gumline done under local anesthetic, usually split across two or more appointments. A re-evaluation follows several weeks later to see which pockets responded. Surgery, gum grafting, and bone work come after that, only where the numbers refused to move.
### The deep cleaning, in plain terms
This is not a regular cleaning done harder. A quadrant of your mouth gets numbed, and the hygienist or periodontist works below the gumline with ultrasonic and hand instruments, removing hardened calculus and bacterial film off the root surfaces and smoothing what’s left so the tissue has something clean to reattach to. Expect soreness for a couple of days and cold sensitivity that can hang around for weeks as the gums tighten and more root sits exposed. Most people describe the appointment itself as long and boring rather than painful.
### Maintenance, and why the interval changes
After treatment your cleaning schedule usually shifts. Bacteria repopulate a treated pocket on a fairly predictable timeline, so maintenance visits get spaced to interrupt that cycle, often every three or four months rather than every six. Some patients alternate between the periodontist and their general office. Skipping maintenance is the most common way a good result quietly comes undone, and it happens to people who feel fine, which is exactly the point.
### Lasers, surgery, and grafts
Some offices use a laser alongside scaling to remove diseased tissue lining the pocket. Protocols vary a lot between practices, so ask what the laser is doing in your case and what the alternative would be without it. Pocket reduction surgery, sometimes called flap surgery, means lifting the gum so the roots can be cleaned under direct vision, reshaping bone where it has been left in an uncleanable contour, and closing the tissue tighter against the tooth. Shallower pockets afterward, and usually more visible root.
Gum grafting rebuilds tissue over an exposed root using tissue moved from elsewhere in your mouth or processed donor tissue, which covers recession and thickens thin gum so it stops receding further. Bone grafting places graft material into a defect, often with a membrane over it, to encourage the body to rebuild in a contained space. When a tooth is beyond saving, removal and an implant becomes the conversation, and the bone site frequently needs preparing before anything can be placed.
If money is the reason you’ve stayed out of a chair, that’s worth naming out loud instead of waiting. There are free and low-cost dental options around St. Louis, including teaching clinics where periodontal work happens under faculty supervision at reduced fees. Slower appointments. Real treatment.

### How does the referral usually work?
Usually there isn’t much to it. Most periodontal offices accept patients who call themselves, so you can book an evaluation without anyone’s permission. Your insurance plan is the part worth checking first, since a few plans want a referral on file before they process specialist claims and others don’t ask at all.
Even where no referral is required, call your general office and ask them to send records ahead. Recent x-rays, the last two or three sets of pocket readings, and any notes about what’s been tried. You avoid retaking films, and the specialist gets to see a trend line instead of a snapshot. A woman in Kimmswick who moved practices twice in four years had no history following her at all, and rebuilding it cost her an extra appointment she didn’t need to spend.
Insurance treats periodontal care differently from a routine cleaning, and understanding the structure saves a lot of frustration. Periodontal procedures are filed under their own codes with their own rules, so they run through the plan on a separate track from the checkup you’re used to. Many plans want documentation before they authorize treatment: a full set of pocket depths, current x-rays, sometimes a written narrative explaining why deep cleaning is indicated. Maintenance visits also sit in a category of their own, and how often a plan will pay for them may not line up with the twice-a-year benefit most people assume they have.
So ask the office to file a pre-treatment estimate with your plan before anything gets scheduled. The plan answers in writing, in advance, about what it will and won’t cover, and you get to make decisions with that document in front of you rather than a surprise afterward. Any office that does periodontal work regularly files these constantly. It’s a routine request, not a difficult one.
Bring your medication list to that first appointment as well. Blood thinners, bone medications, immune-related drugs, anything for diabetes or heart conditions. Some of those change how procedures get planned or timed, and the conversation goes much better before treatment than during it.
### What should you ask at the first periodontal visit?
Ask for your numbers, written down, and what the same teeth measured last time. Then ask what the plan is, what happens if you do nothing for a year, and what the office expects from you between visits. A first appointment is an interview running in both directions.
Good questions to bring with you: Which specific teeth are the problem, and which are fine? What stage am I at? Where has bone been lost, and can you show me on the film? What does the non-surgical plan look like first? What happens at the re-evaluation, and what result would push us toward surgery? Which teeth are you actually worried about five years out? What maintenance interval are you putting me on, and why that one? Write the answers down. Nobody remembers a chair conversation accurately an hour later.
Shortlist two or three practices worth interviewing before you commit to a treatment plan, especially if surgery is on the table. Say plainly what you want: a full set of readings explained to you tooth by tooth, a staged plan that starts with the least invasive option that could work, and a pre-treatment estimate filed with your plan before anything is scheduled. Then compare that against what each office is prepared to provide. The gap is the signal.
One place hands you a printed chart and walks you through it without being asked. Another wants to see how you respond to a deep cleaning before discussing anything further, which is a good instinct. A third opens with surgery before the probe readings have been explained. You’ll know which is which inside of twenty minutes, and it has nothing to do with what anything costs.
Last thing, and it matters more than most patients expect. Ask what they want you doing at home, in specifics. Which tool for which gap, where you’re currently missing, whether interdental brushes suit your spacing better than floss, and what to do about smoking if that applies to you. Treatment buys you a clean starting point. What you do every night decides whether it holds.
