### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Can you go straight to a periodontist?
A.  In most cases, yes. Periodontal offices routinely see patients who call on their own, so you can book an evaluation without going through your dentist first. Check your insurance plan, though, because some plans want a referral on file before they process specialist claims. Either way, ask your general office to forward recent x-rays and your pocket readings ahead of the appointment. It saves a retake and gives the specialist a history rather than a single snapshot.
### Q. How do I tell what stage of gum disease I have?
A.  You can’t tell from a mirror, and that’s the honest answer. Staging needs probe readings at six sites per tooth, recession measured separately, and x-rays showing where the bone sits. Bleeding and puffiness without any bone loss is gingivitis. Once the films show bone loss, it’s periodontitis, and it gets described by how severe it is and how much of the mouth is involved. Ask for your numbers and ask to see the images on the screen.
### Q. How long until gum disease is serious?
A.  There’s no clock you can rely on, because it varies enormously between people. Gingivitis can appear within a few weeks of poor cleaning and clear up just as fast. Progression into bone loss is generally slow and comes in episodes rather than a steady slide, often over months and years, and it runs faster in smokers, in people with uncontrolled diabetes, and in families where teeth are lost early. Being measured is the only way to know where you stand.
### Q. What shrinks gum pockets?
A.  Removing what is living inside them. Scaling and root planing clears calculus and bacterial film off the root surfaces, the inflammation settles, and the tissue tightens back against the tooth, which lowers the reading. Daily home care keeps that film from rebuilding between visits. Pocket reduction surgery physically reduces depth when cleaning alone hasn’t. Some shrinkage is really the gum receding, which trades a better number for more exposed root. No rinse or toothpaste shrinks a deep pocket by itself.
### Q. Can 7mm gum pockets be reversed?
A.  Reduced, often. Reversed is a stronger word than the situation usually supports. A seven means meaningful attachment and bone loss has already happened, and pockets that deep frequently need surgical access because instruments can’t reliably clean the bottom of them otherwise. A good outcome may leave you well below seven without ever returning to a three. Bone already lost doesn’t come back on its own, and whether a regenerative graft suits your defect is a call your periodontist makes from the imaging.
### Q. Can gums grow back from periodontal disease?
A.  Gum tissue lost to recession doesn’t regrow on its own. Tissue follows bone, and where the bone underneath has gone, the gum has nothing to sit on. Treated gums can look slightly fuller because swelling resolves, which is not the same thing as regrowth. Grafting is how coverage and thickness get rebuilt, using your own tissue or processed donor tissue. Whether a given site can be grafted successfully depends on the bone around it, so that assessment has to happen in person.
### Q. How painful is a periodontal cleaning?
A.  Less than people brace for. The area gets numbed with local anesthetic, so the appointment itself is usually long rather than painful. Afterward, expect tenderness for a couple of days and cold sensitivity that can linger for weeks as the gums tighten and root surface sits exposed. Over-the-counter pain relief handles most of it. Tell the office in advance if dental anxiety is an issue, since there are options. Pain that worsens after several days, or swelling, warrants a call.
### Q. Does dental insurance cover a periodontist?
A.  Most plans include some periodontal coverage, but it runs on a different track than a routine cleaning, under its own procedure codes and its own rules. Plans commonly require documentation first: a full set of pocket depths, current x-rays, sometimes a written explanation of why treatment is needed. Maintenance visits sit in their own category too, on a frequency that may not match the twice-a-year cleaning benefit you assume you have. Have the office file a pre-treatment estimate so the plan answers in writing before you schedule.

## What to Order at a Peruvian Restaurant in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-order-at-a-peruvian-restaurant-in-st-louis
The menu arrived at a birthday dinner and the man from Warrenton could not read a line of it. Ceviche. Lomo saltado. Anticuchos. Causa. He knew what none of those words meant, six people were waiting on him, and the server was standing there being polite about the silence. So he ordered the chicken. It was good chicken. It was also the only thing on that page he could have guessed at from his own kitchen.
Different night, different problem. A woman from Marine tried ceviche once at a catered event, where it had been sitting out in a chafing setup for a couple of hours, and what reached her plate was warm, grayish and faintly chewy. She decided she does not like ceviche. What she does not like is ceviche that sat. Those are not the same dish. One of them is barely the dish at all.
Then there is the family out of Wright City with a nine-year-old who eats four foods, all of them beige. They pass the place every week and have never walked in, because the parents assume the whole menu is raw fish and chilies and there will be nothing for the kid. That assumption is wrong, and it gets its own section further down.
What follows is a read of a Peruvian menu, top to bottom, written for somebody who has never eaten this food. What the raw fish dish actually is and why it is not sushi. Why a Peruvian beef dish shows up with soy sauce and french fries in the same pan. Which peppers bite and which ones only look like they will. What the potatoes and the corn are doing there. What to drink. And how to order for a table where two people are game for anything, three are curious, and one wants plain rice.
### What is the most famous Peruvian food?
Ceviche is the one. Raw white fish cut into cubes and cured in fresh lime juice with red onion, chili and salt, served cold with sweet potato and big toasted corn on the side. It is Peru’s national dish, and the cure takes minutes rather than hours.
Peru keeps a national ceviche day on the calendar. That tells you where the dish sits in the culture. It is not a starter somebody added to fill out a menu; it is the thing a cook gets judged on, the way a barbecue place gets judged on brisket. If a kitchen makes one dish with real care, this is usually it.
Lomo saltado runs a close second and probably wins on sheer volume eaten. Pollo a la brasa is the Sunday-dinner, feed-the-whole-house dish. But ask anyone what Peruvian food is and the answer comes back ceviche, every time.
### What exactly is ceviche, and what is leche de tigre?
Ceviche is raw white fish cubed and tossed with fresh lime juice, salt, sliced red onion and chili, then served almost immediately. Leche de tigre is the cloudy liquid left in the bowl: lime juice, fish juices, salt, aji and often a little garlic or ginger. You drink it.
### What the lime is actually doing
The acid denatures the proteins in the fish. The flesh goes from translucent to opaque and firms up, which looks like what heat does and is chemically a different process. This is a cure, not cooking. That distinction matters for food safety, and it matters for how long the fish should sit in the juice.
Classic Peruvian ceviche is a fast cure. Minutes. Some kitchens dress the fish and send it out in under five, so the outside firms while the center stays silky and almost raw. Leave fish in lime juice for an hour and it turns dense and cottony all the way through, which is what happened to that plate at the catered event. Short cure, cold bowl, straight to the table. That is the whole technique.
### Which fish, and how to tell it is fresh
Firm, mild, lean white fish. In Peru the traditional choice is corvina, a sea bass, and flounder, sole, grouper, halibut, snapper, mahi and tilapia all get used depending on what the coast sends in that morning. Oily fish like salmon or mackerel fights the lime instead of working with it, though a few modern kitchens do a salmon version on purpose. Shrimp, octopus and scallops turn up in mixed seafood versions.
Here is the tell. Good ceviche arrives cold, the onion still has snap, the cilantro still looks alive, and the leche de tigre is bright and a little milky rather than watery and separated. It should smell clean, like limes and the ocean, not like fish. If it comes to the table lukewarm, send it back and order something else. Nobody makes this dish well by accident.
### Why there is sweet potato and corn on the plate
Those are not garnish. The lime is aggressive, and a slice of boiled sweet potato is the sugar that takes the edge off it. The corn does the other half of the job. You typically get choclo, a large-kernel Andean corn that is starchy and mild rather than sweet, and cancha, toasted corn kernels that eat like a savory, crunchy corn nut. Fish, acid, sugar, crunch. The plate is balanced on purpose, and eating a bite of each together is the way it was designed to go down.
If raw seafood is not your thing at all, that is a normal place to be, and the rest of the menu does not need you to change your mind. Folks who want their seafood hot and messy instead are usually better served by a crawfish boil around St. Louis, which is a different pleasure entirely.
### What is lomo saltado, and why does it taste a little Chinese?
Lomo saltado is beef strips stir-fried hot with red onion, tomato and aji amarillo, finished with soy sauce and vinegar, then served over rice with french fries tossed right into the pan. It tastes Chinese because it partly is. Chinese immigrants brought the wok to Peru in the 1800s.
That fusion has a name: chifa. Large numbers of Chinese laborers arrived in Peru through the nineteenth century, stayed, opened kitchens, and cooked what they knew using what Peru grew. Soy sauce met aji amarillo. Ginger met potatoes. A wok over high heat met beef and onions. What came out the other side is not Chinese food and it is not pre-contact Andean food. It is its own thing, a couple of centuries old now, and it is one of the most widely eaten cuisines in Peru.
The fries throw people. Rice and potatoes on the same plate reads like a mistake to an American eye. It is not. The fries go into the pan at the end and soak up the soy, vinegar and beef juices, so they arrive half crisp and half saturated, and the rice underneath catches whatever runs off. Order it the first time and you will understand the appeal in about two bites. It is the safest bet on the menu for somebody who wants something recognizable, and it is genuinely one of the great beef dishes anywhere.
### Other chifa dishes to watch for
Arroz chaufa is Peruvian fried rice, usually with chicken or seafood, egg, scallion and soy. Tallarin saltado runs the same treatment over noodles instead of rice. Aji de gallina is not chifa, but it lives in the same comfort-food neighborhood: shredded chicken in a thick, mild sauce of aji amarillo, bread or cracker, milk and cheese, poured over rice and potatoes. Warm, creamy, barely spicy. It converts skeptics.
### What else belongs on a first-time order?
Four dishes carry most first visits: pollo a la brasa, anticuchos, causa and papa a la huancaina. Between them you get roast chicken, grilled skewers, a cold potato terrine and a warm potato starter, which covers a lot of ground without anybody at the table having to be brave about it.
### Pollo a la brasa
Whole chicken marinated in soy, vinegar, garlic, cumin and aji panca, then cooked on a rotisserie spit over charcoal or wood. The skin goes dark and lacquered. The meat stays wet. It usually comes with fries and a simple salad, plus a green sauce, aji verde, made from chilies, herbs and something creamy. That sauce is the point for a lot of people. In Peru this is what families eat on a weeknight or order in for a crowd, and the ordering unit is a quarter, half or whole bird.
### Anticuchos
Skewers, grilled over coals, marinated in aji panca, vinegar, garlic and cumin. Traditionally they are beef heart, and that is worth saying plainly rather than tiptoeing around. Heart is a lean, dense muscle with a clean flavor closer to a good steak than to liver, and marinated and charred over fire it is terrific. Some kitchens also run chicken or plain beef versions. Ask which one you are getting, order it, and decide for yourself.
### Causa
Cold, layered, and prettier than it sounds. Yellow potato is mashed with lime juice and aji amarillo until it is dense and smooth, then pressed into layers with a filling in the middle: chicken salad, tuna, crab, avocado. It arrives chilled, cut like a small cake. Bright, tangy, mild. A good first bite for somebody who is nervous about the whole menu, because nothing about it is challenging and everything about it tastes specific.
### Papa a la huancaina
Boiled yellow potatoes, sliced and covered in a bright yellow sauce of aji amarillo, fresh cheese, milk and crackers or bread, usually with an olive and a hard-boiled egg on top. It is served cool or at room temperature. The sauce tastes like a warm, mild queso with a little fruity chili behind it. Kids eat this. Adults eat it faster.
### How hot do the aji peppers actually run?
Milder than the color suggests. Aji amarillo is bright orange and fruity with modest heat, roughly jalapeno territory. Aji panca is deep red, dried, smoky and nearly mild. Rocoto is the one that bites, and it is used sparingly. Peruvian food is aromatic far more than it is fiery.
Aji amarillo does the most work. It is in the huancaina sauce, in causa, in aji de gallina, in a lot of lomo saltado. What it brings is a fruity, almost apricot-like flavor and a warmth that builds slowly and quits. People who cannot handle a jalapeno will notice it. Most everybody else will just read it as flavor.
Aji panca is the smoky one. Dried, dark red, used as a paste, and it shows up in anticucho marinade and in the rub for pollo a la brasa. Heat is low. What it gives you is depth and color, closer to what a dried ancho does in Mexican cooking than to anything sharp.
Rocoto is different. Thick-walled, apple-shaped, often red, and it carries real heat, hotter than a jalapeno and capable of going further. It turns up in rocoto relleno, a stuffed pepper dish from the Arequipa region, and in table sauces. If a server warns you about something, this is usually what they mean. Take the warning seriously and ask for the sauce on the side.
The comparison people reach for is Mexican food, and it is a useful one as long as you hold it loosely. Both traditions build on chilies, lime, corn and slow-cooked meat. The heat levels and the aromatics land in different places, and anyone who has worked their way through the Mexican food around St. Louis already has the palate for this. Different accent, same language family.
### Why do potatoes and corn get so much attention?
Because both crops were domesticated in the Andes, and Peru still grows them in a variety that is hard to picture from a Midwest grocery store. Native potato varieties run into the thousands, in yellows, purples, reds and blacks, and corn comes in kernels the size of a thumbnail.
Every potato eaten anywhere on earth traces back to that region. Peru kept the diversity that the rest of the world traded away for a handful of commercial types. So when a menu lists papa amarilla, that is not a fancy way of saying Yukon Gold; it is a specific waxy, deep-yellow potato with a texture that holds up in causa without turning to paste. Papas a la huancaina, causa, the potatoes under aji de gallina, the fries in lomo saltado, and in some kitchens a freeze-dried mountain potato called chuno. The potato is not a side here. It is a main ingredient with opinions.
Corn does the same work. Choclo has huge, pale, starchy kernels and gets boiled and served in chunks, sometimes with a slab of fresh cheese. Cancha is a different corn, toasted in oil until it puffs and cracks, salted, and set on the table the way another restaurant sets out bread. Purple corn, maiz morado, is not eaten at all in most preparations. It gets boiled down into a drink, which brings up the glasses.
Killing an hour before dinner? Here is what a local hobby shop carries.
### What should you drink with it?
Three things show up on nearly every Peruvian drink list: chicha morada, a sweet purple-corn drink; Inca Kola, a bright yellow soda that outsells the global brands in Peru; and the pisco sour, a tart cocktail of grape brandy, lime, syrup, egg white and bitters. Try all three eventually.
Chicha morada is the one to order first. Purple corn simmered with pineapple rind, apple, cinnamon and clove, then strained, sweetened and chilled, with fresh lime stirred in. It is non-alcoholic, deep purple, and tastes a bit like a spiced fruit punch that somebody made from scratch and did not oversweeten. Kids drink it by the pitcher. It also happens to be the right foil for lime-heavy food.
Inca Kola is a cultural fact more than a beverage. Golden yellow, wildly sweet, tasting roughly of bubble gum and lemon verbena, and beloved in Peru to a degree that is genuinely unusual for a local soda. Order one. Take a sip. Either you will love it or the table will get a laugh out of your face.
The pisco sour is the serious drink. Pisco is a clear Peruvian grape brandy, shaken with fresh lime juice, simple syrup and egg white, then finished with a few drops of bitters on the foam. It is tart, strong and smooth, and it does what a good sour does next to salty, acidic food. A chilcano is the easier cousin: pisco, ginger ale, lime, ice, tall glass, done.
### How do you order for a table that has never tried this?
Order for the middle of the table, not the edges. One ceviche to share, one lomo saltado, one pollo a la brasa or aji de gallina, and a causa or papa a la huancaina to start. That covers raw, seared, roasted and cold, and nobody gets stuck.
A typical Peruvian dinner is lighter than the American version, because lunch is the large meal of the day. Lunch runs as a set: a soup or a starter, then a main with rice, and something sweet after. Dinner is smaller and later, often built out of sandwiches, skewers, a plate of anticuchos, roast chicken, or whatever the family had at midday. Family-style sharing is normal. So is ordering a starter for the table and letting the mains land whenever they land.
### The picky eater is fine
That kid from Wright City who eats beige food has more options here than at most restaurants. Pollo a la brasa is roast chicken with french fries. Arroz chaufa is fried rice. Papa a la huancaina is potatoes with a mild cheese sauce. Plain white rice sits under half the menu already. Nothing on that list requires courage, and everything on it is actually good, which is a better outcome than the chicken tenders the same kid would have ordered somewhere else.
### Ask two questions and you are set
Ask what the kitchen makes best, and ask what came in fresh. Servers answer both honestly far more often than people expect, and the second question matters a lot for anything raw. If the fish answer is vague, order the lomo saltado and the chicken and come back another day. That is the same instinct that works at a counter on Cherokee Street in St. Louis, where asking what the cook is proud of beats guessing off a board every time.
If the arepa on the next table caught your eye, read what Venezuelan food is and what to order in St. Louis.
One more piece of practical advice for anybody driving in from Lebanon, Marthasville or anywhere else with a long ride home. Call first. Ceviche and pollo a la brasa both have a rhythm, the chicken comes off the spit in batches and the fish depends on a delivery, and a two-minute phone call tells you whether tonight is the night.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Why is Peruvian food so famous?
A.  Geography and immigration, mostly. Peru runs from Pacific coast to high Andes to Amazon basin, so one country grows seafood, thousands of native potato varieties, dozens of chilies and tropical fruit. On top of that sit waves of Spanish, African, Chinese, Japanese and Italian arrivals, each of whom cooked what they knew with what was there. Chifa and Nikkei cooking both came out of that. The result is a cuisine with unusual range that still tastes like one place.
### Q. What do people in Peru usually eat for dinner?
A.  Something lighter than you would guess, because lunch is the big meal. Midday runs as a set course: starter or soup, a main with rice, a little dessert. Dinner comes later in the evening and leans toward sandwiches, anticuchos off a grill, roast chicken, a bowl of soup, or leftovers from lunch. Sharing is normal and portions are smaller. A full multi-course spread at night is a restaurant occasion rather than a Tuesday.
### Q. Is lomo saltado Peruvian or Chinese?
A.  Both, and that is the honest answer rather than a dodge. Chinese immigrants arrived in Peru in large numbers during the 1800s and brought the wok, high-heat stir-frying, soy sauce and ginger. Peruvian cooks married that technique to local beef, red onion, tomato, aji amarillo and potatoes. The tradition it belongs to is called chifa, and chifa is thoroughly Peruvian. You will not find lomo saltado on a menu in China.
### Q. What kind of fish is used in ceviche?
A.  Firm, mild, lean white fish. The traditional Peruvian choice is corvina, a sea bass, and flounder, sole, grouper, halibut, snapper, mahi and tilapia all work well. Oily fish like salmon or mackerel clashes with the lime, though some modern kitchens do a salmon version deliberately. Mixed versions add shrimp, octopus or scallops. Whatever the fish, freshness and cold handling matter far more than the species on the menu.
### Q. Is ceviche healthy to eat?
A.  Nutritionally it stacks up well. Lean protein, fresh lime, raw onion, herbs, a little chili, no added fat, plus the sweet potato and corn on the side. There is no butter, no breading and no fryer involved. The real question is not nutrition but handling, since the fish is raw. Pregnant people, young children, older adults and anyone immunocompromised are generally advised to skip raw seafood preparations entirely.
### Q. Is bacteria killed in ceviche?
A.  Not reliably, and it is worth being clear about this. Lime juice denatures the protein and firms the flesh, which is a chemical cure and not the same as cooking with heat. Acid can reduce some surface bacteria, but it does not dependably kill every pathogen or parasite the way proper cooking does. That is exactly why sourcing, freshness, cold handling and a short cure matter so much, and why high-risk eaters are told to avoid raw preparations.
### Q. What are some common ceviche mistakes?
A.  Marinating too long is the big one, since an hour in lime juice turns silky fish dense and chalky. After that: bottled lime juice instead of fresh, oily fish that fights the acid, warm ingredients or a warm bowl, cutting the fish too small so it overcures, over-salting, dumping everything together and letting it sit, and skipping the sweet potato and corn that balance the acid. Serving it anything other than cold ruins it.
### Q. What is the most unusual food in Peru?
A.  Cuy, which is guinea pig, is usually the answer that surprises visitors most. It has been raised and eaten in the Andes for thousands of years, long before Spanish contact, and it is typically roasted or fried whole. Anticuchos, the beef heart skewers, are the other common answer and are eaten all over the country as street food. Neither one is guaranteed to appear on any given local menu, so ask.

## What You Can Do at a St. Louis Post Office: Passports, PO Boxes, and Shipping
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-you-can-do-at-a-st-louis-post-office
The passport in the junk drawer had expired four years back. A man in Bellefontaine Neighbors found that out on a Tuesday, thirteen days before a cruise his wife had booked as a surprise. He grabbed his keys and drove to the nearest counter with the dead passport and a lot of hope. The clerk was kind about it. She was also booked into the following week.
Across the river, a woman in Venice tapes up six boxes a night. Handmade candles, mostly, sold to strangers online. She’s at the post office so often the staff know her order before she sets the stack down. She still isn’t sure she’s picking the right shipping service, and she suspects she’s overpaying every single week.
A retiree in Sauget needs a money order for rent because his landlord won’t take a personal check. A new arrival in Berkeley wants a PO box after two porch packages walked off in one week. A student out in Maryville just wants stamps and has no idea the machine in the lobby sells them at midnight. Five people, one kind of building, five completely different errands.
Here’s the part most folks miss. A post office does far more than move envelopes, and knowing what happens at that counter before you stand in line saves a wasted trip. Passports, boxes, money orders, mail holds, the whole spread. Let’s walk through what you can actually get done.
### Can I just walk into a Post Office and get my passport?
Sometimes, but don’t count on it. Most post offices around St. Louis that accept passport applications handle them by appointment, and walk-in availability swings by location, day, and how many clerks are trained for it. The post office accepts your paperwork and takes your photo. The U.S. State Department is what actually issues the passport.
That distinction matters more than it sounds. A post office is what the government calls an acceptance facility. Clerks there check your documents, watch you sign the form, seal everything into an envelope, and send it off. They can’t speed up a decision, fix a rejected photo after the fact, or hand you a passport over the counter. Nobody can do that last one except State.
First-time applicants and kids have to apply in person, which is exactly why the appointment system exists. If you’re just renewing and you qualify, you often mail your application straight to State and skip the counter entirely. Two very different trips. Before you drive anywhere, call the specific location or book online, because an unannounced walk-in on a Saturday morning is how people burn an hour and leave with nothing.
Kids add a wrinkle worth planning for. A child’s passport application needs both parents or guardians present, or specific consent paperwork if one can’t make it, and that catches families off guard every summer. If a passport is standing between you and a trip, treat the appointment like the trip itself: booked early, documents stacked the night before, nobody rushing.
### What documents and photos do you need before you go?
Bring more than you think you need. For a first passport you’ll want a completed Form DS-11 left unsigned, proof of U.S. citizenship, a valid photo ID, a photocopy of that ID, one passport photo, and a way to pay. Miss one piece and the whole appointment resets to another day.
Proof of citizenship trips people up the most. A certified birth certificate with a raised or stamped seal works; a hospital souvenir certificate does not. A prior U.S. passport counts, even an expired one, and so does a naturalization certificate. Whatever you bring, the clerk needs the original or a certified copy, not a phone photo and not a plain printout standing in for the real thing.
Don’t sign the DS-11 at home. You sign it in front of the clerk, and a form signed too early sometimes has to be redone. The photo has its own rules too: plain background, no glasses, a recent shot at the right size. Post offices take passport photos on site for a fee, which saves a second stop and cuts the odds of a rejected image.
One more thing that catches people at the register. The State Department application fee and the post office acceptance fee are two separate payments. The State fee usually has to be a check or money order, while the acceptance fee can often go on a card. Rules vary by location, so ask yours what it takes before you’re standing there with the wrong kind of payment.
### How do PO boxes work, and who actually needs one?
A PO box is a locked mailbox you rent inside the post office, sized from a slot that holds a few letters up to one that swallows shoeboxes. You pick the size, pay for a term, and pick up whenever the lobby is open. Setting one up takes two forms of ID and a short form.
Terms usually run in three, six, or twelve-month blocks, and the price rides on box size and the location’s fee group, so a box downtown and a box at a quieter branch can cost different amounts. Rates change, and I won’t guess a number that will be wrong by the time you read this. Ask the branch, or check online for the current rate on the size you want.
Who benefits? Anyone mid-move who doesn’t have a stable address yet. Home-based sellers, like our candle maker in Venice, who’d rather not print a house address on a hundred packages. Folks who travel for weeks at a stretch. And anybody tired of watching deliveries vanish off the front step. Many boxes also come with street addressing, so you get a real street-style address that private carriers will actually deliver to.
If a move is what landed you at the counter, it’s worth knowing the rest of the bill before you sign a lease. We broke down what a local move actually runs in our guide to moving costs across St. Louis, so the total doesn’t blindside you halfway through.

### What can you ship, and which service is right?
Almost anything legal, at a range of speeds and prices. The counter handles letters, flat envelopes, and packages, from a birthday card to a fifty-pound box. The trick isn’t whether they’ll take it. The trick is matching the right service to what’s inside, how fast it needs to land, and how much you’re willing to spend.
For everyday packages, two options cover most needs. Ground Advantage is the budget workhorse for boxes that aren’t in a hurry. Priority Mail runs faster, includes tracking, and often bundles a little insurance, and its flat-rate boxes are a genuine deal when you’re shipping something heavy in a small space. Need it there overnight or close to it? Priority Mail Express is the top tier, with a money-back guarantee on the delivery window.
Books, DVDs, and printed material get their own slow, cheap lane called Media Mail, a quiet money-saver plenty of people never hear about. Letters and thin envelopes go First-Class. And the boxes and envelopes for Priority services are free at the counter, so you don’t buy packaging for those, you just take what you need.
A few add-ons earn the extra coins. Tracking, so you and the buyer both see where it is. Insurance on anything you couldn’t cheerfully replace. Certified Mail when you need proof a letter arrived, which matters for leases, disputes, and anything legal. Our candle seller in Venice cut her costs the day she stopped defaulting to one service and started weighing each box against the flat-rate option.
Shipping overseas is its own animal. Every international package needs a customs form that lists what’s inside and its value, and the clerk will walk you through it, though filling it out online first speeds up the window. Prohibited items and country rules change, so if you’re mailing something unusual abroad, ask before you seal the box.
### The counter services people forget about
Passports and packages get the attention, but the daily bread of a post office is the small stuff. Money orders. Stamps at every hour. Mail holds. A change of address that reroutes your life to a new door. These are the errands that turn a post office into the most useful boring building on the block.
Money orders are the one our Sauget retiree leans on. They work like guaranteed cash for people who can’t or won’t use a personal check, common for rent and deposits, and the post office sells both domestic and international ones up to a set limit for a small fee. Fill it out at the window, keep the receipt, and you’ve got a paper trail if it ever goes missing.
Moving? File a change of address and the post office forwards most of your mail for a stretch while you update everyone who still has the old one. You can do it at the counter or online. It pairs naturally with the rest of a move, and if you’re about to haul boxes yourself, the sizes and prices in our St. Louis moving truck rental breakdown are a good next stop.
The lobby machine and the counter both sell stamps, and the machine doesn’t clock out, so the Maryville student can grab a book of them at midnight. Heading out of town? Put your mail on hold and the carrier keeps it safe at the office until you’re back, instead of stuffing a box that screams “nobody’s home.” Certified Mail, signature confirmation, package drop-off and pickup, PO box package alerts, they all live at that same window.
Not sure which location handles passports, sells money orders, or has the PO box size you need? Hours and services differ from one branch to the next, so it pays to check before you drive. ### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What documents do I need for a U.S. passport?
A.  You’ll bring a completed Form DS-11 left unsigned, proof of U.S. citizenship such as a certified birth certificate or a prior passport, a valid photo ID, a photocopy of that ID, one passport photo, and payment. First-time applicants apply in person; eligible adults renewing by mail skip the counter.
### Q. How long are passports taking right now?
A.  Processing times shift constantly, so the only reliable number is the current estimate posted on travel.state.gov. The clock starts when the State Department receives your application, not the day you visit the counter, and mailing time sits on top of that. Expedited service costs more and moves faster. Check before booking travel.
### Q. How much does a passport typically cost?
A.  You pay two parts: an application fee to the U.S. State Department and a separate acceptance fee to the post office. A passport photo and expedited service cost extra. Because these amounts change over time, confirm the current figures on travel.state.gov before you go, and ask which payment forms your location accepts.
### Q. What are common reasons for passport denial?
A.  Most rejections trace to paperwork, not people. Incomplete forms, an unacceptable photo, weak proof of citizenship, or a name that doesn’t match across documents all send applications back. Certain legal issues, like significant unpaid child support or specific federal court orders, can block approval outright. Check every document against the checklist first.
### Q. What will disqualify me from getting a passport?
A.  Federal law can deny a passport for seriously delinquent tax debt certified by the IRS, child-support arrears above the federal threshold, certain outstanding federal warrants, or a court order that restricts your travel. A passport reported lost or stolen repeatedly can also trigger extra review. Resolve these issues before you apply.
### Q. What three documents do I need for a passport?
A.  Think of it as three items: proof of U.S. citizenship, like a certified birth certificate or prior passport; a valid government photo ID; and a photocopy of the front of that ID. You’ll also need a passport photo and the DS-11 form, but those three documents are the real backbone.
### Q. How much does it cost to rent a PO box?
A.  Box rent depends on the size you choose and the location’s fee group, then multiplies by the term, usually three, six, or twelve months. Because rates change and vary by branch, I won’t quote a figure that will be stale. Ask the specific post office or check online, and bring two forms of ID.
### Q. How do I decide between Priority Mail and Ground Advantage?
A.  Choose Ground Advantage when the box isn’t urgent and you want the lower price. Choose Priority Mail when you need it faster, want tracking baked in, and might use a flat-rate box for something heavy in a small space. Weigh speed against cost per package, and compare both at the counter.

## What a Proctologist Does and When to See One in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-proctologist-does-and-when-to-see-one-in-st-louis
You spotted blood on the paper a couple of weeks back. Figured it was nothing. Too much hot sauce, maybe, or too long sitting in traffic on the way home to Hillsboro. Then it showed up again. Now there’s an ache when you sit down, an itch that won’t quit, and a low hum of worry you keep pushing to the back of your head.
Nobody talks about this at dinner. Bathroom trouble feels private, even embarrassing, so people wait it out, google at midnight, and hope it clears on its own. It’s one of the most common reasons adults quietly avoid a doctor. A proctologist is the person trained to sort out the exact thing you’re too shy to bring up anywhere else.
Let’s walk through what these doctors really do, when a symptom crosses from annoying into call-someone territory, and how to find one near you without burning a month. Quick note before any of that: this is general information, not a diagnosis, and it’s no stand-in for seeing a physician. Anything that worries you is worth running past a doctor in person.
### Why would someone need to see a proctologist?
Most people end up there because something won’t quit. Bleeding. Pain. Itching that keeps them awake. A lump that wasn’t there last month. A change in bathroom habits that’s stuck around too long. A proctologist, more formally a colon and rectal surgeon, diagnoses and treats problems of the anus, rectum, and lower colon — everything from everyday hemorrhoids to the early warning signs of cancer.
The role runs wider than most people picture. These are surgeons, yes, but a big slice of what they do never touches an operating room. They handle the small, miserable problems that drugstore creams never really fix. They catch the serious things early, while those things are still easy to treat. And they work on a part of the body people are too shy to mention at a regular checkup. That shyness is a big reason the specialty exists at all.
So who actually needs one? Anyone whose symptoms hang on past a week or two. Anyone with a family history of colon or rectal cancer. Anyone whose regular doctor spotted something and wants a specialist to take a closer look. You don’t need an emergency to earn the appointment. Persistent and unexplained is reason enough to go.
One more group worth naming: people managing an ongoing condition. Crohn’s and ulcerative colitis both cause rectal and anal problems that flare and fade. Someone who’s had rectal surgery before. Anyone with a repair that needs the occasional check. For them, a proctologist isn’t a one-time visit; it’s part of staying ahead of a condition that likes to resurface.
### What does a proctologist actually treat?
More than you’d guess, and most of it is fixable. The daily bread is hemorrhoids, anal fissures, and abscesses — common, painful, and very treatable. Past those, they handle fistulas, rectal prolapse, warts, stubborn itching, incontinence, chronic constipation, and the screening and surgery tied to colon and rectal cancer. One specialty, a long list.
### The common, fixable problems
This is where most visits live. Hemorrhoids that bleed or won’t shrink back down. A fissure, which is a small tear that turns every bathroom trip into broken glass. An abscess near the anus that’s hot, swollen, and clearly getting worse by the day. Skin tags. Warts. Itching that no cream seems to touch. None of it is glamorous. All of it tends to settle fast once someone who knows the territory takes a proper look.
### The serious end of the list
Proctologists also stand on the front line of colon and rectal cancer. They perform and follow up on colonoscopies, remove suspicious growths, and operate when that’s the right call. A change in the width of your stool, bleeding that keeps returning, weight you can’t explain losing, a strong family history — those put you where a specialist’s exam beats waiting and watching. Caught early, these cancers rank among the more treatable ones there are.
### The treatments that don’t mean surgery
Plenty of what a proctologist does is quick and low-key. Rubber band ligation for hemorrhoids, done in minutes in the office. Ointments and diet changes for a fissure. Draining an abscess. In-office removal of warts or tags. Advice on fiber, fluids, and habits that head off the next flare. Surgery is the last tool they reach for, not the first, and a good one will tell you that plainly.
Worth saying clearly: a proctologist and a gastroenterologist overlap a lot, and plenty of problems could go to either. The proctologist’s edge is the surgical side — they can both diagnose the issue and, when it needs cutting, fix it themselves instead of sending you elsewhere. For a lot of anal and rectal complaints, that one-stop quality saves real time.
### Which symptoms should send you to a proctologist?
Short version: anything that bleeds, hurts, lumps, itches, or changes and won’t settle on its own. One rough day after a spicy dinner is one thing. That same problem running two weeks straight is a different message entirely. Read the pattern, not the single bad night. The pattern is what tells the truth.
### Signs worth booking an appointment
Blood on the paper or in the bowl. Pain or pressure that lingers after you leave the bathroom. Itching or discharge that creams won’t calm. A lump or swelling near the anus. Constipation or diarrhea that drags on. Leaking, or trouble holding gas or stool. Any of these, still around after a week or two, earns a call. You’re not overreacting. You’re paying attention to your own body.
### Signs worth calling this week
Some things shouldn’t wait for a pattern to prove itself. Heavy bleeding, or blood that looks dark. A fever paired with rectal pain, which can point to an abscess. Sudden, severe pain out of nowhere. Weight dropping without reason alongside bathroom changes. Brand-new symptoms if you’re past fifty and overdue for screening. Any of those, move the timeline up and call now. A fast all-clear beats a slow guess.
Trust your gut on this one. If something feels off and it’s lasted longer than it should, that instinct is worth more than a search bar. The worst outcome of going in is reassurance and a small copay. The worst outcome of waiting is the thing you were afraid of, caught later than it had to be.
### What happens if you keep putting it off?
Waiting rarely makes any of this better, and sometimes it makes the fix harder. A fissure that could’ve healed with cream and fiber can turn chronic. A small abscess can grow into a fistula that needs surgery. And the one that keeps proctologists up at night: bleeding written off as “just hemorrhoids” that turns out to be something a scope would’ve caught months earlier.
Here’s the honest math. The exam takes minutes. It’s mildly awkward and over fast. The alternative is weeks of worry, symptoms that creep worse, and treatment that gets more involved the longer you stall. People walk out of that first visit again and again saying the same thing: they wish they’d come in sooner. Almost nobody says they went too early.
None of this means every twinge is an emergency. It means a symptom that keeps showing up deserves a real answer instead of another guess. You wouldn’t ignore a tooth that ached for a month. Same standard applies here, minus the part where you talk yourself out of it because it’s below the belt.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What happens at your first visit to a proctologist?
A.  Mostly talking, then a look. Your provider asks about symptoms, diet, family history, and bathroom habits, then usually does a visual and physical exam of the area. Some offices do a quick scope. Bring your medication list and any questions. Tell the staff up front if you’re anxious — they do this all day.
### Q. Do you need a referral to see a proctologist?
A.  It depends on your insurance, not the specialist. Many HMO plans require a referral from your primary doctor before they’ll cover a visit; most PPO plans let you book directly. Call your insurer or check your plan documents first. When in doubt, the specialist’s office can tell you what they need.
### Q. How much does a proctologist visit cost?
A.  There’s no flat answer, and anyone quoting one is guessing. Cost turns on your insurance, your deductible, and whether the appointment is a simple consult or includes a procedure. A basic office visit costs far less than a scope or surgery. Call the office for an estimate and confirm coverage with your insurer beforehand.
### Q. How to prepare for a proctologist appointment?
A.  Ask the office if any prep is needed — some exams want an enema an hour before, many need nothing. Write down your symptoms, when they started, and your questions. Bring a medication list and your insurance card. Wear clothes that are easy to change out of. Eat normally unless you’re told otherwise.
### Q. What kind of exam does a proctologist do?
A.  Usually a visual check first, then a gloved digital rectal exam that takes seconds. Depending on your symptoms, they may use an anoscope or proctoscope — a short, lubricated scope that lets them see the anal canal and lower rectum. It’s quick and done in the office. A full colonoscopy is scheduled separately.
### Q. Should I see a proctologist or gastroenterologist for hemorrhoids?
A.  Either can help, but they lean different ways. Gastroenterologists manage hemorrhoids with medication and in-office procedures. Proctologists, who are colon and rectal surgeons, handle the same conditions and can also operate when hemorrhoids are severe. For stubborn or recurring cases, a proctologist is often the more direct route. Start with whoever your insurance covers easily.
### Q. Is a proctologist visit embarrassing?
A.  It feels that way beforehand, rarely during. These providers examine this part of the body every single day, and nothing about your situation will surprise them. The exam is brief, you stay draped, and staff are trained to keep it matter-of-fact. Most people leave wishing they hadn’t waited so long out of nerves.
### Q. How soon should you see a proctologist about rectal bleeding?
A.  Don’t sit on it. Bright red bleeding is often something minor like a hemorrhoid or fissure, but bleeding can also signal something serious, and only an exam tells the difference. Book within a week or two for new or ongoing bleeding. Heavy bleeding, dizziness, or dark stool means seek care now.

## When to See a Pulmonologist in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/when-to-see-a-pulmonologist-in-st-louis
The cough started in March and was still hanging on past Memorial Day. A man in Pacific figured it was the tail end of a winter cold, then blamed the pollen, then the dusty drive to the job site. By June he was stopping halfway up his own staircase to catch his breath. His regular doctor listened to his chest, ordered an X-ray, and said something he wasn’t expecting. You need to see a lung specialist.
That word throws people. Pulmonologist. It sounds like a big deal, and sometimes it is, and often it isn’t. A woman in Lake St. Louis spent two years telling herself the snoring and the daytime exhaustion were just middle age. They weren’t. One sleep study later she had a diagnosis, a machine, and the first real night’s sleep she’d had since her forties. Different symptom, same specialist.
A pulmonologist is a doctor who trains for years past medical school in the lungs, the airways, and everything that moves air through them. Here’s what this covers: the symptoms that actually warrant one, the conditions they handle, how you get an appointment around St. Louis, what the first visit looks like, and how to pick one you trust. None of this is medical advice. It’s a map, so you know when a cough is just a cough and when it’s time to make the call.
### What symptoms require a pulmonologist?
Persistent shortness of breath, a cough that lasts more than eight weeks, wheezing, coughing up blood, or chest tightness that won’t quit. Add unexplained weight loss, repeat chest infections, or an abnormal chest X-ray to the list. Sudden, severe breathlessness is different. That’s a 911 emergency, not a specialist appointment.
The tricky part is that lung trouble hides in plain sight. People adjust. You take the elevator instead of the stairs, skip the walk you used to take, park closer to the door, and tell yourself you’re just out of shape or getting older. Sometimes that’s exactly it. But breathlessness that keeps getting worse, or shows up doing things that never used to wind you, is worth a doctor’s ear. Your body is quietly rerouting around a problem, and the rerouting is the symptom.
Some signs deserve a faster call than others. Blood in what you cough up. A wheeze you can hear across the room. Chest infections that keep circling back, three or four in a year. Lips or fingertips that turn a little blue. Any of those, stop guessing and get seen. Most people start with their primary care doctor, who sorts the everyday stuff from the specialist stuff and points you onward when the pattern calls for it.
### When does a lingering cough cross the line?
Doctors draw a rough line at eight weeks. A cough that outlasts a cold, keeps you up at night, or comes with breathlessness has stopped being a leftover and started being a question. Most short coughs clear on their own. The one that won’t is the one to watch.
Think about what a St. Louis year does to a set of lungs. Ragweed in the fall, tree pollen in the spring, that heavy river-valley humidity all summer, and cold dry air rattling around inside a furnace-heated house all winter. A cough can ride any of those and still be nothing. What matters is the shape of it over time. A cough that’s slowly fading, even if it’s annoying, is usually on its way out. A cough holding steady or getting louder after two months is telling you something.
Pay attention to what comes with it, too. A dry cough plus new heartburn points one direction. A wet cough with colored mucus and fevers points another. A cough that only shows up around the cat, or at work, or when you laugh, is a clue in itself. You don’t have to diagnose any of this yourself. You just have to notice the pattern and be able to describe it, because that description is half of what a specialist works from.
### What does a pulmonologist actually treat?
Asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and sleep apnea make up a big share of the caseload, but the reach is wider than that. Lung infections, scarring, blood clots in the lungs, and abnormal spots found on a scan all land on a pulmonologist’s desk. If it involves the airways or the tissue that does the breathing, it’s their territory.
### Long-term airway conditions
Asthma and COPD fill the most appointment slots. Both make air hard to move, and both get managed over years rather than cured in a visit. A pulmonologist fine-tunes the inhalers, checks that you’re actually using them right (most people aren’t), and catches the slow slide before it turns into an ER trip. A steady hand on a chronic condition keeps a lot of people in Wood River and Swansea out of the hospital every winter.
### Sleep and breathing at night
Sleep apnea sits squarely in this world. Loud snoring, gasping awake, a partner who’s clocked you not breathing, waking up wrecked after a full eight hours. A pulmonologist orders the sleep study, reads it, and sets up treatment, often a CPAP machine that pushes air to keep the airway open. Left alone, apnea drags on the heart and the blood pressure, so it’s more than a snoring problem.
### The scarier scans and the sudden stuff
Then there’s the harder end. A nodule on a scan that needs watching or a biopsy. Pulmonary fibrosis, where lung tissue stiffens and scars. Clots that travel to the lungs. Long-haul damage after a bad bout of pneumonia or a virus. This is where the specialist training earns its keep, because these need tools and judgment a family doctor isn’t set up to bring.
### How do you get in to see one in St. Louis?
Usually through a referral from your primary care doctor, though whether you strictly need one depends on your insurance plan. HMO plans tend to require a referral before they’ll cover the visit. PPO plans often let you book directly. Call the number on your insurance card and ask before you schedule anything.
The referral route isn’t just a hoop. A good primary doctor runs the first round of tests, rules out the ordinary explanations, and hands the specialist a head start instead of a blank page. That saves you a visit and them a guessing game. If you don’t have a regular doctor yet, that’s the first call, not the specialist.
Cost and coverage stop a lot of people before they start, and that’s the part worth sorting early. If you’re uninsured or between plans, a specialist bill is a real worry, so start with the groundwork. A clinic can often start the workup and the referral even when a specialist is out of reach on your own dime.
### What happens at the first appointment?
Mostly talking and breathing tests. The pulmonologist digs into your history, listens to your lungs, and usually runs spirometry, a simple test where you blow hard into a tube to measure how much air you move and how fast. Expect questions about smoking, your job, your home, and your family. The first visit builds a picture, it doesn’t fix everything that day.
Come ready and the visit goes twice as far. Bring a list of your medications, including the inhalers and the over-the-counter stuff. Bring any scans or test results you already have, or make sure they’ve been sent over. Write down when the symptoms started, what makes them better or worse, and how they’ve changed. A short honest timeline beats a vague “it’s been a while” every time.
Smoking history comes up, and it pays to be straight about it. Not because anyone’s judging, but because it changes what the doctor looks for and how hard they look. Same with your work. Years around dust, fumes, welding, grain, or paint matter to a lung doctor in a way they don’t to most people. The more honest the input, the sharper the read.

### How do you choose a pulmonologist worth your time?
Line up two or three names, then treat the first calls like short interviews. Ask what they focus on, how the practice handles urgent flare-ups, and how fast you can reach someone between visits. A doctor who mostly manages sleep apnea may not be your best match for a suspicious nodule. Fit matters as much as credentials.
Say plainly what you want out of the relationship. Maybe it’s tight asthma control so you stop landing in urgent care. Maybe it’s a clear answer on a spot the radiologist flagged. Maybe it’s a second opinion on a diagnosis that never sat right. Whatever it is, name it on that first call, then measure what each office actually offers against it. The gap between what you asked for and what they describe tells you where to go.
A few practical questions separate the good fits fast. Is the office in your network, so the visit is covered? How long is the wait for a new patient, and what happens if you get worse before then? Do they run their own testing in-house, or send you across town for every scan? Who calls you with results, and when? None of these are rude to ask. An office that answers them cleanly is showing you how the rest will go.
Location earns a vote too, more than people expect. A lung problem can mean repeat visits, tests, and follow-ups, so a practice a reasonable drive from Weldon Spring beats a big name an hour away in traffic. When you’re short of breath, the last thing you want is a long haul to the appointment. Search the directory, shortlist a few close to home, and start dialing.
### When is shortness of breath an emergency?
When it comes on fast and hard, call 911. Sudden severe breathlessness, chest pain, blue lips, confusion, or the feeling that you can’t get a breath at all is not a wait-for-an-appointment situation. Pulmonologists manage long-run lung disease. Emergencies go to the ER, right now.
This is the one place not to talk yourself down. People downplay breathing trouble because it’s scary to admit, and the delay is the dangerous part. A specialist is for the slow-building problem, the chronic condition, the nagging cough that won’t leave. A sudden crisis is for emergency care. If you’re ever unsure which one you’re in, treat it as the emergency and let the doctors sort it out.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Can I go straight to a pulmonologist?
A.  Sometimes, yes. PPO and many self-pay patients can book a pulmonologist without a referral. HMO and some other plans require one first, or they won’t cover the visit. Call your insurer to confirm before you schedule. Even when you can skip the referral, starting with a primary doctor often saves time and money.
### Q. What are the three conditions treated by a pulmonologist?
A.  Asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and sleep apnea are the three most common. Together they fill much of a pulmonologist’s schedule. The specialty reaches far beyond those, though, into lung infections, scarring, blood clots in the lungs, and abnormal spots on a scan. Anything involving the airways or breathing tissue fits.
### Q. What will a pulmonologist do on a first visit?
A.  Talk, listen, and test your breathing. Expect a thorough review of your history, a chest exam, and often spirometry, where you blow into a tube to measure airflow. Questions about smoking, work, and home are standard. The first visit builds a picture and sets a plan, rather than fixing everything that day.
### Q. Do you need a referral to see a pulmonologist?
A.  It depends on your insurance. HMO plans usually require a referral from your primary doctor before they’ll cover a specialist. PPO plans often let you book directly. Check the number on your insurance card to be sure. A referral also means the specialist starts with your test results already in hand.
### Q. What tests will a pulmonologist do?
A.  Common ones include spirometry and other pulmonary function tests, a chest X-ray or CT scan, pulse oximetry to check oxygen, and blood work. Depending on the case, they may order a sleep study, a bronchoscopy to look inside the airways, or a biopsy. The tests follow your symptoms, not a fixed checklist.
### Q. Do you see a pulmonologist for sleep apnea?
A.  Often, yes. Pulmonologists diagnose and treat sleep apnea, order the sleep study, and set up treatment like a CPAP machine. Sleep medicine doctors and some ENTs handle it too, so the right door depends on your symptoms and your area. If breathing at night is the issue, a lung specialist is a solid start.
### Q. How long does it take to get a pulmonologist appointment?
A.  It varies widely by practice, season, and how urgent your case looks. A routine new-patient visit can take a few weeks; an urgent referral moves faster. Ask about the wait when you call, and ask what to do if you get worse in the meantime. A clinic can often bridge the gap.
### Q. Should I see a pulmonologist or a cardiologist for shortness of breath?
A.  Both can cause it, which is why your primary doctor usually decides. Shortness of breath with coughing, wheezing, or a known lung condition leans pulmonary. Breathlessness with chest pain, swelling, or heart history leans cardiac. Often the two specialists work together. Start with a primary visit so you’re pointed the right way.

## Does Reflexology Work? Missouri’s Hands, Feet and Ears Rule
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/does-reflexology-work-what-to-know-in-st-louis
Gravois traffic is still in your shoulders when the sock comes off. A towel, warm from a cabinet you can’t see, slides under your heel. Then a thumb presses into the arch of your foot - slow, firm, a half-second too deep in one spot - and the breath you’ve been holding since Tuesday leaks out in a sigh you’d be embarrassed by anywhere else.
That sigh is the honest half of reflexology. The other half hangs on the wall: a laminated chart swearing the tender spot under your toes is wired to your head, the arch to your gut, the heel to your lower back. Next to it, a certificate in a gold frame.
Here’s the part nobody in St. Louis tells you. To get a Missouri massage license, the therapist down the street on South Grand had to finish at least five hundred hours of supervised instruction. The person pressing your arch may not need that license at all. Missouri’s massage law exempts “persons who restrict their manipulation of the soft tissues of the human body to the hands, feet or ears” - as long as they file written proof with the state board. So the frame on the wall proves less than it looks, and one sentence on the phone, a few sections down, tells you more than any frame can.
### Is reflexology actually effective?
For an hour of calm, plenty of people feel it all the way up their legs. As a treatment for disease, no. The federal government’s own research center on complementary health says reflexology “is claimed to cause relaxation and healing in those parts of the body, but this has not been proven.” Not even the relaxation part is settled science - worth knowing before anyone sells you a stack of sessions.
Now the twist you’ll want to repeat at Sunday dinner. In a study funded by the National Cancer Institute, women with advanced breast cancer who got reflexology showed improvement in “a few symptoms, such as shortness of breath, but not others, such as nausea or pain.” Read that again. It didn’t touch the pain it’s usually sold for, it eased a symptom nobody puts on the brochure, and it was safe even for the most fragile patients in that study. A real, modest, strange result - and nothing like a chart that says your arch is your liver.
Why can’t science pin it down? You can hand someone a sugar pill that looks exactly like the real one, but you can’t press on a person’s arch in a way that feels like nothing. Warm hands, a hushed room and an hour of undivided attention tangle up with whatever the technique itself does. That leaves you one job: find the person who sells the calm and stops there.
### Missouri’s hands, feet and ears rule
Massage licenses in Missouri go through the Board of Therapeutic Massage, whose office sits in Jefferson City. A practitioner who stays on your feet, hands and ears can skip that license by filing written proof with the board. The certificate in the frame usually means someone finished a private training program. It does not mean Missouri tested them.
So shop like you know the rule. If a place advertises massage alongside reflexology, ask whether the massage therapist holds a Missouri license, and call the board at 573.522.6277 if the answer sounds fuzzy. If a practitioner works only on feet, a blank search can be perfectly ordinary. Ask them plainly, “Did you file your exemption with the massage board?” and “Where did you train, and for how long?” Listen for a straight answer, not a speech. I could not confirm whether the board makes those exemption filings searchable, so don’t let anyone tell you an empty result proves anything either way.
One more Missouri detail with teeth. Missouri’s massage law lets the board file a complaint against a license holder for “use of any advertisement or solicitation which is false, misleading or deceptive to the general public.” So when a licensed therapist’s flyer promises your feet will cure your migraines, that promise has a license riding on it. And if the recliner you’re eyeing sits across the river in Glen Carbon, a Missouri search tells you nothing about it. In a two-state metro, the first question about any credential is which side of the Mississippi it came from.
### Say this one sentence before you book
Since no state license vouches for a reflexologist, the phone call is your real vetting. Call two or three practitioners and say this, word for word: “I’m looking for relaxation and stress relief, not treatment for a medical condition. Is that what you offer?” Then stop talking. The little silence after that question does most of the work for you.
The answer you want sounds plain, almost boring. Something like “Yes, it’s a relaxation session, and it’s not a replacement for your doctor,” followed by practical details - how long the session runs, whether there’s a footbath, that you keep your clothes on, what it costs. That’s the voice of someone who knows exactly what they sell. The answer you don’t want has a pitch tucked inside it: talk of detoxing, clearing blockages, fixing your thyroid or your migraines through your feet, or a push to prepay a stack of sessions before you’ve even met. Thank them. Hang up. Dial the next name.
Then ask one more: “If a spot hurts during the session, what does that mean?” A grounded practitioner says it’s tender or tight, that you should tell them, and that they’ll ease off. If you hear “that means your liver is congested,” you’ve learned something important about the next hour of your life. And here’s the line worth repeating to the skeptic in your family: the reflexologist worth booking is the one who tells you what they can’t fix.
### Your arch is not your liver
Every reflexology room runs on the same map: the feet as a shrunken mirror of the body, toes tied to the head, the arch to the digestive organs, the heel to the lower back and pelvis. Press the zone, the tradition says, and a signal travels through the nervous system to its matching part. It’s a lovely idea and the backbone of the practice. It’s also the piece science can’t verify, which is why the skeptic at Sunday dinner calls the whole thing a foot rub with a horoscope stapled to it.
The map matters most in one moment. You’re drifting, warm, half-asleep, and the practitioner finds a spot near the ball of your foot that makes you suck air through your teeth. So what does it mean when a reflexology point hurts? Usually that patch of foot is tender, or you’re carrying tension there, or you spent Saturday walking the aisles at Soulard Market in the wrong shoes. A sore point is not a message from an organ, no matter what the chart says.
Sharp or lasting pain is a different thing. Don’t grit your teeth through it on a padded recliner just to be polite. Say so right then, and a good practitioner backs off without making it awkward. You should never walk out limping or bruised. If you do, you have your answer about a second visit.
### What happens once the shoes come off?
Less than you’d think, and nothing awkward. You keep your clothes on. You sink into a reclining chair or lie on a table under a light blanket. A short chat comes first - how you’re feeling, whether anything hurts, what you hope to get out of the hour. Then the shoes and socks come off, and sometimes there’s a footbath first, warm enough that you feel the heat climb past your ankles while your toes go pink.
A session usually runs 30 to 60 minutes. The practitioner works your feet with thumbs and fingers, and some work the hands or ears too. From across the room it looks like a focused foot massage, but the touch is different: firmer than a rub, more deliberate, moving point to point instead of kneading one area. Expect a dim, warm room and quiet music. Expect to lose track of time somewhere around the second foot.
Afterward your legs feel heavier than when you walked in and your head a little light, pleasantly underwater. Your feet may stay tender for a while. Plan for that. Don’t book the last slot of the workday and then try to merge onto the highway at rush hour in a fog. Drink a glass of water, skip the heavy drinking, and give the calm an hour or two before you dive into anything demanding. You paid to come down. Don’t spend it white-knuckled behind a semi.
### Who should skip the table, or ask a doctor first?
Most people can lie back and enjoy it. A few should check with a doctor before they book, because pressure and circulation are exactly what make certain conditions worth a quick call. Ask your doctor or nurse first if you have circulation problems in your feet, inflammation or blood clots in the leg veins, gout, foot ulcers, athlete’s foot or another fungal problem, or a low platelet count that makes you bruise easily. If you’re pregnant or managing any ongoing condition, ask anyway. It costs one question.
That isn’t fearmongering. It’s the same caution you’d bring to any hands-on bodywork. If you’re coming off a double shift with ankles so swollen your laces leave red stripes, the question isn’t whether you deserve an hour off your feet. You do. The question is whether that swelling has a cause your doctor should see first.
The bigger risk isn’t physical at all. It’s mistaking a relaxation practice for medical treatment and putting off care you actually need. Reflexology should stand beside your doctor, never in front of them. If anyone ever tells you to skip a prescription because your feet will handle it, pull your socks back on, feel the cold of the parking lot through your soles, and don’t come back.

### Reflexology or a plain foot massage: which is worth your hour?
Which is better, reflexology or foot massage? Neither wins outright, because they overlap so much. A foot massage aims to relax muscles and feels great with no bigger theory attached. Reflexology uses more targeted pressure on specific zones and comes wrapped in the body-map tradition. For pure relaxation, either one gets you to that heavy-limbed, half-asleep place where you forget what you were worried about in the car.
So pick by feel, not by doctrine. Some people love the precise, point-by-point pressure and the little ritual around it - the footbath, the chart, the slow march from heel to toes. Others want broad strokes and warm oil and no talk of zones at all. There’s one practical Missouri difference, though, and you already know it: the hands, feet and ears rule above. Use the phone sentence either way; it sorts massage therapists as cleanly as it sorts reflexologists.
The realistic zone for either one is the same: stress, tension and the wound-up feeling of a hard week. Many people say they feel calmer and lighter afterward, which tracks with any slow, hands-on hour. Where it earns its keep is the same place a slow loop around the Grand Basin in Forest Park does - it pulls you out of fight-or-flight for a while. Some people pair it with a weekly class at one of the yoga studios around St. Louis and treat the two as one stress plan with very different textures.

Clean linens, clear words about what happens next and someone who actually listens matter as much as any certificate on the wall. If a practitioner in Dardenne Prairie makes you feel rushed or leans on packages on day one, that’s reason enough to try somewhere else. How often to go back is your call; there’s no fixed rule, so let your body and your budget set the pace.
