### Frequently asked before the first appointment
### What are the disadvantages of reflexology?
The biggest one is mistaking it for medical treatment and delaying care you need. Beyond that, some points can feel tender, and results are subjective. It’s a relaxation practice, not a cure, so the real risk is overselling it to yourself and skipping a doctor visit that matters.
### How often should you do reflexology on your feet?
There’s no fixed rule. Some people book regularly, some save it for a rough stretch, and gentle self-massage at home is fine whenever it feels good. Let your body and your budget decide - more often isn’t automatically better, and there’s no schedule you have to hit.
### What should you not do after reflexology?
Don’t schedule anything demanding right after. You may feel loose, foggy or thirsty, so a tense meeting or a long highway drive while spacey is a bad idea. Drink water, go easy on alcohol, and give yourself an hour or two before diving back in. The calm is the point - don’t spend it in traffic.
### What does it mean if a reflexology point hurts?
Usually just that the spot is tender or you’re holding tension there. Some practitioners call it a “congested” zone, but that’s tradition, not a diagnosis, and it says nothing reliable about the organ on the chart. Sharp or lasting pain isn’t normal. Tell your practitioner to ease off right away rather than toughing it out.
### Who should not do foot reflexology?
Check with a doctor or nurse first if you have circulation problems in your feet, blood clots or inflamed leg veins, gout, foot ulcers, a fungal foot infection or a low platelet count. If you’re pregnant or managing an ongoing condition, ask too. It’s gentle for most people, but pressure and circulation are exactly why a few conditions deserve a quick medical check.
### Which is better, reflexology or foot massage?
Neither wins outright - they overlap heavily. A foot massage relaxes muscles with no bigger theory attached; reflexology uses targeted pressure on specific zones and carries the body-map tradition. For pure relaxation, both deliver. Choose by which touch you enjoy more and by how honestly the practitioner describes what they do.
### Do you tip a reflexologist?
Usually, yes, when the visit runs like a spa or massage appointment - something in the range you’d tip a massage therapist is normal. In a clinical or medical-style setting, tipping is less expected. Not sure? Ask when you book, or check whether gratuity is already included in the price. Nobody minds the question.

## What to Check When Buying a Used Truck in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-check-when-buying-a-used-truck-in-st-louis
The truck looked perfect in the driveway. Clean bed, fresh wax, tires that still had the little rubber nubs on them. A guy from Imperial drove ninety minutes to see it, handed over cash, and drove home happy. Two weeks later the transmission started slipping on the hill by his house, and the shop found a frame rail so rusted underneath they wouldn’t put it on the lift. The shine was real. Everything under the shine was not.
That gap, between what a used truck looks like and what it actually is, catches good people all the time. Trucks work for a living. They tow, they haul, they sit outside through Missouri winters getting sprayed with road salt. A truck with 120,000 easy highway miles can be a better buy than one with far fewer miles spent dragging trailers up boat ramps in Grafton every summer weekend. Odometer numbers don’t tell you which one you’re staring at. The truck does, if you know where to look.
You don’t need to be a mechanic to catch most of this. You need a routine, a flashlight, an hour of unhurried time, and the nerve to walk away when the truck tells you to. Bring all four.
### What to check when buying a used truck?
Check the frame and undercarriage for rust, crawl under it for leaks, and look hard at the tires and brakes. Test the 4x4 on a truck that has it. Confirm the title and VIN match, drive it cold, then pay an independent mechanic for a pre-purchase inspection before you sign anything.
Do it in that order and let the cheap checks come first. Rust and leaks cost nothing to spot and can end a visit in five minutes, which saves the test drive for trucks that earn one. Everything past the walk-around gets more involved. Start with your eyes and your nose, move to your ears on the drive, and save your wallet for the inspection at the very end.
### How do you check the frame and undercarriage?
Get low and look at the frame rails, the crossmembers, and the suspension mounts with a flashlight. Surface rust that flakes off orange is normal on any Missouri truck. Scaly, thick, flaking-in-layers rust is not. Poke suspect spots with a screwdriver. If metal gives or crumbles, the frame is compromised, and you stop right there.
Road salt is the villain here. St. Louis salts hard from December through February, and a truck that lived its winters outside took years of that spray straight to the underbody. The frame is the one thing you can’t cheaply fix. A rusted brake line you replace. A rusted-through frame rail turns a truck into scrap, no matter how clean the paint is up top.
While you’re under there, hunt for leaks. Fresh oil, red or pink transmission and power-steering fluid, sweet-smelling coolant, a greasy film on the differential. A little seep on an older truck is common. A steady drip, or a fresh puddle where it sat parked, means a repair you’ll inherit. Run a finger along the pan gaskets and the transfer case. Wet is a question. Caked-on grime soaked through is an answer.
### Rust spots that end the deal
Some rust is cosmetic and some is structural, and telling them apart is the whole game. Bubbling under the paint on a fender or rocker panel is ugly but survivable. Rust that has eaten the frame, the cab mounts, the leaf-spring hangers, or the brake and fuel lines is a safety problem and a money pit. Bring a small magnet if you want to catch body filler hiding a rusted panel. Weak pull, or none, means filler, not steel.
### How hard was this truck actually used?
Read the wear, not the odometer. A truck driven gently at 130,000 miles can be sounder than a beaten one at 70,000. Look at the pedal rubber, the steering wheel shine, the driver’s seat bolster, the bed floor, and the hitch. Deep tow scars and a polished ball tell you this thing worked hard for a living.
The bed and the hitch tell the towing story. Deep scratches, a dented tailgate, a receiver worn shiny and scored means the truck pulled weight, often. That isn’t automatically bad, plenty of trucks tow for years with no harm. It just changes what you inspect. Towing loads the transmission, the rear axle, and the brakes. So if the hitch has clearly seen work, spend extra time on how those shift and stop out on the drive.
Tires and brakes cost real money, so check them and price the replacement into your offer. Uneven tire wear, worse on one edge, points to alignment or worn suspension. Feathered tread says the same. Match the date codes on all four; mismatched brands or ages hint at a truck patched up to sell. For brakes, look through the wheel spokes at the rotor face. A deep lip at the edge or bright scoring means pads, and maybe rotors, soon.
Push down hard on each corner and let go. A good shock lets the truck settle in one bounce. Two or three bounces means worn shocks or struts. Grab the top of each front tire and rock it. Play or a clunk points to worn ball joints or wheel bearings, common on trucks that crawled through Cottleville stop-and-go or bounced down gravel roads out past Eureka.
### How do you test the 4x4 and drivetrain?
Only buy 4x4 you’ve actually engaged. With the seller’s okay, shift into four-high while rolling slowly, then four-low while stopped, and feel for clean engagement. Drive a short distance in each. Grinding, a warning light that won’t clear, or a system that won’t engage at all points to expensive transfer-case or actuator work.
Plenty of used 4x4 trucks have systems nobody has touched in years, and the failure hides until you need it in a January storm. Engage it slowly in an open lot or a quiet street. It should click or clunk in, hold, and release cleanly. Then turn a few tight circles on dry pavement in four-wheel drive and listen. Binding, hopping, or a heavy groan can mean drivetrain trouble, though some binding on dry pavement is normal for part-time systems, which is why you keep it brief.
Watch the dash while you do it. A 4WD light that flashes and won’t stop usually means the system tried to engage and couldn’t. Ask when the transfer-case and differential fluids were last changed. Blank stare? Assume never, and add it to your list. A truck sold as four-wheel drive is worth a lot less when the four-wheel drive doesn’t work, and you only learn that by trying it.
Reading the seller as much as the truck? Here’s what a psychic reading costs.
### What should you notice on the test drive?
Start it stone cold, because a warmed-up engine hides hard starts and smoke. Watch the exhaust: blue means oil, white that lingers means coolant, black means fuel. Listen for knocks and ticks. On the road, feel every shift, brake hard once from speed, and lift your hands briefly off a straight wheel to check for pulling.
Ask the seller to leave the truck cold before you arrive. Someone who has it running and warm when you pull up may be hiding a rough cold start, and that’s worth a raised eyebrow on its own. Watch the first thirty seconds. Heavy smoke that clears, loud ticking that quiets, a long crank before it catches, all of it is information you can’t get later.
On the drive, the transmission should shift smoothly and without hunting. Slipping, a hard bang between gears, or a long delay when you drop it into drive points to trouble that gets expensive fast. Get it to highway speed if you can. Let off the gas, then get back on it, and feel for a downshift that never comes or arrives with a lurch.
Find an empty stretch and brake hard once. The truck should stop straight, without pulling to one side, without the pedal pulsing under your foot, without a grind you can feel. Then, on a flat road with no traffic, ease your hands off the wheel for a second. Steady is good. Drift means alignment or worse. Watch the temperature gauge the whole time. A needle climbing toward hot is a red flag you don’t ignore.
### Does the title and VIN actually check out?
Match the VIN on the dash, the door jamb, and the title before anything else. They should be identical. Read the title for a salvage, rebuilt, or flood brand, and confirm the seller’s name is on it. Then pull a history report by that VIN. A clean-looking truck with a messy title is not a clean truck.
A branded title, salvage, rebuilt, flood, follows a truck forever and guts its value and often its safety. Flood trucks are the sneaky ones. They clean up, they smell fine for a while, then the electrical gremlins start months later. Check under the carpet and in the spare-tire well for a waterline, silt, or rust that has no business being there. Missouri and Illinois both brand titles, so a truck that crossed the river still carries its history with it.
The history report by VIN shows past accidents, title brands, and whether a lender still holds a lien. A lien means the seller doesn’t fully own the truck yet, and you do not hand over cash until that’s cleared and you can see how the title transfers. If the numbers don’t match across the dash, the door, and the paper, walk. That mismatch is theft or fraud until proven otherwise.
Buying across the river shifts the paperwork a little, and the dealer-versus-private math moves with it. We walked through that in detail in buying a car across St. Louis, Missouri and Illinois dealerships, and most of it applies straight across to trucks.
### Should you pay for a pre-purchase inspection?
Yes, on any truck you’re serious about. An independent mechanic puts it on a lift, checks compression, scans the codes, and sees what you can’t from a driveway. It costs a fraction of one repair. A seller who refuses to let the truck leave for an hour is telling you something, and it’s rarely good news.
Here’s the part most guides skip. Don’t just ask a seller for a price and a stack of receipts. Interview them. Ask why they’re selling, what’s been fixed, what they’d fix next, and whether you can take it to your mechanic. Then say plainly what you want, a lift inspection, a code scan, a look at the maintenance history, and watch what they’re willing to provide. The gap between what you ask for and what they hand over is the signal. It matters more than the asking price.
Use your own mechanic, not one the seller recommends. An independent shop with no stake in the sale gives you a straight read. If you don’t have a go-to yet, our guide on finding a trustworthy auto repair shop in St. Louis covers how to vet one before you need them. Line up the inspection before you fall for a truck, not after.
Dealers and private sellers each come with trade-offs, and neither is automatically the safer bet. A dealer may offer a limited warranty and handle the title work, usually charging more for it. A private seller in Godfrey or Cottleville often prices lower but sells the truck as-is, with no recourse if it breaks the next day. The inspection protects you either way, so don’t skip it because the lot looks reputable.
Ready to start looking? Browse used trucks and truck sellers on St Louis Near Me Directory, then take any truck you like to an independent mechanic for a pre-purchase inspection before you sign. Say exactly what you want checked, and compare it against what the seller will actually let you do.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What mileage is too high for a used truck?
A.  There’s no single cutoff, and chasing one gets people burned. A well-maintained truck with high highway miles often outlasts a low-mileage one that towed hard and skipped service. Condition, maintenance records, and how the truck was used matter more than the odometer. Judge the truck in front of you, not the number on the dash.
### Q. How to test 4x4 when buying a used truck?
A.  With the seller’s permission, engage four-high while rolling slowly and four-low while stopped, then drive a short distance in each. Listen for grinding and watch for a 4WD light that won’t clear. On dry pavement, brief tight turns reveal binding. A system that won’t engage points to costly transfer-case or actuator repairs.
### Q. What is the best time of year to buy a truck?
A.  Demand shifts with the seasons, so timing can help. Trucks tend to sit longer, and sellers get more flexible, in late fall and winter, when four-wheel drive is less top of mind and outdoor shopping is miserable. Model-year changeovers can also loosen prices. The bigger win is patience: a rushed buyer overpays in any month.
### Q. Should I buy a used car from a dealership or private seller?
A.  Both work, with trade-offs. A dealer may handle title paperwork and offer a limited warranty, usually at a higher price. A private seller often prices lower but sells as-is, with no recourse if something breaks. Either way, a pre-purchase inspection by your own mechanic is what actually protects you, so never skip it.
### Q. What is a red flag when buying a used car?
A.  Several stand out. A VIN that doesn’t match across the dash, door, and title. A seller who won’t let you take it for an inspection. Fresh undercoating hiding rust, a warm engine when you arrive, a branded or missing title, or a lien still on the vehicle. Any one of those is reason enough to pause.
### Q. Which is a drawback to purchasing a vehicle from a private seller?
A.  The main drawback is no recourse. A private sale is almost always as-is, so if the truck breaks down a week later, that’s your problem, not the seller’s. You also handle the title transfer yourself and get no warranty. That’s exactly why an independent inspection before money changes hands matters so much.
### Q. Do I still need an inspection if the truck has a clean history report?
A.  Yes. A history report shows reported accidents, title brands, and liens, but it misses plenty. Unreported damage, worn suspension, a tired transmission, and slow leaks never reach the report. The report and the inspection check different things. Use both, and let an independent mechanic confirm what the paperwork can’t see.
### Q. What paperwork should I get when buying from a private seller?
A.  Get the signed title in the seller’s name, a bill of sale with the price and VIN, and any maintenance records they have. Confirm there’s no lien on the title. In Missouri, you’ll title and pay tax at the license office, so keep every document until the truck is registered in your name.

## How to Choose and Buy a Watch in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-and-buy-a-watch-in-st-louis
The watch arrived in a box that felt exactly right. Solid weight, a little booklet, a warranty card with a serial number printed clean across the bottom. He’d spent most of a paycheck on it, found through an online listing that looked legit, photos and all. Then a jeweler over in Jennings flipped it over, popped the caseback, and went quiet for a second. The movement inside was a bargain quartz unit. The card was run off an inkjet printer. The watch was a good story wearing a nice case.
That gap, between what a watch looks like and what it actually is, trips up careful people all the time. A watch is small. The outside is easy to copy, and most of us have never handled enough genuine pieces to feel the difference. Price won’t save you, either. Someone overpays for a fake while someone else quietly buys a real one at an estate sale, same Saturday afternoon. The case tells you almost nothing on its own. What’s inside, and the paper that comes with it, tells the truth.
You don’t have to be a collector to buy well. You need a plan, a loupe or a decent phone camera, an unhurried hour, and the nerve to walk away when something feels off. Bring all four, every time.
### What should I know before buying a watch?
Decide what you want the watch to do, set a budget, and learn the basics of movements and materials before you shop. Buy from a seller who lets you inspect the piece, verify the serial, and see paperwork. Compare two or three sellers, and never rush a decision you cannot undo.
Start with the job, not the logo. A watch you’ll wear to work every day asks for different things than one that lives in a drawer for weddings. Water resistance, strap comfort, how it reads at a glance, all of that flows from how you actually live. Get the purpose right and every other choice gets easier, fast.
### What makes a watch actually well made?
Good quality shows up in three places: the movement, the case and crystal, and the finish. A well-made watch uses a reliable movement, a hardened crystal like sapphire, solid metal instead of thin plating, and clean details up close. Hold it, feel the weight in your hand, and look through a loupe. Cheap gives itself away.
The movement is the engine, and it’s the part you can’t see from outside. Broadly, watches run on quartz or on mechanical movements, and neither is automatically better. What matters is that the movement is what the seller says it is. A watch sold as a mechanical piece that ticks once a second, the way a battery quartz does, isn’t what the tag claims. That mismatch is your first and loudest warning.
Look at the crystal and the case next. Sapphire crystal resists scratches far better than mineral glass or acrylic, and most quality watches use it. On the case, solid stainless steel or a precious metal feels dense and cool to the touch. Thin plating chips at the lugs and around the caseback, and you can often catch brassy color bleeding through where a watch rubs a wrist.
Then get close. Under a loupe, a well-made dial has crisp printing, evenly applied lume, and hands that line up with the markers. Fuzzy text, a logo sitting slightly crooked, a date wheel that won’t center in its window, those are the tells of a corner-cutting build or a flat-out fake. Quality hides in the details precisely because fakers rush them.
### The weight-and-feel test
Pick it up and close your eyes for a beat. A real metal watch carries a heft that surprises people the first time they hold one. Fakes and low-end builds often feel light and hollow, because the case is thin or the metal is cheap. Weight alone proves nothing, plenty of good watches wear light on purpose. Paired with the other checks, though, it’s a useful gut read.
### Quartz or automatic: which movement fits you?
Quartz runs on a battery and keeps near-perfect time with almost no fuss. Automatic, a type of mechanical movement, winds itself from the motion of your wrist and never needs a battery. Quartz costs less to own and asks less of you. Automatic costs more and needs occasional service, though many people love the way it feels.
Pick based on how you’ll live with it, not on which word sounds fancier. A quartz watch is the low-maintenance choice. Swap the battery every few years and it just works, accurate to a few seconds a month. If you want something you strap on and forget about, quartz earns its keep. There’s no shame in it, and plenty of serious watches run quartz on purpose.
An automatic is a different relationship. A tiny rotor inside spins as your arm moves, winding a mainspring that powers the watch. Leave it in a drawer for a couple of days and it stops, so you reset it or give the crown a wind. The second hand usually sweeps in a smooth glide instead of ticking. People who love mechanical watches love exactly that, the little machine running on its own.
Service is the trade-off nobody mentions at the counter. A mechanical watch needs cleaning and oiling every several years to keep good time, and that adds up over a lifetime of ownership. Quartz mostly needs batteries, though its movement can wear out eventually too. Ask the seller what upkeep the watch you’re eyeing will need, and factor it in before you fall for the romance of gears.
### How do you spot a fake before you pay?
Check the movement, the weight, the printing, and the paperwork together. Fakes cut corners you can catch: a ticking second hand on a supposed automatic, a light hollow feel, blurry dial text, misaligned logos, and warranty cards that look home-printed. One red flag is a question. Two or three, in our experience, are your answer to walk away.
Start where the fakers are laziest, the movement. If you can see it through a display back, or a jeweler can open the case, a real mechanical watch shows finished parts and a smooth-sweeping second hand. A counterfeit often hides a cheap quartz unit inside a case pretending to be mechanical. That one-second tick, on a watch sold as an automatic, has killed more deals than anything else on this list.
Read the dial like a proofreader. Genuine watches get the small stuff right, spelling, spacing, the exact font, the placement of the logo. Counterfeits slip on details: a letter slightly off, uneven gaps between numerals, lume that glows patchy or not at all. Compare the watch against clear reference photos from the maker if you can. A phone camera zoomed all the way in does the loupe’s job in a pinch.
Then handle the paperwork and the box. A real warranty card is printed sharp, often embossed or holographed, with a serial number that matches the one engraved on the watch. Inkjet cards, mismatched serials, or a “no papers, just trust me” seller all raise the stakes. Papers aren’t everything, plenty of honest used watches lost their box years ago. When the papers are there, though, they had better line up.
Trusting your gut on a big buy? See what the research says about reflexology.
### How do you confirm a watch is the real thing?
Match the serial number engraved on the watch to the number on the papers, then take the piece to an independent jeweler who can open the case and read the movement. Many makers can verify a serial through an authorized dealer or their service center. A number that matches nothing, or a seller who won’t let you check, is trouble.
Serial numbers live in a few places, usually engraved on the caseback or between the lugs, and repeated on the warranty card. They should match, exactly. A mismatch means the papers belong to a different watch, or the whole thing was invented. Write the number down and keep it, too, because you’ll want it for insurance and for proving the watch is yours if it ever goes missing.
Here’s the honest limit: a serial number alone doesn’t prove authenticity. Fakers copy real serials off genuine watches, so a valid-looking number can still sit inside a counterfeit. That’s why the number is one check among several, not the whole verdict. Pair it with the movement inspection, the build quality, and the paperwork, and the picture either holds together or it falls apart.
When the stakes are high, pay a professional. An independent jeweler with no stake in the sale can open the case, read the movement, and tell you what you’re actually holding. Some brands confirm a serial through their authorized network, though that can take time. If you’re buying from a shop rather than a stranger, our guide on how to choose a jeweler in St. Louis walks through vetting one before you hand over a dime.
### How should you choose the seller?
Shortlist two or three sellers, then interview them before you buy. Ask where the watch came from, whether you can inspect it and check the serial, and what happens if it turns out not as described. Say plainly what you want, and compare it against what each seller will actually let you do. The gap between the two is your answer.
Don’t just ask for a price and a story. Line up a few options, a jeweler, a watch dealer, maybe a reputable resale shop, and treat the first visit as an interview. Where did this watch come from? Can I bring it to my own jeweler? What’s the return policy if the serial doesn’t check out? A seller who answers straight and hands you the watch to inspect is telling you something good. One who dodges is telling you something too.
State what you want out loud, then watch what they do with it. “I’d like to see the movement, verify the serial, and take a day to think” is a fair ask of anyone selling a genuine watch at a fair price. Some sellers meet all of it. Some meet part. That difference, between what you ask for and what they will provide, matters more than the sticker on the tag.
Buying from a pawn shop or resale spot shifts the math a little, and it can be a smart move if you walk in informed. Those sellers price to move, and they often carry genuine watches taken in as collateral. Know the trade-offs first. Our breakdown of how pawn shops work in St. Louis covers what to expect before you show up with cash.
Whether you shop a jeweler in St. Louis, a dealer out toward Union or Augusta, or a resale counter in St. Ann, the routine holds. Interview, inspect, verify, decide. A watch sold across the river in East St. Louis follows the same rules, only the paperwork for a private sale shifts a bit. The seller changes. What you check does not.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How can you tell if a watch is good quality?
A.  Look at the movement, the case, and the finish together. Quality watches use reliable movements, hardened sapphire crystal, and solid metal instead of thin plating. Under a loupe, the printing is crisp and the hands line up with the markers. Real heft in the hand is a good sign, though never proof on its own.
### Q. What should I consider when choosing a watch?
A.  Start with how you’ll use it. A daily watch needs durability and comfort; a dress watch can lean on looks. Decide on the movement, quartz or automatic, then size, water resistance, and materials. Set a budget that includes future service. Buy from a seller who lets you inspect the watch and verify it.
### Q. What are the common signs of a fake watch?
A.  Watch for a ticking second hand on a supposed automatic, a light or hollow feel, and blurry or misaligned dial printing. Check for uneven lume, a crooked logo, and cheap plating that shows brassy color at the edges. Inkjet warranty cards and serials that don’t match the watch are loud warnings.
### Q. How can I tell if my watch is real or fake?
A.  Have an independent jeweler open the case and read the movement, the single most reliable check there is. Match the serial on the watch to the papers, compare the dial against the maker’s reference photos, and feel the weight. No single test is proof. Several checks agreeing, or clashing, give you the real answer.
### Q. Can I check my watch serial number?
A.  Yes. Find it engraved on the caseback or between the lugs, and confirm it matches the warranty card. Some brands verify a serial through an authorized dealer or service center. Keep in mind that fakers copy real serials, so a valid number isn’t proof by itself. Pair it with a movement inspection.
### Q. How do I identify my watch?
A.  Look for the brand and model text on the dial and caseback, plus any reference or serial numbers engraved on the case. Photograph both sides and the movement if you can. An independent jeweler can identify the model, and the brand’s service network can often confirm details from the reference number.
### Q. What’s the difference between an automatic and a quartz watch?
A.  Quartz runs on a battery and keeps very accurate time with little upkeep beyond a new battery every few years. Automatic is mechanical, winding itself from your wrist’s motion, with a smooth sweeping second hand and no battery. Automatics cost more and need periodic service, but many wearers prefer how they feel.
### Q. How often does a watch need a new battery or service?
A.  A quartz battery usually lasts a few years, then needs swapping by a jeweler to keep the case seal intact. Mechanical and automatic watches need a full service, cleaning and oiling, every several years to run accurately. Ask your seller what the specific watch requires, since intervals vary by movement and use.

## What to Order at an Argentine Restaurant in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-order-at-an-argentine-restaurant-in-st-louis
Smoke first. You catch it in the parking lot before you catch the menu, that low drift of beef cooking slow over wood, and your stomach makes the decision for you. An Argentine kitchen runs on fire and patience. There’s a grill somewhere in back, loaded since mid-afternoon, and a cook who refuses to rush it.
Here’s the thing most first-timers miss. You’re not ordering dinner so much as settling in for an evening. Argentines treat a good meal like a long conversation with meat in the middle. They arrive late, eat slow, linger longer, and nobody checks a watch. Walk in expecting to be out in forty minutes and you’ll fight the whole rhythm of the room.
So what actually lands on the table? Beef, mostly, but that undersells it. Blistered cheese. Little pastry half-moons stuffed with spiced filling. A green sauce you’ll want on everything. Caramel by the spoonful. Wine the color of a bruise. Let’s walk the menu the way a local would, top to bottom, and figure out what to order and how to eat it.
### What is Argentina’s signature dish?
Asado is Argentina’s signature dish, a slow wood-fire barbecue of beef cuts cooked over embers. It’s less a single plate than a whole ritual: short ribs, skirt steak, and sausages grilled unhurried, then served with chimichurri, crusty bread, and Malbec. Order it and you order the country’s heart.
The word covers two things at once. Asado is the food and the event, the cookout and the cook. A friend hosts an asado the way an American throws a backyard cookout, except the fire gets real reverence. The person running the grill, the asador, holds a position of honor. Nobody crowds them. Nobody rushes them.
At a restaurant, asado usually shows up as a parrillada, a mixed grill for the table piled with cuts. Short ribs. Flank. Sweetbreads and blood sausage for the brave. You share it. You pass plates. You argue about which cut won. Whether you’re at a place in Rock Hill or a spot off a main road in Highland, that communal instinct travels with the food.
New to the cuts? A few names worth knowing before you order. Asado de tira is the crosscut short rib, beefy and a little chewy in the best way. Vacío is flank, loose-grained and full of flavor. Bife de chorizo is the sirloin strip, the crowd favorite. Entraña is skirt steak, thin and quick to char. Point at one and you can’t really go wrong.
### Where does an Argentine meal actually begin?
It begins before the beef, usually with empanadas and something molten. Empanadas are hand-held pastry pockets, baked or fried, crimped shut with a rope-like edge called the repulgue. The classic filling is seasoned ground beef with onion, egg, and olive. Order a few. They’re the icebreaker of the whole table.
Then there’s provoleta, and you should not skip it. Picture a thick disc of provolone thrown straight onto the grill until the outside chars and the inside goes soft and stringy. Oregano on top, a little chili flake, and bread to catch it. You tear in while it’s still bubbling. Cold provoleta is a tragedy, so eat it fast.
Choripan bridges the gap between snack and meal. It’s a grilled chorizo split down the middle, tucked into crusty bread, drowned in chimichurri. Street-food royalty. At an asado it comes out early, almost as a reward for showing up, something to gnaw on while the bigger cuts take their time over the coals.
### Which empanada should you try first?
Start with carne, the beef one, because it’s the benchmark every kitchen gets judged against. From there, branch out. Ham and cheese runs mild and crowd-pleasing. Humita, made with sweet corn, leans creamy. Spinach and cheese gives you a break from meat. Each region back home guards its own recipe, so no two menus fill them quite the same.
### How do locals eat asado?
Slowly, and in an order the asador controls. The grill gives up its food in waves. Sausages and sweetbreads first, then the bigger cuts, so the table snacks for a while before the main event lands. Nobody plates their own from a serving station. It comes to you when it’s ready.
The fire itself sets the clock. A proper asado burns wood down to embers first, which can take an hour before a single steak hits the grill. That slow build is the point. Guests show up early, drink something, pick at provoleta and choripan, and let the afternoon stretch. Rush the coals and you ruin it, so nobody does.
Chimichurri is the one condiment that matters, and locals use it with restraint. Parsley, garlic, oregano, olive oil, vinegar, and a hit of chili, chopped fine and left to sit. A spoonful over a slice of steak, not a flood. The sauce brightens the beef, it doesn’t bury it. Argentines rarely reach for anything bottled or sweet.
Doneness runs a notch past what a lot of Americans expect. Beef often arrives cooked through but still juicy, the fat rendered soft rather than left rare in the middle. Ask for it a la parrilla and let the kitchen call it. Pair the whole thing with a young Malbec and you’ve got the standard Sunday table, whether that Sunday happens in Argentina or right here in Ladue.
Feasting late and heavy for weeks? Your body sometimes sends a signal worth checking.
### What should you order beyond the grill?
Plenty, because Argentine food isn’t only fire and beef. Milanesa is the big one, a thin cutlet breaded and fried until it’s crisp at the edges. Order it napolitana and it arrives crowned with ham, tomato sauce, and melted cheese. It’s comfort food, the kind of plate a grandmother makes, and it fills a table fast.
Pasta belongs on the menu too, and that surprises people. A huge wave of Italian immigrants shaped the country’s kitchens, so Sunday can just as easily mean gnocchi or hand-cut ravioli. Argentines call gnocchi ñoquis and traditionally eat it on the 29th of each month, a small superstition tied to payday and good luck. Spot it, get it.
Want something lighter before the meat? A provoleta and a simple salad hold you over. Going all in? Add a side of papas fritas, thin fries, sometimes crowned with two fried eggs when they come a caballo. None of it’s spicy, by the way. Argentine cooking leans savory and herb-forward, not hot.
### Milanesa or milanesa napolitana?
Both are worth your time, but they hit differently. Plain milanesa is the crisp, no-fuss cutlet, great with a squeeze of lemon and a pile of fries. The napolitana version buries it under ham, tomato sauce, and melted cheese, turning a light plate into a heavy one. Hungry and cold outside? Go napolitana. Saving room for dessert? Keep it plain.
### How do Argentines finish a meal?
With something built on dulce de leche, almost always. Dulce de leche is milk and sugar cooked down slow into a thick caramel, and it turns up in nearly every dessert. Flan wears it like a blanket. Panqueques, thin crepes, get rolled around it. Even the coffee alongside tastes like an excuse to keep sitting.
Alfajores are the ones to take home. Two soft cookies sandwiched around dulce de leche, some rolled in coconut, some dipped in chocolate. They’re everywhere back home, sold at every kiosk, and a good bakery version beats anything mass-produced. Ask if the kitchen makes their own. Many do, and it shows.
Coffee closes it out, and it’s taken seriously. A cortado, espresso cut with a little steamed milk, is the standard order. It arrives small and strong, meant to be sipped, not gulped on the way out the door. Pair it with an alfajor or a spoon of flan and you’ve hit the classic ending.
Then comes the part with no food at all. Sobremesa is the stretch of table talk after the plates clear, coffee poured, nobody moving. It can run an hour. This is where the meal actually lives for a lot of Argentines, and a restaurant that honors it won’t rush your check. Let it happen.
### The Argentine table runs on Malbec and mate
Malbec is the pour that made Argentine wine famous, dark and plummy and built for beef. It grows high in the Andes foothills and drinks easy with a fatty cut of steak. You don’t need to know a thing about wine to order it. Ask for a glass of Malbec, say what you’re eating, and let them steer.
Mate is the other national drink, though you’ll meet it more at home than at dinner. A bitter herbal tea sipped through a metal straw from a shared gourd, passed around a circle. One person, the cebador, fills and refills it for everyone. If a local ever offers you the gourd, take a sip and hand it back. Refusing looks cold.
One etiquette note worth carrying in. Argentines eat with the fork in the left hand and knife in the right, European style, and keep both on the plate through the meal. Elbows off, hands above the table. It’s relaxed, not stiff, but tidy. Watch the table around you and follow the pace, especially the slow one.
Argentine spots sit inside a bigger, deeply Italian food scene here, which is no accident given how much Italian blood runs through Argentina itself. Mapping out a night? Our local’s guide to the best restaurants in St. Louis is a solid starting point, and the pasta-and-provoleta overlap makes a detour through where to eat on The Hill feel right at home.
Hungry now? Find and compare Argentine restaurants across the metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, from Town and Country to Valley Park. Check the menu, call ahead to confirm hours, and go hungry, because you’ll be there a while.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is Argentina’s most famous food?
A.  Asado, the wood-fire barbecue of beef, is the most famous by a mile. Empanadas run a close second and travel better, since you can eat them anywhere. If you want the single dish that says Argentina to the world, though, it’s beef over open coals, shared slowly with family and friends.
### Q. What is the Argentinian national dish?
A.  Asado is widely called the national dish, standing in for the whole grilling tradition rather than one cut. Some people give the nod to locro, a hearty corn-and-meat stew eaten on national holidays. Both count. Asado is the everyday icon, while locro carries the patriotic, once-a-year weight.
### Q. What is a typical Argentinean breakfast?
A.  Light and sweet, nothing like a big American plate. Most people have coffee or mate with a couple of medialunas, small croissants glazed a little sweet. Toast with butter and dulce de leche shows up too. There’s no bacon, no eggs, no rush. Breakfast stays small on purpose, since dinner runs so late.
### Q. What do they eat for dinner in Argentina?
A.  Dinner leans on beef, whether that’s a grilled steak, a mixed parrillada, or a milanesa cutlet. Pasta shows up often thanks to Italian roots, and empanadas cover a lighter night. Salad and grilled vegetables round the plate. It’s a substantial meal, eaten late, and usually stretched over a couple of unhurried hours.
### Q. What are the etiquette rules for eating in Argentina?
A.  Keep the fork in your left hand and knife in your right, European style, with both hands above the table. Wait for the host to start, and never rush the meal. Pour wine for others before yourself. If mate gets passed your way, sip it and hand the gourd back without a fuss.
### Q. What time do most Argentinians eat dinner?
A.  Late, by American standards. Dinner rarely starts before 9 p.m., and 10 or even later is normal, especially on weekends. Restaurants often don’t fill up until well after most St. Louis kitchens have closed. Book an early table and expect the room to sit mostly empty until the locals drift in.
### Q. What is chimichurri made of?
A.  Chimichurri is a raw, uncooked sauce of finely chopped parsley, garlic, dried oregano, olive oil, and red wine vinegar, with a pinch of chili flake for warmth. Some cooks add fresh cilantro or a little onion. It’s tangy and herby, not hot, and it exists to lift grilled beef without overpowering it.
### Q. Is Argentine food spicy?
A.  Not really. Argentine cooking leans savory, salty, and herb-forward rather than hot, so heat-sensitive diners can relax. Even chimichurri carries only a faint chili warmth. Love serious spice? You won’t find it built into most dishes, though a jar of chili oil or crushed pepper is usually within reach on the table.

## Art Supplies for Beginners: What to Buy in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/art-supplies-for-beginners-what-to-buy-in-st-louis
Her cart held a small mountain of supplies and she hadn’t drawn a single line yet. Dozens of paint tubes. Brushes in sizes she couldn’t name. A pad of paper so fancy she’d be scared to touch it. She came in to start painting and walked out overwhelmed, lighter in the wallet, and somehow further from the easel than when she started.
That’s the trap. Beginners think the gear is the hard part, so they buy everything, freeze up, and quit before the paint dries. The truth runs the other way. A small, cheap, honest kit gets you making work faster than a drawer full of stuff you’re afraid to ruin. Fewer choices. More marks. That’s the whole game early on.
So here’s the short list, how to buy it without wasting money, and where to find it around St. Louis. Pick a medium. Buy the basics. Start bad. Get better. You don’t need permission or a big budget, just the right handful of things and a reason to sit down.
### What are the essential art supplies for beginners?
Start with one medium and a short list. For drawing, that’s a few graphite pencils, an eraser, a sharpener, and a sketchbook. For painting, add a small set of paints, three or four brushes, a surface, and a palette. Buy student-grade to start, and skip the extras until you actually miss them.
Notice what’s not on that list. No fancy easel. No forty-color set. No paper you’re scared to waste. The essentials are the things that let you make a mark today, cheaply, without a second thought. Everything else is a reward you earn once you’ve filled a sketchbook or two.
Pick the medium that actually pulls at you. Love clean lines and the scratch of a pencil? Start with drawing. Itching to push color around? Start with acrylics. The worst kit is the one you bought for a medium you don’t care about. Follow the pull. It’s what keeps you coming back to the table.
### Which drawing supplies should you buy first?
Drawing is the cheapest way in, and it’s where most artists build their eye. You need three graphite pencils, a couple of erasers, a sharpener, and a sketchbook. That’s the kit. It fits in a coat pocket, costs about the same as a couple of coffees, and it’ll teach you more than any gadget you could pile on top of it.
### The pencils that cover almost everything
Graphite is graded from hard to soft. An HB sits in the middle, a 2B goes darker and softer, and a 4B or 6B lays down rich shadow. Buy those three and you can shade the full range, pale gray to near-black. Skip the twenty-pencil tins for now. You’ll use four of them, and the rest just rattle in the box.
Grab two erasers, not one. A kneaded eraser lifts graphite gently and pulls highlights out of a shaded area, and a firm white eraser cuts clean edges. A cheap handheld sharpener finishes the set. Nothing here is precious, which is the whole point, because precious tools tend to make timid drawings.
### Why paper matters more than the pencil
The surface changes everything, more than most beginners expect. Printer paper pills and smears under any real shading. A basic sketchbook with a bit of tooth grips graphite and survives an eraser without tearing. You don’t need archival cotton paper yet. You need pages you’ll actually fill. Buy the mid-size pad, not the pretty leather-bound one that ends up too nice to use.
One more habit beats any purchase: date the corner of each page and keep every drawing, even the ugly ones. A filled sketchbook is the real beginner supply. It shows you the progress your eye can’t feel day to day, and it costs nothing but the nerve to keep going.
### How do you put together a beginner painting kit?
Painting costs a bit more, but a starter kit still stays small. Get a basic set of acrylics, three or four brushes, a few canvas panels or a pad of paint paper, a palette, a water jar, and a rag. Acrylics are the friendliest place to begin: water clean-up, fast drying, and forgiving of nearly every mistake you’ll make.
### Which paint should a beginner pick?
Acrylics win for most people starting out. They dry fast, rinse off with water, and paint right over their own mistakes, which you’ll be grateful for often. Watercolor costs less and makes less mess, but it’s harder to control. Oils look gorgeous and teach patience, though the solvents and slow drying make them a rougher first date. Start acrylic. Branch out later.
On color, you don’t need the big set. A warm and a cool version of each primary, red, yellow, and blue, plus a white, will mix almost any color you reach for. Learning to mix beats owning fifty tubes. It’s cheaper, it packs lighter, and it trains your eye to see color instead of just grabbing the closest match off the shelf.
### Brushes and surfaces without overspending
Three brushes cover the early going. A small round for detail, a medium flat for filling, and a bigger flat or wash brush for backgrounds. Synthetic bristles are fine and cost little. For a surface, canvas panels or a pad of acrylic paper beat stretched canvas at first, because you’ll paint more when each one feels a little disposable. Cheap surfaces make for brave paintings.
### Should you buy student-grade or artist-grade supplies?
Student-grade, every time, while you’re starting out. Artist-grade paints pack more pigment, purer color, and better lightfastness, and they cost far more per tube. None of that helps a beginner much. What helps a beginner is making a lot of work, and cheap supplies let you do that without wincing at the price of every brushstroke.
Here’s the difference in plain terms. Artist-grade paint carries more pigment and less filler, so the color goes further and holds true for years. Student-grade stretches that pigment with fillers, so it reads a touch chalkier and less intense. For learning to mix, shade, and compose, that gap barely matters. For a piece you plan to sell or frame for decades, it starts to.
Upgrade one thing at a time, once you feel the limit yourself. Maybe your reds keep turning muddy and you spring for a better tube. Maybe a favorite brush frays and you replace it with a nicer one. That’s how a kit should grow, in answer to real frustration, not on day one out of a fear that you picked wrong.
### How much does it cost to start?
Less than you’d guess, if you keep the list short. A beginner drawing kit, three pencils, two erasers, a sharpener, and a sketchbook, is one of the cheapest hobbies you can pick up. Painting runs higher, since paint and surfaces add up, but a small student-grade set still costs a fraction of what an overstuffed cart does.
Real cost depends on the medium and how deep you go. Drawing stays cheap almost forever. Watercolor is gentle on the wallet. Acrylics sit in the middle, and oils climb once you add mediums and solvents. The number that matters isn’t the receipt total. It’s the cost per finished piece, and cheap supplies you use will always beat expensive ones you hoard.
Buy small, then replace what you burn through. Within a month you’ll know which colors you reach for and which brush lives in your hand. Restock those. Leave the rest on the shelf. Your spending grows with your skill, which is the right order, because a bigger budget has never once made anybody a better beginner.

For painting, a small acrylic set, a few brushes, and canvas panels. Pick the medium that excites you, buy student-grade, and make plenty of work before adding anything else.
### Q. What painting supplies do I need for beginners?
A.  You need six things: a basic set of paints, three or four brushes, a surface like canvas panels or paint paper, a palette, a water jar, and a rag. Acrylics are the easiest to learn because they clean up with water and cover mistakes. Keep the color set small and mix the rest.
### Q. What are the 7 essentials of art?
A.  Most teachers mean the seven elements of art: line, shape, form, space, value, color, and texture. They’re the building blocks every drawing and painting uses, whatever the subject. You don’t buy them, you learn to see and use them. Master these, and even cheap supplies produce work that reads as intentional.
### Q. What are the four fundamentals of art?
A.  Definitions vary, but a common set is drawing, value, color, and composition. Some teachers swap in line, shape, form, and perspective. Either way, the fundamentals are skills, not products. They’re what turn a pile of supplies into a picture, which is why practice beats shopping every single time for a beginner.
### Q. How much do art supplies cost?
A.  It depends on the medium, and starting is cheaper than most people fear. A basic drawing kit is one of the least expensive hobbies around. Painting costs more, since paint and surfaces add up, but a small student-grade set stays affordable. Buy little, use it up, and restock only what you actually reach for.
### Q. What art supplies should I get as a beginner?
A.  Get the short list for one medium and nothing more. For drawing: three pencils, two erasers, a sharpener, a sketchbook. For painting: a small acrylic set, three brushes, canvas panels, a palette, and a water jar. Choose student-grade, spend your energy on practice, and add tools only when you genuinely outgrow what you own.
### Q. Is student-grade or artist-grade paint better for beginners?
A.  Student-grade is better for beginners, hands down. Artist-grade carries more pigment and lasts longer, but it costs far more, and none of that helps while you’re learning. Cheap paint lets you work fearlessly and often, which is what actually builds skill. Upgrade to artist-grade later, one tube at a time, as you hit real limits.

## What Makes a Good Bagel: A St. Louis Guide
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-makes-a-good-bagel-a-st-louis-guide
Saturday, a little after eight, and there’s a line out the door in Richmond Heights. Not for coffee. For bagels. The kind that come out of the oven in batches and sell out before eleven. I grabbed the last warm everything bagel one weekend, and the guy behind me actually groaned. That’s a real bagel for you. When it’s good, people build their whole morning around it.
Here’s the blunt part. Most of what gets sold as a bagel isn’t one. It’s a round roll with a hole punched in the middle, soft straight through, no shine, no pull, stale by lunch. A true bagel is a different creature. Once you’ve eaten a proper one, the fakes stop fooling you. So let’s sort out what actually separates the two: what to look for, how the good ones get made, and how to order so you leave with the right bag. A great bagel also anchors a great morning out, which we mapped in our guide to the best breakfast and brunch in St. Louis.
### What is the secret to a good bagel?
A good bagel is boiled, not just baked. That quick bath in kettle water sets a glossy, chewy crust while the inside stays dense and tender. Malt in the dough adds a faint sweetness and deep color. And it’s fresh, same-day fresh, because a bagel starts dying the hour it cools.
Everything else follows from those three moves. The boil is why the surface snaps a little when you bite. The malt is why a plain bagel still tastes like something. The freshness is why a bag from this morning beats a “bakery” bagel that shipped in frozen last Tuesday. Miss any one, and you’ve got bread with a hole.
One more thing the pros know: a bagel is a texture story first and a flavor story second. Get the crackle-to-chew ratio right and even a plain one satisfies. Nail the technique and the toppings become a bonus, not a rescue mission. That’s the whole secret, minus the mystique.
### What should you look for in a good bagel?
Trust your hands and eyes before your first bite. The characteristics of a good bagel show up fast: a burnished, slightly blistered crust, real heft in the palm, and a springy give when you squeeze. It should feel heavier than it looks. Light and fluffy is a dinner roll wearing a costume.
### The crust and the shine
Look for a sheen, almost lacquered, with a few tiny blisters across the top. That gloss comes straight from the boil, and no amount of egg wash fakes it convincingly. The crust should have a thin, crackly resistance, then give way. Pale and matte all over? It probably skipped the kettle. Dark freckles and a little shine mean somebody did the work.
### The chew
Chew is the whole point. A proper bagel pulls back a bit, like it’s arguing with you, then releases clean. That resistance comes from a tight, well-developed dough and, again, the boil. If it tears like a hamburger bun or squishes to nothing, the gluten never built up or the dough got rushed. Good chew is dense without being tough, and it lingers.
### The crumb and the flavor
Tear one open. The inside, the crumb, should be tight and a touch moist, with small even holes, not the big airy pockets of sandwich bread. Flavor should read faintly sweet and a little malty even before the toppings. Salt matters too. A flat, bland bagel usually means a lazy recipe, skimpy on both salt and malt.
### How is a good bagel actually made?
The process is short on ingredients and long on technique. Flour, water, yeast, salt, and malt. That’s basically it. The craft is in the order: mix a stiff dough, let it ferment slow and cold, shape the rings, boil them, then bake hot. Skip a step and the bagel tells on you.
The flour choice matters as much as the method. High-protein bread flour builds the strong gluten network a bagel needs to hold its chew and its shape in the boil. All-purpose flour makes a softer, floppier ring. It’s one more reason a serious shop and a grocery-store six-pack taste worlds apart, even before the first bite.
### Why do bakers boil bagels before they bake them?
Bakers boil bagels before they bake them to lock in the shape and set the crust. The hot water gelatinizes the starch on the outside, which becomes that shiny, chewy shell in the oven. A splash of malt or a pinch of baking soda in the kettle deepens the color. Boil too long and the crust turns leathery. Skip the boil, and you’ve baked a roll.
Time is the quiet ingredient. The best shops give the dough a long, cold rest, often overnight, which builds flavor and that signature chew. Some of the most common mistakes when making bagels come from rushing that rest, over-proofing the dough, or boiling in plain water with no malt. Underbake them and they go gummy. Crowd the kettle and they stick and deflate. None of it is hard. It just refuses to be hurried.
### Does the water really matter?
You’ll hear that New York bagels owe everything to New York tap water. It’s a fun theory, and probably overblown. Water chemistry can nudge the dough, sure. But technique does far more of the heavy lifting: a long ferment, a real boil, hot ovens, and good flour. Blaming the water lets lazy bakers off the hook.
### How do you order a bagel like a regular?
Ask one question first: when did these come out of the oven? A good counter person will tell you straight. Aim for a batch baked within the last few hours, buy a couple extra, and eat at least one before it fully cools. Warm and fresh is the version worth remembering.
Now the toasting debate. A same-day bagel doesn’t need the toaster; the crust already does that job, and toasting a fresh one can dry it out. Day-old is a different story, and toasting brings it right back. As for spreads, a real bagel holds up to a thick schmear of cream cheese without collapsing. If yours goes soggy under a normal layer, that’s the bread talking, not the bagel.
Order enough to have leftovers, because good bagels vanish fast. Plan the drink while you’re at it, since a dark roast cuts the richness of a loaded bagel nicely, and our guide to the best coffee shops in St. Louis is a fair place to start. Ready to find a shop? Search the directory and go early. The best batches don’t last.
A few orders to skip. Don’t buy a bagel that’s been sitting under a heat lamp since dawn; ask for the fresh batch instead. Be wary of one that’s uniformly soft and pale, or that squishes flat the second it hits the bag. And if a shop only sells them pre-sliced and pre-packaged with no baking on site, adjust your expectations before you pay.
Dressing up for a big brunch? See what a tuxedo rental costs.
### Which bagel and spread should you get?
If you’re new to a shop, order plain first. A plain bagel is the honest test; there’s nowhere for a bad one to hide. If it’s great, everything else on the board will be too. From there, the everything bagel earns its crowd-favorite status, and a good cinnamon-raisin proves the kitchen can handle a sweeter dough.
### Spreads that respect the bagel
Cream cheese is the default, and a real bagel takes it thick. Plain, scallion, or veggie all work. Butter on a warm plain bagel is quietly perfect. If you want the full spread, add lox, tomato, red onion, and capers, and let the chewy crust do the structural work a soft roll never could.
### Building a bagel sandwich
For a breakfast sandwich, a sturdy bagel beats every other bread. Egg, cheese, and bacon or sausage sit inside that chew without sliding out or turning to mush. Toast a day-old one for extra grip. The hole is a feature here, not a flaw: it keeps the whole stack from getting too tall to bite.
### What’s the deal with St. Louis bagels?
St. Louis picked a fight with the bagel world and never apologized. The local quirk that went viral is the bread-sliced bagel: instead of one horizontal cut, the whole bagel gets run through a bread slicer into vertical strips. Outsiders lose their minds over it. Around here, plenty of folks shrug and pass the cream cheese.
There’s a reason behind the slice, even if it horrifies New Yorkers. It’s a party move. Bread-cut bagels feed a room, they’re easy to grab at an office spread, and toddlers can handle a strip. It says something honest about the local scene, too: St. Louis has long treated bagels as shareable food, not a religion. You can love a proper boiled bagel and still grab one bread-sliced for the kids’ soccer game.
If you grew up here, you probably have a firm opinion on the slice already. If you’re visiting, order it once for the experience, then get a proper hand-cut one to taste the difference side by side. Both can be good. They’re just built for different jobs: one for sharing, one for savoring.
Good news for us: the metro’s bagel game has climbed. Serious boil-and-bake shops have opened, weekend lines have gotten longer, and you can find a real chew from Oakville out to Washington, and even up in Troy or across in Columbia. The trick is knowing what you’re after. Now you do. Go get the warm one.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are the characteristics of a good bagel?
A.  A good bagel feels heavy for its size, with a glossy, slightly blistered crust and a springy squeeze. The crust cracks lightly, then gives to a chewy, tight crumb inside. It tastes faintly sweet and malty on its own, before any topping. Same-day freshness ties it all together, since a bagel fades fast once it cools.
### Q. What makes a New York bagel different from a regular bagel?
A.  A New York bagel is boiled, hand-shaped, and baked dense, with a shiny, chewy crust that locals credit partly to the water. A “regular” supermarket bagel is usually steamed or simply baked, so it turns out soft, fluffy, and bread-like. The real difference is the boil and the chew, not the shape.
### Q. What are some common mistakes when making bagels?
A.  The usual slips: skipping the cold overnight rest, over-proofing so the dough goes slack, and boiling in plain water without malt. Too long in the kettle makes the crust leathery, while too short leaves it pale. Underbaking causes a gummy center, and crowding the pan flattens the rings. Rushing is the root of most of them.
### Q. Why do you have to boil bagels before you bake them?
A.  Boiling sets the crust and locks the shape before the oven. Hot water gelatinizes the surface starch, which bakes into that signature glossy, chewy shell. It also keeps the bagel from puffing up like a roll. Malt or baking soda in the water deepens the color. No boil, no real bagel.
### Q. What are different styles of bagels?
A.  The big two are New York, larger and puffy-chewy, and Montreal, smaller, sweeter, wood-fired, and boiled in honey water. Beyond those you’ll see kettle-boiled, steamed, sourdough, mini, and flat “flagel” versions. St. Louis adds its own trick: the bread-sliced bagel, cut vertically like a loaf for sharing.
### Q. What is the most popular type of bagel?
A.  Plain and everything trade the top spot depending on who you ask, with everything winning loyalty for its garlic, onion, sesame, poppy, and salt mix. Sesame and cinnamon-raisin round out most lists. The most popular type of bagel, honestly, is whichever one your neighborhood shop nails, batch after batch.
### Q. How do you store bagels and refresh a stale one?
A.  Eat them the day they’re baked if you can. To keep more, freeze them within hours: slice first, bag them, and pull out only what you need. Skip the fridge, which stales bread faster. To revive a firm one, sprinkle it with water and warm it in the oven for a few minutes.
### Q. Why are some St. Louis bagels sliced like bread?
A.  The bread-sliced, or St. Louis-style, bagel gets run through a bread slicer into vertical strips instead of one horizontal cut. The local story is convenience: it feeds a crowd, suits office and party spreads, and is easy for little kids to hold. It went viral online, and opinions about it stay loud.

## What to Order at a Brazilian Steakhouse in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-order-at-a-brazilian-steakhouse-in-st-louis
You sit down and there’s no menu. Just a little disc by your plate, green on one side, red on the other. Someone pours your water. Then a guy in gaucho pants strolls over with a yard of beef speared on a long skewer, shaves a slice onto your plate, and asks if you want more. You do. You have no clue what you just ate. It was some of the best beef of your life.
That’s a churrascaria, a Brazilian steakhouse, and the first visit can rattle you a little. No ordering. No prices on a card. Meat just keeps coming until you say stop. First-timers freeze, pile the salad bar to the ceiling, fill up on cheese bread, and then the picanha finally swings by and there’s no room left. It happens to almost everyone.
Good news: the whole thing runs on one simple system, and once you get it, you relax and eat like you mean it. Below is how a churrascaria works, what to grab first, what to leave alone early, and how to pace a meal that could otherwise flatten you before the best cuts ever reach the table.
### What to eat first at the Brazilian steakhouse?
Eat meat first. Skip the bread, go light on the salad bar, and wave down the picanha, the signature top sirloin, the moment it comes around. Flip your card to green, take the premium beef cuts while you’re hungry, and treat the sides as support, not the main event.
The logic is simple. You’ve got finite room, and the kitchen knows it. Bread, rice, and cheesy fried things are cheap to serve and heavy to eat, so they fill you fast. The picanha, the ribeye, the lamb, that’s what you actually walked in for. Guard the space for it. A little salad early is fine. A giant plate of it is a rookie move.
Show up hungry, too. This isn’t a meal to ease into. Skip the big lunch, drink some water beforehand, and arrive with a real appetite. When you do, those first rounds of beef hit differently, and you get your money’s worth instead of surrendering at round three with a plate of greens you didn’t need. Simple rule: protein before starch. Every time.
### How does a churrascaria actually work?
A churrascaria serves meat rodizio style, meaning continuous rounds carved right at your table until you stop it. You pay one fixed price per person for the whole spread: the salad bar, the hot sides, and unlimited passes of grilled meat. Servers called passadores circle the room with skewers, offering cut after cut.
Here’s the rhythm of a visit. You get seated. You hit the salad bar once if you want. Then you settle in, and the passadores come to you. Each one carries a different cut on a long skewer, names it, and slices it straight onto your plate. You catch the piece with small tongs. No ordering, no waiting on a kitchen ticket. The food finds you.
Good passadores work a loose order, leading with the crowd-pleasers and circling back with the premium cuts as the meal rolls on. You don’t have to wait for your favorite, though. If you want picanha and it hasn’t come by in a while, flag any server and ask. They’ll bring it, or send someone who has it. The parade bends to what the room wants.
The pace is yours to control, which trips people up at first. Nobody’s rushing you, and nobody stops bringing meat on their own. A table from Overland might sit for two hours and never see the parade slow down. That’s the deal you paid for. Your job is to manage the flow, and the restaurant hands you a tool to do exactly that.
### What do the green and red cards mean?
Each diner gets a small two-sided card or coaster, green on one side, red on the other. Green up tells the passadores to keep the meat coming. Red up means pause, you’re full or just catching your breath. Flip it whenever you like. That card is the entire ordering system, no words required.
Use the red side on purpose. When you want to raid the salad bar, sip your caipirinha, or actually taste what’s in front of you, flip to red so a passador doesn’t stack three more cuts on your plate mid-bite. Flip back to green when you’re ready for the next round. The staff read the whole room off those little cards, so keep yours honest.
Green up. Red up. That’s the whole language. A first-timer from Hazelwood can master it in about four seconds, which is part of the charm. You spend zero energy on logistics and all of it on eating.
### Which cuts should you order, and in what order?
Start with picanha, the crown of any churrascaria. It’s the top sirloin cap, ringed by a band of fat that bastes the meat as it grills, and most Brazilians will tell you it’s the best thing on the skewer. Take it first, take it more than once, then branch out into ribeye, filet, pork, and lamb.
### The beef cuts worth chasing
Picanha reaches you a few different ways: a thick crescent, thinner fanned slices, sometimes crusted in rock salt. Say yes every time it passes. Past that, keep an eye out for ribeye, marbled and rich, filet mignon often wrapped in bacon, alcatra, another sirloin, and fraldinha, the deeply flavorful flank. Beef is where a churrascaria makes its name, so lean into the beef and don’t apologize for it.
### Pork, lamb, chicken, and the sausage
Once the beef edge wears off, the rotation opens up. Linguica, the smoky Brazilian pork sausage, wins a lot of fans. So does bacon-wrapped chicken and garlic-rubbed pork loin. Lamb, chops or leg, turns up at the better spots and is worth flagging. Chicken hearts are the traditional deep cut, small and smoky. Try one. You might shock yourself and ask for seconds.
One more thing on ordering: you can request a doneness. If a passador is carving picanha and only the well-done end is left, ask for a rarer slice from the middle. Most will oblige or swing back with a fresh skewer. Same goes for lamb or filet. Speak up. The meat’s better when it’s cut the way you like it.
### What about the salad bar and the hot sides?
The salad bar is a full production, not a token gesture: cured meats, imported cheeses, hearts of palm, marinated mushrooms, and often hot dishes too. The hot sides usually land at your table for free: pao de queijo, crispy polenta, garlic mashed potatoes, caramelized bananas, and rice with black beans. All of it sits inside that one fixed price.
Treat the salad bar like a tasting, not a trough. A few hearts of palm, a slice of cured meat, a spoonful of feijoada, the black bean and pork stew, if it’s out. That’s plenty. The fried bananas and the warm cheese bread are hard to resist, and you shouldn’t skip them cold, but two bites tell the same story as a full plate for a fraction of the stomach room.
One habit worth keeping: taste before you commit. The salad bar rewards a small exploratory plate. If the feijoada is excellent, go back for more. If a marinated vegetable doesn’t grab you, no loss, you only took a spoonful. Grazing wide and shallow beats loading one heavy plate you feel obligated to finish.
St. Louis has a deep food scene well beyond the churrascaria, and it rewards exploring on other nights. Our local’s guide to the best restaurants in St. Louis is a solid starting map. And if a red-sauce tradition is more your speed, the guide to eating on the Hill, the city’s Little Italy points you toward a whole different feast.
### What should you drink with all that meat?
The classic pairing is a caipirinha, Brazil’s national cocktail, made with cachaca, lime, and sugar. It’s bright and sharp, and it cuts through rich beef nicely. Beyond that, a bold red like a malbec or cabernet holds up against the meat. Plenty of diners just stick with water, which keeps room free for more picanha.
Go easy on the sugary sodas and the big beers early. Both bloat you and steal space you want for the skewers. If you’re driving back to Collinsville or Madison after dinner, remember that one caipirinha packs more punch than it tastes like, since cachaca is strong and the lime hides it. Sip slow, keep water on the table, and let the meat be the main show.
For a non-alcoholic option, look for guarana, a sweet Brazilian soda with a berry-ish bite, or a fresh limeade. Both fit the food and won’t knock you out the way a heavy beer can. Coffee at the end, Brazilian and strong, is a fine way to reset before you roll home.
### How do you pace yourself so you don’t tap out early?
Pace it like a long walk, not a sprint. Take one or two slices per round instead of a heaping plate, keep your card red between passes, drink water over soda, and eat the best cuts while your appetite is sharp. The meat keeps coming all night, so there’s no reason to overload any single pass.
The classic mistake is going all-in on rounds one and two. Big salad plate, four cuts stacked, a basket of cheese bread, and by the time the second picanha comes around, you’re waving the white flag. Slow it down. One slice. Taste it. Decide if you want more of that cut or something new. Flip to green. Repeat. That loop keeps you eating well for the long haul.
Save a little room for dessert if that’s your thing. Grilled pineapple dusted with cinnamon is a churrascaria staple, and many places do a papaya cream or a flan. You don’t strictly need it. But after a mountain of beef, something bright and sweet closes the night out right. Small plates, slow rounds, red card when in doubt. That’s the whole strategy.
