### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is a crepe basically a pancake?
A.  Close cousins, not the same thing. Both start with flour, eggs, and milk, but a pancake has baking powder so it rises and gets fluffy, and a crepe has none, so it stays paper-thin and flexible. A pancake is something you stack. A crepe is something you wrap around a filling. That one difference changes how you cook it, fold it, and eat it.
### Q. What is the savory version of crepes called?
A.  A galette, or sometimes a galette de sarrasin, which just means buckwheat galette. It comes from Brittany in northwest France, uses buckwheat flour instead of wheat, has no sugar, and gets folded into a square around fillings like ham, egg, and cheese. Many St. Louis creperies still call it a savory crepe on the menu. Same idea, different flour.
### Q. What do you serve with savory crepes?
A.  Not much, and that’s the point. A simple green salad with a sharp vinaigrette cuts the richness of the egg and cheese. In Brittany the traditional drink is dry cider in a bowl. A cup of coffee or a glass of something dry works too. Skip heavy sides. The crepe is the meal, and a pile of fries next to it just makes everything soggy.
### Q. Do you eat crepes warm or cold?
A.  Warm, always, and ideally within a minute or two of leaving the griddle. That’s when the edges are crisp and the center is tender. A crepe that sits gets limp and a little gummy, and a cold one is chewy. If you take one home, reheat it dry in a hot skillet for twenty seconds a side rather than the microwave, which steams it.
### Q. What do crepes taste like?
A.  A plain wheat crepe tastes faintly sweet and buttery, with a soft eggy tenderness and a hint of browning at the edges, a bit like the thin crispy rim of a pancake without the fluff. A buckwheat galette is darker, nuttier, and slightly earthy, with crispier corners. Both are mild on purpose. The filling does the talking, and the crepe carries it.
### Q. Are crepes healthier than pancakes?
A.  A plain crepe is thinner and lighter than a stack of pancakes, with less flour and no leavening, so on its own it’s the lighter choice. The filling decides the rest. A ham-and-egg galette with a salad is a reasonable lunch. A crepe buried in chocolate-hazelnut spread and whipped cream is dessert, and no amount of thinness changes that. Order by what’s inside.
### Q. Are crepes harder than pancakes?
A.  The batter is easier, the cooking is harder. Pancake batter forgives lumps and thick pours. Crepe batter has to be thin, rested, and poured in one quick swirl before it sets, and the first one always tears. The flip is the real skill and takes practice with a thin spatula. That’s exactly why a creperie is worth paying for. They’ve done the thousand practice ones.
### Q. How many crepes should you order per person?
A.  One savory per person if you’re hungry, or one savory shared between two plus one sweet shared, if you want to taste more. Sizes vary a lot between counters, from dinner-plate galettes to palm-sized street crepes, so glance at what’s going out to other tables first. In my experience, two people splitting one savory and one sweet leave happy and not stuffed.

## Salami on Your Cubano? Where to Find Cuban Food in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/where-to-find-cuban-food-in-st-louis
The bread is from Tampa. That’s the first thing nobody tells you about the cubano so many St. Louisans argue is the best in town. Havana’s Cuisine builds it on loaves from La Segunda Central Bakery, the Tampa bakery that still lays a long, wet palmetto frond across its bread before baking, then presses it on Euclid Avenue until the crust shatters. You hear it first. The lid comes down. Butter hisses at the edges, the Swiss goes glossy and creeps out the corners, and the knife crackles going through. The paper is too hot to hold right. You hold it anyway, shoulders hunched so the yellow mustard misses your shirt.
The woman behind that press didn’t move here to make sandwiches. St. Louis Magazine reported that Tamara Landeiro came to St. Louis from Cuba so her daughter, Thalia, could study at the chess club in the Central West End. Thalia went on to become a grandmaster, an international champion and an Olympic medalist. Her mother kept cooking. She launched a food truck in March 2020, opened a downtown storefront in October 2021, then carried the entire menu to 12 S. Euclid, the old Racanelli’s space, moving the restaurant, in the magazine’s words, closer to where her St. Louis story began. A chess move, of sorts. The sandwich followed the family home.
Here’s how to do it tonight. The restaurant’s own site lists hours of Monday through Saturday, 11 a.m. to 9 p.m., closed Sunday, and a phone number, (314) 899-9977, if you want to check before you drive. Street meters and nearby garages handle parking. At the counter, ask for the Tampa Cuban, which its online menu describes as “Tampa’s classic Cuban sandwich with the addition of salami,” and take the black bean soup as your side. Spoon it while the sandwich cools enough to pick up. If someone at your table wants a plate, point them to the arroz con pollo. Eater describes it as Landeiro’s grandmother’s recipe, yellow rice and chicken cooked in beer, and the smell of it at the next table will change your order. Start with the jamon croquetas, crisp outside, creamy in the middle. Vegans get a real plate too: made-from-scratch black beans with yellow rice, maduros and fried yucca. Can’t sit down? The site offers pick-up, and DoorDash delivers.
And here’s the turn most people miss. Cherokee Street is home to a significant Latine community, but the cubano people argue about never landed there. It went truck, then downtown, then the Central West End, following a family’s story instead of a neighborhood map. If it’s Sunday and the Euclid counter is dark, that’s your night for Cherokee Street, or open the Cuban food listings on St Louis Near Me Directory for other kitchens and trucks.
### What is the most popular Cuban food?
The Cuban sandwich, el cubano, is the Cuban food most Americans meet first: roast pork, ham, Swiss cheese, pickles and mustard on Cuban bread, pressed flat and hot. On a plate, ropa vieja, shredded beef stewed in tomato, is known as one of the national dishes of Cuba.
In St. Louis, the version worth asking about is Tampa’s. Tampa’s version adds salami and South Florida’s usually leaves it out, and Havana’s Cuisine serves a Tampa Cuban that adds salami right here. So when a thin, peppery layer peeks out beside the ham, nobody made a mistake. You got Tampa. Mojo-marinated pork stacked with ham and Swiss, leaned on with a hot plancha until the crust shatters.
Ropa vieja is the plate you want on a gray St. Louis January night, when the wind off the river finds every gap in your coat. The name means “old clothes,” for beef stewed with peppers, onion, tomato, cumin and bay until it falls into soft ribbons, spooned over white rice beside black beans, steam fogging your glasses. It’s known as one of the national dishes of Cuba. At Havana’s Cuisine the plate comes with white rice, black bean soup, maduros and fried yucca, the whole island on one plate.
### Cherokee Street is the fallback, not the finish line
Cherokee Street runs east-west across South City from Grand Boulevard to Broadway, and it’s known for a significant Latine community, restaurants, shops, nightlife, galleries and the storefronts of Antique Row. On a warm evening you hear music leaking out of open doors and smell a grill somewhere up the block before you see it. The same corridor feeds the city’s Mexican food scene, so even on a night without a cubano, you won’t go home hungry.
That’s the real shape of authentic Cuban food near St. Louis: a smaller scene than tacos or toasted ravioli, spread across a truck window here and a dining room there.
So hunt it on purpose. The reward is the moment the paper comes off and the bread cracks under your teeth, and you remember exactly which curb you were standing on.
Some nights you want one perfect sandwich. Other nights, a buffet with no last plate.
### What should you order the first time?
Order two things: a Cuban sandwich and a plate of ropa vieja or lechon asado with rice, black beans and plantains. Between them you get the full range, one pressed and crackling, one slow and saucy. If croquetas are on the menu, add a couple to start. They’re creamy ham fritters about the size of your thumb, crisp outside, and they vanish fast at a shared table.
The plate teaches you the rhythm of a Cuban kitchen. Nearly everything savory lands beside white rice and black beans, sometimes cooked together as congri, sometimes side by side. Then comes the plantain choice: maduros, ripe plantains fried until sweet and jammy, or tostones, green ones smashed flat and fried into salty, crunchy disks. Get both and pass them across the table. Lechon asado, pork shoulder soaked in mojo and roasted until it pulls apart, is the same pork that fills the cubano, served on a plate with its juices pooling into the rice. Vegetarians have a narrower road, but yuca con mojo, black beans, rice and plantains make an honest meal.
If you’ve ever worked your way through a menu at an Argentine restaurant, the same instinct applies here: order the thing the kitchen is known for, then the plate a grandmother would make, and share both.
### A first-timer’s table, in order
Croquetas de jamon. Ham fritters fried gold, creamy inside.
The cubano. Ask for Tampa-style if you want the salami.
Ropa vieja or lechon asado. Shredded beef or mojo pork over rice and black beans.
Maduros or tostones. Sweet and soft, or green and crunchy. Why not both.
Flan and a cafecito. Caramel custard, then a tiny sweet shot of coffee.

### Six ingredients, one hot press, no lettuce
A real cubano is a short list: Cuban bread, roast pork, ham, Swiss cheese, yellow mustard and thin dill pickles. No lettuce. No tomato. No mayo. What turns that list into the sandwich is heat and weight, a plancha that flattens it and fuses the bread into a buttery shell around the melting cheese.
The bread is its own animal. Cuban bread is baked with a little lard or shortening and a thin, soft crust that crisps beautifully under the press, lighter than a baguette and closer to a very soft French loaf. When a shop can’t get it, a hoagie roll or ciabatta stands in, and the sandwich changes character. Still good. Not the same crackle.
And always press. An unpressed cubano is a ham sandwich with extra steps. The press melts the Swiss into the pork, warms the middle all the way through and seals the edges so the whole thing holds together when you bite. That low hiss and the squeak of the lid is the sound of a sandwich being finished properly. The croquetas you ordered on the side have cousins on nearly any Spanish tapas menu in town.
### How can you tell the cooking is real?
Look for mojo, a press and real Cuban bread, then taste for garlic, sour orange, cumin and patience. Authentic Cuban cooking is savory and citrusy and almost never spicy, so a menu drowning in hot peppers is usually borrowing from somewhere else. The clearest tell is the pork: marinated, roasted low, pulling apart in soft, shiny strands you can smell from across the table.
Watch the beans, because they’re what Cubans eat every day. The everyday plate is rice and black beans with a little meat and plantains, so a kitchen that respects its beans respects you. They should taste of garlic, bay, cumin and a splash of vinegar or wine, simmered until creamy. Rice should be separate and fluffy, or cooked with the beans as congri until the grains go soft brown. Under nearly everything sits sofrito, the sauteed base of onion, pepper and garlic. You can taste when it’s really there.
The fast test is small. Maduros should be nearly black at the edges and jammy-sweet, cooked well past the point where an impatient cook would pull them. And the meal should end with coffee. A kitchen that nails those two little things usually nails the big ones.
One recalibration before you go: if you’re expecting the chili burn of Mexican or Thai food, Cuban cooking won’t deliver it. Garlic, citrus, cumin, oregano and bay carry the flavor, with black pepper as the boldest note on the plate. Plenty of first-timers reach for hot sauce out of habit. Taste first.
### The meal ends in a cup the size of a thimble
Finish with Cuban coffee, and keep the drink with the meal cold and simple. A cafecito is a tiny shot of espresso sweetened while it brews, so the sugar whips into a pale foam called espuma on top. A cortadito softens it with a little steamed milk. Either one arrives in a cup barely bigger than a thimble, meant to be sipped slowly after the plates are cleared.
With the food, reach for a batido, a thick tropical shake made with mango, papaya or mamey that drinks like a milkshake and cools a rich plate down, or something cold and plain. Plain sparkling water works too when the pork is heavy.
For dessert, flan is the default, a dense caramel custard every Cuban kitchen makes a little differently. Pastelitos, flaky guava and cream-cheese pastries, are the other classic, and they’re not too sweet. Both were built for that coffee. Save room. The whole meal has been leading to the moment the little cup clicks back down on its saucer.
### Frequently asked questions about Cuban food
### Q. What is a traditional Cuban breakfast?
A.  A traditional Cuban breakfast is short and simple: tostada, buttered Cuban bread pressed flat and toasted, dunked straight into a cafe con leche, strong coffee cut with hot milk. That’s the weekday version. Weekends might add eggs, ham or fruit, but toast and coffee is the morning most Cubans grew up on.
### Q. Is Cuban food healthy?
A.  It can be. The backbone is black beans, rice, garlic, citrus and slow-cooked meat, and a plate of ropa vieja with beans and rice is balanced and filling. The heavier side is the fried stuff - croquetas, maduros, tostones - plus the sugar whipped into Cuban coffee and desserts. Portions and balance decide it.
### Q. What do Cubans eat every day?
A.  Rice and beans, most days. The everyday plate is white rice, black beans, some pork or chicken and fried plantains on the side, with bread and strong coffee covering breakfast. It’s home cooking built on cheap, filling staples and seasoned with garlic, cumin and sour orange instead of expensive ingredients or chili heat.
### Q. What is the most eaten food in Cuba?
A.  Rice and black beans. A typical Cuban meal has both, cooked together as congri until the grains turn soft brown, or served side by side. It’s cheap, filling and flexible next to pork, chicken, eggs or plantains. If you eat one thing every day in Cuba, it’s this.
### Q. What is the most popular Cuban meal?
A.  As a full sit-down meal, it’s ropa vieja: tender shredded beef in a sauce of tomato, onion and garlic, spooned over white rice beside black beans and sweet maduros. The Cuban sandwich is the one you hold in your hands. One is a plate you linger over; the other is lunch you can carry down Euclid Avenue.
### Q. Where can I find authentic Cuban food near St. Louis, MO?
A.  Start with Havana’s Cuisine at 12 S. Euclid Avenue in the Central West End, open Monday through Saturday, 11 a.m. to 9 p.m., and ask for the Tampa Cuban with black bean soup. For other kitchens and trucks, the Cuban food listings on St Louis Near Me Directory are the place to browse.

## Data Entry Services in St. Louis: What to Know
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/data-entry-services-in-st-louis-what-to-know
You’re at a coffee shop in the Central West End with a laptop, a cooling americano, and a job board open in one tab. You typed “data entry” into the search bar because a friend swore she made steady money doing it from her kitchen table in Soulard. The results load. A few look real. Most look like a trap. One promises thirty-plus dollars an hour, no experience, start today, and then asks for a training fee up front. Your gut says close the tab. Your gut is right.
Here’s the tension. Data entry is a real category of work, plenty of St. Louis businesses genuinely need it done, and it’s one of the few jobs a beginner can start with nothing but a keyboard and patience. But the same two words that describe honest work also headline half the scams online. If you can’t tell them apart, you either miss a legit paycheck or hand your bank details to a stranger who was never hiring anyone.
So consider this the plain-talk guide. What a data entry service actually is, what the work looks like on a normal Tuesday, how to start without spending a cent, and how to spot the scams before they spot you. No company names, no invented pay figures, no pretending the work is glamorous. Just what I’d tell a friend before she clicked “apply.”
### What is a data entry service?
A data entry service is a person or company that takes raw information, handwritten forms, invoices, spreadsheets, survey results, and types it accurately into a database or software system. Businesses hire these services to clean up records, digitize paper, and keep information searchable. The work rewards speed, accuracy, and steady attention over any fancy credential.
That definition covers a huge range. On one end, a solo freelancer in The Grove keys receipts for a small firm two evenings a week. On the other, an entire company runs a floor of clerks converting medical charts, insurance claims, or scanned contracts into clean digital files. Same core job, wildly different scale. When a St. Louis business says it needs data entry, it usually means one of three things: get paper into the computer, move messy data into a cleaner system, or keep an existing database current.
The reason the work exists is simple. Information is only useful when you can search it, sort it, and pull a report from it. A shoebox of paper invoices tells you nothing. The same invoices keyed into accounting software tell you who owes what, which vendor overcharges, and where the money went last spring. Somebody has to do that typing, and doing it well is harder than the job ads make it sound.
You’ll also hear related terms thrown around, data processing, transcription, records management, and there’s real overlap. Data entry is the typing-and-verifying core; the others bundle in extra steps like formatting, coding, or interpreting what the data means. For a beginner, the distinction barely matters. The daily work feels the same, and the skills you build in one transfer cleanly to the next.
### What does a data entry clerk actually do all day?
Mostly they type, check, and fix, in that order. A clerk opens a source, a stack of scanned forms, a vendor spreadsheet, sometimes an audio recording, and enters what it says into a target system, one field at a time. Then comes the part beginners skip: confirming the entry matches the source. The good ones catch their own mistakes before anyone else can.
The variety surprises people. One afternoon you’re updating customer addresses; the next you’re transcribing handwritten intake forms, tagging product photos, or cleaning a mailing list riddled with duplicates. Some roles lean into one narrow task all day. Others hand you a little of everything. The through-line never changes: take information in one shape and put it into another, without introducing errors.
The pace is steadier than glamorous. You settle in, put on headphones, and work through a queue. Nobody’s cheering. A quiet, focused shift where the numbers all reconcile at the end is a good shift. If you hate sitting still or drift off during repetitive tasks, this work will grind on you. If a tidy spreadsheet gives you a small hit of satisfaction, you’ll be fine.
There’s also a rhythm to accuracy that takes a few weeks to build. New clerks either race and make errors or crawl and miss quota. The sweet spot is a steady, checkable pace: enter a batch, verify it, move on, so mistakes get caught in small clusters instead of piling into a giant correction job at the end of the week. Managers notice who works that way.
### The three kinds of data entry you’ll run into
People usually group the work three ways, and the labels tell you what tools you’ll touch. Online data entry means working live inside a web app or database with an internet connection. Offline data entry means keying into a local file or form that syncs later. Automated, or software-assisted, entry uses scanning and character-recognition tools for the first pass, then leans on a human to catch what the software got wrong. Most real jobs mix all three.
Online: live keying into a web-based system or cloud database.
Offline: typing into a local file or form that uploads later.
Automated: scanning and recognition software drafts the entry; a person verifies and corrects it.
### How do you start data entry in St. Louis with no experience?
You need four things, and none of them is a degree: a reliable computer, steady internet, typing accuracy you can prove, and a little patience with the search. That’s the honest entry ticket. Most beginners already own the first two, can build the third with free practice, and only lose because they quit the fourth too early or fall for a scam. Let’s take the pieces in order.
### The skills that actually matter
Speed matters less than people think; accuracy matters far more. An employer would rather have forty clean words a minute than eighty sloppy ones they have to correct. Beyond typing, the real skills are attention to detail, basic spreadsheet comfort, reading messy handwriting, and the discipline to double-check your own work. If your spreadsheet skills are shaky, a short course helps more than another resume tweak. Our rundown of computer classes in St. Louis shows where beginners pick up the basics locally.

One more thing worth saying up front: your first data entry job is a foot in the door, not the whole staircase. Take the modest entry-level role, build a track record of clean, on-time work, and you can move into billing, bookkeeping, records management, or administrative roles that pay more. Plenty of St. Louis office careers started with somebody quietly keying data and proving they were reliable.

### How do you spot a data entry scam?
The single reddest flag is money moving the wrong way. A real employer pays you; a scam asks you to pay them. If a listing wants a fee for training, software, a “starter kit,” or a background check you fund yourself, close it. That one rule alone filters out most of the fakes. The rest of the tells are about pressure, secrecy, and pay that’s too good to be true.
### Red flags to walk away from
They ask you to pay for training, equipment, or a starter kit.
The pay is wildly above the going rate for entry-level typing.
The “interview” happens entirely over text or chat, with no call or video.
They want your bank login, Social Security number, or a deposit before you’ve done any work.
The company has no real website, address, or trace beyond the ad.
They mail you a check and ask you to buy gift cards or wire part of it back.
That last one is the classic overpayment scam, and it wrecks people. The check looks real, your bank even shows the funds for a day or two, then it bounces and you’re on the hook for whatever you already wired. No legitimate data entry job ever routes money through your personal account. When in doubt, slow down. Scammers rely on urgency, so the moment someone rushes you, that’s your cue to stop.
Verifying an employer takes about ten minutes and saves you a world of grief. Search the company name alongside the word “scam” or “review” and read what comes back. Check that the address is a real place and the phone number actually answers. Notice whether the listing came through an established agency or a stranger’s direct message. In my experience, honest employers are easy to confirm and the fakes fall apart the second you look closely.
### Is AI going to make data entry obsolete?
Not overnight, but the work is changing fast. Character-recognition and AI tools now handle a lot of the straight typing that used to be a full-time job, especially clean, printed documents. What they still struggle with is messy handwriting, odd formats, judgment calls, and catching their own errors. So the raw keying shrinks while the checking, correcting, and cleanup grows. The job isn’t vanishing; it’s shifting toward quality control.
In practice, that means the smart move is to grow past pure typing. Learn to run the software that does the first pass, spot where it goes wrong, and clean data at scale. A clerk who only types competes with a scanner. A clerk who can verify, reconcile, and troubleshoot a messy dataset is worth keeping. If you’re starting today, treat data entry as a doorway into broader office and data work, not a career ceiling.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How do I start data entry?
A.  Start with what you already have: a computer, steady internet, and typing practice. Build accuracy with free online typing tools, put together a simple resume, and apply through staffing agencies or established job boards. Skip anything that asks for money up front. Your first role will be entry-level, and that’s exactly where you want to begin.
### Q. Can a beginner do data entry?
A.  Yes, and it’s one of the most beginner-friendly jobs out there. You don’t need a degree or prior office experience, just accurate typing, attention to detail, and reliable follow-through. Most employers train you on their specific software. The real barrier isn’t skill; it’s sorting the legitimate openings from the scams that target new job seekers.
### Q. What does a data entry clerk actually do?
A.  A data entry clerk transfers information from a source, paper forms, spreadsheets, or recordings, into a computer system, then verifies it for accuracy. Daily tasks include typing records, updating databases, correcting errors, and cleaning up duplicate or messy data. It’s focused, repetitive, detail-heavy work, and the best clerks catch their own mistakes before submitting anything.
### Q. What are the top 5 skills for data entry?
A.  The five that matter most are typing accuracy, attention to detail, basic spreadsheet and database comfort, reading messy source material, and the focus to stay consistent on repetitive tasks. Speed helps, but employers value clean, correct work over raw pace. Add a little software know-how and you’ll stand out from most entry-level applicants.
### Q. What are the three types of data entry?
A.  They’re usually grouped as online, offline, and automated. Online means keying live into a web app or cloud database. Offline means typing into a local file or form that syncs later. Automated, or software-assisted, entry uses scanning and recognition tools for the first pass, with a person verifying and correcting the results. Most jobs blend all three.
### Q. Will data entry be replaced by AI?
A.  Not entirely, but it’s changing. AI and character-recognition tools now handle much of the straight typing, especially clean printed documents. What they can’t reliably do is read messy handwriting, handle odd formats, or catch their own errors. So the work is shifting from raw keying toward checking, correcting, and cleaning data, which keeps skilled clerks in demand.
### Q. Do you need a degree or certification for data entry?
A.  No degree or formal certification is required for most data entry work. Employers care far more about a typing test, accuracy, and dependability than a diploma. A short typing or spreadsheet course can help you stand out, and some agencies run their own skills check, but you can absolutely start with none of that.
### Q. Is data entry work legit or mostly a scam?
A.  Both exist, which is why caution matters. Real data entry jobs are posted by real businesses, staffing agencies, and directories, and they never ask you to pay to start. The scams borrow the same job title to hook beginners. Verify the employer, refuse any up-front fee, and never route money through your own bank account.

## Dressmakers and Alterations in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/dressmakers-and-alterations-in-st-louis
Say the wedding is eight weeks out and the dress you fell in love with fits everywhere except the places that matter. The bodice gapes. The hem pools on the floor. You bought it online in a size the chart swore would work, and now you’re standing in your bedroom in Lafayette Square wondering who on earth still fixes clothes. A friend says the word “dressmaker” like it’s 1955, and you realize you have no idea what one costs or where to find one.
So you start asking around. Somebody at work swears by a woman near The Hill who takes in wedding gowns. Somebody else mentions a little shop in the Central West End that does custom formalwear. The prices people quote are all over the map, twenty dollars for a hem from one person, four hundred for “alterations” from another, and nobody explains the difference. You just want to know what’s fair and what you’re actually paying for.
That’s what this guide is for. What a dressmaker does, how it’s different from a tailor, what alterations and custom dresses really cost in St. Louis, and how to pick someone who won’t leave you panicking the week of the event. No business names, no sales pitch. Just what I’d tell my own sister before she handed over a dress she loved.
### How much does a dressmaker cost?
Most St. Louis dressmakers charge by the job, not the hour. Simple alterations like a hem or a taken-in seam typically run $15 to $60. A custom dress made from scratch usually starts around $300 and climbs past $1,500 for beaded or bridal work, depending on fabric, fittings, and detail.
Why the wide spread? Because “dressmaker” covers everything from a five-minute hem to a gown built around your measurements over six weeks. The person doing the work, their experience, and how fussy the fabric is all move the number. Silk chiffon and beadwork take longer and cost more than a cotton sundress. A rush job before a weekend event usually adds a fee on top, so timing is part of the price too.
In my experience, the honest shops quote you a flat price after they see the garment, not before. If someone gives you a firm number over the phone without looking at the dress, be a little cautious. A hem on jeans is predictable. A hem on a lined, layered gown is not, and a good dressmaker wants to feel the fabric before promising anything. Ask for the price in writing on the ticket when you drop it off.
### What makes one dress cost more than another?
Three things, mostly. Fabric first: delicate, slippery, or expensive material is slower to handle and easy to ruin, so it costs more to work with. Second, the number of seams and layers, a lined gown with a zipper and boning is far more work than a single-layer shift. Third, fittings. Custom work needs two or three, and every fitting is time. Add beading, lace, or a bustle and the price climbs again.
### What does a dressmaker actually do?
A dressmaker makes and alters clothing that is cut and sewn, and they specialize in dresses, skirts, blouses, and formalwear, usually for women. Some build garments from scratch off a pattern or your measurements. Others focus on alterations, taking in, letting out, hemming, and reshaping something you already own so it fits like it was made for you.
The bread and butter is fit. A dress off a rack is cut for an average body that does not exist. A dressmaker pins it on you, marks where it pulls and where it sags, and rebuilds those seams so the thing hangs right. That’s the whole magic. It is not glamorous work. It is careful, patient, and the difference between a dress that looks bought and one that looks yours.
Beyond fit, a good dressmaker restyles. They can shorten sleeves, change a neckline, add pockets, replace a broken zipper, or turn a mother’s old gown into something a daughter will actually wear. The skill behind that work is real, and a look at what a fashion design school in St. Louis teaches shows how deep it goes. Bridal is its own world, taking in a gown, adding a bustle so the train lifts for dancing, and steaming out every wrinkle before the walk down the aisle.
### Custom dresses versus off-the-rack fixes
These are two different jobs with two different price tags. A custom dress is built for you from the start, you pick the fabric, the pattern, and the details, and you come in for fittings while it takes shape. If you supply your own material, know that buying fabric by the yard is its own small skill. An off-the-rack fix starts with a finished garment and adjusts it. Custom costs more and takes longer, but you get exactly what’s in your head. Alterations cost less and turn something close into something right.
### What’s the difference between a dressmaker and a tailor?
The short version: dressmakers work on soft, feminine garments and dresses, while tailors specialize in structured, tailored clothing like suits, jackets, and trousers. Both sew, both alter, and plenty of shops do both. But the training and the instincts differ. A tailor lives in the world of canvas, lapels, and shoulder seams. A dressmaker lives in drape, gathers, and the way a skirt moves.
It comes down to structure. A men’s suit jacket is engineered, there’s padding, interfacing, and a built shape underneath the cloth that a tailor knows how to take apart and rebuild. A dress is about how fabric falls on a body, so a dressmaker thinks in curves, seams, and flow. Ask a tailor to take in a beaded bodice and they might send you to a dressmaker. Ask a dressmaker to rebuild a suit shoulder and they might do the same.
In practice, the line blurs. Many St. Louis alteration shops handle a wedding gown in the morning and a groom’s suit in the afternoon, and the person at the machine can do both well. If your job is a dress, a gown, or anything with drape, ask for someone who does dressmaking. If it’s a suit or a structured jacket, ask for tailoring. When in doubt, describe the garment and let them tell you if it’s in their lane.
### How much do common alterations cost?
Alterations are priced per task, and most simple fixes land between $15 and $75 in St. Louis. A basic hem or a taken-in waist is cheap. Replacing a zipper, reshaping a lined jacket, or altering a bridal gown costs more because there’s more to take apart. These are typical ranges, not quotes, so always confirm the price when you drop the garment off.
A better-fitting purchase means fewer alterations in the first place, and the guide to shopping for clothes in St. Louis helps you buy closer to your size. When something still needs work, here is what the common jobs tend to run.
Hemming pants or a skirt: typically $15 to $40, more if the hem is lined or cuffed.
Taking in or letting out a waist or a side seam: usually $20 to $50 per seam.
Shortening sleeves: around $20 to $45, higher on a lined jacket with buttons.
Replacing a zipper: often $20 to $60, depending on length and where it hides.
Taking in a dress bodice: commonly $40 to $90 on formalwear.
Bridal gown alterations: frequently $150 to $600 all in, since a gown may need several changes and a bustle.
Why is bridal so much more? Because a wedding gown is rarely one fix. It’s a bodice taken in, a hem shortened over layers of tulle, a bustle added, and cups sewn in, each a separate job, then a final press. Add lace or beading and every seam takes longer because the beads have to come off and go back on by hand. In my experience, the gown price scares people until they see how many hours it hides.
One more thing on cost: rush fees are real. Need it by Saturday and it’s Wednesday? Expect to pay extra, sometimes a lot. The way to avoid that is simple. Bring the garment in early, three to four weeks ahead for regular alterations, and six to eight weeks for a wedding gown. Early is cheaper, calmer, and leaves room for a second fitting if the first one isn’t perfect.
### How long does custom dressmaking take?
Plan on four to eight weeks for a custom dress, and longer for anything bridal or beaded. The clock starts when you settle the design and hand over the deposit, not when you first walk in. Between the pattern, the fabric order, the first fitting, adjustments, and a final fitting, a made-from-scratch dress is a project, not an errand. Rushing it is where mistakes happen.
The fittings are the part people underestimate. A custom dress usually needs at least two, sometimes three. The first checks the rough shape, the muslin or the basic cut. The second checks the near-finished garment. Each one means the dressmaker sets the project down, waits for you, then picks it back up. That’s why your schedule matters as much as theirs. Miss a fitting and the whole timeline slides.
For a wedding, start early, like months early. Gowns get ordered big and altered down, and the shop’s busy season fills up fast. In my experience, the couples who bring the dress in two months out are relaxed, and the ones who show up two weeks out are paying rush fees and holding their breath. Give good work time and it shows up in the fit.
### How do you choose a dressmaker in St. Louis?
Treat it like hiring anyone whose work you’ll wear. Shortlist two or three, bring the garment in, and ask three questions: have you done this exact kind of piece, what will it cost, and when will it be ready. A dressmaker who answers plainly and puts hands on the fabric before quoting is telling you they know the work. Vague answers are a signal to keep looking.
Ask about the fittings. A serious shop schedules a fitting, pins the garment on you, and has you come back to check the result before you pay in full. A place that takes your dress, quotes a flat number sight unseen, and promises it by tomorrow with no fitting is gambling with something you care about. For a wedding gown especially, no fittings is a red flag, not a convenience.
Word of mouth still beats everything here. Ask the person whose tailored coat always fits, or the friend whose wedding photos looked effortless, who did the work. Bridal shops, formalwear stores, and even fabric counters usually know the local dressmakers by name. If you’re starting from scratch, browse who covers St. Louis, then go meet two of them in person before you commit a dress you love.

### Q. What is the difference between a tailor and a dressmaker?
A.  A tailor specializes in structured, tailored garments like suits, jackets, and trousers, with padding and built shape underneath. ## Consular and Passport Services in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/consular-and-passport-services-in-st-louis
Maria found the email on a Tuesday night at her kitchen table in Soulard. Her sister in Guadalajara had finally set a wedding date, ten weeks out, and the group flight was already booked and paid for. She went looking for her passport in the drawer where important things live, the one with the spare keys and the dead phone chargers, and it wasn’t there. When she finally dug it out from behind the tax folder, the little blue book had expired fourteen months ago.
That’s the moment a lot of St. Louisans meet the passport system for the first time, or the first time in a decade. You have to leave the country, the clock is running, and suddenly there are forms with numbers like DS-11, a thing called an acceptance facility, and a fee you somehow pay twice for reasons nobody explains. Somebody at work says “just go to the embassy,” which sounds official right up until you realize there isn’t one anywhere near here.
So this post sorts it out in plain language. What an embassy actually does and why St. Louis doesn’t have one, what a consulate is, how a regular person here gets or renews a U.S. passport without losing a weekend, and who to call when something goes wrong overseas. No legal jargon, no scare tactics. Just what I’d walk a neighbor through before their trip.
### What can a US embassy help with?
A U.S. embassy helps American citizens abroad. It issues emergency passports, provides notary services, and steps in during arrests, hospital stays, or deaths overseas. It shares voting and Social Security information and coordinates evacuations in a crisis. It also represents the United States to a foreign government. What it does not do is handle routine passport renewals for people living here at home.
Here’s the key thing people miss. An embassy exists to serve you when you’re outside the country, not when you’re standing in your own kitchen in Missouri. If you’re in Rome with a stolen bag and no passport, the U.S. Embassy there is your lifeline. If you’re in St. Louis needing to replace a passport that expired, an embassy has nothing to do with you. That single distinction clears up most of the confusion around this whole topic.
Every country runs its embassies the same basic way. The United States keeps one embassy in the capital of each nation it has relations with, staffed with diplomats, and it handles the big government-to-government business plus a citizen-services desk for traveling Americans. Foreign countries do the exact same thing in reverse, and the address for every one of theirs in America is D.C. Not St. Louis, and not anywhere else in Missouri.
### Are there any embassies in St. Louis?
No, and there never have been. Every foreign embassy in the United States sits in D.C., because an embassy’s job is to deal directly with the federal government, and the federal government lives in the capital. St. Louis has plenty of international business, culture, and community, but zero embassies. The nearest ones are close to a nine-hour drive east of here.
What St. Louis does have is quieter and easy to miss: honorary consuls. Several countries appoint a local resident, often a business owner or attorney with roots in that nation, to represent their interests and offer limited help to citizens living in the region. An honorary consul isn’t a full consulate with a passport counter, but they can point people to the right office, witness certain documents, and support their community. Whether a given country keeps one here shifts over time, so it’s worth searching for the current appointee rather than assuming.
For anything a full consulate handles, like renewing a foreign passport or applying for a visa, most St. Louis residents deal with a consulate in another city, frequently Chicago, and usually by mail or online. It’s inconvenient, but it’s completely normal. Cities without a consulate route their paperwork to the nearest one, and a huge share of that business now happens by mail or web portal anyway.
### Why the capital gets the embassies
It comes down to what an embassy is for. An ambassador’s core job is talking to the host nation’s government almost daily, so the embassy has to sit where that government works. D.C. has the State Department, Congress, and the White House, so every country plants its flag there. Consulates and honorary consuls are how nations reach the rest of the country, the Midwest included. That structure is old, deliberate, and the same for every embassy on earth, which is why the map never puts one in a place like St. Louis.
### How do St. Louisans get a U.S. passport?
Through the U.S. State Department, not an embassy and not city hall. First-time applicants fill out Form DS-11 and apply in person at a passport acceptance facility, many of which sit inside neighborhood post offices and public libraries around St. Louis. Renewals are simpler: eligible adults mail Form DS-82, or renew online, without ever standing in a line.
The in-person part trips people up, so here’s how it works. A first-time passport, one for a child, or a badly damaged book has to be witnessed by a certified agent, which is why you go to an acceptance facility instead of mailing it. You bring your unsigned form, your proof of citizenship, your photo ID, a passport photo, and your fees. The agent checks it, watches you sign, seals it, and sends it to the State Department. You do not get your documents back that day; they travel with the application and come back separately.
The two-fee thing confuses everybody. You pay the State Department an application fee, and you pay the acceptance facility a separate execution fee for witnessing the whole thing. They’re different amounts going to different places, sometimes by different methods, so bring a checkbook and a card. Fees change over time, so confirm the current numbers on the official travel.state.gov site before you go rather than trusting an old blog post.
### What documents do you actually need?
Gather these before you leave the house. A missing item is the number-one reason people get turned away at the counter.
Proof of U.S. citizenship: a certified birth certificate with a raised or embossed seal, a prior U.S. passport, or a naturalization certificate. The souvenir certificate from the hospital does not count.
A photo ID: a valid driver’s license or government ID, plus a photocopy of the front and back on one page.
One passport photo: two inches square, in color, on a white background, no glasses, taken within the last six months.
Form DS-11, filled out but not signed. You sign it in front of the agent, on purpose.
Two payments: the application fee and the execution fee, ready in whatever forms each office accepts.
Applying for a child under sixteen adds a wrinkle. Both parents generally have to appear and prove the relationship, or supply the right consent paperwork. If your name changed through marriage or a court order, bring the certified document that proves it. When a supporting paper needs a notary or a certified copy, the guide to getting documents notarized in St. Louis covers where locals go for that.
### How long does it take, and what if the trip is soon?
Plan on weeks, not days. Routine processing runs several weeks, and expedited service shortens that for an added fee, but the timelines shift with demand and get worse ahead of summer and the holidays. Check the current estimate on travel.state.gov the week you apply, not the month before. For genuine last-minute emergencies, the State Department runs regional passport agencies you visit by appointment, and the nearest one to St. Louis is out of state, so build in travel time. The honest fix is boring: apply early. A passport that expires within six months can also block entry to some countries, so check the date now, not the night before. Once the book is in hand, the rest is just logistics, like sorting out where to park at Lambert airport before your flight.
### What is a consulate, and does St. Louis have one?
A consulate is a branch office of a foreign country that handles everyday services for its citizens and visitors: visas, passport renewals for its nationals, document legalization, and notarizations. Full consulates tend to cluster in big cities like Chicago. St. Louis doesn’t host a full consulate, though it has had honorary consuls for various nations over the years.
Think of it as headquarters versus branch. The embassy is the single headquarters in the capital, dealing with the host government and led by an ambassador. Consulates are the branches spread across other cities, led by a consul, and focused on paperwork and people rather than politics. A consulate-general is simply a larger consulate covering a bigger region. All of them, embassy included, offer consular services; only the embassy does the top-level diplomacy.
An honorary consul sits a rung below that. It’s usually a respected local, not a career diplomat, who volunteers to represent a country part-time, promote trade and culture, and give basic help to fellow nationals in the area. They can’t print you a passport, but they can be a first phone call, verify certain documents, and connect someone to the real consulate. St. Louis’s international community has long leaned on people in exactly these roles.
### When a foreign national in St. Louis needs their consulate
If you’re a citizen of another country living in St. Louis, your consulate is who renews your home-country passport, registers a baby born here, or issues documents your home country will recognize. Most of that now runs by appointment and mail through the nearest consulate, often the one in Chicago. When the issue crosses into U.S. immigration law, though, a consulate can’t represent you the way a lawyer can, and the guide to finding a trustworthy immigration lawyer in St. Louis is the better starting point.
### When do you need consular help, and who do you call?
You need consular help when something official happens across a border. For Americans, that means calling the nearest U.S. embassy or consulate abroad, or the State Department at home, if a passport is lost, or someone is arrested, hospitalized, or dies overseas, or a child is caught in a custody dispute between countries. Back in St. Louis, the everyday number is the National Passport Information Center.
For passport questions from home, skip the embassy idea entirely. The National Passport Information Center answers status checks and application questions by phone and email, and travel.state.gov handles the rest. If you’re a U.S. citizen actually overseas and stuck, find the local U.S. embassy’s American Citizens Services desk online, or call the State Department’s emergency line, which runs around the clock for real emergencies like a lost passport or an arrest.
One smart move before any international trip: enroll in the State Department’s free Smart Traveler Enrollment Program, known as STEP, so the nearest embassy knows you’re in the country. It’s how they reach you if there’s a natural disaster, unrest, or a family emergency back home. In my experience, most people never need it, and the handful who do are enormously glad they signed up. It takes five minutes and costs nothing.
Passport sorted? Reward the paperwork with something good. Order sweet or savory in St. Louis.
Need to verify a local detail? Browse embassy and consular resources for the St. Louis area on St Louis Near Me Directory, then confirm current hours, fees, and appointments before you go.
If you’re the notary, passport photo counter or translation office travelers lean on before a trip, this part is about your next customers, so look at the Gold plan.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How do I contact an embassy?
A.  Start with its official website, never a walk-in. The U.S. State Department lists every American embassy abroad, and each foreign embassy in D.C. posts its own phone, email, and appointment links. For passport help from St. Louis, call the National Passport Information Center instead, since no embassy handles routine work for people at home.
### Q. Can I walk into an embassy?
A.  Almost never. Embassies and consulates run on appointments and tight security, so you book online before you show up, even for citizen services. The exception is a true emergency abroad, like a stolen passport or an arrest, which the American Citizens Services desk will handle urgently. For everyday questions, you use the website or the phone.
### Q. What documents do I need for a U.S. passport?
A.  Three essentials, plus payment. You need proof of U.S. citizenship, such as a certified birth certificate or a prior passport, a valid photo ID with a photocopy, and one recent two-inch passport photo on a white background. First-timers also bring an unsigned Form DS-11 and two separate fees. Sign the form only in front of the agent.
### Q. What is the difference between a US embassy and a consulate?
A.  Scale and job. An embassy is the single headquarters in a nation’s capital, led by an ambassador, that manages government-to-government relations. A consulate is a branch office in another city, led by a consul, focused on services like visas and passports for citizens. Both offer consular help; only the embassy handles top-level diplomacy.
### Q. Why would someone need a consulate?
A.  To handle official business with a foreign country without flying there. A consulate issues visas for travel, renews passports for that country’s citizens, registers births and marriages abroad, and legalizes documents so a foreign government will accept them. For a citizen of another country living in St. Louis, the consulate is their home government’s local front desk.
### Q. Do consulates issue visas?
A.  Yes. Issuing visas is one of a consulate’s main jobs. If you’re a St. Louis resident who needs a visa to visit a country that requires one, you apply through that nation’s consulate or embassy, often the one in Chicago, usually online or by mail. The consulate decides who may enter its country and for how long.
### Q. Is there a passport office in St. Louis?
A.  Not a State Department passport agency, no. St. Louis relies on passport acceptance facilities, many tucked inside neighborhood post offices and public libraries, where certified agents accept first-time applications. Those aren’t agencies that print passports on the spot. The nearest regional agency, used only for urgent appointment-based travel, sits outside Missouri, so plan for the drive.
### Q. Do I need a passport or a passport card?
A.  It depends on how you travel. A passport book works for international air, land, and sea travel worldwide. A passport card is cheaper and wallet-sized but only covers land and sea crossings to Canada, Mexico, the Caribbean, and Bermuda, never international flights. Most St. Louis travelers heading overseas want the book; frequent border drivers sometimes add the card.

## French Restaurants and Dining in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/french-restaurants-and-dining-in-st-louis
Your friend books a table for six at a French bistro in the Central West End and calls it her birthday dinner. You show up at seven, hungry, expecting to be home by nine. Three hours later you’re still there, a second bottle is empty, and nobody has brought the check. Nobody will, either, until you ask for it. The waiter has drifted past your table four times without a flicker of urgency, and somehow that’s the whole point of the evening.
This is where a lot of St. Louis diners get tripped up. We treat dinner like a transaction. Order, eat, pay, leave, free the table for the next party. A French meal is built on the opposite instinct. The table is yours for the night, and rushing it isn’t efficient, it’s a little rude. The small rituals that ride along with it, the bread set right on the cloth, the cheese before dessert, the hands kept up where everyone can see them, can feel like a pop quiz you never got to study for.
So here’s the guide I’d hand that friend before the birthday dinner. Where French cooking actually lives around St. Louis, from bistros in the Central West End to a pastry counter in Lafayette Square. What the etiquette is really about underneath the fuss. And how to order like you’ve done it a dozen times. No business names, no prices. Just the parts that surprise Americans, and why almost none of it is as intimidating as it looks from the sidewalk.
### What is impolite to do in France when eating?
The rudest move is rushing. Ask for the check the moment you finish, snap for a server, or start eating before the host says “bon appétit,” and you’ve broken the rhythm. Keep both hands on the table, not in your lap. Don’t split the entrée onto a bread plate. And never, ever ask to take leftovers home.
None of that is snobbery, whatever it looks like from here. It’s a different social contract. In France a meal is time spent together, so the moves that read as polite in the United States, flagging down the server, boxing up leftovers, splitting the bill fast and bolting, come across as cold instead. You’re treating the restaurant like a fuel stop. The fix is almost embarrassingly simple. Slow down, and let the meal arrive in its own order.
A handful of smaller ones land harder than Americans expect. Don’t cut your salad with a knife; fold the leaves with your fork instead. Don’t treat the bread as a buttered appetizer; it’s there to push food onto the fork and mop up sauce, and it sits right on the tablecloth, not on a side plate. Don’t ask for substitutions or sauce on the side. And don’t call “garçon” across the room. It’s condescending. A quiet “monsieur” or “madame” is how you get a waiter’s attention.
### Where can you enjoy French cooking around St. Louis?
French food in St. Louis hides in plain sight, tucked across a handful of city neighborhoods and split into four or five formats. You’ll find white-tablecloth dining rooms, casual bistros, the odd brasserie, pastry counters, and creperies. Each one asks something slightly different of you. Knowing which is which tells you how to dress, how long to block off, and what’s worth ordering when you sit down.
### The bistro and the brasserie
A bistro is small, warm, and short on menu. It does a handful of classics well: steak frites, a roast chicken, a daily plate chalked on a board by the door. A brasserie is bigger, louder, and open long hours, the kind of room built to serve a beer and a plate of mussels at three in the afternoon. If a proper sit-down French dinner is what you want, a bistro is usually the target. If you want oysters and a late bite, look for the brasserie.
### The patisserie and the boulangerie
These are the daytime side of French eating, and St. Louis has more of them than most people realize. A boulangerie is a bread bakery; a patisserie makes the pastries, the tarts, the éclairs, the macarons. Plenty of local spots do both under one roof. A morning croissant and a coffee at a counter in Lafayette Square is French dining too, just the humble, everyday version of it. If that’s your entry point, the bakery guide walks through how to spot a real one.
### Where the rooms actually are
The Central West End is the densest pocket, walkable, a little dressy, and built for a long dinner. The Hill, better known as the city’s Italian heart, hides French cooking on its quieter side streets. Lafayette Square and Soulard lean toward the neighborhood-bistro feel, brick townhouses and small warm rooms. Benton Park has a quieter, chef-driven streak worth chasing. If you’re planning a whole night around the food, the Central West End dining guide maps the walkable options.
### Why does French dining feel slower than American dining?
Because in France the table is rented for the evening, not the hour. American restaurants earn on turns, so the check comes fast and a busser hovers by the water glasses. French restaurants assume you’ll stay two or three hours, so the food is paced, the pauses are built in on purpose, and the bill never lands until you ask. What feels like slow service is the service working exactly as designed.
### The check will not come to you
This one catches every American off guard. Sitting quietly and waiting for the bill in France means you’ll sit there forever, because bringing it unasked is treated as shoving you out the door. When you’re ready, catch the waiter’s eye and say “l’addition, s’il vous plaît,” or mime a little signature in the air. In St. Louis the check tends to come sooner, but at a serious French room, don’t be surprised if you have to ask twice. That’s not neglect. It’s manners.
### The courses have a rhythm
A full French meal moves through a set of stages, and each one gets its moment. It often opens with an apéritif, a small drink to wake up the appetite. Then the entrée, which is the starter. Then the plat, the main. Cheese comes after that, before anything sweet. Then dessert, then a tiny strong coffee, and sometimes a digestif to close it out. You don’t have to run the whole route, but the order rarely changes.
The best service still feels human. Here’s what a machine can’t plate.
### How is a French menu structured?
A French menu reads backward to American eyes. The “entrée” is the starter, not the main event; the “plat” is the main course. A “menu” or “formule” is a fixed multi-course deal at one set price, while “à la carte” means you build the meal dish by dish. Get those four words straight and half the confusion clears before you even sit down.
### The false friends on the page
A few words look English and mean something else entirely. Entrée trips up everyone, since it’s your first course, not your steak. “Plat du jour” is the dish of the day. “Café” means a small black coffee at the end, so ordering one with your meal will earn a raised eyebrow. And “entrée, plat, dessert” printed together is just the three-course spine of the meal. Once you recognize that shape, most French menus stop feeling like code.
### Prix fixe versus à la carte
The prix fixe, or set menu, is usually the smart order for a first visit. You get two or three courses the kitchen has chosen to show off, at a price that beats building the same meal à la carte. It also takes the pressure off. You’re not translating every line; you’re trusting the room. Order à la carte when you know exactly what you want, or when the set menu skips the one dish you came in for.
### What French dishes should a first-timer order in St. Louis?
Start with the classics every French kitchen makes and none can fake: steak frites, coq au vin, French onion soup, moules-frites, and a croque monsieur at lunch. These are the dishes that reveal whether a St. Louis kitchen has the fundamentals down. If the fries come out crisp and the sauce tastes like it simmered all day, you’ve landed somewhere good.
Here’s a short field guide to the ones you’ll see most, in plain terms:
Steak frites. A seared steak with a pile of thin fries, usually under a pat of herb butter or a peppercorn sauce. The house benchmark dish.
Coq au vin. Chicken braised slow in red wine with mushrooms, onions, and bacon. Deep, dark, and forgiving. Comfort food with a passport.
French onion soup. Onions cooked down for hours, beef broth, a raft of bread, and a blistered cap of cheese. Order it when it’s cold out.
Moules-frites. A steaming pot of mussels in wine or cream, with fries to soak up the broth. Messy, cheap, and better than it sounds.
Croque monsieur. A grilled ham and cheese under a blanket of béchamel, broiled till bubbling. Add a fried egg on top and it becomes a croque madame.
Duck confit. A duck leg cooked slow in its own fat until the meat falls off and the skin crisps. Rich, and a little bit of a splurge.
Escargot. Snails baked in garlic-parsley butter. Trust me on this one; the butter is the real dish, and the bread finishes it.
Crème brûlée. Cold vanilla custard under a lid of cracked burnt sugar. The dessert that turned a whole generation into fans of the cuisine.
### The cheese course nobody orders
If the menu offers a cheese course, get it once. In France cheese comes after the main and before dessert, served with a little bread and maybe a smear of something sweet. It’s not an appetizer and it’s not dessert; it’s a course of its own, and most Americans skip right past it. A good St. Louis French kitchen will have three or four cheeses and someone who can tell you about each. Ask. It’s the most French thing you can do at the table.
### What to drink with it
Wine is the default, and you don’t need to know a Burgundy from a Bordeaux to order well. Tell the server what you’re eating and roughly what you want to spend, and let them steer. Before the meal, an apéritif like a kir sharpens the appetite. After, a small digestif settles it. If it’s a special night out, the date-night guide covers the rooms built for exactly that.
### How do French table manners differ from American ones?
The biggest gap is the hands. In France both wrists stay resting on the table edge through the meal, never in your lap, a habit that goes back centuries. Fork stays in the left hand, tines pointed down, knife in the right, and they don’t switch back and forth. Bread lives on the tablecloth. And you wait for “bon appétit” before the first bite.
A few more are worth knowing before you sit down. Don’t cut a bread roll with a knife; tear it with your hands. Don’t drown your food in salt before tasting it, which reads as an insult to the cook. Keep your voice down; a loud table draws stares in a way it never would in St. Louis. And when you’ve finished, lay your knife and fork together across the plate, which quietly tells the waiter to clear it.
None of this needs to make you nervous. Any decent French room in St. Louis has served plenty of first-timers, and nobody’s going to march you out for holding a fork wrong. In my experience, the staff would rather you relax and enjoy the long, slow shape of the meal than fret over which hand your fork is in. Watch the table next to you, mirror what they do, and you’ll blend right in.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it rude to leave food on the plate in France?
A.  Generally, yes. Clearing your plate signals you enjoyed the meal, and leaving a pile can read as wasteful or as a quiet complaint about the food. You don’t have to lick it clean, but portions are usually sized so you can finish. If you truly can’t, leave a little without comment and don’t make a point of it.
### Q. Is it rude to ask for the bill in France?
A.  No, it’s expected. The server will not bring the check until you ask, because doing it early is considered rushing you out. Catch the waiter’s eye and say “l’addition, s’il vous plaît,” or make a small writing gesture in the air. That’s normal and polite. Waiting silently, on the other hand, means you’ll wait all night.
### Q. Do the French eat three meals a day?
A.  Yes, and they hold the line on them. Breakfast is light, often just coffee and bread. Lunch was traditionally the big meal, though that’s shifting. Dinner runs late, rarely before eight. Snacking between meals is far less common than in the United States, and the afternoon “goûter” for kids is the main exception to the rule.
### Q. Is it against the law to eat at your desk in France?
A.  Technically, yes, in many workplaces. A French labor code rule long barred employees from eating lunch at their workstations, meant to protect hygiene and the sanctity of the break. Enforcement is loose and the rule was relaxed during the pandemic, but the culture behind it is real: lunch is a break, not a task you multitask through.
### Q. What is disrespectful in France?
A.  Beyond the table, a few things stand out. Skipping “bonjour” before you speak to someone, especially a shopkeeper, is the big one. Speaking loudly in public, expecting everyone to speak English, and being overly familiar too fast all read as rude. Respect there runs on formality and small courtesies, not on friendliness for its own sake.
### Q. What is the most famous French restaurant?
A.  There isn’t a single answer, but a few names carry global weight. La Tour d’Argent in Paris, dating to 1582, is one of the oldest and most storied. Le Cinq, Guy Savoy, and the late Paul Bocuse’s restaurant near Lyon are others. St. Louis has no equivalent landmark, but its neighborhood bistros hold their own for everyday French cooking.
### Q. Do you tip at a French restaurant?
A.  In France, service is included by law, so the tip is already baked into the price. Leaving a few extra euros for great service is a kind gesture, not an obligation. In St. Louis, though, you’re back in American rules: tip 18 to 20 percent as you normally would, no matter how French the menu happens to read.
### Q. What should you wear to a French restaurant in St. Louis?
A.  It depends on the room. A casual bistro or creperie asks nothing special: clean and put-together is plenty. A white-tablecloth dining room in the Central West End leans dressier, so think collared shirt, a dress, or a jacket. When unsure, err up a notch. In French dining culture, looking like you made an effort is its own courtesy.

## What a Gardener Costs and Does in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-gardener-costs-and-does-in-st-louis
The bed along the north side of my neighbor’s brick two-story in Shaw had gone feral by the second Saturday in April. Hostas the size of hay bales. A peony that hadn’t bloomed since the Blues won the Cup. Bindweed doing whatever bindweed does. She’d called a mowing crew, and the mowing crew had, reasonably, mowed. The bed stayed feral.
What she needed was a gardener. Not a landscaper, not a designer with a drafting table, not two guys with a zero-turn. A person who knows a weed from a seedling and will spend four hours on their knees in that bed. I’ve hired a few over the years, watched friends hire more, and the same questions come up every time: what do they charge, what do they actually do, and how do you tell a good one from a guy with a trowel and a truck? Let’s take those in order.
### How much does a local gardener charge per hour in St. Louis?
Most gardeners around St. Louis quote by the hour or by the visit, and in my experience the hourly rate for real garden work lands well above what a mowing crew charges per visit. That isn’t gouging. A mowing crew runs a route and does the same twenty minutes at forty houses. A gardener does one thing at your house, and it’s skilled, slow, and hard to rush.
Three things drive the number. First, scope. Deadheading and light weeding is one level of effort; digging out a root-bound yew hedge is another. Second, whether it’s a standing arrangement or a one-off. Someone who comes every other week through the growing season will usually give you a better per-visit price than someone you call once in May when the panic sets in. Third, materials. If the gardener brings the mulch, the compost, and the plants, that shows up on the bill, and a fair one will tell you up front whether they mark those up or pass them through.
Expect a minimum. Two hours is common, sometimes three, because nobody wants to drive from Dutchtown to O’Fallon for forty-five minutes of weeding. A few gardeners price a whole-season package instead: spring cleanup, a set number of maintenance visits, fall put-to-bed. That’s often the best math if you have more than a couple of beds.
What I won’t do is give you a dollar figure. Rates in this area shift with fuel, with the labor market, and with how booked a person is in a given month. Anyone quoting a hard number on a blog is guessing. If you want a baseline for the cheaper end of yard help, our piece on what lawn care costs in St. Louis covers the mowing side. A gardener sits above that per hour, and should.
### What’s the difference between a gardener and a landscaper?
A gardener tends what’s already growing. A landscaper builds and installs: patios, retaining walls, sod, drainage, the big shrubs that arrive on a flatbed. There’s overlap, and plenty of people do a little of both, but the instincts are different. One thinks in seasons. The other thinks in projects.
Here’s a quick way to sort it. If the job has a start date and an end date and involves a skid steer, you want a landscaper. If the job is “keep these beds from turning into what they were last August,” you want a gardener. And if you’re not sure what the yard should even look like, that’s a third person entirely; we covered hiring a landscape architect in St. Louis separately.
The money follows the same split. Landscapers bid a project. Gardeners bill time. Mixing them up is how people end up paying a project rate for someone to pull weeds, or expecting a weekly gardener to regrade the side yard.
One more distinction that matters more here than in some places: our dirt. Much of the city sits on heavy clay, and the older neighborhoods, Soulard, Benton Park, Lafayette Square, often have old brick and construction fill a shovel-depth down. A good gardener knows that and amends rather than fights it. A landscaper may just bring in a truck of new topsoil and move on, which works fine until the first hard rain finds the clay underneath.
### What is a professional gardener called?
Mostly, a gardener. The trade never settled on a fancier name, and the people who are good at it rarely want one. You’ll also hear horticulturist, which usually means formal training or a degree in plant science, and fine gardener, a term that drifted over from estate work and means someone who does detailed, hands-on care of ornamental beds rather than general yard maintenance.
Around St. Louis you’ll run into a few other labels. Master Gardener is a volunteer credential run through the University of Missouri Extension. It means the person completed a training course and volunteer hours, not that they run a business. Plenty of professionals have it. Plenty don’t. Garden maintenance specialist, garden care technician, plant health care tech: those are mostly what larger landscape companies call the person they send out to do gardener work.
The name matters less than the questions you ask. I’ve met self-described horticulturists who couldn’t tell a hosta from a hydrangea in March, and a retired schoolteacher in Carondelet who calls herself the plant lady and can diagnose a sick boxwood from across the street. Titles are cheap. Ask what they’d do with your bed and listen to how specific the answer gets.
### What a gardener actually does through a St. Louis year
Gardening here is a twelve-month job with about nine months of dirt under the nails. Our winters are short and jumpy, our springs are wet, and July will kill anything you planted in a hurry. A gardener earns their rate by knowing when each task falls. Here’s the rough calendar.
### Spring: cleanup and the cutback
March and April are the busy season and the hardest time to get on anyone’s schedule. The work: cutting back last year’s perennials, raking out beds, edging, the first round of weeding before things set seed, dividing anything that’s outgrown its spot (hostas, daylilies, irises, ornamental grasses), and mulching once the soil has warmed. A good gardener waits on the mulch. Piling it on cold, wet clay in March just keeps the ground cold.
### Summer: keeping it alive
From June on, the job turns into triage. Deadheading, staking, a watering plan, pest checks (Japanese beetles tend to show up around early summer, and bagworms go after the evergreens), and the endless weeding. Visits often drop to every other week. If you travel in July, this is the month a standing gardener pays for themselves. A week of missed watering in a St. Louis heat stretch can undo a whole spring of work.
### Fall: planting and putting to bed
Fall is the best planting window we have, and a gardener will push you to use it. Trees, shrubs, and most perennials go in from September through early November, when the air cools but the ground stays warm enough for roots to settle. Bulbs go in late. Leaves get managed, not just blown into the street. Tender stuff gets cut back or wrapped. Some perennials get left standing on purpose, for the birds and for something to look at in January, and that’s a judgment call worth asking about.
### Winter: the quiet months
December through February is light: structural pruning while plants are dormant, tool maintenance, and planning. Some gardeners take the winter off entirely. Others will do a January walk-through with you and a notepad. If yours offers that, take it. It’s the cheapest hour you’ll buy all year.
Beds tidy but passport dead? Here’s how consular and passport services work in St. Louis.
### What is the best time to landscape?
Fall, for anything that has roots. Spring is when everyone wants to landscape, which is exactly why it’s the worst time to book anybody and only the second-best time for the plants. In our climate, a shrub planted in early October gets a couple of months of root growth before the ground cools, then a full spring before it has to face July. The same shrub planted in May has to face July at eight weeks old.
Hardscape is a different question. Patios, walls, and drainage work can go in any time the ground isn’t frozen or soup, so late summer and early fall are ideal. Crews are less slammed and the clay is workable. Sod does best in early fall too, and seeding a lawn in this area is a September job, full stop.
If you’re asking a gardener rather than a landscaper, the answer shifts. The best time to start a gardener is late winter. Get on the schedule in February and you’ll have the spring cleanup slot everyone else is fighting over in April.
Buying the plants yourself? Read what to know before buying plants in St. Louis first. The wrong plant in the right season still dies.
### What landscaping adds value to a home?
The honest answer from every agent I’ve talked to in this town: maintained beats impressive. A tidy, healthy yard with a clean edge between lawn and bed, mulch that hasn’t faded to gray, and shrubs that don’t block the windows will do more for a listing than a water feature nobody wants to maintain.
That’s a gardener’s value pitch in one sentence. Landscaping projects can add value, and some do: mature trees placed well, a front walk that doesn’t heave, a patio that turns a useless side yard into a room. But buyers walking a Central West End or Lafayette Square block are pricing the house. The yard’s job is to not subtract. A neglected yard subtracts fast, because it tells a buyer there’s deferred maintenance inside too.
A few things that tend to pay off around here: shade trees on the south and west sides, foundation plantings sized right for the house and not fighting the brick, native and adapted plants that don’t need weekly babysitting, and a front bed that looks intentional from the curb. Things that rarely pay: koi ponds, anything with a pump, elaborate lighting, and a lawn so big the next owner sees a chore.
### How to interview a gardener before you hire one
Treat it like a first visit with a doctor. You wouldn’t ask a doctor for three written estimates before they’d looked at you, and you shouldn’t expect a gardener to hand over an itemized labor breakdown for weeds they haven’t seen. Nobody good will do that. Instead, shortlist two or three people worth talking to, walk the yard with each one, and say plainly what you want and what you expect.
Be specific. “I want the north bed to look like it did in the listing photos, I want the peony to bloom, and I want to not think about it between visits.” Then listen. A good gardener asks questions back: how much sun that bed gets after two in the afternoon, whether the downspout dumps there, and if you actually like the hostas or just inherited them. A weak one nods and quotes.
Compare what you asked for with what each person is prepared to deliver. That gap is the signal. If one of them says the peony’s planted too deep and will never bloom where it is, and the other two say nothing, you’ve learned something the price can’t tell you. In my experience the person who tells you what won’t work is the one to hire.
A few practical things to settle before the first visit: whether they bill hourly or by the visit, what the minimum is, who buys materials and how that’s handled, what happens in a rain week, whether they haul debris or leave it bagged at the curb, and how they want to hear from you when something looks off. You’re not negotiating. You’re finding out if you can work together for a season.
