### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What’s the difference between a gardener and a landscaper?
A.  A gardener maintains what’s growing: weeding, pruning, dividing, mulching, planting perennials, keeping beds healthy through the season. A landscaper builds and installs: patios, walls, drainage, sod, big shrub and tree installations. Landscapers bid a project with a start and an end. Gardeners bill time, usually on a repeating schedule. If the job needs a skid steer, call a landscaper. If the job is keeping the beds from going feral again, call a gardener.
### Q. What is a professional gardener called?
A.  Usually just a gardener. Horticulturist implies formal plant-science training. Fine gardener means detailed care of ornamental beds rather than general yard work. Master Gardener is a volunteer credential through the University of Missouri Extension, not a business license. Larger companies may call the same person a garden maintenance specialist or plant health care technician. The title tells you less than how specific their answers get when you walk the yard together.
### Q. How much for 2 hours of yard work?
A.  Two hours is usually the minimum most gardeners in the area will book, so you’ll pay the hourly rate times two, plus any materials they bring. Whether that’s a bargain depends on what gets done. Two hours of skilled dividing and pruning goes a long way; two hours of general raking, less so. Ask what they’d prioritize in a two-hour block. A good answer lists tasks in order and tells you what will have to wait for next time.
### Q. What are the best low maintenance plants for landscaping?
A.  For this climate, gardeners tend to reach for plants that shrug off clay, heat, and a jumpy winter: coneflower, black-eyed Susan, sedum, ornamental grasses like little bluestem and prairie dropseed, daylilies, hostas in shade, and shrubs like ninebark, viburnum, and dwarf fothergilla. Native or regionally adapted plants generally need less water and fewer rescues once they’re established. Low maintenance still means some maintenance, though. Nothing is zero, and anything is high maintenance in the wrong spot.
### Q. What landscaping adds value to a home?
A.  Maintained beats impressive. A tidy yard with clean bed edges, fresh mulch, healthy foundation plantings sized to the house, and well-placed shade trees does more for a St. Louis listing than a water feature. Buyers price the house; the yard’s job is to not subtract, and a neglected one subtracts fast because it signals deferred maintenance inside. Native and adapted plantings that don’t need babysitting are a plus. Ponds, pumps, and oversized lawns rarely return their cost.
### Q. What is the best time to landscape?
A.  Fall, for anything with roots. September through early November gives trees, shrubs, and perennials warm soil for root growth and a full spring before their first July. Hardscape goes in whenever the clay is workable, so late summer and early fall are ideal. Lawn seeding here is a September job. If you’re hiring a gardener rather than a landscaper, the best time to start is late winter, before the spring cleanup rush fills every calendar in the metro.
### Q. Do I need a gardener if I already have a mowing service?
A.  Depends on your beds. A mowing crew handles turf: cut, edge, blow. Most won’t weed a perennial bed, divide hostas, or notice the boxwood is dying. If your yard is mostly lawn with a few shrubs, mowing is enough. If you have real beds, a border, a vegetable patch, or anything you’d be sad to lose, a gardener a couple of times a month during the season fills the gap the mowing crew leaves. Plenty of homeowners keep both.
### Q. Should my gardener bring the plants and mulch, or should I buy them?
A.  Either works, but settle it before the first visit. If the gardener supplies materials, ask whether they pass the cost through or mark it up, and expect it on the bill. Buying your own saves that markup but risks buying the wrong plant for the spot, which the gardener then has to work around. A common middle ground: the gardener specifies, you buy, they plant. Bulk mulch delivered is usually cheaper than bags either way, and a gardener will know where to get it.

## First Time at a Gay Bar in St. Louis: What to Expect
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/first-time-at-a-gay-bar-in-st-louis-what-to-expect
A Friday in late September, a little after nine. I was standing on the sidewalk on Manchester Avenue with a friend from out of town who had never set foot in a gay bar. He kept adjusting his jacket. The door was propped open, a rainbow flag hung over it, and somebody inside was laughing loud enough to hear from the curb.
He asked me the question everybody asks. “Am I allowed in?” Yes. That was the whole answer then, and it’s the whole answer now.
This guide is for the person standing on that sidewalk. Maybe you’re queer and newly out. Maybe you’re a straight friend who got invited along. Maybe you’re in town for a conference and want a good night out. I’ve spent a lot of evenings in these rooms, and I’ll tell you what I wish somebody had told my friend before he started fidgeting with that jacket.
### Are there any gay bars in St. Louis?
Yes, and more than a first-timer usually expects. The city has had a gay bar scene for decades, and it’s still going. The bulk of it sits in The Grove, the stretch of Manchester Avenue running through the Forest Park Southeast neighborhood. Soulard and the Central West End have long had LGBTQ-friendly spots of their own, too.
They’re not all the same kind of place. Some are neighborhood taverns where the regulars know the bartender’s dog by name. Some are dance clubs with a DJ, a stage, and a drag show most weekends. A few sit somewhere in between: patio in the summer, trivia on a weeknight, a big crowd on Saturday. St Louis Near Me Directory lists them under gay bars, so you can see what’s open and where before you go.
One thing that surprised my friend was the crowd. On a given night you’ll see couples in their sixties, a table of nursing students, a bachelorette party, two guys who clearly just came from a softball game, and a drag queen in full face ordering a water. Nobody’s checking credentials at the door.
### What is the gay area of St. Louis?
The Grove. If you only learn one thing from this post, that’s it. The neighborhood is officially called Forest Park Southeast, and its commercial spine is Manchester Avenue, roughly between Kingshighway and Vandeventer. Rainbow crosswalks, a big painted sign over the street, murals, and a row of bars, restaurants, and shops. It has been the heart of the city’s LGBTQ nightlife for a long time, and Pride-related events have a habit of ending up there.
It’s walkable, which matters. You can start at one end, wander, and hit three or four bars without getting back in a car. It’s also a real neighborhood with real restaurants, so plan on eating. I wrote up my favorites in a local’s guide to eating in The Grove if you want dinner before the bar.
Soulard is the other name you’ll hear. It’s the old French brick neighborhood just south of downtown, known for Mardi Gras and for having more bars per block than anywhere else in the city. Several of them have been LGBTQ-friendly for years, and the Sunday afternoon crowd there is its own thing. The Central West End, up by Forest Park, has a quieter, slightly dressier version of the same idea.
Do you have to go to one of these three? No. Plenty of bars across the city fly a Pride flag and mean it. But if you want the fullest version of the scene on a Friday or Saturday, The Grove is where it is.
### How can you tell if a bar is a gay bar?
Look at the front of the building first. A rainbow flag, a progress flag (the one with the chevron of black, brown, pink, blue, and white), or a trans flag in the window is the plainest signal there is. Bars don’t hang those by accident. Pride month decorations that are still up in November mean the same thing.
Then check the event board or the social media page. Drag brunch. Drag bingo. A weekly show with a named host. A “bears night” or a “ladies night” that reads a little differently than the ones at a sports bar. Karaoke with a heavy showtunes rotation. Any one of these is a tell. All of them together, and you’ve found it.
Listings help too. A bar that describes itself as a gay bar, an LGBTQ bar, or a queer bar in its own bio is telling you what it is. That’s why the directory keeps a category just for them instead of lumping them in with every other tavern in town. Saves you guessing.
One more thing. A bar with a Pride flag in the window in The Grove is a gay bar. A bar with a Pride flag in the window in a strip mall might be an ally bar, a mixed bar, or a place that hung it in June and forgot. Both are fine to walk into. They’re just different rooms.
### Is it normal to go to a gay bar alone?
Completely. Plenty of the people at the bar on a weeknight walked in by themselves, and nobody thinks twice about it. Gay bars have always doubled as living rooms for people who didn’t have anywhere else to be themselves. Solo is the tradition, not the exception.
If you’re nervous, sit at the bar rather than a table. The bartender will talk to you, and the person on the next stool probably will too. Order something, put your phone away for a minute, and watch the room. Within about twenty minutes you’ll have figured out the rhythm of the place.
Go early if a crowd makes you tense. A gay bar at seven on a Thursday is a calm, friendly place where you can see everything. The same bar at midnight on Saturday is a wall of people and bass. Both are great. One is easier for a first visit.
Going alone also means you can leave whenever you want. You don’t owe the room a whole night. Have a drink, get the feel of it, and come back next week if you liked it. That’s how most regulars started.
Buried in paperwork? See what data entry services in St. Louis take off your plate.
### Is it okay for a straight man to go to a gay bar?
Yes. You’ll be welcome, and honestly nobody will be surprised to see you. Straight men show up with their gay brothers, their coworkers, their wives’ friends, their softball teams. The room does not care about your orientation. It cares that you’re decent company.
The one thing to get straight in your head before you walk in: you might get hit on. Probably not, but maybe. If it happens, the correct response is the same one you’d want from a woman you approached at a regular bar. A smile, a “thanks, I’m straight,” and move on. That’s it. Nobody’s going to push, and the guy will likely buy you a drink anyway because you were polite about it.
What gets a straight guy side-eyed isn’t being straight. It’s announcing it every five minutes. It’s standing in the corner with his arms crossed looking like he lost a bet. It’s the loud “no homo” joke. Relax your shoulders, order a drink, and be the same guy you are anywhere else. You’ll be fine.
### What about straight women and bachelorette parties?
Straight women have been going to gay bars for as long as gay bars have existed, and they’re welcome. Bachelorette parties are a slightly more complicated story, and I’ll be honest about why.
The bar is not a theme park. The drag queen is not your personal photo booth. The guys on the dance floor are not props for your night. Groups that treat the room like a novelty tend to get a cool reception. Groups that show up, tip well, cheer the performers, and dance with everyone tend to have the best night of the whole trip. Same bar, same night, two very different experiences. It comes down to how you carry yourself.
Practical version: call ahead if you’re bringing more than six people. Some bars love a big group on a slow night and would rather not have one during a sold-out show. Leave the novelty accessories at the hotel. Do bring cash for the performers.
### What to wear to a gay bar?
Whatever you’d wear to any bar in St. Louis. Jeans and a decent shirt covers almost every room in The Grove on almost every night. Nobody is going to turn you away for sneakers, and nobody is going to look twice at a suit either. Gay bars are, on average, less dress-coded than the cocktail lounges downtown.
That said, the rooms do vary. A neighborhood tavern at five on a Tuesday is flannel and work boots. A dance club at eleven on a Saturday runs flashier: mesh, sequins, harnesses, a lot of bare arms, and at least one person in a full look that took two hours. You’re not required to compete. You’re also not required to hold back if you feel like it.
Two useful rules. First, dress for the weather and the walk. The Grove in July is humid, the patios are packed, and you will sweat. Second, if there’s a theme night, the theme is optional but appreciated. Show up to a leather night in leather and you’ll get compliments. Show up in a polo and nobody will say a word.
Comfortable shoes. I mean it. You’ll be standing more than you think.
### How do tipping and bar etiquette work?
Same as any bar, with a couple of extras. Tip the way you’d tip anywhere: a buck or two a drink, or a normal percentage on a tab. Bartenders in gay bars work hard and remember faces. Tip decently on your first visit and your second visit gets noticeably warmer.
Order efficiently when it’s busy. Know what you want when you get to the bar, have your card or cash ready, and step aside once you’ve got your drink. Standing at the rail chatting while the bartender tries to reach past you is the fastest way to get ignored on the next round.
Watch your drink, and watch your friends’ drinks. That’s not a gay bar thing. It’s an everywhere thing. Don’t accept a drink from a stranger unless you watched the bartender make it.
On personal space: the dance floor gets close, and that’s fine. Touching someone without asking is not. Gay bars are generally quicker than straight bars to throw people out for grabbing, so keep your hands to yourself unless you’ve been clearly invited. If someone’s touching you and you don’t want it, tell the bartender or the door. They will handle it.
If your group wants to sing, some gay bars run karaoke nights that get very competitive. The rules for those are pretty much the same as anywhere, and I covered them in what to expect at a karaoke bar in St. Louis.
### What are the rules at a drag show?
Tip the performers. That is the first rule and the second rule and the third rule. Drag is work. The wig, the makeup, the costume, the rehearsal, all of it costs money and time, and tips are how most performers get paid. Bring cash in small bills. Ones and fives. When a queen or king comes past you during a number, hold the bill out and let them take it. That’s the exchange.
Don’t touch. Not the wig, not the padding, not the costume, not the performer. It looks sturdy. It isn’t, and it was expensive. If a performer takes your hand or sits on your lap, follow their lead. Otherwise keep your hands to yourself.
Stay out of the aisle. Performers use the walkways between tables as part of the stage. If you’re standing in one, you’re in the show, and not in a good way. Find a spot against a wall or at a table and stay there during numbers. Go to the bar between acts, not in the middle of a lip sync.
Do not talk over the host. The host will notice, and the host has a microphone. What happens next is your fault.
Cheer loud. Drag thrives on a loud room. Laugh at the jokes, applaud the death drops, and if a performer nails the note, let them hear it. A quiet, polite audience is the worst thing that can happen to a show.
Be ready for the host to talk to you. If you’re in the front row, you’re fair game for a joke. Take it with a grin. It’s affectionate, mostly, and it means you were noticed.
Phones: filming a short clip for your story is generally fine. Filming a whole number with the flash on is not. Ask if you’re unsure, and don’t post a performer’s face without their okay if they seem to be keeping things low-key.
### How do you stay safe and get home?
The Grove on a weekend night is a busy, well-lit, well-walked strip. It’s a normal city neighborhood, which means normal city sense applies. Stay on Manchester Avenue itself rather than wandering the side streets alone at two in the morning. Keep your phone charged. Know where your friends are.
Parking is on the street and in a few lots, and it fills up. If you’re drinking, don’t drive. A rideshare from The Grove to most of the city is short, and pickups on Manchester Avenue are easy: tell the driver which cross street, and stand on the corner so they can see you. Soulard and the Central West End work the same way.
If you’re visiting, staying somewhere central makes the ride back quick. The Central West End has hotels within a few minutes of both its own bars and The Grove. Downtown is a straight shot up the highway.
If something goes wrong inside a bar, tell staff. Gay bars in this city have been dealing with unruly guests, unwanted attention, and the occasional hostile outsider for a long time, and the door staff are generally quick and firm about it. You will not be brushed off.
And if a night out goes well, which it almost always does, take a walk on the strip afterward. Late-night food is a couple of doors down from nearly everything. My out-of-town friend ended his first gay bar night at a taco window at one in the morning, jacket finally unzipped, asking when we could come back.
Ready to pick a spot? Browse gay bars across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then pick one on Manchester Avenue and get there early enough to grab a stool.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the gay area of St. Louis?
A.  The Grove, along Manchester Avenue in the Forest Park Southeast neighborhood. That’s where the largest cluster of gay bars sits and where the rainbow crosswalks are. Soulard and the Central West End have long had LGBTQ-friendly spots too, with a smaller, more spread-out feel. If you only have one night in town, go to The Grove.
### Q. Is it normal to go to a gay bar alone?
A.  Yes. Gay bars have always been a place people go by themselves, and a solo drinker at the bar is one of the most ordinary sights in the room. Sit at the bar rather than a table, go early if crowds make you nervous, and leave whenever you feel like it. Nobody will notice you came alone, and if they do, they’ll probably say hello.
### Q. Is it okay for a straight man to go to a gay bar?
A.  Yes, and it happens every night. Come with a friend or come alone, order a drink, and act the way you’d act at any bar. If someone flirts, a polite no is all it takes. What earns a bad reaction is treating the room like a joke or making a show of being straight. Be decent and you’ll be treated the same.
### Q. Can a straight woman go to a gay bar?
A.  Of course. Straight women have been part of gay bar crowds for generations. The only caution is for large groups treating the bar as a novelty: the performers and the regulars are not there for your photos. Show up as a guest, tip the drag performers, dance with whoever’s dancing, and you’ll have one of the best nights in the city.
### Q. What to wear to a gay bar?
A.  Whatever you’d wear to any other bar. Jeans and a good shirt work in every room in The Grove. Dance clubs on weekends run flashier, and theme nights are fun to dress for, but none of it is required. Dress for the weather, wear shoes you can stand in for hours, and don’t worry about the rest.
### Q. How can you tell if a bar is a gay bar?
A.  Look for a rainbow, progress, or trans flag on the front, Pride decor that stays up past June, and an event calendar with drag shows, drag bingo, or drag brunch. Check the bar’s own description too. A place that calls itself a gay bar or an LGBTQ bar is one. The directory’s gay bars category takes the guesswork out entirely.
### Q. How much should you tip a drag performer?
A.  There’s no fixed amount, but ones and fives are the standard currency, handed to the performer during a number. Tip every performer whose act you enjoyed rather than just the headliner. If you’re on a budget, a single dollar is still welcome. Bring cash, because most performers can’t take a card in the middle of a lip sync.
### Q. Can you bring a bachelorette party to a gay bar in St. Louis?
A.  Usually yes, and some bars love a big group on a slow night. Call ahead if you have more than a handful of people, especially on show nights. Once inside, tip the performers, leave the novelty accessories at the hotel, and treat the regulars like people rather than scenery. Groups that do that get a warm welcome and usually come back.

## German Food in St. Louis: What to Order and Where It Came From
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/german-food-in-st-louis-what-to-order-and-where-it-came-from
The plate comes down and it hangs off both edges. A breaded cutlet the size of the menu, a wedge of lemon, a mound of something that looks like potato salad but isn’t mayo-based, and a pile of purple cabbage you didn’t ask for. The server says “Jäger” like you should know what that means. You nod. You don’t.
That was me, years ago, in a beer hall on the South Side, and I grew up here. I knew the word schnitzel. I knew the word bratwurst. Past that, the menu might as well have been in Greek, except it was in German, which in St. Louis is a little embarrassing. By history this is one of the most German cities in the country, and most of us can’t order past the first two lines.
So this is the guide I wish I’d had. Why the city is so German in the first place, what the old German neighborhoods were called, what to order the first three times, how a German day of eating is actually built, and how to read a menu without holding up the line. No restaurant names. That’s what the directory is for.
### What is the German area of St. Louis called?
The South Side, historically. Soulard and Benton Park came first, in the decades before and after the Civil War, when German families packed into the brick blocks south of downtown within walking distance of the breweries. Then the population pushed south and west: Dutchtown, Bevo Mill, Carondelet. There’s no single official Germantown in St. Louis today, but that’s where the German churches, breweries and bakeries clustered, and where the food tradition still shows.
Dutchtown is the giveaway. The usual story, and the one most local historians repeat, is that the name is a corruption of Deutsch. English-speaking neighbors heard “Deutsch,” said “Dutch,” and it stuck. Same thing happened to the Pennsylvania Dutch, who are also German. Nobody from the Netherlands was involved.
Bevo Mill is a later chapter. The windmill building the neighborhood is named for went up in the 1910s, built by one of the city’s brewing families, and the “Bevo” part comes from a near-beer they sold through Prohibition. That’s St. Louis in one sentence. Even the neighborhood names are about beer.
Soulard is the one you can still taste. Walk it on a Saturday and you’ll pass the old market, catch the brewery smell on the right day, and see enough brick to build a second city. If you want a full rundown of the eating there, I already wrote one: where to eat in Soulard, a local’s guide. Read that after this.
### Why did Germans immigrate to St. Louis?
Cheap land, a river, and a book. In the 1820s a German writer named Gottfried Duden farmed for a few years along the Missouri River, went home, and published a glowing account of the place. It sold. Germans read it as a promise of vineyards and freedom on the frontier, and a first wave started arriving in the 1830s, mostly farmers and tradesmen, settling St. Louis and the river towns west of it.
Then 1848 happened. Revolutions broke out across the German states, they failed, and a lot of the people who’d fought for them had to leave in a hurry. The ones who landed here are still called the Forty-Eighters. They were educated, political, and loud. They started German-language newspapers, singing societies, and gymnastics clubs, and when the Civil War came they were a big reason Missouri didn’t go with the Confederacy.
By the second half of the 1800s, Germans were the largest immigrant group in St. Louis, and it wasn’t close. Whole parishes ran in German. Schools taught in German. The breweries, dozens of them at the peak, were almost all German-run, because lager is a German invention and the limestone caves under the South Side kept it cold before anyone had refrigeration. That’s the whole reason the industry took root here.
Two world wars sanded most of that down. Berlin Avenue became Pershing. German stopped being taught, the newspapers folded, and a lot of families quietly became just American. But the food never left. It went into church picnics, the backyard, and the sausage counter. Which is where you find it now.
### What is the most popular German dish?
Schnitzel, in the U.S., and it’s not a close race. Every German restaurant in St. Louis sells more schnitzel than anything else on the menu, and I’d bet most first-timers order it. In Germany itself the answer is fuzzier. Bratwurst, currywurst, and schnitzel all get argued for, and sauerbraten gets called the national dish by people who like the sound of it. More on that in the FAQ.
### Schnitzel, and what the adjectives mean
A schnitzel is a thin cutlet, pounded flat, breaded, and pan-fried. That’s it. The word in front of it on the menu tells you the meat and the topping. Wiener Schnitzel is veal, by the strict Austrian rule, and if a place lists it “Wiener Art” that means “Vienna style,” which means pork. Most schnitzel in St. Louis is pork. Nothing wrong with that.
Jägerschnitzel comes with a brown mushroom gravy. Jäger means hunter. Paprikaschnitzel, which older menus list under a name Germany has mostly retired, comes with a pepper-and-onion sauce. Rahmschnitzel gets a cream sauce. Order it plain the first time with a squeeze of lemon, and you’ll understand why the Germans never bothered improving it.
### Bratwurst and the rest of the wurst
Wurst just means sausage, and Germany has something like a thousand of them, so nobody expects you to know them all. Bratwurst is the grilled pork one, usually pale, served with mustard and a roll or with sauerkraut. Knackwurst is short, fat, and snaps when you bite it. Bockwurst is milder and smoother, often boiled. Weisswurst is the white Bavarian one, and there’s a whole ritual: you peel off the skin, dip it in sweet mustard, and, in Munich anyway, you’re supposed to finish it before noon.
Currywurst is the odd one out. It’s a chopped bratwurst under ketchup dusted with curry powder, a Berlin street-stand thing from after the war, and it’s wildly popular over there. If you see it here, get it as a starter to share. Then go buy real bratwurst by the pound. A St. Louis butcher counter is where the good stuff lives, and I’ve already looked at whether a St. Louis butcher is cheaper than the grocery store if you’re curious.
### What else should you order after schnitzel?
Sauerbraten, rouladen, spaetzle, red cabbage, and potato pancakes. That’s your second and third visit, and between the five of them you’ll have hit most of what a German grandmother would cook on a Sunday. Order at least one of the meats and both of the sides. Split them if you have to.
### The meats
Sauerbraten is a pot roast, usually beef, marinated for days in vinegar, wine, and spices, then braised and served in a sweet-sour gravy. A lot of kitchens thicken that gravy with crushed gingersnaps, which sounds strange and tastes right. Rouladen are thin sheets of beef rolled around bacon, onion, mustard, and a pickle, tied up and braised. They look fussy and eat like a stew. Schweinshaxe is a whole roasted pork knuckle with crackling skin, a Bavarian beer-hall centerpiece, and one is dinner for two.
### The sides you should never skip
Spaetzle are little egg dumplings, somewhere between a noodle and a drop dumpling, scraped or pressed into boiling water. Käsespätzle is the same thing baked with cheese and fried onions, and it’s the best thing on many menus that nobody orders. Rotkohl, sometimes listed as Blaukraut, is red cabbage cooked down with apple, vinegar, and a clove or two. Sweet-sour. It cuts through everything fried.
Kartoffelpuffer are potato pancakes, shredded and fried crisp, and the traditional partner is applesauce, not sour cream. Yes, applesauce. Try it before you argue. German potato salad, at least the southern kind, is warm and dressed with vinegar, bacon, and onion, no mayo. And a soft pretzel with butter or sweet mustard isn’t an appetizer so much as a way to hold your beer.
### Dessert
Black Forest cake, Schwarzwälder Kirschtorte if you want to say it, is chocolate sponge layered with whipped cream and sour cherries soaked in kirsch. The real one has enough brandy that you notice. Apple strudel is technically Austrian, but nobody at a German restaurant is going to card it. Thin pastry, apples, raisins, often warm with vanilla sauce. If they’ve got Bienenstich, a honey-almond cake with custard in the middle, get that instead and thank me later.
Dirndl or lederhosen not sitting right before Oktoberfest? A St. Louis dressmaker can fix that.
### What do Germans usually eat for dinner?
Bread. That surprises Americans, but the traditional German dinner is Abendbrot, literally “evening bread,” a cold spread of dark bread, sliced cold cuts, cheese, pickles, maybe some radishes, and a beer or tea. It’s eaten early, around six, and it’s light on purpose. The big hot meal of the day is lunch.
That’s the piece most St. Louis diners miss. In the old structure, Mittagessen, the midday meal, is the main event: the schnitzel, the sauerbraten, the potatoes and cabbage, all of it. That’s why German restaurants here do such a good lunch trade, and why the lunch plates are often the same size as dinner. Modern Germans with office jobs have shifted a lot of that to evening, same as everyone else. The grandmothers haven’t.
Breakfast, Frühstück, is bread rolls, Brötchen, with butter and jam on one side of the plate and cold cuts and cheese on the other. Add a soft-boiled egg in a cup with a tiny spoon, coffee, and on the weekend maybe a sliced tomato or some smoked fish. It looks like a lot for morning. It is a lot for morning. And then there’s Kaffee und Kuchen around three or four in the afternoon, which is exactly what it sounds like and a national institution.
If you want to eat the German way at a St. Louis beer hall, that’s the move: go at noon, order the heavy plate, and treat dinner as a pretzel and a wurst with a beer. Your stomach will thank you around nine o’clock.
### What is German comfort food?
Anything a German grandmother would put on the table on a rainy Sunday. In practice that means the braised meats, sauerbraten and rouladen, plus the dumplings, the potato dishes, and the one-pot stews. It’s food built for a cold climate and a long working day. Fat, vinegar, starch, and cabbage, in some combination, over and over.
Eintopf is the stew category, and the name literally means “one pot.” Lentils with sausage, split pea with smoked pork, potato soup with a sliced wiener floated in it. Frikadellen are pan-fried meat patties, halfway between a meatball and a burger, eaten hot with mustard or cold from the fridge at midnight. Königsberger Klopse are meatballs in a creamy caper sauce, which sounds like something from a hotel and is actually a school-lunch staple.
Then there’s the whole potato department. Bratkartoffeln are fried potatoes with bacon and onion. Knödel are dumplings, made from potato or from old bread, the size of a tennis ball, served under gravy. Kartoffelsalat, the warm one. Pommes with mayo. In my experience the Germans have done more with the potato than anyone but the Irish, and they’d probably argue the point.
Maultaschen deserve a mention. They’re a big square dumpling from the southwest stuffed with meat, spinach, and bread, and the legend is that monks invented them to hide meat from God during Lent. You get them in broth, or sliced and fried with egg. If a St. Louis menu has them, the kitchen is serious.
### How do you read a German menu?
Learn ten words and the rest falls into place. Schwein is pork. Rind is beef. Huhn or Hähnchen is chicken. Kartoffel is potato, Kraut is cabbage, Wurst is sausage, Brot is bread, Käse is cheese. Braten means roast, so Schweinebraten is roast pork and Sauerbraten is, well, sour roast. Gebraten means fried or roasted. Hausgemacht means homemade, and it’s a good sign.
The sections usually run Vorspeisen, starters, then Hauptgerichte, main courses, then Beilagen, sides, then Nachspeisen, desserts. Suppen is soups. If you see Tagesgericht, that’s the daily special, and it’s often the best value on the page and the cook’s favorite. A lot of St. Louis menus print the English under the German, but not all, and the ones that don’t are frequently the ones worth learning the words for.
Beer is the other half of the menu, and you can go deep on it. Helles is the pale Munich lager, easy and clean. Pils is hoppier and drier. Dunkel is dark and malty without being heavy. Weizen or Hefeweizen is the cloudy wheat beer with the banana-and-clove smell. Kölsch is the light one from Cologne served in skinny glasses. A Maß is a full liter in a glass mug, and a Radler is beer cut with lemon soda for people who have to drive. I’ve written a separate piece on visiting a St. Louis brewery taproom, and most of it applies in a beer hall.
One more. If the menu says “mit” it means “with,” and “ohne” means “without.” That’s enough to survive.
### Where does Hermann fit in?
Hermann is the wine-country cousin. About an hour and a half west of the city on the Missouri River, it was founded in the 1830s by a German settlement society that wanted a town where the language and customs could survive intact, and to a surprising degree they did. The hills around it are the Missouri Rhineland, and the wine industry there is one of the oldest in the country. It’s the same immigration story as the South Side, just with grapes instead of hops.
The food in Hermann is what you’d get in the city, with a smaller-town accent: wurst plates, sauerkraut, schnitzel, and a lot of things made in-house because there’s nowhere to order them from. Go for the wine festivals in spring and fall, or for Oktoberfest, which runs every weekend in October and is the closest thing Missouri has to Munich. Book a room early. Everybody has the same idea.
For a regular Saturday, though, the South Side does the job. Soulard for the market and the beer smell, Dutchtown and Bevo Mill for the deep cuts, and any of them for a pretzel the size of your head.
German and Czech kitchens share a border and a lot of the same cold-weather logic, so if the dumplings caught your eye, read what Czech food is and what to order in St. Louis next.
Hungry yet? Browse German food across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then go at noon, order the schnitzel plain the first time, and save the sauerbraten for the second visit.
If you run a business in this line of work, list your business.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Why did Germans immigrate to St. Louis?
A.  A mix of cheap farmland, a river that reached the frontier, and a well-timed book praising Missouri that sold across the German states in the 1830s. The bigger wave came after the failed revolutions of 1848, when political exiles, the Forty-Eighters, fled and many landed in St. Louis. By the late 1800s Germans were the largest immigrant group in the city, running breweries, newspapers, churches, and schools in their own language.
### Q. What is the most popular German dish?
A.  In St. Louis and most of the U.S., schnitzel: a thin, breaded, pan-fried cutlet, usually pork here, veal for the strict Wiener version. It outsells everything else on a German restaurant menu. In Germany the everyday favorite is closer to bratwurst or currywurst, eaten standing up at a stand. If you only order one thing on a first visit, make it schnitzel, plain, with lemon.
### Q. What is Germany’s national dish?
A.  There isn’t an official one, and Germans will argue about it. Sauerbraten, the vinegar-marinated pot roast, gets called the national dish most often, especially by cookbooks. Bratwurst and schnitzel have strong claims by sheer volume, and currywurst is the sentimental Berlin pick. Regional pride matters more than the country as a whole: a Bavarian and a Rhinelander don’t agree on much at the table.
### Q. What do Germans usually eat for dinner?
A.  Traditionally, Abendbrot: a cold evening spread of dark bread, sliced cold cuts, cheese, pickles, and maybe a beer, eaten fairly early. The hot main meal was lunch. Many modern German households have moved the warm meal to evening because of work schedules, but the bread-and-cold-cuts supper is still common, especially with older families. Eating a heavy plate at a St. Louis beer hall at night is more American than German.
### Q. What is German comfort food?
A.  Braised meats and starch. Sauerbraten, rouladen, and pork roast under gravy, with dumplings, spaetzle, or fried potatoes and a pile of red cabbage or sauerkraut on the side. Eintopf, the one-pot stew, is the weeknight version. Frikadellen, pan-fried meat patties, are what a German eats cold out of the fridge. It’s cold-weather food from a place with long winters, and it eats best when it’s gray outside.
### Q. What is a typical German breakfast?
A.  Bread rolls, called Brötchen, with butter and jam on one side and cold cuts and cheese on the other, plus a soft-boiled egg in a cup with a tiny spoon and coffee. Weekends might add sliced tomato, smoked fish, or a sweet pastry. It’s a bigger spread than an American weekday breakfast, but it’s cold, and it’s meant to be eaten slowly with more than one cup of coffee.
### Q. Is Hermann, Missouri worth the drive for German food?
A.  Yes, if you make a day of it. Hermann is about an hour and a half west of St. Louis on the Missouri River, founded by German settlers in the 1830s, and the hills around it are the Missouri Rhineland wine country. The food is the same wurst, kraut, and schnitzel you get on the South Side, with more of it made in-house. Go for a wine festival or an October weekend, and book lodging early.
### Q. What should I order at a German restaurant if I don’t eat pork?
A.  More than you’d think. Sauerbraten and rouladen are beef. Königsberger Klopse are often beef or veal, though ask. Hähnchenschnitzel is chicken, and many kitchens will bread a chicken cutlet on request. Käsespätzle, the cheese-and-onion dumplings, is a full vegetarian meal. Potato pancakes with applesauce, red cabbage, and a pretzel round it out. Just check the potato salad, since the warm southern kind usually has bacon in it.

## When to See a Gynecologist in St. Louis and What to Expect
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/when-to-see-a-gynecologist-in-st-louis-and-what-to-expect
The car is parked outside a medical office building in St. Louis County, engine off, and neither of them has moved. The daughter is fourteen. Her phone is in her lap and she hasn’t looked at it in three minutes. Finally she asks the question she’s been holding since breakfast. “Are they going to, like, examine me?” Her mother, who has been dreading exactly that question, realizes she doesn’t actually know.
That’s the honest state of things for a lot of families here. Nobody sits you down and explains when a first gynecologist visit should happen, what goes on behind the door, or how to tell a good doctor from one who’s just running you through. Women in their thirties wonder the same things. So do women in their seventies who were told, years ago, that they could stop going.
This guide is the conversation in the car, written down. What the timing usually looks like. What a first visit actually involves, and what it doesn’t. Whether it matters if the doctor is a woman. What to do about the bill if you don’t have insurance. And how to spot the doctor who isn’t listening, before it costs you. No clinic names, no made-up prices. Just the plain version.
### When should a woman first see a gynecologist in St. Louis?
The usual guidance is a first visit somewhere between 13 and 15, and that visit is mostly a conversation. A pelvic exam and Pap test typically wait until 21 unless there’s a specific problem. Go sooner for heavy or painful periods, missed periods, pelvic pain, or questions about contraception.
That age range comes from the main professional body for obstetricians and gynecologists in the United States, and it surprises most parents. Thirteen feels young. But the point of that early visit isn’t an exam. It’s an introduction. The teen meets a doctor who handles this part of the body for a living, hears that periods and cramps and questions about her body are normal things to talk about, and learns there’s a place to go when something feels off.
Plenty of St. Louis families skip it, and honestly, plenty of teens do fine getting the same care from a pediatrician or family doctor. That’s a reasonable path too. The thing that shouldn’t wait is a problem. Periods that soak through a pad every hour. Cramps that keep a kid home from school. No period at all by fifteen or sixteen. Pain that isn’t tied to a period. Those earn a visit now, whatever the age.
For an adult woman who never went, the answer is simpler. Go. Twenty-one is when routine cervical screening starts, and if you’re past that with no Pap on record, that’s reason enough. Many offices in the St. Louis area book new-patient visits weeks out, so it helps to call before you actually need to be seen. If you don’t have a regular doctor of any kind yet, our guide to finding a primary care doctor in St. Louis covers where to start.
### What will a gynecologist do on a first visit?
Mostly, talk. A first visit is a health history and a conversation, and for a teen it very often ends there. The doctor asks about periods, general health, family history, and whatever’s on your mind. There may be a basic check of height, weight, and blood pressure. A pelvic exam happens only when there’s a reason for one, or once you’ve reached screening age.
### The conversation part
Expect questions, and expect them to be direct. When did your period start? How heavy, how long, how painful? Are you sexually active? Any discharge, itching, pain, or bleeding between periods? Any medications, any allergies, anything running in the family like breast or ovarian cancer? These aren’t judgments. They’re the doctor building a map. Answer plainly, and if you don’t know something, say that. A good doctor writes it down and moves on.
For a teen, most offices will ask the parent to step out for part of the conversation. That’s standard, and it’s a good sign, not a bad one. It gives the kid a few minutes to ask what she’d never ask in front of her mother. What’s said in that window is generally kept between the teen and the doctor, with the usual exceptions for safety. Parents, let it happen. It’s the whole reason the early visit exists.
### The exam part, if there is one
A general exam is quick and mostly familiar. Heart, lungs, belly. A breast exam, sometimes, depending on age and what came up in the history. If a pelvic exam is on the table, the doctor should say so before it happens, explain what it involves, and explain why. For a first visit with no complaint and a patient under 21, there’s usually no pelvic exam at all.
When one is needed, here’s the honest version. You lie back, feet in footrests, a sheet over your lap. The doctor looks at the outside, then uses a speculum to see the cervix. If it’s a Pap, a small brush collects cells from the cervix. Then a gloved hand checks the uterus and ovaries from the inside while the other presses gently on the belly. It’s a few minutes. Pressure, some awkwardness, not usually pain. If it hurts, say so. Right then, out loud.
Bloodwork or a urine sample may round it out. Vaccines, like HPV, might come up. And then it’s a chair, a pair of shoes, and the question the doctor should always ask: anything else?
### What should you not do before seeing a gynecologist?
For a Pap test, skip intercourse, tampons, douching, and any vaginal creams or medications for 24 to 48 hours beforehand. Those can wash away or hide the cells the test is trying to collect. For a plain conversation visit, there’s nothing to avoid. And the two things people worry about most, being on your period and not being shaved, almost never matter.
Douching deserves its own line, because it’s not just a before-the-Pap issue. Most gynecologists will tell you not to do it at all. It disturbs the normal balance down there and can make an infection more likely, not less. The body handles its own housekeeping. Soap and water on the outside is all it wants.
About the period. Older advice said to reschedule. Many offices now say to come anyway, especially if the flow is light, because a modern Pap can usually still be read. Heavy flow can interfere, so if you’re on day one or two of a heavy cycle and it’s a screening visit, a quick call to the office settles it. If the visit is about a problem, though, don’t cancel. Seeing what’s happening during a period can be useful to the doctor.
And no, you don’t need to shave, wax, or trim. Nobody in that room is grading it. Doctors have seen every variation there is and genuinely don’t notice. Show up clean from a normal shower. That’s the whole list.
One more thing not to skip: bring your questions written down. In the moment, in the paper gown, they evaporate. A note on your phone with three questions is worth more than an hour of reading the night before.
Visit scheduled. Now plan the reward: how a French dinner in St. Louis actually works.
### Is it better to see a female gynecologist?
It’s a personal preference, and either answer is fine. Male and female gynecologists go through the same medical school, the same residency, the same board exams. What differs is comfort, and comfort is a real part of care. If you’ll speak more freely with a woman, choose a woman. If you don’t care, you’ve just doubled your options.
In our experience talking with St. Louis women about this, the honest answer usually isn’t about gender at all. It’s about whether the doctor listens, explains, and doesn’t rush. A woman who never looks up from the screen is not a better fit than a man who pulls up a chair. Some women say a female doctor understands cramps in a way a man can’t. Others have had their pain brushed off by female doctors and taken seriously by male ones. It cuts both ways.
For a teen, though, lean toward whatever she asks for. If a fourteen-year-old says she wants a woman, that’s the answer, no negotiation. The first visit is about making the whole thing feel normal, and it can’t feel normal if she’s bracing the entire time. Whichever way you go, a chaperone in the room during any exam should be offered without you having to ask. More on that below.
Some women also weigh a nurse practitioner or a certified nurse midwife for routine care, and for well visits and Paps that’s a perfectly sound choice. If that path interests you, we’ve written about what a midwife does and how to choose one in St. Louis.
### How much does a gynecologist visit cost without insurance in St. Louis?
There’s no single number, and anyone who gives you one without asking what the visit includes is guessing. Self-pay rates vary a lot from office to office, and a conversation-only visit costs less than one with a Pap, lab work, or an ultrasound. The move is to call ahead and ask for the self-pay price up front, in writing if they’ll give it.
A few things drive the bill. The visit itself, billed by length and complexity. The Pap, which is a lab charge on top. Any tests for infections, which are also lab charges. An ultrasound, if one’s needed. Each of those may come from a different biller, so the number the front desk quotes might not be the whole thing. Ask specifically: does this include the lab? Many offices offer a discount for paying in full on the day, and some won’t mention it unless you ask.
If the quoted price is out of reach, the St. Louis area has community health centers and sliding-scale clinics that charge based on income, and they do routine gynecologic care, including Paps. Some public health programs cover cervical and breast cancer screening at no cost for women who qualify. We don’t name specific clinics here, but a search for sliding-scale or community health in the St. Louis area, or a call to the county health department, will surface them.
One practical note. If you’re uninsured and the visit turns into something bigger, a procedure, a referral, imaging, ask about cost before it’s scheduled, not after. A good office won’t be offended. They deal with this every day.
### What are the red flags for gynecologists?
The big ones: a doctor who dismisses pain, rushes you, won’t explain what’s happening or why, doesn’t offer a chaperone for an exam, or makes you feel ashamed. Any one of those is a reason to look elsewhere. Two or more is a reason to leave before the next appointment. Your body, your call, and there are plenty of doctors in St. Louis.
“That’s normal” is not the same as an answer. Cramps that put you on the floor might be common, but common isn’t the same as fine. A doctor who hears that and says “some women just have painful periods” without a follow-up question has stopped listening. Same for pain during sex, bleeding between periods, or a feeling that something’s wrong that you can’t quite name. You should leave with either a plan or a clear reason there isn’t one.
The chaperone matters more than people think. It’s standard practice for a third person, usually a nurse or medical assistant, to be in the room during a pelvic or breast exam, and the offer should come from the office, not from you. That protects both sides. An office that skips it, or acts put out when you ask, has told you something about how it operates.
Then there’s tone. Comments about weight that have nothing to do with why you came. Raised eyebrows at your number of partners. Lectures instead of information. A teen who leaves a first visit feeling judged may not go back for a decade. That’s a real cost, and it’s the doctor’s failure, not hers.
### Treat the first visit as an interview
Here’s the frame we suggest for choosing any provider. Shortlist two or three doctors worth interviewing. Then treat that first appointment as exactly that, an interview. Before you go, decide plainly what you want: a chaperone offered, time to ask questions, a doctor who explains before touching, someone who takes pain seriously. Say it out loud if you have to. Then compare what you asked for with what the practice actually delivered.
The gap is the signal. If you said you wanted time for questions and got seven rushed minutes, that’s your answer, no matter how good the reviews are. If you asked for explanations and got them, unprompted, you’ve probably found your doctor. Don’t argue with the gap. It’s the practice showing you what it’s prepared to do, and that rarely changes on the second visit.
### Do older women still need to see a gynecologist?
Yes, though the reason changes. Routine Pap screening can generally stop after 65 for a woman with a clean history of normal results, and a woman who’s had a hysterectomy for a non-cancer reason usually stops sooner. But the annual visit isn’t just about the Pap. Menopause symptoms, bleeding after menopause, pelvic floor problems, bone health, breast exams, and vaginal dryness all still need a doctor who knows this territory.
Bleeding after menopause is the one that should never wait. It’s often something minor, but it’s also a common early sign of a problem that’s very treatable when caught early. Any spotting, any time, after twelve months without a period, earns a call the same week. Not next month. Not after the holidays.
The other reason older women keep going is that things get quietly worse when nobody asks. Leaking with a cough. Pain with sex that’s been shrugged off for years. A pelvic heaviness that’s been chalked up to age. Much of it is treatable, and much of it gets missed because nobody brought it up. If your regular doctor handles all of this well, that can be enough. If they wave it off, a gynecologist is still the right call at 73 as much as at 33.
And for women in the middle, the ones trying to get pregnant and running into trouble, the gynecologist is usually the first stop before a specialist. We’ve covered what fertility treatment involves in St. Louis for when that conversation comes up.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it better to see a female gynecologist?
A.  Only if it’s better for you. Male and female gynecologists train identically and pass the same boards, so the medicine is the same. What changes is how freely you talk, and that matters, because the history is most of the visit. Pick whoever you’ll be honest with. For a teen, let her choose. And judge any doctor by whether they listen and explain, not by gender.
### Q. How much is a gynecologist visit without insurance?
A.  It varies a lot, and we won’t invent a figure. A conversation-only visit is the cheapest; a Pap, infection tests, or an ultrasound each add lab or imaging charges, sometimes from a separate biller. Call the office, ask for the self-pay price, and ask whether it includes the lab. Community health centers and sliding-scale clinics in the St. Louis area charge based on income, and some public programs cover screening for women who qualify.
### Q. What should you not do before seeing a gynecologist?
A.  Before a Pap, avoid intercourse, tampons, douching, and vaginal creams or medications for 24 to 48 hours, since they can hide the cells the test needs. Don’t douche at all, really. Don’t bother shaving; nobody notices. Don’t cancel over your period unless the office asks you to. And don’t walk in without your questions written down, because they vanish the moment the gown goes on.
### Q. What are the red flags for gynecologists?
A.  A doctor who dismisses your pain as normal without a follow-up question. One who rushes, won’t explain what an exam is for before doing it, or doesn’t offer a chaperone. Shaming of any kind: about weight, partners, or questions. Any one of those means keep looking. Compare what you asked for on the first visit with what the practice delivered. The gap tells you everything.
### Q. What will a gynecologist do on a first visit?
A.  Mostly ask questions and listen. Expect a health history covering periods, sexual activity, medications, and family history, plus a basic check of blood pressure and weight. A teen’s first visit usually stops there, with the parent stepping out for part of it. A pelvic exam and Pap only happen if there’s a specific problem or you’ve reached 21, and the doctor should explain each step before it starts.
### Q. Does a 73 year old woman need to see a gynecologist?
A.  Yes, even though routine Pap tests usually stop after 65 with a clean history. The visit at 73 is about other things: any bleeding after menopause, which always needs a same-week call, plus pelvic floor problems, leaking, pain with sex, vaginal dryness, breast exams, and bone health. A primary care doctor who handles these well can cover it. One who waves them off is a reason to keep the gynecologist.
### Q. Should a parent stay in the room during a teen’s first gynecologist visit?
A.  Stay for the introductions and the history, then expect to be asked to step out for a few minutes. That’s standard, and it’s the point of the visit: a private window where she can ask what she wouldn’t ask in front of you. What’s said there generally stays between her and the doctor, with the usual safety exceptions. If an exam happens, a staff chaperone should be in the room regardless.
### Q. Can you see a gynecologist while on your period?
A.  Usually, yes. Many offices now say to keep the appointment, especially for light flow, because a modern Pap can typically still be read. Very heavy flow can interfere with a screening test, so on a heavy day it’s worth a quick call to ask. If the visit is about a problem, though, come anyway. Seeing what’s happening mid-cycle can help the doctor more than it hurts.

## How to Tell If Food Is Halal in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-tell-if-food-is-halal-in-st-louis
There’s a small place on South Grand where the halal certificate is taped to the wall right behind the register. Laminated, a little curled at one corner, the date on it about eight months old. I asked the owner about it once. He said, “All the meat. Chicken, lamb, beef. No pork in the building.” Took him four seconds. That, in my experience, is what a good answer sounds like.
Most people never get that far. They see the word halal on a sign, or on a menu, or on a plastic-wrapped tray at a grocery counter, and they either trust it or they don’t. If you’re Muslim, the question comes up every time you eat out. If you’re hosting Muslim guests, a coworker, a kid’s friend, it comes up once and you want to get it right. And if you’re just curious what the word on the awning means, that’s fine too. Here’s how I check, and what the words mean.
### How can I tell if food is halal in St. Louis?
Look for the certificate first. A restaurant that has gone to the trouble of getting certified will usually hang the paper where you can see it, near the register or by the door. Then read the menu. Some places print the word next to each dish, others put one line at the top. Then ask two questions: is all the meat halal, or only some of it, and does the kitchen also cook pork or use wine in anything. A plain, quick answer from the owner is itself a good sign.
Notice what’s not on that list. A Middle Eastern or South Asian menu doesn’t make a place halal. Neither does a Muslim owner. Neither does the word on the awning, if the guy at the counter can’t tell you where the chicken comes from. The paper, the menu, and the answer are the three things I actually weigh. Everything else is decoration.
At a grocery counter the same logic applies with different clues: a certification mark printed on the packaging, a butcher who can name his supplier, and a store where the whole counter is halal rather than one shelf of it. More on that below.
### What does halal actually mean?
Halal is an Arabic word that means permissible. It covers a lot more than food, but at the table it comes down to a short list. Pork is out. Alcohol is out, including wine cooked into a sauce. Blood is out. And for meat and poultry, the animal has to be slaughtered a particular way: by a Muslim (many scholars also accept a Jew or a Christian), with the name of God spoken over it, with a single cut across the throat that drains the blood quickly. The animal is supposed to be healthy, treated decently, and killed one at a time, not in front of the others.
The opposite of halal is haram, forbidden. Between them sits a gray zone people argue about, and this post isn’t going to settle those arguments. Stunning before slaughter. Machine slaughter with a recorded blessing. Gelatin from an unknown source. Vanilla extract with alcohol in it. Some Muslims accept some of these. Some accept none. When you’re feeding someone else, you don’t get to pick their standard for them. You ask.
One more piece of vocabulary. Zabihah (sometimes spelled dhabihah) is the actual slaughter method. When someone says they only eat “zabihah halal,” they want meat slaughtered by hand, by a Muslim, the traditional way, and they don’t accept the looser reading where any meat from “people of the book” counts. You’ll see the phrase on menus around here. It’s a stricter claim, not a looser one.
### What is the difference between halal meat and normal meat?
Same animal. That’s the first thing to understand. A halal chicken is a chicken, a halal ribeye is a ribeye, and nothing about the breed or the feed is different by rule. What changes is the slaughter and the handling. In a standard American plant the animal is stunned, killed, and processed on a line, and nobody says anything over it. In a halal slaughter the animal is faced toward Mecca, the name of God is spoken, and the throat is cut with a sharp knife in one motion so the heart pumps the blood out while it still can.
After that, the rules are about keeping it separate. Halal meat shouldn’t be cut on a block that just had pork on it. It shouldn’t sit in a cooler under dripping pork. In a halal restaurant it shouldn’t share a fryer or a grill with anything haram. That’s why the “does the kitchen also serve pork” question matters so much. The meat can be perfect on the truck and lose its status on the flat-top.
“Normal” meat from a supermarket isn’t dirty or bad. It just wasn’t slaughtered under those rules, and there’s no chain of custody promising it stayed away from pork. For a Muslim diner that’s the whole difference. For anyone else, it’s mostly a question of how much you care about the way the animal died.
### What should you look for at a restaurant?
### The certificate
Certifying bodies in the United States are private organizations, not government agencies. They inspect the supplier chain and the kitchen, and they issue a dated paper. A restaurant that has one will usually display it by the register, sometimes by the front door, occasionally in a frame on the way to the restroom. Read the date. An expired certificate isn’t proof of anything shady, but it’s a fair reason to ask whether something changed.
Plenty of small, honest places skip certification because it costs money and they already buy from a halal butcher everyone in the neighborhood knows. That’s common along Olive and Page out in the county and on South Grand in the city. No paper doesn’t mean no halal. It means you have to ask.
### The menu
Read the menu the way you’d read a lease. “All meat halal” at the top is the clearest version. “Halal chicken available” means the lamb and beef probably aren’t. A little symbol next to some items and not others means exactly what it looks like. If the menu has a bacon cheeseburger on it, the kitchen handles pork, full stop, and the rest of the menu inherits that problem unless they’ve told you how they keep things apart.
### All of it, or some of it?
This is the single most useful question. “Is all your meat halal, or just some dishes?” Owners answer it plainly almost every time, in my experience. Mixed kitchens exist, and some do a careful job with separate grills and separate prep. Others don’t. Either way, you want to know which kind you’re standing in before you order the gyro.
### Pork and wine
Ask about both. Pork is obvious. Wine hides. It’s in the marsala, the coq au vin, the beurre blanc, the deglazed pan under the steak. Beer is in the batter. Some Italian and French dishes can’t be made without it, and a cook may not think to mention it because to him it’s a seasoning. “Does anything on the menu have alcohol cooked into it?” is a fair question, and a good kitchen won’t blink.
### “Halal-style” and other soft words
Watch for hedges. “Halal-style” usually means the dish looks like something from a halal cart, not that the meat was slaughtered halal. “Muslim-owned” is a fact about the owner, not the chicken. “No pork” is nice, but it isn’t the same claim. The word you want is halal, unqualified, with a source behind it. If the language is doing a dance, the meat probably is too.
Locked out after dinner? Here is what a St. Louis emergency locksmith costs.
### How to know if meat is halal at a grocery store?
Start with the package. Certified halal meat sold in a supermarket carries a mark from the certifying body somewhere on the label, often a small logo with the word halal in English and Arabic. It’s printed on, not stickered on, and the brand will match a company that actually does halal processing. A sticker on the shrink-wrap that just says halal, with no logo and no company name, is a claim from the store. That’s a weaker thing.
At a counter with a butcher, ask who the supplier is. You don’t need the name to mean anything to you. You need him to have one ready. A halal butcher buys from a halal slaughterhouse or a distributor, and he knows which, because he’s been asked a thousand times. If the answer is “it’s halal, don’t worry,” worry a little.
Whole-carcass counters versus pre-packaged is the next thing to look at. The small ethnic groceries around South Grand and Dutchtown, and along the Page and Olive corridors out into the county, tend to bring in whole or half animals, or big primal cuts, and break them down on site. That means the butcher can tell you exactly where it came from because he unloaded it. Pre-packaged meat from a distributor is fine too, as long as the label carries the mark. The thing you don’t want is unlabeled meat in a display case at a store that also sells pork ribs three feet away, with nobody on the floor who can explain it.
Those little groceries are also where you find the odd cuts, the goat, the whole chickens with the feet still on, at prices a chain usually won’t match. I’ve written before about whether a St. Louis butcher is cheaper than the grocery store, and the halal counters are a big part of why the answer is so often yes.
### What’s the difference between halal and kosher?
They look alike from the outside and they’re not the same thing. Both forbid pork. Both forbid blood. Both require the animal to be slaughtered by a trained person with a single cut and drained. From there they split. Kosher law forbids mixing meat and dairy in the same meal; halal doesn’t care. Halal forbids alcohol; kosher allows it, and kosher wine is a whole category. Kosher requires an inspection of the carcass afterward and limits which parts of the animal can be eaten, which halal mostly doesn’t. Kosher slaughter is done by a trained Jewish slaughterer. Halal slaughter requires the name of God to be spoken at the moment of the cut, which a kosher slaughterer doesn’t do in the same way.
So kosher meat isn’t automatically halal, and halal meat isn’t automatically kosher. Different rules, different certifying bodies, different marks on the package. Now, some Muslims do accept kosher meat when halal isn’t available, on the reasoning that Jews are people of the book and the slaughter is close enough. That’s a view some hold. Others hold the opposite. I’m not a scholar and I’m not going to rule on it. If you’re buying for a guest, ask the guest.
### Does halal beef taste different?
People argue about this at dinner tables all over the city and nobody has convinced anybody. Here’s the honest version. There’s no chemical reason halal beef should taste different from conventionally slaughtered beef of the same breed, age, feed, and cut. Same muscle. Same fat. Where people notice a difference, and some really do, it usually comes down to two things that have nothing to do with the blessing.
The first is drainage. A quick cut with the heart still beating pumps out more blood than some conventional methods do, and less blood left in the muscle means a cleaner flavor and a longer fridge life. Butchers talk about this. The second is freshness and scale. The halal beef you buy at a small South Grand grocery was probably broken down that week from a carcass the owner picked, not aged in a cryovac bag for a month on a truck. Fresh and small-batch tastes different from industrial. That difference gets credited to the halal label when it really belongs to the butcher.
Cook two ribeyes side by side, one halal and one not, same grade and same age, and I’d bet most people couldn’t tell you which was which. Cook a halal goat shoulder from a neighborhood counter against a supermarket lamb chop and sure, they’ll taste different. But that isn’t the test.
### What about eggs, fish, and vegetables?
Halal by default, all of them. Eggs are halal. Fish is halal, though a few schools of thought quibble about shellfish and fish without scales; anything with fins and scales is fine everywhere. Vegetables, grains, fruit, dairy, all halal unless something haram gets cooked into them. Halal is a rule about slaughter and a short list of forbidden ingredients, not a rule that everything on the plate needs a certificate.
The catch is what they get cooked in and with. Fries in the same oil as the chicken tenders that were breaded next to the pork sausage. A vegetable curry finished with ghee, which is fine, and then a splash of cooking wine, which isn’t. A cheese made with animal rennet from an unknown source, which some people care about and some don’t. Gelatin in the dessert. That’s why the pork-and-alcohol question still matters at a restaurant even for a vegetarian order. At a dedicated halal place it’s already handled. At a mixed kitchen, ask.
### Can anyone eat halal food?
Yes. Halal meat is meat. There’s nothing in it, nothing done to it, and nothing about it that makes it off-limits to a Christian, an atheist, a Hindu who eats meat, or anybody else. Some Christians ask whether eating meat blessed in the name of God under another religion is a problem for them. That’s a question for their own pastor, and different churches have answered it different ways over the centuries. From the food side, it’s a clean-slaughtered animal with the blood drained. Plenty of non-Muslims in St. Louis eat at halal restaurants every week and never think about it, mostly because the food is good.
If you want a low-stakes way to find out what you think, go eat. A lot of the Indian and Pakistani places in my guide to the best Indian food in St. Louis are halal, and so are many of the Mediterranean spots. Order the lamb. Decide for yourself.
### Questions worth asking before you order
Here’s my short list, in the order I actually ask them. None of them are rude. Any owner who takes offense at these has told you something.
Is all of your meat halal, or only some dishes? Where does the meat come from, and do you have a certificate? Does the kitchen cook any pork? Is there wine, beer, or any alcohol in any sauce or marinade? Are the fries and the appetizers fried in the same oil as anything non-halal? Is the gelatin or the cheese in the dessert halal? And, if it matters to the person you’re feeding, is it hand-slaughtered zabihah or machine-processed?
Seven questions sounds like a lot. In practice it’s about forty seconds, and at a real halal place the owner answers the first one in a way that makes the rest unnecessary. “Everything. No pork, no alcohol, all from the same supplier.” That’s the sentence you’re listening for.
Kosher follows its own rulebook, and here’s how to tell if food is kosher in St. Louis when a label is all you have.
Ready to eat? Browse halal restaurants and markets across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then ask the two questions above before you order.
