## What Turkish Food Is and What to Order in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-turkish-food-is-and-what-to-order-in-st-louis
The adana came out on a long metal plate, still hissing, laid over a torn sheet of flatbread that had already gone translucent from the juices. Across the two-top, a man who’d driven up from Hillsboro poked at the pale mound beside it and asked his wife if it was cheese. It wasn’t. Yogurt. She dragged a piece of kebab through it, took a bite, went quiet for a second, and pushed the plate two inches toward him. That was the whole review.
If your only Turkish food so far has been a gyro from a truck, the real thing can feel like a cousin you’ve heard about but never met. The names look hard. The menu runs long. And the person at the counter is so glad you walked in that you don’t want to admit you have no idea what a pide is. Relax. It’s bread with stuff on it.
Here’s what Turkish cuisine actually is, what it tastes like, how it differs from Greek, and what two people should order the first time they sit down at a Turkish restaurant in St. Louis. No restaurant names, on purpose. Kitchens change hands. The dishes don’t.
### What to order from a Turkish restaurant in St. Louis?
Order a mixed grill for two plus one meze plate and warm bread. That covers adana kebab, chicken shish, kofte, rice, and grilled peppers, with hummus or ezme to start. Add ayran to drink and share baklava at the end. If the kitchen lists iskender, one of you should order it instead.
That’s the safe first order, and it works in nearly every Turkish kitchen in the metro. Why the mixed grill? Because it’s a sampler in disguise. You get a skewer of spiced ground lamb, a skewer of chicken, maybe a kofte patty, all charred over flame and set on rice beside a blistered pepper and a wedge of tomato. Nothing on that plate is hot. Nothing needs explaining. The meze keeps the bread busy while the grill works. Skip the soup on a first visit unless it’s red lentil, which is worth it.
### What Turkish food actually is
Turkish food is the home cooking of Anatolia, the wide peninsula that makes up most of modern Turkey, filtered through six centuries of Ottoman palace kitchens. That’s the short answer. The Ottoman Empire ran from the Balkans to the Persian Gulf, and its cooks picked up ideas everywhere they went and sent them back out again. So a Turkish menu sits right where the Mediterranean, the Middle East, the Balkans, and Central Asia overlap.
You can taste the map. Olive oil, lemon, and grilled fish come from the Aegean coast. Bulgur, lamb, hot pepper, and pistachio come from the southeast, near Syria. Yogurt and stuffed dumplings came west with Turkic nomads a thousand years ago. A restaurant in St. Louis usually pulls from all of those at once, with the grill section leaning southeast and the meze list leaning coastal.
One thing it is not: a spinoff of Greek or Lebanese food, even though the three trade dishes constantly. Turkish cooking has its own center of gravity, and that center is yogurt, bread, and meat over a fire. Almost every Turkish kitchen in the metro is a family kitchen, too. What lands on your plate is somebody’s mother’s version. That’s the appeal.
### What does Turkish food taste like?
Smoky, tangy, and mild. That’s the honest three-word answer. Grilled lamb and chicken bring the smoke. Yogurt, lemon, and sumac bring the tang. And almost nothing on the table is hot the way a Sichuan or Thai kitchen means it. Turkish cooks build heat with a dried red pepper called pul biber, and they mostly leave it in a shaker on the table so you can add your own.
Vegetables do more work here than in most meat-heavy cuisines. Eggplant gets roasted until it collapses, then dressed with garlic and oil or folded into a smoky puree. Tomatoes and peppers show up grilled, raw, and chopped into a chunky relish called ezme. Bulgur, the cracked wheat, stands in for rice half the time and has a nutty chew rice doesn’t. Pomegranate molasses, sour and sticky, sneaks into salad dressings. Parsley is a vegetable here, not a garnish.
Layered, but not loud. A first-timer from Spanish Lake once described adana to us as “a burger that went to a better school,” which is about right. If you know Persian food, you’ll notice the shared rice and yogurt; our guide to what Persian food is and what to try in St. Louis covers that cousin. Turkish plates run smokier and less sweet-and-sour than Persian ones.
### What is a typical Turkish menu?
Most Turkish menus in St. Louis follow one shape: cold and hot meze up top, breads and pides in the middle, a long kebab section, a few home-style dishes, then sweets and drinks. Pick what to share first, then one main each, then decide about dessert when you see how full you are.
### Meze, pide, and lahmacun
Meze are small plates, and a table usually orders three or four to pass around. Hummus, yes, but also haydari (thick yogurt with garlic and dill), ezme (that tomato-pepper relish), and patlican salatasi (smoky mashed eggplant). Pide is a boat-shaped flatbread baked with cheese, ground meat, or sucuk on top and sliced into strips; think of it as the Turkish pizza. Lahmacun is thinner and rounder, a paper-crisp disk smeared with spiced ground lamb. Squeeze lemon on it, pile on parsley and onion, roll it up, eat it like a wrap.
### Kebabs, doner, and kofte
Adana kebab is hand-minced lamb with red pepper pressed onto a wide flat skewer and grilled. Urfa is the same thing without the heat. Shish is cubed meat on a stick. Kofte are small grilled patties of seasoned ground beef or lamb. Doner is the big rotating cone of stacked meat, shaved off in ribbons and served on rice, in bread, or in a wrap. Iskender, the one to remember, is doner laid over cubes of toasted pide, soaked in tomato sauce, then finished with browned butter and a heap of yogurt.
### Manti, kumpir, and borek
These are the home-style dishes, and they don’t appear on every menu, so order them when you see them. Manti are tiny lamb dumplings, sometimes no bigger than a fingernail, buried under garlic yogurt and a drizzle of pepper butter. Kumpir is a huge baked potato mashed with butter and cheese inside its own skin, then loaded with whatever toppings you point at. Borek is layered phyllo baked around spinach, cheese, or ground meat, cut in squares or coiled like a rope.
### Baklava, kunefe, tea, coffee, and ayran
Turkish baklava is pistachio-forward and less syrupy than the Greek kind. Kunefe is the dessert to pick if you only pick one: shredded phyllo baked around soft, stretchy cheese, soaked in syrup, served hot so the cheese pulls. Tea comes black and strong in a small tulip-shaped glass, and you’ll be offered it constantly. Turkish coffee is thick and unfiltered; let the grounds settle and leave the last sip. Ayran is salted, thinned yogurt, cold and a little foamy. It’s the drink that belongs with kebab.

### Is Turkish food similar to Greek food?
Yes and no. Both grew up under the same Ottoman roof for roughly four hundred years, so they share a deep pantry: phyllo, eggplant, grilled lamb, stuffed grape leaves, yogurt, honey-soaked pastry. Eat at a Greek table and a Turkish one in the same week and you’ll recognize half the plates. The differences live in the seasoning and the details.
Greek cooking leans on oregano, lemon, olive oil, and feta. Turkish cooking leans on red pepper, sumac, cumin, and mint, with more yogurt on the plate and less cheese. Doner and gyro are cousins. Doner is the older Turkish form, usually lamb or a lamb-beef blend, shaved thin and served over rice or in bread with tomato and onion. Gyro is the Greek adaptation, often pork back home and a pressed beef-lamb loaf in the United States, tucked into pita with tzatziki. Same idea. Different jacket.
Baklava is the argument that never ends. The Turkish version is denser and built around pistachio; the Greek one usually goes walnut and heavier on honey. Want to try the Greek side first? Our local’s guide to the best Greek and Mediterranean food in St. Louis is the place to start. A couple from De Soto told us they keep a running scorecard now. Turkish leads on bread. Greek leads on fish.
### What does a typical Turkish breakfast consist of?
A Turkish breakfast, called kahvalti, is a table full of small plates rather than one big one. White cheese, olives, sliced tomato and cucumber, honey with a slab of clotted cream called kaymak, jam, boiled or fried eggs, and a basket of bread. Tea gets poured without pause. It’s meant to last an hour, and nobody hurries it.
The hot dishes are where it gets good. Menemen is eggs scrambled slowly with tomato, green pepper, and sometimes onion, served soft in the pan it cooked in. Sucuk is a spiced beef sausage, sliced and fried until the fat renders, often with an egg cracked over the top. Simit is the sesame-crusted bread ring stacked by the register, chewy inside and crunchy out, made for tearing and dragging through honey and kaymak.
Not every Turkish restaurant in the St. Louis metro serves breakfast, and the ones that do often keep it to weekends. Check the posted hours before you drive in from Herculaneum for it. When it’s on, the kahvalti spread for two is a dozen tastes on one bill, and the price varies by kitchen. Bring an appetite. Skip lunch.
### What is the etiquette for eating Turkish food?
Bread is a utensil. Tea is a welcome, not an upsell. Meze belong to the whole table. And “afiyet olsun” is what you say when food arrives, or what the cook says to you; it means roughly “may it do you good.” Those four things cover almost everything a first-timer needs. The rest is common sense.
### Bread and hands
Tear the bread; don’t cut it. Use pieces to scoop meze, to drag through the juices on a kebab plate, and to wrap a bite of doner with onion and parsley. Lahmacun gets rolled and eaten by hand. Pide gets picked up by the strip. A fork is fine for rice and salad. The bread just does a better job on everything else.
### Tea, sharing, and the check
When tea shows up after the meal without anyone ordering it, that’s hospitality, not a line on the bill. Take it, or say thank you and decline once. Meze go in the middle of the table, so order with the group in mind. Splitting a big plate like iskender or a mixed grill is normal. If the owner stops by to ask how everything was, that’s normal too, and a real answer beats a polite one. Tipping follows the usual St. Louis rules.
### How to find Turkish food around the St. Louis metro
Turkish kitchens in the metro tend to hide inside bigger labels. Some list as Mediterranean, some as Middle Eastern, some as halal, and a few as a bakery or cafe with a kebab menu in the back. Search all four. The international corridors are densest; our South Grand guide to the international food district maps one. But Turkish spots turn up in strip malls out toward Berkeley too, wherever a family decided to open one.
How do you pick between two? Ask the kitchen what they actually cook. Do they build their own doner or buy the cone? Is the adana hand-minced? Is the bread baked in-house? A kitchen that’s proud of the answer will tell you in detail. Then match that against what you want. A slow dinner with meze and tea calls for a place with real tables and a posted meze list. Doner on a Tuesday? A counter spot will do. Prices vary by kitchen, so read the posted menu instead of trusting a guess.
Online menus go stale. Call. Or walk in and ask what’s good that day. In our experience the answer is whatever the person at the grill is proudest of, and that’s the plate you want.

A.  Smoky, tangy, and mild. Lamb and chicken over charcoal give the smoke. Yogurt, lemon, and sumac give the tang. Eggplant, tomato, parsley, and bulgur fill out the plate, with pomegranate molasses and mint showing up in salads. Heat comes from a dried red pepper called pul biber that usually sits on the table in a shaker, so the base dish stays gentle and you decide how far to push it.
### Q. Are Turkish foods spicy?
A.  Mostly no. Turkish cooking is seasoned, not hot. Cumin, sumac, mint, and paprika do most of the work, and the red pepper flakes that add real heat are often served on the side. Adana kebab and ezme are the two menu items with noticeable warmth, and even those land closer to a mild salsa than a hot wing. Urfa kebab is the no-heat version of adana. Want more fire? Ask for pul biber.
### Q. Is Turkish food similar to Greek food?
A.  Similar enough that you’ll recognize half the plates, since both spent centuries under the Ottoman Empire and share phyllo, eggplant, grilled lamb, stuffed grape leaves, and honey pastries. The differences sit in the seasoning. Greek food leans on oregano, lemon, olive oil, and feta. Turkish food leans on red pepper, sumac, cumin, and a lot more yogurt. Doner and gyro are cousins, and the two baklavas differ in nut and sweetness.
### Q. What is the etiquette for eating Turkish food?
A.  Tear the bread and use it to scoop meze and mop up kebab juices. Order meze for the whole table and share them. When tea arrives after the meal without being ordered, that’s a welcome, so accept it or decline once with thanks. Say afiyet olsun when food lands, or just smile when the cook says it to you. Lahmacun is rolled and eaten by hand. Tipping follows the usual St. Louis rules.

A.  Kahvalti is a spread of small plates: white cheese, olives, sliced tomato and cucumber, honey with clotted cream called kaymak, jam, eggs, and a basket of bread or simit. Hot dishes include menemen, eggs cooked slowly with tomato and pepper, and sucuk, a spiced beef sausage fried until crisp. Tea is poured the whole time. In the St. Louis metro it’s usually a weekend-only offering, so check the posted hours first.
### Q. Are gyros Turkish or Greek?
A.  Gyros are Greek, but they descend from Turkish doner. Doner is the older dish: stacked lamb or a lamb-beef blend roasted on a vertical spit and shaved thin, served over rice or in bread with tomato and onion. Greek cooks adapted it, often with pork at home and a pressed beef-lamb loaf in the United States, and wrapped it in pita with tzatziki. Order doner at a Turkish restaurant and you’re eating the original.
### Q. What is Turkey’s signature dish?
A.  Ask ten Turks and you’ll get ten answers, but kebab is the one most people land on, with doner and adana as the two forms known around the world. Iskender, doner over toasted pide with tomato sauce, browned butter, and yogurt, is the plate many consider the peak of it. Manti and baklava have their champions too. For a first visit in St. Louis, iskender or a mixed grill is the safest showcase.

## How to Eat Out as a Vegetarian in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-eat-out-as-a-vegetarian-in-st-louis
The soup landed on a corner table in Ste. Genevieve looking exactly right. Vegetable soup, the menu said. Carrots, celery, barley, a little dill on top. The woman who ordered it took one spoonful and stopped. Something in the broth tasted like a roast chicken. She asked. The server checked. Chicken stock, the whole pot, every day. Nobody had mentioned it because nobody had ever asked.
That’s the trap, and it’s the whole reason eating out as a vegetarian takes a little skill. The menu isn’t lying to you. It just isn’t telling you everything. Kitchens build dishes around habits, and stock, lard, anchovy, and fish sauce are habits so old that cooks forget they’re there.
Maybe you’ve been vegetarian for twenty years and you’re tired of the plate of sides. Maybe you gave up meat last Tuesday. Maybe your daughter came home from college eating no meat, and the family dinner in Lake St. Louis is Friday. This guide covers how to read any menu in St. Louis, what to ask, and which kitchens make it easy.
### What to eat out as a vegetarian in St. Louis?
Order a full plate, not a pile of sides. Indian, Ethiopian, Lebanese, Thai, Mexican, and Italian kitchens around St. Louis all carry real vegetarian mains. Anywhere else, ask three things: what the stock is, whether there is fish sauce or anchovy in the dish, and whether the kitchen can leave the meat out. Then order with confidence.
That’s the short version. The long one runs on a single idea: interview the kitchen. Ask what they do. Compare it with what you want. A good restaurant answers straight, and one that gets cagey about its stock has answered too.
### What vegetarian means at the table
In practice, vegetarian means no meat, no poultry, no fish, and nothing made from them. Eggs and dairy are in. That’s the lacto-ovo version, and it’s what most people mean by the word. But the term covers a spectrum, and where you land changes how you order. So tell the server which one you are, in plain words.
### Lacto-ovo, vegan, pescatarian, flexitarian
Lacto-ovo vegetarians eat eggs and dairy. Lacto vegetarians skip eggs. Ovo vegetarians skip dairy. Vegans skip all of it, plus honey and usually gelatin, and if that’s you, what vegan food actually means in St. Louis goes deeper. Pescatarians eat fish but no other meat. Flexitarians eat mostly plants and sometimes meat, on purpose. Say which one you are, because a careful kitchen hearing vegetarian might pull the cheese off your pasta.
### How to identify a vegetarian item?
Look for the V symbol first, read the description second, and ask the server third. The symbol is a shortlist, not a guarantee. Some kitchens mark a dish vegetarian because it has no visible meat, then build it on chicken stock. Others mark nothing and still have half a menu you can eat.
### Where the meat hides
In the base, not the topping. Vegetable soup on chicken stock. Refried beans made with lard. Caesar dressing, built on anchovy. Worcestershire, also anchovy, hiding in burger sauces. Fish sauce in Thai curries. Gelatin in panna cotta and marshmallows. Rice cooked in broth. Greens with a ham hock. None of it is listed as an ingredient. It’s just how the dish gets made. Which is why you ask.
### The cheese question
Parmigiano-Reggiano, Grana Padano, Pecorino Romano, and Gorgonzola are made with animal rennet by rule, an enzyme from a calf’s stomach. Some cheddars use it, some don’t, and the menu never says. Plenty of vegetarians eat these cheeses anyway. Plenty don’t. Decide before the pasta arrives, because a strict eater at an Italian table in Weldon Spring will want to ask about the grated cheese.
### The three questions
One: what’s the stock or broth made from? Two: is there fish sauce, anchovy, or Worcestershire in it? Three: can the kitchen make this without the meat, and what goes in its place? Ask in that order. The first catches soups, rice, and beans. The second catches sauces and dressings. The third turns a no into a yes.
### Are eggs considered vegetarian?
Yes, for most vegetarians. Eggs come from a living hen, and a lacto-ovo vegetarian eats them the same way they drink milk. Vegans don’t. Some vegetarians skip eggs on religious grounds, and a kitchen run by such a family may mark egg dishes separately. If the menu is unclear, ask.
Eggs matter at a restaurant because they open up so much of the menu. Frittata. Shakshuka. Egg fried rice. A veggie omelet at a diner in Pacific on a Sunday morning. Fresh pasta is often made with egg, and so are most baked goods, so say which list you’re on.
### Which cuisines make it easy around St. Louis?
Indian, Ethiopian, Lebanese and the wider Mediterranean, Thai, Mexican, Italian, and Vietnamese. In those kitchens a vegetarian main is a dish somebody’s grandmother made on purpose, not a meat dish with a hole in it. Start there when you’re new. Branch out once the three questions feel automatic.
### Indian and Ethiopian
Indian menus are the easiest in the metro, and it isn’t close. Whole sections are vegetarian by tradition: chana masala, palak paneer, dal, aloo gobi. Ghee is dairy, so it’s fine. Ask whether the naan has egg if that matters. Our guide to the best Indian food in St. Louis walks the menu. Ethiopian kitchens nearly always offer a veggie combo of lentils, split peas, and collards on injera.
### Mediterranean and Lebanese
Falafel, hummus, baba ghanoush, tabbouleh, fattoush, stuffed grape leaves, spinach pies. Order a mezze spread and dinner is done. Two things to check: whether the rice pilaf is cooked in chicken broth, and whether the grape leaves are the meat-filled kind.
### Thai and Vietnamese
Tofu versions of most stir-fries and curries exist, and Thai kitchens will usually swap it in. The catch is fish sauce. It goes into the curry paste, early. Ask whether the kitchen can use soy sauce instead. Many can. Some can’t, because the paste arrives premade. Our guide to the best Thai food in St. Louis has more. Vietnamese kitchens often list a tofu pho, but the broth may still be beef. Ask.
### Mexican and Italian
Beans are the question at a Mexican place. Refried beans are traditionally made with lard, and some kitchens still do it that way. Rice may be cooked in chicken stock. Once those are cleared, cheese enchiladas, bean burritos, and chiles rellenos are normal orders. Italian is generous with pasta and pizza, and a margherita is nearly always safe. Watch for pancetta in sauces, anchovy in puttanesca, and rennet in the hard cheeses.
Appetite for heights? Read what first-time skydiving costs and feels like.
### What should I order for dinner as a vegetarian?
Order one dish that stands on its own, with a protein in it, and refuse the row of sides. A real dinner has a center, a starch, and a vegetable. Center: beans, lentils, tofu, paneer, eggs, halloumi, a veggie patty. Starch: rice, bread, potato, pasta, polenta. Vegetable: whatever’s in season. Order that shape anywhere and it feels like dinner.
### At a steakhouse
Steakhouses are better than their reputation. The sides are the strongest part of the menu: creamed spinach, roasted mushrooms, baked potato, a wedge salad. Ask whether the mushrooms are cooked in beef fat and whether the mac and cheese has bacon in it. Then ask for a mushroom plate as an entree. A client dinner in Lake St. Louis doesn’t have to mean bread and a salad.
### At a BBQ joint
Harder. The meat is the menu. But the sides were built to carry it: slaw, potato salad, cornbread, mac and cheese. The beans are the trap, since pit-house beans almost always have pork in them, and the greens usually get a ham hock. Ask. Some pits now smoke a portobello or do a jackfruit sandwich. Otherwise, a loaded baked potato with slaw is honest food.
### At a sports bar
Veggie burger, black bean burger, cheese pizza, nachos, a big salad. Ask whether the bean patty shares the grill with the beef. Then order it with a fried egg on top. Suddenly it’s dinner.
### At a wedding
Tell the couple when you RSVP, or the caterer will hand you the stuffed pepper. Caterers plan a vegetarian plate for every event, and they plan it better with a count. If the invitation didn’t ask, text the host. At the reception, the pasta station and the salad course are usually safe.
### Is it less expensive to eat vegetarian?
At the grocery store, usually. Beans, lentils, rice, eggs, and seasonal vegetables cost less by weight than meat nearly everywhere. At a restaurant, not reliably. Kitchens price by the plate, not the ingredient, and a vegetable entree often sits right beside the chicken on the page. In our experience the gap narrows or vanishes in most St. Louis dining rooms.
Where you do save is in the cuisines above, because those kitchens built their prices around vegetarian dishes. At a steakhouse the vegetable plate is a courtesy, priced like one. We’ve found the best value comes from ordering what a kitchen makes best, not the cheapest line on the page.
### How to eat vegetarian for beginners?
Start in the cuisines that make it easy, learn the three questions, and get comfortable saying them out loud. The first month is about habits, not perfection. Order what you already like without the meat, find a protein you enjoy, and forgive yourself the tortilla soup that turned out to be on chicken stock.
### The first month
Week one: an Indian or Lebanese place, and order whatever you want. No questions needed. Week two: a Thai or Mexican kitchen, and practice the fish-sauce and lard questions. Week three: an ordinary American restaurant, and build a plate from the shape above. Week four: a family dinner where you’re the only one. By then the questions come out on their own.
### Protein, briefly
Every uncle at every cookout in Wood River is going to ask about protein. Short answer: beans, lentils, tofu, tempeh, eggs, dairy, nuts, and whole grains cover it, and one of those at the center of the plate covers a meal. Don’t turn it into a lecture. Don’t let anyone turn it into one for you, either. Order the dal. Eat the dal.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How to eat vegetarian for beginners?
A.  Start in kitchens where vegetarian mains are traditional: Indian, Lebanese, Ethiopian, Thai with tofu, Mexican with beans. Learn three questions and say them out loud until they feel normal: what’s the stock, is there fish sauce or anchovy, can you make it without the meat. Order dishes you already like, minus the meat, and put a protein at the center of the plate.
### Q. What are some good vegetarian dishes to eat at a restaurant?
A.  Chana masala, palak paneer, or dal with rice at an Indian place. A veggie combo on injera at an Ethiopian one. Falafel with hummus and tabbouleh at a Lebanese kitchen. Tofu green curry made without fish sauce at a Thai spot. Cheese enchiladas with lard-free beans at a Mexican restaurant. At an American grill, a black bean burger with a fried egg, or a mushroom plate built from the sides.
### Q. What should I order for dinner as a vegetarian?
A.  Order one dish with a protein at its center, a starch beside it, and a vegetable, and skip the plate of three sides. Beans, lentils, tofu, paneer, eggs, halloumi, or a veggie patty can be the center. If the menu has no vegetarian main, ask the kitchen to build one and be specific. Most St. Louis kitchens will make a mushroom plate or a vegetable pasta on request.
### Q. Are eggs considered vegetarian?
A.  Yes, for lacto-ovo vegetarians, which is most of them. Eggs are not meat, and no animal is killed to produce them, so they sit alongside milk and cheese in the standard definition. Vegans don’t eat eggs. Some vegetarians skip them for religious reasons, and kitchens run by those families may mark egg dishes separately. Say which kind you are, because eggs turn up in fresh pasta, baked goods, and fried rice.
### Q. What cheese can’t vegetarians eat?
A.  Cheeses made with animal rennet, an enzyme from a calf’s stomach, if you’re strict about it. Parmigiano-Reggiano, Grana Padano, Pecorino Romano, and Gorgonzola use animal rennet by rule, and traditional Manchego usually does too. Some cheddars use it and some don’t. Many cheeses now use microbial or plant rennet, and a label that says vegetarian rennet is safe. Decide where you stand, then ask about the grated cheese.
### Q. How to identify a vegetarian item?
A.  Look for the V symbol or leaf icon, then read the description for stock, broth, bacon, pancetta, anchovy, lard, gelatin, and fish sauce, then ask the server. The symbol is a shortlist, not a promise. Meat usually hides in the base of a dish rather than on top: soup stock, refried beans, Caesar dressing, Worcestershire, greens with a ham hock. One question about the stock clears most of it.
### Q. Is it less expensive to eat vegetarian?
A.  At the grocery store, usually yes, since beans, lentils, rice, eggs, and seasonal vegetables cost less than meat by weight. At a restaurant, not reliably. Kitchens price by the plate, and a vegetable entree often sits near the chicken on the menu. In our experience you save most in cuisines that treat vegetarian mains as normal food, and least at steakhouses, where the vegetable plate is a courtesy.
### Q. What is a flexitarian?
A.  A flexitarian eats mostly plants and sometimes meat, on purpose, without calling it a lapse. It’s a style rather than a rule, and it’s the easiest on-ramp for someone cutting back rather than quitting. At a restaurant a flexitarian can order the vegetarian main most nights and the burger when they want it. The three questions in this post still help, because the point is choosing, not guessing.

## What Venezuelan Food Is and What to Order in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-venezuelan-food-is-and-what-to-order-in-st-louis
The man at the counter in Shrewsbury asked for a beef taco. He pointed at a photo on the board, and the woman working the griddle didn’t correct him. She pulled a round of white corn off the heat, split it, packed it with shredded beef and black beans, and slid it across on a paper-lined plate. He picked it up. Looked at it. Then he asked what it was called, and she said arepa, and he said it back twice.
That’s a common first meeting with Venezuelan food in St. Louis. You walk in expecting something Mexican, and it isn’t. No tortilla. No cumin. No heat unless you ask for it. What you get instead is corn, beef, plantain, and a salty white cheese that never melts, and the whole plate leans salty and rich with a little sweetness around the edges.
This guide covers what the food tastes like, why an arepa isn’t a taco, what the national plate is, and what to order your first time at the counter. Just the food, and how to read a menu once you’re standing in front of one.
### What does Venezuelan food taste like?
Venezuelan food tastes mild, hearty, and a little sweet. Corn, beef, black beans, fresh white cheese, and plantain do most of the work. It is not chili-hot; heat comes from a hot sauce on the side, if you want it. Think griddled corn, slow-cooked shredded beef, and fried sweet plantain on one plate.
The country’s cooking comes from three places at once. The Caribbean coast gives it fish, coconut, and plantain. The Andes give it wheat, potatoes, and cool-weather stews. The llanos, the cattle plains, give it beef, and a lot of it. Corn ties all three together: precooked white corn flour, worked into a dough, then griddled or fried. Salt, garlic, onion, sweet pepper, and a touch of raw cane sugar handle most of the seasoning. Simple, and hard to get tired of.
### Why is an arepa not a taco?
An arepa is a thick corn cake, not a flatbread. The dough is precooked white corn flour and water, shaped into a puck, griddled until the outside crisps, then split like a pita and stuffed. A taco wraps a filling. An arepa holds it inside a crust. Different dough, different cooking, different bite.
There’s no direct English word for it. Corn cake comes closest. Griddle cake works too. Ask the counter and they’ll just say arepa, which is fair, because after one bite you won’t need a translation.
### The fillings on almost every board
Five names get you through any Venezuelan menu in St. Louis. Reina pepiada is shredded chicken folded with avocado and a little mayo, cool and rich against the hot corn. Carne mechada is shredded beef, cooked down with peppers and tomato until it’s soft and faintly sweet. Pabellón packs the national plate into one arepa: beef, black beans, plantain, cheese. Perico is scrambled eggs with tomato and onion, the breakfast standard. Domino is black beans and crumbled white cheese, named for the colors.
Eat it with your hands, like a sandwich, first bite from the open side so nothing slides out the back. If the kitchen offers guasacaca, a green avocado sauce, say yes. Hot sauce sits beside it. Optional. Nobody checks.
### What is the most popular Venezuelan dish?
Pabellón criollo is the national plate, and the arepa is the national food. Pabellón is shredded beef, black beans, white rice, and fried sweet plantain, laid out in four quarters on one dish, sometimes with a fried egg on top. Ask ten Venezuelans which matters more and you’ll get a lively argument.
The beef anchors it. It simmers until it falls apart, gets shredded, then cooks again with onion, garlic, tomato, and sweet pepper. A fried egg on top is called a caballo, on horseback, and it’s worth asking for. If you’ve had ropa vieja, you’ll recognize the family resemblance, though the Venezuelan version runs a shade sweeter. Our guide to where to find Cuban food in St. Louis makes a fair companion read.
### The Christmas plate
Hallaca is the dish Venezuelans miss most far from home, and December is the only month you’ll reliably find it. Corn dough colored with annatto, filled with a beef, pork, and chicken stew, dotted with olives, raisins, and capers, wrapped in banana leaf and boiled. A kitchen in Dardenne Prairie or Frontenac posting a hallaca preorder in late November is telling you who’s cooking.
### How is Venezuelan food different from Mexican food?
Venezuelan food has no tortilla, no cumin-and-chili seasoning, and no melted cheese. The corn shows up as a thick cake, the cheese is fresh and salty and crumbles instead of stretching, and sweet plantain lands on nearly every plate. Mexican food is built around the tortilla and dried chiles. Different countries, different pantries.
Mexican cooking runs on nixtamalized masa, dried chile pastes, cumin, oregano, and lime. Venezuelan cooking runs on precooked corn flour, beef, black beans, and raw cane sugar, and the heat lives in a bottle on the table. Mexican cheese melts. Venezuelan queso de mano and queso blanco stay firm and salty, closer to a young feta than to a jack. And plantain, a side dish in Mexico, is nearly a food group in Venezuela.
None of this makes one better. It just means the man in Shrewsbury was ordering from the wrong mental menu. If Mexican is what you actually want tonight, our local’s guide to the best Mexican food in St. Louis is the right page. Different craving, different door.
Weekend project bigger than dinner? See what a garage costs to build.
### What is Venezuelan street food?
Venezuelan street food is fried, handheld, and mostly corn: empanadas, tequeños, cachapas, patacones, and arepas from a cart or a window. Empanadas here are corn dough, not wheat, and they’re fried, not baked. All of it eats fine standing up.
### Tequeños and empanadas
Tequeños are the party food. A finger of salty white cheese, wrapped in thin wheat dough, fried until the outside blisters and the inside goes soft. Empanadas are the corn-dough turnovers, fried to a crackly shell and stuffed with shredded beef, chicken, cheese, or black beans and cheese together. Bite the corner first. Steam comes out. Then the rest.
### Cachapas and patacones
A cachapa is a pancake made from fresh sweet corn, griddled until the edges lace, then folded around queso de mano, a soft, stretchy, hand-pressed fresh cheese. Sweet corn, salty cheese, sometimes a slice of ham or pork. Patacones are twice-fried green plantain slices used as bread: two crisp rounds with beef, chicken, or cheese pressed between them. Messy in the best way.
### What is a typical breakfast in Venezuela?
Breakfast in Venezuela is an arepa with perico, which is scrambled eggs cooked with tomato, onion, and sweet pepper, or an arepa with butter and white cheese. Empanadas and cachitos, a ham-filled bread roll, fill in the rest. Coffee is small, strong, and milky. It’s a salty, corn-first morning, not a sweet one.
The cachito deserves a word. It’s a soft, slightly sweet crescent roll baked around chopped ham, and it’s the closest thing Venezuela has to a breakfast pastry. Around St. Louis, a kitchen that opens early enough for cachitos is usually frying empanadas by seven, and a Saturday drive from Swansea for a bag of both is a fine morning.
### What should you order first at a Venezuelan restaurant in St. Louis?
Order an arepa on your first visit, and make it a reina pepiada or a pabellón. One arepa is a full meal for most people. For a table of three or four, add a plate of pabellón criollo to share, a round of tequeños, and one cachapa, and you’ve covered the whole range in one sitting.
### If you’re eating alone
One arepa and one drink. That’s it. Reina pepiada if you want cool and rich, carne mechada if you want the beef, domino if you don’t eat meat. A second arepa is usually a mistake until you know your appetite.
### What to drink
Papelón con limón is raw cane sugar dissolved in water with lime, served cold, and it’s the drink that makes the most sense next to a fried empanada. Chicha here is a sweet rice drink, thick and cinnamon-scented, closer to dessert. Malta is a dark, non-alcoholic malt soda that Venezuelans either love or grew up loving. A marrón is a small espresso with milk, brown in color; a guayoyo is a lighter, drip-style black cup. Marrón after the meal, guayoyo with breakfast.
### Questions worth asking the counter
Ask anyone who runs a Venezuelan kitchen what they wish first-timers did, and the answer is usually the same: ask. Ask which filling they made this morning. Ask if there’s a daily plate that isn’t on the board. And ask how spicy the house sauce actually is, because the answer runs from mild to serious depending on who made it.
### Finding Venezuelan food around the St. Louis metro
Most Venezuelan food in the St. Louis area comes from small counters, food trucks, weekend pop-ups, and a handful of sit-down places, and they don’t cluster in one neighborhood. You might find an arepera behind a strip-mall door in Frontenac and a truck parked outside a brewery in Festus on the same weekend. The listing tells you which kind you’re walking into.
### The arepera counter
An arepera works like a sandwich shop. Menu board, order at the counter, pick a filling, wait a few minutes while it’s griddled, eat from a paper plate. Fast, casual, and the best format for a first visit, because nobody minds if you ask what everything is.
### The sit-down place
A sit-down Venezuelan restaurant adds the plates: pabellón criollo, asado negro, which is beef braised in a dark caramel-and-wine sauce until it’s sweet and falling apart, and quesillo, a flan with a caramel top. This is where you bring people. Check the posted hours, since many of these kitchens close between lunch and dinner. And if this kind of exploring suits you, our guide to what to order at a Peruvian restaurant in St. Louis is the natural next stop.
The arepa question has two answers — see what to order at a Colombian restaurant in St. Louis.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the most popular Venezuelan dish?
A.  Pabellón criollo is the national plate: shredded beef, black beans, white rice, and fried sweet plantain, sometimes topped with a fried egg. The arepa is the everyday food, eaten at breakfast, lunch, and late at night, split and stuffed with fillings like reina pepiada or carne mechada. Around St. Louis, arepas are easier to find, since a counter can griddle them fast, while pabellón usually shows up at sit-down places.
### Q. How is Venezuelan food different from Mexican food?
A.  Venezuelan food has no tortilla, no dried-chile heat, and no melted cheese. Corn arrives as a thick griddled cake, cheese is fresh and salty and crumbles rather than stretches, and sweet plantain sits on nearly every plate. Seasoning leans on onion, garlic, sweet pepper, and a little raw cane sugar instead of cumin and chile. Mexican cooking is built on masa, chiles, and lime. Different pantries, different plates.
### Q. What are arepas called in English?
A.  There is no direct English word. Corn cake is the closest, and most people just say arepa. It’s a puck of precooked white corn flour and water, griddled until the crust crisps, then split open and stuffed like a pocket. Calling it a corn sandwich gets the idea across at a counter in St. Louis. Calling it a taco does not, since there’s no tortilla involved at all.
### Q. What do arepas taste like?
A.  The arepa itself tastes like toasted corn: mildly sweet, a little salty, crisp on the outside and soft and steamy inside. The filling carries most of the flavor. Reina pepiada is cool and creamy from avocado and chicken, carne mechada is rich, slow-cooked shredded beef, and domino is earthy black beans with salty white cheese. A plain arepa with butter and cheese is the simplest way to taste the corn on its own.
### Q. What is Venezuelan street food?
A.  Fried corn-dough empanadas, tequeños, cachapas, patacones, and arepas from a window or cart. Empanadas are stuffed with beef, chicken, or cheese and fried to a crackly shell. Tequeños are fingers of white cheese wrapped in dough and fried. Cachapas are sweet corn pancakes folded over soft queso de mano. Patacones use twice-fried green plantain as bread. Everything is built to eat standing up, usually with guasacaca or hot sauce on the side.
### Q. What is a typical breakfast in Venezuela?
A.  An arepa with perico, which is eggs scrambled with tomato, onion, and sweet pepper, or an arepa with butter and fresh white cheese. Empanadas and cachitos, soft ham-filled crescent rolls from the bakery, are the other morning standards. Coffee is small and strong, either a milky marrón or a lighter black guayoyo. It’s a salty breakfast built on corn rather than a sweet one built on wheat.
### Q. What drink do they prefer in Venezuela?
A.  Papelón con limón, raw cane sugar dissolved in cold water with lime, is the everyday drink and the best match for fried food. Chicha, a thick, sweet rice drink with cinnamon, is closer to dessert in a cup. Malta is a dark, non-alcoholic malt soda that people either love or grew up loving. Coffee runs all day: a marrón is espresso with milk, a guayoyo is a lighter black cup.
### Q. What is Venezuelan comfort food?
A.  Pabellón criollo on a rainy night, an arepa with perico on a slow morning, and hallaca in December. Asado negro, beef braised in a dark, sweet caramel sauce until it falls apart, is the Sunday-dinner dish. Cachapas with queso de mano fill the sweet-and-salty craving. Ask a Venezuelan living in Festus or Frontenac what they miss most and hallaca usually wins, because it’s tied to family and Christmas.

## What a Good Wig Costs and How to Buy One in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-good-wig-costs-and-how-to-buy-one-in-st-louis
The fitting chair in the back room faced a mirror ringed with soft bulbs, and the woman from Imperial sat down with her coat still on. She’d driven forty minutes. The stylist set three wigs on the counter, one at a time, and said nothing about any of them. Just waited. The second one, a short brown bob with a lace front, went on and got tugged down over the ears. The woman in the chair went quiet. Then she laughed. That was the one.
Nobody tells you how ordinary that moment is. Wig shops around St. Louis see it every week: someone who has dreaded this for a month walks in braced for something clinical and walks out with a bag and a real smile. The dread usually comes from two unknowns. What will it cost? And how do I know I’m buying the right one? Both have honest answers, and neither requires a brand name.
So here are the price tiers in plain ranges, the case for a first fitting in person, what the cap types mean, how long each kind holds up, and the daily routine nobody warns you about. Men weighing a hair system get their own section. And if a diagnosis brought you here, there’s a note on insurance and the phrase cranial prosthesis near the end.
### How much does a good wig usually cost in St. Louis?
It varies widely by shop and hair type. A ready-to-wear synthetic wig usually runs a few hundred dollars. Heat-friendly synthetic costs a bit more. Human hair on a lace-front or hand-tied cap climbs well into four figures, and a custom cranial prosthesis sits at the top. Always ask what the price includes.
Those ranges hold across most shops in the region, but the spread inside each tier is wide. Two synthetic wigs can look identical on the stand and land in different brackets because one has a monofilament crown and the other doesn’t. Treat every tier as a starting point. Not a quote.
### Ready-to-wear synthetic
This is the entry tier and, for many first-time buyers, the right one. The fiber comes pre-styled, holds its shape after washing, and weighs very little. What you pay for is the cap and the fiber quality. Regular synthetic can’t take a curling iron, though. That’s the trade.
### Heat-friendly synthetic
A step up in price for one reason: the fiber tolerates low heat, so you can flat-iron or curl it within limits. It also frizzes a bit faster than regular synthetic and wants gentler care. Worth it if you like changing your look. Not worth it if you plan to wear the same cut daily and forget about it.
### Human hair and premium caps
Here the cost climbs well into four figures, and it climbs for two separate reasons that usually get lumped together. The hair is the first. Human hair takes color, takes heat, washes like your own, and costs real money to source. The cap is the second. Lace fronts, monofilament tops, and hand-tied caps each add hours of labor. Stack all of that on one piece and the number moves fast. Ask the shop which part of the price is hair and which is cap.
### Custom medical pieces
A custom cranial prosthesis, molded to your head and often built on a silicone or vacuum-fit base, sits at the top of the range. It’s made for people with total hair loss who need a secure fit without adhesive, and it’s priced like the medical device it is. That word, prosthesis, matters for insurance. More on that below.
### Ask what the price includes
Before you compare two prices, make them the same price. Some shops include a cut-in, where the stylist trims the piece on your head to frame your face, plus the first styling and a first cleaning. Others sell the piece off the stand and charge for each of those separately. Neither is wrong. But a bare price beside a bundled price tells you nothing until you ask.
### Is it better to buy a wig at a store or online?
For a first wig, a store, and it isn’t close. Online wins on selection and sometimes on price. A shop wins on everything a product photo can’t show: your actual cap size, where your hairline sits, how a color reads by a window instead of a ring light, and whether the piece stays put when you turn your head fast.
### Cap size and placement
Caps come in petite, average, and large, and most people guess wrong. A cap that’s a touch too big slides back through the afternoon. Too small and you’ve got a headache by lunch. A fitter measures, then adjusts the straps or ear tabs so the piece sits where your natural hairline would. That placement is the difference between hair that looks bought and hair that looks grown.
### The four-finger rule
Here’s the trick every fitter teaches, and it’s free. Lay four fingers flat across your forehead with your pinky resting on your eyebrows. The front edge of the wig, or the lace edge on a lace front, should land about where your index finger sits. That’s roughly where a natural hairline starts. Lower and the forehead disappears. Higher and it reads as a costume. Doing this once in a shop mirror with someone nudging your hand beats reading about it ten times.
### Color, light, and the first ten minutes
Screens lie about color. In a shop you can carry the piece to the front window, hold it against your skin, and find out whether that warm brown is really orange. Daylight is the test. The other thing you can’t download is the first ten minutes with the wig in your own hands. Front to back or back to front? Where do the ear tabs go? A fitter walks you through it twice, then makes you do it alone while they watch. Order online and you learn that part in a bathroom mirror, on the morning you needed it to go right.
### What type of wig is most natural looking?
A lace-front cap with a monofilament top, in human hair or a good heat-friendly synthetic, comes closest. The lace front gives you a hairline you can brush back from. The monofilament top lets you part the hair anywhere and shows what looks like scalp. Everything else is a trade between that realism and price, weight, and upkeep.
### Cap constructions, basic to full lace
Basic wefted caps are rows of hair sewn onto elastic strips. Cool, light, cheap, and the part is fixed. Monofilament tops add a sheer mesh panel at the crown where each hair is knotted by hand, so the part looks like skin. Lace fronts add a fine lace strip at the hairline, trimmed and worn against the forehead. Hand-tied caps knot every hair onto soft mesh, which moves the most naturally and weighs the least. Full lace takes that all the way around, so you can wear the hair up. Each step adds hand labor. That’s where the price comes from.
### Synthetic versus human hair
Synthetic holds a style through rain and a wash. Human hair does whatever your own hair does, including fall flat in August humidity. Synthetic is lighter, cheaper, and dries fast. Human hair takes heat, takes color, and lasts far longer with good care, and it costs more up front and more to keep up. There’s no wrong pick. There’s only a wrong pick for how you live. A nurse in Union working twelve-hour shifts wants a different piece than someone who styles every morning.
### How long does a wig usually last?
Roughly speaking, a regular synthetic wig worn daily holds up for several months before the fiber frizzes at the nape and the ends. Heat-friendly synthetic often goes a little less. Human hair worn daily, cared for well, can run a year or more. Rotate two pieces and every one of those windows stretches.
### What wears a wig out
Friction, mostly. The nape against a collar, the crown against a car headrest, the ends against a pillow if you sleep in it. Heat is next: hair dryers, oven doors, the steam off a dishwasher. Then product buildup that never gets washed out. Cut those three down and a piece lasts noticeably longer. Ignore them and even a top-tier human hair wig looks tired sooner than the price would suggest.
### Why fitters push a second piece
A wig worn three days a week ages far slower than you’d expect, because it gets more rest on the stand and fewer washes. So once you’ve found a first piece you love, the shop will probably suggest a second. That isn’t upselling. Two pieces in rotation cost more up front and less per month, and you’re never stuck the week one is drying.
Big move coming? See what a van rental costs in St. Louis.
### What are the drawbacks of wearing a wig?
Heat, itch, upkeep, and money, in about that order. A July afternoon under a full cap in St. Louis humidity is warm work. New wearers often feel an itch at the nape for the first couple of weeks. Every piece needs washing, and every piece wears out. And there’s a confidence curve nobody prices in.
### The confidence curve
The first week, you’re sure everyone can tell. The second week, you catch your reflection in a store window in St. Ann and forget for a second. Somewhere in the first month it becomes hair. Nobody warns you about this part, and it’s also the part that fixes itself. In our experience the people who get through it fastest wore the piece around the house for an evening before wearing it out anywhere.
### The daily routine
Most people take the wig off every night. Sleeping in one crushes the fiber and shortens its life. Set it on a wig stand so the cap keeps its shape and air moves through it. A soft sleeping cap helps if your scalp runs cold or sensitive. Wash a synthetic piece after a week or two of regular wear, human hair a bit more often if you use product, and use the shampoo made for it. Brush from the ends up. Never brush a wet synthetic. And if you need a stand, a wide-tooth comb, or a cap liner before your fitting, our guide to what to buy at St. Louis beauty supply stores covers that aisle.
### Toupees and hair systems for men
A hair system is a wig for the top of the head, and the pricing works differently. You pay once for the piece, which varies by base type. Lace bases breathe and look the most natural at the front. Thin skin bases are tougher and easier to clean. Hybrids split the difference. Then you pay again, on a schedule, for attachment and upkeep.
### Tape, glue, and re-bonding
Tape is faster, cleaner, and easier to remove at home, and it holds for days, sometimes longer depending on your skin. Liquid adhesive holds for weeks and is what most men settle on, but it takes more skill and a stronger remover. Every few weeks the system comes off, the scalp and base get cleaned, and it goes back on. Some men learn to do this at home. Many pay the shop. That visit, repeated all year, is often the true cost of a system, more than the piece itself. Ask for both numbers. And plan on replacing the piece on a rough yearly cycle, since the base thins with each cleaning.
### Showers, pools, and whether anyone can tell
A bonded system stays on in the shower and, with a strong adhesive, in the pool. Chlorine and salt shorten the bond, so rinse right after. As for the question every man asks: yes, people spot a bad system, and no, they don’t spot a good one. What gives it away is a hairline that’s too straight, too dark, or too low, and hair too thick for the man’s age. A careful fitter fixes all four, and the four-finger rule applies here just as much as it does to a lace-front wig. A well-fitted system is the one nobody notices. Including the guy across the counter at the hardware store in Glen Carbon who’s wearing one too.
### Insurance, cranial prostheses, and picking the shop
If your hair loss is medical, ask your doctor to write a prescription for a cranial prosthesis rather than a wig. Some health plans cover part of the cost with that wording and a diagnosis code. Some don’t. Call your insurer, ask the shop whether they’ve billed one before, and don’t assume either way.
### The medical route
Chemo, alopecia, and thyroid-related loss are the usual reasons a plan will even consider it. Ask about the claim process before you buy, because a shop that has done this before hands you an itemized receipt with the right words on it, and one that hasn’t may not. If you’re early in treatment and wondering when to raise the subject, our piece on what happens at a first oncologist appointment in St. Louis covers what to bring up with your care team.
### Interview two or three shops
Treat this like hiring someone. Shortlist two or three shops, call each one, and ask the same questions. What do you stock, synthetic or human hair or both? Do you cut in? Do you offer private fittings? Do you fit men’s systems? What’s included in the price? Then set the answers beside what you told yourself you wanted before you dialed. Want a private room, and a shop only fits on the sales floor? That gap is the signal. Want human hair, and a shop only stocks synthetic? Same. The shop that closes the most gaps wins, even if it’s a longer drive from Grafton.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it better to buy a wig at a store or online?
A.  For a first wig, a store. A fitter measures your cap size, sets the hairline with the four-finger rule, and lets you check the color by a window instead of a screen. You also learn to put it on with someone watching. Online makes sense for a second or third piece once you know your size, cap style, and color code from the first fitting.
### Q. What is the best first wig for a beginner?
A.  A ready-to-wear synthetic in a color close to your own, on a cap with at least a lace front or a monofilament part. It costs a few hundred dollars rather than four figures, holds its style after washing, and forgives mistakes while you learn. Keep the length at or above the shoulder. Long hair tangles more and shows wear faster, which is a hard way to start.
### Q. What type of wig is most natural looking?
A.  A lace-front cap with a monofilament top, in human hair or a quality heat-friendly synthetic. The lace front gives a hairline you can brush away from, and the monofilament crown lets you part the hair anywhere while showing what looks like scalp. Hand-tied and full lace caps go one step further in movement and weight. Every step up adds hand labor, and the price follows.
### Q. What is the four finger rule for wigs?
A.  Lay four fingers flat across your forehead with your pinky on your eyebrows. The front edge of the wig should sit about where your index finger lands, which is roughly where a natural hairline begins. Lower and the forehead vanishes. Higher and it reads as a costume. Fitters use it for lace-front wigs and men’s hair systems alike, and it’s the fastest way to check placement in a mirror.
### Q. How long does a wig usually last?
A.  A regular synthetic worn daily lasts several months before the fiber frizzes. Heat-friendly synthetic often runs a little shorter. Human hair worn daily and cared for well can go a year or more. Friction, heat, and product buildup are what wear a piece out, and rotating two wigs stretches every one of those windows because each gets more rest and fewer washes.
### Q. What are the drawbacks of wearing a wig?
A.  Heat in summer, itch at the nape during the first weeks, ongoing washing and upkeep, and the cost of replacing a piece as it wears. There’s also a confidence curve: the first week you’re sure everyone can tell, and by the end of the first month it’s just hair. Wearing the piece around the house for an evening before going out shortens that curve.
### Q. Do you take your wig off every night?
A.  Most people do. Sleeping in a wig crushes the fiber, tangles the ends against the pillow, and shortens its life. Set it on a stand overnight so the cap holds its shape, and wear a soft sleeping cap if your scalp runs cold or sensitive. A bonded men’s hair system is the exception: it stays on between maintenance visits, which is part of why that route costs more over a year.
### Q. Can you tell if someone is wearing a toupee?
A.  A bad one, yes. A good one, no. What gives a system away is a hairline that’s too straight, too dark, or too low on the forehead, and hair that’s too thick for the man’s age. A careful fitter fixes all four with the four-finger rule, a lighter density, and a slightly irregular front edge. The systems you notice are the badly fitted ones. The well-fitted ones walk right past you.

## How to Get Into Acting in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-get-into-acting-in-st-louis
The folding chair squeaked every time she shifted, and she shifted a lot. Page fourteen sat on her knee, and the woman running the audition in a church basement in Godfrey said, “Whenever you’re ready.” She managed a dental office. Forty-one. She had never read a line aloud to strangers. So she read it. Badly. Then the woman said, “Again, but annoyed at him,” and the second read came from a different person.
That second read is the whole trick, and nobody learns it on a couch. Getting into acting around St. Louis isn’t a mystery. It’s a run of small, slightly embarrassing steps most people never take because the first one feels too big.
Maybe you commute in from Cottleville and have Tuesday nights free. Maybe your teenager in Eureka won’t stop doing voices at dinner. Or maybe you’re past thirty and wondering if the window shut. It didn’t.
### How to get into acting for beginners in St. Louis?
Take one acting class, then audition for a community theater show and say yes to a student film. Get a plain, well-lit headshot and write a short résumé, even a thin one. Rehearse evenings around your day job. Most first roles around St. Louis are small, unpaid or stipend, and they lead to the next one.
### Step one: take a short class
Start small. A drop-in scene-study night or a beginner course that runs a few weeks teaches you to read a scene, take a note, and stop apologizing before every line. You’ll also meet the person who knows a director who needs a tired-looking dad next month. That hallway conversation, in our experience, matters as much as the lesson.
### Step two: audition for a community theater show
Community theaters post open calls listing the roles, the rehearsal dates, and what to prepare. Most want a short monologue or a cold read. Nobody expects polish. They expect you on time, having read the notice, taking direction without a debate. Ensemble parts are where nearly everyone starts, and the rehearsal calendar is built for people with jobs.
### Step three: say yes to a student film
University film programs around the metro need adults on camera every semester. Pay is usually a meal and a copy of the finished cut. Keep that copy. It becomes your first reel clip, and a reel is what a casting person watches before calling anyone in. Treat the student director like a real one.
### Step four: get a plain headshot
After two or three of the above, get a headshot. Plain background, simple light, your actual face, no heavy retouching. Pair it with a one-page résumé listing the shows and shorts you’ve done, your training, and real skills: languages, instruments, sports, a motorcycle license. Thin is fine. Blank is not.
### Is it worth it to take acting classes?
Yes, for reasons that have little to do with talent. A class teaches technique you can’t absorb from watching films. It gives you a group at the same stage who trade audition notices. And it puts you near the people who cast small local things. No single class is a ticket. Several add up.
### What a class teaches, and what it can’t
Breath and voice, so the back row hears you without a shout. Scene analysis, so you know what your character wants and what’s in the way. Listening, the hardest thing in the building. What a class won’t do is get you an agent or get you cast. Be suspicious of any studio that hints otherwise.
### How much do acting classes typically cost?
It depends on the format, and prices vary by studio, so ask what’s included before you pay. Drop-in scene-study nights cost the least per session. Multi-week courses cost more up front and less per hour. Private coaching costs the most per hour. Community-college and university continuing-ed classes often land in the middle and run on a semester clock.
### Drop-in nights versus multi-week courses
A drop-in night is the cheap way to find out if you even like this. A multi-week course asks for more money and more Tuesdays, and in return you get the same faces every week and a teacher who remembers you. Not sure yet? Start with the night.
### Private coaching and continuing education
Private coaching fits a specific problem: a self-tape due Friday, a monologue that keeps dying in the middle. Continuing-ed classes at community colleges and universities tend to be gentlest on price and most structured, and they draw exactly this kind of adult beginner. Ask any studio whether the fee covers script copies, a showcase, or recorded scenes you keep. Some do. Some don’t.
### Is 25 too late to start acting?
No. Twenty-five is early. So is thirty, and so is fifty. The local market around St. Louis casts real-looking adults of every age for commercials, industrials, and training videos, because a client wants a nurse who looks like a nurse. Kids and teens run on a separate track with youth programs of their own.
### Why local casting likes ordinary adults
A patient-intake video for a hospital does not want a twenty-two-year-old model. It wants a fifty-year-old from East St. Louis who reads as someone’s actual uncle. Industrials and local commercials hire that way constantly. Your age is a category, not a barrier, and the least crowded categories are often over forty.
### Kids, teens, and the parent question
Youth programs are a separate world with their own classes, showcases, and rules about parents in the room. A teenager should start with a school production and a summer youth intensive, not adult scene study. Parents, read the fine print and walk away from anything that charges for exposure.
Closing night? Here is what makes a pub different from a bar.
### What is the best way to find acting auditions?
Look in four places: community theater season announcements, university film program casting calls, local casting notices for commercials and background work, and regional casting websites that cover the St. Louis metro. Then build a simple self-tape setup at home, because more first-round auditions now happen on video before anyone meets you.
### Community theaters and open calls
Most community theaters publish a season months ahead and post an audition notice for each show a few weeks before rehearsals start. Sign up for the newsletters of three or four theaters and the notices come to you. Our guide to how to see live theater and performing arts in St. Louis is a decent map.
### Student films, commercials, and background work
Film programs and local indie filmmakers post calls on department boards and social media groups, and they need adults far more than students. Casting notices for commercials, industrials, and background work show up on regional casting websites. Background work teaches how a set runs.
Agencies come later. A talent agency submits you for bigger commercial and corporate jobs, and it wants a headshot, a résumé, and footage first. That’s its own post: St. Louis talent agencies and how to get signed.
### A self-tape setup that works
Phone on a tripod at eye level, horizontal. A plain wall behind you. One light in front, a window works, none behind. Frame from mid-chest to just above your head. Someone off camera reads the other lines in a flat voice. Slate your name and the role if the notice asks.
### What happens at a first audition?
You sign in, hand over a headshot and résumé, wait, then read. The read is usually sides, a page or two from the script, or a monologue you prepared. Sometimes both. The director may give you one adjustment and ask for it again. Then you say thank you and leave.
### Sides, cold reads, and the monologue
Sides sent ahead should be close to memorized. A cold read means you see the page for the first time, and nobody expects fluency. They want to see if you make a choice. The monologue should be contemporary, about a minute, from a real play. Skip the famous speeches. Everyone brings those.
### What to bring
A headshot with your résumé stapled to the back. A pencil. Your calendar, because they’ll ask about conflicts and a vague answer costs you the part. Clothes that suggest the role without being a costume. And a second copy of everything.
### Is acting a well paid job?
For most beginners around St. Louis, no, not at first. Community theater is unpaid or pays a small stipend. Student films pay in food and footage. Local commercials, industrials, and background work do pay, and those rates depend on the job, the usage, and whether it’s a union booking.
### Union and non-union, plainly
SAG-AFTRA is the union for screen and voice work, and joining it is a milestone most beginners are years away from. Almost everyone starts non-union, where nearly all local community theater, student film, and small commercial work lives. Always ask about usage, meaning where and how long the piece runs, since that changes the rate.
### The day job and the rehearsal calendar
Community theater rehearses evenings and weekends because the cast has jobs. Expect several nights a week for a month or more, then a run of performances. Commercials shoot on weekdays, which is the first real tension with a day job and the reason many local actors keep flexible or shift work. Nobody in Augusta quits a job for a first ensemble role.
### What a business pays for when it hires a local actor
Hiring a local actor for a company video? You’re paying a day rate that depends on shoot length and where the video will run. A social clip that lives a month costs less than a training video that runs for years. Ask what the rate includes. Our guide to what video production costs in St. Louis covers the rest of that budget.
### How to choose a class, a coach, or a theater around the metro
Treat it like hiring someone, because you are. Shortlist two or three studios or coaches. Ask each what a single session looks like. Ask who else takes the class: their ages, their experience, whether any of them work locally. Then compare the answers to what you want. Same logic for theaters: see a show first, then audition for the one that feels like a room worth a month of Tuesdays.
