### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it worth it to take acting classes?
A.  Yes, if you pick the right kind. A beginner class teaches breath, scene analysis, and how to take a note, and it puts you beside people who trade audition notices. It won’t get you cast or signed, and any studio hinting otherwise is selling the hint. Take one short course, see if you still want this, and decide on more from there.
### Q. How much do acting classes typically cost?
A.  Prices vary by studio and format, so ask what’s included before paying. Drop-in scene-study nights cost the least per evening. Multi-week beginner courses cost more up front but less per hour. Private coaching is the most expensive per hour. Community-college and university continuing-ed classes usually sit in the middle. Ask whether scripts, showcases, or recorded scenes are part of the fee.
### Q. Is 25 too late to start acting?
A.  No. Twenty-five is early, and so is thirty-five. Local commercials, industrials, and training videos around St. Louis cast real-looking adults of every age, because clients want a nurse who looks like a nurse. Community theater welcomes adult beginners every season. Start with a short class and an open call this year rather than waiting for a better moment. The better moment doesn’t come.
### Q. What’s the best age to start acting?
A.  Whatever age you are now. Kids and teens have their own youth programs, school productions, and summer intensives, and that’s the right track for them. Adults start well at twenty-five, forty, or sixty because the local market needs ordinary-looking people in every bracket. What matters more than age is showing up on time, taking a note, and saying yes to small roles early.
### Q. What is the best way to find acting auditions?
A.  Watch four channels: community theater season announcements, university film program casting calls, local notices for commercials and background work, and regional casting websites that cover the St. Louis metro. Sign up for theater newsletters so notices come to you. Then set up a simple self-tape corner at home, since many first rounds now happen on video before anyone meets you in person.
### Q. How can I get auditions for acting?
A.  Show up to open calls with a headshot, a short résumé, and a one-minute contemporary monologue. Say yes to student films, since they hand you footage for a reel. Tell your class that you’re looking, because word of mouth fills many small local roles. Once you have a reel and a few credits, an agency can submit you for the bigger commercial jobs.
### Q. Is acting a well paid job?
A.  Not at the start, and rarely as a sole income locally. Community theater is unpaid or pays a small stipend, and student films pay in food and footage. Commercials, industrials, and background work do pay, with rates that depend on the job, the usage, and union status. Most St. Louis actors keep a day job or flexible work and build slowly.
### Q. How much does it cost to hire an actor?
A.  It depends on the shoot length and the usage, meaning where the finished video runs and for how long. A short social clip costs less than a training video a company will use for years. Union bookings follow set scales; non-union actors quote their own day rate. Ask each actor what the rate includes, and get the usage terms in writing before the shoot.

## What African Food Is and What to Order in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-african-food-is-and-what-to-order-in-st-louis
The tray came out the size of a bicycle wheel, covered edge to edge with a pale, spongy bread, and nothing on it had a fork beside it. Five small mounds of stew sat on top, each a different color. A man at the next table tore off a strip, pinched up a bite of red lentil, and ate it in one motion without looking down. That was the whole lesson, delivered in about two seconds.
People who have never ordered from an African menu freeze at the same spot. The menu runs long, half the words are unfamiliar, and there is no obvious place to start. Nobody wants to point at a word and guess wrong in front of the table. So they order the one dish with the word chicken in it and leave without meeting the food.
Africa is a continent, not a cuisine. The menus around St. Louis split along real lines, and those lines matter: Ethiopian and Eritrean, West African, Somali and East African, North African. They eat differently. Different breads, different heat, different rules about hands. Here is what sits on each of those menus, what it tastes like, and how to get through a first meal without guessing.
### What to order at an African restaurant in St. Louis?
Order a combination platter. At an Ethiopian table that means injera with several wot stews and vegetable sides, shared from one tray. At a West African counter, start with jollof rice, grilled tilapia or suya, and a swallow like fufu on the side. Ask the server which stew is mildest.
The combination exists because kitchens know you cannot pick. On an Ethiopian menu it might be called a combination, a sampler, or a platter for two, and it is the single best first order in this whole category. You get four to eight things at once. You find out what you like by eating it, not by reading about it.
### The one sentence that works at any counter
Say this: “It’s my first time here, I eat mild, what would you put in front of me?” That’s it. The person taking your order has answered that question a hundred times and almost always answers it well. They will steer you toward the dish the kitchen is proudest of, which is usually also the one that travels best to a new palate.
### What not to do on a first visit
Don’t order four separate entrees for four people. African menus in this metro are built around sharing, and four solo plates cost more and taste like less. Don’t ask for a fork before you have looked at the table. And don’t skip the side salad or the collards, since the cool, sharp stuff is what makes the rich stuff work.
### What is Ethiopian and Eritrean food?
Ethiopian and Eritrean cooking is built on injera, a wide sour flatbread, and wot, the slow-simmered stews you spoon on top of it. You eat with your right hand, tearing bread and scooping. The cuisines are close cousins with overlapping dishes and some real differences, and a St. Louis kitchen may cook either tradition or both.
### Injera, and why it tastes like that
Injera is made from teff, a tiny grain, and the batter ferments for days before it hits the griddle. That fermentation gives it a distinct sour tang, closer to sourdough than to any flour tortilla. The surface is covered in little holes that grab sauce. First bite alone, it can taste strange. With a spoonful of spiced lentils on it, the whole thing clicks.
### Wot, tibs, and kitfo
Wot is the stew family. Doro wot is chicken simmered long in berbere, a red spice blend, usually served with a hard-boiled egg sitting in the sauce. Misir wot is red lentils, and it is the dish most beginners fall for. Tibs are cubes of beef or lamb sauteed hot with onion, jalapeño, and rosemary, served sizzling and often milder than the stews.
Kitfo is the one to know about before you order it. It’s minced raw beef warmed in spiced butter with mitmita, a hot chili blend. Many people love it. If raw beef is not your thing, ask for it leb leb, which means lightly cooked, and nobody will blink.
### The fasting combination, which happens to be vegan
Ethiopian Orthodox fasting days exclude animal products, so nearly every Ethiopian kitchen keeps a full vegetable lineup ready. The veggie combination usually brings red lentils, yellow split peas, cabbage and carrot, collards, beets, and a salad, all on one tray. It is one of the most satisfying vegan meals in the city and it isn’t marketed as vegan anywhere on the menu.
Meatless? Read how to eat out as a vegetarian in St. Louis.
For where to actually go, our local guide to the best Ethiopian food in St. Louis covers the rooms themselves. This post is about the menu; that one is about the address.
### What does West African food taste like?
West African cooking runs on tomato, onion, chili, palm oil, ground nuts, and smoked or dried fish. Think deep, savory, a little oily in the good way, with heat that varies by cook. Nigerian, Ghanaian, Senegalese, Liberian, and Ivorian kitchens all sit in this family, and their staples overlap while their names differ.
### Jollof rice and grilled tilapia
Jollof is rice cooked in a tomato and pepper base until the grains take on the color and the flavor. Smoky, savory, mildly spicy, and beloved to the point of ongoing argument between Nigeria and Ghana about who does it right. Order it with grilled tilapia, a whole fish scored and charred, and you have the most approachable plate in the entire category.
### Egusi, okra, and the soups
Egusi is a thick soup built from ground melon seeds, and it eats almost like a savory, nutty stew with bitter greens and meat or fish worked through it. Okra soup is deliberately slippery, which surprises people the first time. Peanut, or groundnut, stew is rich and slightly sweet, and it is the easiest of the three for a new palate.
A note on the word soup. On a West African menu, soup means a thick sauce you eat with a starch, not something you sip from a bowl with a spoon. Order a soup and you should order a swallow to go with it.
### Fufu and the swallow foods
Swallow is the category name for the soft, dense starches you pull apart by hand and use as an edible utensil. Fufu made from cassava or plantain, pounded yam, eba from cassava flour, amala from yam flour, semolina. They are mild by design, because their job is to carry the soup. Pinch off a piece, dent it with your thumb, dip, and swallow without chewing much.
### Suya, the gateway dish
If one West African dish converts skeptics, it’s suya. Thin strips of beef are coated in yaji, a dry rub heavy on ground peanut, ginger, and chili, then grilled over open flame and served with raw onion and more of the rub on the side. Smoky. Nutty. Hot in a warm, spreading way rather than a sharp one. Order it as a starter and watch the table go quiet.
### What is on a Somali or East African menu?
Somali food shows its Indian Ocean history in every dish: rice cooked with cardamom, cumin, and cinnamon, goat and lamb over anything else, and a bright green chili sauce on the side. It is warmly spiced and rarely fiery. Utensils are normal here, though many people still eat rice by hand.
### Sambusa, bariis, and goat
Sambusa is the triangular fried pastry, usually stuffed with spiced ground beef or lentils, and it arrives hot enough to burn the roof of your mouth. Bariis iskukaris is the signature rice, tinted gold, perfumed with xawaash spice, often studded with raisins. Goat or lamb shank comes alongside, slow-cooked to falling apart, with a banana on the plate.
Yes, a banana. You slice it and eat it with the rice, and the sweetness against the spiced meat makes complete sense after two bites. Basbaas, the green chili and cilantro sauce, is where the heat lives. Add it yourself, a little at a time.
### What is North African food?
North African cooking, from Morocco, Tunisia, Algeria, and Egypt, leans on couscous, slow tagine braises, preserved lemon, olives, cumin, cinnamon, and harissa chili paste. It reads as the most familiar of the four families to an American palate, largely because it shares a Mediterranean shelf with food most people already eat.
### Couscous, tagine, and harissa
Couscous is tiny steamed semolina pasta, light and fluffy, and it usually arrives under a pile of stewed vegetables and meat with broth to pour over. Tagine names both the cone-shaped clay pot and what cooks inside it: lamb with prunes, chicken with preserved lemon and olives, beef with apricot. Sweet and savory sit in the same bowl on purpose, and it works.
Harissa is the heat, a paste of roasted chili, garlic, and caraway. It typically comes on the side rather than in the dish, which means you control the burn entirely. Egyptian menus bring their own staples, like koshari, a carb stack of rice, lentils, and macaroni under tomato sauce and fried onion.
### Is African food spicy?
Some of it, not most of it. Ethiopian berbere stews carry real heat, West African pepper soup and some jollof can run hot, and Somali basbaas will light you up if you pour it on. Plenty of dishes are barely spiced at all. The heat is usually on the side, not baked in.
### Where the heat actually hides
Hot: doro wot, kitfo with mitmita, pepper soup, anything described as pepper anything. Medium: jollof, suya, egusi, tibs. Mild: alicha stews, the yellow split peas, peanut stew, bariis, couscous, most tagines, fufu itself. A kitchen will almost always dial a dish down if you ask before it’s cooked. Ask when you order, not when it lands.
### The palate coolers on the table
Injera absorbs heat. So does plain rice, fufu, and the side salad with its sharp dressing. Ethiopian kitchens pour honey wine, and a lot of West African spots keep malt drinks and hibiscus coolers, both of which do more for a burning mouth than water does. Water just spreads it around.
### How do you eat with your hands?
Right hand only, no utensils, and the bread or swallow does the work. On injera, tear a strip from the edge, use it to pinch up stew without your fingers touching the food, and eat it in one bite. With fufu, pinch a small ball, press a dent, scoop soup, and swallow it mostly whole.
### The mechanics nobody explains
Tear with your fingertips, not your whole fist. Keep the food off your palm. Work from the section of the tray nearest you rather than reaching across somebody. The bread under the stews gets soaked through by the end of the meal and turns into the best part, so don’t leave it. Most places bring a warm towel or point you to the sink first.
### Gursha, and what a shared platter means
A shared platter means one tray, no individual plates, everyone eating from the same surface. It feels odd for exactly one minute. Gursha is the Ethiopian custom of feeding a bite to someone else at the table by hand, an act of affection between people who know each other. Nobody expects a first-timer to do it. Nobody minds if you do.
### How to pick your first African meal around St. Louis
Shortlist two or three places instead of researching one to death. The metro’s African kitchens sit in pockets: some along the South Grand corridor, others north and west through Jennings, Ferguson, Hazelwood, and Overland, with a few scattered toward Rock Hill. Pick two that are close enough to try on a weeknight without it becoming a project.
Then go in and ask plainly. Tell them it’s your first time, say how you handle heat, and ask what they would put in front of you. Compare that answer against what actually arrives. The gap between the two, or the absence of one, tells you more about a kitchen than any list ever will.
### Timing, groups, and the practical stuff
Some dishes cook to order and take a while, doro wot especially. Go when you have an hour. Bring at least two people so you can order a combination and split it. A shared platter for two usually lands in the same range as a mid-priced sit-down dinner, though that varies by kitchen, so look at the menu before you sit.
If you want to walk a block and compare several cuisines at once, our guide to where to eat on South Grand maps that stretch.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What does African food taste like?
A.  It depends on the region, because there is no single flavor. Ethiopian food tastes tangy and warmly spiced from berbere and fermented injera. West African food is deep and savory with tomato, chili, peanut, and smoked fish. Somali food is fragrant with cardamom and cumin. North African food leans sweet-savory with cinnamon, preserved lemon, and olives.
### Q. What is the most common African food?
A.  There isn’t one dish for a continent, but a few show up on menus everywhere in this metro. Jollof rice appears on nearly every West African menu. Injera with wot anchors every Ethiopian and Eritrean table. Starchy staples run through all of it: rice, cassava, yam, plantain, millet, and maize in some form at almost every meal.
### Q. Is African food healthy to eat?
A.  Much of it is, especially the vegetable-heavy plates. The Ethiopian fasting combination is legumes and greens with no animal products at all. Teff, the grain in injera, is naturally gluten-free, though some kitchens blend in wheat flour, so ask. Fried items, palm oil stews, and big starch portions are the heavier end. Balance the tray.
### Q. What does fufu mean in Africa?
A.  Fufu names a soft, stretchy dough made by pounding a boiled starch, usually cassava, plantain, yam, or a blend of them. It belongs to the swallow family, meaning foods you pinch by hand and use to scoop soup. The word travels across West and Central Africa, and the exact starch and texture shift country by country.
### Q. What are some basic Ethiopian foods for a beginner?
A.  Start with misir wot, the red lentil stew, and tibs, sauteed cubes of beef or lamb that tend to run milder. Add the yellow split peas and the collards for balance. Doro wot is the famous chicken dish and it carries more heat. Order all of it as a combination platter so you taste the lineup at once.
### Q. How to properly eat Ethiopian food?
A.  Wash your hands, skip the utensils, and use your right hand. Tear a strip of injera from the rolled pieces on the side, pinch up a bite of stew so your fingers stay off the food, and eat it in one motion. Work from the part of the tray in front of you. Eat the soaked base bread last.
### Q. What is injera called in English?
A.  English has no separate name for it, so injera stays injera on every menu. Descriptions usually call it a sour flatbread, a spongy pancake, or a fermented teff bread. None of those are quite right. It is closer to a soft, tangy crepe with a honeycomb surface that exists to hold sauce.
### Q. What do Ethiopians eat with injera?
A.  Wot stews, mostly. Red lentils, yellow split peas, chicken in berbere, beef or lamb tibs, collard greens, spiced cabbage and carrot, beets, and fresh cheese all get spooned onto the bread. A tomato or green salad usually rides along. On fasting days the whole tray goes vegetable, and rolled extra injera arrives on the side for scooping.

## How to Get to the St. Louis Airport and What It Costs
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-get-to-the-st-louis-airport-and-what-it-costs
The alarm went at 4:10. By 4:40 he was standing at the end of a driveway in Fenton with a duffel on one shoulder, refreshing a rideshare app and watching the estimate climb every time the screen redrew. Six-ten departure. He had budgeted in his head for what a ride costs on a Tuesday afternoon, and this was not a Tuesday afternoon.
That gap is the whole subject here. What a trip to St. Louis Lambert International costs in your imagination and what it costs at 4:40 in the morning are two different numbers, and only the second one hits your card. There are six realistic ways to reach STL. They price out very differently depending on when you fly, how many people are going with you, and how long a car would sit if you drove yourself.
No single answer wins for everybody. The arithmetic does, and you can run it in about ninety seconds.
### What is the cheapest way to get to the St. Louis airport?
For one person, MetroLink is almost always cheapest. The Red Line runs to both airport stations on a flat single-ride fare published by Metro Transit, so the price is the same whether you board downtown or three stops out. A shared-ride shuttle is usually next. Rideshare and taxi cost the most.
### Why the pricing model matters more than the price
Each option charges on a different axis, and the axis decides who it suits. MetroLink charges per person, flat. A shared shuttle charges per seat. Rideshare and taxi charge for the vehicle, so the cost splits across everyone riding in it. Parking charges per day, which means it keeps growing while you sit on a beach doing nothing. Match the axis to your trip and the cheapest option names itself.
### Where cheap stops being cheap
Cheapest on paper is not always cheapest in practice. A flat rail fare stops feeling like a bargain when you have two large suitcases, a car seat, and a five-year-old at 4:30 in the morning. A per-seat shuttle gets expensive fast once your party hits three or four, because you pay four times. And a rideshare fare that looked outrageous for one traveler can land cheaper per head than anything else when four of you split it. Divide before you judge.
### How does MetroLink actually get you to STL?
The Red Line serves the airport directly, with stations at the main terminal and at Lambert East, so you walk off a platform and into the terminal instead of transferring to a bus. Metro Transit publishes the fare, the route map, and the first and last trains of the day. Those three facts are worth checking before you commit to the train.
### Where to get on
You can board downtown, at stations along the line, or at a park-ride lot where you leave the car behind. That last version is the one most locals never think of, and it changes the math completely, since you end up paying a rail fare instead of a daily parking rate. Check whether overnight parking is permitted at the specific lot first. Rules differ station to station, and a week is a long time to guess.
### What the train is good at, and what it is not
Trains are good at predictable. No surge pricing, no driver cancelling on you at 4:15, no white-knuckle traffic on the inbound stretch. What a train is bad at is frequency in the small hours. Service thins out early and late, so a 5:50am flight can easily fall outside the window when trains run often enough to be useful. Compare the first train of the day against your leave time. If those two do not line up, the train is simply off the table that morning, however cheap it looks.
### Bags, and the honest version
One roller bag and a backpack? Easy. Two checked bags, a stroller, and a toddler who has opinions? The train stops being pleasant long before it stops being cheapest. In our experience, people overestimate how much a transfer bothers them and badly underestimate how much they hate hauling luggage up a wet platform ramp in the dark. Be honest about which trip you are actually taking.
### Is a shared-ride shuttle worth it for your group?
A shared-ride shuttle charges per seat, which makes it strong for one traveler and weak for four. Solo, you pay one seat and share the van with strangers. A family of four pays four seats for a vehicle they are nearly filling on their own. That single fact settles most shuttle-versus-rideshare arguments before anybody opens an app.
### The per-seat break point
Run it like this. Take the shuttle’s per-seat rate, multiply by heads, and set that beside one rideshare or taxi fare for the same trip at the same hour. Somewhere between two and three passengers, the vehicle-priced option usually takes over. Exactly where depends on the hour and how far out you live. A solo traveler leaving St. Peters and a family of four leaving Arnold are running two completely different sums with the same two choices in front of them.
### Hotel shuttles and the park-sleep-fly angle
Staying near the airport the night before an early flight? Ask whether the hotel runs its own shuttle and what time the first run leaves. Some do it free for guests, some charge, some go on request only. The park-sleep-fly package, where a hotel in the Bridgeton area lets you leave the car for the length of your trip, quietly competes with airport parking. Ask how many nights the parking allowance actually covers.
### Are they reliable?
Mostly, with a caveat you control. A shared shuttle runs a route with other passengers on it, so it quotes a pickup window rather than an exact minute. That is not unreliability. That is the product working as designed. Real problems come from booking too late, giving a vague address, or letting the phone ring when the driver is at the curb. Confirm the day before. Then answer the phone.
Killing time? Here is how to get into acting in St. Louis.
### When does rideshare or a taxi make more sense?
Rideshare wins on door-to-door speed and on splitting one fare across a full car. Its price is dynamic, set by demand, hour, distance, and how many drivers happen to be online, which is why the same trip costs noticeably different amounts on a Sunday night and a Wednesday at noon. Taxis price on their own terms, so ask the dispatcher before you ride — what a taxi costs in St. Louis walks through the meter.
### What actually drives the number
Four things, mostly. Distance from your door to the terminal. Time of day, since 4:30am and Friday at 5pm are the two thin-supply windows. Live demand right then, which is the surge part everybody complains about. And the airport access fee a platform may add on pickup or dropoff. Three of those are out of your hands. The fourth you handle by knowing it exists and reading the receipt.
### Where the car meets you
Dropping off at departures is simple enough. Getting picked up is where people go wrong, because rideshare pickup at STL is routed to designated zones instead of the curb outside baggage claim. Follow the signs in the app and the ones overhead in the terminal, not your memory of last year. Zones move.
### Should you park at the airport or pay for a ride?
This one is pure arithmetic, and trip length is the variable that decides it. Parking is a per-day charge that compounds for every night you are gone. A ride is a one-time charge in each direction. Multiply the daily rate by your nights, compare that against two rides, and watch the longer trip punish the parking lot.
### Run the break-even
Daily rate times days equals your parking cost. Ride out plus ride back equals your alternative. If parking costs more, get a ride. A weekend trip often favors driving yourself. A twelve-day trip almost never does. For most travelers the tipping point sits somewhere in the four-to-six-day range, though yours moves with your daily rate and your distance from the airport, so use your own numbers rather than anybody else’s. Lot options and current rates live in our guide to where to park at St. Louis Lambert Airport.
### The costs that never show up on a receipt
Parking carries quiet costs. Fuel in both directions. The lot shuttle from an economy space to the terminal, which eats time at both ends of the trip. And the small misery of landing at 11pm, exhausted, hunting for row F with a dead phone. Rides carry quiet costs too, chief among them the 4:15am cancellation with nobody else online to take the job. Neither option is frictionless. They just offer different friction.
### How early should you leave for a 5am flight?
Work backward from the door of the plane, not from the departure time on your ticket. Boarding closes well before pushback, bag drop cutoffs land earlier than most travelers expect, and the security line at STL has a pre-dawn rush of its own. Airlines publish recommended arrival windows for domestic and international travel. Start with theirs, then add your ride.
### The backward math
Begin at your flight time. Subtract the arrival window your airline recommends. Subtract realistic travel time to the terminal, then add a cushion for the thing that goes sideways. The result is your leave time. Subtract again if you are checking a bag, parking in an economy lot and riding a lot shuttle, or traveling with anyone who moves slower than you do. That last one is not an insult. It is a schedule.
### What changes at 5am
Everything tightens. Trains may not be running frequently enough yet. Fewer rideshare drivers are online, so wait times stretch and fares firm up. Shuttle companies fill their earliest runs first, which is why a 3:30am pickup slot vanishes days before the 9am one does. Ticket counters and checkpoints also open at set times, and arriving before the checkpoint opens buys you nothing but a cold bench and a long stare at the departures board. An early flight is a booking problem more than a driving problem. Solve it the week before.
### If somebody is dropping you off
The friend-with-a-car option is free and genuinely the best one whenever it exists. Give them the real leave time, not the polite one. Tell them your airline and your terminal, because STL has two and they are a drive apart, not a walk. Departures is for dropping off, so a long goodbye at the curb earns you a wave from an officer. Send the flight number too, so they can check for a delay before either alarm goes off. Somebody driving in from Valley Park deserves that courtesy.
### How do you choose a shuttle or car service worth calling?
Shortlist two or three and interview them. Call, say plainly what you need, then listen for the gap between what you asked for and what they are prepared to provide. That gap is the signal. Not the quote.
### What to say on the call
Give them your pickup address, your flight time, your head count, your bag count, and the pickup window you want. Then ask what they will commit to. Do they hold a window or a specific time? What happens if the return flight is delayed by three hours? Do they track flights at all? Can four people and four checked bags go in one vehicle, or does that become two runs? Ask what a cancellation costs you, and ask before you need to know.
### What the answers tell you
A service that says “we will get you there” and offers no pickup window has told you something useful. So has the one that asks your airline and terminal before you volunteer it. You are not really testing price. You are testing whether they have done this at 4am on a Tuesday with a stranger who was already anxious. For the wider picture on moving around the region, our guide to getting around St. Louis by rides, shuttles, and MetroLink covers the rest of it.
### Tipping
Tip the driver who handles your bags. Cash is easiest. For a shuttle or car service the convention sits close to what you would tip a taxi driver, with a little more when someone hauls heavy luggage, waits while you sort out a gate change, or runs a pickup in freezing rain. If the operator already adds a gratuity, the receipt will say so. Read it before you pay twice.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is there public transportation that takes you to STL Lambert Airport?
A.  Yes. The MetroLink Red Line serves the airport directly, with stations at the main terminal and at Lambert East, so you walk from the platform into the building. Metro Transit publishes the fare and the schedule, including the first and last trains of the day. Bus routes connect to the line as well. Check the early-morning and late-night timetable before you rely on it.
### Q. Are airport shuttles reliable?
A.  Generally, with one caveat. Shared-ride shuttles carry several passengers along a route, so they quote a pickup window rather than an exact minute. Most trouble traces back to late bookings, wrong addresses, or an unanswered phone at the curb. Confirm the day before, be outside when the window opens, and pick up when the driver calls. Reliability is a shared job.
### Q. How often do shuttles run at St. Louis airport?
A.  It depends on the operator and the hour. Hotel shuttles serving properties near the airport tend to run loops during the day and far less often overnight, sometimes on request only. Shared-ride services to the wider metro run around booked pickups rather than a fixed timetable. Call the specific operator and ask what their schedule looks like on your travel date.
### Q. How early should you get to the St. Louis airport?
A.  Start with your airline’s published arrival recommendation, which differs for domestic and international flights, then add your travel time plus a cushion. ### Q. How much is an Uber from St. Louis Airport to downtown?
A.  There is no fixed fare. Rideshare pricing is dynamic, driven by distance, hour, live demand, driver supply, and any airport access fee the platform adds. The same ride can cost noticeably different amounts at 7am Monday and 11pm Saturday. Open the app and pull a quote for your actual pickup time. That estimate is the only number worth planning around.
### Q. Is an airport shuttle cheaper than a taxi?
A.  Often for one traveler, rarely for four. A shared-ride shuttle charges per seat, so the cost multiplies with your party size. A taxi charges for the vehicle, so the cost splits. Solo, the shuttle usually wins. With three or four people and luggage, run both numbers for your specific trip and hour before assuming anything.
### Q. Do I tip shuttle drivers?
A.  Yes, unless the service already adds a gratuity. Cash is simplest. Tip more when the driver loads and unloads heavy bags, waits while you sort out a delay, or works a pickup in the dark and the ice. Check the receipt or booking confirmation first, since some operators include a service charge and you do not need to pay it twice.
### Q. How early should I book an airport shuttle?
A.  Book as soon as you have a flight number, and treat pre-dawn pickups as urgent. The earliest slots fill first, because every 6am departure wants the same window. A few days ahead usually works for a midday trip. A week or more is safer for holidays, early mornings, and groups large enough to need two vehicles. Confirm the pickup window the day before you travel.

## What It Costs to Build an App in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-it-costs-to-build-an-app-in-st-louis
The printout had been folded and unfolded so many times the crease went soft. Two quotes. Same one-page idea, same rough sketch of four screens on the back, and the two numbers weren’t in the same universe. One shop replied in three days with a flat figure. The other took two weeks, asked eleven questions, and only then put a number on paper.
Neither of them was lying to her.
That’s the part most owners don’t see coming. An app isn’t a product you price the way you price a van wrap or a new sign. It’s a stack of decisions, and every decision moves the number, sometimes a little and sometimes by a multiple. The shop that asked eleven questions was pricing her app. The shop that answered in three days was pricing an app it had already built for somebody else, hoping hers was close enough.
Learn the levers first. Then the quotes stop looking random.
### What does it cost to build an app in St. Louis?
There isn’t one price, and any shop that gives you one before asking about logins, payments, and who maintains it is guessing. Cost tracks a handful of decisions: how many platforms you build for, whether users need accounts, whether you need a server behind the app, and how long you plan to keep it alive.
### Why the same idea produces two different numbers
A quote is a bet on scope. If your page says “customers can book a slot and pay,” one developer reads that as a form and an email notification. Another reads the same sentence as user accounts, a calendar that knows each employee’s availability, card processing, receipts, cancellation rules, and a dashboard where you see tomorrow’s bookings at a glance. One sentence, two products, two honest prices.
The cheap quote isn’t automatically the dishonest one. Sometimes it comes from a developer who plans to build the smallest version that actually works, which may be exactly what you should buy. And the expensive quote often includes things you genuinely need but never thought about, like what happens when a customer loses their phone and wants their account back. You can’t judge either number until you can name what’s inside it.
### Do you need an app, or do you need a good mobile website?
Most local businesses need the website. Ask that question out loud before you spend a dollar. An app only lives on a phone after somebody chooses to install it, keeps it through a storage cleanup, and opens it again next month. A mobile website works the second a person taps a link in search results.
### The install problem is the whole problem
Count the apps you’ve installed this year that weren’t from a company you deal with constantly. A bank. An airline. The grocery chain you visit every week. Now think about how often a customer visits your business. Three times a year? They will not keep your app on their phone. They’ll search your name, tap the first result, and expect a page that loads fast and shows a phone number.
A dentist in Des Peres doesn’t need an app. Neither does a boutique in Brentwood or a landscaper working Ladue and Town and Country. What all three need is a site that loads in a couple of seconds on a phone with two bars, with hours, directions, and a way to book without a phone call. Smaller bill, bigger return. Our breakdown of small business website cost walks through that path and what moves the price on it.
### When an app really is the right call
Real cases exist. You need something a browser can’t do well: dependable push notifications, camera or barcode scanning as a core function, Bluetooth hardware, genuine offline use in a warehouse or a basement. Or your customers use the thing daily and a home-screen icon earns its place. Or the app itself is the product you plan to sell, which is a different business than the one you run today.
Everything else, start with the site. You can add an app later, and most of the plumbing the site needs, the booking logic, the customer database, the payment setup, is the same plumbing the app would have required anyway. Nothing gets wasted.
### Which features move the price the most?
Nine levers do most of the damage: how many platforms you ship to, user accounts, a server and database behind the app, payments, push notifications, maps and location, offline mode, admin tools, and connections to software you already run. Each one adds work. A few of them double it.
### One build or two? Native, cross-platform, or web
Native means two separate builds, one for iPhone and one for Android, written in different languages by people with different skills. Best performance, highest cost, two things to maintain forever. Cross-platform means one codebase that produces both apps, which usually costs meaningfully less and covers what most local businesses need. A mobile web app is a website that behaves like an app, no store approval, no install, cheapest of the three. Ask any developer which of the three they’re quoting, because a quote that doesn’t say is not comparable to one that does.
### Accounts, a backend, and a database
Here’s where budgets quietly double. An app with no login and no saved data is a brochure that lives on a phone, and it’s cheap. The moment users create accounts, you need a server, a database, password resets, security on stored personal information, and a plan for the day somebody tries to break in. That’s a second system, built and hosted and watched. It doesn’t show up on your four sketched screens, but you’re paying for it.
### Payments, push, maps, and offline
Taking money in the app means a payment processor, refund handling, failed-card handling, and the receipts nobody remembers to ask for. Push notifications need a service behind them and rules about what gets sent to whom. Maps and location bring usage costs from the map provider, which land on you monthly, not once. Offline mode is the sleeper: making an app work with no signal and then sync correctly when the signal returns is some of the hardest work in the build.
### The admin side nobody sketches
Someone on your staff has to see the orders, cancel a booking, fix a typo in a listing, and turn off a user who’s abusing the thing. That’s an admin dashboard, and it is effectively a second application you’re commissioning. Same for integrations. Connecting to your point-of-sale, your scheduling software, or your accounting system depends entirely on whether those vendors offer a clean way in. When they don’t, the workaround costs more than the feature.
### What is the second bill nobody warns you about?
Building the app is the first bill. The second one arrives every year and never stops: developer accounts with Apple and Google, hosting for your server and database, map and messaging usage, and the maintenance that keeps the app working as phones change underneath it.
### Store accounts and hosting
Publishing to the App Store requires an Apple Developer account, billed annually. Publishing to Google Play requires a Google Play Console account with a one-time registration charge. Fees change, so check Apple’s developer site and Google’s Play Console pages for current amounts rather than trusting any number in a blog post, including this one. Hosting is separate and monthly, and it scales with use. Ten users cost almost nothing. Ten thousand cost real money.
### The maintenance treadmill
Apple and Google ship new operating systems every year, and both stores raise the minimum requirements an app must meet to stay listed. An app left alone doesn’t sit still. It rots. Features break on new phones, and eventually the stores stop accepting updates to it and pull it from search. Budget for someone to keep it current, every year, for as long as you want it to exist. Owners who skip this line item are the ones who pay twice, because a rebuild from scratch costs more than upkeep ever would have.
### What belongs in version one?
One thing. Version one should do a single job better than your customers can get it done any other way, and nothing else. A shipped app that does one thing beats a full build that never launches, and the second outcome is far more common than anyone in this industry likes to admit.
### The one-thing test
Write down every feature you want. Then circle the one that, if it vanished, would make the whole app pointless. That circled item is version one. Everything else waits for real users to ask for it, and a good chunk of what you listed will turn out to be something nobody wanted. Better to find that out before you’ve paid to build it.
Staging also protects you from the worst version of this story: money spent, nothing launched, no way to tell whether the idea had legs. Ship the small thing. Watch what people actually do with it. Let the next round of work get funded by evidence instead of enthusiasm. And remember that launching is not the finish line, because getting anyone to install it is its own job, closer to digital marketing for small business than to engineering.
Screen fatigue? Here’s what a good wig costs in St. Louis.
### Should you build it yourself or hire someone?
Four paths, four sets of trade-offs: a no-code builder, AI-assisted coding, a freelancer, or a shop. The honest way to choose is to ask two questions about each one. Who owns the code when you’re done? And who answers the phone when the app stops taking payments at eleven at night?
### No-code builders
No-code platforms let you assemble an app from prebuilt blocks with a monthly subscription and no developer. For a simple loyalty card, a menu, or an events list, they work, and they work fast. The catch is ownership. Your app lives inside their system, it does what their blocks allow, and if the company folds or triples its pricing, you have very little you can carry somewhere else. Read the export terms before you build anything on one.
### AI-assisted coding
AI tools can write working code, and a technically curious owner can get a prototype running over a weekend. Genuinely useful for testing an idea. Much harder is everything after: security, payment handling, store submission, and the fact that when something breaks you’re debugging code you didn’t write and don’t fully understand. Fine for a demo you show three people. Risky for anything holding customer data.
### Freelancer, local shop, or offshore
A freelancer costs less and often does excellent work. One person, though, is also one point of failure: one vacation, one illness, one better offer. A local shop in Richmond Heights or anywhere else around St. Louis costs more and gives you a team, a contract, and somebody you can sit across a table from. Offshore teams quote the lowest numbers and can be strong, but the time-zone gap turns a five-minute question into a next-day answer, and specification gaps get expensive fast when nobody can just walk over and ask.
### Who owns the code, and who you call at eleven at night
Settle both in writing before work starts. The contract should say you own the source code outright, and that the store accounts are registered in your business name, not the developer’s. Get access to the code repository while the project is live rather than at the end. Then ask what support after launch looks like, in plain words: what hours, what response time, what it costs monthly, and what counts as a bug they fix free versus new work they bill for.
### How do you interview a developer?
Shortlist two or three and interview them the way you’d interview a surgeon before agreeing to an operation. You’re not collecting paperwork. You’re trying to find out how each one thinks, what they’ve shipped, and whether they’ll tell you something you don’t want to hear.
State plainly what you want. What the app must do on day one. Who owns the code. What happens when it breaks on a Saturday. Who maintains it next year and the year after. Say all of it before anyone quotes, so every quote answers the same brief.
Then compare what you asked for against what each developer is prepared to deliver. The gap is the signal, not the price. A developer who says your idea should be a website, or that version one should lose half its features, has just told you something valuable about how they’ll behave when the project gets hard. Ask to see two apps they built that are still live in the stores today, and open them on your own phone. Ask who did the work, whether that person is still there, and what they would cut if your budget dropped by a third. Someone with a real answer to that last question is worth talking to twice.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much does it cost to set up an app?
A.  Setup splits into two buckets. The build itself, priced from scope, and the running costs that start the day you publish: an annual Apple Developer account, a one-time Google Play registration, hosting for any server behind the app, and usage charges from services like maps. Check Apple’s and Google’s developer pages for current fees, since both change without much warning.
### Q. Can I build my own app for free?
A.  You can build and test one for free using free tiers of no-code platforms and open development tools. Publishing it is where free ends. Both app stores charge for a developer account before your app can appear, and anything storing customer data needs paid hosting. Free gets you a working prototype to show people. It rarely gets you a live product.
### Q. Is it cheaper to build an app yourself?
A.  Cheaper in cash, expensive in hours. Building it yourself on a no-code platform or with AI help means you pay a subscription instead of a developer, and you pay with every evening for months. The real question is what your time is worth and what happens when it breaks during business hours. Many owners build version one themselves, then hire out once it matters.
### Q. What is the cheapest way to develop an app?
A.  Build a mobile web app instead of a native one, or skip the app and improve your website. No store approval, no annual developer account, one codebase for every phone. If you do need an app, the cheapest honest route is one cross-platform build of a single feature, shipped, then expanded only when users ask for more.
### Q. What are the 7 stages of app development?
A.  Most shops work through roughly seven: defining the idea and scope, researching whether people want it, designing screens and wireframes, building the app and any server behind it, testing on real devices, submitting to the stores and launching, then maintaining it as phones and operating systems change. That last stage never ends, and it’s the one owners forget to budget for.
### Q. How can I hire someone to develop a mobile app?
A.  Write one page describing what the app must do on day one. Shortlist two or three developers, local or otherwise, and interview each one against that page. Ask for two live apps you can open on your phone. Settle code ownership, store account registration, and after-launch support in writing before any work starts.
### Q. How much does it cost to hire a mobile app developer?
A.  Rates vary enormously by experience, location, and by whether the job goes to one person or a team, and most developers quote a project fee rather than an hourly rate for defined work. Freelancers sit lowest, local shops higher, offshore teams lowest of all on paper. Bring the same written brief to each and compare what they’ll deliver for it.
### Q. Is it hard to build my own app?
A.  A simple app with no accounts and no payments? Genuinely doable for a determined non-developer using a no-code builder. Add user logins, card processing, or anything storing personal information, and difficulty climbs sharply, because those pieces carry security and legal weight. Build the simple version yourself to test the idea. Hire out anything that touches customer money or data.

## What Armenian Food Is and What to Order in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-armenian-food-is-and-what-to-order-in-st-louis
A guy at the counter had his lahmajun folded like a taco, two hands, parsley sliding out the bottom onto the paper. The woman at the register watched for about three seconds. Then she came around, pulled a fresh one off the tray, laid a stripe of parsley down the middle, squeezed a lemon wedge over the whole thing, and rolled it into a tight cigar. Handed it back without a word.
He ate it in four bites. Then ordered two more.
That is how most first Armenian meals go. One dish, eaten slightly wrong, corrected by somebody who has been eating it since they were five. The menu itself isn’t difficult. It just uses words you haven’t seen before, and nothing on the board tells you which ones are bread, which ones are meat, and which one is a porridge that took eight hours to make.
So here’s the whole plate, in plain terms.
### What to order at an Armenian restaurant in St. Louis?
Start with lahmajun, the thin meat-topped flatbread you roll around parsley and a squeeze of lemon. Add manti, tiny dumplings under garlic yogurt, and a skewer of khorovats. Order a yogurt-cucumber dip, lavash, and an eetch or bulgur salad. Share everything. Finish with tea and something apricot.
### The three-dish first order
Two people, first visit, no idea what anything is? Get one lahmajun each, one order of manti, and one skewer of grilled lamb or chicken. That covers the three things Armenian kitchens are actually known for: thin savory flatbread, dumplings under yogurt, and fire-cooked meat. Add a cucumber-yogurt dip so the table has something cool on it.
### What to add when there are four of you
Four people changes the math. Now you can order sideways instead of stacking mains. Add a plate of basturma or soujouk to start, a bowl of eetch, a few stuffed grape leaves, and a basket of lavash that everybody tears at. Order one thing nobody recognizes. That’s the point of going.
### What are the building blocks of Armenian cooking?
Bulgur instead of rice, lamb and beef over poultry, yogurt and cheese in nearly every course, apricot and pomegranate carrying the sweet-sour note, dried herbs rather than fistfuls of fresh ones, and spice that is aromatic instead of hot. Learn those six things and about eighty percent of any Armenian menu stops being a guessing game.
### Bulgur, not rice
Bulgur is cracked wheat that’s been parboiled and dried, and it is the grain underneath an enormous amount of this cooking. It shows up as pilaf beside a skewer. Ground fine, it becomes the shell of a stuffed kufta. Coarse, it becomes salad. Rice exists on Armenian tables, sure, but it plays backup. If you’ve eaten mostly Persian or Indian food, that inversion is the first real surprise.
### Yogurt, cheese, and the sour note
Yogurt is a sauce, a soup base, a marinade, and a drink. Thinned with water and salted, it becomes tahn, which arrives cold and tastes strange for four sips and then tastes correct forever. Cheese sits on the breakfast table and inside the pastry. The sourness in a dish rarely comes from vinegar. It comes from pomegranate molasses, from dried apricots simmered with lamb, from sumac dusted over onions, from a lemon wedge on the side.
### Spice that smells loud and tastes gentle
Allspice, cumin, coriander, paprika, sumac, black pepper, dried mint. That’s the working shelf. The smell coming off a grill can be enormous while the food itself carries almost no chile heat. Heat, when a kitchen wants it, arrives on the side as a red pepper paste you spoon on yourself. Nobody is trying to hurt you.
### How is Armenian food different from Greek, Turkish, Lebanese, and Persian menus?
The overlap is real, and the differences are specific. Armenian cooking leans on bulgur where Greek leans on rice and phyllo. It uses dried herbs and allspice where Lebanese uses raw parsley, lemon, and garlic. It shares dish after dish with Turkish kitchens under different names. And it almost never reaches for the saffron and long-grain rice a Persian menu is built around.
### Against a Greek menu
Greek cooking runs on olive oil, lemon, oregano, and dill, with feta and phyllo doing heavy lifting. Armenian runs on butter or lamb fat as often as oil, with dried mint where the Greek kitchen reaches for dill, and bulgur where the Greek kitchen reaches for orzo or rice. Both grill meat on skewers. The Greek version is usually seasoned with oregano and lemon; khorovats gets onion, black pepper, and smoke, and the lemon shows up later. Tzatziki and Armenian jajik are cousins. One tastes of dill, the other of mint and garlic.
### Against a Turkish menu
This is where the confusion is thickest, because the dishes are often the same dishes. Lahmajun and lahmacun. Manti and mantı. Soujouk and sucuk. Basturma and pastırma. Dolma on both tables. What differs is proportion and finish: Armenian manti tend to be tiny boat shapes baked until the edges crisp, then drowned in garlic yogurt, while the Turkish version is more often boiled and dressed with butter and pepper. Armenian lahmajun usually tastes more of allspice and parsley than of pepper paste. If you want the other side of that comparison in detail, we wrote what Turkish food is and what to order in St. Louis so this post doesn’t have to re-explain it.
### Against a Lebanese menu
Lebanese menus are mezze-first, lemon-forward, and green. Tabbouleh there is a parsley salad with a little bulgur in it. The Armenian equivalent, eetch, flips that ratio completely: it’s bulgur bound with tomato and pepper paste, onion, and olive oil, with parsley as a garnish rather than the body. Kibbeh and kufta come from the same idea, a bulgur shell around spiced meat, but the Armenian seasoning tilts toward allspice and cumin while Lebanese seven-spice brings cinnamon and clove forward. Hummus appears on both. It isn’t the tell.
### Against a Persian menu
Persian cooking builds outward from rice. Long grain, steamed, saffron-stained, with a crust at the bottom of the pot that people argue over. Fruit does show up in both cuisines, but Persian stews use dried lime, barberry, and pomegranate in slow herb-heavy braises, while Armenian kitchens tend to pair apricot with lamb and call it done. Skewered meat is the shared ancestor. Persian kabab often takes a saffron-and-onion marinade; khorovats is plainer, hotter over the coals, and served piled on lavash that soaks up the drippings.
### The short version
Bulgur plus dairy plus dried herb plus apricot-or-pomegranate sourness equals Armenian. Rice plus saffron equals Persian. Olive oil plus lemon plus oregano equals Greek. Raw parsley plus garlic plus lemon equals Lebanese. Same dish under a different name, usually, equals Turkish. That’s rough, and any grandmother would argue with it, but it gets you to the right order.
### Which Armenian dishes should you know by name?
Ten names cover most menus: lahmajun, manti, khorovats, kufta, dolma, sarma, basturma, soujouk, eetch, and lavash. Learn those and you can read a board in Ellisville or Manchester without pointing. Everything else is a variation, a regional spelling, or a dessert built on apricot and walnut.
### Lahmajun
A paper-thin round of dough smeared with finely ground lamb or beef, tomato, onion, pepper, and parsley, then blasted in a very hot oven for a couple of minutes. It is not pizza. There’s no cheese and the meat layer is thinner than a business card. You eat it by piling on fresh parsley, squeezing lemon over it, and rolling it up. Two is a snack. Four is lunch.
### Manti and the kufta family
Manti are tiny open dumplings, each about the size of a thumbnail, filled with spiced meat and baked until the exposed edges go brown and crunchy. Then garlic yogurt goes over the top and sometimes a ladle of broth, which softens half of each dumpling and leaves the rest crisp. That contrast is the entire dish.
Kufta, also written kyufta, is a shape-shifter. Harpoot kufta is a thin bulgur shell wrapped around seasoned meat and onion, boiled and served in its broth. Chi kufta is raw, pounded fine with bulgur and pepper paste, eaten cold with lettuce leaves. Losh is a flat grilled patty. Same word, four different experiences. Ask which one the kitchen makes.
### Khorovats and the cured meats
Khorovats means grilled over wood or coals: lamb, pork, chicken, and thick rounds of eggplant, tomato, and pepper cooked alongside. The vegetables often get peeled and chopped together into a smoky side. Order it and a pile of lavash arrives underneath, which is not decoration. That bread is the plate.
Basturma is air-dried beef, pressed and coated in a fenugreek-heavy paste, sliced thin enough to see light through. It is intense and a little garlicky and stays with you. Soujouk is a firm, dry, spiced sausage, cooked rather than eaten raw. Both are cured meats. Neither is subtle.
### Dolma, sarma, eetch, and lavash
Dolma broadly means stuffed: peppers, eggplant, tomatoes, hollowed out and packed with meat and bulgur or rice. Sarma means wrapped, most often grape leaves rolled around the same kind of filling, served warm with yogurt or cold with olive oil and lemon. Eetch is the bulgur salad described earlier, and it travels well, which is why it shows up at every gathering. Lavash is the soft, thin, blistered flatbread that comes free and disappears first.
### Why do two completely different foods get called harissa?
Because two unrelated words landed on the same spelling in English. Armenian harissa is a thick, pale porridge of cracked wheat and shredded chicken or lamb, stirred for hours until it goes stringy and smooth, then finished with melted butter and cumin. North African harissa is a fiery red chile paste. Nothing about them is related.
The confusion is common enough that servers expect the question. If you order harissa at an Armenian table and someone brings a bowl of something beige, that is correct. It’s comfort food, cooked for holidays and for people recovering from illness, and it carries real weight in Armenian memory. Eat it with a spoon and a little salt.
Unrelated, but a reader asked: what massage school costs in Missouri.
### What does an Armenian breakfast look like?
Cold, savory, and spread across the table rather than plated. White cheese, olives, sliced cucumber and tomato, butter, apricot or sour cherry jam, hard-boiled or fried eggs, torn lavash, and hot black tea in small glasses. Bread does the work a fork would do elsewhere.
### Soujouk and eggs
The one hot dish worth naming: slices of soujouk fried in a pan until the fat renders orange, then eggs cracked straight in and cooked in that fat. It arrives in the skillet. You tear lavash and drag it through. If a place serves breakfast at all, ask for this.
### Why the tea matters
Tea isn’t an afterthought at the end. It runs alongside the whole meal, poured strong and cut with hot water to taste, refilled without asking. Coffee comes later, small and thick, usually after something sweet. Rushing either one reads as odd.
### How does the table work, and how do you order a first meal?
Everything goes to the middle. Armenian tables are shared by default, so ordering one entree each and guarding it will leave you with less food and a confused server. Order fewer mains than there are people, more small plates than feels reasonable, and let the bread circulate.
### A first order that always works
Say it plainly at the counter or the table: you haven’t eaten this food before, there are two of you, and you want them to pick. Almost every kitchen will do it, and most enjoy being asked. If you’d rather drive yourself, do this: one flatbread, one yogurt dish, one grilled thing, one cold salad, bread on the side.
### Pacing
Cold plates land first, then hot small plates, then grilled meat, then tea, then dessert nobody thinks they want and everybody finishes. Don’t order dessert in advance. Something apricot or walnut-based will turn up on a cart or in a case near the register, and you’ll see it before you need to decide.
### What can you order if you don’t eat meat?
More than the menu suggests. Armenian cooking has a deep meatless tradition tied to fasting periods, so lentils, bulgur, beans, and vegetables aren’t an afterthought. Ask for the vospov dishes, the stuffed vegetables made without meat, and the grilled eggplant. You’ll eat well.
### Dishes to ask for by name
Vospov kufta is a lentil-and-bulgur patty, no meat at all, served cold with lemon. Eetch is meatless. Many sarma are rolled with rice, herbs, and olive oil rather than lamb, and they’re served cold. Grilled eggplant and pepper, mashed together with garlic, is standard alongside khorovats and stands alone fine. Hummus and yogurt dips fill the gaps.
### The one question to ask
Ask whether the stuffed vegetables were made with meat today. Same dish, same name, two versions, and it changes by the day depending on what the kitchen cooked. Vegans should also ask about butter, which finds its way into pilaf and pastry quietly.
### How to shortlist a place around the metro
Pick two or three places worth trying, go in, and say plainly what you want: lahmajun, manti, a skewer, something cold. Then compare that against what they actually put in front of you. The gap is the signal. A kitchen that hands you tight, crisp-edged lahmajun and tiny hand-pinched manti is doing the slow work. A kitchen that swaps in a thick crust and oversized dumplings is doing something else, which might still be good, just not the thing you asked for.
Bakeries and counters matter as much as sit-down rooms here, since lahmajun and lavash travel. Somebody in Oakville or Sunset Hills might drive out, buy a dozen flatbreads, and freeze half. That’s a normal Saturday. If you’re circling the south side generally, our guide to where to eat on South Grand maps the wider international stretch worth walking.
