### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is Armenian food like Greek food?
A.  They share grilled skewers, stuffed grape leaves, and yogurt dips, so the family resemblance is obvious. The seasoning isn’t the same. Greek cooking leans on olive oil, lemon, oregano, and dill with feta and phyllo; Armenian leans on bulgur, dried mint, allspice, cumin, and a sour note from pomegranate or apricot rather than lemon alone.
### Q. What is Armenian food similar to?
A.  Turkish food most of all, since many dishes are literally the same under different spellings, including lahmajun, manti, dolma, soujouk, and basturma. It overlaps with Lebanese cooking through kibbeh, hummus, and bulgur salads, and with Georgian and Persian cooking through grilled meat and fruit-and-lamb pairings. The bulgur-and-yogurt base is what keeps it distinct.
### Q. What do Armenians eat for breakfast?
A.  A cold spread, mostly: white cheese, olives, cucumber and tomato, butter, apricot or sour cherry jam, hard-boiled or fried eggs, and torn lavash, with strong black tea alongside. The classic hot option is soujouk and eggs, sausage slices fried until the fat renders, then eggs cracked into the same pan and brought out in it.
### Q. What is the most famous Armenian dish?
A.  Lahmajun is the one most outsiders meet first, and khorovats is the one most Armenians would name for a gathering. Harissa, the slow-cooked wheat-and-chicken porridge, carries the deepest cultural weight but rarely appears on a menu. If you want the single dish that defines a restaurant’s skill, order the manti and watch the edges.
### Q. How do you eat lahmajun?
A.  Lay fresh parsley across the meat side, squeeze a lemon wedge over it, then roll the whole round into a tight tube and eat it end to end with your hands. Some people add sliced onion, tomato, or a thin smear of pepper paste first. Don’t fold it like a taco. It falls apart.
### Q. What is lahmacun called in English?
A.  There’s no real English name, so menus usually write Armenian pizza or Turkish pizza, and both descriptions mislead. The Arabic root means meat with dough. There’s no cheese, no sauce in the pizza sense, and the meat layer is spread paper-thin across a cracker-thin round. Ordering it by the actual name works everywhere.
### Q. What goes well with lahmajun?
A.  Parsley and lemon go inside, always. Around it, put a yogurt-cucumber dip, sliced raw onion dusted with sumac, olives, pickled vegetables, and a cold glass of tahn, the salted yogurt drink. Hot tea works too. A bulgur salad like eetch rounds out the table without competing, since both lean on the same spice shelf.
### Q. What are some classic Armenian recipes?
A.  Lahmajun, manti under garlic yogurt, khorovats skewers with grilled eggplant and pepper, harissa porridge, harpoot kufta in broth, chi kufta eaten raw and cold, dolma and sarma, eetch, vospov kufta made from lentils, and lavash baked against the wall of a hot oven. Apricot and walnut carry most of the desserts.

## What Army Navy Surplus Stores Sell in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-army-navy-surplus-stores-sell-in-st-louis
The rack is metal, overloaded, and it squeaks when you shove a hanger down it. Third jacket in: olive, four pockets, a hood rolled into the collar. You fold the collar back and hold the label up toward the fluorescent tube, because the print is gray on gray and the store lighting is not on your side. There it is. Or there it isn’t. That one strip of cloth decides most of what you need to know about the coat in your hands.
Here’s what nobody tells a first-timer. Most of what hangs on a surplus rack was never issued to anybody. It was made to look like it was, sold new, and hung six inches from the real thing at a similar price. That isn’t a scam. It’s a different product wearing the same color, and the price tag almost never tells the two apart.
Surplus stores are still worth walking into. A family in Collinsville pulling together winter coats for two kids, somebody in Granite City who needs a container that will haul wet gear out of a boat, a person in Alton who just wants a heavy blanket living in the trunk from November on: all three can do well in one of these places. They only need to know which pile they’re standing in front of.
### What is worth buying at an army navy surplus store in St. Louis?
Wool blankets, wool socks, field jackets with their liners, ponchos and shelter halves, ammo cans, ALICE and MOLLE packs, entrenching tools, and cotton fatigue trousers. Those are the items where government-issue construction still beats what the same money buys new. Skip used boots, old sleeping bags, and anything load-bearing with tired webbing.
Wool is the headline. An issued wool blanket is dense, heavy, and woven to survive a supply system that had no interest in your comfort, and a used one generally undercuts a new blanket of the same weight by a wide margin. Wool socks and wool sweaters follow the same logic. The fiber does not know it’s secondhand. Hold a blanket up to the light, look for moth holes along the folds, and give it a sniff. Musty washes out. Mildew usually doesn’t.
Field jackets are the other reliable win, and the quilted liner that buttons inside is often the better half of the purchase. Liners get separated from their coats in the sorting and end up on a table by themselves, priced low, because shoppers walk past them without knowing what they are. Buy the liner. It works under a rain shell, under a work coat, on its own in a cold garage.
Then the hard goods. Ammo cans are the single most useful thing in most of these stores: a steel box with a gasket lid that keeps damp out of documents, tools, ammunition, dog food, camping stoves, whatever you put in it. Entrenching tools fold, lock, and dig better than a garden trowel. ALICE and MOLLE packs move firewood, sports equipment and moving-day chaos without complaint. Shelter halves and ponchos are heavy compared to modern nylon, and they do not care what you drag them across.
Cotton fatigue trousers deserve a mention too. Deep pockets, reinforced seat and knees, a fabric that gets softer every wash. They are not waterproof and they are not warm on their own. For yard work, garage work, and anything involving a paint can, they are hard to beat.
### Why was most of that rack never issued to anyone?
Because three separate supply chains feed the same store, and they all end up on the same hangers. Sorting them is the whole skill. Once you can do it in about four seconds per garment, a surplus store stops feeling like a maze and starts feeling like a hardware aisle.
### Genuine issued surplus
This is decommissioned government stock: clothing and gear that went through a contract, sat in a depot, possibly got worn, and was later released for sale after being stripped of anything sensitive. It is used, or at minimum stored for a long time. It carries a label sewn inside with a contract line and a national stock number. It is the reason people walk into these stores in the first place.
### Commercial repro sold as mil-spec
A large share of the floor is new production made to military patterns by private manufacturers. The cut is close. The color is close. The stitching is usually lighter and the hardware is usually cheaper. Nothing dishonest is happening here, and some of it is genuinely good, particularly the newer synthetic pieces. It simply never passed through a supply chain, and it should not be priced as though it did.
### Ordinary outdoor and workwear in olive drab
The third pile is regular civilian gear that happens to be green. Camp stoves, work gloves, hiking socks, rain jackets, knives, flashlights, boots from outdoor brands. Often a fair deal, occasionally the best thing in the building, but it has nothing to do with surplus and you should judge it on its own terms, the same way you would at any outfitter.
### How do you tell issued gear from a lookalike?
Four checks, in order, and none of them takes longer than a few seconds. Label, sizing, wear pattern, then the smell and stiffness of the cloth. Any one of them can mislead you alone. Together they are close to decisive.
### Read the label sewn inside
Issued clothing carries a stiff sewn-in label, usually at the collar or inside a pocket bag, printed in blocky capitals. Look for a national stock number, thirteen digits broken into groups, and a contract line identifying who made the item and under what agreement. There will be fiber content and care instructions in the same plain style. Commercial repro tends to carry a brand tag, a barcode, a country of origin, and cheerful marketing language no government contract ever paid for.
### Check the sizing system
This one is fast. Issued clothing rarely uses small, medium and large the way civilian clothing does. It uses its own regimen: small-regular, medium-long, large-short, or a chest and waist measurement in inches with a length code attached. A jacket tagged medium-long was almost certainly made under contract. A jacket tagged M with a brand name above it was made for a store.
### Look at where it wore out
Used issue wears in predictable places. Cuffs and elbows go first on jackets. Knees and seat go first on trousers. Webbing fades unevenly where a buckle sat on it for years. Repro is uniformly new, or it is distressed artificially, which reads wrong because the fading lands where nobody’s arm ever rubbed. Name tapes, unit patches, or the ghost outline of a removed patch are strong signals that a garment actually belonged to somebody.
### Trust your nose and your hands
Long-stored cotton has a specific character. It’s stiff, faintly dusty, and it smells like a warehouse rather than a shop. Sometimes it still has hard creases from folding. New cotton feels softer and smells like sizing chemicals. Rub a sleeve between thumb and finger and you will start recognizing the difference after about a dozen garments. Nobody teaches this. You just pick it up.
### What should you leave on the shelf?
Boots, first. A boot molds to the footstrike of whoever broke it in, and that shape does not reset for you. Used boots are the most commonly regretted surplus purchase there is, and the reason is structural, not cosmetic. Buy boots new. Any brand, any store, just new.
Anything load-bearing needs a hard look before it comes home. Pull on the webbing of a pack or a belt and watch how it responds. Sun-degraded nylon has a chalky look and tears with much less force than it should. Flex every buckle. A cracked buckle is a five-minute replacement if the part is common and a permanent problem if it isn’t. Check the stitching where a strap meets the body of the pack, because that’s where the load actually goes.
Old sleeping bags are usually a pass. Insulation compresses permanently, older synthetic fills break down, and a bag that has been stuffed in a sack for fifteen years has lost the loft that made it warm. You cannot judge that from the outside. Rubber and elastic age the same way: waistbands, gaskets, rain gear, older rubberized ponchos. If the elastic has gone hard or the rubber flakes when you bend it, it’s done.
Helmets and body armor deserve their own warning. Plenty of what sits on those shelves is costume-grade or decades past any useful service life, and older armor in particular should not be treated as protective equipment because someone shelved it near the real thing. If you need protective gear, buy protective gear from a dealer who sells it as such, with a date of manufacture you can read.
One more, softly: anything with visible mold. Not musty. Mold. It spreads to whatever else is in the closet, and it rarely comes out of wool.
Different rabbit hole: what medical weight loss costs in St. Louis.
### Is it legal for a civilian to own military gear?
As a general matter, yes. Surplus that has been demilitarized and released for public sale is ordinary used clothing and equipment once it’s in the retail channel, and buying it makes you the owner of a coat, not a participant in anything. Uniforms, insignia and rank devices are generally lawful to own and to collect in the United States.
The line most people are actually asking about sits at impersonation. Owning and even wearing a uniform is a different thing from presenting yourself as a current or former service member, and claiming decorations you did not earn in order to obtain something of value is where federal law gets involved. Costume use, work use and collecting are not what those rules are aimed at.
Separate categories carry their own rules. Body armor is restricted for certain buyers and regulated differently from state to state. Optics, night vision and some communications equipment sit under export and transfer controls. Anything that was part of a weapon system is its own world entirely. This guide is a starting point, not legal advice, so if a specific purchase matters to you, confirm the current rules with the seller and with a qualified attorney before you buy rather than after.
### Why does surplus sometimes cost more than new gear?
Because the supply is finite and shrinking, and demand for certain items is not. Older issue items exist in a fixed quantity that only goes down. When a particular jacket or pattern gets popular with collectors, reenactors or vintage clothing buyers, the price on the rack starts answering to that market instead of to what the item does.
The channel itself has narrowed. Governments dispose of less usable material than they once did, more of it gets destroyed or recycled rather than resold, and the surplus that does reach the public moves through fewer hands. Stores fill the gap with new commercial stock, which is why the repro pile keeps growing. That’s also why a store can price a genuinely scarce item high and be entirely reasonable about it.
So compare against the job, not against the aesthetic. If you want a warm blanket, price it against warm blankets. If you want the specific jacket your dad wore, you’re in the collector market and the number reflects that. Both are fine. Just know which purchase you’re making before you get to the counter.
### Where does surplus gear earn its keep around St. Louis?
January, mostly. When a cold snap drops in and stays for a week, a wool blanket in the back seat and a field jacket liner in the hall closet stop being novelties. Wool keeps working when it gets damp, which matters here more than raw temperature ratings do, because our cold usually arrives wet.
River-bottom mud is the other proving ground. Anybody who has walked a levee road in Alton after rain, or worked a boat ramp near Granite City, knows that the mud here is the kind that pulls at you. Cotton fatigue trousers and a poncho handle that and wash out afterward. Ozarks camping trips are where shelter halves, e-tools and packs get used the way they were designed to be used, and where the extra weight stops mattering because you’re at a site, not on a thru-hike.
Storage is the underrated one. Basements in this metro get humid, garages swing forty degrees in a day, and ammo cans solve both problems for less than a good plastic tote costs. Seeds, camping stoves, spare fuses, paperwork, ammunition. If you’re sorting out what you actually need before a trip, our guide to what outdoor gear you actually need in St. Louis sorts the real from the aspirational.
### How should you shop a surplus store without guessing?
Pick two or three stores worth walking into, then say plainly at the counter what you’re trying to do with the gear. Not what you want to buy. What you’re trying to do. “I need something that keeps a kid warm walking to the bus in February” gets you a different and better conversation than “do you have field jackets.”
Then listen to the gap. One counter walks you to a rack, flips a collar, shows you the contract label, tells you which pieces are new production and which came out of a depot, and points at the liner you would have missed. Another says everything is military and lets you figure it out. The gap between the two answers is the entire signal, and it takes about ninety seconds to collect.
Check fit before condition. Issued sizing runs differently than you expect, so put the jacket on over whatever you’d actually wear under it, raise both arms, and reach forward like you’re steering. Then work the piece: every zipper, every snap, both cuffs, the inside of both pockets where the corners wear through. Turn it inside out. Pull a seam apart gently and watch whether the thread holds. Ask about returns before you pay, because most of these shops set their own policy and it varies a lot.
Bring a tape measure and a small flashlight if you’re serious. The lighting in these stores is honestly terrible, and a label you can’t read is a label you can’t use. Shops in Highland and Fairview Heights, like the hardware counters we wrote about in what St. Louis hardware stores still do for you, tend to run on staff who know their stock. Use them. That knowledge is the product.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it legal to buy army surplus?
A.  Generally yes. Surplus that has been demilitarized and released for public sale is ordinary used clothing and equipment by the time it reaches a retail shelf. Certain categories carry their own restrictions, including body armor, optics and anything tied to a weapon system. Confirm the current rules for a specific item before you buy it.
### Q. Can anyone buy from a military surplus store?
A.  Yes. These are regular retail stores open to the public, with no service requirement, no ID check and no membership. That is different from an on-base exchange, which does limit who can shop there. If the shop has a street address and a sign, you can walk in like you would at any other store.
### Q. Are army surplus stores cheaper?
A.  For some things, clearly. Used wool blankets, socks, ammo cans, packs and field jacket liners usually cost less than comparable new goods. Other items cost more than new retail, because scarcity and collector demand set the price instead of function. Compare each item against what you actually want it to do, not against the store’s reputation.
### Q. Do army navy stores sell authentic gear?
A.  Some of it, yes, mixed in with a lot that isn’t. Three categories share the same racks: genuine issued surplus, new commercial gear made to military patterns, and ordinary outdoor clothing that happens to be olive. Most stores carry all three without separating them, so the label inside the garment is your best tool.
### Q. Are military surplus stores legit?
A.  Almost always. They are licensed retailers selling legally obtained goods, and the mix of issued and commercial stock is standard practice across the industry rather than deception. The thing to watch is pricing: a new repro jacket priced like a scarce issued one is a judgment you have to make yourself, at the rack.
### Q. Is military surplus new or used?
A.  Both, on the same rack. Genuine surplus is used or long-stored, sometimes unissued but decades old. Commercial reproduction is brand new and never entered a supply chain. Plenty of stores also stock current outdoor and work gear. Price tags rarely distinguish them, so check the sewn-in label and the sizing system.
### Q. How to tell if military surplus is real?
A.  Look for a sewn-in label with a national stock number and a contract line, printed in plain block capitals. Check the sizing: issued clothing uses medium-long or large-short rather than S, M and L. Then look at wear patterns at cuffs and knees, and feel for the stiff, dusty texture of long-stored cotton.
### Q. Why are army surplus stores closing?
A.  The supply has tightened. Governments release less usable material than they once did, more gets destroyed or recycled instead of resold, and what reaches the public passes through fewer hands. Online sellers took a share of what remains. Shops that survive lean on commercial outdoor stock, workwear and staff who know what they are selling.

## What Window Tint Costs and What Is Legal in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-window-tint-costs-and-whats-legal-in-st-louis
The rear glass has gone the color of weak grape soda. One corner has lifted maybe an inch, and pressing it flat with a thumb just moves the bubble somewhere else. Whoever tinted this car did it eight or nine years ago, for somebody else, and you inherited it in the trade.
Peeling rear film is the cheap problem. The front doors are the expensive one, because Missouri puts an actual number on those two windows, and a trooper with a meter cares about the reading, not about what anybody promised at a counter.
So two questions run together here: what am I allowed to put on the glass, and what is this going to cost me. The first has a written answer. The second doesn’t, not a single number anyway, and the shops quoting you aren’t being cagey when they ask about your car before they say a price. Half a dozen things move that number, and one of them is hiding under the film you already have.
### What is the darkest legal tint in Missouri?
On the front side windows, Missouri requires light transmission of thirty-five percent or more, plus or minus three percent, measured through the film and factory glass together. Reflectance has to stay at thirty-five percent or less. Darker than that on the front doors takes a permit issued on a physician’s prescription.
That comes from Missouri Revised Statutes section 307.173, which governs the two windows immediately left and right of the driver. Two limits, not one. Light transmission of thirty-five percent or more, plus or minus three percent. Luminous reflectance of thirty-five percent or less, plus or minus three percent. That second limit is the one people forget, and it rules out a mirrored look on those windows even when the darkness passes.
Read the phrase doing the real work: light transmission through the assembled window. Film plus factory glass, together, as one sandwich. Not the number printed on the box the roll came out of.
Darker film up front is not automatically off the table. The statute provides for a permit issued on a physician’s prescription. Factory-installed tinted glass is exempt, so is its equivalent replacement, and so is the manufacturer-tinted strip across the top of the windshield. Those are not prohibited by this section.
Here’s the part that surprises people. The statute sets no darkness limit for the rear side windows or the back glass. That is why so many cars around St. Louis run near-black behind the front doors and something much lighter beside the driver. Looks like a compromise. It is actually the law being read correctly.
One caution, and take it seriously. Statutes get amended, and this is a plain-language summary rather than legal advice. Pull the current text of 307.173 yourself before you spend money, or have a shop put a meter on your glass, because enforcement runs on the net reading and nothing else.
### Why does the number on the film box not match what the meter says?
Because your door glass was already filtering light before anybody touched it. Most automotive glass carries a faint green or gray cast straight from the plant. Stack film on top and the two effects multiply, so the assembled window always reads darker than the film does on its own.
Which means a roll labeled thirty-five can put you under the limit once it is on the car. Installers who do this all day know it cold. They reach for something a shade lighter than the number you asked for, on purpose, and if one explains why before you bring it up, that tells you something good about the rest of the work.
Ask for a meter reading. Any shop doing volume has one in a drawer, and it takes about four seconds per window. Before and after, if they will do both. The before number shows what your glass was already doing on its own, and the after number is the only one that matters on the shoulder of I-55 at eleven at night.
Factory privacy glass is its own animal. Plenty of SUVs and minivans leave the factory with the rear side glass dyed dark in the glass itself, no film involved. Adding film over that goes darker still, which the statute permits, and which is worth a minute of honest thought anyway. Backing out of a driveway in Mehlville after dark with near-black rear glass, you are leaning almost entirely on mirrors and a camera.
### What actually drives the price of a tint job?
Six things, roughly, and only one of them is the film itself. Glass count and vehicle size, the shape of the back window, whether old film has to come off first, film tier, warranty, and whether the installer comes to you. Ask two shops about the same car and the answers can sit a long way apart.
About ranges. You will find plenty of numbers online, and we are not going to hand you a St. Louis figure as though it were fixed, because it isn’t. A two-door coupe in dyed film and a three-row SUV in full ceramic are not in the same conversation. A quote in Waterloo and a quote in Mehlville on the same truck can land differently for reasons that have nothing to do with quality. Get two or three real quotes on your actual vehicle and compare those.
### How many windows, and what shape are they
Glass count sets the floor. A coupe has fewer panes than a crew-cab pickup, and a minivan with quarter glass plus a liftgate has more still. Sunroofs and windshields usually price separately from a “full car” package, so find out what “full” includes at each shop before you hold two numbers next to each other.
Shape is where the labor hides. A flat side window is a clean cut and a squeegee. A steeply curved back glass has to be heat-shrunk, meaning the installer works the film with a heat gun until it lays down on a compound curve with no fingers and no creases. That is a real skill and it eats time. Some back windows are genuinely nasty, and good shops price them honestly.
### Whether old film has to come off first
This is the expensive surprise. Stripping failed film is slow, filthy work, and almost nobody budgets for it. Old film delaminates as it comes off: the top layer peels away and leaves the adhesive glued to the glass, so somebody has to steam or soak it and scrape every square inch clean before a fresh sheet can go down.
Back glass is worse. Those thin defroster lines are printed on the inside surface, exactly where the scraping happens, and a careless removal lifts a line or two along with the glue. Ask specifically how a shop handles removal on a heated rear window. Removal gets quoted per window at some places and as a flat add-on at others, and on an older car with cooked film the strip can rival the new install.
### Which film tier you pick
Film is what most people focus on and often the smaller slice of the spread on a simple car. Dyed sits at the bottom, carbon in the middle, ceramic at the top, with metalized and hybrid options scattered around. Jumping tiers raises material cost while labor stays roughly where it was.
### Warranty, and who stands behind it
A lifetime warranty on film comes from the manufacturer. A warranty on the installation comes from the shop. Two different promises, and people conflate them constantly. Better film carries a longer guarantee against bubbling, peeling and color change, and that guarantee is part of what the higher price buys. Ask who you call in year four, and whether the coverage follows the car if you sell it.
### Mobile versus in-shop
A mobile installer meeting you in a driveway in Washington saves you a trip, and some of them do excellent work. Dust is the tradeoff. Film shows contamination forever, and a closed bay with a wet floor is a cleaner place to lay adhesive-backed plastic than an open carport on a windy afternoon. Mobile sometimes costs less, sometimes more for the convenience.
### Ceramic, carbon, or dyed: what are you paying for?
Heat, mostly. Darkness and heat rejection are two separate specs, and understanding that one thing will save you money. A cheap dark film can still cook you. A light ceramic can keep the dash noticeably cooler and still pass a meter on the front doors.
Dyed film is pigment suspended in an adhesive layer. It cuts glare, it looks fine on day one, and it is the least expensive thing on the menu. It is also the film that goes purple, because the dye breaks down under sustained UV and the color drifts toward violet as it dies. Every purple window you have ever seen was dyed film reaching the end of its life.
Carbon film swaps the dye for carbon particles. It holds a neutral charcoal tone instead of fading purple, and it turns back more infrared heat than dyed does. Middle of the road on price. For a lot of drivers that is the sensible place to stop.
Ceramic uses nonconductive ceramic particles, and it does the heavy lifting on heat and UV without needing to be dark at all. It costs the most. It also leaves signals alone, which matters because older metalized films can degrade phone reception, GPS, keyless entry and toll transponders. Ever wonder why somebody paid triple for tint that barely looks tinted? That is the answer.
Our summers make the argument. A car sitting in an uncovered lot in Columbia through an August afternoon, humid, no shade anywhere, gets genuinely punishing inside, and the gap between dyed film and good ceramic is something you feel through the steering wheel. Whether that gap is worth the money is your call, not the installer’s.
Flying out Monday? What getting to the St. Louis airport costs.
### What goes wrong with a tint job?
Four failures, and you can spot every one of them from the driver’s seat. Purple color shift, bubbling, edges lifting, and specks of dirt trapped under the film. Three of those are the film or the weather giving up. One is installation, and it shows up early.
Bubbles come in two flavors. Small hazy pockets in the first week are water, they are normal, and they dry out as the adhesive cures. Bubbles arriving in year three are adhesive failure and they never leave. Along the top edge of a door window, lifting usually means the film got cut a hair short or the glass edge never got properly cleaned, and once air finds a way in, the peel walks inward from there.
Trapped dirt is permanent. It is sealed between plastic and glass with adhesive holding it in place. A speck or two on a big window happens to careful installers now and then. A whole constellation means the bay was dirty or the glass never got prepped. Look at your new tint in direct sunlight before you drive away, not under the shop fluorescents.
Curing runs a few days, longer when it is cold or damp, and shops will tell you to leave the windows up until the adhesive sets. Do that. A window dropped on day one can drag the film edge down with it. The haze you are squinting through in the meantime is moisture, not a defect.
Then the one nobody thinks about until it bites. Defroster lines. On back glass, an aggressive strip or a scraper in the wrong hands breaks that printed circuit, and a stripe of your rear window stops clearing in January. Raise it before the work starts, not after.
### How should you pick a tint shop around St. Louis?
Shortlist two or three shops worth interviewing, then actually interview them. Not price-shop them. Say plainly what you want: legal on the front doors with a meter reading to prove it, heat rejection as the priority, old film off the back glass without losing defroster lines, and a warranty you can still use in four years.
Then hold that against what each shop is prepared to deliver. One walks you into the bay, shows you the meter, explains that they will run something lighter up front to land legal through your particular glass, and says flatly that stripping your back window is going to add an hour. Another quotes a flat number and tells you not to worry about the law. The gap between those two answers is the signal. Not the price.
Questions worth asking out loud: how long has the person cutting the film been doing it, plotter-cut patterns or hand-cut, does the shop warranty its own labor separately from the film maker, and what do they do for you if you get pulled over anyway. Ask to see a car they finished this week, outside, in the sun. Tint is a trade where the work is visible and the good ones enjoy showing it off.
That interviewing frame is the same one behind choosing a window company in St. Louis, and it travels well across any trade where the quote shows up before the work. If heat is the thing actually bothering you, understand that house film is a different product under different rules, which is covered in what to know about home window tinting in St. Louis. When shade indoors is the real goal, what window blinds and shades cost in St. Louis is the cheaper comparison. Nothing in 307.173 touches your living room.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Can cops pull you over for tint in Missouri?
A.  Yes. Tint is an equipment matter, and an officer who believes your front side windows read too dark can stop you and meter the glass. The reading comes off the assembled window, film and factory glass together, not off the film spec. A permit issued on a physician’s prescription is the exception the statute provides for darker front film.
### Q. How much does a tint ticket cost in Missouri?
A.  Amounts vary by court and by county, so we will not quote you a figure that might be wrong where you live. Tint is generally handled as a minor equipment violation, and what you pay depends on the local fine schedule plus court costs. Some drivers also get an order to remove the film. Call the court printed on the citation.
### Q. What are the medical exemptions for window tinting in Missouri?
A.  Section 307.173 allows front side film darker than the thirty-five percent standard when a permit has been issued on a physician’s prescription. The statute creates the permit; it does not publish a list of qualifying diagnoses. Photosensitive conditions are the usual reason people ask. Confirm the current application process with the state, and keep the paperwork in the vehicle.
### Q. How long does window tinting last?
A.  Film tier and sun exposure decide it. Dyed film fails first, usually turning purple and bubbling well before better film shows any age at all. Carbon and ceramic hold their color far longer, and quality films carry long or lifetime warranties against exactly those failures. A garage-kept car outlasts one that bakes in an open lot every day.
### Q. What are the downsides of car window tinting?
A.  Night visibility is the honest one, especially reversing or checking a blind spot through dark rear glass. After that: legal exposure on the front doors, the cost of stripping film later, permanently trapped dirt if the install was sloppy, possible signal interference from older metalized films, and a few days of hazy curing you simply have to wait out.
### Q. Is 20 or 35 tint better?
A.  For front side windows in Missouri, thirty-five is the one that keeps you legal, because twenty will not pass a meter on the assembled window. Behind the front doors the statute sets no limit, so twenty becomes a tradeoff between privacy and how much you want to see at night. Heat rejection comes from film tier, not from a darker number.
### Q. Does ceramic tint actually make a car cooler?
A.  Yes, and infrared rejection is the reason rather than darkness. Ceramic particles turn back heat-carrying wavelengths that slip straight through dyed film, so a light ceramic can beat a much darker cheap film on cabin temperature. You notice it most in a car that sits in an open lot. Ask a shop to show you two films under a heat lamp.
### Q. How soon can you roll the windows down after tinting?
A.  Most shops say a few days, and longer when it is cold or damp, because the adhesive needs time to cure fully. Dropping a window early can drag the film edge and start a peel that only gets worse. Haziness and small water pockets during that stretch are normal and clear on their own. Use your installer’s number, not ours.

## How to Hire a Bartender for a Party in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-hire-a-bartender-for-a-party-in-st-louis
It’s 8:14 and the ice is gone. Not low. Gone. The cooler at the end of the folding table holds four inches of gray water with one bottle of tonic bobbing in it, and eleven people are standing in a line that bends around the deck rail. At the head of that line is your cousin, who volunteered to “handle drinks” at three o’clock, has not eaten since, has not sat down, and has not spoken to his own wife in ninety minutes.
He isn’t bartending. He’s trapped.
That trapped-cousin problem is what a hired bartender actually solves, and it’s why the money question is harder than it first looks. You’re not paying somebody to know how to build an old fashioned. You’re paying for the part of a party that breaks first: ice, glassware, the line, the one guest who needs watching, and the cleanup at midnight that nobody else volunteers for. What that runs in the St. Louis metro depends on a short list of things, and hardly any of them are the drinks.
### How to hire a bartender for a private party?
Set your guest count and a firm start and end time, then shortlist two or three bartenders to interview. Tell each one plainly whether they bring the bar, tools, ice and glassware or just themselves, and who buys the alcohol. Confirm liquor-liability coverage and the rules at your venue. Then compare what each is prepared to deliver.
Notice what came first there. Not the rate. Three numbers: how many people, what time the bar opens, what time it closes. Every quote you get back is built on those three, and hosts who call without them get vague answers and then feel misled later. Write them down before you send a single message. It takes four minutes and it changes every conversation you have after.
The second thing to settle is scope, and this is where most of the surprises live. Some bartenders arrive with a portable bar, shakers, jiggers, strainers, a speed rail, coolers, bagged ice, garnish cut and boxed, and racks of rented glassware. Some arrive with a bottle opener and expect your kitchen to be the bar. Both are legitimate businesses. They are wildly different products, and comparing their hourly rates as though they’re the same thing is how hosts end up driving to a store at 4pm on the day of their own graduation party.
Then get quotes. Plural. Rates in this metro move with guest count, total hours, the date on the calendar, how far someone has to drive, and whether the job is a two-person setup or a one-person setup. Anybody who hands you a firm number before asking about those things is guessing, and their guess will get revised.
### How many bartenders do you actually need?
One bartender per fifty guests is the working rule most event staff use for a standard open bar, and it holds up well in practice. Fifty is not a ceiling on what a good bartender can physically pour. It’s the point where the line stops moving and people start drifting toward the kitchen to make their own.
So a backyard fiftieth in Creve Coeur with forty-five people gets by with one. A graduation party with ninety wants two. A wedding reception with a hundred and eighty, full open bar, cocktails rather than beer and wine, is a three-person bar and probably four with support. That math is boring and it is also the single biggest thing separating a party where people talk to each other from a party where people stand in a line.
### What pushes the number up
Drink complexity, mostly. A beer-wine-and-two-batched-cocktails bar moves roughly twice as fast per guest as a full cocktail bar where every order gets shaken to order. Toasts compress everything: a hundred and fifty champagne pours in eight minutes is a different job than a hundred and fifty drinks over four hours. Single-point bars back up worse than two stations placed apart. And a crowd that skews heavily toward drinkers in their twenties will order faster and more often than a family reunion with kids running around.
### When you want a bar back
Somewhere north of roughly a hundred guests, the second body stops being a luxury. A bar back hauls ice, restocks bottles, runs glassware, breaks down boxes and keeps the bartender behind the bar instead of walking to a garage cooler every eleven minutes. Ask whether the person you’re interviewing brings help at your count, and whether that help is billed separately or folded in. It is one of the most common line items hosts don’t know to ask about.
### What does the hourly rate usually cover?
Most private-event bartenders in the metro quote an hourly rate against a minimum number of hours, and the clock they bill is not the clock your guests see. Setup and breakdown are real labor and they get paid for. A four-hour party is generally a five-and-a-half or six-hour booking, and that gap is where hosts get startled.
### Hours booked versus hours worked
Figure roughly sixty to ninety minutes of setup before your stated start: ice in tubs, bottles chilled and arranged, garnish out, glassware unboxed and wiped, a station built so nothing requires a second trip. Then thirty to sixty minutes of breakdown after last call. Somebody has to pour off the melt water, bag the bottles, wipe the surfaces and load a car. If the quote you’re reading says four hours and your party is four hours, ask where setup went. It did not disappear.
### Minimums, travel and the date
Nearly everybody works against a booking minimum, often three or four hours, because a two-hour job still costs a full evening once you count loading, driving and unloading. Travel is its own line. A bartender based in the city driving out to Troy or St. Clair is spending real time on the road, and a mileage or travel charge past a certain radius is normal rather than sneaky. The calendar matters too. Saturday in May, Saturday in October, New Year’s Eve, the weekend of a big local event: those dates get quoted differently than a Thursday in February, and the good people are booked out months ahead for them.
### The line items that move your total
Ask about these one at a time. Bagged ice and how much. Glassware, rented or plastic or yours. A portable bar or a table you provide. Garnish prep, which is an hour of knife work somebody is doing whether or not it shows up in writing. Mixers, juices and syrups. Batched cocktails, which cost prep time and save service time. A second station. Tubs, coolers and trash bags. Whether tip is included or left open. Each one is small. Together they can be a third of your total.
### Who brings the bar, the ice and the glassware?
Depends entirely on who you hire, and it is the question that decides whether your quote is cheap or complete. A bartender who shows up with tools, ice, coolers, garnish and glassware is running a small mobile operation with real overhead. One who shows up with skills alone is charging for skills alone. Neither is wrong.
Say what you have out loud during the interview. “I have a six-foot folding table, a garage fridge, a hose in the back, and no glassware at all.” That sentence does more work than any checklist. A working bartender hears it and immediately tells you what’s missing, because they’ve stood in that exact yard forty times.
Ice is the one people underestimate every single time. Plan on something like a pound to a pound and a half per guest across an evening, more in July, and remember that ice used for chilling bottles in tubs is not ice you can put in a glass. A party for eighty in August wants a lot more bagged ice than anyone expects to buy. Melt is not a rounding error in a St. Louis backyard.
Glassware splits three ways. Real rented glass looks best and comes with a count, a delivery window and a pickup. Decent heavy plastic is cheaper, safer around a pool and completely fine for most backyard events. Your own cabinet is free until forty people are using it and nobody can find the dishwasher. Pick one on purpose. Hosts also tend to forget that a drinks station and a food station want physical separation, the same way a candy buffet in St. Louis needs its own table or it becomes a traffic jam with a spoon in it.
### Does a bartender need a license in Missouri?
Missouri doesn’t issue a statewide bartender license the way a handful of states do. Alcohol here is governed through state liquor control plus local city and county ordinances, and those local rules genuinely differ across this metro. What binds you as a host comes from three places: state and local law, your venue, and insurance.
Start with the distinction that actually matters. Is alcohol being sold, or is it being served free to invited guests? A cash bar, a ticketed event, a donation jar next to the bottles: selling alcohol is a licensed activity, and a caterer or venue that sells or serves alcohol carries its own liquor license. A private host pouring free drinks for guests at their own home sits in a different place. Those two situations are not interchangeable, and the second you charge anybody anything for a drink, you have changed what you’re doing.
Local ordinance is the part nobody can answer for you in a blog post. Rules around permits, hours, public spaces, parks, rented halls and temporary events vary by municipality and by county here, and they change. Call your own city hall or county office and ask about your specific event. Ten minutes on the phone beats a guess. If you’re in a rented venue, a park shelter, a church hall or a country club, the venue’s own written policy is a second and separate layer on top.
What you can absolutely ask the bartender about is insurance and training. Liquor liability coverage, general liability, and whether they carry responsible-serving certification are all fair, normal questions, and plenty of venues require proof of coverage before they’ll let anybody pour on site. A professional will have a certificate of insurance ready and won’t be offended you asked. Somebody who gets prickly about it has told you something useful.
One rule is not negotiable and not local: Missouri’s legal drinking age is 21. A bartender worth hiring will card at a graduation party where half the guests are eighteen, will cut off a guest who needs cutting off, and will do both without making it your problem. That judgment is genuinely most of what you’re buying.
### How much alcohol do you buy for your guest count?
The common planning assumption is about one drink per guest per hour for the first hour or two, then tapering, which for a hundred guests over four hours lands somewhere near three hundred to four hundred drinks total. It’s a starting point, not a promise. Your crowd, your season and your menu all bend it.
In most cases the host buys the alcohol. That’s usually the cheaper path and it keeps the bartender out of licensed-sales territory entirely. A bartender may well build your shopping list, tell you exactly how many bottles of each thing and in what sizes, and hand you a list organized by store aisle. Good ones do this without being asked. What they generally will not do is buy it and resell it to you.
Rough split to argue with: beer and wine tend to carry the bulk of consumption at family events, and a liter bottle of spirits yields somewhere around twenty to twenty-two standard pours depending on how it’s measured. Heat drives beer and anything tall and cold. A December party in a rented hall drinks differently than a June party in a yard in Madison. Limiting the bar to beer, wine and two signature cocktails cuts both the shopping list and the service time, and almost nobody complains.
Buy where you can return what you don’t open. That single habit does more for the alcohol line on your budget than any amount of arithmetic. Ask the retailer about their unopened-return policy before you load the cart, because policies differ. And build the cocktail list with your bartender, not at them. If you want something ambitious, the kind of thing you’d order at one of St. Louis’s best craft cocktail bars and speakeasies, say so early. Batching it is a completely different conversation than shaking it eighty times.
Feeding them too? What African food to order in St. Louis.
### Who tips a private-event bartender?
At a hosted party where drinks are free, the host tips, and the customary range people work from is roughly 15 to 20 percent of the service total. Not the alcohol total. The service total. Some bartenders build gratuity into the quote, some leave it open, and you should know which before the day.
Ask directly during the interview. “Is gratuity included, or should I plan on it separately?” If it’s already in there, tipping again is generous rather than required. If it isn’t, put cash in an envelope the night before and hand it over at breakdown. Doing it then, rather than promising to send something later, is one of those small things that gets you the same bartender next year.
Tip jars are a whole separate decision, and it’s yours to make. Plenty of hosts ask that no jar appear at all, because a jar tells guests they should be paying for something at a party they were invited to. Others let it sit out quietly. Either way, decide it in advance instead of discovering a mason jar full of fives on your table at nine o’clock. And if you’re also tipping a bar back, say so, so the split is clear and nobody is doing awkward math in your driveway.
### How do you choose between two bartenders?
Shortlist two or three people worth interviewing, then interview them and state plainly what you want: guest count, hours, whether they bring the bar, who buys the alcohol, whether you need help at that count. Then compare what each one is prepared to deliver against what you asked for. The gap is the signal, not the price.
Here’s how that plays out. You describe eighty guests, five hours, a yard with a folding table and no glassware. One bartender comes back with a staffing recommendation, an ice quantity, a note that the toast will need pre-poured champagne, a shopping list, a proof of insurance and a question about where the trash goes. The other says yes, sounds great, and gives you an hourly rate. Both may be fine at the actual job. Only one has shown you they’ve done your party before.
Questions that earn their keep in that conversation: How many events like mine have you worked this year? What do you need from me that I probably haven’t thought of? What time do you arrive and what time are you loaded out? What happens if you get sick the week of? Who handles a guest who’s had too much? That last one separates people fast.
Get the agreement in writing, however simple. Date, arrival time, service window, breakdown, guest count, headcount of staff, what they bring, what you bring, deposit, cancellation terms, gratuity. A short written note beats a long phone memory. Then let them run it. A hired bartender who has to be supervised isn’t saving you anything, and the whole point was to get you back into your own party. Rented hall, backyard, a room where the night ends at a karaoke bar in St. Louis after the toast, same principle every time.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much should you pay a private bartender?
A.  There’s no single metro rate, because the number moves with guest count, total hours including setup and breakdown, travel distance, the date, and how much of the bar the bartender supplies. A person who brings tools, ice, coolers, garnish and glassware prices differently than one who brings only themselves. Get two or three quotes against the same written brief and compare scope, not just the hourly.
### Q. How many bartenders per 100 guests?
A.  Two, as a baseline, using the common one-per-fifty guideline. Go to two plus a bar back if you’re running a full cocktail menu, serving a champagne toast, or working a venue where ice and stock live far from the bar. Beer, wine and a couple of batched cocktails can sometimes stretch further. The moment a line forms and stays, you were short.
### Q. What do you pay a bartender for a wedding?
A.  Weddings usually cost more per hour than a backyard party, and the reasons are structural. Longer service windows, a cocktail hour and a reception, a toast that compresses two hundred pours into minutes, rented glassware, premium dates, venue insurance requirements and a larger crew. Ask specifically about the staffing plan for the toast. That single moment breaks more wedding bars than the whole rest of the night.
### Q. Do you have to have a bartender license in Missouri?
A.  Missouri has no statewide bartender license. Alcohol is regulated through state liquor control plus local city and county ordinances, which differ across this metro, and any business selling or serving alcohol needs its own liquor license. What matters for a private host is whether alcohol is being sold, what the venue requires, and whether the bartender carries liquor liability coverage. Confirm specifics with your own city or county.
### Q. What is the 50% rule in bartending?
A.  It isn’t a law or an industry standard. It’s bar-trade shorthand, and more than one version circulates. The reading most event planners use: assume roughly half your guests are actively drinking in any given hour when you size the bar, the ice and the staffing. Useful as a sanity check. Don’t treat it as gospel, and don’t build a shopping list on it alone.
### Q. Is $20 a good tip for a bartender?
A.  For one drink at a bar, that’s generous. For a private event, it’s low, because event tipping runs off the service total rather than per drink. The customary range is about 15 to 20 percent of what you paid for the service. Ask upfront whether gratuity is already built into the quote so you’re not guessing at breakdown.
### Q. Who buys the alcohol, the host or the bartender?
A.  Usually the host. It’s cheaper, and it keeps the bartender clear of licensed-sales territory. Many bartenders will write your shopping list down to bottle counts and sizes, which is worth asking for during the interview. Buy where unopened bottles can be returned, and confirm that policy before you load the cart, since it varies from retailer to retailer.
### Q. Do you need a bar back for a big party?
A.  Past roughly a hundred guests, yes, and sooner if ice and stock are stored far from the bar. A bar back hauls ice, restocks bottles, runs glassware and keeps your bartender behind the bar instead of walking to a garage cooler every ten minutes. Ask whether help is included at your guest count or billed as a separate person.

## What a Backyard Basketball Court Costs in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-backyard-basketball-court-costs-in-st-louis
The hoop is bolted to the garage fascia, slightly crooked, the way they always end up. Ball goes up, rattles the rim, drops, and then keeps rolling, because the driveway falls off toward the street at whatever pitch the builder poured decades ago. Somebody sprints after it. A car slows down. That is the moment a backyard court actually gets decided, with a kid standing in the street holding a ball.
Two phone calls into pricing a real pad out back, most people learn the same thing. The hoop was never the expensive part. You aren’t buying a basketball goal. You’re buying flatwork, and flatwork in eastern Missouri has opinions.
Chalk lines on the grass are a good first move. Mark the footprint, walk it, shoot on the grass for a week and see whether the size feels right. Then start asking about what goes underneath it, because the dirt decides both the price and the lifespan.
### How much does it cost to build a basketball court in your yard in St. Louis?
The slab drives the number, not the hoop. Square footage, how much grading your yard needs, slab thickness, reinforcement, the sub-base under it, and where the water goes matter far more than surfacing or the goal. Prices swing hard by yard and by contractor, so get two or three quotes.
Nobody honest prices this over the phone. Any square-foot figure you found online was quoted in another state, in another year, on a flatter lot, with cheaper trucking. Two yards a mile apart in South County can come back thousands apart and both bids can be correct. One needs a truckload of fill and a drain line. The other needs a skid steer for an afternoon and a broom.
So treat any range you read, including one you hear from a neighbor, as something that varies by yard and by contractor. What you can actually control is knowing which decisions move the number. Court cost is roughly square footage multiplied by site conditions, plus a short list of choices about thickness, steel, joints, drainage and surface. Learn those, then get quotes from people who have stood in your backyard.
### Where does the money actually go on a backyard court?
Into dirt and concrete. On most residential courts, excavation, sub-base, forms, reinforcement and the pour eat the large majority of the budget. The goal, the net and the painted lines are small by comparison. People shop the hoop first because the hoop is the part that photographs well in a catalog.
### Excavation and grading
Your yard isn’t flat. A court has to be. Somebody has to cut into the high side, build up the low side, and either haul the difference off or spread it where it does some good. Cut and fill is the least predictable line on a court budget. A pad area with a two-foot fall across it is a different job from one with an eight-foot fall, and the second may need a retaining wall before anyone talks about concrete at all.
Access changes the math too. If a ready-mix truck can back within a chute length of the forms, great. If it can’t, because the only route to the back of a narrow Tower Grove lot is a four-foot gate, then material moves by buggy, conveyor or pump. That’s labor and equipment, and it shows up in the bid whether or not anybody explains it.
### The sub-base under the slab
Crushed stone, placed in lifts and compacted to a depth your contractor specifies for your soil. This is the layer homeowners cut first, because nobody will ever see it, and it’s the layer doing the most work. It spreads the load across soft spots, and it gives water a path that isn’t the underside of your concrete. Go cheap here and you’ve built an expensive cracker on top of pudding.
### Slab, steel and forms
Thickness is real money. Every extra inch across a pad the size of a three-car garage floor is a meaningful jump in yardage, and the concrete itself is priced by the yard. Reinforcement is a separate decision: welded wire mesh laid flat is cheaper than rebar tied in a grid and held up on chairs, and it doesn’t behave as well over moving soil. Forms, screeding, finishing and curing are labor hours. If that sounds familiar, it should. Our breakdown of what a concrete driveway costs in St. Louis is built on the same handful of variables.
### Everything sitting on top
Surface coating, the goal, its footing, fencing, lighting, lines and nets. Any one of those is modest. Together they can rival a chunk of the slab. One adjustable in-ground hoop with a decent backboard is a manageable purchase. Two goals, black vinyl fence on two sides, and pole-mounted lighting is a second project riding on the back of the first.
### Why does St. Louis clay decide whether your slab survives?
Eastern Missouri sits on expansive clay. Every contractor who pours here knows it, and it’s the quiet reason two identical-looking courts age completely differently. Clay swells when it takes on water and shrinks back when it dries, so the ground under a flat slab rises and settles with the seasons. Now add a St. Louis winter, where a slab can cross the freezing line again and again between December and March. Those two forces, together, are what break flatwork.
Which means the boring items on an estimate are the ones worth your attention. Not the color. Not the net. The dirt, the stone, the steel, the joints and the drain. Every one of those is a fair question to put to your concrete contractor, and the answers tell you a lot about who you’re talking to.
### Ask about the sub-base by name
Say it plainly: what depth of compacted aggregate are you putting under my slab, what material, compacted in what lifts, and why that number for this soil? You’re not quizzing anybody. You’re listening for whether there’s a reason behind the spec or just a habit. Ask what happens if they hit soft clay while they’re digging, because on plenty of lots around here, they will.
### Reinforcement and the joint plan
Concrete cracks. That’s a material property, not a defect, and a court is one big uninterrupted plane of the stuff. Control joints decide where those cracks show up. Tooled or saw-cut, laid out on a grid, at spacing tied to the slab thickness. On a sport surface the joint layout is also a play decision, because a joint running straight through the free-throw line is a spot where a hard dribble skips sideways. Ask where the joints will land relative to the key and the arc, and ask about air-entrained mix for freeze-thaw exposure.
### Where the water goes
You’re about to drop a thousand square feet or more of impervious surface into a yard that used to soak up rain. That water still exists. If nobody decided where it goes, it decides on its own, and its favorite destination is usually a foundation. Occasionally it picks the neighbor’s yard, which turns a fun summer project into a conversation nobody wanted.
Answers vary by lot. A consistent pitch across the pad. A trench drain along the low edge. A swale. A dry well. Pipe daylighted somewhere downhill that isn’t someone else’s problem. The specific solution matters less than the fact that somebody chose one on purpose and can point at it on the ground.
### Is asphalt, concrete, or modular tile the right surface?
Concrete for longevity, asphalt for a lower up-front number, modular tile as a layer that sits on top of either one. They aren’t three competing products, which is where the comparison usually goes wrong online. Two are pavements. One is a covering. A lot of good courts are a combination.
### Concrete
Rigid, long-lived, and the default choice for a residential court in this climate when the budget allows. It costs more going in. It holds a true plane better over clay, it doesn’t soften in August heat, and it accepts tile, coating or paint later. The tradeoff: when concrete does fail, it fails visibly and repairs are patches, not invisible fixes. Get the sub-base and the reinforcement right and that day is decades out.
### Asphalt
Flexible pavement, cheaper to install, faster to put down, and genuinely common on outdoor courts. It moves with the ground instead of fighting it, which sounds ideal on clay until you remember that it also softens in summer, requires periodic sealing, and needs a cure period before anything gets coated over it. Budget for maintenance you’ll actually have to do. An asphalt court that never gets sealed ravels at the edges and starts shedding aggregate.
### Acrylic sport coating
This is the cushioned, colored, textured system you see on tennis and pickleball courts, built up in layers over asphalt or concrete. It plays great, it looks finished, and it turns your pad into something that reads as a court rather than a patio with a hoop. It also needs recoating on a cycle, and it telegraphs any crack that opens up underneath it.
### Modular tile over a slab
Interlocking polypropylene tiles snap together over an existing slab, no adhesive, and the good ones are shock-absorbing and drain through. Nice knees. Nice ball bounce. Easy color and line layout, and you can lift a damaged tile out and replace it. The catch is honest: tile is a surface, not a foundation. Lay it over a slab that heaves and you’ll feel the ridge through your shoes within a season or two.
### How big does the pad need to be, and where can it sit?
A regulation NBA court runs 94 by 50 feet. High school is 84 by 50. Nobody is fitting that behind a house in Ballwin. Actual backyard courts are half courts, narrowed half courts, or a key-and-arc shooting pad, and the useful question isn’t how big it can be. It’s what you want to practice on it.
Here’s the dimensional reality, which is the one part of this post that doesn’t vary by contractor. The free-throw line sits 15 feet from the face of the backboard. The high school three-point arc is 19 feet 9 inches from the center of the rim. The NBA arc is 23 feet 9 inches at the top and 22 feet in the corners. Those distances are fixed, so your pad either contains them or it clips them.
A true half court is 47 by 50 feet. Plenty of families are thrilled with 30 by 50, which keeps the whole arc and gives up the sidelines. A 30 by 30 pad holds the key, the free-throw line and the top of a high school arc with almost nothing to spare, and the corner three disappears entirely. A 20 by 25 pad is a shooting station, and that is a completely legitimate thing to build.
Placement is its own puzzle. Property lines and easements first, then the septic field or lateral lines if you’re on one, then utilities, which must be located before anybody puts a blade in the ground. Watch the trees: roots under a slab are a future crack, and a court under heavy shade stays wet, grows algae and gets slick. Note where your downspouts discharge. Think about which neighbor’s bedroom window faces the spot you want to light. A new-build lot in Wentzville with a flat half acre is a different conversation from a sloped lot with a mature oak in the only open corner.
One more overlap worth catching early. If the flattest part of your lot is also where a future garage or addition would go, price the two together before you pour, because a slab is an awkward thing to demolish. Our look at what it costs to build a garage in St. Louis is a useful comparison if you’re weighing which project takes the good ground.
### What the next owner sees
A court is a taste amenity, and that cuts both ways. A well-built pad with a clean surface, straight joints, a hoop that still adjusts and water that clearly goes somewhere reads as a feature. Some buyers will love it outright. Others see a pad they can turn into a patio, a shop floor or a pickleball setup, which still counts as flexible square footage rather than a liability.
The other version is a cracked, weed-seamed slab with a rusted goal leaning over it and a green stripe where runoff crosses it. That’s not neutral. That’s a removal estimate in the buyer’s head, and demolition and haul-off of reinforced concrete isn’t cheap. Build it well or build it smaller. A modest pad done right ages better than an ambitious one done thin.
### Do you need a permit, and who else gets a say?
Depends entirely on where you live, and this metro is a patchwork of dozens of jurisdictions that don’t agree with each other. Whether a slab, a hoop footing, a fence or a light pole triggers a permit is set by your specific municipality, or by the county if you’re in an unincorporated area. Rules differ on impervious surface coverage, setbacks, fence height and electrical work.
Call your own city or county building department before you spend a dollar. Ask about the slab, the footing, the fence and any wiring as four separate questions, because the answer can be different for each. Ask about impervious coverage limits by name. Get whoever answers to tell you what drawing or site plan they want to see.
Then read your subdivision indentures, because in a lot of St. Louis neighborhoods the trustees are the stricter authority. HOA and subdivision covenants routinely regulate permanent structures, fence type and color, lighting, and sometimes the hoop itself. A project that sails through city review can still get stopped by a covenant from 1978. Better to find that out on a phone call than after the forms are set.
### What do the hoop, the footing, the fence and the lights add?
A real in-ground goal is a small foundation project of its own. The pole sits in a footing, or in an anchor sleeve set in a footing, dug below the local frost depth so seasonal freezing doesn’t heave it out of plumb. That footing usually gets poured before or separately from the slab, with an isolation joint around the pole so slab movement doesn’t torque it.
Ask about extension and backboard while you’re at it. The distance the backboard hangs out past the pole is what keeps a driving player from meeting steel, and the wider, thicker boards behave much better than the budget ones. Height adjustment is worth paying for if you have a seven-year-old, because a rim they can reach is a rim they use.
Fencing is the sleeper cost. Ball containment on the open sides saves you fifty trips into the neighbor’s hostas, and a half-height fence behind the baseline does most of the work of a full one for much less. Rebound netting on posts is a lighter, cheaper option that plenty of families prefer. Lighting means a trench, conduit, a licensed electrician and a real conversation about glare direction and hours. Lines can be painted on, inlaid in a coating system, or laid out in contrasting tile, and that choice is mostly about how permanent you want them.
Feeding the crew after? Try what to order at an Armenian restaurant.
### How do you pick someone to pour it?
Shortlist two or three contractors worth interviewing, then interview them. Not a bid-collecting exercise. An actual conversation in the yard, where you state plainly what you want and expect: this slab thickness, this reinforcement, a joint plan that keeps cuts out of the key, and a drainage solution you can point to on the ground.
Then compare what you asked for against what each one is prepared to deliver. The gap is the signal. Not the price. One contractor tells you why they want more stone than you expected on your particular soil, walks the low corner with you, and explains what they’ll do if they hit soft clay at eighteen inches. Another says concrete is concrete. You just learned something more useful than a number.
Look at their flatwork, in person, on jobs that have been through at least a couple of winters. Fresh concrete always looks good. Four-year-old concrete tells the truth. Ask who actually runs the crew and who’s finishing the surface. Confirm insurance.
