### At what age do kids stop having big birthday parties?
Somewhere around ten to twelve for most families, and the shift is financial as much as social. Whole-class parties are largely a preschool through third-grade phenomenon. After that, guest lists shrink to real friendships, which is exactly when the per-head math stops dominating and a different kind of spending takes over.
The early years are cheap per child and expensive in total. Twenty four-year-olds, a room, pizza, a host, favor bags. The later years invert it. Five twelve-year-olds at a ticketed activity with food afterward is a small guest list and a real per-person cost, because the activities kids want at that age carry adult prices. Fewer kids, pricier kids.
Teenagers change it again. By fourteen or fifteen the party is often a sleepover, a group outing or nothing at all, and the budget is mostly food. A family in Moscow Mills who spent a small fortune on a six-year-old’s party might spend a quarter of it eight years later and get a happier kid. That’s not a discipline story. It’s just what the arithmetic does when the guest list collapses to four people who actually matter to your child.
### How do you pick which place to book?
Shortlist two or three places worth interviewing, then call them and say plainly what you want: your head count, your run time, whether you can bring in your own food and cake, and what happens if fewer kids show than you booked. Compare each answer against what you asked for. The gap is the signal, not the price.
One place will hear “fourteen kids, two hours, I want to bring my own cake” and come back with a package that fits, a note about their minimum, a clear answer on the cake fee, and a question about whether parents are staying, because that changes the seating. Another will quote a per-child rate and stop talking. Both might run a fine party. Only one has told you they’ve hosted your party before.
Questions that earn their keep on that call: How many parties like mine do you do in a weekend? Does a staff host stay with us the whole time or just set up? Where do the parents sit? What’s your rain or closure policy? When exactly does my clock start? How late can I change the head count? That last one is the one that saves money, and the answer varies enormously from place to place.
Book earlier than feels necessary. Four to six weeks out is comfortable for most of the year, and a Saturday in spring or anywhere near a school break wants more like two months. Late bookings cost more, not because anyone raises the price, but because the cheap time slots go first and you end up taking the one that’s left.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is a good budget for a kids’ birthday party?
A.  Set it per child rather than as a lump sum. Decide what you’re comfortable spending on each kid, multiply by your realistic attend count, and let that be the ceiling. Most families find a home party lands near the low end and a booked package with food and favors lands two to three times higher. The per-head frame keeps the decision honest before you ever call a venue.
### Q. How many kids usually come to a birthday party?
A.  Fewer than you invite, and the gap widens with age. A common planning rule is to expect roughly two-thirds to three-quarters of invitations to turn into actual kids, lower during cold-and-flu season and on busy sports weekends. Build the budget on that number, not the invite count. Then confirm with the venue whether you’re billed on bookings or on who walks through the door.
### Q. How far in advance should I plan a kids birthday party?
A.  Four to six weeks covers most dates comfortably. Push to two months for spring Saturdays, anything near a school break, and popular time slots like late morning on a weekend. Invitations go out two to three weeks ahead so families can still get it on a calendar. Booking early doesn’t lower the rate, it just means you get the cheap slot instead of the leftover one.
### Q. Is 2 hours too short for a birthday party?
A.  No, two hours is the sweet spot for most children under about eight. Preschoolers often do better at ninety minutes. The party ends while everyone is still having a good time, which is how it gets remembered well, and it keeps you inside the block you paid for instead of triggering an extra-hour charge that often isn’t prorated.
### Q. How do I estimate party venue costs?
A.  Start from the structure, not the headline. Write down the base package price, the minimum child count, the per-child charge above that, the length of the block, the extra-hour rate, any service or setup fee, and the outside-food fee if you want your own cake. Multiply and add. That total, not the advertised starting rate, is the number to compare across two or three places.
### Q. How much of your budget should your venue be?
A.  Roughly a third to a half is a workable target when the venue is space only. If the package bundles food, drinks, a host and cleanup, expect it to swallow closer to two-thirds, and that can still be the cheaper path overall. Judge it by what the number includes. A high venue share with everything folded in often beats a low one with six separate invoices.
### Q. Do I have to invite the whole class?
A.  Some schools ask for it, most don’t require it, and the policy is worth checking before invitations go out. The common compromise is inviting every child of one gender, or a clearly defined small group, and handing those invitations out away from school. Given that nearly every party line is priced per head, this one decision moves more money than anything else you’ll choose.
### Q. What happens if fewer kids show up than I paid for?
A.  At most booked venues you still pay the minimum, because staffing and food were already set. A few will adjust down to a final count taken a day or two before, which is why the headcount deadline is one of the most valuable things to ask about on your first call. Book to the number you actually expect, not the number you hope for.

## What Boating Costs Near St. Louis and Who Needs a License
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-boating-costs-near-st-louis-and-who-needs-a-license
A pontoon has been sitting in a Byrnes Mill driveway since last September. Tarp on, tires low, cover sagging where the rain pooled and froze. The family bought it in May and got out on the water six times. Six. They still paid the slip fee for a season they half used, the winterizing bill in October, the registration renewal, and twelve months of insurance on a boat that spent seven of those months in a driveway.
That gap is the whole story. The purchase price is the number everybody researches, and it’s the number that matters least once the boat is yours. A season gets priced by storage, slip rent, winterizing, fuel, registration and insurance, and every one of those arrives on its own schedule whether you launched twenty times or twice.
Then there’s the legal question, which people usually ask second and should ask first. Missouri does not issue a boating license the way it issues a driver’s license. The rule is shaped differently, it’s keyed to when you were born, and the agency that runs it is not the one most people expect. This guide walks through that rule, the real shape of a season’s costs, renting versus owning, slip versus trailer, what winter does to a budget, and how to interview a marina before you hand anybody a deposit.
### Can you drive a boat without a license in Missouri?
Missouri doesn’t issue a recreational boating license. What it requires is a boater education card, the Boating Safety Identification Card, and the rule is tied to your date of birth rather than your age today. The Missouri State Highway Patrol administers it. Confirm the current cutoff and which waters are covered before you launch.
The wording matters more than it sounds like it should. People call it a license at the ramp, marina staff call it a license, and then somebody goes looking for a licensing office and finds nothing. There isn’t one. The card is an identification card showing you completed an approved boater education course and passed the test attached to it. It documents education. It isn’t a driving privilege the state scores points against.
Who needs one comes down to a birth date. Missouri sets a cutoff, and operators born after that date have to carry the card to run a motorboat or a personal watercraft on the waters the statute covers. People born before it are generally outside the requirement. We are deliberately not printing the cutoff year here, or the fee, or how long the card takes to arrive, because those are exactly the details that shift and exactly the details you don’t want from a blog post. Ask the Missouri State Highway Patrol, Water Patrol Division. They administer the card and theirs are the boats that pull alongside yours.
Four things worth asking them directly: the exact cutoff date, whether the water you plan to run is covered, what the card costs right now, and whether you have to have it physically aboard while you operate. That last one catches people. A card in a kitchen drawer at home is not a card on the boat.
The river cuts both ways here, too. The metro sits on two states, so a family launching from the Missouri side and a family launching near Roxana on the Illinois side are not reading the same rulebook. Illinois runs its own boating safety education requirement with its own terms. If you trailer across a bridge to launch, or keep the boat on one side and fish the other, check both states rather than assuming your Missouri paperwork travels with you.
### How do you actually get the boater education card?
You take a state-approved boater education course, pass the exam attached to it, and the card follows from that. Courses are generally offered online and in classroom form. The Missouri State Highway Patrol is the agency to confirm which providers are approved, what the current fee is, and how long issuance actually takes.
The course itself isn’t hard. It covers navigation rules, right of way, required safety equipment, what the buoys mean, how to tow a skier legally, and what happens when somebody gets hurt. Most of it is material you assumed you already knew, and a surprising share of that turns out to be wrong. Right of way in a narrow channel trips up nearly everyone.
Here is the part households miss: the requirement follows the operator, not the boat. If your teenager takes the wheel, if your brother-in-law runs the jet ski for an hour, if your spouse drives back to the ramp because you had a beer, each of those people is an operator. One card in the family does not cover the family. Sort that out in April, not in July with a patrol boat idling off your stern.
Ask about exemptions and short-term options as well. Rules like this usually carry carve-outs for supervised operation, for out-of-state visitors, and sometimes for temporary certificates. Whether any of them apply to your household, and on what terms, is a question for the Highway Patrol. It is not a question for a marina employee repeating what a customer told him last summer.
### What does a season on the water actually cost?
Far more than the payment. Storage or slip rent is usually the largest recurring line, winterizing is the one nobody budgets, and fuel, registration, insurance and routine maintenance fill in behind them. Those costs are mostly fixed. They don’t shrink because work got busy and you only launched three times.
Picture a boating year as two piles. The first pile is what it costs to have a boat: storage, slip, insurance, registration, winterizing, spring service, a battery, the fire extinguisher you replace because the gauge dropped. You pay that pile in full at zero trips. The second pile is what it costs to use a boat: fuel, ice, a prop you dinged on a gravel bar, a tow on the day everything goes sideways. That pile scales with use, and for most families it’s the smaller of the two.
We aren’t going to publish dollar ranges for the metro, because a covered slip, an outdoor gravel lot and a heated building are not the same product, and quoting one figure across them would mean inventing it. What holds almost everywhere is the ordering. Storage tends to lead. Winterizing and spring commissioning together often come second. Fuel runs third for a family pushing a big outboard, then insurance, then registration, with maintenance landing wherever the boat decides it should land that year.
Now divide. Take everything you spent last season and divide it by the number of days the boat was in the water. That number is the real price of a boating day, and the first time people run it honestly, it stings. Households plan on twenty-five days. Weather, work, a kid’s tournament schedule and one blown weekend in August turn twenty-five into eight. Eight isn’t a failure. It just tells you which side of the rent-versus-own line you belong on.
### Is a slip or a trailer the cheaper way to keep a boat?
A trailer is cheaper in cash and more expensive in friction. A slip costs more every month and buys back the one thing that decides whether a boat gets used: the twenty minutes between deciding to go and being underway. Which one fits depends on where you live and how spontaneous your boating really is.
### What a slip is actually buying
Convenience, mostly. Also dock power, somewhere to leave gear, and somebody who notices when your bilge pump has been running all night. Ask whether the fee is seasonal or annual, because that single difference moves the math more than the headline rate does. Ask what it includes: haul-out, winter layup, launch, pump-out, a parking pass for the truck. Ask what happens in a flood year, because the Mississippi and the Missouri both have opinions about docks, and a marina that has lived through it will tell you exactly what they did last time.
### What a trailer actually costs
Bearings, straps, lights that fail the week you need them, a tow vehicle rated for the load, and a launch ramp line on a Saturday morning in July. None of that is expensive by itself. Added up, it is the reason a driveway boat in Moscow Mills or Old Monroe gets used less than its owner swore it would. A family that has to hitch up, drive forty minutes, wait for a ramp, then do the whole sequence backwards at dusk will quietly decide, four or five weekends a summer, to stay home.
There’s an honest test for this. Count the trips you cancelled last year, then ask how many of them died at the hitch. If the answer is most of them, a slip isn’t an upgrade, it’s the thing that makes the boat worth owning. If the answer is none, keep the trailer and put the difference into fuel.
### Is it cheaper to rent a boat than to own one?
For metro families who get out fewer than roughly ten days a season, renting wins on arithmetic, and it isn’t close. Ownership starts making sense when that fixed pile of costs gets spread across enough days to shrink the per-day number, or when the boat is doing something no rental counter can do.
Rental pricing has a shape worth learning before you book. Expect a half-day and a full-day rate, a refundable deposit, fuel handled separately and billed on return, a damage waiver that may or may not be optional, and a hard return time with a late fee behind it. A captained option costs more and earns it the first time out, if nobody aboard has run that size of boat. Peer-to-peer rental platforms and membership clubs sit in the middle. You pay for access instead of ownership, and you give up leaving your gear in the boat.
Renting is also the honest way to find out what you want. Two afternoons in a pontoon and one in a deck boat teach a family more about their own preferences than six months of shopping. If those rentals turn into a decision to buy, the paperwork side of that purchase, titles, bill of sale, taxes and what to inspect, is a project of its own, and we walk through it in what to know before buying a used boat in Missouri.
The case for owning is real. It just isn’t financial. It’s the 6 a.m. Tuesday in October when the water is glass and nothing is open to rent. It’s the tackle that lives aboard. It’s fishing one stretch enough times to learn it, and if that’s the direction you’re headed, our roundup of good fishing spots around St. Louis is a reasonable place to start the season. If the plan is sightseeing rather than skiing, a day on the water pairs well with a drive up the river road, and the best stops along the Great River Road covers where to pull over.
Pricing a different family day? Here’s what paintball actually costs
### What happens to the boat between November and March?
It costs money while it sleeps. Winterizing protects the engine and the plumbing from freeze damage, storage protects the hull and the upholstery from weather, and skipping either one can turn a cheap winter into a cracked block in April. This is the line families forget entirely when they price a first boat.
### Winterizing, in plain terms
Water gets out, antifreeze goes in. A shop drains the cooling system, runs non-toxic antifreeze through it, changes engine oil and lower unit gear oil, fogs the cylinders, stabilizes the fuel, pulls the battery onto a trickle charger, and empties the livewell and freshwater lines. Then the boat gets covered or shrink-wrapped and blocked so the trailer tires aren’t carrying the whole load until spring. Some marinas fold this into the slip fee. Plenty don’t. Find out which before you sign, because assuming it’s included is one of the most common billing surprises boat owners run into.
### Storage, cheapest to most expensive
Your own driveway is free and the hardest on the boat, because nobody is watching the cover during a February ice storm. An outdoor lot is the common middle ground: fenced, gravel or asphalt, boats in rows, shrink wrap doing the work. Covered storage keeps snow load and sun off. Heated indoor space is the most expensive and the least stressful, and it’s also the option with a waiting list. A driveway in Truesdale and a heated building sit at opposite ends of both the price range and the risk range.
Can a boat live outside all winter? Yes, and most of them around here do. The conditions are that it’s properly winterized, that water can’t collect anywhere it can freeze, that the cover is tensioned to shed snow instead of holding a pond, and that something is keeping mice out of the upholstery and the wiring. Outdoor storage fails in the same three ways every year: a sagging cover, an undrained system, a rodent nest. None of those are really about temperature.
### The costs that arrive whether you launch or not
Registration, insurance, taxes and maintenance don’t care about your summer. They run on the calendar. A boat that never left the driveway still generated a renewal notice, an insurance premium, a tax bill, and a spring service that had to happen before anyone could safely use it.
Registration is the one people forget until an officer points at the numbers on the hull. Missouri registers boats and that registration has to be current. The title and tax side of ownership carries its own rules, which we handle in the buying guide instead of here. Insurance usually bills twelve months even though the season runs five or six, and it pays to ask your agent what is covered while the boat is in storage, on the trailer, and under tow, because those are three different exposures and one policy does not always treat them the same.
Maintenance is the variable that wrecks budgets. Impellers, plugs, belts, gear oil, a bellows on a sterndrive, trailer bearings, a battery every few years, and the spring commissioning that brings the boat back out of its winter state. Safety gear ages out too. Flares carry expiration dates and life jackets wear out. Add the small items across a season and they stop being small.
### How do you pick a marina or a storage yard?
Shortlist two or three, then interview them. Nobody in this business hands out an itemized written quote, and asking for three estimates gets you nowhere. What works is saying plainly what you need, then listening for the gap between that and what the yard is actually prepared to provide.
Say it out loud in the office. “I want to be in the water by the first weekend in May, out by the end of October, in and out maybe twice a season, winterizing done here, and I want to know what you did the last time the river came up.” Then stop talking. The yard that answers in order, names what it doesn’t do, and mentions a wait list before you ask about one is the yard worth a deposit.
Worth naming out loud: whether the slip fee is seasonal or annual and what happens if you leave mid-season; whether winterizing and shrink wrap are included, optional, or required through their own shop; how in-and-out works and whether each one costs extra; who carries liability while the boat sits; what the flood plan is and how long boats were unusable the last time it mattered; and whether covered or indoor space has a waiting list, since that space tends to fill in late summer for the following winter rather than in November.
The gap is the signal, not the price. A yard that tells you plainly it doesn’t do engine work and points you toward a mobile mechanic has told you something useful. A yard that says yes to every question, fast, has told you something as well.

And if you run the marina, the rental fleet, the storage yard or the mobile repair truck, being the one people and AI assistants name first is the game, so list your boating business.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much does it cost to get a boater’s license in Missouri?
A.  There isn’t a license to buy. There’s a boater education card, and its cost has two parts: whatever the approved course provider charges, and whatever the state charges to issue the card. Provider pricing varies, and some run free or discounted courses. For the current issuing fee, ask the Missouri State Highway Patrol rather than trusting a figure you found online.
### Q. How long does it take to get a boating license in Missouri?
A.  Two separate clocks run here. The course and exam can often be finished in a single sitting online, while classroom sessions follow a schedule and may only be offered on certain dates. Then comes issuance, which depends on state processing and on whether temporary proof is available in the meantime. Confirm both timelines with the Missouri State Highway Patrol before you count on a specific weekend.
### Q. Is it cheaper to buy or rent a boat?
A.  Renting is cheaper for anyone getting out fewer than roughly ten days a season, because ownership costs run whether you launch or not. Storage, slip rent, insurance, registration and winterizing all bill on the calendar. Ownership wins on cost only once those fixed expenses get divided across enough days, or when you need the boat at hours no rental counter is open.
### Q. How much does it cost to store a 20 foot boat?
A.  Storage type drives the price far more than length does. An outdoor gravel lot, a covered rack and a heated indoor building are three different products at three very different rates, and shrink wrap is usually billed on top of the space. Facility pricing in the metro also moves year to year, so call two or three yards, ask what is included, and compare those answers rather than averages.
### Q. Can a boat be left outside in the winter?
A.  Yes, and most boats around the metro are. The conditions are that it’s properly winterized, that every system holding water is drained or filled with antifreeze, that the cover or shrink wrap is tensioned to shed snow instead of pooling it, and that something is keeping rodents out. Outdoor storage fails from sagging covers, trapped water and mice, not from cold air.
### Q. How much is a boat slip usually?
A.  Slips price by length, by whether the dock is covered, by amenities like power and pump-out, and by how the marina bills, since some charge seasonally and others annually. Those variables swing the number widely enough that published averages are close to meaningless. Get current pricing from the specific marinas you would actually use, and ask what each fee includes before comparing them.
### Q. Does my Missouri card cover me if I launch on the Illinois side?
A.  Don’t assume it does. Illinois maintains its own boating safety education requirement, separate from Missouri’s, and the metro straddles both states, so which ramp you back down matters. States often recognize each other’s certificates, but the terms differ and they change. Confirm with the Missouri State Highway Patrol and with the Illinois boating authority before you trailer across a bridge.
### Q. What does winterizing a boat actually include?
A.  Draining the cooling system and running non-toxic antifreeze through it, changing engine oil and lower unit gear oil, fogging the cylinders, stabilizing fuel, pulling and charging the battery, emptying livewells and freshwater lines, then covering or shrink-wrapping the boat and blocking it so the trailer tires aren’t loaded all winter. Ask whether your marina includes it in the slip fee. Plenty don’t.

## What Makes a Restaurant a Brasserie in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-makes-a-restaurant-a-brasserie-in-st-louis
Zinc bar, mirrors on every wall, a waiter carrying four plates up one arm. That’s the picture most people keep for the word brasserie, and it isn’t wrong. It’s backwards. The look is a consequence. Something else is the cause.
What actually makes a brasserie a brasserie is a schedule. The doors open late morning and stay open, and the same full menu runs straight through to late at night. No shutdown at 2:30. No separate dinner card appearing at five. No sign taped inside the glass promising the kitchen reopens at 5:30. One menu, every hour the lights are on.
That single habit explains the rest of the room. Continuous service needs a bar people can eat a full dinner at, tables light enough to push together on ten seconds’ notice, a printed menu nobody rewrites each morning, and a kitchen built to send the same forty dishes at 11:15 in the morning and again at 10:45 at night. Pull that one thread and the bentwood chairs, the crushed ice full of oysters and the beer taps all come along behind it.
### What makes a restaurant a brasserie?
A brasserie is defined by its service model, not its menu. It serves one full menu all day, with no break between lunch and dinner, and it keeps a wide, steady list of classics. The all-day kitchen is the rule. The zinc bar, the beer and the steak frites follow from it.
Hold that against how most restaurants run. A kitchen closes after lunch, the line goes home, prep happens behind a locked door, and a different crew comes back for dinner with a different menu. It’s efficient. It also leaves a hole in the day about four hours wide, right where travelers, shift workers and anybody who ate breakfast at six end up hungry.
A brasserie fills that hole on purpose. Staffing runs continuous, the menu is broad enough to cover a light appetite and a heavy one off the same sheet, and the dishes are chosen because they hold up to being fired at any hour. That’s why the classics repeat from one brasserie to the next. They travel well across a fourteen-hour service.
Size follows from there. Brasseries run big, often far bigger than the small room down the block, because long hours only pay when the space can hold a crowd at the peaks. Big room, long hours, broad menu. Those three arrive as a set, and you rarely get one without the other two.
### Why does brasserie mean brewery?
Because it literally does. The word comes from the French verb brasser, to brew, and a brasserie was a brewery: a place that made beer and sold food alongside it. The restaurant format kept the name long after most of them stopped brewing, which is why beer, not only wine, sits at the center of the thing.
The Paris version took its modern shape in the late 1800s. After the Franco-Prussian War of 1870 to 1871 and the loss of Alsace-Lorraine, Alsatian families moved west into Paris and brought their beer halls with them. Big rooms. Beer on tap. Sausages. And choucroute garnie, which is sauerkraut cooked long with pork and served hot on a platter meant for sharing.
Those dishes are still printed on brasserie menus today, and now you know why. They aren’t Parisian at all. They’re Alsatian, and they arrived with a wave of people who needed somewhere to work.
The useful takeaway sits on the drinks list. A room that calls itself a brasserie and treats beer as an afterthought has kept the word and dropped the reason for it. Real draft taps. A beer list with some thought in it. Glassware that isn’t a shaker pint borrowed from the sports bar. Those are the honest signs, and they cost nothing to check from the doorway.
### What does a brasserie room tell you before you sit down?
Read the room from the entrance. Nearly every physical signature of a brasserie exists to solve a problem that all-day service creates, so each one you spot is evidence the format is real and not just a word painted on the awning.
### The bar you can eat at
A long bar with stools, place settings and menus sitting on it, not a holding pen for people waiting on a table. That’s the tell. A brasserie bar is a dining room in miniature, the spot where a solo diner lands at 4:10 and gets exactly what the tables get. No cutlery on the bar usually means service isn’t truly continuous.
### Mirrors, banquettes and bentwood chairs
Mirrors go up because they double a loud, crowded room visually and let people watch it without craning around. Banquettes run the perimeter because a bench seats two or six equally well with no rearranging. Bentwood chairs are light enough for a server to move one-handed while carrying a tray in the other. It’s all chosen for a floor that reconfigures itself twenty times a day.
### Paper over the tablecloth
White cloth with butcher paper laid over it is a turnover device. Clear the plates, roll the paper, reset in seconds instead of minutes. Some rooms skip the cloth and go straight to paper. Either way it signals a house that expects to seat you quickly and seat somebody else after you, without ever once making you feel rushed.
### Ice, shellfish and a chalkboard
A bed of ice near the door with oysters and crab on it does two jobs. It advertises to the sidewalk, and it announces that a raw bar station runs independently of the hot line, which is precisely how a kitchen keeps food moving through the slow middle hours. The chalkboard beside it usually carries today’s oysters, the plat du jour, or whatever’s open by the glass.
### What is actually on a brasserie menu?
Long, printed and stable. Expect a page or two of dishes that barely move from season to season, a short separate list of daily specials, and a drinks list where beer gets real estate instead of a footnote. Breadth is the whole point, because one sheet has to handle every appetite the clock throws at it.
The recurring cast is remarkably consistent from one brasserie to the next. Oysters and tiered shellfish platters. Charcuterie and pâté. Onion soup under a lid of melted cheese. Frisée salad with lardons and a poached egg. Steak frites in a couple of cuts. Roast chicken. Mussels with a cone of fries. Choucroute and sausages. Croque monsieur. An omelet. A whole fish. Duck confit. Then crème brûlée, profiteroles and a fruit tart.
Nothing on that list surprises anybody, and that’s deliberate. A brasserie sells reliability as much as it sells food. You can walk into one you’ve never seen, in a city you don’t know, order steak frites, and have a fair idea of what arrives and roughly how long it takes.
### What a bistro menu does instead
The opposite play. Short menu, often handwritten or chalked, changed often, shaped by what the chef bought this week and by a kitchen with fewer hands in it. Six mains, not thirty. Fixed lunch and dinner services with the door shut between them. Smaller room, tighter tables, far more of one person’s personality on the plate.
Which is better? Wrong question. They solve different problems. A bistro rewards you for turning up when it’s serving. A brasserie rewards you for turning up whenever you finally got free. For how a French menu is built course by course, and for where to actually eat French food around the metro, our guide to French restaurants and dining in St. Louis handles that ground properly.
### How do you tell a brasserie from a bistro or a café?
One question sorts all three. What happens at three in the afternoon? A brasserie is serving its full menu to whoever walks in. A bistro is dark, or between services with the chairs still up. A café is open and busy, but the kitchen is limited to light food, if it’s cooking anything at all.
### Brasserie
Large room. Continuous all-day service. Long printed menu that stays put. A beer program with real taps behind it. A bar where a full dinner is normal. Late close. Walk-ins absorbed as routine rather than as a favor, because the floor plan was drawn expecting them.
### Bistro
Small room. Fixed lunch and dinner blocks. Short menu that changes. Wine-led rather than beer-led. The chef’s hand visible in every dish. Reservations carry more weight here, and the last seating is often earlier than visitors expect.
### Café
Drinks first, food second. Long hours, but a light kitchen: a sandwich, a croque, a salad, pastry under a dome. Tables turn on coffee, not on entrees. Nobody minds if you sit for two hours with one cup and a notebook. That tolerance is the format’s actual product.
Names get used loosely everywhere, in France and here both. A room can call itself a bistro and run like a brasserie, or the reverse. Look at the posted hours and the length of the menu before you trust the word on the sign. Those two facts tell you more in thirty seconds than the name ever will.
Different counter, same idea: what police supply stores sell
### What is an American brasserie, and how does it differ?
An American brasserie keeps the look and the classics, then quietly rebuilds the engine. The most common change is also the most important one: all-day service gets trimmed back into a lunch block and a dinner block, because paying a kitchen to stand through a dead afternoon is expensive labor almost everywhere in this country.
That isn’t a knock on the restaurants doing it. It’s arithmetic. But it does mean the word on the awning makes a weaker promise here than it does in Paris, so check the hours before anybody drives anywhere.
### What usually gets added
Brunch, which barely exists as a French brasserie service, becomes a major weekend event here. The beer list grows local and much longer. Oysters migrate into a happy hour. Produce and meat get sourced regionally, so the salad follows a Missouri growing season rather than a French one. Portions run larger. Sometimes there’s a burger, which no Paris brasserie of 1900 would recognize.
### What usually gets kept
Steak frites survives everything. So do mussels, onion soup, roast chicken and the raw bar. The room signatures travel intact: the zinc-look bar, the mirrors, the banquettes, the globe lights, the bentwood chairs. And the walk-in friendliness usually survives too, which for a large group turns out to be the single most useful thing the format offers.
Here’s the test, and it takes one phone call. Ask whether the kitchen is serving at 3:30 on a Tuesday. Yes means you’re dealing with the real format and can plan around it. No means you’re in a French-American restaurant with brasserie styling, which can be genuinely excellent and is still a different animal with different rules.
### How should you actually use a brasserie?
Use it for the meals other restaurants can’t take. That’s the practical value of the whole format. Odd hours, unplanned group sizes, solo dinners with no apology attached, and nights that keep going after every other kitchen in town has scraped down the flat top.
### The odd-hour meal
You get out of a long appointment at 3:15 having eaten a gas station coffee and nothing else. Everything good is dark until five. That afternoon is what a brasserie is for, and it’s the better call physically too, since a real plate at 3:30 beats a bag of chips now and a wrecked appetite at eight.
### The solo dinner at the bar
Eating alone at a brasserie bar with the full menu and a beer in front of you is completely unremarkable, which is not true in most rooms. Nobody keeps glancing at the empty stool beside you. Service tends to run faster there, and the bartender is usually the best-informed person in the building about what came in good today.
### The group that didn’t call ahead
Nine people, no reservation, 7:40 on a Friday. Most kitchens simply can’t help you. A brasserie often can, because the room is large, the tables are light and built to push together, and the menu already spans enough ground to feed a table where one person is vegetarian, two want steak, and a seven-year-old will eat fries and nothing else.
### After the show, and the long way home
Late service is the format’s other quiet superpower. Theater, a concert, a shift that finally ended at ten, a drive back into town from Brooklyn on the Illinois side with everyone in the car too hungry to argue about it. The brasserie is frequently the last room still sending out full plates. Building a whole evening around one? Our date night restaurant guide is a useful companion for pacing the night.
### The mismatched table
Two people want entirely different meals. One wants a dozen oysters, a beer and nothing further. The other wants steak, fries and a glass of red. That combination is an ordinary Tuesday for a brasserie and a small crisis for a tasting-menu room. If the steak itself is the whole point of the night, though, how to pick a steakhouse is the better read, because a brasserie steak and a steakhouse steak are aiming at different targets.
### Where the format shows up around here
St. Louis is a beer town with a long German and Alsatian streak running through it, which makes the brasserie idea less foreign here than it sounds. The format needs a big room, a working bar and a kitchen willing to stay lit, so it turns up where those three things already exist: converted corner buildings, old halls, rooms near a theater or a hotel. Drivers coming in through St. John, Vinita Park, Cool Valley or Maplewood Park pass plenty of buildings shaped exactly right for it.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is a bistro vs. a brasserie?
A.  A bistro is small and chef-driven, with a short menu that changes and fixed lunch and dinner services. A brasserie is large, runs one long printed menu all day without closing in between, and treats beer as seriously as wine. The menus overlap heavily. Size and hours are the difference you can actually verify.
### Q. What kind of food is served in a brasserie?
A.  Hearty French classics off a long, stable menu. Oysters and shellfish platters, charcuterie and pâté, onion soup, frisée salad, steak frites, roast chicken, mussels with fries, choucroute and sausages carried over from Alsace, croque monsieur, omelets, a whole fish. Dessert runs to crème brûlée, profiteroles and fruit tarts. Beer belongs with all of it.
### Q. Why are French restaurants called brasserie?
A.  Most aren’t. Brasserie names one specific format, and the word means brewery, from brasser, to brew. Places that brewed beer and served food with it kept the name after the brewing stopped. Alsatian families opened them across Paris in the late 1800s, which is why beer, sausages and choucroute still anchor the menu today.
### Q. What is an American brasserie?
A.  A French brasserie adapted to American operations. Same room signatures, same core classics, usually with a longer local beer list, a serious weekend brunch, regional sourcing and bigger portions. The most common divergence is hours: many US versions split lunch and dinner instead of running the kitchen straight through the afternoon.
### Q. What is a casual French eatery called?
A.  Several words, and they aren’t interchangeable. Bistro means a small, casual, chef-led room with a short menu. Brasserie means a large all-day room with a long menu and beer. Café means coffee first and light food second. Bouchon is the Lyon version, meat-heavy and very much its own thing.
### Q. How is brasserie pronounced?
A.  In French it’s roughly brah-suh-REE, three syllables, weight landing on the last one, with a soft s rather than a z sound. Americans commonly say bra-suh-REE or brass-uh-REE and nobody blinks. The plural, brasseries, sounds identical in French. Saying it confidently matters more than saying it perfectly.
### Q. Can you eat at a brasserie in the middle of the afternoon?
A.  At a true brasserie, yes, and that’s the defining feature. The same full menu runs from late morning until late at night with no gap. Plenty of American versions split lunch and dinner, so check the posted hours or call and ask straight out whether the kitchen serves at 3:30 on a weekday.
### Q. Is a brasserie a good choice for a large group?
A.  Usually one of the best in town. Large rooms, light tables designed to push together, staff accustomed to walk-ins, and a menu wide enough that ten people with ten different appetites all find something. Call ahead when you can. Show up anyway when you can’t, because this format absorbs unplanned groups better than nearly any other.

## What to Order at a British Pub in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-order-at-a-british-pub-in-st-louis
A slab of battered fish hanging off both ends of the plate, a heap of chips under it, and a small pot of something green that nobody at the table ordered on purpose. That’s the British pub meal most Americans remember. The rest of the menu is where the interesting food hides.
British pub cooking gets flattened here into fish and chips plus a burger. The actual list is longer and a lot stranger. Pies with the gravy built in. Sausages named for the sound they made in a wartime frying pan. A boiled egg wrapped in sausage meat and fried. Cheese on toast with a national name attached. Puddings that are not dessert, and one pudding that is made of blood.
None of it is hard to order once the words stop lying to you. That’s the whole job here. A British menu uses plain English to name things an American reader will guess wrong about, and about ten minutes of translation turns a confusing page into an obvious one.
### What is typical British pub food in St. Louis?
Typical British pub food means fish and chips, bangers and mash, meat pies like steak and ale or shepherd’s pie, a full English breakfast, Scotch eggs, and a ploughman’s plate of cheese, bread and pickle. Sunday roast shows up weekly. Cask ale, cider and tea sit alongside it.
Pub is a format, not a cuisine. A public house sells drink first and food second, and the food grew up around that order of business. Small kitchen. Long hours. Dishes that hold well and go out fast. Braises, pies, fried fish, cold plates, a pot of something with mashed potato baked on top. That constraint explains the menu better than any history lesson does. If the line between a pub and a bar still feels blurry, what makes a pub different from a bar lays out the difference.
Around the St. Louis metro, a British-style pub almost always runs two menus stapled into one. Half is genuinely British. The other half exists because a table of six will want wings, a quesadilla and a burger, and no owner wants that argument at seven on a Friday night. Read past the second half.
The British half is where a room shows its hand. A kitchen making its own pie filling, baking Yorkshire puddings to order, and leaving malt vinegar on the table instead of keeping it behind the bar is a kitchen that means it. All three of those are visible from your seat before you order a thing.
### What is the most popular food at a British pub?
Fish and chips, and it isn’t close. Nearly every British pub in America leads with it, and it anchors the menu at home too. Cod or haddock in a beer batter, thick-cut chips, malt vinegar on the side, tartar sauce, and mushy peas if the kitchen cares enough to make them.
The batter is the tell. Beer batter fried properly comes out pale gold and hollow-sounding, and it cracks when your fork goes in rather than bending. Heavy, dark, dense coating usually means the oil was too cool or the fish sat too long under a heat lamp. Ask for it fried to order if the room is slow. Most kitchens will say yes.
Cod gives you big flakes and a mild, clean flavor. Haddock is slightly sweeter and finer-grained, and a lot of British eaters swear by it. Some places offer plaice or pollock. Either of the first two is a safe first order.
### The chips, and what goes on them
Chips are not fries. They’re cut thick, cooked twice, and built to stay soft inside so they can soak up vinegar without collapsing. Skinny, crisp, salted fries are a fine thing and a different thing. A pub serving matchstick fries with its fish has made a choice, and it usually tells you which half of the menu the kitchen actually loves.
Malt vinegar goes on the chips, generously, which surprises first-timers. Salt after. Curry sauce is a legitimate chip-shop tradition, mild and thick and faintly sweet, and it shows up on some American pub menus as a side. Gravy on chips is also real. Nobody in Britain would blink.
### What else sells out first
Bangers and mash runs a steady second: fresh pork sausages, a mound of mashed potato, and onion gravy poured over everything. Pies come next, usually steak and ale or chicken and mushroom, sometimes a shepherd’s pie that is not a pie at all. And on Sundays, the roast. A good Sunday roast is the single best reason to plan around a pub’s schedule rather than your own.
### What do the confusing words on a British pub menu mean?
Six or seven words do almost all the damage. Pudding, chips, crisps, pie, pickle, rarebit and jacket. Each one means something different from what an American reader assumes, and each mistake sends the wrong plate to the table. Learn these and the menu stops being a puzzle.
### Pudding does not mean dessert
Pudding is a category, not a flavor. Yorkshire pudding is a puffed, hollow popover baked in hot beef drippings and served with roast beef and gravy. Black pudding is a sliced blood sausage, dark and mineral and faintly spiced, usually fried for breakfast. White pudding is its milder cousin, made with oatmeal and fat and no blood. Steak and kidney pudding is a savory filling steamed inside a suet crust.
Then there’s sticky toffee pudding, which is a dessert: a dark date sponge drowned in toffee sauce, usually with cream or vanilla ice cream. Spotted dick is a steamed sponge with dried fruit. Both are desserts. The word just refuses to pick a lane.
### Chips, crisps and jacket potatoes
Chips are thick fries. Crisps are what Americans call chips, and they come in flavors that sound made up until you try them: prawn cocktail, salt and vinegar, cheese and onion. A jacket potato is a baked potato, split and loaded, most often with beans and cheese or tuna and sweetcorn. Order one at lunch. It is more satisfying than it sounds.
### Shepherd’s pie is lamb, cottage pie is beef
This one matters. Shepherd’s pie is minced lamb with vegetables under a layer of mashed potato, browned on top. Cottage pie is the same construction with beef. Neither has pastry. If a menu offers shepherd’s pie and the server says it is made with beef, that is a cottage pie wearing a more familiar name, and plenty of American kitchens do exactly that.
Real pies do have pastry. Steak and ale is the workhorse, slow-braised beef in dark gravy under a lid of shortcrust or puff. A proper pie has a bottom crust too, not just a hat. Chicken and mushroom, steak and kidney, and pork pies round out the family. A Cornish pasty is a hand pie, crimped along one edge, filled with beef, potato, onion and swede, which is what the British call a rutabaga.
### Ploughman’s, Scotch eggs and the cold plates
A ploughman’s lunch is a composed cold plate: a wedge of sharp cheddar, crusty bread, butter, pickled onion, and a spoonful of brown pickle, which is a chunky sweet-sour chutney rather than anything resembling a dill spear. Ham, apple slices and a hard-boiled egg often join in. It is widely described as a mid-twentieth-century marketing invention rather than an old farm tradition, so treat the romance with a little salt and enjoy the cheese.
A Scotch egg is a soft or hard-boiled egg wrapped in seasoned sausage meat, breaded and fried. Pork scratchings are fried pork rind, aggressively salty, meant to be eaten standing up with a pint in your other hand.
### Toad in the hole, bubble and squeak, Welsh rarebit
Three names that sound like jokes and describe real food. Toad in the hole is sausages baked into Yorkshire pudding batter, served with onion gravy, and it is the best cold-night order on most British menus. Bubble and squeak is leftover mashed potato and cabbage fried together into a crisp-edged cake, traditionally a Monday dish built from Sunday’s roast. Welsh rarebit is a thick, savory cheese sauce loosened with ale and sharpened with mustard, broiled on toast until it blisters. Not a sandwich. Not grilled cheese. Better than both.
### What’s the difference between a full Irish breakfast and a full English breakfast?
The puddings and the bread. A full Irish usually puts white pudding on the plate next to the black, and it leans on soda bread or a potato farl. A full English leans on toast or fried bread and gives baked beans more prominence. Everything else largely overlaps.
Here is the standard English plate. Two fried eggs. Back bacon, which is cut from the loin and comes out meaty and round rather than as the thin streaky strips Americans grew up on. Pork sausages. Baked beans in a mild tomato sauce, which are not sweet like American baked beans and are much better for it. A grilled tomato half. Mushrooms cooked down in butter. Black pudding. Buttered toast or a slice of fried bread. Sometimes a hash brown, which is a recent and popular intruder. Tea.
Brown sauce goes on it. That is HP or a store-brand equivalent, tangy and fruity and vinegary, and it belongs on the sausage and the bacon. Ketchup on a full English is a live argument in Britain and nobody will stop you.
The Irish plate swaps in soda bread, sometimes adds a boxty or a potato cake, and treats the two puddings as the centerpiece. Scotland does its own version with a tattie scone and sometimes a square sausage. Wales adds laverbread, a seaweed paste cooked with oatmeal, which is genuinely good and almost never shows up here.
One practical note. A full English is a two-hour breakfast and a ruined lunch plan. Order it when the day after has nothing scheduled. If you are hunting for morning food more broadly, how to find good breakfast and brunch in St. Louis covers the wider field.
Different receipt, same homework: what a bike tune-up costs in St. Louis.
### What should you drink with a plate like that?
Cask ale if the pub pulls it, cider if it doesn’t, tea if it is morning. A British pint is 20 imperial fluid ounces, roughly 568 milliliters, which is a fifth larger than the 16-ounce American pint. That difference catches people out by round three.
### Cask ale, and why it is not warm
Cask ale is unfiltered, unpasteurized beer that finishes fermenting in the container it is served from, pulled by a hand pump instead of pushed by gas. That is why it arrives soft and lightly carbonated rather than fizzy. It is served at cellar temperature, meaning cool, not warm and not ice cold. Cold mutes flavor. A bitter served at cellar temperature tastes of bread crust, orchard fruit and dried leaves, and the same beer served at refrigerator temperature tastes of almost nothing.
Look for the tall, curved handles behind the bar. Those are beer engines, and a pub that installed them is signaling something about how seriously it takes this. A half pint is a completely normal order if you want to try two.
### Cider, shandy and everything else
British cider is dry, still or lightly sparkling, and tastes like apples rather than candy. It cuts through fried fish beautifully. A shandy is beer mixed with lemonade, and British lemonade means clear lemon soda, so a shandy lands closer to a beer spritz than to anything sweet. Pimm’s Cup shows up in summer, heavy on cucumber and mint. Black tea with milk is the default non-alcoholic order and the correct partner for a breakfast plate.
### Ordering at the bar, the way it actually goes
In Britain you order at the bar and pay right then. No host stands at the door. No server appears at your table to take a drink order. You find a seat, note the table number, walk up, order food and drink together, pay, and carry your glasses back yourself. That single habit is the biggest adjustment for American visitors.
There is no formal line at the bar, but there is absolutely a queue, and everyone in it knows the order. The bartender tracks who arrived when. Wait to be seen. Do not wave money, do not snap, do not lean over somebody mid-order. Buying in rounds is standard among a group, and when your turn comes you cover everyone. Tipping is not customary for drinks, though offering the bartender one for themselves is an old and appreciated gesture.
American British-style pubs mostly do not run this way. Almost all of them use table service with a check at the end, and normal American tipping applies. Some hybrid rooms take drinks at the bar and food at the table. Watch what other tables are doing for thirty seconds before deciding. It is the fastest read in the room.
One more thing worth knowing. Closing time in a traditional pub is announced, often with a bell and a last call, and the kitchen shuts well before the bar does. If food is the point of the trip, aim early rather than late.
### Where the British plate turns up around St. Louis
The format needs three things: a long bar, a kitchen willing to braise, and a room dark enough to feel like evening at four in the afternoon. Those show up in old corner buildings and converted storefronts all over the metro, not just downtown. Somebody driving in from Caseyville or Bunker Hill passes a dozen buildings shaped exactly right for it.
The British influence here is quieter than the German one, and it shows up in pieces rather than whole rooms. A Scotch egg on a bar menu in Wellston. A steak and ale pie as a winter special. Sunday roast advertised on a chalkboard in Wilbur Park, gone by three. A Black Jack kitchen doing a full English on weekends and calling it a British breakfast so people know what they are getting.
Call before you drive. Sunday roast is the one dish worth confirming by phone, because kitchens run out and they do not restock. Weekend British breakfast service is similarly limited, and if that is the mission, our breakfast and brunch guide is a useful second stop for planning the morning.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are some classic British pub dishes?
A.  Fish and chips, bangers and mash with onion gravy, steak and ale pie, shepherd’s pie, cottage pie, toad in the hole, Sunday roast with Yorkshire pudding, a ploughman’s lunch, Scotch eggs, jacket potatoes, bubble and squeak, Welsh rarebit, Cornish pasties, and sticky toffee pudding for dessert. Most are braised, baked or fried, because that is what a small pub kitchen does well.
### Q. Why do they call it bangers and mash?
A.  Banger is slang for sausage, and the usual explanation traces to wartime rationing, when sausages were padded out with water and rusk filler. Heated in a hot pan, the trapped moisture turned to steam and the casings burst with an audible pop. The nickname stuck long after the recipes improved. Treat the origin story as widely repeated rather than firmly documented.
### Q. What kind of sausage is bangers and mash?
A.  Fresh pork sausage, uncured and unsmoked, with breadcrumb or rusk worked into the mix so the texture stays tender rather than springy. Cumberland is the peppery version, often sold in a long coil. Lincolnshire is seasoned heavily with sage. Both are mild by American standards and both want onion gravy poured over them.
### Q. What is the American equivalent of bangers?
A.  A fresh bratwurst is the closest widely available match, similar in size, pale color and soft texture, though a brat is usually coarser and less bready. Breakfast sausage links share the seasoning but not the scale. Smoked kielbasa and fennel-heavy Italian sausage are both wrong, because bangers are raw when you buy them and mild when you eat them.
### Q. What are the unwritten rules of etiquette in a British pub?
A.  Order at the bar and pay immediately. Respect the invisible queue and wait your turn without waving cash. Buy in rounds and cover everyone when it is your turn. Carry your own glasses, return the empties, and do not block the serving area. Tipping is not expected on drinks. American British-style pubs mostly use table service, so normal tipping applies here.
### Q. What is the American version of a full English breakfast?
A.  The diner platter. Eggs any style, streaky bacon or sausage links, hash browns or home fries, buttered toast, and bottomless coffee. The structure matches: protein, starch, egg, bread, hot drink. What goes missing is black pudding, baked beans, the grilled tomato and the mushrooms, and the bacon switches from meaty back cuts to thin crisp strips.
### Q. Is a Scotch egg served hot or cold?
A.  Traditionally cold, as portable picnic and travel food, with the yolk cooked through. Modern pubs mostly serve them warm from the fryer with a jammy, barely-set yolk, cut in half and plated with mustard or a brown sauce. Both versions are correct. The warm one is harder to make and noticeably better, so order it that way when a kitchen offers it.
### Q. What are mushy peas, and are they worth ordering?
A.  Dried marrowfat peas soaked overnight and cooked down until they collapse into a thick, grassy puree, sometimes with mint or butter stirred through. They are not mashed English peas and they are not sweet. Treat them as a condiment rather than a vegetable side, spooned onto the fish or the chips. Yes, order them once.

## What Commercial Building Maintenance Covers and Costs
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-commercial-building-maintenance-covers-and-costs-in-st-louis
Six-fifteen on a Tuesday, and one corner of the lobby carpet is still damp. Trash gone. Glass clean. Somebody was in the building at eleven the night before and you never saw them, which is exactly the point. Then the invoice shows up with one line on it: MONTHLY SERVICE. That line is where the arguments start.
A maintenance agreement gets sold like a single product. It isn’t one. It’s a stack of separate jobs with separate labor rates bundled into one number, and the bundle shifts from company to company. Two proposals for the same 12,000-square-foot office can land far apart and both be honest, because one carries restroom supplies and quarterly hard-floor work and the other quietly doesn’t.
So the question worth asking isn’t what it costs. It’s what sits inside the number, what drops out the second something breaks, and who eats the 2 a.m. call about water running down a stairwell. Answer those three and the pricing stops feeling like a guess.
### How much does building maintenance cost in St. Louis?
Rates aren’t published, and building maintenance in St. Louis gets quoted four ways: a flat monthly contract for recurring janitorial and preventive work, per square foot for cleaning, per visit for scheduled service, and hourly for reactive repair calls. Square footage, floor type, traffic, restroom count, frequency and after-hours access move the number.
Nobody posts a rate card, and there’s a reason for that. A quote gets built from a walkthrough. How many square feet, how many restrooms, what the floors are made of, how many nights a week, what time a crew can get in the door, and whether you or the vendor buys the paper towels. Move any one of those and the price moves with it. A published number would be wrong for almost every building that read it.
### The flat monthly contract
One number, every month, for a defined list of recurring work. Nightly or three-nights-a-week janitorial, filter changes on a schedule, lamp replacement, a quarterly walk of the roof. Predictable for your budget and predictable for their scheduling, which is why most vendors push it. The risk is vagueness. A flat fee attached to a loose scope is a flat fee attached to nothing.
### Per square foot
Standard for cleaning, usually written as a monthly rate per cleanable square foot. Cleanable is the operative word. Stairwells, mechanical rooms and a warehouse mezzanine are not the same work as open office carpet, and a serious bidder measures what the crew will actually touch instead of copying a number off your lease.
### Per visit
Used for anything scheduled but not constant. Window washing, carpet extraction, strip and wax, gutter clearing, spring and fall HVAC changeovers. Priced per occurrence, so frequency is the lever you control. Four extraction visits a year instead of two is a real budget decision, not a technicality.
### Hourly, for reactive work
The one that surprises people. Repairs outside the scope get billed by the hour, usually with a minimum, and usually at a higher rate nights, weekends and holidays. Parts are separate. If your building is older and things break, this is the line that decides whether the year came in on plan.
Most real agreements mix all four. Flat monthly for the recurring, per visit for the periodic, hourly for the surprises. That’s normal and it’s fine. What matters is knowing which bucket every task lives in before you sign, because the tasks nobody assigned are the ones that turn into an emergency invoice in February.
### What is bundled into a contract, and what gets billed separately?
The bundle is smaller than most owners assume. Recurring, predictable, low-skill-mix work goes inside the monthly fee. Anything that needs a specialty license, a lift, a permit, or a part with a real price tag on it comes out and gets billed on its own. That split is the entire negotiation.
### Usually inside the monthly fee
Trash and recycling pulls. Vacuuming and dust mopping. Restroom cleaning and restocking. Breakroom wipe-down. Glass at entry doors and interior partitions. High and low dusting on a rotation. Lamp and ballast swaps at ordinary ceiling heights. Filter changes. Belt checks. Visual inspection of the roof, the exterior and the mechanical room, with a written note back to you. Salt and shovel work at the entrances, sometimes. Minor plumbing, like a flush valve or a faucet cartridge.
### Usually billed separately
Hard-floor refinishing. Carpet extraction. Window washing above the first floor. Parking lot sweeping, striping and sealcoating. Full snow plowing, which is nearly always its own contract with its own trigger depth. Licensed electrical and licensed plumbing. Refrigerant work. Fire alarm and sprinkler inspection, which are code-driven and go to a licensed specialty firm. Elevator service, always its own agreement. Pest control. Anything behind a locked tenant door. And any part over a stated dollar threshold, which the agreement should name.
Notice how many of those sit under a separate license. That’s not a vendor being cheap with you. Missouri and Illinois both gate real trade work behind licensure, and a good general maintenance company knows where its own edge is. The ones who claim they handle everything in-house are usually subcontracting it anyway, with a markup you never see. Our breakdown of property maintenance services and what they cover maps the same boundary from the property side.
### How much does it cost to clean a 10,000 square foot building?
Square footage alone can’t answer it, and any vendor who quotes off that one number over the phone is guessing. Nobody publishes a local rate. Six variables decide the price of a 10,000-square-foot job, and two buildings of identical size can sit a long way apart on every one of them.
Start with the floors. Ten thousand feet of open carpet is a vacuum and a spot check. Ten thousand feet of VCT is dust mop, damp mop, and a burnisher on a cycle, plus strip and wax somewhere in the year. Polished concrete, sealed terrazzo, ceramic tile in a restroom block, sheet vinyl in a clinic exam room. Each one carries a different labor time and a different chemical. Mixed floors cost more than one floor type does.
Then count restrooms and fixtures. Restrooms are the most labor-dense square feet in any commercial building, and a fixture count tells a bidder more than a floor plan does. Two single-occupancy restrooms in a Pine Lawn storefront and eight stalls across two floors of a Barnhart office are not the same job at the same size.
### The other four levers
Traffic and use type. A dental practice, a machine shop and an insurance office each shed a completely different mess. Frequency, which is the biggest lever you actually control: five nights a week versus three versus one changes the whole structure. Access, meaning what time the crew can get in, whether there’s an alarm code, a dock, an elevator, or a landlord who locks the building at nine. And supplies, because liners, paper, soap and can liners inside the price versus billed at cost is a genuine difference between two bids that look identical.
Want the number to mean something? Make every bidder walk the building, at the hour the work would happen, with your fixture count and your floor types in hand. If you’re comparing cleaning specialists specifically, our guide to top-rated commercial cleaners in St. Louis is the companion read.
Different contract, same math: what a kids birthday party costs
### How long does it take to clean a 10,000 sq ft building?
Nobody can give you an honest hours figure without seeing the building, and the variables that set the time are the same ones that set the price. Floor type, restroom and fixture count, traffic, frequency, crew size and how fast the crew can get through the door. Those six write the schedule.
Frequency does the heaviest lifting. A building serviced five nights a week gets light nightly passes, because nothing has time to build up. The same building serviced once a week needs a longer, harder visit every time, since a week of coffee rings, restroom use and parking lot grit walked across the entry is waiting. Cutting frequency in half rarely halves the total labor hours.
Crew size changes the clock without changing the work. Two people splitting a floor plan finish in roughly half the wall time one person needs, and vendors staff to the window you give them. A tight window costs more because it forces more bodies on site at once. A loose window is cheaper. If a crew can work from seven to midnight, they will price it differently than a building that must be clear by nine.
### What stretches the time out
Hard floors that need machine work. Restrooms, always. Stairwells, because a vacuum and a mop both have to be carried. Glass, which is slow and unforgiving. Buildings with many small private offices instead of one open floor, since every door is a stop, a light switch and a separate trash can. Security procedures, badge-in logs and alarm resets. Elevators that need a key after hours. And a dock or trash enclosure sitting a long walk from the interior.
Here’s the part that gets skipped. Specials aren’t part of the nightly clock at all. Strip and wax, extraction and window washing are separate visits with separate crews and separate hours, and they land on the calendar quarterly or annually. When a vendor tells you the nightly visit takes a certain time, ask what that excludes. The answer is usually everything expensive.
### What actually drives the number up or down?
Building age and mechanical condition drive it harder than anything else, and both show up in the hourly reactive line rather than the monthly fee. A 1970s strip retail building in Freeburg and a five-year-old flex building on the same acreage will produce wildly different annual totals under identical contracts.
### The local factors
St. Louis weather taxes buildings from both directions. Road salt gets tracked across entry floors from December through March and it destroys finish, which means more matting, more frequent scrubs, and sometimes an extra refinish cycle. Summer humidity pushes condensate lines, drain pans and roof drains to the front of the list. Freeze and thaw cycles work on parking lots and on sealant joints. A building with a flat roof and a lot of rooftop equipment carries more scheduled labor than one without, every single year.
### The things you can change
Frequency. Scope. Access window. Whether supplies are your purchase or theirs. Whether you keep the specials in the same agreement or bid them out on their own. Matting at every entrance, which is cheap and directly reduces floor labor. And how fast you approve repair work, because a small leak approved on Tuesday costs a fraction of the same leak on a Saturday after the drywall came down.
### The things you cannot
Square footage. Number of floors and restrooms. Tenant mix. Wage pressure in the local labor market, which nobody controls. Code-driven inspections on fire, sprinkler and elevator systems, which happen on their own schedule whether or not you budgeted for them. Insurance and licensing costs carried by the vendor and passed through in the rate.
One more, and it catches new owners constantly. Read the lease before you shop anything. In a multi-tenant building, a chunk of this work is a common-area expense you recover from tenants, and some of it isn’t recoverable at all. The commercial leasing guide for the St. Louis metro covers how those pass-throughs get written, which determines whether a scope increase is your cost or a shared one.
### How do you tell a real scope from a thin one?
A real scope is countable. It names tasks, frequencies and quantities, and a stranger could audit the building against it without calling anybody. A thin scope uses adjectives. Once you know that single difference, you can sort two proposals in about four minutes.
### Signs the scope is real
Task lists broken out by frequency: nightly, weekly, monthly, quarterly, annual. A fixture count for restrooms. Square footage by floor type, not one lump number. Named specials with named frequencies, priced per occurrence. A stated threshold above which a repair needs your approval. Response times for routine and emergency calls, in hours. A named supervisor and a stated inspection cadence. Proof of insurance and a clear statement of which licensed trades get subcontracted.
### Signs it is thin
The phrase general cleaning as a line item. As needed with no definition. A single square footage figure with no floor types attached. No mention of who buys supplies. Specials listed with no frequency, so they exist on paper and never on the calendar. No after-hours rate stated anywhere. A quote produced without a walkthrough. And a scope that never once says what is excluded, which is the biggest tell of all.
A thin scope isn’t always dishonest. Sometimes it’s a small operator who works on handshakes and does genuinely good work. But it means every disagreement for the next three years gets settled by memory, and memory favors whoever talks faster.
### Interview two or three providers, then look at the gap
Shortlist two or three companies worth an hour of your time. Walk each one through the building. Say plainly what you want, in specifics, then listen to what they are actually prepared to deliver. The gap between those two things is the signal. Not the bottom-line number.
Come to the walkthrough with your own list first. Nightly trash and restrooms, five nights, crew in after six. Hard floors burnished monthly, refinished twice a year. Filters quarterly. Roof inspected after every major storm. A named person who answers the phone. Whatever your building actually needs. Now say it out loud and watch.
### What the good ones do
They push back on something. A vendor who agrees to every item without a single question hasn’t thought about your building, and the disagreement usually lands where you were wrong. They’ll tell you monthly burnishing is too much for that traffic level, or that your entry matting is costing you more in floor labor than the matting would cost to replace, or that they won’t touch the rooftop units and here’s the mechanical company they’d call. That’s a partner. The ones who say yes to everything are selling you the signature and solving the details later, at your expense.
Ask three questions at the end of every walkthrough. Who is the actual person in my building at night, and how long have they worked for you? What happens if a pipe fails at 3 a.m. on a Sunday? And what is on this list that you would tell me to drop? The third one sorts the field faster than anything else, because it asks a salesperson to argue against revenue.
### A note on turnover
Janitorial turnover is high across the whole industry, and it’s the reason good service degrades at month seven. A company with a real supervisor structure and a written inspection cadence survives losing a cleaner. A company where one person does everything does not. Ask how they onboard a replacement, and ask who inspects the work when nobody is watching.
