### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much does a copywriter cost?
A.  It depends on the model and the scope, and anyone quoting a universal figure is guessing. Work gets priced per word, per project, hourly, or on a monthly retainer. The drivers are research depth, customer interviews, page count, revision rounds, turnaround speed and whether strategy is included. To compare two writers fairly, hand both the identical scope and deadline, then judge what each one plans to do with it rather than the number alone.
### Q. Should I hire a copywriter or a marketing agency?
A.  Hire a copywriter when you know what you sell and who buys it, but the words are underperforming. Hire an agency when you need strategy, media buying, design and reporting managed together and you don’t want to coordinate four freelancers yourself. The agency bundle costs more because it includes more. If your only broken link is the message on the page, the bundle is mostly overhead you don’t need yet.
### Q. How long does a copywriting project take?
A.  A single landing page or a short email sequence usually lands in days. A full website or an ongoing campaign runs weeks, sometimes longer, depending on how many interviews and approvals sit in the middle. Delays are almost always on the client side: unscheduled calls, feedback from four people who disagree, silence for a week. Consolidate feedback into one document from one decision maker and the timeline holds.
### Q. What is the 80/20 rule in copywriting?
A.  It’s an old trade rule of thumb: roughly eighty percent of the impact comes from the headline, so give it eighty percent of your effort. Most people read the first line and nothing else, so the headline decides whether the body copy is ever read at all. Treat the number as a reminder rather than a measurement. The practical takeaway is simple — write thirty headlines, keep one.
### Q. Is AI replacing copywriters?
A.  It replaced the bottom of the market and left the top alone. Bulk articles, filler descriptions and thin blog posts got commoditized fast. Customer research, positioning, deciding what not to say, and being accountable for whether a page converts did not. There’s a side effect worth knowing: the more businesses publish machine-default writing, the more a page that actually sounds like a person stands out.
### Q. What skills do you need as a copywriter?
A.  Research and interviewing come first, ahead of writing talent. You need to pull the truth out of a busy business owner, read reviews for patterns, and hear how customers describe a problem in their own words. Then structure, ruthless editing, and enough understanding of how people buy to know which objection to handle first. Add the unglamorous ones: hitting deadlines, taking blunt feedback, and cutting your favorite sentence without sulking.
### Q. Can I be a copywriter with no experience?
A.  Yes, though not by waiting for permission. Build samples without clients: rewrite a local business page and document why you changed each part, write three versions of an email for a product you actually use, publish your reasoning. Pick one narrow area rather than offering everything. Early clients hire evidence of thinking, not credentials, and a folder of sharp spec work beats an empty portfolio with a certificate attached.
### Q. Do copywriters get paid well?
A.  Income varies more in this field than almost any other writing job, and averages hide that completely. The gap usually comes down to what you sell: writing priced by the word pays like typing, while writing tied to a business outcome pays like consulting. Specialization, repeat retainer clients, and the ability to show what your work did tend to separate a comfortable practice from a grinding one.

## How to Choose a Cosmetic Surgeon in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-cosmetic-surgeon-in-st-louis
She has three tabs open and one page of handwriting in a notebook. Tab one is a practice with a wall of before-and-after photos and a countdown clock on a seasonal special. Tab two is a plain physician page, black text on white, no photos at all, which somehow feels less reassuring. Tab three is a review site full of people describing staff who were lovely. Not one of the three screens tells her the fact she actually needs, which is what training the person holding the scalpel finished, and where.
That gap is the whole problem. Elective cosmetic surgery gets marketed the way kitchen remodels and cars get marketed: financing offers, seasonal pricing, a friendly coordinator who calls back inside the hour. The surgery is not a kitchen remodel. It’s anesthesia, an incision, a body that has to heal, and a result you keep.
So handle it as a medical decision. You’re hiring a surgeon, not buying a package. What follows covers how to read credentials, why the job title on the door means less than you’d guess, where the operation happens and why the room matters, and what a consultation should feel like when it’s being run properly. None of it can tell you whether a particular procedure is right for you. Only your own health history and a real examination do that.
### How do you pick a good plastic surgeon?
Verify board certification with the American Board of Plastic Surgery, an American Board of Medical Specialties member board, then ask where the operation happens and whether that facility is accredited. Shortlist two or three surgeons worth interviewing. State plainly what you want. Compare it against what each one is prepared to deliver.
Everything after this is detail hanging off those four moves. Verify. Look at the room. Interview. Compare. Most people run the order backward, falling for a photo gallery first, booking with whoever answered the phone fastest, and getting around to credentials only once they’re already sitting in a paper gown with a marker in somebody’s hand.
Slow down. There’s no emergency in elective surgery. The procedure will still exist in six weeks and the surgeon who is genuinely good will still have a calendar then, probably a fuller one. Any pressure to sign today tells you something about the practice and nothing about your timeline.
### Does it matter if a plastic surgeon is board-certified?
It matters more than almost anything else you can check from a laptop. Board certification documents that a physician finished a full residency in a specialty and passed the examinations that specialty requires. In the United States, the board recognized for plastic surgery is the American Board of Plastic Surgery, which is a member board of the American Board of Medical Specialties.
Here’s where people get tripped. Many boards exist. Some are member boards of the American Board of Medical Specialties, with defined residency requirements and continuing certification. Others are private organizations with official-sounding names, and joining one can be a matter of dues and a short course. Both kinds issue certificates. Both look identical hanging in a hallway, matted and framed, catching the light.
Check the board, not the frame. The American Board of Medical Specialties runs a public verification tool, and the American Board of Plastic Surgery keeps its own directory of who currently holds certification. Look the name up yourself, at home, before the appointment. Two minutes. And it spares you having to ask a stranger an awkward question across a desk.
Other specialties are built the same way, which is useful context if you’re comparing across fields. Our explainer on what an oral surgeon does and what it costs lays out a parallel structure: separate residency, separate board, separate scope of practice. Same logic, different part of the body.
### Why is “cosmetic surgeon” not a protected title?
Because a state medical license licenses a physician, not a specialty. A licensed physician in Missouri or Illinois may legally offer and advertise services outside the field they trained in, and “cosmetic surgeon” functions as a marketing description rather than a credential. That isn’t fraud. It just isn’t the same sentence as “board-certified in plastic surgery,” and the two get used interchangeably in advertising all the time.
Which means the sign, the headline and the business card carry almost no verified information. You’ll find physicians from unrelated specialties offering body contouring. You’ll find practices where the physician of record is rarely on site and the person doing most of the talking is a patient coordinator. None of that is automatically disqualifying. It simply has to be checked instead of assumed.
Ask one flat question, in a level voice. Which board certified you, and in what specialty? A plastic surgeon answers that in a single sentence and moves on. Somebody whose training sits elsewhere tends to produce a longer answer with more words in it, words about experience and volume and continuing education. The length of the answer is the signal.
Worth separating out: plenty of what people want fixed isn’t surgical at all. Texture, pigment, stubborn acne, a mole that changed, sun damage from thirty summers. Those belong with a board-certified dermatologist first, and our guide to when to see a dermatologist in St. Louis covers where that line sits. Starting in the wrong office costs time you could have spent healing.
### Where will the operation actually happen?
In one of three kinds of room, and the difference is not cosmetic: a hospital operating room, a licensed ambulatory surgery center, or an office-based surgical suite inside the practice. Any of the three can be entirely appropriate for the right procedure. What you want to know is whether the facility holds accreditation from a recognized accrediting body, and who is administering the anesthesia.
Office suites are where the questions get sharper. Not because office surgery is unsafe by nature, but because the oversight varies and accreditation there is voluntary in a way hospital licensure is not. A practice that sought accreditation and kept it chose to be inspected by outsiders. That choice tells you something real about how the place runs when nobody is watching.
Then ask what happens if the day goes sideways. Where does a transfer go, and how fast? Does the surgeon hold admitting privileges at a hospital for the same procedure they’re proposing to perform in their own office? Privileges matter because hospitals credential physicians against their documented training. Somebody who can do a procedure inside a hospital has already been vetted by an institution with no financial stake in your booking.
Geography deserves a line here too, because people underestimate it badly. The first couple of weeks after a procedure usually mean follow-up visits, and you won’t be driving yourself to the early ones. A run into the metro from Ste. Genevieve or Wood River is nothing on a normal Tuesday and genuinely rough when you’re sore, swollen and riding in the passenger seat with a pillow against the seatbelt. Count the round trip before you choose.
### What does a real consultation feel like?
Like an appointment with a doctor who is still deciding whether to operate on you. Not a meeting with a predetermined ending. A proper consult has a medical history, a physical examination of the area in question, a conversation where you describe the problem in your own words, and a plain statement about what surgery can and cannot do given your particular anatomy.
It usually runs the better part of an hour once history, exam, photographs and discussion are all counted, though practices differ and complex cases take longer. Wear something you can get in and out of quickly without help, since standardized photographs are routine. Separates beat a fitted one-piece. Bring a written list of your medications, supplements and past surgeries, because trying to recall them under fluorescent light never goes well.
### The questions that get a straight answer
Which board certified you, and in what specialty? How many of these do you perform in a typical month? Where will this be done, is that facility accredited, and who gives the anesthesia? What are the common complications of this specific procedure, and what does your plan look like if one happens to me? Who covers me at two in the morning on day three? Every one of those has a short, direct answer available to a surgeon who does the work regularly.
### What a good surgeon asks you
Plenty. Full medical history, every medication and supplement, nicotine in any form including the ones people don’t count, prior operations, how your weight has moved over the last year, what you’re expecting afterward and why now. A surgeon who never asks why now is not evaluating you. Be straight in your answers. Hiding a supplement or minimizing the vape does not protect you, it just removes information the surgeon needed to keep you safe.
Different subject entirely: what to ask a leasing agent in St. Louis.
### Which answers should make you walk?
The ones that dodge. A vague reply about which board certified them. A refusal to name the facility, or a shrug about whether it’s accredited. Discomfort at the question of who handles a complication. And a promise that nothing ever goes wrong, which no honest surgeon makes, because every operation carries risk and the honest ones say so out loud early.
Sales pressure is its own category. Pricing that expires at the end of the week. Financing paperwork handed over before the examination. A coordinator who does the talking while the surgeon appears for four minutes near the end. A refusal to give you the consent documents to read at home, slowly, with somebody you trust. None of these are medical decisions. They’re conversion tactics, and they belong to a different industry.
One more. Watch what happens when you describe a result the surgeon thinks is unachievable on your anatomy. The good ones say so, plainly, and sometimes talk you out of the whole thing. That sentence costs them a booking. It’s the single most useful thing you can hear in a consultation, and it’s the reason interviewing more than one surgeon is worth the afternoon.
### What disqualifies you from plastic surgery?
Some of it is temporary and some of it isn’t, and only a surgeon who has examined you and read your chart can make the call. In general terms, the issues that pause or stop an elective procedure include uncontrolled medical conditions, active nicotine use, an active infection, a clotting history, a weight that’s still moving, and expectations that surgery cannot meet.
Nicotine is the one people argue about most. Smoking, vaping, patches, pouches: all of it affects blood flow to healing tissue, and surgeons take it seriously enough that many will postpone rather than proceed. Some test for it. That isn’t moralizing. Elective surgery on tissue that can’t reliably heal is a bad trade, and a surgeon who says no to that is doing the job correctly.
Mental health belongs in this conversation too, without stigma attached. Body dysmorphic disorder is a recognized condition in which surgery rarely delivers the relief a person is hoping for, and careful surgeons screen for it and refer rather than operate. Timing counts as well. Grief, a divorce, a job loss: none of it disqualifies anyone, but a good surgeon will ask why now and listen closely to the answer.
### Should you expect to pay for a consultation?
Often, yes, and it’s a normal practice rather than a warning sign. Some surgeons charge a consultation fee, some credit it toward the procedure if you book, and some waive it entirely. Policies vary from office to office, so ask when you schedule and ask what the fee covers before you drive anywhere.
A fee often buys protected time with the surgeon, which is exactly what you came for. Free consultations aren’t automatically worse, but they do raise a question worth holding: if the visit generates no revenue on its own, what is it designed to generate? Sometimes the answer is a genuine practice-building decision. Sometimes it’s a funnel.
Either way, multiply the fee by the number of surgeons on your shortlist and treat that as the cost of doing this properly. Against a permanent surgical result, consulting two or three people is the cheapest quality control you will ever buy. A family in Weldon Spring who budgets for three consults and picks the third surgeon has spent their money extremely well.
### What does recovery really ask of you?
More than the brochure suggests, and for longer. Recovery details depend entirely on the procedure and on your health, so the only reliable instructions are the ones your surgeon writes for you. What’s broadly true across elective surgery is that you’ll need time off, a ride home, an adult with you the first night, and a stretch of doing considerably less than you think you can.
Swelling is the part that surprises people. Final results often take months to settle, well past the point where you feel fine and look mostly normal in a mirror. That in-between stretch is where regret talks loudest, and it is almost always too early to judge anything. Ask at the consultation what the realistic timeline looks like from week one to month six, and write the answer down.
Plan the logistics before the date, not after. Who drives. Who cooks. Who handles the kids or the dog. Whether you can sleep the way you’ve been told to sleep in the bed you actually own. Whether your job lets you sit still. Recovery goes better when the boring arrangements are already made, and it goes badly when you’re solving them on day two with a tight compression garment on.
### How do you compare your shortlist?
Narrow it to two or three surgeons who clear the credential and facility checks, then interview them the way you’d interview any doctor before agreeing to treatment. Say out loud, in ordinary language, what bothers you and what you want to be true afterward. Then listen to what each one is prepared to deliver. The gap between those two things is the signal.
That gap shows up fast once you’re comparing. One surgeon proposes a smaller procedure than you asked for and explains why. Another proposes more. A third declines part of it outright. Disagreement between qualified people is normal and it’s informative, and hearing it is the actual reason to book more than one visit. Second opinions aren’t an insult to anybody. Good surgeons expect them and some will suggest one themselves.
What shouldn’t decide this: price. Not the deposit, not the financing offer, not which office quoted lowest. Cosmetic surgery is one of the few purchases where the cheapest version can cost you a revision, a second recovery, and a result you live with either way. Choosing a cheaper surgeon two exits closer to home is not really a budget decision. It’s a health decision wearing a budget costume.
Trust the quiet stuff too. Whether the surgeon looked at you or at a screen. Whether the staff answered a hard question without glancing at each other first. Whether you felt free to say no in that room, and whether anyone made that feel expensive. You’re about to let this person operate on you. Feeling comfortable saying no is not a soft criterion, it’s a structural one.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What certification should a plastic surgeon have?
A.  Certification from the American Board of Plastic Surgery, which is a member board of the American Board of Medical Specialties. That pairing is the one to look for, because it means a completed plastic surgery residency plus the board’s own examinations. Certificates from organizations outside the American Board of Medical Specialties structure may represent real training, or they may represent a short course and an annual fee. You can’t tell by looking at the frame on the wall, so verify the physician’s name through the board’s own public directory instead.
### Q. Can you be a surgeon but not board-certified?
A.  Yes. A state medical license is what permits a physician to practice; board certification is a separate credential layered on top of it, and it isn’t legally required to operate. Some strong physicians sit in the window between finishing residency and passing their boards. Others never completed a residency in the field they advertise at all. Those two situations look identical on a website. Ask which board, which specialty and which year, then check the answer yourself rather than taking it on trust.
### Q. What not to say to a plastic surgeon?
A.  Anything that hides information. Don’t downplay nicotine, leave medications or supplements off the list, or wave off a prior surgery as ancient history. Those details change the plan and sometimes change the answer. Also skip opening with a celebrity photo and asking for that face, or naming a number and asking what it buys, because both reframe a medical visit as shopping. Describe what bothers you in your own plain words and let the surgeon tell you what is genuinely achievable on your anatomy.
### Q. How long is a consultation with a plastic surgeon?
A.  Longer than a routine office visit. Usually the better part of an hour once the medical history, physical examination, standardized photographs and the actual discussion are all counted, though it varies by practice and by procedure. A brief handshake from the surgeon followed by a long sit-down with a coordinator is a different appointment wearing the same name. You want real time with the person who will operate. If the schedule can’t allow that, book a second visit before you decide anything.
### Q. What do you wear to a plastic surgery consultation?
A.  Something you can get in and out of quickly and without help. There will be an examination of the area you want treated, and standardized photographs are routine, so loose separates work far better than a fitted one-piece outfit. Skip heavy makeup for a facial consultation and skip self-tanner anywhere on the body. Bring a written list of your medications, supplements and past surgeries. Comfort matters more here than looking polished, and nobody in that room is assessing your outfit.
### Q. How can I speed up healing after plastic surgery?
A.  Follow your surgeon’s written instructions exactly, since they were built around your procedure and your history. Broadly, healing tends to go better when people stop nicotine well before and after, sleep in the position they were told to, wear compression if it was prescribed, eat and hydrate properly, and resist going back to the gym early. Attend every follow-up, including the ones that feel pointless. Report fever, one-sided swelling or spreading redness right away instead of waiting to see.
### Q. Should you get a second opinion before elective surgery?
A.  Yes, and a confident surgeon expects it. Booking two or three consultations is ordinary practice for elective procedures, and it’s the cheapest quality control available to you. Different qualified surgeons may propose different approaches to the same concern, and hearing that disagreement out loud is genuinely useful. State plainly at each visit what you want. Then compare the plans side by side. The surgeon who declines to do something the others happily offered is often the one worth listening to hardest.
### Q. Does it matter how far you live from the surgeon?
A.  More than most people expect. The first two weeks generally involve follow-up visits, and you won’t be driving yourself to the earliest ones. A trip in from Ste. Genevieve or Wood River is easy on a normal day and fairly miserable when you’re sore and swollen in a passenger seat. Count the round trip honestly before you choose, and arrange both the ride home and an adult to stay with you the first night well ahead of the date.

## How to Price and Sell Handmade Crafts in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-price-and-sell-handmade-crafts-in-st-louis
A folding table in a Pacific driveway, covered edge to edge in finished work. Forty-some candles, poured over three weeks. A roll of masking tape, a fine-point marker, and a woman standing over the whole spread trying to decide what number to write on the little tags. She’s been at it twenty minutes. Nothing is priced yet.
That exact moment repeats itself across this metro every spring and every fall, and it usually ends the same way. The maker picks a number that feels polite. Writes it forty times. Sells out by early Saturday afternoon, packs up an empty table, and drives home feeling terrific about a weekend that quietly lost money. Selling out fast isn’t a win. Most of the time it’s the first symptom of underpricing, and it’s the most common one there is.
So here’s the ground this covers: the formula itself, why instinct is the expensive part, the line items a booth weekend actually eats, which kinds of handmade work move and which sit untouched all day, what to leave in the car, and how a fair stacks up against selling online or handing your work to a shop on consignment. No numbers invented on your behalf. Your materials, your hours, your town.
### How do I calculate the price of a craft?
Add up materials for that one piece, then pay yourself an hourly rate you would accept from an employer, then add a share of your overhead. That number is your cost. Multiply it for wholesale, then roughly double wholesale for retail, and check it against what comparable work sells for.
Four inputs, in order. Materials, labor, overhead, multiple. Skip any one of them and the number on the tag is a guess in a costume. Most makers get the first input right, fudge the second, ignore the third entirely, and never hear about the fourth until a shop owner asks for a wholesale sheet and the whole structure falls over.
### Materials, counted all the way down
Count the obvious things first. Wax, wick, jar, fiber, beads, clay, glaze, lumber, thread, hardware. Then count the invisible things, because that’s where the leak lives. Sandpaper. Glue. The blade that dulls and gets tossed. Hang tags, the little poly bag, the sticker on the bottom. Freight you paid to get a supply in the door. If you buy in bulk, divide by what the bulk really yields, including the pieces you wrecked. Waste is a material cost. So is the batch you threw out.
Where you restock moves this line more than almost anything else you control, especially on high-volume items. Our guide to where to buy craft supplies in St. Louis covers the shopping side of that, and it’s worth reading with a production mindset rather than a hobby one. Same shelves, very different math.
### Labor, at a rate you would take from somebody else
Pick a real hourly rate and write it down. Not a hobby rate. The test is blunt: if a stranger offered you that rate to do this exact work on their schedule, would you say yes? If the answer is no, the rate is too low, and you’ve been paying customers to carry your work out of the tent.
Then time yourself across a normal batch instead of a good day. Include the fiddly parts nobody counts: trimming, sanding, curing checks, labeling, photographing, wrapping. Include setup and cleanup. Include the piece that cracked. Averaging labor across a whole batch is the honest way to do it, because the batch is how you actually work.
### Overhead, the part nobody tags
Overhead is everything you pay whether or not a single item sells. Studio rent or the basement corner you heat. Tools and their upkeep. Domain and hosting. Insurance, permits, the business banking fee, the software subscription. Application fees for shows that turned you down. Add a year of it, divide by the number of pieces you realistically finish in a year, and attach that slice to every tag. It’s small per item. It’s enormous per year.
### The multiple, and why you run it even if you never wholesale
Materials plus labor plus overhead gives you cost. Cost times a figure around two gives you wholesale, which is what a shop pays you. Wholesale times roughly two again gives you retail, which is what goes on the tag at a fair. Categories vary, and plenty of makers run leaner on one step and heavier on the other depending on what they sell and how fast it moves.
Run both steps anyway. Here’s the reason: if your retail price is lower than the wholesale number the formula spits out, you have already locked yourself out of every shop in the region without knowing it. No boutique can stock work that the maker sells cheaper at a market three blocks away. Last move, the sanity check. Find comparable handmade work, similar materials, similar skill, and see where your number lands against it. Sitting far below isn’t competitive pricing. It’s a subsidy.
### Why is “what feels fair” the expensive mistake?
Because instinct is calibrated to what you would pay, and you are not your customer. Makers anchor hard to the mass-produced version of the object, the one stamped out by the thousand overseas, and then feel embarrassed asking more. That comparison is broken at the root. One of those things was made by a machine in a factory. The other one was made by you, on a Tuesday, in your kitchen.
The second failure mode is sneakier. It’s the hours you enjoyed. “I’d have been sitting there anyway” is the sentence that turns labor into a zero on the tag, and it feels generous right up until you’re stacking unpaid hours every month just to break even on jars. Enjoying the work doesn’t make the work free.
Third problem: a price that’s too low reads as a defect to a stranger walking past. Shoppers use price as a shortcut for quality all the time, whether or not that’s fair to you. A well-made piece tagged suspiciously cheap makes people look for the flaw instead of the craftsmanship. We’ve heard makers describe raising a price and watching the same item start selling, which sounds like folklore until it happens on your own table.
And going up later is genuinely hard. Your repeat customers remember the old tag. The shop that stocked you built a shelf price around it. Setting the number right the first time costs you one uncomfortable afternoon with a calculator. Fixing it two years in costs you a conversation with everybody.
Use sell-out speed as a diagnostic, not a trophy. Empty table by noon on day one of a two-day show? That’s a pricing signal, loud and clear. You just spent two days of fees and travel to sell four hours of inventory at a discount you set yourself.
### What does a booth weekend actually cost?
Far more than the table fee, and the table fee is usually the only line anybody counts. Write every item out before you decide whether a show deserves a weekend. The exercise takes fifteen minutes and it’ll change which shows you apply to next season.
### Before the truck is loaded
Application or jury fee, which you pay whether or not you get in. Booth or table fee. An electricity add-on, sometimes. Temporary vendor registration or a sales tax permit, which varies by municipality, so a show in Festus and a show in Jennings can carry different paperwork. Then the gear you bought once and should be spreading across seasons: tent, weights, tables, covers, grid walls, lights, the wagon. Signage. Bags, tissue, tags, cards.
### The weekend itself
Mileage, both directions, sometimes twice if load-in happens the night before. Lodging if the drive is long. Parking. Food you didn’t pack. Card processing, which takes a percentage of every swipe and occasionally a flat piece on top. Cash you broke for a float. And hours, which is the biggest line and the one that never appears on a spreadsheet: build hours, packing, driving, setup, the selling day, teardown, the drive back.
### After you unload
Unpacking, restocking, laundering the covers, replacing what broke. Then the quiet one, inventory depth. Everything that didn’t sell is money still tied up in wax and wire, sitting in a tote in your hallway until the next show. Depth is necessary, a thin table reads as picked-over by hour two, but it isn’t free. Take the full cost, divide by the number of pieces you honestly expect to move, and you get the floor each item has to clear before you’ve earned anything at all.
One habit worth building: log the weekend while you’re tearing down, not three days later. What sold, in what order, at what hour, and what people picked up and put back. That last column is the useful one.
### Which handmade work moves at a fair, and which sits?
Work that moves is gift-ready, needs no explanation, fits in a tote bag, and sits at a price someone will decide on in under a minute. Candles, soaps, ornaments, simple jewelry, pet items, prints, magnets, stickers, dish towels, small woodwork, and food items where cottage rules allow them. Seasonal anything, in the right season.
Work that sits tends to share a few traits. It needs sizing, so garments are hard. It needs delivery, so furniture is harder. It needs a paragraph of explanation before the value lands. Or it carries a price the crowd in front of you simply isn’t holding that day, which brings up the part most people get backwards.
Match the work to the crowd, not the crowd to your catalog. A Saturday market shopper arrives with a tote, a plan and grocery money, so consumables and small useful goods clear fast while a high-ticket piece gets admired and abandoned. Our guide to St. Louis metro farmers markets by town is a decent map of who shows up where. A holiday bazaar crowd is buying gifts for named people, which shifts everything toward giftable and boxed. A juried art show audience shows up prepared for a bigger number, and the low-price impulse table underperforms there.
Carry a price ladder, too. Something small enough to be an easy yes, a middle tier that does the real volume, and one or two anchor pieces at the top. The anchors often don’t sell. They still work, because they make the middle tier look reasonable, and occasionally somebody has been hunting for exactly that thing for a year.
Nothing to do with this: what to avoid when buying luggage.
### What should you leave at home?
The irreplaceable piece, first. If losing it or watching it get dropped would ruin your month, it belongs in the studio. Outdoor tables get handled, bumped, rained on and packed in a hurry at dusk. That’s the job.
Leave the one-offs you can’t repeat. They’re a trap in both directions: if it sells, you can’t restock the thing that just proved it works, and if it doesn’t, it ate table space all day. Leave fragile work you have no packing plan for. Leave the eleven colorways of one item, because a wall of near-identical choices makes people freeze and walk. Three strong options beat eleven nervous ones.
Leave the half-finished experiments, and leave anything you’re still learning on. Beginners often pack their whole practice run, and it dilutes the table badly. If you’re still in that stage, our rundown of art supplies for beginners in St. Louis is the better place to spend the next month. Show up to sell when you can make the same good thing twice.
One more. Leave the custom-order conversation off the table unless you’ve got a system for it, because “can you make this but in green, by Christmas” will eat your afternoon and frequently ends in nothing. Take the name. Send a note Monday.
### Is a booth weekend better than selling online or on consignment?
Each one trades a different thing. A booth trades your weekend for immediate cash, real faces, and feedback you can’t buy anywhere else. Online trades your evenings for reach without a geographic ceiling. Consignment trades a slice of every sale for shelf space you didn’t have to stand behind.
Booths are the highest gross per hour when a show goes well, and the most brutal when it rains. Fixed hours, weather, and a crowd you didn’t choose. The compensating gift is information: you watch which item people reach for and which one they flip over to check the price, and no analytics dashboard tells you that.
Online shifts the labor rather than removing it. Listing, photographing, writing descriptions, answering messages, packing, shipping, handling the one that arrived broken. Platform fees, payment processing, and ad spend all take a cut before you do. Steady, unglamorous, and it works while you sleep, which the booth never does.
Consignment puts your work in front of a shop’s regulars without a weekend commitment, and the shop keeps a percentage, commonly a meaningful one. You’re typically paid after the sale, not before, and your inventory sits somewhere you can’t see it. Wholesale is the cleaner cousin. The shop buys outright, you get paid up front, and the risk moves to them, but it only functions if your retail number left room for that first multiple. Makers all over this metro hit that same wall constantly: the shop says yes, the math says no, because the retail price was set by feel two years ago.
Most makers who last run two of the three. Fairs during the season for cash and contact, online through the slow months, and wholesale or consignment once a product proves it can be made repeatedly at a number that survives the split.
### How do you test a price without guessing twice?
Change one thing at a time. Take your steadiest seller, raise it at the next show, keep everything else identical, and count units sold rather than dollars taken. If you sell nearly as many at the higher tag, you found free money. If sales fall off a cliff, you found the ceiling, and that’s worth knowing too.
Track sell-through per item across a season rather than judging a single Saturday. One bad weekend might be weather. Four bad weekends is a product. Keep the notes in the same place every time, and be specific about which shows, which hours, which items.
Then recalculate when your inputs move. Material costs drift, your speed improves, your overhead grows the moment you rent space or buy the bigger kiln. A price set eighteen months ago is describing a business you no longer run.
Shopping for handmade instead of making it? Browse crafts around St. Louis on St Louis Near Me Directory, then check hours before you drive, since plenty of makers keep studio time around their market schedule. Prefer to meet the makers face to face? Start with the guide to St. Louis metro farmers markets by town.
If you’re the maker behind the table, list your shop.
Ready to sell between shows? Our guide to where to sell handmade items locally covers the markets, shops and online spots, and where to advertise your business for free maps the rest.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What sells really well at craft fairs?
A.  Gift-ready, tote-sized things that need no explanation and no fitting. Candles, soaps, ornaments, simple jewelry, pet items, prints, stickers, magnets, kitchen textiles, small woodwork, and food items where cottage food rules allow them. Seasonal work does well in its season and poorly outside it. The common thread is a fast yes: the shopper understands what it is, pictures who it’s for, and decides in under a minute. Anything requiring a size, a delivery or a paragraph of context moves much slower on an outdoor table.
### Q. What not to sell at a craft fair?
A.  Irreplaceable one-offs, work you can’t reproduce if it sells, fragile pieces with no packing plan, and garments that need a fitting room. Skip anything priced well above what that particular crowd carries, since a market audience and a juried art audience arrive with different expectations. Skip eleven near-identical colorways too, because too many similar choices makes people freeze and walk away. Leave prototypes and practice pieces in the studio. They dilute the table and they teach shoppers to see your whole display as unfinished.
### Q. Is selling at craft fairs profitable?
A.  Often, but only if you count everything. Real profit is revenue minus the booth fee, application fee, mileage, lodging, parking, packaging, card processing, the amortized cost of your tent and tables, and your hours. Plenty of makers finish a weekend cash-positive and labor-negative, meaning the money covered supplies but paid nothing for the time. The fix is almost never more shows. It’s a price built from materials, labor at a real rate, overhead and a multiple, then a look at which shows actually clear that bar.
### Q. What’s the best way to sell homemade crafts?
A.  A mix, weighted toward whatever your category rewards. Fairs deliver immediate cash and face-to-face feedback you can’t get any other way. Online removes the geographic ceiling but shifts your labor into listing, photography, messages and shipping. Wholesale pays up front and moves volume, while consignment buys shelf space in exchange for a percentage and slower payment. Most makers who stick with it run two channels: shows through the season, online through the slow months, and wholesale once a product proves it can be made repeatedly.
### Q. What are the easiest crafts to sell?
A.  The ones that are repeatable, quick to produce, cheap in materials relative to their price, and instantly understood. Candles, soaps, bath goods, ornaments, simple earrings, printed paper goods, dish towels and small home items all fit. Easy to sell is not the same as easy to profit from, though. Low-cost items also carry the smallest margin per unit, so volume has to do the heavy lifting, which means production speed and inventory depth matter more than they do for higher-ticket work.
### Q. How do I calculate how much I sell my product for?
A.  Same four steps every time. Total the materials for one finished piece, including waste, packaging and the supplies that vanish invisibly. Add your labor, timed across a real batch and paid at an hourly rate you would accept from an employer. Add a per-item share of your annual overhead. That sum is cost. Multiply cost for wholesale, then roughly double wholesale for retail, then compare the result against similar handmade work. Landing far below comparable makers usually means an input got skipped, not that you found an edge.
### Q. How much inventory should I bring to a two-day show?
A.  Enough that the table still looks full on Sunday afternoon. A thin display reads as picked-over, and shoppers skip it. Go deep on your proven sellers and narrow on everything else, keeping restock boxes under the table so you can refill gaps through the day. Remember that depth costs money sitting in materials, so use your own sell-through notes from past shows instead of guessing. If you sold out early at the last one, bring more and raise the price at the same time.
### Q. Is consignment worth it for a small maker?
A.  It depends entirely on the cut and on whether your retail price left room for it. Shops commonly keep a meaningful percentage and pay after the item sells, so your work and your money both sit somewhere you can’t watch. The upside is real: shelf space in front of regular customers without giving up a weekend. Read the agreement for who covers loss or damage, how often you get paid, and how unsold work comes back. If the split breaks your margin, wholesale or your own table is the better route.

## Czech Food in St. Louis: What to Order
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/czech-food-in-st-louis-what-to-order
The tray comes out of the oven with twelve shallow wells pressed into it, each one holding a spoonful of something dark. Prune, mostly. A little apricot at the end of the row. One corner is nearly black with poppy seed, and what rises off the whole thing is butter and yeast and warm fruit, which is the smell of a Czech bakery anywhere on earth at six in the morning.
Those are kolaches. Real ones, not the sausage-wrapped-in-dough object sold under the same name at half the gas stations in America, though we will get to that argument, because it is a good argument. A kolache is a soft enriched roll with fruit or sweet cheese sitting in a dimple in the top. Eat one standing up in a parking lot and you have already understood most of Czech cooking: buttery, plain-spoken, built for cold mornings and long afternoons and people who work outdoors.
St. Louis took in Bohemian immigrants during the same nineteenth-century wave that gave the city its German bakers and its brewers, and that history still shows up in a bakery case once you know what you are reading. Poppy seed. Prune. Sweet farmer cheese. Words on a paper label nobody bothers to translate, because the regulars already know.
So here is what to order, and what the sign is actually telling you.
### What is the most popular Czech food?
Ask in Prague and the answer is svickova: beef sirloin braised and served in a smooth root-vegetable cream sauce with bread dumplings, cranberry and a ribbon of whipped cream. Ask an American and the answer is the kolache. Both are right. One is Sunday dinner, the other is breakfast.
Svickova na smetane is the dish Czech families argue about, because every grandmother built the sauce a little differently. Carrot, celery root, parsley root and onion cook down with the beef and its fat, then get pureed and finished with cream until the whole thing turns the color of pale caramel. It arrives sliced and heavily sauced, a fan of houskove knedliky on one side, a spoonful of cranberry compote on top, and cold whipped cream over that. Sounds wrong. It is not wrong.
The other contender, at least by sheer volume eaten, is vepro-knedlo-zelo. Roast pork, bread dumplings, cabbage. Three words, one plate, and it is what a Czech pub cooks on a Tuesday when nobody asked for anything fancy. The pork is fatty and slow-roasted with caraway. The kraut is often sweetened and thickened rather than sharp, closer to a braise than a pickle. The dumplings are there to mop, and they will.
Then there is the thing most Americans meet first, usually before breakfast, usually in a paper bag.
### What is a famous Czech snack?
Utopenci, which translates to “drowned men.” Fat pork sausages pickled in vinegar brine with sliced onion, bay leaf and whole peppercorns, left alone for a week or two, then eaten cold straight out of the jar with dark bread and a beer. It is the most honest item on any Czech bar menu.
Pickled cheese runs a close second. Nakladany hermelin is a soft ripened round, split and packed into oil with garlic, onion, peppercorn and paprika until it goes sharp and spreadable. Bread comes with it. A fork doesn’t really help. Both of these exist for the same reason: they keep, they suit beer, and they taste better on day nine than on day one.
For something you can eat while walking, chlebicky. Open-faced sandwiches on a slice of baguette, spread thick with potato or egg salad, then loaded with ham, salami, hard-boiled egg, a pickle spear, a curl of butter, sometimes a whole sardine laid across the top. They look like 1960s catering. They are genuinely delicious, and a deli case full of them is a lunch decision rather than a snack.
Then bramborak, the potato pancake: grated raw potato bound with a little flour and egg, heavy on garlic and marjoram, fried until the edges shatter. Cheap, savory, greasy in the correct way. Sausage and kraut overlap hard with the German half of this city, and if that is the aisle you keep wandering into anyway, our piece on German food in St. Louis and where it came from works the same immigrant kitchen from the other side.
### What are the different types of Czech dumplings?
Three families, and they are not interchangeable. Houskove knedliky are bread dumplings, steamed in a log and sliced. Bramborove knedliky are potato dumplings, denser and chewier. Ovocne knedliky are fruit dumplings, a whole plum or apricot wrapped in dough and eaten as dessert.
### Houskove knedliky, the bread dumpling
A yeasted dough of flour, milk and egg with cubes of stale bread folded through it, shaped into a fat cylinder, then simmered or steamed and cut into rounds, traditionally with a thread rather than a knife. The texture is soft and faintly springy, like very fresh bread that decided to be a side dish. Neutral on purpose. Its entire job is carrying sauce from the plate to you, and it does that better than any starch in Europe.
### Bramborove knedliky, the potato dumpling
Potato, flour, sometimes semolina, sometimes egg. Heavier and chewier than the bread version, with a faint sweetness underneath. These usually show up next to smoked meat and cabbage, and some kitchens stuff them with smoked pork so the middle goes salty and the outside stays bland. That contrast is the whole point of the dish.
### Ovocne knedliky, the fruit dumpling
A whole plum, apricot or handful of strawberries sealed inside potato or farmer-cheese dough, boiled, then finished with melted butter, sugar and either ground poppy seed or crumbled tvaroh. Cut into one and the fruit has gone to syrup. Czech families eat these as a main course in summer and nobody apologizes for it. Fair enough. Dessert for dinner is an underrated tradition.
### How do Czech dumplings differ from others?
A Czech knedlik is bread, not a boiled lump of dough. It is shaped in a loaf and sliced into flat rounds rather than rolled into balls, and it is treated as the plate’s starch: the thing you would eat instead of potatoes or noodles, never a garnish floating in soup.
That distinction trips people up constantly. An Italian gnocchi is dense and sauced. A matzo ball is a sphere living in broth. A Southern chicken and dumplings drops soft dough directly into the pot to thicken it. The Czech version is closer to the Austrian and southern German bread dumpling, which makes sense given the shared border and a few centuries of shared empire, but even there the shaping differs.
Eat them the way they are meant to be eaten. Press a slice flat into the sauce with the back of your fork, let it drink for a second, then lift. A good one comes up heavy and stained and slightly falling apart.
Wondering how AI decides which bakery to name first? Here’s how that works
### What is the famous Czech dessert?
Medovnik, the honey cake. Thin spiced layers baked with honey, stacked with a sour-cream or condensed-milk filling, then left to sit for a day so the layers soften into something closer to a torte than a cake. Cut a slice and you can count the lines. Usually eight or nine of them.
Beyond that, the bakery case gets crowded. Buchty are sweet yeast buns filled with jam, poppy seed or tvaroh and baked shoulder to shoulder in a pan so they pull apart. Kolacky, the small cookie-style pastries made with a cream cheese or butter dough, get folded around a dab of filling and dusted heavily with sugar. Vetrnik is a caramel-glazed cream puff the size of a fist. Palacinky are thin crepes rolled with jam.
One honest note about trdelnik, the spiral chimney pastry photographed constantly in Prague. It is commonly described as an ancient Czech specialty, and food writers have spent the last decade pointing out that it is mostly a modern tourist product rather than an old household bake. It tastes good. It just isn’t the heirloom the stall sign implies.
Poppy seed deserves its own sentence, though, because it is the flavor Americans consistently underrate. Ground, not whole. Cooked with milk and sugar until it goes into a dark paste with a taste somewhere between walnut and coffee grounds, in the best possible sense.
### A first order, in three rounds
Round one is the bakery case, because it is the cheapest way to find out whether you like this food at all. Get three kolaches: one prune, one apricot, one poppy seed. Skip the cherry if there are better options, since cherry is the flavor most likely to have come out of a bucket.
Round two is savory and cold. A couple of chlebicky, a jar or a plate of utopenci if anybody near you makes them, some rye bread. This is the round that tells you whether a place is cooking for Czech customers or for the idea of Czech customers.
Round three is the plate. Svickova if it is on the board, vepro-knedlo-zelo if it is not. Both come with dumplings, both take an hour off your afternoon, and both are better in February than in July. Bring a friend who orders the other one.
### Are kolaches just a Texas thing?
No. Texas gets the credit because Czech and Moravian families settled there in large numbers in the 1800s and their descendants turned the pastry into a statewide breakfast, but the same migration put Czech bakers all across the Midwest, including Nebraska, Iowa, Wisconsin, Minnesota and Missouri.
What Texas really did was blur the vocabulary. Somewhere along the way the sausage-filled version stopped being called by its own name and got folded in under “kolache,” and then convenience stores exported that usage to the entire country. Ask for a kolache in Prague and you will be handed something sweet, round and open-faced, every single time.
Around here the older tradition survives mostly in bakeries rather than restaurants, and it survives in home kitchens even more. A kitchen in De Soto with a recipe card written in someone’s grandmother’s handwriting is doing more for Czech food in this region than any menu is. That is how most immigrant baking works. It goes quiet, it goes domestic, and then somebody’s granddaughter opens a shop forty years later.
The spelling fight is real too, if you want to start one. Kolach, kolache, kolaches, kolace, kolacky. Regional, generational, and nobody is winning it.
### How to keep kolaches fresh?
Room temperature for a day, the freezer after that, and never the refrigerator. Cold air stales enriched bread faster than a counter does, which is why a fridge kolache goes dry and tough overnight while the same pastry left in a paper bag on the counter is still soft the next morning.
Day one is the good day. A kolache is at its peak within a few hours of baking, and everything after that is damage control. If you know you can’t finish the box, freeze the extras that same day rather than waiting to see how tomorrow goes. Wrap each one individually so the tops do not weld together, then bag them.
Two exceptions worth knowing. Anything filled with fresh cheese or custard needs refrigeration for food-safety reasons once it has been out a while, so ask at the counter which fillings those are. And loosely covered beats airtight for a day-old pastry, because a sealed container traps steam and the top goes sticky.
To bring one back: unwrap, set it on a sheet pan, low oven, loose foil over the top, eight to twelve minutes until the center is warm. The microwave works for about ten seconds and then punishes you, so if you go that route, eat it immediately while it is still soft.
### How do you tell a real Czech bakery from the sign out front?
Shortlist two or three places worth interviewing, then walk in and say plainly what you want: poppy seed ground on site, prune filling that is not jam, dough made in the building. Compare each answer against what you asked for. The gap between the two is the signal, not the price of a dozen.
Some questions earn their keep at the counter. What time do these come out? Do you make your own poppy seed filling or buy the paste? Is the cheese filling tvaroh or cream cheese? Do you do klobasniky, and do you call them that? Which day is your biggest bake? A baker who lights up at those questions is a baker who cares. One who shrugs has told you something too, and it’s fine to buy one pastry and leave.
Look at the case itself while you wait. Uneven hand-pressed wells, fillings that sit at slightly different heights, a poppy seed that reads dark brown rather than jet black. Those are marks of somebody working by hand. Perfectly identical pastries usually came off a machine, somewhere else.
If judging a case you do not fully understand is a skill you want anyway, it transfers. Get there early. The prune ones go first, and the people who already know that are ahead of you in line.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is a traditional Czech meal?
A.  Soup first, almost always. Then a plate of meat with a sauce, a starch that is usually dumplings, and cabbage or a pickled vegetable on the side. Beer with it, dessert if there is room. The classic full version is svickova or roast pork with bread dumplings, and the whole meal is built around mopping the plate clean rather than around the protein itself.
### Q. What are some classic Czech pastries?
A.  Kolaches lead the list: soft enriched dough with a dimple of prune, apricot, poppy seed or sweet farmer cheese. After that, buchty are filled yeast buns baked together in a pan, kolacky are the small sugar-dusted cookie-pastries, vetrnik is a caramel-glazed cream puff, medovnik is the layered honey cake, and palacinky are thin crepes rolled with jam.
### Q. What is a kolache with meat called?
A.  A klobasnek, plural klobasniky. The name comes from klobasa, meaning sausage, and it describes dough wrapped fully around a savory filling rather than pressed open around fruit. Most American counters sell them as “sausage kolaches” because that’s what customers ask for, but the older name is the accurate one, and bakers who use it usually know why.
### Q. Are kolaches just pigs in a blanket?
A.  No, though the confusion is understandable. A true kolache is sweet and open-faced, with filling visible in a well on top of a soft roll. A pig in a blanket is a sausage sealed inside dough, which makes it structurally closer to a klobasnek. Same bakery case, different pastry, and the sweet original came first by a long way.
### Q. What is the best way to reheat kolaches?
A.  A low oven and loose foil. Set the pastry on a sheet pan, tent it so the top does not dry out, and give it eight to twelve minutes until the center feels warm rather than hot. The microwave works for roughly ten seconds and then turns the dough rubbery, so if you use it, eat the kolache right away.
### Q. How to eat Czech dumplings?
A.  With a fork, pressed into the sauce. Lay a slice flat, push down gently so it soaks, then lift it in one piece. Czech dumplings are the starch of the meal, not a garnish, so treat them the way you would treat bread at a table with good gravy. Sawing at one with a knife is the tourist move.
### Q. What is svickova, and why is there whipped cream on it?
A.  Svickova na smetane is braised beef sirloin in a pureed root-vegetable cream sauce, served with bread dumplings. The whipped cream and cranberry compote on top are traditional, not a flourish: the cream cools and softens a sauce that is already tangy from vinegar and lemon, and the cranberry sharpens the whole thing. Eat a bite with all three together.
### Q. Is Czech food the same as German food?
A.  They overlap heavily and they aren’t the same. Both lean on pork, cabbage, caraway and bread dumplings, thanks to a shared border and centuries of shared politics. Czech cooking runs sweeter and creamier in its sauces, uses poppy seed and prune far more in baking, and treats the dumpling as a sliced loaf rather than a rolled ball.

## How to Choose a Dance Studio in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-dance-studio-in-st-louis
Nine adults lined up at the back of a mirrored room on a Tuesday night, every one of them staring at their own feet instead of the instructor’s. Two had told the front desk they had no rhythm. One had signed up on a dare. Nobody looked at anybody else, because looking at anybody else in a dance studio on your first night feels like asking to be graded.
That room is the whole decision. Not the website, not the trophy shelf in the lobby, not the recital photos from four years ago. Whether a studio fits you gets settled in the fifty minutes after the music starts, and there is no way to learn that from a tuition page.
So the shortlist matters more than the search does.
### What is the best dance to learn as an adult?
There isn’t one answer, but for most adult beginners it’s a social partner style — swing, salsa or basic ballroom — because a few weeks of class gets you functional on a real floor. Want technique instead of a partner? Adult ballet or tap. Pick by what you want to be able to do.
Most adults pick a style by how it looks on video. Ballroom looks elegant, hip hop looks fun, ballet looks like discipline. None of that tells you what the first eight weeks feel like, and the first eight weeks are where beginners quit.
Try a different question. What do you want to be able to do six months from now? Dance at a wedding without dreading the floor. Move better and get stronger. Have somewhere to be on Thursday nights where nobody asks about work. Those three answers point at three different rooms, and a studio that’s excellent for one of them can be a poor fit for another.
Social partner styles get you to usable fastest. Swing, salsa, bachata and the basic ballroom rhythms are built on a small set of patterns that repeat, so a handful of classes really can put you on a floor with a stranger and have it work. Solo styles reward patience instead. Adult ballet, tap and contemporary hand you technique, body awareness and a slow satisfying climb, and they ask you to be visibly a beginner for a good while longer.
### How do you choose a style when you’ve never danced?
Start with whether you want a partner. That one fork sorts most of the confusion, because partner dancing is a conversation and solo dancing is a practice. Adults who call themselves uncoordinated often do better in partner classes, where rotation and a lead give the body something to answer instead of a mirror to fight.
### If you want to dance socially
Swing and salsa are the usual doors. Both run beginner classes that assume nothing, both rotate partners so you don’t need to bring one, and both connect to a scene where people go out dancing afterward. Ask whether the studio hosts those social nights or points you toward them. A partner-dance class with nowhere to use it is a treadmill.
### If you want technique
Adult ballet is the most underrated class in the city. Nobody in that room is auditioning for anything. A good adult ballet or barre-based class rebuilds your posture, your ankles and your patience, and it makes every other style easier later, tap very much included. Progress feels slow for two months. Then something clicks.
### If you mostly want the workout
Hip hop, jazz, heels and cardio-style dance classes carry the least homework. Show up, sweat, leave. They’re also the hardest place to actually learn, because the choreography changes weekly and repetition is what builds a dancer. That’s a fine goal. Just name it honestly, and pick a studio that names it honestly back.
### What is a first dance class actually like?
Louder, sweatier and friendlier than you pictured. Most beginner classes open with ten or fifteen minutes of warm-up, move into a basic step or a short across-the-floor drill, break the material down in pieces, then run it with music at the end. You’ll be lost for stretches of it. Everyone is.
Here’s what nobody tells first-timers: nobody is watching you. They’re watching themselves in the mirror and worrying about their own feet, exactly the way you are. The instructor is watching, which is the entire point, and a good one will fix something small about your frame or your weight transfer inside the first twenty minutes.
Wear clothes you can move and sweat in. Fitted enough that the teacher can see your knees and hips, loose enough that you forget about them. On shoes, ask before you buy. Ballet wants slippers, tap needs tap shoes, partner dance wants a smooth sole that pivots, and hip hop wants clean sneakers that never go outside. Plenty of studios let a first-timer borrow a pair or dance in socks, and a decent front desk volunteers that instead of selling you shoes on night one.
Get there early. Ten minutes in the lobby tells you more than an hour on the website: who greets people, whether the adults talk to each other, whether the class before yours walks out smiling or grim.
Same nerves, different room: how open mic comedy nights work
### How much should I pay for dance classes?
Enough to get a trained teacher in a real dance space, and never before you know what the whole season costs. Pricing arrives in a few different shapes, and comparing two studios on the per-class rate alone is how families get surprised in April. Ask what the season total comes to, not the per-class rate.
Adults usually meet one of three structures. Drop-in by the class, which is the most flexible and the priciest per hour. A class card or punch pass, cheaper per class, with an expiration date worth reading twice. Or monthly and session tuition, which assumes you come every week: best value if you do, worst deal in the building if your job travels.
Private lessons sit in their own category, billed by the half hour or the hour, often sold in packages. They’re the fastest way to learn and the fastest way to spend. For a hard deadline like a first dance in June, a few privates plus a weekly group class beats privates alone, because the group class is where you learn to dance with somebody who isn’t your teacher.
Children’s tuition is built differently. It usually runs as a season roughly tracking the school year, billed monthly or by semester, with a registration fee at the front and a recital at the back. The recital is where the real number hides. Costume fees are charged per routine, so a child in three classes has three costumes, plus tickets, tights, shoes, a photo package and recital week itself. If the studio competes, add entry fees, choreography fees and travel. None of that is a trick. It just isn’t printed on the tuition page. The same pattern shows up in how to choose music lessons in St. Louis, where the recital is smaller and the instrument is the line that bites.
Don’t ask for a line-by-line quote, because no studio hands one over in September. Say it plainly instead: one class a week, and I need to know what I’m committing to through June. How clearly that gets answered tells you plenty about the next nine months.
### Is dance an expensive hobby?
It can be either, and the split falls on one word: performance. An adult taking a single weekly group class with one pair of shoes is running a cheap hobby by any standard. A child in three classes with a spring recital and a competition team is running an expensive one, and almost all of that gap is costumes, fees and travel.
Creep is the thing to watch for. One class becomes two because her friends are in jazz. Two becomes three because a teacher says she’s ready for pointe prep. Each step is small and reasonable. Each one also brings a costume, a rehearsal slot and another night of driving, and the arc looks about the same whether the family lives in Dardenne Prairie or Shrewsbury.
Adults have the opposite problem, which is stopping. A punch pass with an expiration date pressures you into classes you didn’t want, and monthly tuition you skip for six weeks is just a donation with extra steps. Match the payment structure to your real calendar rather than your January intentions.
Cheapest honest path for an adult beginner: one weekly group class, one style, borrowed or basic shoes, for a full session before you add anything. Still going in week eight? Buy the good shoes.
### What should you look for when you watch a class?
The floor and the teacher’s eyes. A sprung or padded floor protects knees and ankles in a way that tile laid over concrete simply cannot, and where the instructor’s attention goes tells you whether corrections actually happen. Watch the weakest dancer in the room. What happens to that person is what will happen to you.
Class size matters more than credentials on a wall. Twelve dancers is teachable. Twenty-eight in the same room is a performance the teacher gives at students. Count bodies, then count how many times the teacher says an individual name out loud. Zero names in fifty minutes is a warning.
Other things worth clocking from the doorway: whether the music is so loud that instruction drowns, whether late arrivals derail everything, whether class ends on time, whether a struggling kid gets corrected kindly or embarrassed in front of friends. Then stand in the lobby at pickup, which is the most honest ten minutes in a studio’s week.
Credentials aren’t nothing, mind you. Training background, years teaching, and whether the person running the class is also the person in the photos all count for something. For children, ask who covers when the regular teacher is out, because across thirty-odd weeks it will happen.
### The questions that reveal a studio’s real character
Ask about the student who struggles. Every studio keeps a polished answer ready for questions about excellence, and almost none has one ready for the child who can’t keep up or the adult who vanished for three weeks. How that gets answered predicts your experience better than anything else you could ask.
Shortlist two or three studios worth interviewing. Watch a class, take the trial, then say plainly what you want: fun, real technique, competition, a first dance by June, or one hour a week that gets you out of the house. Hold that against what the studio is set up to deliver. The gap is the signal, not the price.
Questions that earn their keep: Where do your adult beginners go after this class? Is the recital required, and what happens if we skip it? Do you rotate partners, or should I bring one? What’s the level above this one, and how do people move up? What do you do with a student who falls behind? How many dancers are in this class in February, not September? Can I pause if I travel? Who teaches when the owner is out?
One studio hears “I have never taken a class and I want to dance at my sister’s wedding in June” and comes back with a level, a plan, a social night and an honest caution about the timeline. Another quotes a rate and stops talking. Both might teach well. Only one has told you they’ve had your exact student before.
### What is the most important skill in dancing?
Keeping time. Musicality beats flexibility, memory and even coordination, because a dancer who lands on the beat reads as a dancer and one who rushes never will. In partner styles the skill has a second half: clear leading and honest following, which is communication far more than choreography.
The unglamorous skill matters more, though. Tolerating being bad. Adults leave dance in the first month not because the steps are hard but because the mirror is relentless, and being willing to look clumsy in a lit room full of people is the real gate. No studio advertises that class. Every studio teaches it anyway.
Which makes a room’s culture a technical feature rather than a soft one. A studio where beginners laugh at themselves out loud produces more dancers than a studio with sharper technique and no warmth. We’ve watched people with obvious natural rhythm quit the second kind of room in a month, and people with none stay four years in the first.
### How do you pick between two studios that both look fine?
Pick the one you’ll still be driving to in February. Convenience beats reputation across a nine-month season, and the celebrated studio twenty-five minutes away loses to the good one eight minutes away by the third cold Tuesday. A family in Spanish Lake and a family in Frontenac can look at the same studio and reach opposite answers, because only one of them is crossing the county in the dark.
Test the commitment structure next. Can you leave? A monthly or session arrangement with a clean exit is worth more to a new adult dancer than a discount for paying a year upfront, and a parent enrolling a child for a first season should know exactly what withdrawing in November costs, in money and in costumes already ordered.
Then take the trial. Nearly every studio offers one or lets you observe, and the ones that refuse have told you something useful. Go on an ordinary week rather than during an open house, and go in the time slot you’d actually attend. A Saturday demo class is not the Wednesday-at-seven room you would be living in.
With younger children the weighting shifts toward patience, scheduling and the drive more than pedigree. The roundup of kids music, art and dance classes in St. Louis is a reasonable place to see the options side by side before you start calling.
Ready to start calling? Browse dance instructors and studios around St. Louis on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick two or three, and go watch a class with your questions already written down.
