### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the most popular Filipino food?
A.  Adobo, by most reckonings. Meat simmered in vinegar, soy sauce, garlic, peppercorns and bay leaf until the sauce turns dark and the sharp edge rounds off. It is treated as the unofficial national dish, it exists in a hundred household versions, and it is the safest first order on any board. Lumpia and pancit run close behind, largely because both show up at every party.
### Q. What food do Filipinos eat the most?
A.  Rice, and not as a side. Rice sits at the center of breakfast, lunch and dinner, and everything else is ulam, the dish that seasons it. That relationship explains the portions: a scoop of adobo that looks small on its own is correct over two cups of rice. Fried garlic rice, sinangag, is the breakfast form, almost always with an egg on top.
### Q. What is the difference between an eggroll and lumpia?
A.  Wrapper and family. An American Chinese egg roll uses a thick, bubbled, deep-fried dough shell around cabbage and pork. Lumpia uses a thin crepe-style wrapper you can nearly see light through, so it fries into glass rather than bread. Lumpia is also a whole category rather than a single item, and one branch of it, lumpiang sariwa, never touches hot oil at all.
### Q. What is lumpia called in English?
A.  Spring roll, usually. Fried lumpia gets sold as a spring roll or an egg roll on English menus, and lumpiang sariwa appears as a fresh spring roll. Shanghai rolls is another label you will see. Neither translation is very good. The word itself arrived from Hokkien Chinese through centuries of trade, and most Filipino cooks simply say lumpia when speaking English too.
### Q. What is authentic lumpia made of?
A.  A thin wheat or rice-flour wrapper plus a savory filling. Lumpiang Shanghai is ground pork seasoned with garlic, onion, minced carrot, soy and pepper, rolled pencil-thin and fried. Larger vegetable versions use green beans, cabbage, carrot and mung bean sprouts. Fresh lumpia is built on cooked heart of palm or green papaya and served soft at room temperature under peanut sauce.
### Q. What kind of sauce do you eat with lumpia?
A.  Fried lumpia takes sweet chili sauce or, better, cane vinegar with crushed garlic, black pepper and a chili dropped in. Some kitchens mix a sweet-sour banana ketchup dip instead. Fresh lumpia is another matter: it arrives already dressed in a thick brown garlic-peanut sauce with crushed peanuts over the top and needs nothing added. Vinegar is the traditional answer for anything fried.
### Q. Why is sinigang supposed to be so sour?
A.  Because the sourness is the dish, not a garnish. Sinigang is a thin broth soured hard with tamarind, calamansi, kamias, green mango or guava, then loaded with pork or fish and a heap of vegetables. The acid cuts fat, wakes up plain rice and makes a heavy meal feel lighter in humid weather. A sinigang that doesn’t make you blink slightly is underseasoned.
### Q. What is halo-halo, and how are you supposed to eat it?
A.  Halo-halo means mix-mix, which is also the instruction. A tall glass gets shaved ice, evaporated milk, sweet beans, coconut strips, palm fruit, jellies, leche flan, ube ice cream and often toasted rice flakes on top. Stir the whole thing down into a slush before your first spoonful rather than eating it in layers. Order it on a hot afternoon and use the long spoon.

## Your Coat Still Smells Like Smoke: The St. Louis Fire Damage Paper Trail Nobody Hands You
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/fire-damage-restoration-st-louis-what-to-do
Your coat still smells like a campfire. It’s hanging on the back of a borrowed chair, and every time the furnace kicks on, the room fills with the smell of the house you can’t walk into. Your hair smells like it too, even after the shower. Your phone won’t stop buzzing. And nobody has told you what you’re supposed to do before lunch.
Here’s the part nobody hands you on the lawn. Two clocks started when the trucks pulled away. One is physical: soot and hose water working into the plaster, the oak floors and the mortar between the bricks while the house sits dark and dripping. The other is paper, and in St. Louis it starts with one question: which side of the line is your house on? Since 1876, St. Louis has been an independent city, not part of any county. So where you ask for the fire report depends on which side of the city limits, or the river, your house sits on. Most advice covers the first clock. Here’s the paper one, four moves you can make from that borrowed chair tonight.
1. Tell your agent, and write down the time. Scrawl it on the back of a receipt if that’s all you have, with fingers that still smell like ash. Under Missouri’s claims rule, 20 CSR 100-1.030, your insurer has ten working days from receiving your claim to acknowledge it: by paying, by writing to you, or by calling you and noting the date in your file. Here’s the line worth texting to anyone who’s ever smelled smoke in their own hallway: under that rule, telling your agent counts as telling the insurance company. The clock starts when the agent whose name is on your policy hears from you. If day ten passes in silence, call the Missouri Department of Commerce and Insurance consumer hotline at 800-726-7390 with your claim number and that date in front of you. If you live on the Illinois side of the river, email your insurer and ask which acknowledgment deadline applies to your claim.
2. Email for the fire report. Your adjuster will want the official report, and inside the city limits you don’t stand in a lobby for it. The St. Louis Fire Department posts a one-page Incident Report Request form: fill it in and email it to FDreports@stlouis-mo.gov. The same form requests a fire investigation unit report if investigators came out. In St. Louis County or the Metro East, call the fire department or district that answered your call and ask how it releases reports.
3. Bookmark the permit search. The City of St. Louis Building Division issues building permits and conducts building inspections, and its page carries a Building Permits Search by Address. Weeks from now, standing on a sidewalk that still smells faintly of wet char while a contractor says the rebuild permit is pulled, pull out your phone, type in your own street number and see it with your own eyes.
4. If the claim check comes in light, ask where the rest went. Missouri law lets a city pass an ordinance that makes insurers pay the local government part of the proceeds on a substantially damaged building, to cover demolition if the house is abandoned and never repaired. The Department of Commerce and Insurance list shows St. Louis with that ordinance on file since July 24, 1996. On a bad fire, ask your adjuster in writing whether any money went to the city, then ask the city what it takes to release it.
Tonight still comes first. The Red Cross answers 1-800-733-2767, 24 hours a day, and its St. Louis Area chapter page asks the question you’re living: “Have you been affected by a home fire or other disaster? The Red Cross is here for you.” The chapter’s offices are at 10195 Corporate Square Drive in St. Louis (314-516-2800), with a second office on the Illinois side (618-397-4600). When you call, ask exactly what help is available for your family.
### How long does fire damage restoration take?
A small kitchen fire with light smoke can take a few weeks to clean and repair. A serious fire that reaches the structure often runs several months or longer, because insurance approvals, permits and materials add weeks. Emergency board-up, water removal and drying usually start within the first day or two. Inside St. Louis city limits, two pieces of paper set the pace: the fire report you request by emailing FDreports@stlouis-mo.gov, and the permit the City Building Division issues before the rebuild.
The first phase is loud. A crew boards the broken windows, tarps the roof and pumps out what the hoses left behind. The carpet squelches underfoot. The plaster feels cool and damp under your palm. Water drips through the ceiling light in the hall, and a closed-up house that got hosed down starts to smell like a wet ashtray. That water is its own emergency. The EPA says water-damaged areas and items should be dried within 24-48 hours to prevent mold growth, so the fans and dehumidifiers go in early and drone through the night while everything else waits its turn.
Then comes the slow middle. You walk through in borrowed boots while a tech in a respirator scrubs a wall and the white cloth comes away gray every pass. Assessment, soot and smoke cleaning, odor treatment, and testing to confirm the air and surfaces are actually clean. Reconstruction follows, and that’s where the calendar stretches. Ask your restorer for a phased timeline in writing, and expect the rebuild half to move slower than the cleanup half. In an older city house it moves slower still: matching plaster-and-lath walls, original oak trim and original brick is patient, hand-fitted work, not a weekend of hanging drywall.
Inside the city limits, the rebuild runs through that same Building Division ((314) 622-3313, Permit Section at 1200 Market, Room 425). A permit application needs, at a minimum, the project address and a $25 application fee. In St. Louis County or the Metro East, ask your city or county which office handles it.
Not every week on that calendar belongs to the crew. A restorer who starts drying the night of the fire, then waits three weeks for claim approval before rebuilding, isn’t stalling. That gap is the claim, not the crew, and it’s exactly where the ten-working-day rule above becomes your lever instead of your worry. You have the date. You have the hotline.
### What should you do in the first hours after a fire?
Stay out until the fire department clears the house, then make two calls: one to your insurance company to open a claim, and one to a fire damage restoration company for emergency board-up. Those two calls, in that order, protect your claim and your house at the same time. Everything else can wait until morning.
Do not rush back in. A house that looks fine can hide a weakened floor, smoldering pockets inside the walls, or air that isn’t safe to breathe. Wait for the all-clear. When you’re let in, leave the power, gas and water off until someone qualified checks them. Flipping things back on too early is how a second problem starts the same night.
Before anyone cleans anything, build the record your adjuster will want. Start wide: stand in each doorway and photograph the whole room, then each wall, the ceiling and the floor. Move in close on damage, with a pen or a coin beside it for scale. Open closets, drawers and cabinets and shoot the contents before you touch them. Then take one slow video, room to room, saying out loud what you see. Back everything up somewhere that isn’t your phone, even if that means emailing it to yourself.
Next comes the written log, one line per item: the room, what it is, roughly how old, what it cost or would cost to replace, and the photo number. It will feel endless at midnight. Do the living room tonight and the rest tomorrow. Keep a second page beside it for dates, times, the names of everyone you speak to at the insurer and the restorer, and your claim number. When a claim goes sideways, that page is worth more than your memory.
Bring to the first meeting with the adjuster: your policy, your ID, the claim number, the photo files, the log, and receipts for the hotel, the takeout and the toothbrush you bought at the all-night drugstore A standard policy tends to reimburse those. If it’s safe, grab medications, chargers and a change of clothes, and let the rest sit for the professionals.
What not to do after a house fire is a shorter list than what to do, and every item on it protects your money. Do not wipe soot with a wet rag. Do not eat food or take medicine that sat in heat or smoke. Do not throw anything out before your adjuster has seen it. Do not sign a contract a stranger hands you on the lawn.
Then take care of the people. Call whoever needs to know you’re safe, sort out where everyone sleeps tonight, check on the pets. None of it feels like restoration. All of it is step one.
### Soot is acidic, and in an old city house it keeps eating after the fire is out
Fresh soot looks like nothing: a gray dust on the windowsill, a greasy film you can feel on the pad of your finger. It’s acidic, though, and acid keeps working long after the flames are gone. The fine residue eats into metal, etches glass, yellows countertops and stains anything porous a little deeper every day it sits. Smoke odor sinks into drywall, carpet and insulation. Time is not on your side.
This is why wiping it yourself backfires. Dry soot smears the moment a wet rag touches it, and a smear pushes the residue into the surface instead of lifting it off. Fires leave different soot, too: greasy from a kitchen, dry and powdery from paper and wood, a stubborn plastic film from synthetics. Each calls for a different cleaning method, so a restoration crew tests the residue before it picks the chemicals.
How long toxins stay in the air after a fire depends on the fire and the cleanup. Visible smoke clears fast. Fine ash and soot particles don’t. They stay airborne and settle across rooms the fire never touched, which is why a bedroom down the hall can smell like smoke for weeks. Air scrubbers with HEPA filtration pull those particles out, and proper ventilation clears what’s left. Time on its own rarely does the job.
One more reason to leave it to the pros: your lungs. The mix of soot, ash and whatever burned inside the house isn’t something to breathe without protection, and a few minutes grabbing belongings is a different risk from hours of cleaning. Keep kids and anyone with asthma or a heart condition well clear until the air has been scrubbed and tested. If you must step in, wear a proper respirator, not a paper dust mask.
### What comes back after a fire, and what goes to the curb?
Is anything salvageable after a fire? More than most people assume, but the line runs along one word: porous. Hard, non-porous things such as metal, glass, ceramics, solid wood and plenty of electronics often clean up beautifully. Soft things that drank in soot, smoke and water, like mattresses, upholstered couches and pillows, are usually losses. A good restorer sorts your home into keep, clean and toss before anything hits a dumpster.
Some categories go straight to the discard pile, no matter how new. Food exposed to heat, smoke or firefighting water, tossed. Medicine and cosmetics that sat in the heat, tossed. Anything charred or structurally compromised, gone. Those aren’t judgment calls, they’re safety ones, and an honest crew won’t let you hang onto something that could make you sick.
The surprising saves are worth waiting for. Specialized cleaning, ozone and hydroxyl treatment, ultrasonic baths and document-drying services can bring back photos, books, papers and sentimental pieces you’d have sworn were ruined. It takes time and it isn’t guaranteed. Still, the rule holds: don’t throw anything out before the restorer and your insurance adjuster have both seen it. A discarded item is a denied line on your claim, and that’s why the log matters.

### What is the average cost to rebuild a house after a fire?
There isn’t an honest average, and you should be wary of anyone who offers one. A scorched kitchen and a total loss are not the same project. Cost tracks the square footage affected, how deep the structural and smoke damage runs, local building costs, and any code upgrades a rebuild triggers. I did not find a St. Louis figure I could verify, so I won’t make one up.
Can fire damage be repaired instead of rebuilt? Usually, yes, as long as the structure is sound. Crews clean the soot, strip the smoke odor, dry what the hoses soaked and rebuild the parts that burned. Repair versus rebuild comes down to how far the fire and its heat traveled, and that is the question your restorer and your adjuster will weigh. The number that matters most to you is your policy’s dwelling coverage, not a national statistic.
### Pick a St. Louis restorer before one picks you
Shortlist two or three companies and interview them, rather than signing with the first truck that shows up at the curb. A few phone calls while the house is still wet is a small price. Tell each company exactly what you expect, then listen for the gap between what you asked for and what they’re actually prepared to do.
Say what you want out loud. You want a crew that can respond and board up within a day, technicians trained and certified through a recognized industry body, and someone who will document the damage and work directly with your insurer. You want a written scope and a realistic timeline. A company ready to lay those things in front of you is showing you how it runs. One that dodges the questions is telling you something too.
Then verify the boring stuff. Confirm the company is insured for this kind of work, and be wary of any contract pushed at you the same night. On licensing, ask your city or county what license or permit this work needs, and get the answer in writing. ### How does insurance fit into fire restoration?
Insurance usually pays for most of it, which is why the claim runs alongside the cleanup from day one. Most homeowners policies cover fire damage to the structure and your belongings, plus additional living expenses if the house can’t be lived in. Your deductible and coverage limits decide what lands in your own pocket.
Open the claim the same night if you can. An adjuster will come out to inspect and estimate the loss, so keep those first photos, hold onto damaged items until they’ve been logged, and write down every expense the fire creates. Then send a two-line email: the date you reported the claim, and a request that they confirm in writing they received it. That date is what you’ll point to if the acknowledgment window described earlier passes in silence.
One more detail catches people off guard: what drives the payout is often the policy, not the house. Our piece on what drives your St. Louis home insurance premium explains why replacement cost versus actual cash value matters so much after a total loss. Most claims get paid. Some don’t, or come back far lower than the damage warrants. If a denial or a lowball offer stops you cold, our guide on when to call a St. Louis attorney about a denied claim lays out your options. Read your own policy first. The declarations page is where the real answers hide.
### How do you recover emotionally after a house fire?
Give yourself room, because this is a real loss, not just a repair job. The smoke gets into coats, couch cushions and the inside of the car, and a smell can knock you flat on a Tuesday when you thought you were fine. Being rattled is normal. Lean on family, friends and neighbors, and say yes when someone offers a spare bedroom or a hot meal.
Call that 24-hour Red Cross number without apologizing for it. Keep a simple routine, even a small one: the same breakfast, the same school run if you can manage it. Watch for stress in the kids. And if the weight doesn’t lift after the first few weeks, talk to a counselor. Asking for that help is part of the recovery, not a sign it’s failing.

### Frequently asked questions after a fire
### Q. Can fire damage be repaired?
A.  Usually, yes. If the structure is sound, most fire-damaged homes get restored rather than torn down: crews clean the soot, pull the smoke odor out at the source, dry what the hoses soaked and rebuild what burned. Whether repair or a full rebuild makes sense depends on how far the fire and its heat traveled.
### Q. Is anything salvageable after a fire?
A.  Often more than you’d guess. Metal, glass, ceramics, solid wood and many electronics can come back with professional cleaning, and some photos and papers can be recovered too. Mattresses, upholstered furniture and anything that soaked up soot or water usually can’t. Let the restorer sort it before anything goes in a dumpster.
### Q. What not to do after a house fire?
A.  Don’t go back in until the fire department says it’s safe, and don’t switch the power, gas or water back on. Don’t wipe soot with a wet cloth, which grinds it in. Don’t eat food or take medicine that sat in heat or smoke. And don’t throw out damaged items before your adjuster has logged them.
### Q. How long do toxins stay in the air after a fire?
A.  It varies with the fire and the cleanup. Visible smoke clears quickly, but fine ash, soot particles and odor can hang in the air and settle into surfaces for days or weeks if the home isn’t cleaned and ventilated properly. HEPA air scrubbing and thorough cleaning are what clear it, not waiting.
### Q. Does homeowners insurance cover fire damage restoration?
A.  In most cases, yes. Most homeowners policies cover fire damage to the structure and your belongings, plus additional living expenses if the house can’t be lived in. Your deductible, your limits and whether the policy pays replacement cost or actual cash value shape the payout. Read the declarations page and open the claim early.

## Sending Flowers in St. Louis: A Sympathy and Gift Guide
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/sending-flowers-in-st-louis-sympathy-and-gift-guide
The text comes in on a Tuesday. A coworker’s father has died, and the visitation is Thursday. You’re standing in your kitchen in Hillsboro, phone in hand, and you want to send flowers because that’s what people do. Then the website asks you to pick an arrangement from a photo, and you freeze. Too big? Too cheerful? Too late?
Different week, different reason. Your daughter just had a baby up in Lake St. Louis, and a friend in Swansea is celebrating twenty-five years of marriage the same weekend. Two happy deliveries, two completely different notes, and you have no idea whether roses say the wrong thing to either of them.
And somewhere in St. Ann, someone is refreshing a tracking page at 3 p.m., wondering whether the arrangement will reach the funeral home before the family does. Flowers are a small gesture. Getting them wrong feels enormous. So let’s take the pressure off, one decision at a time.
Here’s the whole thing in order. The sympathy side first, because that’s the part that keeps people up at night. Then the happy occasions. Then the plain logistics of getting a delivery to the right door on the right day. Nothing fancy, just how these decisions actually play out around St. Louis.
### What is the etiquette for sending flowers after someone dies?
Send promptly, but let the family’s wishes lead. Read the obituary first. If it asks for donations in lieu of flowers, honor that. Friends and coworkers send a standing spray or a vase arrangement; the casket spray belongs to the immediate family. A short, plain note, signed clearly, does the rest.
The obituary is the instruction sheet, and most people skip it. It tells you the visitation and service times, the funeral home, sometimes the family’s charity of choice, and now and then a line that says no flowers at all. Read it before you order anything. Two minutes there prevents the two most common mistakes: sending flowers to a service that didn’t want them, and sending them to the wrong building.
There’s a quiet hierarchy to the arrangements, and it trips up people who mean well. The casket spray, the large piece that lies across the top, is traditionally chosen and paid for by the immediate family. It’s not the thing a coworker sends. Friends, neighbors, and workplaces send a standing spray on an easel, or a vase arrangement that can move to the family home afterward. Tell the florist who you were to the person who died, and they’ll steer you to the right piece without you having to know the vocabulary.
One more thing matters more than it should: religion and culture change the rules. Some traditions welcome flowers at the service. Others prefer food sent to the home, or consider certain blooms out of place entirely. If you’re not sure what the family observes, a vase arrangement sent to the house a few days later is almost always safe. It lands when the crowd has gone and the quiet has set in.
### Which sympathy arrangement should you actually order?
Match the piece to your relationship, not to the biggest photo. Coworkers and friends send a standing easel spray or a vase; close friends of the family sometimes send a larger basket or a living plant. The immediate family handles the casket spray. Your money goes further when you name a budget and let a designer build to it.
### Sprays, baskets, and plants
A standing spray reads from across a room, which is why organizations and groups of coworkers tend to choose it. A basket or a vase arrangement is more personal and, dollar for dollar, often looks fuller up close, because none of the budget went into a frame and an easel. A living plant, a peace lily or an orchid, keeps going long after the service and gives the family something to tend. Any of the three is correct. The wrong one is the one that doesn’t fit your place in the person’s life.
### Say a number, skip the photo
This is the single most useful habit in the whole guide. Give the florist three things: a dollar amount, who the flowers are for, and one boundary if you have one. “A hundred dollars, it’s for my coworker’s dad’s visitation, nothing too bright” beats any picture on a screen. A designer at the cooler knows what’s fresh that morning and what will still look right two days later. A photo shot two years ago knows neither. If you want the deeper version of why ordering direct stretches your money, we wrote a whole piece on how to order from a real St. Louis florist instead of a middleman.
### What should the card say, and who signs it?
Keep it short, sign it clearly, and don’t try to fix anything. A sympathy card isn’t the place for a paragraph. A line or two that names the person, offers a small memory or a simple “thinking of you,” and your full name so the family knows who sent it. Grieving people are reading a stack of these. Clear beats clever every time.
The most common card mistake isn’t what people write. It’s the signature. “The Johnsons” means nothing to a widow who knows four families named Johnson. Sign your full name, and add how you knew the person if it isn’t obvious. “Dave Kramer, Tom’s coworker at the plant” tells the family exactly who you are and why you cared. That context is a gift on its own.
As for the words, plain is kind. “I’m so sorry for your loss. Your mother was good to me, and I won’t forget it.” That’s enough. Avoid anything that begins with “at least,” and skip the phrases that try to explain the death away. You’re not there to make sense of it. You’re there to say you noticed, and that you’re standing with them.
Running a business, not a sympathy list? Here’s how to write a press release.
### When flowers aren’t the right call, what is?
When the obituary asks for donations, when the family follows a tradition that skips flowers, or when the house is already overflowing, send something else. A charitable gift in the person’s name, a meal delivered to the home, a grocery gift card, or a basket of practical food all say what flowers do, sometimes louder. The gesture is the point, not the petals.
Donations in lieu of flowers aren’t a hint. They’re a request, and honoring it is the whole etiquette. Give to the charity named, and if the site lets you, note that it’s in memory of the person so the family gets told. That notification means more to them than a vase would. You followed their wishes on a day when very little was in their control.
Food is the other quiet winner, especially in the first hard week. Nobody in a grieving house wants to cook. A tray, a grocery gift card, or a thoughtfully built basket carries the family through the days when casseroles pile up and then vanish all at once. If you want ideas that travel well, our guide to what to actually put in a St. Louis gift basket breaks it down by occasion, including the somber ones.
### How do you send flowers for a happy occasion?
Match the flowers to the moment and the person, then let color do the work. Birthdays, new babies, anniversaries, and get-well deliveries all want brightness and life, which is the opposite of the sympathy palette. The same trick applies: name a budget, name the occasion, name one thing the recipient loves or hates, and let a designer build it.
### Reading the occasion
A new baby in Lake St. Louis and a twenty-fifth anniversary in Swansea call for different arrangements, and not because of the flowers. It’s the note and the scale. A new-parent delivery should be easy to ignore, because those first weeks are chaos—something small that doesn’t need tending. An anniversary can be lush and a little romantic. A get-well arrangement should be cheerful without being loud, and low enough to sit on a bedside table rather than tower over it.
### The stems that stretch a budget
Red roses are the most bid-up flower of the year, especially around Valentine’s Day and Mother’s Day, when a year of demand lands in a 48-hour window. If you want more flower for your money on those weeks, ask for a designer’s-choice arrangement in a color family instead of a dozen red roses. Tulips, ranunculus, and garden-style mixes often cost less and read as more thoughtful. Order five to seven days ahead of the big holidays and you’ll get flowers bought for you, not scraps left at the end of a frantic morning.
### How do you make sure the flowers actually arrive on time?
Call the destination before you call the florist. The building sets the real deadline, not the shop. Funeral homes take flowers into the room before the visitation, hospitals stop accepting deliveries at set times, and some care units restrict fresh flowers entirely. Thirty seconds confirming the window saves a delivery that shows up to a locked door.
For a funeral, the visitation time is your true deadline, and it’s almost always earlier than the florist’s own same-day cutoff. Get the funeral home’s address and the time the family arrives, then give the florist a delivery window rather than a single time. A shop can promise “before the visitation” far more reliably than “by 4:00 exactly,” because a driver’s route bends around traffic and every other stop that day.
Distance is the variable nobody warns you about. A shop close to the recipient can deliver all afternoon. A shop across the metro, or across the river, is making a route decision that morning, and that’s where late deliveries come from. Pick a florist near the destination, not near you. If you’re sending to a hospital in St. Louis and you live forty minutes out, the shop by the hospital is the safer bet every time.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the 3:5:8 rule for flowers?
A.  It’s a design guideline, not an etiquette rule. Arrangers group stems in odd clusters—threes, fives, and eights—so the eye reads the shape as natural instead of stiffly symmetrical. Varied heights and odd numbers are part of what separates a designed arrangement from a bunch stuffed in a vase. You don’t need to know it to order, but it explains why a florist’s work looks fuller than your own.
### Q. What is a good message to send in a sympathy flower?
A.  Short, specific, and signed clearly. A line or two works best: “So sorry for your loss. Your dad always made me laugh, and I’ll miss him.” Name the person if you can, skip anything that begins with “at least,” and sign your full name plus how you knew them. The family is reading a stack of cards, and clear context is a kindness.
### Q. What do you send when someone dies instead of flowers?
A.  A donation to the charity named in the obituary is the first choice, because it honors a stated request. Beyond that, a meal delivered to the home, a grocery gift card, or a practical food basket all carry real weight in the first week, when nobody wants to cook. If you send a donation, ask that the family be notified it was in the person’s memory.
### Q. What flowers do you not send when someone dies?
A.  There’s no universal banned list, but read the family’s culture and faith first, because some traditions treat certain blooms or colors as out of place. When you’re unsure, a tasteful mixed arrangement in soft tones is safer than a bold, bright statement. And avoid anything that reads as a birthday delivery. A designer who knows it’s for a service will steer you clear of the wrong note.
### Q. How soon after death should you send flowers?
A.  For a service, aim to have them arrive before the visitation, which means ordering a day or two ahead once you know the funeral home and the time. If you’ve missed the service, don’t skip it—send a vase arrangement to the family’s home a week or two later. That later delivery often lands harder, because it arrives after the crowd has gone.
### Q. Who delivers flowers for free?
A.  Truly free delivery is less common than the ads suggest. Some local shops fold delivery into the arrangement price within their normal zone, and a few run free-delivery promotions or waive the fee above a minimum order. National gift-service sites usually build delivery into the sticker price rather than removing it. The honest move is to ask the local florist directly what their delivery costs and where they go.
### Q. Is it better to send sympathy flowers to the funeral home or the family’s house?
A.  Both work, and they do different jobs. Flowers at the funeral home support the service and are seen by everyone who attends, so that’s where sprays and easel arrangements belong. A vase sent to the house lands later, when the family is home and the visitors have thinned out. If you can choose only one and you’re close to them, the home delivery is often the more personal choice.
### Q. How much should you spend on sympathy flowers?
A.  Spend what fits your relationship and your budget, not what a website’s photo pushes. A coworker or acquaintance can send a modest, tasteful arrangement without a second thought. Close friends and family tend to send more, or a larger standing piece. Rather than chasing a number, tell the florist your budget and let a designer build the fullest arrangement it will buy.

## Starting a Food Truck in St. Louis: What It Really Costs
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/starting-a-food-truck-in-st-louis-what-it-costs
The used step van has been open in a browser tab for eleven days. A guy in Wildwood keeps coming back to it after the kids are down, running the same math on the back of an envelope and getting a different number every time. The truck looks clean in the photos. The photos are the easy part.
He isn’t the only one doing this tonight. A caterer in Richmond Heights has been asked “do you have a truck?” by three brides in a row and is tired of saying no. A line cook in East St. Louis has a family recipe, a loyal crowd at two church festivals, and a rent number on any storefront that keeps climbing while he waits.
All three picture the same thing: a lunch rush forming outside an office park in Ladue, cash moving, a line that wraps the sidewalk. That picture is real. It’s also the last ten percent of the job. Everything before it is trucks, permits, propane, and a commissary you pay for whether or not you sell a single taco. So here’s the honest cost of getting there, in the order the money actually leaves your hands.
### Can food trucks actually make money?
Yes, but the margins are thinner than the crowds suggest. A well-run truck in St. Louis can clear a real profit once it controls food cost, keeps the schedule full, and stops paying for empty parking. Plenty never get there. The money is made in the boring math, not the busy Saturdays.
Here’s the part nobody posts about. Revenue on a good day looks fantastic. Then you subtract food cost, propane, the commissary rent, card processing, the event fee, fuel, and your own hours, and the great day quietly turns into a fair one. A truck that grosses well can still lose money if it runs a bloated menu and chases every low-paying gig on the calendar.
Profit comes from control, not volume. The owners who last watch food cost like a hawk, keep the menu short enough to run fast, and fill the week with bookings that actually pay. From what local operators describe, the trucks that fold rarely die on one slow Saturday. They bleed out on fixed costs during the weeks nobody photographs.
### What does it really cost to get a food truck on the road?
More than the truck, and the truck is expensive enough. Your biggest upfront number is the vehicle itself, and it swings wildly. A basic concession trailer you tow can start in the low five figures. A fully built, wrapped, inspection-ready truck with cooking equipment installed often lands in the high five figures or beyond. Buy used and you trade money for risk.
Two roads split here. A turnkey used truck gets you selling sooner, but you inherit somebody’s wiring, somebody’s grease trap, and whatever they papered over before the sale. A shell you build out costs less on paper and far more in time, permits, and the parts that never quite fit. Either way, budget for the equipment that makes the truck legal, not just functional: a three-compartment sink, hot water, fresh and gray water tanks, a fire suppression system over the cook line, and a generator quiet enough that events will actually let you run it.
Then the costs that never make the highlight reel. A wrap and signage. Your point-of-sale setup. Starting inventory and packaging. Business registration and an LLC. Insurance binders before anyone will let you park. A deposit on a commissary. First-round permit fees. None of it is glamorous, and all of it clears before you flip the first burger.
### Which permits and licenses do you actually need?
This is where the dream meets paperwork. At a minimum, expect a business registration, a Missouri retail sales tax license, a health permit for a mobile food establishment, a fire safety inspection, and a food safety certification for whoever runs the line. That’s the floor. Individual cities across the metro stack their own vendor permits on top, and no two do it quite the same way.
Start with the state. You register the business, then pull a Missouri retail sales tax license so you can legally collect and send in sales tax on every plate you sell. Our guide to the Missouri sales tax license walks through that step, and it isn’t optional. Skipping it is how a promising first summer turns into a letter from the Department of Revenue.
The health permit is the big one. A local health department inspects the truck, and Missouri’s food code expects a mobile operation to prep, restock, and clean from an approved base rather than living entirely on four wheels. Add a fire inspection for the propane and the cook line, plus a certified food protection manager and food handler cards for staff. Confirm the current rules with the City of St. Louis health department or the county health department where you plan to park, because the details shift and a blog can’t keep them all current.
Here’s the part that surprises everyone. A permit that lets you vend in one city does nothing for you across the line in the next one. Each municipality can require its own license, set its own zoning for where a truck may park, and cap how long you can stay in a spot. The truck that works a lunch route through several towns in a week is quietly juggling several rulebooks at once.
### Why does a commissary kitchen matter so much?
Because across most of the metro you can’t legally run a truck without one. A commissary, sometimes called a base of operations, is a licensed commercial kitchen where you prep food, refill your water, dump gray water, wash equipment, and store inventory overnight. Health departments generally require a mobile vendor to have one, and they want the agreement in writing.
You can rent time in a shared commissary by the hour or the month, split space with another operator, or partner with a restaurant using its kitchen off-hours. Each option trades money for control. A dedicated space costs more and is always open. A shared one is cheaper and fills up on Friday afternoons, right when everybody needs it at once.
Owners underestimate this line constantly. The commissary is a fixed cost that lands every month whether you booked twenty events or two. Factor it into your daily break-even from day one, because it’s one of the biggest reasons a truck can look busy all season and still finish in the red.
### How much does a food truck cost to run for a day?
Add it up before you ever unlock the window. A single service day carries food cost for what you expect to sell, propane, fuel to and from the commissary, a share of that monthly commissary rent, disposables and packaging, card processing on every swipe, staff wages, and whatever the spot itself charges. Even a quiet day starts in the hole.
Card processing deserves its own line, because most of your sales won’t be cash. Every tap and swipe takes a percentage, and on thin margins that cut adds up fast across a season. Our breakdown of credit card processing fees for small business covers what to watch before you sign with a provider.
The number that matters is your daily break-even: the sales you need just to cover the day before you’ve earned a dollar. Know it cold. Owners who can recite their break-even turn down bad gigs without guilt. Owners who can’t say yes to everything and wonder why a full calendar still doesn’t pay.
### Do you have to pay to park at events and festivals?
Almost always, and the way you pay varies. Some events charge a flat vendor fee for the spot. Others take a percentage of your sales. Plenty do both, a smaller flat fee plus a cut off the top. A few private bookings flip the model and pay the truck a guarantee to show up, which is the gig every owner wants.
Recurring spots work differently from one-off festivals. A weekly market or a lunch rotation usually charges a stall or space fee, and the good ones earn back more than they cost because the crowd already shows up. Our guide to St. Louis metro farmers markets by town maps where those crowds gather across the region.
The trap is the free-sounding event. A festival with no vendor fee still costs you a full day of labor, fuel, food, and propane, and if the crowd doesn’t spend, you paid to be there in every way except the invoice. Read every booking as a math problem. What does the spot cost, what will this crowd realistically buy, and does the day clear your break-even with room left over?
Your menu is sales copy, too. See what a copywriter does
### What sells, and what actually makes money?
The most profitable food has a low cost per plate, a price people happily pay, and a build fast enough to keep the line moving. That’s why loaded fries, tacos, birria, gourmet grilled cheese, barbecue, and handheld comfort food show up on so many trucks. Cheap base, strong markup, quick to hand out the window.
Speed is a profit center people forget. A short menu you can run in your sleep beats a long one that stalls the window at the exact moment a crowd forms. Every extra item adds prep, inventory, and waste. The trucks that print money usually do four or five things and do them fast.
Signature beats generic. A truck known for one thing gets remembered, requested, and booked, which is worth more than a wide menu nobody can describe to a friend. Watch food cost as a percentage of the price on every item, cut the losers, and price like a business instead of a friend doing favors.
### Why do so many food trucks close?
Because the costs are relentless and the good days are seasonal. Food service is a famously tough business, and reliable, current failure numbers specific to St. Louis trucks are hard to pin down, so treat any confident percentage online with suspicion. What’s clear is why they fold, and it repeats.
The pattern is boring and consistent. Undercounted fixed costs like the commissary and insurance. A menu too long to run fast. Chasing every free event instead of booking gigs that pay. A brutal weather stretch that wipes out a spring. Burnout, because the truck is a second full-time job stacked on top of the cooking. None of it is dramatic. All of it is fatal in slow accumulation.
The lifestyle is the part the highlight reels skip. You’re the cook, the driver, the dishwasher, the accountant, the mechanic, and the marketer, often before noon. The hours are long, the work is physical, and the weather votes on your income. Go in knowing that, price for it, and the odds get a lot friendlier.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much does a food truck cost for a day?
A.  More than the spot fee, always. A single service day has to cover food cost, propane, fuel, a share of your monthly commissary rent, packaging, card processing on every sale, staff wages, and whatever the event charges. Even a slow day starts in the hole, which is why knowing your daily break-even matters more than the gross.
### Q. Do food trucks pay to park at a small event?
A.  Usually, yes. Small events commonly charge a flat vendor fee, a percentage of your sales, or both. Some private bookings pay the truck a guarantee instead, which is the better deal. Even a no-fee event still costs a full day of labor, fuel, and food, so read every booking as a math problem before you commit.
### Q. What is the failure rate for food trucks?
A.  Higher than most first-timers expect, though a single reliable number is hard to trust. Food service closes at a notoriously high rate in the early years, and trucks are not exempt. Be skeptical of any exact percentage online. The useful question is why they fail: undercounted fixed costs, weak bookings, and burnout, all of which you can plan around.
### Q. What is the most profitable food on a food truck?
A.  The kind with a low cost per plate, a price people gladly pay, and a fast build. Loaded fries, tacos, birria, barbecue, and handheld comfort food fit that shape, which is why they are everywhere. Speed matters as much as margin, since a short menu you can run fast keeps the line moving when a crowd finally forms.
### Q. What are the downsides of owning a food truck?
A.  Long physical hours and relentless fixed costs. You become the cook, driver, dishwasher, mechanic, and marketer at once, often before lunch. Weather can erase a weekend, the commissary bill arrives whether you sell or not, and the season is short. It can absolutely work, but it rewards discipline and stamina far more than a great recipe alone.
### Q. Are there any food trucks for sale in St. Louis?
A.  Yes, used trucks and trailers turn over regularly around the metro through resale listings, restaurant auctions, and owners exiting the business. A used truck gets you selling sooner but carries inherited risk, so bring a mechanic and someone who knows health-code equipment before you buy. Confirm the truck can actually pass a local health inspection as configured.
### Q. How much does it cost to start a food truck in St. Louis?
A.  It varies widely, and honest ranges beat false precision. The truck itself is the biggest line, from the low five figures for a basic trailer to well into the five or six figures for a fully built truck. Then add permits, insurance, a commissary deposit, a wrap, a point-of-sale setup, and starting inventory before you open the window.
### Q. Do you need a commissary kitchen for a food truck in Missouri?
A.  In most of the metro, yes. Health departments generally require a mobile food business to operate from an approved commissary or base kitchen for prep, water, waste, and storage, and they want the agreement documented. You can rent shared kitchen time, split a space, or partner with a restaurant. Confirm the exact rule with your local health department.

## Tuxedo and Formal Wear Rental in St. Louis: A Guide
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/tuxedo-and-formal-wear-rental-in-st-louis
The groom is standing in a bedroom in Des Peres at eleven at night, counting groomsmen on his phone. Six of them, and no two live in the same place. One works nights. One still believes he can walk in the week of the wedding and walk out in a tuxedo. The groom already knows how that ends, because it happened at his brother’s wedding, and the photos still bother him.
A dad in Hazelwood is doing different math. His son’s prom is five weeks out, the kid grew two inches since fall, and the group chat has settled on a color nobody can name out loud. A wedding party driving in from Collinsville wants everyone in the same jacket and the same shade, standing in a line where the camera will catch every hem that sits wrong.
And in Overland, someone opens a closet the morning of a funeral and finds the one dark suit no longer fits. He has a few hours, not a few weeks. Four situations, one question underneath all of them: what does renting formal wear in St. Louis actually cost, and what quietly decides whether the night goes well? This guide takes the price, the timing, and the fitting, in that order.
### How much on average does it cost to rent a tuxedo?
Most tuxedo rentals in the St. Louis area fall into a fairly narrow band: a basic package tends to cost less than a nice dinner for two, while a designer cut, a peak wedding date, or added shoes and accessories pushes it higher. Season, label and add-ons move the number more than anything.
Nobody publishes a rate card you can trust across the metro, so any single figure you read, including one in a guide like this, owes you a written quote. What stays steady is the shape. Price climbs with three things: the label on the jacket, the cut you want, and the calendar. Everything else is detail hung around those three.
The package ladder is easy to follow. A house-brand tuxedo with a standard fit sits at the bottom. A name brand, or a slim modern cut, sits above it. Add real shoes instead of your own, swap in a specialty vest or a colored tie to match a wedding, and each choice nudges the total up a notch. You’re not buying a tuxedo. You’re assembling one, piece by piece.
The calendar is the part people underestimate. Prom season and wedding season squeeze the whole business into a few months, and the popular sizes and colors go first. A tuxedo booked in the quiet season and the same tuxedo booked on a Saturday in May are, in practice, two prices for one rack. Rush handling, when a shop can even do it, costs more again.
It helps to see the rental as one line in a bigger night. The formal wear sits next to the flowers, the photos and the ride, and each of those carries its own minimum and its own surprises. If you’re pricing a prom or a wedding as a whole, our guide to what a limo costs in St. Louis works the way this one does: the headline rate is never the final bill.
### What is the difference between a tuxedo and a suit?
A tuxedo is dressier than a suit, and the difference lives in the details: satin on the lapels, a satin stripe down the trouser leg, and a shirt built for studs instead of buttons. A suit is the everyday workhorse. A tuxedo is the black-tie version, and most people rent one because they wear it about once a year.
That once-a-year part is the whole case for renting. A suit earns its keep because you wear it again, to work, to interviews, to church. A tuxedo mostly sits in a closet losing its fit while your body and the styles both change around it. Renting hands the storage, the cleaning and the going-out-of-date problem to somebody else.
So is renting cheaper than buying? For a single event, almost always, and it isn’t close. A quality tuxedo costs many times a rental before tailoring. The math only flips if you wear black tie several times a year, every year, at which point owning one that truly fits starts to pay for itself. For everyone who reaches black tie once or twice a decade, renting wins on cost and on closet space both.
There’s a middle path worth knowing. Some shops sell off their rental stock, and some offer a buy option on the same pieces they rent. If you’ve got three weddings this year and a reunion next, ask whether buying beats renting four separate times. A good shop will tell you straight, because they’d rather keep you than win one transaction.
### How does renting formal wear actually work, step by step?
Renting runs on a simple arc: you get measured, you pick a package, you leave a deposit, you collect the outfit a few days before the event, and you return it a day or two after. The whole thing is built around your date, and the shop holds your specific sizes so they’re on the rack when you walk in.
### What is included in a tuxedo rental package?
A tuxedo rental package is usually more complete than people expect. Most include the jacket and trousers, a formal shirt, a vest or cummerbund, a tie or bow tie, and the studs and cufflinks a tuxedo shirt needs. Many bundle the shoes, and most include the socks, which, yes, are yours to keep. Ask exactly what’s on the list before you agree to a price, because a package that looks cheap can be missing the shoes, and shoes add up fast.
### How early should you reserve?
Reserve earlier than feels necessary, especially for a wedding party. A few weeks is a reasonable floor for a single rental, and a couple of months is safer when a group has to match. The reason is inventory, not paperwork: the popular sizes, colors and styles get claimed first, and the groomsman who waits until the last week takes whatever is left. For prom and peak wedding dates, the earlier you lock it in, the more you get to actually choose.
### When do you pick it up and drop it off?
Most shops have you collect the outfit two or three days ahead, which leaves room for one last try-on and time to fix anything that’s off. The rental window itself is short, usually a handful of days, with a return deadline printed on the paperwork, often the first business day after the event. Miss it and a late fee starts running, so if the wedding is out of town, ask about the return window before you leave the counter.
### What formal wear can you rent besides a tuxedo?
More than the word tuxedo suggests. Most formal wear shops rent suits as well as tuxedos, in a range of colors for weddings and proms, plus the full kit of accessories: vests, ties, pocket squares, suspenders, shoes and cufflinks. Some carry boys’ and children’s sizes for ring bearers, and many handle hard-to-fit measurements that off-the-rack buying can’t.
For a wedding, the coordination is the real service. A shop can put the whole party in one color and one cut, keep a record of everyone’s measurements, and make sure the groom’s lapel matches the groomsmen’s down the line. That matters more than any single garment, because a lineup where one jacket sits wrong is the frame the camera keeps. Women have rental options too, though the market runs a little differently. Gown and dress rental has grown, and for a one-time black-tie event it solves the same problem a rented tuxedo does: you wear it once, then hand back the storage and the dry cleaning. For prom, plenty of shops dress the whole group, which keeps the colors honest across a dozen photos nobody gets to retake.
Fit range is where a real shop earns its name. Hard-to-fit measurements, big and tall, unusual proportions, a teenager who’s still growing: these are exactly the cases where renting from people who measure for a living beats guessing online. And the accessories are cheap insurance. A tie in the right shade and shoes that match the party pull an outfit together for a fraction of what the jacket costs.

### How do you get a rental tux to actually fit?
Fit is the whole game, and it comes down to one habit: try the entire outfit on, in the shop, days before the event, not an hour before you walk in. Measurements get you close. The final try-on is where a sleeve half an inch too long, or trousers that puddle at the shoe, get caught while there’s still time to swap them.
The most common rental mistake isn’t picking the wrong style. It’s skipping that last fitting. A tuxedo can be reserved in your size and still arrive wrong, because sizes drift between makers and a jacket cut slim runs smaller than the number on the tag. Shops expect this and keep back-up sizes for exactly that reason, but only if you show up early enough to use them.
A few other traps catch people every year. Waiting until the event week, so nothing can be exchanged. Guessing measurements over the phone instead of getting measured in person. Forgetting that a group only matches if every member gets fitted, including the uncle who swears he’s the same size he was in 1994. And skimming the contract, so the deposit, the damage terms and the return deadline all land as surprises later.
Small checks save the night. Do up the jacket button, sit down in the trousers, raise both arms, look at the sleeve length over a watch. Confirm the shirt takes the studs you were handed. Make sure the shoes fit with the socks you’ll actually wear. None of that takes long, and every bit of it is easier to fix on a Wednesday than in a parking lot on Saturday.
### How do you choose a formal wear shop in St. Louis?
Treat the first visit as an interview, because that’s what it is. Shortlist two or three formal wear shops, walk in with your date and your event, and ask each one the same questions. The right shop is the one whose answers are specific and whose fitting process is real, not the one with the best-looking window.
Ask what the all-in price includes and what costs extra. Ask how far ahead they need your order, and when the final try-on happens. Ask what they do if a piece arrives wrong the week of the event, because the honest answer is a back-up plan, not a promise that it never happens. Ask about the deposit, the damage policy and the exact return deadline.
If you’re dressing a group, ask how they handle out-of-town members, since half a wedding party rarely lives in one place. A shop used to weddings can take measurements done elsewhere and still get everyone matching. Ask to see the actual garments, feel the fabric, and look at how a finished rental hangs on the rack. You learn more in five minutes of looking than in any stack of online reviews.
Listen for the red flags too. A shop that quotes a price without asking about your event or your date is guessing. One that can’t tell you plainly what’s included, or waves off the final fitting, is telling you how the night will go. In our experience, the shop that slows down to measure you properly and walk you through the timeline is the one that saves you on the day it counts.

### Q. Is it cheaper to rent a tuxedo or buy a suit?

Buying a suit is a different call, because you actually wear a suit again. The rule of thumb: rent what you need once a year, and buy what you wear often.
### Q. How far in advance should you rent a tux?
A.  Earlier than feels necessary. A few weeks is a reasonable floor for one rental, and a couple of months is safer when a group has to match, because the popular sizes, colors and styles get reserved first. A.  The big one is skipping the final try-on, the last chance to catch a long sleeve or puddling trousers while there’s still time to swap them. ### Q. How long can you keep a rented tux?
A.  Not long. Most rental periods run a matter of days, built around your event date. A.  Usually, yes. Most shops include a new pair of formal socks in the package and expect you to keep them, for the obvious hygiene reason. ### Q. Should the whole wedding party rent from the same shop?

### Q. Can you rent a suit instead of a tuxedo?

A suit rental solves the same once-a-year problem: you wear it for the event, then hand back the storage and the cleaning. Ask about colors and cuts, since suit selection often runs wider than the tuxedo rack.
### Q. What happens if you damage or stain a rented tux?
A.  It depends on the contract, which is why you read it before signing. Normal wear is expected and usually forgiven. A minor spill is often covered by a small damage waiver, if the shop offers one. Serious damage, a burn, a tear, a lost jacket, can bring a repair or replacement fee. Ask what the deposit and damage policy cover before the outfit leaves the shop.

## Frozen Yogurt in St. Louis: What to Know
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/frozen-yogurt-in-st-louis-what-to-know
The cup weighs almost nothing when you pull it off the stack. You fill it yourself, and by the time it hits the scale by the register it costs more than the lunch you ate an hour earlier. A kid in Fairview Heights has just buried two swirls of tart vanilla under gummy bears, three pumps of syrup and a fistful of crushed cookie. The parent is doing the math, and losing.
Maybe you’ve watched this in a strip center in Bridgeton, or in a bright little shop in Alton that was a phone store the year before. Froyo places open fast. They glow for a couple of summers, then turn into a nail salon. One near a busy road in Ferguson lasted two seasons and closed. Another in Granite City is somehow still going, packed every warm Friday night.
The pitch never changes. Lighter than ice cream, a little good for you, and the kids build their own. Some of that holds up. Some of it falls apart the second you weigh the cup. Across the St. Louis area these shops come and go for reasons that have almost nothing to do with the yogurt itself. Here’s what’s actually going on, from the machine to the scale.
### Is frozen yogurt actually healthier than ice cream?
Sometimes, and not by as much as the sign suggests. Frozen yogurt usually carries less butterfat than ice cream, so a plain serving can run lighter in fat and calories. But the tart base is often high in sugar, and once you pile on toppings and fill a giant cup, froyo can easily beat ice cream on both.
The one real difference is fat. In the United States a product has to contain at least ten percent milkfat before it can be sold as ice cream, and the premium brands push well past that. Frozen yogurt is built on milk and cultures instead, with far less cream, so ounce for ounce the plain stuff does tend to carry fewer calories. That part is honest.
Here’s the catch nobody paints on the wall. Fat is what makes a frozen dessert taste smooth and rich, so when a shop pulls the cream out, it usually pours sugar back in to cover the gap. The tart bases are the worst offenders. A plain cup of froyo can hold as much sugar as the scoop of ice cream it replaced, now and then more.
So the straight answer is that froyo isn’t automatically the better choice. A small, plain, tart cup usually beats a scoop of the good ice cream. A large cup loaded at the topping bar usually loses to it. The container does most of the damage, and we’ll get to the container.
### What is frozen yogurt, and what’s in the machine?
Frozen yogurt is milk, yogurt cultures, sugar and a stabilizer, churned with air in a soft-serve machine. Most of what curls out of the nozzle starts as a liquid mix. A few shops build that mix from scratch. Far more pour it in from a bag or carton bought pre-made, then just add the cold and the swirl.
### The mix
Pre-made mix isn’t a scandal. It’s consistent, cheap and easy to store, which is exactly what a small shop needs. But it does mean the flavor you taste was decided in a factory, not a kitchen, and most self-serve bars run the same handful of national mixes as everyone else. That made-here-versus-bought-in question runs through every sweet counter in town. Our guide to how to find a good bakery in St. Louis leans on the very same tell.
### The air, and why your cup weighs what it does
Overrun is the trade word for the air whipped into the mix. More air makes a lighter, fluffier swirl and a taller-looking cup out of less actual yogurt. It’s also why two shops that both charge by weight can feel worlds apart. A dense, cold swirl weighs more per inch than a puffy one, so the airier machine is quietly the friendlier deal once you hit the scale.
### How is froyo different from ice cream and custard?
Three desserts, three recipes. Ice cream is cream-heavy and churned cold. Frozen custard, the St. Louis summer staple, folds in egg yolk and runs dense with very little air, thick enough to hand you upside down without it falling out. Frozen yogurt trades most of the cream for cultured milk, so it tastes tangy and freezes harder and colder.
Around here that middle one matters. Custard is close to the regional default for a frozen treat, and a lot of people who say they don’t like froyo are really just comparing it to a rich, eggy custard and finding it thin. That’s a fair reaction. Froyo isn’t trying to be custard. It’s the tart, lighter, build-your-own cousin, and it lives or dies on that tang.
Texture is the giveaway. Custard is silk. Ice cream is dense and creamy. Froyo has a slight iciness and a clean, sour edge that either refreshes you or doesn’t. None of the three is better in the abstract. They’re answers to different cravings, and knowing which one you actually want saves you from ordering the wrong dessert and then blaming the shop.
### Why do frozen yogurt shops open and close so fast?
Mostly economics, not taste. Self-serve froyo runs on thin margins, a visible corner with real rent, and a season that only truly heats up in the warm months. The format also copied itself half to death in the early 2010s, when a wave of near-identical self-serve shops opened at once. A crowd that big always thins out.
Picture the model. You buy the machines, the mix, the toppings and the pay-by-weight scale, then you hope enough people walk in on hot evenings to cover twelve months of rent with maybe five strong months of traffic. A cold, wet summer hurts. A new shop two miles away splits the crowd. There isn’t much cushion when the weather or the neighborhood shifts.
The self-serve boom crested about a decade ago, then pulled back hard, which is why a spot that felt inevitable in 2013 can feel dated now. That’s the honest reason froyo seems less popular than it once was. It’s not that people stopped liking it. The novelty wore off and the weakest locations closed, leaving the ones with real regulars.
The survivors tend to share a few traits. A loyal local following. Birthday parties and team nights. A spot people pass anyway, near a park or a theater. The froyo is rarely the whole reason those shops last. The habit built around them is.
### Does the self-serve topping bar undo the whole idea?
Often, yes. The base might be light, but the topping bar is where a sensible cup turns into a sundae. Pay-by-weight pricing quietly rewards restraint and punishes the fun stuff, because candy, syrup, cheesecake bites and cookie dough are heavy and loaded with sugar. Fill a large cup with those and you can pass a milkshake on both sugar and price.
### Fruit versus candy
Fresh fruit is the topping that works with the yogurt instead of against it. Berries, mango, a little granola. It adds flavor without turning the cup into candy, and by weight it’s usually cheaper than a scoop of crushed cookies. The syrups are where the sugar and the ounces stack up fastest, so a light drizzle beats a flood every time.
### The cup-size trap
The cup you grab sets your ceiling before you fill a thing. Take the giant one and some part of your brain decides it should look full. Take the small one and the same swirl looks generous. It’s the simplest trick going, and it beats willpower at the scale. If real quality in a small sweet thing is what you’re after, our piece on what makes artisan chocolate in St. Louis different chases the same idea from the candy side.
Craving something savory after all that sugar? Try real Egyptian food
### How do you pick a good cup?
Taste the base before you commit. A good tart base tastes clean and sharp, like cold yogurt, not chalky and not just sweet. Most shops hand out little sample cups, so use them. If the plain tart and the vanilla taste basically the same, the mix is doing the sugar’s work, and you’re about to eat dessert dressed up as a health food.
Watch the machine and the flow. A shop that rotates flavors often and keeps the nozzles clean is turning over fresh mix instead of letting it sit. Icy crystals on the swirl or a sour-off note means old product. Busy is good here. A froyo place with a line is serving mix that hasn’t been sitting in the barrel since last week.
Then be honest about the cup. Grab the small one, taste as you go, and lean on fruit before candy. Froyo is one stop on a much bigger sweet map, and if you like building a dessert to order, what to order at a creperie in St. Louis scratches the same itch with a warmer result.
### Are there really live cultures in that cup?
Sometimes, in small amounts. Frozen yogurt is made with the same live cultures as regular yogurt, but freezing and a sugar-heavy mix are hard on those bacteria. Some survive the cold, plenty don’t, and a cup of froyo is nowhere near a spoonful of fresh yogurt for anything you’d call a gut benefit. It’s dessert first.
If the cultures are your reason for buying, look for a Live and Active Cultures seal on the machine or the mix carton, which signals a minimum amount of living bacteria at the time it was made. Even then, treat any probiotic effect as a small bonus, not the point. You’re there for a cold, tart treat, and that’s a fine reason on its own.
