### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the national dish of Ireland?
A.  Most people point to Irish stew, a slow-cooked pot of lamb or mutton, potatoes and onions, sometimes with carrots. There’s no official, government-declared national dish, though. Bacon and cabbage, colcannon and soda bread all get mentioned in the same breath, and the full Irish breakfast has a strong claim of its own.
### Q. What not to order in an Irish pub?
A.  Skip the shot called an Irish car bomb, and don’t ask for a Black and Tan by that name, since both names touch painful history for many Irish people. On the food side nothing’s off limits, but slow-cooked dishes like stew, coddle and shepherd’s pie usually show a kitchen at its best. The burger can wait.
### Q. What is a traditional Irish breakfast?
A.  A traditional full Irish is fried eggs, rashers of back bacon, pork sausages, black and white pudding, a grilled tomato, mushrooms, baked beans and toast or brown soda bread, with a pot of strong tea. Some versions add potato bread or boxty. It’s a big, slow plate, and many families save it for weekends.
### Q. Do the Irish actually eat corned beef?
A.  Some do, but it isn’t the everyday tradition Americans tend to assume. The classic Irish pairing is bacon and cabbage. Corned beef and cabbage caught on among Irish immigrants in American cities, where brisket was easier to buy. Ireland once exported salted beef, but most ordinary families there ate pork instead.
### Q. What do Irish really eat on St. Patrick’s Day?
A.  Usually a good family dinner rather than a themed one. Bacon and cabbage, a roast, lamb or a hearty stew are all common, with potatoes on the side. The day falls during Lent and has long been treated as a break from fasting, so a proper meal and a drink with friends are part of it.
### Q. What is a simple Irish dish?
A.  Champ is about as simple as it gets: mashed potatoes beaten with warm milk and chopped scallions, served with a well of melted butter in the middle. Soda bread comes close, needing just flour, baking soda, salt and buttermilk. Colcannon, with cabbage or kale folded into the mash, is another easy one for a weeknight.
### Q. What food do Irish people love?
A.  Potatoes, in more ways than you’d guess, plus a proper Sunday roast, brown bread with real butter, a weekend fry-up and fish and chips from the chipper. Tea runs through all of it. Stews and pies carry the colder months, and plenty of Irish families still count bacon and cabbage as pure home cooking.
### Q. What is the difference between colcannon and champ?
A.  Both start with buttery mashed potatoes. Colcannon folds in cooked cabbage or kale, sometimes with scallions too. Champ uses scallions warmed in milk, skips the cabbage, and comes to the table with melted butter pooled in the center. Think of colcannon as the green-flecked one and champ as the oniony one.

## Kayaking in St. Louis: A Guide for Beginners
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/kayaking-in-st-louis-a-beginners-guide
Seven in the morning, and the lake is flat as a kitchen table. A guy in a borrowed life jacket stands ankle-deep beside a bright orange kayak, turning it around twice because he can’t tell which end is the front. His friend is already out there, drifting in a slow circle, laughing, holding her paddle upside down. Neither of them has ever done this. Both of them will be fine.
That’s the part people don’t expect. Kayaking looks technical from the shore, with all the hatches and straps and oddly shaped paddles, but a first trip on calm water asks for surprisingly little. Right water. Right boat. Clothes that won’t turn on you once they’re wet, and a life jacket you actually wear instead of sitting on.
Below is a first-trip plan for St. Louis visitors and locals who’ve never paddled: whether you can go with zero experience (yes, mostly), which kind of kayak to pick, what kind of water to start on, what to pack, and a step-by-step sequence for the day itself. No shop names. No prices. Just the order of operations.
### Can you kayak with no experience?
Yes. Most people can paddle a recreational kayak on calm, sheltered water their first time out, with no lesson beyond a few minutes of basics. The catch is the water you choose. Flat lakes and ponds forgive mistakes. Big rivers with current, barges and cold water do not, so beginners should start small and stay close to shore.
Recreational kayaks are built wide and stable on purpose. They’re hard to tip on flat water, they track reasonably straight, and the basic stroke starts to feel natural after about ten minutes of flailing. Forward is easy. Turning takes a little longer to click. Stopping takes the longest, which is one good reason to practice in open water rather than right next to a dock full of other boats.
Honestly, the real gap for a beginner isn’t paddling technique. It’s judgment. Noticing the wind picking up. Realizing you’ve drifted farther than you meant to. Feeling your arms quit while the launch is still a long way off. Those instincts only come from time on the water, and no amount of video watching gets you there.
### A few basics before you push off
Grip the paddle with your hands a bit wider than your shoulders and your knuckles lined up with the blade edge. The cupped face of each blade should pull toward you, not push. Press your feet into the foot pegs so your core and torso rotation do the work instead of your arms. And sit up tall. Slouching wrecks your stroke and your lower back.
Getting in is the wobbliest moment of the whole day. Set the kayak parallel to shore in shallow water, lay the paddle across the boat behind the seat as a brace, and lower yourself in rear-first before swinging your legs over. Getting out is the same move in reverse. Plenty of people take their first swim right here, in six inches of water. Laugh it off.
### Should you take a lesson first?
It helps, though it isn’t mandatory for flat water. A short intro class or guided paddle teaches rescue basics, like climbing back aboard after a flip, and that’s the one skill almost nobody practices on their own. If moving water is anywhere in your future, a lesson goes from nice to necessary pretty quickly.
### Should a beginner pick a sit-on-top or sit-inside kayak?
For most warm-weather first trips, a sit-on-top is the easier pick. It’s stable, simple to climb back onto after a fall, and it won’t fill up with water. A sit-inside kayak keeps you drier and warmer, which matters in spring and fall, but getting back in after a capsize is harder.
### Sit-on-top kayaks
You sit on a molded seat on the deck with your legs out in the open. Small drain holes called scuppers let splashed water run right through the hull. If you tip, you roll off, flip the boat upright and haul yourself back on belly-first, then twist around to sit. Clumsy the first time. It works, though, which is why so many rental fleets lean on them.
The trade-offs? You will get wet. Your seat will get wet. They tend to run heavier and a little slower, and on a cool, breezy day you’ll feel every gust.
### Sit-inside kayaks
Here your legs slide inside the hull under a deck, and your knees can brace against the sides. That contact gives you more control and a drier ride. Recreational sit-insides usually have big, open cockpits, so you won’t feel trapped. Still, if one flips it can take on water, and you’ll probably have to swim it to shore to drain it.
One small thing that makes a big difference, whichever style you’re in: adjust the foot pegs on land. Knees slightly bent, feet pressing firmly. Five seconds on the bank beats fiddling with them while you drift sideways into a patch of cattails.
### What about length and width?
Shorter and wider means stable and easy to turn. Longer and narrower means faster and straighter, but tippier. For a first lake outing, a short, wide recreational boat is the usual choice. If you’re renting, ask what they’d put a nervous beginner in and take the answer seriously. They see first-timers every weekend.
### Where should a first-timer paddle around St. Louis?
Start on calm, enclosed water: a small lake, a pond, or a sheltered cove without motorboat traffic. Slow, shallow creeks come next, once you can steer. The Missouri and Mississippi rivers come last, not first. Their current, barge traffic, wing dikes and floating debris make them water for experienced paddlers, ideally with a guide.
### Calm lakes and ponds
This is where day one belongs. With no current, you stop moving when you stop paddling, more or less. Wind is the main thing to watch. Launch into the breeze if you can, so the trip home is the easy half, and stay within a comfortable swim of shore. Some public lakes limit or ban big motors, which keeps the water quieter, so check the rules before you go.
A family from Pine Lawn out for a first paddle probably wants exactly this. The whole lake in view. The launch never out of sight. Kids wobbling around in their boats without anybody on shore starting to panic.
### Slow creeks and small rivers
The creek float is the classic Missouri paddle, and plenty of people drive a couple of hours from St. Louis to do one. It feels different from a lake. A gentle current does some of the work, but you’ll also meet gravel bars, low branches and the occasional riffle where water speeds up over rocks. Downed trees that let water through but not people, called strainers, are the real hazard. Steer wide. Always.
Most floats run one way, so you’ll need a shuttle or a second car at the takeout. Water levels swing after rain, too. A creek that’s a lazy drift in August can run fast and muddy after a storm, so check recent conditions and ask someone local before you commit.
### The Missouri and the Mississippi
Beautiful, historic, and not for your first day. Both rivers carry commercial barge traffic, and a tow can’t stop or swerve for a kayak. Wing dikes, the rock structures that jut from the banks to steer the channel, create strong eddies and hidden turbulence around them. The current moves faster than it looks from shore, and after heavy rain, whole trees come floating by. Below St. Louis a single tow can run 30 to 40 barges, and our guide to barges on the Mississippi explains the trade you’d be sharing the water with.
Want big-river paddling someday? Get there through a guided trip after you’ve logged real hours on flatter water. A scenic drive along the bluffs is a good way to take in the scale first, and our list of best stops along the Great River Road lets you look at the river long before you’re floating on it.
Rather see the water from way up? Try hot air balloon rides
### What should you bring on a first paddle?
A properly fitted life jacket comes first, worn and buckled, not stashed behind the seat. After that: quick-dry clothes, water shoes, sun protection, drinking water and a dry bag for your phone and keys. Skip cotton, especially jeans. Wet cotton stays wet, gets heavy, and pulls heat from your body fast.
### Clothing
Paddlers have an old saying: cotton kills. Sounds dramatic until you’ve sat in a soaked hoodie with a breeze coming off the water and nowhere to go. Synthetic or wool layers dry faster and hold some warmth even when wet. A swimsuit or athletic shorts under a quick-dry shirt works on a hot day. On a cool one, add fleece and a windproof shell.
Footwear matters more than people think. Flip-flops float away. Bare feet meet broken glass, sharp rocks and blistering pavement at the launch. Water shoes or sandals with a heel strap stay put in the mud and protect you on gravel bars.
### The small stuff
Sunscreen, sunglasses with a strap, a hat. A full water bottle, even for a short paddle. A snack. A whistle clipped to your life jacket, since it carries farther than a shout. A dry bag or waterproof phone pouch. Dry clothes and a towel left in the car for afterward. That’s plenty for a first outing.
Curious how much of the fancier stuff you’ll really use? Our breakdown of what outdoor gear you actually need in St. Louis sorts the essentials from the impulse buys.
### How do you plan your first kayak trip, step by step?
Plan it in order: pick flat water, check the forecast and water temperature, rent or borrow a stable boat, confirm any launch permit, tell someone your plan, then paddle a short loop and come back. Keep the first trip to an hour or two. Stopping while it’s still fun is the whole trick.
### Step 1: Choose the water a week out
Pick a calm lake or pond reasonably close to home. Look up who manages it, whether that’s a city, a county, a state agency or a private owner, and read their rules. Some parks and lakes want a launch permit or day pass for boats. Others don’t. Rules vary by waterbody and boat type, so the managing agency is the answer that counts.
### Step 2: Check the weather and run the 120 rule
Look at wind first. Anything strong enough to blow your hat off is going to push your kayak around too. Then add the air temperature and the water temperature together. If the total lands under 120°F, plan on cold-water protection like a wetsuit or drysuit, because a sudden plunge can trigger cold shock. Spring fools people here. A warm April afternoon can sit on top of water that’s still bitterly cold.
### Step 3: Sort out the boat and the life jacket
Renting, borrowing or joining a guided outing all work for a first try. Buying can wait. Whatever you paddle, match the life jacket to your size and check the label for Coast Guard approval. Snug is right. If someone can lift it by the shoulders and it slides up past your chin, it’s too loose.
### Step 4: Leave a float plan with someone
Sounds formal. It’s just a text. Tell a friend where you’re launching, when you expect to be off the water, and what to do if you’re not. A cousin back in Fayetteville doesn’t need to know a thing about kayaks to make a phone call when you’re two hours late.
### Step 5: Launch, practice near shore, then loop back
Spend your first five minutes close to the bank. Forward strokes. A wide sweep turn each way. A few reverse strokes to stop. Then head upwind for a short leg, turn around, and let the breeze help carry you home. If there’s other boat traffic, stay out of the middle and keep to the edges.
Quit before you’re tired. Your shoulders, forearms and grip will ache tomorrow in ways that surprise you, and fatigue is exactly when paddles get dropped and bad calls get made. An hour out and back is a great first day. Nobody’s handing out medals for distance.
### Step 6: Practice a flip on purpose
On a warm day, in shallow water, with a friend watching, tip over deliberately. Slide out, flip the boat, climb back on. It’s awkward and a little ridiculous, and it drains the fear out of the one thing you’re most worried about. Do it once. The whole sport feels different afterward.
Ready to get on the water? Browse kayaking rentals and outfitters across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, ask what they’d put a beginner in, and pick calm water for day one.
If you’re the outfitter, being the one people and AI name first is the game when a nervous first-timer searches for somewhere to rent a stable boat, so list your kayak rental.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the 120 rule in kayaking?
A.  It’s a quick cold-water check. Add the air temperature and the water temperature in Fahrenheit. If the total comes in under 120, dress for a swim with a wetsuit or drysuit, not just for the air. Cold shock can make you gasp and lose control of your breathing right after a fall, even if you swim well.
### Q. Do you need a life jacket in a kayak in Missouri?
A.  Federal and Missouri rules generally require a wearable, Coast Guard-approved life jacket aboard for each person, and kids face stricter rules about actually wearing one. Details can change, so check the Missouri State Highway Patrol Water Patrol Division and the Missouri Department of Conservation before you go. Better yet, just wear yours every single time.
### Q. What not to wear when kayaking?
A.  Skip cotton. Jeans, sweatshirts, cotton tees and cotton socks soak up water and stay cold. Leave flip-flops, heavy boots and dangling jewelry at home, too. Wear quick-dry synthetics or wool, a hat, and water shoes or sandals with a heel strap. On cool days, dress for the water temperature instead of the air.
### Q. How likely is a kayak to flip?
A.  In a wide recreational kayak on flat water, not very. Most beginner capsizes happen while getting in or out, leaning too far to grab something, or sitting sideways to a boat wake. Current, wind and narrow boats raise the odds. Keep your weight low and centered, and practice a flip in shallow water so it’s not scary.
### Q. What are the disadvantages of sit-on-top kayaks?
A.  You’ll almost certainly get wet, since you’re sitting out in the open on the deck. That makes them chilly in spring, fall and wind. They’re often heavier and a bit slower than sit-inside kayaks of similar length, and they give you less contact with the boat for control. On warm, calm days, those trade-offs rarely matter.
### Q. Is it safe to kayak on the Missouri River?
A.  For experienced paddlers with the right gear and a solid plan, many people do it. For beginners, no. The Missouri carries barge traffic, strong current, wing dikes that create powerful eddies, and floating debris, especially after rain. If you want to paddle it someday, build skills on calm water first and go with a guide or an experienced group.
### Q. How long does it take to learn to kayak?
A.  You can learn enough to enjoy calm water in one outing, often within the first half hour. Getting comfortable with steering, wind and longer trips usually takes several more times out. Moving water, self-rescue and rolling take real instruction and practice over a season or longer. Everyone’s pace is different, so don’t rush it.
### Q. Do you need a permit to kayak in Missouri?
A.  It depends. Registration and permit rules vary by waterbody and vessel type, and some parks and lakes require their own launch permits or passes. Rather than guessing, check with whoever manages the water you plan to paddle, along with the Missouri Department of Conservation and the Water Patrol, before the trip.

## Buying Knitting Supplies in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/buying-knitting-supplies-in-st-louis
Saturday morning, a kitchen table in Foristell. A ten-year-old has watched one too many videos of somebody finishing a scarf in what looks like twenty minutes, and now she wants in. Grandma digs a pair of needles out of the hall closet, along with half a ball of something dark and fuzzy that’s been in the same bag since who knows when. An hour later nobody can see a single stitch. The yarn’s split twice. The kid’s close to tears.
Bad luck? Not really. Wrong supplies. That fuzzy navy yarn would test a knitter with thirty years behind her, and those skinny needles belonged to a sock project from another decade. Swap in the right ball and the right pair, and the very same afternoon goes a whole lot better.
Here’s what to buy for a first project and why: the yarn weight, fiber and color that make learning easier, the needle size and material that won’t fight you, the little tools people forget, and what a local yarn shop actually gives you compared with a big-box aisle. No brands. No prices. Just what belongs in the basket.
### What type of yarn is best for beginners knitting?
A smooth, light-colored, medium-weight yarn. Look for worsted or aran weight (a 4 in the little ball symbol on the label) in wool or a wool blend. Yarn this thick shows each loop, forgives wobbly tension, and will not split the way loosely plied or fuzzy yarns do. Acrylic works fine too.
### Why medium weight makes learning easier
Weight means thickness, not how heavy the ball feels in your hand. Lace and fingering yarns are thin as thread and pair with tiny needles, so every mistake hides and every row seems to take forever. Super bulky is the opposite problem. It knits up fast, sure, but it’s stiff on the needles and awkward for small hands. Worsted and aran sit right in the middle.
That middle ground matters more than people expect. With a medium yarn on medium needles, you can actually watch a knit stitch form, count your rows, and spot the exact moment something went sideways. Beginners learn by seeing. So give them yarn they can see.
### Why pick a light color?
Dark yarn eats stitches. Navy, black, deep brown and charcoal look great in a finished sweater, but on the needles they blur into one shadowy lump, especially under a kitchen light after supper. Cream, pale gray, light blue, soft yellow, a gentle pink: any of these shows every loop clearly. You’ll catch a dropped stitch before it runs three rows down.
Solid colors help too. Variegated and self-striping yarns are fun, and kids adore them, but the shifting colors can hide the very stitch structure you’re trying to learn.
Save the rainbow skein for project two.
### Wool, acrylic or cotton?
Each fiber behaves differently in your hands. Wool has a little stretch and bounce, so it forgives uneven tension and slides along the needle without much fuss. It’s warm, and it holds its shape. A wool blend, often mixed with acrylic or nylon, keeps most of that give and usually washes more easily. Plenty of teachers reach for smooth wool or a wool blend first.
Acrylic is the easy-to-find, easy-care option. It comes in just about every color there is and tosses in the washer, which matters for anything a kid will wear, chew or drag across the yard. Some acrylics feel squeaky on the needles, though, and a few split more than you’d like. Squeeze several. Pick the one that feels soft and tightly twisted.
Cotton’s the tricky one. It has almost no stretch, so every wobble in your tension shows, and your hands can tire out working it. It’s wonderful for dishcloths and summer tops. Most people find it easier as a second or third yarn, not the first.
### Yarns to skip for now
Leave these on the shelf for a while: fuzzy mohair and eyelash yarns, anything with loose plies that separate when you poke them, very slippery silk or bamboo-fiber yarn, and novelty yarns with bobbles, sequins or ribbons. They aren’t bad yarns. They’re just hard to learn on, and a frustrating first project is exactly how knitting needles end up back in the hall closet for another ten years.
### How do you read a yarn label?
The paper band around a skein tells you nearly everything: weight category, fiber content, length, suggested needle size, gauge, care instructions and dye lot. Learn to read those seven details and you can shop for any pattern with confidence, even in an aisle where every ball looks more or less the same.
### The weight number and the needle size
Many labels carry a small yarn-ball icon with a number from 0 to 7. A 4 means medium, the worsted and aran family. Close by you’ll usually find a needle icon with a suggested size in US numbers, millimeters or both. Treat it as a starting point, not a commandment. Your own tension decides the final fit.
### Yardage and gauge
Length is listed in yards, meters or both, right beside the weight of the ball. Your pattern tells you how many yards it needs. Compare those numbers instead of counting balls, because two skeins that look identical on the shelf can hold very different lengths of yarn.
Gauge usually shows up as a tiny square with numbers along its edges, meaning so many stitches and rows across a set width. For a scarf or a dishcloth, it barely matters. For a hat or a sweater that has to fit an actual human head or body, it matters a lot, and that’s when knitting a small test swatch pays for itself.
### Care symbols and dye lot
Care symbols look like laundry tags because that’s what they are. Hand wash, machine wash, no dryer, lay flat. Superwash wool has been treated so it can go in the machine, while regular wool can felt and shrink with hot water and agitation. For a baby blanket or a pair of kids’ mittens, that’s worth a second look.
Then there’s the dye lot. It’s a code, usually printed near the color name, that tells you which batch the yarn came from. Two lots of the same shade can look slightly different side by side, and you’ll notice it right in the middle of a scarf. Buy all the yarn for one project from one lot, plus an extra ball if you’re unsure. Coming back later is a gamble.
Two rows in and somebody’s hungry. Is there even a St. Louis hot dog?
### What size needles should a beginner start with?
A US size 8, which is 5 millimeters, is the classic starter needle for worsted-weight yarn, and sizes 7 through 9 all work. Pick a length you can hold comfortably, and choose wood or bamboo if you’re worried about stitches sliding off. Match the needle to the yarn label, then adjust if your fabric feels stiff.
Too tight? Go up a size. If the fabric looks loose and holey, like a fishing net, go down one. That’s the whole trick, and nobody gets it perfect on the first try.
### Straight or circular?
Straight needles are what most people picture: two sticks, each with a point on one end and a stopper on the other. They’re simple and easy to understand. Circular needles are two short tips joined by a flexible cable. You can knit back and forth on them just like straights, and the weight of the project rests in your lap instead of pulling on your wrists.
Either one’s fine for a first scarf, honestly. Kids and smaller adults sometimes do better with shorter needles, since long ones bump elbows, couch arms and little brothers. Circulars also pack and travel better, which comes up again further down.
### Wood, bamboo or metal?
Material changes how the yarn moves. Bamboo and wood have a little grip, so stitches stay put while your hands figure things out. Metal is slick and fast, which experienced knitters love and new ones often don’t. Plastic and resin land somewhere in between. There’s more on this further down, but here’s the short version.
Grippy first. Slick later.
### What does a first knitting kit actually need?
Less than the craft aisle suggests. A first kit needs one or two balls of medium-weight yarn, a matching pair of needles, a blunt yarn needle for weaving in ends, a few stitch markers, small scissors and a tape measure. Add a simple pattern and a bag to hold everything, and you’re set.
The yarn needle is the one people forget. It’s a thick, blunt needle with a big eye, sometimes sold as a darning needle, and you’ll use it at the end of every project to hide the loose tails. A sharp sewing needle splits the yarn. A blunt one slips between the stitches instead.
Stitch markers are little rings or clips that ride on the needle or hang in the fabric. They mark the start of a round, a spot where the pattern changes, or the row where you began a decrease. In a pinch, a loop of scrap yarn in a contrasting color does the same job. Kids love the colorful ones. They also lose them. Buy extras.
Any small, sharp scissors will do for snipping yarn. A soft, flexible tape measure beats a metal one because it curves around a hat brim or a sleeve. One optional extra earns its spot, too: a small crochet hook. It’s the easiest way to catch a dropped stitch and pull it back up where it belongs.
### What about all-in-one kits?
Boxed beginner kits can make a nice gift. Some are great. Others pair a novelty yarn with the wrong needle size, or toss in tools that won’t hold up past the first project. If it’s a birthday present, open the box a few days early if you can and check two things: the yarn’s smooth and medium weight, and the needles match its label.
Building your own kit takes a bit longer, but it’s more fun, and you know exactly what’s inside. For a family learning together, one shared pouch of notions plus separate yarn and needles for each person keeps the kitchen table from turning into a single giant tangle by Sunday night.
### Is a local yarn shop worth it over a big-box aisle?
For a true beginner, often yes. A local yarn shop lets you touch the yarn, ask a real person which weight fits your pattern, and get help when a project goes wrong. Many run classes and casual knit nights. A big-box aisle wins on convenience and hours, and plenty of knitters happily use both.
### What a yarn shop usually offers
People who work at an independent yarn shop tend to be knitters themselves. They can glance at a tangled mess and tell you what happened, show you a cast-on at the counter, or steer you toward a yarn that suits the pattern you printed out. Many will wind a skein into a ball for you, too. Small thing. Saves a lot of grief.
Classes and knit nights vary from shop to shop, so ask. A beginner class usually walks you through casting on, the knit stitch, the purl stitch and binding off. A knit night is looser: folks bring whatever they’re working on, chat, and help each other out. Somebody might drive in from Jerseyville or Elsberry just for the company, and for a nervous learner, a room full of patient people beats any video.
### Where the big-box aisle makes sense
Chain craft stores and general retailers stock plenty of acrylic and acrylic-blend yarn in medium weights, along with basic needles and notions. They’re handy when you need one more ball on a Sunday evening. The trade-off is help. Staff may not knit, and the choice of natural fibers usually runs narrower. Shopping for other craft gear as well? Our guide to where to buy craft supplies in St. Louis covers the bigger picture.
### How to walk in as a total beginner
Bring your pattern, or at least a photo of what you want to make. Say it’s your first project. Ask what weight, fiber and needle size they’d pair with it, then ask to feel two or three options. If a shop makes you feel silly for not knowing, that tells you something too. The good ones remember exactly what it was like to start.
### How do you keep a first knitting project affordable?
Start small and buy tools only as you need them. A dishcloth, a headband or a simple scarf uses one or two balls of yarn and a single pair of needles. Borrow what you can, skip the deluxe kits until you know the hobby sticks, and let that first project show you what you actually want.
Yarn is where the money goes, so choose a project that fits your budget. A chunky blanket sounds cozy until you count how many balls it takes. A hat or a cowl gets you a real finished piece without a heavy basket at checkout, and you’ll learn nearly as much making it.
Ask around before you buy a thing. Plenty of families have a bag of old needles and half-used yarn tucked away somewhere, and somebody in your circle probably knits. Estate sales and church rummage sales out around Cedar Hill and New Melle sometimes turn up entire stashes. Check needles for bends and yarn for a musty smell before you haul it home.
Some people fall hard for this hobby, though, and start turning out more hats than they have heads to put them on. If that’s you a year from now, how to price and sell handmade crafts in St. Louis is a good place to start thinking it through.
Ready to shop? Browse knitting supply shops across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, call ahead to ask about beginner classes or knit nights, and bring your pattern along.
If you’re the shop, being the one people and AI name first is the game when a brand-new knitter asks where to find soft worsted wool and somebody patient enough to show them a cast-on, so list your yarn shop.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Should a beginner knit or crochet?
A.  Either works, so pick the one that makes the thing you want. Crochet uses a single hook and keeps just one live loop at a time, which many people find easier to fix. Knitting uses two needles and makes a stretchier, drapier fabric that suits sweaters and socks. Torn? Try a short lesson in each.
### Q. Should I get bamboo or metal knitting needles?
A.  For a beginner, bamboo is usually the safer bet. Its slight grip keeps stitches from sliding off while you learn tension, and it feels warm and light in the hand. Metal needles are slick and quick, which helps once you’re comfortable. Many knitters end up owning both and choosing by yarn: grippy needles for slippery yarn, slick ones for sticky.
### Q. What to look for when buying knitting needles?
A.  Match the size to your yarn label first. Then check the tips, since medium points are easier than very sharp or very blunt ones. On circulars, look for a smooth join where tip meets cable so stitches don’t snag. Choose a length that feels comfortable, and run a finger along the needle to check for rough spots.
### Q. What is the best knitting needle set for a beginner?
A.  Keep it simple. A single straight or circular pair in US 8, which is 5 millimeters, covers most first projects in worsted yarn. Once you’re hooked and trying different patterns, an interchangeable set with several tip sizes and cables often makes more sense than buying pair after pair. There’s no need for the big set on day one.
### Q. Where to buy yarn now that Joann’s is closing?
A.  Joann closed all its stores in 2025, so plenty of St. Louis knitters had to find a new routine. Independent local yarn shops make a great first stop, and other big-box craft chains still carry yarn and needles. Online retailers ship nearly anything, and secondhand stashes from estate sales, thrift stores and friends can stretch a tight budget.
### Q. Why is knitting making a comeback?
A.  People want a break from screens, and knitting gives restless hands something to do besides scrolling. It’s calming, it’s portable, and it ends with something real you can wear or give away. A handmade gift often means more than a store-bought one. And knit nights turn a quiet hobby into a reason to see people.
### Q. Will TSA confiscate knitting needles?
A.  Usually not. TSA generally allows knitting needles in carry-on bags, but the final call belongs to the officer at the checkpoint. Circular needles and bamboo or wood needles tend to draw less attention than long metal straights. Keep any small scissors under four inches, and thread a scrap of yarn through your live stitches so you can save your work just in case.
### Q. How long does it take to learn to knit?
A.  Many people can cast on and work the knit stitch in a single afternoon, especially with someone showing them. Even tension takes longer, often a few projects. Keep practice sessions short and frequent, particularly with kids, and don’t rip out every wobble. A first scarf that looks a little homemade is still a scarf, and it still keeps a neck warm.

## Ted Drewes Is on the List: How to Tell If Food Is Kosher in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-tell-if-food-is-kosher-in-st-louis
Ted Drewes is on the list. The custard stand on Chippewa, where you’ve stood in line on a sticky July night with a cold cup sweating in your hand, shows up on the kosher food list kept by St. Louis’s own certifier. Its certificate letter decides which treats count. A cart at Section 148 of Busch Stadium is on there too. And the cracker box in your hand, a lone K stamped by the flap? It might have nobody standing behind it at all.
You’re in the cracker aisle with that box, the cardboard edge biting your thumb as you turn it over a third time. A text lights up your phone: “Still on for Saturday?” Your new coworker’s family keeps kosher, and you said yes to dinner before you knew what you were saying yes to. The store music keeps playing. You keep staring at one letter.
Here’s what that lone K means. A single letter can’t be trademarked, so any company can print one, and all it tells you is that the maker says the food is kosher. Not who checked. Not whether anyone did.
Learn the local letters: OV. The Vaad Hoeir of St. Louis certifies under the OV symbol from an office at 4 Millstone Campus Drive, 314-569-2770, and its site, ovkosher.org, puts it plainly: “The OV mark is simple.” Its food page is the single most useful thing in town for anyone feeding a kosher guest, because it names the actual places it supervises - eateries, bakeries, butchers, supermarket counters, catering and banquet halls - with a note on each one. You can pull it up on your phone right there in the aisle.
Those notes are where the St. Louis secrets live, the kind you text a friend. The Busch Stadium cart? The Vaad says its supervision applies to weekday games only. The one Schnucks store the Vaad lists for its kosher deli makes fresh kosher salads, sandwiches, sliced deli and hot rotisserie chickens Monday through Thursday, plus fresh kosher sushi Wednesday after 2:00 p.m. and all day Thursday. The Dierbergs at 8680 Olive Blvd. makes kosher sushi Monday through Friday. So if you’re hosting Saturday, that warm rotisserie-chicken smell at the Schnucks deli counter is a Thursday errand. Friday afternoon is too late.
So here’s the week, start to finish. Text your coworker back before you set the box down: “Which kosher marks does your family trust?” Some families accept only certain agencies, so the answer decides everything that follows, and nobody takes the question as rude. It reads as care.
While you wait for the reply, tilt the box under the store lights. The mark is small, usually near the product name or down by the ingredients. An OV, a circled U or another recognized agency logo means someone supervised production. The lone K means only that the maker vouches for itself. Put it back on the shelf.
Thursday, go get the food, and read the fine print even at a store on the list. At The Wine and Cheese Place, the Vaad certifies only items bearing an OV sticker, and at the supermarket bakeries it lists, only items bearing the OVK sticker count. You’re hunting for a little sticker on the wrapper, not trusting the shelf.
Rather hand dinner to a caterer? Ask for the certificate. A certified kitchen can name its agency and show a current one, often posted near the entrance or register. If it says OV, a call to the Vaad confirms it in a minute.
One more thing worth repeating at the table. Four things sound kosher and aren’t, by themselves: a bare K, kosher salt, kosher dill pickles, and a kosher-style Reuben, which stacks corned beef and Swiss cheese on one sandwich. No kosher kitchen would, no matter how good the rye smells.
### What qualifies a food as kosher?
Food is kosher when it meets kashrut, the Jewish dietary law drawn from the Torah. That means permitted animals, slaughtered and prepared a specific way, no meat and dairy together, and every ingredient and piece of equipment traced to a kosher source. On packaged food, a certification symbol is the proof.
Boil it down and the three main rules of kosher are these: eat only permitted animals, slaughter and prepare meat properly, and never mix meat with dairy. Everything else, from certificates to second sets of dishes, grows out of those three.
Permitted animals means land mammals that chew cud and have split hooves, so cattle, sheep, goats and deer, but not pigs. It means fish with fins and scales, so salmon and tuna, but no shellfish. The lox draped over a Sunday bagel passes. The shrimp ring sweating on the office party table does not. And it means birds the community accepts by tradition, like chicken, turkey, duck and goose.
A kosher cow isn’t kosher beef yet. First comes shechita, done by a trained slaughterer called a shochet with one swift cut from a blade with no nicks. Then the lungs are inspected, which is where the word glatt on some packages comes from: it originally meant the lungs were smooth and free of adhesions. Then the meat is soaked and salted to draw out the blood. All that skilled work is slow, so many kosher butchers in the U.S. sell cuts from the front of the animal, which is why kosher filet mignon is so hard to find.
### Can kosher ingredients still make a food that isn’t kosher?
Yes, and this is where home cooks get tripped up. Every ingredient can be kosher and the food still isn’t, if it ran down a line that also handled non-kosher meat, or went into a fryer where shrimp just came out. Heat and shared equipment carry status. So packaged food needs someone watching the whole process, not just a clean ingredient list. Grape wine and grape juice carry their own rules and need supervision through production, which is why kosher wine sits on its own shelf.
Comparing traditions? Neither kosher nor halal is simply stricter, because each forbids things the other allows. Our guide on how to tell if food is halal in St. Louis covers the other side.
### Meat, dairy and pareve: why a kosher kitchen owns two of everything
Every kosher food lands in one of three buckets. Meat, fleishig in Yiddish, covers beef, lamb, poultry and anything cooked with them. Dairy, milchig, covers milk, butter, cheese and anything made with them. Pareve means neither: fruits, vegetables, grains, eggs and kosher fish. Pareve can go with either side.
Why can’t Jews mix dairy with meat? A verse that appears three times in the Torah says not to cook a young goat in its mother’s milk. Rabbinic tradition read that repetition as a reason to build a wide fence around the rule. Meat and dairy aren’t cooked together, eaten together or served on the same dishes. Poultry joined the meat side by rabbinic law, so chicken parmesan is out. So is a turkey sandwich with Swiss.
Open the cabinets in a kosher home and you see the doubling: two sets of pots, pans, plates, silverware and dish towels, sometimes two sinks or two dishwashers. Color coding keeps a hand from reaching for the wrong one. Red for meat and blue for dairy is a common scheme, though every family picks its own.
### How long do people wait between meat and dairy?
Custom sets the clock, not one fixed rule. After eating meat, many observant Jews wait six hours before having dairy. Some traditions wait three. Some communities of Dutch descent wait one. Going from dairy to meat usually takes much less, often just rinsing the mouth and eating something neutral, though hard aged cheeses can call for the longer wait in some homes.
Hosting? Skip the ice cream after a meat dinner. A pareve dessert like sorbet or a fruit plate means nobody has to do math at your table.
### What’s the fine print on pareve?
Two catches. Fish counts as pareve, but many observant Jews won’t eat fish and meat together on one plate, so a kosher menu might serve them as separate courses with fresh utensils. And eggs are pareve only when they’re free of blood spots, which is why plenty of kosher cooks crack each egg into a clear glass first. That small click of shell on glass is the whole safeguard.
### How do you read a kosher symbol on a package?
Look for a hechsher, the certification mark of a kosher agency, usually printed near the product name or on the back by the ingredients. A common one is the OU, a capital U inside a circle, the mark of OU Kosher, the agency founded by the Orthodox Union. The symbol tells you an agency supervised production. Letters beside it tell you meat, dairy, pareve or Passover status.
There’s no single kosher symbol. Each agency has its own trademarked symbol. Hundreds of agencies certify kosher food across the country and the world. Some are national organizations whose marks turn up all over the pantry. Others are regional rabbinical councils that mostly supervise restaurants, bakeries and caterers in their own city. The logos vary a lot: a K inside a star, a K inside a circle, a triangle, Hebrew letters. Each belongs to a specific organization, and each organization answers for what it certifies.
### What do the letters next to the symbol mean?
D, or the word Dairy, means the product contains dairy or was made on dairy equipment. Some agencies print DE to flag dairy equipment with no actual dairy ingredients, a detail that matters to a family serving it after a meat meal. M, Meat or Glatt means meat, or meat equipment. Pareve, sometimes spelled Parve, means neither. A symbol with no letter at all often signals pareve too, though agencies don’t all follow that convention.
P means kosher for Passover. Not pareve. People mix those two up constantly, and it matters, because a product marked P can still be dairy. Some labels also print the word Fish beside the symbol, so shoppers who keep fish and meat apart know what’s inside.
### What does a plain K actually tell you?
Less than you’d hope. The difference between U and K for kosher comes down to who stands behind the mark. The circled U belongs to one agency. A K can be printed by any company, and it means only that the manufacturer says the product is kosher. Some plain-K products are backed by a real rabbi who simply didn’t use a logo. Others aren’t, and the box won’t say which kind you’re holding.
For a guest who keeps kosher carefully, a plain K often isn’t enough alone. Many will want a recognized agency mark, or they’ll contact the company and ask who is behind it. You were right to hesitate in that aisle.
### Who certifies kosher in St. Louis?
The local answer is the Vaad Hoeir of St. Louis, the OV. Its own site describes a kosher certificate as “a guarantee by a kosher agency, such as the Vaad Hoeir of St. Louis, that a product meets the requirements of Jewish laws pertaining to food.” It certifies factories as well as local kitchens, and its industrial clients sign a contract agreeing to inspection of the facility during all operating hours. Call 314-569-2770 and keep the question simple: does this restaurant or caterer hold your certification, and for what?
### What changes at Passover?
Passover adds its own layer. During the holiday, eight days outside Israel and seven inside it, observant Jews avoid chametz, meaning leavened products made from wheat, barley, rye, oats and their close grain cousins. Many Ashkenazi Jews also avoid kitniyot, a group that takes in rice, corn and legumes. Foods marked P or “Kosher for Passover” were made under that tighter standard, and larger grocery stores sometimes stock a special section of them for a few weeks each spring.
### Kosher-style is a menu, not a certificate
Kosher-style describes a cuisine, not a certification. It means the dishes of a Jewish deli counter, the smell of rye, pastrami and pickle brine, plus matzo ball soup, knishes and bagels, made without rabbinical supervision. A kosher-style deli may happily serve a Reuben. A certified kosher kitchen would never put corned beef and Swiss on one bread.
Nothing’s wrong with kosher-style when a place is upfront about it. It’s a real food tradition, and a delicious one, and our guide to types of delis in St. Louis and how to order walks through those counters. Just don’t read a Jewish-sounding menu as a promise. The same goes for “Jewish-owned,” “no pork” and “made with kosher salt.”
Kosher salt is a coarse-grained salt historically used for removing surface blood from meats. It says nothing about the rest of the dish. Kosher dill pickles? Same story. It’s a garlicky brining style, and the jar is certified only if a symbol says so.
Out-of-town cousin needs a bed? What to know about a St. Louis hostel
### Where can you buy kosher food in St. Louis?
Start with the regular aisle. Lots of everyday packaged food already carries a kosher symbol, from cereal and crackers to soda and canned beans. Fresh kosher meat, certified baked goods and prepared meals take more looking, and the Vaad’s food list above is the documented starting point.
Where you live shapes the hunt. A shopper in Hanley Hills or Clifton Heights can stock a pantry from nearly any big store, then make a separate trip for fresh kosher chicken or a challah baked under supervision. Farther out, in Crystal City, say, a cooler in the trunk isn’t a bad idea. Call ahead, too. Kosher shops and restaurants often close early Friday and stay closed through Saturday, and holiday weeks shuffle everything.
Don’t overlook the freezer case. Bigger supermarkets sometimes carry certified frozen meals, soups and meat, which helps when fresh options are a drive away. Read the symbol on each package instead of trusting the sign over the case. And if you want the full in-store experience, here’s what shopping at a kosher grocery store in St. Louis is like.
### What should you ask a restaurant or caterer about kosher?
Ask who supervises, then ask to see the certificate. A certified kosher restaurant or caterer should be able to name the agency and show a current one, often posted near the entrance or register. From there, ask whether the kitchen is meat or dairy, whether a supervisor is on site, and how food reaches your event.
If you keep kosher yourself, you know your standard better than any blog post. Use these questions to check a place against it. Planning for guests who keep kosher? Ask them first which agencies they trust. Their answer shapes every decision after that.
### At a restaurant
Certified kosher restaurants usually pick a side. A meat restaurant won’t serve cheesecake made with real cream. A dairy pizza place won’t put pepperoni on anything. Many close for Shabbat, from before sundown Friday until after dark Saturday, and for Jewish holidays. If a place advertises kosher and is open Saturday afternoon, ask about it politely. It’s a question, not an accusation.
The supervisor who watches a kitchen for the agency is called a mashgiach. Some restaurants have one on site whenever they’re open, while others get regular visits. Ask which. Kosher owners hear the question all the time, and usually answer it in a sentence.
### With a caterer
Catering is where a real interview pays off. Shortlist two or three caterers. Tell each one exactly what you expect: certified kosher, which agency your guests accept, a meat or dairy menu, the venue, and whether that venue has a kosher kitchen. Then listen to what each is prepared to deliver. The gap between what you asked for and what they offer is the signal.
A caterer who answers “we can do kosher-style” when you asked for certified has told you something useful. So has one who explains, without prompting, how meals reach a hall that isn’t kosher. For a hotel ballroom in Lebanon or a banquet room in Winchester, a familiar approach is food cooked in a certified kitchen, double-wrapped and sealed, then opened by the guest at the table, where the steam lifts off the tray. Ask about serving utensils and reheating as well.
Hosting Saturday? Get the food sorted by Thursday. Check the Vaad’s list, then browse kosher food across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, and call each place to ask who supervises and what is certified this week.
If you run the deli, the bakery or the kosher kitchen a family calls before Shabbat, be the name they find before they settle for the supermarket case. A Gold listing puts your certification, hours and menu where neighbors are already searching, so you get more customers from the people who need you most. See what Gold includes, or claim your spot.
### At home, for a guest
Cooking for a kosher guest in your own kitchen is harder than it looks, because your pots and oven aren’t kosher even when every ingredient is. The kindest move is to ask. Many observant guests will gladly eat sealed, certified food served on disposable plates, or whole fruit, or something from a certified bakery left in its packaging. Some would rather bring their own. Neither answer is an insult. Those are just the rules.
### Frequently asked questions about kosher food
### Q. What are the three main rules of kosher?
A.  Eat only permitted animals: cud-chewing mammals with split hooves, fish with fins and scales, and traditionally accepted birds, so no pork and no shellfish. Slaughter and prepare meat properly, through shechita and blood removal. Never mix meat with dairy. Certification, separate dishes and agency symbols all grow out of those three rules.
### Q. Which is stricter, kosher or halal?
A.  Neither, really. Each forbids things the other allows. Kosher bans shellfish outright and never mixes meat with dairy, while many halal traditions permit seafood and have no meat-and-dairy rule. Halal forbids alcohol, while kosher allows supervised wine. Both ban pork and blood.
### Q. What is the difference between U and K for kosher?
A.  The circled U is the trademarked symbol of the Orthodox Union, one of the largest kosher agencies, so it means that agency supervised production. A plain K can’t be trademarked. Any company can print it, and it only tells you the maker claims the product is kosher, without saying who supervised or whether anyone did.
### Q. Is there a universal kosher symbol?
A.  No. No single government office or religious authority issues one mark. Hundreds of independent agencies certify kosher food, each with its own logo, from the circled U to stars, triangles and Hebrew letters. In St. Louis, one local certifier is the Vaad Hoeir. Observant shoppers learn which marks they trust, and many communities keep lists.
### Q. What kosher foods can Jews eat?
A.  Plenty. Fruits, vegetables, grains, beans and nuts are kosher in their natural state, though produce gets checked for insects. Eggs from kosher birds, fish with fins and scales, and meat from kosher animals slaughtered by shechita all qualify. Processed foods work too when they carry a trusted certification, and wine needs its own supervision.
### Q. Is kosher certification worth it?
A.  For a bakery, caterer or restaurant, it depends on who you want to feed. Certification opens the door to customers who keep kosher and can’t eat at uncertified places, and some shoppers who don’t keep kosher read the symbols anyway. It also brings fees, inspections and kitchen changes. Talk with two or three agencies before deciding.
### Q. What does pareve mean on a label?
A.  Pareve means the food has no meat or dairy in it and wasn’t made on meat or dairy equipment, so it can be eaten with either kind of meal. Fruits, vegetables, grains, eggs and kosher fish are pareve. Watch the letters by the symbol: P means Passover, not pareve, and DE means dairy equipment.

## Shopping at a Kosher Grocery Store in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/shopping-at-a-kosher-grocery-store-in-st-louis
The cooler goes in the trunk before the kids do. It’s a Sunday morning in High Ridge, and a dad is working through a list his sister-in-law texted him the night before: two whole chickens, ground beef, a brisket if the price doesn’t scare him, a challah, something pareve for dessert, and “the good grape juice, the one with the symbol.” She keeps kosher. She’s staying a week. He has never once set foot in a kosher grocery store and has no real idea what he’ll find when he gets there.
His kids don’t either. They’re mostly worried about snacks.
That trip is what this guide is about. Not the theology of kashrut, not a full symbol decoder, just the practical part: what a kosher supermarket actually is, what sits on its shelves, how to fill a cart at an ordinary store instead, why the meat bill runs higher, and how to plan around holidays when the shelves empty fast. No store names. No prices. The rules and the labels work the same way across St. Louis, and you can learn them in an afternoon.
### What is a kosher supermarket?
A kosher supermarket is a grocery store where the food on the shelves is certified kosher, usually under the supervision of a rabbinical agency. Fresh meat comes from a kosher butcher, the bakery and deli run under a hechsher, and meat and dairy are kept apart. Some stores are fully kosher; others are regular markets with a kosher department.
The difference between those two setups matters more than it sounds. In a fully kosher store, everything inside has passed through a certifying agency, and the store itself usually posts a certificate near the door or the register naming who supervises it. You can grab almost anything without flipping the box over. In a regular supermarket with a kosher department, that section sits beside everything else, and the job of checking shifts right back to you.
Smaller shops often split the work. One might be a kosher butcher with a few shelves of groceries up front. Another is a bakery that also sells soups from a freezer. A few run as full supermarkets with carts and checkout lanes. Same word on the sign. Very different trips.
Timing is its own thing. Stores under Orthodox supervision typically close before sundown Friday for Shabbat, stay closed through Saturday, and shut for major Jewish holidays as well. Friday mornings get crowded, and the days just before a holiday can be worse, because that’s when families stock up. Want a calm aisle and a butcher with time to talk? Go early in the week.
### What will you find inside a kosher grocery store?
Expect a meat counter or butcher, a deli with sliced meats and prepared dishes, a bakery, separate dairy and meat sections, a deep freezer aisle, and, each spring, a Passover section that can swallow a good part of the store. The mix depends on the store’s size, so a quick phone call before a long drive saves time.
### The meat counter
This is the reason most people make the trip. Kosher beef, lamb, chicken and turkey are slaughtered by a trained shochet, inspected, then soaked and salted to draw out the blood before they ever reach the case. The butcher may sell fresh cuts, sealed trays or both. Front-quarter cuts dominate: brisket, chuck, short ribs, shoulder, rib steaks. Hindquarter cuts are rare in American kosher shops, because removing the forbidden sciatic nerve and fats from the back half takes a great deal of skilled labor.
Talk to the butcher. Ask what’s fresh, what’s coming in later in the week, and whether they’ll cut or grind to order. You’ll also see the word glatt on a lot of packages. Strictly, it refers to a stricter lung inspection on beef, though many shoppers read it as shorthand for a higher standard overall.
### The deli and prepared foods
Behind the glass you’ll often find sliced corned beef, pastrami, turkey and salami, plus trays of ready-made food: roast chicken, kugel, stuffed cabbage, latkes, chopped liver, sides by the pound. For a working parent, that case can be the whole Friday dinner. Remember that the deli sits on the meat side. Anything bought there usually counts as meat, even a potato kugel, if it came out of a meat kitchen. Some stores label their pareve dishes separately. Not sure? Ask.
### The bakery
Challah is the headline. Braided, often sold in pairs for Shabbat, and baked round around Rosh Hashanah, sometimes with raisins. After that come rugelach, babka, cookies, sheet cakes and hamantaschen near Purim. Many kosher bakeries keep most of their goods pareve, made without butter or milk, so dessert can follow a meat meal. Not all of them do, though. If a cake is marked dairy, it means dairy.
### Dairy and meat, kept apart
The layout follows the rules. Meat and dairy live in separate cases, often at opposite ends of the store, and a store with its own kitchen may run separate prep areas for each. Cheese deserves a closer look. Kosher cheese needs supervision from start to finish, largely because of how rennet and equipment are handled, so the cheese case in a kosher store tends to look smaller and less familiar than the one at a regular market.
Milk, butter and yogurt are usually easy to find. Some shoppers also look for cholov Yisroel dairy, meaning milk supervised from the milking itself, and many kosher stores give it a shelf of its own.
### The freezer aisle
Freezers carry more of a kosher store than people expect. Chicken parts, ground beef, schnitzel, fish sticks, blintzes, pizza, soups, whole ready-to-heat dinners. For families who live a long way from a kosher butcher, frozen meat is how a couple of weeks of meals get bought in a single trip. It keeps. It also rides home in a cooler far better than fresh meat does.
### The Passover aisle
Every spring, weeks before the holiday, the shelves change over. Matzo in towers, matzo meal, macaroons, gefilte fish, jarred horseradish, kosher-for-Passover wine and grape juice, cake mixes made without flour, even Passover versions of ketchup and soda. Everything in that section should carry a P or the words “Kosher for Passover.” Regular kosher products don’t qualify just because they’re kosher the rest of the year. That’s the whole point of a separate aisle.
### How do you find kosher items in an ordinary supermarket?
Read the package. A huge share of everyday packaged food, from cereal and crackers to canned beans and soda, already carries a kosher agency symbol somewhere on the label. Larger supermarkets may also group kosher specialty items into one aisle or one freezer case, especially in the weeks before Jewish holidays.
Here’s the catch with that one kosher aisle: it’s mostly specialty stuff. Matzo, gefilte fish, borscht, imported snacks. The crackers, peanut butter and pasta your guest would happily eat are probably scattered across the whole store in their normal spots, each with a small symbol printed on the side. Don’t stop at the international foods aisle.
That dad from High Ridge figured this out by accident. He skipped the drive, went to his usual store first, and found half his list in the regular aisles before he ever reached the kosher shelf.
### Reading labels in the aisle
Flip the box. Check near the brand name first, then on the back near the ingredients or the nutrition panel. The symbol is often tiny. It might be a U in a circle, a K in a star, a triangle or Hebrew lettering. Next to it, look for a letter: D for dairy, M for meat, P for Passover, or the word Pareve. A plain K by itself tells you less, since any company can print one. For every symbol and what each letter means, our guide on how to tell if food is kosher in St. Louis goes much deeper.
Speed comes with practice. On the first trip you’ll flip every box in the cart and feel a little silly doing it, but by the third you’ll know which products you trust, which flavors carry a symbol, and exactly where on the package to glance. Snap a photo of labels you like. Next trip goes faster.
### Fresh produce and bulk bins
Raw fruits and vegetables don’t need a symbol, which makes produce the easiest part of the store. Washed, cut and bagged produce can be a different matter, and kosher kitchens check leafy greens for insects at home anyway. Bulk bins are trickier. Scoops get shared and bins get refilled from sources you can’t see, so many kosher shoppers skip them unless the store posts certification for the bins themselves.
### Ask at the counter
Store staff know more than you’d guess. The meat department can tell you whether any certified poultry or beef comes in, fresh or frozen. Customer service may know when holiday stock arrives. A manager can sometimes special-order a product if enough people ask. Plenty of kosher sections started exactly that way.
Waiting for challah to rise? Knit a scarf. Start with good yarn
### Do big-box and national chains carry kosher food?
Yes, though what shows up varies by store. Big-box retailers, warehouse clubs, discount grocers and national supermarket chains all sell packaged products with kosher symbols, because certification belongs to the manufacturer, not the retailer. Certified fresh meat is far less predictable. Some locations stock it, often frozen, and many don’t. Check the symbol and ask the store.
There’s a simple reason for the gap. A box of crackers gets certified at the factory, so it’s just as kosher on a shelf in any state. Fresh meat has to come from a kosher slaughterhouse and stay in its certified packaging, and a chain has to decide a particular store has enough demand to bother. Two locations of the same chain can carry wildly different selections. One has a full kosher freezer. The other, nothing.
Watch out for repackaging. If a store cuts or rewraps kosher meat in its own ordinary meat room, most observant shoppers won’t treat it as kosher anymore. The certification has to stay intact, usually as a sealed package bearing the agency’s mark, and poultry often carries its own tag or clip. Store brands show the per-product rule nicely. Some private-label items are certified. Others on the very same shelf aren’t.
Heading to a warehouse club before a big hosting weekend? Call first, and ask the meat or grocery department what certified products that location has right now. Two minutes on the phone beats a wasted drive.
### Why does kosher meat cost more?
Kosher meat usually costs more than conventional meat because more skilled work goes into every pound. A trained shochet handles the slaughter, inspectors reject animals with certain defects, workers soak and salt each piece, and an agency supervises the whole chain. Kosher plants also run smaller volumes, and much of the hindquarter gets sold off to the regular market.
Each of those steps is real labor. Salting takes time and floor space. Some animals that pass the standard federal inspection still fail kosher inspection, and they leave the kosher supply entirely. Supervision costs get built into the price. And since demand is small next to the conventional market, kosher suppliers don’t get the economies of scale that a giant national packer running around the clock enjoys.
Pantry goods are another story. A certified box of pasta from a national brand often costs about what any comparable box costs, and frequently there isn’t even an uncertified version, because the regular box is the kosher one. Specialty imports and holiday items can run higher. So can kosher cheese.
### How families plan around the cost
A common approach is to split the list. Pantry staples, produce and certified dairy come from wherever is closest. Meat comes from the kosher butcher or a kosher freezer case, bought in bigger batches and frozen at home. Front-quarter cuts like chuck and brisket reward low, slow cooking, so a slow cooker earns its counter space. Chicken stretches further than beef. A second freezer in the garage? For many kosher households outside the city, that’s standard equipment.
### When should you shop ahead for Jewish holidays?
Start weeks ahead for Passover and the fall holidays, and shop early in the week for Shabbat. Kosher stores close for Shabbat and major holidays, popular specialty items sell out, and holiday shipments arrive on the store’s schedule, not yours. Ask the store when holiday stock comes in, and place meat and challah orders early.
The fall stretch opens with Rosh Hashanah, then Yom Kippur, then Sukkot, often packed into a few weeks of September and October. Round challah, honey, apples, brisket, a pre-fast meal and a break-fast spread. Bakeries take challah orders in advance. Butchers take brisket orders in advance. Show up the morning before the holiday without an order and you may be staring at an empty case.
Passover is the big one. Eight days outside Israel, a seder or two with a crowd, and a whole kitchen that has to switch over to Passover food. The aisle usually opens weeks ahead, and the most popular items can vanish well before the first night. Shelf-stable goods like matzo, wine and grape juice can be bought early. Meat can be ordered for pickup a few days out.
Picture a family in Warrenton hosting cousins for a seder. They’re a long drive from any kosher butcher, so the smart version of their month looks like one big trip a few weeks out for shelf-stable goods, a meat order placed early and collected in a single run with a cooler, and a freezer cleared out ahead of time to make room. Hectic? Sure. But it’s hectic on their terms.
Hanukkah is gentler. Oil, potatoes and flour are sold everywhere, and latkes don’t need a specialty store. Purim brings hamantaschen and gift baskets of treats, and some bakeries do sell out, so an early order never hurts.
### Can you buy kosher groceries online?
Yes. Many kosher butchers, bakeries and specialty grocers ship across the country, and frozen meat usually travels in insulated boxes with dry ice or gel packs. Online ordering suits families far from a kosher store, but shipping costs, delivery windows and order minimums vary. Check the certifying agency on every product page before you buy.
Grocery delivery apps that pull from local supermarkets can help with certified pantry goods too. The problem is that you can’t flip the box. Product photos don’t always show the symbol clearly, and a substituted item may not be certified at all. Turn off substitutions for kosher items if the app lets you.
For shipped meat, be home. A box of frozen brisket sitting on a porch in Glendale on a July afternoon is a real problem. Pick a delivery day when somebody can carry it inside right away, check that everything arrived frozen solid, and get it straight into the freezer. Anything show up soft? Contact the seller before you cook it and follow their guidance.
Online works best as a backup. A local kosher butcher can answer questions, cut to order and tell you what’s good this week. A website can’t.
Planning a kosher grocery run? Browse kosher grocery stores across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, call ahead before Friday afternoon, and ask what the meat counter has in stock.
