### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How to find kosher items in a grocery store?
A.  Check each package for a hechsher, the symbol of a kosher certifying agency, usually printed near the product name or on the back by the ingredients. Many larger stores also group kosher specialty foods into one aisle or freezer case. Ask customer service or the meat counter what they stock, since layouts and selection differ from store to store.
### Q. Which food brands are kosher?
A.  More than most people guess. Plenty of mainstream national brands certify many of their products, so kosher crackers, cereal, soda and canned goods turn up in almost any store. Certification belongs to each product, not the whole brand, though. One flavor may carry a symbol while the next one doesn’t, and certifications can change, so read every package.
### Q. Does Aldi sell kosher products?
A.  Discount grocers, Aldi included, typically stock some packaged products that carry kosher symbols, but there’s no blanket answer for any chain. Certification is printed product by product, and what a given store carries depends on location and season. Look for the hechsher on each item and ask the staff whether that store brings in extra kosher goods before holidays.
### Q. Is Costco meat kosher?
A.  Not by default. Meat at a warehouse club is conventional unless a package is specifically certified, and certified meat carries an agency symbol on its own sealed label. Some warehouse locations may stock kosher meat or poultry, often frozen, while others don’t. Check the label on the package itself and ask the meat department what that store carries.
### Q. Does whole food sell kosher meat?
A.  Natural-food grocers like Whole Foods sometimes carry certified kosher items, but availability varies a lot by location. Don’t assume the fresh meat case is kosher. Look for an agency symbol on a sealed package, and ask the butcher counter whether that particular store stocks kosher poultry or beef, fresh or frozen, and when it usually arrives.
### Q. What to look for when buying kosher?
A.  Look for a recognized agency symbol first, then the letter beside it: D for dairy, M or Meat, Pareve for neither, and P for Passover. On fresh meat, make sure the certified packaging is sealed and wasn’t rewrapped in a regular meat room. Shopping for a guest who keeps kosher? Ask which agencies they accept.
### Q. Are kosher grocery stores cheaper?
A.  Usually not. Kosher meat tends to cost more because of the supervision, skilled slaughter, inspection and salting behind it, and specialty stores buy in smaller volumes than giant chains. Certified pantry staples from national brands often cost about the same as comparable products, so many families buy those anywhere and save the kosher store for meat.
### Q. Is kosher meat actually healthier?
A.  Not necessarily. Kosher rules are religious, not nutritional. The inspection process rejects some animals with certain defects, and people sometimes read that as a health advantage, but there’s no settled evidence that kosher meat is healthier overall. Salting can add sodium. If you’re watching salt or managing a health condition, ask your doctor or a dietitian.

## Laser Eye Surgery in St. Louis: Who Is a Candidate?
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/laser-eye-surgery-in-st-louis-who-is-a-candidate
It’s 6:40 on a weekday morning in Bethalto, and a nurse heading out for a twelve-hour shift is on her knees on the bathroom tile, patting around for a contact lens that just jumped off her fingertip. She finds it. It’s got lint on it. She rinses it, puts it in, blinks hard, and decides, not for the first time, that she’s going to look into LASIK this year.
Then the questions start.
Is she too old at forty-three? Are her eyes too dry? Does it matter that her prescription crept up a couple of years ago? And why do the ads all sound so sure of themselves when her sister-in-law was told flat out she wasn’t a candidate?
This guide walks through how candidacy actually gets decided, what a screening consult checks, the alternatives when laser surgery isn’t the right fit, and what to ask a surgeon before you book anything. No practice names, no prices, no promises. Your eyes are your own, and the only opinion that settles the question is the one from a surgeon who has measured them.
### How do I tell if I’m a candidate for LASIK?
You’re likely a candidate if you’re an adult with a prescription that has held steady for a year or more, healthy corneas that are thick and regular enough to reshape, no significant dry eye or active eye disease, and no health condition that slows healing. A surgeon’s screening exam is the only thing that confirms it.
### Is your prescription stable?
Eyes that are still changing are a moving target. If your glasses or contacts prescription has shifted recently, most surgeons will want to wait, because reshaping the cornea corrects the eye you have today, not the one you’ll have after it drifts again. Dig out your old prescriptions before the consult. They tell a story.
That’s one reason age matters. LASIK in the U.S. is generally limited to adults, and many surgeons prefer patients somewhat past their early twenties, when nearsighted prescriptions often settle down. Is there an upper limit? Not a hard one. Older eyes bring different questions, like early cataracts and presbyopia, and we’ll get to both.
### What about the shape and thickness of your corneas?
The laser removes tissue. That’s the whole trick, and it means your cornea needs enough thickness left over afterward to stay strong. Surgeons also study its shape. A cornea that’s irregular, or shows early signs of keratoconus, a condition where it thins and bulges outward over time, can be a reason to skip LASIK entirely, since removing tissue could make things worse. You can’t judge any of this in a mirror.
Very strong prescriptions run into the same wall. The bigger the correction, the more tissue has to go, and at some point a surgeon may steer you toward a different procedure altogether.
### Do dry eyes rule you out?
Not always, but dry eye is one of the most common reasons a consult slows down. LASIK can make dryness worse for a while because it disrupts corneal nerves that help trigger tears. Someone who already fights gritty, burning eyes by midafternoon might need treatment first, or a different procedure, or a frank talk about whether surgery makes sense at all. Tell the surgeon how your eyes really feel. Downplaying it helps nobody.
### Which health conditions matter?
Healing matters as much as the laser work. Surgeons tend to look closely at autoimmune conditions such as lupus or rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes that isn’t well controlled, anything that weakens the immune system, and eye problems like glaucoma, cataracts or a history of eye infections. Some medications raise flags too. None of that is an automatic no for everyone. It’s a conversation, so bring a full list of what you take.
### What about pregnancy?
Pregnancy and nursing are usually a pause, not a no. Hormonal shifts can temporarily change your prescription and your tear film, so most surgeons prefer to wait until things settle after you’ve finished nursing. Planning a pregnancy soon? Mention it. Timing matters here.
### What does the screening consult actually check?
A good screening consult measures far more than your prescription. Expect corneal thickness readings, a map of the corneal surface, pupil measurements, a tear-film check, eye pressure, a dilated look at the retina and lens, and a long talk about your health history, your job and what you’re hoping surgery will do for you.
Plan on it taking a while. Dilation drops blur your near vision for hours and make daylight feel blinding, so bring sunglasses and, ideally, a driver. Contact lens wearers usually get told to leave the lenses out for a stretch beforehand, because contacts can temporarily change the shape of the cornea and throw off the measurements. How long depends on the lens type. Ask when you book, not the night before.
Sometimes the consult turns up something that needs a medical eye doctor first, like signs of glaucoma or a retina problem. That’s the system working. Our guide on when to see an ophthalmologist in St. Louis covers the difference between routine eye care and a specialist visit.
### What does a no at screening really mean?
A practice that turns you away is telling you something useful. So is one that recommends a different procedure than the one you walked in asking about. Picture a guy from Wellston who’s been saving up for LASIK for two years, only to hear that his corneas are on the thin side and PRK or a lens-based option would be safer for his eyes. Disappointing? Sure. It beats the alternative.
### What if LASIK isn’t the right fit?
LASIK is one option among several. PRK reshapes the cornea without cutting a flap. SMILE removes a small disc of tissue through a tiny incision. Implantable lenses sit inside the eye and remove no corneal tissue at all, and refractive lens exchange replaces your natural lens. Which one fits depends on your measurements, and your surgeon makes that call.
### LASIK
In LASIK, the surgeon creates a thin hinged flap in the front of the cornea, folds it back, reshapes the tissue underneath with an excimer laser, and lays the flap back down. Many people see well quickly, often within a day or so. The flap is also its main tradeoff, since that part of the cornea doesn’t fully regain the strength of untouched tissue.
### PRK
PRK came before LASIK and it’s still widely used. Instead of making a flap, the surgeon removes the thin surface layer of the cornea and reshapes what’s underneath, and that surface grows back over the following days. Recovery is slower. It’s more uncomfortable, too, and vision can take weeks to sharpen fully.
So why pick it? PRK leaves more of the cornea intact, which can make it the better choice for thinner corneas, and there’s no flap to dislodge. People in contact sports, the military or law enforcement sometimes care a lot about that last part.
### SMILE
SMILE uses a femtosecond laser to shape a small lens-shaped piece of tissue inside the cornea, then removes it through a short incision. No flap. It’s newer than LASIK and PRK, it’s approved for a narrower range of prescriptions, and not every practice offers it. Ask whether it applies to your eyes specifically, not just in general.
### Implantable lenses
An implantable collamer lens, or ICL, is a thin lens placed inside the eye in front of your natural lens, a bit like a contact lens that stays put. Nothing gets removed from the cornea. That makes it a common suggestion for very high nearsighted prescriptions or corneas too thin for laser work. It’s surgery inside the eye, though, and it carries its own risks your surgeon should walk you through.
### Refractive lens exchange
Refractive lens exchange removes your natural lens and replaces it with an artificial one. It’s the same basic operation as cataract surgery, just done before a cataract forms. It tends to come up for people in their mid-forties and beyond with high prescriptions, early lens changes or a strong wish to cut back on reading glasses. Bigger step. And unlike a contact lens, you can’t just take it out.
### What happens to your reading vision after 40?
Somewhere in your early to mid-forties, the natural lens inside your eye stiffens and loses its ability to focus up close. It’s called presbyopia, and it catches up with nearly everyone. LASIK reshapes the cornea, not the lens, so it doesn’t stop presbyopia. Plenty of people over 40 still need readers after surgery.
This is the part that surprises people. Say you’re nearsighted at 45 and you’ve been slipping your glasses off to read a menu. That trick works because your nearsightedness happens to offset your aging lens. Correct the distance vision fully and the menu trick disappears, so you may walk out reading highway signs crisply and reaching for drugstore readers at dinner.
### What about monovision?
One workaround is monovision. The surgeon corrects your dominant eye for distance and leaves the other slightly nearsighted for reading, and your brain learns to use each eye for its own job. Some people love it. Others find their depth perception or night driving feels off. Many surgeons suggest trying it with contact lenses first, which makes for a cheap, reversible test drive.
### What changes after 60?
A retiree in Kimmswick asking about LASIK at 62 might hear something different altogether. By the sixties, many people have early cataract changes, and reshaping a cornea that sits in front of a slowly clouding lens may not make much sense. Cataract surgery with a lens chosen to reduce glasses dependence often becomes the better conversation. Age alone isn’t the barrier. The lens is.
### Will insurance pay for any of it?
Most health and vision plans treat LASIK and similar procedures as elective, so they usually don’t cover them. Some vision plans offer member discounts through certain providers. Flexible spending and health savings accounts may help, since refractive surgery is often an eligible expense. Confirm with your plan administrator before you schedule anything at all.
Call the member number on your card and ask three things. Does the plan cover refractive surgery at all? Does it have a discount arrangement, and with whom? What counts as an eligible expense for your FSA or HSA? FSA money often comes with a use-it-or-lose-it deadline, so timing a procedure around your plan year can matter. We’re not tax advisors, though, and your administrator is the one who knows your plan.
The routine eye exams around surgery are a separate question. Plenty of plans cover an annual exam even when they won’t touch the procedure, and our look at eye exam costs with a St. Louis optometrist explains how that usually works. Ask the surgical practice what care comes after the procedure, too, like follow-up visits and what happens if you need a touch-up later.
### What are the real downsides?
Dry eye is the most common downside, and for many people it eases over the following months, though for some it lingers. Glare, halos and starbursts around lights at night are common early on. Serious complications like infection, flap problems or corneal weakening are rare but real, which is exactly why careful screening exists in the first place.
Night vision complaints deserve a straight answer before surgery, not after. People with larger pupils or stronger prescriptions sometimes notice more halos. Drive at night for work? Say so at the consult, and expect the surgeon’s answer to be about your measurements, not a general pat on the shoulder.
Some people also end up slightly under- or over-corrected and need an enhancement, meaning a second, smaller treatment. Vision can drift again over the years as the eye ages. Surgery changes the cornea you have. It doesn’t freeze your eyes in time.
And the stuff nobody prints on the brochure? Recovery-week logistics. You’ll use drops on a schedule, avoid rubbing your eyes, skip swimming and eye makeup for a while, and need a ride home on surgery day. Small things. They pile up fast if you’re a parent or work a physical job.
New eyes, same squint at the grocery label: spotting kosher food
### How should you interview a laser eye surgeon?
Shortlist two or three surgeons and interview them the way you’d interview any doctor you plan to trust with something important. Tell each one plainly what you want and expect from surgery. Then listen for what they’re prepared to deliver for your eyes specifically. The gap between those two things is the signal, not the price.
### Questions worth asking
Am I a good candidate, and for which procedures? A surgeon who explains why you’re better suited to PRK or an ICL, using your own measurements, is showing their work. That’s what you want.
Who performs the surgery, and who handles follow-up? Ask whether the surgeon you meet is the one operating, and who you call if something feels wrong at midnight.
What do you expect my reading vision to look like in five or ten years? That’s the presbyopia question in disguise. A thoughtful, specific answer is a good sign.
What happens if I need an enhancement? Ask how they decide one is needed and how it’s handled.
When would you tell someone like me not to do this? Our favorite. A surgeon who answers without hesitation has probably turned people away before, and that’s reassuring.
### What should make you walk away?
Pressure to book on the spot. A consult that skips the dilated exam or the corneal mapping. Promises of perfect vision or never needing glasses again, because nobody can guarantee that and good surgeons don’t try. The nurse in Bethalto doesn’t need a sales pitch. She needs someone who’ll look at her dry eyes, her forty-three-year-old lenses and her shift schedule, then tell her the truth about all three.
Ready for a screening consult? Browse laser eye surgery across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, shortlist two or three surgeons, and bring your old prescriptions to each consult.
If you’re the shop, being the one people and AI name first is the game when someone tired of fishing contacts off the bathroom floor finally asks whether they qualify, so list your refractive surgery or eye practice.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it worth getting LASIK after 40?
A.  It can be, if you go in knowing LASIK won’t fix presbyopia. Many people over 40 get sharp distance vision and still need reading glasses up close. Monovision is one option, and lens-based procedures may make more sense for some eyes. A screening exam and an honest talk about your daily life decide it.
### Q. Does insurance cover LASIK eye surgery?
A.  Usually not. Most health and vision plans treat it as elective. Some vision plans offer discounts through participating providers, and FSA or HSA funds may be usable, since refractive surgery is often an eligible expense. Call your plan administrator to confirm what applies to you before you pick a procedure date.
### Q. What is the downside of laser eye surgery?
A.  Dry eye is the most common, and it often improves over months but can linger. Glare, halos and starbursts at night are common early on. Some people need an enhancement. Serious complications like infection or corneal weakening are rare but possible, which is why screening matters and why some people get turned away.
### Q. Is there an alternative to laser eye surgery?
A.  Yes. Glasses and contacts are the obvious ones. Surgically, an implantable collamer lens corrects vision without removing corneal tissue, and refractive lens exchange replaces your natural lens, much like cataract surgery. For some people, PRK or SMILE is the better laser choice. Your surgeon’s measurements decide which options you actually have.
### Q. Do you still wear glasses after laser eye surgery?
A.  Many people don’t need glasses for distance afterward, but plenty still reach for a pair sometimes. Reading glasses are common after 40 because LASIK doesn’t stop presbyopia. Some people keep a light prescription for night driving, and vision can shift over time. Ask your surgeon what they expect for your eyes specifically.
### Q. Is 60 too old for laser eye surgery?
A.  Not automatically. There’s generally no firm upper age limit. By 60, though, many people have early cataract changes, and LASIK doesn’t address the lens. A surgeon may suggest cataract surgery or refractive lens exchange instead. Healthy eyes and a stable prescription matter more than the number on your birth certificate.
### Q. Can your vision still deteriorate after LASIK?
A.  Yes, it can. LASIK reshapes the cornea but doesn’t stop the eye from aging. Presbyopia still arrives in your forties, cataracts can develop later, and some people notice a small drift that may call for an enhancement. Keep up with routine eye exams after surgery so changes get caught early.
### Q. What disqualifies you from getting LASIK?
A.  Common reasons include an unstable prescription, corneas that are too thin or irregularly shaped, keratoconus, significant dry eye, certain autoimmune or poorly controlled health conditions, some eye diseases, and pregnancy or nursing, which usually means waiting. Very strong prescriptions can also rule it out. A screening exam is the only way to know.

## How to Prepare for Laser Hair Removal in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-prepare-for-laser-hair-removal-in-st-louis
It’s a Tuesday night in October in Wright City, and a nurse just off a twelve-hour shift is sitting on the edge of her bed reading the prep email from the laser clinic for the third time. Her first appointment is Friday. Underarms and lower legs. The email says shave, but not too early, and don’t wax, and avoid the sun, and bring a list of your medications, and it reads like instructions written for somebody who has already done this twice.
She hasn’t. She shaved this morning. Does that count?
Most first-timers land in that exact spot. The appointment is booked, the money question is settled (if it isn’t, our guide to what laser hair removal costs in St. Louis covers it), and the real question turns practical. What do you actually do between now and the chair? This guide runs in order: the weeks before, the day before, the session itself, the redness afterward, the shedding a couple of weeks later, how sessions get spaced, and why so many people around St. Louis start when the leaves turn. General information only. Your provider’s consult decides what applies to your skin.
### Do I shave before laser hair removal?
Yes. Most providers want the area shaved, usually within a day or so of the appointment, so the laser hits the root and not hair on the surface. Don’t wax, pluck or thread, because the root has to stay in place. Your provider’s own instructions win if they differ.
Here’s the logic, because once it clicks, every other rule gets easier to remember. The laser is aimed at pigment in the hair, and the whole point is to send that energy down the shaft into the follicle sitting under your skin. Hair lying on top of the skin soaks up energy it can’t use. It singes. It smells. It can heat the surface more than anyone wants. A clean shave leaves the pigmented root exactly where the light can reach it.
### How close to the appointment?
Timing is where people trip. Plenty of clinics like a shave the night before or the morning of, while others prefer a day or two ahead so any razor irritation has calmed down before the laser touches it. Neither camp is wrong. Read your own clinic’s instructions, and if they don’t say, call. Thirty-second question.
### What if you miss a spot?
Don’t panic. Many providers will shave a small missed patch in the room before they start. Some charge for that, some don’t, and some will reschedule if a whole area shows up unshaved. The backs of the thighs and the lower back are the usual misses, so a second look in a hand mirror, or a helper, is worth it.
### Why not just wax?
Because waxing pulls out the root, and the root is the target. Same with plucking, threading, sugaring and epilators. Razor yes. Anything that yanks, no. Depilatory creams sit in a gray zone: some clinics allow them between sessions and some don’t, and they can irritate skin right before treatment, so ask before you reach for one.
### What should you stop doing in the weeks before your first session?
Stop waxing, plucking and threading the area, stay out of strong sun, skip self-tanner, and write down every medication and supplement you take. Those are the big four. Exact waiting windows vary by clinic and by device, so treat any number you read online as a rough idea and follow the one your provider gives you.
### The pause on pulling hair
If you’ve waxed for years, this is the adjustment that stings. Clinics commonly ask for several weeks without anything that removes hair from the root before a first session, so the follicles have time to grow a fresh hair the laser can find. Shave in the meantime. It feels like going backward. It isn’t.
### Sun and self-tanner
Tanned skin carries more pigment, and pigment is what the laser is hunting, so a tan puts your skin in competition with your hair. A fresh tan, a sunburn or a coat of self-tanner can raise the chance of burns or of lighter and darker patches afterward. That’s why a provider may turn the settings down, treat more cautiously, or send you home and rebook. Spray tans count. So does that Saturday at the lake.
### Medications and photosensitivity
Some medications make skin more sensitive to light. Certain antibiotics, some acne treatments (especially ones taken by mouth) and a few supplements tend to show up on the lists clinics hand out, though those lists aren’t identical. Retinoid creams on the treatment area can matter as well. Never stop something a doctor prescribed on your own. Bring the full list, doses included, to the consultation and let the provider, and your prescribing doctor if needed, sort out the timing.
A few other things belong in that conversation too, even if they feel unrelated. Cold sores, if you’re treating the upper lip or chin. A tendency toward keloid scars. A recent skin infection, pregnancy, or a new rash that won’t quit. Say all of it out loud. If something on your skin needs a closer look first, a dermatologist is the right stop, and our guide to when to see a dermatologist in St. Louis walks through how that usually works.
### Does your skin tone and hair color change the plan?
Yes, a lot. Laser generally works best when the hair is darker than the skin around it, because the light has an obvious target. Deeper skin tones can be treated with the right device and settings. Gray, white, red and light blond hair usually respond poorly, since there’s little pigment for the laser to find.
The device matters because different lasers use different wavelengths, and those wavelengths interact with melanin in the skin in different ways. Longer-wavelength lasers such as the Nd:YAG are widely used on deeper skin tones, because they tend to pass the skin’s surface pigment more gently on the way down to the follicle. Alexandrite and diode lasers are common for lighter to medium skin. Broad sketch, not a rule. Settings, cooling and the operator’s experience count as much as the name on the machine.
Many providers sort skin with the Fitzpatrick scale, a six-type system based on how skin reacts to sun. Expect to be asked whether you burn or tan, and expect them to look for themselves. With deeper skin, it’s fair to ask straight out: which laser would you use on me, and how often do you treat skin like mine with it? A confident, specific answer is the one you’re listening for.
### What about light or gray hair?
Nobody enjoys this conversation. If the hair holds very little pigment, most lasers just won’t see it, and a good provider says so before taking your money. Electrolysis works on hair of any color, and some providers will point you there instead.
### What should you do the day before and the morning of?
Shave the area on the schedule your clinic asked for, then keep the skin clean and bare. On the day, skip lotion, oil, deodorant, makeup and perfume on the treatment area, and wear loose clothing over it. If you’ve had sun since the consult, tell the provider before the first pulse, not after.
Bare skin matters because products can sit between the light and the hair, and some leave a residue that heats up. Underarms are the classic trap. You swipe on deodorant out of pure habit at seven in the morning and remember it in the parking lot. Many clinics keep wipes on hand for exactly that reason.
Numbing cream is its own question. Some clinics offer it for sensitive areas, some let you apply an over-the-counter version at home, and some would rather you skip it entirely. Don’t slather anything on without checking first, since both the amount and the size of the area covered matter for safety.
Loose clothes. Earrings out if it’s the face. A clean shirt in the bag. That’s the list.
### What does a laser hair removal session feel like?
Most people compare each pulse to a rubber band snapped against the skin, with a quick flash of heat. It’s sharper over bone and in thick, dense hair like the underarm or bikini line, and milder on the legs. Small areas can take minutes. Larger ones take longer, and pain tolerance varies widely.
The room is quiet and a little clinical. You’ll wear goggles or eye shields the whole time, because the light is bright enough to hurt eyes. The provider may draw a white pencil grid on your skin so no patch gets skipped or hit twice. Then comes the cold: a chilled tip on the handpiece, a stream of cold air, or a layer of gel, depending on the device, and that cooling does a lot of the work of making the whole thing bearable.
And the smell. A faint burnt-hair odor, like a match blown out too close to a curl, drifts up with some pulses. Normal. It’s the hair, not your skin.
The first session often stings the most, partly from nerves and partly because there’s more hair soaking up the light. Speak up if a spot feels too hot. That isn’t complaining. It’s information the provider can use, and settings can be adjusted on the spot.
Legs smooth, goggles off. Now pick the internal medicine doctor you’ll actually call.
### What happens to your skin right after, and when does the hair fall out?
Expect redness and small raised bumps around each follicle, a bit like goose bumps crossed with a mild sunburn, which usually settle within hours to a day or two. Treated hairs then tend to shed over the following week or few. Anything that blisters, crusts or keeps getting worse is a call to your provider.
### The first 48 hours
Cool is your friend. A cold compress, or a soothing gel the clinic recommends, takes the heat out. Many providers suggest skipping hot showers, saunas, hot tubs and hard workouts for a day or so, since heat and sweat can irritate freshly treated skin. Hold off on fragranced products and scrubs until the redness fades. Sunscreen goes on every day, on anything the sun can reach.
### The shedding stage
Somewhere around a week or two out, treated hairs start working loose. At first it can look like stubble coming back, with little dark dots under the skin that people call peppering. Then they slide out in the shower or wipe off with a washcloth. Don’t pluck them. Once your provider says it’s fine, gentle exfoliation can help them along, and shaving stays allowed the whole time.
### How far apart should sessions be for each body area?
Sessions are spaced to match how hair grows in each area, so the face often comes back sooner and the body waits longer. Your provider sets the interval after seeing your hair. Going back early doesn’t speed anything up, because the hairs that matter haven’t reached their growth phase yet.
Facial hair tends to cycle faster, so upper lip and chin appointments often come around more quickly. Legs and backs usually run on a slower clock. Underarms and bikini areas land somewhere in between for a lot of people. Treating several areas? Ask whether they can share one calendar or need separate ones, because that answer saves a surprising amount of rescheduling.
Life gets in the way. Slipping a week past your window isn’t usually a disaster, though letting months drift can mean the next session catches fewer hairs at the right stage. Book the next appointment before you walk out. Small habit, big difference.
### Why do so many St. Louis people start laser in the fall?
St. Louis summers are long, bright and spent outdoors, and sun exposure is one of the main things that complicates laser. Starting in fall or early winter means the first several sessions happen while skin is covered and last summer’s tan has faded. By swimsuit season, a good chunk of the work is behind you.
Picture a normal summer here. Day games at the ballpark, lake weekends, yard work in humidity so thick your sunscreen is sliding off by noon. A guy in House Springs who spends his Saturdays on a boat isn’t going to show up to a July appointment with pale shins. His provider knows it. He knows it. Scheduling around the sun is easier than fighting it.
Summer isn’t off limits, though. Plenty of people treat year-round, especially areas that stay covered, like underarms or the bikini line. Faces and legs are harder. Start in warm months and sunscreen, hats and clothing coverage stop being suggestions and become part of the plan.
A bride in Millstadt counting back from a June wedding is doing the same math in reverse, and autumn is usually where it points. Ask at the consultation how far ahead to begin for a fixed date. Be honest about how much sun you’ll get between now and then.
### How do you interview a laser provider before your first session?
Shortlist two or three providers and interview each one the way you would a new doctor. Tell them plainly what you want treated, what your skin and hair are like, what you take, and what your summer looks like. Then listen to what each is prepared to deliver. The gap between those two is the signal, not the price.
Questions worth saying out loud: Which laser would you use on my skin, and why that one? Who runs the device, and what training do they have? Is a physician or other medical professional involved, and how? What do you want me doing the week before and the morning of? What happens if I react badly two days later? Rules about who can operate these devices vary by state, so ask instead of assuming.
A test spot is worth raising too, especially with deeper skin or a history of sensitivity. Many clinics will pulse a small patch and have you wait before the full session. A provider who brings that up without being prompted is telling you something good.
Listen for specifics. A careful provider asks about medications before you mention them, actually looks at your skin, and tells you plainly if your hair color is a poor match. One who promises everything and asks nothing has told you something as well.
Ready to book a consultation? Browse laser hair removal across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, shortlist two or three, and bring your medication list to every conversation.
If you’re the shop, being the one people and AI name first is the game when someone is planning a fall start and wants a provider who explains prep before the first pulse, so list your med spa or laser studio.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it okay to shave 2 days before laser hair removal?
A.  Often, yes. Plenty of clinics are happy with a shave a day or two ahead, and some prefer it because razor irritation has time to settle. Others want it closer, the night before or that morning. The hair should still be short enough that almost nothing sits above the skin. Follow your own clinic’s instructions when they differ.
### Q. Is a little stubble ok for laser hair removal?
A.  A small amount of very short regrowth is usually tolerated, and some providers even like seeing a hint of it to confirm where the hair is. Longer stubble is a different story, because hair above the skin absorbs energy, singes and can heat the surface. If you’re unsure, shave again and let the provider decide.
### Q. How long after laser does hair fall out?
A.  Treated hairs commonly start shedding around one to two weeks after a session, sometimes a little sooner or later. At first it can look like regrowth, with dark dots under the skin, before the hairs slide out in the shower or wipe away with a washcloth. Don’t pluck them. Ask your provider before exfoliating to speed things along.
### Q. Who is not a good candidate for laser hair removal?
A.  People whose hair holds little pigment, such as gray, white, red or light blond hair, often see limited results. Providers may also hold off for someone with a fresh tan, an active skin infection, pregnancy, or certain light-sensitizing medications. That’s a general picture. Candidacy is decided at the consultation, after the provider looks at your skin and your health history.
### Q. How painful is hair laser removal?
A.  Most people describe it as a rubber band snapping against the skin with a burst of heat. Dense, coarse hair and bony areas tend to hurt more, and legs usually hurt less. Built-in cooling helps a lot, and some clinics offer numbing cream for sensitive spots. Tell the provider if a pulse feels too hot, since settings can change.
### Q. How often is each laser hair removal session?
A.  Sessions are spaced weeks apart, matched to how hair grows in each part of the body. Facial areas often come around sooner, while legs and backs usually wait longer, with underarms and bikini areas somewhere between. Your provider sets the interval after seeing your hair. Returning early doesn’t help, because the next wave of hairs isn’t ready yet.
### Q. Will 3 sessions of laser hair removal do anything?
A.  Usually, yes, you’ll notice something. Many people see thinner, patchier regrowth after a few sessions, though hair that was resting during those appointments hasn’t been treated yet. Stopping there tends to leave uneven results. How far a few sessions get you depends on your hair, your skin and the area, so ask your provider what to expect at that point.
### Q. What disqualifies you from laser hair removal?
A.  Usually nothing is permanent, just a reason to wait or change approach. Common pauses include a recent tan or sunburn, an active infection or open wound in the area, pregnancy, and some photosensitizing medications. Very light hair may not respond at all. A provider may also want a doctor’s input first. The consultation, not a checklist online, makes the call.

## The Asterisk Next to Raw Kibbeh Is Missouri Law: Lebanese Food in St. Louis and What to Order
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/lebanese-food-in-st-louis-what-to-order
A plate of raw minced meat slides past your elbow at a St. Louis Lebanese table, glossy under a thread of olive oil, mint leaves on top, a heap of raw onion on the side. Nobody at the next table flinches. They ordered it on purpose. Meanwhile your own table is frozen over a menu that runs for pages, and half the words on it have never been said out loud.
That plate is kibbeh nayyeh. Find it on the menu and look just past the name: there should be a small asterisk, and a footnote at the bottom of the page. That little star is the law talking. Section 3-603.11 of the Missouri Food Code says a kitchen serving beef, lamb or any animal food raw has to tell you in writing, and the reminder works by asterisking the dish to a footnote along the lines of “Consuming raw or undercooked meats, poultry, seafood, shellfish, or eggs may increase your risk of foodborne illness.” No star, no footnote, no table card? Ask before you order.
The rest of the menu is easier than it looks. A Lebanese menu isn’t a list of entrees. It’s a box of parts, and you build the meal in waves. For two people, use the 2-1-1: two cold mezze, one hot, one grill, everything split, pita torn by hand. And if you want to taste those parts made by people who grew up on them, St. Louis has a street literally named Lebanon. At St. Raymond Maronite Cathedral, 931 Lebanon Drive, the parish runs a Wednesday Luncheon of Lebanese and Middle Eastern food; check the parish’s posted kitchen closing dates before you drive, or call the cathedral at 314-621-0056. Over one September weekend, Friday evening through Sunday afternoon, the same cathedral hosts the St. Louis Lebanese Festival, a party nearly six decades old, with kibbe aras, tabbouli, meat pies, spinach pies, cabbage rolls and stuffed grape leaves on the menu, dabke by the cathedral’s youth dancers, and free admission and free parking. The flyer and food pre-order go up on the cathedral’s own site, straymond-mc.org, ahead of the weekend.
### What dishes are typically on a Lebanese menu in St. Louis?
Expect cold mezze like hummus, baba ghanoush, tabbouleh and labneh with warm pita, plus hot mezze like kibbeh and falafel. Then come grills such as shish tawook and kafta with garlic toum, shawarma, and sweets like baklava and knafeh. Order to share: a few cold plates, one or two hot ones, one grill.
Cold plates land first, with a basket of thin pita that doubles as your fork, and they sit happily on the table while everyone talks. Hot plates follow. The grilled meat arrives when the table is already a little too full, and somehow there’s still room. In Lebanon, a traditional mezze table can run to dozens of small dishes and last for hours, with arak, an anise spirit that turns cloudy when water hits it, poured slowly alongside. You don’t need dozens. Five or six plates for four people is a strong start.
### The one line to look for before you order raw kibbeh
Kibbeh nayyeh is minced raw meat worked with fine bulgur and served with olive oil, mint and raw onion. It’s traditional, it’s cold, it tastes clean and green and a little peppery, and it’s exactly what that food-code section has in mind. Under the Missouri Food Code, the written notice can be a menu advisory, a table tent, a placard, a brochure or a label, and the dish itself gets the asterisk. So scan the bottom of the menu and the little card by the napkins. Here’s the part worth knowing: one of the three footnotes the code allows reads “Regarding the safety of these items, written information is available upon request.” See that line? You’re entitled to ask for the written information, so ask. Still can’t find it? Ask the server two things: is it beef or lamb, and when was it ground? A kitchen proud of its nayyeh answers both without a pause. I could not confirm the exact wording any St. Louis restaurant prints, and the city and county write their own food rules on top of the state’s. Curious what St. Louis County’s own Food Code says about raw dishes?
### What a Missouri home kitchen can and can’t sell you
A tin of maamoul from a neighbor’s oven, powdered sugar on your fingers before the lid is all the way off: that one you can legally buy. Under Missouri’s Cottage Law (RSMo 196.298), home kitchens may sell baked goods, canned jams and jellies, and dried herb mixes, per the state health department’s home-based food guidance. Cooked dishes aren’t on the list. So the neighbor who bakes maamoul or baklava for the holidays can legally sell you a box, even online when seller and buyer are both in Missouri. The neighbor whose hummus or kibbeh is the stuff of legend can’t sell it from a home kitchen under that law. Which is why the best baklava of your life might come from a neighbor’s kitchen, while the best kibbeh still comes from a licensed one. Check the state’s current limits before you buy or sell.
### Ordering for two
Call it the 2-1-1: two cold mezze, one hot, one grill, everything split. Hummus and tabbouleh open well, one rich and creamy, the other so sharp with lemon it makes your jaw tingle. Add kibbeh or falafel for crunch, and eat it while it still hisses. Then share shish tawook or a mixed grill, which often comes with rice, grilled tomato and onion, and a cup of garlic sauce. Still hungry afterward? Order dessert, not another dip.
### Ordering for a group
Groups get the best version of this food. With six or eight people you can order a real spread: three or four cold mezze, three hot ones, a mixed grill or two, a stack of extra bread. Plenty of Lebanese kitchens offer a mezze sampler or a family-style feast, and asking the server to “bring us a good spread” is a normal request, not a lazy one. A birthday table that drove in from Sullivan can let the kitchen run the whole show and never open the menu twice. Same logic on Lebanon Drive at festival time: one person in the food line, one holding the picnic table, and nobody eats until the kibbeh lands.
Order in rounds, though. Fried kibbeh sounds different at minute two than at minute twenty: crackle, then nothing. Cold dips hold up fine, so add hot plates as the first ones disappear instead of flooding the table at once.
### Cold mezze: the plates that hit the table first
The pita is warm, the plates are cool, and the first bite is nearly all lemon. These are the typical Lebanese mezze dishes: hummus, baba ghanoush, tabbouleh, fattoush, labneh and stuffed grape leaves called warak enab. Most are vegetarian, all lean on lemon, garlic, olive oil, tahini, parsley and mint, and every one gets scooped up with pita. They double as the popular Lebanese appetizers, though at a Lebanese table they’re less a warm-up than the main event.
### Hummus
Forget the grocery-store tub. Lebanese hummus is chickpeas whipped very smooth with tahini, lemon and garlic, spread in a shallow bowl with a well of olive oil in the center and a dusting of paprika or sumac. Some menus list hummus with meat, topped with sizzling ground lamb or beef and toasted pine nuts. See it? Get it.
### Baba ghanoush
Eggplant gets charred over open flame until the skin blackens and the inside collapses, then it’s mashed with tahini, lemon and garlic. The smoke is the point. Names drift from kitchen to kitchen, and some menus call the tahini version mutabbal and save “baba ghanoush” for a chunkier eggplant salad with tomato and pepper. Unsure which is coming? Ask.
### Tabbouleh
First-timers get a surprise: real Lebanese tabbouleh is a parsley salad, not a grain salad. Finely chopped flat-leaf parsley does the work, with mint, tomato, onion, a small handful of fine bulgur, lemon juice and olive oil. It should taste green, bright and a little sour. A bowl that looks mostly like bulgur is somebody else’s version.
### Fattoush
The salad for people who want crunch. Lettuce, cucumber, tomato, radish and herbs get tossed with toasted or fried pita pieces and a dressing sharpened with sumac, a tart deep-red spice, and sometimes pomegranate molasses. It began as a way to use up yesterday’s bread. Now people fight over the last forkful.
### Labneh
Yogurt strained until it spreads, somewhere between Greek yogurt and cream cheese. It comes swirled on a plate under olive oil, often with dried mint or za’atar. Tangy and cool, it’s the plate you keep dragging bread through after the grills arrive, because it calms the garlic down.
### Warak enab
Grape leaves rolled tight around a filling and simmered. The cold vegetarian kind holds rice, tomato, parsley and onion and is cooked with lemon and olive oil, so each roll comes out soft and tart. Hot versions filled with rice and ground meat exist too, and they usually sit on the hot side of the menu or arrive as a main.
### Which hot mezze should you order?
Listen for the crackle: that’s kibbeh or falafel leaving the oil. Hot mezze are the fried, baked and grilled small plates, falafel, kibbeh, fatayer, sambousek and arayes, and they’re the crunchy half of the table. If you order only one, make it kibbeh.
### Falafel
Lebanese falafel is usually made from soaked, uncooked chickpeas, sometimes with fava beans, ground with herbs, onion, garlic and spices and deep-fried. The outside should crackle. The inside should be green-flecked and tender, never dry. It arrives with tahini sauce and pickles, and rolled into pita with tomato and parsley it makes a sandwich worth the trip.
### Kibbeh
More forms than anything else on the page. The fried kind is a football-shaped shell of bulgur and finely ground meat, stuffed with more spiced meat, onion and pine nuts, then fried dark and crisp. It can also be pressed into a tray, scored into diamonds and baked. Then there’s the raw kind, kibbeh nayyeh, which is why the county note near the top matters.
### Fatayer and sambousek
Fatayer are small baked pies folded into triangles. Spinach is the classic, filled with spinach, onion, lemon and sumac so it bites back with a pleasant sourness; cheese and meat versions are common. Sambousek are their crispier cousins, half-moon pastries, usually fried, filled with spiced meat and pine nuts or salty white cheese. Both travel well, which is why trays of them turn up at so many family parties.
### Arayes
Maybe the most underrated plate on the menu. Pita is stuffed with a thin layer of seasoned ground meat, the same mix used for kafta, then grilled or pressed until the bread crisps and the juices soak through. Cut into wedges. Dip in labneh. Repeat until someone stops you.
### What belongs on a grill order?
Char and garlic reach you before the plate does. The grill section is where the skewers live: shish tawook, kafta and lamb. A mixed grill gives you some of each, which makes it the smartest first-visit order, and it usually arrives with some mix of rice, grilled tomato and onion, pickles, pita and garlic sauce, depending on the kitchen.
### Shish tawook
Chicken cubes marinated in yogurt, lemon, garlic and spices, sometimes with a spoonful of tomato paste, then skewered and grilled. The yogurt keeps the meat tender while the edges char. It’s the safe order that doesn’t taste safe, and one swipe through garlic sauce explains why regulars rarely order anything else.
### Kafta and lamb
Kafta is ground beef, lamb or a blend, worked with chopped parsley, onion and warm spices, pressed onto flat skewers and grilled. Juicy and herby, and the same mixture that fills arayes. Some kitchens also bake it in a tray with sliced potatoes and tomato sauce, a homestyle dish worth grabbing off the specials board. Lamb skewers, chops or a slow-cooked special may appear too; lamb is the meat Lebanese cooking has leaned on for generations, often seasoned simply. Cuts and portions vary, so ask how it’s cooked.
### Toum, the garlic sauce
Garlic, oil, lemon juice and salt, whipped until it turns white and fluffy, a bit like mayonnaise with no egg in it. Fierce. Take too big a swipe and your eyes water, yet people ask for extra cups to carry home, and in a humid St. Louis summer the smell rides in the car with them all the way. Don’t plan a first date around it.
### Shawarma, and what a Lebanese platter really is
Shawarma is marinated meat stacked on a vertical spit, roasted slowly as it turns and shaved off in thin slices. Chicken shawarma usually comes with toum and pickles, while beef or lamb tends to get tahini sauce, onion and parsley. Wrapped in pita it’s a sandwich: a tight roll, pickles tucked inside, sometimes pressed on the grill so the outside crisps and the paper goes translucent with grease. That’s lunch. Piled on a plate, it’s dinner.
### What’s actually on the platter?
A Lebanese platter, sometimes called a plate or a combo, is a whole meal on one dish. Most pair a protein, such as shawarma, shish tawook, kafta or falafel, with rice, a salad, hummus or garlic sauce, and pita. The rice is often cooked with toasted vermicelli, a home-kitchen staple that gives it a nutty flavor. What lands on the plate changes from kitchen to kitchen, so read the description or just ask.
Platters make sense when you’re eating alone or the table can’t agree on anything. Everybody gets a little of everything. Nobody has to share.
Hungry now? Pick one kitchen and order the 2-1-1 tonight. Browse Lebanese food across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, check the hours before you drive, and open with hummus and fried kibbeh while the pita is still warm.

### What do Lebanese people eat for breakfast?
Manakish, a lot of the time, still warm and smelling of thyme. It’s a round flatbread baked with a topping, and the classic is za’atar: wild thyme, sumac, toasted sesame and salt stirred into olive oil and spread over the dough. Cheese manakish, often made with a mild white cheese called akkawi, runs a close second.
Many Lebanese families eat it in the morning, folded around tomato, cucumber, fresh mint and olives, with a glass of hot tea. Some bakers make a half-and-half, za’atar on one side and cheese on the other, so nobody has to choose. Kishk, a fermented mix of yogurt and bulgur, makes another topping with a sour, funky edge. Worth trying once.
Foul, warm fava beans with lemon, garlic and olive oil, is another breakfast classic, scooped up with bread beside labneh and olives. Around St. Louis, manakish mostly turns up at Lebanese bakeries and at restaurants that open early. Go in the morning. Fresh bread doesn’t always last until lunch.
### Which Lebanese dishes work for vegetarians?
More than in most cuisines. The cold mezze are nearly all vegetarian, and hummus, baba ghanoush, tabbouleh, fattoush, labneh and cold warak enab make a full meal on their own. Add falafel, spinach fatayer, cheese sambousek and mujaddara, lentils cooked with rice or bulgur under a heap of deeply browned onions, and nobody misses the grill.
There’s a reason the meatless side runs so deep. Lebanon has large Christian communities with long lenten fasting traditions, and generations of cooks built a repertoire cooked in olive oil with no meat at all. Batata harra belongs on that list: cubed potatoes fried, then tossed with garlic, cilantro, lemon and chili. Crispy, spicy, gone in minutes.
Vegans do well too, since so many plates skip dairy. Double-check anyway. Labneh is dairy, some pastries use butter, rice may be cooked in chicken stock, and falafel might share a fryer with meat. One quick question settles it, and our guide to how to eat out as a vegetarian in St. Louis covers how to ask without making it awkward.

### Lebanese or Greek: how can you tell on a Mediterranean menu?
They share a sea and some ingredients, but the flavors part ways fast. Greek cooking reaches for oregano, feta, yogurt-and-cucumber tzatziki and lemon potatoes. Lebanese cooking reaches for tahini, sumac, za’atar, parsley, pomegranate molasses and garlic toum. A menu labeled “Mediterranean” often mixes both, so it helps to know which side a dish came from.
The gyro and the shawarma make a handy test. In the U.S., a gyro usually means slices off a cone of seasoned ground meat, tucked into thick, fluffy pita with tzatziki, tomato and onion. Shawarma is stacked slices of marinated whole meat in thinner bread, with toum or tahini where the tzatziki would be. Salads split the same way: Greek salad is chunky tomato, cucumber, olives and a slab of feta, while fattoush brings toasted pita and sumac.
Desserts drift apart too. Baklava lives on both sides, but Lebanese versions tend to favor pistachios and a syrup perfumed with orange blossom or rose water, while Greek versions often use walnuts, cinnamon and honey. For the Greek half of the menu, see our local’s guide to Greek and Mediterranean food in St. Louis. Notice some overlap with Armenian cooking? You’re not imagining it, and what Armenian food is and what to order in St. Louis shows how neighboring kitchens trade dishes back and forth.
### Sweets worth saving room for
Syrup on the fingers, pistachio crumbs on the napkin. Baklava is paper-thin pastry layered with chopped nuts and soaked in fragrant syrup. Knafeh is warm, stretchy cheese under a crust of shredded pastry or semolina, drenched in syrup. Maamoul are crumbly cookies filled with dates or nuts, often baked for Easter and Eid.
### Knafeh
Order it hot. Soft white cheese goes under shredded pastry or a semolina crust, the pan bakes until golden, and then it’s soaked in syrup and showered with crushed pistachios. Salty, sweet, gooey. In Lebanon it’s eaten at breakfast too, stuffed into a sesame bread roll. Yes, really.
### Maamoul
Maamoul get pressed in carved wooden molds, so each cookie carries a pattern that often hints at the filling, dates in one shape and nuts in another. Buttery, crumbly, not too sweet. Bakeries often sell them by the box around the holidays, and a holiday box from a neighbor’s oven fits the Cottage Law rule covered near the top: baked goods in, cooked dishes out.
Close with Lebanese coffee, thick and strong and often scented with cardamom. Or mint tea, if you’d like to sleep tonight.
### Frequently asked questions about ordering Lebanese food
### Q. What to order at Lebanese restaurant?
A.  Start with hummus and tabbouleh, add kibbeh or falafel, then share one grill with garlic toum on the side. Use the 2-1-1: two cold, one hot, one grill, split. Order in rounds so fried plates stay hot. Order raw kibbeh only after finding the menu’s raw-food note or asking, and save room for knafeh.
### Q. What is the most famous Lebanese food?
A.  Outside Lebanon, hummus is probably the best known, with tabbouleh, falafel and shawarma close behind. Inside the country, many people point to kibbeh, a mix of bulgur and ground meat that’s fried, baked or eaten raw, as the national dish. Tabbouleh gets plenty of votes too, since it appears on nearly every Lebanese table.
### Q. What are some typical Lebanese mezze dishes?
A.  Cold: hummus, baba ghanoush, tabbouleh, fattoush, labneh and warak enab, the stuffed grape leaves. Hot: falafel, kibbeh, fatayer, sambousek, arayes and batata harra, the spicy garlic potatoes. Olives, pickled turnips, raw vegetables and warm pita fill the gaps between plates, and the whole spread is meant to be shared and eaten slowly.
### Q. What is a Lebanese platter?
A.  A Lebanese platter is a full meal on one plate: a protein such as shawarma, shish tawook, kafta or falafel, plus rice, a salad, hummus or garlic sauce, and pita. The rice is often cooked with toasted vermicelli. Contents change from kitchen to kitchen, so read the menu description or ask before you order.
### Q. What is traditional Arabic mezze?
A.  Mezze is a spread of small shared dishes served together at the start of a meal, or as the whole meal, across Lebanon and much of the Arab world. It mixes dips, salads, pickles, pastries and fried bites, all eaten slowly with bread. In Lebanon it’s often paired with arak, an anise spirit mixed with water.
### Q. What are some good Lebanese dishes for a dinner party?
A.  Choose dishes that hold up on a buffet. Hummus, baba ghanoush, tabbouleh and fattoush can be made ahead, with the fattoush bread added last so it stays crisp. Baked kibbeh, spinach fatayer and a tray of shish tawook or kafta skewers cover the hot side, and baklava or maamoul make an easy dessert.
### Q. What are the top 5 Lebanese dishes?
A.  Ask five Lebanese cooks and you’ll get five lists, but these come up again and again: kibbeh, tabbouleh, hummus, shish tawook and manakish. Plenty of people would add fattoush, shawarma or knafeh. For a first visit, order the first three as mezze and the tawook as your grill, and you cover a lot of ground.

## How to Support Local Businesses in St. Louis for Free
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-support-local-businesses-in-st-louis-for-free
It’s a Tuesday night in Hillsboro, and Dana is sitting on the edge of her bed scrolling back through a group text from three weeks ago, the one where her college roommate announced she’d finally opened the little upholstery shop she’d been talking about for a decade. Dana promised to help. Then rent came due, the car needed tires, and the budget for “helping” shrank to roughly nothing.
So she’s stuck. Wants to help. Can’t buy a sofa.
Here’s the good news, and it isn’t a consolation prize. A lot of what moves a small business forward costs nothing but a few minutes and some attention: a review with real detail, a share at the right moment, a name dropped in the right group chat, a quick check that the listing shows the right hours. Below is the practical list, the stuff you can do tonight from the couch, plus a short note on why it matters. Our earlier piece on why local matters in St. Louis covers the bigger picture. This one’s the to-do list.
### How to support a friend’s small business for free?
Write a specific review, share and save their posts, and recommend them by name whenever a friend asks for what they do. Add real photos, show up to their free events, subscribe to their newsletter, and make sure their directory listing has the right hours and phone number. None of it costs a dime. All of it compounds.
Money is the obvious kind of support. It’s not the only kind, and for a brand-new business it may not even be the most useful kind. A new shop’s biggest problem usually isn’t that the people who know about it won’t pay. It’s that too few people know about it at all. Attention, trust and word of mouth are what you’re really handing over.
### Write a review someone can actually use
“Great place! Five stars!” is nice. It’s also close to useless for the next person reading. A helpful review answers the questions a stranger would ask before calling: what did you buy or hire them for, how did it go, how long did it take, and would you go back? Specifics build trust because they sound like a real customer wrote them, and they give search tools more words to match against what people type.
Try a simple pattern. Say what you came in for. Name one detail you noticed, like the owner explaining your options before starting, or an order being ready a day early. Mention anything a future customer should know, such as parking, walk-ins, or how far they’ll travel for a job. Then say if you’d return. Four or five sentences. Plenty.
One caution. Only review what you’ve actually experienced. If you’ve never been a customer, don’t invent a visit because the owner is your friend, since most review platforms prohibit that and praise that sounds staged can hurt more than it helps. Haven’t bought anything yet? Skip the review for now and work through everything else on this list.
### Add photos people want to see
Photos do quiet work. A clear shot of the finished product, the storefront from the street, the menu board or the waiting area helps a stranger picture themselves walking in. Take them in daylight if you can. Skip heavy filters. And if a staff member or another customer is in the frame, ask them first.
### Answer questions when you know the answer
Some listings and review sites let the public post questions, things like “Do they take Saturday appointments?” or “Is there a ramp at the entrance?” When you know the answer from your own visit, reply. Owners can’t always get to every question quickly, and a customer’s answer often reads as more believable anyway. Not sure? Leave it for the owner.
### Why do saves, shares and comments count more than a like?
Because most social feeds decide who sees a post partly by how people interact with it, and a like is the weakest signal. Shares, saves and real comments generally tell a platform that a post is worth showing to more people, including folks who don’t follow the business yet. It’s free reach. Takes seconds.
### Share it, and tag it
When your friend posts a new product, a holiday schedule or a job opening, share it to your own feed or story and tag the business account so your followers can tap straight through. Add one line of your own. “My friend made our dining chairs look brand new” beats a silent reshare every time, because it tells people why they should care.
Tagging works in the other direction, too. When you post about something you bought, a meal, a haircut, a finished deck, tag the business and, if the platform allows it, the location. Those tags leave a trail of real customers that anyone sizing up the business can follow.
### Save it, then say something real
Saving a post takes one tap, and on several platforms it’s read as a sign the content is useful enough to come back to. Comments work best when they’re more than an emoji. Ask a question. “Do you do custom sizes?” gets the owner talking, and every reply adds to the conversation the platform sees under that post.
Don’t overdo it, though. Commenting on every single post within thirty seconds of it going up starts to look like a friend doing a favor, which, well, it is. Pick the posts you honestly like. A couple of times a week feels natural.
### How do you recommend a business without sounding like an ad?
Recommend it by name, in answer to a real question, and say why. That’s the whole trick. When somebody in a neighborhood group or family group chat asks “anyone know a good tailor?” a reply with the business name, what they did for you and how to reach them carries more weight than a paid post ever will.
Word of mouth has always powered small businesses. It’s just moved online, into community pages, neighborhood apps, church and school parent groups, and the endless family text thread. People in those spaces ask for recommendations constantly. Plumbers. Bakers. Somebody who’ll hem a prom dress by Friday.
### Use the exact name
Give the full business name, spelled the way they spell it. “That lady by the post office” doesn’t help anyone look them up later. Drop a link to their listing or website if the group allows links. Then add the one detail that fits the question: if someone asked about a rush job and your friend turned yours around fast, say exactly that.
### Be the friend who remembers
The best referrals happen offline, standing in a driveway in Marine or waiting in a school pickup line, when a neighbor mentions they need exactly what your friend does. Have the name ready. Better yet, keep the business saved as a contact in your phone so you can text it on the spot. Tiny habit. Pays off for years.
A quiet warning about groups: read the rules. Some community pages ban business promotion outside a set day, and owners who post ads in the wrong place can get removed. A genuine recommendation from a customer answering a question is usually welcome. A copy-pasted ad isn’t.
### What else can you do that costs nothing?
Plenty. Go to their free events, subscribe to their email newsletter, follow them on the platforms they actually use, and tell the owner directly what you liked. Each of those grows the owner’s audience or confidence, and none of them asks anything of your wallet beyond a little time on a Saturday.
### Show up when it’s free
Open houses, ribbon cuttings, free tastings, craft nights, pop-ups at a church fair: small businesses run these to get people through the door. A full room makes the next passerby more likely to stop in. It also gives the owner photos of a crowd, which look a lot better on social media than an empty shop. Bring someone. Two of you doubles the turnout.
### Join the newsletter
An email list belongs to the business. Social platforms can change what gets shown overnight, but a newsletter lands in an inbox the owner can reach without asking anyone’s permission. Signing up costs you nothing, and opening and clicking the occasional email tells them their list is alive. Forward the good ones to someone who’d care.
### Tell the owner what worked
Owners hear complaints fast. Praise travels slower. When something went right, tell them directly and be specific: the careful wrapping, the follow-up call, the way they explained the warranty without rushing you. That tells them what to keep doing, and on a rough week it might be the thing that keeps them going. Honest notes on what didn’t work help too, as long as you say them privately first.
### Help them get noticed by local media
Some owners have a story bigger than the product. A second career. A grandmother’s recipe. A reopening after a flood. If that sounds like your friend, nudge them toward our guide on how to pitch your story to St. Louis local media, and offer to proofread the email. One good feature can introduce a business to people no social post would ever reach.
All this typing earns you a paddle. Beginner kayaking around St. Louis
### How do reviews and listings shape what AI and search recommend?
When someone asks a search engine or an AI assistant “who does upholstery near me,” the answer is built from what’s published online: business listings, directory pages, reviews, photos and the words people use to describe the work. A business with accurate listings and detailed reviews gives those systems more to go on. Thin profiles get skipped.
This is where review detail pays off twice. Say you wrote that your friend reupholstered two wingback chairs and matched the fabric on a cushion from the 1970s. You’ve just put “wingback,” “reupholster” and “fabric matching” right next to their name, so someone asking for exactly that job has a better shot at finding them. Nobody can promise a business will come up first. Detail just improves the odds.
### Check the listing like a customer would
Pull up your friend’s listings on the map apps, review sites and local directories, then read them as a stranger would. Is the phone number right? Do the hours match the sign on the door? Is the address current, or does it still show the old home-based setup? Does the category actually describe what they do?
Wrong details cost real customers. A family drives out on a Sunday and finds the lights off. Somebody dials a dead number and gives up. If you spot a problem, tell the owner first, since they can fix it directly. Many platforms also let the public suggest an edit, which helps when the owner is buried in work.
### Make sure they’re listed where locals look
Some owners never get around to claiming their listings. If your friend isn’t on the local directories people in their area actually check, point it out and offer to help set things up on a slow evening. A laptop, a few good photos and a short description, and most of the job is done. The goal is the same name, address and phone number everywhere, so neither people nor search tools get confused.
### Why does shopping local matter in the first place?
Local owners hire people who live here, buy from nearby suppliers, pay local taxes and tend to sponsor the teams and fundraisers down the street. That’s why the free help above matters. Every customer a small business wins through your review or referral feeds that loop, even in a month when you personally didn’t spend a dollar.
### Where does the money go?
Follow a dollar spent at a locally owned shop. Part goes to wages for employees who live nearby and spend their paychecks here. Part goes to local suppliers: the printer, the bookkeeper, the farmer. The owner lives here too, so profits don’t get shipped off to a distant headquarters. Sales and property taxes help pay for roads and schools. Studies comparing independent businesses with chains have found that more of each dollar recirculates locally, though the exact share varies by study and by business.
### What about local food?
Food grown or made close to home usually spends less time in transit, so produce can be picked closer to ripe. Buying it keeps nearby farms working. And when a market stand in Venice or a bakery down your street knows its regulars, you can ask how something was grown or made and get a real answer from a real person. Try that in a big-box aisle.
None of this means swearing off chains. Budgets are real, and nobody should feel guilty about a cheaper option in a tight month. That’s exactly why the free stuff counts.
Looking for more local businesses to cheer on? Browse the local business spotlight on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick one that deserves a detailed review, and pass it along to someone who needs what they do.
If you’re the shop, being the one people and AI name first is the game when a neighbor asks who to call, and a complete listing with real customer reviews is how you get spotlighted, so list your business.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How can people support local businesses?
A.  Buy from them when you can, and when you can’t, give them attention. Write detailed reviews, share and save their posts, recommend them by name in group chats and neighborhood groups, attend their free events, join their newsletter, and check that their listings show the right hours and phone number.
### Q. What are the best ways to promote local businesses?
A.  The strongest free promotion is a specific, named recommendation from a real customer. After that come detailed reviews with photos, shares with a personal note, tags on your own posts, and accurate listings on the directories and map apps locals use. Helping an owner pitch a local reporter can reach even further.
### Q. What are the advantages of shopping locally?
A.  You usually get more personal service, owners who can answer questions directly, and products or skills you won’t find at a chain. Your spending also supports local jobs, local suppliers and local tax revenue, and it helps keep storefronts in your area open and occupied.
### Q. Why is it better to buy local products?
A.  Local products often travel shorter distances, can be fresher, and come from makers you can actually talk to. Buying them keeps local craftspeople, farmers and small producers working, and it gives your area a character chains can’t copy. It isn’t always cheaper, so buy local where it counts most to you.
### Q. Why should people be encouraged to buy locally produced food?
A.  Locally produced food generally spends less time in transit, so it can be harvested closer to ripeness. Buying it keeps nearby farms in business and farmland in use. You can also ask the grower how it was raised or produced, which is hard to do with food shipped across the country.
### Q. How much money stays local when you shop local?
A.  There’s no single number, and it varies by business. The mechanism is what matters: local owners live here, pay local employees, buy from nearby suppliers and pay local taxes. Studies comparing independent businesses with chains have found that more of each dollar recirculates in the community when the owner is local.
### Q. What should a good review of a small business say?
A.  Say what you bought or hired them for, one specific detail about how it went, anything practical a newcomer should know like parking or turnaround time, and if you’d go back. Four or five honest sentences with real details help the next customer and give search tools more to match.
### Q. Does sharing a small business post on social media really help?
A.  It can. Most social feeds weigh shares, saves and genuine comments more heavily than a quick like when deciding who else sees a post. Sharing with a personal line about why you recommend the business also puts it in front of your own followers, who trust you more than they trust an ad.

## A Missing Rent Receipt Can Shrink Your SNAP. Here’s the St. Louis Fix
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-do-if-your-snap-food-benefits-get-cut-in-st-louis
The new number on the SNAP renewal letter is smaller, and nothing on the page says why. It came to a south city two-family on a Thursday. You read it under the kitchen light while the fridge hums behind you, then read it again. At the table, a kid is asking what’s for supper, and inside that fridge there are eggs, half a loaf of bread and a jar of peanut butter.
That smaller number may be a missing lease, not a cut. Since October 1, Missouri leaves out your rent, utility and child care costs if you can’t prove them on paper, and those costs help set the size of your benefit. Send the proof and the deduction may come back, no appeal needed. No written lease? A rent receipt with your landlord’s contact information, the amount and the date counts. Upload it at mydssupload.mo.gov, fax it to 573-526-9400, or carry it to a Family Support Division resource center: 3101 Chouteau Ave. in the city, 9900 Page Ave. in the county.
### What to do if your SNAP benefits stop in St. Louis?
Get food moving today, then fix the benefit. Dial 211 any hour, or text your ZIP code to 785-503-3310 to find the nearest pantry. Call Operation Food Search at 314-726-5355. If your SNAP was reduced, you have 90 days to appeal, 10 days to keep benefits during it.
A pantry visit is quieter than most people expect: a sign-in sheet, a short wait, and a volunteer handing over a box or letting you pick from the shelves. Nobody asks you to fix your SNAP case first. Some sites want a photo ID or proof of address, so bring both if you have them and call before you drive.
Then make the SNAP you still have go further at Tower Grove Farmers’ Market. Swipe your EBT card at the market’s information booth, and Double Up Food Bucks matches what you spend, up to $25 a market day, in free tokens for fruits and vegetables. The market says it takes EBT year-round.
Mistakes do happen, and Missouri gives you a real window to challenge one. So get food this week, then read the proof and appeal steps below. Free pop-up giveaways move fast, too, so it helps to watch our running list of free food giveaways happening in St. Louis.

### How do you push back on a SNAP cut or denial?
You have more power here than the notice makes it feel. In Missouri you can request a fair hearing within 90 days of the date on your Action Notice, and if you ask within 10 days, your benefits keep flowing while the case is decided. That 10-day window is the one people miss most, so circle it on the calendar right now.
Here’s how to file. Contact the Family Support Division (FSD), say you want a fair hearing on your SNAP case, and put it in writing whenever you can. Any one of the channels below starts the clock.
Missouri Family Support Division: fair hearing Email: IMHearing.FSD@dss.mo.gov Fax: 573-526-4554 Mail: FSD, PO Box 2700, Jefferson City, MO 65102 Phone: 855-373-4636 (855-FSD-INFO); TTY 1-800-735-2966 Deadlines: within 90 days to appeal; within 10 days to keep benefits during the appeal.
You don’t have to do this alone. Free legal aid attorneys in the St. Louis area handle benefit appeals and can represent you at the hearing at no cost; ask FSD for a referral, or dial 211. And if the denial means starting fresh, our step-by-step guide to applying for SNAP in Missouri walks through the whole application.
### What proof do you need for SNAP in Missouri now?
Under Missouri’s new food stamp rules, which started October 1, you need paper proof of your rent or mortgage, utility bills, child or dependent care costs and bank balances when you apply for SNAP, renew it, or add someone to your case. Your word used to be enough. Not anymore. Already on SNAP? Unless you’re adding someone, hold off until your next renewal.
If your amount dropped at a renewal, check this first. A cost you can’t prove doesn’t sink the case. FSD still processes it, just without that deduction, which can shrink your benefit. Send the proof later and the deduction may be added back. You get 10 days to answer any FSD request.
Most of it is already in a kitchen drawer: the lease, the Ameren or Spire bill, the daycare receipt folded into a coat pocket. A clear phone photo works fine.
What to gather Renting: a landlord-signed lease, or a rent receipt with the landlord’s contact info, amount and date Homeowners: latest mortgage or property tax statement Utilities: recent electric, gas, water, sewer, trash or heating fuel bills Care you pay for to work, job hunt or train: the provider’s itemized receipt, a sitter’s signed note of hours and pay, or canceled checks and e-payment receipts Bank accounts: most recent statements No lease, or an informal sitter: a signed note from the person you pay, with their name, phone, address, amount and how often
