### How do you report a change without a penalty later?
Reporting on time protects your future benefits. Missouri asks you to report certain changes by the 10th of the month after they happen: a jump in income, a gambling or lottery win over $4,750 in a single game (a cutoff adjusted each year), or a working-age adult’s hours dropping below 20 a week. Report late, and you may have to repay benefits you weren’t eligible for.
The easiest route is online at mydss.mo.gov under “Report a Change.” You can also call 855-373-4636 or visit an FSD office in person. In the City, the resource center below takes walk-ins during posted hours.

### Food help for seniors, kids, and new parents
Some of the best help is aimed at a specific household, and it stacks on top of everything above. Adults 60 and older can get meals delivered or served nearby. Kids can eat free in summer with no sign-up. Pregnant parents and young children have WIC. If any of these fit your home, use them alongside the pantries, not instead of them.

WIC supports pregnant and postpartum women, infants, and children under five in households at or below 185% of the federal poverty level. It covers specific healthy foods, infant formula, and nutrition support, and it stacks with SNAP and pantries.

### What if your benefits run out before the month does?
Stack your sources, and do it without guilt. Most pantries allow one visit per month each, which means you can visit several different pantries in the same month and legitimately rebuild a week or two of groceries. Layer in free kids’ meals, senior meals, and WIC where you qualify, and a short month starts to fill back in.
Here’s the part people rarely get told out loud: the system is built to be combined. One pantry is a single box of groceries. Four different pantries, plus a WIC appointment and a summer meal site, is close to a month of food. Use the Operation Food Search text line (785-503-3310), 211, or the Foodbank locator to line them up by day and by neighborhood.
For a hot meal with no application and no ID at all, a soup kitchen is often the fastest comfort; see our guide to soup kitchens in St. Louis. And to stretch the benefits you do have, it helps to know which stores treat SNAP and WIC shoppers fairly, which we cover in our look at St. Louis corner stores, SNAP, WIC, and prices.
One last thing, and we mean it. Needing food help is not a character flaw. It’s exactly what these programs exist for, funded by taxes you have paid or will pay. The neighbors who run these pantries want you to walk in. Being found, and finding help, is how a hard month stays just a month. You’ve got this, and the whole St. Louis help and assistance network is behind you.
SNAP can’t buy pet food, but St. Louis has places that give it away. Our guide to pet food pantries in St. Louis covers where to go and what to bring.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Why would my food stamps get cut off?
A.  Sometimes it’s a simple agency error. Other times income rose, a working-age adult’s hours fell below 20 a week, or a lottery or gambling win topped the yearly cutoff, now $4,750 in a single game. Reporting late can also cut you off, and at renewal any rent, utility or child care cost you can’t prove gets left out. You have 90 days to appeal.
### Q. What are the new food stamp rules for Missouri?
A.  The big one started October 1. Missouri now wants proof of rent or mortgage, utilities, child or dependent care costs and bank balances when you apply, renew, or add someone to your case. Unproven costs are left out, which can lower your benefit, but you can send proof later. Already on SNAP? Nothing is due until renewal, unless you add someone.
### Q. Where can I get food today in St. Louis?
A.  Text your ZIP code to 785-503-3310, or call Operation Food Search at 314-726-5355, press 1, to find the closest pantry. You can also dial 211 any hour of the day. The St. Louis Area Foodbank locator at stlfoodbank.org/find-food and the free Plentiful app show hours and let you reserve a slot.
### Q. How to appeal denied SNAP benefits?
A.  Request a fair hearing with the Missouri Family Support Division within 90 days of your Action Notice date. Ask within 10 days if you want benefits to continue during the appeal. Reach them by email at IMHearing.FSD@dss.mo.gov, fax 573-526-4554, mail FSD, PO Box 2700, Jefferson City, MO 65102, or phone 855-373-4636.
### Q. How do I report changes to my food stamps in Missouri?
A.  Report it online at mydss.mo.gov under “Report a Change,” by phone at 855-373-4636, or at a local Family Support Division office. Do it by the 10th of the month after the change, for things like income shifts or work hours dropping. Reporting on time protects you from repaying benefits later.

## Warming Centers in St. Louis: Where to Stay Warm This Winter
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/warming-centers-in-st-louis-where-to-stay-warm-this-winter
It’s a little after seven on a Wednesday in January, and the wind coming off the river has that flat, mean edge that gets under a coat and stays there. Marcus has been walking since the downtown library closed, doing the math everyone in his shoes does. How many hours until somewhere warm opens again? How far can his feet carry him before then? He isn’t asking for much. He’s looking for a door that’s unlocked and a room that’s above freezing.
If that’s you tonight, or someone you love, here’s the short version before anything else. Pick up a phone and dial 211. Then keep reading, because the City of St. Louis, St. Louis County, and St. Charles each handle winter a little differently, and knowing which door to knock on saves time you may not have. This guide is part of our larger St. Louis help and assistance resources hub.
### Where can I go to stay warm in St. Louis tonight?
Call 211 first; they route you to the nearest open site. In the City, Biddle (1212 N. 13th St) and four Peter & Paul locations run 24 hours in severe cold. In St. Louis County, Salvation Army Family Haven (10740 Page Ave) stays open overnight. In St. Charles, call 636-395-0492. Those three phone numbers are the fastest way to a warm room anywhere in the metro.
Keep these numbers where you can reach them. Screenshot them. Write them on your arm if you have to. They work whether it’s noon or two in the morning.
Need a bed for the night, not just a warm room? Start with emergency homeless shelters in St. Louis. Call these first United Way 211: dial 211 or 1-800-427-4626, anywhere in the region. City Housing & Shelter Helpline: 314-802-5444. St. Charles tri-county EWR hotline: 636-395-0492.
If you run a warming site, shelter or ministry that opens its doors on cold nights, this part is for you and the neighbors you serve - you can list it with us.
Nobody freezes because the help isn’t out there. People freeze because they couldn’t find it in time. A phone number you already have is the warmest thing in your pocket tonight.
### When do St. Louis warming centers open, and at what temperature?
It depends where you are. The City runs a four-level “Code Blue” system from December 1 to March 1. Some centers open when the temperature drops below 32°F or wind chill falls under 25°F. More open at 25°F or colder. At 10°F or below, every site opens and transport kicks in. The temperature thresholds are official, though how many beds open can shift night to night.
### How the City’s Code Blue levels work
Level 2 (below 32°F, or wind chill under 25°F): a set of daytime centers open. Level 3 (25°F or colder, or wind chill under 10°F): more centers open and transport becomes available. Level 4 (10°F or colder, or wind chill under minus 10°F): all centers open, plus rally points where you can catch a ride. On the coldest nights, that ride matters as much as the room.
### County and St. Charles thresholds
St. Louis County partners generally activate around 20°F, working through nonprofits rather than one City-style command. St. Charles County’s Emergency Weather Response opens its rotating church sites when the forecast low hits 20°F or lower, roughly mid-November through mid-March. Not sure whether anything is open where you are? Call 211 and ask. That’s exactly what the line is for.
The cheapest warm place is usually the one you already have. If you’re behind on a bill and scared of a shutoff, read our guides to the Missouri Cold Weather Rule, utility assistance programs in St. Louis, and LIHEAP energy assistance. Keeping your own heat on is the first warming center.
### What’s the difference between a warming center and an overnight shelter?
A warming center is a daytime refuge, a warm room with no beds, usually open during business hours. An overnight shelter has beds and typically takes people in around 6 p.m. Libraries and community centers are daytime only. During severe cold, the City runs some sites 24 hours, so the line between the two blurs. When in doubt, 211 sorts out which one you need.
Why does the distinction matter so much? Because a library that saves your afternoon closes at night, and you need a plan for the hours after. If you need a bed tonight, our guide to emergency homeless shelters in St. Louis walks through where to go and how intake works.
### Warming centers in the City of St. Louis
The City has the region’s most developed cold-weather network, with daytime centers, 24-hour severe-cold sites, and library branches all in the mix. Even so, during the recent cold season City shelters ran near 90% capacity, and mobile warming buses were only recently brought back into service (St. Louis Public Radio, January 2026). ### Where can you stay warm in St. Louis County?
Coverage in the County is thinner and leans heavily on nonprofits. The main overnight option is Salvation Army Family Haven (10740 Page Ave), open 24 hours through roughly early November to early March. During the day, a handful of Salvation Army corps and county library branches fill the gap. There’s no County version of the City’s four-level Code Blue, so calling ahead matters even more out here.

### What if you’re in St. Charles County or an outer suburb?
St. Charles and the tri-county area have the thinnest coverage in the metro, run mostly by church volunteers. Your first call is the Emergency Weather Response (EWR) hotline at 636-395-0492. Host churches rotate nightly, so there’s no fixed address to give out; the hotline tells you where the open site is. EWR activates at 20°F or below, roughly mid-November to mid-March, and may arrange a ride.
Emergency Weather Response (EWR) hotline Call 636-395-0492 Overnight church warming sites that rotate nightly across St. Charles, Lincoln, and Warren counties. Activates when the forecast low hits 20°F or below. Transport may be available. Because host sites change each night, there’s no fixed address; the hotline routes you.
St. Peters Rec-Plex (extreme-cold daytime) 5200 Mexico Rd, St. Peters, MO 63376 (636) 939-2386 May open as a daytime warm space in extreme cold. Call ahead or check stpetersmo.net to confirm before you travel.

Salvation Army O’Fallon 1 William Booth Dr, O’Fallon, MO 63366 (636) 240-4969 Mon-Fri, 9 a.m. to 3 p.m.
Across the river, the Illinois side runs its own system. In Alton, the Salvation Army (525 Alby St, Alton, IL 62002; 618-465-7764; Mon-Fri, 9 a.m. to 4 p.m.) is a daytime starting point, and 211 covers the Metro-East too.
### Does the St. Louis metro have enough warming centers?
Honestly, not yet, and the people running these programs will tell you so. The City is the most built out, with its four-level Code Blue system, 24-hour sites at Biddle and the Peter & Paul locations, rally-point transport, and mobile warming buses. Even then, shelters ran near 90% capacity and those buses were only recently revived (St. Louis Public Radio, January 2026).
Coverage thins as you move out. St. Louis County leans on nonprofits, with Salvation Army Family Haven carrying most of the overnight load. St. Charles and the tri-county area are thinnest of all, held together by church volunteers and fragile funding. One recent report put the EWR program’s need near $77,000 against a pending $30,000 county request (First Alert 4, December 2025). None of this is a knock on the people doing the work. It’s a map of where the gaps are, so you know to call ahead instead of assuming a door is open.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Who is eligible to use warming centers in St. Louis?
A.  Warming centers are open to anyone who needs to get out of the cold. Most daytime sites are drop-in, so you can walk in during open hours without a reservation or membership. If you’re unsure whether a site is open near you, call 211 and they’ll route you to the nearest one.
### Q. What is the difference between a warming center and a homeless shelter?
A.  A warming center is a daytime refuge, a warm room with no beds, usually open during business hours. A homeless shelter has beds and typically takes people in around 6 p.m. During severe cold, the City runs some sites 24 hours, so the two blur together. Call 211 to find the right one tonight.
### Q. What do warming centers do?
A.  Warming centers give people a safe, heated place to escape dangerous cold. Daytime sites offer a warm room and a place to sit out the worst hours, open during business hours. During severe cold, some City sites stay open 24 hours. They exist so no one has to wait outside for the next door to unlock.
### Q. At what temperature do warming centers open?
A.  It depends where you are. The City opens some centers below 32°F, more at 25°F or colder, and every site at 10°F or below. St. Louis County partners activate around 20°F. St. Charles County’s EWR opens its church sites when the forecast low hits 20°F, roughly mid-November through mid-March.
### Q. Are libraries warming centers?
A.  Yes. St. Louis Public Library branches are official daytime warming sites, including Central at 1301 Olive St and Schlafly at 225 N. Euclid. St. Louis County libraries serve the same purpose informally. Remember, libraries are daytime only, so line up an overnight option before closing. Hours shift with weather, so call 211 to confirm.
### Q. Who do I call for help staying warm?
A.  Three numbers cover the metro. Dial 211 (or 1-800-427-4626) anywhere in the region for routing to the nearest open site. In the City, call the Housing and Shelter Helpline at 314-802-5444. In St. Charles, Lincoln, and Warren counties, call the EWR hotline at 636-395-0492.
### Q. Is there transportation to a warming center?
A.  Yes, in the City during an activation. Designated rally points run from 5 to 7 p.m., Metro Call-A-Ride offers rides, and mobile warming buses circulate on the coldest nights. In St. Charles County, EWR volunteers may arrange transport to that night’s host church. Ask when you call 211 or 636-395-0492.
### Q. Is New Life Evangelistic Center still open?
A.  No. New Life Evangelistic Center, the shelter many remember on Locust Street, closed in 2017 and no longer operates. Please don’t travel there expecting a bed or a warm room. Use 211, the City Helpline at 314-802-5444, or the sites listed above to find a space that is actually open tonight.
### One last thing before the cold hits
Winter comes back every year, and so does this list. Save the three numbers now, while it’s warm and you’re thinking clearly: 211 for anywhere in the region, 314-802-5444 in the City, and 636-395-0492 in St. Charles. Pass them to a neighbor, a coworker, the person you see at the bus stop. A warm room only helps if someone can find it.
And if you’re the one who’s cold tonight, there’s no shame in any of this. Make the call. You deserve a warm place to sit.

## Emergency Cash and TANF Help in Missouri: A St. Louis Guide
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/emergency-cash-and-tanf-help-in-missouri-a-st-louis-guide
It’s the 28th of the month in Baden, and Nia is doing the math one more time at her kitchen table. Rent is due Friday. The electric bill came with a red stripe across the top. Her hours got cut, the car needed a battery, and the numbers just won’t reach. She keeps hearing the word “TANF” and hoping it’s the fix. She’s about to learn it helps some families a little, some people not at all, and that the real lifeline is a phone number she hasn’t dialed yet.
If that’s close to where you are tonight, take a breath. Being short on cash doesn’t make you a failure, and you don’t have to figure this out alone.
This guide lays out what Missouri’s cash-assistance program actually does, who it’s for, and where St. Louis families and single adults can find one-time help with rent, utilities, and emergencies when the state program isn’t the answer. Real names, real phone numbers, no runaround. For the wider map of local aid, keep our St. Louis help and assistance resources hub open in another tab.
### How can I get immediate financial help in St. Louis?
Start by dialing 211 (or 1-800-427-4626), the free 24/7 United Way line that matches you to rent, utility, and cash help. For families with kids, apply for Missouri Temporary Assistance at myDSS.mo.gov. Then contact the Urban League, CAASTLC, the Salvation Army, or St. Vincent de Paul for one-time aid.
There isn’t one office that hands out emergency money in St. Louis. Help comes from a patchwork: one state program for families, plus a web of nonprofits that each cover certain ZIP codes, certain bills, and certain months until their funds run dry. That sounds discouraging. It isn’t, once you know the order to work the list, and the first move is almost always the same.
Call 211 first. It’s free, confidential, and open 24/7. A real person screens your situation and points you to the closest open funds for rent, utilities, food, or prescriptions, so you’re not burning days calling agencies that are already tapped out. Dial 211 or 1-800-427-4626, or search stl.211helps.org. Prefer to browse yourself? Our guide to findhelp.org shows another free way to find nearby programs.
If you run a food pantry, clinic, ministry or aid agency in St. Louis, the neighbors who need you should be able to reach you - list it with us.
### How do I apply for cash assistance (TANF) in Missouri?
Missouri’s cash program is called Temporary Assistance, and a family of three can receive up to $292 a month, a figure the state has left unchanged since 1991 (Missouri Department of Social Services, Family Support Division). You apply three ways: online at myDSS.mo.gov, by phone at 1-855-373-4636, or in person at any Family Support Division Resource Center.
Here’s the part the name hides. “Temporary Assistance” sounds like an emergency fund. In practice it’s a small, slow, ongoing benefit aimed at very-low-income families with children, not a quick cash injection for this week’s crisis. Knowing that up front saves you from pinning Friday’s rent on a check that may take a month and, even then, won’t cover it.
### How much is Missouri Temporary Assistance, really?
Up to $292 a month for a family of three, which sits at roughly 13% of the federal poverty line (Missouri DSS). That maximum hasn’t moved since 1991. There’s a 45-month lifetime limit, with hardship exceptions for situations like domestic violence, treatment, or a family crisis. Most adults must take part in Missouri Work Assistance and sign a Personal Responsibility Plan.
Miss those work requirements without good cause and the grant can be cut by half. None of this is meant to scare you off, plenty of families rely on it, but go in knowing the check is modest and comes with strings. Treat it as one piece of your plan, not the whole plan.
### Who qualifies for Temporary Assistance?
Temporary Assistance is for low-income families with at least one child in the home, or a pregnant woman (Missouri DSS). You’ll need to meet income and asset limits, be a Missouri resident, and follow the work rules. Childless, non-disabled adults are not eligible, which is the gap we’ll cover next.
### How long does approval take?
Plan on roughly 30 to 45 days after you turn in a complete application, though current timelines shift, so confirm with the Family Support Division. Because it takes weeks, not hours, apply as early as you can and line up the nonprofit help below for bills due right now. You can submit documents to FSD.Documents@dss.mo.gov or by fax to 573-526-9400.
### Is there cash help for adults without children?
Not as an ongoing state check. Missouri has no general-assistance cash program for childless, non-disabled adults (Missouri DSS), so the path runs through other doors: SSI or disability if a health condition keeps you from working, SNAP for food, LIHEAP for energy bills, and the local charities below for one-time rent and utility help. It’s a patchwork, but it’s real.
We hear one myth over and over: that a “township trustee” in the City or County will write you a poor-relief check. In St. Louis City and St. Louis County, that office doesn’t exist. Township-trustee relief is an outstate-Missouri thing, so don’t lose a day chasing it. Put that energy into 211 and the nonprofits instead.
Kids notice when money gets tight. How to talk with them about money.
### Who gives one-time rent and utility help in St. Louis?
A handful of trusted nonprofits do, each with its own turf and its own bills it will cover. In St. Louis City, energy and LIHEAP help runs through the Urban League; in St. Louis County, through the Community Action Agency (CAASTLC). Add the Salvation Army, St. Vincent de Paul, Guardian Angel, Catholic Charities, and St. Patrick Center, and call 211 to be matched fast.
One heads-up before you dial: if an older list tells you to call the Human Development Corporation for energy help, that changed. City residents now go through the Urban League, County residents through CAASTLC. Every one of these funds is finite and can run dry mid-month, so lead with 211 to find what’s open today. Need rent help specifically? Our guide to emergency rent assistance in St. Louis goes deeper.
### Urban League of Metropolitan St. Louis
City of St. Louis energy and LIHEAP help, plus rent and shutoff prevention. Income-based; bring ID, proof of income, and your bill or notice. Address: 1408 N. Kingshighway Blvd, St. Louis, MO 63113 Phone: 314-615-3600 (utility and LIHEAP: 314-615-3632) Web: ulstl.com

### St. Patrick Center

Funds run dry, but they refill. A “no” this week isn’t a “no” next month, so keep working the list.
### What to have ready before you apply
Gathering your paperwork first is the single biggest time-saver, because most of these programs stall on missing documents. Have a photo ID, Social Security numbers for your household, proof of income (or proof you have none), a recent copy of the bill you need help with, and any shutoff or eviction notice you’ve received.
Keep it all in one folder or envelope, so you can answer questions in a single call instead of three. If you’re applying for Temporary Assistance, the Family Support Division also accepts documents by email at FSD.Documents@dss.mo.gov or by fax at 573-526-9400. A little organizing now turns a two-week back-and-forth into a couple of days.
### What about help with funeral or burial costs?
This help is limited, and it’s honest to say so. Missouri has no statewide burial-assistance program (Missouri DSS). The City of St. Louis runs an Indigent Burial Fund for residents who die with no surviving family or means to pay, and the Salvation Army or St. Vincent de Paul may help case by case. Start, again, by calling 211.
If you’re facing this, ask the funeral home directly what public options exist, since they deal with these programs often, and let 211 point you to any church or benevolence fund with money available. It won’t cover everything, but it can ease part of a heavy moment.
### The quiet truth about getting help: you have to be found
In our experience keeping these St. Louis lists current, the most common reason people miss out isn’t that they don’t qualify. It’s that they never reached the one office that still had funds that week. Being seen, by 211, by a caseworker, by the right nonprofit, is half the battle. So make the calls, leave the messages, and follow up until someone says yes.
You’re allowed to ask for help, and asking well, early, organized, and at the right door, is a skill, not a weakness. Nia made two calls the next morning: 211, then the Urban League. It didn’t erase the month. It kept the lights on. Start with one call today, and keep our help and assistance hub handy for whatever comes next.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the $500 direct cash assistance program in Missouri?
A.  Missouri has no single $500 direct cash assistance program you can apply for. Emergency money here comes from a patchwork: Temporary Assistance pays up to $292 a month for a family of three, LIHEAP covers energy bills, and local nonprofits give one-time rent or utility aid. Call 211 to find what’s open.
### Q. What is considered temporary assistance?
A.  In Missouri, Temporary Assistance is the state’s TANF cash-aid program. It’s a small, ongoing monthly benefit (up to $292 for a family of three) for very-low-income families with children or a pregnant woman, not a quick emergency fund. Most adults must meet work requirements to keep it.
### Q. How much can you get in TANF in Missouri?
A.  A family of three can receive up to $292 a month, a maximum Missouri hasn’t raised since 1991 (Missouri DSS). That’s about 13% of the federal poverty line. There’s a 45-month lifetime limit, with hardship exceptions, and most adults must meet work requirements to keep the full grant.
### Q. Who qualifies for cash assistance in Missouri?
A.  Low-income families with at least one child in the home, or a pregnant woman, who meet Missouri’s income and asset limits, residency, and work rules (Missouri DSS). Childless, non-disabled adults aren’t eligible for this program. If that’s you, look instead at SSI or disability, SNAP, LIHEAP, and the charities in this guide.
### Q. Can I get TANF if I can’t work?
A.  Possibly. Most adults must join Missouri Work Assistance, but there are good-cause and hardship exceptions, for situations like domestic violence, treatment, or a family crisis. If a health condition keeps you from working long-term, SSI or disability is usually the better path than Temporary Assistance. Ask the Family Support Division.
### Q. How many years can you get TANF?
A.  Missouri sets a 45-month lifetime limit on Temporary Assistance, roughly three and three-quarter years, with hardship exceptions for situations like domestic violence, treatment, or a family crisis (Missouri DSS). It’s built as short-term help, not a permanent income, so plan to pair it with work supports and the nonprofits in this guide.
### Q. How often do you get paid with TANF?
A.  Temporary Assistance is paid monthly, not as a lump sum, up to $292 a month for a family of three (Missouri DSS). It’s an ongoing benefit, not a one-time emergency check, which is why this guide pairs it with 211 and local nonprofits for bills that are due right now.
### Q. Do I have to pay TANF back?
A.  No. Temporary Assistance is a public benefit, a grant, not a loan, so you don’t repay the monthly help you receive while you qualify. That’s the big difference between assistance programs in this guide and borrowing. The main exception is if the Family Support Division later finds it overpaid you and asks for the difference back.

## Water and Sewer Bill Assistance in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/water-and-sewer-bill-assistance-in-st-louis
Two envelopes sit on Marcus’s kitchen table in Dutchtown, and they don’t agree with each other. One is from the City of St. Louis Water Division. The other, the one stamped “past due,” comes from something called MSD Project Clear. At work, a guy from Ballwin swears his water bill says “Missouri American Water,” a name Marcus has never once seen. So which is it? Who does he actually owe? And who, if anyone, can help him catch up before a shutoff notice turns real?
If that tangle feels familiar, you’re not the confused one. St. Louis really does split water and sewer across different companies, and the help you qualify for depends entirely on which name is printed at the top of your bill. Let’s sort out who bills you, who can help you pay, and one winter myth that could quietly cost you. For the bigger map of local aid, keep our St. Louis help and assistance resources hub close by.
### Why does St. Louis split water and sewer into separate bills?
Because three different utilities divide up the job. Inside the City of St. Louis, your drinking water comes from the City’s own Water Division. Across most of St. Louis County and its municipalities, that same tap water is billed by Missouri American Water instead. Missouri American does not serve the City, so City residents never see that name. Sewer service, the wastewater side, is handled region-wide by the Metropolitan Sewer District, branded as MSD Project Clear.
Here’s why that matters for your budget. Each utility runs its own assistance program, with its own rules, and they don’t share applications. A City household usually has two bills: water from the Water Division and sewer from MSD. A County household also has two: water from Missouri American and sewer from MSD. Catching up means applying to each program on its own. Skip one, and you leave help sitting on the table.
### How can I get help with my water bill in St. Louis?
It depends on who bills you. City of St. Louis residents use the Water Division’s TAP program, worth up to $500 on a past-due water bill. St. Louis County residents apply for Missouri American Water’s H2O Help to Others through CAASTLC. Everyone with a sewer bill can ask MSD about its Customer Assistance Program. Start by calling 211.
That last tip matters more than it sounds. Funds move. One month a particular agency has money for water arrears, the next month it’s gone until the fund refills. Dialing 211, or 1-800-427-4626, connects you, free and around the clock, to whichever agency currently has water or sewer dollars. Then work down your bills one at a time.
United Way 211 — start here Call 211 or 1-800-427-4626 Free, confidential, and available 24/7 Routes you to whichever agency currently has water or sewer funds
### What is H2O Help to Others, and how do County residents apply?
H2O Help to Others is an emergency grant funded by Missouri American Water and customer donations. It exists for Missouri American customers who have fallen behind and face a shutoff, and it can cover both water and wastewater arrears. There’s no published dollar cap; a caseworker weighs your basic needs. Local Community Action Agencies process the applications, which in St. Louis County means CAASTLC.
Two more Missouri American tools are worth knowing. An Installment Plan lets you put 25% down and spread the rest over up to six months. Budget Billing is free and levels your payments into a steady monthly amount, reviewed every three months so you’re never wildly off. Both start with one phone call to customer service.
H2O Help to Others — Missouri American Water (County) Apply through the Community Action Agency of St. Louis County (CAASTLC) 2709 Woodson Rd, Overland, MO 63114 General: (314) 863-0015 Utility & energy line: (314) 446-4420 Hours: Mon–Fri, 8:00 a.m.–3:00 p.m. Missouri American customer service: 1-866-430-0820 (Mon–Fri, 7 a.m.–7 p.m.) Online: amwater.com/moaw, then Payment Assistance
### How do you lower an MSD sewer bill?
Apply for MSD’s Customer Assistance Program, which cuts your sewer rate by 50% for two full years. It’s built for low-income households, seniors 62 and older, and people with disabilities. Because sewer charges hit every City and County household, this is the one program almost everyone reading should check first. The savings compound quietly, month after month.
Qualifying turns on income. The standard ceiling is 200% of the federal poverty level. For 2026 that’s roughly $31,920 for one person, $43,280 for two, $54,640 for three, $66,000 for four, $77,360 for five, and $88,720 for six, plus $11,360 for each additional person. Seniors 62-plus and people with disabilities get a higher ceiling, 250% of poverty, and seniors skip the asset test that otherwise caps liquid assets and real estate at $10,000.
One relief worth repeating: MSD handles sewer only, and it cannot shut off your water. When bills go unpaid, MSD collects through liens and tax certification, not a wrench at the curb. That doesn’t make the debt vanish, but it does mean an overdue sewer bill won’t leave you without running water tomorrow.
MSD Project Clear — Customer Assistance Program (sewer, region-wide) Serves the entire MSD area, City and County CAP & billing: (866) 281-5737 General: (314) 768-6260 Online: msdprojectclear.org, then Customers, Billing, Customer Assistance Program Remember: MSD bills sewer only and cannot disconnect your water
### Behind on your City water bill? What the TAP program can do
City of St. Louis residents have their own lifeline: the Water Division’s Temporary Assistance Program, or TAP. It puts a one-time credit of up to $500 on a past-due City water account and pairs it with a manageable repayment plan through the Collector of Revenue, spread across 12 or 24 months. While you’re active in the program, you’re protected from shutoff.
To qualify, you need to be a City resident with a balance that’s at least 90 days past due, a household income at or below 80% of the area median, and a short hardship self-attestation. Apply online, or grab a paper application at the Water Division office or any of 13 St. Louis Public Library branches.
One honest caveat. TAP is funded through federal relief dollars and runs first-come, first-served until the money is gone. So don’t assume, call. A quick ring to (314) 771-2255 confirms whether funds are still open before you get your hopes, or your paperwork, up.
City of St. Louis Water Division — TAP (water) 1640 S. Kingshighway Blvd, St. Louis, MO 63110 Phone: (314) 771-2255 Email: customerservice@stlwater.com Apply online: logassistance.org/apply/stlwater/introduction Paper applications: the Water Division office and 13 St. Louis Public Library branches Online: stlwater.com
Behind on more than the water bill? Emergency cash and TANF help in Missouri.
### Can your water be shut off in winter in Missouri?
Yes, it can, and this is the myth that catches people. Missouri’s Cold Weather Rule pauses gas and electric disconnections in freezing weather, roughly November 1 through March 31, because losing heat can be deadly. But that rule covers heat, not water. There is no statewide ban on winter water shutoffs. Believing otherwise is how a January surprise happens.
So protect your water on purpose. Enrolling in an assistance program or a payment plan is what actually shields you; City TAP participants, for instance, stay protected while they’re active. If your heat is also at risk, our guide to the Missouri Cold Weather Rule and how to stop a winter shutoff walks through the gas and electric side, and LIHEAP energy assistance in St. Louis can help with those bills.
### Where should you start, and is LIHWAP still an option?
Start with 211, then apply program by program. You may have heard about LIHWAP, the federal water assistance program. Here’s the straight answer: it’s closed. LIHWAP ended in March 2024, and Missouri is not taking new applications, so don’t wait on it or let it stall you. The live help for water and sewer is the three programs above.
Keep the lanes straight, and you won’t waste a phone call. LIHEAP is real and still funded, but it pays for energy, heating and cooling, not your water or sewer. The Urban League and similar agencies also focus mainly on energy bills; check their current details directly before you go. For the wider list of who covers what, see our roundup of essential St. Louis utility assistance programs.
Here’s the part no shutoff notice will tell you: the money to catch you up often already exists, sitting in a fund with your name not yet on it. Being found — by a caseworker, a program, a single phone number — is half the fight. So make the calls. Let yourself be counted.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What if I can’t afford my water bill?
A.  Don’t ignore it, that’s when a shutoff turns real. Call 211 first to reach whichever agency currently has funds, then ask your provider about payment plans and assistance. City residents can try TAP, County residents H2O Help to Others, and everyone can ask MSD about its sewer program.
### Q. What happens if you can’t afford water?
A.  Your water provider can disconnect service for nonpayment, and Missouri has no statewide ban on winter water shutoffs. One relief: MSD handles sewer only and cannot shut off your water, collecting through liens instead. Enrolling in an assistance program or payment plan is what actually protects your service.
### Q. Is there a way to lower my water bill?
A.  Yes. Missouri American offers free Budget Billing that levels payments into a steady monthly amount, plus Installment Plans with 25% down over six months. City residents behind on water can apply for TAP’s one-time credit up to $500. Fixing a hidden leak also trims a suddenly high bill.
### Q. How do I lower my MSD sewer bill?
A.  Apply for MSD’s Customer Assistance Program. It cuts your sewer rate by 50% for two years if you qualify. The income limit is 200% of poverty, about $66,000 for a family of four, and rises to 250% for seniors 62-plus and people with disabilities. Call (866) 281-5737 to start.
### Q. Can I dispute my water bill?
A.  Yes. Disputing a charge is separate from asking for aid, so contact the utility that issued the bill directly. For City water call (314) 771-2255, for County water Missouri American at 1-866-430-0820, and for sewer MSD at (866) 281-5737. A sudden spike often points to a hidden leak worth checking.
### Q. Can my water be shut off in winter in Missouri?
A.  Not necessarily, but it can be. Missouri’s Cold Weather Rule blocks gas and electric disconnections in freezing weather from November through March, yet it does not cover water. There is no statewide winter water shutoff ban. To protect your water, enroll in an assistance program or payment plan. Active City TAP participants stay protected.
### Q. Is there still a LIHWAP water program in Missouri?
A.  No. The federal LIHWAP water program ended in March 2024, and Missouri is not accepting new applications. Don’t wait on it. Instead, use MSD’s Customer Assistance Program for sewer, the City’s TAP program for water, or H2O Help to Others in the County. LIHEAP still helps, but only with energy bills.
### Q. What’s the difference between my water and sewer bill?
A.  Your water bill pays for drinking water, from the City Water Division if you live in the City, or Missouri American Water if you’re in the County. Your sewer bill, from MSD Project Clear, pays to treat wastewater across the whole region. They’re separate bills with separate programs, so apply to each. MSD can’t shut off water.

## How to File for Unemployment in Missouri: A St. Louis Guide
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-file-for-unemployment-in-missouri-a-st-louis-guide
The email came in right before lunch on a Thursday. By two o’clock, Marcus had a cardboard box, a final paycheck, and a badge that no longer opened the door. He took the long way home to Florissant — not because traffic was bad, but because he hadn’t figured out how to walk in and say it out loud yet.
Here’s the part nobody mentions in that first quiet hour: the clock already started. In Missouri, your unemployment claim is dated to the week you file, not the day you lost the job. Sitting with the shock for a week to “get your head straight” can quietly cost you a week of money you’re owed. And this isn’t a handout. It’s insurance your employer paid into for exactly this moment.
So before the shock wears off, let’s walk through it: how to file, what you’ll actually get, the weekly rules that trip people up, and where a real person in the St. Louis area can help you do it for free. If you’re juggling more than one crisis right now, our St. Louis help and assistance resources hub points to food, rent, and utility help too.
### How do I file for unemployment in Missouri?
File online at uinteract.labor.mo.gov as soon as you’re out of work, because your claim starts the week you file, not your last day. Have your Social Security number, 18 months of employer details, and last week’s gross pay ready. Then file a weekly request every week and log at least three job-search activities.
The Missouri Division of Employment Security (DES) runs the program, and the online portal is the fastest way in. If you can’t get online, you can file by phone through the Regional Claims Center at 1-800-320-2519, Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. The St. Louis Regional Claims Center line is 314-340-4950, and translation help is at 573-751-9040.
### What you need before you start
Gather these first so you don’t stall halfway through:
Your Social Security number.
The name, full address, and start and end dates for every employer you had in the last 18 months.
Your DD-214 if you served in the military in the last 18 months.
The gross earnings for the week you file.
### The one mistake that costs people money
File the same week you’re separated. We can’t say this loudly enough. Your benefits are effective the week you submit the claim, so a delay isn’t neutral — it’s a week of payments you simply won’t get back. Create your username and password on your first visit, then keep them somewhere safe, because you’ll be back every single week.
### How much does unemployment in Missouri pay?
Missouri pays a weekly benefit of 4% of the average of your two highest base-period quarters, which lands somewhere between $35 and $320 a week, according to the Missouri DES (labor.mo.gov). The maximum is $320 a week for up to 20 weeks, so the most any single claim pays out is roughly $6,400.
That $320 cap is worth sitting with for a second. It’s one of the lowest maximums in the country, and it hasn’t moved in years. For a lot of households, unemployment covers part of the gap, not all of it, which is exactly why lining up other help early matters. Think of it as a slice of your old paycheck, not the whole thing.
### How the 20 weeks actually work
Your total award is the lesser of 20 times your weekly amount or one-third of your total base-period wages. The “base period” is the first four of the last five completed calendar quarters. If you worked steadily, you’ll usually qualify for the full 20 weeks. If your earnings were uneven, your window may be shorter.
### Am I eligible for Missouri unemployment?
You generally qualify if you’re out of work through no fault of your own and earned at least $2,250 in your base period, per the Missouri DES. That means $1,500 or more in one quarter and $750 across the rest, with total base-period wages of at least 1.5 times your highest quarter.
“No fault of your own” usually means a layoff, a position eliminated, or hours cut. If you quit, you may still qualify when you left for good cause tied to the job itself. Fired for misconduct is a harder road, but don’t assume you’re disqualified. File anyway and let DES make the call. Guessing yourself out of benefits helps no one.
### You also have to stay able and available
Eligibility isn’t just about how you left. Each week, you must be physically able to work, available to take a full-time job, and actively looking. You also have to report any earnings for the week, even from part-time or gig work. Report it honestly — unreported income is the fastest way to turn a benefit into an overpayment you have to pay back.
### What are the weekly rules once you’re approved?
Filing once isn’t enough. To keep benefits coming, the Missouri DES requires you to file a weekly request in UInteract every single week and complete at least three work-search activities. You also need to visit jobs.mo.gov or a Missouri Job Center at least once a month. Miss any of these, and that week gets denied.
### The waiting week
Your first eligible week is a “waiting week.” It’s unpaid at first, but you still have to file for it — skip it and you delay everything. Here’s the part people miss: if you keep drawing benefits through about week 20, that waiting week gets paid out as your final payment. So file it, then forget about it.
### How and when you get paid
Once a weekly request is approved, payment comes by direct deposit or a Money Network Visa prepaid card, usually within a few days. Your amount can be reduced by wages, vacation or holiday pay, severance or WARN pay, a pension, or workers’ comp for the same week. Report it all, and let the system do the math.
### Track your job search
Keep a simple log of your three weekly activities: where you applied, who you contacted, and the date. DES can ask to see it. Job fairs, online applications, interviews, and registering with a Job Center all count. This is where a St. Louis Job Center earns its keep, because it turns a required errand into actual leads.
Short on rent or groceries while the claim clears? Start with our St. Louis help and assistance resources. A Job Center isn’t the unemployment office frowning at you. It’s a free hiring hall. Walking in the door checks your monthly box and puts a real person on your side of the table.
If you’re the staffing agency, workforce program or ministry helping laid-off St. Louisans back to work, list it with us so the neighbors looking for that next job can reach you.
### What if your claim gets denied?
You have 30 days from the date on your determination to appeal, per the Missouri DES — miss it and the decision usually stands. File the appeal through UInteract, or mail or fax the Request for Appeal to the Appeals Tribunal, P.O. Box 59, Jefferson City, MO 65104-0059 (fax 573-751-1321). There are no phone or email appeals.
One thing people forget in the sting of a denial: keep filing your weekly requests while the appeal is pending. If you win, you can only be paid for the weeks you actually claimed. Stop filing, and even a successful appeal leaves money on the table. Write down your determination date the day it arrives so the 30-day clock never sneaks up on you.
Lost the job after getting hurt on it? When to call a workers’ comp attorney.
### Where can you get free, in-person help in the St. Louis area?
Missouri Job Centers help you file, search, and appeal at no cost, and there’s one in every corner of the metro. The statewide line is 1-888-728-JOBS (5627). These centers cover your required monthly visit, and they’re staffed by people who’ve walked hundreds of neighbors through the same portal you’re staring at.
SLATE — St. Louis City Job Center 1520 Market St, Room 3050 (3rd floor), St. Louis, MO 63103 Agency: (314) 589-8000 · Job Center line: (314) 244-2131 Open Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. (Wednesdays open at 9 a.m.). Hours shift, so call before you go. stlouis-mo.gov/government/departments/slate

A counselor can do far more than process paperwork. If you’re reentering the workforce after a conviction, ask about our guide to felon-friendly jobs and re-entry strategies. Over 60 and not ready to stop working? See fulfilling jobs for seniors over 60. And if your old industry is shrinking, trade schools and apprenticeships in St. Louis can open a new lane.
### Will Missouri cut how long unemployment lasts?
As of 2026, the flat 20-week maximum is still the law, per the Missouri DES. You may hear talk of a sliding scale that would tie benefit length to the state’s unemployment rate, dropping it as low as 8 weeks. That idea has been proposed several times, but it is not the current rule.
Here’s the honest version. A 2015 law (HB 150) tried to shorten the window and was struck down in court. Similar bills surfaced again in 2025 (SB 8 and HB 771) without becoming law. So the “will this change?” worry is real, but nothing has moved the 20-week cap yet. Before you file, it’s worth a quick check of labor.mo.gov for the current numbers, since this is the kind of rule lawmakers keep revisiting.
### Your first move today
Losing a job is disorienting, and the paperwork can feel like one more wall. But the system was built for this exact moment, and the single most powerful thing you can do is file today, not next week. Log your three activities, keep your determination dates, and let a Job Center carry some of the weight with you.
Marcus filed that same Thursday night from his kitchen table. It wasn’t much, and it wasn’t everything, but it was a start: a week counted, a door reopened. You deserve the same. For food, rent, and utility help while you get back on your feet, keep our St. Louis help and assistance resources hub close.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How long does it take to start receiving unemployment in Missouri?
A.  Expect a one-week unpaid waiting period first, which you still must claim. After that, each approved weekly request pays out by direct deposit or a Money Network Visa card, usually within a few days. So most people see their first real payment within a couple of weeks of filing, if they file every week.
### Q. How much unemployment can I get in Missouri?
A.  Your total award is the lesser of 20 times your weekly benefit or one-third of your total base-period wages, per the Missouri DES. With the $320 weekly cap running up to 20 weeks, the most a single claim pays is roughly $6,400. Uneven work histories may qualify for a shorter window.
### Q. What disqualifies you for unemployment in Missouri?
A.  Being fired for misconduct or quitting without good cause tied to the job can disqualify you, per the Missouri DES. So can failing to earn at least $2,250 in your base period, not being able and available to work, skipping weekly requests, or hiding earnings. When in doubt, file and let DES decide.
### Q. How long can you stay on unemployment in Missouri?
A.  Under current Missouri law, benefits last up to 20 weeks, per the Missouri DES. Your personal maximum is the lesser of 20 times your weekly amount or one-third of your total base-period wages. Steady earners usually reach the full 20 weeks, while uneven work histories can mean a shorter run.
### Q. Do employers usually fight unemployment claims?
A.  Some do, especially when the separation was a firing or a disputed quit. An employer can contest your claim, but that does not decide it. The Missouri DES reviews both sides and makes the call, so file anyway. If you are denied, you have 30 days to appeal through UInteract.
### Q. What’s the longest you can stay on unemployment?
A.  In Missouri, the longest is 20 weeks, per the Missouri DES, one of the shortest maximums in the country. A proposed sliding scale could drop it as low as 8 weeks, but that is not current law. Extra weeks only appear during special federal emergency programs, which are not active now.
### Q. How much unemployment will I get if I make $40,000 a year?
A.  It depends on how those earnings spread across quarters, but roughly $40,000 a year is about $10,000 a quarter. Your weekly benefit is 4% of your two highest quarters’ average, which pencils out near $400. That exceeds Missouri’s $320 cap, so you would receive the maximum $320 a week, per the Missouri DES.
### Q. How do I file for unemployment in Missouri?
A.  File online at uinteract.labor.mo.gov as soon as you lose your job, since the claim starts the week you file. Have your Social Security number, 18 months of employer details, and last week’s gross earnings ready. Then file a weekly request every week. If you can’t get online, call 1-800-320-2519.

## Daytime Drop-In and Day Centers in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/daytime-drop-in-and-day-centers-in-st-louis
The overnight shelter empties out at seven in the morning. It’s cold, or it’s already hot, and you’ve got a bag, a phone at twelve percent, and roughly ten hours to fill before anywhere will take you back in. That gap, the long daytime hours, is the part almost nobody warns you about. A bed for the night gets the headlines. The day is where it actually gets hard.
This is the guide to that gap. In St. Louis there are real places, open in daylight, where you can take a hot shower, wash your clothes, eat, check your mail, charge a phone, and sit down with someone whose whole job is helping you find the next thing. They’re called day centers, or drop-in centers, and most don’t need insurance, an appointment, or a dime. Below is where they are, what each one actually does, and the numbers that get you in the door. For the wider map of help, start with our St. Louis help and assistance hub.
Need a place to sleep tonight too? Start with emergency homeless shelters in St. Louis. Start here if you need help today. Dial 211 (or 1-800-427-4626) any time for United Way’s 24/7 referral line. For housing and shelter, call the St. Louis Housing Helpline at 314-802-5444, the front door to Coordinated Entry. Both are free, and both can tell you what’s open right now.
If you run a day center, drop-in or outreach ministry here, this part is about the neighbors who are looking for your door, so list it with us.
### Where can a homeless person go during the day in St. Louis?
Daytime drop-in centers offer showers, meals, mail, laundry, and case management while overnight shelters are closed. St. Patrick Center, the St. Louis Empowerment Center, and Bridge of Hope offer showers. The Bridge at Centenary provides a mailing address and meals 365 days a year. Call 211 or the Housing Helpline at 314-802-5444.
Think of the rest of this guide as that answer, unpacked. We’ll go center by center with full addresses and phone numbers, then sort everything by what you actually need: a shower, clean clothes, a meal, a mailing address, an ID, or a person who can help you plan the next step. When you need a bed after dark, our guide to emergency homeless shelters in St. Louis covers tonight.
### What is a day center, and how is it different from an overnight shelter?
A day center, or drop-in center, is a place that offers free daytime services: showers, meals, mail, laundry, classes, and case management. It’s different from an overnight shelter, which gives you a bed at night. The two do opposite shifts. A day center fills the hours a shelter can’t.
Here’s the piece that surprises people: most folks use both. You sleep at an overnight shelter, then it closes in the morning and you head to a day center to wash up, eat, and work on housing or a job. Neither one is the whole answer by itself. Together, they cover the full twenty-four hours, which is really what “getting back on your feet” needs.
A shower, a clean shirt, and a place to sit aren’t small things when you have nowhere else to be. They’re how you stay yourself while you get back on your feet.
### Which daytime drop-in centers serve adults in St. Louis?
St. Louis has a handful of solid adult day centers, and St. Patrick Center is the largest, open Monday through Friday with showers, meals, and case management under one roof. The others each do something specific well. Read the notes below, because what you need decides where you go first.
Heads up: three different places here have the word “Bridge” in the name, and they are not the same organization. The Bridge is a daytime hospitality center at 1610 Olive. Biddle Housing Opportunities Center is run by the Magdala Foundation at 1212 N 13th. Bridge of Hope Ministries is at 4001 Cottage. Different addresses, different phones, different services. Double-check which one you mean before you travel, so you don’t burn a bus fare on the wrong door.
### The Bridge (at Centenary United Methodist Church)
1610 Olive St, St. Louis, MO 63103 Phone: 314-421-3136 Website: bridgestl.org A daytime hospitality center with hot meals served every day of the year, 365 days, plus a mailing address you can use when you have nowhere to receive mail. It keeps long daytime hours, but the schedule can shift, so call first to confirm today’s times before you head over.
### St. Patrick Center
800 N Tucker Blvd, St. Louis, MO 63101 Phone: 314-802-0700 Website: stpatrickcenter.org The largest provider of homeless services in the region, open Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Its Welcome Center takes walk-ins around 8:00 a.m. and 1:00 p.m. You’ll find showers, meals, case management, help with IDs and benefits, rapid re-housing, and utility assistance. In extreme cold or heat, St. Patrick Center also runs emergency day centers.
### Biddle Housing Opportunities Center (run by the Magdala Foundation)
1212 N 13th St, St. Louis, MO 63101 Phone: 314-612-1675 A daytime service center for single adult men that also offers 24-hour overnight shelter. It’s usually reached through the Coordinated Entry system rather than a straight walk-in, so call the Housing Helpline at 314-802-5444, dial 211, or ask at the St. Patrick Center Welcome Center to get connected.
### St. Louis Empowerment Center (DBSA)
907 Dock St, St. Louis, MO 63147 Phone: 314-652-6100 A peer-run drop-in with showers, laundry, lunch and snacks, peer support, employment services, and free Narcan. No insurance and no referral needed. Hours are reported as daily, roughly 9:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m., but confirm by phone, since drop-in schedules change.
### Bridge of Hope Ministries
4001 Cottage Ave, St. Louis, MO 63113 Phone: 314-405-0253 Website: bridgeofhopestl.org A neighborhood drop-in offering showers, laundry, computers, and GED and reading classes. Reported hours are Monday, Tuesday, and Thursday 9:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m., Wednesday 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., and Friday 9:00 a.m. to noon. Call ahead to confirm before you go.
### Employment Connection
2838 Market St, St. Louis, MO 63103 Phone: 314-333-5627 Website: employstl.org Open Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. This is the place for case management, job placement, GED help, and coordinated entry into housing. If your next step is work and a steady paycheck, start here.
### Places for People
1001 Lynch St, St. Louis, MO 63118 Phone: 800-811-4760 (crisis line 314-615-2105) Website: placesforpeople.org A mental-health day program open Monday through Thursday, 7:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m., and Friday, 7:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. It generally serves people enrolled through a central intake rather than anonymous walk-ins, so if you need mental-health day support, call first to ask how to get started.
### Where can I get a shower, laundry, or a hot meal?
Showers for adults are at St. Patrick Center, the St. Louis Empowerment Center, and Bridge of Hope Ministries. Laundry is at the Empowerment Center and Bridge of Hope. Free daytime meals are served at The Bridge every day of the year, at St. Patrick Center, at the Empowerment Center, and at Peter & Paul community meals.
### Showers
For adults, head to St. Patrick Center (800 N Tucker Blvd), the St. Louis Empowerment Center (907 Dock St), or Bridge of Hope (4001 Cottage Ave). Young people can shower at Covenant House and The SPOT. A shower sounds small until you’re walking into a job interview or a benefits appointment. Call ahead so you don’t arrive after the last slot.
### Laundry and clean clothes
The Empowerment Center and Bridge of Hope both offer laundry. For youth, Covenant House, The SPOT, and Restoration House can help, and Restoration House also runs a clothing closet. Clean clothes cost nothing here, and no one needs a reason to want them.
### Free meals
The Bridge (1610 Olive St) serves meals 365 days a year. You can also eat at St. Patrick Center, the Empowerment Center, and Peter & Paul Community Services. For a fuller rundown of where to eat across the city, see our guide to St. Louis soup kitchens.
Drinking or using part of the story? Addiction treatment and free help in St. Louis.
### Where can I get mail, an ID, or help with my benefits?
For mail with no fixed address, The Bridge at 1610 Olive St gives you an address you can use to receive mail, and St. Patrick Center also handles client mail. For an ID or benefits, St. Patrick Center, Employment Connection, and Places for People have case managers, and St. Louis County Library social workers can help for free.
Don’t underestimate the mail piece. A reliable mailing address is the quiet key that unlocks almost everything else: the letter that says your benefits were approved, the reply from an employer, the replacement ID or birth certificate you need before you can get anything else. Without an address, those things never reach you, and it looks like you dropped the ball when you didn’t. Fixing the address often fixes three other problems at once.
### Where can homeless youth go during the day?
Young people roughly 16 to 24 have their own drop-ins, and Covenant House Missouri (2727 N Kingshighway Blvd) is the main one, with showers, laundry, meals, and case management. Other youth options include Epworth in Normandy, The SPOT on Laclede St, Restoration House on Chippewa, and the Center for Youth on the Rise in Spanish Lake.

2727 N Kingshighway Blvd, St. Louis, MO 63113 Phone: 314-533-2241 Website: covenanthousemo.org For young people about 16 to 24. The drop-in runs Monday through Thursday, 9:00 to 11:00 a.m., with a 24/7 crisis line the rest of the time. Showers, laundry, meals, and case management.

7520 Natural Bridge Rd, Normandy, MO 63121 Phone: 314-222-4877 Hot meals plus help with education, employment, and legal needs for youth.

### Who else can help me find day services?
When you’re not sure where to start, two phone numbers and a library will sort it out fast. Dial 211 for United Way’s 24/7 referral line, call the Housing Helpline at 314-802-5444 for housing and shelter, and know that St. Louis County Library has social workers who help for free. A few other places are worth a note too.

Phone: 314-994-3300 Website: slcl.org Social workers stationed at several County Library branches, including Florissant Valley, Lewis & Clark, Natural Bridge, Rock Road, and Weber Road, offer free, private help with housing, food, employment, shelter, and benefits. Note this is the St. Louis County Library system, not the City library. You don’t have to be homeless to ask.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Where can I find homeless shelter in St. Louis?
A.  For a bed, call the St. Louis Housing Helpline at 314-802-5444, the front door to Coordinated Entry, or dial 211 anytime for United Way’s referral line. Biddle Housing Opportunities Center (1212 N 13th St) also offers 24-hour shelter for single men, usually reached through Coordinated Entry.
### Q. Where do I go if I have nowhere to stay?
A.  Start with two numbers: dial 211 anytime for United Way’s 24/7 referral line, and call the St. Louis Housing Helpline at 314-802-5444 for shelter. During the day, drop-in centers like St. Patrick Center and The Bridge offer somewhere warm to sit, showers, and meals.
### Q. Where do homeless people go to take showers?
A.  In St. Louis, adults can shower at St. Patrick Center (800 N Tucker Blvd), the St. Louis Empowerment Center (907 Dock St), and Bridge of Hope Ministries (4001 Cottage Ave). Young people can shower at Covenant House and The SPOT. Call ahead to confirm today’s hours.
### Q. How do I take a shower if I’m homeless?
A.  Head to a daytime drop-in center that offers showers; most need no insurance, appointment, or fee. The St. Louis Empowerment Center (907 Dock St) is peer-run with no referral required. St. Patrick Center’s Welcome Center takes walk-ins around 8:00 a.m. and 1:00 p.m. Call first to confirm shower hours.
### Q. Are there places you can shower for free?
A.  Yes. Showers at St. Patrick Center, the St. Louis Empowerment Center, and Bridge of Hope Ministries are free, and most drop-in centers don’t ask for insurance, an appointment, or a dime. The Empowerment Center needs no referral at all. Call ahead, since drop-in schedules shift day to day.
### Q. Where to go when you are homeless for free?
A.  Nearly every service here is free. Dial 211 anytime for referrals, then head to a free day center like The Bridge (1610 Olive St), which serves meals 365 days a year, or St. Patrick Center for showers and case help. St. Louis County Library social workers also help for free.
### Q. Where can I get mail, an ID, or help with benefits?
A.  The Bridge at 1610 Olive St gives you an address to receive mail, and St. Patrick Center also handles client mail. For an ID or benefits like SNAP and Medicaid, case managers at St. Patrick Center, Employment Connection, and Places for People can help. County Library social workers assist too, at 314-994-3300.
### Q. Where can homeless youth under 25 go during the day?
A.  Covenant House Missouri (2727 N Kingshighway Blvd) is the main youth drop-in, with showers, laundry, meals, and case management for ages 16 to 24. Other options include Epworth in Normandy, The SPOT on Laclede St, Restoration House on Chippewa St, and the Center for Youth on the Rise in Spanish Lake.

## Free and Low-Cost Legal Aid in St. Louis: Eviction, Expungement, Family and Benefits
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/free-and-low-cost-legal-aid-in-st-louis
The envelope came on a Thursday. Marcus knew what it was before he opened it — the county return address, the thin official paper, his name in a little window. He set it on the counter in Baden and let it sit for two days, because opening it felt like making it real. That’s the part nobody warns you about a legal problem: the paperwork is frightening, the clock is already running, and every instinct tells you to look away.
Here’s what Marcus didn’t know, and what this page is for. St. Louis has real attorneys who will help him for free, and the sooner he calls, the more they can do. No scam. No catch. Trained legal-aid lawyers who do this every day — for eviction, for clearing an old record, for a benefits cutoff, for a protection order. You just need their names and numbers. This guide is part of our larger St. Louis help and assistance resources hub, and it exists for one reason: being found is survival, for the people who need help and for the people who give it.
### Where can I get free legal aid in St. Louis, Mo.?
Legal Services of Eastern Missouri (800-444-0514) is the main free civil-law provider, covering housing, benefits, and consumer cases. ArchCity Defenders handles criminal and expungement work, and the SLU and WashU law clinics take family, immigration, and veterans cases. If you earn too much, BAMSL’s referral line finds an affordable attorney.
Think of it as a map, not a maze. Most free legal help in the region flows through a handful of trusted organizations, and each one has a lane. Below are the main doors. Save the numbers that fit your situation, then jump to the section that matches your problem — eviction, a record, family, benefits, or safety.
Legal Services of Eastern Missouri (LSEM) 701 Market St, Suite 1100, St. Louis, MO 63101 Intake (800) 444-0514, main (314) 534-4200 lsem.org
LSEM is the region’s largest free civil-law office. It takes eviction and housing, public benefits like SNAP and Medicaid, consumer problems, immigration, and senior law. It does not handle criminal cases, and it only takes family matters when they’re tied to domestic violence.
ArchCity Defenders 5939 Goodfellow Blvd, St. Louis, MO 63147 (314) 361-8834 or (855) 724-2489 archcitydefenders.org
ArchCity works on criminal, municipal, and civil matters, and it’s a go-to for expungement, meaning clearing an old record. Its team practices holistic defense, so they look at the whole person, not just the charge.
SLU Law Clinics & Catholic Legal Assistance Ministry (CLAM) 100 N. Tucker Blvd, Suite 726, St. Louis, MO 63101 (314) 977-3993 slu.edu/law/academics/clinics
Law students, supervised by faculty attorneys, take civil cases including family law, immigration, veterans, and housing for households at or under 150% of the federal poverty level. One catch worth circling: they take intake calls on Tuesdays, and there are no walk-ins.
Washington University School of Law Clinics law.washu.edu
WashU runs case-specific clinics — low-income taxpayer, immigration, and veterans law. Capacity is limited and there’s no single walk-in line, so start on the clinic pages linked from the site.
BAMSL “Find a Lawyer” (Lawyer Referral Service) (314) 421-4134 or (833) 743-8212 bamsl.org
This one is for people who earn too much for free aid. The Bar Association of Metropolitan St. Louis matches you to a member attorney; the attorney sets the fee, and a free initial consultation is common.
### What should you do the moment you get an eviction notice?
Call for help the same day — do not wait. Missouri eviction cases move fast, and City renters facing eviction have a right to free counsel through HELP STL / Right to Counsel (314-657-1671), delivered by LSEM. The single biggest mistake is ignoring the summons or skipping court. Open the papers, note the date, and call.
This is the section to read twice. An eviction summons is not a bill you can deal with later; it’s a court date with a deadline attached. The people who lose their homes fastest are usually the ones who froze, threw the envelope in a drawer, and missed the hearing. If you do nothing else today, do this one thing.
### Don’t ignore the summons, and appear at your court date
If there’s a court date on the paper, that date is real, and missing it can mean an automatic loss. Even if you think you have no defense, showing up matters. A legal-aid attorney may spot something you can’t — an improper notice, a repair the landlord ignored, a payment that was never credited. You can’t use a defense you never raise.
### Call the moment you’re served, not the day before
HELP STL is free eviction defense for low-income City renters, but it’s underfunded and can’t reach everyone, so apply early. The self-help site MOTenantHelp.org walks you through your options, and the city’s Department of Human Services can help you apply.
HELP STL / Right to Counsel (City eviction defense, delivered by LSEM) Apply (314) 657-1671 or (314) 657-1654 Department of Human Services (314) 612-5900 1520 Market St, 4th Floor #4065, St. Louis, MO 63103 (Monday to Friday, 8a to 5p) Self-help: MOTenantHelp.org
### If the problem is discrimination, or you want to avoid court
Was your Section 8 voucher refused, or were you treated differently because of where your income comes from? The Metropolitan St. Louis Equal Housing & Opportunity Council (EHOC) runs fair-housing and landlord-tenant hotlines, including source-of-income and Section 8 cases. If you and your landlord might still work it out, the Conflict Resolution Center offers free tenant-landlord mediation before things reach a courtroom. For more on vouchers, see our guide to navigating Section 8 in St. Louis City.
Metropolitan St. Louis Equal Housing & Opportunity Council (EHOC) 1027 S. Vandeventer Ave, Suite 600, St. Louis, MO 63110 (314) 534-5800 (confirm the current number on ehocstl.org) ehocstl.org
Conflict Resolution Center (CRC STL) (314) 255-7449 crcstl.org
### How do you clear or expunge a record in Missouri?
You petition the court that sentenced you, under Missouri statute RSMo 610.140. Most misdemeanors and ordinance violations require a one-year wait; most felonies require three years. There’s a $250 filing surcharge that can be waived if you can’t afford it. ArchCity Defenders (314-361-8834) helps people through the process.
An old record follows you into job applications, apartment searches, and volunteer forms, long after you’ve moved on. Expungement seals eligible cases so they stop showing up. The process has waiting periods and paperwork, but it’s doable, and you don’t have to figure it out alone.
### Where to get expungement help
Start with ArchCity Defenders, whose holistic team handles expungement directly. Free expungement clinics also pop up around the region on specific dates, so it’s worth checking whether one is coming up, or whether a program like Expunge STL is currently running one. If clearing a record is part of a bigger fresh start, our guide to starting over after incarceration in St. Louis connects the other pieces.
### Who helps with a domestic-violence order of protection?
The Crime Victim Center and its Legal Advocates for Abused Women program (314-652-3623) give free help filing orders of protection for domestic violence, sexual assault, and stalking across the City and several surrounding counties. Safe Connections runs a 24-hour crisis helpline at (314) 531-2003. LSEM can take related civil matters.
If you’re in immediate danger, call 911. Reach out from a safe place, and use a phone or device the person who is hurting you can’t track. The National Domestic Violence Hotline is free, confidential, and open around the clock at 1-800-799-7233.
An order of protection is a court order telling an abuser to stay away. You don’t need a private lawyer to start one, and advocates can stand with you through the filing and the hearing. If you need shelter, please call a hotline first rather than showing up at an address — shelters keep their locations private to keep the people inside safe. For hotlines, shelters, and a fuller safety plan, see our guide to domestic violence help in St. Louis.
Crime Victim Center / Legal Advocates for Abused Women (LAAW) (314) 652-3623 supportvictims.org
Safe Connections (24-hour crisis helpline) (314) 531-2003 safeconnections.org
### Can legal aid help with SNAP, Medicaid, or disability?
Yes. Legal Services of Eastern Missouri (800-444-0514) handles public-benefits denials and terminations, including SNAP food stamps, Medicaid, and disability appeals. If your benefits were cut or denied, an attorney can represent you at the appeal and the hearing — and deadlines to appeal are usually short, so call quickly.
A benefits cutoff can feel final. It usually isn’t. Agencies make mistakes, paperwork gets lost, and you have the right to challenge a decision. Legal aid does this constantly and knows how to write the appeal and speak at the hearing. Keep the denial letter — the date on it matters.
### Where do you get free family-law help in St. Louis?
The SLU Law Clinics and Catholic Legal Assistance Ministry (314-977-3993) take family-law cases like custody and divorce for households at or under 150% of the federal poverty level. Remember they take intake calls on Tuesdays only. LSEM handles divorce just when it’s tied to domestic violence.
Family law is where a lot of people get stuck, because free help is more limited here than for eviction or benefits. If the clinics are full or you don’t qualify, Missouri courts publish self-help forms at courts.mo.gov, and BAMSL’s referral line can match you with an affordable attorney for the parts you can’t handle alone.
### Do you qualify for free legal aid, and what if you earn too much?
Most free programs use income limits. LSEM generally helps households at or under 125% of the federal poverty level, with room up to 200% in exceptional cases; the SLU and CLAM clinics use a 150% line. Seniors 60 and older and domestic-violence survivors often have expanded access.
If you’re over the limit, you still have options, and you’re not on your own. BAMSL’s “Find a Lawyer” service (314-421-4134) connects you to a private attorney, usually with a free first consultation. LSEM also runs a Senior Law Program for residents 60 and older; ask about it when you call intake, or see our guide to legal services for seniors.
### What to have ready before you call
You’ll get through intake faster with a few things in front of you: your household income, how many people live in your home, a plain description of the legal problem, and any court papers with their dates. Have them ready before you dial. Lines are busy, and being prepared can be the difference between getting a callback and getting missed.
One more thing, and it matters. None of these organizations can help someone they never hear from. The lawyers are there, the programs are funded to do exactly this work, but they can’t knock on your door. The move that changes everything is the smallest one: you pick up the phone. Marcus finally opened his envelope, called HELP STL, and had someone in his corner by his court date. Make the call while the number is still in front of you.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How do I get a lawyer if I have no money?
A.  In St. Louis, free civil-law help starts with Legal Services of Eastern Missouri (800-444-0514) for eviction, benefits, and consumer cases. ArchCity Defenders (314-361-8834) handles criminal and expungement work, and the SLU and WashU law clinics take family, immigration, and veterans cases. You don’t pay these attorneys.
### Q. Who qualifies for Missouri legal aid?
A.  Most free programs use income limits tied to the federal poverty level. Legal Services of Eastern Missouri generally helps households at or under 125%, with room up to 200% in exceptional cases. The SLU and CLAM clinics use a 150% line. Seniors 60 and older and domestic-violence survivors often get expanded access.
### Q. What types of cases qualify for free legal aid?
A.  Free legal aid covers civil matters: eviction and housing, public benefits like SNAP and Medicaid, consumer problems, immigration, and senior law through LSEM. ArchCity Defenders takes criminal, municipal, and expungement cases. The law clinics handle family law, veterans, and taxpayer issues. LSEM takes family matters only when tied to domestic violence.
### Q. What happens if I can’t afford a lawyer?
A.  You still have options. Free programs like LSEM (800-444-0514) cover many civil cases, and City renters facing eviction have a right to free counsel through HELP STL (314-657-1671). If you earn too much for free aid, BAMSL’s referral line matches you with an affordable attorney who often gives a free first consultation.
### Q. Will a lawyer talk to me for free?
A.  Often, yes. Legal-aid attorneys at LSEM and ArchCity Defenders help qualifying clients at no cost. If you earn too much for free aid, BAMSL’s “Find a Lawyer” service (314-421-4134) matches you with a member attorney, and a free initial consultation is common. The attorney sets any fee after that.
### Q. Can I call a lawyer and ask a question for free?
A.  Yes. Start by calling a free legal-aid intake line like LSEM (800-444-0514) or ArchCity Defenders (314-361-8834) and describe your problem. If you don’t qualify for free help, BAMSL’s referral line (314-421-4134) connects you to a private attorney, where a free initial consultation is common before any fee is set.
### Q. What is the maximum income to qualify for legal aid?
A.  Limits are set as a percentage of the federal poverty level, not a flat dollar figure. Legal Services of Eastern Missouri generally helps households at or under 125% of that level, stretching to 200% in exceptional cases. The SLU and CLAM law clinics use a 150% line for eligibility.
### Q. Who helps with eviction in St. Louis?
A.  HELP STL / Right to Counsel (314-657-1671) gives free eviction defense to low-income City renters, delivered by LSEM. The self-help site MOTenantHelp.org walks you through your options. EHOC handles source-of-income and Section 8 discrimination, and the Conflict Resolution Center offers free tenant-landlord mediation before you reach court.
