## Addiction and Substance Use Treatment in St. Louis: Detox, Rehab, and Free Help
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/addiction-and-substance-use-treatment-in-st-louis
If this is an emergency, start here.
Overdose or any life-threatening emergency: call 911 now, then give naloxone (Narcan) if you have it. Missouri’s Good Samaritan law offers limited legal protection to people who call 911 to report an overdose.
Suicidal, mental-health, or substance-use crisis: call or text 988, free and 24/7. In eastern Missouri, 988 is answered by Behavioral Health Response.
St. Louis regional crisis line: 1-800-811-4760 or 314-469-6644, Behavioral Health Response, 24/7.
Free, confidential treatment referrals, 24/7: SAMHSA National Helpline 1-800-662-4357.
It’s a little after 2 a.m. in Affton, and someone is sitting on the edge of the tub with a phone in their hand, typing the same search and deleting it. They already know something has to change. What they don’t know is who to call, whether it costs money they don’t have, or whether the voice on the other end will judge them.
If that’s you, or someone you love, read the box above first. Then take a breath. You’re not too far gone, and you’re not doing this wrong by looking. Reaching out is the hard part, and you’re already doing it.
What follows is a plain, no-shame map of where St. Louis actually offers help: crisis lines, medically supervised detox, residential rehab, outpatient care, medication treatment, and the doors that stay open when you have Medicaid or no insurance at all. It’s part of our larger guide to St. Louis help and assistance resources. Every phone number and address here was checked by hand.
### How do people with no money go to rehab in St. Louis?
Start with BJC Behavioral Health’s Same Day Access walk-in at 314-747-7491, the region’s entry point for people on Medicaid or with no insurance. They assess you and connect you to care on a sliding scale. Federally qualified clinics like Affinia Healthcare (314-814-8700) and CSTAR programs through Preferred Family Healthcare and Queen of Peace Center also offer low or no-cost treatment.
Cost is the wall most people hit first, and it turns them around before they ever start. So let’s clear it now. In Missouri, being broke or uninsured does not mean going without treatment. MO HealthNet, the state’s Medicaid program, now covers the full range of care, from outpatient counseling to medication treatment to residential rehab, for eligible members. You apply at mydss.mo.gov.
No insurance and not sure whether you qualify? That’s exactly what the CSTAR programs and the community clinics below are built for. Many use a sliding fee scale tied to your income, and some draw on state Department of Mental Health funds to cover people who can’t pay. For a wider look at care without coverage, see our guide to free and low-cost health clinics in St. Louis.
### Who do I call right now for a substance-use crisis?
Call or text 988 for any mental-health or substance-use crisis, free and around the clock. In the St. Louis region, you can also reach Behavioral Health Response directly at 1-800-811-4760 or 314-469-6644. If someone is overdosing, call 911 first and give naloxone if it’s within reach. Minutes matter more than anything else.
Behavioral Health Response covers St. Louis City and County plus St. Charles, Franklin, Jefferson, Lincoln, Warren, Iron, St. Francois, and Washington counties. Teens can text BHEARD to 31658. For a free, confidential referral to treatment anywhere in the country, the SAMHSA National Helpline at 1-800-662-4357 runs 24/7 and can filter for Medicaid and sliding-fee options.
### Where can I get free naloxone (Narcan)?
Free, and no strings attached. Missouri mails naloxone to your door through getmonaloxone.com (order form at redcap.link/getsupplies), run by UMSL’s Addiction Science team. Prefer to pick it up? All roughly 20 St. Louis County Library branches, county naloxone vending machines, and county health centers hand it out free, with no ID and no cost. Keeping a dose nearby can buy the time an ambulance needs.
### What’s the difference between detox, residential, outpatient, and MAT?
These four words get used interchangeably, and that confusion costs people time. Here’s the short version. Detox handles the first few days safely. Residential means you live on site. Outpatient means you live at home and come in for treatment. MAT is medication plus counseling. Most people move through more than one of these, in whatever order fits their life.
### Detox
Detox is short-term, medically supervised withdrawal, usually a few days. For alcohol and some other drugs, quitting cold on your own can be dangerous, so this step belongs under medical eyes. Think of it as stabilizing, not curing. It gets your body to a safe baseline so the real work can begin.
### Residential and inpatient
Residential, or inpatient, care means living at a facility around the clock while you focus fully on recovery, often for a few weeks. It pulls you out of the triggers and routines at home. This suits people who need structure, a medically supported setting, or simply distance from a situation that keeps dragging them back.
### Outpatient and IOP
Outpatient means you live at home and come in for scheduled treatment. Intensive outpatient, or IOP, is a heavier version, often several sessions a week for a few hours each. It lets you keep a job, care for your kids, or stay in school while still getting real, structured help.
### MAT (medication-assisted treatment)
MAT pairs FDA-approved medication with counseling. For opioids, that usually means methadone, buprenorphine (Suboxone), or naltrexone; for alcohol, naltrexone and a few others. It isn’t swapping one drug for another, and it’s backed by strong evidence. For many people, MAT is what finally makes recovery hold.
### Where do you find medical detox and residential rehab in St. Louis?
Because detox carries medical risk, start by calling a program directly or dialing SAMHSA at 1-800-662-4357 to check current beds and coverage. The nonprofit and hospital programs below offer medically supervised detox and residential care across the metro, and several take Medicaid or will work with you on cost.
Harris House 2706 S. River Rd, St. Charles, MO 63303 (transitional housing at 8315 S. Broadway, St. Louis, MO 63111) Phone: 314-631-4299 Web: harrishousestl.org Nonprofit medical detox, residential, PHP, IOP, and sober living. Accepts Medicaid and Department of Mental Health funding.
CenterPointe Hospital 4801 Weldon Spring Pkwy, St. Charles, MO 63304 Admissions: 800-345-5407 (main line 636-723-9306) Web: centerpointehospital.com Detox (ages 12 and up), residential, IOP, MAT, and dual-diagnosis care. Accepts Medicare and Medicaid.
Queen of Peace Center 325 N. Newstead Ave, St. Louis, MO 63108 Phone: 314-531-0511 Web: qopcstl.org Family-centered residential and outpatient treatment for women, children, and families, with housing and child care. Medicaid and DMH funded.
Preferred Family Healthcare (which absorbed Bridgeway Behavioral Health) 4066 Dunnica Ave, St. Louis, MO 63116 (314-833-6155) and 4928 Delmar Blvd, St. Louis, MO 63108 (314-899-0846) Web: pfh.org CSTAR outpatient, women’s, children’s, and adolescent residential, and MAT. Medicaid and DMH funded, with a sliding scale.
### Where can I get MAT, methadone, or Suboxone?
Medication treatment is more available here than most people realize, and some doors open the same day. The programs below prescribe and manage MAT, from methadone to buprenorphine (Suboxone) to naltrexone. CenterPointe and Preferred Family, listed above, offer MAT too, so ask whichever program you reach which medications they support.
Assisted Recovery Centers of America (ARCA) 1430 Olive St #100, St. Louis, MO 63103, and 10208 W. Florissant Ave, St. Louis, MO 63136 (North County) Phone: 314-645-6840 Web: arcamidwest.com Outpatient care, MAT (naltrexone and buprenorphine), medical detox and stabilization, an on-site pharmacy, and naloxone. Walk in with no appointment for a free, confidential assessment, plus help enrolling in Medicaid.
St. Louis Metro Treatment Center (New Season) Phone: 877-284-7074 Web: newseason.com MAT and methadone maintenance. Call for the current clinic location and intake hours.
Center for Life Solutions Phone: 314-731-0100 (crisis line 314-302-6728) Web: centerfls.org MAT paired with therapy. Call for the current office location and scheduling.
### How do the uninsured and Medicaid members get care?
There is a “no wrong door” way in, and it starts with a walk-in. BJC Behavioral Health runs the region’s Same Day Access, where you can walk in for an assessment of mental-health and substance-use needs without an appointment. They see you whether you have Medicaid, Medicare, private insurance, or nothing at all, using a sliding scale and state funds for people who can’t pay.
BJC Behavioral Health Phone: 314-747-7491 or 877-729-4004 Web: bjcbehavioralhealth.org The DMH point of entry with Same Day Access walk-in assessments. Serves St. Louis City and County plus St. Francois, Iron, and Washington counties. Call for the nearest site.
Affinia Healthcare Phone: 314-814-8700 Web: affiniahealthcare.org A federally qualified health center offering primary care plus behavioral health, substance-use care, and MAT on a sliding fee scale. Serves the uninsured. Call for the nearest location.
Places for People 1001 Lynch St, St. Louis, MO 63118 Phone: 314-535-5600 (crisis 1-800-811-4760) Web: placesforpeople.org Case management and substance-use counseling with central intake for serious mental-health and co-occurring needs. Medicaid, Medicare, and private insurance.
Prevent+Ed (formerly NCADA) 9355 Olive Blvd, St. Louis (Olivette), MO 63132 Phone: 314-962-3456 Web: prevented.org Not a detox or residential provider. Think of them as navigation: prevention, a confidential helpline, and free assessment and referral to point you toward the right program.
The Salvation Army Midtown also runs men’s inpatient and outpatient programs; call 314-652-3310 for current details. And if your struggle is tangled up with anxiety, depression, or trauma, that’s common, not a personal failing. Our guide to free and low-cost mental-health and substance-use help in St. Louis covers treating both at once.
Here’s the thing nobody says out loud: the help already exists. What’s usually missing is just the one phone number and the nerve to dial it. You now have both.
### Is there help for pregnant women, mothers, and families?
Yes, and this is one area St. Louis does especially well. Queen of Peace Center at 314-531-0511 specializes in family-centered treatment for women, children, and families, combining residential and outpatient care with child care and housing, so a mother doesn’t have to choose between recovery and her kids. Preferred Family Healthcare also offers women’s and children’s residential programs.
The fear of losing custody keeps many mothers from asking for help, which is exactly backward. Getting into treatment is the single strongest step toward keeping or reuniting a family, and these programs are built to protect that bond, not break it. If you’re pregnant, say so when you call, since pregnancy often moves you up the list for a bed.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What number do I call for a substance-use crisis in St. Louis?
A.  Call or text 988 anytime, free and confidential. In the St. Louis region, Behavioral Health Response also answers directly at 1-800-811-4760 or 314-469-6644. If someone is overdosing, call 911 first and give naloxone (Narcan) if you have it. These lines run 24 hours a day, every day.
### Q. Where can I get free Narcan (naloxone)?
A.  Order it free by mail at getmonaloxone.com, using the form at redcap.link/getsupplies, run by UMSL’s Addiction Science team. You can also pick it up free, with no ID and no cost, at all roughly 20 St. Louis County Library branches, county naloxone vending machines, and county health centers.
### Q. Do you have to pay for drug rehabilitation?
A.  Not always. In Missouri, being uninsured doesn’t mean going without care. MO HealthNet covers eligible members, while CSTAR programs and clinics like BJC Behavioral Health (314-747-7491) use sliding fee scales and state Department of Mental Health funds to cover people who can’t pay. Start with a walk-in assessment.
### Q. How much is rehab in Missouri?
A.  Cost varies by program and level of care, and many people pay little or nothing. MO HealthNet (Missouri Medicaid) covers eligible members for outpatient, MAT, and residential rehab. Uninsured? CSTAR programs and clinics use sliding fee scales and state funds. Call a program directly for current pricing and coverage.
### Q. Does insurance pay for addiction rehab?
A.  Usually yes. Most private plans, Medicare, and MO HealthNet (Missouri Medicaid) cover substance-use treatment, from outpatient counseling to MAT to residential rehab. Under Missouri’s substance-use waiver approved in December 2023, MO HealthNet covers the full range for eligible members. Apply at mydss.mo.gov, and ask each program which plans it accepts.
### Q. How do you pay for rehab without insurance?
A.  Several doors stay open. BJC Behavioral Health’s Same Day Access (314-747-7491) sees you with no insurance on a sliding scale. CSTAR programs through Preferred Family Healthcare and Queen of Peace Center draw on state Department of Mental Health funds. ARCA (314-645-6840) also helps you enroll in Medicaid during a free walk-in assessment.
### Q. How to get funding to go to rehab?
A.  Start by applying for MO HealthNet at mydss.mo.gov, since Missouri’s Medicaid now covers the full range of care for eligible members. No coverage? Ask programs about sliding fees and state Department of Mental Health funds. The SAMHSA National Helpline (1-800-662-4357) can filter for Medicaid and sliding-fee options, free and 24/7.
### Q. How long does rehab usually last?
A.  It depends on the level of care and the person. Detox is short-term, usually a few days. Residential or inpatient care often runs a few weeks. Outpatient and IOP let you live at home while attending scheduled sessions, often several a week. Many people move through more than one stage over time.
If you read only one line of this, read this one: the first call is the hardest, and it gets easier from there. You don’t need to have it all figured out before you dial. The person who answers does this every day, and their whole job is to take it from here.
Save a couple of these numbers in your phone right now, while you’re thinking about it: 988, and the SAMHSA helpline at 1-800-662-4357. ## Free and Low-Cost After-School and Summer Programs for St. Louis Kids
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/free-and-low-cost-after-school-and-summer-programs-for-st-louis-kids
You’re standing at the sign-up table, and the number on the flyer is more than a week of groceries. Your kid is tugging your sleeve, eyes lit up, already picturing the friends, the gym, and the summer field trips. And you’re doing the quiet math every parent in this spot knows too well. Here’s what nobody prints on that flyer: in St. Louis, price is almost never the real gate. Sliding-scale fees, scholarships, and flat-out free programs exist across the metro, and asking for them is ordinary, not shameful.
This is the plain-language map to getting your child through the door, even if you can’t pay full price, or can’t pay a dime. We’ll cover who offers sliding-scale fees, who never turns a child away, which programs are completely free, and the two calls that find a seat near your ZIP code. It sits inside our bigger guide to help and assistance across St. Louis. Let’s get your kid signed up.
### Where can St. Louis families find free or low-cost after-school and summer programs?
Start with three front doors: dial 2-1-1, call ARCHS at (314) 534-0022, or search Blueprint4. Then reach programs directly. Gene Slay’s Girls & Boys Club turns no child away, LifeWise StL runs a free after-school program, and the Gateway Region YMCA and Boys & Girls Clubs offer sliding-scale fees and scholarships.
Think of ARCHS as the region’s switchboard for free seats. It doesn’t run a clubhouse you drop your kid at; it funds free after-school programming at other agencies and can point you to an open spot. Recent reporting credited its After School for All Partnership with about $2.5 million funding free programs for roughly 1,900 K-5 students at around 29 sites across St. Louis Public Schools and Jennings (KSDK/St. Louis American, 2024).
ARCHS (Area Resources for Community and Human Services) Address: 539 N. Grand Blvd, 6th Floor, St. Louis, MO 63103 Phone: (314) 534-0022 Website: stlarchs.org
Two more catch-alls belong on speed dial. Dial 2-1-1 (United Way) any hour for a free, confidential referral to programs near you. And Blueprint4, at blueprint4.com, is a searchable directory of free and low-cost St. Louis youth programs you can filter by neighborhood. Being found is the whole game here: the seat already exists, and these front doors connect your child to it.
### How do you get help paying if you can’t afford full price?
Four tools carry most families through: sliding-scale fees, scholarships, formal financial-assistance applications, and the state child-care subsidy. The Gateway Region YMCA alone awards about $2.58 million in assistance each year (gwrymca.org), covering memberships, programs, child care, and camp. You qualify on need, not on a perfect record, and applying is routine.
Here’s how the YMCA process works. Download the financial-assistance application, bring proof of income and dependents to any branch Welcome Center, and expect a decision in about ten business days; you renew once a year. For child-care aid specifically, apply for Missouri or Illinois state child-care assistance first, and if you’re denied, bring the denial letter. Our guide to child care assistance in Missouri walks through that state step.
Gateway Region YMCA (YMCA of Greater St. Louis) Financial-assistance details: gwrymca.org/financial-assistance Association office: 2815 Scott Avenue, Suite D, St. Louis, MO 63103 Phone: (314) 436-1177 Find your nearest branch: gwrymca.org/locations
The Boys & Girls Clubs of Greater St. Louis run on the same sliding-scale idea. Membership listings put the annual fee around $25, with some summer camps near $275, but the clubs don’t publish prices online, so call (314) 335-8000 to confirm and ask about aid. Fees slide with self-reported household income and family size, there’s no registration fee, and scholarships are available for ages 6 to 18.
Its clubs include: Herbert Hoover Club — 2901 N. Grand Blvd, St. Louis, MO 63107 — (314) 335-8100 Mathews-Dickey Club — 4245 N. Kingshighway Blvd, St. Louis, MO 63115 — (314) 382-5952 Adams Park Club — 4317 Vista Avenue, St. Louis, MO 63110 — (314) 335-8203 Teen Center of Excellence — 9200 West Florissant Ave, St. Louis, MO 63136 — (314) 335-8240 Website: bgcstl.org
### Which St. Louis programs never turn a child away?
Gene Slay’s Girls & Boys Club is the clearest answer. Program listings describe a firm policy of “no child turned away” regardless of a family’s ability to pay. Fees slide with self-reported income and household size, there’s no registration fee, and scholarships are available. In 2024 the club served 722 members and 51,276 meals (Blueprint4 listing).
The fee is set once, at registration, so you learn your monthly number up front. It serves ages 6 to 16 for City of St. Louis residents, after school and through the summer. Because that exact policy wording comes from a 211/Blueprint4 listing rather than the club’s own page, confirm it with the membership desk before you count on it.
Gene Slay’s Girls & Boys Club of St. Louis Soulard campus: 2524 S. 11th Street, St. Louis, MO 63104 Main phone: (314) 772-5661; membership desk: (314) 655-9767 Website: gsgbcstl.org
### Are there completely free after-school programs in St. Louis?
Yes, several charge families nothing at all. LifeWise StL (Kingdom House) runs a free Young Scholars after-school program, and ARCHS funds free seats for roughly 1,900 K-5 students at about 29 St. Louis sites (KSDK/St. Louis American, 2024). Free doesn’t mean less; these include homework help, meals, and sometimes a ride home.
Listings describe Young Scholars as free for ages about 6 to 13, Monday through Friday from 3:30 to 6:00 p.m. on the SLPS calendar, with homework help, MAP-test enrichment, a healthy dinner, and free transportation from school and home when needed. Because “free” and the eligible ZIP list appear in secondary listings, confirm current cost and eligibility at (314) 421-0400.
LifeWise StL (Kingdom House) Address: 1321 S. 11th Street, St. Louis, MO 63104 Phone: (314) 421-0400 (Young Scholars intake also cited at (314) 627-1241) Website: lifewisestl.org
The ARCHS-funded free seats, its After School for All Partnership, are aimed at K-5 kids whose parents work, train for a job, or attend school, and who qualify economically for free meals. That’s the door to a no-cost seat, and ARCHS or 2-1-1 can tell you which nearby school or agency has one open.
### What free mentoring and teen programs support St. Louis kids?
Two standouts cost families nothing. Big Brothers Big Sisters of Eastern Missouri matches kids with mentors at no program fee and no application fee; its 2025 impact report cites 9,228 youth served and more than 1,400 active matches. Wyman Center delivers free teen leadership programs through schools and partners. Both wrap around your child rather than replacing daytime care.
Big Brothers Big Sisters serves kids roughly 5 to 17 across St. Louis City and County, St. Charles County, and Jefferson County. Think of it as a steady, caring adult in your child’s corner, not day-to-day coverage. You can start the match at bbbsemo.org/enroll-child.
Big Brothers Big Sisters of Eastern Missouri Main office: 501 N. Grand Blvd, Suite 100, St. Louis, MO 63103 Phone: (314) 361-5900 Website: bbbsemo.org
Wyman Center focuses on teens from tight-budget households, running the Teen Outreach Program, the Teen Connection Project, and Wyman Leaders. These leadership and college-and-career programs are delivered largely free through schools and community partners, so call to find a participating site near your teen.
Wyman Center Address: 600 Kiwanis Drive, Eureka, MO 63025 Phone: (636) 938-5245 Website: wymancenter.org
### Are there free or low-cost programs in St. Charles County or the Metro-East?
Yes. Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Charles County, a separate nonprofit from the city clubs, runs after-school, summer camp, sports, and ACT prep on sliding-scale fees; membership listings run about $25 to $35 by unit (Blueprint4). Across the river, the Bethalto club serves Metro-East Illinois families. City rec centers and the library add still more free options.
Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Charles County St. Charles Unit and admin office: 1211 Lindenwood Avenue, St. Charles, MO 63301 — (636) 946-6255 O’Fallon Unit: 1 Club Way, St. Peters, MO 63376 — (636) 240-9150 Wright City Unit: 100 Wildcat Drive, Wright City, MO 63390 — (636) 251-2099 Website: bgcstc.org
Boys & Girls Clubs of Greater St. Louis — Bethalto Club (Metro-East IL) Address: 324 E Central St, Bethalto, IL 62010 Phone: (618) 377-6030 Website: bgcstl.org
Don’t overlook the free public options either. The City of St. Louis offers free summer camps, outdoor pools, sports, and youth employment; the St. Louis Public Library runs free week-long camps and summer reading; and Beyond Housing’s CDF Freedom Schools hosts a free six-week summer reading program for grades K-5. Check each program’s current-year offerings by phone or website before you plan around them.
Here’s the truth worth holding onto: these programs were built for your family, funded so a child’s afternoon or summer never hinges on a parent’s bank balance. The staff behind these desks want your call. Make the two calls, say the fee question out loud, and let your kid have the chance. If groceries are tight this month too, our guides to WIC food and nutrition help and free food giveaways happening today stack right on top, and the full St. Louis help and assistance network is behind you. You’ve got this.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are some free activities for kids in St. Louis?
A.  Plenty are completely free. The City of St. Louis offers free summer camps, outdoor pools, sports, and youth employment. The St. Louis Public Library runs free week-long camps and summer reading. LifeWise StL’s Young Scholars, Big Brothers Big Sisters mentoring, and Wyman Center’s teen programs also cost families nothing.
### Q. Where can I take my child for free?
A.  Several places charge nothing. LifeWise StL runs a free Young Scholars after-school program, and ARCHS funds free seats for roughly 1,900 K-5 students at about 29 St. Louis sites. City rec centers, outdoor pools, and the public library add more no-cost options. Call ARCHS at (314) 534-0022 to find one nearby.
### Q. Are there free summer camps?
A.  Yes. The City of St. Louis offers free summer camps, and the St. Louis Public Library runs free week-long camps alongside summer reading. Beyond Housing’s CDF Freedom Schools hosts a free six-week summer reading program for grades K-5. Check each program’s current-year offerings by phone or website before you plan around them.
### Q. What documents do I need to apply for a scholarship or sliding-scale fee?
A.  It varies, so call first, but most programs ask for a photo ID, proof of income such as recent pay stubs or a tax return, and dependent verification. Some also want your child’s birth certificate, immunization records, or a recent report card. For YMCA child-care aid, add any state denial letter.
### Q. What are some good summer camps for kids in St. Louis?
A.  Several run on sliding-scale fees or scholarships. Both Boys & Girls Clubs networks offer summer camp, sports, and ACT prep, with some camps near $275. The Gateway Region YMCA runs camp with financial assistance, and Gene Slay’s serves ages 6 to 16 through the summer. Call each site to confirm dates and aid.
### Q. How do parents afford summer camps?
A.  Four tools carry most families: sliding-scale fees, scholarships, formal financial-assistance applications, and the state child-care subsidy. The Gateway Region YMCA alone awards about $2.58 million in assistance each year, and Gene Slay’s turns no child away. You qualify on need, not a perfect record, so ask about aid when you register.
### Q. What if I can’t afford summer school?
A.  Price is rarely the real gate. Sliding-scale fees, scholarships, and formal financial assistance keep summer programs within reach, and Gene Slay’s Girls & Boys Club turns no child away regardless of ability to pay. Start by dialing 2-1-1 or calling ARCHS at (314) 534-0022 to find an affordable seat near you.
### Q. Can I still get help if I was denied state child-care assistance?
A.  Yes. The Gateway Region YMCA asks families to apply for Missouri or Illinois state child-care assistance first, then accepts you with the denial letter and applies its own financial aid. A state denial is not the end of the road. Bring that letter to your nearest branch Welcome Center to keep going.

## Youth and Teen Emergency Shelter in St. Louis: Runaway Help
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/youth-and-teen-emergency-shelter-in-st-louis-runaway-help
It’s late, the phone is down to twelve percent, and the couch you crashed on last night isn’t an option again. Maybe home stopped feeling safe. Maybe a fight went too far, or there was never really a steady home to begin with. If you’re a teenager reading this in the dark, or an aunt, a coach, a teacher, a friend trying to help one, take one slow breath. You are not in trouble for needing a bed. St. Louis has people whose whole job is to open a door for a young person tonight, no lecture attached.
This guide lists the real places, the real phone numbers, and exactly who each one is for, so you can stop searching and start dialing. We keep a wider guide to help and assistance across St. Louis, but a safe place comes first. One thing before anything else: if someone is in immediate danger right now, call 911.
### Where can a homeless or runaway teen get emergency shelter in St. Louis tonight?
For a safe place tonight, Covenant House Missouri (2727 N Kingshighway Blvd) takes walk-ins 24/7 for ages 16 to 24: call 314-533-2241. Younger teens in St. Charles County can reach Youth In Need at 636-946-3771. Anywhere, call the National Runaway Safeline at 1-800-786-2929 or text HOME to 66008. In danger? Call 911.
Think of it as two tracks running at once. Track one is getting somewhere safe tonight, because a walk-in shelter never asks you to have your whole life sorted out first. Track two is everything after: school, family, what comes next. Those can wait until morning. Right now, a bed and a locked door are the only goals that matter.
Which door you knock on mostly depends on age. Covenant House Missouri serves older teens and young adults, 16 to 24. Youth In Need takes younger teens in St. Charles County. Each one is described in full below, with the address and the number that reaches a real person any hour of the night.
### Which St. Louis youth shelters take walk-ins right now?
A walk-in shelter means exactly that: a young person can show up without an appointment, a referral, or a parent on the phone, and staff will help from there. The three below keep a 24-hour door or crisis line for youth. Call first if you can, both to confirm space and so someone is watching for you.
### Covenant House Missouri
Covenant House is the flagship for older teens and young adults with nowhere safe to sleep. It’s open 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, and walk-ins are welcome. Beyond a bed, there’s on-site health care, meals, help with school and work, and case management, all free.
Covenant House Missouri Address: 2727 N Kingshighway Blvd, St. Louis, MO 63113 Phone: 314-533-2241 (local, 24/7) Ages: 16-24 Website: covenanthousemo.org Walk-ins accepted around the clock; all services free.
### Youth In Need (St. Charles County)
Youth In Need runs a small emergency residence for younger teens in crisis in St. Charles. It’s open around the clock, takes walk-in intakes, needs no referral, and charges no fee. Because the age range varies by source, call the 24-hour line first to confirm they can serve the young person’s age tonight.
Youth In Need — Emergency Shelter Shelter: 529 Jefferson Street, St. Charles, MO 63301 24-hour crisis line: 636-946-3771 Main office: 636-946-5600 Ages: roughly 10-18 (call to confirm the current range) Website: youthinneed.org
### Annie Malone Children & Family Services
Annie Malone operates a 24-hour Crisis Center on the city’s north side with emergency shelter, food, clothing, and urgent medical help. Its crisis programs have historically centered on younger children, so call the 24-hour crisis line first to confirm they can take a teen tonight.
Annie Malone Children & Family Services Address: 2612 Annie Malone Dr, St. Louis, MO 63113 Main phone: 314-531-0120 24-hour crisis line: 844-803-7233 Website: anniemalone.org
If the young person is 18 or older and none of these fit, our guide to emergency homeless shelters in St. Louis covers adult options across the metro tonight.
### What if it isn’t safe at home, or a teen is being abused?
If a young person is being hurt at home, or is scared they will be, Missouri has a free hotline that answers 24 hours a day, every day. The Child Abuse & Neglect Hotline takes calls from anyone: the teen, a relative, a neighbor, a teacher. If someone is being harmed right now, call 911 first.
Missouri Child Abuse & Neglect Hotline Phone: 1-800-392-3738 (24/7, anyone may call) Immediate danger: call 911
Can a teen go to a shelter without a parent’s permission? Often, at least enough to get help started. Youth In Need accepts walk-in intakes with no referral, and Covenant House serves 16 to 24 directly. Intake staff explain what happens next and, when the law requires it, help involve family or the Children’s Division. The safest move is to call the shelter’s line and simply ask.
### Where can homeless teens get food, a shower, and clean clothes during the day?
Not every young person needs a bed; some just need a warm, safe place to land in the daytime. The Epworth Drop-In Center offers hot meals, showers, laundry, clothing, and a food pantry, plus help with housing, jobs, and free health screenings. Important: it’s daytime only, not an overnight shelter.
Epworth Drop-In Center & Street Outreach Address: 7520 Natural Bridge Road, Normandy, MO 63121 Phone: 314-918-3470 (Older Youth Services) Ages: 11-20 Hours: Monday to Thursday 12:00-5:00 PM, Friday 1:00-5:00 PM Website: epworth.org
Epworth’s street outreach team also meets homeless teens where they already are, across the region. For more places to warm up, wash up, and regroup during business hours, see our guide to daytime drop-in and day centers in St. Louis.
### Is there free help for a teen being trafficked or exploited in St. Louis?
Yes, and it’s free and confidential. If a young person is being trafficked or sexually exploited, the National Human Trafficking Hotline answers 24/7 at 1-888-373-7888, or text 233733. For a safe place tonight, pair that call with Covenant House Missouri (314-533-2241), which serves trafficked and at-risk youth directly.
For longer-term recovery, two local organizations specialize in this work. Neither is a walk-in emergency shelter; both take young people through a referral into structured, longer-term care, so they’re the next step after the immediate crisis is stable.
The Covering House (referral-based, not walk-in) Serves survivors of sex trafficking and exploitation, roughly ages 12-18. The residential home’s location is kept confidential for safety. Phone: 314-962-6450 Mail: P.O. Box 431, Arnold, MO 63010 Website: thecoveringhouse.org
Marygrove (residential and crisis respite, not self-referral walk-in) Provides 24-hour crisis care and residential programs, usually through the Children’s Division rather than a walk-in intake. Address: 2705 Mullanphy Lane, Florissant, MO 63031 Phone: 314-830-6201 Website: marygrovechildren.org
### Which 24/7 hotlines help runaway youth and worried parents?
When you’re not sure where to start, a hotline is the fastest first move. The National Runaway Safeline is the federally designated line for runaway and homeless youth, free and confidential 24 hours a day. It helps young people and parents alike, and it can even arrange a free bus ticket home.
National Runaway Safeline Call: 1-800-786-2929 (1-800-RUNAWAY) Text: HOME to 66008 Chat: 1800runaway.org, 24/7 Home Free program: a free Greyhound ticket to reunite a youth with family or a safe home.
For a mental-health or suicide crisis, call or text 988. It’s the guaranteed 24/7 line, answered locally by Behavioral Health Response, which also runs a youth line at 314-819-8802 and a crisis line at 314-469-6644 (text BHEARD to 31658). For peer support in the evenings, Kids Under Twenty One (KUTO) is staffed by trained youth volunteers at 1-888-644-5886; pair it with 988 for overnight coverage.
Are you a parent whose teen just took off? Call the National Runaway Safeline for family support, reach out to 988 if there’s a mental-health crisis, and file a police report so your child is entered as missing. There is no waiting period to report a missing minor, and the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children can help at 1-800-843-5678. For ongoing counseling, see our guide to teen mental health and crisis help in St. Louis.
Here’s the truth these organizations live by: being found is survival. A young person who knows one door will open, one number will answer, is a young person who makes it through the night. If you’re that teen, you deserve a safe place, and none of this costs a dime. If you’re the adult who loves one, you just found the list. Save the numbers, then make the call.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Where do I go if I have nowhere to stay?
A.  If you have nowhere safe tonight and you’re 16 to 24, go to Covenant House Missouri at 2727 N Kingshighway Blvd; walk-ins are welcome 24 hours a day. Call 314-533-2241 first if you can. Not sure where to start? The National Runaway Safeline answers 24/7 at 1-800-786-2929.
### Q. Where can a homeless 16 year old go?
A.  A homeless 16-year-old can go to Covenant House Missouri, 2727 N Kingshighway Blvd, which serves ages 16 to 24 around the clock. Beyond a bed, there’s on-site health care, meals, and case management, all free. Walk-ins are welcome; call 314-533-2241 so staff can watch for them.
### Q. Can a 16 year old go to a homeless shelter?
A.  Yes, at least enough to get help started. Covenant House Missouri serves ages 16 to 24 directly, with walk-ins welcome 24/7 and no referral needed. Intake staff explain what happens next and, when the law requires it, help involve family or the Children’s Division. Call 314-533-2241 and ask.
### Q. Where can I find emergency housing in St. Louis?
A.  For a safe place tonight, Covenant House Missouri (314-533-2241) takes walk-ins 24/7 for ages 16 to 24. Younger teens in St. Charles County can reach Youth In Need at 636-946-3771. Annie Malone runs a 24-hour crisis center at 844-803-7233. For adults 18 and older, see our emergency homeless shelters guide.
### Q. What happens to homeless minors?
A.  A homeless minor can get help fast. Youth In Need takes walk-in intakes for younger teens with no referral or fee; call 636-946-3771. Intake staff explain what happens next and, when the law requires it, help involve family or the Children’s Division. If anyone is in immediate danger, call 911.
### Q. What to do with a homeless teenager?
A.  Get the teen somewhere safe tonight first, then sort out everything else in the morning. Covenant House Missouri takes walk-ins 24/7 for ages 16 to 24 at 314-533-2241. Younger teens in St. Charles can reach Youth In Need at 636-946-3771. For guidance, call the National Runaway Safeline at 1-800-786-2929.
### Q. Can a runaway get a free bus ticket home?
A.  Sometimes, yes. The National Runaway Safeline’s Home Free program partners with Greyhound to reunite a young person with family or a safe alternate home at no cost. It starts with a conversation, so call 1-800-786-2929 or text HOME to 66008 to see whether it fits the situation.
### Q. I’m a parent and my teen ran away — who do I call?
A.  Start with the National Runaway Safeline at 1-800-786-2929, which supports families, not just youth. Call or text 988 if there’s a mental-health crisis, and file a police report so your child is entered as missing. There is no waiting period to report a missing minor in Missouri.

## Foster Care in Missouri and Aging Out Support in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/foster-care-in-missouri-and-aging-out-support-in-st-louis
The question can arrive quietly. A caseworker asks a couple, over coffee, whether they’ve ever thought about fostering. Across the metro, in another kitchen, a seventeen-year-old marks a calendar toward a birthday most teens count down to, and she quietly dreads. Foster care in Missouri holds both of those moments at once: the family thinking about opening a door, and the young person about to walk through one alone.
This guide is written for both of you. If you’re weighing whether to become a foster parent, we lay out the real steps, who to call, and what it costs, which is nothing. If you’re aging out, or you love someone who is, you’ll find the health coverage, housing, and college money Missouri keeps ready for former foster youth, including free MO HealthNet coverage all the way to age 26. For the wider picture, keep our guide to help and assistance across St. Louis nearby. Let’s begin.
### What support is available for youth aging out of foster care in St. Louis?
You don’t lose everything at 18. If you were in Missouri foster care around your 18th birthday, you keep free MO HealthNet coverage to age 26. The Chafee Older Youth Program (ages 14-23) adds housing help, and the ETV pays up to $5,000 a year. Start with your caseworker or the Foster & Adoptive Care Coalition at (314) 367-8373.
Here’s what the paperwork rarely says out loud: turning 18 in foster care is not a cliff. Missouri built a bridge, and it runs for years. The catch? Most of it won’t come find you. You have to reach for it, or ask someone to reach alongside you. If you have a Children’s Division worker or an Older Youth Transition Specialist, that person is your fastest door to every benefit below.
### Free health coverage until age 26
This one surprises people, so read it twice. Young adults who were in Missouri foster care around their 18th birthday qualify for free MO HealthNet (Medicaid) until they turn 26, with no income test at all. The Medicaid.gov former-foster-care rule counts youth who were in care any time in the 30 days before turning 18. You don’t have to be broke, employed, or in school to keep it.
Moved here from another state’s foster system? Missouri also covers residents under 26 who spent at least six months in another state’s care and had Medicaid at 18. When you reach 26, reapply through the Family Support Division for a different category so your coverage doesn’t lapse. Ask your caseworker to confirm your enrollment before any birthday sneaks up.
### The Chafee Older Youth Program (ages 14-23)
Missouri’s Older Youth Program is the Chafee “Foster Care Program for Successful Transition to Adulthood.” The state Department of Social Services runs it for youth ages 14 to 23 who are in, or were in, Children’s Division custody. It works across three lanes: Education Services, Help with Independence, and Finance and Life Skills.
An Older Youth Transition Specialist is the person who verifies what you qualify for and connects you to housing help and benefits. If you don’t know who yours is, ask your Children’s Division office, or let the Foster & Adoptive Care Coalition’s Navigator find out for you. One conversation can open several doors at once.
### Money for college and job training: ETV and Missouri Reach
Two programs help foster youth pay for what comes after high school, and you can often use both. The Education & Training Voucher (ETV) covers up to $5,000 a year for tuition, books, supplies, and living costs while you study. Funds are limited and first-come, first-served, so the real advice is simple: ask early.
The ETV application route changed recently, so don’t trust an old online form you find floating around. Ask your Older Youth Transition Specialist or Children’s Division worker for the current ETV application and deadline. They’ll point you to the live process rather than a dead link.
Missouri Reach is the other big one. It waives tuition and fees at Missouri’s public colleges and universities for eligible foster youth. To keep it, you complete at least 100 hours of community service or a public internship each year, and you apply for other non-loan aid first. Most students must apply by their 21st birthday, so put this on your list now.
### Where can a young person who aged out find housing in St. Louis?
Start with Covenant House Missouri, the metro’s round-the-clock anchor for young adults ages 16 to 24. It’s open 24/7, free, and offers emergency beds with private bedrooms plus transitional housing for up to two years. Beyond Covenant House, Epworth, Marygrove, and Annie Malone all run transitional and independent-living programs across the region.
Aging out without a plan is more common than anyone admits, and it’s nobody’s fault. If you need a bed this week, call one of these numbers directly. If you’re facing a true crisis tonight, our guide to youth and teen emergency shelter in St. Louis lists faster options, and for longer-term stability see finding transitional housing in St. Louis.
Covenant House Missouri Address: 2727 N. Kingshighway Blvd., St. Louis, MO 63113 Phone: 314-533-2241 Website: covenanthouse.org Ages 16-24, open 24/7 and free. Emergency shelter (60-90 days), transitional housing up to two years, on-site medical and mental health care, plus employment and education support. LGBTQ+ affirming; walk-ins welcome.
Epworth Children & Family Services Main campus: 110 North Elm Avenue, Webster Groves, MO 63119 Main phone: 314-961-5718 Normandy Drop-In Center: 7520 Natural Bridge Road, St. Louis, MO 63121; 314-222-4877 Website: epworth.org Runs the Chafee program, transitional and independent living, a youth drop-in center, and street outreach for at-risk youth.
Marygrove Address: 2705 Mullanphy Lane, Florissant, MO 63031 Phone: (314) 830-6201 Website: marygrovechildren.org Transitional and independent living with scattered-site apartments and houses where young adults (roughly ages 17-20) live on their own with support as they leave care.
Annie Malone Children & Family Services Address: 2612 Annie Malone Dr., St. Louis, MO 63113 Phone: (314) 531-0120 Website: anniemalone.com A St. Louis institution since 1888. Transitional and independent living, plus an Economic Mobility Program for youth 16-21 that blends academics, job training, and mental health support.
Foster & Adoptive Care Coalition — Older Youth Readiness Program Phone: (314) 367-8373 Website: foster-adopt.org A Navigator helps youth ages 13-24 secure housing, food, clothing, jobs, medical care, and continued education. Serves St. Louis City and County plus Jefferson, Franklin, and St. Charles counties. Full address in the agencies section below.
### How do you become a foster parent in Missouri?
You need to be at least 21, and it costs you nothing. The Missouri Department of Social Services charges no fee for the foster-parent license or for the background checks it runs. You’ll apply, complete free pre-service training, host a home study, and pass a health physical. Call the Children’s Division at 800-554-2222 to begin, or work with a local licensing agency.
Wondering whether you’re “qualified” enough? Most people who ask that question already have what matters most: steady ground and room to care. The formal requirements are practical, not perfect-family fantasies. Here’s the honest checklist.
### What are the requirements to foster in Missouri?
Be at least 21 years old. Pass background checks, which apply to every household member age 17 and up. Show adequate income to cover your own household, since foster payments support the child, not your bills. Have room in your home, and complete pre-service training, a home study, and a health physical. That’s the core of it.
Notice what’s not on the list. You don’t need to be married, own a home, or have a big income. Singles and renters foster all the time. If you’re raising your own kids, working full-time, or new to the area, a licensing agency can look at your situation and tell you what to expect. Fostering can sit alongside a busy life; if child care is part of your plan, see our guide to child care assistance in Missouri.
### What does it cost, and how long does it take?
The license itself is free, and so are the background checks and the required training. What it asks for instead is time: an application, a training series, a home study visit, and a health check. Timelines vary by agency and by how quickly paperwork moves, so the best move is to call and ask your agency for their current schedule.
A quick tip from families who’ve done it: pick one agency and let them guide you, rather than juggling several. Every licensed agency in the metro can walk you through the exact same state process, so you’re free to choose the one whose people you click with.
### Which St. Louis agencies license and support foster families?
Several trusted agencies handle licensing across the metro, and the Foster & Adoptive Care Coalition serves youth and families in five counties: St. Louis City, St. Louis County, Jefferson, Franklin, and St. Charles. The Missouri Children’s Division is the state licensing authority, but you rarely need to drive to Jefferson City. Start with a phone call to any name below.
Missouri Children’s Division (Department of Social Services) Become-a-foster-parent line: 800-554-2222 Child Abuse & Neglect Hotline: 800-392-3738 Website: dss.mo.gov/cd/foster-care The state authority that licenses foster parents and runs the Older Youth/Chafee transition program. Licensing happens through regional and county offices across the St. Louis area, so call the 800 line to be routed locally.
Foster & Adoptive Care Coalition Address: 1220 N. Lindbergh Blvd., St. Louis, MO 63132 Phone: (314) 367-8373 Website: foster-adopt.org Recruitment and licensing support for foster and adoptive parents, plus the Older Youth Readiness Program for young people leaving care. Known for national models like Extreme Recruitment and 30 Days to Family.
KVC Missouri — St. Louis office Address: 330 N. Gore Ave., Webster Groves, MO 63119 Phone: (844) 424-3577 Website: missouri.kvc.org Foster-parent licensing, case management, family strengthening, children’s mental health care, and independent-living support. KVC Missouri took over the former Great Circle operations in Missouri in 2023 and now serves families from the Gore Avenue site.
Lutheran Family and Children’s Services of Missouri (LFCS) Address: 9666 Olive Blvd., St. Louis, MO 63132 (call ahead to confirm the current suite) Phone: (314) 787-5100 (toll-free 866-326-5327) Website: lfcsmo.org Foster care, adoption, counseling, and youth mentoring across Missouri.
Epworth Children & Family Services and Marygrove, both listed with full contact details in the housing section above, also license and support foster families. Don’t rule them out if their location or programs fit your family better.
Whether you’re opening your home or leaving one, the same truth holds: nobody does this alone, and being found is how a hard season stays just a season. Make one call this week, to an agency, a caseworker, or a Navigator, and let a real person carry the next step with you. For everything else a St. Louis neighbor might need, keep our guide to help and assistance across St. Louis close.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are the requirements to foster a child in Missouri?
A.  You must be at least 21, pass background checks (every household member 17 and older is screened), show adequate income, and have room in your home. You’ll also finish pre-service training, a home study, and a health physical. Marital status and home ownership are not requirements, per the Missouri Department of Social Services.
### Q. What disqualifies someone from being a foster parent?
A.  Missouri screens every household member age 17 and older with background checks, so a serious criminal or child-abuse history can be a barrier. What doesn’t disqualify you: being single, renting, having a modest income, or not owning a home. Singles and renters foster all the time, so ask your agency about your own situation.
### Q. What age is best to become a foster parent?
A.  There’s no single best age. Missouri’s only age rule is that you must be at least 21, with no upper limit, so people foster in their twenties through their sixties and beyond. What matters more than age is stable income, safe space, and time. If you’re 21 or older, you can start today.
### Q. How much money do foster parents get in Missouri?
A.  The state provides foster payments meant to cover the child’s needs, not your own bills. That’s why Missouri asks you to show adequate income for your household before licensing. The license itself, the required training, and the background checks all cost nothing. Ask your licensing agency for the current payment rates when you apply.
### Q. Can you choose to foster only babies?
A.  You can share the ages you feel ready to parent with your licensing agency, and they’ll weigh it during your home study. Keep in mind the young people in this guide, though: teens and older youth aging out of care are often the ones who most need a stable home. Ask your agency where the need is greatest.
### Q. What is the hardest part of fostering?
A.  Every family’s answer differs, but two hard truths run through this guide. Placements can be uncertain, and you may not know how long a child will stay. And the young people who reach 18 still in care can face adulthood with too little support. That’s exactly why the aging-out help here matters.
### Q. What benefits do youth get when they age out of foster care in Missouri?
A.  Free MO HealthNet (Medicaid) coverage to age 26, Chafee Older Youth services for housing help and life skills, Education & Training Voucher money up to $5,000 a year, and Missouri Reach tuition waivers at public colleges. Your Children’s Division worker or Older Youth Transition Specialist confirms exactly what you qualify for.
### Q. Where can a young person who aged out of foster care get housing in St. Louis?
A.  Covenant House Missouri (2727 N. Kingshighway) houses youth ages 16-24 around the clock, with transitional housing up to two years. Epworth, Marygrove, and Annie Malone run transitional and independent-living programs too. The Foster & Adoptive Care Coalition’s Navigator can line up a bed and benefits. Walk-ins are welcome at Covenant House.

## Teen Mental-Health and Crisis Help in St. Louis: Who to Call
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/teen-mental-health-and-crisis-help-in-st-louis
Maybe it’s the bedroom door that stays shut now, or a text you weren’t meant to read. Maybe your teenager said the words out loud, and the floor dropped out from under you. Or maybe you’re the teenager, reading this late at night because everything feels like too much and you don’t know who to tell. Wherever you’re standing, take one breath. Help in St. Louis is closer, kinder, and more real than it can feel right now, and you don’t need the perfect words to reach it.
This guide keeps it simple. The exact number to call in a crisis, where a teen can talk to someone free and confidential, and how to find counseling that doesn’t hinge on having insurance or money. It covers the City, the County, St. Charles, and eastern Missouri. We keep a broader guide to help and assistance across St. Louis, but if tonight is hard, start with the first number below.
### What number do you call for a teen mental-health crisis in St. Louis?
Call or text 988, the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, any time. In St. Louis, local counselors at Behavioral Health Response answer it, free and around the clock. For a counselor who works specifically with young people, call BHR’s Youth Connection Helpline at 314-819-8802. If a teen is in immediate danger, call 911. LGBTQ+ teens can also reach The Trevor Project at 1-866-488-7386.
Here’s the part that matters most: a teen can reach any of these on their own. No parent has to be in the room, and the call or text is confidential. If you’re a parent, you can call too, to talk through what you’re seeing and what to do next. These are the numbers to keep on the fridge and saved in a phone.
988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline Call or text 988, or chat at 988lifeline.org. Free, confidential, 24/7. In the St. Louis region a local BHR counselor answers. Press 1 for Veterans, Press 2 for Spanish.
Behavioral Health Response (BHR) Address: 5501 Delmar Blvd., Suite B300, St. Louis, MO 63112 Local crisis line: 314-819-8811 Youth Connection Helpline: 314-819-8802 (toll-free 844-985-8282) Web chat: bhrstl.org Free, all ages, 24/7, no insurance needed. BHR is Missouri’s largest 988 provider and runs mobile crisis outreach across the region.
The Trevor Project (LGBTQ+ young people under 25) Call 1-866-488-7386, text START to 678-678, or chat at TheTrevorProject.org. Free, confidential, 24/7, with counselors trained on LGBTQ+ experiences.
Call 911 for immediate danger to life: an active suicide attempt, an overdose, or a serious injury.
### What happens when a teen calls or texts 988, and will they send the police?
You reach a trained local counselor, not a dispatcher. The large majority of 988 contacts are handled entirely by phone or text, start to finish. Emergency services are sent only in the smaller number of cases where someone is in imminent danger to life. The call is free, confidential, and a teen can end it whenever they want.
We say this plainly because the fear of police showing up is the single most common reason a teen won’t pick up the phone. The counselor’s whole job is to listen, help the moment settle, and figure out a next step together. Sometimes that’s a plan for the night. Sometimes it’s a follow-up call. Only rarely is it anything more.
### 988 or 911: which one do you use?
Call 911 or head to the nearest emergency room when life is in immediate danger, an active attempt, an overdose, a serious injury. Call or text 988 for an emotional or mental-health crisis, frightening thoughts, or when a teen simply needs someone to talk to. Not sure which fits? 988 counselors can help you decide, and connect you to mobile crisis help when it’s needed.
### Is there a crisis line just for teens in St. Louis?
Yes. BHR’s Youth Connection Helpline (314-819-8802, toll-free 844-985-8282) connects young people to counselors trained for their age, free and 24/7. KUTO, Kids Under Twenty One, runs a helpline answered by trained teen and young-adult volunteers, so a struggling teen can talk to a peer who actually gets it. Both are free and confidential.
KUTO (Kids Under Twenty One) Crisis Helpline: 314-644-5886 (toll-free 888-644-5886) Business office: 314-963-7571 Free, confidential, youth-to-youth peer support for teens, LGBTQ+ youth, and parents across Missouri. Hours vary, so call to confirm when the helpline is staffed. For overnight or immediate help, use 988. Website: kuto.org
Crisis Text Line Text HOME to 741741, or text HOLA to 741741 in Spanish. Free, confidential, 24/7, staffed by trained volunteer counselors. Texting can feel easier than talking out loud, and that’s completely okay.
### Where can your teen get free or low-cost counseling in St. Louis?
More places than you’d expect, and cost should not be the wall it seems. Youth In Need offers counseling at no cost for kids under 19. Compass Health Network, Provident, and Saint Louis Counseling all use sliding-scale fees and accept Medicaid (MO HealthNet). CHADS Coalition offers youth suicide-prevention counseling through partner schools. Our guide to free and low-cost mental-health help in St. Louis goes wider still.

### How do you know when a teen needs help right now?
Trust the shift you can feel. Watch for talk of death, suicide, or being a burden; giving away treasured belongings; pulling away from friends and the things they used to love; big changes in sleep or eating; new drug or alcohol use; self-harm; deep hopelessness; or a sudden, eerie calm after a dark stretch. Any talk of suicide is a reason to call 988 today, not next week.
You will not “plant the idea” by asking directly. Ask the plain question: are you thinking about hurting yourself, or about dying? Naming it out loud, gently and without panic, tells a teen they can finally put the weight down. If drugs or alcohol are part of the picture, our guide to addiction and substance-use treatment in St. Louis can help you find the next door.
### Where to start if it isn’t an emergency
Start with the people who already know your teen. A pediatrician can screen and refer. A school counselor sees them five days a week. NAMI St. Louis can point you toward the right kind of support, and the sliding-scale providers above take new clients without a referral. You don’t have to diagnose anything to make the first call.
NAMI St. Louis Address: 12125 Woodcrest Executive Dr., Ste 205, St. Louis, MO 63141 HelpLine: 314-962-4670 (Mon-Fri 8:30am-5pm) Free peer support groups, family education like Family-to-Family, and “Ending the Silence” presentations for middle and high schoolers. This is information and referral, not a crisis line, so use 988 for emergencies. National NAMI HelpLine: 800-950-6264, or text “NAMI” to 62640. Website: namistl.org
### A last word, for the parent and for the teen
You found this page. That already counts for something. Reaching out isn’t weakness or failure, it’s the bravest, most ordinary thing a person can do on a hard day. Every number here exists because someone believed a young life is worth answering the phone for, at 3 a.m. or 3 p.m., insurance or no insurance.
Being found, and finding help, is how the worst night stays just one night. Save 988 in the phone right now, before you close this tab. Then, when you’re ready, our full St. Louis help and assistance network is here for whatever comes next, from housing to food to counseling. You are not doing this alone.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How to help a teenager with mental health issues?
A.  Trust the shift you feel, and ask directly; you won’t plant the idea by asking. Start with people who know them: a pediatrician can screen and refer, a school counselor sees them daily, and NAMI St. Louis can guide you. Any talk of suicide means calling or texting 988 today.
### Q. What to do when your child needs mental help?
A.  For a crisis, call or text 988; local BHR counselors answer, free and around the clock, and a teen can reach them alone. If it isn’t an emergency, a pediatrician or school counselor can refer, and sliding-scale providers take new clients without one. BHR’s Youth Connection Helpline is 314-819-8802.
### Q. What are some signs that a teenager might have mental illness?
A.  Trust the shift you can feel. Common signs include pulling away from friends, big changes in sleep or eating, new drug or alcohol use, giving away belongings, self-harm, deep hopelessness, or talk of death and suicide. A sudden, eerie calm after a dark stretch can also be a warning.
### Q. What are 5 warning signs of depression in teenagers?
A.  Five to watch: pulling away from friends and the things they used to love; big changes in sleep or eating; deep hopelessness; self-harm; and talk of death or being a burden. These overlap with crisis warning signs, so any mention of suicide means calling or texting 988 today, not next week.
### Q. What is the best treatment for teen depression?
A.  There’s no single fix, but professional counseling is the usual starting point. A pediatrician can screen and refer, and sliding-scale providers like Youth In Need, Compass Health Network, Provident, and Saint Louis Counseling offer teen therapy, many accepting Medicaid. For a crisis, call or text 988 before anything else.
### Q. Where can I send my troubled child for free in Missouri?
A.  Youth In Need provides counseling at no cost for young people under 19 across St. Louis, St. Charles, and Lincoln Counties, no referral needed. CHADS Coalition offers free youth suicide-prevention counseling through partner schools. For free, confidential crisis support any time, a teen can call or text 988 or the Youth Connection Helpline.
### Q. What happens when you call or text 988, and will they send the police?
A.  You reach a trained local counselor, in St. Louis that’s BHR. The large majority of contacts are handled entirely by phone or text. Emergency services are sent only when there’s imminent danger to life, a small share of cases. It’s free, confidential, and you can hang up any time.
### Q. Is there a crisis line for LGBTQ+ teens in St. Louis?
A.  Yes. The Trevor Project is free and 24/7 for LGBTQ+ young people: call 1-866-488-7386 or text START to 678-678, with counselors trained on LGBTQ+ experiences. KUTO also serves LGBTQ+ youth. Note that 988’s dedicated LGBTQ+ youth “Press 3” option ended in July 2025.

## Free Tutoring, GED, and Dropout Help for St. Louis Youth
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/free-tutoring-ged-and-dropout-help-in-st-louis
Picture a kitchen table at 8 p.m. A tenth-grader stares at an algebra worksheet, you want to help, and the last tutor you priced cost more than a week of groceries. Here’s the part almost nobody says out loud: in St. Louis, some of the best tutoring costs nothing at all. A library card can put a live tutor on your kid’s screen tonight. A diploma is free to prepare for. And leaving school early is not a locked door.
This guide is only the free help, no paid learning centers and no monthly memberships you can’t swing. We pulled together the real programs across the City, the County, St. Charles, and the wider metro, with the addresses and phone numbers you can use today. It lives inside our broader guide to help and assistance across St. Louis. Let’s get your student unstuck.
### Where can I get free tutoring in St. Louis?
Any student with a St. Louis Public Library or St. Louis County Library card gets free live online tutoring, grades K-12, through Brainfuse. Nonprofits like Gene Slay’s Girls & Boys Club, Boys & Girls Clubs of Greater St. Louis, UrbanFUTURE, and College Bound add free in-person homework help. For a diploma, free GED and HiSET prep runs through several colleges.
Start with the fastest free win. If your family already has a library card, you already have a tutor. Both major systems here, the City’s and the County’s, pay for a live online service called Brainfuse, and your card unlocks it from any laptop or phone. No appointment, no fee, no income check. That is the whole point of this page: you do not need money to get your kid help tonight.
### St. Louis County Library — Brainfuse HelpNow
St. Louis County Library gives every cardholder free access to Brainfuse HelpNow: live online tutoring, homework help, and test prep in a secure virtual classroom. It covers grades K-12, with extra resources for early-college students, adult learners, job seekers, and veterans. Get a card at any branch, then log in through slcl.org and connect with a tutor.
St. Louis County Library (Brainfuse HelpNow) Address: 1640 S. Lindbergh Blvd, St. Louis, MO 63131 Phone: 314-994-3300 Website: slcl.org (service page: slcl.org/news/brainfuse-online-tutoring) Free with any St. Louis County Library card.
### St. Louis Public Library — free online homework help
The City’s system, St. Louis Public Library, also offers free online homework help to cardholders in grades K-12. Local coverage describes a Brainfuse-style tutoring service with evening hours, but the library’s tutoring page moves around, so we’d rather you confirm than trust a stale link. Call 314-241-2288 or check slpl.org for the current service and hours before you count on them.
St. Louis Public Library (Central Library) Address: 1301 Olive Street, St. Louis, MO 63103 Phone: 314-241-2288 Website: slpl.org Free online homework help with a City library card; call to confirm current tutoring hours.
### What free after-school tutoring and homework help exists for St. Louis kids?
More than most parents realize, and it is woven into after-school and summer programs kids already enjoy. Four nonprofits stand out: Gene Slay’s Girls & Boys Club, Boys & Girls Clubs of Greater St. Louis, UrbanFUTURE, and College Bound. Each folds one-on-one or small-group homework help into free or low-cost programming, so the tutoring feels less like a chore and more like belonging.
### Gene Slay’s Girls & Boys Club of St. Louis
This Soulard club builds one-on-one and group homework help right into its after-school and summer programming. Membership is the entry point, and staff can walk you through age bands and sign-up when you call. It is a warm, low-pressure place for a kid who needs steady help and a snack more than another lecture.
Gene Slay’s Girls & Boys Club of St. Louis Address: 2524 South 11th Street, St. Louis, MO 63104 Phone: 314-772-5661 Email: gsgbc@gsgbcstl.org Website: gsgbcstl.org Free club programming for youth; ask about current age ranges at intake.
### Boys & Girls Clubs of Greater St. Louis
Boys & Girls Clubs of Greater St. Louis runs daily academic support and tutoring through its Power Hour program, alongside mentoring, sports, and wellness. The focus is underserved youth across North St. Louis, with several club sites. Call the main office to find the nearest club and confirm ages and hours for your child.
Boys & Girls Clubs of Greater St. Louis Address: 2901 North Grand Blvd, St. Louis, MO 63107 Phone: 314-335-8000 Website: bgcstl.org Free and low-cost programming, K-12; ask which club sites serve your neighborhood.
### UrbanFUTURE
UrbanFUTURE pairs middle-schoolers, mainly grades 6-8, with two free programs: INSPIRE for mentoring and IMPACT for tutoring. The goal is to get urban students ready to thrive in high school and beyond. Because the website was intermittent during our research, call 314-480-3725 to confirm the current site and that enrollment is open before you visit.
UrbanFUTURE Address: 2823 Olive St., St. Louis, MO 63103 Phone: 314-480-3725 Website: urbanfuturestl.org (confirm the site is live) Free for students, grades 6-8; call to confirm current enrollment.
### College Bound
College Bound supports promising students from under-resourced backgrounds with free tutoring, academic coaching, ACT prep, early college credit, and mental-health and stabilization support. It is application-based and aimed at the long game: high school success that carries into college. Call 314-361-4441 to ask about eligibility and how to apply.
College Bound Address: 110 N. Jefferson Ave, St. Louis, MO 63103 Phone: 314-361-4441 Website: collegeboundstl.org Free; application-based for students from under-resourced backgrounds.
### How do I get my GED in Missouri?
Missouri accepts two high school equivalency tests, the GED and the HiSET. You create your own account and schedule directly with the publisher at GED.com or HiSET.org, because a test center cannot book the exam for you. Free prep classes are widely available, and the statewide locator lives at ael.mo.gov. You must be 17 to test, or 16 with an approved age waiver.
Here is the reassuring part: you do not have to take a class before you test. Some people study on their own and schedule when ready. Others want the structure of a free class, and that is a smart choice too. Either way, passing one of the two tests earns the same result, a high school equivalency that colleges and employers accept across Missouri.
What about cost? The test itself carries a fee, commonly around $120 for all subjects, though fees change and fee assistance exists. The prep classes, though, are free. For current fees, testing rules, and the essentials, the state keeps two plain-language sites: hse.mo.gov for high school equivalency and ael.mo.gov to find free classes near you. You can also reach the Missouri Department of Elementary and Secondary Education at 573-751-4212.
### Where are the free GED and HiSET classes in St. Louis?
Three well-run programs offer free GED and HiSET prep across the metro: St. Louis Public Schools Adult Education, St. Louis Community College’s FastTrack, and St. Charles Community College. All follow Missouri’s adult-education rules, generally age 17 and up, out of high school, with some 16-year-olds eligible under specific conditions. Classes are genuinely free; only the final test carries a fee.
### St. Louis Public Schools — Adult Education & Literacy
SLPS runs free HiSET and GED preparation, along with literacy, ESL, and workforce-readiness classes, in both day and evening sessions Monday through Thursday, with some Friday classes. It is open to the community, not just SLPS families. Call 314-231-3720 to ask about the next start date and how orientation works.
St. Louis Public Schools Adult Education & Literacy Address: 801 N. 11th St, St. Louis, MO 63101 Phone: 314-231-3720 Website: slps.org/AdultEd Free HiSET and GED prep; Missouri adult-education eligibility applies.
### St. Louis Community College — FastTrack HiSET
STLCC’s FastTrack is an accelerated, free HiSET path for out-of-school adults, and it goes further than most: it provides HiSET testing vouchers, gas cards, and bus tickets to help you actually finish. Classes meet at Forest Park, Tuesday through Thursday. You will need a 9th-grade reading and math level and to attend orientation first.
STLCC FastTrack (Adult Education & Literacy) Address: STLCC-Forest Park, West Building Room W317, 5600 Oakland Ave, St. Louis, MO 63110 Contact: Susan Ryffel, 314-951-9432, sryffel1@stlcc.edu Website: stlcc.edu (Adult Education & Literacy) Free; includes testing vouchers, gas cards, and bus tickets.
### St. Charles Community College — Adult Education & Literacy
In St. Charles County, the community college offers free High School Equivalency prep, HiSET or GED, plus ESL, with morning and evening classes. Eligibility is 17 and up, not enrolled in high school, with a Missouri address; 16-year-olds who have earned 16 high school credits may enroll with withdrawal and transcript documents. If childcare is your hurdle, see our guide to child care assistance in Missouri.
St. Charles Community College Adult Education & Literacy Address: 4601 Mid Rivers Mall Drive, Cottleville, MO 63376 Phone: 636-922-8411 Website: stchas.edu/ael Free HSE classes; morning and evening options.
### My teen dropped out of high school — what are the options in St. Louis?
Leaving school early is not a dead end, and here is the part that surprises families: two St. Louis programs will essentially pay a teen to come back. St. Louis Job Corps and SLATE’s youth services combine education with job training, stipends, and support for young people ages 16 to 24. Add free GED or HiSET classes, and there are at least three real paths forward.
### St. Louis Job Corps Center
Job Corps is a free education and career-training program for low-income young people ages 16 to 24. Students can earn a high school diploma or equivalency while training for a career, and the program can include housing, meals, health care, a living allowance, and childcare. Confirm current enrollment and on-site status at stlouis.jobcorps.gov or by calling before you go.
St. Louis Job Corps Center Address: 3860 Lindell Blvd, St. Louis, MO 63108 Phone: 1-800-733-5627 Website: stlouis.jobcorps.gov (confirm current enrollment and site status) Free for eligible low-income youth ages 16-24.
### SLATE Missouri Job Center — Youth & YouthBuild
SLATE offers education and employment services to youth ages 17 to 24 who are at risk of leaving school or already have. That includes Out-of-School Youth services, YouthBuild, and summer employment for ages 16 to 24. It is a free public workforce program and a solid first phone call for a young adult figuring out a path back to a diploma and a paycheck.
SLATE Missouri Job Center (Youth Services) Address: 6347 Plymouth Avenue, St. Louis, MO 63133 Phone: 314-622-4800 (main); 314-406-0175 (youth program line) Website: stlouis-mo.gov/slate Free public workforce program for youth ages 17-24.
A few honest words for the young adults reading this. If you are also job hunting or between jobs, our guide to filing for unemployment in Missouri can steady the ground while you study. And if you are rebuilding after time away, including incarceration, our guide to starting over after incarceration in St. Louis walks the road with you. A diploma is not the finish line. It is the door.
One last thing, and we mean it. Needing free help to learn is not a shortcoming; it is exactly what these programs were built and funded to do. Librarians, tutors, and teachers across this region want your student to walk in and log on. Being found, and finding help, is how a hard semester becomes just a semester. The whole St. Louis help and assistance network is behind you.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How to get a tutor for free?
A.  Start with your library card. Any St. Louis County Library or St. Louis Public Library cardholder gets free live online tutoring through Brainfuse, grades K-12, with no appointment or income check. Get a card at any branch, then log in from a laptop or phone and connect with a tutor tonight.
### Q. Where can I find a free tutor?
A.  Two places. Online, the libraries’ Brainfuse service covers grades K-12 free with a card. In person, four nonprofits build homework help into free programming: Gene Slay’s Girls & Boys Club, Boys & Girls Clubs of Greater St. Louis, UrbanFUTURE for middle-schoolers, and College Bound. Call each to confirm ages and enrollment.
### Q. Does the government pay for tutoring?
A.  In effect, yes. St. Louis City and County public libraries pay for the Brainfuse online tutoring service, so any cardholder uses it free, grades K-12, with no income test. That is the clearest public funding for tutoring in this guide: a free library card is all it takes to connect with a live tutor.
### Q. Can I get a GED without taking classes?
A.  Yes. In Missouri you do not have to take a class before you test. Some people study on their own and schedule the GED or HiSET at GED.com or HiSET.org when ready. Others prefer the structure of a free prep class. Either way, passing earns the same high school equivalency.
### Q. How much does a GED cost in Missouri?
A.  The test carries a fee, commonly around $120 for all subjects, though fees change and fee assistance exists. The prep classes, though, are free through SLPS Adult Education, STLCC FastTrack, and St. Charles Community College. STLCC FastTrack even provides testing vouchers. Check hse.mo.gov for current fees and any help available.
### Q. How to get your GED in Missouri for free?
A.  The prep is free; only the test has a fee. Enroll in free GED or HiSET classes through SLPS Adult Education, STLCC FastTrack, or St. Charles Community College. Find more classes statewide at ael.mo.gov. STLCC FastTrack adds testing vouchers, gas cards, and bus tickets, and fee assistance can cover the test.
### Q. What is the minimum age requirement to get a GED in Missouri?
A.  You must be 17 to test in Missouri. Sixteen-year-olds can qualify with an approved age waiver, for example after earning 16 high school credits or through the Missouri Option Program. Rules and paperwork vary, so confirm your situation at hse.mo.gov before scheduling a GED or HiSET test date.
### Q. Does St. Louis Community College offer free classes for adults?
A.  Yes. STLCC’s FastTrack is an accelerated, free HiSET path for out-of-school adults, meeting at Forest Park Tuesday through Thursday. It even provides testing vouchers, gas cards, and bus tickets. You will need a 9th-grade reading and math level and to attend orientation first. Call 314-951-9432 to start.
