The name is the story. The land was part of a World War II ammunition plant, and the county started elk and bison herds there in 1948. When the federal government took the land back, the herds were destroyed for safety reasons, and county history dates that to 1958. One bull elk survived. The park opened to the public in October 1971. Same arc as Weldon Spring: military ground turned into a wildlife drive anyone can take. Give the bison room, and leave the dog home, because pets aren’t allowed here, even inside a vehicle. I’m working from the county’s own summary, so call 314-615-4386 to check before you go.
Bluff Road in Columbia, Illinois. The Illinois side has a second bluff drive most people never try, about 25 to 30 minutes from the Arch. The official Great River Road listing says Bluff Road runs along the bluffs from Palmer Road in Columbia. It’s a quiet back road, so drive it slowly.
Pere Marquette State Park. The Great River Road ends its run at Grafton, and the park sits there at 13112 Visitor Center Ln, about 60 minutes from the Arch. From November through March its visitor center is open Monday through Saturday, 8 to 3:30, and closed Sundays. Call 618-786-3323 for the rest of the year. Our guide to things to do in Grafton covers the town.
### How do you turn a scenic drive into a cheap weekend getaway near St. Louis?
The cheapest weekend is a campsite and a full tank. Klondike Park sells tent sites at $10, and Washington State Park has a campground, so Saturday can be Route 94 and Sunday can be Highway 21. The Weldon Spring platform and the petroglyph deck charge nothing. What you actually spend is gas and lunch.
Looking for good places to take a road trip from St. Louis? Pick by direction. Which city is an hour away depends on where you point the car: Mt. Olive is about 55 minutes north, Grafton about 60 up the river, Augusta about 70 to 75 west, and Ste. Genevieve about 80 south. Of the prettiest towns in Missouri within that circle, Augusta, Washington and Ste. Genevieve are the three I’d drive to first.
Next time someone tells you St. Louis is flat, you’ll know about the staircase, the miners’ monument and the carvings off Highway 21. Check the MDC report Thursday night, pick a direction Saturday morning and go find the view the lists missed.
Hungry at the end of the drive? Browse where to eat around St. Louis on St Louis Near Me Directory before you’re an hour from home with nothing open.
If you’re the tasting room, the diner or the shop on Route 94, old 66 or Highway 21, claim your spot and turn the people already driving past into customers.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the most scenic drive in Missouri?
A.  Statewide lists send you to the Ozarks, and those drives are lovely. Inside about 80 minutes of St. Louis, though, the Missouri Department of Conservation names state highways 94 and 21 for fall color. Take Route 94 west from Weldon Spring toward Augusta in mid-October, climb the free staircase first, and finish at Klondike Park, which closes half an hour after sunset. MDC posts its color reports weekly, usually by Thursday evening, so check the latest before you pick a Saturday.
### Q. What is the closest national park to St. Louis, Missouri?
A.  Gateway Arch National Park, on the downtown riverfront, is the closest. Next is Ste. Genevieve National Historical Park, about 80 minutes south, which became the 422nd unit of the National Park Service on October 30, 2020. It protects the French colonial houses of Missouri’s first permanent European settlement, established by 1750. The park is fee-free. Free house tours take 15 people at most, with same-day sign-up in person at the Welcome Center, 66 S. Main St.
### Q. What are some good places to take a road trip from St. Louis?
A.  Start with the four runs on this page: Route 94 to Augusta, old Route 66 to Mt. Olive, Highway 21 to Washington State Park and the Great River Road to Grafton. Each has a stop worth the gas, and all sit within about 80 minutes. If you’ll drive farther, our roundup of the best day trips from St. Louis within two hours covers the longer runs. Leave early, though: the Weldon Spring interpretive center and the West End station in Edwardsville both close at 4 on weekends.
### Q. What are some cheap weekend getaways near St. Louis?
A.  Build one around a campsite. Klondike Park near Augusta has tent sites at $10 and cabins at $65 a night with a two-night minimum, and Washington State Park has a campground. Missouri state parks charge no admission, and the Weldon Spring platform is free too. Your real cost is gas and lunch. Klondike’s shower house is closed from November 1 through March 31, so plan around that, and confirm rates with the park before you book.
### Q. What city is 1 hour away from St. Louis?
A.  Pick a direction. Mt. Olive is about 55 minutes north on old Route 66, Grafton about 60 minutes up the Great River Road, and Augusta about 70 to 75 minutes west on Route 94. To the south, Washington State Park and Ste. Genevieve each run about 80 minutes. Each sits at the end of a drive on this page, which is the point: make the road the trip. Those times are free-flow estimates from the Arch, so add a cushion on a fall weekend.
### Q. What are some of the prettiest towns in Missouri?
A.  Close to St. Louis, start with three on these drives. Augusta sits in the wine-country hills on Route 94 and was the first federally recognized American Viticultural Area, on June 20, 1980. Washington has a working riverfront across the Highway 47 bridge, and Ste. Genevieve still has French colonial houses from the late 1700s. Drive the bluff road between the first two and judge for yourself. Plan on about 70 to 75 minutes to Augusta, and call ahead for tasting-room hours, which I could not confirm.
### Q. What is the most beautiful state park in Missouri?
A.  It’s subjective, but close to St. Louis the strongest case is Washington State Park near De Soto: the largest group of petroglyphs found in Missouri, Ozark overlooks and stone buildings laid by an African American CCC company in the 1930s. It’s about 80 minutes south on Highway 21, free to enter, and open from 7 a.m. to sunset year-round, with camping if you want to stay over. Guided petroglyph tours run only from Memorial Day weekend through Labor Day weekend, usually Saturdays at 2 p.m.
### Q. Can you walk on top of the Weldon Spring disposal cell?
A.  Yes. A staircase climbs the roughly 75-foot cell to a crushed-gravel walkway and a viewing platform with viewfinders. The Department of Energy says the site is free and open to the public, and the cell is open from dawn to dusk. The interpretive center at the base is open weekdays 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. and weekends 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Keep dogs leashed, and out of the buildings.

## Hidden Gems in St. Louis: Rare Water Towers, Ruins You Can Legally See, Free Art
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/hidden-gems-in-st-louis
We’ll admit it: the first version of this page read like every other St. Louis list. It sent you to the same handful of places every roundup sends you, in roughly the same order. Meanwhile three of the last seven standpipe water towers left in the United States stand in our own city, and the one those lists still tell you to climb has been locked for years.
So we started over. This version is for the person who has done the big weekend more times than they can count and wants the places that never make the roundups: a 154-foot Corinthian column on Grand that hasn’t been used since 1912, two stone towers standing out in the Mississippi like something off the Rhine, the last surviving mound in a city once nicknamed Mound City, and a burned hotel that Henry Shaw turned into fake ancient ruins. Almost all of it is free. Most of it is visible from a car window, which is exactly why people drive right past it.
If you’ve already worked through the small towns outside St. Louis, this is the same idea pointed back at the city and the county. Everything below was checked this month, and where something is closed or gone, we say so.
### What are some underrated places to visit in St. Louis?
Start with what the lists skip: three of the last seven standpipe water towers in the U.S., castle-like intake towers standing in the Mississippi, a burned hotel’s stones arranged into ruins in Tower Grove Park, Ulysses S. Grant’s free White Haven farm, and a walk-in Richard Serra spiral at the free Pulitzer museum.
Here’s the short list, roughly in the order we’d hand it to a friend who swears they’ve seen everything:
The three standpipe towers. Compton Hill on the south side, plus the Bissell Street “Red” tower and the Grand Avenue “Old White” tower a few minutes apart in north city. One morning, one car, three landmarks.
The Chain of Rocks intake towers. Two stone towers in the river off north St. Louis, built to draw water for the city’s Chain of Rocks waterworks and best seen from the old bridge.
The Ruins in Tower Grove Park. Fire-damaged stones from the 1867 Lindell Hotel, arranged by Henry Shaw into three “ancient” clusters.
Richard Serra’s Joe. A torqued steel spiral you can walk into, in the courtyard of a museum that charges nothing.
White Haven. The farm where a young Army officer named Grant met Julia Dent. Entry and house tours are free.
Jefferson Barracks. The 1826 Army post where Grant, Lee and Sherman all served, with three small museums that ask only for a donation.
Bellerive Park. A 1908 overlook in Carondelet where nearly every bench faces the river.
The Mural Mile. A riverfront floodwall that graffiti artists have been painting since 1997.
Notice what’s missing from most of that list: a ticket. That’s the pattern. The places St. Louis overlooks tend to be the ones nobody is selling.
One more belongs on this list even though you can’t walk onto it, and it may matter more than anything else on the page.
The last mound in Mound City. St. Louis got that old nickname from the earthen mounds that once stood here, hundreds of them across the area, built centuries before the city existed. Settlers turned some into house sites and beer gardens, then leveled the rest. By 1875, according to the Osage Nation, nearly all of them were gone. One survived. Sugarloaf Mound, on Ohio Avenue in south city, went up sometime between AD 600 and 1200, and it’s the oldest known human-made structure in St. Louis. In 1928 somebody built a house on top of it.
The Osage Nation, which considers the mound sacred, bought the first third of it in 2008 and spent 17 years getting the rest back. It bought the house on the summit in 2009 and took it down in 2017. On September 22, 2025, the Nation announced that the entire mound was under its control again, with help from Counterpublic, the arts nonprofit behind this fall’s citywide exhibition. The plan now is to remove the remaining structures, stabilize the mound and build an interpretive center.
Until that center exists, this isn’t an outing. It’s sacred land and it isn’t open to visitors. If you want to see it, see it from the public street, briefly and quietly, the way you’d pass a cemetery, and if it moves you, the Osage Nation is raising money for the preservation work. For the region’s even older story, head south of the county line to the Kimmswick Bone Bed, where a stone spear point turned up among mastodon bones. It’s where our list of things to do in Arnold, MO starts.
### Can you legally climb a water tower in St. Louis?
Not right now, and that’s the part the other lists get wrong. The only St. Louis water tower that ever opened for public climbs is Compton Hill, at Grand and Russell, and it has been shut for years. Tours stopped during the pandemic in a pause that was supposed to be temporary. St. Louis Magazine reported in September 2025 that masonry deterioration and falling debris had kept it closed for several years, and Nine PBS’s Living St. Louis dates the closure to 2019. The preservation society’s own website now says the tower is closed for preservation.
Here’s the trap. The city’s park page for Compton Hill Reservoir Park still lists climbing hours: the first Saturday of the month and full-moon evenings, April through November. At least one travel article published this year repeats them. Anyone who trusts those pages is planning a night around a door that stays locked. The other two aren’t open to climbers either, and going up any water tower without permission is trespassing, on top of being a good way to get hurt 179 feet off the ground.
What you can do is see all three from the ground, and that’s better than it sounds once you know what you’re looking at. A standpipe tower is a disguise. Inside each one stood a tall iron pipe that soaked up the surges from the pumps and kept the city’s water pressure even. The brick, stone and terra cotta around it were there to make plumbing look like a monument. Only seven of these towers are left in the country. St. Louis kept three.
Compton Hill (1898). Harvey Ellis designed it: 179 feet of Romanesque brick and terra cotta on a stone base, with 198 steps inside. The city decommissioned it in 1929, when it moved to a more modern water system. A 2025 structural assessment found weathering in the limestone base, spalling on the terra cotta and water getting into the upper shaft, and the Water Tower & Park Preservation Society says a phased restoration plan is being worked out. The park around it is open from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m., and it rewards a walk even with the tower locked. The reservoir wall has steps and fountains laid out like an Italian villa garden, and near Grand stands the Naked Truth, a bronze unveiled in 1914 to honor three editors of the German-language Westliche Post, with its inscription in German and English. For a reopening date, watch watertowerfoundation.org and ignore any calendar that doesn’t come from there.
Bissell Street “Red” tower (1885). William S. Eames drew it as a Moorish minaret, red brick under a copper roof gone green, at Bissell Street and Blair Avenue in Hyde Park. During World War II, St. Louis Magazine recounts, city leaders called it useless to anyone but the scrap-metal dealers, and the city came close to losing it. Kids in the neighborhood grew up calling it a castle.
Grand Avenue “Old White” tower (1871). The oldest of the three stands at 20th Street and Grand in College Hill. George I. Barnett designed it as a 154-foot Corinthian column during the postwar waterworks expansion led by Thomas Whitman, the poet Walt Whitman’s brother, and it was once declared the largest free-standing Corinthian column in the world. It was retired in 1912. In the 1920s and ’30s beacons on top helped pilots find the airport. When a 1933 recommendation proposed tearing it down, Mayor Bernard Dickmann said wrecking it would “verge closely on an act of sacrilege.”
Make it a loop. Old White and the Red tower are a few minutes apart, and Compton Hill is a straight run south on Grand. Keep one more name in your pocket for the drive: William Eames, the architect behind the Red tower, also designed the first of the two water intake towers standing in the Mississippi. That’s where the next section starts.
### What are some abandoned places in Saint Louis, Missouri?
Plenty, and most of them are a bad idea. An abandoned building still belongs to someone, whether that’s an owner, a bank or the city, and walking into one is trespassing before you even get to the rotten floors. So this list sticks to places that look abandoned, ruined or salvaged and that you’re allowed to see.
The Ruins in Tower Grove Park. In 1867 the Lindell Hotel, the largest hotel in America at the time, burned to the ground. Henry Shaw was about to deed the land for Tower Grove Park to the city, and he looked at the fire-damaged blocks and saw ancient ruins. He had the stones arranged in three clusters, and they’ve stood in the park ever since: a fake ruin made from a real disaster. Go on a weekday. The park says wedding parties line up there for photos on Saturdays.
The intake towers at Chain of Rocks. Just south of the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge, close to the Missouri shore, stands Intake Tower No. 1. William Eames designed it in a Richardsonian Romanesque style, it was finished in 1894, and the city’s landmark page compares it to the Mouse Tower on the Rhine near Bingen. When it couldn’t keep up with the city’s thirst, a second intake followed in 1913. You can’t reach either one, and the water around the Chain of Rocks is no place for a boat or a swimmer. You don’t need to. The view from the bridge is the point.
The National Building Arts Center, Sauget. Across the river sits a campus full of buildings that no longer exist, much of it St. Louis: terra cotta, cast iron and carved stone salvaged from demolitions. It isn’t a walk-in museum. You see it on a ticketed campus tour. Its 2026 calendar listed tours on Saturday, October 10, and Saturday, November 14, both at 11 a.m. In 2026 it’s also a Counterpublic exhibition site through December 12, and its Route 66 exhibition, City 66, is listed through October 17. Book through the center’s events page, and check the details there before you cross the bridge.
The Mural Mile. The riverfront floodwall between Victor Street and Chouteau Avenue, south of the Arch, has been painted since 1997, when the Paint Louis gathering began drawing graffiti artists from around the country. More than 250 have left work on it. The city owns the wall, and paint-overs come with the territory, so what you see this year won’t match the photos from five years ago. This fall Counterpublic added a new painted work nearby, Yatika Starr Fields’s Melted Destiny, at 1450 S. Wharf Street. The same flood wall carries the St. Louis Riverfront Trail north of the Arch, and it held through the Great Flood of 1993 with less than three feet to spare.
That’s the honest version of urban exploring in St. Louis. You get the ruin, the salvage and the paint, and nobody has to call a lawyer.
### What to do in St. Louis, MO for free?
The usual free answers are the big museums in the big park. They’re fine, and you’ve done them. These are the free ones the lists leave off.
Walk into a Richard Serra. The Pulitzer Arts Foundation, at 3716 Washington Boulevard in Grand Center, is a Tadao Ando building with free admission and free parking. The museum keeps short hours, Thursday through Sunday from 10 to 5 and until 9 on First Fridays. Joe stands in its outdoor courtyard, a torqued steel spiral Serra made for the building and named for Joseph Pulitzer Jr., and you walk its leaning walls around and around until you reach the center. Plan on museum hours for that one. The rest of the outdoor campus, including Park-Like, a native garden across the street, and the Spring Church, an open-air stone pavilion, is open every day from sunrise to sunset.
See Grant’s St. Louis farm. Most cars on Grant Road are headed somewhere else. Turn in at 7400 Grant Road instead. Ulysses S. Grant National Historic Site preserves White Haven, the Dent family farm where Grant, fresh out of West Point, met Julia Dent, the sister of his roommate. Entry is free, the house tours are free, and the visitor center is open daily from 9 to 5 except Thanksgiving, Christmas and New Year’s Day. Ulysses and Julia picked the house’s Paris Green exterior themselves in 1874, which is why it’s that startling shade of green. The Park Service is direct about the hard part, too: by 1850 Julia’s father enslaved upwards of 30 people on two St. Louis properties, 17 of them at White Haven, and Grant himself freed the one man he is known to have enslaved, William Jones, in 1859.
Then go where he was stationed. Grant reported to Jefferson Barracks in 1843, and it was from that post that he rode out to White Haven. The post opened in 1826 as the country’s first Infantry School of Practice, and Lee, Sherman, Sheridan and Jefferson Davis served there too. Its northern 420 acres became a St. Louis County park in 1950, on the bluffs in south county, open from 7 a.m. until half an hour past sunset. Stone buildings from the old post hold three small museums, the Ordnance Room, the Powder Magazine and the Visitors Center, open Wednesday through Sunday from noon to 4. Admission is free with a suggested donation. County hours can shift, so check before you go.
See a citywide art show for nothing. Counterpublic 2026, titled Coyote Time, is free and on view through December 12. It puts about 50 new commissions in public places across the city: along the riverfront, in The Ville, in Tower Grove Park, in Grand Center and across the river in Sauget. Much of the riverfront work is grouped at 101 Chouteau Avenue. The organizers bill it as one of the largest public art exhibitions in the country, and it only comes around every three years, so fall 2026 is the window.
Sit on a bench that faces the river. Bellerive Park costs nothing and gives you the best quiet river view in south city. More on that below. If you’re working the free list in the inner suburbs too, our guide to free things to do in Webster Groves picks up where this one stops.
Touring the towers? Here’s where to eat in St. Louis.
### Where can you watch the Mississippi without the riverfront crowds?
Skip the crowded steps downtown. Three quieter spots do it better: one south, one north and one across the water.
Bellerive Park, south. The city set this 8.67-acre park aside in 1908, first as Riverside Park, to give the public a scenic viewpoint over the river, then renamed it for an early French governor of St. Louis. It sits at 5570 S. Broadway in Carondelet, and the city’s own description is blunt: nearly every bench faces the Mississippi. A crescent drive off Broadway climbs to a pavilion with an overlook, and the view runs south down the river. Bring coffee and watch the barges work. There are no bike racks, so plan to walk the last bit or lock up elsewhere.
Chain of Rocks Park, north. Great Rivers Greenway’s park at 10840 Riverview Drive is the Missouri-side front door to the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge, open from 7 a.m. to 30 minutes after sunset. Walk out onto the bridge and look downstream, and the two intake towers stand in the river just south of you. Two warnings for this fall. The canal bridge on the Illinois side closed for construction on June 22, 2026, cutting off the Illinois approach until it reopens, so plan to come from Missouri and check the greenway’s park page for the current status. And the westbound I-270 exit to Riverview Drive is temporarily closed; the greenway’s posted detour uses the Lilac Avenue exit and Dunn Road. The bridge itself, a mile of old Route 66 with a bend in the middle, gets its full due in our guide to historic sites in St. Louis.
Malcolm W. Martin Memorial Park, across the river. In East St. Louis, this park has an elevated river overlook that its managers call the best view in the region of the St. Louis skyline. It’s also where the lists are wrong a second time. The Gateway Geyser there, a fountain built to reach 630 feet to match the Arch, was the tallest fountain in the country and went off at noon on summer days. In late 2023 the Metro East Park and Recreation District announced the end of it: nearly 30 years had worn out the pumps, the generators and the pond liner. Some travel pages still tell you to show up at noon. Don’t bother. The park itself is open daily from 7 a.m. to 10 p.m., it’s free, and the view hasn’t gone anywhere. If you’re on the Illinois side anyway, our guide to parks in Fairview Heights covers the next stop east.
Want a river from higher up, on foot? The bluff trails around the county do that best. Start with our easy family-friendly hiking trails around St. Louis, or head to Emmenegger Nature Park’s bluff trails in Kirkwood, where a short, steep climb ends at a rocky outcrop over the Meramec.
### Where do the quieter lists lead past the city limits?
Mostly west and south, to places that sit a few minutes off a highway everyone takes for something else.
The Black Madonna Shrine and Grottos, Pacific. About eight miles outside Eureka, at 100 St. Joseph Hill Road, a set of grottos built from Missouri tiff rock sits in the woods, part of a shrine that traces back to six Franciscan brothers from Poland in 1927. The shrine says it’s about a 40-minute drive from west county. The grounds are open from 9 to 5 from April through October and from 9 to 4 from November through March. Admission isn’t posted online, so call the office at 636-938-5361 before you go. It pairs well with the rest of our list of unique things to do in Eureka.
Next time somebody tells you they’ve done St. Louis, ask them which water tower is the oldest, or where Henry Shaw put a burned hotel. You’ll be the one who knows the climb is closed, the geyser is off and the mound is back in Osage hands. Pick one this weekend.
Planning a north-side tower loop or a weekday morning at the Ruins? Check where to eat around St. Louis on St Louis Near Me Directory and put lunch near the stop.
If you run a café, gallery or shop within a few blocks of one of these places, the people reading this are deciding where to stop next, so list your business with us.
Want the intake towers from mid-river? Our Chain of Rocks Bridge guide covers parking, the bend and which side is open.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Why are secret towers in the Mississippi River?
A.  They’re water intakes, not secrets. The two stone towers off north St. Louis, just south of the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge, were built to draw river water into the city’s Chain of Rocks waterworks. Intake Tower No. 1 dates to 1894 and was designed by William Eames, who also drew the Bissell Street water tower, and the second followed in 1913. See them from the bridge.
### Q. What was the original purpose of the water tower?
A.  In St. Louis, pressure control. Each of the city’s three historic standpipe towers hides a tall iron pipe that absorbed surges from the pumps and kept the water pressure even. The decorative shells were architecture wrapped around plumbing: the Grand Avenue tower’s 154-foot Corinthian column hides a standpipe about five feet across, and it hasn’t been used since 1912.
### Q. How illegal is it to explore abandoned places?
A.  Illegal enough to skip. In Missouri, knowingly entering or staying unlawfully in a building is trespass in the first degree under RSMo 569.140, generally a class B misdemeanor, and entering someone else’s land unlawfully is second-degree trespass under 569.150, an infraction. This isn’t legal advice. It’s the reason every place on this page is one you can see legally.
### Q. What are some strange and unusual things to do in St. Louis?
A.  The famous-weird circuit, City Museum and the rest, lives in our guide to unique things to do in St. Louis. This page is the quieter list: a 1914 bronze called the Naked Truth, a fake ruin built from a burned hotel, and a Mississippi water intake that looks like a castle on the Rhine.
### Q. What to do in downtown St. Louis today?
A.  Walk the Mural Mile, the painted floodwall that runs along the riverfront south of downtown between Chouteau Avenue and Victor Street, then come back to the Counterpublic works grouped at 101 Chouteau Avenue, part of the free 2026 exhibition (on view through December 12, 2026). Yatika Starr Fields’s new painted work is close by at 1450 S. Wharf Street. Check counterpublic.org for each site’s hours first.
### Q. What are some hidden places to visit in Missouri?
A.  Start with the river towns and small places most people only drive through. Our guide to day trips from St. Louis maps the ones within two hours. Closer in, the Black Madonna Shrine’s rock grottos near Pacific are about 40 minutes from west county.
### Q. Why are there so many abandoned buildings in downtown St. Louis?
A.  Mostly because the city lost most of its people. St. Louis had about 857,000 residents in 1950, according to the Census Bureau, and the 2020 census counted 301,578. The buildings stayed while the population moved out, and the vacancies that followed show up downtown and across the whole city, not only in the core.
### Q. Can you visit Sugarloaf Mound?
A.  Not as an attraction. Sugarloaf Mound, on Ohio Avenue in south city, is sacred Osage Nation land. The Nation announced in September 2025 that the whole mound was back under its control, and it’s working to remove the remaining structures, stabilize the mound and build an interpretive center. Until then, view it briefly from the public street, and if you want to help, support the Osage Nation’s preservation effort.

## Things to Do in St. Charles, MO: Chicago's Founder, Christmas Lights, Stocked Lakes
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-st-charles-mo
Every listicle’s wrong about St. Charles. They park you on Main Street, point you at the fudge and the cobblestones, and never mention that the man who founded Chicago moved here in 1810, died here in 1818, and, since September 16, has had an 8.5-foot bronze head watching over the same brick street they just sent you to.
His name is Jean Baptiste Pointe DuSable. He spent about 20 years building the trading settlement that became Chicago, then came to St. Charles to be near his family. Missourinet called him someone “many Missourians have never heard of.” That’s the recycled top-10 list in a nutshell. The best stories in this town sit in plain sight, and the lists walk right past them.
So this guide skips the brochure loop. It’s for the local who has done Main Street twice and the parent hunting a cheap Saturday: what’s actually free, where the neighborhood Christmas lights are, the Halloween stuff grown-ups like, the city lakes that get stocked every year, the trails beyond the Katy, and where to duck in when it rains. St. Charles belongs on any list of the small towns outside St. Louis worth a day, and it hides more than most of them. For addresses and the basics, our St. Charles, MO city guide keeps them in one place.
### What are some free things to do in St. Charles, MO?
The best free stuff is what the lists skip. Find Chicago’s founder twice (a 1968 memorial marker on Randolph Street, a new 8.5-foot bronze head on Main), fish three stocked lakes at Fountain Lakes Park, ride 4.2 miles of island singletrack at Bangert Island, walk McNair Park’s Braille Trail, and catch free summer band concerts in Frontier Park.
Start with DuSable, because nobody else will tell you to. The sculpture is called Explorer, and it stands outside the St. Charles County Historical Society at 101 S. Main, in a building from the 1880s. Fox 2 put it at ten times the scale of a typical human head. It stays at least two years and then moves on to its next home, so this is a see-it-now thing.
Then take the short drive west to St. Charles Borromeo Cemetery, 2400 W. Randolph St. A stone marker for DuSable stands there, placed in 1968 by the Illinois Sesquicentennial Commission, right beside the marker for Louis Blanchette, the man who founded St. Charles. Two city founders. One plot. DuSable died on August 28, 1818, and the marker itself says that, according to tradition, his remains were moved twice before they reached this cemetery, so treat it as a memorial rather than a pinpointed grave. It’s an active Catholic cemetery. Go in daylight and keep it quiet.
One more DuSable detail most locals miss: the riverfront park in Frenchtown is officially Jean Baptiste Point DuSable Park. Its Eco Park section has a 1.08-mile sand trail and 1.82 miles of crushed rock trail with outlooks over the Missouri River, open dawn to dusk, and nobody charges you a thing.
The free music is the other thing visitors overlook. The St. Charles Municipal Band has been playing since 1870, and in summer it plays Thursday nights at 7:30 on the Jaycee Stage in Frontier Park, June through August. Bring a lawn chair. Music on Main runs the third Wednesday of each month from May through September, 5 to 7:30 p.m., in the 100 and 200 blocks of North Main. Visiting in fall or winter? Pencil it in for May. And through November 28 in 2026, the Saint Charles Market fills Main Street between Clark and Adams every Saturday from 7:30 a.m. to 1 p.m. Browsing costs nothing.
A few honest caveats on “free.” Most adults need a Missouri fishing permit to fish the city lakes. The Shrine of St. Philippine Duchesne asks a $5 suggested donation for tours. And the Friday ghost walk on Main Street is a paid tour. The rest of this list costs you gas.
### Where are the best Christmas lights in St. Charles, MO?
On people’s houses, mostly. The listicles answer this question with the Main Street festival and stop there. Locals answer it with an address list, and the city hands you that list at no charge.
It’s called City Lights. Every December the City of St. Charles runs a lighting contest open to residents and businesses, judges the displays and posts the winners on the city website. The 2025 categories tell you what to hunt for: Best Overall, Most Festive, Best Theme, Best Street/Neighborhood, Best Business and Mayor’s Choice. Residents got a vote, too. And it isn’t a new idea. New Town’s community website billed the 2022 contest as the 19th annual, which puts the first one around 2004.
Timing is the whole trick. The city posted its 2025 winners on December 18, so the last week before Christmas is when the list is fresh and every winning display is fully lit. Pull up the winners page, plot a loop and go after dark. One courtesy note: the city publishes the winning home addresses, so we won’t reprint them here. Drive slowly, stay on the street or the sidewalk, and kill the high beams. The 2026 contest hadn’t been announced as of early October, so check the city site in late November.
Start in New Town. The St. Charles tourism bureau’s own lights guide sends people there because so many residents take decorating seriously, and in 2025 one New Town display ran across five townhouses in a row, each with its own theme. The 2025 Best Business winner was in New Town as well: BobaQue, at 3331 Rue Royale. That’s the move. Get dinner there, then walk the lit blocks off.
Yes, Christmas Traditions happens here too: Main Street, Fridays through Sundays from Thanksgiving weekend to Christmas Eve (November 27 to December 24 in 2026), named the Merriest Main Street in America by the Today Show in 2024, and covered by nearly every holiday guide in the metro. The part fewer people know about is Wednesday night. From 6 to 8:30 p.m. on Wednesdays, the festival stages “A Christmas Carol” Stroll, and Main Street turns into the foggy Dickens-era streets of the book under its gas lamps. Same bricks, different show. If you’re going for the glow and not the shopping, that’s your night.
Here’s how we’d stack a St. Charles lights night. Park near Main by 6 p.m. on a Wednesday and catch the Carol Stroll while the gas lamps are the main event. Drive to New Town for dinner at BobaQue (check its hours first). Then work the City Lights winners list with the heater on. If the winners post around the same date as 2025’s, the last Wednesday before Christmas is the night all three line up (December 23 in 2026). Confirm the stroll schedule and the winners page that week, then go.
Bringing kids? Santa sits inside the historic Katy Depot in Frontier Park on opening day, Saturdays, Sundays and Christmas Eve, and the festival offers a free Sensory-Friendly Experience for guests who find the crowds and noise too much. Check the festival site for those dates before you go.
Want a drive-through instead? St. Charles County’s big ones are next door. The O’Fallon Christmas lights at Fort Zumwalt Park are the classic, and Wentzville runs a one-mile Holiday Night Lights display of its own. For the rest of the region, we’ve already done the legwork: our guide to drive-through Christmas lights around St. Louis covers the car-window shows, and our roundup of the best Christmas lights in St. Louis covers the big walk-through displays too. This page sticks to what only St. Charles has.
### What is there to do for Halloween in St. Charles?
Two things, and neither one is a haunted house. St. Charles does Halloween as history, which is exactly why grown-ups like it.
The first is Legends & Lanterns, the October festival on Main Street. It’s free, with no tickets. Villains, witches and spirits from history and folklore wander the brick street, and the Victorian Mourning Museum walks you through how 19th-century families grieved. The 2026 dates: Saturday, October 10 (11 a.m. to 6 p.m.), Sunday, October 11 (noon to 5), Saturday, October 17 (11 to 6), Sunday, October 18 (noon to 5), then the Pumpkin Glow weekend, Friday, October 23 from 5 to 8 p.m., Saturday, October 24 from 11 a.m. to 8 p.m., and Sunday, October 25 from noon to 5. Main Street closes to cars from Boone’s Lick Road to Jefferson Street during Pumpkin Glow, so park early. In 2026 the Saturday market on October 17 is set to double as the city’s Pumpkin Festival, with a live carving demo and a pumpkin pie contest.
The second is the one the lists skip: the St. Charles Haunted History Trail. It’s a self-guided video walking tour. During Legends & Lanterns, signs with QR codes go up at each stop, and the videos stay online all year, so you can pull them up and walk the route on a random Tuesday in March. Stops include the spot where witches met along Main Street, the grounds of a lost cemetery, the old post office, a former funeral parlor and Edgar Allan Poe’s St. Charles connection. We won’t spoil that one.
Want a live guide instead of a phone? Macabre Main Street walking tours run Friday evenings (through October 30 in 2026), with a “spirit host” leading you through tales of treason, the legendary witch house and the jails that once had Main Street addresses. It’s a paid tour with limited spots, so reserve ahead. And the Historical Society’s Dinner With The Dead sold out all three of its 2026 dates. That tells you how this town feels about its ghosts. Book early when the next dates go up.
Ghost walk first, dinner after? Where to eat in St. Charles
### Where can you go fishing in St. Charles, MO?
Fountain Lakes Park, and it isn’t close. The city stocks every lake there each year, and there are three of them plus a pond across 145 acres: Kluesner Lake (30 acres, with a fishing dock), Moore Lake (20 acres), Skate Park Lake (15 acres) and a 2-acre pond. The forums keep asking where to fish in St. Charles. This is the answer they keep missing.
Know which end you want before you go. Kluesner and its dock are reached from the north end of the park. Moore Lake and the skate park are at the south end. A 4.74-mile gravel and natural trail ties the two halves together by running underneath Interstate 370, which is about as odd and useful as a park trail gets. Hours are dawn to dusk, and the restrooms close for the season after November 14.
For bigger water, go to the Missouri River. Blanchette Landing in DuSable Park, at 100 Olive Street, has a boat ramp that’s open 24 hours a day, and the city also lists the river along Frontier Park as fishing access, which makes it the walk-up option. The river is still the river: check the level and the current before you go, especially after a wet week upstream.
Two small spots work for kids or a quick hour. Fox Hill Park has two connected ponds, about 2 acres combined, with a paved loop around them. Wapelhorst Park has a 1.7-acre lake circled by a 0.28-mile paved trail, short enough that a 6-year-old won’t mutiny. Heatherbrook Park has a fishing pond, too.
The fine print: most adults need a Missouri fishing permit, and the Missouri Department of Conservation sets the limits. Fountain Lakes isn’t the only lake along I-370, either. Fishing at 370 Lakeside Park in St. Peters is the next one over.
### Where do locals hike and bike in St. Charles besides the Katy Trail?
The Katy gets the attention. Bangert Island gets the locals who ride. It’s 160 acres wedged between the Katy Trail and the Missouri River just south of downtown, and trail builders have squeezed 4.2 miles of singletrack onto it. The main loop is a figure 8 laid out for beginners with almost no elevation change, and the Sandy Loop weaves through the drainage troughs along the river’s edge for a change of pace. Park on Old South River Road. One hard rule: the island floods, and once the river reaches 23 feet, the bridge onto it is no longer accessible. Check the river gauge first.
The Fountain Lakes trail is the long walk: 4.74 miles of gravel and natural surface past three fishing lakes, ducking under I-370 to join the two halves of the park.
For river views without the mud, DuSable Park’s Eco Park section pairs its sand trail with crushed rock and outlooks over the Missouri. Paved and long? The Boschert Greenway runs 4.15 miles, and the Centennial Greenway adds 2.7 more.
Then there’s the one that stops people. McNair Park, 98 acres at 3100 Droste, has a Braille Trail and garden in its southwest corner, an amenity the city itself calls unique. Pair it with McNair’s 1.75-mile paved loop and its disc golf course and you’ve got a full morning. If you want bluffs instead of river bottoms, the Goat Cliff Trail at Pere Marquette is the climb on the Illinois side of the Mississippi.
### What to do in St. Charles, MO with kids?
Discovery Playground at Jaycee Park, 2805 Elm Street, is the famous one, and it earned that. It opened in 2012, and from May 1 through September 30 its water feature runs from 7 a.m. to 9 p.m., weather permitting. The restrooms there stay open year-round, which every parent reading this just noted.
Fox Hill Park, 3400 Kister Drive, does something smarter with a walk. Its Storybook Walk sets a children’s story along 16 posts around two connected lakes, and the story changes every month through a partnership with the St. Charles City-County Library Foundation. The park also has a new playground for ages 2 to 12, and the paved loop runs 1.45 miles. Go once a month and it’s a different outing every time.
Older kids want the skate park at Fountain Lakes: 13,000 square feet of concrete with three bowls, at 3740 Huster Road. Bring helmets. Then there’s the winter one nobody lists. On days with snow on the ground, Blanchette, Jaycee, McNair and Wapelhorst parks may stay open until midnight for sledding. Blanchette, at 1900 Randolph, was the city’s very first park, acquired on September 26, 1914, and it still has a dedicated sledding hill.
### What can you do in St. Charles on a rainy day?
Head for Frenchtown, just north of the Main Street historic district. Two of the best indoor stops in town sit on North Second Street, and a third is a few blocks away on North Main Center.
The Frenchtown Heritage Museum shares a restored fire station at 1121 N. Second St. with Good News Brewing. You can tour the museum whenever the brewery is open, so St. Charles history, craft beer and wood-fired pizza all come under one roof. Rain or not, it’s the most St. Charles afternoon there is.
Down Second Street, the Shrine of St. Philippine Duchesne at 619 N. Second St. is the quiet stop. Duchesne opened a log-cabin school for girls here in 1818, and in 1988 she was canonized as the fourth United States saint. Her marble sarcophagus sits in an alcove facing the altar, and visitors can see the small room where she died at 82, plus relics from that first school. The shrine is open for personal prayer Monday through Friday, 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., and usually closed on the first Friday of the month outside summer. Tours are by appointment, booked at least 24 hours ahead.
The Foundry Art Centre, 520 N. Main Center, keeps its exhibitions free and open to the public. As of October 2026, its main galleries had work by Melissa Whiteman, Igor Karash and Anna Schenker on view through November 21, and First Fridays add extended evening hours from 5 to 8 p.m. And if you want to go deeper on DuSable, the Historical Society behind the statue is open Monday, Wednesday and Friday from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. Its lease on 101 S. Main is set to end December 31, 2026, and in 2026 it was raising $600,000 to buy the building, so ask about that while you’re there.
Start with the bronze head on Main this month, while it’s still here. Come back in December with the city’s winners list in your phone. By spring you’ll be the one telling everybody else where to go in St. Charles.
If you’re making a night of the lights or the ghost walk, St Louis Near Me Directory’s guide to where to eat in St. Charles covers dinner before or after.
If you run a business along that Main Street route, list it with us so the quarter of a million people who come for Christmas Traditions each season can find you.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are the must-see attractions in St. Charles, MO?
A.  The headliners are real. They’re just not the whole story. Historic Main Street, the First Missouri State Capitol (St. Charles was the state capital from 1821 to 1826), the Lewis & Clark Boat House and the Katy Trail are the big four, and every guide covers them. Add the two this one is built around: DuSable’s bronze head outside the Historical Society and his memorial marker beside Louis Blanchette’s on Randolph Street.
### Q. Where is Frontier Park in St. Charles?
A.  At 500 S. Riverside Drive, on the Missouri River at the foot of Main Street. It’s 16 acres, the Katy Trail runs straight through it, and it holds the historic Katy Depot, a 15-foot Lewis & Clark statue and the Jaycee Stage, where the Municipal Band plays free summer Thursday concerts. It’s open from dawn to midnight, and its restrooms stay open year-round.
### Q. What is the nightlife scene like in St. Charles?
A.  Main Street has bars, and the tourism bureau lists them. The after-dark plans worth knowing are different: First Fridays at the Foundry Art Centre (free, 5 to 8 p.m.), the Friday-night Macabre Main Street ghost walk (through October 30 in 2026), the Wednesday “A Christmas Carol” Stroll in December, and, if it snows, sledding hills that may stay open until midnight.
### Q. What are some free events happening in St. Charles, MO today?
A.  It depends on the day, but the free calendar repeats. Saturdays bring the Saint Charles Market on Main Street (through November 28 in 2026). October weekends bring Legends & Lanterns (October 10 to 25 in 2026). First Fridays at the Foundry Art Centre run 5 to 8 p.m. Summer adds Municipal Band concerts on Thursdays in Frontier Park and Music on Main on the third Wednesday, May through September.
### Q. Which town in Missouri is considered the most Christmas-themed?
A.  St. Charles makes a strong case. NBC’s Today Show named its Christmas Traditions festival the Merriest Main Street in America in 2024, the festival’s 50th season, and the tourism bureau says it draws about a quarter of a million people each year. It runs from Thanksgiving weekend to Christmas Eve (November 27 to December 24 in 2026).
### Q. What is Saint Charles famous for?
A.  Being Missouri’s first state capital, from 1821 to 1826, plus its brick Main Street and its Lewis and Clark history. What it should be famous for: Chicago’s founder, Jean Baptiste Pointe DuSable, spent his last eight years here, and his memorial marker stands beside the one for St. Charles founder Louis Blanchette.
### Q. What are some free things to do in St. Charles County?
A.  Inside the city, start with the parks in this guide. Fountain Lakes, Bangert Island, McNair and Fox Hill cost nothing to use, and the Foundry Art Centre’s exhibitions are free. Next door, O’Fallon and St. Peters each have their own free lineups, and our town guides for both, linked above, cover them.
### Q. Can you go sledding at night in St. Charles parks?
A.  Sometimes. On days with snow on the ground, the city says Blanchette, Jaycee, McNair and Wapelhorst parks may extend their hours to midnight for sledding. Blanchette and Jaycee both have dedicated sledding hills. Because it’s a “may,” check with St. Charles Parks and Recreation before you load the sleds.

## Things to Do in Grafton, IL: Ferry All Winter, Eagle Tours, Goat Cliff Trail
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-grafton-il
Outdated Grafton lists cost you the whole winter. Plenty of them still describe the Grafton Ferry as a Friday-to-Sunday boat that ties up for the year in mid-November, and the top Google result for things to do in Grafton still calls it seasonal. That stopped being true on April 10, 2026.
The City of Grafton bought the boat with a $1.458 million state grant. It now crosses the Mississippi from St. Charles County seven days a week, January included, for $10 a car. Five to 10 minutes on the water. It lands next to the Grafton Lighthouse.
That one change turns Grafton from a summer-Saturday town into a Tuesday-in-February town, and February is exactly when the eagle tours at Pere Marquette State Park run. Every one of the 2027 tour dates falls on a weekday. Reservations for them are set to open November 16, 2026. Of all the small towns outside St. Louis, Grafton rewards the person who knows the calendar better than the crowd does. So here’s the calendar, starting with the boat.
### Is the Grafton-Illinois ferry running?
Yes. Since April 10, 2026, the city-owned Grafton Ferry runs year-round, seven days a week, weather permitting: 5 a.m. to 9 p.m. Monday through Thursday, 5 a.m. to 10 p.m. Friday and Saturday, and 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. Sunday. A car costs $10 one way or $19 round trip. Ice or high water can pause it.
The schedule is the news. Before this year, the Calhoun Ferry Company owned the boat and carried passengers only Friday through Sunday, from mid-April to mid-November. Now the city owns it, the same company runs it on the city’s behalf, and the first weekday crossing leaves at 5 a.m. for commuters. The regional tourism bureau said as much when it opened: weekday visits to Grafton are finally an option.
Where it runs: the Illinois landing sits by the Grafton Lighthouse and the public boat ramp off Market Street. The Missouri landing is at the end of Grafton Ferry Road, just off Highway 94 in St. Charles County. You’re allowed out of your car during the crossing, which is the best seat for watching the bluffs come closer. From St. Charles County, the boat saves more than 30 minutes over driving around through Alton.
One thing the new schedule can’t fix is the river. “Weather permitting” is in every official notice, and winter is when it bites. The free state ferry about a mile west of town shut for ice floes in late January 2026. After a week of hard cold, check the ferry’s status before you leave the house, because the fallback is the long way around.
### How much is the ferry in Grafton, Illinois?
A car or small truck is $10 one way or $19 round trip. Motorcycles are $7 one way or $13 round trip, a bicycle is $6 one way, and a foot passenger pays $5 one way. If you cross a lot, the 10-trip commuter pass is $70, which works out to $7 a crossing. The boat takes cash, checks and credit cards. Those are the posted fares as of October 2026, so check before you count on the exact number.
Now do the math on a winter morning. Two people, one car, ferry both ways: $19. The alternative from St. Charles County is the drive around through Alton, more than half an hour longer by the tourism bureau’s count. For an 8:30 a.m. eagle program, that half hour is the difference between coffee on Main Street and jogging into the visitor center late.
Don’t confuse it with the Brussels Ferry. That one is a different boat on a different river. The Illinois Department of Transportation runs it across the Illinois River about a mile west of town, around the clock, and it costs nothing. Riding it over and straight back is a free way to see the bluffs from the water. For that crossing plus every stop on the way up, we mapped the full Alton-to-Grafton drive, stop by stop.
### What is there to do in Grafton in winter?
More than the lists admit, and most of it happens on weekdays or after dark. Winter used to be the season the Missouri side mostly skipped, because the boat wasn’t carrying passengers. Here’s what’s on from November through March, with dates we confirmed in early October 2026.
### When do Pere Marquette’s eagle tour reservations open?
Pere Marquette State Park runs Bald Eagle Days every winter: a video and a talk at the visitor center, then an observational drive along the Illinois River to find eagles in the trees. Reservations are required. For the 2027 tours, the phone line at (618) 786-3323, extension 1, is set to open November 16, 2026. Every program starts at 8:30 a.m. at the visitor center, 13112 Visitor Center Lane.
The 2027 dates are Wednesday, January 20; Tuesday through Friday, February 2 to 5; and the Fridays of February 26, March 5 and March 12. Eight dates. Not one on a weekend. Under the old ferry schedule, no passenger boat crossed from Missouri on any of them. For the 2027 tours, you can roll onto the ferry before 8 a.m. and reach the park, a few miles west of town, with time to spare. Reading this after March 12? Call the park for next winter’s dates.
Bring a full tank, binoculars and boots that don’t mind mud. The program has been free in past winters, but confirm that when you call. If a weekday won’t work, the Bald Eagle Festival and Bird Show at Pere Marquette Lodge was set for Sunday, January 31, 2027, from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. In the 2025-26 winter it was free to walk in, and the live raptor shows cost $5. One trap: the park’s visitor center keeps winter hours, Monday through Saturday from 8 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., and it’s closed Sundays.
### Where can you ice skate in Grafton?
At The Loading Dock, which occupies the 1928 Grafton Boat Works building on the riverfront. The 2026-27 season is set to run from November 21, 2026, through February 28, 2027. An all-day skate pass is $10.50, rentals are $5, and a season pass is $75. Posted hours are Saturday from noon to 10 p.m. and Sunday from noon to 5 p.m., plus 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Martin Luther King Jr. Day (January 18, 2027) and Presidents Day (February 15, 2027). Past seasons have added Friday evenings, so check before you plan around one. A riverfront rink at a 1928 boatyard is a different night out from a mall rink.
### When is the Grafton Winter Lights Parade?
The 2026 date: Saturday, December 19, and it’s free. Floats line up at 4:30 p.m. at the Hawg Pit and step off at 5:30, roll down Water Street and finish at The Loading Dock, where the skating keeps going. The Sunday before (December 13 in 2026), Pere Marquette Lodge holds its Holiday Market from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. If you’re crossing the river for one December night anyway, pair it with the Christmas lights in St. Charles on the Missouri side.
### What time are Grafton’s New Year’s Eve fireworks?
In 2026 they were set for 10 p.m. on Thursday, December 31, over the river from Lighthouse Park. Here’s the catch: the ferry’s posted Thursday hours end at 9 p.m. Unless it announces special holiday hours, anyone who came over from St. Charles County is driving home the long way through Alton. Check the ferry schedule that week, or settle the route before the first glass.
### Which Pere Marquette trail has the best view?
Ask the park and you get a straight answer. In its own trail guide, the park’s staff picks the Goat Cliff Trail, calling it “our most popular trail with a fantastic view at the top.” It’s about 2 miles round trip and climbs along the limestone bluff to McAdams Peak, where the Illinois River and its backwater lakes spread out below you.
Pere Marquette is the largest state park in Illinois at nearly 8,000 acres, with about 12 miles of marked trails open from sunup to sundown. Most of what ranks online for this question covers one loop, or a hike someone took years ago. The short version holds up: if you only have an hour, it’s Goat Cliff.
Go in winter if you can. With the leaves down, the river shows through the trees for much of the climb instead of only at the top, and the trails are quieter on a weekday. Want a guide? The visitor center books guided hikes at (618) 786-3323. Afterward, walk into the stone lodge for a look at its 700-ton fireplace.
### Can you ride horses at Pere Marquette?
Yes, at the riding stables on Route 100, run by St. Louis Trail Riders. A ride is 45 to 50 minutes over about 2.5 miles of park trail, and it costs $55 a person, $5 less in cash. Rides leave on the hour from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Riders must be at least 8 years old and under 250 pounds, and there are no doubles. The season usually runs May through October with Tuesdays off, so this month is the last chance of the year. Call ahead.
Ferry over hungry? Here’s where to eat in Grafton before the last boat.
### Where can you fish around Grafton, and which license do you need?
Start at Stump Lake. The state’s Stump Lake Fish and Wildlife Area has a boat ramp just north of Pere Marquette that opens onto four backwater lakes: Flat, Long, Fowler and Upper Stump. The Illinois Department of Natural Resources rates the complex excellent for bluegill, crappie and bullhead. That’s a rating from the state’s own biologists, not a forum rumor.
For the big water, boat ramps at Grafton and at Pere Marquette put you on the lower Illinois River. The city posted a rehab notice for its ramp at Evans and Water streets earlier this year, so confirm it’s open before you tow. Bank anglers have it easier. The Mississippi River Fish and Wildlife Area has plenty of bank fishing spots, and its office at (618) 376-3303 can point you to them. Waterfowl management areas may be closed to fishing as posted, which matters from fall into winter.
Now the number that should get your attention. IDNR’s fact sheet for this stretch says two former world-record blue catfish, one at 124 pounds and one at 130, were caught just a few miles downstream of the Illinois River’s mouth. The mouth of the Illinois is Grafton. The same sheet says blue catfish numbers are rising in the lower river and sends anglers to the deep holes and the main channel border near structure. One advisory to keep in mind: the state recommends no more than one meal a week of channel catfish over 16 inches from the lower Illinois.
Which license? It depends on the water. Missouri’s reciprocal rule lets a Missouri-licensed angler fish the flowing Mississippi, its adjacent backwaters, and from the Illinois bank. It doesn’t cover tributaries in a state where you aren’t licensed. The Illinois River is an Illinois tributary of the Mississippi, so by that rule the Illinois River and Stump Lake call for an Illinois license. That’s our reading of the Missouri Department of Conservation’s rule, so confirm with IDNR at 217-782-6302 before you cast. If the Grafton ramps are jammed, here’s where to fish in Alton, about 15 miles downriver.
### What can you do in Grafton for free?
A surprising amount, for a town of fewer than 700 people. On summer Thursdays, Music in the Park puts local bands in Grove Memorial Park, at Market and Main, from 7 to 9 p.m. The 2026 season ran 18 weeks, May 28 through September 24, the longest yet. Bring lawn chairs and a cooler. The 2027 dates aren’t posted, but expect late May through September.
Lighthouse Park has more of a story than it looks. The lighthouse went up in 2007 to mark Grafton’s survival of the 1993 flood. The Snapper turtle sculpture came in 2020, and the park flies the largest American flag on the river. It’s also where the ferry lands, so you can sit and watch the boat come across.
Then stack the rest. Ride the Brussels Ferry over and back. Hike Goat Cliff. Catch the Winter Lights Parade, and the eagle programs if they stay free. Bike the Sam Vadalabene Bike Trail, about 20 paved miles between Alton and Pere Marquette. Each June, Pere Marquette also hosts a free Family Fishing Fair, where kids fish for live fish, get the catch cleaned and cooked, and make gyotaku fish prints. The 2026 fair was June 6, so watch for the 2027 date in spring.
Besides those, Eckert’s Grafton Farm sells field access by ticket for its fall apple and pumpkin picking, so that part isn’t free, though the country store costs nothing to browse. Heading home across the river on a budget? Line up these free things to do in St. Peters on the Missouri side.
### What are some fun things for adults to do in Grafton, Illinois this weekend?
That depends on the weekend, so here’s the fall and winter run, dated as of early October.
Witches on the Water is Grafton’s big grown-up party of the fall, and the 2026 date is Saturday, October 17. It’s 21 and over, and you need a wristband, with the proceeds going to the National Memorial of Military Ascent. Expect costume contests, artisan vendors, live music in several venues and a bonfire on the riverfront. The official listing gives two different time windows, 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. and 10 a.m. to 11 p.m., so check before you go.
For something quieter, the Grafton History and Ghost Tales walking tour runs about an hour for $25 a person, with up to 15 guests. It meets at the gazebo in Grove Memorial Park. Stops include the Ruebel Hotel, whose walnut bar was shown at the 1904 St. Louis World’s Fair, and the old Boat Works. Book through the tour listing and check open dates.
Pere Marquette Lodge runs a full grown-up calendar of its own. Its 2026 Halloween events were set for Friday, October 30: GRIP Paranormal leads a paranormal investigation of the lodge from 8 to 10 p.m., while the Moonlight Mixer Halloween party runs from 6 to 10 p.m. in the lodge’s winery. The December 2026 calendar has a murder mystery dinner on the 4th and a Christmas with Elvis dinner show on the 11th, listed at $60. From January through April, a wine pairing dinner lands once a month.
And yes, the wineries, the SkyTour gondola and the riverfront bars carry on most weekends. Every list already covers those. The point of this one is the night you’d never have found on them.
### What to do near Grafton, IL?
Use the ferry as the hinge. On the Illinois side, Alton sits about 15 miles down Route 100, close enough for a fishing morning and a Grafton afternoon. On the Missouri side, the landing drops you into St. Charles County, which is why the ferry turns Grafton and St. Charles into one trip now. For more winter-ready outings, our list of day trips within two hours of St. Louis covers the rest of the region.
Coming up from the city, the river has two more stops worth the detour: where the Missouri and Mississippi rivers meet, and the steps, trail and boats of the St. Louis riverfront.
Most people who say they’ve done Grafton did it on a summer Saturday, through Alton, in traffic. You’ll be the one rolling off the boat on a Wednesday in January with an eagle tour booked and the bluff to yourself. Call the park when reservations open (November 16 in 2026).
Crossing over for dinner? Pick the table first with the where to eat in Grafton guide on St Louis Near Me Directory, then time the drive home around the ferry’s 9 p.m. close Monday through Thursday.
If you run a Grafton business that stays open through the winter, the people reading this just learned they can reach you on a Tuesday in January, so list it with us where they’re already planning the trip.
Downriver toward Alton, free eagle watching at Clifton Terrace in Godfrey sits right on the same bike trail.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Where does the Grafton Ferry go to?
A.  It crosses the Mississippi between Grafton and St. Charles County, Missouri. The Illinois landing is beside the Grafton Lighthouse and the public boat ramp off Market Street. The Missouri landing is on Grafton Ferry Road, just off Highway 94. The ride takes five to 10 minutes and saves more than 30 minutes over driving around through Alton. For the other boats on this stretch, from the free Brussels Ferry to the Golden Eagle, see our guide to ferries near St. Louis.
### Q. What is the schedule for the Brussels Ferry in Grafton, Illinois?
A.  The Brussels Ferry is free and runs 24 hours a day, seven days a week. The Illinois Department of Transportation owns and operates it, crossing the Illinois River about a mile west of Grafton off Route 100. It does shut down for ice or high water, as it did for ice floes in late January 2026, so check its status during cold snaps.
### Q. Where can I fish in Illinois without a fishing license?
A.  Anywhere in the state during Illinois Free Fishing Days, held the third weekend of June. In 2026 that ran Friday, June 19, through Monday, June 22, with no license, salmon stamp or inland trout stamp needed. Near Grafton, the free Family Fishing Fair at Pere Marquette State Park in early June is the easiest way to try it with kids.
### Q. What river runs by Grafton, Illinois?
A.  Two of them. Grafton sits at the confluence, where the Illinois River, after flowing 273 miles across the state, enters the Mississippi. That meeting point is why the town has eagles in winter, record-size catfish downstream and a long history of floods, including the 1993 flood its riverfront lighthouse now commemorates.
### Q. What is the history of Grafton, Illinois?
A.  Brothers James and Paris Mason founded Grafton in 1832, and it’s the oldest town in Jersey County. Quarries and boatbuilding fed a mid-1800s peak of more than 10,000 residents, and the steamboat era supported 26 saloons. Fewer than 700 people live there now. Grafton limestone went into the Eads Bridge in St. Louis.
### Q. Is Grafton worth visiting?
A.  Depends on the season, and that’s the point. Fall weekends are crowded, so go on a weekday. Winter is quiet, the ferry still runs, and you get eagle tours, skating and bluff trails with the leaves down. Spring brings high water, so check river conditions first. Summer has free Thursday concerts. Go when the thing you want is happening.
### Q. What are some good places to shop in Grafton, Illinois?
A.  Main Street is the shopping strip, lined with small, locally owned stores. River Bank Gifts sits in the 1871 building that held Grafton’s first bank, at 225 E. Main St. Up on the bluffs, Eckert’s Grafton Country Store sells homemade pies, jams, apple butter, pumpkin butter and cider, open Tuesday through Sunday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.
### Q. Can you use a Missouri fishing license at Grafton?
A.  On the Mississippi, yes. Missouri’s reciprocal rule covers the flowing river, its adjacent backwaters and fishing from the Illinois bank. On the Illinois River and the Stump Lake lakes, no, because those are Illinois tributary waters and the rule bars fishing tributaries in a state where you aren’t licensed. That’s our reading; confirm with IDNR at 217-782-6302.

## Things to Do in Alton, IL: 4 Million Drive-Through Lights, Park Concerts, Catfish
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-alton-il
Why do the top-ten lists keep selling Alton as a ghost tour and a giant statue? In summer 2026 the Alton Municipal Band played its 132nd consecutive season of free concerts, Thursday nights in the Riverview Park gazebo and Sunday nights in Haskell Park, and the lists walked right past it. Same with Halloween. Alton’s Halloween parade has been running for more than a century. It steps off at 7 p.m. on October 31. It costs nothing to watch.
That’s the pattern here. Alton’s best stuff is old, cheap or free, and it’s sitting in city parks that day-trippers drive straight past on the way to the bluffs. The town is about 25 miles up the Mississippi from downtown St. Louis, and it’s one of the small towns outside St. Louis where the locals work from a very different list than the one online.
So this guide skips the scenic-drive itinerary and the haunted-house roundup. It’s built around what people actually search once they’ve done the obvious: which parks are worth the trip, where to drive through 4 million Christmas lights, where to fish, Halloween for grown-ups, what’s free, and what’s open after dark.
### What are the best parks in Alton, Illinois?
Start with Gordon F. Moore Park: 704 acres, a 13-acre lake the Illinois DNR stocks, and a rose garden with 1,600-plus bushes and Sunday carillon concerts. Riverview and Haskell parks host the free Alton Municipal Band each summer, Rock Spring Park lights up for Christmas Wonderland, and Russell Commons anchors the dog park and Confluence Trail.
Each park does a different job, and that’s the whole trick. Pick by season, not by star rating.
Gordon F. Moore Park (4550 College Ave.) is the big one, and there’s no charge to get in. Most visitors only ever see the ball fields. Keep driving to the south side. That’s where the memorial rose garden sits: dedicated in 1980, about an acre, more than 150 varieties, blooming from late May or early June until the first hard freeze. A carillon in the garden plays every half hour, and from Memorial Day through September the carillon guild gives a concert every Sunday at 5 p.m. Bring your own chair. Next to it, a walkway crosses a bridge and loops past a koi pond, a waterfall and a pagoda in the Oriental Garden, and a quarter-mile accessible nature trail starts and ends right there. The same park holds the stocked fishing lake and an Arnold Palmer-designed public golf course, so one park can cover four very different afternoons.
Riverview Park (491 Park Ave.) and Haskell Park (1211 Henry St.) are the band parks. Riverview has the gazebo where the full municipal band plays Thursdays at 7:30 p.m. in summer. Haskell hosts the Sunday 7 p.m. concerts near its Lucy Playhouse. More on the band below, because it’s the best free night in town.
Rock Spring Park (College Avenue, just west of Washington Avenue) is quiet most of the year, apart from an 18-hole disc golf course that’s been there since 2008. Then the day after Thanksgiving it turns into Christmas Wonderland, which gets its own section next.
Russell Commons Park is the trail-and-dog park. The MCT Confluence Trail starts here, and so does the city’s 3-acre fenced dog park. Riverfront Park, a footbridge walk from downtown over Landmarks Boulevard, has the 4,000-seat Alton Amphitheater, a summer splash pad, walking paths and the best ground-level look at the Clark Bridge. City parks are open dawn to dusk. The bridge has a better story than its looks, a 1994 cable-stayed span that PBS’s NOVA filmed for “Super Bridge,” and our guide to bridges in St. Louis tells it.
### Where can you see drive-through Christmas lights in Alton, IL?
At Christmas Wonderland in Rock Spring Park, 2116 College Ave. It’s a drive-through display of more than 4 million lights. It opens the day after Thanksgiving, which falls on Friday, November 27, in 2026, and runs through late December. Getting in is free, with a suggested donation of $10 per car, cash only.
Here’s what makes it Alton’s. The display is built by area grandfathers and volunteers who call themselves the “Grandpa Gang.” They start hanging lights the second week of September and put in four hours every weekday morning until opening night, so if they keep their usual schedule, they’re out there right now. The money at the gate covers operating costs, and the rest goes to local nonprofits. In 2024 that came to about $75,000.
Search for Alton’s Christmas lights and the results mostly hand you other towns’ displays and an old news item. The real thing is 4 million bulbs, a donation bucket and a crew of grandpas on ladders.
What the drive is like. You roll through the park at a crawl with your headlights off, past lighted trees, cascading waterfalls and hundreds of light displays. Halfway through, you can pull over to see Santa. Kids get a photo and can write him a letter. Near the end, you vote for your favorite of the 15 or so Christmas trees decorated by local organizations, and the top three win a prize. Last season Santa took Christmas Eve and Christmas Day off, so plan the kids’ visit before then.
Hours: 6 to 9 p.m. weeknights, 5 to 9 p.m. Saturdays and Sundays.
Cost: a suggested $10 per car or small van, in cash. Vehicles carrying 10 or more people are asked for $1 a person.
Season: in 2025 it ran November 28 through December 28. Expect a similar window in 2026 and confirm before you go.
Walk-through night: one night a season the park opens to people on foot. In 2025 it was Monday, December 1, from 6 to 9 p.m., with parking at Alton Middle School and a $1-per-person donation. Watch for each season’s date. It’s the night for strollers and slow photos.
A few ways to do it right. Bring cash, because it’s the one thing people forget. Pick a weeknight if lines bother you. Then make it a whole evening: dinner downtown first, the lights, and home over the Clark Bridge with the river black below you. Want to help instead of watch? The Grandpa Gang takes donated lights, and it takes volunteers. Last season they told people to stop by Rock Spring Park on a weekday morning between 8 a.m. and noon to ask.
One display rarely satisfies a lights family. The tourism bureau pairs this one with Bethalto Christmas Village, a free walk among lit cottages in Bethalto’s Central Park and arboretum. Alton’s Madison County neighbor runs its own season too, so add Christmas lights in Edwardsville to the list, and our guide to drive-through Christmas lights around St. Louis covers the Missouri side.
### Where to fish in Alton, IL?
Two very different places. One is the 13-acre lake in Gordon F. Moore Park, which the Illinois Department of Natural Resources stocks. The other is the Mississippi itself, especially the tailwater below Melvin Price Locks and Dam, where catfish anglers have worked the wing dams for years. One needs an Illinois license. The other might not, if you already carry a Missouri one. The dam itself is worth the stop: our guide to Melvin Price Locks and Dam covers the free lock tours and the museum beside it. The river here has produced bigger surprises, too. In 1937 two commercial fishermen brought in a bull shark near town, still the only accepted record in the upper Mississippi, and our story of sharks in the Mississippi sorts that one from the hoaxes.
The park lake. This is the easy bank-fishing option: a free city park and fish the state put there. It sits beside the Oriental Garden on the south side of the park, so anyone in the group who doesn’t fish has a koi pond and a nature trail to wander. Because it’s an inland Illinois lake, the river deal below doesn’t cover it. You need an Illinois fishing license.
The tailwater. Below the dam, the wing dams hold big catfish, and cut shad is the classic bait. How seriously does the region take its Mississippi catfish? In 2024 the King Kat tournament trail added Alton as a brand-new stop, with teams launching off the riverfront and the captains’ meeting at the amphitheater. Obey the posted restrictions around the dam and the locks, and fish only where it’s open.
Your Missouri license. This is the part St. Louis anglers miss. Under the reciprocal agreement on the Mississippi, a properly licensed Missouri angler may fish the river’s flowing water on either side, its adjacent backwaters, and from the Illinois bank. Two catches. You follow Illinois rules while you’re in Illinois, and the stricter of the two states’ rules applies. Tributaries and inland lakes don’t count. The Missouri Department of Conservation’s reciprocal fishing page spells it out, and it’s worth a fresh read before each season.
Rather stay on the Missouri side? The fishing lakes in St. Charles are an easy swap.
### What Halloween events happen in Alton?
The big one is free: the Alton Halloween Parade, held on Halloween night itself, which is Saturday, October 31, in 2026, at 7 p.m. Around it, the town stacks a month of grown-up Halloween, from haunted beer walks to a museum of oddities to a live Rocky Horror. Here’s the short list, with 2026 dates.
The Alton Halloween Parade. The local tourism bureau bills it as one of the oldest Halloween parades in the country, running for more than a century. It starts at Washington Avenue and Broadway, rolls down Broadway to Piasa Street, then turns right on Piasa to 9th Street. Expect 40-plus entries: floats, bands and costumed marchers. Get to Broadway early for a curb spot, and park a few blocks off the route.
Haunted Craft Beer Walks (21+). Alton Odyssey Tours and Old Bakery Beer Company run these on Friday nights in October: the 9th, 16th, 23rd and 30th, at 8 p.m., for $50 a person. You start at the Historic Grand Theater, 230 Market St., with a quick ghost-hunting primer and a look at the equipment, then walk to five spots, including the Underground Railroad tunnels at the Enos Sanitarium, the Old Post Office and the Hilltop Room at the Stratford Hotel. Each stop comes with an Old Bakery beer. Bring ID, wear shoes for hills and stairs, and book early, because spots are limited.
Troy Taylor’s American Oddities Museum. It’s at 301 Piasa St., open Thursday through Sunday from noon to 5 p.m. (last admission 4:30), $7, and free for kids 10 and under. Inside are objects from the Enos Apartments and the McPike Mansion, Victorian vampire-killing kits, a taxidermied “mermaid” and a collection of quack medicine. Taylor also leads a Haunted Alton Zombie Pub Crawl from the museum; the 2026 dates are October 24 and October 30.
The Rocky Horror Show. Alton Little Theater’s 93rd season puts it on October 29 through November 1, 2026. It’s the indoor pick for Halloween weekend, so check the box office for tickets.
The Great Godfrey Maze. Next door in Godfrey, at Glazebrook Park (1401 Stamper Lane), the corn maze stays open after dark on Friday and Saturday nights into early November. Everyone needs a flashlight, and they’re $3 at the concession stand if you forget. General admission is $8 for adults, and the regular plus haunted maze combo is $10. It’s alcohol-free and family friendly, so it’s the one stop here for the kids.
Alton has run ghost tours since 1992, so the classic haunted walk is easy to find. This list is for the night you want something else.
Hungry after all that? Where to eat in Alton
### What free things can you do in Alton, IL?
Start with the band. The City of Alton says the Alton Municipal Band is in its 132nd consecutive season of summer concerts, and they’re free. The full band plays Thursdays at 7:30 p.m. in the Riverview Park gazebo and Sundays at 7 p.m. near the Lucy Playhouse in Haskell Park. In 2026 that ran from early June to late July. Guest soloists sit in, kids get the traditional kiddie march through the park, and smaller groups from the band turn up around town, including at the Saturday farmers market. This year’s season is over. Put next June on the calendar now.
The rest of the free calendar, in the order the year hands it to you:
Carillon concerts in the Gordon F. Moore Park rose garden, Sundays at 5 p.m. from Memorial Day through September. Bring a chair.
The September Sunset Series at the Alton Amphitheater on the riverfront: Friday-night concerts, 6 to 9 p.m., every September. Blankets, outside food, non-alcoholic drinks and leashed dogs have all been welcome. Watch for next fall’s lineup.
The Alton Farmers’ and Artisans’ Market, in its 34th season in 2026, Saturdays 8 a.m. to noon at Landmarks Boulevard and Henry Street. Admission is free, and the last 2026 dates are October 10 and 17.
The Alton Military Prison ruins at William Street and Broadway. Only a short restored section of wall is left, but more than 11,700 Confederate prisoners passed through in three years, and the official military death toll was 1,354 as smallpox, influenza and dysentery swept the place.
