Lincoln-Douglas Square downtown, near where Market Street meets Broadway, where life-size bronzes mark the final Lincoln-Douglas debate of 1858 and the 6,000-plus people who came to hear it.
Free mulch. Really. The city’s park and forestry crews grind up branches, and the mulch is free for the taking near the Learning Center at Gordon F. Moore Park. Bring a truck bed and a shovel.
### Where can you bike or walk the river in Alton?
Two long river trails start in Alton, and they point in opposite directions.
Downriver: the MCT Confluence Trail. It runs 20.5 miles from Russell Commons Park to the McKinley Bridge, right along the Mississippi, on a mix of asphalt, oil-and-chip and rock. Along the way you pass the Clark Bridge, the National Great Rivers Museum, a 900-foot bridge over Wood River Creek and the Lewis and Clark Interpretive Center. The part almost nobody on the Missouri side knows: a 3-mile extension reaches the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge and connects to the Riverfront Trail in St. Louis, and the McKinley Bridge bike lane links up too. You can ride from an Alton park to the St. Louis riverfront on connected trail. Park at Russell Commons or at the museum. A spur at New Poag Road also joins the MCT Riverbend Trail toward East Alton.
Upriver: the Sam Vadalabene Bike Trail. About 20 paved miles from Alton to Pere Marquette State Park, tucked under the limestone bluffs. Park at Piasa Park on Route 100, where the Piasa Bird is painted on the rock face, and ride north. It’s open dawn to dusk. What’s at the far end is another town’s story, and if you’d rather do it by car, our guide to the Great River Road drive from Alton to Grafton has every stop.
In winter, watch the sky over the Confluence Trail. Bald eagles winter along this stretch of river, and MCT’s own trail page mentions them as a cold-weather bonus. Eagle season is a bigger deal upriver, and it’s a big part of the things to do in Grafton in winter.
With a dog, the Alton Dog Park at Russell Commons sits right at the Confluence trailhead: three acres, three separate fenced runs, obstacles and play stations. It isn’t a drop-in park, though. You need an annual pass from the City Hall Treasurer’s Office or the Parks and Recreation Office at 2 Emma Kaus Lane (the Alton Marina takes applications evenings and weekends), plus proof of rabies and booster shots and proof your dog is spayed or neutered. Kids under 16 can’t go inside the runs.
### What is there to do in Alton at night?
More than ghost tours. Alton’s after-dark list is short, specific and runs late.
Game Over, 1022 East Broadway, is an arcade bar and grill with more than 200 games, from old shooters and fighting cabinets to pinball and VR, plus a full bar that pours alcoholic slushies. It’s open seven days, from 11 a.m. to 1 a.m. early in the week and as late as 3 a.m. on weekends. Credits start at $20 for 80. Bringing anyone under 21 after dark? Check their age policy first.
Alton Little Theater calls itself the oldest continuous community theater in Illinois. In its 93rd season, Rocky Horror is followed by The Outsider, a political comedy, November 13 to 22, 2026, and Come From Away, opening January 22, 2027.
Summer evenings belong to the Alton Night Market, Thursday nights in June and July, roughly 7 to 10 p.m., and to the free Sunset Series at the amphitheater in September. The market has moved around over the years, so check the summer schedule for the spot. October Fridays are the haunted beer walks above, and on Halloween night itself the parade fills Broadway.
### What can you do indoors in Alton on a rainy day?
Skate. The East Alton Ice Arena, 631 Lewis and Clark Blvd. in East Alton, lists its hours as 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. every day, with public skating, stick-and-puck times and drop-in sessions on its online calendar. The Village of East Alton owns it, and SIUE and a lot of local high school hockey teams play their games there. A rainy Saturday on the ice beats a rainy Saturday in the car. Check the calendar for public skate times and prices before you go.
Get weird. The American Oddities Museum is the best rainy hour downtown, Thursday through Sunday afternoons, and kids 10 and under get in free. Decide for yourself how much medical quackery your 8-year-old needs.
Play. Game Over works at lunch, too. It opens at 11 a.m., the grill runs burgers and wings, and 200-plus games eat a wet afternoon fast.
River history, indoors. The National Great Rivers Museum, beside the Melvin Price Locks and Dam, is the other classic rainy-day stop, and our Great River Road guide covers it in detail.
None of this makes the lists that send everyone to the same statue and the same bluff. Fine. You’re the one who knows the band plays the gazebo on Thursdays, which lake the state stocks, and that a gang of grandpas starts hanging 4 million lights on College Avenue every September. Put the day after Thanksgiving on the calendar (November 27 in 2026) and bring cash. When you need addresses and phone numbers, the Alton city guide has them.
Making a night of the lights or the parade? Line up dinner first with St Louis Near Me Directory’s where to eat in Alton guide.
And if you run an Alton business, the families creeping down College Avenue in December are looking for somewhere to go next, so put your Alton business where they’re searching.
Just upriver, free eagle watching at Clifton Terrace in Godfrey is one of the easiest winter eagle stops on the river.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What time does the Alton Illinois Halloween parade start?
A.  7 p.m. on Halloween night, which is Saturday, October 31, in 2026. It starts at Washington Avenue and Broadway, runs down Broadway to Piasa Street, then turns right on Piasa to 9th Street. It’s free to watch and has run for more than a century. Plan to park a few blocks away and walk in.
### Q. What river runs through Alton, Illinois?
A.  The Mississippi. Alton sits on the Illinois bank between two big confluences: the Illinois River joins the Mississippi upstream at Grafton, and the Missouri River joins it a few miles downstream. Fittingly, the trail that heads south out of town along the water is called the Confluence Trail.
### Q. Is Alton, IL worth visiting?
A.  Yes, if you plan around the calendar instead of a quick photo stop. Summer has band and carillon concerts, October has the Halloween parade and haunted beer walks, late November brings Christmas Wonderland’s 4 million lights, and winter has eagles along the river trail and a skating rink next door in East Alton that opens every day. It’s about 25 miles from downtown St. Louis.
### Q. What is Alton, Illinois famous for?
A.  Robert Wadlow, the tallest man ever recorded, was born here, and a statue downtown honors him. Alton also hosted the final Lincoln-Douglas debate in 1858, is where abolitionist editor Elijah P. Lovejoy was killed defending his press in 1837, and markets itself as one of the most haunted small towns in America.
### Q. Is there anything to do in Alton?
A.  Plenty, once you look past the top-ten lists. Fish a state-stocked lake, ride 20 miles of river trail in either direction, catch a free band concert in a park gazebo, skate any day of the week in East Alton, play arcade games until 3 a.m. on a weekend, or drive through 4 million Christmas lights hung by retirees.
### Q. Did Abraham Lincoln live in Alton, Illinois?
A.  No. Lincoln lived in Springfield. Alton hosted the seventh and final Lincoln-Douglas debate on October 15, 1858, in front of the old city hall at Broadway and Market, and more than 6,000 people turned out. Life-size bronzes of the two men mark the spot today at Lincoln-Douglas Square, and it costs nothing to stop.
### Q. What are some fun activities for kids in Alton?
A.  Walk the koi pond and nature trail in Gordon F. Moore Park, fish its stocked lake, skate at the East Alton Ice Arena, cool off at the Riverfront Park splash pad in summer, or join the kiddie march at a municipal band concert. In fall, the Great Godfrey Maze is family friendly. In December, Christmas Wonderland has Santa halfway through the drive.
### Q. Can you fish the Mississippi at Alton with a Missouri fishing license?
A.  Yes, on the river itself. Missouri’s reciprocal agreement with Illinois lets licensed Missouri anglers fish the Mississippi’s flowing water, its adjacent backwaters and from the Illinois bank, as long as they follow Illinois rules and the stricter of the two states’ limits. Inland waters like the Gordon F. Moore Park lake need an Illinois license. Confirm current rules before you go.

## Things to Do in Edwardsville, IL: Free Band Nights, a 1978 Movie Set, Bank Fishing
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-edwardsville-il
St. Louis grown-ups, the Edwardsville listicles have been shortchanging you. Every recycled top-10 sends you to the same campus garden and the same Saturday market, then calls the town done. Not one of them mentions that most of Stingray, a 1978 Corvette car-chase movie, was shot on these streets. Or that the City Park lawn where the film staged its rock-concert stampede still fills with folding chairs for free band nights every summer Thursday.
That’s the Edwardsville this guide is about. It’s the Madison County seat and a college town about half an hour from downtown St. Louis, and it’s one of the small towns outside St. Louis worth a whole day instead of a pass-through. The Gardens at SIUE and the Watershed Nature Center boardwalk are lovely. Every list already has them, so they get a line here and no more.
Everything below is built around what people actually search for once the obvious stops are used up: free things to do, a rainy afternoon, fishing without a boat, Christmas lights, free concerts, a grown-up night out. Hours and prices were checked against the city, the township and the venues themselves in October 2026. Some will move. We flag the ones most likely to.
### What are some free things to do in Edwardsville, Illinois?
Plenty, and the best of it isn’t on campus. The Municipal Band, a tradition dating to the 1880s, plays free in City Park every summer Thursday. Add a real Navy A-7 jet at Township Airplane Park, a free Route 66 service station museum, two stocked fishing lakes at Joe Glik Park and a 0.02-acre park honoring five governors.
Start with the band, because it’s the thing locals would miss most. It plays the City Park bandstand, 101 S. Buchanan St., at 7:30 p.m. on summer Thursdays. In 2026 it added one free fall show there, set for Sunday, October 11, at 2 p.m. The full concert rundown is further down.
Then go see the jet. Edwardsville Township’s community park on Center Grove Road is the one everybody here calls Airplane Park, and the reason sits on the lawn: a U.S. Navy A-7E Corsair II attack jet, on loan from the National Museum of Naval Aviation and on display for more than 20 years. Volunteers and the Edwardsville Community Foundation are restoring it. The park is at 6368 Center Grove Rd. Its posted 2026 hours: 8 a.m. to 7 p.m. through October 31, and 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. from November 1. It costs nothing to walk up and stare.
The West End Service Station has the best plot twist of any free stop in town. This corner of Route 66 sold gas from 1927 until 1964, and the station standing there now dates to 1939. When the highway bypassed Edwardsville, the building was sold and filled with dental offices. Dentists worked there for the next 55 years. The city and the Great Rivers & Routes tourism bureau bought it in 2022 and reopened it in June 2023 as a free Route 66 interpretive center at 620 St. Louis St., open Wednesday through Sunday, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. In September 2026, with the Mother Road turning 100, it won a Landmarks Illinois preservation award.
Two of the oddest free stops share a street. Hotz Park, at St. Louis and Randle streets, measures 0.02 acres, and the city calls it one of the smallest parks in the United States. It’s basically one huge stone with a bronze plaque for the five Illinois governors who lived in Edwardsville: Edward Coles, Ninian Edwards, John Reynolds, Thomas Ford and Charles Deneen. A short walk up Randle, Lusk Memorial Park at No. 535 is the city’s oldest cemetery. It’s a shady, quiet park now, and the remains of several original headstones are still visible near the entrance. A historical marker went up in 2024.
The trails are free, and downtown is a trailhead. The MCT Quercus Grove Trail starts at Schwarz and Springer streets and runs 18.9 miles north on asphalt and limestone toward Hamel, with parking at the MCT Park & Ride on Hillsboro Avenue. The 28.5-mile Nickel Plate Trail heads south toward Pontoon Beach and passes Glen Carbon’s Miner Park, part of a Madison County Transit network of about 138 miles. Besides those, the SIUE gardens and the Watershed boardwalk cost nothing and open daily. You knew that.
### What movie was filmed in Edwardsville, IL?
Stingray, a 1978 action comedy starring Christopher Mitchum, was filmed mostly in Edwardsville. Its writer and director, Richard Taylor, ran the motion picture production department at SIUE, and he gave up the job to make it. Cameras rolled from August 1 to October 7, 1977, on a budget of roughly a million dollars.
The story is one long chase. Two buddies buy a red Corvette Stingray off a used car lot, not knowing a drug gang hid a fortune inside it, and the gang spends the rest of the movie trying to get it back. Alton was supposed to be the main location, since its hills suit car stunts, but the mayor refused, and Edwardsville ended up carrying most of the picture. Wood River and Alton still appear. The finale was shot in East St. Louis, and the big stunt is a plunge off the Eads Bridge into the Mississippi.
The scene to know is the rock concert, filmed on the City Park lawn. The band on stage was miming, played by members of the production staff. The extras weren’t paid. Most were retirees and parents, and the crowd work dragged past eight hours. When Taylor needed the audience to stampede, he fired a blank without warning anybody. He got his shot.
Edwardsville never let it go. Taylor kept his own print, with the violent footage that was cut in 1978 to land a PG rating. It fed a restored director’s cut that premiered on April 20, 2019, at the Wildey, the 1909 movie house at 252 N. Main St. That’s a tidy loop, because a 2026 review clocks the Wildey’s own marquee on screen about 29 minutes in. And during the city’s America 250 week in summer 2026, Samm’s Last Chance Saloon at 1013 N. Main, which the city says the movie filmed inside, played Stingray on repeat all week.
So here’s the night we’d plan. Watch it first. It has turned up on free streaming services like Tubi, so check what’s carrying it now. Then drive over on a summer Thursday, catch the band on the same lawn where the extras ran, walk up Main past the Wildey’s marquee, and finish at Samm’s. The Post-Dispatch critic in 1978 said the film mostly worked as a regional travelogue. Forty-eight years later, that’s the best reason to watch it. If a car movie puts you in a drive-in mood, Belleville’s Skyview Drive-In is about half an hour south and usually runs movies into October.
Planning the Stingray night? Here’s where to eat in Edwardsville first.
### What is there to do in Edwardsville on a rainy day?
Skate, then go back two centuries. Edwardsville’s indoor options run deeper than its size suggests, and the best one is open all year.
The R.P. Lumber Center, 6289 Tiger Dr., has a year-round indoor ice rink with public skate sessions on a monthly calendar. Admission is $8 for District 7 residents and $10 for everyone else, rental skates are $3, and select Friday sessions drop to $5 with the rental included. The rink sits around 60 degrees, so wear long sleeves and bring gloves. Watching costs nothing, which matters when only half the family wants to skate. Session times shift month to month, so check before you drive.
The 1820 Col. Benjamin Stephenson House, 409 S. Buchanan St., is the oldest brick home in Madison County, and it doesn’t tell a tidy story. Indentured servants helped build it, and the house is direct about enslavement and indentured servitude in early Illinois, including inside the Stephenson household. Its 2026 hours, through December 13: Thursday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. and Sunday from noon to 3, with no tours after 2 p.m. Admission is $10 for adults and $5 for kids; children 5 and under get in free. The house said in 2026 that it was short-staffed, so call 618-692-1818 to make sure a docent will be there, and confirm prices while you’re at it.
Up on North Main, the Madison County Historical Society runs the 1836 Weir House Museum at 801 N. Main St., with guided tours of eight rooms and the basement, Wednesday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. and Sunday from 1 to 4. Next door in Glen Carbon, the Heritage Museum fills a former schoolhouse on the National Register at 124 School St. with coal-mining tools, Native American stone tools and the toys local kids once played with. Since this fall it’s open Monday through Friday, 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., and closed on weekends.
The Route 66 station from the free list works in the rain too. It’s indoors, and it’s free. With small kids, the Children’s Museum in the old Leclaire Academy building and the bowling and arcade at Edison’s are the standbys every family list already covers.
### Where can you fish in Edwardsville without a boat?
Three places, and none of them needs a boat. Two are city parks with easy bank access. The third is a campus lake holding better bass than most people would guess.
Leclaire Lake sits in Leclaire Park, 900 Hale Ave., inside the neighborhood N.O. Nelson laid out in 1890 as a model village for his factory workers. It’s a 2-acre lake with a lighted waterfall fountain and a sidewalk looping the park, so you can fish it from the edge. An IDNR urban fishing coordinator has said the fish here run small “but the population is tremendous.” Every summer, the Illinois Department of Natural Resources runs free weekday fishing clinics at the lake, with bait and gear provided and no registration. In 2026 they ran July 21 through August 13, from 9 to 11 a.m. or 1 to 3:30 p.m. Adults are welcome, which surprises people.
Joe Glik Park, 710 E. Lake Dr., covers more than 42 acres and has two stocked fishing lakes with a concrete fishing deck, the easy pick for kids or anyone who’d rather not scramble down a bank. The city’s free spring derby for kids 15 and under, catch and release, was held here on May 30, 2026. City parks are open 6 a.m. to 10 p.m., and Joe Glik also has a fenced, shaded off-leash dog park if the dog rode along.
Cougar Lake, on the SIUE campus, is the sleeper. In the latest IDNR survey posted for the lake, biologists caught largemouth bass at 33 per 30 minutes, above the agency’s goal of 30, and a high share of them were larger fish. Redear sunfish rated good, mostly 4 to 8 inches. Channel catfish and crappie are in there too, though bluegill rated poor. IDNR says the lake lacks good formal public access, but people do walk in and fish from the bank. The Cougar Lake Recreation Area, a peninsula off the Delyte Morris Trail, is the obvious place to start. SIUE requires a valid Illinois fishing license and bans boating, swimming and wading.
Anyone 16 or older needs an Illinois license at all three. If you’d like more water on the Missouri side, our guide to the best fishing spots in St. Louis picks up where this leaves off.
### Where can you see Christmas lights in Edwardsville?
Downtown, mostly, and on two Saturdays more than any others. Edwardsville has no big drive-through display. What it has is a short run of walkable lighting nights that St. Louis Christmas lists almost never mention.
On the 2026 calendar, the first is Saturday, November 28, Small Business Saturday, and it makes a two-stop date night. From 4 to 7 p.m., the Stephenson House holds its Christmas Candlelight Tours of the 1820 house. Then drive a few minutes to the Glen Carbon Heritage Museum, where the Heritage Winter Market runs 5 to 8 p.m. with live reindeer, local vendors and a tree lighting at 6. The night also opens the Glenfestival of Trees, a schoolhouse full of decorated trees and wreaths that visitors vote on.
The second, on the 2026 calendar, is Saturday, December 5. The city’s Winter Market Festival fills City Park from noon to 5 p.m. with artisan vendors, Santa, a free kids’ craft and the annual tree lighting. In 2025 it drew more than 60 booths, handed out free s’mores kits at the fire pit and lit the tree at 5:30. The same day, the Municipal Band plays a free holiday concert at the Wildey. The start time hadn’t been set in early October 2026, and seats go first come, first seated, so watch the band’s Facebook page. Reading this after December 5? Check the city and the band’s page for next year’s dates.
The rest of December fills in around those two. Santa has visited Nickel Plate Station, 610 Troy Rd., on select December days, the R.P. Lumber Center holds Skate with Santa in mid-December, and the West End Service Station has put up a holiday exhibit. None had posted 2026 dates by early October. Glen Carbon’s Lighted Christmas Parade ran December 6 in 2025; its 2026 date wasn’t confirmed by early October. As for the lit-up houses on hobbyist light maps, they change every year and they’re private homes, so we leave the addresses to their owners.
Want a display you can drive through? The drive-through Christmas lights in Alton are about 25 minutes west, and our roundup of the best Christmas lights in St. Louis covers the Missouri side.
### Are there free concerts in Edwardsville in the summer?
Yes. Two free series share the same lawn on back-to-back nights, and a free outdoor movie fills in once a month. A summer week here can mean a community band on Thursday and a rock cover band on Friday without spending a dollar on either.
Thursdays belong to the Edwardsville Municipal Band, a tradition the city traces to the 1880s. Concerts start at 7:30 p.m. at the Cleaon Etzkorn Bandstand in City Park, weather permitting, and the 2026 season ran every Thursday from June 4 to August 20. The band added a Sunday afternoon show at the Leclaire Park bandstand in August 2026, and one more City Park show was set for Sunday, October 11, at 2 p.m. After that, find it marching in the Halloween parade on October 31 and the Veterans Day parade on November 11.
Fridays are Concerts in the Park, run by Parks and Recreation as part of its Arts in the Park series. Shows start at 8 p.m. on Friday nights in June and July. The 2026 lineup gives you the flavor: an ’80s tribute band, a Motown set, the Steve Ewing Band (Ewing fronted the St. Louis band The Urge), a folk and blues group and a dueling-pianos night. A bonus show on August 14 kicked off the Rotary Criterium weekend.
Movies in the Park take over the same bandstand one Saturday a month, June through September, at dusk. In 2026 that meant Shrek and Jurassic Park among others. Bring chairs or a blanket and your own snacks. When weather threatens, Parks and Recreation posts cancellations on its Facebook page, so check it before you leave St. Louis.
### What to do in Edwardsville, IL for adults?
Make it a night, not an errand. The Stingray plan above is the headliner. These fill out the rest.
Stagger Inn Again, 104 E. Vandalia St., calls itself Edwardsville’s oldest continuously operating drinking establishment. It’s a restaurant by day and a bar with live bands Thursday through Sunday at night, and it marked 40 years in December 2024. Check its Facebook page for who’s playing. Samm’s, the Stingray bar, is up on North Main.
Skating with no kids underfoot is a better date than it sounds. The R.P. Lumber Center schedules adults-only public sessions for anyone 18 and older; they’re on the rink’s monthly calendar.
October is when Edwardsville gets fun for grown-ups. The Stephenson House’s 2026 exhibit, “Mourning Col. Stephenson,” looks at how people grieved in the early 1800s and is up through October 31. Its Ghosts in the Parlor evening, set for Saturday, October 10, 2026, from 5 to 8 p.m., brings parlor games, food and local folklore into the 1820 house after hours. It’s ticketed, so book ahead. Then comes the Halloween parade at 6:30 p.m. on October 31, which the Edwardsville/Glen Carbon Chamber of Commerce has staged for more than 100 years. Thousands line downtown for roughly 100 floats, and the 2026 theme, Mother Road Memories, leans into Route 66’s centennial. It leaves Lincoln Middle School at Schwarz and West streets, heads east on St. Louis Street, then north on Main to High Street.
Summer’s grown-up event is the Rotary Criterium, a day of bike racing on the streets of downtown every August. In 2026, its 16th year, it ran from 2 to 11 p.m. on August 15. The top pro race started at 9:35 p.m., well after dark, with live music, free kids’ races earlier in the day and an open-container perimeter, so you can watch with a drink in your hand. Organizers bill its prize money as one of the region’s largest one-day race payouts, which is why fast riders show up.
Next time somebody tells you there’s nothing across the river but a campus and a market, you’ll be the one who knows about the jet, the 0.02-acre park, the bass in Cougar Lake and the City Park lawn that once staged a stampede for a Corvette movie. Keep our Edwardsville city guide handy for the local shops and services around all of it. And if you’re stringing river towns together, our page on Grafton Ferry hours and fares covers the crossing that gets you home to the Missouri side the long, pretty way.
Line up dinner before band night or the parade with St Louis Near Me Directory’s guide to where to eat in Edwardsville.
And if you run a shop or restaurant on Main Street, the Stingray crowd and the parade crowd both start their night with a search, so list it with us where they’re already looking.
About 10 miles south on Route 159, the parks in Collinsville include a free farm with donkeys and goats.
