### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is Edwardsville, Illinois known for?
A.  It’s the Madison County seat, the home of SIUE and a Route 66 town; the old highway ran through its streets until 1964, and 2026 is the road’s centennial. Locals will also point you to the five Illinois governors who lived here, the 1890 Leclaire model village, the 1820 Stephenson House and Stingray, the 1978 movie filmed mostly in town.
### Q. What is the movie Stingray about?
A.  Two easygoing buddies, played by Christopher Mitchum and Les Lannom, buy a red Corvette Stingray off a used car lot without knowing drug dealers stashed a million dollars and a load of heroin inside. The gang’s boss, Abigail, played by Sherry Jackson and first seen disguised as a nun, chases them all over the region. It’s a PG action comedy from June 1978. MGM had a Corvette movie coming the same month, wanted the Stingray title and lost, so it renamed its picture Corvette Summer.
### Q. What’s going on in Edwardsville this weekend?
A.  Check the city’s online calendar at cityofedwardsville.com, where Notify Me alerts will email you new events, and the Wildey’s schedule for films and concerts. In summer the answer is easy: the Municipal Band on Thursday, Concerts in the Park on Friday. In October 2026, the big dates are Ghosts in the Parlor on the 10th, the band’s free City Park show on the 11th, Halloween Party in the Park on the 24th and the parade on the 31st.
### Q. What kind of fish can you find in Illinois lakes?
A.  Mostly the warm-water regulars: largemouth bass, bluegill, redear sunfish, crappie and channel catfish. Edwardsville’s lakes are a fair sample. IDNR’s survey of Cougar Lake at SIUE found good numbers of largemouth bass and redear sunfish, with channel catfish and crappie present, and Leclaire Lake holds bluegill, catfish and bass. Anglers 16 and older need an Illinois fishing license.
### Q. What’s the etiquette for using paved bike trails?
A.  Keep right, pass on the left, and call out “on your left” or ring a bell before you go by. Walkers and runners get the right of way, so slow down around them, ride single file when someone’s coming, and keep dogs on a short leash. On the MCT trails through downtown Edwardsville, the Quercus Grove and Nickel Plate cross city streets, so stop at the road crossings. Taking a break? Pull all the way off the path.
### Q. How do you find free local events?
A.  Go to the source. In Edwardsville that means the city calendar with its Notify Me email alerts, the Parks and Recreation Facebook page, which also posts concert and movie cancellations, and the Municipal Band’s own Facebook page. The Great Rivers & Routes tourism bureau keeps a regional events calendar too. Big event sites tend to lag, and they miss small stuff like a Sunday band concert.
### Q. What are some fun things to do in Edwardsville?
A.  For a daytime or family outing: the free splash pad at Leon Corlew Park (9 a.m. to 8 p.m. daily from Memorial Day weekend to Labor Day), the All-Abilities Playground that opened at 610 Troy Rd. in July 2026, the jet at Township Airplane Park, the fishing lakes at Joe Glik Park and the indoor rink at the R.P. Lumber Center. The Gardens at SIUE, the Watershed boardwalk and the Children’s Museum round it out.
### Q. What does Edwardsville do for Halloween?
A.  A lot, for a town its size. The Halloween parade steps off at 6:30 p.m. on October 31 and has run for more than a century. The 2026 Halloween Party in the Park, set for Saturday, October 24, brings a candy walk to City Park from 10 a.m. to 12:30 p.m., a free costume contest at noon with a pets category, and downtown trick-or-treating from 12:30 to 2:30. Neighborhood trick-or-treating runs October 30 and 31, noon to 9 p.m., and the evening of the 30th is the busy window.

## Things to Do in Washington, MO: Arrive by Amtrak, Walk the River Bridge, Fish Lions Lake
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-washington-mo
Ever wonder why every Washington, MO list reads the same? Corncob pipe museum, antique mall, wine bar, drive home. Those lists were written from behind a windshield, and it shows. Leave the car at the Kirkwood station instead. The 8:39 a.m. Missouri River Runner rolls into Washington’s 1923 depot, steps from the riverfront park, and the 8:24 p.m. train takes you back the same night. Check the current Amtrak timetable before you book, because schedules change.
That’s about 11 hours on the ground with nothing to park. The town happens to be built for that kind of day. A 10 foot walking and biking path crosses the Missouri on the Highway 47 bridge, and it has only existed since 2019. There’s a city fishing lake with a mile loop around it, a 3 mile greenway through the middle of town, an arcade bar on Main Street, and a volunteer-run train museum whose oldest working engine is a 1926 Lionel. Of all the small towns outside St. Louis, Washington is one of the few you can do properly without a set of keys.
Everything below was checked against city, state, Amtrak and organizer pages in October 2026, and it’s sorted by what you came to do.
### What are some fun things to do in Washington, Missouri?
Fun things to do in Washington, Missouri include arriving by Amtrak from Kirkwood with no car, walking the Highway 47 bridge path over the Missouri, fishing Lions Lake or the riverfront bank, following the 3 mile Busch Creek Greenway, playing arcade games at The Alley on Main Street, and greeting Santa when he arrives by train in December.
Notice what isn’t on that list. Besides the Missouri Meerschaum corncob pipe museum, which every other guide leads with (the company has made pipes in town since 1869, and it’s worth a stop), Washington has a second layer that only shows up when you walk it. Here’s how a car-free day actually runs.
The ride out. The Missouri River Runner boards in the middle of downtown Kirkwood, the same blocks we cover in our list of things to do in Kirkwood, at 8:39 a.m. It runs daily, and the ride along the river takes under 40 minutes. Bring a bike if you want one. The train carries bikes in racks inside the coach cars, but Amtrak requires a bike reservation with your ticket, caps bikes at 50 pounds and 2 inch tires, and wants you at the station 30 minutes early to pull off bags and baskets.
Morning on the river. The depot doubles as the Washington Visitor Center, at 301 W. Front St., and Rennick Riverfront Park is steps away, with picnic shelters, restrooms and the start of the Rotary Riverfront Trail. No bike? Revolution Cycles in Washington rents them, with posted full day rates (10 a.m. to 6 p.m.) of $60 for a regular bike and $110 for an e-bike. Call ahead and confirm current rates.
Midday downtown. Walk up to the Washington Historical Society Museum at 113 E. Fourth St. It’s free, it fills two floors, and it holds the best footnote in Missouri beer history: brewery pieces from John B. Busch, Adolphus Busch’s older brother, who co-founded the Washington Brewery here in 1855. Lunch is a few blocks in any direction.
Afternoon, pick one. Walk out onto the Highway 47 bridge path for the long view up and down the Missouri. Take the Busch Creek Greenway inland from the riverfront trail. Or ride out to Lions Lake with a rod. All three are below.
Evening. The Alley, at 7 W. Main St., is a few blocks from the depot and open late, so the arcade, the self-pour taps and the pool tables cover the stretch between dinner and the 8:24 p.m. train. On the second Thursday of the month in season, the free Music at the Market concert ends at 8, about a block from the platform. Leave yourself a cushion, and check the timetable that morning.
### What parks and trails does Washington, MO have?
More than most people expect. The City of Washington counts roughly 15 miles of trails and 580 acres of parks, and the best of it links together. One quirk first: search for parks here and the map may show Washington State Park. That one isn’t in Washington at all. It’s down near De Soto. The parks below are in town.
Rotary Riverfront Trail. The flat one. Ten feet of asphalt starting at Rennick Riverfront Park and running about 3 miles east with the river on one side, open to walkers, bikes and skates. It’s the easiest out-and-back in town and the one to push a stroller on.
Busch Creek Greenway. City leaders said this one was 25 years in the making. It opened in October 2022, months ahead of schedule: a 3 mile path that connects the riverfront trail to Washington High School and Jefferson Street, with its start at Jefferson and Eighth. It’s how you see the neighborhoods instead of the water.
Miller Post Nature Reserve. The wooded one. Sixty-seven acres off Grand Avenue, entrance on Post Drive, free admission and parking. The loop runs about 2.1 miles with roughly 230 feet of climbing, according to AllTrails, which you’ll feel on a humid day. Leashed dogs are welcome. It isn’t wheelchair accessible.
Lions Lake and the All Abilities Park. A 1 mile walking loop circles the lake, and the All Abilities Park beside it was built so kids with special needs and kids without them can play on the same equipment. There’s another playground, swings and pavilions you can rent.
South Point Bark Park. The town dog park is at 101 Kingsland Drive. City rules: open sunrise to sunset, dogs vaccinated and spayed or neutered, a separate area for dogs under 20 pounds, and no kids under 10 inside the off-leash area.
### Where can you go fishing in Washington, MO?
Two places, and they couldn’t be more different. Lions Lake is a quiet 11.5 acre city lake. The Missouri is the Missouri.
Lions Lake. The Missouri Department of Conservation lists it as Washington (Lion’s Lake) and names sunfish, catfish, crappie and black bass. It sits off Veterans Drive near the fairgrounds. One warning: fishing apps sometimes mix it up with a same-named lake elsewhere in Missouri, so trust the MDC listing over an app pin. The walking loop around the bank means the non-anglers in your group have something to do.
The Washington riverfront. This is the one the lists miss. MDC’s own fishing prospects for the lower Missouri name the Washington Riverfront as great bank fishing for anglers without a boat. And the river holds real fish. MDC sampling turns up lots of blue catfish in the 25 to 35 inch range, anglers report trophies of 80 to 100 pounds, and flatheads run up to 45 inches. Blues hold along current breaks near dike tips and on rock-lined banks with fairly swift current. MDC suggests cut shad or skipjack herring, and says spring water around 60 to 65 degrees is prime.
Two rules before you cast. You need a Missouri fishing permit unless you’re exempt. And if you hook a lake sturgeon, a fish that can grow 4 to 8 feet and live past 100, release it right away. It’s endangered, and shovelnose is the only sturgeon you can legally keep from the lower river.
Rennick Riverfront Park has free parking and restrooms. The city is renovating it in 2026, with fishing benches by the river and a better launch for kayaks and canoes in the plans, so check the parks department’s page for closures before you haul gear down. For more water closer to home, see our picks for the best fishing spots in St. Louis, or the fishing lakes in St. Charles, where MDC flags the riverfront for bank fishing too.
### Is Washington, MO on the Katy Trail?
Not quite, and that trips up a lot of riders. The Katy Trail runs along the north bank of the Missouri. Washington sits on the south bank. The Highway 47 bridge connects them, and the bridge sits about 1.8 miles from the trail.
That bridge is newer than most of the lists that mention Washington. The current span opened Dec. 3, 2018, with a 10 foot walking and biking path on its west side. On April 11, 2019, crews blew up the old 1934 bridge beside it, and the path opened to walkers and cyclists that May. Walk to the middle and you get a long look at the river in both directions, with nothing between you and the water but a railing. It costs nothing. Wear decent shoes.
Getting from the north end to the trail is the catch. There’s no separated path yet on that last stretch, and riders describe fast traffic on the Highway 47 shoulder. Experienced road riders manage it. Everyone else should take the shuttle. Revolution Cycles runs Katy Trail shuttles from Washington for up to four riders and bikes, with posted prices for one or two riders of $25 to the nearest Katy Trail trailhead across the river, $30 to Marthasville and $40 to Augusta. Call or text ahead to book, and confirm the price.
From that nearest trailhead, ride west toward Marthasville or east toward Augusta’s wine country. Katy Trail State Park is 240 miles long with 26 trailheads, and Missouri State Parks lists the grounds as open sunrise to sunset. If you’re riding home on the 8:24 p.m. train, that sets your clock: be off the trail, back across the river and at the depot before dark.
Off the morning train and hungry? Where to eat in Washington, MO
### What can you do for free in Washington, MO?
Quite a lot, if you time it. The bridge walk, every trail above, Miller Post and the riverfront park cost nothing. So do these.
Washington Historical Society Museum. Free, at 113 E. Fourth St., open Tuesday through Saturday 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. and Sunday noon to 4. It closes from Dec. 23 to Feb. 28, so don’t build a holiday visit around it. Inside are corncob pipes, Schwarzer zithers, John B. Busch Brewery pieces, Missouri River history and a local history library on the lower level.
Gary R. Lucy Gallery. Lucy paints Missouri River history, and his gallery at 231 W. Main St. is open to browse Monday through Friday 9 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. and Saturday 9 to 5.
Free concerts. Music at the Market runs 5 to 8 p.m. on the second Thursday of May, June, July, September and October at the Farmers’ Market, 317 W. Main St. The series wraps on the second Thursday of October (Oct. 8 in 2026). Food, beer and wine are for sale, and the chamber says no pets or coolers. Sunset on the Riverfront fills Rennick Riverfront Park on fourth Thursdays from about April through September; the 2026 season wrapped Sept. 24. In the dead of winter, Cajun Night brings live music and dancing to the City Auditorium at 211 High St. on the first Saturday of February, free at the door. Watch the chamber’s site for each year’s date.
The Farmers’ Market itself. Saturdays 8 a.m. to 1 p.m., April through October, at 317 W. Main St. Browsing is free. The tomatoes are not.
The December run. In 2026, Washington packs its free holiday events into eight days. The Holiday Parade of Lights starts at 6 p.m. Friday, Nov. 27, 2026, with more than 70 lit floats and a tree lighting at Main and Elm. Olde Fashioned Christmas follows on Sunday, Nov. 29, from 3 to 5 p.m. at the Farmers’ Market: free, with live reindeer, trolley rides, marshmallow roasting, and Santa and Mrs. Claus. Then on Friday, Dec. 4, Santa and Mrs. Claus ride Amtrak into the depot at 301 W. Front St. The chamber pours free cocoa from 4 p.m. and hands out numbered tickets for photos, and it posts the train’s arrival time on its Santa on Amtrak page. Same rails you rode in on. Reading this after Dec. 4? Check the chamber’s site for next year’s dates.
### What is there to do in Washington, MO on a rainy night?
Rain moves Washington indoors, and two places do most of the work.
The Alley. At 7 W. Main St., The Alley is part arcade, part bar: more than 50 arcade games, VR, a redemption counter, a digital sandbox room for little kids, pool, darts and eight self-pour taps for the grown-ups. It opens at 11 a.m. daily and stays open until 1 a.m. on Fridays and Saturdays. October is its big month. Every Friday and Saturday in October 2026 there’s a haunted maze, with a “Not So Scary” run from 6:30 to 8:30 p.m. and “Alley Frights” from 9 to midnight, and Zombie Prom closes the month on Saturday, Oct. 31. Once a month, Country Night brings line dancing and a mechanical bull at $5 a ride. Check the calendar before you go.
Iron Spike Model Train Museum. For the daytime version of a rainy day, this volunteer-run museum at 1498 High St. is the find. Its oldest piece is a 1910 wind-up American Flyer, and its oldest train that still runs is a 1926 Lionel Standard Gauge 318E. Hours are Wednesday and Thursday 10 a.m. to 3 p.m., Friday noon to 5, Saturday 10 to 5 and Sunday noon to 5, with last admission an hour before close. It’s closed Monday and Tuesday. Want to see the layouts running on a Wednesday or Thursday? Call 24 hours ahead, and ask about current admission while you’re at it.
The other Busch brewery. Here’s the story to tell over a drink. John B. Busch co-founded the Washington Brewery in 1855, and it grew into the biggest brewery in town. When Prohibition hit, it stayed alive making ice, soda water and potato chips. After repeal in 1933 it became a bottler for Budweiser, and it closed for good in 1953. The surviving buildings on Busch Avenue are on the National Register of Historic Places and now run as a private event venue, so look from the street.
In December, two ticketed evenings fill downtown. Crawlin’ Around the Christmas Tree, a 21-and-over pub crawl, was set for Saturday, Dec. 5, in 2026. The Downtown Holiday Tour opens decorated historic homes; its 2026 date is Sunday, Dec. 13, from 4 to 7 p.m., with tickets on sale from Nov. 2.
### Nearby, on the same river and rails
Washington sits at the eastern edge of Missouri wine country, and the wineries around Augusta and New Haven are the reason most people drive out. We kept them off this page on purpose and gave them their own: our St. Louis winery day trip guide covers that side of the river. If you do drive, try the long way once. Cross the Missouri at Chesterfield, follow Highway 94 west through Augusta, and come into Washington over the Highway 47 bridge. On the way home there are good places to walk around Chesterfield if anyone still has legs left.
Next time somebody tells you there’s nothing to do past the county line, you’re the one who knows the 8:39 leaves from Kirkwood, the bridge has a path, and the riverbank holds blue cats longer than your arm. Pick a Saturday. Check the timetable. Go.
Between the bridge walk and the 8:24 train home, our guide to where to eat in Washington, MO lists the diner, brewery and riverfront kitchens a few blocks from the depot.
If you run a bike rental, a bait counter or a Main Street shop that train riders walk past, list it with us so they find you before the ride home.
Seven miles south on Route 47, the things to do in Union, MO include free live steam train rides.
About 12 miles upriver, the Walt Theatre in New Haven still shows movies on the screen it opened with in 1940.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is Washington, Missouri close to St. Louis?
A.  Yes. Visit Washington puts the drive at about 50 minutes: take I-44 to exit 251, then Highway 100 west for about 10 miles. Without a car, the daily Missouri River Runner leaves Kirkwood at 8:39 a.m. and heads back at 8:24 p.m. Check the current Amtrak timetable before you go.
### Q. What is Washington, MO known for?
A.  Corncob pipes, first. Missouri Meerschaum has made them in Washington since 1869. It’s also a German river town with a brick downtown on the Missouri, the place where Adolphus Busch’s older brother ran his own brewery, and home of the Washington Town & Country Fair, held the first Wednesday through Sunday of August.
### Q. Does Amtrak stop in Washington, Missouri?
A.  Yes. The Missouri River Runner stops daily at the 1923 depot at 301 W. Front St., which doubles as the Washington Visitor Center, a short walk from downtown and the riverfront. Bikes ride in racks inside the coach with a bike reservation made with your ticket. The October 2026 timetable shows the 8:39 a.m. from Kirkwood and the 8:24 p.m. back; check the current timetable before you book.
### Q. What is The Alley in Washington, Mo?
A.  It’s a family entertainment center and bar at 7 W. Main St. with more than 50 arcade games, VR, a redemption counter, pool, darts and self-pour taps. It opens at 11 a.m. daily and runs until 1 a.m. on Fridays and Saturdays, with trivia, karaoke, music bingo and a monthly Country Night on the calendar.
### Q. What concerts are happening in Washington, MO?
A.  The free Music at the Market series plays 5 to 8 p.m. on second Thursdays in season, with the season closing on the second Thursday of October (Oct. 8 in 2026) at the Farmers’ Market. Sunset on the Riverfront normally plays Rennick Riverfront Park on fourth Thursdays from about April through September, and the free Cajun Night lands on the first Saturday of February. The Alley also books live music on first Fridays.
### Q. Is there a craft fair in Washington, MO?
A.  Yes. In 2026 the Craft & Gift Expo was set for Saturday, Nov. 21, from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. at the Elks Lodge, 1459 W. Fifth St., organized by the Washington Farmers’ Market. The bigger Fall Festival of the Arts & Crafts, with 90-plus booths, comes back the fourth weekend of September.
### Q. What fall festival is held in Washington, MO?
A.  Pumpkin Palooza takes over downtown for a day; the 2026 date is Saturday, Oct. 24. The giant pumpkin weigh-in runs 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Main Street, pumpkin rolling races start at Main and Cedar at 12:30, and costume judging follows at 1:30, with a candy crawl through downtown shops. September brings the Fall Festival of the Arts & Crafts.
### Q. Is it safe to walk the Katy trail at night?
A.  It isn’t open at night. Missouri State Parks lists Katy Trail State Park grounds as open sunrise to sunset, so plan to finish in daylight. From Washington, that means booking your shuttle pickup, or riding back over the Highway 47 bridge, well before dark.

## Things to Do in Kirkwood, MO: Walker Lake Trout, Emmenegger Bluff Trails, a Textbook Quarry
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-kirkwood-mo
Confession: we believed the lists. Every Kirkwood roundup we read sent us to the same depot, the same Saturday market and the same few blocks of Argonne, so that’s where we went, for years. Not one of them mentioned that a 9.5-acre city park off Marshall Road is, by the city’s own marker, the “type locality” for the Meramecian Series: the reference site a U.S. Geological Survey geologist chose in 1904 for a whole series of North American rock. Or that the state stocks rainbow trout in a two-acre lake in Kirkwood Park every November.
Kirkwood sits about 12 miles southwest of downtown, and most people only know the slice of it you can see from a parked car. The rest runs down to the Meramec: a quarry wall with 1890s drill holes still in it, a bluff loop that shares a property line with a Lemp family estate once licensed as a federal game farm, and a fall calendar that includes a ham radio swap meet on Halloween morning. All of it is public. None of it makes the lists. If you’re working your way through the small towns outside St. Louis, this is the Kirkwood worth a day.
### What are some fun things to do in Kirkwood, Missouri?
Start where the lists stop. A quarry park off Marshall Road is where a federal geologist defined the Meramecian Series of rock in 1904, and the state stocks rainbow trout in Walker Lake every November. Hike Emmenegger’s bluff loop above the Meramec, catch a free summer concert, join the Witches Walk and watch Santa arrive by train.
Besides the Magic House and the farmers’ market, which you already know, here’s the rest of the short list, roughly in the order we’d do it:
The Meramec Highlands Quarry at Dee Koestering Park, 1703 Marshall Road: fossils you can spot without a lens, and a steep 0.8-mile walk to the overlook.
Walker Lake in Kirkwood Park: winter rainbow trout from early November, catch-and-release on flies and artificial lures through January.
Emmenegger Nature Park: flat paved loops in a creek valley, then a dirt climb to a rocky ridge over the Meramec.
Greentree Park: a Meramec boat ramp and the start of a flat, shaded 3.6-mile greenway.
Free music: Saturday nights in Kirkwood Park in summer, Thursday nights at Station Plaza in season.
Fall and early winter: the Witches Walk, a Halloween costume skate, a ham radio swap meet, a wine walk and Santa by train.
Two of those are the reason to come at all. They go first.
### Why do geologists care about a quarry in Kirkwood?
Because of one paragraph written in 1904. A U.S. Geological Survey geologist named E.O. Ulrich described the limestone layers exposed in these walls and proposed a name for them, the Meramec Group. According to the city’s marker at the overlook, that made the Meramec Highlands Quarry the type locality for what geologists now call the Meramecian Series. A type locality is the reference section, the place other exposures of that rock get compared against. This one sits in a Kirkwood city park that the city itself describes as having no services.
The rock is old enough to be hard to picture. The marker dates the layers to roughly 320 to 360 million years ago, laid down when shallow seas covered what is now St. Louis County, and it splits the walls into two formations: St. Louis Limestone and the Salem Formation. Most of the fossils are microscopic. Some aren’t. The city says you can pick out the remains of prehistoric sea creatures with the naked eye, and the thin, dark, shaly bands are what’s left of old tidal mud flats.
Then there’s the human layer. In the 1890s this was the working quarry for the Meramec Highlands, a river resort built by a St. Louis businessman named Marcus Bernheimer. Its “Meramec Blue Stone” went into the 125-room Highland Inn, the Meramec Station railroad depot, the school and the store. At its peak the quarry turned out 500 to 1,000 feet of rock a day with steam drills and gang saws. The resort had a steam yacht, 50 rowboats and a dance hall called the Sunset Hill Pagoda, which served nickel beer and drew crowds during the 1904 World’s Fair. The quarry shut down for good in 1905.
Walk down and you’ll see what it left behind. Several hundred tons of cut stone still sit stacked in the quarry, and the slabs carry round drill holes 1.5 to 2 inches across, where workers split the rock with wedges. One massive shelf still shows the cuts of a stone saw. The stacks have turned into habitat, and the marker’s own wildlife list runs from blue-tailed skinks to copperheads. Watch where you put your hands.
Getting there: park in the lot off Marshall Road and follow the signs 0.8 miles to the overlook, where the Kirkwood Rotary Club built the interpretive display. The marker calls it a very steep trail that isn’t recommended for everyone, and dogs, bikes, scooters and anything motorized are banned. The city bought the land from Dee and Ernie Koestering in 2001 and opened the park in 2003. Look, photograph, and leave the stone where it is.
### What can you see at Emmenegger Nature Park?
A creek valley, a bluff over the Meramec and a property line shared with a 1911 Lemp estate. Emmenegger sits at 11991 Stoneywood Drive, next door to a far busier state nature center, and gets a fraction of the attention. The city lists 125 acres. The trailhead has parking, restrooms and a pavilion with grills, which is more than the quarry can say.
Start on the paved path heading north from the lot. Within a couple hundred feet it crosses a big bridge over the creek and skirts two short paved loops that work for wheelchairs and strollers. That’s the easy half of the park. Keep going and a post marks the start of the dirt trail, the route AllTrails lists as the Bluff Creek Trail. It follows the creek through bottomland woods, crosses a smaller bridge, then climbs about 100 feet to a ridge above the river. A rocky outcrop near the top looks out over the Meramec valley. The descent drops you back onto the paved path near the lot.
Backpacker magazine mapped that loop at about 1.4 miles. Hikers who add the side trails log closer to two. Wear real shoes, because the climb is short, steep and full of roots and rock.
Now the neighbor. The park borders Cragwold, the estate Edwin A. Lemp built in 1911, one of four country estates that wealthy St. Louisans with brewing and German-American ties put up near the Meramec between 1910 and 1920. According to the National Park Service, the roughly 11,000-square-foot house was designed around a central atrium full of tropical plants and exotic birds, and by the 1920s the grounds held more exotic birds and hoofed animals from many continents. Lemp ran it as an exotic animal farm, licensed as a Federal Game Farm. It joined the National Register of Historic Places in 2009. The house is private, so enjoy the story from the trail and stay on park land.
Two rules before you go. The Missouri Department of Conservation (MDC) says Emmenegger allows leashed dogs, unlike Powder Valley next door, which bans pets. Bikes aren’t allowed on Emmenegger’s trails, but there are bike racks at the greenway trailhead across Stoneywood Drive, and that trailhead is the part most visitors miss. Its lot opens at 7 a.m. and closes at 9 p.m. From there a walking and biking bridge crosses the Meramec, and the paved Meramec Greenway runs 5.1 miles between Unger Park and George Winter Park, one of the Meramec River access points in Fenton. It’s flat, with a mix of sun and shade, and an easy way to turn a short hike into a long morning.
If you’ve already walked everything in our guide to easy family-friendly hiking trails around St. Louis, Emmenegger is the next lot over and the better view. Grant’s Trail has a Kirkwood trailhead too, at Leffingwell and Holmes, with street connectors to Kirkwood Park.
### Where can you catch trout in Kirkwood?
Walker Lake, in Kirkwood Park at 111 S. Geyer Road. It’s about 2.2 acres, it shares the park with the ice rink and the community center, and MDC lists it as one of its winter trout fishing areas. MDC stocks rainbow trout there beginning in early November. The department pitches the program as trout fishing minutes from home instead of hours away at an Ozark trout park, and on a gray weekday morning, trout fishing at Walker Lake in Kirkwood is exactly that.
The rules change with the calendar, and they’re specific enough that it pays to read them before you rig up. From November 1 through January 31, trout are catch-and-release only. You can use flies, artificial lures and unscented soft plastics, one pole per angler, no chum. That quietly rules out the scented dough bait most people bring to a stocked pond. From February 1 through October 31 any legal bait works, but you have to stop fishing, for every species, once you have four trout in possession.
Permits trip people up too. Anyone 16 through 64 needs a Missouri fishing permit, and keeping a trout takes a trout permit on top of it, at any age.
Two numbers to save. The St. Louis fish stocking hotline, 636-300-9651, is updated right after each stocking run with where the fish went and how many. As of early October, MDC hadn’t announced this season’s stocking dates, so call it before you drive over in November. The second number is ten. MDC said last November that it adds several brood-stock lunkers to its urban winter trout lakes, some as large as 10 pounds. That’s a program-wide statement, not a promise about Walker Lake. It does mean the next fish on a light rod could surprise you.
A few practical notes. Kirkwood’s city code keeps the park open from sunrise to sunset between November 1 and March 31, so winter trout is a daylight sport here. Boats aren’t allowed on park lakes, which keeps Walker a bank-fishing lake, and swimming and wading are banned. MDC also lists black bass, catfish, sunfish and white bass in Walker Lake, so it earns its keep in summer.
Want moving water instead? Greentree Park, 2150 Marshall Road, gives you 89 acres on the Meramec with a boat ramp and bank fishing, plus the start of the Meramec Greenway: 3.6 flat, shady, paved miles past Simpson Park’s 72-acre lake to Arnold’s Grove in Valley Park. Two warnings. The riverside park floods seasonally, and Great Rivers Greenway says the Greentree restroom is closed indefinitely. For the rest of the metro’s stocked lakes, our guide to good fishing spots in St. Louis has the bigger picture.
### What free things can you do in Kirkwood?
More than the lists give it credit for, and most of it happens outdoors. The quarry, Emmenegger, Walker Lake and Greentree cost nothing to walk into. So does the music. The Kirkwood Arts Commission’s Making Music series, which ran its 23rd season in 2026, puts free concerts on Saturday nights at 7:30 at Lions Amphitheater in Kirkwood Park from June into August. Bring your own food and drinks if you like; a beverage truck usually parks on site.
Downtown, the Station Plaza series runs free Thursday shows from 6:30 to 9 p.m., and you bring the chair. The 2026 schedule wraps with a twice-postponed show on October 8. It usually starts again in late May.
Three more that cost nothing:
Trainwatching at the 1893 depot, 110 W. Argonne. The city calls it the third-busiest Amtrak station in Missouri, and its restoration plan names watching the daily freight and passenger traffic as one of the building’s uses. The restored depot had its ribbon-cutting on September 15, 2026.
Historic Quinette Cemetery, 12188 Old Big Bend Road, a 1.75-acre city park with an interpretive display, about 0.3 miles from the quarry. The city calls it the oldest African-American cemetery west of the Mississippi: it was offered as a free burial ground starting in 1866, and about 150 people rest there, five of them veterans. Go quietly. It’s a burial ground first and a history stop second.
Live music at the farmers’ market on Saturday mornings, 10 to noon, in season.
### Where do adults celebrate Halloween in Kirkwood?
Downtown, on a Thursday, in a pointed hat. In 2026 the Witches Walk lands on Thursday, October 15, per Downtown Kirkwood’s events list. You sign in at the farmers’ market, collect a “witch’s brew potion,” then work through participating shops and restaurants for spooky specials. There’s a best-dressed-witch contest with Downtown Kirkwood gift cards on the line, and in 2026 the Bedlam Brothers play the market from 5 to 8 p.m. Reading this after Halloween? Check Downtown Kirkwood’s events list for next year’s date.
The same evening is a Night Market on Argonne. The farmers’ market stays open late, Argonne closes to cars out front, and food trucks and dozens of vendors fill the street. The event page lists 5 to 8 p.m., and admission is free.
Then it gets stranger. Kirkwood’s all-volunteer community theater guild has staged plays since 1931, and its 95th season brings Arsenic and Old Lace to the Kirkwood Community Center from October 23, 2026. Two sweet old aunts, a cellar and a great deal of elderberry wine: it’s a black comedy, and at $27 a ticket it’s the best Halloween date night in town. Evening shows are at 7:30 on October 23, 24, 29 and 30, with 2 p.m. matinees on October 25, 31 and November 1. The Halloween performance is a matinee, so book dinner after.
In 2026 the ice arena’s Halloween Costume Skate was set for Sunday, October 25, from 3:15 to 5:15 p.m.; pre-register through the city. And the 33rd Halloween Hamfest, a ham radio swap meet put on by the St. Louis Amateur Radio Club and sanctioned by the ARRL, was set for Saturday, October 31, 2026, from 8 a.m. to 1 p.m. at the Kirkwood Community Center. A room full of radio operators trading gear on Halloween morning won’t show up on anyone else’s list. That’s the point.
For the kids, The Summit All Seasons Market on East Argonne runs a pumpkin patch and fall fun zone daily through October 31.
Making a night of it? Start with where to eat in Kirkwood.
### When does Santa arrive by train in Kirkwood?
At 8:40 in the morning. For 2026 that’s Saturday, November 21, the day of Downtown Kirkwood’s Holiday Walk. Santa and Mrs. Claus arrive downtown by train, and Santa poses for photos inside the train station from 9 a.m. to noon. The 2025 schedule also had Mrs. Claus telling stories in Ken Connor Park, carolers working the sidewalks from 11 to 1 and a dance troupe at Station Plaza at noon. The posted times are from 2025, so check them the week of. Get there early. A train-station Santa is the kind of photo people line up for. Reading this after November 21? Check Downtown Kirkwood for next year’s Holiday Walk date.
Two weeks earlier, the Fall Wine Walk (Saturday, November 7, in 2026) sends ticket holders through more than 20 downtown businesses for tastings from 1 to 5 p.m. Tickets are $25 in advance or $30 at the door, check-in starts at 12:30 at the Kirkwood Performing Arts Center, and it’s 21 and up. Part of the proceeds goes to the St. Louis Area Foodbank, which by the organizers’ count has received $48,266.07 from the walk over the past few years. You keep the glass.
The first Kirkwood Festival of Trees was set for 2026, in the Kirkwood Performing Arts Center lobby from November 21 through December 4. Local businesses and groups decorate trees and wreaths, and you buy $5 raffle tickets online and pick the one you want to win. The drawing is Friday, December 4 at 2 p.m., and winners take the tree home that day. Viewing runs 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. on weekdays, 10 to 4 on November 21 and 28, and an hour before and during performances at the center. Santa drops by the lobby from 1 to 2 p.m. on opening day. Proceeds go to the Kirkwood Arts Foundation and KirkCare.
In 2026, December 12 brings Holiday Cheer, with carolers downtown from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m., and The Summit runs a Christmas tree lot and Gingerbread Shoppe daily from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., November 21 through December 23. One honest gap: Kirkwood doesn’t put on a big Christmas lights display. For that, head next door for Christmas lights in Webster Groves.
### What can you do in Kirkwood on a cold or rainy day?
Skate. The Kirkwood Ice Arena at 111 S. Geyer Road came back this season with a new skating surface and new refrigeration, from a $5.3 million rink renovation that capped an $11 million overhaul of the community center. Public skate costs $6 for Kirkwood or Glendale residents with ID and $7 for everyone else, and skate rental is $3. Session times shift month to month, so check the calendar on the city’s ice arena page. Skate aids are first come, first served, mostly for kids 8 and under.
Then watch someone go fast. The Gateway Speed Skating Club practices at the Kirkwood rink from September through March and says it’s open to all ages. Speed skating in a suburban rec center is about as far from a listicle as Kirkwood gets. Group lessons for ages 4 and up run in seven- to ten-week sessions all winter, and registration for the November session opens in early October.
Indoors and quieter: Mudd’s Grove, the 1859 Greek Revival house at 302 W. Argonne, is headquarters for the all-volunteer Kirkwood Historical Society, which dates to 1961 and has digitized more than 21,000 artifacts. The society has invited the public to stop in, and on September 30 it launched a Save Mudd’s Grove fundraising campaign. There are no posted hours, so check before you go. On Kirkwood’s western edge, the National Museum of Transportation is the familiar backup.
If the rain hits on the third Friday of the month, the same community theater guild behind the Halloween show runs a monthly improv night, Recipes for Ice, at the Steamboat Room, 314 S. Clay. Doors open at 7, the show starts at 8, and it skips December.
### What else is near Kirkwood?
Across the Meramec, Fenton picks up the river story with boat ramps and fishing lakes, and the greenway bridge by Emmenegger gets you there on foot or by bike. Webster Groves is next door to the east. For addresses and more local listings, our Kirkwood city guide keeps the details in one place.
Next time somebody calls Kirkwood a train station with some shops around it, you’ll be the one who knows where the fossils are, which lake gets rainbow trout in November and what time Santa’s train pulls in. Pick one this month.
Planning a Kirkwood Saturday around the quarry or the lake? See where to eat in Kirkwood on St Louis Near Me Directory for lunch close to the trails and dinner before a show.
If you own a Kirkwood shop that pours at the Fall Wine Walk or decorates a tree for the Festival of Trees, list your business with us so the people deciding where to stop can find you.
Up the Meramec, the best trails at Castlewood State Park start in Valley Park, past the ruins of an old river resort.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Does Walker Lake have fish in it?
A.  Yes. MDC lists trout, black bass, catfish, sunfish and white bass in Walker Lake, and it stocks rainbow trout there each winter starting in early November. From November 1 through January 31, trout are catch-and-release only, on flies, artificial lures or unscented soft plastics. Call MDC’s stocking hotline, 636-300-9651, for the latest run.
### Q. Is Walker Lake safe to swim in?
A.  Swimming isn’t allowed, so don’t plan on it. Kirkwood’s city code bans swimming, bathing and wading in park waters except the Meramec River, and it bans boats on park lakes, though model boats are fine. Treat Walker Lake as a fishing lake.
### Q. Is there a fee to enter Kirkwood Ice Rink?
A.  Yes. Public skating at the Kirkwood Ice Arena costs $6 for Kirkwood and Glendale residents with ID and $7 for non-residents, and skate rental is $3. Stick-and-puck and freestyle sessions run $6 or $7 an hour. Session times change monthly, so check the city’s ice arena calendar before you go.
### Q. What is Kirkwood, Missouri famous for?
A.  Mostly its trains: the city calls its restored 1893 depot the third-busiest Amtrak station in Missouri. The better answers are less famous. A city park off Marshall Road is the type locality for the Meramecian Series of rock, Walker Lake gets MDC rainbow trout every winter, and Emmenegger Nature Park borders Cragwold, Edwin A. Lemp’s 1911 estate and onetime federal game farm.
### Q. How far is Kirkwood from St. Louis, MO?
A.  Kirkwood is about 12 miles southwest of downtown St. Louis in a straight line, or roughly 14 to 15 miles by road. Most of the drive is I-44, and it usually takes about 20 minutes outside rush hour. Amtrak’s Missouri River Runner also stops at the Kirkwood depot.
### Q. What events are happening in Kirkwood, MO this weekend?
A.  It depends on the week, but the rhythm is steady: music at the farmers’ market on Saturday mornings in season, free Thursday concerts at Station Plaza in summer, and the city and Downtown Kirkwood calendars online. For fall 2026, the dates to know are the Witches Walk and Night Market on October 15, Arsenic and Old Lace from October 23, the costume skate on October 25 and the Halloween Hamfest on October 31.
### Q. What are some parks in Kirkwood, MO?
A.  Kirkwood Park, home to Walker Lake, the ice rink and Lions Amphitheater, is the big one. Emmenegger Nature Park has the bluff trail over the Meramec, Greentree Park has river access and the Meramec Greenway, the Meramec Highlands Quarry at Dee Koestering Park has the fossil walls, and Historic Quinette Cemetery is a 1.75-acre history stop.
### Q. Can you bring a dog to Emmenegger Nature Park?
A.  Yes, on a leash. MDC notes that Emmenegger allows leashed pets, while Powder Valley next door doesn’t allow pets at all. Leave the dog home for the quarry trail at Dee Koestering Park, which bans dogs, and keep it out of Walker Lake, since city code keeps dogs out of park lakes except the Meramec.

## Historic Sites in St. Louis: Oldest Buildings, Famous Graves, Civil War Sites
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/historic-sites-in-st-louis
1,500 buildings went up for the 1904 World’s Fair, and the plan was to keep two. The rest were built mostly of staff, a plaster and fiber mix that was never supposed to outlive the party. Every recycled top-10 list stops at those two famous survivors and moves on. Our guide to the St. Louis World’s Fair covers every piece that is left.
They miss the one that never stopped working. Francis Olympic Field, on Washington University’s campus, was built in 1902 and hosted the 1904 Olympics, the first Games held outside Europe. The International Olympic Committee calls it the oldest Olympic stadium still used regularly for official sporting events. WashU’s Bears still play football on it.
That’s how St. Louis history works. The famous pieces get the photos, and the stranger, more human stories sit where the lists never send you: a convent church in Florissant, two cemeteries on West Florissant Avenue, an unmarked grave off Lucas and Hunt Road, a WPA staircase down to the river that swallowed Lewis and Clark’s last campsite. Most of them are free.
This one is for the St. Louisan who has done the big-name museums and wants what’s underneath.
### What is the oldest part of St. Louis?
The downtown riverfront, where Pierre Laclède’s party started the village in 1764. Nothing from the colonial village survives. The oldest building left on that ground is the Old Cathedral at 209 Walnut St., built from 1831 to 1834. It sits on the Gateway Arch grounds, a short walk from the river.
### What is the oldest building in St. Louis you can still walk into?
The oldest building in the City of St. Louis is one you can’t enter: the Lewis Bissell Mansion on Randall Place, built around 1823 to 1828, once a dinner theater and now private property. To get inside something older, head to the county. Taille de Noyer in Florissant has a log core from about 1800, the Thomas Sappington House dates to 1808, and Old St. Ferdinand Shrine went up from 1819 to 1821. Inside the city limits, your best bet is the Old Cathedral, built from 1831 to 1834.
Old St. Ferdinand Shrine, 1 Rue St. Francois in Old Town Florissant, has the oldest Catholic church and convent in Missouri, and the parish dates to 1789. St. Rose Philippine Duchesne arrived from France at 49 to teach frontier girls and made this her home; the shrine says she was the fourth saint canonized from the U.S. Tours are free (donations welcome); book by calling 314-837-2110.
Taille de Noyer, 1896 S. New Florissant Road, on the grounds of McCluer High School. The log cabin at its core grew into the Mullanphy family’s country estate, and when the land was sold around 1960, the whole house was moved to save it from demolition. The Florissant Valley Historical Society opens it Sundays from 1 to 4 p.m., except January through March, for a small fee.
While you’re in Old Town, two private homes from around 1790, Casa Alvarez and the Aubuchon-Herbst House, are older than anything standing in the city. Look from the sidewalk, then use our Florissant city guide for lunch and the rest of the town.
Thomas Sappington House, 1015 S. Sappington Road, south St. Louis County. Built in 1808, it’s the oldest brick house in St. Louis County. The museum and library open Wednesday through Friday from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. and on the third Saturday of the month, with the last tour at 1:30; call 314-822-8171 to reserve. This year there’s a bonus: the 1816 log house of his cousin, Joseph Sappington, is being raised again on the same grounds, log by log.
The Old Cathedral, 209 Walnut St. downtown. Built of Joliet limestone from 1831 to 1834, it’s the oldest church in the city, it survived the clearing of the old riverfront blocks around it, and it’s still an active parish.
If your own house has you wondering, here’s how to find the history of your St. Louis house.
### Where are famous people buried in St. Louis?
Mostly in two cemeteries side by side on West Florissant Avenue. Bellefontaine holds explorer William Clark, writer William S. Burroughs, bridge builder James B. Eads and the 1904 fair’s president, David R. Francis. Next door, Calvary holds Dred Scott, Tennessee Williams, Kate Chopin, Gen. William Tecumseh Sherman and Auguste Chouteau, one of the city’s founders.
Bellefontaine Cemetery and Arboretum, 4947 W. Florissant Ave., opened in 1849. It covers 314 acres with 14 miles of paved roads, and about 87,000 people are commemorated there. It bills itself as the oldest garden cemetery west of the Mississippi and Missouri’s first Level III arboretum. Pick up a map at the office or follow the White Line Tour on your own. What to look for:
William Clark’s monument, a 35-foot granite obelisk with his bust, near the Broadway entrance. Clark died in St. Louis on September 1, 1838.
William S. Burroughs, whose modest stone sits beside his inventor father’s obelisk. Fans leave pens on it.
The Perpetual Mourner, George Julian Zolnay’s bronze of a shrouded, grieving woman over the Francis family plot.
Chris von der Ahe, owner of the team that became the Cardinals. The statue on his grave once stood outside his own ballpark.
The Girl in the Glass Box, Herman Luyties’ marble figure, sealed behind glass because by the time she arrived the cemetery allowed only granite monuments.
The Wainwright Tomb by Louis Sullivan, plus the Lemp and Busch mausoleums, for the architecture alone.
The strangest stop runs on the sun. At solar noon on the spring and fall equinoxes, the obelisk of the Severson Monument works as a sundial and throws a cross of light on the ground. The cemetery invites people to watch at solar noon on the solstices and equinoxes; in 2026 the winter solstice falls on Monday, December 21. Confirm on its event calendar first. Guided trolley tours, including a Black History Trolley Tour, need registration.
Calvary Cemetery, 5239 W. Florissant Ave., opened next door in 1854 and is far bigger: about 470 acres and more than 300,000 graves. Dred Scott’s grave is one of its most visited, and a new memorial was dedicated there in 2023. Tennessee Williams, Kate Chopin, General Sherman and Auguste Chouteau, who helped lay out the village of St. Louis in 1764, are here too.
These are working cemeteries. Go in daylight, follow the posted rules, and give funerals a wide berth.
Two cemeteries before lunch? Where St. Louis locals actually eat
### Where are the Underground Railroad sites in St. Louis?
Start at the Mary Meachum Freedom Crossing on the riverfront, then the Freedom Suits Memorial downtown, Greenwood Cemetery, where Harriet Scott is buried, and Archer Alexander’s grave on Lucas and Hunt Road. The National Park Service’s Network to Freedom lists more than 800 sites nationwide, and the Archer Alexander Memorial Foundation counts 14 of them in the St. Louis region.
Mary Meachum Freedom Crossing, on the Mississippi Greenway riverfront trail north of the Merchants Bridge (use 28 E. Grand Ave. for directions). On the night of May 21, 1855, a small group of enslaved people met at Mary Meachum’s home and set out to cross the river to free Illinois. At least five were caught, and Mary was charged for helping them. The Park Service recognized the site in 2001.
The free annual celebration is the time to go. The 24th was set for Saturday, October 10, 2026, from 2 to 4 p.m., and for the first time in 23 years the 20-actor production moved off the crossing site to the downtown riverfront. Bring a chair or a cushion for the steps.
Freedom Suits Memorial, on the east plaza of the Civil Courts Building downtown. Preston Jackson’s 14-foot bronze was unveiled on June 20, 2022, for the hundreds of enslaved people who sued for their freedom in St. Louis courts between 1806 and 1863. Dred and Harriet Scott filed their own suit in 1846 a few blocks away, at the Old Courthouse in St. Louis.
Greenwood Cemetery, 6571 St. Louis Ave., St. Louis County. Organized in 1874, it was the first commercial non-sectarian cemetery for African Americans in the St. Louis area, and more than 50,000 people are buried on its 31.85 acres. Harriet Robinson Scott, Dred Scott’s wife and co-plaintiff, is here. So is Lucy Delaney, whose memoir is the only first-person account of a freedom suit. The Park Service added Greenwood to the Network to Freedom in October 2023. Call ahead about tours.
Archer Alexander’s grave, St. Peter’s United Church of Christ Cemetery, 2101 Lucas and Hunt Road, St. Louis County. You’ve probably seen him without knowing it. In 1863, enslaved in St. Charles County, he overheard Confederate sympathizers plotting to destroy a North Missouri Railroad bridge, warned the Union troops, and escaped across the frozen river. He reached the home of Rev. William Greenleaf Eliot, a founder of Washington University, and was freed that September. In 1876 he became the model for the kneeling freedman on the Emancipation Memorial in Washington, D.C.’s Lincoln Park. The foundation also identifies him as Muhammad Ali’s great-great-great-grandfather.
He died in 1880, and his burial place was lost until St. Charles historian Dorris Keeven-Franke traced it here. The grave is still unmarked. His foundation is raising money for a memorial by St. Louis sculptor Abraham Mohler and holds a free service at the cemetery every September. Don’t go hunting for the plot on your own; go to the service.
One more for this list: Quinette Cemetery, a small city park in Kirkwood with an interpretive display, which the city calls the oldest African-American cemetery west of the Mississippi. It’s in our guide to things to do in Kirkwood.
### What Civil War sites can you visit in St. Louis?
Three, all a short drive apart in south St. Louis County: the Missouri Civil War Museum, the free museums in Jefferson Barracks Park, and Ulysses S. Grant’s home at White Haven, a free National Park Service site.
Jefferson Barracks is the thread. The post opened in 1826 as the Army’s first Infantry School of Practice and stayed active until 1946, and its roster of officers reads like both sides of the war: Grant, Sherman, Philip Sheridan and Stephen W. Kearny, and also Robert E. Lee and Jefferson Davis, the future Confederate president.
Missouri Civil War Museum, 222 Worth Road. It fills Jefferson Barracks’ restored 1905 post exchange and gymnasium. Hours are Tuesday through Saturday 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. and Sunday 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. Adults pay $9, with discounts for seniors, veterans and students. By the museum director’s count, more than 1,000 battles were fought in Missouri, more than any state but Virginia and Tennessee.
Jefferson Barracks Park museums, 345 North Road. St. Louis County Parks runs the 1851 Old Ordnance Room and the Powder Magazine as small museums, open Wednesday through Sunday from noon to 4 p.m. They’re free; donations are suggested. The park opens at 7 a.m. and closes half an hour after sunset.
Ulysses S. Grant National Historic Site, 7400 Grant Road. White Haven was the Dent family farm, where Grant lived with Julia in the 1850s. Entry is free, the visitor center is open daily from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. except Thanksgiving, Christmas and New Year’s Day, and rangers lead tours of the house, the last at 4 p.m. One tip straight from the Park Service: GPS apps often send drivers to the wrong gate, so use the directions on the park’s own site.
### Are there free historic sites in St. Louis?
Yes, and most of the best ones are. These cost nothing to walk into:
Fort Belle Fontaine Park and its WPA staircase, 13002 Bellefontaine Road
Ulysses S. Grant National Historic Site and the Jefferson Barracks Park museums
The 1904 World’s Fair gallery at the Missouri History Museum, with free tours Thursdays and Sundays
Soldiers Memorial Military Museum, 1315 Chestnut St., Wednesday through Sunday, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.
Bellefontaine Cemetery’s self-guided White Line Tour
Old St. Ferdinand Shrine tours
The Freedom Suits Memorial and the Mary Meachum Freedom Crossing
A walk across the Eads Bridge, James B. Eads’ 1874 span, which still carries pedestrians
The one almost nobody has heard of is Fort Belle Fontaine, in the Spanish Lake area of north St. Louis County. Built in 1805, it was the first U.S. military post west of the Mississippi, and the Lewis and Clark story bookends here. Per the National Park Service, the Corps of Discovery’s first camp, on May 14, 1804, was on an island opposite the mouth of Coldwater Creek, where the fort would rise. On September 22, 1806, home from the Pacific, they camped just below the new fort, its artillery fired a 17-round salute, and the next day they were back in St. Louis. The river has since shifted and erased the campsite. What’s left is a 305-acre county park, open dawn to dusk, and the grand limestone staircase the WPA built down the bluff in 1936.
One paid upgrade is worth it: the Landmarks Association’s downtown walking tours, Saturdays at 9:30 a.m. (through November 21 in the 2026 season), capped at 15 people. Tickets are $20, and kids under 12 go free. If ruins are more your speed, we keep a separate list of abandoned places in St. Louis you can legally see.
### Which towns near St. Louis hold pieces of its history?
Three stand out: Ste. Genevieve, St. Charles and Kimmswick.
Ste. Genevieve, about an hour south, is where to go when even 1808 feels new. Its Green Tree Tavern, built around 1790, is the oldest house in Missouri dated by tree rings, and in May 1780 militia from Ste. Genevieve helped defend St. Louis when British-allied forces attacked. Our guide to things to do in Ste. Genevieve sorts out which houses earn a ticket.
St. Charles was Missouri’s capital from 1821 to 1826. Jean Baptiste Pointe DuSable, who built the trading settlement that became Chicago, moved there in 1810 and died there in 1818, and since September 16, 2026, an 8.5-foot bronze head of him has watched over Main Street. Our list of free things to do in St. Charles shows where to find it.
Kimmswick, about 25 miles south, holds a piece of St. Louis itself. The wrought-iron truss at the south end of Mill Street carried Carondelet traffic over the River des Peres from 1874 to 1928, and it’s the oldest known wrought-iron span in Missouri. It has been closed to foot traffic since February 2026 while the Kimmswick Historical Society works out how to keep it standing, so admire it from the bank. Here’s more on Kimmswick’s 1874 iron bridge.
For more places like these, our guide to the small towns outside St. Louis worth a day goes town by town.
Pair a cemetery morning or a Florissant house tour with lunch nearby: St Louis Near Me Directory has where-to-eat guides for every town and neighborhood.
And if you run a business in Old Town Florissant, on West Florissant Avenue or near any stop on this list, the people working through it are deciding where to go next, so list your business with us.
For a newer landmark with an older-looking secret, St. Louis City Hall turned out to be pink granite under 40 years of soot.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the oldest neighborhood in St. Louis?
A.  It depends how you count. Carondelet was founded as its own village in 1767, three years after St. Louis, and joined the city later. If you mean a neighborhood that grew up as part of St. Louis itself, the federal Advisory Council on Historic Preservation calls Soulard “the oldest residential district in the city.” Our Carondelet neighborhood guide covers the south side’s claim.
### Q. Is there a Civil War Museum in St. Louis?
A.  Yes. The Missouri Civil War Museum is at 222 Worth Road in south St. Louis County, in Jefferson Barracks’ restored 1905 post exchange. It’s open Tuesday through Sunday, and adult admission is $9. The free Jefferson Barracks Park museums are minutes away, so check current hours and do both.
### Q. What is the history of St. Louis, Missouri?
A.  St. Louis began in 1764 as a fur-trading post that Pierre Laclède and his stepson Auguste Chouteau laid out on the Mississippi, just below where the Missouri River comes in. It passed from French to Spanish to American hands with the 1803 Louisiana Purchase, outfitted Lewis and Clark in 1804, and grew into one of the country’s biggest cities by the late 1800s, which is how it landed the 1904 World’s Fair and Olympics.
### Q. What are some attractions along Route 66 in St. Louis?
A.  Start at the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge, the old Route 66 crossing you can still walk. Ted Drewes Frozen Custard still serves on Chippewa Street, part of the 1932 alignment, and the Route 66 State Park visitor center in Eureka sits inside a 1935 roadhouse.
### Q. Are there any Route 66 signs in St. Louis?
A.  Yes, and 2026 is the year to look, since Route 66 turns 100. The World’s Largest Amoco sign stands at Skinker Boulevard and Clayton Road, on the 1926 alignment. The Park Plaza Courts neon sign at 10709 Watson Road in Sunset Hills was relit in April 2024 for the first time in about 50 years. Route 66 signs and state-line markers also stand on the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge. Before you go, check our guide to Old Chain of Rocks Bridge parking and which side is open.
### Q. Where did Route 66 go through St. Louis?
A.  Through at least five alignments between 1926 and 1977, which is why people still argue about it. The 1926 route crossed the McKinley Bridge and ran out Manchester Road. From 1932, the main route followed Gravois, Chippewa and Watson Road. To follow it west, stop at the Route 66 State Park visitor center in Eureka.
### Q. Which neighborhood in St. Louis is historically Black?
A.  The Ville, in north St. Louis. Sumner High School opened in 1875 as the first high school for Black students west of the Mississippi and moved to the Ville in 1910; Chuck Berry, Tina Turner and Arthur Ashe went there. Annie Malone’s Poro College and Homer G. Phillips Hospital stood here too. The area is still rebuilding from the May 2025 tornado, so visit respectfully. Our guide to the Ville has more.
### Q. Where is Harriet Scott buried?
A.  At Greenwood Cemetery, 6571 St. Louis Ave. in St. Louis County. Harriet Robinson Scott died in 1876. Her husband, Dred Scott, is buried at Calvary Cemetery on West Florissant Avenue, so the couple who sued for their freedom together rest in different cemeteries a few miles apart.

## Things to Do in Chesterfield, MO: What the Usual Lists Miss
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-chesterfield-mo
A 188-acre park sits behind The District’s parking lot, and you could park there for bowling a dozen times without knowing it exists. Walk under half a mile on crushed limestone and the trees close in around a lake. There’s a fishing dock off a shelter, two boardwalks, a mulched side trail, and bat boxes a local Boy Scout built so the bats would stay and eat the mosquitoes. It’s called River’s Edge Park. It isn’t on the recycled top-10 lists.
Those lists keep sending everyone to the same carousel and the same outlet stores, then call it a day. Besides Faust Park, which you’ve probably done twice, Chesterfield has roughly 600 acres of city parkland, a levee trail that crosses the Missouri River, two fishing lakes with opposite rules, and a city-run amphitheater where the summer concerts are free and you’re allowed to bring your own drinks. People drive past all of it on the way to somewhere else.
So this guide skips the brochure. It’s built around what you actually want to do: walk, fish, catch a show, get through a rainy Saturday with kids, or find something to do after dark. Every place below was checked against official city, county or business pages in October 2026. Hours and prices change, so check before you go.
### What are some good places to walk around Chesterfield?
Start at River’s Edge Park, where under half a mile of crushed limestone leads to a 1.6-mile loop around a tree-lined lake. For distance, the flat, paved Monarch-Chesterfield Levee Trail runs about 11 miles. For shade, try the Riparian Trail along Chesterfield Creek or the boardwalk at the Wetland Trails.
River’s Edge is the one to start with. Park in the lot it shares with The District (the park’s address is 17125 N. Outer 40 Road), follow the limestone path north toward the river, and the lake loop runs the full 1.6-mile circumference with two boardwalks and a mulched trail branching off. The city calls it a passive park, which is a polite way of saying nobody’s selling you anything. It’s open sunrise to sunset, all year. Bird watchers come for the woodland songbirds and woodpeckers. There’s also a newer off-road bike trail through the woods if you brought knobby tires.
For shade, head to Central Park. The Riparian Trail is 1.57 miles of crushed stone, boardwalk and pavement that follows Chesterfield Creek through the woods. Park at the Chesterfield Family Aquatic Center lot or at the trailhead off Old Chesterfield Road. It’s one piece of a five-phase plan that will eventually tie into the levee trail, so you’re walking the start of something bigger.
The Wetland Trails are the summer move most people never find. The city maintains 43 acres of wetland on the north side of the levee, just north of the A2 field at the Chesterfield First Community Athletic Complex (17925 N. Outer 40 Road), with a nature trail and boardwalk looking out over a Missouri River slough. On a July afternoon, that shade feels like a different county.
Central Park’s own one-mile trail is the easy stroll, past the lake, pedestrian bridges and a run of public sculptures. At Chesterfield Parkway and Park Circle Drive, a bearded aluminum giant is pulling himself out of the ground. That’s The Awakening, a Seward Johnson sculpture 70 feet long and 17 feet tall, unveiled there on October 10, 2009. Chesterfield Arts says you’re welcome to climb on it. Kids do.
Two smaller parks round it out. Eberwein Park (1627 Old Baxter Road) has a 0.82-mile trail, the family’s preserved red barn, a storybook walk, and a one-acre native prairie that volunteers seeded in 2014. The W.F. Dierberg Meditation Park on Olive Boulevard is two acres of paths, benches, a butterfly garden and a fountain. That’s about as quiet as West County gets.
### Where do you get on the Monarch-Chesterfield Levee Trail?
The levee trail runs about 11 flat, paved, sunny miles around the Chesterfield Valley, and parking is half the battle. The city lists four trailheads.
Railroad Park Trailhead, 17634 Edison Ave.
River’s Edge Park Trailhead, 17017 N. Outer 40 Road.
Chesterfield First Community Athletic Complex Trailhead, 17891 N. Outer 40 Road, with restrooms and a drinking fountain.
St. Louis Premium Outlets Trailhead, 18575 Outlet Blvd., with restrooms during store hours.
The city’s suggested routes are a good gauge of effort. Railroad Park to Baxter Road and back is 4.25 miles. The Athletic Complex around River’s Edge and back is 7.5. The big one, River’s Edge across the Boone Bridge to the Duckett Creek Trailhead and back, is 15 miles, roughly two and a half hours on a bike.
That bridge is the part people miss. A walking and biking path crosses the Missouri River on the Daniel Boone Bridge, the I-64 span, with bump-outs where you can stop and look up and down the water. Great Rivers Greenway, which runs the regional greenway system, points out that you can’t get that view from a car. From the outlets it’s about three-quarters of a mile across to the Katy Trail. Their parking tip: use the northwest corner of the outlet lot near the levee, then walk up the short gravel road to the paved trail.
One more stop on the levee. Park at the Railroad Park trailhead, walk about a quarter mile toward Chesterfield Bottoms, and take the concrete path on the right to an 18-hole disc golf course the city opened in 2022. Dogs are allowed. There’s no drinking water and no restroom, so fill a bottle first. A mowed-grass trail close to a mile long runs through the same park.
The levee itself has almost no shade. A few benches, a few shade structures, and that’s it. In summer, go early.
Want more trails like these? See St. Louis’s best outdoor spots.
### Where can you fish in Chesterfield?
Chesterfield has two city fishing lakes with opposite rules, and most people only learn the difference from a sign. Central Park Lake (16365 Lydia Hill Drive) is catch-and-release only. The city lists bass, bluegill, sunfish and catfish in it, which makes it a solid first-fish spot for a kid with a bobber.
River’s Edge Park Lake is the opposite. It is not catch-and-release, so state limits apply and you can keep what’s legal. The city stocked it, there’s a dock attached to the park shelter, and you can paddle a kayak or canoe there. No motorized boats.
Both lakes share the same house rules: no fishing off paths or bridges, no trapping or jug fishing, and either lake can close to fishing during special events. Great Rivers Greenway also notes you can reach the Missouri River itself from River’s Edge, if you’d rather fish moving water.
Here’s what older fishing threads get wrong. Howell Island, the big conservation island across Centaur Chute, used to be a walk-in spot reached from the Chesterfield side. The causeway is gone. The Missouri Department of Conservation now says the island is still open but can only be reached by boat.
You’ll need a Missouri fishing permit unless you’re 15 or younger or a Missouri resident 65 or older. MDC currently lists the annual resident permit at $14 and a daily permit at $9.
### Are the concerts at the Chesterfield Amphitheater really free?
Some are, and the free ones come with a perk most people don’t expect. The city-run Chesterfield Amphitheater, which goes by the ChAmp, opened in 2011 beside Central Park at 631 Veterans Place Drive and holds up to 3,000 people. It runs two kinds of nights: ticketed national acts, and the city’s Sounds of Summer series, which is free with no ticket required.
Now the perk. At free events, the venue’s own entry rules allow your own snacks (no full meals), your own beer or wine as long as it isn’t in glass, small or medium coolers, and dogs on a leash no longer than eight feet. Ticketed shows ban outside food, alcohol and pets. Blankets have to be throw size, 50 by 60 inches or smaller, and lawn chairs come out of their bags at security.
The 304 fixed seats down front are first come, first served at free events. Doors have been opening at 5:30 p.m., and food trucks park inside the gate. The 2026 series leaned on tribute nights, including a Beatles show in late July and an Eric Clapton set in June.
The same free-event rules cover Movies Under the Stars, the outdoor movie nights, where the film starts on the stage at dusk. The last one of the 2026 season is Hotel Transylvania on Wednesday, October 7. Park in the Central Park lot at Lydia Hill and Veterans Place drives, or on the surrounding streets: Veterans Place, Park Circle, Lydia Hill and Burkhardt Place. Kids 5 and under get into general admission free, even at ticketed shows.
### What is there to do in Chesterfield at night?
Most of it lives on one stretch of North Outer 40 Road. The District, the old Taubman Prestige Outlets site, is now an entertainment strip. The Factory books touring concerts. The Hub STL runs outdoor watch parties and events. Main Event (17027 N. Outer 40 Road) has bowling, laser tag, billiards, a ropes course and a bar, and Game Show Battle Rooms puts groups of six or more in a custom arena playing three TV-style game shows in an hour. Topgolf is a short drive down the road at 16851 N. Outer 40 Road and stays open late on weekends.
The oddball pick is on Edison Avenue. Slick City, an indoor slide park built for kids, runs an Adults Only Night for ages 18 and up on select evenings. It’s exactly what it sounds like: grown-ups racing each other down slides more than 20 feet tall. Check its calendar for dates.
For a quieter night, the free ChAmp shows are the date. Bring a blanket and drinks in cans or plastic, walk the one-mile Central Park trail before the opener, and stay for the headliner.
### What can you do in Chesterfield on a rainy day?
Slick City (17379 Edison Ave.) is the obvious one for kids. It’s a hall of indoor slides with names like the Mega Launch and the Hyperloop, plus air courts for bouncy basketball and dodgeball and a Junior Jungle soft-play area for kids 5 and under. Regular tickets are for ages 4 and up, grip socks are required, and it runs Sensory Hours with lower music and smaller crowds. When we checked, 90 minutes cost $27.99, so look before you go. Main Event works for wet days too, and Game Show Battle Rooms is built for a group of six or more.
The free option is the Samuel C. Sachs Branch of St. Louis County Library at 16400 Burkhardt Place, one of the streets that wraps around Central Park. A 2016 renovation rebuilt its children’s area, and Chesterfield Arts has placed sculpture at the branch, so a library stop and a quick look at The Awakening make a decent hour between showers.
The classic wet-weather move is still the Butterfly House at Faust Park, a warm glass conservatory full of free-flying butterflies even in January. Its hours shift with the seasons, so check before you drive out.
### What can kids do in Chesterfield for free?
Start with the storybook walks. The city sets out a picture book along the paths at Central Park, Logan Park (1859 Schoettler Road) and Eberwein Park, so a walk turns into a read-aloud. Logan Park also has a small accessible playground.
Then go climb the giant. The Awakening is fair game for climbing, and Central Park’s playground nearby was resurfaced with rubber instead of mulch, which makes it easier for kids using walkers or wheelchairs and for anyone pushing a stroller. At the Athletic Complex, the Catch-22 Miracle Field is a baseball field built for children with disabilities.
The city’s free events are the other half. Movies Under the Stars and the Sounds of Summer shows cost nothing. Trucks and Treats at Central Park (it ran October 3 this year) is a free morning of climbing into emergency vehicles and heavy equipment, and it opens with a quiet hour for kids who don’t love loud noise.
Not free, but close: a $5 Parks Passport Bottle from City Hall or the parks admin office at 17891 N. Outer 40 Road. There are nine stickers to collect, one for each park or facility, and you earn each one by showing a photo of yourself there at City Hall or the Aquatic Center. It turns nine park visits into a scavenger hunt.
### What’s happening in Chesterfield this fall and at Christmas?
Here’s the city’s own calendar for the rest of 2026, straight from its event pages:
Saturday, October 10, 2026: Yappy Howl-O-Ween, a dog costume afternoon at the Eberwein Park dog park, 2 to 3 p.m., free for dog park members.
Saturday, October 17, 2026: the free Chesterfield Fall Festival at the amphitheater from 1 p.m., with carnival rides, a pumpkin patch and hayride, a petting zoo, a Clydesdale meet and greet, and live music until 6.
Thanksgiving Day (Thursday, November 26, in 2026): the 27th annual Turkey Trot 5K at the Athletic Complex, 8:30 a.m., with a kids’ fun run at 9:30.
Friday, December 4, 2026: Cookies with Santa at City Hall, 6 p.m., $10 per child ages 2 to 12, adults free.
Saturday, December 5, 2026: the Candy Cane Hunt at Central Park, 10 a.m., $10 if you preregister or $15 that day, with crafts and treats after.
As for Christmas lights, Chesterfield doesn’t run a public drive-through display of its own, whatever the search results suggest. The closest big one is St. Louis County’s Winter Wonderland at Tilles Park in Ladue, which ran from late November into early January last season. Private neighborhood displays change every year, so the county show is the safer bet.
### Where else is worth going near Chesterfield?
Cross the Boone Bridge and you’re on the Katy Trail in St. Charles County, and about a mile west the paved Busch Greenway climbs the bluff toward Weldon Spring Conservation Area. Stay on the Chesterfield side and the levee keeps going roughly three miles past the outlets to Centaur Road. For the businesses in town, the Chesterfield, MO city guide lists who’s here, and the rest of the region is mapped in our complete local guide to things to do in St. Louis by town.
Next time someone tells you there’s nothing to do in Chesterfield but shop, you’ll know about the lake behind the bowling alley. Take them there.
