### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is Chesterfield, MO known for?
A.  Most people know Chesterfield for shopping in the Chesterfield Valley and the entertainment strip at The District. Locals would add the Monarch-Chesterfield Levee Trail, the free summer shows at the Chesterfield Amphitheater, and The Awakening, the 70-foot giant sculpture climbing out of the ground beside Central Park.
### Q. What are some free activities to do in Chesterfield?
A.  Walk the lake loop at River’s Edge Park, ride the levee trail across the Boone Bridge, or take the boardwalk at the Wetland Trails. Climb The Awakening, play the 18-hole disc golf course at Railroad Park, and catch a Sounds of Summer concert or a Movies Under the Stars night at the amphitheater.
### Q. What are some fun things for adults to do in Chesterfield, Mo.?
A.  Catch a touring act at The Factory, bowl or shoot pool at Main Event, or book a Game Show Battle Rooms session with five or more friends. Topgolf stays open late on weekends. Slick City’s 18-and-over Adults Only Night is the strangest good time in town.
### Q. What are some good date night ideas in Chesterfield, MO?
A.  Walk the River’s Edge lake loop an hour before sunset, since the park closes at sunset, then eat in the valley. In summer, take a blanket and your own drinks (no glass) to a free Sounds of Summer show. For a double date, a game show room needs at least six players.
### Q. Where to take kids in Chesterfield?
A.  Slick City’s indoor slides on Edison Avenue, the storybook walks at Central Park, Logan Park and Eberwein Park, and The Awakening for climbing. Central Park Lake is catch-and-release with bluegill and sunfish, which makes it a good first-fishing spot, and the Sachs library branch covers a rainy hour for free.
### Q. What are some fun activities to do in Chesterfield?
A.  Walk the 1.6-mile lake loop at River’s Edge Park, fish the two city lakes, or ride the levee trail across the Boone Bridge to the Katy Trail. For something livelier, catch a free Sounds of Summer show at the amphitheater, bowl at Main Event, or race down Slick City’s indoor slides.
### Q. What happened to the Chesterfield Mall in St. Louis?
A.  It closed in August 2024 and was demolished starting that October. The 96-acre site is now Downtown Chesterfield, a roughly $2 billion mixed-use project by The Staenberg Group. Grading and roadwork are under way, and the first residents are expected around 2029, so there’s nothing to visit there yet.
### Q. How far is Chesterfield from downtown St. Louis?
A.  Chesterfield is about 25 miles west of downtown St. Louis on I-64, usually a 30 to 35 minute drive outside rush hour. That’s close enough for an evening concert at the amphitheater or a morning on the levee trail without planning a whole day around it.

## Things to Do in Wentzville, MO: What the Top 10 Lists Skip
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-wentzville-mo
St. Charles County locals, here’s the Wentzville every recycled top-10 list sells you: the Renaissance Festival in October, a drive-thru light show in December, and an I-70 exit the rest of the year. Those lists aren’t wrong. They quit early. They skip the free telescope night every Friday, the hall of fame that holds relics from White House horseshoe games, and the little red caboose downtown that once hosted children’s parties for McDonald’s.
All of those share one ZIP code, 63385. So does the first Vietnam veterans memorial in the United States, which began in December 1967 as a Christmas tree of lights. What follows is the Wentzville that people living off Pearce Boulevard already know, checked against city, county and state sources for fall 2026 and sorted by why you’re driving out.
### What are some fun things to do in Wentzville?
Fun things to do in Wentzville include free Friday-night stargazing at Broemmelsiek Park, the National Horseshoe Pitchers Hall of Fame at Quail Ridge Park, a caboose museum and the nation’s first Vietnam memorial downtown, public skating at the Wentzville Ice Arena, the Renaissance Festival on fall weekends, and the Holiday Night Lights drive-thru each holiday season.
Most of that costs little or nothing. Our Wentzville city guide covers the basics, from what the town is known for to where Chuck Berry lived. This page is the other half. It’s what to actually do with a Friday night, a rainy Saturday, a fishing morning, an October weekend in costume or a December car full of kids in pajamas.
### What is there to do in Wentzville at night?
Start with the sky. Every Friday night, weather permitting, the Astronomical Society of Eastern Missouri sets up telescopes at the Broemmelsiek Park Astronomy Viewing Area, 1615 Schwede Road, where Schwede meets Wilson Road, and lets anyone take a look. It’s free. Viewing starts at dark or 7 p.m., whichever comes later, and runs about two hours. Rain cancels it. A few clouds or a cold night usually won’t.
St. Charles County Parks lists the Friday sessions straight through December 2026. ASEM posts weather cancellations in a news flash on its website, so check before you leave, and email the club ahead if you’re bringing a big group so it can staff enough scopes. Bring a camp chair. Bring a warmer layer than you think you need.
Two more after-dark plans from the 2026 calendar. Frights & Bites, the city’s last outdoor movie night of 2026, was set for Friday, Oct. 16, starting at 5:30 p.m., with food trucks at Heartland Park. And once the Holiday Night Lights drive-thru opens (Nov. 27 in 2026), you can stack a clear Friday in December: light tunnels first while the sky darkens, then the telescopes at 7.
### What activities are available at Quail Ridge Park?
Quail Ridge Park, the St. Charles County park at 560 Interstate Drive, is where most list-writers stop at “nice trails.” The trails are nice: more than seven miles of paved and natural-surface paths through pasture, wooded hillsides and the bottomland along Peruque Creek. But the real reason to come sits off Bluestem Way inside the park.
That’s the National Horseshoe Pitchers Hall of Fame and Museum, open here since 2007. It’s a 21,000-square-foot building with 16 indoor and 16 outdoor courts, steel shoes and memorabilia going back to the 1800s, and items from George H.W. Bush’s White House horseshoe games. Missouri’s state tourism office lists free public hours on weekend afternoons. The Quail Ridge Horseshoe Club runs the place, keeps the outdoor courts open to the public year-round and arranges weekday museum tours, so call the club before a weekday visit.
The rest of the park earns a full afternoon. There’s an 18-hole disc golf course, fishing lakes and ponds, playgrounds and shelters, and a 2.5-acre off-leash dog area split into large-dog and small-dog sides, with a covered shelter and water near the parking lot. The cedar Quail Ridge Lodge books weddings for up to 180 guests, so on some Saturdays you’ll share the park with a wedding party.
### What is there to see in historic downtown Wentzville?
Plenty, once you get off the interstate. William M. Allen laid out Wentzville in 1855 as a narrow strip seven blocks long beside the new railroad, and he named it for Erasmus Livingston Wentz, the New York engineer who supervised building the line. That railroad spine is still the best walking route.
Start at 209 W. Pearce Boulevard. The Vietnam Veterans Memorial there began in December 1967 as a tree of lights that residents used to raise money for Christmas gifts to local servicemen in Vietnam. People stood through cold, pouring rain at the dedication. Today it’s a column of red Missouri granite topped by a carved eagle and inscribed “Whither thou goest, I will go,” and the Run for the Wall motorcycle ride stops here every year on its cross-country trip to the Vietnam Veterans Memorial Wall.
A short walk west, the Wentzville Historical Museum fills the old City Hall at 310 W. Pearce. It’s open Tuesday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. and the first Sunday of each month. Then cross the tracks to East Main Street for the red caboose. Built around 1942, it later served McDonald’s as a children’s party room at its St. Peters location, and when a local arts council bought it in 2000, a faded outline of Ronald McDonald still showed through the paint. The historical society rotates exhibits inside. It opens during festivals or by appointment.
The Crossroads Arts Council’s mural walk ties the rest together. Find the History of Tobacco mural at 1 E. Allen Street: by the Civil War, seven area factories were turning out tobacco products, and Caleb Dula, who owned a factory here, became the first president of Liggett & Myers. There’s a Civil War mural on East Pearce marking a July 1861 skirmish near town. And in Bicentennial Park, 22 W. Pearce, a stone marks a time capsule buried in 1976 and set to be opened Aug. 10, 2046.
Two timing notes. The Wentzville Flea Market, run by the Wentzville Community Club at 500 W. Main Street, opens every Sunday from 7 a.m. to 1 p.m., rain or shine, with vendors indoors and out. And Wentzville Days, the free three-day street festival with a carnival and live bands, takes over Main Street in May. It ran May 15 to 17 in 2026.
### Where do you take kids in Wentzville on a rainy day?
A wet Saturday doesn’t have to mean another drive in to City Museum. The Wentzville Rec Center, which the city calls the WREC, has an indoor natatorium with a 4,000-square-foot leisure pool and a water slide, plus a six-lane, 25-yard lap pool kept at 80 degrees. Upstairs, a 1/8-mile elevated track has an incline and a decline, so you get a hill without the weather, and the gym holds two full-size courts. Daily admission runs about $10 to $12 for an adult, depending on residency. Public swim times don’t match building hours, so check the swim schedule first.
One quirk catches first-timers. Every Wentzville Parks and Recreation facility requires a pass, a Resident Card or a Nonresident Card to get in, and nonresidents need the card even when paying the daily fee. Ask about it when you pay, before anyone is in a swimsuit.
The Wentzville Ice Arena is the other indoor answer. The city-owned rink runs year-round. Public skate is $7 for residents and $8 for nonresidents, and rental skates are $3, from toddler size 8 up to adult size 14. Skate-aid trainers are free for wobbly beginners, and Wee & Me sessions are built for kids 5 and under skating with a grown-up. A rainy weekend afternoon is also the right time for the horseshoe hall of fame’s indoor courts.
Dunkin’ for Pumpkins floats pumpkins in the WREC pool for kids to swim out and claim. In 2026 it was set for Friday, Oct. 9, from 5:30 to 7 p.m. Preregistration is required. When the problem is heat instead of rain, Splash Station Aquatic Center on Peine Road has a lazy river, a spiral slide, a deep diving well and a zero-depth kids’ area. Its 2026 season ended Sept. 7, so save that one for summer.
### Where is the best place to fish without a boat near Wentzville?
Search “Wentzville fishing” and you get fishing-app pins and old forum threads. Here’s the short list that holds up. Inside town, Quail Ridge Park’s lakes and ponds and Heartland Lake at Heartland Park are shore fishing close enough to squeeze in before dinner.
The big-water option is the August A. Busch Memorial Conservation Area off Route D near Weldon Spring, and our O’Fallon, MO guide covers its winter trout lakes.
North of town near Troy, Cuivre River State Park’s 55-acre Lake Lincoln is stocked with largemouth bass, bluegill and channel catfish and has multiple access points from shore. Mind the calendar, though. In 2026 the park is set to close from 3 p.m. Oct. 30 until 7:30 a.m. Nov. 2 for a managed deer hunt, and only registered hunters get in.
### Where’s a longer, wooded hike near Wentzville?
When Quail Ridge feels too familiar, head just west to Indian Camp Creek Park at 2679 Dietrich Road in Foristell. At 603 acres it’s the largest park St. Charles County runs, with more than 10 miles of paved and natural-surface trails shared by hikers, bikers and horseback riders. The part kids remember is the observation silo you can climb for a look out over prairie and wooded hills. There’s also camping, disc golf, fishing and a big destination playground.
For a full day, Cuivre River State Park outside Troy trades suburban paths for wilder, hillier ground, and its Lakeside Trail follows the Lake Lincoln shoreline, so anglers and hikers share it. Closer in, the city’s Tree Talk is a guided walk through Peruque Valley Park about native trees and invasive species. In 2026 it was set for Saturday, Oct. 17. It’s a good fit for the kid who asks what every plant is.
Want more trails like these? Try our easy St. Louis family hikes.
### Where is the Renaissance Festival in Missouri?
The St. Louis Renaissance Festival is in Wentzville, at Rotary Park, 2577 W. Meyer Road, and 2026 is its 28th season. The 2026 dates: Saturdays and Sundays from Sept. 12 through Oct. 25, plus Monday, Oct. 12, from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., rain or shine. That’s seven weekends plus the holiday Monday.
The twist most write-ups miss is the setting. Instead of the usual English village, the grounds become Petite Lyon, a town in southern France in the 1520s, with King Francois, Queen Claude and Queen Katherine of Aragon holding court over jousts, music, food and craft vendors. If you went once years ago and decided you’d seen it, the French setting is a fair reason to go back. The same field hosts the St. Charles County Fair in summer and the Holiday Night Lights in winter, which is why locals can drive West Meyer Road half asleep.
### When do the Wentzville Christmas lights start?
Wentzville’s Holiday Night Lights is a drive-thru at Rotary Park. The 2026 run: nightly from Friday, Nov. 27, through Dec. 30. You wind through a one-mile route of lit scenes and light tunnels. For 2026 the city added new displays and moved the opening time 30 minutes earlier, and the lights stay on until 9:30 p.m. Reading this after Dec. 30? Check with the city for next year’s dates.
Tickets are $15 per vehicle for up to six people when you buy ahead, plus $1 for each extra passenger, or $20 per vehicle on-site. Plan around the 2026 gaps: no drive-thru on Dec. 13 and 14, when the route switches to a walk-thru event, or on Christmas Day, and on Dec. 6 the lights come on around 7 p.m. after the Holiday Night Lights 5K. Vehicles longer than 30 feet can’t make the tight turns. On Saturdays, stop at the Kolb Building near the end of the route to visit Santa.
Here’s the detail that turns a light show into a Wentzville story. The nation’s first Vietnam veterans memorial started as this exact kind of thing, a tree of lights on Pearce Boulevard in December 1967. Drive the tunnels, then stop at 209 W. Pearce on the way home. For the rest of the region’s displays, our guide to drive-through Christmas lights in St. Louis maps them out.
### Where else should you go near Wentzville?
Wentzville sits about 40 miles west of downtown St. Louis, right where I-64 runs into I-70, so it’s the far end of most day loops. Next door, things to do in O’Fallon, MO covers the neighboring city, and Lake St. Louis, Foristell and Troy are all short drives. For every town on our list, start from the complete local guide to things to do in St. Louis by town.
Next time somebody says there’s nothing to do out where the interstates meet, you’re the one who knows about the Friday telescopes, the horseshoe hall of fame and the caboose. Pick a clear Friday. Go.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is Wentzville a suburb of St. Louis?
A.  Yes. Wentzville is in western St. Charles County and part of the St. Louis metro area, about 40 miles west of downtown along I-70, at the spot where I-64 ends. The city puts its population at about 47,500. It still has its own railroad-era downtown, laid out in 1855, long before the subdivisions arrived.
### Q. What’s going on in Wentzville, Missouri?
A.  The fall 2026 calendar: the St. Louis Renaissance Festival on weekends through Oct. 25 at Rotary Park, Dunkin’ for Pumpkins in the WREC pool on Oct. 9, Frights & Bites with a movie and food trucks at Heartland Park on Oct. 16, and free Friday stargazing at Broemmelsiek Park. Holiday Night Lights: Nov. 27 through Dec. 30.
### Q. Is there a Renaissance Fair in Wentzville?
A.  Yes. The St. Louis Renaissance Festival, spelled festival rather than faire, sets up at Rotary Park on West Meyer Road every fall. The 2026 season: Saturdays and Sundays from Sept. 12 to Oct. 25, plus Monday, Oct. 12, from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., rain or shine. Tickets are sold through the festival’s official website.
### Q. Is Quail Ridge Park free to enter?
A.  Yes. Quail Ridge is a St. Charles County park, and there’s no entry fee for the trails, playgrounds, disc golf course, fishing lakes or the off-leash dog area. The National Horseshoe Pitchers Hall of Fame inside the park is listed as free to visit, too. You pay only for reserved extras, such as renting the Quail Ridge Lodge.
### Q. Is Quail Ridge Park dog-friendly?
A.  Very. The park has a 2.5-acre fenced off-leash area with separate large-dog and small-dog sides, a covered shelter and water near the parking lot, and there’s no charge to use it. Dogs need current immunizations and must stay leashed outside the fence, and the county caps it at three dogs per person. Kids under 8 aren’t allowed inside the off-leash area.
### Q. Where can I see dark sky near St. Louis?
A.  Closer than most people think. Every Friday night, weather permitting, the Astronomical Society of Eastern Missouri sets up telescopes at the Broemmelsiek Park Astronomy Viewing Area, 1615 Schwede Road in Wentzville, and anyone can look for free. Viewing starts at dark or 7 p.m., whichever is later, and runs about two hours. Rain cancels it.
### Q. What are some fun activities for kids in Wentzville, Mo?
A.  Start with the WREC’s indoor leisure pool and slide, public skating and Wee & Me sessions at the Wentzville Ice Arena, and Jake’s Field of Dreams at Heartland Park, an all-inclusive playground with ramps to the very top of every play element. Add Splash Station’s lazy river in summer. In December, it’s the drive-thru lights and Santa on Saturdays.
### Q. What can a family do for free?
A.  In Wentzville, quite a lot. Friday-night stargazing at Broemmelsiek Park is free, and so are Quail Ridge’s trails, dog park and horseshoe hall of fame, the climb up Indian Camp Creek Park’s observation silo, the Vietnam memorial and murals downtown, and Wentzville Days each May. Pack a picnic, pick two, and you’ve filled a Saturday without opening your wallet.

## Things to Do in Belleville, IL: What St. Louis Lists Skip
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-belleville-il
Missouri-side listicles cost you things, and you never see the bill. A 1949 drive-in that USA Today ranked the No. 1 drive-in in the country two years running. An orchestra that’s been playing since 1867. A free horse-drawn trolley that loops a German Christmas market on holiday weekends. A brand-new dirt track where sprint cars race under the lights. They lose all of it the same way: by treating the Mississippi like a wall and stopping at the riverbank.
Belleville is about 20 minutes from downtown St. Louis on I-64. It’s the largest city in the Metro East and the seat of St. Clair County, and by 1870 roughly nine in ten residents were German-born or of German descent. To most St. Louisans it’s an exit sign. To the people who actually cross over, it’s where the good stuff is that nobody else bothers to write up.
So this guide skips the obvious. The shrine shows up where it earns its place, in December. Everything else is built around what people search for once they’re done with the usual list: Christmas lights, a night out, small museums, antiques, fruit you pick yourself, and things that cost nothing.
### Is there anything to do in Belleville?
Yes, and most of it never makes the St. Louis lists. Belleville has a 1949 drive-in, an orchestra that’s played since 1867, five small museums, a drive-through Christmas display in its 57th year, a new dirt track that races at night, pick-your-own orchards, and a downtown square that throws a festival nearly every season.
The catch is timing. Belleville’s best stuff runs on a calendar, and the town doesn’t spend much advertising it to the Missouri side. Apples, pumpkins and a lighted jack-o’-lantern trail own September and October. Sprint cars hit the new track this fall. The drive-in runs from spring into October. December belongs to the lights, the Christkindlmarkt and that trolley you don’t pay a cent to ride.
Pick the season first. Then pick the night.
### What is there to do for Christmas in Belleville, IL?
Christmas in Belleville is a whole night, not one stop: a drive-through light display in its 57th year, then a downtown circuit with a German Christmas market, a free horse-drawn trolley, what the city calls the largest holiday parade in Southern Illinois, and a block of gingerbread windows. Here’s how it fits together.
Start with the Way of Lights. The National Shrine of Our Lady of the Snows has staged it since 1970, and it runs from the Friday before Thanksgiving through December 31 (November 20 to December 31 in 2026, its 57th year), with more than a million lights telling the story of the journey to Bethlehem along a route you drive at a crawl. Driving through is free. Donations keep it going, since it’s the shrine’s largest fundraiser, and the extras cost a little: camel and pony rides, a petting zoo, kettle corn and funnel cakes. In past seasons the display ran about 5 to 9 p.m., so check the shrine’s site for each season’s dates and hours. Weeknights are the safer bet for a short line.
Then don’t drive home. Drive downtown.
Downtown Belleville runs its own holiday circuit, and almost none of it shows up on St. Louis Christmas lists. The Santa Parade steps off the day after Thanksgiving (Friday, November 27, at 10 a.m. in 2026), floats and marching bands and all. The 13th annual Belleville Christkindlmarkt, an open-air German Christmas market on the Public Square, was set for November 27 through December 23 in 2026, Thursday through Sunday, 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. (Sundays close at 6). On holiday-season weekends (through December 20 in 2026), a 26-passenger horse-drawn trolley circles the decorated square and the downtown shopping blocks. It’s free. No reservations. On Fridays it runs 5 to 8 p.m., after dark, which is exactly when you want to be on it.
Two smaller traditions are worth circling on the calendar. The 36th annual gingerbread contest fills downtown shop windows from late November into early January, and it costs nothing to walk the block and judge for yourself. And the Old Belleville Historical Luminary Walk lines the Abend and Garfield Streets neighborhood with candlelight; in 2026 it was set for Saturday, December 12. That’s the same old neighborhood as the Gustave Koerner House, home of the Lincoln confidant who helped write the 1860 Republican platform, still mid-restoration and worth seeing from the sidewalk.
One display is never enough. Here are St. Louis’s best Christmas lights.
### When does the Skyview Drive-In open?
The Skyview usually opens for the season in late March or early April and runs into October, with movies starting at dusk. Late in the year the schedule thins out. By late September 2026 it was down to Fridays and Saturdays, so check the website or Facebook page before you load the car.
And yes, it’s staying open. In June 2026 the Bloomer family listed the Skyview for sale at $975,000, and plenty of people read that as a closing notice. It wasn’t. The family and its realtor said plainly that the drive-in isn’t shutting down, and it kept showing movies all summer while they look for a buyer to carry it on.
Some context for how rare this place is. Wesley, Frank and Tom Bloomer opened the Skyview in 1949, when it held up to 900 cars and admission was 60 cents. St. Louis Public Radio counts fewer than 350 working drive-ins left in the entire country. USA Today ranked this one No. 1 in 2024 and again in 2025, and No. 5 in 2026. You pull in at 5700 N. Belt West, tune the sound to an FM station, and watch from your own front seat.
In June, admission was $13 for adults and free for kids under 12. If the season’s already over when you read this, put it at the top of next spring’s list. Losing the Skyview to a sale someday would hurt. Missing it because a listicle never mentioned it is worse.
### What are good date night ideas in Belleville, IL?
Skip the dinner-and-a-chain-movie default. Four places carry most good Belleville evenings, and the Missouri side barely knows two of them.
The Lincoln, the movie palace at 103 E. Main St., opened on October 6, 1921, and it still runs first-run films plus concerts and touring acts on the old stage. Wednesdays are the cheap night; recent promotions have offered $5 seats with popcorn, so check what’s running. The building alone is worth the ticket.
Belle-Clair Fairgrounds Park Speedway is the newest thing in town and the least known across the river. The old fifth-mile track, built in 1948 with walls made of railroad ties, ran its last race in 2021 and came down after that. In its place, St. Clair County built a $13.9 million quarter-mile dirt oval that opened in 2026. The World of Outlaws sprint cars are set to race there for the first time ever on Saturday, October 17, 2026. Reserved seats for that one went on sale in August, so on big race nights, don’t wait on general admission.
Eckert’s Belleville Farm stays up later than people think. The Cider Shed is open until 10 p.m. on Fridays and Saturdays. On select nights in September and October, Jack’s Lighted Trail sends you down a half-mile path of glowing jack-o’-lanterns and lit corn stalks, with a Spook-Easy bar for the grown-ups. It’s ticketed, and the gate price runs $35, so buy online.
Then there’s the Philharmonic Society of Belleville, in its 161st concert season as of 2026 and one of the oldest continuously operating orchestras in the United States. It played its first concert on January 26, 1867, and it has owned Philharmonic Hall on North Jackson Street since 1897. Dinner first? Here’s where to eat in Belleville, sorted so you can land near the Public Square or out by the farms.
### What museums are in Belleville, IL?
Five, and each is small enough that whoever shows you around probably knows the building’s whole life story. Most keep short hours. Call first.
The Labor & Industry Museum, 123 N. Church St., sits in the Conrad Bornman House, an 1837 building the city’s preservation commission pulled back from the wrecking ball. It tells the story of the foundries and factories that made Belleville the “Stove Capital of the World,” back when Illinois industry ranked third in the nation. The biggest piece in the collection is Jumbo, a 12,000-pound steam engine. It’s open Saturdays, 10 a.m. to 2 p.m., with group tours by appointment.
The Victorian Home Museum at Heritage Square on East Washington Street was built in 1866 for Belleville businessman Morris Dobschutz and has been a museum since 1968: parlor, library, dining room and bedrooms set the way a well-off family lived. The St. Clair County Historical Society runs it and says tours are limited by staffing, so call ahead. The Daphne Sumner History Discovery Center on the same grounds keeps weekday hours, 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. The society also opens the Emma Kunz House, 602 Fulton St., by appointment. It’s a “German street house,” the plain brick cottage Belleville’s immigrants built first, furnished the way a mid-1800s working family had it.
The strangest of the five is the Museum of Mid-Century Modern Architecture & Design at 6 Oak Knoll Place, off West Main. Belleville architect Charles E. King designed it in 1952 for Terry and Thelma Blazier, a couple who loved to throw parties. Then the house spent decades as a funeral home. By the time the Belleville Historical Society bought it at auction in 2015, doorways had been widened for caskets. They’ve been narrowed back, the terrazzo floors restored, and a complete 1956 General Electric Wonder Kitchen installed. Tours are free by appointment. For a 2026 art show, the house also added Sunday hours, 1 to 3 p.m., through November 15. You can even rent the attached apartment on Airbnb and sleep in 1952.
The same society runs the Historic Garfield Street Saloon Museum in the Abend and Garfield Streets neighborhood, covering early city life and the town’s brewing history. That history goes back a long way. Illinois’s first brewery was in Belleville. Tours are by appointment.
### Where can you shop for antiques in Belleville?
Go big first. The Belleville Flea Market at the Belle-Clair Fairgrounds runs the third full weekend of every month, all year, indoors and out, with 300 to 400 vendors spread across more than 600 tables. Parking is free and so is admission. Hours are 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. Saturday and 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. Sunday. The October 2026 dates: the 17th and 18th, the same weekend the sprint cars were booked at the speedway on those grounds, which makes for a strange and excellent Saturday. The St. Louis Antique Festival fills the fairgrounds in spring too; in 2026 it ran April 25 and 26.
Then go small. Downtown, antique and vintage storefronts mix in with cafes along East Main, inside a historic district full of the brick German street houses and 1800s commercial blocks that put the Belleville Historic District on the National Register in 1976. Inventory turns over constantly, so it’s the kind of browsing that rewards a second lap. Building a whole day around vintage? Our guide to St. Louis vintage, thrift and antique shops worth the trip covers the Missouri side too.
### Where can you go apple picking in Belleville, IL?
Most St. Louis families default to one famous farm. Belleville has two, and the older one is the one people miss.
Braeutigam Orchards, out on Turkey Hill Lane, belongs to a family that’s farmed here since 1831. The seventh and eighth generations run it now, and they’ve grown fruit commercially since the 1940s. The pick-your-own list is long: peaches, cherries, blueberries and blackberries in summer, apples and pumpkins in fall, plus tomatoes, peppers, corn, squash and more. Pumpkins usually open for picking around the third week of September. Call before you go, because what’s ripe changes week to week.
Eckert’s Belleville Farm on South Green Mount Road is the bigger operation. In fall, apples and pumpkins are both pick-your-own, with field passes sold online, and the fall festival runs every Saturday and Sunday through October with pony rides, carnival rides, farm animals and live music. In 2026, Christmas trees are set to go on sale November 14. Spring brings tulips and strawberries. Summer brings peaches and sunflowers. Weekday mornings are the quiet window at both farms.
### What are some free things to do in Belleville?
Plenty, and a few of them rank among the best things in town.
Walk or bike the Richland Creek Greenway. The city’s 2-mile path follows the creek through a string of parks, North End, Optimist, Hough, Rotary and South Side among them, past public sculpture along the way, and it ties into the longer MetroBikeLink Trail that runs beside the MetroLink tracks. Fishing is allowed at the pond in South Side Park.
Bellevue Park, the city’s first park, has 27 acres, a 3-acre fishing lake, a one-mile fitness trail and a stone lodge from the WPA years. In summer, its band shell hosts an evening concert series that’s been a Belleville habit for a long time.
Art on the Square costs nothing to walk. The juried fine art show fills the Public Square every May, and it ranked No. 1 in the country for artist sales six times between 2006 and 2017. Mark May 14 to 16, 2027, its 25th anniversary year.
December stacks up the most free stuff of all. The Way of Lights drive, the horse-drawn trolley, the parade and the gingerbread windows don’t cost a dime, and the midcentury museum’s tours are free year-round by appointment.
Next time somebody in your group says there’s nothing to do but the usual, you’ll be the one who knows better. Pick one night: the trolley in December, the sprint cars in October, a cheap Wednesday movie at the Lincoln. Keep our Belleville city guide handy for the local shops and services around all of it.
