### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are some unique things to do in Belleville, Illinois?
A.  Tour a 1952 midcentury modern house that spent decades as a funeral home, watch a movie from your car at the 1949 Skyview Drive-In, ride a free horse-drawn trolley around the Christkindlmarkt, or see Jumbo, a 12,000-pound steam engine, at the Labor & Industry Museum. Most of these need a quick call or a schedule check first.
### Q. What are some fun things for adults to do in Belleville?
A.  Catch sprint cars at the new Belle-Clair speedway, split a cider at Eckert’s Cider Shed (open until 10 p.m. Fridays and Saturdays), see a concert or a cheap Wednesday movie at the 1921 Lincoln, or hear the Philharmonic in its 161st season. In December, the Christkindlmarkt serves food and drinks on the Public Square Thursday through Sunday.
### Q. Where is the best place to drive through Christmas lights in Illinois?
A.  For anyone in the St. Louis area, the strongest Illinois answer is the Way of Lights at the National Shrine of Our Lady of the Snows in Belleville. It’s free to drive through, runs from the Friday before Thanksgiving through December 31 (November 20 to December 31 in 2026, its 57th year), and has more than a million lights. Pair it with the free downtown trolley on a Friday night.
### Q. What are some popular festivals in Belleville, Illinois?
A.  Art on the Square in May, Oktoberfest, the Belleville Chili Cook-Off in October (the 42nd was set for October 9 and 10, 2026, with more than 60 vendors, many raising money for nonprofits) and the Christkindlmarkt from late November to December 23. The Santa Parade, which the city calls the largest holiday parade in Southern Illinois, opens the season the day after Thanksgiving.
### Q. Is Belleville a German town?
A.  Historically, very much so. Belleville was the center of Illinois’s first major German settlement, and by 1870 an estimated 90 percent of residents were German-born or of German descent. Many were university-educated refugees of the 1848 revolutions, nicknamed “Latin Farmers.” The Christkindlmarkt, the brick street houses and a sister city in Paderborn, Germany, keep that heritage visible.
### Q. What is Belleville, Illinois famous for?
A.  Its German roots and its factories. Belleville was once called the “Stove Capital of the World,” had Illinois’s first brewery, and is home to the state’s oldest public library. The candy company known today as Jelly Belly was founded here in 1868. These days it’s also known for the Skyview Drive-In and the Way of Lights.
### Q. Who is the most famous person from Belleville, Illinois?
A.  Tennis great Jimmy Connors is the name most people know. Music fans will point to Jay Farrar and Jeff Tweedy, Belleville natives who founded the alt-country band Uncle Tupelo before Son Volt and Wilco. Actor Buddy Ebsen and 1968 Masters champion Bob Goalby are on the list too.
### Q. How do you get to Belleville from St. Louis without driving?
A.  Take the MetroLink Red Line east. Belleville has three stations, Memorial Hospital, Belleville and College, and the MetroBikeLink Trail runs right alongside the tracks if you want to bring a bike. By car, it’s about 20 minutes from downtown St. Louis on I-64.

## Things to Do in Fenton, MO: Meramec Access, Fishing Lakes, Pinball
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-fenton-mo
What did the last “things to do near St. Louis” list say about Fenton? A shopping center, a go-kart track, an exit number on I-44? Then why does a town that size keep four public fishing lakes, close a 125-acre nature preserve every fall for managed archery deer hunts, and host a pinball museum whose owners drove more than 10,000 miles to hand-pick the machines?
Because those lists get written from the highway. Fenton was laid out in 1818 on 408 acres along the Meramec, and the river still runs the weekend here: which ramp the jet skis get, where the bank anglers set up, which stretch of trail is under water after a hard rain. The lists keep recycling the Arch and the Zoo. This is the other kind of Saturday. None of it is secret. You just have to take the exit.
### Where are the Meramec River access points located in Fenton?
Fenton’s main Meramec access is George Winter Park on Allen Road, a St. Louis County park with two boat ramps. Paddlers can also launch at Minnie Ha Ha Park, one river mile upstream. Bank anglers use the paved Meramec Greenway from Fenton City Park, and Route 66 State Park in Eureka has a free ramp farther upstream.
Here’s the full set, upstream to downstream, using the public ramps Great Rivers Greenway maps for paddlers:
Route 66 State Park, Eureka: free state park ramp off South Outer Road. Leave before the gates close; they no longer let cars out automatically after hours.
Meramec Landing, Valley Park: ramp and parking off Cal Hedrick Way.
Minnie Ha Ha Park: ramp off Old Gravois Road, one river mile above George Winter Park.
George Winter Park, Fenton: two ramps off Deer Lodge Road, onto a wide lake that opens to the river.
Meramec Greenway at Fenton City Park: walk-in bank access along a paved path, no ramp.
Flamm City Access: the next public ramp downstream, off Telegraph Road.
George Winter Park is the one to know. The county is candid about its history: by 2003 the lake was silting up, and today one of the two ramps can be limited to Jet Skis depending on the water level. The other still puts boats and kayaks onto the lake and out to the Meramec. Expect a small per-boat launch fee collected on site, and watch the clock. The gates open by 8 a.m. and the park closes a half hour after sunset.
The greenway is the walk-up option, and it’s where most people first notice the river is fishable at all. A paved path leaves Fenton City Park and follows the Meramec toward the Highway 30 overpass, with mini shelters along the way, a boardwalk the city built from recycled materials, and a playground and restrooms near the start. The city lists the whole stretch as river fishing access. Bring a folding chair and a heavier rig than you’d use on a pond. This is current.
### Where are the public fishing lakes in Fenton, MO?
There are four, all open to the public for bank fishing, all managed under a cooperative agreement between the city and the Missouri Department of Conservation. That’s the detail the top-ten lists skip, and it’s the best reason to keep a rod in the trunk when you drive through a suburb.
Preslar Lake is the main event. It sits inside the 125-acre Fabick Nature Preserve, reached by Fabick Lane off Larkin Williams Road, and at seven acres it’s the biggest still water in town. MDC lists black bass, crappie, catfish, sunfish, and white bass there. Boats aren’t allowed. The city calls Preslar the most popular and easiest to reach of the preserve’s two lakes; the other, Upper Fabick, takes a little more walking.
Westside Park Lake is the opposite: one acre, tucked at the end of the Woodridge Trails subdivision off Bowles Avenue. You can walk the whole shoreline in a few minutes, and it’s where a youth fishing derby ran this past May. Bud Weil Lake, behind City Hall on Gregory Lane, rounds out the four. If you want a fifth, Simpson Lake in Valley Park is a short drive away in a county park, runs under the same MDC limits, and has a ramp off Grand Glaze that paddlers use.
Read the signs before you keep anything. On Preslar, Upper Fabick, and Westside, MDC’s St. Louis-area rules allow two black bass a day with an 18-inch minimum, four catfish combined, 15 crappie, and ten of everything else. Most bass you hook here go back in the water. Anyone 16 or older needs a Missouri fishing permit, currently $14 a year for residents or $9 for a single day, unless they’re a resident 65 or older.
Then the thing almost nobody mentions. Fabick closes. MDC coordinates managed archery deer hunts in the preserve, and the city shuts it to everyone else on hunt dates. The fall 2026 hunt dates: October 8-15, November 5-12, and December 10-17. Plan a fall fishing morning around those weeks, or fish Westside and Bud Weil instead. For bigger water across the metro, our guide to good fishing spots in St. Louis covers the rest.
### Is the Meramec River good for floating?
It is, if you match the trip to the river. Around Fenton the Meramec runs wide and, at normal levels, slow, closer to a flatwater paddle than the gravel-bar float trips people drive hours for. What it offers is easy logistics close to home. Great Rivers Greenway, the regional greenway agency, lays out the public ramps in day-trip segments:
Minnie Ha Ha Park to George Winter Park: one mile, about half an hour. A good first paddle.
Route 66 State Park to Meramec Landing in Valley Park: 11.5 miles. Plan on six hours.
George Winter Park to Flamm City Access: 11.6 miles, also about six hours.
There are no lockers or supply stores at these ramps, so bring everything and stage a car at the take-out before you launch. Regional outfitters rent canoes and kayaks, but not all of them include a shuttle, so ask. The rules that matter most are boring and non-negotiable: wear a life jacket, tell someone where you’ll come out, and check the river the morning you go. The USGS runs a streamgage called Meramec River at Fenton, station 07019210, and the National Weather Service posts forecasts for the same reach. If the level is jumping after a storm, the river can wait a day.
Not ready to go solo? St. Louis County Parks runs guided canoe and kayak floats that meet at Meramec Landing, with boats and paddles provided. The October 25, 2026, color float sold out, which tells you how many people already know this river is worth a Sunday. Watch the county parks calendar for the next one.
### Which small Fenton parks are worth the detour?
Fenton City Park gets the traffic: 96 acres, seven softball fields, eight soccer fields, and the greenway trailhead. It’s fine. The smaller parks have the better stories.
Bud Weil Memorial Park, at 990 Gregory Lane, starts with one. In 1929 a stonemason named Gregory Domijan, an immigrant from Croatia, bought 60 acres here, and the city bought the park site in 1979. You still reach the Domijan Shelter by climbing a stone stairway. There’s the fishing lake, a short informational nature trail, and a new playground the city just finished. Shelter rentals are residents-only now. The lake and trail are open to everyone.
Westside Park has something odd for a neighborhood park: a small shelter designed by students from Washington University’s School of Architecture. The rest is simple and good, with the pond, a mile of paved trail, a basketball court, and a playground. Fabick Nature Preserve is the wild one, with 1.7 miles of gravel and wood-chip trail through 125 acres, and the city and MDC have spent the past few years pulling invasive honeysuckle, clearing dead trees, and planting native grasses and flowers along Fabick Drive. Valiant Park, across the street from both Fenton City Park and Fabick, is a two-and-a-half-acre playground stop with a shelter and restrooms. Olde Towne Plaza, a brick path with benches on Ware Street, doubles as the trailhead for the Great Rivers Greenway connector.
### What are the best rainy day things to do in Fenton?
Start at the Lazarus Pinball Museum, 26 Western Plaza. A family opened it in 2023 with a single machine and has since traveled more than 10,000 miles through several states hand-picking the rest. There are more than 40 machines to play now, plus arcade games, and you pay for a block of time instead of feeding quarters. Hours are short, so check before you go: Wednesday evenings, Friday and Saturday from noon, Sunday afternoons, closed Monday, Tuesday, and Thursday. On the last Monday of each month there’s a parent-and-child competition at 6:30 p.m.
The RiverChase YMCA at 990 Horan Drive is the all-weather backup, with an indoor pool, an indoor track, a hot tub, two full basketball courts, and indoor pickleball. Its outdoor aquatic center is members-only, but guest passes can use the indoor pool, so call ahead about a day visit. Sky Zone, at 631 Gravois Road, handles the kids who need to bounce off something: dodgeball, a foam zone, a ninja course. Its $12 Tuesday walk-in jump is the budget move right now, and jump socks cost extra.
For a quieter hour, the Fenton History Museum at #1 Church Street in Olde Towne is run by volunteers from the Fenton Historical Society and opens Wednesdays and Saturdays, 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Ask about William Lindsay Long, who platted the town in 1818 and named it for his Welsh grandmother, Elizabeth Fenton Bennett.
Still raining? Here are St. Louis’s best indoor activities for any weather.
### What’s happening in Fenton this fall?
Halloween in the Park fills Fenton City Park with live music, food trucks, and a crowd in costume. In 2026 it was set for Friday, October 16, from 5 to 8 p.m. Come dressed. In 2026, Fabick is set to close October 8-15 for the deer hunt, so don’t plan a leaf walk there that week; the greenway and Bud Weil’s nature trail stay open.
Spring and summer fill the same park again. The Fenton Community and Farmers’ Market runs Thursdays from 4:30 to 7 p.m., May through September, at the Meramec Greenway Pavilion, and Friday Food Truck Night takes the park on the third Friday of each month from April through September, 5 to 8 p.m., with live music. Bring chairs and a cooler.
### Where can you see Christmas lights in Fenton, MO?
At City Hall, first. The Board of Aldermen approved November 20 for the 2026 Annual Lighting Ceremony. The 2025 version filled City Hall and the Community Development Building on New Smizer Mill Road with a winter market, a food truck, Santa, and a Lindbergh school choir. Two weeks after the 2026 lighting, the RiverChase YMCA’s fifth annual Holiday Craft Fair was set for Saturday, December 5, from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., with Santa there from 9 to noon. Reading this after the holidays? Check with City Hall for next year’s lighting date.
Fenton doesn’t have its own drive-through light show, and that’s the honest answer for anyone searching for one. The big display nearby is Santa’s Magical Kingdom at Jellystone Park in Eureka, off I-44 at exit 261, a drive-through of millions of lights that has opened around November 20 and run into early January. Confirm each season’s dates before you load the car, and see our guide to drive-through Christmas lights in St. Louis for the rest of the circuit.
### Where does Route 66 fit into a Fenton day?
A short drive west on I-44, Route 66 State Park in Eureka turns the river into a history lesson. The visitor center is the old Bridgehead Inn, a 1935 roadhouse that sat on the original Route 66, and it’s lined with displays about the road. The ground under the park has a harder story. In the early 1970s, waste oil laced with dioxin was sprayed on the dirt streets of the river town that stood here to keep the dust down. The EPA announced a buyout in 1983, and after a long cleanup the state opened the 400-plus-acre park in 1999.
Then look at the bridge. The 1932 Meramec River U.S. 66 Bridge is a Warren deck truss, and the National Park Service counts it as one of only four rigid-connected bridges of that type left in Missouri. It’s been closed since 2009, and its deck came off in 2010 to take weight off the aging steel, but the truss still spans the river inside the park. More than 175 bird species have been identified here. For Route 66’s 100th birthday, the park scheduled a Route 66 Centennial Celebration for November 7, 2026. The ramp is free, which makes it a natural put-in for the long float down to Valley Park.
### What else is near Fenton?
When you come off the river hungry, our guide to where to eat in Fenton covers the independents, from a scratch bakery-cafe to Shanghai-style soup dumplings near Gravois Bluffs. Downstream, the Meramec runs on toward Arnold and its meeting with the Mississippi. For every other town on the map, start with our complete local guide to things to do in St. Louis by town.
Next time someone says there’s nothing out by the Fenton exit, you’ll be the one who knows which preserve closes for bow season, which ramp the jet skis get, and where to play pinball on a Wednesday night. Pick one this week.
Planning a day in Fenton? See where to eat in Fenton on St Louis Near Me Directory for lunch near the ramps, dinner after the parks, and local spots close to the river.
If you run a Fenton business, the people reading this are planning a Saturday in your town right now, so put your business where they’ll find it.
Upriver, the best trails at Castlewood State Park start in Valley Park, past the ruins of an old river resort.
Near where the Meramec meets the Mississippi, Cliff Cave County Park in Oakville runs ranger-led trips inside its cave in summer.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is Fenton, MO known for?
A.  Fenton markets itself as the City of Parks, and the river is the reason. William Lindsay Long laid the town out in 1818 on 408 acres along the Meramec and named it for his Welsh grandmother, Elizabeth Fenton Bennett. Today locals know it for George Winter Park’s boat ramps, four public fishing lakes, the RiverChase YMCA, and the Gravois Bluffs shopping district.
### Q. How far is Fenton, MO from STL?
A.  Fenton is roughly 20 miles southwest of downtown St. Louis by road, usually a 25- to 30-minute drive on I-44 outside rush hour. That’s close enough for an after-work session at Westside Park Lake or a Wednesday night at the pinball museum, and closer than most people assume.
### Q. What are some fun things to do in Fenton, MO with kids?
A.  Fish the one-acre pond at Westside Park, picnic at Bud Weil Memorial Park, where a new playground was just finished, or sign up for the parent-and-child night at the Lazarus Pinball Museum on the last Monday of the month. On wet days, try Sky Zone or the RiverChase YMCA’s indoor pool. Swing-A-Round Fun Town on Skinker Lane covers go-karts, mini golf, batting cages, and an arcade.
### Q. Does Fenton City Park have a playground?
A.  Yes. The main shelter area has a playground with restrooms and a concession stand, the Hitzert Shelter in the middle of the park is within walking distance of play equipment, and the Meramec Greenway has its own playground and restrooms next to the park. Valiant Park, across Larkin Williams Road, adds another small playground with a shelter.
### Q. Is there parking at Fenton Park?
A.  Yes. Fenton City Park, at 1215 Larkin Williams Road, has lots by the main pavilion and another off River Road near the city’s free mulch and compost pile. With seven softball fields and eight soccer fields, the lots fill fast on tournament weekends and during events like Halloween in the Park, so arrive early or plan to walk in from the far end.
### Q. What are the current water levels in the Meramec River at Fenton?
A.  They change by the hour, so check live data instead of a number in an article. The USGS streamgage Meramec River at Fenton, station 07019210, reports current stage and flow online, and the National Weather Service posts forecasts for the same reach. The USGS has also published flood-inundation maps for the Fenton stretch that show which low-lying areas go under at each river stage.
### Q. Is it safe to swim in the Meramec River?
A.  It’s riskier than it looks. The lower Meramec has currents stronger than they appear, sudden drop-offs, and submerged trees, and it rises quickly after heavy rain. If you get in at all, wear a life jacket, which is Great Rivers Greenway’s first rule for anyone on the water, stay out after storms, never swim alone, and look for posted health advisories before wading in.
### Q. Can I fish in Missouri without a license?
A.  Sometimes. Anyone younger than 16 can fish with pole and line without a permit, Missouri residents 65 and older are exempt, and everyone can fish without one during MDC’s Free Fishing Days, traditionally a weekend in June. Everyone else needs a permit, currently $14 a year for residents or $9 for a single day. On Fenton’s city lakes, the posted MDC limits still apply.

## Things to Do in O'Fallon, MO: Free Picks, Christmas Lights and Late Nights
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-ofallon-mo
Bedroom suburb? Not even close. That’s the label the recycled top-10 lists hang on O’Fallon, right before they send you back downtown to the same five attractions everybody has already photographed. The numbers say otherwise. O’Fallon has more than 90,000 residents, and the 2020 census made it the seventh-most populous city in Missouri and the largest in St. Charles County, bigger than St. Charles itself.
A city that size doesn’t shut off at dinnertime. It runs a one-mile drive-through light show that’s been going every winter since 1991. Its ballpark sells $2 tickets on summer Tuesdays. It keeps a 17-foot monument cut from World Trade Center steel outside City Hall, a heated indoor pool with a 185-foot slide, and a lake where you can keep four catfish and everything else goes back in. Locals know all of it.
The listicles skipped it. So here’s the version for the person who has done the obvious weekend twice: what’s free, where to fish, what to do after dark or when it rains, and exactly how to beat the line at the Christmas lights.
### What are some free things to do in O'Fallon, MO?
Plenty. Fish Lake Whetsel at Fort Zumwalt Park, play the free 18-hole disc golf course there, walk the one-mile loops at Dames Park, let kids loose on O’Day Park’s adventure playground, see the 17-foot 9/11 memorial made from World Trade Center steel, and catch free Tuesday Jammin’ concerts at Civic Park in summer.
Start with the memorial, because almost nobody outside O’Fallon knows it’s here. The city dedicated it on September 11, 2005: a 17-foot monument built from 22 tons of steel salvaged from the World Trade Center, with a plaque honoring the firefighters and police officers who died trying to reach people trapped in the towers. Walk inside City Hall and there’s a second piece, a section of the towers’ red steel core in a Plexiglas case. New York City sent both to O’Fallon in 2001. If City Hall’s Main Street entrance is still closed for storm repairs when you go, use the Sonderen Street side.
Across town, the Veterans Memorial Walk does something no brochure prepares you for. A platoon of cast bronze boots is set as if it’s marching, one solitary pair stands at the foot of the POW/MIA flag, and an eternal flame burns around the clock. It’s free and open 24 hours a day. Go at dusk.
Then get outside. Besides the lake, Fort Zumwalt Park has The Fort, O’Fallon’s only disc golf course: 18 holes looping through the woods, with no charge for open play and the course map on the UDisc app. Up in north O’Fallon, 59-acre Dames Park pairs a one-mile asphalt path with two things most visitors walk right past: a Native American burial mound near the south fields and the Omer Dames War Memorial, which honors St. Charles County soldiers killed in Vietnam.
And if you have kids, O’Day Park off Highway DD is the one. The city calls it the area’s first adventure playground, and it earns the title with a rope course, group swings, log climbers, a creek play area and a Teen Overlook, so the older ones have somewhere to pretend they didn’t come with you. The hillside amphitheater below O’Day Lodge hosts free concerts and performances, including Fall into the Arts, a free juried art fair held there in September.
Older kids and teens need something louder. Just over the line in Dardenne Prairie, St. Charles County’s Kinetic Park costs nothing to enter. There’s an outdoor skate course, a vert ramp, a bike skills course and an asphalt pump track the county bills as the largest in North America, plus an 80,000-square-foot playground built around a custom cave with stalactites, plus a seated zipline. Helmets are required for any riding, and kids under 12 need an adult along.
### When do the O’Fallon Christmas lights open, and how do you beat the line?
The display is called Celebration of Lights. Every winter since 1991, the city has turned Fort Zumwalt Park into a drive-through holiday show, and every scene in it is designed and paid for by a local church, business or community group. More than 13,000 vehicles roll through each season. The 2026 run: nightly from Friday, November 27, the day after Thanksgiving, through December 30, from 6 to 9 p.m. Reading this after December 30? Check with the city for next year’s dates.
The rules trip up first-timers. Tickets are sold online only, never at the gate: $18 per car, $40 per van, $65 per bus. You can use your ticket almost any open evening without a reservation, but it covers one trip through. The 2026 closures: no cars on November 30 and December 6, 7, 8 and 14, and no one at all on Christmas Day. You can’t get out for photos. There are no restrooms on drive-through nights. And nobody rides in a pickup bed, because the road looping through the park, Jessup Lane, is a city street.
Here’s the part the event listings bury. On Fridays and Saturdays, the city says the wait plus the drive can take 60 to 90 minutes. Pick a Monday through Thursday instead.
If nobody in your group wants to drive, book a specialty ride at least two weeks out. Enclosed, heated trolleys run Thursday through Sunday at 6, 7 and 8 p.m. ($18 for 2026), boarding from the Alligator’s Creek Aquatic Center lot at 403 Civic Park Drive. A hay-filled wagon for up to 20 people runs Monday through Thursday for $165. The city train runs on just two nights (November 30 and December 14 in 2026), at $85 per car for up to five adults and five kids.
The best night of the season doesn’t involve a car at all. During the Old-Fashioned Holiday Stroll (December 6, 7 and 8 in 2026), the park closes to traffic and you walk the paved loop on foot, which the city measures at exactly one mile. There’s Santa, there are hot drinks, and fireworks go up over Lake Whetsel at 7 and 7:45 p.m. Tickets are $10 a person, free for kids 2 and under, sold in advance only, and they go on sale in early November. Park at Fort Zumwalt West High School, 1251 Turtle Creek Drive, and take the free shuttle. The city notes 2026 stroll details can change, so confirm before you buy.
One more thing locals learn the hard way: once light setup starts in mid-October, the city typically closes the park to vehicles, and the disc golf course and playground close with it, though you can usually still park at the front entrance to walk or fish. Building a whole December out of nights like this? Our guide to drive-through Christmas lights around St. Louis lines up the rest.
### Where can you fish near O’Fallon, MO?
Inside city limits, it’s Lake Whetsel, the 3.5-acre lake at the center of Fort Zumwalt Park. It was made in the 1970s by damming a spring on the property, and it’s named for Ed Whetsel, the parks board member who championed it. Read the sign before you cast. You can keep four channel catfish a day, and everything else is catch and release. It’s pole and line only, two poles per person, no wading or boats, and anyone 16 to 64 needs a valid Missouri fishing permit. Don’t feed the ducks, either. The city asks, and it has reasons.
For a real fishing day, head a short drive south to the August A. Busch Memorial Conservation Area off Route D, run by the Missouri Department of Conservation right next to the Weldon Spring Conservation Area. It’s a numbered-lake system, and the numbers matter. Lake 12 is MDC’s pick for family fishing with kids. Lake 33 holds flathead catfish over 20 pounds. Lake 35 is the muskie lake: MDC sampled two fish over 40 inches there in spring 2025, and an angler landed a 47-inch master angler muskie in November 2024. Lakes 1, 2 and 15 are reserved for education programs, so skip those.
Now the timing almost nobody writes about. Starting in November, MDC stocks rainbow trout in Lakes 3, 7, 21, 22 and 23. Lakes 7 and 21 are catch and release, artificial lures only, through January, while Lakes 3, 22 and 23 let you keep fish right after stocking under statewide rules. Check MDC’s current regulations and permit requirements before you keep a single trout. For river and lake spots farther out, see our roundup of the best fishing spots around St. Louis.
### What is there to do in O’Fallon at night?
In summer, Tuesday is O’Fallon’s night. The O’Fallon Hoots, a Prospect League collegiate team, play about 28 home games a season at CarShield Field from late May into early August, with a 6:35 p.m. first pitch. On Two Dollar TWOsday, general admission is $2, and so are select food items, soft drinks and select alcoholic drinks. The club won a league-best 41 games in 2025, including a league-record 17-game winning streak, so the baseball is better than the price suggests. The 2026 schedule came out in January, so watch for 2027 dates around then.
Or skip the ballpark for the free Jammin’ concerts at the Civic Park Bandstand, Tuesdays from 6:30 to 9 p.m., late May through mid-August. Admission and parking cost nothing. Bring lawn chairs, bring a cooler, even bring your own beer, as long as nothing’s in glass. Leashed dogs are welcome. The city sprays the park for bugs before every show, which tells you how seriously they take a summer evening here. The 2026 season wrapped in August, and the city has already promised a 2027 run.
In fall, the after-dark move is a tractor-pulled hayride through the same wooded park that hosts the lights, followed by a bonfire where you can bring your own food and drinks. The 2026 schedule: October 8 through 25, Thursdays and Fridays at 6:30 p.m. and weekends at 5 and 6:30 p.m. Each lasts about 30 minutes. Book at least two weeks ahead.
The rest of the year, the late-night move is laser tag. 18 North Central, on North Central Drive, runs iCombat tactical laser tag in an 8,000-square-foot indoor arena built to look like a village, plus an outdoor field, and the owners compare it to a real-life Call of Duty. You don’t need a full squad. Buy a single spot and you play once at least six people sign up for the session. Each one runs 90 minutes, with about an hour of actual play after gearing up and training. Players under 14 need an adult, and weekend sessions can fill weeks ahead. Dress light and wear closed-toe shoes.
Want a band instead? Brewskeez Smokehouse & Music on Keaton Crossing Boulevard books live music on weekends and stays open until 1:30 a.m. on Wednesdays, Fridays and Saturdays, with pool tables and darts for the set breaks.
### Where should you go for a date night in O’Fallon?
Begin in north O’Fallon, just off Main Street, at Interruption Public House & Brewery on Sonderen Street. It took over the old Good News Brewing space in 2026, and it started the way good breweries do: as a homebrew project poured one small batch at a time from a single tap. The opening plan called for 10 taps, seven of them house beers, plus handmade sodas for whoever’s driving, and a menu built around wood-fired pizza and sandwiches. It’s closed Mondays and opens at 3 p.m. Tuesday through Thursday and at noon Friday through Sunday, so check hours before you go. Want a sit-down dinner instead? Our local guide to where to eat in O’Fallon covers the rest of the town’s tables.
Then go throw something. 18 North Central bills itself as the place where grown-ups come to play, and it comes with a backstory: it’s run by the Moss family, whose Barn Dinner Theater opened on New Year’s Eve 1971 as the first dinner theater in St. Louis. Mike Moss, who managed the Barn, turned his O’Fallon marketing business into this place in 2014. The date-night pick is the digital-target axe throwing: $25 a player for an hour, $40 for two, with open play Thursday through Sunday. Throwers have to be at least 14. Bringing another couple or two? Book Demo Ball, a game for up to 10 players that mixes lacrosse, hockey and bumper cars, at $115 for a half-hour on the court. Outside food and drinks aren’t allowed, but there’s an appetizer and drink menu on site.
Pizza and a pint, then an hour of trash talk at the axe lanes for $50 for two. That beats another dinner and a movie, and you’ll both remember who won.
### What can you do in O’Fallon on a rainy day?
Go to the Renaud Center at 2650 Tri Sports Circle, a 66,000-square-foot city recreation complex that most people outside O’Fallon assume is members-only. It isn’t. Day passes are sold at the front desk, and everyone who passes it pays daily admission, spectators included. What you get for that is a heated 121,000-gallon indoor pool with a 185-foot water slide, a lazy river with four water features, a water vortex, zero-depth entry and a raised catch pool with two waterfalls. Adults can walk the climate-controlled indoor track, a tenth of a mile per lap, while the kids wear themselves out. Got a climber instead of a swimmer? Kinetic Park in Dardenne Prairie has an indoor climbing gym, with a fee for climbing passes.
Timing matters in October. At the Renaud Center’s Pumpkin Plunge, kids search the pool for a floating pumpkin, then decorate it poolside before jumping back in. In 2026 it was set for Friday, October 16. There’s an 11 a.m. session for the littlest swimmers and evening sessions at 5:30 and 7 p.m. Listings put the cost around $8 to $18, and registration runs through the city.
And remember the free option from earlier: the World Trade Center steel inside City Hall is indoors, takes ten minutes, and gives older kids something to actually talk about on the ride home.
Rain moving in? Here are St. Louis’s best indoor play places for kids.
### Which walking trails in O’Fallon are worth it?
Be honest with yourself here. O’Fallon’s in-town trails are short, paved and good for a loop with a stroller, a dog or a podcast. The city has mapped the paths in four parks, measured to within one foot, and they’re worth knowing by name. The paved loop around Lake Whetsel is exactly one mile. Dames Park splits into a figure eight: a north loop of roughly 0.4 miles with a hill in it and a flat south loop of about 0.6 miles, so you can choose your hill. Civic Park has a quarter-mile, ADA-accessible path along a rocky stream, past the bandstand and the O’Fallon Historical Society’s log cabin. Six-acre Knaust Park rounds out the list.
Want real mileage? That’s past the city line: Broemmelsiek Park south of Wentzville has more than nine miles of trails and free Friday telescope nights, and our guide to things to do in Wentzville covers it.
### Is Lake St. Louis open to the public?
No, and it catches a lot of people off guard. The City of Lake Saint Louis says it plainly: its two lakes are private, owned by members of the Lake Saint Louis Community Association. That’s 625 acres of water on the big lake and 75 more on the smaller Lake St. Louise, plus the marinas, boat launches and three beach areas, and the association runs all of it for members. If you don’t live inside the association’s boundaries, you can’t just show up with a kayak or a fishing rod.
What you can do is go on a Saturday morning. The Lake Saint Louis Farmers & Artists Market sets up at The Meadows, near Highway 40 and Lake Saint Louis Boulevard, from 8 a.m. to noon, rain or shine, and the 2026 season is set to run through October 31. Lake Saint Louis borders O’Fallon on the west, so a market morning and an O’Fallon afternoon fit in the same day.
Need a local business while you’re out here, from a tire shop to a pediatric dentist? Our O’Fallon business directory and city guide lists who’s in town. For every other town, start with our complete local guide to things to do in St. Louis by town.
So the next time someone writes O’Fallon off as a place people only sleep, let them. You’ll be the one walking the lights on foot while everybody else idles in line, or on a blanket at Civic Park with a cooler on a summer Tuesday. Start with the easy win: put the Holiday Stroll on your calendar now, and buy tickets the day they go on sale.
Planning an O’Fallon night out? St Louis Near Me Directory’s guide to where to eat in O’Fallon covers dinner before the lights or after the ballgame.
If you run an O’Fallon business, list it with us so the 13,000-plus carloads that drive the Celebration of Lights each holiday season can find you.
Up US-61 near Troy, camping at Cuivre River State Park starts at $14 a night.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is O'Fallon, MO a suburb of St. Louis?
A.  Yes, technically. O’Fallon sits about 30 minutes west of downtown St. Louis, where I-70 and I-64 both cross St. Charles County. Calling it a bedroom suburb undersells it, though. At the 2020 census it was the seventh-most populous city in Missouri and the largest in St. Charles County, with more than 90,000 residents and a full festival calendar of its own.
### Q. What is O'Fallon, MO famous for?
A.  Around St. Louis, mostly the Celebration of Lights, the drive-through holiday display at Fort Zumwalt Park that has run every year since 1991 and draws more than 13,000 vehicles. It’s also known for its 9/11 memorial made from 22 tons of World Trade Center steel, the bronze-boot Veterans Memorial Walk, and summer Hoots baseball at CarShield Field.
### Q. What are some fun things for adults to do in O'Fallon, MO?
A.  Bring a cooler to a free Tuesday Jammin’ concert at Civic Park in summer, catch a $2 Tuesday Hoots game, or get a pint and wood-fired pizza at Interruption Public House on Sonderen Street. In October, book one of the city’s fall hayrides, with a bonfire after. Any Thursday through Sunday, an hour of axe throwing at 18 North Central runs $25 a player.
### Q. What are some fun things to do in O'Fallon this weekend?
A.  It depends on the season, so check the city’s parks and events calendar first. The 2026 calendar: the city’s fall hayrides Thursday through Sunday through October 25, the Lake Saint Louis Farmers & Artists Market on Saturday mornings through October 31, and the Celebration of Lights nightly from November 27 to December 30, with a few dates closed to cars.
### Q. Can you fish at Fort Zumwalt Park?
A.  Yes. Lake Whetsel, the 3.5-acre lake in the middle of the park, is open to anglers during park hours, dawn to dusk. You can keep four channel catfish a day, and all other fish are catch and release. It’s pole and line only with a two-pole limit, no boats or wading, and anglers 16 to 64 need a valid Missouri fishing permit.
### Q. Can you swim at Lake St. Louis?
A.  Only if you’re part of the Lake Saint Louis Community Association. The city describes both lakes as private, owned by association members, and the beaches at the Clubhouse, the Main Marina and Jefferson Point are association amenities. If you know a member, ask about guest rules. Otherwise, the Renaud Center’s heated indoor pool in O’Fallon sells day passes year-round.
### Q. What are some free family activities in St. Louis?
A.  Out in O’Fallon, many of the best ones cost nothing: fishing Lake Whetsel and playing the 18-hole disc golf course beside it, O’Day Park’s adventure playground and creek play area, the one-mile loops at Dames Park, and free Tuesday concerts at Civic Park in summer. City and county parks across the region fill in the rest.
### Q. What are some fun things to do at night in St. Louis?
A.  If you’ll drive about 30 minutes west, O’Fallon’s nights are underrated. Drive the Celebration of Lights from late November, catch a summer Hoots game under the lights at CarShield Field, play tactical laser tag or throw axes at 18 North Central, or catch a weekend band at Brewskeez Smokehouse & Music, which stays open until 1:30 a.m. on Fridays and Saturdays.

## Things to Do in Ste. Genevieve, MO: What the Usual Lists Miss
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-ste-genevieve-mo
Three of five. That’s how many of the country’s known surviving poteaux-en-terre houses stand in Ste. Genevieve, according to the National Park Service. The name means posts in the ground: upright logs sunk straight into the dirt, the way French colonists built along the Mississippi in the late 1700s. Nobody put them behind glass. They sit on ordinary streets, a few minutes’ walk from wherever you park.
The usual top-10 list walks right past them. It tells you to tour the national park, taste some wine, maybe hike, and a lot of those lists still point you to wineries that have stopped pouring, like the saltpeter-cave tasting room at Cave Vineyard and the Chaumette estate, which closed in August 2025. Follow one and you’ll drive an hour to a tasting room that isn’t there.
Here’s the part St. Louis never hears about. In May 1780, when British-allied forces attacked the village of St. Louis, reinforcements from Ste. Genevieve helped bring its defenders to roughly 300 men. One of the young militia officers in that fight, François Vallé fils, built a house here in the 1790s. It’s open to visitors now, and the exhibit inside is called Saving St. Louis.
So this guide is for the St. Louisan who has done the Arch, done the usual weekend loop, and wants the Ste. Genevieve that locals use. Which houses earn a ticket. Which wineries are open this fall. Where to eat a liver dumpling, when the town throws its best parties, and how to cross the Mississippi for five bucks.
### What festivals are held in St. Genevieve, Missouri?
Ste. Genevieve’s calendar runs all year: the King’s Ball in February, the French Heritage Festival in June, Jour de Fête in August, the Fly with the Hive honey festival in September, Rural Heritage Day and a lantern cemetery tour in October, Pecanapalooza in November, the Holiday Christmas Festival in December, and La Guignolée on New Year’s Eve.
Here’s the full year in one place, with the dates as they usually fall. Most of these run downtown and cost nothing to walk into.
February: the King’s Ball (Bal du Roi), first full weekend, at the VFW Hall. Colonial dress, the old dances, and whoever finds the figure baked into the king cake reigns for the year. Ticketed.
April and October: the Milice Encampment, usually the second Saturday, when the LeMeilleur House grounds become a working 18th-century militia camp with gun building, spinning, and leatherwork. Free.
April through October: the 4th Friday Art Walk, 6 to 9 p.m., when the downtown galleries stay open late. The season’s last one is the fourth Friday of October (October 23 in 2026).
May: the Master Gardeners’ Garden Walk, the weekend after Mother’s Day, with a rare look behind the gates of historic gardens.
June: the French Heritage Festival, second Saturday, which ends with dancing in the lantern-lit gardens of the historic houses.
July: fireworks over Pere Marquette Park around the Fourth, then the Ste. Genevieve County Fair and its truck pull on the second full weekend.
August: Jour de Fête, the second full weekend, with more than 150 craft vendors filling the historic district. 2026 was its 58th year.
September: Fly with the Hive, a free honey festival on Merchant Street that held its second run on September 12, 2026.
October: Rural Heritage Day at the Felix Vallé House and the Déjà vu Spirit Reunion, a lantern-light cemetery tour, both on the fourth Saturday. In 2026 that’s October 24.
November: Pecanapalooza, a pecan street festival, and the Robin Hood-themed Sherwood Forest Festival on Merchant Street. The 2026 dates: November 7 and November 14.
December: the Holiday Christmas Festival on the first weekend, then La Guignolée on New Year’s Eve.
If you can only do one fall weekend, pick the one that pairs an Art Walk Friday with the Saturday heritage events. In 2026 that’s October 23 and 24. Walk the galleries Friday night, watch apple pressing and soap-making Saturday afternoon, then take the cemetery tour by lantern after dark. Dates drift a little year to year, so check the organizer’s page before you commit a Saturday.
### Which historic houses in Ste. Genevieve are worth touring?
Start at the Welcome Center, 66 S. Main St. It’s free, it’s where rangers hand out same-day tickets for the National Park Service houses, and it holds a 12-by-12-foot diorama of the whole town as it looked in 1832. The park tours cost nothing but cap at 15 people, first come, first served. On a fall Saturday, get your tickets before you get coffee.
Green Tree Tavern, 244 St. Marys Road, is the one to see if you only see one. Built in 1790, it’s the oldest building still standing in town, and over two centuries it has been a home, a tavern, an inn, a tobacco shop, and a Masonic lodge. It’s also one of the few places where you can plainly see the vertical logs that make up the walls. The park lists it as open daily for self-guided visits, with ranger programs on top.
The Bauvais-Amoureux House, built around 1792, is one of the three post-in-ground survivors, and it looks out over le Grand Champ, the Big Field whose rich bottomland drew French farmers here in the first place. Its story runs through Pelagie Amoureux, who inherited the house after her husband died. The Jean Baptiste Vallé House at 99 S. Main shows the other method, poteaux-sur-solle, where the logs stand on a sill instead of in the dirt. Keeping the wood out of wet ground is a big reason more of those houses lasted.
Then walk over to Market Street. The Centre for French Colonial Life, 198 Market St., sells tickets for guided tours of the Louis Bolduc House and the Bolduc-LeMeilleur House at 10:30 a.m., 1:30 p.m., and 3:30 p.m. (no 10:30 tour on Sundays). The Centre bills Bolduc as the only authentically period-furnished French colonial house open to tour in town, and it shows. The same desk sells tickets for the François Vallé fils House, the militia officer’s home, with guide-led visits at 11:30 a.m. and 2:30 p.m. Monday through Saturday, and 12:30 and 2:30 on Sunday.
The Felix Vallé House State Historic Site at 198 Merchant St. is the after picture. Built in 1818 in the American Federal style and furnished the way it would have looked in the 1830s, it shows how fast French Ste. Genevieve changed after the Louisiana Purchase. Missouri State Parks runs tours at set times through the day. Reserve online or walk up.
Short on time? Do Green Tree Tavern for the logs and Bolduc for the furniture. Those two tell the story better than any five-stop checklist. On Saturdays from late March through the first weekend of November, the Linden House across Main from Bolduc adds living history demonstrations from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.
### Which Ste. Genevieve wineries are still open?
The Route du Vin changed faster than the lists that describe it. Cave Vineyard’s Facebook page says its winery and cave are permanently closed. Chaumette Vineyards & Winery shut down on August 15, 2025, after 25 years; Life Teen International, a Catholic youth ministry, bought the property for a campground called Camp Cana. Crown Valley on Route WW is shut too, and online winery guides now list it as permanently closed. The little downtown Lewsi Winery closed back in 2022. If a guide still sends you to any of the four, close the tab.
Here’s what’s pouring as of fall 2026, going by the town’s tourism office and the wineries’ own pages:
Brix Urban Winery & Market, 245 Merchant St. Downtown, under a grape arbor. Mead flights, wine slushies, and craft beer, and the Star Lite River Restaurant kitchen inside opens at 6 a.m. with pastries and coffee. Closed Mondays.
Charleville Brewery & Winery, 16937 Boyd Road. High above the Saline Creek valley on the county’s west side. You tap a wristband at a 24-tap self-serve wall of beer, wine, and Charle-Ritas and pay for what you pour. There’s an 1860s log cabin you can rent for the night. Wednesday through Sunday.
Chateau Sainte Genevieve Winery, 8921 Jackson School Road, north of town. Family-run, with every wine made and bottled on-site next to its own vines. Its site lists daily hours of 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. and free tastings and tours.
Weingarten Vineyard, 12323 Rottler Road, west of downtown. Reopened under new owners with a full restaurant, Garten Haus. Late-week and weekend hours.
One more name you’ll see: Watertower Winery on Route M. These days it shows up mostly as a venue for concerts and private events, so call before you count it as a tasting stop. Seasonal hours shift everywhere on the trail. Brix and Weingarten make the easy pairing since both sit close to downtown. Charleville is a drive, and it’s also the one with the view, so save it for a clear day and bring a designated driver.
Skip the closed cave. Plan real pours with our winery day trip guide.
### What’s worth finding in the downtown Ste. Genevieve shops?
The downtown grid is small enough to cover on foot, and the best stops aren’t museums. At ASL Pewter Foundry, 183 S. Third St., Tom and Patricia Hooper have spent close to 40 years making pewter by hand, some of it cast in molds from the 1700s, and you can watch them work. Their pieces turned up in HBO’s John Adams miniseries. The studio lists daily hours, but it’s a two-person shop, so call if you’re making a special trip.
Rust Artisan Shop, 173 N. Main St., turns corrugated tin pulled off old Missouri barns into lamps and luminaries that throw patterned shadows across the ceiling. It’s open Friday through Sunday. On the fourth Friday of each month from April through October, the galleries stay open from 6 to 9 p.m. for the Art Walk, and some pour drinks and put out food while you browse. It’s the closest thing this town has to a date night block.
Two more details most visitors miss. The Old Brick House at 90 S. Third St. is generally cited as the oldest brick building west of the Mississippi, put up around 1780 (some sources say as late as 1785), and it was a courthouse, a school, and a fur trading post before it became a restaurant in 1940. And at the corner of Merchant and Main, the Civil War living history day in late August has staged Federal troops taking money from the town bank, an early-war episode that really happened here, with a camp set up in the Felix Vallé House yard.
### Where can you get liver dumplings in Ste. Genevieve?
Start with the dish nobody in St. Louis has heard of. Liver dumplings came over with German immigrants: minced liver worked into dumpling dough and simmered in broth. They’re on menus all over town, and the tourism office’s app even maps out a liver dumpling tour. Order them once. You’ll either get it or you won’t.
The Old Brick House runs a buffet with fried chicken and liver dumplings Thursday through Monday, 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. Its owners also run the Anvil Saloon & Restaurant at 46 S. Third St., which serves liver dumplings too and has sold them cooked or raw to take home. Between the two, you can eat lunch in a building older than the Constitution and dinner a short walk away.
Audubon’s, at 9 N. Main St., fills the old Palace Bar building with a menu that runs German, Cajun, French, and Italian to match the town’s mix; the pork schnitzel is the dish people talk about. Mornings take more planning, because the coffee spots keep short hours. Common Grounds, 10 S. Third St., is a coffee house that employs people with special needs, serving coffee, quiche, wraps, and pastries on weekdays and Saturdays. Birdies Coffee + Bakery on North Main keeps weekend-morning hours, Friday through Sunday the last time we checked, and the homemade oatmeal cream pie is the order. Up at dawn? The kitchen at Brix starts at 6 a.m. Our full rundown of where to eat in Ste. Genevieve covers the rest of the downtown tables.
### What’s on in Ste. Genevieve for Halloween, Christmas, and New Year’s Eve?
Late October is the sleeper. On the fourth Saturday of the month, the Foundation for Restoration of Ste. Genevieve holds the Déjà vu Spirit Reunion in Memorial Cemetery, which it bills as Missouri’s oldest cemetery. You walk the graves by lantern light while costumed “spirits” tell you who they were. Recent tickets ran $5 to $10. That same Saturday, Rural Heritage Day at the Felix Vallé House shows apple pressing, spinning, lace-making, and soap-making; the state parks calendar lists it for October 24, 2026. Call it Halloween for grown-ups who’d rather hear a good story than stand in line for a haunted house.
The Holiday Christmas Festival takes over the first weekend of December, and the 2025 edition was the 41st. AAA magazine has ranked it among the top two Christmas celebrations in the Midwest. Expect a parade, music from Renaissance sacred pieces to jazz inside the old churches, Santa photos, and craft workshops. Nearly all of it is free. It pairs well with the city lineup in our guide to Christmas events in St. Louis.
New Year’s Eve is the night you can’t get anywhere else around here. La Guignolée is a French begging-song tradition still practiced in only two U.S. towns. In Ste. Genevieve, singers in old-fashioned, sometimes masked costumes traditionally set out from the American Legion Hall, work their way through restaurants, bars, and nursing homes asking for food and drink in song, and finish at midnight at the Knights of Columbus Hall. The lyrics jokingly demand the household’s oldest daughter. Nobody hands her over.
### What can you do in Ste. Genevieve for free, or close to it?
A lot, because the biggest attraction in town doesn’t charge admission. The national historical park is fee-free, so the ranger-led tours of Green Tree Tavern, the Jean Baptiste Vallé House, and the Bauvais-Amoureux House cost nothing; you only need a same-day ticket from the Welcome Center. The 1832 diorama there is free too. So is watching the Hoopers work pewter, the Art Walk, the Milice Encampment, most of the Christmas festival, and the Fourth of July fireworks. Chateau Sainte Genevieve lists free tastings.
Then spend five dollars on the best view of the trip. The river ferry, which locals call the French Connection, has crossing records going back to at least 1798, carried whole rail cars on cradles starting in 1904, and has run as a modern passenger ferry since 1997. Walk on at the Missouri landing, 8205 Little Rock Road, for $5 each way and you’re on the Illinois bank 10 to 15 minutes later. Cars pay $20 one way and $10 for a same-day return; bikes and horses pay $5. It’s one of only a handful of car ferries left on the river near St. Louis; our guide to ferries near St. Louis has the rest, all the way down to the Dorena-Hickman Ferry.
The summer schedule is Wednesday through Saturday, 6 a.m. to 5:30 p.m., and Sundays from 9 a.m.; it’s closed Monday and Tuesday, and in winter it drops to Friday through Sunday. Be at the landing 30 minutes before closing for the last run. River levels can shut it down, so call the Welcome Center at 573-880-6970 the morning you go. Cyclists know it as the official Great River Road crossing, and it’s the only way over the river along a roughly 60-mile stretch.
### Where else should you stop on the drive back?
The drive home runs up I-55 through a string of Jefferson County towns. Our Arnold guide covers the stretch closest to the city, and the full guide to things to do in St. Louis, town by town, maps the rest. Stacking trips? Our list of day trips from St. Louis has more within two hours.
Next time somebody at work says they did Ste. Genevieve, ask whether they saw logs standing in the dirt, ate a liver dumpling, or rode the ferry just for the view. You’ll be the one who knows the cave tasting room is gone, the Bolduc tour leaves at 1:30, and the best night of the year is December 31. Pick a Saturday. Check the calendar. Go.
Heading south? Use the St Louis Near Me Directory guide to where to eat in Ste. Genevieve to line up lunch between house tours before you leave the city.
If you run a winery, an inn, or a shop on Main Street, the day-trippers driving down I-55 are already asking Google and ChatGPT where to stop, so list your business where they’re looking.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is Ste Genevieve, Missouri known for?
A.  It’s known as Missouri’s oldest town, established by 1750 according to the National Park Service, and for the vertical-log French Creole houses that survived here after they vanished almost everywhere else. Three of the five known post-in-ground houses left in the country stand in town. Locals would add liver dumplings and La Guignolée, the costumed New Year’s Eve singing tradition.
### Q. Where to eat in St. Genevieve, MO?
A.  For the local dish, the Old Brick House at 90 S. Third St. serves a fried chicken buffet with liver dumplings Thursday through Monday, and the Anvil Saloon & Restaurant at 46 S. Third St. serves them too. Audubon’s on North Main handles dinner with schnitzel and Cajun plates. For breakfast, try Common Grounds, Birdies on weekend mornings, or the early kitchen at Brix. Hours change, so call ahead.
### Q. What are some fun things to do in Sainte Genevieve, Missouri?
A.  Ride the car ferry across the Mississippi just for the view, watch Tom and Patricia Hooper make pewter at ASL Pewter, pour your own tastes from the wristband tap wall at Charleville, and step inside Green Tree Tavern, where the 1790 vertical logs are still visible. In late October, take the lantern-light cemetery tour. On New Year’s Eve, follow the La Guignolée singers from bar to bar.
### Q. What is there to do in Ste Genevieve?
A.  More than a day’s worth, and most of it is walkable from the Welcome Center at 66 S. Main St. Pick up free same-day tickets for the National Park Service houses there, add a guided tour at the Bolduc House or the Felix Vallé House, eat lunch downtown, then choose an afternoon: a winery or two, the river ferry, or the trails at Hawn State Park out in the county.
### Q. How many wineries are in Sainte Genevieve, Missouri?
A.  Fewer than older lists claim. As of fall 2026, four are pouring in town or a short drive out: Brix Urban Winery & Market downtown, Charleville Brewery & Winery, Chateau Sainte Genevieve Winery, and Weingarten Vineyard. The tourism office’s Route du Vin list adds a couple of stops farther out. Cave Vineyard, Chaumette, Crown Valley, and Lewsi have all closed.
### Q. Is there a ferry in St. Genevieve, Missouri?
A.  Yes. The Ste. Genevieve ferry, locally called the French Connection, carries cars, bikes, horses, and walk-on passengers across the Mississippi to Illinois from a landing at 8205 Little Rock Road. The crossing takes 10 to 15 minutes, and a standard vehicle pays $20 one way. It doesn’t run Mondays or Tuesdays, and river conditions can close it, so call the Welcome Center at 573-880-6970 first.
### Q. How far is Ste Genevieve from St. Louis?
A.  About 60 to 65 miles south of downtown St. Louis, roughly an hour down I-55 without traffic. That’s an easy day trip. Still, the Friday night Art Walk, the evening lantern tour in October, and the La Guignolée route on New Year’s Eve all make a strong case for booking a room and staying the night.
### Q. What is the oldest town in MO?
A.  Ste. Genevieve. The National Park Service calls it the first permanent European settlement in Missouri, established by 1750. The original village sat on the river bottom about three miles from today’s downtown; after the flood of 1785, residents moved to the higher ground where the historic district stands now. Its oldest standing building, Green Tree Tavern, dates to 1790.

## Things to Do in Arnold, MO: Mastodon Bones, Meramec Fishing and River Trails
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-arnold-mo
The listicles lose Arnold at the exit ramp. They file it under two I-55 interchanges and a strip of Jeffco Boulevard storefronts, the town you pass on the way to somewhere that earns a paragraph, and the southbound traffic takes the hint at highway speed. What gets lost is oddly specific. A public boat ramp onto the Meramec. A river trail laid over the streets of a neighborhood the 1993 flood took back. A Saturday-only museum that will tell you Buffalo Bill Cody got married here. And a few exits south, the creek bottom where a stone spear point turned up among mastodon bones.
None of that makes the top-10 roundups. Locals have known about it for years.
If you’ve done the Arch and the Zoo enough times to give the tour yourself, this is the other list: the Arnold that people who live off Jeffco Boulevard actually use, sorted by what you came to do. Fish. Paddle. Walk a river loop. Stand on the spot where Ice Age hunters met a mastodon. Burn a rainy Saturday without burning much money.
### What are some fun activities to do in Arnold, Missouri?
The best things to do in Arnold are the ones the lists skip: launch a kayak onto the Meramec at Flamm City Park, walk the 3.7-mile river loop at Arnold City Park, fish its 8-acre lake, then drive south to Mastodon State Historic Site, where a Clovis spear point turned up among mastodon bones.
That’s a full day, and most of it costs nothing but gas. The city lake, the river loop, the two dog parks and the Mastodon trails are all free to walk onto. The one real ticket is the Mastodon museum, and kids 12 and under get in free there.
Some context helps. Arnold is Jefferson County’s biggest city, a little over 21,000 people, about 20 miles south of downtown St. Louis, and it sits right where the Meramec River runs into the Mississippi. That geography is the whole story. Two rivers, a floodplain the city turned into parkland, and limestone bluffs a short drive south. The town even traces itself to a 1776 trading post on the old road between St. Louis and Ste. Genevieve, so people have been stopping here on the way somewhere else for a long time. The trick is to stop on purpose.
### What to do at Mastodon State Park?
Start here, because this is the stop with a story the textbooks had to catch up to. Mastodon State Historic Site sits right off I-55 at Exit 186 in Imperial, a few minutes south of Arnold, and almost everybody calls it Mastodon State Park. Its 431 acres protect the Kimmswick Bone Bed, a fossil deposit where people have been pulling mastodon bones out of the ground since the 1800s.
The bones alone would make it worth the drive. What changed the science happened in 1979, when paleontologist Russell Graham’s team found a stone Clovis spear point lying in direct association with mastodon remains. It was the first solid evidence in eastern North America that people and mastodons were here at the same time, and that people were hunting them. Ten minutes from the Jeffco Boulevard strip, that lands differently than it does in a book.
Here’s how to spend the visit:
The museum. A full-size mastodon skeleton replica, cases of fossils and artifacts, and a 15-minute film that usually runs about once an hour. Admission has been $4 for ages 13 and up and free for 12 and under, so check before you go.
Wildflower Trail. The short one, under half a mile, with stairs down to the spot where the bones and the spear point were excavated. There’s no open dig to peer into. You’re just standing on the spot, which turns out to be enough.
Spring Branch Trail. About 0.8 miles of packed gravel through bottomland woods, following Rock Creek for a stretch. On hot summer days this is where the kids end up, ankle deep in the creek.
Limestone Hill Trail. A rugged 2-mile loop along the base of a limestone bluff, then up through oak, hickory and cedar woods to hilltop views. Budget about two hours and expect roots, rocks and washouts.
Timing matters more than people expect. The grounds and trails are open every day from 8 a.m. until half an hour after sunset. The museum keeps its own schedule. From March 16 to November 15 it’s closed Mondays and Tuesdays, and from mid-November to mid-March it opens only Thursday through Sunday. Show up on a Tuesday and you’ll get the trails without the skeleton.
The site turned 50 in 2026, with an anniversary celebration on September 5, and the fall 2026 calendar lists a Hunter’s Moon Hike on October 26 plus Toddler Thursday programs on October 22, November 19 and December 17. Leashed dogs are welcome on the grounds, just not inside the museum. There’s a playground by the picnic area too, which buys you twenty minutes of quiet after the film.
### Where can you fish in Arnold, MO?
Two kinds of water, a few minutes apart. Arnold City Park, off Jeffco Boulevard on Bradley Beach Road, wraps around an 8-acre lake with a paved half-mile loop and four pavilions. It’s bank fishing, plain and easy, and what most anglers report pulling out of it is catfish and sunfish. Bring a folding chair and a bucket and you’ve got an evening. City rules ban swimming, wading and boating in park waters, so this one is shoreline only.
Every September, Arnold Days turns the park into a three-day carnival with rides, live music and fireworks over the lake, and the Saturday morning brings a free kids’ fishing derby. This year’s ran September 19, with registration opening at 7 a.m. If you’ve got a kid who has never caught anything, put next September on the calendar now.
The bigger water is the Meramec. Flamm City Park, at Telegraph Road and the river, is a 36-acre cluster of public land with a paved lot sized for boat trailers and a ramp straight into the current. Right beside it, Teszars Woods Conservation Area adds about 180 acres of bottomland woods that the Missouri Department of Conservation leases to the city, with hiking, birding, and catfish and crappie on its fishing list. This is where you go for river catfish instead of park-pond catfish. For more water across the metro, see our guide to the best free public fishing spots in St. Louis.
On permits: anglers 16 and older need a Missouri fishing permit, with an exemption for Missouri residents 65 and older who carry proof of age and residency. Kids under 16 fish without one. There’s also a daily permit if you only get out once in a while, and on Free Fishing Days, the Saturday and Sunday after the first Monday in June, anyone can fish state waters without a permit.
Most lists stop at the exit ramp. Try scenic drives around St. Louis.
### Can you kayak the Meramec from Arnold?
You can, and the Flamm City ramp is the obvious put-in. Paddling directories rate it a beginner launch with mild current in normal conditions, with the best season running March through November. The catch is what’s downstream. Arnold sits at the mouth of the Meramec, the Mississippi confluence is below you, and that is not water to drift into without a plan.
So do three things. Check the National Weather Service gauge for the Meramec River at Arnold before you load the boat. Paddle upstream first, so the trip back is the easy half. And skip it entirely after heavy rain, when the river comes up fast and carries debris. Do that, and you’ve got an evening paddle under half an hour from downtown that most people in the city never think to try.
### Are there hiking trails in Arnold Park?
Yes, and the best one has a backstory. Arnold City Park has a paved half-mile loop around the lake, but the trail locals mean is the river loop that starts at the gravel road in the park’s northeast corner. Walk the whole thing and it’s about 3.7 miles, flat, close to the Meramec, mostly under trees.
Pay attention to the pavement. It doesn’t feel like a trail because it wasn’t built as one. Hollywood Beach Road and Bradley Beach Road were lined with homes and river clubhouses until the 1993 flood swamped this side of Arnold, and the damaged properties were bought out and cleared. The city kept the old streets and let the woods move back in. You’re walking through a neighborhood the river reclaimed. Our story of the Great Flood of 1993 covers what that summer did across the region.
A few honest notes. An active rail line crosses one of the old roads, so watch for trains. The stretch closed to cars isn’t maintained like a city sidewalk, it gets muddy after rain, and a low section floods in spring. Part of the loop shares a slow park road with light traffic. City parks open half an hour before sunrise and close half an hour after sunset, which answers the question every evening walker eventually asks.
Back near the lake there’s a 9-hole disc golf course that’s been in since 2009, short and mostly flat. Across town, Strawberry Creek Nature Area is the quiet one: 118 acres on Upper Tenbrook Road, about half a mile past Highway 231, with a pond, four walking trails and a creek winding through the whole property. There’s no running water or electricity out there, just a portable restroom and a small pavilion near the entrance, so pack what you need.
Dog owners get their own loop. The Ozark Drive Paw Park, at 1839 Ozark Drive, connects to Ferd B. Lang Park by a half-mile walking trail and a bridge, so you can walk the dog in, let it run, and walk back out. Both of Arnold’s Paw Parks are fully fenced, split into areas for dogs under and over 25 pounds, and run on donations.
### What is free to do in Arnold, MO?
More than the event calendars suggest. The dog parks, the trails and the disc golf course cost nothing, and so do the Mastodon grounds. Jim Edwards Archery Park, at 1136 Telegraph Road, is an ADA-accessible range with year-round targets for bows only, open regular park hours except Tuesday mornings, when it closes until noon for maintenance. The Arnold Jaycees Skate Park covers skateboards and skates.
Saturday mornings from May through the last Saturday in October, the Arnold Farmers Market sets up at Arnold City Park with around 80 vendors selling produce, eggs, honey, farm meats and baked goods. Walking it is free, and the 2026 season’s last Saturday is October 31. The one Saturday it skips is the Saturday of Arnold Days.
Parents should know about the library too. The Jefferson County Library’s Arnold branch shares a 23-acre campus with the rec center and runs free story times and kids’ programs, some of which need registration. Pair a story time with a lap around the lake and you’ve filled a morning for nothing.
### Where can you see Christmas lights in Arnold, MO?
Arnold does Christmas the small-town way, which is the point. The city’s Christmas in the Park at Arnold City Park was set for Saturday, December 5, 2026, from 4 to 7 p.m. It started in 2023, so 2026’s is the fourth one, and it’s been free and built squarely for families. Reading this after December 5? Check with the city for next year’s date.
For a show you watch from the car, First Baptist Church of Arnold, at 2012 Missouri State Road, runs Lights of Christmas: you park, the light show plays out in front of you, and the church’s guest services team comes by with hot cocoa and a treat. It ran on December evenings last year and has been free in past seasons. Check the church’s site for this year’s dates before you go.
Then there are the houses. Arnold’s subdivisions carry a handful of serious residential displays, and one was bright enough that local light hunters reported spotting it from I-55 at highway speed. That’s a fitting twist for a town most people only ever see from the interstate. Slow down for once.
### What can you do in Arnold on a rainy day?
Head for the Arnold Recreation Center at 1695 Missouri State Road. The indoor pool is the draw: a lazy river with a vortex, a bubble bench, a slide and a children’s play area. Fall open swim runs Monday and Wednesday evenings plus Saturday and Sunday afternoons, and a daily fee, about $6 for most ages at last check and free for kids 4 and under, gets you in without a membership. Kids 13 and under need an adult with them the whole visit, and anyone 14 or older buying a day pass needs a photo ID.
On Saturday afternoons, the Arnold Historical Society Museum opens at 1723 Jeffco Boulevard from noon to 4, with a $5 donation requested. It’s small and volunteer-run, and more interesting than its size suggests. There’s an 1873 Bible carried across the Atlantic by a German settler, a 1906 Victrola that still plays records through its horn, and the story Arnold likes to tell best: Louisa Frederici, born on a farm here in 1844, married William F. Cody at her parents’ home on March 6, 1866, about a year before anyone called him Buffalo Bill.
Make it a double feature. The Mastodon museum is indoors too, and on a Saturday both are open. If the kids need to burn energy instead, Cactus Pete’s Family Fun Center in Imperial runs arcade games and laser tag, started by two Jefferson County dads who were tired of driving their kids to South County, Fenton and St. Charles for the same thing; check its hours before you go. Rain on the trails, a skeleton in the museum, Buffalo Bill on Jeffco Boulevard. That’s a better wet Saturday than another lap around a mall.
### When is the Kimmswick Apple Butter Festival in 2026?
October 24 and 25, 2026, from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. both days. It’s always the last full weekend of October, and it’s the reason a tiny river village a few minutes past Arnold fills up every fall. The Kimmswick Historical Society’s apple butter is the headliner, with hundreds of craft and food vendors and live music around it.
Go in knowing it gets crowded. The local paper estimated about 120,000 people over the two days in 2021, so expect street closures and shuttle parking rather than a curb spot on Main Street. Arrive early, eat late. If you want the village without the crowd, our full guide to things to do in Kimmswick covers the quieter weekends, and Mastodon is five minutes away either way.
### What’s near Arnold for a longer day?
Arnold works as a base because of where it sits. Take Highway 141 northwest and you’re in Fenton, where our guide to things to do in Fenton picks up the thread. Stay on I-55 south past Imperial and Kimmswick and you’ll eventually reach Ste. Genevieve, the old French town at the far end of the same road Arnold’s trading post served in 1776, covered in our Ste. Genevieve guide. For every other town on the map, start with our complete local guide to things to do in St. Louis by town.
Next time somebody says there’s nothing to do south of the Meramec, you’ll be the one who knows about the river streets, the Saturday museum and the spear point. Pick one this weekend and go.
Spending the day in Arnold? Before you leave the house, check where to eat in Arnold, MO on St Louis Near Me Directory for lunch near the lake or a coffee on the way to Mastodon.
And if you run a business in Arnold, the families and anglers already driving past at highway speed should be able to find you, so list your business where they’re searching.
