### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are some fun activities for kids in Arnold, MO?
A.  Fish the 8-acre lake at Arnold City Park, swim the lazy river at the Arnold Recreation Center’s indoor pool, and save a day for Mastodon State Historic Site, where kids 12 and under get into the museum free and summer wading happens in Rock Creek. In September, circle the free kids’ fishing derby during Arnold Days.
### Q. What are the current hours of operation for the Mastodon State Historic Site?
A.  The grounds and trails are open every day from 8 a.m. until half an hour after sunset. The museum keeps its own schedule: from March 16 to November 15 it’s closed Mondays and Tuesdays, and from mid-November to mid-March it opens only Thursday through Sunday. Show up on a Tuesday and you’ll get the trails without the skeleton.
### Q. Can I get a one-day fishing license in Missouri?
A.  Yes. The Missouri Department of Conservation sells a Daily Fishing Permit to residents and nonresidents, and you can buy it for more than one day if you’re in town for a long weekend. Prices change, so check MDC’s permit page. If you’re a Missouri resident planning several trips to the Meramec this year, the annual permit usually works out cheaper.
### Q. Can you swim at Mastodon State Park?
A.  There’s no swimming beach or pool at Mastodon State Historic Site. What people do on hot days is wade in Rock Creek along the Spring Branch Trail, which draws families all summer. Treat it as wading rather than swimming, keep small kids within arm’s reach, and remember there’s no lifeguard on duty.
### Q. How do I get to the creek at Mastodon State Park?
A.  Take the Spring Branch Trail. It’s about 0.8 miles of packed gravel through bottomland woods and follows Rock Creek for a short stretch, which is where summer visitors stop to wade. It’s the easiest of the site’s three trails, so it works for small kids and for anyone skipping the rugged Limestone Hill loop.
### Q. Are there any American mastodon skeletons on display?
A.  Yes. The museum at Mastodon State Historic Site in Imperial displays a full-size replica of an American mastodon skeleton, alongside real fossils and artifacts from the Kimmswick Bone Bed and a 15-minute film. It’s a replica, not the original bones, and Missouri State Parks calls it “a sight that is not easily forgotten.” Check museum days before you drive.
### Q. Is Kimmswick worth visiting?
A.  Yes, if you go with the right expectations. It’s a small, walkable river village of old storefronts and shops a few minutes past Arnold, best for a slow half-day paired with Mastodon State Historic Site. Festival weekends, especially the Apple Butter Festival on the last full weekend of October, bring huge crowds. Quiet weekends are the better bet for wandering.
### Q. What is the current Meramec River level at Arnold, MO?
A.  It changes daily, so check it live rather than trusting a guide. The National Weather Service tracks the Meramec River at Arnold on its water prediction site, and the Army Corps of Engineers posts the same gauge. Look at the reading the morning you go, and if the river is up or rising after rain, save the kayak for another day.

## Things to Do in Clayton, MO: Free Art, Bell Concerts and Quiet Parks
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-clayton-mo
What do you picture when someone says Clayton? Glass office towers. The county courthouse. A parking meter ticking down while you sit through jury duty. That’s the Clayton the recycled top-10 lists keep selling, and most of them run out of ideas somewhere around the steakhouses.
Try a harder question. Why is the courthouse in Clayton at all? Because two farmers gave away land for it in the 1870s, and one of their farmhouses is still standing on a quiet residential street. Where’s the free museum on Clayton’s doorstep with a Henry Moore and a Keith Haring on view this fall? Which Clayton tower holds 49 bells, and on what night of the week do they play for anyone who shows up with a blanket? And what happened to the Saturday farmers market the internet still lists?
If you can’t answer those, that’s not on you. The lists never asked. Start with the market, because it shows how stale the usual advice has gotten.
### Does Clayton have a farmers market?
Not one we could confirm for 2026. The downtown Clayton market that used to run Saturday mornings on Forsyth Boulevard is missing from this year’s area market guides and the city’s event calendar. The closest weekly markets are The Boulevard in Richmond Heights on Sundays and the U City Farmers Market in Heman Park on Saturdays.
That surprises people, because a few market directories online still list a Saturday Clayton market, and one even shows 2026 dates. We couldn’t find a single current source to back that up, and St. Louis Magazine’s 2026 farmers market guide doesn’t include Clayton at all. If you remember buying tomatoes on Forsyth on a Saturday morning, you’re not imagining it. It just isn’t running now, as far as anyone can confirm.
The replacements are close. The Boulevard market sets up Sunday mornings from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. through late October, a few minutes south of downtown Clayton. The U City Farmers Market runs Saturday mornings from 8:30 to 12:30 in Heman Park at 7210 Olive, and its season stretches into late November. Dates shift every year, so check both before you go. Once you’re there, our guide to buying fresh produce in St. Louis covers whether market produce really costs more and whether haggling is ever okay.
### What are the best free things to do in Clayton?
Start with the art, because there’s more of it than the business district lets on. The St. Louis Artists’ Guild, around since 1886, runs free galleries behind green doors at the corner of Forsyth and Jackson. They’re open Tuesday through Friday from 10 to 6 and Saturday from 10 to 4. Park in the two-hour retail spots, not the visitor spaces. The Guild spent 20 years inside Oak Knoll Park before moving downtown in 2015.
Then cross to the Wash U edge of town for the Mildred Lane Kemper Art Museum, on the east end of the Danforth Campus near Skinker and Lindell, directly west of Forest Park. Admission is free. It’s open 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. every day but Tuesday, and it’s a short walk from the Skinker MetroLink stop. Founded in 1881, the Kemper is one of the oldest teaching museums in the country, and its two big fall 2026 shows, one on Argentine modern art from 1935 to 1950 and one from the artist Carolina Caycedo, are set to stay up through January 4, 2027. The coffee bar sells Sugarwitch ice cream sandwiches. On a warm afternoon that alone justifies the trip.
The rest of the free list is outdoors, and it runs on the calendar. Clayton’s Musical Nights concerts at Oak Knoll Park happen one Sunday evening a month from late June through September, 5 to 7 p.m., no ticket. Concordia Seminary’s carillon concerts are free too, at 7 p.m. every Tuesday in June. And here’s the detail that changes the math on any evening out: street parking across Clayton is free after 5 p.m. on weekdays, all day on weekends, and on city holidays. The meters are for the lunch crowd.
### What are the best parks in Clayton, MO?
Clayton has a dozen city parks, and the biggest one gets nearly all the attention. For a slow hour, Oak Knoll Park is the better pick. It covers 14.5 acres at the northwest corner of Clayton Road and Big Bend Boulevard, became a park in 1958, and takes its name from a native stand of post oaks the city puts at about 150 years old. A half-mile path loops past a rain garden, a sunken garden and the Uchitelle Garden of Reflection, then drops you at a pond with a lighted fountain. Look for the turtles. They sun themselves on an old stump in the water. There’s a large playground by the picnic tables, two early-1900s stone mansions still standing on the grounds, and the park is open from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.
Bring binoculars in spring. Clayton was named a Bird City Missouri community in 2026, only the second city in the state to earn it, and Oak Knoll is where its World Migratory Bird Day event was held this spring.
Want something smaller? Wydown Park is a half-acre square at 7619 Wydown Boulevard, just east of Hanley Road, with cafe tables, vine-covered pergolas, a Little Library and a stone sculpture called “Youth” by Todd Frahm. Get a coffee nearby and sit. Remembrance Park, the city’s smallest, is a pocket park the city pitches for a workday break or a game of chess. And if you’d rather cover miles than minutes, the Centennial Greenway starts at a trailhead in Shaw Park and runs about two and a half paved miles north toward Olive Boulevard, tying Clayton to University City and Ladue.
Tired of the usual list? See offbeat St. Louis for grown-ups.
### What are some unique things to do in Clayton, MO?
The strangest good answer is a seminary. It holds a lot more than most people expect from a campus they’ve only ever driven past. Concordia Seminary has sat on 72 acres in Clayton since 1926, and when it was dedicated it was the largest Protestant seminary in the United States. The stone quad looks like it was lifted from an old East Coast college, and the seminary openly invites visitors to stroll the grounds.
Look up first. Luther Tower rises 156 feet over the east side of the main quad. It was drawn into the original 1922 plans, but it wasn’t finished until the funding came through in 1966, 44 years later. At the top hangs a 49-bell carillon. The biggest bell weighs two and a half tons; the smallest weighs 17 pounds. The seminary’s dean of chapel calls it one of only 175 such instruments in North America. It chimes on weekdays before chapel, and every Tuesday in June at 7 p.m. a visiting carillonneur plays a free concert while people spread blankets on the quad or near the Luther statue with a picnic. If it rains, the crowd shelters under the tower and its covered passages.
Then walk the rest. The bronze Luther statue stands more than nine feet tall on a granite base taller than that. It’s a replica of the famous one in Germany and has been on this campus since 1926. Beside the library sits a log cabin, a 1938 replica of the 1839 cabin school the seminary grew out of. Inside that library, among more than 6,000 rare items, is Johann Sebastian Bach’s personal Bible. It’s part of the rare book collection, not a lobby display, so ask the library before you plan around it. Still. Bach’s own Bible is sitting in a library in Clayton.
Mark one more date. The seminary’s 2026 Advent Lessons and Carols was set for Tuesday, December 1, at 7 p.m., and its fall 2026 music series also lists a choral evening prayer for All Saints’ Day on Sunday, November 1, at 4 p.m., plus a recital dedicating the seminary’s new Steinway on November 15. All of it is free.
### Where should you go for a date night in Clayton?
Skip the downtown dinner rush and go to DeMun. It’s a short, leafy stretch of DeMun Avenue near the seminary, and it’s where the regional coffee chain Kaldi’s got its start: the original coffeehouse opened there in 1994 and still overlooks little Concordia Park. For dinner, Louie at 706 DeMun takes reservations online or by phone, and its patio tables go first come, first served when the weather cooperates.
The other block worth knowing is where Wydown Boulevard meets Hanley Road. Pick up something warm to drink, carry it to the cafe tables in Wydown Park, and you’ve got a better first hour than most rooftop bars can sell you. That’s also the start of a good slow Saturday: coffee on DeMun, a lap around the seminary quad, the Artists’ Guild galleries before they close at 4, then an early dinner back on DeMun or Wydown. Total weekend parking cost? Nothing.
Summer evenings are where the free parking really pays off. Pack a picnic for Musical Nights at Oak Knoll or a June Tuesday under the carillon, then head to dinner after. Downtown, the city throws two free street parties on North Brentwood Boulevard: the Music & Wine Festival in early June and the Clayton Jazz Festival in early October, both from 5 to 10 p.m. This year’s jazz night, the sixth, was October 3. Put next fall’s on the calendar now.
### Why is Clayton the county seat?
Because of a land gift you can still go look at. When St. Louis County split from the city in 1876, the new county needed a seat. Farmer Ralph Clayton donated 100 acres, and his neighbor Martin Franklin Hanley gave four more. The downtown you know grew out of that donated farmland.
Hanley’s 1855 brick farmhouse still stands at 7600 Westmoreland Avenue, the oldest surviving home in Clayton and a National Register property. The city bought it in 1968 and opened it as a museum in 1971. It closed in 2020, went through masonry and waterproofing repairs, and held a ceremonial reopening in May 2026, with public tours expected to resume next year. Until then it’s a walk-by, so check with the city before you plan on going inside. When it does open, look for the original furnishings and the family letters still tucked in a desk. Out back stands something rarer: a detached brick kitchen and the preserved quarters of the three people the Hanleys enslaved, including a woman named Lydia Jackson. It’s an honest piece of county history on a street most people never turn onto.
### What are the best seasonal events in Clayton?
Work backward from the calendar and Clayton gets a lot more interesting than its office hours suggest.
Fall. Party in the Patch, a family Halloween night with a candy hunt, hayrides and inflatables, is held in Shaw Park, hosted by the Clayton and Brentwood parks departments. In 2026 it was set for Friday, October 16, from 6 to 8 p.m. Kids register ahead for the hot dog dinner. The Kemper’s fall 2026 shows are set to stay up into January 2027. Reading this after Halloween? Check with the Clayton parks department for next year’s Party in the Patch date.
Winter. Advent Lessons and Carols at Concordia Seminary (December 1 in 2026) is the quiet, free alternative to a packed light show, and it’s indoors.
Spring. Migration. Oak Knoll’s pond and old oaks are the place to look, and the city has made a point of planting native habitat for birds.
Summer. The busy stretch. Music & Wine on North Brentwood in early June, carillon concerts every Tuesday in June, and Musical Nights at Oak Knoll from late June through September.
September. The Saint Louis Art Fair filled downtown for its 33rd year on September 18 to 20, 2026, with 233 artists. Admission is free. Friday runs 5 to 10 p.m., which makes it an easy after-work stop.
### What’s near Clayton for a longer day out?
Clayton makes a good base. The Kemper puts you on the edge of Wash U’s campus for a longer walk, U City’s Saturday market in Heman Park is about ten minutes north, and The Boulevard’s Sunday market is just south in Richmond Heights. For the shops, services and businesses in between, our Clayton city guide lists what’s open in town. Heading west on I-64? Our Chesterfield guide covers the next town out. ### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is Clayton, Missouri known for?
A.  Clayton is the seat of St. Louis County and the area’s second downtown, a cluster of office towers around the county courthouse. Locals also know it for the Saint Louis Art Fair each September, Concordia Seminary’s 156-foot Luther Tower and its 49-bell carillon, and a dozen city parks. Part of Wash U lives there too: everything south of Forsyth Boulevard, including the South 40 dorms, is inside Clayton.
### Q. Is Clayton a nice part of St. Louis?
A.  Clayton is its own city, separate from the City of St. Louis, about 15 minutes west of downtown. It’s compact and walkable, with a dozen parks and a new Bird City Missouri designation. For a visitor, the nicest parts are the quiet ones: Oak Knoll Park, the DeMun block, the Wydown business district and the seminary grounds.
### Q. What are some fun activities to do in Clayton, Missouri?
A.  Walk the half-mile loop at Oak Knoll Park, see the free galleries at the St. Louis Artists’ Guild, catch a June carillon concert at Concordia Seminary, have coffee where Kaldi’s started on DeMun, and drive past the 1855 Hanley House. Add the Saint Louis Art Fair in September and the free Jazz Festival in early October if your timing lines up.
### Q. Is Clayton, MO part of St. Louis County?
A.  Yes. Clayton is the county seat of St. Louis County, and has been since shortly after the county split from the City of St. Louis in 1876. Two farmers, Ralph Clayton and Martin Franklin Hanley, donated the land for it. The City of St. Louis is a separate jurisdiction that isn’t part of any county.
### Q. Is Clayton, MO affluent?
A.  Yes, Clayton is one of the more affluent communities in the St. Louis area, and its home prices and dinner checks show it. A day there doesn’t have to cost much, though. Street parking is free on weekends and after 5 p.m. on weekdays, and the art galleries, seminary grounds, park concerts and carillon recitals don’t charge admission.
### Q. What do couples do for fun at night?
A.  In Clayton, the easy answer is something outdoors followed by dinner on DeMun or Wydown. In summer that means a Sunday Musical Nights concert at Oak Knoll Park or a Tuesday carillon recital at Concordia Seminary in June. In early December, Advent Lessons and Carols at the seminary makes a quiet date. Street parking is free after 5 p.m.
### Q. Should I bring cash to a farmers market?
A.  Bring some. Plenty of vendors take cards or phone payments now, but smaller growers don’t always, and cash keeps the line moving. That goes for both markets closest to Clayton, The Boulevard on Sundays and the U City Farmers Market on Saturdays in Heman Park. Small bills help.
### Q. When is the Saint Louis Art Fair in Clayton?
A.  The Saint Louis Art Fair takes over downtown Clayton for one weekend each September. The 2026 fair, its 33rd, ran September 18 to 20, open Friday 5 to 10 p.m., Saturday 10 a.m. to 9 p.m. and Sunday 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Admission is free. Watch the fair’s website for next year’s dates.

## Things to Do in Creve Coeur, MO: Public Ice Skating, Curling, Night Fishing
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-creve-coeur-mo
Wrong town, listicles. Most lists of things to do in Creve Coeur start at Creve Coeur Lake, which sits just over the city line in Maryland Heights, and then retell a lovesick-maiden legend that St. Louis County’s own history page calls “obviously spurious.” Meanwhile, the best Saturday night inside the actual city happens on its own ice rink. That’s where the St. Louis Curling Club, which bills itself as the only place to curl in the St. Louis metro, slides granite stones down the sheet while anyone who wanders in watches from the bleachers for nothing.
You’ve walked the lake loop. Maybe twice. Creve Coeur has more going on than the Olive Boulevard exit suggests: a city rink with public skating seven days a week, a 1962 church built from stacked concrete arches, an 1880s farmhouse built for $260 in labor plus room and board, and a lake that stays open until 11 p.m. one Saturday a month. The town’s real broken-heart story isn’t the one on the lake sign, either. It’s in Creve Coeur’s first park, and the city now tells it in its own words.
So this guide skips the brochure. It answers what people actually search for: whether you can fish the lake, when the rink is open, what’s free, where to walk, what to do when it rains, and what’s on the calendar this fall. Creve Coeur has earned a spot among the small towns outside St. Louis worth a day, even if it’s really a suburb, and our Creve Coeur city guide keeps the addresses and basics in one place. Every place below was checked against city, county, club or museum pages in October 2026. Hours and prices change, so check before you go.
### Can I fish in Creve Coeur Lake?
Yes. Creve Coeur Lake is a 320-acre St. Louis County lake, just over the city line in Maryland Heights, with crappie, white bass, black bass, catfish and sunfish. You need a Missouri fishing permit, boats run electric motors only, and from April to October the bank stays open until 11 p.m. on the second Saturday of each month.
That last part is the one regulars plan around. St. Louis County calls it Late Night Fishing: on the second Saturday of every month from April through October, Creve Coeur Park stays open until 11 p.m. so you can fish from the bank with your own poles, bait and light. On an ordinary day, MDC lists the area’s hours as 8 a.m. to a half hour after sunset, so this is how you fish it after dark without breaking park rules. The season closes on October’s second Saturday (October 10 in 2026), from 6 to 11 p.m. After that, the series picks back up in April.
Read the posted signs at the lot before you set up. The County limits where in the park you can fish, and MDC puts this lake under its own St. Louis region limits: two black bass a day with an 18-inch minimum, four catfish, 15 crappie and 10 of everything else combined. Statewide rules still apply on top of that, which means three unlabeled poles per person. Bringing a boat? There are public ramps on the north side at Sailboat Cove and on the south and west sides.
Here’s the part the lists never mention. Invasive bighead and silver carp rode Missouri River floodwater into the lake before 2009, crowded out native fish, hurt the crappie and even leaped at people on the water. In early 2018, MDC and its partners netted 47,000 of them, 119 tons in all, and biologists estimated they’d removed about 85 percent. A second push with the U.S. Geological Survey was planned for mid-March through April 2026. It didn’t go as hoped. State and federal crews ran out of time before they could net the big schools they were after, and the Post-Dispatch headline said the sweep “comes up largely empty.” The carp aren’t gone.
One more stop before you pack up: Dripping Springs, the small waterfall a few steps from the Taco Bell Shelter lot. It runs best after a rain, and the rocks around it stay slick. For more water across the metro, our guide to the best fishing spots around St. Louis covers the lakes and river access points beyond this one. From November through January, trout fishing at Walker Lake in Kirkwood is a short drive south on I-270.
### When is public ice skating at the Creve Coeur Ice Arena?
Every day of the week, but mostly in the morning. The Creve Coeur Ice Arena is the city’s own indoor rink, open year-round in the Dielmann Recreation Complex at 11400 Olde Cabin Road, the same complex as the city golf course. The 2026 recreation guide lists public skate on Monday from 8:15 to 11:15 a.m., Tuesday and Thursday from 9:15 a.m. to 1 p.m., Wednesday from 9:15 to 11:15 a.m., Friday from 9 to 11:15 a.m., Saturday from noon to 2 p.m. and Sunday from 2:30 to 4 p.m.
Read that schedule twice. Public skating here is a weekday-morning thing. The weekend windows are two hours on Saturday and 90 minutes on Sunday, and hockey, lessons and figure skating share the ice, so sessions shift. Check the city’s online ice calendar the morning you go, or call the Recreation Department at 314-432-3960.
The prices, per the city: public skate is $7 for non-residents and $5 for Creve Coeur residents (bring the city’s resident ID card), and Maryland Heights residents get the $5 rate too. Seniors 55 and up pay $3.50 as residents or $5.50 otherwise. Skate rental is $3, and kids 4 and under skate free with a paying adult. Two non-resident adults with rentals come to $20. To see how that compares, read our breakdown of what ice skating costs around St. Louis, and if the weekend windows don’t fit your week, look at the times for public skating at the Webster Groves ice rink.
Saturday night is when this rink turns into something else. The St. Louis Curling Club, founded in 2010, plays its season from September to April on this ice, and several times a season it opens the sheets to beginners. A Learn to Curl class runs about two hours and costs $40: instructors teach you to deliver the stone, sweep and think through strategy, then you play a short game. A Try Curling class is about an hour for $25. Kids 5 and up can join in, and they throw lighter stones.
You don’t need gear. They fit grippers over your shoes and supply the equipment. The rink sits around 40 degrees, so wear layers, loose pants, a hat, gloves and clean flat-soled shoes. Can’t get down low to throw? The club keeps delivery sticks, a bit like a shuffleboard cue, so you can do it standing up.
The October 10, 2026, class sold out, all 40 spots. The public Learn to Curl dates after it: Saturday, November 28, 2026, listed from 8:45 to 11 p.m., then February 20 and March 5, 2027. They fill fast, and the club keeps a waitlist. Can’t get in? Go anyway. Bleachers overlook the sheets, watching costs nothing, and club members will happily explain what you’re seeing. As cheap date nights go, an hour of strangers sweeping like mad in front of a sliding granite stone is hard to beat.
Curling after dinner? Where to eat in Creve Coeur
Two more reasons to stop by. Spooky Skate’s 2026 date is Saturday, October 31, from noon to 1:30 p.m.: kids 13 and under in costume skate free with a paying adult (rental not included), and the city asks you to leave weapon props at home. And on your way in, look for the red heart. Low-Poly Heart No. 4 (Red) by m.l. duffy stands outside the Dielmann complex on loan through the Sculpture on the Move program from 2026 to 2028. A red heart outside the rink, in a town whose name is French for broken heart. Make of that what you will.
### Why is Creve Coeur’s first park named for Dr. H. Phillip Venable?
Because the city took his land to build it. Dr. H. Phillip Venable was a Black ophthalmologist, and he and his wife, Katie, wanted to build their home in Creve Coeur. In proceedings between 1956 and 1960, the city acquired their land by eminent domain. The Venables fought it in state and federal court, lost, and sold the land to the city. It became Creve Coeur’s first park, dedicated in June 1961.
The city doesn’t soften what happened. Its own history page says city and court records showed the people leading the effort to obtain Dr. Venable’s land were “motivated by bigotry and racial animus” and sought to keep the Venables from building their home in the city because of their race. For decades the park went by another name, Beirne Park. The city says its origins “had been forgotten for many years” until members of the public brought the facts to the City Council in 2019.
On December 9, 2019, the council approved Resolution 1467. It renamed the park Dr. H. Phillip Venable Memorial Park, acknowledged and apologized for what the city calls the abhorrent actions of its predecessors, and recognized the Venables’ effort to oppose the misuse of government authority. A rededication followed on September 18, 2021. In March 2022, the podcast 99% Invisible told the story in an episode titled “Broken Heart Park.”
Since April 2026, the park has a permanent memorial. It’s called Home in Sight, by artists Oletha DeVane and Christopher Kojzar, and its central element is modeled on an ophthalmic lens flipper, a tool from Dr. Venable’s own field. The City Council chose it on the recommendation of a jury, after input from stakeholders that included the Venable family. A fundraising committee raised $50,000 toward it, the city added $150,000, and a $400,000 HDR Foundation grant is paying for the wider park renovation.
The park is at 10630 Country View Drive, open dawn to dusk, and free. It covers seven and a half acres with a half-mile paved trail, playgrounds and tennis courts, and the city counts it among its busiest parks, so expect neighbors. The city’s 2026 guide lists the soccer field as closed this year. Walk the loop, then give the sculpture some time. If you want to hear the story from Dr. Venable himself, the city’s history page links his 1987 oral history interview with the Missouri Historical Society.
### What are some unique things to do in Creve Coeur, MO?
Start with a church that seems to float. The Abbey Church at Saint Louis Abbey, the Benedictine monastery on South Mason Road, was designed by Gyo Obata of HOK and consecrated in 1962. Its round facade is three tiers of thin, whitewashed concrete parabolic arches, with the top tier doubling as the bell tower, and the arches appear to rise straight up off the lawn. The Priory calls it a name-making project for HOK, which grew into one of the world’s largest architecture firms. Inside are a 7-ton granite altar, a 14th-century Madonna and Child and a 17th-century holy water font in the Della Robbia style.
This is a working monastery with a school on the grounds, so don’t treat it like a museum. The respectful way in is Mass. Masses in the Abbey Church itself are Saturday at 4:30 p.m., Sunday at 7:30 and 9 a.m., and weekdays at 7:30 a.m. and 5:30 p.m. The Sunday 11 a.m. and 5:30 p.m. Masses are in the Parish Chapel, so pick your time with that in mind.
Next, the farmhouse. The Tappmeyer Homestead in Millennium Park, 2 Barnes West Drive, is a Victorian Italianate house built from 1880 to 1884, and four generations of Tappmeyers lived there for more than a century. The family drove wagonloads of potatoes into St. Louis and came back with the lumber to build it. It was moved to the park in 2003. Admission is free, but it only opens on the second and fourth Sundays of June, July and August from noon to 4 p.m., plus summer concert nights, so put it on next summer’s list.
Then cross the city line for the lake’s real history, which beats the legend. Around 1900 the upper park was Electric Park, an amusement park at the end of a streetcar line, and the County says original rail ties are still visible near the maintenance building. In the summer of 1904, the Olympic rowing races were held on this lake on July 29 and 30. When that year’s World’s Fair closed, a 255-foot observation tower was moved here from the fairgrounds. It’s gone now. By the end of Prohibition, the County says, the lakefront had become a gangster hideout, and in 1945 it became St. Louis County’s first park.
Two more finds sit over the line in Maryland Heights. The St. Louis Rowing Club still keeps a boathouse on the lake and runs an adult Learn to Row course each spring. And at Creve Coeur Airport, the Historic Aircraft Restoration Museum keeps 49 aircraft in four hangars, mostly from the Golden Age of Flight between 1920 and 1939. Its 2026 season opened May 1 with hours Friday through Sunday from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., and weekday visits by appointment. Admission is $10 for adults and $5 for ages 5 to 12. The hangars aren’t climate controlled, so call 314-434-3368 before you drive over. Our Maryland Heights city guide covers the rest of that side of the lake.
### Where can you hike in Creve Coeur besides the lake loop?
Malcolm Terrace Park is the one to start with. It’s 25 wooded acres at 11370 St. Paul Street, off South Mosley Road, with a mile and a half of nature trails. Find Serenity Grove, a densely planted corner with a rock creek and shaded seating, and you’ll forget I-270 is a few minutes away. Like every city park, it’s open dawn to dusk.
For an easy, flat loop, Conway Park at 12301 Conway Road, just west of I-270, has a one-mile paved path around a pond lined with wildflower and native plantings, plus two pickleball courts. Millennium Park has a 0.6-mile paved trail, and Venable Park adds a half-mile paved loop that passes the new sculpture.
Want a workout instead of a stroll? Cross into Creve Coeur Park for the 220 steps, the locals’ stair climb that starts across the road from the lot nearest Dripping Springs and climbs to the upper park. Do three laps and your legs will tell you about it. If you’d rather have hills on dirt, Bootleggers Run in the same park is about 2.5 miles. The paved Lakeview Loop around the water runs about 3.7 to 3.8 miles, and our roundup of easy family-friendly hiking trails around St. Louis already covers it. Heading west afterward? Here are the places to walk around Chesterfield.
### What can you do in Creve Coeur on a rainy day?
Spend the afternoon at the St. Louis Kaplan Feldman Holocaust Museum, 36 Millstone Campus Drive. It reopened in late 2022 after a $19.8 million renovation, and it’s a visit that deserves unhurried time. It’s open Wednesday through Monday from 10 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. (closed Tuesdays, last ticket at 3:40). Admission is $12 for adults, $10 for seniors, college students and veterans, and $6 for ages 10 to 17. Educator-led tours run Sundays at 2 p.m., and Bank of America cardholders get in free on the first full weekend of each month.
The rink is the other answer, since it’s indoors and has a public session every day. On a wet Saturday night, the curling bleachers are dry and free, though you’ll want a jacket at 40 degrees. A weekday 5:30 p.m. Mass in the Abbey Church is a quiet stretch out of the weather, too.
### What are some free things to do in Creve Coeur?
More than you’d guess, and one thing you’d assume is free isn’t. The free list: Venable Park and Home in Sight, the trails at Malcolm Terrace and Conway Park, watching curling from the bleachers, and in summer, the Tappmeyer Homestead and the city’s free Summer Concert Series in Millennium Park. The concerts run on second Thursdays from May through September, usually from about 6 or 6:30 to 8:30 p.m. Bring a cooler (no glass), and the Kiwanis sell barbecue. The 2026 season wrapped on September 10, so look for it again in May. One summer heads-up: the Millennium Park splash pad is closed for all of 2026.
The catch is the dog park. The fenced Creve Coeur Dog Park at Conway Park is members only, and membership costs money (the FAQ below has the numbers). If you just want to watch, the Dog Park Costume Contest (Friday, October 30, in 2026, from 5 to 6 p.m.) is free for spectators.
### What’s happening in Creve Coeur this Halloween and holiday season?
Here’s the short calendar, in order.
Saturday, October 10, 2026: the season’s last Late Night Fishing at Creve Coeur Park, 6 to 11 p.m., and the sold-out Learn to Curl at the rink.
Friday, October 30, 2026: the Dog Park Costume Contest at Conway Park, 5 to 6 p.m. Members’ dogs compete, and anyone can watch.
Saturday, October 31, 2026: Spooky Skate, noon to 1:30 p.m. Costumed kids 13 and under skate free with a paying adult.
November 1 to 10, 2026: Festival Week of the St. Louis Jewish Book Festival & Speaker Series, in its 48th year, at the J’s Staenberg Family Complex, 2 Millstone Campus Drive. The season starts in October, and author events continue through the year.
Saturday, November 28, 2026: a public Learn to Curl, listed from 8:45 to 11 p.m.
What you won’t find is a city Christmas light display. Creve Coeur doesn’t run one, so for lights you’ll be driving to another town. December here belongs to the ice: curling season is in full swing, and a night in the bleachers still costs nothing.
Next time somebody says there’s nothing in Creve Coeur but a lake that isn’t even in Creve Coeur, you’ll know better. You’ll know about the curlers on Saturday night, the lens-flipper sculpture on Country View Drive and the one night a month the bank stays open until 11. Take them with you.
For a meal before a morning skate or after a night of curling, start with St Louis Near Me Directory’s guide to where to eat in Creve Coeur.
If you run a business near the Dielmann complex on Olde Cabin Road, the skaters and curlers reading this are planning their Saturday right now, so list it with us where they’ll find it.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How many steps are at Creve Coeur Park?
A.  There are 220. The staircase starts across the road from the parking lot nearest Dripping Springs and climbs to the upper park, and locals use it as a free stair workout. KSDK profiled one of its regulars in 2022. Creve Coeur Park is a St. Louis County park just over the line in Maryland Heights.
### Q. How long is the trail around Creve Coeur Lake?
A.  The paved Lakeview Loop runs about 3.7 to 3.8 miles, depending on whose measurement you trust, and it’s flat enough for strollers and bikes. Plan on a little over an hour at an easy walk. If you want hills and dirt instead, Bootleggers Run in the same park is about 2.5 miles.
### Q. How deep is Creve Coeur Lake in Missouri?
A.  About 10 feet on average, and that depth is man-made. By the 1970s the lake averaged just 18 inches deep. A dredging project from 1974 to 1981 moved more than 4.6 million cubic yards of slurry, deepening it to about 10 feet and growing it from 220 to 320 acres. The sand it turned up became the 1,600 feet of beach along Marine Avenue.
### Q. Is it illegal to fish at night in Missouri?
A.  MDC’s statewide rules don’t ban it, and they spell out how you can use lights while you fish: above the water for any method, and underwater with pole and line. What usually stops you is the property’s hours. MDC lists Creve Coeur Park Lake as open from 8 a.m. to a half hour after sunset, which is why the County’s Late Night Fishing Saturdays matter. Check each area’s rules before you go.
### Q. How many rods are you allowed to fish with in Missouri?
A.  Three, unless you label the rest. MDC says anyone using more than three poles at a time must label the extra ones with a full name and address or Conservation Number. You also can’t use more than 33 hooks in total, or more than three hooks per pole. On the Mississippi River the numbers change to two unlabeled poles and 50 hooks.
### Q. Where is Creve Coeur, Missouri?
A.  In the middle of St. Louis County, along I-270 and Olive Boulevard, about 15 miles west of downtown St. Louis. The lake that shares its name is next door in Maryland Heights, which is why Creve Coeur Lake Memorial Park doesn’t have a Creve Coeur address. The city’s own six parks and its ice rink are all inside the line.
### Q. What can I do with my kids that’s free?
A.  In Creve Coeur, walk the wooded trails and rock creek at Malcolm Terrace Park, loop the pond at Conway Park, or spend an hour at Venable Park’s playgrounds and sculpture. Watching curling from the rink bleachers costs nothing. In summer there’s the free concert series and the Tappmeyer farmhouse, and at Spooky Skate (October 31 in 2026), costumed kids 13 and under skate free with a paying adult.
### Q. Is the Creve Coeur dog park free?
A.  No. The 2.5-acre fenced dog park at Conway Park is for registered members only. An annual membership is $30 for a resident’s first dog and $15 for each additional dog, or $80 and $25 for non-residents. You’ll need current rabies and Bordetella records plus spay or neuter paperwork. Memberships run through December 31, and fees paid after July 1 are cut in half.

## Things to Do in Fairview Heights, IL: Parks, a Lost Log Cabin, Adult Nights Out
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-fairview-heights-il
Gone since 2023, and the top-10 lists never noticed. The two-story Kinsella log cabin in Pleasant Ridge Park, the last structure left from a farm started by an Irish immigrant who fled the potato famine, came down when its 160-year-old logs finally gave out. The city recorded the loss on page 3 of a park master plan. Almost nobody else did.
That’s how Fairview Heights usually gets written up: as an exit sign. A mall, a food court, maybe a movie, then back across the river. Meanwhile the park the cabin stood in, 95 acres of woods, ravines and sledding hills just north of St. Clair Square, has been fenced off since March 23 for a rebuild the city said in October 2026 was coming that month. And here’s the part the lists skip entirely. Fairview Heights has no city property tax, so the dinner tab you run up near the mall is part of what’s paying for it.
So this guide leaves the mall alone. It goes where the recycled lists don’t: the one city park that stays open after dark, a lake you can look at but can’t fish, an indoor lazy river, a $10 Friday climbing night and a fall calendar most St. Louisans never hear about. Fairview Heights belongs on any short list of the small towns outside St. Louis that pay off for people who actually take the exit.
### What to do in Fairview Heights, IL for adults?
Skip the mall. Grown-ups climb The REC’s Clip ’N Climb walls, float its indoor lazy river on a day pass, race a 500-piece puzzle at the free library, walk Moody Park’s lake paths after dark (it’s the only city park open past sunset), and ride the city’s 21-and-over bus trips to tours, shows and holiday light displays.
None of that shows up in the usual write-up, which stops at the parking lot. Here’s how each piece works.
The REC, 9950 Bunkum Road. The city’s rec center sells day passes to anyone, $12 for resident adults and $17 for non-residents, and the pass includes an indoor lazy river you can float while it sleets outside. Climbing costs extra. Clip ’N Climb, which the city calls the area’s only Clip ’N Climb wall, runs $10 per 30 minutes for non-members ($5 for members), Fridays 4:30 to 7:30 p.m., Saturdays 10:30 to 4:30 and Sundays 11 to 3. Book online, because sessions fill. And wear closed-toe shoes or you won’t get into the arena.
The 21-and-over bus trips. This is the part almost nobody outside Fairview Heights knows about. Parks and Rec runs adults-only day trips that leave from The REC parking lot, and the fare covers the bus and the tickets. The 2026 Halloween Tour of Alton, set for Thursday, October 22 (9 a.m. to 4 p.m., $70 for members, $75 for non-members), starts at the American Oddities Museum, then boards a two-hour guided history tour packed with ghost stories, followed by food, games and music downtown. Registration closes a week before every trip, so for the 2026 Alton trip that’s October 15. December brings the Brewery Lights trip, which is down in the Christmas section.
The library, 10017 Bunkum Road. Every event at Fairview Heights Public Library is free. The 2026 Puzzle Race, set for Saturday, October 24, puts teams of two to four (ages 14 and up, at least one adult per team) against a 500-piece puzzle. The clock starts at 1 p.m. and stops at 3, or the moment the first team finishes. Mah Jongg players meet Tuesdays at 2, with a separate beginners’ table that takes registration. A Community Music Jam was set for October 20, 2026, from 4:30 to 6, and singers and listeners are welcome too. The evening book club meets the second Tuesday of the month at 6; the October 2026 banned-books pick is Kurt Vonnegut’s Slaughterhouse-Five.
Moody Park after dark. Every other city park closes at sunset. Moody Park, at 525 South Ruby Lane, stays open until 9 p.m. from October through April and until 10 p.m. from May through September, and that’s written into city code. In October, that buys you a couple of hours past sundown for a slow lap around Lake Mitchell after work.
Late August, the art comes to you. Midwest Salute to the Arts brings nearly 100 juried artists to Moody Park, with free admission and free parking. The 38th ran August 28 to 30, 2026.
Leaving the car at home? Fairview Heights Station is the eastern end of MetroLink’s Blue Line, and the Red Line from Lambert Airport stops there too.
### What parks are in Fairview Heights, IL?
Fairview Heights runs six city parks plus The REC complex: Moody Park, Pleasant Ridge Park, Old Lincoln Trail Park, French Village Park, Lexington Park and Fox Creek Mini Park. Moody is the big one and the only one open after sunset. Pleasant Ridge, the wooded one with the hiking trails, has been closed for a rebuild since March 23, 2026.
Here’s a loss the lists hand you without meaning to. Some of them still count Longacre Park and Moody Park as two separate stops. They’re the same 60 acres. Longacre Park was officially renamed Everett Moody Park in October 2007, after a former Fairview Heights mayor, with about 100 people on hand for the ceremony. If a list sends you to both, nobody has checked it in years.
Moody Park, 525 South Ruby Lane. The city’s park map packs a lot in: Lake Mitchell with walking paths around it, five pavilions (Pavilion 5 has a kitchen), two playgrounds, sand volleyball, pickleball and tennis courts, a football field, the North and George Lanxon baseball fields, a dog park and the Miracle League Field. That last one is home to the Miracle League of Fairview Heights, which plays baseball for children and adults with disabilities. Most city events land at Moody, from an October pumpkin carving night to the August art fair. Pavilions rent April through October. The rest of the year they’re first come, first served.
Old Lincoln Trail Park, 9820 Old Lincoln Trail. A neighborhood park with a playground, restrooms, pavilions and a gazebo, and leashed dogs are welcome. With Pleasant Ridge closed, it’s one of only two parks taking pavilion rentals this season. Moody is the other.
French Village Park, 1725 Sycamore. Playground, restrooms, picnic tables and its own dog park, which matters more than usual right now.
Lexington Park (1 Richmond Drive) and Fox Creek Mini Park (823 Columbia Avenue). Small neighborhood playgrounds, both pet friendly on a leash. You walk to these. You don’t drive to them.
Which park for what? For an evening walk after work, Moody, since nothing else is open past sunset. For a party pavilion this season, Moody or Old Lincoln Trail. For an off-leash dog, Moody’s dog park or French Village. For a real woods hike, Pleasant Ridge, once it reopens. For a lake you can actually fish, leave town for Frank Holten (details below).
A few rules catch visitors off guard. Every park except Moody opens at 7 a.m. and closes at sunset, and playgrounds don’t open until 8. Animals aren’t allowed in pavilions or on playgrounds. And renting a pavilion doesn’t let you bring a DJ, a band or a bounce house. For the shops and services around all of this, keep our Fairview Heights city guide handy.
### What happened to Pleasant Ridge Park, and when does it reopen?
Pleasant Ridge Park, at 401 Pleasant Ridge Road, closed on March 23, 2026, for a full rebuild. The city’s page for it still reads “Coming October 2026,” with no exact reopening date announced as of early October. The other change got far less attention. The park’s log cabin, the last structure left from the family farm the park was carved out of, was demolished in 2023.
The story sits in the city’s Pleasant Ridge Park Master Plan, dated March 4, 2024. William Kinsella left Ireland in the 1840s, during the potato famine, and settled in Caseyville Township. He was working nearby for the B&O Railroad when he fell for this land, bought it and named it Pleasant Ridge for its views and its hills. Kinsellas lived and farmed here from the 1860s on, generation after generation. One photo in the plan shows the family gathered in front of the cabin in 1945 to welcome Cy Kinsella home on leave from the war.
The city bought 95 acres of the farm in 1973 to keep it as a nature park. In 1976 it rebuilt the cabin to stretch the life of the last building left on the farm. That bought decades, not forever. By 2023, the plan says, the original logs, more than 160 years old, had deteriorated enough that the cabin had to come down for public safety. The plan calls for a commemorative plaza marking where it stood, with interpretive signs about the Kinsella farm, the early settlers and the Native Americans who lived here first, plus a barn-style event pavilion next to it. That’s the long-range plan, though. Nobody has confirmed the plaza is part of this year’s build, so look for it when you go.
Here’s what is confirmed for 2026. The Belleville News-Democrat reported three new restrooms, including one open all season, three new pavilions and an updated playground. The city’s own project page adds expanded dog run areas and new walking paths. Then there’s who pays. The Pleasant Ridge rebuild and The REC’s new Field House together cost about $14 million, paid with bonds and the city’s food and beverage tax. Mayor Mark Kupsky told KMOV in February that “we do not have a city property tax,” so the city funds everything through retail sales and food and beverage taxes. Every dinner check near St. Clair Square chips in.
Why it’s worth the wait: the master plan calls these trails the only natural hiking trails in the Fairview Heights park system. Picture roughly a mile of rough dirt path dropping through ravines, over log footbridges and along a creek. The valley is a popular sledding spot too, with families parking on both sides and riding down either one. A nearby homeowner who usually trail-runs there told KMOV he’d spent a cold February morning skiing it, weeks before the fences went up. And its open field is the city’s designated off-leash dog area, which the plan calls the only large area in town where dogs can run freely.
It’s due back in October 2026. Check the city’s parks page or its Facebook before you go, because construction dates slide.
### Can you fish in Fairview Heights?
Not on your own, and that surprises people. Lake Mitchell in Moody Park looks made for a lawn chair and a bobber, but city code bans fishing in any park waterway without the Parks Director’s permission. The same code bans boating and walking or skating on the ice. For a legal line in the water, drive to Frank Holten State Recreation Area in East St. Louis.
The city does open Lake Mitchell a couple of times a year, and it’s for kids. Family Fishing Day lands during Illinois Free Fishing Days, the long weekend each June when the state waives the license requirement (2026’s ran June 19 to 22). The most recent one the city lists ran June 14, 2025, for ages 5 to 13, free for residents and catch-and-release only. The city’s own listing calls it a rare opportunity. It isn’t exaggerating. Each September there’s also a Kids’ Fishing Rodeo for resident children 5 to 13 (it cost $10 in 2024). Watch the Parks and Rec calendar in late spring for both.
Grown-ups go to Frank Holten. The Illinois Department of Natural Resources site has two lakes, Whispering Willow and Grand Marais, with 208 acres of water and 5 miles of shoreline between them. Whispering Willow was rehabilitated in 1983 and stocked with largemouth bass, bluegill and channel catfish. You can fish from the bank or a boat, as long as the motor is a trolling motor or 10 horsepower or less. On the east side there’s a covered, ADA-accessible fishing pier about 90 feet from paved parking, with an accessible restroom nearby. An Illinois fishing license applies outside Free Fishing Days, and some species carry creel and length limits, so check with the site office first. The park’s 18-hole Grand Marais Golf Course is right there if half your group doesn’t fish.
Want more bank spots farther north? Our Edwardsville guide covers fishing in Edwardsville without a boat.
Lake Mitchell won’t feed you. Where to eat in Fairview Heights
### Where are the dog parks in Fairview Heights?
Fairview Heights has two dog parks open right now: the one inside Moody Park at 525 South Ruby Lane and the one at French Village Park, 1725 Sycamore. Two more are off the table for the moment. Pleasant Ridge’s off-leash area is closed along with the rest of that park, and The REC’s dog park is shut while the Field House goes up.
Moody’s comes with a catch. Under city code, dogs are allowed in Moody Park’s dog park area only and banned everywhere else in the park, service dogs excepted. So you can’t walk your dog around Lake Mitchell and then let it loose. Park, head straight to the dog area, and save the lake loop for a day without the leash.
French Village is the quieter pick, a neighborhood park with a playground, restrooms and its own dog area. Outside that area, dogs stay on a leash.
The big one is coming back. Pleasant Ridge’s off-leash field is, in the master plan’s words, the only large area in the city where dogs can run freely, and the 2026 rebuild expands the dog run areas. The plan even sketched a small parking lot, restroom and shade pavilion just for dog owners, so nobody has to walk a loose dog past the playground. Whether that piece made this phase, you’ll see when it opens.
The same rules apply in every park. County registration and vaccination tags on the collar. No more than three dogs per handler. No dogs within 20 feet of any playground. No tying a dog to a tree, a bush or a shelter. Pick up after it. For off-leash options across the rest of the region, see our guide to the best dog parks in St. Louis.
### What can you do indoors in Fairview Heights on a rainy day?
Head to The REC at 9950 Bunkum Road. Its indoor Aquatic Center has a 4-lane zero-depth pool, a two-story waterslide, a splash pad, a vortex and a lazy river, and Clip ’N Climb runs Friday through Sunday. A short way up Bunkum Road, every program at the public library is free. Between the two, a wet Saturday costs very little.
Pool hours run 7 a.m. to 7:30 p.m. on weekdays, 7 to 4:30 on Saturday and 10 to 3:30 on Sunday. Day passes are $8 for resident kids and $12 for non-resident kids, and $35 or $42 for a family of two adults and three kids. One rule trips up visitors. Non-members under 18 need an adult 21 or older with them for the entire visit, or the desk won’t sell the pass. At Clip ’N Climb, climbers have to be at least 3 years old and between 25 and 300 pounds, and anyone under 13 needs an adult along.
The real money-saver is Family Fun Night. On select Fridays from 4 to 7:30 p.m., $10 for non-members ($5 for members) buys unlimited Clip ’N Climb, bounce houses, Nerf games and pool access. Do the math. On a normal Friday, that same $10 buys 30 minutes on the walls. Its late-2026 dates: October 9, November 13 and December 11, then January 8, 2027.
At the library, the free calendar leans young on weekday mornings: Fall Storytime on Wednesdays at 10:30, a sensory playgroup for ages 0 to 4, and a music-and-movement hour called Sing & Stomp. Teens get Dungeons & Dragons on Monday evenings, and the October 2026 calendar added Frankenstein’s Toy Box on the 12th, where they build creepy creatures out of spare toy parts. Kids who’d rather bounce than read have Urban Air down the road, which our roundup of indoor play places for kids in St. Louis already covers.
### What is there to do in Fairview Heights with kids this fall?
Plenty, and most of it is free or close to it. The city and the library pack October with a cryptid hunt, a pumpkin carving night and a costume parade around a running track, and November brings a drive-in movie where the kids build the cars. Here are the dates.
Cryptid Hunt, Saturday, October 10, 2026. Drop by Moody Park anytime from 9:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. and hunt down the cryptids the library has hidden around the park. Find them all for a small prize. Free.
Pumpkin Glow, Wednesday, October 14, 2026. From 5 to 7 p.m. at Moody Park’s Pavilion 5. The city supplies the pumpkins, stencils and carving tools and does the cleanup, which might be the best part. Early registration closed October 1, 2026, and after that it’s $15 a pumpkin instead of $10.
Track of Treats, Friday, October 16, 2026. Kids 12 and under come in costume and parade around The REC’s outdoor track from 5 to 6:30 p.m., collecting candy from booths run by local businesses and groups. It’s free, it drew more than 500 guests in 2025, and Clip ’N Climb and the bounce houses stay open late afterward.
Kid’s Drive-In Experience, Saturday, November 14, 2026. This one’s clever. Each child, ages 4 to 10, gets a big cardboard box to turn into a car with paint and stickers, then watches a movie from inside it with a snack pack of popcorn, juice and a treat. It’s a drop-off program from 1 to 5 p.m. in The REC’s Holland Room, $35 for members and $55 for non-members, which means four free hours for the grown-ups. If the kids fall for it, the full-size version is a short drive south: Belleville’s Skyview Drive-In reopens each spring. Reading this after November 14? Check The REC for next fall’s lineup.
Year-round at Moody Park. The Miracle League Field gives children and adults with disabilities a real ballfield of their own, and the city runs a fall Tee Ball Clinic there for ages 4 to 7 ($50 for members, $60 for non-members). Check the city calendar for the next session.
### Where can you see Christmas lights in Fairview Heights?
In town, the 2026 season starts Saturday, November 7, when the city lights its tree at 5:45 p.m. at the Market Place Roundabout. 2026 marks only the second year of the tradition. For the big displays, the city puts you on a bus: The REC’s Family Light Tour (December 4 in 2026) and a 21-and-over Brewery Lights trip (December 11).
The tree lighting caps a 3 to 7 p.m. kickoff with bounce houses, crafts, library story time, food trucks, vendors and music from school bands and church choirs. It’s free. The 2026 holiday parade is set for Wednesday, November 18, at 6 p.m. The route hadn’t been posted in early October 2026, so check the city’s holiday page closer to the date. All season, giant walk-in snow globes pop up at businesses around town as photo spots. Step inside, take the picture, go find the next one. Reading this after the holidays? Check the city’s holiday page for next year’s dates.
Family Light Tour, Friday, December 4, 2026. The bus leaves The REC lot at 5 p.m. and gets back around 10 after three stops: the Shrine of Our Lady of the Snows, Candy Cane Lane and Tilles Park. It’s $45 for one, $90 for two, $120 for three and $160 for four, plus $40 for each extra person. You have to register at least a week ahead. Nobody in the family has to drive, and nobody has to fight for a parking spot at the Shrine.
Brewery Lights, Friday, December 11, 2026, ages 21 and up. From 5 to 11 p.m., the bus takes adults to see the Clydesdales and the Brewery Lights displays, with live singers and samples, then on to St. Charles for an evening of holiday shopping, dinner and drinks. It’s $60 for residents and $65 for non-residents, with transportation and Brewery Lights tickets included. If you’d rather plan that night on your own, start with our guide to Christmas lights in St. Charles.
Next time somebody says there’s nothing in Fairview Heights but a mall, you’ll know better. You’ll know about the cabin that isn’t there anymore, the lake nobody’s allowed to fish and the one park that stays open after dark. Pick one thing this month. Then, when the Pleasant Ridge gates open, be the one who walks that creek trail first and knows what used to stand beside the park road.
Before the climbing wall, the lazy river or the light tour, line up dinner with St Louis Near Me Directory’s guide to where to eat in Fairview Heights.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Where to bring your dog for a walk?
A.  In Fairview Heights, take a leashed dog to Old Lincoln Trail Park, Lexington Park or Fox Creek Mini Park, all listed by the city as pet friendly. Skip Moody Park for a walk, since dogs are banned there outside the dog park. Keep dogs out of pavilions and 20 feet from playgrounds, and don’t bring more than three at once.
### Q. Is it illegal to not pick up dog poop in Illinois?
A.  In Fairview Heights parks, yes. City code requires owners and handlers to clean up after their animals and either drop it in a proper trash can or carry it out of the park, and violations get reported to the authorities. Other Illinois towns and parks post their own rules, so read the sign at the entrance.
### Q. What are some free activities I can do in Illinois?
A.  In Fairview Heights alone: every program at the public library, the library’s Cryptid Hunt at Moody Park, the Track of Treats costume parade, the November tree lighting (November 7 in 2026) and the Midwest Salute to the Arts each August. During Illinois Free Fishing Days in June, you can fish without a license anywhere in the state, Frank Holten included.
### Q. Where to catch catfish in Illinois?
A.  The closest public answer to Fairview Heights is Whispering Willow Lake at Frank Holten State Recreation Area in East St. Louis, which the state stocked with channel catfish, largemouth bass and bluegill after rehabilitating it in 1983. Fish from the bank or from the covered ADA pier on the east side. Bring an Illinois fishing license and check the site’s limits.
### Q. What are the best months to fish in Illinois?
A.  Locally, June and September, because those are the only times Fairview Heights opens Lake Mitchell, for Family Fishing Day and the Kids’ Fishing Rodeo. Statewide, fall trout season opens at 5 a.m. on the third Saturday of October (October 17 in 2026) at 60 stocked ponds, lakes and streams, with a daily limit of five trout. Check the state’s list for sites.
### Q. What are some fun places to visit in Illinois with kids?
A.  Start with The REC in Fairview Heights for the indoor lazy river, the waterslide and the Clip ’N Climb walls, then Moody Park for its two playgrounds and the Miracle League Field. Once Pleasant Ridge Park reopens, its creek trail and sledding hills make the best free outdoor afternoon in town. Family Fun Nights bundle most of The REC for $10.
### Q. Why is Moody Park called Moody Park?
A.  It’s named for Everett Moody, a former mayor of Fairview Heights. The 60-acre park was Longacre Park until October 2007, when the city officially renamed it at a ceremony about 100 people attended. That’s why some older lists still send you to Longacre and Moody as if they were two parks. They’re one.
### Q. Can non-members use The REC’s pool and climbing wall?
A.  Yes. A day pass covers the indoor Aquatic Center: $12 for resident adults and $17 for non-residents, $8 or $12 for kids, and $35 or $42 for a family. Non-members under 18 need an adult 21 or older on site for the whole visit. Clip ’N Climb is priced separately, at $10 per 30 minutes for non-members, so book it online ahead of time.

## Things to Do in Festus, MO: Crites Park Light Shows, Night Fishing and the Twin City Parade
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-festus-mo
Why is there a Festus at all? The recycled top-ten lists never stop to ask. They give you a historic downtown, a big city park and a drive time, then move on to the next town. The real answer sits on the Twin City Area Chamber of Commerce’s own history page, and it beats anything on those lists. After 1877, Crystal Plate Glass Company held complete control over the land and buildings of Crystal City. It allowed no saloons, no homes for people who didn’t work for the company and no private businesses of any kind. So a second settlement grew up just past the line. People called it Limitsville. Then Tanglefoot.
When the new town wanted a more dignified name, the story goes that a local businesswoman named Elizabeth Posch opened her Bible and promised to take the first proper name she came to. Acts 25:1. Festus. The city incorporated on February 8, 1887, and that’s why two towns sit where you’d expect one, sharing a chamber of commerce, a Christmas parade and a nickname: the Twin City.
Here’s the part that matters this month. On Sunday, October 4, a free Halloween light show opened in Crites Park, synced to music you pick up on your car radio, and it runs every evening through Halloween night. You won’t find it on the recycled lists. That’s Festus in a sentence: the good stuff is local knowledge.
So this is the other list, for the person who has done the Arch twice and wants the spot nobody else at work has heard of. Festus is one of the small towns outside St. Louis that pays you back for knowing where to park.
### Where is Crites Park in Festus, Missouri?
Crites Park is the old West City Park, renamed Larry G. Crites Memorial Park, on the west edge of Festus along Joachim Creek, about a mile off I-55. Its 100-plus acres hold Al Brown Lake, where city code allows fishing around the clock, a 20-hole disc golf course, a 1.5-mile bike trail and the free Lenhard Family light shows.
The name trips up almost everyone, Google included. The city renamed West City Park as Larry G. Crites Memorial Park, and locals now just say Crites. Search either name and Google Maps can hand you two separate places, one called West City Park and one called Crites Park. Tripadvisor still lists it as West City Park. So does the city’s own fishing ordinance, and so does the web address of the city’s park page. It’s one park. Same lake, same ball fields, same light shows.
For directions, the city lists 2221 Sunshine Drive. Local light-show coverage gives the location as Old Highway A instead, since the park runs along it. Inside, it spreads past 100 acres, bordered on the east by Joachim Creek, with a three-acre lake, a fairgrounds area, a long list of numbered pavilions, a big ball field complex, Mayor Mike’s Stage and a 1.5-mile bicycle trail.
The disc golf course is no beginner loop. UDisc rates its 20 holes “Very hard,” with water in play on half of them, about 2.4 miles of walking and an estimated round of 2 hours 22 minutes. It opened in 2007, it’s free, and dogs are allowed. One of its five layouts is named Flood Bypass. Players were still logging rounds there on October 4. If you’d rather not feed discs to a pond, Jokerst Memorial Park at 525 South Mill Street has a shorter nine-hole course plus six regulation pickleball courts under mature oaks.
Then there’s the barn. Stand on the bank of Al Brown Lake and you’re looking at a red dairy barn the Peterein family built in 1932, back when this patch of ground was known as Silica, Missouri. They shipped their milk to St. Louis on the railroad a few steps away, and when the work was done, barn dances filled the hayloft. The city bought the land in 1981 and used the barn for parks storage for years. In 2024 it was restored with federal American Rescue Plan Act money, and the work won a Preserve Missouri Award. It’s a rental hall now, not a walk-in museum, so enjoy it from the shore. You’ve probably seen it without knowing. It’s the barn that keeps turning up in Firecracker Festival fireworks photos.
One practical note. Festus city parks are open dawn to dusk under city code, with exceptions for events, lighted courts and fishing. Crites happens to hold the two best exceptions in town: the light shows and the fishing rule, both below.
### Is there a Halloween light show in Festus?
Yes, and it’s free. The Lenhard Family Light Show, Halloween Edition, takes over the stage field at Crites Park every October. The 2026 run opened Sunday, October 4, according to the family’s Facebook page, and it plays on a continuous loop from 7:30 to 10 p.m. through Halloween night. The city’s event page still calls this year’s schedule tentative, so check the Lenhard Family Light Show page on Facebook before you drive down, especially if storms are in the forecast.
Getting in is easy once you know the drill. Enter the field at the top of the hill, to the right of the stage. Park on the stage field or back in against the trees to the right of the road, and keep the road itself clear. Tune to 99.7 FM. When you’re done, leave from the far end of the field, where orange traffic cones mark the exit.
The scale is the surprise. The city puts it at about 120,000 pixel lights, each able to produce more than 16 million colors, strung on 2 miles of cable and run by 19 computers. Twelve 350-watt spotlights can be seen for miles when the air is clear. Two 30-foot cones carry 5,000 lights apiece. Every song takes 40 to 60 hours to program, and while the city’s page counts 17 songs, the family’s own posts list 18 for 2026. The city describes the whole thing as one family’s hobby, given to the town as a gift.
Two tips. It’s most crowded right when it opens, so the city suggests coming later in the evening. And bring a few dollars even though it’s free, because donations go to the Jefferson County Rescue Mission.
When the cones come down, the park has one more fall night. Camp Crites is the city’s once-a-year chance to camp in the park. The 2026 date: Saturday, November 7, starting at 4:30 p.m. The Festus Fire Department tends the bonfire, the parks crew runs hayrides, yard-sized games come out, and there may be family-friendly ghost stories. Bring sticks, s’mores supplies, a cooler and lawn chairs. For the rest of the season, our roundup of Halloween events around St. Louis picks up where Festus leaves off.
### What’s going on in Festus, Missouri this weekend?
That depends on the weekend, but Festus runs on a calendar that barely moves from year to year. Learn the rhythm once and you won’t need an events feed. Here’s what’s left in 2026, in order:
Saturday, October 10, 2026: Main & Mill Streetfest. The organizers call it OktoberFestus: live music, food and drinks on Festus Main Street from 11 a.m. to 11 p.m., all ages. The event listing also mentions October 12 and a 1 p.m. start, so confirm on the Twin City events calendar first.
Every evening through October 31, 2026: the Lenhard Halloween light show at Crites Park, 7:30 to 10 p.m.
Saturday, November 7, 2026: Camp Crites from 4:30 p.m. in the park, and Ladies Night on Main Street from 2 to 8 p.m.
Saturday, November 28, 2026: the Stocking Stroll on Main Street at 2 p.m.
The Monday after Thanksgiving (November 30 in 2026): the 77th Christmas Parade at 7 p.m. The details are in the Christmas section below.
Saturday, December 5, 2026: WinterFest on West Main.
Saturday, February 6, 2027: the third annual Mardi Gras Parade, at noon on Festus Main Street.
And here’s the rest of the year, so you can plan ahead:
Mother’s Day: Swingin’ Under the Stars. A free big-band night with the Missouri Big Band. The next one is Sunday, May 9, 2027.
Summer Saturdays at dusk: Movies Under the Stars on the main stage at Crites.
Late June: the Twin City Firecracker Festival. The 37th ran June 26 and 27, 2026, with a patriotic drone show Friday, fireworks Saturday and Pam Tillis headlining.
The weekend after Labor Day: Twin City Days. It ran September 10 to 12 in 2026.
Late September: the George Portz Traditional Music Festival at Crites. The 36th was September 26, 2026, at $12 a ticket, with kids 10 and under free and primitive camping at $10 a night.
September Sundays: Sundays at Sunset. Free concerts from 6 to 8 p.m. in Sunset Park. The 2026 series ended on October 4 with the Funky Butt Brass Band and should return next September.
Early fall: the Four Brothers Mead Viking Festival on East Main, free and all ages. It fell on October 3 this year.
Sunset Park is worth a walk on any weekend, concert or not. It sits near City Hall at 816 Parkview Drive, under soft maples and white oaks the city puts at 100 years old, and its wooded bird sanctuary is crossed by a stone arch bridge the city calls ever popular. Bring lawn chairs and a cooler for the concerts. The covered bandstand is where Sundays at Sunset happens, and the park is open 7 a.m. to 11 p.m.
### Where can you see Christmas lights in Festus?
Back at Crites Park. The Lenhard show returns as its Christmas Edition, with two 30-foot Christmas trees in place of the Halloween cones and a 6 to 10 p.m. loop on 99.7 FM. When we checked, the city hadn’t set the 2026 dates, so the 2025 run is your best guide. The 2025 show opened on Thanksgiving night, ran November 27 to 30, took a few days off, then came back December 5 through 31. Justin Lenhard told the Jefferson County Leader it carried more than 163,000 lights matched to music. The family also added a lighted entrance sign, bought partly with a Festus Tourism grant, because people from out of town kept driving right past the turn. It’s free, and donations again go to the Jefferson County Rescue Mission.
The parade is the best way to see the whole Twin City story in one evening. The Twin City Area Chamber of Commerce Christmas Parade steps off at 7 p.m. on the Monday after Thanksgiving. The 2026 parade, the 77th, falls on Monday, November 30. It starts at North Taylor and Bailey Road in Crystal City, heads to Festus Main Street and finishes on West Main in front of the Festus Library. The company town and the town that grew up outside its rules, in one parade. The 2026 theme is “Christmas Along Route 66,” for the highway’s 100th anniversary. Reading this after November 30? Check with the Twin City Area Chamber of Commerce for next year’s parade details.
Two rules are worth knowing before the kids line the curb. Nobody in the parade may hand out candy, an insurance rule, so don’t promise a haul. And the chamber allows exactly one Santa in the whole parade, its own, so little kids never spot two.
After the parade, December mostly happens on Main Street:
Santa’s House, at the corner of Main and Mill. Visits are free, and you take your own pictures, since there’s no photographer. Well-behaved, leashed pets are welcome. Bring canned food for the Ozark Food Pantry. Santa’s 2026 hours: Tuesday through Friday, December 8 to 11 and 15 to 18, from 6 to 8 p.m., plus Saturdays, December 12 and 19, from noon to 5.
WinterFest, Saturday, December 5, 2026. Breakfast with Santa runs 8 to 10:30 a.m. at First United Methodist Church for a freewill offering. Then craft and food vendors fill West Main and the library parking lot from 10 to 4, with a petting zoo, pony rides and inflatables until 5. The decorated cookie challenge pays $50 in each of three age groups: 13 and under, 14 to 17, and 18 and over.
Fridays in December. Santa reads kids’ letters on the city’s YouTube channel.
Building a whole December out of small-town Christmas? Pair a night at the Festus lights with the Kimmswick Cookie Walk and Christmas Festival on another day, a short drive north on I-55.
### Where can you fish in Festus, MO?
Start with the fish that made the news. On March 19, 2024, George Chance of Festus was bank fishing for catfish on the Mississippi at a spot he visits often, south of town between the Ameren plant and the Holcim plant. Whatever took the bait needed a while to bring in. It was a 97-pound bighead carp, landed from the bank on pole and line. The Missouri Department of Conservation lists it as the state record, and news reports said it topped the world-record weight for the species. Chance took it home, chopped it up and fertilized his tomatoes and cucumbers with it. Bighead carp are invasive, and MDC encourages anglers to harvest them.
You don’t need the big river, though. The ponds at Crites Park come with a rule most anglers never hear about: city code allows fishing there 24 hours a day, as long as you park in the designated spaces outside the park gates. The rest of the rules are short.
A Missouri fishing license is required.
Rod and reel only, and no minnows for bait.
Daily limits: 3 bass with a 15-inch minimum, 5 catfish, 10 fish total.
No wading, swimming, boats or ice skating, and no private stocking.
Al Brown Lake is the one in front of the red barn, and the barn’s deck looks out over the North Lake. Once a year the kids get first crack at it. On Firecracker Festival Saturday the city runs a free Kids’ Hooked on Fishing Derby at Al Brown Lake from 8 to 10 a.m., then a Seniors’ Fishing Derby from 10 to noon, both with attendance prizes.
For the Mississippi without a boat, drive south from Crystal City on Highway 61 about 6.8 miles, turn east on Route AA, then follow Big Hollow Road across the railroad tracks to the river. That’s Truman Access, 19.8 acres run by MDC, with bank fishing on the Mississippi and walk-in access to Harlow Island, part of the Middle Mississippi River National Wildlife Refuge. MDC lists white bass, catfish, crappie, black bass and sunfish. The area is open 4 a.m. to 10 p.m., fishing is allowed around the clock, and leashed pets are fine. Camping isn’t. The boat ramp is still closed from flood damage, though the parking lot has reopened, and MDC treats the whole access as closed when water, heavy mud or flood debris covers the road. After a river rise, check before you go.
Fishing your way up I-55? Fishing in Arnold adds an 8-acre city lake and a ramp onto the Meramec, and our guide to the best fishing spots in St. Louis covers the rest of the metro.
### What can you do in Festus at night?
There’s a nice irony in where Festus spends its evenings now. The town that started life just outside a saloon ban keeps three good night stops within about 140 street numbers of East Main.
Boxed In Escape Rooms, 102 East Main, locks your group in a themed room for 60 minutes of puzzles, and every room is booked privately. Its last bookings run as late as 10:30 p.m. on Fridays and Saturdays. Four Brothers Mead, 124 East Main, is a veteran-owned meadery started by four brothers, who make their mead with raw, unpasteurized local honey and no sulfites. The tasting room is open Thursday and Friday 4 to 9, Saturday noon to 9 and Sunday noon to 5. Main & Mill Brewing, 240 East Main, opened on October 15, 2015, after three years of renovation. It’s the beer stop on the walk. Hours at all three shift, so check before you go.
Dinner first? Here’s where to eat in Festus before the East Main walk.
Just over the line in Crystal City, Quonset Lanes at 2004 North Truman Boulevard runs Cosmic Bowling every Friday night, in a 7 to 9 p.m. session, a 9:30 to 11:30 session, or the full 7 to 11:30 stretch. On a rainy night, B&B Theatres Festus 8 at 1522 Parkway West has heated luxury recliners, RealD 3D and a full-service Marquee Bar, so the drink and the movie happen in one building.
And don’t forget Crites after dark. In October and December the light shows run until 10. The rest of the year, the park’s ponds stay open to anglers all night, as long as you leave the car in the designated spaces outside the gates. Bring a headlamp.
### What is there to do in Crystal City?
Start by knowing what you’re standing on. Crystal City was founded to make glass. In 1868 a mineralogist found high-grade silica sand near the mouth of Plattin Creek, and Captain Ebenezer B. Ward started the American Plate Glass Company in a river town he named New Detroit. Crystal Plate Glass of St. Louis bought the plant in 1877, the town became Crystal City as its glass reputation spread, and in 1895 Pittsburgh Plate Glass, later PPG Industries, bought the factory, the town and everything in it. The city says its Crystal City Works Nine became the largest plate glass plant in the world. It stayed a company town until 1906, when PPG began selling lots to private citizens.
The ending is quieter. The last plate glass was made in Crystal City in 1972. On the Monday after Christmas 1991, Union Electric shut off the power to Works Nine for good. Today the only pieces of the plant still standing are the company headquarters building and the hospital, both put to other uses.
To see what that era looked like, time a visit for the first Sunday of the month. The Crystal City Historical Society runs a small museum of artifacts in the old Girl Scout House just south of the Crystal City football field, open noon to 4 p.m. that day, with exceptions for holidays. The last two open Sundays of 2026 are November 1 and December 6. Check the society’s Facebook page in case a holiday moves one.
Quonset Lanes sits on this side of the line too, and the Christmas parade starts here before it crosses into Festus. One thing to skip: the old advice to tour the Crystal City Underground. The FAQ below explains why.
### What’s near Festus for a longer day?
Go just north first. In Herculaneum, at Shot Tower Park, 345 Dunklin Drive, a marker points to the cliff where the first shot tower west of Pittsburgh went up in 1809.
