Shot made by dropping molten lead from that tower, along with bullets molded from lead smelted nearby, went to American troops in the War of 1812, including the Battle of New Orleans on January 8, 1815. It’s a free stop and takes about as long as reading the plaque.
Heading home, Mastodon State Historic Site and Arnold sit up I-55, and Kimmswick’s river village is just off the highway. Heading the other way, the old French colonial town is down I-55, and our guide to things to do in Ste. Genevieve picks up the thread.
Next time somebody tells you there’s nothing to do in Festus, you’ll be the one who knows the town exists because of a saloon ban, that the city lake stays open to anglers all night, and that the best seat for the light show is your own car with the radio on 99.7. Pick a night this month and go.
Making a night of the Halloween light show or the Streetfest? Check where to eat in Festus on St Louis Near Me Directory first, so dinner on Main Street is settled before the lights come on.
And if you run a shop along the parade route between Crystal City and the Festus Library, the people planning their Twin City Christmas are searching right now, so list your business with us where they’ll find you.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is there to do in Festus, MO?
A.  Start at Crites Park, the renamed West City Park, for the free Lenhard light shows in October and December, a 20-hole disc golf course and city ponds you can fish around the clock if you park outside the gates. Then walk East Main for an escape room, a veteran-owned meadery and a brewery. Add Friday cosmic bowling or the Christmas parade, depending on the season.
### Q. What is Festus, Missouri known for?
A.  Being half of the Twin City with Crystal City, and an unusual origin. The glass company that owned Crystal City banned saloons and private businesses, so a settlement grew up just outside it, first called Limitsville, then Tanglefoot, and finally Festus, a name a local businesswoman is said to have found in her Bible. Today it’s known for the Firecracker Festival and the Lenhard light shows.
### Q. Is there a Viking Festival in Festus, Missouri?
A.  Yes. Four Brothers Mead, a veteran-owned meadery at 124 East Main Street, holds a free, all-ages Viking Festival each fall. The 2026 edition was Saturday, October 3, from noon to 9 p.m., with steel-weapon combat demonstrations, shield-wall tactics and an artisan market. The meadery has also hosted a spring Viking festival. Check its website for 2027 dates.
### Q. Why is Crystal City, Missouri called Crystal City?
A.  Because of glass. The town was founded to make plate glass after silica sand turned up near the mouth of Plattin Creek in 1868, and it was first called New Detroit. As the glassworks grew and its reputation spread, the name changed to Crystal City. Its PPG plant, Works Nine, became the largest plate glass plant in the world, according to the city.
### Q. Where is Crystal City in Missouri?
A.  In Jefferson County, on the Mississippi River, about 27 miles south of St. Louis by the city’s own count. It runs directly into Festus, so you can cross from one town into the other without noticing, which is why locals call them the Twin City. Most people reach both from I-55 or Highway 61.
### Q. What cities are near Festus, MO?
A.  Crystal City shares its border. Herculaneum is just north, and De Soto and Hillsboro lie to the west. Up I-55 you’ll pass Kimmswick, Imperial and Arnold on the way back to St. Louis, and Ste. Genevieve is the natural next stop if you keep driving south.
### Q. Is the Crystal City Underground open?
A.  No, not for regular visits. As of early October 2026, its own website says it has been closed by flooding, that no reopening date is set and that it’s open for special events only. The Marsan Kayak and Canoe outfitter listed on its site is closed too. Older lists still tell you to tour it, so don’t plan a trip around it until the owners announce a reopening.
### Q. Can you fish at night at Crites Park in Festus?
A.  Yes. Festus city code allows fishing at the park’s ponds 24 hours a day, as long as you park in the designated spaces outside the park gates. You’ll need a Missouri fishing license, it’s rod and reel only, and minnows aren’t allowed as bait. The limit is 3 bass of at least 15 inches, 5 catfish and 10 fish total.

## Things to Do in St. Peters, MO: Kayak Dardenne Creek, Free Light Shows, 370 Lakeside Fishing
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-st-peters-mo
Here’s the secret every recycled top-10 list for St. Peters leaves out. From a lake park off Highway 370, you can slide a kayak into Dardenne Creek and follow a mile-marked county water trail toward the Mississippi River. The lists don’t mention it. They send you to Mid Rivers Mall, wave at the rec center and move on to the next town.
Locals know better. They know the 140-acre lake at 370 Lakeside Park didn’t exist until a grading crew dug 6 million cubic yards of dirt out of the ground in 12 months. They know which St. Peters home turns into a free light show twice a year, synced to a radio station. They know the dog park by the lake has its own platform so dogs can wade in. And they know the Rec-Plex pool was built in 1994 to host the U.S. Olympic Festival’s aquatic events.
So this is the St. Peters for people who have already done the Arch and the Zoo and are tired of the same five weekend plans. Every fee, date and rule below was checked against city and county sources in October 2026. If you’re working through our guide to the small towns outside St. Louis worth a day, this is the one most people drive past on I-70.
### What can you do for fun with no money in St. Peters?
Plenty, and none of it is the mall. Walk the 5.5-mile trail around 370 Lakeside Park’s 140-acre lake, browse the Cultural Arts Centre galleries at City Hall, let kids loose at Ollie’s Fun Forest, and park for Hidden Lake Lights, a free synchronized show on 90.1 FM with a Halloween run and a Christmas run (2026 opening nights: Oct. 10 and Nov. 28).
Start with the lake loop. The city lists a 5.5-mile walking trail around the lake at 370 Lakeside Park, 1000 Lakeside Park Drive, and the park is open from sunrise to sunset. Walking in costs nothing. The city charges for the extras, like fishing and boating passes, archery, rentals, camping and the dog park. Go late in the day. The park sells itself on its sunsets over the water, and that’s fair.
Then cross town to City Centre Park, 101 City Centre Park Drive off Mexico Road. Ollie’s Fun Forest, which the city built in 2022, is a fully inclusive, ADA-compliant playground with wide ramps, shaded seating at each play area, calm corners next to the loud ones, and permanent fencing around the whole thing. Parents notice the restroom: there’s a separate family room with an adult-size changing table. Behind the playground, a Sensory Trail is built for people of all abilities.
The same park holds the Judy Bateman Arboretum, five acres of City Centre Park’s 78 planted with dozens of native tree species. It has earned Level 1 accreditation from ArbNet, the arboretum accrediting program. Bring the kid who asks what kind of tree that is. The city posts a map of the arboretum online.
For a story the brochures skip, drive to 141 Gatty Drive, across from Olde Towne Park, the city’s original park and more than 100 years old. The two-story log cabin there was built by Jacob Sattler around 1835 near Belleau Creek Road. In 1995, it was about to be razed for a new development. Sattler’s descendants donated it instead, it sat in storage for four years, the city gave it a new homestead on donated land, and it reopened in December 2005 with the first of the city’s annual Santa visits.
One cheap exception is worth knowing about. The archery range at 370 Lakeside is open year-round from sunrise to sunset, with ground shooting positions, elevated platforms and 3D targets. A non-resident adult day pass is $7, and residents with a Resident Privilege Card pay $5. Youth passes only come with an adult pass.
### How do you kayak the Dardenne Creek Blueway from St. Peters?
Put in at 370 Lakeside Park or Woodlands Sports Park, follow the mile markers down Dardenne Creek and take out at Riverside Landing Park near the Mississippi River. No boat? Rent one at Riverside Landing and paddle up the creek and back. Either way, check the water level first, and skip the access point that’s closed.
The blueway belongs to St. Charles County Parks, which calls it the county’s first completed blueway. The City of St. Peters is the partner. Its newest launch, at Woodlands Sports Park, was a joint city and county project, and three of the six access parks the county lists sit inside St. Peters.
Here’s where the official pages disagree. The county now describes about 19 miles of paddling with six access points: Bluebird Meadow Park in Dardenne Prairie, O’Fallon Sports Park, Woodlands Sports Park, Lone Wolff Park, 370 Lakeside Park and Riverside Landing Park. The city’s page still says 8.7 miles and calls the two upstream parks future access points. One paddler’s trip log, last updated in October 2025, explains the gap. It measures 5.2 miles from Lone Wolff Park to 370 Lakeside and about 3.5 more to Riverside Landing, which adds up to the city’s 8.7.
Don’t plan on Lone Wolff. The county lists that access as closed for maintenance, and the same trip log says its concrete stairway collapsed into the creek. At 370 Lakeside, the city lists two launches, one on Dardenne Creek and one on Sandfort Creek. The log reports that the Sandfort side often runs dry and that a newer 370 Lakeside entry bypasses it. Aim for the Dardenne Creek side.
Woodlands Sports Park, at 1 Woodlands Parkway, has the newest launch. The city’s directions: follow the new road alongside Soccer Field 7, park in the lot built for the launch, then walk south on the paved trail to the water.
If you own a boat, the cleanest St. Peters trip is a two-car shuttle. Leave one car at Riverside Landing Park, 101 Riverport Lane in St. Charles, which has a boat ramp the county doesn’t charge for and opens at 7 a.m. and closes half an hour after sunset. Then put in at 370 Lakeside and ride the creek about 3.5 miles down to it. That’s a relaxed afternoon, not an expedition.
No kayak? The county runs a self-serve Paddle Share station at Riverside Landing. A kayak costs $20 a session and a tandem $30, and the rental windows are 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. and 2 to 6 p.m. daily. You book online, get a code and punch it into the machine. There are two catches. Every rented kayak has to come back to the Riverside Landing station, and the county says its kayaks aren’t for use on the Mississippi or Missouri rivers. So a rental trip is an out-and-back: up Dardenne Creek, turn around, and paddle back down, with the boat secured at least five minutes before your window ends to avoid a late fee.
Timing matters in the fall. The county’s other paddle stations run April 1 to Oct. 31, and the Riverside Landing season wasn’t posted for 2026 when we looked, so check the booking page before you count on a late-fall paddle.
Read the creek before you go. The trip log warns that Dardenne Creek floods, can back up from the Mississippi, and hides snags both above and below the waterline. The current picks up fast after rain upstream, so check the stream gauge for Dardenne Creek at St. Peters the morning you go. Near the river end you’ll share the water with bigger boats, though the log notes the route is posted idle speed, no wake, because of the private docks along the banks.
One more county detail worth packing. Through the Missouri Stream Team’s Stash Your Trash program, the county hands out red mesh trash bags at no cost to people out on local waterways. Pack out what you bring, grab any litter you pass, and drop the bag in a trash can or back in a Stash Your Trash box when you’re done.
First time in a kayak? Start on the lake instead. 370 Lakeside rents a single kayak for $15 the first hour and $7.50 each hour after, a two-person kayak for $20, a Kay Park paddleboat for $22 and an aqua cycle for $25, from sunrise until 90 minutes before sunset. Life jackets are provided, the person signing the waiver has to be 18 or older, and card payments carry a 3% fee. You can reserve online.
Paddled out and starving? Here’s where to eat in St. Peters.
### Where can you fish in St. Peters, MO?
At the 140-acre lake in 370 Lakeside Park, as long as you stop at the RV check-in station before you cast. Every angler and every boat has to check in there first. Non-residents pay $2 per angler and $2 per watercraft for a day pass, St. Peters residents fish free with a Resident Privilege Card, and kids 6 and under are free. Seasonal passes are sold too.
Then the rules the listings skip. Bass, bluegill and channel catfish are catch-and-release. Other fish may be kept under city rules and Missouri law. Gas engines aren’t allowed, so it’s paddles or an electric trolling motor. And the lake closes to fishing and boating from December through February, which means your last cast of 2026 on this water happens in November. The city posts status changes on signs at the check-in station and by the boat ramp, so read them before you unpack.
Now the part that surprises people. None of this water is old. The contractor on the Lakeside 370 development, Kolb Grading, says it moved 6 million cubic yards of dirt and created the 140-acre lake in 12 months. It placed another 3 million cubic yards of fill to build a four-mile levee. The park opened on May 19, 2011. The shoreline, the levee and the lake itself were all built, not found.
Laurel Park has two fishing ponds inside its 40 acres, plus a 9-hole disc golf course and 1.93 miles of paved trail. Read the fine print, though. City park rules say residents and their guests may fish designated city lakes, so visitors without a St. Peters host should stick to 370 Lakeside, where non-residents can buy a day pass.
Want bigger water? Our roundup of the best fishing spots around St. Louis covers the rest of the region.
### When do the Hidden Lake Lights and St. Peters Christmas events start?
The 2026 dates: Hidden Lake Lights opens its Halloween show on Saturday, Oct. 10, at 7 p.m., and its Christmas show on Saturday, Nov. 28, at 7 p.m. The city’s 37th Tree Lighting follows on Friday, Dec. 4, and Breakfast with Santa is Saturday, Dec. 12. Reading this after Dec. 12? Check the city’s calendar for next year’s dates.
Hidden Lake Lights is the one the lists miss. It’s a free synchronized light show at a private home in St. Peters. You park, tune your radio to 90.1 FM and watch from the car. The Christmas show runs 24,990 lights, and the Halloween version runs 22,440. A local teenager started it in 2018, when he was 15, and donations go to Sts. Joachim and Ann Care Service. The show reports $13,255.88 raised since 2018.
The address is on the show’s website. It’s a residential street, so park legally, keep it low-key and respect the neighbors, which is what the show asks. For Halloween, it runs 6 to 9 p.m. Monday through Thursday, 6 to 10 p.m. Friday and Saturday, and 6 to 9:30 p.m. Sunday, through Halloween night. It’s the rare October plan that works as a date night and with a car full of kids.
The Christmas schedule shifts an hour earlier: 5 to 9 p.m. Monday through Thursday, 5 to 10 p.m. Friday and Saturday, and 5 to 9:30 p.m. Sunday. Christmas Eve runs 5 to 11 p.m., Christmas Day 4 to 11 p.m., and New Year’s Eve goes from 5 p.m. to midnight. The site posts a live show status, so check it on rainy nights.
The Tree Lighting is free and runs 5:30 to 8:30 p.m. at St. Peters City Hall, with live performances, photos with Santa and the community countdown. This year it grows. The new Holly-Day Market brings local vendors with handmade gifts. At the Children’s Market, kids Shop with a Cop alongside St. Peters police officers, buying presents for their families. Santa’s Mailbox takes letters and sends replies. And the city’s first Gingerbread House Contest, with an America 250 theme, puts its entries on display inside City Hall, where every vote supports Meals on Wheels at the Mayor Tom Brown Senior Center.
Breakfast with Santa runs 9 to 11 a.m. at the Rec-Plex North Food Court for kids 2 to 8. It’s $16 per child and $11 per adult for the public, or $14 and $9 for Rec-Plex members, with a continental breakfast, donut decorating and photos with Santa. Bring your own camera. The 1835 Sattler log cabin also hosts the city’s annual Visit With Santa each December, but the 2026 date wasn’t posted when we checked, so watch the city calendar.
Searching for a St. Peters drive-thru display? There isn’t a city-run one. The closest are next door: our O’Fallon guide covers the O’Fallon Christmas lights at Fort Zumwalt Park, and our guide to things to do in Wentzville covers its Holiday Night Lights. Do one, then swing back for Hidden Lake Lights on the way home.
### What can you do in St. Peters on a rainy day?
Go to the Rec-Plex, and know what you’re walking into. The building opened in 1994 to host the aquatic events of the U.S. Olympic Festival, and for its 10th anniversary it hosted the 2004 U.S. Olympic Diving Trials. It was expanded in 2007. That history rarely makes the lists, and it’s a good thing to tell a kid on the way in.
You don’t need a membership. A non-resident day pass is $13 for an adult, $11 for anyone under 18 or 55 and up, and $38 for a family of four. It covers the pools, the ice rink, the indoor track, the gym and the fitness rooms. Ice skate rental is $3.50 during public skate sessions, and so is a game controller rental. Kids 8 and under need a guardian who’s at least 13. Hours vary by area of the building, so check the schedule before you go.
Here’s the money tip. St. Charles City residents with a Parks Passport and Cottleville residents with a Cottleville Privilege Card pay the resident rate, $11 per adult and $26 for a family of four. It’s spelled out on the Rec-Plex’s Plan Your Visit page.
Around Halloween, the Rec-Plex Halloween Carnival is the rainy-day pick for kids 10 and under. The 2026 date: Saturday, Oct. 24, 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. in the Rec-Plex South gyms. It’s $5 for the public and $3 for members, and both kids and adults have to register. Wear a costume and you get a treat at check-in. Family-friendly costumes only.
For a quieter hour, walk into City Hall at One St. Peters Centre Boulevard. The Cultural Arts Centre’s galleries hang original work by local artists, and much of it is for sale: watercolors, acrylics, oils, ceramics, jewelry and photography. The work changes about every 53 days, so the walls you saw in August are a different show by October. Visitors vote for a People’s Choice award on paper ballots outside the office. Looking costs nothing.
The galleries keep long hours: 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. Monday through Thursday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Friday and 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. Saturday. They’re closed Sunday. When the rain finally quits, Ollie’s Fun Forest at City Centre Park is a short drive away.
### Is the St. Peters dog park free?
No. The St. Peters Rotary Club Dog Park, at the north end of 370 Lakeside Park, is fenced, off-leash and members-only. Non-residents pay $70 a year for the first dog and $35 for each additional dog. Residents pay $40 and $20, and senior residents pay $40 for up to two dogs. There’s a limit of three dogs per address.
The timing trick is in the fine print. Memberships run on the calendar year and all expire Dec. 31, and anything bought on or after July 1 is half price. Join in the spring and you pay full price for a full year. Join in the fall and the half-price rate applies, but the clock runs out at New Year’s. There are no refunds.
Here’s what the fee buys. The park covers just over two acres, split into a small-dog side for dogs 24 pounds and under and a large-dog side. There are 11 agility stations, seven on the large side and four on the small, plus key-code gates, water hydrants that run year-round and a covered pavilion with picnic tables. Members get two members-only events a year, around Easter and Halloween. The feature that sells it is the lake: a platform with walkways and steps lets dogs get in and out of the water. Hours are sunrise to sunset.
To join, apply online through the city’s CitizenServe portal with your dog’s spay or neuter records and current rabies records, plus a Resident Privilege Card if you want the resident rate. Animal control checks the records, approval takes up to seven days, and you pick up the tag at the 370 Lakeside check-in station.
Want a free off-leash option instead? Our guide to the best dog parks around St. Louis covers no-cost county parks and membership parks across the metro.
### Is there a farmers market in St. Peters?
Yes, on Saturdays in season. In 2026, the St. Charles Lions Farmers Market, which dates to 1991, moved to the Sunset Pavilion at 370 Lakeside Park. It runs Saturdays from 8 a.m. to 1 p.m., May 2 through Oct. 31, 2026. The market has shifted its hours for special dates, including an afternoon market in September, so check its page the week you go. After Oct. 31, watch for the 2027 season.
The same lakefront hosts the city’s free Sunset concert series. In 2026, Sunset Fridays ran 6:30 to 8:30 p.m., with food and drink vendors opening at 6. That season is over. Its Sept. 19 finale was cancelled for heat near triple digits. But the 2027 dates are already posted: a new Sunset Saturday opener on May 8, Sunset Fridays on May 14, 21 and 28 and June 4 and 11, then Aug. 20 and 27 and Sept. 3 and 10, and a closing Sunset Saturday on Sept. 18. Notice the gap. There are no concerts from mid-June to mid-August, so plan around spring or late summer.
So the next time somebody calls St. Peters the mall exit, let them. You’ll be the one sliding a kayak into Dardenne Creek at 370 Lakeside while they merge back onto I-70. Riverside Landing sits on the St. Charles side of the blueway, and if you finish the paddle wanting more, our list of free things to do in St. Charles picks up where the creek ends. Don’t leave it too late in the year, though. The 2026 Hidden Lake Lights Halloween show runs through Oct. 31, and the lake closes to paddlers on Dec. 1.
If you come off the creek or the lake hungry, St Louis Near Me Directory’s guide to where to eat in St. Peters covers dinner close to 370 Lakeside Park.
If you run a St. Peters business, list it with us so the paddlers, anglers and Saturday market crowds coming off Highway 370 can find you on the way home.
Up Dardenne Creek, the things to do at Legacy Park in Cottleville include a log cabin, lakes and a bark park.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is 370 Lakeside Park free to enter?
A.  Yes. The city lists no entry fee to walk into 370 Lakeside Park, use the 5.5-mile lake trail or have a picnic. You pay for extras: non-residents pay $2 per angler and $2 per watercraft, and archery day passes, equipment rentals, camping and dog park memberships all cost money. Anyone fishing or boating checks in at the RV check-in station first.
### Q. Is swimming allowed in 370 Lakeside Park?
A.  No. St. Peters city code and park rules prohibit swimming in city-owned lakes, and that includes the 140-acre lake at 370 Lakeside Park. Ice skating on city lakes is banned too. For water play, the park has a sprayground, and the indoor pools at the St. Peters Rec-Plex sell day passes.
### Q. How long is the trail around Lakeside 370?
A.  The city lists a 5.5-mile walking trail around the lake. The park rents bikes from $8 for the first hour, plus trike bikes and surreys. Great Rivers Greenway is rebuilding the Dardenne Greenway between Mexico Road and Dardenne Park from August 2026 through August 2027, and later phases are planned to link the greenway to Old Town St. Peters and the 370 Lakeside trails.
### Q. What kind of fish are in Lakeside Park?
A.  The city names bass, bluegill and channel catfish, and all three are catch-and-release at 370 Lakeside. Other fish may be kept, subject to city rules and Missouri law. Non-residents need a $2 day pass from the RV check-in station, and the lake is closed to fishing from December through February.
### Q. What time does 370 Lakeside Park close?
A.  At sunset. The park opens at sunrise, rental equipment goes out until 90 minutes before sunset, and RV check-in runs 24 hours a day. The park itself stays open in winter, but the lake closes to fishing and boating from December through February.
### Q. What are some fun things to do in Saint Peters, Missouri?
A.  Paddle the Dardenne Creek Blueway from 370 Lakeside Park, fish the 140-acre lake, catch Hidden Lake Lights on 90.1 FM in October and December, swim in the Olympic-history pool at the Rec-Plex, browse the Cultural Arts Centre galleries and walk the 5.5-mile lake trail. From May through October, add Saturday mornings at the farmers market.
### Q. What is St. Peters known for?
A.  Around St. Charles County, two things. The Rec-Plex, built in 1994 for the U.S. Olympic Festival’s aquatic events, hosted the 2004 U.S. Olympic Diving Trials. And 370 Lakeside Park is the city’s largest park at 500 acres, built around a 140-acre lake that a grading crew dug in 12 months. The city has nearly 60,000 residents.
### Q. Can you rent a kayak at 370 Lakeside Park?
A.  Yes. A single kayak is $15 for the first hour, a two-person kayak $20, a paddleboat $22 and an aqua cycle $25, rented from sunrise until 90 minutes before sunset. You can reserve online. Life jackets are provided, the renter has to be 18 or older, and card payments carry a 3% fee. The lake closes to boating December through February.

## Things to Do in Webster Groves, MO: Ice Skating Prices, Christmas Lights, Free Sculpture Walks
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-webster-groves-mo
One hundred seasons. That’s where the Theatre Guild of Webster Groves stands this fall, and by its managing director’s account nobody has ever been paid a dime to work there. In 1936 the guild’s one-act playwriting contest gave first place to a young St. Louis writer named Thomas Williams, for a short play called The Magic Tower. Three years later he started signing his work Tennessee.
His prize was an engraved plate. He reportedly wasn’t impressed and tossed it to his mother, and that’s how it stayed in the St. Louis area. His niece still has it, and the guild says it plans to put the plate on display. The centennial season’s November 2026 show is Arthur Miller’s A View From the Bridge, opening Nov. 6.
None of the recycled top-10 lists mention any of that. They send you to the Arch, file Webster Groves under “cute shops” and move on. Even the most-searched place in town gets shortchanged. The Webster Groves ice rink draws more than 3,000 Google searches a month, and the top three results are a Facebook album, a Yelp page and a job posting. You have to dig to learn what a session costs.
This is the other list: what Webster Groves locals actually do, with prices and dates checked in early October 2026. It’s one stop in our guide to the small towns outside St. Louis worth a day, and it starts at the rink.
### How much is one session of ice skating in Webster Groves?
Public skating at the Webster Groves Ice Arena costs $7 for non-residents and $5 for city residents ages 4 and up. Kids 3 and under skate free, rentals are $2, and Friday and Saturday cosmic skate nights run $8. The indoor rink at 33 E. Glendale reopened in October 2025 after a rebuild the city priced at $4 million.
Two things trip people up. Resident rates need a Webster Groves recreation ID card, which costs $5 at the recreation complex and takes a photo ID plus a piece of current mail, a lease or an occupancy permit. And the rental skates come in whole sizes only, youth 6 through adult 14, from a stock of more than 500 pairs. If you’re a half size, wear thick socks.
Seniors 62 and up pay the same $5 or $7. Public session times change month to month, so check the city’s skate calendar, posted each month as a PDF, before you drive over, and know the city says its fees can change. Regulars should run the season-pass math. The non-resident pass is $195, so it pays for itself on your 28th session at $7. Residents break even at 29 sessions on the $145 pass. A senior resident pass is $50.
The rink is a full 200-by-85-foot sheet, the same footprint as an NHL rink, with seats for 900. It’s also serious money for the city: the Webster-Kirkwood Times reports it’s Webster Groves’ largest source of non-tax revenue, about $800,000 a year. The rebuild came out of the $22.1 million “Destination WG!” package voters passed in April 2024 with more than 66% of the vote. The first estimate for the rink was $1.75 million. By March 2025 the city had raised it to $4 million for a new ice sheet, refrigeration equipment, cooling tower and bleachers. Then the reopening slipped 10 days, because one section of the new ice wouldn’t freeze. Contractors found a partial blockage in a refrigerant line, fixed it, and skaters were back on Oct. 6, 2025.
Hockey players get their own windows. Stick and Puck sessions cost $6 for residents and $8 for non-residents, cap at 28 skaters, and require a helmet, gloves, a stick, your own skates and your own pucks, with full pads for anyone under 16. Players 16 and older can join the no-referee pickup scrimmages, in full gear, for $6 or $10.
One name to know before you walk in. The complex is named for Benny Gordon Jr., a Webster Groves resident and business owner who challenged the whites-only rules at the city’s Memorial Pool after it opened in 1949. The city credits his persistence with opening the pool to all residents in 1953. The City Council voted unanimously in 2024 to put his name on the building, and it was dedicated this past May. In summer the same complex runs the new Webster Groves Water Park (see the FAQ). To see how these prices stack up against rinks around the metro, read what ice skating costs in St. Louis.
### Where can you see Christmas lights in Webster Groves?
October comes first, and it’s full. The 2026 dates: Old Webster’s Walktober Fest on Saturday, Oct. 17, from 10 to 5, and the Old Orchard Fall Festival on Big Bend Boulevard Oct. 24 and 25, 10 to 6 both days, with more than 55 vendors. Keep your jack-o’-lantern afterward. You’ll want it for the Pumpkin Smash (Nov. 7 in 2026).
Then the lights. The display locals keep pointing people to is the red-ribbon house on West Jackson Road. The decorations wrap the whole place, around the side and onto the garage: an archway of gift-box presents, red ribbons and icicles, a reindeer team pulling a sleigh, elves to hunt for and a little train. The presents are wrapped in foil floral paper because it survives the rain and throws the light back. It looks as good by day as it does at night. Leave a letter to Santa with a self-addressed, stamped envelope, and a reply comes back in the mail. The display was up for the 2025 season, so check before you go this year. It’s a private home. Stay on the sidewalk and keep it neighborly.
The town’s season runs on a pattern. The Old Webster Holiday Open House falls on the second Sunday in November, which points to Sunday, Nov. 8, in 2026; confirm it on the city calendar. Expect carolers, Santa, carriage rides and a trolley looping the district, with the streetscape already hung in wreaths and garland. The same day, the Webster Groves Historical Society fills the greenhouse at Rolling Ridge Nursery, 60 N. Gore, with a Christmas Market of about 60 handmade-goods vendors, and the society says every visitor can pick up a free fir sapling there. The family behind Rolling Ridge has run a business on that site since 1894, and the original stable is still standing.
Early December brings the tree lightings. In 2025 the city’s Holly Jolly Holiday Fest had Santa light the tree at the Benny Gordon Recreation Complex on a Friday at 6:30 p.m., with hot chocolate, an ornament craft table and a toy drive for the Siteman Kids at St. Louis Children’s Hospital. Admission was free with pre-registration. The next evening, Old Orchard lit its tree at 5 p.m. in Gazebo Park, after a morning that opened with Elf Yoga. Later in the month, the Holiday Night Market ran 4 to 9 p.m. across two lots on Big Bend. None of the 2026 dates were posted when we checked, so watch the city calendar.
The ticketed one sells out. The Hixson Middle School PTO’s Holiday House Tour, 32 years running, opened nine decorated homes on Sunday, Dec. 7, 2025, from 1 to 5 p.m. for $35, and tickets were gone three days early. One stop was a brick bungalow holding six model train sets, seven Christmas trees and 80 Nativity displays. Another was billed as the second-oldest home in Webster Groves, at 174 years. Buy the minute 2026 tickets post. For the rest of the metro, our roundup of the best Christmas lights in St. Louis covers the big displays, and south county drivers can add Christmas lights in Arnold to the same night.
### What can you do for free in Webster Groves?
Start on Kirkham Avenue, where three free stops sit a few blocks apart. The Gerry Welch Sculpture Garden, at Kirkham and North Gore, is a winding 0.8-acre path built in 2013 with eight pieces along it, including two by Ernest Trova, the St. Louis sculptor behind the Falling Man series, and Catharine Magel’s Inflorescence. Last October the city renamed it for Gerry Welch, mayor from 1998 to 2022 and the longest-serving in city history.
A few blocks away at Elm and Kirkham, Barbre Park holds an 11.5-foot bronze by Preston Jackson honoring North Webster, one of the oldest African American communities in the region. Look down at the base. It’s set with stones from the 1845 Rock Hill Presbyterian Church. Shady Creek Nature Sanctuary, at 112 W. Kirkham, rounds out the walk. For the longer story, the historical society posts self-guided walking tours, including a 1.75-mile route past sites tied to the town’s historic African American community.
Over on the east side, Backflip Park at 520 E. Lockwood is a wedge of lawn built around one sculpture, Allen Jones’s Backflip, installed in 2007 with The Gateway Foundation and relit in 2018. It’s a two-minute stop. Make it anyway. If the sculpture walk is your speed, there’s more free art in Clayton a short drive north.
Free music and film run on the calendar. The Old Orchard Gazebo Music Series wrapped its 21st season in September 2026 with six free Friday concerts at 7 p.m. in Gazebo Park, including Jake’s Leg, billed as the longest-running Grateful Dead tribute band in the country. Bring a chair when it comes back in August. On the film side, the 2026 standout: Webster University’s Film Series screening of Andrea Callard’s short films, made from 1974 to 2026, on Sunday, Nov. 1, at 7 p.m. Admission is free. And every event the Webster Groves Nature Study Society runs is free and open to the public, which matters more than it sounds. More on that below.
### Where can you see a play in Webster Groves besides The Rep?
The Rep is the answer everybody gives, and it’s a good one. It plays at the Loretto-Hilton Center on the Webster University campus, which opened in 1966, and it’s in its 60th season. The stranger stage in town is on a residential side street.
The Theatre Guild of Webster Groves has owned its building at 517 Theatre Lane since 1951, and the building came with a past. It went up in 1909 as a music school. Two men later leased it for a print shop and went to jail for printing counterfeit trolley tickets. A doctor owned it after that and, as the guild tells it, cut them a good deal. Before the guild had a home, most of its 1930s shows ran at The Monday Club of Webster Groves, which still operates.
The Tennessee Williams story gets better up close. The guild started its one-act contest in 1931 for Webster Groves residents, and it grew until entries came in from all over the country. Williams won in 1936 with The Magic Tower, which the guild staged that October. He entered again in 1937 and didn’t place, and the guild has never tracked down a copy of that second script. The guild’s managing director also knocks down the legend that The Magic Tower turned into The Glass Menagerie. Similar themes, she says. Different plays.
For the 100th season the guild picked the plays it has produced most often, one for every two decades of its history. The last four of the season: A View From the Bridge, Nov. 6 to 8 and 13 to 15, 2026; Proof, Jan. 15 to 17 and 22 to 24, 2027; Night Must Fall, March 12 to 14 and 19 to 21; and Inherit the Wind, May 14 to 16 and 21 to 23. Tickets are sold on the guild’s website, so check current prices there. One honest warning: the 1909 building has 31 steps inside and out, and the guild itself says access is hard for guests with limited mobility.
Since it’s October, one more thing. The building is considered one of the most haunted in town. It gets a full chapter in Patrick Dorsey’s 2015 book Haunted Webster Groves, ghost hunters have come from as far as Chicago, and a former board member says a backstage ghost named Bud, Gus or Charlie used to tug on one actress’s shirt right before her entrance. Then there’s Mrs. H., who watches from the back left of the house. The guild says she came with the seats it bought from the University of Michigan in the ’80s.
### What can couples do in Webster Groves at night?
Start with a movie you’ve probably never seen on a big screen. The Webster University Film Series runs in the 240-seat Winifred Moore Auditorium at 470 E. Lockwood, and the October 2026 lineup reads like a film-school syllabus: Network on Oct. 13, All the President’s Men on Oct. 20, Robert Bresson’s Au hasard Balthazar on Oct. 24 and White God on Oct. 25. Tickets are $10, or $9 for seniors, Webster alumni and students from other schools. Some sites still show an older $8 price, so go by the university’s own calendar.
Then do something you haven’t done since you were twelve. Cosmic skate runs Friday and Saturday nights at the ice arena for $8, plus $2 for rental skates. Two film tickets and two cosmic skates come to $40 for the whole evening, before dinner.
Or make it a Friday at the guild. Its November 2026 show, A View From the Bridge, opens Nov. 6, and an Arthur Miller tragedy in a 1909 building with a resident ghost beats another night of scrolling for something to watch. Eat first, close by, and walk in with time to spare.
Hungry after the movie? Where to eat in Webster Groves
### Where can you go birding or walk a trail in Webster Groves?
Blackburn Park is the one most people drive past. The nearly 36-acre park at Edgar Road and East Jackson Road keeps a bird sanctuary in its southeast corner, and it’s listed on the Great Missouri Birding Trail. Margaret Blackburn gave the land to the city in 1949 in honor of her husband, Jasper, an inventor whose company later became ITT. It’s also where the Pumpkin Smash happens.
If you want company, and someone who can tell a Cooper’s hawk from a sharp-shin, find the Webster Groves Nature Study Society, usually called WIG-NESS. It started in 1920 with 85 adult and 30 junior members and has about 400 now. Its ornithology group leads bird walks on Thursdays and Saturdays, weather permitting, usually meeting at 8 a.m. and finishing between 11 and 1; the meeting spot goes out on the MO-Birds email list and the group’s own list. From September through April, the society meets monthly at 7 p.m. at the Webster Groves Public Library, 301 E. Lockwood. It has also organized the area’s Audubon Christmas Bird Count for 75 years. In a recent count, 15 teams and 50 people covered 176.6 square miles of St. Charles and St. Louis counties.
For a walk without binoculars, take the Deer Creek Greenway. It runs about 2 miles through Webster Groves itself, tying together Deer Creek Park, Barnickel Park, the Marshall Avenue trailhead and Lorraine Davis Park, and Great Rivers Greenway plans to extend it east through Maplewood to the River des Peres Greenway. Two smaller spots fill out a morning: the 3-acre Plant Wildlife Sanctuary at West Swon and Jefferson, set up in 1939 by Nellie Plant, and Shady Creek on Kirkham. Ready for hills? Kirkwood next door has Emmenegger Nature Park’s bluff trails above the Meramec.
### What is the oldest house in Webster Groves?
There’s no official answer, and the famous one got 10 years younger in 2022. The Hawken House, a Federal and Greek Revival brick farmhouse at 1155 S. Rock Hill Road, was long dated to 1857; a 2022 brick-invoice find now puts it at 1867. Museum manager Ginger Fletcher Krueger was going through donated papers when she found, in an unmarked manila folder, an order for bricks dated Dec. 7, 1866.
That one sheet undid a 50-year story. Docents had told visitors the bricks were made on the property by an enslaved man, from clay out of a nearby pond. The invoice showed they were bought, and the research that followed found no enslaved people held on the Hawken property at all. The society rewrote its tour script and got a new 1867 U.S. flag. Its phone number still ends in 1857.
The house has moved, too. It first stood on Big Bend Boulevard. When it faced demolition, the Webster Groves Historical Society, founded in 1965 with saving it as its first goal, bought it. In July 1970 the house was split in half and trucked to a new foundation in Southwest Park, and it opened as a museum on Oct. 2, 1971. Tours are by appointment only, $5 for adults and free for kids under 12, led by volunteer docents, so give the society at least a day’s notice. On second Mondays from June through September the society also holds lawn concerts with pop-up food in the Hearth Room, the 1989 event space behind the house. Pencil in next June.
So is it the oldest? Probably not. Last December’s Holiday House Tour billed one private home as the second-oldest in Webster Groves, at 174 years, which would date it to about 1851. If that count is right, at least two private homes are older than the Hawken House. The honest answer is that the oldest house you can actually walk into is the Hawken House, by appointment.
That’s Webster Groves past the shop windows. For the rest of the town’s businesses, start with our Webster Groves city guide. Next time somebody calls it a cute shopping street, you’ll know what the rink charges on a Friday night and which volunteer company gave Tennessee Williams a prize. Pick one date from this page and go.
Planning a Webster Groves night out? Settle dinner first with the where to eat in Webster Groves guide on St Louis Near Me Directory, then park once near the rink or the film series and walk.
If you run a Webster Groves business, the people reading this are deciding where to spend the hour before cosmic skate or the drive home from the house tour, so list it with us where they’re already looking.
Follow the Deer Creek Greenway west and it ends at Brentwood Park in Brentwood, MO, which is free and open sunrise to sunset.
Just north in Maplewood, the oldest bowling alley in St. Louis has been upstairs on Sutton since 1916.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is Webster Groves known for?
A.  Its age, mostly. Webster Groves incorporated in 1896 when five railroad communities merged, which makes it one of the oldest suburbs of St. Louis, and its tree-lined streets of old homes show it. Locals would add the 100-year-old community theater guild, Webster University, the Old Webster and Old Orchard shopping districts, and the city’s ice rink and water park on East Glendale.
### Q. Is Webster Groves walkable?
A.  Yes, in pockets. Old Webster, around Lockwood and Gore avenues, and Old Orchard, around Big Bend Boulevard and East Lockwood to the east, are both park-once shopping districts. Add the free Kirkham Avenue sculpture walk and the 2-mile Deer Creek Greenway. Outside those areas it’s a leafy residential suburb, and most people drive between stops.
### Q. What can I do for Christmas with no money?
A.  In Webster Groves, quite a lot. Walk the Old Webster Holiday Open House on the second Sunday of November for carolers and Santa, pick up a free fir sapling at Rolling Ridge Nursery that day, go to the city’s Holly Jolly Holiday Fest tree lighting, which was free with pre-registration in 2025, and visit the red-ribbon house on West Jackson Road, where a letter to Santa with a stamped envelope gets an answer.
### Q. What are unique free attractions in St. Louis?
A.  A lot of them sit outside the city limits. In Webster Groves, a free sculpture garden on Kirkham Avenue holds two works by Ernest Trova, a park a few blocks away has an 11.5-foot bronze set on stones from an 1845 church, and the Webster Groves Nature Study Society leads free bird walks twice a week. Allen Jones’s Backflip on East Lockwood is another quick stop.
### Q. Is it cold inside an ice skating rink?
A.  Yes. The air over the ice stays cold enough that you’ll want layers, gloves and long socks even in July, and spectators get chilly faster than skaters because they aren’t moving. The Webster Groves Ice Arena is fully indoors, so wind and rain don’t matter, but bring a jacket you can shed once you warm up.
### Q. Can a 70 year old ice skate?
A.  Plenty do. Start at a public session, stay near the boards until your balance settles, and think about a class: the Webster Groves skating school runs Learn to Skate USA classes for all ages and skill levels. Seniors 62 and up pay the same $5 resident or $7 non-resident rate, and a senior resident season pass is $50. If balance or bone health worries you, check with your doctor first.
### Q. Does Webster Groves have a water park?
A.  Yes. The $12.1 million Webster Groves Water Park opened in 2025 beside the ice rink at 33 E. Glendale, with a toddler pool, a leisure pool with a small lazy river, an 8-lane lap pool with a Ninja Course, and a slide the city bills as the tallest stand-up slide in North America. Daily admission is $8 for residents and $17 for non-residents. The 2026 season ran May 23 to Sept. 7.
### Q. When is the Pumpkin Smash in Webster Groves?
A.  The 2026 date: Saturday, Nov. 7, from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. in the Jackson Road parking lot at Blackburn Park, and it’s free. Strip off candles, wax, paint, stickers and googly eyes, then smash your pumpkin with a baseball bat into a dumpster so it can be composted. Brentwood, Maplewood and Sunset Hills take part too, and the dumpster stays for drop-offs through Nov. 13.

## Things to Do in Eureka, MO: Route 66 State Park, Wolf Howls, River Floats
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-eureka-mo
Ever wonder why a town would be named after a newspaper? In 1926 the St. Louis Times was handing out lots on the Meramec River to anyone who took a six-month subscription and paid $67.50 more. That town was Times Beach. Its old roads still run through Route 66 State Park in Eureka, and not one of the recycled top-10 lists that send you to the Eureka exit for roller coasters will tell you which exit actually gets you there. There are two. They lead to different halves of the same park.
That’s Eureka in a nutshell: the good stuff sits a little sideways from where everybody’s pointed. Wolves that howl back at you after dark. A stocked city lake where every fish goes back in the water. A four-mile float on a stretch of the Meramec with exactly one outfitter. A Christmas light show that won’t take your card. None of it is secret. Locals just know which turn to make, the same way they know the rest of the small towns outside St. Louis worth a day.
### What are some unique things to do in Eureka, MO?
Walk the old roads of Times Beach, the 1926 newspaper-giveaway town that is now Route 66 State Park. Then howl with endangered wolves after dark at the Endangered Wolf Center, cast for catch-and-release bass at Hilltop Lake, float the Meramec from Allenton Access in summer, and pay for Santa’s Magical Kingdom in cash on the way out.
The wolves are the one most people have never heard of, and the Evening Wolf Howl is built around sound, not sight. You sit by a campfire for stories, walk about a half mile round trip in the dark toward the habitats, and howl. The center says its wolves usually answer. You won’t see them on this program. That’s the point.
Hilltop Lake is a city lake that was dredged in 2024 and restocked in 2025, so it’s young water with rules to match. The Times Beach roads are free and open every day of the year from 7 a.m. And the light show is the one everybody knows, run by people who still want cash. What follows goes in the order you’d actually use it: the park first, because it’s the one that confuses people, then the water, the trails, the dog park, the grown-up fall plans and the winter lights.
### How do you visit the Route 66 State Park visitor center?
Start with the strangest fact in the park: there’s no direct road from the visitor center to the park it serves. The building is the old Bridgehead Inn, a 1935 roadhouse on the east bank of the Meramec, and it’s the only Times Beach building still standing. Most of the park’s roughly 400 acres, the old town itself, sit across the river on the west side. The 1,008-foot Route 66 bridge between them has had no deck since 2010, so the only way from one half to the other is back out onto I-44. The longtime park manager told St. Louis Public Radio in 2019 that attendance dropped by about 40,000 a year once the bridge closed, because people who found one half rarely found the other.
Here’s how to get to each:
Visitor center: Exit 266 (Lewis Road), from either direction. Follow the outer road past the West Tyson County Park entrance to the stop sign at Lewis Road. Cross it, and the old roadhouse is on your left.
The park itself: Exit 265 (Williams Road). Eastbound, take the exit and make the first left onto South Outer Road, then keep going past the car dealership and you’re in. Westbound, there’s no direct move. The park’s posted directions have you exit at 264 (Highway 109), get right back on I-44 east, and ride a quarter mile to Exit 265.
On foot or by bike: Kircher Park. The city’s Kircher Park at 25 Williams Road, open 7 a.m. to dusk, connects to both Flat Creek Trail and the state park, so you can leave the car by the playground and walk in.
Time it right. The visitor center is open 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. daily from March through October, and then it goes dark for winter with one exception: it reopens the second week of December for holiday shopping. That week is the move if you want a Route 66 gift nobody else in the family thought of, since the shop carries hundreds of Route 66 items. Inside, the display room covers the road’s Missouri years and gives a small exhibit to Times Beach. The roadhouse itself went through four names: the Bridgehead Inn in 1935, Steiny’s Inn in 1946, the Bridgehead Inn again in 1972 and the Galley West in 1980. The park side keeps its own clock, 7 a.m. to a half hour after sunset, every day of the year. Both halves are free.
Then head over to the park side and look for the town. Most of the trails follow old Times Beach roads, which is why they’re so flat, and the outer loop runs about 3.2 miles, picking up old Riverside Drive along the river. On the short W Trail you’ll pass a capped monitoring well and a long, grassy rise that isn’t in the brochures. It’s known as the town mound. It’s roughly the size of four football fields, and the town’s houses, churches and even its water tower are buried under it. One regular rider told the station she’s noticed surprise lilies blooming where front yards used to be.
Is it safe? The EPA came back in 2012 at the state’s request, sampled the soil with newer methods, and reported no significant health risk to park visitors or workers. The longer story of the dioxin and the buyout is told in our Fenton guide, the one that maps the Meramec River access points in Fenton, along with the all-day float from this park’s free ramp down to Valley Park.
Now the bridge, because it could change all of the above. It was built in 1931 and 1932, it’s one of four Warren truss bridges left in Missouri, and the Missouri State Parks Foundation says engineers estimated the truss had only seven years of structural life left. MoDOT planned to tear it down if no reuse plan appeared by the end of 2016. Missouri State Parks took ownership instead. A 2021 study priced a restoration for people walking and biking at about $9 million, and Great Rivers Greenway says that in 2026 it and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers are working to complete the permits. No reopening date has been announced. When it does open, the visitor center gets its park back, and you’ll walk from the roadhouse to the town mound without a car.
Route 66 turns 100 in the fall of 2026, and the park marks it with a free Route 66 Centennial Celebration. The 2026 date: Saturday, November 7, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.
### Where can you fish near Eureka, MO?
Four places, and each one has a rule that trips people up.
Hilltop Lake is the city’s lake, inside 34.7-acre Hilltop Park at 17180 Hilltop Ridge Drive, on the corner of Meramec Boulevard. Eureka dredged it in 2024 and stocked it in 2025 with bass, bluegill, redear sunfish, catfish and minnows. Here’s the catch: it’s catch-and-release only until further notice, single hook, artificial lures only. So no live bait. No boats, no swimming and no restrooms either, and it’s open dawn to dusk. Leave the treble-hook lures at home; a jig or a soft plastic on one hook does the job.
Allenton Access is the Missouri Department of Conservation’s 9.8-acre landing on the Meramec, 3.8 river miles above the Big River junction and 6.9 below Pacific Palisades. The area is open 4 a.m. to 10 p.m., but MDC allows fishing and boat launching there 24 hours a day. If you want to sit on the river after dark with a catfish rig, this is the place near town to do it. Expect sunfish, catfish, crappie and black bass.
The river at Route 66 State Park is open to anglers from sunrise to sunset. The park points out that more than half of Missouri’s fish species live in the Meramec, and all three black bass are in play along with catfish, panfish and trout. What you can’t do is fish the park’s ponds. That’s prohibited, so walk past them to the river.
Young Conservation Area, south of town in Jefferson County (Route W south, then Route FF west 3 miles), is the one for curious anglers. It sits in the LaBarque Creek watershed, which MDC says holds at least 54 species of fish, almost three times the diversity of any of the other 15 Meramec tributaries below it. Two small ponds near the parking lot hold sunfish, black bass and white bass if you just want to dip a line.
Most anglers 16 and older need a Missouri fishing permit at all four. For stocked trout, the trout fishing at Walker Lake in Kirkwood is a short drive east on I-44, and our guide to good fishing spots in St. Louis covers the bigger water around the metro.
### Can you float the Meramec River from Eureka?
Yes, and it’s closer than most people think. Eureka Floats, run out of Brookdale Farms on Twin River Road, buses you to the put-in and lets you drift back to the farm. The standard trip is 4 miles from Allenton Access and averages about three hours, depending on the river and how many gravel bars you stop on. Tubes, rafts, kayaks and canoes all run that route. The outfitter says it’s the only float operation on this stretch of the Meramec, which is the whole appeal: you get bluffs and swimming holes without a river full of strangers.
For a full day, the 8:30 a.m. slot is held for an 11-mile canoe and kayak run that launches from Pacific Palisades and averages six to eight hours. Posted prices, which the outfitter says can change, run $30 for a tube Monday through Thursday and $40 Friday through Sunday, $45 for a kayak and $65 for a two-person canoe, with rafts priced by size. Floats run Tuesday through Sunday because Mondays are held for private groups. Everyone has to be off the water by 5 p.m., and kids under 13 bring their own life jackets. Dogs can ride along if they wear booties.
It’s a warm-weather business, and the site doesn’t post season dates, so check the booking calendar before you plan around it. If the river runs high after a storm, they’ll cancel and give you a rain check. Have your own boat? Allenton Access and the free ramp at Route 66 State Park are both public.
Off the river and hungry? Where to eat in Eureka
### Where can you hike and bike in Eureka?
Eureka’s trails are mostly flat, and that’s a feature. The spine is Flat Creek Trail, which runs from Legion Park to Kircher Park, connects into Route 66 State Park and ties into the Meramec Greenway. The city finished the first phase in April 2013 and the second in February 2020, and it won a $263,713 federal grant toward the next piece, a Legion Park to Route 66 State Park connection with off-road underpasses at Central Avenue and Highway 109. The plan is a walking and biking route across town south of I-44, from the Old Town district to the state park.
Inside Route 66 State Park, the trails follow the old town’s roads, paved or crushed gravel, open to walkers, bikes and horses. It’s the easiest long walk around for a stroller or a kid on training wheels, and the state calls the trails a good fit for visitors with disabilities. The South Loop, the one piece south of I-44, starts on the paved old South Outer Road that once led into Times Beach and runs about 1.4 miles.
For hills, go two directions. South, Young Conservation Area has about six miles of trail, with the lowland Taconic Loop and the LaBarque Hills Trail up top, and you cross a small bridge over the creek right at the start. West, Greensfelder County Park sits next door off Exit 261, 1,734 acres of ridges behind the theme park, with trails shared by hikers, mountain bikers and riders on horseback. Only have 20 minutes? The Forby Road Nature Trail is a quarter mile along Clifty Creek, and Berry Park’s one-third-mile trail connects to Eureka High School.
### Is the Eureka Dog Park free?
Yes. The Eureka Dog Park in Berry Park, 401 Forby Road, is free for all, in the city parks department’s own words. No membership needed. What you do need is paperwork: the city requires proof of your dog’s rabies, Bordetella and distemper (DHLPP) shots plus spay or neuter, and the parks department asks you to have current vet records on hand if someone asks to see them.
Inside there’s a shared area and a separate small-dog area, agility equipment, benches, shade structures, waste stations, and drinking fountains for people and pups. Hours are dawn to dusk. Afterward, Berry Park’s trail makes an easy cool-down walk.
Where else can the dog go? Leashed dogs are welcome on the Route 66 State Park trails, and Eureka Floats lets pets ride in its boats with booties. Leave the dog home for The Hollows, which bans pets and even service dogs because the trail is so dark.
### What to do in Eureka for adults?
Book the Evening Wolf Howl. The Endangered Wolf Center on Tyson Valley Road was founded in 1971 by Marlin Perkins, the Wild Kingdom host, and his wife, Carol, and it still cares for endangered wolves, foxes and African painted dogs. The howl is an evening program: stories about wolf communication around a campfire, a half-mile round-trip walk to an area near the habitats, and then everyone tries to get the wolves to sing. They usually do. Light refreshments and the gift shop come after. It’s the rare date night where the best part happens in the dark.
Would you rather see them? Wolf Fest is the day for it. The 2026 date: Saturday, October 17, from 10:30 a.m. to 4 p.m., with keeper chats at the habitats, stuffed pumpkins handed out to the maned wolves and foxes, live music and a howl competition. A car pass is $75 for up to seven people.
For a real scare, The Hollows at Brookdale Farms is a haunted trail through the woods, about 50 minutes to an hour on foot, with four new scenes in 2026: The Camp, The Graveyard, Fighting Dead and Ghost Town. Tickets are marked 18 and up. Presale is $20, general admission $25 and the gate $30, and the 2026 season runs through Sunday, November 1. No pets, no strollers, no outside food or drinks. Pair it with Brookdale’s Campfire Nights, since a four-person bundle covers both for $100.
For something quieter, drive a few minutes west to the Black Madonna Shrine and Grottos in Pacific. Brother Bronislaus Luszcz, one of six Franciscan Brothers who came to Missouri from Poland in 1927, built its grottos out of Missouri tiff rock and covered them in mosaics. It’s also one of the places pilgrims can visit for the Jubilee Year of St. Francis, through January 10, 2027. It opens at 9 a.m., and donations keep it going. And if screaming on a coaster is the plan, Mid America Adventure, the park that was Six Flags St. Louis until August, runs its 2026 Fright Fest on select days through November 1.
### Where can you see Christmas lights in Eureka, MO?
Santa’s Magical Kingdom gets the attention, so start with the parts the ads skip. The 2026 season runs every night from November 20 through January 3 at Jellystone Park St. Louis Eureka, Exit 261, opening at 5:30 p.m. and closing at 10:30 through Christmas Eve, 10 p.m. after that. Admission is by the carload: $35 for a family vehicle, $40 on Saturdays, $60 for a 12- to 15-passenger van, limo or small bus. It’s cash only, and you pay at the booth on the way out, not on the way in. Forgot? There’s an ATM inside Kringle’s General Store. Vehicles over 12 feet tall or 30 feet long can’t go through.
Two more things nobody mentions. The campground takes no overnight guests during the show, so there are no cabins or RV sites to book for a lights weekend. And the wagon and train rides through the lights sell out, so buy those ahead. Weeknights are calmest; the park says Saturday nights in December before Christmas are its busiest.
Eureka’s own lights cost nothing. The city’s Holiday Tree Lighting (Saturday, November 21, in 2026) runs from 5 to 8 p.m. at the Central Avenue Spur, 394 South Central Avenue, with hot cocoa, crafts, a stage and Santa. The good part is the walk in: you park at Geggie Elementary and follow the lights along Flat Creek Trail to the Spur.
Then there’s Forest Run Lights, a private home display on Forest Run Drive that has been running for more than ten years, synced to music on 92.9 FM and free to drive past. In the 2025 season it ran a Halloween show through October 31 and its Christmas show through January 3. A September 2026 post on its Facebook page hinted at a 2026 season, but dates weren’t up when we looked, so check the page before you go. It’s somebody’s house. Drive slowly, keep the music in the car, and don’t block driveways.
One more for the list-makers: the Route 66 visitor center opens for holiday shopping the second week of December. For the rest of the region’s drive-through shows, see our guide to drive-through Christmas lights in St. Louis.
### What’s near Eureka for a second day?
Eureka sits where three good day trips meet. Downstream, the river and its ramps run on through Fenton. East on I-44 is Kirkwood. Keep driving west and you reach Washington, where our guide to things to do in Washington, MO plans a second day on the Missouri River.
Next time somebody tells you Eureka is just the roller coaster exit, you’ll be the one who knows there are three ways into Route 66 State Park, which ponds you can’t fish, and where the wolves answer back. Pick one and go this week.
Planning the two-exit Route 66 day? See where to eat in Eureka on St Louis Near Me Directory for lunch between the visitor center and the river.
If you run a Eureka business, the people reading this are working out which exit to take right now, so put your business where they’ll find it.
West on old Route 66, Jensen’s Point Overlook in Pacific is a 1939 stone lookout, and east along the Meramec, the best trails at Castlewood State Park start in Valley Park.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is Eureka, Missouri known for?
A.  Most people know it for the theme park off I-44, Mid America Adventure, which was Six Flags St. Louis until August 2026. The name is the better story. The city’s history says that when Missouri Pacific Railroad crews came around the bend in the 1850s and saw level land with no rocks and very little dirt to move, they shouted “Eureka!” The village was laid out in 1858 and incorporated as a city in 1954. Locals know it just as well for Route 66 State Park and the river.
### Q. Is Route 66 State Park free?
A.  Yes. There’s no entrance fee for the grounds, the trails, the visitor center or the boat ramp, which Missouri State Parks lists as free. You’d only pay to reserve a picnic shelter. The grounds are open 7 a.m. to a half hour after sunset year-round, and the visitor center keeps shorter hours, 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. from March through October plus the second week of December.
### Q. Can you visit Times Beach, Missouri?
A.  Yes. Times Beach is Route 66 State Park now. The town was bought out and razed after dioxin was found on its roads, and the state opened the park on the site in 1999. Take Exit 265, walk the old town roads on the outer loop, and look for the grassy town mound along the W Trail. EPA soil sampling in 2012 found no significant health risk to visitors.
### Q. What to do in Eureka today?
A.  In October, start with the longer runs. The 2026 schedule: the Route 66 visitor center through the end of the month, the Brookdale Farms Fall Festival Wednesday through Sunday until November 8, and The Hollows on select nights through November 1. Then come Wolf Fest on October 17, the free Route 66 Centennial Celebration at the state park on November 7, and the lights season opening November 20. Check each schedule the day you go.
### Q. Is it illegal to fish at night in Missouri?
A.  No. Missouri has no statewide ban on night fishing. Conservation areas like Allenton Access are open to visitors 4 a.m. to 10 p.m., but MDC allows fishing and boat launching there 24 hours a day. Local rules can be tighter: the river at Route 66 State Park is sunrise to sunset, and Hilltop Lake is dawn to dusk.
### Q. How many rods are you allowed to fish with in Missouri?
A.  There’s no fixed cap on poles. The rule is about labels and hooks. If you use more than three poles at once, or more than two on the Mississippi River, the extras must carry your full name and address or your Conservation Number, and you can’t have more than 33 hooks in the water at one time, or 50 on the Mississippi. At Hilltop Lake, each line gets a single hook.
### Q. What to see on Route 66 in Missouri?
A.  Close to St. Louis, start in Eureka: the 1935 Bridgehead Inn visitor center, the 1,008-foot Meramec River bridge and the old Times Beach roads inside Route 66 State Park. In the city, the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge carried Route 66 over the Mississippi and is now a walking and biking bridge with a famous bend in the middle. West of Eureka, the old road runs on through Pacific.
### Q. Is Santa’s Magical Kingdom cash only?
A.  Yes. Admission is cash only at the ticket booth, and you pay as you exit, not on the way in. It’s $35 per family vehicle, $40 on Saturdays and $60 for vans, limos and small buses, tax included. If you’re short, there’s an ATM inside Kringle’s General Store. Wagon and train rides are sold separately, and they go fast.

## Things to Do in Kimmswick, MO: The 1874 Iron Bridge, Cookie Walk and River Trail
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-kimmswick-mo
Pie, then leave. That’s the entire Kimmswick plan on every recycled list: park near Market Street, split a slice of the ten-pound apple pie, grab a jar of apple butter and be back on I-55 inside twenty minutes. Follow it and you walk right past the best thing in town. At the south end of Mill Street, a riveted wrought-iron truss stands over Rock Creek. It carried Carondelet traffic across the River des Peres from 1874 to 1928, it’s the oldest known wrought-iron span in Missouri, and since February 2026 it has been closed while a five-person committee works out how to keep it standing.
Here’s the catch. The city’s own bridge page and the state tourism listing still tell you to stroll across it. Don’t. The Kimmswick Historical Society, which owns the bridge, shut it to all foot traffic after volunteers clearing brush underneath found a support that was badly distorted, and it was still fenced and signed in July. The committee’s order of business is blunt: keep it from falling down first, then fix everything else.
The bridge is one piece of a pattern nobody mentions. A surprising amount of Kimmswick was somewhere else first. The bridge came from St. Louis. Starting in 1970, log buildings from around St. Louis County were taken apart, their logs numbered, and rebuilt on a single Kimmswick block in a restoration launched by a 7-Up heiress. The post office is fitted out with the interior of a dismantled post office from the mid-1800s. For a town of 133 people, that’s a lot of rescued history. Almost none of it makes the lists.
So treat this as the other list, the one for people who get out of the car and stay. Kimmswick is one of the small towns outside St. Louis that pays you back for walking it slowly.
### What are some fun things to do in Kimmswick?
Skip the 20-minute pie stop. Walk the riverside trail at Kimmswick Park, find the 1874 Windsor Harbor Road Bridge that once crossed the River des Peres in Carondelet, tour the free Historical Society museum on a weekend afternoon, and time a visit for Witches Night Out, Food Truck Friday or the December Cookie Walk.
That’s a full day, and most of it is free. Here’s the short version, with the details further down:
The 1874 bridge and its flood marker. Study the riveted Pratt truss from the north end on Mill Street, then find the 2021 marker on the bridge that shows how high the Mississippi has climbed.
The Historical Society museum. A former Baptist church at 6000 Third Street, free, open 1 to 4 p.m. on most weekends.
The Burgess-How House. The oldest log building in town, furnished as an 1850s farmhouse, open most Sundays through October.
City Hall’s jail cells. Two cells finished in 1909 sit inside a building where the city still does its business. The bars show on the small back windows.
The river trail. Kimmswick Park runs a natural trail north along the Mississippi, with a boat-shaped playground at the trailhead. Open 8 a.m. to 8 p.m., free.
The Anheuser Estate. An 1867 house on 23 acres above the river, with $10 walk-in tours on Thursday afternoons through November.
The fall and winter calendar. Witches Night Out on the second Saturday of October (October 10 in 2026), Deer Widow’s Weekend in mid-November, then the Stocking Stroll, the Cookie Walk, the Christmas Festival and a kids’ Elf Hunt.
Food Truck Friday. The third Friday of the month, 5 to 9 p.m., free, with movie and live-band nights mixed in.
Some geography helps. Kimmswick sits on the Mississippi where Rock Creek runs in, about 25 miles south of downtown in Jefferson County, and Theodore Kimm founded it in 1859. The river built the town and keeps testing it. In 1993, 2012, 2015 and 2019, residents, merchants and volunteers sandbagged a temporary levee and rented pumps to hold the water back, and every time, two of the town’s three roads went under. Most of what’s worth seeing sits within a few blocks of the Visitor Center at 314 Market Street, in the Maul House, built around 1872. Park once. Walk. Our story of the 1993 flood in St. Louis covers what that summer did across the region.
### When are the Kimmswick Cookie Walk and Christmas Festival in 2026?
The Kimmswick Cookie Walk runs Thursday, December 3 through Sunday, December 6, 2026, and the free Christmas Festival fills the same streets December 4 to 6. Cookie Walk tickets go on sale in October, and the 2026 price hadn’t been posted when we checked, so keep an eye on the Visitor Center’s event page. You start at the Visitor Center, 314 Market Street, where you trade your receipt for a gift bag, a map and a holiday cookbook, then work your way through town collecting sweets from each participating shop. Reading this after December 6? Check the Visitor Center’s event page for the next dates.
The cookbook is the keeper. It’s filled with the shop owners’ own favorite sweet recipes, so long after the cookies are gone you can still bake the ones you liked best.
The festival around it has one rule that explains its whole feel. Kimmswick allows no outside vendors at the Christmas Festival, only the town’s own merchants, which makes it the opposite of the Apple Butter weekend’s hundreds of booths. The town is firm enough about it to warn people not to trust anyone on social media selling vendor spots. What you get instead is luminaries along the walks, carolers, carriage rides, Santa, and the shops themselves dressed for December. Walking in costs nothing.
Kimmswick has a title to defend, too. In River Travel Magazine’s 2020 contest, which drew 75 river towns from 10 states, it was named Best Holiday River Town among towns under 500 people.
The Cookie Walk is one stop on a month-long run. Here’s the whole 2026 Christmas calendar in order:
Saturday, November 21, 2026: Christmas Parade and Open House. The parade steps off at 11 a.m., shops stay open from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m., restaurants stretch their hours, and the River Town Sound Quartet sings its way around town. Free.
Small Business Saturday (November 28 in 2026): Stocking Stroll. 2026 is its second year, and it’s built like the Cookie Walk. A $35 ticket, good from 10 a.m. to 7 p.m., gets you a holiday bag that 17 shops each drop a stocking stuffer into, more than $100 in gifts by the end. 2026 tickets were already on sale when we checked.
Thursday to Sunday, December 3 to 6, 2026: Cookie Walk. Ticketed. Cookbook, gift bag, map and treats.
Friday to Sunday, December 4 to 6, 2026: Christmas Festival. Free, merchants only, Santa included.
December 12 and 13, then 19 and 20, 2026: Elf Hunt. A ticketed kids’ event from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Children get an activity book of riddles that point to an elf hidden in each store, and when they find it, the register hands over a small prize. Donate a toy and you get a $5 gift card good at participating merchants. The toys go to Jefferson County families.
Any day of the year: the Christmas Haus. The shop at 311 Elm Street bills itself as the area’s largest year-round Christmas store, with more than 40 decorated trees and ornament personalization.
Two timing tips. If you want the Cookie Walk without the festival crowd, go on the Thursday (December 3 in 2026), since the free festival doesn’t start until Friday. And if you’re bringing young kids, the Elf Hunt weekends give them a reason to walk into every shop with you instead of waiting by the door. Building a whole December around lights? Pair Kimmswick with Christmas lights in St. Charles on another night, or browse our guide to Christmas events in St. Louis for the rest of the season.
### Why is a Carondelet bridge sitting in Kimmswick?
Because St. Louis was done with it and Jefferson County wasn’t. The Keystone Bridge Company, the Andrew Carnegie firm that erected the superstructure of the Eads Bridge, built this 123-foot Pratt truss in 1874 and 1875 to carry traffic over the River des Peres at Ivory Avenue in Carondelet. The city and the county split the bill, and the city’s share was $6,500. It’s the same age as the Eads Bridge, from the same builder.
It stood there until 1928, when a new crossing replaced it. Two years later, Jefferson County re-erected it over Rock Creek at the south edge of Kimmswick. Cars eventually moved to the modern bridge next door, and in 1983 the old span went on the National Register of Historic Places. That didn’t save it. In 1985 the county planned to demolish it for scrap, and the Kimmswick Historical Society stepped in and took ownership instead.
For decades after that it was a footbridge and the town’s favorite photo backdrop. Prom couples, high school seniors and wedding parties all lined up on it. That ended in February 2026. A society board member had the growth under the bridge cleared, the crew spotted a structural support that was distorted badly, and the society closed the bridge to foot traffic and formed a committee to save it. Committee chair Steve Kalisch told the Leader the plan is to stabilize it, then go through the bridge looking for other defects and repair them.
Here’s how to see it now. Walk to the north end, where Mill Street meets Front Street near the Blue Owl, read the plaque, and stay off the span. Bolted to the same bridge is a second marker worth the stop: a 2021 flood marker from the Missouri Department of Public Safety and the Silver Jackets, showing the highest the water has reached on record and telling the story of those four floods. The Blue Owl even named its Levee High apple pie after the 1993 levee. Then walk about a third of a mile to Jefferson Square Park, where a red granite boulder set by the Missouri Daughters of the American Revolution in 1917 marks El Camino Real, the Spanish Royal Road between Ste. Genevieve and St. Louis and the oldest road in Missouri. The boulder was moved to the park in 2008. Like the bridge, it’s history that got relocated here and stayed.
If you grew up near the River des Peres, our Carondelet neighborhood guide covers the end of the city this bridge came from. And if you want to help, the society posts updates on its Facebook page and keeps its museum open on weekend afternoons.
Saw the bridge? Now find lunch: where to eat in Kimmswick.
### What historic buildings in Kimmswick can you actually go inside?
More than you’d expect from a town this size, as long as you come on a weekend afternoon.
Kimmswick Hall and Museum. The Kimmswick Historical Society runs its museum out of a former Baptist church at 6000 Third Street, at Vine. It’s free and open from 1 to 4 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays, most weekends. The society’s monthly meeting, the first Monday at 7 p.m., is open to anyone, and it’s the fastest way to hear where the bridge effort stands.
The Burgess-How House. At Third and Elm, this was the first log building ever moved into Kimmswick, in 1970, and it’s the oldest log building in town. It came in from elsewhere in Jefferson County and is furnished as an 1850s farmhouse full of primitive antiques. It opens most Sundays from 1 to 4 p.m., April through October. Outside that season, call 636-223-0453 to set up an appointment.
The log block. Walk the block bounded by Second, Elm, Third and Oak streets and look closely at the cabins. In 1970, Lucianna Gladney-Ross, heiress to much of the 7-Up fortune, launched the restoration the city credits with saving Kimmswick. Log buildings from around St. Louis County were dismantled, numbered log by log, and reassembled here. A few streets over, LaChance runs its restaurant in The Old House, a log house the winery dates to around 1770, roughly 90 years before Kimmswick existed.
City Hall. The one-story frame City Hall at 6041 Third Street still holds two jail cells completed in 1909, and official city business still happens inside. You don’t need to go in. Walk around back and you’ll see the bars on the small rear windows.
The post office. The building at 6057 Front Street dates to about 1914 and was restored in 1974 with the interior of a dismantled mid-1800s post office.
