The carriages are the one ticketed part: tickets go on sale at 5:30 p.m., first come, first served, and they’re non-refundable. In between the two, the city’s 2026 calendar also listed the Sweet & Savory Stroll on Nov. 14 and Small Business Saturday on Nov. 28. Check current dates for all of them. For a second night of lights, Christmas lights in Webster Groves are right next door.
### Is there still a farmers market in Maplewood, MO?
Yes, but not where a lot of listings say. The market that used to set up on Schlafly’s lot lost its sponsor in February 2020, and its vendors took it over and renamed it the SOL Food Farmers Market, for Sustainable, Organic, Local. It’s producer-only, so the person behind the table grew or made what’s on it. It now runs Wednesdays from 4 to 6:30 p.m., May through October, in the Living Room lot at 2810 Sutton Blvd. That leaves the remaining Wednesdays of October 2026 for this season, so check the market’s page before going.
Two warnings when you search. Some map listings still send people to the old Maplewood Farmers Market at Schlafly, which moved off that lot years ago; the Schlafly lot’s market now is Sundaze, which sells art, not tomatoes. And most results for a Maplewood farmers market are about the Maplewoods in New Jersey and Minnesota. For every other market around the region, see our guide to St. Louis metro farmers markets by town.
### Nearby, down the old Route 66
Maplewood is small, and it shares borders with good company. Webster Groves is just south, where The Focal Point got its start. Brentwood is just west, tied in by the Deer Creek Greenway. And if you follow the 1926 route out Manchester Road through Rock Hill, you reach Kirkwood, where our list of things to do in Kirkwood leads with winter trout at Walker Lake.
Next time someone tells you Maplewood is a place to grab dinner and leave, you’re the one who knows the bowling alley upstairs is older than Route 66, the score sheet takes a pencil, and the fourth Sunday starts at a parking-lot art market and ends with a tango lesson on a maple floor. Pick a fourth Sunday. Call Saratoga first. Then go.
Between the last frame and the walk back to the car, our guide to where to eat in Maplewood, MO covers the whole-animal butcher on Sutton, a 30-seat tasting-menu room on Manchester and the late-running pub kitchen right on the plaque blocks.
If you run a shop on the 7200 or 7300 block of Manchester, where the Route 66 plaques walk people right past your window, list it with us so they know to come inside.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is Maplewood known for?
A.  Saratoga Lanes, first: eight lanes upstairs on Sutton Boulevard since 1916, billed as the oldest bowling alley west of the Mississippi. Maplewood is also known for sitting on the original 1926 to 1933 alignment of Route 66, for a business district the city calls the nation’s first Green Dining District, for The Focal Point’s folk concerts and dance nights, and for two breweries, Side Project and Schlafly Bottleworks.
### Q. What is the history of Maplewood, MO?
A.  Maplewood marked its centennial in 2008. From 1926 to 1933, the original Route 66 ran through town on Manchester Road, and Maplewood grew into a busy retail hub serving the traffic. By the late 1950s, malls and newer suburbs had drawn shoppers away. A revival began in the late 1990s, led by locally owned shops and restaurants. The city’s free self-guided tour, “A Stroll Through Time,” covers its late-19th-century neighborhoods.
### Q. What is the history of Saratoga Lanes?
A.  It opened in 1916 on the second floor of a new office building owned by Albert Carl Blood of the Maplewood Planing Mill, who put the lanes upstairs to give a saloon game some respectability. By its own account it was the only alley in St. Louis County to survive Prohibition and the Depression. The Stein family ran it for decades, it added automatic pinsetters in the 1950s, and it joined the National Register of Historic Places in 2008.
### Q. Is there a bowling hall of fame in St. Louis?
A.  Not anymore. The International Bowling Museum and Hall of Fame was a downtown St. Louis fixture from 1984 until it closed to the public on Nov. 8, 2008. It reopened in Texas in January 2010. For bowling history you can still play on, go to Saratoga Lanes, where Hall of Famer Otto Stein Jr. and his Maplewood teammates took on visiting champions.
### Q. Why are bowling alleys closing down?
A.  At Saratoga, the pressure has been leagues. Its owner has watched league bowling decline over his decades there, and the alley has made up for it with private events, including a surprise wedding. It has also survived by changing just enough. Automatic pinsetters went in during the 1950s, when big suburban bowling centers were opening. What it never changed was the pencil scoring, and that’s a big part of why travelers still find it.
### Q. What’s the best time to go to the farmers market?
A.  In Maplewood, Wednesday afternoon. The SOL Food Farmers Market runs 4 to 6:30 p.m. on Wednesdays from May through October at 2810 Sutton Blvd. Get there in the first half hour for the best pick, since a producer-only market sells what the vendors brought and nothing gets restocked. October ends the season, so check the market’s page before your last trip of the year.
### Q. What are some free activities I can do in St. Louis, Mo.?
A.  In Maplewood alone, walk the Route 66 plaques on the 7200 and 7300 blocks of Manchester Road, browse Sundaze at Schlafly on fourth Sundays from April through December, watch the free Morris dance practice at The Focal Point on Sunday afternoons, let the kids loose on the rocket ship at Deer Creek Park, and come back for the Great Pumpkin Glow in October and the Christmas Tree Walk in December. Free trivia runs Tuesday and Wednesday nights at Schlafly Bottleworks.
### Q. How much does it cost to bowl at Saratoga Lanes?
A.  Saratoga’s posted open-bowling rate is $40 an hour per lane on weekdays and $45 an hour on weekends, plus $5 for shoes, and it prorates your time to the minute. Pool is $6 per person per hour, with an $18 cap per table. Call (314) 645-5308 before walking in to make sure a private party hasn’t booked the whole place, and confirm current rates while you’re on the phone.

## Things to Do in Glen Carbon, IL: Miner Park's Caboose, Schon Park Fishing, the World's Fair Brickyard
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-glen-carbon-il
Confession: we skipped Glen Carbon for years. Every recycled top-10 list files it as the exit before Edwardsville, so we kept driving, right up until we read one entry in SIUE’s Madison Historical encyclopedia. According to it, the St. Louis Press Brick Company in Glen Carbon supplied brick for the Palace of Fine Arts at the 1904 World’s Fair, and one building of that palace went on to become the Saint Louis Art Museum.
Most of us have walked through that museum. Few of us have heard of the brickyard that helped build it. At its peak the yard employed 200 to 300 people, and in 1894 it reportedly signed a contract for 40 million paving bricks. A fire in 1906 destroyed most of it. Nobody rebuilt.
What’s left is a paved rail trail through the old company town, and one of the 17 history panels along it tells the brickyard’s story. The trail is free. So is nearly everything else in this guide. A 12-foot pink steel canary stands on that trail for the miners. Residents pushed a caboose into Miner Park by hand. The fire district almost burned an 1850s log cabin in a 1989 training exercise, because siding hid the logs, and residents rebuilt their Bicentennial covered bridge after arsonists torched it the same year it went up. Of all the small towns outside St. Louis, this one posted its history on signs along a bike path. The lists still haven’t read them.
Everything below was checked against the Village of Glen Carbon, Madison County Transit and SIUE’s Madison Historical in October 2026. It’s sorted by what you came to do.
### What to do in Glen Carbon?
In Glen Carbon, ride the MCT trails past 17 coal-and-railroad history panels and a 12-foot pink steel canary, find the caboose residents pushed into Miner Park by hand, fish the stocked pond at Ray M. Schon Park, drive through the covered bridge on Main Street, see the 1850s Yanda Log Cabin and tour the always-free Heritage Museum.
That’s the short version. The long one starts around 1801, when this valley was the Goshen Settlement and Col. Samuel Judy was its first American settler, according to Madison Historical. Railroads followed the valley in the 1870s. Then came coal. Workers from the Madison Coal Corporation and the St. Louis Press Brick Company joined 78 locals to petition for a village, and Glen Carbon was incorporated on June 6, 1892.
It was a company town in the plain sense. The brick company built salt-box rental houses for its workers along Main Street. By 1895, the village’s own history says, Glen Carbon had 13 taverns and no churches, and that year it passed a misdemeanor ordinance. Two depots carried residents into St. Louis by train. The mines and the brickyard are long gone. Some of the old rail beds are trails now.
If you’ve already toured the buildings left from the 1904 World’s Fair, this is the other end of that story. Here’s the plan. Miner Park for the caboose and the trailhead. Schon Park for the fishing. The Heritage Museum and the 1910 jail a block away for a weekday when it rains. The trails for the brickyard panel and the canary. Then the cabin and the covered bridge on Main Street. October and December add a ghost walk, a model railroad and a winter market.
### What are some things to do at Miner Park in Glen Carbon?
Start with the caboose, because it has the best story in the park. Gulf, Mobile & Ohio caboose No. 2890 came to Glen Carbon in 1977, donated through State Rep. Everett Steele and delivered near the site of the old No. 2 mine. Getting it into place, by the village’s own account, “required gathered citizens manually pushing the caboose.” Kiwanis members, steelworkers and retirees restored it afterward. It still sits in the park.
The park was a bargain, too. The village bought the land in 1974 for $15,500 and opened it in August 1977 with a party called Glenfest. Miner Park sits in Old Town, behind the American Legion post, and Judy Creek splits it in two, with a footbridge joining the halves. Around them you’ll find pavilions, a bandstand, two lighted tennis courts, basketball and ballfields.
The storybook walk. A children’s book is laid out along the path, so small kids read their way around the park. It’s the cheapest bribe in Madison County for getting a four-year-old to walk a loop.
The miners’ memorial. A 1987 plaque honors miners killed in mine accidents. Read it first. The canary up the trail makes more sense afterward.
The Bark Park. Miner Park’s dog park is back. On March 19, 2026, the village posted that repairs had been made and the dog park was open again. Check the posted rules when you arrive. If your dog has worn out the usual spots, our roundup of the best dog parks in St. Louis covers the rest of the metro.
The trailhead. Miner Park is a parking point for the MCT Nickel Plate Trail, so riders coming down from Edwardsville roll right through it. Walk a short way up the Heritage Trail toward Main Street and you’ll meet Cole, the pink canary. More on him below.
Here’s how an hour goes. Park at Miner Park. Walk the storybook path, cross the footbridge over Judy Creek, read the plaque and visit the caboose. Then head up the trail to the canary and back. Total cost: nothing.
### Can you fish at Ray M. Schon Park in Glen Carbon?
Yes. In October 2021 the village announced that fishing was now permitted at Schon Park Lake, under rules posted at the water. A stocked pond, free to fish with a license, and it’s the park the lists forget.
The license. Anglers 16 and older need an Illinois fishing license. That’s state law, and it applies here the same as on any lake in Illinois.
The rules. Read the signs at the lake before you cast; they set the terms. Questions go to the Glen Carbon Parks Department at 618-288-2650.
The pond. The village describes it as a stocked pond. Bring a light rod, bait and a folding chair, and fish from the bank.
The park around the water is worth the drive by itself. Ray M. Schon Park covers 69 acres on Glen Carbon Road, across from Village Hall and St. Cecilia’s. The village bought the land from the Schon family in 2005 and opened the park in 2013, so it’s young: walking trails, pavilions, a playground and the village’s first electric vehicle charger. Charge the car while you fish.
New courts this fall. A $1.4 million expansion is adding eight courts, four of them dedicated to pickleball, plus tennis and basketball. Construction began in March with a target of the end of October 2026, The Intelligencer reported. The courts are scheduled to open this fall, so check before you bring paddles.
Chalk This Way. The 2026 date for Schon Park’s second annual chalk art day with District 7 schools: Saturday, Oct. 10, from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Chalk artists compete, and there are free caricatures and face painting, vendors and a bounce house. Check the village calendar that morning in case weather moves it, and again for next year’s date.
Want more water? Our list of the best fishing spots in St. Louis covers lakes and river access around the metro.
### Is the Glen Carbon Heritage Museum free?
Always. Admission to the Glen Carbon Heritage Museum is free for every visitor, and the parking out front on School Street is free, too. The catch is the calendar. As of this fall the museum is open Monday through Friday, 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., and closed on weekends and federal holidays. Saturdays open only during events or by appointment at 618-288-7271. Older listings around the web still show Saturday hours, so check current hours before you plan a weekend around it.
The building is half the visit. It went up in 1914 as the Glen Carbon School, at 124 School St., and in 2014 it became the first building in Glen Carbon on the National Register of Historic Places. Look for the window where the fire escape slide used to be. Students rode it down. The tin ceilings and hardwood floors are original. Accessible parking, a ramp and an elevator are at the back of the building.
Three exhibits do the heavy lifting.
Valley of Coal. The company town, told through what it left behind: carbide lamps, union meeting minutes and actual coal. If the trail panels made you curious about the mines, this is the room with the answers.
The Heritage Store. A child-size play grocery built from artifacts out of the old Main Street stores. Small kids get to play shopkeeper. Grown-ups get a look at what Main Street used to sell. On a wet Tuesday, that’s an hour handled.
Glen Carbon Veterans. An exhibit on the village’s service members. It pairs with Honor Roll Park on Main Street, covered below.
The 1910 jail a block away. Walk over to the Old Village Hall & Firehouse at 180 Summit Ave. It was built in 1910 on land the Madison Coal Corporation donated, and it was the fire engine house, the village hall and the jail all at once. Volunteers replaced the bell tower in 1990, and its bronze bell still chimes the hour. It joined the National Register in 2018. The museum, this old village hall and the Yanda Log Cabin all sit within a few blocks of each other, so one parking spot covers all three.
Inside, the Metro East Model Railroad Club runs an HO layout of roughly 18 by 27 feet, with about 1,000 feet of track. The upper level is Glen Carbon in the 1940s. The lower levels hold the club’s own Glen Carbon Central railroad, a steel mill and a coal mine. The public gets in at free open houses, and the 2026 holiday dates are in the Christmas section below.
One more indoor stop sits just off the Heritage Trail’s Main Street end: the Glen Carbon Centennial Library, which holds Read with a Dog on the second Thursday of the month at 6 p.m. (Oct. 8 and Nov. 12 in 2026).
### Which bike trails run through Glen Carbon?
Three Madison County Transit trails meet here: the Ronald J. Foster Heritage Trail, the Nickel Plate and the Goshen. They belong to an MCT network of more than 138 miles, and they’re paved and free. The trail maps tell you where they go. They don’t tell you what you’re riding past, and in Glen Carbon that’s the good part.
The 17 history panels. MCT and the Glen Carbon Historical and Museum Commission put up 17 interpretive panels along the Heritage and Nickel Plate trails in Glen Carbon and unveiled them on Nov. 5, 2021, 30 years after the first signs went up in 1991. Each one is 36 by 24 inches, set on an accessible pad, with a QR code for more. The titles read like a map of the old company town: Railroad Control Tower, Coal Washer, Rescue Station No. 2, Ethnic Neighborhoods, Coal Mine No. 4, the East St. Louis and Suburban Railway streetcar, Mont Station and the St. Louis Press Brick Company, the brickyard from the top of this page.
The route. MCT publishes its own Heritage Trail History Run: 8.34 miles out and back on the Nickel Plate and Heritage trails, starting from the MCT Glen Carbon Park & Ride. MCT puts it at about an hour and 45 minutes. Stop at every panel and it takes longer. That’s fine.
Cole the Canary. Where the Heritage Trail meets Main Street stands a 12-foot, hot-pink canary made of 10-gauge steel by Texas sculptor Jeffie Brewer. It went up in November 2023 as a nod to the canary in the coal mine, the bird miners carried underground as an early warning of bad air. Cole is one of MCT’s 12 Trail Critters, and if you message MCT’s Facebook page, it will mail you a Trail Critters Adventure Book for tracking down the other 11.
The Heritage Trail itself. The village built it in 1991 on the old Illinois Central corridor, one of the first 500 rails-to-trails projects in the country, and named it for Ronald J. Foster, a village trustee from 1965 to 1981 and mayor from 1981 to 2001. It runs 12.2 miles of asphalt from Main Street near the Glen Carbon Centennial Library to Marine Village Park, over nine bridges. TrailLink notes a 150-foot tunnel under Troy Road about 2.5 miles out, a second tunnel at Old Troy Road and a 340-foot trestle over Silver Creek farther east. Park on Daenzer Drive.
Mont Station. On the way out, Mont Station Park, at Old Troy Road and Mont Station Road, holds the Valier & Spies grain elevator, built in 1913. MCT lists Mont Junction as a parking point on the Heritage Trail.
The Goshen Trail. MCT calls it the spine of its trail system: 19.5 miles, 10 tunnels and 8 bridges, running from Kyle Road in O’Fallon through Troy, Maryville, Glen Carbon and Edwardsville. At the south end, pair a ride with the free things to do in O’Fallon, Illinois. Along the way the Goshen connects with Collinsville’s Schoolhouse Trail, which we cover with the other parks in Collinsville.
Greenspace East. For a walk with no bikes at all, step off the Heritage Trail at South Trace Road and Paddock Lane. Greenspace East covers about 80 acres, with roughly 9,500 feet of asphalt paths and covered picnic stations. It’s for walking, jogging and hiking only. Bicycles are prohibited.
The rules. MCT trails are open sunrise to sunset. Leashed dogs are welcome on leads 6 feet or shorter. Pedal-assist e-bikes are allowed at the 15 mph limit; gas engines, horses and alcohol aren’t. Check MCT’s trail closures page before a long ride.
Back off the trail and hungry? Where to eat in Glen Carbon
### Can you go inside the Yanda Log Cabin?
Yes, on the right day, and 2026’s regular open-house season is already over. The village calendar listed open houses on the third Saturday of each month from April through September, 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Some tourism listings still say the season runs through October, so trust the village calendar. Off-season, you can look through the glass doors and read the display on the porch. Groups can book a private tour at 618-288-7271.
There are two more ways in. Cabin Day is the free annual open day in early October (Oct. 3 in 2026), and the library set its 2026 Spooky Pajama Storytime at the cabin for Wednesday, Oct. 21, at 6:30 p.m., with s’mores if the weather cooperates.
The cabin survived by one question. William and Anna Yanda, Bohemian immigrants, built it around 1853 along Goshen Road and ran a blacksmith shop for travelers. A saloon was added in 1883. The family sold the place in the 1940s, and over the decades siding and additions swallowed the logs until nobody could see them.
By 1989 the Glen Carbon Fire Protection District had the building scheduled for a training burn. The Historical and Museum Commission asked to look under the siding first, and found the logs. The village bought it, and volunteers restored it in 1990 with white oak and square nails. When archaeologists dug where the saloon had stood, they turned up broken steins and five-cent pieces.
The cabin’s garden is just as strict about the past. It grows only plants that were in Illinois in the 1850s, sorted into six categories by use, and the G.L.E.N. Committee raises every one from seed.
The covered bridge. A short walk down Main Street, you can drive through Glen Carbon’s covered bridge over Judy Creek. Volunteers built the first one, 34 feet long, between March and May of 1976 for the Bicentennial. That September, arsonists burned it. Residents rebuilt it. In 2008 it was rebuilt again, larger, with state and county grants, and it got a new cedar-shake roof in 2023 and 2024. It still carries Main Street traffic, so you can drive through a covered bridge on the way to dinner.
Honor Roll Park. Beside the bridge at 195 S. Main St., this small veterans’ memorial sits on land Sophia Lawson donated in October 1944. Memorial bricks honor Glen Carbon veterans.
### What’s happening in Glen Carbon for Halloween and Christmas?
More than the town’s size suggests, and almost all of it is free.
Ghosts of Glen. The village’s Haunted History Walking Tour had four nights on its October 2026 calendar: Friday and Saturday, Oct. 9 and 10, and Friday and Saturday, Oct. 23 and 24. Check in at the Heritage Museum at 7 p.m. The tour steps off at 7:15, breaks at the library from 8:30 to 9 and wraps up around 10. Guests get to try real paranormal-investigation equipment, and the route changes every year, so last year’s crowd gets a new walk. Tickets are $25 a person through Eventbrite or at the museum, if any remain. Anyone under 18 needs a parent along. It’s the one ticketed event in this guide. Reading this after Oct. 24? Ask the Heritage Museum about next year’s dates.
Spooky Pajama Storytime. The 2026 date: Wednesday, Oct. 21, at 6:30 p.m. at the Yanda Log Cabin. Pajamas are the point. The Edwardsville/Glen Carbon Chamber of Commerce’s Halloween parade (Oct. 31 in 2026) is an Edwardsville event.
Model railroad open houses. The Metro East Model Railroad Club opens the Old Village Hall & Firehouse for free holiday open houses; the 2026 dates are Saturdays, Nov. 21, Dec. 5 and Dec. 19, from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. It’s the chance to see 1940s Glen Carbon in HO scale with the trains running.
Heritage Winter Market. The 2026 date: Saturday, Nov. 28, from 5 to 8 p.m. at the Heritage Museum. It’s free, with vendors, live reindeer in Santa’s sleigh and a community tree lighting by the mayor. Snow canceled the 2025 market, so check the village’s page that afternoon. To make a night of it, our guide to Christmas lights in Edwardsville pairs the market with candlelight tours a few minutes away.
A Dec. 5 double. In 2026, that Saturday stacks two free events: the model railroad open house from 10 to 3 and the library’s Holiday Open House at 1 p.m., with Santa and cookie decorating. Library registration opening date: Nov. 1.
Lighted Christmas Parade. The Glen Carbon Fire Protection District and the village run a lighted parade down Main Street in early December. The 2025 parade, the fourth, was on Saturday, Dec. 6. The 2026 date hadn’t been posted when we checked in October, so watch the village calendar.
### Nearby, down the same trails
The trails don’t stop at the village line, and your Saturday doesn’t have to either. Ride the Nickel Plate north and you’re in Edwardsville, where our guide to free things to do in Edwardsville picks up with band nights and bank fishing. Take the Goshen through Maryville and Troy toward O’Fallon, or follow the Heritage Trail east until it runs out at Marine.
Next time somebody calls Glen Carbon the exit before Edwardsville, you’re the one who knows about the brickyard that helped build the World’s Fair art palace, the caboose that came in by hand and the cabin that nearly went up in smoke. Pick a weekday for the museum and a Saturday for the trail. Then go.
After a loop past the brickyard panel and the canary, our guide to where to eat in Glen Carbon runs from a pub and a tea room to a frozen custard stand and a coffee roaster.
If you run a bike rental, a repair stand or a Main Street shop that Heritage Trail riders pass, list it with us so they find you before they ride home.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is Glen Carbon, IL known for?
A.  Coal, then brick, then trails. Glen Carbon grew up as a company town: workers from the Madison Coal Corporation and the St. Louis Press Brick Company joined 78 locals to petition for incorporation, granted on June 6, 1892. The valley had been the Goshen Settlement since about 1801. Today it’s known for the MCT trail hub at Miner Park, the covered bridge on Main Street, the Yanda Log Cabin and a Homecoming that dates to 1925.
### Q. Is Glen Carbon a city?
A.  No. It’s a village, officially the Village of Glen Carbon, in Madison County, Illinois. It was incorporated on June 6, 1892, and it sits between Edwardsville and Maryville.
### Q. Why are e-bikes not allowed on trails?
A.  On the MCT trails through Glen Carbon, they are. MCT’s rules allow pedal-assist e-bikes, along with e-scooters, Segways, hoverboards and one-wheels, as long as riders keep to the 15 mph limit. Gas-powered bikes and anything with a combustion engine are banned, and the trails are open sunrise to sunset. Where other paths ban e-bikes, speed around walkers is usually the reason. The local exception is Greenspace East, where no bicycles of any kind are allowed.
### Q. What is the longest bike path in Illinois?
A.  The Hennepin Canal State Trail in northwest Illinois usually gets the title. The Illinois Department of Natural Resources describes the Hennepin Canal Parkway as a 104.5-mile linear park, and American Trails counts 93.5 miles of bike trail along it. Closer to home, the longest MCT trail is the 28.5-mile Nickel Plate, and Glen Carbon is where it meets the Heritage Trail.
### Q. What happened to the Nickel Plate Road?
A.  It merged away. The railroad nicknamed the Nickel Plate Road became part of the Norfolk and Western on Oct. 16, 1964. Glen Carbon’s link runs through the Clover Leaf line, which joined the Nickel Plate in 1922 and had a station here. One of the trail’s history panels, Coal Mine No. 1 and Clover Leaf Station, marks the spot. Sources disagree on which old rail lines the MCT Nickel Plate Trail follows, so don’t assume you’re riding the original Nickel Plate grade.
### Q. What is the oldest known log cabin in the United States?
A.  That title usually goes to the C. A. Nothnagle Log House in New Jersey, built by New Sweden settlers between 1638 and 1643. Glen Carbon’s Yanda cabin is about two centuries younger, from around 1853, and it only survived because local historians asked to look under its aluminum siding before a 1989 fire-training burn.
### Q. When is Glen Carbon Homecoming?
A.  Father’s Day weekend, on Main Street. The 2026 Homecoming was billed as the 100th, the Glentennial, and ran June 19 and 20 with a carnival, a Saturday parade and the Covered Bridge 5K. The first one was held in 1925 in Henry’s Park, where the library stands today. A photo exhibit, Glentennial: 100 Years of Homecoming, has been on display at Village Hall during business hours.
### Q. Is the Glen Carbon model railroad open to the public?
A.  Yes, at free open houses. The Metro East Model Railroad Club’s 2026 holiday open houses are Saturday, Nov. 21, Saturday, Dec. 5 and Saturday, Dec. 19, from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m., at the Old Village Hall & Firehouse, 180 Summit Ave. The club also invites visitors to its Thursday evening work sessions, but that page hasn’t been updated in years, so email the club before you show up.

## Things to Do in Oakville, MO: Inside Cliff Cave With a Ranger, the Nims Mansion, Bee Tree Lake
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-oakville-mo
Closed since 2004. That’s the steamboat museum that used to fill the stone mansion in Bee Tree Park, and the county’s own Bee Tree history page still says the house is leased to it. Old information hangs on out here, and it costs you. The bigger loss is the line nearly every write-up about Oakville repeats: the cave at Cliff Cave Park is gated and closed. It is gated. It isn’t closed to you. Every summer, St. Louis County park rangers open the bat gate and lead small groups inside, and this year all 20 sessions sold out.
Oakville is an unincorporated stretch of south St. Louis County, about 36,300 people at the 2020 census, on the bluffs where the Meramec runs into the Mississippi. Most of the region knows it as Telegraph Road. Between that road and the river sit two county parks that hold a cave with an 1868 wine company’s stone walls still at its mouth, a paved greenway that climbs to a river overlook, a stocked lake on the grounds of a 1929 mansion that’s been empty for years, and overlooks the county itself lists for spotting winter bald eagles. Of all the small towns outside St. Louis worth a day, Oakville may hide the most below its own bluffs.
Everything below was checked against St. Louis County Parks, the Missouri Department of Conservation, Great Rivers Greenway and the St. Louis County Library in October 2026. One warning before you search: results mix this Oakville up with a much bigger one in Canada, so if a listing mentions a province, it isn’t this one.
### Is there a cave at Cliff Cave Park?
Yes. Cliff Cave County Park in Oakville has a real limestone cave, more than 4,700 feet of surveyed passage that stays about 57 degrees year-round. It has been gated since 2009 to protect endangered Indiana bats, but St. Louis County park rangers lead small groups inside on summer programs that need reservations and fill fast.
Plenty of people who say they’ve done Cliff Cave walked the paved loop and looked at the gate. Here’s what’s on the other side, and how to get there.
Cliff Cave Capers is the way in. That’s the county’s name for the ranger trip. A park ranger takes up to 10 people per session through the gate to talk about the cave’s history and geology and show you what lives underground. The 2026 season ran May through September, with sessions from 10 a.m. to noon and 1 to 3 p.m., for ages 7 and up at about $15 a person. Helmets and lights are provided. You will get wet and muddy, and you’ll wade through shallow water, so wear clothes and shoes you don’t mind ruining. The county’s caving policy, revised in 2024, says Cliff Cave may be entered only during these ranger-run programs. This is the one legal way in.
Why you plan it in winter. When the 2026 season wrapped in September, the county posted that all 20 sessions had sold out, taking 105 people underground. It said registration for next year is expected to open in January or February. Reservations go through the parks department at 314-615-8822. The county’s own posts say the program typically sells out, so set a reminder for early January now, and check the 2027 fee and dates when they’re announced.
The crawl, for people who’ve done it once. Finish Capers and you can sign up for the Wild Cliff Cave Crawl. A ranger leads the group to the cave’s second entrance, where the ceiling drops to about 18 inches for a belly crawl of roughly 150 feet through water. You bring long sleeves, long pants, gloves and closed-toe shoes. The county supplies helmets, headlamps and pads. In 2026 it ran on two summer afternoons, July 18 and Aug. 2. Sources disagree on the minimum age, 9 or 13, so ask when you call.
What’s at the mouth. You don’t need a reservation to walk up to the entrance, and the history there is still visible. It was first known as Indian Cave. The county says French fur trappers ran a tavern by the river in the 1700s and kept their beer in the cave. In 1868 the Cliff Cave Wine Company bought the site and built the stone walls at the entrance, and those walls still stand. By 1870, local histories say, the cave could store 100,000 gallons of wine, and around 1910 a brewery leased it to store beer. Late in the 1800s, volunteer soldiers from Jefferson Barracks even built a saloon right in the cave’s mouth.
Who lives inside now. The gate went up in October 2009 for endangered Indiana bats. Big and little brown bats, eastern pipistrelles and cave salamanders use the cave too, and the county says bat numbers have grown since it closed. At 4,723 surveyed feet, it’s the second-longest cave in St. Louis County, and it holds that steady 57 degrees in July and January alike. The park around it opened in spring 1977. It’s one of five county Heritage Parks under a 1986 referendum that limits development.
Can’t wait for January? Illinois Caverns near Waterloo is a wild cave you explore on your own, with your own lights, across the Jefferson Barracks Bridge and south into Monroe County. It runs on a season of its own, so check its dates before you drive.
Out of the cave and starving? Where to eat in Oakville, MO
### How long is the trail at Cliff Cave Park?
About 7 paved miles, depending on who’s counting. St. Louis County lists 7.1 miles of the Mississippi Greenway inside the park. Great Rivers Greenway, the regional trails agency, puts it at 6.7. Either way, it splits into two rides that feel nothing alike, with dirt trails on top.
The floodplain loop. Down on the river bottom, the greenway makes a flat loop of about 5 miles with little shade. The county’s 10-10 Bikes program calls it roughly a 5-mile loop and suggests riding it twice for a flat 10. It’s the easy stretch, and our guide to easy family-friendly hiking trails around St. Louis already covers it as a family walk. Bring water and a hat in summer. There’s almost no cover.
The climb to the overlook. This is the newer half, and the better one. A 2.04-mile extension, finished in May 2018, leaves the bottoms, climbs the bluff under real tree cover and reaches a scenic overlook, then connects to Telegraph Road at Erb Road. That gives you a way onto the greenway from the Telegraph side. Ride it downhill first and you’ll earn the climb home.
Dirt, if you want it. River Bluff Trail runs about a mile of earthen path along the bluff top, and the river view from it won the Riverfront Times’ Best View of the Mississippi in 2009. Spring Valley Trail climbs to a karst plateau, the cave-and-sinkhole upland that explains why there’s a cave here at all. The county lists Spring Valley at 1.8 miles and Great Rivers Greenway says 3, so check the county’s park map. Mountain bikers use the trails at the upper end, and the park has equestrian trails too.
What changes by season. Great Rivers Greenway says hundreds of migratory birds pass through in spring and fall, with great blue herons and egrets in summer. After a snowstorm, it says, the area is perfect for cross-country skiing. Two cautions. The lower park floods when the Mississippi runs high, so check with the county after heavy rain upstream. And an active rail line runs through the park, so take every crossing seriously.
Cliff Cave Park is at 806 Cliff Cave Road. It’s open dawn to dusk, with gates open by 8 a.m., and there’s no entry fee.
### What is the history of Bee Tree Park?
It starts with a swarm. According to the historical marker St. Louis County and its parks foundation placed at the park, a 1936 St. Louis Post-Dispatch article said a nephew, Thomas Ratcliffe, named the estate for bees swarming in a grove of white oaks. The estate belonged to Eugene Nims, a Southwestern Bell telephone executive, and his wife, Lotawana. In 1929 they built a Tudor Revival house on the bluff as a weekend retreat, designed by Maritz & Young and built of stone from a quarry less than 2 miles away. Lotawana planted more than 10,000 daffodils on the bluff below it.
How it became a park. St. Louis County bought the 199 acres in April 1968. The $197,000 came through the Open Space Foundation, raised by Lindell Gordon and R. Walston Chubb, with a federal match on top. Gordon was dying while he raised it. His memorial fountain carries a line worth reading in person: “The imprint of a dying leaf is wondrous to behold.”
The Frisbee Shelter has nothing to do with the disc. It’s named for Emmett Frisbee, a D-Day and Battle of the Bulge veteran who went to work for the county parks department in 1951. It’s also where you’ll find the park’s year-round restroom.
The museum years. In 1974 the Golden Eagle River Museum moved into the mansion. It took its name from the Steamer Golden Eagle, the last overnight packet boat out of St. Louis, which sank on May 18, 1947. Volunteers ran it from May to October for 31 years, among pilot wheels, riverboat bells, steam whistles and boat models. Before Bee Tree, the club had shown its collection around town, including inside Cherokee Cave. By 2002 the volunteer pool was aging and shrinking, and in October 2004 the members voted to close and split up the collection. The farewell party was held on Oct. 31, 2004. Papers, photographs and artifacts were divided between a regional museum in southeast Missouri and the Herman T. Pott National Inland Waterways Library at the St. Louis Mercantile Library. A history of the museum published by Southeast Missouri State University says the club itself never disbanded and kept an office at the Carondelet Historical Society.
The empty house now. The mansion was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2017, and it has sat empty for years. In July 2026 the county put a roof replacement out to bid. You can’t go inside, but the grounds are open during park hours, and the Mansion Garden and the Overlook are both booked as wedding sites. From the Chubb Memorial Overlook you look straight across the Mississippi to the Illinois bluffs.
### Does Bee Tree Park have a lake or river?
Both, but you fish only one of them. Bee Tree Lake is a 9-acre lake the Missouri Department of Conservation stocks under a management contract with the county. The Mississippi runs below the park’s bluff, and at Bee Tree it’s the view. For river fishing, Cliff Cave is the better bet.
The lake. MDC lists white bass, sunfish, catfish, crappie and black bass. The county deepened the lake in 2000 and added an accessible fishing dock, so anglers who can’t manage a steep bank still have a spot. Boats aren’t allowed. It’s a bank-and-dock lake, and a gravel trail circles the whole shoreline, so you can work every side of it in one morning.
The rules. Anglers 16 through 64 need a Missouri fishing permit, and Missouri residents 65 and older are exempt. For other lakes and the full rundown on permits, see our picks for the best fishing spots in St. Louis.
The river. For the Mississippi, drive a short way north to Cliff Cave Park. The county lists Mississippi River fishing among that park’s features, and Great Rivers Greenway says plainly that you can fish the river there. The Riverside Shelter has a year-round restroom and can be reserved for a group. If it’s the Meramec you’re after, cross it. Arnold sits on the far bank, and our guide to fishing in Arnold covers that side.
### How to spend a day in Oakville, MO?
Build it around the cave in summer and around the eagles in winter. Here’s the summer version, since that’s the one you have to book.
Morning, underground. Take the 10 a.m. Capers session if you can get it, and plan to come out around noon wet to the shins. Leave a full change of clothes, a towel and a plastic bag for your shoes in the car. Cliff Cave’s gates open by 8 a.m., which leaves time for a lap of River Bluff Trail before you go underground.
Midday, Telegraph Road. Lunch is up the bluff on Telegraph, where Oakville’s family-owned restaurants cluster.
Afternoon, the overlook. Bike or walk the greenway extension up the bluff. It’s the shaded half of the trail, which matters in July.
Late day, Bee Tree. Drive south to Bee Tree Park with a rod. Fish the dock for an hour, walk up to the Nims Mansion grounds and the Gordon fountain, and finish at the Chubb Memorial Overlook, facing the Illinois bluffs across the river while the sun goes down behind you.
The winter swap. The cave trips stop after September. In January and February, trade the headlamp for binoculars and start at the bluff overlooks. The next section has the exact spots.
### What are free things to do in Oakville, MO?
Almost everything on this page except the cave trip. Neither county park charges admission, and the best free show of the year needs no ticket at all.
Bald eagles from the bluffs. In January 2026, St. Louis County Parks posted its own list of places to see bald eagles, and two Oakville parks made it: Cliff Cave Park, at the Mississippi Greenway overlook or the Riverside Shelter, and Bee Tree Park, at the Crow’s Roost Trail overlook. January and early February are the window, before the birds head north. Dress for wind on the bluff. Bring binoculars.
Sunset on River Bluff Trail. The bluff-top path behind that 2009 best-view award costs nothing. Get there an hour before sunset. The park closes at dusk.
The trails. About 7 paved miles of greenway at Cliff Cave, plus Spring Valley, plus four short trails at Bee Tree. All of it is open dawn to dusk at no charge.
Fishing. Bee Tree Lake and the Mississippi bank at Cliff Cave cost nothing beyond your state fishing permit.
The library’s calendar. The Cliff Cave Branch of St. Louis County Library, at 5430 Telegraph Road, runs free events, and its 2026 highlight for small kids is a Halloween Party and Costume Parade for ages 0 to 6 on Friday, Oct. 30, at 10 a.m. Check the library’s event calendar before you go, since details can change. Reading this after Halloween? The same calendar lists what’s next.
### What can you do in Oakville on a rainy day?
Rain pushes Oakville indoors, and Telegraph Road has two good answers, plus one you can do from the couch.
A library that shakes. The Cliff Cave Branch library puts a fun fact on its own web page: it’s built near two active quarries, and on blasting days you can hear the blast and feel the vibrations. The branch opened in 1980 and was renovated in 2016, when it gained a more open floor plan, a new children’s area and a large south-facing window that looks out on the branch’s community garden. It’s open Monday through Thursday 9 a.m. to 8 p.m. and Friday and Saturday 9 to 5, and closed Sundays.
Free-roam VR on Telegraph. STL Virtual Reality, at 5626 Telegraph Road in the Dierbergs plaza, runs wireless Quest 3 headsets in a free-roam space where up to six players see and play with each other in real time. There are co-op games, player-versus-player games and VR escape rooms, which makes it a good rainy-day date or a teen birthday that isn’t another trampoline park. It’s open Thursday 2 to 7 p.m., Friday 2 to 8, Saturday noon to 8 and Sunday noon to 7, and closed Monday through Wednesday. It charged $35 for 45 minutes when it opened in 2023, so check current pricing. For more ideas across the metro, see our list of indoor activities in St. Louis.
The steamboat museum, from the couch. The Golden Eagle River Museum collection is held at the St. Louis Mercantile Library at UMSL, and the UMSL Digital Library has scanned riverboat photographs credited to the museum that you can browse online. It’s the closest anyone can get now to the rooms that filled the Nims Mansion for 31 years.
Museums a short drive north. If the rain lets up, Jefferson Barracks Park, just north of Oakville, has military museums of its own, and our guide to historic sites in St. Louis covers them.
### Nearby, across the Meramec and the Mississippi
Oakville ends at the Meramec. Cross it and you’re in Arnold. A few miles farther down the river, Kimmswick’s 1874 iron bridge once carried Carondelet traffic over the River des Peres, the same Carondelet where the Golden Eagle club set up its office. Head east over the Jefferson Barracks Bridge instead and you’re in Illinois, on the road to Waterloo’s caves.
So the next time somebody tells you Oakville is just Telegraph Road traffic, you’re the one who knows a ranger walks people through the bat gate at Cliff Cave every summer, that the steamboat museum moved out in 2004, and which bluff the county itself sends you to for eagles. Set the January reminder now. Next summer, you’re the one with the cave trip booked, not the one reading about the gate.
After a muddy morning in the cave or a cold one on the bluff, our guide to where to eat in Oakville, MO maps the family-owned rooms on Telegraph Road, from a 50-year Italian institution to a barbecue kitchen that serves German dumplings.
If you run a bait shop, an outfitter or a Telegraph Road kitchen that cavers and anglers pass on the way to Cliff Cave and Bee Tree, list it with us so they find you before they head home.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What happened at Cliff Cave Park?
A.  On July 23, 1993, during that summer’s record Midwest floods, a flash flood filled Cliff Cave while seven people from a local boys’ home group were inside. Six of them drowned. A 13-year-old boy survived the night on a ledge above the water and was rescued the next day. Today the cave stays gated, and the county allows entry only on ranger-led programs.
### Q. What time does Bee Tree Park open?
A.  Bee Tree Park is open from dawn, which the county defines as half an hour before official sunrise, to dusk, half an hour after sunset. The gates open by 7 a.m. Cliff Cave Park keeps the same dawn-to-dusk hours, with its gates open by 8 a.m.
### Q. Are there hiking trails at Bee Tree Park?
A.  Yes, four short ones, going by published trail notes. Fishermen’s Trail is a gravel loop of about 0.8 mile around the lake. Crow’s Roost Trail runs about 0.8 mile along the bluff overlook and down to the lake. Paw Paw Trail covers about half a mile in the woods, and Cedar Trail is a short, steep spur. Check the county’s park map for current lengths.
### Q. Where is Bee Tree Park located?
A.  Bee Tree Park is at 2701 Finestown Ave. in Oakville, St. Louis 63129, on the bluff just above where the Meramec meets the Mississippi. MDC’s directions: take Telegraph Road south from I-255, turn left on Becker, then follow Finestown down to the park.
### Q. What is the best cave to visit near St. Louis?
A.  It depends on how much mud you want. For a real wild cave with a guide, Cliff Cave Capers runs May through September, with registration expected in January or February. For a short walk-in with no reservation, the county’s caving policy lists Mud Cave, about 75 feet long, in Greensfelder County Park. For a full day of self-guided caving, Illinois Caverns near Waterloo is the trip. Missouri had about 7,300 documented caves as of 2018, the second most of any state, according to the Missouri Speleological Survey.
### Q. What are the popular attractions near Bee Tree Park?
A.  The closest is Cliff Cave Park, a short drive north, with its ranger cave trips, about 7 miles of paved greenway and River Bluff Trail. Up on Telegraph Road you’ll find the Cliff Cave Branch library and STL Virtual Reality. Across the Meramec are Arnold and Kimmswick, and the Jefferson Barracks Bridge puts the Illinois side of the river in easy reach.
### Q. Is the Golden Eagle River Museum still open?
A.  No. The museum opened in the Nims Mansion in 1974, ran on volunteers for 31 years and closed with a farewell party on Oct. 31, 2004. Its collection was split between a regional museum in southeast Missouri and the Herman T. Pott National Inland Waterways Library at the St. Louis Mercantile Library, where researchers can still use it.
### Q. Can you go inside the Nims Mansion?
A.  Not for tours. The 1929 house is on the National Register of Historic Places but has stood empty for years, and in July 2026 the county put out a bid to replace its roof. The grounds are open during park hours, and the Mansion Garden and the Overlook are both bookable wedding sites.

## Things to Do in Elsberry, MO: Ted Shanks, Clarence Cannon Refuge, Snow Geese
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-elsberry-mo
Ever wonder why every eagle-watching list sends St. Louis across the river to the same Illinois bluffs? The lists copy each other. Meanwhile, on one day in December 2022, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service counted 77,076 ducks on a free federal refuge about 10 miles north of Elsberry, and on Feb. 13, 2023, its survey logged 30,000 snow geese on the same ground. Those counts come from the refuge’s 2022-23 season, which is the latest the agency has posted, so check its survey page for a newer table before you plan around them. None of the recycled lists mention the place.
The refuge is named for a man born in Elsberry in 1879. Clarence Cannon went on to serve 41 years in Congress, punched a fellow congressman in the face during a 1945 argument, and came home in 1964 for a funeral that brought a sitting president to a field outside town by helicopter. Hardly anyone connects the name on the refuge sign to a Lincoln County town of 1,937 people at the 2020 census. Farther up the same highway, Ted Shanks Conservation Area adds 6,705 acres of marsh, oxbow lakes and river bluffs that the eagle lists skip entirely.
Of all the small towns outside St. Louis worth a day, Elsberry is the one that sits between three public wetlands on the Mississippi Flyway. Everything below was checked against U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Missouri Department of Conservation, USDA and city pages in October 2026, and it’s sorted by what you came to see. Bring binoculars. Let everybody else fight over the Illinois pull-offs this winter.
### What is Elsberry, Missouri known for?
Elsberry is the Lincoln County river town where Congressman Clarence Cannon was born in 1879 and buried in 1964, with a sitting president at his funeral. It sits at the edge of the Mississippi floodplain, with the wetlands of B.K. Leach Conservation Area just south and the free Clarence Cannon National Wildlife Refuge about 10 miles north.
Start with Cannon, because the town does. He was born on April 11, 1879, and Elsberry itself was surveyed and platted that August, so the boy and the town grew up together. His father ran a general store and later served as the town’s second mayor. Cannon became House parliamentarian, compiled the rulebook still known as Cannon’s Precedents, and chaired the House Appropriations Committee for about 19 years in all. He also had a temper. In 1945 he punched Rep. John Taber of New York during an argument, and years later he mocked the space program as a “moondoggle.”
When he died in May 1964, the funeral came home to the First Baptist Church in Elsberry. President Lyndon Johnson flew into St. Louis and took a helicopter to a field on the edge of town to join the motorcade. Former President Harry Truman came too. About 4,000 people filled the streets, some with lawn chairs, ladders and packed lunches. Cannon is buried in Elsberry City Cemetery, and visiting the grave costs nothing.
Then there’s the ground under the town. The 1888 county history put Elsberry “fifty-eight miles north of the city of St. Louis” on the old railroad, and it described two halves that people called “on the hill” and “under the hill.” The hill half sits on a bench of the bluffs, with what that history called a view of the Mississippi Valley and the hills on the Illinois side. The flat bottomland below the bluff is why the birds come. It’s also why two state conservation areas and a federal refuge line Highway 79 north and south of town.
### What can you do at Ted Shanks Conservation Area?
Hike, fish, camp at a primitive site, watch birds and, in season, hunt ducks, on 6,705 acres where the Salt River runs into the Mississippi. It’s the biggest of the three wildlife areas on this stretch of Highway 79, and the longest drive on this page: about 45 road miles north of Elsberry, straight up Highway 79 and then east on Route TT. Fill the tank in town.
The land has a pedigree St. Louis should care about. Zebulon Pike charted the mouth of the Salt River in 1805. MDC says the area was a hunting and battle ground for the Sac and Fox from the north and the Osage from the south. In 1799 it was granted to a man named Saucier, and it passed from him to Auguste Chouteau, one of the founders of St. Louis, and then to Neree Valle, a name tied to the founding of Ste. Genevieve. The state bought it in 1970 and 1971, and a federal excise tax on guns and ammunition paid 75 percent of the original purchase.
What’s out there. The area borders 8.75 miles of Mississippi River frontage, 4.75 miles of the Salt River and 2.25 miles of river bluffs. Inside that line, MDC manages bottomland hardwoods, open marsh, oxbow lakes, sloughs, old fields and upland woods. It also runs plumbing most visitors never notice: 35 miles of levees, three pump stations, nine miles of canals and 45 water-control structures, split into 25 management units. That machinery lets the state flood fields on cue for migrating birds, and Visit Missouri puts the seasonally flooded acreage at about 4,000.
Hiking and the overlook. MDC lists hiking among the area’s uses, and its area map marks a hiking trail, a scenic overlook and a picnic area. Vehicles stay on the gravel and paved roads and in the parking lots, and the speed limit is 45 unless posted otherwise. Pick a clear morning and take the binoculars up to the overlook first.
Camping. Ted Shanks is one of the conservation areas where MDC allows camping, at designated sites. The statewide rules apply: no more than 14 consecutive days in any 30-day period, quiet hours from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m., and a special use permit for groups of more than 10. Seasonal closures can cover campsites too, so check the area map before you pack the tent.
Fishing. MDC lists white bass, sunfish, catfish, crappie and black bass. A concrete boat ramp drops into the Salt River, and the area holds more than 500 acres of fishable water, Horseshoe Lake among them. On lakes and ponds under 70 acres, only electric motors are allowed. On bigger water, outboards over 10 horsepower have to run at slow, no-wake speed.
Birds and other wildlife. MDC’s short what-to-look-for list for the area names the mallard, the bald eagle, white-tailed deer and the North American snapping turtle. In spring and fall, the managed units turn into a rest stop for whatever is moving up and down the river.
Hunting. Waterfowl hunting runs on a daily morning draw. Deer hunting is archery only, and the list also covers turkey, rabbit, squirrel, dove and quail. Shotgun hunters must use nontoxic shot. Lead is banned on the area.
The calendar that matters. Ted Shanks is open from 4 a.m. to 10 p.m. But portions close to protect waterfowl every year from Oct. 15 through March 1, and during duck season only authorized hunters may be inside the waterfowl shooting areas, where shooting ends at 1 p.m. MDC also posts a standing warning that the area floods, so check local conditions and never drive onto a flooded road. Call (573) 248-2530 before a long drive. If you’re reading this in early October, Oct. 15 is the date to circle. Go before it for the full run of roads, or after it for the birds and a view from the edges.
### What can you see at Clarence Cannon National Wildlife Refuge?
Big flocks of ducks in late fall, geese through the winter, shorebirds in spring and nesting bald eagles, on 3,750 acres of Mississippi floodplain that cost nothing to visit. It’s about 10 miles north of Elsberry. Take Highway 79 north, then go one mile east on Pike County Road 206 to the headquarters at 37599 Pike 206. The refuge invites you to call ahead at (573) 847-2333 and ask what’s moving that week, so do it.
The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service bought the land in 1964 with duck stamp money, the federal stamp waterfowl hunters buy every season, and named it for Cannon, who the agency says was “influential in its establishment.” It used to be farmland in an agricultural levee district, and all but a few hundred acres still sit behind a levee. The refuge’s job is narrow and stated plainly: a feeding and resting area for migratory birds. FWS says nearly 300 bird species use it during migration.
How to see it, by the clock. FWS gives visitors a time menu, and it’s a good one. With 15 minutes, stop at the headquarters and visitor contact station, finished in 2008, where exhibits tell the story of the Mississippi Flyway. With an hour, drive the auto route. With half a day or more, hike, bird or photograph. The nature trail is unpaved and open all year, unless it’s posted closed for weather or to protect eagles nesting nearby. A pair of bald eagles built the refuge’s first nest in 1991.
Hours and the fine print. Refuge lands, roads and trails are open from a half hour before sunrise to a half hour after sunset. The visitor contact station keeps weekday hours, 7:30 a.m. to 4 p.m., Monday through Friday except federal holidays, and it may close for flooding or winter weather. The only restrooms are inside, during those hours. Many parts of the refuge are reachable on foot only, and weather can ruin the roads, so dress for mud.
When to go: read the survey table. Refuge staff count birds through fall and winter and post the results online. As of October 2026, the latest season posted is fall 2022 through winter 2023. Treat these dated counts as a pattern, not a forecast for this year:
Read it the way a fisherman reads a tide chart. In that season the ducks went from a dozen in early October to 77,076 on Dec. 6, 2022, then fell to 1,100 three weeks later. That’s a narrow window. If the pattern holds, late November and the first half of December are the duck weeks, and the geese hang around longer. Check the FWS survey page for a newer table before you go, because a wet fall or an early freeze can move everything.
One more surprise. This headquarters also runs two other refuges, Great River and Middle Mississippi River, and the Middle Mississippi refuge’s island divisions sit far downriver near Ste. Genevieve. A lot of the federal refuge land along this river is managed from a building on a county road north of Elsberry.
### Where can you see snow geese near St. Louis?
At Clarence Cannon National Wildlife Refuge, on the Mississippi floodplain north of Elsberry, where the survey counted 30,000 snow geese on Feb. 13, 2023, the biggest snow goose count in the latest season the agency has posted. Here’s what that same survey says about timing, since snow geese don’t keep a schedule.
In the 2022-23 season, the first 2,000 snow geese showed up on the Nov. 29, 2022 count. The flock grew to 7,000 by Dec. 19, 2022, dropped off the count over the holidays, came back at 3,200 on Jan. 9, 2023, and then hit 30,000 on Feb. 13, 2023. A week later the survey found none. That’s the whole lesson. The big push can last about a week, so watch the weather in February and call the refuge before you drive. The same table logged 22,000 greater white-fronted geese on Dec. 19, 2022, and trumpeter swans twice, 4 on Dec. 13, 2022 and 8 on Jan. 4, 2023. Those are the newest numbers posted, not this winter’s.
MDC calls the snow goose a common migrant and an uncommon winter resident in Missouri. Its field guide adds two things worth knowing before you go. Snow geese fly day and night and prefer clear days with no rain or snow, so a clear, dry day is your best shot at seeing a flock in the air. And they’re an important winter food for bald and golden eagles. Where the geese pile up, keep one eye on the tree line.
The closer option: B.K. Leach. You don’t have to drive all the way to the refuge. B.K. Leach Memorial Conservation Area starts about six miles from town: Highway 79 south 3 miles, then Route M east 3 miles to the main tract. Our Troy guide, the one built around camping at Cuivre River State Park, already covers its size, hours and fall closure, so here’s only what that guide skips. MDC’s birding trail page says 234 species have been documented on B.K. Leach, and the rare king rail is known to breed there. Bittern Basin, the separate unit on Highway P across from the turnoff to Prairie Slough Conservation Area, is the spot to know, and MDC’s map marks waterfowl hunting and viewing blinds plus a disabled-accessible blind. There are no designated trails, and the ground is wet. MDC’s own tip is the best one: use your car as a blind, sit still, and let the birds get used to you.
Cold from the levee? Where to eat in Elsberry, MO
### Where do bald eagles winter near Elsberry?
Along the river and around the refuge wetlands, from late December through early February. MDC lists the bald eagle as a common winter migrant, counted more than 600 active nests in Missouri in 2025, and tells eagle watchers to look for birds perched in large trees at the water’s edge. Go early. Mornings are when they’re flying and fishing.
Three spots on this stretch of river are worth an early alarm.
The refuge. Eagles have nested there since that first pair in 1991, and the nature trail can close when a nest is active nearby. Take that as good news. In the latest survey season posted, the refuge counted seven adult bald eagles on Dec. 13, 2022, a week after the duck count peaked.
Ted Shanks. MDC names the bald eagle on its short list of what to look for there. Bring a spotting scope to the overlook and scan the big trees along the water.
Lock and Dam 25. It’s on MDC’s statewide list of best places for winter eagle viewing, on the Mississippi south of Elsberry. The lock opened in 1939, and the Army Corps of Engineers says it’s preparing for major construction on a new 1,200-foot lock, so check access before you go.
Most eagle guides send you straight to Illinois, and the Illinois bluffs are good. If you want that side too, Pere Marquette’s eagle programs are in our guide to things to do in Grafton in winter. This page stays on the Missouri bank.
### What is there to do on the Missouri side of the Great River Road?
Drive Highway 79. Say “Great River Road” in St. Louis and most people picture the Illinois bluffs. On the Missouri side it’s Route 79, which carries the Great River Road north from I-70 at the O’Fallon and St. Peters line, and Elsberry sits about 29 miles up it. The northern 30 miles of the route form the Little Dixie Highway of the Great River Road, a National Scenic Byway since 2002, and Ted Shanks is one of its listed stops.
Here’s the run, with nothing on it you’d find on a postcard rack.
The oldest plant materials center in the country, by its own account. The USDA’s Elsberry Plant Materials Center, established in 1934, sits on Highway 79, and an NRCS brochure calls it “the oldest Center in the nation.” Its 243 acres are a working research station that has developed more than 80 conservation plants for Missouri, Illinois and Iowa, among them big bluestem, sideoats grama and pale purple coneflower. It isn’t set up as an attraction, so don’t count on a tour. If you want to ask about one, call 573-898-2012 first.
A native-plant nursery you can shop. Forrest Keeling Nursery’s garden store, at 88 Forrest Keeling Lane, is open to the public Monday through Saturday. Its website lists 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., and its Facebook page has shown a later close, so check before you go. The nursery says it grows more than 250 species of native trees and shrubs, and it calls itself the largest producer of native plants in North America. It was also a partner on the 2001 wetland deal that added 2,900 acres to B.K. Leach. Fall is planting season, which makes October a good month to fill the trunk.
The wildlife string. B.K. Leach south and east of town, the refuge about 10 miles north, Ted Shanks about 45 road miles north. That’s nearly 14,800 acres of public wetland and woods along one highway, and you don’t pay to get into any of it.
The view. Stop on the hill in Elsberry and look east. The 1888 county history promised a view across the valley to the Illinois hills, and you can test that claim from the bench of the bluffs where most of the town still lives.
When the river rises. Route 79 runs close to the Mississippi, and floods in 2019 closed stretches of it. When the river is high, check MoDOT’s traveler map before you leave.
For the other bank, our guide to the Illinois side of the Great River Road from Alton to Grafton covers the bluffs and the ferry, and our roundup of scenic drives around St. Louis has more routes for a fall color day. To cross from here without driving to a bridge you need a boat, and our guide to ferries near St. Louis covers the Golden Eagle Ferry and the Winfield Ferry, the backup that runs when ice or high water closes the Golden Eagle.
### What free things can you do in Elsberry?
More than you’d expect from a town this size, and most of it is history you can put your hand on.
The Old Calaboose. In the 200 block of North 2nd Street stands a limestone town jail, believed to date from about 1896. It replaced a wooden one that burned after a prisoner set newspapers on fire to get attention and nearly died before anyone let him out. According to the town’s history, the stone came from a quarry on the old Page Branch Road run by two African-American brothers, Ira and Tom Smith, and it was hauled into town on a sled pulled by oxen. Each block is 36 inches long and 17 inches on a side. Inside you’ll find one iron-barred cell and a potbellied stove. Only four or five calabooses are left in Missouri, and this one made Missouri Preservation’s Places in Peril list in 2015. A 2019 visitor guide listed it as free to see from dawn to dusk. The Elsberry Historic Preservation Society opened its museum next door free during this year’s Fall Festival, so watch its page for the next open day.
Cannon’s grave. Elsberry City Cemetery. Stand there a minute and picture 4,000 people and two presidents in a town this size.
Page Branch Park. The city’s newer park, on 5th Street, has a walking trail, a playground and a pavilion. It takes its name from the same creek the calaboose stone came out of.
A rainy-day plan. The Joseph R. Palmer Family Memorial Library is at 502 Broadway. Its posted hours don’t match across its own pages, so check current hours before you go. On a weekday, the refuge visitor contact station’s flyway exhibits are free and dry. And The Pickle Barrel, at 401 Broadway, keeps pinball and arcade machines next to its ice cream counter, which is the best way we know to end a cold morning on a levee.
The town calendar. The Elsberry Fall Festival lands on the first Saturday of October at City Park on Broadway. The 74th ran on Oct. 3, 2026, so expect the 75th on the first Saturday of October 2027, and check dates. Christmas in the Park ran on Dec. 6, 2025, with Santa from 3 to 4:30 p.m. in the Methodist Church Hall, a 5 p.m. parade and vendors. The 2026 date hasn’t been posted, but it’s usually early December, so check the city’s page. In summer, the Elsberry Community Growth Association runs free concerts at First Mid Park, 402 S. 4th St. The 2026 series, its ninth, played June 13, July 3 and Aug. 8 from 6 to 9 p.m. Bring chairs. The 2027 dates haven’t been announced.
Heading home? Highway 79 drops you back on I-70 at the O’Fallon and St. Peters line, and if there’s daylight left, our list of free things to do in O’Fallon, MO is right on the way.
Next time someone tells you eagle season means Illinois, you’re the one who knows whose name is on the refuge sign, that the 2022-23 survey, the latest posted, counted 77,076 ducks there on one December day, and that a snow goose flock can come and go in a week. Check the survey page. Call the refuge. Then drive north.
After a cold morning on the refuge auto route, our guide to where to eat in Elsberry, MO covers the warm-up stops on Broadway and North Main.
If you run a bait shop, a guide service or a Broadway storefront that birders and duck hunters pass on Highway 79, list it with us so they find you before they head home.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How far is Elsberry, MO from St. Louis?
A.  About 58 road miles from downtown St. Louis, which happens to match the 1888 county history’s figure of “fifty-eight miles north” by rail. The usual route is I-70 west to Highway 79, then about 29 miles north on 79 from the O’Fallon and St. Peters line. Plan on more than an hour from downtown, and check your map app for traffic before you leave.
### Q. What time of year do snow geese migrate?
A.  In Missouri, fall through late winter. At Clarence Cannon National Wildlife Refuge north of Elsberry, the 2022-23 survey, the latest season the agency has posted, found the first 2,000 snow geese on Nov. 29, 2022, then 7,000 on Dec. 19, 2022, and a peak of 30,000 on Feb. 13, 2023. MDC calls them a common migrant and an uncommon winter resident. They spend the winter in the southern part of their range, Missouri included, and nest on the Arctic tundra from Nunavut east to Hudson Bay.
### Q. Is it rare to see a bald eagle in Missouri?
A.  No. MDC lists the bald eagle as a common winter migrant and counted more than 600 active nests statewide in 2025. That’s a long way from the early 1960s, when the whole Lower 48 was down to 417 nesting pairs. From 1981 to 1990, MDC and its partners released 74 young eagles to rebuild Missouri’s nesting population, and it still lists the bird as a species of conservation concern. For the best odds near Elsberry, go from late December through early February, early in the morning.
### Q. What is not allowed in National Wildlife Refuges?
A.  It depends on the refuge, because each one allows only uses that fit its purpose. At Clarence Cannon, the posted rules ban camping and fires, ATVs and UTVs, alcohol, target shooting, and collecting shed deer antlers, mussels, clams, crayfish, frogs or turtles. Dogs must be on a leash, and lands close a half hour after sunset. Fishing is by boat only in Bryants Creek and the Mississippi and its side channels, and gas motors are banned everywhere except Bryants Creek. Berries and mushrooms are fine for your own table.
### Q. Is a national wildlife refuge the same as a national park?
A.  No. A national wildlife refuge is run by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service for wildlife first, and every activity has to fit the reason the refuge exists. Clarence Cannon was set up in 1964 as a feeding and resting area for migratory birds and bought with duck stamp money. It charges no fee and allows no camping. Visitors get an auto route, a nature trail and a weekday visitor contact station instead.
### Q. Can you camp anywhere on conservation land in Missouri?
A.  No. On Missouri Department of Conservation areas, camping is allowed only where the area’s page lists it. Ted Shanks Conservation Area has designated camping sites, while at B.K. Leach, just below Elsberry, camping is prohibited. Where it’s allowed, you can stay 14 consecutive days in any 30, and no more than 30 days a year across all MDC areas without a special use permit. Quiet hours run from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m., and groups of more than 10 need a permit.
### Q. Where are the best duck hunting conservation areas in Missouri?
A.  We won’t rank them, since a good season depends on water and weather. Here’s what we can tell you. MDC runs managed wetland areas with a daily morning draw, and two of them are near Elsberry. B.K. Leach and Ted Shanks are both on MDC’s list of 19 areas where waterfowl hunting on designated portions ends at 1 p.m., hunters need a Daily Waterfowl Hunting Tag, and the areas close to waterfowl hunting on Dec. 25. Nontoxic shot is required on both. Hunting at Clarence Cannon refuge follows refuge and state rules.
### Q. Where does Great River Road start and end?
A.  It follows the Mississippi from Minnesota to the Gulf of Mexico through 10 states. North of St. Louis on the Missouri side, it rides Highway 79 from I-70 at the O’Fallon and St. Peters line, past Elsberry, and its northern 30 miles form the Little Dixie Highway of the Great River Road, a National Scenic Byway since 2002. Across the river near St. Louis, the Illinois route follows the bluffs from Alton to Grafton.

## Things to Do in New Haven, MO: Public Telescope Nights, $5 Movies at the Walt, John Colter's Lost Grave
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/things-to-do-in-new-haven-mo
Forget the wineries. Every recycled New Haven list leads with a tasting room that closes by 5, and a widely circulated one still sends readers to a winery that retired in 2023. The New Haven worth the drive starts after dark. On scheduled Friday nights from March through November, a volunteer astronomy club opens a 30-inch telescope in a field two miles west of town to anyone who walks down the rock road at dusk. Downtown, an Art Deco movie house that opened in 1940 still projects onto its original screen, and a ticket still costs $5, cash or check.
New Haven sits on the south bank of the Missouri River in Franklin County, 11 miles west of Washington on Highway 100 and about 64 miles from downtown St. Louis. It has 2,414 people, a short downtown on Front Street, a levee you can walk on, and a reputation as a wine-and-gin stop that empties out once the tasting bars close. Of all the small towns outside St. Louis, it’s the one most people leave an hour too early.
Everything below was checked against the astronomy club’s, the theater’s, the Missouri Department of Conservation’s, the chamber’s and the organizers’ own pages on Oct. 6, 2026. Small-town schedules move. Check before you drive.
### Is there anything to do in New Haven MO?
Yes, and the best of it happens after the tasting rooms close. New Haven, MO has a 1940 Art Deco movie house where tickets are still $5, a 30-inch telescope a club opens to the public on scheduled Friday nights, a levee river walk past John Colter’s memorial, and a Pumpkin Glow and Christmas by Moonlight downtown.
Besides Röbller Vineyard and Pinckney Bend Distillery, which lead every list and which our guide to where to eat in New Haven, MO already covers, the town runs a second shift. For everything else, here’s New Haven sorted by when you’d go:
Friday nights, March through November: Big Blue, the 30-inch telescope, on the club’s scheduled dates. Friday, Saturday and Sunday, most weeks: a first-run movie at the Walt for $5. Any daylight hour: the levee walk and the cluster of historical markers at John Colter Memorial Park. Rainy afternoons: theater seats facing a glass furnace at Astral Glass, and two free museums in an 1883 schoolhouse. October: the Scarecrow Festival and Pumpkin Glow downtown, plus a U-pick pumpkin patch out on Highway E. December: two free Fridays of Christmas by Moonlight.
A lot of that is free. The movie is five dollars.
### How much is a movie at the Walt Theatre in New Haven?
Five dollars. That’s the ticket price at the Walt Theatre, 111 Front St., and children 2 and under get in free. The box office takes cash or check only, so bring cash. Shows run Friday and Saturday at 7 p.m. and Sunday at 5 p.m., and the box office opens 30 minutes before each one. The Walt plays first-run movies, meaning current releases, plus the occasional special screening.
Here’s why it’s worth the trip. The Walt opened on Nov. 14, 1940, with three showings of the western “Wyoming,” starring Wallace Beery. Kids paid 10 cents. Adults paid 25. More than 85 years later the theater still has the same marquee out front, and it still projects onto the same white screen that first movie played on. The one big change came in the summer of 2014, when it switched from 35mm film to digital; the first digital show was Friday, Aug. 29, 2014. It’s a fully restored Art Deco house, and it’s locally owned and operated.
Do the date-night math. Two tickets cost $10. The Sunday 5 p.m. show has you back in St. Louis at a reasonable hour before the work week starts.
One 2026 date: on Saturday, Oct. 17, from 7 to 9 p.m., the Walt is set to screen “The Trail State,” a documentary about how Missouri turned a flooded rail line into the Katy Trail, America’s longest rail-trail. Gov. Mike Kehoe proclaimed Sept. 22 Trail State Day, the day the film premiered at the Missouri History Museum. Seeing it in a 1940 theater, in a river town that sits across the water from the trail, beats watching it at home. Its 2026 schedule also had the Walt closed Oct. 9 to 11 and on Oct. 18, so check the Now Showing panel on its homepage before you drive.
For cheaper seats closer to home, our guide to cheap movie tickets in St. Louis covers discount days and the independent single screens around the city. The Walt is the long-drive version of the same idea, with a better marquee.
