Each one holds a quote from a former resident, set inside, so you have to lean in and look for it. Great Rivers Greenway says Davis wanted visitors to put in the effort to unearth those voices. A granite slab nearby lists the name, age and occupation of everyone who lived on that block of Market Street, with a map that marks the four surviving buildings in gold. Benches and plantings trace the old lot lines, and the pre-demolition address of each parcel is etched into the concrete. A tactile model with braille is part of it. The stretch west to Harris-Stowe opened on April 13, 2026, St. Louis Public Radio reported. It’s outdoors and free.
2. The Stars Park marker and ballfield, 3100 Market St. Keep walking west on the greenway to Compton. Harris-Stowe’s baseball field sits close to where Stars Park stood, and the marker the Society for American Baseball Research dedicated there in 2007 tells the Stars’ story. A baseball historian told MLB.com it’s one of the few 1920s Negro Leagues sites still played on as a diamond. St. Louis ArtWorks students painted a St. Louis Stars mural along the new stretch.
3. The Vashon Center at Harris-Stowe. The 1937 community center reopened in April 2023 as home to the Don and Heide Wolff Jazz Institute and the National Black Radio Hall of Fame. Harris-Stowe lists the jazz institute’s gallery as free and open to the public. Call the university to confirm hours before you go.
4. The Legacy of Mill Creek, at Grand and Lindell. Four panels by St. Louis artist Cbabi Bayoc, on faith, business, music and sports, surround the fountain at the southeast corner of Grand and Lindell on SLU’s campus. SLU dedicated them on Sept. 10, 2024, and calls the corner a historic entrance to the old neighborhood. Read the backs, too. Each one carries a handwritten note from the artist.
5. The Scott Joplin House State Historic Site, 2658 Delmar Blvd. Joplin lived in the second-floor flat from 1900 to 1903, a few blocks north of the valley’s Olive Street edge. Missouri State Parks runs guided tours; check current hours and fees before you go. It’s the closest you’ll get to the ragtime world that filled Market Street.
If you want to dig. The State Historical Society of Missouri’s St. Louis research center at UMSL holds the John Goldston Photograph Collection, 1958-1963, which documents the destruction of Mill Creek Valley. The Missouri Historical Society’s online collections search well on “Mill Creek,” and its Library and Research Center is at 225 S. Skinker Blvd. UMSL’s digital humanities students built online exhibits and a driving tour of more than 20 sites. Washington University’s open scholarship site posts the 1958 Redevelopment Plan for Mill Creek Valley Project as a free PDF, if you want to read the city’s own words. And Gibson’s book is still the best first read.
One thing you can’t see anymore: the Missouri History Museum’s exhibit Mill Creek: Black Metropolis ran from Nov. 15, 2025, to July 12, 2026, and has closed. The museum has said its Josephine Baker collection will appear in new signature galleries planned for 2027. For more of the city’s surviving past, our guide to the oldest buildings in St. Louis picks up where this leaves off, and our list of underrated places to visit in St. Louis keeps going in the same spirit.
### Could moving the Poplar Street Bridge or I-64 bring Mill Creek back?
Not under any plan that exists today. We checked every proposal we could find on Oct. 6, 2026, and none of them would return Mill Creek’s land or rebuild the neighborhood. Here’s what’s real, and what it does and doesn’t do.
The Poplar Street Bridge and downtown highways. The Gateway Arch Park Foundation wants the region to study capping, burying or removing downtown highway sections near the Arch. Its executive director, Ryan McClure, told First Alert 4 on Sept. 30, 2026, that the Poplar Street Bridge, the I-64 double-decker and the elevated lanes by Laclede’s Landing will need replacing within about 15 years. St. Louis Magazine reported in December 2025 that major work on the bridge is on track to begin in 2040. MoDOT told First Alert 4 there are no plans yet: a regional study of the downtown area hasn’t started, and its scope is still being worked out. That conversation is about reconnecting downtown to the Arch grounds, well east of Mill Creek.
I-64 through Mill Creek itself. MoDOT’s Future64 study opens with the history of Mill Creek and aims to ease the highway’s barrier effect. The money that’s actually committed rebuilds the interstate where it stands: a roughly $120 million project to replace the eastbound bridge over Vandeventer and update the Grand interchange, with eastbound lanes between Vandeventer and Compton closed for about a year starting in fall 2027 and the work finished by late 2029, St. Louis Public Radio reported in April 2026.
A federal reconnection grant. In March 2024, Great Rivers Greenway won $9.9 million from the U.S. Department of Transportation’s Reconnecting Communities and Neighborhoods program for a Brickline Greenway bridge that threads between the two decks of I-64 at Spring Avenue, linking the Grand MetroLink station to SLU. Its CEO, Susan Trautman, tied the grant directly to what happened in Mill Creek. Construction is expected to start in 2027. It reconnects people on foot and on bikes. It doesn’t give back any land.
Recognition and repair. On Feb. 10, 2023, the Board of Aldermen passed Resolution 189, commemorating Mill Creek and the disproportionate and unjust impact of its demolition on Black St. Louisans. It’s a statement, not a program. In October 2024, the city’s Reparations Commission recommended up to $25,000 for Black former residents of Mill Creek Valley, or their direct descendants. In March 2025, then-Mayor Tishaura Jones told St. Louis Public Radio that direct cash payments would violate the state constitution. We found no record of any payments since.
The ground itself is spoken for. Saint Louis University, Harris-Stowe, the stadium district, businesses and the highway sit on it. When five I-64 ramps there closed for good in February 2020, the space went to the stadium district. So the honest answer to the question is no. What’s growing is the effort to remember, and Mill Creek isn’t the only lost Black neighborhood getting that attention. Our guide to things to do in Brentwood, MO tells the story of Evans Howard Place, which stood by the I-64 and I-170 interchange where a shopping center is now.
Next time someone calls Mill Creek a slum that had to go, you’re the one who knows about the 27-to-1 vote, the ballpark where Cool Papa Bell played center field, the sidewalk where Josephine Baker danced for money, and the names cut into granite on Market Street. Pick a dry afternoon. Start at the pillars at 22nd and Market, walk the greenway west to Compton, and read every quote.
When the walk is done, our Midtown neighborhood guide covers where to eat and what’s open around Harris-Stowe, SLU and Grand Center.
If you run a business in Midtown or Downtown West, on ground that was once Mill Creek Valley, list it with us so the people walking the Brickline Greenway can find you.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the history of Mill Creek Valley?
A.  It started as a mill site. UMSL historians date the first mill on the creek to 1765, and by the mid-1800s railroads had followed the creek bed and turned the valley into an industrial district. German immigrants settled there first. Free Black families and people who escaped slavery arrived before the Civil War, more came after it, and the Great Migration filled the neighborhood. By the early 1950s nearly 20,000 people lived there, about 95 percent of them Black. The city began clearing it in 1959.
### Q. Which neighborhood in St. Louis is historically Black?
A.  Several. Mill Creek Valley was, in curator Gwen Moore’s words, the center of Black life and the largest concentration of Black St. Louisans. The best known today is The Ville in north St. Louis, home to Sumner High School, Homer G. Phillips Hospital and Annie Malone’s Poro College. JeffVanderLou, where Vashon High School moved in 1963, has a long Black history too.
### Q. Who benefits most from urban renewal?
A.  In Mill Creek, the institutions and developers that got large, cleared, subsidized parcels in the middle of the city: Saint Louis University, which spoke up for the land first, plus industrial and commercial builders and the highway. Mayor Joseph Darst wrote in 1950 that the federal law would bring down the cost of land in slum areas and make it attractive to investors. The residents paid the price. They lost homes, churches and businesses all at once.
### Q. Why did urban renewal fail?
A.  In Mill Creek, the land sat empty for years, so the promised jobs and tax base came slowly. The displaced families crowded into north side neighborhoods and public housing, including Pruitt-Igoe, whose demolition began in 1972. Even the city’s own 1971 report on renewal conceded that relocation contributed to the mounting problems of other areas of the city. The plan treated a community as a set of buildings to remove.
### Q. What are the criticisms of urban renewal?
A.  That it destroyed working communities instead of repairing them, fell hardest on Black neighborhoods, gave too little help to the people it moved and often left cleared land empty for years. Mill Creek fits every one. Terry Jones, who watched it come down as a SLU student editor, later called it a missed opportunity to strengthen a community in place with public and private money instead of rooting it out.
### Q. Is gentrification the same as urban renewal?
A.  No. Urban renewal, as practiced in Mill Creek, was run by government: the city used eminent domain and federal money to take and clear whole blocks at once. Gentrification is usually gradual and driven by the market, as rising rents and property values push longtime residents out. Both displace people. In Mill Creek, the bulldozers did it in a few years.
### Q. What is another name for urban renewal?
A.  Officials in the 1950s called it slum clearance or redevelopment, and St. Louis ran Mill Creek through its Land Clearance for Redevelopment Authority. Critics used a blunter name. In a 1963 television interview with psychologist Kenneth Clark, writer James Baldwin said urban renewal meant “Negro removal,” and the phrase stuck because projects like Mill Creek fit it.
### Q. Was Josephine Baker from Mill Creek Valley?
A.  Yes. She was born in St. Louis on June 3, 1906, and grew up in Mill Creek Valley, the Missouri Historical Society says. As a girl she danced on the sidewalk by the Booker T. Washington Theatre on Market Street. At 15 she joined a traveling troupe, and she went on to stardom in Paris, wartime work for the French Resistance and a speech at the 1963 March on Washington. In 2021, France honored her in the Panthéon.

## St. Louis City Animal Control vs County: Who to Call, What Getting Your Dog Back Costs, the Attic Raccoon Neither Will Remove
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/animal-control-in-st-louis-city-vs-county
“Just call animal control.” Every national how-to says it, as if a metro gets one phone number and one pound. St. Louis doesn’t. Which agency picks up depends on which side of a line drawn in 1876 the dog is standing on, and inside St. Louis County it can depend on the town, too.
A loose dog in Dogtown and a loose dog in Florissant are two calls to two different health departments, with two shelters, two fee schedules and two after-hours numbers. A loose dog in Hazelwood is a third call, because Hazelwood keeps its own officer. Dial the wrong one and you spend the afternoon getting transferred while the dog keeps walking.
This is the map. Everything here was checked on Oct. 7, 2026, against the City of St. Louis Department of Health, the St. Louis County Department of Public Health and its animal control ordinance, CARE STL, the Humane Society of Missouri and St. Louis Public Radio. Hours and fees change, so confirm by phone before you drive anywhere.
### Is it a good idea to call animal control?
Yes, when someone could get hurt: a bite, an aggressive or injured animal, a pet in visible distress, or a bat inside your living space. For a friendly loose dog, call second. Most lost pets live close by, so check for a tag, get a microchip scan at a vet, and knock on a few doors first.
The danger list is short, and it’s the reason these agencies exist. A dog that has bitten someone, a dog charging people on the sidewalk, an animal hit by a car, a pet locked in a hot car, a bat in the bedroom: call right away. On the City side, an animal in distress goes to Animal Care and Control at 314-657-1500 on weekdays from 8 to 5, or to the police non-emergency line, 314-231-1212, after hours. In the County, it’s 314-615-0650 during shelter hours and 636-529-8210 after them.
The friendly dog trotting down your block with a collar on is a different problem, and here’s the part the national advice skips. The City’s shelter has told the public, in writing, that it can’t take found pets walked in by residents. CARE STL, the nonprofit that runs it, says it has operated beyond capacity for more than a year, on pop-up kennels, and has to save its space for animals brought in by animal control officers. Its found-pet page asks finders to keep the dog at least 48 hours, get it scanned for a microchip at a vet clinic, and hang signs where it turned up. The County’s lost-and-found page says the same thing: a pet kept close to where it was found has a better shot at getting home.
So the honest answer is yes, in the right order. Danger, phone immediately. Friendly stray, neighborhood first, phone second. And if you can’t safely hold the animal for even one night, call anyway. That’s what the system is for.
### Which animal control do I call in St. Louis, city or county?
Call the agency that covers the ground where the animal is, not the one on your mailing address. Inside the City of St. Louis, that’s the City’s Animal Care and Control division. Anywhere in St. Louis County, check your own town’s website first, because some towns employ their own officer, then call St. Louis County Animal Care and Control.
The split is older than anyone reading this. In 1876 the City of St. Louis voted to separate from St. Louis County, and it has belonged to no county since. A century and a half later the line still runs through backyards; St. Louis Public Radio marked the 150th anniversary in January by visiting a family whose house sits right on top of it. Animal control follows the same border. Two governments, two health departments, two rulebooks.
The trap is the mailing address. Plenty of County homes put “St. Louis, MO” on their mail. Even the City’s own list of area shelters prints a St. Louis, MO 63146 address for the Humane Society of Missouri’s Maryland Heights campus. If your police department and property tax bill come from the City of St. Louis, you’re a City call. If your police are a town department or St. Louis County Police, you’re in the County.
On the City side, Animal Care and Control is a division of the Department of Health. Routine reports, like a stray roaming loose, a neighbor keeping more pets than the law allows, or dog waste piling up in a yard, go through the Citizens’ Service Bureau at 314-622-4800 or the City’s online request form. The shelter is at 2801 Clark Avenue, run under contract by CARE STL, and its line is 314-612-5310.
On the County side, Animal Care and Control sits inside the Department of Public Health, with its shelter at 10521 Baur Boulevard in Olivette, listed as open weekdays from 10 to 6 and weekends from 10 to 4. That building has had a busy few years. After an independent audit faulted the County’s handling of the shelter, the Animal Protective Association of Missouri ran it from December 2022 under a five-year, $16 million deal, and the County took it back in February 2025, according to St. Louis Public Radio and Fox 2.
Inside the County, check your town first. St. Louis County has close to 90 municipalities, and they don’t all handle animals the same way. Hazelwood employs a full-time certified animal control officer at 314-838-5000, ext. 1. Maryland Heights has its own officer who also covers Bridgeton, at 314-373-3873 on weekdays, with the County covering nights and weekends. University City’s animal control line is 314-505-8508. Florissant sends residents straight to the County. Your town’s website will say which kind you live in, usually on the police department’s page.
Fees come from the City’s Animal Care Center page and Chapter 611 of the County code as posted in October 2026. Both governments revise them, so check again before you go.
### Why won’t the City shelter take the stray you found?
Because it’s full, and it has been for a long time. CARE STL calls itself the only open-admission shelter in the City of St. Louis, which means animal control officers can bring it any animal, at any hour, and it has to take it. To keep that promise, it stopped accepting animals that members of the public carry through the door.
The numbers explain why. CARE STL told St. Louis Public Radio in July 2026 that the shelter has about 70 kennels and has held as many as 100 dogs at times. Its own site counts 3,098 animals taken in during 2023 and 2,782 in 2024. The City renewed CARE STL’s contract in July for another year, worth about $1 million, and the shelter says that covers staff salaries while donors carry most of the rest.
So CARE STL asks for a finder who acts like a foster. Keep the dog at least 48 hours. Get it scanned for a chip. Hang signs near the spot you found it, post it on Petco Love Lost, PawBoost and Nextdoor, and file a found-pet report on the shelter’s website. If you’ll keep fostering through the City’s required five-day stray hold, CARE STL says it will provide veterinary care and supplies at no cost, and the animal becomes eligible for adoption if nobody claims it.
It can sound like the shelter handing the job back to you. Look at it from the owner’s side, though. Most lost dogs don’t wander far from home, so the family is out searching the same few blocks where you found theirs. A sign on the pole at the corner reaches them faster than a kennel card across town. CARE STL says it bluntly: when lost pets are brought to shelters, reclaim rates by their families are typically low.
Cats get their own rule of thumb. Many outdoor cats belong to someone, and CARE STL suggests leaving a healthy-looking one where it is. A cat with a tipped ear has already been through trap-neuter-return, which the City has allowed by ordinance since 2014, and it’s meant to be outside. The County’s code exempts ear-tipped cats from impoundment altogether.
For what happens once a dog is admitted, from the intake exam to the adoption paperwork, our guide to St. Louis animal shelters walks through it.
### What does St. Louis animal control do, and what won’t it do?
Both agencies are public health departments first. Their core jobs are rabies control, bites, strays, animals in danger, and enforcing local animal ordinances. Neither one is a free wildlife removal service, and that catches people off guard every spring.
What they handle. In the City, the Citizens’ Service Bureau takes reports of bites, welfare checks, injured or sick animals, dead animals in the right-of-way, stray dogs at large, prohibited animals, a household with more than four pets, and unsanitary yards. In the County, Chapter 611 lets officers impound dogs and cats running at large, animals without a rabies vaccination, animals that have bitten a person or another animal, dangerous dogs that aren’t properly confined, and animals nobody is feeding, sheltering or taking to a vet.
Wildlife is where the line gets drawn. The City’s Animal Care and Control says plainly that it doesn’t respond to reports of nuisance wildlife. It will come for injured wildlife or a wild animal that poses a safety or health issue, and otherwise it suggests calling a pest control company. The County will remove a wild animal from the living area of your home, but says it isn’t licensed to remove wildlife that’s outdoors or in attics, crawl spaces, basements or garages. Maryland Heights tells its residents the same about raccoons in the attic. For animals outside, the County points people to the Bi-State Wildlife Hotline at 636-492-1610 and the Missouri Department of Conservation. A raccoon nesting over the garage usually ends with one of the pest control companies in St. Louis that do wildlife exclusion.
Bats are the exception worth memorizing. If a bat turns up inside your house in the County and anyone in the household, people or pets, might have touched it, or you aren’t sure, keep it confined. Turn the room’s lights on so it stops flying and call 314-615-0650, option 6. The County will capture it for rabies testing. Its health department notes that a bat bite can be hard to feel or see, and that bats and skunks make up most of the animals testing positive for rabies in Missouri.
Rats, mice and mosquitoes aren’t animal control’s job in the City either. They go to the Health Department’s Vector Control unit, also through the Citizens’ Service Bureau.
Rats or mice instead? What pest control costs in St. Louis
The pet limit changes at the line, too. The City allows no more than four pets, counting dogs, cats and rabbits, on a residential parcel unless the owner gets a non-commercial kennel permit, and the limit is per parcel, not per person. University City caps single-family and two-family homes at two adult pets. If you’re counting noses before you adopt, our breakdown of how many dogs you can have in St. Louis County covers the town-by-town rules.
### How do I get my pet back from St. Louis animal control?
Move fast and check everywhere, because a dog that slips out in one jurisdiction can be picked up in another. Call or visit both public shelters, CARE STL at 314-612-5310 and the County at 314-615-0650, plus the private ones the City itself lists: the Humane Society of Missouri’s campuses on Macklind Avenue and in Maryland Heights, the Animal Protective Association of Missouri on South Hanley Road, and Stray Rescue of St. Louis. If your town has its own officer, call that officer too. The County posts strays on hold through its 24PetConnect page, and CARE STL posts found pets on its website and Facebook. The City’s advice is to walk through each shelter in person, more than once.
The clock. Both public shelters hold a stray for five days. The County’s ordinance adds the fine print: County holidays don’t count, and an animal that arrives after 6 p.m. starts counting the next day. The County has to try to identify and notify the owner within 72 hours, every impounded dog and cat gets a microchip scan, and an owner who disputes the impoundment or the charges can request a hearing within 48 hours of being notified. After five unclaimed days, a County animal can be adopted out, moved to a licensed rescue, or euthanized under shelter policy.
What it costs. In the City, the impound fee is $20 for the first three days, then $10 for each additional day. If your pet isn’t registered, you’ll handle that too: $50 for an intact pet or $4 for a spayed or neutered one. The shelter can add $10 for a rabies shot, $10 for a microchip, and more for other vet care. The City says fees may be waived case by case with proof of low income or hardship, such as a SNAP, SSI, TANF or WIC award letter.
In the County, the shelter service fee is $25 for the first day or part of a day and $15 for each additional day, plus any citation fees, and the director can waive them. Side by side, a dog held four days runs about $70 in County shelter fees before any citation, against about $30 in City impound fees before registration or vet charges. If your pet’s rabies shot has lapsed, the County will vaccinate it at the shelter or release it on the condition that your own vet does it within 72 hours.
What to bring. Proof of rabies vaccination and anything that shows the animal is yours: vet records, the microchip number, recent photos. CARE STL asks owners to email those details, with face and body photos and any identifying marks, to info@icarestl.org. Then go look in person anyway.
If the search runs past a few days, our guide to lost pets in St. Louis covers the flyers, the Facebook groups and the microchip follow-up that bring most pets home.
### How do I report a stray, a bite or neglect in St. Louis?
A stray. In the City, file it with the Citizens’ Service Bureau at 314-622-4800 or online, and you’ll get an email with a request ID to track it. In the County, call 314-615-0650, or your town’s own officer. Have the address or nearest intersection, a description, and the time you saw it. If the animal is hurt or in danger, skip the form and use the direct lines.
A bite. The wound comes first. The County health department says to flush it with soap and water for 15 minutes and get medical care. Get the owner’s name, address and phone number if it’s someone’s pet. Then report it. In the City, an officer will interview you and any witnesses, find the animal, and check its rabies vaccination and registration. In the County, you don’t file the bite form yourself. A doctor, a police officer or County animal control staff files it, so tell whoever treats you that you want it reported.
Either way, the animal that bit you goes into a 10-day rabies observation, and the County explains that a dog or cat that stays healthy through those 10 days didn’t have rabies. In the City, the observation can happen at the owner’s home if approved, at a vet’s office or at the City’s animal facility, where the fee schedule lists $50 for it. The City adds a rule most owners don’t hear about until they’re in it: before a biting animal is released, it must be spayed or neutered and microchipped, and a dog gets evaluated against the City’s definitions of a potentially dangerous or dangerous dog.
Neglect or cruelty. Call the Humane Society of Missouri’s Animal Cruelty Task Force at 314-647-4400. It says it’s the only St. Louis area animal welfare agency on call 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, in both the City and the County, and its ten investigators field more than 20,000 reports of suspected abuse or neglect a year across Missouri. Give the address or exact directions and a specific description of what you saw. For a dog in a hot car, the task force asks you to call the police and its hotline.
### Who answers after hours and on weekends?
This is the question people actually face at 9 p.m. on a Sunday, so here it is in one place.
City, an animal in distress or unresponsive: the St. Louis police non-emergency line, 314-231-1212, or 911.
County, an urgent animal call or a wild animal loose inside your living space: the County police non-emergency line, 636-529-8210. Ask for an animal control officer.
Either side, abuse, neglect or an injured stray: the Humane Society of Missouri hotline, 314-647-4400, staffed around the clock.
City, a friendly found dog at night: CARE STL says to put it in a spare room or a crate, email info@icarestl.org, and call the shelter the next day.
Most people learn all of this the hard way, standing on a sidewalk holding a stranger’s dog by the collar with a phone in the other hand. You won’t. You know which side of the line you’re on, which number answers at night, which shelter to walk through when your own dog slips the gate, and which calls belong to a pest control company instead. Save the two shelter numbers in your phone tonight. The neighbors will start asking you.
And for the better side of owning a pet around here, our guide to dog-friendly places in St. Louis covers where your dog is welcome.
Found a dog and need somewhere to scan it for a chip or take it in? Browse animal shelters around St. Louis on St Louis Near Me Directory and call ahead, since space changes daily.
And if you run a shelter, rescue, kennel or vet clinic that scans found pets for microchips, list it with us so the finder holding a leash at 9 p.m. can find you.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What services does CARE STL provide?
A.  CARE STL, the Center for Animal Rescue and Enrichment, runs the City of St. Louis animal shelter on Clark Avenue under contract and takes in every animal the City’s officers bring. It also handles adoptions, foster homes, including people fostering a stray they found, volunteers and a Doggy Day Out program. It runs a pet food bank during business hours, gives out donated supplies, offers behavior advice, and provides low-cost wellness care by appointment for animals adopted there, such as a $10 rabies shot or a $50 exam. Check its site for current prices.
### Q. Is St. Louis city in a county?
A.  No. The City of St. Louis voted to separate from St. Louis County in 1876 and has been an independent city ever since, part of no county. It runs its own county-level offices, and Missouri lists it alongside its 114 counties. It’s one of only three independent cities in the country outside Virginia; Baltimore and Carson City are the others. For pet owners, that means two separate animal control agencies with different phone numbers, shelters and fees.
### Q. What happens when animal control is called?
A.  Your report gets logged and an officer is sent based on urgency. In the City, a Citizens’ Service Bureau report generates a request ID by email so you can follow it. In the County, you call the shelter line during business hours and the police non-emergency line after them. What happens next depends on the animal. A tagged or chipped pet may go straight home, an unidentified stray goes to the shelter for its five-day hold, a biting animal goes into a 10-day observation, and an owner breaking an ordinance may get a warning or a ticket.
### Q. What is the point of animal control?
A.  Public health, mostly. In St. Louis both agencies sit inside health departments, and rabies control is the backbone of the job: vaccination tags, bite investigations, 10-day observations, bats captured for testing. The rest is public safety and animal welfare, from strays and dangerous dogs to animals left without food, water or shelter. A public shelter can’t pick and choose, either. When the County reopened its Olivette shelter in 2025, its public health director told Fox 2 that it takes in roosters, chickens and sheep, too.
### Q. What happens if your dog is reported to animal control?
A.  An officer looks into the complaint, and the first question is usually rabies. In the City, every dog and cat must be vaccinated and registered, and skipping registration can bring a ticket and a fine. In the County, a dog without a current rabies tag or certificate, one running at large, or one that has bitten can be impounded under Chapter 611. If the report is a bite, expect the 10-day observation, and in the City a spay or neuter and a microchip before release. Keep your rabies certificate where you can find it.
### Q. Does animal control charge you if you call them?
A.  Neither side lists a fee for reporting a stray, a bite or an animal in distress. The bills land on owners. In the City, that’s $20 for the first three days of impound and $10 a day after, $50 for a bite observation at the shelter, and $150 to surrender an owned dog or cat to Animal Care and Control. In the County, it’s $25 for the first day and $15 for each additional day, plus citations. Both say fees can be waived in some cases, so ask before you pay.
### Q. Does animal control tell who called?
A.  Neither the City nor the County publishes a promise that your name stays private, so ask before you give it. The City’s online form sends a request ID to the email you provide. For abuse and neglect, the Humane Society of Missouri says it keeps reporter information confidential unless the case goes to law enforcement or a subpoena or court order requires disclosure, though it needs a witness name and number for allegations of physical abuse. And if a complaint ends up in court, the person who saw it may be asked to testify.
### Q. What happens to dogs that go to animal control?
A.  They’re scanned for a microchip, checked over, and held five days so an owner can claim them. After that, County dogs can be adopted, sent to a licensed rescue or euthanized under shelter policy; County adoptions cost $80 and include vaccinations, a microchip and a spay or neuter. CARE STL told St. Louis Public Radio that City shelter dogs aren’t euthanized for space, even over capacity, though dogs flagged for behavior, a long stay or declining quality of life get 40 days, plus a possible 15-day extension, to find a home. To help one, our guide to St. Louis pet rescues is a good place to start.

## Cat Cafes in St. Louis: Five Lounges, What an Hour Costs, and 1,300 Cats Sent Home
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/cat-cafes-in-st-louis
Ignore the latte reviews. The number that tells you what a St. Louis cat cafe actually does sits on a page most visitors never open. Mauhaus, the lounge on Sutton Boulevard in Maplewood, keeps a numbered Wall of Fame on its website listing every cat that left the lounge for a home. No. 1 is a cat named Hazlitt. When we checked in October 2026, the list ran past 900 names, and the newest was Teddy.
Cat Zen, on North Main Street in St. Charles, keeps score a different way. Its homepage carries a counter: 428 adoptions and counting. Two storefronts, more than 1,300 cats placed. Neither one is a shelter.
That’s the part the cute-photo roundups skip. They grade the pastries, praise the lighting and send you off for a novelty hour, as if the cats were part of the decor. Around here a cat cafe works more like an adoption floor with a coffee counter bolted to the front. The cats are fostered there by a rescue. Your hourly fee pays their rent. And the quiet person on the bench next to you may be on a third visit to the same shy tabby, working up the nerve to apply.
So this guide covers what the lists leave out. Where the five lounges are. What an hour costs, and where that money really goes. Which ones will take a toddler, which rescue stands behind each room, and how a visit turns into a cat carrier riding home on your passenger seat.
### Is there a cat cafe in St. Louis?
Yes, five. Mauhaus in Maplewood, The Cheshire Grin on Cherokee Street, Whisker Station in Kirkwood, Cat Zen in St. Charles and MeowTown across the river in Alton all let you sit with adoptable rescue cats for a small fee. Book ahead on weekends, and nearly every cat in the room is adoptable through a partner rescue.
Here they are in the order they opened, which is the only fair order. Each one is tied to a different rescue, and that matters more than the menu.
Mauhaus Cat Cafe & Lounge, 3101 Sutton Blvd., Maplewood. Opened in November 2016 and calls itself St. Louis’s first permanent cat cafe. Its cats come from Stray Haven Rescue, the bakery menu changes daily, and it’s open Wednesday through Sunday.
The Cheshire Grin Cat Cafe, 1926 Cherokee St., in the city. Opened in August 2019 and runs as its own nonprofit rescue, The Green Paw Rescue, which pulls cats from animal control euthanasia lists and from partner rescues. Open weekends only, Saturday and Sunday from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., and every pastry is plant-based, with the lineup changing weekly.
Whisker Station Cat Cafe and Lounge, 212 N. Kirkwood Road, downtown Kirkwood. Opened in November 2021 in a renovated former travel agency and houses 15 to 25 cats at a time from Heartland Humane Society of Missouri, a foster-based rescue. Closed Mondays.
Cat Zen Cafe and Lounge, 319 N. Main St., historic St. Charles. Opened in November 2022 as the first cat cafe in St. Charles and fosters 12 to 20 cats at a time for Smelly Cat Rescue.
MeowTown, 301 W. Elm St., Alton, Illinois. Opened in December 2023 with cats from Metro East Humane Society and cookies baked in house. Closed Monday and Tuesday.
Cherokee Street actually has two cat rooms. Farther west on the same street, Tenth Life Cat Rescue runs an adoption lounge at 3202 Cherokee St. It isn’t a cafe. It opens by appointment for adoption meet-and-greets, plus one “Caturday” each month when visitors can reserve time with 10 or more adoptable cats in a living-room setup. Fittingly, Tenth Life supplied the cats when Mauhaus first opened in 2016.
Hours shift with the seasons at several of these rooms, and Cat Zen has posted separate fall hours in past years. Check the cafe’s own site the day you go. And if your household runs on dogs as much as cats, our guide to pet-friendly St. Louis covers where the rest of the family is welcome.
### What does a St. Louis cat cafe visit cost?
Plan on $10 to $15 per adult for 30 to 60 minutes with the cats, based on the rates the cafes posted in October 2026. Some fold a drink into the ticket. Others sell snacks separately.
Mauhaus: $15 per person 13 and older, $11 for 65 and older, $9.50 for kids 2 to 12, and nothing for children under 2. That buys an hour in the lounge and a house drink.
Whisker Station: $15 for an hour in the lounge. Prepackaged snacks and bottled drinks are sold on the side.
Cat Zen: $15 for 60 minutes or $10 for 30, tax included. The hour comes with a complimentary beverage.
MeowTown: $11 per person for a 50-minute visit that starts at the top of the hour.
The Cheshire Grin: doesn’t print a lounge rate on its homepage. Every guest books separately through its online scheduler, so check the price there.
Ten years ago the same hour at Mauhaus cost $10, and the fee counted toward your food bill. Whisker Station charged $12 when it opened in 2021. Blame the building, mostly.
Here’s the detail most visitors never hear. At Cat Zen, every adoption fee goes to the rescue partner, and the cafe says it receives no outside funding. So the lounge fee is what covers staff, rent, utilities, food, litter, vet bills, medications, cleaning supplies and the furniture the cats shred. When Mauhaus opened, co-owner Dana Huth told St. Louis Public Radio the cafe needed two insurance policies, one for a restaurant and another of the kind petting zoos carry, and that the whole thing cost more than she expected. Your $15 is the cats’ rent. The coffee is the tip.
A few extras worth knowing. Whisker Station rents out its cat room for 90-minute private parties at $250 Tuesday through Thursday and $300 on Friday and Sunday, before tax, for up to 25 people with no more than 10 kids. The Cheshire Grin hosts private events of up to 20 guests. Mauhaus sells gift certificates in $15 and $25 amounts, in the store only. Any of it can change, so confirm on the cafe’s site before you plan around a number.
### Can you adopt a cat from a St. Louis cat cafe?
Yes, and that’s the whole point of the room. You aren’t adopting from the cafe, though. You’re adopting from the rescue that fosters the cat there, so the application, the fee and the approval all belong to that rescue. Expect days, not minutes.
Mauhaus sends you to Stray Haven Rescue for the application. Once you’re approved, you come back to the cafe for an interview, then pick a date to bring the cat home. The cafe says plainly that it doesn’t do same-day adoptions. If nobody in the lounge clicks with you, the Mauhaus site notes that Stray Haven has more than 200 other cats waiting in foster homes.
Cat Zen works through Smelly Cat Rescue, an all-volunteer group. You apply online, approval isn’t first come, first served, and the process can take one to two weeks or longer. Pickups typically happen on Sundays from 3 to 5 p.m., you bring the carrier, and applicants must be 21 or older. The fee is $175 per cat, which covers the spay or neuter, vaccines, deworming, a microchip and a triple snap test.
Whisker Station uses Heartland Humane Society’s online application and lists adoption pricing at $190. Call ahead if your heart is set on one particular cat. Cats leave, and the cafe asks you to confirm before you drive over.
The Cheshire Grin asks every would-be adopter to fill out an application with its rescue and talk with a staff member first. Kittens six months and younger go home in pairs unless you already have a young cat in the house.
MeowTown runs adoptions through Metro East Humane Society, with an application and a phone interview, and you can start the paperwork the same day you visit.
Two rules repeat across the region, so plan for both. Kittens tend to go home in pairs, a firm policy at the Cheshire Grin and at Tenth Life, with Cat Zen giving preference to pair applications. And several rescues, Smelly Cat and Tenth Life among them, require adopters to be 21. Tenth Life’s own fees run $160 for an adult cat and $185 for a kitten six months or younger, with $50 off when you adopt two at once.
Why meet a cat here instead of in a shelter kennel? The Cheshire Grin’s founders spent years working in shelters, and their site puts it bluntly: kenneled cats tend to come across as stressed and scared, while the same cats in a free-roaming room purr, talk, play and show who they really are. Whisker Station owner Sara McGinnis made the same argument to Kirkwood High School’s student paper shortly after she opened. You see the cat’s real personality instead of its worst day. If you’d rather start with the big adoption floors, our guide to St. Louis pet rescues lays out where to look.
### How many cats have St. Louis cat cafes sent home?
More than 1,300 from two of them alone, by their own public counts. The Mauhaus Wall of Fame passed 900 names this fall, and the Cat Zen counter reads 428. Whisker Station, The Cheshire Grin and MeowTown don’t post a running total online, so ask at the counter. They know the number.
The pace is the surprising part. Mauhaus says two to four cats tend to leave for homes every week, which is why the lineup on any cafe website runs slightly behind. When we compared the Mauhaus list of adoptable cats with its Wall of Fame in early October 2026, 10 of the 14 cats still listed as available had already moved onto the wall.
Even the worst year kept moving. In August 2020, with normal traffic gone and the business losing money for roughly four months, Mauhaus told FOX 2 it had still placed 80 cats that year, 25 of them after the pandemic began. The co-owner said they weren’t closing their doors. They didn’t, and the Mauhaus site says it no longer keeps resident cats at all. Every cat in that lounge is looking for a home.
Think of a cat cafe in this town as a foster home with a door to the street. Every paid hour keeps a bed open for the next cat a rescue pulls.
### Which cat cafe fits your visit: kids, reservations, St. Charles?
Match the room to the people you’re bringing. The rules differ more than you’d guess, and the age cutoffs are firm.
Bringing a toddler. Mauhaus allows children of all ages, with one adult for every two kids 12 and under and at least one person 18 or older in the party. Kids under 2 don’t need a ticket. Whisker Station saves a Guardian & Me hour for kids 6 and under, from 11 a.m. to noon Tuesday through Friday and Sunday, and 10 to 11 a.m. on Saturday. Cat Zen lets all ages book its 30-minute slots, while its one-hour slots are for ages 7 and up, no exceptions.
Kids who are 6 or 7. MeowTown’s cat lounge is open to ages 6 and up. The Cheshire Grin doesn’t allow anyone under 7 in the lounge except for adoptions, and it asks for one adult per two children.
Teenagers on their own. Whisker Station lets kids 7 to 12 in with an adult and teens 13 and up without one, though anyone under 18 needs a waiver signed by an adult first.
You hate waiting. Reserve. Mauhaus takes reservations at least two hours ahead and refunds cancellations made 24 hours or more out. Cat Zen suggests booking at least a day early, because it caps the room and turns walk-ins away at capacity. Whisker Station allows 15 people in the cat room at a time, and the Cheshire Grin also caps at 15 per hour. Weekend afternoons fill first everywhere.
Someone in your group is sensory-sensitive. Mauhaus runs Low-Sensory Nights on the third Wednesday of each month from 6 to 8 p.m., currently for adults 18 and older. The music goes low or off, the lights dim, fewer guests get in, and espresso comes off the menu for the night because the grinder is loud.
You’re in St. Charles County. Cat Zen is the stop, on North Main Street in the historic district, and it runs monthly events like yoga with cats and painting with cats. Its snacks are mostly prepackaged, and the cafe encourages guests to bring food from nearby businesses, so make an afternoon of it with our guide to coffee shops in St. Charles.
You live in the Metro East. MeowTown in Alton saves you the bridge. The last lounge visits of the day start at 6 p.m., and the family that runs it bakes the cookies in house from its own recipes.
You want a weekday afternoon in Kirkwood. Whisker Station is open Tuesday through Sunday, hosts weekly cat yoga and a guided watercolor pet-portrait class, and sits a short walk from the rest of downtown. It sells packaged snacks rather than a full menu, so pair it with things to do in Kirkwood or our rundown of coffee shops in Kirkwood and Webster Groves.
Parking and access. Mauhaus has street parking along Sutton and a small lot just south of the cafe. Downtown Kirkwood offers free two-hour parking, and Whisker Station’s back entrance is wheelchair accessible. MeowTown asks guests to use the lot across the street.
Here for the coffee, not the cats? Coffee shops in Maplewood, MO
### What are the rules inside a cat cafe?
Sign the waiver, sanitize your hands, and let the cats come to you. Those three cover most of it. Each cafe adds its own list, and the reasons behind the rules are more interesting than the rules.
Don’t pick them up. Mauhaus explains it simply. Not every cat wants to be held, and with hundreds of visitors on a weekend, all that handling would leave the cats agitated. If one settles on your lap anyway, the cafe’s advice is to consider yourself lucky.
Don’t feed them. Diets are managed. Mauhaus asks guests not to bring outside treats, and Cat Zen welcomes outside food for you as long as none of it goes to the cats. When a cat jumps on a table for your scone, a Mauhaus lounge manager once told St. Louis Public Radio, the fix is to move the food, not the cat.
Don’t bring your cat. Every cafe says this, some with feeling. Your cat hasn’t been through the rescue’s health screening, and a stranger in the colony stresses everybody. The Cheshire Grin puts it in terms any cat owner gets: a trip to a cafe is about as much fun for your cat as a trip to the vet.
Give the shy ones room. New arrivals at the Cheshire Grin sometimes settle in from an open acclimation crate before they join the room. Sit low, stay put and let a nervous cat watch you for a while. That’s how it decides about you.
Watch the kids. Every cafe expects adults to supervise young children, and most set or recommend one adult per two kids. A child sitting on the floor with a wand toy gets far more cat time than one chasing tails.
No surrenders, no strays. None of these cafes takes cats in directly. Mauhaus, Whisker Station and the Cheshire Grin turn away owner surrenders, and Cat Zen says it can’t accept a stray you found because it isn’t a licensed rescue. If you need to rehome a cat, start with St. Louis animal shelters rather than the cafe counter.
### Why is there a glass wall between the coffee and the cats?
Because the health department wants one. A cat cafe is two businesses sharing a wall, a food service and an animal facility, and regulators treat it that way.
When Mauhaus opened, health department rules required a double door between food prep and the cat lounge. The cafe also put a glass wall between the two rooms, and its kitchen staff don’t go into the lounge at all. That’s why you order at one counter and carry your drink through a little airlock to reach the cats.
Across the river, Alton’s health officials weren’t sure what to make of MeowTown at first. Its owners told Feast Magazine the department finally classified the cat room the way it would a zoo. In the city, Cat Heaven Cafe needed permits, a virtual public hearing and an inspection from the Missouri Department of Agriculture before its first cats arrived in 2021, when it turned a Bevo Mill bar into a cat room. It now shows as closed.
Stack up the second insurance policy, the rescue vetting, the separate rooms and a lounge that holds only a handful of guests at a time, and the math gets tight. A coffee shop can squeeze in another table on a busy Saturday. A cat lounge can’t, and shouldn’t.
Which is the case for booking the hour even if you never adopt. Cat Zen says plainly that you don’t need to be shopping for a cat to visit, and that your time in the lounge helps socialize the cats for their next home. Sitting on a cushion with a purring stranger is the volunteer work.
### What do you need before a cafe cat comes home?
A carrier, a vet and a quiet room. The rescue handles the medical basics before a cat ever reaches the lounge, but the first weeks at your house are on you.
The carrier. Cat Zen asks adopters to bring one to pickup, and a sturdy carrier with a top door makes every vet visit after that easier.
The vet. Book a wellness visit in the first couple of weeks and bring the rescue’s records, so the clinic has vaccine dates and the microchip number on file. Our guide on how to choose a vet in St. Louis covers what to ask before you book.
The quiet room. Even a cat that greets strangers all day at the cafe may hide under a bed for the first few days at your place. Being used to people isn’t the same as being used to your house. Start it in a bathroom or spare room with litter, food, water and somewhere to hide, then widen its territory as it settles.
The first trip. Line up care before you need it. Our guides to pet sitters in St. Louis and cat boarding in St. Louis lay out what each option costs. Cat Zen’s owner, for what it’s worth, also runs a cat-only boarding resort in the St. Charles area.
Then send the cafe a photo. Mauhaus adds every graduate to its Wall of Fame, and there’s always room past the last number. You walked in for a coffee and an hour with the cats, and you were the one who knew what the room was really for.
Want to meet more adoptable cats before you decide? Browse pet adoption services around St. Louis on St Louis Near Me Directory and set up a second meeting with your shortlist.
If you run a cat lounge, a rescue or a shop that hosts adoption days, list it with us so the next person who searches for a cat cafe near me finds your adoption floor and not only a latte.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Are there any cat cafés in Missouri?
A.  Yes. Four sit on the Missouri side of the St. Louis area: Mauhaus in Maplewood, The Cheshire Grin on Cherokee Street, Whisker Station in Kirkwood and Cat Zen in St. Charles. Kansas City has its own cluster, starting with Whiskers Cat Cafe and Coffeehouse, which KCUR reported opened in 2018 as that metro’s first. Lineups change, so check before a road trip.
### Q. Why are cat cafés closing?
A.  Mostly money. A cat cafe carries restaurant costs and animal costs at once: separate rooms and double doors for the health department, two kinds of insurance, vet bills, litter and staff, while the cat room holds only a few guests at a time. Adoption fees usually go to the rescue, not the cafe. Mauhaus nearly went under in 2020, and Bevo Mill’s Cat Heaven Cafe is now listed as closed.
### Q. Are cats in cat cafés treated well?
A.  At a well-run one, yes, and you can check. Look for cats that arrive spayed or neutered, vaccinated and microchipped through a rescue, high shelves and hideaways they can retreat to, and staff who enforce no-pickup and no-feeding rules. The Cheshire Grin says any cat that shows signs of unhappiness goes to a foster home instead. Ask any cafe what its version of that policy is.
### Q. What do cat cafes do with the cats at night?
A.  Usually the cats just stay put. Cat Zen says its cats sleep in the lounge on beds, perches and cat trees, and aren’t kenneled unless health or safety calls for it. The setup works like a large foster home, and the Cheshire Grin calls itself a giant foster house. A new arrival may keep an open crate as a safe spot while it settles.
### Q. Do cats enjoy being in cat cafes?
A.  Some clearly do and some tolerate it, which is why room design matters. A 2025 study in the journal Animals observed 27 cats in a Swedish cat cafe for 227 hours. The cats chose elevated spots and cat-only rooms more often when the cafe got busy, and for about 44 percent of the observation time no cat was interacting with a person at all. Good cafes give cats a way to opt out.
### Q. What is the 3-3-3 rule for cats?
A.  It’s a rough adjustment timeline rescues use for newly adopted cats: about three days to decompress, when hiding and skipped meals are normal, about three weeks to learn the household’s routine, and about three months to feel truly at home. Every cat runs on its own clock. Treat the numbers as a guide, and call your vet if a cat stops eating for more than a day or two.
### Q. Is there a free cat cafe in St. Louis?
A.  No. Every cafe here charges for lounge time, because that fee pays for the cats’ care. You can still buy a drink up front at Mauhaus or Cat Zen without entering the cat room. For time with adoptable cats and no lounge fee, visit a shelter’s adoption area, or reserve a spot at one of Tenth Life’s monthly Caturday visits on Cherokee Street.
### Q. Can I bring my own cat to a cat cafe?
A.  No. Mauhaus, Cat Zen and the Cheshire Grin all say so directly. An outside cat hasn’t been through the rescue’s health screening, it stresses the resident colony, and the car ride alone is hard on most cats. Leave yours home and bring back a good story instead.

## Dog-Friendly Restaurants in St. Louis: The 2007 Patio Law, Brunch Spots, Custard Pup Cones
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/dog-friendly-restaurants-in-st-louis
Every dog-friendly restaurant list in St. Louis does the same thing. It hands you a few dozen names, wishes you a nice afternoon, and skips the one rule that decides where your dog can actually sit.
That rule has a birthday. By early 2007 the city health department was threatening action against the Boathouse in Forest Park, a lakeside restaurant whose patio had become a regular stop for dog walkers, because the code back then kept animals off a restaurant’s premises, patio included. Owner Mark Erker sent out an email asking for help. Within months Missouri had a new state law, and St. Louis had become the first city in the state to let dogs sit with their people at outdoor restaurant tables.
Nineteen years later, that ordinance still shapes every patio in the city. It explains why your dog stops at the door, why the server admires her from two feet away, and why the answer shifts once you cross into the County. Below: the rule in plain English, then the patios, brunch tables and custard windows that say yes, checked on Oct. 7, 2026. This page is one piece of our guide to dog-friendly places in St. Louis.
### Can I take my dog to restaurants?
Usually yes, to the patio, if the restaurant allows it, and almost never inside. In the City of St. Louis, a 2007 ordinance lets restaurants welcome leashed dogs in outdoor dining areas, as long as the dog comes in from outside and stays off chairs and tables. Indoors, only trained service dogs have a legal right to enter.
So you need two yeses, not one. The first comes from the law where you’re eating. The second comes from the restaurant, and that one can be no for any reason at all: a packed patio, a manager who broke up a scuffle between two retrievers last month, a landlord who doesn’t want it. A dog-friendly reputation from 2019 is not a yes in 2026.
Here’s how the first yes breaks down around the metro:
City of St. Louis: written into the food code since 2007, with eleven conditions that the restaurant and you both have to meet.
St. Louis County: dogs sit on plenty of patios, but the County’s published food code doesn’t spell out a patio exception the way the City’s does. The restaurant’s own policy is the word you’re leaning on.
The Illinois side: since March 2024 the state food code lets pet dogs into outdoor dining areas when the local health department approves.
Service dogs: allowed wherever customers can go, inside or out, under the Americans with Disabilities Act. Emotional support dogs don’t get that right.
Everything on this page was checked against the ordinance text, the codes themselves, visitors bureaus and the restaurants’ own posts. Policies still change with a new manager or one bad Saturday. Call before you drive.
### Why can dogs sit on a St. Louis patio but not inside?
Because the city wrote a narrow exception for patios and nothing at all for dining rooms. The model food code that health departments adopt starts from a flat ban: live animals may not be allowed on the premises of a food establishment. Then it lists exceptions. Aquarium fish. Patrol dogs. Service animals. A pet dog on a patio wasn’t on that list in 2007, which is how the Boathouse ended up in trouble.
The fix took two governments. State Sen. John Loudon of Chesterfield answered Erker’s email and carried the language in Senate Bill 22, which passed on the last day of the 2007 session and was signed by Gov. Matt Blunt. It became Section 67.316 of Missouri’s statutes. That section lets any county or city pass an ordinance allowing patrons’ pets in designated outdoor areas of restaurants, and it requires each restaurant to hand over a diagram of the patio first: its dimensions, the tables, the entrances, any fences, the sidewalk line.
Technically the state law reaches past dogs. It leaves out caged pets like gerbils and hamsters, which led a Missouri Municipal League official to joke at the time that gerbils needed a better lobbyist. The city only ever wrote its rule for dogs.
The city moved first. Alderwoman Lyda Krewson, who later became mayor, sponsored the bill. The Board of Aldermen passed it 25 to 1 in July 2007, and Ordinance 67611 took effect on Aug. 24, 2007. Its conditions read like a seating chart:
The restaurant posts a sign, somewhere you’ll see it, saying dogs are allowed in the outdoor dining area.
Waterless hand sanitizer is out for customers and staff, or available on request.
You and the dog reach the patio straight from outside. The dog never walks through the building.
The dog stays on a leash that keeps it close, under your control.
No dog on a seat, a table, a counter or anything like them.
No contact with plates or utensils.
No food is prepared on the patio, and no open food sits out except what’s being served.
The restaurant cleans up any mess a dog makes, right away.
The operator can ask any dog to leave, at the operator’s sole discretion.
When the city replaced its food code in 2021 with one built on the federal 2017 model, it carried the patio rule forward as a named exception: dogs in outdoor patio establishments that meet all requirements of Ordinance 67611. The federal model didn’t catch up until its 2022 edition, which says pet dogs may be allowed in outdoor dining areas if the local regulator approves. St. Louis got there about fifteen years early.
One quirk survives on paper. The 2007 ordinance exempted seven of the city’s old 28 wards. The city has since redrawn itself into 14, so if a patio near you seems oddly strict, the Health Department’s Food and Beverage Control program is the office that can tell you what applies on that block.
Inside, the logic is simpler. A dining room is where plates, open food and kitchen traffic all meet, and the code keeps animals out of it. The same federal model says food employees may not care for or handle animals that are present, apart from narrow exceptions. That’s why a good server tells your dog she’s gorgeous and keeps her hands on the tray.
### Do the patio rules change in St. Louis County and the Metro East?
Yes, and the change is bigger than most dog owners guess. St. Louis County runs its own food code, separate from the City’s, covering unincorporated areas plus the cities and towns inside the county. That code is still built on the federal 2005 model, adopted by the County Council in 2006. The 2005 model has no patio-dog exception, and the County’s published chapter, codified through early 2026, doesn’t add one that we could find. We also couldn’t find a County ordinance passed under the 2007 state law.
Out in the real world, dogs lie under patio tables in Kirkwood, Clayton and Webster Groves every warm weekend. So read it this way. In the County, a restaurant’s welcome is a house policy, and a manager can change it overnight. If you run a County patio and want to put the bowls out, the County health department’s food program is the office to ask first. Other pet rules change at the city line too, from leash laws to licensing, and our page on how many dogs you can have in St. Louis County lays them out.
Across the river, Illinois took the federal route. The Illinois Department of Public Health adopted the 2022 FDA Food Code, with amendments effective March 22, 2024, and that edition lets pet dogs into outdoor dining areas when the regulatory authority approves. Before that, the only Illinois statute on the subject, a 2008 law, let cities of a million people or more authorize patio dogs. In practice that meant Chicago. Eating in Edwardsville, Alton or Belleville? The local health department’s approval and the restaurant’s yes are what count.
St. Charles County runs its own health department as well. We didn’t find a published patio-dog provision either way, while St. Charles’s own visitors bureau happily lists patios where pets are welcome. Same advice: ask the restaurant.
### Which St. Louis restaurants have dog-friendly patios?
These are places where dogs on the patio were confirmed recently by the restaurant, a local visitors bureau or a 2026 local roundup, sorted by where you’ll be. Breweries and beer gardens are left out on purpose, since our guide to dog-friendly patios and breweries already covers them. Treat every line here as “call first.”
In the city
Rooster, South Grand: the crepe and brunch cafe at 3150 South Grand welcomes dogs at its outdoor tables. Brunch is the draw, so check the current hours before you go.
Russell’s on Macklind: at 5400 Murdoch, a neighborhood bistro with a big tree-shaded patio, and diners have mentioned staff keeping water bowls filled. It’s closed Monday and Tuesday, with weekend brunch from 9 to 2.
Zoomies Pet Cafe: the coffee house and boutique at Macklind and Rhodes avenues was built around dogs. They’re welcome inside as well as out, which makes it the rare exception on this page, and there’s a fenced backyard for off-leash play once your dog is registered.
In St. Louis County
Taco Buddha, University City: the corner spot at Pershing and Jackson avenues has a dog-friendly patio. The second location, on Manchester Road in Kirkwood, has patio seating too, so ask about dogs there before you go.
Billy G’s, Kirkwood: at 131 W. Argonne, across from the train station, a shaded patio known for water bowls. The kitchen opens at 10 a.m. on weekends and 11 a.m. on weekdays.
Mr. Wizard’s Frozen Custard: 2101 S. Big Bend Blvd., with a handful of outdoor tables. More on custard below.
In St. Charles
Magpie’s Cafe and Bike Stop Cafe: St. Charles’s visitors bureau names both for coffee and brunch with your pet. Bike Stop sits on the riverfront by the Katy Trail, which makes it a natural turnaround on a long walk.
Savor and Salt + Smoke: the same bureau lists both for lunch or dinner on pet-friendly patios.
In the Metro East
The Loading Dock, Grafton: a riverfront deck right on the water, open seasonally. Check this year’s hours before the drive up the Great River Road.
And the patio that started it all? The Boathouse restaurant is closed for renovations through 2026, though boat rentals continue on Post-Dispatch Lake. Watch for the reopening before you plan a lakeside lunch.
Patio season without the dog? The best patios in St. Louis
### Where can you take your dog for brunch or frozen custard?
Brunch is the hard one. Weekend patios fill first, tables get pushed close, and a dog under a two-top at 11 a.m. on a Sunday is a dog with a server’s feet six inches from her tail. Show up at opening. Russell’s weekend brunch starts at 9, and Rooster is built around brunch, so its early hours are the calm ones. Ask for a corner or edge table where the dog can lie against a wall instead of across the walkway. For the food side of the decision, our guide to the best breakfast and brunch in St. Louis has the menus.
Frozen custard is the easy one. A walk-up stand has no dining room to cross. You order at a window outside, you eat outside, and the dog never has to set a paw in a building. Ted Drewes needs no introduction, but it’s far from the only window in town.
Andy’s Frozen Custard serves a Pup Cone, and the company was still promoting it on National Dog Day in August 2026. The Kirkwood stand is at 311 S. Kirkwood Road, and there are others around the metro. Whether it’s free varies, so ask at the window.
Mr. Wizard’s on South Big Bend has a few outdoor tables and closes for part of the winter, so check its social posts before a February craving.
Clementine’s Naughty & Nice Creamery offers dog ice cream when it’s in stock, made with Kansas City’s Mixed Mutt Creamery in three flavors: Banana Peanut Butter Dream, Barking Maple Bacon and Blueberry YumYum. It launched at $5 a cup in 2021, so check the current price.
Picasso’s Coffeehouse in St. Charles is the visitors bureau’s pick for a pup cup on that side of the river.
A word from the vet side. A lick of plain vanilla is a treat. A whole cup is a lot of sugar and dairy for a 20-pound dog, and some dogs don’t handle dairy at all. Skip anything chocolate, and skip sugar-free products sweetened with xylitol, which is toxic to dogs. If your dog needs to burn off the walk first, our guide to dog parks in St. Louis covers off-leash space in every corner of the metro.
### Which restaurants put out water bowls or a dog menu?
Water bowls, often. A real dog menu, almost never. The best-known one in town belonged to the Boathouse, which in 2024 was offering dogs cheeseburger patties, bacon strips and a frozen dog-treat cup. It’s closed for renovation this year, and nobody has stepped in with a full dog menu at a sit-down restaurant that we could confirm.
What you’ll actually find is quieter. Water bowls on the patio at Billy G’s. Staff at Russell’s keeping them filled. Pup cups at custard and ice cream windows. Zoomies, where the whole place is set up for people who brought a dog. That’s the real currency of a dog-friendly restaurant here, and it’s worth more than a cute menu.
Don’t count on the bowl, though. On a 95-degree July afternoon the communal bowl is warm, half empty and has been shared by six other dogs since noon. Bring a collapsible bowl and your own water. Brick and concrete patios hold heat long after the sun moves, so take the shaded table, or wait for evening.
### How do you check a patio’s dog policy before you go?
Start with the sign. In the city, a restaurant that allows dogs on its patio has to post one where customers will see it, so a city patio with no sign is a question, not a yes. Outside the city there’s no sign rule to lean on, which makes the phone call matter more.
Call, and ask three things:
Is the patio open today? Wind, rain, a private party or a short-staffed lunch can close it.
Can we reach the patio without walking through the restaurant? In the city that’s the law, and anywhere else it’s the difference between a smooth arrival and a hostess blocking the door.
Any limits? Ask about a cap on the number of dogs, size rules, or hours when dogs aren’t allowed.
Then check the restaurant’s own posts from this season rather than any roundup, this one included. The restaurant’s Instagram from last week beats a list from 2023. And if you’re in town with the dog for a few nights, line up pet-friendly hotels in St. Louis before the restaurants, because the room is the harder booking.
Timing matters as much as policy. A Tuesday lunch at 1:30 is a different patio from a Saturday dinner at 7. If your dog is new to restaurants, start with the quiet shift and work up to the busy one.
### What gets a dog asked to leave a St. Louis patio?
Most of what gets a dog asked to leave is spelled out in the 2007 ordinance, whether or not anyone on the patio has read it. Paws on a chair. A dog licking a fork you lowered to her. A long leash stretched across the path servers use. The ordinance hands the call to the operator at their sole discretion, so there’s no appeal and there shouldn’t be.
The fixes are boring and they work. Walk the dog and let her relieve herself before you sit down, not after. Bring a mat so she has a spot that’s clearly hers. Shorten the leash and loop it under your chair leg, not around the table, because a dog that bolts after a squirrel will take the table with her. Order her water before your drink. And don’t feed her from your plate, since contact with plates and utensils is literally on the city’s list.
Then there’s barking. One alert bark at a passing dog is life. Steady barking at every bicycle on the block means today isn’t her day, and the kind move is to box the food and go. Missouri has also made it a misdemeanor since 2020 to pass a pet off as a service dog, so a vest bought online won’t get a nervous dog into the dining room either.
The regulars who keep a patio dog-friendly are easy to spot. Their dog is asleep under the table before the drinks come, and the next table doesn’t notice her until they stand up to leave. That’s the whole goal: be the reason the manager keeps the sign up.
Picking the neighborhood before the patio? Our guide to where to eat in the St. Louis region breaks it down town by town, so you can find a spot near wherever the walk ends and call ahead about the dog.
If you run a restaurant whose patio welcomes dogs, that water bowl by the gate is already doing half your marketing, so list it with us and let dog owners find you before they leave the house.
Celebrating a dog birthday? Our guide to dog bakeries in St. Louis covers custom cakes and treats.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Can a dog sit at the table in a restaurant?
A.  No. In the City of St. Louis, Ordinance 67611 bars dogs from seats, tables, countertops and similar surfaces, and from contact with plates or utensils. The same goes for service dogs, in a sense: the ADA guarantees a service dog’s access, but restaurants aren’t required to let any animal sit on a chair or be fed at the table. Floor level only.
### Q. Can dogs sit on restaurant patios?
A.  In the City of St. Louis, yes, when the restaurant chooses to allow it, posts the required sign and meets the ordinance’s conditions. Elsewhere it depends on the local health code and the restaurant’s policy. In Illinois, the state food code has allowed pet dogs in outdoor dining areas with local health department approval since March 2024.
### Q. Why are dogs not allowed in restaurants?
A.  Food safety. The model food code keeps live animals off a food establishment’s premises, then allows narrow exceptions, such as service animals, only where contamination of food, clean equipment, utensils and linens can’t result. Dining rooms never got a pet exception. Patios did, in places like the City of St. Louis, because outdoor seating can be kept apart from food preparation.
### Q. Can you take your dog to a restaurant?
A.  To the patio, usually, with planning. Pick a restaurant that confirms dogs are welcome, call to make sure the patio is open, arrive at a quiet hour, and bring water, a bowl and a mat. Walk the dog first. Keep the leash short and the dog on the ground, and be ready to leave if she’s having an off day.
### Q. Which states allow dogs in restaurants?
A.  About 23 states allowed dogs on restaurant patios by state law or regulation as of 2025, according to Michigan State University’s Animal Legal & Historical Center, and more are following as they adopt the FDA’s 2022 Food Code. Missouri chose local control in 2007, letting each city or county decide. Illinois adopted the 2022 code in March 2024.
### Q. Are dogs allowed on restaurant patios in St. Louis County?
A.  Many County restaurants allow them, from Kirkwood to Clayton. The County’s published food code, though, is based on the federal 2005 model and doesn’t include the patio exception the City wrote in 2007, as far as we could find. Treat each restaurant’s welcome as its own policy, and call ahead.
### Q. Can you take an emotional support dog into a restaurant?
A.  Not inside. The ADA covers only service animals, dogs individually trained to perform a task for a person with a disability. An emotional support dog is treated as a pet, so it can go where pets can go, which usually means a dog-friendly patio. Staff may ask only whether a dog is a service animal required because of a disability and what task it’s trained to perform.
### Q. Is it illegal to say no to an emotional support animal?
A.  Not for a restaurant. Emotional support animals have no public-access right under the ADA, so a restaurant can turn one away from its dining room. Housing is different: federal fair housing rules treat them as assistance animals. And in Missouri, misrepresenting a dog as a service dog has been a misdemeanor since 2020.

## Puppies for Sale in St. Louis: Check the State License, the Inspection File and the Horrible Hundred
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/puppies-for-sale-in-st-louis-what-to-check
Family-raised. Vet-checked. Ready now. Those three phrases cost a seller nothing to type, and not one of them is a credential. Missouri has something that is: a state license number that starts with the letters AC, tied to an inspection file any buyer is allowed to read.
You have to ask for it. That gap is where puppy mills make their money, and Missouri has more of them on the national watch list than any other state. Humane World for Animals, formerly the Humane Society of the United States, put 31 Missouri dealers in its 2026 Horrible Hundred report. That’s the 14th year in a row Missouri led the list.
Here’s the part St. Louis buyers miss. Not one of those 31 kennels is in the St. Louis metro. By FOX 2’s count, more than half sit in the greater Springfield area, a good 200 miles down I-44. Distance doesn’t protect you, though. The report says more than half of its listed breeders hold USDA licenses, which lets them sell to pet stores and online without ever meeting the buyer. A website, a store counter or a parking-lot handoff closes those 200 miles in an afternoon.
So this isn’t a list of where to buy a puppy in St. Louis. It’s how to check whoever you buy from, using records Missouri already keeps and will hand to anyone who asks.
### How to find out if a dog breeder is a puppy mill?
Ask for the breeder’s Missouri license number, confirm it with the Department of Agriculture, and request the inspection reports under the Sunshine Law. Search the USDA database and the Horrible Hundred report. Then visit: meet the mother, see where the puppies live, read the vet records. A breeder who refuses any of that has answered you.
Paperwork first, puppies second. Once you’ve held a puppy you stop reading carefully. Everybody does, and sellers know it. That’s why the photos come first in a listing.
Missouri gives you more to work with than most states. Under the state Animal Care Facilities Act, anyone who breeds dogs or cats or sells their offspring and keeps more than three intact females needs a state license. The Missouri Department of Agriculture says every licensed facility is inspected at least once a year or on complaint, and that the inspection reports are available to the public on request.
The federal layer is thinner than people assume. According to the 2026 report, the USDA only licenses dog breeders who have five or more breeding females and sell sight unseen, to pet stores, brokers or online buyers. A breeder who sells only face to face never needs a USDA license at all, even with hundreds of dogs. So “USDA licensed” on an ad tells you how a breeder sells. It doesn’t tell you how the dogs live.
Then there’s the record nobody advertises. In states that inspect kennels, Missouri included, the report’s researchers found puppy mills with long strings of state violations and no USDA violations over the same stretch. The state file is often the more honest one. Read it.
The visit settles what paper can’t. Go to where the puppies were born, not a gas station halfway between. Ask to meet the mother. Look at the floor the puppies live on, notice the smell, and watch how the adult dogs react when the breeder walks in. Dogs who shrink from the person who feeds them are telling you something no inspection report will.
### Why does Missouri keep topping the Horrible Hundred list?
Two reasons, and the second one works in your favor. Missouri has a big commercial dog-breeding industry. It also inspects that industry and hands over the records. The report’s own methodology says the large number of listings in some states is partly due to the greater availability of records there, while states that don’t inspect kennels leave little paper to find.
Here’s Missouri’s count in every report since 2014, taken from the reports themselves. Each list holds 100 dealers (the 2014 edition, titled 101 Puppy Mills, held 101), so Missouri alone fills a fifth to nearly a third of it.
Look at what doesn’t move. The count swings between 19 and 31, and the state on top never changes. The first report, in 2013, put Missouri on top too. A good year for Missouri is still a first-place year.
The 2026 entries read like a checklist for your own visit. Inspectors found a coughing, lethargic puppy at one Missouri kennel who had been given a livestock medication instead of a trip to a veterinarian. Another Missouri kennel needed six inspection attempts over 104 days before state inspectors could finish a routine visit. A third is on the list for the sixth time. Across the whole report, about half the breeders are repeat offenders.
Some of this is history. In November 2010, Missouri voters narrowly passed Proposition B, the Puppy Mill Cruelty Prevention Act, which capped breeders at 50 breeding dogs. On April 27, 2011, less than six months later, Gov. Jay Nixon signed Senate Bill 113, which dropped the cap and renamed the law the Canine Cruelty Prevention Act. The 2014 report called the replacement weaker than Prop B, while granting that it still raised kennel standards above where Missouri had been five years earlier.
Eighteen state field staff now cover every licensed breeder, boarding kennel, shelter and pet shop in Missouri, according to the department. That’s the system that keeps landing Missouri at the top of the list. It’s also the system that lets a St. Louis buyer check a breeder before paying, which most states can’t offer. Use it.
### How do you check a Missouri breeder’s license and inspection report?
It takes a phone call, one online form and a few days of waiting. Here’s the sequence.
