Ask for the number. A licensed Missouri breeder has an Animal Care Facilities Act license number that starts with AC (the department’s own example is AC000ABC). A small show breeder may hold a hobby or show registration instead. A seller with more than three intact females who can’t produce either shouldn’t be selling puppies in Missouri at all.
Confirm it’s current. Every license expires January 31 and has to be renewed. Call the program office at (573) 751-3076 or email acfa@mda.mo.gov with the number and kennel name, and ask whether it’s active.
Request the inspection file. The department says all of its ACFA records, including inspection reports, complaints and investigative reports, can be obtained through a Sunshine Law request. File one on the department’s open records form and ask for the last few years of inspections for that license number.
Search the federal database. If the breeder ships puppies or sells online, look the name up in the USDA Animal Care Public Search Tool, which lists licensees and their inspection reports.
Check the watch list. Search the kennel name and the owner’s name in the current and past Horrible Hundred reports. Repeat appearances tell you more than one bad year.
Call the vet. Licensed breeders must keep a written program of veterinary care signed by an attending veterinarian, who should visit the premises at least once a year. Ask for that vet’s name, then call the clinic and confirm the relationship is real.
That last step sounds paranoid until you read the 2026 report. In one Missouri entry, state inspectors had found in 2024 that the signature of a breeder’s attending veterinarian wasn’t authorized by the vet. A phone call to the clinic showed the vet hadn’t been to the kennel since December 2021. One call. That’s all it took.
When the file arrives, read it for patterns, not a grade. One citation for peeling paint is a maintenance note. The same citation on three straight visits is a choice. Look for repeat violations, official letters of warning, reinspection fees, and any note that inspectors couldn’t get in. Missouri charges a reinspection fee when a problem goes uncorrected through consecutive inspections, so a fee in the file means somebody was told twice and didn’t fix it.
Hobby and show registrations work differently, and the limit matters. A registered hobby or show breeder keeps ten or fewer intact females, has to show proof of at least one public, competitive show a year, and isn’t inspected annually. The state only investigates when someone complains. A registration tells you the breeder shows dogs. It doesn’t tell you anyone from the state has been inside lately.
If something looks wrong, say so. Missouri takes complaints about unlicensed or substandard breeders through a webform called Operation Bark Alert, linked from the department’s program page. Know before you file that complaints, names included, are public records under the Sunshine Law. Suspected cruelty goes somewhere else. Missouri law gives abuse and neglect cases to local law enforcement, so call the police or sheriff where the kennel sits.
### Where can you buy a puppy in St. Louis?
Five places, and each one leaves a different amount of homework to you.
Shelters and rescues carry the least risk and arrive with the most vet work done. The Humane Society of Missouri, the APA Adoption Center, Stray Rescue of St. Louis, St. Louis County’s shelter in Olivette and Open Door Animal Sanctuary in House Springs all place puppies, alongside dozens of smaller and breed-specific rescues. The tradeoff is less control over breed and age. Our guide to St. Louis pet rescues sorts out who takes what.
A breeder you visit is the right route if you need a specific breed for allergies, work or sport. Start with the breed’s national club, which often keeps breeder and breed rescue contacts, and with dog shows. Missouri requires registered hobby breeders to show their dogs at least once a year, so a show ring is a fair place to meet people who breed for the dog rather than the sale. The Purina Event Center at Purina Farms in Gray Summit hosts shows through much of the year and says spectators can attend free unless a listing notes otherwise. Check the calendar first.
Pet stores are legal puppy sellers in Missouri. The 2026 report found that more than 20 percent of its listed dealers had sold to Petland or its affiliated stores, or had been listed on Petland’s website as breeders, and it describes Petland as the only national pet store chain in the country that still sells puppies. That’s a finding about breeders, not a verdict on any single store. It does hand you the question to ask at any counter: which breeder, which license numbers, for this puppy? Then check them yourself.
Online listings and social media are where the risk piles up. Humane World for Animals tells buyers to refuse any breeder they haven’t met and screened in person, and to skip pet stores, internet sales and third-party handoffs like flea markets. A parking-lot meetup offered to save you the drive is a convenience for the seller. It also guarantees you never see the kennel.
A neighbor’s surprise litter is the fifth source, the one nobody plans. It can be a perfectly good way to get a dog. Ask for the mother’s vet records and book a first exam before the puppy comes home, because nobody inspected anything.
### What changes if you buy a puppy across the river in Illinois?
More than most Metro East buyers realize. Since February 23, 2022, Illinois pet shops may only offer dogs and cats obtained from an animal control facility or an animal shelter, and those shelters can’t get their animals from breeders, brokers or auctions. That’s Public Act 102-0586, signed in August 2021. A pet store in Belleville or Edwardsville can’t sell you a commercially bred puppy. One in Missouri can.
Illinois also makes pet shops hand buyers a written disclosure before the sale: the price, the breed and age, any vaccines or treatment, where the animal came from, the store’s state license number and its return policy, with a remedy written into state law if the animal turns out to be sick. Missouri has no pet purchaser protection law like it. The state-by-state table kept by Michigan State University’s Animal Legal & Historical Center lists Illinois and leaves Missouri off.
The border changes the paperwork too. Missouri requires dogs entering the state to travel with a certificate of veterinary inspection issued within 30 days. A puppy moving within Missouri needs no certificate at all. So a puppy from an Illinois breeder should arrive with a vet certificate by rule, and a puppy from a Missouri breeder arrives with whatever records you insist on. Insist.
### What should a puppy cost, and what does a too-low price mean?
Google’s related searches for puppies for sale in St. Louis read like a list of price ceilings: under $300, under $500, free. That’s the exact search a scammer hopes you’ll run.
The Better Business Bureau has been tracking this since a 2017 study that estimated at least 80 percent of sponsored ads in an online pet search may be fraudulent. Its 2020 update, which quoted the head of BBB St. Louis, put the median loss reported to BBB Scam Tracker that year at $750 and noted payments had moved from wire transfers to apps like Zelle and Cash App. The BBB puppy scam study and its updates are public.
The script barely changes. A photo, a sweet backstory, a price a few hundred dollars under everyone else’s, and a reason you can’t visit. Pay once and a second bill shows up: a special crate, pet insurance, a shipping fee. The BBB’s advice is to see the pet in person before paying anything, run a reverse image search on the photo, and learn what a fair price for the breed looks like, because a purebred puppy offered free or deeply discounted may be the bait.
So what should the price buy? Not a number. A list. From a careful breeder, the price usually covers the first vaccines and deworming, a vet exam, a written contract, records on both parents, and a promise to take the dog back if you can’t keep it. In breeds with known inherited problems, good breeders health-test the parents and show you the results without being asked twice. If the price is low and the list is short, you aren’t getting a deal. You’re paying later, at the vet.
Deposits are normal for a planned litter. Paying a stranger by gift card, payment app or wire before you’ve met isn’t. Use a payment method with a dispute process, and get a receipt with the breeder’s name and license number on it.
Puppy home soon? See the real dog training cost in St. Louis
### Is adopting cheaper than buying a puppy in St. Louis?
Usually, because the adoption fee bundles vet work you’d otherwise pay for one appointment at a time. At the Humane Society of Missouri, a puppy younger than nine months is $325, and the fee includes spay or neuter surgery, a microchip, the first DHPP and Bordetella vaccines, first deworming and an initial flea treatment, with a $10 rabies tag fee on top. Open Door Animal Sanctuary lists $150 for dogs and puppies, covering spay or neuter, vaccinations, a microchip and heartworm and flea preventatives. St. Louis County’s shelter in Olivette raised its fee from $40 to $80 in late 2025. Fees change, so check current prices before you go.
Compare that with a breeder’s puppy, where the spay or neuter, the microchip and the rest of the vaccine series are usually yours to book and pay for afterward. If money is tight either way, our guide to low-cost vet care in St. Louis covers the clinics and programs that shrink those bills.
Adopting doesn’t excuse you from the homework. Ask what the shelter or rescue knows about the puppy’s history, whether the mother came in too, and what help it offers if things don’t work out. Good rescues answer all three without blinking.
Either way, the first-day shopping list is the same, so here’s what to buy for a new puppy before pickup day. Once the vaccines are done and your vet says go, our guide to dog-friendly places in St. Louis covers where the new arrival can tag along.
### What should you get in writing before you pay?
All of it. Missouri has no puppy lemon law, so on this side of the river the contract has to do the job that law does in other states. Anything a breeder promises out loud is worth exactly what’s on paper.
The breeder’s full name, kennel name, address, and Missouri license or registration number.
The puppy’s birth date, sex, breed, color and microchip number, and whose name the chip is registered to.
Vaccination and deworming dates, with the name of the clinic that gave them.
A health guarantee that spells out what’s covered, for how long, and what happens if your vet finds a problem: refund, exchange or vet costs.
A set number of days to get your own vet exam, with a stated remedy if the exam turns something up.
A take-back clause, so a dog you can’t keep goes back to the breeder rather than to a stranger or a shelter.
Registration papers if you’re paying for them, knowing that papers record parentage, not how the dogs were kept.
Book the vet visit before pickup day, not after. An exam in the first few days gives you a dated record of the puppy’s health on arrival, and that record is exactly what a guarantee claim needs.
Check the household side while you’re at it. If this is your second or third dog, look up how many dogs you can have in St. Louis County, because the limit can change from one municipality to the next.
Finding a puppy is the easy part. Anyone can have one by Saturday. The buyer who asks for the AC number, reads the file and drives out to the kennel is the one whose money stops paying for the next litter on that list. Be that buyer. Start with the number.
Book that first exam before pickup day: find veterinarians around St. Louis on St Louis Near Me Directory and ask whether they can see a new puppy within a day or two of purchase.
If you run a vet clinic, training school or grooming shop that meets new puppies every week, list it with us so new owners find you before day one.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How do I tell if my puppy came from a puppy mill?
A.  Start with the paperwork you were handed. Ask the seller, or the store, for the breeder’s name and state and USDA license numbers, then look them up exactly as you would before buying. Commercial kennels often sell through brokers, stores and websites, so a missing breeder name is a clue on its own. Your vet’s first exam fills in the health side. If the puppy is sick, Humane World for Animals suggests reporting it to the USDA and to the breeder’s state agriculture department.
### Q. How to find a puppy not from a puppy mill?
A.  Adopt from a shelter or rescue, or buy from a breeder you’ve met where the puppies were raised. Both routes put you in front of the people and the conditions. In Missouri, add a records check: a license or registration number, the state inspection file through a Sunshine Law request, and a call to the breeder’s attending vet. Skip any seller who will only meet you in a parking lot.
### Q. What classifies a breeder as a puppy mill?
A.  Puppy mill is a description, not a category in Missouri’s breeder law, which regulates by headcount instead. Humane World for Animals uses the term for an inhumane breeding operation that churns out puppies for the pet trade, with dogs often caged and given little attention. Under state law, more than three intact females means a license, and eleven or more brings the Canine Cruelty Prevention Act’s stricter space, outdoor access and vet care rules.
### Q. How to tell if a breeder is a backyard breeder?
A.  Backyard breeders tend to be small and casual: a litter or two from the family dog, little or no health testing of the parents, no contract, and no plan if the puppy doesn’t work out. In Missouri, a breeder with three or fewer intact females needs no state license, so a missing license number proves nothing at that size. Ask about health testing, the parents’ vet records and a take-back promise. Vague answers are the answer.
### Q. How to spot a bad breeder?
A.  Watch what they won’t do. A bad breeder won’t let you visit, won’t show you the mother, won’t give you a license number or a vet’s name, always seems to have puppies of several breeds, and wants payment before you meet. Missouri inspection files add a second test: repeat violations, reinspection fees and refused inspections. In one 2026 report entry, state inspectors needed six attempts over 104 days to get inside.
### Q. What is the difference between a backyard breeder and a puppy mill?
A.  Mostly scale and business model. A puppy mill breeds in volume for the pet trade, often selling through brokers, stores or websites to people it never meets. A backyard breeder is small, usually sells directly, and often skips health testing. Missouri draws the line by headcount: no license at three intact females or fewer, a state license above three, and the stricter Canine Cruelty Prevention Act rules at eleven or more.
### Q. What are red flags in a dog breeder?
A.  Puppies always available, several breeds at once, no visits, a meeting spot instead of a home address, a price far below what other breeders charge, payment by gift card or app before you meet, pressure to decide today, and no contract or health records. In Missouri, add one more: a seller with more than three breeding females who can’t give you a state license or registration number.
### Q. Which states banned puppy mills?
A.  None has banned dog breeding outright. Several have banned pet stores from selling commercially bred dogs and cats, and Illinois is one of them: since February 23, 2022, Illinois pet shops may only offer dogs and cats from animal control facilities or shelters. Missouri has no statewide rule like that, which is why pet stores here can still sell breeder puppies. Missouri relies on breeder licensing and inspections instead.

## Lost Pets in St. Louis: Which Shelter Has Your Dog, How Long Strays Are Held, and Where to Look First
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/lost-pets-in-st-louis
Generic lost-pet advice assumes your town has one pound. St. Louis has a City shelter in Midtown, a County shelter in Olivette, Humane Society of Missouri campuses in the City and Maryland Heights, the APA in Brentwood, and County towns where a stray can sit at city hall for a few hours before anyone else hears about it. All of it is split by a boundary the City drew around itself in 1876. A terrier who slips her collar near Skinker Boulevard, which tracks the City’s western edge, can change jurisdictions just by crossing the street.
Then there’s the part the share-it-everywhere advice never mentions. The metro’s one shared lost-pet database, STL Lost Pets, pulls found animals from the Humane Society of Missouri, the APA and St. Louis County Animal Care & Control. The City’s own Animal Care Center isn’t on it. And CARE STL, the nonprofit that runs that City shelter, says on its website that it can’t currently accept strays carried in by the public at all. Only animals brought by City animal control officers.
So a Facebook post isn’t a search. It’s a flare. The search is your feet, your block, and a handful of buildings you walk into in person, because the national numbers say your dog is far more likely to be a few streets over than sitting in a kennel. Here’s the St. Louis version, in order.
### What do I do with a lost pet?
Search your own block on foot right away, because most lost dogs and cats turn up close to home. Then file a lost report with STL Lost Pets, flag your microchip as lost, put up big flyers, and visit shelters in person on both sides of the City and County line, starting the same day.
The first hour matters more than anything you type. Walk, don’t drive, and bring a leash, a bag of something that smells loud (a rotisserie chicken works). Check the places a scared animal wedges itself: under porches and decks, behind the water heater, in the window well, inside a neighbor’s open garage. The APA and the County shelter both list those spots first.
Talk to the people who are outside all day. The mail carrier. The crew mowing three houses down. The neighbor with the six o’clock dog walk. CARE STL tells people who find a pet to ask exactly those neighbors when they’re hunting for an owner, which means they’re also the people most likely to have watched yours go by.
Leave a way home. CARE STL’s advice for a lost dog is plain: put out food, water and its bed or a piece of your clothing, because there’s a good chance the dog comes back on its own. A garage door cracked a foot. A crate with the door wired open. Your worn sweatshirt on the back step.
Then do the paperwork, in this order:
Call your microchip company, confirm the phone number on file still works, and report the pet as lost. Don’t know the company? The chip number is in your vet’s records.
File a lost pet report with STL Lost Pets, which alerts the Humane Society of Missouri, the APA and the County shelter.
Email the City shelter separately at info@icarestl.org with your phone number, clear photos of your pet’s face, body and markings, and the microchip number or vet records. CARE STL says shelter staff monitor that inbox.
Print flyers and get them up within a few blocks before dark.
Walk into the shelters yourself, starting today.
That last step is the one people skip, and it’s the one the research rewards. In a study of 187 lost dogs around Dayton, Ohio, owners who called an animal agency got their dogs back at roughly twice the rate of owners who didn’t, and owners who visited one did nearly as well. Among the dogs that came home, the median wait was two days. Calling helped. Showing up helped. Hoping didn’t show up in the data at all.
### Which St. Louis shelters and pounds should you check first?
Start with the shelter that covers the spot where your pet went missing, then check the rest anyway. Animals cross the line. So do the people who pick them up.
Lost in the City of St. Louis. The City’s Animal Care Center at 2801 Clark Avenue in Midtown takes in the animals that City Animal Care and Control officers pick up. CARE STL has managed it since 2019 and calls it the only open-admission shelter in the City. The shelter number the City lists is 314-612-5310, and Animal Care and Control itself is 314-657-1500 during business hours. CARE STL posts found animals on its lost and found pets page and in a daily Facebook post, and its strays show up in a CARE STL feed on PawBoost. They do not show up on STL Lost Pets.
Lost in St. Louis County. St. Louis County Animal Care & Control runs the County shelter at 10521 Baur Boulevard in Olivette, 314-615-0650. When we checked, it was open 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. on weekdays and 10 to 4 on weekends, so confirm before you drive. Its strays are listed on the County’s stray pets page. One wrinkle worth knowing: the APA ran this building under contract from December 2022 until the County took operations back on February 21, 2025, and some municipal websites still tell residents the APA is in charge there. It isn’t anymore.
Before the County shelter, try city hall. Some County municipalities pick up strays themselves and hold them for a few hours first. St. John, for one, tells residents to call City Hall at 314-427-8700, extension 3, because it has no place to keep animals overnight and sends unclaimed ones on to Baur Boulevard. If you live in one of the County’s smaller towns, call your police department’s non-emergency line and ask a blunt question: did anybody bring in a dog today?
Then the private shelters. The Humane Society of Missouri has a City campus at 1201 Macklind Avenue (314-951-1562) and a campus in Maryland Heights at 11660 Administration Drive (314-951-1588). The APA Adoption Center sits at 1705 South Hanley Road in Brentwood (314-645-4610). Stray Rescue of St. Louis, at 2320 Pine Street (314-771-6121), is on the City’s own list of places to check.
Here’s why you check both sides. When we looked at the County’s stray list in early October 2026, one dog’s found location read Jefferson and Olive, ZIP code 63103, well inside the City limits. That dog was sitting in a kennel in Olivette. An owner who checked only the City shelter would have walked right past the answer.
Outside the two Missouri systems, St. Charles County runs its own Pet Adoption Center in St. Peters (636-949-7387), and Illinois counties run their own animal control, so a dog lost in Belleville or Edwardsville means a separate set of calls. For the full split between the City and the County, our breakdown of St. Louis city animal control versus the County’s covers who answers which call.
### Where do St. Louis lost-pet posts actually get seen?
Where the shelters themselves look. Every major shelter in the metro points people to the same short list. Use all of it.
STL Lost Pets is the shared database run by the Humane Society, the APA and the County. Its found-dog and found-cat lists refresh once an hour, and a lost report there alerts all three partners at once. The site says 90% of lost, stray and unwanted pets in the area end up at one of its agencies. Read that line with the City shelter in mind. It isn’t one of them.
PawBoost, Petco Love Lost and PetHarbor fill the gaps. PawBoost is listed on both the County’s and CARE STL’s lost-pet pages. Petco Love Lost, which matches photos of lost and found animals, is recommended by CARE STL, the APA and the County alike. The County also sends people to PetHarbor. Post on all three.
The APA’s text line is the fastest checklist in town. Text JOIN to 844-752-3642 and it sends back step-by-step actions, a resource list and a link to describe where your pet was lost.
Facebook still matters, if you post it right. Share to the STL Lost Pets page, the big metro lost-and-found groups, and the Buy/Sell/Trade group for your own municipality, and paste your flyer’s text into the post itself, not only the image, so the words can be searched. Nextdoor and the Ring Neighbors app reach the people physically closest to where your pet vanished.
Paper still wins, though. In the Ohio study, neighborhood signs brought home about 15% of the recovered dogs, and fewer than half of the owners bothered to hang any. Kat Albrecht, who has trained lost-pet recovery specialists since 1998, builds searches around giant neon posters, and lost-dog volunteers boil the design down to one photo, the words LOST DOG, a phone number and DO NOT CHASE. A driver stopped at a four-way can read that from the car. Nobody reads a Facebook post at a stop sign.
One warning that STL Lost Pets prints on its own homepage: no one will call you from a shelter and demand money up front to return your pet. Anyone who does is running a scam. Leave your home address off the flyer, and hold back one identifying mark so you can test a caller who says they have her.
### How long do St. Louis shelters hold a stray?
Assume you have days, not weeks, and act like you have hours. CARE STL describes a required five-day stray hold for City animals, after which an unclaimed pet becomes eligible for adoption. Back in 2012, the Humane Society of Missouri described the same five-day window for strays, with ten days for a dog wearing a tag or carrying a microchip while staff tried to reach the owner. Each agency and municipality sets its own rule, and rules change, so ask for the current number the first time you call.
Getting your pet back costs money, and the City publishes its fees. On the City’s posted fee table, impoundment is $20 for the first three days and $10 for each day after that, plus any vaccines or vet care the shelter provided. The same page says the Health Commissioner can waive fees case by case with proof of hardship, such as an award letter for SNAP, SSI, TANF, WIC or disability. If money is what stands between you and your dog, ask about the waiver at the desk. Fees change, so check the current table.
Bring proof. Photos of you with the pet, vet records, the microchip number, an adoption contract. CARE STL asks owners for the same items. Ask on the phone whether you’ll also need proof of a current rabies shot, so you aren’t sent home to find it.
Then walk every row, because online lists are only as good as the person typing them. When we checked the County’s stray list in October 2026, 16 of the first 30 animals were labeled terrier mix. Your schnauzer, your pit mix and your scruffy whatever-she-is could all be wearing that label. Plenty of entries also read In Foster Care, which means the animal isn’t in a kennel you can walk past at all. Ask the front desk to check foster placements against your description, and leave a flyer behind the counter.
Our look at what St. Louis animal shelters actually do explains intake, stray holds and why space runs tight.
Passports, PO boxes, shipping: what a St. Louis post office actually does
### Does a microchip really bring a lost pet home?
It more than doubles the odds, as long as the phone number behind it still rings. In a study of more than 7,700 microchipped strays entering 53 shelters, the chipped dogs went home 52.2% of the time, against 21.9% for stray dogs overall. For cats the gap was enormous: 38.5% against 1.8%. STL Lost Pets cites the same figures on its own microchip page.
The catch sits in the same study. The biggest reason shelters couldn’t reach an owner was a wrong or disconnected phone number in the registry. A chip is only a pointer, and a pointer to a phone number you gave up two moves ago leads nowhere.
Fix that tonight, before you need it. Find the chip number in your vet records, run it through the AAHA Universal Pet Microchip Lookup to see which registry holds it, and update your phone number plus a backup contact there. If your pet came from a shelter or rescue, ask whether the chip was ever transferred into your name.
Keep a tag on the collar too. In the Ohio study, dogs wearing a license tag were more likely to be recovered, and a 2025 survey of 1,500 dog owners by the pet-licensing company DocuPet found that 45% of lost dogs weren’t wearing a collar when they went missing. A neighbor can read a tag in a driveway. Reading a chip takes a scanner and a trip. In the City, registration for a spayed or neutered pet is listed at $4 on the City’s fee table, and the tag that comes with it is one more way back.
If your pet isn’t chipped yet, STL Lost Pets lists the APA, the Humane Society of Missouri’s Animal Medical Center of Mid-America and the County shelter as places that do it, along with most vet clinics. Our guide to low-cost vet care in St. Louis covers the cheaper routes.
### Why does a lost cat need a different search than a lost dog?
Because a lost indoor cat usually isn’t traveling. It’s hiding, silently, close by. In a 2018 study of more than 1,200 missing cats, indoor-only cats were found a median of 39 meters from where they got out, about 130 feet. Cats with outdoor access went farther, a median of 300 meters. Three out of four cats overall turned up within 500 meters.
That changes the whole search. A frightened cat won’t answer your voice and won’t come trotting down the alley. Search slowly, after dark, with a flashlight, because eyes shine back. Look under the porch, behind the AC unit, under the neighbor’s deck, in the window wells and gangways of a brick block in Tower Grove South or Dogtown. In that same study, 11% of recovered cats were inside somebody else’s house, most often in a garage. Ask the neighbors on both sides and behind you to open the garage and the shed and actually look.
Don’t write off the shelter, and don’t wait on it. In the ASPCA’s national survey, 59% of cat owners who got their cat back said it came home on its own, and only 2% found theirs at a shelter, which is exactly why cat owners sit tight. The Ohio researchers found cat owners waited about three days before contacting a shelter, against about a day for dog owners, and warned that some cats who never came home may have been in a shelter the whole time. Report a missing cat to STL Lost Pets and the City shelter on day one, the same as a dog.
### What if you find a lost dog in St. Louis?
Don’t chase it, and don’t rush it to a shelter. Both feel like helping. In St. Louis right now, neither one usually is.
Start with your body, not your voice. Kat Albrecht’s rule for a loose, scared dog is to stop calling it, because calling while you walk straight at a frightened dog reads as a threat and can send it into traffic. Sit or lie down sideways, look away, crinkle a food bag, and toss treats short of yourself. A friendly dog will come over on its own. A panicked one at least won’t bolt.
Once you have the dog, look for a tag, then get it scanned for a microchip. The County and CARE STL both send finders to a vet clinic for the scan, and the County shelter will scan one as well. Call the clinic first.
Then keep it close if you can. CARE STL asks finders to hold a found dog for at least 48 hours, hang signs near where it turned up, and post it online. Its website says it’s unable to accept animals brought in by the public because it has been operating beyond capacity for more than a year. The County says keeping a found animal near where it was found raises the chance of a reunion, and the APA says the same. If you’re willing to foster, CARE STL says it can cover supplies and vet care at no cost while you search.
File a found report so the owner’s search leads to you. STL Lost Pets takes found-dog and found-cat reports from people keeping the animal at home, and CARE STL has its own found pet report. Post a photo on PawBoost and Petco Love Lost. If the dog is hurt, don’t handle it: STL Lost Pets tells City and County residents to call the Humane Society of Missouri at 314-647-4400, and an emergency vet in St. Louis can stabilize it.
Found one after hours in the City? CARE STL says to email info@icarestl.org, keep the pet in a spare room or a crate overnight and call the shelter the next day, or report it on the police non-emergency line at 314-231-1212. In the County, the after-hours non-emergency line the shelter lists is 636-529-8210.
Be careful who you hand the dog to. A real owner can show photos, vet records or a microchip number that matches. If somebody’s story doesn’t hold together, call one of the shelters before you give the dog up. And if it’s a healthy-looking cat strolling your street, CARE STL’s advice is usually to leave it be. Plenty of outdoor cats belong to someone and know the way home.
If nobody comes forward after the hold, surrendering the dog isn’t your only move. Our guide to St. Louis pet rescues covers who places dogs and how fostering works.
The people who get their dogs back in this city usually aren’t the ones with the most shares. They’re the ones at the Baur Boulevard counter when it opens with a flyer in hand, then on the phone to Clark Avenue, then back in their own alley at five in the morning with a flashlight and a bag of chicken. Now you know which doors to knock on. And once she’s home and asleep on your feet, our guide to dog-friendly places in St. Louis is where the two of you go next.
Want every place a stray might land in one list? The animal shelters around St. Louis on St Louis Near Me Directory cover both sides of the river, so you can call straight down the list this afternoon.
If you run a vet clinic, groomer or boarding kennel that will scan a found dog for a chip, list your business with us so the neighbor holding somebody’s terrier knows your door is open.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What usually happens to missing dogs?
A.  Most get home. In the ASPCA’s national survey, 93% of lost dogs were recovered: about half because the owner searched the neighborhood, 15% because of an ID tag or microchip, and only 6% from a shelter. Dogs that land in a St. Louis shelter go on a stray hold, then become eligible for adoption, foster or transfer if nobody claims them.
### Q. What is the best way to find a lost dog?
A.  Search on foot immediately, put large signs at nearby intersections, and contact shelters the same day. Those are the moves the research rewards: in the Ohio study, calling an agency, visiting one and posting signs all raised the odds of recovery. Around St. Louis, that means a report to STL Lost Pets, a separate email to CARE STL for the City shelter, and in-person visits on both sides of the City and County line.
### Q. How far will a lost dog wander?
A.  There’s no reliable single number. A friendly dog often ends up on the nearest porch, while a frightened one, spooked by fireworks or a car crash, can cover miles. CARE STL notes that most lost dogs don’t wander far from home. Search in widening rings, and if sightings start coming from farther out, move your flyers and your feeding station to follow them.
### Q. Where do lost dogs hide during the day?
A.  Scared dogs usually lie low in daylight in quiet cover: under decks and porches, in sheds and open garages, in brush along creeks and rail lines, and on the wooded edges of parks. Around St. Louis that can mean the greenway along the River des Peres or the creek corridor beside Grant’s Trail. Check those spots quietly. Calling out and crashing through the brush can push a hiding dog farther away.
### Q. How to attract a lost dog back home?
A.  Make home easy to find. CARE STL tells owners to put out food, water and the dog’s bed or a piece of their clothing, because there’s a good chance the dog returns. Leave a garage or gate cracked where that’s safe. If you spot your dog, don’t call or chase. Sit or lie down, look away, crinkle a food bag and toss treats until the dog comes to you.
### Q. How long do dogs usually stay missing?
A.  Most recovered dogs come back fast. In a study of 187 lost dogs around Dayton, Ohio, the median dog was home in two days, though some took three weeks. The St. Louis County shelter notes that pets are reunited after days, weeks or even months of searching. Keep checking shelters past the first week, because the stray hold at the City shelter is only five days.
### Q. What do lost dogs do at night?
A.  Frightened dogs tend to move once the streets go quiet, traveling and looking for food and water after dark and around dawn. That’s when doorbell cameras tend to catch them. Ask the people near any sighting to check their overnight footage, and set up a feeding station with a trail camera there so you learn the dog’s schedule. Lost-pet recovery specialists use exactly that setup before they set a humane trap.
### Q. Where is a lost dog most likely to go?
A.  Somewhere close and familiar. Nearly half of the dogs in the ASPCA survey were found by owners searching their own neighborhood. Outgoing dogs often walk up to the nearest person or into the nearest open garage, which makes neighbors and mail carriers your best scouts. Scared dogs look for cover near food and water. And some ride away in a stranger’s car, which is why the shelter visits matter too.

## Pet Sitter Cost in St. Louis: What $30 a Day Buys and Who Needs a License
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/pet-sitter-cost-in-st-louis
Thirty dollars a day sounds like a fair price for pet sitting, right up until you ask what the thirty dollars buys. In St. Louis it might buy one 30-minute visit from an insured local company. It might buy a day and a half of drop-ins from a sitter you found on an app. It buys nowhere near a night with somebody sleeping on your couch. The number isn’t the problem. The yardstick is.
And here’s the part no price tag mentions. In Missouri, a sitter who takes your dog home to her spare room for the weekend and gets paid for it is supposed to hold a state license, pass an inspection before the first boarder arrives, and pay the state a dime per animal per boarding day. A sitter who lets herself into your house three times a day with your key needs nothing from the state at all. Same kind of listing. Same smiling profile photo. Opposite rules.
So this guide does two jobs. It lays out what St. Louis sitters actually publish, company by company, with the math for a weekend, a week and a holiday. Then it hands you the checks Missouri won’t run on your behalf, so the rate you pay buys what you think it buys. Every figure below comes from a published rate page, a booking app’s own St. Louis data or a state agency as of October 2026, and every one of them can change, so confirm the current rate when you book.
### Is $30 a day good for pet sitting?
It depends on the animal. For a healthy adult cat needing one visit a day, $30 is a fair St. Louis rate, about one 30-minute professional visit. For a dog it usually falls short: most dogs need two or three visits a day, and an overnight sitter costs more than $30 a night almost everywhere in the metro.
Run the numbers both ways. A single visit in St. Louis typically runs $15 to $25 from independent sitters on booking apps and $24 to $34 at the established local companies that publish prices, so $30 lands squarely in the fair zone for one cat visit, with a little left over for a second cat. A dog is a different job. 4 Legged Kids, which has done in-home pet care around St. Louis since 1997, requires at least two visits a day for a dog on a weekend trip and three a day on anything longer. At app prices, three visits come to $45 to $75 a day. At company prices it’s roughly $72 to $102.
So $30 for a dog buys one visit. One visit means your dog spends something like twenty-three and a half hours alone, holding it, watching the door. That’s the real answer hiding inside the question. Thirty dollars is a fine price. It’s the price of the wrong amount of care.
Overnights break the $30 frame completely. A sitter sleeping at your house runs $35 to $60 a night for a dog on one national booking app’s St. Louis data, and Fetch! Pet Care’s St. Louis location lists in-home overnights starting at $90. Anybody offering a full night for $30 is a friend, a beginner building reviews, or somebody worth a few more questions.
### How much does a pet sitter cost in St. Louis?
Expect $15 to $25 a visit from independent sitters on booking apps, $24 to $34 a visit from established local companies, and $35 to $90 or more for a night in your home. Those two tiers aren’t a typo. They’re two different products wearing the same job title.
Start with the app tier, because it sets the floor. One national booking app reports a St. Louis average of $22 per drop-in visit as of October 2026, with most bookings between $13 and $33 and a median of $20. Its June 2026 rate guide for the city puts dog drop-ins at $15 to $25, house sitting in your home at $35 to $60 a night, and boarding in the sitter’s own home at $30 to $50 a night. Then read the checkout screen: the app adds an 11% booking fee plus taxes on top of the sitter’s rate.
The company tier publishes less, which tells you something on its own. Fetch! Pet Care’s St. Louis location lists 30-minute pet-sitting visits from $24, a midday add-on visit at $22, an “almost overnight” package from $74 and full in-home overnights from $90. 4 Legged Kids lists pet-sitting visits starting at $34. Others post no prices at all and quote after an intake call, so ask for that quote in writing, with your exact schedule on it.
For a reality check on both tiers, a scheduling-software company that serves professional pet sitters publishes average rates drawn from the businesses using it. For the St. Louis region it shows about $27 for a 30-minute pet-sitting visit and about $41 for an hour, against $29.48 for 30 minutes statewide and $39.17 nationally (October 2026). St. Louis is a cheaper market than most of the country. Good for your budget. Also a reason to ask hard questions of anyone pricing far below it.
What does the gap between a $15 visit and a $34 visit buy? Mostly risk that somebody else carries. Liability insurance that pays if your dog gets hurt or bites another dog. A bond that covers theft from your house. Background checks on every employee. A second and third sitter who already know your house when the first one gets the flu. An office that picks up at 4 p.m. on a Friday when your flight slips. 4 Legged Kids, for example, says on its FAQ page that it carries a liability policy and a bonding policy, background-checks its staff and assigns each household two to four caregivers in its area.
Plenty of independent sitters carry some of that, and plenty are wonderful with animals. The difference is who checked. With a company, the company did. With an independent, you do. And if you’re still sorting out where your dog is welcome around town, start with our guide to dog-friendly places in St. Louis.
### How much does a cat sitter cost in St. Louis?
Less than a dog sitter, because the job is shorter. The same app’s June 2026 data puts St. Louis cat drop-ins at $15 to $25 a visit, about $7 more for each additional cat on a 30-minute visit, and $40 to $64 a night for a sitter who stays over. The software company’s figure for a professional 30-minute cat visit in the St. Louis region averages about $32.
Most healthy adult cats do fine with one visit a day, and that’s the minimum 4 Legged Kids books for cats. Two a day starts to make sense for kittens, seniors, a cat on a twice-daily medication, or a house where one cat bullies the other away from the bowl. Before you pick, ask yourself one thing. If something went wrong at 9 a.m., how long before anybody noticed?
That question matters more for cats than people expect. Cats hide illness well, and the first sign usually shows up in the litter box or the food bowl rather than on the cat. A cat who stops eating, or a male cat straining in the box, is a call-the-vet-today problem. A sitter who reports what she actually sees in the box and the bowl, every visit, is worth more than one who sends a cute photo of a cat on a windowsill.
The money favors sitters for cats almost every time. Cat boarding on that same app runs $30 to $45 a night plus about $15 for each extra cat, so two cats boarded for a week can cost roughly double what a daily visit costs, and the cats never see a carrier. If your cat genuinely handles a change of scenery better than an empty house, compare cat boarding in St. Louis before you decide.
### Drop-in visits or overnight stays: which do you need?
Drop-ins are enough for most cats and for adult dogs who sleep through the night without fuss. Overnights earn their price for puppies, seniors, anxious dogs, tight medical schedules and houses that shouldn’t sit dark. The deciding question is the gap: how many hours will your pet be alone between the last visit of the night and the first one of the morning?
With drop-ins, that gap usually runs ten or eleven hours. Last visit around 8 p.m., first one around 7 a.m. Most adult dogs sleep through it. A dog who paces, howls or chews the door frame once the house goes quiet does not, and that dog’s owner pays for it later in drywall.
Here’s the detail almost nobody checks: “overnight” isn’t a standard unit. 4 Legged Kids describes its overnight as about nine hours, roughly 9 p.m. to 6 a.m., with daytime visits booked separately. Fetch! Pet Care’s St. Louis location describes its in-home overnight as roughly 7 p.m. to 8 a.m., about thirteen hours, with a midday visit available for $22. Those are different products under one word. Ask for arrival and departure times in writing, and ask whether a midday visit is included, because a dog alone from 6 a.m. until a 5 p.m. visit has had a very long day.
There’s a middle option, too. Some companies sell a long evening visit plus a morning visit instead of a sleepover. Fetch! calls its version “almost overnight”: a two-hour evening visit and walk, then an hour the next morning, starting at $74. 4 Legged Kids sells a “Bed & Breakfast” visit built the same way, about two hours in the evening and a return for breakfast. For a calm dog who mostly wants company at dinner and a walk before bed, it covers what matters for less than a full night.
St. Louis adds its own reasons to book the overnight. The Fourth of July, when the fireworks start at dusk and roll on for hours. A January ice storm that keeps a drop-in sitter off the roads. A house sitting empty for ten days in August with the mail piling up on the porch. And high water: 4 Legged Kids says it went keyless in 2017, keeping access on each client’s property, after a flood left one client’s house reachable only by boat. Whatever you book, have a plan for the morning your regular sitter can’t get there.
Coming to town with the dog instead of leaving him home? Start with pet-friendly hotels in St. Louis, then ask the front desk whether your pet may stay in the room alone and whether an outside sitter can come up for a midday visit.
### Does Missouri license pet sitters?
Only the ones who keep your pet at their place. Missouri’s Animal Care Facilities Act requires a license for anyone who boards dogs or cats overnight, for pay, somewhere other than the owner’s home, and the Missouri Department of Agriculture classifies home-based boarding under a pet-sitter license. A sitter who comes to your house falls outside the program entirely.
Read that again with an app listing in mind. Boarding in the sitter’s own home is one of the most common things those listings sell, at $30 to $50 a night in St. Louis. Under the Department’s own guidance, the person selling it is supposed to hold an ACFA license, and the state regulation says boarding covers all boarding activities regardless of the name used, pet sitters included. Trainers and groomers get the same treatment. Training and grooming aren’t regulated in Missouri, but the moment a trainer or groomer keeps your dog overnight, a license is required.
Here’s what that license involves, per the Department’s ACFA page. A $125 application fee. A prelicense inspection before any license is issued. Routine inspections at least once a year after that, unannounced, usually between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. on weekdays. A per-capita fee for boarders of ten cents per animal per boarding day, so ten dogs for ten days comes to $10. And a renewal every year before January 31. Eighteen field staff cover the whole state, for breeders, shelters, pet shops and boarders alike.
It’s a real program with real paperwork. Inspection reports are available to the public through a Missouri Sunshine Law records request, and the ACFA office answers at (573) 751-3076 or acfa@mda.mo.gov. Some St. Louis companies say outright that they hold one: 4 Legged Kids states on its FAQ page that it’s licensed by the Missouri Department of Agriculture for pet sitting and private boarding. Ask any home boarder for her license number. A licensed one can give it to you on the spot.
Now the uncomfortable half. For a sitter who comes to your house, Missouri keeps no license, no inspection and no file. Nobody from the state has ever looked at her. The only checks are the ones you run yourself: a certificate of insurance you’ve actually seen, a bond if she carries one, a background check, and references from people whose houses she’s been inside. The vetting questions in our guide to dog walkers in St. Louis work for sitters word for word.
Crossing the river changes the rulebook. Illinois licenses kennel operators who keep dogs for a fee for more than twelve hours or overnight, under its own Animal Welfare Act, and the Illinois Department of Agriculture lists a $350 application fee per license type. If your sitter boards at her house in Belleville or Edwardsville, ask which license she holds, and check the current fee with the state if it matters to you.
The other bill nobody budgets: dog groomer prices in St. Louis
### Pet sitter or boarding kennel: which costs less in St. Louis?
For one dog, a kennel or an app house sitter usually costs the least, and drop-ins cost the most. Every extra pet tilts the math toward the sitter, because kennels charge per animal and sitters charge per visit. For cats, the sitter wins almost every time.
The kennel side is easy to price. Metro kennels that publish their rates charge about $34 to $60 a night for one dog, according to our breakdown of dog boarding in St. Louis. St. Louis Muttropolitan on Fyler Avenue, the lowest published rate we’ve found, lists $34 a night for one dog, $62 for two and $96 for three. Sled & Breakfast in Fenton lists $60 for a standard kennel. Confirm both before you book, since kennel rates move every year or two.
Now a five-night trip with one dog, using the published ranges above:
Kennel at $34 to $60 a night: $170 to $300.
App house sitter at $35 to $60 a night: $175 to $300, plus the 11% booking fee.
App drop-ins, three a day at $15 to $25: $225 to $375, plus the fee.
Company drop-ins, three a day at $24 to $34: $360 to $510.
Company overnights from $90 a night: $450 and up, before any midday visits.
Add a second dog and the picture moves. On the app data, a second dog adds about $11 to each drop-in and about $24 to a night of house sitting, while that cheapest kennel goes from $34 to $62. Add a third, and a house sitter at typical app rates lands in the same range as the kennel’s $96, with the dogs sleeping in their own beds. The crossover sits somewhere around the second or third animal, and it comes sooner if your dogs don’t board well together.
Then add what each side leaves off the sticker. Kennels typically want rabies, distemper and parvo, and bordetella records, often a temperament evaluation before the first stay, and many add a holiday surcharge of around $10 a night. Sitters add booking fees on apps, holiday rates, extra-pet fees and sometimes a lockbox deposit. 4 Legged Kids asks a $25 deposit for its lockbox and refunds it when the lockbox comes back. None of this is hidden if you ask. All of it is easy to miss if you don’t.
### What makes a St. Louis pet sitter charge more?
Holidays, extra animals, longer visits, puppies, medication, short notice and distance. Most of those are predictable, which means most of them are avoidable if you book like somebody who’s done this before.
Holidays first. The app’s June 2026 data shows St. Louis holiday averages around $25 for a drop-in, $54 a night for dog house sitting and $60 for cats, and its holiday list runs longer than most owners expect: Martin Luther King Jr. Day, Presidents Day, Memorial Day, Juneteenth, the Fourth of July, Labor Day, Thanksgiving, Christmas and New Year’s Day. Companies tighten their terms at peak times too. 4 Legged Kids notes that its cancellation terms require more notice during peak periods.
Timing is the cheapest fix. On that same app, St. Louis owners typically lock in a house sitter about ten days ahead for a dog and twelve days ahead for a cat. Holiday weeks need far more runway than that. Book the sitter the same week you book the flight.
Then the add-ons. In the app’s figures, a puppy drop-in averages about $22, a 60-minute drop-in adds about $11, an extra dog adds about $11 a visit and an extra cat about $7. Daily injections, insulin, or a dog who has to be carried down the back steps usually move the rate, and that’s fair. Ask for it priced up front instead of discovered on the invoice.
Distance matters in a metro this spread out. Companies draw service areas by ZIP code or county, and a house in Wildwood or Eureka can sit at the edge of somebody’s map. Ask whether your address is on the regular route. A sitter driving forty minutes each way, three times a day, will eventually be late.
Last, cancellations, where policies vary more than prices. 4 Legged Kids asks for more than three business days’ notice to cancel a trip, and canceling within 24 hours of the first visit forfeits the first 24 hours of fees. On the booking app, sitters pick their own policy, anywhere from same-day to seven days. Know which one you agreed to before your plans change, not after.
### What should a pet-sitting agreement cover?
Everything you’d want settled if your phone died the day you left, starting with what overnight means in actual hours and who can approve a vet bill. Get it on paper, or at least in one email you can both find later.
A good agreement covers, at minimum:
The visit schedule, with arrival windows, visit length and the exact hours of any overnight.
Feeding, medication and walk instructions for each animal, including what to do if a pet refuses food.
A vet authorization on file at your clinic, a dollar ceiling the sitter can approve without reaching you, and the after-hours hospital you’d choose.
Access: a lockbox or a code issued only to the sitter, never a key under the mat, and what happens to that access when the job ends.
A backup plan: who comes if the sitter can’t, and what changes in an ice storm or a heat advisory.
Proof of insurance and bonding, plus the ACFA license number if your pet stays at her place.
Cancellation, early return and holiday terms, in the sitter’s own words.
What every visit report includes: times, photos, food eaten, and litter box or bathroom notes.
The vet piece is the one people skip and regret. A sitter standing at an emergency desk at 11 p.m. without written permission is a stranger with no authority to approve treatment and no way to pay for it. Pick the clinic before you leave, using our guide to finding an emergency vet in St. Louis, and put its address in the agreement.
Splitting the trip between a pro and a neighbor? Expect paperwork. 4 Legged Kids says it doesn’t recommend sharing a trip with a friend or relative but has done it, and when it does, it asks clients to sign a hold-harmless clause and wants a note left after every visit the company didn’t make. That’s a business protecting itself. It’s also a hint. When two people share a job, nobody owns it unless the paper says who does.
Your pet can’t tell you how the week went. The paper can. Be the owner who wrote it down.
Ready to build a shortlist? Start with dog walkers around St. Louis, since the companies that walk dogs at noon are usually the same ones doing drop-ins and overnights when you travel.
And if you’re the pet sitter these owners are about to call, list your pet-sitting business with us with your insurance, service area and license up front, no public address required.
