Write the answers down. A week from now, when the cat is under the bed and the van is ten minutes out, you’ll want them in one place.
Most people in this metro will spend years wrestling a yowling carrier into the back seat because somebody online said nobody makes house calls here. You know better now. Find the practice that covers your street, save the number before you need it, and let the vet do the driving.
For the overnight stay, the x-ray and the 2 a.m. call a van can’t cover, browse veterinarians around St. Louis on St Louis Near Me Directory and pick a clinic close to home.
If you run a house-call or mobile practice and your trip fee only lives on a voicemail, the families searching for a vet who comes to them are reading this page, so list your practice with us.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much does it cost for a mobile vet to come to your house?
A.  Expect a trip fee on top of the exam. The one general-practice mobile vet in the area we found posting its rates online, Pet Country in Sullivan, starts its house call fee at $56 for the first 10 miles and charges $46 per exam. Most others quote by phone, so ask for the trip fee and the per-pet exam fee as two separate numbers, and check current rates.
### Q. How does a mobile vet work?
A.  You book a time window rather than an exact minute, because traffic and the stop before yours decide when the vet pulls up. The vet either works from a fitted-out van parked in your driveway or carries equipment into your home. Have cats in carriers early, pay at the visit or beforehand depending on the practice, and expect a referral to a hospital for anything that needs an overnight stay.
### Q. What are the disadvantages of mobile vets?
A.  Higher cost per visit, limited days and service areas, and no hospital behind the van at 2 a.m. Most can’t hospitalize a pet or take after-hours emergencies. Some lab work goes out and comes back a day later. You may owe the trip fee if you’re not home when they arrive. And a Missouri vet can’t work in Illinois without an Illinois license.
### Q. Is a mobile vet good?
A.  A mobile vet holds the same state license as a clinic vet and works under the same rules, so the care can be every bit as good. It’s strongest for anxious cats, large or senior dogs, homes with several pets and people without a car. It’s the wrong call in an emergency. Before you book, look the vet up on Missouri’s or Illinois’s license lookup.
### Q. How much does it cost to have a pet put to sleep at home?
A.  Around St. Louis, most published prices for the in-home visit run from about $370 to $475, going by the practices’ own sites in October 2026, and cremation adds roughly $100 to $480 depending on size and whether the ashes come back to you. Weekends, evenings and homes outside a practice’s main area usually cost more. Confirm current pricing when you call.
### Q. How long does an at-home euthanasia procedure take?
A.  Plan on 30 to 60 minutes from the moment the vet arrives, which is the range Home with Dignity gives for most visits. The sedative usually takes 5 to 15 minutes to work fully. The passing itself takes seconds to a few minutes after the final injection. The rest of that hour belongs to you, and a good vet won’t rush it.
### Q. How far out to schedule euthanasia?
A.  Call a few days ahead if you can. Most in-home practices can book within days, and several try for same-day visits, but same-day is never guaranteed, and weekends and holidays fill first and cost more. Pets at Rest urges families to reach out before a crisis. A phone consult, $150 at Pets at Rest, can help you decide whether it’s time.
### Q. Will a Missouri mobile vet come to Illinois?
A.  Only if that vet also holds an Illinois license. The 2014 federal law that lets vets carry sedatives and euthanasia drugs to your home covers only states where the vet is licensed. On the Illinois side, look to house-call practices based there, such as Metro-East Home Vet Care in Belleville or Daniel Randall Veterinary Clinic in Godfrey, and confirm they cover your town.

## Low-Cost Vet Care in St. Louis: Free Spay Days, County Vouchers, Vet Bill Help
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/low-cost-vet-care-in-st-louis
Same dog, same surgery, two posted prices. A female dog under 50 pounds, six months or older, can be spayed through SNIP, the Humane Society of Missouri’s subsidized program, for $59.95. The animal hospital inside the PetSmart on Lemay Ferry Road posts $540.95 for that spay, plus a $74.95 office visit. Both numbers sit on public web pages right now.
Part of that gap buys real things. The hospital package includes routine bloodwork, an IV catheter and fluids. Part of it is a subsidy. The same nonprofit clinic that runs SNIP charges $189.95 for that dog at its regular rate, and donors and grants carry the price the rest of the way down.
Search “low cost vet St. Louis” and neither price comes up. You get a page of clinic homepages calling themselves affordable. The real low-cost system here doesn’t look like a cheaper vet at all. It’s a county coupon, a nonprofit surgery line on South Jefferson, a Brentwood wellness clinic that has no x-ray machine, a drive-through rabies clinic capped at 100 dogs, and a few charity funds whose rules you only learn after you’ve paid the bill. Here it is on one page, with the posted prices and the catches.
### What is the cheapest way to get vet care?
Split the job. Buy vaccines, microchips and spay or neuter surgery from a nonprofit or shelter program, where St. Louis prices run a fraction of a full-service bill, and keep one regular vet for sick visits. If money is tight and your pet isn’t fixed yet, start there, because several local aid programs require it.
Vet care is really three jobs with three price structures. Prevention, meaning shots, a chip, and flea and heartworm control, is close to a commodity, and the nonprofits sell it cheap: Carol House Quick Fix Pet Clinic posts a $25 rabies shot. Routine surgery on a healthy animal, mostly spay and neuter, is where the subsidies run deepest. Diagnosis is the expensive job. Working out why a dog stopped eating takes an exam, bloodwork and sometimes an x-ray, and that’s exactly the work most low-cost clinics are set up not to do.
So the household that spends the least isn’t the one that found a bargain vet. It’s the one that buys each job where it’s cheapest. Shots at a wellness clinic or a pop-up. Surgery through a subsidized program. One regular vet for the day something is actually wrong.
Then there’s the rule that ties the whole St. Louis safety net together: get the pet fixed first. Inside the City, an unaltered dog or cat costs $50 to register and an altered one costs $4, according to the City’s pet registration rules, and that registration renews every one or three years along with the rabies shot. The Animal Protective Association’s vet-bill fund won’t help an owner who doesn’t want to spay or neuter. The Bi-State Pet Food Pantry asks new clients for proof of at least one spay or neuter on the very first visit. The cheapest surgery in town turns out to be the key to most of the other help.
If you haven’t brought a pet home yet, the cheapest vet care is the kind that’s already done. The St. Louis County Pet Adoption Center lists an $80 adoption fee that includes up-to-date vaccinations, a microchip and the spay or neuter (check the current fee before you go). Our guide to St. Louis animal shelters explains how the shelters work and what happens to the animals that come through the door.
For everything else that comes with owning a pet here, from patios to parks, start with our guide to pet-friendly St. Louis.
### Where are the low-cost vet clinics in St. Louis?
Five places around the metro post low-cost prices in public, and each one does a specific job. None of them is a cheaper copy of a full-service hospital. The fastest way to waste a morning is to show up at one with the wrong problem.
Carol House Quick Fix Pet Clinic, 1218 S. Jefferson Ave., is a nonprofit that opened in 2012 and says it has done more than 150,000 spay and neuter surgeries since. Surgery is by appointment at 314-771-PETS. Wellness runs on online reservations plus limited walk-ins on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and the posted wellness prices include a $25 exam, a $25 rabies shot, $20 distemper shots and a $35 microchip ($30 if it goes in during surgery). It doesn’t require proof of vaccines before surgery and lists no residency requirement. It doesn’t see sick or injured pets. Cash, debit, Visa or Mastercard, no checks. Spay and neuter prices aren’t posted online, so call and ask about its income-based discounts.
The APA Wellness Clinic, 1705 S. Hanley Rd. in Brentwood, is the Animal Protective Association’s appointment-only clinic. It gives vaccines, sells flea and heartworm prevention, and treats small problems: fleas, a mild ear or skin infection, an eye infection, an ingrown nail. It has no x-ray, no bloodwork and no surgery, and the APA says plainly that if your pet needs more, you’ll be referred out and still pay the exam fee.
Animal Medical Center of Mid-America, the Humane Society of Missouri’s veterinary partner, runs SNIP at 1201 Macklind Ave. in the city and 11660 Administration Dr. in Maryland Heights. SNIP is for Missouri residents, up to three pets per household a year, at $49.95 for cats, $59.95 for dogs under 50 pounds, $79.95 from 50 pounds and $99.95 from 100 pounds. The catches: a $50 nonrefundable deposit, a pet at least four months old, and rabies and distemper shots given by a licensed vet at least two weeks before surgery. The program runs on donations and grants, and the clinic warns that when the money runs out, SNIP appointments may not be available. Call 314-951-1534.
Five Acres Animal Shelter in St. Charles does surgery on Tuesdays with no residency or income requirement. Its posted fees are $100 for a cat neuter, $110 for a cat spay, $175 for a dog under 50 pounds and $225 for a bigger dog. You pay when you schedule.
St. Charles County’s Division of Humane Services runs a once-a-month low-cost surgery day at its Pet Adoption Center for county residents who can show proof of need: $40 per cat, $65 per dog, with a rabies shot included if the pet needs one, plus $5 for the tag. Book ahead at 636-949-7366. On the Illinois side, Operation SPOT says it runs free or low-cost spay and neuter programs across St. Louis and the Metro East.
Here’s how the posted prices line up for one ordinary patient, a dog under 50 pounds. Subsidized prices move with the grant money, so check each source before you book.
### How does the St. Louis County spay/neuter voucher work?
It works like a coupon. St. Louis County Animal Care and Control gives county residents a voucher that knocks a fixed amount off the surgery at a participating vet: $50 for a cat neuter, $60 for a cat spay, $70 for a dog neuter and $80 for a dog spay. You pay the rest of the bill yourself, and the County tells you to confirm the vet takes the voucher when you book.
The order of steps trips people up. You need proof of the surgical appointment to get the voucher, so book the surgery first. Then take a valid ID showing County residency, a current rabies certificate and that appointment proof to the Pet Adoption Center at 10521 Baur Blvd. in Olivette. The surgery has to be scheduled and done within 30 days of picking up the voucher. Questions go to 314-615-0650.
Because the voucher is a flat dollar amount, it covers a bigger share of a modest quote than a big one. Get the clinic’s price first, and ask whether it takes the County voucher in the same call. No rabies certificate yet? Fix that before anything else, since the County won’t issue the voucher without one.
Before you use it, check the free option. The County also holds Community Spay and Neuter Clinics at the Pet Adoption Center on the fourth Wednesday of every month, free for County residents. To get on the waiting list, email SpayNeuter.dph@stlouiscountymo.gov with your full name, your address, and your pet’s name and description. If you can wait for a slot, free beats a coupon. If you can’t, the voucher is the faster road.
The voucher is County only, which leaves City residents and everyone else looking elsewhere. Two volunteer-run groups fill a lot of that gap. BARC has subsidized more than 83,000 spay and neuter surgeries since 2003, with no residency restriction; its help is for privately owned family pets, not rescues or breeders. Pound Pals pays partner vets directly for surgeries on owned cats and dogs whose people need financial help, across the St. Louis metro and nearby Illinois. Carol House’s income-based discounts and St. Charles County’s $40 and $65 surgery day round out the list.
### Where can you get cheap vaccines and microchips in St. Louis?
Watch the visit fee, not the shot. The Banfield hospital inside the Lemay Ferry Road PetSmart posts a rabies vaccine at $28.41, which looks cheap until you read the line above it: every vaccine requires an office visit, posted at $74.95. Carol House charges $25 for the rabies shot and lists a $25 wellness exam fee. The Vetco vaccination clinic inside the Petco on Watson Road lists rabies at $41 and a microchip at $38, by appointment, and handles routine vaccines and preventive tests only.
The cheapest shots around come from pop-ups. Five Acres Animal Shelter’s 2026 low-cost vaccine clinics charge $20 each for a one-year rabies shot, distemper, Bordetella and a microchip. Cash only, first come first served, 9 to 11:30 a.m. or until supplies run out. Two dates are left this year: Saturday, Oct. 17 at the City of St. Charles Animal Shelter, and Saturday, Nov. 14 at The Academy of Pet Careers. Check the page for changes before you drive out, and plan on sitting in your car for about half an hour.
Free beats $20, and St. Louis County has been running free ones. With the Humane Society of Missouri, it held two drive-through clinics in August and September 2026, each offering rabies and DHPP shots plus a microchip to 100 pre-registered County dogs. The September clinic hit capacity, and HSMO told the overflow to watch its social media for the next one. When a date is announced, register that day.
For a microchip on its own, the best posted price is St. Charles County’s: $10 at its Pet Adoption Center during regular business hours, no appointment needed (call 636-949-7387 to confirm it’s open to you if you live outside the county). Otherwise, have the chip put in during the spay or neuter, while your pet is already under anesthesia. Carol House drops its chip price to $30 at surgery. Then register the chip with your phone number, the step people skip. A chip with no contact information can’t call anybody, and our guide to lost pets in St. Louis covers what to do if that day ever comes.
One City wrinkle. If a pop-up outside the City vaccinates your pet, you still owe the City registration. Its Animal Care and Control office at 1520 Market St. registers pets vaccinated by vets who don’t carry City tags: $4 for an altered pet, $50 for an unaltered one. Bring the rabies certificate.
Need care for yourself too? Free and low-cost health clinics in St. Louis
### What can you do if you can’t afford a vet bill?
Start in the exam room, before any money moves. Ask for an itemized estimate, ask which items have to happen today and which can safely wait, and ask whether there’s a less expensive version of the plan. It’s a normal question, and a good vet will answer it straight. That answer is worth more than any fund on this page, because nearly every fund has the same first rule: apply before the treatment, not after.
The local fund is the APA’s Heads to Tails Hope Fund. It’s needs-based and covers care beyond routine visits, meaning treatment, surgery and medication, and a grant typically covers up to half of the estimate, capped at $1,000. The fine print matters. It doesn’t fund emergency services or care already under way, it pays the vet directly, it helps a household one time, and it won’t fund an owner who doesn’t want the pet spayed or neutered (the APA says it can help arrange the surgery). You’ll need proof of income. Call 314-645-4610, ext. 167.
RedRover Relief’s Urgent Care grants are national and small on purpose. The average is around $250, meant to close a gap that’s keeping an animal from care, and RedRover can’t help if the gap is $500 or more. Household income has to be $60,000 a year or less, it’s one grant per household, and you need a diagnosis, a treatment plan and an estimate from the treating vet. The application closes at 4 p.m. Pacific every Friday, which is 6 p.m. in St. Louis, and reopens Monday morning. One line in its rules deserves a second read: if the same care is available nearby for much less, RedRover may ask you to get another estimate, and its example is staying at an ER for care a general practice could safely handle.
The Killuminati Foundation, a Missouri nonprofit, takes applications for non-routine care and, if it approves one, grants up to half the cost depending on need and funding. Stack these. Half from one fund plus a small gap from another can turn an impossible estimate into a payment you can actually make.
Financing comes last, and it’s the one to read slowly. Ask whether the clinic takes CareCredit or Scratchpay. CareCredit’s no-interest offers are deferred interest: if the promotional balance isn’t paid in full by the deadline, interest is charged all the way back to the purchase date at the card’s standard rate, which its posted terms listed at 32.99% when we checked. Divide the bill by the promo months before you sign, and read the current terms.
Money for the vet and money for the food bowl often run out together. Our guide to pet food pantries in St. Louis covers where to pick up food, and the Bi-State Pet Food Pantry says it offers financial support toward the spay or neuter it asks for. If you need help beyond the pet, dial 2-1-1 for United Way’s referral line.
### When is low-cost care the wrong choice?
When the animal is sick. Carol House doesn’t see sick or injured pets, and the APA Wellness Clinic publishes the list of problems it sends to a full-service vet: weight loss, lethargy, loss of appetite, vomiting, wounds that need stitches, heavy drinking or urinating, accidents in the house, trouble breathing, a coughing cat, seizures, limping, weakness in a leg, a swollen ear flap, a head tilt or stumbling, and any chronic condition. Pin that list to the fridge. It costs nothing, and it’s clearer than most of what turns up in a late-night search.
When it’s an emergency, skip everything on this page and go. Our guide to finding an emergency vet in St. Louis covers the signs that can’t wait until morning.
When the patient carries more risk under anesthesia. The SNIP price doesn’t include pre-anesthetic bloodwork; AMCMA recommends it for every pet and sells it as an add-on. Some full-service packages build it in, which is part of why they cost more: the Lemay Ferry hospital’s spay package includes routine bloodwork, an IV catheter and fluids. For an older pet or one with a known health problem, pay for the bloodwork, or ask your regular vet whether that surgery belongs somewhere with more backup.
When the dog is big and young. Banfield’s own spay guidance says large and giant breeds may benefit from waiting until 12 to 18 months, because hormones play a part in bone and joint development. A cheap early surgery isn’t a bargain if it’s the wrong age for that dog. Ask a vet about timing before you book.
And when you need a relationship rather than a transaction. Pop-ups and wellness lines don’t follow your pet across ten years. Keep every receipt and vaccine certificate in one folder, and find one regular vet for the sick days; our guide on how to choose a vet in St. Louis walks through it. If the hard part is getting there rather than the price, mobile vets in St. Louis come to you.
The mistake runs the other way, too. Paying ER prices for something a regular vet could safely handle the next morning is the most expensive vet bill in town, and even RedRover’s grant rules flag it. Knowing which door to walk through is the whole skill: a free County slot, a $20 pop-up, a fund that pays half, or a full-service vet who already knows your dog. None of those doors has a sign out front. Now you know where they are, and the next neighbor who asks gets the short version from you.
Need a regular vet for the sick days the low-cost lines won’t take? Browse veterinarians around St. Louis on St Louis Near Me Directory and call two with your pet’s records in hand.
And if you run a clinic, a house-call practice or a vaccine day of your own, being the name pet owners and AI tools find first when money is tight is the game now, so list your practice with us.
Two routine bills that catch owners off guard: puppy shots in St. Louis and dog teeth cleaning cost in St. Louis.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Where can I find low-cost spay and neuter services in St. Louis?
A.  The main options are Carol House Quick Fix Pet Clinic on South Jefferson Avenue, the Humane Society of Missouri’s SNIP program at AMCMA’s Macklind Avenue and Maryland Heights clinics, Five Acres Animal Shelter in St. Charles, and St. Charles County’s monthly surgery day. St. Louis County residents can also get a voucher worth $50 to $80 off at participating vets. Prices move with grant funding, so call before you book.
### Q. Where can I find a free spay and neuter clinic in St. Louis?
A.  St. Louis County holds free Community Spay and Neuter Clinics for County residents on the fourth Wednesday of every month at its Pet Adoption Center on Baur Boulevard, and you join the waiting list by email. Outside the County, BARC and Pound Pals help pay for surgeries for families who need it, and Carol House offers income-based discounts. Ask each one what it covers right now.
### Q. What is the cheapest way to get a dog spayed?
A.  If you live in St. Louis County and can wait, the free monthly County clinic. If you can’t wait, SNIP posts $59.95 for a dog under 50 pounds, for Missouri residents whose dog had its shots at least two weeks ahead. St. Charles County residents with proof of need pay $65. If even those prices are out of reach, apply to BARC or Pound Pals.
### Q. Where is the cheapest spay and neuter clinic?
A.  Around St. Louis, the lowest posted fees belong to programs with eligibility rules: free for St. Louis County residents who get a monthly clinic slot, $40 per cat and $65 per dog for qualifying St. Charles County residents, and SNIP’s $49.95 cat and $59.95 dog rates for Missouri residents. With no residency rule at all, Five Acres posts $100 to $225, and Carol House quotes by phone.
### Q. What is the average price to get a female dog spayed?
A.  Banfield’s own spay guide says dog spays and neuters typically run $250 to $600, depending on size, age, health and the vet. In St. Louis, posted prices for a dog under 50 pounds run from $59.95 through SNIP to $189.95 at AMCMA’s regular rate and $540.95 for a full package at a chain hospital. Ask what each quote includes before you compare them.
### Q. How much does a spay cost at PetSmart?
A.  PetSmart stores don’t do surgery themselves; vet hospitals inside some stores do. Banfield Pet Hospital inside the PetSmart on Lemay Ferry Road posts dog spay packages from $469.95 for a puppy under six months to $618.95 for an adult over 50 pounds, and cat spays at $326.95 to $383.95, plus a $74.95 office visit. Packages include bloodwork, an IV and fluids. Check current pricing.
### Q. Does Petco offer spaying?
A.  At its full-service Vetco Total Care hospitals, yes. Around St. Louis, they’re inside the Petco stores on Eager Road in Brentwood and on Mid Rivers Mall Drive in St. Charles. Surgery needs a consultation first and can’t be booked online, and no spay price is posted. The Vetco vaccination clinics, like the one in the Watson Road Petco, do vaccines and preventive tests only.
### Q. Will a low-cost clinic see a sick pet?
A.  Usually not. Carol House doesn’t see sick or injured animals, and the APA Wellness Clinic treats only minor problems like fleas or a mild ear infection, with no x-rays, bloodwork or surgery on site. Vomiting, lethargy, limping, trouble breathing or seizures need a full-service vet, or an emergency hospital if it can’t wait. Low-cost clinics are built for prevention.

## Exotic Vets in St. Louis: Bird, Reptile and Rabbit Vets, 24/7 Exotic ERs, Missouri vs Illinois Pet Laws
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/exotic-vets-in-st-louis
Stale vet lists fail at night. A rabbit stops eating at nine on a Friday, somebody in Ballwin types “exotic vet near me” into a phone, and what loads first is a list compiled years ago and never checked since. Some of those numbers ring clinics that closed at six. Some ring practices where the one doctor who saw rabbits has moved on.
House Rabbit Society, the national rabbit welfare group, draws the line at 12 hours: a rabbit that hasn’t eaten or pooped in that long is an emergency. Birds and reptiles are worse at telling you. Many hide illness until it’s advanced. That’s why the list you need isn’t the one a search engine hands you at 9 p.m. It’s the one you built on a slow Tuesday, with three numbers you’ve already called.
St. Louis adds a twist that a vet guide for Denver or Dallas never has to handle. This metro straddles a state line, and the river changes more than the area code. Under Missouri law, a pet monkey is a registration question. Inside the City of St. Louis, it’s banned outright. Cross the Poplar Street Bridge and Illinois has barred new pet primates since January 1, 2011.
So this guide maps both sides: who treats birds, reptiles, rabbits and pocket pets, which hospitals take them at 2 a.m., how to find out what a visit costs, and what you can legally keep where you live. Everything here was checked against clinic websites, state statutes and city pages in October 2026. Exotic care follows doctors, not buildings. Call before you drive.
### How to find an exotic vet?
Start with the vet-finder lists kept by the Association of Avian Veterinarians, the Association of Exotic Mammal Veterinarians and the Association of Reptile and Amphibian Veterinarians. Then call and ask which doctor sees your species, how often, and where they send exotic patients after hours. Do it before your pet is sick.
Those three groups are the professional homes of vets who chose this work on purpose. Each runs a public search: Find-A-Vet at the avian association, Find a Vet at the exotic mammal association (rabbits, ferrets, guinea pigs, chinchillas, rats), and Find A Vet at the reptile and amphibian association. Membership tells you a vet has a real interest in the species. It doesn’t tell you that vet still works at the address listed, so treat every result as a lead to confirm, not an answer.
One level up is board certification. The American Board of Veterinary Practitioners certifies specialists in Avian Practice, Exotic Companion Mammal Practice, Reptile and Amphibian Practice and even Fish Practice, and its Find a Specialist search shows who holds the title. Diplomates are rare in any metro. You don’t need one for a guinea pig’s nail trim. You might want one for a cockatoo with a lump on its chest.
Local rescues are the shortcut most owners miss. A rescue that fosters parrots or rabbits puts its own animals in front of exotic vets every week, and it learns fast which practices pick up the phone on a Saturday. St. Louis Avian Rescue, known as STAR, publishes its partner vets and its emergency partners on its website. For bird owners, that’s about as close to a vetted local list as you’ll get.
Then make the call. These five questions separate a real exotic practice from a dog-and-cat clinic willing to “take a look”:
How many animals of my species did your practice see last month? A clinic that sees bearded dragons every week answers without hesitating.
Which doctor sees them, and on which days?
Can you keep my pet overnight if it needs to be hospitalized, and who checks on it?
Where do you send exotic patients when you’re closed?
For rabbits: do you carry the RHDV2 vaccine? The U.S.-licensed version starts as two doses about three weeks apart, and whether your rabbit needs it is worth a conversation.
The second question is the one that saves you. At several metro practices, the exotic service is one named veterinarian. Animal Emergency Clinic names Dr. Ferry on its exotic care page. Fairview Heights Animal Clinic announces that Dr. Craig Thacker “is now seeing exotic pets.” When exotic care rides on one person, it can disappear the month that person leaves, and nobody updates the old lists. Ask for the doctor by name, and ask again at every annual exam.
If you’re also picking a practice for a dog or cat in the same house, our guide on how to choose a vet in St. Louis covers the routine-care side.
### Which St. Louis vets see birds, reptiles, rabbits and pocket pets?
Each practice below says on its own website, as of October 2026, that it treats exotic species. The list runs by side of the metro, not by any ranking, and it’s a starting map rather than an endorsement.
West County. Kersting Animal Hospital, which also operates as Bird Medicine and Surgery, sits in the Four Seasons Shopping Center in Chesterfield and calls birds its specialty, from parrots and cockatiels to raptors and waterfowl, with reptiles and small mammals seen too. Tri-City Animal & Bird Clinic in Ellisville has been open since 1961 and lists birds and exotics of all types. Fox Creek Veterinary Hospital, with West County locations including Wildwood and Manchester, lists guinea pigs, rabbits, ferrets, sugar gliders, hedgehogs, hamsters, rats, mice, chinchillas, reptiles and amphibians.
Mid County. Creve Coeur Animal Hospital on Olive Boulevard says it has more than 20 years of experience with reptiles: nonvenomous snakes, turtles, tortoises, bearded dragons, iguanas, chameleons and geckos, plus pocket pets. Notice the word nonvenomous. Owners of hot snakes need a different plan, and inside the City of St. Louis they can’t legally keep one at all.
South City. St. Louis Hills Veterinary Clinic on Hampton Avenue, family owned since 1974, treats dogs, cats, birds and other exotic species, and its site lists hours until 7 p.m. Monday through Wednesday. St. Louis Veterinary Center, also in South City, lists exotic animal care among its main services.
North County. Howdershell Animal Clinic in Florissant says it handles small animals, birds and exotic pets of all kinds, and it offers house calls (call for details). It serves Florissant, Hazelwood and the rest of north County.
St. Charles County. Bryan Road Animal Hospital in O’Fallon, Missouri, describes itself as caring for pocket pets and exotics, and it’s one of STAR’s partner vets for birds. Animal Emergency Clinic’s O’Fallon location books wellness and sick visits for exotics: birds including backyard poultry, ferrets, rabbits, pot-bellied pigs, guinea pigs, chinchillas, hamsters, gerbils, sugar gliders, hedgehogs, lizards, turtles, tortoises and snakes. It asks exotic owners to call ahead.
Metro East. Hawthorne Animal Hospital runs a 24/7 hospital in Glen Carbon, next door to Edwardsville, and treats rabbits, pocket pets, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish. Fairview Heights Animal Clinic and its sister practice, the Animal Hospital of O’Fallon in O’Fallon, Illinois, see small mammals, pocket pets and reptiles through Dr. Thacker, who has worked with exotics for more than 20 years. Village Veterinary in Collinsville offers exotic wellness and exotic surgery for birds, reptiles and small mammals, and recommends twice-yearly exams for every exotic pet.
A clinic missing from this list may still see your pet; we just couldn’t confirm it on the clinic’s own site. If your regular vet already handles your hamster well, keep that vet. Learn where they’d send it at midnight.
### What do you do in an exotic pet emergency after hours?
Call before you drive, every time. Three emergency practices on the Missouri side and one in the Metro East say they take exotics after hours, but which doctor is on shift matters far more for a parrot than for a Labrador. A two-minute call lets the team get ready.
VEG Brentwood at 2101 South Brentwood Boulevard and VEG St. Peters at 250 Mid Rivers Mall Circle are open 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. Both take walk-ins with no appointments, both say they treat birds, reptiles, turtles, snakes, lizards and other exotics, and both let you speak with a doctor by phone. VEG still recommends calling first.
Animal Emergency Clinic runs 24/7 emergency care at 9937 Big Bend Road in Kirkwood and 334 Fort Zumwalt Square in O’Fallon, Missouri. Its exotic service is described at the O’Fallon site, and the clinic asks exotic owners to call ahead so it can fit your pet in.
Hawthorne Animal Hospital at 5 Cougar Drive in Glen Carbon is the Illinois-side option. It describes itself as the only 24/7 emergency hospital in the St. Louis Metro East with the capability to care for exotics.
STAR lists AEC O’Fallon and both VEG hospitals as its emergency partners for birds. That’s a useful tell. A rescue with parrots in foster homes every night has every reason to know where a bird can be seen at 3 a.m.
What counts as an emergency? Hawthorne’s exotic team lists respiratory distress, discharge from the mouth or nose, popping or clicking sounds when breathing, traumatic injury, inability to move, vomiting, seizures or tremors, straining to urinate or defecate, any prolapsed tissue, and swollen joints or limbs. For rabbits, add House Rabbit Society’s 12-hour rule on eating and droppings. When in doubt, call. The phone call costs nothing.
On the way in. Bring your pet in a secure carrier; Animal Emergency Clinic asks that every exotic arrive properly secured in one. Keep a sick bird warm and away from other pets, which is the clinic’s own home-care advice. Then take three photos: the enclosure, the heat and light setup, and the food. Exotic vets ask about habitat constantly. Creve Coeur Animal Hospital, for one, reviews husbandry and nutrition at every wellness or sick visit.
Dog or cat emergency tonight? Start with the emergency vet in St. Louis guide.
Save these numbers today, under a contact name you can find with shaking hands. “Exotic ER, Missouri” and “Exotic ER, Illinois” work fine.
### What does an exotic pet exam cost in St. Louis?
Nobody posts it. None of the exotic service pages we checked for this guide, on either side of the river, lists an exam price, so the real number comes from a phone call. Ask for three figures instead of one: the exam fee for your species, what a first visit usually adds, and the exam fee at the emergency hospital you’d use after hours.
The exam fee is the floor. Some practices charge the same for a rabbit as for a dog. Others charge more for exotics, since the appointment runs longer and the doctor has extra training. Neither is a red flag. A clinic that won’t give you a number on the phone is a different story.
What a first visit adds depends on the animal. For birds, St. Louis Avian Rescue describes a wellness exam that can include bloodwork, radiographs and gram stains on top of the hands-on exam. Reptile visits tend to turn into a habitat review. Rabbits may start the RHDV2 vaccine series. Pocket pets often need a tooth check, and Fox Creek notes that guinea pigs and rats are especially prone to dental problems.
How often you go drives the yearly bill more than any single fee. Hawthorne recommends a yearly wellness exam for exotics and more frequent visits for pets that are elderly, chronically ill or naturally short-lived (under 10 years). Village Veterinary in Collinsville recommends exams twice a year. STAR says birds should be seen at least once a year, and some twice. Budget for the schedule your vet recommends, not the cheapest one you can talk yourself into.
Emergency visits cost more than daytime ones nearly everywhere, and a hospitalized bird or rabbit adds daily care charges on top. That’s the bill that hurts, and the best argument for the annual exam.
### Which exotic pets are legal on each side of the river?
Most of what people actually keep, rabbits, guinea pigs, parakeets, bearded dragons, ball pythons, is legal in both Missouri and Illinois. The split shows up at the dangerous end of the list, and it’s sharper than a glance at the map suggests.
Missouri, state level. Missouri doesn’t ban most dangerous wild animals. It requires registration. Under RSMo 578.023, anyone keeping a lion, tiger, leopard, ocelot, jaguar, cheetah, margay, mountain lion, Canada lynx, bobcat, jaguarundi, hyena, wolf, bear, nonhuman primate, coyote, or any deadly, dangerous or poisonous reptile (or a dangerous reptile over eight feet long) outside a zoo, lab, veterinary hospital or similar institution must register it with the local law enforcement agency in the county where it lives. Skipping that step is a class C misdemeanor.
Big cats and nonnative bears carry a second layer. Missouri’s Large Carnivore Act requires a permit from the state Department of Agriculture for each animal, a microchip, at least $250,000 in liability insurance, and an owner who is 21 or older, with a permit fee of up to $2,500. Federal law now caps the whole category anyway. The Big Cat Public Safety Act, signed in December 2022, bars private ownership and breeding of lions, tigers, leopards, snow leopards, clouded leopards, jaguars, cheetahs and cougars, except for owners who registered existing animals with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service by June 18, 2023.
The City of St. Louis. The City’s Animal Care and Control page lists pets prohibited within City limits, a list far stricter than the state’s that includes all bears, big cats, all nonhuman primates, foxes, wolves, coyotes and their hybrids, alligators, crocodiles and caimans, all venomous snakes, and any constrictor snake over eight feet long. The City also caps a residential parcel at four domestic animals without a kennel permit, and its examples of pets that count toward the four include rabbits. One pot-bellied pig per parcel is allowed inside that four. Our guide to how many dogs you can have in St. Louis County covers the limits on the County side.
St. Louis County and its cities. Dozens of municipalities inside the County write their own animal ordinances, and a city can be stricter than the state. Before you bring home anything on Missouri’s registration list, call your city hall, or St. Louis County Animal Care & Control if you live in unincorporated County, and get the answer in writing.
Illinois. Cross the river and the dangerous list becomes a ban. Illinois law (720 ILCS 5/48-10) says no one may keep a lion, tiger, leopard, ocelot, jaguar, cheetah, margay, mountain lion, lynx, bobcat, jaguarundi, bear, hyena, wolf or coyote, or any nonhuman primate, except at a zoo, licensed exhibit, university, research lab, veterinary hospital or similar facility. The only private pet primates still allowed are ones owned before January 1, 2011 and registered with local animal control by April 1, 2011. Every day of a violation counts as a separate offense.
Illinois handles reptiles in a separate law, the Herptiles-Herps Act. Venomous species require a Herptile Special Use permit from the state, and the keeper must carry $100,000 in liability insurance or a surety bond per animal, up to $1 million. The approved venomous list is mostly species native to the U.S., minus several rattlesnakes and coral snakes. Boas, pythons and anacondas are exempt from the permit, the fee and the insurance, as long as the state’s care standards are met.
### Can you keep a turtle you found in Missouri or Illinois?
In Missouri, often yes, within limits. The state Wildlife Code (3 CSR 10-9.110) lets a Missouri resident take and keep up to five of a native species alive without a permit, but those animals can’t be bought or sold, and endangered species and a short list of protected animals are excluded. A three-toed box turtle from your own backyard can be a legal keep. Selling its offspring isn’t. Public land can carry its own rules, so check before you pick anything up there.
Illinois is tighter, and it comes with a twist: you need a fishing license. Under the Herptiles-Herps Act, an Illinois resident may keep no more than four of any native reptile or amphibian species and no more than eight in total, and collecting one from the wild requires a valid sport fishing license. On public land, the agency that manages it also has to allow collecting. Going over the limit takes a state permit, wherever the animals came from.
The part Missouri families miss is the nonresident rule. Illinois says nonresidents may not keep herptiles collected from the wild in Illinois unless they first get a scientific collection permit. So a turtle picked up on a day trip to Horseshoe Lake State Park near Granite City isn’t a legal souvenir for a family from Florissant. Leave it where you found it.
If you’re buying a reptile instead of finding one, our guide to fish stores in St. Louis covers where local keepers shop, and any of the turtle-seeing clinics above can do the first exam.
### How can you tell an exotic pet is sick before it’s too late?
Often you can’t, which is the whole case for the annual exam. Animal Emergency Clinic points out that many pet birds are prey species that hide signs of illness as a defense against predators. Hawthorne says many exotics are sick before they start showing symptoms, and lists the early signs as poor appetite, lethargy, weight loss and shedding issues. STAR warns that by the time you notice symptoms in a parrot, the bird is often already quite ill.
So watch the boring things, every day. Is the food bowl as empty as yesterday? Are the droppings the usual size, number and color? Is the animal in its usual spot at its usual hour? Weigh it weekly on a kitchen gram scale and write the number down. A scale is cheaper than one exam, and it catches a slow slide before your eyes do.
Then act on small changes. A rabbit with no droppings by morning. A bird that stops talking and stays on the cage floor. A bearded dragon that skipped two meals and won’t bask. Each is a same-day call, not a wait-and-see weekend.
### Can a mobile vet or house call handle an exotic pet?
Sometimes, and for a stressed bird or a nervous rabbit, skipping the car ride is a real plus. Howdershell Animal Clinic in Florissant offers house calls, and Fox Creek Veterinary Hospital advertises mobile visits; ask either one whether the house-call doctor sees your species before you book. Our guide to mobile vets in St. Louis covers what a house call can and can’t do.
Know the limit. X-rays, anesthesia, surgery and overnight care still mean a hospital, and a real emergency means the ER list above, not a van in the driveway. A house call is best for wellness exams, nail and beak trims, and the end-of-life visit you’d rather keep at home.
The whole plan fits in one afternoon. Pick a primary exotic vet, confirm the doctor by name, save one ER on each side of the river, and weigh your animal once a week. That makes you the owner who already knows which door to drive to at 2 a.m., while everyone else is still scrolling a list that went stale years ago. For the rest of the metro’s animal map, from patios to parks, start with our guide to pet-friendly St. Louis.
Building your list now? Browse veterinarians around St. Louis on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call and ask the five questions above.
If you run a practice that sees birds, reptiles or rabbits, list it with us and say so plainly, because the owner searching late on a Friday is looking for exactly that line.
Thinking about a rabbit? Our guide to rabbit adoption in St. Louis covers the adoption side before you need an exotic vet.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much does a visit to an exotic vet cost?
A.  It depends on the species and what the visit adds. Expect an exam fee, usually a parasite check, and for birds possibly bloodwork and radiographs, and expect an emergency hospital to charge more than a daytime clinic. None of the St. Louis exotic service pages we checked posts a price, so call and ask for the exam fee for your animal plus the usual first-visit tests.
### Q. Are exotic pets legal in Missouri?
A.  Many are. Missouri requires registration with the county’s local law enforcement agency for animals such as big cats, bears, wolves, nonhuman primates and dangerous reptiles (RSMo 578.023), a state permit for big cats and nonnative bears, and federal law bars new private big cats. Cities can go further. The City of St. Louis bans primates, venomous snakes and big constrictors.
### Q. Are exotic pets legal in Illinois?
A.  Common ones like rabbits, parakeets, ball pythons and bearded dragons are. Illinois bans keeping big cats, bears, wolves, coyotes, hyenas and nonhuman primates outside zoos, labs and similar facilities, with only registered primates owned before 2011 grandfathered in. Venomous reptiles need a state Herptile Special Use permit and $100,000 in liability coverage per animal.
### Q. Is PetSmart an exotic vet?
A.  No. PetSmart is a pet retailer. Many PetSmart stores house a Banfield Pet Hospital, which is a separate veterinary company, and Banfield’s exotic services vary by location. Some Banfield hospitals list birds, rabbits and reptiles, while many focus on dogs and cats. Check the individual hospital’s page, then call and ask which doctor sees your species.
### Q. What is the easiest exotic pet to own?
A.  The one a vet near you already treats. Rabbits and guinea pigs are seen by most of the exotic-capable practices in this guide, while a hedgehog or a chameleon narrows the field quickly. None of them is low maintenance. If you’re set on a rabbit or guinea pig, check St. Louis pet rescues before a breeder, since small animals end up in shelters too.
### Q. Are exotic pets expensive?
A.  The animal is often the cheap part. Lighting, heat, enclosures and specialty food drive the setup cost, exotic exams can cost more than a dog or cat visit, and long-lived species like large parrots and tortoises can need care for decades. Insurance helps for some species. Nationwide sells an avian and exotic plan, though it isn’t offered in every state.
### Q. Which US states allow exotic pets?
A.  Nearly every state allows common exotics such as parakeets and many reptiles. The real differences sit at the dangerous end. Missouri regulates animals like primates and wolves through registration and permits, Illinois bans them outright, and the federal Big Cat Public Safety Act bars new private big cats in every state. Cities and counties add their own rules, so check locally.
### Q. What is the most exotic pet I can own?
A.  In St. Louis, that depends on your address more than your ambition. Missouri law lets some dangerous animals be kept with county registration, but the City of St. Louis bans primates, big cats, bears, venomous snakes and big constrictors, County cities set their own rules, and Illinois bans the whole dangerous list. The most exotic pet worth owning is one a vet will see at 2 a.m.

## Pet Food Pantries in St. Louis: Where to Get Free Dog Food, What to Bring, Why SNAP Won't Pay
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/pet-food-pantries-in-st-louis
SNAP won’t buy a single can of cat food. Not one. The USDA files pet food under “nonfood items,” in the same list as cleaning supplies and paper products, so the card that covers your groceries stops working at the edge of the pet aisle.
Here’s what rarely gets said. The letter proving you get SNAP is one of the papers St. Louis pet food pantries ask to see. Bi-State Pet Food Pantry lists food stamps as proof of need. The Jefferson County Pet Food Pantry asks for a Food Stamp Determination letter by name, and across the river Gateway Pet Guardians accepts an Illinois Link card. The benefit that can’t buy the kibble is the paperwork that gets it for free.
The harder problem is finding a pantry that’s actually open. When we searched “pet food pantry St. Louis” in October 2026, one of the top results was a pantry in Lindenhurst, New York, out on Long Island. Another was a 2013 newspaper story giving an address that isn’t the pantry’s pickup site today. A third promised Saturday walk-ins, while that pantry’s own website says one Sunday morning a month, with paperwork. Lists go stale when nobody checks them, and you’re the one who burns the gas finding out.
So every program below was checked in October 2026 against its own website, its own recent posts or a government page. Donated food runs out and dates move, so call before you drive. And if this is your first time asking for help with a pet, you’re in good company.
### How to get dog food when you have no money?
Use a pet food pantry. Around St. Louis, Bi-State Pet Food Pantry, CARE STL, Stray Rescue, Five Acres, Metro East Humane Society and county programs hand out free dog and cat food. Most ask for a photo ID, proof of need such as a SNAP or Medicaid letter, and proof your pet is spayed or neutered.
The practical version has four steps, in this order.
1. Pick by calendar, not just by distance. Most pantries here don’t run like a grocery store. Bi-State hands out food one Sunday morning a month. The Jefferson County pantry also runs one Sunday a month. Five Acres in St. Charles opens its pantry every Saturday morning, and Metro East Humane Society takes walk-ins most afternoons. The closest pantry might be three weeks from its next distribution while one twenty minutes farther is open tomorrow.
2. Put three papers in one folder tonight. A photo ID. A benefits letter or other proof of need. A vet record showing your pet is spayed or neutered. That folder gets you through the door at nearly every pantry on this page.
3. Call first. Pantry shelves run on donations, and they empty. Stray Rescue posted in May 2026 that its pantry was looking bare. Five Acres says it’s serving more families than it has donated food for. A two-minute call saves a wasted trip.
4. Switch foods slowly. Pantry food is whatever got donated, which is rarely your dog’s usual brand. Bi-State’s own application warns that a new food can upset a pet’s stomach and suggests mixing it in gradually with what you already have. So don’t finish the old bag first. Blend the two.
Need food before any pantry opens? Dial 211, the United Way’s line for basic needs; the person who answers may know a church pantry or giveaway with donated pet food that week. And don’t fill the bowl from the people pantry without checking first. The ASPCA lists grapes, raisins, onions, garlic, chocolate and xylitol among the people foods to keep away from pets.
### Where are the pet food pantries in St. Louis?
Ten programs, sorted by where you live. Hours, dates and rules are what each one published as of October 2026.
In the City of St. Louis
Bi-State Pet Food Pantry. All volunteer. Its founders started by handing out pet food on the stoop of a small restaurant, and at their first distribution in August 2010 they gave away more than 300 pounds. By 2017 the pantry said it was helping about 200 families a month. Pickup is at 4950 Connecticut Street, St. Louis 63139, from 9 to 11 a.m. on one Sunday a month, and you need to be in line by 11. The dates left on its 2026 calendar are October 18, November 15 and December 20. Each animal gets roughly a month of food, up to 40 pounds, for up to five animals per household. The rules: you must be 18 and the owner, have had the pet at least six months, come in person (no delivery) and visit once a month at most. New clients, and anyone who hasn’t been in for a year, fill out an application first. Phone: 314-596-2128.
CARE STL. The nonprofit that runs the city’s animal shelter under contract with the City. Its website says it keeps a pet food bank for families during business hours and hands out donated supplies when it has them. If you need a specific item, it asks you to call and see whether it’s in. CARE STL has been stretched thin for a while, so call 314-696-2444 before you head over.
Stray Rescue of St. Louis. The shelter at 2320 Pine Street downtown runs a pet food pantry that gives free dog food to families going through a rough stretch. Its one stated condition, in a May 2026 post: your pets need to be spayed or neutered. The same post said the shelves were looking bare, so call 314-771-6121 first.
In St. Louis County
APA Adoption Center, Pet Partners program. For any St. Louis County resident, the APA lists pet food, flea prevention and other supplies as available on request. Call 314-645-5169. In six North County ZIP codes (63033, 63121, 63135, 63136, 63137 and 63138), the same program adds spay and neuter surgery, microchips and vaccines. The APA has also stocked pet food at North County human food pantries, including TEAM Food Pantry, Helping Hands Food Pantry and the Dellwood Recreation Center, so ask which partners have food right now.
In St. Charles County
Five Acres Animal Shelter, AniMeals pantry. 1099 Pralle Lane, St. Charles. Open every Saturday from 8 to 11 a.m. To enroll, bring a photo ID and one proof of need: a letter from the Department of Family Services, a referral from a human food pantry or social services group, or a letter from a church leader explaining your situation. Bring vet records if you have them. Once you’re enrolled you can pick up once a month for six months, for up to four pets, then renew with a new letter. Phone: 636-949-9918.
St. Charles County Pet Adoption Center. The county’s Division of Humane Services runs a monthly pet food pantry at 4850 Mid Rivers Mall Drive in St. Peters, handing out dry food as supplies allow. It’s for county residents, and you register ahead by calling 636-949-7387. Bring a photo ID, proof of county residency, proof of need, proof of a current rabies shot for each animal and proof of spay or neuter, or be ready to set the surgery up when you register. Bring a container that holds at least 3 pounds of food, too.
In Jefferson County
Jefferson County Pet Food Pantry. 4150 Old State Road M in House Springs, off Old Highway 21 behind the Dollar General. Distribution is one Sunday a month, now 9 a.m. to noon, and the pantry posts each month’s date on its website; in September 2026 it was the 20th. You need to be 18, live in Jefferson County or a nearby rural area, show a photo ID, prove all your pets are fixed and bring proof of low income: a Social Security letter, a Medicaid letter, a Food Stamp Determination letter or an unemployment letter. Phone: 636-215-0416.
Open Door Animal Sanctuary. A no-kill shelter founded in 1975, at 6065 Duda Road in House Springs. Its pantry gives about two weeks of food per month as a supplement, once a month, while supplies last. You’ll need proof of low income, such as a Social Security, unemployment or disability award letter or a medical card, plus verification that every animal is spayed or neutered. If one isn’t, Open Door runs a low-cost spay and neuter program for qualifying owners. Phone: 636-671-3643.
In the Metro East
Metro East Humane Society, Riverbend Pet Food Pantry. The fewest hoops on this page, and that’s by design. MEHS says every pet parent in the Metro East is eligible regardless of income, with no ZIP code rules. You need a valid ID to enroll, and after the first month you need proof of spay or neuter to keep coming. Walk-ins are welcome during open hours at MEHS Edwardsville, 8495 Illinois Route 143, and MEHS Highland, 510 W. Monroe. From April through December that’s 11:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. daily, with shorter days January through March. Dog portions go by size: 8 pounds a month for a small dog, 16 for medium, 24 for large and 32 for extra large, capped at 80 pounds and four pets per home. Phone: 618-656-4405.
Gateway Pet Guardians. 725 N. 15th Street, East St. Louis. Its monthly pantry serves families in ZIP codes 62201, 62203, 62204, 62205, 62206 and 62207, for up to four pets, with proof of residency, proof of need (a Link card, medical card, W2 or pay stub) and proof that every pet is fixed. Bigger news for everyone else: Gateway hands out pet food at the St. Louis Area Foodbank’s Food On The Move distributions, and its website says those come with no residency, income or spay/neuter requirements. The Foodbank’s calendar lists the next one at Gateway’s own building on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, from 10 a.m. to noon, then on first Tuesdays after that. Groceries and dog food, same parking lot, same morning. Confirm pet food is on hand that day before you go. St. Louis Public Radio reported in November 2025 that Gateway’s pantry had seen nearly a 50% jump in families needing pet food each month in about a year. Pantry questions: 618-687-8007, ext. 712.
Read those ten together and one thing stands out. Nearly every one gives the same reason for existing: to keep pets in their homes and out of crowded shelters. Picking up a bag there keeps one more dog out of a kennel.
### What do St. Louis pet pantries ask you to bring?
Almost every pantry above asks for the same three things. Get them together once, keep them in one envelope, and next month gets easier.
A photo ID. Bi-State’s application asks for an ID with your current address at each visit, and the county programs use it to prove residency.
Proof of need. A benefits letter does the most work here: SNAP or food stamps, Medicaid, Social Security or disability, unemployment. Bi-State also accepts a tax return showing low income. Five Acres takes a referral from a human food pantry or a letter from a church leader. Gateway takes an Illinois Link card or a pay stub.
Proof of spay or neuter. A vet record, or an adoption contract if the pet came from a shelter, showing your name and the pet’s name. Bi-State says it may call the vet listed to confirm.
The spay/neuter rule catches people off guard. These pantries are trying to keep the pets already in St. Louis homes fed, and a surprise litter in a house that’s already short on dog food is the exact problem they’re working against. The rule isn’t meant as a wall, though, and the details vary:
Bi-State wants proof for one pet at the first visit, then one more each month, and its application says it offers help paying for the surgery.
St. Charles County lets you arrange the surgery when you register, and Metro East Humane Society gives you the first month.
Open Door, Metro East Humane Society and Gateway Pet Guardians run low-cost or free spay and neuter programs of their own.
Bi-State’s fine print is easier to hear now than in line. Pantry food can’t be resold. Breeders, feral colony feeders and rescue foster parents aren’t eligible. You can’t add animals while getting help, and no animal can be kept outside, tethered or chained around the clock. If one of those is a problem, call and explain; Bi-State says it can make exceptions based on need.
Two places also want rabies records: St. Charles County asks for proof of a current rabies shot for each animal, and Bi-State’s application asks you to verify rabies vaccinations.
### Why won’t SNAP pay for pet food, and what fills the gap?
Because SNAP is built to buy food for the people in your household, and nothing else. The USDA’s page on what SNAP can buy says it covers “any food for the household,” then puts pet foods first on its list of nonfood items it won’t pay for, ahead of cleaning supplies and hygiene products. Missouri’s Department of Social Services says it in plainer words: an EBT card can’t be used for “non-food items, such as paper products, soap, or pet food.” Treats count as pet food.
There’s one honest workaround on the same card. Missouri’s Department of Social Services notes that an EBT card can also be used to withdraw a Temporary Assistance cash benefit. If you get that cash, it isn’t limited to SNAP’s food list, and a bag of dog food is a perfectly good use of it. If you don’t get Temporary Assistance, the pantries are the gap.
And the gap runs mostly on donated kibble moving through small hands. Shelters run the pantries. Volunteers staff them. The bags come from food drives, a radio station’s collection drive for Stray Rescue, and neighbors dropping off what their own dog refused to eat. Even here, in the city Purina calls home, the APA wrote in 2022 that Purina supplies the food for its shelter animals while its outreach program for families runs entirely on donated food. The help is real. It’s also stretched thin.
Ask at your regular food pantry, too. Some keep donated pet food but won’t think to offer it unless you mention the dog.
If your own benefits are what just changed, start there, because a fed household feeds its pets. Our guide to what to do if your SNAP benefits get cut in St. Louis covers appeals, reporting changes and where to find food this week. If you aren’t on SNAP and think you might qualify, here’s how to apply for food stamps in Missouri, and the approval letter doubles as your pantry paperwork. For rent, utilities and the rest, our St. Louis help and assistance resources guide has the numbers to call first.
Skipping meals so the dog eats? Find food pantries in St. Louis.
### Which programs help with vet bills too?
Food is the monthly problem. A vet bill is the sudden one, and Gateway Pet Guardians’ director told St. Louis Public Radio in 2025 that vet costs are one reason more people are surrendering pets.
Routine care at low cost. Carol House Quick Fix Pet Clinic, 1218 S. Jefferson Ave., does spay and neuter by appointment and tells owners to ask about its income-based programs. Its wellness clinics list prices such as $25 for a rabies shot and $35 for a microchip, though wellness days and times change week to week (314-771-7387). It doesn’t see sick or injured pets. In St. Louis County, the Pet Adoption Center in Olivette runs a spay/neuter voucher program that takes a set amount off the surgery at participating clinics (314-615-0650).
Help with a bigger bill. The APA’s Heads to Tails Hope Fund pays toward care beyond the routine: treatment, surgery, medication. A grant typically covers up to half of the vet’s estimate and tops out at $1,000, and the money goes straight to the clinic. The catches: it doesn’t fund emergencies or anything already underway, so the care has to be able to wait for approval. Your pet has to be spayed or neutered, and the APA can help arrange that. You’ll show proof of income. And it’s one grant per family, one time. Call 314-645-4610, ext. 167.
Emergencies. The Missouri Coalition of Animal Care Organizations keeps a list of funds that help with emergency and urgent care, including Armani’s Angels and the Killuminati Foundation for Missouri pets, Saving St. Louis Pets for local emergency and urgent cases, and RedRover for any pet in the country. The Coalition’s own advice is the line to remember: one group is unlikely to pay a whole bill, so apply to more than one. Gateway Pet Guardians also runs a full-service clinic in East St. Louis with lower prices and interest-free payment plans, according to St. Louis Public Radio.
For the clinics, vouchers and payment plans in more depth, see our guide to low-cost vet care in St. Louis.
### What are your options if you can’t keep feeding a pet?
Start with the option people skip: tell the pantry everything. Bi-State’s guidelines say outright that it can make exceptions to how much or how often it gives, based on need. A volunteer can’t solve a problem you didn’t mention.
If the trouble is temporary, look for temporary care before anything permanent. Stray Rescue points active and retired military families to PACT for Animals and Dogs on Deployment, which help find temporary homes for pets. Hospice patients can ask whether their provider takes part in Pet Peace of Mind. And if housing is the issue, you’re far from alone. Gateway Pet Guardians’ director told St. Louis Public Radio that a lack of pet-inclusive affordable housing is the biggest reason more pets are coming through its doors.
If you do need to rehome, try to do it yourself first. CARE STL, which runs the city shelter, says rehoming straight from your home is easier on a pet than a shelter stay. It suggests a few good photos, an honest write-up of your pet’s best qualities and a free profile on Adopt-a-Pet’s Rehome site. If your pet came from a shelter or rescue, call them before anyone else. Some adoption contracts require it, and Open Door Animal Sanctuary, for one, has a lifetime return policy for every animal it adopts out.
Surrender is the last door, and right now it’s a crowded one. St. Louis Public Radio reported in November 2025 that CARE STL had 109 dogs in a facility built to house about 61 comfortably. In the city, CARE STL is the open-admission shelter. In St. Louis County, call the County Pet Adoption Center at 10521 Baur Blvd. in Olivette (314-615-0650). Stray Rescue doesn’t take owner surrenders at all. Our guide to St. Louis city animal control sorts out who covers which address, the guide to St. Louis animal shelters explains what happens after intake, and if a rescue group fits better, start with St. Louis pet rescues.
Feeding a dog through a bad month with help from a pantry is what a responsible owner does when money is tight. Pick the pantry that fits your calendar, put the three papers in an envelope tonight and make the call in the morning. When things turn around, our guide to dog-friendly places in St. Louis is a good place to plan the next outing.
Most of the pantries on this page are run by shelters and rescues, so browse animal shelters around St. Louis on St Louis Near Me Directory to find the one nearest you.
And if you run a pet supply or feed store here, these pantries live on donated bags and the families they carry through a hard month are your customers when it turns, so list your store with us and be the name they find.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Can I get EBT for my dog?
A.  No. SNAP benefits on an EBT card can’t buy pet food or treats. The USDA classes them as nonfood items, and Missouri’s Department of Social Services names pet food outright. Two things still help. If your card also carries a Temporary Assistance cash benefit, you can withdraw that cash and spend it on dog food. And your SNAP approval letter counts as proof of need at pantries like Bi-State and the Jefferson County Pet Food Pantry.
### Q. What to do if I have no money for dog food?
A.  Work in order of speed. Today, call a pantry with open hours, such as Metro East Humane Society or CARE STL, or dial 211. This week, get to the next scheduled distribution with a photo ID, a benefits letter and spay/neuter proof. And skip people food until you’ve checked what’s toxic to dogs.
### Q. How to get free dog food today?
A.  Call first, then go. In Illinois, Metro East Humane Society’s pantry in Edwardsville and Highland takes walk-ins during open hours, daily from April through December, regardless of income, with a valid ID. In the city, CARE STL says its pet food bank is open during business hours. On Saturday mornings, Five Acres in St. Charles runs AniMeals from 8 to 11; bring a letter showing need to enroll. Otherwise, 211 can check what’s near you.
### Q. Where can I get free dog food vouchers?
A.  None of the St. Louis programs we checked hand out pet food vouchers. They hand out food, which is usually faster anyway. For anything voucher-like, try 211, a church or social service agency you already work with, and pet food brands’ apps and email lists, which sometimes send coupons. Be wary of any website that wants money or personal details in exchange for “free” pet food vouchers.
### Q. What is a pet grant?
A.  A pet grant is a one-time payment from a nonprofit toward a vet bill, usually sent straight to the clinic rather than to you. Locally, the APA’s Heads to Tails Hope Fund typically covers up to half of an estimate, capped at $1,000, for non-emergency care that can wait for approval. Nationally, The Pet Fund and RedRover run similar programs. Expect to show proof of income and a vet’s estimate. The APA’s fund doesn’t cover food.
### Q. Where can I get free dog food samples?
A.  Ask at your vet’s front desk first. Clinics often have sample bags of the diets they carry and will hand one to a client who asks. Independent pet stores sometimes keep trial bags, too. A sample is a few meals, not a month’s supply, so treat it as a bridge to your next pantry visit and blend it in slowly so your dog’s stomach keeps up.
### Q. What if my pet isn’t spayed or neutered yet?
A.  Go anyway, and say so up front. Several pantries here will work with you while you get it done. Bi-State only needs one pet’s proof at the first visit and offers help paying for surgery, St. Charles County lets you schedule it at registration, and Metro East Humane Society gives you a month. Carol House Quick Fix, the APA’s North County program, Open Door and the St. Louis County voucher all lower the cost.
### Q. Where can I donate pet food in St. Louis?
A.  Start with the pantries on this page, since they run on donations. Stray Rescue accepts unopened dog and cat food, wet or dry, at 2320 Pine Street. Five Acres takes opened dry food as long as it’s still in the original bag, and Metro East Humane Society accepts open bags too. If your own dog just turned up its nose at a 30-pound bag, that bag can keep somebody else’s dog fed for weeks.

## Pet Laws in St. Louis City and County: How Many Dogs, Leash Rules, License Fees
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/pet-laws-in-st-louis-city-and-county
Four dogs, one house. On a rowhouse lot in Tower Grove South, inside the City of St. Louis, that household is legal, sitting right on the line. Move the same four dogs to a cul-de-sac in Oakville, in unincorporated St. Louis County, and the fourth one turns the house into a kennel under the County’s zoning code. Meanwhile the national pet-law roundup you skimmed last night says Missouri has no limit at all.
All three answers are right. That’s the trouble with every one-number list that tries to sum up pet law by state. Around St. Louis, Missouri hands the question down to the City, the County and 88 municipalities, and each of them answers it a little differently. The rule that matters is the one attached to your parcel. Not your state. Not your mailing address either, because Oakville, Mehlville and Affton all get mail addressed to St. Louis, MO without being in the City at all.
What follows are the actual numbers, pulled from the City’s Revised Code, St. Louis County’s ordinances and the Missouri statutes, with section numbers so you can check every one. A plain warning up front: this is a guide, not legal advice. Codes get amended and the office that enforces a rule gets the final word, so confirm anything you’re about to act on.
### How many dogs can you legally have in Missouri?
Missouri itself sets no number. The state’s Canine Cruelty Prevention Act says plainly that it places no numerical limit on dogs you own but don’t breed for sale. Limits come from local law: four dogs and cats combined per parcel in the City of St. Louis, three dogs in unincorporated St. Louis County.
The state language is unusually blunt. That act, RSMo 273.345, started life as Proposition B in 2010 and was amended by the legislature in 2011. It sets care standards for anyone keeping more than ten intact female dogs to breed and sell puppies as pets. Then it says it “shall not be construed to place any numerical limits” on dogs that aren’t used for breeding, and in the same paragraph it leaves local governments free to pass animal laws of their own. They did.
Where the state does count, it counts breeding females. Under the Animal Care Facilities Act, RSMo 273.325, a person who keeps more than three intact females mainly to breed animals for sale is a commercial breeder, and RSMo 273.327 requires an annual license from the Missouri Department of Agriculture for that, with fees the statute sets between $100 and $2,500 a year. None of it touches the family with three spayed rescues and a sagging couch.
So the honest state answer is short and a little useless: as many as your local government allows. The rest of this page is about what your local government allows.
### How many dogs can you have in St. Louis County?
Three, if you live in unincorporated St. Louis County. The cap isn’t in the animal control chapter at all. It hides in the zoning code’s definition of a kennel, SLCRO 1003.020, which counts a property as a kennel when it keeps four or more dogs over four months old, six or more cats over four months old, or more than five dogs and cats combined.
Turn that around and you get the household limits. Up to three dogs. Up to five cats. No more than five of the two together. Three dogs and two cats works, and so do two dogs and three cats. Three dogs and three cats is a kennel. So is a fourth dog of any size, including the thirteen-year-old beagle who sleeps twenty hours a day and hasn’t barked at the mail carrier in years.
The age cutoff matters more than people expect. Puppies and kittens four months old or younger don’t count toward any of those numbers, and the definition says outright that selling the young your own animals produce at that age isn’t the kind of selling that makes you a kennel. Neither is an isolated sale of an older animal. Where it bites is the family that keeps one puppy from a litter and forgets the headcount changes at four months and a day.
Here’s the part the national lists never get to. A kennel is a land use, and the County zoning code lists kennels as a conditional use in only three districts: NU (Non-Urban), KP (Karst Preservation) and R-1, the one-acre residential district. It also permits them in the C-7 commercial district. In the denser residential districts, R-2 through R-8, the code doesn’t list a kennel as something you can apply for. Weighing a fourth dog? Ask the County’s Department of Planning how your parcel is zoned before the dog comes home.
This zoning code governs only land outside city limits, so it’s the rule for a few hundred thousand people in places like Oakville, Mehlville, Affton, Lemay and Spanish Lake, not for anyone inside Kirkwood or Florissant. It looks current, too: the Municode version is dated May 12, 2026, and a 2026 County Council zoning bill reprints the same kennel definition word for word. Zoning bills move, so check the live version.
### How many pets can you have in the City of St. Louis?
Four, and the City counts dogs and cats together. Section 10.20.011 of the City’s Revised Code says no more than four domestic animals may be kept on any parcel in a residentially zoned district. The City’s Animal Care and Control laws page puts it in plain terms: the limit is set by parcel, not person. Two roommates with two dogs each are at the limit together. One cat later, the house is over.
The definition is where City households get caught. Under 10.20.010, a domestic animal is a dog or cat, including any puppy or kitten, more than six weeks old. Six weeks, not the County’s four months. A two-dog house with a surprise litter of five is legal the day the puppies arrive and well over the limit a month and a half later, and it stays over until the litter is placed.
The City’s page also lists rabbits among the pets that may count toward the four, and allows one pot-bellied pig per parcel inside that same total. The code is fussy about the pig: purebred, spayed or neutered by set ages, and licensed like a dog. Roosters aren’t allowed at all under 10.20.015. Neither are cattle, sheep, goats or ordinary swine, and neither is any dog bred from a wolf or coyote.
Going over four is possible, up to a hard ceiling of eight, with a noncommercial kennel permit from the Health Commissioner. The process in 10.20.013 is not casual: an application, a $60 inspection fee, a home inspection, and a permit good for one year that costs another $60 inspection to renew. The animals have to be personal pets, not bred and not offered for sale, and they have to stay indoors, in a fenced yard or on a leash. Confirm the current fee with the Health Department before you apply.
Apartment dwellers get a different formula. In a building with more than four units, the City doesn’t apply four per parcel; it’s fine as long as the total number of dogs and cats in the whole building doesn’t exceed the number of units, and the code puts the duty to stay under that number on the building owner. Your lease can be stricter.
If the City finds a parcel over the limit, 10.20.014 lays out the order: an inspection, a notice of violation by regular mail, and 14 days to fix it before the matter goes to the City Counselor. A conviction under 10.20.020 carries a fine of $100 to $500, up to 90 days in jail, or both.
### Do the rules change again inside your own St. Louis County town?
Yes, and in two directions at once. St. Louis County has 88 municipalities, and each one writes its own zoning code, which is where pet-count limits usually live. When a street is a city boundary, a dog can be legal on one side and over the line on the other. Read your own city’s code or call its city hall.
Some towns add paperwork on top of the County’s. Florissant, the County’s largest city at roughly 51,000 people by recent Census estimates, issues its own dog and cat tags. Its tag page asks for proof of a current rabies shot and, for any dog it calls a pit bull, proof of spay or neuter as well. The same page says Florissant’s city code holds pets to a leash no longer than six feet once they’re off the owner’s property.
The other direction almost nobody hears about: the County’s animal control chapter reaches inside town limits. Under SLCRO 611.020, the County’s rabies registration rules apply across the County except in towns that enforce their own matching rabies ordinance. Its rules on animals at large, nuisances, cruelty and dangerous animals apply in unincorporated areas and in every municipality except one with 75,000 or more residents that runs its own organized health department. Florissant, the biggest, isn’t close. Towns can add rules that fit with the County’s. They can’t pass ones that conflict.
As written, that means the County’s tethering hours and its at-large definition, both covered below, follow you into Kirkwood, Webster Groves and Ballwin, even though the County’s three-dog zoning number stops at their city limits.
Then there’s the address trap. Oakville, Mehlville, Affton, Lemay and Spanish Lake are unincorporated, which puts them under the County’s zoning and animal rules directly, yet the mail there says St. Louis, MO. Plenty of people in those neighborhoods assume the City’s four-pet rule is theirs. It isn’t. Your real estate tax bill or the County’s property records should show whether a municipality is attached to your parcel. And if you live in a subdivision, read the indenture: trustees and HOAs can be stricter than any government.
### Do you need a pet license in St. Louis?
Yes, on both sides of the line, and in both places the license rides along with the rabies shot. Your vet gives the shot, fills out the certificate and hands you a numbered tag. That tag is the license. What it costs depends almost entirely on whether your pet is spayed or neutered.
