In the City, every dog and cat has to be vaccinated against rabies and registered, and the City’s registration page says puppies and kittens should get both between three and four months old. Under 10.04.070 the fee is $50 for an intact animal and $46 less, or $4, for one that’s spayed or neutered. Same fee for a one-year or three-year vaccine. New arrivals get 30 days, and if your vet had no City tags, you register in person at Animal Care and Control, 1520 Market Street, Suite 4051, with proof of the shot.
In the County, SLCRO 611.050 requires the shot and registration by four months of age, but not before three. The posted fees for a certificate and tag: $8 for one year or $20 for three if the animal is spayed or neutered, $16 or $40 if it isn’t, on top of the vet’s charge for the shot. Newcomers get 30 days.
Put the two fee schedules side by side and the policy is hard to miss. The City charges an intact dog twelve and a half times what it charges a fixed one. The County charges double. The City’s $46 gap comes back with every renewal. Call it a nudge.
The tag isn’t decoration in either place. Under County code a dog or cat found without one may be treated as unvaccinated, and a missing tag alone is grounds for the County to impound it unless you can produce a rabies certificate. The City wants the tag on the collar at all times and the certificate on hand for any officer who asks. That number also ties back to your name and phone number, which matters the day a dog slips a gate; our guide to lost pets in St. Louis picks up from there.
If the cost of the shot is the sticking point, our guide to low-cost vet care in St. Louis covers cheaper ways to get vaccines done. Prices change, so call ahead.
Car windows have a legal limit too. Window tint laws in St. Louis
### What are the leash laws in the city and county?
In the City of St. Louis, a dog in any street, park or other public place has to be on a secure leash no more than six feet long, held continuously in the hands of someone capable of controlling it. That’s section 10.04.220 of the City’s dogs and cats chapter, and the six-foot cap is hard to square with a sixteen-foot retractable run all the way out. The exceptions are short: a dog shut inside a car or an enclosed lot, permitted dog shows and trials, and the City’s designated fenced dog exercise areas.
Those exercise areas have rules of their own in the same section. Open 6 a.m. to one hour after sunset. No more than three dogs per person. No aggressive or sick dogs, and the owner is legally responsible for any injury the dog causes. Our roundup of dog parks in St. Louis covers where to find them.
St. Louis County writes it differently. Under SLCRO 611.200, a dog or cat is at large whenever it’s outside a cage or building unless it’s on a leash held by a person who can control it and actually is, inside a vehicle it can’t escape, or on its owner’s own property. Cats sit in the same sentence as dogs. The County chapter doesn’t set a leash length, though some towns do.
That own-property clause cuts both ways. Under the County definition your unfenced front yard counts as your property, so a dog dozing on the lawn isn’t at large. The second it trots onto the sidewalk to bark at a jogger, it is. A dog in heat is a separate case: she’s at large unless she’s kept inside where other animals can’t reach her, or leashed and supervised on your property, and the County’s impound section adds that an electronic fence doesn’t count as a secure enclosure.
County fines climb fast, and they cost more if the dog isn’t fixed. Under 611.240, a citation for one of the listed violations is $25 the first time in a twelve-month stretch, $100 the second, $200 the third or fourth, and $500 for the fifth, which also goes to the county counselor for prosecution. For an at-large dog with no proof of spay or neuter, the first offense starts at $50 and the second jumps to $200.
Both governments make you pick it up, too. The City requires removing pet waste from public or private property (10.04.310), and the County lists waste left on someone else’s property as a nuisance unless it’s removed right away (611.210). Whoever holds the leash on weekdays is bound by the same rules, so bring them up when you’re interviewing dog walkers in St. Louis. For where a leashed dog is actually welcome on a Saturday, start with our guide to dog-friendly places in St. Louis.
### How long can a dog be tied up outside in St. Louis?
Ten continuous hours in the City, and no more than 12 hours total in any 24. In the County it’s eight continuous hours and nine total. Those are the tethering caps in City section 10.04.285 and County section 611.180, and they’re a clean example of why one statewide answer doesn’t exist.
The equipment rules match almost word for word: a tether at least 15 feet long with a swivel at both ends, on a properly fitting nylon or leather collar or harness, that can’t tangle or keep the dog from food, shelter and clean water. Both codes add that the water has to be cool in summer and unfrozen in winter.
Temperature is where they split. The County bars leaving a dog or cat tethered outdoors unattended when the actual or effective temperature is 32 degrees or lower, or 90 degrees or higher. The City’s rule is broader and kicks in a little later on the hot end: no dog or cat left unattended outside, tethered or not, below 32 degrees or above 93, or during a severe weather warning or a heat or cold advisory. In that weather a closed garage, basement or car without temperature control counts as evidence of a violation. Separately, no dog or cat left unattended can go more than 30 minutes without adequate food, water and shelter.
The City even defines what a doghouse has to be. Appropriate shelter, under 10.04.010, means cover with bedding such as straw, hay or wood shavings, small enough for the animal to hold its body heat and big enough to stand, turn around and lie down. An empty plastic igloo with no bedding doesn’t meet that.
Underneath both sits state law. Missouri’s animal neglect statute, RSMo 578.009, makes failing to provide adequate care a class C misdemeanor, and RSMo 578.005 defines adequate care as wholesome food, clean water, shelter and health care.
One more line both codes share, and few owners know it. Declawing a cat is banned in the City (10.12.070) and in the County (611.180) unless a licensed vet does it under anesthesia because it’s medically necessary. The City’s version says outright that convenience doesn’t count. Neither does the sofa.
### What happens if your dog is picked up or a rule gets broken?
It depends on which side of the line the dog was found. A dog running loose in the City can be taken up under 10.04.140 and held at the City’s shelter at 2801 Clark Avenue. Getting it back costs $20 for the first three days and $10 a day after that, and after five days the City can move on without you. The code adds a step that surprises people: no dog or cat is supposed to be finally released until procedures for spaying or neutering and microchipping have been followed (10.04.150 and 10.04.160).
In the County, impounded animals go to the County shelter at 10521 Baur Boulevard in Olivette, which holds them five days, not counting County holidays. The fee written into 611.090 is $25 for the first day and $15 for each day after, plus any citation fees. Fees get revised, so check before you go.
The heaviest rules land on a dog officially found dangerous. In the County, 611.190 requires a securely locked fenced enclosure the dog can’t jump or climb over, squeeze through or crawl under, and says an electric shock containment system doesn’t qualify. The owner has to post a sign with letters at least two inches tall, microchip the dog and report the number, and have it neutered. Notice what’s missing from both codes. A breed. Neither the City’s Title 10 nor the County’s animal control chapter names one.
For who to call, how intake works and what each office will and won’t do, see our guide to St. Louis city animal control and its County counterpart. If you’re on the other end of it, wondering what happens to a stray after intake, our explainer on St. Louis animal shelters walks through it.
None of this is hard once you know which rulebook is yours. Find out whether your parcel sits in the City, in unincorporated County or in one of the 88 towns, read that one code, and register the tag with the next rabies shot. Then you’re the person on the block who answers the four-dog question with a section number instead of a guess.
When the rabies shot and registration tag come due, find veterinarians in St. Louis and ask when you book whether they issue the City or County tag with the vaccine.
If you run a clinic that issues those tags, or any pet business new residents need in their first 30 days, list it with us so the people moving in with a dog and a registration deadline can find you.
Renting? See renting with pets in St. Louis. For assistance animals, see service dogs and emotional support animals in Missouri.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is 7 dogs too many?
A.  Legally, across most of the St. Louis area, yes, unless you hold a permit. Seven is more than double unincorporated St. Louis County’s three-dog line, which makes the property a kennel under the zoning code, and the County lists kennels as a conditional use only in its NU, KP and R-1 districts. In the City, seven is over the four-animal limit, but a noncommercial kennel permit allows up to eight dogs and cats in total, so seven dogs and one cat is the ceiling.
### Q. Is it illegal to leave a dog outside 24/7?
A.  No single law orders a dog indoors, but the rules around outdoor dogs make true round-the-clock outdoor living hard to do legally here. In the City, a dog can’t be left unattended outside below 32 degrees or above 93, and a tether is capped at 10 straight hours. In the County it’s eight hours, and no tethered dog left alone at 32 or below or 90 or above. Both require real shelter. Report concerns to the City at (314) 657-1500 or the County at (314) 615-0650.
### Q. My neighbor’s dog is barking at 6 AM. What should I do?
A.  Talk to the neighbor first; someone who leaves at 5:45 may honestly not know. If it keeps up, log dates, times and how long it lasts. In the City, excessive animal noise is a violation under 10.04.285, but the code requires a neighbor who will state in writing that they’ll testify under oath, so be ready to sign. Report it through the Citizens’ Service Bureau at (314) 622-4800. In the County, excessive barking, howling or meowing is listed as a nuisance under 611.210; call County Animal Care and Control at (314) 615-0650.
### Q. Can you have chickens in St. Louis County?
A.  It depends on where in the County you live. Each of the 88 municipalities sets its own rules, and many require a permit. In unincorporated County, start with the Department of Planning, since the zoning chapter doesn’t spell out a backyard hen count the way the City code does. Across the line in the City of St. Louis, 10.20.015 allows up to eight fowl per parcel, no roosters, coops kept out of the front yard. Read your subdivision indenture too: FOX 2 and Missourinet reported that a Cole County judge struck down a 2024 state law limiting HOA chicken bans in October 2025.
### Q. How many dogs am I legally allowed to own?
A.  As many as the government over your parcel allows, since Missouri sets no statewide number. In the City of St. Louis that’s four dogs and cats combined, or up to eight with a noncommercial kennel permit. In unincorporated St. Louis County it’s three dogs, with no more than five cats and five animals combined. Inside one of the County’s 88 municipalities, check that city’s code, then your lease or HOA rules.
### Q. What pets can you not own in Missouri?
A.  Missouri regulates more than it bans. Keeping a lion, tiger, bear, wolf, coyote, nonhuman primate, venomous reptile or a dangerous reptile over eight feet long requires registration with local law enforcement under RSMo 578.023, and big cats and nonnative bears need a state permit under the Large Carnivore Act, RSMo 578.600 to 578.624. Native wildlife falls under the Missouri Department of Conservation, which says many wild animals can’t be possessed without a permit. The City of St. Louis goes further and prohibits bears, big cats, primates, wolves, foxes, coyotes and their hybrids, crocodilians, venomous snakes and constrictors over eight feet.
### Q. Is there a pitbull ban in Missouri?
A.  Not statewide. Missouri has no breed ban in state law, and neither the City of St. Louis code nor St. Louis County’s animal control chapter names a breed; both handle dangerous dogs by behavior. Some municipalities do write breed into their rules. Florissant, for one, requires proof of spay or neuter before it tags a pit bull. Bills to stop cities from passing breed rules have come up in Jefferson City more than once, so check your town’s current code.
### Q. What exotic pets are legal in Missouri?
A.  Most of what a pet store sells. State law targets specific animals, the dangerous wild animal list in RSMo 578.023 and the big cats and bears in the Large Carnivore Act, so animals like bearded dragons, corn snakes, ferrets and parrots aren’t on either list. Native wildlife needs MDC permits. City residents also face the City’s own prohibited list and its four-pet count, which the City says can include rabbits. Line up a vet who treats the species before you buy.

## Powder Valley Said No. The Park Next Door Said Yes.
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/dog-friendly-places-in-st-louis
The gate says no, and the dog is already leaning out the window. You’d pulled onto Cragwold Road in Kirkwood with the leash on the passenger seat and a Saturday with nothing in it, and Powder Valley’s oak and hickory woods sat right there. The rule is one line. The area does not allow pets. Not on a leash. Not at all.
Here’s the part that saves your morning, and it’s sitting in plain sight. The Missouri Department of Conservation’s own listing for Powder Valley gives the answer in one line: “The area does not allow pets but our neighboring property Emmenegger Nature Park does allow pets on a leash.” Two neighboring properties, opposite answers. Drive over, and the dog still gets its walk. Powder Valley sits at 11715 Cragwold Rd, and the number for questions is 314-301-1500.
St. Louis does this to dog owners constantly: the yes and the no sit one property line apart. Here’s the rule of thumb worth texting to every dog person you know. If a place is built around wild animals, the dog stays home, and at Lone Elk Park that means not even inside your parked car while you watch the bison. If it’s a park or a greenway, bring the leash. If it has a roof, call first. And the number almost nobody mentions: the City charges $4 to register a spayed or neutered dog and $50 for one that isn’t. That gap is the cheapest win on this page. Your vet hands you the City tag at the rabies shot, or you can register in person at Animal Care and Control, 1520 Market St, 314-657-1500.
### Is St. Louis a dog friendly city?
Mostly yes, as long as you carry a leash. Forest Park and Tower Grove let a leashed dog in. The Arch grounds and Laumeier do too. Shaw and the Zoo say no to pets.
Clip the leash on at the car door and most of this city opens up, nails clicking the whole way. Then the fine print bites. The Arch grounds take a leashed dog but keep it out of the reflecting pools. Laumeier, free and dog-friendly most days, turns dogs away on Art Fair weekend. One phone call before you leave beats a wasted drive.
### Where can your dog go in St. Louis, and where does it get turned away?
Parks and greenways, yes, on a leash. Nature preserves and wildlife parks, usually no. Indoors, ask first. Here’s how that plays out at real gates, starting back where we began.
### Powder Valley says no. Emmenegger says yes.
Gravel crunches under four paws on the neighboring property, and the dog that just got turned away is suddenly the happiest animal in the county. That’s Emmenegger Nature Park, and the Missouri Department of Conservation’s own Powder Valley listing is what sends you there: Emmenegger allows pets on a leash. Powder Valley’s no is just as firm: the area does not allow pets.
### Is Forest Park in St. Louis dog friendly?
Forest Park on a Sunday sounds like bike bells, a far-off ball game and somebody yelling a dog’s name across the grass. Your dog hears every bit of it and wants to meet all of them. The one rule that matters: a leash no more than six feet long, in the hand of someone who can actually hold it. Tower Grove Park’s rule is shorter still: “Dogs must remain on leash.”
### Can dogs go in the St. Louis Arch?
The dog hauls you toward the water the moment the Arch grounds open up in front of you, and there’s a rule for exactly that: dogs may not swim in the reflecting pools. Inside is a firm no, because service animals are the only animals allowed in the buildings, so there’s no tram ride for the dog. Out on the grounds, the leash can be no more than 6 feet long.
### Laumeier Sculpture Park: free, leashed, and closed to dogs on Art Fair weekend
Your dog will sniff a giant sculpture exactly the way it sniffs a fire hydrant, completely unimpressed, and Laumeier is fine with that. It gets a ground-level view of every piece in Laumeier’s outdoor galleries, as long as it’s leashed at all times and you pick up after it. The park is free and open from 7 a.m. until 30 minutes past sunset. Dogs aren’t allowed during some special events, including the Annual Art Fair and Laumeier After Dark, and the park closes for Art Fair weekend in May.
The best fun things to do with dogs in St. Louis barely touch your wallet. Laumeier is free year-round, the greenways ask only for a short leash, and Purina’s Pups Play Yard takes reservations for its limited spaces. That’s a whole Saturday with a dog and no admission line.
### Shaw Nature Reserve: no, not even on a leash
Air rushes through the open windows on the drive out I-44 to Gray Summit, and at Shaw Nature Reserve the dog’s day ends at the gate. Shaw’s own FAQ answers the leash question in six words: “No, not even on a leash.” Service animals are welcome and pets are not. The reserve is at 307 Pinetum Loop Rd, 314-577-9555, open 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. daily with last entry at 4:30, and closed Mondays in January and February. Admission is $5 for ages 13 and up, $3 for seniors 65 and older, and free under 13. Parking is free.
### Purina Farms: reserve before you drive
You know the drive, you know the lot, the dog knows the smell of the place, and this time the doors are locked. Purina Farms’ Visitor Center remains temporarily closed after tornado damage, so any plan that starts with walking through the lobby needs a new first step. The tornado that hit the farm damaged the Visitor Center, Pet Center, Pet Barn and Incredible Dog Arena. Our Purina Farms visitor guide has the longer version.
What’s still open: the Purina Event Center, which hosts hundreds of dog and cat shows and performance trials a year, most of them free and open to the public. Dogs can also explore the farm’s nature trail, or you can reserve one of the limited spaces in the Pups Play Yard, where dogs run, play and try light agility equipment. The Play Yard is free, but online registration is required, and visiting dogs must be at least 4 months old with age-appropriate vaccinations. Book the spot before you load the car.
### Lone Elk Park: elk and bison, no dogs
A dog’s nose presses to the window the second it smells something wild, and at Lone Elk Park, a County park with herds of elk and bison, that window seat is off limits: domestic animals aren’t permitted, even if they stay confined to your vehicle. The dog stays home for this one.
### Is the Saint Louis Zoo dog friendly?
The kids are already running ahead and Zoo admission is free. The dog still can’t go in. Dogs and other pets are prohibited, and emotional-support animals aren’t allowed either. Service animals are permitted except in the Cypress Swamp (the 1904 Flight Cage) and the Bird House. At the gate: 1 Government Dr, 314-781-0900.
### The fine print behind the yes list
Here’s the part you’ll want in the glove box, because rules sound different when someone in a park uniform is reading them back to you and your dog is sitting there panting. Off your own property in the City, a dog stays on a leash held by a responsible person, everywhere except the designated dog parks. Tower Grove Park’s leash rule is City Ordinance 66384, its posted hours run 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. with a curfew from 10 p.m. to 5 a.m., and it sits at 4257 Northeast Dr, 314-771-2679. Forest Park closes from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m., and Forest Park Forever answers questions at 314-367-7275. A loose dog gets reported to City Animal Care and Control at 314-657-1500.
At the Arch, the grounds are open 5 a.m. to 11 p.m. at 11 North 4th Street. Dogs can’t root around in the garden beds or be left unattended in a vehicle, and rangers have run B.A.R.K. Ranger programs for dogs, so ask 314-655-1600 for the current schedule. Laumeier is at 12580 Rott Road, 314-615-5278, and service animals are allowed in all public areas.
Back in Kirkwood, Powder Valley is at 11715 Cragwold Rd, 314-301-1500, with the area open daily 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. and the building open Tuesday through Saturday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. For Emmenegger, read the sign at the entrance before you start down the trail.
Between the parks, the greenways run on one simple ask. Great Rivers Greenway wants “a fixed leash, 6 feet or less, preferably on the right.” St. Louis County Parks puts it plainly: dogs and cats must be kept on a 6-foot leash.
### The 30-second gate check
Screenshot this before you leave the house. Laumeier doesn’t charge a cent at the door, and the rows below sort the places that decide a Saturday.
Three questions sort most gates before you leave the driveway. Is it built around wildlife? Powder Valley, Shaw and Lone Elk all say no. Is it a big attraction or a building? Those mostly say no, and stores say yes only after a call. Is there an event today? Laumeier’s Art Fair and Laumeier After Dark both clear the dogs out. Any yes, call first.
Zoo days, Shaw days and Lone Elk days don’t include the dog. For the hours it stays home, browse pet services around St. Louis and call two or three close to home before the tickets are bought.
If you’re the groomer, the kennel or the one-person dog-walking crew, the owners reading this are building exactly that call list. List your pet business with us and put your name where those customers are already looking.
### Where can a dog run off leash?
A dog that has spent a week on a 6-foot leash runs differently the first time the clip comes off. The County’s answer is Tails and Trails, a membership-based, 5-acre park inside Queeny Park with separate areas for large and small dogs, a water feature and permanent agility and skill stations. An annual membership or a daily pass comes from the Greensfelder Recreation Complex. Call first: 314-615-8472, and ask what the membership costs and which shot records to bring.
Inside the City, several off-leash yards run on memberships too. The Southwest City Dog Park’s own list names Fox, Lucas Gardens and Water Tower in Compton Heights as membership parks, along with McDonald in Tower Grove South. Fox Park’s yard is open to anyone with proof of shots who agrees to the rules. Southwest City itself, in Willmore Park, calls itself the largest dog park in the City, and right now its site says “Registrations temporarily closed” and keeps a waitlist. Our guide to the dog parks in St. Louis compares the rest of the metro.
One thing runs through every off-leash gate on this list: the paperwork. In the City, the vet hands you the registration tag at the rabies shot, and Fox Park’s yard wants proof of shots before you join. Snap a photo of the vet records on your phone and you’re ready at every desk.
### Which indoor dog friendly places in St. Louis let a dog through the door?
Walk a dog through a set of automatic doors and you find out in two seconds whether the answer was yes. Fewer places say it than you’d hope, and every yes comes with a call first. Bass Pro Shops calls its stores pet friendly, with pets allowed “except where specifically prohibited by state or local laws.” Call first: 3600 S. Lindbergh Blvd, 314-946-2000.
Soulard Market is the sharp no. Its rule reads, “Animals and smoking are prohibited anywhere on Soulard Market grounds.” Leave the dog home. Call first: 730 Carroll St, 314-622-4180.
Around the holidays, some malls set aside a pet night for photos with Santa. Ask the mall for this season’s date before you line up a dog in a bow tie.
Food and drink is where most dog outings start, so those get their own guides. For beer gardens and brewery yards, start with our roundup of dog-friendly patios and breweries. For brunch, frozen custard and restaurant patios, go to dog-friendly restaurants in St. Louis, which also explains why a dog can sit on the patio but not one step inside. Coming in from out of town? Pet-friendly hotels in St. Louis sorts out pet fees, weight limits and two-pet caps before you book.
Cat people get an outing too, minus the leash. The cat cafes in St. Louis guide covers what a visit costs and how adopting from one works.
### What does a pet cost here, starting with a $4 tag?
The first sound a new City dog makes is a tag clinking, and it costs $4. That’s the City of St. Louis registration fee for a spayed or neutered dog or cat, against $50 for one that’s intact. The difference is written straight into the fee schedule, and a replacement tag is $1. Rabies inoculation is the only vaccination City ordinance requires.
At the gate: Animal Care and Control, 1520 Market St, Suite 4051, handles registration Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., at 314-657-1500. New arrivals get 30 days to register, and visitors don’t need a City tag unless the pet stays longer than 30 days. Fees change, so check the City’s registration page before you pay.
Room to run costs more. Tails and Trails and several City yards are membership parks, so ask what it costs before you sign up. The off-leash section above covers the rules that come attached.
Nationally, the American Pet Products Association put a year of U.S. pet spending at $158 billion, with $41 billion of it going to vet care and vet products. Food is the steady line. The vet and the care while you’re away are the lines that swing.
Care while you’re away is usually the first surprise. See what pet sitters in St. Louis charge for drop-ins versus overnights, how dog boarding in St. Louis prices kennels and daycare, and how cat boarding in St. Louis works, including how to check a cattery’s state inspection.
Mobile vets in St. Louis bring the exam to your living room, which matters for a cat who panics in the carrier or a senior dog who can’t manage the front steps. If your pet has scales, feathers or a cage, exotic vets in St. Louis covers who sees birds, reptiles, rabbits and pocket pets.

Read puppies for sale in St. Louis before you pay anybody, because Missouri licenses commercial breeders and that license is worth asking about before any deposit changes hands. Aquarium and reptile keepers can start with fish stores in St. Louis. Two recurring lines are easy to underestimate: dog training cost in St. Louis and dog groomer prices in St. Louis.
### Your dog can’t see the city line. What changes when you cross it?
Nothing out the car window tells you the City just ended, and the dog in the back seat certainly doesn’t notice. Almost everything behind its tag changes anyway. The City of St. Louis split from St. Louis County in 1876 and never went back. Many of the County’s 88 municipalities then add their own pet rules on top.
Inside the City, Animal Care and Control is at 1520 Market St, Suite 4051, and the shelter is at 2801 Clark Ave, open daily 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Both answer at 314-657-1500. The household cap is four domestic animals per parcel in any mix, so two roommates with three dogs each are over the limit together. A tethered dog also can’t be left out more than 10 continuous hours, or 12 in any 24.
Cross into the County and the agency becomes St. Louis County Animal Control, which takes bite reports at 314-615-0650, Monday through Friday, 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. In unincorporated areas, the County zoning code treats four or more dogs over four months old, six or more cats, or more than five dogs and cats combined as a kennel, and cities inside the County write their own rules on top. One dog, two governments, two phone numbers.
The details live in three companion guides. How many dogs you can have in St. Louis County lays the County’s limits, licenses and leash rules next to the City’s. St. Louis city animal control explains which agency to call for a stray, a bite or neglect. And if your dog slips out, lost pets in St. Louis lists the shelters to check first and how long each one holds a stray.
The best skyline walk for a leashed dog is on the Illinois side
### The Illinois side: a skyline walk for a leashed dog
Across the river the whole skyline lines up like a postcard, and the dog only cares about the grass. Malcolm W. Martin Memorial Park, on the Illinois side, answers “Dog Friendly?” with “Yes (Leash Required),” and it’s open daily from 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. Ask about events before you cross. Call first: MEPRD, 104 United Drive, 618-346-4905.
### Where can St. Louis pet owners get help when money is tight?
The bag of kibble is getting light and payday is a week out. Nobody should decide a pet’s future from that spot, and more places help than most people check before they give up a pet. The help splits three ways: cheaper surgery, food, and a soft landing at a shelter if it comes to that.
Surgery first, because spay and neuter is the bill that prevents the next ten. The Humane Society of Missouri runs Operation SNIP, a low-cost spay and neuter program for the pets of Missouri residents. Call HSMO and ask what it costs right now. Our guide to low-cost vet care in St. Louis lays out the free spay days, the County vouchers and what to do when a vet bill lands that you can’t cover.
Food is the part people are most embarrassed to ask about, and it has the clearest rule. SNAP benefits can’t buy pet food, because the USDA lists pet foods among the nonfood items households cannot buy with SNAP. That gap is why the Bi-State Pet Food Pantry exists, with emergency pet food to keep pets and their people together. Distribution days and paperwork change, so check its site before you go. Pet food pantries in St. Louis lists the other pantries and what each one asks you to bring.
If keeping the pet truly isn’t possible, a shelter is a far better landing than a parking lot or a stranger from an online post. St. Louis animal shelters explains what happens after intake. Ready to take one home instead? St. Louis pet rescues covers where the adoptable dogs and cats are.
### The checkerboard that made St. Louis a pet town
The name changed to Ralston Purina in 1902, the checkerboard trademark came with it, and the pet food business behind it grew up here. In 1894 William H. Danforth founded the animal feed business known as the Robinson-Danforth Commission Company, which became Ralston Purina, and the company’s headquarters went by the name Checkerboard Square. Nestlé bought Ralston Purina in 2001, and Nestlé Purina still keeps its headquarters in St. Louis.
Purina’s research didn’t stay downtown. In 1926 the company set up the Purina Dog Care Center at Gray Summit, and the Purina Event Center now stands on that same footprint, hosting hundreds of dog and cat shows and performance trials a year. You can go to a dog show just to watch, and most are free and open to the public. The Incredible Dog Challenge started on the property in 1998.
For three decades, the historic Jarville House in Queeny Park held the American Kennel Club’s Museum of the Dog. It moved there from New York in 1987, spent more than 30 years in Queeny Park, and reopened in New York on February 8, 2019. The AKC Museum of the Dog now stands at 101 Park Avenue in New York City, 212-696-8360. It’s open Wednesday through Sunday, 11 a.m. to 6 p.m., adult tickets are $15, and pet dogs are welcome every Friday.
Queeny Park didn’t stop being a dog place when the paintings left: Tails and Trails is inside it now. The same park that held the AKC’s Museum of the Dog now has dogs tearing around its agility stations, which is about as St. Louis as a story gets.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is the Saint Louis Zoo dog friendly?
A.  No. The Saint Louis Zoo lists dogs and other pets among its prohibited items. Emotional-support animals aren’t allowed either. Service animals are permitted except in the Cypress Swamp (the 1904 Flight Cage) and the Bird House. Admission is free. The Zoo is at 1 Government Dr, and the number is 314-781-0900.
### Q. Can dogs go in the St. Louis Arch?
A.  Not inside. Service animals are the only animals allowed in the Arch’s buildings, so there’s no tram ride for the dog. The grounds are open to leashed dogs from 5 a.m. to 11 p.m., on a leash no more than 6 feet long. Dogs may not swim in the reflecting pools, root around in the garden beds or be left unattended in a vehicle. The number is 314-655-1600.
### Q. Is Forest Park in St. Louis dog friendly?
A.  Yes, Forest Park allows dogs on a leash. The leash may not be more than six feet long and must be held by a responsible party capable of controlling the animal. The park is closed from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. Forest Park Forever is at 314-367-7275, and loose dogs should be reported to City Animal Care and Control at 314-657-1500.
### Q. What are some indoor dog friendly places in St. Louis?
A.  Fewer than you’d hope. Bass Pro Shops on South Lindbergh (314-946-2000) calls its stores pet friendly except where state or local law prohibits it, so call first. Some malls hold a pet night for photos with Santa, so ask for this season’s date. Soulard Market bans animals on its grounds, and Purina Farms’ Visitor Center is closed.
### Q. What are some fun things to do with dogs in St. Louis?
A.  Pick by mood. For art, walk the outdoor galleries at Laumeier Sculpture Park, where leashed dogs are welcome. The park is free and open from 7 a.m. to 30 minutes past sunset. For distance, take a greenway, where the leash is 6 feet or less. For a skyline walk, cross to Malcolm W. Martin Memorial Park in Illinois. For a real run, try a City dog park or Tails and Trails at Queeny Park, 314-615-8472.
### Q. Is there a dog museum in St. Louis?
A.  No. The AKC Museum of the Dog moved to Queeny Park in St. Louis County in 1987 and spent more than 30 years there, then reopened in New York in February 2019. Queeny Park kept a dog connection, though: St. Louis County’s membership dog park, Tails and Trails, sits inside it.
### Q. Where is the AKC Museum of the Dog located?
A.  At 101 Park Avenue in New York City, not in St. Louis. The number is 212-696-8360. It’s open Wednesday through Sunday, 11 a.m. to 6 p.m., and closed Monday and Tuesday. Adult admission is $15, and pet dogs are welcome in the museum every Friday during regular hours.
### Q. Can you go to a dog show just to watch?
A.  Yes. Around St. Louis the place to do it is the Purina Event Center at Purina Farms in Gray Summit, which hosts hundreds of dog and cat shows and performance trials a year, and most are free and open to the public. Check each event listing before you go, and leave your own dog home unless the listing says pets are welcome.

## Purina Farms: What Is Still Open, Free Dog Shows and When Your Dog Can Come
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/purina-farms-gray-summit-visitor-guide
Old travel lists still send St. Louis families to Purina Farms for the red barn, the hayloft and the dogs that launch themselves into a 50-foot heated pool. One big review site was still telling visitors it would see them back at the farm in spring 2025. That spring never came. On the night of March 14, 2025, an EF-2 tornado hit the property and wrecked the Visitor Center, the Pet Center, the animal barn and the Incredible Dog Arena. They’ve been closed ever since.
Here’s what those lists miss. Purina Farms never shut down. The building everybody remembers did. About 250 yards away, the Purina Event Center took minimal damage and kept doing what it has done since 2010: hosting dog and cat shows that pull exhibitors from across the country, most of them free to walk in and watch. In 2026 the property turned 100. Dog people never stopped driving to Gray Summit. Plenty of St. Louis families did, because nobody told them what was still there.
So this is the update. What’s open right now, what it costs, which days your own dog can come along, and the one rule that turns pet owners around at the door. It’s written for St. Louis pet owners, so it pairs with our map of dog-friendly places in St. Louis. Every hour, price and date below comes from Purina, MoDOT, the AKC or an event organizer as of October 2026. Any of it can change, so check Purina Farms’ own pages before you load the car.
### Is Purina Farms open?
Partly. The grounds are open dawn to dusk and the Purina Event Center hosts dog and cat shows year-round, most free to watch. The Visitor Center, animal barn, Pet Center and Incredible Dog Arena have stayed closed since a March 2025 tornado, so check Purina’s site before you drive out.
Here’s the split, building by building, the way Purina’s visit page lists it:
Open: the grounds, from dawn to dusk.
Open: the Purina Event Center, all year, with hours set by whichever club is running that weekend’s show.
Open on weekends: a dog-friendly walking trail of about a mile, Saturdays and Sundays, dawn to dusk.
Open by reservation: the Pups Play Yard, two fenced pens you book online by time slot.
Closed: the Visitor Center, the Pet Center, the animal barn and the Incredible Dog Arena.
The damage was real. Purina’s statement the next day said all four of those buildings were significantly damaged, that every employee on site was safe and every animal accounted for, and that the Event Center, sitting about 250 yards from the damage, had come through with very little. A month later Purina said the Visitor Center would stay shut for the 2025 season and that it was reviewing plans for the future of the damaged area.
Then came the centennial, and still no reopening date. Purina’s visit page kept the Visitor Center marked temporarily closed through the anniversary year, and the organizers of the October 2026 Purple Leash 5K answered the question flatly in their race FAQ: the Visitor Center won’t be open on race day. When rumors spread in 2025 that the damaged buildings might never come back, Purina pushed back on them, according to the Missourian. Pushing back on a rumor isn’t the same as announcing a date. Until Purina posts one, plan your visit around the Event Center, the trail and the play yard.
One more stale detail to unlearn. The Incredible Dog Team didn’t retire when its arena closed. In 2026 the team took its agility, disc and trick shows downtown to St. Louis Union Station, performing Thursday through Sunday into September. Where it performs next spring is one more thing to confirm before you promise the kids.
### What can you still do at Purina Farms while the Visitor Center is closed?
More than the old lists suggest, and most of it costs nothing. The catch is that almost all of it is built for dogs and the people who love them, not for the farm-animal field trip a lot of St. Louisans grew up on. If you remember milking a cow and crawling through hay tunnels, adjust the pitch before you tell your kids where you’re going.
Walk the trail. Purina lists a dog-friendly walking trail of roughly one mile, mostly grass, open to guests Saturdays and Sundays from dawn until dusk, with expansions promised during 2026. It’s leash only. Grass means wet paws in March and burrs in October, so throw a towel and a comb in the back seat.
Book the Pups Play Yard. Two fenced pens with light agility equipment, free, by online registration only. You reserve a time slot, you get a gate code, and the yard is yours: one household at a time, up to four dogs, and only dogs that already know each other. The registration rules require current rabies, DHLPP and Bordetella vaccines, bar dogs in heat and aggressive dogs, and ban food and treats inside for dogs and people alike. Purina releases dates and times week by week.
Watch a show. The Purina Event Center runs dog and cat shows and performance trials through the year, from conformation rings to agility, obedience, rally, FastCAT sprints and dock diving. Purina says most are free to attend. It’s the best free thing on the property by a mile, and the section below shows you how to do it right.
Go on an event day. Purina’s public calendar runs fuller than most people realize. Recent years have included:
Responsible Pet Owners Day, usually a Sunday in late February, run with Operation SPOT. Purina’s 2026 listing priced microchips at $30 and vaccinations at $20 each. Cats are welcome at this one.
The Purina Pro Plan Incredible Dog Challenge National Finals, the dock diving, agility and flying disc competition that started on this property in 1998. In 2026 the Finals were set for Saturday, October 10, with free admission, a parking ticket bought in advance and no day-of sales.
The Purple Leash 5K and Fun Run, new in 2026 and set for the next day, with $5 of every registration going to RedRover’s Purple Leash Project, which helps domestic violence shelters make room for family pets.
Cold-Nosed Candids in December: pet photos with Santa. In 2025 it ran across two weekends, with a session just for cat families and a $5 parking registration that included a printed and a digital photo.
Smaller dates, like a Petfinder adoption event and blood drives, that shift from year to year.
The centennial added one big night: the Bark Tie Gala on August 22, 2026, which raised money for the Coalition for Pet Progress, an alliance of regional animal nonprofits, and brought adoptable animals from local rescues. If that leaves you wanting to help without adopting, read up on fostering pets in St. Louis.
Leave a mark. Two brick walkways lead into the Event Center: the Walk of Champions, for titled dogs, and the Path of Honor, for any pet, person, kennel or breed club. Engraved pavers support the AKC Canine Health Foundation. Purina also keeps the Remember Me Furever memorial fence, where owners hang a late pet’s ID tag for a suggested donation to the Missouri Veterinary Medical Foundation. Its description mentions replica tags sold in the Visitor Center gift shop, which is closed, so call 1-888-688-7387 on a weekday before you drive out just for the fence.
### Can you bring your dog to Purina Farms?
Yes, to most of the property. No, to the thing it’s most famous for. That second half surprises people every weekend. Purina’s visiting-pet guidelines say visiting pets are only allowed at the Purina Event Center during events designated as pet-friendly for the general public, unless they’re competing. On an ordinary show weekend, the building full of other people’s dogs is not the place for yours.
So the most dog-famous address in Missouri works like this. Your dog can walk the trail on a weekend, play in the reserved yard, and come along on public pet-friendly event days, such as the Incredible Dog Challenge Finals, the Purple Leash 5K and Cold-Nosed Candids. On a regular show day the exhibitors’ dogs are inside, and yours stays home. Not in the car. Home.
Every visiting dog, on any day, has to clear the same bar. From Purina’s guidelines and the play yard rules:
At least 4 months old.
Puppies need rabies plus two rounds of the puppy series. Adults need rabies and DHLPP. Purina recommends Bordetella and canine influenza on top of that, and the play yard requires Bordetella.
Current flea and tick prevention, and a collar with ID tags.
A fixed leash, 4 to 6 feet preferred. Retractable leashes are banned everywhere on the property.
Healthy and friendly. A dog with a runny nose or a cough, or one that shows aggression, gets asked to leave.
No pets in the café.
Carry proof of the rabies shot even if the tag is on the collar. The 5K organizers, for one, accept a copy of the rabies certificate when the tag is missing, and a photo of the certificate on your phone covers you if anyone asks.
Now the local detail that makes Purina’s modest little trail matter more than it looks. The two best-known nature spots in this corner of Franklin County don’t take dogs. Shaw Nature Reserve, just off I-44 in Gray Summit, welcomes service animals but not pets, apart from rare staff-led Hiking With Rover mornings that sell out (the October 18, 2026, date did). Engelmann Woods Natural Area, on Route T past the turnoff for St. Albans, is a Missouri Department of Conservation area whose posted rule is blunt: pets and hunting dogs are prohibited. Drive 40 miles for a weekend walk in the country with your dog, and the trail that says yes is Purina’s.
Picture a St. Albans family with a young Lab who has been cooped up all week. Engelmann Woods looks like the obvious walk. It’s the wrong answer. The Purina trail on a Saturday morning, followed by a booked slot in the play yard, burns the same energy and nobody gets turned around at a trailhead sign. On a weekday, when the trail is closed, skip the drive entirely and use one of the off-leash dog parks in St. Louis closer to home.
### How do you watch a dog show at the Purina Event Center?
Walk in, find a spot by a ring, and ask before you touch anything with fur. That’s most of it. Purina says spectators are welcome unless the Event Calendar notes otherwise, and most shows are free. What separates a great morning from a confusing one is timing, because a dog show is really dozens of small competitions running on a published schedule.
The building is worth the trip by itself. The Event Center opened in August 2010 with 84,000 square feet under one roof, including a 45,000-square-foot Great Hall on padded sport flooring, lit to approximate natural sunlight so coats look true to the judges. Out back sit full-service RV spaces with water, sewer and 30- and 50-amp hookups, which tells you how long some exhibitors stay.
At a conformation show, judges compare each dog to the written standard for its breed. Breed winners move on to their group, and at an all-breed show, the group winners meet for Best in Show. You’ll see handlers gait dogs around the ring so the judge can watch them move, then stack them for a hands-on exam, with the small breeds lifted onto a table. Performance trials are louder and easier for kids to follow: agility against the clock, obedience and rally, FastCAT sprints, dock diving.
Here’s the trick almost nobody outside the dog world uses. AKC shows are run by a licensed superintendent or a show secretary, and they post a judging program shortly before the show. It lists every breed, its ring and its start time. Golden retrievers might go into the ring at 8 a.m. and be done by 9:30, so the family that strolls in at noon sees an empty ring. Find the club’s name on Purina’s Event Calendar or the AKC’s event search, look up the superintendent listed for it, and download the program. Then plan the morning around the breed your kid can’t stop talking about.
National specialties are the ones to circle. A national is a single breed’s championship week, run by its parent club, and it brings that breed’s serious owners and breeders to one building for days. The AKC’s national specialty list shows the American Bouvier des Flandres Club starting October 15, 2026, the Giant Schnauzer Club of America on October 17 and the English Setter Association of America starting November 3, all at Purina Farms. The 2027 list already includes the American Shetland Sheepdog Association in late March, the Bernese Mountain Dog Club of America at the end of April and the Dachshund Club of America in May. Local clubs fill the winter, too. The Golden Retriever Club of Greater St. Louis is listed for January 22 to 24, 2027.
A few habits make you the spectator handlers are glad to see:
Ask the owner before you pet any dog or cat. Purina asks it of every visitor, and handlers mean it, since a dog minutes from the ring may have just been groomed for an hour.
Keep clear of ring gates and grooming areas.
Bring a folding chair. Purina has invited spectators to bring their own in the past, and ringside seats go quickly at a big show.
Plan to buy lunch. The Checkerboard Café serves food at shows, and Purina’s Event Center page says no outside food is allowed on the property.
Leave your dog home unless the event is listed as pet-friendly for the public.
Shopping for a purebred puppy? A show is the best free research you’ll ever do. Breeders who show will talk health testing and temperament between rings, and you’ll see adult dogs of the breed in person instead of in a filtered photo. Before you hand anyone a deposit, though, run the checks in our guide to puppies for sale in St. Louis.
### What does a Purina Farms visit cost?
For most visits, nothing but gas. Purina lists no admission charge for the grounds or the trail, the Pups Play Yard is free with a reservation, and most Event Center shows are free to watch. Money comes in on big event days, at lunch and if you stay the night. Here’s the rundown from the most recent published prices:
Grounds and the weekend trail: no fee listed.
Pups Play Yard: free, by online time slot.
Most dog and cat shows: free, unless the Event Calendar notes otherwise.
Big public events: often free admission with a parking ticket you book in advance. The Incredible Dog Challenge Finals charged $10 a car in 2022, and Cold-Nosed Candids charged $5 a car in 2025.
Purple Leash 5K: $35 to $45 in 2026, rising as race day got closer, with no on-site registration.
Responsible Pet Owners Day: microchips at $30 and vaccinations at $20 each on Purina’s 2026 listing.
Lunch on a show day: whatever the Checkerboard Café charges, since outside food isn’t allowed.
For a sense of scale, the National Dog Show that Purina presents on Thanksgiving television is held in Pennsylvania, and its 2026 tickets run $20 for adults and $10 for kids 4 to 11. In Gray Summit, a national specialty is usually free to walk into, unless the calendar says otherwise. Same sport. Different price tag.
The real cost is the wasted drive. It’s roughly 80 miles round trip from downtown, and showing up on a Wednesday with a dog, expecting the barn, gets you a parking lot and a long ride home. Three checks prevent it: the Event Calendar for what’s on, the day of the week if you want the trail, and the play yard registration if you want the pens.
### How do you plan the drive from St. Louis to Gray Summit?
Take I-44 west to exit 253, the Gray Summit exit. Go north on Highway 100 for half a mile, turn left onto Route MM and head west about a mile. The entrance is on your left. It’s about 40 miles from downtown. Purina describes it as 30 minutes west of St. Louis, and from downtown on a clear Saturday you should plan on 40 to 50 minutes, depending on traffic.
Put 500 William Danforth Way, Gray Summit, MO 63039, in your phone. That’s the address on Purina’s visit page and on the 2026 race listing. Older event listings still show 200 Checkerboard Drive, and the exit 253 directions get you to the same gate either way.
If you tried this drive in late 2025 and hit barricades, that’s fixed. MoDOT closed Route MM, the road that runs between Gray Summit and Labadie, in summer 2025 for curve widening, a box culvert, a retaining wall and resurfacing near the railroad bridge. It reopened on April 22, 2026.
That reopening matters if you like to make a loop of it. Keep going west on MM after a Saturday trail walk and you’re in Labadie, where Point Labaddie Brewery on Thiebes Road is listed by pet travel sites as welcoming leashed dogs in its outdoor space. Policies change, so call before you bring yours. And if you’re taking the back roads out past St. Albans, remember what the sign at Engelmann Woods says, and save the dog walk for Purina’s trail.
Staying over for a multi-day national? Exhibitors don’t commute from the city every night. Some park on the full-service RV lot. Others rent close by. In Villa Ridge, one owner runs three dog-friendly rental houses on a shared gravel drive, the Hound Haus, the Setter Haus and the Fox Haus, about 8 to 10 minutes from the Event Center by the owner’s own estimate, at $25 a night for each approved dog and a special rate for show dogs on request. Check current rates when you book. Purina also posts a pet-friendly lodging list on its Event Center page, made for exhibitors and handy for anybody.
Staying for a two-day national? Here’s what to expect at a bed and breakfast
Rather sleep closer to the city? Compare pet fees and weight limits in our guide to pet-friendly hotels in St. Louis. If the show is just the excuse and a few days away with the dog is the real plan, our roundup of dog-friendly getaways from St. Louis picks up from there.
Most people still picture Purina Farms as the barn they visited in second grade. You know better now. The barn is closed, the best show in Gray Summit is usually free, and the closest trail that welcomes your dog is on Purina’s own property. Check the Event Calendar, pick a breed, and go on a Saturday.
If your own pet is staying home while you spend the day ringside, line up a sitter, groomer or boarding kennel through pet services around St. Louis before you go.
