### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Why are Purina Farms temporarily closed?
A.  An EF-2 tornado hit the property on the night of March 14, 2025, and significantly damaged the Visitor Center, the Pet Center, the animal barn and the Incredible Dog Arena. No employees were hurt and every animal was accounted for. Those buildings have stayed closed since. The Purina Event Center, about 250 yards away, took minimal damage and still hosts shows.
### Q. Has Purina Farms reopened yet?
A.  Partly. The grounds, the weekend walking trail, the Pups Play Yard and the Purina Event Center are open. As of October 2026, the Visitor Center, Pet Center, animal barn and Incredible Dog Arena remain temporarily closed, and Purina hasn’t announced a reopening date. Check the Purina Farms visit page, or call 1-888-688-7387 on a weekday, for the latest.
### Q. How much does it cost to go to Purina Farms?
A.  Usually nothing. Purina lists no fee for the grounds or the trail, the Pups Play Yard is free with an online reservation, and most dog and cat shows are free to watch. Big public events often charge for a pre-booked parking ticket instead of admission, like the $5 a car Cold-Nosed Candids charged in 2025. Check each event listing for the current price.
### Q. What is Purina Farms?
A.  It’s Purina’s property in Gray Summit, Missouri, which began in 1926 as a research farm where the company studied animal nutrition; Purina calls it the first pet nutrition and care center. Today it’s best known for the Purina Event Center, which hosts dog and cat shows year-round, and for the Incredible Dog Challenge, which started there in 1998. It turned 100 in 2026.
### Q. Where is Purina Farms located?
A.  At 500 William Danforth Way in Gray Summit, Missouri, in Franklin County, about 40 miles west of downtown St. Louis. Take I-44 west to exit 253, go north on Highway 100 for half a mile, then turn left onto Route MM and drive about a mile west. The entrance is on the left.
### Q. What is there to do at Purina Farms?
A.  Right now you can watch free dog and cat shows at the Purina Event Center, walk the leashed dog trail on weekends, book the fenced Pups Play Yard, and come out for public events such as the Incredible Dog Challenge Finals in the fall and pet photos with Santa in December. The barn, the Pet Center and the arena dog shows are closed until Purina says otherwise.
### Q. What dog shows are happening in Missouri?
A.  Near St. Louis, the busiest venue is the Purina Event Center in Gray Summit, which hosts all-breed shows, breed specialties and national specialties through most of the year. Its fall 2026 nationals include the American Bouvier des Flandres Club from October 15 and the English Setter Association of America from November 3. For a full statewide list, search events by state on the American Kennel Club’s website.
### Q. Where is Purina Farms dog show?
A.  Inside the Purina Event Center, an 84,000-square-foot indoor hall on the Purina Farms property at 500 William Danforth Way in Gray Summit. Shows use the Great Hall and the smaller Gateway Hall, and some events use the outdoor show fields. Spectators are welcome unless the Event Calendar says otherwise. Don’t mix it up with the Thanksgiving National Dog Show Purina presents, which is held in Pennsylvania.

## Cat Grooming in St. Louis: Lion Cut Prices, Cat Specialists, and When a Vet Sedates
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/cat-grooming-in-st-louis
National price guides put cat grooming at a tidy $50 to $70, as if a cat were a small dog with a bad attitude. Call around St. Louis and that number comes apart in your hand. A south city salon lists a bath and brush for a short-haired cat from $40. A cat-only spa on Hampton Avenue won’t post a base price at all, but it will tell you that matting adds $20 to $75 before anyone picks up a comb. And a feline-only vet clinic in west county does full-body shave-downs, but only for cats so matted they have to be sedated first.
The averages miss what actually sets the bill. The haircut is the cheap part. You’re paying for the condition of the coat when the carrier opens, for how your cat behaves on the table, and for whether the person holding the clippers was ever taught to groom a cat. Missouri doesn’t check that last one. The state Department of Agriculture says it in a single line: dog or cat grooming is not regulated in Missouri.
Below: what St. Louis groomers actually publish, where the surcharges hide, why every sedated groom we found runs through a vet, and which cats never need a groomer. Prices come from each business’s own page or listing as of October 2026, so check current before you book. For parks, patios and pet rules, see our guide to pet-friendly St. Louis.
### How much does it cost to groom my cat?
At St. Louis salons that publish cat prices, a bath, comb-out and nail trim runs about $40 to $54, and a lion cut about $50 to $68. Matting adds $20 to $75 at one cat-only spa, and a shave-down under sedation happens only at a vet clinic, priced as a vet visit. Check current prices.
Shops price a cat three different ways, and it helps to know which one you’re looking at.
Some shops publish a menu. St. Louis Muttropolitan, a dog-and-cat salon on Fyler Avenue that has groomed in south St. Louis since 2008, posts cat prices on its Care.com business listing: a bath and brush runs $40 to $48 for a short-haired cat, $44 to $50 for medium hair and $46 to $54 for long hair, and a lion cut or a full shave runs $62 to $68. Biters and problem cats add $10 to $22. Its own website says to call for a price, since prices vary with breed, coat type and condition, so treat that menu as a floor. It also takes 20% off grooming for seniors 60 and older on Wednesdays.
Some price by the clock. Mrs. Anderson’s Pet Grooming on Watson Road has groomed pets since 1960 and keeps a dedicated cat groomer, Jerilyn, who the shop says has specialized in cats for more than 30 years and gets referrals from veterinarians. Cats are priced by the time the groom takes. An archived 2023 copy of its grooming page put most small and medium cats around $50 to $55 for a clipper cut “without matting, fleas or bad behavior.” Read that clause twice. It’s the whole pricing model of cat grooming in six words. The same page listed nail trims at $10, or $15 with grinding.
And some won’t quote until they’ve met the cat. Happy Cat Hotel & Spa, the cat-only hotel and grooming spa at 3460 Hampton Ave., starts every appointment with an in-person consultation and a price estimate before any grooming begins. What it does publish is the surcharges: $20 to $75 for matting, depending on severity and how well the cat tolerates removal, and a possible $30 fee for a cat that turns aggressive, who may also have to wear soft nail caps for the groomer’s protection. Its Spa Club costs $60 a year per cat and takes 20% off standard rates, though matting and aggressive-handling fees don’t get the discount.
A few other line items show up around town:
Walk-in nail trim and filing at Kennelwood Pet Resorts: $20, with a sanitary trim also listed at $20. Call to ask whether your location takes cats as walk-ins.
Nail trims and sanitary shaves at the vet: The Cat Clinic, a feline-only practice on Schuetz Road, does both by appointment.
A shave-down under sedation, done at a veterinary clinic and billed as veterinary care. Neither clinic we found posts that price online, so ask for an itemized estimate.
Now run the math the way your cat will run it. Say you live in Sappington with a long-haired cat who mats along the belly and the back legs every summer. A lion cut every 8 to 12 weeks, the schedule Happy Cat recommends for that cut, means four to six cuts a year. At $62 to $68 a cut, that’s roughly $250 to $410 a year. Skip the schedule and wait for felted mats, and the same cat costs a base groom plus a $20 to $75 matting fee at the spa, or a sedated shave-down at the vet. Happy Cat calls matting “100 percent preventable” and has a zero-tolerance policy for repeats: a second round can bring doubled matting fees or a refusal of service.
That’s the real answer under the question. The cheapest cat groom in St. Louis is the one you book before the mats form.
### Why does grooming a cat cost more than grooming a dog?
Pound for pound, it does. A short-haired cat’s bath and brush at $40 to $48 lands right beside Silver Maple Pet Center’s small-dog bath at $42 to $58, and the cat is the harder job. Four things push a cat’s price up. None of them is the shampoo.
Time comes first. Cats get groomed one at a time, start to finish, with breaks when they need them. Happy Cat says a typical groom runs 45 minutes to two hours depending on behavior and coat, and since many cats need a break partway through, a cat may stay a couple of hours. Love Cats Grooming builds its whole business around one cat at a time. A dog salon can bathe one dog while another dries. A cat groomer mostly can’t.
Then the skin. Cat skin is loose and elastic, so when a mat lifts, the skin can lift right along with it. A veterinarian writing for PetMD warns that mats can sit so close to the skin it’s hard to tell where the hair ends and the skin begins, which is why professionals take tight mats off with clippers rather than scissors. Happy Cat adds that removing mats hurts even when it’s done gently. Slow, careful clipper work gets billed by the minute.
Then the teeth. Mayo Clinic researchers reviewed 193 patients treated there over three years for cat bites to the hand, and 57 of them, 30 percent, ended up hospitalized, for an average stay of 3.2 days. That’s the arithmetic behind every handling fee on a St. Louis price list, from Muttropolitan’s $10 to $22 to Happy Cat’s $30. A groomer’s hands are the whole business.
Last, training. This is where cats and dogs split for real. The National Cat Groomers Institute awards its Certified Feline Master Groomer title only after nine exams, four written and five hands-on, each passed at 85% or better. Two of the five practical exams are lion cuts. The exam fees alone come to $585, before the hands-on training the institute recommends. A groomer who paid for all that prices like it. One who learned on dogs and takes the occasional cat may charge less, and you’ll be the one who finds out why.
Dog-first shops are honest about the difference. Kennelwood Pet Resorts, with nine grooming spas around St. Louis, says it specializes in dog grooming while its groomers also bathe and cut cats. Before you book a cat into any mixed shop, ask how long it will be on site and where it waits.
### What is a lion cut, and when does a cat need one?
A lion cut shaves the body short and leaves the head, the ruff and usually the tip of the tail full, so the cat looks like a very small lion who has had a long week. At Happy Cat, it means a body shave down to 1/16 of an inch, taken to the elbow and hock joints, with a moderate mane and a choice of a full tail or a shaved tail with a pom-pom. It’s a real technique with real standards: the National Cat Groomers Institute tests a standard lion cut and a lion cut variation as two separate practical exams.
Most cats who get one need it for one reason. The coat got ahead of them. Happy Cat says a lion cut may be required when matting is severe, and calls it a good option for cats prone to matting. The PetMD veterinarian points out that cats who normally keep themselves groomed can start matting when illness, pain or arthritis makes grooming harder. The Cat Clinic adds weight to the list, noting that losing weight may help a heavy cat groom itself more often.
Picture a long-haired senior in Crestwood who used to keep herself immaculate. Arthritis sets in. She stops reaching her lower back, and by spring she has felted pads along her spine and under both front legs. That cat doesn’t need a style. She needs the mats off without pain, and then a vet visit, because the mats were the symptom.
Mats tend to start where the coat rubs. PetMD’s list: behind the ears, under the legs and around the armpits, the collar or harness line, between the toes, and around the tail and hindquarters. Check those spots once a week and you’ll catch tangles while they’re still tangles.
A lion cut isn’t the only option, and it isn’t right for every cat. Happy Cat says it may not suggest one, depending on a cat’s health and personality. For owners who want less fur without the shaved look, it sells a plush trim, a short trim all over that isn’t a shave, on an 8 to 12 week cycle. Bark & Mane’s mobile menu splits it further: a kitty cut that keeps the coat fluffy, a belly shave that clears only the underside, the lion cut, and a very short shave down it reserves mostly for severe matting, skin issues or extreme heat.
A good groomer will tell you the rest. A lion cut is a reset. Book it to get out of trouble, then book the comb-outs that keep you out.
### Can a groomer sedate a cat, or does it take a vet?
It takes a vet. Every sedated groom we found in St. Louis runs through a veterinary practice, and the groomers say so themselves. Happy Cat calls itself an anesthesia-free facility and says it never sedates cats for grooming. Four Pretty Paws, a mobile service, says it doesn’t perform sedation grooms. Kennelwood says it can’t administer medication at all.
On the vet side, the options are specific. The Cat Clinic, a feline-only hospital at 1919 Schuetz Road in west county, whose veterinarian is certified as a feline specialist through the American Board of Veterinary Practitioners, offers full-body shave-downs for cats that are very matted and require sedation. For cats that don’t need sedation, it sends owners to a professional groomer who handles cats. Kingsbury Animal Hospital, which says its grooming service dates to 1978, grooms dogs and cats and lists pets requiring grooming under sedation among the cases it takes, with veterinary staff on hand. Neither posts a price online. Both ask you to call.
There’s also a middle path most owners never hear about: medication your vet prescribes and you give at home. Kennelwood asks owners to give calming medication about two hours before the appointment, to mention it when booking, and to expect a handling fee, since a second team member helps with the groom. One drug veterinarians increasingly prescribe for this is gabapentin. In a small 2017 study in the Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association, 20 stress-prone cats given gabapentin 90 minutes before a vet trip showed fewer stress behaviors, less aggression and more cooperation than on a placebo. That was a vet exam, not a groom, and the dose is your veterinarian’s call, never a leftover pill from another pet.
Say you’re in Lemay with a cat who has bitten her way out of two grooming appointments. Don’t book a third groomer and hope. Call your vet, ask whether a pre-visit medication or a sedated shave-down makes more sense, and get the estimate itemized: the exam, the sedation, the monitoring and the groom itself. No vet you trust yet? Start with how to choose a vet in St. Louis.
And walk away from any groomer who offers to sedate your cat on the premises. None of the groomers we found will do it, and that’s the right answer.
Cat’s shaved. Should you shave before laser hair removal in St. Louis?
### Salon, cat-only groomer or mobile van: which suits your cat?
Match the setting to the cat first and the price second. Each one solves a different problem.
Cat-only shops suit the cat who flattens at the sound of a bark. Happy Cat Hotel & Spa on Hampton Avenue is cats only, front to back, and books spa sessions with or without a hotel stay, so a cat boarding for a week can go home groomed. If you’re pricing a stay too, compare cat boarding in St. Louis first. Love Cats Grooming is run by a Certified Feline Master Groomer who works one cat at a time, either in a salon across the Missouri River or in your home, with owners welcome to stay.
Dog-and-cat salons with a cat person on staff suit the easygoing cat and the owner watching the budget. Mrs. Anderson’s on Watson Road, a short drive from Crestwood, has its 30-year cat specialist, and Muttropolitan on Fyler Avenue publishes the cat menu above. Silver Maple Pet Center lists lion cuts for long-haired cats right on its dog price page, with a note that yes, it grooms cats too. Kennelwood grooms cats at its dog-focused spas, including the one on Baptist Church Road in south county, and PetSmart grooms cats only at select salons, so call ahead to make sure a certified Cat Stylist is working.
Mobile vans suit the cat who yowls the whole way down Gravois, the senior with bad hips, and the house with three cats and one carrier. Bark & Mane of Central and South St. Louis, the mobile franchise that used to be Aussie Pet Mobile, grooms cats in its van in your driveway, from a bath and blowout to lion cuts and belly shaves, and offers an automatic rotation, typically every four to six weeks. Four Pretty Paws grooms cats too, with conditions worth reading before you book. Its Cat Pampering service is for cats with mild temperaments who are used to grooming, it doesn’t sedate, there’s one groomer per van, and your cat has to be in a carrier before the van pulls up. Anyone who has chased a cat under the bed at the sound of a doorbell knows why.
Mobile has limits. One groomer means no second set of hands, which is why mobile shops screen for calm cats. If your cat needed two people at the last salon, a van won’t fix that. Weighing the same trade-off for the dog? Compare mobile dog grooming in St. Louis.
The quick sort:
Panics around dogs: a cat-only spa or an in-home cat groomer.
Calm and short-haired, needs nails and a de-shed: a dog-and-cat salon with a cat specialist, or a walk-in nail trim.
Hates the car, or too stiff to ride comfortably: a mobile van, if the cat is calm with strangers.
Matted to the skin, or has bitten a groomer: your vet, first.
### Does Missouri license cat groomers?
No. The Missouri Department of Agriculture’s Animal Care Facilities Act program puts it in one sentence: dog or cat grooming is not regulated in Missouri. A license kicks in only if the groomer also keeps animals overnight, which makes the place a commercial kennel in the state’s eyes. The person shaving your cat on a Tuesday afternoon needs no license, no inspection and no cat training of any kind.
That makes you the inspector. The one cat-specific credential that means something is voluntary: the National Cat Groomers Institute’s Certified Feline Master Groomer, or CFMG. The institute’s own groomer locator draws the line for you. It recommends CFMGs, and it warns that people listed simply as members may be working toward certification or may be brand new to grooming cats. A membership is a subscription. The certification is nine passed exams.
Read other credentials for what they are. PetSmart says its safety-certified stylists have more than 800 hours of hands-on experience with dogs and cats, and Bark & Mane advertises AKC S.A.F.E. certified groomers. Both are real training. Neither is a cat-specific master certification.
Before you hand over the carrier, ask:
Are you certified for cats, and how many do you groom in a week?
Are cats groomed one at a time, and where does my cat wait before and after?
How do you dry cats? Four Pretty Paws, for one, advertises no crates and no crate drying.
What happens if my cat gets upset partway through? Do you stop, take a break or call me?
Will you give me the matting or handling fee before you start?
Which vaccines do you require? Kennelwood and Kingsbury both list rabies and FVRCP for cats.
Can I stay? Some cat groomers, Love Cats among them, welcome it.
A groomer who answers all of that without flinching has done this before. One who bristles at the questions just answered the most important one. Grooming the dog too? The same red flags apply, and our guide to dog groomer prices in St. Louis walks through them.
### Which cats need a groomer, and which never do?
Most healthy short-haired cats never need a professional groom in their lives. They need their nails trimmed and an occasional brushing, and that’s about it. The Cat Clinic says most cats don’t require regular bathing at all; the exceptions it names are hairless or thin-haired cats with oily skin, and older cats who aren’t grooming themselves well.
Picture a young short-haired tabby in Lemay who spends her afternoons in a sunny window. She needs a nail trim about once a month, which is what The Cat Clinic recommends, and maybe a rubber brush during spring shedding. Paying for a full groom would mean paying for a bath she doesn’t need and won’t forgive.
The cats who do need help fall into a few groups:
Long-haired breeds. Happy Cat recommends monthly grooming for Persians, Ragdolls and Maine Coons, and roughly every eight weeks for domestic shorthairs that need it.
Seniors. The Cat Clinic notes that older cats don’t shed their nails as well and can end up with thickened, curled nails.
Overweight cats. The Cat Clinic says losing weight may help a heavy cat groom more often.
Cats with dandruff. The Cat Clinic says it can come from poor grooming or diet, and can also be a sign of internal disease such as diabetes.
Any cat that suddenly quits grooming. That’s a vet visit first. A groomer can take the mats off, but only a vet can find out why they formed.
Here’s where the two sides of St. Louis cat care disagree, and it’s worth knowing. Happy Cat argues that a groom needs a real bath, because oily skin and dead hair are the root of matting, and it won’t shave or comb out mats without a full groom. The Cat Clinic says most cats don’t need regular baths. They’re describing different cats. A healthy shorthair keeping herself clean is the vet’s cat. A long-haired cat whose coat has gone greasy and clumped is the spa’s.
Bringing home a new one? Start brushing and handling paws in the first weeks, while it’s still a game, and see our guide to getting a kitten in St. Louis for the rest of that first year.
Your cat can’t book her own appointments. Be the owner who books the comb-out in March instead of the shave-down in July.
Ready to compare? Browse pet groomers around St. Louis and call two or three with the same three questions: cats only or cats too, one cat at a time, and what mats cost.
And if you’re the cat groomer these owners are vetting, list your grooming business with us with your certification, your setup and your matting fee up front.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Why are cat groomers so expensive?
A.  Every cat is a slow, one-at-a-time job with risk at both ends of the comb. Mats sit tight against elastic skin and come off carefully, with clippers. Of 193 Mayo Clinic patients treated for cat bites to the hand, 30 percent were hospitalized. The surcharges for mats and handling are where bills jump.
### Q. How much is normal grooming for a cat?
A.  A standard groom is a bath, blow-dry, comb-out, nail trim and ear cleaning, plus a sanitary trim for long-haired cats. At Muttropolitan, a south city salon that lists cat prices, a bath and brush runs $40 to $54 depending on coat length. Cat-only spas quote after a consultation. Add a matting fee if the coat has knotted, and check current prices.
### Q. How much does a haircut for a cat cost?
A.  At St. Louis salons that publish numbers, a lion cut or full shave runs about $50 to $68. Muttropolitan lists $62 to $68, and an archived Mrs. Anderson’s page put most small and medium cats around $50 to $55 for a clipper cut. Severe matting adds a fee, and a shave-down under sedation at a vet clinic is billed as vet care. Check current prices.
### Q. How often should a cat get a haircut?
A.  Only as often as the coat needs. Happy Cat books lion cuts every 8 to 12 weeks, and its plush trim runs on the same cycle. Bark & Mane’s automatic rotation is usually every four to six weeks for a groom. Plenty of short-haired cats never need a haircut at all, just nails and brushing.
### Q. Can I groom my cat myself?
A.  Mostly, yes. Brushing and monthly nail trims are home jobs for most cats; The Cat Clinic suggests an undercoat tool for short hair, plus a rake and comb for long hair. Leave tight mats alone, though. Never cut them out with scissors, because they sit so close to the skin it’s easy to cut the cat. Animal clippers or a professional are the safe route.
### Q. What kind of grooming does a ragdoll cat need?
A.  Less than the fur suggests. The Cat Fanciers’ Association breed standard calls the Ragdoll coat naturally non-matting, with abundant guard hairs and minimal woolly undercoat, and Ragdolls don’t reach full coat until about age three. Mats still form under the legs and around the hindquarters, so Hill’s recommends daily brushing and Happy Cat suggests a monthly professional groom.
### Q. Does PetSmart groom cats?
A.  Yes, at select salons. PetSmart says its cat services, from baths and brush-outs to nail trims and nail caps, are offered only at some locations, so call ahead to make sure a certified Cat Stylist is working. Prices vary with breed, coat condition and service time.
### Q. What vaccines does a cat need before grooming?
A.  Rabies and FVRCP, the feline distemper combination shot, are the usual pair. Kennelwood Pet Resorts and Kingsbury Animal Hospital both list those two for cats, and Happy Cat won’t confirm a first appointment until it has your cat’s vaccination records. Bring the paperwork, or have your vet send it, a few days ahead.

## Getting a Kitten in St. Louis: Best Age, Shelter Fees, Why Free Costs More
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/getting-a-kitten-in-st-louis
Free kittens, ready now. Some version of that post turns up in St. Louis neighborhood groups every summer. Picture the photo: a litter piled in a laundry basket, and a note that they have to be gone by Sunday. It gets two things wrong before you finish reading it. The age. And the price.
Start with the age. A kitten who’s “ready” at six weeks is two weeks short of the eight-week floor vets use, and as much as six weeks short of the age plenty of them would rather see. Then the price. In St. Louis, a kitten that’s already spayed or neutered, microchipped and started on its shots goes home from five of the region’s main shelters and rescues for $80 to $175, and for nothing at all on the fee-waived days several of them run when the cat rooms overflow. The free kitten in the laundry basket needs every bit of that work bought one piece at a time. At the lowest prices nonprofit clinics in town post, that runs roughly $195 to $215, and still about $145 if you land a slot at the County’s free monthly spay clinic.
So the cheapest kitten in St. Louis usually isn’t the free one. It’s the one a shelter already paid to fix. This is one of the cat chapters in our guide to pet-friendly St. Louis. Fees and rules below come from each organization’s own pages and from City and County code as of October 2026. They change, sometimes by the week, so check before you drive over.
### What age is best to get a kitten?
Between 8 and 12 weeks. Eight weeks is the floor: a kitten is weaned, eating on its own and about two pounds. Twelve weeks is often the easier start for a first-time owner, because the extra weeks with its mother and littermates build cat manners, like a softer bite. Earlier than eight weeks is too young.
Eight weeks is a floor for good reasons. By two months, the ASPCA notes, a kitten eats on its own, weighs around two pounds and runs and plays with real coordination. Before that it still needs its mother, for milk and for lessons: how hard is too hard to bite, when to back off from a hiss, how to use a litter box by copying. A kitten pulled at five or six weeks hasn’t finished that course. You become the substitute teacher, and your hands become the chew toy.
VCA Animal Hospitals puts the sweet spot at 8 to 12 weeks and adds a detail that matters at the top end. Kittens mature socially faster than puppies, and by 12 weeks they’re already less flexible about new people, places and sounds. So a kitten who comes home at nine or ten weeks gets used to the vacuum, the kids and the carrier while it barely notices. A kitten at 12 weeks or older arrives with more of its personality showing, which helps if you want to know whether you’re getting a lap cat or a curtain climber.
Shelters settle part of the question for you. Every kitten from the five shelters and rescues below goes home already spayed or neutered, so the youngest you’ll meet are usually around eight weeks and two pounds, and many are older.
One more piece of the answer has nothing to do with age. Think about getting two. During its July 2026 cat surge, APA President and CEO Sarah Javier put it plainly: “Kittens do better in pairs.” Two kittens wrestle each other instead of your ankles and learn bite control from someone with fur. Two St. Louis organizations price it in. At the APA, one kitten is $175 and two are $300. At Stray Rescue, one is $125 and a pair is $200. The second kitten costs $125 or $75, less than the vet work already done on it.
### When is kitten season in St. Louis?
Roughly March through October, with the heaviest stretch in late spring and summer. Cats breed as the days lengthen, and Missouri shelters commonly put kitten season at March to October. In St. Louis the numbers show up fast. The APA Adoption Center took in about 700 cats between May 1 and early July of 2026, and said its cat intake was running 15 percent ahead of the year before, with no sign of slowing.
Seven hundred cats in about ten weeks, at a building the APA says houses around 200 animals at a time. Foster homes are what let it more than double that. That’s kitten season here: months when the shelters are full, the overflow lives in volunteers’ spare bedrooms and fees start dropping to make room. For you, that plays out three ways:
Choice peaks in summer. From about June through September you’ll usually find the most kittens at the most ages. Late summer tends to be the sweet spot, when spring litters hit 8 to 12 weeks and shelters are fullest.
So do the deals. Full shelters waive fees to make room. The APA did it for cats and kittens for three days in July 2026, and CARE STL and the County shelter run fee-waived events too. The dates are in the FAQ below.
Winter is quieter. From about November to February you’ll meet fewer tiny kittens and more four-to-eight-month-olds, still kittens, with most of their goofy first year ahead.
One City rule catches kitten-season households off guard. Inside the City of St. Louis, a kitten counts as a domestic animal from six weeks old, and the City caps a residential parcel at four dogs and cats combined. A two-cat house whose unspayed cat has a litter of four is over the limit about a month and a half after the kittens arrive. Our rundown of pet laws in St. Louis City and County covers the County version and the permit route. The fix is the same on both sides of the line: spay before the first litter. The ASPCA warns that cats can start breeding before they’re six months old.
### What should you do if you find kittens outside?
Usually, nothing yet. Watch from a distance and wait. The APA’s advice to anyone who finds a litter is blunt: please don’t kitten-nap. Mother cats leave their kittens for hours at a time to eat, and kittens get the best care from her. The ASPCA suggests leaving them where they are and checking back over a few hours to see whether she returns.
Say it’s late May in Normandy and you hear mewing from behind the air-conditioner unit. Three or four kittens, eyes barely open, no mother in sight. The instinct is to scoop them into a box and drive them somewhere. Hold that thought. If they’re clean, quiet and round-bellied, she’s probably close by, watching you and waiting for you to leave. If they’re in real danger, in a window well that floods or the path of a mower, move them a few feet to somewhere safer where she can still find them. Then step back far enough that she’ll come in.
Kittens that look cold, dirty, thin or listless, or that cry for hours with no mother showing up, are a different story. They may really be orphaned, and very young ones need help that day. Call a vet clinic or one of the shelters below before you try feeding anything.
Here’s what surprises most finders. Dropping the litter at a shelter often isn’t an option. CARE STL, the City’s only open-admission shelter, says it has been operating beyond capacity for more than a year and can’t accept animals brought in by the public, because every open kennel goes to animals Animal Control officers bring in. It asks finders to foster instead, and it supplies what they need.
The ASPCA’s timeline makes that doable. Once kittens eat wet food on their own, at around four to five weeks, you can bring them inside and foster them until they’re old enough to adopt out, while the mother gets trapped, spayed and returned if she isn’t friendly. The Humane Society of Missouri says most of its fosters are young puppies and kittens, the average stint runs one to three weeks, and it provides all food, medical care and supplies. Its City foster line is 314-802-5710. Our guide to fostering pets in St. Louis walks through each program.
And that Normandy litter behind the air conditioner? Fostered, fixed and chipped, those are exactly the kittens a shelter hands to somebody else at eight weeks.
### Where do you get a kitten in St. Louis: shelter, rescue, foster or neighbor?
Most St. Louis kittens move through five organizations, and their posted kitten fees run from $80 to $175. Every one of those fees includes spay or neuter surgery, a microchip and age-appropriate vaccines. The differences are price, hours and whether you can walk in and meet a kitten at all.
St. Louis County Pet Adoption Center, 10521 Baur Blvd.: $80 for any animal since the County Council doubled the fee from $40 in October 2025, with spay or neuter, vaccines and a microchip included. It can’t turn animals away, so it runs full in summer.
CARE STL, 2700 Walnut Place: $100 for every animal, kittens included. Walk-ins are welcome 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. daily.
Stray Rescue of St. Louis, 2320 Pine St.: $125 for a kitten under six months, or $200 for a pair. Here’s the detail most people miss: every puppy and kitten under six months lives in a foster home, not at the shelter. You apply, staff screen the application, and the foster family contacts you directly.
Humane Society of Missouri, 1201 Macklind Ave., plus a second campus in west St. Louis County: $150 for a kitten under nine months, plus a $10 rabies tag fee. The fee covers spay or neuter, a microchip, the first FVRCP shot, a feline leukemia test and a starter bag of food.
APA Adoption Center, 1705 S. Hanley Rd.: $175 for a kitten or two for $300, and variable pricing may apply. The fee covers spay or neuter, a microchip, vaccines, deworming and flea prevention. Kittens must leave in a secure carrier; bring one or buy one there, $5 for cardboard or $30 for plastic.
Those are posted prices as of October 2026, and promotions change them often, so check before you go. Then look at what the fee actually buys. The APA says its average cost to care for an animal is $500, and that its fees cover only about a quarter of the medical bills and care. A shelter fee isn’t the price of the kitten. It’s a partial refund on vet work somebody already did.
Beyond those five, smaller foster-based cat rescues place kittens all over the metro. Our guide to St. Louis pet rescues covers the bigger groups and their applications, and our roundup of cat cafes in St. Louis covers the lounges that double as adoption floors. One hour there shows you which kitten climbs into laps and which one lives behind the cat tree.
Renting changes the order of operations. Picture someone in Breckenridge Hills who falls for a gray kitten online on a Tuesday night. If she rents, Stray Rescue needs written approval from her landlord, including any size or breed limits, before it moves her application forward. Get that email first, then go shopping. Our guide to renting with pets in St. Louis covers the lease side.
Then there’s the neighbor with a litter. Plenty of great cats started that way. It simply moves the vet bill from the shelter to you.
### Is a free kitten cheaper than a shelter kitten?
Usually not, once you count the vet work. A shelter kitten comes home fixed, chipped and started on its shots. A free kitten needs every piece of that bought separately, and at the lowest posted nonprofit prices in St. Louis, the basics come to roughly $195 to $215. That’s more than the regular kitten fee at all five of the big shelters and rescues above.
Here’s the math. Say a neighbor in Riverview hands you a healthy ten-week-old kitten, free. This is the cheapest route to where a shelter kitten starts:
Wellness exam at Carol House Quick Fix Pet Clinic on South Jefferson: $25.
FVRCP distemper shots at $20 each. Kittens get a series, every three to four weeks until about 16 weeks old under the AAHA and AAFP feline vaccination guidelines, so two or three shots: $40 to $60.
Rabies shot: $25. The City and the County both require it, along with registration, between three and four months of age.
FIV and feline leukemia test: $20.
Microchip: $35.
Spay or neuter through SNIP, the Humane Society of Missouri’s subsidized program at Animal Medical Center of Mid-America: $49.95 for a cat.
That’s $194.95 to $214.95, and it assumes everything goes your way. SNIP is for Missouri residents, takes pets at four months or older, wants rabies and distemper shots from a licensed vet at least two weeks before surgery plus a $50 nonrefundable deposit, and warns that when its donation and grant money runs out, appointments may not be available. Live in St. Louis County? The County runs a free spay and neuter clinic for residents on the fourth Wednesday of each month, off a waiting list. Land a slot and the total drops to about $145 to $165, still more than the fee at the County shelter, CARE STL or Stray Rescue. Then add dewormer, flea treatment and a rabies tag. These are October 2026 prices, so call to confirm.
Then there’s time: four or five separate trips over about two months, and a window between roughly four and six months old when an unspayed female can already get pregnant. The shelter kitten skipped all of it. It may still need a booster or two after it comes home, but the surgery, the chip and the first shots are done and paid for.
None of this makes the neighbor’s kitten a bad choice. It makes it a $200 kitten, which is worth knowing before you say yes. And if the mother cat isn’t fixed, the kindest thank-you is helping get her spayed before the next litter. Our guide to low-cost vet care in St. Louis lists the clinics, the County voucher and the free spay days.
### What does a kitten cost in the first year?
Plan on something close to $2,000 in year one and a little over $1,100 a year after that. Those are the ASPCA’s estimates, the most widely cited national figures: $1,904 for a cat’s first year, made up of $1,149 in yearly costs, $455 in one-time startup costs and $300 for grooming and dental extras. Every year after the first, it budgets $1,149.
Those figures date to a 2021 update, so treat them as a floor. Here’s how they line up with St. Louis prices:
The kitten: $0 to $175 at a shelter or rescue with surgery, chip and first shots included, against roughly $145 to $215 to buy the same work for a free kitten.
Food: the ASPCA budgets $225 a year. Kittens eat three or four small meals a day until about six months, so the early months run heavier.
Litter: $150 a year in the ASPCA’s figures. Two cats, more litter.
Routine vet care: $160 a year for checkups and vaccines, plus $140 for flea and other preventive medicine. Locally, Carol House posts a $25 exam and $20 distemper shots, and the APA runs an appointment-only wellness clinic for shots and minor problems.
The rabies tag: in the City, $4 for a spayed or neutered cat and $50 for an intact one. In St. Louis County, $8 for one year or $20 for three if the cat is fixed, $16 or $40 if not.
Startup gear: carrier, litter box, scratching post, bowls, toys. A hard plastic carrier earns its price on the first vet trip.
Look hard at that tag line. In the City, an intact cat pays $46 more at every renewal, before you count a single unplanned litter. And budget for the visit you can’t schedule. Kittens chew cords and swallow things they shouldn’t, and a small cushion set aside in year one beats a credit card at midnight.
Kitten already shredded the couch? Start here: free furniture in St. Louis
### What should a new kitten’s first week look like?
Small, quiet and a little boring, on purpose. Set up one room before the kitten arrives, with food, water, a litter box, a scratching post, a bed and a couple of toys, and let the kitten live there for the first several days. The APA recommends exactly that for any new cat: one quiet room, something familiar from the shelter, no forced cuddling, indoors only. Open the rest of the house once the kitten is eating, using the box and coming to you on its own. A reasonable shape for week one:
Day 1: Carrier into the room, door open, you on the floor. Let the kitten come out when it’s ready, and keep feeding whatever it ate at the shelter or foster home.
Days 2 and 3: Hiding is normal. Keep play short and use a wand toy. VCA advises toys rather than hands or feet, because a kitten who learns fingers are prey grows into a cat who bites them.
Days 3 to 7: Book the first vet visit and bring the shelter’s paperwork, so the vet can schedule boosters every three to four weeks until about 16 weeks. Rabies and registration are due between three and four months of age in both the City and the County.
All week: Cords, string, rubber bands and hair ties off the floor. Toilet lids down. Check the recliner before you sit. And no lilies in the house; the ASPCA lists them as toxic to cats.
Work full time? Plan a lunch-hour visit for the first few months, since kittens under four months shouldn’t be left alone much more than four hours. Then let the 3-3-3 rule run its course. Some kittens own the place by day two. Others need the whole three months. Bringing home a puppy instead? Dogs get their own version, and our checklist of what to buy for a new puppy explains the 7 7 7 rule.
The best kitten stories in St. Louis tend to start the same way. Somebody skips the laundry-basket post, waits the extra two weeks, and drives to Walnut Place or Macklind Avenue or Baur Boulevard for a kitten that’s already fixed, already chipped and maybe already somebody’s foster success story. Be that person. Then send this page to the next neighbor who posts “free kittens.”
Ready to meet kittens in person? Start with pet adoption services around St. Louis, and ask each one what its fee covers and which kittens are living in foster homes right now.
And if you run a rescue or adoption program, the people reading this are comparing fees, what each fee includes and how to meet a kitten who lives in foster care, so list your adoption program with us with all three spelled out.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the 3-3-3 rule for kittens?
A.  It’s a rule of thumb shelters use for any newly adopted cat: about three days to decompress, three weeks to learn the household routine and three months to feel fully at home. The APA calls week three a make-or-break point, when new behaviors show up and friction with other pets is common. Treat it as a guide, not a deadline.
### Q. Is 12 weeks too old to get a kitten?
A.  No. Twelve weeks is the top of the 8-to-12-week window VCA Animal Hospitals recommends, and the extra weeks with a mother and littermates help. Kittens do get less flexible about new things around then, so start gentle handling, carrier practice and household noise right away. A three- or four-month-old from a St. Louis shelter is still a kitten, and already fixed.
### Q. What is the hardest age for a kitten?
A.  For many households it’s the stretch from about four months to a year. Adult teeth replace baby teeth between roughly three and a half and six months, so everything gets chewed. Energy peaks. And the ASPCA notes that cats can breed before six months, which is how an unspayed female has a litter while still looking like a kitten. Timely spay or neuter, daily play and a sturdy scratching post handle most of it.
### Q. Where can I find free kittens in St. Louis, Mo.?
A.  At shelter fee-waived events, which cluster in summer and fall when cat rooms are full. In 2026 the APA waived all cat and kitten fees July 8 through 10 and scheduled a fee-waived weekend for October 17 and 18 that includes kittens. CARE STL says it often waives its fee, and the County Pet Adoption Center has too, within limits the County Council set in 2025. Dates change every year, so watch each shelter’s site.
### Q. Where’s the best place to get a free kitten?
A.  A shelter’s fee-waived event, because the kitten is free and already spayed or neutered, microchipped and vaccinated. A neighbor’s litter is the other route. If you go that way, meet the mother cat, wait until the kitten is at least eight weeks old, and budget roughly $145 to $215 for the vet work a shelter would already have done.
### Q. Where is the cheapest place to get a kitten?
A.  Among the big five, the St. Louis County Pet Adoption Center on Baur Boulevard has the lowest regular fee at $80, then CARE STL at $100. Adopting two lowers the per-kitten price at Stray Rescue, $200 a pair, and the APA, $300 for two. Stretch the word kitten and the Humane Society of Missouri lets you pick your price, $35 minimum, for cats nine months and older. Check current fees first.
### Q. What disqualifies you from adopting a cat?
A.  Usually the basics. CARE STL, Stray Rescue and the Humane Society of Missouri require adopters to be at least 18, and the APA asks for an ID. Renters at Stray Rescue need written landlord approval, and CARE STL reserves the right to deny any applicant or ask for a home visit. Local limits count too: the City caps a home at four dogs and cats combined, and in unincorporated St. Louis County a sixth cat over four months makes your house a kennel under the zoning code.
### Q. Can I leave my 4 month old kitten alone for 8 hours?
A.  Not routinely, at least not without a midday check. Vet-reviewed guidance says kittens under four months shouldn’t be left much more than four hours, and kittens need three or four meals a day until about six months. For an eight-hour workday, set up a kitten-proofed room with water, litter and toys, and arrange a lunch-hour visit from you, a neighbor or a pet sitter.

## Mobile Dog Grooming in St. Louis: Real Prices, What the Van Carries, Who It Suits
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/mobile-dog-grooming-in-st-louis
The top Google result for mobile dog grooming in St. Louis isn’t a groomer. It’s a machine-written summary of a social media thread, and it tells you full grooms start around $60 and nail trims around $25. Then you start calling vans. Pups Mobile Spa’s published price for a full bath starts at $89, and that’s for its smallest dogs. Furry & Fabulous starts its bath service at $100. Four Pretty Paws says its grooms start at $100. We didn’t find a single St. Louis grooming van that publishes a $60 full groom.
That summary isn’t inventing the number. It’s flattening it. It even says where the number came from: one commenter who charges $60 a dog, and another groomer explaining that all she needs from you is a bathtub, room for a table and an outlet. That’s a real business. It’s also a different business from a 20-foot-plus van that pulls into your driveway carrying its own water, power and air conditioning. Two jobs share one word, and the robot averaged them.
The number that actually sets the price is parked at the curb. Wag’n Tails, an Indiana company that has been building grooming vans since the 1990s, lists two of its current models at about $124,000 and $140,000. Each carries 50 gallons of fresh water and 50 gallons of dirty water. A groomer working alone in one gets through somewhere around six dogs on a full day. One groomer, one dog, one driveway at a time. That’s the whole cost story.
So the real question isn’t whether mobile grooming costs more. It does. The question is whether your dog is the kind of dog that premium was built for. If you’re still sorting out where your dog is welcome around town, start with our guide to dog-friendly places in St. Louis. Every price here comes from a groomer’s or builder’s own page as of October 2026. Prices move, so confirm the current one when you book.
### Is mobile grooming more expensive than regular grooming?
Yes, usually by half again to more than double for the same dog. Published St. Louis menus show van baths starting around $89 to $100, against salon baths that start in the $40s. The premium pays for a self-contained van, the drive to your door and a groomer who works on one dog at a time.
Put one dog through two menus and the gap is plain. Take a 40-pound dog with a long coat, a shih tzu mix, say. At Pups Mobile Spa, which prices by coat type and weight, a bath and blow-dry for that dog is $127 and a full haircut is $159. Silver Maple Pet Center, a West County salon that posts its whole menu, lists a medium bath at $54 to $62 and a medium haircut at $72 to $98. Size tiers never line up perfectly between two businesses, so treat it as a rough match. Still: the van runs about 60% to 120% more for the haircut and roughly double for the bath.
None of that gap buys a better haircut. A good salon groomer and a good van groomer learned the same trade and use the same clippers. What you’re paying for is everything around the haircut. PetSmart says a grooming appointment can last two to four hours, as NerdWallet’s tipping guide reports. Pups Mobile Spa and Four Pretty Paws both say a van groom usually takes one to two. No car ride. No lobby. No kennel row, and no other dog in the room.
The rest of the bill is arithmetic. A salon can work several dogs at once, with bathers, dryers and somebody answering the phone. A van groomer can’t. The grooming expert NerdWallet quotes puts it plainly: mobile groomers can typically care for only one dog at a time, and the price has to cover gas, maintenance, permits and specialized equipment. Spread a $124,000 to $140,000 truck across six dogs a day and a $100 starting price stops looking greedy.
The premium shrinks in exactly one place: a house with more than one dog. The drive costs the groomer the same whether one dog climbs into the van or three do, and some menus show it. Pups Mobile Spa charges $40 for a nail-trim visit for the first dog and $25 for each one after that, and $40 then $20 for a de-shedding brush visit. Ask any van for its multi-dog math before you book.
If a salon turns out to be the better fit, our guide to dog groomer prices in St. Louis covers salon rates, red flags and how often each kind of coat needs a groom.
### What does mobile dog grooming cost in St. Louis?
Plan on about $89 to $241 for a full visit from a St. Louis van, set by your dog’s coat and weight, plus add-ons and condition fees. Nail-only visits start around $40. Doodles, poodles and double-coated shepherds land at the top of the price charts.
Here’s what the vans that publish prices were listing in October 2026:
Pups Mobile Spa, which works a cluster of inner-ring suburbs west and southwest of the city: a bath and blow-dry from $89 for a short-coated dog up to 15 pounds to $190 for a double-coated dog of 61 to 90 pounds, full haircuts from $110 to $241, and a puppy groom at $85 to $105. Its price page breaks every service out by coat type and weight.
Furry & Fabulous, dogs only: a bath from $100, a bath and trim from $110 and a full haircut from $130, with nails, ears and de-shedding folded in, per its services page.
Four Pretty Paws: grooms from $100, priced breed by breed on its site, plus a long-coat fee for coats kept longer than an inch and a convenience fee on credit card payments.
Bark & Mane of West St. Louis: quotes on request through its booking page.
Then come the fees that never make the headline price. Pups Mobile Spa’s menu is unusually candid about them: $25 to $50 to de-mat a coat that has to come off short, $10 to $50 for special handling when a dog needs extra time because of aggression, anxiety or physical limits, $35 to $50 for a tick treatment that ends in a deep sterilization of the van, and a $200 charge if fleas show up unannounced and the rest of the day’s appointments have to be canceled while the van gets fumigated. It also weighs your dog at every visit and adjusts the price if the dog has moved up a tier.
Read that list as a schedule of what goes wrong, priced in advance. That’s useful. A groomer who prices matting up front is a groomer who’s going to tell you the truth about matting.
Coat type moves the price more than size does. At Pups, a bath for a 40-pound short-coated dog is $101. For a 40-pound curly-coated doodle it’s $143. Call it the doodle tax, and it compounds: curly coats mat, mats mean shaving, and shaving means the de-matting fee on top. Regular visits every four to six weeks are what keep a curly coat out of de-matting territory. Pups adds nail buffing and paw balm at no charge for clients who pre-book a full year at six-week intervals or tighter.
What we didn’t find on any of these menus is a separate trip fee. The drive is baked into the price. That can change at the far edge of a route, where a groomer may add a charge or simply say no, so mention it if your house is a long way from the usual stops.
Payment and cancellation rules are cost, too. Four Pretty Paws charges for appointments canceled less than 48 hours ahead, per its FAQ page, and adds a convenience fee to card payments. Put both in the math before the first visit.
### What does a mobile groomer do in the van?
The same work a salon does, in about 20 feet of truck, on one dog. The groomer parks, walks your dog out to the van, bathes, dries, clips and trims it there, then walks it back to your door, usually within one to two hours. The van brings its own water, power, heat and air conditioning, so it needs nothing from your house but a place to park.
Read the spec sheet of a purpose-built van and the price starts making sense. Wag’n Tails’ Supreme Groom Van, built on a Mercedes-Benz Sprinter, runs 22 feet 10 inches long and stands 10 feet tall with its rooftop air conditioner. Inside there’s a one-piece stainless tub big enough for large breeds, a 50-gallon fresh-water tank and a 50-gallon gray-water tank, an electric table that drops to 16 inches off the floor and lifts 250 pounds, and a walk-over bridge so a big dog never gets hoisted from table to tub. A 15,000 BTU air conditioner and a 20,000 BTU propane furnace keep the box comfortable without idling the engine.
Power is where the vans are changing. Older rigs run a generator, and you can hear it from the sidewalk for the whole groom. Newer builds run on lithium battery packs that charge overnight from an ordinary outlet. Wag’n Tails sells its battery system partly on the neighbors, promising no generator noise in the driveway.
Drying is the other big difference. Busy salons often park a wet dog in a kennel dryer so the groomer can start on the next one. Four Pretty Paws says outright that it doesn’t crate or crate-dry at all; its groomers fluff-dry with warm, low-heat air. In a van there’s no next dog waiting. The dog on the table is the only job.
St. Louis weather tests all of it. August is why that rooftop air conditioner exists, and January is why the furnace does. Ice is the one thing a van can’t fix, so book winter appointments expecting a reschedule call on glazed-over mornings.
Parking is the question nobody asks until the van shows up. In Glencoe, out past the Meramec off Route 109, a lot of homes sit back on wooded lots, some at the top of drives that curve, climb or narrow to one lane of gravel. A truck that size, eight feet wide at the mirrors, needs somewhere flat to open its doors, ideally close enough that an old dog doesn’t have to walk far. Describe your drive when you book. A groomer will tell you in about ten seconds whether the street works better.
### Which dogs do better with mobile grooming?
Anxious dogs, seniors, dogs who get carsick, dogs who come apart around other dogs, and households with two or three dogs to do at once. The poorest fits are dogs heavier than the van’s weight limit, dogs one groomer can’t safely handle alone, and any pet that needs sedation to get through a groom.
For a nervous dog, a salon visit stacks the stressors: the car, the lobby, strangers, barking from the kennel row, a long wait for pickup. The van strips out nearly all of them. The only new things are one person and one quiet room parked 30 feet from home. Four Pretty Paws pitches its vans squarely at dogs with separation anxiety, and Pups Mobile Spa asks that an adult stay home and reachable for the whole appointment, so the owner is close by if anything goes sideways.
Seniors may gain the most. Picture a 13-year-old Lab mix in Glencoe whose back legs have given up on car rides. A salon day means lifting her into the car, a drive, a few hours in a building full of noise and another lift at the end. The van means a short walk down the drive, a table that lowers almost to the floor, and her own couch again in under two hours. For that dog it isn’t a luxury. It’s the difference between getting groomed and going without.
Glencoe is on at least one West County route, too. A 2025 local magazine roundup listed it by name among the areas served by the franchise that was then called Aussie Pet Mobile. It now operates as Bark & Mane of West St. Louis and lists the city Glencoe sits inside.
Big dogs are where vans run out of room. Four Pretty Paws grooms dogs up to 89 pounds. Pups Mobile Spa’s price chart stops at 90 pounds for most services. A St. Louis forum thread asked for exactly the job those limits squeeze: a mobile groomer for a 70- to 80-pound German shepherd who just needed a bath and nails. That dog fits, barely, and at Pups a bath for a double-coated dog that size lists at $190. A 120-pound Newfoundland may not fit anywhere. Furry & Fabulous says it runs a larger van for bigger dogs, so ask about the unit, not just the company.
Then there are the dogs who bite. A van holds one groomer and no second pair of hands. Pups Mobile Spa recommends a consult groom first for a highly anxious or reactive dog and says it may end a groom early if the dog can’t be handled safely. Four Pretty Paws doesn’t do sedation grooms. If your dog needs medication to get through a groom, start with your vet, and if even the car ride to the clinic is the problem, there are mobile vets in St. Louis too.
Cats are a narrower yes. Four Pretty Paws takes mild-tempered cats who are used to grooming, already in a carrier when the groomer arrives. Furry & Fabulous doesn’t take cats at all. Our guide to cat grooming in St. Louis covers the rest.
And if your dog is simply dirty, a van may be more than the job needs. A self-serve dog wash in St. Louis costs a fraction of a groom and gets the mud off just fine.
### Which parts of the metro do St. Louis mobile groomers cover?
Mostly the south and west sides of St. Louis County, plus a corridor running into the city. That’s where the published service areas we found cluster. North County barely shows up on any of them, and the Illinois side has fewer vans. Every route is drawn around drive time, so check your ZIP code before you get attached to a groomer.
Here’s how the vans describe their own maps. Four Pretty Paws, grooming since 2018, says it covers south and west St. Louis County, the suburbs across the Missouri River and parts of the city, and it keeps a separate Illinois booking page. The 2025 magazine roundup described Furry & Fabulous’s area as stretching from West County east to the Central West End. Pups Mobile Spa works a cluster of inner-ring suburbs west and southwest of the city and keeps a waitlist for addresses outside it. Bark & Mane of West St. Louis lists West County suburbs.
North County is the gap. None of those descriptions names it, and that matters if you live or work out where I-70 meets the Missouri River. Say your office in Earth City lets dogs come in on Fridays. Four Pretty Paws and Furry & Fabulous both say they’ll groom at a workplace if the van can park safely, and an Earth City business park has exactly the kind of flat, wide lot a van that size wants. What it may not have is a groomer whose route runs past it. Call before you plan around it, and ask whether a stop out there is a regular thing or a favor.
Illinois runs on its own map. Four Pretty Paws began taking new Illinois clients in the fall of 2025 through its own Illinois booking page and a 618 number, with a route through the Metro East suburbs. If you’re in Shiloh, near the air base, ask that line directly whether your subdivision is on it and how often the van comes your way. A Missouri van crossing the river at rush hour for a single house is a hard sell to any groomer. One who already works your side of the river is usually the easier booking.
There’s a reason the maps look this lopsided. A grooming van has no storefront and no sign on a busy road. It lives on a phone number, a ZIP list and word of mouth, one street at a time. Groomers pack appointments close together to save fuel and hours; Four Pretty Paws switched to two-hour booking windows specifically so it can route efficiently. When three houses on a block book the same groomer, that block joins the route. So ask the neighbor whose dog always looks freshly done.
Same no-storefront problem, no van: how coaches get found and booked in St. Louis
### What should you ask a mobile groomer before you book?
Ask about five things: the route, the size limit, the water, the price and the house rules. Those answers sort out most bad fits before the van ever pulls up.
Route. Is my ZIP code a regular stop, and how wide is the arrival window? Four Pretty Paws asks for two hours either side, so plan the day around it.
Size and coat. What’s the weight limit for the van that would come to me, and is there a long-coat or curly-coat surcharge?
Water. Do you carry your own fresh water and power, and where does the gray water get emptied? The right answer is a sanitary sewer drain, never the curb or a storm grate. MSD Project Clear’s rule for the whole district is only rain to the storm drain, and shampoo water isn’t rain.
Price. What’s included, what costs extra, and what’s the cancellation window? Get the matting, handling and flea fees in writing.
House rules. Which vaccines do you require, and do I need to stay home? Pups Mobile Spa asks for current rabies, distemper and parvo shots and an adult on site. Ask about training, too: Furry & Fabulous and Pups both say their groomers are certified in pet first aid and CPR, and Bark & Mane says its groomers hold the American Kennel Club’s S.A.F.E. certification.
Here’s why that list matters more than any review. Missouri doesn’t regulate dog or cat grooming. The state Department of Agriculture says so in plain words on its animal care page, and it steps in only if a groomer starts boarding pets overnight. No state inspector checks a grooming van’s tub, tanks or table. Your questions are the inspection.
You don’t need the cheapest van in St. Louis. You need the one whose route, limits and rules fit your dog, and a ten-minute phone call will tell you which one that is. Be the owner who asked before the van pulled up.
Ready to make those calls? Browse pet groomers around St. Louis on St Louis Near Me Directory and run each one through the five questions above.
And if you run a grooming van, list your mobile grooming business with us and answer the service area, weight limit and gray water questions before the phone rings.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are the disadvantages of mobile pet grooming?
A.  Price first: published St. Louis van menus run half again to more than double a salon’s. Then logistics. Four Pretty Paws asks clients to be available two hours either side of the booked time, Pups Mobile Spa wants an adult home for the whole groom, weight limits sit around 89 to 90 pounds, one groomer works alone, and ice days bring reschedules.
### Q. Are mobile groomers sanitary?
A.  The good ones are, but Missouri won’t check for you, since the state doesn’t regulate dog or cat grooming. Ask how the van is cleaned between dogs and what happens with fleas; Pups Mobile Spa fumigates and closes its van for the rest of the day when it finds them. Ask where the gray water goes, too. In the MSD district, only rain belongs in a storm drain.
### Q. Do mobile dog groomers bring their own water?
A.  Van groomers do. A typical purpose-built van carries about 50 gallons of fresh water, a 50-gallon tank for the dirty water and its own power, so it needs nothing from your house but a parking spot. Some in-home groomers work differently and use your tub and your outlet, so ask which kind you’re booking.
### Q. How much do you tip a $70 dog groomer?
A.  About $10.50 to $14, using the 15% to 20% that etiquette guides commonly cite. Go higher for a matted coat, a difficult dog or a holiday booking. In St. Louis, $70 is usually a salon price. The same dog in a van more often runs $100 to $125, which puts a 15% to 20% tip around $15 to $25.
### Q. What not to say to a dog groomer?
A.  Don’t say he’s fine with strangers if he isn’t, and don’t ask a groomer to save the length on a matted coat, because mats close to the skin usually mean a short cut and a de-matting fee. Don’t keep fleas a secret either. One St. Louis van charges $200 when surprise fleas wipe out the rest of its day.
### Q. Why do groomers squeeze glands?
A.  Because owners ask, and because full anal sacs can make a dog scoot and smell. Most healthy dogs empty them on their own when they poop, VCA Animal Hospitals notes, and a veterinarian writing for groomers warns that squeezing from the outside can irritate a gland that was fine. If your dog keeps scooting, that’s a vet visit; here’s how to choose a vet in St. Louis.
### Q. How much is a mobile dog grooming trailer?
A.  A basic grooming trailer from one Georgia builder starts around $16,000, and loaded ones run $36,000 or more, before the truck that tows it. Purpose-built vans cost far more: new Wag’n Tails models list near $124,000 to $140,000, and its used vans have been listed from about $89,000. Missouri itself doesn’t license groomers, though local business licenses can still apply.
### Q. What does FFF mean in dog grooming?
A.  Face, feet and fanny: a bath plus a tidy trim around the eyes, paws and sanitary area, without a full haircut. Four Pretty Paws sells it as an in-between groom, and Pups Mobile Spa calls it a face, feet and sani trim. In a van it isn’t a bargain. For a curly-coated dog, Pups prices it within about $5 to $15 of a full haircut.

## Self Serve Dog Wash in St. Louis: Raised Tubs From $9.99 and a Pet Bay at a Car Wash
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/self-serve-dog-wash-in-st-louis
Bathtubs weren’t built for dogs. They sit too low for your back, they’re too slick for four paws, and the drain was never meant to swallow a whole shedding season of undercoat. Then the dog shakes. Water on the mirror, hair in the grout, and a pile of wet towels that smells exactly like the thing you were trying to wash off. Most owners do it anyway, every month or two, on their knees.
St. Louis has a better room for this job, and it’s tucked inside places you already drive past: a car wash on Watson Road, a farm store in Jefferson County, a pet shop in Lafayette Square, a row of storefronts on Manchester Road. Walk in with a dirty dog, pay one price, and you get a waist-high tub, warm water, shampoo, towels and a dryer. Somebody else mops. At most of them, the price is the same for a terrier as it is for a Newfoundland.
The hard part is finding them. Search for a dog wash near you and the map lumps full-service groomers, who bathe the dog for you at size-based prices, in with the few places that actually hand you the sprayer. This guide sorts them out: where you can wash your own dog around St. Louis, what it costs as of October 2026, what to bring, and the question that comes before all of it, which is whether your dog needs a bath at all. If you’re still mapping where your dog is welcome around town, start with our guide to dog-friendly places in St. Louis.
### How do you know when your dog needs a bath?
Your dog needs a bath when the smell survives a good brushing, the coat feels greasy or gritty, or there’s mud or something worse in the fur. Most dogs land somewhere between weekly and every three months, the ASPCA’s minimum. If the odor comes back within days, check ears and teeth, then call your vet.
That three-month figure is the ASPCA’s floor: bathe at least once every three months, and more often for a dog who spends a lot of time outdoors or has skin trouble. Coat type moves you from there. The American Kennel Club says oily-coated breeds like Basset Hounds may need a bath as often as once a week, while water-repellent coats like a Golden Retriever’s and thick double coats like a Malamute’s should be washed less often and brushed a lot more. A groomer quoted by the AKC offered the simplest test of all: wash them “when they are no longer huggable.”
The signs are usually obvious once you know where to look:
The smell is still there after a brush-out. Brushing lifts dirt and spreads the coat’s natural oils, so if your hand smells like dog afterward, the coat itself needs washing.
The coat feels tacky, greasy or gritty when you run a palm down the back, or it looks dull and clumped instead of loose.
There’s mud, burrs, pond water or something dead in the fur. That bath doesn’t wait for the schedule.
Somebody in the house is allergic. The AKC notes that owners who react to dander can often manage it with a weekly bath.
St. Louis weather moves the schedule, too. A veterinarian writing for PetMD notes that warm, wet months bring greasier coats, more doggy odor and more fleas and ticks, which is why July baths land closer together than January ones. A dog who swims in a creek or a farm pond needs a rinse in clean water afterward, even if the full shampoo can wait. A wet morning at one of the dog parks in St. Louis can go either way. Winter is a different job. The ASPCA recommends washing paws in warm water after walks to get rock salt and chemical ice melt off before your dog licks it, and that’s a paw rinse in the kitchen sink, not a bath.
One more check before you book a tub. If the smell comes back within a few days of a bath, the coat probably isn’t the source. The ASPCA says to check the ears and teeth first, since both commonly harbor odor-causing bacteria, and to see a veterinarian if your dog smells consistently stinky no matter how you groom. Red skin, scabs, bald patches and nonstop scratching belong at the vet’s office too. If the bill is what’s holding you back, start with our guide to low-cost vet care in St. Louis.
Picture two dogs in one Cottage Hills house. The retriever spends Saturday down in the river bottoms and comes home wearing half of them. That’s a bath today, whatever the calendar says. The short-coated mutt who napped through the same weekend might go two months between baths and smell fine. Same house, different schedules. The coat and the week decide.

### What should you bring to a self-serve dog wash?
A leash, a towel for the car, a pocket of treats, and your own shampoo only if your vet prescribed one. Most St. Louis washes supply everything else, down to the apron.
A leash and a collar or harness you don’t mind soaking. You’ll be walking a slippery dog back through a store or across a parking lot.
An old towel or seat cover for the ride home. Even a good dryer can leave a damp undercoat.
Small, soft treats for the step up into the tub and the first blast of the dryer.
Medicated shampoo, if your vet prescribed it. Four Muddy Paws drops the wash to $12 when you bring your own, Treats Unleashed allows it, and Pet Supplies Plus asks you to bring yours or buy it there. If you need to stock up first, here’s where to buy pet supplies in St. Louis.
Clothes you can get wet. Most places hand you an apron. Your shoes are on their own.
Nothing sharp. Treats Unleashed bans outside equipment and trimming tools, and Four Muddy Paws says no scissors, clippers or sharp tools in the wash area.
Once you’re in, the routine is simple. Brush first: Washington State University’s veterinary teaching hospital points out that wet fur mats more than dry fur and is harder to untangle. Put a cotton ball in each ear, as the ASPCA suggests, wet the dog from the neck back, and wipe the face with a damp cloth instead of spraying it. Rinse until the water runs clear, because leftover shampoo itches. Towel hard, then dry. The AKC’s advice for any blow dryer is to skip the hottest setting and hold it at least a foot from the skin, and Four Muddy Paws lists professional no-heat dryers at its drying station.
One timing trap matters in tick season: topical flea and tick treatments. Frontline’s own guidance is to apply only to a completely dry coat and then wait 48 hours before you bathe, shampoo or let the dog swim. So wash first, dry fully, then treat. Other products have their own windows, so read the label on yours.
### Self-serve wash or full groom: which does your dog need?
A self-serve tub handles washing. It doesn’t handle mats, haircuts, nails on a dog who fights you, or anything that needs scissors, and the places that rent you a tub won’t let you bring clippers anyway.
Book a groomer when the coat needs cutting, when there are tight mats you can’t brush out, or when it’s time for a seasonal shave-down. A PetMD veterinarian notes that groomers have special tools for tight knots and sticky messes like bubblegum, the kind of job a rented tub can’t fix. Doodles and other coats that grow without stopping usually land here too, on a schedule your groomer sets.
Use the tub between grooms. That’s the gap Pamper Your Pooch’s owners say they built for: washing dogs in between groomer visits without wrecking a bathroom. It’s also the right call for the muddy emergency, the heavy shedder in spring, and the dog who’s fine with water but miserable in a kennel. Four Muddy Paws even sells a $20 DIY de-shed treatment for that spring blowout.
There’s a middle option, too. Dirty Dog Wash adds a nail trim to a self-wash for $10 more, so you do the scrubbing and a pro handles the part your dog hates most. Shakers sells a full-service Complete Bath with a nail trim, ear cleaning and a paw trim that takes about 90 minutes, which is shorter than the two-to-four-hour window a big salon quotes.
Some dogs can’t handle a store at all. The noise, the other dogs, the strangers. For that dog, the better answer may be a groomer who comes to the driveway: one dog, one van, no kennel. Our guide to mobile dog grooming in St. Louis walks through what that costs and who it suits.
### How do you bathe a big dog at home without wrecking the bathroom?
Set up before the dog is wet, keep the water shallow and warm, and stop the hair before it reaches the drain. The ASPCA suggests three to four inches of lukewarm water. The AKC says to check that it’s warm, not hot, and to fill it to about knee height.
A detachable shower sprayer makes the job much easier, the AKC says, and a big plastic pitcher works if you don’t have one. Lay a rubber mat or towel in the tub so your dog isn’t scrabbling for footing, and another on the floor for the exit. Put a mesh hair catcher over the drain. Wet dog hair clumps, the same reason the AKC tells owners to vacuum a dog bed before it goes in the washer. Brush the coat out first and less of it ends up in the pipe.
Big dogs bring a lifting problem. Don’t hoist an 80-pound dog over a tub wall if you can help it. A walk-in shower works better for a lot of big dogs, and on a warm St. Louis afternoon a garden hose and a kiddie pool in the yard are fair game, once you’ve let the hose run until the sun-warmed water in it cools down. Dry in a warm room. The AKC suggests letting your dog finish drying somewhere warm and sunny, and a damp dog shouldn’t head out on a January night until the undercoat is dry.
Then there’s the meter. Every home bath runs through your water bill, rinse after rinse, and a thick-coated dog takes a lot of rinsing.
Home baths run the meter: water and sewer bill assistance in St. Louis
Your dog doesn’t care where the bath happens. Your back, your drain and your Saturday do. The owners who’ve figured this out don’t kneel on tile anymore. They know where the tub is.
When the coat needs more than a bath, compare pet groomers around St. Louis before the mats get worse.
And if you run a wash room or a grooming shop, the owners reading this want three things before they load a wet dog into the car: your tub height, whether you take walk-ins and what a big dog costs, so list your dog wash with us with all three spelled out.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it okay to give a dog a bath once a week?
A.  For most healthy dogs, yes, with a gentle shampoo made for dogs. Washington State University’s veterinary teaching hospital says a weekly bath with veterinary shampoo is generally safe, but bathing too often can strip the coat’s protective oils. Oily-coated breeds may genuinely need it weekly. If the skin turns dry or flaky, space the baths out and ask your vet.
### Q. How long can I go without bathing my dog?
A.  The ASPCA’s guideline is at least once every three months. A PetMD veterinarian puts the healthy range anywhere from once a week to a few times a year, depending on the coat and the dog’s life. Brushing carries more of the load than people expect: it lifts dirt, spreads natural oils and shows you fleas early, so a well-brushed dog goes longer between baths.
### Q. What’s the best time to give a dog a bath?
A.  After the dirty part of the day, not before it. Bathe after the hike or the dog park, when there’s time to dry the coat completely before your dog goes back outside, which matters on a cold St. Louis evening. If you use a topical flea treatment, wash first and let the coat dry fully, then wait 48 hours after applying before the next bath, or follow your product’s label.
### Q. How often should a dog bed be cleaned?
A.  Weekly is the standard to aim for. The AKC notes that the CDC and researchers writing in the Canadian Medical Association Journal recommend washing dog bedding weekly to cut the spread of parasites and diseases that pass from pets to people, and that the EPA advises a deep clean every two to three weeks to control fleas. Vacuum off the hair first, then wash on the hottest setting the fabric allows.
### Q. How often should I wash my sheets if my dog sleeps with you?
A.  Every three to four days, according to the Sleep Foundation, which recommends that pace for anyone who lets pets sleep in the bed, compared with about once a week for everyone else. A washable blanket on top of the comforter, just for the dog, catches most of the hair and lets the heavy bedding go a little longer.
### Q. Can I wash my dog at PetSmart?
A.  Not yourself, as a rule.
