PetSmart’s services site sells salon grooming plus a Quick Wash walk-in bath, listed at $29.95, where a salon associate bathes and blow-dries your dog in about 30 minutes while you shop. It excludes doodles and some coat types, and vaccine requirements apply. PetSmart doesn’t advertise self-wash tubs, so for a do-it-yourself bay, use the list above and call ahead.
### Q. Do you need an appointment for a self-serve dog wash?
A.  Usually not. Four Muddy Paws, Shakers, Dirty Dog Wash, Pet Supplies Plus and Tractor Supply all take walk-ins, and Four Muddy Paws says waits usually run under 15 minutes except around holidays. Treats Unleashed asks you to call and book a suite, with a one-day cancellation policy, though its own blog says walk-ins are welcome when a tub is free. Going on a weekend? Call first.
### Q. Can you wash a cat at a self-serve dog wash?
A.  Sometimes. Dirty Dog Wash says its self-wash is open to cats, and Treats Unleashed says its suites work for a brave kitty. Call first anywhere else, bring a harness rather than a collar, and keep the dryer on its lowest setting. A cat who fights water is a job for a groomer who handles cats, not a rented tub.

## Ticks in Missouri: Protecting Your Dog From Lone Star Ticks, Ehrlichia and Seed Tick Swarms
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/ticks-in-missouri-protecting-your-dog
Most tick advice online was written for Connecticut. It warns you about the deer tick, tells you to watch for a bull’s-eye rash, and treats Lyme disease as the whole story. Follow it in St. Louis and you’ll spend the summer guarding your dog against the wrong tick.
Here’s what Missouri found when it actually asked. In a two-year study that began in April 2021, the Missouri Department of Conservation and A.T. Still University had people across the state mail in the ticks they pulled off themselves, their pets and their homes. The mail brought 17,466 usable ticks. Seventy-one percent were lone star ticks. Twenty-six percent were American dog ticks. Blacklegged ticks, the deer tick from all that Connecticut advice, came to 2 percent. And the lone star, the tick that runs this state, has never been shown to transmit the Lyme bacterium. The CDC notes its saliva has been shown to kill it.
So this guide starts from Missouri’s own numbers: which ticks ride home on a St. Louis dog, which months they bite, what they carry for the dog and for you, and which prevention covers the tick that matters here. If your dog lives for trails and patios, our guide to dog-friendly places in St. Louis is the fun half of this story. This is the half that keeps the fun from ending at the vet.
### How bad are the ticks in Missouri?
Bad, and mostly not the kind Lyme-focused advice warns about. Lone star ticks made up 71 percent of the 17,466 ticks Missourians mailed to a state study, and Missouri ranks among the states with the highest ehrlichiosis rates. Activity peaks in June and July, but some life stage bites here nearly year-round.
The study behind that first number went further than a head count. Of the ticks the lab tested for disease-causing bacteria, about 5 percent were positive. Five percent sounds small. Then you count how many ticks one dog brushes past in a June afternoon. Missouri’s Department of Health and Senior Services wrote in a 2024 health advisory that the state is among those with the highest rates of ehrlichiosis and tularemia, both carried by the lone star, and among those with the most alpha-gal syndrome, the tick-bite meat allergy.
Living in the city doesn’t exempt you. Washington University researchers dragging white cloths through the brush at the university’s Tyson Research Center, on the western edge of St. Louis County, reported in 2023 that about one in every 150 lone star ticks in the St. Louis area carries Bourbon virus. The same team says lone stars are most common here from March through October. And the state health department’s own guidance says ticks turn up in neighborhoods and backyards, not only in heavy woods.
So the honest rating is this. Missouri isn’t much of a Lyme state. It’s an ehrlichiosis state, a lone star state, and a state where the tick on your dog matters to everybody on the couch.
### Which ticks live around St. Louis?
Three hard ticks do nearly all the biting here, and a fourth specializes in dogs. MDC’s field guide lists the first three as common statewide. Learn their backs, because that’s where the field marks are.
Lone star tick. The female wears a single white dot in the middle of her back; males have pale streaks or dots around the edge. It’s the most common tick in Missouri, and the CDC says it bites aggressively as a larva, a nymph and an adult. MU Extension’s entomologist adds that it lives in tall grass, weeds and brushy patches as readily as in the woods.
American dog tick. Brown with ornate white mottling on the back, turning gray when a female fills with blood. In the state study it was the tick people most often found inside their homes, many of them in beds, according to KBIA’s reporting on the project.
Blacklegged tick. The deer tick. Black legs, a dark upper body, very small. Present across Missouri but only 2 percent of the state sample, and it’s the one that carries Lyme.
Brown dog tick. The odd one out. MU Extension says it feeds only on dogs and can become an indoor pest once a dog carries it inside, and the CDC notes it can infest homes and kennels. A house that keeps finding ticks in January with no trail walks in the picture should ask the vet about this one.
Size is the trap. MDC describes adults as roughly sesame-seed size, 1/16 to 1/4 inch, and larvae, the so-called seed ticks, as about the size of a poppy seed, with six legs instead of eight. Nymphs aren’t much bigger, and the CDC singles them out as hard to see. On a black Lab, a nymph is a speck of nothing.
Picture a June Saturday on the Katy Trail at Defiance. The trail is crushed limestone, and your dog has no interest in it. He wants the weedy shoulder where the grass meets the trees, and that edge is exactly where ticks wait. MDC’s tick researcher told KBIA that edge areas, where fields meet woods, are the likeliest place for people and animals to pick them up. Ticks don’t jump, fall or fly, the state health department notes. They climb a stem, hang on with their back legs, stretch out the front pair and grab whatever brushes past, usually within three feet of the ground. For you, that’s ankles and knees. For a beagle, that’s the whole dog.
### When is tick season in Missouri?
Officially, spring through fall. Practically, any warm day. MDC says most ticks are most active April through July but can show up nearly any time of year, and MU Extension calls June through September peak season, with numbers topping out around June and July. For a dog owner, the more useful view is which stage is biting when, because the threat changes shape across the calendar.
March and April. Lone star adults and nymphs come out. Washington University’s researchers put the St. Louis lone star season at March through October.
May through July. The peak. Adults and nymphs are out, the grass is tall, and the unmowed edges are where they wait.
Late July through September. Seed tick season. MU Extension says lone star larvae stay active from late summer into early fall. One female lays thousands of eggs, so larvae can carpet a single spot, even a mowed lawn where a fed female dropped off a passing animal.
October and November. MU Extension’s urban entomologist calls fall prime time, because deer, a main tick host, move around during the rut. The CDC says blacklegged adults are most active in fall and early spring.
December through February. Quiet, rarely empty. MU Extension’s line is that ticks have no off-season and come out whenever they sense warmth.
Seed ticks are the late-summer surprise. Say you let the dog run a mown field edge near Dutzow at the end of August and she trots back with what looks like ground pepper on her belly. If the pepper moves, it’s larvae, possibly hundreds. Don’t pick at them one by one in the car. Get her home, wash her, make sure her preventive is current, and call your vet if they’re already attached in numbers. Then deal with yourself. MU Extension says to strip in the laundry room, run the clothes through a hot wash and a high dryer, and shower, because a tick that has already attached won’t rinse off.
Which is why the real question isn’t when to start prevention. It’s whether there’s any month you can safely stop, and in Missouri the people who study ticks for a living keep answering no.
### How do you check a dog for ticks after a walk?
With your fingertips first and your eyes second. Run your fingers slowly over the whole dog, against the lie of the fur, and stop at any bump the size of a seed. Then part the hair and look. The CDC’s pet guidance says to check every day a dog spends time outdoors, and it warns that ticks are hard to spot on long or dark coats. Its diagram of where ticks bite dogs is a good checklist:
In and around the ears, including inside the flap.
Around the eyelids.
Under the collar. Take it off for this.
Under the front legs, in the armpits.
Between the back legs.
Between the toes.
Around and under the tail.
To pull one off, use fine-tipped tweezers or a tick tool. The CDC’s method works on a dog the same as on a person: grab the tick as close to the skin as you can, pull straight up with steady, even pressure, and don’t twist or jerk. Skip the petroleum jelly, the nail polish and the hot match. The CDC says those tricks can agitate the tick and force infected fluid into the bite, Clean the spot, wash your hands, and keep looking, because one tick usually means the dog walked through more.
Then keep the tick. Disposal advice often says to flush it, but MU Extension notes some ticks survive a long time underwater, so drop it in rubbing alcohol or seal it in tape instead. Better yet, use the trick MDC published: tape it to the wall calendar on the day you found it, and toss it if nobody feels sick after ten days or so. MU Extension’s version is an index card with the date and place, kept in a sealed container in the freezer for about six months. If your dog or anyone in the house gets sick later, the vet or doctor knows what bit and when.
Do the check before the dog reaches the couch, not after. After a romp at one of the dog parks in St. Louis with tall-grass edges, or any trail day, two minutes on the porch beats a ten-minute hunt across the bedspread.
Squinting at poppy-seed ticks? Read up on laser eye surgery in St. Louis
### What diseases do Missouri ticks give dogs?
Ehrlichiosis leads. Rocky Mountain spotted fever and anaplasmosis are on the list too, and Lyme is possible but uncommon. That’s close to the reverse of what a New England dog owner frets about.
Missouri’s dogs have the paper trail. A 2003 study in the Journal of Clinical Microbiology carried the blunt title “Predominance of Ehrlichia ewingii in Missouri dogs.” A 2020 analysis of canine blood tests sent in by veterinarians nationwide from 2013 through 2019 found dog exposure to Ehrlichia climbing in Missouri, along with other central and southeastern states. And when a University of Missouri veterinary research poster tallied 18 months of screening tests at the university’s own veterinary hospital, it counted 74 new Ehrlichia positives against 6 for the Lyme bacterium.
The unsettling detail from that same poster: the vast majority of the Ehrlichia-positive dogs showed no obvious signs at all. When dogs do get sick, the Merck Veterinary Manual lists fever, swollen lymph nodes, loss of appetite, low energy, stiffness or reluctance to walk, and, as platelets drop, nosebleeds or easy bruising, often seen on the gums. With E. ewingii, the strain long documented in Missouri dogs, a classic sign is lameness that shifts from one leg to another, along with stiff, swollen joints. A long-term form of ehrlichiosis can also develop, and Merck notes German shepherds are especially prone to it.
Timing fools people. The CDC says signs may not show for 7 to 21 days or longer after the bite, long after you’ve forgotten which walk it was. That’s the other reason to keep the taped tick. Diagnosis takes a blood test, and treatment is usually a course of antibiotics. One common in-clinic screening test checks a single blood sample for heartworm plus Ehrlichia, Anaplasma and the Lyme bacterium, so ask whether your dog’s yearly heartworm test is that combined version.
Rocky Mountain spotted fever, which MU Extension says is spread in Missouri mainly by American dog ticks and lone stars, sickens dogs as well as people. Lyme is the one to keep in proportion. Missouri’s health department describes Lyme risk as concentrated in the Northeast and upper Midwest, and in the MDC study the Lyme bacterium and anaplasmosis together turned up in about 3 percent of the blacklegged ticks tested. Possible, then. Not the main event. Merck’s manual adds a point to tape to the fridge: a dog diagnosed with a tick disease is proof the infected ticks live where you walk.
### What can the ticks your dog brings home do to you and your cat?
Your dog is the shuttle bus. The CDC’s pet page puts it simply: pets carry ticks from outside to inside, where those ticks may bite people. The study’s finding that American dog ticks turned up most often in homes, many in beds, is what that looks like in a real house. Missouri’s health department also lists dogs, along with deer and small rodents, among the reservoirs for ehrlichiosis.
Here’s what the household is up against, drawn from the state’s own list of tickborne illnesses reported in Missouri:
Ehrlichiosis. Fever, headache and aches, usually 7 to 14 days after a bite. The state health department puts the fatality rate around 2 percent and flags people 40 and older as higher risk. Doxycycline treats it, which is why telling your doctor about the tick matters.
Rocky Mountain spotted fever and tularemia. Both reported in Missouri, both carried by ticks that are common here.
Heartland virus. First found in Missouri in 2009 and spread mainly by lone stars. The CDC says there’s no vaccine and no medicine for it.
Bourbon virus. Named for the Kansas county where it was identified in 2014. In 2017 a woman admitted to Barnes-Jewish Hospital in St. Louis died of it. When Washington University later tested blood from 1,500 St. Louis-area residents, five carried antibodies, a sign that milder infections slip by unnoticed.
Alpha-gal syndrome. A lone star bite can leave some people allergic to red meat and other mammal products, with reactions that typically arrive two to six hours after eating and range from hives to anaphylaxis.
STARI. A red, expanding rash around a lone star bite that sometimes looks like a bull’s-eye. The CDC says it closely resembles the Lyme rash but isn’t caused by the Lyme bacterium, so a bull’s-eye in Missouri doesn’t automatically mean Lyme.
None of that is a reason to keep the dog off the trail. It’s a reason to treat the dog’s tick prevention as a household health decision, and to mention the dog’s ticks if anyone at home runs a fever or grows a rash within a few weeks.
Then there’s the cat. Cytauxzoonosis, better known as bobcat fever, spreads through lone star ticks that have fed on bobcats, and it was first described by professors at the University of Missouri. An MU small-animal internist told KBIA it’s nearly 100 percent fatal in house cats without treatment, and even intensive treatment saves only up to about 60 percent. A veterinarian in the same story warned about hitchhiker ticks carried in by the family dog, and the story cites research showing transmission can take up to 36 hours. Your daily dog check protects the cat, too.
One more cat rule, and it trips up people who mean well. Some dog spot-ons contain permethrin, and the American Association of Feline Practitioners warns it can poison cats: dog products typically run 45 to 60 percent permethrin, cat-safe ones under 0.1 percent, and cats have been sickened just by grooming a freshly treated dog. In a house with a cat, tell your vet before you pick a product, and never put a dog product on a cat.
### What tick prevention works for Missouri dogs, and what does it cost?
A veterinary tick product, given on schedule, plus the daily check. The CDC’s position is blunt: dogs are very susceptible to tick bites and tick diseases, vaccines don’t exist for most of those diseases, and no vaccine stops a dog from carrying ticks indoors, so use a tick preventive. Your vet’s job is matching the product to your dog. Yours is never missing a dose.
The main options, as you’ll hear them at the clinic:
Oral chews. Most current prescription tick chews belong to the isoxazoline class, whose active ingredients end in -laner: afoxolaner, fluralaner, sarolaner, lotilaner. Some are monthly, some last longer, and several fold heartworm prevention into the same chew.
Collars. A long-lasting choice for dogs that won’t take a chew. Read the label for which ticks it covers and for how long, and follow its fitting instructions to the letter.
Topical spot-ons. Applied to the skin between the shoulder blades. This is the category where the permethrin products live, so it’s the one to steer around in a house with cats unless your vet signs off.
The Lyme vaccine. The only vaccine for a tickborne disease in dogs, per the CDC. With Missouri’s low Lyme risk, it’s a question to ask your vet rather than a default, and it matters more for a dog that travels to Lyme country. Planning a new puppy’s first year? Our guide to puppy shots in St. Louis covers the core schedule.
Now the Missouri-specific question almost nobody asks at the counter: does this product’s label cover lone star ticks, and for how long? Labels name the tick species they’re approved against, and the timing isn’t always equal. Fluralaner chews, sold as Bravecto, are labeled to kill blacklegged, American dog and brown dog ticks for 12 weeks, but lone star ticks for 8. The maker’s once-a-year fluralaner injection covers most ticks for 12 months and lone stars for 8. In a state where seven of every ten ticks are lone stars, that line in the fine print decides when the next dose is really due.
Ask about side effects, too, and speak up if your dog has ever had a seizure. The FDA considers isoxazoline products safe and effective and says most dogs and cats have no neurologic reactions, but it has warned that some animals have had muscle tremors, loss of coordination and seizures, including animals with no seizure history.
On cost, expect the price to depend on the product and your dog’s weight band, so a 75-pound dog costs more per dose than a 15-pound one. As one published reference point, a national nonprofit clinic network lists $17 for a single monthly flea and tick dose and $22 for a combined flea, tick and heartworm dose. St. Louis clinics, online pharmacies and stores set their own prices, and every one of those numbers changes, so ask for a 12-month total at your dog’s exact weight and check it against the clinic’s online pharmacy and any manufacturer rebate. If the total is what’s stopping you, start with low-cost vet care in St. Louis. If you’re still picking a practice, the questions in our guide on how to choose a vet in St. Louis apply here word for word.
### How do you make your yard and weekend spots less tick-friendly?
Take away the shade and the leaf litter. MDC notes that ticks avoid bare ground and prefer leaf litter, and it points landowners toward mowing, landscaping and, on bigger properties, prescribed burning. MU Extension adds the reason: ticks dry out easily and keep retreating to the base of plants to stay moist. On a city or suburban lot, that comes down to a few habits.
Keep the grass short where the dog actually goes, especially along the fence line.
Rake leaves and cut back brush at the edges, where lawn meets trees.
Give the dog an open, sunny route to the spots he uses every day.
Don’t feed wildlife near the house. Deer are a main tick host, and Washington University’s virologist ties new urban green space to the deer and coyotes that bring ticks with them.
Spraying the whole yard is the step MU Extension is least excited about. Its tick guide calls chemical control in yards usually not recommended and only marginally effective, and if you try it anyway, the label has to list ticks on lawns and kids and pets stay off until it dries. The dog’s own preventive goes everywhere the dog goes. A sprayed lawn doesn’t.
Weekends away need their own plan. Picture an October weekend at a lake cabin in Innsbrook: leaves down, deer moving through the woods at dusk, a dog delighted by all of it. That’s fall tick season in full swing, right when most owners have mentally closed the season. Pack the tweezers and an index card, keep the preventive on schedule, and do the porch check before the dog goes in for the night. If you’re still deciding where to take him, our guide to dog-friendly getaways from St. Louis can help you choose. This checklist goes either way.
The dog doesn’t know any of this. He knows the grass at the edge of the trail smells incredible. Knowing which tick is on him, and what it carries, is your half of the deal. Start tonight, with your fingertips, before he finds the bed.
When you’re ready to pick a clinic, or want a second opinion on a dog that seems off after a tick bite, start with veterinarians around St. Louis and ask each one which products cover lone star ticks and what a year costs at your dog’s weight.
And if you run a veterinary practice, the owners reading this are about to ask which preventives you stock, whether your yearly heartworm test also screens for Ehrlichia, and what a year of protection costs by weight, so list your clinic with us with those answers up front.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Does Missouri have deer ticks?
A.  Yes. The blacklegged tick, the deer tick, lives statewide, and MDC counts it among Missouri’s common ticks. It just isn’t the main one. In the state’s two-year mail-in study it made up only 2 percent of 17,466 ticks, against 71 percent lone stars. The CDC says adults of this species are most active in fall and early spring, so October and March walks count.
### Q. Which ticks usually carry Lyme disease?
A.  Blacklegged ticks: Ixodes scapularis in the eastern United States and the western blacklegged tick along the Pacific Coast, per the CDC. Lone star, American dog and brown dog ticks can’t transmit the Lyme bacterium. The CDC also says an infected tick generally has to stay attached more than 24 hours to pass Lyme on, which is one more argument for the nightly check.
### Q. What’s the worst month for ticks?
A.  In Missouri, June and July, according to MU Extension, inside a peak season that runs June through September. MDC puts most activity from April through July. Lone star larvae, the seed ticks, then swarm from late summer into early fall, and fall brings another push as deer move during the rut. No month is truly safe; MU Extension says ticks have no off-season.
### Q. What kills ticks immediately?
A.  For a tick you’ve already pulled off, rubbing alcohol: the CDC lists dropping it in alcohol as a disposal method, and MU Extension suggests wiping crawling seed ticks off skin with an alcohol-soaked cotton ball before they attach. On clothing and gear, Missouri’s health department says permethrin kills ticks. Don’t bother crushing one. The shell is tough, and MU Extension warns crushing can expose you to its fluids.
### Q. What smell do ticks hate most?
A.  No scent works like magic, but the closest real answer is grapefruit. Nootkatone, the compound behind grapefruit’s smell, was developed by the CDC and registered by the EPA in 2020 as an ingredient that repels and kills ticks. For people, MU Extension calls DEET, picaridin and oil of lemon eucalyptus effective. For dogs, skip homemade essential-oil sprays: Pet Poison Helpline says tea tree oil is the most common essential-oil poisoning it sees in dogs, and pennyroyal can cause liver failure.
### Q. What is a ticks worst enemy?
A.  Probably not the opossum. The popular claim that opossums eat thousands of ticks traces back to a 2009 lab study of five captive animals. When researchers in central Illinois examined the stomach contents of 32 wild opossums for a 2021 study, they found no tick parts at all. A tick’s real enemies are bare, sunny ground, which it avoids because it dries out, and an owner who checks the dog daily and never skips a dose.
### Q. Do dogs need tick prevention in winter in Missouri?
A.  Usually, yes. MDC says ticks can turn up nearly any time of year, MU Extension says they come out whenever they sense warmth, and the brown dog tick can live indoors. Stopping in November and restarting in spring leaves gaps, so ask your vet whether year-round dosing makes sense for your dog.
### Q. Can my dog give me a tick-borne disease?
A.  Not by itself. For Lyme, the CDC says there’s no evidence dogs or cats pass the infection straight to their owners. The route is the tick: a dog carries unattached ticks inside, and those can crawl off and bite people. A current preventive and a daily check protect the whole household.

## Where to Buy Pet Supplies in St. Louis: Local Stores, Autoship Math and the 13th Free Bag
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/where-to-buy-pet-supplies-in-st-louis
Thirty-five percent off. It’s on the autoship banner at Chewy, at PetSmart and at Petco, and it’s the number that sells a lot of people on pet food delivery. Read the terms and the number shrinks. All three cap that first-order discount at $20, so the full 35 percent only holds up to a cart of about $57. After the first box, Chewy and PetSmart both drop the discount to 5 percent from then on.
Now walk into a locally owned pet shop and ask the question almost nobody asks at the register: do you punch a frequent buyer card on this food? On a lot of premium brands the answer is yes. Buy 12 bags, take the 13th home free, and you’ve knocked about 7.7 percent off every bag you carry out. That beats the 5 percent. And it comes from the store that lets your dog try on the harness before you pay for it.
The star-rating lists that rank pet stores never show you that math. This guide does: where St. Louis’s independent stores actually are, how big box, online and local stack up on the bag you buy every month, what the tax takes on each side of the river, and which stores wash dogs, host adoptions or bring in a vaccine clinic. Every program and price below comes from the company’s own page or filing as of October 2026, and any of them can change, so check the current terms before you commit to a 30-pound bag. If you’re also figuring out where the dog is welcome once the shopping’s done, start with our guide to dog-friendly places in St. Louis.
### Where’s the cheapest place to buy pet supplies?
It depends on what you’re buying, so compare price per pound, not price per bag. For food you buy every month, the discount you stack matters most: online autoship takes 5 percent off after the first order, while many St. Louis independents punch a buy-12-get-1-free card worth about 7.7 percent on brands that carry one.
Start with the division, because bag sizes aren’t built to make it easy. Two bags of the same food in different sizes can sit side by side at prices that look close, and the only number that matters is the one you get by dividing price by pounds. Do it on your phone. Then go one step further and figure cost per day. The feeding chart on the back tells you how many cups your dog needs, and a denser food that calls for fewer cups can cost less per day even when it costs more per pound.
Next, look at who makes the food. Plenty of premium brands publish a minimum advertised price policy. Canidae posts its own on its website, and it applies to internet and brick-and-mortar sellers alike. That’s a big reason the same premium bag so often shows up at nearly the same sticker price in a neighborhood shop, a big-box store and a website. When the stickers match, no store wins on price. The program stacked on top of the price does.
Canidae’s policy even explains the online number. Retailers running a subscription or automatic-reorder program may advertise Canidae food up to 5 percent below its minimum advertised price, and no lower. So when an autoship page promises 5 percent off, that figure isn’t generosity. On brands with rules like this one, it’s the ceiling. The policy covers advertised prices only, so the total in your cart can still differ.
Store brands play by different rules. A warehouse club’s or a grocery chain’s house-label kibble isn’t sold anywhere else, so the only fair comparison is per pound and per daily serving, against whatever else your vet is comfortable with. For a lot of healthy adult dogs, that’s a perfectly good answer.
Then your household changes the answer. Picture two 70-pound dogs in Cahokia Heights working through a big bag every couple of weeks. That’s more than 20 bags a year, enough to fill a buy-12-get-1 card well inside any deadline, so the free bag works like a second discount layered on the shelf price. A single cat in South Roxana eating one small bag every six weeks is a different problem. Twelve bags takes that cat about 17 months, and some cards expire at 12. For that household the card might never pay out, and autoship’s steady 5 percent is the surer thing.
### Where are St. Louis’s independent pet stores?
In the city, look in Lafayette Square, the Central West End and on The Hill. In the county, look along Manchester Road and Olive Boulevard. Farther out, a homegrown chain and a couple of national brands with local storefronts fill in the map. Here’s what each store we verified publishes about itself as of October 2026. Hours shift, so call before you drive.
Four Muddy Paws, 1711 Park Avenue in Lafayette Square. Founded in 2004 and in its early-1900s building since 2007, it sells natural food and offers grooming across three connected storefronts. Longtime manager Stephanie Windsor and her husband, Jesse, took over as owners in 2025, according to a pet trade magazine’s report on the ownership change.
The Healthy Pet House, 7316 Manchester Road. The store says it was formerly known as Airedale Antics, cites more than 25 years in pet education, and offers grooming and nutritional counseling next to the shelves.
Wolfgang’s Pet Stop, 328 North Euclid in the Central West End. Family owned since 2004 and, in its own words, never a franchise. Grooming, daycare and small-group training classes run alongside the store, which posts weekday hours of 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.
Treats Unleashed, a St. Louis-grown chain that started in 2002 baking apple cinnamon treats. Its locations page lists 15 St. Louis-area stores, from 22 North Euclid in the Central West End out to the far western suburbs. Every one of them lists grooming and a self-serve dog wash, and the treats and pet cakes are made from scratch in the shops.
Ciao Chow, 1923 Marconi Avenue on The Hill. A small shop selling food, toys and treats that says it specializes in enrichment, nutrition and its own homemade bakery items and bandanas.
EarthWise Pet, 12730 Olive Boulevard in west St. Louis County. It belongs to a national family of pet store brands. This one lists grooming plus a self-wash with waist-high tubs, ramps or steps and air dryers, and the brand says its nutrition consultations are free in most cases.
Pet Supplies Plus, a national brand with a local twist. The store on Manchester Road near Sappington Road names its owners on its store page, calls itself locally owned and operated, and lists about 40 natural food brands, a grooming department and a self-serve wash. Two more Pet Supplies Plus stores, in the Oakville Shopping Center and Southfield Center, show up on Fromm’s store finder.
That store finder is a shortcut most shoppers never think to use. Fromm describes the St. Louis shops that carry its food as independent and locally owned, and lists five: Four Muddy Paws, The Healthy Pet House, Treats Unleashed’s Central West End store and those two Pet Supplies Plus locations. It doesn’t rank anybody by stars. It just tells you who stocks the bag, which was the question you had in the first place.
Shopping for fish, reptiles or the crickets that feed them? That’s a specialty trade with its own rules, and we cover it in our guide to fish and reptile stores in St. Louis.
### Big box, independent or online: where does food cost less?
On the sticker, often nowhere in particular. Premium foods tend to list close to the same price everywhere, and store brands only exist in one chain. What separates the three is what gets stacked on top of the sticker, and what shipping, delivery fees and your own gas add back.
Online’s strength is the subscription. Chewy and PetSmart each publish the same structure: 35 percent off your first Autoship order up to $20, then 5 percent off future orders, with free shipping at $49. Petco advertises the same 35 percent first-order discount with the same $20 cap, and its Autoship page says customers can use that first-order discount twice a year. Near carbon copies. When three rivals run the same offer, the discount clearly isn’t where they’re competing.
Big box’s strength is range on a single trip: the giant bag, the store brand, the cheap tennis balls, and at some stores an adoption room or a vaccine clinic on the right day. More on those below.
The independent’s strength is the card, plus everything that can’t ride in a box: somebody who will talk you out of the wrong food, a trial-size bag, a return made across a counter. Those frequent buyer cards are usually run by the food makers, not the store, and the fine print matters. The terms one St. Louis chain posts cover cards for Fromm, Farmina, Stella & Chewy’s, Ziwi, Taste of the Wild and others. Most say all purchases must happen at the same store or chain, most are valid in store only, Ziwi’s is limited to local pet food stores and independent chains, and Taste of the Wild’s to the maker’s approved retailers. A bag bought from a national website won’t count toward a card you’re filling at a local shop.
### How does autoship math compare with a frequent buyer card?
Per bag, over the long run, the card wins: about 7.7 percent against 5. In the first year online actually comes out ahead, because the $20 welcome discount lands on day one and the free bag doesn’t arrive until month 13. Over time, a local store that offers both autoship and the card beats either one alone. Here’s the arithmetic.
Say your dog eats one $60 bag a month, before tax. Three ways to buy a year of it:
Online autoship on Chewy or PetSmart terms. The first order’s 35 percent would be $21, so the $20 cap kicks in. The next 11 bags save $3 each. Year one: $53 saved. Every year after: $36.
A local buy-12-get-1 card. Twelve bags cost $720 and the 13th goes home for just its sales tax. That’s $60 saved per 13 bags, about 7.7 percent, or roughly $55 a year once you’re in the rhythm. The catch is timing. The first free bag doesn’t show up until month 13.
Local autoship plus the card. Treats Unleashed posts 5 percent off every autoship order and says local-delivery autoship still counts toward its buy-12-get-1 program, with a 30 percent first-order code on top. Stack 5 percent on 12 bags ($36) with the free 13th ($60) and you land near $96 saved per 13 bags, about 12 percent.
Then subtract the friction. Treats Unleashed delivers the same day on orders placed before noon, free over $75 and $9.99 below that, with a $25 minimum. One $60 bag on local delivery pays the fee, and $9.99 wipes out most of a month’s savings. Add a second item to clear $75, or grab it curbside. Its posted terms also say ground-shipped subscriptions don’t count toward the free bag, and that redeeming the 13th bag through autoship takes an additional purchase.
Distance is the last variable. A dog owner in Hartford should check whether a Missouri store’s delivery zone reaches across the river before counting on doorstep delivery, and Treats Unleashed’s delivery page has a ZIP code checker for exactly that question. If the zone stops at the river, the math tilts back toward a website with free shipping at $49, or toward one big in-person run that fills the card faster.
Notice which number mattered least over time: the 35 percent. It’s a one-time $20 at most. The percentage you pay on bag 30, bag 60 and bag 90 is the number that decides where your money goes.
### Is pet food taxed like groceries in Missouri and Illinois?
No, on either side of the river. Missouri’s reduced 1.225 percent state rate covers only food that SNAP can buy, and SNAP can’t buy pet food, so kibble pays the full 4.225 percent state rate plus local tax. Illinois taxes pet food as general merchandise, at 6.25 percent plus local.
The Missouri rule comes straight from the Department of Revenue: the 3-point reduction applies to food items that may be purchased with food stamps, and the USDA’s SNAP list puts pet foods under the nonfood items households can’t buy. On a $60 bag, the state share alone is about $2.54. At the grocery rate it would be about 74 cents. Twelve bags a year, and that gap tops $21 before any local tax. Our guide to pet food pantries in St. Louis covers what that same SNAP rule means for families who need help feeding a pet.
Illinois made the contrast sharper this year. Since January 1, 2026, the state charges no state sales tax on groceries, though cities and counties can add 1 percent by ordinance, and the Department of Revenue defines groceries as food for human consumption. So in a Cahokia Heights checkout lane, the family’s cereal may carry a 1 percent local grocery tax while the dog’s food in the same cart pays the 6.25 percent state rate plus local tax.
Buying online doesn’t dodge it anymore. Since January 1, 2023, Missouri has required out-of-state sellers with more than $100,000 a year in Missouri sales to collect its tax on orders shipped in, and the big pet sites clear that bar without trying. Check the tax line on your next receipt.
And the free 13th bag isn’t tax-free. Most of the frequent buyer terms we read say the customer pays the sales tax on the free item at redemption. Budget a few dollars for bag 13.
### Which St. Louis pet stores run adoption days, washes or vaccine clinics?
More of them than most people realize, though rarely every day. Some chain stores keep standing adoption rooms, most of the independents above run self-serve washes, and vaccine clinics rotate through partner stores on a schedule. Check the calendar before you load the car.
Adoptions first. PetSmart Charities says more than 1,600 PetSmart stores have Everyday Adoption Centers, where local animal welfare groups host adoptions, and that more than 11 million pets have found homes through the program. Locally, Stray Haven Rescue, a volunteer-run, foster-based cat rescue, lists two in-store adoption centers: the Petco at MacKenzie Pointe, at Watson and MacKenzie, and the South County PetSmart at Lemay Ferry and I-270. You can meet cats there, but each adoption runs through the cat’s foster, so send the application before you fall in love at the glass. The rescue asks for at least 3 to 5 days for a reply, and adopters must be 21 or older.
Independents host events on their own rhythm. Treats Unleashed’s calendar page promises free samples, pet adoptions and parties, but its October 2026 listings were a pumpkin spice goat milk tasting, a 25 percent off chew sale and a Halloween costume party, so read the month you’re actually shopping. The Pet Supplies Plus on Manchester lists Saturday afternoon events from late October through mid-December.
Washes are the easy win. Treats Unleashed charges $20 per pet for its self-serve wash, which covers shampoo, conditioner, ear wash, a dryer, towels, brushes and an apron, and the staff cleans the tub after you. It has a 24-hour cancellation policy, so book it like an appointment. EarthWise Pet’s west County store lists waist-high tubs and air dryers, and the Pet Supplies Plus on Manchester lists a self-serve wash too. For a dog who just needs the mud off, a $20 bath you do yourself beats paying for a full groom. Our guide to self-serve dog washes in St. Louis covers the rest of the map.
Vaccine clinics are the sleeper. VIP Petcare runs preventive clinics inside partner stores, including Tractor Supply and Pet Supplies Plus, for vaccines, microchips and testing, with upfront pricing and no appointment needed. It says plainly that it isn’t an emergency clinic. Tractor Supply bought VIP Petcare from PetIQ on May 28, 2026, according to its SEC filing. Clinic days rotate, so look up the store nearest you on VIP Petcare’s site before you go, and if it’s a new puppy, line the visits up with our guide to puppy shots in St. Louis.
One more service most shoppers walk right past. The Pet Supplies Plus on Manchester says it accepts flexible plastic pet food and treat bags from every brand, for every species, bought from any retailer. Call first, since programs like that change.
### What should you buy local?
Anything that has to fit, anything you need today, anything frozen, and any food you’re not sure about yet. The heavy, boring repeat purchase your pet already eats happily is the one that travels well in a delivery box.
Fit first. A harness bought online is a guess about your dog’s chest. Bought in a store, it’s a fitting, and a wrong size goes back across the counter instead of into a return box. If you’re outfitting a new puppy, that whole first-week list lives in our guide to what to buy at a pet store for a new puppy. This page is about where the money goes after that.
Then the food you haven’t committed to. The frequent buyer terms quoted above keep excluding trial sizes, which tells you something handy: the makers produce trial-size bags. Ask for one before you buy 25 pounds of a food your dog might refuse, and ask whether the store takes back an opened bag if it goes badly.
Sample-before-you-buy, human edition: what to buy at a cheese shop in St. Louis
Frozen and raw diets belong in your freezer within the hour. Treats Unleashed delivers frozen food but recommends having someone home to take it, and says it isn’t responsible for frozen items that spoil after sitting out. On a St. Louis porch in July, that’s not a technicality. Buy frozen in person, with a cooler in the trunk.
Advice is the last reason, and the one that saves the most. The Healthy Pet House lists nutritional counseling, and EarthWise Pet advertises consultations with pet dietitians. One conversation that stops you from buying three wrong bags in a row is worth more than any 5 percent.
The banner wants you to remember 35 percent. You’ll remember the $20 cap, the 13th bag and the tax line instead, and that makes you the one in your house who knows what the dog food really costs.
Comparing shelves near you? Browse pet stores around St. Louis, then call two of them with the exact bag you buy and ask three things: the price, whether they punch a frequent buyer card on it, and when that card expires.
And if you run a pet store, those are the questions your next regular is about to ask, so list your pet store with us with your card brands, wash hours and clinic days spelled out.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the cheapest pet supply store?
A.  No single store wins every cart, so be wary of anyone who names one. Premium foods often carry nearly identical sticker prices everywhere because many makers set minimum advertised prices, which means a frequent buyer card or an autoship discount usually decides it. Store-brand kibble can only be compared per pound and per daily serving. Price your exact bag at two or three stores and one website, with tax and shipping included.
### Q. What is the cheapest pet shop?
A.  For supplies, it’s the shop whose programs fit how you buy: a frequent buyer card on your brand, trial-size bags before you commit, and a $20 self-serve wash when a bath is all your dog needs. If you mean the animal itself, a rescue’s adoption fee is usually lower than a pet shop’s price and often covers vaccines and spay or neuter surgery, so ask what’s included before you compare.
### Q. How to save money on dog supplies?
A.  Divide price by pounds, then figure cost per day from the feeding chart. Put the food you’ll buy for years on a frequent buyer card or autoship, and watch the card’s deadline. Don’t pay a delivery fee on a single bag. Wash at a self-serve tub between grooms. And if the budget itself is the problem, St. Louis pet food pantries hand out dog and cat food to families who qualify.
### Q. What is the cheapest online pet store?
A.  It changes daily, so compare carts, not logos. Chewy and PetSmart publish the same autoship terms, 35 percent off the first order up to $20 and then 5 percent, and both list free shipping at $49. Petco advertises the same capped first-order discount and says you can use it twice a year. Put your exact bag in each cart, add Missouri or Illinois tax, and include local stores that deliver.
### Q. What is the most popular pet store?
A.  By reach, the national chains. Chewy reported 21.3 million active customers for its 2025 fiscal year, and PetSmart Charities says more than 1,600 PetSmart stores host adoption centers. Popular isn’t the same as right for your pet, though. Around St. Louis, the homegrown chain with storefronts across the metro is Treats Unleashed, with 15 area stores on its own list, alongside single-store independents in Lafayette Square and the Central West End.
### Q. Why is Chewy so cheap?
A.  Part of the answer is in its own numbers. Autoship customers accounted for $10.5 billion of Chewy’s $12.6 billion in fiscal 2025 net sales, 83.3 percent, according to its March 2026 earnings release. Repeat orders that predictable let a seller without a chain of retail stores plan inventory and shipping at enormous scale. Cheap isn’t automatic, though. Many premium brands keep advertised prices close everywhere, and the ongoing autoship discount is 5 percent.
### Q. Do pet stores take back empty pet food bags?
A.  Some do. The Pet Supplies Plus on Manchester Road near Sappington Road says it accepts flexible plastic pet food and treat bags from all brands, for all species, purchased from any retailer. Programs vary by store and change without much notice, so call your nearest store before you save up a trunkful.
### Q. Is pet food cheaper in Illinois or Missouri?
A.  The shelf price doesn’t care about the river, but the tax does. Missouri taxes pet food at its full 4.225 percent state rate and Illinois at its 6.25 percent general merchandise rate, and local taxes on both sides add more and vary by address. On a $60 bag, the state share alone is about $2.54 in Missouri and $3.75 in Illinois. Check the combined rate at the store you actually use.

## Is Pet Insurance Worth It in St. Louis? The $1,321 ER Night Test
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/is-pet-insurance-worth-it-in-st-louis
The most popular advice about pet insurance fits in one sentence: skip it, put the premium in a savings account, and pay the vet yourself. It sounds responsible. It’s half right, and the half it gets wrong is the expensive half, because a savings account starts at zero on the day you open it, and any policy you buy after your pet’s first diagnosis will exclude that diagnosis for good.
So start with the number that actually decides this in St. Louis. One rough night at an emergency vet, for a dog that needs an exam, bloodwork, an ultrasound and an overnight stay, comes to about $1,321 on published averages. That’s more than 13 months of setting aside $100. It’s also about 19 months of the average accident-and-illness premium for a dog in the U.S. Which of those you’d rather have in hand at 2 a.m. is the whole question.
This guide runs the math both ways: what a policy costs in Missouri, how a claim actually pays out, what policies leave out, and the timing trap that makes “save first, insure later” the priciest plan of all. It also covers the part almost nobody mentions. Missouri has no pet-insurance law of its own, so the fine print is your only protection. Every figure here comes from an industry report, a veterinary group or a published cost survey as of October 2026, and premiums move every year, so check current quotes before you buy. And if your dog goes everywhere you go, from patios to trailheads on our list of dog-friendly places in St. Louis, count every outing as one more chance at a cut paw or a swallowed corncob.
### Should I get pet insurance or just put money aside?
If a $1,300 vet bill tomorrow would mean a credit card you can’t pay off, get insurance and save on the side. A savings fund starts empty, and anything diagnosed before you buy a policy is excluded as pre-existing. Owners with several thousand dollars set aside just for the pet can reasonably skip it.
Savings handle the predictable side of owning a pet very well. Vaccines. A dental cleaning. The flea and heartworm prevention you buy every month, and an ear infection now and then. Those are bills you can see coming, and paying a premium so an insurer can hand part of it back to you, minus its costs, is a poor trade. Insurance earns its keep on the other kind of bill: the one that arrives all at once, at night, with four digits on it.
The trouble with saving instead comes down to speed and timing. Speed first. Put $100 a month into a pet fund and it takes more than a year to cover one rough ER night, and a torn knee ligament, at a national average of $3,525 per knee for the surgery, would take you nearly three years. Your dog doesn’t know the fund is still filling up.
Timing is worse. Pet insurers exclude pre-existing conditions, meaning anything a vet advised on, treated, or noted signs of before the policy began. So the household that plans to save now and buy coverage later is really planning to insure everything except whatever shows up first. And whatever shows up first, allergies or a bad knee or a thyroid problem, is often the thing that keeps showing up.
Insurance has an honest catch too. Across all customers, it pays back less than it takes in. NAPHIA, the industry’s trade group, counted about $3.07 billion in U.S. claims paid in 2024 against $4.74 billion in premium, which works out to roughly 65 cents back for every premium dollar. The rest covers the insurer’s costs and profit. Think of the premium as the price of handing your unluckiest year to somebody else.
Here’s where we land. For most St. Louis households, the strongest setup is both: an accident-and-illness policy with a deductible high enough to keep the premium down, plus a small fund that covers that deductible and the routine stuff. If you already have several thousand dollars set aside for the pet, and you’d spend it on a surgery without losing sleep, self-insuring is a reasonable call. Just make it a decision, not a default.
### What does a St. Louis emergency vet visit cost without insurance?
About $1,321 for one bad night with a dog, and about $1,106 for a cat, if you add up published averages for the usual pieces: an emergency exam, a basic blood count, an ultrasound and one night in the hospital. The exam is the cheap part. The rest is where the bill lives.
Here’s how the dog version stacks up, using the figures in our guide to finding an emergency vet in St. Louis, which come from CareCredit’s published cost data:
Emergency exam, Missouri average for a dog: $115. The national average is $135.
Basic blood count (CBC), national average: $104.
Ultrasound, national average: $483.
One night in the hospital at a veterinary clinic, national average: $619.
For a cat, the same four lines run $122, $79, $323 and $582. That’s a modest emergency, the kind where your pet ate something questionable and comes home the next afternoon. Add emergency X-rays and the survey’s average of $334 joins the bill. If the vet finds a blockage, surgery to remove it averages $2,217 for a dog. A stay at an emergency clinic rather than a regular practice averages $1,323 in the same data. These are averages, not quotes, so ask for a written estimate before treatment starts.
Where you live changes the odds, too. Picture a family in West Alton, where the Mississippi and Missouri rivers meet and high water is a regular visitor. The CDC says leptospirosis risk climbs after floods, and that dogs exposed to contaminated water are at higher risk. A dog who laps from a flooded field and spends several days on IV fluids isn’t a one-night bill anymore. Every extra night repeats the hospital line.
And here’s the St. Louis detail that should change your math. The local help most owners count on mostly doesn’t reach the ER. The APA’s Heads to Tails Hope Fund doesn’t fund emergency services or care already under way, and RedRover’s urgent care grants can’t help if the gap is $500 or more, as our guide to low-cost vet care in St. Louis lays out. For the 2 a.m. bill, your real options are what you’ve saved, what you can charge, and what a policy will hand back afterward.
### How does pet insurance actually pay a vet bill?
After the fact. With most policies you pay the clinic in full, send the insurer the itemized invoice, and get a check or deposit back once the claim is approved. The AVMA, the national veterinarians’ association, tells owners exactly that in its pet insurance guidance: these are generally reimbursement plans, so ask how claims are processed and how long payment takes before you sign up.
Three dials set how much comes back, and you choose all three when you buy:
The deductible: what you pay each policy year before the insurer pays anything. A higher deductible means a lower premium.
The reimbursement rate: the share of each covered bill the insurer pays after the deductible. Common choices are 70%, 80% and 90%.
The limit: the most the policy pays. Usually it’s per year, but some policies cap each condition or the pet’s whole lifetime instead, which matters far more than it sounds.
Run the $1,321 night through a policy with a $250 deductible and 80% reimbursement. The insurer subtracts $250, then pays 80% of the remaining $1,071, which comes to $856.80. You’re out $464.20 that night, plus whatever you’ve paid in premiums. Turn the dials to a $500 deductible at 70% and the check drops to $574.70. Have a second covered emergency later in that same policy year, and the deductible is already met, so the insurer pays its full percentage from the first dollar.
Two details move real money. Some insurers apply the percentage before the deductible instead of after, which on this bill would shave $50 off your check. And some policies don’t reimburse the exam fee, which stings most on small claims. Ask about both, in writing, before you pay a premium.
Notice what reimbursement doesn’t solve. You still need $1,321 on a card or in the bank that night. That’s why the small fund matters even with a policy. It’s also why one question for your clinic is worth asking early: does it accept direct payment from any insurer? A few insurers can pay participating practices at checkout, and if your vet already works that way, that answer can be worth more than a lower premium somewhere else.
### What does pet insurance cost in Missouri?
Nationally, the average accident-and-illness policy cost $836 a year for a dog in 2025, about $70 a month, and $435 for a cat, about $36 a month, according to the North American Pet Health Insurance Association’s 2026 State of the Industry report. Missouri owners appear to pay less than that. Treat both as a starting point, not a quote.
Here’s why we say less. In the same report, Missouri accounts for about 1.1% of the country’s insured pets but only about 0.8% of the premium written. When a state’s share of the money is smaller than its share of the pets, its average policy costs less than the national one. Here that gap works out to roughly a quarter less, though both shares are rounded, so read it loosely. It lines up with vet prices: CareCredit’s data puts Missouri’s average emergency exam for a dog at $115 against $135 nationally, and the NAIC lists where you live among the things that set a premium.
NAPHIA tracks three kinds of policy, and the 2025 U.S. averages show how far apart they sit:
Accident only: $190 a year for dogs and $112 for cats. NAPHIA’s own description covers things like swallowed objects, cuts, car accidents, ligament tears and poisoning.
Accident and illness: $836 for dogs and $435 for cats. It adds illnesses such as cancer, infections and digestive problems, and it’s what most people mean by pet insurance.
Insurance with wellness built in: $1,414 for dogs and $859 for cats. It adds routine care such as vaccines and screenings.
Whatever you pay this year, plan on paying more next year. The average dog accident-and-illness premium has climbed every year since 2021, from $625 to $836, and it jumped 11.5% in 2025 alone. Age pushes it up as well. The AVMA tells owners to find out, before buying, how premiums rise as a pet ages and whether filing claims raises them.
Accident-only coverage gets overlooked, and for some pets it’s the right buy. Picture a young Lab in Portage des Sioux who spends every summer on the riverbank and in the brush. The eastern copperhead is the most common venomous snake in Missouri, according to the Missouri Department of Conservation, and a bite means an ER trip even if the dog seems fine at first. A policy around $190 a year is built for that dog. It won’t touch the stomach trouble, ear infections and skin problems that top the industry’s dog claim list, though, so think of it as a floor.
Your own quote turns on species, breed, age, ZIP code and the three dials you pick. Get at least three quotes on the same deductible, reimbursement rate and limit, so you’re comparing prices instead of plans. Keep wellness add-ons in their own column, too. A plan that prepays vaccines and checkups is a budgeting tool, and the same math we run on clinic wellness plans in our guide on how to choose a vet in St. Louis applies to it.
### What does pet insurance leave out?
More than the ads suggest. Every policy is different, but these are the usual gaps in an accident-and-illness plan:
Pre-existing conditions, judged by what a vet noted, advised on or treated before coverage started or during the waiting period.
Anything that starts during the waiting period. Illness waits commonly run 14 to 30 days, and knee and hip problems can carry six months to a year.
Routine and preventive care such as vaccines, checkups and flea or heartworm prevention, unless you add wellness coverage.
Spay and neuter surgery, plus breeding and pregnancy costs on most plans.
Routine dental cleanings. Some plans cover dental illness or a broken tooth, but the yearly cleaning usually comes out of your pocket, and our guide to dog teeth cleaning cost in St. Louis covers that bill.
Cosmetic procedures, prescription food and supplements on many plans.
Hereditary or congenital conditions on some plans, and on many, the matching knee, hip or eye on the other side once one side had a problem before coverage. Policies call that a bilateral exclusion.
Exam fees and behavioral treatment on some plans, or only with an add-on.
Now the Missouri part. In 2022 the National Association of Insurance Commissioners, the group of state insurance regulators, adopted a Pet Insurance Model Act. In states that have passed it, the law bans waiting periods for accidents, caps illness waiting periods at 30 days, puts the burden of proving a pre-existing condition on the insurer, stops a condition covered one year from turning pre-existing at renewal, and gives you 15 days to return a new policy for a full refund if you haven’t filed a claim.
About 16 states have adopted it, by one count of the NAIC’s state chart in late September 2026. Missouri isn’t one of them, and neither is Illinois. According to that chart, neither state has a pet-insurance-specific law at all. That doesn’t make the policies sold here bad, and plenty of insurers write similar terms everywhere. It means none of those protections is guaranteed by statute on either side of the river. In Missouri, the policy wording is the protection.
So read it before you pay. Ask for the full sample policy, not the brochure, and find five things: the waiting periods for accidents, illness and orthopedic conditions; the definition of pre-existing; whether a cured condition can be covered again; whether this year’s claims can change your coverage at renewal; and how many days you have to cancel for a refund. If a claim goes sideways later, the Missouri Department of Commerce and Insurance takes consumer complaints at 800-726-7390.
### Why does waiting to buy pet insurance cost the most?
Because the first diagnosis sets the exclusion, and it usually arrives sooner than anyone expected. Policies generally treat a condition as pre-existing if a vet gave advice about it, treated it, or recorded signs of it before coverage began or during the waiting period. Your pet’s medical record is the evidence, and insurers ask for it when you claim.
Knees show how expensive that gets. The American College of Veterinary Surgeons says 40% to 60% of dogs with cruciate ligament disease in one knee will develop it in the other one later. Surgery averages $3,525 per knee in CareCredit’s data. If the first knee goes before you buy, many policies will exclude the second under that bilateral clause, so a dog who needs both is a $7,050 problem you carry alone. Buy before the first knee and both can be covered claims.
Not every exclusion lasts forever. Some insurers will cover a cured, curable problem again, a urinary infection or a bout of vomiting, say, after a stretch with no symptoms or treatment, commonly six to twelve months. Chronic conditions like allergies, diabetes or kidney disease generally stay excluded for the life of the policy. Ask which rule your insurer uses before you assume either one.
Older pets make the trap easy to walk into. Picture a retired couple in Lake St. Charles who adopt a 10-year-old cat whose shelter records mention slightly high kidney values. Kidney disease is among the most common cat claims insurers see, per NAPHIA, and those records mean it’s almost certainly excluded from day one. Some insurers also stop enrolling pets past a certain age, the NAIC notes. For that couple, a policy would cover the next new problem and almost none of the likely one. That’s a real decision, and it might reasonably end with a savings fund instead.
The cheapest moment to buy is the first month you own a young, healthy pet, while the medical record still says healthy. It’s also the moment insurance feels least necessary. Funny how that works.
### When does pet insurance stop making sense?
When the policy can no longer pay you back for the bills you’re actually likely to face. That happens in a few predictable situations, and none of them depends on what anybody’s brother-in-law said about his claim.
The likely problems are already excluded. A senior dog with arthritis, allergies and a heart murmur on record is buying coverage for everything except those three. Pay for that only if the premium is small and the new risks are big.
The premium is closing in on the payout. Add a year of premiums to the deductible, then compare that with what the policy would realistically pay in a bad year once the exclusions come out. When the two numbers get close, you’re prepaying your own vet bills with a markup.
You have the cash and the nerve to use it. A dedicated fund of several thousand dollars, kept apart from everything else, does for most owners what a policy does, minus the insurer’s cut. The nerve matters as much as the cash. A fund you’d hesitate to spend at the ER desk is a savings account with good intentions.
You already know where you’d stop. This one is hard to say out loud. If you know you wouldn’t approve a $5,000 cancer treatment for a 15-year-old cat, a policy built to pay for $5,000 treatments isn’t buying you much. And it’s not a made-up number: CareCredit’s data puts average cancer therapy at $5,254 for a dog and $4,269 for a cat.
Need the vet fund to grow faster? Flexible work-from-home income for St. Louis parents
If you drop a policy, keep the plan. Switch to accident-only if your pet still roams, keep the fund growing every month, and decide now which card or financing you’d use, after reading its deferred-interest terms. The owners who get through a 2 a.m. emergency without a financial hangover made their call before the drive. Make yours this week, while your pet is asleep on the couch and the record still says healthy.
Picking a vet before you need one? Start with veterinarians around St. Louis, and ask each clinic two questions: does it accept direct payment from any pet insurer, and which financing does it take.
And if you run a practice, the owners reading this are about to call with exactly those two questions, so list your clinic with us and answer them before the phone rings.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are the downsides of having pet insurance?
A.  You pay the vet first and wait to be reimbursed. Premiums rise most years and as your pet ages; the U.S. average for a dog’s accident-and-illness policy went up 11.5% in 2025 alone. Pre-existing conditions, routine care and problems that start in the waiting period aren’t covered. And across all customers, insurers pay back less than they collect, about 65 cents per premium dollar in NAPHIA’s 2024 figures.
### Q. Is $10,000 enough pet insurance?
A.  For most years, yes. CareCredit’s averages put knee surgery at $3,525 per knee, cancer therapy for a dog at $5,254 and colon tumor surgery with chemotherapy at $8,733, so a $10,000 annual limit covers nearly any single bad year. The rare worst cases go far higher: the top dog and cat claims NAPHIA listed for 2025 ran from about $24,500 to $66,600. Check whether your limit resets each year or applies per condition or for life.
### Q. What do vets recommend for pet insurance?
A.  The AVMA endorses pet insurance as a concept but recommends no company. Its policy favors plans that let you use any vet, including specialists and ER hospitals, use licensed vets to review claims, stay out of medical decisions, and spell out limits, deductibles, exclusions and how fast reimbursement arrives. Ask your own vet which insurers’ claims go smoothly at that clinic. They see the paperwork every week.
### Q. How much does pet insurance typically cost?
A.  In 2025 the U.S. average accident-and-illness policy cost $836 a year for a dog, about $70 a month, and $435 for a cat, about $36, according to NAPHIA. Accident-only plans averaged $190 and $112. Missouri’s share of the premium suggests policies here run below the national average. Your quote depends on species, breed, age, ZIP code and the deductible you choose, so check current prices.
### Q. What does pet insurance not pay for?
A.  Pre-existing conditions, anything that starts during the waiting period, routine care like vaccines and checkups without a wellness add-on, spay and neuter, and routine dental cleanings. Many plans also skip cosmetic procedures, prescription food and exam fees, and some exclude hereditary conditions or the opposite knee or hip once one side has a problem. In Missouri, which has no pet-insurance law, the policy wording decides.
### Q. What breeds of dogs will insurance not cover?
A.  Breed rarely blocks enrollment outright; insurers mostly price the risk into the premium. The AVMA cautions that some providers won’t insure a breed they consider high risk, though, and breed shows up in the fine print another way: some policies exclude hereditary or congenital conditions, which lands hardest on breeds known for hip, airway or heart problems. Some insurers also cap the age at which they’ll enroll a new pet.
### Q. At what point is pet insurance not worth it?
A.  When a year of premiums plus the deductible starts to rival what the policy would realistically pay after its exclusions. That usually means an older pet whose likely problems are already on record, or an owner with a dedicated fund big enough to absorb a $3,000 to $5,000 bill. If that’s you, look at accident-only coverage before dropping protection altogether.
### Q. Does pet insurance cover a behaviorist?
A.  Sometimes. Anxiety, behavioral and neurological issues were the fourth most common claim category for both dogs and cats in NAPHIA’s 2025 data, so insurers do pay behavior-related claims. When a policy includes behavioral coverage, it usually applies to diagnosis and treatment by a veterinarian or veterinary behaviorist, sometimes with its own cap or as an add-on, and trainers rarely qualify. Before you book a dog behaviorist in St. Louis, read your policy’s behavioral clause.

## Puppy Shots in St. Louis: The Schedule, the Real Cost, and the One Shot the Law Requires
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/puppy-shots-in-st-louis-schedule-and-cost
Twenty-eight dollars and forty-one cents. That’s the posted price of a dog’s rabies shot at the Banfield hospital inside the PetSmart on Lemay Ferry Road, and it’s accurate. It’s also nowhere close to what the shot costs you. Read one line up on the same price list: every vaccine requires an office visit, and the visit is $74.95.
Now run a puppy through the whole core series there. Three rounds of the distemper-parvo combination, two leptospirosis doses and one rabies shot come to $197.29 in vaccines. The three office visits come to $224.85. The visits cost more than every shot combined. Across town, a nonprofit clinic on South Jefferson Avenue posts a $25 exam, a $20 combination shot and a $25 rabies shot, which puts the same three visits at about $160. Same puppy. Same diseases. A $262 gap, and most of it sits on the line nobody quotes you over the phone.
Then there’s the rule the national vaccine charts skip. The City of St. Louis requires exactly one puppy shot, and its own registration page says so: rabies is the only vaccination City ordinance requires. Parvo, the virus that actually kills puppies, isn’t required by anybody. Missouri doesn’t even require rabies statewide. Drive less than an hour southeast to Red Bud or Marissa and Illinois law does.
Below: the schedule visit by visit, the series priced at three real St. Louis clinics from their posted numbers as of October 2026, and the line between what the law requires and what keeps a puppy alive. They’re two different lists. Prices and clinic dates change, so confirm before you book.
### What is the vaccination schedule for a puppy?
Under AAHA guidelines, a puppy gets a distemper-parvo combination shot every 2 to 4 weeks from 6 to 8 weeks old until at least 16 weeks, two leptospirosis doses starting at 12 weeks, and rabies at 12 to 16 weeks, with boosters within a year. St. Louis requires rabies and a tag by four months.
AAHA is the American Animal Hospital Association, and its 2022 canine vaccination guidelines are the reference schedule many U.S. vets build from. For a puppy who comes home at eight weeks, it usually lands on the calendar like this:
8 weeks: the first distemper-parvo combination shot (you’ll see it called DHPP, DAPP or the 5-in-1), usually with a fecal test and a deworming.
12 weeks: the second combination shot and the first leptospirosis dose, plus Bordetella if the puppy will board, go to daycare or see a groomer.
16 weeks: the third combination shot, the second lepto dose and rabies, with the City, County or Illinois county tag that comes with it.
Within a year of the last puppy shot: one combination booster, one lepto booster and the second rabies shot. After that, AAHA spaces the combination shot every three years and lepto every year, and rabies follows the vaccine label and local law.
Why three shots of the same vaccine? The series isn’t a dose being built up like a savings account. A puppy starts life with antibodies borrowed from its mother’s milk, and those borrowed antibodies block the vaccine along with the virus. They fade on a timetable nobody can see from the outside, and the week is different for every puppy. Each shot is another chance to land after they’re gone. That’s why AAHA keeps the shots coming every 2 to 4 weeks until the puppy is past 16 weeks, and why it notes that finishing at 18 to 20 weeks may be the better call where distemper and parvo run high.
The World Small Animal Veterinary Association’s 2024 guidelines go a step further, recommending a booster at 26 weeks instead of waiting for the first birthday, to catch the minority of puppies whose mother’s antibodies were still in the way at 16 weeks. Vets differ on which approach they follow. Ask which one yours uses, because it changes when the next bill arrives.
Here’s where the calendar goes sideways in real life. A family in Red Bud brings home a seven-week-old from a farm litter, and the seller hands over a card that says “first shots” with a date and nothing else. No product name. No lot sticker. No signature. Plenty of vets won’t count a dose they can’t identify, and AAHA’s rule of thumb for unknown history fits on a sticky note: when in doubt, vaccinate. The series starts over at visit one. Before money changes hands for a puppy, ask for the vaccine sticker or a vet-signed record, one of the checks in our guide to puppies for sale in St. Louis.
And once the last shot is in, our guide to dog-friendly places in St. Louis picks up where this one stops, with the patios, trails and stores that welcome a vaccinated dog.
### Which shots does Missouri law require?
At the state level, none. Missouri law doesn’t require pets to be vaccinated against rabies, a state health department official told Missourinet in December 2025, and local governments fill the gap. In the City of St. Louis and in St. Louis County the requirement is one shot, rabies, given by a licensed veterinarian between three and four months of age, with a registration tag that rides along with it.
The City says it more plainly than any national chart. Its Animal Care and Control registration page states that rabies inoculation is the only vaccination required by City ordinance. Puppies have to get their first rabies shot and be registered between 3 and 4 months old, and only a licensed veterinarian can give it. The vet hands you a certificate and a tag; if your vet doesn’t carry City tags, you register in person at 1520 Market Street with proof of the shot. Registration is $4 for a spayed or neutered pet and $50 for an intact one, renewed every one or three years along with the vaccine. A four-month-old who hasn’t had surgery yet is intact on paper, so ask your vet which fee applies and what changes after the spay or neuter.
St. Louis County runs the same idea on different numbers. County code requires the rabies shot and registration on or before four months of age but not before three. The posted fee for a certificate and tag is $8 for one year or $20 for three if the pet is spayed or neutered, and $16 or $40 if it isn’t, on top of the vet’s charge for the shot. A dog found without the tag can be treated as unvaccinated.
Now read what neither government requires. Not parvo. Not distemper. The shot that protects your neighbors from your dog is the law. The shot that protects your dog from the sidewalk is your call.
That second shot is the one that matters most in the first six months. Cornell University’s Riney Canine Health Center says parvovirus most often hits puppies between 6 weeks and 6 months old, shrugs off many household disinfectants, and can survive in the right conditions for up to a year. Infected dogs shed it in their stool for up to two weeks before they look sick. Cornell’s summary of untreated cases is short: most patients won’t survive without treatment.
Cross the river and the state steps in. Illinois’ Animal Control Act requires every dog 4 months or older to be vaccinated against rabies by a licensed veterinarian, with a second rabies shot within a year of the first. It also restricts the vaccine itself: rabies vaccine can be sold to, and used by, only licensed vets. The numbered tag comes from county animal control, through your vet. A puppy in Marissa or New Athens registers with St. Clair County, where Animal Services lists registration at $15 for a spayed or neutered dog and $35 for an unaltered one. A Red Bud puppy registers with Randolph County, which sets its own fee, so ask when you book.
The Illinois side also shows what the paperwork is for. St. Clair County’s policy says a dog or cat that bites a person must be confined for 10 days. A pet that’s currently vaccinated, or under 4 months old, may be released for confinement at home with a vet check. An unvaccinated one over 4 months has to be confined at Animal Control or with a licensed vet. Ten days in a clinic kennel is a hard way to learn the rabies shot was overdue. For the rest of the local rulebook, from pet limits to leash length, see our guide to pet laws in St. Louis City and County.
### What do puppy shots cost in St. Louis?
Posted prices for the core puppy series run from about $160 at a nonprofit wellness clinic to $279 for a retail vaccine-clinic bundle to $422.14 at a full-service chain hospital, as of October 2026. More than half of the gap between the cheapest and the priciest is the fee for walking in the door.
Here are the three, priced from their own pages:
Carol House Quick Fix Pet Clinic, the nonprofit on South Jefferson Avenue: a $25 wellness exam, $20 for its combination shot (DHLPP, where the L is leptospirosis) and $25 for rabies. Three visits with three combination shots and one rabies shot come to about $160. Kennel cough (Bordetella) adds $20, and dewormer is priced by weight.
Vetco Vaccination Clinic, inside the Petco stores on Watson Road and Telegraph Road: a $279 Puppy Bundle covering three distemper-parvo shots, two lepto doses, one Bordetella, rabies, two dewormings and a fecal test. Bought visit by visit it’s $99, $105 and $115, or $319. Rabies alone is $41.
Banfield Pet Hospital, inside the PetSmart on Lemay Ferry Road: a $74.95 office visit, then $39.98 for DAPP, $24.47 for leptospirosis and $28.41 for rabies. Three visits covering three DAPP shots, two lepto doses and rabies come to $422.14, or $456.34 with a $34.20 Bordetella.
Those totals aren’t three prices for one product. Carol House gives a vet exam at each wellness visit but won’t see a sick pet. Vetco’s packages list a vitals check, and Petco says the clinics do only routine vaccines and preventive tests. Banfield’s visit is a full exam at a hospital that can treat a sick puppy. If a puppy vomits on the exam table, only one of the three is built to do much about it.
Then there’s the bill a lot of owners forget: the first-year booster. At Carol House, one exam, one combination shot and one rabies shot come to $70. At the Lemay Ferry Banfield, an office visit with DAPP, lepto and rabies comes to $167.81. Put that number in the budget now, not next fall.
Most independent St. Louis practices don’t post puppy prices at all. Call two and ask both the same question: what does the whole series cost, visits included, from the first shot to the rabies tag? A clinic that answers with the price of one vaccine hasn’t answered.
