If you’re weighing a policy too, our breakdown of whether pet insurance is worth it in St. Louis runs the numbers on the bigger bills.
### Where can you get low-cost puppy vaccines in St. Louis?
Three kinds of places: a nonprofit wellness line, retail vaccine clinics inside pet stores, and free drive-through clinics St. Louis County runs with the Humane Society of Missouri. Each one has a catch worth knowing before you load the puppy in the car.
Carol House Quick Fix Pet Clinic at 1218 S. Jefferson Ave. is best known for spay and neuter surgery, more than 160,000 since it opened in 2012, by its own count. Its wellness line runs on reservations you can make up to midnight the night before, plus a limited number of walk-ins on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Days and times change week to week, so check the calendar on its site, and expect a line if you walk in. No residency requirement. Cash, Visa or Mastercard, no checks. No sick or injured pets.
There’s a money detail on that page most people scroll past. Carol House books technician appointments on Wednesdays and Fridays for boosters a clinic vet has already approved, for pets one of its vets has seen in the past 12 months. Rabies can’t be given at those visits and the page lists no price, so ask before you book rounds two and three there.
Vetco Vaccination Clinics sit inside the Petco stores at 7279 Watson Road and 3158 Telegraph Road and post the same puppy menu at both. Appointments only, and Petco notes that vet availability varies, so book rather than walk in.
The catch there is the building, not the price. Cornell’s Riney Canine Health Center lists pet stores right beside dog parks as places to avoid while a puppy is unvaccinated, because parvo spreads without any dog-to-dog contact and outlasts most household cleaners. Carry the puppy in, or bring a crate. Don’t set an eight-week-old down on the floor by the dog food.
Free beats cheap, and St. Louis County has been offering free. Its Animal Care and Control ran a drive-through clinic with the Humane Society of Missouri on Sunday, Sept. 13, 2026, at the North County Recreation Complex: canine rabies and DHPP shots, a microchip on request, County residents only, the first 100 registrations. It filled, and HSMO told the overflow to watch its social media for the next one. Register the day a date is announced, and ask whether they’ll vaccinate a puppy your dog’s age, since one free shot covers a single round of the series, not the series.
On the Illinois side, St. Clair County Animal Services keeps a resource page of low-cost vaccine and spay options for Metro East owners, with phone numbers. The listings carry no dates, so call before you count on a price. For spay and neuter programs, vet-bill funds and the rest of the safety net, see our guide to low-cost vet care in St. Louis.
### Which optional puppy shots make sense in St. Louis?
Bordetella if your puppy will board, go to daycare, see a groomer or join a membership dog park. Leptospirosis for nearly every dog, which is why AAHA moved it to core. Lyme disease and canine influenza by lifestyle. List where your dog will actually spend this year, then ask your vet which shots match the list.
Lepto is the one people still call optional, and AAHA no longer does. Its 2022 guidelines put leptospirosis in the core group, recommended for dogs 12 weeks and older who go outside in rural, suburban or urban settings across North America: two doses 2 to 4 weeks apart, then a booster every year. The bacteria spread through the urine of infected animals, wild animals and rodents included, and survive in contaminated water or soil for weeks to months, according to the CDC. People catch it too.
Picture a puppy in New Athens. The Kaskaskia River State Fish and Wildlife Area, more than 20,000 acres of it, surrounds the village. Summer evenings mean a creek bank, a deer trail and a puddle that never quite dries. That dog is the textbook lepto candidate. A city dog isn’t off the hook either; AAHA’s recommendation names urban dogs too.
Bordetella, the main kennel cough vaccine, is the shot businesses ask for. Southwest City Dog Park won’t accept a membership without records of a vet-administered rabies and Bordetella vaccine, and boarding kennels and daycares commonly want it on file before the first stay. It comes as a nose drop, an oral dose or an injection. The nose and mouth versions are a single dose; the injected one takes two, 2 to 4 weeks apart. A family in Marissa booking a kennel for Thanksgiving week should ask in October how far ahead of check-in the kennel wants it.
Lyme and canine flu are AAHA noncore shots, two doses 2 to 4 weeks apart and then yearly. Lyme comes down to ticks, and our guide to ticks in Missouri covers which ones live here and what they carry. Canine influenza is worth asking about for a dog who boards or spends a lot of time in a crowd of other dogs; Banfield’s posted price is $54.13 a dose.
Puppy’s calendar, done. The kids’ afternoons: free and low-cost after-school and summer programs
### When can a St. Louis puppy go to a dog park?
Not before 4 months at the gated city parks that post their rules, and realistically not until a week or two after the last puppy shot, which puts most puppies at about 17 or 18 weeks. Puppy class is a different question with a different answer.
Two city dog parks spell it out. Southwest City Dog Park takes no dogs under 4 months, wants vet-administered rabies and Bordetella records with the membership application, and lives by a “No SWCDP tag, No admittance, No exceptions” rule. Shaw Dog Park bars puppies under 4 months and wants proof of rabies vaccination, or approved titers, before it mails out the tag and the gate code. Our roundup of dog parks in St. Louis covers which parks need a membership and which don’t.
The wait is about the ground, not the other dogs’ manners. A fenced acre where hundreds of dogs of unknown vaccine status relieve themselves is about the worst floor in town for a puppy halfway through the series.
Now the part that gets lost. The American Veterinary Society of Animal Behavior says puppies can start socialization classes as early as 7 to 8 weeks, with at least one set of vaccines seven days before the first class, a first deworming, and shots kept current through the course. Its reasoning is stark. The first three months are the main window when a puppy’s sociability outweighs its fear. Behavior problems are the top reason dogs get surrendered to shelters, and AVSAB says behavior issues, not infectious disease, are the number one cause of death in dogs under three.
So the old advice to keep a puppy indoors until every shot is done trades a small risk for a bigger one. AVSAB’s middle path is a class held on an easily cleaned indoor floor, with puppies whose shots are current, and no dog parks or other heavily used ground where nobody knows the other dogs’ vaccine status. When you compare trainers, ask how they check vaccine records and what the floor is made of, and see our guide to dog training cost in St. Louis for the rest. Between classes, the crate, gate and chew toys do the heavy lifting; our checklist of what to buy for a new puppy covers day one.
Get the calendar right and the rest follows. The tag on the collar by four months. The last shot at 16 weeks or later. The first dog park visit a couple of weeks after that. Be the owner whose puppy walks into class at nine weeks and through the dog park gate at eighteen, with every record already in your phone.
Ready to book the first round? Compare veterinarians around St. Louis and ask each one for a written estimate of the whole puppy series, office visits included, not just the price of the first shot.
And if you run a clinic or a vaccine day, the owners reading this are about to ask whether your exam fee is charged at every visit and whether you hand out the City or County tag with the rabies shot, so list your practice with us with both answers up front.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much is a full set of puppy vaccines?
A.  In St. Louis, posted prices for the core series run from about $160 at Carol House Quick Fix Pet Clinic (three exams, three combination shots and rabies) to $279 for Vetco’s Puppy Bundle to $422.14 at the Banfield on Lemay Ferry Road, as of October 2026. Budget again for the first-year booster, $70 to $167.81 at those two clinics. Prices change, so ask for the whole-series total before you book.
### Q. How many shots do puppies usually get?
A.  Usually six or seven core injections over three or four visits, or fewer where lepto is combined into the same shot: three or four distemper-parvo combination shots every 2 to 4 weeks until at least 16 weeks, two leptospirosis doses starting at 12 weeks, and one rabies shot at 12 to 16 weeks. Bordetella, Lyme or flu add to that by lifestyle. Then come boosters within a year of the last puppy shot.
### Q. How many 5 in 1 shots do you give a puppy?
A.  At least three, given 2 to 4 weeks apart between 6 and 16 weeks of age, under AAHA’s guidelines, with the last one at 16 weeks or later. A puppy who starts at six weeks often gets four. The 5-in-1 covers distemper, two types of adenovirus (one causes canine hepatitis), parainfluenza and parvovirus. One booster follows within a year, then AAHA spaces it every three years.
### Q. How long after the 2nd vaccination can a puppy go out?
A.  It depends on where out is. Your own yard, a car ride or a friend’s vaccinated dog are fine now, and AVSAB says a well-run puppy class is fine a week after the first set of shots. Dog parks and pet-store floors should wait until the series is done, about one to two weeks after the final shot at 16 weeks or later. Southwest City and Shaw dog parks bar puppies under 4 months anyway.
### Q. Can my 8 week old puppy go outside?
A.  Yes, into your own yard if unknown dogs don’t use it, and potty training starts now. Carry the puppy, or use a crate, anywhere strange dogs walk. Cornell’s Riney Canine Health Center lists dog parks and pet stores as places to avoid until the shots are done. Meeting calm, vaccinated dogs and new people is good for an eight-week-old; AVSAB calls the first three months the main socialization window.
### Q. Is 12 weeks too late to vaccinate a puppy?
A.  No, but don’t wait any longer. Parvo most often hits puppies between 6 weeks and 6 months, so a 12-week-old with no shots is unprotected inside the danger window. Your vet will start the combination series now and repeat it every 2 to 4 weeks until the puppy is past 16 weeks. Rabies is due between three and four months in St. Louis.
### Q. Can I give my puppy vaccinations myself?
A.  Not rabies. The City of St. Louis says only a licensed veterinarian can give a rabies shot, and Illinois law lets only licensed vets buy or use rabies vaccine. Some farm and feed stores sell combination shots over the counter, but you’re on your own for storage, technique and the exam. Records may not count either: Southwest City Dog Park requires vet-administered rabies and Bordetella, and boarding kennels commonly want vet records.
### Q. What will happen if I don’t vaccinate my puppy?
A.  Medically, you’re betting against parvo, which Cornell says most untreated dogs don’t survive. Legally, skipping rabies can mean a City ticket and fine or an impound risk in the County. It gets worse after an exposure. Missouri sees rabid animals every year, mostly bats, and national rabies guidance says a never-vaccinated dog exposed to a rabid animal should be euthanized or held in strict quarantine for four months. If your puppy shows vomiting or bloody diarrhea, find an emergency vet in St. Louis now.

## Rabbit Adoption in St. Louis: $15 to $75 Fees, the 3-3-3 Rule, Why Bunnies Get Dumped in June
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/rabbit-adoption-in-st-louis
The $35 baby bunny is the expensive rabbit. It shows up every spring in a cardboard box on a farm-sale table or in a listing timed for Easter baskets, and it goes home unfixed, usually unvaccinated and too young for anybody to promise how big it’ll get, or even whether it’s a boy or a girl. The rescue rabbit across town costs $15 to $75 and arrives spayed or neutered, vet-checked and usually litter trained. Run the numbers on the first year and the cheap one loses.
Nobody selling the baby mentions the summer, either. Rabbits hit puberty somewhere between three and six months old, so the soft little thing from April is spraying, growling and boxing by June. That’s when they get dumped. In June 2022 a St. Louis rabbit rescue told St. Louis Public Radio it was fielding about 60 surrender requests a week and had run out of pellets. Four Junes later, KMOV reported the same rescue was getting about 150 a week.
So this guide runs in the order a good adoption does: how a new rabbit settles in, who adopts rabbits around St. Louis and for how much, the first year priced line by line, and the Easter-to-June pipeline that keeps every local rabbit rescue full. Rabbits barely register in most guides to pet-friendly St. Louis, and that’s part of how the problem stays out of sight. Every fee below comes from the group’s own published page as of October 2026. Fees change, so confirm before you go.
### What is the 3-3-3 rule for rabbits?
It’s House Rabbit Society’s rough timeline for a newly adopted rabbit: about 3 days of hiding and stress, about 3 weeks before the rabbit settles in and shows its real personality, and about 3 months before it trusts you and feels at home. Some rabbits move faster, some slower, so treat it as a guide.
The rule comes from House Rabbit Society, the national rabbit welfare group founded in 1988. In the first three days, it says, expect a rabbit who’s overwhelmed: skittish, scared, not interested in you, and likely to leave a trail of territorial droppings as it works up the nerve to explore. Around three weeks, the real personality starts showing. By three months the rabbit should be used to your home and building a genuine bond with you.
Here’s why the timeline matters more for a rabbit than for a dog. Rabbits are prey animals. To a rabbit, being scooped up feels like being caught, which is why House Rabbit Society tells new owners to resist handling them early and why most rabbits never learn to love being held. A new owner who spends week one chasing the rabbit around the living room for a cuddle is teaching it exactly the wrong lesson. Then, on day eight, the rabbit gets called mean.
What works instead is boring. It also works. Sit on the floor. Read, scroll or watch TV down at rabbit level. Let the rabbit come to you, and when it does, hand over a few pellets or a leaf of romaine from your open palm. Talk so it learns your voice. If you plan to add a second rabbit later, House Rabbit Society suggests waiting a day or two before any introduction, and always on neutral ground.
St. Louis rescues build part of the 3-3-3 into the adoption itself. Missouri House Rabbit Rescue won’t let you meet its rabbits until you’ve sat through its free class on rabbit care and behavior, which runs two-plus hours. Dolly’s Dream Home Rabbit Rescue requires every adopter to take its free virtual course first. That means a family in Staunton can do the homework at the kitchen table on the Illinois side of the river before anybody gets in the car. And because Dolly’s rabbits live in foster homes, you can ask the foster how that rabbit handled its own first three days, three weeks and three months under a stranger’s roof.
Not sure your household is ready for a ten-year animal? House Rabbit Society suggests fostering as the trial run, and our guide to fostering pets in St. Louis explains how it works here.
### Where can you adopt a rabbit in St. Louis?
At two rabbit-only rescues and at the region’s big general shelters, which list rabbits alongside guinea pigs and hamsters. The rabbit rescues charge more and include more. The shelters charge less and can move faster.
Missouri House Rabbit Rescue. Its legal name is House Rabbit Society of Missouri, it’s been active in Missouri for more than 27 years, and it has rescued over 7,000 rabbits by its own count. It’s all volunteer and runs the Bunny House, a 6,600-square-foot shelter on four acres in southwest St. Louis County. There are no walk-ins. You attend the class, then book an appointment to meet rabbits, and you have to be 21 or older to apply. Anyone younger who lives at home needs a parent to fill out the application.
The fee is $75 for one rabbit and $125 for a bonded pair. The rescue spells out what that buys: a well-bunny check from a vet who specializes in rabbits, both shots of the RHDV2 vaccine, a 30-day health guarantee, the spay or neuter, parasite treatment, litter box training or a good start on it, and a year’s membership with free nail trims, access to bunny boarding and a members-only supply store. One line on its adoption process page deserves a highlight: don’t buy housing or supplies before the class. A pet-store cage is the classic first mistake, and the rescue would rather tell you before you spend the money.
Dolly’s Dream Home Rabbit Rescue. Started in late 2020 and a licensed nonprofit since 2021, Dolly’s is foster based, so its rabbits live in volunteers’ homes in and around St. Louis instead of a shelter building. It says it has taken in more than 2,000 rabbits, and every one is spayed or neutered, vetted, microchipped, socialized and litter trained before adoption. Every adopter takes the free virtual course, and since the rabbits live with fosters, the foster is the person who can tell you what that rabbit is really like at 10 p.m. Its site doesn’t post the adoption fee, so ask when you apply. Adopters get free nail trims at its supply store, where everyone else pays $10.
Humane Society of Missouri. The lowest published rabbit fee we found. HSMO’s adoption fee page lists rabbits at $15, guinea pigs at $10, and ferrets and chinchillas at $50, and the small-animal fee includes the spay or neuter plus a nail trim. Bring a real carrier. HSMO warns that rabbits chew through its temporary cardboard boxes, and it sells plastic carriers at its St. Louis City gift shop.
APA Adoption Center. The Animal Protective Association of Missouri, on South Hanley Road, lists small animals and birds at $30, with variable pricing, and its fees include spay or neuter surgery. Small pets have to leave in a secure carrier. Bring your own or buy one at the counter: $5 for cardboard, $30 for plastic.
Other shelters. General shelters across the metro take in rabbits as strays and owner surrenders, and they tend to file them under small animals or “other” next to the birds and reptiles, so they’re easy to miss. If you’re flexible on age and color, check those lists every week or two. Our roundup of St. Louis pet rescues covers the wider network.
Which one fits? For a first rabbit, the rabbit rescues. The class, the litter training and a year of support are worth far more than the $45 to $60 you’d save, and the volunteers you’ll call when something looks wrong have seen it before. If you’ve kept rabbits for years and know what you want, the shelters are a fine, cheaper route.
### What does a pet rabbit cost in the first year?
Plan on roughly $800 to $1,000 for a rescue rabbit’s first year and $1,150 to $1,600 for a pet-store or backyard baby, using Missouri House Rabbit Rescue’s own cost sheet. The gap is almost entirely the spay or neuter. The rescue fee already covers it. The baby still needs it.
The rescue’s published breakdown, as of October 2026:
Purchase price: $35 to $100
Cage or pen: $80 to $200
Food and water bowls: $15 to $20
Litter box: $10 to $12
Nail trimmers: $7 to $10
Brush: $10 to $40
Pellets, hay and greens: about $50 a month
Vet visit: $45 to $60
Spay or neuter: $150 to $500
Now build two first years. Adopt from the rescue at $75, add $122 to $282 for setup, $600 for twelve months of food and one checkup at $45 to $60, and you land around $840 to $1,020. HSMO’s $15 rabbit pulls that down to about $780 to $960, if the right rabbit is there when you are.
Now the spring baby. Picture a family in Alhambra that picks one up for $35 at a farm sale in March. Same setup, same hay, same checkup. Then the surgery. The rescue’s cost sheet puts a spay or neuter anywhere from $150 to $500, and its adoption page says rabbit-savvy vets routinely charge $350 to $550. Use that second range and the cheap bunny’s first year runs about $1,150 to $1,590, before the two-shot RHDV2 series the rescue rabbit already had. The $35 rabbit ends up costing several hundred dollars more than the $75 one.
Skipping the surgery isn’t the savings it looks like. House Rabbit Society says most rabbits with bad litter box habits aren’t fixed, that spaying or neutering curbs biting and scratching, and that studies put unspayed females at high risk of reproductive cancers as they age, somewhere between 40% and 80% depending on age. An unspayed female can also have a litter of one to 12 kits every 30 days if she meets an intact male. And sexing a rabbit at four to eight weeks old is hard enough that the local rescue warns adopters about it. Two “sisters” from the same box aren’t always two sisters.
Then budget for the bill nobody plans. The rescue’s health pages list what GI stasis, a gut slowdown and maybe the most common reason rabbits see a vet, tends to cost: $50 to $75 for the visit, about $90 per X-ray view, more than $200 for a procedure and more than $100 in medications. One bad night can pass $400 fast. A small monthly rabbit fund turns that night into an inconvenience instead of a decision.
Two more lines. A bonded pair from the rescue costs $125 instead of $150 for two singles, and two rabbits keep each other company while you’re at work, though they go through twice the hay. And if you travel, the rescue boards members’ rabbits for $14 to $27 a day, depending on crate or pen size and how many rabbits share it.
### How do you set up a St. Louis home for a rabbit?
Indoors, in a roomy pen, with every cord covered and the thermostat under 75. That’s the short version. The long one starts with unlearning the hutch.
Hutches were designed for rabbits on meat farms, Missouri House Rabbit Rescue says, and a rabbit living in one is a lonely, frightened animal. Outdoors, a rabbit is exposed to predators, parasites and weather. House Rabbit Society puts a rabbit’s comfort zone at 60 to 75 degrees, with heat stroke a risk above 75, and a St. Louis July afternoon blows well past that. A rabbit in a backyard hutch in summer, or shut in a garage, is in real danger. KMOV’s June 2026 story on Dolly’s featured Cobbler, a rabbit rescuers found barely alive with heat stroke after being locked in a hot garage all day. He recovered. Now people fly in from other states to meet him.
Skip the pet-store cage, too. The rescue says most are too small and many have wire floors that hurt rabbits’ feet. Its suggestions are a large dog crate, a homemade cube setup or an exercise pen. House Rabbit Society’s shopping list starts with a foldable exercise pen, washable floor covering, a litter box in the pen plus one in the running space, heavy bowls, a hidey house, unlimited hay and a rabbit-safe litter. Paper pellets are on both its list and Dolly’s. No clumping or clay litter. The local rescue also wants rabbits out of the pen at least two to four hours a day.
Then get down on the floor and look at the room the way a rabbit does. Every charger, lamp cord and speaker wire at rabbit height is a chew toy. Baseboards, couch corners and the bottoms of door frames come next. House Rabbit Society’s list calls for wire covers, baseboard protectors, couch covers and baby gates.
Bunny chewed the charger? What to do with old electronics in St. Louis
If the rabbit is mostly for the kids, go in clear-eyed. The local rescue tells parents that the adult is expected to be the primary caregiver, House Rabbit Society notes that many young children lose interest within a few weeks, and both say bigger rabbits do better around small children. Missouri House Rabbit Rescue doesn’t recommend rabbits under four pounds for homes with small kids, because most dwarf rabbits hate being held and one badly placed hug can seriously hurt one.
Renters, one more check before the rabbit moves in. Ask your landlord, since many leases treat any animal as a pet. Inside the City of St. Louis, the Animal Care and Control laws page lists rabbits among the pets that may count toward the four-animal limit per residential parcel. Our guides to pet laws in St. Louis City and County and renting with pets in St. Louis cover the fine print.
### Why do so many rabbits get surrendered after Easter?
Because the bunny bought for the basket grows up. Rabbits mature at roughly three to six months, and the cuddly baby from April turns territorial, sprays, nips and boxes by early summer. Owners told a rabbit is an easy starter pet decide they got a bad one, and the surrender calls start.
The Humane Society of the United States has called rabbits the third most popular pet in America and the third most abandoned, according to a National Geographic investigation. In the same report, a Georgia chapter of House Rabbit Society said its abandoned-rabbit calls jumped from one or two a week to three or four a day in the six weeks after Easter. Chapters in Illinois and Idaho saw their spike later, in summer, as the Easter bunnies hit puberty.
St. Louis runs on that summer clock. Look at the dates on the local reporting. St. Louis Public Radio’s story on rabbit rescues at capacity ran in June 2022, when Dolly’s was out of pellets, almost out of carriers and taking about 60 surrender requests a week, a surge its founder blamed on Easter gifts and quarantine impulse buys. KMOV’s profile of the same rescue ran in June 2026, at about 150 requests a week. Dolly’s own site says it typically gets 150 to 200 surrender and dumped-bunny requests a week and can’t keep up. Missouri House Rabbit Rescue says its rescue team most often captures rabbits released outside by former owners and breeders.
Released is the wrong word for what happens next. Pet rabbits are domesticated European rabbits, a different species from the cottontails in your yard, and both local rescues say flatly that they can’t survive outdoors. Picture a big lop-eared rabbit sitting in a yard in St. Jacob in July, barely bothering to move when people walk by. That’s probably somebody’s Easter rabbit. Dolly’s founder told St. Louis Public Radio that cottontails are smaller, with longer and thinner snouts, and run completely differently. She asked people to send photos and video to a rescue before trying to trap one.
It’s also against the law. Missouri’s animal neglect statute, RSMo 578.009, makes it an offense to knowingly abandon an animal anywhere without making provisions for its adequate care, a class C misdemeanor the first time. Rescues bring it up for a reason. A domestic rabbit left in a park has no provisions at all.
The fix starts before the purchase. Adopt instead of buying a baby. If someone you know wants an Easter rabbit, hand them a chocolate one and the rescue’s class schedule. And if a rabbit already isn’t working out, call a rescue before you give up. Dolly’s says it tries to keep bunnies in the homes where they’re loved, and plenty of “bad rabbit” problems turn out to be a neuter and a bigger pen away from solved.
### Which vets see rabbits in St. Louis?
Fewer than you’d think. Missouri House Rabbit Rescue’s vet page says it plainly: most small-animal vets work only with cats and dogs, and rabbits are exotics that need someone trained in their physiology. Find that vet before you need one, not on the night your rabbit stops eating.
Start with the rescue’s own short list of St. Louis-area rabbit vets it knows and trusts. Then widen it with our guide to exotic vets in St. Louis, which maps which practices see rabbits during the day and which emergency hospitals take them after hours.
When you call a practice, ask four things. Does a specific doctor see rabbits, and on which days? Do you carry the RHDV2 vaccine? How many rabbit spays and neuters do you do in a month? And where do you send rabbits when you’re closed? The vaccine question isn’t a formality. Even the rescue’s own vet list flags one practice that doesn’t carry it.
RHDV2, rabbit hemorrhagic disease virus type 2, is a highly contagious and usually fatal rabbit virus that has been spreading across North America since 2020. It can ride into a house on shoes, clothing or insects, so an indoor rabbit isn’t automatically safe. The vaccine is two shots three weeks apart, then a yearly booster. Missouri House Rabbit Rescue vaccinated every rabbit in its shelter and foster system as soon as Missouri’s state veterinarian approved the vaccine, and it now requires proof of a current shot for boarding, nail trims and its events. Report any sudden, unexplained rabbit death to your vet.
Learn one emergency rule cold. Any rabbit that isn’t eating needs a vet right away, the rescue says. Rabbits can’t burp or vomit to relieve gas, and a stomach blockage can be life threatening. Teeth grinding, a hunched posture or an empty litter box are reasons to call that day, not next week.
The family that leaves the class with a supply list, a pen in the right corner and a rabbit vet already saved in their phone isn’t lucky. They skipped the Easter listing. Be the one who knew to, then give your new rabbit its three days, three weeks and three months.
Ready to start looking? Browse pet adoption services around St. Louis and ask each one whether it takes in rabbits, since many file them under small animals where you’d never spot them.
And if you run a rescue or adoption service that places rabbits, list it with us with your rabbit fee and your class schedule up front, because those are the first two things the families reading this will ask.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What to do with a rabbit you can’t keep?
A.  Call a rabbit rescue before you do anything else, and ask for help with the problem, not only for a surrender slot. Biting, spraying and missed litter boxes are often hormonal and fixable with a spay or neuter and a bigger setup. If money is the problem, Dolly’s runs a bunny food pantry for owners who take its free course. If you adopted from a rescue, your contract likely requires returning the rabbit there. Never turn it loose outside.
### Q. Where is the best place to rehome a rabbit?
A.  The rescue you adopted from, first. Missouri House Rabbit Rescue’s adoption contract asks adopters to bring rabbits back, and Dolly’s Dream Home takes requests through a surrender form on its site. Both stay full, and Dolly’s alone fields 150 or more requests a week, so reach out early. Bring vet records and an honest description of the rabbit’s temperament.
### Q. What is the average lifespan of a bunny?
A.  Eight to 12 years for an indoor house rabbit, according to Rabbit.org, and some reach 14 or even 16. Outdoor domestic rabbits live only about three to five years. That’s as long as many dogs and cats live.
### Q. What breed of bunny makes the best pet?
A.  For most St. Louis households, the best one is an adult, spayed or neutered rabbit whose foster already knows its personality. Breed matters less than size and hormones. A pet-store baby can grow up to weigh 2 pounds or 10, Missouri House Rabbit Rescue warns, and nobody can promise which. With small children in the house, bigger rabbits usually handle noise and movement better.
### Q. What is the calmest breed of rabbit?
A.  No breed guarantees calm, but size and age help. House Rabbit Society says big rabbits generally have a more confident, easygoing temperament, and the local rescue says larger rabbits are less skittish around sudden movement. One Dolly’s volunteer shares her house with Moose, a free-roaming Flemish Giant. A fixed adult with a known temperament is still the calmest bet.
### Q. Can I leave my rabbit home alone for 2 days?
A.  Not without someone checking in at least once a day. A rabbit that stops eating needs a vet right away, and a tipped water bowl or a hot house can turn serious fast. Hire a sitter who knows rabbits, or board. Missouri House Rabbit Rescue boards members’ rabbits for $14 to $27 a day with 48 hours’ notice and proof of RHDV2 vaccination, and Dolly’s offers bunnysitting with its trained fosters.
### Q. Do pet rabbits poop all over the house?
A.  In the first few days, some, yes. House Rabbit Society says new rabbits often leave territorial droppings while they explore. After that, spayed and neutered rabbits usually learn near-perfect litter box habits, and most rabbits with bad habits aren’t fixed. The droppings are dry, round and easy to sweep, and a box of paper litter can go straight into the compost.
### Q. Is it illegal to release a pet rabbit outside in Missouri?
A.  Knowingly abandoning an animal without making provisions for its care counts as animal neglect under RSMo 578.009, a class C misdemeanor for a first offense. It’s also close to a death sentence for the rabbit, since pet rabbits are a different species from wild cottontails and can’t fend for themselves. A rescue’s surrender list is the legal route, and the kinder one.

## Dog Behaviorist in St. Louis: Who Earns the Title, What It Costs, Why Pain Comes First
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/dog-behaviorist-in-st-louis
Anyone can call themselves a dog behaviorist. Missouri doesn’t license dog trainers, and nothing stops a person with a weekend certificate and a ring light from putting “canine behaviorist” on a website. The one group that can’t use the word freely is veterinarians. The American College of Veterinary Behaviorists says a vet may call herself a behaviorist only after earning its board certification, and it points out that no such limit applies to trainers or anyone else.
Sit with that for a second, because it flips the usual logic. On a dog pro’s website, the job title is the least reliable line on the page. The letters after the name are the most reliable. And which letters you need depends on what your dog is actually doing.
Picture three dogs. In Winfield, a two-year-old heeler mix who’s a sweetheart on the couch and a screaming, lunging wreck the moment another dog rounds the corner. In Foley, a young lab who howls for most of an hour after the car pulls out and has chewed the trim off the back door. In Grover, a nine-year-old shepherd who never growled at anybody until this summer, when a grandchild leaned on his back end and he snapped. All three owners will type the same words into a search bar. They need three different people, and the shepherd probably needs a vet before anyone else.
This guide sorts out who does what, what St. Louis owners actually pay, and the checks to run before anyone takes your deposit. It’s about problem behavior: aggression, reactivity, fear and separation anxiety. For puppy class and everyday manners, our breakdown of dog training cost in St. Louis covers that side, and our guide to dog-friendly places in St. Louis covers where a calmer dog can go once the work pays off. Every fee below comes from a published price page or fee schedule as of October 2026. Fees change, so confirm before you book.
### When should a dog see a behaviorist?
See a behaviorist when the problem could hurt someone or won’t budge with ordinary training: any bite or near-bite, growling over food or toys, lunging on leash, panic when left alone, or a sudden change in a dog who used to be fine. Start with your regular vet, since pain or illness drives many cases.
The signs that an ordinary obedience class won’t touch the problem:
A bite that broke skin, or a snap that stopped short on purpose.
Growling, freezing or going stiff over a food bowl, a bone, a toy, the couch or one particular person.
Lunging, barking or spinning on leash at dogs, people, bikes or cars.
Panic when left alone: howling, drooling, clawing at doors or window frames, accidents from a dog who’s house-trained. The Merck Veterinary Manual notes these signs are often worst in the first 15 to 30 minutes after you leave.
Fear that runs the dog’s day: hiding from visitors, trembling on walks, shutting down at the vet.
Compulsive loops, like tail chasing, shadow chasing, snapping at flies that aren’t there or licking a leg raw.
Any sudden change in a dog who used to be easygoing, especially a senior.
Aggression tops that list for a reason. Merck says the most common behavior problems in dogs are the ones tied to aggression, and that most of those cases involve a dog trying to put distance between itself and a situation. It also tells owners to get help from a veterinarian as soon as any sign of aggression shows up, because of the risk of injury and the risk of the aggression getting worse. A growl is a dog asking for space before it decides to take it.
Timing is where owners lose ground. Most people wait for the second bite, or the neighbor’s complaint. By then the dog has rehearsed the behavior dozens of times, and every rehearsal makes it easier. The American College of Veterinary Behaviorists names behavior problems as a leading cause of dogs and cats being surrendered to shelters in the United States. Most of those dogs didn’t start out hopeless. They started out as a fixable problem handed to the wrong person, or to nobody.
Notice the order in that short answer, too. Vet first. Then the right behavior professional. Skip the first step and you can spend months of training money on a dog whose real problem is a sore back.
### Trainer, behavior consultant or veterinary behaviorist: who does what?
Think of it as tiers, sorted by how deep the problem goes and whether medicine might be part of the answer. Every tier can refer up. The good ones do it without being asked.
The trainer. Trainers teach skills: sit, down, loose-leash walking, a recall that holds up with a squirrel in play. Look for the CPDT-KA from the Certification Council for Professional Dog Trainers, or the Accredited Dog Trainer credential from the International Association of Animal Behavior Consultants. A skilled, reward-based trainer handles plenty of mild reactivity and nuisance behavior well. Trainers get into trouble with aggression and panic, the problems that need a diagnosis before they need a plan.
The certified behavior consultant. This is the tier most St. Louis families with a reactive or aggressive dog actually need, and two credentials carry real weight. The CCPDT’s CBCC-KA, short for Certified Behavior Consultant Canine, Knowledge Assessed, requires at least 300 hours of behavior consulting on fear, phobias, compulsive behavior, anxiety and aggression within the previous three years, a signed attestation from a CCPDT certificant or a veterinarian, and a 200-question exam. The IAABC’s Certified Dog Behavior Consultant, or CDBC, is aimed at consultants with three or more years on complex cases, and its exam is writing-heavy, built on case studies and scenario answers. IAABC credential holders then owe 36 continuing education units every three years. Neither credential lets a consultant diagnose a medical problem or prescribe a drug. A good consultant tells you that on the first call.
The separation anxiety specialist. Separation anxiety has its own credential, the Certified Separation Anxiety Trainer, or CSAT, from a program founded by trainer Malena DeMartini. Her team works with clients in other countries, and her program says the work goes better when the trainer doesn’t come to your house, so the practice absences you rehearse look like real ones. For the owner in Foley, that means the best-qualified person for that howling lab might live several states away and still be the right hire.
The applied animal behaviorist. The Animal Behavior Society certifies Applied Animal Behaviorists, CAAB after the name: a doctorate in a behavioral or biological science plus five years in the field, or a veterinary degree plus a behavior residency and three more years. An associate level, ACAAB, covers master’s-level behaviorists. One without a veterinary license can’t prescribe.
The veterinary behaviorist. A Diplomate of the American College of Veterinary Behaviorists, DACVB after the name, is a licensed veterinarian who then finished at least one year of internship or general practice, at least three years of case supervision under an established Diplomate, original behavior research published in a peer-reviewed journal, three case reports approved by a committee of Diplomates, and a two-day board exam. This is the person for dangerous aggression, panic that medication might help, a dog whose medical problems are tangled into the behavior, or a case that has already worn out two trainers.
Every one of those credentials can be checked. The CCPDT and the IAABC both keep public directories of their certificants, and the ACVB runs a Find a DACVB search on its website. If somebody says they’re certified and you can’t find them, ask why.
Then ask about methods, because a credential doesn’t settle that by itself. Merck is blunt here: punishment isn’t helpful and may backfire, and physical punishment, including prong collars and electric shock collars, can make an already aggressive dog worse. A behavior pro who reaches for either one with a frightened dog has told you what you need to know.
### How rare are veterinary behaviorists around St. Louis?
Rarer than most owners would guess. The ACVB says there are currently more than 100 board-certified veterinary behaviorists in the world, and it warns that not every state has one. Its advice for owners without one nearby is to search the neighboring states, and it adds that many Diplomates will consult over the phone with your regular vet. More than 100, for the whole planet.
Missouri’s piece of that list is thin, and partly out of date. The ACVB’s directory still files a Diplomate under “Missouri CVM” at the address of the building that housed Mizzou’s satellite clinic, out I-70 on the metro’s far western edge, a site the university once said offered pet behavioral services. Today the building’s tenants are private cancer and dermatology practices, one of which notes that MU has announced changes to its location there, and neither lists behavior appointments. Mizzou’s main teaching hospital lists no behavior service among its small animal departments either. The closest thing is its Community Practice team, which names behavior problems among the conditions it focuses on. Missouri has one veterinary college, so that gap is the whole state’s gap. Call the Small Animal Hospital at 573-882-7821 and ask what’s offered now before you plan around it.
In practice, St. Louis owners reach specialist-level help in three ways:
A vet-to-vet consult. Ask your regular vet to reach out to a Diplomate about your dog. You skip the drive, and your own vet stays in charge of any prescription.
A referral appointment. Your vet sends records to a behavior practice, and you book a long first visit. Plan for a wait and a deposit.
A general-practice vet who takes behavior seriously. Some St. Louis clinics publish behavior consultation pages. Heritage Veterinary Hospital describes a consult that reviews the pet’s history, includes a physical exam and diagnosis, and ends in a treatment plan, trying behavior modification first and adding medication when it helps. Southwick Veterinary Hospital lists anxiety, noise phobia, aggression, cognitive dysfunction and house soiling among the problems its team takes on.
Neither clinic page describes a board-certified behaviorist on staff, and for a lot of dogs that’s fine. A general-practice vet with a real interest in behavior can rule out pain, start medication and refer up when a case outgrows the clinic. Just know which tier you’re booking.
### What does behavior help cost in St. Louis?
Plan on about $150 for a first behavior evaluation with a credentialed local trainer, roughly $600 to $700 for a first appointment with a board-certified veterinary behaviorist, and several thousand dollars for an aggression board-and-train. Only the first number is a one-time cost. The other two are the opening bill on a plan that runs for months.
Local trainers publish the fewest prices, and when they do, it’s usually the intake. The Persuaded Pooch, a St. Louis in-home training company whose trainers are certified through the Karen Pryor Academy, lists its Initial Behavior Evaluation at $150 and waives it if you buy a private training package. Most behavior consultants work the same way: a paid intake, then a package quoted for your dog. Get that quote in writing, with the session count and what support you get in between.
Board-and-train sits at the top of the local range. Modern K9 Solutions, which serves the St. Louis metro, lists a six-week aggression stay-and-train program at $7,999 and a four-week program for fearful dogs at $5,995, each with a private go-home lesson and ongoing lessons included. Before you pay for any program where the dog leaves home, ask the question our training cost guide raises: the dog learns the trainer, not you, so how exactly does the training get handed back to you?
No veterinary behaviorist in the St. Louis area that we found publishes a fee schedule, so use the published ones as a yardstick. Tufts University’s veterinary school lists $605 for a 90-minute new-client behavior consultation. A specialty hospital in Michigan with a board-certified behaviorist on staff publishes its whole 2026 schedule:
First dog consultation, two hours: $665, and a second dog may add $332.
Rechecks, 50 minutes: $197 within six months of the last visit, $250 within a year, $305 after that.
Technician coaching sessions: $111 to $140.
Deposit: half the consult fee to hold the appointment.
Now the math nobody shows you. That Michigan practice recommends rechecks every two to three months during the first year, which works out to four to six of them. At $197 apiece, year one comes to roughly $1,450 to $1,850 before a single prescription or technician visit. Next to a $150 evaluation, that’s sticker shock. Next to one dog bite, one lost lease or one dog surrendered to a shelter, it reads differently.
Two ways to soften it. First, check your pet insurance before you assume the answer is no. Some policies reimburse behavioral treatment a veterinarian diagnoses, some sell that coverage only as an add-on, and plenty of basic plans leave it out entirely, so read the behavioral line in the policy itself. Our guide to whether pet insurance is worth it in St. Louis walks through the rest of that decision. Second, start with the cheap steps. The Humane Society of Missouri keeps a free online Pet Care and Behavior Library with handouts on aggression, fear, barking and more, and an exam with your regular vet is the least expensive diagnostic step there is.
Rewards beat punishment for struggling students too: free tutoring in St. Louis
### What happens at a first behavior consult?
A long conversation about your dog’s history, with your dog in the room or on video. Expect an hour and a half to two hours, homework before you arrive, and a written plan when you leave.
The work starts before the appointment. The Michigan practice above requires a detailed behavior questionnaire seven days ahead and cancels the consult, deposit and all, if it doesn’t arrive. Tufts asks for your dog’s medical records in advance and invites videos and photos. Fill out every form honestly.
Video is the most useful thing you can bring, as long as you don’t stage it. Film what already happens, from a safe distance: the lunge at the corner, the stare over the food bowl, the first ten minutes after you walk out the door. Never provoke a growl to catch it on camera. You’re documenting, not testing.
In the room, the specialist walks back through when the problem started, where it happens, what the dog’s body does in the seconds before, and everything you’ve already tried. Bring everyone who lives with the dog. The Michigan practice asks all involved family members to attend, because a plan only works if the whole house runs it. Tufts says you leave with recommendations plus an estimate of how many follow-ups to expect.
The plan itself usually has three parts. Management keeps everyone safe starting today: baby gates, a closed door at mealtime, walks at quieter hours. Behavior modification changes how the dog feels about its trigger, slowly, through techniques like desensitization and counterconditioning. And sometimes medication lowers the anxiety enough for the learning to stick. If your dog goes on a behavior prescription, expect regular rechecks. The Michigan practice requires an exam at least every six months for any patient on medication.
For the heeler in Winfield, that plan can look almost boring on paper. Walks at 6 a.m. instead of 5 p.m. Turning around before the other dog gets close enough to set him off. A treat every time a dog appears at a distance he can handle, until another dog starts to predict something good. If a walker covers the middle of the day, it has to be a solo walk, never a pack of six, and our guide to finding a dog walker in St. Louis covers how to ask for one.
For the lab in Foley, the first rule surprises most owners. Separation anxiety plans generally ask that the dog not be left alone longer than it can handle while treatment is underway. That might mean a sitter, a neighbor, daycare or a work-from-home stretch while the absences get built up a few minutes at a time. Inconvenient? Very. It’s also the part that makes the rest of the plan possible.
### When is it a medical problem, not a training problem?
More often than most owners expect. In a 2020 paper in the journal Animals, an international group of behavior specialists reviewed 100 recent dog cases from their own caseloads and concluded that, conservatively, about a third of referred cases involved some kind of painful condition. In some caseloads the figure ran close to 80 percent. Musculoskeletal pain was a common thread, and painful stomach and skin conditions showed up too.
Pain isn’t the only hidden driver. Merck lists kidney and liver disease, neurologic disease and hormone disorders, including adrenal and thyroid problems, among the medical causes that can lead to aggression. Heritage Veterinary Hospital’s behavior page gives the everyday version: a sudden change in personality might trace back to abnormal thyroid levels.
Back to the shepherd in Grover. Nine years old, never a growl, then a snap when somebody leaned on his hips. That’s the classic shape of a medical case: an older dog, a sudden change, a reaction tied to touching one part of the body. A trainer could spend six weeks teaching him to tolerate handling and never touch the reason he hurts. A vet with an orthopedic exam, and maybe an X-ray, might find it in an afternoon.
Signs that send a case to the vet’s office first:
The behavior started suddenly, or in a senior dog.
It’s tied to touch, lifting, stairs, jumping into the car or lying down.
It comes with changes in appetite, sleep, thirst, gait or bathroom habits.
The dog licks, chews or guards one spot on its body.
A dog who’s been house-trained for years starts having accidents.
The authors of that 2020 paper push vets to err on the side of caution. When pain is suspected, they argue, it’s worth watching how the dog responds to a trial of pain medication, even if no specific injury turns up. If your dog’s behavior lines up with any of the signs above, ask your vet about that directly. And if the cost of the exam is what’s holding you back, our guide to low-cost vet care in St. Louis lists clinics and programs that keep it affordable.
### What should you do the day your dog bites someone?
Separate the dog, make sure the person gets care, and be straight with everyone who needs to know. Then start the clock on two things: a 10-day observation period and a behavior plan.
Confine the dog behind a closed door or in a crate while adrenaline is high. Get the injured person’s name and number, share yours, and have your dog’s rabies certificate ready. The CDC says even a vaccinated animal should be observed for 10 days after it bites or scratches a person. Where that observation happens, and who has to be told, depends on whether you live in the City or the County, and our guide to animal control in St. Louis City vs. County sorts out which office takes the call.
Then the part that feels backward. Don’t punish the dog for the bite, and never punish a growl. Merck says punishment isn’t helpful and may be counterproductive, and behavior professionals warn that a dog punished for growling can learn to skip the warning. The next bite then arrives without one.
Start muzzle training this week, before you need it. A basket muzzle, introduced slowly with treats until the dog pokes its nose in on its own, gets you through vet visits and walks safely while the real work happens. And book the vet visit and the behavior professional now, while the details are fresh. The questionnaire will ask exactly what happened in the two seconds before the bite. Write it down tonight.
The owners with the best outcomes usually noticed early, called the right tier and kept notes. You’re reading this, so you’ve already done the first one.
Ready to build a shortlist? Start with dog trainers and behavior consultants around St. Louis, and ask each one which credential they hold and how they work with your vet.
And if you’re the CBCC-KA, CDBC or CSAT these owners are hunting for, list your behavior practice with us with your credential and the cases you take spelled out up front, since that’s the first thing a worried owner checks.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What does a behaviorist do for a dog?
A.  Figures out why the dog does what it does, then builds a plan to change it. That means a long history, watching the dog, checking for medical causes, and writing a plan built from management, behavior modification and, when a veterinarian is involved, sometimes medication. Then the behaviorist coaches you, since you’re the one running the plan at home. A board-certified veterinary behaviorist can diagnose and prescribe. A certified behavior consultant can’t, and works alongside your vet.
### Q. Is a dog behaviorist worth it?
A.  For aggression, separation panic or fear that runs a dog’s life, usually yes. The American College of Veterinary Behaviorists names behavior problems as a leading cause of dogs and cats being surrendered to U.S. shelters. In St. Louis, a credentialed trainer’s first behavior evaluation can run about $150, while a specialist’s first year can pass $1,450 before medication. Either is cheaper than a bite, a lost lease or giving up a dog you love.
### Q. How much do vet behaviorists cost?
A.  Published first-visit fees run about $600 to $700. Tufts lists $605 for a 90-minute consult, and a Michigan specialty practice lists $665 for a two-hour dog consult, with rechecks at $197 to $305. With rechecks every two to three months, the first year runs roughly $1,450 to $1,850 before medication. Ask your St. Louis vet about a vet-to-vet consult with a Diplomate, which can save you the drive.
### Q. Can fear aggression be trained out of a dog?
A.  It can usually be improved a lot, and it’s rarely erased. The realistic goal is a dog who feels less afraid of its triggers and a bite risk pushed as low as it’ll go, with management like gates, distance and a muzzle kept in place where needed. Behavior modification does the heavy lifting, and medication sometimes helps. Punishment doesn’t. Merck warns that physical punishment can make an aggressive dog worse.
### Q. What is the most common behavioral disorder in dogs?
A.  Aggression. The Merck Veterinary Manual says the most common behavior problems in dogs are the ones associated with aggression, and that most cases involve a dog trying to put distance between itself and a situation. Separation anxiety, thunderstorm and noise phobias, and compulsive habits like tail chasing also show up on the common-problem lists that St. Louis vet hospitals publish on their behavior pages.
### Q. What dog breed has the most behavior problems?
A.  Breed predicts far less than people think. A 2022 study in Science, drawing on thousands of dogs in the Darwin’s Ark project, found breed explains only about 9 percent of the variation in behavior between individual dogs. History, socialization, pain and handling matter more. St. Louis City and St. Louis County see it the same way: both handle dangerous dogs by behavior, not breed.
### Q. At what age are dogs worst behaved?
A.  Adolescence, around eight months old for many dogs. A 2020 study in Biology Letters found the odds of a dog repeatedly ignoring “sit” from its own caregiver were about twice as high at eight months as at five. Like a human teenager, the dog is going through a stage. Keep training through it, keep the rewards generous, and don’t read a stubborn eight-month-old as a dog who’s broken.
### Q. Can my regular vet prescribe anxiety medication for my dog?
A.  Yes. Any licensed veterinarian can prescribe behavior medication, and some St. Louis general practices advertise behavior consultations. Medication works best alongside a behavior modification plan, never in place of one. For a complicated case, ask your vet to consult a board-certified veterinary behaviorist by phone, which the ACVB says many Diplomates will do. Expect regular rechecks for as long as your dog takes it.

## Service Dogs and Emotional Support Animals in Missouri: The 2026 Landlord Shift, Real ESA Letters, Fake Vests
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/service-dogs-and-emotional-support-animals-in-missouri
Twenty-four hours and about a hundred dollars. That’s the pitch from some of the emotional support animal letter sites that show up when you search for Missouri ESA rules, and several of them still close the sale with the same promise: no pet deposit, no pet rent, no landlord allowed to say no. The federal guidance that promise leaned on is gone. HUD withdrew it on September 17, 2025. On May 22, 2026, the head of its fair housing office told investigators to back animal complaints only when the animal is trained to do something for the person’s disability.
Service dogs have the opposite problem. Anyone can order a vest and an official-looking ID card online, and Missouri got tired enough of it in 2020 to make putting that vest on a pet a crime. The people paying for every fake are the handlers whose dogs are real: the ones a St. Louis nonprofit spends $40,000 to $50,000 to raise and train, then places after a wait that can run two years.
Here’s how the three kinds of animals, three federal laws and Missouri’s own statutes sort out as of October 2026. It’s plain English, not legal advice, so if your lease or your dog’s access is on the line, talk to a lawyer or a fair housing agency first. Looking for where your everyday, untrained dog is welcome instead? Start with dog-friendly places in St. Louis.
### Can a landlord deny an emotional support animal in Missouri?
Yes, in more cases than most ESA websites admit. A Missouri landlord can refuse an emotional support animal without reliable documentation, when the animal threatens safety or property, or in an owner-occupied building of four units or fewer. And since May 2026, HUD has stopped bringing charges over untrained ESAs, though tenants can still sue.
Start with what hasn’t changed. The federal Fair Housing Act and the Missouri Human Rights Act both require a housing provider to make reasonable accommodations in its rules when a person with a disability needs one to use and enjoy a home. Waiving a no-pets rule is the textbook case. For years, HUD guidance stretched that to untrained emotional support animals, pet fees waived, and many courts went along.
Then HUD rescinded its 2013 and 2020 assistance animal notices on September 17, 2025, and its May 22, 2026, enforcement memo finished the job. HUD now finds reasonable cause only when an animal is individually trained to do work or perform tasks tied to the person’s disability. The memo says untrained ESAs account for more than 20% of its fair housing complaints, and it promises a formal rule matching the ADA’s definition, with no date attached.
What the memo didn’t do matters as much. Congress didn’t amend the Fair Housing Act, state law is untouched, and the memo itself says a tenant can still sue within two years of a denial. A renter with an untrained ESA lost the cheapest way to enforce the right, a HUD investigation, without losing the right. Landlords’ own lawyers are warning them that denying every ESA request is still a legal risk.
Under any reading, a landlord can say no when:
The disability or the need for the animal isn’t obvious, and you won’t provide reliable documentation of both.
This particular animal poses a direct threat to other people’s safety, or would cause substantial damage, and no other accommodation fixes that.
The request would impose an undue financial and administrative burden, or fundamentally change how the housing operates.
The building is exempt from fair housing law in the first place.
That last one is the St. Louis surprise. Both the Fair Housing Act and the Missouri Human Rights Act exempt a building of four or fewer units when the owner lives in one, plus some single-family houses an owner rents out without an agent. That covers a lot of the two-family and four-family flats this city is built on. A landlord living upstairs in his own two-family flat may owe you no ESA accommodation under either law, though the ban on discriminatory ads still applies. Federally assisted housing also answers to Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, which the memo says it doesn’t address.
Trained dogs stand on firmer Missouri ground. A state law on the books since 1977, RSMo 209.190, gives a person who is blind, deaf or physically disabled full and equal access to rental housing with a guide dog, hearing dog or service dog, bars the landlord from charging extra for the dog, and exempts only a homeowner renting out a single room. No Missouri statute says anything like that about emotional support animals.
Illinois does. Take a renter in Okawville whose therapist of three years wrote a letter for her cat. Under Illinois’ Assistance Animal Integrity Act, in force since 2020, a qualifying assistance animal can’t be charged a pet deposit, pet fee or other pet assessment, even in a building that charges everyone else. Then she takes a job downtown and rents across the river. Same cat. Same letter. Missouri has no statute like that, HUD stopped backing untrained-animal complaints in May, and her new landlord may slide the pet addendum across the table anyway. Before you sign one, read our guide to renting with pets in St. Louis.
One more catch. The Governor’s Council on Disability publishes the landlord and tenant flyer that state law requires, and as of October 2026 it still says tenants pay no fee or deposit for an assistance animal, emotional support animals included, and can file with HUD. That’s the withdrawn HUD guidance talking, so don’t treat the flyer as the last word.
If a Missouri landlord turns you down, get the denial in writing. You have 180 days to file with the Missouri Commission on Human Rights, one year to file with HUD, which still takes trained-animal cases, and two years to sue under the Fair Housing Act. Paraquad, the St. Louis center for independent living, does disability rights advocacy and referral if you need help choosing.
### Service dog, ESA or therapy dog: what is the legal difference?
A trained task. A service dog is individually trained to do specific work for its handler’s disability. An emotional support animal helps simply by being there and needs no training at all. A therapy dog is a pet trained to comfort other people in hospitals and schools. Only the first one gets into restaurants, stores and airplane cabins by right.
The ADA sets the definition, and the Justice Department’s examples are concrete: guiding a person who is blind, alerting a person who is deaf, pulling a wheelchair, protecting someone during a seizure, calming a person with PTSD during an anxiety attack. Comfort alone doesn’t count. Under the ADA a service animal is also a dog, with a separate rule for trained miniature horses, while an emotional support animal can be a cat, a rabbit or a parakeet.
The line people trip over is anxiety, so the Justice Department drew it with an example. If a dog has been trained to sense an anxiety attack coming and take a specific action to head it off or blunt it, that’s a service animal. If the dog’s presence is what helps, it isn’t. The difference is whether somebody taught the dog to do something.
Picture two retired airmen near Scott Air Force Base, both with PTSD from the same deployment. The first one’s Labrador is trained to wake him from nightmares and to plant itself between him and whoever crowds him in a checkout line. The second one’s mutt sleeps at the foot of his bed, and he sleeps better for it. Same diagnosis. Same relief at 3 a.m. Only the first dog does a trained job, so only the first is a service dog, and in 2026 that difference follows both men to the leasing office.
Missouri’s definition, in RSMo 209.200, uses the same task test and names the familiar types, from guide and hearing dogs to psychiatric service dogs. It also lists two most people have never heard of: a dog trained to keep a person with a mental disability, autism included, from getting lost, and a professional therapy dog that works with a trained handler as part of that person’s profession. Volunteer visiting dogs are expressly left out, certified or not.
Volunteer therapy dogs are the odd category: more formal training than most pets, fewer legal rights than either of the others. Duo Dogs’ therapy teams, for example, finish a six-week obedience class, a six-week prep class and twelve weeks of therapy training before visiting approved hospitals, schools and libraries. Off the clock, the dog is a pet with no more right to enter a restaurant than the beagle next door.
### Where can a service dog go that an ESA can’t?
Nearly everywhere the public goes. A service dog can enter stores, restaurants, hotels, hospitals and city and county offices in St. Louis, and ride in the airplane cabin. An emotional support animal has no public access right anywhere. It goes where pets go, and that’s it.
When it isn’t obvious what a dog does, staff may ask exactly two questions: is the dog a service animal required because of a disability, and what work or task has it been trained to perform. No questions about your disability, no ID card or training papers, no demonstration. Allergies and fear of dogs aren’t valid reasons to refuse, and a business can’t charge a pet fee for a service dog, though it can bill for real damage.
The handler’s side is control. The dog must be leashed, harnessed or tethered unless that interferes with its work or the disability prevents it, and staff can remove it for only two reasons: it’s out of control and the handler doesn’t fix it, or it isn’t housebroken.
Restaurants and grocery stores must generally admit service dogs in public areas even where health codes ban animals, self-serve lines included. The dog stays on the floor, though, never on a chair or in a cart. Churches are the big exception, since religious organizations are exempt from the ADA.
Hotels can’t steer a service dog into pet rooms, charge a cleaning fee for dog hair, or let the guest leave it alone in the room. Emotional support animals get whatever the hotel’s pet policy says, and local chains split on that, as our guide to pet-friendly hotels in St. Louis lays out fee by fee.
Missouri goes one step past federal law on training. The ADA doesn’t cover a dog that’s still learning, but RSMo 209.152 lets a trainer from a recognized training center bring a dog in training into the same public places at no extra charge. That’s why you may see a young Lab in a program cape learning the cereal aisle.
Flying is where the ESA era ended first. The Department of Transportation’s Air Carrier Access Act rule, in effect since January 2021, says an emotional support animal isn’t a service animal, so airlines may treat an ESA as a pet, which usually means a carrier and a pet fee, if they take pets at all. For a trained service dog, an airline can require DOT forms on its health, behavior and training, up to 48 hours before departure on an advance booking, cap you at two dogs and require the dog to fit in your foot space. It must treat a psychiatric service dog like any other. Check your airline’s current rules before you fly out of St. Louis Lambert International Airport.
And a service dog is still a dog to animal control. The Justice Department says service animals follow the same local vaccination and licensing rules as any dog, so the requirements in our guide to pet laws in St. Louis City and County apply to a working Lab too.
### What makes an ESA letter legitimate?
A real professional relationship. A legitimate ESA letter comes from a licensed health care or mental health professional who actually knows you and your condition, says in writing that you have a disability, and explains how the animal helps with it. A certificate, an ID card or a spot on an online registry is none of those things.
Start with the registries, because they’re pure decoration. There is no official government registry for service dogs or emotional support animals. The Justice Department says the certificates and registrations sold online convey no rights under the ADA, and it doesn’t accept them as proof that a dog is a service animal.
Missouri’s law speaks to the letter itself. Under RSMo 209.204, assistance animal documentation has to come from a qualified professional as the Fair Housing Act allows, and it’s a crime to knowingly create or hand out a document falsely calling an animal an assistance animal, or to knowingly lie to a health care provider about a material fact to get one. Read that last part twice. In Missouri, gaming your own therapist for a letter is a misdemeanor.
Illinois wrote the clearest test into law, and it’s a good yardstick on either side of the river. Its Assistance Animal Integrity Act wants the documentation in writing, from someone with a therapeutic relationship with you, describing your disability-related need for the animal. An outfit that issues a certificate without a meaningful assessment doesn’t count. The letter doesn’t have to name a diagnosis, and a landlord may verify that it’s authentic.
HUD noticed the overnight-letter business too. Its May 2026 memo footnoted a seller’s promise of an ESA letter in 24 hours as evidence that a whole industry had grown up to turn pets into emotional support animals.
A letter that holds up usually has these:
The writer’s license type, number and issuing state, so a landlord can look it up.
A writer who treats you now or evaluated you meaningfully, not a quiz with a checkout button.
A plain statement that you have a disability and how the animal helps with it. The diagnosis itself can stay private.
The animal you’re asking about.
A date, and contact details that reach the actual writer.
Now the honest part the letter sellers skip. In 2026, even a flawless letter carries less federal weight for an untrained animal than it did a year ago. It’s still your best evidence before the Missouri Commission on Human Rights or a judge, and one from a clinician who has treated you for two years will hold up far better there than one bought overnight.
And if your animal could be trained to do something specific for your disability, like interrupting a panic attack or waking you from a night terror, that trained task moves you from the weakest category to the strongest in housing, public places and airplane cabins at once.
### What happens if you fake a service dog or ESA in Missouri?
It’s a crime. Under RSMo 209.204, knowingly passing off a dog as a service dog, or any animal as an assistance animal for housing, is a class C misdemeanor, punishable by up to 15 days in jail and a $750 fine, plus civil liability for any actual damages. A second offense is a class B misdemeanor, with up to six months and $1,000.
The statute lists what counts, and it’s specific. For service dogs:
Knowingly creating documents that falsely say a dog is a service dog.
Knowingly giving someone else documents that say so.
Knowingly fitting a dog that isn’t a service dog with a harness, collar, vest or sign of the type service dog handlers use.
Knowingly calling a dog a service dog when it hasn’t finished training to do disability-related work or tasks.
The housing version covers any animal passed off as an assistance animal, with the same clauses plus the one about lying to a health care provider. Another makes it a crime to pretend to have a disability to get service dog accommodations. All of it took its current shape in 2020.
Look closely at the vest clause. In Missouri the vest isn’t evidence of a crime. Knowingly putting it on a pet is the crime.
Why lawmakers cared shows up one section earlier, in RSMo 209.202. Harassing or chasing a dog you know is a service dog is a class B misdemeanor, and so is knowingly letting your animal chase or harass a working one enough to interfere with its job. Knowingly letting your animal seriously injure or kill one is a class A, with civil damages that can cover an equally trained replacement. When a nonprofit has $40,000 or more in one dog, a fake in a vest lunging at it in the pharmacy line can end a working career.
Business owners get tools from the same statute: it tells the Governor’s Council on Disability to publish a window placard saying service dogs are welcome and misrepresentation breaks Missouri law, plus a brochure on the questions you may ask. Ask the two questions, accept the answers, remove only a dog that’s out of control or not housebroken, and you’ve done what the law asks.
Thank the shop that got it right: support local businesses in St. Louis
### Where do St. Louis service dogs get trained?
Mostly through two local nonprofits, Duo Dogs and CHAMP Assistance Dogs, which place fully trained dogs without charging the client for the dog after an application and a wait, or through owner training, which the ADA allows. Private trainers teach task work too, but Missouri doesn’t license dog trainers, so the vetting is on you.
Duo Dogs has done this in St. Louis since 1984 and is accredited by Assistance Dogs International. It trains Labrador retrievers as mobility dogs, hearing dogs and PTSD dogs for veterans, and says each costs $50,000 to raise and train, none of it passed to the client. Per its FAQ, you pay a $100 application fee, about $400 to $900 for an equipment kit at placement, and $37 for a background check. Mobility and PTSD dogs go to people within 120 miles of its facility on Linpage Place in St. Louis County, and there’s no fixed wait time. The retired airman near Scott Air Force Base fits its PTSD program on both counts.
CHAMP Assistance Dogs, based in northwest St. Louis County, puts nearly $40,000 into each dog and also places at no cost to the recipient, under tighter rules. Applicants need a physical disability other than loss of vision or hearing, must live within 50 miles of its office, and in almost all cases need a physically fenced yard. No new pets during the application or for a year after. Public access dogs go to adults and are recertified yearly. CHAMP doesn’t place seizure or diabetic alert dogs, and it puts the average wait at about two years.
Run those two maps from the Illinois side. Say you live in Albers, and multiple sclerosis has turned dropped keys and heavy doors into a daily fight. Duo’s 120-mile radius takes you in easily. CHAMP’s 50-mile circle puts Albers close enough to its edge that you should call and ask before you assume you’re in or out. Apply to both, and use the wait to get the yard, the vet and the routine ready.
Owner training is legal too, since the ADA doesn’t require a professional program. The hard part is the in-between months. A dog in training has no ADA access right, and Missouri’s training access in RSMo 209.152 is written for trainers from a recognized training center and members of a trained service dog team. An owner working alone with a half-trained dog isn’t clearly covered, so practice in pet-friendly places until the dog is finished.
Hiring a private trainer for task work? Get three things in writing before any deposit: the specific tasks, how public access manners will be tested, and what happens to your money if the dog washes out. CHAMP’s public access dogs pass the Assistance Dogs International public access test, a fair benchmark to ask about. A dog that reacts to strangers or other dogs usually needs a dog behaviorist in St. Louis long before it needs a vest. For what ordinary obedience runs, see our breakdown of dog training cost in St. Louis.
The vest, the certificate and the overnight letter are the three things that never made an animal legitimate. A trained task and a professional who knows you are the two that do. Walk in with both.
Ready to start on task work, or just on manners? Look through dog trainers around St. Louis, and ask each one for a written task plan and how they test public access before you put money down.
And if you run a dog training business, list it with us and say up front whether you teach disability-related tasks, public access skills or both.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What qualifies you for emotional support animal?
A.  A disability plus a disability-related need for the animal. Under fair housing law, a disability is a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits a major life activity, and a licensed professional who knows you has to say both things in writing. A diagnosis that doesn’t limit your daily life isn’t enough, and neither is loving your dog.
### Q. Do landlords verify ESA letters?
A.  Many do, and they’re allowed to. A Missouri landlord can check a Missouri license on the state’s MOPRO license search, call the writer, and ask follow-up questions when the letter doesn’t establish both a disability and the need. Illinois law says outright that landlords may verify authenticity. A letter from an out-of-state provider who never treated you draws a second look.
### Q. What disqualifies a dog from being an emotional support animal?
A.  Behavior, mostly. There’s no breed or training test for an ESA, but a landlord can refuse a specific animal that poses a direct threat to others or causes substantial damage that no other accommodation fixes. A dog that has bitten a neighbor gives a landlord the cleanest reason to say no. So does a request with no documented disability-related need behind it.
### Q. Does anxiety qualify for an emotional support animal?
A.  It can, if it rises to a disability, meaning it substantially limits things like sleeping, working or concentrating, and a professional who treats you documents that. If your dog is trained to do something specific when anxiety hits, like interrupting a panic attack, it may be a psychiatric service dog instead, with stronger rights in housing, stores and airplane cabins.
### Q. Can you just say your dog is an emotional support animal?
A.
