It works at city scale. Denver made hazing its main response to coyote problems, and its parks department reported that direct encounters between people and coyotes fell more than 75 percent from 2009 to 2010, as MDC’s magazine recounted.
Three habits keep hazing safe and effective. Stay big, loud and visible until the coyote actually leaves, because a half-hearted shout it ignores teaches the wrong lesson. Never corner it; you want a coyote that chooses to leave, not one pinned against a fence. And skip hazing a parent near an active den in spring. Change your route instead.
If one stands its ground, don’t run. Colorado Parks and Wildlife’s guidance is to face the coyote, get as big and loud as you can, and back away slowly if it still won’t leave. The warning signs of real aggression are raised hackles, bared teeth and growling. A coyote showing those, or one that keeps approaching people after repeated hazing, is the one to report.
Then recruit the neighbors. Hazing works best as a block-wide habit. If one house yells and the next leaves kibble on the porch, the coyote learns the second lesson. Which brings us back to that Facebook thread. One post asking everybody to bring in pet food, hold the trash until pickup morning and blow an air horn on sight will do more than two hundred comments about calling someone.
### What does Missouri law allow you to do about a coyote?
More than you’d expect on a farm, and much less than you’d expect in town. Missouri treats the coyote as a furbearer and game mammal, and for 2026 the hunting season runs all year with no daily limit for small game permit holders, with catches: no daylight hunting from April 1 until spring turkey season opens, turkey methods and an unfilled turkey permit during turkey season, and an unfilled deer permit for daylight hunting in the November firearms deer portion. New this year, artificial light, night vision and thermal gear are legal for coyotes January 1 through September 30, except during spring turkey season. Trapping runs November 15, 2026 through February 28, 2027, plus a private-land extension from March 1 to April 14 for foot-hold, foot-enclosing and cage traps only. The dates move every year, so check MDC’s current regulations first.
Out of season, there’s the landowner rule. Under 3 CSR 10-4.130 of the Wildlife Code, wildlife that is, beyond reasonable doubt, damaging property may be shot or trapped by the property owner or a representative at any time without a permit, on the owner’s property only. Two strings come attached. Anything captured or killed has to be reported to an MDC agent within 24 hours, and it’s disposed of only as the agent instructs. Trapping a coyote and quietly letting it go in a park isn’t your call to make.
Picture a small hobby farm outside Richwoods where a coyote has started taking chickens. That’s the case the rule was written for: damage beyond reasonable doubt, on the owner’s land, in unincorporated country. The same coyote in a city backyard is a different legal animal.
In town, gunfire is the problem. Missouri’s Blair’s Law, in effect since August 28, 2024, makes it a crime to recklessly fire a gun within or into the limits of any municipality, a class A misdemeanor the first time. Its exceptions include hunting during an open season, nuisance-wildlife control as permitted by MDC, defending a pet from an attack that’s actually underway, and shooting more than a mile from any occupied building, and even the hunting exception lets a city restrict gunfire within a quarter mile of an occupied structure. Cities stack their own rules on top. St. Louis updated its illegal-discharge ordinance in November 2024, city police have reminded residents that firing a gun inside city limits is illegal, and MU Extension notes that most cities have ordinances against shooting. A coyote trotting down a south city alley isn’t a hunting opportunity.
Trapping in town has its own fences. In Missouri communities of 10,000 people or more, only cage-type or foot-enclosing traps may be set within 150 feet of a home or occupied building. Snares on dry land are illegal without MDC authorization, and no trap may go in a path used by people or pets. MDC’s biologists add that coyote traps can catch cats, dogs or even children, which makes them unsafe in populated areas, and that most coyotes are too wary to walk into a cage trap anyway. MDC’s hunting and trapping rules also say furbearer dens aren’t to be molested or destroyed, so if you find one under your deck, call MDC before you touch it.
And the biggest legal hammer may not fix anything. Remove the coyote and another takes the spot. That’s why MDC and MU Extension put food removal, fencing and hazing first, and save lethal control for specific animals doing specific damage. This is a plain-language summary rather than legal advice; for your address, ask MDC and your local police department.
### Who do you call about a coyote in St. Louis?
It depends on what the coyote is doing. One passing through, or showing up now and then, needs no call at all. Haze it and fix the food.
A coyote that keeps hanging around, acts bold or is causing real trouble is MDC’s department. The St. Louis Regional Office answers at 636-441-4554. MDC’s coyote control page says your county conservation agent can usually name a local trapper, and the regional wildlife damage biologist can sometimes help with instruction or equipment. MU Extension notes that MDC’s wildlife damage program has served Missourians since 1945 and often makes traps and scare devices available at cost.
A sick, injured or threatening coyote depends on where you live. In the City, file a report through the Citizens’ Service Bureau; City Animal Care and Control says it doesn’t respond to nuisance wildlife but will respond to injured wildlife or wildlife that poses a safety or health issue. In the County, animal control points residents with outdoor wildlife to the Bi-State Wildlife Hotline at 636-492-1610 and to MDC. Our breakdown of animal control in St. Louis City vs. County sorts out which agency covers your address. If a person is hurt, call 911.
If your pet is hurt, go to a vet now, even if the wound looks small. That same emergency-vet group warns that small puncture wounds can hide deeper injury and infection, and a wild-animal bite can mean a rabies booster. Press a clean cloth firmly on any bleeding, add layers rather than lifting the soaked one, and drive. Never reach in with bare hands to break up a fight; use a hose, a stick or a trash can lid. After hours, here’s how to find an emergency vet in St. Louis.
For hands-on work, like coyote-proofing a fence line or a trapper for a rural property, City Animal Care and Control itself suggests a pest control company. Ask whether they handle coyotes, which traps they use near homes, and whether they report to MDC as the Wildlife Code requires.
Coyotes aren’t leaving St. Louis. The ones that last here are the ones that learned where the easy meals are. Be the house on the block that taught them yours isn’t one.
Need hands-on help with a den under the deck or a yard that needs coyote-proofing? Start with wildlife and pest control companies around St. Louis and ask whether they take coyote calls before you book.
And if you run a wildlife removal or exclusion company, the pet owners reading this want to know whether you work through April and May and which Missouri trap rules you follow, so list your wildlife control business with us with your service area and coyote work spelled out.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What month are coyotes most aggressive?
A.  In Missouri, April and May. MDC says conflicts between people and urban coyotes peak then because parents are feeding pups, and coyotes with pups sometimes turn aggressive toward dogs that come near a den. Breeding season in February and early March brings more sightings and howling, but less trouble.
### Q. Can you shoot coyotes anytime in Missouri?
A.  Not quite. The 2026 season is open all year with no limit for permit holders, but daylight hunting closes from April 1 until spring turkey season opens, and turkey and deer seasons add method rules. A coyote damaging your property can be taken on your own land without a permit if you report it to MDC within 24 hours. Inside city limits, state law and local ordinances usually make firing a gun illegal.
### Q. What smell do coyotes hate the most?
A.  None has proven reliable. MDC lists repellents for coyotes as not recommended because none are known to be effective, and MU Extension says home remedies like ammonia and urine haven’t been scientifically proven. Taking away food, cover and easy access works better than any smell.
### Q. Will motion lights scare coyotes?
A.  For a while. MU Extension calls frightening devices a short-term fix, and a light that flicks on with nothing else happening stops meaning much. Use motion lights to check the yard before your pet goes out, which fits MDC’s advice to keep pet areas well lit, and back the light up with a person making noise.
### Q. Will a coyote chase you if you run?
A.  Don’t give it the chance. Colorado Parks and Wildlife says not to run or turn your back on a coyote. Face it, be big and loud, and back away slowly if it doesn’t leave. Most coyotes retreat from a confident person. With a small dog along, pick the dog up first.
### Q. What is a coyote’s weakness?
A.  Its caution. MDC’s coyote booklet says coyotes that are hunted and trapped stay very wary of people, and city coyotes lose that wariness when nobody pushes back. Hazing rebuilds it. They’re also smaller than people expect: MDC puts Missouri coyotes at 18 to 30 pounds.
### Q. Can a coyote jump a 6-foot fence?
A.  Some can. MDC’s yard advice is a fence at least six feet high and dug six inches into the ground, and its livestock guide calls for woven wire at least seven feet tall when a fence has to be truly predator-proof. Rollers on the top rail help. Supervise small pets anyway, because a fence slows a coyote down more than it guarantees anything.
### Q. Are coyotes dangerous to people in St. Louis?
A.  Rarely. MDC’s coyote booklet says there have been no documented cases of coyotes attacking people in Missouri. Never feed one, keep small children supervised where coyotes are active, and report any coyote that approaches people or won’t leave when hazed to MDC’s St. Louis office at 636-441-4554.

## Dog Bakeries in St. Louis: Custom Dog Cakes, Homemade Treats and What Not to Buy
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/dog-bakeries-in-st-louis
Stale map listings are still sending St. Louis dog owners to a bakery that isn’t there. Search for a dog bakery in St. Louis and two of the top results point to a Three Dog Bakery at Town and Country Crossing, hours and all. A shopping-center directory marks that store as closed, and the chain’s own store finder now lists exactly one Missouri bakery, near Kansas City. If you’ve ever pulled into a parking lot with a birthday dog in the back seat and found an empty storefront, that wasn’t bad planning. That was a bad list.
The second trap is closer to home. It’s the slice of people cake sitting on the counter after the kids’ party. The FDA warns that xylitol, a sugar substitute that can also go by birch sugar or wood sugar, turns up in cakes, muffins and pies, especially sugar-free ones, and that in-store bakeries sell baked goods made with it. In a dog it can crash blood sugar within 10 to 60 minutes. Chocolate frosting and raisin filling bring their own trouble. A real dog cake skips all of it, and the St. Louis area has more people baking them than the listings let on.
So here’s the plan. Where to order a custom dog cake, which shops actually bake in-house, what a dog-safe cake is made of, which treats to leave on the shelf, the Missouri rule that tells you a homemade treat is legit, and how to run a birthday your dog will enjoy. It’s one piece of our bigger guide to dog-friendly places in St. Louis. Prices and hours below come from each business’s own pages as of October 2026. All of them change, so check before you drive.
### Where can I get a custom dog cake?
Order from a pet bakery that bakes in-house. Treats Unleashed makes personalized dog cakes at its St. Louis-area stores with at least 24 hours’ notice, and Four Muddy Paws in Lafayette Square bakes custom cakes for in-store pickup. Ask what the frosting is made of, and skip any bakery cake made for people.
Treats Unleashed is the easy place to start, because it’s close to almost everybody. The family-owned chain began in 2002 as a small mall kiosk in St. Louis selling a single batch of Apple Cinnamon Heart treats, and its locations page now lists 15 stores around the metro, from the Central West End out to Wentzville, Wildwood and Oakville. Every store bakes on site. Cakes are made to order, need at least 24 hours’ notice before pickup, and go out for pickup or local delivery only. They don’t ship.
The menu is short, and refreshingly clear. On the chain’s website in October 2026, a personalized mini bone cake, roughly 8.5 by 4.75 inches with a message of three words or fewer, listed at $16.99. A personalized 6-inch round listed at $19.99 and a 10-inch bone at $24.99. A birthday bundle with a cake, a party hat, a bandana sewn by a local crafter and a plush cake toy listed at $39.99. The cake itself is honey, wheat flour, white flour, canola oil, oats, whey and eggs, finished with peanut butter, carob or a vanilla yogurt shell, and the store says it keeps a week in the fridge or a month in the freezer. Confirm the price when you order. Bakery prices drift.
Four Muddy Paws, a healthy-pet market at 1711 Park Avenue in Lafayette Square, bakes its own treats from scratch and lists fresh-baked custom cakes, with a birthday bone cake at $16.99 in its online shop. One catch matters for planning: the store says its custom cakes are in-store pickup only and aren’t eligible for its delivery service. The shop opened in 2004 and changed hands in 2025, when longtime manager Stephanie Windsor and her husband, Jesse, took over from the founders. Call (314) 773-7297 and ask about lead time before you pin a party to a specific day.
Whoever bakes it, ask three questions before you pay. What’s in the frosting? How long does it keep? And can they write the dog’s name in fewer letters than you were planning, because a mini cake fits about three words and a Great Dane’s full registered name won’t fit on anything.
### Where are the dog bakeries in St. Louis?
Fewer than the search results suggest, and not always where they say. Here’s what checked out in October 2026, with what each place actually sells. Treat every hour and price as a starting point.
Treats Unleashed, 15 metro stores. Treats and custom cakes baked in every store; the chain lists hours of 9 a.m. to 8 p.m. Monday through Saturday and 9 to 6 on Sunday.
Four Muddy Paws, 1711 Park Avenue, Lafayette Square. Treats baked from scratch, custom cakes for pickup, grooming and a self-serve dog wash. Listed hours run 9 to 7 on weekdays, 9 to 5 Saturday and 10 to 5 Sunday.
Tilted Heads Pet Bakery & Coffee Shop, 2961 Dougherty Ferry Road, Suite 110, Valley Park. A dog bakery with a coffee bar for the humans, open as a storefront since May 2025. Its hours have shifted since opening, so check its social pages first.
Ciao Chow, 1923 Marconi Avenue on The Hill. A small pet shop that lists its specialties as enrichment, nutrition, a homemade bakery and bandanas. Call (314) 410-8377 to ask what’s in the case that day.
Tilted Heads is the one with a story. Co-owner Heather Zumwalt started baking because her German shepherd couldn’t tolerate store-bought treats, according to a December 2025 profile in St. Louis Magazine. She and her husband, Michael Kammer, sold homemade and freeze-dried treats at the Arnold Farmers Market starting in 2021, then opened the Valley Park shop. The case now holds biscuits made with local honey, single-ingredient freeze-dried treats from local farms and butchers, and chicken jerky, next to a pastry case for people and a full coffee menu. Zumwalt’s motto, per that profile: “Canines, caffeine, and chaos.”
Here’s a detail almost nobody on the Illinois side knows. Tilted Heads’ own website says it can sell its treats only to Missouri residents, because every state sets its own requirements for selling dog treats, and that its treats are lab tested and registered with the Missouri Department of Agriculture. So a family in Worden planning a birthday for a gray-muzzled Lab should ask before counting on a Missouri bakery for an online order. The paperwork stops at the river, in both directions. More on why in a minute.
And the bakery the map listings keep sending people to? Three Dog Bakery, the chain founded in Kansas City in 1989 that bills itself as the original bakery for dogs, did have a franchise at Town and Country Crossing. That storefront is the one a shopping-center directory now marks closed, and the chain’s store finder shows a single Missouri location, on the Kansas City side of the state. Its packaged treats still turn up in big-box pet aisles and online. The St. Louis bakery counter doesn’t.
Shopping for more than cake? Our sibling guide on where to buy pet supplies in St. Louis covers the stores for food, chews and everything else on the list.
### What goes into a dog-safe birthday cake?
Flour, oats, eggs, a little honey or fruit, and a frosting made from peanut butter, plain yogurt or carob. That’s the whole trick. A dog cake is a dense, barely sweet muffin wearing a party hat, and its ingredient list should read like one.
Look again at that Treats Unleashed cake: honey, two flours, canola oil, oats, whey and eggs, with no added salt or refined sugar, per the store. The frosting choices are peanut butter, carob or vanilla yogurt. Each one stands in for something from a people cake that doesn’t belong in a dog.
Carob instead of chocolate. Chocolate carries methylxanthines, theobromine and caffeine, which the ASPCA says can cause vomiting, panting, an abnormal heart rhythm, tremors, seizures and even death in dogs, with dark and baking chocolate the most dangerous. Carob comes from the pod of a Mediterranean tree. It looks and bakes like cocoa without the theobromine and caffeine, which is why dog bakers reach for it.
Peanut butter instead of buttercream. Dogs love it, and plain peanut butter is fine in small amounts. The catch is the jar. The FDA lists some peanut and nut butters among products that may contain xylitol, so the label should say peanuts, maybe salt, and nothing sweeter.
Yogurt or pumpkin instead of sugar frosting. Plain yogurt and pure pumpkin add color and a little tang. Go easy on the dairy, though. The ASPCA notes pets don’t make much lactase, the enzyme that breaks down milk sugar, so a big helping can mean an upset stomach.
Baking at home works if you keep it that simple. A retired couple in Benld making a cake for their terrier’s eighth birthday really needs four things: whole wheat or oat flour, an egg, plain pumpkin or mashed banana, and a spoonful of xylitol-free peanut butter. Bake it in a muffin tin so every dog gets one portion and nobody fights over the corner piece. Frost with plain yogurt. Skip sprinkles and candy decorations, and skip anything from the baking aisle labeled sugar-free.
Then cut small. The American Kennel Club’s rule of thumb is that treats should make up no more than 10 percent of a dog’s daily calories, and birthday cake counts. Its own example: a small dog eating about 182 calories a day has roughly 18 calories to spare for extras. A real slice of party cake blows through that in two bites. That’s why the mini bone cakes exist, and why the muffin tin beats the 9-inch pan.
And the leftover sheet cake from the kids’ party? Put it up high. The FDA’s xylitol warning names cakes, muffins and pies, especially ones where the baker swapped in another sweetener for sugar. Signs start with vomiting and can move to weakness, staggering, collapse and seizures, and the FDA says serious effects sometimes don’t show up for 12 to 24 hours. If your dog gets into anything sugar-free, call your vet or an emergency vet in St. Louis right away, or the ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center at (888) 426-4435, which answers around the clock. The ASPCA says a consultation fee may apply.
### What dog treats are not to buy?
Skip anything with xylitol or birch sugar on the label, processed bone treats, chews too hard to dent with a fingernail, and homemade treats sold without a real label. Add chocolate, grapes, raisins, macadamia nuts, onions and garlic in any form, and you’ve covered most of the emergency visits that start in a treat bag.
Sweeteners that aren’t sugar. The FDA notes xylitol may be listed as birch sugar or wood sugar, and it shows up in sugar-free candy, baked goods, chewable vitamins and some nut butters. A treat made for a dog has no reason to contain it.
Grapes, raisins, macadamias, onions and garlic. The ASPCA links grapes and raisins to kidney damage in dogs and points to tartaric acid as the culprit. Macadamia nuts can cause weakness, vomiting, tremors and overheating within about 12 hours. Onions and garlic can damage red blood cells. Trail mix and anything oatmeal-raisin stay people food.
Processed bone treats. In 2017 the FDA warned owners about smoked or baked bone treats sold in packages, after about 68 reports involving roughly 90 dogs, about 15 of which died. The reported problems included choking, blockages in the gut, cuts in the mouth and bleeding. Products in the reports carried names like Ham Bones, Rib Bones and Smokey Knuckle Bones.
Chews harder than teeth. Veterinary Dental Specialists of Missouri in O’Fallon, whose Dr. Robert Ulbricht is Missouri’s first board-certified veterinary dentist, offers a simple test on its website. Press your fingernail into the chew. If it dents, it’s flexible enough. If your nail bends and the chew doesn’t, it’s too hard. The practice names antlers, cow hooves and natural bones as some of the most common causes of fractured carnassial teeth, the big shearing teeth toward the back of the mouth.
Mystery bags. A cellophane bag with a ribbon and no ingredient list, no guaranteed analysis and no name or address looks charming at a craft fair. In Missouri it’s missing what the state requires on a treat label. More on that below.
The tooth problem deserves a second look because it’s expensive and quiet. Dogs hide mouth pain well. The O’Fallon practice says a fractured tooth treated within 24 hours can sometimes be saved with vital pulp therapy, and after that the choices are pulling it or a root canal with a metal crown. Compare that with routine care in our guide to dog teeth cleaning cost in St. Louis and the rubber chew starts to look like a bargain.
Got a new puppy? Our checklist of what to buy at a pet store for a new puppy makes the case for holding off on bulk training treats until you learn what this particular dog will work for. Good advice for bakery runs, too. Buy one small bag before you buy the big one.
Garlic toum is for you, not the dog: Lebanese food in St. Louis
### Who is allowed to sell homemade dog treats in Missouri?
Anyone who gets licensed and registers each product. Missouri regulates dog biscuits as commercial feed, under the same law that covers livestock feed, and the Missouri Department of Agriculture’s Feed and Seed Program says its rules apply to anyone making pet food or treats, in a commercial kitchen or in their own home.
Here’s what that means in practice, per the department’s own guide to making and selling pet treats:
A Missouri Commercial Feed License, $35 a year and valid July 1 through June 30, for anyone who makes, distributes or puts their name on pet treats. A store that only resells treats already labeled by a licensed maker doesn’t need one.
Registration of every product sold in packages of 10 pounds or less, at $90 per product per year. A maker whose total gross sales stay at or under $5,000 a year can apply for a reduced $25 fee.
A guaranteed analysis worked up by an animal feed testing lab, listing minimum crude protein and crude fat and maximum crude fiber and moisture, in that order.
A label carrying the product name, the species it’s for, the ingredients in order by weight, feeding directions, the net quantity and the maker’s name and address.
The state backs it up with seven feed inspectors who can walk into manufacturing sites and retail stores, pull samples and send them to the department’s lab. Rawhides and plain bones are generally exempt. That changes the moment the package makes a nutrition claim like “high protein” or “made with real chicken,” at which point the department wants it registered and labeled like any other treat.
Illinois runs a parallel system through its own Department of Agriculture: a $30 license, $90 for each registered product sold in containers of 10 pounds or less, and a label that must say snack or treat and carry a guaranteed analysis. Illinois licenses and registrations expire every December 31, and the state’s FAQ says that even giving treats away counts as distribution. So a baker in Moro who wants to sell pumpkin biscuits at a fall craft fair needs Illinois paperwork. A Missouri license doesn’t carry over.
For buyers, the payoff is a two-second check. Flip the bag over. A treat made under these rules shows a guaranteed analysis and the maker’s name and address. The Treats Unleashed cake listings, for instance, print their guaranteed analysis right on the product page: 6 percent crude protein minimum, 11 percent crude fat minimum, 28 percent moisture maximum. A bag at a market table with none of that may still be lovingly made. It just hasn’t been through what the state asks for, and it’s fair to ask the seller about it.
If you think a treat made your dog sick, the Missouri department lays out the order: call your vet first, check the FDA’s recall list, then file a complaint with the Feed and Seed Program, which you can reach at (573) 751-4310. Keep the bag. A lot number is worth more than a description.
### How do you throw a dog birthday party in St. Louis?
Keep it small, short and out of the heat of the day, with one portion of dog-safe cake per dog and a plan for the humans. Dogs don’t care about the theme. They care about who’s there, what’s on the ground and whether anybody steps on their tail.
Two or three dogs your dog already knows beat a yard full of strangers. Do introductions on neutral ground before the party, not during it. Set out more water bowls than seems necessary, pick up toys that cause guarding, and give one human a single job: watch the dogs’ body language. Party energy in dogs can look a lot like the opening seconds of a scuffle, and a calm person who calls a break early saves the afternoon.
Picture a backyard in Moro on a Saturday morning in May. A shady patch of grass, three dogs, a 6-inch cake cut into three pieces, and everyone headed home before the afternoon warms up. That’s the whole template. Summer changes the math around here, because July and August afternoons wear dogs out fast and pavement soaks up heat. Hot-month parties belong in the morning, in deep shade or indoors.
Want to take the party out? A bakery stop makes a good outing on its own, and Tilted Heads pours coffee next to the dog treats, so the humans are covered. Or book a patio. The patio rules, and the spots that welcome dogs, are in our guide to dog-friendly restaurants in St. Louis. Call ahead with the head count, dogs included. A table for six with four dogs is a different ask than a table for two.
For favors, a bag of biscuits from a local bakery, split into small portions, beats anything mystery-baked. Each dog goes home happy. No owner ends up squinting at a blank label in the car.
Do it this way and you’re the owner who knew which bakery was actually open, ordered the cake two days early and read the label before the candle went in. Your dog won’t know any of that. Your dog will just know it was a very good day.
Planning the shopping trip? Browse pet stores around St. Louis to find the bakery case, the safe chews and the party hat in one stop.
And if you run a dog bakery, list your bakery with us and put your lead time, cake sizes and state registration where owners can see them.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Where can I buy homemade dog treats?
A.  At St. Louis shops that bake in-house. Every Treats Unleashed store bakes daily, Four Muddy Paws in Lafayette Square bakes treats from scratch, Tilted Heads in Valley Park sells honey biscuits and freeze-dried treats, and Ciao Chow on Marconi Avenue lists a homemade bakery. At markets and craft fairs, look for a label with a guaranteed analysis and the maker’s name and address, which Missouri requires.
### Q. What are the cleanest dog treats?
A.  The ones with an ingredient list you can read out loud in one breath. Single-ingredient freeze-dried treats, like chicken or beef, are about as clean as it gets. For baked treats, look for flour, oats, eggs, peanut butter or pumpkin and very little else, with no xylitol and no artificial colors, plus a guaranteed analysis on the label so you know a lab has tested it.
### Q. What is the number one dog treat?
A.  There’s no official ranking. The practical number one is whatever your dog will work hardest for at the fewest calories. For a lot of dogs that’s a pea-sized piece of freeze-dried meat. For others it’s a single piece of their own kibble. Buy two or three small bags and let your dog vote.
### Q. What dog treats do dogs love the most?
A.  Dogs pick with their noses, so strong-smelling, meaty treats usually win: freeze-dried liver or chicken, jerky made for dogs, or a lick of plain, xylitol-free peanut butter. Run a taste test with two or three tiny pieces side by side and watch which one gets the head tilt. Then keep the winner small, since treats should stay under about 10 percent of daily calories.
### Q. What’s the healthiest brand of dog treats?
A.  No single brand wins for every dog. The healthiest treat is the one that fits your dog’s calories, allergies and teeth. Check the calories per treat, keep treats under 10 percent of the day’s calories, favor short ingredient lists, and ask your vet if your dog has a weight, allergy or kidney issue. A local bakery biscuit can hold its own against any national label.
### Q. What are some of the best dog treats made in the USA?
A.  Start with the ones made down the street. Treats Unleashed bakes in each of its stores, and Four Muddy Paws and Tilted Heads bake their own. For packaged treats, flip the bag: Missouri requires the maker’s name and address on a treat label, so you can see who stands behind it and where they’re based. Where it’s made tells you less than what’s in it, so read both.
### Q. Can dogs eat regular birthday cake?
A.  It’s a bad idea. People cake is heavy on sugar and fat, and some versions hide ingredients that are dangerous for dogs: chocolate, raisins, macadamia nuts, or xylitol in sugar-free recipes. The FDA says in-store bakeries sell baked goods made with xylitol. If your dog eats a sugar-free cake, call your vet or the ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center at (888) 426-4435 right away.
### Q. How far ahead should you order a dog birthday cake?
A.  At Treats Unleashed, at least 24 hours before pickup, according to its cake listings. For a weekend party, ordering two or three days ahead is the safer move, since every cake is baked to order. Four Muddy Paws custom cakes are in-store pickup only, so call the Lafayette Square shop at (314) 773-7297 to ask about its lead time.

## Renting With Pets in St. Louis: Pet Rent, Breed Lists and the Deposit Missouri Doesn't Cap
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/renting-with-pets-in-st-louis
The “pet friendly” checkbox on a St. Louis rental listing answers the least useful question you have. Yes, a pet can live there. It doesn’t say which pet, how heavy, how many already live in the building, or what you’ll pay every month for the privilege. And it never mentions the one sentence in Missouri law that decides whether your pet money is protected at all.
That sentence sits at the bottom of RSMo 535.300, the state’s security deposit law. The law caps a deposit at two months’ rent, gives the landlord 30 days to return it with an itemized list, and lets a tenant recover twice whatever is wrongfully withheld. Then its last line says the term security deposit “does not include any money or property denominated as a deposit for a pet on the premises.” That line is written into the statute itself, not tucked into a regulation. So the word on your lease, deposit or fee or rent, quietly decides which rules apply to your money.
Below: what St. Louis landlords actually publish for pets, with the twelve-month math, the breed lists and the insurance bill behind them, and the rules on both sides of the river as of October 2026. It’s plain English, not legal advice, and prices change, so confirm everything in writing before you sign.
### How to find pet friendly rental properties?
Use the rental sites’ pet filters to build a list, then get each landlord’s written pet policy before you pay an application fee: pet limit, weight cap, breed list, deposit, one-time fee and monthly pet rent. Property managers usually have one ready. In the City of St. Louis, also ask how many animals the building already has.
The filters are the easy part. The big listing sites sort for cats, small dogs or large dogs, and that’s about where their help ends. The rules that decide whether your dog gets approved live in the listing remarks or a separate policy page. One St. Louis property management company says on its own help page that pet rules vary by property at the owner’s discretion, and that it may prioritize applicants who don’t have pets. Read that twice before you pay three application fees in one weekend.
So call or email first and ask for the pet policy in writing. A real one answers six questions: how many pets, which species, the weight limit (per pet or combined), the breed list, the one-time money and whether any of it comes back, and the monthly pet rent. If nobody can answer, the owner may never have decided, which can work in your favor.
Then ask a question almost nobody thinks of, because in the City of St. Louis it can matter more than the listing does. City code caps dogs and cats at four per parcel in residential zones. A two-family or four-family flat usually sits on one parcel, so every unit in the building shares those four. If the upstairs tenant has two dogs and the couple downstairs has two cats, a genuinely pet friendly landlord has nothing left to give you. Buildings with more than four units get a different formula under Section 10.20.011: the total number of dogs and cats can’t exceed the number of units, and the code makes keeping that count the building owner’s duty. Ask how many animals already live there. It explains a lot of no’s that sound personal and aren’t.
In unincorporated St. Louis County the number is three, since a fourth dog makes a house a kennel under County zoning. Our breakdown of pet laws in St. Louis city and county has the full headcount rules for both. New in town and picking a neighborhood around the dog? Start with dog-friendly places in St. Louis before you tour a single unit.
Keep the pet paperwork in one folder you can email the same day a policy checks out. If your move-out and move-in dates don’t line up, pet-friendly hotels in St. Louis can cover the gap for a few nights without boarding the dog.
### What do St. Louis landlords charge for pets: deposit, fee or pet rent?
The published St. Louis pet policies we found pair a one-time, non-refundable pet fee of about $325 to $350 per pet with monthly pet rent of $40 to $50. A refundable pet deposit shows up less often. Those are three different charges with three different fates, and only one of them can ever come back to you.
Pet deposit. Money held against damage and returned, in whole or in part, when you move out. It’s the only one of the three you can get back.
Pet fee. A one-time charge, usually at move-in, that the landlord keeps. Some policies call it a “non-refundable deposit,” which is a fee wearing a deposit’s name.
Pet rent. A monthly charge added to your rent for as long as the pet lives there. It never comes back.
Here’s what local landlords publish as of October 2026. Suson Pines, an apartment community in south St. Louis County, lists a $325 pet fee for one pet and $425 for two, plus monthly pet rent of $40 for one or $50 for two, with a two-pet maximum and a 100-pound combined weight limit. Another complex in southwest St. Louis County posts the identical schedule. Complete Realty Solutions, a St. Louis property manager, charges a $350 non-refundable payment per pet, capped at $700, plus $50 a month per pet, capped at $75. Deca Property Management, a family-owned St. Louis firm since 1990, runs every pet through a third-party screening profile that costs $30 by card or $25 by bank transfer, and the pet’s resulting FIDO Score sets its non-refundable fee. Check each one current before you apply.
Now run a full year, because the monthly number is the one that piles up:
One dog at $325 plus $40 a month: $805 the first year, then $480 every year after.
One dog at $350 plus $50 a month: $950 the first year.
Two pets at $425 plus $50 a month: $1,025 the first year.
A dog and a cat at $700 plus $75 a month: $1,600 the first year.
That’s the honest answer to whether a $500 pet deposit is a lot. A one-time $500 sits above the $325 to $350 per-pet fees these St. Louis landlords publish. But if it’s refundable, it may be the cheapest pet money on the table, because pet rent is where the real cost hides. Stay three years at $40 a month and the pet rent alone comes to $1,440. None of it comes back.
Some landlords split the difference. Select Leasing & Management, a St. Louis property manager, wrote in a 2016 landlord-education post that it makes pet deposits half refundable and half non-refundable, so a careful tenant gets something back, and it put typical pet rent at $25 to $50 a month. Quoted a flat fee? Ask for that structure instead.
And watch the word on the paperwork. If any of your pet money is supposed to come back, the lease should say how much, when and on what conditions, for a reason the law section below explains.
### Which breeds and weights do St. Louis rentals restrict, and why?
The usual lists start with pit bull types, Rottweilers and Doberman Pinschers, and weight caps run anywhere from about 30 pounds a dog to 100 pounds combined. The reason is mostly insurance. A dog bite is a liability claim, and insurers price, limit or refuse the breeds they consider the biggest risk.
Deca Property Management publishes one of the longer lists in town. Its listings marked no aggressive breeds exclude 13: pit bulls, Staffordshire terriers, Chows, Doberman Pinschers, Cane Corsos, Siberian Huskies, Great Danes, German Shepherds, Rottweilers, wolf hybrids, Alaskan Malamutes, Presa Canarios and Mastiffs. Complete Realty Solutions takes a different route. It allows dogs over 50 pounds, and breeds like pit bulls, Dobermans and Rottweilers, only when the tenant carries renters and liability insurance. Weight rules swing just as widely. Suson Pines caps two pets at 100 pounds combined, while a St. Louis real estate investor writing advice for landlords suggested a limit of 30 or 50 pounds per dog.
Follow the money and the lists make sense. According to the Insurance Information Institute, insurers paid $1.86 billion on 28,450 dog-related injury claims in 2025, an average of $65,450 a claim. Triple-I says some insurers won’t cover homeowners who own breeds they classify as dangerous, with pit bulls as its example, and others decide dog by dog after a bite. It names only two states, Pennsylvania and Michigan, with laws that stop insurers from canceling or denying some policies over breed. So a landlord’s breed list is often the insurance company’s list wearing the landlord’s name. Complete Realty says it outright: it limits breeds and sizes because of liability and insurability risks.
Those lists screen the breed on paper, not your dog’s temperament. Check what your vet records and adoption papers list as the breed before you send them, because that line is what a screener reads.
Say you’re taking a job in Nashville, Illinois, and bringing a 60-pound pit mix. The rental house you like belongs to one owner, and the no may really be coming from that owner’s insurance policy. Ask directly whether the policy excludes the breed or just charges more for it. Illinois runs hot on these claims: Triple-I counted 1,283 dog-related injury claims there in 2025, averaging $79,596, well above the national figure. Offering to carry your own liability coverage, and to list the owner as an interested party on your renters policy, can turn a flat no into a yes with conditions.
One more layer. Missouri has no statewide breed ban, and neither the City nor St. Louis County’s animal code names a breed, but some municipalities write breed into their ordinances. Deca tells applicants with a listed breed to check the property’s municipality first. Do that even when the landlord says yes.
### How do you win over a landlord who says no pets?
Answer the fear behind the no. Landlords worry about damage, noise, a bite on their property and a unit that’s hard to re-rent, so bring proof for each one: vet and vaccination records, a reference from your last landlord, renters insurance with liability coverage, and an offer of a refundable pet deposit.
Small landlords are where this works best. A large complex has a policy and a leasing agent who can’t bend it. The owner of a single house or a two-family flat may have written “no pets” years ago and never been asked again. Ask whether no means never, or not without more information.
Then hand over a one-page pet resume. It should cover:
Name, age, breed as listed on the vet records, weight and a recent photo.
Spay or neuter status and current vaccinations, with the rabies certificate attached.
A reference from a previous landlord who’ll confirm the pet caused no damage or complaints.
Training: a finished class, or an AKC Canine Good Citizen certificate, which a dog earns by passing a 10-skill test with an approved evaluator.
Your renters insurance declarations page showing personal liability coverage, and whether the policy covers your dog’s breed.
A plan for your work hours: crate training, a midday walker or daycare.
If the training line is empty, our guide to dog training cost in St. Louis covers what classes run and how to pick a trainer.
Next, put money where the fear is. Offer a refundable pet deposit in writing, return conditions spelled out. In Missouri a deposit labeled for a pet doesn’t count against the two-month cap, so a landlord can legally take it on top of a full security deposit. Offer a longer lease, too. An owner who dreads turnover may value your second year more than a second fee.
Picture a renter in North Venice with two indoor cats and a landlord who once spent a month airing out a unit after a cat owner left. A cat resume reads differently: proof both cats are spayed or neutered, how many litter boxes you keep and where, and an offer to pay for a professional carpet cleaning at move-out, receipt included. Specific beats sincere.
Two moves backfire. Sneaking a pet in breaks the lease, and in the City it can push a building over the headcount its owner is legally responsible for. Buying an emotional support animal letter online to dodge a pet fee burns trust even faster. HUD’s own May 2026 enforcement memo complains that “an entire industry has emerged to convert pets into emotional support animals.” Landlords read the news too.
Fostering for a rescue? A foster dog is still a dog under your lease, and under City code an animal you feed and shelter for more than seven days counts as kept on the property. Clear it with the landlord first, then see our guide to fostering pets in St. Louis for the rest.
Pet deposit ate the move-in budget? Try free clothing closets in St. Louis
### What does Missouri law say about pets in rentals (and what about service animals and ESAs)?
No Missouri law requires a landlord to accept pets, so the lease controls. The state’s deposit law caps a security deposit at two months’ rent and sets a 30-day return rule, but it expressly leaves out money labeled a pet deposit. Assistance animals fall under federal fair housing law, where HUD’s guidance changed in 2025 and 2026.
Start with what RSMo 535.300 does for a regular security deposit. The landlord can’t demand more than two months’ rent. Within 30 days after the tenancy ends, the landlord must return the deposit or send an itemized list of damages along with whatever balance is left. Deductions are limited to unpaid rent, damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, and losses from a tenant who didn’t give proper notice. You get written notice of the move-out inspection and the right to be there. And if a landlord wrongfully withholds any of it, the tenant recovers twice the amount wrongfully withheld.
One subsection reads as if a pet owner wrote it. A landlord can withhold actual carpet cleaning costs only if the lease sets that up and warns you that you may owe for carpet cleaning beyond ordinary wear and tear, and the landlord has to hand you a receipt for the cleaning within 30 days. Find that clause before you sign.
Now the line from the top of this guide. Because the definition leaves out money labeled a pet deposit, the two-month cap doesn’t limit it, and the 30-day rule and double-damages penalty are written for security deposits, not pet deposits. Read plainly, that makes the lease your main protection for pet money. If a landlord holds a pet deposit and won’t return it, your claim is most likely a breach of the lease, which Missouri small claims court hears up to $5,000. Legal Services of Eastern Missouri’s housing law program can tell you how it applies if you qualify.
If you own rentals, the same sentence hands you a choice. Label the pet money a pet deposit and you can collect it above a full two-month security deposit. Fold it into the security deposit and it counts toward the cap, but everybody works from the statute’s clear return rules. Either way, write the refund conditions down. Vague pet terms are how a $300 disagreement becomes a court date.
Lease a house in Roxana and the rulebook changes at the river. Illinois sets no statewide cap on how much deposit a landlord can take. Since January 1, 2024, its Security Deposit Return Act has covered every residential landlord, not just buildings of five units or more. A landlord who deducts for damage owes you an itemized statement with receipts within 30 days of move-out, or the full deposit within 45 days. Skip the statement or use it in bad faith and hold the money past the deadline, and a court can award twice the deposit due plus costs and attorney’s fees. Illinois’s act carries no pet deposit carve-out like Missouri’s. And for new leases signed from January 1, 2027, Public Act 104-0479 requires every non-optional fee to appear on the first page of the lease, and a tenant doesn’t owe a fee that isn’t there. Illinois property managers are reading that to cover pet fees and pet rent.
Service animals and emotional support animals follow different rules, and federal guidance on them changed in 2025 and 2026, so check what’s current before you lean on it. HUD withdrew its 2013 and 2020 assistance animal notices on September 17, 2025, and a May 22, 2026 enforcement memo says the agency will now pursue animal complaints only when the animal is trained to do disability-related work or tasks. The Fair Housing Act itself didn’t change, tenants can still sue, and state laws are untouched. For the details, including how ESA letters hold up now, read our guide to service dogs and emotional support animals in Missouri.
### How do you get your deposit back after renting with a pet?
Record the unit on day one, fix pet damage before you leave, show up for the move-out inspection and get every refund term in writing. In Missouri the security deposit comes back within 30 days or with an itemized list of damages. A pet deposit comes back on whatever terms your lease sets.
Start the day you get the keys. Walk every room with your phone recording and narrate as you go: the scratches already on the back door, the stain by the radiator, the worn carpet in the hallway. Email the video and a written list to the landlord that week so there’s a date on it. A year later, nobody remembers whose dog scuffed what.
Know where the statute draws the line. Ordinary wear and tear isn’t chargeable: faded paint, carpet worn flat between the couch and the kitchen. Damage beyond that can be: chewed window trim, a door clawed through the finish, urine soaked into the pad. Fix what you can before the inspection, and a professional carpet cleaning with the receipt in hand answers the most common pet deduction before anyone makes it.
Missouri gives you the right to attend the move-out inspection, and the landlord has to tell you the date and time in writing. Go, and bring the move-in video. Leave a forwarding address in writing too, since the landlord meets the 30-day rule by mailing the list and payment to your last known address.
If the security deposit doesn’t come back and no itemized list shows up within 30 days, send a short written demand citing RSMo 535.300 and its double-damages provision. Missouri small claims court handles cases up to $5,000, and Legal Services of Eastern Missouri posts self-help tenant material at MOTenantHelp.org.
The renters who get their pet money back aren’t lucky. They’re the ones holding a video, a receipt and a lease that spells out what happens next. Be that tenant, and the next landlord’s first question gets easy: can I call your last one?
Want a landlord whose pet policy is already written down? Start with property management companies around St. Louis, since the firms that manage dozens of rentals usually have a pet policy they can email before you pay an application fee.
And if you run a rental business yourself, list your property management company with us and put your pet policy in writing where renters will find it.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is $500 pet deposit a lot?
A.  For St. Louis it’s on the high side for a one-time charge, but not out of line. Local landlords publish one-time pet fees of $325 to $350 per pet. What matters more is whether the $500 is refundable. A refundable deposit can cost you nothing if you leave the place clean, while $40 a month in pet rent costs $480 a year no matter what.
### Q. How to avoid a pet fee?
A.  Legally, by negotiating. Owner-managed rentals bend more than big complexes, so offer a refundable deposit or a longer lease in place of the fee. A trained service animal is generally exempt as a fair housing accommodation. Don’t hide a pet or buy an online letter to dodge the charge. Either one can cost you the lease.
### Q. Why do landlords charge so much for pets?
A.  Because pet damage is expensive to fix and pets add liability. Replacing urine-soaked carpet and pad, refinishing clawed doors and treating for fleas between tenants all come out of the owner’s pocket, and dog-related injury claims averaged $65,450 apiece in 2025, according to the Insurance Information Institute. Pet rent also covers the extra ordinary wear that Missouri’s deposit law won’t let a landlord deduct.
### Q. What dog breeds do landlords not like?
A.  The breeds that show up most on St. Louis lists are pit bull types, Staffordshire terriers, Rottweilers, Doberman Pinschers, German Shepherds, Chows, Cane Corsos, Huskies, Malamutes, Great Danes, Mastiffs, Presa Canarios and wolf hybrids. One local manager excludes all 13 from properties marked no aggressive breeds. Another allows pit bulls, Dobermans and Rottweilers if the tenant carries renters and liability insurance. The driver is usually the landlord’s insurer.
### Q. Is pet rent ridiculous?
A.  It can feel that way, since it never comes back and isn’t tied to any repair. At the St. Louis landlords we checked it runs $40 to $50 a month for one pet, or $480 to $600 a year. Whether it’s fair depends on the rest of the package. Pet rent with no fee and a refundable deposit can be a decent deal. Pet rent stacked on a $350 non-refundable fee is the expensive version.
### Q. What do landlords fear the most?
A.  Tenants who stop paying, and damage that costs more than the deposit covers. Pets add a third fear: somebody getting bitten on the property. One St. Louis property manager says it limits breeds and sizes because of liability and insurability risks, and that it may prioritize applicants without pets. Answer those fears with records, references and insurance, and you’re a much easier yes.
### Q. What laws do landlords have to follow in Missouri?
A.  The Missouri Attorney General’s landlord-tenant guide lists the basics: make the home habitable before move-in, pay for repairs from ordinary wear and tear, never shut off a tenant’s utilities, give written notice when the property changes owners, and don’t discriminate. RSMo 535.300 governs deposits, a month-to-month tenancy ends on one month’s written notice, and RSMo 441.234 lets a tenant of six months or more who is current on rent fix certain code violations and deduct the cost after 14 days’ written notice.
### Q. Does a pet deposit count toward Missouri’s two-month deposit limit?
A.  No. RSMo 535.300 caps a security deposit at two months’ rent, but its definition of security deposit excludes money labeled a deposit for a pet. So a Missouri landlord can collect a full two-month security deposit plus a separate pet deposit. The flip side is that the statute’s 30-day return rule is written for security deposits, so get the pet deposit’s refund terms into the lease.

## Ten Dollars Puts Your Car on a Mississippi River Ferry: A St. Louis Riverfront Field Guide
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-riverfront
Your car is parked on a boat, and the Mississippi is sliding past on both sides. Ten dollars one way, per car. No bridge involved. This is the Grafton Ferry, a city-owned boat upriver from St. Louis that still makes the crossing seven days a week.
Closer to town, the river asks for shoe leather instead. About sixty-five steps drop from the Arch grounds to the cobblestone levee, where the riverboats tie up a few steps from fast water. What you’re looking at is what USGS calls “excess river flow from 13 States and part of Canada.” Just north, under the Eads Bridge, a gauge installed in 1861 has been reading it ever since.
Then comes the number that stays with you. On Aug. 1, 1993, that gauge read 49.58 feet, still the record. The top of the west-bank floodwall sits at 52.0 on the same gauge. The crest came, in USGS’s words, “just 2.5 feet below the floodwall.” Two and a half feet. That was the margin.
This guide is for getting to that water instead of squinting at it from a car window. Rivers don’t keep schedules, so every hour and fare below comes with the same advice: phone first.
### Where is the best place to see the Mississippi river in St. Louis?
Wind off the water, an engine humming up through the deck: the best way to meet this river is to get onto it. Every viewpoint below shows you the Mississippi from the bank, and each is worth the stop. A ferry or a riverboat puts you on the river itself, so start there if the schedule lets you, and use the bank spots when it doesn’t.
At the levee you’re at eye level with the current, and the riverboats tie up a few steps from fast water. The Arch grounds above it are open “from 5:00am - 11:00pm year round,” the National Park Service says, and walking down is free. Just north, under the Eads Bridge, the cobblestones give way to the brick of Laclede’s Landing, nine blocks of historic buildings beside the bridge that carries the river gauge.
For height, cross to the Illinois bank. At Malcolm W. Martin Memorial Park, directly across from the Arch, the Mississippi River Overlook stands about 40 feet tall and keeps the Arch straight across the water. The park is open daily 7 a.m. - 10 p.m. For the river under your feet, walk the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge: about a mile of old Route 66, closed to cars, with the water below. It’s open to walkers and cyclists daily from 7 a.m. to 30 minutes after sunset.
To watch two rivers become one, follow the short interpretive trail at Confluence Point State Park, at the end of Riverlands Way on the peninsula north of the city. It’s open 7 a.m. to a half hour after sunset. To get out on the water, board a riverboat on the downtown levee; daily sightseeing cruises run March to November. To put your car on the river, ride a ferry upriver, with fares and hours in the ferry section below. Save Columbia Bottom for later: public access there is currently limited to the boat ramp.
### What is waiting on the riverfront, about 65 steps below the Arch?
Under your shoes the original levee cobblestones tilt toward the water, and the wind comes straight off the river. Wear shoes you don’t mind scuffing. Nobody sells you a ticket. The Arch grounds are at 11 N. 4th St., and the National Park Service answers at 314-655-1600.
Behind you, the Grand Staircase is the part visitors misjudge. It drops about 65 steps, with handrails, from the Arch grounds to the boulevard, and the National Park Service lists two ramps beside it. Driving? The Arch’s own directions say to enter “The Mural Mile” in your GPS to reach the levee. Parking there is “for a fee (card only),” the Arch doesn’t run it, we couldn’t find the amount posted, and it “may be unavailable due to river conditions.” The spaces on the cobblestones themselves are “not accessible due to the slope.”
Your fallback is the Stadium East garage at 200 S. Broadway: $11 for the first five hours if you prepay, according to the Arch’s riverfront parking page, though rates can move.
The boulevard you came down to is newer than it looks. Great Rivers Greenway led a $33 million rebuild of 1.5 miles of it, from Biddle Street to Chouteau Avenue, and the road came back an average of 1.9 feet higher, St. Louis Public Radio reported at the ribbon cutting on June 2, 2016. Work started in November 2013. What it left is plain and useful: protected walking and bike paths, benches, bike racks, a street-level stage and those cobblestones.
One catch the cruise listings tend to bury: at high water, the ramps from the levee road can be cut off. The National Weather Service says flooding begins near the Eads Bridge underpass on Leonor K. Sullivan Boulevard when the river gauge hits 34 feet. Those 1.9 feet of extra height were never decoration. For garages, food and everything up the hill, our guide to downtown St. Louis picks up where the cobblestones end.
### How high is the Mississippi river in St. Louis right now?
Walk north from the levee and the Eads Bridge swallows the light, with shade overhead and your footsteps echoing. Somewhere on that bridge sits the reason St. Louis knows what its river is doing: USGS gauge 07010000, installed in 1861, the reading behind the city’s river flood warnings. Our guide to bridges in St. Louis covers the bridge itself.
This page won’t print a number, because the number changes by the hour. For the live reading and forecast, use the USGS gauge page or the National Weather Service page (ID EADM7). What you’re reading is the river’s stage, in feet above a reference zero on the gauge, not the depth of the water. That’s why it can go negative: the record low is minus 6.2 feet, set Jan. 16, 1940.
To turn that number into what you’ll actually see, use the National Weather Service’s own markers:
28 feet: action stage.
30 feet: flood stage.
32 feet: flood panels go in at Carr and Poplar.
34 feet: flooding begins near the Eads Bridge underpass on Leonor K. Sullivan Boulevard.
35 feet: moderate flooding.
36.5 feet: water reaches the base of the floodgates at Poplar and at Chouteau.
38 feet: the Coast Guard “will consider closing the St. Louis harbor to navigation above this level.”
40 feet: major flooding.
47 feet: businesses along North Commercial Street in Laclede’s Landing begin flooding.
Check the city’s flooding street-closures page too before a levee trip after heavy rain upstream. The gauge tells you what the river is doing. That page tells you whether the boulevard is open.
### The summer the river stopped 2.5 feet short of the floodwall
Stand on the levee and the air off the water smells of river mud. In the summer of 1993, that same river was moving 1,080,000 cubic feet per second, “sufficient to fill Busch Stadium about every 65 seconds,” USGS estimated. The water came within 100 feet of the Arch memorial, and the river spent 144 days above flood stage that year.
So how deep is the Mississippi river at the Arch in St. Louis? It depends on the day. At low flow USGS puts the deepest water under 30 feet, with a current under 3 mph. At the 1993 peak it estimated 87 feet at the deepest and a current of up to 7.6 mph.
Here’s the detail that should bother you. The NWS says the floodwall was built for the flood of 1844, when roughly 1,000,000 cubic feet per second of water reached an estimated 41.32 feet. In 1973, less water, 851,000 cubic feet per second, crested at 43.23 feet. Less water, higher river. Hydrologists blame development on the floodplain, which leaves the river less room to spread out. The second-highest crest is recent: 46.02 feet, on June 9, 2019.
Off the levee after dark and hungry? Where to eat in Lafayette Square
The rest of that summer, from the levee breaks to the propane tanks that floated loose off South Broadway, is in our story of the 1993 flood in St. Louis. For the numbers behind it, read USGS’s 1995 fact sheet and the National Weather Service’s 1993 flood page.
### What is Laclede’s Landing now?
Cobblestones knock under your shoes as you walk north from the riverboat dock, pass under the Eads Bridge and reach the brick warehouses. This is the district that shows up at the top of that flood ladder, at 47 feet. It calls itself “home to 17 historic buildings and seven restaurants” across nine blocks, and it’s named for Pierre Laclede, the fur trader who founded St. Louis. The office is at 707 N. 2nd St., Suite 102. We couldn’t find posted hours or parking.
Ask a few longtime St. Louisans about the Landing and you’ll hear about a night out years ago, not last weekend. So what’s there now? Our Laclede’s Landing guide covers it. The district also sits on the walk between the riverboats and the trail: head north, and the Biddle Street trailhead waits past the MLK Bridge. Wear real shoes.
### Does St. Louis have a riverwalk?
Ride the Riverfront Trail and the floodwall slides past at your shoulder, the pavement is flat and there is little shade. The trail runs on both sides of the wall, so you ride along the working river instead of through a park built for postcards. It’s not a shop-lined riverwalk, but it is a long one. Great Rivers Greenway’s Riverfront Trail is a paved 16.19-mile trail, a total that counts the Old Chain of Rocks and McKinley bridges, and it runs from the Chouteau riverfront to the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge. Some stretches are levee roads you share with business vehicles.
Start at the Biddle Street trailhead, a few blocks north of the MLK Bridge, and the cobblestones give way to levee and floodwall fast. Bring water. Then bring a little more. Our guide to the St. Louis Riverfront Trail has every trailhead and the detours.
The big lots are at the north end: 55 spaces at Chain of Rocks Park, with no overnight parking, and 90 more across two lots at North Riverfront Park, just south of the bridge. Great Rivers Greenway also flagged concrete barriers at Maline Creek during repairs, so its trail page is worth a look for detours before you ride.
The Mary Meachum Freedom Crossing. About halfway between Biddle Street and the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge, at 28 E. Grand Ave., the trail passes the most important spot on the whole riverfront, and it’s easy to ride right past it. On May 21, 1855, eight or nine enslaved people tried to cross the river by boat to Illinois. Five were captured. Mary Meachum, the widow of the founding pastor of First African Baptist Church, was prosecuted for helping them, the National Park Service records.
In 2001 the Park Service accepted the site into its Network to Freedom, the first in Missouri. Stop and face east. That far bank was the whole plan. Great Rivers Greenway holds a celebration of the crossing every year, so watch its events page for the next one.
The Mural Mile. The riverfront’s other landmark is painted. Paint Louis, at the floodwall at 1000 S. Wharf, is “named in the Guinness Book of World Records as the longest graffiti wall in the world,” and the wall keeps changing. It’s the same name the Arch’s directions give you for your GPS, so you may already have typed it.
### Can you walk out over the Mississippi?
Stand on the old bridge with the wind coming off the water and look down. You’re looking at the reason barges avoid this stretch. The bridge, at 10840 Riverview Dr., is about a mile long, closed to cars, and part of Route 66 from 1936, according to the National Park Service. It’s open daily from 7 a.m. to 30 minutes after sunset, and Great Rivers Greenway answers at 314-436-7009.
Right now, in Great Rivers Greenway’s words, “The Old Chain of Rocks Bridge is OPEN and accessible from the Missouri side only.” The closure of the canal bridge on the Illinois approach began June 22, and we couldn’t find an end date. Treat the walk as an out-and-back from Missouri, and ask Great Rivers Greenway whether that has changed. The restrooms are portable and out only from April to November. The westbound I-270 exit to Riverview is closed, so use Lilac Avenue (exit 33).
Coming from the Illinois side? That closure matters most to you. Our guide to things to do in Granite City, Illinois has more to do on that bank. Our Old Chain of Rocks Bridge guide covers the walk itself.
Below you, tows bypass 17 miles of rock ledges by taking the Chain of Rocks Canal, and Lock 27, at the canal’s lower end, is the southernmost lock on the Mississippi, the Army Corps of Engineers says. The Corps calls the river north of St. Louis a “locking river” and the river south of it an “open river,” with no locks or dams all the way to the Gulf. St. Louis is where the river changes jobs. Upriver, Melvin Price Locks and Dam has its own guide, and our guide to barges on the Mississippi explains why the tows downtown look so different from the ones up there.
Downtown, drivers cross on the Eads, the MLK, the Poplar Street and the Stan Musial Veterans Memorial bridges, and the McKinley Bridge, farther north, is part of that trail count. Our guide to bridges in St. Louis covers each crossing.
### What does the Arch look like from across the river?
Climb the Mississippi River Overlook and the river opens out below you, with the Arch straight across the water. The ADA-accessible overlook stands about 40 feet tall at Malcolm W. Martin Memorial Park, 185 W. Trendley Ave. in East St. Louis, Illinois. The park is “open daily, 7 a.m. - 10 p.m.,” and its number is 618-581-5811. Skip the Gateway Geyser: it’s closed. Live in Brooklyn or elsewhere on the Illinois side? This is your easiest look at downtown, no bridge required. Our Mississippi River Overlook guide has the rest.
### Are there any ferries that cross the Mississippi River?
Roll onto a river ferry and the engine hums up through the deck while the Mississippi runs past on both sides. Yes, there are ferries, and they work upriver from the city. The Grafton Ferry and the Golden Eagle Ferry carry cars across the Mississippi itself, while IDOT’s free Brussels Ferry crosses the Illinois River near Grafton. Pick the wrong one for your trip and you’ll end up on the wrong river, so here they are one at a time.
The Grafton Ferry, a Mississippi crossing. You wait at the landing, watching the current, and the river decides whether you go: “Heavy ice on the rivers or strong winds could keep the ferry from running some days.” The Missouri landing is on Grafton Ferry Road, off Highway 94. Here’s what to expect:
Hours: Mon-Thu 5 a.m. - 9 p.m., Fri-Sat 5 a.m. - 10 p.m., Sun 8 a.m. - 9 p.m.
Fares: $10 per car one way, $19 round trip, $5 on foot, $6 with a bicycle.
Payment: cash, check and card.
The city of Grafton bought the boat for $878,000 with help from an IDOT grant, and it reopened to run seven days a week, year-round, with the Calhoun County Ferry Co. operating it for 20 years, St. Louis Public Radio reported. We found no ferry-specific phone number we could confirm, so our Grafton Ferry hours and fares guide is the best place to start, and the weather decides the rest.
The Golden Eagle Ferry. When river conditions stop this boat, word that it’s running again can arrive by way of the sheriff’s office, relayed by local outlets. That’s exactly why ferry news is so hard to find. A tourism-bureau listing gives 618-535-5759 and these hours: Mon-Thu 5 a.m. - 9 p.m., Fri-Sat 5 a.m. - 2 a.m., Sun 8 a.m. - 9 p.m. Expect about $10 a car one way, cash only. The listing text still shows older prices, so confirm by phone.
The Brussels Ferry, free but on the Illinois River. On paper, this boat never sleeps: IDOT operates it “24 hours a day, seven days a week,” across the Illinois River, one mile west of Grafton, linking Illinois Route 100 to Calhoun County. Is the Brussels Ferry free? Yes, at no charge, and it’s the one that trips people up because it isn’t on the Mississippi. It’s one of two free IDOT ferries on the Illinois River, and the other is at Kampsville. IDOT lists no ferry-specific phone, so use its general line, 217-782-7820, or check its ferry page during a cold snap, because ice has stopped the boat in past winters.
Why go to the trouble? Because the ferries turn a drive up the river into a loop: over the Illinois on the free boat, through Calhoun County, and back across the Mississippi to Missouri without retracing a mile. Skip them and you’re driving back down to the nearest bridge. Our guide to ferries near St. Louis keeps every boat in one place, and the river towns along the way are in our guide to small towns outside St. Louis.
Before the levee, the bridge or the boat, pick your table from our guide to where to eat in St. Louis.
If you run a riverfront restaurant, a bar on Laclede’s Landing or a tour or charter boat, the walkers, cyclists and cruise passengers this page sends to the water are visitors already headed your way, so list your business with us and turn more of them into customers.
### Which rivers meet in St. Louis?
Walk out to the tip of the peninsula at Confluence Point State Park and the land runs out into moving water, because “a short interpretive trail leads directly to the point at which the Mighty Mississippi and the Big Muddy merge into one.” The two rivers are the Missouri and the Mississippi, just north of the city, and USGS puts the Missouri River’s mouth 15 river miles upstream of the Eads Bridge gauge.
The park’s official name is Edward “Ted” and Pat Jones-Confluence Point State Park, and it sits at 1000 Riverlands Way in West Alton, Missouri. It’s open daily, 7 a.m. to a half hour after sunset, year-round, and no fee is listed. Call 636-899-1135; messages are monitored 7 to 8 a.m., Monday through Friday.
Climb the Lewis and Clark Confluence Tower on the Illinois bank and three decks, at 50, 100 and 150 feet, put you above the meeting of the rivers. The tower stands at 435 Confluence Tower Dr. in Hartford, off Illinois Route 3, and admission is $10 for ages 6 and up and free for ages 5 and under. Hours are the tricky part. One listing says “May - October and January, Thursday - Sunday 10 a.m. - 5 p.m.,” which would leave the tower closed after October until January, while a press release says Wednesday through Sunday, 10 to 4. Call 618-251-9101 first.
The view a lot of locals remember is mostly closed. The Missouri Department of Conservation says public access to Columbia Bottom “is currently limited to the boat ramp,” and its number is 636-441-4554. Even after full access returns, parts of the area close every Oct. 15 to March 1 for waterfowl. Our guide to Columbia Bottom Conservation Area will say when the gates open again. Which view is worth the drive, and how to time it, is the job of our guide to where the Missouri and Mississippi rivers meet.
### Can you ride the river?
Step off the cobblestones onto a riverboat deck and the skyline starts to slide. Gateway Arch Riverboats docks at 50 S. Leonor K. Sullivan Blvd. and answers at 877-982-1410. Daily sightseeing cruises “operate from March to November,” and December is holiday cruises only. The boats go rain or shine, and a weather cancellation earns a one-year voucher, not cash.
The one-hour Riverfront Cruise was $26 for adults, $16 for kids 3-15 and $24 for seniors 60+ when the season opened, with children under 3 free, and fares move, so confirm before you book. Dogs are allowed on the one-hour cruise only.
The Becky Thatcher, which started life as the Capt. JP in 1987, carries up to 400 passengers across three decks. Bi-State paid $549,500 for the boat and spent $3.2 million on the renovation. One of the captains is even “ordained to marry couples,” the line says, and it bills itself as the oldest Mississippi excursion boat company in St. Louis, with a home port here since 1917. Prices change by cruise and by date, and our guide to what a riverboat cruise costs walks through them.
Paddling is the other way on, and the downtown Mississippi is a hard place to learn. USGS estimated the current at up to 7.6 mph at the 1993 peak. At low flow it slows to under 3 mph, but add barge tows and floating debris and this is still water for experienced paddlers with a plan. Beginners should start with our guide to kayaking in St. Louis.
Can you swim in the Mississippi river in St. Louis? We found no city ordinance either way, and you still shouldn’t. Wetting a line from the bank instead? Our list of fishing spots in St. Louis has places to cast.
### Where should you start?
Go to the levee an hour before sunset, feel the cobblestones under your shoes and the light going low over the water, then walk north under the Eads Bridge into Laclede’s Landing, and you have one good evening. Got a whole Saturday? Start on the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge, reach Confluence Point by midday and finish on the cobblestones at dusk, maybe aboard a riverboat cruise. Feeling adventurous? Drive up to Grafton and put the car on the boat. Columbia Bottom can wait until you’ve checked its access, and Columbia Bottom Conservation Area has the details.
Most people who grew up here know the river as the blur below the Poplar Street Bridge. You now know a free boat still crosses the Illinois, the Eads Bridge holds the city’s official river height, and Mary Meachum’s crossing sits beside a bike trail by the water. Pick a clear evening, park by the levee and walk north until the cobblestones run out.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Which rivers meet in St. Louis?
A.  The Missouri and the Mississippi, just north of the city, about 15 river miles above the Eads Bridge gauge, according to USGS. The Illinois River joins the Mississippi farther upstream, and the Meramec comes in 19.2 river miles below the gauge, south of the city. For a land view of the main meeting, use Confluence Point State Park (7 a.m. to a half hour after sunset) or the Lewis and Clark Confluence Tower, and call the tower at 618-251-9101 first.
### Q. Can you swim in the Mississippi river in St. Louis?
A.  We found no city ordinance either way, and you still shouldn’t. USGS estimated the current at up to 7.6 mph at the 1993 crest, and at low flow it’s still under 3 mph, with barge tows and floating debris in the channel. In 2005, the chair of the Missouri Clean Water Commission called the fast current and heavy barge traffic a “great hazard” to swimmers. Enjoy it from the levee or a riverboat deck.
### Q. How deep is the Mississippi river at the Arch in St. Louis?
A.  It depends on the day. At low flow, USGS puts the deepest water under 30 feet. At the 1993 crest, it estimated a maximum depth of 87 feet. The Army Corps of Engineers maintains a navigation channel 9 feet deep and 300 feet wide for barges, and the gauge on the Eads Bridge tells you which river you’re looking at today.
### Q. How high is the Mississippi river in St. Louis right now?
A.  Check the official gauge: the USGS page for station 07010000 or the National Weather Service page for EADM7. Flood stage is 30 feet, and the riverfront boulevard starts flooding near the Eads Bridge underpass at 34. Action stage is 28, moderate flooding is 35 and major flooding is 40. Check the city’s flooding street-closures page before you drive down after heavy rain upstream.
### Q. Does St. Louis have a riverwalk?
A.  Not a shop-lined one, but a long one: a paved, 16.19-mile Riverfront Trail, counting the Old Chain of Rocks and McKinley bridges, with little shade. Downtown adds benches, bike racks and the original cobblestones on the rebuilt boulevard, and the Mary Meachum Freedom Crossing, at 28 E. Grand Ave., is a stop on the trail to the north. Our St. Louis Riverfront Trail guide covers the trailheads and parking.
### Q. Are there gators in the Mississippi river?
A.  Not at St. Louis. We found no credible report of wild alligators here, and the Missouri Department of Conservation calls alligators non-native; the ones found in Missouri have been released or escaped pets. The river does hold alligator gar, a long, toothy fish that MDC lists in Missouri only in the Mississippi, from St. Louis downstream. For the one bull shark on record near here, and the rest of what lives in the river, see sharks in the Mississippi.
### Q. Are there any ferries that cross the Mississippi River?
A.  Yes, upriver from the city. The city-owned Grafton Ferry runs every day and charges $10 per car one way, $19 round trip and $5 on foot. The Golden Eagle Ferry costs about $10, cash only, so confirm at 618-535-5759. IDOT’s free Brussels Ferry nearby crosses the Illinois River, not the Mississippi. Wind or heavy ice can stop any of them, so confirm before you drive.
### Q. Is the Brussels Ferry free?
A.  Yes. The Illinois Department of Transportation runs it at no charge, 24 hours a day, seven days a week, across the Illinois River one mile west of Grafton, linking Illinois Route 100 to Calhoun County. It is one of two free IDOT ferries on the Illinois River, and the other is at Kampsville. Ice has stopped it in past winters, so check IDOT’s ferry page during a hard freeze.

## Columbia Bottom Conservation Area: What Is Open Now, Sunflowers and Catfish
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/columbia-bottom-conservation-area
Stale review pages still describe Columbia Bottom Conservation Area like a park somebody forgot about. One review on a travel site went further and said the place “should be permanently closed.” As of October 9, 2026, it mostly is. Nobody gave up on it, though.
