## Where the Missouri and Mississippi Rivers Meet: Confluence Point State Park and the Lewis and Clark Confluence Tower
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/where-the-missouri-and-mississippi-rivers-meet
The confluence moved. When the Corps of Discovery pushed off from its winter camp on May 14, 1804, and turned up the Missouri, it entered that river about 2 miles upstream of where the two rivers meet today, by the count of the Missouri Department of Natural Resources. And the camp? The National Park Service says the Mississippi’s channel shifted east and the Missouri’s mouth shifted south, so the ground where Clark’s men spent that winter is likely under the river now, or on the Missouri side of it. A camp built in Illinois may have changed sides without moving an inch.
Search the question and the top answers come from a bank’s blog, a pair of Facebook posts and a travel forum. They’ll get you to the water. What they skip is the part that changes your day: there are three classic places to watch the Missouri pour into the Mississippi near St. Louis, and right now only two of them are open.
Here’s the short version. Confluence Point State Park puts you on the tip of the peninsula, on the Missouri side. The Lewis and Clark Confluence Tower and the Lewis and Clark State Historic Site, about a mile apart, look across from the Illinois bank. The third, the viewing platform at Columbia Bottom, is closed, and on September 8, 2026, the Missouri Department of Conservation shut the whole area around it.
It’s part of our larger guide to the St. Louis riverfront. Every hour, fee and date below was checked against state, federal and operator pages in October 2026. Any of it can change, so confirm before you drive.
### Where do the Missouri and Mississippi rivers meet?
The Missouri River flows into the Mississippi just north of St. Louis, at the tip of the peninsula between them. You can stand at the point itself in Confluence Point State Park on the Missouri side, or look across from the Lewis and Clark Confluence Tower and State Historic Site on the Illinois bank off Illinois Route 3.
That’s the map. The Missouri Department of Conservation puts the meeting point just north of St. Louis and says the Missouri adds nearly half the flow of the Mississippi below it. The viewpoints on each bank work differently, so it helps to know which one fits your day:
Confluence Point State Park, Missouri side: the view at water level, at the end of Riverlands Way. No admission fee.
Lewis and Clark Confluence Tower, Illinois side: the view from above, with a top deck at 150 feet.
Lewis and Clark State Historic Site, Illinois side: the story, with a full-scale keelboat replica and a colonnade facing the confluence.
Columbia Bottom Conservation Area, Missouri side: closed as of October 2026, with no reopening date posted.
Which should you pick? To stand where the water meets, go to the state park. To see the line between the rivers from above, go to the tower. Doing both takes one day, and the last section lays out the drive.
### Can you see the two colors meet?
Often, yes, because the two rivers carry very different loads of silt. The U.S. Geological Survey measured a median of 427 milligrams of suspended sediment per liter in the lower Missouri, against 139 in the Mississippi, roughly three times as much. Side by side, the Missouri reads as the browner river.
The Missouri Department of Conservation calls the upper Mississippi “relatively clear” and describes the Missouri as still “muddy-looking.” Still is the word to notice. Dams upstream have already cut the Missouri’s sediment load to about 20 to 25 million tons a year, by the department’s estimate, and it remains the muddier river anyway. There’s a reason it goes by Big Muddy.
Here’s the detail that surprised us most. The two rivers don’t blend the moment they touch. A 1965 U.S. Geological Survey report found them still unmixed as they passed St. Louis, with water along the west bank carrying up to 2,400 parts per million more sediment than water near the Illinois shore. For miles below the point, two rivers share one bed.
So where do you look? At the state park you’re at the tip, close to the water, with the two currents coming together in front of you. From the tower you look down on the river rather than across it, which should be a better angle for spotting a line on the surface. Nobody we found publishes a forecast for it, though, so treat the line as a bonus rather than a promise.
### What is at Confluence Point State Park?
About 1,100 acres of river bottom and a short walk to the point. The Missouri Department of Natural Resources describes a path of about a quarter mile, part pavement and part compacted gravel, from the parking lot to the confluence overlook. There’s no admission fee, and the park is open daily, year-round, from 7 a.m. to a half-hour after sunset.
The full name is a mouthful: Edward “Ted” and Pat Jones-Confluence Point State Park, at 1000 Riverlands Way. That road runs out across the peninsula from US-67, past the Audubon Center at Riverlands, and ends at the park. Follow it until it stops.
What’s out there is spare. Interpretive displays and a vault toilet sit at the parking area, and a short interpretive trail leads straight to where the rivers merge. No visitor center, no gift shop. The state lists the route on its accessibility page, and a path of pavement and packed gravel should suit most strollers.
The best story about this ground comes from the day it became a park. At the dedication in May 2004, St. Louis Public Radio reported, benefactor Pat Jones touched both rivers at once. That’s the point in one picture: the land narrows until there’s nothing left but water on either side.
There’s a newer piece that older write-ups miss. A half-mile walking and biking trail named for Ted and Pat Jones runs along the Mississippi levee, and the state held its ribbon-cutting on October 5, 2024. That ceremony had first been planned for May. Flooding postponed it.
Which brings up the one real drawback. The park is day-use only because it’s floodplain, and the river doesn’t always stay out. Since 2007, high water had topped the 7-mile Kuhs agricultural levee six times by early 2021, Terrain magazine reported, and the closure after the 2019 flood dragged into 2021. The concrete path came back as crushed rock. The state now describes the route as pavement and compacted gravel.
When we checked on October 9, 2026, we found no closure notice. Still, after any big rise on either river, check the state park page before you drive out.
### Is the Lewis and Clark Confluence Tower worth the climb?
Yes on a clear day, and you don’t actually have to climb. The tower has decks at 50, 100 and 150 feet, reached by stairs or an elevator, and its posted admission is $10, with kids 5 and under free. From the top deck at 150 feet, you’re looking down on the confluence instead of across it.
It stands on the Illinois bank off Illinois Route 3, run by the local village together with the Great Rivers & Routes Tourism Bureau. The view runs three ways: the confluence, downtown St. Louis to the south and the Clark Bridge to the north. On very clear days, the National Park Service says, you can pick out the Gateway Arch.
The tower went up for the 200th anniversary of the expedition, and the Park Service dates its completion to May 14, 2010. It later closed for about a year of renovation and reopened on May 14, 2026, with an expanded park, new murals and a children’s playscape, the tourism bureau announced.
Look at those dates again. May 14 is also the day in 1804 that the Corps of Discovery pushed off from Camp River Dubois, so the reopening landed 222 years to the day after the expedition left. We don’t know whether anyone planned that. It makes a good trivia question for the elevator ride.
Now the catch. The tower keeps a season, May through October plus January, and it closes on holidays. Two official pages list different days and hours, so we won’t guess for you. Check current hours: (618) 251-9101. If you’re reading this after October, call before you assume it’s open. Bringing a scout troop or a family reunion? Groups of 12 or more pay $5 a person.
Is it worth $10 a head? For two adults and two kids over 5, that’s $40. Our take: it’s the one paid stop on this trip, and it earns the money. The state park gives you the meeting point at ground level, and the colonnade at the Historic Site gives you a quieter look. Only the tower puts you 150 feet up, where the whole shape makes sense: two rivers coming in, one going out.
### What is at Camp River Dubois today?
A state historic site that re-creates the camp, about a mile from the tower. The Illinois Department of Natural Resources runs the Lewis and Clark State Historic Site, where an interpretive center of about 14,000 square feet holds a 55-foot, full-scale replica of the expedition’s keelboat. The state lists no admission fee and points visitors to a donation page.
The keelboat is the reason to go inside. It’s cut away to show how the supplies were packed, and standing next to it does more for a ten-year-old than any map in a textbook. Fifty-five feet sounds like plenty of boat. Then you see what had to fit in it.
Outside stands a replica fort built to the Army’s 1803 regulations for a military post, with a settlers’ cabin nearby. Clark reached the camp site on December 12, 1803, according to the National Park Service, while Lewis spent that winter in St. Louis gathering supplies.
Then walk out to the colonnade. Eleven columns overlook the confluence, one for each state the expedition crossed, according to the Illinois DNR. Count them with the kids, then see who can name all eleven.
And the original camp? The Park Service says the channels moved, the Mississippi east and the Missouri’s mouth south, so the real campground is likely under the river now or on the Missouri side. The fort you walk through is a careful model standing near history rather than on top of it.
Hours follow the season. From September through May the site is open Wednesday through Sunday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. From Memorial Day to Labor Day it’s open daily, same hours. The address is 1 Lewis & Clark Trail, on the Illinois bank off Illinois Route 3, and the phone number is 618-251-5811.
### Why can’t you get to the Columbia Bottom platform right now?
Because the Missouri Department of Conservation closed all of Columbia Bottom on September 8, 2026, and only its Missouri River boat ramp has reopened, on September 30. The platform was shut even earlier: in April, St. Louis Public Radio was already sending readers to the state park instead. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers is targeting the end of 2026 to demolish the old levee, and no reopening date has been posted. That stings. In 2003, the same station billed this spot on the south bank of the Missouri, right at its mouth, as the first Missouri-side platform looking straight at the confluence. Our guide to Columbia Bottom Conservation Area tracks the closure.
### Did Lewis and Clark start at St. Louis?
No, though St. Louis was their supply base and their finish line. According to the National Park Service, the boats left Camp River Dubois, on the Illinois bank, on May 14, 1804, and camped six miles up the Missouri that night. Day one of the expedition began in Illinois.
The full party didn’t come together for another week. The boats worked up the Missouri to a river town, where Lewis joined them from St. Louis on May 20, and the whole Corps left there on May 21, 1804. So where did it start? Take your pick: the Illinois bank, a river town up the Missouri, or St. Louis, where Lewis spent the winter gathering supplies.
St. Louis does own the ending. The Park Service says the Corps came back about noon on September 23, 1806, landing on a spot that’s now inside the Gateway Arch grounds. That was two years, four months and nine days after the boats pushed off from the Illinois bank.
Why go at all? A land deal. The Louisiana Purchase is what sent Lewis and Clark west, and the city that outfitted them didn’t forget it.
The Louisiana Purchase finally got its party: the 1904 St. Louis World’s Fair
Back at the water, that 2-mile shift is the thing to tell whoever’s standing at the point with you. The boats of 1804 turned into the Missouri 2 miles upstream of today’s meeting, on banks the rivers have since rearranged. If the history has you hooked, our guide to the oldest buildings in St. Louis picks up the city’s side of the story.
### How do you see the confluence from both banks in one day?
Start on the Missouri side and finish on the Illinois bank. US-67 crosses the Missouri on the Lewis Bridge and the Mississippi on the Clark Bridge, and the drive from Confluence Point State Park to the tower takes roughly 20 to 30 minutes: across the Clark Bridge, then south on Illinois Route 3. The Historic Site is about a mile from the tower.
Your first stop is the Audubon Center at Riverlands, 301 Riverlands Way, on the road out to the point. It sits inside a 3,700-acre sanctuary with more than 300 bird species on its list, on land the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers owns and manages. The center is open Tuesday through Sunday, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., admission is free with donations welcome, and it may close for floods. The dam beside the sanctuary is Melvin Price Locks and Dam, where free tours take you to the top of the lock.
In winter, this is the stop that makes the trip. Trumpeter swans tell the comeback story here: from 5 birds in 1991 to 870, St. Louis Public Radio reported in 2021. They peak from late December into early January, and the best looks come within an hour of sunrise. From December through February the center adds winter programs, eagle meet-and-greets among them.
A Saturday in January, the one winter month inside the tower’s published season, could run like this:
Sunrise: swans at Riverlands. Bring a thermos and a warm hat.
8 a.m.: the Audubon Center opens. Warm up and ask what’s been spotted.
Mid-morning: drive to the end of Riverlands Way. The state park opened at 7, so it’s ready when you are. Walk the quarter mile to the point.
Late morning: US-67 north over the Clark Bridge, then south on Illinois Route 3 to the tower. Call first to confirm it’s open.
Early afternoon: the Historic Site and its keelboat, then the colonnade on your way out.
Choose the day of the week with care. The Audubon Center closes Mondays. Outside summer, the Historic Site closes Monday and Tuesday. The tower’s two published schedules disagree, but both include Thursday through Sunday, so Thursday to Sunday is your safest window. A call to (618) 251-9101 settles the rest.
Coming from the Illinois side, run it backward. Picture a grandmother in Bunker Hill with two grandkids and a Saturday to fill. She reaches the Illinois bank first, so she starts at the Historic Site when it opens at 9, then the tower once a phone call confirms it’s open, then the Clark Bridge into Missouri for the point and Riverlands. Families from Gillespie or Brighton can run the same loop.
The I-270 Chain of Rocks bridges are being replaced, so expect work zones if you head home that way. Downriver, the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge and Chouteau Island make a second river day of their own, and upriver from the Clark Bridge the Illinois bluffs line the Great River Road.
The recycled lists treat the confluence as a photo stop on the way to somewhere else. You know which bank is open this fall, and that the river mouth Clark’s boats entered in 1804 lies 2 miles from the meeting in front of you. You’re the one who knows the river is open for business. Pick a clear day and start at the point.
Coming down off the tower around lunchtime, look through our guide to places to eat on the Illinois side of the confluence before you cross back over the Clark Bridge.
If you run a restaurant, a bait shop or a tour business near the confluence, the families driving between the state park and the tower are already headed your way, so list your business with us and turn that drive into more customers.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. When was the Lewis and Clark Confluence Tower built?
A.  It was built for the 200th anniversary of the expedition, and the National Park Service dates its completion to May 14, 2010. After about a year closed for renovation, it reopened on May 14, 2026, with an expanded park, new murals and a children’s playscape. Its decks sit at 50, 100 and 150 feet, reached by stairs or an elevator.
### Q. Which river is larger, Missouri or Mississippi?
A.  By length, the Missouri: the National Park Service puts the Mississippi at 2,350 miles and the Missouri about 100 miles longer. By water, it’s close. USGS median daily flows for 1996 to 2000 were 91,300 cubic feet per second on the lower Missouri and 94,700 on the Mississippi just below the Illinois River’s mouth, a figure that may include the Illinois River’s flow.
### Q. What river joins Mississippi at St. Louis?
A.  The Missouri. It flows into the Mississippi just north of St. Louis, according to the Missouri Department of Conservation, at the tip of the peninsula where Confluence Point State Park sits. The department says the Missouri adds nearly half the flow of the Mississippi below the confluence, so the river that passes the city is carrying both.
### Q. What is a nickname for the Missouri River?
A.  Big Muddy, a name the Missouri Department of Conservation uses too. It fits. The U.S. Geological Survey measured a median of 427 milligrams of suspended sediment per liter on the lower Missouri, about three times the Mississippi’s 139, and the department says the Missouri still looks muddy even after dams cut its load to about 20 to 25 million tons a year.
### Q. What did Native Americans call the Missouri River?
A.  In 1673, Marquette recorded an Algonquian name for it, Pekitanoui, and the meaning “muddy water” belongs to that name, according to a 1999 article in the journal Names. The word Missouri has a different root. It means roughly “people with dugout canoes.” One name described the water. The other described the people.
### Q. What is the only US river longer than the Mississippi?
A.  The Missouri, by the National Park Service’s figures: the Mississippi runs 2,350 miles and the Missouri about 100 miles more. Agencies measure rivers differently, so you’ll see other lengths quoted, and the gap between the two varies. Taken together as one system, the Park Service says, they run 3,710 miles, the fourth-longest river system in the world.
### Q. Where did Lewis and Clark actually end?
A.  Back in St. Louis. The National Park Service says the Corps returned about noon on September 23, 1806, landing on a spot that’s now inside the Gateway Arch grounds. That was two years, four months and nine days after the boats left Camp River Dubois on the Illinois bank. The Park Service traces the full trail at about 4,900 miles.
### Q. What is so special about the Missouri River?
A.  Length and mud, mostly. By the National Park Service’s figures it runs about 100 miles longer than the Mississippi, and by USGS medians its water carries roughly three times as much suspended sediment per liter. It was the road west for Lewis and Clark. And its meeting with the Mississippi has moved: today’s confluence sits 2 miles downstream of where the Corps entered the Missouri in 1804.

## $37.71 a Click, or Free: Where to Advertise Your St. Louis Business
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/where-to-advertise-your-business-for-free-st-louis
The phone on the dash hasn’t buzzed since breakfast. It’s Tuesday, the truck smells like pipe dope and cold coffee, and twenty free profiles carry the same name, the same number and the same three photos. Meanwhile, somewhere in Wilbur Park, a homeowner stands in a basement with cold water soaking through her socks, thumbing four words into her phone: plumber near me today. Swap the truck for a salon chair or a bakery counter and the silence sounds the same.
Here’s the part that stings. She isn’t comparing anyone. She’s cold, she’s in a hurry, and she’ll call whoever answers first. The owner who loses that call never even sees it. Plumbers draw about 8,100 searches a month in the St. Louis metro, per Google Ads data we pulled for our what St. Louis is searching for page. That page also prices a plumber’s paid click at $37.71. Thirty-seven dollars rents her attention for one tap. Say that number out loud the next time someone tells you free listings are enough.
Blame the advice, not the owner. The “list yourself everywhere” guides, and the sites that reward a mention over an answer, collect a name, an address and a phone number, send back a confirmation email and call it advertising.
Listed isn’t chosen. A free profile puts your name in the pile. An answer, posted where she can tap it, is what makes her phone dial yours.
Start where you can touch it. Soulard Farmers Market, at 730 Carroll St, rents stands by the day or by the year, and a daily renter has to be approved by the market manager before setting up a single jar. It isn’t free. The city puts a yearly stand at roughly $1,400. But a stand is an ad read in two seconds by someone holding a paper sack of tomatoes, and nobody needs a login. Here’s the St. Louis date no free-advertising list mentions: food vendors sign a one- to three-year lease, leasing begins in November, and if there are openings, Parks staff go through the inquiry folder and choose. If you bake, the folder fills before the holidays do.
Now thumb open the Explore St. Louis event form. The cost field takes “Free or 0.” The photo must be exactly 780 pixels wide by 520 pixels high, and the form promises only “potential inclusion” on the calendar. No spot is guaranteed. That’s an honest door. Set it beside that plumber’s click: $37.71 for one tap from a stranger, or $0 and a photo cropped to 780 x 520 for a shot at the city’s own calendar. Screenshot that for the next time a sales rep calls about “premium placement.”
Then open Craigslist, the board everyone mentions, and the St. Louis math turns odd: $5 to advertise your plumbing, nothing to rent out an apartment, because Craigslist only bills for apartment rentals in the Boston, Chicago and New York City areas.
Those are real doors, and worth knocking on, in this order. Tonight, open your own Apple Maps and Google cards and fix any wrong hour or stale photo. Tomorrow, call the Soulard market manager at (314) 622-4180 and ask whether a stand is open, and if you sell food, get your inquiry into the folder before November. This weekend, send your next event through the Explore St. Louis form with a 780 x 520 photo, then post the same date on a profile you control.

### Why do twenty free profiles still leave the phone quiet?
Because listed isn’t chosen. Every one of them says the same five things. Name, address, phone, hours, a category. Open Google Maps, type your trade and thumb down the first screen: the cards read like photocopies of each other. That proves you exist. It gives nobody a reason to call you today instead of the shop two miles closer.
Here’s the part the free-advertising lists skip. People now ask ChatGPT, Gemini and Copilot the things they used to type into Google, and they ask in full questions: who’s hiring near Wilbur Park, who can take a Saturday appointment, who’s running a first-visit deal. An assistant answers by citing pages that hold the answer. Twenty profiles repeating your name and number hand it twenty copies of a mention and zero answers. So it names the business that posted the opening, the date or the deal. A page full of followers doesn’t change that.
Followers aren’t phone calls. Why social media isn’t enough on its own

And some review sites run ad programs that let other businesses display their pages on related business pages, yours included, so a customer reading your page can be shown a rival. None of that is the owner’s doing. The advice, and the sites built around it, did it.

A.  Google, Bing and Apple Business profiles cost nothing. In the Google Ads data we pulled, a plumber’s paid click costs $37.71. An ad stops when the money does. A good post keeps answering.
### Q. How do I advertise my business with no money?
A.  Claim every free profile once, ask happy customers for reviews and answer each one, and post something useful to your Google profile every few weeks so it never looks abandoned. Then lean on referrals. Our guide to winning customers without paying for ads has the full playbook.

St Louis Near Me Directory works the same way: Gold doesn’t require a public address. Check Craigslist before you post, since it charges $5 for services ads.

## Free Classified Ad Sites: Where St. Louis Businesses Post, and What Actually Gets a Call
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/free-classified-ad-sites-st-louis
Free classified sites aren’t why your ad went quiet. It wasn’t the wording, the photo or the Tuesday you posted it. The ad failed for a plainer reason: the person reading it had no way to check who you were.
Picture a two-truck roofing crew in Dorsey. Good work, steady referrals, and a slow stretch once storm season ends. The owner writes a decent services ad for the St. Louis Craigslist site, pays the fee that category carries, and watches it sink as newer posts land on top of it. By the weekend it’s a page deep. The one reply he gets offers to pay with a check for more than the estimate and asks him to send back the difference.
He didn’t do anything wrong. The old advice did. It says post everywhere for free and customers will find you, and it treats a classified board like a storefront. It isn’t one. It’s a bulletin board in a stranger’s hallway: your card goes up between a lost cat and a futon, new cards cover it every hour, and nobody walking past can tell whether the number on it rings a real business or someone who’ll disappear with a deposit.
This guide is one stop on our larger map of where to advertise your business for free around St. Louis. It covers classified ads: where a business can post them, what each kind of site actually lets a business do, and why the same few lines get more calls when they’re attached to a profile people can check.
### Where can I post free classified ads online?
Craigslist, Facebook Marketplace, OfferUp, local Facebook groups and newspaper classifieds all take local ads. For a business, read the rules first: as of October 2026, Craigslist charges for services, jobs and dealer posts, and Marketplace is built for person-to-person sales. An ad attached to a real business profile gets more calls.
Each one works differently, and the differences matter more to a business than to someone selling a couch. Here’s what each site’s own rules say as of October 2026. Check current terms before you post, because platforms change them often.
Craigslist. Its fee page says all postings are free except a short list, and for a business that list covers most of the useful part: services, jobs, gigs, every for-sale-by-dealer category, cars and trucks, and commercial real estate carry a fee in the US. Service offerings may only go in the services category. Craigslist also asks you to post to the single area closest to you, so a shop in Dorsey or French Village lands on the same St. Louis site as the rest of the metro.
Facebook Marketplace. Meta’s commerce policies say Marketplace is intended for consumer-to-consumer sales. The same policies don’t allow job listings in commerce content, limit event tickets to approved sellers, and restrict service listings to the WhatsApp Business app or Appointments on Facebook and Instagram. It suits selling a piece of equipment you own outright. A “services offered” ad isn’t what it’s set up for.
OfferUp. Items, plus service listings with their own list of prohibited services, from childcare to real estate agents. Its posting rules keep website links out of listings, and phone numbers and email addresses too unless you’re a verified business, so buyers usually reach you through the app’s messages. It also sells a paid business program.
Local Facebook groups. Town and neighborhood buy-and-sell groups. Each group’s admins write the rules, including whether business posts are welcome at all, so read the pinned post before you share anything.
Newspaper classifieds. The region’s papers still run classified sections next to their display ads. Our guide to St. Louis newspapers and magazines walks through how print advertising is priced and when it fits.
A hyper-local business directory. On St Louis Near Me Directory, a classified posts from your business profile instead of standing alone. It’s a Gold feature, and the section on how it works explains what that includes.
If you’re comparing places to list the business itself rather than a single ad, our roundup of the best free local business listing sites covers that side of it.
### Why does a classified ad on a free board go quiet so fast?
Because a board is built for one-off sales between strangers, and a business needs something a board can’t give it: a reputation that stays put. Three things happen to almost every business ad, and none of them is the owner’s fault.
It expires. Craigslist’s own help pages say free postings stay live for 7 to 45 days and paid postings for 30. A paid post can’t be moved back to the top; you buy a new one or a repost. Post the same thing more than once every 48 hours and it can be removed for overposting. The work you put into the ad has a shelf life, and the clock starts the minute it goes up.
It slides. In Craigslist’s words, “All postings move down the listings as new postings are published.” Your ad is the newest for an hour. Then it’s the second, then the fortieth.
It can’t be checked. This is the one that costs the call. A classified is a few lines, a photo and maybe a number. There’s no About section, no history, no photos of last month’s jobs, no sign the business will still be around next year. Some apps keep your number out of the listing entirely and route buyers through in-app messages. That’s a sensible safety rule, and it also means the buyer learns about you only from the ad. For someone deciding whether to let a stranger on the roof, or drop a kid off for a lesson, that gap is the whole decision.
Run the Dorsey roofer’s week again with that in mind. His ad didn’t lose to a better roofer. It lost to doubt. A homeowner read it, couldn’t tell whether he was licensed, insured or even local, and kept scrolling to a name they recognized.
None of that makes the boards bad places. Selling a used trailer on one is a fine idea. Building a business on them is where the old advice breaks, because a board was never designed to hold who you are. If the real worry is budget, our guide to getting customers without an ad budget covers the moves that pair well with any ad.
### What should a St. Louis business actually post as a classified?
Post what a customer can act on this week: a service with open dates, a class with open seats, equipment you’re selling, a block of tickets, a wholesale lot. Leave the garage clean-out to your personal account. A business classified works when it’s one specific offer from a business people can look up.
Our classifieds board is organized into 20 categories, and the ones built for owners line up with what actually moves:
Services Offered and Professional Services: a gutter crew with openings before the leaves drop, a bookkeeper taking on two new clients before tax season.
Classes and Lessons: music, tutoring, art, fitness, a first-aid class with seats left.
Wedding and Party Services: tents and tables, a DJ, a photographer whose Saturday just opened up.
Health and Wellness Services: a new practitioner introducing a service.
Home Improvement Supplies: a contractor’s leftover pavers, overstock tile, a pallet of hardware from a cancelled job.
Tickets for Sale or Trade: a venue or promoter moving a block of seats.
Community Announcements: a grand opening, new hours, a move to a bigger space.
Say you teach guitar out of a converted garage in French Village and you’ve got three Saturday-morning slots open. The ad itself is easy: beginner and intermediate, ages 8 and up, Saturdays, here’s the number. The hard part is the parent reading it. Their first question isn’t price. It’s who are you, and would I leave my kid in your garage for an hour? A board can’t answer that. A profile with your About section, photos of the room and last spring’s recital, and a phone that rings a real business can.
Record crate in the classifieds? What to look for when buying vinyl
Equipment and wholesale lots deserve one more note. A business selling gear it owns, like a bakery replacing a proofing cabinet or a landscaper selling a trailer after upgrading, often uses the same apps people use for personal sales, so check each app’s business rules first. Craigslist’s dealer categories carry a fee, so if you sell equipment regularly, plan for it.
### What makes a buyer trust a classified enough to call?
Proof they can check in under a minute. A business name that matches a real profile, a phone that rings a business, photos of real work, an About section that sounds like a person, and other posts that tell the same story. The ad starts the conversation. The profile behind it is what settles the doubt.
On the Illinois side of the river, the law already leans this way for one trade. Illinois’ Roofing Industry Licensing Act says a licensed roofer may not advertise roofing services unless the ad includes the state roofing contractor license number and the licensee’s name as it appears on the license, and knowingly running an ad without them is a misdemeanor, with each day counted as a separate offense. So the Dorsey crew’s classified needs that number in it, on Craigslist, on Facebook, anywhere. Missouri has no statewide roofing license; licensing there comes from cities and counties, so check with yours before you advertise.
Think about what that rule is really for. It hands the homeowner a way to verify the roofer before the first phone call. Every trade gains from the same move, licensed or not: put the proof where the buyer is already looking.
Here’s where it gets bigger than one ad. Customers, and the AI assistants they now ask, aren’t looking for a mention. They’re looking for an answer. Who teaches beginner guitar near French Village on Saturdays? Who can look at a leaking roof in Dorsey this week? A three-line post that’s gone in a month gives an assistant very little to stand behind. A business whose name, phone, About section, photos and posts all line up on pages it can read gives it an answer it can repeat.
A mention is not an answer. That’s the whole shift. The old way scattered you across boards you don’t control. The way that gets more customers puts every ad, offer and opening in one place that people and AI can read, and lets each new post point back to the same business.

### How do you write a classified ad that gets a call?
Lead with the job and the place, put the proof in the ad, and give one clear next step. The rest is discipline.
Headline the job, not the company. “Roof leak repair, Dorsey and nearby” tells a buyer more than a business name in capital letters.
Say who it’s for and when. “Beginner guitar, ages 8 and up, Saturday mornings” filters out the wrong calls before they happen.
Put proof in the ad. Your license number where the law requires it, your years in business, and a photo of your own work. OfferUp’s rules bar stock photos and catalog images, and buyers everywhere read them the same way.
Price it honestly. A real price or a real “starting at” beats a token price meant to game the sort, which Craigslist lists as a reason for removal.
Skip the keyword pile. A string of every service you can think of reads as spam to a buyer, and Craigslist removes keyword spamming.
Post once, in one area, and refresh with news. Craigslist flags overposting and posts outside your own area. Instead of reposting the same words, post something new: an opening, a season, a finished job.
Point to your profile. Where a site allows a link, use it. Where it doesn’t, use your exact business name so a search lands on the profile.
Guard the payment. The FTC is blunt about it: don’t accept a check for more than the selling price. Seeing the funds in your account doesn’t mean the check is good, and a bank can take weeks to spot a fake.
The roofer in Dorsey doesn’t need a cleverer ad. He needs the ad to lead somewhere a homeowner can check him out: his license, his crew, the job he finished a few streets over last month, and a phone number that answers. That’s the gap between an ad people scroll past and a business people call.
Hiring? See real openings on our jobs board and read where to post job openings.
Selling something you make? Browse items for sale and see where to sell handmade items locally.
Leasing a space or a rental? Start with our real estate profile and our guide on where to list commercial property for lease.
If a parent found your ad today, what could they check about you before they called? Where will that ad be three weeks from now? And when a neighbor asks an AI who does what you do nearby, what would it have to quote? Post yours where it stays up: the classifieds board.
If you run a business that posts classified ads, these questions are for you. See who AI names instead of you. See what Gold includes. See how it works. Refuse to be invisible.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Do people still use classifieds?
A.  Yes, though the board has moved. Craigslist still runs a St. Louis site with jobs, apartments, for sale, services, community and events sections, Facebook Marketplace and OfferUp carry local listings in their apps, and the region’s papers still print classified sections. What changed is the buyer. People check a business before they call, so a classified now works best as the front door to a profile, not the whole house.
### Q. What do people use now instead of Craigslist?
A.  For personal items, many people use Facebook Marketplace, OfferUp and local Facebook buy-and-sell groups, which run inside apps they already have open. Businesses spread out further: their own profiles, local directories and the social accounts where customers already follow them. Craigslist is still active, though. For a business, the better question is where a buyer can verify you once they’ve seen the ad.
### Q. Is it safe to use classified ads?
A.  Mostly, if you know the FTC’s warning signs. The classic seller scam is overpayment: a buyer sends a check for more than your price and asks you to send back the difference. The FTC says don’t accept a check for more than the selling price, and notes that seeing funds in your account doesn’t mean the check is good. Keep conversations on the platform until you’re sure, and take payment in a way you trust.
### Q. What are examples of classified ads?
A.  For a business: services offered like lawn care or roof repair, classes and lessons, professional services such as bookkeeping, wedding and party services, home improvement supplies like overstock tile, event tickets, wholesale lots, and community announcements like a grand opening. Personal classifieds cover used furniture, cars, rentals and lost-and-found. The business versions work best when each ad is one specific offer with a date, a place and a way to check you out.
### Q. Are classified ads free?
A.  On many sites, for many categories. As of October 2026, Craigslist’s fee page says all postings are free except a list that includes services, jobs, gigs, for-sale-by-dealer, cars and trucks, and commercial real estate in the US. Other apps charge fees on some sales or listings, or sell business programs. On St Louis Near Me Directory, classified ads are a Gold feature; the free basic listing holds only your name, address, phone, three images and About section.
### Q. Do classified ads still work?
A.  They work when the buyer can verify you fast. A classified that’s specific, current and tied to a real business profile gives people something to act on and something to check. One that’s vague, repeats every week or leads nowhere tends to get skipped, or answered by the wrong people. The ad is the hook. The proof behind it is what turns a reader into a call.
### Q. What should you avoid in classified ads?
A.  Avoid vague headlines, keyword piles, token prices that don’t match the real one, stock photos, and posting the same ad over and over or in several areas. Craigslist lists overposting, keyword spamming and posting outside your area as reasons for removal. In Illinois, a roofer’s ad must carry the state license number. And never accept a check for more than your price, which the FTC flags as a scam.
### Q. What is a classified ad site?
A.  A website or app where people and businesses post short ads sorted by category and area, usually with the newest on top. Craigslist, Facebook Marketplace and OfferUp are well-known general ones. Some local directories add a classifieds board tied to business profiles, so each ad links back to the business that posted it instead of standing alone on the board.

## Free Event Listing Sites: Where to List a St. Louis Event So People Show Up
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/free-event-listing-sites-st-louis
Free calendar listings expire. Not after a year, and not after somebody reviews them. On most community calendars, the morning after your event, the listing that brought people to your door slides off the upcoming list, and the neighbor who goes looking for something to do next month never learns you exist.
Picture a bakery owner in New Baden planning a Saturday cookie-decorating class. She does what every guide says. A Facebook event. A post on her Google profile. A flyer taped by the register. A submission to the regional tourism calendar her county sends visitors to. The class fills. By Sunday afternoon every one of those listings is gone or pointing at a date that already passed, and the people who almost came, the ones who would have booked the next class, have nothing left to find.
She didn’t do anything wrong. The old way did. “List it everywhere for free and people will find it” treats an event like a flyer on a telephone pole: useful for a week, then a rusty staple. This guide covers the free event listing sites worth your time around St. Louis, which local calendars will actually take a small-business event (several won’t), and how to make each event leave something behind. It’s one piece of our bigger map of where to advertise your business for free. If you need the promotion plan itself, timing, partners and how to word the description, our guide on how to promote an event in St. Louis County covers it. This page is about where the listing goes.
### Where can I list my event for free?
Start with three places that take almost any public event at no cost: a Google Business Profile event post, a Facebook Page event and Eventbrite, which charges no fees on free tickets. Then submit to the local calendars your event qualifies for. Calendar listings fade with the date, so point each one back to a profile you keep.
Those three cover most of what a workshop, tasting, class, open house, trunk show, fundraiser or networking night needs. Here’s what each one asks of you, as of October 2026. Platforms change their terms often, so check before you post.
Your Google Business Profile. Choose Posts, then Add post, then Event. Google asks for a title plus start and end dates and times, and you can add a description, a photo, a video and a button. Once it’s live, the post shows on your profile in Search and Maps. Google’s help page on Business Profile posts walks through it.
Your Facebook Page. Switch into the Page, open Events from the left menu and choose Create new event. Every event a Page hosts is public, and people can answer Going or Interested.
Eventbrite. Publishing an event costs nothing, and there are no fees on free tickets. Fees start when you sell paid tickets or add-ons or accept donations, and by default attendees pay them at checkout unless you choose to cover them yourself.
Local calendars. The City of St. Louis, Explore St. Louis, county tourism offices on both sides of the river, your chamber of commerce, your library branch, and the community calendars run by local newspapers, magazines, TV stations and public radio. Each one has its own rules, and the next section is about those rules.
One more that people forget: your own customer list. An email to the people who already bought from you, or a sign at the counter, fills more seats for a small event than most strangers ever will. None of it is glamorous. All of it costs nothing.
### Which St. Louis calendars will actually take a small-business event?
Fewer than you’d think. The official calendars around St. Louis were built for festivals, tourism and nonprofits, and several spell out rules that leave a shop’s workshop or tasting off the list. Read the fine print before you spend an evening on forms.
The City of St. Louis calendar. The City’s event calendar submission page is clear about who belongs there. The event has to be inside City limits and open to the public, and it has to be non-commercial and not-for-profit, or a for-profit event with an approved special use permit. The City’s own example of the permitted kind is a farmers market. One nice touch: if you pick a neighborhood on the form, the event also shows up on that neighborhood’s page. For a charity fundraiser inside the City, this is one of the best fits on this list, and if fundraising is your whole year, our marketing for nonprofits in St. Louis work is built for exactly that.
Explore St. Louis. Explore St. Louis’s Submit an Event form is for “potential inclusion” on its event calendar, which means someone reviews it and it isn’t automatic. It asks for images at exactly 780 by 520 pixels, so size the photo before you start. Browse the calendar first and you’ll see what it tends to carry: exhibitions, festivals and big seasonal draws.
VisitMO, the state’s tourism site. The Missouri Division of Tourism lists tourism-related events on VisitMO.com free of charge, and its listing criteria are refreshingly plain about who gets in. Events should draw visitors from more than 50 miles away. Events aimed mainly at the local community may not be listed. Seminars and workshops sit on the not-eligible list by name, and so do regularly recurring events that are part of normal business operations. A monthly class at your shop fails three of those at once.
Say you run a pottery studio in Cedar Hill, out along Route 30, and you host a beginners’ wheel night once a month. The state calendar’s rules leave it out. The Jefferson County Tourism Commission’s Current Events page works differently: it asks you to email your flyer as a JPG. Do it. Just notice how the page is laid out, month by month, and plan on that flyer having a short life.
The Illinois side. Cross the river and the map changes. VisitMO and the City’s calendar don’t cover a New Baden event at all. Clinton County Tourism’s Events button sends visitors to the Discover Downstate Illinois calendar, whose western region is the stretch close to St. Louis, and that bureau has its own Submit an Event form. If you sit near the line, your customers cross the river every day. The calendars don’t.
Media, chambers and libraries. Local newspapers, magazines, TV stations and public radio all run community calendars, most of them through a web form that an editor reviews. Chambers of commerce usually keep a member calendar and a weekly email. Ask what it takes to get in, and ask early.
### What does each free event listing site actually get you?
Reach, mostly, and for a short window. Each platform puts your event in front of its own audience in the days before the date. Most of them weren’t built to hold on to the people who find you there, and that’s the gap to plan around.
A Google Business Profile event post has one big advantage: it sits on your own profile, next to your hours, your reviews and your phone number. Google reviews every post before it goes live, and its help page notes two things worth knowing. Posts with a phone number in the description can get rejected if Google can’t connect that number to your business, so keep the number on the profile rather than in the post. And posts older than six months get archived unless a date range is set.
A Facebook Page event reaches the people who already follow your Page and the friends they share it with. Going and Interested give you a rough headcount, which is more than most calendars offer.
Eventbrite runs its own discovery marketplace, where people browse for things to do near them, plus registration, automated reminders, waitlists and mobile check-in. The event page lives on Eventbrite, with your business listed as the organizer.
Google’s event results are the box that appears when someone searches for things to do. Per Google’s own event documentation, events get in through pages marked up with event structured data, or through ticketing and social sites that already take part. The rules matter for small hosts. The event needs a physical location. It has to be open to the general public, so anything that needs a membership or an invitation is out. Each event needs its own page. And Google doesn’t guarantee any of it will show. A members-only networking breakfast won’t appear there no matter where you post it.
Google Calendar is for the people already coming. Google’s instructions are short: click Create, add a title and the details, click Save, and add guests by email if you want it on their calendars too. Great for reminders. It won’t introduce you to anyone new.
### What happens to your event listing the day after?
On a calendar, it drops off the upcoming list. On a ticketing page, sales end. On social media, it sinks under newer posts. What should survive is the thing the event was supposed to build in the first place: people who now know your name and want the next one.
Think about who searched for your event. Somebody typed “cookie decorating class near me” or “beginner pottery Saturday” into a phone. That was a customer raising a hand. If the only page that answered was a calendar entry, the hand goes back down with the date. They don’t remember the calendar. They barely remember the class. They remember they couldn’t find it again.
This is the part the “list everywhere” advice skips. Every site above was built to serve its own visitors first. That’s its job, and a fair one. It just means the relationship your event created lives on their page, under their name, next to whatever they show people next. Scatter ten listings across ten sites and you’ve built ten small rentals, each with a lease that ends the day after the event.
The fix isn’t to stop using them. Use every one that takes your event. Then make sure each listing points to one place that doesn’t expire. The event ends. The profile it lives on doesn’t. A person who finds the class there also finds your phone number, your About section, the next date and anything else you’ve posted.
Give them a reason to come back while you’re at it. An event-night offer works well here: a gift with purchase for anyone who mentions the class within a week, or a complimentary add-on on their next visit. Our coupon ideas for small business guide has more to pick from.
Want guests lingering past the cheese tray? Read this before you book a magician
### Why do people and AI pass over some event listings?
Because a mention isn’t an answer. A calendar entry gives a title, a date and a link. People, and the AI assistants more of them now ask, are looking for answers: who’s hosting, what it costs, whether kids can come, where to park and who to call with a question.
Somebody in Cedar Hill asks an assistant what’s happening Saturday for a beginner who wants to try pottery. The assistant can only name what it can read and trust. A one-line calendar entry gives it a title and a date and not much else to go on. A page that answers the obvious questions gives it something to repeat. Whoever wrote the clearest answer is the one that gets named, and getting named is most of the game now.
So whatever site you list on, write the listing like you’re answering the phone:
The date and the start and end time, typed out in the text, not only on a flyer image
The full street address, plus where to park and which door to use
Who it’s for: total beginners, kids 8 and up, couples, members of the public
What it costs, or that there’s no charge, and what’s included
How to sign up, and what happens when it fills
A phone number and a real person to ask
What to bring and what to wear
Google’s event guidelines read the same way: a real place, open to the public, each event on its own page. Notice that none of that is about the platform. It’s about the page answering the question before anyone has to ask.
### Why put your events on your own business profile?
Because a profile keeps working after the date, and a calendar entry doesn’t. Your Google Business Profile is one place you own outright. A directory profile that holds your events, offers, openings and story together is the other. An event on your St Louis Near Me Directory profile sits next to your phone number, your About section and everything else you post, so the person who came for the class finds the rest of your business too.

Events get filed under the categories people browse, from Educational Workshops and Networking Events to Pop-Up Shops and Markets and Charity Fundraisers. That’s the difference between a calendar entry and a listing that works like your own website. The workshop, the offer, the job opening and the story about why you started all live on one page that people and AI can read.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Where to post community events for free?
A.  Around St. Louis, start with the City of St. Louis calendar if the event is inside City limits and nonprofit or permitted, then Explore St. Louis’s submission form. In Jefferson County, the tourism commission takes flyers by email, and on the Illinois side Discover Downstate Illinois has its own form. Add your library, your chamber and local media calendars, and post it on your Google and Facebook pages.
### Q. How can I advertise my event for free?
A.  Use the channels you already own first: a Google Business Profile event post, a Facebook Page event, your email list and a sign at the register. Ask any co-host or vendor to share it, and submit it to the local calendars it qualifies for. Give every listing the same complete details and one link back to the page where people can reach you.
### Q. How do I add an event to Google Calendar?
A.  On a computer, open Google Calendar, click Create at the top left, add a title and the event details, and click Save. To put it on someone else’s calendar, add them as a guest by email before you save. Google Calendar is good for reminding people who already said yes. A private calendar event won’t put you in front of anyone new.
### Q. Can I post my event for free on Eventbrite?
A.  Yes. Eventbrite’s help center says, as of October 2026, that publishing an event costs nothing and free tickets carry no fees. Fees start when you sell paid tickets or add-ons or accept donations, and attendees pay them at checkout unless you choose to cover them. Ads and a Premium subscription are optional extras. Check the current terms before you publish.
### Q. What is a cheaper alternative to Eventbrite?
A.  For an event with no admission charge, Eventbrite already costs you nothing, so price isn’t the question. For a paid event, some owners skip ticketing altogether: they take RSVPs through a Facebook Page event or a Google Business Profile event post with a sign-up button, then collect payment at the door or through the card reader they already use. Compare the fees before you decide.
### Q. How to host an event with no money?
A.  Borrow what you’re missing. Co-host with a business that has the room, or with one that has the audience. Offer a vendor a table in exchange for samples. Partner with a local nonprofit, and if you’re inside City limits, the City’s calendar may take it. Then list it everywhere that costs nothing, starting with your own Google and Facebook pages.
### Q. How do I post an event on a Facebook page?
A.  On a computer, click your profile photo, choose See all profiles and switch into your Page. Click Events in the left menu (you may need See more first), then Create new event. Add the name, date and time, choose In person or Virtual, fill in the details and click Create Event. Events a Page hosts are always public.
### Q. Why can’t I post an event on Facebook?
A.  Usually it’s access. Creating events for a Page takes Facebook access to that Page, with full or partial control, and you have to be switched into the Page first. Task access, which owners often hand to helpers, covers content, messages, ads and insights, but Meta’s help page doesn’t list events among its tasks. Ask whoever has full control to check your access.

## Where to Sell Handmade Items Locally in St. Louis: Markets, Shops and a Storefront That Never Closes
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/where-to-sell-handmade-items-locally-st-louis
St. Louis makers, you know the Saturday routine by heart. Load the car in the dark. Set up the tent, lay out the work, sell for six hours, then pack every unsold piece back into the bins and drive home. Sunday night, the leftovers go up on an online shop built to ship to strangers three states away.
That’s the old way: a weekend booth plus a scattered online shop. It isn’t wrong to start there. It just leaks. Every good Saturday ends with your business cards in other people’s coat pockets, and nothing in that setup brings those people back.
Picture a soap maker in New Melle who has a great fall market. One woman buys three bars for her sister and takes a card. In December she wants three more as gifts, but the card went through the wash. So she asks her phone who sells handmade goat milk soap near St. Louis, and the answer names somebody else, because nothing about the soap maker’s work exists anywhere a phone can read it.
This guide is the map for that problem: where St. Louis makers actually sell, what each venue asks of you, the tax paperwork on both sides of the river, and the one storefront that stays open after the tent comes down. It’s one piece of our bigger look at where to advertise your business for free. If you’re still working out what to charge, our guide on how to price handmade crafts owns that math. This one is about where.
### Where can I sell my handmade items?
Sell where your crowd shops: Soulard Market’s daily stands, a makers-only Saturday farmers’ market, holiday shows like the Print Bazaar on Cherokee Street, and local shops that stock makers. Add Etsy or Facebook Marketplace for reach. Then give your best pieces a product post on your own business profile, so buyers can find them after the market packs up.
Each of those gets you something different, so be blunt about what:
Farmers’ and artisan markets get you foot traffic and instant feedback, plus a fixed schedule, a tent to haul and weather you don’t control.
Maker and consignment shops put your work on a shelf while you’re home. The shop chooses what it carries, keeps a share or buys at wholesale, and the customer mostly belongs to the shop.
Pop-ups and holiday fairs get you one big day in front of gift buyers. One day.
Facebook Marketplace gets you neighbors shopping nearby, one listing at a time.
Etsy gets you buyers searching the whole country, inside a marketplace that sets the fees and the rules.
Shops rarely post a sign-up form. Walk in on a slow weekday, buy something, and ask who handles new makers. Some close a whole year’s intake early.
Now notice what’s missing. None of them is a page that belongs to you, stays up all year and answers the question a St. Louis buyer actually asks. Hold that thought. First, the venues.
### Which St. Louis markets actually take handmade work?
Four are worth knowing by name. All four are in the city, and every detail below comes from the organizer’s own pages as of October 2026, so check current terms before you load the car.
Soulard Market. The city runs it and rents daily stands to non-food vendors; food vendors need a longer lease. Email the market manager first to ask whether there’s room for your type of product, because Parks staff keep the mix of wares varied. If you’re approved, the city’s stand rental page lists what to bring: a Missouri retail sales tax license, a City of St. Louis business license, liability insurance naming the City as an additional insured, and a description of what you sell. Saturday sign-in starts at 6:30 a.m., stands go first come, first served, and you rent by the half stand, roughly eight feet by four. There’s no electricity, so charge the card reader the night before.
The makers-only Saturday market in the park. STL-FM runs a Saturday farmers’ market in a south city park with about 130 vendors in its April-to-November season. Its vendor FAQ is refreshingly direct: made by you within 150 miles of St. Louis, nothing resold, designs your own. Right now it wants home goods like table linens, reusable kitchen cloths, functional ceramics and refillable soaps, and it isn’t taking plastic-based work such as 3D printing or acrylic engraving, or permanent jewelry. New-vendor applications open January 1. It even suggests a season at one of its smaller markets first, which is honest advice most organizers never give.
Best of Missouri Market. It’s happening this weekend, October 9 through 11, 2026, at the Missouri Botanical Garden, which says it draws more than 25,000 shoppers over three days. Participation is by invitation, most vendors are Missouri artists and producers, and the 2026 window has closed. The vendor information page already takes 2027 applications, and if you don’t have a website, it asks you to email product photos instead. Read that line twice. The first thing an invitation-only show wants is somewhere it can look at your work.
Print Bazaar on Cherokee Street. The 19th annual edition runs Saturday, December 5, 2026, from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m., with more than 150 artists spread through more than 30 storefronts and venues on and around Cherokee. It’s built around printmaking, though prints on fabric and pottery count, and so do paintings and collage. Artist applications opened September 23, and the organizers warn that spots fill fast.
See the pattern? A date. A sign-in time. A tent that comes down when the day ends. Those are good days. They’re just days.
### Is Etsy or Facebook Marketplace enough to reach St. Louis buyers?
They’re useful, and neither was built to send a St. Louis neighbor to your door. That’s not a knock. It’s what they’re for.
Etsy is built for reach. Its own help page on finding local sellers tells buyers to open the filters and pick their country under Shop Location. Their country. By that filter, a soap maker in New Melle and one in Oregon are equally local to a buyer in Soulard. Adding your city does help in local searches, Etsy says, so fill it in. Then read the fee policy, updated October 5, 2026: a possible one-time set-up fee, a listing fee whether or not the item sells, a transaction fee on price plus shipping, payment processing, and an Offsite Ads fee you can opt out of only while your shop stays under a sales threshold. It also bars moving a sale off the platform, so a buyer you meet through Etsy is a buyer you serve through Etsy. Check current terms, and if your shop already lives online, see our guide to reaching local customers when you sell online.
Facebook Marketplace works the other way around: local by default, one item at a time. Meta’s Marketplace safety page lists what you can’t sell, including digital products, animals and ingestible supplements, and points sellers to its Commerce Policies for the rest. A quilt or a cutting board isn’t on that list. Food is different, and health rules matter long before Facebook’s do. The real limit is shape. Each listing sells one thing through a private message, and once it’s marked sold, that listing has done its whole job.
Instagram and TikTok sit in a similar spot. A reel of you trimming wicks pulls views from everywhere, and views from everywhere don’t walk up to a stand in Soulard.
Filming your process anyway? Here’s how creators turn local views into customers.
### What happens to your customers when the market packs up?
Most go back to their lives. Some come looking for you later, which is the whole game, and that’s where the old way quietly drops them.
Say you turn walnut cutting boards in a Carlinville garage. All summer you sell at small Saturday markets, and a man from the city buys one in July. In December he wants two more as gifts. He doesn’t remember your name. He remembers walnut, and Illinois. So he asks his phone, or an AI assistant, who makes handmade walnut cutting boards near St. Louis.
What comes back is built from pages that answer that question in plain words: what the item is, who made it, roughly where, what it costs and whether it’s available. Your booth answered it perfectly, for six hours, to the people in front of it. Your card answered it for one coat pocket. None of those says, about you, in St. Louis: here’s what I make and how to get one.
That’s the difference between a mention and an answer. A mention is a booth, a card, a price tag, a name dropped in a group thread. An answer is a page a person or an AI can read later and act on. Buyers don’t search for mentions. They ask questions. Who makes custom dog collars by Friday? Who sells hand-thrown mugs I can pick up this weekend? Who can paint our house on a Christmas ornament?
So if the season ends and the phone goes quiet, you’re not doing it wrong. The old way is. Listing everywhere and hoping, scattering profiles you don’t control, renting a crowd from platforms that keep the customer, counting on referrals as a plan: none of it was built to hold on to the people who already loved your work. It was built to get you through the weekend.
### What does a product post on your own business profile do that a booth can’t?
It stays. A product post is a page about one thing you make, on your own business profile, with photos, a description in your words and a price, and it’s still there on a rainy Tuesday in February. ### What paperwork do you need before your first St. Louis market?
In Missouri, a sales tax license, even if it’s a hobby. The Department of Revenue’s special event sales FAQ asks the question every new maker asks, whether you have to collect sales tax when this is just a hobby, and answers yes if you’re selling retail to the public. Occasional event sellers apply with Form 2643S, the Missouri Special Events Application, and the department asks unregistered vendors to get in touch three to four weeks ahead. The license covers every city and county in Missouri.
One exception: if you or your spouse is at least 65 and handicraft sales are no more than half of your annual income, you may be exempt from collecting, as long as you pay tax on your materials and display Form 2478, the handicraft exemption certificate.
The city adds its own layer. Soulard Market asks for a City of St. Louis business license on top of the state license. Food is its own world: STL-FM says home bakers at its city market can sell under a Cottage Law health permit, which the market processes for vendors it accepts.
Selling on the Illinois side, out of that Carlinville garage? The Illinois Department of Revenue’s page on fairs, markets and craft shows says it plainly: full-time business or hobby, the same requirements apply. At an event the department has registered, you’re handed a reporting form. Otherwise you register directly, and if you travel to events through the year, you register as a “changing location” filer.
Etsy says it collects and remits sales tax on orders shipped to U.S. buyers. Everything here is current as of October 2026, and it’s a map, not tax advice. Call the department before your first event, not after.
