### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is couponing still a thing in 2026?
A.  Yes, it just moved to phones. In a February 2025 nationally representative Consumer Reports survey of 2,015 U.S. adults, 36 percent of grocery shoppers said they use coupons or member discounts frequently and another 38 percent occasionally. Consumer Reports also notes digital redemptions passed print back in 2020. For a local business, that means your offer has to be somewhere a phone can find it.
### Q. How can I create coupons for my business?
A.  Decide the one thing you want the customer to do: a first visit, a referral, a return trip. Pick the offer type your margin can carry, then write the headline, the terms and an end date in plain words. Add a short code so you can track it. Post it where customers check you out, such as a Gold listing with us, an Offer post on your Google Business Profile, and a card at the counter.
### Q. Can you give me an example of a coupon?
A.  Here’s one a Truesdale tutor could post: “New students: first 45-minute session on the house. Call to book and mention code FIRSTMATH. One per family, grades 3 through 8, expires December 31.” It names who qualifies, what they get, how to redeem it and when it ends, so nobody walks in confused and nobody argues at the door.
### Q. How do discounts attract customers?
A.  They lower the risk of trying someone new. A first-time customer isn’t weighing your price so much as the chance you’ll disappoint them, and a discount or a complimentary first consultation makes that bet cheaper. Discounts also reward habits. Consumer Reports’ February 2025 survey found 80 percent of Americans who shop for groceries belong to at least one store loyalty program. People like being rewarded for coming back.
### Q. What are the downsides of couponing?
A.  Three big ones. A deep discount can wipe out your profit on every sale it touches. Deal-site coupons tend to draw people loyal to the deal, not to you. And an offer that never ends trains customers to wait for it. Loyalty programs can sour too: in that same Consumer Reports survey, the top complaint among dissatisfied members was that the discounts weren’t as good as expected.
### Q. Do stores lose money from coupons?
A.  On the coupon sale itself, often yes, and that’s fine if it’s planned. A coupon is a marketing cost, the price of a first visit. It turns into profit when the customer returns at full price or sends a friend. The shops that lose money for good usually picked a discount too deep for their margin, or ran it somewhere customers had no reason to come back.
### Q. What are some creative coupon code ideas?
A.  Make the code do two jobs: describe the offer and tell you where it came from. A salon might use NEWLOOK on its listing and NEWLOOKCARD at the register. A landscaper could run SPRINGFIRST for early bookings, and a bakery DOZENPLUS for a gift with purchase. A Fayetteville diner might try RIVERMORNING for its anglers. Keep codes short, easy to say aloud, and skip look-alike characters like 0 and O.
### Q. What are the best coupon websites?
A.  For shoppers, the big categories are store apps, coupon-code browser tools and daily-deal sites. For an owner, the best one is the page where your customer meets you, not a middleman. That means your Google Business Profile, which lets you post an Offer with a coupon code and terms, and a listing you control, where coupons and offers are included with Gold and sit beside your phone number and reviews.

## Does Blogging Help SEO for a Small Business? The 2026 Answer for St. Louis Owners
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/does-blogging-help-seo-for-small-business-st-louis
Somebody gets quoted. Tonight a homeowner in Mt Olive will type a question about her house into her phone, and the answer that comes back will borrow its explanation from somebody’s page. Maybe a page written by someone in her own county. More likely a national site that has never once mentioned Macoupin County.
Here’s her question. She just closed on an older house in a town with coal-mining roots, and a line in her insurance paperwork mentions mine subsidence. Does she need that? Can she drop it? Now picture an insurance agent a few minutes from her front door who could answer it half asleep. Macoupin is one of 34 Illinois counties where mine subsidence coverage is automatically included in a property policy, and an owner who doesn’t want it has to reject it in writing, according to the Illinois Mine Subsidence Insurance Fund. That agent has explained it across a desk more times than she can count.
She has never once written it down anywhere a search engine, or an AI assistant, can read it.
That’s the real question hiding inside “does blogging help SEO.” Forget whether blogs are fashionable. What matters is whether the answer you give out loud every week exists anywhere in writing, so the next person who asks a machine gets your answer and not a stranger’s.
You’ve probably heard that blogging is dead. What died is the post that could have been written for any town on earth: “5 Tips for Choosing the Right Insurance Agent,” padded out to whatever length somebody swore Google prefers. Google says flatly that it has no preferred word count. What it does publish is a long list of questions about whether a page shows first-hand expertise and tells readers something beyond the obvious. The filler flunks them. The agent’s answer about mine subsidence passes without trying.
Still sorting out where your business should show up at all? Start with our map of where to advertise your business for free, then come back for the part those sites can’t do for you.
### Are blogs still relevant in 2026?
Yes, for a small business, as long as each post answers a question your customers really ask. Generic “top tips” filler is what died. A page that answers one real question, with details only you know, is the kind of page Google says it wants to reward, and the kind AI answers draw from.
Forget the online-diary picture. For a business, a blog post is a page that answers one question in writing, under your name. People never stopped asking questions. More of them now ask an AI assistant instead of clicking through ten links, and that assistant still has to read somebody’s page to answer.
What changed is the bar. For years a business could publish a thin post on a popular topic and pick up a trickle of traffic. Google’s guidance on helpful, people-first content now reads like a checklist aimed squarely at that habit. Its warning signs include content made mainly to attract search visits, pages that mostly summarize what others already said, and writing to a particular word count. On the other side of the ledger sit original information, first-hand expertise, and a reader who leaves having learned enough to reach their goal.
Read that list as an owner and something flips. You can’t outspend a national publisher. You can out-know one. Nobody writing generic advice for every zip code in the country has sat across from a Mt Olive homeowner holding a mine subsidence form. You have. That first-hand detail is the one thing filler can’t fake, and it’s exactly what Google says it’s looking for.
So yes, relevant. Different, though. Fewer posts, and every one of them carrying something only you could have written.
### Does blogging help SEO for a small business?
Yes, when each post answers a specific question better than anyone else nearby has. No, when it’s filler. SEO is a long name for a simple idea: showing up when someone searches. Every useful post is one more page that can show up, for one more question, in front of one more person who’s about to call somebody.
In plain words: your listing or homepage shows up for a short list of searches, mostly your name, your trade and your town. It can’t answer two hundred different questions. A post can answer one, all the way down. Publish a couple dozen over a few years and you’ve built a couple dozen extra doors into your business, each standing on the exact words somebody typed.
The posts help each other, too. A post on mine subsidence links to one on insuring an older home, and both link back to your profile and your phone number. Search engines follow those links the way readers do. Google’s advice on its AI features lists making content easy to find through internal links as one of the fundamentals that still matter.
What a blog won’t do is fix the basics. If your hours are wrong and your phone number is two numbers ago, a post won’t save you. It won’t pay off in a week, either. Our guide to content marketing for small businesses covers where to start and the honest timeline, so this page won’t repeat it. The short version: think in months, and know that the slow start is where a lot of owners give up.
### How does an AI answer decide whose page to quote?
It needs a page that answers the question, and then it shows the reader where that answer came from. Google says a page has to be indexed and eligible to appear in Search with a snippet to be shown as a supporting link in AI Overviews and AI Mode, and that there are no additional technical requirements. Translation: the same kind of page that can rank can be quoted.
The part most owners haven’t heard is how those answers get assembled. Google describes a “query fan-out” technique, where the AI may run several related searches across subtopics and gather supporting pages from each. So the Mt Olive homeowner might ask something broad, like what to know before insuring an older house in her part of Illinois. Behind the scenes, that can splinter into narrower searches, and one of them lands on mine subsidence. That narrow search is where a small local page can win, because almost nobody else bothered to write the narrow answer.
Other assistants work along similar lines when they search the web. OpenAI, for one, says it runs a crawler called OAI-SearchBot to surface websites in ChatGPT’s search features. None of these companies publishes a formula for who gets cited, so anybody promising you a guaranteed spot in an AI answer is guessing. What they all need is the same raw material: a public page that says the thing clearly.
Which is why a mention is not an answer. A listing that says “insurance agent, Mt Olive” is a mention. It tells a machine you exist. A post explaining how mine subsidence coverage works in Macoupin County, what it means for a buyer and what to ask before turning it down, is an answer. Machines quote answers. And since the post sits on its own page, a stranger can land on it from an AI answer without ever having heard of you, or of us.
### What does a blog post worth quoting look like?
It reads like your best answer across the counter, typed up. Before you publish anything, run one test: could a competitor in another city post it by swapping out the town name? If yes, it’s filler, however polished it sounds.
Take a tax preparer in Washington Park, the small Metro East village with its own MetroLink stop. Lots of people on that side of the river work on the other side of it, and every spring some of them walk in asking the same thing: I live in Illinois and get paid in Missouri, so where do I file?
The filler version is called “Top Tax Tips for the New Year.” Seven bullet points. Keep good records. Don’t miss the deadline. It could run on any website in America.
The version worth quoting is titled with the question itself and answers it in the first two sentences. Then it says the thing a Metro East preparer says every spring. According to the Illinois Department of Revenue, Illinois has reciprocal agreements with four states, Iowa, Kentucky, Michigan and Wisconsin, and Missouri isn’t on that list. For a lot of households that means a Missouri return plus an Illinois return that claims a credit for the Missouri tax, and working from home can change the picture, so the post tells readers to check their own situation. That one paragraph outweighs the seven bullets combined, because nobody finds it on a page written for everywhere.
Posts worth quoting tend to share the same bones:
The title is the question, worded the way customers actually say it.
The first two or three sentences answer it, plainly, before any backstory.
At least one detail only somebody local and in the trade would know.
A real job, with no names and all the details: what the customer asked, what you found, what happened next.
Cost in words, not numbers. What pushes the price up, what keeps it down, what people regret skimping on. Prices change; the reasons don’t.
Your name and your business at the bottom. Google’s guidance encourages accurate bylines, and readers trust a post signed by the person who does the work.
Tempted to let ChatGPT write it? Teach it to sound like you first
About drafting with AI, since everybody asks. Google says generative AI can be useful for researching a topic and adding structure to original content, and that using it to churn out many pages without adding value may violate its spam policy on scaled content abuse. It also says to fact-check everything AI produces before you publish. Treat it like an assistant taking dictation. The local fact, the real job and the opinion still have to come from you, because those are the parts a machine can’t know.

### Is a blog worth the time for a one-person business?
Only at a pace you’ll actually keep. A blog has three real costs, and all three land on the owner.
Time. A post worth quoting takes a real evening: thinking it through, writing it, checking the facts, reading it out loud once. Picture the Mt Olive agent after a day of renewals and claims calls. That evening has to come from somewhere.
Consistency. One strong post a month, month after month, beats ten in January and silence until next year. Customers notice the rhythm. So does anyone deciding whether you’re still active.
The abandoned blog. This one stings. A customer clicks your blog and the newest post is three years old. Nobody thinks “busy owner.” They wonder whether you’re still open. An abandoned blog can look worse than none at all, and changing the dates won’t fix it. Google lists updating a page’s date to make it seem fresh, when the content hasn’t substantially changed, among its warning signs.
Here’s the reframe. You’re not behind because you never blogged. The old way told you to list everywhere and wait for the phone. It never mentioned that the answers you give away every single day are the most valuable marketing you own, or that each one disappears the second the customer hangs up. Writing one of them down a month is a smaller job than it sounds.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is blogging a dead trend?
A.  Blogging as an online diary faded as people moved their personal updates to social apps. Blogging as a business answering its customers’ questions in writing is very much alive, because search engines and AI assistants still need pages to read. What’s fading is the generic post that could belong to any company in any city.
### Q. What is replacing blogging?
A.  Short video, social posts, newsletters and AI answers all compete for attention now, and each has a place. None of them replaces a written answer, though. AI assistants pull from pages they can read, and a video lands better when a written page explains the same thing. Most businesses do best treating the post as the anchor and everything else as the way people discover it.
### Q. Are blogs still worth it in 2026?
A.  For a business that can answer real customer questions with first-hand detail, yes. A strong post keeps working for years, can rank for the exact words customers type, and gives AI answers something specific to cite. It isn’t worth it if every post would be generic filler or if you’ll stop after a month. Pick a pace you can keep before you start.
### Q. What are the downsides of having a blog?
A.  Time, consistency and the risk of neglect. A post worth reading takes an evening of real thought, results build over months rather than days, and an abandoned blog with a three-year-old latest post can make customers wonder if you’re still open. Google also lists changing dates to look fresh, without real updates, as a warning sign. Commit to a pace you can hold.
### Q. How often should I post my blog?
A.  As often as you can produce a post worth reading, which for many one-person businesses means once or twice a month. Steady beats frequent. Google says piling on new content mainly to make a site seem fresh won’t help its rankings, and it publishes no magic schedule. A monthly answer to a real customer question will outlast a burst of rushed posts.
### Q. What is the 80/20 rule for blogging?
A.  It’s a rule of thumb, not an official rule, and people use it two ways. One version says spend about 20 percent of your effort writing and 80 percent getting the post in front of people. The other says keep about 80 percent of your content helpful and 20 percent promotional. For a local business both point the same direction: answer first, sell second, and share every post.
### Q. Does anyone blog anymore?
A.  Plenty of businesses do. They rarely call it that. Any page that answers a specific question about a trade, a cost or a local rule is a blog post by another name. Readers arrive through Google, AI answers and shared links rather than by checking a blog’s homepage every morning, which is why each post has to stand on its own.
### Q. Are blogs old fashioned?
A.  The name is. The idea is current. A page that answers one question clearly, signed by someone who knows the subject, matches what Google’s own guidance says it wants to reward. Call it a blog, an article or an answer page. What matters is that it exists, it’s accurate, and it sits next to the phone number of the person who wrote it.

## Your Car Tax Bill Finds You. Your Unclaimed Money Won't.
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-money-guide
The envelope has been on the kitchen counter for a week, under the car keys, and the bill inside is for the car those keys start. Not the loan. The car. Missouri taxes it every year you own it, the bill is due December 31, and if it goes unpaid, the clerk at the license office slides your plate renewal right back across the counter. Own your home and a second bill, for the house, comes due the same December 31.
Then there’s the paycheck. Work inside City limits and 1% of every check usually goes to the City of St. Louis before it ever reaches your account, even if you drive home to the County every night. Work some of those days from your kitchen table instead and part of that 1% can come back on Form E-1R, the refund commuters miss. The City gives you one year from the April 15 due date to ask for it, and not a day more.
The tax office never loses your address. The money owed to you does. A utility deposit that never came back after a move, a refund mailed to an apartment you left years ago, a bank account you forgot you had: Missouri’s State Treasurer is holding more than $574 million of it under St. Louis County and the City, close to 4 million separate items, and none of it comes with an envelope. You have to go get it.
If you do one thing today, make it that search. Go to treasurer.mo.gov, open the unclaimed property search and type your last name, then every other name you’ve gone by. Keep a list of old addresses next to you, because the record may sit under one you left years ago. It’s free, it takes about ten minutes, and if your name comes up, you file the claim on the same site. Stuck? The Treasurer’s office answers 573-751-0123 from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Then come back for the bills that find you.
### What are the taxes in St. Louis?
Five, and each one lands somewhere different: a line on your pay stub, an envelope on the counter, a few extra coins on every receipt. The state takes income tax, topping out at 4.7%. The City takes 1% of the pay of everyone who lives there and everyone who works there. The car in your driveway draws a personal property tax bill every year you own it. The house draws a real estate tax bill, or the landlord folds it into your rent. And sales tax rings up at the register: 7.738% in unincorporated St. Louis County, 9.679% in the City and more inside special districts, topping out at 13.238% in stacked districts in north St. Louis County, the highest rate on the state’s entire table.
Taxes are only one line in the cost of living in St. Louis and they carry the most fine print. Take them in the order they hit your wallet.
The bills that find you
### Who pays the St. Louis earnings tax?
Check the deductions on a pay stub from any job inside City limits and you’ll usually find it: a local tax line, 1% of what you earned. Everyone who lives in the City of St. Louis pays 1% of their earnings, wherever they work, and so does anyone who works inside City limits, wherever they live. That’s how the Collector of Revenue puts it. A County resident with a County job never pays it. A County resident who drives downtown every morning does, usually straight out of each paycheck, on a line most people stop reading by February.
It taxes earned income only. The City’s non-taxable list includes pensions, Social Security, interest, dividends and unemployment benefits. On a $60,000 salary it’s $600 a year. Missouri law has barred any new city earnings tax since the end of 2011, so only St. Louis and Kansas City still levy one, and City voters must re-approve it every five years. They did again in April 2026.
Here’s the trap. Individual returns on Form E-1 are due April 15, and the City does not allow individuals to file extensions at all. Your federal extension doesn’t reach City Hall. Our guide to the St. Louis earnings tax covers the forms and that work-from-home refund.
### Why do you pay tax on your car every year in Missouri?
Because Missouri taxes personal property, meaning cars, trucks, motorcycles, boats and trailers, based on what you owned on January 1, every year you own it. State law sets the taxable amount at one-third of its value (RSMo 137.115), and your local rate, built from your school district, fire district and other taxing bodies, applies to that third.
Here’s the math inside that envelope on the counter, in round numbers: an $18,000 car is assessed at $6,000. At a combined rate of $8 per $100 (a made-up figure; your real one prints on your bill), you’d owe $480. Next year the car’s worth less, so the bill usually shrinks.
One local wrinkle: St. Louis County wants your declaration by March 1, while the City’s deadline is April 1, with a 10% penalty if you miss it. Bills are due December 31 in both. Then the part that ambushes new residents: to renew plates, Missouri requires a paid receipt or a statement of non-assessment (a waiver) for the previous year, or two years on a two-year registration. Our guides cover St. Louis County personal property tax and the personal property tax receipt or waiver.
### How is property tax on a house figured in St. Louis?
Multiply your home’s market value by 19%, and your tax rate applies to that assessed value. The City Assessor’s example: a $100,000 home is assessed at $19,000. Values reset as of January 1 of every odd-numbered year under the same statute, so the notices that rattle people arrive in odd years. The bill is due December 31.
A value notice is not a bill, even if your stomach drops when you pull it out of the mailbox, and it’s the piece you can push back on. If the number is higher than your house would sell for, ask for an informal review, then appeal to the Board of Equalization with recent comparable sales; the County takes appeals through its revenue and assessment portal. Deadlines are short, so read our guide to a St. Louis County property tax appeal the week your notice arrives. Renters pay property tax too, folded into the rent, and that can qualify them for a credit in part two.
### Same couch, two receipts: why sales tax changes by the store
Missouri’s sales tax is a stack, and the stack depends on the store’s exact address. The state’s share is 4.225%, or 1.225% on most groceries. Counties, cities and special districts add their own. On the Department of Revenue’s current rate table, unincorporated St. Louis County totals 7.738% and the City of St. Louis totals 9.679%.
Then come the districts. A Community Improvement District (CID) or Transportation Development District (TDD) can add its own sales tax inside a single shopping center, and nothing on the shelf tag tells you. You find out when the receipt prints. Inside some City districts the total reaches 11.679%. In stacked districts in north St. Louis County it hits 13.238%, the highest rate on the state’s entire table. On a $1,000 couch, that’s $77.38 in unincorporated County and $132.38 in the priciest district. Same couch. $55 apart.
Check any address with the state’s sales and use tax lookup; the state reissues its table every quarter. Our guide to the St. Louis sales tax rate breaks down each layer.
Waiting on a refund with a thin pantry? Here’s what to do if SNAP gets cut.
### How much is Missouri state income tax?
You meet this one once a year, W-2 in hand, and the surprise is hiding in the brackets. Missouri’s top income tax rate is 4.7% for the 2025 tax year, and it applies to every dollar of taxable income over $9,191. That threshold is the part nobody mentions. The lower brackets are so narrow that most of a full-time worker’s income lands in the top one. Someone with $50,000 of Missouri taxable income owes about $2,174: $256 on the first $9,191, plus 4.7% of the rest. Brackets are indexed for inflation, and the Department of Revenue posts the current table each year.
Two newer breaks matter. Missouri became the first state to fully exempt capital gains for individuals, starting with the 2025 tax year, which changes the math on capital gains tax on selling a house in Missouri. And from the 2024 tax year on, Missouri doesn’t tax Social Security for people 62 and older, at any income, part of how Missouri taxes retirement income. The full walk-through is in our guide to the Missouri state income tax rate.
Federal and Missouri returns are due April 15. An extension moves filing to October 15 but never moves the payment date, as the IRS spells out on its extension page. Here’s how to file a tax extension in Missouri without stacking penalties.
Here’s the whole stack on one card, the kind worth taping inside a kitchen cabinet door.
Have a mortgage? You may never see the real estate bill at all. The lender pays it quietly out of an escrow account built into your monthly payment. Two traps stand out. The earnings tax and Missouri income tax are separate returns, so an extension on one does nothing for the other. And the receipt for the car tax matters more than the bill: without it, or a waiver, the license office won’t renew your plates, and you’re back at the end of the line.
The money you have to go find
### How do you find unclaimed money in Missouri?
Search your name on the Missouri State Treasurer’s unclaimed property search, then file the claim online. That’s the whole process. The Treasurer holds more than $1.5 billion, says 1 in 10 Missourians has some, and puts the average return at $300. Its county totals list $387.7 million under St. Louis County and $186.4 million under the City, spread across close to 4 million separate properties. More than $574 million, sitting in Jefferson City with St. Louis names on it.
What is it? Money that went quiet. A utility deposit you never got back after you handed in the keys to an old apartment. A government refund mailed to an address you left years ago. A forgotten bank account, stock, bond or insurance payout, or the contents of a safe deposit box. Holders must turn it over after it sits untouched with no owner contact, generally for five years, according to the Treasurer’s FAQ.
The Treasurer keeps it in trust forever, so there’s no deadline, and interest-bearing accounts can earn up to seven years of interest. Searching is free. Claiming is free; the office says it never charges to return property. Search like you mean it:
Every name you’ve used, plus your first initial with your last name.
Every address you’ve had, since the record may sit under an old one.
Parents or grandparents who have died; heirs can claim.
Any business you’ve run under its own name.
Now the part somebody is counting on you not knowing. Letters from “finders” offer to recover your money for a cut. You never need one. Missouri law (RSMo 447.581) makes a finder’s fee agreement unenforceable if it’s made within 12 months after the money reaches the Treasurer, caps the fee at 10%, 15% or 20% after that depending on how long it has sat, and requires finders to register. Ten minutes on the official site does the same job for nothing.
### Who qualifies for the Missouri property tax credit and the senior freeze?
The Missouri Property Tax Credit (MO-PTC) goes to renters and homeowners with limited income who are 65 or older, 100% disabled, or 60 or older and receiving surviving-spouse Social Security. For 2025 claims, full-year owners qualify with household income of $30,000 or less ($34,000 married filing combined), and renters with $27,200 or less ($29,200 married). It tops out at $1,100 for owners and $750 for renters, per the state’s qualification chart.
If a parent or grandparent opens a tax bill on a fixed income, read this part to them out loud. Three details turn this into real money. You can file it alone, on Form MO-PTC, if you don’t otherwise have to file a Missouri return. You can claim a past year within three years of its original due date, says the Department of Revenue. And a 2025 law raises the income limits and credit amounts starting January 1, 2026 (summary), so check the newest chart before deciding you earn too much. Renters in a building that pays no property tax aren’t eligible.
The senior freeze is a different program, and St. Louis has two. The City’s Senior Citizen Property Tax Freeze Credit covers homeowners 62 and older whose home is worth $528,392 or less, takes applications March 1 through June 30, and must be renewed yearly. St. Louis County runs its own for owners 62 and older who live in the home; in August 2026 the County Council passed a bill ending yearly renewals for seniors already approved, and new applications are closed until the next window opens. The County’s version holds the line on nearly every taxing district on the bill. The City’s covers only City levies, so school, library and zoo taxes can still rise. Our guide to the St. Louis County senior tax freeze and the state credit walks through both.
### Can you get St. Louis earnings tax back for days you worked from home?
Yes, if you live outside the City. Nonresidents owe the earnings tax only on work done inside City limits, so if your employer withheld 1% on days you worked from your kitchen in the County or the Metro East, you can ask for it back on Form E-1R. Your employer verifies how many days you worked outside the City.
Take a claims adjuster who lives in the County, earns $70,000 and has $700 withheld, but works from home two days a week, laptop on the kitchen table. About 40% of her working days were outside the City, so she’s looking at something near $280 back; the form does the exact math. City residents can’t do this.
The deadline is the tightest on this page: one year from the original return due date. Not three. One. Email it to earningstaxcor@stlouis-mo.gov, fax 314-622-4847, or mail the Collector of Revenue, 1200 Market St., Room 410, St. Louis, MO 63103.
One more refund that’s easy to forget: Missouri lets drivers of vehicles up to 26,000 pounds claim back the gas tax increase. On the current Form 4923-H, that’s 12.5 cents a gallon, filed July 1 through September 30 for the prior July-to-June year. See gas prices in St. Louis, Missouri vs. Illinois.
### Where can you get your taxes done for free in St. Louis?
Through volunteer programs the IRS backs, usually set up in libraries, schools and community centers, where you sit down with your W-2s and an IRS-certified volunteer does the return. VITA sites prepare returns free for people who generally make about $70,244 or less, and TCE sites focus on people 60 and older, per the IRS. Find one with the IRS locator or at 800-906-9887; the list updates February through April. Our guide to free tax preparation in St. Louis covers the local sites and the Earned Income Tax Credit.
Volunteers don’t take every return. A rental, a tangled side business or an IRS letter you can’t decode is where a paid preparer earns the fee; here’s what a tax preparer costs in St. Louis. If the letter mentions a levy or a lien, read when you need a tax attorney in St. Louis first.
Before the next April 15, compare tax preparers around St. Louis and ask one question up front: do you file the City’s E-1 and the E-1R refund, or only federal and state?
If you’re the CPA, enrolled agent or preparer a neighbor should be calling, see who AI names instead of you and put your practice in front of more customers.
Before you borrow
### What borrowing really costs in St. Louis
Know the price before you sign. The most expensive debt is usually the easiest to get, and it feels like relief the day you sign. The price is the APR, or annual percentage rate: the yearly cost of borrowing, interest plus certain fees, as one number. The Federal Reserve’s latest figure puts the average rate on credit card accounts that are paying interest at 22.36%. Carry $3,000 at that rate and you pay about $670 a year just to stand still.
Payday loans cost more, and Missouri allows them. State law (RSMo 408.500 and 408.505) covers unsecured loans of $500 or less for 14 to 31 days. A loan can be renewed up to six times, each renewal must cut the principal by at least 5%, and total interest and fees are capped at 75% of the original loan. On $500, that’s $375. Our breakdown of how payday loans work in Missouri and what they cost shows how fast that ceiling arrives. A title loan puts your car title up as collateral, so falling behind can cost you the car you drive to work.
Better doors exist. Credit unions are member-owned cooperatives, worth checking first for a small loan; start with the local credit unions in the St. Louis metro, and if fees keep draining the account, here’s how to avoid bank fees in St. Louis. Debt consolidation helps only when the new rate is truly lower and the old cards stay at zero. When debt has outrun any plan, what happens when you file bankruptcy in Missouri explains what it erases.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Does St. Louis have a city tax?
A.  Yes. The City of St. Louis levies a 1% earnings tax on everyone who lives in the City, wherever they work, and on nonresidents for work done inside City limits. Pensions, Social Security, interest and dividends aren’t taxed. St. Louis County has no earnings tax, so a County resident who works outside the City never pays it.
### Q. Is MO a high tax state?
A.  Not at the state level. Missouri’s 4.225% state sales tax is lower than Kansas’ 6.5%, and its 4.7% top income rate for the 2025 tax year sits below Illinois’ flat 4.95% and Kansas’ top 5.58%. What makes St. Louis feel expensive is the local stack: the earnings tax, the yearly car tax and sales taxes that top 13% in a few districts.
### Q. What city in Missouri has the highest tax rate?
A.  For sales tax, the top combined rate on the Department of Revenue’s statewide table is 13.238%, inside stacked special districts in north St. Louis County. For taxes on wages, only St. Louis and Kansas City levy a city earnings tax, both at 1%, because state law has blocked new ones since the end of 2011.
### Q. Is it better to live in Kansas or Missouri for taxes?
A.  It depends on how you earn and spend. Missouri’s income tax is lower: a 4.7% top rate for the 2025 tax year against Kansas’ 5.2% and 5.58%, and Missouri now exempts capital gains. Kansas wins at the grocery store, where its state food tax has been 0% since January 2025, while Missouri still charges 1.225% plus local tax.
### Q. What are taxes like in St. Louis?
A.  Layered. The state takes a modest cut, then local bills stack up: 1% of your pay if you live or work in the City, a personal property tax bill each December for every car, real estate tax split among dozens of districts, and sales tax that changes by address. Newcomers usually get blindsided by the car tax.
### Q. How can I contact the Missouri Department of Revenue?
A.  For individual income tax, the department lists 573-751-3505 for refunds and general questions, 573-751-7200 if you owe, and income@dor.mo.gov. You can also schedule a tax call online. Its only walk-in Tax Information Office is in Jefferson City; St. Louis-area license offices handle plates and driver licenses, not income tax.
### Q. Is it really free to claim unclaimed property in Missouri?
A.  Yes. The Treasurer’s office says it never charges to return unclaimed property, and searching its website is free. Paid finders exist, but Missouri law won’t enforce a finder’s agreement made within 12 months after the money reaches the Treasurer, caps the fee at 10% to 20% after that, and requires finders to register.

## St. Louis County and City Personal Property Tax: How It's Figured, How to Pay, and What Late Costs
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-county-personal-property-tax
Your sold car still gets a tax bill. Picture a nurse in Winchester who traded in her old silver sedan in March, signed the title over and never gave it another thought. In November an envelope shows up from the Collector of Revenue with that sedan printed on it and a December 31 due date. She calls to explain the car is gone. Doesn’t matter.
Missouri taxes the cars, trucks, boats and trailers you owned on January 1, with no refund for the months after you let one go. St. Louis County’s Assessor says vehicles bought, sold or moved out of the county mid-year don’t qualify for adjustments, and the City makes the whole year’s assessment as of January 1. The bill explains none of it. That’s the real trouble with personal property tax: a once-a-year cycle with four dates, two governments and a formula, and nobody walks you through it. Not school. Not the dealership.
So here’s the walk-through for both sides of the city-county line: the assessor’s math, why the same car costs more in one place than another (even on two streets of one small town), every date that matters, and what late really costs. Juggling more than this one bill? Our St. Louis money guide lays out the rest of the local money calendar.
### Do I pay personal property tax on my car every year in Missouri?
Yes. If you own a car, truck, motorcycle, boat or trailer on January 1, it’s taxed every year where you live. You declare it early in the year (by March 1 in St. Louis County, April 1 in the City), the bill comes in November, and it’s due December 31. Selling later doesn’t cancel that year’s bill.
It’s the yearly tax on things you own that aren’t real estate, and for most households that means vehicles. The County Assessor’s list of personal property also covers trailers, mobile homes, boats and boat motors, aircraft, livestock and farm machinery. Your couch and your clothes aren’t on it. State law exempts household goods, furniture and clothing you use in your home.
And it’s every year, not once at purchase the way sales tax works. A car you keep ten years produces ten bills, though each one should shrink as the car ages, since the tax follows its value. Moved to Missouri after January 1? You owe nothing for that first partial year. You’ll get a waiver to register the car instead, which our move-in setup checklist puts in order with your other first-month errands.
Where you lived that day decides who bills you; the County Collector says your bill is based on where you lived on January 1. Move from the City to the County in February and the City still sends that year’s bill.
### Why does a car I sold in March still get a tax bill?
Because the tax is a snapshot, not a meter. You’re billed for the whole year based on what you owned January 1, with no proration for the months a car was gone. So the nurse in Winchester owes a full year on the sedan she traded in March. The SUV that replaced it isn’t on this year’s bill at all. It shows up next year.
The rule cuts both ways, and that’s the part nobody mentions. Buy a car on December 30 and it’s on next year’s bill. Buy it January 2 and it isn’t taxed until the year after. Over a lifetime of car buying it mostly evens out. In the year you feel it, it doesn’t feel even. Our guide to buying a car from a St. Louis area dealership covers the rest of the purchase math.
Where people really get burned is the next declaration. That form lists what the office thinks you own, and in the County’s own words, what you file determines your personal property tax bill. Cross off anything you didn’t own on January 1, add anything you did, and send it back. County residents with an existing account can file online. In the City, a first declaration goes on paper, and you can switch to online filing after that.
Bill shows a car you didn’t own on January 1? In the County, the Assessor’s Office fixes accounts when you bring proof of the sale, trade, loss or repossession. In the City, only the Assessor’s Office can change the vehicles on a bill; the Collector just collects. Either way, ask right away. The tax is still due December 31 while you wait.
### How does the assessor figure what I owe on a car?
Three numbers: the car’s value, one-third of that value, and your local tax rate. The formula is identical in the City and the County. Only the rate changes.
Value. State law tells assessors to use the trade-in value from the October issue of a used-car guide the State Tax Commission picks, and not to go above the average trade-in figure without physically inspecting the car (cars two model years old or newer are the exception). Not what you paid. The trade-in number, which usually runs well below retail.
Assessed value. Personal property is assessed at 33 1/3% of that value. A car the guide puts at $15,000 has an assessed value of $5,000.
Rate. Every taxing district covering your address, from the school district to the library, fire and zoo-museum districts, sets a rate per $100 of assessed value. Added together, that’s your composite rate.
Bill. Divide the assessed value by 100 and multiply by the composite rate.
Here’s the City version, using the City’s 2025 personal property rate of $8.1122 per $100. A $15,000 value divided by 3 is $5,000 assessed. Divide by 100 and you get 50. Fifty times $8.1122 is $405.61. That’s one year on a $15,000 car in the City, before any penalties, and the City’s own personal property page uses the same $15,000-to-$5,000 example.
Now the newer part, and it matters if you watched used-car prices climb. A change to state law that took effect January 1, 2026 says that for a vehicle with a true value under $50,000 as of January 1, 2025, the assessor can’t assess it for more than it was assessed the year before, as long as last year’s assessment was done properly. In plain terms, the assessment on most everyday cars can hold or drop. It can’t climb.
Think the value’s wrong anyway? Appeal to the Board of Equalization, in the County between May 1 and the second Monday in July and in the City in writing by that same Monday. Bring real evidence. In one St. Louis County appeal, an owner argued his former rental SUV was worth less because of an accident, scratches and a dented door. The State Tax Commission kept the assessor’s number: the title was clean, and that wear fit the guide’s definition of average condition. Average already assumes some dings.
### Why does the same car cost more in the City than in the County?
Because the rate isn’t one number. The City of St. Louis charges a single personal property rate at every address, $8.1122 per $100 for 2025. St. Louis County’s Collector bills for more than 200 taxing districts, and your rate depends on which school, fire, sewer and city districts overlap at your address. The school district is usually the biggest slice.
Winchester shows how fine-grained it gets. The tiny town sits in two school districts, so neighbors a few houses apart can pay different school levies on the same car. Here’s a $15,000 car, assessed at $5,000, run through the school levy alone on each side of that line, next to the City’s full rate:
Then the fire, library, sewer and county levies stack on top, and a County bill can land near the City’s or past it. The school district is the swing. It’s the biggest slice, it changes at a line on a map, and on a car assessed at $5,000 every extra dollar of school levy per $100 adds $50 to the bill. Same car. Same year. A different bill, set by which side of a district line your driveway sits on.
One more wrinkle: a district can set different rates for different kinds of property, so the rate on your car can top the rate on your house. Parkway’s 2025 school levy was $3.1636 per $100 on homes and $4.2609 on vehicles and other personal property. Same district. Same year. Same household.
To find your own number, the County’s tax rate lookup shows composite rates by school district and sub code through 2024, the Collector of Revenue posts the current year’s rate book, and the City publishes its rates each October. Rates reset every year, so last year’s figure is a guide, not a promise. Comparing City and County living? Factor in the St. Louis earnings tax on City residents’ pay, too.
Tax follows the car. Finance the next one cheaper: credit union or bank?
### When is personal property tax due in St. Louis City and County?
December 31, on both sides of the line, and a mailed payment counts as on time if the postmark is on or before the due date. But the cycle starts eleven months earlier, and the County and City run slightly different clocks:
January 1. The snapshot. What you own and where you live that day set the whole year’s bill.
January. Declarations go out. The City mails individual declarations in January, and the County mails one to every active account.
March 1. County declarations due. Miss it and state law has the assessor send a second notice between March 1 and April 1. The County’s late penalty applies only if your list still isn’t back before May 1.
April 1. City declarations due, or the next business day if April 1 lands on a weekend. An April 1 postmark counts.
May 1 to the second Monday in July. The County’s appeal window. The City’s appeal deadline is that same Monday.
October. The County posts final tax amounts online.
November. Paper bills arrive in the City and the County.
December 31. Due, paid or postmarked.
January 1, again. Penalty and interest start, and the next snapshot is taken.
If one big December payment is the hard part, the County runs a pre-payment plan at no cost. It splits last year’s tax into four payments due March 31, June 30, August 31 and December 31, then adjusts the last one to this year’s actual bill. Your taxes must be current to enroll, pre-paid money earns no interest, and payments go by mail or in person at the main office, not online.
In the City you can pay through PayIt St. Louis, by phone, by mail or at City Hall, Room 109. The payment page lists a 2.45% card fee and $1.25 for an ACH bank payment, so a card adds about $9.94 to a $405.61 bill. The City won’t take a check for delinquent taxes.
### What does it cost to file late or pay late?
There are two separate late penalties, and people mix them up. One is for filing your declaration late. The other is for paying the bill late. You can get hit with both in the same year.
Filing late first. In the City, a declaration received after April 1 adds a 10% penalty to your assessed value, so $5,000 assessed becomes $5,500 and the $405.61 bill becomes about $446. In the County, state law sets a flat penalty by the assessed value you failed to report, from $15 (up to $1,000) to $105 ($9,001 and up). A $5,000-assessed car draws $55. The assessor must waive it in a few cases, like military service outside Missouri or no form ever mailed to you.
Paying late is where it compounds. After December 31 the County charges up to 18% interest per year plus a 2% penalty, both set by state law. The City adds penalty and interest from January 1, with more interest on the first of each month from January through September, for every year the tax stays unpaid. On a $400 bill, the 2% penalty is $8 and a full year at the 18% cap is $72. Up to eighty dollars on a four-hundred-dollar bill. County partial payments go to fees, interest and penalties first, and the bill isn’t marked paid until it’s paid in full.
Then come the consequences that cost more than interest. You can’t renew your plates: Missouri wants proof of paid personal property tax for the previous year, or two years on a two-year registration, and the City won’t license a vehicle until every year is paid, oldest first. Our guide to the personal property tax receipt and waiver walks through that license-office trip. And the Collector can sue. The City says court costs and attorney’s fees get added, and partial payments won’t stop a suit.
### Do boats, RVs, trailers and business equipment get taxed too?
Yes, all of them. If it’s titled, or it’s equipment a business uses, it generally belongs on the declaration. The City’s examples include autos, trucks, motorcycles, boats, motors, RVs, campers, trailers, conversion vans, buses and airplanes.
Boats can land on the bill more than once: the boat, the motor and the trailer can each be a line. Budget for that every year, and read our guide on buying a used boat in Missouri before you commit. RVs are the bigger number. An RV with a $45,000 trade-in value is $15,000 assessed, and at the City’s 2025 rate that’s $1,216.83 a year. Our piece on what first-time RV buyers should know covers the other ownership costs.
Historic vehicles get a real break: a car registered with historic plates is assessed at 5% of its value, so a $15,000 classic is assessed at $750, not $5,000.
Run a side business? Office equipment, computers, tools, furniture and vehicles titled in the business’s name go on a business declaration, due March 1 in the County and April 1 in the City. Leasing is its own case. The state wants the receipt for a leased vehicle in the leasing company’s name, so check your lease for how that tax reaches you.
### Who doesn’t have to pay, and how do you prove it?
Anyone who didn’t own a taxable vehicle on January 1 owes nothing for that year, plus a short list of exemptions. The proof is a statement of non-assessment, which everybody calls a tax waiver, and the license office takes it in place of a paid receipt.
St. Louis County issues waivers to new Missouri residents (bring a title in your name or a current out-of-state registration), first-time vehicle owners (a title showing the sale date, or a signed bill of sale) and people leasing a vehicle (the lease agreement). Active-duty service members whose home of record isn’t Missouri take their Leave and Earnings Statement to a state license office. Lived in another Missouri county on January 1? That county issues the waiver.
The City issues a tax waiver at no charge if you’re new to Missouri, or if you didn’t own a vehicle on January 1 of the prior year and don’t owe back taxes. Bring the title or bill of sale and a photo ID to City Hall, Rooms 115 and 117, or email copies to the Assessor’s office.
What doesn’t exist is an age-based break on vehicles. The County’s senior tax freeze covers the home you live in, not your car; our guide to the St. Louis County senior tax freeze and Missouri property tax credit explains who qualifies. Mapping your whole retirement tax picture? Start with how Missouri taxes retirement income.
This is general information, not advice for your situation. A CPA or enrolled agent can apply it to your own bills and records, and our St. Louis Financial directory is a place to start.
Holding a bill that doesn’t match what you owned on January 1? Tax preparers around St. Louis can check it against your declaration, flag a car that should have come off, and tell you whether an appeal is worth the trip.
And if you run a tax or bookkeeping practice, the neighbor staring at that envelope is asking who can sort it out, so list your practice.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How does Missouri calculate personal property tax on vehicles?
A.  The assessor takes the average trade-in value from the October issue of the used-car guide the State Tax Commission selects, multiplies it by 33 1/3% to get assessed value, and applies your local rate per $100. A $15,000 car is assessed at $5,000; at the City of St. Louis’s 2025 rate of $8.1122, that’s $405.61.
### Q. What happens if you don’t pay personal property tax in MO?
A.  Penalty and interest start January 1, and you can’t renew your plates, because Missouri requires a paid receipt or waiver for the prior year, or two years on a two-year registration. The collector can also sue. In the City, court costs and attorney’s fees are added, and partial payments don’t stop a suit.
### Q. What is the penalty for late personal property tax in Missouri?
A.  In St. Louis County, taxes paid after December 31 carry up to 18% interest per year plus a 2% penalty, set by state law. The City adds penalty and interest after December 31, plus monthly interest through September. A late declaration is separate: 10% added to assessed value in the City, or $15 to $105 in the County.
### Q. How do I look up my personal property tax in Missouri?
A.  In St. Louis County, search your account on the Collector of Revenue’s online tax inquiry and payment page; personal property account numbers start with the letter I. In the City, the Collector’s online receipt page finds your account by address, name or account number. Elsewhere in Missouri, start with your county collector’s website.
### Q. Who is exempt from personal property tax?
A.  Household goods, furniture and clothing used in your home are exempt under state law. You also owe nothing for a year if you didn’t own a taxable vehicle on January 1, such as a new Missouri resident, and you prove it with a waiver. Active-duty members whose home of record isn’t Missouri use their Leave and Earnings Statement.
### Q. Does Missouri still have personal property tax?
A.  Yes. The tax on vehicles is still state law, and bills still go out every November. Lawmakers keep filing proposals to shrink or end it, and one limit took effect January 1, 2026: a vehicle worth under $50,000 as of January 1, 2025 can’t be assessed above its proper prior-year assessment.
### Q. How much is car personal property tax in Missouri?
A.  It depends on the car’s value and your local rate. Take one-third of the average trade-in value, divide by 100 and multiply by your rate. On 2025 rates, a $15,000 car runs about $405 a year in the City of St. Louis. In St. Louis County it depends on the districts at your address; the Rockwood school levy alone on that car is about $194. A $30,000 car roughly doubles that.
### Q. What is the personal property tax rate in St. Louis?
A.  The City of St. Louis charged $8.1122 per $100 of assessed value for 2025, one rate for every City address. St. Louis County has no single rate; it depends on your school, fire, sewer and city districts. The school levy is usually the biggest slice: Rockwood’s 2025 school levy alone was $3.8816 per $100, and Parkway’s was $4.2609 on vehicles.

## Personal Property Tax Receipt or Waiver in St. Louis: What the License Office Wants and How to Get It Fast
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/personal-property-tax-receipt-and-waiver-st-louis
Next window, please. Picture yourself finally reaching the counter at a Missouri license office with a folder you were proud of: the title, the insurance card, the inspection slip, a driver’s license with your new St. Louis address. The clerk thumbs through it, looks up, and asks for one more thing. Your personal property tax receipt. Or, if you didn’t owe one, a statement of non-assessment. You’ve never heard either phrase in your life, and the person behind you just sighed.
Nobody warns you about this paper. Missouri taxes the cars and trucks people own every year, based on what they owned on January 1, and the state won’t register a vehicle until you prove last year’s bill was paid or that there wasn’t one. The people stuck at that counter usually aren’t careless. They’re new to Missouri, or bought a first car, or moved from another county, and the system assumed they already knew.
Here’s the twist almost nobody explains. In St. Louis, the license office can often see a tax bill you paid, because St. Louis County and the City are both on the state’s list of places that send paid personal property tax records to the Department of Revenue. It can’t see a waiver. The state says flatly that a statement of non-assessment “cannot be accessed or verified online” (Department of Revenue). So the one paper the clerk can’t pull up is the one most newcomers need. Get it before you take a number, and carry it in your hand.
Below: which paper you need, how the County and the City hand them out, how far back the clerk looks, and the fix when you paid but the system says you didn’t. It’s one piece of our St. Louis money guide, the stuff nobody taught us in school.
### How to get a personal property tax waiver in St. Louis County?
Apply online through St. Louis County’s customer service portal, visit an Assessor’s office, or book an in-person or virtual appointment. You qualify if you owed the County no personal property tax for the year being checked, usually because you were new to Missouri or had no vehicle on January 1. Bring your title, out-of-state registration or bill of sale.
A statement of non-assessment is what most people at the counter just call a tax waiver. It’s the County’s written word that you didn’t owe it personal property tax for a specific year, and it stands in for a paid receipt. One quirk worth knowing: in St. Louis County the Assessor’s Office prepares the statement and the Collector of Revenue’s Office issues it, so don’t be thrown if both offices come up in the same conversation.
What you bring depends on why you owed nothing. The County’s list, where any one item on a line will do:
New Missouri resident: the vehicle title in your name, your current out-of-state registration, or a Missouri Department of Revenue title receipt.
First-time vehicle owner: the title in your name, filled out by buyer and seller with the date of sale; a Missouri title application; or a bill of sale signed by both of you with complete vehicle information.
Leased vehicle: the lease agreement or the out-of-state registration.
Active military whose home of record isn’t Missouri: skip the waiver and show your Leave and Earnings Statement at the license office.
The online route runs through the County’s customer service portal, linked from that waiver page. In person, the County Assessor’s main office is on the third floor at 41 S. Central Ave., open Monday through Thursday, 8:00 to 3:30, with phones at 314-615-2555. Business waivers need an appointment or a spot in line there, and bankruptcy waivers must be picked up there in person. The County doesn’t post a fee or a turnaround time, so ask when you apply if your plates are close to expiring.
One rule catches people who move within Missouri. If you lived in a different Missouri county on January 1 of the year being checked, St. Louis County can’t write your waiver for that year. That county has to. Same if you owed tax there: the receipt lives with that county’s collector, not ours.
### Do you need a paid receipt or a waiver?
It comes down to one date. On January 1 of the year the clerk is checking, did you live in Missouri and own a vehicle? If yes, a bill was owed, and you need the paid receipt. If no, you need a waiver. The State Tax Commission puts it in a sentence: the waiver comes from your county or City assessor if you didn’t own or possess personal property on January 1.
Here’s how that rule lands on the situations that send people home from the counter:
You moved here from another state this year. Last January 1 you weren’t a Missouri resident. Waiver.
You bought your first car in the spring. No vehicle on January 1. Waiver.
You sold one car in March and bought another in October. You owned a car on January 1, so that year’s bill stands. Receipt. The County says vehicles bought or sold mid-year don’t qualify for adjustments.
You moved to St. Louis from another Missouri county. Receipt or waiver from the county you lived in on January 1.
You lease. The state wants proof in the leasing company’s name. Ask your leasing company which paper it supplies before you go.
Notice what’s missing from that list: whether you’re good with money. This is a calendar rule, not a character test. Most people who get sent home from the counter never heard that January 1 was the day that counted.
### How do you get a waiver in the City of St. Louis instead?
Through the City Assessor, not the County. The City of St. Louis isn’t part of St. Louis County; it keeps its own Assessor and its own Collector, with their own rules. The City says you qualify for a tax waiver if you’re a new resident of Missouri, or if you didn’t own a motor vehicle on January 1 of the prior calendar year and have no tax delinquency. There’s no fee.
You can get it two ways:
In person: City Hall, 1200 Market St., Rooms 115 and 117, weekdays 8:00 to 5:00. Register for the Assessor’s Virtual Lobby first, then bring the title or bill of sale and a driver’s license or photo ID. Questions go to (314) 622-4171.
Online: email the Assessor’s personal property office copies of your driver’s license, each car title and each registration or renewal (front and back), plus confirmation of your current address. City residents only, not County.
Here’s the catch hiding in the online option. Waivers processed online are mailed by USPS, and the City says they can’t be emailed. Put that next to the state’s rule that a waiver can’t be verified online, and the math is plain: if your plates expire this week, an emailed request may not beat the deadline. Going downtown in person takes the mail out of the equation.
Moved into the City recently? Same January 1 logic. The City says you get the waiver from the county you lived in on January 1, not from the City.
Side by side, the two systems look like this:
### How many years of receipts does the license office check?
One year or two, depending on the registration you’re renewing. The Department of Revenue asks for proof for the previous year if it was a one-year registration, and for the previous two years if it was a two-year registration. Buying new plates for a car you just bought takes a paid receipt or a waiver for the previous year.
Two-year registrations are only offered when the model year and the calendar year are both even or both odd. So a renewal that asks for two years isn’t a mistake.
The receipt itself has to pass a quick inspection. Under the state’s rules, it must be in one of the owners’ names, list each vehicle you own, and be stamped “PAID.” An original, a photocopy, a fax copy or an internet confirmation screen all work, as long as it’s legible. If a company owns the vehicle, the receipt has to be in the company’s name.
Walk one hypothetical newcomer through it. Say you move to the County from out of state in June and title your car in July with a one-year registration. The clerk checks the previous year. You lived elsewhere that January 1, so a County waiver covers it. Next January 1 you’re a County resident with a car, so a bill follows, due by December 31. At the next July renewal, the answer is a paid receipt. Same counter. Different paper.
The title runs its own clock. New residents get 30 days to title a vehicle, and a car you just bought has to be titled within 30 days of purchase or a $25 penalty starts, capped at $200, per the Department of Revenue. Still shopping? Our guide to buying a car in St. Louis covers the dealer side.
### Where do you get a copy of a paid receipt in St. Louis?
Online, at no charge, in both the County and the City. Paper at the counter costs a dollar.
St. Louis County. The County stopped needing paper receipts for registration: it says the state’s license offices now accept electronic proof of paid personal property tax, and it no longer mails receipts automatically. Want one anyway? Print an official receipt from the County’s tax payment site by searching your property number, name or address, or get one for $1.00 at a County Revenue office.
City of St. Louis. Start at the City’s personal property tax receipt page and search by account number, address or owner name. The account number is the most reliable search; an address has to match the record exactly. Then use Print Account for each year you paid. Online receipts cost nothing and are accepted at Missouri license offices. An official duplicate at City Hall, Room 109, is $1.00.
One dead end to know about. If you never filed a declaration and never got a bill, there’s no receipt to print. The State Tax Commission says you have to file with your assessor first.
Waiver handled? Here’s the rest of your St. Louis move-in checklist.
### Why can’t the license office see a tax bill you already paid?
Usually it’s timing. Sometimes it’s a typo. The state’s online system only knows what your county collector sent it, and the Department of Revenue lists three reasons a paid bill doesn’t show up: the county’s records haven’t reached the state, you paid after the county had already sent its records, or the details you entered don’t match the receipt exactly, down to the spaces, commas and dashes.
December makes it worse. The County says online payments generally post within two business days, but mailed payments pile up at year’s end and processing runs well into January. A check mailed December 30 might not show as paid until sometime in January or later. If your plates expire in January, the County’s own advice is to pay early or pay online.
The fix is boring, and it works. Print the receipt from the County or City site and bring it, or have it ready on your phone. Check three things first: your name, every vehicle you own, and the word PAID. Wrong car on it? That’s an Assessor fix, not a Collector one. The County corrects it with the title or registration for the vehicle to add and proof of the sale, trade, loss or repossession for the one to remove.
Don’t let a correction delay payment, though. County taxes have to be paid or postmarked by December 31. After that, state law adds up to 18% a year in interest plus a 2% penalty. On a $400 bill, the 2% alone is $8 before a single day of interest. Small money. Still money you lost because nobody explained the calendar.
### What should you bring to renew your plates in St. Louis?
Five things, according to the Department of Revenue:
Your renewal notice, or a printed Form 184 if the notice never came.
Your paid personal property tax receipt or statement of non-assessment: the previous year for a one-year registration, the previous two years for a two-year registration.
A current insurance ID card, whether original, copy or electronic, as long as it’s legible.
A safety and/or emissions inspection certificate no more than 60 days old, if your vehicle needs one. St. Louis City and County are inside the emissions area, and our guide to what fails a Missouri car inspection covers the rest.
The registration and processing fees.
Cars in their first ten years after the model year, with under 150,000 miles, skip the safety inspection. You can renew up to six months early and have until the last day of the expiration month. After that, it’s a $5 penalty.
Renewing online skips the line, but not everyone qualifies. The state’s FAQ says you can’t renew online if your proof is a personal property tax waiver or the vehicle is leased, and card payments carry a 2.0% plus 25 cent convenience fee. To see exactly what your registration needs, run it through the state’s Renewal Requirements Inquiry before you go.
### What happens the year after you get a waiver?
You go on the list. The State Tax Commission notes that asking for a waiver also adds you to the assessment roll for the next tax year. Think of the waiver as this year’s pass and next year’s sign-up sheet, printed on the same piece of paper.
Next comes a declaration: the list of vehicles and other taxable personal property you owned on January 1. In the City, declarations go out in January and are due April 1, with a 10% assessment penalty after that, and first-time filers must use the paper form. For county assessors, state law sets a March 1 filing date and a late penalty of $15 to $105 depending on assessed value, waived if the list comes back before May 1 after a second notice. Go by the date printed on your form.
Then the bill, due by December 31. How that number gets built is its own story, and our guide to St. Louis County personal property tax walks through the math. For this paper chase, one habit does most of the work: the day you pay, save the receipt as a PDF somewhere you’ll find it. Next year it’s the first thing the clerk asks for.
This is general information about how the County, the City and the state handle these papers, not advice for your situation. A CPA or enrolled agent can apply it to yours, and our St. Louis Financial directory is a place to start.
A move left you with bills in two places, or a receipt that lists the wrong car? A tax pro can untangle it before your next renewal, so start with tax preparers around St. Louis.
And if you run a tax practice or a title-and-tag service, the neighbor stuck at that counter needs someone today, so see who AI names instead of you.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How do I get my St. Louis County personal property tax receipt?
A.  Print it yourself from the County’s tax payment website by searching your property number, name or address, or get a printed copy for $1.00 at a County Revenue office. You may not need paper at all: the County says the state’s license offices now accept electronic proof of paid personal property tax. Online payments generally post within two business days.
### Q. Can I get a copy of my personal property tax receipt online in Missouri?
A.  In St. Louis, yes, at no charge. County residents print from the County’s tax payment site, and City residents use the City’s property tax portal and its Print Account option for each year paid. The state accepts a receipt that’s an original, a copy or electronic, as long as it’s legible. Elsewhere in Missouri, ask your county collector how its lookup works.
### Q. Can the Missouri DMV look up personal property tax?
A.  For paid bills, often yes. St. Louis County and the City are both on the Department of Revenue’s list of places that send paid personal property tax records to the state, which is what makes online renewal possible. A waiver is different. The state says a statement of non-assessment can’t be accessed or verified online, so that one has to come with you on paper.
### Q. Do I need a tax waiver to register a car in Missouri?
A.  Only if you didn’t owe personal property tax for the year the license office checks. New Missouri residents title and register with a statement of non-assessment from their county or City assessor. If you owned a vehicle and lived in Missouri that January 1, you need the paid receipt instead. Active military whose home of record isn’t Missouri show a Leave and Earnings Statement.
### Q. How to get a personal property tax waiver in St. Louis City?
A.  Go to the City Assessor at City Hall, 1200 Market St., Rooms 115 and 117, with your title or bill of sale and a photo ID, or email copies of your license, titles, registrations and proof of address to the Assessor’s personal property office. There’s no fee. Waivers requested online come back by USPS mail only, so leave time before your plates expire.
### Q. What is a personal property tax declaration?
A.  It’s the yearly list you give the assessor of the vehicles and other taxable personal property you owned on January 1. The assessor values what’s on it, and the collector bills you from that. In the City, forms go out in January and are due April 1, with a 10% assessment penalty after that. First-time City filers have to use the paper form.
### Q. Can I apply for a personal property tax waiver in Missouri online?
A.  In St. Louis, yes. St. Louis County takes waiver applications through its online customer service portal, and the City accepts requests by email with copies of your documents, then mails the waiver by USPS. Other Missouri counties set their own process, so check with your county assessor. Keep the paper once it arrives, because the license office can’t verify a waiver online.
### Q. What if I moved to St. Louis from another Missouri county?
A.  Your paper comes from wherever you lived on January 1 of the year being checked. If that was another Missouri county, its assessor issues the waiver, or its collector holds your paid receipt, even though you live in St. Louis now. Both the County and the City say so on their waiver pages. Once you’ve spent a January 1 here, the bills start coming from here.

## St. Louis Earnings Tax: Who Pays the City's 1%, Who Doesn't, and How to Get Some Back
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-earnings-tax
Box 19. Look for it on your next W-2. If you live in the City of St. Louis, or drive into it for work, that box holds a number labeled local income tax, and odds are nobody at new-hire orientation ever told you what it was, who decided it, or that some of it might belong back in your pocket.
The City has its own name for it: the earnings tax. It’s 1% of your pay, it’s been 1% since 1959, and it brings in 36% of the City’s general revenue, according to the Collector of Revenue. Your employer takes it before you ever see the check. That’s the whole explanation most people get. No letter. No form. No mention that a commuter who worked whole days somewhere else may have paid tax that was never owed, or that a City resident whose job is out in the county can owe the full 1% with nothing withheld at all.
Neither one is a character flaw. It’s a local tax with local rules that nobody teaches in school, run by an office that mails a bill without a lesson attached. This page, one stop in our St. Louis money guide, walks through who pays, what income it skips, which form does what, the one-year clock on refunds, and why City voters get asked about it every five years.
### Who pays St. Louis city earnings tax?
Two groups pay it. Everyone who lives in the City of St. Louis owes 1% on all their earned income, wherever their employer is. Everyone who works inside City limits owes 1% on the pay for that work, wherever they live. Businesses owe 1% of net profits from City activity, and retired and unemployed people don’t pay it.
The City’s individual earnings tax page spells out the edges. A resident files on 100% of earnings, even when the employer sits across the river or the job happens on a laptop at the kitchen table. A non-resident who works for a business located in the City, or who works inside the City, owes on that pay. People who move in or out during the year owe only on wages earned while they lived or worked in the City. College students who study somewhere else but keep a permanent City address still file on what they earn.
Then there’s the rule that surprises commuters most. If any part of a workday happens inside the City, the City counts the whole day as a City day. A two-hour meeting downtown before you head to a job site in the county? City day.
Employers carry most of the load. A business located in the City withholds the 1% from its employees’ pay, and the City’s withholding rules say it has to withhold on every employee, regardless of where that employee works. On top of that, the employer owes its own 0.5% payroll expense tax on wages earned in the City, which comes out of the company’s pocket, not yours. That blanket withholding is the reason refunds exist at all. The paycheck system takes 1% first, and the person who worked part of the year elsewhere has to ask for the difference.
### How much is the St. Louis earnings tax, and what income does it skip?
It’s a flat 1%. No brackets, no standard deduction, no sliding scale. Earn $50,000 in wages and the City’s share is $500, whether you’re a first-year teacher or a vice president. That flatness is exactly why people forget it’s there. It never changes, so nobody ever explains it.
What counts is earned income, meaning pay for work, and the City publishes its own list of taxable and non-taxable items. A few of its calls:
Taxed: wages, salaries, tips, bonuses, commissions, severance pay, and vacation and sick pay.
Taxed: active-duty and reserve military pay. Combat pay is not.
Not taxed: pensions and Social Security, which is why retirees owe nothing on their retirement checks. Our guide to how Missouri taxes retirement income covers the state side.
Not taxed: dividends and interest, unemployment compensation, workers’ compensation, scholarships, and alimony or child support you receive.
Not taxed: gambling and lottery winnings. The City leaves your casino night alone.
One more line matters if you’re leaving a City job. The instructions on the City’s refund form say annual leave, sick leave and separation pay from a workplace in the City are taxable in the year you receive them, with no exceptions based on where you earned them or where you live. A final payout of unused vacation gets the 1% even if you’ve already started somewhere new.
Keep the layers straight, too. The City’s 1% sits on top of Missouri’s state income tax rate, which is figured on a separate return with its own brackets and its own rules. Two governments, two forms, two sets of rules.
### Do you have to file your own St. Louis city tax return?
Only if your employer didn’t withhold the full 1%. When the tax comes out of your paycheck correctly, the City’s filing page says you don’t file or pay separately. When it doesn’t, you file Form E-1 yourself, and it’s due April 15.
Here’s who gets caught. Say you rent a flat in Dutchtown and take a job with a company whose only office is out in the county. That employer has no City location, so it may never withhold a cent of St. Louis tax. You owe it anyway, because you live in the City. On $48,000 of wages that’s $480, due April 15, on a form nobody mailed you.
The City’s deadlines are stricter than most people expect. Three things to know before April:
No extensions for individuals. The City says plainly that it doesn’t allow them, so a federal or state extension, the kind covered in our guide to filing a tax extension in Missouri, doesn’t buy you time with City Hall.
Late tax costs 5% a month, up to 25%, plus interest of 1% a month until it’s paid. On that $480, three months late adds $72 in penalty and about $14 in interest.
You can’t e-file the E-1 yet. You can pay online, then mail, fax or email the return, and the City matches the payment to the return when it arrives. Card payments carry a 2.45% fee, and ACH payments, which come straight from your bank account, carry a $1.25 flat fee.
