### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Does Missouri have a W4?
A.  Yes. Missouri uses its own Form MO W-4, separate from the federal W-4, so a new hire fills out both. It has four lines: filing status, additional withholding, reduced withholding and exempt status. Your employer sends the Department of Revenue a copy within 20 days of hiring you.
### Q. Do you still claim 0 or 1 on W4?
A.  No. The federal W-4 stopped using allowances with the 2020 version, and Missouri’s current form doesn’t use them either. Both work in dollars now: extra withholding in federal Step 4(c) or Missouri line 2, deductions in Step 4(b), credits in Step 3. A form asking for allowances is an outdated version.
### Q. What is a pay stub supposed to look like?
A.  Most show gross pay, each tax and deduction, and net pay, often with a column for this check and one for the year to date. Missouri’s wage law, section 290.080, requires corporations doing business here to give workers at least a monthly statement of total deductions.
### Q. What percentage is usually taken out of your paycheck for taxes?
A.  No single number, but some pieces are fixed. Social Security and Medicare take 7.65% up to the yearly Social Security cap, Missouri withholding runs from 0% to 4.7% after a standard deduction, and the City adds 1% if you live or work there. In this page’s illustrative example, taxes came to about 18.5% of gross.
### Q. How to fill out W4 to not owe taxes?
A.  Start with the IRS Tax Withholding Estimator, which turns your pay stub and household details into W-4 entries. Two jobs or a working spouse means completing Step 2. Income with no withholding can go in Step 4(a), or extra withholding in Step 4(c). Owing under $1,000 at filing generally avoids the IRS underpayment penalty.
### Q. Is it better to claim 1 or 0 allowances on state taxes?
A.  In Missouri, neither, because the current MO W-4 has no allowances. State withholding depends on the filing status box you check and any dollar amount on line 2 or line 3. The box matters most: “Married (Spouse does not work)” doubles the formula’s standard deduction to $32,200.
### Q. What is a MO W-4 withholding?
A.  It’s the Missouri income tax your employer takes from each paycheck based on your MO W-4. The state formula annualizes your pay, subtracts a standard deduction tied to your line 1 box, applies rates from 0% to 4.7%, divides by your paydays and rounds to the dollar. It’s a prepayment, not the final bill.
### Q. Why is my first paycheck smaller than my offer letter?
A.  The offer letter quotes gross pay. The stub subtracts pre-tax deductions like a 401(k), then federal income tax, Social Security, Medicare, Missouri withholding and, for City jobs and City residents, the 1% earnings tax. In this page’s illustrative example, a $2,000 check became $1,531.

## Side Hustle Taxes in Missouri: 1099s, Estimated Payments and the $100 Line Nobody Mentions
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/side-hustle-taxes-missouri-1099-and-estimated-payments
Paid every week, warned never. The delivery app dropped money into your account all year, for the Soulard dinner rush and the late runs through the Central West End, and not one of those deposits had a cent of tax taken out. No screen said April. No pop-up said Missouri. The money looked like yours, and most of it was.
That silence is how the system is built. When an app or a client pays you as an independent contractor, nobody withholds anything, so the IRS calls what you owe estimated tax: tax on income that isn’t subject to withholding. The federal form for it, Form 1040-ES, lists self-employment earnings, “including gig economy work,” as its very first example. Nobody mails you a reminder, either. The Missouri Department of Revenue says it in five words, printed on its own estimated-tax worksheet: “You will not be billed.”
Then the law made the silence louder. For payments made in 2026, the line that triggers a 1099-NEC from a client jumped from $600 to $2,000, and payment apps are back to sending a 1099-K only after you pass $20,000 and more than 200 transactions. Lots of side hustlers will never see a form. The tax didn’t move an inch.
None of that means you’re bad with money. It means nobody sat you down and explained that a St. Louis side hustle can answer to three tax collectors (the IRS, the Missouri Department of Revenue and, if you live in the city, the Collector of Revenue) and that none of them sends a bill before the due date. This page does the explaining, with the numbers taken straight off the official forms. It’s one chapter of our St. Louis money guide, the plain-English money stuff school skipped.
### How do I calculate my estimated taxes in Missouri?
You estimate the year’s profit, then figure two bills. Federal: self-employment tax of 15.3% on 92.35% of profit, plus income tax at your bracket. Missouri: run taxable income through the MO-1040ES rate chart. Subtract withholding from each. If Missouri’s remainder reaches $100, or the IRS’s $1,000, pay in four installments: April 15, June 15, September 15, January 15.
Here’s the same math as steps, using the 2026 versions of both forms. Rates, brackets and deductions are adjusted each year, so check the current form before you run your own numbers.
Profit first. Add up everything the apps and clients will pay you for the year, form or no form, then subtract business costs. What’s left is net profit, the number everything else runs on.
Self-employment tax. Multiply profit by 92.35%, then by 15.3%. On $10,000 of profit that’s about $1,413. The Form 1040-ES worksheet runs exactly this calculation.
Federal income tax. Add profit, minus half of that self-employment tax, to your other income and apply your bracket. On the 2026 rate schedule, a single filer’s 12% bracket covers taxable income from $12,400 to $50,400, and 22% runs from there to $105,700.
Subtract withholding. Whatever your day job will withhold for the year comes off. If you still expect to owe $1,000 or more, the IRS expects estimated payments.
Missouri. The MO-1040ES worksheet starts from your federal adjusted gross income after Missouri’s own adjustments, including a 20% business income deduction on Schedule C profit, subtracts the Missouri standard deduction ($16,100 for a single filer on the 2026 form) and taxes every dollar of Missouri taxable income over $9,436 at 4.7%. Subtract Missouri withholding. If what’s left is $100 or more, Missouri expects a declaration and payments.
Divide by four, or by however many due dates are left in the year.
Look at that Missouri step again, because it’s the local trap. Missouri’s line is one-tenth of the IRS’s. At 4.7%, it takes only about $2,130 of extra Missouri taxable income to produce $100 of tax. So if your day-job withholding already covers your wages, a side gig netting roughly $2,900 can put you over Missouri’s line, while owing the IRS $1,000 takes roughly $3,300 to $4,300 of profit, depending on your bracket and using the worked example below. It’s easy to stay current with the IRS and miss Missouri entirely.
### Do you owe tax on side hustle income if no 1099 shows up?
Yes, from the first dollar. The IRS’s gig economy tax center says gig income has to be reported even when it isn’t on a 1099-K, 1099-NEC, 1099-MISC or W-2, and even when you’re paid in cash, property or virtual currency. The form is a receipt, not a permission slip.
What changed is who gets a form. Two thresholds moved:
1099-NEC, from clients who pay you for services: $600 for payments made before 2026, $2,000 for payments made in 2026, with an inflation adjustment after that, according to the IRS’s information return filing page.
1099-K, from payment apps and online marketplaces: required only when your payments top $20,000 and more than 200 transactions. The IRS says the One, Big, Beautiful Bill retroactively reinstated that older threshold. Card processors, by contrast, have no threshold at all.
You can still get a form below those lines. And a 1099-K reports only gross payments, before the fees the platform kept or the refunds you gave. Its number is a starting point, not your taxable income.
The line that matters more is $400. Once your net earnings from self-employment reach $400, the IRS’s gig work guidance says you must file a return, with Schedule C for the profit and Schedule SE for the self-employment tax. A summer of weekend dog walking can get there.
### Why is self-employment tax so high?
Because you’re paying both halves. On a regular paycheck, Social Security and Medicare take 7.65% of your wages, and your employer pays a matching 7.65% you never see. Work for yourself and you’re the employer too. The self-employment tax is 12.4% for Social Security plus 2.9% for Medicare: 15.3% in all.
Two things soften it, and both are printed on the IRS forms. First, the tax applies to 92.35% of your net profit, not all of it. Second, you deduct the employer-equivalent half of the tax when you figure adjusted gross income, which lowers your income tax (not the self-employment tax itself). On $10,000 of profit, $9,235 is taxed at 15.3% for about $1,413, and about $706 comes off your adjusted gross income.
The Social Security piece stops at a wage base, $184,500 of combined wages and self-employment earnings for 2026, and day-job wages count toward it first. Medicare has no cap, and an extra 0.9% Medicare tax applies above $200,000 for single filers. If your combined pay is nowhere near those figures, ignore them.
Here’s why it stings. Income tax has a standard deduction standing in front of it. Self-employment tax doesn’t. It starts at $400 of net earnings, so someone who owes zero income tax can still owe the 15.3%. That’s the bill the app never mentioned.
### Which side hustle expenses actually shrink the bill?
Ordinary costs of doing the work, subtracted from what you were paid: business miles, parking and tolls, the business share of your phone, supplies you used up, platform fees. Every real expense comes off profit, and profit is what both the 15.3% and your income tax run on. One deduction, two smaller bills.
Mileage. The IRS standard mileage rate for business was 72.5 cents a mile for January through June 2026, then 76 cents from July 1, a mid-year raise. At 76 cents, every 1,000 business miles takes $760 off your profit. The Schedule C instructions let you add parking fees and tolls on top, but not depreciation, lease payments or gas and repairs when you use the standard rate. The rate is reset each year.
Your phone. Only the business share counts. If the phone is half work and half life, the personal half stays personal, and a preparer will ask how you arrived at the split.
Supplies. Insulated delivery bags, a ring light, packaging, ink for invoices. Schedule C allows supplies to the extent you actually used them in the business.
Platform fees. Since a 1099-K shows gross payments, the fees the platform kept come off through your own records.
The catch is proof. The IRS tells gig workers to collect and keep records and receipts during the year, not rebuild them in March. A mileage log kept as you drive is worth far more than one pieced together from memory. If the shoebox is winning, here’s what a bookkeeper costs and why Missouri doesn’t license them.
One more tax lives next door. If you sell physical products rather than services, check whether you need a Missouri sales tax license. That’s a separate tax on your customers’ purchases, with its own filing schedule.
Paying tax on creator income? Make your following earn more of it.
### How much of every payout should you set aside?
In the worked example below, the honest number lands between 26% and 35% of profit, which is roughly 18% to 23% of every dollar the app deposits. Setting aside about 30% of profit is a workable starting point in the 12% bracket, closer to 35% if a day job already puts you in the 22% bracket or you live in the city. Treat it as a first draft and let a preparer tune it.
Picture a nurse in Bevo Mill who drives deliveries three nights a week. Say the app pays her $15,000 over the year, and her business miles, phone share and supplies come to $5,000. Net profit: $10,000. Her hospital paycheck withholding already covers the tax on her wages, and she files single. Here’s what the side gig adds:
Self-employment tax: $10,000 times 92.35% times 15.3% is about $1,413.
Federal income tax: profit minus the $706 half-of-SE-tax deduction leaves $9,294. The qualified business income deduction, which lets many sole proprietors deduct up to 20% of that business income and which recent legislation made permanent, trims about $1,859 more. Roughly $7,435 is left: about $892 of tax at 12%, about $1,636 at 22%.
Missouri income tax: The federal deduction doesn’t carry over, but Missouri has its own: a 20% business income deduction on Schedule C profit, claimed on Form MO-A. That takes $2,000 off the $9,294, so about $7,294 lands at 4.7%. Call it $343.
City earnings tax, if she lives in the city: 1% of net profit, about $100.
Add it up. Outside the city in the 12% bracket, about $2,648, or 26% of profit. Inside the city at 22%, about $3,492, or 35%. Against the $15,000 the app actually deposited, that’s 18% to 23% of each payout. Not one dollar of it was withheld.
The way to keep that number from ambushing you is boring on purpose: a separate savings account, a transfer the day each deposit lands, four calendar alerts. Come April, the money’s already sitting there.
### When are federal and Missouri estimated payments due?
Both use the same four dates: April 15, June 15, September 15 and January 15 of the following year, moved to the next business day when one falls on a weekend or holiday. They’re called quarterly, but they aren’t evenly spaced. The gaps run two months, then three, then four. June 15 arrives fast.
Federally, you generally avoid the underpayment penalty if withholding and on-time payments cover the smaller of 90% of this year’s tax or 100% of last year’s, or 110% of last year’s if your adjusted gross income topped $150,000 ($75,000 married filing separately). That prior-year rule is why a first-year side hustler with a well-withheld day job can owe no penalty at all and still owe a four-figure bill in April. The rule protects you from the penalty. It doesn’t make the tax smaller.
There’s a quieter federal option if you also hold a job: more withholding. File a new W-4 at work and ask for an extra amount per paycheck. IRS Publication 505 treats one-fourth of your year’s withholding as paid on each installment date, unless you choose to count it on the actual dates, so extra withholding added in the fall still counts toward April and June. Our guide to the Missouri W-4 and reading your pay stub walks through the form.
Missouri runs on the same dates with its own rules. The MO-1040ES instructions skip the extra charge when each installment is on time and your payments reach either last year’s Missouri tax (from a full 12-month return that showed tax) or 90% of this year’s. Otherwise Missouri adds a charge figured at its current interest rate from the first underpaid installment. If the side gig starts mid-year, Missouri’s first due date moves with it: June 15, September 15 or January 15, depending on when your estimated tax changes.
City residents have one more stop. The Collector of Revenue’s E-234 instructions say a City resident who is self-employed owes the 1% earnings tax on 100% of business net profit, even for work done outside city limits, and that all 1099-NEC and 1099-MISC income goes on that return. It’s due April 15. A federal extension won’t cover it: the city wants its own Form E-8, received before the deadline, because the IRS doesn’t tell the city about federal extensions. Our St. Louis earnings tax guide covers the rest, and our page on filing a tax extension in Missouri covers the state and federal side.
### How do you pay taxes on self-employment income?
In installments during the year, then at filing time on Form 1040, with Schedule C for the profit and Schedule SE for the 15.3%. The IRS takes estimated payments through your online account, IRS Direct Pay from a bank account at no cost, EFTPS, a debit or credit card (the card processor charges a fee) or a check with a 1040-ES voucher. Missouri accepts estimated payments online by e-check or card, or by check with the MO-1040ES voucher mailed to P.O. Box 555 in Jefferson City.
The part nobody explains is that you start the payments yourself. There’s no account to wait on and no bill coming. You figure the number, pick the installment, and send it. That’s the whole system. The second time through, it’s routine.
When the side income gets real, a pro can set your quarterly numbers once, and from then on you just follow them. Here’s what a tax preparer costs in St. Louis. And if the gig is turning into something bigger, our guides to turning a St. Louis side hustle into a real business and drawing customers online without a storefront pick up where the tax part leaves off.
This is general information, not tax advice for your situation. A CPA or enrolled agent can apply it to your numbers, and our St. Louis Financial directory is a place to start.
Want a second set of eyes before the next due date? Start with accountants and tax preparers around St. Louis, and ask each one two questions: do you work with gig and 1099 clients, and will you set my quarterly numbers for the IRS and Missouri both?
And if you’re the bookkeeper or CPA who already does exactly that, the next driver searching at midnight, or asking an AI, should hear your name before anyone else’s, so list your practice.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. At what point do you have to pay taxes on a 1099?
A.  As the money comes in, in practice. The tax is owed on the year’s profit, but the IRS and Missouri both expect it in installments by April 15, June 15, September 15 and January 15 once you’ll owe enough: $1,000 federally, $100 for Missouri. Skip them and the IRS can charge an underpayment penalty and Missouri adds an interest-based charge, even if you pay in full in April.
### Q. Is DoorDash income taxable?
A.  Yes. The IRS lists driving for booked rides or deliveries as gig work, and gig income is taxable whether or not a form arrives. Delivery apps that pay drivers as independent contractors don’t withhold tax, so the 15.3% self-employment tax and income tax are yours to pay, figured on profit after business miles, phone share and other real costs.
### Q. What is the minimum income to file taxes for self-employed?
A.  $400 of net earnings from self-employment. At that point the IRS requires a return with Schedule SE, even if you’d owe no income tax, because self-employment tax has no standard deduction in front of it. Missouri’s estimated payments are a separate question: they start when your expected Missouri tax, after withholding, reaches $100.
### Q. How much money can I make on a 1099 before I have to pay taxes?
A.  For self-employment tax, the line is $400 of net earnings. Income tax depends on your whole year: the 2026 standard deduction is $16,100 for a single filer federally and in Missouri, so someone with no other income owes no income tax below that, though the 15.3% still applies. The $2,000 1099-NEC line only decides whether a form gets sent.
### Q. What is taxable income on a 1099?
A.  Profit, not the number on the form. Start with everything you were paid, form or no form, then subtract ordinary business costs: business miles at the IRS standard rate, parking and tolls, the business share of your phone, supplies you used up and platform fees. A 1099-K shows only gross payments, so fees and refunds come off using your own records.
### Q. What is the difference between a 1099 form and a W-9 form?
A.  Direction. A W-9 goes from you to the company paying you, handing over your name and taxpayer ID, and the form itself says not to send it to the IRS. A 1099 comes back after the year ends, reporting what they paid you, and a copy goes to the IRS. Being asked for a W-9 usually means you’re being paid as a contractor.
### Q. Do I need Missouri estimated payments if my day job already withholds?
A.  Possibly. Missouri measures its $100 line against your expected Missouri tax after withholding and credits. If your paycheck withholding only covers your wages, a side gig netting about $2,900 can push the gap past $100 at the 4.7% rate. Raising Missouri withholding at work is another way to close it, and a preparer can tell you which route fits.
### Q. Does a federal extension cover my City of St. Louis earnings tax return?
A.  No. The Collector of Revenue’s E-234 instructions say extension requests go on the city’s own Form E-8 and must arrive before the deadline, because the IRS doesn’t notify the city of federal extensions. The return is due April 15, penalty and interest apply if the extension prepayment falls short of 90%, and late tax runs 5% a month, up to 25%, plus 1% a month interest.

## Missouri Minimum Wage: What It Is Now, Who Is Exempt, Tipped Pay, and What Happened to Paid Sick Leave
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/missouri-minimum-wage
$15.00 an hour. That’s the Missouri minimum wage, and it has been since January 1, 2026. What changed around it is the part nobody pinned to the break-room wall. For nearly two decades, Missouri law always had the next cost-of-living adjustment written in. A 2025 law deleted it, and the same law ended the paid sick days that came with the ballot measure that got you to $15.
So the floor is higher than it’s ever been, and it’s also frozen. Nobody mails you that. You find out when a friend across the river mentions her paid leave, or when a slow night of tips leaves you wondering who covers the gap. This is what the law says now, and what to do when a check comes up short. It’s one chapter of our St. Louis money guide, the plain-English version of what school skipped.
### Is the minimum wage in Missouri $15 an hour?
Yes. Missouri’s minimum wage is $15.00 an hour for most workers, and current law schedules no raise after it. Tipped workers can be paid $7.50 an hour in cash wages if tips bring them to at least $15.00. Retail and service businesses grossing under $500,000 a year are exempt from the state rate.
The $15.00 rate took effect January 1, 2026, a $1.25 step up from the $13.75 that applied through 2025, under Section 290.502 of Missouri’s statutes. The Missouri Division of Labor Standards posts the same figure. It covers full-time, part-time and temporary hours alike, and there’s no automatic teen rate: the Division’s minimum wage FAQ says a lower training wage for learners or apprentices requires a hearing on that specific exception first. Looking for a first job? Our roundup of summer jobs in St. Louis for students shows who’s hiring.
Overtime runs on the week, not the day. Missouri requires time and a half after 40 hours in a workweek, and a ten-hour shift doesn’t trigger it by itself, per the Division’s wages and hours guidance. At minimum wage that’s at least $22.50 for every hour past 40. You also can’t trade overtime away for straight time. An employer who asks is breaking the law.
The federal minimum is still $7.25 an hour, where it’s sat since July 24, 2009. Missouri pays a little more than double that. The statute has a safety valve, too: if the federal minimum ever climbs above Missouri’s, the higher federal rate becomes the Missouri minimum immediately.
Commute across the river? The two states match on the headline number and split on almost everything else:
Illinois figures come from the Illinois Department of Labor.
### Is Missouri’s minimum wage going up again?
Not under current law. The statute sets $13.75 for 2025 and $15.00 for 2026, then stops. No step, no formula, no date. The number moves again only if lawmakers or voters change the law, or the federal minimum passes it.
That’s new. Voters wrote a cost-of-living formula into the wage law with Proposition B in November 2006. Before that, the state minimum simply matched the federal one. Starting January 1, 2008, the rate was adjusted every year by a federal price index, rounded to the nearest nickel. Some years it barely moved: the Division’s rate history shows $7.65 in both 2015 and 2016, then $7.85 in 2018.
Then voters went back to the ballot twice. Proposition B in November 2018 set yearly steps from $8.60 in 2019 to $12.00 in 2023, with the formula picking back up after that, which is how 2024 landed at $12.30. Proposition A in November 2024 raised it to $13.75 for 2025 and $15.00 for 2026, restarted yearly adjustments on January 1, 2027, and created statewide paid sick time. So why is Missouri’s minimum so far above the federal one? Voters put it there by petition, three times.
In 2025 the legislature passed House Bill 567, effective August 28, 2025. It kept the $15.00. It cut the 2027-and-after adjustments, repealed the sick time law, and added one more line: the wage section now applies to public employers, which the statute defines to include the state, counties, cities and school districts. The Revisor of Statutes keeps every version of Section 290.502 online, back to 1990.
A frozen floor is simple arithmetic. Rent, groceries and bus fare can keep rising while $15.00 stays $15.00, so the same check buys a little less every year prices climb. Running a small business instead? Our guide to hiring your first employee in Missouri covers what an employer owes now.
### Who is exempt from Missouri’s minimum wage?
The biggest exemption is about size. A retail or service business with annual gross sales under $500,000 doesn’t have to pay the state rate, and the Division says employers outside the law can pay “wages of their choosing.” Think corner store, two-chair salon, tiny family diner. A cashier at a shop like that could earn $10 an hour, assume the owner is breaking the law, and be wrong, at least under Missouri law.
Here’s the catch. The Division’s FAQ notes that the federal Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA, the national wage law) doesn’t have this exemption, so it may still apply. If it does, the floor at that small shop is $7.25, not $15.00. If neither law reaches the job, the owner sets the wage. That’s why one question belongs in every small-business interview, said out loud: does this job pay the Missouri minimum?
The statute also carves out specific jobs and situations in Section 290.500. Among them:
Bona fide executive, administrative and professional employees, the salaried exemption covered next.
Volunteers at charities, churches and other nonprofits where no real job relationship exists.
Staff at a children’s day or resident camp working less than four months a year.
Occasional work at a private home, six hours or less each time, and casual babysitting.
Casual or occasional golf caddies and newspaper carriers.
Commission salespeople whose hours and work locations the employer doesn’t substantially control.
Students working for a school in exchange for tuition, housing or fees.
People incarcerated in Missouri Department of Corrections facilities.
One group moved the other way. Earlier versions of the statute said the voter-approved raises didn’t apply to public employers. Since August 28, 2025, the section says it does, so a part-time job with a city, a county or a school district sits under the same $15.00 floor as a big-box stockroom.
### Can a salaried job pay less than $15 an hour?
Only if the job is truly exempt, and a salary alone doesn’t make it exempt. The Division’s FAQ says Missouri’s minimum can apply to a salaried worker who doesn’t fit an exemption and whose pay doesn’t equal $15.00 for every hour worked that week.
The executive, administrative and professional exemption runs on federal rules, and Missouri’s overtime statute points straight to them. Three tests have to hold. The salary has to be at least $684 a week, or $35,568 a year. It has to be paid as a true salary, not docked hour by hour. And the actual duties have to fit the exemption, whatever the title on the badge says.
Run it on a common setup. Say a store offers a “salaried assistant manager” job at $650 a week and the schedule runs 50 hours. That’s $13 an hour, and $650 sits below the $684 federal line, so the exemption fails the salary test. Under Missouri’s minimum, those 50 hours are worth at least $750 before overtime enters the picture. Now flip it. A job that clears $684 and passes the duties test can legally work out to $13.68 an hour over the same 50 hours. That’s the trade an exempt salary makes, and the math belongs in the offer conversation, not after the first paycheck.
### How much do tipped employees make in Missouri?
At least $15.00 an hour, counting tips. Under Section 290.512, an employer can pay a tipped worker as little as half the minimum, $7.50 an hour, in cash wages. Cash wage plus tips still has to reach $15.00 for every hour worked, and if tips fall short, the employer makes up the difference.
On a pay stub, it looks like this. Picture a server who works 30 hours in a week. Her legal floor for the week is $450. Her employer pays $225 in cash wages at $7.50. In a good week she pulls $300 in tips, lands at $525, and the employer owes nothing extra. In a slow week she makes $150 in tips. Now she’s at $375, and the employer has to add $75. If that $75 never shows up, that gap is exactly what a wage complaint is for. Our guide to reading your pay stub and filling out a Missouri W-4 shows where those lines appear and what comes out before payday.
Overtime for tipped workers is figured on the full minimum, not the $7.50. The Division puts it at a total of at least $22.50 an hour for every hour past 40. And the tips have to actually be yours: the statute speaks of tips the worker “receives and retains,” and federal law bars employers, managers and supervisors from keeping workers’ tips.
The river matters here more than anywhere. Federal law lets employers pay tipped workers a cash wage of just $2.13 an hour. Missouri requires $7.50. Illinois lets employers pay 60% of its $15.00 minimum, which is $9.00, so a server in the Metro East starts every shift $1.50 an hour ahead of one doing the same work in Missouri, before a single tip.
And the “80/20 rule” you may have heard about? It’s the nickname for a federal limit on non-tipped side work, the setup and cleanup that keeps a dining room running. A 2021 U.S. Labor Department rule said that once that support work passed 20% of the workweek or 30 straight minutes, the full minimum wage applied. A federal appeals court vacated that rule on October 29, 2024, and the department restored its older regulation. Missouri’s statute sets no percentage of its own.
Fired after asking where your tips went? Here’s when to call a lawyer.
### What happened to paid sick leave in Missouri?
It’s no longer required statewide. Since August 28, 2025, Missouri employers don’t have to provide earned paid sick time, though they can still choose to, according to the Division’s paid sick time FAQ. Whether you get sick days now depends on your employer’s policy or your contract.
For one short stretch, it was the law. Proposition A gave workers one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, starting May 1, 2025, or the first day on the job if that came later. Employers with 15 or more workers had to allow up to 56 hours of use a year; smaller employers, up to 40. House Bill 567 repealed those sections effective August 28, 2025, and the statute page now just says “Repealed.” Count it out: workers earned that time for less than four months, May 1 through August 27, 2025.
Two things still hold. The Division says an employer may offer sick and vacation pay to some groups and not others, but not based on age, race, sex, religion or national origin; that complaint goes to the Missouri Commission on Human Rights. And your employer’s written policy, or any contract you have, is where your sick days live now. Read it before you’re the one running a fever.
Cross into Illinois and it flips. The state’s Paid Leave for All Workers Act lets workers earn one hour of paid leave for every 40 hours worked, up to 40 hours a year, for any reason. Two jobs paying the same $15.00, a short drive apart, can come with very different time-off rules.
### Is $15 an hour a livable wage in St. Louis?
For one adult with no kids, not by MIT’s measure. The MIT Living Wage Calculator puts the St. Louis living wage at $21.79 an hour for a single adult, or $45,320 a year before taxes. Full-time at $15.00, which MIT counts as 2,080 hours, comes to $31,200. Our breakdown of the cost of living in St. Louis shows where the money goes.
Household shape moves the answer more than the wage does. Two adults who both work full time with no kids need $14.89 an hour each, so two $15.00 paychecks clear the bar by 11 cents an hour apiece. Add two children and each parent needs $27.28. A single parent with one child needs $38.52, more than two and a half times the minimum wage. MIT last updated these figures on February 15, 2026, and they cover basics like food, child care, housing and transportation.
The hourly rate isn’t what lands in your account, either. Taxes come out first, and depending on where you live and work, the city may take a cut too. Our guide to the St. Louis earnings tax covers who pays it.
### How do you file a wage complaint in Missouri?
Start with the Missouri Division of Labor Standards. Its online minimum wage complaint form covers unpaid minimum wage and overtime, or you can call 573-751-3403 or email minimumwage@labor.mo.gov. The Division investigates and calculates the back wages owed at the minimum wage rate.
Then comes the part that catches people off guard. The Division says it “does not have the legal authority” to make an employer pay, and its FAQ is blunt: Missouri has no wage collection law. The state can find that you’re owed. It can’t collect for you. If the employer doesn’t settle up, the Division points workers to small claims court for amounts under $5,000, where it’s easier to proceed without a lawyer, and to circuit court above that.
The law gives that move real teeth. Under Section 290.527, an employer who pays less than the Missouri minimum is liable for the unpaid wages plus an additional amount equal to twice the unpaid wages as liquidated damages (a set penalty written into the statute), along with court costs and reasonable attorney fees. Shorted $1,000? The statute puts that at $1,000 owed plus $2,000 in liquidated damages, before fees. A side deal to work for less is no defense. The deadline is three years.
Two more protections. Firing or otherwise punishing a worker for reporting to the Division or taking part in a wage case is a misdemeanor under Section 290.525, and the Division keeps investigation records confidential unless a court orders them released. If the job is covered by federal law, you can also reach the U.S. Wage and Hour Division at 1-866-487-9243.
Already let go? Missouri makes earned wages due on the day of discharge. If they aren’t paid, a written request starts a seven-day clock, and after that the wages keep running as a penalty for up to 60 days under Section 290.110. Our guide to your rights when you’re fired in Missouri covers the rest. Either way, keep your own record: a phone note of every shift’s start and end, a photo of each posted schedule, every pay stub and tip report. Paper beats memory.
This is general information about how Missouri and federal wage rules work, not legal advice for your situation. An employment attorney can apply it to yours, and our St. Louis Legal directory is a place to start.
Shorted on hours, tips or a final check? Gather your pay stubs and your own log of shifts, then talk with employment attorneys around St. Louis before that three-year clock runs down.
And if you run an employment law or payroll practice, the next worker with a wage question needs a name to call, so see who AI names instead of you.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the lowest you can legally get paid?
A.  For most Missouri jobs, $15.00 an hour. Tipped workers can receive a cash wage as low as $7.50 if tips bring their total to $15.00. Employees of retail or service businesses under $500,000 in annual gross sales aren’t covered by the state rate, though the federal $7.25 may still apply. A few situations, like casual babysitting and genuine volunteering, fall outside Missouri’s law.
### Q. Who does not qualify for the minimum wage?
A.  Missouri’s law excludes bona fide executive, administrative and professional employees, nonprofit volunteers, seasonal youth camp staff, occasional household help, casual babysitters, commission salespeople who control their own hours and locations, work-for-tuition students and incarcerated workers. Employees of retail or service businesses under $500,000 in annual gross sales are excluded too, though the Division notes federal law may still cover them.
### Q. What if your employer doesn’t pay you minimum wage?
A.  File a complaint with the Missouri Division of Labor Standards online or at 573-751-3403. It investigates and calculates back wages but can’t force payment, so collecting is up to you: small claims court under $5,000, circuit court above that. Missouri law lets a worker recover the unpaid wages plus twice that amount in liquidated damages, costs and attorney fees, within three years.
### Q. What is the 80/20 rule for tipped employees?
A.  It’s the nickname for a federal limit on non-tipped side work. A 2021 Labor Department rule said that once support work passed 20% of the workweek or 30 straight minutes, the employer owed the full minimum wage instead of the tipped cash wage. A federal appeals court vacated that rule on October 29, 2024, and the department restored its older regulation. Missouri sets no percentage of its own.
### Q. Is there a minimum wage for salaried?
A.  Yes, unless the job is exempt. To be exempt as an executive, administrative or professional employee, federal rules require a salary of at least $684 a week plus duties that fit the exemption. A salaried worker who doesn’t qualify must be paid at least $15.00 for every hour worked in Missouri, so long weeks can drag a modest salary below the legal floor.
### Q. What are the rules around sick pay?
A.  In Missouri, paid sick leave is now up to your employer or your contract. The statewide requirement voters approved in Proposition A applied from May 1, 2025, and was repealed effective August 28, 2025. Employers may still offer it, and the Division says they can treat employee groups differently as long as they don’t discriminate. Illinois law still lets workers earn up to 40 hours a year.
### Q. Can my employer take a register shortage out of my pay?
A.  Sometimes. The Division of Labor Standards says Missouri employers may deduct for cash register shortages, damaged equipment and similar losses, but only if the deduction doesn’t push your pay below the minimum hourly rate. On a 30-hour week paid exactly $450, there’s no room for any shortage deduction at all. A pay cut generally needs 30 days’ written notice first.
### Q. Does Missouri require lunch breaks?
A.  No. Missouri doesn’t require meal or rest breaks for most workers, including most teens; the Division leaves them to company policy or agreement. The exception is young people working in the entertainment industry, who must get a meal break before working more than five and a half hours, plus a 15-minute rest after every two hours of continuous work.

## Debt Consolidation in St. Louis: Loan, Credit Counseling or Something Else? The Honest Math
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/debt-consolidation-st-louis
Consolidation doesn’t shrink debt. It moves it. The ads in your feed lead with one number, a smaller monthly payment, and skip the two that decide whether you come out ahead: the new rate with every fee folded in, and the balance on your old cards a year from now. Get both right and consolidating can save you thousands. Get either one wrong and you’ve paid someone to rearrange the same pile.
Picture a home health aide in Dutchtown with $15,000 spread over three cards. She pays something to everybody every month, and the balances barely move. Then the mailers start. One loan, one payment, “lower your bills today.” A few come from credit unions. Others come from companies that want her to stop paying her cards altogether.
They all use the same word for four very different tools. A consolidation loan or balance transfer swaps your debt for new debt at a lower rate. A nonprofit debt management plan keeps the debt but gets the interest cut. Debt settlement tries to pay less than you owe, at a real cost to your credit. Bankruptcy is a court process with its own rules. Here’s the honest math on each, plus the Missouri rules the ads leave out. It’s part of our St. Louis money guide, the stuff nobody taught us in school. If this feels confusing, that’s not on you. Somebody makes money when it stays confusing.
### Is there a downside to debt consolidation?
Yes. Consolidation moves debt; it doesn’t erase it. It saves money only when the new APR, fees included, beats what you pay now and the old cards stay near zero afterward. Stretch the term, pay a big upfront fee or run the cards back up, and the move can cost more than it saves.
Start with the rate. APR, or annual percentage rate, is the yearly cost of borrowing with the lender’s fees built in. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau describes it as the interest rate plus fees such as origination charges, which is why you compare APR to APR, never APR to a bare interest rate.
Then the term. A lower payment usually means a longer loan, and the CFPB’s guide to consolidating card debt warns that a longer repayment period can cost considerably more overall. Some low rates are teasers that climb later. And a home equity loan changes the stakes completely, because your house becomes the collateral.
Then the habit, the part nobody wants to hear. That same CFPB page says many people don’t succeed in paying off debt by taking on more debt unless they lower their spending. A consolidation loan pays your cards to zero. It doesn’t close them. If whatever filled them is still around, a transmission, a short paycheck, a school bill, they fill again, and now you’re carrying two debts instead of one. The ad told you a third of the story.
### Is it better to pay off my credit card debt or consolidate my debt?
Consolidate only if the new APR is clearly lower and you can leave the old cards alone. Otherwise a steady payoff on the cards you already have can beat a loan that looks better on paper. Run one household’s numbers several ways and it gets obvious.
Our Dutchtown aide owes $15,000 at 22% APR, close to the 22.36% average the Federal Reserve reported for August 2026 on card accounts charged interest. She can put $500 a month toward debt. The loan rows use 12%, near the Fed’s 11.90% average for a 24-month personal loan at a commercial bank. Illustrative round numbers, not quotes:
The straight loan wins: about $4,040 less interest, and she’s debt-free eight months sooner. Now look at the third row. Stretching the same loan to five years drops the payment to $334, which feels like relief. It also keeps her in debt 16 months longer than simply paying the cards at $500, and it gives back more than half the savings. The lower payment is the bait. The term is the price.
The fee row is sneakier. If the lender keeps 5% at closing, she has to borrow about $15,790 to clear $15,000 of cards. The loan still wins, but by roughly $3,100 instead of $4,040. That’s why APR, which counts the fee, is the number to compare.
Then the row that doesn’t fit in a box. A year after consolidating, her loan is down to about $10,580. If $5,000 has crept back onto the cards, she owes about $15,580, more than she started with, split between a loan payment and card bills at 22%. That’s exactly the failure the CFPB warns about.
A balance transfer card runs the same math with a twist. Say she gets 0% for 18 months with a 3% fee, and the issuer grants a $15,450 limit. The fee adds $450 on day one. At $500 a month, about $6,450 is still owed when the regular rate kicks in. Clearing it in time takes about $858 a month. The CFPB flags two more traps: new purchases on that card get no grace period, and paying more than 60 days late can let the issuer raise the rate on all balances, the transferred one included. Our explainer on how credit card interest works covers the mechanics.
Where you borrow matters too. Federal credit unions are generally held to an 18% ceiling on loan rates, a temporary cap above the normal 15% limit that the NCUA board extended through September 10, 2027. Even that ceiling sits below the average card rate, and our rundown of the best local credit unions in the St. Louis metro covers who can join each one.
### What is the difference between debt consolidation, credit counseling and debt settlement?
They sound alike and pull in opposite directions. Consolidation replaces your debts with one new debt. Credit counseling, usually from a nonprofit, helps you budget and can set up a plan that cuts interest on what you already owe. Debt settlement, usually sold by for-profit companies, tries to get creditors to accept less. The CFPB’s side-by-side adds that many lenders won’t negotiate with settlement companies, and those companies usually can’t get better terms than you could by calling the creditor yourself.
Consolidation loan or balance transfer: fits when your credit still earns a clearly lower APR and your income covers the payment.
Nonprofit debt management plan: fits when your credit has slipped too far for a good loan, but your income can repay the full balance at lower interest.
Debt settlement: for people who truly can’t repay in full, with credit damage, fees and possible taxes attached.
Bankruptcy: a federal court process for debts you can’t repay on any realistic timeline. Our guide to what happens when you file bankruptcy in Missouri walks through Chapter 7 and Chapter 13.
A payday loan or car title loan isn’t on that list on purpose. Rolling card debt into a payday loan trades a 22% problem for a far pricier one, as our breakdown of how payday loans work in Missouri shows, and a title loan puts your car on the line, as our guide to title loans and repossession in Missouri explains.
### What is a debt management plan?
It’s a repayment plan run by a credit counseling agency. You make one payment to the agency each month, and it pays your creditors, usually after they’ve agreed to lower your interest or waive some fees. That’s how the CFPB describes it. You still repay the full balance, and the National Foundation for Credit Counseling says plans typically run three to five years. The FTC adds that plans cover unsecured debts like cards and medical bills, not a house or car, and that you may have to stop using or applying for credit until you finish. Before you send an agency a dime, the CFPB says to confirm with your creditors that they’ve accepted the plan.
Now the Missouri part, the one almost nobody mentions. Missouri’s debt-adjuster law, section 425.010, caps what a paid provider can charge to run a debt management plan: no more than $50 to set it up, then no more than $35 a month or 8% of what’s paid to your creditors that month, whichever is greater. Run it both ways. If the plan sends $500 a month to creditors, 8% is $40, so $40 is the ceiling. If it sends $300, 8% is only $24, so the ceiling is $35. The same chapter lets any organization run a plan free of charge.
Nonprofit isn’t a guarantee, though. The CFPB’s warning signs: an agency that pushes a plan before looking at your finances, charges for basic information, turns you away because you can’t afford its fee, or pays counselors more when you buy more. It suggests starting with members of the NFCC or the Financial Counseling Association of America. The Justice Department also keeps a list of approved credit counseling agencies for the Eastern District of Missouri, the federal court district that covers St. Louis. That list exists for pre-bankruptcy counseling, so treat it as a screen, not an endorsement.
The cheapest loan here needs a membership first: how joining works.
### What are the risks of debt relief?
With debt settlement, the risks are big and mostly land on you. Many programs have you stop paying creditors and save into an account, so the company can later offer each one a lump sum. Meanwhile late fees and interest pile up, your credit takes the hit, and creditors can step up collections or sue. The CFPB warns settlement may leave you deeper in debt than when you started, and some creditors won’t deal with these companies at all.
A lawsuit is where it turns expensive. A creditor that wins a judgment can go after your paycheck, and our guide to debt collectors in Missouri covers garnishment and the statute of limitations here. Most negative information, late payments included, can stay on your credit report for seven years.
Then the tax bill nobody budgets for. When a creditor forgives part of what you owe, the IRS generally treats the canceled amount as taxable income for that year, and lenders that cancel $600 or more generally file Form 1099-C. Say a card company settles a $10,000 balance for $4,000. The $6,000 it forgave can land on your return as income unless an exclusion applies. The big one is insolvency: under IRS Publication 4681, you can exclude canceled debt to the extent your total debts topped the fair market value of everything you owned right before the cancellation.
And the fees. Settlement companies often charge expensive ones, the CFPB says. The real question is when they’re allowed to collect.
### How can you tell a debt relief company is breaking the rules?
Ask when they get paid. Under the federal Telemarketing Sales Rule, a company selling debt relief by telemarketing can’t take any fee until it has renegotiated, settled, reduced or otherwise changed at least one of your debts under an agreement you signed, and you’ve made at least one payment under that deal.
Here’s the Missouri wrinkle. The federal rule is a telemarketing rule. Missouri wrote its own version into state law, section 425.043, and nothing in it limits the ban to phone sales. Any debt adjuster, meaning anyone offering debt relief for a fee, has to wait for the same two things: one debt resolved and one payment from you under the plan. Before you agree to pay, it must tell you how long results will take, how much you must save before it makes each settlement offer, and that skipped payments can hurt your credit and bring lawsuits. If it holds your savings, you own that money and can withdraw it anytime, getting it back minus fees already earned within seven business days. One carve-out: under section 425.040, Missouri-licensed attorneys aren’t debt adjusters, so if a pitch comes through a law office, ask exactly who you’re hiring.
The CFPB’s red flags. Walk away from any debt relief company that:
Charges any fee before it settles your debts.
Guarantees it can make your debt go away.
Tells you to stop communicating with your creditors.
Claims it can stop all collection calls and lawsuits.
Promises your unsecured debts paid off for pennies on the dollar.
Pitches a “new government program” to erase card debt.
If one crosses the line, report it. The Missouri Attorney General’s Consumer Protection Hotline is 1-800-392-8222, or file a complaint online with copies of your contract and payment records. Copies, never originals.
### When does bankruptcy beat debt consolidation?
When the honest math says you can’t repay the full balance on any realistic timeline, even at a lower rate. Consolidation and a debt management plan both assume you’ll repay every dollar. Settlement assumes you can save lump sums while your credit sinks. Bankruptcy is the one route here where a court order ends eligible debts.
It’s no shortcut. A bankruptcy can stay on your credit report for up to ten years, per the CFPB, and you’ll need counseling from an approved agency before you file, which is what that Justice Department list is for. St. Louis cases go to the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Eastern District of Missouri at the Eagleton courthouse downtown. One quiet difference from settlement: the IRS excludes debt discharged in bankruptcy from income, while settled debt can be taxed.
### What should you ask before you sign with anyone?
Treat it like an interview, because it is one. You’re hiring someone to handle the biggest bill in your house, and the good ones expect questions. It’s the same habit that works for choosing a financial advisor in St. Louis: learn how they’re paid before you hear what they’ll do.
For a credit union or other lender:
What’s the APR with every fee included, for this exact amount and term?
What will I pay in total over the life of the loan?
Can you pay my card companies directly, so the money never sits in my checking account?
Is there any penalty for paying it off early?
For a counseling agency or settlement company:
Are you a nonprofit, and which national association are you a member of?
What do you charge to start, and each month after?
When exactly do you get paid, and what has to happen first?
Which of my creditors have agreed to work with you?
Listen to how they answer. A good counselor starts with your budget. A good loan officer shows the total cost without being asked twice. Anyone who rushes you or dodges the fee question has told you what you need to know. You’re not bad with money. Nobody sat you down and ran these numbers. Now you have.
This is general information, not advice for your situation. A nonprofit credit counselor, a credit union loan officer or a bankruptcy attorney can apply it to yours, and our St. Louis Financial directory is a place to start.
Ready to price a consolidation loan? Start with credit unions around St. Louis, bring your latest card statements, and ask each one for the APR with every fee included on the same amount and term.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is a debt consolidation personal loan?
A.  It’s an installment loan from a bank, credit union or other lender that pays off several debts, usually credit cards, leaving one fixed payment and a set end date. It saves money only when its APR, fees included, beats what you pay now and the old cards stay paid down. Under the NCUA’s current ceiling, federal credit unions are generally held to 18% on loans.
### Q. Is debt consolidation better for your credit?
A.  It can help if you pay on time. Payment history matters most, and the CFPB says experts advise using no more than 30% of your total credit limit, so moving card balances onto an installment loan can bring that usage down. A new application counts as fresh credit activity, and settlement, which usually involves missed payments, damages credit.
### Q. What disqualifies you from debt consolidation?
A.  Lenders weigh your credit history, income and debt-to-income ratio, all your monthly debt payments divided by your gross monthly income. Recent missed payments, a high ratio or income too uneven for the new payment can mean a denial or a rate too high to help. A nonprofit debt management plan isn’t a loan, though each creditor still has to accept it.
### Q. Are credit counselors worth it?
A.  A reputable nonprofit counselor usually is. Counseling groups commonly offer free or low-cost education, a good session starts with your whole budget instead of one product, and Missouri caps what a paid provider can charge to run a debt management plan. Walk away from any agency that pushes a plan before reviewing your finances or charges just for information.
### Q. What charities can help people with debt?
A.  Nonprofit credit counseling agencies are the main ones. The CFPB points people to members of the National Foundation for Credit Counseling, which lists 800-388-2227 on its site, and the Financial Counseling Association of America. The Justice Department keeps a list of approved agencies for the Eastern District of Missouri. Check any agency with the Missouri Attorney General before paying a fee.
### Q. Does a debt management plan work?
A.  It works for people whose income can cover the full balance once the interest drops, and who can stick with a plan that typically runs three to five years, per the NFCC. It falls apart when creditors never accepted it, so confirm with each one first, or when new card debt piles up alongside it. It lowers the payment, not the balance.
### Q. What is the smartest way to pay off debt?
A.  Pay every minimum on time, then send each extra dollar to the highest-APR balance first, which saves the most interest. Paying the smallest balance first costs a bit more but delivers quick wins that keep some people going. Either beats minimums alone. Consolidate only if a lower APR, fees included, speeds that up.
### Q. Is debt consolidation the same as debt settlement?
A.  No. Consolidation replaces your debts with a new loan or card, and you repay every dollar, ideally at a lower rate. Settlement tries to get creditors to accept less, usually after you’ve stopped paying them, which damages credit and can turn forgiven debt into taxable income. In Missouri, a debt relief company can’t charge you until at least one debt is resolved.

## Title Loans in Missouri: What They Really Cost and Your Repossession Rights
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/title-loans-in-missouri-and-car-repossession
Sized to your car, not your paycheck. That’s the title loan in one line, and it’s the whole business model: the lender’s safety net is parked in your driveway, so the deal can work out fine for the lender even when it falls apart for you. A 2016 study by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) of single-payment title loans found that one in five borrowers had the car or truck seized. More than four in five of those loans were renewed the day they came due.
Missouri’s rules push back harder than the storefront lets on. The law makes a title lender weigh whether you can repay when it sets the size and length of the loan. It caps any single loan at $5,000. And before a repossession, the lender generally has to send you a written notice and give you 20 days to catch up. The poster the law makes every lender hang by the counter doesn’t have to mention any of it.
Below: what a title loan costs in plain math, exactly when a repo can happen, what a repo agent can’t do in your driveway, and what you owe after the car is sold. It’s part of our St. Louis money guide, built for the money stuff nobody covered in school. You’re not bad with money. Nobody hands you Chapter 408 at the counter.
### Can I get a car title loan in Missouri?
Yes. Missouri allows title loans from lenders licensed by the Division of Finance, up to $5,000, for terms of at least 30 days, if you’re 18 or older with a clear title. The law sets no interest-rate cap, and before repossessing, a lender generally must give you 20 days to catch up.
The rules live in sections 367.500 to 367.533 of the state statutes, and the Missouri Division of Finance in Jefferson City licenses and examines every title lender. Before you walk in:
Check the license. The Division’s licensee search lists title loan companies as their own license type. A loan from an unlicensed lender is void under the statute, and the borrower owes back only the principal.
The title has to be clear, meaning no other lender holds a lien on the car, and you have to be at least 18, under section 367.527.
Every owner listed on the title has to sign off on the pledge, under the Division’s title loan rule.
Mobile home titles are off the table.
Before you sign, the lender has to hand you a notice in bold type warning that you may lose your automobile, and you sign to say you read it. The contract must carry the federal Truth in Lending disclosures, including the APR (annual percentage rate, the yearly cost with interest and required fees rolled in) and the monthly interest rate. And look at the wall. Every Missouri title loan office has to post the maximum rates it’s currently charging, in 14-point bold type.
One line in that contract deserves a circle. Missouri lets you cancel at no cost by returning the full principal before the close of the lender’s next full business day. That’s your exit, and it closes fast.
### How much can I borrow on a title loan?
No more than $5,000 on a single Missouri title loan, whatever the car is worth. Below that ceiling, the number is supposed to depend on you as well: the statute says the lender “shall take into consideration” your financial ability to reasonably repay when it decides the size and length of the loan.
The Division of Finance reads that rule as reaching past the first payment. Its regulation says the lender must consider whether you can make the required principal paydowns later on, and that ignoring the requirement can bring fines or the loss of a license. A loan sized only to the car isn’t what Missouri law describes.
Nationally, the CFPB found the typical title loan ran about $700. Small check, big collateral.
Picture a home health aide in Dutchtown who needs $900 to keep the rent current. Her paid-off SUV could secure a lot more, and a bigger check feels like breathing room. It isn’t. Missouri’s paydown rule is figured as a share of the original loan, so every extra dollar borrowed raises both the interest and the payments you’ll owe later. Borrow the bill, not the car.
### What does a Missouri title loan really cost?
Whatever you agree to. Missouri sets no interest-rate cap on title loans. The title loan law points to a general lending statute that allows simple interest “at rates agreed to by the parties.” The CFPB put the typical title loan APR at about 300%, so that’s the number to run.
Set that beside Missouri’s other short-term loan. The state caps everything a payday lender can collect on one loan at 75% of the amount borrowed, renewals included, and our guide to how payday loans work in Missouri and what they cost walks through those rules. The title loan law has no such ceiling:
Now the plain math, in round numbers. Say you borrow $1,000 at the 300% APR the CFPB found typical. Missouri’s rule has interest figured daily, which comes to about $247 for every 30 days. Then take the slowest path the law allows on 30-day terms: renew twice paying only interest, then pay interest plus $100 of principal at every renewal after that.
After three months, you’ve paid about $740 in interest and still owe $900.
The balance finally reaches zero at the end of month 12.
Total interest comes to about $1,849, so roughly $2,849 to retire a $1,000 loan.
On top of that, section 408.140 allows an origination fee of up to 10% of the loan, capped at $100, late charges that top out at $50, and the reasonable costs of towing, storing and selling the car if it comes to that. Pay faster and the total drops fast.
And the renewal rule has teeth. The Division treats paying off a title loan and borrowing again in the same visit as a renewal: walk in owing, walk out owing, and it counts. Paying off and reborrowing the same afternoon won’t reset the paydown clock.
### How many months late until repossession?
In Missouri it’s closer to one month than several, and the clock has rules. A missed payment is a default, whether it’s an installment or the payoff due at the end of the term. After you’ve been in default for 10 days, the lender can send you, and any cosigner, a notice of default and right to cure. Then it has to wait 20 days after giving that notice before it can repossess or demand the whole balance. Ten days plus 20 days: about 30 days from the missed payment, at the earliest.
That protection comes from Missouri’s consumer credit code, and the title loan law applies it to every title loan in the state. The Division of Finance even publishes a repossession checklist for lenders that reads like a borrower’s bill of rights. Is the account 10 or more days past due? If not, wait. Did the notice give at least 20 days to cure? If not, send one that does. After the repo, did the customer get a notice of the planned sale with at least 10 days to redeem the car? Did any surplus go back to the customer?
The notice itself is short. It lists an AMOUNT NOW DUE and a LAST DAY FOR PAYMENT. Pay that amount by that date and the statute says you’re restored as though you’d never been late. The 20 days start when the notice is delivered or mailed to your last known address, not when you open it, so keep your address current with the lender.
Two catches. The protection runs out: once you’ve defaulted twice on the same loan with the same lender, even if you caught up both times, the lender isn’t bound by the notice rule the next time. And it doesn’t apply if you hand the car over voluntarily, which lets the lender move ahead right away.
### What counts as a breach of the peace in a Missouri repo?
Missouri lets a lender take the car without going to court only if it acts “without breach of the peace,” in the words of the state’s version of the Uniform Commercial Code. The statute doesn’t define the phrase, so courts decide it case by case. The CFPB describes it as generally meaning threatening or using physical force, removing a vehicle from a closed garage without permission, or continuing a repossession after you’ve resisted or refused.
You can’t sign that protection away. Missouri’s UCC says a borrower can’t waive the lender’s duty to repossess without a breach of the peace, and the title loan law separately bars a lender from accepting a waiver of any borrower right. Whatever the fine print says, those rules stand.
Saying no is different from fighting, though, and courts look hard at the facts, including how far along the repo was. In a 2021 ruling, the federal court in Springfield applied the test used by the Eighth Circuit, the federal appeals court covering Missouri: an officer who only keeps the peace isn’t taking part in a repo, but one who steps in so it happens when it otherwise wouldn’t can be. There, the car was already hooked and lifted when a deputy told the owner, sitting inside it, to get out or face arrest. The court ruled for the deputy.
So the safer play looks like this:
Keep the car in a closed, locked garage if you have one, and don’t hand over keys.
If an agent shows up, say clearly that you don’t consent, then step back. Don’t grab the truck, the chains or the person, and don’t climb into the car.
Record from a distance, and write down the company name and the time.
If it turns into a confrontation, call the police. The CFPB says you can contact law enforcement if a lender breaches the peace.
Then call a consumer attorney. A breach of the peace may give you a claim for damages or a defense that lowers what you owe after a sale, the CFPB says, and when a lender breaks these rules on a personal vehicle, Missouri sets a minimum recovery of the finance charge plus 10% of the principal.
Courts, not this page, decide where the line falls in a particular driveway.
Title loan to fix the AC? Read free AC help in St. Louis.
### What can I do if I can’t pay my title loan?
Move before the due date, and put it in writing. Missouri’s title loan law says the lender shall renew the loan when you ask in writing and pay the interest then due. That buys time, not freedom. Can’t cover even the interest? The Division’s rule recognizes that a lender may waive part of it so the loan can renew. That’s the lender’s call, but asking costs nothing.
Then work the exits, cheapest first:
Refinance at a credit union. Federal credit unions offer payday alternative loans, or PALs, of $200 to $1,000 over one to six months at no more than 28% APR, with an application fee capped at $20, and you generally need to be a member for at least a month. On a $1,000 PAL paid off over six months, the interest comes to about $83. Our comparison of credit union and bank auto loans in St. Louis covers how membership works.
Free up the cash the loan was covering. Rent, utility and food help can take a bill off the table; start with our list of help and assistance resources in St. Louis.
Put something other than the car on the line. A pawn loan risks an item, not your ride to work; here’s how pawn shops work in St. Louis.
If several debts are stacking up at once, read about debt consolidation in St. Louis before you sign anything new.
If a cure notice arrives, pay the amount it lists by the last day and the loan goes back to normal. If the repo has already happened, you can still redeem the car before it’s sold by paying everything you owe plus the lender’s reasonable repossession expenses. That’s the whole balance, not just the missed payment.
Bigger trouble has bigger tools, and our guide to what happens when you file bankruptcy in Missouri explains one of them. Legal Services of Eastern Missouri runs a consumer law program and gives free civil legal help to low-income residents and seniors in 21 eastern Missouri counties; its intake line is 314-534-4200. And if a lender broke the rules, file a complaint with the Division of Finance, which contacts the company for a response in a process it says generally takes about 30 days.
### What happens if you never pay off a repo?
The car gets sold, the money gets applied, and any shortfall, called a deficiency, becomes a debt the lender can sue you for. It doesn’t vanish because the car did. But Missouri puts real conditions on that debt, and lenders don’t always meet them.
Start with the sale. Before selling, the lender has to send you a notice of its plan, and a Missouri title lender can’t store a repossessed car more than 15 miles from the office where you signed. To get a new Missouri title stamped “Repossessed Title,” it must first give the owners 10 days’ written notice. Every part of the sale has to be commercially reasonable. The money goes first to the costs of repossessing, storing and selling, then to the loan, and anything left over is yours.
Then the shortfall. Missouri lets a lender collect a deficiency only if the amount financed was more than $500 and at least $300 was unpaid when you defaulted. Borrowed $500 or less? There’s no deficiency to chase. Before suing, the lender must send you the required sale notice, and a court can’t enter a default judgment unless the lender backs its claim with a verified petition or sworn testimony. You can also demand a written explanation of how the deficiency was figured, and the lender has 14 days to send it.
Ignore a deficiency and it can follow you a long way. After a judgment, Missouri lets the lender keep collecting the contract’s interest rate, as simple interest, until the judgment is paid. On a loan written near 300%, that’s a reason to answer the lawsuit, not hide from it. A judgment can also lead to wage garnishment, which our guide to debt collectors, the statute of limitations and garnishment in Missouri breaks down.
So check the paperwork against the rules before you pay a dime on a deficiency. A missing cure notice. A sale with no notice. A car stored too far away. A surplus nobody returned. Each one matters, and a consumer attorney can tell you how much.
This is general information, not legal advice for your situation. A consumer attorney can apply it to your contract and your notices, and our St. Louis financial services directory is a place to start.
Want a way out of a title loan, or a way to never need one? Compare auto lenders and credit unions around St. Louis, and ask each one what it would take to refinance a car you already own.
And if you run a credit union or a consumer law practice, the neighbor holding a cure notice tonight is asking an AI who can help, and being the name it gives first is the whole game, so see who AI names instead of you.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Can I refuse a repo?
A.  You can refuse consent, and a lender repossessing without a court order must do it without a breach of the peace, a duty you can’t waive. Keep the car in a closed, locked garage and say no clearly. Don’t physically block the agent or climb into the car. If the lender goes to court instead, a judge decides.
### Q. Do police get involved in repo cars?
A.  Usually only to keep the peace. Police don’t repossess cars for lenders. Under the test the federal appeals court covering Missouri applies, an officer who just keeps order isn’t part of the repo, but one who steps in so it happens when it otherwise wouldn’t can be. If an agent uses force or threats, the CFPB says you can contact law enforcement.
### Q. How does voluntary repossession work?
A.  You arrange with the lender to turn the car in. Missouri lets you surrender it any time after a default, but surrender skips the 20-day right-to-cure wait, and the lender can then call the whole loan due. It must tell you that you could still owe money after the sale. Surrender ends the repo, not the debt.
### Q. What disqualifies you for a title loan?
A.  In Missouri, a lender can’t lend to anyone under 18 or anyone who appears intoxicated, and it needs a clear title, so a car with another lender’s lien on it won’t qualify. Every owner on the title has to sign, and mobile home titles aren’t accepted. Because the lender must weigh your ability to repay, your income can shrink the offer or end it.
### Q. What is the statute of limitations for car repossession in Missouri?
A.  The deadlines people usually mean apply to lawsuits over the money, such as a deficiency. Missouri allows 10 years for an action on a written promise to pay money and five years for most other contract claims; which fits depends on your paperwork. The CFPB warns a court may still enter judgment if you don’t show up and raise the deadline yourself.
### Q. Is a charge-off better than a repossession?
A.  Neither is a fresh start. A charge-off is the lender writing the debt off as a loss on its own books, but the CFPB says a debt doesn’t generally disappear until it’s paid. A repo costs you the car and can still leave a deficiency. If either lands on your credit report, most negative information can be reported for seven years.
### Q. Can a title lender keep my car instead of selling it?
A.  Only by accepting the car as full payment, which wipes out the debt, and only if you agree in writing after default or don’t object within 20 days to its written proposal. On a consumer loan it can’t keep the car as partial payment. And once you’ve paid 60% of the principal, Missouri’s UCC generally requires a sale within 90 days.
### Q. Can I get my belongings back after a repo?
A.  Yes, and move fast. The CFPB says to contact the lender right away to set a time to collect your things, and to write down what was in the car and roughly what it was worth. If the lender or repo company demands a fee first, talk to an attorney; the CFPB has called that practice unfair in a public enforcement action.

## Debt Collectors in Missouri: How Old Is Too Old, Your Rights on the Phone, and What Garnishment Can Take
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/debt-collectors-in-missouri-statute-of-limitations-and-garnishment
Phone buzzing again? Same number as yesterday, asking about a debt you barely remember, and the voice on the line sounds sure of everything except the one date that matters: when the account went bad. Old debt in Missouri runs on clocks written into law. Once you know which clock you’re on, those calls get a lot less scary.
Here’s the gap collectors count on. Almost nobody was taught that there are two separate clocks. One decides whether you can be sued. The other decides how long the account sits on your credit report. A single small payment can restart the first while leaving the second exactly where it was. That trap is what this guide is built around, and it’s one chapter of our St. Louis money guide, the plain-English version of the stuff nobody covered in school.
### How long before a debt is uncollectible in Missouri?
Never completely, because Missouri’s deadlines end the right to sue, not the debt. Most contract debts carry a five-year lawsuit limit, and a written promise to pay money gets ten. After that, a collector can still ask but can’t sue or threaten to. A court judgment is different: it lasts ten years and can be revived.
The five-year rule lives in RSMo 516.120, which covers lawsuits on “contracts, obligations or liabilities, express or implied.” The ten-year rule is in RSMo 516.110, for an action “upon any writing” for the payment of money. Which one fits a given account isn’t always obvious, and lawyers argue about it. If a collector’s paperwork leans on the longer clock, that’s a question for an attorney, not a guess.
When the deadline passes, the debt doesn’t vanish. The federal collection rule, Regulation F, calls it time-barred and says a collector “must not bring or threaten to bring a legal action” to collect it. Letters and calls asking for money are still allowed. Nothing in that rule makes the collector warn you the debt is too old to sue on. You have to know.
A judgment runs on its own clock. Under RSMo 516.350, a Missouri judgment is presumed paid after ten years, but the creditor can revive it, and a payment entered on the court record restarts the count.
### What restarts the clock on an old debt in Missouri?
Two things, and Missouri treats them differently. A promise or admission has to be on paper: RSMo 516.320 says an acknowledgment or promise doesn’t revive a contract claim unless it’s in a writing signed by the person who owes. A payment is another story. RSMo 516.340 says that rule doesn’t lessen “the effect of a payment” of principal or interest, and the federal consumer bureau warns that a partial payment or acknowledging an old debt can restart the time period.
Picture it. A collector calls about a store card from years back and asks for a small “good-faith” payment to show you’re serious. Twenty dollars. It feels like a peace offering. On a debt near its deadline, or past it, that twenty dollars can hand the collector back the right to sue you for the whole balance.
So the dates come first. The validation notice, covered below, has to show an itemization date, such as the last statement, the charge-off or the last payment, and that’s where the clock math starts. If the balance began as a short-term loan, our breakdown of how payday loans work in Missouri shows how those balances balloon before a collector ever calls.
### Can I be sued for a debt over 7 years old?
Yes, in some cases, because seven years is the credit-report clock, not the lawsuit clock. A debt built on a written promise to pay money has a ten-year lawsuit window in Missouri, a payment can restart the five-year clock, and a judgment can be revived. Seven years tells you when the account should leave your credit report. It doesn’t tell you when you’re safe from a lawsuit.
The seven-year rule comes from the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act. Section 1681c bars credit reports from carrying collection and charged-off accounts older than seven years, counted from a fixed point: 180 days after the delinquency began. Because the start is anchored to when you first fell behind, a later payment doesn’t move it. Federal Trade Commission staff said as much in an advisory letter: a payment, a dispute or the sale of the account doesn’t stretch the reporting period.
