And if your bathtub overflows on a Saturday morning and the water comes through the ceiling of the apartment downstairs, the landlord’s policy won’t pay that bill for you either. That one can land on you, with a lawyer attached.
If you believed otherwise, you’re in big company. Missouri’s own insurance regulator says most tenants skip renters insurance because they assume the landlord’s coverage protects them, when landlords typically insure only the building they own. Nobody hands you an insurance briefing with the keys. The fine print just sits in a drawer, waiting for the worst day of your year to explain itself.
So here’s the briefing: what Missouri law requires, who pays when water goes through a floor, and the three disasters a renters policy refuses in writing, all of which have a St. Louis address. It’s part of our St. Louis money guide, plain-English explainers on the money stuff nobody taught us in school.
### Do you have to have renters insurance in Missouri?
No. No Missouri law requires tenants to carry renters insurance, but a lease can, and a signed lease is a binding contract. Either way, your landlord’s policy covers the building. It doesn’t cover your belongings, your hotel bill after a fire, or your liability if you damage someone else’s unit.
Start with the law. No Missouri statute makes a tenant buy renters insurance. The state Department of Commerce and Insurance (DCI) describes it as coverage renters “should consider,” and the Attorney General’s guide to Missouri landlord-tenant law lists a tenant’s legal duties (pay rent on time, use reasonable care, dispose of garbage properly, don’t add occupants or sublease without written permission) without a word about insurance.
The lease is a different story. A landlord can write a renters insurance requirement into it, whether the building is a big complex in the Central West End or a four-family in Dutchtown. Once you sign, the Attorney General’s guide is blunt: a signed lease is a binding legal contract, and a tenant isn’t excused from it for not reading it or not understanding it. Violating a condition of a written lease is one of the reasons the guide lists for a landlord ending one.
Read the insurance clause the way you’d read the deposit clause. Look for the liability amount it asks for, when proof is due, and whether it names a particular insurer or lets you shop. Our walk-through on renting an apartment in St. Louis covers the rest of the lease, line by line.
### Who pays when your bathtub floods the apartment downstairs?
You might, and that’s the exact job of the liability part of a renters policy. The Missouri Attorney General’s guide draws the line plainly: landlords should pay for repairs from ordinary wear and tear and natural forces like weather, and tenants should pay for damage caused by their own negligence or a guest’s.
Picture a second-floor flat in a brick two-family in Bevo Mill. You start a bath, the phone rings, and twenty minutes later water is dripping from the light fixture in your downstairs neighbor’s kitchen. Their ruined rug goes on their renters claim, if they have one. The soaked ceiling goes on the landlord’s. Then either insurer, after paying, can pursue whoever caused it. The industry calls that subrogation, which Missouri DCI’s insurance glossary defines as the insurer’s right to recover what it paid on a loss from a negligent third party who caused it.
The third party is you.
Without a policy, that claim comes out of your own pocket. With one, liability coverage answers it. The Insurance Information Institute (III) describes it as protection against lawsuits for bodily injury or property damage that you or your family cause to other people, and DCI adds that it covers unintentional damage you cause to the landlord’s property, using a kitchen fire as its example. The policy pays for your legal defense and any court award up to the limit, and the III says liability limits generally start around $100,000.
Now flip the floors. If the tenant upstairs leaves the tub running and ruins your things, the III’s renters insurance guide lists that exact scenario as water damage a renters policy covers. The landlord’s policy fixes the ceiling. Yours replaces the couch. Nobody else’s will.
### What does renters insurance actually cover?
Three things: your belongings, your liability to other people, and the extra cost of living somewhere else if a covered disaster forces you out. Everything after that is detail, and the detail is where claims get decided.
Personal property. DCI’s consumer guide to renters insurance lists fire and smoke, windstorm and hail, lightning, vandalism and theft, the weight of ice, snow or sleet, and damage from a car. Coverage follows your things, so a laptop stolen from your car can count, though DCI warns coverage away from home may be limited. The III’s example: on a $25,000 policy, off-premises losses might be capped at $2,500.
Liability. Covered above, plus a small no-fault medical piece, generally $1,000 to $5,000, so a friend who trips on your rug can send the medical bills straight to your insurer without anybody suing anybody.
Additional living expenses, also called loss of use. If a covered fire makes the place unlivable, the policy pays toward hotels, temporary rentals and restaurant meals. The III says most policies pay the difference between those costs and your normal spending, usually with a dollar cap or a time limit.
Then come the sublimits, the caps inside the cap. The III says jewelry and similar valuables are generally covered up to about $1,500. DCI suggests a rider (an add-on that raises the limit for a specific item) for jewelry, antiques and firearms, plus a separate add-on if a side business keeps its gear in your bedroom.
### Which three disasters does a Missouri renters policy refuse to cover?
Floods, earthquakes, and sewer or drain backup. Missouri DCI names those three on its renters page, and its printed guide adds normal wear and tear, the building itself and cars parked on the property. Here’s the uncomfortable part for St. Louis renters. None of the big three is a someday risk here. All three have a local address.
Flood. On July 26, 2022, 8.64 inches of rain fell at Lambert airport, a new all-time daily record that broke the 6.85 inches from August 20, 1915, according to the National Weather Service in St. Louis. The service issued a Flash Flood Emergency, a warning it reserves for high-end flash flooding, for parts of the city and county. Water like that can fill a garden-level apartment nowhere near a river, and a standard renters policy won’t pay for any of it. The fix is a separate policy. The National Flood Insurance Program sells renters contents-only coverage for belongings up to $100,000, and FloodSmart says it takes effect 30 days after purchase, with a few exceptions. A policy bought while the rain is falling is a policy for the next storm. Our guide to flood insurance in St. Louis goes deeper.
Earthquake. Missouri is the third-largest earthquake insurance market among the states, behind only two West Coast states, according to DCI. The department cites a U.S. Geological Survey estimate that the New Madrid zone has a 25 to 40 percent chance of a quake larger than magnitude 6 within 50 years. A standard renters policy leaves that out. The III says earthquake coverage can be a separate policy or an endorsement, meaning an add-on, to your renters policy.
Sewer and drain backup. When heavy rain overfills a public sewer, it can push sewage back into a building, which is how a basement unit gets ruined in an afternoon. The Metropolitan St. Louis Sewer District (MSD) runs its own program for this. If an overcharged public sewer discharges into your building, MSD will reimburse up to $3,000, with a $100 deductible, and if a collapsed or blocked public line caused it, MSD reimburses the adjusted losses. You have to contact MSD within 30 days, and its 24-hour emergency line is (314) 768-6260. Two cautions. MSD’s page is written for homeowners, so a tenant should ask directly whether belongings in the unit qualify. And a backup from the private lateral line, the pipe from the building to the public sewer, isn’t MSD’s to pay. MSD itself says damage can exceed its cap, and DCI’s guide lists a sewer and drain backup endorsement you can add to a renters policy.
Two quieter gaps catch people too. Cars aren’t covered by renters insurance at all; the vehicle needs its own auto policy. And living with someone doesn’t put them on your policy. The III says a domestic partner generally isn’t automatically insured the way a spouse is and has to be specifically named. If a roommate’s things burn, your policy wasn’t written to replace them.
Flood took the furniture and no policy? St. Louis furniture banks can help.
### How much does renters insurance cost in Missouri?
Less than most people guess. The average Missouri renters policy cost $173 for the year in 2022, about $14 a month, according to National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) figures published by the III. That’s next to the national average of $171, and roughly a tenth of the $1,668 the average Missouri homeowner paid that year.
You’ll see other numbers, and they don’t match. DCI’s renters page says premiums average $8 to $21 a month for $20,000 to $30,000 of coverage. Its own printed guide, updated in 2023, puts the average at $32 a month for that same range. They weren’t published at the same time, and neither page says how its figure was measured. Every source agrees on one thing, though: this costs tens of dollars a month, not hundreds.
What moves your quote:
Deductible, the amount you pay on a claim before the policy pays. DCI says a $1,000 deductible costs less than a $500 one, and the III says moving to $1,000 can cut a premium by as much as 25 percent. You pay it on every claim, so the right number is one you could cover tomorrow.
Replacement cost. About 10 percent more than actual cash value, per the III. The next section shows why that’s money well spent.
Limits and add-ons. More property coverage, a higher liability limit, a sewer backup endorsement or a jewelry rider each adds to the price.
Discounts. DCI lists monitored fire or burglar alarms, fire extinguishers, sprinklers, deadbolts on exterior doors, and buying auto insurance from the same company.
DCI’s own advice is to get several quotes, since Missouri’s insurance market is highly competitive, and to compare prices every two years. The levers work the same way they do on a house, and our breakdown of what drives home insurance premiums in St. Louis goes deeper on deductibles. Still deciding where to live? Budget the premium right next to rent with our guide to how much rent you can afford in St. Louis.
### Replacement cost or actual cash value: which one actually rebuys your stuff?
Replacement cost does. Actual cash value pays what your things were worth the moment they were destroyed, after depreciation, which is the drop in value from age and use. Replacement cost pays what it takes to buy a similar item new today.
DCI’s guide runs the numbers on two items:
Now put both in a kitchen fire with a $500 deductible. On actual cash value, you’d collect $1,260, which is $1,760 minus the deductible, toward $3,600 of shopping. On replacement cost, you’d end up with $3,100. DCI explains the sequence: the company pays the actual cash value first, then settles up after you replace the item and send the receipt. Keep the receipts.
At about 10 percent extra, replacement cost on a policy near the Missouri average works out to something like $17 a year. The couch alone makes that look cheap. If a fire does happen, our guide to fire damage restoration in St. Louis covers the first hours and how the insurance side fits into cleanup.
### Does renters insurance cover it if your dog bites someone?
Usually, up to your liability limit, and in Missouri that limit matters more than dog owners tend to think. Under Missouri Revised Statutes section 273.036, the owner or possessor of a dog that bites someone without provocation, on public property or lawfully on private property, including the owner’s own home, is strictly liable for the damages, regardless of the dog’s past behavior or what the owner knew about it.
Translation: under that statute, “he’s never done that before” doesn’t get you off the hook. Damages shrink if the bitten person was partly at fault, and the law adds a fine of up to $1,000.
Then look at the size of these claims. Dog bites and other dog-related injuries averaged $65,450 per liability claim nationally in 2025, according to the III, and that average nearly doubled from 2016. Typical liability limits run $100,000 to $300,000, and anything above the limit is the owner’s to pay.
Two catches. Some insurers won’t cover certain breeds or charge more for them, and after a bite a company may raise the premium, decline to renew or exclude the dog. And DCI’s guide notes that damage your pet does to the rental itself is generally not covered, so chewed trim and clawed floors can come out of the deposit, not the policy. Our guide to renting with pets in St. Louis covers breed lists, pet rent and pet deposits.
### How do you set up a claim to pay before anything goes wrong?
Make a home inventory now, while everything is still where it belongs. DCI publishes a room-by-room home inventory checklist, and its tips are the useful kind:
Record specifics. The checklist warns that without the brand, model and serial number, you might get a lower-priced replacement.
Walk each room with your phone recording, opening closets and drawers as you go.
Group the small stuff, like cookware, linens and toys. Bought all at once, it adds up fast.
List what leaves the apartment with you: phone, laptop, tablet, watch, jewelry.
Keep a copy somewhere else, at a relative’s place or in an email to yourself, and update it every year and after big purchases.
When something does happen, the III’s list is short. Report a theft to the police and get the report. Call your insurer right away, because claims have filing time limits. Photograph the damage and don’t throw damaged items out before the adjuster sees them. If you have to move out during repairs, keep every receipt.
And if a claim stalls? Take the problem to the company first, note the name and date of every call and keep copies of everything in writing, the way DCI asks. Then call the department’s Insurance Consumer Hotline at 800-726-7390, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. weekdays, or file a complaint online. DCI forwards complaints to the company, requires a response and reviews it against Missouri insurance law. It can’t act as your lawyer or decide what your claim is worth.
This is general information, not advice for your situation. A licensed insurance agent can apply it to your lease, your belongings and your address, and our St. Louis Financial directory is a place to start.
Ready to price it? Get two or three quotes from home and renters insurance agents around St. Louis, and bring this page’s questions: replacement cost or actual cash value, what liability limit, and whether sewer backup, flood and earthquake coverage can be added.
If you’re the independent agent, the St. Louis renter weighing those questions, or asking an AI who can answer them, is really deciding who to call, and being the name that comes up first is the whole game, so list your agency.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What are three things that renters insurance typically does not cover?
A.  Missouri DCI names three: floods, earthquakes and sewer or drain backup. Flood coverage for belongings is sold separately through the National Flood Insurance Program, up to $100,000, and DCI and the III say sewer backup and earthquake coverage can be added to a renters policy as endorsements.
### Q. What is a fair price for renters insurance?
A.  In Missouri, the average renters policy cost $173 a year in 2022, about $14 a month, according to NAIC data published by the III. A fair price is one that buys replacement cost, a liability limit that fits your life and a deductible you could pay tomorrow. The only way to know you’ve found it is to compare at least three quotes.
### Q. Is renters insurance tax deductible?
A.  Not for a typical renter. IRS Publication 529 lists home repairs, insurance and rent among nondeductible personal expenses. The exception is someone self-employed who uses part of the home exclusively and regularly for business: Publication 587 allows a business share of rent and insurance. Employees working from home can’t take it. A CPA or enrolled agent can say whether a home office qualifies.
### Q. Is it legal to rent without renters insurance?
A.  Yes, as far as Missouri law goes. No state statute requires tenants to carry it. But if your lease requires a policy, going without breaks a lease term, and the Missouri Attorney General’s landlord-tenant guide lists violating a condition of a written lease among the reasons a landlord can end a lease.
### Q. Who should get renters insurance?
A.  Anyone who couldn’t replace their belongings out of pocket or absorb a lawsuit, which describes most renters. Add up the list the III suggests, furniture, clothing, electronics, appliances, kitchen gear and even bedding, and the total usually dwarfs a year of premiums. Dog owners have extra reason in Missouri, where state law holds owners strictly liable for unprovoked bites. College students living off campus usually need their own policy.
### Q. What are my rights as a renter in Missouri?
A.  The Attorney General’s guide covers the basics. A security deposit can’t exceed two months’ rent, and the landlord has 30 days after the lease ends to return it with an itemized list of deductions. Landlords handle ordinary wear and tear, can’t cut off your water, electricity or gas, and can’t evict without a court order. Tenants pay for damage they or their guests cause.
### Q. How much does $20,000 worth of renters insurance cost?
A.  Missouri DCI has published two averages for $20,000 to $30,000 of coverage: $8 to $21 a month on its website and $32 a month in its 2023 printed guide. NAIC data put Missouri’s overall average at $173 a year in 2022. Your price depends on the deductible, the liability limit, replacement cost and discounts, so quote the exact limit you want.
### Q. Does my roommate’s renters insurance cover me?
A.  Usually not, unless you’re named on it. The III says rules vary by state and company, some insurers let people who live together buy joint coverage, and a partner usually isn’t automatically insured the way a spouse is. With Missouri premiums averaging about $14 a month, your own policy is often the simpler fix.

## Flood Insurance in St. Louis: The 30-Day Wait and the Basement Gap Nobody Mentions
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/flood-insurance-st-louis
Your homeowners policy almost certainly excludes flood. The line sits in the exclusions section, a few pages past the part anyone reads, and Missouri’s insurance regulator doesn’t soften it: a standard homeowners or renters policy typically does not cover flooding damage. Water that rises out of the ground, rolls in off the street or comes over a riverbank belongs to a different policy entirely.
And that policy has fine print of its own. A new policy from the National Flood Insurance Program, the federal program FEMA runs, takes effect 30 days after you buy it. Thirty days. So the evening the river forecast scares you, when the crest prediction on the news keeps climbing, is the evening it’s already too late. The wait is longer than the warning. Nobody taught that in school, and it’s why so many St. Louis families find out what their insurance pays for while standing on the bottom basement stair.
Here’s the local number that ought to stop you. FEMA’s count of single-family homes carrying a federal flood policy on August 31, 2023 came to 182 in the entire City of St. Louis and 2,190 in St. Louis County. That’s the whole list. About a year before that count, on July 26, 2022, Lambert airport logged 8.64 inches of rain in one calendar day, its all-time record, in what the National Weather Service called the most prolific rainfall event the St. Louis metro has seen since records began in 1874. No river had to crest for that one.
This page is one chapter of our St. Louis money guide, the plain-English series on the money rules nobody walked us through.
### Is flood insurance worth the money?
Usually yes, if your home sits near a river or creek, takes on water in heavy rain, or carries a mortgage in a high-risk zone. Homeowners policies exclude flood, a new federal policy waits 30 days to start, and nearly a third of flood claims come from outside high-risk areas. The case is weakest for upper-floor condos.
Run the math the way an adjuster would. FEMA’s own agent materials put roughly $25,000 of damage on one inch of water in a home. Drywall wicks it up. Flooring buckles. Against that, the median single-family flood policy in the City of St. Louis cost $948 a year in FEMA’s 2023 data, so a single inch of water would eat about 26 years of that premium. And floods rarely stop at an inch.
The odds aren’t small where the maps say they’re high. Inside FEMA’s high-risk zones, a home has a 1 in 4 chance of flooding at least once over a 30-year mortgage. Outside those zones the chance drops. It doesn’t disappear.
Where it’s honestly a weaker buy: a condo several floors up, or a house high on a ridge with no basement. Even then, get a quote. The federal program now prices each home on its own risk, so a genuinely low-risk house tends to get a lower price.
### Why can’t you buy flood insurance when the river starts rising?
Because the federal policy’s coverage starts 30 days after the purchase date, and the rule doesn’t bend for a scary forecast. FloodSmart, FEMA’s consumer site, lists only four ways around the wait:
No wait if you buy the policy while making, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage.
No wait when you change your coverage at the policy’s renewal.
A one-day wait if your property was just mapped into a high-risk flood zone and you buy within 12 months of the map update.
A one-day wait for flooding caused or worsened by a wildfire on federal land, a rule that rarely touches St. Louis.
Notice what’s missing. No exception for a wet spring or a flash flood watch on your phone. River floods here usually come with days of warning, and none of those days buys coverage. The moment flood insurance feels urgent is the moment it can’t help with this flood.
Two more pieces of fine print change the plan. Building coverage and contents coverage are bought separately, with separate deductibles, so a policy on the house alone pays nothing for the couch. And the federal policy runs one year at a time, with a 30-day grace period to renew and pay in full. Let it lapse past that and you’re buying a new policy, with a new wait.
There’s a bigger version of the same risk. The program itself has to be reauthorized by Congress, and FEMA says that during a lapse in that authority it would stop selling and renewing policies, though it could still pay valid claims. One more reason the right day to buy is a dry one. Missouri’s Department of Commerce and Insurance takes policy and claim questions at 800-726-7390.
### Does St. Louis flood away from the Mississippi?
Yes, and that’s the part people miss. The Mississippi is the river everyone pictures, and its numbers are real: on August 1, 1993 it crested at St. Louis at 49.58 feet, the highest stage on record, and the 52-foot floodwall held it back with just over two feet to spare. That flood broke records set by the Mississippi in 1973 and the Missouri River in 1951. But the riverfront has a wall. A basement two miles from any river doesn’t.
The Meramec rewrote its own record book in the winter of 2015. On December 30, 2015, U.S. Geological Survey crews recorded 18 preliminary record-high flood measurements along the Meramec. Then it came within a foot of doing it again. At one lower-Meramec gauge the National Weather Service tracks, the two highest crests on record arrived 16 months apart: 44.11 feet on December 31, 2015, and 43.31 feet on May 3, 2017. Major flood stage at that gauge is 27 feet.
Then there’s the water that never touches a river. The July 2022 storm dropped 7.68 inches in six hours, a total the Weather Service puts at a 1-in-1,000 chance in any given year, and it issued a Flash Flood Emergency for parts of the city and county. Interstates went under. Homes took water. Crews ran water rescues. Creeks and storm channels that barely trickle most of the year can rise in an hour, and the federal policy counts that rain-driven water as a flood, as long as it covers two or more acres of normally dry land or two or more properties.
That’s why FloodSmart keeps repeating that from 2014 to 2024, nearly one-third of the program’s claims came from outside high-risk flood areas. Low risk is a map label, not a promise.
### What is not covered in flood insurance?
The biggest hole is the basement, and in a region where so many homes sit on one, that’s the clause to read first. The federal policy covers a basement’s working parts and almost nothing you’d call finished. FloodSmart’s guidance says these items qualify below grade only if they’re installed and connected to power:
Under building coverage: the furnace, water heater, cooling units, sump pump, and electrical outlets and switches.
Under contents coverage, if you bought it: a washer, dryer, freezer and the food in it, and window air conditioners.
What doesn’t qualify is the part people spent real money on. Finished walls and flooring. The sectional. The TV. The boxes of photographs. FloodSmart lists finished basements and home improvements, couches, televisions and keepsakes as not covered, and the policy defines a basement as any area with its floor below ground level on all sides, which can include the lowest level of some split-level houses.
Then there’s the list that applies on every floor. The federal policy won’t pay for cash, precious metals or valuable papers; cars and most self-propelled vehicles; anything outside the building, like landscaping, decks, patios, fences, septic systems and pools; temporary housing while repairs drag on; or lost business income. Valuables such as original art and furs are capped at $2,500. And the limits top out at $250,000 for the building and $100,000 for contents.
Two practical moves follow. Photograph the basement now, while it’s dry, and write down the make, model and serial number of the furnace, water heater and appliances, the same habit we walk through in what to do in the first days after fire damage. Second, anything you’d grieve losing doesn’t belong below grade.
### What type of water damage is not covered by insurance?
It depends on where the water came from, and that single question decides which policy pays, if any. Water that starts inside, like a burst supply line or a failed water heater, is generally a homeowners claim. Water that comes from outside and spreads, like rain pooling and pouring in or a creek over its banks, is flood. And water that comes up through the floor drain is a sewer or drain backup, which is the one that falls through the cracks.
Missouri’s insurance department says a standard homeowners or renters policy doesn’t protect against floods or sewer and drain backup. Sewer backup coverage is a separate add-on to the homeowners policy, usually called an endorsement, with its own limit and terms that vary by company. It isn’t flood insurance, and flood insurance isn’t it.
Here’s where it gets expensive. A flood policy pays for sewer backup only when a flood caused the backup, meaning a general condition of water covering two or more acres of normally dry land or two or more properties. A clogged line on an ordinary Tuesday isn’t that. Neither is a sump pump that can’t keep up during a hard rain if the street outside never actually flooded. Without a backup endorsement, that’s the water most likely to land in the gap between the two policies.
The other quiet exclusion is slow water. Groundwater that seeps through basement walls over days generally isn’t a flood claim, and seepage is a common homeowners exclusion too, which is why Missouri’s regulator tells people to check their exclusions for words like “water damage,” “seepage” and “runoff.” To see how an add-on like this moves your bill, our breakdown of what drives a St. Louis home insurance premium covers the homeowners side.
Same storm drop a limb on the garage? Here’s what tree removal costs.
### What does flood insurance cost in St. Louis?
In FEMA’s data for single-family homes insured on August 31, 2023, the median policy in the City of St. Louis cost $948 a year and the median in St. Louis County cost $988. FEMA also calculated what the same policies would cost at their full risk-based price. The gap is wide.
Source: FEMA, single-family policies in force August 31, 2023, yearly premiums. Why two prices? In 2021 the federal program switched to the pricing system known as Risk Rating 2.0, which prices each home on flood frequency, distance to water and the types of flooding that reach it, heavy rainfall included, plus its elevation and cost to rebuild. New policies got the new price on October 1, 2021, and the rest moved over at renewals starting April 1, 2022. For existing policyholders, the law says most rates can’t rise more than 18% a year, so plenty of older policies are still climbing toward their full price.
Here’s what that climb looks like. Picture a city policy priced at the $948 median whose full-risk price matches the $2,077 median. At the 18% maximum it rises to about $1,119 the next year, about $1,320 the year after, and needs five straight years of increases to reach full price. That’s a budget line, not a one-time bill. When an agent quotes an existing policy, ask for both numbers: this year’s premium and the full-risk price it’s heading toward.
Two more things about price. Every company that sells the federal policy offers the same rates, so shopping agents won’t change the federal price; shopping private insurers might. And if you’re buying a house that already carries a federal flood policy, the seller can assign it to you, and FEMA says any discount on it can transfer to the new owner. Ask before closing.
### What is the 50% rule in FEMA?
If repairing a home in a high-risk flood area would cost 50% or more of the building’s market value before the damage, the home is declared substantially damaged, and the whole structure has to be brought up to current floodplain rules before it’s rebuilt. Often that means elevating it. The same 50% test applies to big remodels and additions, which FEMA calls substantial improvement.
Three details catch people. First, all damage counts toward the 50%, whether it came from flooding, straight-line winds or a tornado. Second, FEMA doesn’t make the call and neither does your insurer. Your community’s building official or floodplain administrator does, and a community can set a stricter line, such as 45%. Third, the number that matters is the building’s value. Say the structure is worth $120,000. Repairs of $60,000 cross the line, and suddenly you’re pricing an elevation job instead of new drywall.
The federal policy has a built-in answer for this. Increased Cost of Compliance coverage pays up to $30,000 to elevate, relocate or demolish a home in a high-risk zone that floods have substantially or repeatedly damaged. It’s filed as its own claim, on top of the regular building claim, as long as the policy hasn’t hit its $250,000 limit. It only exists if you had the federal policy before the flood. Without it, the code upgrade comes out of pocket.
### Do you have to buy flood insurance with a mortgage in St. Louis?
Yes, if the home is in a high-risk zone and the mortgage is government-backed. FEMA’s maps mark high-risk areas with zones that start with A or V, and FloodSmart says a home there with a government-backed mortgage must carry flood insurance. Lenders typically collect it through escrow; our guide to how escrow and PMI work in St. Louis explains that account. Zones B, C and X are moderate to lower risk, and coverage isn’t federally required there, though a lender can still ask for it.
Check your own address before anyone tells you. The FEMA Flood Map Service Center lets you search by address and pull up the official flood map panel for it, zone included. Two cautions. A zone line on a map isn’t a wall in a storm, and the July 2022 flash flood didn’t check anyone’s zone first. And maps change; if your home is newly mapped into a high-risk zone, buying within 12 months of the update gets you the one-day wait instead of 30.
### Is private flood insurance an option in Missouri?
Yes. Private insurers write flood policies outside the federal program, and federal banking regulators have required regulated lenders to accept qualifying private flood policies since July 1, 2019. Because the company writes its own contract, the limits, waiting period, price and exclusions are whatever that company’s policy says. Prices, and the basement and sewer backup language, can differ a lot from the federal policy’s.
The federal policy charges the same rate through every seller and carries Increased Cost of Compliance coverage. A private policy is only as good as its own wording. Ask an agent to put a federal quote and a private quote side by side, and to show you in writing how each one handles basements, sewer backup and the start date.
This is general information, not advice for your situation. A licensed insurance agent can quote your address and read your actual policy with you, and our St. Louis Financial directory is a place to start.
Before the next wet season, get two numbers on paper: a flood quote for your address and the price of a sewer backup endorsement on the policy you already have. Home insurance agents around St. Louis can price both in a single conversation, and a dry Tuesday is the cheapest day to have it.
And if you’re the independent agent or a flood restoration contractor, the neighbor reading this is about to ask someone, or some AI, who to call, and being the name that comes up first is the whole game, so list your agency.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much is flood insurance in Missouri?
A.  In FEMA’s data for single-family homes insured on August 31, 2023, the median Missouri policy cost $827 a year, a little above the $786 national median. The median full risk-based price was $1,422, so many existing policies are still rising toward it, by up to 18% a year. Your own price depends on elevation, distance to water and what it would cost to rebuild.
### Q. Can anybody buy flood insurance?
A.  Almost anybody. Missouri’s insurance department says anyone can buy flood insurance if their community participates in the National Flood Insurance Program, regardless of where the home or business sits. Owners, renters and businesses all qualify, with or without a mortgage, in a high-risk zone or out of one. Private flood policies are another route.
### Q. How can I lower my flood insurance premium?
A.  Raise the deductible; FEMA says moving to $10,000 can cut premiums by up to 40%. Elevate the furnace, water heater and other covered equipment to at least the floor above the first floor, add proper flood openings to a crawlspace, and get an elevation certificate. Communities in FEMA’s Community Rating System earn 5% to 45% off every policy.
### Q. Can I write off flood insurance on my taxes?
A.  Not on the home you live in. IRS Publication 530 lists insurance, including fire and comprehensive coverage, among nondeductible payments. On a rental property, insurance is a deductible rental expense. Uninsured flood losses on a personal home are deductible only if tied to a federally declared disaster, after $100 and 10%-of-AGI reductions, per Publication 547.
### Q. How to estimate flood insurance?
A.  Start with FloodSmart’s online quote tool, which asks a few questions about the property and returns a personalized estimate, then confirm it with an agent. For a local yardstick, FEMA’s 2023 data put the median single-family policy at $948 in the City of St. Louis and $988 in St. Louis County. Elevation, distance to water and rebuild cost drive your real number.
### Q. Why would insurance deny a water damage claim?
A.  Usually because the water came from a source the policy excludes. Homeowners policies exclude flood, and sewer backup without an endorsement. Flood policies need a general flood covering two or more acres or properties; FEMA upheld one denial where owners couldn’t show that and missed the 60-day proof of loss. Here’s when to call a St. Louis attorney.
### Q. Is flood insurance always included?
A.  No. Flood is excluded from standard homeowners and renters policies and is always a separate purchase, from the federal program or a private insurer. Even inside a flood policy, building and contents coverage are separate, with separate deductibles. Lenders require it only for homes in high-risk zones with government-backed mortgages, and FEMA’s 2023 count found only 182 single-family homes in the whole city carrying a federal policy.
### Q. Can renters buy flood insurance in St. Louis?
A.  Yes. A renters policy excludes flood just like a homeowners policy does, but renters can buy a federal contents-only flood policy covering belongings up to $100,000, with the same 30-day wait. A landlord’s flood policy, if there is one, covers the building, not your things. Our guide to renters insurance in Missouri covers the rest of the policy.

## Missouri Car Sales Tax: What You Pay at the License Office, Private Sales, and the 30-Day Rule
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/missouri-car-sales-tax-at-the-license-office
Nobody billed you yet. You signed at the dealership, drove home on a paper tag, and the sales tax on that car is still unpaid, because in Missouri it usually isn’t the dealer’s to collect. You pay it yourself, at a license office, at the rate for the street where you live. And the clock started the day you bought.
Here’s the part nobody explains at the desk. Two neighbors buy the same $16,000 car from the same lot on the same afternoon. One lives in the city of St. Louis and owes $1,548.64 in sales tax. The other lives in unincorporated St. Louis County and owes $1,238.08. Same car. Same seller. A $310.56 difference set entirely by a home address, and neither of them pays a cent of it at the dealership.
That’s the system nobody covered in school. No office mails you a bill with the math worked out. You’re expected to know your rate, show up with the right papers, and pay before day 31, when a late penalty starts stacking. This is the license-office side of buying a car, one chapter of our St. Louis money guide. Still shopping? Our guide to buying a car from a St. Louis dealership handles doc fees and the finance office. This one starts after you sign.
### Do you pay sales tax at the dealership or DMV in Missouri?
At the license office, under the current process. Missouri tells buyers to title the vehicle and pay the state and local sales tax at any Missouri license office within 30 days of the purchase date, whether a dealer or a private seller sold it. The rate is 4.225% state plus the local rate where you live.
The Department of Revenue’s buying-a-vehicle page puts it plainly: you have 30 days from the date of purchase to title the car and pay the tax. State law backs that up from both ends. RSMo 144.020 places the vehicle sales tax on the person titling the car, not on the seller, and RSMo 144.070 has the owner pay it when applying for title, with the title held until it’s paid. No tax, no title. No title, no plates.
What most people call the DMV is, in Missouri, a license office. The offices are run by independent contractors under the Department of Revenue’s oversight. Any of them can take your title application, and the license office locator shows the ones near you. Mailing it to the Motor Vehicle Bureau in Jefferson City also works, though the mail eats into your 30 days.
Bring the whole stack the first time. For a car getting new plates, the Department’s list comes down to this:
The title signed over to you, or the Manufacturer’s Statement of Origin on a brand-new car.
A signed Application for Missouri Title and License, Form 108.
A safety inspection, generally no more than 60 days old. Cars within their first ten model years and under 150,000 miles are exempt.
An emissions inspection if you live in the city or St. Louis County. Our guide to Missouri car inspections in St. Louis covers what fails.
Proof of insurance.
Last year’s paid personal property tax receipt, or a statement of non-assessment. Here’s how to get the personal property tax receipt or waiver.
Any bill of sale or Notice of Sale that supports a tax credit, covered below.
You can pay with cash, a check, a money order or a card. Cards carry a vendor convenience fee of 2.0% plus $0.25 per transaction, so putting a $1,238 tax payment on plastic adds about $25.
### Why does your address set the rate instead of the dealer’s?
Because Missouri law ties it to you. RSMo 144.069 imposes the sales tax on a titled vehicle at the rate in effect at the owner’s address, and has the Department of Revenue collect any local sales taxes based on that address too. The dealership’s ZIP code doesn’t enter into it. Neither does the private seller’s. The Department’s refund form adds a detail worth knowing before you sign anything: taxes are assessed on the address written on the title assignment at the time of purchase.
So the real number lives on a document most buyers never see, the Department’s Motor Vehicle Sales Tax Rate Chart. It’s reissued for each three-month period, it lists a local rate for every county, city and district that taxes vehicles, and that local rate is added to the state’s 4.225%. On the current chart, two St. Louis lines matter most:
City of St. Louis: 5.454% local, for 9.679% combined.
St. Louis County, for addresses outside city limits: 3.513% local, for 7.738% combined.
That 1.941-point gap is what separated the two neighbors above. Inside the county it can widen, because cities stack their own tax on top: one municipal line on the current chart lists 7.263% local on Missouri-dealer sales, or 11.488% combined. Live in an incorporated city? The county number isn’t yours.
The current chart also shows something new for unincorporated county addresses. Several fire-district areas, listed separately and marked new or increased, now carry 4.513% local instead of 3.513%. Here’s the twist: the extra point appears only on the Missouri-dealer line. For the same address, when the car came from anyone else, a private seller or an out-of-state dealer, the line still reads 3.513%.
Why two lines? Under RSMo 32.087, most local governments had to ask voters about taxing vehicles bought from a source other than a licensed Missouri dealer, and places that skipped that vote by the November 2022 election had to stop applying their local sales tax to those purchases.
The cleanest way to get your own number is the Department’s motor vehicle tax calculator. Enter your street address, ZIP code and net price, say whether a Missouri dealer sold the car, and it estimates the state and local tax, not counting title fees or penalties. The rate at a store register is a separate question, answered in our guide to the St. Louis sales tax rate.
### How much tax is due on a $5,000 or $16,000 car in St. Louis?
Multiply the net price by the state rate plus your local rate. Net price means the purchase price minus any trade-in allowance or rebate. Here are two common price points at the current chart’s rates, no trade-in:
Here’s the math once, so you can check any quote. A $16,000 car titled at a county address outside city limits: $16,000 times 4.225% is $676.00 for the state, $16,000 times 3.513% is $562.08 for the county, and together that’s $1,238.08. In the city, the local share is $16,000 times 5.454%, or $872.64, for $1,548.64 in all. If the county address sits in one of those fire-district areas and a Missouri dealer sold the car, the local share becomes $722.08 and the total $1,398.08.
Then add $17.50 for the title, an $8.50 fee plus $9 for processing. Picture a nurse in Bevo Mill who buys a $5,000 commuter car from a coworker. She walks into the license office owing $483.95 in tax and $17.50 for the title, before plates. If she walks in on day 45 instead of day 25, add a $25 penalty.
### What happens if you miss the 30-day window?
A penalty lands on day 31, and it grows. Under RSMo 301.190 and the Department’s titling page, the late title penalty is $25 on the 31st day after purchase and another $25 for every 30 days after that, capped at $200. The statute lets the director extend the deadline or waive the penalty for good cause. That’s a request you make, not a plan.
The penalty is the small part. The tag is the bigger trap. A Missouri temporary permit runs 30 days from the purchase date, costs $5 plus a $9 processing fee at a license office, and the Department allows only one per vehicle. When it expires, the car has no valid tag until the title work is finished.
And the state will know a sale happened. Private sellers must report it within 30 days on a Notice of Sale or Bill of Sale showing the date and net price. Skipping it is an infraction with a fine up to $200, or a class C misdemeanor up to $300 if it was meant to help the buyer dodge titling or fees.
Most late titles are a lienholder slow to release a title or a buyer who assumed somebody else had it handled. If paperwork is stuck, the Department’s motor vehicle line is 573-526-3669. Call before day 30.
New plates, first dent? Here’s how to read a body shop estimate.
### Can selling your old car yourself still lower the tax?
Yes. RSMo 144.025 gives a private sale the same tax treatment as a trade-in, as long as you sell the old vehicle within 180 days before or after you buy the next one. The actual sale price comes off the new car’s price before state and local tax is figured. A trade-in isn’t the only way to get the break.
Run it on the $16,000 car. Say you sold your old sedan to a neighbor for $6,000 two months before buying. Bring that bill of sale to the license office and you’re taxed on $10,000, not $16,000. At the county rate outside city limits, that’s $773.80 instead of $1,238.08, a $464.28 difference that stays on the counter without the paperwork.
Sold the old car after you’d already titled the new one? The window still covers you. The Department’s Form 426 lists a 180-day credit refund for that case, filed with your title receipt and the signed Bill of Sale or Notice of Sale. The same form handles a local rate charged in error.
The details that trip people up, from the Department’s titling manual:
The window runs both ways: 180 days before or 180 days after the date the old vehicle is sold.
It doesn’t have to be like for like. Sell a boat and buy a car, or the reverse, and the credit still applies.
At least one owner’s name has to match between the vehicle sold and the one being titled.
The bill of sale or Notice of Sale doesn’t need a notary.
More than one sale can count. Since a December 2019 change to the statute, the sale prices of one or more vehicles, boats or trailers sold inside the window can come off the new purchase, as long as every bill of sale is presented at titling.
A totaled car works much the same way: the insurance settlement plus your deductible can come off a replacement bought within 180 days of the insurer’s payment, with a statement from the insurer.
### Do family gifts and private sales get taxed the same way?
No. A real gift isn’t taxed at all, and a private sale is taxed like any other purchase. The Department’s instructions for sellers say the new owner of a gifted vehicle won’t pay state or local tax, as long as the paperwork shows it’s a gift:
The giver writes GIFT in the sale price area of the title. The Department specifically says not to use a sale price of $1.
The giver signs a General Affidavit, Form 768, or a written statement that the vehicle was a gift. Neither needs a notary.
The gift still gets reported to the Department within 30 days on a Notice of Sale or Bill of Sale.
The giver must have paid their own tax on the vehicle for the gift to pass tax-free.
Picture a grandmother in Carondelet handing her 12-year-old hatchback to a grandson. Done as a gift, he pays title and plate fees and no sales tax. Done as a $1 sale, it’s neither a clean gift nor an honest sale, and the titling manual says the Department can ask for more documentation any time a price looks questionable. When a price is undisclosed or unconvincing, RSMo 144.070 lets the director set it by appraisal.
A private sale from a neighbor, a coworker or an online listing carries the same 4.225% state rate plus your local rate, all paid at the license office. Only the local line changes, since the seller isn’t a licensed Missouri dealer, and for city addresses and the county’s base line, the two match. Our checklist for checking a used car before buying covers the car itself, and a vehicle won at a public auto auction runs on the same 30-day clock.
### What if you bought the car outside Missouri?
You still pay Missouri tax when you title it here, minus what you already paid. The Department’s titling FAQ says tax paid to another state is credited toward the Missouri amount, and if that state’s tax was lower, you’re assessed the difference. Bring proof. If the out-of-state title doesn’t show the tax paid, you’ll need a tax receipt from that state.
A trade-in at an out-of-state dealer needs proof too, such as a copy of the trade-in title or an invoice on the dealership’s letterhead. Moving here with a car you already own is a different case. New residents get 30 days from becoming a Missouri resident to title, and if the vehicle was titled in your name in another state for more than 90 days, no Missouri sales tax is assessed.
### How much do title, plates and registration add?
Far less than the tax, but they add up. Every title carries the $8.50 title fee and the $9 title processing fee. Plates are priced by taxable horsepower, the figure printed on your title, under the Department’s fee chart for passenger vehicles:
Each registration adds a processing fee, $9 for one year or $18 for two. Moving plates over from a car you sold or traded costs a $2 transfer fee, and they can ride on the new car for 30 days before that transfer is due.
So the $16,000 car at a county address outside city limits, titled on time with new one-year plates in the 24-to-35 bracket, comes to $1,238.08 in tax, $17.50 for the title and $33.25 for plates and processing. That’s $1,288.83 at the counter.
Then comes the bill nobody mentions at the counter. The car is now personal property, so it will show up on your St. Louis County personal property tax bill, or the city’s. Same car, second tax.
### What is changing about how Missouri collects vehicle sales tax?
Dealer sales are moving to point-of-sale collection, just not yet. Senate Bill 28 took effect August 28, 2025, and the Department of Revenue said at the time that once the second phase of its new FUSION computer system is running, buyers purchasing through a dealership will pay the sales tax at the point of sale. Temporary tags go away. You’d get a paper copy of your new plate at purchase, and the metal plate, with the same number, comes by mail.
That release projected late 2026 or early 2027. The Department’s dealer newsletter now puts the FUSION launch in mid-February 2027. State law already anticipates the switch: RSMo 144.070 says licensed dealers will collect and remit the tax once a modernized, integrated system is in place. Until it’s live, the Department says the current process stays in effect for dealer and private purchases alike.
Two things won’t change. Private-party buyers will still pay at a license office. And the Department has told buyers to be ready to pay the full sales tax at the time of a dealer purchase, so money you once had 30 days to gather will be due the day you sign.
This is general information, not tax or legal advice for your situation. A CPA or enrolled agent can apply these rules to your own purchase, an attorney can untangle a stuck title or an estate transfer, and our St. Louis Automotive directory is a place to start.
Before you sign anywhere, run your street address through the DOR calculator so you know the tax you’ll owe at the license office, then compare out-the-door prices at car dealerships around St. Louis with that number already in hand.
And if you run a dealership or a title and tag service, the buyer reading this is about to ask who can walk them through the paperwork, and when a neighbor (or the AI they ask) wants that help, the shop named first gets the call, so list your dealership where they’re looking.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the sales tax rate for cars in St. Louis county?
A.  It depends on your address. On the Department of Revenue’s current vehicle chart, county addresses outside city limits carry 3.513% local plus the state’s 4.225%, or 7.738% combined. Some fire-district areas show 4.513% local on Missouri-dealer sales, and cities inside the county add their own taxes. The city of St. Louis runs 9.679%.
### Q. How much is tax and title on a car in Missouri?
A.  Tax is 4.225% state plus your local rate, on the price after any trade-in or rebate. The title adds an $8.50 fee and a $9 processing fee. A $16,000 car at a St. Louis County address outside city limits comes to $1,255.58 before plates. In the city of St. Louis, it’s $1,566.14.
### Q. How much do plates and registration cost in Missouri?
A.  It depends on the taxable horsepower printed on your title. One-year registration for a passenger vehicle runs from $18.25 for under 12 horsepower or an electric vehicle to $51.25 for 72 and up, plus a $9 processing fee. Two years costs double, with an $18 processing fee.
### Q. How to avoid sales tax on a car in Missouri?
A.  You can’t skip it, but legal rules shrink it. A trade-in or rebate lowers the taxable price, and so does selling your old vehicle yourself within 180 days before or after buying. A genuine gift from someone who paid tax on the car isn’t taxed. A made-up low price can bring an appraisal instead.
### Q. What are the recent changes to the Missouri vehicle sales tax law?
A.  Senate Bill 28, effective August 28, 2025, moves sales tax collection to the dealership for dealer sales and ends temporary tags once the Department of Revenue’s FUSION system is running. Its dealer newsletter puts that in mid-February 2027. Private-sale buyers will still pay at a license office, and until launch, everyone does.
### Q. Do you pay sales tax on vehicles in Missouri?
A.  Yes. Missouri taxes the person titling a vehicle at 4.225% state plus the local rate where the owner lives, on the price after any trade-in or rebate. Dealer and private sales alike are paid at a license office within 30 days. A gift from someone who already paid tax on it is the main exception.
### Q. How much sales tax will I pay on a $5,000 car in Missouri?
A.  The state share is $211.25. At a St. Louis County address outside city limits, with 3.513% local, the total is $386.90. In the city of St. Louis, with 5.454% local, it’s $483.95. Subtract any trade-in or qualifying sale of your old car first, then add $17.50 in title fees.
### Q. What is the sales tax on a $16,000 car?
A.  In Missouri, the state share is $676.00. At a St. Louis County address outside city limits, the total is $1,238.08; in the city of St. Louis, it’s $1,548.64. Sell your old car for $6,000 within 180 days and the county figure drops to $773.80, because only $10,000 is taxed.

## Lease vs Buy a Car: The Real Math, Mileage Traps, and When Gap Insurance Is Worth It
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/lease-vs-buy-a-car-and-gap-insurance
What is that lower lease payment actually buying you? Not a car. It buys the right to drive through the most expensive stretch of that car’s life, the first few years, when its value usually falls fastest, plus a finance charge written as a tiny decimal that federal rules won’t let the leasing company call an annual percentage rate. And if the car is totaled in month eight, the insurance check and what you still owe turn out to be two different numbers. Somebody covers the difference. Unless you planned for it, that’s you.
None of this is hidden. It’s in the federal lease disclosure the dealer slides across the desk, written in words nobody taught us in school: capitalized cost, residual value, rent charge. The finance office uses them all day. You see them once every few years, after a long test drive. That’s the house edge, and it has nothing to do with being bad at money.
Below: what a lease payment is made of, one lease-versus-buy example with the math shown, the Missouri tax rules that shift it, and the gap decision. Our guide to a credit union versus bank auto loan in St. Louis covers the basics of owing more than a car is worth. This goes further. The St. Louis money guide has the rest of the series.
### What are the disadvantages of a lease car?
You build no ownership. Lease payments cover the car’s steepest years of value loss plus a rent charge, and unless you buy it at the end, you hand it back with no equity. You also accept a mileage cap, charges for wear beyond the lessor’s standard, and an early termination bill that can reach several thousand dollars.
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau puts the core trade bluntly: leasing is like renting, and your payments don’t go toward owning the car unless the lease includes an option to buy it.
Mileage. Most leases cap you at 10,000 to 15,000 miles a year, the CFPB says, and charge for every mile over.
Wear. The leasing company usually decides what counts as excessive. Federal rules require its standards to be in the lease and to be reasonable, which isn’t the same as lenient.
Getting out early. You can’t simply return the car and stop paying. Federal Regulation M requires a consumer vehicle lease to warn that ending it early may cost a substantial charge, possibly several thousand dollars.
A payment that never ends. Lease, turn in, lease again.
The early-months hole. For a while, the car is usually worth less than it would cost to end the lease. That’s what gap coverage is for.
In fairness, leases have real upsides: a lower payment for the same car, no selling or trade-in haggling, and in a closed-end lease, if the car ends up worth less than the lessor predicted, that’s the lessor’s loss. You still owe excess wear and mileage charges. The trouble starts when the monthly payment is the only number anyone discusses.
### What are you actually paying for in a lease payment?
Two things: the value the car loses while you drive it, and a rent charge for the money tied up in it. Federal rules require your lease disclosure to show the four terms that set both.
Capitalized cost: the car’s price inside the lease, plus anything rolled in. Negotiate it like a sale price.
Capitalized cost reduction: your down payment, trade-in credit or rebate.
Residual value: the lessor’s forecast of what the car is worth at the end.
Rent charge: the lease version of interest.
Depreciation is plain division: capitalized cost minus residual, spread over the months. The rent charge is where the fine print lives. The Federal Reserve’s leasing guide says it’s usually set with a money factor, a decimal like 0.0025, multiplied by the capitalized cost plus the residual, and that the money factor typically isn’t disclosed to you. Regulation M adds a twist: a lessor that quotes a rate at all may not call it an “annual percentage rate.”
So translate it yourself. Multiply the money factor by 2,400 for a close stand-in for an APR, the yearly interest rate you’d compare on a loan. A money factor of 0.0025 is about 6%. One of 0.0040 is about 9.6%. Why 2,400? The formula adds the starting and ending values, which is twice the average amount financed, so you divide out that 2 and the 12 months, then multiply by 100 for a percentage: 2 x 12 x 100. In the example below, the exact rate behind 0.0025 comes to about 6.03%.
Get the money factor in writing and hold the result next to a bank or credit union loan rate on the same car. A few points higher means you’re paying for that friendly monthly number in interest. These disclosure rules cover consumer leases with a total contractual obligation up to $73,400, a ceiling adjusted each year.
### Is it cheaper to lease or buy the same car?
Over three years, it’s closer than most people expect. Over six, buying pulls far ahead, if you keep the car. Here’s an illustrative example in round numbers, before taxes and fees.
The car has a $40,000 negotiated price. The lease runs 36 months with nothing down, a $24,000 residual and a money factor of 0.0025, about 6%. The loan is $40,000 at 6% APR for 60 months.
The lease math: $16,000 of depreciation ($40,000 minus $24,000) divided by 36 is $444.44. The rent charge is 0.0025 x ($40,000 + $24,000), or $160. Together that’s $604.44 a month, which over the term is $16,000 for the value you used plus $5,760 in rent charges.
The buyer pays $773.31 a month and, after 36 payments, still owes about $17,448. If the car is worth the $24,000 the lessor predicted, the buyer could sell it, clear the loan and keep about $6,552. Take that from $27,839 in payments and three years cost about $21,287. Within $500 of the lease.
That’s what nobody explains at the desk. A fairly priced lease isn’t a trick. It charges the same depreciation and roughly the same interest a loan would, sliced smaller because you pay only for the part you use. The real differences are who carries the risk that the residual guess is wrong, and what happens after month 36.
Stretch it to six years. Two back-to-back leases on the same terms cost $43,520 and leave you with no car. The buyer pays the loan off at month 60, about $46,399 in all. Say the car is then worth $15,000. Net cost: about $31,399, roughly $12,100 less than leasing, and the difference grows every month the paid-off car stays on the road. The buyer does pay for the repairs that come with age.
### What do mileage caps, wear charges and early exits really cost?
More than the payment suggests. Federal rules make the lessor disclose the excess-mileage charge, or how it’s figured, before you sign. A 36-month lease at 12,000 miles a year allows 36,000. A 25-mile commute each way across the metro, five days a week for 50 weeks, is 12,500 miles a year before a single weekend errand. Drive 15,000 a year and you return the car 9,000 miles over. At an illustrative 25 cents a mile, that’s $2,250 on turn-in day.
Buying miles up front can cost less. The Federal Reserve’s leasing guide walks through a case where a higher mileage allowance negotiated at signing beat paying the overage at turn-in, because the extra miles were priced into a lower residual. Guess high on your driving.
Wear works the same way. Regulation M requires the lease to warn that you may be charged for excessive wear based on the lessor’s standards for normal use. Read those standards at signing, not the week before turn-in. Kids, a dog and a tight garage all show up at inspection. Many lessors also charge a disposition fee at return to cover part of the cost of cleaning, inspecting and selling the car, while others build it into the payment. Regulation M requires charges like that to be itemized.
Leaving early costs the most. The Federal Reserve says the early termination charge is typically what you still owe on the lease minus the amount credited for the car, often a wholesale value, plus fees. Early on, the car has usually lost value faster than your payments covered, so the charge is biggest then. A baby, a job in another state, a layoff: none of them stop the meter.
Lease turn-in day is payday for detailers. How St. Louis detailers build a business
### How does Missouri tax a leased car?
Differently from a car you buy. Buy one, and Missouri collects 4.225% state sales tax plus your local sales tax on the purchase price, less any trade-in allowance, when you title the car at a license office within 30 days. On a $40,000 car with no trade-in, the state portion alone is $1,690, all at once. Our guide to Missouri car sales tax at the license office covers that visit.
Leases run on a different track. Missouri law lets an approved leasing company either pay the tax when it registers the car or collect sales tax on each lease payment while the car is based here. On the payment route, a 2024 Department of Revenue letter ruling says each payment is taxed at the rate where the lessee is located when it’s made, and the payments stop being subject to Missouri’s motor vehicle sales tax once the lessee moves out of state. That ruling answered one taxpayer, but it shows how the department reads the law.
On our example lease, $21,760 in payments at the same 4.225% state rate is about $919, paid a little at a time, against $1,690 up front to buy. That’s three years of driving, not a car you keep, but it shows the shape. Local tax stacks on both. If the lessor paid at registration instead, ask how that cost reaches you.
Personal property tax trips up lessees at plate renewal. Cars here are taxed every year as personal property, and on a lease the leasing company holds the title. The Department of Revenue says that to register or renew a leased vehicle, the paid personal property tax receipt must be in the leasing company’s name. Ask at signing how the lessor handles that tax and whether it bills you, then keep its receipt with your renewal notice. Our guide to the St. Louis County personal property tax covers the bill itself.
Buying the car at lease end is a purchase, and titling a purchase is when Missouri collects sales tax. Ask the license office how your buyout will be taxed before you sign.
### What happens if a leased or financed car is totaled in month eight?
Your insurer pays what the car was worth, not what you owe. The CFPB says standard auto insurance only pays up to the value of your vehicle. Any balance above that is still yours, on a car headed for salvage.
Run month eight on our example. The $40,000 loan has about $35,330 left after eight payments. Say the insurer values the car at $32,000 and your deductible is $500. The lender gets $31,500 and you still owe about $3,830. Gap would typically cover the roughly $3,330 between balance and value, but the Federal Reserve notes that in most cases it doesn’t cover your deductible.
The lease is worse. Eight payments into our zero-down lease, ending it costs roughly $36,700, depending on how the lessor figures it, so the same $32,000 valuation leaves a hole of about $4,700. The Federal Reserve’s own illustration shows the pattern: on a $22,000 vehicle in month one, a $2,700 gap on the lease against $1,000 on a loan with more money down.
The good news: the Federal Reserve says many leases include gap coverage as a standard feature at no separate charge. Read yours before paying for gap twice.
Know what gap won’t touch. The same guide lists your down payment or capitalized cost reduction, past-due payments, and amounts like personal property taxes or parking tickets. Rolled-in debt digs the hole deeper, too. Put $5,000 of old balance into our example and month eight shows about $39,750 owed on that same $32,000 car, a gap near $7,750.
### Gap insurance or a gap waiver: which one are you buying, and from whom?
Three places sell it, and the product changes with the seller. From your auto insurer, gap is an add-on that sits on top of your collision and comprehensive coverage. From a dealer or lender, it’s a contract attached to the loan or lease, sometimes called a waiver or an addendum. Missouri’s statute lumps them together as a “deficiency waiver addendum, guaranteed asset protection, or a similar product.”
Your auto insurer. The CFPB says your own insurer may offer GAP, so price it there first. Not every insurer sells it.
Your lender. Some direct lenders offer it too, per the CFPB, so ask the bank or credit union making the loan.
The dealer’s finance office. It’s one of several optional add-ons a dealer will likely offer. Told it’s required for financing? Ask where the contract says so. Our guide to what the finance office is selling you covers the rest of that menu.
Missouri adds protections the national explainers skip. Under section 408.380 of state law, GAP or a deficiency waiver sold as part of a loan with collateral needs your written consent, with a reasonable cost disclosed in the loan contract. You can cancel within 15 days of buying it for a complete refund, a right that must be disclosed in 10-point type. If the product ends before the loan’s scheduled maturity, the refund is figured pro rata, in proportion to the time left. The CFPB lists selling, refinancing and paying off early as times a refund may be owed.
One caution. Dealer-arranged financing is typically a retail installment contract, which Missouri governs under a separate motor vehicle time sales law, so don’t assume section 408.380 applies word for word. Your contract’s cancellation section should spell out the refund math. If a refund never arrives, gap sold by an insurer goes to the Missouri Department of Commerce and Insurance, which takes complaints about insurers and agents. Gap that came with your loan is a lender matter, and the CFPB takes complaints about auto loans.
### When does a lease make sense, and when is it a trap?
A lease fits when your miles are predictable and under the cap, you want a newer car every few years and accept a payment that never goes away, and you’d rather hand the residual gamble to the lessor. That’s a fair price for predictability. It turns into a trap when:
Your miles are unpredictable, or a new job could double your commute.
You might need out early: a move, a baby, shaky work.
You’re rolling negative equity into the lease. That old balance lands in the capitalized cost and raises the payment.
The monthly payment is the only number on the table.
You keep cars six years or longer.
Either way, a car payment is a monthly obligation lenders see when you apply for a mortgage, and our look at why it’s easier to buy a car than a house explains how it weighs on a home loan. Before you sign anything, get the capitalized cost, the money factor, the per-mile charge and every add-on price in writing. Then sleep on it. Nothing about a lease improves at nine o’clock at night in a finance office.
This is general information, not advice for your situation. A licensed insurance agent can price gap against your own policy, a loan officer can quote the financing side, and our St. Louis automotive directory is a place to start.
Shopping your next car payment? Line up a loan quote and a gap quote before you visit a lot, then compare auto lenders around St. Louis against whatever the finance office slides across the desk.
And if you’re the dealer, credit union or insurance agent those families are comparing, being the name a St. Louis neighbor, or the AI they ask, hears first is the whole game, so list your business where they look.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it better to lease a car for 24 or 36 months?
A.  Neither wins on its face. A 24-month lease squeezes the car’s fastest-falling stretch of value into fewer payments, so the monthly number usually runs higher. A 36-month lease spreads that depreciation out and lowers the payment, but adds a year of mileage and wear exposure. Compare total cost: everything due at signing plus all payments, divided by the months you drive.
### Q. Can you customize a leased car?
A.  Check the lease first, because the leasing company owns the car. Add-ons you can remove before turn-in carry less risk. Permanent changes are the lessor’s call, and anything outside its wear-and-use standards, which Regulation M requires it to disclose, can turn into a charge at inspection. When in doubt, ask in writing first.
### Q. How does gap insurance work if a car is totaled?
A.  Your insurer declares a total loss and pays the car’s value, minus your deductible, toward the loan or lease. Gap then covers the difference between that value and the remaining balance. Per the Federal Reserve’s leasing guide, it typically won’t pay your deductible, past-due payments or your down payment.
### Q. Is gap insurance really worth it?
A.  It earns its price when the hole is big and you couldn’t cover it from savings: little or nothing down, a long loan, rolled-in negative equity, or a lease without gap built in. The hole shrinks each month as you pay down the balance, so gap is worth the most at the start.
### Q. When not to get gap insurance?
A.  It has little to do when you owe less than the car is worth from day one, thanks to a big down payment or a short loan, or when you pay cash. Check your lease, too, since the Federal Reserve says many include gap at no separate charge. Once your balance drops below the car’s value, gap has nothing left to pay.
### Q. Can I purchase just gap insurance by itself?
A.  Not as a replacement for car insurance. Gap only fills the difference between a total-loss payout and your balance, so it rides on top of collision and comprehensive coverage. You can buy it apart from the car deal, though: the CFPB says your own insurer may offer it, some direct lenders sell it, and you can decline the dealer’s version.
### Q. Can I get a gap insurance refund?
A.  In many cases, yes. The CFPB says a refund may be owed if you sell, refinance or pay off the loan early. For GAP sold with a secured loan, Missouri’s section 408.380 requires a complete refund if you cancel within 15 days and a pro rata refund if the product ends before the loan’s scheduled maturity.
### Q. Should I keep gap insurance after I paid off my car?
A.  There’s little reason to. With the loan paid off, there’s no balance for gap to cover. If it’s an add-on to your auto policy, ask your insurer to remove it. If you bought it as a contract with the loan, ask the provider whether any unused portion is refundable. The CFPB says you can cancel optional add-ons at any time.

## How to Budget on a St. Louis Paycheck: 50/30/20, Real Local Costs and an Emergency Fund That Fits
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-budget-on-a-st-louis-paycheck
First paycheck in St. Louis? Then you’ve probably met the budget template, the free one from the internet with tidy rows for rent, utilities, groceries, phone and fun. Picture someone who moves here for a new job, rents a one-bedroom in Bevo Mill, and fills in every row on a Sunday night. It balances. There’s even money left for savings, and for about eight months it feels like winning.
Then the calendar turns, and two local bills surface that the template never had a row for. The first is the City of St. Louis earnings tax, 1% of everything a City resident earns, wherever the employer sits. Her company’s only office is out in the county, so nothing came out of her checks, and the City still expects a return and payment by April 15. The second shows up in November: a personal property tax bill on the car she owned on January 1, due December 31.
Neither one means she’s bad with money. Nobody teaches this in school, the offices that mail these bills don’t explain them, and a template built for the whole country can’t know that St. Louis taxes your paycheck and your car on its own calendar. So here’s the budget built the local way, from take-home pay, with both lines baked in. It’s one stop in our St. Louis money guide, and every number links to the agency behind it.
### How should a beginner budget?
Start with take-home pay, the amount that actually lands in your account, not your salary. List every fixed bill, turn once-a-year bills into monthly set-asides, and give each leftover dollar a job: needs, wants, or savings and debt. Track one full month, then adjust. In St. Louis, add two lines most templates skip: the City earnings tax and the yearly tax on your car.
Why take-home? Because gross pay is a rumor. Federal and Missouri income tax, Social Security and Medicare, health premiums, retirement and, for many people, the City’s 1% leave before you see a dime. Budget from the offer letter and you’re spending money that was never yours. If the stub is a mystery, our guide to the Missouri W-4 and your pay stub walks it line by line.
The pieces are the same for everybody. Income. Fixed bills. Spending that moves around. Savings and debt payoff. And the irregular stuff that wrecks whatever month it lands in. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s free Your Money, Your Goals toolkit has a worksheet for each, from a spending tracker to a bill calendar, and suggests tracking a whole month, long enough for every paycheck and bill to show up.
The bill calendar is the sleeper. Mark each payment day early, at least seven days ahead for anything you mail, then line those dates up against your paydays. Most budgets don’t fail on the total. They fail on timing, when rent is due on the 1st and the check lands on the 5th.
### What does a realistic St. Louis monthly budget look like?
Something close to this, if you rent a one-bedroom and bring home $3,600 a month, about $1,660 every other payday. The figures are illustrative, but the rent line isn’t a guess. It’s HUD’s fiscal year 2027 fair market rent for a one-bedroom across the St. Louis metro: $1,104 a month.
HUD sets that figure at the 40th percentile, so about 40% of standard-quality rentals taken by recent movers went for less. And it’s gross rent, meaning it already includes tenant-paid utilities except phone, cable and internet, per HUD’s own definition. The year before, the same figure was $995. That’s a $109-a-month jump in one update, and it’s why last year’s budget advice can already be stale.
Health insurance and retirement aren’t listed because they came out before the deposit. Phone and internet get their own row because HUD’s rent figure leaves them out. The $34 car-tax line is the City math on a $15,000 car. And the forgot-it line is real, because every budget misses something the first month.
How does that compare with actual households? The Bureau of Labor Statistics’ latest St. Louis consumer spending release, covering 2023-24, found the average metro household spent $77,694 a year. Housing took 29.1%, well under the national 33.2%. Transportation took 17.3%, a shade above the nation’s 17.0%, and households here kept 2.1 vehicles to the country’s 1.9. Housing is gentler here than nationally. The car is where St. Louis money leaks, and that’s exactly the template’s blind spot. Our look at the real cost of living in St. Louis and our guide to how much rent you can afford cover the housing side.
### Which St. Louis bills does a budget template forget?
Two, mostly: the City of St. Louis earnings tax, when your employer isn’t withholding it, and the yearly personal property tax on your car. Both are real money. Both run on a schedule nobody explains. Both are easy once they become a monthly line.
Start with the earnings tax.
