The City’s individual earnings tax page says the 1% is owed by residents of the City regardless of where their employer is located, and by people who work for businesses in the City, wherever they live. If your employer withholds it, it’s already out of your take-home. The trap is the City resident whose job sits outside City limits, because the City holds the taxpayer responsible whether or not the employer withheld. Form E-1 is due April 15, individuals get no extension, and late tax draws a 5% penalty per month, up to 25%, plus 1% a month in interest.
The fix is a set-aside. On $60,000 of wages the 1% is $600 a year, or $50 a month moved to savings on payday. Not sure yours is withheld? Call the Collector’s earnings tax office at (314) 622-4101 with your W-2. Our guide to the St. Louis earnings tax covers commuter refunds and the rest.
Now the car. The City’s personal property page lays out the cycle: declaration forms go out in January and are due April 1, bills are mailed in November, and payment is due by December 31. Vehicles are assessed at one-third of their value, and the City prints the example itself: $15,000 of value is $5,000 assessed. Multiply by the City’s 2025 personal property rate of $8.1122 per $100 and that car owes $405.61 for the year. Divide by 12 and you get the $34 line in the table. The County bills at its own rates, and our guide to personal property tax in the County and the City runs that math.
Skip the set-aside and the bill finds you anyway, in December. It has teeth, too: the Department of Revenue won’t renew your plates without a paid receipt or a statement of non-assessment, the waiver new residents get. That’s the ambush. A newcomer gets the waiver, so there’s no bill the first year. It starts the year after, right when the budget finally felt settled.
### Does the 50/30/20 rule work on a St. Louis paycheck?
Often, yes, as a starting check. The rule splits after-tax pay three ways: 50% for needs, 30% for wants, and 20% for savings and debt payments beyond the minimums. On $3,600 that’s $1,800, $1,080 and $720. It breaks in two predictable places.
The first is housing. At $3,600 take-home, the metro’s $1,104 one-bedroom figure is 31% of pay. Workable. At $2,800, the same apartment eats 39%, which leaves about $300 of the needs half for groceries, the car, the phone and every minimum payment combined. That doesn’t fit, and it isn’t a character flaw. The wants bucket shrinks until the math closes.
The second is debt. The average rate on bank credit card accounts that were charged interest was 22.36% in August 2026, according to the Federal Reserve’s consumer credit report. At that price, the 20% bucket should lean hard toward the card. A budget that dutifully saves 20% while a balance compounds at 22% balances on paper and loses in real life.
The illustrative budget above lands near 58/22/20, and that’s a healthy budget. Rent wasn’t the problem. The car, the student loan and the yearly car tax were, which is the usual story in a metro where the average household keeps more than two vehicles. Treat 50/30/20 like a check-engine light. It tells you where to look. It doesn’t grade you.
Got a kid in club soccer? Here’s what that budget line really costs.
### What is zero-based budgeting, and when does it beat 50/30/20?
Zero-based budgeting means income minus every planned dollar equals zero. Not zero in the bank. Zero unassigned. Savings, the car-tax set-aside and the forgot-it line all count as assignments, so the month is spoken for before it starts.
It beats percentage rules in three spots. When money is tight, because a percentage can’t say which bill to pay first and a priority list can. When income moves with tips, commissions or a side gig, because you budget the month you’re actually in. And during debt payoff, because every spare dollar gets aimed at a balance on purpose.
On payday, write the deposit at the top. List what must be paid before the next payday, in order: housing, utilities, food, transportation, minimum payments. Then the set-asides, savings and wants, until the remainder hits zero. The CFPB’s cash flow budget applies a similar idea week by week, and the toolkit says it matters even more when income is irregular or seasonal.
One quirk helps. Paid every two weeks? That’s 26 checks a year, so two months bring a third. Build the budget on two checks a month and give each extra one a job in advance. In the illustration, a single third check of about $1,660 would cover the CFPB’s $1,000 starter goal by itself.
### How much emergency fund do you need in Missouri?
Start with $500, then $1,000, the starter goals in the CFPB’s toolkit. After that, the common target is three to six months of essential expenses, not total spending. In the illustrative budget, essentials run $2,100 a month, so three months is $6,300 and six months is $12,600.
Why such a small first goal? Most emergencies aren’t layoffs. A 2022 CFPB report, citing JPMorgan Chase Institute research, notes the typical expense spike or income dip runs about three weeks of income, and the typical family hits more than one a year. A $1,000 cushion covers the tire, the copay, the furnace call, and keeps them off a card charging 22%.
The bigger number is for losing a job, and here’s the Missouri math no template includes. The state’s maximum unemployment benefit is $320 a week, for no more than 20 weeks in a benefit year. Your weekly amount is 4% of the average of your two highest-paid quarters, so plenty of people get less. Even at the full $320, that’s about $1,387 a month. HUD’s fair market rent for a two-bedroom in the metro is $1,349. Do the subtraction. The best-case check covers a family’s rent, leaves about $38 for everything else, and stops after 20 weeks.
So three months of essentials is the floor for a household with one steady paycheck. Six fits a single income with kids, a field where searches drag, or pay that swings. Missouri eligibility runs on wages from an insured employer, so if most of your income is freelance or gig work, plan as if that $320 won’t come. On the Illinois side, the state runs its own program with its own numbers.
### Where should you keep an emergency fund?
Somewhere insured, boring and one step away from your debit card. The CFPB’s guide to building an emergency fund calls a bank or credit union account generally one of the safest places for your money, and says to keep the fund where you won’t be tempted to spend it on things that aren’t emergencies.
Insured is the key word. FDIC deposit insurance covers $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, for each account ownership category, across checking, savings, money market deposit accounts and CDs. Stocks, bonds, mutual funds and crypto aren’t covered, even when a bank sells them. At a federally insured credit union, the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund covers individual accounts up to $250,000 as well.
Then put it on autopilot. The CFPB suggests automatic recurring transfers from checking to savings, plus all or part of a tax refund. Watch the fees, because a $5 monthly charge on a $500 fund eats 1% of it every month. Compare a credit union or two against your bank, and read the fee schedule first. Our guide to avoiding bank fees in St. Louis lists every charge to ask about. And keep this money out of the stock market. Its job is to be there on the worst day, not to grow.
### When is a full year of emergency savings worth it?
For most people with one steady paycheck, a year is more than they need, and the honest reason is cost. Every dollar past six months is a dollar that could be paying off a 22% card, collecting an employer’s retirement match, or working toward the next goal. Insured savings is safe. Safe doesn’t pay much.
A year stops being overkill when income could vanish for a long stretch. That covers the self-employed and gig workers who can’t lean on Missouri unemployment, commission and seasonal earners, single-income families with kids, specialized fields where a search can outlast the 20-week benefit cap, and anyone close to retirement who’d rather not sell investments in a down market.
Take a self-employed photographer in Soulard with $3,000 a month in essentials. A slow winter plus a dead camera can cost her four months of income, and no state check is coming. For her, a year of essentials, $36,000, isn’t paranoia. It’s her sick leave, her severance and her unemployment insurance in one account.
Everyone else can take the middle path. Build three to six months first. Once high-rate debt is gone and you’re getting any match on offer, decide whether the next dollar buys a longer cushion or bigger goals. That’s a good question for a planner, and our guide to what a financial planner costs in St. Louis explains the fee models first.
### What are the biggest budgeting mistakes?
Budgeting from gross pay, forgetting the yearly bills, and building a plan so strict it breaks by the second weekend. Most failed budgets trace back to one of those, and none of them is a willpower problem.
Budgeting the offer letter. The salary isn’t the deposit.
Forgetting the once-a-year bills: here, the car tax, plate renewal and, for some City residents, the earnings tax. Divide each by 12.
No room to be human. A budget with $0 for fun lasts about as long as a New Year’s resolution.
Calling everything an emergency. Christmas comes every December. Give it a set-aside.
Saving hard while a card compounds at 22%. Keep the starter fund, then aim the extra at the balance.
Quitting after one bad month. The first month is a rough draft.
And when a month goes sideways for reasons no budget could fix, a layoff, a hospital bill, a shutoff notice, the region has more help than most people hear about. Our list of St. Louis help and assistance resources covers housing, utilities, food and more.
This is general information, not advice for your situation. A licensed financial advisor or a CPA can apply it to yours, and our St. Louis Financial directory is a place to start.
Want a second set of eyes on your numbers? Financial planners around St. Louis can build the budget and the emergency fund target around your real paycheck, so bring a recent pay stub and three months of statements.
And if you run a coaching practice that helps people through exactly this, list your practice so the newcomer holding a surprise tax form can find you.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the 50/30/20 rule budget?
A.  It splits take-home pay three ways: 50% for needs like housing, utilities, groceries, transportation and minimum payments, 30% for wants, and 20% for savings and extra debt payments. On $3,600 a month that’s $1,800, $1,080 and $720. Treat it as a quick check. The illustrative St. Louis budget on this page lands nearer 58/22/20 once the car is counted.
### Q. Does the 50/30/20 rule actually work?
A.  As a starting point, yes. It works best when housing stays near a third of take-home pay and you aren’t carrying high-rate debt. It strains when rent eats 40% of the check or a card compounds near 22%. Then a zero-based budget, which gives every dollar a job in priority order, usually fits better.
### Q. What are the 5 basics to any budget?
A.  Take-home income, fixed bills, variable spending, savings and debt payoff, and irregular bills turned into monthly set-asides. The fifth is the one people miss. In St. Louis it includes the yearly personal property tax on your car, plate renewal and, for some City residents, the 1% earnings tax.
### Q. What bills do most adults pay monthly?
A.  Rent or a mortgage, utilities, phone and internet, groceries, car costs, health premiums, minimum debt payments and subscriptions. In St. Louis, treat two yearly bills as monthly too: the personal property tax on your car, about $34 a month for a $15,000 car at the City’s 2025 rate, and the City earnings tax if your employer doesn’t withhold it.
### Q. Is $10,000 a good enough emergency fund?
A.  It depends on your essential monthly costs, not your income. With $2,100 a month in essentials, like the illustrative budget here, $10,000 covers nearly five months, inside the usual three-to-six-month range. A family with $4,500 a month in essentials gets a little over two months. Divide $10,000 by your own essentials to see where you stand.
### Q. Is a 1 year emergency fund overkill?
A.  For most households with one steady W-2 paycheck, yes. Three to six months of essentials covers the usual risks, and extra cash does more against high-rate debt or toward a retirement match. A year makes sense for the self-employed, commission or seasonal earners, single-income families and people near retirement, especially with Missouri unemployment capped at $320 a week for 20 weeks.
### Q. What is the meaning of emergency fund?
A.  The CFPB defines it as “a cash reserve that’s specifically set aside for unplanned expenses or financial emergencies.” Think car repairs, a medical bill, a furnace that quits in January or a gap between jobs. Holidays and the yearly car tax aren’t emergencies, because you know they’re coming. They get their own set-asides.
### Q. How much should I save if I make $3,000 a month?
A.  If $3,000 is take-home, 50/30/20 says $600. Whether that’s realistic depends on rent. A one-bedroom at HUD’s $1,104 metro figure is 37% of that check, so a realistic start might be $150 to $300 a month, moved automatically on payday, until the $1,000 starter fund is built. Then raise it each time a debt is paid off.

## What Causes Inflation? A Plain Explanation From the City That Hosts the St. Louis Fed
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-causes-inflation-st-louis-fed
One of twelve. That’s how many regional Federal Reserve Banks the country has, and one of them sits downtown at Broadway and Locust. St. Louis was among the 12 cities picked in 1914, when the banks opened for business that November. Today the St. Louis Fed’s research department runs FRED, a data site it has kept since the early 1990s that now holds hundreds of thousands of economic data series. The same price charts economists pull up are sitting right there. You can look up how fast prices are rising in St. Louis in about two minutes.
Most of us never got that tour. School covered the water cycle and the Louisiana Purchase, then sent us out into a world where the same cart of groceries costs more every year and nobody explains why. The receipt shows the total. It never shows the reason. So prices start to feel like weather, or like somebody running a con, and the only time we think about it is when a bill lands.
You’re not bad with money. Nobody showed you this part. Here’s the plain version, from the city that hosts one of the twelve, right down to where to click for the St. Louis numbers. It’s one chapter of our St. Louis money guide, the series on the money stuff school skipped.
### Why are prices increasing?
Prices rise for three main reasons: shoppers and businesses try to buy more than the economy can produce (demand-pull), costs like fuel, materials and wages climb and get passed along (cost-push), and people expect higher prices and act on it. A sudden jump in one item, like gas or eggs, often traces to a supply problem.
Lately, energy is doing most of the shoving. The Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Consumer Price Index report for August 2026, released September 11, showed overall prices up 3.4% from a year earlier. Gasoline alone was up 27.4%. Take food and energy out and everything else rose 2.4%, a much calmer number.
St. Louis is running a little cooler. BLS publishes a separate Consumer Price Index for the St. Louis area, covering the city and the surrounding counties on both sides of the river, and it comes out every two months. For the 12 months ending in August 2026, area prices rose 2.9%. Energy was up 12.9%, food 2.1%, and everything outside food and energy 2.2%.
Those figures go stale within weeks. That’s fine. The point is knowing where the next ones live.
One definition first, because it clears up half the confusion. Inflation isn’t one thing getting expensive. The Federal Reserve describes it as a general increase in the overall price level of goods and services. A spike in egg prices is a price problem. Rent, insurance, haircuts, daycare and car repairs all inching up together, month after month, is inflation.
### What actually pushes prices up: too much spending or higher costs?
Both, and they feel different at the register. Demand-pull is the classic. The St. Louis Fed’s Page One Economics describes it as demand outrunning what producers can supply, or in the old shorthand, too much money chasing too few goods.
Picture a spring when half the households in the county decide to redo a bathroom at once. Contractors book out for months. Tile runs short. Quotes go up, and not because tile got harder to make. Everybody just wants it at the same time. Spread that across the whole economy and you have demand-pull inflation.
Cost-push runs the other way. A business’s own costs climb, for fuel, ingredients, freight, insurance or wages, and some of that gets handed to the customer. Nobody suddenly wanted more of anything. It just cost more to make.
Here’s where living in a Fed city pays off: the St. Louis Fed asks businesses about this directly. In its August survey of firms in the Eighth District, the seven-state region the bank covers, businesses said the prices they charge rose about 3% over the previous 12 months, and they expect about the same pace over the next 12. Almost half said their nonlabor costs were higher than a year earlier. Firms said they pass higher costs along whenever possible, though only about a third said they’d actually managed it.
The fine print is shifting, too. In the same survey, 24% of firms saw suppliers adding temporary fees or surcharges, 27% saw suppliers changing prices more often, and 18% saw price quotes staying valid for less time. If a contractor’s estimate now expires in a week instead of a month, that’s cost-push showing up in the paperwork.
Then there’s the third engine: expectations. A business that expects its costs to keep rising marks prices up ahead of time. A worker who expects groceries to cost 4% more next year hears a 2% raise as a pay cut, the same point a St. Louis Fed economist makes in the bank’s explainer on inflation expectations. So workers push for more, employers pay it and raise prices to cover it, and prices climb partly because everyone braced for them to. Economists call that loop a wage-price spiral.
That’s why the Fed watches what people expect almost as closely as what prices do. When expectations sit near 2%, the same explainer notes, the Fed may not need to move rates as much. When they come loose, getting inflation down tends to cost more jobs.
### Why do gas and eggs jump while rent just creeps?
Because some prices sit on a hair trigger and others move like a barge on the Mississippi. Food and energy swing hard on news unrelated to the rest of the economy, so economists also track core inflation, which leaves those two out. The Fed’s explainer says such items go up and down in price dramatically or often.
Eggs are the textbook case. The USDA’s Food Price Outlook says an avian flu outbreak that began in 2022 pushed egg prices up by shrinking laying flocks and cutting egg production. Fix the supply and the price can fall fast. In its September 2026 update, USDA forecast egg prices to drop 29.4% for 2026.
Gas works the same way on a bigger stage. Gasoline follows crude oil, which trades on a world market no St. Louis station controls. There’s a local layer on top, too, which is why gas usually costs more on the Illinois side.
Rent and services are the barge. Leases reset once a year. Pay at a barbershop or a daycare changes gradually. Insurance gets repriced at renewal. Nationally, the shelter index rose 3.0% over the 12 months ending in August, a quieter number than gasoline’s, but one that lands on nearly every household every month.
So when a headline says inflation ticked up, ask which kind. A gas spike can fade within months. A services climb tends to linger: looking back at past slowdowns, St. Louis Fed economists concluded that goods inflation tends to fall quickly, while the last stretch depends on services, which take longer.
### How can you look up St. Louis inflation yourself?
Here’s the two-minute version, on the St. Louis Fed’s own data site.
Open FRED’s page for the national Consumer Price Index, series CPIAUCSL. That’s the CPI for All Urban Consumers, the headline number BLS releases every month.
Click Edit Graph. Under Units, switch Index to Percent Change from Year Ago. The line on your screen is now the inflation rate, month by month, going back decades.
Still in Edit Graph, add a second line: Personal Consumption Expenditures: Chain-type Price Index, the Fed’s preferred gauge, set to the same units. A FRED blog post notes CPI has generally run above PCE, by about half a percentage point on average since 1960.
Bring it home. Search FRED for St. Louis CPI and open the All Items index for St. Louis, MO-IL. FRED shows it as half-year averages, while the bimonthly St. Louis release lives on the BLS St. Louis CPI page.
Hit the Download button above any graph to save it as an image or a PowerPoint slide, or the numbers as an Excel or CSV file.
While you’re there, look at the raw index before you switch units. Both the national and St. Louis indexes are set to 100 for 1982 to 1984. The national index read 334.1 in August 2026, so a basket that cost $100 back then costs about $334 now. The St. Louis index averaged about 298 in the first half of 2026. Same starting line, so prices here have climbed noticeably less than the national average over four decades. That doesn’t prove things are cheaper here today, since the index only tracks change. For actual price levels, see what it really costs to live in St. Louis.
One thing the CPI won’t hand you is your own number. BLS records the prices of about 80,000 items a month, mostly through data collectors who visit stores in person, and its own CPI questions and answers say the index does not necessarily measure your own experience with price change. A retiree whose budget leans on medical care can run hotter than the headline. Your bank statement, set beside the same month last year, is the closest thing to a personal CPI you’ll get.
### Why does the Fed aim for 2% inflation instead of zero?
Because zero leaves no cushion. The Federal Reserve’s longer-run goal is 2% inflation, measured by the annual change in the PCE price index, which its policy committee judges most consistent with maximum employment and price stability. Page One Economics calls 2% a compromise, high enough to provide a buffer against deflation, which is a general, sustained fall in prices.
Deflation sounds great at the register. It’s rough on everything behind the register. The St. Louis Fed’s Open Vault blog says many economists consider it harmful, though that claim is disputed. One worry: when people expect prices to fall, they may wait to buy things, which can feed a loop of lower spending, lower incomes and more unemployment.
The Fed’s main tool is the federal funds rate, the rate banks pay for overnight borrowing. The Fed explains that changes in it influence other interest rates, and those set borrowing costs for households and businesses. Raise it and borrowing gets pricier, spending cools, and demand-pull pressure eases. Cut it and the reverse happens. The catch is timing. The links from policy to inflation are not direct or immediate, so the Fed is always steering by forecast.
You feel that lever in two places. One is a home loan, and our guide to how mortgage rates work walks through that side. The other is plastic. Many credit cards carry a variable APR, the yearly interest rate on a balance, which the CFPB says changes with an index such as the prime rate. Since Fed moves ripple into other rates, a card balance can get pricier without you doing a thing. Our explainer on how credit card interest works runs the math.
And St. Louis has a chair in the room. The Federal Open Market Committee, which sets that rate, holds eight scheduled meetings a year. All 12 Reserve Bank presidents join the discussion, while votes rotate, and the Fed’s published rotation gives St. Louis a vote again in 2028.
Prices steer behavior, even at the curb. How pay-as-you-throw cuts trash.
### If inflation slows down, why don’t prices go back down?
Because a slower inflation rate still means rising prices. The St. Louis Fed’s Page One Economics puts it plainly: when the inflation rate decreases, prices do not. A falling inflation rate is called disinflation, meaning the price level is still rising, just more slowly. Prices as a whole only fall during deflation, when the inflation rate itself turns negative.
Picture a gallon of milk that climbed from $3 to $4 during a rough stretch. If inflation cools from 6% to 2%, the milk doesn’t slide back to $3. It goes to about $4.08 next year instead of $4.24. That’s what winning against inflation looks like on a receipt, and it’s why the news can say inflation is down while your cart insists otherwise.
Single items can fall. Eggs are forecast to, by the USDA numbers above. The whole basket almost never does, and when it has, it wasn’t good news. That same Page One piece notes the U.S. saw slight deflation in 2009, and the bank’s earlier explainer warns that falling prices can signal a weak economy.
So the real way out isn’t lower prices. It’s paychecks that grow faster than prices, so the same groceries take a smaller bite of the week. That hasn’t been happening lately. The BLS real earnings report shows average hourly pay, adjusted for inflation, down 0.3% from August 2025 to August 2026. That gap is the squeeze you’ve been feeling. It’s measured, not imagined.
### Who comes out ahead when prices rise, and who falls behind?
It depends less on how much money you have than on what you hold and what you owe. Inflation quietly shifts value away from people holding fixed dollars and toward people paying back fixed dollars.
Take a fixed-rate loan. The St. Louis Fed’s Open Vault walks through a bank holding a 6% fixed-rate mortgage: if inflation suddenly rose from 3% to 7%, the bank would lose out, because it’s being repaid in dollars that buy less than it planned. Run it backward, with inflation unexpectedly falling, and the borrower becomes the one who’s worse off. A household with a fixed-rate mortgage and pay that keeps up with prices sits on the comfortable side of a price surge.
Savers sit on the other side. Cash in an account paying less than the inflation rate loses buying power every month, even though the balance never drops. The number looks the same. It buys less.
Fixed incomes take it straightest. A pension or annuity that pays the same dollar amount every month buys about 3% less after a year of 3% inflation, and about 26% less after ten years of it. If you or a parent rely on one, find out whether it carries a cost-of-living adjustment before the next price jump, not after.
The worst mix has its own name. Stagflation is high inflation plus a stagnant economy. The 1970s were the American lesson, and the wave crested in 1980, when the CPI inflation rate briefly topped 14%, its highest since 1947. Prices race while hiring stalls, and paychecks get squeezed from both sides.
### What can a St. Louis household do with all this?
Knowing how inflation works won’t shrink a grocery bill. It does change which moves make sense.
Price your own basket. Pull three months of bank or card statements from a year ago and compare them with the last three. That’s the rate your budget actually lives on, and our guide to budgeting on a St. Louis paycheck shows how to build a plan around it.
Know which debts float. Fixed-rate debt gets lighter in real terms as prices rise. Variable-rate debt can get heavier when rates climb to fight inflation, so a big card balance can get hit twice. Your loan papers and card agreement say which kind you have.
Check what your savings earn against the latest CPI. Below inflation, the balance buys less every month.
See it in person. The Economy Museum at the St. Louis Fed, inside the bank at Broadway and Locust, has free admission on weekdays from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. Visitors over 18 need a government-issued photo ID, and everyone goes through X-ray screening.
This is general information about how inflation works, not advice for your situation. A licensed financial advisor or planner can apply it to yours, and our St. Louis Financial directory is a place to start.
Want a second set of eyes on how rising prices hit your savings, debt and retirement plan? Start with financial advisors around St. Louis, and bring the FRED chart you just made.
And if you’re the planner families call, these are the exact questions your neighbors (and the AI they ask) are typing right now, and the advisor named first gets the call, so list your practice where they’re already looking.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is stagflation?
A.  Stagflation is high inflation and a stagnant economy at the same time: slow growth, weak hiring, and prices still climbing. It’s hard to fix because the usual medicine pulls in opposite directions. Raising rates to cool prices can also cool hiring, and cutting rates to help jobs can keep prices running hot.
### Q. How do central banks control inflation?
A.  Mostly through interest rates. In the U.S., the Federal Reserve sets a target for the federal funds rate, the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans, and that ripples into other borrowing costs. Higher rates make borrowing costlier, which cools spending and eases demand pressure. The effect isn’t immediate, so the Fed acts on forecasts and works to keep inflation expectations near 2%.
### Q. What is demand-pull inflation?
A.  Demand-pull inflation happens when people and businesses want to buy more goods and services than the economy can produce, so sellers raise prices. The St. Louis Fed’s shorthand is too much money chasing too few goods. It tends to show up in an expanding economy, when households have more money and want to spend it. Its counterpart is cost-push inflation, where rising production costs push prices up.
### Q. Can inflation be a good thing?
A.  A little can be. The Federal Reserve aims for 2% a year, not zero, because a small positive rate leaves a buffer against deflation, a broad fall in prices that can feed a cycle of delayed spending and job losses. Mild, predictable inflation also lets households plan. Trouble starts when inflation runs high or jumps unexpectedly, because paychecks, savings and fixed incomes fall behind.
### Q. Do the rich get richer during inflation?
A.  Not automatically. Inflation sorts people more by what they own and owe than by income. People with fixed-rate debt, like a fixed mortgage, repay with dollars that buy less, which helps them. People holding cash, savings earning less than inflation, or a fixed pension lose buying power. Households that own assets and carry fixed-rate debt can come through better than renters living paycheck to paycheck.
### Q. Will prices ever come down again?
A.  Some will. Prices for single items like eggs or gasoline can drop when a supply problem eases, and USDA forecast egg prices to fall sharply in 2026. The overall price level rarely falls, though. When inflation slows, prices keep rising, just more slowly. That’s disinflation. Real relief usually comes from wages growing faster than prices, not from prices returning to where they were.
### Q. What is creeping inflation?
A.  Creeping inflation is a slow, steady rise in prices, low enough that it barely registers month to month. There’s no official cutoff. The worry is that it adds up and can speed up. A Federal Reserve speech from 1957, titled “The Myth of Creeping Inflation” and archived on the St. Louis Fed’s FRASER library, shows how long that debate has run.
### Q. How often does BLS publish inflation numbers for St. Louis?
A.  Every two months. The Bureau of Labor Statistics releases a Consumer Price Index for the St. Louis area, covering the city and surrounding counties in Missouri and Illinois, for even-numbered months. The national CPI comes out monthly. On FRED, the St. Louis Fed’s data site, the St. Louis index appears as half-year averages you can chart next to the national number.

## Grants vs Loans for College in Missouri: Pell, Access Missouri, A+, Fast Track and When to Borrow
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/grants-vs-loans-for-college-missouri
Loans aren’t aid. Not the kind the word promises, anyway. Open a college financial aid offer and you may find a Pell Grant and a federal loan sitting in the same column, added together under one friendly heading. One of those you keep. The other comes back with interest, usually starting six months after you leave school and running ten years or longer.
Nobody taught most of us this. The letter isn’t lying, exactly. It’s counting everything a school can arrange and leaving the sorting to an 18-year-old and a tired parent. So here’s the sorting, cheapest first: free money, then work, then the cheapest borrowing, with private loans dead last.
The Missouri layer is where families quietly lose money. The state’s biggest need-based grant, Access Missouri, guarantees an award only to eligible students whose FAFSA is in by Feb. 1. File in March with the exact same income and you’re counting on leftover funding. That one date is worth up to $3,500 a year at a four-year school. Nobody mails you a reminder.
This page is one stop on our St. Louis money guide. If you want the actual list of awards to apply for, our guide to scholarships for St. Louis students has the verified programs. This page is about the order you use them in, and the loans you take only after the free money runs out.
### Is it better to get a loan or a grant?
A grant is better every time you can get one, because grant money generally isn’t repaid and a loan is repaid with interest. Take free money first: grants and scholarships, then work-study. Borrow only for the gap, starting with federal subsidized loans, then unsubsidized, then parent PLUS, with private loans last.
Here’s the whole ladder, top rung first:
Grants and scholarships. Pell, Missouri’s programs, school money and outside scholarships. Generally never repaid.
Federal Work-Study. A part-time job paying at least the federal minimum wage. You earn it, so you don’t owe it.
Direct Subsidized Loans. For undergraduates with financial need. The government covers the interest while you’re enrolled at least half-time and for six months after.
Direct Unsubsidized Loans. Same rate, but the interest is yours from day one.
Parent PLUS Loans. A higher rate, a much bigger fee, a credit check and, since July 1, 2026, fewer ways out.
Private loans. From a bank or other lender, priced on your credit or a cosigner’s.
Why the order matters in dollars: a $1,000 grant makes college $1,000 cheaper. A $1,000 loan makes it more expensive than $1,000, because interest runs on it and, on federal loans, a fee comes off the top before the school ever sees the money. On a parent PLUS loan that fee is 4.228%. Borrow $10,000 and about $9,577 actually reaches the school, while the balance you owe is the full $10,000, at a fixed 9.07% for loans first paid out between July 1, 2026 and June 30, 2027, according to Federal Student Aid’s rate and fee tables.
One honest footnote: a few grants carry strings. A TEACH Grant must be repaid if you skip the teaching service it requires, and any federal grant can be partly clawed back if you withdraw early, per the Education Department. Read the conditions once. Then take the money.
### Is there a way to get free college tuition in Missouri?
Yes, for a lot of St. Louis students, at least at the community college level, and the math is almost embarrassingly simple once you line it up. St. Louis Community College charges $127 per credit hour in-district for fall 2026 through spring 2027, the rate for city and St. Louis County residents. A full-time year of 30 credit hours comes to $3,810 in tuition. The federal Pell Grant runs from $740 to a maximum of $7,395 for the 2026-27 award year. For a student who qualifies for the top award, Pell alone is nearly double a year of STLCC tuition.
Then Missouri stacks its own programs on top, each aimed at a different kind of student.
A+ Scholarship, for recent high school graduates. Graduate from an A+ designated high school with a 2.5 unweighted GPA, 95% attendance, 50 hours of unpaid tutoring or mentoring and a qualifying Algebra I score, and the state reimburses tuition and general fees at a participating public community college or technical school. For 2026-27 the cap is $240 per credit hour, nearly twice STLCC’s rate. You sign the A+ agreement before graduation, enroll full-time, file a FAFSA every year, and the clock runs out 48 months after you graduate.
Here’s the part that confuses families. A+ is a last-dollar award. It pays the tuition and general fees left after Pell and other non-loan federal aid, so a student whose Pell covers tuition can see an A+ award of zero. The state says so on its own page. That’s not the program failing you. Pell simply got there first, and the school can pay out what’s left of it for books, a bus pass or living costs.
Access Missouri, need-based money at any participating Missouri school. If your Student Aid Index (SAI, the need number the FAFSA produces) is $12,000 or less and you enroll full-time, you’re in range. The statute sets awards of $500 to $1,700 a year at a public two-year college and $1,750 to $3,500 a year at a public four-year university, State Technical College of Missouri or a private school, and the state can pay less if funding falls short, according to the Access Missouri program page. There’s no separate application; the state pulls your FAFSA. One wrinkle: if you also get A+, Access Missouri drops by the A+ amount.
Fast Track, for adults going back. You may qualify if you’re 25 or older (or haven’t been enrolled in high school or college for two years), have lived in Missouri at least two years, don’t hold a bachelor’s degree, and your adjusted gross income is $40,000 or less, or $80,000 or less filing jointly. Fast Track then covers tuition and fees left after other grants for at least half-time study in a high-demand field like health care, computer science, transportation or accounting. If other aid already covers tuition, it can still pay up to $500 toward books, housing or transportation. You apply through the state’s financial aid portal (the 2026-27 deadline is May 15, 2027) and file a FAFSA too.
And a myth worth retiring: older articles warn that Fast Track turns into a loan if you leave Missouri after you finish. Not anymore. The state says the loan conversion ended after the 2022 legislative session. Recipients now report their job and residence to the department for three years after completing the program instead.
Bright Flight, for top test scores. An ACT of 32 or higher earns up to $3,000 a year, and a 30 or 31 up to $1,000, at an approved Missouri school for students who enroll full-time the year right after graduation, per the Bright Flight page.
If you’re still deciding between STLCC and a four-year campus, our guide on choosing a college or trade school in St. Louis walks through the transfer path. If the goal is a trade, the trade schools and apprenticeships guide covers programs that pay you while you train.
### How late is too late to fill out FAFSA?
For federal aid, you have until June 30 at the very end of the school year the form covers: the 2027-28 FAFSA is accepted until 11:59 p.m. Central on June 30, 2028, per the federal deadline page. For Missouri money, too late comes much sooner. Feb. 1 is the state’s priority date, and April 1 is the last day you’ll be considered at all.
That gap is the most expensive thing on this page. Access Missouri runs the same way every year. Eligible students who file by the Feb. 1 priority deadline are guaranteed an award. After that, the state sets an award deadline between Feb. 1 and April 1, depending on how far the money stretches, and anyone who files after it gets nothing from the program that year. Two families with identical paychecks can end up thousands of dollars apart over four years because one filed in January and one filed in March.
Colleges set their own dates too, so ask each one what its deadline means. The calendar:
Fall: the next year’s FAFSA opens. Federal law now requires a launch by Oct. 1, and the 2027-28 form went live Sept. 23, 2026, per the Education Department. It uses tax information from two years back, so the 2027-28 form asks for 2025 taxes.
Feb. 1: Missouri’s priority date (Feb. 1, 2027 for the 2027-28 school year).
April 1: Missouri’s final date for state aid consideration.
July 31: Missouri’s cutoff for FAFSA corrections that affect Access Missouri, if your form was in on time.
June 30: the federal deadline, more than a year after the Missouri dates have passed.
One practical note for a family with a senior: the FAFSA doesn’t need an acceptance letter. You can add up to 20 schools to the online form before you’ve heard from any of them, and remove one later, according to studentaid.gov. Waiting for admissions decisions before filing is an easy way to slide past Feb. 1 without noticing.
A counselor costs money too. Here’s what St. Louis families pay.
### What order should you borrow in?
Federal before private, subsidized before unsubsidized, and the student’s loans before the parent’s. Here’s how the federal options compare for loans first paid out from July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027, using the current federal rates and fees:
Dependent undergraduates can borrow up to $5,500 in the first year (no more than $3,500 of it subsidized), $6,500 in the second ($4,500 subsidized) and $7,500 each year after that ($5,500 subsidized), with a $31,000 total cap for undergraduate study ($23,000 subsidized). Those student limits didn’t change when federal loan rules were rewritten on July 1, 2026, per Federal Student Aid’s loan limits guidance. The parent side did change, and that’s the next section.
What “subsidized” is worth in plain numbers: take a $3,500 loan at 6.52%. Subsidized, the in-school interest is the government’s bill. Unsubsidized, the same loan builds about $228 of interest a year while you’re sitting in class, and you owe every cent of it. Four years of school puts roughly $900 on top of that single first-year loan.
Work-study sits above every loan. You trade hours instead of interest. The award depends on when you apply, your need and your school’s funding, so apply early. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau notes that working more than 20 hours a week is linked to lower grades, which is a fair ceiling to keep.
Private loans come last because federal loans generally carry lower rates and fees, and a student with no credit history will usually need a family cosigner, whose credit is then on the line for years. Our explainer on how interest works and how credit gets built shows why that matters.
### What changed for parent PLUS loans?
Parent PLUS loans now have a ceiling and fewer exits. When a student starts a new program or takes a first federal loan for a program on or after July 1, 2026, parents can borrow no more than $20,000 a year for that student, all parents combined, and $65,000 across the student’s whole undergraduate career, according to Federal Student Aid’s parent PLUS page. Families already borrowing for a student who stays in the same program at the same school can keep the old rules for now, which allowed borrowing up to the full cost of attendance minus other aid.
The bigger change is what happens after graduation. A parent who takes out, or consolidates, a PLUS loan after July 1, 2026 can repay only on the Tiered Standard Plan, with no income-driven repayment and no Public Service Loan Forgiveness. And the loan can’t be handed to the student later. It stays the parent’s debt, start to finish.
Picture a parent in north county, a few years from retirement, signing for $16,000 a year over four years. That’s $64,000 of debt, each year’s loan at that year’s rate (9.07% right now), and at today’s 4.228% fee about $2,700 of it never reaches the school. If that parent’s income drops later, there’s no income-driven plan to fall back on. That’s why PLUS sits below every dollar the student can borrow.
PLUS also requires a credit check. If a parent can’t get the loan at all, the student may qualify for extra unsubsidized loans instead, up to $9,500 in the first year rather than $5,500, at the lower student rate. Reaching the PLUS cap doesn’t unlock that. Being turned down does.
### How do you compare two financial aid offers?
Split every offer into two piles before you compare anything: money you never repay (grants, scholarships, work-study) and money you borrow (every loan, parent PLUS included). Subtract only the first pile from the cost of attendance. What’s left is what that school really costs this year, whether you cover it from savings, a paycheck or a loan.
The CFPB’s planning tool, Your financial path to graduation, builds its whole worksheet that way. Grants, scholarships and work-study land in a non-debt subtotal; federal, private and PLUS loans land in a separate debt subtotal. Run each offer through it and the “total aid” number stops doing the talking.
Then ask each financial aid office four questions drawn from that CFPB checklist:
Is each grant renewable, and what GPA does it require?
What happens to my aid if I win an outside scholarship? Some schools cut aid they already offered, which the CFPB calls scholarship displacement.
Do I have to take every loan? No. You can accept less, or none.
Will my total debt at graduation top my likely first-year salary? The CFPB treats that as a warning line.
If your family’s money changed since the tax year the FAFSA used, ask the aid office for an adjustment; the school’s decision is final. Then put the monthly loan payment next to a real budget. Our guide to budgeting on a St. Louis paycheck shows how one holds up.
### Are 529 contributions tax deductible?
Not on your federal return, but yes on your Missouri return. The IRS says 529 contributions aren’t federally deductible, though earnings come out tax-free when they pay qualified education costs. Missouri lets you deduct contributions to MOST, the state’s 529 plan, up to $8,000 per person or $16,000 for a married couple filing jointly, according to MOST’s tax page.
Three details matter once college is close. The FAFSA counts education savings accounts as investments, so have the balance ready when you sign. A withdrawal for something that isn’t a qualified expense can bring federal tax plus a 10% penalty on the earnings, and Missouri can recapture your deduction. And MOST says up to $10,000 can go toward repaying student loans. For the K-12 question, our guide to how St. Louis families afford private school tuition covers it.
This is general information, not advice for your family’s situation. A school’s financial aid office, a licensed financial advisor or a CPA can apply it to yours, and our St. Louis Education directory is a place to start.
Shortlist two or three schools, get the FAFSA in before Missouri’s Feb. 1 priority date, then sit down with each offer split into free money and borrowed money. When you’re ready to compare campuses side by side, start with colleges and universities around St. Louis.
And if you run a college admissions counseling practice or a tutoring center: when a St. Louis parent asks a neighbor, or an AI, who can help with applications, the name that comes up first gets the call, so list your practice.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Do I have to pay back grant money?
A.  Usually not. You may owe part of a federal grant back if you withdraw early, drop from full-time to part-time, get outside aid that lowers your need, receive Pell from two schools at once, or skip a TEACH Grant’s service requirement. Your school will tell you, and you then have 45 days to repay or set up a repayment arrangement, or you lose eligibility for more federal aid.
### Q. Can I get a grant instead of a loan?
A.  Not by swapping lines on the offer, but you can shrink the loan line. Decline any loan you don’t need, ask the aid office whether more grant or work-study money is available, and if your family’s income dropped after the tax year the FAFSA used, ask for an adjustment. The school makes that call, and its decision is final.
### Q. What disqualifies you from getting a Pell Grant?
A.  Already holding a bachelor’s degree (with narrow exceptions), using up 12 full-time semesters of Pell, or a Student Aid Index at or above twice the maximum award, which is $14,790 for 2026-27, per the Education Department. Starting that year, Pell also stops for any period when non-federal grants and scholarships (state, school or private) equal or exceed your cost of attendance.
### Q. What is the #1 most common FAFSA mistake?
A.  There’s no official ranking, but the costly one is an unfinished form. A FAFSA isn’t complete until every required contributor, usually a parent, signs and consents to the IRS data transfer, and without that consent the student can’t get federal aid at all. In Missouri, every week past Feb. 1 can also cost state grant money. Using the wrong tax year is another one.
### Q. Does FAFSA check your bank account?
A.  No. The FAFSA doesn’t log into your bank. You enter the current balances of your checking and savings accounts, plus cash over $1,000, as of the day you sign, and your tax information comes from the IRS with your consent. The home you live in and retirement accounts aren’t reported as investments, per studentaid.gov. Keep the statements you used.
### Q. What is the maximum money FAFSA will give you?
A.  The FAFSA itself pays nothing; it unlocks aid. The largest federal grant is Pell, up to $7,395 for 2026-27, and some students can get up to 150% of their yearly award by taking classes in an extra term. A dependent first-year student can add up to $5,500 in federal loans. Missouri and your school layer their own grants on top.
### Q. How many years does FAFSA cover?
A.  One. Each FAFSA covers a single award year, July 1 through June 30, so you file again for every year you’re in school. Pell has its own lifetime limit of 12 full-time semesters, roughly six years, which the Education Department tracks as 600% of one year’s award. Access Missouri caps out at 10 semesters, or five at a two-year school.
### Q. Does the Fast Track grant turn into a loan if I leave Missouri?
A.  Not anymore. Missouri’s higher education department says the rule that converted Fast Track grants into loans ended after the 2022 legislative session. Recipients now report their employment and residency to the state for three years after finishing their program. Older articles that warn about repayment are describing the old rule, so check the department’s current page.

## Power of Attorney in Missouri: Durable vs Health Care, Notary Rules, and How to Set One Up
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/power-of-attorney-missouri
The bank won’t talk to you. That’s the sentence St. Louis families hear the week a parent has a stroke, a bad fall, or a slow slide into dementia that finally tips over. Picture walking into the branch with your dad’s checkbook, his ID and a past-due gas bill, and hearing the teller say, kindly and firmly, that she can only discuss the account with the account holder. He can’t sign. You can’t sign for him. The mortgage is due on the first.
One document would have changed that conversation: a durable power of attorney. Without it, the main way in runs through the probate division of the circuit court. The judge appoints a lawyer for your parent, the family proves incapacity by clear and convincing evidence, and a conservator files an accounting with the court every year after. St. Louis County’s probate court posts a 34-page packet for these cases, and its first line says the materials are there to assist attorneys.
Here’s what nobody explains at the kitchen table. In Missouri, a power of attorney survives incapacity only if it’s titled “Durable Power of Attorney,” contains one of two sentences the statute spells out, and is acknowledged the way a deed is. A downloaded template that skips those words can go quiet on the exact day you need it. This page is part of our St. Louis money guide.
### Does a POA need to be notarized in Missouri?
Yes, if it’s meant to keep working after the person who signed it can’t manage their own affairs. Missouri law says a durable power of attorney must be signed by the principal, dated and “acknowledged in the manner prescribed by law for conveyances of real estate.” For nearly every family, that means signing in front of a notary public.
That rule lives in section 404.705 of the Revised Statutes of Missouri, the core of the Durable Power of Attorney Law of Missouri. Missouri’s health care power of attorney law borrows section 404.705 directly, so a medical POA needs the same acknowledgment. A plain, non-durable POA isn’t covered by that rule, but it pauses when the signer loses capacity, and if it touches real estate it still has to be acknowledged and recorded like a deed.
A living will plays by different rules. Section 459.015 says a health care declaration must be in writing, signed and dated and, unless it’s entirely in the signer’s own handwriting, signed in front of two or more witnesses who are at least 18. That section never mentions a notary. The Missouri Bar’s free health care form follows the same split: a notary for the health care POA, two witnesses for the directive, both if you complete both. Our guide to where to get a document notarized in St. Louis covers what to bring.
### What makes a Missouri power of attorney durable?
Three things, and all three have to be on the paper. The document must be named a “Durable Power of Attorney.” It must contain one of two statements from the statute. The shorter one reads: “This is a durable power of attorney and the authority of my attorney in fact shall not terminate if I become disabled or incapacitated or in the event of later uncertainty as to whether I am dead or alive.” And it must be signed, dated and acknowledged like a deed.
Leave the durability sentence out and the document isn’t worthless. It’s fragile. Under section 404.714, a power of attorney that isn’t durable is suspended while the principal can’t receive or evaluate information or communicate decisions. So the paper works while Mom can still handle things herself and stops the week a stroke takes that away, which is the whole reason she signed it.
Durable doesn’t have to mean immediate. The same section lets authority begin on a future event the document describes, a springing power, though someone then has to prove the trigger happened. And families from the Metro East get a break: under section 404.730, a power of attorney that was durable under the law of the state where it was signed can be enforced in Missouri.
### Why do most families need two powers of attorney, not one?
Because Missouri splits money and medicine into separate laws, and the agent for one has no automatic say in the other. The financial POA falls under sections 404.700 to 404.737, the health care POA under sections 404.800 to 404.872, and most families add a written directive so the medical agent isn’t guessing.
The Missouri Bar’s free form comes with a HIPAA privacy authorization, and its booklet explains why you want both. A health care POA only takes effect after you can’t make or communicate decisions, and it doesn’t authorize release of your medical information to your agent while you’re still competent. The Bar page offers no matching financial form, so the money half takes a separate document.
The doctor count surprises people. Unless the document says otherwise, section 404.825 starts a health care agent’s authority only when two licensed physicians certify, after examining the patient, that the patient is incapacitated. The Bar’s form lets you pick one physician instead, and its booklet warns that a second doctor can be hard to find at some facilities during after-hours emergencies.
Then feeding tubes. Under section 404.820, an agent can stop artificially supplied nutrition and hydration only if the document specifically grants that power. A traditional Missouri living will doesn’t reach it either, because section 459.010 leaves nutrition and hydration out of its definition of a death-prolonging procedure. Missouri has history here. In Cruzan v. Director, Missouri Department of Health, the U.S. Supreme Court in 1990 upheld Missouri’s demand for clear and convincing evidence of an incapacitated patient’s wishes before artificial nutrition and hydration is withdrawn. The remarks to a former housemate that the case turned on never spoke in those terms. Write it down. Initial the box.
### Which powers have to be spelled out in writing?
The ones that change who ends up with your property. General powers “for all lawful subjects and purposes” let an agent do almost anything you could do yourself. But section 404.710 lists powers an agent gets only if the document expressly names and authorizes them, including:
Making or revoking gifts of your property
Creating, changing or revoking a trust, or funding one you didn’t create
Creating or changing survivorship rights on property
Naming or changing the beneficiaries who receive property at your death
Consenting to an autopsy, making organ donations, or controlling burial or cremation
Nominating a guardian or conservator, or naming a substitute agent
Why would an ordinary family care? If a parent may someday need Medicaid to cover a nursing home, which our guide on how to pay for a retirement home in St. Louis covers, the planning an elder law attorney does often runs on gift or trust powers. Boilerplate that says “all lawful purposes” won’t supply them. One practical exception: an agent with general powers for all lawful purposes can withdraw from a joint bank or brokerage account without the survivorship power.
And no Missouri power of attorney can let an agent make, change or revoke your will or your living will declaration, force you to act against your will, or do anything you specifically forbade while you were competent.
### When does a Missouri power of attorney stop working?
At death, first and always. Section 404.717 ends the agent’s authority when the principal dies, with a narrow carve-out that keeps expressly granted powers over an autopsy, organ donation or burial alive for a reasonable time. Section 404.714 then requires the agent to promptly deliver the principal’s property to the estate’s personal representative. What takes over is the will, any trust, beneficiary designations and, if needed, probate. Our guide to when a parent dies in Missouri picks up the story there.
The same statute lists the other endings:
A termination date or condition written into the document itself.
The principal telling the agent, out loud or in writing, that the power is changed or revoked.
A written revocation notice filed with the recorder of deeds where the principal lives.
The agent no longer qualifying to serve.
A divorce filing between the principal and an agent spouse, unless the document says otherwise.
If the named agent drops out, a successor named in the document steps in. Plenty of homemade POAs leave that line blank.
Filing for divorce usually ends a spouse’s POA. Need a family law attorney?
### Why do banks still push back on a power of attorney?
Because Missouri law protects a bank that says yes far more clearly than it punishes one that stalls. Section 404.719 shields a business that relies on a POA in good faith and says that, unless it actually knows otherwise, it has no duty to investigate whether the agent is acting properly or whether the principal is still alive. It can ask for signature specimens and require protection against a forged POA, by bond or otherwise. What the section doesn’t contain is any penalty for saying no.
Missouri does state a policy. Section 404.710 says an agent with general powers gets the same rights as if the principal were present, and it voids any waiver to the contrary. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s guide for agents under a power of attorney lays out the play: hand over copies, never the original, get certified copies, ask for a supervisor, then call a lawyer. It also names the trap. A bank may want the parent to sign its own form, which is a problem once the parent can’t act. The easy fix is a branch visit while the parent can still come along.
Social Security and VA checks. The CFPB guide says an agent can’t manage those benefits without a separate appointment from the agency, as a representative payee or VA fiduciary.
The house. Section 442.360 says a POA used to convey or affect real estate must be acknowledged, certified and recorded like other real estate documents, with the City of St. Louis Recorder of Deeds or the St. Louis County Recorder of Deeds. Once recorded, section 442.370 says it isn’t revoked until the revocation is recorded in that same office.
### What does Missouri law expect from the agent?
Trustee-level loyalty. Section 404.714 makes the agent a fiduciary much like a trustee: act for the principal’s benefit, avoid conflicts, no self-dealing and, unless the document authorizes otherwise, use “a high degree of care in maintaining, without modification, any estate plan.” Section 404.712 adds two housekeeping rules. Clearly show you’re acting as agent. Keep the principal’s property separate from everyone else’s. The Missouri Bar shows the signature: your parent’s name, then “by,” then yours, then “POA.”
The CFPB boils the job down to four duties: act only in the person’s best interest, manage the money carefully, keep it separate from yours, and keep good records. Missouri allows reasonable pay and expenses unless the document or an agreement says otherwise, under section 404.725. Keep a log anyway. Section 404.727 lets an adult family member ask the probate court for an accounting once the principal is disabled, incapacitated or dead, and the court can remove an agent who breaches a duty.
An agent who commits willful misconduct or fraud can owe damages, attorney’s fees and punitive damages under section 404.717. If you suspect someone is draining a parent’s accounts with a POA, Missouri’s Adult Abuse and Neglect Hotline takes financial exploitation reports at 1-800-392-0210, and our guide to money scams in St. Louis and how to report them lists the other places to call.
### What happens if a parent can’t sign and there’s no POA?
The family asks a judge. A guardian handles the person’s care, a conservator handles the money, and both run through Chapter 475 in the probate division of the county where the parent lives.
Under section 475.075, the court immediately appoints a lawyer for the parent, the petitioner can’t nominate that lawyer, and the lawyer’s fee is taxed as a cost of the case. The parent can demand a jury, choose whether the hearing is open or closed to the public, and appeal. The family must prove incapacity or disability by clear and convincing evidence, and the court has to apply the least restrictive alternative.
Then the paperwork never really stops. A conservator posts a bond paid from the estate before taking charge, and section 475.270 requires a settlement of accounts every year, within 60 days after the anniversary of the appointment. Guardians file yearly reports too.
St. Louis County’s adult guardianship and conservatorship packet lists the filings: a petition with a financial statement, interested persons and a witness list, a medical affidavit with the diagnosis, and a bond letter when there are assets beyond a Social Security account. The court’s posted fee schedule lists a $115.50 cost deposit to open an adult case, plus $36 for each person the sheriff serves. That’s the cheap part. Lawyers, the bond and years of annual filings are where the money and the months go.
Even then, a durable POA matters. Under section 475.050, a person nominated in a durable power of attorney signed before the incapacity ranks right behind the parent’s own current choice when the court picks a guardian or conservator, ahead of spouses and children.
### How do St. Louis families set one up without wasting money?
Start with the person, not the paper. Section 404.707 qualifies anyone who isn’t barred from serving as a guardian or conservator, which rules out minors, people who are incapacitated themselves and a short list of others. For health care, section 404.815 also rules out your attending physician and the staff of a facility where you live, unless they’re related to you within the second degree. The best pick is usually organized, nearby, honest about money and able to deliver bad news to siblings.
Name one agent and a successor for money, and the same for health care.
Check that the financial POA is titled “Durable Power of Attorney” and carries one of the statute’s durability sentences.
Decide which spelled-out powers you want: gifts, trusts, beneficiary changes, nominating a conservator.
Fill out the Missouri Bar’s health care form and HIPAA authorization, choosing one physician or two and initialing one of the feeding tube boxes.
Sign the POAs before a notary and the directive before two adult witnesses.
Give copies to the agent, the doctors and the bank, and keep the original where the agent can reach it.
If real estate is involved, record the financial POA with the city or county Recorder of Deeds.
Do you need a lawyer? Nothing in the statute requires one, and the Missouri Bar says its health care form can be completed without one. The financial side is where homemade documents break: no durability sentence, no successor, no gift power when Medicaid shows up. For what local attorneys charge for the full set, see what a will or trust costs in Missouri. Money tight? Legal Services of Eastern Missouri runs an Advocates for Older Adults program for people 60 and older, consistent with available resources, and it lists powers of attorney and health care directives among its services. Intake is 314-534-4200. More options: legal services for seniors.
This is general information about Missouri law, not legal advice for your family. An estate planning or elder law attorney can apply it to your situation, and our St. Louis Legal directory is a place to start.
Get it signed while everyone can still sign. Talk to estate planning attorneys around St. Louis and ask whether the financial POA will carry the durability sentence plus spelled-out gift and beneficiary powers.
And if you run an estate planning or elder law practice, the family just turned away at a bank counter needs someone tonight, so see who AI names instead of you.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Does a power of attorney need to be recorded in Missouri?
A.  Usually not. Section 404.705 says a durable power of attorney doesn’t need recording to be valid. The exception is real estate: if the agent will sell, mortgage or otherwise affect property, section 442.360 requires the POA to be recorded like a deed, and a recorded POA isn’t revoked until the revocation is recorded too.
### Q. Can a person do a power of attorney without a lawyer?
A.  Yes. Missouri’s statute sets requirements, not a lawyer requirement: the durable title, a durability statement, a signature, a date and an acknowledgment. The Missouri Bar offers a free health care form for the public. The risk is what a template leaves out, like a successor agent or the gift and beneficiary powers that must be spelled out.
### Q. What are the four types of power of attorney?
A.  Usually general, limited, durable and springing. In Missouri terms, a general power covers all lawful subjects, a limited one covers only the subjects it lists, a durable one survives incapacity using the statute’s wording, and a springing one starts on a future event the document describes. Health care powers sit in a separate law.
### Q. What’s the difference between a POA and a durable power of attorney?
A.  Whether it survives incapacity. A durable power of attorney keeps working after the principal becomes disabled or incapacitated; a non-durable one is suspended while the principal can’t evaluate information or communicate decisions. To be durable in Missouri, the document must carry the durable title and one of the statute’s durability statements, and be acknowledged like a deed.
### Q. Does power of attorney give access to bank accounts?
A.  If it grants general powers for all lawful purposes, yes, including joint accounts to the same extent the principal could act. Banks may still ask for signature specimens and protection against forgery. Without express wording it can’t change payable-on-death beneficiaries, and it doesn’t reach Social Security or VA payments, which need a separate agency appointment.
### Q. Am I responsible for my parent’s debt if I have power of attorney?
A.  The debts stay your parent’s, and the CFPB’s agent guide says to pay them from your parent’s funds, not yours. What can pull you in is how you sign. Missouri law says an agent must clearly show they’re acting as agent, and the Missouri Bar warns that signing only your own name could make you responsible for a bill like the hospital’s.
### Q. What three decisions cannot be made by a legal power of attorney?
A.  Missouri actually lists four. Under section 404.710, no power of attorney can let an agent make, amend or revoke the principal’s will; make, change or revoke a living will declaration; force the principal to act, or not act, against their will; or do anything the principal forbade while competent.
### Q. Can a power of attorney withdraw money from a bank account after death?
A.  No. A Missouri power of attorney ends when the principal dies, apart from a narrow exception for expressly granted autopsy, organ donation and burial powers. The agent’s duty then is to turn property and records over to the estate’s personal representative. Good-faith acts by an agent who didn’t know about the death are protected, but the money itself moves through the estate or beneficiary designations.

## When a Parent Dies in Missouri: Probate, the Small Estate Affidavit and What Skips Court
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/when-a-parent-dies-in-missouri-probate-and-small-estates
The funeral’s over. Picture two grown kids at their late mother’s kitchen table in a brick bungalow in Bevo Mill, a stack of her mail between them and a plan that sounds simple: sell the house, pay what she owed, split the rest. By Friday the plan is in pieces. The bank won’t release a dollar from her checking account, not even to the son who paid her bills for six years. The real estate agent asks a question nobody at the table can answer. Who signs the deed? And her mortgage payment still comes due on the first.
Nobody explained any of this to them. Not the funeral home, not the bank, not one class in twelve years of school. Missouri’s rules for the weeks after a death live in a probate code whose bones date to 1955, and they show up only when you need them. You aren’t bad at this. Nobody showed you.
So here’s the money side: what passes straight to family, what freezes, the $40,000 shortcut and its St. Louis catch, and who really owes the debts. It’s one piece of our St. Louis money guide.
### What happens if you don’t file probate in Missouri?
Anything your parent owned alone, with no co-owner or named beneficiary, stays frozen: the house can’t be sold and the account can’t be released. Missouri also runs a one-year clock. A will not presented to the probate court within a year of death is forever barred, and letters of administration generally can’t issue after that.
Read that last part twice. Under section 473.050, a will has no legal effect until a probate court admits it, and when no estate was opened, it has to be presented within a year of the death or never. The same section bars letters of administration unless someone applies within that year. St. Louis County’s probate division puts it plainly in its general FAQ: the will can be filed any time, but the petition to probate it is due within one year of the date of death.
So what happens to a house when the year passes and nobody filed? The state doesn’t take it. Title passed to the heirs the moment your parent died (RSMo 473.260), but the deed still shows a dead owner, and nobody alive holds paperwork saying who inherited what. If there was a will that never reached the court, it no longer counts. Missouri’s intestacy law picks the heirs instead: with no surviving spouse, the children share equally, and a child who died earlier is represented by their own kids.
To clear title after that first year, an heir petitions the probate court for a determination of heirship. The court publishes notice once a week for four consecutive weeks, holds a hearing, and issues a decree that gets recorded against the property. It works. It’s also slower, public, and every heir has to be accounted for, including the half-brother nobody has an address for.
Sitting still doesn’t keep anyone else from moving, either. If nobody with the right to serve applies within 20 days of the death, Missouri lets any interested person ask the court to open the estate, including a creditor with a sworn claim (RSMo 473.020).
### What skips probate when a parent dies in Missouri?
Anything with a beneficiary or a surviving co-owner built into the title skips probate, and for a lot of St. Louis families that’s more of the money than the will ever touched. Missouri’s Nonprobate Transfers Law says property with a beneficiary designation passes to that beneficiary “by operation of law” at death. No court. No waiting on letters. Here’s how the usual pieces sort out.
Two traps hide in that table. First, a beneficiary deed only works if it was signed and filed with the recorder of deeds before your parent died. One found in a desk drawer after the funeral doesn’t work as a beneficiary deed. For a city property, the Recorder of Deeds offers a free online search of recorded land documents; for a county house, the St. Louis County Recorder of Deeds holds the record.
Second, a will can’t override a beneficiary form. Say Mom’s will splits everything three ways, but the POD on her savings names only one daughter. The POD wins. Missouri law says a will can’t revoke or change a beneficiary designation unless the designation itself allows it (RSMo 461.033). That one blindsides families.
### Why can’t the family sell the house or touch the bank account?
Because nobody has legal authority yet. Property passes at death to the heirs or the will’s beneficiaries, but it stays subject to the executor’s or administrator’s possession and on the hook for the estate’s bills. The family owns it and still can’t hand anyone clean title. Authority comes from paper: letters from the probate court, a small estate affidavit with the clerk’s certificate, or after a year, an heirship decree.
The power of attorney won’t bridge the gap. A power of attorney ends at death, and the Missouri Department of Revenue’s guidance for families says every power of attorney, durable ones included, stops being valid when the person dies. The son at that kitchen table has exactly as much say over his mother’s checking account today as a stranger does.
The car in the driveway is stuck too, unless it had a TOD beneficiary. The DOR lets a surviving spouse or unmarried minor child move one vehicle out of a deceased owner’s name without probate, using Form 2305. Adult children don’t get that path. For them, the department’s titling FAQ requires letters or a small estate affidavit before ownership can transfer.
Meanwhile, the mortgage doesn’t pause for probate. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s report on homeowners after a death says adult children who inherit a family home have to act quickly on payments to avoid foreclosure, that the servicer must tell them which documents prove ownership, and that they can keep paying without taking over the loan.
### When does Missouri’s $40,000 small estate affidavit work?
When everything in your parent’s name alone is worth $40,000 or less after subtracting liens, debts and mortgages, and at least 30 days have passed since the death. That’s the core of section 473.097. It lets an heir collect the property, real estate included, without a full probate case. Anything that already skipped probate, like a POD account or a jointly owned account, doesn’t count toward the limit.
The net figure is where families misread it. Say Mom’s bungalow would sell for about $150,000 and still carries a $118,000 mortgage. That’s $32,000 of equity. Add $6,000 in a checking account with no POD and the estate comes to $38,000, under the line. Now picture the same house paid off. Same checking account, $156,000 total, nowhere close. The house your parents spent decades paying off is the one that needs full probate.
The statute also calls for a bond, a guarantee bought from a surety company that the debts get paid, though the court can waive it. Above $15,000, the clerk publishes a notice to creditors for two weeks. And the signer’s personal liability for unpaid bills is capped at what they received.
Now the St. Louis catch. National articles pitch this as the do-it-yourself route, and Missouri’s statute does let an heir make the affidavit (or, if a will was filed, the executor it names). Locally, it runs through a lawyer. St. Louis County’s probate division (21st Judicial Circuit) states on its small estate packet that the affidavit “cannot be done pro se,” meaning without an attorney. The City of St. Louis probate division (22nd Judicial Circuit) builds an attorney’s signature and bar number into its own small estate form. The bond differs too: the county waives it automatically at $15,000 or less, while the city’s checklist asks for a corporate surety bond covering all the property, rounded up to the next thousand.
The county does leave one door open. If one of you paid for the funeral, Missouri treats you as a creditor for this purpose (RSMo 473.090), and a creditor’s application for refusal of letters is one of the few probate filings St. Louis County accepts without an attorney. It reaches up to $15,000 of personal property when there’s no surviving spouse or unmarried minor child. The county’s creditor packet wants the itemized funeral bill marked paid in full with your name as the payer, and it can’t move real estate. Keep that receipt.
### Can you clean out a house before probate?
Not the valuable parts, and not yet. Locking up, keeping the heat on and emptying the fridge protect the place. Selling furniture, splitting up jewelry or hauling the contents to the curb before anyone has authority is where families get hurt, because Missouri gives the court-appointed personal representative the right to take possession of all of a parent’s personal property (RSMo 473.263).
Here’s why it matters on paper. Within 30 days of appointment, that personal representative files an inventory of everything the parent owned, furniture and household goods included (RSMo 473.233). A missing ring shows up as a gap.
