In January 2025, the farm cooperative CHS won exclusive rights to move fertilizer through the city’s Municipal River Terminal.
Grain is the cargo to watch this fall. For the week ending Oct. 3, 2026, grain barge movements at Lock 27 ran 60 percent below the same week last year and 42 percent under the three-year average, USDA’s Grain Transportation Report found. Freight went the other way. USDA put the St. Louis barge rate at $28.85 a ton on Oct. 6, 53 percent above a year earlier.
### Where is the port of St. Louis, and who runs it?
Along the city’s riverfront. The St. Louis Port District covers 19.3 miles of riverbank, from river mile 171.9 to 191.2, and the wider Port of Metropolitan St. Louis covers 70 miles of both banks, according to the Missouri Port Authorities website. The St. Louis Port Authority, part of the St. Louis Development Corporation, is the landlord.
The public dock most people mean is the Municipal River Terminal, about 1.5 miles north of downtown. SCF Lewis and Clark Terminals, an Ingram company, runs it under a 25-year lease signed in 2015, on a 2,000-foot dock with direct rail. About 18 million tons of freight move through it each year, the Illinois Business Journal reported in 2025.
The city calls the terminal “the northern-most lock- and ice-free port on the Mississippi River.” Read that next to the St. Paul dates above and it clicks. North of here, every barge waits its turn at a lock, and the top of the river waits out the ice. St. Louis does neither. As we read it, that goes a long way toward explaining the size of the harbor.
How big is the port? Depends who’s counting, and which year. The newest ranking we found comes from the St. Louis Regional Freightway in March 2025, using 2022 Corps data: the region is the most efficient inland port district in the U.S., moving 369,309 tons per river mile against an average of 92,863 for the other eight districts. Its five metro ports along 70 river miles handled nearly 26 million tons that year. Older pages still quote rankings built on older data, so check the date on whatever you read.
### Can you take your own boat through the locks?
Yes, and it costs nothing. Pull the signal cord on the approach wall or call the lock on VHF channel 14, the Minnesota DNR’s Mississippi River boating guide says, and hold your lines by hand instead of tying off. Federal rules give commercial tows precedence, but if pleasure boats can’t lock through within the time of three other lockages, they get one of their own.
Going all the way? The National Park Service puts the Mississippi at about 2,350 miles from Lake Itasca, and you can’t float every mile. Up around Minneapolis, the Coon Rapids Dam and the Upper St. Anthony Falls Dam have no working locks, so every boater portages around them. The St. Anthony Falls carry alone runs 1.54 miles.
Near St. Louis, the advice for small boats is firm: stay out of the Chain of Rocks Canal. The Mississippi River Water Trail calls it narrow, with “no safe place to pull aside if barge traffic is heavy.” Its route keeps to the main river and, when the St. Louis gauge reads below 16 feet, makes a 200-foot portage on river left, the Illinois side, at Chouteau Island, near river mile 190.3.
Add barge tows and floating debris to the current and the river downtown is water for experienced paddlers with a plan. New to paddling? Start with our guide to kayaking in St. Louis. Pricing a boat first? Our breakdown of what boating costs near St. Louis covers the money and who needs a license. And if you’d rather spend the day beside the water than on it, find a beach near St. Louis instead.
### When does the river close to barge traffic?
Only at the extremes, and it wasn’t closed as of Oct. 10, 2026. That day the St. Louis gauge read about 16.3 feet, and we found no Coast Guard restriction on the harbor. USDA’s Oct. 8 grain report called river levels supportive of “generally reliable navigation.” Floods and droughts are what shut it.
High water first. Above 38 feet on the St. Louis gauge, the National Weather Service says, the Coast Guard will consider closing the harbor to navigation. Above 45 feet, it will consider closing the river to all vessel traffic from downtown St. Louis to Chester, Illinois. The harbor closure isn’t hypothetical. On May 3, 2019, and again on May 23, the Coast Guard closed the harbor between river miles 179 and 184 for “extremely high water levels and fast-moving currents.”
Low water shuts the river a different way. In dry years the Coast Guard caps how deep barges can load and how wide tows can run, and sometimes it closes stretches outright. In early October 2022, it closed the river near Stack Island, Mississippi, and the Associated Press reported more than 2,000 barges waiting there. At St. Louis, the Corps kept its 9-foot channel open, but loads had to be lighter, a Corps spokesman told St. Louis Public Radio.
This year has swung both ways. Last winter the St. Louis gauge bottomed out at minus 4.49 feet on Jan. 21, 2026, its lowest reading since 2013, NWS records show. The gauge’s zero is a reference mark, not the riverbed. Then came this fall. The gauge read minus 0.9 feet on Sept. 11 and 23.9 feet on Oct. 6, a rise of nearly 25 feet in 26 days by our count from National Weather Service data. The forecast issued Oct. 10 had it sliding back to about 2 feet by Oct. 24.
Planning a lock tour or a paddle for late October? Check the NWS gauge for St. Louis, ID EADM7, the morning you go.
### How deep does the water need to be, and how fast do tows move?
The Corps’ St. Louis District maintains a channel 9 feet deep and 300 feet wide on 300 miles of the Mississippi, from Saverton, Missouri, to Cairo, Illinois, plus the lower 80 miles of the Illinois River and the lower 36 of the Kaskaskia. When the St. Louis gauge falls below 1 foot, the NWS says, barges may need to lighten loads, and dredging may be needed to hold that depth. Locks add a margin of their own: under federal rules, a vessel’s draft must be at least 3 inches less than the depth over the sills.
Speed is fuzzier than you’d expect. No agency we checked publishes a current official tow speed, so treat these as rough: about 3 to 6 mph pushing upstream and about 10 to 12 mph downstream, depending on current, load and tow size. Those ranges lean on river guides, Corps averages from the 1970s and a 2024 NTSB report that clocked one southbound tow at 12.9 mph over the ground.
Why the gap? Going south, ACBL’s Hettel said, a towboat has to move faster than the water to keep steering; going north, it burns much more fuel. The river itself runs under 3 mph at St. Louis at low flow and reached an estimated 7.6 mph at the 1993 crest, according to USGS. Near lock gates, a Corps navigation notice holds tows to 2 mph, the “rate of a slow walk.”
### What do barge crews earn, and how do the schedules work?
Solid money, on a hard schedule. Federal 2025 wage data on the Labor Department’s O*NET site puts the median for sailors and marine oilers, the job group that includes deckhands, at $57,450 in the St. Louis metro, against $51,520 nationally. Captains, mates and pilots earn a metro median of $94,990, and $92,460 nationwide.
Ship engineers do better still, with a national median of $109,530, though O*NET lists no Missouri figure for them. The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects water transportation jobs to grow 4 percent from 2025 to 2035, with about 8,600 openings a year.
The schedule is the real adjustment. At Golding Barge Line, the standard for deckhands is 28 days on the boat and 14 days off, and the whole crew lives, eats and works aboard. ACBL told the federal webinar that its lower Mississippi towboats run 28 days on and 28 off, while harbor boats work 14 on and 7 off. BLS puts it plainly: crews on barges “may spend weeks or months away from home and work on board for long periods 7 days a week.”
So do deckhands get days off? Yes, in blocks of weeks at home rather than weekends. The ladder can be short, too. Golding says a deckhand who moves up to tankerman in about 12 to 18 months more than doubles the starting deckhand wage. One line on its hiring page is worth knowing before anything else: applicants have to be able to swim.
Not ready for 28 days on a towboat? Start earning with no experience
### What sank in the river around St. Louis?
Plenty, and low water keeps bringing it back. The best-known wreck is the USS Inaugural, a World War II minesweeper that served as a museum ship here from 1968. During the August 1993 flood it broke loose from its moorings, took on water through a breach in its hull and rolled onto its side, the National Park Service says.
The ship had cleared 82 mines and earned two battle stars, and it was a National Historic Landmark from 1986 until 2001. It still lies partly submerged south of the Poplar Street Bridge, and low water exposed it in 2012, 2015, 2021 and 2022. For the flood that put it there, see our story on the Great Flood of 1993.
The Missouri River has its own. The 250-foot steamboat Montana, built in 1879 for the Missouri River trade, struck a pier of the Wabash Railroad Bridge on June 22, 1884, and sank with no lives lost, Waterways Journal recounts. Low water uncovered the wreck again in 2012 and 2022.
Fire did worse. On May 17, 1849, the Great Fire began aboard the steamboat White Cloud and burned 23 steamboats, 15 square blocks and more than 400 buildings, St. Louis Magazine reported. Three deaths were confirmed, among them fire captain Thomas Targee.
The deadliest happened downriver. On April 27, 1865, the steamer Sultana exploded near Memphis. Licensed for 376 passengers, it was carrying more than 2,400, most of them soldiers just freed from Confederate prison camps, with one lifeboat aboard. The Coast Guard calls it “the worst marine disaster in American history.” Estimates of the dead conflict, but the toll was well over 1,000.
Most people in this city know the barges as slow gray shapes in the corner of somebody’s skyline photo. You’re the one who knows why a tow downtown can run twice the size of one at the locks, where the harbor parks up to 1,750 barges and what the crew on that towboat takes home. Next clear afternoon, walk the levee and count the barges in the first tow that passes. Then drive up to the locks for the 3 p.m. tour and count again.
If an afternoon of counting barges has you wanting a hull of your own, start with the boat dealers and boating businesses in St. Louis we list.
If you run a towing company, a fleeting operation or a marine repair shop that hires deckhands, list your business with us and put your company in front of the readers who just learned what a 28-day hitch pays and want to know who’s hiring on this harbor.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much do barge workers make on the Mississippi river?
A.  Federal 2025 wage data on O*NET puts the median for sailors and marine oilers, the group that includes deckhands, at $57,450 in the St. Louis metro and $51,520 nationally. Captains, mates and pilots earn a metro median of $94,990. Golding Barge Line says moving up to tankerman can more than double starting deckhand pay.
### Q. Do deckhands get days off?
A.  Yes, in blocks rather than weekends. Golding Barge Line’s standard deckhand schedule is 28 days on the boat and 14 off, with the crew living aboard. ACBL has said its lower Mississippi towboats run 28 days on and 28 off. While aboard, BLS notes, crews may work seven days a week for long stretches.
### Q. Is the Mississippi river closed to barge traffic?
A.  Not as of Oct. 10, 2026. The St. Louis gauge read about 16.3 feet, we found no Coast Guard restriction on the harbor, and USDA called levels supportive of “generally reliable navigation.” Closures come at the extremes: above about 38 feet the Coast Guard considers shutting the harbor, and in drought it caps drafts and tow widths.
### Q. How fast does a barge go on the Mississippi river?
A.  There’s no official figure, so treat these as approximate: roughly 3 to 6 mph pushing upstream and about 10 to 12 mph downstream, depending on current, load and tow size. The ranges come from river guides, 1970s Corps averages and a 2024 NTSB report. Near lock gates, tows slow to about 2 mph.
### Q. How deep does a river have to be for a barge?
A.  On the Mississippi from Saverton, Missouri, to Cairo, Illinois, the Army Corps of Engineers maintains a channel 9 feet deep and 300 feet wide. Barges load to about 11.5 feet of draft where the river allows, ACBL says. Below 1 foot on the St. Louis gauge, the NWS warns, barges may need to lighten loads.
### Q. Where is the port of St. Louis?
A.  Along the city’s Mississippi riverfront. The St. Louis Port District covers 19.3 miles of riverbank, river miles 171.9 to 191.2, and the wider Port of Metropolitan St. Louis spans 70 miles of both banks. Its main public dock, the Municipal River Terminal, sits about 1.5 miles north of downtown, run by an Ingram company.
### Q. What are some examples of sunken ships in the Mississippi river?
A.  At St. Louis, the USS Inaugural, a World War II minesweeper turned museum ship, broke loose in the 1993 flood and still lies on its side south of the Poplar Street Bridge. The Great Fire of 1849, which began on the steamboat White Cloud, burned 23 steamboats. Near Memphis, the Sultana exploded in 1865 carrying more than 2,400 people.
### Q. Can you take a boat the entire Mississippi River?
A.  Not without carrying it. The National Park Service puts the river at about 2,350 miles from Lake Itasca, and around Minneapolis the Coon Rapids and Upper St. Anthony Falls dams have no working locks, so boaters portage. Locking through elsewhere is free. Near St. Louis, paddlers skip the Chain of Rocks Canal and portage on Chouteau Island when the gauge is below 16 feet.

## Sharks in the Mississippi at St. Louis: The One Real Bull Shark, Stray Gators and Giant Catfish
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/sharks-in-the-mississippi-river-st-louis
Forget the headlines. In July 2021, a wave of stories announced that two bull sharks had swum up the Mississippi all the way to St. Louis. TV station websites ran it. Science blogs ran it. It was a terrific summer story, and that same year a Missouri Department of Conservation biologist took a closer look at one of the two fish. It wasn’t a bull shark.
So here’s the honest count. One bull shark. It came out of the river on the Illinois side in 1937, and it’s still the only accepted bull shark record anywhere in the upper Mississippi. The second “St. Louis shark” was a different species entirely, probably a hoax or a dumped fish, and the researchers who had counted it published a correction in 2023. Plenty of the 2021 stories are still online, still saying two.
The true version is a better story anyway, and it opens onto a bigger one. This stretch of river holds a 124-pound catfish record, a fish whose paddle-shaped snout senses electricity, and a World War II minesweeper lying on its side on the riverbed. This page sorts the real from the viral using biologists’ papers, state wildlife agencies and USGS surveys, checked in October 2026. It’s one chapter of our guide to the St. Louis riverfront, written for the kid who asked “are there sharks in there?” and the grown-up who wasn’t sure what to say.
### Has there ever been a bull shark found in the Mississippi river?
Yes, once. In late summer 1937, two commercial fishermen caught a 5-foot, 84-pound bull shark on the Illinois side of the Mississippi, about 20 river miles above downtown St. Louis. Biologists confirmed it from photographs and published it in the journal Copeia in 1977. It remains the only accepted bull shark record in the upper Mississippi.
Every version of the story agrees on the size and argues about the rest. Herbert Cope and Dudge Collins fished commercially on that stretch of the river. In one account, credited to the old Illinois Department of Conservation, something kept wrecking their wood-and-mesh fish traps, so they built a heavy wire trap, baited it with chicken guts and found the shark inside the next morning. Another account says it got tangled in a seine. Either way, two working fishermen ended up with a fish nobody expected.
They put it on display at a fish market, and it drew crowds for days. Some people smelled a hoax even then. Forty years later, three researchers, J.E. Thomerson, T.B. Thorson and R.L. Hempel, concluded from the photographs that it was a bull shark and wrote it up for Copeia.
What the record lacks matters, too. There’s no preserved specimen in a museum jar. Nobody pinned down the exact date or the exact spot, and “late summer 1937” is as close as it gets. A descendant’s family legend says Collins bought the shark at a St. Louis fish market and showed it around as his own catch. Scientists who revisited the case in 2023 didn’t buy it. They wrote that the record “has never been satisfactorily falsified,” and that no first-hand evidence against it has surfaced in 85 years.
How far had it come? By the river-mile charts that USGS and the Army Corps keep, the catch site sits more than 1,100 river miles from the Gulf. That’s a long haul upstream for an animal most of us picture in the ocean. The bank where it happened makes a full day on the Illinois river road, and the shark is a good story for the drive.
### What happened to the second shark in the 2021 headlines?
It wasn’t a bull shark. The second fish, about 3 feet 2 inches long and taken off a power-plant intake screen at Rush Island in Jefferson County in 1995, was re-examined in 2021 by Missouri Department of Conservation (MDC) fisheries biologist Robert Hrabik. He identified it as an Atlantic sharpnose shark, a species never reported from rivers.
His conclusion was blunt. The fish was most likely “an improperly dumped individual if not an outright hoax.” Translation: somebody probably put it there.
The mix-up had a paper trail. A 2004 USDA Forest Service report listed the Rush Island fish as a bull shark that did “not appear to be the product of a hoax.” In spring 2021, researchers R. Shell and N. Gardner leaned on that listing in a study of bull shark movement in the upper Mississippi, counting just two upper-river specimens in the entire 20th century. That’s where the July 2021 “two bull sharks” stories came from.
To their credit, Shell and Gardner went back. Their 2023 follow-up, written with Hrabik, printed the 1995 photo and formally retracted the earlier acceptance. The 1937 fish was left standing alone as the only known record in the upper basin. That’s how science is supposed to work. The headlines never got a second edition.
Missouri has seen sillier shark scares. In October 2019, a prank site’s story about a bull shark pulled from the Osage River spread across social media, and MDC’s response was “BULL SHARK? BALONEY!” The department said no bull sharks had been caught in Missouri waters. Federal fish biologists added that decades of sampling on the Mississippi along eastern Missouri had never netted a shark of any kind.
So when the next shark clip makes the rounds, ask two things. Where, exactly? And which biologist looked at it? The 1937 fish had photographs and three scientists behind it. Most viral sharks have a caption and a lot of exclamation points.
### How can a saltwater shark survive in a river?
By making its kidneys work overtime. In fresh water, a bull shark has to hold onto salt and shed extra water, so it lowers the urea in its body and puts out about 20 times more urine, with much less salt in it, than it does in the sea, according to the University of Texas program Science and the Sea.
Yes, kids, that means a shark in fresh water spends a lot of its day peeing. It burns plenty of energy doing it, too. The Save Our Seas Foundation describes a whole-body job, with the gills, rectal glands, blood, hormones and kidneys all taking part.
The Florida Museum of Natural History says bull sharks “readily move into freshwater” and can stay there for long periods. That’s why a bull shark is everyone’s first guess when a shark turns up somewhere it shouldn’t. Some travel astonishingly far. The University of Texas program reports bull sharks more than 2,000 miles up the Amazon. Next to that, 1,100 miles up the Mississippi sounds almost modest.
### Why is a bull shark this far upriver so rare?
Partly because the trip is rare to begin with, and partly because of the dams. A 2023 paper by Shell, Gardner and Hrabik found nothing verified upriver since the locks and dams went in, which “strongly suggests” those structures limited the bull shark’s upriver range for much of the 20th century.
The dates line up. The Army Corps built the original Lock and Dam 26, about 2 miles upstream of today’s structure, between 1934 and 1938. The 1937 shark came through while that dam was still going up. Its replacement, Melvin Price Locks and Dam, went into operation on October 10, 1989, and the old dam came down in 1990. Those locks now lift and lower the tows pushing barges on the Mississippi, and no shark has been verified following them through.
Cold water is the answer most people guess. It isn’t the whole story. Shell and Gardner noted in 2021 that the river near the 1937 catch site reaches or beats the bull shark’s average preferred temperature for a large part of the year. Summer water here is warm enough for a shark.
The plainest answer is that these long trips are, in the 2023 paper’s words, “exceptional and rare events.” Most young bull sharks presumably stay in the lower reaches of rivers. A 1938 report put bull sharks about 300 kilometers up the Mississippi in Louisiana. There are records from the Red River, and an 1829 “white shark” caught at Natchez, Mississippi, was probably a bull shark, judging by its size and the fresh water it came from. Beyond the 1937 fish, though, nothing north of Louisiana has been confirmed anywhere in the Mississippi basin.
How far north is that on a map? The 1937 catch site sits at about 38.9 degrees north, the farthest upstream accepted record in the Mississippi system. Bull sharks have been farther north, just not by river. Summer migrations along the Atlantic coast carry them to Chesapeake Bay and off New England.
So if a kid won’t wade in at a beach near St. Louis because of sharks, you can honestly say the only confirmed one around here was caught in 1937. Save your respect for the Mississippi’s current. At the 1993 flood crest, USGS estimated it downtown at up to 7.6 mph, and that, not a fin, is the river’s real hazard.
### What really lives in the Mississippi at St. Louis?
Bigger fish than the shark, for a start. Tim Pruitt’s blue catfish, caught just below Melvin Price Locks and Dam in May 2005, weighed 124 pounds, 40 more than the 1937 bull shark. It was a world record then and is still the Illinois record, says the Illinois Department of Natural Resources.
Pruitt’s fish measured 58 inches with a 44-inch girth, and the Associated Press reported that it dragged his boat during a fight of more than half an hour. It died on the way to an aquarium afterward. One correction for the internet, since a bad number keeps circulating: the 143-pound blue catfish behind today’s world record came from Kerr Lake, Virginia, in 2011. A 130-pound blue caught on the Missouri River north of the city in 2010 set a Missouri record. Neither came out of the Mississippi.
Giant blues aren’t new. MDC says fish over 100 pounds were common in Missouri before 1900, and reports from the 1800s run as high as 315 pounds. The twist is that blue catfish have nearly disappeared from the Mississippi above the mouth of the Missouri River, partly because dams hamper their seasonal runs upstream. Sound familiar? The same structures may have stopped the sharks.
The rest of the cast, from MDC’s field guides:
Flathead catfish. Commonly 1 to 45 pounds, up to about 100. It hunts live fish and crayfish at night and isn’t a scavenger.
Paddlefish. Missouri’s official state aquatic animal, up to about 7 feet and 160-plus pounds. The paddle is an electrosensory organ that finds plankton, and since the Chinese paddlefish was declared extinct in 2022, it’s the last living member of a family about 120 million years old.
Pallid sturgeon. Endangered under federal and Missouri law. It lives at least 40 years, and if you hook one, it goes back unharmed.
Lake sturgeon. Up to 8 feet and 300 pounds, and it can live 150 years. MDC started stocking them in 1984, and the first confirmed spawning in Missouri came in 2015, below Melvin Price.
Silver carp. An invasive fish whose adults leap out of the water at any disturbance and can injure boaters. One female can produce 500,000 eggs.
Freshwater drum. It grunts, using muscles on its swim bladder, and its ear bones get collected as “lucky stones.”
Freshwater mussels. Called “the livers of the rivers” because they filter water. Missouri has about 69 native species, and nearly 42 percent are species of conservation concern.
The strangest visitor in the record books wasn’t a shark at all. In fall 2006, a West Indian manatee about 10 feet long swam more than 1,200 kilometers up the Mississippi to near Memphis. It was first spotted on October 23, slipped past federal, state and SeaWorld search teams using sonar and infrared, and was found dead 49 days later. It’s a sad ending to a remarkable swim.
Want to try for a big blue yourself? Our list of fishing spots in St. Louis includes places on the Mississippi. Pack a heavy rod and a kid who doesn’t mind waiting.
### Should you eat the fish you catch here?
Yes, in moderation. The Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services advisory, last updated March 2024, tells everyone to eat flathead, channel and blue catfish over 17 inches and common carp over 21 inches from the Mississippi no more than once a week, because of PCBs, chlordane and mercury. Shovelnose sturgeon and buffalo: once a month.
Never eat sturgeon eggs, the advisory says. Stricter limits apply to pregnant women, women of childbearing age, nursing mothers and children under 13, including one meal a month of those catfish once they pass 30 inches. A meal, by Missouri’s count, is 8 ounces of uncooked fish for a 150-pound adult and 3 ounces for a 40-pound child.
Cross the river and the same water gets different rules. Illinois’s advisory, updated April 2026, sets common carp at one meal a week and shovelnose sturgeon at one a month for everyone. It has carried no catfish advisory on the Mississippi since 2023. Its statewide mercury rule asks pregnant or nursing women, women who may become pregnant and kids under 15 to stick to one meal a week of predatory fish, gar and flatheads included.
Both states agree on the easy wins. Fillet the fish, take the skin off and trim the fat. That cuts your exposure, though trimming does nothing for mercury. Keep the smaller legal fish and, as Missouri puts it, “release the lunkers.” PCB manufacturing stopped in 1977 and chlordane was banned in 1988, but both still persist.
Craving fish nobody pulled from the Mississippi? Poke bowls in St. Louis
### Where do the alligators spotted around St. Louis come from?
From somebody’s house. The Missouri Department of Conservation says alligators aren’t native wildlife in Missouri, and the species’ natural range ends in northeast Arkansas. The gators found around St. Louis are escaped or dumped pets, and the Bi-State Wildlife Hotline’s director says she’s done more alligator rescues than she can count.
The local cases read like a neighborhood group chat. In July 2021, an alligator about 4.5 feet long lived for roughly two weeks in a creek behind a home in west St. Louis County after escaping its enclosure. The hotline caught it and returned it to its owner. In June 2022, a 2.5-foot pet named Zurich got out of its outdoor pen on Wyoming Street in south St. Louis during storms, and police handed it over to city animal control.
Is owning one even legal? Depends which side of the river you live on. Illinois bans pet alligators except for specific educational purposes, and a gator of any size is illegal in the City of St. Louis, hotline director Angel Wintrode told St. Louis Public Radio in August 2026. Missouri state law lets someone keep a dangerous reptile without a permit until it reaches 8 feet. After that, it has to be registered with county law enforcement.
Crocodiles are an easier no. In the United States, they live only in south Florida, and there are none in the Mississippi. If you do spot a gator around town, the hotline and animal control are the people who handle it.
### What is the alligator gar, the “gator” that belongs here?
A native fish. MDC says alligator gar can reach 10 feet and 300 pounds, far bigger than any other gar, and once lived in the Mississippi at least as far upstream as the mouth of the Illinois River. There are no authenticated attacks on people. In Missouri the species is critically imperiled and protected.
It’s an old design. Fossils date the species to the early Cretaceous, so alligator gar were swimming while dinosaurs walked. Like all four of Missouri’s gars, it gulps air into a lung-like swim bladder. One warning for curious cooks: MDC says the eggs are highly toxic to warm-blooded animals, people included.
In 1923, a Field Museum curator wrote that alligator gar were “common in the Mississippi River about to St. Louis.” Then they mostly vanished. The last one caught in Illinois before reintroduction came out of a diversion channel in Alexander County, at the state’s southern tip, in 1966. It was about 7 feet long and weighed about 130 pounds.
Here’s the detail no shark post mentions. In spring 1937, the same year as the bull shark, an alligator gar about 6.5 feet long and about 130 pounds was captured on the Monroe County, Illinois, floodplain, and another 25 to 30 big gar were seen nearby, according to a 2019 paper in the Journal of Applied Ichthyology. So 1937 was a two-monster year on this river. Only one of the monsters became a legend.
Both states are bringing the gar back, partly because it’s one of the few native fish big enough to eat invasive carp. MDC began stocking in 2007 at Mingo National Wildlife Refuge and expanded to Bootheel conservation areas in 2013. Illinois stocked 21,665 alligator gar into 12 water bodies from 2010 to 2025. We couldn’t find a recent record of one near St. Louis. Hook one in Missouri, and it goes back in the water.
### What’s lying on the riverbed at St. Louis?
Mostly moving sand. A USGS sonar survey at the Poplar Street Bridge in August 2020 found the bed shaped into underwater dunes covered with smaller dunes and ripples, and bridge plans show roughly 71 to 92 feet of loose sand and gravel above bedrock near one pier. South of that bridge, a World War II minesweeper lies on its side.
Think of a sand desert, only underwater and always on the move. USGS sorts these dunes by height, and medium ones stand 5 to 10 feet tall. The deepest channel that day ran along the Illinois bank, 12 to 15 feet deeper than the rest of the bed, and the lowest point was a scour hole at one of the bridge piers. The report notes that scour is the leading cause of bridge failures in the U.S.
How deep does it get? At low flow, the deepest water is under 30 feet, USGS says. At the 1993 crest, the river near the Arch ran an estimated 87 feet deep.
Then there’s the ship. The USS Inaugural cleared 82 mines in World War II and earned two battle stars, and from 1968 it was a floating museum on the riverfront. On August 1, 1993, at the crest of the 1993 flood in St. Louis, it broke loose, rolled onto its side and sank. The National Park Service declared it a total loss. Low water has exposed the wreck in 2012, 2015, October 2021, when the gauge read 3.85 feet, and again in fall 2022.
The next time a shark post makes the rounds and somebody in the comments swears an uncle saw a fin, you’ll know the real count. One bull shark, in 1937. One Atlantic sharpnose that never belonged in a river. And a 124-pound catfish that outweighed the real shark by 40 pounds. You’re the one who knows what actually lives in the Mississippi. Take the kids down to the bank with a rod, a copy of the fish advisory and a good story, and see what bites.
Before that first trip, find bait, tackle and someone who knows the river among the fishing shops and guides in St. Louis we list.
If you run a bait shop or guide anglers after the big blue catfish below the locks, list your business with us and reach more customers: the families this page turns from shark hunters into first-time catfish anglers are already headed your way.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Are there sharks in the Mississippi at St. Louis today?
A.  None have been verified. The only accepted upper Mississippi record is the 1937 bull shark. The 1995 Rush Island fish turned out to be an Atlantic sharpnose shark and a probable hoax, and MDC said in 2019 that no bull sharks had been caught in Missouri waters. Treat any new viral video with suspicion until a biologist confirms it.
### Q. How far north are bull sharks in the Mississippi river?
A.  In the Mississippi system, the farthest accepted record is the 1937 bull shark caught on the Illinois side about 20 river miles above downtown St. Louis, at roughly 38.9 degrees north. Nothing has been verified that far upriver since the locks and dams went in, which a 2023 paper says “strongly suggests” the dams limit how far they get.
### Q. Has a bull shark ever been found in Illinois?
A.  Yes, once. In late summer 1937, two commercial fishermen caught a 5-foot, 84-pound bull shark on the Illinois side of the Mississippi, upstream of St. Louis. Biologists confirmed it from photographs, and it remains the only accepted bull shark record in the upper Mississippi. We found no record from the Illinois River itself.
### Q. Does the Mississippi river have crocodiles or alligators?
A.  Not wild ones near St. Louis. MDC says alligators aren’t native to Missouri, and their natural range ends in northeast Arkansas. The gators found around St. Louis, like a 4.5-footer in a west St. Louis County creek in 2021, were escaped or dumped pets. In the U.S., crocodiles live only in south Florida. The native “gator” here is the alligator gar, a fish.
### Q. Is an alligator gar dangerous to people?
A.  No. MDC reports no authenticated attacks on humans, even though alligator gar can reach 10 feet and 300 pounds. The one real warning is about the eggs, which are highly toxic to warm-blooded animals, people included. In Missouri the fish is critically imperiled and protected, so any alligator gar you hook goes back in the water.
### Q. What kind of fish do you catch in the Mississippi river?
A.  Big catfish lead the list: blue, flathead and channel cats all appear in Missouri’s Mississippi River advisory, along with common carp, buffalo and shovelnose sturgeon. Freshwater drum and paddlefish live here too. The Illinois record blue catfish, 124 pounds, came from just below Melvin Price Locks and Dam in 2005. Release any pallid sturgeon: they’re endangered.
### Q. Is it okay to eat fish out of the Mississippi river?
A.  Yes, within limits. Missouri’s advisory, last updated March 2024, says to eat flathead, channel and blue catfish over 17 inches and carp over 21 inches from the Mississippi no more than once a week, shovelnose sturgeon and buffalo once a month, and sturgeon eggs never. Kids under 13 and pregnant or nursing women get stricter limits. Illinois’s rules differ slightly.
### Q. What is at the bottom of the Mississippi river?
A.  At St. Louis, mostly moving sand. A 2020 USGS sonar survey at the Poplar Street Bridge found the bed shaped into underwater dunes, and bridge plans show roughly 71 to 92 feet of loose sand and gravel above bedrock near one pier. The wreck of the USS Inaugural, a World War II minesweeper that sank in the 1993 flood, lies on its side south of that bridge.

## A Pope Came Back for It: Polish Food in St. Louis and What to Order
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/polish-food-in-st-louis-what-to-order
Thirty years after his first bite, a pope asked for a St. Louis smoked sausage again. Karol Wojtyla tried it in 1969, when he was still a cardinal. When he visited St. Louis in 1999 as Pope John Paul II, he asked for it again. The family shop that made it, Piekutowski’s European Style Sausage, tells the story on its about page as plainly as you’d mention that a regular likes extra mustard.
You can taste why without leaving your kitchen. Lay a link of that smoked kielbasa in a hot pan and inside a minute the room smells of garlic and hickory. The skin tightens and shines. Fat spits at the edge of the pan. Then your fork goes in and the casing snaps, and a little steam comes out with it. That snap tells you most of what you need to know about Polish food in this city.
The shop is open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. and Saturday from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m., and it’s closed on Sundays. Call (314) 254-0499 before you drive over, and ask what’s in the case that day.
It doesn’t live on a restaurant row. You won’t find a block of Polish bistros the way you find red sauce and toasted ravioli on The Hill. Polish St. Louis eats in parish halls, out of butcher-paper bundles and from freezer cases at a sausage counter, and it keeps a calendar instead of a menu. The best of it shows up on parish festival days, on Christmas Eve, and in the sugar-dusted days before Lent. Miss the date and you’re eating frozen pierogi from the supermarket, wondering what the fuss was about.
Below is what to put on your plate, from pierogi and kielbasa to barszcz and a jam-heavy pączek, and the days St. Louis still serves them. The nearest one is Sunday, November 8, at the Polish Heritage Center next to St. Stanislaus Kostka, a church close to downtown that was established in 1880 to serve the Polish community. The fall celebration runs from 11:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. Get there early if you want the sampler plate; it goes until it’s sold out.
### What is a typical Polish meal?
A typical Polish meal is smoked sausage, sauerkraut, a filled dumpling, a beet soup and good bread: sour, salty, filling and built to get you through a winter. In St. Louis the clearest picture of it is the sampler plate at St. Stanislaus Kostka’s festivals, which the parish has listed at $15 for Polish sausage, bread, sauerkraut, pierogi, borscht, and beets or applesauce.
Look at that plate and you’re looking at a whole country’s pantry. The sausage is pork, garlic and smoke, with a casing that snaps when your fork goes in. The sauerkraut is cabbage that sat in brine until it turned sharp enough to make your jaw tighten. The pierogi are soft half-moons, still glossy with butter. The borscht, barszcz in Polish, is beets, and it bleeds pink into the edge of the paper plate. Nothing on it is fancy. All of it was built to keep.
Now stand in that line on festival day. The hall at the Polish Heritage Center is warm before you reach the table, and the air is hickory smoke and sour cabbage. The pierogi land on your plate still slick with butter, the sausage goes on beside them, and the paper sags in your hand on the walk to a folding chair. Here’s the line to repeat to whoever you dragged along: fifteen dollars buys the Polish sampler meal, sausage to borscht, served by a parish that a St. Louis judge ruled controls its own church property. Carry-outs are available, too, so buy a second plate to go. That’s tomorrow’s lunch, already paid for.
And if you only get one thing on your first try, make it the plate with everything on it. You’ll learn more in ten forkfuls than in any menu description, including this one.
### Who kept Polish food alive north of downtown?
A parish that refused to close. St. Stanislaus Kostka was established in 1880 to serve the Polish community in St. Louis, and it became the mother church for three more Polish parishes: St. Casimir, St. Hedwig and Our Lady of Czestochowa. In 1928 a fire destroyed its center dome and almost all of the original interior, and the dome was never rebuilt. The church still stands at 1413 North 20th Street, a City Landmark since 1976 and on the National Register of Historic Places since 1979.
Karol Wojtyla came here too. The church’s Wikipedia entry records that Karol Wojtyla visited St. Stanislaus in 1969, the same year he first tasted that kielbasa. The Polish families had mostly moved away from the surrounding streets by the 1950s, but the parish kept its people. By the 1970s the buildings were badly deteriorating, so the parishioners restored the church themselves, bought up land around it, and later built the Polish Heritage Center next door, which opened in 2005.
Then came the fight over who controlled the parish and its property. In 2012 a St. Louis judge sided with the parish, writing one memorable line: “The archbishop may own the souls of wayward St. Stanislaus parishioners, but the St. Stanislaus Parish Corporation owns its own property.” A 2013 agreement made St. Stanislaus an independent church, outside the archdiocese and the Roman Catholic Church.
Today it calls itself, on its own parish page, “The Little Polish Church That Refuses to Die.” Its Sunday Mass is at 10 a.m. in English, Polish and Spanish, three languages, one set of pews. On its fall celebration day, $15 buys a Polish sampler plate: sausage, bread, sauerkraut, pierogi, borscht, and beets or applesauce, on a paper plate that bends under the weight. That’s not a quirk of St. Louis, either. After World War II, freshly cooked pierogi became a staple of ethnic church fundraisers in America. A church-hall pierogi isn’t the backup option. It’s the real thing.
Totally different aisle: ever stood confused in a kosher grocery store?
### The sausage a pope came back for
Piekutowski’s has been making sausage in St. Louis since 1940, when Ted Piekutowski Sr. took over the shop he had apprenticed in. Four generations of the family have run it since. The shop says it sticks to natural casings and slow hickory smoke, and hickory is the first thing you taste when the casing snaps.
Here’s what to ask for, straight off the shop’s own menu:
Smoked Polish sausage (kielbasa). Fully cooked, edible casing, made with beef, pork, garlic, salt and pepper. Warm it and slice it. This is the one the pope asked for.
Fresh Polish sausage. Uncooked, sold in the store only, and the menu calls it “a big tradition for the Polish heritage to use at holidays.” Brown it in a pan or bake it.
Kra-Kow. Hand-cut pork and beef, smoked, sliced thin for sandwiches.
Pierogi, 12 to a pack. Fillings run from cheese and cheese potato to kraut, mushroom, meat and kraut mushroom.
Cabbage rolls, four to a container. Sold in the store only, so plan to carry them out yourself.
Call (314) 254-0499 before you go, and call early in December. The shop’s own FAQ tells customers to order early for Christmas and Easter, its busiest times of year, and its menu says mail orders will not be available from December 16-25. If you’re feeding a crowd on Christmas Eve, that week is not the week to discover the line.
### So what actually makes a pierogi, and how do you eat one?
What makes a pierogi a pierogi is simple: unleavened dough wrapped around a filling and cooked in boiling water. The dough is rolled flat and cut, the filling goes in the middle, the dough folds into a half circle, and the seam gets pressed shut so nothing leaks. That pinch along the edge, done with a thumb dusted in flour, is the whole craft. The word itself goes back to an old Slavic root for “feast,” and the recipe dates back to at least 1682, to Poland’s first cookbook.
The filling most people mean when they say pierogi is potato with farmer cheese and fried onion. In Poland that’s pierogi ruskie, “Ruthenian” pierogi, often mistranslated as Russian. Sauerkraut, mushroom and ground meat are the other classics. Sweet pierogi get fruit, most often strawberries or blueberries.
Now, how do Polish people eat pierogi? Boiled first, until they float. Then, very often, fried in butter until the edges turn gold and blister. Savory ones come with sour cream, fried onions, or bacon fat and little bits of bacon. Sweet ones get sour cream stirred with sugar. That’s it. No dipping sauces, no sriracha drizzle. The butter hissing in the pan and the onions going soft and brown are the entire production.
If you bring home a frozen pack from the sausage counter, do exactly that: drop them into a pot of salted, simmering water, wait until they rise, lift them out, then give them a few minutes in a hot pan with butter and a sliced onion. Serve them next to a few rounds of warmed kielbasa and a spoonful of sauerkraut and you’ve built the same plate the parish hall sells.
One more thing worth knowing. U.S. pierogi eating is concentrated in a region dubbed the “Pierogi Pocket,” an area including New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Indiana, Chicago, Detroit, parts of the northern Midwest and southern New England, which accounts for 68 percent of annual U.S. pierogi consumption. Missouri isn’t named in it. That’s why our pierogi hide in church halls and freezer cases instead of on every corner, and why you have to know where to look.
Can’t wait until the next parish festival for a plate of pierogi? Start with Polish Food on St Louis Near Me Directory and find a kitchen, deli or market that cooks it any week of the year.
If you’re the deli, the bakery or the kitchen that still pinches pierogi by hand, the people reading this page are hungry and already looking for you, so list your business where they can find your counter and get more customers from it.
### What is a traditional Polish Christmas Eve meal?
A traditional Polish Christmas Eve meal, called Wigilia, is twelve dishes with no meat, in memory of the twelve Apostles, and it doesn’t start until the first star has been sighted. Before anyone eats, everybody breaks a thin Christmas wafer called opłatek and wishes each other blessings for the coming year. Sometimes there’s a handful of hay under the tablecloth, for the manger. And there’s an extra place set for the “unexpected guest.”
That empty chair has a St. Louis echo. St. Stanislaus quotes an old saying from Poland on its parish page: “When guests arrive, God arrives.” It’s the same idea, a seat kept warm for whoever comes in from the cold.
Why is it meatless? Because the supper follows a day of Catholic abstinence, and the abstinence carries right onto the table: no meat, so fish becomes the main dish. That one rule explains half the Polish menu you’ll ever see. It’s why there are mushroom pierogi and sauerkraut pierogi, why the beet soup is made without a bone, why herring and carp matter so much, and why the stuffed cabbage on that night is filled with mushrooms and rice instead of meat.
The dishes run roughly like this. Soup first: red barszcz with uszka, tiny dumplings filled only with dried wild mushrooms, or a wild mushroom consommé. Then herring in different forms, then carp, which has been the central dish for decades. Pierogi filled with sauerkraut and dried mushrooms. Cooked sauerkraut with yellow split peas. Kutia, sweet with poppy seeds, honey, raisins and nuts. Dried fruit compote, then poppy seed cake. By the time the first star is up, the whole house smells of mushrooms, sour cabbage and fried fish, and the windows are fogged from the inside.
In St. Louis, Wigilia is cooked at home, not ordered off a menu. So plan it like a project. Get your kraut-mushroom pierogi and anything smoked from the sausage counter before the December rush. The Polish Roman Catholic parish, St. Agatha at 9th and Utah in south city, was named the only official Polish church in St. Louis on July 1, 2005, and still holds its Polish Mass at 10 a.m. on Sundays. After Mass is a good moment to ask a parishioner where they buy their opłatek wafers.
### A St. Louis Polish calendar: what to order, and when
Polish food in this city runs on dates. Put these on yours:
Fat Tuesday: pączki. Heavy, sugar-dusted fried doughnuts filled with stewed plum jam or wild rose petal jam, made to use up the lard, sugar, eggs and fruit in the house before Lent. In Poland they’re eaten especially on Fat Thursday. St. Louis keeps Pączki Day on Fat Tuesday. Call your bakery a week ahead and ask when they start frying.
July: the St. Stanislaus Summer Polish Picnic. This year it ran July 12 from 11:30 a.m. to 4 p.m., with a Polish sampler meal, Polish beer, Polish pottery, and free admission and free parking.
Sunday, November 8: the St. Stanislaus Day Fall Celebration. The celebration runs from 11:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. at the Polish Heritage Center: the Polish sampler meal until it sells out, Polish beer and bakery, pottery and a kids’ booth. Carry-outs available, free admission. Go early; the sampler sells out.
Early December: call the sausage counter. Mail orders will not be available from December 16-25, and the shop’s FAQ says Christmas and Easter are its busiest times of year. Mailing a box to family out of town? Get it ordered before the 16th.
Christmas Eve: Wigilia at home. Twelve dishes, no meat, and nobody eats until the first star has been sighted. Watch the sky.
Mark November 8 first. It’s the day the whole menu is in one room, steaming, with a band playing somewhere behind it.
### What else should you order besides pierogi?
Once you’ve had the dumplings, go deeper. Bigos, hunter’s stew, is considered a Polish national dish: chopped meats of several kinds stewed for hours with sauerkraut and fresh cabbage. It’s considered best after it has been repeatedly refrigerated and reheated, which makes it the rare dish that improves while it waits for you. If you see it at a festival table, take it.
For Polish comfort food in its purest form, order gołąbki, cabbage rolls: boiled cabbage leaves wrapped around a filling of minced pork or beef, onions and rice. They show up at weddings and on Christmas Day. It’s the kind of dish that fogs a kitchen window on a January Sunday.
For a starter, try herring salad, the fish cold and slick with oil and chopped onion. And for dessert you have a real choice. Pączki, if it’s late winter. Makowiec, the rolled poppy seed cake. Sernik, a baked cheesecake made with twaróg, the Polish farmer cheese. Or kremówka, puff pastry filled with cream. In June 1999, the same year he asked for that St. Louis kielbasa again, John Paul II recalled eating cream cakes with friends in his hometown after his final school exams. The man had a long memory for food. St. Louis is lucky it fed him well.

### Frequently asked questions about Polish food in St. Louis
### Q. What is the national dish of Poland?
A.  Bigos, hunter’s stew, is considered a Polish national dish: chopped meats of several kinds, often including kielbasa, stewed slowly with sauerkraut and fresh cabbage. It’s considered best after it has been repeatedly refrigerated and reheated.
### Q. Why is Polish Christmas Eve dinner meatless?
A.  The supper follows a day of Catholic abstinence, and the meal itself excludes meat. Fish becomes the main dish, which is why carp, herring and mushroom or sauerkraut pierogi carry the Wigilia table.
### Q. What makes a pierogi a pierogi?
A.  A pierogi is unleavened dough wrapped around a filling, folded into a half-moon, pinched shut and boiled. After that it’s often fried in butter. The filling can be potato and farmer cheese, sauerkraut, mushroom, meat or fruit.
### Q. How do Polish people eat perogies?
A.  Boiled until they float, then often pan-fried in butter. Savory pierogi come with sour cream, fried onions or bacon bits; sweet ones with sour cream mixed with sugar. A few slices of kielbasa and some sauerkraut make it a full plate.
### Q. What is a popular Polish dessert?
A.  Pączki, fried doughnuts traditionally filled with stewed plum jam or wild rose petal jam, are the famous one, and St. Louis celebrates Pączki Day on Fat Tuesday. Makowiec (poppyseed roll), sernik (cheesecake made with twaróg) and kremówka (cream-filled puff pastry) are close behind.
### Q. What are some popular Polish appetizers?
A.  Herring is the classic, often as a salad with oil and chopped onion. A small bowl of barszcz, the beet soup, or a few slices of smoked kielbasa with rye bread also opens a Polish meal well.

## Same Fish, Different Grandmother: Portuguese Food in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/portuguese-food-in-st-louis-what-to-order
Why does Nonna’s fridge smell like the sea every December?
Open it on The Hill the week before Christmas and you see why. A glass baking dish on the bottom shelf, filled to the lip with cold water, and lying in it a slab of fish that went in stiff as a shingle. The water is cloudy. Somebody pours it off over the sink, morning and night, and fills it again from the cold tap, and the whole kitchen carries that faint, clean smell of a harbor. By Christmas Eve the slab has gone soft and pearly, the oil is warming, and there are more coats on the bed upstairs than there are hooks in the hall.
That fish is baccalà, and it is not one family’s quirk. In December 2006, Sauce Magazine ran a Christmas Eve story that put it plainly: baccalà, dried salted cod, is the most common Christmas Eve dish for southern Italians, and you soak the fish for a day or two to get rid of the salt. The same story remembered Maryann Coletti of The Hill celebrating at her grandmother’s house with 20 to 30 family members and friends, the women in the kitchen most of the day. Another cook in the piece, born in Sicily, said the fish tradition began as a way to save money, since it was cheaper than buying meat. “The ocean is free,” she said.
Here is the turn. Carry that dish of cold water across the Atlantic to Portugal and the fish keeps its shape and changes its name. There it is bacalhau. And it is not a side note in Portuguese cooking. It is the national dish of Portugal.
Sit with that for a second. A lot of St. Louis families have been making Portugal’s best-known food every Christmas Eve for generations, in Italian, without ever calling it Portuguese. The stiff slab, the bowl, the patience, the garlic and olive oil at the end. Same fish. Different grandmother.
Want that bowl in your own fridge this week? Start here. A Portuguese buying guide gives a thick center-cut loin, the cut most home cooks want, 48 to 55 hours in cold water with 6 water changes. Small pieces sold as migas need only 6 to 8 hours. Then pick up the phone. DiGregorio’s Italian Market sits at 5200 Daggett Ave. on The Hill, (314) 776-1062, open Monday through Saturday from 8 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. and closed on Sunday. I could not find salt cod listed on its website, so call before you drive and say it plainly: “Do you have baccalà in? Bone-in or boneless? How thick are the pieces, and how many days would you soak them?” If they have it, ask for the stiffest, thickest piece in the box, the one that knocks like a board when you tap it.
That is the real story of Portuguese food in this city. It mostly turns up under other names. Baccalà on a Hill holiday table. Pudim and feijoada at a Brazilian kitchen in Benton Park. A blistered custard tart in a bakery case labeled “egg tart.” Once you learn to spot the family resemblance, you can eat it here, and you can cook it here.
Start with the kitchen. Yemanja Brasil, at 2900 Missouri Ave. in Benton Park, bills itself as fine Brazilian dining in the Midwest, and its owners say they are from Brazil. To be plain, it is a Brazilian restaurant, not a Portuguese one. Brazilian cooking carries a lot of Portugal in it: the caramel flan called pudim, the collard greens shaved thin, the slow onion-and-oil base called refogado. It opens Thursday through Saturday from 5 to 10 p.m. and Sunday from 4 to 9 p.m. Plan for it.
### Which is the national dish of Portugal?
The national dish of Portugal is bacalhau, salted cod. The Portuguese call it fiel amigo, the faithful friend, and on The Hill you already know it by its Italian name, baccalà.
The saying goes that there are 365 ways to cook it, one for every day of the year. It can be baked, fried, grilled or boiled. One Portuguese home cook’s guide says it has been known in Portugal as the “meat of the poor,” which is the same logic as that Sicilian line about the free ocean. Cheap. Keeps for months without a fridge. Feeds a full house if you have the pot for it.
Here’s the part people forward to their cousins. The cod in most bacalhau never swam anywhere near Lisbon. That same buying guide notes that most bacalhau in Portugal comes from Norway or Iceland. The salt, the drying and the waiting are what make it Portuguese. The fish is just the raw material, which is exactly why the bowl in a Hill fridge and the bowl in a Lisbon kitchen look the same.
### What does bacalhau taste like?
Properly soaked, bacalhau tastes mild, savory and gently salty, with big moist flakes that peel apart in layers. It is firmer and meatier than fresh cod, closer to the bite of a good pork chop than to a flimsy fillet. It does not taste “fishy” the way a tin of sardines does.
Raw and dry, it is another animal. Open the box and the smell is sharp and briny, a little like a dock at low tide. The fillet is so stiff you could knock on it. That smell fades in the water, and after a long soak the flesh goes from chalky white to pearly and soft under your thumb. Anyone who has stood in a Hill kitchen on Christmas Eve knows that change by feel.
Get the soak wrong and you taste it right away. Too short, and every bite is a mouthful of brine that dries your tongue and has you reaching for water. Too long, and it goes flat, like boiled paper. The cook behind that Portuguese buying guide says the salt cure changes the fish’s texture and taste and lifts it “to celestial heights.” That only happens in the middle, which is why the soaking section below matters more than any recipe.
The simple check: before you commit the whole fillet to a dish, poach a thumb-sized piece for a minute and taste it. Salty like a potato chip is about right, since the potatoes and eggs will soak some up. Salty like seawater means it needs more time in the bowl.
### How do Portuguese eat bacalhau?
In every way you can think of, and a few you can’t. One Portuguese food guide lists the classics: bacalhau à Brás, shredded with onions, eggs and potatoes; bacalhau com natas, with cream; and bacalhau à lagareiro, roasted with garlic and olive oil. Then there are the little fried balls called bolinhos de bacalhau, the bar snack that converts skeptics.
If you see bolinhos on a menu, order them first. The shell crackles, a puff of steam comes out, and the inside is soft potato threaded with salty flakes. They are the friendliest way into the whole cuisine, and they tell you in two bites whether the kitchen soaks its fish right.
Bacalhau à Brás is the one to order for a first real plate. A tangle of straw-thin fried potatoes gone soft in barely set egg, with flakes of cod all through it, chopped parsley on top and black olives at the edge. It eats like the best scrambled-egg breakfast you ever had, only salty and golden. It is also the most forgiving dish to cook at home, because the egg covers small mistakes, which makes it the right second act for any baccalà left over after Christmas Eve.
Bacalhau com natas is the cold-night order: the cod and potatoes baked under cream until the top browns in spots and the edges bubble against the dish. Lagareiro is the showpiece. A thick loin roasted until the flakes split open, swimming in olive oil and garlic you will want to mop up with bread. If a menu offers it, ask how thick the loin is. Thick is the whole point.
### The Portuguese thread already running through Benton Park
Walk into Yemanja Brasil on a Friday evening and the first thing you notice is the noise of a dining room that is actually having fun, then the smell of black beans that have been going for hours. The restaurant says its family is committed to the community and that it brings in fresh seafood daily, shipped straight from the docks. It is a Brazilian kitchen, not a Portuguese one, and it does not pretend otherwise. But if you want to taste where Portuguese cooking traveled, this is the closest door I found in the city.
Look at its event buffet menu and the thread is right there. The feijoada is black beans stewed with Brazilian dried beef, smoked sausage and smoked pork ribs, served with rice, farofa, orange slices and collard greens. There is a dish called Pescada Miranda, sautéed cod in a refogado and coconut cream sauce, topped with fried bananas and provolone. And the dessert is pudim, a traditional flan: baked egg custard under a light caramel sauce. That custard is the same family of sweets as the Portuguese tart people cross town for.
Two practical notes. First, the cod dish appears on the menu the restaurant posts for events, so if you want it, ask about it when you book a party. The buffet starts at $38 per person plus tax and gratuity. Second, the restaurant also runs a food truck called Brazil Express, worth following if your cravings land midweek. The appetizer menu for events lists shrimp empanadas at $8 a piece, fried pastry with rock shrimp and a creamy Brazilian filling.
Check the posted menu before you go, because dine-in dishes and prices change. If you are new to the cuisine, our guide to what to order at a Brazilian steakhouse in St. Louis covers the grill side of the story.
### How long do you soak salt cod before you cook it?
Anywhere from 6 to 8 hours for small pieces to 72 hours for extra-thick jumbo loins, with the water changed the whole time. A thick center-cut loin, the cut most home cooks want, lands at 48 to 55 hours. This is the step that decides whether dinner tastes like Lisbon or like a salt lick, and it is the step those Hill kitchens in the Sauce story already had down.
The Portuguese buying guide breaks it down by cut. Small pieces sold in 400 to 500 gram packs, called migas, need 6 to 8 hours, changing the water every hour. Thick center-cut loins need 48 to 55 hours with 6 water changes. Extra-thick jumbo loins, usually from a cod weighing more than 3 kilograms, need 72 hours, with the water changed every 6 to 8 hours. A seafood supplier’s tutorial says most recipes call for 24 hours, warns that this is risky and may leave the fish too salty, and calls about 48 hours a better bet. Its trick is a good one: prop the fish up on something inside the container so the salt has somewhere to go, and change the water every few hours.
Here is how that looks in a real St. Louis week. Buy a thick loin on Wednesday after work. Rinse off the loose salt, set it on a rack in a deep container, cover it with cold water and slide it onto the bottom shelf of the fridge. Change the water morning and night, more when you remember. By Friday evening, poach your test piece. If it tastes right, you are cooking bacalhau à Brás for Saturday breakfast, and your fridge smells like Nonna’s for the week.
Buying it is the harder part in this city, which is why DiGregorio’s gets a phone call before it gets a drive. On The Hill, the Italian markets are the first places to ask. My guess, and it is only a guess, is that December is when you are likeliest to find a box on the shelf. Our guide to where to eat on The Hill will put you on the right blocks. Add one more question to that call: is it dry-salted, or sold frozen and already desalted? That one matters. The buying guide says to thaw frozen desalted cod in the fridge for 24 hours before use, so if that is what you find, skip the soak entirely.
At the counter, trust your hands and eyes. A good piece is thick through the middle, ivory under the salt, and stiff without crumbling. Thin tail pieces are fine for bolinhos. For lagareiro you want the fattest loin in the box.
### Where did pastel de nata originate?
In Lisbon, with Catholic monks at the Jerónimos Monastery. One Portuguese food guide traces its history to the 18th century in Lisbon and says the monks used egg whites to starch their clothes and turned the leftover yolks into the custard filling. Pastéis de Belém says it began making the original tarts in 1837, following an ancient recipe from the Mosteiro dos Jerónimos.
A good one is loud. The pastry shell shatters into flakes that end up on your shirt. The custard underneath is barely set, trembling, still warm, and the top is blistered with dark scorch marks that taste like the edge of a crème brûlée. You eat it in three bites, standing up, and reach for the second before you have finished chewing. That same food guide calls it “the mother of all custard tarts,” and once you have had a warm one, you understand why.
You do not need a plane ticket for one. Pint Size Bakery & Coffee, at 3133 Watson Rd. at Arsenal in south St. Louis, (314) 645-7142, sells pasteis de nata it describes as little Portuguese custard tarts with a lemon and vanilla custard in a flaky puff pastry, sprinkled with cinnamon and powdered sugar. Lemon brightens the custard. The powdered sugar gets on your fingers before the shell even cracks. Go early: one listing puts the doors open at 7 a.m. Tuesday through Friday and 8 a.m. on Saturday. Call before you make it a special trip.
That tart sits at the top of the popular Portuguese desserts, but it has company. There is pudim, the caramel flan you can already eat in Benton Park. There is salame de chocolate, a log of chocolate and crushed biscuits that looks like salami when you slice it. If you are chasing the tart in St. Louis bakery cases, read the labels for “Portuguese egg tart” and pick the one with the darkest spots on top. Pale means underbaked.
And when the weather turns, Portuguese comfort food is what you want on the stove. Caldo verde is a soup of potatoes, kale, onions, garlic and chorizo or linguiça, with the greens sliced so fine they melt into the broth. Arroz de pato, duck rice, is one of Portugal’s most indulgent comfort foods. Both are easy to make in a St. Louis kitchen with ingredients from any good grocery, which is more than you can say for a perfect nata shell. For the bakery side, our guide on how to find a good bakery in St. Louis tells you what to look for in the case.
Want the salt cod, the flan and the custard tart without calling around all week? Start with the Portuguese Food page on St Louis Near Me Directory, and check back as more kitchens and markets add their listings.
If you’re the baker pulling nata out of the oven or the Hill market keeping salt cod in the back cooler, the people in this guide are already searching for you, and a listing puts your name where they look. List your business and get more customers who already know what they want.
### Your order, start to finish
Here is the whole guide on one screen, for the moment you are standing at a counter or staring at a menu.
At a bar or café: bolinhos de bacalhau first, to see if the kitchen soaks its fish right.
For a first real plate: bacalhau à Brás, the egg-and-potato tangle.
On a cold night: bacalhau com natas, baked under cream.
If you see it: lagareiro, and ask how thick the loin is.
In Benton Park, Thursday through Sunday: the Pudim de Carioca at Yemanja Brasil.
On Watson Road, Tuesday through Saturday morning: pasteis de nata at Pint Size.
At a bakery case: the “Portuguese egg tart” with the darkest top.
At home: a thick loin, a rack, cold water and about 48 hours.
One last thing about bacalhau. The soak is not a chore you rush. It is the cuisine. Those Hill kitchens knew it: the fish went into the water well ahead of the feast, and the house ran on its schedule. Give it the time, and the reward is a fish that pulls apart in silky layers and fills the kitchen with garlic and olive oil. The same smell, in two languages.
Side note, nothing to do with cod: is your gynecologist visit overdue?
