### Frequently asked questions about Portuguese food
### Q. What is Portuguese comfort food?
A.  Caldo verde is the classic: a soup of potatoes, kale, onions, garlic and chorizo or linguiça, popular in the colder months as a starter or a main course. Arroz de pato, duck rice, is one of Portugal’s most indulgent comfort foods. Bacalhau com natas, salt cod baked under cream, belongs on the list too.
### Q. What is a typical Portuguese breakfast?
A.  Coffee and something small, usually at a café. A galão, a tall glass that is about a quarter coffee and three quarters milk, with a torrada, thick buttered toast, is the classic pairing. The quicker version is a bica, a short espresso, with a pastel de nata.
### Q. What are popular Portuguese desserts?
A.  Start with the pastel de nata, the custard tart created by Catholic monks at the Jerónimos Monastery. Pudim, a baked caramel flan, and salame de chocolate, a sliced log of chocolate and crushed biscuits, are close behind. In St. Louis, Yemanja Brasil, a Brazilian restaurant in Benton Park, lists Pudim de Carioca, a traditional flan, as a dessert on its buffet options menu.
### Q. Is Portuguese food expensive?
A.  Not at its roots. Bacalhau has been called the “meat of the poor” in Portugal, and most classics are built on potatoes, eggs, beans, greens and olive oil. Cooking it at home costs mainly time. Eating out in St. Louis, Yemanja Brasil’s event buffet with feijoada and flan starts at $38 per person plus tax and gratuity.
### Q. What is a typical lunch in Portugal?
A.  Lunch, almoço, is the main meal of the day, usually eaten between 12:30 and 2:00 p.m. It often starts with soup, moves to a hearty plate of meat or fish with rice or potatoes and vegetables, and ends with a small dessert or fruit, with bread, olives and a glass of wine or juice on the table.

## That Earnings Tax Line on Your Stub Starts Professional Development in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/professional-development-in-st-louis-where-working-adults-start
That earnings tax line on your paycheck stub, the one you squint at every two weeks and grumble about, is a library card. Slide the stub across a St. Louis Public Library desk, the paper still soft and curved from your back pocket, and the person behind the counter can hand you a card even if you sleep outside the city limits. The rule sits right on SLPL’s get-a-card page: if you work in the City of St. Louis, bring a work ID, a business card or your most recent paycheck stub showing St. Louis City taxes taken out, and you’ll get a card that’s good for one year.
Most working adults get professional development backwards. They think it’s for people with free evenings and a company that pays, or for people who are out of work and have hours to fill. So they put it off, at the kitchen table after a double, coffee gone cold, the dryer thumping in the next room, quietly sure they can’t afford to get better at anything. You can. You don’t have to be jobless, and for the library you don’t even have to live in the city. In St. Louis, the classroom part can cost you nothing but a bus ride and a stub that’s already folded in your wallet.
Here’s how it actually goes. You come in out of the wind with the stub still warm from your pocket, wait behind somebody returning a tote bag of picture books, and slide it across. They’re looking for one line, the one showing St. Louis City taxes taken out. Then you’re back on the sidewalk with a card in your hand that opens thousands of courses you can start on the bus ride home. That’s the part people get backwards: the class is the cheap part. The expensive part is the year you spend waiting until you feel ready.
What follows is for the working adult who wants a raise, a better shift, a different job, or just the feeling of not being stuck: three St. Louis doors, what each one asks you to carry in, and what to say once you’re standing at the counter.
### What are examples of professional development programs in St. Louis?
The strongest examples in the city are free or close to it: SLATE’s WIOA-funded training, which can put up to $10,000 toward tuition, books and supplies for eligible St. Louis City residents, and a St. Louis Public Library card, which gets you LinkedIn Learning’s over 16,000 online video courses plus instructor-led Gale Courses that are free for cardholders. And if you’re at least 25, or haven’t been in school for two years, Missouri’s Fast Track grant can help with tuition and fees.
Each door fits a different kind of week. A LinkedIn Learning video plays on a cracked phone screen on the bus down Grand, one earbud in, the other ear on your stop. A SLATE-funded program means real classroom hours and a manila folder that gets thicker every visit. A Fast Track certificate is a whole semester and a credential with a school’s name printed across the top.
Start with SLATE, the St. Louis Agency on Training and Employment, because it holds the biggest number. The city’s own page says that if you’re a resident of St. Louis City, you may be eligible for up to $10,000 to help cover tuition, books, supplies and more. The help runs through the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act, or WIOA, and it comes with things a course catalog never gives you: skills assessments, workshops on resume writing and interview skills, and individualized career guidance. The number to call is (314) 589-8000.
Here’s the part almost nobody tells you. You don’t have to be out of work to qualify. Most people hear “job center” and figure it’s for the guy who just got his last check, not for someone who has to be back on the clock by three. But SLATE’s eligibility list includes “any employed person who meets low-income eligibility criteria,” right next to people who have been laid off. If you’re working full time at a wage that still makes the light bill feel like a threat, you may be exactly who this money was set aside for.
The second door is already in your wallet: the library card from the top of this page. For a city worker who lives out in the county, the stub with the earnings tax line is the whole application. Through SLPL you get LinkedIn Learning, which the library lists with over 16,000 online video courses, plus Gale Courses, interactive, instructor-led online courses with a syllabus you read before you enroll. You also get resume and cover letter help, and computers you can reserve at any of the library’s 15 locations. Walk into a branch on a weeknight and you’ll hear it: the soft click of keyboards, a printer warming up, somebody whispering a cover letter out loud to check how it sounds. Plenty of those people are doing exactly what you’re thinking about doing.
The third door is for the person who wants a credential with a school’s name on it. Missouri’s Fast Track Workforce Incentive Grant is designed to give adults the education and skills to enter the workforce in high-demand fields, and it serves both students and apprentices. You qualify if you’re at least 25, or if you haven’t been enrolled in school in the last two years, and if your adjusted gross income is $40,000 or less, or $80,000 or less filing jointly. You also can’t already hold a bachelor’s degree, and students need two years of Missouri residency first. For students at a public two- or four-year school, the grant is designed to make sure tuition and fees are fully covered when it’s combined with other state and federal non-loan financial aid.
Which one first? If you have a library card or a city paycheck, start there this week, because it costs nothing and tells you fast whether you actually like the subject. If you already know the field you want and need real money for tuition, call SLATE. If you’re aiming at a full certificate and you’re at least 25, or two years out of school, check Fast Track before you borrow a dime.
### Can you get training paid for while you’re still working?
Yes, and the paperwork is less scary than the waiting room you’re imagining. SLATE’s training help is open to St. Louis City residents who are 18 or older, authorized to work in the U.S. and registered for Selective Service if that applies to them. The other condition is one of these: you’re unemployed, you’ve received a layoff notice, or you’re employed and meet the low-income criteria. The city lays out the start in a handful of steps:
Register, or update your registration, in MoJobs, the state’s job site.
Attend a WIOA Orientation, where you’re assigned a Career Advisor. Check the SLATE training page for the next date before you go, because the schedule changes.
Gather the documents your Career Advisor asks for and turn them in.
Keep showing up. Enrollment is decided by your paperwork, your assessments and your continued engagement with the staff.
The Job Center itself is at 1520 Market St., 3rd Floor downtown. It’s open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m.-5 p.m., except Wednesdays, when it opens at 9 a.m. The phone is (314) 589-8000. If you work days, Wednesday morning is the one slot where you might sleep a little later and still make it before your own shift.
Carry the documents in your hand, not in your inbox. A paper folder, the stubs flattened under a heavy book the night before, your ID clipped to the front. You’ll feel the elevator-and-hallway nerves anyway. Holding the folder gives your hands something to do, and showing up with everything your Career Advisor asked for is how the next visit turns into the one where you hear a start date.
Walk in with questions, not just a form. Treat the Career Advisor the way you’d treat anyone you’re about to trust with your next year: say plainly what you want (“I want to move from warehouse floor to a forklift lead,” “I want out of food service and into medical billing”), then ask which approved programs fit that goal, which ones run at night, and how long people usually wait to start. Then compare two or three programs on what each will actually deliver, the hours, the credential and the job they point at, before you pick one.
Gums that bleed every time you floss? That’s a periodontist question, not a toothbrush one.
### What does a St. Louis library card actually unlock for your career?
More than most people who own one have ever used. On SLPL’s courses and training page, LinkedIn Learning (formerly Lynda.com) is listed with over 16,000 online video courses in software, creativity and business skills. On your phone, download the LinkedIn Learning app and enter the library ID stlouispubliclibrary, all lowercase, because it’s case-sensitive. That one detail is where most people give up at 11 p.m. with the app spinning. Now you won’t.
Gale Courses are the part nobody in your break room has heard of. They’re instructor-led, they’re free for cardholders, and new six-week sessions start on the second Wednesday of every month. Read the fine print before you enroll, because the library can’t drop or transfer you once you’re in. If you don’t visit the week 2 class within 13 days of the start of the course, you’re automatically dropped. There’s no penalty, and you can enroll in the same course again in the next six-week session. You get one 10-day extension after the final exam date. That structure is the point. A deadline is what turns “someday” into Thursday.
The same card gets you $5 of free printing each month, which covers a stack of resumes on good days, plus job and career prep help with resumes and cover letters. Questions about whether you qualify go to the library at 314-241-2288.
### Should your employer pay for training?
Often, yes, and the tax code gives your boss a reason to say so. Under section 127 of the Internal Revenue Code, an employer with a written educational assistance plan can pay for your tuition, fees, books, supplies and equipment, and you won’t pay tax on the first $5,250 of those benefits in a year. After that, the IRS says the amount is adjusted for increases in the cost of living in later tax years. The detail that changes the conversation: the payments don’t have to be for work-related courses.
That knot in your stomach before you ask? Swap it for one plain sentence. The IRS itself says your employer can tell you whether there’s a section 127 plan where you work. So you’re not asking for a favor. You’re asking about a benefit. Try this, by email so there’s a record, typed with your thumbs in the break room while the vending machine hums behind you: “Do we have a section 127 educational assistance plan, and if not, would you consider paying for this course if I bring back what I learn to the team?” Attach the course link and the price. Name the problem at work it would solve.
If your employer trains people in groups, point HR to St. Louis Community College. Its workforce solutions team builds training for St. Louis companies, including incumbent worker training to build new skills and short-term workforce credentials, delivered on campus, at the job site or in flexible formats. For a manager, that’s a much easier yes than a one-off reimbursement form.
Choosing a private trainer, coach or course provider on your own? Shortlist two or three, interview them, tell each one exactly what you want to be able to do when you finish, and compare that against what each says it will deliver: the hours, the format, who teaches and whether you leave with anything you can show an employer. The right one will answer those questions without flinching.
You don’t need permission to get better at your job, only a first class. Browse trainers, coaches and classes near you in Professional Development on St Louis Near Me Directory, then shortlist two to interview this week.
If you’re the trainer, tutor or career coach who teaches working adults after hours, the people reading this page are already looking for someone like you, so list your business where St. Louis learners can get more customers to your door.
### The 70-20-10 rule, translated for a St. Louis shift
The 70-20-10 rule for learning emerged from over 30 years of the Center for Creative Leadership’s Lessons of Experience research into how executives learn, grow and change over their careers. It says people tend to learn about 70 percent of what they know from challenging experiences and assignments, 20 percent from developmental relationships and 10 percent from coursework and training. It was built from studying how managers grow, but the shape fits a warehouse, a hospital floor or a kitchen line just as well.
Here’s what that looks like in real life. The 70 is volunteering to run the inventory count nobody wants, the beep of the scanner in a cold aisle at 5 a.m., and learning the system cold because you had to. The 20 is the shift lead who lets you shadow the schedule, or the cousin in medical billing who answers your texts. The 10 is the Gale Course or the SLATE-funded certificate that names what you’ve been doing and makes it official. CCL says well-designed coursework and training programs have an amplifier effect, clarifying, supporting and boosting the other 90 percent of your learning. So don’t take a class instead of asking for the harder assignment. Take it so you can ask.
### How do you make a career development plan that survives a double shift?
A career development plan doesn’t need a binder. It fits on an index card stuck to the fridge, and it should, because you’ll see it every time you reach for the milk:
The job you want next, not in ten years. One title, one place you’d like to do it.
The one skill standing between you and that title. Ask someone who has the job; they’ll tell you in one sentence.
Your 70: one stretch task to ask for at work this month.
Your 20: one person to buy a coffee for and learn from.
Your 10: one course, with a start date. A Gale session starting the second Wednesday is a ready-made deadline.
The money question: library, SLATE, Fast Track or your employer, in that order of effort.
Look at the card every payday. Cross things off in pen. The scratch of the pen is the whole reward system, and it works better than any app.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What qualifies as professional development?
A.  Anything that builds a skill you use at work and can point to afterward. A course, a certificate or an apprenticeship counts, but so does a stretch assignment or a mentor who teaches you the next job. In St. Louis, if you live in the city, SLATE may put up to $10,000 toward tuition, books and supplies.
### Q. What is the 70-20-10 rule for learning?
A.  It’s a guideline from the Center for Creative Leadership: people tend to learn about 70 percent from challenging experiences and assignments, 20 percent from developmental relationships and 10 percent from coursework and training. The class is the smallest slice, but it sharpens the other two.
### Q. What are some good professional development courses?
A.  Start with what’s free. Through the St. Louis Public Library you get LinkedIn Learning, listed with over 16,000 online video courses, and Gale Courses, instructor-led online courses that are free for cardholders. If you need a credential, SLATE keeps a list of approved occupational training programs and, in some cases, offers financial assistance if you’re eligible.
### Q. Should an employer pay for training?
A.  Often, yes. Under a section 127 plan, an employer can cover tuition, fees, books and supplies, and the first $5,250 a year is tax-free to you. The courses don’t even have to be work-related. Ask HR whether a plan exists where you work.
### Q. What to put in professional development on a resume?
A.  List the course or credential, who offered it and when you finished, then one line on what you can now do with it. A finished six-week instructor-led course reads stronger than a pile of half-watched videos, so list what you completed.
### Q. How to make a career development plan?
A.  Name the next job, the one skill blocking it, one stretch task at work, one person to learn from and one course with a start date. Then pick how you’ll pay: library, SLATE, Fast Track or your employer. Review it every payday.
### Q. Why is continuing professional development important?
A.  Because the job you have now keeps changing, and the people who get the better shift or the promotion are usually the ones who learned the new thing first. Steady small learning also gives you proof to bring to a raise conversation.
### Q. What is the difference between professional learning and professional development?
A.  People often use the terms loosely. Professional learning usually means the ongoing, everyday learning you do on the job and with colleagues. Professional development usually means the planned courses, credentials and programs. The 70-20-10 rule says you need both.
### Q. Do I have to live in the city to get a St. Louis Public Library card?
A.  If you work in the City of St. Louis, bring a work ID, a business card or a recent paycheck stub showing St. Louis City taxes taken out, and SLPL will issue a card that’s good for one year.

## Don't Pay to Haul It: Decluttering Mistakes Before a Professional Organizer in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/decluttering-before-a-professional-organizer-in-st-louis
$14 a month already paid for the three kitchen chairs leaning at the edge of your alley to disappear. The City of St. Louis picks up up to three bulky items a month from your curb or alley, set out by 6:00 a.m. on the Monday of your collection week, and the service is included in the $14 solid waste fee collected quarterly on your water bill.
Stand there with that bill in your hand for a second. One chair has a split seat that pinches the back of your leg. One wobbles like a bar stool at last call. The third came with the house. The garage door groans up behind you, the cold smell of concrete and old cardboard rolls out, and somebody says the sentence that costs real money: “We’ll just call a hauler for the big stuff.” Don’t. You already paid for them to leave.
Here’s the short version, before anything else. Find your bulk week with the address search on the Refuse Division page, which shows your collection days for trash, recycling, bulky items and yard waste. Put no more than three items out by 6:00 a.m. that Monday. More than three? Every year, St. Louis City residents can bring up to 12 loads of trash, yard waste and bulk items to a transfer station: the North Transfer Station at 71 Angelica St. or the South Transfer Station at 4100 South 1st Street, Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. Paint and chemicals take a third door, the regional household hazardous waste drop-off, where an appointment is required. To make a reservation, the city lists the Saint Louis City phone as 314-622-4800, or you can begin online at hhwstl.com.
Most people find out after they’ve paid someone else. Or after the pile has lived in the back hall for six weeks, bags slumping against the radiator, while everyone in the house learns to step over it in the dark. It isn’t a willpower problem. It’s a logistics problem dressed up as a character flaw, and fixing it before a professional organizer ever knocks keeps the hours you pay them for on shelves and systems, not on dragging chairs.
### What are the biggest decluttering mistakes in St. Louis?
The biggest decluttering mistakes are sorting without an exit plan, paying to haul what your city trash bill already covers, tossing paint and chemicals in the cart, donating furniture a thrift store can’t sell, and tossing papers you still need. Every one of them comes from the same root: you decided what to get rid of before you decided where it goes.
Start with the exit plan, because it’s the one that quietly wrecks everything else. You open the hall closet. Coats that smell like a winter three years gone, a box of tangled cords, a stack of mail held with a rubber band, a vacuum that wheezes. You sort it into three neat piles on the hardwood and feel great for about an hour. Then the piles sit. The donate bag goes in the trunk and rides around for three weeks, thumping every time you hit a pothole on Gravois. The toss pile is too big for the roll cart. The “maybe” pile migrates back into the closet one item at a time, like it never left.
That’s the most common way a decluttering push fails, and it fails before an organizer arrives. When you finally book one, you’re paying for hours of sorting through the same stuff you already sorted once. Not because you did it wrong. Because nothing had anywhere to go.
The second mistake is the expensive one. You hire somebody with a truck to take away the couch, the broken window unit and a bed frame, when the city’s monthly bulk pickup would have taken three of those for nothing beyond the bill you already pay. If the load is bigger, city residents can bring up to 12 loads a year to a City transfer station, also included in the trash fee. A private hauler is the right call sometimes. A piano. A whole basement in one day. A closing date. But it should be a choice, not a reflex.
The third mistake is chemical. Half-empty paint cans, a jug of weed killer, the gas can from a mower you sold years ago. People bag it with everything else because it’s right there and the cart lid is open. Household hazardous waste has its own drop-off with its own rules, and the city says HHW is not accepted at its transfer stations. More on that below.
The fourth one stings because it comes from a good place. You load the loveseat with the cat-shredded arm into a borrowed van and drive it to a thrift store, sure somebody will want it. The charity can’t sell it, so the charity won’t take it. Now you’re standing in a parking lot next to a loveseat.
And the fifth mistake makes its noise later, usually in April. You toss the shoebox of papers with the rest of the junk, and the one statement you needed was in it.
### Your trash bill already bought three couch pickups a month
Here’s the city’s math, because it changes how you plan the whole job. The Refuse Division’s collection rules spell out what the flat fee buys: at least one weekly trash pickup, weekly yard waste pickup from March through December, and monthly pickup of bulky items like furniture, appliances, tires, waste motor oil and car batteries. All of it is in the $14 per month per dwelling unit, collected quarterly on your water bill.
The bulky pickup has rules, and they’re the kind people break by accident. Items go out by 6:00 a.m. on the Monday of your collection week. Not Sunday afternoon in a hopeful heap two weeks early. If your trash goes out front, bulk goes to the curb. If you’re on an alley, it goes in the alley behind your home, kept away from the trash containers. Collectors aren’t allowed to pick up anything on private property, so the couch sitting just inside your back gate in Benton Park stays exactly where it is.
A few more details from the city’s bulk page that will save you a second try. Refrigerator doors must come off. Smaller loose items go in a container or a bundle, and no container or bundle can weigh over 100 pounds, run longer than 6 feet or be more than 2 feet in diameter. Don’t put bulky items in your trash container, and don’t pile regular bagged trash on top of the bulk. And give the crew the whole week. The city asks you to allow the entire week before you report anything missed.
Think about what that means for a weekend purge in a Dutchtown two-family. You don’t need a dumpster. You need a calendar. Three items this month, three next month, the transfer station for the overflow. The city also says it’s against the law to throw car batteries, motor oil, appliances like refrigerators and air conditioners, and vehicle tires out with the trash, and those BOAT-E items can go out during the same monthly bulk pickup. The dead chest freezer humming its last in the basement is a pickup, not a problem.
### Where does the stuff you let go actually go in the city?
Sort into five piles, not three, and give every pile an address before you start. That’s the whole trick. The organizing world loves the keep, donate, toss trio, and it works, but in St. Louis city the toss pile splits three ways and each one leaves the house by a different door.
Keep stays. Donate goes to a charity that can sell it. Bulk goes to the alley or curb on your Monday. Hazardous goes to a reserved drop-off. Trash goes in the cart. When you hold up a sweater, a lamp or a can of deck stain, you aren’t asking “do I love it?” You’re asking “which door does it leave by?” That second question is faster, and it kills the maybe pile.
The donate pile. St. Vincent de Paul in St. Louis takes new or gently used clothing, home goods and furniture at its thrift stores, and you can schedule a donation pickup. Read the furniture rule before you lift anything. They ask that donated furniture be clean and in good condition, which they spell out as no pet hair, dirt, dust, rips, stains, burns, odors, peeling, cracking or broken parts. Wood pieces have a size limit of 6 feet high by 6 feet long. For pickup, the piece sits at ground level, in front of your home on a paved path or inside a clear garage, and the driver inspects it before accepting. Run a lint roller over that armchair. Put your face in the cushion and breathe in. If it smells like the basement, it’s a bulk item, not a donation.
The bulk pile. Three items to the curb or alley by 6:00 a.m. on your collection Monday. Overflow goes to a transfer station: the North Transfer Station at 71 Angelica St. or the South Transfer Station at 4100 South 1st Street, open Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., closed weekends. Both take bulk furniture, bedding, scrap metal and household items. If you’re hauling the old refrigerator, the tires or a printer, go south: the city lists BOAT-E items as accepted at the South station only.
Bring your driver’s license or state ID and a recent combined Water/Solid Waste Fee statement if you own the home. Renters bring ID and another recent utility bill, and the property owner has to be paying the solid waste fee or the renter isn’t eligible. The load can’t be bigger than what fits in a half-ton pickup, and the vehicle can’t be larger than 5 feet by 8 feet by 4 feet high. A buddy with a truck who’s doing it for cash is out of luck too: the city says anyone suspected of hauling for hire gets rejected.
The hazardous pile. Household hazardous waste does not go to the transfer station. The city sends you to the regional program at hhwstl.com, open to residents of St. Louis City, St. Louis County and Jefferson County, and an appointment is required. To make a reservation, the city lists the Saint Louis City phone as 314-622-4800. The first 50 pounds of HHW are free with each visit, any additional HHW materials over 50 pounds cost $1.70 per pound, and there’s a 500 pound limit per drop off. Here’s the detail nobody mentions: latex paint has its own price tag. If you bring latex paint, you’re charged the recycling fee of $.50 per pound, so those twelve crusted gallons from the last three bedroom colors are a bill, not a freebie. Bring proof of address, stay in the car, and bring a card, because the facilities take credit and debit only.
The trash pile. The cart. And if you’re tempted by the vacant lot down the block, don’t. The city’s illegal dumping page says it tracks and fines the violation, and the St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department’s Environmental Investigations Unit targets dumping in alleys and lots.
Basement dust left you coughing for weeks? See when a lung doctor helps.
### What should you not throw out when decluttering?
Don’t throw out tax records you might still need, anything hazardous that belongs at a drop-off, or the one thing you can’t replace. The first one is where real money hides. The IRS’s record-keeping guidance says to keep records for 3 years if situations (4), (5) and (6) on its list don’t apply to you, so read that list before anything goes in the shredder. The shoebox of W-2s and receipts doesn’t go in the toss pile on a Saturday afternoon. It goes in one labeled folder, and you sort it at the kitchen table with a cup of coffee and the radio on, not on your knees in a hot attic.
Photos, letters and anything in a grandparent’s handwriting get the same rule. Pull them aside. Don’t decide on the spot. The worst decluttering regrets aren’t about money. They’re about the birthday card with the shaky cursive that went out with the junk mail.
And don’t toss what the city wants handled separately. Car batteries, motor oil, appliances and tires can’t legally go out with the trash. Paints, pesticides and gasoline are on the city’s list of household hazardous waste the drop-off accepts, by appointment. Separate them first, before the bags fill up and nobody remembers which one has the can of stripper in it.
### How do you get a bulky item hauled away this month?
Do it in this order, and the dresser is gone before the organizer’s first visit.
Look up your bulk week. The Refuse Division page has an address search that shows your collection days for trash, recycling, bulky items and yard waste.
Pick your three. Not more than three items per monthly pickup. Take the door off if one of them is a refrigerator.
Bundle the small stuff. Loose pieces go in a container or bundle, under 100 pounds, no longer than 6 feet, no more than 2 feet in diameter.
Set them out by 6:00 a.m. on the Monday of your collection week, at the curb or in the alley behind your home, away from the trash containers and not blocking the alley.
Wait the week. If they’re still there at the end of it, call the Citizens’ Service Bureau at 314-622-4800 and name the items that were missed.
Over the limit and own your home? The city’s drop-off page asks homeowners for a driver’s license or state ID and a recent combined Water/Solid Waste Fee statement.
That’s the whole process. The Refuse Division also answers at refuse@stlouis-mo.gov and works out of 1900 Hampton, Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
One timing tip for anyone in a Soulard rowhouse with a narrow gangway: move the heaviest piece first. Wrestling a sleeper sofa through a doorway two inches narrower than the sofa is the part that eats an afternoon, and you want it in the alley Sunday night, not wedged in the hall at 5:45 Monday morning while the truck growls two blocks over.
### Why does the pile come back after you clear it?
The root cause of clutter usually isn’t too much stuff. It’s stuff with no home and no exit. Things come in faster than they leave, and the house has no door built for leaving. Mail lands on the counter because there’s no spot for mail. Outgrown sneakers pile up by the back steps because nobody knows when the donation run happens. The broken lamp waits for a bulk week nobody looked up.
City life adds its own twist. The city ended alley recycling after over half of the recycling it collected in fiscal year 2025 was rejected at the sorting facility, and it says recycling costs it almost five times more per ton than trash. If you’re on alley service, the cardboard from every new organizing bin you buy now needs a ride to a drop-off site. The city says it added 13 more so every resident has one within one mile of home. Find yours before you order a single storage tote.
That’s why the best decluttering method is a calendar, not a heroic weekend. Bulk week once a month. One donation run on the same day. A reservation at the hazardous drop-off when the bin in the garage fills. The house starts breathing out on a schedule, the same way it breathes in.
### What should you have done before the organizer rings the bell?
Walk the house with a roll of painter’s tape and a marker. Tape the furniture that’s leaving and write BULK or DONATE on it. Get the first three bulk items out on your Monday. Book the hazardous drop-off for the paint and chemicals. Pull the papers into one folder. Then call the organizer, so the hours you’re paying for go to systems, shelves and the way your family actually lives, not to dragging out a recliner you could have set in the alley yourself. If you’re still weighing whether to hire one at all, our guide to what a home organizer costs in St. Louis covers that.
When you’re ready, shortlist two or three organizers and interview them. Tell them what you’ve already cleared and what’s left. Ask how they handle the last mile: do they haul donations away with them, will they work around your bulk week, will they leave you with a routine for keeping it clear? Then compare what each one says they’ll deliver with what you want the house to feel like on a Tuesday night. Pick the one whose answer sounds like your house, not a catalog.

If you’re the professional organizer who knows which Monday bulk goes out in Dutchtown, homeowners halfway through a purge are already looking here for someone like you, so list your business and get more customers from the people standing in their half-empty closets.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the 12-12-12 rule for decluttering?
A.  It’s a quick room-by-room challenge: you pick twelve items to throw away, twelve items to donate, and twelve items to put away. In St. Louis city, check that throw-away dozen before it hits the cart: household furniture can go out with the monthly bulk pickup, and paints are on the city’s household hazardous waste list.
### Q. What should you not throw out when decluttering?
A.  Keep tax records until you’ve checked the IRS list: it says to keep records for 3 years if situations (4), (5) and (6) don’t apply to you. Keep irreplaceable photos and letters too. And pull out paints, pesticides and gasoline, which the city lists as household hazardous waste for the appointment-only drop-off.
### Q. What are the 5 steps of organizing?
A.  A practical version: clear everything out of one space, sort it into keep, donate, bulk, hazardous and trash, get the outgoing piles out of the house that week, give every keeper a home, then set a monthly routine so new stuff leaves as fast as it comes in.
### Q. Do professional organizers also clean?
A.  Don’t assume either way. Ask on the interview call. Some will wipe a shelf as they reset it, others expect a clean space to work in, and if deep cleaning matters to you, say so up front and compare what each organizer says they’ll actually do.
### Q. What is the root cause of clutter?
A.  Usually it’s not the amount of stuff. It’s stuff with no home and no exit route. When things come in faster than they leave, piles form. Giving each category a place inside the house and a scheduled way out is what keeps it from coming back.
### Q. What happens if my bulk items aren’t picked up in St. Louis?
A.  The city asks you to give the Refuse Division the entire collection week. If your items are still out at the end of it, report them to the Citizens’ Service Bureau at 314-622-4800 and note which items were missed.

## Is the Red Stuff Going to Hurt? Malaysian Food in St. Louis, Ordered Right
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/malaysian-food-in-st-louis-what-to-order
Is the red stuff going to hurt? That’s the question sitting at the table before the plate even lands. A dome of rice so white it almost glows. A smear of brick-red paste on the side. A scatter of tiny fried fish, crisp as potato chips, and a smell of coconut and toasted chili rising off all of it like heat off a radiator in January. You came for something new. You’d also like to taste the rest of your dinner.
In St. Louis, the best answer to that question isn’t on a website. Akar, chef Bernie Lee’s small dining room at 7641 Wydown Blvd, has no menu online. You have to call for a reservation, at (314) 553-9914, and that phone call is the whole trick. The red stuff there has shown up folded into a rich, silky sambal-spiced demi-glace over short ribs that Sauce Magazine called insanely tender when it put Akar on its Sauce 75 list of the essential St. Louis restaurants. The dishes change constantly, so don’t memorize one. Memorize a sentence instead, and say it to whoever picks up the phone: “Can I get the sambal on the side, and how hot does it run tonight?” Say that, and you’re the one holding the spoon.
Here’s the St. Louis fact that changes how you hunt for this food. This city had a Chinatown, called Hop Alley, and in 1966 it was demolished for Busch Memorial Stadium. The tea shops and noodle counters that might have grown into a block of Malaysian kitchens went down with it. What’s left of that cooking here is scattered, one chef, one grocery aisle, one curry at a time, which is exactly why you have to know what to ask for. Want the flavor at home tonight? Call Olive Supermarket at 8041 Olive Blvd, (314) 997-5168, before you drive, and ask three things by name: sambal in a jar, belacan, a bundle of pandan. Thirty seconds on the phone saves you a wasted trip down Olive in rush hour.
The red stuff is sambal. It can sting. And you control exactly how much of it lands on your spoon. Touch a fingertip of it to a corner of coconut rice and you’ll feel the order it arrives in: sweet first, then salt, then a warmth that climbs the back of your throat, sits there a few seconds and lets go. Your first order, word for word, if you’re nervous: “Roti canai with the curry, and the chicken rice with the chili on the side.” Neither one will hurt you. Both will tell you whether you want to go further.
And here’s the one to repeat at your next dinner party: a Hainan chicken rice that Sauce Magazine called iconic in Malaysia and Singapore was cooked inside an old Taco Bell on Woodson Road, and the real menu there was written entirely in Chinese. The people who ate it were the ones who asked. The rest of this page is how to be one of them, dish by dish.
### What is the most famous Malaysian food?
Start with nasi lemak: in Malaysia it is considered the national dish. It’s rice cooked in coconut milk and pandan leaf, served with sambal, fried anchovies and cucumber, and most often eaten for breakfast. Nasi is simply the Malay word for rice, and the pandan gives it a rich fragrance. One bite tells you the rest: the coconut makes every grain rich, faintly sweet and soft enough to cling to the spoon.
Here’s how the first good bite goes. Your spoon cuts into warm rice that gives like a pillow. You drag the edge through the sambal, add two anchovies and a peanut, and lift. The anchovies crack first, loud enough to hear, and salt floods your tongue. Then the coconut rice smooths everything over. The sambal arrives last, sweet, then hot, a slow burn at the back of your mouth, and that’s when you reach for the cucumber, cold and wet, and the fire steps back. Break the boiled egg and the yolk softens the next spoonful. A restaurant in Penang might set spicy squid beside it, but the order of that bite doesn’t change: crunch, cream, heat, cool.
Now the St. Louis twist: Akar, where Bernie Lee cooks from his Malaysian heritage, works without a fixed menu, so don’t count on a plate of nasi lemak waiting for you. Build it in your own kitchen instead. Pandan, a can of coconut milk, a jar of sambal, a bag of dried anchovies fried until they crackle and jump in the pan. You’ll know the rice is right before you taste it: the kitchen smells like warm sweet hay with coconut underneath. Lift the lid when the pandan hits the coconut milk and the steam smells like a bakery and a beach at once. If it smells like plain rice, the pandan never made it into the pot.
Make it for dinner the first time. Rice, chili and fish at seven in the morning sounds like a lot if you grew up on toast and coffee. By the third bite you’ll understand why a whole country is happy to start the day this way.
### St. Louis once had a Chinatown, and a stadium took it
Ask around for Chinatown here and you’ll mostly get a shrug. From 1869 until 1966, Hop Alley sat near downtown in the blocks bounded by Seventh, Tenth, Walnut and Chestnut streets, until the wrecking crews came for the stadium. If you’ve walked from a Cardinals game up toward Chestnut Street, you’ve crossed ground where people once ironed shirts and poured tea.
It started with one man. Alla Lee, born in Ningbo near Shanghai, arrived in St. Louis in 1857, and he was the only Chinese immigrant in the city until 1869, when a group of about 250 arrived looking for factory work. Hop Alley grew up around them. Its Chinese hand laundries made up more than half of the city’s laundry businesses, and the blocks also held groceries, restaurants, tea shops and barber shops. Think of the steam rolling out of those laundry doors on a February morning and you’ve got the feel of the place: hot starch, wet cotton, and somewhere under it, a wok.
Why does that matter on a page about Malaysian food? Because Malaysian cooking is the cooking of a crossroads. Malaysia’s population divides roughly among three major groups, Malays, Chinese and Indians, and a Malaysian menu carries all three on one page. The noodle soups and the toast shops lean Chinese. The flatbreads and curries lean Indian. The coconut rice, the sambal and the spice pastes are Malay.
Here’s the part most St. Louisans have never heard: the story didn’t end at the ballpark. In recent decades, efforts have been made to establish a successor to the old Chinatown. Drive Olive Boulevard and you’ll see what that looks like now: a number of Asian grocery stores and restaurants line the stretch between I-170 and Skinker Boulevard. Hop Alley had its groceries and tea shops downtown. Olive has them today, and that’s where a Malaysian craving turns into a shopping list. Ask for sambal in a jar, belacan in a hard little brick, a bundle of pandan from the cooler. Open that shrimp paste in your own kitchen and the whole house will know it; fry it in hot oil and the smell turns from fierce to savory, almost meaty, in front of you.
### Which laksa is the creamy one, and which one bites back?
Laksa is a spicy noodle soup, but the word covers two very different bowls, and ordering the wrong one is how people decide they don’t like laksa. One is built on rich coconut milk. The other is soured with tamarind. Same name. Different planet.
Curry laksa is the coconut one, and it’s the bowl most people picture: a broth the color of a sunset, glossy on top, thick enough to coat the back of your throat. The Kuala Lumpur version comes loaded with deep-fried tofu, cockles, long beans and mint, over yellow egg noodles, rice vermicelli or both. Those tofu puffs are the secret. They drink up the broth, and when you bite one, hot coconut curry bursts out and runs down your chin. It tastes rich first and warm second; the heat builds over the bowl instead of punching you on the first sip.
Asam laksa, the Penang specialty, is the one that surprises people. There’s no coconut milk in it at all. The soup is made with mackerel that’s poached and flaked, soured with tamarind, and piled with things like cucumber, onion, red chili, pineapple and mint. It smells like the sea and tastes like a squeeze of something sharp: sour, salty, fishy in the good way, and bright enough to wake you up on a gray St. Louis afternoon.
A rule of thumb that works: if you love Thai tom kha or a creamy curry, start with curry laksa. If you’re the person who squeezes lime over everything, go straight to asam. And if the menu just says “laksa,” ask one question: “Is it the coconut one?” A cook who knows laksa will answer before you finish the sentence.
### How hot is this going to be, really?
Less than you fear, if you order with your eyes open. Malaysian food and Thai food are relatives, not twins. Malaysia shares culinary ties with Indonesia, Thailand and the Philippines, and some dishes cross the border, like tom yam, which picks up a Malaysian accent once it moves south. But the center of gravity is different. A lot of Thai cooking chases a bright, sharp balance of lime, fish sauce and fresh chili. Malaysian cooking tends to run rounder and deeper: coconut, slow-fried spice pastes, and belacan, a shrimp paste that smells fierce in the jar and turns savory and almost meaty once it hits a hot pan.
The heat usually lives in one place on the plate, the sambal or the chili sauce, rather than being cooked into everything. That’s good news for a nervous eater. If you want a gentle first night, these are the plates to point at:
Hainanese chicken rice. Chicken over rice that, in Malaysia, is usually flavored with pandan, with the chili sauce served on the side for dipping. Clean, soft, comforting.
Roti canai with dal. A flaky flatbread torn by hand and dunked in a lentil curry. Butter, crunch, warmth.
Nasi goreng. Fried rice, usually seasoned with sweet soy sauce. Smoky and a little sweet; ask for it mild.
Satay. Skewered, grilled meat, served mainly with peanut sauce. Charred edges, sweet nutty sauce.
Kaya toast. Toast with kaya, a coconut jam. Breakfast or dessert, your call.
Ais kacang. Shaved ice with colored syrup and evaporated milk. The fire extinguisher at the end of the meal.
And nasi lemak itself? It’s only as hot as the sambal you take. Ask for it on the side, taste a corner of rice with a fingertip of it, then decide. That small move is the whole difference between a great first night and a glass of water you can’t drink fast enough.
### Why does one Malaysian menu feel like three countries?
Because it’s three kitchens sharing one counter. Read a Malaysian menu with that in mind and it suddenly makes sense.
Start with the two rice dishes that confuse everybody. Nasi lemak is rice cooked in coconut milk and then served with the sambal, anchovies, egg and cucumber arranged around it like a little map. Nasi goreng is fried rice with meats, vegetables and spices, usually seasoned with sweet soy sauce, so it comes out of the wok brown, smoky and glazed. Its roots are thrifty: in the cultures that gave us fried rice, it was taboo to throw food away, so the previous day’s leftover rice was often recooked in the morning. One dish is gentle and creamy and built around sides. The other is a single hot jumble straight from the pan. If you remember nothing else, lemak is the rich one and goreng is the fried one.
Then the bread. Roti canai is an Indian-influenced flatbread. Indians brought it during the era of British Malaya, when it was sold at street stalls called mamak stalls, and it’s typically served with dal or curry. Watch one get made if you ever can: the dough slapped and stretched thin as paper, folded, then crisped on a flat griddle until it shatters when you tear it. You pull off a piece, the layers come apart in your fingers, and you drag it through the curry. No fork. Don’t even look for one.
And then the drink, which might be the most Malaysian thing on the table. Teh tarik, “pulled tea,” is a strong brew of black tea blended with condensed milk, poured back and forth between two vessels from a height until it wears a thick, frothy top. In 2024 teh tarik was designated as a Malaysian contribution to intangible cultural heritage, listed by UNESCO under Malaysia’s breakfast culture. Sweet, milky, a little bitter underneath. It’s also the best thing you can drink after a spoonful of sambal that was bigger than you meant it to be.
Put those together and you’ve got the Malaysian morning: coconut rice from the Malay table, flatbread from the Indian stall, noodles and toast from the Chinese coffee shop, and pulled tea for everybody. One counter. Three kitchens. A whole country eating breakfast side by side.
### Where to find Malaysian cooking in St. Louis
Start with Akar, at 7641 Wydown Blvd. Chef Bernie Lee cooks from his Malaysian heritage, and “Akar” means “roots.” It’s a 44-seat room, and it isn’t a nasi lemak counter: there’s no fixed menu, and the dishes change with what’s fresh, so the Malaysian notes show up reimagined rather than served street-style.
The plate that comes closest to a mamak stall is the roti. The Infatuation told diners to start with the impossibly flaky roti and long bean curry, and said if the curry was available as a drink, they’d knock it back. That’s the Malaysian move in one line: tear the bread, drag it through the sauce, don’t leave any behind. St. Louis Magazine found the short ribs braised in soy sauce instead of red wine, pot roast soft, with a demi-glace spiked with Indonesian sambal adding a vinegary edge. That’s the red stuff again, cut with something sharp so it never just burns.
Sauce Magazine pointed diners to Rangoon stuffed with huge chunks of lobster and served with a spicy-sweet mango sauce, and to a cocktail called the Serai, made with lemongrass-infused tequila. Serai is the Malay word you’d smell before you read it: lemongrass, sharp and green, the same note that runs through a good laksa paste. Reservations are by phone only. Use the call. Ask what’s on tonight that tastes like the chef’s home. Ask how hot it runs. You’ll learn more in two minutes on the phone than in twenty minutes of scrolling photos.
Now the full story behind that Taco Bell. In 2015 chef Ying Jing Ma opened the first Chef Ma’s Chinese Gourmet inside a disused Taco Bell at 2336 Woodson Road, where the “real” menu was written entirely in Chinese. The plate his fans remember is Hainan chicken rice, a dish Sauce Magazine called iconic not only in China’s Hainan province but in Hong Kong and Southeast Asian nations like Malaysia and Singapore. St. Louis Magazine described the rice as flavored with chicken fat, ginger and broth, its fragrance and color like saffron. Ma died at 59. The lesson isn’t an address. It’s that one of the most Malaysian plates this city ever ate sat on a menu most diners couldn’t read, and the people who found it were the ones who asked.
Treat every Malaysian craving that way. Make a short list of two or three places: a Malaysian-rooted kitchen, a Thai or pan-Asian spot on South Grand, a newer place that just opened. Call each one. Tell them exactly what you’re after: “I want something with coconut and not much heat,” or “Do you ever make laksa or roti canai?” Then compare what each one says it can actually put on a plate tonight. The places that light up when you say the word laksa are the ones worth the drive.
Hungry for coconut rice and a bowl of laksa tonight? Start your short list with Malaysian Food on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two or three kitchens and ask what they can make.
If you’re the cook behind a Malaysian, Singaporean or pan-Asian kitchen in St. Louis, this one’s for you. Diners hunting for roti canai and laksa are already looking here, so list your business where they search.
### How do you eat it without looking lost?
Nobody at the next table is grading you, but a few small moves make the food taste better, and they’re the moves people who grew up on it make without thinking.
With nasi lemak, use the spoon as your main tool and the fork to push food onto it. Build each bite: a little rice, a little sambal, two or three anchovies for crunch, a slice of cucumber when your mouth needs cooling. Break the egg early so the yolk runs into the rice. Don’t eat the parts one by one like a sampler; the dish only makes sense when coconut, chili, salt and crunch land on your tongue at the same moment.
With laksa, lean in. Chopsticks for the noodles, the soup spoon for broth and tofu, and yes, slurp. Curry laksa splashes; wear the dark shirt. With roti canai, use your hands and tear. With satay, pull the meat off the skewer with your teeth and drag it through the peanut sauce on every pass.
If you’re hungry to keep exploring the flavors next door to Malaysia, these guides pick up the thread:

Chinese food and dim sum in St. Louis
What Filipino food is and what to order
Where to eat on South Grand
Last thing, and it matters: order one dish you’re sure of and one you’re not. The safe plate keeps dinner from going sideways. The other one is how you end up with a new favorite and a story to tell.
Coconut rice can wait a minute: is your gynecologist appointment overdue?
Then go back to the table, where the teh tarik is still frothy and the sambal is still sitting there, waiting to see how brave you feel tonight.
### Frequently asked questions about Malaysian food
### Q. What does laksa taste like?
A.  Depends which laksa you get. Curry laksa tastes rich and creamy from coconut milk, with a slow-building warmth, tofu puffs that soak up the broth, and noodles underneath. Asam laksa, the Penang style, has no coconut milk at all: it’s a sour tamarind and mackerel broth with pineapple, cucumber, onion and mint, sharp and bright rather than creamy.
### Q. What is the difference between nasi goreng and nasi lemak?
A.  Nasi lemak is rice cooked in coconut milk and pandan leaf, served with separate sides like sambal, fried anchovies, cucumber, peanuts and a boiled egg. Nasi goreng is fried rice with meats, vegetables and spices, usually seasoned with sweet soy sauce. One is rich coconut rice with sides; the other is a single dish straight from the wok.
### Q. How do I eat nasi lemak?
A.  Use the spoon as your main tool and the fork to push. Build each bite with a little rice, a little sambal, a few anchovies and a slice of cucumber, and break the egg early so the yolk runs into the rice. If you’re worried about heat, ask for the sambal on the side and add it a bit at a time.
### Q. Is Malaysian food like Thai food?
A.  They’re related but not the same. Malaysia shares culinary ties with Thailand, and dishes like tom yam cross the border. Malaysian cooking tends to lean on coconut, slow-fried spice pastes and belacan shrimp paste, while a lot of Thai cooking chases a sharper balance of lime, fish sauce and fresh chili.
### Q. Does STL have Chinatown?
A.  St. Louis had one, called Hop Alley, near downtown. It was bounded by Seventh, Tenth, Walnut and Chestnut streets and lasted from 1869 until 1966, when it was demolished for Busch Memorial Stadium. In recent decades, efforts have been made to establish a successor, and a number of Asian grocery stores and restaurants now line Olive Boulevard between I-170 and Skinker Boulevard.

## A $95 Million Mall Sold for $12.7 Million: Which St. Louis Malls Are Still Open
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-malls-whats-still-open
A $95 million mall, sold off for $12.7 million. Most of us blame the suburbs for killing the mall, but that one sat right on Washington Avenue, and when it opened in 1985, St. Louis Centre was the largest urban shopping mall in the United States. Four stories. A green, white and glass front. More than 150 stores and 20 restaurants under one roof, with a Famous-Barr at one end and a Dillard’s at the other.
If you rode those escalators as a kid, you remember the sound before you remember a single store. The low rubber hum of the handrail. Hard shoes clacking on tile. Somebody’s little brother yelling across the atrium while a parent hissed his name. Then the same building became an almost-empty “dead mall,” and in 2006 it closed.
Here’s the part people get backwards. They picture the malls dying from the outside in, the far-flung ones first, the big central one last. St. Louis did it the other way around. Northwest Plaza, once the largest enclosed mall in the state of Missouri, closed on January 1, 2011. Size didn’t save anybody.
Whether you’re after a gift, a dry place to walk when it’s sleeting, or just the mall you remember, here is the honest map, dark corridors included, plus the early-morning habit the regulars already know.
That secret first, because it’s the most useful thing on this page. Monday through Saturday, the Saint Louis Galleria opens its stores at 10 a.m., but walkers get in at 8. The mall says plainly that it supports mall walkers, and they can come in through the north parking garage entrance at 8 a.m. On most mornings that’s two quiet hours of climate-controlled floor before the first gate rattles up. Just you, your sneakers, and the faint squeak of rubber on a floor somebody mopped last night. At 8 you can hear the escalators running for nobody. By 10 it’s gates clattering up, the first stroller wheels, and the pretzel ovens warming. Before your first morning, call the front desk at 314-571-7000 and confirm the walker door, because a locked garage at 7:55 is a cold way to start.
Now the rest of the map.
### What malls are still open in St. Louis?
The Saint Louis Galleria is open 10 a.m. to 7 p.m. Monday through Saturday, and West County Center and Mid Rivers Mall are open 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. Monday through Saturday. All three open 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. on Sunday. St. Louis Centre closed in 2006 and Northwest Plaza in 2011.
The Galleria keeps its hours on its own page. It sits at 1155 Saint Louis Galleria, St. Louis, MO 63117, about 10 miles from downtown, and you can reach the front desk at 314-571-7000. West County Center’s hours page notes that stores with their own outside doors may keep different hours.
Out along I-70, Mid Rivers Mall opened in 1987, lists over 140 shops and posts its hours online. That’s a real enclosed mall for anyone already heading that way.
If your memory is of a roof, a skylight and a pretzel smell drifting down a long tiled corridor, those three are where it still lives.
### So where did downtown’s giant mall go?
What happened to St. Louis Centre mall is a story about money and timing. It was a $95 million complex. It drew crowds for a few years. Then, in 1991, the old Westroads Shopping Center out west was rebuilt into the Saint Louis Galleria, and the downtown mall suddenly had a shinier rival with easy parking. By the mid-1990s, the Dillard’s end had turned into a clearance store, and that store shut for good in 2001.
Walk through it in your head in those last years and you can feel how empty it got. Rows of pulled-down metal gates. The echo of a place built for thousands, holding a few dozen. A single open shop with its lights on, like a porch light on a dark street. In 2006 the “dead mall” closed outright.
The ending wasn’t pretty. A developer bought it with plans for condos and shops, then went under in 2008. The bank foreclosed in 2009, and the whole thing sold for $12.7 million. That’s the number that makes people stop: a $95 million mall, sold for about an eighth of what it cost. That same year, the building was about 85% vacant.
In May 2010, crews started turning part of it into a 750-car parking garage and a retail and entertainment space called Mercantile Exchange. The skybridges that had carried shoppers over the street came down so the two downtown streets underneath could see sky again, and one newspaper headline at the time reported that a party was planned as the downtown skybridge fell to the wrecking ball. A party. For a demolition. That tells you how most of downtown felt about a building that had turned its back on the sidewalk.
If you park in that garage for a night downtown, you’re driving up ramps where people once bought jeans.
Malls close quietly. So do gums. Bleeding when you floss is worth a look.
### The north county malls that went dark
Northwest Plaza opened in 1965 as an open-air shopping center, got a roof later, and grew into the largest enclosed mall in the state of Missouri. At its peak, Northwest Plaza held nine anchor stores and more than 210 shops. If you grew up nearby, you probably remember the parking lot more than anything: a sea of asphalt so wide you wrote down the row number on your hand. The mall closed on January 1, 2011. The site lives on as The Crossings at Northwest, a mixed-use center with retail and office space instead of a food court.
Jamestown Mall opened in 1973 and never quite recovered once tenants started drifting away in the early 2000s. It closed in July 2014. For years it sat there, windows going cloudy, until it was demolished from 2023 to 2024. The site has been slated for redevelopment as an open-air center.
St. Louis Mills is the one that stings, because it was so new. It opened on November 13, 2003, with a food court designed to resemble the 1904 St. Louis World’s Fair, and in 2006 it was 99% occupied. Then the stores thinned out. After years of struggles with tenants and upkeep, it closed in 2019. A sports complex called POWERplex STL ran there from 2019 to 2023, and in 2023 the interior was gutted and redeveloped into a business park, an industrial warehouse and office building. Kids who ate lunch in that World’s Fair food court are now old enough to ask where it went.
### Which St. Louis mall died once and came back?
The answer is West County Center: the first version opened on February 20, 1969, on the site of an old drive-in movie theater that many people remember for the Easter sunrise services held there. Think about that for a second: families in folding chairs and car hoods at dawn, and then, a few years later, a mall on the same ground.
That original mall closed on January 27, 2001, and it was demolished, all except the JCPenney building, which got remodeled. A brand-new mall opened on the same site on September 20, 2002, a $230 million project with a two-story Nordstrom, a food court and three parking garages. So the mall you walk into there today is not the mall your parents walked into. It was torn down and rebuilt on purpose, which is a big reason it’s still standing while others aren’t.
By the numbers, West County Center lists 1,209,649 square feet and more than 150 stores. The Galleria lists 1.2 million square feet. Those two are a coin flip in size and a different feel entirely: the Galleria leans polished and dressy, West County leans family errand day with a stop for pretzels.
### Before the gates go up: the walkers’ hour
Are mall walkers still a thing? At the Galleria, yes, and the mall says so in writing. The doors at the north parking garage open to walkers at 8 a.m. That means you can walk around the mall before it opens, as long as you come in that way and stay in the common corridors while the stores stay dark.
Picture the actual feel of it, because it’s nothing like a Saturday. The air is cool and still. The escalators are running for nobody. Behind the metal gates you can see shelves half-lit, a manager counting a drawer, a mannequin with no arms waiting for its sweater. Your footsteps are the loudest thing in the building. A couple of regulars nod as they pass you for the second time. Nobody is trying to sell you anything.
A few practical things help. Wear real walking shoes, since the floors are hard. Bring a water bottle, because the food court won’t be serving yet. Park on the north side so you’re not hiking across the lot in the cold. If you want company, start with a friend on a fixed morning each week; a standing date beats good intentions every time.
If West County Center or Mid Rivers Mall is closer to you, call the mall office and ask about early walking before you show up at dawn. Ask the office, not the internet.
Don’t burn a Saturday driving to a gate that’s already down. Check which stores and shopping centers are actually open near you on the Malls page on St Louis Near Me Directory before you grab your keys.
If you’re the shop owner paying rent under a mall skylight, you already know foot traffic isn’t what it was. More St. Louis shoppers start by searching for what’s open and close by, so see who AI names instead of you and put your store where they are looking.
### When is the mall actually worth the drive?
The best time to go to the mall, if you want a calm one, is a weekday morning right after the doors open. The stores are freshly stocked, the fitting rooms are empty, and the only line is at the coffee counter. By late afternoon the after-school crowd arrives, and the noise climbs.
Weekends are a different animal, and the Galleria plans for it. On Fridays and Saturdays, kids 16 and under must be with an adult after 2 p.m. If you’re a parent planning to drop off your teenager for an afternoon, that rule decides your weekend for you. If you’re a grown-up who wants quiet, it’s a hint to go early.
Sunday is the short day at all three, 11 a.m. to 6 p.m., so a late Sunday trip gives you less time than you think. And if you’re hunting one specific item, call the store first. It’s a 60-second call that can save you a 40-minute round trip and a parking garage you’ll circle twice.
### What about Union Station?
For a while, Union Station was a mall. The old train station was renovated in the 1980s as a hotel, shopping center and entertainment complex, and the mall side reopened in 1985, the same year St. Louis Centre opened downtown. The mall chapter ended in 2016. In 2019 the building got its next life as the home of the St. Louis Aquarium, so the corridor where you once bought a souvenir T-shirt now leads to fish tanks.
That’s the pattern across the whole region. The buildings rarely just vanish. They become parking, offices, warehouses, an aquarium. If you want to see what a place turned into, it’s worth the drive. Stand where the entrance used to be. You’ll be surprised what your body remembers: the turn you used to make toward the arcade, the spot where the cold air hit you coming in from August heat.
