### Frequently asked questions about St. Louis malls
### Q. What happened to St. Louis Centre mall?
A.  It opened downtown in 1985 as the largest urban shopping mall in the country, lost shoppers after the Saint Louis Galleria was rebuilt in 1991, and closed in 2006 as an almost-empty dead mall. After a 2009 foreclosure it sold for $12.7 million, and part of it became a 750-car parking garage and retail space called Mercantile Exchange.
### Q. Is St. Louis Galleria still open?
A.  Yes. The Saint Louis Galleria is open 10 a.m. to 7 p.m. Monday through Saturday and 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. on Sunday, at 1155 Saint Louis Galleria, St. Louis, MO 63117. The main number is 314-571-7000. Check the mall’s hours page before a special trip.
### Q. What is the largest mall in St. Louis?
A.  By listed floor area, West County Center comes in at 1,209,649 square feet and the Saint Louis Galleria at 1.2 million, close enough to call it a tie. Northwest Plaza was once the largest enclosed mall in the state of Missouri, and it closed on January 1, 2011.
### Q. Are mall walkers still a thing?
A.  Yes. The Saint Louis Galleria says outright that it supports mall walkers and lets them in through the north parking garage entrance at 8 a.m., two hours before the stores open. Wear real walking shoes, bring water, and expect a quiet, cool building with the gates still down.
### Q. Can I walk around the mall before it opens?
A.  At the Galleria you can, starting at 8 a.m. through the north parking garage entrance. At any other mall, call the office before you go.
### Q. What is the best time to go to the mall?
A.  For a calm trip, go on a weekday morning right after the 10 a.m. opening. Weekend afternoons are the busiest, and at the Galleria, kids 16 and under need an adult with them after 2 p.m. on Fridays and Saturdays. Sundays are short, closing at 6 p.m.
### Q. How many malls are there in St. Louis?
A.  Of the enclosed malls in this guide, the Galleria is open until 7 p.m. and West County Center and Mid Rivers Mall until 8 p.m., Monday through Saturday.
### Q. Is Union Station still a mall?
A.  Union Station was renovated in the 1980s as a hotel, shopping center and entertainment complex, and its mall closed in 2016. Since 2019 it has been home to the St. Louis Aquarium.
### Q. Can teenagers go to the Galleria without a parent?
A.  On Fridays and Saturdays, children 16 years or under must be accompanied by an adult after 2 p.m. at Saint Louis Galleria, so plan weekend drop-offs for earlier in the day.

## Your Jeans Won’t Button? When to Start Buying Maternity Clothes in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/when-to-start-buying-maternity-clothes-in-st-louis
First Friday in August, a red light on Gravois, the car still hot from the parking lot. You pop the top button of your jeans and feel your whole stomach exhale. The button has been pressing a red ridge into your skin since lunch, the seat belt has settled somewhere new, and you’re quietly counting how many more days these jeans have left. You have no idea that since 12:01 this morning, every pair of maternity jeans in Missouri priced $100 or less has been tax-free.
Almost nobody in that car knows it. At 12:01 that morning, Missouri’s Back-to-School Sales Tax Holiday started, and it runs until midnight Sunday. For those three days, any article of clothing with a taxable value of $100 or less is exempt from all state and local sales tax. Read the rule slowly. The state defines clothing as any article of wearing apparel intended to be worn on or about the human body. It doesn’t say kids’ clothing. Nobody at the register asks whether anyone in your house is starting second grade. And the local cut is gone too: the state’s own FAQ says that starting January 1, 2023, the holiday exempts all state and local sales or use taxes, so a register in Soulard or on Cherokee Street rings up the same zero as one anywhere else in Missouri.
Maternity jeans are clothing. So is the stretchy dress you’ll wear to three baby showers and a wedding. Most expecting parents in St. Louis never hear that, because the weekend gets advertised with backpacks and crayons. Two catches before you load the cart: the law leaves out scarves, headbands, jewelry and handbags, and items normally sold in pairs can’t be split up to slip under the $100 line. Not sure a piece counts? The Missouri Department of Revenue takes questions about the taxability of items at 573-751-2836. Call before the weekend, not from the fitting room.
So do one thing today, whatever month you’re in. Put the first Friday in August on your phone with an alert for 12:01 a.m. Then let your body, not the calendar, tell you the rest. By the time a coworker notices the bump, the question has already changed from “when should I buy maternity clothes” to “what am I wearing tomorrow.” This is the schedule nobody hands you: the week the waistband turns on you, what to buy first, what to borrow, and the one St. Louis rule that saves the most money. Buy for the month you will be biggest, not the month you are in.
### What month should you start buying maternity clothes in St. Louis?
Start buying real maternity clothes when the bump starts to show and your regular waistbands quit. In a first pregnancy, the first signs of a bump usually appear early in the second trimester, between weeks 12 and 16, and someone carrying one baby may not show until after 3 or 4 months.
Smaller through the middle, closer to 12 weeks. More weight there, closer to 16. Either way it shows up sideways: the bathroom mirror, the hair dryer running, a curve under your shirt that wasn’t there last week. Face the mirror and it’s gone. Turn again. Still there.
That curve means a few pieces, not a wardrobe. After the first trimester most people gain about 1 pound a week for the rest of the pregnancy, so the top that lies flat and perfect in the fitting room at week 16 is pulling across your ribs by week 26. Buy the one with stretch to spare.
And in St. Louis, the month on the calendar matters almost as much as the week of the pregnancy. If your fourth month lands in late July, the tax-free weekend is days away and worth waiting for. If it lands in November, you’re shopping for a body that grows every week of a Missouri winter, and the first thing that stops closing won’t be your jeans. It’ll be your coat.
### Why do your clothes get tight before you even show?
Clothes get tight in pregnancy earlier than the bump can explain. Plenty of people feel the waistband dig in during the first trimester, weeks before anyone at work could guess, and assume they’re gaining fast. Usually they aren’t. Most people gain just 2 to 4 pounds during the first trimester. That little weight doesn’t close a button gap or open one. For a lot of people, that early squeeze is bloat and a midsection quietly changing shape, the same puffy, end-of-the-day tightness many know from their period, only it doesn’t go away on Monday.
Sitting is where you find out. Standing at the counter, the jeans feel fine. Then you slide into a booth on The Hill, a plate of toasted ravioli lands in front of you, and the waistband draws a hard line straight across your stomach. You spend the rest of dinner leaning back like you’re in a recliner.
This is the stretch where you should spend almost nothing. The cheapest fix in pregnancy is a hair tie. Loop a ponytail holder or rubber band through the buttonhole and around the button, and the elastic gives you an inch or more of breathing room. Pull a long tank top or a stretchy belly band over the open zipper and nobody sees the trick. It costs nothing, and it buys you weeks.
The hair tie stops working when the button sits right on the bump instead of under it. That’s the day. When the waistband no longer has anywhere to go, your regular pants are done, and the first real maternity purchase earns its money.
### Can you just size up instead of buying maternity clothes?
You can size up for a while, and for some pieces it’s the smartest move you’ll make. But sizing up only adds width, and a pregnant body mostly needs length in the front. A regular shirt one size bigger hangs loose at the shoulders, the sleeves slide past your wrists, and the front hem still rides up over the bump. Reach for a cereal box on the top shelf and there’s a stripe of skin showing above your waistband, cold air from the freezer aisle hitting it.
Maternity tops are cut differently, with extra fabric in the front so the hem stays level as the bump grows. That one detail is most of what you’re paying for.
Pants are where sizing up fails fastest. A bigger size gaps at the back of the waist, the seat sags, and the waistband still has to sit somewhere, which is usually right across the lowest part of the bump. You’ll be hitching them up every time you stand.
So split it. Size up on the pieces that are already loose by design and that you’ll keep wearing after the baby: knit dresses, wrap dresses, long cardigans, a partner’s oversized button-down that smells like their laundry soap. Buy true maternity cuts for pants, fitted tops and anything you’ll wear to work. That split is how most people keep the total spend small without spending five months tugging at their own hem.
### Buy for the month you will be biggest, not the month you are in
Count forward to your due date. Your final weeks are when you’ll be biggest, and in St. Louis those months land in one of two very different worlds.
If you’re due in September or October, your biggest weeks are a St. Louis summer. You know that air. Step out of an air-conditioned store into a parking lot in August and it’s like opening a dishwasher mid-cycle. Your thighs stick to the car seat. The backs of your knees sweat at a Cardinals game before the first pitch, and a slow loop around the lake in Tower Grove Park leaves your shirt stuck to the small of your back. Carrying a bump through that, every extra layer of fabric feels like a wool blanket. Full-panel pants that felt like a hug in April feel like a wetsuit by August.
For a summer finish, buy loose and breathable: cotton or linen-blend dresses that hang from the shoulders, under-the-bump shorts, tank tops with long front hems, sandals a half size roomier because feet can swell in the heat. Skip anything thick, shiny or tight across the belly. And if your biggest months land in late summer, the tax-free weekend on the first Friday in August is timed almost perfectly for you. Any article of clothing with a taxable value of $100 or less is exempt from state and local sales tax that weekend, so a $90 pair of maternity jeans rings up at $90.
If you’re due in February or March, your biggest weeks are a St. Louis winter, and the problem is the coat. You zip it up in the car and the zipper stops two inches short of the top of the bump, wind off the river cutting straight through the gap while you wait at a bus stop on Grand. A full maternity coat is expensive for a few months of use. A coat extender panel, a partner’s big parka or a long, heavy cardigan layered over a warm top will usually get you through to the due date.
Spring and fall finishes are the easy ones, except for Missouri’s habit of swinging from coat weather to T-shirt weather inside a single week. Layers win: a stretchy dress, a cardigan you can peel off, leggings with a fold-over waist.
The money point is simple. Clothes bought for the season you’re in will be too small by the season you finish in. Buy most of your later-pregnancy wardrobe for the weather of your final weeks, and it gets worn the most.
That cough you keep blaming on ragweed might deserve a lung doctor.
### What should you buy first, and what should you borrow?
The first maternity purchase should be the piece you’ll wear the most days in a row. For most people, that’s pants. Everything else can wait a few weeks or come out of somebody else’s closet.
Buy these yourself, because fit matters and you’ll wear them constantly:
One or two pairs of maternity pants or jeans you actually like, either over-the-bump panels or under-the-bump bands. Try both if you can. Some people love the full panel, and some can’t stand the feeling of fabric over the bump.
Two or three stretchy tops with extra length in the front, in colors that go with those pants.
One knit dress that works for an office, a baby shower and a wedding, depending on what shoes you put with it.
A bra that fits the body you have this month, not the one you had before.
A belly band to stretch the life of your regular pants and cover the gap.
Borrow the things you’ll wear for only a few weeks or a single event: the dressy outfit for a wedding, the winter coat, the biggest third-trimester sizes and anything for a season you’ll only be pregnant in briefly. In a lot of St. Louis families, maternity clothes travel. A sister or a friend from church hands over a stuffed trash bag in the driveway, everything folded, all of it smelling like somebody else’s dryer sheets. Say yes to it. Wash it, keep what fits, and pass the rest along when you’re done.
Resale racks are worth a look for the same reason: maternity clothes get worn for months, not years, so a lot of them come in barely broken in. Check the stretch panels for loose elastic and the knees for pilling before you buy.
### Your maternity closet, in the order you’ll need it
Taped inside a closet door in Dutchtown or the Central West End, this is the whole plan on one sheet:
Today: set the phone alert for the first Friday in August at 12:01 a.m.
Waistband digs, no bump yet: hair tie through the buttonhole, long tank over the zipper, spend nothing.
Bump shows, usually weeks 12 to 16 in a first pregnancy: one or two pairs of maternity pants and two or three long-front tops.
Hair tie quits: count to your due date and buy the rest for the weather of your final weeks.
Before you buy a coat or a wedding outfit: ask your sister, your cousins and your friends from church first.
After the baby: wash it all, fold it into the same trash bag, and hand it to the next person.
### Why is it so hard to find maternity clothes in an actual store?
It isn’t your imagination. In October 2019, Destination Maternity, the company behind its namesake stores and Motherhood Maternity, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection and said it planned to close 183 stores. In a court document, the company blamed the retail industry’s turmoil, declining birth rates, high rents and leadership turnover. A lot of maternity clothing moved online after that, or shrank down to a single rack in the back corner of a bigger store.
Online works fine for leggings. It’s a gamble for everything else, because maternity sizing is a guess layered on top of a guess. You order your usual size, the box sits on the porch in the sun, and the jeans that come out fit your hips but not the bump, or the bump but not your legs. Then it’s back to the post office, standing in line with your hand on your lower back.
Trying things on in person still wins, especially for pants. In the fitting room you pull on the jeans, sit down on the little bench, stand up, turn sideways, and you know in thirty seconds whether you’ll live in them for five months.
To make the trip worth it, shortlist two or three shops that carry maternity clothing, whether that’s a boutique, a resale shop or a department store with a maternity section. Call each one before you drive. Tell them how far along you are, your due month and what you need the clothes for, whether that’s a work wardrobe, a wedding or just pants that don’t hurt. Ask what they have on the rack right now in your size and how returns work. Then compare what each shop can actually put in your hands. The one that listens to the question is usually the one worth the gas.

If you’re the boutique or resale shop with a maternity rack, this reader is already shopping for you. Expecting parents across St. Louis are searching here for exactly what hangs on that rack, so list your business and get more customers through your door.
### Frequently asked questions about maternity clothes
### Q. When can you start wearing maternity jeans?
A.  Whenever your regular jeans stop working, which for many people is early in the second trimester, between weeks 12 and 16. Some people switch in the first trimester simply because a soft waistband feels better than a button, and that’s a fine reason.
### Q. Can you just size up when pregnant?
A.  For loose pieces like knit dresses, cardigans and oversized button-downs, yes. For pants and fitted tops, sizing up usually fails, because a bigger size adds width everywhere while the bump needs extra length in the front. Expect gaping at the back of the waist and a hem that rides up.
### Q. When in pregnancy do clothes get tight?
A.  Often in the first trimester, before there’s a visible bump. Most people gain only 2 to 4 pounds in those first months, so early tightness is usually bloat and a changing midsection rather than weight. A hair tie looped through the buttonhole of your jeans buys a few weeks.
### Q. Why are stores no longer selling maternity clothes?
A.  Destination Maternity, the company behind Motherhood Maternity, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in 2019 and planned to close 183 stores, blaming the retail industry’s turmoil, declining birth rates, high rents and leadership turnover. A lot of maternity clothing moved online, which is why calling a local shop before you drive saves a wasted trip.
### Q. Where can I find a maternity clothing sale?
A.  Look at the calendar first. Under Section 144.049 of Missouri law, the Back-to-School Sales Tax Holiday starts at 12:01 a.m. on the first Friday in August and runs through Sunday, and during it any article of clothing with a taxable value of $100 or less is exempt from state and local sales tax, and maternity clothes are clothing. Resale shops and hand-me-downs from friends are the other big savings.
### Q. When did you switch to maternity clothes in your second pregnancy?
A.  Usually sooner than the first time. After a first pregnancy, stretched abdominal muscles don’t always return to their original size, and it’s not uncommon to see a bump in the first trimester. If you’re carrying twins, you might show as early as 6 weeks. Keep your first-pregnancy clothes handy.

## Monday, Then Thursday, Then Nothing: How to Tell If a St. Louis Business Is Reputable
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-tell-if-a-st-louis-business-is-reputable
Monday, the text said. Then Thursday. Then nothing. The check torn out at the kitchen table, still smelling faintly of the pen, cleared days ago, and now a blue tarp snaps against the roof every time the wind comes up off the river and you lie awake listening to it.
You are not the only one up there listening. 1,800-plus complaints in one year, and you can almost hear the voicemails that started them. That is how many complaints the Missouri Attorney General’s office received about home repair, construction and real estate, which put the category fifth on the office’s list of Missourians’ top consumer complaints. The office says what they often involve in one flat line: home repair contractors who ask for money up front and provide little to no work.
Here is the part nobody paints on the side of a van: Missouri has no statewide general contractor license. None. General contractors are licensed at the county and city level instead, so when a friend from another state tells you to “look up their state license number,” you come up empty and think you did it wrong. You didn’t. Inside the city limits, business licenses come from the License Collector, and they quietly die every May 31. The paperwork that separates a real business from a smooth talker is public, and most of it sits one search box away from the couch you’re sitting on. Almost nobody looks.
So here is the check, in the order a careful neighbor would run it: the city’s business license search on stlouis-mo.gov, the state’s free business filing search at bsd.sos.mo.gov, and the city’s permit search by address, where the contractor’s own name sits next to the jobs they pulled permits for. Save two numbers in your phone tonight, before you need them: the License Collector at (314) 622-4528 and the Attorney General’s Consumer Protection Hotline at 800-392-8222. Then comes how to read reviews so they tell you the truth, and what to ask when the person is standing on your porch with a clipboard and a smile.
### How to check if a business is reputable in St. Louis?
Check three public records before you pay anyone: the City of St. Louis business license search, the Missouri Secretary of State website to see whether the business is registered with the state, and the city’s building permit search by address for past jobs. Then read the reviews from the middle out, interview two or three providers, and keep the big deposit in your pocket until a business clears all three.
You can run them on your phone at the curb while the estimate is still warm in your hand and the truck is still idling. A business that is the real thing passes without trying, because it has been filing the paperwork quietly for years. A business that isn’t tends to trip on the very first one.
Why bother when the guy seems great? Because seeming great is the entire skill set of the worst ones. They are friendly. They are fast. They work the old St. Louis icebreaker on you before you’ve asked a single question, and by the time you’ve said the name of your high school they somehow know your cousin. Paperwork doesn’t care how charming anybody is. In this town the first question is always where you went to high school. Make the second one: are you on the city’s license list?
There is help after the fact, too. The Attorney General’s advocates try to mediate complaints between consumers and businesses, and when there are credible allegations of a violation of the Missouri Merchandising Practices Act, investigators look into it and attorneys can file suit. That matters. But it is help after the money is gone. The five minutes is help before.
### The city license that quietly expires every May 31
Start at City Hall without getting off the couch. The porch light is still on and the estimate is balanced on the arm of the sofa. Open the city’s business license search. Every sole proprietor, partnership and corporation that conducts business in the City of St. Louis has to get a city business license for that activity, and this is where the License Collector’s Office shows who has one.
Two details make it far more useful than it looks. First, a city license runs on a fiscal year: it is valid starting June 1 and expires May 31 the following year, and the search only shows businesses licensed for the current year. A company that was legit two summers ago and then folded will not show up as current. Second, the database is updated nightly. If someone says they “just renewed yesterday,” you can look again tomorrow morning and see whether it was true. A license expires every May 31. A smile never does.
Type part of the name, not all of it. The city’s own search tips say you can search using any part of the name, and that business licenses are issued under legal names. The friendly name on the magnet sign may be filed under something longer with LLC on the end. Try the shortest distinctive word and scan the list.
The rule, as the city words it, covers all persons who conduct business in the city. So a roofer who drives in from Coulterville, Illinois, to work on a Benton Park two-flat should be looking at the same search you are, the same as the shop around the corner on Cherokee Street.
One honest limit. The search covers the city’s graduated business license only, not license types that other departments handle, and it covers the city, not every town around it. If a business you trust doesn’t show up, call the License Collector at (314) 622-4528, or walk into City Hall at 1200 Market Street, Rooms 102-104, Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., before you assume the worst. Names get filed in strange ways, and a two-minute call beats a sleepless night.
### Is the name on the truck the name on file in Jefferson City?
The second record lives with the Missouri Secretary of State, whose office sits at 600 West Main Street in Jefferson City. The city itself points you there: you can verify whether a business is registered with the State of Missouri on the Secretary of State’s website, and searching the state’s business filings is free at bsd.sos.mo.gov. Your thumb hovers over the search button. Ten seconds later you know whether the company on the estimate exists on paper.
Here is the little-known part. Missouri law requires any person or business that transacts business in the state under a name other than their own “true name” to register that business name with the Secretary of State as a Fictitious Name Registration. In plain words, the name painted on the truck door should lead back to a real person or a real company. If the name on the truck, the name on the estimate and the name on the state file are three different names, ask why. Sometimes the answer is boring. Sometimes it isn’t.
And remember the missing state contractor license from the top of this page. If the state search turns up a company but no contractor license, that empty spot is not a red flag. It is just how the state works. For the trade-by-trade version, see how to check if a contractor is licensed in Missouri.
Need a palate cleanser? Try a first trip to a St. Louis kosher grocery.
### Has this crew ever pulled a permit in the city?
This is the check almost nobody runs, and it may be the best one. The City of St. Louis publishes its building permit data, and the fields include the contractor’s name, the contractor’s phone and a contractor license number. Electrical permits are published the same way. Put simply, the city keeps a running record of who did permitted work, and at which addresses.
Here is how to use it. Say the contractor tells you they redid the porch two doors down. Walk over. Stand in the gangway and look at the new railing, the paint still sharp enough to smell. Then type that address into the city’s building permit search by address, which finds past permits issued for a property. If a permit comes up with their name on it, you just got a reference nobody coached.
The search box asks for one thing: a street address or parcel. Type the house number and street the way it reads on the mailbox, hit search, and give it a few seconds, because the page itself warns it may take a few seconds to process. Then scroll the list of past permits and look for the contractor’s name next to the work.
And the city keeps more than building permits. Its Building Division also publishes demolition, electrical, mechanical and plumbing permit data, with the plumbing and mechanical sets broken out by neighborhood and ward, plus a list of all vacant buildings its inspectors track. So if a plumber swears he has done a dozen jobs in Soulard, there is a public file that can tell you whether Soulard has ever heard of him.
If they say they do “tons of jobs in the city” and their name is nowhere in the records, treat it as a question, not a verdict. Ask whether your job needs a permit, and who pulls it. A reputable contractor answers in one sentence and doesn’t blink. A shaky one changes the subject to how soon they can start.
Notice what this check does that reviews can’t. A review is somebody’s opinion. A permit is a record the business created with the city, under its own name, about a real address on a real block in Dutchtown or the Central West End. Nobody fakes their way into a permit file to look good on a Tuesday night.
### What do the reviews actually tell you, and what don’t they?
Reviews are the check everyone runs first, and the one that fools people most. Start with the size of the problem. Google says that in a single year its systems and analysts blocked or removed more than 292 million policy-violating reviews on Maps, while publishing more than 1 billion helpful ones, and removed more than 13 million fake Business Profiles. That is the short answer to why so many Google reviews are being removed: a lot of them were never real, and some of the businesses weren’t either.
To look up Google reviews for a business, search its exact name plus “St. Louis” in Google, or open it in Google Maps, then tap the star rating to open the full list and sort by newest. Then read it like a neighbor, not like a scoreboard. A 4.9 tells you less than three honest sentences from someone who lives on your side of Grand.
Read the three-star reviews first. They are usually written by people who aren’t furious and aren’t family.
Watch the dates. A burst of glowing reviews in one week, then a long silence, is a pattern worth a second look.
Look for specifics. A street, a season, the first name of who showed up, the mud on the stairs. Real customers remember details. Fake ones remember “great service.”
Read the owner’s replies. Calm and specific beats defensive every single time.
One more thing that confuses people. If a busy shop suddenly shows a strange gap, Google says that when it sees a sudden spike in spam reviews, it removes the fake content, pauses new reviews on the profile, alerts the owner and shows a banner telling customers why. A pause is not a verdict on the business. Sometimes it means the business was the target.
Because yes, owners get hit too. Google says it has upgraded its systems to be even faster at stopping new kinds of scams, like attempts to demand payment in exchange for removing fake one-star reviews. Think about the stomach drop of a shop owner on South Grand opening an email like that over the morning register. Keep that in mind the next time a single furious review sits alone on an otherwise steady page.
Want to hear from St. Louis pros before anyone is standing on your porch? Read how local tradespeople explain their own work in plain English on Local Expertise Article on St Louis Near Me Directory, then bring their questions to your interviews.
If you’re the roofer, the remodeler or the one-truck crew who renews every June, let people see it. More St. Louis homeowners are already looking here for someone they can check out before they call, so list your business right where they are searching.
### Shortlist three, then interview them on the porch
Once a business clears the records and the reviews, stop researching and start talking. Shortlist two or three. Invite each one out. Tell every one of them the same thing, in your own words, about what you want done and what matters most to you, whether that is the budget, the timing or keeping the dog calm. Then compare what each one says they will actually deliver.
Watch how they look at the job. A good one climbs the ladder, presses a palm flat against the soffit, and tells you something about your own house you didn’t know. A bad one never takes his hands out of his pockets. You will feel the difference in your chest before you can explain it.
Questions worth asking each of them:
Who exactly will be working at my house, and are they your people?
Does this job need a permit, and who pulls it?
What does the deposit cover, and when do the materials show up in my driveway?
What happens to the schedule if it rains for a week?
Can I see a job you finished in the city in the last year?
Skip the demand for a line-by-line quote; good pros price whole jobs and many won’t play that game. What you want is a clear written scope, a clear deposit, and a start date in ink. The Attorney General’s complaint pattern is money up front and little or no work, so a deposit that matches what has actually arrived at your curb is the cleanest protection you can ask for.
### Where does a complaint go if it goes wrong anyway?
Sometimes you do everything right and it still goes sideways. The phone stops ringing. The dumpster sits in the alley, half full, collecting leaves. When that happens, file a complaint with the Missouri Attorney General at ago.mo.gov or call the Consumer Protection Hotline at 800-392-8222. Keep every text, every receipt and every photo, with dates. Then read what to do when a contractor won’t finish the job.
Your complaint also does a quiet favor for the next family on the block. The Attorney General’s office describes the reports it gets as tools to identify misconduct and stop bad actors. The five-minute check protects your house. The complaint protects your street.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How to find a local business?
A.  Search the service plus your neighborhood, like “tuckpointing Soulard” or “plumber The Hill,” in Google Maps, browse a local directory such as St Louis Near Me Directory by category, and ask the people on your block who just had the same work done. Then look up whoever lands on your shortlist in the city’s business license search, which shows only businesses considered currently licensed.
### Q. Where can I read business reviews?
A.  Google Maps is the usual first stop, since you can write reviews there for places you visit, and local listings like St Louis Near Me Directory show what the business says about itself in its own words. The most honest source is still a neighbor: ask for the address of a recent job, go look at it, and check the permit history for that address in the city’s building permit search.
### Q. Why are so many Google reviews being removed?
A.  Because a lot of them break the rules. Google says that in one year it blocked or removed more than 292 million policy-violating reviews on Maps and took down more than 13 million fake Business Profiles. Reviews that are fake, paid for or posted in a spam burst are what usually disappear, which is why a rating can drop overnight.
### Q. Why can’t I see Google reviews on a business?
A.  The business may be new and simply have none yet, or you may be looking at a second listing for the same place, so search the exact address too. Google also says that when it spots a sudden spike in spam reviews, it pauses new reviews on the profile and shows a banner explaining why. A pause is not proof the business did anything wrong.
### Q. How do I look up Google reviews for a business?
A.  Search the business’s exact name plus “St. Louis” in Google, or open it in Google Maps, and tap the star rating to open the full list. Sort by newest, read the three-star reviews first, and look for specific details like a street, a date or a name, which fake reviews almost never have.
### Q. What should I do if a St. Louis contractor took my deposit and disappeared?
A.  Gather every text, receipt and photo, with dates, and send the contractor one calm written request to finish or refund. If that goes nowhere, file a complaint with the Missouri Attorney General at ago.mo.gov or call the Consumer Protection Hotline at 800-392-8222. Advocates there try to mediate complaints between consumers and businesses.

## Saturday at 1 p.m. Is a Trap: When to Shop St. Louis Outlet Malls and What to Skip
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/when-to-shop-st-louis-outlet-malls
Your sneakers are standing on old floodwater. The ground under St. Louis Premium Outlets, off I-64 out west, sat underwater during the Flood of 1993, and both outlet sites you can see from that highway did. Now your thumb is flipping a price tag over to do the math again, a stroller wheel bumps your heel, the fitting-room line bends around the end of the display table, and somebody’s kid is asking, loudly, whether you’re done yet. It’s early afternoon on a Saturday, and the medium you wanted is gone.
Come back at 10 a.m. on a Monday and you can hear the hangers slide on the rail. Settle three questions from the kitchen table tonight, before the car leaves the driveway. The hour: in Google’s busy-times tips reported by Real Simple, shopping centers are least busy at 10 a.m. Monday and busiest 1-2 p.m. on Saturdays, and the outlets open at 10 a.m. Monday through Saturday, with free parking. The weekend: Missouri’s Back-to-School Sales Tax Holiday runs from 12:01 a.m. on the first Friday in August to midnight that Sunday, and it now exempts all state and local sales or use taxes on qualifying clothing, school supplies and computers. The habit: look up what the same item costs at the brand’s regular store before you go, because the Federal Trade Commission warns that many stores sell products at their outlets made exclusively for those outlets, and they may be of lower quality.
Here’s the line to text the family group chat. The tax-free limit for clothing is $100 per item, not per cart, and it’s all or nothing. In the state’s own example, $98 jeans go tax-free while a $114 sweater is taxed on its full cost. Go $14 over and you pay tax on all $114.
And here’s the St. Louis story most shoppers never hear: St. Louis got not one new outlet mall but two that year, and Urban Review STL sized them up side by side. Taubman Prestige Outlets opened August 2, 2013. St. Louis Premium Outlets opened August 22, three weeks later. St. Louis Public Radio called it what it was: the outlet mall battle.
In April 2018, St. Louis Magazine reported the rival was being sold to The Staenberg Group, which planned to turn the shopping center into an entertainment destination. That story, and the bigger one about St. Louis Mills off Route 370, carries a lesson about timing, too. We’ll get there.
Write the hours on a sticky note and slap it on the dashboard. St. Louis Premium Outlets is open 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. Monday through Saturday and 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. on Sunday, according to St. Louis Roamer’s visit guide.
### What is the least busy time to go to the mall in St. Louis?
The least busy time to go to the mall is 10 a.m. on a Monday. In Google’s busy-times tips reported by Real Simple, shopping centers are least busy then and busiest 1-2 p.m. on Saturdays. St. Louis Premium Outlets opens at 10 a.m. Monday through Saturday, so a Monday at opening is your quiet window.
Walk in at opening on a weekday and you feel the difference before you reach a store. Parking there is free, and you’re choosing a spot instead of stalking one. The fitting-room doors stand open. You can hear the music playing in the store. That last one sounds like a small thing until you’ve tried to talk a teenager out of a third hoodie over the noise of a full Saturday crowd.
The people who write about the place agree. St. Louis Roamer, a local guide site, visited on a Saturday afternoon in mild weather and was “surprised how busy it was,” adding that the walkways “can get a little congested on busy days.” Their tip for anyone who wants a pleasant walk there: go earlier on a weekday, when it isn’t too crowded.
December sharpens the curve, and you can feel it in the crawl of brake lights on the exit ramp. Sensormatic, which counts shoppers walking through store doors, says early afternoon will be the busiest time of day for in-store shopping throughout the holiday season, with traffic likely to peak between 2 and 3 p.m. So in December, arrive at opening and be back on the highway before that 2 o’clock surge starts circling for spots.
For any single store, check Google Maps before you leave. Pull up the outlet center, or the one store you came for, and scroll to the popular times graph. Google says the graph “shows how busy your location typically is during different times of the day,” and when it has enough data, a live bar sits on top showing how busy the place is right now. Check it from your kitchen table, coffee in hand, before you start the car.
### Which weekend takes the sales tax off the receipt?
The one St. Louis parents circle is the weekend of sticky car seats and a back seat full of new sneaker boxes. Missouri’s Back-to-School Sales Tax Holiday begins at 12:01 a.m. on the first Friday in August and ends at midnight on the following Sunday. For those three days, qualifying clothing, school supplies and computers come off the tax roll. Put it on the calendar now: find the first Friday of August, and that’s your weekend.
Here’s the part a lot of St. Louisans still carry around wrong. For years, the holiday came with an asterisk: local sales tax didn’t always take the weekend off, so the savings depended on which side of a city or county line you were standing on. Not anymore. The Missouri Department of Revenue says that starting January 1, 2023, the holiday exempts all state and local sales or use taxes. The outlet register out west and a neighborhood shop on Cherokee Street play by the same rule now.
Now the part that turns the weekend into real money or a wasted trip: the limits are per item, not per cart. Each article of clothing has to have a taxable value of $100 or less. The state’s own example is worth reading twice. A shopper buys $98 jeans and a $114 sweater. The jeans go tax-free. The sweater is taxed on its full cost, not just the $14 over the line. School supplies cap at $50 per purchase, graphing calculators at $150, computer software at $350, and personal computers and peripheral devices at $1,500.
So what does the no tax weekend include at an outlet center? The state’s clothing list runs from coats, jackets and hats or caps down to socks, undergarments and shoes or boots. Belts count. Belts with buckles count. A belt buckle sold by itself doesn’t, because Missouri’s definition of clothing excludes watches, watchbands, jewelry, handbags, handkerchiefs, umbrellas, scarves, ties, headbands and belt buckles. Translate that into a real cart. The sneakers under $100 ride free. The charm bracelet you’ve been eyeing at Pandora doesn’t, and neither does a handbag, no matter which weekend you buy them. If jewelry or a bag is the whole point of the trip, there’s no reason to fight the August crowd for it.
Two more lines from the state’s FAQ save arguments at the register. You don’t have to be a Missouri resident to buy tax-free that weekend, which is worth texting to the cousin across the river in Illinois. And something put on layaway during the holiday doesn’t qualify unless the final payment lands inside the holiday, too.
### Is Black Friday worth the drive to the outlets?
Black Friday is a good day for deals and the worst day for elbow room. Sensormatic predicted that Black Friday would again be the holiday season’s busiest in-store shopping day, with the last two Saturdays before Christmas close behind. Google’s traffic data, per Real Simple, shows roads busiest on Black Friday between 11 a.m. and 2 p.m. And St. Louis Roamer notes the outlet center is closed on some major holidays, including Thanksgiving and Christmas.
Then comes the number that should change how a St. Louis family plans that weekend. Placer.ai, which draws on a panel of tens of millions of devices, broke the Black Friday weekend down day by day in its November mall index. On the Friday itself, outlet malls were essentially flat compared with the year before, and Saturday and Sunday traffic declined. Across Black Friday week, visits to indoor malls and open-air centers flattened or even dropped, which Placer.ai read as many shoppers moving their trips to earlier in November, when mall retailers had begun rolling out early Black Friday promotions. It also suggested some shoppers used those earlier visits to scout specific items or sizes.
Put those together and the smart play is boring and effective. Scout in early November, on a weekday morning, when the early promotions are already up and the lot is quiet. Know your sizes, know the regular price and know which two stores matter. If you still want the Black Friday ritual, the cold air on your face, the coffee in a paper cup, the bag handles cutting into your fingers on the long walk back to the car, go at opening, stay off the roads during the 11-to-2 rush and treat it as an outing, not a mission.
Selling the family plumbing company someday? Here is when a banker earns the fee.
### The habit that decides whether you saved anything
The tag in your hand has two numbers on it, and the one that matters isn’t printed there. It’s what the same brand charges at its regular store or on its regular website. The Federal Trade Commission’s advice to outlet shoppers includes a plain step: make a list of the stores you want to visit. Then the warning: if you’re only saving a few dollars at the outlets, you may want to buy at the regular stores, especially if quality matters.
Why quality? Because the FTC also says many stores sell products at their outlets made exclusively for those outlets, and those items may be of lower quality than what’s sold in the regular stores. Its examples are the kind you can check with your fingers right at the display table: a jacket that isn’t fully lined, stripes that don’t match up at the seams, a t-shirt in lighter-weight fabric, shoes made with synthetic materials instead of real leather. Run your thumb along the inside of the jacket. Hold the shirt up to the light. Five seconds, and you know what you’re buying.
None of that is a reason to skip the outlets. The FTC puts it fairly: if it’s the brand, style or look that’s key, you may be in the right place. It’s a reason to shop with your phone in one hand. Screenshot the regular price at home the night before. Compare it at the table. Buy when the gap is real, and walk when it isn’t. Putting a shirt back on a table you drove across the county to reach is the single most profitable move in outlet shopping, and it feels terrible for about ten seconds.
The habit has a second half: ask about the return policy before you pay. The FTC notes that some outlet stores have 30- to 90-day return policies, some don’t allow returns at all, and many regular retail stores won’t take returns from their outlet stores. That last one stings when the wrong size means a second long drive instead of a quick stop near home in South City. Ask at the register. It takes ten seconds.
### What happened to St. Louis’s other outlet malls?
Ask a St. Louisan of a certain age about outlet shopping and you may get a story about the other place. St. Louis Mills, off Route 370, opened November 13, 2003. It cost $250 million to develop. Its food court was designed to resemble the 1904 World’s Fair. It had Ice Zone, a 1,200-seat indoor ice arena that served as the official practice facility of the St. Louis Blues, plus a NASCAR Speedpark with a go-kart track and an ESPN Skate Park that opened with the mall. Think of the noise under one roof: the slap of pucks on the boards, the whine of go-karts, the smell of the food court drifting down the concourse.
So why did the St. Louis Mills mall shut down? It lost its footing at the top before it lost its shoppers. In 2006 it was 99% occupied. But its developer, the Mills Corporation, ran into financial struggles and an SEC investigation, and Simon Property Group and Farallon Capital acquired its assets in a deal completed in April 2007. In August 2012 a new owner took the mall through foreclosure, and that fall it was renamed St. Louis Outlet Mall. In February 2016 it sold for $4.4 million, roughly 98% off its original construction cost.
Then the slide got fast. Occupancy was 77% in 2016 and 48.4% by late December 2017. On May 24, 2019, the owner sent the remaining tenants an eviction notice giving them 30 days, and the mall closed in September 2019. The building’s interior was gutted in 2023, and it lives on as an industrial warehouse and office building.
Out west, the 2013 rivals told a shorter version of the same story. When Taubman Prestige Outlets opened, St. Louis Public Radio reported the 310,000-square-foot mall was about 80 percent leased. In April 2018, St. Louis Magazine reported that Taubman Centers planned to sell it to The Staenberg Group, which planned to turn it into an entertainment destination.
The lesson for your next trip is quieter than the headline: stores come and go. Before you leave the house, check the center’s own store directory for the two or three brands you actually want.
### Which months are quiet enough to hear the store music?
Retail exhales after the holidays. Shopify’s guide to slow retail months says sales are typically slowest in January and February. For an outlet shopper, that’s the off-season worth knowing about: room in the lot, open doors on the fitting rooms, and associates with time to go check the back for your size.
The flip side is real, too. St. Louis Premium Outlets is an outdoor shopping space, so a February trip means walking store to store in whatever the sky is doing, collar up, hands jammed in your pockets, ducking into the next doorway for that blast of warm air at the threshold. St. Louis Roamer puts it plainly: it isn’t an ideal spot in bad weather, and St. Louis has its share of that. Check the forecast, dress for the walk instead of the store, and park near the stores you came for, since some sit farther from parking than others.
Sunday hours are shorter, 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. If the weekend is your only window, check the popular times graph for the stores on your list before you go.
### The one-trip plan for a busy family
Most families don’t get Monday at 10 a.m. Saturday is a 9 a.m. soccer game, a birthday party at 3 and the outlets squeezed in between, with the cleats still rattling around the back seat. Fine. Here’s the one-trip plan, built from everything above, for the family that has one free Saturday and a list:
The night before, pick the two or three stores that matter and look up what the same items cost at the brand’s regular store or website. Screenshot the prices.
Call or look up those two or three stores to make sure they’re still open.
Arrive at opening: 10 a.m. Monday through Saturday, 11 a.m. on Sunday.
At the table, feel the lining, check the seams and compare against your screenshot.
Ask about the return policy before you pay.
Be back in the car before the early-afternoon peak.
And if the trip is really a family outing, a walk in the fall air and a snack from the food court, go whenever you like. Just know which kind of trip you’re taking before you leave the driveway.

### Frequently asked questions about outlet shopping in St. Louis
### Q. What day are malls least busy?
A.  Monday, especially in the morning. In Google’s busy-times tips reported by Real Simple, shopping centers are least busy at 10 a.m. Monday and busiest 1-2 p.m. on Saturdays. At St. Louis Premium Outlets, that means showing up at the 10 a.m. opening on a weekday.
### Q. What is the quietest day of the week to go shopping?
A.  It depends on where you’re shopping. In the same Google tips reported by Real Simple, a shopping center is least busy at 10 a.m. Monday, but a grocery store is least busy at 8 a.m. on Sundays. For any single store, the popular times graph in Google Maps shows how busy it typically is by hour.
### Q. What month do people shop the least?
A.  January and February. Shopify’s retail guide says sales are typically slowest in those two months, right after the holiday rush. For an outlet trip, that means more room to browse, but at an outdoor center like St. Louis Premium Outlets you’ll be walking between stores in winter weather, so dress for it.
### Q. What does no tax weekend include?
A.  In Missouri, the Back-to-School Sales Tax Holiday runs from 12:01 a.m. on the first Friday in August through midnight Sunday, and since January 1, 2023 it covers local sales tax too. It covers clothing at $100 or less per item, including shoes, school supplies up to $50 per purchase, graphing calculators up to $150, software up to $350, and computers and peripherals up to $1,500. Handbags, jewelry, watches, scarves and ties are excluded.
### Q. Is Black Friday a good day to go shopping?
A.  For deals, yes. For crowds, it’s the worst. Sensormatic predicted Black Friday would again be the busiest in-store shopping day of the holiday season. Placer.ai’s November mall index found outlet-mall visits essentially flat on the Friday of Black Friday weekend, and read the softer week as many shoppers moving their trips to earlier in November, when early Black Friday promotions began. A weekday morning in early November is the calmer scouting trip.
### Q. What stores do St. Louis Premium outlets have?
A.  Clothing dominates. St. Louis Roamer’s visit guide lists stores including Aerie, Hollister, Lids, Crocs and Nike, plus jewelry and accessories at Claire’s, Pandora and Jared, and shops selling mattresses, luggage and kitchenware. There’s an indoor food court, too. Stores change, so check the center’s directory before you go.
### Q. Why did the St. Louis Mills mall shut down?
A.  St. Louis Mills opened in 2003 at a cost of $250 million, but its developer, the Mills Corporation, hit financial trouble, and the mall went through foreclosure in 2012 and was renamed St. Louis Outlet Mall. It sold in 2016 for $4.4 million, occupancy fell below half, and the owner gave tenants 30 days to leave in May 2019. It closed that September.

## $7.99 a Pound: The Nihari Shank Behind Pakistani Food in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/pakistani-food-in-st-louis-what-to-order
Why does one bowl of stew take all night? On Page Avenue the answer comes with naan. The gravy is dark and glossy. A piece of shank sits in it with the bone still showing, and a little plate of ginger slivers, chopped cilantro and green chilies waits beside it so you can finish the bowl yourself. It smells like beef and pepper and a long night. The naan goes soft the second it touches the gravy, the marrow leaves your lips a little sticky, and somewhere near the bottom of the bowl you start doing math: could I make this at home?
You can, and the surprise is where the shank comes from. St. Louis Halal Meat, at 10276 Page Ave., prints it on the beef side of its raw meat price list: Nihari/Shank, $7.99 a pound on the list we read, one line above the payas, and the store notes its prices move with the market.
Raw shank, $7.99 a pound. A small cooked tray of nehari, $50. The difference is one night of somebody’s sleep.
Rather let someone else lose the sleep? Then here’s the whole script. Call (314) 427-8500 before you drive (the store takes orders for pickup or delivery, and its posted hours list Mondays as closed) and ask, using the menu’s own spelling, “Is the nehari on today?” Lunch is easiest: the buffet runs Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday, 11:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. Walk in at 11:30, while every pot is still full.
If the answer is no, don’t walk out. Order off the daily board instead: goat biryani at $14.99 and a chicken seekh roll at $8.99, then ask for the Bihari kebab, which St. Louis Magazine called one of Baba’s specialties: thin strips of beef tenderloin, marinated and tenderized overnight. Ask for extra naan. Ask for green chilies on the side. Tear the bread, fold it around a strip of beef still shining with marinade, and you’ve ordered a Pakistani lunch like a regular.
Same menu, different country? You’ve read the board at a curry counter, seen biryani and korma and naan, and quietly filed Pakistani food under “Indian, basically.” Then that bowl lands in front of you. One spoonful and the filing system falls apart. The two kitchens share a family tree. They don’t share a center of gravity.
Here’s the local history most people at those tables have never heard. St. Louis has had a mosque since 1957, according to St. Louis Public Radio’s reporting on the area’s Muslim community, and the first real wave of Muslim immigrants arrived after 1965, when immigration laws were relaxed. The station found families here from Pakistan, India, Iran, Iraq, Afghanistan, Somalia and Sudan, and many of those communities were already second, even third generation, with children born and raised here. One of the people who fed them is Syed M. Hussain, who started St. Louis Halal Meat in 2003 because, in the store’s own words, there was a need for fresh zabihah halal meat and authentic food from Pakistan and India.
### Is Pakistani food the same as Indian food?
No, though they share dishes: korma, a classic dish of Mughlai origin, is very popular in Pakistan too. The difference is the center of the plate: a Pakistani kitchen builds around beef, goat and chicken, eats every main dish that isn’t rice with bread, and halal rules keep pork and alcohol off the table entirely.
You can taste the difference before you sit down. To reach the steam table on Page Avenue you walk past a butcher case, and the board above it is goat qorma, goat keema, chicken charga, one meat after another. The surprise for most St. Louisans is how often the star is beef. Nihari is classically a beef shank dish, and Pakistani cooks reach for goat, lamb, mutton and chicken the way a South City barbecue joint reaches for pork.
The second difference is on the table, not in the pot. Every main dish that isn’t rice is eaten with bread. Think less fork, more hand: you tear a piece of naan, still blistered from the tandoor, fold it into a little scoop and pull up a mouthful of gravy and meat together. Rice gets its own showpiece dishes, and those are the ones people argue about.
Third, the bowl tastes of what went into the pot. If you’ve only had the creamy, tomato-heavy curries of American takeout, the first spoonful of a Pakistani stew tastes of meat and the broth it cooked in, and the heat comes from what you add at the table.
None of this means one kitchen is better. It means you order differently. At an Indian place you might build a spread of four curries and a bread basket. At a Pakistani counter on Page Avenue, the move is one great slow-cooked stew, one rice dish, something off the grill, and more bread than you think you need.
### What is special about nihari?
Time. Nihari is meat, mainly beef shank, simmered for hours with bone marrow until the meat gives up at the touch of a spoon. Its name comes from a word meaning morning in Arabic and Urdu, because it was originally eaten by nawabs in the Mughal Empire as a breakfast course following Fajr prayer, the dawn prayer. That means the pot was going all night. One telling of its origin, from the Lucknow tradition, says it was invented for construction laborers and prepared overnight in huge vessels so the workers could be fed in the morning. Another tradition places its birth in Delhi. Either way, it was built to carry somebody through a hard day.
Its signature flavor comes from long pepper, a relative of black pepper with a warmer, almost sweet bite. Nihari spread through Pakistan after the partition of India in 1947, when Urdu-speaking Muslims from northern India moved to Karachi and opened restaurants serving it. In Karachi it became a large-scale success, and today nihari is considered the national dish of Pakistan, at least by the many cooks and food writers who say so.
Then there’s the part that gets screenshotted. In some restaurants, a few kilograms of each day’s leftover nihari is added to the next day’s pot. That carried-over portion is called taar, and it’s believed to give the stew its depth. Some nihari shops in Old Delhi claim to have kept an unbroken chain of taar going for more than a century. Think about that the next time someone brags about a sourdough starter.
So what does it actually taste like? Deep, beefy and peppery, with a warmth that builds slowly rather than biting all at once. The gravy is silky from the marrow and the long cook, and it clings to bread. The garnish matters more than people think: ginger, cilantro and green chilies go on at the table, and each one cuts the richness in a different direction. The ginger is sharp and clean, the cilantro is bright, the chilies wake the whole bowl up.
One St. Louis detail worth knowing before you call anyone: on St. Louis Halal Meat’s beef menu it’s spelled nehari, and it’s sold cooked by the tray, paired with haleem: $50 for a small tray, $95 for a large. Fifty dollars for a pot somebody tended all night. Spellings wander from nihari to nehari to nahari across South Asian menus, so if a search comes up empty, try the other two.
People often ask how nihari differs from korma, since both are rich, meaty Mughal dishes. Korma is meat or vegetables braised with yogurt, water or stock and spices into a thick sauce, usually chicken or mutton. Nihari is a long, slow shank stew with marrow and long pepper, no yogurt-forward sauce, and it is traditionally a morning dish. Korma is the polite dinner guest. Nihari is the dish you crave on a cold Saturday in January.
### What is the difference between yakhni pulao and biryani?
Look at the plate before you taste it. Yakhni pulao is one even color, a toasted brown, because the rice is cooked in the meat’s own broth. Biryani is layered, so your spoon comes up with grains of white, yellow and orange tangled together, a piece of meat, maybe a whole cardamom pod you’ll want to set aside.
Yakhni means stock. In Pakistani cooking, yakhni pulao is meat and stock added to rice, which creates a brown rice. Pulao in Pakistan is made with fragrant basmati cooked in a seasoned meat or bone broth, and it’s typically non-spicy. It’s a one-pot dish. The flavor is gentle and savory, closer to the best chicken soup you ever had, turned into rice.
Biryani is the louder sibling. A biryani is two layers of rice with a layer of meat in the middle, while pulao is not layered. Biryani’s rice and meat can be cooked separately, the layers can be colored with turmeric or saffron, and the spicing is stronger and more complex. Biryani often has a light layer of scorched rice at the bottom of the pot, which in plenty of families is the piece everyone fights for.
The argument is old. The Mughal text Ain-i-Akbari, written between 1589 and 1596 in the time of the emperor Akbar, already mentions pilau and biryani as two rice dishes, listing ingredients with quantities for each. Food writers still say the two are sometimes almost impossible to tell apart, and they still disagree.
Here’s the practical version for your table. Order both. Eat a spoonful of the pulao first, while your palate is clean, so you can taste the broth. Then go to the biryani. In one bite you’ll understand what no menu description can tell you: pulao is about the stock, biryani is about the spice.
### Is Pakistani food generally more spicy than Indian food?
Not as a rule. Spice in Pakistani cooking runs by region, and the map isn’t what people expect. Karachi’s food is known for bold, spicy flavors, while Pashtun cuisine is traditionally non-spicy and Sindhi food is typically not spicy. Ask the cook where the family is from and you’ll learn more about the heat than the menu tells you.
What surprises newcomers is that much of the heat lives on the side. Pickles made from mango, carrot, lemon and other fruits and vegetables sit on the table so each person can push the heat as far as they like. Green chilies come with the nihari. The pot itself is often milder than you braced for, and the burn is yours to add.
So if you love heat, say so out loud, and ask for the pickle. If you don’t, a yakhni pulao or a plate of seekh kebab with raita is a calm, deeply flavored way in. Karahi, a spicy curry cooked in a wok-like vessel, is where the kitchen usually shows its teeth. You’ll hear it before you see it, sizzling in the pan as it comes out of the kitchen.
### Where do you find Pakistani food in St. Louis?
Start on Page Avenue, at the same store where the shank came from. Located inside Saint Louis Halal Meat, Grocery & Foods, Baba’s offers a range of South Asian and Middle Eastern dishes, so lunch comes after the butcher case and the grocery shelves. One calendar note: every Ramadan, Baba’s does catering only, for events and mosque iftars, so in that month call before you drive.
Then there’s Biryani House. St. Louis Magazine counted more than 35 variations of biryani across the subcontinent and found seven of them on its menu, from beef to paneer, including the Sindhi style. The specialty is Hyderabadi, and the dum-cooked goat version comes in a copper-bottom matka, the traditional pot. Haleem is a specialty here too, and it’s the bowl to order on a gray afternoon.
For the most St. Louis version of all, there’s a gas station at 9680 Olive Blvd. Behind the counter, Nazia Afzal, who came from Chichawatni in Pakistan in 2014, was issuing lottery tickets one minute and dipping back to a makeshift kitchenette the next. What comes out is samosa chana chaat: a vegetable samosa smothered with chickpea curry, chopped tomato, onion, jalapeno and cilantro. She cooks chicken tikka masala, chana masala and basmati rice from a couple of slow cookers. “I can do two things: teach and cook,” she said. Gas station hours move, so call first.
And for the pulao side of the argument, cross the border. The same St. Louis Magazine guide sent readers to Sameem Afghan Restaurant, the first Afghan restaurant in St. Louis, for Qabelli Pallow, also spelled Kabuli pulao: rice with caramelized carrots and raisins and your choice of meat. It’s not Pakistani, but it’s the next pot over, and eating it beside a yakhni pulao is the fastest lesson in how rice travels.
To see who else is cooking, the Pakistani Food page on St Louis Near Me Directory keeps local spots in one place so you’re not stitching it together from a dozen tabs. These guides make good companions when you’re planning a food weekend:
Best Indian food in St. Louis: a local’s guide
