Where to eat on South Grand
A word on timing. Slow-cooked dishes sell out; they can’t be rushed back onto the steam table at 7 p.m. If you want the cook’s attention and a full pot, go early and call first. If you want the energy of a full room, the clatter of steel trays and kids weaving between tables, go later and accept that the nihari might be gone.
### How to order a Pakistani meal in St. Louis without guessing
Most of the best Pakistani cooking in town is quiet about itself. A short menu, a steam table, a cooler of mango lassi, a cook in the back who will tell you exactly what’s good today if you ask. These are the questions that turn a decent lunch into the meal you tell your friends about.
Ask which days the nihari is made. It takes hours, so some kitchens make it in batches or only on certain days. Say “Is the nehari on today?” and you’ll sound like you’ve done this before.
Build the table in three parts. One slow stew (nihari or haleem, a rich porridge of wheat, lentils and meat), one rice dish (yakhni pulao or biryani), one thing off the grill (seekh kebab, chicken tikka or a chapli kabab, a crisp, spiced minced-meat patty). Then double the bread.
Ask about the meat. Beef, goat or chicken changes the dish. Goat biryani and chicken biryani are different evenings.
Set the heat yourself. Tell them how hot you like it, then ask for pickle and green chilies on the side.
Ask how the meat is sourced. If halal matters to you, ask plainly. A good kitchen will tell you exactly where its meat comes from.
Order one more container than you need. Slow-cooked stews often taste even better the next day.
Feeding a crowd? Catering a party with Pakistani food works the same way hiring any good kitchen does. Shortlist two or three places, call each one, and tell them your headcount, your date and the dishes you want. Many kitchens think in trays, not plates. St. Louis Halal Meat’s beef menu sells biryani, korma and nehari by the large, medium or small tray, from $50 for a small tray of nehari to $110 for a large tray of beef biryani. Ask what they recommend for your group, then compare what each kitchen says it will actually deliver. The cook who asks you questions back, how spicy, how many kids, is usually the one to book.
Your bowl of nihari is closer than you think. Pick the dish you want tonight, then see who’s cooking it on Pakistani Food on St Louis Near Me Directory and call ahead to ask which days the pot is on.
If you’re the cook who starts the nihari before sunrise, St. Louis diners are already looking for your kitchen. Put your menu where those hungry neighbors search and get more customers with a list your business spot on St Louis Near Me Directory.
### The slow dishes are worth planning around
There’s a reason the dishes in this guide all share one ingredient you can’t buy: hours. Nihari needs the night. Haleem needs patience at the stove. Even a good yakhni starts with bones simmering long before the rice goes in. When you order them, you’re eating somebody’s early alarm, and the kitchens that still cook this way are worth going back to.
Take some home and you’ll see it. The next morning, the nihari in your fridge has set into a firm, shining jelly from all that collagen. Warm it slowly in a small pot, tear up yesterday’s naan, scatter on whatever ginger and cilantro you have left, and eat it the way it was first meant to be eaten: for breakfast.
Totally off the menu: here’s when a gynecologist visit really can’t wait.
And when you find the kitchen that gets it right, tell people. Small family places live on word of mouth, and the best review you can give a cook who stayed up all night is to bring a friend next weekend and order the same pot.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the national dish of Pakistan?
A.  Nihari, the slow-cooked beef shank stew, is widely considered the national dish of Pakistan. It became hugely popular in Karachi after 1947 and spread across the country from there.
### Q. What is the most popular Pakistani dish?
A.  Biryani is one of the most popular dishes in South Asia and among the South Asian diaspora, and it’s commonly served in Pakistan in regional styles such as Lahori and Sindhi biryani. In St. Louis, Biryani House carries seven versions, and its specialty is the Hyderabadi style.
### Q. Which meat do Pakistanis eat most?
A.  Beef, by the numbers. One analysis of Pakistan’s meat market put beef at 55% in 2010, with poultry at 25% and mutton at 20%, though chicken has been climbing fast from a mere 2 to 2.5% in 1971. Beef and goat star in the celebrated dishes, like beef nihari and goat biryani.
### Q. What does nihari taste like?
A.  Deep, beefy and peppery, with a slow warmth from long pepper and a silky gravy from bone marrow and hours of cooking. It’s eaten with naan and finished at the table with fresh ginger, cilantro and green chilies, which cut through the richness.
### Q. What is the difference between nihari and Korma?
A.  Korma is meat, usually chicken or mutton, braised with yogurt, water or stock and spices into a thick sauce. Nihari is beef or other shank simmered for hours with bone marrow and long pepper, traditionally eaten in the morning. Korma is creamy and mild, nihari is deep and peppery.

## Legally a Tattoo: Permanent Makeup in St. Louis, Before You Book
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/permanent-makeup-in-st-louis-what-to-know-before-you-book
In Missouri, that faint scratch above your eye, like a fingernail drawn slowly across a paper bag, is legally a tattoo. You’re lying back on crinkly table paper, the numbing cream has gone thick and tingly, and a gloved hand rests cool and faintly powdery on your forehead. The scratch is a small blade opening your skin one stroke at a time, and pigment goes into every line.
Not a gentler cousin of a tattoo, not a spa facial with a little color. State law defines a tattoo as pigment or ink inserted under the skin “with the aid of needles or blades,” and that new definition arrived with Senate Bill 70, which became effective August 28, 2023. A brow blade is a blade.
None of that is a reason to cancel. Plenty of people wake up for years to brows they don’t have to draw on, eyeliner that survives a sweaty August walk through Forest Park, lips that don’t look washed out in winter. It is a reason to book it the way you would book a tattoo on your face, because that is exactly what it is. A Cleveland Clinic dermatologist put it plainly: the color fades as skin cells turn over, but getting it out is “a long, painful, expensive process,” and sometimes it never fully leaves.
Here’s the St. Louis part almost nobody knows. Inside city limits, a tattoo studio can’t just hang a sign and start booking. According to the city’s tattoo parlor permit instructions, the application goes to the City of St. Louis Health Department for inspection, then to a Board of Public Service hearing, and the studio files a drawing of its tattoo chairs. The city’s conditions say a licensee “shall not increase the number of tattoo chairs over the number specified in the drawing filed with the Board of Public Service.”
Here’s what that means while you’re standing at the front desk, smelling rubbing alcohol and studying the healed-brow photos on the wall. That permit serves as the studio’s business license, so a city studio that went through all of this has something to show you. Ask to see it. If the answer is a shrug, keep your deposit in your pocket until you get one.
You can start your own check tonight, before you pay a deposit. Email the state tattoo office at tattoo@pr.mo.gov, or call 573.526.8288 once the office opens, with the artist’s name spelled exactly as the booking page spells it, and ask whether that person holds a practitioner license. Then ask about the studio, because the owner/operator needs its own establishment license. If the answer is no, or a long pause, keep your deposit in your pocket. And at the consultation, ask the one question that sorts careful artists from the rest: will you write down the color, manufacturer and lot number of the pigment you put in my face? The American Academy of Dermatology says artists should record exactly that.
### What’s the difference between microblading and permanent makeup?
Microblading is one kind of permanent makeup: the artist uses a small blade to draw fine strokes into the brow and lays pigment into them. Other permanent makeup, which doctors call micropigmentation, uses a needle in a pen-like instrument or a standard tattoo machine to place pigment in the brows, along the lash line or across the lips.
In the chair, the difference is mostly sound and feel. The blade is that dry, papery scratch. The machine is a steady hum close to your ear, a little like an electric toothbrush running on the sink. Cleveland Clinic describes the needle version going a few millimeters into the dermis, the middle layer of skin, carrying an iron oxide pigment with it. Either way, color ends up below the surface, where a makeup wipe will never reach it.
Here is the part the menus at brow bars rarely mention. Missouri’s statute defines a tattoo as a mark made on the body of another person “by the insertion of a pigment, ink, or both pigment and ink under the skin with the aid of needles or blades using hand-held or machine-powered instruments.” Blade, needle, hand tool, machine: the statute names every one of them. The state’s own rules spell out that “permanent cosmetic tattooing” covers eyeliner, eyebrows, lip liner, full lip color, repigmentation and camouflage. So the useful question is never which technique sounds softer. It is who is holding the tool, and whether the state knows their name.
Clients also hear words like “semi-permanent” and relax. Cleveland Clinic calls lip blushing a semi-permanent tattoo, “just like microblading.” Semi-permanent means it fades. Fading is not the same as leaving. Treat the first session like a decision you will see in the mirror every morning for a long time, because you will.
### The law that quietly rewrote brow appointments in Missouri
The state’s tattoo page carries a heading in capital letters: “Microblading Licensure Law.” Under it, the amended law requires anyone providing services that fall within the new definition of tattooing to obtain a practitioner license, and the owner/operator of the establishment to obtain an establishment license from the Division of Professional Registration, Office of Tattooing, Body Piercing and Branding.
There is a catch worth knowing. On that same page, the office says it “legally cannot make a determination for you” about whether a particular service falls inside the definition. Translation: the state will not tell an artist over the phone that their technique is exempt. If someone in a Central West End suite or a South Grand storefront tells you their method “isn’t really tattooing,” that is their reading, not the state’s blessing.
Two more lines in Missouri’s tattoo statute, sections 324.520 to 324.526, matter to clients. No one may tattoo a minor without the prior written informed consent of a parent or legal guardian, and the parent or guardian must sign that consent in the presence of the artist or an employee or agent of the artist. And no one may tattoo a person who is under the influence of alcohol or a controlled substance. That second rule is why a careful artist will send you home if you show up after two glasses of wine at a friend’s place on The Hill. A violation of sections 324.520 to 324.526 is a misdemeanor with a fine of not more than five hundred dollars.
Inside the city limits, a studio answers to City Hall as well. City of St. Louis Ordinance 70813 governs the operation of tattoo facilities, and the city’s permit page says no practitioner may practice and no establishment may operate without a license issued by the License Collector. The studio must maintain a Missouri license and a City of St. Louis business license at all times. I could not confirm whether the city treats every brow suite as a tattoo facility, so ask. A studio in Soulard or on Cherokee Street that can point to both licenses on the wall by the front desk, next to the aftercare cards, has nothing to hide.
When the American Academy of Dermatology reviewed permanent makeup rules, it found seven states with no state regulations for cosmetic tattooing at all, and formal training courses in some places as short as four hours. Four hours, for a needle working a breath away from someone’s eye. Missouri is not one of the seven. Cross the river and the rules change again. If you live in Pierron or anywhere else on the Illinois side, the Illinois Department of Public Health requires body art establishments to register and inspects them after they apply, so ask an Illinois studio about that registration the same way you would ask a Missouri artist about a license.
A license does not make anyone talented. It means the state has the person on file, and it gives you somewhere to send a complaint if something goes wrong. Checking takes less time than choosing a brow shade. The whole check, for your notes:
Email tattoo@pr.mo.gov or call 573.526.8288: ask about the artist’s practitioner license, then the studio’s establishment license.
Inside the city, ask to see the studio’s City of St. Louis business license, and count the chairs: the studio can’t add one beyond the drawing it filed with the Board of Public Service.
If something has already gone wrong, the state’s tattoo page at pr.mo.gov/tattooing.asp lists Complaint Forms in its menu.
Quick detour: when did a dentist last measure your gums with a tiny ruler?
### What can actually go wrong, and how often?
Most people ask about pain. The better question is about the ink. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration says it has not approved any pigments for injection into the skin for cosmetic purposes, and its fact sheet goes further: many pigments used in tattoo inks are not approved for skin contact at all, and some are industrial grade colors suitable for printers’ ink or automobile paint. Think about the little dropper bottle on the steel tray, a few inches from your eye, while the cold air hums overhead.
That is why the downsides of permanent makeup are worth reading slowly, not skimming. The FDA lists infection from unsterile equipment or contaminated ink, and it notes recalls of contaminated inks in 2012 and again in 2017. Allergic reactions are rare, the agency says, but can be stubborn because the pigment is hard to remove, and occasionally a reaction shows up on a tattoo someone has had for years. The body can also wall off pigment it treats as foreign, forming small bumps called granulomas. People prone to keloids can scar.
Lips carry their own risk. Cleveland Clinic’s dermatologist points out that lip color is usually a shade of red, and “Red is one of the most common allergenic tattoo colors.” Eyes carry theirs too: work along the lash line can cause loss of eyelashes, severe eyelid injury, crusting and ectropion, where the lid turns away from the eye.
Then there is the MRI question. The FDA has reports of swelling or burning in tattooed areas during MRI scans, and of permanent eyeliner interfering with images of the eyes, but it says this seems to happen only rarely and the risks of avoiding an MRI your doctor recommended are likely much greater. Tell the technician about your eyeliner and get the scan.
And here is the one nobody puts in the brochure. According to the dermatologist quoted in the academy’s announcement of that review, the most common complication is simply being unhappy with the results: regret, unrealistic expectations, ink placed wrong. That one is about choosing the person and saying out loud what you want.
### Is your face ready for this right now?
Timing matters as much as technique. If you are wondering who should avoid permanent makeup, start with the people the risks above land on hardest: anyone who forms keloid scars, anyone with a known reaction to tattoo pigment, and anyone planning fillers or Botox soon, since the academy warns those treatments can distort the look of permanent makeup. In Missouri, a parent or guardian must sign written informed consent in front of the artist or staff before anyone under 18 can be tattooed. And if you are young and chasing a look you saw last week, Cleveland Clinic’s warning is worth taping to the mirror: full lips and thick brows flood social media now, but that may not be the case five or ten years from now, and faces change with age.
As for what not to do before permanent makeup, the list is short and practical. Don’t drink beforehand; Missouri law says no one may tattoo a person who is under the influence of intoxicating liquor or a controlled substance, and the city ordinance says the same. Don’t skip the patch test; Cleveland Clinic says a test spot behind the ear can show a reaction before it is on your face. Don’t keep quiet about cold sores if you are getting lip color, or about medications, past surgeries and allergies. And don’t walk in with only a filtered screenshot. Bring a photo of yourself on a good day, bare-faced, in plain morning light by a kitchen window.
That last part is the leverage point most clients miss. The artist is not trying to recreate a stranger’s brows from a phone. They are mapping your face with a pencil and string, the cool thread pulled taut across your forehead, marking where your brow wants to start, arch and end. If you have never sat still for that mapping and looked at it in a hand mirror for a long minute before any blade comes out, you are not ready to book the procedure yet. You are ready to book the consultation.
Book the consultation first, then the procedure. Shortlist two or three artists on Permanent Makeup on St Louis Near Me Directory, sit through each mapping, and choose the one whose healed work looks like you on your best morning.
If you’re the brow artist, the lash-and-brow studio or the tattooer who does cosmetic work between bookings, this part is for you. Clients are already searching here for someone they can trust with their face, and a listing helps you get more customers who show up with their questions answered, so see who AI names instead of you with a free audit.
### How do you pick an artist in St. Louis without regretting it?
Pick two or three artists. Maybe one is a cosmetic tattoo specialist in the Central West End, one works out of a quiet studio off South Grand, and one is a tattooer on Cherokee Street who does brows and liner on the side. Book a consultation with each, tell them exactly the look you want, and compare what each one says they will actually deliver.
Then interview them. Cleveland Clinic and the American Academy of Dermatology give you most of the script, and a good artist will be glad you asked:
How long have you done cosmetic tattooing, and can I see your Missouri license?
Can I see healed photos, months later, not just the glossy same-day shots?
How do you sterilize your tools, and can I see the room where you work?
Will you record the color, manufacturer and lot number of the pigment you use on me? (The academy recommends artists do exactly that.)
Do you do a patch test, and when?
How many sessions will this take, and what is your follow-up and touch-up policy?
Am I a good candidate, and are my expectations realistic?
The artist who pulls up a binder of healed work, flips to a client with your coloring and says “this is about where yours would land” is giving you something real. The one who changes the subject to a same-day discount is giving you something else. Before you leave, run one more check Cleveland Clinic suggests: after visiting, talking and watching, ask yourself whether you feel confident going forward. If the answer is a shrug, the dermatologist’s advice is to delay or forgo it until you find a good fit.
### What it costs, and what keeps the color where it belongs
Prices are set artist by artist. For a national reference point, Cleveland Clinic puts lip blushing at $500 to $1,500 per session, depending on where you live. Cleveland Clinic calls micropigmentation an elective, cosmetic procedure that you pay for on your own. Some people need more than one treatment to get the result they want, and touch-ups come later as the pigment fades. So when you compare artists, ask each one what the first visit, the follow-up and a future refresh will cost, and weigh that against the healed work you saw.
Keeping the color is mostly about the first few weeks and the sun. Cleveland Clinic says sun exposure and smoking speed up fading on lips, and anyone who has stood in a frozen-custard line on Chippewa in July knows how hard St. Louis summer sun hits a face. Plan the appointment around it if you can, and keep a hat in the car.
Aftercare is simple and boring, which is the point. The academy’s dermatologist advises washing your hands before you touch a healing tattoo, using only fragrance-free products, and contacting both your artist and a board-certified dermatologist if signs of infection appear. Cleveland Clinic says to contact your cosmetic specialist immediately if you have excessive swelling, pain or redness, if you develop a fever or rash, or if the area feels excessively hot or burns. Expect some swelling and crusting. Do not pick.
Done right, the payoff is small and daily: rolling out of bed, catching your reflection in the dark microwave door, and recognizing your own face without reaching for a pencil.

### Frequently asked questions about permanent makeup in St. Louis
### Q. What is the average cost of permanent makeup?
A.  Prices vary by artist and by what you are having done. ### Q. What are the downsides of permanent makeup?
A.  It is hard to remove, and the FDA has not approved any pigment for injection into the skin for cosmetic purposes. Risks include infection, allergic reactions that can appear even years later, granulomas, keloid scarring and, around the eyes, lash loss or eyelid injury. The most common problem dermatologists see is simpler: people unhappy with the result.
### Q. Who should avoid permanent makeup?
A.  Think twice if you form keloid scars, have reacted to tattoo pigment before, or plan fillers or Botox soon, since those can distort the look. In Missouri, a parent or guardian must sign written informed consent in front of the artist or staff before anyone under 18 can be tattooed. And if you are unsure about the shape or color, wait until you are sure.
### Q. What not to do before permanent makeup?
A.  Don’t drink beforehand; Missouri law says no one may tattoo a person who is under the influence of intoxicating liquor or a controlled substance. Sit through the brow mapping and study it in a mirror before you agree to start.
### Q. How long does semi-permanent eyeliner typically last?
A.  No trustworthy source gives a single number, because it varies person to person. Cleveland Clinic says the ink never washes off but fades over the years as skin cells are replaced, so you may need touch-ups to keep the look. Plan for it as permanent, because removal is difficult.
### Q. Can you get eyeliner tattooed?
A.  Yes. Missouri’s rules list eyeliner as a form of permanent cosmetic tattooing, so the artist needs to be licensed for it. ### Q. What is the most popular permanent makeup?

### Q. What is the most natural looking permanent eyebrow?
A.  The one that asks for the least. Cleveland Clinic’s dermatologist says it is very difficult to mimic the appearance of eyebrow hair with tattoo ink and advises starting minimal, because less is more. Ask to see healed brows on clients with your coloring, months after the appointment, before you choose a technique.
### Q. Does Missouri require a license for microblading?
A.  Yes. Since Senate Bill 70 took effect on August 28, 2023, the artist needs a practitioner license and the studio needs an establishment license from the state Office of Tattooing, Body Piercing and Branding.

## His Blanket Goes In, the Wooden Box Stays: Pet Cemetery Burial in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/pet-cemetery-burial-in-st-louis-what-to-know
A hinge squeaks. It’s the little wooden box from the garage, the one that used to hold drill bits, and someone has wiped it out with a dish towel and set it on the kitchen table. Next to it sits the plaid blanket from the end of the couch. It still smells like him. The water bowl is on the floor by the back door, a third full, and nobody in the house has been able to pick it up yet.
You fold the blanket. You unfold it. You fold it again, smaller, because folding is the only thing in the room you know how to do right now.
Then somebody says the thing out loud. Where does he go?
The backyard feels like the obvious answer. It’s where he barked at squirrels and wore a path along the fence. But in St. Louis, the backyard is the answer that runs into the most trouble, and almost nobody hears why until after the hole is half dug. Missouri’s dead-animal law is Section 269.020. Read word for word, it wants any burial site at least 300 feet from any existing neighboring residence. That’s 100 yards. Walk out your back door in Dutchtown or Benton Park and look at how close the next kitchen window is. You can probably hear their screen door.
And that wooden box? If the plan is a pet cemetery, there’s a second surprise waiting. The oldest pet cemetery in the area does not accept wooden caskets at all. That same cemetery, by the way, was once rescued from overdue county taxes by the grieving families whose pets were already buried there. St. Louis pet people do not let go easily.
If you have to make the call today, three answers will make it shorter. First, whole body or ashes: do you want him buried as he is, or cremated? Second, where is he right now, at home on the blanket or still at the vet? Third, do you want to see him once more before the lid closes, or would you rather it be sealed before you arrive? Write those three answers on the back of an envelope. Then dial. Memory Park Pet Cemetery answers at 314.576.3030. One phone call starts its visit to your location, and if your pet is still at the vet, Memory Park will pick your pet up there. Imperial Crown Pet Cemetery, the oldest one, is at 314-921-1558, tucked toward the rear of a parking lot it shares with a battery store on Lindbergh. Zion Cemetery, the historic one that keeps niches for pet ashes, is at 314-721-8631. And keep one number in your head while you dial: Missouri gives you 24 hours from the moment you know.
Two more things nobody mentions until the shovel is already out. If he was put to sleep, the drug that made it peaceful stays in his body. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service says the same drugs used to bring a quick and humane end of life for family pets linger after their use and can be lethal for scavenging wildlife and domestic animals. Eagles, hawks and ravens are on its list. So is the neighbor’s dog that digs under the fence.
And the money, because it’s sitting on your chest whether you say it or not. The one price posted in plain sight is $300, for a niche for pet ashes at Zion Cemetery, with special pricing for service animals. The others ask you to call, and there’s a reason: Memory Park’s caskets alone run from 6 inches to 52 inches. A parakeet and a shepherd are not one price.
### How do pet cemeteries work in St. Louis?
A pet cemetery burial in St. Louis starts with one phone call: the cemetery can pick your pet up at home or at the vet, or you can bring them in yourself. Your pet goes into a sealed casket, you can hold a short viewing, and the grave gets a temporary marker and a flower until you order a permanent stone.
That’s the outline. The texture is gentler than most people expect. At Memory Park Pet Cemetery, the casket can stay open for a visitation with your pet laid in a sleeping position on a silk pad and pillow, or it can be sealed before you arrive if you’d rather remember them some other way. Someone will say a short prayer if you want one. Then you choose: leave, or stay and watch the casket go into the ground and get covered. Memory Park will come to your house after one phone call. If the loss happened at your vet, it will be in touch with the vet, pick your pet up there, and then call you to set up the burial.
Older still is Imperial Crown Pet Cemetery, which calls itself the oldest pet cemetery in the Saint Louis area. A veterinarian, Dr. Charles F. Bauer, founded it in 1924. Its middle chapter is the part worth knowing. After decades of changing owners, the cemetery fell into disrepair and the county taxes went seriously overdue. So the people who already had pets buried there did something about it. On October 23, 1992, they incorporated the Friends of Imperial Crown Pet Cemetery as a not-for-profit and went to work on the lawns and the old monuments. A cemetery for pets was saved by grieving pet owners who refused to let the graves go to weeds. That’s a St. Louis story if there ever was one.
Their burials run on the same rhythm. A short service with viewing for family and friends is part of it unless you say otherwise, and you can walk with your pet to the grave site. A temporary marker and flowers go on the grave after it’s closed. The grounds are open year round during daylight hours, and the cemetery says plainly that it may postpone a burial when the weather turns bad. In a St. Louis January, with sleet coming sideways off the river and the ground hard as a sidewalk, that is not a small detail.
Then there’s the stone, which comes later on purpose. Imperial Crown suggests waiting a while and then ordering a granite headstone. Memory Park lists colors like Salisbury Pink, Gray, Missouri Red and Black, and it can set a weather-resistant photo into the face of the stone. Some families pick a slant marker. Some pick a flat one that sits flush with the grass so the mower rolls right over it. Nobody needs to decide that the same week.
### Missouri’s backyard rule was written for a farm, not a city lot
Here’s the text that surprises people. Section 269.020 of the Missouri statutes says every person owning or caring for any animal that has died from any cause has to dispose of it within 24 hours of learning about the death. It doesn’t carve out cats or beagles. It lists the ways that count: buried, incinerated, composted, or disposed of in a manner the state veterinarian approves.
So how long can you leave a dead pet before burying it? Under Missouri law, the clock is 24 hours from the moment you know. That’s one more reason the cemetery call tends to happen the same day, and why the vet’s office will usually ask what you want done before you leave the parking lot.
Then come the burial conditions, and this is where a city yard falls apart. The animal has to be covered right away with at least six inches of soil and a final cover of at least 30 inches. The site can’t sit in a low spot that floods. And the distances are the kicker: at least 50 feet from the neighbor’s property line, at least 300 feet from any well, spring or sinkhole, and at least 300 feet from any existing neighboring residence.
Pace off 300 feet sometime. On most blocks in the city, from Soulard to South Grand, the house next door is close enough that you can smell their dinner. So can I legally bury my pet in my backyard? On a typical St. Louis lot, not by the letter of that statute.
Now the honest part, because you deserve it. That law was plainly written with livestock in mind. Its loading limits are counted per acre: one bovine, six swine, seven sheep, and seventy turkey carcasses or three hundred poultry carcasses. And the Missouri Department of Agriculture says its Animal Health Division does not respond to reports about pets. Nobody from the state is likely to knock on your gate over a cat under the hydrangea.
But “nobody checks” is not the same as “it’s fine.” The distances in that law exist for real reasons: groundwater, wells, the neighbor’s kids, and what animals dig up. And there’s one more reason that the law doesn’t mention, and it matters most if your pet was put to sleep.
Switching gears: when does a St. Louis business owner actually need an investment bank?
### What does the euthanasia drug do after the grave is filled?
The last appointment at the vet is quiet. A soft room, a blanket on the table, your hand on their side as the breathing slows. The drug that makes it peaceful is usually sodium pentobarbital, and it doesn’t leave when your pet does.
The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service puts it bluntly: the drugs used for a humane end of life linger afterward and can be lethal to scavenging wildlife and domestic animals. The drug spreads through the whole body. Organs like the liver can carry especially high concentrations. A lethal dose for a bird is generally much lower than the amount used to euthanize the pet, and eagles, hawks and ravens are particularly at risk. That’s the warning from the opening, in the agency’s own detail.
This is why you should think twice before you bury your pet in the backyard, even where it’s allowed. The federal agency’s first choice is incineration or cremation. Its second is immediate deep burial, and it notes that most regulations require at least three to four feet of cover. Look back at Missouri’s number. The state’s minimum final cover is 30 inches, which is two and a half feet. A grave dug only to the state minimum can still be shallower than the cover the wildlife service describes.
A pet cemetery solves this without you having to think about it. The grave is dug by people who do this for a living, the casket is sealed, and the ground isn’t sitting under a bird feeder a few steps from your patio.
### Will the cemetery take the box you already found?
Back to the kitchen table. That wooden box was a loving instinct, and it may not make the trip.
At Imperial Crown, a casket is required for every whole-body burial, and the cemetery uses only heavy styrene plastic because it holds up over time. Wooden caskets are not allowed. You get two choices: a strong single-walled, two-part casket that most families use, or a Deluxe style with a fully lined interior and a display skirt. Memory Park uses the same kind of material. Its high-impact styrene caskets come in sizes from 6 inches up to 52 inches, which covers everything from a parakeet to a big shepherd, and once sealed they’re air-tight and impermeable to water. You can add a silk pillow and pad.
Here’s the good news inside the bad news. The blanket goes with him. Imperial Crown says outright that you may put your pet’s favorite blanket, toy or other personal item in the casket. So the plaid blanket you kept folding gets to stay folded around him.
And the box? Keep it. The pet-loss guidance from Humane World for Animals suggests making a memory box with your pet’s collar or favorite toys. Put the collar in it, the tags that jingled at the door, the last tennis ball with the fuzz chewed off. The box was never meant to go in the ground. It was meant to stay on the shelf.
If you do end up burying at home on land where the rules allow it, the same Memory Park caskets and urns are sold for use elsewhere too. A sealed styrene casket is a better barrier against digging animals than a cardboard box or a pillowcase.
### How much does a pet cemetery burial cost in St. Louis?
Straight answer: you will likely have to call. Imperial Crown asks families to inquire for current pricing at 314-921-1558, and Memory Park describes its stones as available at all price ranges. The one firm number posted is at Zion Cemetery, which lists niches for pet ashes at $300 and offers special pricing for service animals.
That gap is not a trick. A whole-body burial bill is built from pieces, and the pieces move with your pet’s size and your choices: the casket size and style, the grave, the opening and closing, a pickup from your home or vet, a viewing, and later the stone and maybe a vase. Imperial Crown also points to a perpetual care fund that keeps the grounds tended after you’re gone. A small cat in a regular casket and a big lab in a Deluxe one are not the same bill, and a cemetery that guessed over email would be guessing.
The way to get a real number without wearing yourself out is simple. Shortlist two or three cemeteries. Call each one and tell them exactly what you want: whole-body burial or ashes, home or vet pickup, a viewing or not, and roughly how big your pet is. Then ask what they will do for that and what it comes to. Lay the answers side by side. You’re not shopping for the cheapest hole in the ground. You’re looking for the place that answers the phone kindly and tells you plainly what happens next.
### Burial or cremation: you don’t have to pick just one
Families tend to frame it as one or the other. In St. Louis, the cemeteries quietly blur the line. Imperial Crown allows cremation burials, so ashes can have a grave and a stone. Memory Park can return the cremains to you in an urn within a few days, or place them in a burial plot. Zion keeps those $300 niches for ashes.
Zion is worth a second look for a reason that has nothing to do with price. It’s a historic St. Louis cemetery, certified by the Green Burial Council, and its 49 acres are pet-friendly, with several miles of walking trails over gently rolling hills. Open sunrise to sunset, every day. Think about what that means. You can bring the dog you have now, on a leash, and walk the trail on a cool October morning past the spot where the dog you lost is resting. Gravel under your shoes, leaves coming down, a nose working every inch of the path. Grief and the walk, together.
Memory Park has its own kind of peace: six acres on sloping hills with big shade trees, evergreens, benches and a pond. Its website lists dogs, cats, parakeets, rabbits, monkeys and turtles among the pets buried there, and describes champion show dogs lying side by side with pets that had no pedigree, “for the place is purely democratic.” Read that twice. It might be the best sentence ever written about a cemetery.
If you’re leaning toward cremation instead, our guide to pet funeral and cremation in St. Louis walks through that side in detail. And remember what the wildlife service said: cremation is its preferred method, so if the backyard was the plan, ashes buried in the garden can be a gentler compromise than a whole-body grave.
### What should you settle before you call a St. Louis pet cemetery?
The call is easier with a few answers already in your pocket. Talk these over at the kitchen table first:
Whole-body burial, or cremation with the ashes buried or kept at home?
Where is your pet right now, at home or at the vet, and do you need a pickup?
Do you want a viewing, a short prayer, or just to be there when the grave is closed?
Who needs to be there, and is there a day this week everyone can make it?
What personal things go in the casket: the blanket, a toy, a note from the kids?
Do you want to visit often? Then pick a place you can reach easily and that keeps hours you can use.
Then, when you call, ask each cemetery the same few things: what kind of casket they require, whether they can pick up from your vet, how soon they can do the burial, what their perpetual care covers, and what the whole plan you described will come to. Write the answers down. Grief scrambles memory, and you’ll be glad you did.

### Frequently asked questions about pet cemetery burial
### Q. How much does a pet cemetery burial cost?
A.  It depends on your pet’s size, the casket, pickup and the stone. Around St. Louis, Imperial Crown asks families to call for current pricing, and Zion Cemetery lists niches for pet ashes at $300 with special pricing for service animals. Call two or three cemeteries, describe exactly what you want, and compare what each will deliver.
### Q. Can I legally bury my pet in my backyard?
A.  Missouri’s statute 269.020 requires a burial site at least 50 feet from the property line and 300 feet from any neighboring residence, with at least 30 inches of final soil cover. Most St. Louis city lots can’t meet that. The state’s Animal Health Division says it doesn’t respond to reports about pets, but the rule is on the books.
### Q. Is it better to bury or cremate your pet?
A.  Both are loving choices. If your pet was euthanized, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service calls incineration or cremation the preferred method, because the euthanasia drug can poison scavenging animals. A pet cemetery gives you a grave without that risk. Imperial Crown allows a cremation burial and Zion keeps niches for pet ashes, so you can do both.
### Q. What is the best thing to bury a pet in?
A.  A sealed casket. Imperial Crown requires heavy styrene caskets and does not allow wooden ones, and Memory Park’s styrene caskets run from 6 to 52 inches and become air-tight once sealed. You can still wrap your pet in a favorite blanket and add a toy inside.
### Q. How long can you leave a dead pet before burying it?
A.  Missouri law says an animal that has died must be disposed of within 24 hours after you learn of the death. In practice, call your vet or a pet cemetery the same day. Imperial Crown, for example, lists pickup from your veterinarian’s office or your home.
### Q. Is it bad to keep pet ashes at home?
A.  No. Humane World for Animals lists reserving a place in your home for your pet’s ashes and photos as one healthy way to memorialize them. If you change your mind later, Imperial Crown accepts cremation burials and Zion Cemetery offers niches, so the ashes can still get a permanent place.
### Q. How to help a teenager with the loss of a pet?
A.  Tell the truth, in plain words. Humane World for Animals warns that softening it, like saying the pet ran away, keeps a young person from grieving in a healthy way. Let them say goodbye if the death is expected, show your own grief so sadness feels allowed, and invite them into a ritual like writing to the pet or choosing what goes in the casket.

## Your $5 Napkin Is a Bid: What to Expect at a Piano Bar in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-expect-at-a-piano-bar-in-st-louis
Nobody goes to a St. Louis piano bar to hear the piano. You go to be heard. By the second chorus your throat feels scraped, your palms sting from clapping, and there’s a napkin under your hand with a song title printed in block letters and a folded bill pressed flat beneath it. Keypers Piano Bar, at 2280 S. Jefferson Ave., puts the house rules on its own website: “Drink responsibly. Sing loudly. Tip your bartender.” Three orders, and not one of them is “sit still and listen.”
Then there’s the money, and first-timers get it backwards: in a dueling room the jar on the piano isn’t a courtesy, it’s an auction. One dueling-piano company spells out the math. Somebody asks for “Piano Man” with $5, and a table that hates it can stop it cold with $6. Another act’s rule book calls a request with no tip a “Suggestion,” played only if nothing else is in the stack. The second that napkin leaves your fingers, it stops being a wish and becomes a bid, and the bartender’s tip is a separate thing entirely.
This kind of night has a St. Louis address. Tom Turpin opened the Rosebud Bar at 2220 Market Street, and the State Historical Society of Missouri says that saloon “became a focal point for the ragtime music scene.” The crowd was the point then, and it still is.
And here the night can legally run long. The general Missouri rule closes a by-the-drink bar at 1:30 a.m. on weekdays. But a separate statute, headed “Convention trade area, St. Louis City,” lets a bar licensed to sell by the drink “in a city not located within a county” apply for a special permit to remain open until 3:00 a.m. Not every room holds that permit, so ask before you promise the birthday table a finale. The rooms that do can hand you an extra hour and a half of choruses, and an extra hour and a half for your voice to go to gravel.
Two south-side rooms show the range today. Keypers is open 2 p.m. to 1:30 a.m. Monday through Saturday, with Piano with Patty on Thursdays and Piano Potpourri on Saturdays, both 8 to 11 p.m., discounted martinis on Thursdays and, in its own words, “no pretenses, no dress code.” The Hideaway, at 5900 Arsenal Street, calls itself “a piano bar in South City St. Louis” and has been around since 1954, with live music, trivia weekly and meat bingo the first Monday of every month.
The review The Hideaway chose to post on its own site tells you what the room feels like better than any ad could. The decor is “largely unchanged from its previous life as a working-class neighborhood bar,” and “the paintings behind the bar take you on quite the journey.” The same review gives the practical warning: “No food, no beer on tap.” So eat on the way, and order a local bottle once you’re in. The site lists hours of 3 p.m. to midnight Monday, 3 p.m. to 1 a.m. Tuesday through Saturday, and noon to 10 p.m. Sunday, and the number is (314) 645-8822. Calendars change, so call the week you go.
And if you want a request that belongs to this town, write “St. Louis Blues” on your napkin in big block letters. It’s a 1914 song by W.C. Handy, older than anyone in the room, and it was written about the city you’re singing in.
### What do you do at a piano bar in St. Louis?
You request, you sing and you tip. The crowd runs the room here: a song title in ballpoint on a napkin or slip, a bill folded under it, set on the piano lid, and the players work that stack all night, trading songs, teasing tables and turning one stranger’s birthday into a full-room chorus.
Everything else follows from that. You don’t need to know the words, because somebody in the room does, and loudly. You don’t need to sing well. Nobody sings well by the third round, and the players are counting on it. What you need is a willingness to be loud in public with strangers for a couple of hours, which is rarer than it sounds and exactly why it feels so good.
There are two kinds of room. In a dueling room, two pianos face each other and two players trade songs, finish each other’s jokes and occasionally sabotage each other on purpose, swinging a slow ballad into a polka halfway through because somebody at a back table paid them to. In a single-player room, one piano holds court, the pace is slower, and the requests lean toward standards and sing-alongs. At bottom they work the same way. The players read the room, read the napkins, and build the night out of whatever the crowd hands them.
So your job as a guest is to hand them something. A song, a name, a reason. Whose birthday it is, and why this song, gives a player far more to work with than a bare title, so it tends to land bigger.
### St. Louis Had a Saloon Piano Long Before Anyone Said “Piano Bar”
Here’s the part most visitors never hear. The bar piano in this town isn’t a Las Vegas import or a souvenir from Bourbon Street. It’s home-grown, and it’s more than a century old.
Go back to the Rosebud on Market Street. Turpin’s “The Harlem Rag,” from 1897, is considered the first published rag by an African American. When Scott Joplin moved to St. Louis in 1901, he walked into a scene that already had a bar with a piano at the center of it. He is considered the “King of Ragtime Writers.”
You can still hear what that sounded like. At the Scott Joplin House State Historic Site at 2658 Delmar Blvd., an authentic player piano fills the modest flat where Joplin rented a room in 1902 with his melodies. Stand in that small room and watch the keys go down with nobody touching them. Then go out that night and watch a dueling player pull a request off a napkin. It’s the same deal, a long century apart: a piano, a room, a crowd that wants a song, and money changing hands to get it.
So when a friend from out of town asks what music St. Louis is known for, most locals say blues, and they’re not wrong. But the piano answer is ragtime, and the piano bar is its loud, sing-along grandchild. Tell that to the table at 11 p.m. and watch somebody look it up.
Belted every chorus? Fine. Gums that bleed when you brush need a periodontist.
### How does the request napkin actually work?
Here’s the ritual. Grab a napkin or one of the request slips if the bar sets them out, and write three things: the song, the artist if it’s obscure, and the reason. Bring your own pen. The bartender’s pen is the most fought-over object in the building by ten o’clock. Fold a bill inside or under the napkin, carry it up, and set it on the piano lid or hand it to a player between songs. Don’t reach across the keys mid-song. You will be called out, by name if they can read it off your napkin.
Then wait. The stack is a queue, and only the players know its order. In most dueling rooms a bigger tip moves a request up the pile, and a napkin with nothing folded inside may sit until the night slows down, or never come at all. That isn’t greed. The jar is a big part of how the people at the keys get paid for a long night of singing over a crowd.
Watch for the counter-moves, too. In a lot of dueling rooms you can pay to stop a song somebody else asked for, and the other table can pay to keep it going. It turns into an auction. The room picks sides and starts chanting. Somebody’s power ballad becomes a bidding war, and every dollar of it lands in the same jar, which is exactly how the players like it.
A few things worth knowing before your napkin goes up. Print in big letters, because the light is low and the player is reading it while singing something else. If the players say a song is banned for the night, believe them; it has probably been requested over and over already. And if you ask for the same song every visit, they will remember you, and they will make fun of you, with real affection.
### How much are you supposed to tip at a bar?
Two different tips happen at a piano bar, and mixing them up is how people leave feeling cheap or feeling fleeced. The first is for the bartender. The Emily Post Institute’s tipping guide puts it at $1-2 per drink or 15-20% of the tab, and that holds here like anywhere. The bartender hauling buckets of beer through a room that’s screaming “Piano Man” has earned every dollar of it.
The second tip is the jar on the piano, and it plays by different rules. The same guide lists tip jars as “No obligation,” and at a coffee counter that’s right. On a piano lid it’s still technically true; nobody chases you to the door. But at a piano bar the jar isn’t a courtesy. It’s the request system. A table that sings all night and never feeds it tends to hear a lot of the players’ own picks.
The $5 in that dueling-piano example is a starting point, not a St. Louis price list, so here’s the honest rule: the tip is the price of the moment. A song for your table to sing while you finish a drink is worth a small bill. A song that has to happen right now, because the bride just walked in the door, is worth more, and the players will happily tell you how much more. Bring cash in small bills. Digging for a card at the piano while the whole room watches is its own kind of karaoke.
And the question everyone asks quietly: is 10% insulting? The Emily Post guide puts a bar tab at 15-20% and saves its 10% line for buffet service. So on a bar tab, the low number reads as short, and the bartender will notice. In the piano jar there’s no percentage at all. There’s just whether your napkin gets played.
Got a birthday, a bachelorette or one friend who swears she can hit the high note? Pick your room before the good tables are gone: browse Piano Bars on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call ahead about tables for your group.
If you’re the dueling-piano duo or the bar that keeps a piano tuned for the late crowd, the groups planning their big night are already searching here, and a listing puts your name in front of them so you get more customers; see who AI names instead of you.
### What to wear at a piano bar?
Whatever you can stand in and sweat in for three hours. That’s the real dress code, and the room explains it the moment you open the door: a wall of warm air, bodies shoulder to shoulder, a floor that’s gone tacky under your shoes by eleven. Cardinals red and Blues blue fit right in. So do bachelorette sashes, light-up birthday tiaras and the one guy in a sport coat who came straight from a wedding.
A few practical calls. Wear shoes you can stand in, because the best spot is often standing room near the pianos, and in Soulard the walk from where you parked can mean blocks of old brick sidewalk. Dress in layers in fall and winter; you’ll be cold for the walk and roasting by the second chorus. Leave the white silk at home, because somewhere in that crowd is a beer with your name on it. Keypers says flat out it has no dress code. If you’re planning something dressier elsewhere, check that bar’s own page or call; some rooms lean more cocktail than college.
### Is there dancing at a piano bar?
Sometimes, and usually not the way you picture it. Most piano bars are table-and-chair rooms built for singing, not dance floors. The dancing happens anyway: in the aisle when “Shout” drops into its slow, crouch-down-low part, at your table with your arms around strangers during “Don’t Stop Believin’,” and up front when the players call a birthday or bachelorette group to the piano and make them perform.
If a real dance floor matters to your group, ask the bar before you book. And keep your feet off the furniture unless the staff waves you up. The players will happily get you on stage; the bouncer will less happily get you off a chair.
### Last Call in St. Louis Can Come Later Than You Think
Under RSMo 311.290, the Missouri section titled “Time fixed for opening and closing premises,” a bar licensed to sell by the drink “shall be and remain a closed place” between 1:30 a.m. and 6:00 a.m. on weekdays. That’s why the lights snap on and the players launch into a closing number while you’re still mid-sentence.
St. Louis is different on paper. In 1876, voters approved separating the city from St. Louis County, and the city’s own history page notes it was “separated from any county.” That oddity matters at last call, because a separate statute, RSMo 311.176, headed “Convention trade area, St. Louis City,” says a bar licensed to sell by the drink “in a city not located within a county may apply” for a special permit to remain open until 3:00 a.m., if it meets the statute’s requirements.
So some city bars stay open later than others; Keypers, for one, posts a 1:30 a.m. close. Before you promise the group a late finale, call the bar and ask one question: do you hold the 3 a.m. permit? And settle the ride home before the first drink, not after the last one. If half your table drove in from out of town for the birthday, that long dark drive home is no place to discover nobody agreed on a driver.
### Want the pianos at your own party instead?
Dueling pianos travel. Two players, two keyboards or a pair of rolled-in pianos, a sound system, and suddenly a basement, a parish hall or a backyard under string lights is a piano bar for one night. It’s a popular pick for milestone birthdays, reunions, fundraisers and wedding receptions, and the cost swings widely with how many players you want, how many hours, who brings the instruments and sound, the travel, and the date.
Here’s how to get a straight answer. Shortlist two or three acts. Interview each one: how many players come, who brings the pianos and the sound gear, how much room and power they need, whether there are stairs at load-in, how requests and tips work at a private party (do guests tip the jar, or does the host cover a request budget), and whether the set runs clean or rowdy. Then tell them exactly what you want: the crowd size, the mood, three songs that must happen and one that must never be played. Compare what each act says it will deliver for your night, not just the bottom line.
The act that asks you the most questions back is usually the one that will read your room best. That’s the whole job, after all.

### Q. Is there dancing at a piano bar?
A.  Usually not on a real dance floor. People dance in the aisles, at their tables and up front when the players call a birthday or bachelorette group to the piano. If dancing matters to your group, ask the bar before you book a table.
### Q. How much to rent dueling pianos?
A.  It depends on how many players, how many hours, who brings the pianos and sound gear, travel and the date. Shortlist two or three acts, interview each about what’s included and how guest requests and tips work at a private party, tell them exactly what you want, and compare what each will deliver.
### Q. How much are you supposed to tip at a bar?
A.  The Emily Post Institute’s guide puts a bartender tip at $1-2 per drink or 15-20% of the tab. At a piano bar that covers the bartender only; the tip jar on the piano is separate, and it’s what moves your song request up the stack.
### Q. How much should you tip an artist?
A.  There’s no fixed rate for live performers. At a piano bar, treat the tip as the price of your song: one dueling-piano company’s own example starts a request at $5, so a small bill for a sing-along, more for a request that has to happen right now. ### Q. What music is St. Louis known for?
