### Q. Is 10% tip insulting?
A.  The Emily Post Institute’s guide puts sit-down wait service and a bar tab at 15-20%, and lists 10% for buffet service. So on a bar tab, the lower number reads as short. In a piano bar’s tip jar there’s no percentage at all, only whether your request gets played.
### Q. Can you request any song at a piano bar?
A.  Almost. The players know a huge catalog and can fake their way through more, but they can pass on a song, ban one for the night after one request too many, or play yours in a style you did not see coming. A name and a reason on the napkin always help.


## Your Nose Needs a Parent, Your Ear Doesn’t: Getting Pierced in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/getting-pierced-in-st-louis-what-to-know

$500. That’s what Missouri can fine a piercer for putting a needle through a minor’s nostril without a parent standing at the counter. Not a text from Mom at work that says yes. A parent, in the room, holding the pen, signing the consent form in front of the piercer or someone who works there. The fine and the rule both live in Missouri statute 324.520, and a careful studio treats it like the license on the wall depends on it, because it does.

Now the line people screenshot: in Missouri, your nose needs a permission slip and your earlobe doesn’t.

The same statute defines body piercing as “the perforation of human tissue other than an ear for a nonmedical purpose.” The ear is written out. So the ear sits outside that definition. Here’s the twist: lobes tend to heal in about six to eight weeks, while a helix or tragus can take six to 12 months. The piercing with the longest heal is the one the consent law skips.

A real St. Louis counter fills in what the statute leaves blank. TRX Tattoos & Piercing on South Grand says it straight in its own FAQ: Missouri law lets a studio pierce at any age, as long as there’s appropriate parental consent. The minimum age was left to the shop, and this one wrote its own. Its posted minor piercing policy starts earlobes at 5, nostril, helix and septum at 14, conch and tragus at 15, and daith, eyebrow, navel, lip, industrial and rook at 16. Everything else waits for 18. And the parent, the consent and the photo IDs apply to the earlobe, too. The law skips the ear. That counter doesn’t.

Whatever you get, your body tells the story the same way. The cold swipe of antiseptic. A tiny purple dot, checked twice in a mirror. A breath held a beat too long. Then the hot, fast pinch, eyes watering whether you meant them to or not, and a throb that rides home with you, keeping time with your heartbeat at every red light. The next morning there’s a little crust on the stud. For weeks after, it’s you at the bathroom sink with a can of saline: the hiss, the cool mist, a paper towel cupped under your chin. Get the studio and the aftercare right and one morning you forget the stud is there. Get them wrong and you spend a month poking a swollen lump in the mirror, wondering whether it’s infected.

A shop that tattoos needs a city permit on top of its state license, and getting one means a City of St. Louis Health Department inspection first, then a hearing before the Board of Public Service, held on Tuesdays at 1:45 pm. TRX on South Grand, for one, tattoos and pierces under one roof. So if your piercer works in a shop that also tattoos, that room went through an inspection and a city hearing to get its permit. Ask to see it. A studio that’s proud of how it runs points to the wall before you finish the question.

The city permit is written for tattoo parlors, but every studio in Missouri, piercing-only included, needs a state license, and you can check it before you ever smell the antiseptic. From the driver’s seat, thumb on your phone, open the Division of Professional Registration site and tap its Licensee Search link. Prefer a phone? The state’s Office of Tattooing, Body Piercing & Branding answers at 573-526-8288, and inside the city the City of St. Louis Health Department answers at (314) 612-5100, Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.

### What is the legal age to get a body piercing in Missouri?

Under Missouri law, anyone under 18 is a minor, and no one may knowingly pierce a minor without the prior written informed consent of a parent or legal guardian. That parent has to sign it in the presence of the piercer or one of the piercer’s employees or agents.

Read that last part again. In the presence. Not a permission slip folded into a back pocket. Not a video call from the car. A parent standing at the counter with a pen, close enough to hear the paper crinkle, while someone from the studio watches them sign. If your 16-year-old wants a nostril stud for her birthday, plan on driving her yourself and staying until the paperwork is done.

So pack the folder the night before and set it on the passenger seat. The statute only says a parent or guardian signs in person, so call the studio ahead and ask for its list. TRX’s list shows what to expect. The parent brings a valid photo ID, state-issued or a passport. The kid needs a photo ID with their photo and their first and last name on the same document: a permit or driver’s license works, and so does a school ID, a library or YMCA card, or a yearbook from the last 2 years. If the parent’s last name is different from the minor’s, TRX will additionally need a birth certificate or marriage license, divorce papers or adoption papers to verify you are the minor’s parent or guardian.

Adults don’t get a pass, either. TRX says it won’t pierce anyone without proper ID present, no matter how old you are, even if the staff knows you or has worked on you before. Bring the ID every single time. The statute itself makes it a class B misdemeanor to fraudulently pass yourself off as a parent. So the older cousin who could “totally pass for her mom” isn’t a workaround.

A piercer may not pierce anyone who is under the influence of intoxicating liquor or a controlled substance. And nobody under 18 can perform a body piercing on someone else, which covers the friend at a sleepover lining up a safety pin with your nostril.

Why are good studios so strict about all of this? Money and a license. A violation is a misdemeanor with a fine of up to $500. A second violation within a year runs $500 to $1,000. A studio that waves a 15-year-old through without a parent present is telling you something about how it handles everything else, including the needles.

### The law skips the ear. A good studio doesn’t.

Back to that earlobe line, because it cuts both ways. It isn’t a green light. A studio is free to set its own age rules and turn you away anyway, the way TRX holds earlobes to age 5 and up.

You probably remember the sound. The loud click of a piercing gun at a mall counter, a sting, a throb, a pair of starter studs. Earlobes are the most pierced body part in the country, and Cleveland Clinic says 84% of women and 64% of men in the U.S. rock pierced lobes. The trouble, Mayo Clinic warns, is that reusable piercing guns can’t be properly sterilized. That’s a small risk on a fleshy lobe. It’s a bigger one on cartilage.

### What does a clean piercing studio look like up close?

Walk in and use your eyes and nose before your wallet. A good room smells like almost nothing. The counters are clear. The piercing area is its own space, not a chair in the corner of a retail floor. And somewhere in the back you may hear the low hum and click of the sterilizer running a cycle.

There is paperwork behind that room, too. Missouri requires every practitioner of body piercing to hold a license, and every establishment where piercing is done to hold one as well, both issued through the Office of Tattooing, Body Piercing & Branding in the Division of Professional Registration.

And if the room doesn’t match the paper, if the counter is sticky, the needle comes out of an open drawer, or nobody can point to a license, the state office’s own page lists Complaint Forms. Inside the city, the Health Department’s Community Sanitation program responds to complaints about health hazards, and the Citizens’ Service Bureau, which registers and routes city service requests, answers at (314) 622-4800, Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Then watch the station itself. Mayo Clinic says to look for:

A fresh pair of disposable gloves for each piercing, put on after the piercer washes their hands.

A sterile, disposable needle instead of a reusable piercing gun.

A heat sterilizer, called an autoclave.

Hypoallergenic jewelry in surgical stainless steel, titanium, niobium, or 14- or 18-karat gold.

That last point matters more than the sparkle. Cleveland Clinic notes that allergic reactions to metal piercings are more common than infections, and that up to 20% of people may have a nickel allergy. A cheap starter stud can turn a clean piercing into an itchy, rash-red ring that looks infected and isn’t.

Here’s what that looks like on a real St. Louis price board. TRX posts its piercing prices online, with classic titanium jewelry included and tax not: a nostril starts at $69, a septum at $69, cartilage at $70, an eyebrow at $75 and a first-position lobe at $110. Jewelry on its own starts at $10 for a smaller classic titanium ball. The shop says it carries only implant grade titanium jewelry for piercings, and it works up a quote before you go back, so you know what you’re paying before anyone opens a needle. Getting more than one? It takes $5 off each additional piercing, up to 4 in a session.

So how do you choose? Interview the piercer: tell them exactly what you want, where on your body, and what metal you’re hoping for, then ask them to walk you through how they would do it, from the needle to the aftercare they send you home with. Ask for a sit-down before you commit; TRX says its one-on-one consultations carry no charge. Compare what each one says they’ll deliver with what you saw on the counter. And if a piercer tells you your navel isn’t shaped for it, that’s a good answer, not a brush-off. TRX says it declines a piercing when the anatomy won’t let jewelry heal, and always checks anatomy first for a bridge, industrial, tongue or navel.

Breathing hard on the Art Hill climb in October? Ask a lung doctor why.

### What should you actually clean a new piercing with?

Twice a day, you’ll stand at the sink, and the whole ritual takes about a minute. A short hiss from the can. A cool mist on skin that still feels warm and tight. A clean paper towel pressed under it to catch the drip. That’s it. Mayo Clinic says to clean around a skin piercing twice a day with a saline solution made for wound cleaning, or with soap and water, and to wash your hands before you touch it.

So is saline or salt water better for piercings? Sterile saline from the store wins. Cleveland Clinic says normal saline solution, which is .9% sodium chloride, can be used to clean a new piercing, and that experts recommend store-bought sterile saline over homemade. The reason is simple and annoying: homemade salt water is easy to make too salty, and too much salt dries out a delicate piercing and slows the healing. When you buy it, flip the can over. Sodium chloride and purified water should be the only two ingredients on the label. And grab it from the first-aid aisle, not the eye-care shelf. TRX’s aftercare guide warns that the saline should be made for wound care, and that contact lens solution is not the same thing and can have a negative impact on your piercing.

What not to put on it matters just as much. Mayo Clinic says to skip hydrogen peroxide, iodine and other harsh products, which can injure the pierced skin. Cleveland Clinic’s family physician on ear piercings doesn’t advise antibiotic creams or tea tree oil either: some people can have allergic reactions to them, and they don’t help you heal any faster. The fizzy brown bottle from the back of your parents’ medicine cabinet stays in the cabinet.

### What does the first week feel like, and what should you skip?

The first morning, you’ll find a little crust on the stud and maybe a faint spot on the pillowcase. That’s normal. Mayo Clinic says a new piercing can be swollen, red and tender for a few days and might bleed slightly. TRX’s aftercare guide lists a whitish-yellow fluid that forms some crust on the jewelry as normal during healing, and says it’s not pus. It looks gross and it means your body is doing its job.

It’s also the stretch that counts most. Cleveland Clinic says the highest risk of infection for a new nose piercing is in the first week, so that’s the week to be fussy.

Can you shower with a new piercing? Yes. TRX’s aftercare guide says that in the shower you just gently rinse the piercing site off when you’re done showering normally, so warm water does the softening and nothing gets picked or scraped. Then pat it dry. The guide says to pat it gently with a clean, disposable paper towel, because cloth towels can harbor bacteria and snag the piercing, and the bath towel hanging on the door has been everywhere.

What you skip is open water. Mayo Clinic says to stay out of pools, hot tubs, rivers, lakes and other bodies of water while a piercing heals. In a St. Louis summer that means no Meramec float trip, no lake weekend and no hotel hot tub until you’re healed, so if you have one on the calendar, schedule the piercing after it.

The rest of the what-not-to-do list after a fresh piercing is about your hands. Don’t twist it. Cleveland Clinic says rotating a piercing regularly used to be recommended, and that’s not recommended anymore; it’s better to wait until healing is well underway, which may be weeks to months, before purposefully spinning a piercing. Don’t take the jewelry out, even at night; Mayo Clinic says to leave it in place the whole time it heals.

### How long until a new piercing stops being a wound?

Longer than the soreness lasts. That’s the trap. The ache fades in days, and you start treating it like it’s healed when it’s still an open wound underneath.

For a nose, one university health service’s piercing guide says not to remove the stud for 8 weeks and that healing may take 12-24 weeks, depending on where it sits. The same guide also warns that nose piercings can close within hours, so never leave one empty. That’s the panic moment people don’t see coming: the stud pops out in the shower, rolls into the drain, and by dinner the hole has started to shrink. Keep a spare in the medicine cabinet.

Ears run on the lobe-and-cartilage clock from up top. Cleveland Clinic lists the signs of a healed piercing, and they’re worth taping to the mirror: it doesn’t hurt, it’s not red or swollen, it’s not crusty, scabby or flaking, and you can rotate the jewelry easily.

### When a piercing goes wrong in St. Louis

Most don’t. But it isn’t rare, either. Cleveland Clinic reports that nearly 1 in 4 people with body piercings outside the earlobe have had an infection or other medical issue. The main signs of infection it lists are pain, redness, swelling, thick yellow pus and warmth. You’ll know the feeling: the spot is hot to the touch and throbs with your heartbeat when you lie down.

Mayo Clinic says that if swelling, redness and bleeding last longer than a few days, you should contact your healthcare professional. A fever is another level. Cleveland Clinic says you shouldn’t have a fever with a mild infection; a fever usually comes with a more severe one, which is rare but serious, and you should immediately seek medical attention. Leave the jewelry in until a professional tells you otherwise, and call the studio that pierced you, too; a good piercer wants to know. If the studio itself was the problem, the complaint routes from the clean-studio section above still apply. If you’re weighing where to go, these St Louis Near Me Directory guides can help:

Urgent care vs. the ER in St. Louis, and what each one costs

When to see a dermatologist in St. Louis

How to choose a jeweler in St. Louis

The best tattoo studios in St. Louis

The best piercing you’ll ever get starts with a long, slow look at the room. Make your shortlist of two or three local studios from Piercing on St Louis Near Me Directory, then go see the gloves, the needles and the license for yourself.

If you’re the piercer with the autoclave humming in the back room, people in St. Louis are already looking for you. Put your studio, your license and your aftercare where they search and get more customers: list your business.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. How old do you have to be to get a nose piercing in Missouri?

A.  Missouri draws the line at 18: the law defines a minor as a person under the age of eighteen. A minor needs written informed consent from a parent or legal guardian, signed in front of the piercer or a studio employee, so a texted OK from home won’t do.

### Q. How much should I tip for a $50 piercing?

A.  TRX on South Grand answers it in its own FAQ: nothing is expected, and anything is appreciated, and it’s not like the restaurant business with a standard percentage. Do what you feel comfortable with. Want to tip but short on cash? The shop says making them something as a gift will always put a smile on their face, and it admits the crew likes baked goods.

### Q. Is saline or salt water better for piercings?

A.  Store-bought sterile saline is the better choice. Cleveland Clinic says homemade salt water can be too salty for a delicate piercing, which dries it out and delays healing. Look for a label that lists only sodium chloride and purified water.

### Q. Can I shower with a new piercing?

A.  Yes. TRX’s aftercare guide says to gently rinse the piercing site when you’re done showering normally, then pat it dry with a clean, disposable paper towel. What you avoid is soaking it in pools, hot tubs, rivers or lakes until it heals.

### Q. What not to do after a fresh piercing?

A.  Don’t touch it with unwashed hands, twist it, or take the jewelry out, even at night. Skip hydrogen peroxide, iodine and other harsh cleaners, and stay out of pools, hot tubs and lakes until it heals.

### Q. What happens if you don’t clean a new piercing?

A.  You raise the odds of infection, and for a new nose piercing the highest risk is in the first week. Watch for pain, redness, swelling, warmth and thick yellow pus. Cleveland Clinic lists scarring or an enlarged hole among the possible complications of an infected nose piercing, and says a fever usually means a more severe infection that needs medical attention right away.

### Q. How to heal a fresh piercing fast?

A.  There is no shortcut, only consistency. Clean it twice a day with sterile saline or soap and water, keep your hands off it, and leave the jewelry in. A Cleveland Clinic family physician doesn’t advise antibiotic creams or tea tree oil, because they don’t help you heal any faster and some people react to them.

## The $15 Sandwich With No Bread: Puerto Rican Food in St. Louis and What to Order
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/puerto-rican-food-in-st-louis-what-to-order

$15 buys a sandwich with no bread. At Mayo Ketchup in Midtown, the jibarito comes with steak, pork or grilled chicken, and the cheese, lettuce, tomato and garlic mayo are layered between twice fried green plantains where the bun should be. The first bite cracks like a cracker and then gives. The garlic mayo finds your wrist before you find a napkin.

Here’s the part that wins the table: the jibarito isn’t from the island. WTTW reports that a Puerto Rican-born Chicagoan, Juan C. Figueroa, created the sandwich at his Humboldt Park restaurant, Borinquen, in 1996, as a riff on a plantain sandwich recipe he found in a Puerto Rican newspaper. So the jibarito you order on Olive Street was invented by a Chicagoan in Humboldt Park. Say that out loud over the plates and somebody puts their sandwich down to argue.

Downtown, Puerto Rican sandwiches are headed for Wash Ave. St. Louis Magazine reports that 787 Subs, named for one of Puerto Rico’s area codes, will see Jose and Cynthia Ramos fill the downtown hall’s final full kitchen with slow-roasted meats, tripletas and fried yuca. The Wash Ave Food Hall has announced a late-October soft opening, then a grand opening the weekend of November 5-8.

Which means a lot of St. Louisans are about to stand at a counter they’ve never stood at, read the words mofongo, pernil and arroz con gandules, and do the thing almost everybody does the first time. Point. Say “that one.” Hope it’s the pork.

Say this instead: “Pernil bowl, a side of maduros, extra mayo-ketchup.” At Mayo Ketchup that bowl is $14: roasted pork, arroz con gandules, grilled onions, avocado, lime and tostones. The maduros are $4.50 more. Salty twice fried plantains, sweet maduros, pink sauce over everything, in one breath. Save it to your phone.

Read the board like a map. Mayo Ketchup’s own page says that as a team, they bring the flavors of Puerto Rico, Colombia, the Dominican Republic and Cuba to life, so the Puerto Rican plates share the board with food from three other countries. The same page invites people to find it on game days at Busch Stadium section 168 and at Energizer Park section 110, which means the pork you ate on Olive Street at lunch can follow you to a Cardinals game. The restaurant itself is at 3135 Olive Street, open Monday through Thursday 11 to 8 and Friday and Saturday 11 to 9; check its page the day you go.

### What does a mofongo taste like?

Mofongo tastes like garlic first, then salty pork, then the deep, starchy chew of green plantain that has been fried and mashed into a dense, savory mound. It isn’t sweet at all: the classic version is deep-fried green plantains mashed with salt-cured pork, garlic and butter, so think garlic mashed potatoes with crackling folded in, not banana bread.

The first forkful is heavier than you expect. The outside of the mound has a thin crust where the plantain met the oil. The inside is soft and warm, close to a stiff dough, with salty bits of pork that crunch between your teeth. Then the garlic lands at the back of your throat and decides to stay. Nobody eats mofongo quickly. You slow down, you reach for a drink, you go back in.

It’s a meal, not a garnish. It can show up as a side or as the whole entree, and it’s often topped with shrimp. Some cooks stuff it with stewed chicken, octopus, crab meat or stewed vegetables, which is why you’ll see it listed as “mofongo con” and then a protein. The mound is the base. The protein is the crown.

One St. Louis menu shows exactly how it’s meant to land. Fresh & Chill on Beck Avenue calls itself a Latin-Caribbean brunch spot where Dominican soul meets Central and South American classics, and its menu lists Mofongo & Shrimp: garlic-mashed plantains mixed with pork cracklings, topped with sautéed shrimp and chimichurri, served with a bowl of chicken broth for drenching. That broth is the tell. You spoon a little over the mound as you go, so the last bite is as soft as the first. When I checked, though, its site said the kitchen was temporarily closed, with a reopening to be announced on social media. Check those pages before you plan a brunch around it.

I’ll be straight with you: mofongo was the hardest dish in this guide to pin down in St. Louis. I couldn’t confirm it on the printed menu of a kitchen that was open the day I looked. So if you see it on a specials board or hear it called out at the counter, don’t think about it. Order it.

### Green or sweet: which plantain is on your plate?

Every Puerto Rican menu is quietly a plantain menu. The catch is that a plantain changes completely depending on how ripe it is, and the menu won’t always warn you which one you’re getting.

Green means savory. At Mayo Ketchup, tostones con aguacate are $9: twice fried plantains with smashed avocado, pickled red onion, cilantro and lime. Fried plantain coins like these come to the table salty, crisp at the rim and starchy in the middle, built for dragging through sauce. The green plantain does something stranger in the jibarito, where it stands in for the bread, layered with cheese, lettuce, tomato and garlic mayo. Smashed avocado on it is $3 more.

Ripe means sweet. Puerto Rico Activities describes amarillos as ripe plantains fried until the outside is almost blackened while the inside stays soft and sweet. The edges go sticky. The middle tastes like caramel that remembers it was a vegetable. On Mayo Ketchup’s menu the sweet ones are maduros, listed as sweet plantains, a $4.50 side.

Here’s the trick that makes you look like you’ve done this before. Order one of each. A salty, crunchy tostón next to a soft, dark, sweet maduro on the same plate is the whole cuisine in two bites, and it tells you instantly which one you’ll be ordering for the rest of your life. Mofongo, for the record, is made with the green ones. That’s why it tastes like garlic and salt instead of dessert.

Somewhere in your kitchen, a junk drawer refuses to close. Start there.

### Why is arroz con gandules next to everything?

Because it’s considered the national dish. Serious Eats puts it plainly: arroz con gandules, rice with pigeon peas, is considered the national dish of Puerto Rico. If a Puerto Rican plate has a center of gravity, it’s this rice, and it’s why nearly every pork plate you order will arrive leaning against a gold-tinted pile of it.

It starts with sofrito, which Serious Eats describes as an aromatic seasoning base of peppers, onions, garlic and herbs. Lift the lid off a pot of it and that’s what hits you first, green and sharp and savory, before the rice even comes into view. The peas are the surprise. Pigeon peas are small, dense legumes with a nutty taste, closer to a firm little bean than the soft green peas you grew up pushing around a plate.

That rice is also the answer to the question people type into their phones at the counter: what do Puerto Ricans eat pernil with? Rice first. Serious Eats notes that arroz con gandules is commonly served in large quantities during the holiday season with pernil, the slow-roasted pork, and pasteles. In St. Louis you can taste that pairing at lunch: Mayo Ketchup’s pernil bowl is $14 and puts roasted pork over arroz con gandules with grilled onions, avocado, lime and tostones. Squeeze the lime over the pork. Eat the onions. Use a tostón as a spoon.

Pernil and lechón get mixed up constantly, so here’s the difference. Lechón asado is the showpiece, and Puerto Rico Activities describes it as a whole pig marinated in adobo, a mix of oregano, black pepper, garlic, vinegar and water, then slowly roasted over coals for several hours until the skin is crisp and the meat is juicy. Pernil is slow-roasted pork, which is why it fits in a lunch bowl. On the 787 Subs menu, St. Louis Magazine lists other sandwiches beyond the tripleta, including pork shoulder seasoned with Caribbean adobo and garlic, then finished with mojo sauce.

When it’s done right, you hear it before you taste it. The skin snaps under the fork, the meat underneath pulls apart in long, wet strands, and the garlic in the marinade has gone soft and sweet in the oven. Ask for a piece with skin on it. If they have it, they’ll know exactly what you mean.

### Where can you eat Puerto Rican food in St. Louis right now?

Start in Midtown. Mayo Ketchup is at 3135 Olive Street, open Monday through Thursday 11 to 8 and Friday and Saturday 11 to 9. Its menu lists Pernil at $14, Pork, Steak and Grilled Chicken Jibaritos at $15, a $4 side of arroz con gandules described as yellow rice and pigeon peas, and La Tripleta.

La Tripleta is the sandwich to know by name. At Mayo Ketchup it’s $18 and stacks steak, pork, ham, cheese, bell pepper, onion, lettuce, tomato and potato sticks with mayo ketchup on toasted Cuban bread. Steak, pork and ham, a crunch of potato sticks and a pink sauce that drips onto the paper. Get extra napkins before you sit down, not after.

Then downtown. The Wash Ave Food Hall announced a late-October soft opening and a grand opening weekend of November 5-8, and 787 Subs will fill its final full kitchen. Its menu is led by La Tripleta Boricua, slow-roasted pork, grilled steak and ham on toasted bread with Swiss cheese, crispy potato sticks and mayo-ketchup sauce. Every sandwich comes with fried yuca instead of fries, served with house-made mayo-ketchup. There’s a plant-based one too, the Bori-Green, with plant-based ham and dairy-free cheese.

The cook behind it has the résumé to back up the name. St. Louis Magazine reports that Jose Ramos trained as a chef in Puerto Rico and worked in fine dining restaurants and hotels in New York before the family moved to St. Louis nearly eight years ago. His line on the food: “We marinate, we slow cook, and we give the flavors time to develop.” That’s the whole philosophy of the pork in one sentence.

And on game days, remember section 168 at Busch Stadium, where Mayo Ketchup invites fans to find it. Hot pork and plantains beat a cold pretzel in the seventh inning, and you’ll be the one in your row who knew.

Menus change, kitchens pause and food halls shuffle vendors, so call or check the restaurant’s own page before you drive across town for one specific plate. That goes double for mofongo.

### How do you order without pointing at the menu?

Use one sentence with three parts: the protein, the plantain and the sauce. “Pernil bowl, add maduros, extra mayo-ketchup.” “Pork jibarito and a side of arroz con gandules.” “What’s the mofongo today?” That’s it. You’ve just told the person at the register that you know what you’re eating, and the line moves faster for everybody behind you.

Say the words out loud once at home so they don’t catch in your throat at the counter. Mofongo is mo-FOHN-go. Pernil is pair-NEEL. Arroz con gandules is ah-ROHS kohn gahn-DOO-lehs. Tostones is tohs-TOH-nehs. Nobody is grading your accent. They’re just glad you tried.

Then there’s the sauce, which is the real password. Mayo-ketchup is pink, creamy and everywhere, and St. Louis Magazine calls it a version of the pink condiment found throughout Puerto Rico. Ask for it with tostones, with yuca, with the pork, with anything fried. It is salty, creamy, faintly sweet, and it turns a plate of plantains into something you keep picking at long after you said you were full.

Ask one more question and you’ll eat better than most first-timers: “What would you order?” Not “what’s good,” which gets you the bestseller. “What would you order” gets you the plate the cook is proud of today.

Feeding a crowd? Mayo Ketchup caters events. Before you book any kitchen, make a short list, talk to each kitchen, tell them what you want on the table and how many people are coming, then compare what each will actually deliver. Pernil, arroz con gandules and a tray of tostones feeds a room the way it feeds a family on the island.

### The order that teaches you the whole cuisine in one sitting

If you’re two people and it’s your first time, don’t each order an entree. Share. Get a pernil plate or bowl with arroz con gandules. Get a jibarito or a tripleta. Get one side of tostones and one of maduros. Get the mayo-ketchup. That’s the island on one table: slow pork, gold rice, green plantain and sweet plantain, with the pink sauce running between all of them.

Eat it in that order. The pork and rice first, while the skin is still crisp. Then the sandwich, while the plantain “bread” still crunches. Then trade tostones and maduros back and forth until somebody admits which one they like better. It’s loud food. It’s shared food. It’s food that expects you to lick a finger.

If mofongo is on the board, swap it in for the sandwich, spoon the broth over it if they bring some, and save the last bite for whoever drove.

Hungry now and not sure which kitchen is open tonight? Browse Puerto Rican Food on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick a spot, and call ahead to ask what’s coming out of the oven.

If you’re the cook behind a Puerto Rican kitchen, truck or catering table, people are already searching for your pernil. Put your menu where they’re looking and get more customers: list your business on St Louis Near Me Directory.

### Breakfast, coquito and the sweet end of the meal

A typical Puerto Rican morning is smaller and sweeter than lunch. The classic is a mallorca, a soft, sweet roll showered with powdered sugar, torn open and dipped into coffee. King Arthur Baking describes mallorcas as a fluffy, yeasted sweet bread made with lard and topped with confectioners’ sugar, commonly found in Puerto Rican bakeries all over the island. The writer of that piece put the feeling better than I can: “I feel instantly connected whenever I rip into a freshly baked mallorca and dip it into my morning café con leche.”

The sugar gets everywhere. On your fingers, your shirt, the table. That’s how you know you did it right. The same piece notes that the oldest and most famous mallorca bakery in Puerto Rico, La Bombonera Puig y Abraham, was founded in 1902 and ended its 110-year run in 2012, which is a reminder that a pastry like this lives or dies on whether people keep buying it.

If you ever spot mallorcas in a St. Louis pastry case, buy two. This is a breakfast worth crossing town for.

At the other end of the day, there’s coquito. Puerto Rico Activities describes it as a white rum drink made from evaporated milk, condensed milk, coconut milk and cinnamon, similar to eggnog but with a Puerto Rican flair, and it also comes in flavors like pistachio, guava and chocolate. It’s cold, thick and sweet, and the rum arrives a second after the coconut. Tembleque, a pudding-like dessert made from a coconut base, is the gentler choice for the table. It wobbles when you set it down.

Holiday season is also when the pork and rice get serious. The big holiday spread is the same pairing you can order at lunch, pernil and arroz con gandules, just in quantities meant for the whole family and whoever else wanders in.

### Q. What is Puerto Rico’s national dish?

### Q. How are you supposed to eat mofongo?

## A Dime for Being Right: Race Tracks Near St. Louis and What to Know
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/race-tracks-near-st-louis-what-to-know

$2.10. The gate clangs open for race 3 at Fairmount Park on September 1, the favorite Be Lucky Again runs exactly the way the 2/5 morning line said he would, and the $2 show ticket in your hand cashes for $2.10 on the posted results. A dime of profit, for being right. Later on the same card, a 15/1 morning-line shot named More Than Destiny won, and his $2 show ticket paid $9.80, his win ticket $47.20. Same window. Same two dollars. The favorite gives you a dime and a cheer; the long shot buys dinner on The Hill.

Nobody tells you that at the glass. The two-dollar bill, folded once, slides under the window at Fairmount Park in Illinois, and the teller is already looking at you, waiting for the words. Behind you, horses are walking toward the starting gate. The race program in your other hand has gone soft at the edges because you have been squeezing it for ten minutes. You know which horse you like. You have no idea what to say.

Racing around St. Louis runs on its own clocks, and this month they cross. Fairmount’s live races run Tuesdays and Saturdays through October 27. Tickets for the Gateway Dirt Nationals, the December race on a track laid down inside The Dome at America’s Center downtown, go on sale October 20. The horses are finishing their season just as the dirt opens its box office. Miss the calendar and you miss the race. One driver even connects the two sides of the river: Kyle Larson won the Enjoy Illinois 300 at World Wide Technology Raceway on September 13, and the Gateway Dirt Nationals’ list of past champions has him as the 2019 midget winner inside the Dome.

### How much does a $2 win place show bet cost?

A $2 win, place, show bet costs $6, because an across-the-board bet is really three separate wagers on the same horse: a win bet, a place bet (first or second) and a show bet (first, second or third). If your horse finishes third or better, you earn money.

Horseplayers call it betting “across the board.” It’s the gentlest way in. The ticket goes damp in your fist as the field turns for home, the crowd noise climbs a notch with every stride, and your horse can get caught at the wire and still leave you holding something that cashes. A place bet pays if your horse finishes first or second; a show bet pays if it finishes first, second or third. Third or better is the line for getting something back, and you’ll find out how much you cared about an animal you met twenty minutes ago.

If $6 feels like a lot for a first try, bet $2 to show. A show bet pays if your horse lands anywhere in the top three. The payout is small. You still walk back to the window holding a slip of paper that is worth more than it was a minute and a half ago.

Now the twist hiding in the small print of Fairmount’s September 1 card. The race listings carried a 10-cent superfecta, a 50-cent trifecta with a $1.00 minimum wager, and a $1.00 daily double, so some of the hardest bets on the board cost less than a $2 show ticket to try. Minimums can vary from track to track and race to race, so ask the teller what the minimum is before you hand over your money. It’s a normal question. Nobody will blink.

### What do you actually say at the betting window?

The teller’s hand rests on the counter while you thumb the program for a number, and the line behind you shifts its weight. Here are the rules for betting on horse races that nobody hands you at the door, and they fit in one breath. First, find your horse’s program number, the big number on its saddle cloth, not its name. Then walk up and say it in this order: track name, race number, bet amount, bet type, horse number. At Fairmount on September 1, backing the favorite in race 3, the whole sentence would have been: “Fairmount, race 3, $2 to show on number 1.” That is where the folded two-dollar bill goes. Under the glass, with those words, in that order, and the printer hands back your ticket.

Check your ticket before you step away. Wrong horse, wrong race: far easier to fix at the window than after the gate opens. Get your bet in before the starting gate opens. After that, the race belongs to the horses.

Carry the rewards card? The track’s racing page says to give it to the teller when you place your bets. If you would rather talk to a machine than a stranger, the same page lists auto-teller machines: insert cash, swipe your rewards card and place your wagers there. No line building behind you. No blurting “place” when you meant “show.”

Should you bet win, place or show? It depends on what you want out of the afternoon. Win cashes if your horse comes in first and carries the most upside. Show cashes if it comes in first, second or third. Some bettors use what they call the “80/20 rule”: 20% of the stake on a horse to win and 80% on the same horse to place, for steadier returns with a little upside left in. For your first day, show bets keep you in the game longest, and staying in the game is the point.

Decide your limit before you park, not at the window. Bring that amount in cash and leave the card in the car. The afternoon is better when the number is already settled, and the horses will run again whether you chase a loss or not.

### Where do the horses actually run near St. Louis?

Fairmount Park, just over the river on the Illinois side, has been racing Thoroughbreds since 1925, and its own newsroom calls it Illinois’ only “racino” venue that puts live horse racing and casino gaming under one roof. The track marked its hundredth year with a three-day celebration for a place a lot of people only know as the lights they pass on the way to somewhere else.

Remember a different name on the sign? The track changed its name as part of a partnership with FanDuel for a stretch. Today, type Fairmount Park Casino & Racing into your map.

Fairmount bills itself as Illinois’ only Thoroughbred racetrack and casino, and this June the place got quieter in one corner: FanDuel said it was closing the retail sportsbook that took football and baseball bets there. The general manager’s answer was short. Horse race betting will continue. The window you walk up to is the horse window.

Here is the part that matters for your calendar. Fairmount’s posted live-racing schedule this season runs Tuesdays and Saturdays, first post 1:30 p.m., through October 27. The live meet is seasonal, and the track pairs it with what it calls all-day simulcast wagering. You can learn to bet that way. You just can’t feel the ground move.

And it does move, a little. Stand at the rail when a field turns for home and you hear it before you see it, a low drumming that gets louder and closer until it is right in front of you, a blur of silks and dirt clods, and then gone. Fairmount’s own copy talks about “the thunder of hooves,” and for once the marketing undersells it.

General manager Vince Gabbert made the track’s pitch plainly when the casino added live table games: “We’re the only place for many people within a 5-6 hour radius to come watch horse races and play games in a casino.” That’s a casino man talking, so weigh it accordingly. Still, for a St. Louisan who wants to watch live Thoroughbreds this afternoon, it’s the obvious first stop.

Come hungry. The track says it has a new country-western-themed restaurant with a BBQ menu, plus a deli and concessions, and the posted hours for Longshots, its trackside restaurant, start at 11:30 a.m. Monday through Sunday. Eat before first post and you can watch the horses parade to the gate with sauce still on your fingers.

One more quiet perk. Fairmount runs a racing rewards program: every $10 you wager on racing earns 1 point, and 100 points turn into $1 in free slot play or food credit. Do the math: that is a dollar back for every thousand wagered. It won’t change your life. But the track says the rewards card is free to join, you have to be 21 or older with an active card, signing up takes a valid ID at the entrance, and the points land whether your horse wins or runs dead last.

### Is the NASCAR race really a St. Louis thing?

You feel a Cup field before you properly hear it: a push of air against your chest as the pack goes by, then the sound catching up and filling the grandstand until the person next to you is just a moving mouth.

Yes, it’s a St. Louis thing: the September 13 Cup race drew a fifth consecutive sellout crowd. St. Louis does have a NASCAR track: World Wide Technology Raceway on the Illinois side hosts the Cup Series race called the Enjoy Illinois 300. When it ran on September 13, Kyle Larson snapped a 51-race winless streak by surviving two overtime restarts. The track’s own announcement said the future of NASCAR in the St. Louis market is bright, and the empty-seat count backs it up.

Think about what a sellout means for you. It means the lazy, spur-of-the-moment version of NASCAR weekend doesn’t exist here. The people in those stands bought early. If you want in next time, the track’s homepage offers its Track Talk newsletter to “stay in the know.” Get on it now, instead of waking up race week to an empty ticket page and a long face.

Outside Cup race day, the same property has a drag strip as well as its oval track, and its upcoming-events list still showed several October dates when I checked. Drag racing is a different animal. It’s loud in a way you feel in your sternum, each run is over almost before you can blink, and you can watch the whole thing from one seat. For a first-timer with a short attention span, or a kid who has one, that’s a feature.

One name ties the two seasons together. Kyle Larson, the driver who won the Enjoy Illinois 300 at World Wide Technology Raceway on September 13, is also on the Gateway Dirt Nationals’ list of past champions as the 2019 midget winner inside the Dome. In September he was in a Cup car across the river. In 2019 he was throwing a midget sideways through the clay under the same roof where you may have sat through a convention.

### Why is there dirt inside the Dome in December?

The smell reaches you on the concourse before the cars do: race fuel, with nowhere to go but back down on the crowd.

Because the Gateway Dirt Nationals bring the racetrack indoors. FloRacing, which streams the event, says the Gateway Dirt Nationals are held on a temporary fifth-mile oval inside The Dome at America’s Center in downtown St. Louis, the building at 901 N. Broadway, and the past winners list runs from super late models to open wheel modifieds throwing clay under a roof.

So yes, dirt racing at the Dome is on the calendar: the Gateway Dirt Nationals run December 3-5. Tickets go on sale October 20 at 10 a.m. Central in 3-day packages, 2-day packages and single days. If you want to sit together as a family, that is the morning to set an alarm for. Tickets will also be available on-site each day, but the good seats won’t wait for you.

Inside, it’s sensory overload in the best way. This is the room where Larson won. Clay comes off the tires in clumps. The engine noise doesn’t drift off into the sky the way it does outdoors; it bounces back at you. Bring ear protection, for the kids and for yourself. The event is strict at the door: bags are not permitted except medical bags and diaper bags for those with a child, and outside food, drinks and coolers are prohibited. Children under 2 can sit on a lap without a ticket. Can’t make it downtown? Every lap streams live on FloRacing.com.

Quick detour: a contractor who won’t give a street address is telling you something.

### The dirt oval 8 miles from downtown

Not every dirt night needs a ticket packet and a parking plan. Tri-City Speedway sits just across the Mississippi from St. Louis, about 8 miles from downtown, and it’s the opposite of the Dome: open sky, a 3/8-mile dirt oval with 10 degrees of banking in the corners, and a main grandstand with 5,000 seats.

The track’s FAQ says races generally start at 7:15 p.m. and last about four hours, so plan on a late one. Tickets are sold at the front gate only, cash or card, and there’s an ATM on site. No coolers, no outside food, no alcohol carried in. You may bring a stadium chair, and you should, because 4 hours on a bleacher is long. At the concession stand, the track says nachos and chili cheese fries seem to be the most popular. Eat them in the stands on a dry night and you may be brushing grit off the cheese by the third heat. That is the experience, and nobody who loves it would trade it.

Watch the super late models if you can. Gordy Gundaker holds the track record for that class at 14.017 seconds a lap, a 96.311 mph average, on an oval shorter than half a mile. When a pack dives into turn one at that pace, the cars are sideways and the dirt comes off the outside in a sheet.

One honest note. When I checked, the track’s schedule page still described a past season, so check its social pages before you drive over and call it a race night only once you see a date posted. That is also my answer to anyone asking where the cheapest dirt racing is: a regular race night at a local oval like this one costs you a gate ticket and a tank of gas, while the Dome’s December event is the splurge.

### What to carry, and what gets turned away at the gate

Every gate around here has its own rules. Here is the short packing list for each.

Fairmount Park: a valid ID, because Fairmount Rewards is free to join and you sign up with a valid ID at the entrance, cash for the window, and something to circle your picks with. Racing post times are Tuesday and Saturday at 1:30 p.m. during the live meet.

World Wide Technology Raceway: tickets bought well ahead for the Cup race, which drew a fifth consecutive sellout crowd on September 13, plus ear protection.

Gateway Dirt Nationals at the Dome: bags are not permitted except medical bags and diaper bags for those with a child, and outside food, drinks and coolers are prohibited. For ADA seating, the event says to call The Dome at America’s Center at (314) 342-5201.

Tri-City Speedway: cash or card at the front gate, a stadium chair, and nothing that clinks. Its list of items not permitted starts with coolers of any size and glass containers.

Which one first? For a date or a slow Saturday, the horses: a show ticket, an afternoon in the sun, a plate of barbecue. For a kid who loves loud things, the drag strip or a dirt night. For a story you’ll still be telling in January, the Dome in December. Whichever you pick, the second trip to the window is easier than the first, and by the third you are the one telling a stranger to say the program number.

### Frequently asked questions about race tracks near St. Louis

### Q. Does St. Louis have a NASCAR track?

A.  Yes. World Wide Technology Raceway in Illinois ran the NASCAR Cup Series’ Enjoy Illinois 300 on September 13, before a fifth consecutive sellout crowd, so buy tickets early.

### Q. Is there dirt racing at the Dome in St. Louis?

A.  Yes. FloRacing says the Gateway Dirt Nationals are held on a temporary fifth-mile oval inside The Dome at America’s Center in downtown St. Louis, at 901 N. Broadway. This year’s dates are December 3-5, and tickets go on sale October 20 at 10 a.m. Central.

### Q. What is Fairmount Park called now?

A.  Fairmount Park Casino & Racing. The track went by FanDuel Sportsbook and Horse Racing during its partnership with FanDuel, and FanDuel later announced it was closing its retail sportsbook there.

### Q. How much do tickets cost to attend Fairmount Park racetrack?

A.  For its centennial celebration, Fairmount listed general admission as free. If you want a better seat, the track says you can book a private box or table in the grandstand. Check the track’s site before you go, since event pricing can change.

### Q. Should I bet win place or show?

A.  Win cashes if your horse comes in first, place if it comes in first or second, and show if it comes in first, second or third. For a first visit, show keeps you in the race longest, while win carries the most upside.

### Q. What is the lowest amount you can bet on a horse?

A.  On Fairmount’s September 1 card, the superfecta was a 10-cent bet and the trifecta a 50-cent bet with a $1.00 minimum wager. For win, place and show, Churchill Downs lists a $2 minimum. Minimums vary by track, so ask the Fairmount teller.

### Q. What is the cheapest dirt track racing to get into?

A.  A regular night at Tri-City Speedway, about 8 miles from downtown St. Louis, skips the ticket packages: you pay at the front gate, cash or card, and races generally start at 7:15 p.m. I couldn’t find a posted gate price, so check the track’s social pages before you drive over.

## Your Rug Didn’t Shrink: How to Choose an Area Rug for a St. Louis Room
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-an-area-rug-in-st-louis

Why is your sofa still standing on bare wood? You got the new rug home, heard it slap down on the boards, dragged the coffee table onto it, and stood back. The sofa sat there with all four feet on bare wood like it was waiting for a bus. Your stomach dropped a little. On the showroom floor that rug looked enormous, a whole field of wool under those bright lights. It didn’t change size in the car. Your room just did the math the store never asked you to do.

Here’s the fix, and it costs a roll of blue painter’s tape. Before you set foot in a shop, tape an 8-by-10 rectangle on your living room floor, 8 feet deep and 10 feet across the front of the sofa. Slide the sofa so its front legs sit just inside the line. Then live with it for a day. Carry the laundry through it, put your coffee on the table in the middle, and watch where your feet land when you stand up. If the tape looks like a postage stamp, run a second line out to 9 by 12 and live with that one too. By the next evening you’ll know your size in your gut, and you won’t have spent a cent finding out.

Now the old rug, the flat, faded one the dog has slept on for years. If you live in the city, the fee for its ride out is already on your water bill. The City of St. Louis Refuse Division picks up bulky items once a month, and the service is included in the $14-a-month-per-unit solid waste fee that rides on your water bill. Here’s the catch nobody mentions until the truck rolls past your alley: no container or bundle can be over 6 feet long, over 2 feet across or over 100 pounds. Roll an 8x10 the way everybody does and you’ve built an 8-foot log, two feet too long.

So fold it in half first, then roll it. It comes out about 4 feet long, dust in your nose and grit on your forearms, and you tie it off and drag it out back by 6 a.m. on the Monday of your collection week, up to three items a pickup. Not sure it qualifies? The Refuse Division’s number is (314) 622-4800.

Your old rug’s funeral is already on your water bill. It just can’t be longer than 6 feet.

Most people buy a rug in the opposite order. You fall for a rug first. The color hits you, or the softness under your palm, or the way it makes you picture a winter evening with your feet tucked under you. The logic comes after, and it’s there to protect the feeling: tape the room, flip the corner before you pay, read the little sewn-in tag, and interview the shop before you hand over a card.

If you live in an older brick house, a Soulard rowhouse, a South Grand four-family, one of the big places in the Central West End, you may already know the sound problem. Footsteps ring off the walls. A sock foot finds the one board that creaks. A rug in a house like that earns its keep. It softens the echo. It protects the floor. And it pulls a room of mismatched furniture into one place where people want to sit. Get the size wrong and it fails at every one of those.

There’s a reason so many of those houses are brick, and it starts with a mattress. On the night of May 17, 1849, an ember smoldering in a mattress on the steamboat White Cloud set its cabins burning at the riverfront. According to St. Louis Magazine, the fire claimed 15 square blocks, more than 400 buildings and 23 steamers, and a newly instituted building code called for fire-resistant materials, including plenty of brick. So the ring in your front room has a pedigree. Hard brick, hard plaster, hard boards, and every sound bounces until something soft catches it. In a lot of St. Louis houses, the rug is the softest thing in the room. Your echo started on a burning boat. Your rug is how you finish the story.

### Should I get a 5x7 or 8x10 rug?

For most living rooms, get the 8x10. A 5x7 works when you want every furniture leg off the rug in a small room or a reading corner, while an 8x10 is sized so the front legs of your sofa and chairs can rest on its edge, and that one move is what makes a seating area look like it belongs together.

Start with the sofa, not the room. Lift the front of the couch, slide the rug under, and set it down: the front feet thump onto the wool edge, the coffee table and the chairs suddenly line up around it, and the room pulls together like somebody finally sat down in it. A rug narrower than your couch does the opposite and leaves the couch floating, cut loose from everything in front of it. One sizing guide puts it in plain numbers: under a standard 84-inch sofa, an 8-foot-wide rug, which means an 8x10, is the minimum, and a 9x12 is ideal. So the question people type into their phones at midnight, whether a rug should be bigger or smaller than the couch, has a short answer. Bigger. Almost always bigger.

Then look at the edges. The same guide suggests leaving 18 to 24 inches of exposed floor around the rug. That strip of wood is the frame around the picture. Run the rug nearly wall to wall and it starts to look like carpet somebody forgot to finish. Leave a wide moat of floor all the way around and the rug looks like a bathmat that wandered down from upstairs.

If you’re torn between two sizes, go up. The guide says a too-small rug can make a sweeping space feel cramped, while a larger rug will give even tiny rooms a spacious, coordinated look. You’ll feel the difference the first time you get up from the sofa barefoot on a January morning and your heel lands on wool instead of the cold edge of a board.

The 5x7 still has a job. Tuck it under a coffee table between two armchairs, slide it in front of a fireplace, or put it in a narrow front room where a bigger rug would curl up against the radiator. Just choose it on purpose, with the legs deliberately off, rather than because it was the one on sale.

### Why does every rug look bigger in the store?

Because the store is a warehouse, and your living room isn’t. A showroom has high ceilings, wide open floor and rugs hanging on racks or stacked in piles with no sofa next to them. Your eye has nothing to measure against. At home it has everything: the sofa, the radiator, the doorway to the dining room, the spot by the window where the dog sleeps in the sun.

That’s why the tape test works. It puts the ruler back in the room. And if you can’t decide between the two outlines after a day, go with the one your feet liked. The kids and the dog will have crossed it twenty times by then, and the tape peels up with a little tearing sound when you’re done.

Then stand in the doorway and take a photo of the taped room, the way a guest first sees it. Carry that photo into the shop. It’s worth more than a page of measurements, because it shows the person helping you the room you actually live in: the light from the bay window, the color of the floor, the fireplace that eats one whole wall, the sofa your aunt gave you that isn’t going anywhere.

### What does the back of a rug tell you that the front won’t?

Almost everything. Flip the corner. That’s the whole trick, and hardly anyone does it in a store because it feels a little rude, like checking a stranger’s teeth. Do it anyway. Fold the corner back, put your fingers on the underside, and look.

On a hand-knotted rug, the pattern shows clearly through on the back and you can see the individual knots, like stitches you could count. One rug dealer’s guide to spotting hand-knotted work describes the other case: on a hand-tufted rug, the back is covered entirely by a canvas cloth that hides the construction, and if you can’t see the pattern on the reverse at all, it isn’t hand-knotted.

Now fold it over your arm. The same guide says a hand-knotted rug folds softly and unevenly, while a stiff, board-like fold usually means there’s a backing. Your hands will know the difference before your head does. One drapes like a heavy wool coat. The other bends like a cereal box.

Check the fringe last. On a hand-knotted rug the fringe isn’t decoration. It’s the warp, the foundation threads the whole rug is built on, coming out at each end. On many machine-made rugs the fringe is sewn or glued on afterward as a finishing touch. Look where the fringe meets the pile. If you see a seam or a band of stitching, you know which kind of rug you’re holding.

None of this makes a tufted or machine-made rug a bad buy. It makes it a different thing at a different price, and you deserve to know which one you’re paying for. That’s what high quality really means once you’re standing in the shop: a rug that is exactly what the person selling it says it is. And don’t panic over a rough-looking back. Knot density varies enormously between regions and periods, so a coarser back does not mean a lesser rug. Honest beats perfect.

### What is that little fiber tag really telling you?

Somewhere on the back, usually near a corner, there’s a small sewn-in label. Most people never read it. It should.

Under the Federal Trade Commission’s textile rule, that label has to list the generic names and percentages by weight of the fibers in the product, for every fiber present at 5 percent or more. So “100% wool” isn’t a mood or a marketing word. It’s a statement somebody is on the hook for.

Here’s the part almost nobody knows. For a floor covering with a backing, the rule says the fiber disclosure has to make clear that it relates only to the face, pile or outer surface, and not to the backing, filling or padding. The rule’s own example label reads: “100% Nylon Pile, 100% Cotton Back.” In plain English, the soft part you run your hand across can be one thing, and the layer holding it together can be something else entirely. A tag that says wool is talking about what you touch, not what’s touching your floor. Which is one more reason to fold that corner.

Want to train your eye before you shop? Go look at rugs nobody will ever try to sell you. According to St. Louis Magazine, local lore says a St. Louisan named James F. Ballard fell for rugs one day in 1905, captivated by an oriental rug in a shop window, and the Saint Louis Art Museum ended up with the larger share of his collection: 110 carpets. Admission to the Saint Louis Art Museum is free every day. One fragment of a Mughal court carpet Ballard donated is labeled simply “wool and silk,” which is the museum version of the tag sewn on your rug. I couldn’t confirm which of his carpets are on view on a given day, so check with the museum before you go. Even an hour in the galleries teaches your eyes what a centuries-old knot looks like up close.

That’s also the honest way to think about the blend question people ask most, whether all-wool beats a wool blend. Read the small print first. Under the same rule, a fiber present at less than 5 percent of the total fiber weight can’t be listed by its generic name. It has to be designated as “other fiber.” So the tag tells you the big players in the pile, not every guest at the party. Wool does earn its place in a muggy St. Louis summer, though. The Woolmark Company says wool fibers can absorb large quantities of moisture vapor and allow it to evaporate, which is the cool, dry, never-clammy feel you get when you sink your toes into a good wool pile in July. It doesn’t tell you how that rug will wear in your front room with a dog, two kids and a radiator. So don’t argue percentages with yourself in the aisle. Ask the shop why the blend is there, which room they’d put it in, and how it has held up in homes like yours. A good shop answers that without blinking.

### Will a rug hurt the old wood floor underneath?

It can, and the damage hides until you move the rug. You roll it up a few years later to repaint, and there it is: a pale rectangle, or a cloudy, slightly tacky patch the exact shape of the rug, like a shadow that stayed behind after the rug left.

The usual suspect is the backing, not the wool. Flip the rug one more time. If the underside is a solid sheet of rubber, a slick plastic grid, or a stiff coating that smells like a new tire, ask the shop plainly what it will do to a finished wood floor over a long, sticky St. Louis summer. Ask what pad they’d put under it and what that pad is made of. If the answer is a shrug, keep shopping.

In an older house this one is personal. If your floor has been refinished before, there’s only so much wood left to sand, and a rug that marks the finish costs you a lot more than a rug. So the answer to what rugs to avoid on hardwood floors comes down to three habits: read the back, ask about the pad, and lift the rug now and then to let the boards air out and see what’s going on underneath. If you’re still deciding what goes on the floor itself, our guide to hardwood vs. laminate in St. Louis is a good place to start.

### Lighter or darker than the floor is really a question about light

People ask whether a rug should be lighter or darker than the floor. What you’re really choosing is contrast. A light rug on a dark-stained floor reads crisp and bright. A darker rug on pale oak anchors a room that otherwise feels like it’s drifting. Match the two too closely and the rug disappears, which is a lot of money to spend on something nobody notices.

Then think about the light you actually get. A north-facing front room in a brick house goes gray by mid-afternoon in January, and a dark rug in there turns into a hole in the floor. A sunny back room off the kitchen can carry a deep red or a navy that would sulk anywhere else. And if you want a small room to feel bigger, a lighter rug with a quiet pattern helps, but size helps more. A big, calm rug opens a room in a way a small loud one never will.

Last, think about what walks across it. A golden retriever who sheds like it’s his job. A toddler with a grape popsicle. Boots in from a slushy January sidewalk on Cherokee Street. The prettiest cream rug in the store is a different rug in that house. A soft pattern, a mid-tone color and a little visual noise forgive a lot of life.

### Fall for it first, then interview the shop

Price follows construction, which is why two 8x10 rugs that look the same from across the room can be far apart on the tag. A hand-knotted pile rug can take months on a loom. A hand-tufted rug is made with a tool that punches yarn through a canvas backing in a fraction of the time. Neither is a rip-off at the right price. Either one is at the wrong price.

So don’t walk in asking for the cheapest 8x10. Shortlist two or three local rug shops and go in with your taped-room photo and your measurements, ready to interview them. Tell each one what you want: the room, who walks on it, the floor underneath, and how you want it to feel under bare feet on a cold morning. If you live in an old brick house, say so. Tell them the boards are old, the walls aren’t square, the radiator sits where it sits, and the house rings when the kids run. Then ask whether they’ve laid rugs in houses like yours, and what they put underneath. Ballard fell in love through a shop window. You get to do the falling and the asking.

Then listen. Ask what the rug is made of, front and back, and ask them to flip the corner for you. Ask what pad they’d pair with your floor, whether you can see the rug in your own room before you commit, and how they clean and repair what they sell. Then compare what each shop says it will deliver, the rug, the pad, the advice and the care after the sale, against what you told them you wanted. A good price for an 8x10 is the one where those two lists match.

Your taped-up floor and that doorway photo are the best shopping list you’ll ever carry. Bring them to two or three local shops you find under Rugs on St Louis Near Me Directory, and let them show you what fits the room you actually live in.

If you’re the rug shop, the rug cleaner or the one-person repair crew who flips corners for a living, St. Louis homeowners are already looking for you. More customers are searching this page for exactly what you know, so list your business where they can call you.

And before you say yes, put your hand flat on the rug and close your eyes for a second. It feels silly in a store full of people. It isn’t. You’re going to touch this thing every day for years, and your palm knows more than the price tag does.

### When it finally comes home

It’ll arrive rolled tight and maybe curled at the ends, and the old one goes out to the alley folded in half. Give it a few days flat. Roll a stubborn corner backward against the curl. Put the pad down first, then square the rug to the sofa rather than the walls if your walls aren’t quite straight, which in an older house they often aren’t.

Brain full of rug math? Go eat something red and Malaysian.

Then sit on the sofa and look at it from where you’ll see it most. If the front legs rest on the rug, the edges have their strip of bare wood, and your feet land on something soft when you stand up, you chose well. If the rug still looks small, now you know exactly why, and exactly what to ask for next time.
