### Frequently asked questions about choosing an area rug

### Q. Should area rug be bigger or smaller than couch?

A.  Bigger. A rug narrower than the sofa makes the sofa look like it’s floating. One sizing guide says that under a standard 84-inch sofa, an 8-foot-wide rug, an 8x10, is the minimum and a 9x12 is ideal, with at least the front legs of the sofa resting on the rug.

### Q. How can you tell if a rug is high quality?

A.  Fold the corner back. A hand-knotted rug shows its pattern and knots on the back and folds softly, while a tufted rug hides its construction under a canvas cloth and folds stiffly. Neither is automatically better. Quality means the rug is what the shop says it is, so ask them to flip it for you and explain what you’re looking at.

### Q. What rugs to avoid on hardwood floors?

A.  Be wary of rugs and pads with a solid rubber or plastic backing, especially on an older floor with a finish you want to keep. Ask the shop what the backing is made of, what pad they recommend for your floor and why, and lift the rug now and then to check the wood underneath.

### Q. Should a rug be lighter or darker than the floor?

A.  Either works if there’s contrast. A light rug brightens a dark floor, and a darker rug anchors a pale one. A rug that matches the floor too closely tends to disappear. Let your room’s light and who walks across it, kids, dogs, winter boots, decide how light you can go.

### Q. Is 100% wool carpet better than 80%/20?

A.  The tag can’t settle that by itself. The federal textile rule requires the label to list each fiber at 5 percent or more by weight, and on a backed floor covering that disclosure covers only the face or pile. So read the label, then ask the shop why the blend is there and how it has held up in rooms like yours.

## Ukrainian on Paper, Russian on the Menu: Russian Food in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/russian-food-in-st-louis-what-to-order

Borscht lands the color of a church window with the sun behind it, deep magenta, a thin shine of fat on top and a little hill of chopped dill. Steam comes off it smelling of beets and broth and something sour underneath. You drop in a spoon of sour cream and drag it once. The white goes pink in a long, lazy ribbon. Bread waits on the side, dark and heavy, and the first spoonful is sweet, then sharp, then warm all the way down to your belt.

Now the part most St. Louisans have backwards. Ask around and that bowl is Russian. Ask UNESCO and it’s Ukrainian: the culture of Ukrainian borscht cooking went onto the List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding in 2022, filed as a case of extreme urgency, because the war displaced the families who carry the recipe and cut communities off from the vegetables that go into it. The soup on your spoon is a soup somebody is trying to save.

In St. Louis, that borderland showed up in a church on Gravois long before it showed up on a menu. Its Russian Orthodox church, named for the Archangel, was founded in October 1909, and its parish was made up of immigrants from “Austria-Hungary, Galicia and Russia” who had come looking for work in the mining areas of Illinois and Missouri. They couldn’t afford a church at first, so they rented stores for services. Then they bought a house at 1125 Hickory Street for $7,000 and stacked a whole parish inside it: services on the first floor, the priest living on the second, a meeting hall on the third. Outside, Gravois was a cobblestone street, and the Bellefontaine streetcar rattled down it.

Visitors are welcome anytime. The parish stands at 1901 Ann Avenue, on the corner of Ann and Gravois. Divine Liturgy is at 10:00 a.m. on Sundays, the services are in English, and the parish holds a coffee hour right after. Parking is on the street only, the church line is 314-884-0394, and its website says it plainly: “Visitors are welcome anytime!”

So where do you go tonight? Start at Astoria Bistro, also known as Astoria Kabob House. One diner called it “a lovely jewel box of a restaurant” and wrote down exactly what landed on the table: the currant compote, the borsch, the Olivier salad, the bliny with meat and the cherry dumplings. Order it in that sequence and you can feel the meal turn. A cold, sweet-tart sip of compote first. Then beet steam on your face. Then the cool crunch of potato salad, a warm pancake folded around meat, and last a dumpling that splits under your fork and bleeds dark cherry into the sour cream. Ask for the sour cream on the side, and say yes to the bread.

The receipt: 12949 Olive Arcade Plaza. Its MapQuest listing shows it closed Sundays and Mondays and opening at 4 p.m. Tuesday through Saturday, so this is a dinner plan. Its menu runs to homemade comfort food: borscht, pelmeni, beef stroganoff, chicken Kiev and stuffed cabbage rolls. Small family kitchens change hours without warning, so call 314-878-7711 before you drive.

Here’s the one idea that changes how you order. Russian food in St. Louis has always been a borderland table. The same hands rolled the dumplings whether the grandmother called herself Russian, Ukrainian or something the census never had a box for. Don’t walk in asking whether a dish is “really” Russian. Ask who made it, how, and what goes on top. That last answer is almost always sour cream.

### Is borscht Ukrainian or Russian?

In 2022, UNESCO inscribed the Culture of Ukrainian borscht cooking. The same record says there are many versions. Each kitchen swears its version is the real one. Each grandmother is right.

One detail from the UNESCO record will stay with you. In the Podillia region, the third day of a wedding has kept its ritual name do nevistky - na borshch, which means “visit daughter-in-law to eat borscht.” The new bride’s soup is how the family takes her measure. Think about the nerves on that stove.

### What goes into a real bowl of borscht?

UNESCO’s record says borscht is cooked with broth combined with beetroot, sugar beet or fermented beet juice, and that last one is where a sour edge can come from. Most kitchens build from there with cabbage, potato, carrot and onion, cut small enough to fit on a spoon. Many add beef and let the bones do the work. Some go meatless. A good cook adds something sour near the end so the red stays bright instead of fading to brown, and you can tell when they didn’t: the soup looks like weak tea and tastes like boiled vegetables.

So what is traditional borscht made of, if you have to say it in one breath? Beets, broth, cabbage and a little sour, finished with dill and sour cream. Everything else is family argument.

What is usually eaten with borscht? UNESCO says borscht is typically served with bread or garlic buns. In a Russian or Ukrainian home that often means dark rye, torn rather than sliced, and the garlic buns are soft little rolls brushed with garlic and oil that you pull apart and drag through the bowl. Sour cream goes on top, a pinch of fresh dill, and maybe a clove of raw garlic rubbed on the crust if the cook trusts you. At a St. Louis restaurant, ask for the bread before the soup comes. Nobody will think you’re greedy. They’ll think you’ve done this before.

### Why is there sour cream on everything?

Because almost everything on a Russian table is either rich, sour or both, and sour cream settles the argument. It cools a hot soup. It softens the vinegar in a pickle. It turns a plate of plain boiled dumplings into something you’d fight your brother for. Our own Russian Food category page says it plainly: sour cream and dill show up throughout by design. St. Louis should get this faster than anyone. Sour cream is Russia’s Provel, minus the argument.

The sour cream at a Russian table is heavier than the tub at the grocery store. It sits on the spoon in a slow curl and doesn’t run. It tastes of cream first and tang second. When it melts into borscht the soup goes from sharp to silky in one stir, and that change in your mouth is half the reason people order the soup at all.

Dill is the other constant. Fresh, feathery, chopped fine and scattered without much ceremony on soup, dumplings, potatoes and salads. If you think you don’t like dill, it’s probably because you’ve had the dried kind. Fresh dill on hot buttered dumplings smells like a summer garden somebody carried indoors.

Unrelated, but have you ever eaten a stew that cooked all night?

### Pelmeni are small on purpose

Pelmeni are the dumpling that tells the kitchen you know what you’re doing. They’re little, about the size of the end of your thumb, made of thin dough pinched around a raw meat filling. The raw meat cooks inside the tightly fastened dumpling, so it fills with its own juices. Bite carelessly and it runs down your chin.

Small is the point. They come glossy with melted butter, and you eat them fast and hot, three to a forkful if nobody’s watching. They freeze beautifully, too, so a bag in the freezer is the plan for the night nobody wants to cook.

What do Russians eat pelmeni with? Butter and sour cream, mostly, often both at once. Some people splash on a little vinegar to cut the richness. Some like a smear of hot mustard. Some eat them floating in the broth they boiled in, with dill on top, which is the Russian answer to chicken noodle soup on a sick day.

Pelmeni vs pierogi is the question every St. Louisan with a Polish grandmother asks first. Pierogi are larger half-moons with fillings like potato, cheese or fruit, and they’re commonly fried in butter. Pelmeni are smaller and rounder, with a thinner dough and a raw meat filling. If that’s the dumpling you’re craving, look on the menu for vareniki: dough folded over the filling into a half-moon, filled with potato and onions, cheese or cherries. If you grew up on church-basement pierogi in South City, vareniki will taste like home with a different accent.

Even the parish on Gravois ran on dumplings. The parish’s own history thanks the “Piroghi workers whose work is really a labor of love” and says they “keep our freezers filled with this popular food item for many people to enjoy.” That’s the borderland table, rolled by hand on Gravois.

### What do you order first at a Russian table?

Not the main course. Russian hospitality starts with zakuski, the little bites often described as Russia’s answer to tapas. Traditionally they meet guests coming in from the cold: pickles of all sorts, salted herring, Salat Olivier, blini and caviar. Order two or three to share, and listen for the pickle that cracks when somebody bites it.

Look for seledka, salt herring, usually laid out with raw onion and boiled potato. It’s oily and briny and much milder than you’re afraid it will be. Look for the Olivier salad, a cold potato salad with peas, pickles, carrots and mayonnaise, a holiday-table favorite that tastes like somebody’s childhood. If red caviar is on the menu, it comes on buttered bread or rolled in blini, and the little orange beads pop against your teeth like warm sea salt.

Then the soup. Borscht if it’s your first time. If the server mentions solyanka, say yes: it’s a sour, salty soup of pickles and several kinds of meat, often with a slice of lemon and an olive floating on top, and it tastes like the best thing that ever happened to a pickle.

Then one hot plate for the table. Pelmeni. Beef stroganoff over noodles or potatoes. Stuffed cabbage rolls. Chicken Kiev, which arrives looking innocent and squirts hot herb butter across the plate the second your knife goes in, so cut it pointing away from your shirt.

Here’s the ordering script that gets you the good stuff. Ask, “Are the pelmeni made here?” Handmade pelmeni have slightly uneven edges and a thinner skin, and a kitchen that makes them by hand is proud to say so. Ask for sour cream on the side so you can use as much as you want. Ask what the cook would order. Then say yes to the bread.

Craving a bowl of buttered pelmeni before the weekend is out? Start your shortlist with Russian Food on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two or three kitchens and ask which dumplings they roll by hand.

If you’re the cook behind a Russian, Ukrainian or Eastern European kitchen, the people craving your borscht are already searching. Put your menu where they look and list your business so more of those hungry neighbors end up at your door.

### Where can you eat Russian food in St. Louis?

Fewer places than you’d hope, which is why the good ones are worth the drive. For a sit-down dinner, start with Astoria. Bring the friend who isn’t sure about any of this; the kabobs on the same menu are the safe harbor while they steal a spoon of your borscht.

For the night you cook at home, go to Global Foods Market, an international grocery you can reach at 314-835-1112. The store says it carries deli meats and sausages from Turkey, Poland, Russia and Ukraine. Stand at the counter long enough and the cold smell of smoked sausage follows you to the car. Ask what came in this week, then build your own zakuski board with dark bread, a jar of pickles and a tub of sour cream.

The same rule works anywhere: shortlist two or three spots, call and tell them what you want, a first-timer’s borscht and dumpling dinner, then compare what each kitchen says it will put on the table. The one that gets excited on the phone is usually the one to visit.

If you’d rather meet the community than a menu, go back to that parish on Gravois. Its history also remembers the Bazaar, begun in October 1975, as the one event that brought many visitors and friends into its hall. Call the church line from the top of this page and ask when the next one is. Go for the welcome, not to shop for dumplings, and you’ll still leave knowing more about this food than a menu could teach you.

For more of the city’s old-country tables, these guides pair well:

### Save room for blini, tea and something sweet

Blini are crepe-like pancakes, and they swing both ways on a menu. Savory, they’re folded around ground meat or rolled with red caviar and sour cream. Sweet, they come with jam, honey or farmer’s cheese. A plate of them with a glass of hot tea is the Russian version of coffee and a doughnut, only slower.

Look for syrniki, small golden pancakes made from farmer’s cheese, crisp outside and tender in the middle, served with sour cream and jam. And if the menu has cherry vareniki, order them: purple juice seeps out of the dough when you cut one, and with a spoon of sour cream they taste like a cherry pie that wandered into a dumpling.

Drink the compote. It’s a cold drink made by simmering fruit, often currants or cherries, and it tastes like the end of summer in a glass. Then finish with tea, strong and hot. Nobody at a Russian table rushes this part of the meal, and neither should you.

### Frequently asked questions about Russian food

### Q. What is Russia’s national dish?

A.  There’s no single winner, and Russians will happily argue it over dinner. The answers you’ll hear most are pelmeni, the small meat dumplings, and the soups: shchi, the old cabbage soup of the countryside, and borscht, which UNESCO lists as Ukrainian heritage. If you want one plate that tastes like Russia, order pelmeni with butter and sour cream.

### Q. What is Russian comfort food?

A.  Hot, heavy and cheap to make: pelmeni in butter, borscht or cabbage soup with dark bread, buckwheat kasha, mashed potatoes with dill, cabbage rolls baked in tomato sauce, and blini with sour cream. It’s food built for cold kitchens and long winters, and almost all of it gets a spoon of sour cream before it reaches the table.

### Q. What is traditional borscht made of?

A.  Broth and beets are the heart of it. UNESCO’s record describes borscht as cooked with broth combined with beetroot, sugar beet or fermented beet juice. Most cooks add cabbage, potato, carrot and onion, often beef, and a little sour to keep the color bright, then finish the bowl with dill and sour cream.

### Q. What is usually eaten with borscht?

A.  UNESCO notes borscht is typically served with bread or garlic buns. Dark rye is common, and soft garlic rolls are a treat worth asking for. On top: a spoon of sour cream and fresh dill. Some families also put out raw garlic or a plate of pickles.

### Q. What is Russian pelmeni made of?

A.  Thin unleavened dough made from flour, water and often egg, wrapped around raw ground meat, usually beef or a beef and pork mix, seasoned with onion, salt and black pepper. The meat cooks inside the dough as the pelmeni boil, which is why every bite comes with its own little spoonful of broth.

### Q. What is pelmeni vs pierogi?

A.  Pelmeni are small, round, meat-filled dumplings that are boiled and served with butter or sour cream. Pierogi are larger half-moons with fillings like potato, cheese or fruit, and they are commonly fried in butter. If you want something closer to pierogi, look for vareniki: half-moon dumplings filled with potato and onions, cheese or cherries.

### Q. What do Russians eat pelmeni with?

A.  Melted butter and sour cream, often both. Some add a splash of vinegar to cut the richness, a smear of hot mustard, black pepper or fresh dill. Others eat pelmeni in the hot broth they cooked in, like a dumpling soup. Ask your server which way the kitchen likes them and try that first.

### Q. What are some popular Russian desserts?

A.  Syrniki, little farmer’s cheese pancakes with jam and sour cream; sweet blini with honey or jam; cherry vareniki; and pryaniki, spiced honey cookies served with tea. To drink, look for compote, a cold drink of simmered fruit such as currants or cherries.

### Q. What is a typical Russian breakfast?

A.  Often kasha, a warm porridge, with buckwheat the classic, topped with butter or milk. Syrniki and blini are weekend favorites. Many people eat farmer’s cheese with jam or sour cream, or an open-faced sandwich of bread, butter and cheese or sausage, all with a strong cup of black tea.
